[GODEFRID OF ADMONT.]

[Col. 0009]

## DISSERTATION ON THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF THE VENERABLE GODEFRID

[Col. 0009A]

**I.** The very celebrated Benedictine monastery of Admont in Styria, founded and dedicated in the seventy-fourth year of the eleventh century of Christ by the most holy Gebehard, archbishop of Salzburg, as the old Admont chronicler testifies [Note: [Col. 0009] Vol. II, *Script. Rer. Austr.*, col. 180 ff.], has, from that time down to the present, been a nursery of men eminent in religion and learning. This could very easily and readily be demonstrated, if an account of this place and institution were required. But here we must speak of Godefrid alone, the first abbot of that name, who, if he did not surpass all the rest in learning, certainly did so by the greatness of deeds gloriously and most holily accomplished; and whose outstanding homilies, after fully six hundred years, we now for the first time make public.

**II.** The old and contemporary writers, so far as I know, are indeed silent concerning the origin of this great man. Yet Gabriel Bucelinus, a learned monk of the distinguished monastery of Weingarten [Note: [Col. 0009] Part I, *Germania Sacra*, p. 93.], makes him a lord of Venningen. He therefore deserves so much the greater credit because the ancient charters and records of his own monastery, over which, as we shall shortly see, Godefrid presided for several years under the title of abbot, were more fully known to him.

He had a brother, Irimbert, that celebrated interpreter of the Holy Scriptures, who succeeded him in the abbacy of Admont after Liuthold and Rudolf; concerning whose life and writings see what we have discussed at length elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0009] Vol. II, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, preface to Part II.]. Near the end of the eleventh century, he professed the monastic life according to the Rule of St Benedict and the customs of Hirsau, in the once highly renowned monastery of St George in the Hercynian Forest. From that monastery, at nearly the same time, came forth many men most illustrious by holiness of life and distinction in learning.

The remarkable progress Godefrid made under their eyes, both in the pursuit of virtue and in the knowledge of divine things, was soon made clear by his excellent deeds, whose fame filled all Germany.

**III.** Captivated by his piety, prudence, and learning, the monks of Weingarten, when, after Abbot Chunon—steward of Waldpurg and count of Thann, under whom a great number of princes, counts, and barons, and at least eight members of the family of the Counts of Thann alone, flourished at Weingarten—they were considering the choice of a successor, found no one more worthy than Godefrid to entrust with the government of their house.

Bucelinus does not state the exact year in which Godefrid was designated and created abbot of Weingarten, being content to observe that he flourished in the year of Christ 1130. Nor do we have from him anything more certain concerning how many years he illumined the monastery of Weingarten by his piety and learning. But whatever the case may be, it is established that Godefrid’s governorship at Weingarten did not extend beyond the year 1138. For in that same year the Admont chronicler already calls him prior of the monastery of St George, to which he had withdrawn from the monastery of Weingarten. In speaking of his election as abbot of Admont, the chronicler writes distinctly in the cited passage:

> Lord Godefrid, prior of St George’s, having been elected abbot of Admont, was sought by the messengers and letters of Archbishop Conrad and brought to us.

The biographer of St Gebehard, archbishop of Salzburg, likewise a monk of Admont, agrees with the chronicler of Admont, in Henry Canisius [Note: [Col. 0010] Vol. VI, *Antiquae Lectiones*, p. 1243.]:

> Therefore, when our aforesaid father Wolvold, after many fruits of monastic religion, had at last happily been taken from this light on the Kalends of November in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1137, the twenty-third year of his rule, the brothers, by common election, chose as their abbot Lord Godefrid, formerly prior of the monastery of St George. Through our monks, the aforesaid Odalric and Witilo, sent by the community on his behalf, they obtained this bishop through Lord Theodwin, cardinal of St Rufina.

**IV.** Now, as soon as Godefrid assumed the government of the monastery of Admont, it is incredible how much advantage, illumination, and glory immediately accrued to that church. The biographer of St Gebehard recounts the entire matter. Although his words are somewhat lengthy, we reproduce them all the more willingly because he was nearer to those times and thus more trustworthy. He relates as follows:

> Accordingly, this man, diligently fulfilling the name of shepherd by his deeds, watched carefully over the flock entrusted to him, so that by God’s gift and his providence, and also by the labours and exertions of the oft-mentioned lord Archbishop Conrad of pious memory, the place, as though receiving a new beginning once more, perhaps grew stronger than all the monasteries of Germany, not only in various ways but especially in the glory of its reputation, the strictness of its observances, the offerings and gifts of the faithful, and its most noble multitude of monks and sisters.
>
> Finally, among the other memorials of the excellently accomplished deeds of Father Godefrid himself, and among the benefits of the great prosperity of the monastery in his time, he obtained from two apostolic pontiffs, Innocent and Lucius, privileges of the Roman See: namely, the protection of the Apostolic See and the perpetual confirmation of the grants of the blessed pontiffs Gebehard and Thiemo, and of Lord Conrad himself.

This ancient author then adds by whose particular work, zeal, and piety Godefrid was aided in carrying through and completing such an excellent and arduous undertaking:

> At that time certain good emulators of the spiritual life encouraged and cooperated in the pursuit of religion; by their reputation and example they drew many others. These were the aforesaid Prior Raban and those four unlearned men (*illiterati*, that is, converts or lay brothers) mentioned above: Odalric of Elsendorf, Long Odalric, Maganus, and a certain religious man named Witilo; also Wernher, who held the office of second prior and armarius, and later governed the monastery of Brul with distinction; and Perchtold, later abbot of the monastery of St Emmeram.
>
> There were also many others who, because of the distinction of their merits, were later appointed over various monasteries. For thirteen abbots were taken from our monastery to other houses in that period. Besides these, other religious persons were then conspicuous among us: Odalric, priest and sacristan; Perchtold, an excellent scribe, who copied with his own hand no small number of books for our monastery; Lambert, likewise a most diligent scribe; and Gotschalk, precentor under Father Godefrid and under the rule of the three succeeding abbots, and himself an excellent scribe; and Salmann, who administered the pastoral care of a parish.
>
> Likewise, there were three unlearned men, formerly nobles in the world: namely Reginher, who, coming to conversion with his equally noble wife and his son Leutold—a boy of good disposition who later became abbot of our monastery—conveyed to us no small estates; Arbo of Byberch; Wernhard of Urle; and also Isinric, who, holding the office of cellarer, by his own care and that of the other cooperating religious brothers, greatly improved the resources of the monastery.
>
> At that time also Henry of Nazawe, a ministerial of St Rudbert, came to conversion with his wife and four sons and offered to the monastery, with the hand of Lord Archbishop Conrad, the estates and benefices that he had possessed in great number.

Thus far the writer of the Life of St Gebehard, on the school, as it were, and gymnasium of holiness and learning that flourished at Admont under Godefrid’s presidency.

**V.** As for those thirteen abbots whom the anonymous author just cited reports to have been taken from Admont under Abbot Godefrid for the administration of other monasteries, the following, besides those already named, are known to us from ancient Admont documents.

Reinbert, Reginbert, or Reimbert, was first prior at Admont [Note: [Col. 0011] Vol. IV, *Antiquae Lectiones*, p. 1243.], later abbot of the monastery of St Peter at Salzburg, and then advanced to the bishopric of Brixen. Otto likewise passed from being prior of Admont to become abbot of Millstatt. Dietmar, paternal uncle of Ekbert the elder, count of Putten, was a distinguished abbot at Ossiach. Engilschalk was abbot of Benediktbeuern in Bavaria.

Some think that this Engilschalk is one and the same as the Engilschalk who succeeded Sigibald, the first abbot of Melk, in the government of that house. But the chronology itself shows them to be greatly mistaken. For Engilschalk of Melk governed his monastery from 1116 until 1121, when Godefrid—through whose influence, nevertheless, Engilschalk is supposed to have received Melk—could not yet have assumed the government of the abbey of Admont.

Irimbert, brother of Godefrid, was called to the abbacy of St Michael at Bamberg. Jacob Gretser, the learned Jesuit theologian, published in the Appendix [Note: [Col. 0011] P. 486.] to the *Saints of Bamberg* several highly honourable letters about him from Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, and Conrad, bishop of Passau.

John was placed over the monastery of Göttweig. The old Chronicle of Admont says of him under the year 1157: “Lord John, formerly a monk of Admont, becomes abbot of Göttweig.” Isinric was abbot of Biburg, of whom the same Chronicle makes mention in these words: “In the year 1169, Lord Isinric is elected abbot of Biburg.” Godefrid was no longer alive in that year; nevertheless Isinric is deservedly and rightly counted among those whom Godefrid sent out to preside over other monasteries, having been formed by his long instruction and guidance so as eventually to be judged worthy of that office and position.

Someone adds Hartmann and Ambrose, the former abbot of Fulda and the latter of Campidonum. But concerning their selection from Admont, there is deep silence among both ancient and modern writers.

**VI.** Nor were Godefrid’s merits confined to monasteries of men. If he discovered that any sacred communities of virgins had departed from their former, holier discipline, he laboured to lead them back into the way by sending out virgins and teachers from his own convent of women at Admont.

In this respect there was the exceptional and most learned Regilendis, or Regilla, of whom the Chronicle of Admont records under the year 1156 [Note: [Col. 0011] Vol. II, *Script. Rer. Austr.*, col. 188.]: “The monastery of Bergen, that is Berg, near Neuburg on the Danube, is established by the men of Admont under Lady Abbess Regilla.” This is the same Regilindis who used to attend wholly to the exposition of Scripture from the lips of Irimbert and to commit his sayings to writing in Latin. A lasting memorial of this remains in Irimbert’s Commentary on Judges, chapter 19.

Nor should we omit the noteworthy passage of the same Irimbert, where he speaks as follows of the sacred studies of the virgins of Admont [Note: [Col. 0012] Prologue to the Commentary on Judges, Vol. IV, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*]:

> Some years ago, because I had expounded to the sisters of Admont the history of the concubine who was cut into twelve parts, and also the history of Ruth, two of them devoted the diligence of their studies to preserving the memory of my interpretation. Therefore I judged it fitting to append to this little work a brief exposition of the same histories, as arranged by the sisters themselves.

Elsewhere the same Irimbert handed down to posterity the following concerning the life and conduct of the nuns of Admont, who flourished under Abbot Godefrid:

> Throughout the whole year, summer and winter, they rise with the brothers at the sound of the bell for the morning vigils, and throughout the winter season they continue the order of the vigils until daylight. They observe the same fasting and the same silence as the brothers throughout the yearly cycle. None of them wears linen garments, except the little girls alone, if any are being brought up among them. They hold their chapter among themselves every day, with the mistress or her deputy presiding. On feast days, when the abbot cannot come to them, there are persons among them appointed to give a word of exhortation.
>
> For they are very learned and wonderfully trained in the knowledge of Holy Scripture. Since after their first entrance they never leave the monastery, unless they are carried out dead or perhaps transferred alive to another monastery, where they are protected by like custody; and since they never see anything of worldly vanities and rarely hear anything of secular matters, why should they not possess knowledge of heavenly mysteries, they who fast from every participation in worldly pleasures?
>
> And although daughters of most noble princes and others born of illustrious lineage are among them, they contend with one another in a great contest of humility, because any woman among them would be considered utterly detestable if she were touched by any mark of pride or boasting.

These are the words of Irimbert, whose complete little work *On the Life of the Virgins of Admont* we published in the *Ascetic Library* [Note: [Col. 0013] Vol. VIII.].

**VII.** Such was the condition of the convent of Admont under Abbot Godefrid when Sophia, daughter of Béla, king of the Hungarians, withdrew into it after abandoning her royal betrothed. The biographer of St Gebehard recounts it in these words [Note: [Col. 0014] Vol. VI, *Antiquae Lectiones* of H. Canisius, p. 1245.]:

> At the same time, namely in the year 1200, Sophia, daughter of Béla, king of the Hungarians, had been betrothed to the son of Conrad, king of the Romans, and sent to him with incalculable wealth in royal fashion. But since the world loves what is its own, that is, temporal goods, and neglects faith and truth, this aforesaid queen, having been treated in a manner unworthy of royal dignity, exchanged an earthly kingdom for the heavenly one.
>
> By the counsel and assistance of Liukardis, countess of Regensburg, she sought the monastery of Admont, and thereafter lived a celibate life among God’s sacred virgins in a most humble conversion and manner of life. Some princes and counts, and many nobles too, offered their daughters there to serve God under regular discipline, making that monastery more celebrated than almost all convents of nuns in Germany, as we said above.

**VIII.** While Godefrid thus enjoyed favourable circumstances, a violent storm suddenly burst upon Admont, overthrowing in one night the whole monastery that had until then been preserved and enlarged by so much effort. The year was 1152 when, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, before dawn, a grievous and terrible fire consumed all the monks’ buildings.

Irimbert describes the history of this destruction in the above-mentioned work as follows:

> While the solemnity of Matins was being celebrated in the choir with watchful attention and a measured rendering of the psalmody, I and the brother assigned to assist me in writing, after the morning praises had been completed in the chapel of St Mary, had sung the Office of that same Lady of ours as far as the lesson. Then, hearing the cry of a certain servant, we were astonished, because at Admont we were not accustomed at night to hear any noise of disturbance.
>
> He cried out a second time, and his repeated cry made us suspect some evil. We rushed from the chapel; and although we saw nothing, we heard a great commotion around the infirmary. For the servant who had cried out was heating the infirmary. But through his negligence a violent wind, blowing from the region of the wilderness, had struck that building from outside; and, driven by the wind, the flame had already increased with astonishing speed beyond the power of resistance.
>
> I ran to the monastery. In the choir they were already chanting, in a very measured melody, the psalm, “Why do you glory in malice?” I brought the dreadful news: outside, fires were already blazing. The outer brothers first ran out; I found nearly all of them standing attentively in prayer. For it is their custom to keep watch during the night psalmody, lest, by sitting continually, they languish in the torpor of sleep.
>
> The flame, growing beyond measure, began fiercely to tear at the chapel of St Mary from the infirmary, because, owing to the magnitude of the fire and the violence of the wind, no one could bring aid in the danger. Mourning arose among all, and the brothers’ Matins were interrupted. At the beginning of the second Nocturn, when they received the signal from me, the sisters laid aside Matins and prostrated themselves in litany supplication with an incomparable outpouring of tears.
>
> On one side the flame seized the monastery; on the other it spread into the cloister, scarcely anything like which could be found in those mountainous regions, since it had been constructed of most precious marble at the expense of Lord Archbishop Conrad of blessed memory, and at the same expense the precious columns of the monastery rose high.
>
> Seeing the fire grow and seize all the workshops of the monastery beyond recovery, the lord abbot went to the monastery of the sisters, because he feared that it too could no longer escape. He sat for a time before the doors of the church and watched the flames, driven by the wind, grow beyond measure. Despairing that the sisters could remain in the monastery, he asked that the prior, to whom he had entrusted the keys of the same monastery, be sought more diligently.
>
> But because he could not be found—for, all having left the monastery, and in the darkness of night, one did not know where another might be—the abbot, shaken by the roar of the flames [Col. 0015] and the terror of the flying sparks, had the locks of the sisters’ monastery broken open and granted them permission to leave if the danger of the fire could not be avoided.
>
> When Lady Agnes, daughter of Count Otto, brother of the bishop of Regensburg, tearfully asked him where they were to go, he himself answered tearfully: “Wherever the mercy of the highest Father shall lead you,” etc.

**IX.** Hardly anyone will doubt that this tragedy tore Godefrid’s heart apart. But far more sharply, as is customary, the differing opinions and judgments of people tormented the holy man. Irimbert does not conceal this at all, but concludes his tragic narrative with the following defence:

> Perhaps different people say different things; and though the Apostle declares God’s judgments inscrutable, they themselves undertake to be searchers of divine judgments. Accordingly, perhaps they do not hesitate to assert that negligence or pride was the cause of so great a desolation, and add the blow of their tongues to the wound of divine chastisement.
>
> But if anyone conscious and loving of the spiritual purpose had seen, before the ruin caused by the fire, the state of that monastery—how great was the fervour burning day and night in divine service, how they competed with one another in continence and humility—he would certainly not hesitate to judge of them that they had stirred up Leviathan against themselves and, like blessed Job, had been handed over into the hands of the tempter not for condemnation but for testing.
>
> What others think, I do not know. I know one thing: those who had previously devoted themselves to continence and humility, girded with God’s scourge, were more and more adorned in the beauty of continence and humility; for, according to the Apostle’s testimony, “all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8).

These are Irimbert’s words—an eyewitness and an authoritative writer. Yet however bitter this affliction may have been, the generosity of Godefrid’s supporters was so abundant that almost the entire establishment of Admont was restored within about a year.

**X.** Among these benefactors, St Eberhard should rightly be counted first. Since he had been appointed to succeed Conrad I in the archbishopric of Salzburg principally through Godefrid’s efforts, he never afterward ceased to show his grateful disposition toward the monastery of Admont.

The writer of the Life of St Gebehard is a full witness to everything. After recounting Conrad’s death and his exceedingly great services to the monastery of Admont, he adds the following concerning Eberhard [Note: [Col. 0015] *Antiquae Lectiones*, p. 1245.]:

> After the death of Lord Archbishop Conrad of blessed memory, the clergy and people of the Church of Salzburg, by divine inspiration, as there is no doubt, and especially through the intervention of Lord Godefrid, abbot of Admont, chose Lord Eberhard, abbot of Biburg, as archbishop by unanimous election and vote, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1148, under King Conrad, in the tenth year of his reign.
>
> This Eberhard, beloved by God and men, born of noble and religious parents, had first been a canon of Bamberg, then a monk of Prüfening, and afterward had been made abbot of Biburg. He and his brothers had founded that monastery with the help and cooperation of Otto, bishop of Bamberg, of happy memory.
>
> Thus, by divine grace and the aid of the merits of his virtues, when he had been ordained archbishop, he strove to preside over the flock entrusted to him not only by the word of instruction, but also by the example of a most holy life. … More than all the other places and churches of his bishopric, he loved, cherished, and enlarged the monastery of Admont, following the practice of his predecessors.
>
> When it had miserably collapsed in the fire, he expended thirty pounds of silver annually until it was rebuilt, and aided it in a fatherly way from his own revenues to the value of more than sixteen marks. He also greatly augmented the possessions of that monastery by his gifts, especially grants of tithes, and fortified it with privileges.

**XI.** In the year 1164 Conrad II succeeded Eberhard in the archiepiscopal dignity, no less in generosity toward the monastery of Admont. He was the son of St Leopold, margrave of Austria: a man indeed most noble in royal descent, learning, and uprightness of conduct. So says the biographer of St Gebehard, who also reports that when pressures of tribulation assailed Conrad on every side, he regularly withdrew privately and familiarly to the monastery of Admont, finding there some respite from worldly disturbances.

> He never ceased, he says, day by day to assist that place by counsel and every kind of aid, and to work for its advancement. For the support of the poor who arrived every day, he also bestowed certain tithes upon the Hospital.

I pass over the benefactors of lesser name: Godefrid of Wietting and his wife Adela; Count Frederick, advocate of Regensburg; Count Berthold of Andechs; the noble Wichard of Truna; Gunther of Hohenwart; and very many others. Their conveyances, gifts, and benefices, made to the monastery of Admont under Abbot Godefrid, may be seen in the Diplomatic Codex of Admont [Note: [Col. 0016] Vol. III, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*.].

**XII.** Moreover, Godefrid stood in the highest repute for learning and erudition among very many learned men of his age; and it is incredible how much weight accrued to any cause to which he attached himself.

The exceptionally learned bishop of Bamberg, Eberhard, always held him in the highest esteem. We shall shortly publish from the Admont codex Eberhard’s dogmatic letters *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, written against Gerhoh. And Gerhoh himself, that most celebrated provost of Reichersberg, dedicated to Godefrid his so-called *Prologue with Helmet* to his exposition of the Psalms, or his little book against two heresies of his time:

> “To be approved where it pleases,” as Gerhoh himself says, “and corrected where it reasonably displeases.”

Finally, St Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, considered Godefrid most worthy to employ his counsel, fairness, and prudence above all in resolving the grave controversy that arose in 1157 between Otto I, bishop of Freising, and Hartwic, bishop of Regensburg, concerning the boundaries of their respective dioceses.

A striking testimony to this survives in the *History of Freising*, recently written and published with the greatest thoroughness by the most distinguished and learned Father Charles Meichelbeck, Benedictine of Benediktbeuern, p. 334. There, however, a typographical error has entered: in the record of the settlement, Gotehard appears in place of Godefrid, or Gotfrid.

**XIII.** The Admont records place the death of this great abbot in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1165, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July. The old Chronicle of Admont, most recently published by the Reverend brother in Volume II of the *Writers of Austrian Affairs*, says:

> In the year 1165, Abbot Gotfrid of happy memory died; in his place Lord Liutold, his fosterling and professed monk, was elected.

Extracts from two Admont necrologies [Note: [Col. 0017] Vol. III, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, col. 204.] for the seventh day before the Kalends of July state:

> Godefrid, abbot of our congregation, founder of this monastery.

But best of all is the writer of the Life of St Gebehard in Henry Canisius, Volume VI of the *Antiquae Lectiones*:

> In the second year of the pontificate of Conrad II, archbishop of Salzburg, namely from the Incarnation of the Lord 1165, the reverend Abbot Godefrid of Admont—a man of great glory and authority in the Church of Christ and father of many monasteries—after producing manifold fruits for the Lord both in his own way of life and in the abundant edification of others, in the twenty-eighth year of his rule, closed his last day in a good old age on the seventh day before the Kalends of July. Amid the tearful lamentation of his sons and daughters, his body was committed to the earth with due veneration on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

**XIV.** Godefrid left to posterity illustrious memorials not only of his industry and holiness, but also of his intellect: namely, these two volumes of homilies, which you have before your hands and eyes, for Sundays and the solemnities of the saints, arranged according to the order in which they were celebrated in the Catholic Church in his age.

They are contained in four parchment volumes of large format, written in a contemporary and most elegant hand. Until now they had benefited only certain learned and devout men within private walls; but at last, through the most gracious approval of the most reverend, most illustrious, and most eminent Lord Antonio—Godefrid’s true successor both in rank and in deed, and a most generous patron of all solid learning—and through the care and effort of the very reverend, distinguished, and learned Father Sigismund Munich, subprior and librarian of that same celebrated religious house, they were brought to me.

As soon as I had sampled them, and other learned men also approved my plan, I immediately determined to commit them to the press. Several of my brethren, enduring in labour and devoted to the common good, notably advanced my undertaking, promptly applying themselves to transcribe those volumes.

Nor should the very Reverend Father Benedict Walner, monk and senior of the Cistercian monastery of Seisenstein, my fellow-countryman, be deprived of singular praise. He was so captivated by the sweetness of Godefrid’s teaching that, though already about sixty-three years old and with a trembling, faltering hand, he prepared for the press the greater part of the first volume. But that good old man did not see the fruit of his truly religious labour, having departed almost two years ago to the heavenly realms, as I hope with affection.

XV. In the Admont manuscripts the homilies have for the most part been copied without any order. For the reader’s convenience, we have arranged them so that those which the subject itself indicates were delivered on definite days of the ecclesiastical year are placed on those days, while all the rest are relegated to the Appendix. On Sundays several homilies are very often given, not always on the same Gospel, but either on the Epistles customarily read at Mass or on the readings usually recited first in the nocturnal office. In all these Godfrey is entirely consistent with himself. Everywhere he pursues allegory, tropology, or anagogy, applying himself chiefly to that aspect which he judges most suitable for correcting and perfecting the morals of monks. Hence, in order to attain and stir up the more tender movements of the soul—what more recent writers call compunction, inward turning, and the anointing of the spirit—he bends almost all the figures and sayings of Holy Scripture to this end, perhaps at times more forcibly than the passage permits. He is constant in inculcating the expiation and confession of sins; and it is sufficiently clear that this holy man was thoroughly persuaded that, without a clear and complete confession of sins, nothing holy, nothing solid, nothing perfected is to be expected from religious persons. In teaching moral conduct he imposed upon himself this rule: that he should be neither too rigid and severe nor too lax and indulgent. “Whenever the words of the Lord,” he says [Note: [Col. 0018] Homily on the Sixth Sunday after Pentecost], “sound with such strictness and severity that they can scarcely, or not at all, be fulfilled, there the weight of his words must be moderated by sound judgment. But whenever they abound with such gentleness and sweetness that the weak and slothful, because of the gentleness of his words, become through laxity of conduct prone to evil, there it is necessary that they be seasoned with some moderation of strictness.”

Throughout Godfrey one may find statements concerning grace and gratuitous predestination to glory—the very doctrine which the Thomistic school later commendably taught, and which it boasts, with laudable zeal, that it drew from the holy doctors Augustine and Thomas and that it is consonant with the word of God, the decrees of the supreme pontiffs and councils, and the sayings of the Fathers. Thus the most holy and most wise pontiff Benedict XIII wrote most solemnly in his letter of 6 November 1724 to all the professed brethren of the Order of Preachers [Col. 0019], against the calumnies directed at the teaching of Saints Augustine and Thomas.

XVI. There is only one thing I should wish absent from Godfrey’s homilies: namely, the assertion of original sin, from which the most holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary was not exempt. This may seem all the more surprising to everyone because the zeal for her maternal and virginal honor shines out so fervently in all Godfrey’s homilies concerning Mary. Yet anyone who remembers that the devout opinion concerning the Immaculate Conception of the holy Mother of God became established with such force long after Godfrey’s age that, without prejudice to the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, no one may oppose it; and who at the same time considers what was permitted to St Bernard of Clairvaux, in his letter to the people of Lyons, on this very question—such a person will not dwell unduly upon Godfrey’s opinion.

If this man, so devoted to the Mother of God, could have seen the hosts of most learned men who now splendidly defend the devout opinion concerning the immaculate conception of the Mother of God, he would doubtless have gone over wholly—“with hands and feet,” as they say—to views other than those he wrote. This was precisely why I added marginal notes at all the passages in which he departed from the devout opinion, and referred readers to the present dissertation. I wished thereby to cut off every occasion of stumbling, especially for those who hunt down almost every syllable and punctuation mark in the little works I edit, in order to arouse and foment hatred against ecclesiastical writers, and envy and calumny against me. But I leave it to others to judge how admirably such people serve the Catholic Church.

Certainly, if only those ancient ecclesiastical writers in whom no blemish is found are to be brought to light, then the case of nearly all the Fathers from the second century onward is lost and beyond hope. For who among them all is there who, in matters still obscure and not defined either by the judgment of the Church or by the agreement of learned men, has not displayed some human weakness in some subtler question? Foolish and barbarous, therefore, are all who fix their eyes upon merely one or another blemish of some ancient writer and, neglecting all the excellent sayings which he also offers, universally cry out for nothing but perpetual prisons or the stake.

Moreover, anyone will be wholly unfair to me who believes that I regard as certain and sound everything found in the ancient writers whom I publish merely because no observation has at once been written in the margin. Many things in them must be left to the judgment of readers; and some things are so plainly evident at first sight, as to what they are or what place they deserve, that they are evident to everyone except the utterly crude and unlearned. And what else would it be to draw the reader’s attention to these things than to misuse leisure and good paper, and, in addition, to reproach our learned age with ignorance?

As regards my own faith, before the good God it has hitherto been, and will be, no other than that which, while still a youth, I vowed always to retain: namely, that which the holy Roman and apostolic Church holds, and which the holy Council of Trent set forth to Christ’s faithful. Whatever differs from this faith, whether it occurs among ancient or modern writers, I detest from my heart; but whatever agrees with it, whether handed down by ancient or recent writers, I embrace with my whole mind. But enough of these matters. I now proceed to describe the other little works of our Godfrey.

XVII. Besides the homilies published here, Godfrey also composed a little work *On the Blessings of the Patriarch Jacob*, by which Jacob, at the point of death, described the future lot of his sons. It appears in the Appendix, drawn from the same manuscripts from which the homilies were copied; and the author seems to have delivered it as a sermon to his disciples. Certainly by the same Godfrey is the book *On the Ten Burdens in Certain Chapters of Isaiah*, composed from mere homilies, which I published in the *Treasury of Anecdotes* [Note: [Col. 0019] Vol. II, Part I] under the name of Irimbert. There you may see, in the Introductory Dissertation, p. XVI, the occasion of my error. But because it is now most certain to me that all those homilies with which this book is intermixed in the Admont manuscript belong not to Irimbert but to Godfrey, this little work must be restored to its true author, although it does not bear his name.

In a manuscript at Tegernsee we also found a letter of Godfrey to O., formerly his monk, whom he asks to send him for copying Josephus’s work, the destruction of Jerusalem, the celebrated triumph of Vespasian and Titus at Rome, and other books of better quality. We shall publish this in volume V or VI of the *Treasury*. For although there are some who judge such old scraps, especially when woven in a rather harsh style, unworthy of publication, we who labor to enlarge the glory and remembrance of great men in the Catholic Church think very differently.

I conclude this short dissertation with the words of the learned Jacob Gretser, most experienced in this kind of study [Note: [Col. 0020] *Observations on the Eystettensian Miscellanies*, book II, p. 316]:

> You, my reader, attend not to the words but to the matter. The words are cheap, but what lies beneath the words is great. The shell is not food, but the kernel is sweet. Heretics—especially Illyricus in his *Catalogue*, and those who in later years expanded Illyricus’s catalogue twofold, if not threefold or fourfold—most zealously hammer into public view whatever rhymes and little verses they find in any corners against Catholics and the pope; and for that very reason the rhymes are sufficiently elegant and polished, because they attack, tease, and tear apart the pope, clergy, monks, nuns, and rites of the Church. Why should we not with similar diligence bring to light things once written for the glory of saints by men better than they were eloquent?

[Col. 0021]

# Sunday Homilies of the Venerable Godfrey, Abbot of Admont

[Col. 0021]

## Homily I. First Homily for the First Sunday of Advent

[Col. 0021A]

“When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives” (Matt. 21).

Concerning the Gospel reading read on the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent—wherein it is related that the Lord came to Jerusalem upon an ass and was received by crowds of people with palm branches—very many wonder, and may well wonder, why it is read at this time, since according to the letter this reading seems in no way suited to the present season. But because the words of the Lord, which are the words of the Gospel, are, as he himself says, “spirit and life” (John 6:63), let us, according to the command of the Law, remove the skin from the victim and cut its limbs into pieces (Lev. 1:7); that is, setting aside the letter [Col. 0021B], let us seek the spiritual meaning in the sacred words. Perhaps we shall find something which we may fittingly apply to the Lord’s daily advent to his faithful.

To touch briefly upon the sum of the Gospel reading: by the ass is signified the soul of each faithful person, which at each person’s death is brought to the Lord, and, with him seated upon it, is introduced into the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, eternal rest—where it is solemnly received by the multitude of holy angels coming to meet it, with joys and songs, as though with palms. In order that we may perceive this more clearly in the Gospel reading, let us reread its text more attentively and, as far as we can, with God’s grace assisting, examine it more diligently.

“When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem and came [Col. 0021C] to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives.” This most desirable season of the Lord’s Advent, for which all the saints from the beginning longed, is celebrated each year for this reason: both so that the remembrance of the Lord’s Nativity may not be erased from human hearts, and so that we may be recalled to remembrance of his terrible advent, which daily draws near to us, when, at the Lord’s command, each blessed person is led from this valley of tears to the homeland and to the region of everlasting brightness. For the more diligently that advent of his which took place among men is honored and observed, the more bearable will this advent be; because the more blessed each blessed soul is found at its end, the greater a fullness of glory it will receive. So, as it seems to me, the whole present Gospel reading proceeds—which is read at this advent of the Lord because it appears to announce the daily advent of death that threatens us all.

By Jerusalem, which is interpreted “vision of peace,” is understood every blessed assembly of the righteous. It is called Jerusalem because, although it sojourns on earth, it nevertheless possesses within itself the vision of peace, while it hangs in desire upon that place where there is the vision of everlasting peace. The Lord draws near to this Jerusalem when, through the affliction of sickness, he announces to someone within it that death is near. He comes to Bethphage, which is called “house of the jaw,” [Col. 0022A] when, as death approaches, each person to be saved discloses his sins in confession. “To the Mount of Olives”: by oil, which floats above all liquids, is signified the mercy of God, [Col. 0022B] which surpasses all his works. To this Mount of Olives, to this mountain of mercy, every person has recourse at the hour of death, that the heavenly physician may pour the oil of mercy into his wounds, may exalt mercy over judgment, because he judges that through his own merit he has little or nothing by which he may be saved and redeemed. It follows:

“Then he sent two disciples, saying to them: Go into the village that is opposite you.” The two disciples are, I think, bodily weakness and the pain of death. It is rightly and fittingly said to them, “Go into the village that is opposite you,” because bodily weakness and the pain of death are contrary to a human being by the nature of the flesh. Thus the Lord says to Peter: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (John 21:18). When these disciples come, an ass tied up is found, and a colt with her. The tied-up ass is the flesh, I think, brought low by weakness; the colt with her is the human spirit placed in distress. “Untie them,” says the Lord, “and bring them to me.” It is as if he said: Let the soul be loosed and separated from the body by my command, and, when loosed from the body, brought to me. Let no alien hand touch it, but let it be brought to me, its maker and rewarder.

“And if anyone says anything to you, say: The Lord has need of them.” These objectors are, I think, evil spirits, who at the hour of death insert themselves by many and varied objections; and, by false accusations, they strive, if they can, to bring it about that a person does not reach the reward. He wills that the soul of the righteous be led to himself from heaven by his messengers, namely the holy angels, as one known to him, as one of his household. On the other hand, the devil with his own wishes to hurl this soul down into hell and everlasting death [Col. 0023A].

But amid these things, while this and that are objected by evil spirits, “Say,” he says, “that the Lord has need of them.” It is as though it were said: He who is absolutely Lord of all chose to be Lord of this soul and body; and therefore [Col. 0023B] he has need that, for those whose Lord he chose to be in their toil and service, he may be Lord in rest and reward. “And immediately he will let them go.” He lets them go immediately because, in the case of anyone of whom these things may truly be said, the power of the ancient enemy to prevail against him at the hour of death is taken away. It follows:

“All this happened that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you meek, sitting upon a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.” What is this “all” that happened? Surely, when each blessed soul reaches the presence of its rewarder, there “all” has happened, because there all that was said or promised to it concerning Christ in the present life through the mouths of the prophets—that is, doctors and preachers—has been fulfilled. There it will truly be said to the daughter of Zion, to that watchful soul which longed to behold God: “Behold, your king comes to you meek.” For although he now comes meekly to the hearts of his own, he comes and withdraws almost in a moment. But when the dissolution of body and soul has occurred, then he will come wholly with meekness and sweetness; having come [Col. 0023C], he will not depart, but will sit upon the ass and colt: for he will possess and fulfill the spirit in its release, and the body in its resurrection.

“The disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them.” The disciples go when prolonged bodily weakness brings on the pain of death. The garments of the disciples are laid upon the ass and colt when the flesh is worn down and afflicted by varied sufferings. For the garment of one disciple is, it seems to me, bodily pain; the garment of the other disciple is dissolution itself and the fear of death, which lead a person to Jesus. Upon these garments the disciples cause the Lord to sit, because when a person has received from the Lord’s hand double punishment for all his sins—outwardly through the labors of pains, inwardly through the fear of death—he deserves through this prolonged purgation and cleansing to have the Lord as his rider, whose fellowship in brightness he will possess face to face forever. But how much zeal and concern the faithful on earth devote to the hour of a blessed soul’s departure, and with what rejoicing [Col. 0023D] and glory it is received in heaven, is, as it seems to me, indicated by what follows.

“Now a very great crowd spread their garments in the road; others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the road.” The very great crowd is, I think, the assembly of spiritual people, called “very great” because among them are diverse and numerous merits. I judge that all the garments of this crowd are the offices and commemorations which they perform at the funerals of the dead: the solemnities of Masses, the holy offering at the altar, vigils, alms, the continuous recitation of psalms, scourges, and other things offered and sacrificed to God the Father for the rest of the deceased. These garments are spread in the way when, at the hour of the death of any blessed soul, it is met with brotherly love through prayers and aided by tears. That road, I say, by which it departs from the body is strewn with garments when the mercy of angels, archangels, and all God’s saints is implored to help it, so that, its adversaries excluded, it may pass freely into the way of peace.

Accordingly, when the very great crowd—that is, the weaker part of Christ’s body which still sojourns on earth—has done thus and thus, [Col. 0024A] when one human being has commended another, ash to ash, to the Lord God, what occurs above is indicated, as I think, by what the Evangelist says: “Others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the road.” These others, stronger and more powerful, who cut branches from the trees, are, I think, the holy angels, who rejoice and exult with a particular kind of gladness in their assemblies over the assumption of blessed souls. For at the advent of every holy and God-beloved soul, the entire army of the heavenly host rushes out to meet it, receives it joyfully, and gloriously and magnificently recounts and narrates to the Lord all that it accomplished gloriously here. There they cut branches from the trees and spread them in the road.

It is pleasing to consider what the branches of the trees are, and what is the road along which they are spread. As it seems to me, by the branches we may understand the two natures—divine and human—of Jesus Christ, God and man; by the trees from which these branches come forth, God the Father [Col. 0024C] and the incorrupt Mother of his only-begotten Son, the Son of God; and by the road, him who says of himself: “I am the way” (John 14:6). The divine and human nature may fittingly be understood by the branches: just as a branch comes forth while the tree remains sound and whole, so God the Father, before all ages, while Deity remained intact, begot the branch—that is, the Son coeternal and consubstantial with himself. And him whom he thus brought forth eternally from himself, he willed at the end of the ages to be born from the flowering and fruitful tree, the perpetual Virgin Mary, while the seal of virginity remained intact. He who was the only-begotten Son of God the Father in heaven without a mother, deigned on earth to become the firstborn son of his virgin Mother without a father.

The holy angels “cut,” that is, distinguish, this divine and human nature from the trees, because they praise the Son of God for their own strengthening, and praise the son of the Virgin for the liberation of souls; and they spread the same branches in the road when they ascribe all things to the divine and human nature. It follows.

“The crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” The crowds that go before are, I think, legions of angels and saints coming at the departure of a holy soul and receiving it with great ceremony. The crowds that follow are the multitude of faithful persons hastening together on earth. All these cry out [Col. 0025A] with one voice, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David.” Those below cry, “Hosanna”—that is, “Save, O Lord, this soul”—you who, because of your excessive love for humankind, deigned to become the Son of David. Those above sing in harmony and meet the arriving soul, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Or they give praise to the Son of David because they sweetly remember how he received it when it repented and did not disdain, as once with David, to grant this blessed soul pardon for its offenses. They offer the joyful praise of blessing, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”; that is, blessed be he alone who comes in the name of the Lord, because by his blessing and grace all these things come to be and have come to be in you—he whose honor and dominion remain unto ages of ages.

[Col. 0025B] Such is the sequence of this most sacred Gospel reading, which, assisted by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we have run through in exposition as far as we could. It is read each year in the Advent of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ so that, admonished and awakened by it, we may always keep before our eyes that advent of the Lord to the soul, of which we have now spoken, when summoned from the prison-house of this life it must meet its Savior; and that we may now carefully provide what manner of persons we shall then be found to be.

For the Apostle Paul also admonishes us to this in today’s reading, saying: “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day: not in revelry and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, [Col. 0025C] not in strife and envy” (Rom. 13:12). Therefore we must mortify the flesh through abstinence; we must draw near to God through chastity of body and mind; we must burn with love for God and neighbor. For if, having cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light in this manner, we discipline our souls in this advent of the Lord which we commemorate yearly, then at his final advent, when we are called forth from the body, we shall meet him joyfully and unencumbered; and, received into that glory of eternal blessedness which is without failing or misery, we shall reign with him forever. May he deign to grant this—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily II. Second Homily for the Same Sunday

[Col. 0025D]

“When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then he sent two disciples, saying to them: Go into the village opposite you, and immediately you will find an ass tied up and a colt with her” (Matt. 21).

The whole sequence of this Gospel reading, full of sweetness and wonderfully profound in mysteries, offers no small material for spiritual life and teaching. In it we discern not merely the present and visible advent of the Lord, by which he is read to have come once then to Jerusalem, but rather that invisible and wondrous advent by which he daily comes, now more familiarly to the clean of heart, now more fittingly and sweetly to the filthy and unclean in order to make them cleaner. For whatever is heard outwardly, we perceive that he deigns to bring about frequently within us, if we are willing to follow the life-giving spirit in the letter.

“When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem.” Jerusalem, which is called the vision of peace, signifies not that temporal Jerusalem but the Jerusalem above, which is free, our mother: the seat and foundation of eternity, where he who “made both one” (Eph. 2:14) prepared for his heirs the vision of abiding peace. To this Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace—the rational soul is rightly compared. In the region of unlikeness it strives, according to its measure, to become like those standing before the face of the Creator, groaning and sighing to be conformed to them by living well, though it is not yet able [Col. 0026A–B] to join them in beholding the King in his beauty.

It will not, however, first begin to be and to be called Jerusalem until our Lord Jesus Christ—our Savior—deigns to draw near to it by secret inspiration, having been pleased by his hidden counsel to predestine it to eternal life; so that she who was once the most rejected of the rejected may become the most beloved of the beloved, and she who was formerly turned away may become a praiseworthy imitator of heavenly conduct and discipline. Worthily joined to the assembly of those who serve God, she denies herself, takes up Christ’s cross, longs to follow the footsteps of his life, and eagerly learns by what path of actions she must proceed. For the worthy accomplishment of these things, the places here expressly named are to be sought spiritually. Hence the Evangelist continues:

“And he came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives.” Bethphage is interpreted “house of the jaw.” It was a house of priests, where they continually rendered to the Lord the voice of praise and confession. Therefore let the blessed and faithful soul which has resolved, leaving all things, to follow him “whose ways are beautiful,” first come to Bethphage, approach the house of the jaw, and disclose with devout lips what it has conceived in a devout heart. Let it beneficially utter in the voice of humble and pure confession a conscience still biting it and reproving it for its past vanity and transgression. Then, watered by tears of repentance and no longer despairing of pardon and salvation, let it have recourse to the Mount [Col. 0026C–D] of Olives, to the rich and fertile mountain, to the Son of Oil; hanging upon God’s abundant blessing, let it now dare to beg that some little of the oil of mercy and compassion be given to it.

For what is signified by oil, which floats above all liquids, except the mercies of the Lord, which are above all his works? (Ps. 144:9 [Vulgate]).

But it should be noted that, just as there is a great, sweet, inexhaustible mercy of God, so also there is a small, temporal, and failing mercy of God. When the Lord graciously provides the supports of temporal life, this is indeed called small mercy, though it is necessary. Of this mercy it is said through the prophet: “Your mercy is like a morning cloud, and like dew passing away in the morning” (Hos. 6:5). For all these things pass away like a morning cloud; they pass and do not remain, and therefore perhaps are to be sought less. But God’s great mercy is, I say, a great and lofty mountain: when God does not forget to have mercy on the unworthy and sinful, but refreshes them with the oil of mercy, anoints them with the anointing of grace, enriches and fattens them. And the more this oil is hungered for through his gift, the more the mind is kindled to seek it. David begs that the richness of this oil, the greatness of this mercy, be granted him, saying: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50:1 [Vulgate]). The following words immediately indicate in what order these things should be begun and with what zeal they should be completed.

“Then he sent two disciples, saying to them: Go into the village opposite you.” Who are these two disciples except certain faithful messengers of the soul: fear [Col. 0027A–B] and love? Fear, when every person to be saved is pierced by sorrow for sins and dread of judgment; love, when that wholly desirable One alone is embraced and sought in sweet affection. Fear is indeed the beginning that brings repentance; but love, having cast out fear, strengthens souls chosen by God in the perfection of virtues. Thus, among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, the first degree is placed as fear, by which the sad recollection of sins troubles and torments the sinner’s mind; but the final degree is wisdom, which is love, by which the ardent lover, trained through the successive degrees of virtues, has leisure only to contemplate the benefits of the Creator.

Where these disciples—these two movements of the soul—are to be sent, and what benefit they confer when sent, the Lord who sends them himself indicates, saying:

“Go into the village opposite you, and immediately you will find an ass tied up, and a colt with her.” When almighty God, by a wondrous work, had created all things from nothing, at last he made humankind from the slime of the earth in Paradise with such dignity and blessedness that, if humanity had chosen rather to live more blessedly than to sin, it should have been the dwelling-place of its Creator without end—as we believe we shall one day be when he who will be all in all has wholly possessed us. But now, subject to sins and entangled in the crimes of old Adam, we are no longer what we were happily created to be. And when we return to ourselves within ourselves, we see that we have done many things contrary to the fear and love of God, many things altogether abject and unworthy; we find our ass tied up and a colt with her. For what do we understand by the ass except the foolish and stupid soul? It is rightly said to resemble an ass because, when it despised possessing knowledge of God alone, it remained foolish and insensible, enslaved to animal life. David, seeing its glory of beauty changed into disgrace, testifies thus, saying: “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” [Col. 0027C–0028A] (Ps. 48:13 [Vulgate]).

It should also be noted that this our ass is by no means free or unencumbered, but bound and entangled in harsh knots of chains. By what chains, I ask, or by what cords? Certainly by wicked deeds and crimes, which make a cord exceedingly long and tangled. David declares with groaning words that he is constrained by these cords of sins: “The cords of sinners have encompassed me” (Ps. 118:61 [Vulgate]).

“And a colt with her.” By the colt may be understood the rational spirit, which, while it longs to seek earthly things more than spiritual, loses in a certain manner the likeness stamped upon it of God’s image. But amid these darknesses of blindness, amid these miseries of life, will the Lord reject us unto the end? Assuredly, because he is “a helper in due time, in tribulation,” he does not despise those whom he created, but, merciful and compassionate, commands them to be loosed and brought to himself.

“Untie them,” he says, “and bring them to me.” It is as though Truth plainly said: You who were once captives in death, bound in harsh chains of sins: constrained by the remembrance of my fear, free yourselves by fitting repentance to receive the hope of pardon. But bring yourselves through love, so that you may no longer be fearful in seeking to escape the torments of Gehenna, but, filled with my inestimable sweetness, may not begrudge working diligently to gain eternal things. And what does it mean that he commands them to be loosed and brought to himself—saying, “Untie them and bring them to me”—except that thanksgiving must be rendered to him who works all things in all, to him who loosens the fettered and raises the fallen; that no merits of ours, if there are any merits, are to be imputed by us to ourselves, but praise and glory due to the sole author and giver must be rendered, as the Psalmist says: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” [Col. 0028B–C].

But before these things are fulfilled in us, how many temptations and adversities arise is openly declared in what follows. It continues:

“And if anyone says anything to you, say: The Lord has need of them.” Whoever have at any time resolved to renounce this world know better than any speech can express how many temptations and contradictions they have endured through the suggestion of evil spirits or wicked people; how often they have changed their good intention; how often they have resolved to undertake the way of good action; how often, timid and faint-hearted, they have planned to evade it. Hence David, lest the deceitful tongue of worldly people, hostile to good intention and action, should ever become harmful, prays to the Lord, saying: “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 119:2 [Vulgate]).

But amid these very contradictions, once anyone has attained the habit of holy conduct, can that person then, placed in safety, escape the missiles of temptations? By no means. Rather, he suffers and endures innumerable battles of the tempter; he hears manifold words of contradiction which the tumultuous crowd of thoughts introduces. Hence Solomon, desiring to make everyone cautious and watchful, admonishes thus: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). Indeed, if we consider attentively, we are assaulted by a twofold temptation, which arises either from the depression of adversity or from the exaltation of prosperity. Solomon expresses these customary kinds of temptation when he says: “The turning away of the simple will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. 1:32). When a person insufficiently perfected in the Lord is affected by the slightest movements of injuries, he slips by that means toward worse things; but when prosperity follows, attributing it to his own merits, he exalts himself above others [Col. 0028D–0029B]. But by what means or methods we may withstand these troublesome temptations, let us hear the Wisdom of God the Father himself, who selects a few things from many. For he says:

“And if anyone says anything to you, say: ‘The Lord has need of them.’” Here Christ, our wise one, whose wisdom is without number, made this known in few words. As his praise accords with his name, so his speech and teaching are full of truth and praise. For, as Isaiah says, “The Lord makes a shortened word upon the earth” (Isa. 10:23; Rom. 9:28): brief indeed in number of words, but containing within itself the weight of life and salvation. What, then, does it mean to say, “The Lord has need of them,” except that the righteous, for whom all things work together for good [Col. 0029C], are accustomed not only to rejoice but also to give thanks amid the persecutions of adversity, and declare themselves worthy to be crushed by the Lord’s scourges, saying: “The Lord has need of these things”? “The Lord,” they say, “who works salvation in the midst of the earth, who knows all things before they come to pass, has need to crush us with the troubles of adversity—us whose restless mind and disordered conduct knew how to do nothing but works of the flesh. He has need that we be reduced to nothing in the sight of men, as though despised and trampled underfoot—we who, puffed up, thought ourselves something when we were nothing.”

If this is what the humble and kindly mind says amid adversity, what, we may suppose, will it say amid prosperity and tranquillity? “It is the Lord’s work,” it says; “if I possess any good action, any knowledge, I ascribe it all to him; I owe it all to him, from whom comes everything that I possess.” Therefore, when amid prosperity and adversity we have begun, by God’s favor, to maintain an inviolable and unshaken constancy and evenness of mind, we shall immediately be dismissed, free and released, and be able to approach the author of life. “And he will immediately dismiss them.” For we are immediately dismissed if we are humbled in prosperity. We are immediately dismissed if we are so raised up by humility that we do not fail in adversity. It follows:

“All this took place, that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: ‘Say to the daughter of Zion.’” All this took place—all, I say, that we have heard; by sure experience we know how true it is—and the faithful prophecy of the preachers is fulfilled, who are ready to announce to the daughter of Zion the glory of the King who is to come from above [Col. 0030A]. What, then, do those established in the contemplation of eternity prophesy to the daughter of Zion? “Behold,” they say, “your King comes to you, meek.” Behold, without delay your King will come to you meek; he will come, the One to one alone; the King will come to the queen, I say, with such meekness and sweetness that you may enter, through contemplation, into the joy of your Lord and search out his sweet secrets. He will not come empty, he whose fullness you desire to receive; and such an occasion for holy daring will be granted that you may even, insofar as is permitted while you are still clothed in mortal flesh, investigate what knowledge of eternal life is. The Lord reveals the blessedness of this knowledge and love when speaking to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

How, then, will he come to you? “Sitting upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.” For he gladly dwells wherever he finds a seat and habitation worthy of the presence of his majesty: not a place which he visits for an hour or now and then—for “there is none who can hide himself from his heat” (Ps. 18:7)—but one in which he deigns to dwell in familiar and continual residence, as he says elsewhere: “We shall come and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Thus the Lord sits upon the ass and the colt when, by dwelling within our spirit and soul, he possesses them; and they recover in themselves the likeness of the image of God, long since effaced, and, with the flesh subjected to the lord of the mind, they raise one another without any disturbance to exercise the strength of good work [Col. 0030C]. Hence it is fittingly added:

“And the disciples went and did as Jesus had commanded them; and they brought the ass and the colt, and laid their garments upon them, and made him sit thereon.” What can we understand by the disciples but fear and love, as we said before? For each of the elect, once he has recognized the great works of God’s goodness, does not yield to torpor or negligence; rather, aided by the grace of the fear and love of God, he strives to advance by the tireless steps of virtues. They also bring the ass and the colt and likewise lay their garments upon them, when, clothed and adorned with the finest virtues, they prepare in their hearts a seat for Christ. For, as it is written, the soul of the righteous is the seat of Wisdom [Col. 0030D]. Therefore, if he finds it naked and not clothed in the equipment of virtues, the Beautiful and Splendid One will by no means be able to sit there in delight.

“But a very great multitude spread their garments in the way; and others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the way.” Let us see why it is said that not merely a multitude, but a very great multitude, spread its garments in the way. Let us see which multitude goes before and which follows; who acts first, and what the following multitude makes known by its cry. The very great multitude, then, is present when the hearts of the elect are sometimes afflicted, in vehement fear, by an excessive agitation arising from the memory of past sins; when, continually returning to themselves, they severely afflict themselves even for a slight transgression; and when, troubled and disturbed in mind, they have learned how they ought formerly to have lived [Col. 0031A], and grieve that they have passed over, even for a moment, the growth of some good. This indeed is the very great multitude of thoughts which spreads its garments in the way, because, bowed down and humbled, it receives the garment of sanctification and piety; clothed and adorned with this, it directs a way for the Lord to its own heart. But because amid the turbulent movements of thoughts other thoughts sometimes follow when the grace of love has gone before, it is rightly added:

“But others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the way.” They cut branches from the trees when, within the house of the mind, they gather whatever they see worthy of imitation in the examples of the saints who have gone before, and whatever they see praiseworthy in the conduct of those who are still living in the flesh. For what are trees except souls worthy of God, lofty and eminent in the summit of virtues [Col. 0031B]? Is not the ever-Virgin Mary recognized as a tree, flowering and fruitful with the twofold abundance of chastity and humility? Is not John the Baptist a tree outstanding in the height of humility, as were all those already made participants in his blessedness? As they labor to pluck branches of holiness from these, striving themselves in every respect to be humbled and to attain chastity, without which no one shall see God, they cut down the delightful fruits of the trees, by which they make a pleasant way for the author of life, walking in them and dwelling in them.

“And the multitudes that went before and that followed cried out, saying: ‘Hosanna to the Son of David. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’” The multitudes which precede [Col. 0031C] and follow are, as has often been said, thoughts born from the twofold tinder of fear and love. As they differ among themselves in diverse quality, so they seem to meet the King of Hosts with diverse cries. For the one whom the memory of a sinful conscience gnaws, whom the punishment of avenging flame terrifies, cries “Hosanna” to the Son of David in voice—indeed, in great devotion. Wounded by the blow of sin, pressed down and humbled by inward sickness, he earnestly implores with a mighty cry the grace of the Savior, whose nature is goodness, in order to obtain the gift of pardon and salvation: that he who, through the tenderness of his mercy, did not once despise David when he was a transgressor—indeed, when he was penitent—may not disdain to grant pardon to that person’s sins with the same merciful regard.

[Col. 0031D] But the multitude of following thoughts—that is, thoughts which do not accuse but defend—which, freed from the snares of vices, is accustomed with entire intention to search out and investigate the things above, does not seek one who saves from sins. Rather, it meets the Lord of virtues, who rules and reigns most powerfully within it, with this cry and jubilation of exultation: “Blessed,” it says, “is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Whenever, I say, the blessed soul in the exile of this pilgrimage receives God as he visits it graciously and mercifully, it offers the joyful praise of blessing, until in the joy of eternity it may be permitted always to possess in present reality its beloved—not then won by tears or acquired by any contrition of mind and body, but held forever by the firm lot of everlastingness [Col. 0032A]. To him be honor and dominion through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY III. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

“When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, unto the Mount of Olives, then he sent two disciples, saying to them: ‘Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find an ass tied, and a colt with her; untie them and bring them to me’” (Matt. 21).

The reading of the holy Gospel, which is fittingly read on Palm Sunday because of the sequence of the letter, is fittingly repeated on the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent because of the eminence of the allegory hidden in the letter. For the Son of God draws near to Jerusalem [Col. 0032B] when, at the end of time, he administers for the restoration of the heavenly Jerusalem the mystery of its redemption, arranged before the ages with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Thus he comes to Bethphage when, in the diverse prefigurations of patriarchs and prophets, he declares to the world that mystery of its redemption. For Bethphage is interpreted “house of the mouth,” by which name the bread of angels, one day to be eaten by humankind, is signified. Bethphage is written to be at the Mount of Olives, by which is expressed the greatness of that mercy through which the Son of God himself is brought down from the heights of heaven to the depths of earth. Hence the Psalmist says: “His mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9).

Therefore, when he had drawn near to Jerusalem, when he had come to Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, “then he sent two disciples, saying to them: ‘Go into the village that is opposite you’” [Col. 0032C]. Since disciples are so called from learning, the two disciples rightly signify the natural law and the written law. Both are wondrously instructed through the illumination of the Holy Spirit concerning the mystery of the redemption to come, while he who, coming in the flesh, declares himself to be the light of the world is prefigured in marvelous and innumerable ways by the eternal mountains. He himself sends these two disciples, since by the mystery of his incarnation he fulfills all the prefigurations of the patriarchs and prophets. Accordingly he speaks to them when, through the instruction of the Holy Spirit, he trains both the natural law and the written law for the ministry of his future redemption. “Go,” he says, “in diverse prefigurations into the village opposite you,” that is [Col. 0032D], exposed and set before your sight: into that most fortified and most holy temple of the Holy Spirit, into that enclosed garden and sealed fountain of the Virgin Mother. For this village was set before both natural and written law, since this almond-tree of virginity was, from the beginning of the world, exposed to the expectation of patriarchs and prophets. Hence the Son of God himself, present in the flesh, says to his disciples: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke 10:24).

“And immediately,” when you have begun to proceed through the diverse prefigurations, when you have entered the village set before you, “you will find” the redemption of the world which you seek [Col. 0033A]. What, then, is this redemption? “An ass tied, and a colt with her.” The tied ass is the most holy flesh, joined to the Word of God in the Virgin’s womb by the incomprehensible and ineffable bond of union. The colt with her is the rational soul assumed by the Word in the flesh, as is said in the Catholic faith:

> Perfect God, perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0033D] That is, in the Athanasian Creed.]

Of this ass or colt the patriarch Jacob speaks when, in the Spirit, he beholds Christ who would one day be born from the tribe of Judah: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations, binding his ass to the vine and, O my son, his colt to the vine-stock” (Gen. 49:10). Hence he of whom we speak says to his disciples at supper [Col. 0033B]: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman” (John 15:1); and again: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (ibid., 5).

The most holy flesh of Christ is rightly signified by the ass, which is known to be a beast of burden, since it was voluntarily burdened with the weight of many labors for the cleansing of our sins, as the prophet Isaiah declares concerning him: “Truly he bore our infirmities, and he carried our iniquities” (Isa. 53:4). Hence he himself says through the Psalmist, when describing the extremity of his Passion: “Sinners built upon my back” (Ps. 138:3). Likewise, the most holy soul of Christ is rightly understood by the colt, in which the marks of youth are evident. By its unique innocence it cleanses all faithful souls of the contagions of every oldness and restores to them, as it were, the marks of youth belonging to ancient freedom [Col. 0033C]. Therefore the Son of God himself says to his disciples, when he points natural law and written law toward the testimony of his redemption: “Untie them and bring them to me.” With the keys of your prefigurations untie the mystery hidden from the ages, and bring it to me, bearing witness to the future redemption which will be to the glory of my name.

“And if anyone says anything to you”—that is, if the world, which lies in evil because it is devoted to unbelief, contradicts the testimony of your faith and preaching—“you say,” you, I say, my fellow-councilors, declare by your signs and writings that “the Lord has need of them”: that the Son of God, Creator of time, must become man in the fullness of time, in order by his humanity to free the human race from death. “And immediately he will dismiss them,” that is, believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation, he will subject himself in due veneration to the divinity and humanity of the Son of God [Col. 0033D].

For that word, “dismissal,” occurs frequently in the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments, bearing witness to Christ’s divinity and humanity. Thus Jephthah’s daughter says to her father: “Dismiss me, that I may go about the mountains for two months” (Judg. 11:37). By Jephthah, whose name means “opening,” Christ the Lord is signified, by whose blood paradise is opened to the thief and to all the faithful. By Jephthah’s daughter the humanity of Christ is designated, which he protects by the governance of his divinity, as a father protects his daughter [Col. 0034A]. Thus the daughter says to the father; Christ’s humanity speaks to God the Father: “Grant me only this which I ask, by which I attain both the fruit of your love and of my submission, the effect of human redemption: dismiss me; make my divinity and humanity known to the world. Let me go about the mountains for two months”: that in the consummation of the two Testaments, in the salvation of two peoples, in the salvation of soul and body, in love of God and neighbor, in the active and contemplative life—for the type of all these is contained in two months—I may go about the mountains, so that I may fulfill the prefigurations of the patriarchs and prophets by the mystery of my redemption.

Thus David, in the type of Christ, says to Michal, by whom the Synagogue is understood: “Dismiss me; confess me as true God and true man, otherwise I shall kill you” (1 Sam. 19:17)—that is, I shall justly deliver you over to eternal death because of your unbelief. Thus David, in the type of Christ, says to Jonathan, through whom the prophetic order is designated: “Dismiss me,” that is, “attest my divinity and humanity by your preaching, that I may quickly go to Bethlehem” (1 Sam. 20:6), that I may have a place of faith and a seat of rest in the Church of the Gentiles. It follows:

“Now all this was done, that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: ‘Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your King comes to you, meek, and sitting upon an ass and a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’” All this took place, which saved the whole world, that in the fullness of time what had been foreshadowed through the prophet at the beginning of the age might be fulfilled [Col. 0034C]. Who was this prophet who sang beforehand the mystery of the future redemption to both natural law and written law? Surely it was that first-created man, the *protoplastēs*, who, placed in paradise and awakened from sleep, as one foreknowing things to come, celebrated the work of woman’s creation in these praises: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.
