She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:4–5).

When Adam uttered these songs of prophecy in paradise, he spoke, as it were, these words to the faithful who would be generated from his flesh in the world: “You patriarchs, placed under natural law; you prophets, joined to the written law: say in your prophecies and writings to the daughter of the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 0034D], which is the mother of all the faithful—to the Church of the Gentiles sighing upon the earth—of the Son of God, who shall be the expectation and salvation of the Gentiles: ‘Behold, your King comes to you, meek.’” That glorious Son of God comes as a humble man, entering the world in silence, like Gideon, who, fearing the people of his city because he had to destroy Baal’s altar at God’s command, took ten of his servants and did not wish to do it by day, but completed everything by night (Judg. 6:27).

Gideon, whose name is said to mean “going about in the womb,” signifies Christ the Lord, who embraces all things in the circuit of his majesty, yet for the redemption of the human race is enclosed in the womb of the Virgin Mother [Col. 0035A]. Gideon destroys Baal’s altar when the Son of God, made man, overthrows the antiquity of carnal ceremonies. Gideon takes ten men from his servants when the Son of God joins a rational soul and human flesh to his divinity in the unity of person. For there are five senses of the outward human being, and likewise five senses of the inward human being. These are represented as ten men by the ten lines by which the sun returns backward on the sundial of Ahaz. For by the sundial of King Ahaz, whose name means “he grasps God” (Isa. 38:8), the mystery of Christ’s incarnation is expressed; through it, as through a timepiece, the course of times and the condition of the elect and the reprobate are distinguished, as Simeon says to the blessed Virgin: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted” (Luke 2:34).

Gideon fears his father’s household because Christ recoils from the unbelief of the Jewish people. He fears the people of that city, which is wholly given over to the delight of the world or of the flesh. He does not wish to act by day because, having become man, he does not wish to make his majesty known [Note: [Col. 0035D] That is, to make it known.]. “For,” says the Apostle, “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). Gideon completes everything by night [Col. 0035C], because the Son of God accomplishes the redemption of the world under, as it were, the silence of night, in the design of assumed humanity and humility: sitting upon the ass, ruling by his divinity the flesh he assumed; and upon the colt, the foal of a beast of burden—the rational soul, which was the life of the flesh assumed through obedience to the Father. It follows:

“And the disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them; and they brought the ass and the colt, and laid their garments upon them, and made him sit thereon.” The disciples go because the natural and written law come forth in their own times. They do as Jesus commanded them because they serve the dispensation of the Son of God for the redemption of the world by their prefigurations and preaching. They bring the ass and colt when, by their testimonies, they establish that the true Son of God would one day become the true Son of the Virgin and would assume an animate body in his Mother’s womb. They lay their garments upon them when they adapt the adornments of their prefigurations and preaching to the humanity of the Redeemer. They make him sit thereon [Col. 0035D] when all patriarchs and prophets, and all believers of natural law and written law, beseech with continual sighs and tears that the Son of God may come in the flesh.

“But a very great multitude spread their garments in the way; and others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the way.” The very great multitude is the innumerable multitude of virtues and graces. They spread their garments in the way when they heap the insignia of their beauty upon him who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). For whatever virtues or graces there could be, or will be, from the beginning to the end of the age in the whole body of the faithful, flow from him as from the head, like the ointment which flows down upon the beard [Col. 0036A] and descends to the hem of the garment.

“But others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the way.” Who are these others but the ministering spirits sent from heaven to us for the service of salvation? They are rightly called “others,” because they are alien to us who are condemned in the prison of this exile, by reason of the difference of eternal blessedness, immortality, and exaltedness. They cut branches from the trees and spread them in the way when, in honor of him whom they acknowledge to be their Creator, whom they behold descending from heaven to earth for humankind’s sake, they bring to his faithful, from those trees of eternal knowledge flowering in the heavenly kingdom, innumerable and fragrant delights of divine meanings. Hence the Apostle declares that in him are hidden all treasures of wisdom and knowledge [Col. 0036B] (Col. 2:3), which he himself mercifully distributes to his elect until the end of the age. It follows:

“And the multitudes that went before and that followed cried out, saying: ‘Hosanna to the Son of David. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’” The multitudes who go before can rightly be called the holy angels, who precede human beings both in the dignity of creation and in the immutability of blessedness. The multitudes who follow are understood to be the remnant of the elect among humankind, who follow, as it were, the footsteps of those who have gone before from afar, when they are eventually transferred, through the countless labors and difficulties of this life, into the fellowship of the holy angels. Or the multitudes who go before are the fathers and faithful of the Old Testament; the multitudes who follow are the fathers and faithful of the New Testament.

Whether, then, they are holy angels [Col. 0036C], elect human beings, or fathers and faithful of both Testaments, they cry out the glory and mercy of the Son of God coming in the flesh. The angels cry out to Christ born in Bethlehem: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14). The elect from the beginning to the end of the age offer thanksgivings to Christ the Redeemer. Or both holy angels and elect human beings cry out in the present and speak in the future: “Hosanna to the Son of David. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Blessing to the incarnate One; brightness to the One born; wisdom to the One baptized; thanksgiving to the One dying; honor to the One rising again; power to the One ascending; strength to the One who judges all things justly—to you, our Creator’s most unconquered Son. Blessed are you, who sanctified us with an eternal blessing when you expiated the curse of the first parent by your blood; who came in the name of the Lord [Col. 0036D] when you freed your creature from the evil enemy and dedicated it to yourself, the true Lord. To you, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, be praise and glory through the infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY IV. ON THE SAME FIRST SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“The voice of my beloved knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove,’” etc. (Song of Songs 5).

The Advent of the Lord and Savior, now commemorated throughout the world by the faithful with solemn rejoicing, is the season of grace and salvation. All the ancient fathers and prophets always sighed for it with burning desire [Col. 0037A], and longed with great sorrow, tears, and groans to remain in the flesh in order to receive that grace. Had they indeed obtained their desire, there is no doubt that they would have prepared themselves with the greatest diligence to receive worthily the advent of our Lord and Savior. Since almost none of them merited to see or hear him in the flesh, they greeted his advent from afar; and all who, illuminated by the Spirit of God, could foresee the future commended everywhere in their words the grace of salvation which would come to the world through him and through his blessed Mother.

Among them, Solomon, wisest of men, composed a book in praise and honor of this same Lady, our Mary: namely, the Song of Songs. Though it may be referred to the holy Church and to each faithful soul [Col. 0037B], it belongs especially to her through whom the salvation of the world appeared to believers. For as this solemnity belongs especially to our Lord Jesus Christ, so it belongs especially to his Mother, with whom the Lord and Redeemer himself willed to work the salvation of the human race. In this book, therefore, we find written twice: “The voice of my beloved, the voice of my beloved.” The first occurrence is stated simply: “The voice of my beloved.” In the second is added: “The voice of my beloved knocking.” This is not without mystery, because by the first phrase, given without addition—“The voice of my beloved”—we may understand the desire of the holy fathers and prophets. Everything that they spoke prophetically or enacted figuratively was a kind of voice of their desire, by which they called and proclaimed the Lord who was to come to earth. But when our Lord Jesus Christ resolved to satisfy their desires, what follows was fulfilled: “The voice of my beloved knocking.” For one who knocks surely knocks with his hand; and in a sense the Lord knocked with his hand when, by assuming flesh, he fulfilled in deed that which they had long desired [Col. 0037C].

God, therefore, as we have said, wishing by his birth to aid lost humankind, immediately addressed his beloved Mother, whom he had chosen and taken up for accomplishing this work of human redemption, as the following text indicates: “Open,” he says, “to me, my sister.” If we examine these words more closely, a certain sequence of the Gospel Annunciation and of the Lord’s incarnation is woven into obscure language. Although the words differ, they agree in mystical meaning with the words of the Evangelist: “The angel Gabriel was sent to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph” (Luke 1:26), and he said to her: “Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son” (ibid., 31). Therefore, that she might incline the ear of her heart toward this heavenly embassy and not doubt the oracle as though unbelieving, he who spoke to her through his angel admonishes her in these words: “Open to me.” It is as though he said: “Open to me through faith; do not doubt my words, for it can fittingly happen to you that, by conceiving and bearing a son, the human race may be saved through the blessed fruit of your womb” [Col. 0038A]. Why she ought to give faith is openly explained in what follows.

“My sister,” he says. Why does he call her sister? The Son of God was promised to two fathers, namely Abraham and David, as one who would be born of their seed. For when Abraham, obedient to the Lord’s command, did not hesitate to offer his only son in sacrifice, this obedience pleased God so greatly that he confirmed by oath that he would give him his Only-begotten Son (Gen. 22). Thus our Lady Mary is rightly admonished to believe the Lord’s words without doubt, because she is Abraham’s sister—indeed, his daughter—and derived her true origin from his offspring, from whose seed the Lord himself, as he had promised, was to be born. He further calls her by other names which fittingly accord with her merits.

[Col. 0038B] “My friend,” he says, “my dove, my spotless one.” She was God’s friend through faith, because she believed the angel announcing that she would conceive and bear the Son of God for the redemption of the human race. She was also a dove through simplicity, for though she was chosen by God so that the salvation of the world might come from her, she sought from this nothing but the honor of God and the salvation of humankind. The Gospel plainly indicates this where she is said to have told the angel: “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 2:38). For there would have been a certain duplicity in her, and in some sense she would not have been a dove without gall, had she sought her own praise or honor from this. She was also spotless through purity of life [Col. 0038C]. Indeed, she was spotless in heart and body, she through whom the stain which clung to the whole human race through the fault of the first parent was to be cleansed and abolished. Had she not possessed these names—or rather, these insignia of virtues—she could by no means have become a dwelling-place of divinity. But because she was perfectly adorned with them, she was judged worthy to receive the fullness of grace, concerning which it is added:

“For my head is full of dew.” By Christ’s head we must understand his divinity, which, never becoming greater or smaller, always abounded from the beginning in itself with unchangeable mercy; but not in such a way that this mercy reached us and freed lost humankind from penal dominion. Why is the head said to be full? Just as we call a vessel filled with water superabundantly full when the water poured into it flows outward, so truly, when the time came of which the Apostle says, “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4), and of which the Psalmist says, “You shall arise, O Lord, and have mercy upon Zion, for it is time to have mercy upon her; for the time has come” (Ps. 101:14), then that eternal divinity was in some sense made so full of mercy and grace that it would not, and could not, hold itself back within, unless, coming forth, it flowed out upon the earth. It first poured itself into the Virgin’s womb, as the angel entering said to her: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 2:28) [Col. 0039A]. It is as though he said: “The Lord, the inhabitant of heaven, is now full of grace for saving humankind; and your virgin womb is now filled with the fullness of this grace, because he himself is to be born from you.” Nor should it be passed over that the head is said to be full of dew; for dew falls from heaven upon the earth. Certainly this ineffable grace came not from human beings but from above. And because the blessed Mary conceived and bore true God and true man, it is suitably added:

“And my locks with drops of the night.” Locks are hair intertwined and joined together. By locks we can fittingly understand that union of divine and human nature which took place in the womb of the inviolate Virgin Mary. Yet no mortal ever has known, or can know or investigate, how human nature was united to divinity; nor did the Virgin’s own consciousness know this mystery. But by locks, which are also called twisted hair, something else may be understood: namely, the twisted and contorted limbs of the assumed man. For our Lord Jesus Christ spent all the days of his life amid many labors and sufferings; and at last, hung on the cross and pierced with nails, he was condemned to a most shameful death—the kind of death by which not even the most wicked thief or robber is usually punished. Therefore these locks, by which we understand Christ’s humanity, are said to be full of drops of the night. What can be expressed by “drops of the night” except the cleansing of sins? For where a drop trickles, it washes and cleanses the place. And indeed, whoever strives to reach eternal salvation must be cleansed by certain drops [Col. 0039C].

Let us see, then, how the cleansing of the beloved was first accomplished by drops. The drops of Christ’s blood which flowed from his most holy side as he hung upon the cross cleansed and washed away the sins of the whole human race. There are also the drops of baptism, by which a person is made clean from every original or actual sin when washed. But whoever, defiled again by sins, loses the innocence received in baptism must be baptized anew and cleansed by drops of tears, which the eyes bring forth from a penitent heart. Therefore, after the glorious words of an unheard-of greeting, after the mysteries of so great a promise—that by receiving the fullness of grace, of which we have spoken, she ought to conceive and bear a son—the blessed Mother of God Mary, ignorant of the divine dispensation but conscious of her own chastity, speaks as follows:

“I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” By this tunic we believe carnal concupiscence is signified, prefigured in the first parents, as we read written in Genesis: “The Lord God made coats of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them” (Gen. 3:21). Both had been created so that, dwelling in the paradise of delight and sharing the angelic life, they would beget children without any carnal concupiscence [Col. 0040A]. But when, persuaded by the devil, they became disobedient to the Lord’s command, they were immediately cast out of paradise and clothed in coats of skins, so that in conceiving offspring they might be defiled by carnal concupiscence. This carnal concupiscence continued in all their descendants in such a manner that, apart from the Virgin’s Son alone, there is no human being upon earth conceived without concupiscence of the flesh. Thus the perpetual Virgin Mary had stripped herself of this tunic, namely carnal concupiscence.

And rightly it is said, “I have put off.” For one who despoils another takes away from him what ought to have been his. Thus too blessed Mary, by despoiling herself, inflicted upon herself, so to speak, a kind of violence; and, as it were doing violence to her body, deprived it of its proper right [Col. 0040B]. It would indeed have been natural for her to take delight in carnal desire, since she too had been conceived in that desire, like other human beings. But what ought to have been hers by the law of original sin [Note: [Col. 0039D] On this opinion of Godfrey, which was commonly held among the ancients but has now almost been abandoned and refuted [Col. 0040D], see our preliminary dissertation to this work.], she made wholly foreign to herself by mortifying her members with their vices and desires. For we may believe, although we find nothing at all written of it in the Gospel, that by continual abstinence and many labours she disciplined her virginal body, lest the vice of carnal desire ever approach her. And just as she had cut away from her flesh every carnal desire, so she had entirely excluded the same from her heart, as she herself declares in the following words:

“I have washed,” she says, “my feet; how shall I defile them?” By the feet we understand the affections of the inward person [Col. 0040C], which that same incorrupt Virgin so washed and cleansed from every stain that not even the pleasure of carnal desire ever touched her virginal heart. Therefore what she says—“I have put off my garment; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?”—though it differs in the letter, nevertheless agrees in spiritual meaning with the words of the Gospel, where she is said to have answered the angel announcing the divine birth to her: “How shall this be,” she says, “since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1:34). This is as though she said: “I have cut away all things of the flesh from my flesh and spirit, and have resolved to keep myself undefiled in heart and body for the eternal Bridegroom of incorruption. But that I should be joined in marital union through the desire of producing offspring [Col. 0040D], and thus violate my purpose and willingly experience the defilements of flesh and spirit which I have rejected—this I shall never consent to. Yet because I still do not know the heavenly mystery, I ask you the manner of conception. Make known how and in what order it must come about that a virgin, conceiving contrary to nature, may give birth without a man’s intercourse.” And the angel answered and said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (ibid., 35). In these words, assuredly, what follows was immediately accomplished:

“My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my womb trembled at his touch.” In this passage the Holy Trinity, which altogether worked in the one flesh of the Virgin for the conception and birth of the Son of God for the redemption of humankind, is prefigured by a hidden mystery [Col. 0041A]. By the beloved we may understand God the Father; by his hand, his consubstantial Son; and by the opening, the Holy Spirit. This beloved, then—that is, the almighty Father—sent his hand, namely his Only-begotten Son, when he ordained that he should be incarnate for our salvation. And through what did he send his hand? Through the opening. This eternal incarnation of the Son of God was effected through the opening, that is, through the Holy Spirit. For when he came upon the Virgin and overshadowed her by his power, she conceived and bore the Father’s Only-begotten himself.

Nor should it seem unfitting that we have said the Holy Spirit is signified by an opening [Col. 0041B]. For just as, through a wall that remains whole, no trace of light is visible unless it is pierced, so in some fashion a wall had been firmly fixed between us and God, so that none of mortals could see God, who dwells in inaccessible light. But this wall was broken down when, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, the Son of God assumed flesh and became visible, so that humanity might draw near to him and see him. When the blessed mother conceived him, true God and true man, she broke out into this cry, saying:

“And my womb trembled at his touch.” When a woman conceives a child, she does not immediately perceive that she has conceived, until after some time the child himself begins to live [Col. 0041C]; and often the mother’s womb trembles at the movement of the living body. Blessed Virgin Mary did not, I say, conceive our Lord Jesus Christ in this way. For when she heard from the angel, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you,” she immediately conceived true God and man with body and soul, so that in that very hour she could proclaim: “And my womb trembled at his touch.” Rightly indeed did she tremble who enclosed within the narrow chamber of her womb the Lord of such majesty, as the Church also sings in his praise: “For him whom the heavens could not contain, you bore in your womb.” Concerning this new and unheard-of miracle, the prophet Jeremiah, marvelling, had long before foretold: “Behold, the Lord will create a new thing on earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:21).

Therefore, the Holy Spirit coming upon this Mother of God made her free from every original sin [Note: [Col. 0041D] See what I noted a little earlier on a similar passage, at note 20.] and cleansed her from every actual sin, if any such sin there was, as she herself plainly indicates when she says:

“I arose, to open to my beloved.” “I arose,” I say, in body and soul, free from every original or actual sin. Nor was this done for my own sake, as though I, surpassing others in merits of virtue, were worthy to be exalted by such a gift; but “to open to my beloved”—that is, to become for him a gate through which he might pass to humanity with the flesh taken from me.

30. “My hands dripped with myrrh; my fingers were full of the finest myrrh.” By the hands of blessed Mary [Col. 0042A] we may understand her deeds; and by myrrh, the mortification of the flesh. And truly her hands dripped with myrrh, because, even if the stain of some sin had clung to her before she conceived the Son of God, it was so mortified in her by the power of the Holy Spirit that, after she had conceived and borne the Saviour of the world himself, she could thereafter be touched by no contagion of sin.

“And my fingers were full of the finest myrrh.” By her fingers we may understand her power of discernment. For with great discernment she distinguished God’s works from her own works, so that she attributed the magnificent deeds which God worked with her not to any merits of her own, nor to her chastity or humility, but to divine grace alone. It follows:

“I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved, but he had withdrawn [Col. 0042B] and passed on.” By the bolt her integrity may be understood; by the door, her faith. She says, then: “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved,” which is as if she said: “By true faith I opened to my beloved, not doubting his promises; indeed, I opened to him alone, so that, as he willed, he might be born from me while I remained intact and did not lose the seal of virginity.”

“But he had withdrawn.” Our same Redeemer had indeed withdrawn very far, had emptied himself very greatly from his exalted and transcendent divinity, when, born of a Virgin, he was placed in a narrow manger—he whose majesty neither the immensity of heaven nor the breadth of earth can contain.

“And passed on.” With this profound inclination of humility he passed through the world; he passed beyond every sin [Col. 0042C]; he passed beyond death; he passed beyond the devil, the prince of death. And by passing thus, he also granted to us, if we wish to follow him, to pass beyond all sins and vices, so that by this blessed passing, laying aside the burden of the flesh, we may at last attain him in a blessed end. May he deign to grant this—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto all ages of ages. Amen.

31. HOMILY V. FOR THE SAME FIFTH SUNDAY.

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch; and a king shall reign and be wise, and shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth. And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our righteousness” (Jer. 23).

[Col. 0042D] The most holy season of the Lord’s Advent, which we now celebrate, Holy Mother Church fittingly observes with a special observance because this season is a season of grace and mercy, in which he who in his eternity was outside time willed, at the end of time, to become temporal man for human beings. This is that pleasant and desirable time which all those hoped for and desired who, enlightened by the Spirit of God, foresaw with the prophetic eye of the heart that the Son of God would come to earth.

Among these chosen prophets of the Lord was the prophet Jeremiah, who foretold in these obscure words the salvation and grace which would come in the last times through the Incarnation of the Son of God: “Behold,” [Col. 0043A] “the days are coming,” says the Lord. By these days may be understood all that time in which the Day of eternity himself, incarnate for us, willed to dwell among human beings. For the time before the coming of this Day could be called not day but night, because there was no one so righteous and holy as to be able to attain the true light of the heavenly homeland; but after the end of the present life they descended, so to speak, into a land of darkness covered by the gloom of death.

By these days we may also understand the patriarchs and prophets themselves, who before Christ’s coming supplied the light of their preaching to those seated in the region of the shadow of death, affirming through words and enigmas that Day would come through whom the entire human race was to be enlightened and healed.

[Col. 0043B] To these days, then, what follows is aptly suited: “Says the Lord.” For the Lord truly spoke through them, and made known to them and through them to us in mystical words the plan which God the Father had undertaken for humankind’s restoration, as he says in what follows:

32. “And I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch.” When the shoot of any fruit first springs from the earth, it is a small and fragile thing, yet from it arise the beginning and hope of the fruit to follow. And what could we more fittingly understand by this Branch than the Son of God himself, who for our sake emptied himself, taking the form of a servant? He was like a little shoot in his conception, because he whom heaven and earth could not [Col. 0043C] contain made himself so small that he could be contained in the womb of a tender Virgin. He was in some fashion a little shoot at his birth, because he who holds the thrones of heaven and encloses the earth in his palm willed, born of a virgin mother, to be laid in a lowly manger. He was likewise a little shoot throughout his entire life, because in the days of his flesh he appeared before human eyes not as Lord of all, but humble and despised, and as the lowest of men. Yet in this little shoot, in this true God and man, was the beginning and hope of the fruit to follow, because he was the true salvation of the whole human race.

And it should be noted that he does not say simply “a branch,” but adds, “a righteous Branch” [Col. 0043D]. And rightly so: for he was not only righteous but righteousness itself, making all righteous, without whom no one ever was, is, or can be righteous. Or he is called a righteous Branch because every human being is conceived and born in sins; but he alone was conceived and born without sin, and therefore alone was free from sins.

And this righteous Branch is called the Branch of David, who, as is known, is said to mean “strong of hand,” or “desirable in appearance.” For although he appeared to the world humble, despised, and frail as a human being, yet he was truly strong of hand—indeed, the strongest of spirits—who, coming as the stronger one, overcame that strong armed man on the side on which he was humble, and destroyed his kingdom. He is also desirable in appearance. For though, appearing in the form of a servant, his appearance was as if hidden, he is nevertheless fairer in form than the children of men, the King of powers and glory, into whom even angels desire to look [Col. 0044A]. How this righteous Branch, springing up so small—that is, coming into the world so humbly—lived in the days of his flesh can be understood from the following words.

“And a king shall reign and be wise.” Since he is King of kings and Lord of lords, ruling and governing all things in heaven and on earth, yet in the humanity which he assumed for us he was especially King over himself. For he governed that noble kingdom—namely, the senses which he willed to have in his humanity—with such power of his divinity that it could not be touched even by the slightest stain in thought, word, or deed [Col. 0044B]. And what shall we say of his wisdom, whose wisdom is without number? He himself is the power of God and the wisdom of God, to whom it is most truly said: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24); and he governs and rules with wise ordering all that he created by the greatness of his wisdom.

He who in his first coming came humble and gentle, not to judge but to save the world—how stern a judge he will come at the final judgment, to render to each according to his works, the order of the following text seems to indicate:

“And he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth.” For he will execute judgment upon the reprobate, consigning them to eternal punishments; he will execute righteousness in those being saved, making them exalted by the glory of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0044C]. And this will be done in the earth, namely in the human flesh which he assumed from the substance of our earthly body. For although he will come in his majesty, he will nevertheless judge the world in the form of a servant which he assumed, as he himself testifies when he says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

After that universal judgment, then, in which each person will receive according to his merit, the elect, beholding the wonderful righteousness of their Lord, will endlessly praise the name by which they have been saved, singing with one voice: “The Lord our righteousness.” So long as we remain in the misery of this mortality, we cannot know or investigate the abyss of God’s judgments. There, when the veil of mortality has been put aside [Col. 0044D], we shall perfectly know the judgment and righteousness of our Redeemer: that by a most righteous judgment he condemned the reprobate, and that according to the multitude of his mercy he glorified the elect with the rewards of the heavenly kingdom.

All these things which he willed either to suffer or to perform in the humanity assumed for us, he does not disdain still to perform with every human being who is being saved, whom he causes to come from the darkness of ignorance of God and of himself into the light of perfect knowledge and true faith. “Behold, the days are coming,” says the Lord. For in order that a human being may be freed from the night of this world, it is necessary that the splendour of the eternal Father kindle his heart with the grace of his light, and that he whose very speaking is doing begin to speak with an invisible tongue in that person’s heart, and by hidden inspiration teach and instruct him what he ought to avoid [Col. 0045A] and what he ought to do. Therefore it fittingly follows at once:

“And I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch.” By the branch, which at its first emergence is small and fragile, we may understand a human being’s good will, which is tender and frail when it has not yet produced the effect of a good work. But just as in a branch is given the beginning and hope of the ensuing fruit, so in a person’s good will there is shown a certain beginning of a life that may one day be perfected. But in order that it may attain the fruit of good works, it is necessary that the true David, truly strong of hand, hold it with the hand of his power, raise it up, and sustain it, advancing the person from good will to good action, so that, progressing from virtue [Col. 0045B] to virtue, he may be fully able to fulfil what the following argument declares.

“And a king shall reign and be wise.” Since a king is so called from ruling, that person may fittingly be called king who restrains his kingdom—his body and soul, his inner and outward senses—under such discipline of strictness that he permits no contagion of vices to reign with wicked domination in his body and soul. Whoever orders and governs the kingdom of his body and soul by such rule is sometimes raised to the glory of a more exalted life, namely to that true wisdom which is from above. For he begins to relish and understand what he formerly rejected as tasteless and abominable; he also begins in this present life to taste beforehand how great is the abundance of that sweetness [Col. 0045C] which, after this exile, the eternal wisdom of the divine Father has prepared for all his elect.

Delighted by the glory of this eternal blessedness and enlivened by the grace of this inestimable sweetness, he will, as follows here, “execute judgment and righteousness in the earth”: he becomes a strict judge of himself, closely examining his thoughts and actions, and whatever he remembers having done wrong in unlawful thoughts, words, or deeds, he strives to correct with the worthy fruit of repentance, punishing in himself in the present what he fears will be punished in the future. He will also “execute righteousness in the earth,” in his earthly body. For wherever he remembers that he has been defiled by earthly deeds, he does not cease to blot this out by making satisfaction through works of righteousness [Col. 0045D]. Whoever proceeds in the present life in this order, as we have said, when he has at last passed into the inner joys of everlasting happiness, with what glory and honour he will be received is plainly indicated when it is immediately added:

“And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our righteousness.” Who are those who, raising the person delivered from the dominion of death with such reverence of praise, honour him with the glory of this name? They are surely the angelic spirits, who, unceasingly enjoying the vision of almighty God, marvel that a human being dwelling in the dust of death has merited such blessedness. “The Lord,” they say, “our righteousness.”

We must consider, dearest brethren, how inestimable is the glory of this dignity: the blessed hosts of heavenly spirits, wholly free from the stain of bodily corruption, judge the human being taken up from the prison of death and rescued from the countless defilements of carnal life [Col. 0046A] not only worthy to be made like to their own dignity, but worthy of a more excellent merit, and call him their Lord. And why is this? Surely because they behold human nature already made immortal in the head of all the elect; and therefore, magnifying every member of that Head, they honour and love it. They also marvel, and in marvelling magnify, that a human being—earth and ashes—has obtained by his merits, in this frail body, what they themselves, strangers to corruption and frailty, possess from the free goodness of God alone. There too will truly be fulfilled what is added here in fitting order:

“In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely.” By Judah, whose name is said to mean “confessing,” is fittingly expressed the person who reveals his ways to the Lord in confession and repentance for previous sins, or who shows himself a praiseworthy confessor of the divine name by magnificent merits of virtue [Col. 0046B]. Such a confessor of the divine name will truly be saved in those days, receiving as his reward what Israel signifies in its name. For Israel is said to mean “the man who sees God.” And everyone who in the present life has confessed God by the merits of a praiseworthy life, when that day of eternity shines forth, will rejoice without end in the blessed vision of his Creator.

There too he will dwell securely, whereas so long as we are in this manifold misery of mortality, we cannot be free and without fear. There we shall be granted perfect freedom, where we shall no longer have warfare with spiritual wickedness, where neither the pleasure of the flesh nor the adversity of the world will assail us any more, but there will be an everlasting festival in the vision of almighty God [Col. 0046C]. May he bring us to these joys, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

37. HOMILY VI. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY OF ADVENT.

“In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills, and all nations shall flow unto it” (Isa. 2).

The Lord our God, who has provided for human salvation in many ways [the codex reads *praevidit*, “foresaw”] [Col. 0046D], established certain principal times in the year in which a person should keep himself more diligently and carefully from every unlawful thing, amend the negligence of his body, and exercise himself more earnestly in the work of spiritual devotion. Among these is also this festal season which we observe, called the Advent of the Lord.

It would indeed be proper for us, who are designated by a spiritual name, to be prepared at every time with eager expectation for the coming of the Lord, never proving ungrateful for the grace of his visitation. But because it is not within human capacity for the mind to remain at every moment so fixed upon God, at least during this time, which, as we have said, is called the Lord’s Advent, let us be watchful and solicitous concerning the work of our salvation [Col. 0047A], so that when he comes we may not be found unprepared by him.

That acceptable season, full of every sweetness, might one day come: the ancient Fathers, awaiting Christ’s presence in the flesh, desired it and sighed for it from the depths of their hearts day and night. For the promise of this birth had kindled in them such desire that they could not restrain themselves from prophesying, in the desire of their soul, concerning the joy of this promise, wishing not to be deprived of participation in so great a sweetness. And many perfect persons who lived at that time did not prophesy about it in words, but nonetheless kept their eyes fixed upon this promise and had burning desire. Although, filled with the spirit of prophecy, they knew very well that this most salutary and most desired birth would not find them here [Col. 0047B], nevertheless they left us their writings, for whom the manifestation of this grace was reserved; they uttered their words for the use of our salvation, as the Apostle Paul declares: “Whatever things were written,” he says, “were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4).

Accordingly, one of those who foresaw that Christ would come in the flesh said in the gladness of his heart: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared.” By these last days of which he spoke, he signified the time in which the Saviour was to be incarnate. We are in these last days—days, indeed, of salvation and joy, in which God willed to become human; we, I say, who exist at the end of the ages, as the Apostle just cited says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). Thus it is rightly called “days,” because the ancient shadow of night has passed into the light of truth: that is, because we now behold with our eyes the work of our redemption which was then foretold in the hidden and obscure words of the prophets and prefigured by enigmas [Col. 0047C].

It is very fittingly called the last days, as we have said, because in this grace-filled time, when the figure has passed away, the reality has shone forth; the shadow has been driven back, and the light of truth has arisen. “In the last days,” he says, “the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared.” By the mountain in this place may be understood the lofty and most transcendent divinity; by the house of the Lord, the humanity of Christ. And rightly—indeed, most truly—the humanity of Christ is called the house of the Lord, because, according to the Apostle’s words, “all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” in it (Col. 2:9). Let us now hear in what follows where this mountain of the Lord has been prepared for us:

“Upon the summit,” he says, “of the mountains.” By the summit, which rises above every part of the body, may be understood our Lady, the perpetual Virgin Mary. For this same blessed Mother of God is called the summit of the mountains because by the privilege of her humility and purity she surpasses all saints from the beginning—who can be represented by the name of mountains on account of their most excellent merits of virtue—except only the Son whom she bore [Col. 0048A]. For the fullness of God’s manifold grace, from which we have all received, was poured out wholly upon her, because it was fitting that the precious charisms of full grace, distributed among the other saints and elect, should all at once be infused into her with a special sweetness of love: in her and through her, above all mortals, the Son of God deigned to work things so great and such as these. In her, therefore, whom we have called the summit of the mountains, that most noble mountain of the house of the Lord—namely, God and man—was prepared for us.

How, then, was he prepared for us? His whole life, his entire, I say, human conduct in this world, was a preparation for human salvation. So long as God and man dwelt among human beings, he was prepared for this purpose: that we who could not attain the height of his divinity might draw near to him through the humility of his incarnation and be saved by participation in him [Col. 0048B]. And though he was prepared for us throughout all the days of his flesh, he was especially so at the time when he deigned to drink for us the cup of his Passion. This was in some manner the completion of the preparation, when the righteous one suffered the death of the cross for the unrighteous, the innocent for sinners. He was truly being prepared for us when his body, scourged and torn, was stretched out upon the wood of the cross. There, indeed, he was, so to speak, cooked and roasted for us, as we sing of him in the commemoration of his Passion [Note: [Col. 0047] The hymn *Ad coenam agni candidi*, at Vespers for the first Sunday after Easter, or Quasimodo Sunday.]: “Whose sacred little body, roasted upon the altar of the cross.” Thus he was prepared for us through the torment of the Passion, so that we now feed in the Church upon his flesh and drink his blood [Col. 0048C]. For as among human beings, when rich or poor people are about to eat, if the food to be set before them has not been cooked or roasted, it is customary to say, “It is not prepared”; or, if it has been so prepared, “All things are ready”: so we speak spiritually concerning our food, namely the bread of angels, that he, fried and roasted in the fire of the Passion, was prepared for us so that we may employ him for our benefit—namely, feed upon his flesh and blood. And let this be the provision of our warfare, by which we are sustained on this way lest we fail.

Thus, yes, thus for us who are in the last days, this mountain of the house of the Lord has been prepared; but not in the same way for the ancient Fathers, although they too awaited him who was to come in the flesh and with worthy faith hoped for the eventual accomplishment of those things which we believe to have been done by Christ. Abel, the first martyr, fell slain by his brother for innocence. Noah, righteous in his generation, pleased the Lord. Abraham and David likewise, beloved by the Lord, merited the promise of the grace now manifested; and many others in those times pleased the Lord in holiness and righteousness. Yet the Son of God was not prepared for all of them as he has been for us, because they all departed bodily before this preparation in Christ was to be completed [Col. 0049A]. Still in praise of this most noble mountain of the house of the Lord, it is fittingly added:

“And it shall be raised above the hills.” A hill, as is clear, rises somewhat above level ground. Thus by hills may also be represented those who by good conduct and the pursuit of spiritual life excel others who savour earthly things. And that this may be understood soundly as we say, the Psalmist indicates when he says: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness” (Ps. 71:3). What could we understand more suitably by the name of mountains than patriarchs, prophets, and apostles? For they were lofty mountains because they were powerful in merits of virtue beyond other mortals, and, aflame with heavenly desire, rejected all earthly things. When those mountains received peace for the people—that is, preached the Lord’s command by word and example—there began likewise to arise in the Church people who were hills: those, namely, who raised themselves from earth, that is, from the common life of human beings, by the knowledge and love of God [Col. 0049B]. Above all these is raised this mountain of the house of the Lord, the Redeemer of the human race, because none of the saints ever could or will be equal to him.

There is also another meaning which can be understood by this raising. Christ’s raising is properly called his exaltation on the cross. Why is this called an exaltation, when it might rather be called humiliation? What height is there in such humility? What is elevated in such contempt? Never did he appear so despised by human beings as when he bore the shame of the cross. But truly, if we consider rightly, it was an exaltation, because then for the first time he won a noble triumph over the enemy: hanging on the cross, he suspended eternal death; fastened to the wood, he fastened down the world that had been bound to perpetual death; stretched out as a man upon the gibbet, he drew all things to himself. This exaltation was long before marked in Isaiah’s prophecy: “The government,” he says, “has been made upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9:6) [Col. 0049C]. What does he call “government” but the wood of the cross? Government was made upon the shoulder of the Lord Jesus when he carried the cross laid upon him and died fastened upon it; and while on it he received bodily death, he killed the death of the souls of all believers. Therefore the cross itself was not merely his instrument of punishment but also his government, because through it he mightily defeated the prince of darkness and showed himself to be the Son of the most mighty God, and the prince of all strength and every virtue, when by wonderful power he took from him the human being whom he held captive. Therefore, though Christ had been born in the flesh, before the victory of the cross the devil nevertheless exercised his power over all human beings; but after Christ died upon the cross, he lost his tyranny over all the elect.

Therefore it is rightly said: “And it shall be raised above the hills.” As in the preceding sense we said that by hills all the saints may be represented because of their excellence in virtue, so now too by hills we may understand evil spirits because of their pride. Above [Col. 0050A] these, this mountain of the house of the Lord was wondrously raised by the summit of his Passion in power; and, having taken away their tyranny, he rules his own creature.

We may also understand by the often-mentioned exaltation his resurrection and ascension.

After this exaltation it is accordingly added: “And all nations shall flow unto it.” Not without the mystery of a certain reason did the prophet prefer to say that all nations “shall flow” to him, rather than “shall come” to him. For in the Spirit he foresaw the sacrament of baptism—which now exists in Holy Church—without which there can be no access to God and no entrance into the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, when we are born, even if we are born of Christian parents, we are called and are nations before this flowing is accomplished in us [Col. 0050B], that is, before each of us is reborn through the water of the font. In that rebirth we renounce the pomps and works of the devil, that thereafter we may walk in newness of life. But if by sinning we again refuse to be doers of this profession, we are nevertheless designated before God by the name of nations.

The prophet also here signifies another flowing, by which it is fitting that, after the washing of the first baptism, we who have again become entangled in Gentile error—that is, become liable to sins—should return to Christ and to innocence of life. For after the violation of our profession in the first baptism, we return to God by flowing again when we strive to renew by the baptism of tears a conscience polluted by sins. Without doubt no hope exists for anyone of coming to the mountain of the house of the Lord—that is, to Christ—unless that person flows to him by these two modes of baptism [Col. 0050C].

Let us now briefly recapitulate what has been said and see how these same things have been prefigured in other passages of Scripture. This prophet says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared.” We also sing, when we begin the proclamation of divine praise in the Antiphonary, that another man, foreseeing that God would assume human nature, said: “Looking from afar, behold I see the power of God coming, and a cloud covering the whole earth.” What is there called a mountain is here more plainly called the power of God. What is there signified by the house of the Lord is here signified by the cloud. We have said that by the mountain may be signified Christ’s divinity, and by the house of the Lord the humanity of our same Redeemer. The one who says, “Behold I see the power of God coming, and a cloud covering the whole earth,” expresses this same thing in other words [Col. 0050D]. For in the Spirit he foresaw that the one who was to assume humanity for our salvation would possess all the fullness of divinity.

“And a cloud,” he says, “covering the whole earth.” By the cloud, as we have said, we may understand Christ’s flesh. This cloud—that is, Christ’s human nature—was such and so great that it could cover and abolish the whole earth, that is, every guilt which humanity had contracted from earthly contagion. For human divinity and divine humanity are now joined to humankind through compassion in such a way that they cover the whole earth: that is, exclude from the grace of remission no one, however heavily oppressed by earthly deeds, provided only that such a person acknowledges himself by amending his conduct [Col. 0051A].

We may render these same words, “upon the tops of the mountains,” as referring to her whom, we said, may be understood as our Lady, Mary, perpetual Virgin. Nothing prevents us from understanding the overshadowing cloud as the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the angel also said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1:35). For she was that noble earth which this cloud wholly covered and overshadowed on every side, lest the stain of actual sin, in thought, word, or deed, should touch her who had proceeded under the hereditary taint of original sin [Note: [Col. 0051D] See note 20.], but that the whole dwelling-place might be holy, in which God might dwell for the full nine months [Col. 0051B], so that the material from which the Son of God would incorruptibly assume the body of His glory might be wholly pure.

Let us strive to draw near, by the merits of good works, to this true tabernacle of the virginal womb, to which no scourge of sin could approach—although we are wounded by countless scourges of sins—so that she, full of piety and mercy, may fortify us by her protection amid the storm and misery of this world. And when He whom the true Virgin and Mother bore as the propitiation for our sins comes at His second advent to judge the living and the dead, may He exalt mercy above judgment, so that through her intercession we may attain the glorious joys of the heavenly kingdom. May our Lord [Col. 0051C] Jesus Christ deign to grant this—He who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

44. HOMILY VII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY OF ADVENT.

“There shall be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and upon the earth distress of nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and its waves; men withering away for fear and expectation of what shall come upon the whole world” (Luke 21).

Because the day of the final judgment that is to come will be exceedingly great and terrible, the merciful and compassionate Lord foretold that day to us by evident signs: “There shall be,” He says, “signs in the sun and moon and stars.” The signs which Truth itself foretold as to come have, our own age remembers, already occurred in large part [Col. 0051D]. Yet by these signs which He foretold would come in the sun, moon, and stars, He indicates to us something else, very great and eminent. By the name of the sun He signifies Himself, the Sun of righteousness, who enlightens every person coming into this world. In that very Sun—that is, in the Redeemer of humankind—signs of a new wonder were wrought when He became obedient for us even unto death. These signs, I say, of great and wondrous salvation are the wounds of the crucified and pierced Redeemer, when, hanging upon the instrument of the cross, He displayed the horns of the nails in His hands. By these signs death, as though struck by the Sun’s dart, was swallowed up in victory. Hence in a fitting order there immediately follow signs in the moon and stars [Col. 0052A]. For what is more rightly understood here by the moon than the Bride of the Lamb, namely the holy Church? And what by the stars except the brightness of apostolic splendor?

For although the moon has no brightness of its own, the sun in some manner illumines it with the ray of its splendor. So that Sun which knows no setting illumined the darkness of the whole Church with the most desirable light of His countenance. But because that Sun was to be raised up and the moon had to remain in its own order, He chose to adorn it with such stars as, shining amid a crooked nation, would never know how to withdraw their splendor, and by whose illumination very many might attain the true Light, which is Christ. By these stars, as was said before [Col. 0052B], the holy apostles are to be understood, whom the Light itself called the light of the world. When their preaching went out to the ends of the earth, great signs and wonders were wrought among the people.

45. “And upon the earth distress of nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and its waves.”

For after the light arose in darkness through apostolic preaching, a health-giving distress of nations began to occur upon the earth. Those who formerly savored only earthly things, desiring to savor the things above, strive to drive out and suppress within themselves the wicked nations of vices. Hence a grievous flood of storm immediately assails the mind because of the confused roaring of the sea and waves. For a confused sound of clamor arises in the mind when perverse thoughts press in from every side [Col. 0052C]. And because human strength is not sufficient to restrain these waves of the sea-storm, He alone, to whom none among the mighty is like, can calm the motion of its waves, as He says: “Thou rulest the power of the sea, and thou stillest the motion of its waves” (Psalm 88:10).

But because He said that such waves are calmed in part, not wholly removed, let us hear what the Evangelist adds concerning the expectation of them:

“Men withering away for fear and expectation of what shall come upon the whole world.”

For when any of the faithful behold waves swelling over them, when they perceive some succeeding others in turn, they rightly tremble with grievous expectation of fear, fearing lest, descending even to the depths, their soul should waste away amid evils [Col. 0052D]. There is also another sense in which this expectation that shall come upon the whole world may be understood. For the expectation of the final judgment causes the good and bad to wither in different ways. The perverse fear, and by fearing wither; for they recognize that they will perish as the world perishes. Yet, while adding sins to sins, they tremble there in fear where there is no fear.

There is also, in the good, another kind of fear—better, I say, and nearer to salvation: in them is the holy fear of the Lord, “whose praise endureth for ever and ever.” They fear to offend Him whom they love by fearing; and, loving Him, they always do what pleases Him [Col. 0053A]. But because a person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, withering through holy fear they fear all their works, and always set divine judgments before their souls.

This vessel of the Lord, so desirable, was filled to the very brim with this spirit of fear—namely, the Apostle Paul, who said: “I chastise my body and bring it into bondage” (1 Corinthians 9:27). Though he was so great and such a man that, while still placed in the flesh, he deserved to share in heavenly secrets, he nevertheless preferred, through humble self-estimation, to fear rather than, presumptuously thinking highly of himself, to entertain lofty thoughts. Holy David also humbly asks this spirit of fear from the Lord, saying: “Pierce my flesh with thy fear” (Psalm 118:120). Thus the inner person desires that every pleasure of the flesh and every inclination of the interior sense be pierced with the fear of the Lord [Col. 0053B], so that, as though fastened with nails, he may remain strong and immovable against every enticement of vices.

“For even the powers of heaven shall be moved.” By the powers of heaven the choirs of angels are to be understood. The love of that unchangeable eternity has so united them to itself that no will to sin can ever arise in them. Hence it is pleasing to consider more deeply on what ground those angelic orders are to be moved. They are moved not for themselves but for us, by an affection of pious compassion; and they believe that, apart from the vision of divine contemplation alone, nothing is more desirable than that their number should be made complete through our restoration.

There are also some in this life who seem to stand over others at so lofty a summit of virtues that, in the judgment of many, they are considered as it were powers of heaven [Col. 0053C]. But because they delight in the windy favor of flatterers, they receive in the present their reward for their labor. These, surely, shall be moved at the coming of the strict Judge, when the oil of the sinner will be unable to enrich their head.

“And then they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.” All flesh shall indeed see the coming Son of Man, but the joy of those who see Him will not be alike. The elect shall see Him in order that they may rejoice without end; the reprobate also shall see Him, in order that they may be confounded and perish. For the wicked shall suddenly be taken away, lest they see the glory of God. Of this manifest vision of the dreadful Judge, holy David sounds forth with prophetic voice: “God shall come manifestly, our God, and shall not keep silence” (Psalm 49:2). God, I say, of all things through the power of His divinity [Col. 0053D]; but our God through the substance of our frailty which He assumed. This our God, to whose hands the Father gave all judgment, shall one day come manifestly and shall not keep silence.

But it must be known that He will not hold mutual conversations with us as one human being with another; rather, there will be another manner of questioning and answering, exceedingly fearful. Seated upon the throne of His majesty, He will openly show us His wounds, through which all flesh shall be judged by its own conscience. For then every person will bear witness concerning himself as to how, by living rightly in this life, he answered to those wounds. Those for whom at present the word of the cross is a stumbling-block and folly shall then be condemned without mercy by judgment and justice [Col. 0054A]. But the one who, bearing about in his body the mortification of Jesus, has conformed himself to Christ’s sufferings, will go forth secure and rejoicing, without any danger of fear, to meet the crucified Lord. Therefore the Son of Man accordingly promises this to those who love Him, saying:

“When these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draweth nigh.” What, then, does it mean that they are commanded to look back with eyes turned behind them, except that, seeing their works, they may receive a sure hope of confidence? Having looked upon these things, they are also commanded to lift up their heads—that is, to make their hearts glad with hope and joy. For as soon as the Lord appears in glory, the redemption promised to them shall draw near.

To confirm the certainty of all that has been foretold [Col. 0054B], He immediately sets forth the fitting comparison of the fig tree. “Behold,” He says, “the fig tree and all the trees.” What is this fig tree except the Synagogue, long barren? This, I say, is that fruitless fig tree whose barrenness the Lord cursed, because He found in it no fruit of good work, when, hungering for its salvation with the hunger of mercy, He sought it. But behold, days shall come when, at the end of the world, the chill of unbelief having been shaken off, it shall bear the fruit of faith and love, as is said through the Psalmist: “They shall return at evening, and shall suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go round about the city” (Psalm 58:7).

48. At the end of the world, as at evening, the Jews shall indeed be converted, and shall suffer hunger and thirst, like dogs, to hear the word of God. When they have been satisfied with the bread of faith and the solid food of the Scriptures [Col. 0054C], desiring to incorporate others still unbelieving into the members of the Church, they shall go round about the very city of the Church through preaching and teaching. Like continual barking, they shall make the voice of their preaching resound throughout all lands, awakening from the sleep of death those who slumber in sins.

Truth itself immediately confirms, by a certain reason, how unquestionably all these things ought to be believed:

“Amen I say to you, this generation shall not pass away till all things be fulfilled.” What generation is more rightly understood here than the generation of the righteous, whose seed shall be directed for ages of ages? For through God’s favor, even at the very end of the world there will not be lacking those who seek the things pleasing to Him. But lest any doubt remain in the hearts of His hearers, Truth itself again added by way of affirmation: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” [Col. 0054D].

This is certainly not to be understood as though these elements will, after the end of the world, be reduced to nothing; rather, they shall be renewed into a better state by purifying fire. For the prophetic voice plainly declares with what brightness this aerial heaven—whose splendor now seems to be altered by the varied passage of clouds—shall then shine in the light of sun, moon, and stars: “The light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days” (Isaiah 30:26). And if insensible elements shall possess such beauty of brightness, what splendor can there be for those placed at God’s right hand? For then all the elect, conformed to the body of Christ’s glory, shall shine like the sun in heavenly power [Col. 0055A].

Therefore, that we may be able to attain this vision of brightness, let us strive in this life to be children of light and children of the day, He granting and helping who is the true light and the blessedness of all the blessed, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

49. HOMILY VIII. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE SAME SUNDAY OF ADVENT.

“There shall be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and upon the earth distress of nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and its waves; men withering away for fear and expectation of what shall come upon the whole world” (Luke 21).

When the Lord was asked by His disciples concerning the end of this world, as the order of the present Gospel reading indicates, He gave certain signs of the coming judgment from all the elements of the same world: from heaven, in the sun [Col. 0055B], moon, and stars; from earth, distress of nations; from the sea, confusion caused by the roaring of that sea and its waves. Thus, when they should see these things coming to pass, they might believe that the day of His advent was not far away.

And when He added, “Men withering away for fear and expectation of what shall come upon the whole world,” He showed that dreadful and terrible peril of the final judgment, in which not only those who are of the earth—that is, people who have committed deeds deserving trembling and terror—but even the holy angels themselves, who shall never be separated from God and from the repose of eternal tranquillity, will be moved and terrified by the misery of humankind which they shall then behold. Therefore the Lord says: “For the powers of heaven shall be moved.” But why shall they be moved? They shall fear not for themselves but for us, when they behold the most just judgment of God’s unbending equity so strictly hanging over the entire human race [Col. 0055C], where the consciences of all are searched and not only people’s deeds but their thoughts also are examined.

Hence it is added: “And then they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.” At that time each person shall feel more strictly upon himself the force of the power and majesty of the Son of God coming in the cloud, to the degree that he now shows himself ungrateful toward His mercy and patience. The following words disclose what hope remains for God’s elect amid these things:

“But when these things begin to happen,” He says, “look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draweth nigh.” According to the words of blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0055] St. Gregory, Book I, Homily 1, Homilies on the Gospels, Homily 40, vol. LXXVI of the *Patrologia*.], they are commanded to lift up their heads—that is, to gladden their hearts—because [Col. 0055D], just as the eternal damnation of the reprobate draws near when the terrors of God’s strict judgment come upon them, so eternal salvation draws near for God’s elect.

But so that they might know more clearly the time of that day of the Lord and, knowing it, make provision, He spoke to them a parable: “Behold the fig tree and all the trees. When they now put forth fruit of themselves, you know that summer is near.” By the fig tree we understand the Synagogue; by all the trees, the multitude of the nations. The fruit of the fig tree is the conversion of the Synagogue which is to come at the end of the world. Or, as some say, the fruit of the fig tree is Antichrist, the head of all the wicked, who is to be born from the Jews. For when, after it has produced from itself the shoot of iniquity and wickedness which is Antichrist [Col. 0056A], Judea, now barren in faith in Christ, shall be converted to God and shall begin, by believing and preaching that same faith, to bring forth fruits of faith—fruits, I say, of righteousness and truth—and when the multitude of the nations shall have entered in, it is certain that summer is near: that He is near who, removing the wicked lest they see the glory of God, is to bring His coheirs into that most serene tranquillity of heavenly rest.

These are the words of the only-begotten Son of God, by which He then prepared them to recognize beforehand the coming of His strict judgment through the preceding signs of the world’s end. By these same words He nevertheless teaches and instructs us, and all who are truly His disciples and wish to be so, how signs ought to occur in us, so that, when He comes [Col. 0056B] to visit us in the present life or to judge us after this present life, He may be received by us without fear, with gladness and exultation.

“There shall be signs,” He says, “in the sun, moon, and stars.” By these three—the sun, moon, and stars—we may understand the whole person. For there is in us something that may be referred to the sun, something that may be compared with the moon, and something that may be prefigured by the stars. The Apostle expresses this still more plainly when he says: “May the God of peace sanctify you wholly, that your spirit and soul and body may be kept sound at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:23). By the sun, therefore, we may fittingly understand the human spirit; by the moon, the human soul or mind; and by the stars [Col. 0056C], the human body or bodily senses.

The signs which must be wrought and present in such a sun, moon, and stars in order to foresee and escape the strict judgment of the coming examination are the signs of sacred Scripture, which marks out and sets forth for us both the endless glory of eternal salvation and the endless pain and misery of eternal damnation. These signs ought to be in the sun, so that we may nourish the living perception of our spirit through continual meditation upon sacred Scripture. These signs ought to be in the moon and stars, so that we may apply our soul, which is the moon, to the teachings of sacred Scripture, and may not be reluctant to exercise our bodily senses, which are the stars, in hearing, reading, and teaching sacred Scripture.

When signs of this kind have been made in the sun, moon, and stars, there also comes to be upon the earth a distress of nations [Col. 0056D], which is the distress of vices; for from frequent reading and meditation there gradually arises in the earth—that is, in the earthly members of the human being—restraint of sins. Although one cannot utterly destroy these nations, one nevertheless suppresses them and subjects them to one’s dominion so that one cannot be overcome by them.

The addition, “because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and its waves,” is not to be passed over lightly. For by the sea the world is signified, and by the waves we may understand the changeable desires of carnal pleasures. When these two—the remembrance of the world and carnal desire—meet in a person’s heart [Col. 0057A] and throw each other into confusion, they produce there a deadly sound. It is therefore necessary for a person who is to be saved to take thought beforehand concerning the sea and waves; that is, before the love of the age, mingled and confused in the human heart with carnal desires, begins to roar mortally and carries off the human mind as if by certain waves, one must fortify oneself through frequent reading—which are the signs in the sun, moon, and stars—and through restraint of sins—which is the distress of nations upon the earth.

But since neither frequent reading nor restraint of sins can endure long unless supported and strengthened by abstinence of the flesh, eternal Wisdom added after these things:

“Men withering away for fear and expectation of what shall come upon the whole world.” Two things shall come upon the whole world: the salvation of the righteous and the damnation of the reprobate. People wither away through fear and expectation when, because of future evils whose fear terrifies them and future goods whose expectation consoles them, they give themselves less freely to food, drink, sleep, amusements, and the other things in which the flesh delights [Col. 0057B]. They now dry up and weaken themselves so that afterward, flourishing anew through Christ in Christ in the delightfulness of eternal blessedness, they may rejoice without end.

Nor are they deprived in the weariness of this present life of the reward of their labor, as is mystically indicated when the Lord immediately adds: “For the powers of heaven shall be moved.” In the powers of heaven we may fittingly understand two chief virtues in a person: humility and love [charitas]. The powers of heaven are moved when, through true humility and the twofold love of God and neighbor—which is acquired by the efforts of the preceding labors, namely, frequent engagement with the Scriptures, restraint of sins, and abstinence of the flesh—a person is moved and raised up to the inward grace of divine visitation and sweetness [Col. 0057C].

The Prophet experienced this movement of the powers in himself when he said: “I humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Psalm 34:13). When the soul has been humbled by fasting and the other afflictions of the flesh, a person’s prayer returns into his own bosom when he so prays outwardly that inwardly he receives and tastes the fruit of prayer, namely the savor of divine love.

When the powers of heaven have thus been moved, the following is fittingly added: “And then they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.” The Son of Man—made human for humankind, the Father’s Only-Begotten—comes in a cloud when He visits the human heart through the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the cloud signifies, and waters it with tears of compunction unto the sweetness of His love [Col. 0057D]. He comes with great power when He makes the one whom He visits strong and able to resist vices; and with majesty when, after the aforesaid afflictions of labors, He refreshes that person with the sweetness of His Spirit. It follows:

“But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draweth nigh.” He did not say, “When these things have been done,” but, “When these things begin to happen” [Col. 0058A], so as to give greater consolation by this to those who put their hope in Him: for all these exercises of spiritual labors effect a person’s eternal redemption not only when they are completed but when they are begun.

Nor should we pass over His saying: “Look up.” It is as though He said: If it now seems difficult and harsh to seek through the temporal contests of labors the promised joys of redemption, turn the eye of your heart back to the times of your past life. Consider how nothing is what you have lived, and what the time has given you which you spent amid bodily pleasures and softness. Toward this insatiable sweetness and joy of the Son of Man coming in the cloud, which you desire—to this, I say—lift up your heads; direct toward it the attentions and desires of your mind [Col. 0058B], because your redemption draweth nigh. There you shall truly be redeemed, not only from sins and vices, but also relieved from the present corruption of soul and body.

The Lord teaches us, in the following comparison, how each person who is to be saved ought to observe within himself the time of this redemption, this grace:

“Behold,” He says, “the fig tree and all the trees.” What above was the moon, here is the fig tree: namely, the human soul. What there was the stars, here are the trees: namely, the human senses. Nor is the soul unjustly signified by the fig tree, for it has something in itself suitably referable to the soul: the double fruit which it bears, which figuratively expresses a certain double fruit of the soul [Col. 0058C]. And not unjustly; for first it sends out its *grossi*, immature and bitter fruits, and then produces figs, fruits that are sweet and ripe. So too the soul: since every age is inclined toward evil from its youth, almost every soul first produces bad fruit, bitter fruit, which are sins and vices. Then, when it begins to be watered by the grace of divine visitation, it produces the fruit of sweetness, namely the fruit of righteousness and truth.

What does it mean, then, that we are commanded to behold the fig tree, except that we must earnestly apply every safeguard of watchful care to our soul, lest anything from the thoughts and desires of this age or from its pleasures settle upon it and be able to hinder the eye of the mind from the inward vision of the Son of Man coming in the cloud? Hence Solomon says: “With all watchfulness guard thy heart” [Col. 0058D] (Proverbs 4:23).

With no less diligence and no less vigilance, we must guard our outward senses, which, as we said, are signified by the trees, so that they may bring forth to God fruits of righteousness. Otherwise we shall not attain that summer-like and delightful serenity of divine warmth and love, concerning which the Lord says in what follows: “When they now put forth fruit of themselves, you know that summer is near.” What is this fruit? Surely that fruit of which the Apostle says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is peace, joy, kindness,” and the rest like these (Galatians 5:22). When by God’s grace we begin to produce fruit of this sort, it is certain that summer is near: the fervent and serene brightness of divine visitation [Col. 0059A].

Therefore the Lord added and said: “So you also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.” When we see these things occurring in us in this way—that our soul attends to good senses and our body applies itself to good actions—this is a certain assurance by which we are assured of the kingdom of God, which is begun in a person here through the splendor of His visiting grace and is accomplished and consummated more gloriously in the life to come. It follows:
