“Amen I say to you, this generation shall not pass away till all things be fulfilled.” This generation is the generation of the holy Church, which shall not pass away until all these things are fulfilled. Again, this generation which shall not pass away can be understood as the generation of good works, the generation of holy virtues. But how does He say, “shall not pass away”? What has passed is no longer, and what seems no longer to be is considered, as it were, to have perished [Col. 0059B].

The Lord therefore consoles His elect by these words, lest they fail in their labors: whatever zeal or labor they expend for God in frequent study of the Scriptures and holy meditation, in restraint of sins, or in abstinence of the flesh—even if it is now no longer present, even if it has perished from their sight because it has passed—it shall never perish from God’s memory, never perish from God’s presence, until all things are fulfilled. That is, until it brings a person so far that the powers of heaven are moved within that person, and that he deserves to see, as has been said, the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.

But because it seems, as indeed it is, hard and difficult to weaken and afflict the body with continual labors, and to constrain the mind inwardly by unceasing watchfulness [Col. 0059C], the Lord admonishes us always to keep before our eyes what we are and what we ought to become. “Heaven and earth,” He says, “shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.” By heaven and earth we may fittingly understand the human spirit and body. Heaven and earth pass away when, the body being dissolved by death, the human spirit is snatched upward and the flesh is reduced to the dust of earth.

It is as though the Lord said: Since you shall pass away and cannot stand and endure amid the corruptibility of this mortality, strive, while you now stand, that through the labors of a passing life you may be able to attain the stable promises of my kingdom, which shall remain without end. For heaven and earth—that is, your spirit and body—shall pass away when dissolved by death [Col. 0059D]; but my words shall not pass away. They shall be fulfilled for you in the present life unto consolation or justification; they shall be fulfilled for you in the future life unto the glorification of bodies and souls.

These are the most sacred mysteries of the Gospel reading, by which the eternal Wisdom of God has instructed us: by what signs and by what labors and merits we ought to anticipate the day of final judgment. But may He who taught what we should do help us to accomplish it, so that we may deserve to be marked by the signs of His sacred Scripture; so that we may suppress in ourselves the nations of vices; so that, through abstinence of the flesh, we may please God [Col. 0060A]; and so that, when we see Him coming in a cloud with great power and majesty, we may see Him not trembling but secure—not condemned with the wicked, but eternally glorified with all the saints and elect in eternal blessedness. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

56. HOMILY IX. THIRD HOMILY FOR THE SAME SUNDAY.

“In the year when Tharthan entered Azotus, when Sargon king of the Assyrians had sent him and he had fought against Azotus and taken it: at that time the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah son of Amos, saying: Go, loose the sackcloth from thy loins and take off thy shoes from thy feet. And he did so, going naked and barefoot” [Col. 0060B] (Isaiah 20).

If we understand these words according to the letter alone, we shall be able to derive little or even no profit from them. But because they are words of the Holy Spirit, let us strive to seek their spiritual meaning; and, with His help and gift, let us see how they spiritually express the sacred advent of God and our Savior Jesus Christ. For this is why the Apostle exhorts us in today’s reading, saying: “Whatsoever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15:4).

What does it mean, “to have hope through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures”? A human being, consisting of soul and body, has been so created by God that one can never, or rarely can, avoid suffering some adversity or trouble—now in soul, now in body—either from the devil, from oneself, or even from other people. Therefore all that has been written has been written for our instruction, so that we, who cannot pass through the present life without the adversities of temptations, may continually have recourse to sacred Scripture, learn patience from it, and seek in it and from it consolation to relieve the weariness of our mortality [Col. 0060C]. For the patience and consolation of the Scriptures animate and strengthen us unto hope, so that we may never be able to despair of the mercy of divine compassion.

Therefore now, since the Apostle has taught us this, let us follow his teaching. In this prophetic Scripture set before us [Col. 0060D], let us seek our consolation; let us examine and see what it signifies spiritually with regard to the advent of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the consolation of eternal life has been restored to us. For, as the same Apostle says, “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). Therefore, leaving the killing letter and following the life-giving spirit, let us first distinguish the interpretations of the names. For in these lies the greatest force of spiritual understanding.

“In the year,” he says, “when Tharthan entered Azotus, when Sargon king of the Assyrians had sent him.” Tharthan is interpreted “gave a tower”; Azotus, “fire of conflagration”; Sargon, “prince of the garden.” In Azotus human nature, which began in Adam, may be understood. It could quite fittingly be called Azotus, that is, “fire of conflagration,” when unhappy Eve, inflamed as though by a mighty fire through desire for the forbidden fruit, began to burn so fiercely that she neither wished nor was able to refrain from putting forth her hand toward the prohibited tree, eating, and inclining her husband’s mind to eat [Col. 0061A].

But when, or how, did this happen? Certainly “in the year when Tharthan entered Azotus.” In this year we may understand the whole time of the present life, which began when the first human being was created. Before humanity was created, there were neither times nor years; when humanity was created, times were created at the same time. And all the time from the first human being to the last is like one year [Col. 0061B] running through equal days and months. It was in this year, then, that Tharthan entered Azotus, in a manner of speaking.

By his name Tharthan, which, as stated before, is interpreted “gave a tower,” aptly expresses the height of pride and self-exaltation. Through this our first parents, in the year—that is, in the time—when they were nobly created, were miserably deceived and cast down. The unhappy woman, at the voice of the serpent—or rather, of the devil speaking in the serpent—and saying, “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil,” heedlessly swelled with pride in the honor and dignity for which God had created her. Not content, desiring to know what it was not permitted to know, she wished to become like God. This was indeed the blind exaltation of mind which, as has been said, was that Tharthan, namely the messenger of the devil [Col. 0061C], whom he sent into Azotus and through whom he first set the woman aflame with the fire of his conflagration—that is, with desire for the forbidden fruit. Afterwards, through her, he struck down and supplanted that noble first-formed human, Adam. For he was the author and instigator of so great a crime, as the text immediately following adds concerning him.

“When Sargon, king of the Assyrians, had sent him,” he says. By the name Sargon, which, as we have said, means “prince of the garden,” the devil may aptly be understood. The garden, whose fruit both grows quickly and passes away and fails still more quickly, suitably signifies this unstable world, or the unstable and transitory pleasures and delights of the world; and the devil is rightly called their prince. For through them he ensnares and deceives the unwary minds of men. He is also called—and is—the king of the Assyrians. The Assyrians, whose name means “those directing,” [Col. 0061D] may signify all people unwilling humbly to submit to God their Creator, who direct themselves according to the pleasures and desires of their flesh and are unwilling to be directed by others in humble obedience for God’s sake.

When this Sargon, king of the Assyrians, sent Tharthan against Ashdod, fought against Ashdod, and took it—that is, when he first fought against that noble creature by the tower of pride and arrogance, took her, and cast her down when she had been set aflame by the fire, that is, the desire, of the forbidden tree—then the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah son of Amos, saying: “Go, loose the sackcloth from your loins, and remove the sandals from your feet.” In Amos, whose name means “strong,” God Almighty, who by the strength and power [Col. 0062A] of His divinity upholds all things and fills all things, may very fittingly be understood. In Isaiah, son of Amos, the only-begotten Son of God may worthily be understood.

That word which the Lord spoke by his hand was that command and obedience which God the Father, in counsel shared with the same Son and the Holy Spirit, gave Him when He ordained that He should become man in order to repair and restore His noble work—namely, the whole human race, which had perished in Adam.

“Go,” He says, “and loose the sackcloth from your loins.” From the loins proceeds bodily generation. And by Isaiah’s loins—that is, by the loins of our Lord Jesus Christ—we may aptly understand His fathers, namely the patriarchs and prophets, from whose seed He willed to be born according to the flesh. [Col. 0062B] The sackcloth hanging over those loins was the guilt of original sin. All from Adam to Christ bore this sackcloth with excessive toil, because, although they lived holy and just lives in this world, nevertheless after death they all inherited hell.

At last, at the end of the ages, the Lord, beholding the affliction of His people, sent His Only-Begotten into the world, saying to Him, as it were: “Go.” As though He said: “The grave offence of original sin, by which the whole human race is held bound, can by no means be loosed except through You. You will bear it; You will pay the penalties it has deserved. You alone will make satisfaction to Me for all. But because this cannot be done in the power of Your divinity, by which You are coequal and consubstantial with Me, it is necessary that You go. Go from the eternity of divinity [Col. 0062C] to the temporality of human mutability; go by assuming the form of human nature. Take the sackcloth from Your loins, freeing by Your death, from the knot of the old guilt, those from whom and for whom You are to be born.”

“And remove your sandals from your feet.” If, by Christ’s loins, we have said that the patriarchs and prophets are to be understood, from whose seed He willed to be born, then by His feet we fittingly understand the holy apostles. They were indeed His feet, because by preaching Him and steadfastly teaching faith in Him, they bore Him, as it were, throughout the whole world. From these His feet He removed the sandals, when, having abolished in His blood the original guilt which we understood by the sackcloth, He also cleansed and purified them—after His death, resurrection, and ascension—when they had been anointed and imbued with the new and unheard-of gift of the Holy Spirit, from actual sins likewise, which are aptly understood through sandals, since sandals are made from dead animals. [Col. 0062D] For after the Holy Spirit had filled and intoxicated them with so great a grace of His own, little or nothing, as we may believe, could thereafter cling to them from actual sins.

Holy Scripture indicates these feet of the Lord elsewhere when it says: “The devil shall go forth before his feet” (Hab. III, 5). This rightly applies to the holy apostles, because, as they went 60 throughout the world and preached, the devil could not stand before them; he could no longer remain in the accustomed dwelling-places—the hearts of unbelievers—once these had been kindled and inflamed with the heat of faith through their preaching. After setting forth the Father’s command, which He gave His Only-Begotten for the restoration of humankind, the prophet now shows what the Son did, immediately adding and saying in His person:

“And he did so, going naked and barefoot.” He did so: that is, He obeyed the Father by taking upon Himself the miseries of our humanity, as the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7).

Nor should we pass lightly over the fact that it says, “going.” One who goes passes from place to place. And this word “going” rightly shows the mutability of our humanity, which the Only-Begotten Son of God came to assume in Himself. For He who, according to the substance [Col. 0063B] of His divinity, dwelt in inaccessible light and could neither be moved, changed, nor seen, willed to become mobile, changeable, and visible in the form of humanity assumed for our sake. He of whom it is written, “But thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail” (Ps. CI, 28), who had no accident in His divinity—being never less, never greater, never older, never younger—became, for our sake, as one going.

Going, I say, from the bosom of the Father into the womb of His mother; going by being born of the Virgin; going by undergoing beneath His Virgin mother the conditions of infant age. Thus He passed through each stage of life until He rose to the strength of manhood. Thus He was going for the sake of human beings, yet going not as other human beings do: going naked and barefoot—naked from original [Col. 0063C] sin, barefoot from every actual sin.

And the Lord said: “As my servant Isaiah walked naked and barefoot, it shall be a sign and portent for three years over Egypt and Ethiopia, so the king of the Assyrians shall threaten the captivity of Egypt and the deportation of Ethiopia, of young and old alike, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered—the shame of Egypt.” By the number of three years, I think that three times are to be understood: the time before 61 the Law, the time under the Law, and the time under grace; and by Egypt and Ethiopia, the Gentile people and Judea. The Only-Begotten Son of God came by His advent to visit and console not only those whom the time of grace found here, but also those whom the time before the Law and under the Law had sent to hell with true faith and hope.

[Col. 0063D] Nor without reason did He add: “It shall be a sign and portent over Egypt and Ethiopia.” In Holy Scripture, a sign is often taken in a good sense, a portent in an evil one. He was a sign to the Gentiles, a portent to the Jews; a sign to believers and those to be saved, a portent to unbelievers and those to be condemned. For all, whether from among Gentiles or Jews, who received His humble advent in the flesh with humble faith and upright living, found in Him a sign of eternal salvation. But to those who rejected Him by unbelief, or who received Him yet strayed from true faith by not living rightly—and were found in that condition—He was a portent of eternal damnation.

By the king of the Assyrians, however, of whom it is added, [Col. 0064A] “Thus the king of the Assyrians shall threaten the captivity of Egypt and the deportation of Ethiopia,” we may aptly understand the devil, the ancient enemy. He is indeed king and lord of all who direct themselves not according to God but according to the pleasures and desires of the flesh; for “Assyrians” means “those directing.” The captivity of Egypt is the multitude of the Gentile people; the deportation of Ethiopia is the multitude of the Jewish people.

Nor is this unfitting. Egypt means “affliction that constrains”; Ethiopia, “darkness” or “gloom.” The Gentile people are rightly marked by the captivity of Egypt, while the Jewish people are figured by the deportation of Ethiopia. For the devil afflicted and constrained the Gentile people as though under his yoke and power, and held them as captives, because he powerfully bent them to whatever shameful acts he wished, since they were utterly ignorant of God and their Creator. But the Jewish people, darkened by the gloom of pride and unbelief, as it were voluntarily departed from God; for they rejected the Only-Begotten Son of God, whom they had heard from the Law and the Prophets would come in the flesh, when He had now come and was showing the way of life by teachings and examples. 62 They refused to believe Him to be God and Savior. Thus, plainly, Christ’s advent was for that people departing and persisting in its departure, as it were, a portent of eternal damnation. But for the Gentile people, who escaped the devil’s captivity through the sacrament of faith and baptism, Christ’s advent was a sign of eternal salvation.

As for the words added after “the captivity of Egypt and the deportation [Col. 0064C] of Ethiopia,” namely “of young and old,” I think the same two peoples are to be understood. The Jewish people were, as it were, older because they were chosen first; the Gentile people were, as it were, younger because they were later in being chosen. Scripture indicates them elsewhere too when it says: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. XXV, 23).

But just as Christ came to save Jews and Gentiles—that is, all who believe and join upright works to upright faith—so here He who was always at rest in His divinity, naked from original sin and barefoot from every actual sin, deigned in the humanity assumed for our sake to walk, that is, to labor, by suffering and dying. Thus the devil, who, “like a strong man armed, guarded his court” and had possessed the whole human race in peace, rages and raves more [Col. 0064D] after Christ’s advent than before it, threatening and attacking not only the captivity of Egypt and the deportation of Ethiopia, young and old—that is, not merely Gentiles and Jews—but also the naked and barefoot: namely, the multitude of those who have been freed from original and actual sin by baptism, or who, after violating baptism, have been purified and cleansed through repentance and satisfaction.

But how does he threaten them “with buttocks uncovered, the shame of Egypt”? That is, by the indecency and shamefulness of the flesh and fleshly pleasures, which are the shame of Egypt. By and toward this shame of Egypt he threatens them, and he does not cease to threaten until the end of the world—not only Gentiles, Jews, and bad Christians, who willingly live according to the flesh and its desires, but even those who have renounced worldly pleasures, who, by vigils, fasts, and other devout labors, mortify their flesh for God’s sake and strive to please God in purity of heart and chastity of body. He does this by bringing before them things they once did shamefully, 63 or by suggesting now for thought and now for action things which they have never done or even thought of. Thus he now threatens Gentiles and Jews, evil and good alike.

At last, at the end of the world, when the fig tree and all trees begin to flourish, when the fullness of the Gentiles shall enter and all Israel shall be saved, then what is here added will finally be fulfilled:

[Col. 0065B] “They shall fear and be ashamed because of Ethiopia, their hope, and because of Egypt, their glory.” At the end of the world, I say, when Judea—which now lies rejected and cast off in the darkness and gloom of its unbelief—shall be gathered to Christ and faith in Christ, and when the Gentile world, which has not yet believed in God, shall be fully converted through it, as was said of them through the prophet: “They shall return at evening, and suffer hunger like dogs, and go round about the city” (Ps. LVIII, 7), then that prince of demons and all his attendants, the evil spirits, will at last fear and be ashamed because of Ethiopia, their hope—that is, because of the Synagogue, which they never expected to lose—and because of Egypt, their glory, that is, the Gentile world, over whose perdition they expected always to boast and rejoice before their prince. [Col. 0065C]

“And the inhabitant of this island shall say in that day.” By the name “island” fleshly desire, or the human being himself who lives carnally and loves the desires of the flesh, may fittingly be understood. The inhabitant of this island—that is, the inhabitant of each person lying in fleshly desire—may not unfittingly be understood as any evil spirit that incites and inflames him to shameful acts. On that day of the complete conversion of Jews and Gentiles, this will, it is believable, be the voice of evil spirits mourning and grieving at the salvation of the elect:

“Behold,” they say, “this was our hope, to whom we fled for help, that they might deliver us from the face of the king [Col. 0065D] of the Assyrians. Behold, these, by whose faith and conversion we are suddenly terrified and confounded, are surely those whom we thought would aid and deliver us from the face of the king of the Assyrians, on whose account we hoped to be honored before our prince. They are now wholly converted; now 64 all have believed in Christ, whom we reckoned to be assigned with us to eternal punishment.”

“And how shall we escape?” To whom shall we flee, since we have now lost those whom we always held under our power? What they say—“How shall we escape?”—shows us what we find elsewhere in Holy Scripture: that those demons who have less power in deceiving human beings are tormented with greater reproaches and punishments [Col. 0066A] before their prince, whereas those more active in deceiving people are exalted with greater honor before him.

But since we are celebrating the advent of the Lord, the words of this reading rightly accord, according to the interpretation of the mystery set forth above, with that same Lordly Advent. I mean not that advent when He will come terribly to judge, but that in which He came mercifully to save. This advent of His was sweet, kind, and lovable; that one will be grave, strict, and terrible, according to the prophecy of David: “A fire shall burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him. He shall call heaven from above, and the earth, to judge his people” (Ps. XLIX, 2). This advent of His was in mercy; [Col. 0066B] that advent of His will be in justice alone.

This first advent of His, by which we have been saved and delivered, we honor—and ought to honor—each year with hymns, praises, and such services as we can offer, so that we may be deemed worthy mercifully to escape the strictness and severity of His second advent. For now, stretched out upon the wood of the cross, He shows us, as it were, His open hands to receive the repentant; now He has His arms extended, that He may gather and bind to Himself all who flee to His mercy. Let us flee beneath these arms of His and cast ourselves into His most holy hands, lest that future tempest of strict judgment snatch us away and swallow us up with the ungodly; but may He Himself gather us, with the just and those to be saved, into the bosom of His mercy—He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

65 HOMILY X. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY OF ADVENT.

“When John had heard in prison of the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Art thou he that is to come, or do we look for another?’” (Matt. XI.)

This third Sunday of the Lord’s Advent, on which blessed John the Baptist is related to have been in chains for his invincible assertion of the truth—and on account of which his fortitude is commemorated by the Lord to the crowds, in that he was neither a reed shaken by the wind nor a man clothed in soft garments—teaches that we ought not to be a reed shaken by the wind. For it is necessary that, amid prosperity and adversity alike, we so strengthen [Col. 0066D] the condition of our mind that we are neither carried beyond ourselves by the wind of self-exaltation nor cast down beneath ourselves, disturbed by the wind of detraction; but, humble in prosperity and patient in adversity, we should await the invisible advent of the Creator in unshaken tranquility of mind.

We are also warned not to be a man clothed in soft garments: that is, not to neglect ourselves for the softness of the flesh and the pleasure of fleshly desires, but willingly to subject ourselves for God’s sake to the hard and rough labors of this present life. For this reason, I also think, the fast of the Four Seasons has been placed in this third week of the Lord’s Advent: that those who at other times have lived less cautiously and less diligently may now at least, in order to deserve and receive the splendor of the Son of God coming in the flesh, flee softness of flesh through abstinence and continence, and strive tirelessly to exercise themselves through every kind of diligence in good works [Col. 0067A].

The present reading from the Holy Gospel finally encourages and instructs us in this, saying: “When John had heard in prison of the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Art thou he that is to come, or do we look for another?’” By John, whose name means “the grace of God,” or “in whom is the grace of God,” may fittingly be understood that person whom Christ’s grace has anticipated by a visitation of inward sweetness.

But because the human mind, still weighed down by its earthly dwelling, cannot remain long in those things which it has scarcely tasted even a little beforehand, John is rightly described as being in chains when, the grace of customary visitation having been withdrawn, the human heart becomes hardened. Thus, as though entangled in certain bonds, it hears only—whether outwardly from a human voice or inwardly through divine inspiration—the works of Christ, which He wrought in the midst of the earth for human salvation by being born, dying, rising, and ascending. [Col. 0067B] It also hears—that is, it weighs with inward consideration of the heart—the works of Christ, the works, namely, of compassion and grace: that in His freely given mercy He does not disdain to save very many bound in sins.

Encouraged, then, by this hope, although inwardly ensnared in chains and unable to raise itself to inward contemplation as it desires, it nevertheless sends disciples as messengers of its intimate sorrow—namely, the outward performance [Col. 0067C] of good works—as the sequence of the Gospel reading immediately indicates: “Sending two of his disciples, he said to him.” For in asserting that he sent two of his disciples, it clearly appears that he had more disciples. But what can we more fittingly understand here by the name of two disciples than faith and hope? Any person constrained by the hard bondage of the heart must direct these disciples to God.

Without doubt, he sends faith when, though inwardly oppressed by a heavy burden of sorrow, he nevertheless does not cease outwardly from good work. He also sends hope when, in the good works he performs, he seeks only the glory of eternal recompense or the restoration of the grace of inward visitation which he has lost. But the third messenger, namely charity, which is the grace of God, cannot be sent by him, because it lies, as it were, bound in the inward person. Yet, using these two messengers, he makes known his sorrow to the Searcher of hearts in these words:

“Art thou he that is to come, or do we look for another?” “Art thou,” he says, “the one who is to come into my heart, with that grace of sweetness by which Thy merciful clemency once deigned to visit me? But if Thou disdainest to do so, perhaps I await another greatly opposed to me.”

“And Jesus answering said to them.” God’s answering is when, by the hidden grace of inspiration, He gives the human faculties counsels of pious admonition. “Go,” He says, “and report to John what you have heard and seen.” As though He plainly said: Go through the desire of good devotion; [Col. 0068A] go through zealous pursuit of the good work you have begun; report to John what you have heard through understanding and seen through experience.

For to report to John is to bring a person back to remembrance of how he once knew the hidden mysteries of Scripture by spiritual understanding, and how great an abundance of sweetness he experienced through the grace of inward visitation. It follows:

“The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor receive the Gospel. And blessed is he who shall not be offended in me.” The human faculties are, as it were, blind when they attend only to images of earthly vanity and cannot see things of the light. But they see when, God having gone before them and inspired conversion, the mist of earthly occupation is dispelled and they regard all earthly things as nothing.

The lame walk when those who once limped away from the paths of justice begin at last, through worthy action, to tread straight paths. Lepers are cleansed when those who, because of the contagion of vices, were as lepers in the inward person afterward deserve, through pure confession, to receive true cleansing. The deaf hear when those who formerly had no ears for hearing the teaching of sound preaching, after the ear of the heart has been opened, are able beneficially to attend to what is said. The dead rise when those who were certainly once dead with the death of the soul, weighed down by the burden of sins, afterward, being anticipated by divine mercy, begin through true knowledge [Col. 0068C] of sin—mortifying vices within themselves—to live praiseworthily for justice.

The poor receive the Gospel because those who thus attain, through knowledge of sin, to true humility of heart are rightly said to receive the Gospel. For certainly whatever they receive outwardly from the mouth of one preaching will all advance their salvation. “And blessed is he who shall not be offended in me.” To cause scandal is to provide an occasion for sinning. But who ever could or can be offended in the Lord, who alone is free from sins and is by nature supremely good? Yet if these words of His are examined with subtle consideration, clear evidence will show who is offended in Him. Whoever, for these benefits of the Lord which we have mentioned, renders no thanksgiving and proves ungrateful, wishing to glory in himself by attributing them to his own merits rather than to the Lord, is truly said to be offended in Him.

Therefore eternal and supreme Goodness indicates to every person established in such hardness of heart as we have described the source of his grievous bondage. It is as though He openly said: “Because, with the grace of My visitation withdrawn, the chains of dire affliction now constrain you in the inward person, consider with diligent attention whence you deserved the severity of so great a bondage. For by the illuminating grace of My Spirit I once caused your blind faculties to know the true light; I gave strength of good action to their lameness, true wholeness of cleanness to their leprosy, healthful hearing to their deafness; and, by granting true knowledge of sin, I raised the dead in sins from their vices, and thus finally made them poor—that is, truly humble. [Col. 0069A] But because you ascribed to your own power all these things divinely bestowed upon you, lifting yourself above yourself, you have in a sense been offended in Me and are now burdened by the harsh constriction of the mind.”

But when God speaks all these things in the heart of a person through the hidden grace of inspiration, what the Evangelist then added indeed takes place:

“But when they had departed, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John.” “When they had departed,” he says—that is, when the disciples mentioned above persevere in the exercise of good works and the desire of pious devotion—Jesus begins to speak concerning John to the crowds, that is, to the disturbed faculties of the human person. God’s speaking is His acting, when by a secret visitation He makes a person know how great a grace of spiritual gifts he has lost and how great a misery of calamity he has found. 69 And it should be noted that the Evangelist does not say “he spoke,” but “he began to speak,” because once the inward grace of the Redeemer has anticipated the heart, only then can one attend to oneself and ponder, in bitterness of heart, that which had previously been wrongly sweet and pleasant, as the words of the Gospel reading here recall:

“What went ye out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” In some passages of Scripture, the wilderness signifies the present world, because it seems in a sense empty of the fruit of worthy action. [Col. 0069C] A person is said to go out into this wilderness when, with the guard of the mind relaxed, he wanders too freely and wrongly amid earthly things. But when, returning to himself, he begins to consider what harm he has done to his soul by going out in this way, with the groaning voice of his heart he reproves his faculties thus: “What went ye out,” he says, “into the wilderness to see?” As though he said: “O wretched and miserable inward faculties of mine, what advantage, what profit have you gained in this wilderness into which you have gone out so often in wandering about? What fruit, I ask, do you now have in those things in which you sometimes delighted through wrongly directed thought?”

For all these things have conferred no progress, no grace whatsoever, except a reed—that is, a soul dry from every spiritual grace; a reed, I say, shaken by the wind—that is, a soul restless in windy instability. For that soul is not unfittingly said to be shaken by the wind which in prosperity is lifted up by the wind of self-exaltation, but in adversity cast down by the storm of anger and indignation. When the inward person goes out and is distracted in this way by wandering amid earthly vanities, it follows that, delighting in them, he will miserably go out again, as the following sequence of words declares:

“But what went ye out to see? A man clothed in soft garments?” To be clothed in soft garments is to foster the corruptible body with fleshly desires. A person is said to be clothed in soft garments when he wishes to foster and nourish within himself, through wrongful and sweet delight, those things which he has inwardly conceived in his mind by vain thought. What danger to the soul it incurs by going out in this manner, the Gospel reading immediately recounts in fitting sequence. “Behold,” it says, “they that wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses.” Here by “kings” we must understand the powers of vices that wickedly rule. Whoever, then, are devoted to fleshly desires and refuse to resist their pleasures have not one but many kings ruling wickedly within them, because they are certainly slaves to as many masters as there are powers of vices which they permit to reign in them.

It should further be noted with what fitting order three departures are expressed in this Gospel reading. The first departure occurs in thought; the next in delight; [Col. 0070B] the third in action, as follows: “But what went ye out to see? A prophet? Yea, I say unto you, and more than a prophet.” When a person has, in the manner described, miserably gone out through thoughts and delights, it commonly happens that he goes out again a third time in a worse manner: that is, he begins to commit in deeds the unlawful things which he had formerly turned over in the secret place of his heart through the evil habit of thought and delight.

But when any person who is to be saved returns to himself and begins to attend to himself, he becomes not only a prophet but more than a prophet. He becomes a prophet when, with the tearful eye of the heart, foreseeing the evils of future damnation which he must undergo for the works of wicked action he has committed, he prophesies to himself. But he becomes more than a prophet when, anticipating God’s judgment by strict satisfaction, he himself punishes in the present that for which he recognizes he will otherwise be punished in the future judgment. Thus, thus, when everyone recognizes in himself these destructive departures and mourns with frequent lamentation that he has gone out so wretchedly and miserably in thought, delight, and deed, then what the Evangelist added indeed comes to pass:

“For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before thy face, who shall prepare thy way before thee.’” Here the name “angel” may aptly figure the sweetness of spiritual grace. By “face,” through which any person is recognized, knowledge of God is rightly understood. The angel, therefore, is sent before the person’s face because when spiritual grace anticipates the heart of a person by sweetly visiting it, then he can truly know both himself and God. [Col. 0070D] He also prepares the way because he fully instructs the person how, while walking in the way of truth, he may prepare a way to his heart for his Creator.

But note that He does not say, “This is he of whom it was said,” but “of whom it is written.” For everything that is said passes away, but what is written remains fixed. If, then, anyone has advanced in the order described and, in repentance, recognized the misery of his calamity, it is not said but written of him that this angel preparing the way before his face is sent, because, insofar as is possible in this time of mutability, he has enduring sweetness of spiritual grace within himself.

[Col. 0071A] We have discussed these matters from the Gospel reading as we have been able, the Lord granting it. Let us now add a few words concerning the reading and office of this same Sunday, for the edification of the hearers. The first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent is assigned especially to the Gentile people, because in this advent He is known to have especially called the Church from the Gentiles. The second Sunday, on which “People of Zion” is sung, especially marks the Jewish people, because they too, though in second place after the Gentiles, ought to have hope of salvation in the Lord’s advent. But the present Sunday may, with sound faith and understanding, be believed to concern both peoples.

But that we may hear something further useful to us concerning Gentiles and Jews, let us call the Jews in the Church the innocent and the Gentiles the penitent. The whole body of the Church consists of these two orders: it advances and increases daily through the medicine of repentance among the penitent, and rejoices and glories among the innocent through their daily progress in virtues. Paul admonishes all these in today’s office, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice.” As though he said to those healed by the medicine of repentance: “O you whom God by His grace has rescued through repentance from the filth of sins, rejoice in the Lord, not attributing what you are to your own merits but simply ascribing it to His gift.”

And rejoice also, you who have not been corrupted by capital crimes. Rejoice in the Lord, not in yourselves; preserve the good things granted you by His clemency, and do not despise as inferior to yourselves those unequal to you in virtues. For God is able, in a single moment, through the satisfaction of repentance, to lead those who are lying in sins today to great perfection in good works. It follows:

“Let your moderation be known unto all men.” Moderation means not only bodily chastity, by which a person refrains from unlawful acts; this too is called moderation: that a person regulates the whole of life, in prosperity as in adversity, by a certain good measure, so that if he rejoices, he does not rejoice excessively, and if he is saddened, he is not saddened beyond measure, but in both cases, by God’s gift, steadfastly maintains fitting measure or temperance. This moderation ought to be known to all people.

It is clear that one person’s good action cannot be known to all people; but it is as if he said: “Let such be the measure and temperance in every part of your life that all among whom you live may receive examples of good progress from your upright way of life.” Why we ought to possess this moderation he openly declares when he adds:

“The Lord is near.” The Lord, from whom nothing can be hidden, is near you; He is always and everywhere present with you, beholding and considering all your works. Therefore show yourselves such that you may worthily please the eyes of His majesty. Or he says that the Lord is near because the most sacred time of the Lord’s Incarnation is imminent, in which we ought, more diligently than on other days, to exercise our hearts and [Col. 0072A] bodies in good works.

“Be anxious about nothing.” Anxiety is any superfluous care. A person is anxious when he becomes entangled in earthly and transient things. We must recall our minds from this superfluous concern, since we ought not to cling to present and perishable things beyond what necessity requires. “But,” he says, “in every prayer, supplication, and thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known before God.” The worthiness of prayer consists in three modes. We pray when we implore God’s mercy in order to obtain forgiveness for our sins. We supplicate when, with the continual sighings of prayers, we entreat God for the necessary acquisition of virtues. We render thanksgivings when we preserve in true humility the gifts granted us [Col. 0072B]. In this prayer, supplication, and thanksgiving our petitions are made known before God, because, if at the time of prayer a heart distracted by many things does not depart from us—or rather, if the voice of the mouth accords with the lips of the heart—then we shall truly deserve to be heard by the Lord and shall obtain the effect of our petition.

The blessed Apostle also admonishes and exhorts us to this in today’s Lesson, when he says: “Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Cor. IV). For in all that we do, we must present ourselves in such a way that we please God inwardly and do not displease our neighbour outwardly; so that, while by deeds and words we aim either at God’s honour or at our neighbour’s edification, we may prove ourselves to be true ministers of Christ [Col. 0072C]. But if anyone contradicts us, if anyone blasphemes, if anyone judges us beforehand, we must make light of it and endure it patiently for the Lord’s sake, saying with Paul: “But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself” (1 Cor. III). For we must neither yield to human accusations nor place confidence in ourselves because of human favour, so that, while we strive to please him alone from whom we have our being, we may deserve to have our Lord Jesus Christ himself as ruler in the present life and rewarder in the life to come—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XI. ON THE SAME SECOND SUNDAY

[Col. 0072D]

“And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah that Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, went up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them” (Isa. XXXVI).

Whenever in the prophets, or in the Lord’s sayings through the prophets themselves, we find the expression “and it came to pass,” we do not doubt that something great and memorable is being indicated. Therefore this event, which the great prophet of the Lord Isaiah placed at the beginning of this present history, mystically signifies a great work of divine compassion, which the merciful Lord mercifully performs with sinners. For *Hezekiah* is interpreted “the strength of the Lord” or “one who lays hold of the Lord” [Col. 0073A]. And a sinful man may rightly be called Hezekiah when, raised up and strengthened by the Lord, he resolves to abandon sins, so that by the merit of a spiritual life he may somehow be able to recall and lay hold of him whom he drove away, whom by sinning he alienated from himself.

The mystical number of the fourteenth year mystically indicates when and how this occurs. Since it is perfect, it fittingly directs us to the perfection of the four Gospels, to the observance of the ten commandments, or to the excellence of the four cardinal virtues. Hezekiah is said, as it were, to reign in the fourteenth year when he strives to govern and order his life and conduct according to the sacred teaching of the Gospel; when he exercises himself in observing the ten commandments; when he seeks to advance praiseworthily in every progress of virtue [Col. 0073B]. Since this is indeed a great and memorable work of divine mercy, the phrase “and it came to pass” rightly ought to have been prefixed and inscribed to the following history. But let us see what follows.

“Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, went up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them.” Sennacherib, whose name is interpreted “one who removes deserts,” signifies the devil, who subjects and claims for his own dominion hearts deserted by God. He went up against all the fortified cities of Judah, by which we may understand all persons who possess within themselves the confession of God—the confession, that is, which they received in baptism, when, renouncing the devil and his pomps, they vowed to live for God alone [Col. 0073C]. They are rightly called fortified cities, because it is a great and supreme defence to be marked in baptism by Christ’s seal through the remission of sins. Yet all who, after baptism, neither adorn nor preserve this confession of faith and defence of that seal by good and perfect works provoke Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, to come up against them. He captures them, though fortified by baptismal grace, when, after the seal of faith has been corrupted by sins, he begins to enslave them to his own dominion.

In this way he goes up and reigns over those who are in the world and live worldly lives. Yet he does not forget to pursue those who dwell in Jerusalem—those who, imitating Hezekiah in merit and name, hasten in heart and mind toward the vision of everlasting peace [Col. 0073D]. Therefore it is immediately added: “And the king of the Assyrians sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a heavy hand; and he stood by the conduit of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller’s field.”

Sennacherib, signifying the devil, as we have said, is king of the Assyrians: that is, of those persons who direct themselves according to their own will and disdain being directed by others through obedience; for *Assyrians* is interpreted “those directing.” Sennacherib therefore sends his envoy into Jerusalem, that is, into every holy way of life where are gathered, and continue to be gathered, those who, aided by divine mercy, strive to make peace for themselves from their sins. *Jerusalem* is interpreted “vision of peace.” But who is this envoy, and what is his name? Rabshakeh [Col. 0074A], namely, from Lachish.

By the name Rabshakeh, interpreted “kissing prince” or “abundant in kissing,” the spirit of carnal desire is suitably signified. He rightly bears the name “kissing prince,” because he arouses and inflames in the human heart the love of carnal desire, which may be understood through a kiss. He is also called “abundant in kissing,” because his suggestions, which incite and entice wretched humanity to the pleasures of carnal delights, are many and innumerable. He comes from Lachish, which is interpreted “he stands between” or “a man for himself.” This interpretation of the name fittingly applies to Rabshakeh, that malignant spirit. For he stands between God and the human being, obstructing, as it were, the path of one tending toward God. He is also a man for himself, because with great and, as it were, manly strength he attacks and oppresses the human being, as the following text plainly declares when it says:

[Col. 0074B]

“With a heavy hand.” His hand is truly heavy, because no person can resist him without God’s powerful assistance; for one whom he cannot bend to vices while awake, he does not fear to disturb by his unclean assaults while asleep. Yet what it is by which this heavy hand is restrained and overcome, the subsequent text seems aptly to indicate to us:

“And he stood,” it says, “by the conduit of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller’s field.” By the upper pool we may understand compunction of heart, which is rightly called an upper pool when it arises from the desire for heavenly goods [Col. 0074C]. The conduit of the upper pool suitably signifies the constancy of compunction. If this is on the road of the fuller’s field, the invisible Rabshakeh cannot pass into Jerusalem—that is, he cannot accomplish his malicious will in the human being.

By the name of the fuller, who by his labour makes black and filthy garments beautiful and white, we rightly understand almighty God, the Father of mercies. By the regard of his heavenly compassion, he reforms the human heart and body—deformed and defiled by the accumulated manifold stain of sin—to their former state of beauty and comeliness. A human being is rightly called this fuller’s field when, in the manner of a shrewd farmer, he strives to exercise the outward senses of the body—namely, eyes, feet, and hands—in good works, and to cultivate inwardly without ceasing by sacred meditations and reflections upon the word of God [Col. 0074D].

By such works a person undoubtedly earns from God the grace to have ready to hand the conduit of the upper pool of which we spoke a little earlier; this prevents the said Rabshakeh from passing into Jerusalem—that is, prevents him from harming and prevailing against the soul that tends toward the vision of eternal peace. For by constancy in compunction the devil is conquered; the human being becomes more and more strong and fortified against his fiery arrows, as is more clearly signified by the words that follow:

[Col. 0075A] “And,” Scripture says, “Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, went out to him.” These three men—Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah—signify one human being: the person who, through the exercise of good labour and devotion to holy meditation, has become the field of that noble fuller of whom we have spoken, and who has been divinely washed and cleansed from the filth of his former life through the sweet and desirable conduit, that is, through the merit of continual compunction.

For *Eliakim* is interpreted “the Lord rising,” a name aptly applying to one who, rising in newness of life, has deserved to rule over sins and vices. Thus, by rising and ruling, he becomes a son of Hilkiah—a son, that is, of almighty God, whom Hilkiah fittingly expresses by his name [Col. 0075B]. Indeed, *Hilkiah* is interpreted “God the Lord.” He also becomes Shebna the scribe, which name is said to mean “sitting” or “returning,” when, having turned away from the path of iniquity and returned to God with all his heart and body, he walks quietly and humbly before God and human beings in accordance with the sound teaching of sacred Scripture.

He becomes a scribe when he diligently writes divine commandments upon his heart in order to keep them; he becomes one sitting when he advances in every humility so as to please the humble God; he becomes one returning when he withdraws and restrains himself from outward and perishable things so that, with the whole desire of his heart, he may be able to pass over into God. Thus he may deservedly also be called Joah, which is interpreted “brother here,” “brother of the Lord,” or “making of a brother,” when, though by creation he is the servant of almighty God, he becomes his brother through good and praiseworthy conduct [Col. 0075C]. He is also a “making of a brother” by renewing day and night in his soul the form of the divine likeness and image.

That such great grace can be acquired only through humble and voluntary obedience is plainly gathered from the fact that the aforementioned Joah is described as “son of Asaph, the recorder.” For by the name Asaph, interpreted “gathering,” any good teacher and master who fears God is fittingly figured; he carefully gathers and assembles from the records—that is, the expositions of sacred Scripture—what may enable him to renew the image of God in himself and in his son, namely, his good subordinate.

Therefore everyone who has deserved to be called Eliakim by rising in newness of life, Shebna by advancing in true humility, Joah by reforming in himself, as far as he is able, the making of a brother—that is, the image of God—and son of Asaph by obedience in humble subjection, may boldly go out and fight against the invisible Rabshakeh [Col. 0075D]. For, fortified by divine assistance, he will by no means have to succumb to him. But the higher a person rises in spiritual conduct and in the glorious practice of virtues, the more harshly he is attacked by the stings of temptations, as the oft-mentioned Rabshakeh declares in the following words:

“Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians: What is this confidence in which you trust, or by what counsel or strength do you intend to rebel? In whom do you have confidence, that you have withdrawn from me?” [Col. 0076A]

The great king, king of the Assyrians, is the devil, as we have said: the head of all wicked persons. When he sees the blessed man, designated by Hezekiah, withdrawn from him, and cannot otherwise overthrow him, he reproaches him with the wretchedness of carnal malice and frailty. He says: “What is this confidence in which you trust, or by what counsel or strength do you intend to rebel, because you have withdrawn from me?” As though saying: “Since in comparison with my wondrous strength you are shown to be a little dust and ash, by what confidence, or by whose counsel, have you withdrawn from me? Or by whose strength have you determined to resist me, whom neither the weakness of flesh oppresses nor the need of sleeping, eating, or drinking ever delays or hinders?”

“Behold, you trust in this broken reed-staff, in Egypt” [Col. 0076B]. Egypt, whose name means “darkness” or “constricting tribulation,” suitably signifies in this place any spiritual way of life. To the eyes of foolish and worldly people this life appears exceedingly dark, because they judge it altogether foolish and absurd to leave the world, despise and reject the flesh and its desires. This same holy way of life is also rightly called constricting tribulation, because it afflicts its dwellers and lovers here through true repentance and constrains them through worthy satisfaction pleasing to God; then, after temporal sorrow, it conveys them to the unending glory and joy of eternal delight.

Since the ancient enemy is well aware of this, he goes about day and night and labours so that, if he cannot entirely turn a person away from his good resolve [Col. 0076C], he may at least render the labour undertaken fruitless and useless. “Behold,” he says, “you trust in a broken reed-staff.” In the staff by which a person is beaten is suitably expressed the strict discipline of spiritual life. This may rightly be called a broken reed-staff because it beneficially dries and breaks the human body from the fatness of sins. Grieved by this dryness and breaking, the enemy speaks inwardly to the human being through his aforesaid envoy: “Behold, you trust in a broken reed-staff.” As though saying: “Behold, because you have hidden yourself in the darkness of this spiritual way of life, abandoning the temporal light of pleasure; behold, because you do not spare yourself, drying your body through frequent fasts and breaking it through the difficult constancy of vigils [Col. 0076D], do you imagine that you can escape my hand? It will not be so; this vain labour will not turn out well for you. For whoever leans upon this reed-staff, it will enter into his hand and pierce it.” As though saying: “Your fasts, vigils, and scourges, by which you afflict yourself, are vain, because they will benefit you in nothing, except that they exhaust and take away your strength and all the vigour of your body.”

“So is Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to all who trust in him.” By Pharaoh, king of Egypt, any person living spiritually in the spiritual life is suitably designated. When he begins, by pursuing sins, to govern his conduct and actions according to the will of God, he may fittingly be called both Pharaoh and king. For *Pharaoh* is interpreted “pursuing,” “destroying,” or “scattering” [Col. 0077A]. These names well suit the person tending toward perfection, who, as we have said, pursues vices in himself and strives to scatter and destroy the devil’s kingdom in his own soul.

But Rabshakeh provokes him by inwardly addressing him in this manner so that he may cease to be both Pharaoh and king of Egypt: “So is Pharaoh to all who trust in him.” As though saying: “Whoever rises against himself with such cruelty, whoever treats his flesh without mercy, will thus, as I have said, be worn down and broken, and will render himself useless both to himself and to all others.” The accursed Rabshakeh speaks such words in the ears of the human heart when, as the steadfastness of spiritual fervour grows cold, he introduces into a person such a thought [Col. 0077B] that, disturbed within himself, he begins to waver and often doubts that he can endure or complete what he has laudably begun unless the strictness of his spiritual resolution is relaxed.

But if someone is of such integrity and virtue that, placing his hope in the Lord and despising all the labours of this present life in view of the heavenly homeland, he cannot be overcome by this first temptation, then Rabshakeh still opposes him in another way, craftily insinuating himself and saying:

“But if you answer, ‘We trust in the Lord our God’: is he not the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed, and [Hezekiah] said to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You shall worship before this altar’?” But what are these words of the devil except this: when the person rooted and founded in the Lord has not yielded to the aforesaid temptation, overcome by no bodily labour, but acts manfully and answers the tempting enemy that he can do all things in the Lord, the enemy then sets before him the magnitude of his sins, in case he may cast him down from the state of uprightness by wearying him with despair [Col. 0077C].

“You trust,” he says, “in the Lord? Are you not the one who has now become Hezekiah and thinks that you have laid hold of the Lord and can resist my lord by the Lord’s strength? Are you not, I say, the one who removed his high places and altars?” But, I ask, what are the Lord’s high places and altars? If we examine closely, the Lord has in us certain high places, certain higher places, and certain highest places. It was certainly a great high place that he created us from nothing in his own image and likeness. We may call it a higher thing that, through the washing of regeneration and the remission of sins, he re-formed in us his image and likeness, which had been effaced. But we most suitably call it the highest thing that we received, by the gift of his grace, the sense and understanding to distinguish good from evil [Col. 0077D]. For our creation and re-creation would have profited us nothing unless, enlightened through the understanding of the mind, we had been permitted, at least after our fall, to be restored through knowledge of sin and repentance.

A person removes and destroys in himself these high, higher, and highest things of the Lord when he forgets God his Creator and Re-creator, his Lord and Redeemer, and knowingly and willingly plunges into the abyss of sins. He also removes the Lord’s altars when he offers him no sacrifice of worthy satisfaction for what he has committed. Thus the malignant enemy says to the converted person: “You removed the Lord’s high places and altars,” because you spoiled and scattered in body and soul the accumulated gifts of divine mercy bestowed upon you through the innumerable enticements of a lustful life; and, in addition to all this, you reconciled the Lord to yourself by no offering of amendment and satisfaction proportionate to such great crimes [Col. 0078A]. “And now you say to Judah and Jerusalem”—that is, to your own soul and body—“If you worship before this altar, if you are truly humbled in this holy way of life, you will be able before God to wash away all former transgressions and excesses. But by such a thought you deceive and mislead yourself, because, unworthy of God your Creator and ours, you are rightly enslaved as a despairing sinner to our dominion.”

[Col. 0078B]

“Therefore now hand yourself over to my lord, the king of the Assyrians, and I will give you two thousand horses, though you cannot furnish riders for them from yourself.” By horses, as we often read in the Holy Scriptures, we may suitably understand the lust of the flesh, as the Prophet testifies: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI [32]:9). The number of two thousand horses, consisting of and signifying perfection, expresses full and perfect pleasure of mind and body. The same spirit of uncleanness, the instigator of every malice and wickedness, promises and instils this by his suggestions.

“Hand yourself over,” he says, “to my lord, the king of the Assyrians: relax the cruel rigour of bodily abstinence; shake off the servile yoke of obedience by which you are weighed down; do not consume yourself in superfluous labour, because, being tender, soft, and exceedingly delicate, you cannot finish what you have begun [Col. 0078C]. I will therefore give you two thousand horses, because I shall make sweet and delightful to you the carnal desires which you now abhor because of the continual contrition of heart and body. And when inwardly you are made joyful by consent to and desire for their delight, you will not lack my aid outwardly in the flesh for carrying out works of wickedness.” For the first thousand horses is, as it were, pleasure conceived in the heart, or the will to do evil; the second thousand is the ability supplied by the devil to accomplish the evil one desires.

What follows—“though you cannot furnish riders for them from yourself” [Col. 0078D]—indicates to us the importunity of diabolical suggestion, by which the devil first recalls a person from divinely conceived fervour of mind to carelessness and lukewarmness, and from the devout exercise of spiritual labour to negligence and transgression of God’s commandments. “You cannot furnish riders for them from yourself.” As though saying: “Your bodily frailty itself plainly shows that you cannot stand or persist amid these intolerable and continuous tribulations. Therefore you must seek to treat your body more gently, so that when at last I have brought you to what I desire, you may, with bodily strength at your disposal, be able to carry out the things of the flesh with some sweetness and enjoyment.”

“And how will you withstand the face of one governor from among the least servants of my lord?” By the face of one governor among the devil’s lesser servants we may understand every lesser and lighter temptation [Col. 0079A]. Thus the wicked spirit says—or, by his prompting, the person says inwardly to himself: “It is better to satisfy my flesh by sparing it than to be thus vainly consumed and make progress neither in body nor in spirit. For when I fled to God with my whole heart and had the greatest hope and confidence in this holy way of life, in the most holy teaching of God, and in the devout guardianship of the holy angels, I have become as I was at the beginning, when the Lord did not rule over me; for, as it seems, I am in every way unworthy of his mercies, and cannot resist even the least temptations of the devil.”

[Col. 0079B]

When the profane Rabshakeh has inwardly disturbed a person by introducing this thought, he rises against him with greater darts of temptation, saying:

“But if you trust in Egypt, in chariots and horsemen, and now have I gone up against this land without the Lord, to destroy it?” By Egypt, as we have said, we may understand any spiritual life; by chariots, either the four cardinal virtues or the four Gospels. By horsemen we may understand the most noble company of holy angels, as the prophet testifies when he says: “You ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. III:8). The holy angels are indeed like most valiant horsemen, for day and night they stand by the wretched and defenceless human being, and with devout care preserve, protect, and fortify him lest, succumbing to the devil’s fiery arrows, he perish [Col. 0079C].

A person is rightly said to trust in Egypt, chariots, and horsemen when, drinking deeply with a thirsty breast the streams of evangelical teaching, and carefully entrusting himself at all times to the sweet guardianship of the holy angels, he advances courageously in spiritual life according to the righteous commandments of the Lord. In order to turn him away from the steadfastness of this spiritual fervour, the ancient enemy continually disturbs him inwardly with words of this kind: “But if you trust in Egypt, in chariots and horsemen, have I now gone up against this land without the Lord, to destroy it?” As though saying: “If by tirelessly labouring in this holy way of life you trust that in God’s strength and in the protection and defence of his holy angels you can resist me, do you imagine that I too came without the Lord to seduce you, destroy this purpose of yours, and bring it to nothing [Col. 0079D]? I also have a lord, who said to me: ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’ Since he is strong and has sent me, his messenger of such strength, you who are earth and ash cannot resist my power.”

“And Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to Rabshakeh: Speak to your servants in the Syrian language, for we understand it.” What is meant by “Speak to those who are your servants”? Speak to those who, devoted to flesh and fleshly pleasures, have chosen to serve you, unclean spirit. Speak in the Syrian—that is, lofty—language. For we who are servants of the Most High, who have resolved, despising all temporal things in hope of a better life, to serve our God in holiness and righteousness [Col. 0080A], will not be overcome by you while he protects us. “For we understand”: enlightened by the light of divine knowledge, we know what you are and what you say, because you are false and speak false things; you are unclean and suggest to those who hear you nothing except uncleannesses and wickednesses.

“Do not speak to us in Jewish in the ears of the people who are upon the wall.” Do not speak Jewishly—that is, in the manner of those who confess you—to us, who stand upon the firm height of this holy, just, and spiritual way of life; to us, I say, who in our higher part, which is our spirit, seek and desire nothing except God. We shall not receive your words, but shall always obey him alone who is above all, who can crush both you and your lord beneath our feet.

When the malignant enemy perceives that he and his suggestions are repelled with such great courage and constancy of soul by any perfect and proven person, designated, as we have said, by Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah, he cunningly withdraws and conceals himself—not in order to cease tempting, but so that he may more easily overthrow that person when he is less watchful and less solicitous for himself [Col. 0080B]. Hence it follows:

“And Rabshakeh said to them: Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you to speak all these words, and not rather to the men who sit on the wall, so that they may eat their own dung and drink the urine of their own feet with you?” As though saying: “I was not sent to you and your lord, for I know that I cannot prevail against you either in flesh or in spirit. [Col. 0080C]

But there are those who do not at all resist my embassy: namely, the men who sit upon the wall. Though going in and out with you, they display the appearance of men only in their outward dress; inwardly they are effeminate and deprived of all manly steadfastness. They are, as it were, sitting, because they know, seek, and desire nothing but things of the flesh. I confess that I was sent to such people, that they may eat their own dung and drink the urine of their own feet with you.”

By dung we may rightly understand the filthy and unclean sins of the flesh, which emit a most foul stench before God, his angels, and all the saints; this makes a person abominable to eternal chastity and purity, which is God, if he neglects quickly to wash and cleanse the stains of his defilements by true repentance and worthy satisfaction [Col. 0080D]. By feet we may understand the perceptions and affections of the unstable heart; by the urine of the feet, unchaste thoughts flowing from the unchaste motions and affections of the heart.

The wretched person eats his own dung when he sweetly and pleasurably recalls in himself the foul crimes of his former life, not to mourn or repent of them, but because he may be able to commit them again, or similar acts, in accordance with the counsel of the malignant enemy inwardly inflaming him; or at least because, delightfully rehearsing the past, he may somehow satisfy the lusts of the flesh. He drinks the urine of his feet when, by unclean thoughts issuing from evil affections and desires, he strives more and more to kindle in himself the thirst for evil pleasure [Col. 0081A]. Wherever such persons are found, that malignant enemy raises over them the joyful sound of his cry, by which he immediately provokes and impels them to open works of wickedness. Therefore the following is immediately added in his person:

“And Rabshakeh stood and cried with a loud voice in Jewish, and said: Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians. Thus says the king of the Assyrians: Make a blessing with me, and come out to me; and each of you eat his own vine, and each his own fig tree, and each drink the water of his own cistern, until I come and take you to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards.”

By a person’s vine the soul may be designated; by the fig tree, the body; by the water of the cistern, the fluid impulses and effects of evil thoughts [Col. 0081B]. The fact that he who is “abundant in kissing” provokes with so many circumlocutions of words the people sitting on the wall—that is, the person proceeding negligently and uselessly in spiritual life—to come out and make a blessing with him signifies nothing other than that those whom he has inwardly captured by consent to depraved pleasure he also strives to cast out and drive, in body as in heart, into open crimes from the very state and habit of their profession.

“Make a blessing with me,” he says: that is, carry out with outward acts, along with me, what I call good and what I inwardly suggest to you as useful. Yet often the wretched person, now overcome by the enemy’s importunate suggestion, now by the flesh’s sweetly evil pleasure, resolves to go out to satisfy his desires, but cannot accomplish what he desires because he is prevented by the difficulty of time or place. But the malignant enemy immediately confronts him in this manner: “Let each,” he says, “eat his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink the water of his own cistern” [Col. 0081C].

Since we have said that the vine designates the soul, by wine, which grows from the vine, we may suitably understand carnal love. The fruits which grow from the fig tree—that is, the body—may suitably be understood as illicit bodily acts. Rabshakeh therefore urges all those who have gone out to him by consent that each may eat his own vine and fig tree: that is, that each may meanwhile feed and nourish his own soul in himself by the delightful pleasure of carnal love, and that, by outward bodily act and habit, he alone may strive in himself to serve his desires—“until I come,” he says, “and take you to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards.”

The malignant spirit comes to take a person to a land like his own when he joins and associates him with a person like himself, who equally loves what belongs to the earth and tends toward the earth. Such a person may rightly be called not simply land, but a land of grain, because from that mutual alliance brought about by diabolical suggestion the wretched person wretchedly receives grain—that is, a kind of fruit of his mind [Col. 0081D]. He is likewise called a land of wine when he supplies ardently, [Col. 0082A] according to the appetite of his lust, everything belonging to earthly love and carnal sweetness to one who formerly ate only his own vine and fig tree. Thereafter he is deservedly called a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards, when, enticed and corrupted by continual habit of sin, he delights more and more, both in heart and body, in wickedness.

## HOMILY XII. FIRST [HOMILY] ON THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John, to ask him: Who are you?” (John IV.)

Although these three Sundays which we have celebrated since the Advent of the Lord stand out with a particular excellence of mysteries and heavenly teaching, today’s Sunday is yet more excellent by as much as it is nearer to the Nativity of the Lord and of Christ our Redeemer [Col. 0082B]. Since it is wholly spiritual, it concerns spiritual persons alone: those who, alienated from this world, labour so that they may inwardly experience in themselves the Nativity of Christ which they celebrate outwardly. Therefore every spiritual person who desires spiritually to bring Christ to birth from his own heart must carefully attend to, and zealously fulfil, what this Sunday prescribes and teaches us. But before we proceed to its exposition, let us consider how rightly and fittingly the four cardinal virtues may be assigned to these four Sundays.

To the first Sunday, then, on which the she-ass is read of as having been brought to the Lord, prudence is suitably referred. For the she-ass is the animal-like soul, which is indeed unreasoning in itself, but in some manner [Col. 0082C] becomes prudent when it has merited to have God as its possessor. To the second Sunday, however, on which, after the signs in sun, moon, and stars have been set forth, there is added: “Men withering away from fear and expectation of what shall come upon the whole world,” temperance is appropriate. For when a man, through abstinence of the flesh, restrains himself from sins and vices, this is in some sense to wither away from those things in which he formerly grew fat. To the third Sunday, moreover, on which blessed John the Baptist is praised by the Lord because he was neither a reed shaken by the wind nor a man clothed in soft garments, the third virtue, fortitude, may fittingly be referred. For it is necessary that the man who is prudent and temperate should also be strong: he must learn not to be a reed shaken by the wind, [Col. 0082D] so that he may be carried away from himself neither by the wind of self-exaltation nor cast down beneath himself by the wind of detraction. After these comes the fourth Sunday, to which the fourth virtue, justice, is rightly assigned. Now justice is to render to each what is his own. For when the man who is prudent, temperate, and strong attributes, not to himself but humbly to him from whom he received them—to almighty God—both his prudence, his temperance, and his fortitude, this is true and perfect justice. This virtue, indeed the virtue of humility, being near to Christ, fittingly belongs to this fourth Sunday, which is near to Christ’s Nativity, because it makes a man truly near to Christ. Let him be prudent, temperate, strong: he does well, he pleases Christ. But unless the fourth be added to these three, so that he may also be just [Col. 0083A]—that is, humble—he does not become near to Christ. Since, therefore, there is nothing in man that God so loves as humility, and nothing in man that the devil so attacks as humility, the present reading from the holy Gospel aptly declares this. It indicates those varied and manifold alternations of temptations by which unclean spirits assail a man tending toward true justice, which is true humility.

For those Jews who sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John are malignant spirits, which at all times spread the snares of their faithlessness in order to deceive the man who desires salvation, who is figured by John, whose name means “in whom is the grace of God.” For the person whom they cannot tempt through carnal [Col. 0083B] vices, they take from the very good deeds he performs material for seduction. This is indicated to us by the phrase: “They sent from Jerusalem.” Jerusalem, indeed, is interpreted “vision of peace,” and by it is figured the spiritual life in which a man labours toward the joys of peace and of eternal vision. But what did they send from Jerusalem? Priests and Levites. The priests represent the pure and continual prayers which the blessed man sends up to God by day and night. The Levites represent the holy works in which he unceasingly exercises himself, that he may be able to please almighty God. Thus malignant spirits send priests and Levites when they take from the very virtues present in a man material and occasion for temptation, so that what ought to have served salvation becomes a fault, and those who ought to have been our protectors begin to be [Col. 0083C] our assailants and tempters. This is what it means for the Jews to send priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John.

Why? “That they might question him”—that is, tempt him. The temptation which malignant spirits send upon a man proceeds from virtues and virtuous deeds: it is an exaltation of mind, so that they may at least overthrow through pride the man whom they cannot overcome through vices of the flesh. Hence they say: “Who are you?” As though they said: “What a man you are! How greatly you abound in good! Prudence is subject to you; temperance is not lacking; you are strong in fortitude, because you endure perseveringly in uprightness.” Blessed John teaches us by his own example what a man ought to do against this embassy of malignant spirits.

[Col. 0083D] “And he confessed,” says the Evangelist, “and did not deny. And he confessed: I am not the Christ.” The words “and he confessed” are placed twice, because the confession by which this exaltation of mind must be emptied and overcome ought likewise to be twofold. For if the phrase, “Who are you?” has so sounded in the ears of his heart through the embassy—that is, through the sending and suggestion—of demons that he took delight and pleasure in it, then in humility, penitence, and contrition he must confess to God in prayer and confess to his superior in confession, so that the inward fault of exaltation, through which he was not ashamed to sin before the Lord, may be washed away by the shame and confusion of humble confession.
