If a man humbly does this, he has fulfilled [Col. 0084A] the phrase that follows: “And he did not deny.” Blessed Job shows us what this denial is in his book: “If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon advancing brightly, and my heart rejoiced in secret, and I kissed my hand with my mouth—this is a very great iniquity and a denial against the Most High” (Job 31:26). He who praises, extols, and magnifies himself because of his own works—this is to kiss his hand with his mouth—commits a very great iniquity and a denial against the Most High. For he acts unjustly who attributes to himself rather than to God what belongs to God; because, when he desires to be known and praised for what he has received, he denies him from whom he received it. But he does not deny who, because of the grace of God’s gifts received, praises and magnifies not himself but God. The Evangelist therefore says:

“And he confessed: I am not the Christ. And they questioned him: What then? Are you Elijah? And he said: I am not. Are you the prophet? And he answered: No.” John is questioned about three things, because there are also three matters concerning which the spiritual man is tempted by the devil through pride. Through his ministers, the malignant spirits, he tempts him concerning anointing, or the inward sweetness of the heart, which is Christ. For Christ is called “the Anointed One.” He tempts him concerning the fervour of bodily discipline, which is Elijah. He tempts him concerning prelacy, which is the prophet. Malignant spirits tempt him concerning anointing when by their suggestions they raise him within himself above himself, so that, while he is sweetly refreshed inwardly by the grace of the inward sweetness arising from the visitation of the Most High, he may begin to exalt himself above other people, who seem to him [Col. 0084C] inferior in this grace. Humility must be set against this temptation. John’s humility teaches us this when he says: “I am not the Christ.” As if he said: “If at any time the power of the Most High has inwardly touched me with the sweetness of inward anointing, this is not I, because I cannot possess that from my own being; rather, it is the gift and grace of him who can give it when he wills and take it away.” When he answers thus, when he resists the vice of exaltation by humility, they attack again and strive to cast him down by another kind of temptation. Therefore it follows:

“And they questioned him: What then? Are you Elijah?” As if they said: “If you deny that you are Christ, clearly you cannot deny that you are Elijah. For just as [Col. 0084D] that man, zealously zealous for the Lord, slew four hundred men who were adversaries of the truth (3 Kings 18), so you have laboured after his example. By persevering in good works, you have diligently and steadfastly endeavoured, in the fervour of good zeal, to cut away in yourself and in others, by detesting it, whatever you believed displeased God.” Yet he easily restrains this vice of exaltation also if he answers: “I am not.” He must answer “I am not,” believing and confessing that by himself he has power neither to oppose evils zealously nor to perform good works.

When these two temptations have been conquered, at last a third follows, with them saying: “Are you the prophet?” They assert that he is a prophet while inwardly stirring him up toward prelacy and teaching; for when a man is frequently visited inwardly by God through the anointing of the heart, and when he is outwardly strengthened in God by [Col. 0085A] the continual fervour of bodily discipline, it is difficult for the desire of prelacy not to creep in. Hence they say: “Are you the prophet?” As if they said: “Experienced in inward things and not ignorant regarding outward matters, you could possess authority of governance; you could provide very usefully for the welfare and salvation of others.” But whoever imitates John humbly excuses himself even from this vice, saying: “No.” To say “No” is to judge oneself altogether useless and unworthy for the office of prelacy, choosing rather to be subject in humility for God’s sake than proudly to desire to preside against God. But because malignant spirits are such that, when defeated, they are not put to shame but are more inflamed to tempt man by their very repulse, it is rightly added still further:

[Col. 0085B] “They said therefore to him: Who are you, that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say of yourself?” By this answer we may understand consent to sins. For if they inclined toward that consent, they would surely give a glad answer to those who sent them. For so long as consent is avoided, no answer is carried back by unclean spirits. Even if they cannot bend a man to the full act of sin, it would suffice them if they could cast him down from the standing of his uprightness even through consent. But humility alone passes over their very diverse snares, as the following order of words mystically indicates:

John says, “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said.” A voice accomplishes nothing of itself, because it is not from itself [Col. 0085C] but from a person: when the person wishes it to sound, it sounds; but when he wishes, he restrains it, so that it cannot be heard. Whatever a man can do, whatever good he possesses, whether inwardly from sweetness of heart or outwardly from the merit of good action, is like a certain voice; it is the voice, I say, of him who cries in the wilderness—almighty God, who in his mercy works this in the man whose heart is truly deserted by this world. And because it is within a person’s power to utter and suppress his voice, so it is likewise within God’s power to bestow upon a man the gifts of his mercy according to his good pleasure and to take them away. Thus, humbled within himself, the blessed man rightly says: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” As though he were answering the malignant spirits that incite him [Col. 0085D] to the boastfulness of exaltation: “If there is any good in me, it is not from me; and therefore I ought not to attribute it to myself, but to him from whom I have it, whose voice I am, without whom I can do nothing; who works his mercy in me when he wills, and withdraws it from me when it pleases his omnipotence. He is the one who cries in the wilderness, in hearts deserted by this world: ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.” Isaiah is interpreted “salvation.” “My salvation,” he says, “is Christ. In order that his way may be able to come to my heart, I must make it straight through humility, not repel him from my heart through the haughtiness of exaltation, as you malignant spirits suggest.” It follows:

“And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees.” Pharisees are called “divided.” Malignant spirits are rightly called divided [Col. 0086A] because all their labour tends solely to divide a man from God and subject him to the devil, to divide him from virtues and subdue him to vices and crimes. Therefore they add and say: “Why then do you baptize, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?” This questioning of theirs, therefore, is, as we have said, their untiring temptation. They tempt him still, in case they may perhaps be able to make him guilty before the Lord in some respect; and the man whom they cannot overthrow through the vice of exaltation, they seek to draw back from the very fervour of his austerity, as though he laboured uselessly. “Why then,” they say, “do you baptize?” As though they said: “Why do you wear yourself out, afflicting yourself with such tears and sighs, when you are neither Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet? What do your tears profit you, [Col. 0086B] since you neither presume yourself to be God’s anointed one, nor call yourself strong in action, nor believe yourself worthy of prelacy?”

John answered them, saying: “I baptize in water; but one stands in the midst of you whom you do not know.” This answer is the answer of a penitent man humbly acknowledging the guilt of his offence. It is as though he said: “I rightly wash my sins with tears, since my manifold transgressions cannot be abolished except through manifold tears and groans. For, as you enemies of salvation suggest to wretched me, I do not seek from my penitence, nor ought I to seek, the favour of human praise or the honour of any dignity; but I strive for this alone: that perhaps through the clemency of almighty God I may merit to obtain pardon for my sins. For I, wretched man, am that person whom you now do not know—the person whom you strive, as though just and innocent, to raise above himself. I stood in your midst through the pride of my heart when I consented to you in whatever you suggested to me: now to the empty joy of prosperity, now to impatience in adversity, now to luxury and wickedness, now to every evil of vices. From this I fear the future judgment of almighty God and the punishment of eternal damnation. Why? Because he who was made before me is to come after me, and I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal. I fear, indeed, that the man I formerly was, when I lay subject to so many and such great evils of vice, will come [Col. 0086D] before God on the day of judgment to receive the sentence of eternal punishment deserved by my merits.

“But why does this fear press upon me? Because I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal. For throughout all the years in which I serve almighty God in this spiritual life, I am unable, by any of my labours, to attain the point at which I am worthy to loosen from myself, and overcome in myself, the carnal and mortal vices that cling to me from the man I formerly was. Therefore, because this fear distresses me, I must now by weeping and groaning forestall the strict judgment of almighty God, in case I may perhaps be found worthy for God at least on that day to deign to save me through his mercy.” These are the teachings of the Gospel reading, by which the spiritual man is armed and instructed against [Col. 0087A] the momentary temptations of malignant spirits; for the end of the Gospel shows that this warfare in the spiritual life is not uncommon but daily:

“These things,” says the Evangelist, “were done in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.” Bethany is interpreted “house of obedience,” by which the spiritual life is rightly figured; through the Jordan, which is called “descent,” humility is expressed. Nor is it without reason that it is placed: “In Bethany beyond the Jordan.” Those who are in the spiritual life, even if at times they pass beyond the virtue of humility through the swelling of pride—which the phrase “beyond the Jordan” signifies—nevertheless return to themselves within themselves by penitential satisfaction, washing away the stains of crime with tears, as is immediately added concerning them: “where John was baptizing.” For while they are daily cleansed within themselves by the fountain of tears, they are renewed as though baptized in Christ.

Therefore, since we have heard that all these things are said to have happened, and daily to happen, not in the world but in Bethany, in the spiritual life, it is necessary that every spiritual person, with the watchful and provident eye of the heart, carefully and attentively look about to see how he may escape the dangerous snares, the most subtle temptations of malignant spirits of which we have heard—spirits that always and everywhere lie in wait for us, never leave us, and everywhere stretch before us inevitable snares of deception and destruction. Since we cannot resist them by our own strength, in today’s prayer we invoke the help of him who knows, is strong, and has power—almighty God—saying:

[Col. 0087C] [Note: [Col. 0087D] Prayer at Mass for this Sunday.] Stir up thy power, O Lord, and come; and assist us with great strength, so that, through the help of thy grace, which our sins obstruct, the pardon of thy propitiation may be hastened.

This is great strength: great humility, which is also called the power of Christ, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Most gladly will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9). This is that great power which drew the Only-begotten Son of God from heaven to earth, into the womb of the Virgin; she herself bears witness in her canticle, saying: “For he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). It establishes the heavens; it renews the earth. Those who did not possess this power fell from heaven. For the devil himself, although he had been glorious in all wisdom and knowledge, nevertheless, because [Col. 0087D] he did not have humility, could not remain in heaven; but cast down with his followers, he became the lowest of all. But those who possessed this power remained with God in their glory: namely, the holy angels, who were so established through it in him that they can never be separated from him. In order that he may deign, by this great strength, to assist us against the great and manifold deceits of malignant spirits, we must cry to God with voice of heart and body, saying: “Stir up thy power, O Lord, and come; and assist us with great strength.” For since the Only-begotten Son of God crushed the devil’s pride through his humility—for in that respect in which he willed [Col. 0088A] to become humble, coming upon him as the stronger one, he destroyed his kingdom—nothing so casts the devil down as humility; nothing so prevails against temptations as humility.

The Introit of the Mass also teaches us this virtue of humility, in which we say: “Remember us, O Lord, in the favour of thy people” (Ps. 105:4). This is the voice of the spiritual man crying to God with a humble heart. It is as though he said: “I am, O Lord, thy people, because, so far as I can by thy grace, I share in habit and action with thy people, the people that serves thee. But I beseech thee, remember me, that I may be in the favour of thy people; that I may be a people pleasing to thee, seeking nothing apart from thee in all my works. And because this cannot come to pass unless [Col. 0088B] thy mercy goes before us, visit us with thy salvation” (*ibid.*), pouring into us the most sweet grace of thy sweetness, “that we may see the goodness of thy chosen ones” (*ibid.*), so that, enlightened by the splendour of thy grace, we may so see and know what pleases thy goodness and what displeases thy justice, that, pursuing good and avoiding evil in that goodness by which thy chosen ones serve thee, we may merit to be joined to thee “in the joy of thy nation” (*ibid.*), in the repose of eternal blessedness, “that thou mayest be praised with thine inheritance” (*ibid.*)—that is, with thy holy angels and just souls, who are thy inheritance, because thou shalt remain in them and they in thee without end. In the misery of this life thy praise is neither stable nor perfect; but when we have come into the joy of thy nation, when we have been joined to [Col. 0088C] thine inheritance in the number of the holy angels and all thy redeemed, there thou shalt truly be praised, there thou shalt be glorified eternally without end.

But because we cannot be admitted to this inheritance of God unless, through the visitation that comes with God, we merit to be cleansed here from sins and vices, we rightly add the Alleluia, saying: “Come, O Lord, and do not delay; forgive the crimes of thy people.” But since no virtue obtains the coming of God if humility is absent, we rightly ascribe the Offertory that follows the Gospel to the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, who alone among all mortals was founded and filled with the virtue of humility, saying: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee.” By this we are admonished that we can overcome the most subtle wiles of diabolical temptation [Col. 0088D] that Gospel authority sets before us only through humility; only through humility must we ascend to praise God with his inheritance and to share and partake of the unchangeableness of eternal blessedness with angelic spirits and all the elect. Therefore, that through the intercession of her who, because of the incomparable merit of humility, bore incarnate from herself the Word of God, we may be able to advance toward true justice, toward true humility, which is true and perfect justice, through which, after conquering the snares of the crafty tempter, we may sometime merit to be enrolled in the inheritance of God: may he grant this to us, Jesus Christ [Col. 0089A] our Lord, the author of humility, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

97 HOMILY XIII. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD.

“Joseph and Mary, the mother of Jesus, were marvelling at the things that were said” (Luke 2).

Since the coming of the Saviour proved to be the most certain cause of salvation for all who are to be saved, all who are to attain the lot of eternal inheritance must take care not to observe only in passing whatever the writings of the Gospel recall concerning our Redeemer or his parents. The Evangelist therefore says: “The father and mother of Jesus were marvelling.” It is pleasing to consider what these four [Col. 0089B] persons signify: Joseph and Mary, namely, Simeon and Anna, whose names are set down in the present Gospel.

Joseph and Mary designate any one of the faithful; Simeon, the order of prelates, who know well how to preside through word and example; while Anna signifies divine grace, by which the Lord is accustomed sweetly to visit the hearts of his elect. Joseph and Mary may also suitably be understood as our body and soul: Joseph as the body, Mary as the soul. For just as Joseph was guardian and servant of the perpetual Virgin, offering her sweet services continually, so surely our body ought to give assistance to our mother—that is, the soul—through the practice of good works, so that she may be able to conceive and bear the Son of God in the bridal chamber of her heart. This body, indeed, serves its superior—the soul—so much the more diligently as the soul rules more fittingly that which is subject to it.

“They marvelled, therefore, at the things that were said.” Whatever is known by experience is not an object of wonder; but what is unknown is the object of earnest investigation by one who wonders. Thus surely the mind of the elect, which is rightly called the mother of Christ, when it contemplates the works of his humanity, full of marvellous sweetness, is more ardently raised up to investigate the unsearchable power of his divinity. But because it cannot comprehend the incomprehensible One as he is, it always has reason to marvel. Therefore, although it does not arrive by searching, it does not know how to grow weary of him whom it loves above all things; rather, day by day, by searching and investigating, it desires somehow to receive from the treasures of his knowledge and divinity, because the force of love multiplies the intensity of inquiry. But the merciful Lord, whose mercies toward the soul that seeks him do not fail, does not cease to provide the aid of knowledge and consolation to relieve the weariness of his beloved through the words of preachers, as the Gospel narrative relates in what follows:

98 “And Simeon blessed them.” What is signified by Simeon, whose name means “hearing sorrow,” except the order of teachers, who through the word of exhortation pour the grace of divine blessing into the hearts of grieving subjects? For their blessing is to sustain and refresh the desiring and ardent soul with the food of inward refreshment. Therefore, when they bless, let us hear what they say and to whom they say it. It follows:

“And he said to Mary his mother.” Here it is suggested that the faithful soul may fittingly be understood through the Lord’s mother, because the preaching of teachers is directed principally toward the instruction of the faithful soul, so that it may be taught both rightly to be subject to its superior, namely God, and rightly to preside over its inferior, namely the body. Therefore preachers must teach that men can approach God for the knowledge of truth only by the steps of humility, saying: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel.” The Lord stood when, invisibly hidden with himself in the repose of heavenly secrecy, he had not yet taken on the deformities of our corruption; [Col. 0090B] but he sat when, descending from the height of his power, he came to take upon himself the burdens of our weakness; and he was laid low exceedingly when, captured for our sins, he endured the disgrace of the cross. For who in this world’s exile was laid low as was the most gracious lover of humankind? Going forth from the height of heaven, he so humbled himself to the earth that in the whole world, placed under his dominion, he had nowhere to lay his head; and he who is great and immense beyond measure became humble and small even unto the passion of the cross. When they set these traces of humility before the minds of the elect as examples to be imitated, there comes about a fall and resurrection of many.

For in contemplating so great a Creator, they begin to think nothing of themselves except what is lowly; and through these foundations of humility, the destruction of pride and exaltation happily occurs in them. There also comes about a resurrection of many in Israel: those who, as true Israelites, raised to life by the thunder of the heavenly word, merit to have their minds lifted on high. And it should be noted that he does not say “of all,” but “of many in Israel.” For, as the Apostle says, “not all who are of Israel are Israelites” (Rom. 9:6). Rather, that stream flowing forth through the mouths of preachers gladdens the city of God when it wills, and at times, visiting not the hearts of all but of those whom it wills, raises them to life. Thus they declare that the Lord himself of death and life is set as a sign that shall be contradicted.

[Col. 0090D] “Behold,” they say, “this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be contradicted.” The sign of Christ is the Lord’s cross, upon which he offered himself to death for the human race, through which death, that is, he willed his own to be restored to life. Hence the image of the same Redeemer, that it may be recognized among other images, is marked beforehand by the sign of the cross. Every blessed soul embraces that sign more intimately, fondly dwelling on it in frequent weeping and tears, because it touches more deeply its inward remembrance that he who is the author of eternal sweetness tasted such bitterness for its redemption. The cross of Christ is the sign of complete mortification, which the holy mind ought to bear and carry about. And just as death kills the outward senses of the body to every appetite, [Col. 0091A] so it is necessary that the soul which has died with Christ strive to mortify within itself every act and consent of sin. Thus, contemplating the cross of Christ—that is, the Lord’s passion—in it and through it the soul learns what right works it should do, striving to imitate him from whom it has its being, lest it hear of the Redeemer’s passion without receiving the fruit of redemption, but may join to it works worthy and necessary. Yet this sign of such constant and perfect mortification is contradicted by every sex and every age, because, as long as one lives in this life’s exile, no one will be of such perfection as to escape even the least contagions of sin amid those pious vows and desires. Nevertheless, preachers ought not grow weary of presenting this through continual exhortations, as is made clear in what follows:

[Col. 0091B] “And a sword shall pierce thine own soul.” Here the sword signifies the force of powerful preaching, by which each person is happily slain so that he may die to fault. Paul indicates how this sword divides and pierces the soul: “The word of God,” he says, “is living and effectual, and more piercing than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul, and joints and marrow, and discerning thoughts and intentions” (Heb. 4:12). When the sword of the heavenly word kills everything in us that savours of the flesh, the thoughts of many hearts are indeed revealed, because there is a more subtle examination not only of what lies hidden as perverse in deed, or idle in speech, but also of what lies hidden as foul in thought. It follows:

[Col. 0091C] “And there was Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher.” Anna, whose name echoes the grace of God, can signify the inward sweetness of the heart, which almighty God mercifully customarily inspires in his elect who have been wounded by the sword of pious love. She is not unfittingly called a prophetess, because she knows how to prophesy to the very hearts of the just concerning the punishments of the future judgment and concerning the ineffable delights of blessedness to be received one day. Nor should it be passed over that this same Anna is described as the daughter of Phanuel. Phanuel is interpreted “face of God.” And what can be expressed by the face of God except the knowledge of our Creator? When this knowledge of God is sought through reading, prayer, and meditation, the grace of divine love is sometimes generated from the very diligence of the inquiry. But because it is generated not in all but the merit of such a virtue is granted by God to very few of the elect, Anna is also aptly said to have descended from the tribe of Asher. Asher, indeed, is interpreted “blessed.” Such a meaning of the name belongs only to the elect, whom the gift of heavenly mercy especially makes blessed. Blessed, then, and exceedingly blessed in tribe and lot—in heavenly generation, that is—are those who have learned to possess God in knowledge through the study of sacred Scripture, persistence in prayer, and the watchfulness of continual meditation, and who for this reason have merited to taste the sweet grace of contemplation. But because the grace of the Holy Spirit is accustomed to work these great gifts of God in a person gradually and through the progress of time, [Col. 0092A] the Evangelist adds this, describing the praiseworthy life of Anna.

“This woman,” he says, “had advanced in many days.” For the blessed soul advances as though through many days when, though still devoted to earthly affairs, it resolves and determines to take up the path of good action; and what at first it is still too weak to accomplish, it repeatedly desires in the heart, that it may someday begin and be brought to completion. And because will is fruitless if just and pure works do not follow, she is rightly described as having lived with her husband seven years from her virginity. 101 For she lives seven years—all the days, that is, of life, which is turned through cycles of seven days—as barren and sterile with her husband, so long as she is occupied with the actions of this world. She cannot beget for God the spiritual offspring of virtues while she has not yet been joined to her bridegroom Jesus Christ through renunciation of the world. But when, through God’s prevenient grace, she has perfectly abandoned all earthly things in mind and habit, so that, truly widowed and stripped of all worldly enticements, she begins to long only for her bridegroom Jesus Christ, it is rightly added:

“And she was a widow until eighty-four years of age.” That the faithful soul may be understood by the widow is suggested by truthful Job, who, describing the works of any wicked person, says: “He fed the barren woman who does not bear, and did not do good to the widow” (Job 24:21). For it belongs to the perverse to feed the barren woman—that is, to nourish with wicked delights the flesh that is unfruitful in good actions. But they do not do good to the widow, because they do not attend to what benefits the soul that will live [Col. 0092C] eternally. Therefore the blessed and faithful soul that tends toward its heavenly bridegroom alone is like a widow, desolate in this world; and when it sees that the Only-begotten of the Father, likewise its sole and only beloved in every respect, laid down his beloved soul for his sheep, it cannot ever admit consolation until it merits to see the glory of him who reigns, whose shame upon the cross it so often beholds in exile. She is rightly said to have been a widow for eighty-four years, because this number appears by no means devoid of mystery. For seven times twelve makes eighty-four, and through this number of twelve and four apostolic and evangelical teaching shines forth. By this teaching, in the present time, the weariness of the faithful soul that sighs and groans in exile is relieved; and lest it ever lose the bright and splendid light of truth, it has the certain guidance of the Scriptures. But when it has arrived at the years of eternity, all the testimonies of love that it received from evangelical and apostolic teaching it shall worthily see, face to face, as more truly and perfectly manifest through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit; and by seeing, it shall obtain them.

But what soul, I ask, will be so holy and blessed that, once it has attained the vision of the supreme Godhead, it will find such great rewards laid up for it? Surely one such as this widow, who did not depart from the temple, serving the Lord with fastings and prayers by day and night. What is this temple but that of which the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17)? [Col. 0093A] The temple of God, therefore, is the holy and undefiled mind, into which the supreme High Priest enters, seeking a place of sanctification; and, if he is to appear to the pure in heart, he requires the brightness of integrity and purity. A person departs from this temple when scattered by unclean thoughts, and does not restore it adorned with the splendours of virtues, if by wicked deeds he repels the Son who comes with the Father and desires to make his dwelling there. For nothing unclean ought to be admitted where the wondrous condescension of the King deigns to have the place of his most welcome seat.

He too serves night and day, persisting in fastings and prayers, who not only abstains from bodily food but also—what is chief and most pleasing to God—so applies himself to bodily restraint that he fasts yet more carefully from vices and sins. He prays and entreats without ceasing [Col. 0093B] who carries out his works with such foresight and circumspection that they may deservedly be called, and truly be, like a fervent and pure prayer before God. That our service ought not to be lax and unstable but persevering unto the end is indicated when she is said to have served in the temple by day and night. What is usually signified by night except adversity, and by day except prosperity? It is fitting, indeed, that adversity should not break the beloved soul, nor prosperity exalt it beyond measure; but that, amid adversity and prosperity alike, it should not omit the offices of due reverence in holiness and righteousness.

Again, in another sense, these same words may be referred to Christ. “She had advanced,” he says, “in many days, and had lived with her husband seven years from her virginity.” By “many days” many saints may be understood: namely Abel, [Col. 0093C] Noah, Shem and Japheth, Abraham, David, and many others besides. In all of these Anna had advanced through the merits of virtues—that is, the grace of God had made some progress—but she did not have them as her lawful husband, for her lawful and sole husband was our Lord Jesus Christ. With him she had lived, as it were, seven years: that is, in him rested the fullness of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Yet all this was from her virginity, that is, from her incorruption, since no corruption whatever was ever found either in him or in her. That grace was incorrupt, because at no time or moment was it found lesser or more imperfect in him. 103 He too was incorrupt, because no stain of sin corrupted in him [Col. 0093D] that same grace.

And she was a widow until eighty-four years of age, she who did not depart from the temple, serving the Lord by day and night with fastings and prayers. For when Christ died on the cross, she became, and remains, as it were a widow until eighty-four years—that is, as long as this present and changeable age continues to roll on—because in this mortal life she could not, and cannot, find such and so great a husband in whom she might have so stable and firm a dwelling. Moreover, when the Lord ascended, that same grace was a widow so long because it worked nothing in the apostles until, after the Holy Spirit had been sent from heaven, the mysteries of the eight beatitudes and the four Gospels began through them to be preached throughout the whole world. She never departed from the temple, because as long as the present age endures she will persevere in [Col. 0094A] the elect and with the elect, who serve the Lord by day and night with fastings and prayers: fasting, that is, abstaining from evils; praying, that is, persevering in good works. It follows:

“And she, coming in at that very hour, gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Jerusalem [otherwise: Israel].” What, then, does it mean that at the hour when Simeon blessed Joseph and Mary, Anna came in, gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke to all who awaited the redemption of Jerusalem, except that the elect, when pierced by the goads of preaching, come into their higher part—that is, into their own soul—and confess themselves all the more blameworthy in proportion as they deserve to receive through the mouths of preachers a greater light of grace? [Col. 0094B] For the more sweetly the mind is touched by God entering it, the more healthfully is it pierced with compunction for its past sins; and that pleasant inward compunction itself becomes a certain praiseworthy confession of sins. The fact that it is not at all related what she said or confessed is undoubtedly because the holy mind which conceals itself in spiritual things and tramples earthly things beneath its exalted mind cannot fittingly explain or utter what it has sometimes perceived of God while raised up amid tears.

“And when they had performed all things according to what was written in the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own city Nazareth.” 104 Although, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, an overflowing knowledge of Scripture may gladden by its infusion the mind of whoever receives it, still no one in the exile of this pilgrimage observes with perfect conduct of life what he perceives concerning God. Yet he is said to have fulfilled all the commandments of the law who is never convicted of having lost the desire of a good will, even if works are lacking. Such a person, without doubt, when the course of this life is ended, returns to his own city, Galilee, [Col. 0094C] where, his migration completed, he beholds without the stain of reproach him to whose sweetness and love he preferred nothing in this world. He will dwell also in Nazareth, where that unique flower of purity will appear in the beauty of divinity to those pure in heart and body. For nothing defiled shall enter there; but the pure and shining go forward before the virgin purity [Col. 0094D] of the flower, where, standing more familiarly in attendance, they shall joyfully behold him who looks upon them. There will be perfectly fulfilled in us what immediately follows:

“But the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom.” That most pure innocence of supreme purity grows and is strengthened in the elect, where Christ himself will be our righteousness and wisdom. He will give the great abundance of his sweetness to those who hope in him; we shall possess it not by measure but in fullness. “And the grace of God was with him.” The sheer goodness of almighty God will freely bestow all these things, where the reward will certainly be greater than any merit can demand, and where our reward alone will be he whose dominion endures without end.

Again, in another sense: “But the child grew and was strengthened, [Col. 0095A] full of wisdom, and the grace of God was with him.” So long as we continue amid the labours of the present life, God in a certain manner grows within us, until we all come “to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ.” He grows, I say, amid good things and prosperity; he is strengthened amid evils and adversities. He is full of wisdom, because the savour of divine sweetness causes a person to grow in virtues; and the grace of God—that is, true humility—will furnish the patience necessary in adversity. May we deserve to attain this humility through the granting of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

105  
## HOMILY XIV. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF EPIPHANY

[Col. 0095B]

“When Jesus was twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, and when the days were completed, as they returned, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it” (Luke 2).

Because our Lord and Redeemer, who is the splendour and image of the Father’s glory, emptied himself by taking the form of a servant in order to make many people co-heirs of his kingdom, he set before those same co-heirs of his kingdom for following and imitation all that he did in the humanity he assumed. Therefore we must carefully and attentively consider those things which the present reading of the holy Gospel relates to us concerning that same Son of God.

“When Jesus was twelve years old.” This ascent of the Lord to Jerusalem [Col. 0095C] plainly admonishes and instructs us how we ought spiritually to ascend by the steps of virtues. For Jerusalem, which is interpreted “vision of peace,” bears the type of that heavenly Jerusalem in which the souls of the elect, now freed from the body of this death, enjoy an abundance of eternal peace and full security. To the blessed vision of that eternal city every one of the elect, though still a pilgrim in the body, now frequently ascends by the intention of the mind; because, as they recognize and lament that they are exiles in this world, they strive through diligent prayer and continual meditation, insofar as is possible in this time of mutability, to taste beforehand what are the joys of the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0095D] There is also another Jerusalem: the blessed city beloved of God—namely, every holy and faithful soul. It may truly be called a vision of peace when, setting aside all earthly things, it savours only what is above, and contemplates the form of its Creator more clearly in proportion as it is less struck back by the tumult of earthly vanity. Yet one ascends to the summit of such lofty dignity not easily, but by exceedingly arduous labour. 106 For those who desire to draw near to the divine brightness must put away from their souls every desire for worldly things and every enticement of the carnal life. But when will frail and weak humanity be judged worthy by the Lord of the gift of so great a height? Truly, when it has spiritually reached the age of twelve years through progress in virtues. By this number twelve we may understand perfection of life, just as by the number seven we understand the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. For as the sum of the number seven consists of three and four, so likewise, if we multiply three by four or four by three, we find the perfection of the number twelve. Therefore, as we have said, the fullness of heavenly gifts and perfection of the spiritual life may fittingly be understood by this number twelve. Whoever, then, desires through the grace of a contemplative mind to ascend to Jerusalem must carefully provide for himself that he may attain the sum of this number; that is, being rooted [Col. 0096A] and grounded in the gifts of virtues, and persisting in pious works, he must strive to fulfill what is said here in what follows:

“According to the custom of the feast day.” To keep a feast day is to shape the mind for the repose of spiritual discipline after the crowds of useless thoughts have been removed; to be free from harmful works; to be restrained from all superfluities. For the mind which desires to see him whose purity could never be touched by even the slightest stain ought to be very unencumbered and free. Very blessed are those who order their whole life according to this custom of the feast day: who despise in mind and body everything in the world that seems delightful and pleasant, and who, as long as they bear the body that weighs down the soul, desire, in order to lighten the weariness of their exile, to have only the inward visitation of the one Creator [Col. 0096B] himself. For those who grieve that they are pilgrims away from the Lord count it a great benefit of consolation if they may at least behold, as though in a mirror and in an enigma, him whom they cannot yet see eye to eye.

But it must be known that there are some who, although they seem through meditation on the law of the Lord to ascend spiritually to Jerusalem, nevertheless do not deserve to receive the taste of inward sweetness, the banquet and delights of divine contemplation. Conversely, there are some whom the strength of mighty love so carries beyond themselves, so to speak, to contemplate the form of the eternal Creator that, as though present to God, they feel themselves in some manner absent from the body. Of these it may rightly be said that they celebrate in Jerusalem the joys of the solemn [Col. 0096C] day, since such inward sweetness is opened to them that they can rightly say with the Prophet: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord!” (Ps. 30:20).

Yet, however much any person blessed in the spirit of his mind strives always to reach upward, so long as he bears the corruptible body, so long, I say, as flesh taken from dust wounds and weighs down the mind, he cannot cling long to the author of incorruption. Hence what follows is rightly said:

“And when the days were completed, as they returned.” To return when the feast days have passed is, after the joys of inward rest, to fall back upon the business required by bodily necessity. This mournful return is very burdensome for those groaning in this valley of tears. It is grievous, I say, and deeply pitiable, after joys to return to miseries, after light to darkness, after tasting the sweetness of the heavenly homeland to return to the mournful bitterness of pilgrimage. Yet all the elect turn this return toward the advancement of their own salvation, because they return not to the vices of their former life but to the exercises of pious labour and God-pleasing action, so that [Col. 0096D] by bodily exertion they may deserve to receive the consolation of the desired visitation. Therefore, as we return in this way from Jerusalem—that is, from the vision of peace—the Evangelist declares in what follows where he whom, so to speak, we leave without leaving, remains:

“He says, ‘The child Jesus remained in Jerusalem.’” When we return, as we have said, to our own affairs, the Lord remains in Jerusalem, because he with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration can remain nowhere but in Jerusalem—in the city of the living God, in the vision of eternal peace. It follows:

“And his parents did not know it.” Under the figure of the Lord’s parents our soul and body may fittingly be understood. In blessed Mary, who bore the Son of God, the soul may be understood; through Joseph, who was the guardian of that Virgin, the body may be figured. And blessed Virgin Mary, who bore our Saviour while preserving her virginity, aptly represents every blessed soul which, impregnated by the Holy Spirit, conceives the Son of God within itself. Joseph, however, who cared for the outward needs [Col. 0097A] of that same Virgin, fittingly figures our body, which does not cease by pious labours diligently to render service to the soul giving birth to God. Therefore these parents of the Lord—that is, all who serve the Lord in faith and truth—do not in a certain manner know whither the Beloved turns aside; because although in the time of prayer they have sweetly embraced him in the embraces of inward love, nevertheless, as long as they are in the body, they can in no way know or investigate with what merciful regard he comes to them, how long he remains, or how suddenly he passes away. Hence in another place of the holy Gospel it is said: “The Spirit breathes where he wills; and you hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3:8). They indeed feel, so to speak, a certain touch of the heavenly visitation; but their mind, still burdened by the darkness of human misery, cannot clearly discern whence this graciousness of divine inspiration comes, or whither it turns when passing from them.

109 “But supposing him to be in the company, they went a day’s journey.” What does it mean that, returning from Jerusalem—namely, turning themselves from inward rest to outward actions—they judge that they have Jesus in the company, except that by unceasing recollection they ponder within themselves the abundance of his sweetness which they deserved to taste beforehand in the hour of contemplation? Because their soul, inflamed with heavenly desire, is always intent upon spiritual delights, they believe that they remain inwardly within the joys of contemplation even when [Col. 0097B] they do something outwardly; for, while they call to mind what they received in the hour of prayer, they burn more and more with the longing of holy love. Of such persons it may rightly be said that they travel a day’s journey, because they most earnestly shun travelling the journey of night—that is, doing the work of sin—who have chosen Jesus, the splendour of the eternal Father, as the guide of their journey.

But because, as long as one lives in this life, as long as mortal humanity is oppressed by the miseries of life and the gathering darkness of temptations, the joy on which the blessed soul feeds in God cannot remain stable, all the elect whose mind has once been truly inflamed by the fire of divine love cannot remain long in the coldness of their own torpor when they feel the light of inward visitation extinguished within them. Therefore, considering the lives of the saints who went before, whom they know to have been inflamed with a like fervour of love, they vigilantly search their words and writings to see whether they may find some inward light in their words, as the following words declare:

“And they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintances.” The kinsfolk of our Saviour may fittingly be called the Fathers of the Old Testament, from whose race he deigned himself to derive the true origin of his flesh. By his acquaintances we understand the ministers of the New Law, who deserved to be exalted above the other saints more eminently by the Lord of virtues himself, through their devotion to a more perfect life and the gift of greater knowledge. Therefore we anxiously and vigilantly seek the Beloved among these kinsfolk and acquaintances of the Lord [Col. 0097C] when, with the eager attention of the mind, we examine the words and writings of the Fathers who went before, so that our mind may gather something from them by which it may be stirred to tears of compunction.

But it sometimes happens that the hardened mind, while remaining cold within itself, conceives no warmth from heavenly words; for when it is not inwardly touched by the very author of sweetness, whatever is said outwardly about God sounds in vain and without sweetness. When the elect are placed in this miserable desolation and intolerable anguish of spirit, what they must do or whither they should turn—when every joy apart from him seems sorrowful and bitter—the Evangelist instructs by the words that follow:

“And not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem [Col. 0097D] seeking [otherwise: seeking again] him.” For if the writings of the Fathers who preceded do not suffice for contemplating the form of our Creator, Jerusalem must be revisited: we must return to ourselves within ourselves and diligently examine our ways and actions, lest this Beloved have withdrawn the presence of his vision because of some deformity of morals or some frivolity of flesh or mind. And if we discover in any respect the guilt of our negligence, let us wipe it away by continual laments of repentance; let the fervent flood of tears burn away what the rust of vices has made impure and foul. Thus—thus when we have been consumed by health-giving sorrow, thus purified by the burning flame of repentance—the Beloved will at last appear, who withdraws himself in order that he may be sought; he wishes to be sought in order that he may be found; he is found with labour in order that he may be held [Col. 0098A] with more burning love. For immediately follows:

“And it came to pass that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers.” We fittingly undertake the journey of three days when we wash away the contagions of words, thoughts, and works through worthy fruits of repentance. “Sitting,” he says, “in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them.” We behold the Lord sitting in the midst of the teachers when, after the dryness of our heart has been watered by divine mercy, we draw with a thirsty breast from holy teachers the streams of wholesome doctrine—him, I say, the true fountain of knowledge—for our edification. He too is said to listen to and question the teachers because through him we are made both hearers and questioners. [Col. 0098B] For when his invisible anointing, which is perfect compunction of heart, begins inwardly to teach us, it opens our understanding with such breadth 110 that our mind can keenly savour and investigate the profound mysteries of the Scriptures which, formerly closed and hidden, it could scarcely comprehend even by hearing. The power of compunction discloses to us higher and subtler things concerning the hidden mysteries of Scripture than any diligence of teachers can teach us. It follows:

“All who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.” All our faculties are awestruck at the utterly unfamiliar sweetness of the divine savour; we ourselves, who are enlightened, marvel within ourselves at the unprecedented new abundance of wisdom which, after the rain of compunction, will be given us by the Father of lights. In this time of visitation, in this splendid illumination, what is immediately added here will be most truly fulfilled:

“And his mother said to him: ‘Son! Why have you done this to us?’” By the Lord’s mother, as we said above, we may understand the soul of any elect person; it is rightly called the Lord’s mother when it is made pregnant through receiving the Word of God. When this blessed Mother has at last found the Beloved, sought long and with much labour, she holds him more closely in the embraces of love and frequently addresses him in these words, with an affection both tender and sorrowful: [Col. 0098C] “Son, why have you done this to us?” As if she said: That I dare call you Son I ascribe not to my merits but to your ineffable mercy; though you are most worthy, you did not disdain, in the wondrous condescension of your compassion, to become the son of one most unworthy. “Why have you done this to us?” Why, my Beloved, has the abundance of your compassion held itself back from me so long that the presence of the vision of your face did not somewhat lighten the heavy burden of my pilgrimage? In your vision is given the hope of eternal life, while your absence is calamity and misery.

“Behold, your father and I [manuscript: ‘behold, I and your father’] were seeking you in sorrow.” My body, I say, which rendered me the service of its ministry so that I might deserve your visitation, has been almost exhausted by continual exertion. I too, an exile and pilgrim, thirsting for you, the living fountain, have miserably dried up in my thirst; for when the long-sought joys of your countenance do not lift up the inner parts of the heart, human frailty cannot sustain itself. For I burn so violently with love for you that the present life is a burden, and nothing apart from you is pleasant, because there is no true pleasantness apart from you. When, therefore, the blessed soul has uttered the grief of its heart in such a mournful voice before the sight of divine compassion, the words that immediately follow show what answers, and of what sort, it receives from him:

“What is this, that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in those things which are my Father’s?” As if he plainly said: Since I, the indweller of hearts, rest nowhere except in humble hearts, why do you seek me in what is foreign and not in what is your own? For the house of my Father is the bridal chamber of your breast. If your watchful mind had always kept it clean and undefiled for me, it would without doubt have had me as its perpetual indweller, because “my delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8:31). [Col. 0098D] But the human mind, which has not yet perfectly come to know itself and cannot preserve true innocence through the observance of life, does not grasp this saying. Hence what immediately follows is rightly added:

“And they did not understand the word which he spoke to them.” Since we were conceived and born in iniquities, as long as we bear the corruptible body we shall never be able to be entirely free from sins. Therefore, whenever we lapse into the contagion of sin, however slight and small, we drive the author of purity from the dwelling of our heart. But God alone, without sin and most graciously knowing human frailty, sees that in this mortal flesh we cannot retain the merit of perfect innocence; and he who created nature kindly helps our weakness. This the Evangelist seems well to indicate in the narrative that follows:

“And he went down with them and came to Nazareth.” For when, through the goodness innate to him, he weighs the misery of mortal life, the supreme Majesty stoops from that inaccessible height of his so that human weakness may be able to have some approach to divine power. Nevertheless, though the Creator of all things descends in compassion for our miseries, he turns aside nowhere but in Nazareth, which is called the flower of purity. For that unique flower of purity can rest only in the lodging of a pure heart; nor is there any house worthy of his Majesty except a mind unstained and flourishing in innocence and purity. What, then, [Col. 0099A] and how great the reward will be which the author of purity himself gives as recompense to the pure in heart will be declared by the words that follow:

“And he was subject to them.” The gracious Majesty of the Creator then deigns in some manner to be subject to our will, when, our desire being fulfilled, we are fed with the inward sweetness of God, long sought with tears. Hence Jacob is read to have conquered the Lord in the figure of an angel and, by violently persisting, to have brought him to what he wished. Thus also, when we persevere in spiritual conflict and, as it were, use force upon the divine Majesty, the kindness of God, in some manner wearied and delightfully fatigued, sometimes yields when, as has been said, it abundantly pours into those who seek and knock opportunely and importunately the savour of heavenly joys. Happy is the soul; most blessed the conscience that has deserved thus to rule its Ruler! But whence, I ask, comes to it such glory of power, that the supreme Majesty deigns to be subject to it? Truly from what the Gospel reading adds here:

“And his mother kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.” Because she stores the divine sayings deep in her memory, pondering them in her heart, she rightly has him familiarly subject to her in time of need, whose words she strives to store within herself with such intimacy and devotion. Therefore, when we have made ourselves such through such advances in virtues that we are worthy to be refreshed by the food of eternal sweetness, what is said in what follows concerning our Author will already be fulfilled in us:

“The child Jesus advanced in age, and wisdom, and grace before God and men.” One is said to advance in age who surpasses childish age by the gravity of morals, and from whom neither inconstancy of mind nor disorderliness of action and bearing can easily steal away. This advance in age, [Col. 0099B] this perfection of maturity, will someday be brought about in us through the Lord’s cooperation, so that in all that we do, say, and think, nothing of vanity may intrude, but the countenance of holy gravity pleasing to God may appear.

“And in wisdom,” he says. Prudence is understood as knowledge of outward things, and belongs only to those who cleave to and concern themselves with worldly things. Wisdom, however, is an inward savour by which we savour and understand those things which are of God or pertain to the salvation of the soul. Therefore the grace of advancing in wisdom is given us, so that we who trample the desires of secular life may, while still living in the flesh, taste in some measure what are the joys of the heavenly life.

“And in grace before God and men.” We advance in grace before God when, on account of the merit of a praiseworthy life, he deigns to anticipate us through gratuitous goodness with blessings of sweetness. For often, without any industry of our own labour, the hour of prayer anticipates us with free goodness, so that our spirit, overflowing with spiritual delights, can fittingly say: “In your sweetness, O God, you have prepared for the poor” (Ps. 67:11).

[Col. 0099C] Or Jesus advanced in age through the progress of time, in wisdom through the increase of knowledge, in grace through the increase of virtue; before God and men—before God in conscience, before men in reputation; before God in order to be rewarded, before men in order to be glorified. Since, therefore, we have now learned in part with what diligence the Beloved must be sought, with what sweat he must be found, and with what bonds of love he must be held—the Son of the Beloved—let us take the greatest care to serve this author of sweetness with such sweetness of character that, when his sweetness, here tasted a little, is someday perfectly beheld, it may become for us a full satiety of every good. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

115  
## HOMILY XV. FOR THE SAME SUNDAY, SECOND HOMILY

[Col. 0102A]

“When Jesus was twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, and when the days were completed, as they returned, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it” (Luke 2).

In the twelve years of the age of the Lord Jesus, which are recorded for us in the present Gospel, may be understood the faith of the Holy Trinity, or the mystery of the four Gospels of the Son of God, by which we are instructed and led to faith in Christ. For whether four threes or three fours are counted, twelve are nonetheless found. Therefore the Lord Jesus is rightly said to have become twelve years old when he preached to the world faith in the Holy [Col. 0102B] Trinity and declared to the age the perfection of evangelical truth. Then, as he preached the new law and new ordinances, the Jews, inflamed by the torches of envy and hatred, burned so fiercely that they delivered the Author of life to death, as is immediately said in what follows:

“As they went up to Jerusalem.” This Jerusalem, called the vision of peace, signifies the flesh and body of the Lord, free from every defilement of sin, into which nothing flowed from the law of sin that could have disturbed that most peaceful peace. For in no human being could there ever be found, nor can there be found, such peace as was in our Mediator, because he alone, conceived without sin and born without the sprinkling of sin, remained undefiled in thought, word, and deed. Thus, according to the humanity he assumed, he himself was Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace.

But let us now consider who those were who went up into this Jerusalem, since they are not expressly described but are here mentioned covertly. “As they went up,” it says, “to Jerusalem.” Therefore, just as elsewhere in the Gospel, where “they” is used not expressly but indefinitely, we generally understand either good or evil angels, so in the present place we may understand evil spirits. These evil spirits, by their perverse suggestions and persuasions, stirred up and inflamed the Jews to such a degree that in their pride and cruelty they ascended against Christ. They did this, indeed, [Col. 0102C] when they laid hands upon him and, delivering the Author of salvation to death, crucified him. But God the Father permitted this ascent against his Son; God the Son permitted this ascent against his flesh, so that that feast day might follow of which what follows speaks:

“According to the custom of the feast day.” This feast day signifies the common life and holy manner of living which began in the primitive Church after Christ’s death and ascension, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; and no one called anything his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32). This feast day—that is, the common life—was rare in the Church before Christ’s coming, but after Christ’s passion it became customary. For it was rare for the faithful, setting aside all the riches, indeed all the business, of the world, to follow the Lord alone. But this feast day first began in the apostles, then in the martyrs, afterwards in the confessors; now, with God’s help, this feast day has reached us and has grown abundantly in the Church. It follows:

“And when the days were completed, as they returned.” These days of which it is said here were the days of Christ’s nativity, passion, burial, resurrection, and ascension. They deserved to be called days because they not only drove away the darkness of this age but also penetrated heaven, earth, and hell with their light. When these days of our salvation and redemption had been completed, [Col. 0102D] the Jews returned to their own things—to their own malice, plainly, and their former hardness—because they refused to believe in the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. For, as the Gospel itself testifies, when he died on the cross they asked Pilate the governor, because of their malice, to order the tomb guarded, lest perhaps his disciples take away the body. But when they knew with complete certainty that he whom they had crucified had risen from the dead, they gave money to the soldiers 116 so that they might spread abroad the report that, while the soldiers slept, his disciples had stolen him away.

Therefore, when they had returned, as we have said, to their cruelty and malice, where, I ask, did the Lord Jesus remain? “The child Jesus,” says the Evangelist, “remained in Jerusalem.” Thus the child Jesus remained and remains in Jerusalem, that is, in the Church. And he rightly says, “Child Jesus,” because it is the part of a child to fear his lord and master. For Jesus is a child in the present Church, which is his body, so long as it lives here under fear, so long as it is governed here under guardians and stewards, until it comes to that holy fear of which the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for age upon age” (Ps. 18:19). This holy fear is love beginning from fear and ending in love, which will endure in the elect in eternal life, never to be terminated, never to be ended. It follows:

And his parents did not recognize him. Who are the parents of the boy Jesus but the Jews, from whose stock [Col. 0103D] he descended, from whose flesh he came forth, having become flesh? For our Lady, the perpetual Virgin Mary, mother of that same Redeemer, was a Jewess through all her kindred, descended both from wicked and from righteous parents, as is recorded in the genealogy of that same generation: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1). Hence the Jews gloried that they were descended from the nobility of that seed, saying to the Lord: “We are Abraham’s seed, and have never been slaves to anyone” (John 8:33). And that blessed Samaritan woman, with whom he was speaking while seated by the well, said: “Our father Abraham gave us this well” (John 4:12). Therefore these parents of the Lord—the Jews, that is, sprung from Abraham’s seed—did not recognize, nor do they wish to recognize, that the Lord Jesus himself remained in his Church. But what do they do?

“Thinking that he was in the company, they travelled a day’s journey, and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances.” Therefore the Jews think not that the Lord has gone before them, but that [Col. 0104A] he, who has already gone before them, ought still to accompany them. For they suppose that Christ will come in the flesh, will still be a human being, and will give them earthly and temporal 118 glory and dwell with them. “They travelled a day’s journey, and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances.” The Jews now make a journey of one day, because they do not worship idols, but worship and venerate God the Father alone, God their Creator alone. But they do not reach the second day—to God the Son, of whom it is said through the prophet: [Col. 0104B] “Declare his salvation from day to day” (Ps. 95:2)—because they refuse to believe in God the Son, God the Redeemer.

In another sense also, they make a journey of one day, because they desire to obtain only the honour and prosperity of this present age, which they often indeed deserve to attain; but eternal blessedness and the prosperity of future joy they neither seek nor know how to seek. Thus, travelling the journey of one day, they seek him among relatives and acquaintances. The relatives, certainly, were the patriarchs, from whose stock and kinship he was born. The acquaintances, however, are the holy prophets, of whom the Jews boast that they have much knowledge according to the letter; but they despise and count as nothing our knowledge or understanding, which is according to the Spirit. Hence [Col. 0104C] it follows:

“And, not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking him.” For as long as they seek him in the patriarchs and prophets, they do not find him, until they return to the Catholic Church and find him there, as is said in the present passage: “They returned to Jerusalem, seeking him.” Thus, in the present time Jews return to the faith and unity of the holy Church, though few in number; but near the end of the world their whole multitude will fully return, as is said through the Psalmist: “They shall return at evening, and suffer hunger like dogs” (Ps. 58:7). Isaiah the prophet likewise, foreseeing their faith and conversion, said: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand which is on the shore of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isa. 10:22). Of this same conversion Paul the Apostle also says: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25). It follows:

119 “And after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, hearing them and questioning them. And all who heard him were astonished at his wisdom and his answers.” In these three days, of which we have just heard, three times may be understood: those before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. After these three days, after these three times, or after the knowledge of the holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—this great event will occur: the Jews, perfectly converted to the Lord and seeking him [Col. 0105A] in the temple, that is, in the Church, will find him.

“Sitting,” he says, “in the midst of the teachers.” Sitting is the posture of one judging. Therefore they will find the Lord Jesus sitting—that is, judging—when they recognize that he is the one who will judge the whole human race, the judge of the living and the dead. And it is rightly said: “Sitting in the midst of the teachers.” For Jesus sits in the middle among the Fathers and teachers of the New and Old Testaments, because he whom Moses and the other prophets foretold and taught would come in the flesh before Christ’s birth, the teachers of the New Testament believe, confess, and testify to have come.

But let us now see to what work he is devoted, and how they declare him to be sitting among the teachers. “Hearing,” [Col. 0105B] he says, “and questioning them.” Although this sense is allegorical, it nevertheless has a moral fragrance, and the mysteries of allegory themselves are not without the sweetness of moral instruction. The Lord hears the teachers when he carefully observes how, and with what zeal, every prelate and master teaches those subject to him: whether the discourse of his exhortation proceeds from earthly or heavenly matters; whether he destroys by the examples of his life what he preaches in speech; or whether he himself, by living well and perfectly, fulfils in works what he advises and exhorts others to do in words. Thus, in hearing the teachers, he in some sense also questions the hearers: how they have stored in the secret place of the heart what they have received by hearing the Lord’s words. Again, he questions them when he strictly examines why they have sinned. He questions them [Col. 0105C] again when he wishes to know how they have spent the time of life granted to them, how they have passed every single moment. After this hearing, after this questioning, the Gospel saying quite fittingly follows:

120 “And all who heard him were astonished at his wisdom and his answers.” Astonishment is an alienation of the mind, by which the human mind is drawn outside itself either through fear or love. What we have said makes the hearer astonished: that the Lord is so provident in hearing, so strict and subtle in questioning. Everyone who has sound understanding is struck with astonishment on hearing these things: that such and so great is the providence and wisdom of God, who so providently hears [Col. 0105D] how we are instructed by our teachers and masters through the word of preaching, and so diligently considers how our conduct and life correspond to their teaching. Whoever therefore has right understanding, on hearing this thunderclap of God’s word makes himself a stranger to earthly desires; and, if his mind had first been occupied with any sins, he strives with the utmost desire to remove them utterly from his own heart, and is immediately compelled by fear to return to his heart.

He is indeed astonished also at the Lord’s answers, when he hears that the Almighty examines all human works so strictly and minutely, permitting nothing to pass without examination; but answers the good according to their merits, and answers the evil with just recompense according to their sins. In short, as blessed Gregory says, no moments of time pass [Col. 0106A] without a determination of recompense. Hence it is well added:

“And, seeing him, they were astonished.” And since we have briefly digressed into the moral sense, let us now return to the allegory and see how these things too are fulfilled in the Jews. “They found him,” he says, “in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, hearing and questioning them.” Therefore, when the Jews, as we have said, have taken refuge in the faith of the holy Church, they find Jesus hearing the teachers and questioning them. Struck and stirred by the word of preaching, they at last awaken so as to consider how carefully almighty God hears the words of his preachers, how he demands and requires from them an answering return of good works after the preachers’ words. They also hear [Col. 0106B] him questioning, when they hear the force of the heavenly strictness with which he examines every human work, and how justly he repays good and evil.

Hence it is rightly added: “And all who heard 121 him were astonished at his wisdom and his answers.” They are astonished at his wisdom and providence because, when they hear God’s provident scrutiny, they are stunned and desire in mind to become alienated from earthly desires. They are also astonished at his answers, when from the pages of the Old and New Testaments they consider how strict he comes in judgment, how subtly he examines each person’s merits, and how justly he answers each according to those merits. And, seeing these things, they will be greatly astonished. They will indeed marvel at the unsearchable and inscrutable abyss of God’s judgments: why, after first rejecting the Gentiles, he called the Jews; then, after rejecting the Jews, received the Gentiles; and finally chose both to be converted to himself at the end of the world. And because they cannot investigate these matters by reason, they will be astonished when they see them.

“And his mother said to him: Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I sought you in sorrow.” In Jesus’ mother the Synagogue is signified, which is to be converted near the end of the age. When it has come to perfect knowledge of the faith, and has perceived with the eye of the heart that all things formerly prophesied of Christ have been fulfilled in him, it will grieve deeply that, though the Gentiles were enlightened, it itself and all its fathers were so blinded. Yet it will not be able [Col. 0106D] to comprehend [Col. 0106D] by what judgment of God this was brought about; and therefore, with a spirit greatly contrite, it will say to the Lord: “Son, why have you done this to us?” As though it said: “O beloved Son, who were willing to assume the material of flesh from our offspring, why have you so long continued over us the multitude of your compassion and mercies? Why have you done this to us, leaving us in such blindness of mind and permitting us to remain through so many times and ages in such hardness of heart? Behold, I, your mother the Synagogue, and your father the Jewish people, sought you in sorrow. The sorrow which has come upon us by your just judgment is wholly unbearable. We grieve that we ourselves were left in this blindness and were rebellious against God for so long; and we grieve also for our fathers, whom we know [Col. 0107A] descended to hell in this misery of blindness and received from the hand of the just Judge the sentence of eternal condemnation.”

These are the words of Jews grieving deeply 122 over their blindness, by which they address their beloved Son, begotten from their flesh.

Great indeed will be the grief and lamentation of those who consider these things and cannot comprehend God’s hidden judgment. The Apostle Paul, beholding this abyss of divine judgments, could not comprehend by what judgment of God it came about that, while the Gentiles were left in unbelief, the Israelite people was first chosen by God; but afterward, as justice and mercy worked, the people of the Gentiles was received into Christ’s faith after the Jews had been rejected. Thus, failing in [Col. 0107B] this contemplation, he finally cried out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). Therefore, when the Jews, as we have said, grieve so deeply and repent so bitterly, the Lord finally answers:

“Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in those things which are my Father’s?” As though he said: “You sought me sorrowfully, as you say; but because you did not seek me rightly in the Church, where I remained and where you ought to have sought me, you were certainly not worthy to find me. Indeed, I must be in those things which are my Father’s: namely, in the blessed souls that are in the Church, who truly are the house of my Father.”

[Col. 0107C] “And they did not understand the word which he spoke to them.” In sacred Scripture, “Word” frequently refers to divinity and “flesh” to humanity. Thus blessed John says in the Gospel: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14). So long as the Jews persist in their unbelief, they do not understand this Word, because they do not believe that Christ, the Word of God, was incarnate—he whom the Lord had nevertheless long ago declared through Moses and through the mouths of all his prophets would one day be incarnate. It follows:

“And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them.” He goes down with them when he deigns to come into their heart, visits them by enlightening them, and kindles them in his love. He also comes [Col. 0107D] with them to Nazareth because he will rejoice and delight in the purity of their faith and the sincerity of their perfect love. And he will be subject to them, because he 123 will remain among and with them. Such will be the end of the Church as was its beginning; and as great will be the fervour and love toward God at the Church’s end as is known to have existed in the primitive Church. Hence it is well added:

“And his mother kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.” The Lord’s mother has often already been said to be the Synagogue. Converted near the end of the age and strongly enkindled in love of the Lord by the heat of faith, it will keep in its heart all the words of both the New and Old Testaments. For those converted, according to the Psalmist, “shall return at evening, suffer hunger like dogs, and go round about the city” [Col. 0108A] (Ps. 58:7). With such devotion of faith and such constancy of soul will they seek the Lord that, even while seeking him, they will suffer hunger: hunger, indeed, for faith, hunger for righteousness, hunger for truth. They will also go around the city—the holy Church, that is—so that wherever they find unbelievers, they may convert them to faith by the word of their preaching; and whomever they see sluggish and indolent in God’s love, they may awaken and inflame to the love of God by their exhortations.

Finally, they will be preachers so outstanding and perfect, being filled with such abundant knowledge of both the New and Old Testaments, that no wiser or more perfect 124 preachers will have existed in the holy Church since the word of God began to be proclaimed. Then they will perceive with the eye of faith how those two [Col. 0108B] cherubim look toward the oracle, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat. For they will know most fully that all sacred Scripture, both New and Old Testament, looks to Christ alone. At that time, certainly, what is immediately added here will be fulfilled:

“And Jesus increased in wisdom and age and grace before God and men.” In the Church now present, the Lord Jesus seems as it were a child, because it is still governed by fear. But in that Church which will exist at the end of the age, perfectly converted to God, Jesus will make a certain increase. He will increase in wisdom through growth in knowledge; in age through maturity of perfection; in grace through eternity of reward: before God, because God is the one who works [Col. 0108C] this increase; before men, because God works this increase in and with human beings. May our Lord Jesus Christ bring us to that increase—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.
