## HOMILY XVI. THE FIRST, FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

“A marriage was held at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. And Jesus and his disciples were invited to the marriage” (John 2).

Through this sacred Gospel text, in which the beginning of the signs of our Lord and Saviour [Col. 0108D] is commended to us, is prefigured that memorable and saving beginning by which everyone who is to be saved is first initiated into the joys of eternal salvation. Just as bodily marriages can nowhere be held unless bridegroom and bride are present, so the joys of spiritual marriage cannot be celebrated without those same persons: God as bridegroom, and the faithful soul as bride. The place where festive banquets for these marriages are customarily prepared is the chosen congregation of those who serve God, in which, by God’s cooperation, are found those who are worthily admitted, according to their merits, to the bridal chamber of the eternal King.

What sort of blessed soul this ought to be, which desires to be called and to be the bride of the immortal Bridegroom, is plainly taught by the fact that these marriages are described as having taken place at Cana of Galilee. [Col. 0109A] For *Cana* is interpreted “zeal,” and *Galilee* “migration.”

125 But it should be noted that many are in Cana who are not in Galilee, and conversely a great many appear to be in Galilee who do not deserve to have a dwelling-place in Cana. Those, indeed, are as though in Cana but not in Galilee who, as commonly happens among secular people, after committing adultery, murder, or some other grave crime, undertake penance for a time and zealously pursue, as it were, the sins they have committed; but when the time of satisfaction has passed, they become entangled again in their former sinful errors. Such persons, because they are zealous but not persevering, penitents but not converts, do not deserve a place in the wedding chamber of the eternal King.

Conversely, many [Col. 0109B] come into Galilee but not into Cana: those, namely, who abandon the harmful paths of their former conduct and flee to the delights of spiritual life. Yet, because they think that mere migration away from sins suffices for the perfection of eternal salvation, they are not inflamed with any spiritual fervour or with any firm zeal of penance, as would be fitting, to pursue the crimes of their former bestial [Col. 0109C] life. Since these are migrants but not zealous, converts but not fervent, they are likewise excluded from the banquet of the heavenly Bridegroom. Therefore only the person truly dwells in Cana of Galilee who, making a praiseworthy passage from vices to virtues, does not neglect always and tirelessly—not merely for an hour or for a time—to punish, with the worthy fervour of spiritual constancy, those things in which he remembers having acted wickedly. Truly blessed and beloved of God is the soul that has in this way made itself worthy of divine marriage. For the Evangelist makes clearer in the following words how great is its blessedness and dignity before the eyes of divine majesty:

“And,” he says, “the mother of Jesus was there.” The mother of Jesus is the same as the bride: the faithful soul, a bride by loving, and a mother by spiritually begetting from the spiritual womb of its heart that same Jesus whom it loves. But how can one who is mere dust possess such power to beget from its heart its own begetter, unless, as the Evangelist testifies, it was there—that is, in Cana of Galilee? For to be in Cana of Galilee is, by zeal and migration, to remain with firm constancy in the Lord’s marriage.

[Col. 0109D] 126 Yet by the Lord’s mother we may also understand a good prelate, without whom spiritual marriages are not brought to completion: one who ought, by his life and teaching, to commend and make known to the faithful soul Christ, the bridegroom of the bride, and to instruct the bride in how she ought to love that same bridegroom, Christ, and attain his embraces.

“And Jesus and his disciples were invited to the marriage.” The Lord must indeed be invited by holy desires and chaste thoughts, so that, coming through the hidden grace of his visitation, he may grant it bridal love; and through that love may more fully instruct by his commandments all its senses, which we understand under the name of disciples, so that it may know what guardianship it ought to exercise with its eyes and [Col. 0110A] hands, mouth and ears, lest, by doing anything unlawful through these, it incur the offence of its bridegroom and lover.

But because it is impossible for anyone, at the beginning of conversion, to attain either perfect self-guardianship or the desired sweetness of divine knowledge, the Evangelist consequently adds:

“And when the wine failed, the mother of Jesus said to him: They have no wine.” By wine we may fittingly understand either the fervour of love or the grace of devotion which arises in a person from the knowledge of God. Therefore the mother of Jesus—namely, a good prelate or a faithful soul—laments the failure of wine, when either a prelate humbly entreats the Lord because of the lack of spiritual fervour which he sees in those subject to him, or the soul itself does so because of the slothfulness of its own torpor. But the pious and merciful Lord does not disdain the soul humbly persevering in the cry of such supplication as though he did not hear it; rather, by the invisible word of his response he graciously makes known to it what produces such a failure and by what means it may avoid it:

“What,” he says, “is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” When Jesus says these things to his mother, he plainly suggests to us, as though he did not recognize her as his mother, that the soul placed in spiritual marriage ought to reject every carnal affection from itself, lest, while care for its carnal parents troubles it, it be less diligent in spiritual exercise. For as long as we are in the world, we are admittedly indebted to our parents. But after we have left ourselves, [Col. 0110C] we ought also to be free from concern for them.

Nor should what he says be passed over: “Woman, my hour has not yet come.” By “woman,” a word derived from softness, may be understood fickleness of mind. Unless the soul casts this away and rejects it, Jesus’ hour does not come: it is not yet the time, I say, for him to admit it to the bridal joys of his sweetness. When the faithful soul, moved by desire for its bridegroom, inwardly perceives this from the grace of his visitation and inspiration, it girds itself manfully for a greater fervour of spiritual constancy, as the Evangelist figuratively shows when he says:

“And Jesus’ mother said to the servants: Whatever he tells you, do.” These servants are all its senses, which it then diligently summons [Col. 0110D] and binds together within itself, so that by their service and assistance it may attain what it desires. “Whatever,” she says, “he tells you, do.” As though she said: “I have indeed heard many things about God, but because of my own sloth—indeed, yours as well—I have never taken care to fulfil them in action. Therefore now, whatever he tells you, do. Whatever the Lord commands, fulfil effectively in works, since we cannot obtain this grace of divine sweetness which we seek except by the exertion of devout action.” It follows:

“Now there were six stone water-jars set there, according to the purification of the Jews.” By these six water-jars we may understand the observances instituted by the holy Fathers for cleansing the hearts of those who confess; and, unless I am mistaken, we can find them all here [Col. 0111A].

The first water-jar is the continence of chastity, by which whatever lust has previously defiled is washed away.

The second is fasting, so that abstinence may now cleanse what gluttony had stained.

Through sloth and idleness also, which are enemies of the soul, we have contracted many stains, eating, contrary to God’s sentence, bread in the sweat of another’s face rather than our own. For this reason a third water-jar is also set before us, so that those stains may be washed away by manual labour.

Likewise, through sleepiness and the other works of nights and darkness we have sinned greatly; 128 therefore a fourth water-jar, the observance of vigils, is set there, so that, rising at night to confess the Lord, we may redeem—not [Col. 0111B] good nights—the nights of past time.

Moreover, who does not know how greatly the tongue has defiled us through idle chatter and lies, detractions and flatteries, malicious and boastful words? For all these a fifth water-jar is necessary: namely, silence, the guardian of religion and the place in which our strength lies.

The sixth water-jar also is discipline, by which we live not according to our own judgment but another’s, so that whatever we have sinned through undisciplined living may be wiped away. These are stone jars: they are hard, but we need to be washed in them, unless perhaps we wish to receive from the Lord a bill of divorce because of our foulness. Yet in their being called stone, not only hardness but, much better, solidity may be understood, since these things do not wash [Col. 0111C] unless they remain with steadfast stability.

Nor should we pass over his statement: “Each holding two or three measures.” In the two measures we may understand a twofold fear: one by which a person fears to be eternally condemned; another by which one fears to be deprived of eternal life. The third measure, however, is a third and much more commendable love, by which one fears to be defrauded of daily grace—that is, inward grace. Whoever has been filled with this fear has certainly added the third measure to the two measures.

But in another sense these six water-jars also suitably signify the six ages of the world, with which [Col. 0111D] our six ages—namely infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, and decrepitude—are fittingly compared. In the first age of the world God placed the first man in paradise, never to die if he had remained obedient. But because he did not keep God’s commandments, he brought upon himself and all his posterity the misery of perpetual death. Our first age, called infancy, may rightly be likened to this first age: in it God places a person as it were in paradise when, having been freed from original sin through baptism, he restores that person to eternal salvation. But because no one remains in this dignity without transgressing the Lord’s command after baptism as Adam did, this first water-jar is rightly called the water-jar of transgression.

129 In the second age, holy Noah entered the ark which he had built at the Lord’s command, intending to escape the waters of the flood [Col. 0112A]. By this he signified to us that everyone who has drunk from this first water-jar of transgression, of which we have spoken, should put his hand to the second water-jar of the second age: he should approach the Lord’s ark, that is, the place of holy conduct, in which he may wash away by the cleansing flood of tears whatever he sinned outside the ark. This second water-jar is not unfittingly called the water-jar of conversion. If in that conversion one advances by humbly repenting, then with God’s help one will at last be able to reach the third water-jar of the third age, which begins with Abraham. Abraham, humbly obeying God, was willing to sacrifice his only son; but being forbidden by the divine voice, he sacrificed not his son but a ram.

And this third water-jar should be called the water-jar of perfection [Col. 0112B], because no perfection can be greater or more acceptable to God than when a person, by mortifying the flesh—which is understood through the ram—and its desires, begins to despise it, and, having given life to the spirit through good works, turns attention solely to heavenly things.

To this, indeed, the fourth water-jar of the fourth age will be added most fittingly and justly. In that age holy David, because of reverence for his great humility, was raised, by God’s appointment, to royal power. This fourth water-jar may be called the water-jar of prelacy: God then gives drink from it to one making such progress, when, because of the merit of a praiseworthy life, he raises that person to the honour of a teaching dignity as an example to others.

But if the person lives perfectly in his office and according to [Col. 0112C] God’s will, the fifth water-jar of the fifth age must immediately follow: namely, the water-jar of tribulation, which may rightly be understood through the Babylonian migration that occurred in the fifth age. For Babylon, which means “confusion,” signifies the tribulation of the present world, into which a good prelate is sometimes compelled to fall and suffer for love of the holy bodies and likewise of the chaste souls whom God has entrusted to his care and governance in both bodily and spiritual matters.

Yet if he acts patiently and perseveres manfully in labours undertaken for God, then at last, in the sixth age, which begins with the coming of the Lord, he will drink joyfully from the sixth water-jar as well, when, after the laborious end of this life, he is crowned with the glory of eternal reward [Col. 0112D]. But no one can reach this sixth water-jar, which we may call the water-jar of deliverance or reward, unless he considers and examines with the watchful eye of his heart his own six water-jars—his six ages, that is, of which we spoke above. For this is why the holy Evangelist admonishes and exhorts us in his words, testifying that the water-jars now under discussion were set there according to the purification of the Jews.

First, therefore, a person must consider how he has lived in each of his ages, which almighty God has assigned—that is, granted—to him so that he might live in them according to the purification of the Jews: according to the example, that is, of those who, purified in this life through true confession and the merit of holy action, now rejoice in heaven, immortal inhabitants of the bridal chamber of the eternal King [Col. 0113A]. When a person begins carefully to do this in himself, he finds that all his water-jars have been nothing other than stone. For stone is hard and cold. He sees how hard and cold-heartedly he has passed all his days: neither taking care to avoid evil for fear of the Lord, nor to do the good that ought to have been done for love of him.

He also sees how all his water-jars held only two or three measures apiece, when, carefully considering all his ways, he finds in himself nothing except that, in every age, in words, deeds, and even [Col. 0113B] wicked thoughts—things which are as it were two or three measures—he has been in all respects contrary to the divine will. The Lord immediately adds in what follows what such a person must do:

131 “Fill,” he says, “the water-jars with water.” As in the preceding passage wine signifies knowledge of God, so here water may signify knowledge of oneself. Therefore, to fill the water-jars with water is to know oneself perfectly in all one’s actions, and to offer God worthy fruits of repentance for every excess of sin. Whoever obeys this command—indeed, this counsel—of divine mercy will easily be able to rise to what follows.

“And they filled them to the brim.” They likewise fill their water-jars to the brim who, enlightened by divine illumination [Col. 0113C], diligently set before themselves not only their sinful acts, but also their will and desires, as well as the time and place in which they sinned and how often they committed the same sins. But because inward knowledge is insufficient unless true and perfect confession of the mouth follows as well, the Lord immediately added:

“Draw now, and carry it to the steward.” This steward signifies any good prelate, who is rightly called *architriclinus*, as it were “ruler of the dining hall,” because he presides over the three orders in the congregation: the innocent, penitents, and perfect [Col. 0113D]. The innocent, I say, are those who, living innocently from the flower of their earliest age, have clung to God alone. The penitents are those who, the farther they had departed from God by sinning, have submitted themselves the more humbly to divine mercy through repentance. The perfect are those who, both innocent and penitent, love God more sweetly because they have deserved to taste more intimately his inward sweetness. All these prepare in themselves a dining hall pleasing to the Lord, because they labour to please him alone in soul, spirit, and body.

Or the Lord honours him with the title of steward because in all his words, deeds, and thoughts he labours to please the eyes of God alone. “Draw,” he says, “and carry it to the steward.” As though he said: “Whatever pestilential thing lies hidden within, draw out from the hidden depths of the breast through true self-knowledge and repentance; and carry it in the hands of perfect confession to this [Col. 0114A] steward whom I have set over you.” Therefore, as soon as God speaks these things invisibly within a person, 132 what is said next comes about in a wonderful manner: “And they carried it.” They carry a drink pleasing to the steward when, confessing truthfully, they draw out from the abyss of their own heart what they long poured in by sinning.

“But when the steward tasted the water made wine.” It is well and fittingly said, “when the steward tasted,” since it is exceedingly sweet and delightful to a prelate who fears God when he understands, in the humble and truly penitent heart of those subject to him, water made wine: that is, when he inwardly perceives that through true and perfect knowledge of themselves they have also been divinely enlightened with knowledge of God. “And he did not know,” says the Evangelist, “whence it was. But the servants knew, who drew [thus the codex] [Col. 0114B] the water.” The servants—the humble subjects, namely—know by how many labours they have obtained these things, and by what guarding of the heart and discipline of the body they have deserved this grace before God. But because the prelate cannot know whether a subject does what he does from fear and love of God alone, he calls that person the bridegroom, addressing him in these words:

“Every person sets out the good wine first.” These words are certainly a fatherly exhortation, by which a kindly teacher urges a disciple who is making good progress toward a greater perfection of spiritual [life] [codex: “urges spiritual perfection”]. He calls him bridegroom when he continually sets before him the voluntary [Col. 0114C] pledge by which he has joined himself to God, admonishing and exhorting him that, by always advancing toward what is better, he may remember with what constancy he came to God and with what humility of heart and body he pledged himself to serve God. “Every person,” he says, “sets out the good wine first.” As though he said: “It is indeed the custom of many who take up the arms of spiritual warfare first to set out good wine: that is, at the beginning of their conversion, to gird themselves manfully with the good zeal of fervour; but when people have become intoxicated, then they set out what is inferior.”

Source/review notes: The final proposed edit is not needed; the draft contains no unresolved substantive omission or mistranslation after the listed corrections.

133. People are said to become intoxicated, indeed, not with a good intoxication, when, desiring to run with a joyful heart in the way of God’s commandments, they are assailed either by the snares of the devil, or by the wrongs of their neighbours, or even by the weakness of their own bodies. But when they are unwilling or unable to resist their temptations, they often do what is worse. For what could be worse than to set aside the praiseworthy zeal of one’s first fervour and to yield by wrongly consenting to temptations?

“But you have kept the good wine until now.” You, I say, who, with your own conscience as witness, have kept the good wine within yourself until now to such an extent that you have never brought forth anything good from your heart or body for the service of divine praise: do not judge that you should live after the example of such persons. Rather, proceeding steadfastly in all things in the fear and love of God, carefully restraining yourself, strive, as you began, always to advance [Col. 0115A] from good to better. It follows:

“This beginning of signs Jesus performed at Cana of Galilee, and he manifested his glory.” We are accustomed to call it a sign when we see either the blind restored to light or the dead returned to life. Yet it may much more truly be called a sign when, through the inward radiance of divine illumination, someone enlightened from the blindness of the heart comes to know the death of his own soul, and, giving himself life through good works, merits to rise to the true life, which is Christ. That beginning of conversion is rightly called the beginning of Christ’s signs, because he alone works it in Cana of Galilee—that is, in the soul that is both zealous and passing over. He also manifested his glory to that soul, namely the glory of forgiveness, when [Col. 0115B] he mercifully justified it after cleansing it from the stain of sins. After the glory of justification there immediately follows the power of perfection; hence it is said:

“And his disciples believed in him.” The disciples therefore believe in God when the blessed soul, subject with all its senses to divine discipline, so pours the whole affection of its heart into God that it loves nothing besides God and begins to do everything it does for the honour and love of God alone. May the almighty Lord bring us to this power of perfection, so that, justified from all sins, we may love him in this present life in such a way that we may merit to reach him there, where we shall never be torn away from the wholeness of his love, through the favour of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the same Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0115C] through all ages of ages. Amen.

135. HOMILY XVII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY.

“And when Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him; and behold, a leper came and worshipped him, saying: Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Matt. 8).

Our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, desiring to save the human race lost from the beginning, came down from the mountain when, descending from the height of his divinity, he stooped down to the depths of our mortality; [Col. 0121D] when, in order to redeem the human being whom he had created, he did not hesitate to take upon himself the form of our humanity. By the great crowds that followed him after this descent, [Col. 0115D] the crowds of the faithful, the crowds of the holy Church, are signified. For he whom Judaea alone first followed was afterwards followed by the multitude of the nations gathered to faith in Christ; and this is fittingly called a great crowd because of the prerogative of love by which it is loved by God.

Those two sick persons who then came to him figuratively represented two peoples: the people of the nations and the people of the Jews. Nor without reason is the people of the nations, defiled by the worship of idols, represented by the leper; while by the paralytic lying in bed is represented the Jewish people, which, living in desires and according to the desires of the flesh, sought, loved, and awaited only the prosperity of temporal things. It was indeed then saved in part, but later—that is, at the end of the world—[Col. 0116A] when the fullness of the nations has entered, it will be saved more fully and perfectly. For so that these two sick persons might be healed—that is, so that the nations and the Jews might be freed through faith in him from the sickness of eternal condemnation—the only-begotten Son of God descended from the bosom of the eternal Father into this misery of our mortality. For this reason he was willing to taste, in the humanity assumed for us, every kind of pain and misery except sin alone.

But in this leper who was healed in the open country may also be understood the secular person, who is commanded to show himself to the priests and to offer the gift commanded by Moses, because he ought to be healed through confession and satisfaction. By the paralytic, however, who lies in bed, I consider that the spiritual person [Col. 0116B] may fittingly be understood: he wastes away as though weakened by paralysis when inwardly he fails and grows lukewarm in fervour for God.

In these two persons we may also understand, more particularly, every individual human being, whom the Lord cleanses by his grace from outward and inward sins. The vices of the flesh, which a person contracts outwardly through the body, are like a kind of leprosy because they defile the flesh. But the vices of the mind, contracted through the lukewarmness and sloth of the heart, are like a kind of paralysis, by which the inner person is weakened and fails away from his God. Having briefly set these matters before us, let us first consider both the manner of the leper’s healing and the words by which the truly sinful person is instructed in what order he ought to come to God and how he may obtain the grace of the desired healing—[Col. 0116C] namely, the forgiveness of his sins.

“And behold,” says the evangelist, “a leper came and worshipped him, saying: Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” The leper comes to God when the sinner, polluted by sins and vices, begins to recognize the infection of his sins. For to go away from God is not to know oneself; but when he thoroughly considers the greatness of his sins, and on this account begins thoroughly to humble himself before God, this is truly to come and to worship. Nor should we pass over what he says: “And behold.” *Behold* is a demonstrative adverb, and by this word we are mystically shown that the only reason the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, came down from the mountain—that is, from the height [Col. 0116D] of his divinity—to the depths of our mortality, was that the leper might be healed, that through his coming in the flesh the sinful human being might be set free. This “behold” still endures, because from the time when he deigned to become human for humanity, there has been no time in which the way of salvation and grace was not open to sinners who humbly acknowledged their sins. And this “behold” is prolonged even to the end of the world, because he who came to redeem always is, and always will be, ready to forgive. Let us therefore hear what this leper said:

“Lord,” he says, “if you will, you can cleanse me.” This prayer is the prayer of a person who is truly penitent and knows himself in true humility. It is as though he said: “Lord, who made and redeemed me, I acknowledge your power. I know that you are able to cleanse me. However great [Col. 0117A] the leprosy of my vices may be, it is not impossible for you to heal me. I do not doubt your power, but your will; for, when I consider the enormity of my crimes, I fear that you may not wish—and ought not to wish—to cleanse and heal me. You can, Lord, if you will; but if you do not will it, your judgment is right. I blame not you but myself. For it is my iniquities, my crimes and offences, that have caused this; they resist your mercy, so that you ought rightly not to will it. Therefore, because I acknowledge and believe the omnipotence of your majesty, I seek only your will; for if you merely will, my iniquity yields to your power, and by your will alone the leprosy and foulness of my crimes can be purged.”

Almighty God does not despise this humble prayer of the leper, his humble sinner; but, since he is gracious and [Col. 0117B] merciful, he hears and answers it graciously and mercifully, as the evangelist subsequently adds:

“And stretching out his hand,” he says, “he touched him, saying: I will; be cleansed.” The Lord’s hand is, as it were, not stretched out but held back when he allows a person to follow his own lusts and serve the pleasures and desires of his flesh. But he stretches out his hand when, by his operation, he outwardly manifests in a person that grace to which from eternity he foreknew and predestined the person: that is, when he grants a person the power of self-restraint, which is the beginning of eternal salvation, begun here and to be completed in the life to come. He touches him [Col. 0117C] when he visits him through his fear, so that he begins to fear his sins and to displease himself in them, and so that the one who was formerly an incontinent person, a sinner, and a carnal person begins to be self-controlled, righteous, and chaste. For this righteous will of the human being causes God to subject his will to the human will. He therefore answers and says: “I will; be cleansed.” It is as though he said: “Because you have not doubted my ability, but have believed that my will alone is sufficient to heal and cure the leprosy of your crimes, I will what you will: be cleansed as you will.”

“And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.” He aptly says “immediately,” because as soon as God grants a person good will—that is, when, touched by his fear, he makes that person self-controlled—his leprosy is cleansed: inwardly and invisibly he is purged from every infection of crimes. [Col. 0117D] He felt this operation of divine power within himself who said: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31:5). And another prophet says: “At whatever hour you turn back and groan, you shall be saved” (Ezek. 33:12). But because this inward grace, this invisible cleansing, does not suffice for full and perfect salvation unless outward cleansing is added—the cleansing, that is, of the body—unless a person makes loving penitential satisfaction to God with the same body by which he committed sins, Jesus rightly adds after the leprosy has been cleansed, saying:

“See that you tell no one.” “See,” he says, “by diligently attending to yourself; see by keeping yourself in true humility; see that you do not at any time speak of the grace wrought in you [Col. 0118A] in such a way as to attribute or ascribe it to your own merits. But go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” Go, I say, through the devotion of mind you have begun; show yourself to the priest through true confession; offer the gift through humble bodily satisfaction. And he aptly added: “which Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” For when one does not shrink from making satisfaction to God for one’s sins, by constant and unceasing labour, with the very body by which one sinned, through true and perfect confession, this is truly the gift offered according to Moses’ commandment, according to the teaching of the sacred law. It is the evident testimony of one’s salvation to follow in eternal life. It follows:

“And when he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came to [Col. 0118B] him, begging and saying.” By Capernaum, which is interpreted “village of consolation,” any spiritual manner of life is aptly represented, in which, if a person lives rightly, he can find the consolation of eternal life. The Lord enters Capernaum when he causes the person whom he has purposed to save to enter upon a spiritual way of life. For whatever good a person does is ascribed to the person of him who, through his mercy, works it in that person.

Nor is it without mystery that, after the Lord’s entry into Capernaum, the centurion came to him. A centurion is one who commands a hundred soldiers. Nor without reason may perfection be understood by the number one hundred, which is perfect. Through the purpose of spiritual life, signified by Capernaum, a person in some measure approaches God. For one who had withdrawn far from him by living badly and adding crime to crime draws nearer to him daily through the labour of spiritual life. One also becomes a centurion when, by the gift of God’s grace, one advances to such perfection that, according to the Lord’s evangelical command, one renounces for God both bodily and mental things: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, and follow me” (Matt. 19:21). Thus, thus, when, leaving all things, one strives toward that alone which is above all things—namely, the grace of God’s inward sweetness—yet cannot attain it according to one’s desire because the frailty both of body and mind still resists, one breaks forth in humble entreaty as though in these words:

[Col. 0118D] “Lord, my servant lies paralysed at home and is grievously tormented.” It is as though he said: “You know, Lord, that I love you alone above all things and thirstingly pant after that inward grace of your sweetness, by which you are accustomed to refresh the soul that loves you. But my servant—my sense and affection—because it is not manly but childish, lies paralysed at home; it lies weak and afflicted in my body. For now bodily weakness, now lukewarmness of heart, prevents me from rising to you. Nor do I grieve only because I lack the grace of your divine sweetness; rather, because the multitude of harmful thoughts that succeed one another in my heart weakens and dissolves me inwardly like a kind of paralysis, so that I cannot stand firm in you. This is the torment by which my soul is grievously tormented.” This [Col. 0119A] prayer is indeed the prayer not of a carnal but of a spiritual person; it is so much loftier than the preceding prayer as it is nearer to God, being wholly spiritual. Nor does it ever pass without effect, as the evangelist subsequently shows when he adds:

“And Jesus said to him: I will come and heal him.” Jesus’ speaking is Jesus’ doing. He speaks when he grants the soul its desire. What does he say? “I will come.” He comes when, by the grace of his sweetness visiting the soul that desires him, he manifests himself to it; and thus, while here the soul merits the fulfilment of its request, it is assured of the grace of future blessedness, in which it will dwell with him not momentarily but continuously, not transiently but eternally. The apostle Paul bears witness to this when he says: “He who gave us the pledge of the Spirit” (2 Cor. 1:22). [Col. 0119B] For that brief grace of heavenly visitation, tasted here in a moment, is a kind of pledge of that grace which is reserved without end for the person in the life to come. This is what the Lord shows us when he says not in the present, “I am coming,” but, “I will come and heal him.” It is as though he said: “When you have passed through the miseries of mortal life, when, laying aside the burden of flesh, you are to be freed from the straits of this laborious struggle, I will come through the power of my divinity; I will heal you, because by myself I will cure you from every infirmity of mind and body which you now suffer.” From this ineffably gracious divine conversation, perceived not by the bodily ear but by the ear of the heart, the person himself begins to understand that he can never attain in this life the full sweetness of God’s grace. [Col. 0119C] Hence he answers and says:

141. “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed.” It is as though he said: “I am unworthy, Lord, as long as I bear the roof of this wretched mortality and ignorance, to be able to know you as you are, or to rest as I desire in you, in whom alone is my rest. But only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed. Speak only the word—speak, I beseech you, who are the Word of the Father—so that, when the roof of this ignorance and mutability has been removed, I may merit to see the excellence of your divine majesty. For there my servant will be perfectly healed, where you yourself will be the spirit of my soul and the health of my body, you who will remain without the corruption of mutability in your elect without end. [Col. 0119D] Lord, you have given me, your unworthy sinner, hope of this mercy and grace in the many and great compassions that you have shown in me.

“For I too am a man under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another [the manuscript: *to another person*], ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” I am indeed a human being—not such as I once was, when I lived without you and against you—but a person under authority, bearing for love of you the yoke of obedience, the yoke of spiritual observance and strict discipline. “Having soldiers under me,” because my senses and affections, which once were above me while they fought against me and against the salvation of my soul, I now hold beneath me by the gift of your grace, so that I am able by your power to refuse and repel the harmful and useless thoughts that force themselves upon my heart, [Col. 0120A] and likewise wicked and unlawful desires. “And I say to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes,” because, when vain thoughts and evil desires yield place, I am able by the gift of your generosity to delight in spiritual perceptions. “And I say to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it,” because I subject my body to myself and reduce it to slavery, lest it grow sluggish through harmful freedom, but instead not shrink from exercising itself through good works. These, Christ, are the gifts of your grace. I attribute none of them to my own merits, but humbly ascribe everything in me that I perceive to be pleasing to your will to grace that goes before and follows after.

“And Jesus, hearing, marvelled, and said to those following him: Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.” Jesus’ marvelling is Jesus’ approving and loving. “Hearing,” he says, [Col. 0120B] “he marvelled.” For he himself, the author and teacher of humility, gladly hears words that proceed from a truly humble heart, approves them with special kindness, and loves the speaker, as the evangelist shows when he adds: “And he said to those following him.” Who are those following the Lord except the multitude of holy angels and elect human beings? To all these the Lord commends his humble one. “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.” By Israel, whose name is interpreted “a man seeing God,” we may understand the apostate angels, who, since they were created to see eternally the face of God, can fittingly be called Israel. It is as though he said: “This incomparable power of faith, which this man formed from frail matter offers and renders to me, who submits himself to my power in such profound humility of heart that whatever virtue he has ever acquired through the labours of his own body he attributes wholly not to himself but to my name and grace—this faith, I say, I have not found in Israel, among my angels, who showed themselves ungrateful to me when they exalted themselves against me above that for which they were made. My first angel, created by me perfect in beauty, exalted himself against me, saying: ‘I shall place my throne above the stars of heaven; I shall be like the Most High’” (Isa. 14:14). “This man, wholly subject to my will, humbles himself and exalts me.”

“Amen, I say to you that many shall come from east and west, and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob [Col. 0120D] in the kingdom of heaven.” These many who come from east and west are to be understood as the elect, who may fittingly be called “many” because they are great and honourable in God’s sight. Those who come from east and west—that is, in whom the light of God’s grace rises and, with the assistance of that same grace, sins and vices set—shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, because they shall become heirs of the heavenly kingdom together with faith, hope, and charity, which seem to be denoted by the names of these three patriarchs. “But the children of the kingdom shall be cast into the outer darkness.” By the children of the kingdom, therefore, we understand the same beings as by Israel: namely, evil spirits. They are called children of the kingdom because they were created so that, if they had persevered in humility and subjection to God, they should have been inhabitants of God’s kingdom [Col. 0121A] without end. As they have now been cast into inner darkness, because they will never wish to return to the light of the knowledge and love of God, so also on the final day of the great judgment they shall be cast into outer darkness, where they shall be subject to eternal condemnation and perpetually tormented in unquenchable fire. After the explicit condemnation of proud spirits, the recompense of humble elect persons is mystically indicated when there immediately follows:

“Jesus said to the centurion: Go, and as you have believed, let it be done for you.” These are words of consolation and grace which every elect person who has fought bravely here merits to hear from God at the hour of death. “Go,” he says, as though he said: “Go; leave the instability of this wretched mortality, leave the valley of weeping, [Col. 0121B] and enter the place of exultation and joy. And as you have believed, let it be done for you. Everything that you have hoped for from my mercy you shall possess with me eternally in my eternity.” After this sweet voice of divine invitation, when the blessed person has been removed from the miseries of this life, what follows will be truly and perfectly fulfilled:

“And the servant was healed from that hour.” For from that hour in which every elect person, having laid aside this body of corruption, is taken up into the light of eternal glory, the spirit—which is that person’s servant—will be so established by God in God in a kind of perpetual health that it will never change and never decay. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who became weak for us, bring us to the perpetuity of this health—he who [Col. 0121C] lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

144. HOMILY XVIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY.

“When Jesus had gone up into a little boat, his disciples followed him; and behold, a great commotion arose on the sea” (Matt. 8).

Because the evangelist foresaw that a mystical meaning abounds in every single word of the Gospels, in the present passage he chose to use *navicula*, “little boat,” rather than *navis*, “ship.” By it is understood every humble soul, which in its own eyes considers itself, as it were, small and despised. In accordance with the literal quality of the words, it would seem more suitable to say that Jesus descends into such a soul than that he ascends, since his grace descends from above, from the citadel of the Father, into the human heart. Yet Jesus is fittingly said here to ascend, since he deigns at times to establish various ascents of virtues in a soul made subject to him by good will. When this has taken place, his disciples—that is, the human senses—truly follow him, as, constrained by the discipline of divine fear, they are directed from earthly to heavenly things. The disciples, whose name derives from learning, may rightly be understood as the human senses, because, after the happy stage of ascent just described, one becomes remarkably capable both of understanding and of hearing God’s word—one who previously could neither hear such things fruitfully nor understand them sweetly. But the evangelist immediately recounts what this blessedness brings:

[Col. 0122A] “And behold, a great commotion arose on the sea.” The sea may also be understood as the heart made bitter, not by anger or hatred or any other vices, but made bitter because the sweet bitterness of penitence makes it bitter. For when a truly penitent person calls to mind all his sins, this great commotion arises in his heart, as he is stirred within himself through compunction of heart, not partially but wholly. No one can bring about this happy and great commotion in the human heart except the one great and praiseworthy Lord. In this commotion the little boat is covered by waves, as is said in what follows:

“So that the little boat was covered by waves.” By these flooding waves are denoted the tears of the truly [Col. 0122B] penitent soul, flowing not from a cold but from the most fervent affection of the heart, and received as wholly acceptable in the divine sight. The prophet Jonah recognized that these waves had passed over him when, led to penitence for the guilt of disobedience, he uttered words of this kind: “Your waves passed over me, and I said: ‘I have been cast out from your sight’” (Jonah 2:4). Thus we also, who often incur offence against the Lord by transgressing divine commandments, ought frequently to say these words after the example of that prophet: “Your waves passed over me, and I said: ‘I have been cast out from your sight.’” That is to say: “Over me—that is, over my higher part, namely my soul—your waves, the waves of compunction, passed; and they have now made me recognize, in a manner of speaking, perfectly that I have been cast out from your sight.” [Col. 0122C] For no one can see his own expulsion, indeed his own misery, so rightly and clearly as in that hour of visitation when he merits to have these waves pass over him.

Just as what is covered is not seen, so certainly, although all our sins are naked and open before the divine majesty, [Col. 0122D] when washed by these waves of tears they will be as though unknown and covered before him. Hence David says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31:1). Since we incur original sin not through our own guilt but contract it from the nature of our parents, it is forgiven in baptism through divine grace alone going before, without the exercise of our labour. But when we reach mature age, because, alas, by our own will in serving sins we have made void the vow of baptism, it is right that each of us should strive unceasingly to cover the sins he has committed by his own choice through pure confession and worthy satisfaction, by the labour of his own body. With the balanced measure of just moderation, he should lament them with as much bitterness as he remembers having committed them with the wickedly sweet pleasure of the flesh. Therefore, to one who perseveres in these practices as constantly as possible, the Lord will not impute sin at the end of life. For just as one who falls beneath the material sword for Christ enters heaven free, most certainly cleansed from every stain of sins by blood, so likewise [Col. 0123A] one whose flesh is in this manner crucified with its vices and desires shall without doubt be crowned eternally in heaven, as is fitting, with the splendid glory of martyrs. It follows:

“But he was sleeping.” Whoever labours to persevere vigilantly in the practices we have mentioned, and guards these devout works of labour with profound humility of heart, has the Lord truly deign to sleep—that is, to rest sweetly—in his heart. The Lord himself declares this through his prophet: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). Now, just as the wicked, by adding sin to sin, always become worse, so also the elect, advancing daily from good to better, become better, [Col. 0123B] as is said through John: “Let the one who is filthy become filthier still, and let the one who is holy be sanctified still” (Rev. 22:11). The evangelist therefore rightly now adds these words:

“And they came and awakened him.” Who are the disciples coming to Jesus except, as we noted at the beginning of the reading, our senses, which, after all these things have been numbered, come to Jesus with great constancy of resolve? For just as one withdraws from him through evil desires, so one happily approaches him through good desires. Therefore we ought to approach him through devout and holy desires, indeed through good will, and awaken him through praiseworthy action; we ought to knock by continual prayer, saying: “Lord, save us; we perish.” [Col. 0123C] It is as though we said: “Lord, save us—that is, preserve firmly within us this great commotion, these delightful waves of tears, this most sweet sleep of yours—for we are surrounded by so frail a body and tossed by so unstable a heart that, unless these things are preserved in us by your grace, they will certainly soon perish through our inconstancy.” Or otherwise: “Lord, save us; we perish,” because, even if we have done something good, we know it to be so imperfect that we cannot merit to obtain the salvation of our souls unless we are saved especially through the provision of your mercy.

147. “And he said to them: Why are you fearful, you of little faith?” It is as though he said: “You are fearful because you are of little faith. If you were not of little faith, you would have no need to fear.” Let us now see what little faith is. For we read that the Lord distinguishes in the Gospel a threefold division of faith: the least, the little, and the great. He reproves his disciples, as it were by admonition, for the least faith, when he addresses them in these words: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat, or what shall we drink?’” (Matt. 6:32). But for little faith he rebuked Peter, walking upon the sea but wavering as a strong wind rushed upon him, saying: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:21). He praised great faith in the Canaanite woman, who, for her patient endurance of the Lord’s long refusal, finally merited to hear from him: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (Matt. 15:28).

[Col. 0124A] Secular people are said to have the least faith: to them it seems exceedingly difficult and wholly impossible ever to set aside the customary pleasure of the flesh and undertake the labour of a stricter life for the redemption of their souls. Although in some manner they believe in God, they nevertheless demonstrate completely by their works that they have the least faith, as we have said. But those who undertake the summit of spiritual life are found almost all alike to have the faith of Peter just mentioned—that is, little faith—because, while at the beginning of conversion they resolve with great constancy of mind to endure every adversity patiently, when certain winds of temptation suddenly rush upon them, they begin, just as Peter began to sink while wavering on the sea, to depart from the steadfastness of purpose they had set before their minds. [Col. 0124B] Moreover, if some favour, divine or human, comes to them, their heart immediately and rashly grows proud; and so they become empty through prosperity and lukewarm through adversity, so that in the things of God they remain as though inexperienced and cold, and in matters concerning their neighbour they prove bitter and cruel. Great faith, therefore, is neither to be lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity.

But who are those who hold this great faith, so that they are neither raised up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity? Who is equal to these things? Who is wise enough to keep [them]? This virtue belongs to few. Yet although we who are weak and unstable are in no way equal to these things, there are nevertheless some, with God’s help, who are of such perfection that, by keeping these things, they are neither raised up by prosperity nor broken by adversity. Therefore, whoever [Col. 0124C] is made worthy of such great and exalted blessedness, to that person, insofar as it can be done in this life of corruption, every salvation and every blessing shall without doubt come as he wills, as the author of mercy himself said to the aforesaid Canaanite woman: “Let it be done for you as you wish.” Yet the evangelist clearly intimates that, amid all these things, however great and wonderful, no one can attain perfect salvation in this life. He therefore adds that great and memorable event of the future resurrection, saying:

“Then, rising, he commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm came about.” “Then”—that is, when this time of mortality has passed and ended—the saved will be able powerfully to command the winds and the sea. By the sea [Col. 0124D] we understand our heart; by the winds are understood the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. For in the universal resurrection of the dead, when the elect rise perfectly to eternal life both in soul and body, imperial power is granted to them. Just as it belongs to emperors that what they command by word is immediately accomplished in deed, so these persons will use, according to their desire and with great power of virtue, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which they could never obtain while placed in this life by any labour whatever. When these things have been attained, a truly great tranquillity of mind and body will arise. For although the perfect often have tranquillity with Christ in this world, it cannot at all be called “great,” because the manifold variety of temptations so often interrupts it. But in eternal life [Col. 0125A] there shall be a very great and wondrous tranquillity, where neither bodily frailty nor the perversity of the ancient enemy can do further harm. Hence the evangelist immediately adds:

“Moreover, the people marvelled, saying: What kind of man is this, that he commands the winds and the sea, and they obey him?” Then with great and ineffable amazement of praise they say: “How great and what kind is this one—how sweet, how desirable! While we were still established in mortal flesh, we heard again and again of the greatness of his sweetness, but never such things as we now behold, by his favour, with the eyes of mind and body. The winds and sea obey him”—the sea, namely, our heart; the winds, the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For our heart, filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, will obey him eternally. [Col. 0125B] May Jesus Christ bring us to this true and stable security of life, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY XIX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY.

On the five spiritual ages of the soul.

In the five Sundays which we have celebrated from the time when he who was eternal deigned, for our sake, to become temporal, we may quite fittingly understand five ages: infancy, childhood, adolescence or youth, old age, and decrepit old age. In his Godhead Christ had no age, but eternity. But from the time when he who was eternal [Col. 0125C] descended from his divinity into humanity, or temporality, he began, together with humanity, to have an age, so that he might make us ascend from humanity to the eternity of his divinity. Although he did not reach old age and decrepit old age, he nevertheless appeared in that nature in which it was possible for him to reach those ages. But since each one of us advances bodily through these same five ages, we should like, if God grants it, to relate them to the spiritual ages of the inner person, in which we ought to advance before God, so as to be found worthy of him.

The first age, namely infancy, we may call knowledge of God, which that good thing—the teaching of God—produces in the soul. The second age, namely childhood [Col. 0125D], we may call obedience to God’s commandments, which fear of God brings to perfection. The third age, called adolescence or youth, we call the preaching of the word of God, which that good thing—the love of God and neighbour—brings forth. The fourth age, called old age, is perfect purity of body and heart, generated and produced by the practice of good works. The fifth, namely decrepit old age, we may call complete victory over the world and the glory of heavenly life, which true perfection of life forms and produces in us. To these five praiseworthy and proven ages of the soul we can assign the individual Gospels and offices, in which the mystery and correspondence of the same meaning shines forth.

[Col. 0126A] The first age of the soul is fittingly called, as I think, knowledge of God, because while a person is still ignorant of God and of himself, he is in some sense as though at the age of infancy. But when the teaching of God approaches, knowledge of God also approaches. For unless the good of teaching is added, the gift of knowledge of God and of oneself will likewise remain far away. The office leads us to this understanding: “While all things kept deep silence, and night in its course was halfway through, thy almighty Word, O Lord, came from heaven, from the royal thrones” (Wisdom 18:14). For what is meant by “While all things kept deep silence,” except that, as though in the first age of infancy, a person is in silence while he is in ignorance? And this ignorance continues until the almighty Word comes from the royal thrones. The hearts of good prelates may aptly be called royal thrones [Col. 0126B], since by the almighty Word which comes from heaven their hearts are visited and delivered from their former blindness.

The words of the holy Gospel answer and accord with this: “The father and mother of Jesus were wondering at the things that were being said, and Simeon blessed them.” Simeon can signify a prelate, who blesses when he offers sound and wholesome teaching of exhortation. On hearing it, as it penetrates and rightly enlightens the heart, the chosen soul predestined to life begins greatly to marvel at what is said. Since, as we have said, knowledge of God comes through the teaching of prelates, the Collect rightly and fittingly teaches how prelates ought to pray for the more tender and weaker age of their infants. They pray well indeed, and most excellently, for their infants [Col. 0126C]. For an *infans* (“infant”) is so called as though *non fans* (“not speaking”), because he cannot speak; and therefore, since their infants cannot pray, they ought diligently and continually to implore God the Father for them in these words: “Almighty and everlasting God, direct our actions according to thy good pleasure, that in the name of thy beloved Son we may deserve to abound in good works.”

This is as though they said to God the Father: “O Lord, who hast taken us up and chosen us for this purpose, that we might provide for our infants—that is, for those subject to us—direct our actions according to thy good pleasure, so that our actions may please thee alone and not human beings, in order that, in the name of thy beloved Son, we and those subject to us may deserve to abound in good works: we by teaching them for thy sake, they by hearing us for thy love, and by obeying us.”

[Col. 0126D] After this first age of the soul follows the second age of the soul, which we have called obedience to God’s commandments. Fear of God effects and begins this second age. For, instructed and formed by the teaching of God, a person receives the gift of fear, through which he begins to fear God, to guard against the punishments of Gehenna, and to consider and dread the hour of death. From this praiseworthy fear there consequently arises vigilant obedience to God’s commandments. The Gospel can fittingly be assigned to this age: “When Jesus was twelve years old.” There it is said of him who became for us a pattern and mirror of life that “he went down with them and was subject to them.” To whom? Certainly to his parents, to whom, while still a child, he did not refuse to be subject and obedient.

The office of the Mass looks to this meaning, where the one [Col. 0127A] who passes from fear of God to obedience to God’s commandments sings and says: “I saw a man seated upon a lofty throne, whom a multitude of angels worship, singing together: Behold, the name of whose dominion is everlasting.” It belongs to children always to fear their teacher, as though they saw him seated on a lofty throne. By this comparison, therefore, every chosen person ought always to stand in awe of and fear his Lord and Teacher for the sake of obedience to the commandments of God. “Whom a multitude of angels worship”—that is, whom a multitude of good subjects reverence—“singing together,” namely praying in unanimous concord, that he may so hold the authority of his present rule that at some time the name of his dominion may remain for ever.

The Collect looks to this [Col. 0127B] age when, after they have received knowledge and obedience to God’s commandments, which arises from fear of God, prelates entrust to the Lord God not merely their infants but their children, ready to obey God’s commandments, saying in their Collect: “We beseech thee, O Lord, continue thy heavenly gift to the vows of thy suppliant people, that they may both see what ought to be done and be strengthened to fulfil what they have seen.” It is as though they said to the Lord: “O Lord, since our children now offer their vows to thee, graciously attend them as they supplicate thee with thy heavenly gift, that they may see what must be done—that is, that they may know thy commandments—and that, faithfully and eagerly obeying thee, they may strive to fulfil and accomplish those same things which they have known.”

After these two ages follows the third age, namely adolescence [Col. 0127C] or youth, which we have called the preaching of God’s word. That virtue which is love of God and neighbour fittingly and beautifully effects and works this age in the soul. For whoever has knowledge of God and obedience to God’s commandments fittingly tends toward the third age, adolescence or youth; for just as in adolescence a person is fit for marriage, so, having passed through these two ages, a person is suited to receive the dispensation of God’s word. Once he has received this preaching of God’s word, it is necessary that the virtue of love of God and neighbour accompany him. For if the preaching of God’s word bears and produces any fruit in those subject to him, it is fitting that the love of God alone should establish and perfect that fruit; because in preaching God’s word [Col. 0127D] a prelate ought to seek or desire nothing except the love of God alone and the edification and salvation of those subject to him.

Therefore, because in youth and adolescence a person is suited to marriage, the Gospel, “A wedding took place at Cana in Galilee,” which treats of a wedding, can suitably be assigned to this age. In spiritual marriage, which is signified through bodily marriage, the spiritual bridegroom is the prelate, while his bride is the congregation committed to him, which Christ betrothed to him and gave a pledge through the preaching of God’s word. Since it is most fitting and most necessary that constant peace and continual love should endure between prelate and subject, we fittingly say in the Collect: “Almighty and everlasting God, who governest both heavenly [Col. 0128A] and earthly things, mercifully hear the prayers of thy people, and grant thy peace in our times.” What are the heavenly and earthly things which almighty God governs? The heavenly things are, I think, prelates; the earthly, those subject to them. Or the heavenly things are those exalted and heavenly words of preachers; the earthly things are the good works which arise and are born in the hearts of subjects through the heavenly words of prelates. We therefore ask that he who governs heavenly and earthly things may grant his peace in our times: that is, that he may make peace and concord between prelate and subjects. For even if something else should arise between them, it will be corrected sooner and, with God’s help, turned aside sooner, provided only that peace and continual love are maintained between them.

Nor does the Mass office disagree with this meaning: “Let all the earth worship thee, O God, and sing to thee; let it sing a psalm to thy name, O Lord.” “All the earth” means every prelate and subject, who, each worshipping God, shall declare glory and give praise to thy most high name. And what is meant by the addition in the Gradual, “The Lord sent his word and healed them,” except that the Lord sends his word when he opens the mouths of preachers, through words of exhortation, to heal the hearts of subjects? Once that word has been sent, the verse fittingly follows: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wondrous works to the children of men.” For what is it to confess to the Lord except, after words of preaching have been uttered, to perform good and praiseworthy deeds?

[Col. 0128C] The fourth age, called old age, follows these three ages. Through it is understood that beautiful and praiseworthy age of the soul which is perfect purity of body and heart. That beautiful and praiseworthy age of the soul is produced and perfected by the virtue which is the practice of good works. This purity of body and heart is mystically denoted in the following Gospel, “When Jesus came down from the mountain,” where the leper is cleansed and the paralytic healed. Bodily impurity is not unjustly compared with the impurity of leprosy. A person is delivered from it when, in body, he is cleansed from evil works, and, in heart, he is healed from harmful, vain, and superfluous thoughts—which is paralysis. Therefore, that we may be delivered from this twofold infirmity of heart and body and, through the practice of good works, may attain perfect purity of body and heart, we implore the help of heavenly assistance [Col. 0128D], saying: “Almighty and everlasting God, look graciously upon our weakness, and stretch out the right hand of thy majesty to protect us.” We quite worthily ask almighty God to look upon our weakness, because the infirmity of this leprosy—that is, the impurity of evil works—and paralysis—that is, the superfluity of harmful thoughts—are never driven away from us unless he looks graciously upon us and stretches out the right hand of his majesty to protect us from them.

When this fourth age has happily been passed through, the fifth age, namely decrepit old age, is set forth. Through this age may be understood the age of the soul which we have called complete victory over the world and entrance into heavenly life. [Col. 0129A] Perfection of life effects and perfects this praiseworthy age; and in this age every disturbance is stilled: the Lord rises, commands the winds and sea, and there is a great calm. Finally, in the death of the blessed, all the movements of vices are stilled; the contrary winds of temptations are driven away by the Lord’s rising and command; and whoever has advanced through these ages of the soul in the order we have described will receive, after this life, complete victory over the world and will possess glory in heaven for ever.

And because the hour of death is terrible and to be feared, when a hard conflict must be endured with malignant enemies, the Collect sounds quite terrifying, in which, in order that we may be freed from the terror and deceits of unclean [Col. 0129B] spirits, we pray thus: “O God, who knowest that, placed amid such great dangers, we cannot stand by reason of human frailty, grant us health of mind and body, that, with thy help, we may overcome the things which we suffer for our sins.” We pray, finally, that the punishment and bitterness of fear impending then at death may become the cause of our purification, so that, tested and purified through the imminent fear of death, we may arrive free and secure at the vision of heavenly peace. It is as though we said: “O Lord, because thou knowest that, placed amid such great dangers, we cannot stand by reason of human frailty, thou who art supremely good, grant us health of mind and body, that, with thy help, we may so overcome the things we suffer for our sins that we may deserve entrance into heavenly life.”

Therefore, since all the elect, at the end of death and after departing this life, when the movements of vices have been stilled and the winds of temptation calmed, must receive complete victory over the world and possess everlasting glory in heaven, the rejoicing of the angels at the reward of the elect is well and fittingly denoted throughout the excellence of today’s office. In the Introit it is sung: “Worship God, all his angels; Zion heard and rejoiced, and the daughters of Judah exulted.” For our redemption is the worship and rejoicing of angels. They praise and worship God not only because of their own confirmation, by which God the Father established and strengthened them so that they could not sin; rather, they worship and glorify God more sweetly and devotedly, in a sense, because they have received us as their fellow citizens and see that we have arrived at the same glory which they possess.

[Col. 0129D] What then will the multitude of the elect do in this worship and rejoicing of the angels? It follows: “Zion heard and rejoiced.” On hearing the wonderful exultation and praise of the angels concerning their salvation and redemption, that holy Zion—that is, the multitude of saints who behold God—rejoices and shares their joy. The daughters of Judah also will exult there: I mean all those who now, through a good confession of faith, have made themselves near to God in this world.

But it should be noted why this office is sung for two Gospels. First, for that in which, as Jesus comes down from the mountain, the leper is cleansed and the centurion’s servant healed; then again for that in which he enters the boat and a great [Col. 0130A] storm arises on the sea, where at last he rises, commands the winds and the sea, and there is a great calm. It seems to me that, since we have said that the fourth Sunday pertains to the fourth age of the soul, namely perfect purity of body and heart, the person who has arrived at perfect purity of body and heart sings there in hope what he has not yet received in actuality. For we must always hold in hope what we shall one day receive in actuality. If we do not first possess it in hope, we shall never receive it in actuality.

Thus, in the fourth age of the soul, namely perfect purity of body and heart, we now sing this office in hope; but when the fifth age of the soul, namely complete victory over the world and the glory of heavenly life, has come, then we shall truly sing this Mass in actuality, because what we now hold in hope will be received [Col. 0130B] in actuality. What glory will then belong to sinful but converted prelates and subjects is proclaimed by the words of the Gradual after the Introit: “The nations shall fear thy name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth thy glory.” By kings may be understood prelates; by nations, subjects; or by nations, sinners who once lived as Gentiles and were saved through repentance; and by kings, those who knew how to rule themselves well in this world. All these will fear the Lord’s name in the glory of heavenly life, not with servile fear but with the fear of filial love.

And because in this present life the Lord has built Zion—that is, the multitude of saints—through the preaching of his word and the practice of holy virtues, the verse fittingly follows: “For the Lord has built Zion, and he shall be seen in his majesty,” because there he shall be seen in his majesty by all. There will be praise and jubilation there for everlasting ages, as the following Alleluia indicates: “Praise God,” it says, “all his angels; praise him, all his powers.” For his angels praise him, and his powers also praise him: namely, the holy souls of the elect, who deserved to become partakers of such great blessedness not by their own power but by his power alone.

[Col. 0130C] As they behold their glory, what, I ask, will those heavenly ranks of angels do except what the following words of the Offertory contain? “The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me: I shall not die, but live, and shall declare [Col. 0130D] the works of the Lord.” Beholding the works of the saints, they extol with praises the Lord God, author both of merit and giver of reward; and to him who has wrought strength they ascribe everything, saying, “The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength.” But that blessed multitude of saints, thinking humbly of itself, replies as it were to its fellow citizens, as follows: “The right hand of the Lord has exalted me.” It is as though they said: “It was not the magnificence of our work that raised us to such distinctions of honour and glory; the right hand of almighty God alone exalted us. It supplied all that was great in what we did and all that was worthy in the reward we received; and therefore, living through the ages, we shall declare not our own works but his.”

In all these things, in this excellence of divine fear [Col. 0131A], the following words of the Communion will truly be fulfilled: “All marvelled at the things which proceeded from the mouth of God.” What are the things that proceed there from God’s mouth? They are wonderful, sweet, and ineffable. When that sweet voice proceeds from his mouth—“Come,” he says, “blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you by my Father”—will they not marvel? They will indeed marvel, because they will receive greater things and behold more excellent things than were announced to them here through sacred utterances. They also marvel then at the things proceeding from God’s mouth when, introduced into all the fullness of the knowledge of God, they deserve to hear from God’s mouth secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak. Then, when the five ages of the soul have been well passed through and completed, they ascend from humanity to the eternity of divinity. May he who lives and reigns through endless ages of ages bring us to these goods. Amen.

## HOMILY XX. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY OF SEPTUAGESIMA

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20).

In this Gospel reading the eternal wisdom of God distinguishes three orders of those called: the first is that of the innocent, the last that of penitents, and the middle that of the obedient. But let us see from the beginning of this present reading how the first calling, that of the innocent, occurs.

“The kingdom of heaven,” says the evangelist, “is like a householder.” By the name “kingdom of heaven” we may here understand any faithful soul [Col. 0131C], which that supreme householder—God, who is both God and man—makes in some sense like himself when he begins invisibly to work in it the things that follow.

“He went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard,” says the evangelist. By “early morning” we may understand a person’s infancy or childhood. Thus the Lord is said to go out as though early in the morning when, in the very years of childhood, he gathers to himself and into his vineyard a person taken away from this world, lest that person be defiled by worldly conduct, but so that, in the spiritual life signified by the vineyard, he may adhere to and serve the innocent God innocently and simply.

But one must note what it is to hire labourers for the vineyard. Almighty majesty, to whom neither the will nor the power to save sinners is lacking, wishes that the very person whom he saves should be his fellow worker in being saved [Col. 0131D]. This is not because he cannot by himself accomplish what he wills, but so that he may reward more gloriously the merit of one who cooperates with him by free choice. Therefore this hiring belongs jointly to God and to the human being. It belongs to him mercifully to anticipate us; it belongs to us devoutly to obey him who anticipates us.

But since those who are called early in the morning—that is, infants and children—do not know how to cooperate with God through this voluntary devotion, because their childish age hinders them, but all that is done with them is done as though they neither knew nor willed it, the following words rightly apply to them:

“Having made an agreement for a denarius a day, he sent them into the vineyard.” There is, then, from the beginning a certain separation between God [Col. 0132A] and the human being on account of original sin. Because of this, every person is separated from his Creator until he deserves to be regenerated through the Holy Spirit in baptism. There, when the original guilt has been removed, a true and intimate agreement is made between God and the human being concerning the daily denarius. In the denarius, upon which the image of the king is impressed, is fittingly expressed the image of God recovered through innocence. It can quite worthily and rightly be called a daily denarius, because, as long as a person is in sins, he is said to dwell as though in the darkness of night. But when, in baptism, he has cast off the night of sins and has received this daily denarius of which we have spoken—when, I say, he has returned through innocence to the true image of God—he is said to remain as though in daylight: in such a day as that from which every good thing and every element of eternal salvation is begun and perfected.

This is truly that pleasant and desirable agreement of God and humankind. Once it has been made, they are immediately sent into the Lord’s vineyard, when either, through the faith they professed in baptism, they are incorporated into holy Church, or when, still in childhood, they are introduced through their parents’ hands into a place of holy and spiritual life, there to serve the Lord for ever. But having set forth the first order of those called, namely the innocent, let us also see how the calling of those whom we have called obedient immediately follows.

“And he went out about the third hour.” In the third hour a person’s adolescence is to be understood. Because it is always inclined toward evil, it has every need of this going out by the Lord. For the following sequence of words declares what fruit of grace [Col. 0132C] and salvation all who are saved receive from this second going out of his: “He saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them.” God’s seeing is God’s having mercy; his speaking is his calling. He sees them and, seeing them, has mercy, because he perceives that they have become other than he made them through the sacraments of baptism. He also sees them standing idle in the marketplace, namely idle from every good work. For by the marketplace, in which things pleasing to the flesh are bought, carnal desires are fittingly expressed. But because, according to the testimony of Scripture, “every idle person is in desires” (Prov. 21:25), those who are called about the third hour are rightly said to be standing in the marketplace, because, with the neck of their heart raised proudly against God, they neither wish nor know how to humble themselves beneath his mighty hand.

Yet the pious and merciful Lord by no means passes them by as though despising them; rather, those whom he deigns to see with the hidden eye of his mercy, he also calls through the grace of his inward inspiration: “Go,” he says, “you also into my vineyard.” But because it is exceedingly hard and difficult for a person to despise his flesh and its pleasures and to submit himself in heart and body to divine service, he deigned to soften the labour to come through the promise of a subsequent reward. “Whatever is just,” he says, “I will give you.” It is as though he said: “If you come willingly, if with voluntary devotion of heart you obey him who calls, I will give you what is just.”

But what is this justice which eternal Truth promises to give to these middle ones, namely the obedient, when in the first and last calling he added nothing about the justice of the reward to follow?
