Those who are called into the vineyard of spiritual life early in the morning and at the eleventh hour are saved, in a sense, not by any justice of their own but as though by God’s goodness and mercy alone. The first, namely the innocent, entered the Lord’s vineyard not by the choice of their own will but at the command of their parents; while the last, persisting in sins almost to decrepit old age, finally ceased from sinning only when they were no longer able to sin. Therefore what is given to these two by mercy is given, in a sense, to the middle group by justice. For their justice before the Most High is voluntary confession of sins. Since the Lord seeks and loves this spontaneous decision of free will above all things in his labourer, he rightly added to their calling these glad words of promise: “Whatever is just, I will give you.” It is as though he said: “My justice—indeed yours as well—requires this: that you who have voluntarily left the sweet joys of this present life in comparison with the sweetness of me, should be raised by my consolation in the present and should eternally be glorified with me in the future.”

Thus, yes, thus, when that heavenly householder inwardly addresses a person with the invisible language of his inspiration, there wonderfully comes about what is said next: “But they went away.” They go away when they pass from bodily to spiritual life, beginning joyfully, in heart and body, to work for God alone in a holy manner of life.

“And again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour [Col. 0133C], and did likewise.” By this going out of the Lord at about the sixth and ninth hour is signified that praiseworthy and saving departure from sins which the same merciful Lord mercifully effects in persons still of more advanced age—namely youth and old age—which we understand through the sixth and ninth hours. Although the evangelist does not state in what words or in what place this calling occurred, nevertheless, from his assertion that he did likewise, there is no doubt that he found these people, like the former ones, standing in the marketplace. This may quite fittingly be referred to those who are called into the Lord’s vineyard in youth or old age, since they too undoubtedly appear spiritually to be standing in the same marketplace.

Their standing in the marketplace is to be troubled by that same marketplace-noise of carnal desires, which seems to assail people, whether unwilling or willing, continuously from adolescence itself until decrepit old age. Yet those who freely leave this same marketplace, whether in youth or in old age, will not be deprived by the pious and merciful Lord of the same grace of reward which he promises the earlier workers. There are, however, some who do not obey the voice of the calling Lord even in old age, but add sins to sins with so much the greater confidence as, by living wickedly for longer, they have proved useless both to God and themselves. Yet the kindly lover of humankind does not permit very many of these to perish; but, as though desiring even their labour in his vineyard, he calls them, in order that through this he may find an occasion to save them. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0134A] “About the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing, and said to them: Why are you standing here idle all day?” By the eleventh hour, in which decrepit old age is understood, are not unfittingly expressed those who have committed grave crimes liable to death and, through evil habit, have become as though decrepit in them and lost all manly strength of mind. But then, as though at the eleventh hour, the Lord mercifully goes out when, to those who have grown old in sins in the manner described, he grants through the grace of his hidden mercy that, recognizing themselves and finally putting an end to vices and desires, they may happily go out from them and, abandoning deadly idleness, may not delay to return, through the humble satisfaction of repentance, to him from whom they had departed by standing—that is, by living proudly.

Therefore, as soon as the Lord has gone out in them in this way and they have gone out in the Lord, they can profitably hear the words of the Lord’s subsequent rebuke: “Why are you standing here idle all day?” God says this, as it were, to a person at the moment when the person himself, touched inwardly by sorrow through the grace of God breathing upon him, begins to review all his days and years in the bitterness of his soul. For then he truly and repeatedly presses these same words upon the ears of the eternal Judge with the groaning voice of his heart: “Why are you standing here idle all day?” It is as though, humbly confessing to the Lord alone, he said: “I confess, Lord, and do not deny, that I, wretched man, with every one of my faculties, have stood here all day—that is, throughout the whole time of my life—wickedly exalting myself against thee.”

[Col. 0134C] For “here” is put as though for the present, and consequently in this same word delight in present things is not unfittingly understood. And what else do true penitents mourn and bewail except that they have stood here idle all day, that in all their actions they have sought temporal rather than future joys? “It is true,” they say, “true, Lord, that, given until now to the deadly idleness of bodily pleasures, we have taken no care to render to thee, our Creator, the service we owe. But whence, merciful Lord, whence came to us such unheard-of delight in bodily enticement? Certainly because no one hired us. No one, I say—that is, no human being hired us—because it was not the weakness of human flesh but the incomparable malignity of our proud heart that led us to so many and such great wicked acts [Col. 0134D]. For we did not fall through human sin, but were seduced by diabolical pride. For it was human to have sinned; it is diabolical to have persevered in sins until now.”

Thus, while they stand in this way, while they continually recount their miseries in the ears of eternal mercy, at last the Lord’s voice says inwardly to them:

“Go also into the vineyard.” He commands them to go into the vineyard when he inspires in them so perfect a renunciation of carnal desires that they regard it as a crime if they should ever return to them even in thought. But why is it that these last, of whom we have now spoken, are called to cultivate the Lord’s vineyard and yet no reward is stated for the labour to be expended there? Nothing, I think, is more truly suggested to us by this than what is still invisibly occurring in the hearts of those who are truly humble and humbly repentant. Although they labour in every way they can to reconcile divine clemency to themselves, they nevertheless give no thought to the future reward of their labours, considering it a great thing if, by God’s mercy, they can finally escape the penal torments of hell.

Such, then, is the last order of those called: namely, the order of penitents. Joined with the two orders already mentioned—the innocent and the obedient—it can worthily be called the chosen vineyard of the Lord of hosts, in which sweet cups of divine wine are mingled daily, seeming sweet and delightful in draught to the heavenly householder. Nevertheless, the following words of the holy Gospel clearly declare that no vineyard of God, no congregation of righteous persons, is found so chosen and perfect that it does not sometimes suffer morning and sometimes even evening:

[Col. 0135B] “When evening came, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: Call the labourers.” The elect of God have morning as long as they remain unshaken in the spiritual light of fervour through the practice of righteousness. But that sweet morning turns, as it were, into evening when the shadow of temptation follows the light of rectitude. Moses indicates these alternations of varied change when he says: “And evening came, and morning came: one day” (Gen. 1:5). The whole human condition groans under the loss caused by this mutability until that supreme morning rises, in which, when every shadow of mortality has been banished, the Psalmist glories that he will behold the author of light himself: “In the morning,” he says, “I will stand before thee and will see” (Ps. 5:4).

Yet meanwhile, while that morning is delayed, the merciful Lord does not so leave his own in the gloom of this mortality that he does not often illuminate and comfort them with the light of his sevenfold Spirit. He himself is the steward of the Lord’s vineyard; he himself is the one by whose inspiration the labourers working in it are called by the Lord, and by whose fire, once the evening of sins has been driven away, they who are already wearied are sweetly refreshed inwardly.

We may also understand by this same steward of the Lord, mentioned above, any good preacher appointed over the Lord’s vineyard. Through him the Lord commands his labourers to be called—that is, to be diligently exhorted by the continual word of his preaching to earnestness in God’s work. “Call,” he says, “the labourers, and pay them their wages.” It is as though he said: “Do you see the burning sun of righteousness setting in the hearts of those subject to you? Do you see them falling from the fervour of divine love into the shadow of inward cold?

[Col. 0135D] “But call them; cry out, I say, and do not cease, so that, awakened by the constant cry of your preaching and exhortation, they may grow warm again inwardly and, at your call, may burn with their accustomed zeal to seek their wage—namely, the grace of my sweetness—which they have lost.” For by saying, “Pay them their wages,” he clearly shows that they once possessed this same wage but have ceased to possess it through the torpor of creeping negligence.

In what manner, then, or in what order the calling just described ought to be made to the hearts of those subject to him, the same Lord of the vineyard indicates to his beloved steward in the following words: “Beginning from the last even to the first.” Certainly the steward of the Lord’s flock ought to begin with the last—that is, with sins. He ought, I say, first to rebuke firmly the sins and vices of the persons subject to him; and then, ascending even to the first—that is, to exhortation to the virtues—he should unceasingly urge them toward the constancy of divine fervour which they have lost. For by such an ordering of the words of his teaching, under God’s direction, that spiritual reward will at length be paid to the cultivators of the Lord’s vineyard which seems to be signified spiritually in what follows. [Col. 0136B]

“But when they came,” says the Evangelist, “who had come about the eleventh hour.” A person comes when he finds himself. And rightly those who came about the eleventh hour—that is, the humble and penitent—are said as it were then to come, when, intent in heart and body upon heavenly teachings, they inwardly find themselves by rightly knowing themselves from the word of God which they hear. Thus, having been found by themselves within themselves, when they perceive that they possess nothing but sins, through the coming of divine mercy they receive each the denarii of whom the Evangelist speaks. “And they received,” he says, “individual denarii.”

But why is it said, “They received individual denarii,” when, according to common usage, it might more suitably be said: “They each received a denarius”? To receive individual denarii, then, is to recognize individual sins, to do penance for individual sins, and through true repentance to return to true innocence—which is the image of God.

“But when the first came, they thought that they would receive more.” The first likewise—that is, the innocent—when they see converted sinners receiving so great a grace of compunction from hearing the word of God, they too come, believing that they will receive more than they. This “more,” which those first persons believe they will receive from the honey-sweet teaching of the preacher, is the most sweet compunction of love; compared with it, the laborious compunction of fear is far less and far inferior. For they are always desiring, always looking out for this: that amid words of exhortation they may deserve to hear something concerning heavenly things by which their minds may burn more powerfully with love of heavenly joys, and the present world and its desire may wither more and more in their hearts. [Col. 0136D]

Yet it often happens that, while they desire to receive the upper watering, they can scarcely obtain even the lowest watering below. For while they wish to be watered by that desirable compunction which flows solely from longing for things above, they scarcely at times find tears with which to bewail their daily transgressions. Hence it follows: “And they too received individual denarii.” They indeed receive individual denarii just as the last do, when, recognizing each of their negligences, they finally burst into tears; and they become so much the humbler as they see themselves the weaker in attaining what they desire. [Col. 0137A] Hence it follows:

“And, receiving, they murmured against the householder, saying: ‘These last have worked one hour, and thou hast made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.’” That is called murmuring when a person suffers some trouble or indignation in the secrecy of his heart which he does not dare, or is unable, to utter in open words. And rightly by such murmuring is understood that hidden pain of heart by which these first persons, after recognizing the steadfast constancy of the penitent in the fear of God, are inwardly afflicted and tormented—not because they envy them the mercy divinely bestowed, but because, on account of the guilt of their own sluggishness and negligence, they see themselves deprived of the taste of inward sweetness. “These last,” they say, “have worked one hour, and thou hast made them equal to us?” Thou hast made them equal to us, Lord, in gifts. For what we possess through innocence, they have obtained, as it were in the moment of a single hour, through humble repentance, granted by thee. And thou hast judged our case and theirs justly, Lord. For they are last: new, indeed, through repentance; last, moreover, through humility. But we are those “who have borne the burden of the day and the heat,” because we have been neither humble in prosperity nor patient in adversity. For whether prosperity smiled upon us or adversity threatened, the whole burden of our souls was heavy, because it wretchedly weighed them down lest they should be raised to thee.

“And he answered one of them and said: ‘Friend, I do thee no wrong. Didst thou not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is thine and go.’” All who seek heavenly converse, so long as they are many and manifold through thinking many things, do not receive the one thing which they seek from the depths of their heart: the word of the Godhead. But if all their intention is made one with the Lord, then the Creator’s word gently addresses their one spirit: “Friend,” saying, “I do thee no wrong.” Friend, whom I know so well by the familiar constancy of thy service, whom I have found so tested by integrity of life and conduct, that the judgment both of my justice and of my mercy requires me to honour thee with the name of friend: I do thee no wrong, nor do I withhold anything from those things due to thee. For I, whose works are all faithful, shall not deprive thee—whose friendship has greatly pleased me—of the denarius for which thou didst agree with me; because I shall mercifully grant the gift of the compunction thou seekest, now as is expedient, and at times as thy desire asks.

But if thou desirest to become richer in the gift, as one who hast been more devoted in service, “take what is thine and go.” As if he said: Whatever thou art able to do, whether in virtues of the mind or virtuous works of the body, is not thine but mine. For from me thou hast whatever thou hast. But if thou hast mingled something of thine with that which is mine—that is, if, from that which my grace has wrought in thee, thou hast attributed something to thine own powers or to thine own praise—take what is thine, leave what is mine; remove utterly from thyself whatever the desire for vain glory has introduced through pride. What thou hast from me, humbly attribute to me alone; and go, advancing from virtue to virtue, progressing from good things to better, so that he who is the fountain of purity and the summit of incorruption, having now made thee conformed to himself in all things, may judge that none of his sweetness ought to be withheld from thee. [Col. 0138A]

“But I will give to this last one also as to thee. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I will? Is thine eye evil because I am good?” I will, I say, bestow upon this last and humble one the same benefit of mercy, the same grace of inward visitation, as upon thee. For I am rich and abundant, since I fill heaven and earth. And all that I will, I am permitted to do, because power is at hand whenever I will it. But the weak eye of thy mortality cannot fully search out how inestimable are the treasures of my goodness: that I, who am accustomed to give good things to the just according to the merit of their justice, should choose to grant the same things to those less worthy solely through the obligation of my compassion. Here the “evil eye” is to be understood not as wicked or double-minded, but rather as weak: unable to foresee the counsels of the Most High or to comprehend them by reason. For the gracious majesty of the Creator does not accuse of malice or duplicity one whom he has truly decreed to honour with the name of friend. It follows:

“So shall the last be first, and the first last.” Truly, when they behold the merits of the first, the last become first, since they strive to imitate, according to their ability, those whose innocence they revere; and in their reflection they stretch themselves to every work of truth even beyond the powers of the others. [Col. 0138C] Likewise the first, beholding the last, become lowest and most humble, since they wisely consider with what weight the Godhead values even the small offering which the humility of the last brings from their labours, and how much more precious in these persons is the devotion of humility in proportion as the exercise of pious labour is more abundant. By this mutual consideration, by this reciprocal imitation, the last shall be first and the first last; thus in both parties the accumulation of perfection increases.

But what is said at the conclusion of this parable is very terrible: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” There are indeed many who, renouncing the affairs of the world, become last—that is, most humble through contrition of spirit; and there are still more who, living in a good resolve, seem first through their approved conduct. Such persons are very numerous and many among the called. But those who rise to this merit of election, so as to appear perfect in both respects at once—namely, that those whom fervour of purpose has made first may also be made last by profound humility of heart, or that those whom a conscience mindful of sin has made last may be made first by an ever-increasing abundance of good works—such elect persons are few and rare. [Col. 0138D]

But since it is most certain that every best thing in the treasures of glory and immortality is given to the elect, let us make provision with every endeavour that the lot of recompense may one day receive us into the number of the elect. And let us take care, through earnestness in good work, to be joined to the merits of the first; while through the pursuit of inward humility we strive especially to become conformed also to the last. May he deign to grant this, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0139A]

## HOMILY XXI. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE SAME SUNDAY

“The kingdom of heaven is like a man who is a householder, who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20).

This man, the householder, is God the Son of God, the man Christ Jesus, who is rightly called the Householder because he is the Father of many households: namely, of all those who worthily serve him. Therefore the kingdom of heaven—that is, the holy Church, or any congregation of those who live devoutly, or each faithful soul—is fittingly said to be like him. For all who receive the fruit of salvation must be made like this man, the Householder, so that they may strive to conform themselves, according to their measure, to the holiness of his conduct by imitating it—a conduct in which is the true and perfect pattern of all virtues. Blessed John the Apostle aptly admonishes this when he says: “He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). [Col. 0139B]

“Who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard.” Our Redeemer indeed went out when, proceeding from his hidden divinity in order that he might be seen by human beings, he was born as visible man from the blessed and virginal flesh of the blessed and undefiled Virgin Mary.

[Col. 0139C] And note that it says, “Early in the morning.” For just as, when morning rises, darkness departs and light begins to draw near, so at Christ’s birth the whole world, which before his coming had been in the darkness of ignorance and the darkness of sins, was illuminated by the light of the newly born Saviour. For at Christ’s birth that joyful morning began to dawn in which the new star appeared to the world, drawing from the distant ends of the earth those Magi, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, to faith in him.

He therefore went out to hire labourers for his vineyard. He hired labourers because by both the word of truth and the example of holy and religious conduct he revealed the truth of God to those ignorant of it and unacknowledging of the good. If he had merely preached, he would indeed have led them, not hired them. But because he showed by example what he taught in word, the Evangelist quite fittingly declares that he hired labourers for the vineyard:

“Having made an agreement with the labourers for a daily denarius, he sent them into his vineyard.” Where or when was this agreement made? In the cross and passion of Christ. For there was great disagreement and separation between God and man because of original sin. But when he, the Mediator between God and men, ascended the cross and by the passion of his death wiped out original sin with his blood, there the true agreement between God and man was made by means of the daily denarius. The daily denarius was that man whom he assumed from the Blessed Virgin Mary: a true denarius, I say, because in him was the true likeness of God the Father, which no ignorance and no stain of sin had ever darkened. [Col. 0140A] He was fittingly compared to a denarius because, just as in former times the image of the king was stamped upon a denarius, so that noble and spotless man, the son of an incorrupt mother, had in himself the true image of the true and highest King, God the Father. For our first father Adam and our first mother Eve, both made in the image of God, could be called denarii; but because by sinning they had violated that same image of God in themselves, neither of them was a daily denarius, but each was in some manner a nocturnal one. Once this agreement had been made, as we have said, through the daily denarius, he sent them into his vineyard; for just as Eve was fashioned in paradise from the side of the sleeping Adam, so the Church was fashioned from the side of Christ sleeping upon the cross. [Col. 0140B]

It may also be understood otherwise when it says, “He sent them into his vineyard.” For when the same most glorious conqueror of death descended to hell and rescued his elect from the infernal prisons, he sent them into his vineyard—that is, after the long ages of hell, he led them back to the eternal joys of his paradise. It follows:

“And he went out about the third hour.” What was that going out? This going out took place at the third hour, at which hour also the Holy Spirit came upon the Apostles. After the surpassing grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out upon the children of adoption, let us hear what fruit of human salvation immediately followed: “He saw others standing idle in the marketplace.” By these other labourers we may understand the Gentiles, who indeed stood as it were in the marketplace because they had raised the neck of their proud mind against God; devoted to the life of the marketplace—that is, to carnal desires—they knew and sought only earthly things, and thus, being sluggish in every good work, neglected to labour for their salvation. The almighty God undoubtedly saw them when he began to have mercy on them; for God’s seeing is his having mercy. [Col. 0140C]

Yet we nowhere read that our Redeemer, appearing in the flesh and living and teaching only among the Jews, ever preached to the Gentiles or conferred upon them any grace of his kindness, except upon the centurion’s servant, whom he restored to health, and the daughter of the Canaanite woman, whom he freed when she was afflicted by a demon. He also commanded his disciples: “Do not go,” he said, “into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10:5). But when the Holy Spirit had been sent, he spoke through the mouths of the Apostles to all the nations scattered throughout the whole world. For, instructed by that same Holy Spirit, they knew and were able to speak in every language, and “their sound went forth into all the earth.” This is plainly indicated by the words of the Gospel when it adds:

“And he said to them: ‘Go you also into my vineyard, and what is just I will give you.’” As if he openly said: Enter my Church through the right faith, and I will give you what is just. It is just before God to repay the righteous according to their righteousness and, after the end of life, to reward those who live rightly in this world and persevere in goodness with the rewards of the heavenly kingdom. This justice of God had been far removed from the ancient Fathers because of Adam’s transgression. For to Abel the righteous man, innocently slain because of him; to Noah, who had served him in the ark amid many dangers; to Abraham, who in obedience to his command had left his land and kindred; and to the other holy Fathers who faithfully served him—he gave not what was just, that is, the kingdom of heaven, but, after their perfect righteousness, he denied them the honour of the kingdom and gave them hell. [Col. 0141A]

But to the Gentiles who were to be converted he says, “What is just I will give you.” This is as though he said: My justice—that is, the glory of my kingdom—I never gave before my passion; it is this that I have resolved to give to you Gentiles. Hence also, after his resurrection, sending his disciples to teach all nations, he said: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). The holy reading continues:

“But they went away.” In this passage it is plainly shown how devoutly the Gentiles, obedient to faith, abandoning the error of idolatry, were converted to the Lord through the saving teaching of the Apostles. Therefore after this going out, which took place through the coming of the Holy Spirit, it immediately adds:

“And again he went out about the sixth and ninth hour, and did likewise.” By the sixth hour we may fittingly understand the time of the martyrs, which came after the times of the Apostles. Nor is it unfitting that this hour should designate the times of the martyrs labouring in the contest of suffering. For the heat and fervour of the sun are usually stronger at the sixth hour than at the other hours of the day. [Note: [Col. 0141D] This is our present twelfth hour, or noon.] [Col. 0141C] So indeed the most glorious martyrs of both sexes were, one might almost say, more fervent in love for God than nearly all Christ’s elect. For, tried by diverse kinds of torture, while they were beaten with exceedingly harsh scourges, flayed alive, and even burned by flames applied to them, they could never have endured with equanimity the fire burning them outwardly unless they had inwardly burned with the most ardent fire of divine love.

At the ninth hour, however, when the sun still shines clearly but inclines toward setting, we may understand mystically the times of the confessors. When the fury of persecution had now ceased, these most holy confessors lived a quiet life in the peace of the Church; but, despising present things, they proclaimed the eternal homeland by word and conduct. Being found worthy of God in all things, they were in their own days great lights of this world through holy instruction and examples of good works. Thus it may rightly be said of that same householder, who worked in them and through them: “And he did likewise.” [Col. 0141D] For just as through his Apostles he converted the Gentiles to the grace of faith, so also through martyrs and confessors he brought no small multitude of that same people both to the knowledge of his name and to love. Thus the Evangelist, following in order the times of the Apostles, martyrs, and confessors, immediately added:

[Col. 0142A] “About the eleventh hour he went out.” This eleventh hour signifies our times. For by the number eleven, which exceeds ten, transgression is figured; and, alas, the life of the present age, filled with countless evils, exceeds the perfection of the Decalogue, in which nearly all transgress the commandments of the Lord. But although the whole world is now set in wickedness, the kindly Householder—our Redeemer—still goes out about the eleventh hour, because even in our times he gathers labourers worthy of himself into his vineyard. Hence it aptly adds: “And he found others standing, and said to them: ‘Why stand ye here idle all the day?’” All those who now raise themselves against God through pride of life are the others standing; and to them the divine voice says: “Why stand ye here idle all the day?” Why, he says, do you waste in vain, without good work, the present time granted you for the remedy of your souls? And they are rightly rebuked for standing idle all day, because in that faculty wherein they ought to have been day—namely, the understanding and intelligence of the enlightened heart which they received from God—they turn themselves to iniquity and pride, not to the honour of God or the benefit of their neighbours. [Col. 0142B]

But let us consider what answer those questioned give. They say to him: “Because no one has hired us.” This answer is the cry of the people to God. “Lord,” they say, “no one has hired us, because no one shows us, wandering as we are, the way of righteousness by preaching; and even if at times we are taught by good exhortations, we have no good example of good conduct.” These indeed are words which, alas, may truthfully be said of almost all rulers of the Church. For if there are some who desire to hear good things, those who speak them are lacking; and if there are those who teach rightly, exceedingly few are found who do what they say. Hence the Psalmist, groaning, says: “They have all turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none that doeth good” (Ps. 13:3). [Col. 0142C]

He says to them: “Go ye also into the vineyard.” This command of the calling Lord is the mercy of his inspiration, whereby our most kindly Creator causes those whom he has resolved to save eternally to come, even though it is about the eleventh hour, to some life of good conduct; there, even if they do not have one who teaches rightly, they themselves may nevertheless be saved by living rightly. [Col. 0142D]

“But when evening had come.” This evening of which he speaks is rightly understood as the consummation of the age. As the very end of the world approaches, indeed, what the Evangelist immediately adds takes place: “The Lord of the vineyard said to his steward: ‘Call the labourers.’” The Lord of the vineyard may here be understood as God the Father, who says to his steward—that is, to his coeternal Son, or perhaps to Elijah or Enoch, who are to come into the world before the Judgment to preach, or to some shepherd of the Church—“Call,” he says, “the labourers, so that all who are still held in the ignorance of unbelief may, through thy preaching, teaching, and assistance, be summoned by faith to the Church.” For before the end of the world many from Jews and Gentiles are to be gathered into the unity of faith. [Col. 0143A]

“And pay them their wage.” This wage which he commands to be given them is the knowledge of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as the incarnate Wisdom of God, speaking to the Father, says: “And this is eternal life, that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John 17:2). It fittingly adds: “Beginning from the last even to the first.” For the last are the Gentiles, who will be converted to the Lord through faith; but the first are the Jews, whom the kind and merciful Lord calls to the knowledge of himself after the Gentiles have already been converted. The Gentiles are therefore rightly placed before the Jews, because it cannot happen that the Jews should precede the Gentiles in conversion; rather, after the calling of the Gentiles, they too are saved according to the election of grace, as blessed Paul says: “When the fullness of the Gentiles shall have entered in, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25). Hence it plainly follows:

“When therefore those came who had come about the eleventh hour, they received individual denarii.” The Gentiles, still to be converted, will come as it were about the eleventh hour, since they will remain in unbelief until the end of the world. But then they receive individual denarii when, instructed through faith in the Holy Trinity, they begin to know their Redeemer, who before the ages deigned to become man for them at the end of the ages. [Col. 0143B]

“But when the first came, they thought that they would receive more.” These first, as we have mentioned above, are the people of the Jews, who are called first because they were first chosen and called; but afterward, when Christ came in the flesh, they refused to believe him and were rejected by him. When, after the fullness of the Gentiles has been converted, they finally come to the unity of faith, they think that they will receive more. It is well said, “they thought,” not “they think,” because now they certainly suppose that they are sometime to be preferred to the Gentiles and, as beloved and pre-elected sons, ought by hereditary right to be exalted above them with a greater glory of dignity.

“But they too received individual denarii.” For in conversion they receive nothing further than the knowledge of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. They receive individual denarii, indeed, because the Father is a denarius, the Son is a denarius, and the Holy Spirit is a denarius; and by one and the same way of true faith, they and the Gentiles are led to the heavenly homeland. [Col. 0143D]

“And, receiving, they murmured against the householder.” This murmuring is humble acknowledgment and hidden grief, which they will have in their heart when they come to know God in truth, groaning and grieving in an overwhelming affliction of spirit because God so long abandoned them and so long left them blind in their error. In the tearful voice of the heart they will say: “These last have worked one hour, and thou hast made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.” As though they said: “O Lord and Ruler, thou art just and thy judgment is right, because what we who were first called possessed in our fathers, and what we received long before in the Law and the Scriptures, these last—that is, the Gentiles—have done in one hour, because they believed in thee upon one preaching of the Apostles. And therefore thou didst rightly in making them equal to us. For we are those wretched persons who bore the burden of the day and the heat. Whatever good we received from thy grace in prosperity, whatever adversity we endured by thy judgment, was in some manner a heavy burden upon our miserable souls. For neither in prosperity did we render worthy thanksgivings to thee, the Giver of all good things, for benefits received; nor in adversity, when thou didst bring evils upon us in accordance with the merit of our iniquity, did we humble our souls beneath thy righteous judgment.” [Col. 0144A]

## HOMILY XXII. THIRD HOMILY FOR THE SAME SUNDAY

[Col. 0144B] “Therefore the Lord God formed man from the slime of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Gen. 2).

Every human being conceived and born in sins, so long as he lies in the filth of sins, so long as he is defiled by the mud of earthly contagion, appears in some manner unformed in the sight of the divine majesty. For when, with the whole intention of his mind, he remains fixed in the mud of the present life; when, I say, he knows only how to desire and love those things which the foul delight of the slippery world wickedly offers him—what could more rightly be said than that he is a man formed from mud? But when the prevenient grace of almighty God determines to form—that is, reform—a person from such misery, according to the goodness innate to him he mercifully breathes into that person the knowledge of God and of himself, according to the account of the following text.

“And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” By the face, through which every person is recognized, knowledge of God is sometimes signified in sacred speech. By the breath of life, however, we may not unfittingly understand the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore when almighty God, as we have said, decides to reform a person from the formlessness of sins, he breathes into his face the breath of life; that is, through the grace of the Holy Spirit he brings the person to knowledge of God and of himself, so that he may truly know his Creator and, by worthy repentance, be able to recognize how deformed he has been in sins. [Col. 0144C]

But after the knowledge of God and of himself has been received, when a person begins to consider himself carefully and, ashamed of his own formlessness, determines to come to conversion into a new life, it may rightly be said of him:

“And man became a living soul.” For as long as a living person in sins makes no endeavour to mortify within himself the vices of the flesh, which are truly works of death, he becomes not a living soul but, in a manner, a dying soul. But after he begins to mortify these things in himself and resolves to live praiseworthily in the Lord, it may properly be said of him that he has become a living soul, whereas before he had become in a manner a dying soul. What it means for man to be made a living soul may be gathered from the Lord’s own words, who at the very beginning of human creation says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” [Col. 0145A]

A person is said to be made in the image of God when he who formerly violated God’s image in himself through sinning desires, by living well, to be reformed in the spirit of his mind. He is said to be made in God’s likeness when he desires to become like him: that is, just as God himself has in all things been supremely good, so he too strives to attain the example of that goodness; just as God was pure—indeed, the author of all purity—so he strives to be pure in heart and body; and just as God appeared meek and humble, so he presents himself to all who see him as humble and meek.

Whoever, therefore, has thus been formed from the mud of the earth—that is, from the mud of earthly conduct; whoever, through the inspiring grace of the Holy Spirit and having received knowledge of God and of himself, has been made from a dying soul into a living soul; and whoever recognizes himself as thus reformed in the image and likeness of God, so that, renewing God’s image in himself, he watches and delights with the whole effort of mind and body to become like him by examples of goodness, purity, and meekness—such a person has great need to become altogether estranged from the passing world. For if he wishes to remain in it longer, as the occupations of turbulent affairs gradually arise, the mind sometimes grows sluggish in the progress of virtuous work and casts itself down into the failure of an indolent manner of life. Hence it aptly follows at once:

“But the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight [Col. 0145C] from the beginning.” By paradise, which is called a garden of delights, the spiritual life may not unfittingly be understood, in which are gathered delicate souls, souls overflowing with the delights of heavenly sweetness. There are also some in secular life who strive to please their Creator through the merits of good works; but because they do not detach themselves from lowly goods, they can neither taste beforehand nor receive the grace of spiritual delights. Therefore they cannot offer to the very Author of sweetness the taste of the sweetest refreshment. For just as delicate and tender food restores and invigorates the human heart with a sweeter taste than hard and cheap food, so likewise souls delicate in Christ, so to speak—nourished, I say, with spiritual delights—prepare for the throat of the Beloved himself a taste of greater sweetness than those who strive to serve God only through outward good works. [Col. 0145D]

And this paradise is rightly said to have been planted “from the beginning”: that is, ordained by divine providence, from him who is the Beginning, for every person called to the salvation of eternal life. This is well made clear by the words which immediately follow:

“In which he placed the man whom he had formed”—namely, the man whom he had reformed from that formlessness of sins, from a dying soul, I say, into a living soul. Almighty God, therefore, places the man formed from the mud of the earth into paradise—that is, into the spiritual life—so that he may bear the fruit of good works more abundantly in proportion as he is known to be free and unencumbered from the tumult of earthly occupation. This also seems plainly indicated by the order of the following text.

“And the Lord God brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant for food.” By the earth in this passage we may understand the humble heart of any penitent person who has turned to the Lord. When such a person humbly recalls before the eyes of the mind the formlessness of his sins, he becomes humble and lowly in the sight of his own self-examination. From this noble earth—that is, from this humble heart—the Lord sometimes brings forth every tree: namely, the strength and excellence of good works. [Col. 0146A]

And note that he does not say merely “every tree,” but adds a qualification: “beautiful to behold and pleasant for food.” Truly, an action proceeding from a genuinely humble heart is called a beautiful tree. For whoever humbles himself from his whole heart, whatever he performs through the outward discipline of the body is certainly beautiful in the sight of the divine majesty, beautiful and pleasing in human estimation; it will also be useful for the edification of neighbours. For whoever lacks true humility, even if he performs any good works whatever, what has been done without the beauty of humility cannot be called beautiful. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). [Col. 0146B]

“And pleasant for food,” he says, because the work which proceeds from humility is pleasant for living and will likewise be pleasant for other people to imitate. “The tree of life also in the midst of paradise” is the human reason placed in the centre of the heart. Human reason is that power of the soul by which one contemplates God alone and heavenly things. A person is said to have his reason in the centre of his heart when, supported by divine help, he wisely knows how to distinguish what is above from what is below: namely, so that he fears, reveres, and loves God, who is above him, as Lord and his own Maker; while he subjects what is below him, namely his body, as a servant to his own authority. Whoever thus gives to what is above and below him what belongs to each—that is, whoever offers his Maker the reverence of due submission and knows how to allow his body what is necessary with just moderation—may truly be said to have the reason of his soul in the centre of his heart. [Col. 0146D]

Yet however much any spiritual person may, by the prevenient grace of God, continually strive upward through these and other exercises of virtues, as long as he bears the body which weighs down the soul, there is no doubt that again and again he feels within himself the troubles of temptations: namely, the delight of carrying out those things which his own will seems to suggest. Hence, after the tree of life was placed in the midst of paradise, it was immediately added:

And the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. By the tree of the knowledge of good and evil a person’s own will may be understood, when, as we have said, anyone flourishing in the advances of virtues takes greater delight in being exalted by human favor [Col. 0147A] than in being content to remain hidden in the secrecy of his own conscience. But when a person is vainly occupied with these and similar thoughts, it sometimes happens that he appears dry and deprived of divine sweetness, and feels no increase of solid virtue within himself. Therefore it is greatly necessary that almighty God should again look upon with the eyes of divine mercy the person whom, as we mentioned above, he formed from the clay of the earth, and should deign to water and moisten the dryness of that earth with the dew of the Holy Spirit. This following verse seems fittingly to explain this:

And a river went out from the place of delight to water Paradise. Three things seem here to have been set down: river, place, and delight; through these we may also understand the threefold confession of the divine name [Col. 0147B]—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. In “delight,” namely, the Father; in “place,” the Son; in “river,” the Holy Spirit. And the Father is rightly signified by delight, for he is the true and unfailing fountain of all delight, the fullness itself of all grace and sweetness; from the torrent of his delight he not only satisfies and intoxicates the companies of heavenly powers, but also delights, refreshes, and strengthens human hearts.

The Son of the eternal Father is also rightly understood through the place of delight, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwelt and dwells bodily, and in whom alone—and above whom alone—the Holy Spirit rested with all his gifts. By the river, moreover, we have said that the Holy Spirit is designated. For as a river, by watering dry [Col. 0147C] earth, makes it sprout, so the Holy Spirit, by pouring the stream of his grace into dry human hearts, brings them to produce fruits of worthy action. Therefore the river goes out from the place of delight, because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, as the Lord himself says to Philip in the Gospel: “Do you not believe,” he says, “that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:10).

But for what purpose this river goes forth is disclosed when it is added: “To water Paradise”—that is, to water the dry and hard heart of a human being; to water and cultivate the soil of the unfruitful mind, which has already withered from thirst and cannot of itself bring forth the fruit of a virtuous shoot. What power, grace, and perfection this river accomplishes as it goes forth may be understood [Col. 0147D] from what follows: “Which is divided there into four heads.” By the four heads the cardinal virtues may quite suitably be understood, upon which, and from which, the other virtues depend and stand. This the interpretation of the rivers themselves will make plain with evident proof.

“The name of one is Phison.” *Phison* is interpreted “the mouth of the pupil.” Since, as everyone knows, we speak with the mouth and see with the pupil, the first virtue, called prudence, is rightly designated through this first river, Phison, which is called “the mouth of the pupil.” For that person may most truly be called prudent who does not fear to confess with his mouth what he believes in his heart. Thus the apostle Paul says in his Epistle: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness; but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” [Col. 0148A] (Rom. 10:10).

Phison is also called “the alteration of the mouth,” which likewise rightly suits prudence. For that person may truly be called prudent who, through “the alteration of the right hand of the Most High,” begins, so to speak, to speak in new tongues: that is, one who formerly used to utter words of arrogance with a proud mouth now begins to speak humbly; one who formerly recklessly loosened the bridle of his tongue for idle talk now sets a guard over his mouth, and endeavors to utter, for the edification of his neighbors, words seasoned with the salt of wisdom. Of this river it is further said: “It is that which goes around all the land of Hevilath, where gold is produced; and the gold of that land is excellent.”

Hevilath is called “suffering” or “giving birth”; and by “giving birth” we mean, as it were, bringing forth with desire. Phison, [Col. 0148B] that is, prudence, goes around the whole land of Hevilath when a person learns through prudence to grieve for the sins he has committed and to desire to bring forth good works by which he may make satisfaction to God. There too gold is produced, by which we may understand human intelligence. Thus, in the land of Hevilath—that is, in the heart of one who grieves and desires good—gold is in a sense produced when, by God’s grace, understanding of the highest virtue is given to a person. “And the gold of that land is excellent.” That person truly has excellent understanding who always grieves for sins and always desires to bring forth works of virtue. For there are some in secular life who indeed possess great understanding through God’s grace; but only that understanding is called excellent [Col. 0148C] which is born in the land of Hevilath, that is, in the heart of one who grieves and desires good.

“And there are found bdellium and the onyx stone.” Bdellium is an aromatic tree, black in color but said to shed a bright tear, bitter in taste and fragrant; if it is steeped in wine, it will give off a sweeter scent. The onyx stone resembles a human fingernail. By bdellium, which has a black color but is said to exude a bright tear, we may quite suitably understand compunction of heart. For whoever, in true compunction of heart, considers the guilt of his wicked manner of life, appears indeed black to himself; but his tear—that is, his repentance—appears in some way bright in the sight of divine [Col. 0148D] majesty. Bright, I say, because it makes bright and clean the soul blackened by the darkness of sins.

The onyx, however, which resembles a human fingernail, suitably expresses the perfection of life. For the nail, in the part where it first becomes visible, displays whiteness; in its middle, blood appears mingled with the whiteness; but the part which is usually cut away from the flesh appears pure. If all these things are understood in a subtle and mystical sense, the perfection of life is rightly expressed through them. Therefore by that part which appears bright, innocence may be understood, whether received through baptism or through repentance. For a person is truly called bright when he deserves to recover, through the fruit of worthy repentance after falling into sins, the innocence which he received in baptism [Col. 0149A].

By the middle part, in which redness is mingled with whiteness, imitation of Christ’s sufferings is prefigured. For after receiving through repentance the brightness of innocence, a person must endeavor to become a participant in Christ’s sufferings and strive to bear his mortification in his own body. If, as we have said, using prudent counsel, he does not cease to mortify the works of the flesh in his body, he will rightly be compared to that part which appears wholly hard. For if in this present life he strives through devout exertions to be cleansed from every contagion of sin, and endeavors vigilantly to retain, insofar as it is possible in this time of mutability, the perfection of life, then, when he has at last laid aside this corruptible body [Col. 0149B], he will be altogether pure and free at the strict judgment.

It follows:

“And the name of the second is Gehon. This is that which goes around the land of Ethiopia.” Gehon is called “the severed-off,” while Ethiopia is interpreted “darkness.” What, then, is understood by Gehon, called “the severed-off,” except the virtue named fortitude? Without doubt a person may then be called strong when, acting manfully in the Lord, he forcefully cuts away from his body everything he formerly loved, everything which he nourished and cherished with evil-sweet delight in his hidden places. Gehon, that is, fortitude, goes around the whole land of Ethiopia when a person, as we have said, forcefully cuts away from his body the dark works of wicked habit.

“The name of the third river is Tigris; it goes against [Col. 0149C] the Assyrians.” Tigris is interpreted “arrow,” while Assyrians are interpreted “those who direct.” Therefore through Tigris we may rightly understand the virtue called temperance. By the Assyrians, moreover, evil spirits are to be understood. For Tigris, that is, temperance, goes against the Assyrians because the person who knows how to restrain himself from vices sends, as it were, an arrow against evil spirits when he vigorously resists their wicked suggestions.

“The fourth river, however, is Euphrates.” By Euphrates, called “fruit-bearing,” we may designate the virtue called justice. For whoever, with the Lord’s help, has struggled devoutly and steadfastly to stand in the three above-mentioned stages of virtue [Col. 0149D], will eventually deserve to attain that virtue by which, living commendably in justice, he continually brings forth to the Lord from himself the fruit of good works, so that he may rightly be called fruit-bearing.

In these four rivers we may also understand four orders: through the first, Phison, those who understand; through the second, Gehon, penitents; through the third, Tigris, those who fight; through the fourth, Euphrates, those who are perfected. Every elect person must advance through these four orders: first, that he may prudently understand how he has offended the mercy of his Creator and what satisfaction he owes to God for his sins. Then, when he has begun to sacrifice himself through repentance, fortitude will be greatly necessary to him, so that by the lamentations of vigorous repentance [Col. 0150A] he may forcefully cut from his body the works of ingrained wicked habit.

But after, in the constancy of repentance of this sort, he has somewhat mortified the vices of the flesh, since he cannot possibly be free from the temptations of evil spirits, he must put on the armor of that virtue called temperance, so that temperance itself may fly ahead like an arrow against the darts of adversaries. For it meets their darts like a certain arrow whenever a person, by vigorously resisting vices, continually endeavors to guard against the snares of their wicked suggestion. Therefore, whoever has become strong in battle in this way must now strive to complete in the Lord the course of the good contest. For if he endeavors to live in the justice which he has once embraced until death, he may now rightly be called fruit-bearing through the good fruits of justice.

Whoever has been raised by the Lord through these gifts of virtues in the spiritual life is also fittingly described by what the following text immediately adds:

“Therefore the Lord God took the man whom he had formed and placed him in the Paradise of delight.” When it says that he “took him,” this is as though it said that he raises him in the spiritual life, making him exalted through merits of virtue increasing day by day. He raises him, I say, from earthly desires to the desire of heavenly things, so that nothing in the present life now pleases him, but he fixes the whole intention of his soul, his entire hope and desire, above, where God himself abides [Col. 0150B].

“That he might work,” it says, “and keep him” [the manuscript: “it”]. For one whom the Lord thus raises and lifts up in the spiritual life ought not to be idle; rather, he must himself be a co-worker with the divine grace working in him. That is, he must perform works of virtue and keep watch lest he lose them through exaltation of mind [Col. 0150C].

“And he commanded him, saying: ‘From every tree of Paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat.’” It is as though he said: “Diligently imitate and carry out, with the attentive intention of a watchful mind, every pursuit of virtuous action and every example of devout conduct which you see practiced in the spiritual life. But do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—that is, never seek to fulfill your own will, so as to attribute the gifts of my generosity to your own merits and seek the glory [Col. 0150D] of human praise.

“Do not eat,” he says, “from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” Knowledge of good and evil is experience of good and evil. It is one thing to know evil and another to experience evil. To know evil without experiencing it is not to consent to evil; but to experience evil is to proceed to an evil act. The one who endeavors to resist evil deeds knows evil but does not experience it. Therefore the Lord forbids the human being to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; that is, he forbids him to misuse his own will so as eventually to experience evil. He experiences evil when he does not fear to fulfill in action what his own will suggests, when he desires vainly to be exalted by human praise for things bestowed upon him by God.

[Col. 0151A] And notice what is said: “Do not eat.” For whatever a person eats by chewing somehow adheres to the body when assimilated to it. It is as though he said: “If the appetite for human favor entices your mind, take care not to eat; that is, do not receive it so delightfully, do not permit thoughts to linger in your heart for so long that you eventually consent to the delight.” But if delight prevails and, using force against you, persuades you to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, “on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.” On whatever day, whatever night, hour, or moment you eat from it by consenting to voluntary delight, you shall die by death: that is, strive so to mortify it within yourself that you too may become entirely dead to sin.

What is said, “On whatever [Col. 0151B] day you eat from it, you shall die by death,” may also be understood otherwise. If, I say, you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil by obeying your own will as far as consent, then, on whatever day—that is, whenever the day of some knowledge or some divine visitation dawns in your heart—you shall die by death: that is, by truly acknowledging and worthily repenting, strive so to mortify it within yourself that it may appear to exercise no further power in you.

“The Lord God also said: ‘It is not good for the man to be alone.’” Since any person who has been raised by God to so great an excellence of virtue, if he felt no stirrings of temptation within himself, would easily be subject to the vice of boastfulness by exalting himself above himself, God himself, who providently orders all things and foresees his salvation, says: “It is not good for the man to be alone.” [Col. 0151C] It is as though he said: “This person, who stands in the glory of such an eminent life, is in some sense alone, because he feels nothing of the wretchedness of his own vileness. For the dignities of virtues which he has within him are not his own and are not to be attributed to his own merits, because he has them solely from our abundant goodness. If he remains thus alone and feels nothing within himself of that fragility which is his own, he will, being ungrateful to us, attribute to his own virtue the virtues which he has from our generosity.”

“Therefore, because it is not good for him to be so alone, let us make him a helper like himself”—that is, let us make for him such a helper as will not bring him an impediment but will stir him up to devout labors; such a helper as will not crush and destroy [Col. 0151D] the steadfastness of his good works but will make him stand more robustly in firmness. “Like himself,” that is, so that he may feel something in himself by which, remembering his own fragility, he may learn not to be proud of the grace of virtues but humbly to trust in the help of our goodness. Hence it is rightly added:

“Therefore the Lord God, having formed from the ground all the animals of the earth and all the birds of heaven, brought them to Adam.” The Almighty forms all animals and birds of heaven and brings them to Adam when he opens the eyes of the human heart so that a person may recognize his animal and changeable life. Thus one who formerly seemed righteous and perfect to himself, believing himself free from wicked deeds, may at last, divinely inspired, be able to consider [Col. 0152A] how animal-like and how changeable his life has been: namely, that he has immersed himself in the mire of vices by living irrationally, like a brute beast devoid of sense; and that through a changeable life—that is, through a swollen and proud manner of life—he has grievously offended his Creator.

“That he might see,” it says, “what he would call them.” After all these have been formed in the human heart—that is, before the person has perceived all these things with the eye of provident consideration—the almighty Lord wishes to see what he would call them; that is, he desires to see and know how the person decides to make satisfaction for them, how he endeavors through pure confession truly to disclose the deeds of his shameful transgression, how he does not delay severely to accuse the exaltation of his swollen mind, and then at last to make satisfaction to God for all these things through devout exertions [Col. 0152B]. For if a person truly acknowledges his sins and is not ashamed to confess them purely and fully, he will deserve to attain the grace of full pardon. This the following order of words seems rightly to indicate.

“For whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name.” The kind of satisfaction a person offers in confession will be the kind of grace he receives in the remission of sins. For as is the confession, so will be the remission. It follows:

“And Adam gave their names to all the animals of the earth, to all the birds of heaven, and to all the beasts of the earth.” Having recognized through God’s grace the innumerable defilements of sins, he begins humbly to confess his injustice against himself; and he gives [Col. 0152C] their names to all the animals, birds of heaven, and beasts of the earth when, in pure confession, he does not fear, so to speak, to set forth each individual sin by name.

“But for Adam a helper like him was not found. Therefore the Lord God caused a sleep to fall upon Adam.” A sleep is sent upon Adam when, by the hidden judgment of God, a person is allowed to grow sluggish in good works. For what is sloth in good work but a kind of sleep of the lazy mind? If the human mind makes no effort to shake itself free from the indolence of this torpor, it sometimes happens that even the very strength is taken away by which it had formerly persisted in good actions, so that it finds within itself nothing but the softness of carnal frailty. This is well indicated by the sense of the following passage:

“And when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs.” A rib is taken from him when the strength by which he had formerly been accustomed to work profitably is withdrawn. Thus strength is filled with flesh when the one who had lately been firm and steadfast in exercises of virtue begins to feel carnal frailty within himself [Col. 0152D].

“And the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam.” That rib too is built into a woman when, as we have said, the person who once seemed to flourish in the glory of the highest virtue is so subjected to womanly softness that he now feels nothing virtuous within himself, but becomes, so to speak, soft and weak in regard to every pursuit of spiritual virtues. This woman too is brought to Adam when, by the grace of divine visitation, a person is brought back inwardly to himself, so that with the watchful gaze of his heart he may consider the misery of his calamity. And every person who is to be saved, when he recognizes that he has been diminished in this way in virtuous deeds and in the sweetness of desired contemplation, quickly returns to himself and prudently recognizes whence he has deserved the misery of so great a fall. And, as follows here, he addresses himself inwardly with the groaning voice of his heart [Col. 0153A].

“And Adam said: ‘This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.’” It is as though he said: “The swelling of my exalted mind, which now heavily weighs down and depresses me inwardly, cast down by the Lord, so that neither bodily exercise nor the intention of a devout mind can be practiced as formerly, has arisen from my bones—that is, from my strong works. For because, after receiving the grace of the divine gift, I vainly exalted my soul by seeking human praise, the boastfulness of such vanity strongly draws me back, cast down inwardly, from the pursuit of my customary activity. And ‘flesh,’ he says, ‘of my flesh.’ The weakness which has now enfeebled my strength came from the frailty of flesh made wickedly weak: namely, because I did not take care to subject to the law of the mind the law of the flesh resisting the spirit [Col. 0153B].

“She shall be called *virago*, because she was taken from her man.” This weakness, then—this frailty of weak flesh—shall be called *virago*, that is, “acting as a man,” because it drives from the mind, by manly action, the favor of human praise; for it was taken from man, namely from manly action, from the height of virtuous conduct. Since, moreover, as long as a person bears this corruptible body, this conflict between spirit and soul does not cease, what he must chiefly do may be gathered from the following words.

“For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife.” In this passage we may understand the spirit by the father, the flesh by the mother, and the softness of the flesh itself by the wife. Therefore a person must leave father and mother and cleave to his wife: that is, he must powerfully humble within himself the exaltation of the spirit, which sometimes savors high things [Col. 0153C]; he must despise, by always acting manfully, the softness of the flesh suggesting the repose of evil security; and, mindful of his own frailty, he must never exalt himself on account of good works, but humbly place his hope in God and in the power of his might. “And the two shall be one flesh”: the spirit and soul, conscious of human frailty, always recognize before the Lord that they ought to humble themselves [Col. 0153D].

## HOMILY XXIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR SEXAGESIMA SUNDAY

“When a very great crowd was gathered together, and they were hastening to him from the cities, he spoke in a parable: ‘The one who sows went out to sow his seed’” (Luke 8).

This man who went out to sow his seed signifies him who is speaking these words, our Lord Jesus Christ. He is rightly compared to a man sowing. For he is the one who sowed everything that exists. He is the one who formed and created all things that exist. But why does he say, “He went out”? Where was he, or whence did he go out? In a sense he was within, because the invisible God remained unknown to humankind in the invisible substance of his divinity. But he went out when, descending from the bosom of the Father into the womb of the Virgin Mother, he assumed the form of humanity, through which the invisible God appeared to the world as visible man [Col. 0154A].

But in another way he was within when, in the very form of the humanity he had assumed, he concealed himself for thirty years, so that he revealed to the world the omnipotence of his divinity neither by signs nor by teaching. But he went out to sow his seed when, with miracles flashing forth, he began to preach to the world. He also goes out daily in his preachers, in the teachers of truth, to sow his seed, while his mercy goes beforehand through the words of teachers to the hearts of hearers. For everyone who preaches labors in vain unless almighty God goes before and opens the human heart by his blessings. For he is the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens.

“And while he was sowing, some fell beside the way, and it was trampled down, and the birds of heaven ate it.” Human frailty does not presume to investigate words which, as blessed Gregory says, Truth itself expounded [Note: [Col. 0153D] St Gregory, *Forty Homilies on the Gospels*, book I, homily 15, vol. LXXVI of the *Patrologia*.]. Yet it would be necessary for us if someone could make that exposition clearer for us. For those chosen disciples, the holy apostles, who were wise—as men who shared day and night in the living fountain of eternal Wisdom and knowledge and therefore grasped and understood much from little—these few words sufficed [Col. 0154C]. But for us wretches, slow of heart, who from many words scarcely grasp and understand even a few at times, not merely the parable, but the explanation of the parable itself, is exceedingly obscure.

But if we were imitators of apostolic life, we might hope that the word spoken to them in answer to their inquiry concerning the mystery of this parable had likewise been spoken to us. “To you,” he says, “it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables.” He then spoke these words to them bodily; he likewise speaks the same words daily to us, that is, to spiritual persons, spiritually [Col. 0154D]. By the mystery of the kingdom of God is understood the mystery of Holy Scripture, which is not unsuitably likened to the kingdom of God, since God truly is in Holy Scripture and is truly known from Holy Scripture. Holy Scripture, which speaks mysteries of the kingdom of God to spiritual persons, is like a parable to worldly people.

And note what he says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God.” He affirms that it has been given to us to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, to know the mystery of Holy Scripture, not merely that we may know it, but that we may endeavor to fulfill in action what we know. For knowledge of the Scriptures will not benefit us if good action does not accompany good knowledge [Col. 0155A]. Indeed, it harms more than it benefits, as the Lord testifies when he says: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:47); and as the apostle says: “To one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (James 4:17).

What he further added—“That seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand”—we judge may not inappropriately be understood of the learned and the unlearned. Those who know the mysteries of Scripture are rightly called “seeing”; those who do not know but await the word of God from others are rightly denoted by “hearing.” Those who see do not see when, by reading the Scriptures, they see through knowledge but not through experience. Those who hear do not understand when they hear [Col. 0155B] through instruction but have no wisdom through efficacy. Having briefly set these points before us, let us see what are the three things which the eternal Wisdom of God has proposed to us in this reading. First he set down the way; after the way, the rock; after the rock, thorns.

“And while he was sowing,” he says, “some fell beside the way, and it was trampled down, and the birds of heaven ate it. And some fell upon the rock; and when it sprang up, it withered because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns sprang up with it and choked it.”

By the way we may understand negligence of mind; by the rock, hardness of heart; by thorns, avarice of heart. These are the three things through which the seed of the Word of God, sown in the field of our heart, perishes, unable to spring forth into growth through the fruit of good action. Seed is cast beside the way when the Word of God is preached to a negligent person. Therefore the Lord says: “Those beside the way are those who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word from their hearts, lest they believe and be saved.” Those are beside the way who are not solicitous about guarding themselves. Solomon says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4:23). Whatever is sown beside that way is trampled down, because, when the guard has been removed—that is, the vigilant watchfulness of the mind—harmful, useless, and vain thoughts succeed one another, freely enter and proceed. Thus the human heart becomes like a trodden road; and even if the seed of the Word of God falls into it, it cannot germinate there [Col. 0155D]. Rather, the birds of heaven eat it, because unclean spirits, signified by the birds, entering and departing through suggestions and unclean thoughts, lay waste and consume even whatever good they find rising in that heart.

After the way he rightly set down the rock, by which we understand hardness of heart. For when the sluggish and negligent mind restrains itself by no watchfulness, it is, by God’s just judgment, so hardened and blinded within itself that even when it wishes, it cannot return into itself through remembrance of sins or desire for eternal things. Hence the Lord rightly added, after saying, “And some fell upon the rock”: “And when it sprang up, it withered because it had no moisture.” This moisture is the moisture of tears [Col. 0156A], by which the conceived seed of the Word of God must continually be watered. For the Word of God is conceived when it is heard; it is born when it is brought to the effect of good action. But if the moisture of tears is lacking, what has been born withers: because whatever a person brings forth, whether of good will or good action, from hearing the Word of God, withers as though newly born through the dryness of a hard heart, lest it grow and gain strength into the fruit of perfect action.

Therefore the Lord says: “Those upon the rock are those who, when they have heard, receive the word with joy; but these have no roots, because they believe for a time and in the time of temptation fall away.” There are some who receive the Word of God with joy—those, namely, who gladly hear it and resolve to follow what they have heard. But because they are rock and have no roots, lacking the virtues of humility and perseverance, which are roots, they at some time begin to fulfill and carry out in deeds what they have heard. But when temptation comes upon them—if anger or envy seizes the mind, if some prosperity or adversity presents itself—they abandon what they had well begun and return to their former habit of instability and inconstancy in vices. This is to believe for a time and to fall away in a time of temptation [Col. 0156B].

Since the human heart is such that it can never be without loving something, when it neglects and despises God and the things of God, it begins to love and strive to obtain the world and the things of the world. Hence, after the way and after the rock, he rightly set down thorns.

“And some,” he says, “fell among thorns, and the thorns which sprang up with it choked it.” We have said that avarice is to be understood by thorns. But avarice is not only of money, but also of honor and pleasure, as the author of truth himself proves, saying: “That which fell among thorns are those who have heard; and as they go, they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and bring no fruit to maturity.” What are the cares, riches, and pleasures of life but avarice? These are the three tyrants that assail us, that always call us back and delay us from producing and bringing forth the fruit of righteousness and truth: namely, the devil, the world, and the flesh which we bear. The devil assails us with cares when he troubles and disturbs us with his suggestions. The world assails us [Col. 0156D] with riches, namely with the favors and honors of this present life. Our flesh assails us with pleasures, so that, resisting the spirit, we may love deeds of the flesh. These are the wickedly piercing thorns which, if they strike root in a human heart, choke the seed of the Word of God when it is sown and springs up there, so that it may not bear fruit and may be unable to rise to the pursuit of good action.

Against these three—the way, the rock, and the thorns—the Psalmist prayed, saying: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice” (Ps. 118:36). Against the way he placed this word, “incline,” by which humility is signified, because the heart founded in humility bars from itself, through the virtue of humility, the entrance of evil spirits, lest it become impassable or passable to their suggestions and assaults [Col. 0157A]. Against the way, against negligence of mind, he prayed, saying, “Incline my heart.” Against the rock, against hardness of heart, he prayed by adding, “to your testimonies,” through which meditation on Holy Scripture is expressed. For there is nothing that so softens the human heart as meditation on God’s testimonies, from which is generated watchful observance of God’s commandments.

Once a person has avoided these two—the way and the rock—through humility and observance of God’s commandments, the third, which is avarice, will not prevail against him. For a humble heart, solicitous in observance of God’s commandments, though assailed by the devil with cares, by the world with riches and honors, and by the flesh with pleasures, is nevertheless not overcome; but, as the seed of the Word of God grows strong within it, it is daily encouraged to bring forth fruit worthy of God [Col. 0157B]. Therefore the Lord added and said:

“And some fell into good ground, and when it sprang up it yielded fruit a hundredfold.” What he signified by the good ground and the hundredfold fruit he himself explains when he says: “That in the good ground are those who, hearing the Word of God in a good and excellent heart, retain it and bear fruit in patience.” Good ground signifies the good person; by the good heart is figuratively denoted the heart of fear, and by the excellent heart the heart of love. These two—fear and love—are rightly opposed to the two preceding things, the way and the rock: fear against the way, love against the rock. For fear of God restrains a person lest he be a way, lest he be negligent in guarding his heart; love of God softens a person lest he be a rock, that is, stony ground parched by the moisture of inward sweetness [Col. 0157C].
