Therefore we may call the good heart the heart fortified by watchfulness, and the excellent heart the heart softened by the grace of love.

And he rightly says: “Those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, retain it.” The Word of God is heard in a good heart and retained in an excellent heart. For it is good to hear the Word of God; it is excellent to retain it—that is, to fulfill it in works. From these two, from the good and excellent heart, from divine fear and love, there springs that fruit in which God delights and on which he feeds. This fruit is the fruit of love for God and neighbor, and it is designated by the hundredfold fruit because, when God is loved above all things and love of neighbor is preserved in all things for God’s sake, the reward of eternal blessedness is made a hundredfold. But because neither love of God nor love of neighbor can be practiced without the adversities and disturbances of the present life, the Lord adds still further and says:

“And they bear fruit in patience.” By these few words the Lord admonishes us, 196 that, moved neither by prosperity nor adversity, we should not grow slack in the love of God; that no disturbances arising from the occasions of diverse events should make us fall away from the love of God; but that we should always bear our fruit in patience. Did not the vessel of election—Paul, I mean, the apostle—bear this fruit, the fruit of the love of God and neighbour, in patience? For, because of the love of God with which he burned, he so blazed in love for his neighbour [Col. 0158A] that no adversities or labours of this present life could recall him from his purpose, by which he laboured for the salvation of his neighbours. What he endured, and how he laboured more than all Christ’s disciples, he himself enumerates in today’s reading, where he says: “From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck. A night and a day I was in the depths of the sea; often on journeys, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brethren, in labour and hardship, in many watchings, in cold and nakedness.”

Let us, dearest brethren, imitate this man, such as he was and so great—a man whom we, who ought to be imitators of the apostolic life, must imitate. [Col. 0158B] Let us strive not to be a path, not to be a rock, not to be thorns choking within us the seed of God’s word; let us not be those to whom the Lord speaks in parables, but those to whom he opens the mystery of his kingdom. In it we are taught to be good soil, which hears and retains God’s word in a good and excellent heart, and bears fruit in patience that remains without end. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## 197. HOMILY XXIV. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY OF QUINQUAGESIMA

Jesus took his twelve disciples and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things that have been spoken through the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled” (Luke 18).

[Col. 0158C] We fear to be reproved by many for rashness or presumption because we venture to say or expound something upon the words and sentences of blessed Gregory, that distinguished and eminent teacher. But, considering that blessed Gregory then spoke not to spiritual persons but to secular people, according to the place and condition of the time, we believe that we detract nothing from his honour or praise if we devote the effort of our labour and discourse to adapting, for the profit and edification of those living in monasteries, matters which he either passed over or expounded for ordinary people as suited them.

For we know that we, being unlearned and poor in ability, can in no way attain to his understanding and wisdom. Yet, humbly following his footsteps [Col. 0158D] with sound faith and sound understanding, we offer, as the Lord grants, words of humility and charity for the edification of those who serve God. Therefore the Evangelist says:

“Jesus took his twelve disciples and said to them: ‘Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things spoken through the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled.’” Our Lord and Saviour Jesus takes to himself a person predestined for eternal life when that person, formerly far from him, is visited by him in his salvation and is made concerned for his own salvation; and thus, through inward inspiration, he gives that person the will to leave the world and enter the school of spiritual life. But he ought not to come to this school alone; rather, he must hasten there with the twelve disciples. [Col. 0159A] The ten disciples may be understood as the senses of the inner and outer person; the remaining two are to be understood as body and soul. With these, one coming to conversion, and intending there to serve God, submits himself to divine discipline. 198

But because it is very difficult and laborious for a person to leave the world and enter upon a purpose of spiritual strictness, God immediately sets consoling words before him, saying:

“Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem.” Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” Under its figure may be understood the whole Church collectively, or each blessed congregation individually, or any faithful soul. But in this place the congregation of believers is to be understood. Although the ascent to it is grievous and laborious, an even more grievous [Col. 0159B] and laborious conflict remains. For just as one who enters the arena has no rest until the end, but tirelessly either tries to strike his opponent or fears being struck by him, so it is indeed in the spiritual contest, in which we shall fight the devil until our end. If we act too slackly, we succumb to the tempter; but if, through God’s grace, we are more fervent, we resist the tempter. Hence Solomon says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). To come to God’s service is to ascend to Jerusalem. And because whoever reaches this Jerusalem cannot possibly be without the labour of temptations, God rightly consoles him with these words: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem.” [Col. 0159C] As though he said: Do not fear or be dismayed. You shall not ascend there alone; behold, I shall ascend with you, I shall be with you in tribulation, I shall bear with you all your labour, and whatever you suffer there I shall endure with you.

Concerning these temptations also, which a person is to suffer in this life, it is immediately and rightly added:

## 199. “And all things written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled.”

Because Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and humankind, is our head, while we are his members, all things foretold through the prophets concerning the Son of Man—begun indeed, as it were, in our head himself—are fulfilled daily and until the end of the age in his members, as the apostle Paul says: “I fill up in my flesh what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ” [Col. 0159D] (Col. 1:24). For whatever was foretold of the Lord Jesus and was not fulfilled bodily in his own person will be fulfilled invisibly each day in his elect. But, to make what we have said clearer, let us touch briefly upon some matters which were done bodily in him but ought to be fulfilled spiritually in us.

For when he was still of tender age, fleeing Herod’s cruelty, he was carried by his own parents into Egypt. This had long before been prophesied of him and was bodily fulfilled in him. But it then signified how every blessed person, still of tender age—that is, at the beginning of conversion or good works, while not yet practising perfect righteousness—ought to flee into Egypt, [Col. 0160A] that is, into darkness. For one ought to conceal one’s good works from malignant spirits and from human favour, lest, if they are publicized, they quickly perish through human praise. These things, as we have said, prophesied of the Lord Jesus and fulfilled in him, will also be fulfilled in his faithful people; and very many other things, too numerous to enumerate, will be fulfilled until the end of the age in his members incorporated into him through faith. Hence it follows:

“For he shall be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon.” In these four words—“he shall be handed over,” “mocked,” “scourged,” “spat upon”—four stages of sin may be understood: namely, suggestion of sin, delight, consent, and action, through which malignant spirits tempt and deceive people. [Col. 0160B] A person is handed over to the Gentiles, that is, to vices, through the suggestion of sin; mocked through delight in sin; scourged through consent to sin; and spat upon through sinful action.

It should be noted 200 that suggestion suitably corresponds to being handed over, delight to mockery, consent to scourges, and action to spittle. For just as one who wishes to hand someone over first works through suggestions, seeking how he may hand him over, so malignant spirits first assault us with their suggestions in order to hand us over to vices. If, at their prompting, we slip into delight in sin, exposed to their derision and reproach, we are truly mocked. But if, delighting in sin, we incline as far as consent, then without doubt we are scourged. For just as the flesh is visibly wounded by scourges, so [Col. 0160C] the soul is invisibly wounded through consent to sin. Finally, when wounded, we are spat upon when we are brought to the very action of sin, which is fittingly likened to spittle cast from the mouth. For although we have been handed over through suggestion, mocked through delight, and scourged through consent, we are still in Christ’s body. But when we fall into the open action of criminal sin, we begin to be cast out from Christ’s body like spittle from the mouth, because through the uncleanness of sin we become abominable to God. It follows:

“And after they have scourged him, they will kill him; and on the third day he will rise again.” After he has been scourged, therefore, he is killed through the defence of sin, when one who formerly used to commit sins with fear and trembling comes so far as not merely to commit sins heedlessly and without fear, but even begins to defend them. [Col. 0160D] But because the Lord knows who are his, and because, according to the saying of the apostle Paul, “all things work together for good to those who love God; for those whom he foreknew he also predestined; and those whom he predestined he also called; and those whom he called he also justified; and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Rom. 8:28), this person, though miserably killed, will nevertheless rise on the third day according to the Gospel narrative.

The first day is knowledge of sin; the second, confession of sin; the third, satisfaction for sin. When this has been accomplished, the one who had been killed shall rise. It follows:

“And they understood none of these things; and this saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand the things which were said.” At the beginning of conversion, a person understands none of the things foretold. For he does not know whether what is required of him will result in condemnation or salvation. Being in bitterness, 201 [Col. 0161A] he seeks at least to be refreshed by some good word; he also seeks in the Lord’s word something from which he may receive consolation. But when preaching comes, the word is hidden from his eyes—namely, the sweetness that is in God’s word. He hears or reads the Lord’s word, just as many who come from the world and are well trained in literary studies read and understand the Scriptures; but they do not yet understand by experience. How they may come to understand all these things is brought about only by God’s favour and providence. Hence it is added:

[Col. 0161B] “And it came to pass, when he drew near to Jericho, that a certain blind man sat by the way begging.” No one can work this wonderful deed in a person except he alone whose omnipotence subjects to itself whatever he wills. But this deed is fulfilled in a person when the Saviour begins to draw near to Jericho. Jericho is interpreted “moon,” by which an unstable soul may be represented: through its instability it changes like the moon, and Jesus draws near to it through grace. The way is Christ, beside whom the one sits who recognizes his blindness through humility.

Wonderful, therefore, is the power of humility. The apostle Paul was so concerned to commend it to believers that he called it the power of Christ: “That the power of Christ,” he says, [Col. 0161C] “may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9). Although he possesses all virtues and is himself the power and wisdom of God, he nevertheless especially claims this virtue for himself, saying to his apostles: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). He commanded that this virtue alone, together with gentleness—which is patience—be learned from him, because patience is truly the daughter of humility, always opposed by the plague of pride. Through pride, indeed, an angel was cast from heaven to earth: though created in great sublimity, because he refused to submit to God with a humble will, he could not long remain in that high station. Thus the first human being, Adam, formed in God’s image and likeness and placed with honour in paradise, because he proudly raised himself against God, was expelled into the exile of this world. Hence the virtue of humility is exceedingly necessary. The Psalmist again commends it, saying: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.”

Whoever, therefore, [Col. 0161D] as we have said, recognizes his blindness in humility is said to sit beside the way—that is, Christ. Yet he is certainly not permitted to sit there idle, but must beg after the example of this blind man.

## 202

We should consider that the person who begs, having nothing in his own house, seeks from others a supply for his need. But even if he has some little thing, yet believing that it does not suffice for him, he begs in order that he may abound more and more. Thus, the one who humbly recognizes the blindness of his wretched life seeks the aid of prayer from other persons whom he finds richer than himself in God’s gifts, [Col. 0162A] so that, helped by their prayers, he may obtain the assistance of divine grace. He also counts it a great thing if he is sometimes comforted by some small visitation, as it were, of the Lord’s mercy. It follows:

“And when he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was.” While established in this humility, he hears the crowd passing by when he understands his past sins, by which he had long offended God. Thus he sits by humbling himself; begs by desiring; asks by praying; and cries out by confessing sins. “He asked what this was.” He prays to God that, through the help of God’s grace, he may repent and weep over his sins as he remembers having acted against God.

“But they told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by.” [Col. 0162B] “And he cried out, saying: ‘Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.’” By those who tell this blind man, as he asks, that Jesus of Nazareth is passing by, we may especially understand almighty God, who inwardly speaks to a person about his salvation. We may also understand thoughts inspired by him, which sometimes speak these same words within a person, as if a sorrowing soul lamented and groaned within itself: “Now, O wretched soul, what will you do? That Jesus of Nazareth, who is the flower of purity, has passed from you! You have lost through your sins him who ought to preserve your purity and chastity. You will now remain forever without salvation and happiness unless that one alone returns, on whom alone all your joy and sweetness [Col. 0162C] depend.” 203

Hearing such answers within himself, the person at last begins to cry out. He cries, I say, with saving confession, to him in whom he has placed the salvation of his soul, and to whose teaching he has submitted himself; he recounts the magnitude of his former offences. Crying out in this way in confession, he turns again to God and says to him in prayer: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.”

It should be noted that, believing and confessing him to be true God and true human being, he calls him Son of David because David was sinful and wicked, and he recognizes in a humble heart that he himself is such. David, indeed, committed both adultery and murder. Moreover, Scripture records that he gravely [Col. 0162D] sinned against the Lord in the census of the people which he caused to be taken through the pride of his heart. For this reason he calls him Son of David, that, reminded of this grace, the Almighty may more graciously and kindly have mercy also upon him. And he aptly calls him Jesus, that is, his Saviour, holding faith in him and showing that he believes he will be saved by him from his sins. He also shows that he has hope, asking him to have mercy on him.

We likewise must constantly maintain faith, hope, and charity in our confession. Faith: because we must faithfully and without any doubt believe that we can obtain from the Lord forgiveness of our sins if we confess them perfectly with a contrite heart. Hope must be held in this: that this Saviour, who has forgiven us our sins, will also [Col. 0163A] abundantly bestow his mercy upon those who hope in him after the absolution of their offences. Between these two—faith and hope—charity is joined as a middle and, as it were, mediating element. Having obtained it, a person begins to love God with perfect love, and likewise deserves to be bound to God by no lesser affection of charity. It follows:

“And those who went before rebuked him, that he should be silent. But he cried out all the more: ‘Son of David, have mercy on me.’” Who, then, are those said to go before us, if not sinful impulses and evil desires, which first come into a person’s heart and afterwards draw him into committing evil deeds? These perverse desires and impulses, which formerly went before a person prior to sins, after the confession of perverse acts cry within, persuading and exhorting him to keep wholly silent about them. 204 [Col. 0163B] For he says in his heart that there is absolutely no way for him to confess so many evil impulses and so many perverse desires which, as his conscience bears witness, he remembers having often entertained against God.

But again, aided by God’s grace, he begins to cry out all the more in confession, accusing his desires and bringing forth from the depth of his heart the diverse impulses to sin—with a cry, I say, stronger than the one with which he had earlier cried out over his deeds—so that in a wondrous way he may cause Jesus to stand for him, as follows:

“But Jesus, standing still, commanded that he be brought to him.” Note that in the earlier confession of deeds he invokes Jesus as Son of David; but here, where he bewails sins of thoughts [Col. 0163C] and desires, he calls him not Jesus but only Son of David, asking only that he have mercy on him, lest he be utterly overwhelmed by the sins of his thoughts. With God’s help, we can indeed in this life be saved from wicked and dead works; but it is exceedingly difficult for one dwelling in this exile to be thoroughly cleansed from the defilements of one’s thoughts, according to the saying of the apostle Paul: “For who shall boast that he has a pure heart?” Again the Psalmist says of this: “Who understands transgressions? Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Ps. 18:13).

At last the Lord Jesus stands for the one crying in this manner, as we have said. This is fulfilled in us when, lifted up to God in the stronghold of inward [Col. 0163D] prayer, we stand with him; and this standing is exceedingly sweet to the Lord. But because that standing cannot long persist in a person, so that the mind is always intent upon prayer, one must at least, by good thoughts that cling to him, always return to the heart, examining and searching every hour how our heart is holding itself within. For if we do this, we shall unquestionably have the Lord standing within us. But even if we fall into some wicked thought—which, through the frailty of human nature, 205 we cannot avoid—we nevertheless do not lose him, God willing, provided that we return more quickly to the heart through repentance.

Thus, standing within us, the Lord commands that we be brought to him. He commands, I say, the holy angels, who share in mutual love, [Col. 0164A] to bring us to him, with that charity and sweetness by which a bride is usually brought to her bridegroom. But in another way he commands that we be brought to him: when we strive to fulfil his commands and precepts, we ourselves in some manner gladly bring ourselves to him.

“And when he had come near, Jesus said to him: ‘What do you want me to do for you?’” We draw near to the Lord when we approach him not with a lukewarm heart but with a burning one. We are asked what we wish him to do for us when he raises our will toward his own will, so that we may agree with him in one will. But let us see what this blind man, thus questioned by the Lord, wishes, asks, and seeks. “Lord,” he says, “that I may see.” This blind man desired neither gold nor silver from the Lord, but [Col. 0164B] asked only for the restoration of two lights. 206 If we too can obtain these eyes from God, we shall indeed be blessed. For the two eyes of the soul are understanding and affection. Whoever has understanding without affection, or affection without understanding, is as though seeing with only one eye. Yet it is better to see something than nothing. But it is far happier and more delightful to possess both eyes, namely affection and understanding. Let us also seek these eyes from the Lord, saying: “Lord, let me see with the eye of understanding and be wise with the eye of affection.” If, then, we ask God in faith for these eyes, he will answer us as he is described as having answered this blind man.

[Col. 0164C] “Receive your sight; your faith has made you well.” As if he said: Receive sight through understanding, because your faith has made you well. We call a person faithful who knows not to abandon his friend either in prosperity or adversity, but remains faithfully with him in both. Conversely, one is called unfaithful who loves his friend in prosperity but, abandoning him in adversity and distress, withdraws from him. Thus the Lord calls this person faithful, because he did not abandon faith in the Lord whether handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, spat upon, or killed; and therefore by this faith he deserved to receive sight through understanding. Hence it follows:

“And immediately he saw, and followed him, glorifying [Col. 0164D] God.” Immediately, therefore, he sees with the eye of understanding; he follows with the eye of affection; he glorifies God through the effect of his work. It follows: “And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.” Thus, as we have said, when we see by understanding, follow by the affection of the heart, and glorify by the effect of our works, all our people give praise to God; for not only our greater works but every least work ought to give praise to God. We must attribute nothing to our merits, reckon nothing to ourselves, seek no praise from people, but refer everything to the praise of God and the honour of his grace, from whom we have received all that we possess. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## 207. HOMILY XXV. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

[Col. 0165A]

Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry (Matt. 4).

Because today we begin the most holy commencement of Lent, today’s reading from the holy Gospel is rightly read to us. In it we find the temptations of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he wished to endure for us sinners. We also find how, through labours and fasts, he prepared himself against the assaults of the ancient enemy who was fighting against him; and by what means he finally overcame and cast down that same tempter. [Col. 0165B] In the same reading there is also set before us the insolent and obstinate pride of the tempting devil, and it is shown at the same time that, when he presumed to assail with his temptations the one to whom no stain of sin had ever clung, he withholds the hand of his malice and wickedness from no human being, however holy or innocent that person may be. For he is always tempting, always striving and seeking how he may overcome and cast down a person.

The pride of the tempting devil, therefore, and the victory of the Lord tempted for our sake, by which he cast down the tempter, are set before us so that we too may learn from them, after the Lord’s example, to prepare ourselves against the temptations of the malignant enemy rising against us, not only through abstinence of the flesh but also through patience, humility, and purity of heart.

[Col. 0165C] Although he lies in wait for human salvation at every time, nevertheless during these holy days he rages most fiercely, in order that he may obstruct and cast down a person—especially a spiritual person—and turn him away from the fervour of divine love. Such a person is recognized as having withdrawn from the world under Jesus’ guidance 208 chiefly so that, as though in the wilderness of spiritual life, he may resist the devil’s temptations more confidently and strongly. Therefore, that we may clearly know the order of those temptations with which the devil shamelessly and continually fights against Christ and against Christ’s members, let us carefully consider in order the reading of the holy Gospel.

The Evangelist says: “Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, [Col. 0165D] to be tempted by the devil.” First let us see, according to the allegorical sense, when our Lord Jesus Christ was led into the wilderness and tempted; and, harassed by daily temptations, let us follow the one tempted by the devil according to our measure. For, as Luke relates, he was baptized by John when he was beginning to be about thirty years old, and immediately was led by the Holy Spirit into the wilderness, where he endured the deceits of his tempter. He endured them not for himself but certainly for us, in whom God the Father placed the iniquities of us all. Although he was the Holy of holies and had no sin at all, after receiving baptism he nevertheless wished by fasting to make satisfaction to God the Father for us, in order to instruct us by his example that, after receiving in baptism the remission of all [Col. 0166A] sins, if strength of ability is available, we should completely renounce all the pomps and works of the world. But because not all receive—or indeed can receive—this word of complete renunciation of the world, one may be said, so to speak, to renounce the world who keeps careful watch lest he fall into its dead works.

## 209

“Jesus,” he says, “was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil.” I ask: what need was there for so great a Lord to be tempted, when by a single word he could have plunged his tempter into the abyss? He wished to be tempted in every respect according to our likeness, yet without sin, so that a wretched person, amid his miseries and temptations, might be encouraged by greater confidence of hope and might not complain that he had been forsaken and abandoned by him who never forgets to show mercy. Thus it was that, against most blessed Job, whom God himself approved with special praise, declaring that there was no one on earth—not merely greater, but not even like him—the Lord gave the crafty enemy permission to tempt. [Col. 0166B] The enemy burned his flocks, destroyed his household, crushed his sons and daughters, struck the health of his body, so that, sitting on a dungheap, he scraped away his discharge with a potsherd; and, to increase the temptation, he preserved the tongue of his wife. Yet as many wounds as the raging enemy inflicted, so many victories did he unwittingly furnish to the holy man.

Moreover, we must know with what weapons of virtue our King armed himself to shatter the darts of the wicked tempter; and with what weapons Christ’s soldiers ought also to arm themselves, that, bearing the standards of their King, they may be recognized by him [Col. 0166C] and follow him. These are not a visible shield, a bronze helmet, or a material sword, but fasting and the example of outstanding and great humility. Hence the Evangelist continues:

“And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry.” That he was able to do this through divine power inherent in his human nature is not especially astonishing, since he made Moses and Elijah admirable and renowned by a similar deed. For how could Moses, beloved of God, desire visible and earthly bread when for forty days and forty nights he had before him the bread of life and spoke with God as a friend is accustomed to speak with his friend? Likewise Elijah, satisfied by a cake baked in ashes and divinely given, [Col. 0166D] walked in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights as far as Horeb, the mountain of God.

But this fast, which bestowed upon them in a special manner a singular gift of God, is not to be understood by us as though we should entirely abstain from all food, since neither reason counsels this nor the necessity of human nature 210 permits it. Therefore, when the number of forty days and nights had been completed, he to whom, according to his divine nature, no misery of suffering can come, began, according to the mortality of his human nature, to be hungry and to challenge the proud enemy to a singular contest.

“And the tempter came and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.’” Here the highest wisdom and the highest malice, two beings strongest of all, entered upon [Col. 0167A] a very hard conflict. And that supreme malice laboured to discover whether that supreme wisdom had clothed itself in flesh by coming forth from the Virgin’s womb. But this truth was always hidden from its eyes. For, as the apostle says, “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). Seeing him teach wonderful things, do wonderful things, and abstain from food for so long, the enemy thought him the Son of God. Yet on the other [hand], seeing him grow weak, be sorrowful, sleep, and suffer hunger, he disdained to think that that supreme majesty could ever have stooped to such miseries.

“If you are the Son of God,” he says, “command that these stones become bread.” As though he said: I see that you suffer hunger, and I doubt whether you are the Son of God or not. Command, therefore, that these stones become bread, so that you may drive away your hunger through the immoderate gluttony of your belly.

[Col. 0167B] He answered and said: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” Our Lord Jesus chose to oppose his tempter only with the testimony of Holy Scripture, in order thereby to indicate that, when we are tempted, we too should know it to be most healthful and profitable to strive, armed with the shield of Holy Scripture, to pursue him until he fails. It follows:

“Then the devil took him into the holy city, set him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down.’” Oh, with how great fear, wonder, and indignation our mind is shaken on hearing that he whom cherubim [Col. 0167C] and seraphim tremble before, whom dominions, principalities, and powers adore, 211 together with all the host of heaven, did not disdain to be touched by the hands of this impious one. Yet our proud mind, which despises every unclean person and sinner and is indignant, is greatly confounded and rebuked by this. For if the companionship or sight of any unclean person displeased us, perhaps, driven away by our kicks, he would depart shamefully.

But our God is not such: far unlike us sinners—indeed, more righteous than all righteous people and holier than all holy people—yet he alone, together with his mother alone, was always in his own eyes humbler and more despised than all mortals. For he, utterly pure in himself, descended into the deepest mire of our sins, in order to raise his precious pearl from the mire: namely, the human being who had fallen voluntarily, [Col. 0167D] and to place him again in the purest and beloved place, there to serve thenceforth (*serviturum*; cod.: *serviturus*, “about to serve”). For such love of the human race he patiently endured spittle, blows, scourges, insults, and reproaches; and finally he died between two thieves.

And because he did not refuse to suffer all these things, which he endured through the devil’s members, what wonder is it that he allowed himself to be held by a bloodthirsty beast, set upon the pinnacle, and led onto a mountain? Some maintain that the pinnacle was the teachers’ chair, or the battlement of the temple where soldiers stand and defend the city from enemies. Therefore, in order that the Son of God might cast himself down from the pinnacle out of desire for empty glory, the devil, the head of all evils, persuaded him and, with words very true though a malicious heart, adduced testimonies of Scripture, saying:

[Col. 0168A] “For God has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.” From the time he was conceived and born and dwelt among human beings, angelic spirits rendered at every hour and moment the service due to their Creator, and watched lest he should ever strike his foot against a stone. Understand by “stone” the harshness of the Law. Against this the Son of God did not strike his foot, because he never wished either, through acting too leniently concerning sins, to nullify the strictness of the Law, or to lose the sweetness of mercy and loving-kindness by which he cherished and refreshed his own. Let us see how [Col. 0168B] 212 his foot stood evenly and straight, and in no way struck against the stone.

When the scribes and Pharisees bring before him a woman caught in adultery, he does not immediately command that she be stoned according to the precept of the Law, but first commands her accusers to examine themselves, saying: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7). If any one of them, foolish and mad, had attempted this, he would doubtless have heard, to his confusion, from him who searches hearts and reins a fitting accusation of his own sins. But he who is true truth and true mercy so weighed his words that he neither abandoned mercy for the sake of truth nor lost truth through the gentleness of mercy.

Jesus said to him: “Again it is written: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.” [Col. 0168C] A person is said to test another when he questions him in order to discover whether the one questioned knows or does not know, so that, if he finds him ignorant of what was asked, he may perhaps mock him. The Lord Jesus Christ would in some sense have tested God the Father if, puffed up by empty glory, he had cast himself down as though to be saved by God the Father. Thus it is as if he said: “For those things which I can accomplish through my own powers and understanding, I neither wish nor ought—since the Law forbids it—to test God.” In this too he gave us an example, that we should act in the same way. For a person who has received rational understanding and natural ability from God ought to order his life and actions according to the sense and understanding granted him by God. But when he can proceed no further by his own understanding, [Col. 0168D] he ought to entrust himself and all that is his to God alone. If he does not do this, he in some sense tests God—something which the Law altogether forbids. It follows:

Again the devil took him up onto a very high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.” How true is the saying of the prophet David: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73:23). Having been defeated in the first two temptations—namely gluttony and vain glory—the wicked one now dares for a third time to lift up his head. He who sees everything lofty does not fear to show all the kingdoms of the world 213 and their glory to him to whom only lowly things are pleasing, in case he might bend him toward desiring the honours and earthly elevations [Col. 0169A] of those kingdoms.

“All these things,” he says, “I will give you, if, falling in body, you worship me in mind.” He would indeed have worshipped in mind if such a suggestion had taken root in his soul; he would have fallen in body if he had sought temporal dignities and glories in any manner whatever. Therefore, no longer enduring his tempter, he rebuked him most imperiously, saying: “Begone, Satan. For it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.”

We may also understand the three temptations as three persecutions. By the first, that persecution which the Son of God deigned to suffer in himself; by the second, that which began in the primitive Church, namely against the apostles and martyrs; by the third, that which is to come upon the whole world under Antichrist. Although [Col. 0169B] we have evangelical authority that our Lord Jesus Christ was tempted by no more than the three temptations commemorated in the present Gospel, we should nevertheless suppose that, according to the weakness of human nature, he underwent other temptations also—not human temptations, I mean, such as human fault and vice suggest, but those which compassion for nature requires. For as there were two natures in him, divine and human, so he also had two wills, divine and human. I call divine the will by which he wished to suffer; human, that by which he grieved deeply over the destruction of the Jews who were to do this. Was it not as though a temptation to him when, seeing the city of Jerusalem, he wept over it with an affection of mercy and humanity? He had indeed come to suffer, but [Col. 0169C] he grieved greatly that this should be done through the hands of the Jews.

Seeing this, the enemy—who, from his antiquity and the subtlety of angelic nature, knows many things and has learned many things by most subtle inquiry—seeing, I say, how at Christ’s death the Jews were to be rejected and the Gentiles called, did not fear to test Christ in this matter, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves.” It is as if he said: “You grieve indeed over the destruction of the Jewish people, because they are your flesh and your bone. Command, then, that these stones—that is, the Jews, who 214 have become hard after the manner of stones—become loaves: that is, pass into your faith and into your body.” Thus even at Christ’s death he laboured by every means to prevent him from being delivered over to death, for this very cause and reason: lest the Jewish people be left liable for his death, and the multitude of Gentiles [Col. 0169D] that was to be spread throughout the earth be called to faith.

Hence we read in the Gospel according to Matthew that, while Pilate was sitting on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man; for I have suffered much today in a dream because of him” (Matt. 27:19). His divine will rejected this, and he wished to fulfil the dispensation for which he had come; and therefore he not unfittingly said to his tempter: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” This is as if he said: “It is not enough for me that God should be known only in Judaea. I desire my word to be preached among all nations, so that, called into my marvellous light, they may become a holy nation, a people for possession.”

[Col. 0170A] In the second temptation may be understood the persecution of the martyrs. The devil persuaded them to cast themselves down when, through his members, they were compelled to worship idols; yet though they were tested in many ways and tried by diverse torments, they could in no way be bent into denying their Creator. For it was a great temptation when all who killed the saints thought that they were offering service to God.

When this temptation had been overcome, the enemy grieved that he had been defeated by the patience and perseverance of the martyrs. He therefore turned elsewhere and introduced the incurable wound of hypocrisy, which today creeps through the whole body of the Church. By the pinnacle, which is the teacher’s chair, we understand the prelates. At the devil’s persuasion, they cast themselves down through hypocrisy, [Col. 0170B] when they present themselves outwardly as humble ministers of Christ but serve Antichrist all the more. All seek what is their own; all devote themselves to greed; yet, going about honoured, they do not render honour to him to whom they owe it.

215 But the final temptation denotes the persecution which will be under Antichrist, when there will be tribulation such as is called a very high mountain, because he is exalted and lifted above everything called God or worshipped. From that mountain all the kingdoms of the world are shown, when all the proud and reprobate are made ready for his service. Through their hand he exercises his tyranny upon the elect, and those whom he cannot capture through terrors he attempts to seduce through the world’s glory and riches.

[Col. 0170C] Having briefly set these matters forth according to the letter, let us now enter upon the moral sense [manuscript reading: *litterae*, “of the letter”]. Just as the Gospels which, by the ordering of the Holy Spirit, are read on the principal Sundays display in their beginning the beginning of conversion, and at their end the end and departure from this world of those who pass to the land of the living, so also the present reading from the holy Gospel indicates what the beginning of conversion is, what end follows, and what reward awaits those perfectly converted. But the intervening words of the same reading make known to those who seek and investigate the battles of the impending temptations against which we meanwhile contend with the spiritual forces of wickedness, until it is taken out of the way.

> [Note: [Col. 0169D] That is, until mortal life comes to an end.]

[Col. 0170D] “Jesus,” he says, “was led into the desert.” Since, as the Apostle says, almighty God “predestined” some, “called” them, and “justified” those whom he called (Rom. 8:30), Jesus is led in order that the ungodly may be justified and the proud humbled, when, at his coming, the sinful person is pierced by sorrow for sin and terror of judgment, and through fear of sin is converted to knowledge of God and of himself.

But whither is the Creator of all led? Into the desert. By the desert is understood the human heart, abandoned by its true and holy inhabitant, the Holy Spirit. In it are small animals with great: the animal and bestial excesses of carnal desires; a bestial brood and offspring of savage and useless thoughts; a seed-bed [Col. 0171A] of wicked words and deeds. Into this desert Jesus—that is, our Saviour—is led when the sinful soul, converted to its Saviour, who is Christ, vigilantly considers what and how great remedies of salvation are necessary for its wounds, and begins to ponder and meditate how the contritions and sorrows of its soul may be soothed and healed by its Saviour, that is, Christ. But lest it suppose that it conceived such an inspiration and desire of heart through itself or from itself, it is rightly added: “by the Spirit.” For he who fills all things with his goodness inspires these things, illuminating and watering the human being from above with the spirit of his mercy.

Finally, God works in some through the spirit of mercy, drawing them, snatched from the prison of the world and the jaws of the devil, [Col. 0171B] after himself toward the heavenly kingdoms, and bringing them into the place of the holy congregation and of the multitude beloved by him. But others, who seemed better, more perfect, and stronger than most, both in knowledge and in virtues, he wondrously and miserably permits, not without his true and just judgment, to be defiled by worldly actions. When the soul reflects and meditates anew upon this work of mercy and compassion, it must with continual thanksgiving bring before the eyes of its mind the benefits conferred on it by the Lord.

Why, then, is Jesus led into the desert? Surely because of what follows: “That he might be tempted by the devil.” Thus also the person into whose desert Jesus comes, whom he has already begun inwardly to draw to himself by internal inspiration, is led to spiritual conversion—not that he may rest, [Col. 0171C] but that he may work; not toward softness and bodily pleasures, but toward works of laborious discipline to be exercised within himself; not that he may enjoy his life amid abundance and delight, but that he may endure countless labours and struggles of the present life.

Yet amid these things there occurs something which greatly consoles the holy and spiritual soul: namely, that he whose dwelling and being are in the elect acknowledges that he is tempted in that soul and with it. To establish this more clearly for our consolation, and that we may believe it true, let us hear what he once said to his persecutor Saul: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). The one and same Lord has now ascended into heaven who descended from heaven, and [Col. 0171D] yet he declares that Saul injures and persecutes him. For whatever the members united to their head—that is, to Christ—suffer, he himself suffers and suffers with them. He who is the being of all things, without whom all things are nothing, conquers in his own, glories in his own, and whatever gifts he has bestowed on them from the nobility of virtues innate to himself, he works and perfects with them and through them. Therefore, when he comes in judgment, he will say to those who have endeavoured to serve his least members: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:45).

We should know, moreover, in what ways and for what causes a person is tempted; in these, if he does not yield, he will someday deserve to be rewarded as the faithful combatant of his Lord. A person is tempted in two ways: by days and by nights—that is, by prosperity and adversity. For it often happens [Col. 0172A] that, when someone resolves in mind and disposition to pass over to spiritual things, greater prosperity from the seductively flattering world smiles upon him, greater and sweeter comforts from friends follow, or perhaps he is pierced by the stings of greater adversity, so that, impeded by these, he may not enter from the mire of Egypt into the promised land. Therefore, lest he be recalled from the very entrance to heaven, if the winds of adversities blow, let him fix the anchor of hope in Christ, lest he be broken or scattered. If joy in prosperity occurs, let him not yield, but remain fasting with the Lord his God through days and nights, as the evangelist subsequently says:

“And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry.” A person fasts by day when he does not desire prosperity; he fasts by night [Col. 0172B] when he likewise despises every adversity. Hence David says: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song” (Ps. 41:9). He indeed sings a song to the Lord day and night who, standing equally firm in adversity and prosperity, does not recoil from himself through either. This the most blessed Job, of whom we spoke above, truly fulfilled: righteous before the scourges and adversities, he remained more righteous after the scourges had been inflicted. After loss of possessions, after the deaths of his children, after wounds of his body, he gives thanks for his preceding blessings, saying: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away” (Job 1:21). But concerning the imminent 218 pains and temptations, he sounds in the ears of the Lord of Hosts a kind of song, as it were, of joy and exultation, when he says: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not [Col. 0172C] endure evil things?” (Job 2:10). “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

If a person journeying toward the heavenly homeland has fasted in this way—that is, has not recalled his mind from its purpose either through present goods or adverse evils—he will afterwards begin to suffer a blessed hunger. For he seeks the sustenance of eternal salvation; he seeks to be satisfied among the guests of the Lord’s table. He hungers and thirsts for nothing other than the Lord’s justice. Of this hunger and thirst the Word of God says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6). Therefore, when those whom God the Father foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son judge it wholly unworthy to be conformed to this passing age, the snares of the tempter immediately [Col. 0172D] approach, as the words of the evangelist indicate:

“And the tempter,” he says, “came near.” To whom, I ask, does he come near? Surely to the Holy Spirit and to the human person. For just as the approach of the Holy Spirit to the soul—by inspiring good things and supplying good things—is good and sweet, so, conversely, there is an evil approach of the devil to the soul. He desires, as though it concerned him personally, to hinder its good; and if he cannot do so openly, he comes secretly.

“If you are the Son of God,” he says, “command that these stones become loaves.” The crafty tempter, having sufficiently discovered that the person recoils from manifest evil, attempts to overthrow him by a false good. For he conceals what is and lies about what is not. Hence Herod, by whom the devil is signified, when he could not extinguish the desire of the three Magi seeking Christ, sends them to seek the child with counterfeit goodness, saying: “Go and inquire diligently concerning this child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him” (Matt. 2:8). [Col. 0173A] He sends them to worship the one whom he intends to kill by his deceit and malice. Thus also the tempter, unable to deceive a person by his malice, falsely recommends good things. For he is confident that one whom he has not captured upon the level and secular 219 road, advancing afterwards to the lofty citadel of studies and virtues, he may hurl down to the depths—so that he may fall the more grievously, the higher he has surpassed the way of human conduct by living well.

“If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves.” It is as though the cunning ambusher inwardly addresses the person: “You ought to make known to all the aim [Col. 0173B] of your good will, inspired by God; tell and proclaim it to everyone—command, I say, that these stones become loaves.” By the stones we can understand soul and body, which are like stones insofar as they remain strong and immovable against the devil’s devices; these are changed into the sweetness of bread when they are transferred into Christ’s body. Hence that ancient serpent, the enemy of the human race, trained in a thousand arts of injury, speaks to the person more smoothly the more he seeks to cast him down from a higher place: namely, that, despising all things, he may transfer himself into Christ’s body and, on this account, rightly not doubt that he is and is called the Son of the highest Father.

Meanwhile it is necessary for the prudent mind to examine itself watchfully and diligently, and, wholly [Col. 0173C] fixed and trusting in God, to resist its tempter strongly and not turn back until he fails. For, as Scripture says, no one will be crowned unless he has contended lawfully (2 Tim. 2:5). To contend lawfully is to persevere in the conflict of contest until one deserves to carry off triumph over the enemy. Let the blessed soul fortify herself wholly, impress herself with the word of God, with which, when occasion requires, she may strike her tempter; and let her take up the very words of her tempted Lord, to be tested and proved, saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” This is as if she said: “I have resolved to leave all worldly things in mind and disposition; but man does not live by bread alone—that is, it is not enough for me [Col. 0173D] that I wish to become Christ’s bread and pass into his body, unless I also strive to obey every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

For there are some who think it sufficient for the salvation of the soul merely that they have escaped the common life of this world, and do not know how much imperfection they still have before the eyes of the highest Judge, both in word and in deed. But in the time of good conduct, gradually advancing from virtue to virtue, they desire that all that they are, live, and understand should live, understand, and please God alone; and according to the words and counsels of the Lord’s mouth, they endeavour to adorn themselves by nobility of conduct and exercise of virtues. By the Lord’s mouth good prelates [Col. 0174A] may be understood, as is elsewhere said concerning some who presumed to do things that should not be done and did not consult the mouth of the Lord (Josh. 9:14). For they are the Lord’s mouth who ought, by their preaching and the testimony of good works, to guard the flock entrusted to them. Therefore, those consult the Lord’s mouth who hasten to obey every word proceeding from the mouth of a good teacher by devout and holy works. It follows:

“Then the devil took him into the holy city, set him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down.’” The holy city of the Lord is the assembly or congregation of whatever holy souls; the pinnacle is the good teacher; the temple, the good and perfect subject. The pinnacle, according to some, is called the teacher’s chair, from which, standing [Col. 0174B] or sitting, he offers the people counsels of salvation. Thus I judge that the pinnacle not inappropriately signifies the teacher and master himself, who ought continually to preside over his subjects, who are the Lord’s temple, both by the authority of instruction and by the example of good conduct.

The Red Sea has now been crossed; the holy city—that is, holy conduct—has now been reached. In the very beginning of this way of life, the person has received great consolation from God’s sweetness; yet very harmful temptations still meet him, which may block the path he has begun. Hence it is not inaptly said: “The devil took him.” For while a person tends toward God through God’s grace preceding and following him, the devil, on the contrary, confronts him with the stings of temptations. Whom God takes up toward [Col. 0174C] perfection, the devil takes up toward temptation.

After the first temptation, therefore, 221 which each person suffers through zeal and love for conversion, this second temptation subsequently arises: that he is set upon the pinnacle of the temple. A person is set upon the pinnacle when he lifts and raises himself harshly above his teacher, and, while reproving that teacher’s judgments, neglects to consider himself. Thus it comes about that the prelate, outwardly honoured, is inwardly held in profound contempt by his subject. For the latter thinks that, if the care of rule fell to him, he would conduct everything better and more acceptably. And it is well said, “he set him,” because he cannot easily be torn away from this stubborn obstinacy. But if the one who presides seems less learned or less fit for this office, nevertheless, because he has been chosen for it by God’s ordering, he must not be judged and must not go unheard. Hence the Lord exhorts his disciples, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ chair. Do whatever they tell you” (Matt. 23:2). Likewise the Apostle says: “Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance, and there is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13:12).

Meanwhile, let us hear what that lion lying in ambush in secret, to seize the poor, says: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down.” For he recommends hypocrisy, that the person may seek the appearance of perfect holiness and seem to be what he is not. “Cast yourself,” he says, “down.” To cast oneself down [Col. 0175A] is outwardly to display the holiness of humility while inwardly wasting away with bitterness of heart and the zeal of envy. Let us further hear what the enemy, lying in wait by secret suggestion, says to the heart:

“Because God commanded his angels concerning you, and they will bear you in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.” It is as though a person says within himself, not knowing what he says: “You ought indeed to cast yourself down because God commanded his angels concerning you, and they will bear you in their hands. That is: you have renounced the world and worldly vices with such perfection; afterward, in this holy way of life, you have lived with such strict observance and guardianship of God’s commandments, that you are worthy for God so to guard and fortify you with the protection of holy angels, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone”—that is, lest (I mean knowingly and willingly) you fall into any offence against God, but “lest perhaps,” that is, by some accidental occurrence, you offend the eyes of his majesty.

In response to these things, let Christ’s soldier stand undaunted, cast down the enemy, and strive to fulfil in deed what the Creator of life has said. It follows:

Jesus said to him: “Again it is written: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.” This word *tento* (“I test”), a frequentative verb, is derived from *temno, temnis*, which means “I test frequently.” Therefore, let the person raised up inwardly repent that he has acted foolishly and thought foolishly against himself, and let him strictly restrain himself lest, through frequent contempt for prelates, he offend God. After this second temptation follows a third, in which whoever, having been tested, is not overcome will, when the term of this world has ended [Col. 0175C] and the battles of all enemies have been put to flight, be endowed with the fullness of everlasting reward. For it is most certain that the Lord prefigured all this under a certain dispensation. He permitted himself to be tempted only after baptism, in order to signify a future pattern of conduct and to show that, after his members advance toward God, they must then endure sharper snares of temptations. Hence it is added:

“Again the devil took him up onto a very high mountain.” The very high mountain is the marks of chastity and humility. Whoever, by God’s favour, has conquered the things we have already mentioned is shown to be truly harmless and humble, truly innocent in hands and pure in heart. [Col. 0175D] He is now reckoned not like any of the lesser persons, but as one of the mountains—that is, as one among the number of the perfect. Yet the devil takes him up again in a remarkable manner, because the higher and more sublime God has made him by taking him up through grace, the more eagerly the enemy presents himself to deceive and destroy him, so that he may corrupt and scatter by the wind of self-exaltation everything which excellence in chastity and humility had gathered in him. He now begins, because of the praiseworthy prerogative of virtues which he sees in himself, to desire honours, favour, and dignities; to extend himself above what he is; and, through ambition, as it were to possess what he cannot actually attain.

233 “And he showed him all the kingdoms of the world.” Understand the world as the person himself. Hence the human being is called a *microcosmos* [μικρὸς κόσμος], a “lesser world.” [Col. 0176A] By the kingdoms of the world understand all the members of the body. And the human person is rightly understood by “the world.” For if human dignity were not spread throughout the circuit of the world, what would there be from which the world might rejoice and take pleasure? The whole world, then, is the human being; and all the kingdoms of this world are, as I have said, all the members of the body, in which the person takes pleasure in himself, wishing through these to please and conform himself to this age.

“And their glory,” he says. To show the world’s glory is to seek the honour of pre-eminence; to show the world’s glory is to deliberate and ponder all the things that one might have accomplished pointlessly in deed, clothing, or manner of life. For he unhappily broods upon them and, as it were, chews and ruminates with certain teeth why, while still remaining [Col. 0176B] in the world, he did not do or say this or that. He reflects, in case he should somehow still be there, how praiseworthy he might have been in speech, how glorious in deeds, how splendid in clothing, how skilful and well-composed in every respect, and in all other similar things which this world seeks.

After such unclean desires of suggestion, let us hear the poisonous words of the wicked one:

“All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.” What things? Namely, the kingdoms of the world: that you may have bodily members so fit and well-composed that you take pleasure in yourself in them; and their glory: that you may now desire to possess this or that adornment and worldly glory. And in what way will I give them? “If, falling in body, you worship me in mind.” To worship (*adorare*) is said, as it were, to be akin to praying (*orare*). [Col. 0176C] One falls in body who commits sin in deed, but does not worship in mind if, quickly returning to himself, he washes it away by fitting satisfaction. But he worships and falls who consents to his own desires and pleasures and, by consenting, carries them out. The Lord’s chosen one David did not do this. He left to all a model and manner of repentance: he fell indeed in body, but did not worship in mind, because the repentance that taught him quickly wiped away what he had committed in deed.

But this temptation, of which we have spoken—the showing of kingdoms and their glory, where illicit things are sought and things hateful to God are desired—must be expelled all the more swiftly and forcefully because it is more dangerous and wicked. For unless such thoughts are quickly driven out of the heart, [Col. 0176D] evil deeds often follow, unless God is a helper in times of need. The following order of the Lord’s words therefore shows with what zeal and feeling the adversary who suggests such things must be cast out and abhorred. It follows:

Then Jesus said to him: “Begone, Satan. It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” For, as we have said, the enemy who introduces illicit things must be rejected and driven away; and our Lord Jesus Christ must be worshipped, established with us, and given the chamber of our heart—the one to whom all the members of our body ought to render their due service.

“Then the tempter left him, and angels came and ministered to him.” When these three temptations have at last been overcome, [Col. 0177A] it will then be joyful, because, by God’s command and help, that destroyer will vanish when he leaves the soul. He will leave it, I say, in such a way that he will not dare or be able to tempt it as much as he wishes and desires, though he does not cease to pursue the soul until the end of life. As he does not leave it while living, so he does not leave it while dying. For at the death of each person he is present, maliciously bringing forward whatever he can, in order to block the way of life.

Holy angels too are present as helpers and defenders of the soul: they are present to defend it from the death-bearing ravager; present to convey it, on the oarage of their wings, to the palace of the eternal King; present at its right and left as companions. When they have presented it to the Son of God, they abundantly minister to it from all the goods of its Lord—that is, so that it may possess eternal life most abundantly. [Col. 0177B] Then the tempter will truly and perfectly leave it, because when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption, it will experience no further temptation or imperfection, either in mind or body, from the devil or the world. May our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages, bring us to these goods. Amen.

225 HOMILY XXVI. FOR THURSDAY AFTER THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What is this proverb that you use among yourselves in the land of Israel, saying: ‘The fathers ate sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge’?” (Ezek. 18).

[Col. 0177C] The chosen and beloved prophet of the Lord, foreseeing with the prescient eye of his heart the present condition of the holy Church among prelates and subjects, seems in this compressed discourse to point out what harm the life of prelates who do not conduct themselves worthily brings upon their subjects. He likewise prescribes and demonstrates, in proper order, by what preceding merits of an approved life the one whom divine predestination raises to the summit of governance ought to advance, and what he ought thereafter to be in his teaching.

Therefore the prophetic spirit, foreseeing that there would be some in the Church who by the frivolity of their life and character would offer their subjects more occasions of scandal than any progress in edification and salvation, sets forth in these words the murmur of malice and detraction made by subjects—a murmur not pleasing to the eyes of the divine majesty: “What is this proverb that you use among yourselves in the land of Israel, saying: ‘The fathers ate sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge’?” These fathers are to be understood as the prelates of monasteries. For just as one who begets a son from his own flesh is called and is a father, so those who beget spiritual children for God are not inappropriately called and are fathers. A grape is the fruit of the vine. By the vine we may understand the spiritual life. This saying, therefore, concerns fathers and sons—that is, prelates and subjects.

For fathers eat sour grapes when prelates, setting aside the sweetness of divine contemplation, do not fear to entangle and stretch the whole intention of their mind in the bitter and empty [Col. 0178A] cares of the world. And when the fathers—that is, the prelates—eat sour grapes as we have said, it sometimes happens that the children’s teeth too are set on edge. By the teeth of the children may be understood the thoughts of the subjects. The children’s teeth—that is, the thoughts of the subjects—are set on edge because, just as one who has eaten something bitter, such as the hard and immovable fruit of trees, has his teeth so dulled by its very bitterness that they cannot be fitted to take sweet food, so indeed where such prelates exist, who attend more to earthly than heavenly things, when the time requires them to offer a word of exhortation, their speech not only becomes cheap in the estimation of their subjects, but also brings more bitterness [Col. 0178B] than edification and divine sweetness.

Thus it happens that they sometimes turn this parable into a proverb among themselves, because in place of the word of God they adopt words of disparagement and detraction for their own use. In silent thought, the weak mind of a subject sometimes murmurs against a prelate of this kind, and does not fear rashly to judge his life, because it is insufficiently circumspect, with this malicious reproach. “This man,” they say, “does not himself fulfil, by living worthily and laudably, the pattern of righteousness about which he instructs us in preaching. For he is insufficiently diligent in prayers, insufficiently watchful and attentive in sacred reading; and, since he himself is by no means careful and provident in guarding his own life, what benefit can he bring me, or what edification can his teaching [Col. 0178C] offer me?” That this rebuke of imprudent detraction is in no way pleasing to the divine sight, he himself immediately declares in the following words, as though reproving them:

“As I live, says the Lord, this parable shall no longer be a proverb among you in Israel.” It is as if he said: “So long as you do not fear to rage in the flame of kindled anger and indignation against your prelate, stirred by the gall of bitterness—if you wish to be what I am, that is, if you wish to possess eternal life—cease rashly examining and criticizing another’s life, and turn the eye of your mind toward examining the negligences of your own conduct.”

“Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins, that same soul shall die.” [Col. 0178D] Leave another’s life to be examined by my judgment, and provide carefully and diligently for your own souls. For just as the soul of the one whom you do not fear to judge through rash criticism is in my hand, so your soul also is subject to my power. “The soul that sins, that same soul shall die.” If he sins, he will receive the sentence of just condemnation; if you sin, you will experience the same punishment through my just judgment.

What sort of life he ought to have—he whom divine predestination raises to the summit of governance—and by what height of virtuous action he must strive upward, the text of the following passage openly indicates.

“And if a man is righteous and does judgment and justice.” [Col. 0179A] He is truly called and will be righteous when, renouncing the world and its desires, he recognizes what he truly is: namely, a sinner. Since this knowledge alone does not suffice for perfection, he must raise himself to a higher way; that is, he must do judgment and justice. He does judgment when, strictly judging himself for his sins, he punishes in himself in the present that for which he recognizes that he must be punished in the strict judgment. He also does justice when, making satisfaction to God for sins and diligently persisting in just works, he begins to live commendably. One raised to this height of good works must take the greatest care lest that occur which the following sequence of words declares:

[Col. 0179B] “He has not eaten upon the mountains.” To eat upon the mountains is to seek human praise for the manner of one’s praiseworthy life. Notice that it says “to eat,” that is, to seek human praise out of love and deliberate choice. For there are some whose minds are at times unexpectedly touched by a desire for praise; yet they do not eat upon the mountains, because they do not welcome this desire with love and delight, but, so far as they can, resist the temptation with God’s help. Conversely, there are some who are rightly said to eat upon the mountains, because for their righteous works they seek with all their affection and all their desire the favour of men. Whoever, then, as we have said, does not eat upon the mountains—that is, whoever, living worthily and praiseworthily, does not seek praise from [Col. 0179C] human lips—should also endeavour to avoid what the following text plainly indicates.

“And has not lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel.” Pagans who do not know God make and worship idols, bestowing upon works made by human hands the honour that they owed to God their Creator. We may also understand by the bodily eyes the inclination of ambition. Thus he lifts up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel who raises the eyes of his heart to the inclination of ambition, who desires with every wish to receive power and dominion over others, so that the honour and reverence owed to God may be rendered to him by his subjects. For just as a person who wishes to worship someone prostrates himself upon the ground, so likewise one who seeks the height of rule not for the gain of souls but solely from love of temporal glory desires, in a sense, to be worshipped, since he wishes to be revered by his subjects bowing humbly before him. And indeed, if it should happen that the care of others is entrusted in such a manner to him—not because God ordains it, but because He permits it—then what the text of the following passage seems to signify will sometimes be fulfilled.

229 “And has not violated his neighbour’s wife.” Our neighbour is our Creator and Redeemer himself. The wife of this neighbour may be understood as any congregation. Therefore, whoever has obtained a position of rule through the love and inclination of ambition violates his neighbour’s wife, because, serving not that neighbour—that is, our Redeemer—but his own desires, he does not gather spiritual gains in the congregation entrusted to him, nor [Col. 0180A] diligently sends ahead to the heavenly kingdom the fruit of his daily labour. It follows:

“And has not approached a menstruous woman.” A menstruous woman is defiled by her own flesh. Therefore, by the menstruous woman may be understood that congregation whose life and conduct appear base and reprobate to everyone. For there are some so eager for honour and glory that they neither fear nor blush to be set over a congregation made filthy by its own vices, provided only that they may acquire for themselves the name of honour. But if someone has received a place of rule not by his own will but by divine dispensation, the prophet indicates in the following words what he ought to be like in his teaching:

“And has not grieved a man.” When a superior hears the confession of his subjects, he must take the greatest care [Col. 0180B] not to grieve or trouble a person confessing his sins. He hears of the lives of some, at whose innocence he may rejoice; he also hears the grievous sins of others, for whom he ought to feel compassion and with whom he ought to suffer. He should indeed console the sinner, and, lest the enormity of his sins bring him into the abyss of despair, promise, to one who humbly confesses, hope of obtaining salvation and pardon from the Lord. The following statement is then added concerning this:

“He has restored the pledge to the debtor.” To restore the pledge to the debtor is, as we have said, to promise hope of forgiveness and grace to the sinner who humbly confesses. Hence, in Deuteronomy, the Lord commanded the children of Israel through Moses, saying: “You shall not take the upper [Col. 0180C] or lower millstone as a pledge” (Deut. 24:6). The upper and lower millstone are hope and fear. Therefore the upper or lower millstone is forbidden to be taken in place of a pledge, because one who preaches to a sinner must frame his preaching with such wise discernment that he neither removes fear by giving hope without profit, nor, by removing hope, leaves him in fear alone; rather, enlivened by hope, the sinner should be more and more kindled to seek heavenly things, while by fear he should be frightened lest he begin anew to repeat his former ways.

So that a superior may be able to impress this hope and fear upon the hearts of his subjects, he should strive, as is immediately added, to agree with the holy interpreters in his preaching. “He has taken nothing by violence.” To take nothing by violence is not to turn the meaning of Sacred Scripture away from the truth. He is said to seize Sacred Scripture by violence who, disagreeing with the holy interpreters, tries rashly to expound it not with sound understanding but according to his own pleasure. For if he does this—namely, if he confirms and strengthens his preaching by the testimonies of the saints—he will be able profitably to fulfil what follows here.

“He has given his bread to the hungry, and has covered the naked with a garment.” What is it to give bread to the hungry and cover the naked with clothing? He gives bread—the nourishment, that is, of heavenly teaching—to the hungry when he refreshes and instructs by the word of preaching a hearer who is receptive and attentive. But when he sees someone naked—that is, when he perceives someone to be without this grace, neither receptive nor attentive to hearing the word of God, [Col. 0181A] and naked also of spiritual knowledge and good works—he must, as blessed Benedict says, preside over such a one by a twofold teaching: he must labour to show what is good and holy not only by preaching, but also by living well.

But when, as we have said, he has given his bread to the hungry and covered the naked with clothing, the following words show with what intention and humility he ought to guard himself:

“And has not lent at interest.” Interest is to give one’s own and demand what belongs to another. He lends the bread of teaching at interest who seeks in his subjects not only the fruit of good works, but also desires that praise be offered to himself by them. Hence it is further said below: “And he has not received more.” He desires to receive more [Col. 0181B] than he ought who seeks his own honour more than God’s honour, and more than the benefit and salvation 231 of his neighbours. The prophetic discourse has already indicated and prescribed in the words we have noted what a superior ought to be like in his teaching; now, in what follows, it shows in fitting order what his life ought to be like.

“He has turned his hand away from iniquity.” Since works are customarily signified by hands, he in some manner turns his hand—that is, his work—away from iniquity when, for a good work, he gives praise and honour not to himself but to God. “He has executed true judgment between man and man.” A superior executes true judgment between man and man when he judges between God and himself in such a way that he leaves glory to God alone and attributes nothing to himself from his good works. Again, in another sense, a superior ought to execute true judgment between man and man: he should render submission to God, and equality and love to his subjects; so that, although he knows himself to be set above others by God’s ordinance, he himself may fear and love his superior, who is Christ. All these things which we have mentioned above are truly the Lord’s commandments, truly the Lord’s judgments, of which it is immediately added:

232 “And has walked in my commandments and kept my judgments, to do truth: he is righteous.” Whoever, therefore, is a good and perfect superior, walking in these commandments of the Lord in the order we have described—because he has not eaten upon the mountains by seeking human praise [Col. 0181D], because he has not lifted up the eyes of his heart to the idols of the house of Israel, that is, to the inclination of ambition, because he has not violated his neighbour’s wife, namely the congregation entrusted to him, by governing it badly; and likewise because he has done truth, by executing true judgment between man and man, that is, between God and himself—may fittingly be called righteous. Such a person will also attain, here and in the future, with praiseworthy and blessed effect of works, what follows:
