“He shall surely live and shall not die.” For he will have within himself, so far as is possible in this time of changeability, him who is Life living in himself; and when this corruptible body “puts on incorruption,” he will be endowed with such eternal glorification that he will remain in God and God in him without end.

## HOMILY XXVII. FOR FRIDAY AFTER THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

[Col. 0182A]

“It was a feast day of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now at Jerusalem there is a sheep-pool, called in Hebrew Bethsaida, having five porticoes” (John 5).

Beloved, Sacred Scripture is not inappropriately compared to the earth, which almighty God willed to create in order that all living creatures might be fed from it: human beings, domestic animals, beasts, birds, and creeping things. For it produces grass and herbage, which are food for animals; it produces grain and wine, which are food and drink for human beings. Thus Sacred Scripture too is like a certain earth: it produces [Col. 0182B] grass and herbage for those who are animals—that is, worldly people who live in an animal-like manner—when it simply teaches and instructs them how each should flee and avoid grievous and deadly sins. Nevertheless, it produces grain and wine for those who are human beings: namely, spiritual persons who recognize that they have been made in the image and likeness of God.

Herbage and grass grow without human labour; grain and wine are laboriously cultivated and obtained, now by ploughing, now by digging, as the Lord says to the first man: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3:19). Grain and wine signify the spiritual meaning and mystical understanding of Sacred Scripture, which is truly food and drink for every blessed soul; but it cannot be acquired [Col. 0182C] or found except through labour.

This grain and wine—surely the desirable refreshment of our souls—we shall be able, with God’s help, to find more abundantly in the earth now before us, that is, in this Gospel reading, if we seek diligently. For if it suggested to us nothing else than that simple mercy of our Lord and Saviour which he showed to a man sick throughout so many years, whom he mercifully healed when neither the man himself asked, nor another interceded for him, it would still be great refreshment and great consolation for those people who willingly labour for their salvation, who day and night implore his mercy as much as they can with the powers of their body and the affections of their heart. [Col. 0182D] For how would he not help those who ask, when he helped one who did not ask? How would he not save those who hope in the clemency of his mercy, when he saved one who did not hope for salvation from him?

But this sacred reading also contains something else that is not without refreshment for spiritual souls. For we—we are those who celebrate, and ought to celebrate, for the Lord this feast day of which we heard at the beginning of the Gospel. Although, burdened with the mortal body that we bear, we cannot completely avoid sins, yet, with God’s help, we are free from grievous vices. This is that feast day to which the prophet David exhorts us when he says: “Be still, and see that the Lord is gracious; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. 33). This feast day of the Lord is celebrated not in the tumult of the world, [Col. 0183A] but in the spiritual life, where people are gathered who resist vices and, as much as they can, devote themselves to virtues, seeking to be free for God alone and somehow to attain his vision.

Those two sisters Mary and Martha duly celebrate this feast day, because there are some souls which, with Mary, give themselves to divine contemplation, and others which, with Martha, apply themselves and minister to good action. Those with Martha labour humbly to render services to those in need; those with Mary are still and see that the Lord is gracious. Those with Martha are occupied with outward things; those with Mary contemplate inward things. The Lord gladly goes up to this feast day, because, although he is everywhere and in all places, he nonetheless dwells especially with and among those whom he finds free for himself, [Col. 0183B] whom he sees striving courageously, with such labours as they can, toward the vision of eternal peace. He is everywhere through the power of his majesty; he is with these through the clemency of his mercy. Of them it is aptly further said:

“Now at Jerusalem there is a sheep-pool, called in Hebrew Bethsaida, having five porticoes.” *Probaton* [πρόβατον] means “sheep.” The sheep-pool is, as it were, a pool for livestock, because the priests used to wash in it the animals that were to be offered to the Lord as a burnt offering. Bethsaida, moreover, is interpreted as “house of fruits” or “house of hunters.” This pool could rightly be called a house of fruits, because those who simply offered to the Lord for their sins the sacrifices made with animals received from them those fruits—that is, refreshment [Col. 0183C] and consolation—because they received pardon for their sins. But those who had a more elevated understanding and, through God’s inspiration, could recognize what those sacrifices prefigured, drew from them more abundant fruits, sweeter food, and refreshment for their souls.

That sheep-pool signifies the holy and righteous soul, which washes and cleanses within itself whatever it resolves to offer God from the affection and sweetness of its heart, lest any stain of pride or vain glory cling to it. The five porticoes which the pool has signify the five senses of the human being, which bring either good or evil to the soul. But because no one is found so holy as to be innocent in these five senses—for who among us has not seen with his eyes what it was not lawful to see, heard with his ears what harmed him to hear, or contracted many unlawful and harmful things through his other senses, namely taste, smell, and touch?—the Evangelist aptly adds:

235 “In these lay a multitude of sick persons, blind, lame, and withered, waiting for the moving of the water.” What mystery or meaning this order of words contains, our own misery can teach us; for however many sins we have contracted through sight of the eyes, hearing of the ears, taste, smell, and touch, so many sick persons, as it were, lie in our porticoes. Notice that he says: sick, blind, [Col. 0184A] lame, withered. We are sick in affection, blind in understanding, lame in action, withered in prayer.

Indeed, we are sick in affection when, as God’s grace fails within us, we grow torpid inwardly from love of him. A certain good soul felt and lamented this harmful sickness of the soul when she said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I am sick with love” (Song 5:8). By her we too are taught and admonished that, as soon as we feel ourselves becoming sick in the love of God, we should hasten to the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the delicate souls of the righteous, whether those now placed in the vision of eternal peace and glorying with Christ, or those still pilgrims in the misery of this life—in order to make known to our Saviour this sickness and sorrow of ours, and humbly implore the aid of their intercession. Unless this sickness is quickly healed by God’s mercy, a more grievous evil will follow: namely, hardness and blindness of heart. For as the inward light of former understanding and knowledge declines, one can recognize neither oneself nor God. When the inward light of the heart is darkened and withdrawn, one also begins to limp in action; for, like a lame person walking not on two feet but on one, if such a person performs anything good, he defiles and destroys it by many other evil actions.

After this multitude of sick, blind, and lame persons, there enters a multitude of withered persons when someone begins to become so dried up within himself that he can have no sweetness of inward savour in prayer, but, dry and withered, continually falls into worse things. Those who said, “Our soul is dry,” were held by this dryness. David asked to be preserved from this dryness when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow 236 and fatness” (Ps. 62:6). He immediately added what fruit he would receive from this inward sweetness of richness, saying: “And my mouth shall praise you with lips of exultation” (ibid.). As if he said: “If you fill me inwardly with the marrow and richness of your sweetness and grace, I shall praise your name, Lord, with joy and exultation.”

But to recognize and lament in themselves this multitude of sick, blind, and withered persons belongs only to spiritual people humbly waiting for the moving of the water. This movement of the water signifies the grace of compunction, which they desire and await all the more ardently because they find less outwardly in which to delight and rejoice. For what else is their day-by-day expectation—what they labour for, for which they mortify their bodies day and night—than that they may find this fruit of their labour? Yet the merciful and compassionate Lord does not despise the labour and expectation of his humble servants, as the Evangelist adds:

“But an angel of the Lord, at a certain time, came down into the pool, and the water was moved.” This angel signifies the grace of God. The angel of the Lord comes down into the pool when almighty God visits a blessed soul through his hidden grace, moving in it the water of long-desired compunction, through which it may burn more ardently in hope and desire of heavenly love. Since this grace is granted to a person not according to human will and desire, but according to the will and mercy of almighty God, it is rightly said, “at a certain time.” For often, while people await God’s mercy with every affection of their hearts and every labour of their bodies, persevering in vigils, fasts, disciplines, and other good works, and think that God will visit and console them magnificently, they find less than they seek, because the inward consolation for which they laboured comes more slowly. But sometimes, when they expect it less, they receive a more abundant grace of inward sweetness.

We may also understand differently the words “at a certain time.” Time is fear, or the delay of things. [Col. 0185B] That hour of heavenly visitation is fittingly compared to time, which passes swiftly, because it is brief: whatever a person receives there by tasting inward sweetness happens wholly, as if in haste and in passing. It cannot be possessed for long; yet, however brief it may be, it never passes without the effect of healing, as the Evangelist immediately adds:

“And he who first went down into the pool after the moving of the water was made whole of whatever infirmity held him.” We understand these words as we also believe them: whatever sin a person first recalls after that moving of the water which occurs when the angel of the Lord descends—that is, when God’s grace visits his heart—if he repents of it perfectly, he is without doubt cleansed and healed from it. For just as we know and believe that all a person’s sins, namely original sins and whatever actual sins there may be, are removed through baptism, so we ought truly and without hesitation to know that for whatever sin a person is perfectly compuncted in that hour of heavenly visitation, he is truly cleansed from it through God’s mercy. This is our faith and hope, which we have from the mercy of almighty God speaking through the prophet: “At whatever hour you turn and groan, you shall be saved” (Ezek. 18:21).

Whenever the person whose pool is within himself, who can continually possess from God’s grace that water of inward compunction, sins, so often may he also be healed. If he sins again, let him again have recourse to the laments of repentance; and he should know that in whatever state he endures and is found, in that state he is to be saved or condemned. But because there are some in the spiritual life who can neither recognize nor possess this movement of the water, that sick man of thirty-eight years, who could not go down into the pool yet deserved to be healed by the Lord’s command alone, consoles them. For the Evangelist says:

“Now there was a certain man there, who had been thirty-eight years in his infirmity.” Ten counted three times make thirty. The ten commandments are signified by the number ten; by the number three, those three—faith, hope, and charity—or again thoughts or wills, words, and actions. That man [Col. 0186A] who had thirty-eight years in his infirmity signifies the person who has sinned against the Lord in faith, hope, and charity; or in his thoughts and wills, words and deeds; or likewise by despising and transgressing God’s commandments. Eight is fittingly added to thirty, by which resurrection is figured, when the sinner who has thus grown old, who has persisted so long in sins, utterly despairs of himself and altogether doubts whether he can ever be renewed in God and rise again to hope of life. Yet the merciful Lord does not despise one so old in sin, so despairing, as the Evangelist immediately adds:

“When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him: ‘Do you wish to be made whole?’” The Lord asks the man lying in sins whether he wishes to be healed of his infirmity when, according to the customary clemency of his compassion, he mercifully supplies to him the will and ability to rise from his iniquity. Hence shortly afterward he added: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk.” He rises when, awakened by the Lord’s command—which comes inwardly to a person through God’s hidden inspiration—he raises himself from the deadly death of his sins. He takes up his bed and walks when, through continuous bodily labours in the spiritual life—the body being signified by the bed—he strives to remove the crimes of his former life, and thereby deserves to be restored to full health of soul.

Such a person must carefully beware the snares of the Jews, that is, of evil spirits, who plot against his salvation all the more subtly as they see that, if he falls, he can rise again only with greater difficulty. For if those who, through innocence and purity of heart and body, cleave to divine contemplation, are deceived by the devil into some transgression, they can rise more swiftly and be healed more easily, because they immediately return to the pool, immediately to the familiar remedy of customary compunction. But those who have grown old in sins, if after recovering health and receiving from God forgiveness for the ungodliness of their sins they fall, can rise again with all the more difficulty because they have been less worthy to attain the oft-mentioned movement of the water. Hence the Lord says:

“Behold, you have been made whole. Sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.” For before God, the fall [Col. 0186D] incurred in the spiritual life after renunciation of the world is believed to be graver and worse than all previous sins.

Therefore, because without God’s mercy and help we can neither worthily weep for past offences nor avoid future ones as is necessary, let us humbly implore him who can do all things, that he may deign to visit our pool through his angel. For unless his gift and grace come down to us and within us, the water of our heart cannot be moved unto health. It accords indeed, and accords greatly, with his goodness and mercy that he himself should deign to visit and gladden us—the one to whom alone we look—since we have and seek no other joy than that which we can possess in him and with him. For if he once descended from heaven to earth in order to free and bring forth the souls of his own from the darkness of hell, should he not, by the obligation of that same mercy, imprint and offer to us—to those who desire and seek him—the pledge of his love? What punishment of Gehenna could be greater or more cruel than that which occurs when what is awaited is not received, when what is hoped for, sighed for, and desired every day and every hour is withdrawn?

Let this angel, then, come down—come down to us—so that, cleansed and healed from our infirmity, having passed these holy days with every safeguard, care, and watchfulness, and bearing a joyful triumph over our enemy, we may deserve to attain the glory of the Lord’s resurrection. May our Lord himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

240 ## HOMILY XXVIII. FOR THE SATURDAY BEFORE THE SECOND SUNDAY OF LENT

[Col. 0187B]

“Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother” (Luke 9).

The more abundantly these Gospel words overflow with the grace of heavenly sweetness, the more carefully they must be investigated by us with mystical understanding. “Jesus took,” says the Evangelist, “Peter, James, and John his brother.” The Lord Jesus takes up those whom he has disposed by his grace to bring to the summit of this perfection, which is mystically signified by these three names: namely, that they may possess knowledge of God and of themselves, strive to overthrow vices within themselves, and, with the filth of vices uprooted, deserve to taste [Col. 0187C] how sweet the Lord is.

“And he led them,” he says, “apart up a high mountain.” Therefore Jesus leads apart up a high mountain all whom he saves when he advances them to the sublimity of the spiritual life and of good works. He leads them apart when, through inward inspiration, he begins to separate them from the sinful condition of their former life. Then what follows occurs:

“And he was transfigured before them.” Certainly all the sacraments enacted in a faithful person in the holy Church may be called a figure of Christ, such as the washing of holy baptism and other such things established as remedies for the soul. Even unbelievers receive these in faith; they sometimes come to the thresholds of the Church and fortify themselves with the sign of the holy cross. But the faith that appears outwardly remains utterly empty within of good works. Therefore, when by evil living they contradict those things which, as we have said, they received in faith, they behold the Lord Jesus, as it were, in a foul figure. But when, leaving the world, they strive to preserve in character and life those same things which they received in the sacraments, the Lord Jesus is immediately transfigured before them in another figure, and through zeal for good works they themselves are conformed to him.

“And his face shone as the sun.” Since it is evident that a person is recognized more by his face than by another part of the body, by the face may be understood all who are perfect: those who strive to advance from virtue to virtue in the spiritual life, so that in them it may be recognized more clearly than light [Col. 0188A] that they truly belong to Christ’s body. Though they are never chosen to instruct others by the word of teaching, through their diligent pursuit of a praiseworthy life they nonetheless offer to all who see them a great lesson or example of perfect conduct.

But more properly and particularly, prelates are figured by the face: those, that is, who labour to preside over their subjects in such a way that God may be recognized in their character and life. Such people may not inappropriately be compared to the brilliance of the sun, because, just as the sun has by nature both properties—namely, to enlighten and to warm—so they in a sense enlighten and kindle, because they preside by word and example. They enlighten when they drive the darkness of ignorance from the hearts of their hearers by the word of their teaching. But when they strive to practise in their own life and conduct what they teach in words, they undoubtedly kindle those whom they enlighten to accomplish good works. It follows:

“His garments became white as snow.” If we understand prelates by the face, we may not unfittingly understand subjects by the garments. Therefore, just as a garment does both things—it covers nakedness and adorns a person—so all perfect subjects established in the spiritual life strive to cover their former sins before God’s sight by daily lamentations or by any good works, and labour to adorn themselves with the merits of virtues. Thus these garments become white as snow. Snow is by nature cold, [Col. 0188C] but when it is warmed by the sun’s heat, it melts and is immediately changed into water. Likewise those who formerly persevered in sins and remained entirely cold toward God’s love, when warmed by the word of preaching, are immediately melted into tears through the grace of the Holy Spirit; and being melted, they are undoubtedly made white.

Then follows what the Evangelist adds:

“And Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.” By Moses, who was a lawgiver, the Law itself is understood; by Elijah the prophets are figured. Therefore Moses appears to all the perfect who, as we have said, have been enlightened, when they already perfectly know what the Law forbids or commands them to do; namely, when they strive inwardly to imitate in themselves, by typological understanding, what the letter of the Law seems outwardly to command, and again observe in a mystical sense what the same Law forbids, and are unwilling of their own accord to admit anything from the unlawful things it prohibits.

They also behold Elijah appearing, because, taught through the Law in the manner we have described, they now begin to prophesy to themselves concerning the hope of future goods. Moses and Elijah therefore appear not silently, but speaking with him about the very things mentioned above. For while a person was still given over to worldly acts, whatever perhaps he perceived outwardly by hearing from the Lord’s Law was in a sense mute to him and did not speak [codex: “and with”] with him, because he did not strive inwardly to practise by good works what he heard outwardly. But when, enlightened as we have said, he has come [Col. 0189A] to the knowledge of God, he will now be able to use Peter’s words:

“Lord,” he says, “it is good for us to be here,” as though any blessed person should say to the Lord: “Lord, where we were before, when we lived according to the judgment of our own will, it was evil for us to be. But here—that is, in the purpose of spiritual life which we have undertaken through your inspiration—it is good for us to be. It is good for us, I say, to be here”: that is, for both our human elements, soul and body, henceforth to cleave to your commandments.

“If you will,” he says, “let us make here three tabernacles: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” By these three tabernacles spirit, soul, and body may be mystically figured. For by the words “one for you” love is fittingly understood, because Christ, the new man coming into the world, did not inflict the punishment of terror, but rather taught those things that belong to sweetness and love, when in his honeyed voice he proclaimed: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. 3:2). Conversely, by the words “one for Moses,” fear may be understood, because in the Law which God gave to the children of Israel through Moses no promise of the kingdom of heaven was given; sins alone are commanded to be punished, as it says there so often: “Whoever does these or other things shall die the death.”

By Elijah, moreover, any teacher or preaching itself may be understood, because Elijah the Lord’s prophet not only foretold future things, but also strove to call God’s people back from error to the way of truth. Every blessed person makes three tabernacles: one for love, one [Col. 0189C] for fear, one for preaching. Since the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, we ought to know why in this passage love is placed before fear. It is put first in dignity, because love, so to speak, holds primacy. For what belongs to supreme perfection reaches the sweetness of inward contemplation through love; fear holds, in a sense, a lower place, because those who are less perfect know only to fear the punishment of eternal damnation and have not at all tasted the joys of inward sweetness.

Since, therefore, we know this to have been placed in this mystical order, let us in proper order put fear before love. Each person makes a tabernacle for fear when, from dread of death or future punishment, he strives to abandon past sins and turns to the laments of repentance. But he builds a tabernacle for love when, setting aside servile fear and quieting the tumult of carnal desires, he does not cease to labour day and night in good works, now longs for the vision of his Creator, and hastens to attain the joys of eternal contemplation. Then he will also be able to make a tabernacle for preaching, because then he perfectly prepares his mind for understanding the sacred word; and, with his mind gathered in God, he always preserves by reading and recollection what he has heard, and does not lose from memory the commandments of life which his understanding can grasp.

Let every blessed person, then, say—let him say: “Let us make here three tabernacles: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” For, as is clear, the tabernacles are called the encampments of soldiers. Though three tabernacles are named here, they are spiritually made one when these three—spirit, soul, and body—are united harmoniously in Christ’s soldiery. Therefore, when any of the perfect resolve within themselves to make these tabernacles, what the Evangelist adds occurs in this blessed resolve:

And while he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. We know indeed that a cloud has by nature both properties: it brings rain and casts shade. What can more fittingly be understood by the cloud than the irrigating grace of the Holy Spirit? For as rain soaks and drenches the earth, so the grace of the Holy Spirit abundantly waters the human heart with its many gifts [Col. 0190B].

It should also be noted that it is not said simply, “a cloud overshadowed them,” but “bright” is added; for this same grace, having filled the mind, drives away the blindness of vices and illumines it. It also overshadows: just as shade refreshes one scorched by the fierce heat of the sun, so it grants refreshment—that is, forgiveness of sins—to the mind which it illumines and which formerly burned with carnal desires. Finally, when this cloud—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—has thus flooded, illumined, and overshadowed the human heart, that desirable voice immediately sounds forth, namely the voice of inward visitation, which says:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” This, I say, is the spiritual understanding [Col. 0190C] which, through the inspiration of divine grace, you have now received: it is beloved by me and, without doubt, pleasing to me. This I love within you; this I truly praise and approve. Listen to it. If it suggests any virtue or good work, strive to follow it; but whatever another understanding—that is, the carnal understanding—may attempt to persuade you, turn away the ear of your heart.

“And when the disciples heard this, they fell upon their faces, and were greatly afraid.” Therefore, when any who are to be saved, having deserved to taste the grace of this visitation, hear this delightful voice speaking within, they indeed fall upon their faces: that is, in the deep humility of their hearts they prostrate themselves before God and in a manner lie upon the ground before the Lord. For they no longer maintain a stance of pride; rather, in consideration of their weakness [Col. 0190D], before the eyes of the supreme Majesty, they humbly cast themselves down and make further progress in divine fear.

“Then,” he says, “Jesus came and touched them, and said to them.” What and how great this approach is, how sweet and delightful, human speech cannot express; experience alone teaches it. He approaches because he joins himself to chosen souls; and those whom he first touched so that they might fear, he then awakens so that they may love. He touches with the touch of love those whom formerly, by his inspiration, he taught to be perfected solely in his fear.

“Rise,” he says, “and do not be afraid.” Rise—that is, lift your hearts upward; henceforth place confidence in my mercy. Until now you have laboured under the compulsion of servile fear; in service you have toiled day and night [Col. 0191A]. But now do not be afraid: love me as a most gentle Father, whom formerly you strove to fear as a most severe Lord and Judge. As previously it pleased you to serve me with trembling, so now, setting aside penal dread, let it please you to accomplish every good work in love.

“And lifting up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone.” In this place intellectual rather than bodily eyes are to be understood. To what do these blessed persons, and those destined for blessedness, who have experienced the things of which we have spoken, lift their spiritual eyes except to things above? And when they direct them there, they behold no one except Jesus alone, because in that blessed hour they find in themselves nothing apart from their salvation. Or, if we wish to understand it simply [Col. 0191B], when they have thus been illumined through the Spirit of love, whatever they behold among outward things becomes wholly salvation to them, because they draw it to their own salvation.

But since the human mind cannot remain long in contemplation, and, repelled by the immensity of such height, quickly falls back into itself, it is now rightly said:

“As they were coming down from the mountain.” In the sublimity of contemplation, because the weakness of corruption cannot, as we have said, sustain itself there for long, they descend to lower things; they return to outward good works; they are nourished by the memory of God’s sweetness which they have tasted beforehand—outwardly by devout deeds, inwardly by holy desires.

“And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them [Col. 0191C], saying: Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man rises from the dead.” In this divine command we are taught that God’s elect, after tasting beforehand the sweetness of heavenly contemplation, ought always to preserve themselves in humility. They should not seek the glory of human favour through it, nor delight in taking up a position of rule; rather, they should keep themselves within themselves, lest, by displaying to their neighbours too soon goods still tender, they lose them.

“Tell the vision to no one,” he says, “until the Son of Man rises from the dead”: that is, let silence please them until they rise to such perfection that they are neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity. But when the Son of Man has risen from the dead—that is, when the spirit is so quickened in the Lord that it neither falls when raised by praise [Col. 0191D], nor withers when struck by reproach—then at last they fittingly and in due season announce to their neighbours that blessed vision of contemplation which they themselves could see, at least, through a mirror and in an enigma; and they kindle their neighbours’ souls to love of the heavenly homeland.

## 247. HOMILY XXIX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY OF LENT

“Jesus went out and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders and cried, saying: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David. My daughter is grievously troubled by a demon” (Matt. 15).

In all the words of sacred and Gospel reading, if we look more carefully, the whole salvation of the human being is found: first, what the beginning of conversion ought to be; and after the beginning of conversion, what degree of perfection, with God’s help, ought to be sought [Col. 0192A]. This is also commended to us by the present reading of the holy Gospel, in which the Holy Spirit so narrates what was outwardly done by the Lord as also to indicate what he daily works invisibly.

“Jesus,” he says, “went out and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon.” Jesus, our Saviour or salvation, is said in a manner to be within when he permits a person to live unlawfully according to the will and desires of his own heart, and sets before one rushing toward every crime no impediment by which he might come to his senses. Then salvation is hidden and remains within, while nothing is done for the soul’s salvation, and the person is boldly carried headlong into everything that endangers and destroys him [Col. 0192B]. But then the Lord Jesus, who has long kept silence and remained within, comes out by a marvellous condescension when, in his hidden ordering, he determines to work a person’s salvation.

By this blessed and memorable going out he withdraws into the region of Tyre and Sidon. Tyre means “distress,” Sidon “useless hunting.” In mercy, therefore, the Lord who goes out withdraws into these regions when, by his inspiration, body and soul—which may be understood by Tyre and Sidon—begin to tear themselves away from each other [codex: *evellere*, “to tear out”], having formerly maintained unanimous consent in the vices and sins of the flesh. Tyre, which is the soul, begins to be distressed over the useless hunting of Sidon, which is the body. For in the bitterness of its soul [Col. 0192C], it considers how it has spent the whole time of its life living like a beast, and has subjected its body, occupied with the useless hunting of sins, to shameful and criminal actions.

When a person is thus anticipated by God’s abundant grace, when, I say, the Lord Jesus goes out and withdraws into the region of Tyre and Sidon in the manner described, what follows takes place from heaven:

“And behold, a woman.” Behold—that is, without delay the woman comes out: namely, the soul divinely softened and converted, which had formerly been hardened by sins after it had set aside fear and love of God. And this woman was a Canaanite. The addition that this woman is called Canaanite is not superfluous. Canaanite, indeed, is interpreted “moved,” “trader,” or “little poor woman.” As I see it, the soul is fittingly called moved when, now possessed by desire, it longs—despising the foulness of its offences—to renounce worldly vanities. It also becomes a trader, desiring to sell useless and shameful works in order to acquire the precious adornments of virtues. For everyone who sees gives what is cheap in order to buy something dearer. Thus this soul also, a good trader, gives the useless and cheap price of sins, in order to possess the noble and beautiful merchandise of merits. It also becomes a little poor woman when, in true humility of heart, it recognizes and repents of the innumerable crimes it has committed. Hence it follows:

“Coming out from those borders, she cried, saying: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” It should be noted that she is said to have come out from those borders [Col. 0193A]. There are three stages of sins: beginning, middle, and end. The beginning of sinning is consent; the end is the completed act; between these two extremes is the middle, the concupiscence of the flesh. The Apostle Paul calls this the law of the members, which resists the law of the mind (Rom. 7:23), because, like a certain tinder of sin, it importunately intrudes even upon the soul of the perfect.

Therefore, this Canaanite woman, having come out from those borders—from consent to sin and from the act of sin—yet still often troubled by the intermediate pleasure of sin, what will she do? It follows:

“She cried, saying: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David. My daughter is grievously troubled by a demon.” Let us see in what order this soul advances and by what acts or dispositions it shapes itself [Col. 0193B]. First it came out by abandoning evil. Secondly, it cried, confessing with the inward desire of its heart, in order to receive the salvation for which it hoped. For the heart’s desire and confession are before God a kind of cry uttered by a living voice, just as Moses, silent with his mouth yet crying in his heart, is told: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14:15).

Therefore this Canaanite woman cries—namely, the soul moved away from the world, skilled in trading, a little poor woman, that is, humble in its own eyes—saying: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” As though it said: “Although, Lord, I have hope and trust in you, because you are merciful unto thousands, taking away iniquity and sins, nevertheless I know and consider that with your two feet—mercy, namely, and judgment—you traverse the ends of the earth; and therefore I tremble and groan, knowing and recalling in my mind [Col. 0193C] that you who never forget to show mercy also never abandon your most righteous judgment.”

Thus the Psalmist, mentioning both feet, says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1). For he did not affirm that mercy without judgment, or judgment without mercy, befits the just God; rather, he declared that he would sing to the Lord of both mercy and judgment. Hence every blessed soul prays, lest, mercy being withdrawn, it be condemned by the sentence of the just Judge, saying: “Lord, if I am examined by you with pity set aside, I perish. Therefore, draw back and remove the foot of justice, and mercifully extend the foot of mercy, which, embracing and kissing, I may breathe more confidently upon account of your infinite mercies. Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.”

For I call you Son of David in this hope and confidence: that as you forgave grave crimes to David your servant, so you may likewise mercifully deign to be propitiated for my iniquities [Col. 0193D]. Or for this reason, my God, I call you Son of David: that you may deign to remember that you are my Creator, and that you yourself were created for my sake, made human for me. Have mercy on me, Lord.

“My daughter is grievously troubled by a demon.” I would indeed correct my sins by making satisfaction to you, but I cannot, because my daughter is grievously troubled by a demon. In saying that her daughter is grievously troubled by a demon, she shows that some are troubled beneficially and some grievously. Blessed Job deserved to be troubled beneficially—indeed, to be tested—because in temptations he remained the same person he had been before, and therefore through temptation he was judged worthy to be crowned [Col. 0194A]. Judas was tested grievously and to no purpose, because, consenting to the temptation of avarice, he was rejected and condemned by God.

Therefore one is grievously troubled who cooperates, through consent and pleasure, with the devil as he persuades and suggests; but one is beneficially troubled who is found not to consent at all to the devil who troubles and persuades. This is the one of whom it is written: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he shall receive the crown of life” (Jas. 1:12). Thus the sinful soul grieves that it is troubled grievously and not beneficially, when it yields through consenting to temptation. Therefore it cries with a strong cry, speaking to the Lord with the inward desire of its heart: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” But because it often happens that amid so many groans and cries it is not heard according to its wish, the text rightly continues:

“But he did not answer her a word.” What Word? He did not answer—that Word, assuredly, which is accustomed sweetly to touch a person within, concerning whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), through whom all things were made. Again it is said of him: “He sent his Word and healed them” (Ps. 106:20). Therefore the Word does not answer as long as inward sweetness is not sent, and thus the power of healing is sometimes delayed.

But *word* is also used for *deed*, as in the passage: “And there was not,” Scripture says, “a word in his house which he did not show them” (Isa. 39:2). The almighty Lord does not answer a word [Col. 0194C] when he does not yet allow a person to bring the desire of good will to pure and righteous works. But if that person perseveres in good will, greater gifts of salvation come to him through God’s inspiration. Hence it fittingly follows:

“And the disciples came.” Since the name and authority of a master call forth a disciple’s fear, the senses of fear are aptly expressed through the disciples. For the more frequently the sinful soul examines itself, the more it will be filled with the grace of divine fear. These senses of fear indeed never cease from prayers, but continually ask the Lord, as Paul says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17). No one can always devote himself to prayer. But the person truly prays without ceasing who, whether eating or drinking, sleeping or doing anything else, strives so to do everything in the Lord’s name that it may rightly be called prayer before the Lord [Col. 0194D].

Therefore, what do the disciples—that is, the senses of fear—ask as they come? “Send her away.” As though they said: “Send her away”—that is, make her free from sins; send her away and make her attain her petition. For no one will be able to hold or hinder her if your gracious and good will permits her to follow you. “For she cries after us”: therefore send her away, that she may be able, by your power, to possess us. Or she thus cries after us because she hopes for heavenly things, but body and soul still seek earthly things.

While God invisibly accomplishes all these things and has hitherto concealed himself and not answered [Col. 0195A], “even though he does not give because he is a friend, yet because of her persistence he rises and gives her whatever she needs.” Hence it follows:

“But he answered and said: I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” Here the Spirit of counsel, which among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit enumerated from the first Sunday of Septuagesima is assigned to this fifth Sunday, gives wholesome counsel to the soul which seeks him. “I was not sent,” he says, “except to the sheep.” By sheep are figured innocence, or simple and harmless thoughts. Therefore, the lost sheep are those who at one time lost their innocence, but, changed from wolves into lambs, live meekly and innocently in the house of Israel. They themselves have now become the house of Israel: that is, they seek with a pure heart to contemplate and see the Lord [Col. 0195B].

“I was not sent except to the sheep.” As though the Angel of great counsel said to a person: “You press me urgently, seasonably and unseasonably begging from me salvation and counsel for your soul. Behold, if you desire to be freed from the death of sins, you must imitate the innocence, simplicity, and purity of heart of those whom I have described, and seek the fellowship of their household. For I was not otherwise sent by the Father, nor does my soul delight except in such persons.”

Hearing this, the prudent and faithful soul does not despise the Lord’s commands, as follows:

“But she came.” From where, or whither, did she come? She came by leaving the world; she came in body; she came also in mind; she came also by doing whatever good she could. Nor content with this, she also worships: that is, preserving her good works in humility; she worships by prostrating her mind before God or her Master with all devotion; she worships also by humbling herself before all. And though she does not physically lie at everyone’s feet, nevertheless, in the innermost depths of humility, she subjects herself to all [Col. 0195C].

“Lord,” she says, “help me.” First she had said, “Have mercy on me”; secondly, the senses of fear had said, “Send her away”; now, thirdly, she implores the Lord’s help, saying: “Lord, help me.” For where the battle is greater, the greater protections of the Saviour must be sought. What is the warfare of the whole spiritual life except an unceasing conflict with the enemy? “Lord,” she says, “help me.” As though she said: “Lord, placed amid my enemies, I contend alone in the struggle, and as long as breath remains in me I must engage in this duel. Prepare for me your accustomed help, for I have no consolation apart from you; grant that my enemies may never have dominion over me” [Col. 0195D].

Having received such a petition, he again exhorts her to advance toward better things, saying:

“It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs to eat.” These words are truly words of the Holy Spirit, uttered from the Father’s eternal wisdom. The children’s bread is the great and sublime teaching of the elect; or the children’s bread is the inward sweetness of the peacemakers, concerning whom the Gospel says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5:9). This bread must certainly not be thrown to dogs. For in the Old Testament, where clean animals are distinguished, the dog is reckoned among unclean animals. Therefore dogs signify those who sin insolently and proudly [Col. 0196A]. It should be noted that he does not say “to a dog,” but “to dogs,” in order to signify those unclean in both persons: namely, in heart and in deed.

Thus this bread is thrown to dogs when the Lord’s word is received with heart and body unclean, and the eye of the heart is not cleansed in order to taste its inward sweetness. Therefore the Lord admonishes each person and says: “If you wish to eat the bread of my children, keep yourself undefiled inwardly and outwardly, because it is not good to throw this bread to defiled souls and bodies. Rather, receive my word by hearing in such a way as to produce in deed the fruit of good action.”

As the Lord thus exhorts and admonishes, the blessed soul, receptive and eager for such teaching, replies within itself from the deep humility of its heart in the words of this blessed woman:

“Yes, Lord. It is altogether as you affirm, Lord, and so it ought to be. But even the little dogs eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.” As dogs signify those who sin proudly, so little dogs may signify humbled sinners; crumbs, slight grace; the table, abundant sweetness; and masters, the rank of prelates and of other perfect persons.

For the Lord and our Saviour prepared a certain table for his children, on which are set various courses of delights: the surpassing sweetness of God, as I have said, and understanding of the mystery of God’s kingdom, which is the hidden and profound knowledge of the Scriptures. The little dogs—that is, those who are humble sinners in their own eyes—do not approach this table, nor do they seek this seat in order to eat the children’s bread. Rather, persevering in a humble and contrite heart, they sometimes say within themselves [Col. 0196C]:

“We, Lord, who were once dogs by sinning insolently, are now little dogs—that is, sinners humble in our own eyes. Give us crumbs; give us a little grace from the immeasurable grace of your elect; give us crumbs which fall from the table of our masters. They, having experienced great benefits within themselves, do not consider it a great thing to be comforted by a small grace of your sweetness. But for us, weighed down by the burden of sins, even the smallest portion of your grace would suffice, if our wretched life could in some way merit it from you. We do not say, Lord, that they do not commit sins; rather, they judge it wicked and abominable even sometimes to think of sins, and for this reason they worthily await from you the reward of no small recompense [Col. 0196D]. If any hope or confidence were granted us that we might escape the very torments of Gehenna, we would believe ourselves fully satisfied.”

Again, in another sense, the children’s bread may be understood as the spirit of love, which is ministered and set forth from above in an overwhelming abundance of sweetness only to God’s beloved and elect children. When the sinful soul, which has not yet deserved by repentance to attain the spirit of fear, desires to receive this children’s bread—that is, the spirit of intimate love—it fittingly hears from him who knows how to provide for everyone’s salvation: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.”

“It is not good,” he says [Col. 0197A]—as though to say, “It is not good because it is not just, nor does it accord with my equity, that you who have imitated the life of a dog by sinning proudly and insolently, and who have not yet learned through worthy satisfaction of repentance how you ought to fear me, should receive even a little of the sweet bread by which I customarily satisfy my children.”

While the Lord thus says inwardly in the human heart that it is neither worthy nor just to throw the children’s bread to dogs, the humble and truly repentant soul agrees with the Lord as just Judge, replying in these words: “Yes, Lord, but even the little dogs eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.” As though, in great contrition of heart and spirit, the soul said [Col. 0197B]:

“I know, Lord, that it is fair and fitting, as you affirm, that the sweet bread of your children should not be given to dogs—that is, to the unclean and defiled. Yet little dogs may eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.” By little dogs, as we said above, understand humble sinners; by crumbs, every slight transgression; by the table, a heart abounding in the sweetness of the Holy Spirit.

Crumbs fall from the table when children of God, visited by the abundant sweetness of the Spirit of love, strictly judge and rebuke themselves for even the slightest faults of thought, work, or speech. They thus punish small faults as though they had committed the greatest crimes, and, insofar as mortals may, in true humility offer and preserve their lives blamelessly before God [Col. 0197C]. But meanwhile, when humble penitents see their masters—that is, each of the innocent—strangely pierced with compunction and wonderfully tormented with tears over even the slightest faults, they begin in a manner to eat from the crumbs. For, having received the spirit of fear, they take from them a praiseworthy example of how they ought to repent of and mourn every graver sin, and make worthy satisfaction to God for them.

This is done not by dogs—that is, those who sin proudly and insolently—but by little dogs, namely humble sinners who recognize the weight of their sins and thus, through the spirit of fear, finally make progress to the spirit of love. When any blessed soul, instructed to such a degree, advances in the order we have described and is humbled from the deep root of its heart in both word and deed, then Jesus answers; then he bursts forth into the voice which brings the long-desired blessing. For upon whom does God rest except upon one humble, quiet, and trembling at his word? Then he answers and says:

[Col. 0197D] “O woman, O soul softened by grace: let it be ascribed to my name that I mercifully softened you, once stiff-necked and impenitent in heart. Yet reward is also due to your work, because great is your faith, which you have merited through great humility.” We must understand what is called little faith and what great faith. Blessed Peter had little faith when, as the sea’s wave arose, he abandoned the anchor of hope and did not believe at all that he could be saved. Therefore he is rebuked by the Lord as having little faith, when the divine voice says to him: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31).

Whoever is now excessively cast down by a breath of detraction or vainly exalted by the favour of praise possesses this little faith of Peter [Col. 0198A]. But the one is distinguished by the praise of great faith who, cleaving to God, is found strong in adversities and humble in prosperities. The perfection of this faith is rewarded with great blessedness, as follows:

“Let it be done to you as you wish.” What is meant by “Let it be done to you as you wish”? Those who have experienced it know how, when heavenly love and desire have touched the heart to its depths, an overflowing abundance of God’s sweetness gladdens the heart; how it attains its desired longings according to its wish; and with what fervour it may linger in tears.

[Col. 0198B] “O woman, great is your faith. Through the ardour of great faith, let it be done to you as you wish. In whatever measure you wish, overflow and feast upon my delights.”

“And her daughter was healed from that hour.” From that hour the daughter—that is, the soul—is truly healed. Although still surrounded by mortal flesh and unable to escape every infirmity of sin, from that hour, when it becomes one spirit with the Lord, it receives such great and perfect health as removes everlasting condemnation and infirmity.

These same words are also deservedly heard by every holy and perfect soul which has fought bravely to the end of life, finished its course, and kept the faith, when it is taken from the prison-house of the flesh and raised to heaven. “O woman, great is your faith.” As though the Lord said [Col. 0198C]:

“I, the Lord who search hearts and reins, know the weakness of your powers; I know that you were a mass of clay and a fragile creation. But because you have shown me great faith and love, let it be done to you as you wish. For you always sought the presence of my glory with a thirsting breast; now, taken out of the world’s exile, you shall dwell with the Son of God. See, not through a mirror and an enigma, but face to face, him whom you desired to see. Embrace and enjoy him whom you always loved.”

“And her daughter was healed from that hour.” For from then on, when it possesses that supreme good which is God, it will be granted whole and perfect health in both soul and body, because no stain of corruption will thereafter harm it; instead, the ineffable joys of everlasting health will come to it [Col. 0198D]. May Jesus Christ our Lord, the author of health, bring us to that health: he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## 257. HOMILY XXX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FRIDAY AFTER THE SECOND SUNDAY OF LENT

“Joseph said to his brothers: Hear my dream. I thought that we were binding sheaves in the field, and that my sheaf, as it were, rose and stood, while your sheaves stood around and worshipped my sheaf” (Gen. 37).

These brothers of Joseph, who afterwards sold that same Joseph by malicious treachery, suitably signify evil spirits. We call them brothers because both they and we were created by the one God, the Creator [Col. 0199A]. To these brothers every spiritual Joseph in some manner relates the dream that he saw when, through the good will which he conceived by God’s inspiration, he opposes their perverse suggestion.

For by a dream, which a person ordinarily sees not while awake but while asleep in the night and, as it were, unwittingly, may be understood the hidden and, so to speak, unexpected grace of divine visitation. By this grace a person yet to be saved, still placed in the darkness of ignorance and with no preceding merits of his own, is inwardly visited and illumined by gratuitous goodness and somewhat recalled to recognition of his sins. Since he begins to be displeased with himself because of the evils he has committed, he says, as though contradicting and renouncing the perversity of evil spirits: “Hear my dream which I have seen. I now disdain [Col. 0199B] any further hearing of the counsels of your wicked plotting, because I strive to fulfil in deed the dream of salvation which I saw—the good which I have proposed in my mind through divine inspiration.”

“I thought,” he says, “that we were binding sheaves in the field.” *I thought* is the word of those who doubt. For when a person is touched by inward visitation, he is not immediately converted to God; but first he meditates and reflects within himself with a certain hesitation, not knowing what he ought chiefly to choose. For good will urges him to be converted and abandon worldly things, but weak flesh on the other side draws him back to love of the world [Col. 0199C].

“I thought,” he says, “that we were binding sheaves in the field.” He determines to enter the field of spiritual purpose, where he may gather sheaves of holy thoughts, heavenly desires, good understandings, and righteous works. He appropriately says, “I thought that we were binding sheaves in the field,” because he is not alone in going to enter the field of holy life: his brothers will likewise enter with him in order to fight—most powerful warriors who gather innumerable sheaves of temptations, by which they strive to disturb and unsettle the tranquillity of his mind. Hence it is necessary that he, on the contrary, gather such a strong sheaf of patience and perseverance that he may make it rise and stand against the surrounding sheaves of his enemies, and make them, as it were, bowing before his sheaf, humbly prostrate themselves upon the ground before him.

“His brothers answered: Shall you indeed be our king, or shall we be subjected to your rule?” This answer of the perverse brothers is their hard and powerful struggle, because they attempt by every means to turn and call him back from the good will which he has undertaken. They fear lest, after abandoning the kingdom of vices, he may deserve to obtain the kingdom of virtues and they, rendered powerless and weak, be subjected to his dominion [Col. 0199D].

“This, therefore, was the cause of dreams and words that supplied the fuel of envy and hatred.” It produces the fuel of envy and hatred in unclean spirits when they perceive that the causes of dreams and words—that is, the grace of hidden visitation and inward address—are being received beneficially and fruitfully and brought to the effect of action. Hence it follows:

“Again he saw another dream [Col. 0200A], which he related to his brothers, saying: I saw in a dream as it were the sun, moon, and eleven stars worshipping me.” This spiritual Joseph sees another dream when he now strives to fulfil in deed that which he had proposed in his heart through hope of eternal reward. For this is, as it were, to relate it to those perverse brothers who oppose and resist him: namely, to prove the purpose of good will by works.

The sun—that is, those who contemplate; the moon—that is, those who are continent; and the stars—that is, those who confess—will in a manner worship him while he is working well in the field of spiritual life, when they magnify him for his good conversion and praiseworthy manner of life.

“When he had related this to his father and brothers, his father rebuked him and said: What does this dream which you have seen mean?” He relates it to his father, God his Creator, by giving thanks; he relates it to his aforesaid brothers by provoking their envy through good works. But his father does not praise him for relating such things; he rebukes him. This rebuke is to be understood as an insinuating temptation. For he permits him to be tempted in order to humble him, and, after he has been humbled, to exalt and raise him more highly.

“Shall I,” he says, “and your mother and your brothers worship you upon the earth?” Shall I—the true sun of contemplatives—and your mother, the Church of the continent, and your brothers, namely the multitude of those who confess, worship you upon the earth? He would also be worshipped, as it were, upon the earth if he were held equal to contemplatives, the continent, and those who confess in every grace of virtue [Col. 0200C]. Again, in another sense, he would be worshipped upon the earth if he were permitted to be disturbed by no annoyances of temptation. It follows:

“Therefore his brothers envied him, but his father kept the matter silently in mind.” While those wicked brothers envy him and rise up against him more and more through temptation, God the Father silently considers the matter because he patiently endures and awaits the outcome of the temptation. He is silent because he does not aid one labouring in temptation; he is silent because he neither drives away nor restrains those envious and plotting brothers. Yet the following text expresses that this very temptation will finally, through God’s mercy, turn to his salvation:

“And when his brothers were staying in Sichem, feeding their father’s flocks [Col. 0200D], Israel said to him: Your brothers are feeding the sheep in Sichem. Come, I will send you to them.” By Sichem, which is interpreted “shoulder,” bodily labour is rightly signified. Therefore the flocks of so great a Father—that is, those gathered to Christ who despise the world—are rightly said to remain in Sichem, where they are brought under spiritual servitude through devout labours. There those frequently mentioned brothers in a manner feed them, because through temptations they make them advance all the more. To that place every blessed Joseph is sent by God the Father for the increase of his salvation, as the text immediately proceeds.

Sent from the valley of Hebron, he came to Shechem; and he found him wandering in the field and asked him what he was seeking. Hebron means “everlasting increase”; Shechem, [Col. 0201A] as has already been said, means “shoulder,” by which the labor of the present life seems not unfittingly to be signified. The useful discipline of the present life is indeed an increase of everlasting blessedness; yet when this Joseph is sent to Shechem, when he is commanded to set the shoulder of heart and body to pious labors, he is found, as though wandering in a field, by a man—that is, by some teacher—because, although he has chosen to dwell in Shechem, the varying error of temptations nevertheless intrudes itself upon his heart at the beginning of conversion. But the man of virtue, namely the teacher of eternal truth, when he finds this man wandering, when he has recognized the errors of temptation by which he is disturbed, announces to him that yet more grievous snares of temptations remain, when he says:

“I heard them saying: ‘Let us go to Dothaim.’” [Col. 0201B] As though he said: “Your brothers, malignant plotters, desire to go to Dothain—that is, to failure—because they hasten to draw you away with them, not into progress but into failure.” Hence it follows: “When they saw him from afar, before he came near to them, they planned to kill him; and they spoke to one another: ‘Behold, the dreamer is coming. Let us kill him and cast him into an old cistern; and we shall say: “A most savage beast has devoured him,” and then it will appear what profit his dreams bring him.’”

They see him not from nearby but as coming from afar; that is, he has not yet consented to their malice and suggestion. Therefore, rising against him in a great onset, they rush upon him and desire cruelly to kill the dreamer of good things with the death of the soul, so that, once slain, they may cast him into the old cistern: that is, so that by apostatizing from God they may make him put on again [Col. 0201C] the old man with his deeds. Then, exulting like most powerful victors over his destruction, they may say: “A most savage beast has devoured him.” The most savage beast is lust, or the concupiscence of the flesh; it is said to devour the spiritual Joseph when, after conversion, he falls back again into the pleasure of the world.

But Reuben, hearing this, endeavored to free him from their hands and said: “Let us not take his life, nor shed his blood; but cast him into the cistern which is in the wilderness, and keep your hands innocent.” By Reuben, whose name means “mouth of vision,” we should understand the prince and author of all diabolical perversity. Seeing that his ministers and fellow-brothers prevail nothing by such plots, [Col. 0201D] he gives advice for a new craftiness and deception, by which the man may more easily be cast headlong into destruction. “Do not kill him,” he says; “do not turn him away from his spiritual purpose; but cast him into the cistern which is in the wilderness.” The cistern of solitude is the secrecy of holy conduct. Cast him into this cistern, not in heart but in body, so that he may appear deceitfully only under the outward appearance of holiness, while seeking and loving every delight and every concupiscence of the flesh; and so, drawn away and enticed by evil desires, he may be returned to his father—namely, the world and the devil.

## HOMILY XXXI. FOR THE SATURDAY BEFORE THE THIRD SUNDAY OF THE FIRST LENT

“A certain man had two sons; and the younger said [Col. 0202A] to his father: ‘Father, give me the portion of the substance that falls to me’” (Luke 15).

The man who is said to have had two sons is understood to be God the Father; I mean, his two sons were two peoples. The elder son represents the Jewish people, who was, as it were, always with the Father because he worshipped the one God. The younger son, however, is to be understood as the people of the Gentiles. Having, as it were, received the portion of substance that fell to him, he went into a far country when, abandoning the true God, he enslaved himself to the vain worship of idols.

For the portion of substance which he received and with which he departed is rational understanding, through which he ought to have known and loved his Creator, God almighty, from whom he received it. To know the Redeemer belonged to few; every human being [Col. 0202B] could plainly know the Creator both from himself and from the things that have been created. For, as the Apostle says, “the invisible things of God are perceived by being understood through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20). For heaven, earth, stars, seas, and all things made that are seen under heaven plainly speak of him by whom they were made. They would not exist unless they existed from someone; they would not have been created unless they had a Creator. Therefore every human being could know God from the natural capacity that he had received from God.

But this younger son, namely the people of the Gentiles, after not many days, having gathered all things together, departed as though into a foreign country when, abandoning him by whom he was created, he withdrew far from the grace of God through the worship of idols. There he truly squandered his substance by living dissolutely. [Col. 0202C] For when, abandoning inward things, he began to serve with pleasure outward, that is earthly, desires and pleasures, and to love the creature rather than the Creator, this was in some manner to squander miserably the substance of the divine gift—that is, the excellence of natural capacity and rational understanding.

After this there is fittingly added: “And after he had squandered everything, a severe famine arose 263 in that country, and he began to be in want; and he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country.” The one citizen to whom that needy man attached himself represents the devil, to whom all Gentile peoples attached themselves before Christ’s coming, having abandoned the Creator. Under him they labored intensely under a severe famine of the word and knowledge of God; and “he desired to fill his belly with the husks which [Col. 0202D] the swine ate, and no one gave to him.” By the husks are signified the foolish wisdom of the world and the pursuit of secular learning, in which that ancient people of the Gentiles chiefly toiled; these were indeed food for swine, namely malignant spirits. For they delighted in these things and were refreshed by them. It is rightly added, “and no one gave to him,” because however much labor they spent upon such husks, upon the studies of empty philosophy, they could never perfectly attain what they sought. But when the time of grace had come, he at last began to be filled through God’s mercy, as follows:

“But, returning to himself, he said: ‘How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here with hunger! I will rise and go to my father.’” [Col. 0203A] This return took place in Christ’s incarnation, when God sent his Only-begotten Son into the world to save the human race. This younger son truly returns when, having heard the preaching of the Gospel after the passion, resurrection, and ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, he is converted to faith.

That good father, in the grace of such sweetness, received his son as he returned after long wanderings; clothed him in the first robe, adorned his hands with a ring and his feet with shoes, and finally admitted him to eat the fatted calf slain for him amid such joy and exultation. All this prefigured for us that spiritual joy which is now in the house of God, namely the holy Church gathered from the Gentiles. It has been adorned by God the Father with purity of innocence, integrity of faith, and constancy in evangelical preaching—these being the first robe, ring, and shoes. [Col. 0203B] In this house, indeed, that fatted calf, the only-begotten Son of God, once sacrificed for us upon the altar of the cross, is daily slain, because his most holy body and blood are daily consecrated and received therein for the salvation of believers. In this house too a certain sweet harmony and choir resound daily, because through the sacrifice of this calf, through the most sacred offering of Christ’s body and blood, the holy Church daily approaches God the Father in the unanimous concord of faith and the constant harmony of divine praise.

The elder son, namely the Jewish people, hears this harmony and choir. He now dwells, as it were, in the field [Col. 0203C] because he is uselessly occupied only with external and perishable things. He hears, but is angered and refuses to enter, because he refuses, by believing in the Son of God, to share in the unanimity of the holy Church. “But his father came out and began to entreat him.” This coming out of the Father signifies the future calling of the Jewish people near the end of the world. For then God the Father will, as it were, go out to entreat the elder son, the Jewish people, when through his preachers he makes their calling manifest and, by the wondrous grace of his visitation, perfectly illumines them to believe in his Only-begotten Son whom he sent. Then, with heart and body weeping, they say:

[Col. 0203D] “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment; and you have never given me a kid, that I might feast with my friends. But after this son of yours, who squandered his substance with harlots, came, you killed the fatted calf for him.” They will indeed marvel and torment themselves with immeasurable pain of repentance, because they, whom God first chose in their fathers, were so blinded and rejected at the coming of the only-begotten Son of God, while the Gentiles, who had not known God, were chosen and called by the wondrous ordering of almighty God into so great a grace of blessedness. For by the kid, through which sin is expressed, the Son of God was prefigured; he willed to be made sin for us when he took upon himself the miseries of our mortality.

[Col. 0204A] Having briefly run through these matters according to the allegorical sense, let us turn the eye of the mind upon ourselves and consider what this parable morally suggests to us. For the Lord says:

“A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father: ‘Father, 265 give me the portion of substance that falls to me.’” All the parables of our Lord Jesus Christ are full of wondrous depth and excellence of mysteries, since they were uttered from the mouth of him who is the wisdom of God the Father. Therefore no mortal can attain or comprehend by his own understanding the full and perfect truth hidden in them. One of these is this present parable of the Lord, wholly full of grace and sweetness. Although we cannot, nor are worthy to, reach its depth perfectly [Col. 0204B] by our understanding, yet, by his gift, we may infer something from it that may promote the progress and salvation of our souls.

This man who had two sons bears the type of almighty God. By his two sons we may not inappropriately understand the one and same human being, composed of soul and body. For although he willed that we should have a father and mother on earth, from whose flesh he ordained that we should be born, yet he himself is the supreme and true Father, from whom we subsist and from whom we have received spirit, soul, and body.

His younger son signifies the human spirit, which is not unjustly called the younger son since, through God’s mercy, it is daily renewed within itself. [Col. 0204C] Of this youth the Psalmist says: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102:5). It belongs to youth, by its nature and the heat of the blood, always to be fervent within itself. Nor is it without reason that, by that fervent blood, is represented that fervent love through which the human spirit, continually renewing itself, is shown to love God above all things and beyond all things in the grace of spiritual sweetness. This youth the aforementioned prophet David laments that he once possessed but lost, saying elsewhere in the psalm: “I was young; indeed, I have grown old” (Ps. 36:25). For a person wastes away in miserable old age when inwardly he grows cold from the fervor of divine love.

But the younger son—the human spirit ever more fervent day by day in the love of God—[Col. 0204D] seeks nothing apart from him whom he loves. Hence, with the suppliant voice of heart and body, he cries to the ears of his Father, almighty God:

“Father, give me the portion of substance that falls to me.” The portion of this substance which he requests appropriately signifies the gifts of spiritual virtues and graces. Yet, more excellently still, by this portion of substance which he requests, we may worthily understand communion in the divine gift, namely in the life-giving body and blood of Christ. The spiritual person always longs for this portion of substance; that he may be able to receive it worthily, he labors day and night with vigils, fasts, and other pious works. Thus, whenever he approaches to receive [Col. 0205A] this portion of substance, or even thinks of the day or hour in which he is to approach, he beseeches God the Father: now from the love by which he desires the sweetness of so great a refreshment, now from the fear by which he fears lest he appear unworthy of so great a gift of divine mercy. “Father,” he says, “give me the portion of substance that falls to me. Holy Father, merciful Father, Father of great mercy, give me a portion of that substance which is truly my substance: namely, the portion of the body and blood of Christ your Son, by which I subsist and by whose price I have been redeemed. Give it so that it may touch me, so that it may touch me inwardly through the spiritual sweetness of grace, in order that the visible reception of that same body and blood may become an invisible and spiritual refreshment for my soul. [Col. 0205B] For it will profit bodies little to touch this portion of substance if the savor and power of spiritual sweetness and grace do not inwardly touch my soul.”

God the Father does not at all despise this humble supplication of his son. Hence the Evangelist immediately adds: “And he divided the substance between them.” He divides the substance when he grants a person the effect of prayer. He divides it to body, and divides it also to spirit. He divides it to body when, by the gift of his grace, a person shares in the heavenly mysteries in such a way that he shows love for his neighbor bodily, so far as he can. He divides it also to spirit when the person can approach in true love of God.

Those who truly are the sons of God know this division of the divine substance: those who love [Col. 0205C] before all things him who is above all things, desiring this alone and preferring this alone to all the joys of the present life, while amid the dishes of heavenly food they are granted to taste beforehand certain joys of spiritual gladness. Hence we may also judge that the reading from the holy Gospel was placed in this Lenten season by the ordering of the Holy Spirit for this reason: that the sons of God, who now, applying themselves more strictly to vigils, fasts, and other labors, mortify the flesh, may strive to long more ardently for the portion of substance of which we have spoken—for the refreshment of this spiritual nourishment. For all who are admitted to it in such a way that they are often inwardly touched by the heavenly savor of sweetness found in it easily despise whatever outward afflictions [Col. 0205D] they undergo.

Nevertheless, wretched man, who never remains in the same state, is unable to remain long in this grace. For he has those who always persecute him; he has those who always endeavor to cast him down: namely, the ancient enemy, who everywhere and always plots against him; the world, in the midst of which he lives; and his own body, from which he can nowhere escape. The Evangelist therefore added:

“And not many days after, the younger son, having gathered all things together, departed into a far country, and there squandered his substance by living dissolutely.” Many days are many continual illuminations; if a person deserved to have them frequently, he would not wander in a far country. But because these days—alas!—are few, not many; rare, not continual, it is rightly said: “And not many days after, having gathered all things together.” [Col. 0206A] By “having gathered all things together” we may understand good and evil. The younger son gathers all things together not many days later when, as the illuminations of heavenly visitation become infrequent within him, his spirit grows cold and lukewarm from the fervor of divine love. Then indeed he gathers all things together when he heaps evils upon goods: that is, when, after the effect of prayer, he keeps less careful watch over himself, and gathers every evil and useless thing into that heart in which he had first received the grace of heavenly sweetness. Through these things he falls miserably into a failure of spiritual joys.

And when he begins in this manner to be alienated from the grace of God, this is, as it were, to dwell as a stranger in a far country. For just as a stranger knows no one and is known by no one, so the one who alienates himself thus from God neither knows God nor is known by God. God indeed knows everything that exists by the power of his divinity, [Col. 0206B] and he knows this person too, but not in the grace of his former goodness and sweetness. Thus comes what follows:

“And there he squandered his substance by living dissolutely.” For when, forgetful of spiritual grace, he gives his mind to unclean thoughts, evil desires, and harmful pleasures, it may rightly be said of him that he squandered his substance by living dissolutely. After this miserable dissipation, he commonly falls into such want that he is deprived of all spiritual gifts; and thus what follows is fulfilled:

[Col. 0206C] “And he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his field to feed swine.” By this one citizen to whom he attached himself the devil may not unfittingly be understood, and he is not unjustly called our fellow-citizen. For we were so created that we ought jointly to have inhabited one country, namely the dwelling of the heavenly kingdom. A person estranged from God begins to attach himself to this citizen when he contradicts that citizen’s will in nothing. And because a field (*villa*) is said to derive from baseness (*vilitas*), that one citizen sends him into his field when he powerfully subjects him to every baseness, every uncleanness of evil thoughts, and the frivolity and wickedness of shameful desires.
