“To feed swine”—that is, malignant spirits, who are [Col. 0206D] understood by the swine. For they feed and are refreshed upon such uncleannesses and wickednesses. A human being’s deception is their food and refreshment; human ruin is their exultation. They are always vigilant, never eat, never rest, and are always inflamed to overthrow a person who wishes to live devoutly. But what finally follows?

“And he sought,” says the Evangelist, “to fill his belly with the husks which the swine ate.” By the belly is understood a person’s memory. He seeks to fill his belly with the husks which the swine eat when he fills and burdens his memory so thoroughly with unclean thoughts and pleasures—which are truly the food of demons—that he willingly lingers over them, delights in returning to them frequently, and thus subjects himself to them by consent, so that, if it were possible, he would willingly perform in deed what he entertains in his mind. [Col. 0207A] But the pious and merciful God, who is “a helper in due season, in tribulation,” comes to the aid of the one whom he has decreed to save with his customary mercy: recalling him as he wanders, and mercifully helping him so that he may be able and willing to return. Hence it follows: “Returning to himself, he said.”

Observe all these matters of which we have spoken. They are in a manner outside themselves, not in themselves, because nothing except God can be within the human soul. He returns to himself when, abandoning the things that are outside himself, he humbly returns in repentance to his Father, almighty God, from whom he had withdrawn by sinning.

“How many hired servants,” he says, “in my Father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here with hunger!” [Col. 0207B] In the Lord’s house there are some who are called hired servants, and there are some who receive the name of sons. The hired servant serves because of fear, for he fears being deprived of his reward. The son serves because of love, because he expects the honor of the paternal inheritance. Nor is it unfitting that the name of hired servants here designates those who, because of the fear of hell and of the punishment they have deserved, have abandoned the world, subjected themselves to divine service, and, to gain that reward which is the remission of sins, daily eat the bread of tears and gladly afflict themselves with the laments of repentance.

When the one who was formerly a son sees them—he who once received the portion of paternal substance in accordance with his soul’s desire—he is afflicted with a pain so much more grievous as he remembers having lost a greater [Col. 0207C] sweetness of spiritual grace. “How many hired servants in my Father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here with hunger!” They feed, indeed, in the spirit of fear upon the bread of repentance and compunction; but I perish here with hunger because I am unable to attain either the spirit of fear or the spirit of love.

“I will rise and go to my father.” As though he said: “Why, wretched man, have you deprived yourself of so great a good? What profit is it to you to have spent your days in this way? What profit is it to you to have defiled your soul with so many uncleannesses? I will rise from this sloth, from this idleness of life, and go to my Father, the Father of mercies, and say to him: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer [Col. 0207D] worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.’”

“Holy Father, most merciful Father, you raised me above heavenly things because you once admitted me more familiarly to the sweetness of heavenly grace. Yet I have sinned against heaven because I made myself utterly unworthy of so many benefits of your fatherhood. I have also sinned before you because I was not ashamed before the face of your majesty, present with me everywhere, forever and everywhere beholding the filth of my iniquity. I am no longer worthy to be called your son because I know that I have grievously strayed from the path of filial love; and I neither ask nor presume to ask ever again to receive the grace of that sweetness by which you are accustomed to cherish your sons. Because I judge myself unworthy, make me as one of your hired servants by giving me the spirit of fear, [Col. 0208A] so that, since I cannot have, nor am worthy to have, the spirit of love, I may at least deserve through fear to be stirred to some repentance and satisfaction for my sins.”

“And rising, he came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father, seeing him, was moved with mercy; and running, he fell upon his neck and kissed him.” Because words are uttered through the neck, confession of sins is not unfittingly understood in the neck. God the Father sees from afar the one rising from the depth of iniquity and coming to him along the way of saving repentance and satisfaction—for God’s seeing is God’s loving—and, moved with mercy, runs to him when he aids him through the gentleness of his mercy. He falls upon his neck when, by his inspiration, he teaches him inwardly [Col. 0208B] that, just as he remembers having sinned shamelessly, so he should not be ashamed to confess as unreservedly, truly, and perfectly before God and before God’s vicar, to whom he has been entrusted.

After this it is aptly added: “And he kissed him.” For when someone thus shames himself without reserve for God’s sake, it often happens that this very shame produces within him a certain spiritual love of God, which may fittingly be compared to a kiss. Hence it follows:

“But the father said to his servants: ‘Quickly bring out the first robe and clothe him; put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet.’” By the first robe, which he commands to be brought out, charity may not unfittingly be understood; God the Father truly clothes his son in it when he restores him to the perfect sweetness of his [Col. 0208C] former love. After the first robe, a ring is also placed upon his hand when he strives to preserve in all things an integrity of right faith toward his heavenly Father. For faith is called not only that by which we believe in God, but also the effort to have a faithful heart toward God in all things. After receiving this ring of faith, he is clothed with shoes when true and perfect hope for the remission of sins is granted him.

And charity is rightly placed first, faith next, and hope last, because through the perfect charity by which a person loves God before all things and above all things, he advances to preserve for God that faith which knows no stain of faithlessness; and that faith produces in a person such hope that he can never despair of [Col. 0208D] God’s mercy. After this he is admitted more intimately to the heavenly banquet of that fatted calf and is refreshed more sweetly, as is immediately added:

“And bring,” he says, “the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat and feast.” The fatted calf is our Lord Jesus Christ, who is brought to him and slain when, in the same heavenly sweetness and the same delight of spiritual joy which he had formerly possessed with God, he is spiritually refreshed at the life-giving banquet of Christ’s body and blood. For that good father, who says, “Let us eat and feast,” shows this figuratively in the following words. There are some who eat and feast, and some who eat but do not feast. [Col. 0209A] Those eat and, eating, feast at that heavenly banquet who worthily receive Christ’s body and blood bodily and are inwardly animated by the savor of his divinity through an abundance of inward sweetness. But those eat without feasting who receive bodily indeed, but inwardly lack the taste of the heavenly sweetness contained in it. It follows:

“Now his elder son was in the field.” By the elder son, who is in the field, the human body may not unjustly be understood; it is rightly said to remain in the field when it strives always to exercise itself in good works. This elder son, namely the outward person, having heard the harmony and choir—that is, the exultant jubilation of spiritual delight, by which the spirit exults in the Lord when it recognizes that it has merited, by none of its own merits, so great a condescension of divine mercy toward itself—humbles itself before God in a certain humble thanksgiving and says:

[Col. 0209B] “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment; and you have never given me a kid, that I might feast with my friends. But after this son of yours, who devoured his substance with harlots, came, you killed the fatted calf for him.” These are the words not of one who is indignant or hateful, but of one truly repentant and loving. For when he considers the negligence of his whole life, he marvels at so great a mercy of divine compassion toward himself.

“Behold,” he says, “for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment.” He does not say “commandments,” but “I have never transgressed your commandment.” [Col. 0209C] For no one can be found faithful in all the Lord’s commandments. The keeping of this one commandment is a person’s perseverance in the spiritual life. And by adding, “and you have never given me a kid,” he signifies perfect repentance for sins, as though he said: “Behold, for so many years I have served you and have never transgressed your commandment, because even if I have lived uselessly, I have nevertheless never departed in habit and body from the path of spiritual life which I undertook. And you have never given me a kid, because I have never yet been able perfectly to attain perfect repentance for my sins, by which I deserved your wrath. But after this son of yours, who devoured his substance with harlots, came, you killed the fatted calf for him,” because you have mercifully deigned, according to the multitude of your mercy, to admit my wretched spirit—lost to you, prostituted to unclean thoughts, most wicked pleasures and desires, carried away as though captive, and justly deserving to be deprived of every grace of spiritual sweetness which it had received—to the sacrament of reconciliation amid an abundance of its former sweetness.

[Col. 0209D] This, as we have said, is a certain humble thanksgiving of a person truly repentant, who humbly recognizes his own misery and God’s mercy. The way God the Father answers this son at the end of his life is fittingly shown also at the end of this holy Gospel.

“Son,” he says, “you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was fitting to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and [Col. 0210A] has been found.” As though he said: “Son, who have kept for me the integrity of filial faith, while still placed in a mortal body you have always been with me, because you remained with me by faithfully serving under the rule of my dominion according to your measure. All that is mine is yours because the good and evil, favorable and adverse things which befell you in that life came from me. If I received you mercifully, I did it for the sake of your salvation; if I left you for a time exposed to temptations and worn down by labors, I nevertheless intended your salvation through this as well.

“But now all that is mine is yours because these things have brought you to the glory in which you will hereafter dwell with me, where you will always feast with me in the joys of eternal blessedness. There this brother of yours, this spirit of yours which was dead, will be so clothed in blessed immortality [Col. 0210B] that it will never die again; and the one who was lost will be found in such a way that it will never again be separated from my eternal vision.”

These are the words of the Gospel reading, which we have run through in exposition according to our measure, as the Lord himself has deigned to grant. Let us humbly beseech the very Father of mercy that we too may deserve to hear their conclusion at our own end: so that, by his gift, we may serve and cleave to him in the present in such a manner that at the end of our lives we may rightly hear this most sweet voice: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours”; where, feasting and rejoicing with him in glory, we may fear no torments of death. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0210C] through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXII. FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY OF THE FIRST LENT

“Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute. And when he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled” (Luke 11).

In the Gospels the spirit of understanding rightly pertains to this Sunday; indeed, it is altogether necessary in this holy Gospel reading, because unless it is present to grant us understanding of the mysteries of this sacred reading, we shall be able to discern in it nothing worthy of it, nothing suited to our instruction.

[Col. 0210D] The Scripture of the Old Testament, in which we read and heard at night of Joseph, fittingly agrees with the Gospel. When Joseph recognized his brothers descending to him in Egypt to buy food, he was not recognized by them; but, as if speaking to strangers, he addressed them harshly, saying: “You are spies; you have come to see the weaker parts of the land.” And a little later he added: “By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not depart from here until your youngest brother comes” (Gen. 42:9 ff.).

This Joseph signifies Christ, who, in order to become our brother, deigned to descend from the height of his divinity to the depths of our mortality. We must descend to this our brother in order to buy the necessities of sustenance, because we [Col. 0211A] ought always to seek from him and in his words the food of our souls. But he often speaks harshly to us, as Joseph did to his brothers. In a manner he speaks to us on this subject in the holy Gospel reading now before us; for it is hard and difficult to understand and expound.

But lest we leave untouched what Joseph says: “You are spies; you have come to see the weaker parts of the land,” we may understand ourselves under the name of spies. Nor is this inappropriate: for what else are we than spies when we diligently search out and investigate the words of Holy Scripture, to see whether we may find in it anything bearing upon our instruction, consolation, and salvation? We have come to see the weaker parts of the land when we seek the plainer passages of the same Holy Scripture, through which [Col. 0211B] an entrance may be opened for us to the firmer and more difficult ones. But while we are thus exploring and seeking to see the weaker parts of the land, let us hear what our Joseph says to us: “By the life of Pharaoh,” he says, “you shall not depart hence until your youngest brother comes; bring your youngest brother to me.” And, taking Simeon, he bound him before their eyes. Joseph, as we have said, signifies Christ; his brothers signify the various spiritual virtues, among which two are chief, and these may suitably be understood through those two brothers Simeon and Benjamin—one of whom is bound, so that the other may be obtained. Through Simeon, whose name is interpreted “hearing sorrow,” fear is understood; through Benjamin, who is called “son of the right hand,” love is understood. Or, through Simeon the present life may be understood, and through Benjamin, the son of the right hand, the right hand—that is, eternal life—which is always on the right and admits nothing left-handed. And this word “hearing sorrow” suitably agrees either with the present life or with fear, which is altogether necessary in the present life. For what is it to hear sorrow except to fear sins and the eternal punishments which the sinner hears are laid up after this life? When Simeon is bound, Benjamin is brought; when Benjamin has been brought, Simeon is released. God, who is the true Joseph, binds—indeed, binds to himself—humankind first through fear, so that through the bonds of fear he may bring them to the liberty of sweetest love. “Bring your youngest brother to me.” How can the spirit of love, than which nothing is more excellent or more worthy, be called the least? It could indeed be called the greatest, since nothing is more excellent than it. [Col. 0211D] Yet it is rightly called the least, because it makes the human heart truly least, truly most humble. For a person is never so humbled by the spirit of fear as by the spirit of love. Therefore, when Simeon has been released—that is, when fear of the present life has been emptied out—we shall receive the inheritance of eternal life through Benjamin, through the perfect love of God and neighbour.

Nor should we pass over what he says: “By the life of Pharaoh you shall not depart hence until your youngest brother comes.” Pharaoh signifies the devil. He fittingly says, “by the life of Pharaoh,” as though against Pharaoh’s life; for, while we range through Holy Scripture by searching it out in order to buy what is necessary for our sustenance, we act altogether against the salvation of the ancient enemy [Col. 0212A] signified by Pharaoh. But when he adds, “You shall not depart hence,” he shows by this that although we can enter into Holy Scripture, we can never depart from it having fully and perfectly understood the sweetness hidden in it—something that nourishes and refreshes us when contemplated. So too the words of the present holy Gospel, although the Lord speaks harshly in them, although they sound harsh outwardly, are nevertheless full of instruction for human life, full of consolation and grace. For the Evangelist says:

“Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute.” By the name of this demon, love of the world may not inappropriately be understood. This demon is in a sense mute because, as long as anyone is held possessed by the ruinous love of this world, he can speak neither those things which concern his salvation [Col. 0212B] nor those which look to the praise and honour of God. Jesus casts it out when the grace of his mercy compassionately anticipates the human heart; and, when the love of the world and of vices has been expelled, the person rises to his love and to the desire of holy conduct. Thus comes about what follows:

“And when he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke.” The mute man speaks when a person, set free from the world, loosens mouths long silent to praise of the Creator and to words of confession [the text breaks off: *ora relax-*].

“And the crowds marvelled.” By the marvelling crowds we may suitably understand the troubled senses of a person. They marvel now through joy and love, now through fear and dread. A person marvels through joy and love when he rejoices and is glad that he has been freed [Col. 0212C] from the world and from the sins of the world. He marvels through fear when he begins to be afraid and anxious about how he may stand firm amid the various temptations that arise. For while a person is in this world and lives in a worldly and pleasure-seeking manner, he is in a kind of rest. But when he has left the world and entered the warfare of spiritual life, he undertakes a difficult and laborious contest, which will never end except with death. Hence Solomon says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). And the Lord says in another Gospel: “Which of you, having a servant ploughing or feeding cattle, when he returns from the field, will say to him at once, ‘Come and recline at table’? Does he not rather say to him, [Col. 0212D] ‘Prepare my supper, gird yourself, and serve me’?” (Luke 17:7–8). Let us see how Paul, his chosen disciple, when he returned from the field, did not immediately come and recline, but laboured by enduring the stings of diverse temptations. For he himself says concerning himself: “Lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Cor. 12). Thus Paul, who was caught up even to the third heaven and heard secret words which a human being is not permitted to utter, could not live without the contest of temptations. Thus none of Christ’s servants can live in this life without the adversities of succeeding temptations. The following words of the Gospel indicate and suggest, in part, these adversities and varieties. For it continues:

[Col. 0213A] “But some of them said: ‘He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons.’” By demons evil works are understood; by Beelzebub, which is interpreted “man of flies,” may not inappropriately be understood the strength of filthy thoughts. This is suitably called the prince of demons, because every evil work is first initiated from evil and filthy thoughts. For it often happens that, when by the mighty mercy of almighty God a person is snatched from demons—that is, from evil and demonic acts—he is oppressed by such strength of filthy thoughts as he does not remember having endured when he was still set amid the world and its sins. Therefore, drawing sighs from the depths, he often breaks out into these words: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons”; as though he said: “O merciful Lord, by your mercy you have cast out demons and rescued me from demonic deeds, and yet this has been done by Beelzebub, prince of demons, since an intolerable tumult of filthy thoughts weighs and presses upon me. What has it profited me to have cast away the filth of evil works, if I was to endure such great filth of unclean thoughts?”

“But others, testing him, sought from him a sign from heaven.” These words, it seems to me, indicate another temptation not unlike this one, which arises in a similar way in the heart of one and the same person. For [Col. 0213C] [the manuscript: *appetens*, “desiring”] while he grieves and groans that he is at one time attacked by filthy thoughts, at another he desires to become heavenly—that is, to possess, and to appear to possess, a heavenly and perfect life—as though he were seeking a sign from heaven. And this is, in a sense, to test God. For this ought not to be so; rather, it is expedient for a person to be humbled through the labours and temptations by which he is exercised and instructed, and thus through true humility to advance to true perfection. Scripture elsewhere also indicates this to us, saying: “These are the nations which the Lord left, in order that he might instruct Israel by them” (Judg. 3:1). Therefore, as we have said, a person can never be without temptations. And what wonder is that? For these are the devil’s pursuits and works: he always follows close upon his fugitive, because, grieving that he has lost someone, he is accustomed to assail him with diverse adversities in order to cast him down. He cares little for worldly people; all his striving is to deceive the spiritual and the despisers of the world. “He shall swallow up the river,” as blessed Job says, “and shall not wonder; he trusts that the Jordan may flow into his mouth” (Job 40:18). Yet, lest they fail amid tribulations, the Lord compassionately consoles them in the words that follow. For it continues:

“He, seeing their thoughts, said to them: ‘Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste.’” Every kingdom is every human being; and every human being is either a kingdom of God or a kingdom of the devil, either a kingdom of righteousness or a kingdom of unrighteousness. This whole kingdom remains in a sense undivided when the person as a whole—that is, body and heart alike—is possessed by love of the world. But it is divided against itself when, according to [Col. 0214A] the Apostle, the flesh begins to desire against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh; when, through God’s grace and temptation, the kingdom of unrighteousness, which is the kingdom of the devil, ceases to be ruled by the love and pleasures of the world and becomes the kingdom of righteousness, which is the kingdom of God. Having undergone this good division, it is also laid waste with a good and salutary desolation: it is well, I say, laid waste when, having left the world and the consolation of friends, it turns itself wholly to God and places all its hope and consolation in him alone. There is then fulfilled what follows:

“And house falls upon house.” There is a house of the flesh and a house of the mind. The upper house, which is the house of the mind, falls upon the lower house, which is the house of the flesh, when one has been truly humbled before God in heart and body. [Col. 0214B] Yet even then the devil does not leave him, but attacks now through these things, now through those, now through sad things, now through pleasant; and thereby his kingdom in the person is destroyed, as the Lord’s following words show when he says:

“If Satan also is divided against himself, how shall his kingdom stand?” After a person’s conversion, Satan is divided against himself when he attacks that person with diverse temptations of such kinds as are mutually contrary. To mention a few out of many: the pleasure of the flesh, anger and envy, avarice, and the like are entirely contrary to one another—especially since some delight and make a person cheerful and pleasant, while others make the mind sad and troubled. Nor is this question of the Lord devoid of the grace of mercy:

“How shall his kingdom stand?” One who asks surely asks in order to know what he asks. But the Lord’s question is not of that kind, because he knows all things and understands all things before they occur. He asks, then, in order to make us who are ignorant knowledgeable by his question. “How,” he says, “shall his kingdom stand?”—as though he said: “If Satan is divided against himself, attacking you now with these, now with those temptations which are mutually contrary, you will know from this that his kingdom will not stand—that is, it will not endure—in you.” Therefore his kingdom, which is the kingdom of unrighteousness, will not stand—indeed, it will be destroyed in you—because you say [Col. 0214D] that I cast out demons by Beelzebub. “But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” That is to say: If it seems to you harsh and intolerable that, after I have cast out the demons of evil works, I permit you to be troubled by tumults of filthy thoughts, look to your sons. Return to yourselves; look within yourselves at the intentions of your thoughts. Consider carefully, I say, how you receive them. They are indeed a sign of perdition to you if you love them, if you take delight in them; they are an indication of salvation to you if, rejecting them, you are grieved by them. But because I know that you do not love them but rather reject them, therefore they themselves shall be your judges. Those very sons of yours—that is, the intentions of your thoughts—which [Col. 0215A] testify to you that you cast them out and do not willingly receive them, shall judge you worthy of eternal life, worthy of the eternal crown and glory.

“But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.” That is, whatever I have done with you, I have done in the Holy Spirit and through the Holy Spirit. And if this is so—if I, indeed because I, who am true and perfect truth, have by the finger of God, that is, by the Spirit of God, rescued you from the world and its acts—then, although you are now tempted, this is not a sign of danger. For surely the kingdom of God has come upon you. How does he say, “the kingdom of God”? What is the kingdom of God? The kingdom of God, as the Apostle says, is “righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 14:17). And it is as though the Lord said: “Let not whatever you suffer while the devil tempts and attacks you trouble you. For by this, once the devil’s kingdom has been destroyed in you, you shall attain righteousness—that is, remission of sins; by this, peace being given you from above, you shall advance from vices to joy, which is in the Holy Spirit: the joy, indeed, of contemplation.” The Lord then makes clear in the following words why a person who is set in the kingdom of God—that is, in the spiritual life—suffers such great uncleanness of filthy thoughts as he never endured while he appeared to be in the devil’s kingdom:

“When a strong man armed guards his court, those things which he possesses are in peace.” This strong armed man may not inappropriately be understood as the devil, the enemy of humankind; and he is rightly called both strong and armed. He is strong [Col. 0215C] by nature, strong by wisdom, strong by his own malice; but armed through human consent. For he could not prevail over a person by any strength of his own if the person did not himself supply him with weapons by consent. The court of this armed strong man may rightly, I think, be understood as the heart of the sinner; while the devil dwells there freely, as though guarding it, those things which he possesses are in peace. But this peace is evil peace, namely the peace of the devil altogether opposed to God’s peace: the peace between the devil and a person, when the person’s will so agrees with the devil’s will that the devil suggests little or nothing which the person does not carry out through delight, consent, or even the act of sin.

[Col. 0215D] “But when one stronger than he comes upon him and overcomes him, he shall take away all his weapons in which he trusted, and shall distribute his spoils.” This strong one may not inappropriately be understood as the Holy Spirit, who, coming in the strength of his grace, conquers the devil when by his splendour he enlightens and kindles the human heart so that it may know and be able to resist the devil, its evil guardian and possessor. Having conquered that armed strong man in this way, he takes away all his weapons in which he trusted when he withdraws from the devil and subjects to his own authority and dominion the inward senses of the person, which, by delighting in and consenting to the counsels and suggestions of the devil, helped and further strengthened his power.

And he rightly says, “his weapons, in which he trusted.” [Col. 0216A] For the ancient enemy’s confidence is the consenting will of the person. He does not care greatly, nor rejoice greatly, in the outward act of sin if the will and consent to sin are not present in the heart. For a person sometimes falls through weakness of the flesh, sometimes through a sudden impulse, without any deliberation of the mind. But the devil does not put great confidence in this. Such a person is not his armour-bearer. Where there was prior deliberation of sin, there are his weapons in which he trusted. For anyone whom he has captured and possessed through consent is someone in whom he puts great confidence. His “trusting” is nothing other than that hope and joy which he has that the person may perish with him eternally and never be able to be snatched from his power.

But when that stronger one, the Holy Spirit, comes upon him [Col. 0216B] and, having conquered him, has taken away all his weapons in which he trusted, as has been said, he will also distribute his spoils. Just as we understood the inner senses of the person by “weapons,” so we may understand the outward members of the person by “spoils.” And he rightly says, “his spoils.” For nothing in a human being belongs to the devil, since the human being is God’s creature and image; but by stealth and fraud the devil, as though stripping a person of possessions, snatches him from his Lord when he subjugates the deceived person to his own dominion through the malice of his deception. Yet that stronger one, the Holy Spirit, coming upon him, distributes these spoils powerfully—that is, he assigns them to diverse good works, for the beauty, honour, and glory of his house—as David says: “To divide the spoils for the beauty of the house” (Ps. 67:13 [Vulgate]). For when a person, stripped by the devil and taken away from God, is recalled by the coming [Col. 0216C] of the Holy Spirit and begins faithfully to serve his Creator alone with both the senses of the heart and the members of the body, then both what he has lived and what he lives are wholly ascribed to the praise and honour of God; all is reckoned for the adornment of God’s house. But because a person always has the devil as an adversary, who, envying his salvation, always labours to discover how to deceive him, the Lord immediately teaches us with what diligence in good works and what watchful guarding of the thoughts of the heart we must keep vigil against his snares. For he adds:

“He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters.” As long as a person lives in sin, his being is not with God but against [Col. 0216D] God. Nor does he gather with God so long as, scattered within himself among vain and harmful thoughts, he dissipates himself uselessly. Therefore, when he says, “He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters,” he arms and instructs his soldier so that, if he is tempted, he may neither endure temptation further nor be overcome while enduring it; rather, he may make his being to be with the Lord, always gather with God, be with him in the work of good, be with him in consenting to good, and gather with him by keeping the most watchful guard over his thoughts. And he must do this not for an hour nor for a time, but persevere in these things to the end of his life; for as the devil always scatters, so it is fitting that the person always gather. For the Lord teaches him more plainly in what follows that he must never be secure in this life, but must always have something against which to fight and from the harsh encounters of that aforesaid armed strong man receive a crown:

[Col. 0217A] “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it walks through waterless places seeking rest, and does not find it.” By the unclean spirit we may suitably understand the spirit of lust. It then goes out from a person when that person leaves the world and is converted to the Lord, because the first thing a person who desires salvation wishes for himself is that, having left the act of sin, he may henceforth strive to live chastely. But because this spirit is such that it dares to attack even holy and perfect persons, the Lord rightly adds: “It walks through waterless places.” What are these waterless places except the hearts of those living soberly and righteously, who, through love and desire of the heavenly homeland, daily make themselves dry and, so far as lies in human power, receive no waters of carnal desire? It walks through these waterless places when it labours by its suggestions and assaults to recall them from the good and praiseworthy dryness of their chastity and purity, and to defile them with the waters of carnal desire, so that it may rest in them as in moist places. But because this cannot readily happen, the Lord aptly adds and says: “Seeking rest, and not finding it.” For it can trouble them by its attacks, but it cannot rest in them or remain with them. Hence it says:

“I will return to my house from which I came out.” The house from which it came out is the heart of the sinner, which, as said above, it left when it was conquered by the coming of that stronger one, the Holy Spirit. It returns, indeed, to this [Col. 0217C] house when it strives again to bend the person back to the disgraces of his former life. The following sequence of words mystically suggests what prevents it from this return. It continues:

“And when it comes, it finds it swept clean and adorned.” These brooms by which the heart—that former house of the devil—is cleaned and adorned are confession of sins and satisfaction for sins: by confession a person is cleansed, by satisfaction adorned. But to be cleansed and adorned in this way will not profit greatly unless the person keeps himself in true humility. For through pride an occasion is given to the unclean spirit to return to its own house, as the Lord’s following words more plainly indicate:

[Col. 0217D] “Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and, entering in, they dwell there.” There are seven principal vices, through which seven malignant spirits ruling over those same vices may be understood: anger and envy, avarice and pride, vainglory, sloth, and gluttony; lust is the eighth. The spirit presiding over this vice is fittingly called the unclean spirit, since it has all the others beneath itself. But why does he say, “It takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself”? They are indeed the same in act, but different in habit, when they cloak themselves through hypocrisy in order to overthrow the person more ruinously. They also become more wicked than themselves—than their former selves, that is. “And, entering in, they dwell there” when they begin through hypocrisy to return to and inhabit that house, that heart, from which they had gone out; and they subject the person, covertly and through hypocrisy, to those vices which formerly reigned openly in him. For example, one who was openly proud becomes proud again, but does not wish to be known as proud; and thus, having taken those seven spirits of wickedness, made more wicked than themselves through hypocrisy, the unclean spirit returns into him in a worse state than it departed, when it makes him both proud and hypocritical. Thus what follows is fulfilled:

“And the last state of that person is worse than the first.” His former state was evil when he exalted himself through pride; his last state is worse than his former when, while feigning a humility that he does not possess, he becomes both proud and hypocritical.

[Col. 0218B] “And it came to pass, when he said these things, that a certain woman from the crowd, raising her voice, said: ‘Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked.’” Often, where “it came to pass” is read in Holy Scripture, some great and memorable work of almighty God is signified. And truly a great, truly magnificent thing comes to pass in whatever soul almighty God has wrought all these things that we have already heard by the hidden hand of his mercy and inspiration; a soul which, inwardly instructed in this way, he has advanced so far through the grace of his mercy that it begins to know all these things within itself. This name, “a certain woman,” suitably belongs to such a soul. For she becomes as it were a certain and singular woman before God when, truly softened toward the love of God and the desire of heavenly life, she savours nothing outside [Col. 0218C] God. United to God in this wholesome sweetness of delight, she often magnificently raises her voice from the crowd when, animated by the taste of divine contemplation and having cast down that thought which she previously had, she gathers herself wholly to love God and raises the voice of heart and body in praise of the Creator: “Blessed,” she says, “is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked.” By the name “womb” is understood the human memory; by the two breasts either the two Testaments or the two kinds of compunction are suitably represented. And it is as though she said: “O Lord, source of all sweetness and grace, I now know by your gift how sweet it is always to meditate upon you, so that that soul is altogether blessed which bears you continually in the womb of its memory, which, made pregnant by you, abides diligently in you. And the breasts which you sucked”—the soul which gathers within itself the mysteries of the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments offers sweet milk, as it were, for you to suck. Yet it is nourished from her still more sweetly and delightfully when, either pierced by the remembrance of sins or sweetly inflamed by the desire of eternal life, and intoxicated by a mighty fountain of tears, it is raised to God. This is what the blessed woman—that is, the blessed soul, having experienced it within herself—calls blessed and praises when she says: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked.” The Lord confirms her speech by his answer when he says:

“Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.” As though he said: “Truly it is as you affirm. [Col. 0219A] Yet those too are blessed—those, indeed, worthy of the reward of eternal blessedness—who bend the ear of the body to God’s word with devout eagerness, and who inwardly keep and store vigilantly and carefully in the depths of the heart what they have received through outward hearing, until, with God’s help and co-operation, they become strong enough to fulfil by the effect of good work what they have grasped by the understanding of the mind.”

Whatever soul it may be which, as we have heard, inspired and aided by God, can truly say while raising its voice from the crowd, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked,” can joyfully take up the pleasant Introit of the Mass and say: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord, because he himself shall pluck my feet out of the snare” (Ps. 24:15 [Vulgate]). For the more clearly it lifts up the eyes of its heart to see and love God, the more mercifully it recognizes that by his grace alone it has escaped the diverse snares of the aforesaid temptations which it endured at the beginning of conversion. And the more it has been united to God through true humility and purity of mind, the more confidently it asks that the gaze of divine mercy may be present to it, saying: “Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor” (Ps. 24:16 [Vulgate]). And indeed, to this one and poor spirit—that is, to the spirit united [through humility] to God—the following verse suitably applies: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in whom I trust, I shall not be put to shame” (ibid., 1–2). For when, despising things that pass with time, it has perfectly lifted its soul to God through desire for eternal things, then for the first time it truly trusts in God. For from God’s mercy it conceives a certain hope and confidence which it did not previously know.

But because, after conversion, a person often remains long in the spiritual life before advancing to this grace, or even after receiving it the devil again renews the weapons of his malice, whether by the same temptations or similar ones, to attack and overthrow him, he must have the following Gradual ever to sing: “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail; let the nations be judged in your sight” (Ps. 9:20 [Vulgate]). Or: “When my enemy is turned back, they shall be weakened and perish before your face” (ibid., 4). “Arise, O Lord.” For if [Col. 0219D] you arise—if, to defeat the devil who attacks me, you strengthen me with the arm of your might—man shall not prevail, and the nations of vices, the nations of vicious thoughts, shall be judged in your sight. For when my enemy has been turned backward and overcome by the visiting grace of your mercy, they shall be weakened and perish before your face.

After this, the prayer rightly follows: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens” (Ps. 122:1 [Vulgate]); because the more one sees divine help to be necessary, the more humbly and devoutly one asks and awaits mercy from God with the eyes of mind and body, as it were, lifted up to him. And he adds and says: “Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of the maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. Have mercy on us, O Lord; have mercy on us” (ibid., 2–3).

The Prayer for today also accords with the supplication of this faithful soul, in which we ask God both to look upon the vows of the humble and to stretch out the right hand of his majesty for our defence. At last heard and liberated from temptations by the outstretched right hand of the divine majesty, and also instructed by the hidden and inexpressible language of God’s inspiration against the manifold snares of the enemy, according to the foregoing reading of the holy Gospel, he will joyfully sing the Offertory and say: “The ordinances of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts, and [judgments] sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; for your servant also keeps them” (Ps. 18:9–12 [Vulgate]).

[Col. 0220B] The Communion is then very fitting for one who keeps God’s ordinances; it says: “The sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest where she may lay her young” (Ps. 83:4 [Vulgate]). Thus, lifted up by desire for eternal things, she flies beyond all earthly things, thirsting for God alone throughout the days of her life, so that by cleaving to him there without ceasing or failing, among those blessed ones who will praise him for ages of ages, she may enjoy his eternal unchangeableness without any failure of contemplation, without any interval of change. May he bring us to this blessedness who is the blessedness of all the saints, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

288. HOMILY XXXIII. FOR MONDAY AFTER THE THIRD SUNDAY OF LENT.

[Col. 0220C] “In those days Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man before his lord and honoured” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 5).

By Naaman, whose name is said to mean “beauty” or “stirring,” may not inappropriately be signified any person who loves not the beauty of God’s house but the beauty of this present world. For one who seeks and loves the beauty of worldly loveliness, and desires to be adorned not in virtues but in the vanities of this life, may in a sense be called and named a beauty not good but evil. When, however, by God’s mercy, he is stirred toward salvation and repentance after harmful beauty has been removed and laid aside, he will deserve to be called a good, not an evil, stirring. For under this mystical name of stirring is expressed that salutary stirring, the stirring of contrition and repentance, by which a person becomes healthfully angry with himself and is moved in humble repentance because he has neglected the beauty and loveliness of the inward person while lavishly adorning his flesh—which will shortly perish and be consumed by decay and worms.

Yet before this salutary stirring arises in him, he will be commander of the army of the king of Syria. By Syria, interpreted “height,” we may understand a lofty and exalted heart. The king or lord of this lofty Syria is to be understood as the proud and arrogant spirit of the person. While this Naaman, still evilly beautiful, serves in its army as a glorious commander, he considers himself great and honoured before this same lord [Col. 0221A] of his. For because before his lord, before his own proud spirit, he honours and magnifies himself in his own eyes, he likewise desires to be magnified and honoured by all. Therefore what follows is very remarkable: it is written that through him the Lord gave salvation to Syria:

“Through him,” it says, “the Lord gave salvation to Syria. But he was a strong and wealthy man, yet leprous.” In this place we may consider the wonderful and ineffable great works of divine mercy. For although this Naaman is strong in evils, rich in sins, and deformed by the leprosy of sins, through him salvation will nevertheless be given by the Lord to Syria: salvation, I mean, of humility to the lofty heart. This happens when, as said above, the outward person is stirred through repentance from the adornment of vanity to the adornment of good works, [Col. 0221B] and thus the heart, formerly lofty and exalted, is bent down to humility.

“Now raiders had gone out from Syria and had carried away captive from the land of Israel a young captive girl, who was in the service of Naaman’s wife.” Once the aforesaid salvation of humility has begun in a person, there go out—that is, from the heart formerly very lofty—like certain raiders, thoughts which are not great or high but humble and small. From the land of Israel, that is, from spiritual conduct, they bring a little girl: a good will, but still slight and imperfect, and therefore in a sense captive. One who is held and constrained captive by another is not permitted to serve his own will or his own freedom. So too a good but still little will is called captive because it cannot yet fulfil, through perfection of work, the good which it wills and which lies before it. Yet this same will, although little and captive, will be energetic and constant in the service of Naaman’s wife. By Naaman’s wife we may understand the soul itself, to which the aforesaid girl of good will renders faithful service when she addresses her in these words: “Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria; surely he would heal him of his leprosy.” By Samaria, interpreted “guarding,” we rightly believe that the guarding of holy conduct is signified; and by the prophet who is in that Samaria we may understand the Lord of prophets himself. Thus it is as though the repentant soul said: “Would that my lord—my spirit, that is—were in Samaria! Would that he were so perfect and attentive in every watchfulness of spiritual life that he sought or desired nothing earthly, nothing passing away, but desired and loved the Lord of prophets alone and cleaved to him alone. For then indeed that same Lord and prophet would cleanse him from his leprosy,” [Col. 0221D] from every defilement and uncleanness of his sins.

Naaman therefore entered to his lord and reported to him, saying: “Thus and thus has the girl from the land of Israel spoken.” Since, by the little girl, we have said that a good but slight thought is to be understood, and by the land of Israel a good manner of life, what can we understand by Naaman entering to his lord and reporting what the same girl had said? Naaman—the outward man, that is—enters to his lord, namely to his spirit, and in a manner reports the words spoken by the girl when body and spirit agree with one another, when they meet in harmonious devotion, so that they do not delay to enter the land of Israel, the land of holy conduct, as that girl—that is, good will—has long secretly suggested. Hence it follows:

And the king of Syria said to him: “Go, and I will send letters to the king of Israel.” To say this is to do it. The often-mentioned king of Syria—that is, the human spirit—commands the outward man to go, to come to conversion, and swiftly to accomplish the good which he has proposed. “And I will send,” he says, “letters to the king of Israel.” To send letters to the king of Israel [Col. 0222B] is to make known in words to a spiritual master whatever that aforesaid girl has spoken and meditated secretly within him through divine inspiration.

When he had set out and had taken with him ten talents of silver, six thousand gold pieces, and ten changes of clothing, he brought letters to the king of Israel in these words: “When you receive this letter, know that I have sent to you Naaman my servant, that you may cure him of his leprosy.” This Naaman, who is to be saved and cleansed, brings with him ten talents of silver, desiring worthily to repent his transgression of the Decalogue; he also brings six thousand gold pieces—that is, his senses, made most pure by perfect will. He also brings letters to the king of Israel, when he firmly inscribes good will upon his heart, discloses it in words to his spiritual father, and asks to be received [Col. 0222C] by him into the fellowship of holy conduct, so that by worthy repentance he may be cleansed from the contagion of his sins.

291 And when the king of Israel had read the letter, he tore his garments and said: “Am I God, that I can kill and make alive, since this man has sent to me that I should cure a man of his leprosy?” The spiritual king of Israel, hearing the will and desire of penitent Naaman, in a manner tears his garments—that is, he resolves to alter his habits and deeds for the better—so that he may assist this wretched penitent by teaching and example, and also by the help of his intercession. “Am I God,” he says, “that I can kill in this sinful man the sins and vices which live in him [Col. 0222D], raise him from the death of the soul, and cleanse him from the most foul leprosy of sins?”

“Take note and see how he seeks an occasion against me.” You, that is, my faculties, take note and see that through abstinence, fasts, vigils, and labours I must rise up against myself, so that I may be able not only usefully to govern but also healthfully to benefit, in word and deed, this wretched and sinful man who repents humbly and confesses truthfully.

When Elisha, the man of God, heard that the king of Israel had torn his garments, he sent to him, saying: “Why have you torn your garments? Let him come to me, and let him know that there is a prophet in Israel.” The true Elisha, truly the man of God, truly the Son of God the Father, hearing that the king of Israel had torn [Col. 0223A] his garments—that is, had changed his works for the better—sends him messengers of his compassionate support and cooperation, saying: “Why have you torn your garments?” God’s questioning is his approval. It is as though he said: “I know for what reason you tore your garments, and how strictly you have resolved to order your life. Since it pleases me that you have acted and resolved thus in your heart, let this Naaman come to me. Let him come to me, I say, and receive from you, for love of my name, the habit of holy conduct. For I shall be your fellow-worker; I shall cure him of the leprosy of his sins, so that he may know and perceive that I am a prophet in Israel”—indeed, such a prophet as says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 33:11). It follows:

[Col. 0223B] Therefore Naaman came with horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha’s house. And Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying: “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan.” By the horses and chariots we may understand the faculties of both the outward and inward man, which this Naaman gathers to himself within himself; and, coming, he stands at the door of Elisha’s house, that is, he makes a firm profession of a spiritual purpose. The true Elisha commands him to wash seven times in the Jordan, which means “descent,” admonishing and exhorting him to humble himself both in heart and body, so that through the descent of profound humility he may deserve to receive the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

But because, after the beginnings of conversion, various phantasms of temptations sometimes arise, the following text immediately indicates that the often-mentioned [Col. 0223C] Naaman, complaining in sad murmuring, says: “I thought that he would come out to me, stand and invoke the name of the Lord his God, touch the place of the leprosy with his hand, and cure me.” As though he said: “Wretched man that I am, I thought that if I renounced this wicked world and entered the land of Israel, the land also of the spiritual life, that true Elisha would come forth to meet me through mercy and consolation; that he would deign to protect and defend me from the tumults of rising temptations; that, standing, he would invoke his name over me—that is, establish in me steadfast humility and patience, reveal to me the knowledge of his name in an abundance of sweetness, and so cleanse me from every defilement of flesh and spirit.”

[Col. 0223D] “Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel, that I should wash in them and be cleansed?” Abana means “stones”; Pharpar, “scattering” or “digging,” or “moles”; Damascus is said to mean “drinking blood.” It is as though he said: “While I still served carnal desires and opposed a hard, stony heart to truth; while by evil living I scattered every sense and understanding; while, digging like a mole, I laboured by every means to attain the things of the world; while I drank blood—that is, the sins of this age—with a thirsting heart—did not tears flow more abundantly for me, and did I not delight in a greater sweetness of divine savour? But now, after I have offered myself and all that is mine to God [Col. 0224A], after I have resolved to serve him alone in heart and body, I cannot accomplish the good that I will; instead I endure new and unfamiliar struggles of temptation. Therefore I judge it better and more useful to return to worldly business, so that, if I cannot attain heavenly goods, I may at least delight pleasurably in temporal goods.” It follows:

Therefore, when he had turned away and was departing angrily, his servants approached him and said: “Father, even if the prophet had told you some great thing, surely you ought to have done it; how much more, since now he has said to you: ‘Wash, and you shall be cleansed’?” Therefore, when, as we have said, the often-mentioned Naaman groans and suffers under temptations rising against him, murmurs, and thinks of forsaking the spiritual life and returning to the world, his servants—that is, his inward faculties, divinely stirred and enlightened—at once approach. Having driven away vain and various thoughts, the inward man exhorts himself in these words: “If the prophet—indeed, the Lord of prophets—had commanded you some great thing, that is, if he had permitted you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, should you not have endured it patiently, since your iniquity has deserved things far heavier and harsher? Why then do you murmur against God with such impatient grief because the sweetness of inward compunction is lacking to you, when you might consider it a great thing if, through worthy [Col. 0224B] satisfaction, you deserved to be cleansed from sins and freed from the punishments of hell?”

Thus, yes, thus the wretched man, when tempted and troubled, rebukes himself as though taking counsel with himself; and by God’s mercy it surely comes about, as the present text subsequently indicates, when it says:

Then he went down and washed seven times in the Jordan according to the word of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was cleansed of his leprosy. Descending, he washes seven times in the Jordan because, ever more humbled through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, he is mercifully cleansed from the leprosy of pride. And his flesh—that is, the inward man—becomes like the flesh of a little child: of a child, I say, through innocence; of a little one, through the true grace of humility.

And he returned to the man of God with all his company, came and stood before him, and said: “Truly I know that there is no other God in all the earth except the Lord God of Israel alone.” With all his company—that is, with every affection of the virtues—he returns to the performance of every good work [Col. 0224D], and strives to stand firm in his spiritual purpose with steadfastness of mind, saying: “Truly I know; I have learned by experience that the Lord shows particular mercy and favour to those dwelling in the land of Israel, that is, in the spiritual life, because there one who is perfectly converted can worthily make satisfaction for sins and has fitting time, day and night, for doing good works.”

295 HOMILY XXXIV. FOR FRIDAY AFTER THE THIRD SUNDAY OF THE FIRST LENT.

Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychem, near the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph (John 4).

[Col. 0225A] This most holy season of Lent which we observe, just as it has been specially chosen and set apart from the other seasons of the year for the salvation and remedy of souls, must likewise be observed with the diligence of special discipline. Thus, we who cannot live as we ought at other times may at least strive during these days to please God through the guarding of mind and body. The Apostle commends this season to us, saying: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). For in this season a person may obtain that throughout the whole remaining year his life may prosper in the Lord and in progress in spiritual virtues; he may also obtain that he may increasingly fall and fail in every grace of spiritual advancement.

For, to take an example from outward matters, now the ground is broken by the plough and sown; now vines are pruned and prepared for the future fruit expected from them. Nor was this ordained by God merely so that we should look to and seek that fruit alone—for food from the earth and drink from the vine—but he wished to prefigure that special good which surpasses all goods, which at this season he began to prepare and make ready for his Church: namely, his most holy body and blood, which are made from bread and wine.

We too are admonished and taught by these outward things to break up our own soil—that is, at this season to exercise our body through the pursuits of spiritual labours, and to bear in it and from it the seed of virtues, the seed of good works; to prune our own vine, cutting away from our soul the branches [Col. 0225C] of useless thoughts, evil pleasures, and desires, and planting in it good desires, virtues, and holy delights. For just as a farmer who is idle in ploughing now does not receive fruit in its season, so we too, if we neglect ourselves now, if we live carelessly and uselessly in these days, shall be found empty and vacant when the time of fruit, the time of Paschal joys, arrives; we shall be left without the grace of spiritual joys.

Let us therefore see to it that we do not receive the grace of God in vain. Let us labour now for God, so that then we may rest with God and in God. Let us now weep worthily in repentance for our sins, so that then, having received forgiveness of sins, we may rejoice with Christ. For this is what we are stirred, admonished, and urged toward day and night in all that we read and sing. For as the compassionate physician of souls wished that something should be withheld from the body during these days, so too he wished that the soul’s food and refreshment should be added and increased. Each day, indeed, we have distinct and new offices, readings, and Gospels in the celebration of Mass, abounding in spiritual food and drink; refreshed by these, the friend who loves God ought to be raised from earthly things to heavenly ones.

Thus this entire week abounds in heavenly nourishment. Rightly, moreover, this Sunday, which is the sixth from Septuagesima Sunday, corresponds to that sixth gift of the Holy Spirit—the gift, namely, [Col. 0226A] of understanding. On it we heard how Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute; how, when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke; and the other things there read, for grasping and spiritually understanding which the spirit of understanding was altogether necessary. But let us first see what understanding is.

297 True and perfect understanding is that a person should know God and know himself. This twofold knowledge—of God, certainly, and of oneself—is exceedingly necessary for every person who is to be saved, because neither can avail without the other. For who is the person who rightly knows himself? One who, considering his days and nights, his months and years, rightly recalls his transgressions and negligences, and is more able to despair than dare promise himself any hope of everlasting life. Conversely, who is so despairing as not to be able to rise to the hope of life, if he rightly knows the mercies of God? [Read: quin.] “His compassions,” says the Prophet, “are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9). For his mercy surpasses all human sins. Therefore, it is necessary for a person, in addition to knowledge of himself, to possess knowledge of God, so that, while knowledge of himself disturbs, casts down, and terrifies him, knowledge of God may give him something by which to breathe again and be comforted.

Everything which we read in this week has reference to the gift of understanding, namely to this twofold knowledge of God and self of which we have spoken. It is to this that pertains what we read on Monday about Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria. Coming leprous from Syria to Samaria to Elisha the prophet, he first grew angry when the prophet answered that he should wash seven times in the Jordan; afterward, as his servants pressed him and said, “Father, even if the prophet had told you some great thing, surely you ought to have done it,” he consented, went, and washed seven times in the Jordan according to the word of the man of God. Cleansed of his leprosy, he returned to the man of God, came and stood before him, and said: “Truly I know that there is no other God in all the earth except the Lord God of Israel alone” (4 Kings 5:15). When he said these things, he had already received in part the gift of the Holy Spirit, namely understanding, since amid the darkness of paganism he recognized the light of truth: he knew, believed, and deserved to confess God as his Creator and the Lord [Col. 0226D] of the whole earth.

What we read on the third day about that woman whose husband had died, and who cried out to Elisha when the creditor came to take her two sons; when he asked her, “What have you in your house?” and she answered, “Your handmaid has nothing in my house except a little oil, with which I may anoint myself” (4 Kings 4:2)—she was commanded to borrow from all her neighbours many empty vessels, to shut the door upon herself and her sons, to pour the oil into all those vessels, and, once they were full, to sell the oil and repay the creditor—all these things which we heard there are fittingly referred to the same gift of understanding, which, as we have said, is the twofold knowledge of God and self. For by the little oil of which that woman said, “Your handmaid has nothing except a little oil with which I may anoint myself,” may be understood that knowledge by which a person knows himself. But in the fact that this little oil, poured into all those vessels, grows and multiplies, the knowledge of God is aptly figured. A person has, as it were, a little oil with which he is anointed when he is compuncted by recollection and knowledge of his sins. But that little oil grows immeasurably when, after his sins have been recognized and, through continual repentance and satisfaction, in part purged and healed, he advances to the knowledge and love of God. Through this he is both freed from the creditor and quickened unto life.

Having received this grace, the reading of the fourth day fittingly follows, in which it is said: “Honour your father and your mother; you shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness against your neighbour” (Exod. 20:12), and the rest, by which one is sufficiently instructed in the observance of God’s commandments. For unless a person first begins to know and love both himself and God, it is impossible for him either to hear the commandments of God profitably or to observe them rightly.

After knowledge of God and self, after the observance of God’s commandments, the reading of the fifth day rightly follows. It is read there of the Shunammite woman who, after her son’s death, came to Elisha on Mount Carmel, grasped his feet, and said: “As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you” (4 Kings 4:30). He rose and followed her; entering [Col. 0227C] the house, he shut the door upon himself and the child, went up and lay upon the child, and placed his mouth upon the child’s mouth, his eyes upon the child’s eyes, and his hands upon the child’s hands (ibid., vv. 33–34). Elisha signifies Christ, who places his eyes upon the eyes of the dead child—that is, upon the spirit of a person dead in sins—when by his grace he grants him to see his own death and, seeing it, to weep for it. 299 He places his mouth upon the mouth when he inwardly touches him by his interior inspiration, so that he may usefully speak to God in prayer and truthfully confess to his superior the sins that he sees and recognizes. He places his hands upon the child’s hands when, after the knowledge and confession of sins, he mercifully advances and leads him to good works. Thus the spirit of understanding is signified in all that we read on each of these days.

But it is more clearly indicated, and works more fully and mercifully, in today’s reading of the holy Gospel. There we read how Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychem, near the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Samaria means “she-ass” or “guarding”; Sychem is said to mean “shoulder.” And because burdens are carried on the shoulders, Sychem fittingly signifies the labour of the present life. The city of Samaria represents the holy Church, which strives to please God through the keeping of his commandments. It is also not unfittingly called Sychem, because through the various conflicts of labour which it endures for Christ, it hastens toward the future joys of eternal rest.

The estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph, I consider to mean the kingdom of heaven. Jacob, God the Father, gave this estate to his son Joseph, our Lord Jesus Christ, because the Son possesses all that the Father possesses, not only according to divinity but also according to humanity. Thus, after rising from the dead, he said to his disciples: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). In his divinity he possessed all things eternally with the Father; in his humanity all things were given to him by the Father. What things? “That at his name every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10).

The city of Samaria called [Col. 0228B] Sychem may also be understood as any spiritual way of life, every holy congregation, which is exercised in this life through the keeping of its rule of life, the discipline of spiritual strictness, and the constancy of daily labours. This city of Samaria is rightly said to be near the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph. For all who in the holy Church labour perseveringly for God in the observance of the spiritual life, although, burdened as they are by a mortal body, they cannot yet enter that estate—the kingdom of heaven—are nevertheless near it. For after the miseries of mortal life have run their course, they are received into it, where they shall rejoice eternally among the choirs of angels. Unjust and perverse people are by no means near this estate, but far from it; for those who do not wish in this life to approach the kingdom of heaven through good desires and works will one day be far from it. It follows:

There was there a fountain of Jacob. By the fountain, by which stains are washed away and the thirsty refreshed, either the power of tears or knowledge of the sacred Scriptures is figuratively expressed, and not without reason. The fountain of tears washes away the filth of sins; knowledge of the Scriptures abundantly refreshes the thirst of the soul that loves God. This fountain is Jacob’s fountain—that is, the fountain of almighty God—because from him comes the power of tears and from him proceeds knowledge of the Scriptures. This fountain is found nowhere but in the city of Samaria called Sychem, where dwell those people who, through the pursuit of daily labour, know how to seek and find within themselves the sweet water of constant compunction. The Lord willingly and often comes to this city; God delights to dwell with and in such people. His dwelling and rest are not among worldly people and lovers of the world, but among spiritual people who steadfastly despise and cast aside the things of the world for love of him. He is with the former through the power of his divinity; with the latter through the mercy of his compassion. Hence the Evangelist immediately adds:

Jesus therefore, weary from the journey, was sitting thus by the fountain. In the substance of his divinity he could never become weary; in the substance of his humanity he could become weary, because he willed to take upon himself and experience every misery of our weakness except sin alone. Because he accepted in himself that in which he could become weary for the salvation of humankind, he willed not without cause, weary from the journey, to sit there where he knew that she would come upon whom he had determined to have mercy: where that Samaritan woman—not a noblewoman, not a king’s daughter, but a sinful, poor, and despised woman—would find him, and where he would more intimately impart to her the gift of his Spirit, namely the gift of understanding of which we have begun to speak.

Even now, moreover, Jesus is in a manner daily on a journey and grows weary from the journey when his word and teaching are presented by his ministers, namely holy preachers, to unworthy hearers. Their evil life and perverse conduct are a great weariness to him. Weary from the journey, he seeks where he may sit; [Col. 0229B] he seeks where he may find that fountain—that is, a soul possessing the water of compunction, a soul fervent with heavenly desire—so that he may rest in it and make it rest in himself.

Nor should we pass over what he says: “He was sitting thus by the fountain.” He sits thus because he conforms and adapts himself to every soul in whatever way he judges useful and necessary for its salvation. He sits thus because he both consoles the soul and does not disdain to be consoled by the soul. He sits thus, now stirring the soul through knowledge of itself to repentance for sins, now raising it through knowledge of God to inward sweetness and love of the heavenly homeland. This grace of almighty God, working its work in the blessed soul in such a manner, is fittingly expressed in the following words, when it is immediately added:

The hour was about the sixth. The Evangelist John notes this same hour where he says: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8:1). It is rightly called an hour, because whatever may be grasped and tasted of God’s compassion and sweetness in that brief moment when God visits a soul beloved to him is exceedingly slight and brief. Yet that hour, though very brief, is most sweet. It surpasses all the joys of the present life, because whatever perfection is ever effected in a person, that hour effects and teaches it. Nor should we pass over that he did not say, “The hour was the sixth,” but “The hour was about the sixth.” The number six, which consists of a perfect number, signifies perfection. But because complete perfection can neither be acquired nor possessed in this life, “about” is rightly added, since in this life no one is fully perfect, but only, as it were, perfect. The fullness of perfection is reserved for us in eternal life, where, once the “as it were” has been removed, no imperfection will remain. Yet that perfection begins here, as is mystically indicated when it is immediately added:

302 A woman came from Samaria to draw water. That woman is the soul softened by God’s grace, which comes, as it were, from Samaria when it seeks daily to draw near to God through strict keeping of its manner of life. But why does it come? To draw water. By water we may understand both evil and good desires. For it comes to draw into itself from the fountain of God’s mercy good desires, and by the assistance of God’s grace to draw evil desires out of itself.

Jesus said to her: “Give me to drink.” His request that the woman give him drink signifies the gift of his compassion, because a person can do nothing by himself unless he who can do all things supplies both the willing and the ability to do what is good. Thus, when he says, “Give me to drink,” this must not be referred only to that person who is in the city of Samaria called Sychem, who knows through guarding and labour in the present life sweetly to refresh God within himself by drawing good things in and drawing evil things out. He also often speaks the same words to a person still lying in sins, from whom he asks to drink as though thirsty, when by inner inspiration he inwardly stirs that person to thirst for and desire the remedy of salvation. It follows:

The Samaritan woman said to him: “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask drink from me, who am a Samaritan woman?” As though she said: “By your compassion working in me, Lord, I desire to be saved; but I do not know how I ought or can be saved. But since you are a Jew, since according to the multitude of your mercies you have declared: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live’ (Ezek. 33:11), show me through the grace of your compassion how I may rise from the pit of destruction and return to the way of salvation. For I am a Samaritan woman, defiled and made old in the crimes of a beastly life; and unless you grant and inspire me to know how I can live, I shall by no means be able to reach that water by which you may both be refreshed in me [Col. 0230C] and refresh me.”

Jesus answered and said: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me to drink,’ perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” As though he said: “You have come in part to knowledge of yourself, because you have recognized yourself to be a Samaritan woman; but it remains for you to know me also, who have worked these things in you. For if you knew who it is that says to you, ‘Give me to drink’; if you tasted and understood that I am the fountain of life, the fountain of sweetness and grace; perhaps you would ask me, and I would give you living water. There is, as it were, dead water when a person is compuncted for his sins and dead deeds. There is, as it were, living water when he is compuncted not only for evils committed [Col. 0230D] but also for goods neglected, and when, made alive within himself, he is moved by joy for eternal blessedness.”

The truly penitent soul considers itself altogether unworthy of this water. But, knowing itself better and better, it adds: “Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep; whence then have you living water?” As though she said: “Lord, you ought to have in me and from me that water which would delight you and heal me. But the well is deep: that is, so great is the depth of my sins that I do not judge myself worthy ever to attain that living water, the life-giving grace of your sweetness.”

Jesus answered and said to her: “Everyone who drinks of this water shall thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water [Col. 0231A] which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.” By this water, after drinking which a person thirsts again, may fittingly be understood the desire and pleasure of the world: the more a person drinks from it, the more he thirsts. But the water given by him who is the fountain of mercy signifies holy delights and sweet desires for everlasting life. This water makes the drinker not thirsty. “But it shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.” A person, indeed, after the fashion of one who springs from place to place, raises himself from the earth when, having somehow tasted the delights of the heavenly homeland, he passes beyond all earthly things by sweet desires, ardently seeks heavenly things, and transfers himself, as it were, from place to place. He does this when he begins to go from virtue to virtue, when after holy thoughts and holy desires he courageously girds himself for good and righteous works. And it becomes in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life, because after such leaps of virtue, after he has passed through the mortality of this life, he will spring across into the eternity of heavenly joys.
