This blessed woman had gradually begun inwardly to taste the flavour of this water when she said:

“Lord, give me this water, that I may not thirst nor come here to draw.” Every blessed soul still says and ought to say the same words: “Lord, give me this water, that I may not thirst.” As though it said: “Give me, Lord, in the sweetness of your goodness, this your water, which may become in me a fountain of water springing up into eternal life, so that, refreshed and renewed by the delight of spiritual virtues and by desires for heavenly goods [Col. 0231C], I may no longer thirst for what I once thirsted for, what by evil living I used to draw from the desires and pleasures of the world.”

Jesus said to her: “Go, call your husband, and come here.” As though he said: “In order that, by my gift, you may attain the grace which you desire: go, persist manfully in good works; call your husband, your understanding, by diligently attending to the practices of prayer; come here, gathering your whole self inwardly.”

The woman answered and said: “I have no husband.” This answer of the woman is the answer of a penitent soul, which declares that it has no husband when, through the visiting and inspiring grace of God, increasingly recognizing itself, it complains that it lacks the manly discernment and understanding by which it ought to know God. God approves this humility. Hence he says afterward:

“You have spoken well, saying, ‘I have no husband’; for you have had five husbands, and he whom you now have is not your husband.” The five husbands may be understood as the five senses of a person. The soul then has these five senses as five husbands ruling and commanding it when it delightfully sees unlawful things with its eyes; willingly hears what is not beneficial with its ears; willingly says with its mouth what offends God; does not restrain its hands from unlawful touch; and does not endeavour to draw back its feet from wicked steps. A sixth, as it were, succeeds these five husbands when a person falls into error by either not recognizing or even defending such excesses of the outward senses as we have just heard. This is what he means when he says: “And he whom you now have is not your husband.”

305 The woman said to him: “Lord, I perceive that you are a prophet.” It is the prophet’s office to know and speak of past and future things. The soul sees the Lord within itself as a prophet when, by the prompting of his inspiration, it begins to see, to prophesy and preach to itself, both the future goods it has lost and the future evils it has deserved. Therefore it judges nothing more useful than humbly to flee to the aids of prayer. But because it still does not know the manner of perfect prayer, it suppliantly implores the very Father of mercies to teach it. This is signified for us by the following words spoken by this woman:

[Col. 0232B] “Our fathers worshipped on this mountain, and you say that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship.” This woman was not foolish, but wise, because eternal Wisdom, which spoke to her outwardly, taught her inwardly. Therefore, to her prudent question about how and where God should be worshipped, Jesus gives a wise answer:

“Woman, believe me: the hour is coming when you shall worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth.” Certainly, in these words of the questioning woman and answering Lord, the Lord teaches us also what and how we ought to pray: no prayer is useful and perfect unless it is made in confession of the true and undivided Trinity. He indicates its distinction in these words when he says: “But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers shall worship in spirit and truth.” He names the Father and the Spirit; by “truth” he signifies himself, the Son consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

We may also understand otherwise what he says: “They shall worship the Father in spirit and truth.” We must worship the Father in spirit, gathering our spirit inwardly to ourselves, so that we do not dissipate ourselves among useless things, but gather all our faculties toward him whom we worship and whose grace of compassion and mercy [Col. 0232D] we implore. We must worship in truth, so that in our prayers and good works we seek nothing other than that true and highest good, to which no falsehood or doubleness attaches. God loves such worshippers, as he himself says in what follows:

“For the Father also,” he says, “seeks such as worship him.” What a man seeks, that he loves; what he does not love, that he does not seek. Therefore God’s seeking is God’s loving. And he rightly says: “For the Father also seeks such as worship him,” because, whatever they may be before men, however far they may have fallen from him and perished through sinning, those whom he foreknew and predestined would become such, he seeks because he loves. Whatever pit of sins they may be submerged in, from there [Col. 0233A] he will draw them out through the mercy of his loving-kindness, because he gathers them to himself through true and perfect repentance. It follows:

“God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.” God indeed, who is spirit, is truly worshipped when he is worshipped in spirit and truth; that is, when temporal and perishable things have been excluded, and, as we have said, a person has gathered his spirit inwardly to himself, so that in prayer he seeks nothing but the supreme and true Good alone, which surpasses every good. When a person has ascended this exalted degree of perfection, he may rightly say with this blessed woman:

“I know that Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will declare all things to us.” For there [Col. 0233B] he receives that full gift of the Holy Spirit, namely the gift of understanding; there he advances from true knowledge of himself to knowledge of God. For when that true Messiah who is called Christ, through the anointing of his inspiration, in a sense declares all things to him, no teacher’s tongue instructs a person so greatly as does that hour of prayer, the hour of heavenly infusion. For there a person truly speaks with God, and God with the person, as is subsequently added; for it follows:

Jesus says to her: “I am [he] who speaks with you.” We read in the Gospel that the Lord asked his disciples: “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13). When they had set forth the various opinions of men about him, Peter said: “You are [Col. 0233C] Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16); and the Lord answered: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 17). He commended the disciple’s confession, yet he did not manifest himself to him, or to any of his disciples, in words so explicit as to say, “I am,” as he did to this blessed woman, to whom he said: “I am [he] who speaks with you.” In this he was already giving us an example and foreshadowing that ineffable mercy which he still works daily with sinners: first, through the grace of his visitation, he enlightens them to know themselves; afterwards, in the sweetness of his goodness, he mercifully raises them even to know him. It follows:

[Col. 0233D] “And immediately his disciples came, and they marvelled that he was speaking with a woman. Yet no one said, ‘What do you seek?’ or, ‘Why do you speak with her?’” They loved him as sons love a most sweet father; they feared him as disciples fear a most venerable master. Therefore, though they marvelled that he spoke with a woman, they did not dare ask what he was saying with her, because they rendered due reverence and honour to so awe-inspiring a master. And because he did not wish Peter, James, John, or any of his disciples to be present or take part when he intended to lead and teach this sinful woman toward knowledge and confession of her guilt, in this he gave us a clear example and instruction concerning how great the intimacy and secrecy between confessor and penitent [Col. 0234A] ought to be: no one but the penitent and the hearer ought to be present, and confession ought never to be made public or spread abroad. And because his conversation with her to whom he spoke was her instruction and salvation, it is rightly added:

“The woman therefore left her water-jar, went into the city, and said to the men: ‘Come and see a man who told me everything that I have done.’” Yet even now, every day, the woman—that is, every blessed soul softened by the grace of his visitation and inspiration—leaves her water-jar when she completely abandons the world’s desire and avarice, which may be understood through the water-jar. Once the water-jar has been left behind, she can go into the city; she can usefully aid the salvation of others by preaching and teaching. [Col. 0234B] Hence it is fittingly added: “And she said to the men: ‘Come and see a man who told me everything that I have done.’” But because avarice and desire consist not only in riches and money, but also in favour and empty glory, whoever desires—even while living rightly and teaching others rightly—to benefit others, must cast away his water-jar in such a manner that he desires not himself but God to be praised and magnified in his deeds and words, and seeks not his own honour but God’s. Only then can his teaching be useful and fruitful, as the evangelist subsequently added:

“And they went out,” he says, “from the city and came to him.” The Samaritans go out from the city when sinful people, awakened by the preaching of God’s word, pass away from citizenship, so to speak, and neighbourhood with vices [Col. 0234C] toward God, and begin to live justly and commendably. It follows:

“Meanwhile the disciples asked him, saying, ‘Rabbi, eat.’ But he said to them: ‘I have food to eat which you do not know.’” Christ’s food is our salvation. They did not yet know this food of his. Hence they said: “Has anyone brought him something to eat?” Jesus says to them: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, that I may complete his work.” It was the will of God the Father that the human being whom he had created in his own image and likeness should be recreated through the passion of his Only-begotten; for his work was in some sense incomplete so long as humanity had not been redeemed through the death of his Son. But since the time was now at hand [Col. 0234D] when God the Son was preparing himself to complete this same work of God the Father, he disclosed this redemption to those whom he wished to have as fellow-workers and ministers in the salvation of the human race, when he said:

“Do you not say that there are still four months, and then the harvest comes?” In these four months may fittingly, in my judgment, be understood either the four cardinal virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—or the four periods: the time before the Law, the time under the Law, the time under grace, and the time of future judgment. When that fourth month has elapsed, namely on the day of dreadful judgment, that desirable and joyous harvest will come, in which all who are predestined to life will be cut down from the field of this mortality [Col. 0235A] and stored and laid up in the granaries of heavenly blessed immortality. But because he wished this harvest, begun by the patriarchs and prophets, to be brought to completion and fulfilment through the blessed apostles themselves, he added and said:

“Behold, I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see the fields, how they are already white for harvest.” As though he plainly said: Behold, I who descended into this world for the salvation of the human race do not wish to remain long in the world. I wish my work to be completed through us. Behold, I say to you: “Lift up your eyes.” “For blessed are the eyes that see what you see.” For it was said of you: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5; Rom. 10:18). And see the fields, [Col. 0235B] that is, the various nations of peoples, how they are already white for harvest: through your ministry they are to be whitened and renewed by the faith which they will receive through your preaching in the regeneration of baptism.

“And he who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto eternal life, so that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.” By the one who sows he signified the order of patriarchs and prophets; by the one who reaps he intended the apostolic order to be understood. For what the patriarchs and prophets sowed in sorrow and groaning, the apostles reaped in joy and exultation. Did not Abraham sow in sorrow and labour? In order to obtain that seed in whom all nations were to be blessed, he went out [Col. 0235C] from his land and kindred, lived as a stranger in a foreign land, had his wife taken away, and endured many harsh adversities. They sowed indeed by generating one another from their flesh, as it is written: “Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob” (Matt. 1:2). They sowed by preaching Christ’s future incarnation, prefiguring and foretelling it by figures and enigmas. But they did not reap what they sowed, because they did not see in the flesh the coming of him whom they awaited, our Lord Jesus Christ; rather, sad and groaning, they descended into hell with all their descendants. But because he was also to save and console them through his death, he rightly said: “And he who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto [Col. 0235D] eternal life, so that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.” As though he had said: You, by baptizing and by preaching and teaching my faith to the fields—that is, to the nations of those whom I will save—shall reap; you shall receive the unfading crown, the reward of eternal blessedness; and you shall gather fruit unto eternal life, so that both they—namely my patriarchs and prophets who sowed—and you who reap may rejoice together; that is, that you may alike exult over your salvation and that of the whole human race through the infinite ages of ages. Amen.

311  
## HOMILY XXXV. ON THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF LENT, THE FIRST

“Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee, which is [the Sea] of Tiberias.” (John 6.)

Today’s Sunday, which is exalted and honoured with such festivity in chant and reading, [Col. 0236A] seems to announce the joyful and renowned delights of the life to come. For the whole excellence of today’s office sets forth the measure of a singular and great joy—a joy that will have no measure—and, if I may say so, even anticipates in its chant the solemnities of Easter Day. For where, or when, can the Introit truly and with true joy be sung: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her,” except when our great and true High Priest, Jesus Christ, adorned with all his pontifical vestments, has entered within the Holy of Holies? Daily, as it were in part, he is clothed and adorned in sacred and precious garments whenever he deigns to clothe the souls of his elect, freed from this prison of death, in the beauty of his robe of immortality. [Col. 0236B] Yet while another portion of his members is still wandering on earth, our High Priest by no means proceeds fully and perfectly adorned before his people. But when, in the general resurrection, he has gathered all his members to himself and brought them to the longed-for glory of their reward, then, truly adorned in his entirety, he will proceed to the altar to celebrate his Mass, where thousands upon thousands, joined with the chanting choirs of angels, ought to resound and rejoice, beginning thus: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her; rejoice with joy.” What does it mean to say, “rejoice with joy”? It would have sufficed to say, “rejoice.” But he added “with joy” in order to indicate that they rejoice both in body and soul. For if they rejoiced in body and not in soul, or [Col. 0236C] in soul and not in body, they would not truly rejoice with joy. But they shall rejoice with joy, because in body and soul alike they will possess the full, certain, secure joys of eternal happiness. [312] They shall also be satisfied from the breasts of consolation of that heavenly city, where, with every desolation wiped away, they will suck the milk of perpetual consolation—a milk by which they are always nourished, always given drink, and made drunk.

And as for what is added in the verse, “I rejoiced in those things which were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121:1); and likewise in the Gradual, “I rejoiced in those things which were said to me”—what is this but that this twofold chant signifies the twofold glory of body and soul? [Col. 0236D] Today’s reading from the holy Gospel, which recalls that five thousand men were satisfied with five loaves and two fishes, teaches and leads us toward obtaining these joys. These are truly figures of that satisfaction which shall be without surfeit and of that desired vision which shall be without weariness. But the fact that the subsequent words of this Gospel reading are read at another time, while the preceding words are omitted, whereas now the subsequent words are recited together with those preceding, seems to me to have this reason: the four sacraments of the Lord—his passion, death, resurrection, and ascension—which we are soon to celebrate, are sufficiently expressed in them. Each of us ought so to contemplate and venerate them that through them he may deserve to attain the vision of God and perfect knowledge of him.

The evangelist says: “Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee, [Col. 0237A] which is [the Sea] of Tiberias.” With great aptness and suitability, the sea signifies the world. For just as the sea is named from bitterness, because it is salty and bitter, so this world is not unfittingly designated by the name of sea because of the bitterness of sins. In these the entire human race has so been immersed and wasted away that there would be no one able to escape the bitterness of death and Gehenna. But for our Lord Jesus Christ this sea was the Sea of Galilee, which means “passage,” because he so went across the sea of this world that, alone conceived and born without the stain of sin, [313] he sinned neither in word, deed, nor thought throughout his life. Thus, living in the humanity assumed for us, he went across the Sea of Galilee by perfectly turning away from evils. The excellence of his passion is indicated [Col. 0237B] by the word “Tiberias.” For Tiberias is interpreted “his goodness.” That goodness and mercy of his which caused him to put on the death-bound condition of our flesh—his goodness and the vision of his goodness likewise caused him, the innocent, to be willing to suffer and die for the guilty, the just for the unjust, so that, abolishing enmities in his flesh, he might provide access to God the Father, blot out original sin, and grant forgiveness of sins. Therefore, while he thus went away, while he thus willed to suffer, die, and rise again, what follows came to pass:

“And a great multitude followed him, because they saw the signs which he performed upon those who were sick.” In this great multitude the primitive Church, which began in the apostles, may be understood. [Col. 0237C] It is called great because it was great both in number and in merit. Of this multitude it is also written that “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). This great multitude followed the Lord upon seeing his signs: the signs, I say, of his humility and abasement, of mockery, scourges, death, and resurrection. These signs were performed upon those who were sick, because he exposed his body to torments and punishments in order to remove every infirmity of our souls and restore and renew every strength and health. But when the dispensation for which he had come was accomplished,

as the evangelist says, “He went up onto the mountain, and there he sat [Col. 0237D] with his disciples.” The Lord went up onto the mountain when, after the joy and triumph of his resurrection, he ascended victorious and sat at the right hand of the Father. There, taken away from us, he remains with his disciples—that is, with the holy angelic spirits—with whom he has continual festivity, solemn joy, perpetual and happy fellowship. Of their feast day it is immediately added:

“Now the Passover, the feast day of the Jews, was near.” Passover means “passage.” This passage may signify the departure and transition of our life. [314] It is truly near, because, although the labour of our present exile may seem to weave out lengthy delays for us, certain and imminent death nevertheless threatens and presses upon everyone. Do you not see, beloved, how those who were with us last year have now been taken away [Col. 0238A] from us? Thus those who are with us today perhaps pass away tomorrow and do not remain. They are suddenly taken from us and are found no more. But when this passage has been made and finished, all the blessed arrive at the feast day of the Jews. In the Jews’ feast day we may understand the brightness and joy of the angels, who are Jews—that is, confessors—because with unceasing voice they praise and glorify the name of God the Father. To this splendour of the unending festive day possessed by the holy angels, the elect pass after Passover, where morning or evening shall not come. In the present life, indeed, evening and morning exist: evening, I say, when we are so hindered by the frailty of our flesh, the temptations of the devil, or the adversities or prosperities of the world that we cannot see God clearly; [Col. 0238B] morning, however, when, our torpor shaken off, some small light of divine brightness has shone upon our hearts. But in that joy of eternal life neither morning nor evening will come; rather, there will be one feast day of the Jews, namely of the holy angels and souls who perpetually confess and praise God. In order to bring us, confessing and praising, to this feast day, from the beginning he has always lifted up the eyes of his mercy, as the Gospel says in what follows:

“When therefore Jesus had lifted up his eyes and saw that a very great multitude was coming to him.” What is now said simply as “when he had lifted,” but as “when he had lifted up,” seems to me to signify that it was always hidden from the beginning in what way God hidden would deign to become man manifest [Col. 0238C] at the end of the ages. And because all who are saved were in his predestination, it is rightly said that he lifted up his eyes and saw the greatest multitude coming to him. In this greatest multitude the holy apostles may be designated, who are worthily and rightly called the greatest multitude because of the eminence of their merits: they surpassed all patriarchs and all prophets. They truly [315] had blessed eyes and blessed ears, by which they deserved to see and hear God, and to whom he made known, as to his friends, all things which he had heard from the Father. Yet not only they, but all their imitators, who despised earthly things and became not merely despisers of the world but exposed their bodies to diverse and countless punishments even unto death, [Col. 0238D] are called the greatest multitude. Hence the greatest multitude before the Lord were and are also those who strove to obey not only the Lord’s command but also his counsel, of whom the apostle Paul says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:25). Therefore, because God the Father has provided at every time for the salvation of all humanity, he sent his preachers at every time—before the Law, under the Law, and under grace—and, seeing this greatest multitude, he says to Philip:

“Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?” By Philip may be understood the preachers of the Old Testament, in whom and through whom God spoke in promising his advent; by whom God the Creator was believed in, and salvation and redemption were expected from him. Yet how that same salvation was to be fulfilled and accomplished was not known to the other faithful, save for a few to whom it was singularly given as a gift to know that he would be born from a virgin. [Col. 0239A] And because faith in Christ’s incarnation and passion has always existed in the Church of God from the beginning, and those who knew these things were never lacking, though they did not deserve to see and comprehend them in their fulfilment, the evangelist fittingly adds:

“But this he said, testing him. For he himself knew what he was going to do.” For the patriarchs and prophets, it was a great trial to know and not know: to know that he would come at some time, but not to know when and how it would be. God the Father alone knew, while the patriarchs and prophets were ignorant, the time and hour in which he had decreed that his Son would come for the restoration [Col. 0239B] of humankind, so that humanity might receive again the good for which it had been created from the beginning. But if we wish to refer to Philip what is said, “for he himself knew what he was going to do,” this may be understood: the patriarchs and prophets knew well that they ought to declare [316] in obscure and hidden utterances, until the time when these things were to be manifested in truth. This is also indicated in Philip’s response, when he says:

“Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not enough for them, that each might receive a little.” In the two hundred denarii understand the Law and the Prophets. For the Law had, as it were, bread worth a hundred denarii; the prophetic word had bread worth a hundred denarii, because, as we have said, it proclaimed and taught belief in God and in the Saviour to come in the flesh. [Col. 0239C] But these loaves were not sufficient for salvation until each person should deserve to receive and see a little something—that is, him who, according to divinity, is incomprehensible, made little and small in his humanity. Hence Moses, once sent to free the Israelite people, declaring that he was not fit for this work, prayed that he might come who would save both Moses and all others, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4:13). Isaiah too, burning with the same desire, cried out: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and come down!” (Isa. 64:1). But when those heralds had ceased, the preachers of the New Testament came forward; through Andrew they may be understood, and by them are proclaimed both the manner of redemption [Col. 0239D] and the character of the Redeemer’s person.

The evangelist says: “One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, says to him: ‘There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fishes.’” By Simon, which is interpreted “obedient,” and Peter, which is interpreted “knowing,” understand one and the same Son of God: he who truly was Simon, that is, obedient to God the Father unto death, and who is truly called Peter, that is, knowing. For he knows all things before they happen; he alone searches and penetrates the abyss of the human heart. Andrew’s brother—namely, the holy apostles especially, and other preachers—were and are his brothers; he himself deigned to call them his brothers, saying: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. 28:10). Likewise, elsewhere: “I will declare your name to my brothers” [Col. 0240A] (Ps. 21:23). What do these brothers of the Lord God proclaim? “There is one boy here,” they say. “Behold, a boy has been born to us; a son has been given to us” (Isa. 9:6). For all their preaching concerns this boy, this one boy, our Lord Jesus Christ. [317] He is rightly and most fittingly called a boy because he was wholly pure, wholly sound, wholly unstained; and he is called not only a boy, but one boy, because he was one in divinity and one in humanity. And he who was thus one and singular boy did not refuse also to be a boy here. This word is demonstrative and infinite, by which is indicated that the eternal and immortal became temporal and mortal for us. He had five barley loaves and two fishes. In the five barley loaves, as [Col. 0240B] we have often said and heard, may be understood the five books of Moses or the five senses of the human being.

Yet we may understand something still more elevated in these five loaves. Holy Scripture, the treasury of the supreme King, abounds in such riches that it bestows much and is nevertheless always found inexhaustible. In these five loaves we may understand the five senses of the Lord’s body—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—which, as other human beings do, he deigned to possess in the humanity he assumed for us. But why do we call these loaves not of fine wheat flour but of barley? For this reason: barley has something in it which, with sound faith and sound understanding, can be applied to Christ. As you know, barley is rough and pure. [Col. 0240C] In a certain respect Christ was this: not indeed austere to others, harsh or hard toward anyone—for he was gentle and merciful toward all people—but austere to himself; he was very hard toward himself. For every desire of worldly pleasure, though it is sweet and delightful to the flesh, he utterly excluded from his five senses, so that he never admitted to them anything which the flesh caresses and seeks; rather, he kept them in all justice and holiness beyond all people. He was hard toward himself when, having contracted no sin requiring purification by fasting, he completed a fast of forty days and forty nights. He made himself hard and austere in his passion when so great a Lord was willing, for his servants, to be tortured, struck, spat upon, bound, and scourged by the judge Pilate, and at last deigned to die as though a thief, between two thieves, [318] on the altar of the cross.

[Col. 0240D] Nor should it be passed over that barley is fodder for beasts. Christ too is the fodder and refreshment of his beasts, namely of those who desire to be his beasts, who offer and render him assistance through the zeal of good and praiseworthy conduct. David declares that he is a beast of this Lord, saying: “I became as a beast before you” (Ps. 73:23). Likewise, concerning the same beasts: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 35:7). The men are good prelates; the beasts are subjects. Both are saved if the manifold mercy of almighty God deigns to look upon them. These things may be understood concerning the five loaves; let us now see what may be meant by the two fishes.

[Col. 0241A] In the two fishes the divinity and soul of Christ may be understood. Nor is it unsuitable for Christ’s divinity and soul to be understood by the fishes, because, just as fishes customarily lie hidden in waters, so no mortal could know or investigate by what union Christ’s divinity and soul were one person in him. But when that ineffable joy comes, in which we shall at last delight after Christ’s body has been gathered together in heaven, these two fishes will be drawn, as it were, out of the waters and set before us for knowing, loving, and praising. But because among these matters no mortal may rightly know perfectly what will someday be revealed concerning Christ, they fittingly add:

[Col. 0241B] “But what are these among so many?” As though they say: O Lord, great and most glorious things are said of you; splendid and ineffable things are told of you and of the glory of your kingdom. But we, little and weak as we are, wonder what these things are among so many—among so many, namely, princes of heaven, angels and archangels, and other blessed spirits, seated in whose midst you reveal and display yourself, as you are, in your delights. But oh, when shall it be granted to us, least and unworthy as we are, to see and possess these things among so many? After these sighs, after these desires of the heart, the Lord subsequently teaches by what power we ought to come among so many, saying to the apostles:

[Col. 0241C] [319] “Make the people recline.” He rightly and truly reclines who, not thinking high things of himself, lowers himself in the deep humility of his heart. From our ancient father Adam we learned rather to be exalted than humbled; from the new Adam, our Father, we hold nothing but the measure and pattern of humility, of which it is immediately added:

“Now there was much grass in the place.” What does the much grass mean except the much, great, and precious flesh of Christ? This much grass was in a place—but in what place? Namely, in the womb of the blessed and undefiled Virgin Mary, from whom he was conceived and born. He who according to his divinity was eternal, immortal, incomprehensible, and not localized, willed to become temporal and localized. All who went before us and attained the kingdom of heaven imitated these traces of humility; [Col. 0241D] for by great perfection of humility they pleased God, as follows:

“The men therefore reclined, about five thousand in number.” By their example, brothers, let us recline; let us be humbled in heart and body, because if we are humbled in this way, we shall truly be found men, truly strong before the Lord. But it should be noted that the reclining men are about five thousand in number. For we are now not in complete humility, but as it were in a certain likeness of humility; and so, meanwhile, until “the *as it were*” is taken away, let us flee exaltation and love humiliation, that we may deserve to come there where we are without “as it were,” and are in truth what we are. But because it is difficult to be humbled, in order that we may imitate and follow his humility he did what follows:

[Col. 0242A] “Jesus therefore took the loaves.” He took from us what is ours, because he became man for human beings: this is Jesus’ taking the loaves.

[320] “And when he had given thanks, he distributed [them] to those reclining.” Our Lord Jesus Christ gave many thanks, for he showed and bestowed the diverse and infinite graces of his goodness on the entire human race. Did he not give pre-eminent thanks when he descended from heaven into the Virgin’s womb? Did he not give saving thanks when he went forth from the womb of the same Virgin as a bridegroom from his bridal chamber? Did he not give many thanks throughout the whole time when he dwelt with people, praying, healing, and preaching? [Col. 0242B] Yet he never gave full and perfect thanks except at that hour when he willed to suffer and die and deigned to lay down his beloved soul for those who loved him. When these thanksgivings had been completed and accomplished, it was beautifully and aptly said that he distributed to those reclining. For he distributed himself both to the living and to the dead; he apportioned himself to those reclining when he left his wounded and pierced body in the world to his humble ones—namely, to his chosen mother Mary, to Mary Magdalene, who was anxious about his burial, to Joseph, Nicodemus, the apostles, and others who loved him. He distributed himself to those reclining when he visited his humble ones in hell with his divinity and soul. He distributed himself when he willed to be laid in the tomb, so that he might not be absent even there, [Col. 0242C] but might rest beside the bodies of other saints. With divinity and soul he was present in hell, where he filled and healed those awaiting him, as much as they wished and desired, with the two fishes—that is, the presence of his divinity and holy soul. And he rightly distributed from the two fishes as much as they wished, because those elect and holy persons—Abel, Noah, Moses, Abraham, and very many others—who had long awaited Christ among the dead, did not receive from the beginning of the world until the hour of his descent to hell what they desired; but only then were they satisfied, and received it, with him present, as much as they wished.

“And when they were filled.” They were filled with every good when they saw him in hell; they were filled with every joy when they recognized him, because, as he himself says, “this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). They were filled with all abundance of his goods when he led them from hell into paradise, and from paradise into heaven. But the living too were filled with every good and joy, especially those who deserved to see and hear him, to whom he himself said: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10:24). They were filled with all sweetness and delight when they saw him risen from the dead. They were filled and satisfied with ineffable [321] [Col. 0242D] good when, after his ascension, they received the wondrous and unheard-of gifts of the Holy Spirit. When they had thus and in this manner been filled, he said to them:

[Col. 0243A] “Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they perish.” What and of what kind were the fragments of these loaves? And where or when were they made? These fragments are the five wounds of the Lord’s body, by which, so to speak, he broke his soul from his body when, crying out on the cross, he expired. Of these fragments it was properly said, “they remained over,” because through them the devil was overcome, hell shattered, original sin blotted out, and the gate of the kingdom opened. These fragments would indeed have perished if the apostles had not made them known to the whole world. For we would be like the Gentiles and Jews who do not believe, if the fragments—that is, the sacraments of his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension—had been hidden from us. Hence the Lord commanded the apostles to gather them when, having sent them into [Col. 0243B] the world to preach, he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). And likewise: “You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

“Therefore they gathered [them], and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves which remained over for those who had eaten.” Indeed, they gathered Christ’s fragments with every diligence and care, and filled twelve baskets with fragments when they made clear to their hearers’ hearts what faith ought to be held. They gathered these fragments with quite diligent zeal when they composed the Creed, “I believe in God,” in which all Christ’s fragments, namely all his sacraments, are found distinctly recited and set forth. But the words, “from the five loaves which remained over for those who had eaten,” omitting also the two fishes, seem to signify that these five loaves, namely the senses of the Lord’s [322] body, remained over for those who were in hell, because they saw only Christ’s divinity and soul, as has been stated. The blessed disciples gathered all these things.

Let these things therefore be an example to us, so that we too may do likewise. Let us gather up all that he did and said for us, and all that he deigned to suffer; let us carry the fragments of his bread in our baskets—that is, in our hearts—doing inwardly what is customarily done outwardly in baskets. Dung is customarily carried in baskets, by which the earth is enriched and cultivated. So too, [Col. 0243D] most beloved, let us carry in the baskets of our hearts good dung: the dung of humility and self-contempt, by which the soil of our heart may receive the richness of good work. Let us implant before and above all things in the chief place of our heart him who set forth in himself the pattern of humility; let us cling to him, be united with him, carry him diligently in our memory, as far as lies in us, and preserve him. For we are those people of whom the Gospel continues, saying:

“Those men therefore, when they had seen the sign which he had done, said: ‘This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.’” We therefore—we, dearest brothers—are denoted by those men; we, I say, [Col. 0244A] are those who see the signs which he performed: the signs of his death, burial, resurrection, and ascension; and we too can say: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world, to condemn the wicked and to reward the elect.” Let us earnestly entreat him that in the life to come he may deign to fill us with these loaves and fishes—that is, with his divinity and humanity—and, since the feast-day of the Passover of the Jews is near, that after our passage and departure from this life he may grant us to arrive at the feast-day of the angels, where we too may be found in the one city of those who live and praise God through endless ages of ages. Amen.

323

## HOMILY XXXVI. ON THE FIFTH SUNDAY OF LENT, OR THE FIRST SUNDAY OF THE PASSION

[Col. 0244B]

“Which of you will convict me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? He who is of God hears the words of God” (John 8).

The whole life and teaching of Christ are the rule and instruction of his children. Therefore, if we attend carefully to the words of this holy Gospel, they are, so to speak, a warning and an exhortation concerning our salvation. The Son of God indeed knew that his words and discourse would bring little or no benefit to the wretched Jews; and therefore whatever he said, taught, and did, he said and did for the sake of his elect.

“Which of you,” he says, “will convict me of sin?” Who could ever convict Christ—the power of God and the wisdom of God—of sin, he who was wholly holy, wholly undefiled throughout all his life? For this reason he assumed the reality of flesh and [Codex: “but”] the likeness of sin: that through him humanity might learn how it ought to exchange and attain heavenly things for earthly, eternal things for transitory. This is well attested by today’s reading, which seems very much to accord with the words of the holy Gospel, in which God’s exceedingly great love toward us is thus commended. “Christ,” says the Apostle Paul, “appearing as High Priest of the good things to come.” Christ is called our High Priest because, when he clothed himself in flesh for us as a mighty helper, he in some manner offered and made himself a bridge for us, by which we might return to our own country, which we once lost when Adam, our first parent, sinned.

[Col. 0244D] For our country was the pleasant and delightful region of Paradise, from which, as we have said, through the pride and disobedience of the first human being, we were cast down into the land of this mortality. Between these two regions lay a great river—namely, original sin—by whose obstacle none of mortals could pass over to the desired place, until Christ himself, clothed in human nature, entered the waters of this world and made and offered himself to us as a bridge for crossing this river. Whoever touches this bridge by believing the mystery of his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension, and moreover adorns faith with good works, will have a completely free passage and return [Col. 0245A] to his own country—that is, the land of the living. For without this faith, as the Apostle says, it is impossible for a human being to please God (Heb. X, 6). Hence some among the Gentile peoples, although they may live chastely and, like the Christian people, be bound among themselves by a great devotion of faith and love, nevertheless cannot be saved at all because they do not touch this bridge through faith.

We must therefore consider what our true High Priest, who through life and teaching made himself a bridge for us, says in the reading of this holy Gospel:

“Which of you will convict me of sin?” By these words he conveys to us nothing other than this: those who ought to be preachers and witnesses of his word should present such a life that they cannot truthfully be convicted by others of the sin for which, when preaching to others, they rebuke and accuse them. For although, so long as we groan in this dwelling of the body, we cannot escape and avoid sin—as John testifies: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8); and the prophet David: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11), that is, every human being is a sinner—yet every preacher must observe with the utmost care and all vigilance of soul that he does not fall into deeds so wicked and criminal that he may publicly be accused and convicted, and that scandal and an occasion for sin may be offered to others.

Whoever does this will be able to bear fruit pleasing and acceptable to God in the hearts of those subject to him whenever he utters the voice of exhortation. Since this is so, our Lord Jesus Christ, whom no one could convict of any sin, said to the faithless and unbelieving Jews:

“If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” And why they did not believe, he immediately adds: “He who is of God hears the words of God.” Here the children of God and the children of the devil are distinguished. “He who is,” he says, “of God hears the words of God.” Those who proceed wholly from God and from a heavenly birth hasten to hear the word of the Lord, and not merely to hear it, but also, as far as lies in them, to preserve with watchful custody of heart whatever commands of the same Lord they proclaim and enjoin.

And indeed, whatever soul has this in its conscience—that it gladly hears the word of God, preserves and loves what it hears, and fulfils it according to its measure—however much anyone may object that it is not of God and cannot become an heir of his kingdom, let it not despair or be afraid. Let it know that, being born as it were from God, it will at some time possess those things which belong to its Father. Conversely, the children of the devil, who do not deign even to hear the words of God with the hearing of their ears, and, if they do hear them, do not fear to oppose and contradict them by wicked deeds—however great a hope may be held out to them and however worthy of God they may be judged by others—should know, with the Lord himself testifying, that they are not of God and therefore cannot share in his good things hereafter.

“Then the Jews answered and said: ‘Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?’” See, brothers, how sin swells, increases, and grows. “You are a Samaritan,” they say, “and have a demon.” In saying, “You have a demon,” they could devise nothing more perverse or hateful to say. If they had called him a thief or a robber, it would seem something more tolerable, so to speak; but in saying that he had a demon, they were affirming that all vices were in him, as though he were worse than all other human beings.

But we must observe why they called him a Samaritan. For the Samaritans, as is known, are neither wholly Jews nor wholly Gentiles, but observe a rite partly of Judaism and partly of Gentilism. Of their number was that Samaritan woman who came to draw water at the well and wondered that Christ, a Jew most noble in every respect, had asked her for a drink; for “the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans” (John 4:9), but wholly despise and disdain them. For this reason the Jews falsely call our Lord a Samaritan—that is, as though he had sprung from an ignoble Jewish stock—though he was born from the most noble tribe of Judah. For that lady, our perpetual Virgin Mary, although she was not among the rich but was poor and needy in this world, yet descended by royal seed from David’s line.

But because *Samaritan* means “guardian,” the Lord was unwilling to deny that he was a guardian, for he cannot deny himself. For he is the one who, by the governance of his guardianship, preserves, rules, and defends all things that are in heaven and on earth. He knew that he was the true Samaritan who, seeing that wounded man, was moved with mercy, and, drawing near, bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine—him whom the priest and Levite had passed by, because they were unable to render help by themselves. Therefore he not undeservedly affirms in silence that he is a Samaritan; but he denies, not as one angered or provoked, but most gently and patiently, that he has a demon, saying:

“I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me.” If someone said to any one of you, “You have a demon,” how many fits of rage, how many pains of heart, do we suppose, would he conceive? And if he could not return insults for insults, he would call upon God, the just rewarder and avenger, with empty words to answer for these things. But God is not so: patient, gentle, and meek in all things. And what did he say? “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me.” As though he said: “I am unwilling to render curse for curse or abuse for abuse, since I ought always to honor my Father who sent me; and you have dishonored me.”

Why does he say, “You have dishonored me,” when he himself is honor—indeed, the honor of all his host, namely angels and human beings? It is therefore as if he said: “You can indeed dishonor me in no way, nor inflict upon me anything unworthy of my majesty. But in that I gave you the honor of innocence, when I created you for the praise and honor of my name, you have in some manner dishonored me because you did not preserve this honor in yourselves, and by acting faithlessly took away what ought to have been mine in you.”

“I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.” The whole life of Christ was the glory of God the Father. He was equal to the Father, God from God, God with God, coeternal and consubstantial; and yet he sought not his own glory but the Father’s. What shall we say, what shall we do in response to this, who, whenever we do any good thing, despise God by seeking our own glory and attribute these few good things to our own merits? Of such people the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2). Let us therefore seek the glory of him from whom we have received all grace. For if we do not seek our own glory here, he will concern himself with our glory; he will glorify those who glorify him; he who is the judge of the living and the dead will judge our cause rightly. It follows:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death.” The Jews were slandering; servants were pursuing the Lord, sinners the Just One, the creature its Creator. But he whom God the Father sent does not delay to render obedience to the Father amid these very reproaches; rather, again and again he took up his word, although they did not receive it, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death.”

The Lord’s word is evangelical teaching; the Lord’s word is the utterances of the prophets; the Lord’s word is the authority of all sacred Scripture, which proclaims and preaches nothing except those things which concern Christ. Whoever keeps this word of the Lord, holds it in a devout and faithful mind, and demonstrates by the evidences of good works what he holds in his heart, shall never see death. For the words of the Lord are those various healing and noble spices and remedies which the faithful soul ought to preserve within itself for driving out the various sicknesses of the mind: for example, if pride comes and inflates the mind, it should immediately seek the remedy of humility by which to heal the disease of pride; if anger comes, it should set against it the good roots of patience; if disobedience, the remedies of obedience; if lust, it should gather the sweet-smelling spices of chastity, by which it may drive out the pestilence of lust. Thus, by doing this in every case, it should know that it will never see death.

What death? I mean the death of the soul, not the body. For what we call death is not death, but the leaving of the body, the laying down of a heavy burden, a certain journey and road from prison to a kingdom. But there is another death which must be feared and dreaded: when a human being, given over to diverse vices and sins, loses and forfeits Christ, the life of his soul. Whoever preserves his words and teaching in faith, rendering and imitating in deed whatever he has learned from the words of this same Lord, will escape that death. The Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, spoke spiritual things and preached spiritual things. But because the Jews were carnal and predestined to everlasting death, they did not understand spiritual things.

[Col. 0248A] And, indignant, they answered abusively and said [Note: [Col. 0247D] The Vulgate has: “The Jews therefore said: ‘Now,’ etc.”]: “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets; and you say: ‘If anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death.’ Whom do you make yourself?” Could he not have replied to these venomous words most authoritatively and freely: “I make myself your Lord; I make myself the Creator of heaven and earth”? Yet he did not wish to return abuse for abuse; indeed, he said:

“If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing.” As though he said: “If I wish to glorify myself and boast how great I am, my glory is of no account.” Amid these words let us return to ourselves, enter within ourselves, consider and look upon ourselves. If any one of us—dust and ashes that we are—were told by another: “Whom do you make yourself? Consider who you are, and cease to exalt yourself above others,” would not his breast, filled with furies, find no rest day or night, and would he not, overestimating himself, boast of merits which perhaps he did not possess?

Let us therefore behold our Lord Jesus Christ, who left himself to us, and all his words and deeds, as a living image of virtues, so that we may learn and hear from him what we wretched people ought to do and say: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing.” Let the human being also say: “If I think myself something when I am nothing, and wish to glorify myself, my glory is nothing, and I shall be granted no blessedness of reward by the Lord.”

“The Father is,” says the Lord, “who glorifies me, whom you say is our God; and you have not known him. But I know him; and if I say that I do not know him, I shall be a liar like you. But I know him and keep his word.” The Father glorifies the Son because the Son knew and knows the Father—that is, loved him—and kept his word, becoming obedient to him unto death, even death on a cross.

“Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.” I would like to say briefly something about the day of the Lord which Abraham saw and rejoiced in; may the Lord himself grant that we too may deserve to see that day. At the Lord’s command Abraham went out from his land and from his kindred. And once established in the land of his pilgrimage, one day three angels appeared to him in the very heat of the day; seeing three, he worshipped one, because he recognized and believed one in substance and three in persons. Having received them as guests, the man offered to God what he could: he commanded Sarah quickly to mix three measures of fine flour, offered butter, and killed a calf (Gen. 18:2 ff.). All this signifies something which it is fitting for the true sons of Abraham to imitate.

By Abraham the faithful human being may be understood; by Sarah, reason, or soul, or body. And not inappropriately is every believer understood by Abraham, who is called the father of all believers, if by equalling that same Abraham in good works he proves himself to be his son. To such a person, lifting up his eyes in the very heat of the day—that is, at noon—three angels appear when he is graciously visited by the advent of the holy Trinity. This visitation rightly occurs at noon. For as the day is illuminated and kindled by noonday light, so a human being must first be illuminated through knowledge and kindled through the fervor of love. Thus he shines as it were with noonday light and inwardly glows and burns with noonday fervor, to whom God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit do not disdain to appear, insofar as is permitted during this time of mortality.

Illuminated through knowledge and burning with the fervor of love, he ought to desire what Abraham desired and carry out in deeds what Abraham did. “Do not pass by your servant,” he says, “but let me bring a little water, that your feet may be washed” (ibid., 4). A little water may be called compunctive remembrance, which arises for sins; it is small and slight in comparison with the sweet remembrance of God’s benefits. In this water our feet—that is, evil affections—ought certainly to be washed, so that they may be cleansed before God. Or the Lord’s feet are mercy and truth; we pour water upon them when, with worthy sorrow of repentance and a stream of tears, we wash away whatever we have done or sinned against God’s mercy or his truth.

Once the Lord has been received and his feet washed, a banquet must be prepared and set forth in which he may delight, rejoice, and be refreshed. At Abraham’s command, three measures of fine flour must quickly be mixed; a most tender and excellent calf must be killed; butter and milk must be offered. And what is it to hasten one’s work except, having cast off bodily sluggishness, to hurry toward the fervor of the heart? With sluggishness cast off, three measures of fine flour must be mixed. A *sat* is a kind of measure. In this threefold measure understand the gifts of three virtues: faith, hope, and love, which the clean soul, signified by fine flour, ought firmly to hold. They are rightly commanded not merely to be mixed but to be mingled—that is, all three must be held together, each with the others; for no one of them can be perfect without the other. For if faith is held without hope, or hope without faith, or love without the first two, fullness of perfection is not possessed. One must believe faithfully, hope strongly, and love fervently: this is to mingle the three measures.

After this one must run to the herd, so that the most tender and excellent calf may be sought and killed. The herd is called the flock of sinners. And what is expressed by the herd except the movements of wanton and foolish thoughts? He therefore runs to the herd who, with a contrite and humbled heart, gathers back into himself all the vanities of his life, all the wantonnesses and follies of all his ways, and seeks most carefully how he may make worthy satisfaction to God for them.

In the calf which is first killed and then cooked, pride or humility, or the mortification of the flesh, may be signified. Nor is it surprising that I have said that pride, humility, or mortification may be signified by the calf, which must first be killed and afterwards cooked. For the fact that this calf is first killed and afterwards cooked signifies, as it seems to me, that the pride of the heart must be killed through the mortification of the flesh, so that where pride is slain the true virtue of humility may be raised up.

Nor should it be passed over that it must be most tender. For the calf is in some sense killed tenderly when a person is pierced with compunction for evils committed; more tenderly when he is humbled for good deeds neglected; but most tenderly when he is humbled neither for evils he has done nor for good things he has neglected, but solely and wholly for the love of God. This calf is most tender and excellent, because it is best to taste and see how sweet the Lord is. There butter is added, because the richness of the Holy Spirit, which is butter, is sent from above; by it the person is inwardly fed, enriched, and refreshed. David asks to be filled with this richness, saying: “May my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. 62:6). When such a banquet has been prepared, the joyful promise to the Lord immediately follows. For the son of blessed promise, namely Isaac, whose name is interpreted “laughter,” is promised to be born, because that ineffable joy—which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—will be given to them at their arrival.

This was the day in which Abraham saw the Lord: he saw and rejoiced. This is the day in which a person, having conquered sins, is illuminated, as we have said, through the knowledge of God and of himself, and thereby kindled with the fervor of inward love. But because the Jews bear the type of malignant spirits, who today cause Christ to suffer in his members, the Jews’ answer is the answer of malignant spirits wishing to lead a human being into despair.

“You are not yet fifty years old,” they say, “and have you seen Abraham?” By fifty, repentance is signified; it is as though they say: “You have not yet deserved to know what the measure of perfect repentance is, and do you now aspire to see the day of the Lord—that is, his splendor, which shines forth only upon devout minds?” Amid these words of malignant spirits, let us hear the consoling answer of the Lord God:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham was made, I am.” This is the same as if he said: “What you cannot do through yourself, you can do through me. If you are powerless, I am powerful. Only trust in my mercy; I can help you through the strength of my divine power.”

“The Jews took up stones to throw at him.” By stones understand the impenitent heart. A person takes up stones when he has a stony and impenitent heart; but he does not take up stones when he endeavors to wash away his sins through the satisfaction of repentance, and in this way always finds God merciful. For he is always ready to forgive those who repent, to have mercy, and to spare his suppliants. Nor is this remarkable or unworthy of his goodness. For just as the devil, according to his wickedness, hastens to lead all human beings into ruin and the destruction of eternal damnation, so conversely he whose nature is goodness turns all things toward grace and salvation, if only the human being does not take up stones.

We have now heard what Christ suffered from the Jews. Let us hear what he still suffers in his members. Christ has now ascended as victor; the Jews are dead. But the instigators of the Jews—that is, malignant spirits—still live, and make him suffer in his members those same things which he once suffered in himself. Some are tempted and overcome; some are tempted and not overcome. There are four ways in which we sin: by will, action, thought, and speech. While we are tempted in these four ways, it remains for us, when tempted, to be fortified and instructed by the words and examples of our Lord Jesus Christ.

In the fact that the Jews say twice to the Lord, “You have a demon”—first in doubt, when they say, “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”; secondly in affirmation, when they say, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets”—they wish to convict the Lord of lying and falsehood. And this aptly suggests that they do not cease to tempt and attack a human being in these same ways. For by “demon” we may understand evil desires, impure pleasures, and perverse wills, through which a blessed person is sometimes more tempted and attacked in the spiritual than in the secular life. Whoever receives these same evil desires, pleasures, and harmful wills in consent and brings them to the unlawful act of sin undoubtedly has a most evil demon. But whoever does not receive the pleasure of fleshly concupiscence and does not seek, by giving assent to evil wills, to commit works of sin, rightly and excellently protests truly with his Lord God that he does not have a demon but honors the Father who is in heaven, saying: “I do not have a demon.”

But malignant spirits, as soon as they see that they cannot overcome a human being by will, desire, or wicked action, attack him instead through lying and falsehood. Is not lying a great evil when a human being arrogates and attributes to himself what belongs to God and the Lord alone? For after evil desires, depraved pleasures, and perverse wills have been overcome, they provoke a human being by lying—which we may call vainglory—so that he may now seek praise in thought, attribute to himself whatever good he has done, and not reserve and render glory to him alone who alone works in a human being whatever good the human being does. And because useless and vain speech generally breaks forth after useless thoughts, they bring it about that he later vaunts and extols in speech his own merits for the sake of the praise which he had sought again and again in thought.

Accordingly, we are taught by the Lord’s answer what we should do and say against this vice: “If I glorify myself,” says the Lord, “my glory is nothing.” Let the human being also say: “If I do or possess any good thing, I ought not to attribute it to myself by glorifying myself. My Father is the one who glorifies me; for if I do not seek my own glory, he will seek it, and will judge it here and in the present as he wills.”

The excellence of today’s divine office accords well with this Gospel reading. The Collect also accords with it, in which we pray thus to be delivered from the temptations mentioned above: “We beseech you, almighty God, graciously look upon your household, that by your bounty it may be governed in body against evil action, and by your protection guarded in mind against evil will.” The Tract of the Mass agrees with all these things; those who are joyful victors over the aforesaid temptations can offer it to the Lord, singing in their hearts: “Often have they attacked me from my youth; let Israel now say: often have they attacked me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me. Sinners have built upon my back” (Ps. 128:1–3).

Who are those fighting against and attacking us except malignant spirits? For what person belonging to Christ is not troubled by various temptations? Daily the devil and his angels contend with him, lest he be perverted by some pleasure or evil action. But because he who protects us is strong, let Israel now say—that is, the person desiring to see God—“Often have they attacked me from my youth; sinners have built upon my back,” that is, they have built upon my flesh, and, like a craftsman striking frequently upon an anvil, afflict us by tempting us. They press upon us in every manner in order to cast us down. But let us not fear, because “the righteous Lord will cut the necks of sinners” (ibid., 4).

Thus, for those who fight in this manner, hope in God their protector, and cast away stones—that is, the impenitent heart—the following good thing will occur which happened to the Jews as an evil: “Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.” For Jesus—that is, our true Savior—hides himself in the blessed person through humility of heart, and makes a good departure through good and holy action of the body.

Then, truly incorporated into Christ, he will be able to sing the words of holy communion: “This body, which shall be given for you.” For, made the body of Christ and a member from a member, he will be rendered fit to drink the blood of the New Testament, because he will receive divinely the good and sound senses of holy Scripture, from which and through which he may have continual recollection of God. Therefore, that we may deserve to be incorporated into Jesus Christ our Savior, and may have continual recollection of him, may he himself help us—Jesus Christ our Lord—who gave himself over to death for us, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

337

## HOMILY XXXVII. ON THE SAME SUNDAY, SECOND [HOMILY]

“Christ appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hands, that is, not of this creation, and not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9).

These are the words of the blessed Apostle Paul, in whom and through whom Christ truly spoke. Though they are few and brief, they are nonetheless full of the excellence of heavenly mysteries. For if we wish to examine and investigate them with careful reflection, we can find all the mysteries of Christ expressly set forth in them. When he says, “Christ appearing as High Priest of the good things to come,” by this the mystery of Christ’s incarnation may be understood. According to the excellence of his divinity, by which the Son of God is consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal with God the Father, he was always High Priest, making and preparing for us in his eternal predestination that bridge by which we were to return to future goods, namely to the blessedness of eternal salvation. But he who was High Priest only in predestination became for us an appearing High Priest in his most holy incarnation.

And this word *appearing* rightly accords with Christ’s incarnation. For *appearing* is said as though “standing by to help.” The human nature which he assumed in himself for our salvation stood by him, as it were, to help, because the dispensation ordained from the beginning for human restoration had to be accomplished not by the divine nature, which was incapable of suffering, but by human nature.

After thus signifying and prefiguring Christ’s incarnation, he mystically indicates also his most holy life in this world when he immediately adds: “Through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands, that is, not of this creation.” By the greater and more perfect tabernacle, Christ’s soul and body can very suitably be understood. This tabernacle can truly be called greater, truly more perfect: greater in love, more perfect in action. For no soul has ever been found so great, so expanded in the sweetness and love of God; no body has ever been found so pure and so perfect in action.

But from what came such vastness and perfection of this tabernacle? Surely because it was not made by hands—that is, not of this creation: it was brought forth from the blessed Virgin Mary, not by human operation but by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit. It was not of this creation because, contrary to the manner and custom of human generation, by which absolutely all human beings are begotten from sin and in sin, he alone was conceived and born without sin, and he alone lived in this world without sin.

[Col. 0253D] Hence it follows:

“Nor through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption.” In goats we may understand the uncleanness of the flesh, which occurs in action; in calves, the wantonness of the heart, which works especially in thought. And because no stain of sin ever clung to his most holy body in action, and no wantonness could ever touch his most holy mind in thought, it is rightly said: “Not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood.”

By Christ’s own blood we understand Christ’s own will. For no human being, however righteous or holy, can possess himself so wholly in his own power as always to have a will upright and directed toward God, without often being drawn away from the good which he wills to the evil which he does not will. Our Lord Jesus Christ alone possessed himself entirely in his own will, so that nothing whatever could happen to him unless he himself willed it. Yet we also rightly understand by Christ’s own blood Christ’s most holy passion, in which, according to the abundance of his mercy, not unwillingly or under compulsion, but by his own will, he shed upon the cross his blood, by which the entire human race might be washed and redeemed.

But when it is added, “He entered once into the holy places,” his holy resurrection is not inappropriately understood; for he truly entered into the holy places when, having conquered death and despoiled the prince of death, he rose from the dead and so united and joined his most holy soul with his most holy body that it could never again be separated from it. After this glorious entrance into the holy places, there consequently follows: “Having obtained eternal redemption,” because in these words, as far as I can see, the glorious ascension of Christ may not unjustly be understood. For where he sat at the right hand of the power of God, there eternal redemption was truly obtained—a redemption which could not be fully or perfectly obtained or known in the incarnation, passion, or resurrection.

340

## HOMILY XXXVIII. FOR TUESDAY AFTER THE FIRST SUNDAY OF THE PASSION

[Col. 0254C]

“The Babylonians gathered together before the king and said to him: ‘Hand Daniel over to us, who destroyed Bel and killed the dragon; otherwise we shall kill you and your household’” (Daniel 14).

The most holy observance of Lent, and likewise the season of the Lord’s Passion which we commemorate, has been especially set apart and chosen above the other times of the year for this purpose: that the spiritual person, who at other times is unable to live as he ought, may at least in these days strive for his salvation with all the powers of body and affections of heart. For just as the true and merciful physician of souls willed and ordained that during these days something should be taken away from the body, so he also arranged that food and refreshment should be added to and increased for the soul. For every day we have distinct and new offices, Lessons, and Gospels in the celebration of Mass, so that the soul which loves God, refreshed by this abundant spiritual food and drink, ought to be raised from earthly things to heavenly things. Thus also in the Lesson now before us, if we seek diligently, we shall, with God’s help, be able to find the desirable refreshment of our souls.

“The Babylonians gathered to the king,” he says, “and said to him: Hand Daniel over to us—Daniel, who destroyed Bel and killed the dragon.” By Daniel, whose name means “judgment of God,” is fittingly signified that person who, because of the offenses of his wicked manner of life, becomes a strict judge of himself, judging and punishing in himself, here and now, the guilt of his own conscience with subtlety and severity, so that on that fearful day of final judgment he may appear free and unburdened before the eyes of his Creator. Whoever, therefore, is such a person—who, as we have said, forestalling the divine judgment, punishes in himself in the present that for which he recognizes that he must someday be punished—does not cease invisibly to perform, by the praiseworthy effectiveness and constancy of his works, what this Daniel accomplished with manly steadfastness in destroying Bel and killing the dragon. By Bel, which was an idol of shamefulness, we may understand the impurity of the flesh; but by the dragon, which is of excessive cruelty and malice, we may understand the malice of the heart.

These two foul and abominable vices—namely, lust and malice—especially reign and work among worldly people, to whom it is sweet and pleasant to pass the days of this present life in luxurious living. For from what does this come, except from great malice of heart: that they pursue robbery with such pleasure, wickedly seize the property of others, envy one another, and are always ready for quarrels and lawsuits? But a person who, through the prevenient mercy of almighty God, has turned from the common way of worldly life to the warfare of spiritual life, labors and keeps watch with all his strength in order to destroy Bel, that is, the idol of shamefulness, and to kill the dragon. He destroys Bel when he washes away the stains of his shamefulness by fitting tears of repentance, and when he who was formerly so entangled in the contagions of sins that it is shameful and disgraceful even to confess them to another person devotes himself to chastity and purity. Thus, cleansed and justified by God’s grace, he applies himself through devout labors to killing the dragon, because he turns the former malice of his heart—hatred, envy, and bitterness—into compassion and sweetness, so that he no longer has the will to harm any person, but, full of tender compassion, strives to offer the affection of charity to all.

The evil spirits, enemies and foes of human salvation, bear this change of the right hand of the Most High—that is, this glorious progress of a human being—with difficulty; and this is openly intimated to us by the words of the present Lesson.

“They gathered,” he says, “the Babylonians to the king, and said to him: Hand Daniel over to us.” By this king we may understand our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who truly is King of kings and Lord of lords. The Babylonians, however, may fittingly be understood as evil spirits. But how, or with what appropriateness, ought we to understand that the Babylonians—that is, perverse enemies—are said to gather against this King of glory? For he, seated on the lofty throne of his majesty, rules both heavenly and earthly things; nothing can resist his divine power, and therefore no vexation from anything that happens can disturb him. Yet because he is our head and we are his members, when any chosen member of his is afflicted by tribulations, he does not disdain to declare that he himself suffers. For he rejoices in us; he is saddened in us. He rejoices in us when, applying ourselves to good works, we work out our salvation; he is saddened in us when we do not fear to perform things contrary to our salvation.

Therefore the Babylonians gather and rise up against this king when the enemies of the human race desire that the person who strives by good works to become a member of Christ should be exposed to their temptations. For these evil spirits have no power to tempt a person except such as God permits. Thus, if a person, supported by divine assistance, proceeds successfully in his spiritual purpose and felt no trace of his own weakness in himself, he would easily exalt himself above himself by ascribing God’s gift to his own merits. Therefore the Lord of knowledge, in provident goodness, sometimes permits him to be tested by temptations, as the text of the following passage indicates.

“The king therefore saw that they rushed upon him violently, and, compelled by necessity, handed Daniel over to them.” What is this that we say, or how should we understand that God is compelled by necessity? We cannot, nor ought we, investigate the hidden judgments of almighty God; rather, we speak in this human fashion. For he, the knower of hidden things, knows and understands that the person whom he has raised by progress in spiritual virtues, if he were altogether free and untroubled by temptation, would easily ensnare himself in a chain of graver guilt, corrupted by the vice of pride. Therefore, as though compelled by a certain necessity, the compassionate and merciful Lord beneficially permits a person to be tempted; because, lest something worse happen to him—that is, lest, secure and unguarded, he rush headlong into the vice of pride—he hands him over to enemies, that is, he permits him to be tempted by enemies. This is not because he satisfies their malice and impiety, but because he provides for human salvation: so that, legitimately trained and instructed in the contest of temptations, he may gird himself more strongly and worthily for the work of his own salvation and, conscious of his own weakness, may not glory in his virtues, but may know and recognize that he ought to humble himself under the mighty hand of God.
