When this provident and salutary handing-over has taken place by almighty God, the words of the following passage show to what blindness of mind the very princes of darkness bring a person.

“They sent him into the den of lions.” By the den, which receives no trace of light, blindness of mind may be understood; by the lions, which are of excessive cruelty and fierceness, bitterness of mind may be understood. Evil spirits send a person into this den of misery, this blindness and harshness of mind, when they so envelop him in the darkness of temptations that his inward sight, blinded by the shadows of ignorance, is altogether unable to see what should be seen or to taste, as it ordinarily does, the grace of inward sweetness. And because, so long as we remain in this time of mutability, we cannot possibly be free from temptations, the words which immediately follow seem rightly to instruct us.

“And he was there for six days.” During these six days—that is, so long as we bear the body which weighs down the soul—we cannot be wholly delivered from the temptations of our enemies. For the devil assails us by suggestion; our flesh assails us by pleasure; the world assails us by prosperity and adversity. Yet amid this calamity and misery of temptations, divine compassion and mercy sometimes graciously look upon, console, and help the faithful; and, lest they succumb to temptations, they sustain and strengthen them by the power of their arm. But who those are whom the evil spirits themselves will receive into their body in order to devour them is made clear by the following words:

“Moreover, there were seven lions in the den, and two bodies and two sheep were given to them every day.” By the two bodies we may fittingly understand those who, with a reprobate mind, relish only the things of the flesh and do not fear to fulfill the desires of the flesh in its lusts. By the sheep, although elsewhere simple and innocent persons are understood, in this place are signified the slothful, enfeebled by the softness of the flesh, who do not strive to expend even the slightest labor for love of the heavenly kingdom. These, then, are cast before the lions—that is, the evil spirits—because those whose temptations they do not resist in the present will be their portion and inheritance forever, as the Psalmist attests when he says: “Like sheep they are placed in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. XLVIII [49]:15).

But divine mercy does not permit the person whom, forestalling him with the blessings of its sweetness, it has predestined for eternal life to be tempted beyond what he is able to bear; rather, it will make with the temptation also a way out, that he may be able to endure it. And according to the goodness innate to it, it does not disdain to visit and console, through some chosen and God-beloved teacher, the misery and grief of his desolation. Thus, just as, according to the multitude of his mercy, he delivered Daniel, placed in the den of lions, from the danger of hunger by sending him bodily refreshment of food through the prophet Habakkuk, so indeed he who does not despise the desire of the poor does not disdain to visit and refresh with spiritual food this poor and needy person who looks to the abundant hand of his goodness. How this occurs is plainly indicated by the following sequence.

“Now the prophet Habakkuk was in Judea, and he had crushed bread in his trough, in order to carry it to the reapers.” By the prophet Habakkuk a spiritual father and prelate may be understood; the reapers may be understood as his subjects, who in the Lord’s field—that is, in a spiritual way of life—do not cease to reap and gather the fruit of eternal salvation, the fruit, I say, of virtues and good works. The bread which the prelate carries to these reapers, namely his subjects, he grinds in his trough when he gathers and prepares in his humble heart the bread of God’s word, spiritual food of refreshment, by which he may gladden, console, and refresh souls that hunger and thirst for God. This spiritual refreshment is brought, by the providence of divine compassion, to Daniel placed in the den of lions, when the person whose soul was placed in such bitterness as we have described, and whose mind had been estranged from itself by the troubles of temptations, receives from the words of a devout teacher the strength of spiritual refreshment. Rekindled thereby toward the customary grace of divine sweetness, he begins to be renewed in the spirit of his mind, so that he can fittingly employ the words of Daniel in a voice of exultation and thanksgiving: “You have remembered me, O God, and have not forsaken those who love you.”

Thus the whole course of this present life turns and passes through this diversity of alternation: now we are enveloped in the darkness of temptations; now we are illuminated by the splendor of divine visitation. There is no one born of woman who can remain in a firm and unchanging state of mind. But when the seventh day comes—that is, when the person who is to be saved, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, has put off the tent of his earthly dwelling—then what is immediately added here will truly be fulfilled:

“The king came therefore on the seventh day to mourn for Daniel.” For on the seventh day the heavenly King and Lord comes to mourn for Daniel when, at the hour of the departure of any blessed soul, he presents himself to it as he is: full of compassion, full of grace and mercy. That mourning which he makes over it is the inestimable sweetness of paternal consolation, by which he will eternally glorify it, freed from the body of death, through the blessed vision of himself. But the text of the following passage indicates what punishment of condemnation awaits the enemies and foes of the human race.

“Moreover, he brought in those who had been the cause of his destruction.” When the Lord, Creator of all things, comes as the strict Judge in the general judgment, having gathered to himself all his members in eternal glory, he will bring their enemies—that is, evil spirits—into the pit of his wrath, the pit, I say, of eternal condemnation. By his power he will so reduce to nothing the devices of their malice and wickedness that they will be unable to exercise any art of their customary perversity against God’s elect; rather, for the troubles of temptations which they inflicted, unquenchable fire will be their inheritance forever.

## HOMILY XXXIX. THE FIRST HOMILY FOR PALM SUNDAY

“The children of Israel came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees; and they pitched camp beside the waters” (Exod. XV).

This present Lesson is fittingly read, as we think, on this day on which the Passion of our Savior is commemorated with solemn devotion. For in this same Lesson we can find the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion mystically prefigured, as well as the pride of the Jews, who from the beginning always provoked the Lord, and their calling, by which they were to be converted to faith at the end of the world.

“The children of Israel,” he says, “came to Elim.” The children of Israel—namely, those Jews whom the Lord chose as his own special people—did not come by a good path to Elim, which means “ram.” For by the ram, which leads the flocks, we rightly believe that their pride is signified. They certainly came badly to this pride when, on account of the good things divinely bestowed upon them, through which they ought to have been humbled, they vainly exalted themselves as though they were above the other nations.

“Where,” he says, “there were twelve springs of water.” By the twelve springs the twelve patriarchs—the sons, that is, of Jacob—seem to be understood, from whom the whole multitude of the Jewish people undoubtedly arose. They therefore gloried in having these twelve springs of water: namely, because they had been born from the noble lineage of holy patriarchs. This was the first cause of their pride, as we have already said: that they knew themselves to have been born of holy and righteous fathers. And immediately another cause follows, in which they gloried with no less pride:

“And seventy,” he says, “palm trees.” Seven times ten and ten times seven make seventy. And by this number the Decalogue may fittingly be expressed, for it was written and composed by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. They received this Decalogue from the Lord as seventy palm trees, that, instructed and trained through knowledge of the Decalogue, they might learn how, by resisting vices and lusts and by fighting against the devil, the world, and sins, they ought to obtain the palm of victory. But they, glorying more and more and exalting themselves as though on account of the singularity of the law they had received, sought from these things no salvation of soul or progress in spiritual understanding. Hence it immediately follows:

“And they pitched camp beside the waters.” Camps belong to soldiers; the camps in which they ought to have served God their Creator were their bodies and souls. Therefore, as has been said, the Decalogue was given them so that through its teaching they might learn how to guard and defend these same camps for the service of their Creator. But they pitched camp—that is, they changed—beside the waters, namely beside carnal desires. For in the camps of body and soul, in which they ought to have served God alone, they served carnal desires. Thus, while serving badly in these camps, they had already fallen into worse things, as is made clear in what follows.

“And they departed from Elim.” This departure must not be thought good. For to depart from Elim—that is, from pride—is rather to decline. For the more they advanced in pride, the more they failed in good things. Hence the Psalmist says: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. LXXIII [74]:23). For to rise in pride is rather to descend. And so the things immediately added clearly show how great a decline they descended into after this advance of pride.

“And the whole multitude of the children of Israel came into the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month.” What is the fifteenth day of the second month? What is the first month? What is the second month? We may say that the first month is the illumination of the law, while the second month is evangelical perfection. In the first month, which was the law, a certain illumination took place. For before the law they had no light of knowledge except insofar as they were illuminated by the natural law; but after they received the law, they were illuminated in part, so that they knew how, if they wished, to preserve themselves from sins. Yet this illumination was neither full nor perfect, because remission of sins and the reward of eternal life did not follow this illumination.

But the second month—that is, evangelical perfection—fully contains in itself what the fifteenth day mystically teaches and expresses. This fifteenth number consists of seven and eight. By seven, the present life is to be understood; by eight, eternal reward. Therefore, when the second month came, which is evangelical perfection, the full illumination of the fifteenth day took place. For then they were illuminated so perfectly that in this present life, signified by seven, they might live justly and devoutly; or, if they sinned, they might make such worthy satisfaction for their sins as to receive true remission and someday possess the reward of eternal life, which is signified by eight.

This perfection or illumination of evangelical grace is found prefigured elsewhere, where the Old Testament says: “The water was fifteen cubits higher than all the mountains” (Gen. VII:20). By cubits, as we suppose, perfection may be understood; by water, sacred Scripture; by mountains, all the righteous and perfect, lofty and exalted in the eminence of virtues. Thus it is as though it were said: Although all the righteous and perfect, divinely illuminated by evangelical grace, grow and advance in mystical understanding, nevertheless the water of sacred Scripture surpasses all their sense and understanding. For although they see and understand much concerning the perfection of this life and much concerning eternal reward, this water will always be higher than they are, because they never so attain the height of this water as to reach perfect knowledge of evangelical teaching.

But when this evangelical doctrine appeared and came, then the whole multitude of the children of Israel came into the wilderness of Sin, which means “temptation.” For because of their pride, such a great temptation rushed upon them that they were deserted and abandoned by the Lord. For they always resisted the word of truth and refused to believe that he could take away the sins of the world. When they heard that he preached forgiveness of sins and even granted it to certain persons, they said: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” (Luke VII:49).

What they suffer, or will suffer, for so proud a temptation of perversity and malice is plainly shown by the statement that the wilderness of Sin lies between Elim and Sinai. Elim, as was said at the beginning of the Lesson, means “ram,” by which Jewish pride is understood; Sinai means “jar,” by which the measure of eternal condemnation may be understood. For every temptation which that people had, and still has, against God was and is between Elim and Sinai. For those who, from benefits bestowed on them by God, burst forth into such pride that they did not fear to exercise such great malice against the same Savior, and who were or are found in this same pride—for them, without doubt, a grievously harsh jar is reserved, that is, the measure of eternal condemnation. But the following passage clearly indicates whence, or from what time, they came into this misery.

“After,” he says, “they came out of the land of Egypt.” This coming out is, as we suppose, the fall of the first human being. For by Egypt, which means “darkness,” we may fittingly understand paradise, in which there was good darkness: while our first parents knew nothing evil; while they did not see the serpent suggesting the sin of disobedience; while they did not see the tree, pleasant to look upon and sweet for food, in such a way as to desire to eat it. But when, after transgression, their eyes were opened, they were expelled from the excellent land of this Egypt and came from good darkness into evil light, where they always saw nothing except what was evil and grievous.

And because the whole human race, expelled in them, lost good darkness and entered the light of misery and sorrow, he then expresses the tearful voice of all the elect:

“And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness.” This murmuring is hidden sorrow. In hidden sorrow, indeed, the entire multitude of the elect has always groaned from the beginning as though murmuring: because without any fault of their own, in their first parents they had been cast down from the land of Egypt, from good darkness, into the evil light of this world, where they had eyes always open to see and know evil things. And why did they murmur secretly concerning this? They knew that God’s judgment, by which they had been cast out, was just; and therefore they did not dare to rebuke or accuse his just judgment. Yet, in hidden grief, they lamented their miseries, as though murmuring against Moses and Aaron—that is, against our Lord Jesus Christ.

These two names, Moses and Aaron, suitably apply to our Lord Jesus Christ. For Moses means “drawn from water,” while Aaron means “mountain of strength.” Our Redeemer may fittingly be called Moses, that is, “drawn from water,” because, insofar as he is the Son of the Virgin, he was drawn from water, namely from human nature. Why he should be called Aaron, that is, “Mountain of strength,” no one can doubt: for by the strength of his divinity he contains and governs all things. Against this Moses and Aaron—against God our Savior Jesus Christ—all the children and elect of God, who, by revelation of the Holy Spirit, knew that he who was to come was true God and true man, murmured in the wilderness in sorrow and groaning. They murmured, I say, because he delayed so long in coming for the redemption of the human race, because he left the poor so long as strangers in the wilderness.

A miserable person came into a great wilderness when, expelled from paradise, he fell into this pit of wretched pilgrimage, though while still placed in paradise he had been in great abundance of delight and joy. For he came into a wilderness exceedingly sad and bitter when he was left to himself, having lost the true fullness, which is God. And because all the children of Israel—that is, all the holy and elect—had lost this blessed fullness, they all said with groaning:

“Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt!” Death which occurs by the hand of the Lord, by the power and mercy of the Lord, is a good and precious death when the person who is to be saved dies to vices and sins and merits to have within himself the true life, which is Christ. “Would,” they say, “that we had died this blessed death in the land of Egypt, in the land of paradise, where we knew no evil and saw no evil! Would that in this good darkness we had died by the hand of the Lord and had not come into this miserable light, to know these innumerable evils!”

“When we sat over the pots of meat.” The pots of meat may be understood as carnal bodies and carnal souls, in which carnal desires boil and are cooked. A person in a sense sits over these pots when by such powerful strength of spirit he restrains body and soul that carnal desires cannot prevail against him. “Over the pots of meat,” they say, “over the pots of carnal pleasures, while still placed in paradise, we sat with such powerful mastery that we could feel no carnal desire.”

“And we ate bread to the full.” The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are bread most greatly to be desired. We somehow ate this bread of wonderful sweetness to the full when, insofar as was possible, we were deemed worthy to see the presence and glory of the holy Trinity. There are also other breads, namely angelic spirits, which we likewise ate to the full when together with them we praised God the Creator with unceasing voice. We had these breads and all these good things in the land of Egypt, in that good land; and now, because of the sins of our parents, we have come to this misery of calamity.

This murmuring, which the ancient fathers then uttered tearfully, still persists in the hearts of the elect when, because the law of the flesh resists them, they are unable to do what they wish and feel the flesh always desiring against the spirit, according to the words of the Apostle: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; and these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever things you wish” (Gal. V:17). Thus even now, together with those ancient Fathers, they repeat their murmuring in a mournful voice, saying:

“Why have you brought us into this wilderness, to kill the whole multitude with hunger?” Behold, they address the holy Trinity, who is one God in three persons, with sad and groaning murmuring; and they complain why they have been brought into the wilderness of this world. “Why,” they say, “have you brought us—why have you permitted us to be brought—into this dreadful wilderness, where we are deprived of every good and burdened with every evil; where cruel beasts of vices and sins meet us on every side; where the manifold snares of evil spirits are spread before us? Did you bring us in so as to kill the whole multitude with hunger? We labor under hunger for God’s word, and, as though killed, we fail through our labor, because we are not yet able to hear and see that Word which was in the beginning. We suffer hunger of good desire, but cannot be filled, because we do not yet have him whom we desire, him who is true fullness; nor shall we obtain him before life’s setting, because in our first parents you so miserably killed—that is, permitted to be killed—the whole multitude of the elect.”

Thus, thus, while all the elect labor from the beginning to the end of the age, has the Lord forgotten to show mercy? It follows:

“The Lord said to Moses.” This speaking of the Lord God the Father to Moses, his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, means that he never could or can forget his mercy, but always was and will be ready to have mercy upon the human race. Accordingly, three periods are here subsequently prefigured: before the law, under the law, and under grace. In each of these periods, as he willed, the Lord marvelously showed mercy to the human race.

The period before the law is prefigured by the following words: “Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven for you.” The period under the law is: “Let the people go out and gather what is sufficient for each day.” The period under grace is: “But on the sixth day let them prepare what they bring in.”

Concerning the first period, which was before the law, eternal divine Wisdom fittingly says:

“Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven for you.” He somehow rained bread from heaven when by his heavenly mercy he sent into the world such persons as loved their Creator himself and fed their neighbors, by the example of good works, as with a kind of heavenly food—such as Abel, Abraham, Noah, Isaac, Jacob, and others like them. But it should be noted that he declares that such persons rain from heaven. Rain descending drop by drop upon the earth is a small and slight thing. Thus those Fathers who lived before the law may rightly be compared to rain, as small and slight in comparison with the apostles and those who imitate the apostles, because they were not spiritual but carnal.

Though they were righteous in their generation and did many things worthy of imitation, they could not attain that apostolic perfection by which, as the apostles and their imitators did, and some still do, they might leave behind the things of the world and love the virginal life. Hence it is said of one of them: “Noah was a righteous man in his generation” (Gen. VI:9), that is, in a carnal generation. Like Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and certain others, though righteous in their generation, were nevertheless carnal because they had wives and children.

But after the merciful Lord willed to increase the work of his mercy, he said to those who were to come under the law:

“Let the people go out and gather what is sufficient for each day.” From what was the people under the law commanded to go out, or where were they to gather? It was commanded to go out a little from carnal ignorance and to gather from legal knowledge. For before the law that people was so entirely carnal that in sexual union it did not know how to distinguish mother from sister. Indeed, even [with regard to] this matter it had received absolutely no command, as this people did, to whom the law commands: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother” (Lev. XVIII:7); and again: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister” (ibid.). It was commanded to gather these and similar things from the law given to it; and because it could not be sufficient if it gathered only from the written law, it was commanded to gather each day as much as could suffice.

The person gathers sufficiently for himself day by day if he takes an example of virtue from each of the ancient Fathers. Whoever wishes to live chastely should strive to imitate Isaac, the husband of one wife. Thus, thus he finds examples of obedience, humility, patience, and other virtues to imitate, if he strives to gather day by day with diligent care. There are also other days—namely faith, hope, and charity—which he must gather, because no one can be saved without these three virtues. But why he commands him to gather all these things is shown by the following words, when he says:

“That I may test him, whether he walks in my law or not.” What does “that I may test him” mean, except that, by testing him, he may make him know whether he walks in my law or not? He walks if he advances; he walks if he strives to imitate others. Some walk in the law of the Lord. Those who stand are those who do only what the law commands; those who walk are those who do not merely what is commanded, but also gather from each person things which they can imitate. Thus, thus, mercifully providing for those under the law, he commanded them, as it were, to gather a single portion from each person.

But he willed that we, who are under grace, should gather a double portion, saying:

“But on the sixth day let them prepare what they bring in, and let it be double what they used to gather each day.” The sixth day is the time of grace. For the sixth day may be understood as the sixth age of the world, in which the Son of God, incarnate for us, came into this world. And what prepared thing ought we to bring in during this sixth age? In the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary, the immaculate body of our Redeemer and his whole manner of life among human beings began to be prepared for us. This was a great preparation for our salvation. But at the end his sacred little body was fully prepared, roasted and cooked upon the altar of the cross in the burning fire of manifold suffering and pain. We ought beneficially to bring it in for ourselves thus prepared: so that, when we receive his body and blood under the form of bread and wine, we may believe without hesitation in the true divinity and humanity hidden within.

“And let it be double,” he says, “what they used to gather each day.” What is it to gather a double portion except to believe him to be true God and true man? Those who were before the law and under the law somehow gathered a single portion, because they believed him to be true God only. But we gather, as it were, a double portion because we believe him to be true God and true man. We also gather, as it were, a single portion each day when we believe that each day—that is, each of the ancient Fathers—though great and outstanding in virtues, was nevertheless a mere human being; but we believe our Lord himself to be not only true man, but also true God.

That he willed, as has been said, to be prepared for us upon the cross, and that we must gather this double portion by believing and confessing him to be true God and man, our same Savior proclaimed and taught before his Passion. Therefore the time of his preaching is immediately added, when it is said:

And Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel: “In the evening you shall know that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt.” What Moses and Aaron—our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ—in his eternity with God the Father determined and foreordained, [Col. 0265C] he declares that he will mercifully fulfill at the end of time, when he says: “In the evening you shall know that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see his glory.” Here, by “evening,” the dishonor of the Passion is indicated, and by “morning,” the glory of the divine Resurrection.

“In the evening,” he says, “you shall know.” When that evening of my Passion comes, and I, lifted up upon the cross, shall commit my spirit into the hands of the Father and descend to the lower regions to set you free, then you shall know—what you are now unwilling to know—that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt: that my divinity descended with my soul to the lower regions and delivered you from the darkness of eternal condemnation. For you believe me to be merely a pure human being and refuse to believe that I am true God and man. “And in the morning you shall see his glory.” In the evening of the Passion you shall know the lowliness of my humanity [Col. 0265D], and in the morning of the Resurrection you shall see the power of my divinity; for, if I were merely a pure man and not true God, I could not rise from the dead after suffering and death.

He had often foretold these same things about the dishonor of his Passion and the glory of his Resurrection to his disciples before his Passion, as where he said: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man shall be delivered to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and spat upon. And after they have scourged him, they shall kill him, and on the third day he shall rise again” (Matt. XX, 19). The words of this reading agree quite clearly [358] with these words, in which it next says:

“For he has heard your murmuring against the Lord.” Your murmuring—that is, your grief—God the Father has heard [Col. 0266A], and he sent me, his Son, who am true God and man, for your redemption. But you attend only to the form of a servant which I have received, and do not believe that I am true God. “But what are we, that you murmur against us?” I say this to you in the form of a question, so that by my question I may cause you to know what you do not know: that I am true God and man. “We” refers to my humanity, because I am compounded of two essences, that is, soul and body; but “what,” which is ineffable, pertains to my divinity, which you refuse to believe. Therefore I say: “But what are we, that you murmur against us?” That is: if that “what,” which is ineffable and pertains to divinity, were lacking to me, what benefit would my humanity—to which “we” refers—[Col. 0266B] give you? How could it set you free?

The statement which Peter made by Christ’s own inspiration agrees with these words: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16). Martha also affirms this when she says: “I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who came into this world” (John XI, 27). Many others believed and confessed this, being divinely inspired by him. It follows:

“And Moses said: The Lord will give you flesh to eat in the evening, and bread in the morning to the full.” This is said not by Moses and Aaron, as in the preceding passages, but by Moses alone: Christ Jesus, that man, alone; alone, I say, he spoke—that is, he acted alone. For to speak was his to do. And how was it his to do? Whatever he foretold concerning his Passion, he alone accomplished in his human nature [Col. 0266C]; and because his divinity was impassible, he endured in the experience of human nature spittings, blows with the fist, bonds, scourges, wounds, and nails. In that evening when he supped with his disciples, and in that evening of the Passion, he gave us his flesh, roasted and cooked upon the altar of the cross.

“And bread in the morning to the full.” [359] Just as before his Passion he revealed himself to some, so also after the Resurrection. When the morning of the Resurrection had passed, he gave bread to the full, because he revealed by faith to certain persons who doubted concerning him the Holy Trinity, which we may understand through the breads. Some doubted concerning his humanity, others concerning his divinity. Thomas doubted concerning his humanity, saying: “Unless I see in his hands the mark [otherwise, the fastening] of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.” [Col. 0266D] Those also doubted whose unbelief and hardness of heart he rebuked, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen from the dead. It follows:

“Because he has heard your murmurings, by which you murmured against him.” Because God the Father heard the murmurings of your grief, he therefore sent me, his Son, true God and man, for your redemption; and now, in the same humanity in which I died and was buried for you, I have risen from the dead through the power of my divinity. Therefore you ought not to doubt either my divinity or my humanity. “But what are we?” he says. This repetition of the Lord’s words [Col. 0267A] is, I think, a certain confirmation of the truth. For the earlier question containing these same words was, so to speak, a manifestation of his divinity, by which he revealed himself before his Passion and Resurrection to some who doubted his divinity. And because, after his Passion and Resurrection, doubt concerning both his divinity and his humanity remained in many hearts, he wished to repeat the same words once more in question form, so as to show that he had risen as true God and true man: “But what are we?”

“We,” I say, in respect of humanity, because I am compounded of soul and flesh; “what,” in respect of divinity, because I am God. Therefore you must believe without doubt both the power of the divinity and the dispensation of the assumed humanity.

“And your murmur,” he says, “is not against us, but against God” [Col. 0267B]. As if he said: If you do not believe that I am compounded of divine and human nature, [360] then your murmur is not only against my humanity, to which “we” refers, but also against the Lord—that is, against my divinity. And because the Jews resist this faith above all others, yet are to be converted near the end of the world, therefore, just as their pride and rejection were signified at the beginning of this reading, so their calling is signified at its end. Hence it follows.

“Moses said to Aaron: Say to the whole congregation of the children of Israel.” By Moses, as we have often said, Christ’s humanity is signified; by Aaron, whose name means “mountain of strength,” his divinity is signified. Therefore Moses’ saying this to Aaron is the devout supplication of Christ’s assumed humanity [Col. 0267C] to his divinity for the remnant of the children of Israel. Thus the humanity of our Redeemer, sitting at the right hand of the Father, where it also intercedes for us, does not cease to entreat its own divinity, which is equal to the Father, for the salvation of the remnant of Israel.

“Say to the whole congregation of the children of Israel: Draw near before the Lord.” As though he said: Lord Father, I assumed from that mass, namely, from the Jewish people—who have been forsaken by you and have long been deprived of your grace—this human nature which you see in me, your Son, and which you have placed at your right hand above every creature. But remember your mercies [Col. 0267D], Lord Father, and look graciously upon this people. Since it has now almost wholly perished, let at least the remnant be saved. Say therefore, Lord Father, through the inspiration of your grace, that they may draw near through faith before you, their Lord and Creator; that they may know you in truth as God the Father, and me, your only-begotten Son, whom you sent into the world for their redemption.

You have heard, Lord Father, their murmur of unbelief, by which from the beginning they have never ceased to murmur against you. You have heard the murmur of your servants, namely their fathers, who murmured before you not wrongly but rightly, lamenting their children’s faithlessness with great grief. There are also still some among them, though few, who, converted to the faith, murmur in sorrow for those [361] [Col. 0268A] who continue in unbelief and the blindness of their hearts. Speak, Lord Father, and cause all their murmuring to cease; and let those who are still in darkness return to the light of your truth.

Thus, indeed, when our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the eternal Father, pleads and intercedes for his people, it shall at some time come to pass, when the time of their salvation arrives, as the following text plainly states:

“And while Aaron was speaking to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness; and behold, the glory of the Lord appeared in a cloud.” For when that supreme Aaron, God the Father, begins to speak in their hearts by faith and illumines the darkness of their blindness with the light of his visitation, troubled and saddened, they shall look toward the wilderness [Col. 0268B]: that is, they shall consider that they had thought our Redeemer not to be God, but merely a pure human being. And when they look upon this wilderness with so blessed a regard, behold, the glory of the Lord shall appear in the cloud, that is, in Christ’s flesh; for they shall believe and preach with great faith the glory of Christ’s divinity, though formerly they had refused to believe and confess him to be God and man, born of a virgin mother.

And because the conversion of the Jews prefigured at the end of this reading has not yet taken place but is still to be hoped for, the chant which follows after the reading has ended seems not unjustly to accord with the same reading:

“The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council and said: What are we doing? For this man performs many signs.” Just as the chief priests and Pharisees visibly assembled against the Lord Savior at the time of his Passion [Col. 0268C], so now too nearly all the Jews who still remain assemble against that same Savior, now seated at the right hand of the Father. Daily they gather a council of malice and faithlessness against him, and they shall not cease to gather it until the end [362] of the world; for with malicious and hardened heart they oppose, as far as they can, the true faith, saying:

“What are we doing? For this man performs many signs.” What, they say, are we doing, since we see this man performing so many signs throughout the world? They grieve and are filled with great hatred because this man—Christ Jesus, whom they regard not as God but merely as a man—has performed, and daily performs, so many signs of salvation and grace, [Col. 0268D] so many signs of heavenly mysteries in the Church, and because almost the whole world believes in him.

For they have now been scattered throughout all lands and have lost their place and nation, in which the Romans—whose name means “thundering ones,” that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—dwell powerfully through the mysteries of faith. And because, as we have said, they never cease to assail the faith which is in Christ Jesus, they continually gather their council of perversity against the Lord Savior, now reigning eternally in heaven. Quite fittingly we sing the aforementioned chant, “They gathered,” every year at the time of the Lord’s Passion, as though mocking those same faithless Jews; and until their universal conversion takes place at the end of the world [Col. 0269A], we shall never cease to sing it. But after their general conversion has taken place, when they have been united and joined to the children of the Church, they too shall sing the same chant with us in the name of the crucified Savior, with equal harmony and one faith. And him whom their fathers mocked in his Passion, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews,” they shall praise and confess with the true faith of confession as reigning and living for ages of ages. Amen.

## 363. HOMILY XL. FOR THE SECOND PALM SUNDAY

“The children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, who strengthened Eglon king of Moab against them. And they served him eighteen years, and afterward cried out to the Lord” (Judges III).

[Col. 0269B] The venerable day of today’s feast—the Day of Palms—is for this reason commemorated by holy Church with splendid proclamations of praise: on this day the children of the Hebrews went forth with palms to meet the Lord as he came to Jerusalem. For this is the illustrious day on which he, because the salvation of the whole human race had come, was preparing himself for the work of our redemption, namely, to overcome the ancient enemy, leaving his faithful in this an example of how, triumphing over the adversary, they might attain the glory of heavenly joys.

The chief reason why that crowd met so great a Lord with such glory was that it had Lazarus in its company, whom he himself had raised from the dead after four days. At that procession the Lord was then bodily and visibly present [Col. 0269C]. But we trust and hope that in our procession today he may deign to be invisibly present in mercy and compassion. In it there are found not one but many Lazaruses, whom he has restored through penitential conversion from the death of the soul to life—a work truly greater and more glorious in divine mercy.

This magnificent glory of the Lord’s Passion and triumph has been prefigured, albeit obscurely, [364] in many places of sacred Scripture. Of these we shall recount one memorable instance, which seems not unfitting for the present solemnity:

“The children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, who strengthened Eglon king of Moab against them. And they served him eighteen [Col. 0269D] years, and afterward cried out to the Lord.”

Eglon means “their calf”; Aod [Ehud] is interpreted as “strength” or “military service.” By Eglon, king of Moab, the ancient enemy may appropriately be understood, who after the transgression of the first human being had subjected the entire human race to his dominion. Although he reigned freely among the Gentiles and the other nations of the earth, who did not know God and did not possess the Law and the prophets, and violently crushed them, he nevertheless exercised the greatest force of his tyranny among the Jewish people. For, though they possessed the prophets, the Lord’s Law, and religious ceremonies, at his instigation they devoted everything belonging to the worship of God to the acquisition of temporal goods.

But the elect of that time, grievously afflicted by the oppression of humankind [Col. 0270A], interceded with God the Father in mighty cries for its liberation, and for so long assailed him with importunate prayers that, looking down from heaven, he sent them a Savior and [365] champion, according to the account of the following text.

“He raised up for them a Savior, named Aod, illustrious, who used either hand as his right.” By Aod, who, as we have said, means “strength” or “military service,” our Lord Jesus Christ is understood; and it is rightly said of him that he used either hand as his right. His right hand was his divinity, but his left his humanity. With his right hand—that is, in his divinity—he created heaven and earth; but with his left, namely his human nature, which, as we have said, he used as his right hand, he possessed such strength that he never did anything sinister [Col. 0270B], but was wholly holy, wholly just, pure and unstained in all his works; and in that same humanity he restored fallen man from death to life. How he lived in the days of his flesh and how he taught may be understood from the words that follow shortly.

“He made himself a two-edged sword, having in the middle a hilt the length of a hand’s palm.” By Christ’s sword his preaching may be understood, of which sword David says: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. XLIV, 4). He is truly described as a two-edged sword, that is, sharp on either side, because what he taught in words he set forth with the testimony of good works. He taught people to despise riches and worldly glory, and to embrace voluntary poverty for the heavenly kingdom, as in: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3); and what he admonished by word, he confirmed by examples.

“Having,” he says, “in the middle a hilt the length of a hand’s palm.” In the hilt, as is well known, the sign of the cross [366] is shown [Col. 0270C]. Christ’s cross, however, was not only that upon which he hung before human eyes. Rather, throughout all the days of his life he in some manner bore a cross, because he steadfastly endured countless miseries of toil and suffering, and the manifold injuries of poverty and persecution. He also set forth this cross for his imitators to follow, saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Matt. XVI, 24). It follows:

[Col. 0270D] “And he was girded beneath his cloak on his right thigh.” Since sons are born from the thigh, Christ’s holy humanity may be understood through his right thigh; from it noble sons arose, namely, the holy apostles. The Lord was girded with the sword beneath his cloak on his right thigh because he taught that the pleasures of carnal life, which are to be understood through the cloak, must be despised not only by himself but also by his sons, that is, by the apostles.

“Now Eglon was exceedingly fat.” The enemy of the human race was indeed exceedingly fat, because before Christ’s Passion he violently drew both elect and reprobate after death into his belly and swallowed them. And although, as we have said above, he drew many powerfully to himself from among the Gentiles, he had nevertheless placed, as it were, the chief throne of his kingdom among the Jewish people [Col. 0271A], as the sequence of words that follows suggests.

“Now he was sitting alone in a summer upper chamber.” Because in summer the fruits of the earth and the blossoms of trees emerge, which had lain concealed in winter, the Jewish people may rightly be signified by the summer upper chamber. At that time they abounded in the greatest joy of prosperity, enjoyed riches, glory, and abundance in every respect. Since, in their abundance of all good things, they despised God [367] and devoted themselves to pleasure and the desires of the flesh, the enemy of the human race had established for himself a sweet resting place in their hearts. But how our Lord and Redeemer, mercifully providing aid for the misery of human ruin, crushed his violence by strength may be understood from the account that follows [Col. 0271B].

“And he said: I have a word of the Lord for you.” As though he said: That Word which I have, this Word which was made flesh—namely, the human nature which I bear—is against you; for by it, triumphing over you, I shall dissolve and reduce to nothing the power of the former condemnation.

“Who immediately rose from his throne.” For when he saw that the whole life and teaching of our Lord and Savior was utterly contrary to himself, he in a sense rose from his throne [368] in opposition to him, inciting those same Jews, among whom he sat and reigned, to persecute him. Our Lord Jesus Christ continued this conflict of persecution with the adversary until he came to the gibbet of the cross [Col. 0271C].

Upon that very gibbet, as the following sequence of words declares: “Aod stretched out his left hand, took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly so forcefully that the hilt followed the blade.” Aod stretched out his left hand because our Lord and Savior gave his holy humanity, which he assumed for us, over to the contests of suffering and to the punishment of the cross.

## 369. HOMILY XLI. FOR THE THIRD PALM SUNDAY

“Caleb said: ‘Whoever strikes Kiriath-sepher and lays it waste, to him I will give my daughter Achsah as wife.’ And when Othniel, son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, had taken it, he gave him his daughter as wife” (Josh. XV).

[Col. 0271D] The venerable feast of this day, dearest brothers, must be celebrated by us with great rejoicing. On it the Son of God, glorious above all things, sitting meekly upon an ass’s back, deigned today to come to the place of his Passion, where he would offer himself to God the Father as an acceptable sacrifice, a fragrant offering, for the salvation of the whole human race. Let us therefore rise and go out to him beyond the camp, not being ashamed of his reproach—that is, of his cross. And just as the crowds of poor people and children met him as he came to Jerusalem with green branches and sang royal praises to him as though he were already triumphant, so let us do likewise: if we are his members, let us follow the head; let us imitate Christ himself in poverty, and, humbly cleaving to him, meet him with the greenness of good works. Let us meet him through compassion; let us die with him through the mortification of vices; let us venerate him, weak for our sakes, while recognizing that in himself he is exceedingly exalted and glorious. If he perceives in us a devout affection toward himself, then in humility he will show himself loving and merciful to his servants; lofty and immeasurable, he will reveal himself glorious to his poor.

These true joys of our salvation, which we now celebrate, were long ago prefigured in many different figures and enigmas. From them all it is pleasing to bring forward two examples, and, according to our measure, to show how the light of truth lay hidden beneath the shadow of the letter.

[Col. 0272B] “Caleb said: ‘Whoever strikes Kiriath-sepher and lays it waste, to him I will give my daughter Achsah as wife.’” By the name Caleb, which means “heart,” God the Father may be understood; by Othniel, whose name signifies “his time of God,” the Son of God; by Achsah, which means “limping” or “angry,” the soul of Christ; and by Kenaz, which means “a contemptible possession,” the Synagogue.

Caleb, whose name means “heart,” fittingly represents God the Father, who from his heart uttered and begot the good Word, that is, his Son, coeternal, co-omnipotent, and consubstantial with himself. God the Father promised—and indeed gave—his daughter Achsah as wife to this Son of his heart when he who was perfect God chose to become perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh; he alone stood ready to strike and lay waste Kiriath-sepher, that is, the city of letters. That is, he so struck the carnal understanding of the Law that the understanding of the spiritual sense made it alive; he so utterly laid it waste that the new grace of the Gospel transformed the harsh precepts of the Law [Col. 0272C].

“And when Othniel, son of Kenaz, had taken it, he gave him his daughter Achsah as wife.” Through Othniel, whose name means “his time of God,” the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, may consistently be signified. Every time of his life was God’s time, since in all things he obeyed the will of God the Father. He alone was innocent in hands and pure in heart, meek, good, and gracious toward all; yet he chose to be found among the imperfect, because, though like a sinner he had nothing of sin, he did not refuse to suffer and die. He is rightly called son of Kenaz, whose name signifies “a contemptible possession,” because according to his human nature he was son of the Synagogue, which is truly a contemptible possession. For just as the Church is a beloved possession, so the Synagogue is a contemptible possession, because it does not receive faith in the Savior. Othniel therefore took the city of letters, because Christ transformed the killing letter [371] into the life-giving Spirit [Col. 0272D].

Achsah, whose name is interpreted “limping” or “angry,” is joined to him in marriage. In the assumed humanity God the Father joined and gave him a rational soul. I confess that this soul was not feebly limping or improperly angry; rather, I see that it limped and was angry in the best possible way [Col. 0273A]. You know that one who limps rests one foot on the earth and holds the other raised above the earth. Thus, indeed, Christ’s soul rested one foot, so to speak, upon the earth when, as Paul says in today’s reading, “Christ was made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. II, 7). And: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (ibid.). Remaining in that form, he did not reject sinners who came to him; he had compassion on the weak and conformed himself mercifully to the imperfect. Yet his soul held its other foot far raised above the earth, because through the power of divinity it strongly guarded itself so that not even the faintest stain of sin might share in the weakness of our sins. It also possessed good anger and exercised praiseworthy wrath, because at all times it was accustomed to be angry with sins and to forbid sins with great severity.

This soul of Christ is well and most fittingly called the daughter of God the Father, because besides this soul alone there was and shall be no soul—not even that of the blessed Virgin Mary—which could so please the eyes of God the Father. For she too was conceived and born in sins, though afterward the Holy Spirit received her into his own in such a way that sins should not approach her. But this soul of Christ [370] alone, among all and in all respects, was chosen and pre-chosen; the Holy Spirit wonderfully praises and proclaims it in the Song of Songs, saying: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number; my dove, my perfect one, [Col. 0273C] is one, the only one of her mother, chosen by her who bore her. The daughters of Zion saw her and called her most blessed; queens and concubines also praised her” (Song VI, 7–8).

What are the queens but those noble souls joined to the eternal King, the immortal Bridegroom, through union of faith, correction of conduct, and praiseworthy practice of virtues? What are the concubines but sinful souls who, now cleansed through penitence [372], themselves approach the king’s bed and are at last found worthy to bear spiritual children to God within themselves? What are the maidens but souls fervent in Christ’s love? Among all these souls, though good and holy, the soul of Christ alone has no equal: it alone is the dove; alone, I say, because it knows no duplicity; a dove, because it does not swell with the bitterness of gall; perfect, because it is unstained in word, deed, and thought; the only one of her mother, because it alone is praiseworthy and immeasurable to that heavenly multitude of angels and saints; and chosen by her who bore her, because it is more admirable and beloved than all saints to the whole Church which still journeys on earth.

Thus it fittingly follows: “The daughters of Zion saw her.” Zion means “contemplation.” And what are the daughters of Zion but the heavenly multitudes of angels and saints, beholding with unveiled face the glory of the Lord? These saw Christ’s soul and proclaimed it most blessed. And queens—that is, perfect souls belonging to the heavenly inheritance—and concubines—that is, souls once sinful but now penitent—praise and proclaim Christ’s soul with all their hearts [Col. 0274A].

“As she was proceeding on the way, her husband instructed her to ask her father for a field.” He who in his divinity was in heaven without journey or change, when born into the world began to have a journey, because he chose to advance from infancy to childhood, from childhood to adolescence, and from adolescence to youth; so that he who, remaining in his exaltation, could not be comprehended, might begin to be known in his humility. Elsewhere we read of this journey that a certain Samaritan was journeying, and, coming near a sick man, moved with compassion, poured in oil and wine (Luke X, 34). This Samaritan is Christ himself, who made a journey when he deigned to become a participant in our nature; and, as one loving and merciful toward us, [Col. 0274B] his sick ones, he poured wine and oil into us: wine, by loosening sins through penitence; oil, by conferring gifts of virtues through grace.

Thus, as she proceeded on the way, her husband—that is, the divine nature—instructed her to ask her Father for a field. What, I ask, does this field signify? What fruit and honor is there in asking this field from the Father? [373] It is surely a great fruit and a great condescension that the soul of the Son of God asks this field from the Father, because this is the field which the Lord has blessed: this field is the holy Church gathered from the Gentiles. God the Father gave it as a gift to his Son, saying to him through the prophet: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. II, 8). For it was not sufficient for the Son of God that God was known only in Judaea and his name was great in Israel [Col. 0274C], since he had come to taste death and lay down his life for all.

“And as she sighed while sitting on the ass, Caleb said to her: ‘What do you have?’ And she answered: ‘Give me a blessing.’” In the ass upon which Achsah sat we may understand human nature, in which the young Son of God sighed throughout all his days and all his time, because he chose to suffer in his flesh many kinds of misery for us. And when his Passion was imminent, he drew deep sighs in fear and anguish of death, saying: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Mark XIV, 34). Again in another place: “Now my soul is troubled; and what shall I say?” (John XII, 27).

We may also simply understand in this ass the animal upon which the King of Heaven, sitting, deigned today to come to Jerusalem, as the prophet had long before foretold, saying: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your King comes to you, meek, sitting on the colt of an ass, the offspring of beasts under the yoke” (Zech. IX, 9).

Thus Achsah, sitting on the ass—that is, the soul of Christ clothed, as we have said, in human nature—when she sighed, when she was thus sorrowful and troubled, is shown by the words, “Give me a blessing,” not to have been troubled and sighing for herself, but for the redemption of humankind.

As though the Son said to God the Father: I, your Son, have become a servant; coeternal with you, I have come under time; I have assumed a rational soul; I do not refuse to suffer things unworthy and abject for the salvation of humankind [Col. 0275A]. [374] Grant me, I pray, this blessing: that through my blood all things in heaven and on earth may be made peaceful and reconciled to you. Paul commends this blessing when he says: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself,” and “he gave him as Redeemer of the world, making peace between things in heaven and things on earth” (II Cor. V, 19).

“You have given me dry land; give me also land watered with waters.” You, Lord, my Father, ask what I have—why I have uttered so many sighs for thirty years and more. Behold, I tell you: you have given me dry land, namely Judaea; give me also land watered with waters. Cause your Church, spread throughout all lands, to begin through the grace of faith to thirst for you, the fountain of life; let it not delay to run to you and follow you [Col. 0275B].

“Therefore Caleb gave her the upper watered land and the lower watered land.” What may we understand by the upper watered land except the multitude of angels, and by the lower watered land except the multitude of human beings? God the Father gave both these watered lands to his Achsah, his daughter. For he subjected all things beneath the feet of his Son, because he is the one before whom every knee bends—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—because he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.

These things, as you have heard, beloved, foretold this joyful season. These are the yearly feasts of our redemption, in which that true Lamb was slain and sacrificed, with whose blood our doorposts are consecrated. His Passion is recited on these days [Col. 0275C] so that we may attend, see, and remember what so great a Lord deigned to suffer for his servants, knowing that if we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him; and if we die with him, we shall also rise with him. May he grant this, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## 375. HOMILY XLII. FOR THE FOURTH PALM SUNDAY  
### On Samson and Delilah (Judges XVI)

This day, dearest brothers, is rightly called the Day of Palms, on which our King and Lord Jesus Christ, in order to triumph over the devil and win the palm of victory, deigned today to raise the banners of the cross and, like a most strong and glorious champion, hasten to the place of Passion and contest. It is pleasing, insofar as God grants, to set forth how another man prefigured all his deeds [Col. 0275D] and the mysteries of his incarnation, Passion, descent to hell, burial, and Resurrection—I mean Samson, who in all his actions displayed and bore the likeness of the true Samson, the true Nazarite, our Lord Jesus Christ, consecrated from his mother’s womb, and who through his wondrous strength expressed the work of divine might and power.

The history relates that he loved a certain woman who lived in the valley of Sorech, whose name was Delilah. At the urging of the Philistines, she agreed to deceive him and discover from him wherein he possessed such great strength. She tested him a first, second, and third time [Col. 0276A], but did not prevail; on the fourth she finally deceived him and prevailed. At last, after his seven locks had been shorn, he was seized by the Philistines; his eyes were gouged out; he was led to Gaza; shut in prison, he was compelled to grind. Thus, when he had been deceived, the Philistines offered magnificent sacrifices to their god Dagon; rejoicing at their feasts, they ordered that he be summoned and made sport before them. They made him stand between two columns; and he, calling upon his God and seeking vengeance for the loss of his two eyes, shook the columns violently and, dying with them, killed the Philistines, his enemies. He killed far more by dying than he had previously killed while alive.

In this Delilah, whom Samson loved, the whole of human nature, which the true Samson, Christ the Lord, [Col. 0276B] wondrously loved [376], may be understood. It consists partly of the elect and partly of the reprobate: the good Delilah is the good part of the elect; the evil Delilah, the evil part of the reprobate. This Delilah—that is, human nature, which began in our first parents Adam and Eve—is rightly said to have dwelt in the valley of Sorek. Sorek is a most excellent kind of vine, and is interpreted “chosen” or “best vision”; by it that garden of delights, Paradise, is figured, in which, before the transgression of Adam and Eve, the wine of joy was offered to all to drink; where the cup of eternal life, bringing neither death nor sin in its train, was offered; where there was the best vision, because there was the delightful and sweet vision of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and the frequent and solemn coming of the holy angels was pleasing.

While human nature [Col. 0276C] thus flourished in Paradise, burning with love for the true Samson alone, the princes of the Philistines came to her and said:

“Deceive him, and learn from him wherein he has such great strength, and how we may overcome him and afflict him when bound.”

Human nature in some fashion deceived God when, at the prompting of the foreigners—that is, evil spirits—it did not render the submission and obedience which it owed to God its Creator. And it is quite properly said: “Deceive him.” For one is said to deceive who neglects to fulfill in deed what he vows and promises. This Adam and Eve did, who then set snares of deception against God, when they believed the deceiving serpent rather than God who made true promises; and they made void what they had promised, when they became transgressors of the Lord’s commandment. “And learn,” they say, “from him wherein he has such great strength, and how we may overcome him and afflict him when conquered.”

Even if the serpent—or rather that evil Philistine, that is, the devil [377] [Col. 0276D] in the serpent—did not speak in these very words, the meaning is nonetheless equivalent. For it resembles what he said: “Why has God commanded you not to eat from every tree of Paradise? On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III, 1). It is as though he had said: “In this way you will deceive God concerning yourselves: eat from the tree from which he commanded you not to eat; and if you do what I have persuaded you to do, you will learn from him wherein God himself has such great strength—that is, you [Col. 0277A] too will be like gods, knowing good and evil. And when you do this, we too shall be able to know how—that is, by what means—we, having become superior in you, may make him inferior and afflict him, bound by your sins and those of all your posterity, with many miseries, until we condemn him to a most shameful death.”

“If you do this, O human nature, we shall give you eleven hundred pieces of silver.” These two things promised by the Philistines, the greater and the lesser, signify that twofold pledge of the devil: by the thousand, which is the greater, “you shall be like gods”; by the hundred, which is the lesser, “knowing good and evil.”

Therefore, after our first parents had been deceived and, with all their posterity, excluded from the joys of Paradise, the whole multitude of the elect, [Col. 0277B] descended from the first Delilah before the Law, saw its own calamity and spoke to Samson, seeking the mystery of the incarnation of the true Samson, through which the lost inheritance of the kingdom of heaven might be restored to them. And what did they say to their Samson and ours?

“Tell me, I beseech you, wherein your greatest strength lies, and what it is by which, if bound, you cannot break free.”

“Your greatest strength,” they say, “is your humility. If you deign to empty yourself and become man, we, who cannot comprehend you in the exaltation of divinity, shall glory that you, bound to human nature, are our Redeemer and Liberator. Therefore, O Lord, we ask that for our sake you put on that by which, once bound, you cannot break free.”

Thus, to Delilah praying and pressing him—the true Samson before the Law—he began through the patriarchs to promise his coming, prophesying and answering thus: “If I am bound with seven fresh cords, not yet dry but still moist, I shall be weak like other men.” The seven fresh cords rightly signify the time before the Law [378], [Col. 0277C] when, throughout that whole period measured by the sevenfold number of days, every person was a law unto himself; and those cords were not yet dry, because neither the fire of legal observance nor the sun of righteousness and evangelical teaching had dried them. Rather, they were still moist, because they were defiled and infected by the moisture and flow of sins. “If,” Christ the Lord says, “I am bound by these cords—that is, if, born and bound in human nature, I bear the sins of the world—I shall be weak [Col. 0277D] and, like other men, able to die.”

But the promised and expected one then delayed his coming. Therefore this Delilah—that is, the part of the elect—continually broke forth in the cry: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” “Your noble creature,” they say, “whom you created for the praise and honor of your name, has wholly degenerated; it has wholly descended into hell, because the Philistines are upon you—that is, evil spirits hold the higher place, and have made you, who alone ought to rule, inferior to your creature.”

“He broke the cords as one breaks a thread of tow twisted from the husk of yarn when it has caught the smell of fire; and it was not known wherein his strength lay.” In these words the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion is prefigured and foretold. But we must consider [Col. 0278A] what the cords, the thread of tow, the yarn, the husk, and the smell of fire signify.

Our yarn was Adam and Eve, who were noble yarn while they remained in their original state and delighted in the delights of Paradise. The husk, however, which is a section of this yarn, is the whole human race, cut off and propagated from those first parents of ours. This yarn, namely Adam and Eve, was turned into tow when by sinning they degenerated and, excluded from the joys of Paradise, lost that nobility in which they had been created. From that mass, from that ignoble tow, was drawn the noble thread, the Son of God, who broke the cords of original and actual sin. How did he break them? In this way: he who was true God did not disdain to become a thread of tow; God the Father, by his goodness, sent his Son; and God the Son obeyed that same Father even unto death in order to redeem us. And this thread is rightly called “twisted from the husk of yarn,” because he who was perfect God became perfect man, and [379] [Col. 0278B] the two natures, divine and human, were so mutually twisted and united that neither is separated from the other.

That noble thread received the smell of fire when it was roasted in the fire of the Passion; and from this fire of the Passion a most sweet fragrance penetrated the heavens, whereas from the beginning the stench of iniquity rather than the fragrance of sweetness had continually risen. Such was the immensity of this most sweet fragrance that through it the human race was redeemed and forgiveness of sins bestowed. That noble thread was broken on the cross [Col. 0278C] when, after the side of the crucified Lord had been opened by a soldier’s spear, blood and water came forth for the redemption of our salvation. “And it was not known wherein his strength lay,” because they did not recognize him to be God when they saw him dying as a man. These things were promised and prophesied to Delilah—that is, to the elect who were before the Law—but our Samson accomplished all things in truth with us.

Therefore, just as in Samson’s first answer—where he foretells that, if bound with seven fresh cords, he would be weak like other men—we should understand a reference to the time before the Law, so in his second answer, where he says: “If I am bound with new cords, which have never been used in work,” the sins of the second period, [Col. 0278D] which was under the Law, are figured. For new sins, which were the new cords, were added to the old ones under the transgression of the Law. New sins accrued to that people through the Law; for where there was no Law, sin was not imputed, as Paul says: “I did not know sin except through the Law. For I did not know covetousness unless the Law said: ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me every kind of covetousness” (Rom. VII, 7–8).

These cords are said never to have been used in work because, although some obeyed the Law, nevertheless the Law brought no one to perfection. “If,” Christ says, “I am bound with these new cords—that is, if under the time of the Law I am bound by the bonds of human nature—I shall be weak and like other men, [Col. 0279A] though according to divinity I am immutable God. Yet at that time it is not my will to come.”

Thereupon Delilah again cried, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” That is, when those elect who were under the Law grieved and offered God the cry of their heart because evil spirits held the higher place in God’s creature, there was foretold and shown beforehand [380] the future power and glory of the Lord’s descent into hell in what follows: “He broke the cords as threads of a web.” In the first breaking, in which Christ was broken in his body through Passion and death, the bonds of sins were broken; in the second breaking, in which his soul descended into hell, the bonds of punishments were broken.

He is mystically said to have broken the cords. For one who breaks something tears and divides the whole thing. Thus God the Father broke the threads of the human race when he took some—namely, the elect—from hell, but left others there to be eternally condemned.

And because at every time there was always some good Delilah, [Col. 0279B] that is, some good soul devoted to God and desiring his coming, in the third answer, in which Samson says, “If you weave the seven locks of my head with a web and fasten into the ground the peg wrapped round them, I shall be weak,” and when Delilah had done so said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson,” the grace of the third time is manifested: that in which God deigned to become man, assuming what he was not while remaining what he had always been.

In the seven locks we may understand the soul of Christ, full of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit; [Col. 0279C] in the web, the flesh; in the peg, the strength of divinity; in the ground, the blessed Virgin Mary. Nor is it unfitting that the blessed soul of Christ be understood in the locks; for as the number of hairs is infinite, so an infinite and numberless multitude of virtues was implanted in Christ’s soul. “If,” he says, “you weave the seven locks of my head—that is, my holy soul, full of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit—with the web of human flesh, and fasten the peg of divine strength, wrapped round it, into the ground—that is, into the virginal ground, the womb of the Virgin Mary, from whom I have determined to be conceived and born in the time of grace—I, who have in myself no cause why I should die, shall be weak and mortal.”

[Col. 0279D] And it should be noted that he says: “If you fasten the peg, wrapped round it, into the ground,” because he so put on, so wrapped and fastened to himself, that garment which he assumed from the Blessed Virgin that he will never wish to put it off, and never can or will separate human nature from divinity. The glory of his resurrection is also commended in what follows:

“Awakening from sleep, he drew out the peg together with the locks and the web.” [381] Christ the Lord began to sleep when he fell asleep upon the cross; he arose from sleep when he rose from the dead. He drew out the peg together with the locks and the web when, by the strength of divinity, he resumed the same soul and body, though with a different grace. In that human nature he wished to eat and drink and associate with people, as before [Col. 0280A] the Passion, so that he might establish in himself the foundation of our faith and grant us the spirit of resurrection.

All this was a kind of prophecy concerning the incarnation, Passion, descent into hell, and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ; and the truth, which was to appear in the fullness of time, had not yet appeared. Therefore, because all these things had been prophesied, Delilah—namely, the whole Church—was always from the beginning laboring to discover wherein his greatest strength lay. For where the weakness of humanity appeared, there the strength of divinity lay hidden. And therefore, so long as the human race was not redeemed through the power and strength of his divinity, it complained that he who is true and faithful in all his words had, in a manner of speaking, lied in his promise, saying:

“You have lied to me three times, and have not wished to tell me wherein your greatest strength lies.” When this our Samson, promised in many ways, kept delaying his coming for a long time, this Delilah—namely, the whole multitude of the elect—began to trouble him, as is said in what follows: “And since she was troublesome to him and clung persistently to him for many days, granting him neither space nor rest, his soul failed and was wearied even unto death.”

Was she not troublesome to him when it was said in anxious, complaining voices: “Command, command again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little here” (Isa. XXVIII, 13)? Again: “Give a reward, O Lord, to those who wait for you, that your prophets may be found faithful” (Ecclus. XXXVI, 18). Again: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I, 1). “I wait,” she says, “not for another, [Col. 0280C] not for an angel, not for a man; but let him himself kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. Long ago the Lord spoke to me through the mouths of his prophets; let him come himself, humble and empty himself, and kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Was not one of these Delilahs the blessed Mary, Mother of God, whom we believe to have sought the kisses of such love [382] with an urgency [so much] greater than that of all other human beings insofar as she burned beyond all mortals with a greater desire of love for God and neighbor? He sought this kiss who said: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down!” (Isa. LXIV, 1.)

[Col. 0280D] “Since she clung to him continually in this way and that, and granted him neither space nor rest, his soul failed and was wearied even unto death.” How and when did his soul fail? Surely when, having compassion on his own, he descended, made man in the weakness of our flesh. How was he wearied who, in his divinity, did not admit mutability or weariness? He was wearied by assuming our weariness; and for this reason he deigned to know and experience it in himself, so that the Creator might know how to condescend to his creature, considering in his own weariness that our weariness and weakness did not allow us to stand with him.

Then, revealing the truth of the matter, he said to her: “Iron has never come upon my head, because I am a Nazarite—that is, consecrated to God—from my mother’s womb.” Born into the world, our Lord Jesus Christ revealed himself to the worthy and showed who he was, [Col. 0281A] saying: “Iron—that is, any corruption—has never come upon my head, that is, upon my divinity, because I am true and immutable God, and true man, who am a Nazarite—that is, consecrated—from the womb of my mother Mary: never corrupted in her conception, never corrupted in my birth, nor afterwards, living in the world, did I contract anything of the stain of sin.”

The truth of this was apparent to Peter, who said: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16). The truth of it was apparent to Martha, who said: “I have believed that you are Christ, the Son of the living God” (John XI, 27), and to certain others to whom he deigned to reveal himself. What our Samson was willing to suffer from the other Delilah—that is, from the part of the reprobate Jews—is indicated in his saying:

[Col. 0281B] “If my head is shaved, my strength will depart from me; I shall fail and become like other men.” The head of Christ is the divinity of Christ, as we have said. Christ’s head was shaved and stripped bare in death when, as the soul was separated from the body, his strength so departed and failed that the strength of divinity [383] withdrew its aid from humanity. He became like other men when, as the hour of Passion approached, he chose to fear, be weary, and be sorrowful, saying: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Mark XIV, 34).

“When she saw that he had confessed to her all his heart, she sent to the princes of the Philistines and gave them word, saying: ‘Come up here once more, because he has now opened his heart to me.’” Our Samson confessed all his heart to that Delilah, namely the treacherous and unbelieving Synagogue, when among them he performed so many and such great signs, healed the sick, raised the dead, and displayed and showed other incomparable benefits. Although this treacherous Delilah knew that things so glorious and magnificent, done and spoken by him, could be accomplished only through the Son of God—as when, marveling at his teaching, she said: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks” (John VII, 46)—she nevertheless refused to believe in him. Instead, she sent to the princes of the Philistines [Col. 0281C] when she admitted evil spirits into her heart; at their prompting the chief priests and elders of the people assembled and stirred up the whole people against our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0281D] This Delilah commands the Philistines, saying: “Come up here once more, because he has now opened his heart to me.” When the Jews, after seeing his signs and miracles, wickedly and stubbornly pressed him, saying, “How long do you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John X, 24); and, “Whom do you make yourself?” (John VIII, 53), then at last, in the Passion, when the high priest adjured him to say whether he was the Son of God’s chosen one, he opened his heart when he said: “You have said it, for I am he” (Matt. XXVI, 64; Mark XIV, 62).

“They came up, taking the money which they had promised.” This verse has a double sense. We said above that evil spirits may be understood by the Philistines. They came up in the Lord’s Passion, taking the money which they had promised.
