Their money, which they promised our first [Col. 0282A] parents in Paradise, was eleven hundred pieces of silver: a thousand when they said, “You shall be like gods,” and a hundred, “knowing good and evil.” The money which they then promised was given and received in the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, because then the eyes of the entire human race were truly opened and enlightened. Men became gods because God, having become man, bestowed his divinity upon us. They became knowers of good and evil: good, because forgiveness of sins and redemption from death and hell were given; evil, because Christ endured for us the punishment of the cross.

But we may also understand the money of the Philistines—that is, of the Jews—to be the Law and prophecy. Taking this, they came up when they gathered a council [Col. 0282B] to kill our Lord Jesus Christ, lest perhaps, if they allowed him to remain thus, all should believe in him, and the Law and prophecy be taken away from them.

“But she made him sleep upon her knees and rest his head in her lap; she called the barber, shaved his seven locks, and began to cast him off and drive him away from her.” The knees of Jesus Christ are called the holy apostles. That harlot, the Synagogue, made him sleep upon those knees when, sending a cohort with swords, she ordered the Lord Jesus to be seized and bound; for he then so fell asleep in them that not even Peter himself, who had said, “I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke XXII, 13), remained with him, but all abandoned him and fled.

[Col. 0282C] Thus, while he slept upon her knees, she also made him rest his head in her lap. Did she not incline and humble his head too much in her lap when, despising and forgetting the glory of his divinity, she led him into her council, where she defiled his angelic face with filthy spittle, struck him with blows, and veiled his face? Or did she not wickedly and cruelly incline and despise him when she sent him to Herod, and Herod with his army despised and mocked him, clothing him in a white garment? “She called the barber, shaved his seven locks, and began to cast him off and drive him away from her.”

That barber was Pilate, who is rightly called a barber because he then, so to speak, sheared that most gentle Lamb and deprived him of his fleece when he laid the most bitter scourges upon his most holy body—scourges [Col. 0282D] which in their enormity and cruelty surpassed all his previous punishments. For his sweating blood in agony, his sorrow unto death, his being spat upon, his being struck with blows—all this, so to speak, was tolerable in comparison with the scourges he endured from the judge Pilate. There his seven locks were shaved.

What may be understood in the locks of Jesus Christ but what is understood in his knees: namely, the holy apostles? They are quite appropriately called the locks of his head, because as the hair of the head is an ornament, so they became an ornament of his divinity by later teaching and preaching what they had seen and heard concerning him. But these locks were in some sense shaved from Christ’s head when, at the crisis of the Passion, they denied him and fled, abandoning him.

[Col. 0283A] “And she began to cast him off and drive him away from her.” Judea cast Christ off and drove him away when, Pilate asking, “Shall I crucify your king?” (John XIX, 15), they answered, “We have no king but Caesar” (ibid.); and, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (ibid., 12). After all this it is fittingly added: “Immediately his strength departed from him.” When, I ask, did strength depart from the true Samson, to whom none is like among the strong? Christ was God and man; and according to his human nature he could not have suffered unless the strength of divinity had withdrawn its aid from humanity.

In all these things it was not that worst Delilah, but the good and chosen Delilah—that is, the multitude of holy souls [Col. 0283B] still sitting in hell and in the region of the shadow of death—who cried and said: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson.” This is to say: “O Lord, although you now suffer for us, although you endure so many and such great evils, the Philistines are still upon you—that is, evil spirits remain superior to your creature. And we shall endure this evil until you pour out the noble price of your blood and, by your coming, take and rescue us from here.” Not scorning their prayers and desires, he did what follows:

“He, rising from sleep, said in his heart: ‘I shall go forth as I did before and shake myself free,’ not knowing that the Lord had departed from him.” Truly our Samson rose, as it were, from sleep when, putting aside all bodily sweetness and rest, he hastened to the labors of the Passion. That he suffered not unwillingly but voluntarily [Col. 0283C] is indicated by what he says: “I shall go forth as I did before and shake myself free.” What is “I shall go forth” [386] but “I will lay down my soul upon the cross”? What is “I shall shake myself free” but “having suffered and died, I shall rise with my elect”? “Not knowing,” it says, “that the Lord had departed from him.” Why is he who knows all things said not to know that the Lord had departed from him?

He certainly did not know because he did not wish to know how contemptible was the ignominy of death, how grievous the insults, how bitter the endurance of death. He did not know because he did not wish to know that he would be abandoned by the power of divinity, which, unless it had withdrawn and hidden itself for a time, he could in no way have suffered death. And thus, not wishing to know the ignominy of death, he offered himself for us [Col. 0283D] as a living and spotless sacrifice.

We may also understand in another sense the phrase: “Not knowing that the Lord had departed from him.” To know God is to love God; not to know God is not to love God. These two—the knowing of God and the not knowing of him—belong to the two wills which he had at the very point of the Passion. For as he was God and man, so he had two wills: one of divinity, by which he intended and desired what was necessary for the salvation of the human race; the other of humanity, by which he feared death, by which his soul was distressed and wished to remain in the flesh, as he also prays in the Passion, saying: “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.” This saying shows that he did not know—that is, did not love—that the Lord had departed [Col. 0284A] from him, namely, that the strength of divinity should withdraw its aid from humanity. But when he immediately says, “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done,” he knew—that is, loved—according to the divine will, that the Son should suffer and the world be saved.

“When the Philistines had seized him, they immediately tore out his eyes.” Samson’s eyes were torn out; and the eyes of the true Samson, consecrated from the womb, the Lord and Savior, were also torn out. The two eyes of Jesus were the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles; his two eyes were Adam and Eve; or his two eyes were Peter and Judas. The two eyes, Adam and Eve, were torn out when Adam, who was God’s right eye, did not fear to sin in Paradise. His left eye, Eve, was torn out when she who formerly had looked upon God with upright eyes looked to the left by obeying the serpent. He lost [387] [Col. 0284B] his right eye when Peter denied him three times at the voice of the maid at the door; he lost his left when Judas, who betrayed him, hanged himself with a noose.

“Samson was led to Gaza,” which is interpreted “strength.” Christ too was led to Gaza when he was led to the altar of the cross to be offered for us, where he completed a work of such strength that the strong man armed was made unarmed and powerless. “Shut up in prison, he ground,” because the power of love that had made him ascend the cross also made him seek the prison and horror of Gehenna. There, like one grinding, he began to grind diligently: he gathered with himself, leading them forth, the good and chosen grains—namely, his saints—ground pure; but he left the evil grains, namely the wicked and sinners who were unworthy of him, in the devil’s mill.

[Col. 0284C] “Now his hair began to grow again.” We said above that the apostles may be understood by the Lord’s hair. They began to grow again when they washed away with loving repentance the fact that they had yielded somewhat through fear of death; and therefore they deserved to grow and be renewed upon the head of Jesus.

“The princes of the Philistines gathered together to offer magnificent sacrifices to their god Dagon.” The elders of the people, chief priests, and scribes also gathered together to offer sacrifices to Dagon, which is interpreted “fish of sorrow,” when they so vomited forth the hatred which deadly sorrow was producing in their hearts that their voices grew hot in saying: [Col. 0284D] “Away with him, away with him, crucify him” (John XIX, 15). They were thoroughly satisfied and rejoiced when Pilate adjudged that their petition be granted and, releasing Barabbas, delivered Jesus to their will (Luke XXIII, 25). There indeed they offered magnificent sacrifices to the devil; there, filled with wicked vows and desires, they praised their god, saying: “He has delivered our enemy Samson into our hands.”

“Rejoicing at their feast, after the meal had now been taken, they commanded Samson to be summoned and to play before them. Brought out of prison, he played before them.” When, I ask, did our Samson play before these Philistines? Surely when he did not disdain to be blindfolded by those striking him, did not reject the reed placed in his hand as a scepter by those mocking him, and did not spurn the scarlet cloak [388], the crown of thorns placed upon his head, or the Roman soldiers bending their knees before him and hailing him with laughter as king of the Jews. After he had played enough in such things—for all these things were joy and gladness to his heart—he began again to play in another manner, as follows:

“They made him stand between two pillars.” These two pillars are the two arms of the cross, upon which the limbs of the heavenly King were stretched and suspended. There Samson, playing, was expected by a house full of men and women, because the whole Church of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal applauded this spectacle, through which it hoped soon to be gladdened and redeemed.

“He said to the boy guiding his steps: ‘Let me go, [Col. 0285B] that I may touch the pillars upon which the whole house rests, that I may lean upon them and rest a little.’” The boy who directed the steps of our Samson was divinity, which ordered every work of humanity and which at that time appeared to unbelievers to be nonexistent. But it was not nonexistent; rather, it was great and was already working secretly. “Let me go,” he says, “that I may touch the pillars.” It is as though he said to God the Father: “O my strong and most mighty divinity, permit me to ascend the tree of the cross, upon which the whole house of my Church rests, without which nothing is strong, nothing holy, nothing safe, that I may lean there and rest a little. For unless there, with bowed head, I surrender my spirit and sweetly rest, I cannot lead forth and free so many thousands of my elect from hell.”

[Col. 0285C] “But he, having invoked his God, said: ‘Lord God, remember me, and now restore to me my former strength, that I may take vengeance upon my enemies and seek one vengeance for the loss of my two lights.’” It is as though our Lord Jesus Christ, hanging upon the cross with his hands nailed fast, invoked God the Father and said: “Lord Father, remember your Son hanging upon the cross. Grant that, with the former strength which I exercised in heaven in casting down the devil and his angels, so that he may never again be restored [389], I may now likewise cast him down and crush him by that same strength in my death: that as he was condemned and cast out of heaven, unable to have seat or place in heaven, so he may also be crushed and have no seat upon earth—that is, in the hearts of [Col. 0285D] my elect—and may likewise be crushed in hell, unable to have power over the souls of my elect.

“And for the loss of my two lights: Adam and Eve, who were my eyes in Paradise and whom he tore out from me when he deceived them, I shall receive one vengeance upon them. Moreover, I shall take away from them my other eyes—Job, my eye, and Moses, my eye—who are placed in hell, restoring them to Paradise and heaven.”

“And seizing both pillars on which the house rested, holding one with his right hand and the other with his left, he said: ‘Let my soul die with the Philistines.’” Our Samson seized both pillars when he spread out his hands upon the cross. He held one with his right hand—that is, with the power and providence of divinity—by which he blotted out the crimes of original sin and opened heaven; the other [Col. 0286A] with his left—that is, the obedience which he rendered to God the Father even unto death. He said—indeed, he prayed: “Let my soul die with the Philistines.” “I will,” he says, “that the human nature which I assumed should die; and not only die, but die with the Philistines.” “How, O Lord, may your soul die with the Philistines?” “That my death,” he says, “which I endure innocently, may so rule over and prevail against them that their power may be utterly destroyed and perish.”

“And, shaking the pillars violently, the house fell upon all the princes of the Philistines; and in dying he killed many more than he had killed while alive.” When the pillars of the holy cross were shaken—that is, when the Lord gave up the Spirit—signs of such an event shone forth: the veil of the temple was torn in [Col. 0286B] two from top to bottom, rocks were split, tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose.

But we may also say simply that our Samson shook the pillars of the cross when he cried out and expired. For some whom we often see suspended upon a gallows, while they are still very strong and vigorous, at the moment of death, bracing themselves against the gallows, shake the timbers of the cross very violently. Thus our Lord himself, because he was young [390] and strong, as his soul departed, violently shook the timbers of the cross. There the house fell upon all the princes of the Philistines. This house signifies the holy Church, which then underwent a good falling when Christ, who is the head of the body of the Church, fell in death. The saving ruin of this holy house fell upon the princes of the Philistines because the evil spirits, formerly superior, became inferior; and, through this fall, the Philistines—that is, the invisible enemies—having been overthrown and annihilated, the Church began to be superior and preeminent.

[Col. 0286C] Then our Lord, our Samson, killed many more in dying than he had killed while alive. For although in his life he taught every good and holy thing, showed and did every good thing, the Philistines were nevertheless not thereby utterly killed. But when these pillars were shaken, where he tasted death, he killed many more in dying than he had killed while alive, because they shall never again reign over the human race with such dominion as before. Hence it is that, if one whom throughout the whole course of his life [Col. 0286D] they gloried to possess as their own while living wickedly and disgracefully should repent in his heart while drawing his last breath, they grieve that he is numbered not among the torments of Gehenna but among the fellow citizens of heaven.

Now, dearest brothers, you have heard of the incarnation, Passion, descent into hell, and resurrection of our Lord; and now observe what is added concerning his burial.

His brothers, he says, and all his kindred came down, took his body, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol. The brothers of our Samson were his apostles and other disciples; his brothers were Joseph and Nicodemus, who, having received his body from Pilate, bound it in linen cloths with spices and placed it in his own tomb. But what is meant by the statement that he was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol? It signifies something, if we inquire into the interpretation of the names themselves. Zorah is interpreted as “coals”; Eshtaol, “fire giving birth.” What are signified by the coals, if not we wretches, we coals of desolation? What by the fire giving birth, if not those fiery stones—that is, the multitudes of angelic powers? Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ was placed and buried between us, who are Zorah, that is, coals, **391** [Col. 0287A] and Eshtaol, which is the burning angels. Yet we possess and attend to our buried one not in the same but, indeed, in a different manner. For they possess him in reality, we in hope; they near at hand, we far off; they in fullness, we in part; they rejoicing, we grieving; they burning, while we in this world, as in a foreign [Col. 0287B] house, scarcely acquire even a spark of charity. Nevertheless, in the meantime let us faithfully keep our buried one; let us honour him with such services as we can, until, after the exile of this life, we too exchange imperfection for fullness, image for truth.

Meanwhile, I am inclined, so far as God grants, to draw the oil of morality from the rock of this history, and briefly explain in what order these things related as done to Samson take place in us. Many of us detest this Delilah because of her wickedness. But if we look upon ourselves, we cannot deny that what she once visibly did to Samson, we have often done to our Samson, Christ, and daily do—alas! O how often, after his sweet kisses and covenants of love, do we cast him away and drive him [Col. 0287C] from us, summoning the Philistines—that is, evil spirits—giving them the higher place, and constructing in our hearts many devices of impiety for deceiving and destroying the lover of our soul! By Delilah, whose name is interpreted “bucket,” our flesh is understood, which always carries the water and honour of fleshly desire. Samson, however, whose name is interpreted “their sun,” is any faithful person illuminated by the true Sun of righteousness through knowledge of faith and the choosing of merit. After he has slain many thousands of vices and sins, after the sweet embraces of divine love, this Delilah—that is, the flesh—sometimes deceives such a faithful person when, by consenting, he yields to carnal desires which he ought to resist. She shaves his hair when she takes from a person good affections [Col. 0287D] and holy thoughts, which may be understood by the hair; she shaves his hair when she distracts his heart from innumerable and continual meditations upon Holy Scripture; she shaves his hair when she intercepts that inward sweetness of prayer and of the taste of God, and makes it alien to the Spirit.

**392** After this she exposes Samson in bonds—that is, the human mind—to the Philistines, namely, the impious demons. Seizing him and joyfully surrounding him, they strive to deprive him of both eyes. The two eyes of a person are the spiritual and literal senses; or the two eyes are understanding and memory. These two eyes are wretchedly torn out when, fleshly desire ruling in a person, neither spiritual precepts can be understood [Col. 0288A] nor literal knowledge retained in memory. Thus, thus, when we have been wretchedly cast down and confounded, we must not despair; rather, our child—that is, humble understanding—must be summoned without delay, so that humility may sit in the heart, enlighten us in action, and cause us truly to know and see what we ourselves are; and if this child is present, our feet will be directed into the right way.

For when the time of heavenly visitation dawns upon such persons, they say to their child—that is, to their humbled spirit: “Let me go, that I may touch the pillars on which the whole house rests, that I may lean a little upon them and rest.” These two pillars, which a person desires to touch and upon which to rest a little, are the two goods that can free him from fleshly desires: bodily continence and the guarding of the heart. [Col. 0288B] Having touched them by the hand of holy action through God’s mercy, he must keep watch in bodily continence, maintain most diligent guard over the heart, and lift up to the Lord the voice of prayer, saying: “Lord God, remember me, and now restore to me my former strength, that I may take vengeance upon my enemies, and for the loss of my two lights seek one act of vengeance.” This is to say: “Lord my God, I received from you, my Creator and benefactor, two lights—understanding and memory; but because my sins demanded it, I have lost these lights. If, therefore, in your just judgment I am not found worthy before you to receive them back, at least now restore to me my former strength: grant that now, as I was once able to do through your gift, I may resist vices [Col. 0288C] and strive to exercise myself in good deeds.”

After this, by shaking the pillars, he killed far more in dying than he had killed while alive. **393** He shakes the pillars when, withdrawing from the slothfulness of the heart, he presses on to the labour of good action, and from the good action of the body to the guarding of the heart; and he so joins these two—bodily continence and the guarding of the heart—that afterwards he cannot easily lose them. Thus he kills far more in dying than he had killed while alive, because, although he may at some time have pursued vices in himself, yet because he did not do so in humility, he in some measure had to lose what he did not preserve in humility; and then he kills vices all the more [and] more powerfully, the more perfectly and truly he chooses to humble himself before God.

[Col. 0288D] Therefore let us implore our Lord Jesus Christ, whose feast this is, in which he willed to humble himself unto death, that he may grant us true humility and cause us so earnestly to attend to the sorrow of his death that we may be pierced with compunction, suffer with him, and die with him, so that we may also at some time rise again and reign with him through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## 394 HOMILY XLIII, FIFTH HOMILY FOR PALM SUNDAY

> The word which came from the Lord to Jeremiah, saying: “Arise, and go down to the potter’s house; and there you shall hear my words” (Jer. 18).

The time of the Lord’s Passion is the singular [Col. 0289A] and pre-eminent time of our salvation and restoration; it also receives a special designation in Holy Scripture. For it is called the Passion of the Lord, not because the Lord suffered for fourteen days, but because during these days the insults of words and the injuries of many kinds of suffering which he received at the hands of the Jews are related more expressly.

We should understand that we celebrate this Passion of the only-begotten Son of God for fourteen days because he suffered for us in both parts of humanity, in soul and body. In soul, indeed, he suffered for us through the exceeding compassion which he inwardly bore toward the affliction and misery of the human race; but in body he suffered for us by enduring many injuries and reproaches, finally [Col. 0289B] by dying for us upon the cross in the very bitterness of death. For the only-begotten God did not suffer for us only when, crucified, he gave himself over to death; rather, his entire life and conduct, through which he lived in this life for thirty-three years, was in some manner a harsh passion to him, because utterly estranged from every prosperity, pleasure, and delight of the present life, he began under persecution and ended this life under persecution. For, as we read of him in the sacred books of the Gospels, while still tender and crying, still nursing at his mother’s breasts, he fled into Egypt because of Herod’s persecution, carried there by his parents’ service; and thus, spending the whole period of his life under persecution, he finally completed that venerable life by the passion of the cross.

[Col. 0289C] Long before, Jeremiah the prophet prefigured this Passion of the Son of God by his name and his life. Chosen by God as a prophet and sanctified in his mother’s womb before he was formed in the womb, he shone among the other prophets with a certain singular holiness and innocence. Isaiah, David, and the other prophets, although holy and chosen, nevertheless lawfully made use of this world while joined in marriage. But Jeremiah, when the Lord commanded and said to him, “You shall not take a wife in this place, nor shall you have sons” (Jer. 16:2), remained in virginity; and, having endured many tribulations, distresses, and sufferings from the Jews for truth and righteousness, he signified by his name and his passion the singular Lamb of innocence. For Jeremiah is interpreted [Col. 0289D] “the exalted Lord.” Who can more fittingly be expressed in this exalted Lord than the only-begotten Son of God the Father, who, according to the excellence of his divinity, is Lord of angels and human beings? To this exalted Lord the word of the Lord came, concerning whom we read thus in Jeremiah:

> The word which came from the Lord to Jeremiah, saying: “Arise, and go down to the potter’s house; and there you shall hear my words.”

When this word, “Arise,” is spoken to someone, that person is certainly understood to be either sitting or lying down. Sitting or lying belongs to one at rest; arising or standing belongs to one who labours and fights. Therefore the only-begotten Son of God sat at rest, lay at rest in the bosom of God the Father, in the repose of his eternity, before he became visible, before he appeared as a human being made in [Col. 0290A] flesh. To him, then, resting in this manner, reclining thus amid the delight and pleasures of his divinity, God the Father invisibly and ineffably, by his hidden judgment and counsel, admonished with a secret word that he should arise. When he caused him to be incarnate for the salvation of the human race, he addressed him with these words: “Arise, and go down to the potter’s house.” As though he were saying: “Because in your divinity, in which you are coeternal and coequal with me, you cannot endure the pains and sufferings by which you must restore and renew fallen humanity, arise from this sweet and delightful rest and prepare yourself for the contest of labours and tribulations, and for the bitterness of death. Thus, by arising, go down into the potter’s house by assuming flesh, so that through the labours and afflictions of the humanity you assume [Col. 0290B] you may aid fallen humanity.”

But let us now see who can be understood by this potter, or what may be understood by the house of this potter. This potter is God the Father; this potter also is the Son of God according to his divinity, who, according to the power of his divinity, fashioned and created all things with God the Father. This all-powerful potter, creating and forming all things with God the Father according to divinity, was, according to his humanity, the house of this potter, because according to the assumed human nature he was created by God the Father. And because the potter fashions and shapes the vessel he wishes to make from clay, the assumed humanity of the Son of God may rightly be signified by the potter’s house. Although it was incorrupt and undefiled, he nevertheless willed to assume an unstained body from the clay of human nature and condition, that is, [Col. 0290C] to unite it to his divinity. **396** For just as the first man, Adam, formed by God, was fashioned from the clay of the earth, so also the second Adam, the man Christ Jesus, was in a certain manner formed by God the Father from the clay of the earth, because from virginal flesh, descended from the same clayey mass, he assumed the material of flesh.

We may also understand by the potter’s house the blessed Mary, Mother of God, in whom that same potter, the Son of God, by assuming flesh dwelt as though in his own house. It follows:

> And there you shall hear my words.

This is the same as if God the Father had said to his Son, dwelling in his divinity: “You cannot fulfil in your divinity my words that will benefit the salvation of the human race, because in [Col. 0290D] your divinity you cannot suffer afflictions and miseries for humankind. But if you descend into the potter’s house, if you become human, there you shall hear my words; there indeed you shall obey my words, because you will endure in the assumed human being the sufferings and pains which divinity cannot admit.” These words, as we said before, are the words of God the Father addressing his Son in eternity. But the words that follow are the words of the only-begotten Son of God, voluntarily obedient to God the Father in his assumed humanity for the salvation of human beings. Hence it follows:

> “And I went down,” he says, “to the potter’s house; and behold, he was making a work upon the wheel.”

“I went down,” says the Son of God, obeying the Father, and in that obedience assuming a mortal body; and thus, as I went down, behold, the potter himself was making a work upon the wheel. This noble and excellent work which our potter, God the Father, wrought was the most holy body of the only-begotten Son of God. By the power of his divinity he deigned so to work it in the blessed Virgin that, without corruption of virginity and without intercourse with a man, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit alone working in [Col. 0291A] her flesh, the Virgin should give birth to God and man. **397** And this work, in which the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God is signified, is rightly said to have been made upon the wheel. For this work is so splendid and pre-eminent that by its excellence and sublimity it surpasses all the works of the Lord which he has wrought either in heaven or on earth. It is said to have been made upon the wheel. [Col. 0291B] For by the wheel, which turns and by its revolution continually descends to lower places, the human race may quite fittingly be signified. This wheel—that is, the whole human race—was turning from the beginning of the world and sinking down into original fault, because no mortal from the beginning of the age could avoid being conceived and born in original sin. Thus the order of generation had descended and continued as far as Christ: each person was conceived and born from another in sin, and no one could remain in this life so holy and innocent as not, after the end of this mortality, to descend to the depths of hell as one born in sins. But he alone, the mediator between God and humankind, the man Christ Jesus, was above this wheel, [Col. 0291C] because he alone was conceived and born without sin. And because in these words of the prophet three mysteries are expressed to us—of the incarnation, Passion, and resurrection—having set forth the mystery of the incarnation, he now proceeds to relate the mystery of the Passion and resurrection. For it follows:

> And the vessel which he was making from clay with his hands was broken.

In this vessel the Lord’s body must be understood; that most holy body was the vessel of the divinity dwelling within it. Yet God the Father, the craftsman, had made this noble vessel from clay with his hands. He made this vessel from clay because, as we said before, from the clayey mass of the human condition he caused the unstained body of his only-begotten Son to be conceived and born without sin and without intercourse [Col. 0291D] with a man. And this he did with his hands—that is, by the strength and power of his divinity. This vessel of divinity was broken when, for the salvation of the human race, he allowed the holy body to hang upon the cross as it succumbed to death, while the holy soul, released from the flesh, descended to the gates of hell.

**398** Thus, when this vessel had been broken, when Christ Jesus had suffered on the cross, the holy prophet, full of the prophetic Spirit, immediately turns his words to the glory of the resurrection, saying:

> And turning, he made that vessel another, as it pleased him in his eyes to make it.

Because of the disobedience of the first parent, God the Father had turned away from the whole human race. This wall of enmity between God and humankind remained firmly established until the Son of God himself, by his Passion and death, paid to the eternal Father Adam’s [Col. 0292A] debt. For although, when our Lord Jesus Christ was baptized, the Father’s voice had thundered from heaven over him, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17), all still descended into hell, as they had descended before Christ’s incarnation, and no human being, however righteous and holy, could enter the kingdom of heaven. But when this vessel was broken, when our Saviour was crucified in the flesh and his side opened by the soldier’s spear, while blood and water flowed out, then at last, original sin having been erased and remission of sins accomplished, God, appeased by the death of his Son, turned from his wrath to the reconciliation of the human race. Thus, having turned from wrath through the death and Passion of his Son, he made the body of his only-begotten Son in the resurrection [Col. 0292B] another vessel—in glory indeed another vessel, but the same in nature—as it had pleased the divine majesty before the foundation of the world to glorify his only Son with glory and honour after the triumph of the resurrection. Of this glorification the apostle Paul says: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9). Therefore in his resurrection and glorification he gave us also hope of the future resurrection, since we too shall rise in the same body in which we now live, though we shall be another vessel in glory, when, endowed with the gift of incorruption and immortality, we are crowned by him in the resurrection—he who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## 399 HOMILY XLIV, SIXTH HOMILY FOR PALM SUNDAY

[Col. 0292C]

> I said: “I will climb the palm tree, and I will take hold of its fruits” (Song of Songs 7).

The commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, which holy Church has undertaken to celebrate with solemn devotion for fourteen days, has not been arranged without cause; rather, we believe that, by the ordering of the Holy Spirit, the work of our redemption is celebrated for two weeks because something mystical lies hidden in them, which, with God’s help, will be accomplished in Christ’s faithful both in the present and the future life.

Therefore in the first week, in which we begin the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, a week entirely full of grief and sorrow, we may understand the whole time of the present life, in which the Lord’s elect, conformed to Christ’s sufferings, [Col. 0292D] grieve and are distressed amid the misery and labour of this exile. When this mournful life has been completed at the end of a person’s life, the second week follows, which indeed begins in joy but is nevertheless mingled with mourning and sorrow. Thus the first day of this week—the day of Palm Sunday, celebrated in great gladness and exultation—may signify the end of every elect person, when, released from the bonds of this life, he or she departs free from this world. Such a departure will truly be joyful and festive for the Lord’s elect, because, recognizing through God’s grace that they have conquered their own flesh, the world, and the devil, they joyfully meet the Lord with the palm of victory. [Col. 0293A] The holy angels, applauding them and coming forth to meet them with palms, receive them with joy and lead them into the palace of the eternal King.

Holy Scripture has not been silent about this celebrated day of palms, but foretold through the mouth of King Solomon in the Song of Songs that it would be so, saying: “I said: I will climb the palm tree, and I will take hold of its fruits.” In the palm tree is signified the victory of the holy cross. Yet in the palm tree, if we wish to take the plain sense, we can perceive that the present day was also prefigured, **400** on which the Saviour, ascending to Jerusalem—which, of course, is situated in a more elevated and higher place—willed there to be honourably received by crowds of the faithful with palms, hymns, and praises. For if in these words he had wished to signify only the victory of the holy cross, [Col. 0293B] he could surely have said just as suitably, “I will climb the cross,” as he said, “I will climb the palm tree.” But the glory of this day, on which he ascended to Jerusalem in order to suffer for us, was briefly prefigured by the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Son of God said long ago that he would climb the palm tree, when, established in his eternity, he had long before agreed and ordained with God the Father that, for the salvation of humankind, he would ascend the palm tree of the holy cross, where he would free the human race from the devil’s power and make it subject to his own dominion. Therefore, when he climbed the palm tree, when he hung upon the cross with outstretched hands, he took hold of the palm tree’s fruits. And what are the fruits of this palm tree except the whole human race, which he then took hold of when, dying on the cross, he joined it to himself by his Passion and death?

[Col. 0293C] And he rightly says, “I will take hold.” For what is taken hold of is known first to have fled. For all human nature had fled God by sinning, and could not be saved, not only before Christ’s coming but even after Christ’s birth. Though the Lord had been born for sinners, had enlightened them by the grace of his teaching, and had shown many signs, yet after all these things had been done he had by no means taken hold of them: all still fled from him, because the elect descended into hell together with the reprobate. But finally, when he died upon the cross, then he truly took hold of those who had fled from him and joined them to himself so firmly that not only the righteous and innocent but also sinners, if they repent before death, may deserve entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0293D] **401** To obtain and perfect this grace for the human race, the Lord ascended to Jerusalem on this day, where he was solemnly received with palm branches. Through this joyful day, as we have already said above, may be signified the end of our life, at which, passing from this life with the palm of victory, we shall be received by the holy angels. Other days follow this glad and glorious day, somewhat mingled with sadness and grief, because the Lord’s elect, who could not attain full perfection and purification in this life, commonly must be cleansed after life’s end by purgatorial fire. There is another cause of the sorrow which the Lord’s elect, released from the flesh, experience after the end of this life. So long as they do not deserve to receive into the fellowship of their joy their faithful fellow-combatant—namely, the body [Col. 0294A] in which they laboured for the Lord—as immortal and incorruptible, they are sorrowful for this reason. But this sorrow will be abolished on the eighth day of Easter, the day of the Lord’s resurrection, when, death swallowed up in victory, they will rise in the Lord, having obtained a twofold joy, of body and soul. Therefore, in today’s procession we are clothed not in copes but in white garments, because, leaving their bodies, the souls of the saints now rejoice and receive their reward in the soul alone, while the body still lies in the dust of the earth. In the singers who receive the congregation with verses, and who are clothed in white garments and copes, we may understand the holy angels, ordained by God to receive the souls of the elect. The cope suitably belongs to them, since it is broad and open in its [Col. 0294B] front part, because they, free from every corruption and misery of the present life, enjoy full blessedness. We too shall someday be clothed in these copes, when on the day of our resurrection we are made glad by rising with body and soul, when the body—which is now a burden—will have become an honour, adorned with immortality and incorruption. There the soul will be rewarded with such freedom and glory that, wherever it wishes, the body will immediately be present without any impediment or weight.

But because every human being, before attaining this height, must suffer many deceits and snares of the enemy and tribulations at life’s end, it is fitting that **402** on this day we sing at the Blessing of the Palms: “The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council and [Col. 0294C] said: ‘What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him. Perhaps the Romans will come and take away our place and nation’” (John 2:48 [as cited]). By the chief priests and Pharisees we may understand the evil spirits who draw near at the hour of death of every faithful person. They gather their council when they prepare various devices and many snares for that person, so that they may wretchedly deceive him after casting him down from the hope of eternal blessedness. For this alone is their aim: that, deceived by their counsel and suggestions, he may be dragged with them to torments. Therefore, having gathered the council, they say: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs.” For when they perceive that a sinful person is being changed from a wretched life to a better [Col. 0294D] one, and is preparing himself toward life’s end through confession and other good works, these are the signs which evil spirits greatly abhor to see performed by a human being. Seeing such signs, they fear that, having escaped from their dominion and fellowship, he may become a partaker of the heavenly kingdom and be found in Christ Jesus our Lord. Moved by this fear and grief, the evil spirits fittingly add: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him.” “If,” they say, “we permit this sinner, now repentant, to escape from us in this way, if we do not overthrow him with perverse suggestions and snares, we shall suffer loss not only in this one person, but shall lose the other sinners as well, who will be recalled to repentance by the example of his conversion. For they too will believe that they can be saved through repentance, [Col. 0295A] and thus all whom we hold under our power will escape from us.”

“Perhaps,” he says, “the Romans will come and take away our place and nation.” “Romans” is interpreted “thundering ones,” by whom we may understand the holy angels. Therefore the evil spirits fear that, if they permit the repentant person to rest from temptations, the holy angels will come and take away the place which they had prepared for themselves in such persons’ hearts, and utterly lose the nation of vices which they had nurtured in them through evil deeds. **403** Troubled by these suspicions, the evil spirits consider and deliberate how they may prevail against that person. Hence it follows:

> Therefore, from that day they planned to kill him.

From that illumination by which he has been visited by God, [Col. 0295B] they are so alarmed that they strive by every means to kill with their deception and wiles one now near to eternal life. Caught amid these distresses and snares, the person must direct prayers to God from the inmost affection of the heart, lest, abandoned by his help, he perish; and, as we sing today in the Introit of the Mass, must cry out to God, saying: “Lord, do not put your help far from me; look to my defense; deliver me from the lion’s mouth, and my humility from the horns of unicorns” (Ps. 21:20–22). When the Lord has heard that person crying to him, freed him from the snare of this world, and commanded him to come to him, he will offer worthy thanksgiving to his deliverer, saying in the Gradual: “You have held my right hand; in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. [Col. 0295C] 72:24). As though he said: “You, Lord, held my right hand, for you did not permit me to fall amid this life’s temptations; and leading me in your will, you overcame by the strength of your arm the tempter, lest he prevail against me; and now you have received me with glory to see you.”

Thus offering devout thanks to his saviour and deliverer, having beheld in the Gradual his Lord whom he desired, he wonderfully adds in the Verse: “How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart!” (Ibid., v. 1). Immediately after marveling at God’s goodness, he turns the eyes of his heart back to consider his own misery from which he emerged, saying: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped, **404** because [Col. 0295D] I envied sinners when I saw the peace of sinners” (Ibid., v. 2). As though the blessed soul said: “Indeed, Lord, established amid the world’s temptations, I would have perished utterly; placed in the danger of death, I would have despaired completely, unless you, Lord, had helped me by your grace and, protecting me by your aid, had not allowed me to slip.”

All that follows in the Mass—the Tract, Offertory, and Communion—also pertains to these further temptations which the soul will suffer at the point of death. Does not the soul, placed in agony and surrounded by death’s distresses, fittingly sing this Tract, saying: “My God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me? The words of my sins are far from my salvation!” (Ps. 21:2). Indeed, no one lives so holy and innocent a life [Col. 0296A] in the present world as not to be distressed, grieved, and afraid when the hour of death approaches. Hence the Offertory fittingly follows: “Reproach and misery awaited my heart; and I waited for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; I sought one to comfort me, and I found none; and they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:21–22). At that time the soul seeks one to comfort it, but finds none, because its comfort depends upon God’s judgment alone. Knowing and fearing this, the provident soul prays at the end of the Mass, as though at the end of its life, saying: “Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (Matt. 26:42). This is the same as saying: “I know, Lord Father, that, as the decree of your divinity ordains, I cannot pass from this world [Col. 0296B] unless I experience death’s harshness and endure its stings. Therefore, because it is impossible that I should not drink this cup, let your will be done, because your will is good and glorious.”

## 405 HOMILY XLV. FIRST, FOR THE PASCHAL SEASON. [Note: Thus the codex; Col. 0295D.]

> Achish said to David: “I know that you are good in my eyes, like an angel of God; but the princes of the Philistines said: ‘Let him not go up with us into battle’” (2 Kings 28).

The feast of the holy and venerable Paschal solemnity, now celebrated throughout the whole world, was prefigured long ago in our fathers, and especially foretold in the words and deeds of those two patriarchs Abraham and David, to whom the Son of God was also formerly promised in a singular and special manner. For that distinguished psalmist David, both by mystical deeds and prophetic words, signified more particularly him who became the stock and root of David. [Col. 0296C] In all his prophecy he did not omit the testimony of a single psalm without saying something concerning Christ, his Lord and his Son. Let us briefly hear when and how this David was conquered in the figure of the true David.

We read that the Hebrew people, whom the Lord chose for himself from the whole multitude of all peoples as his own possession, had teachers, as he appointed for them: first Moses and his successors, then Samuel, who judged them justly and royally, not in the vanity [Col. 0296D] of self-exaltation but in the Spirit of God and in truth. Because in their pride they were unwilling to remain content and subject under these men, they asked that a king be appointed for them. Their request displeased the Lord, and he said to Samuel: “Hear the voice of this people in all that they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them” (1 Kings 8:7). Although this word displeased him, he nevertheless allowed it to happen. For one thing is what he permits to happen through human wickedness; another is what he mercifully ordains and graciously disposes to happen. Hence that saying in the psalm: “And I dismissed them,” he says, “according to the desires of their hearts; they shall go in their own inventions. If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways, perhaps I would have humbled [Col. 0297A] their enemies with no effort [*pro nihilo*, literally “for nothing”] and laid my hand upon those afflicting them” (Ps. 80:13–15). Therefore he gave them Saul as king, under whose power they suffered great punishment and great humiliation, as they deserved. Yet, although he gave them a king in his wrath, he did not forget his customary mercy and compassion. For he sent Samuel secretly to anoint the boy David as king, concerning whom he himself said: “I have found a man after my own heart,” who would be leader and ruler over his people.

By this wicked people, who asked for Saul as king, the enemy of God, is expressed the whole human race, which sinned in our first parents, Adam and Eve, when they transgressed. These first parents of ours [Col. 0297B] had been created so nobly that the Lord himself willed to be their sole Father, protector, and king. But, dissatisfied with this good, they made themselves subject to the dominion of wicked Saul—that is, the devil—when, deceived through the serpent, they ate the forbidden fruit. Hence all their succeeding posterity endured countless evils under that king until David, “strong of hand,” that is, Christ, the new king, should be born into the world, undertake to conquer that Philistine—that is, the devil—in a wondrous contest, and, swinging the sling in his hand this way and that, cast the living stone—that is, send forth his holy soul, twisted by innumerable sufferings—saying to the Father: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46), and thus overthrow [Col. 0297C] and destroy our adversary.

Therefore, as we have said, they were held under the power of this demonic king until the merciful Lord descended from the bosom of the Father; and, just as David of old was secretly anointed king, so he himself deigned to be born exceedingly secretly and in concealment.

407 For the rulers of this world were unaware of his glorious birth, since they did not yet understand or recognize by what path, in what order, and by what power he intended to destroy the devil’s kingdom. Yet, having been born, he remained and lived within the devil’s kingdom. Why do I say that he was in the devil’s kingdom? I do not mean that he was in the devil’s kingdom in such a way as ever to have sinned by will or deed [Col. 0297D]; rather, I say that he was in the devil’s kingdom because he dwelt with us in the world—which was wholly the devil’s kingdom—and lived and moved among us sinners, free from every sin.

Under that king, during the days of his flesh, he suffered many adversities and persecutions. For Herod began persecuting him as soon as he was born; while still a tender little child, he fled into Egypt from Herod’s hands. Throughout all the days of his life, under Saul—that is, the devil—and his members, he suffered with us pain and temptation, yet without sin. For the opposition to his teaching, the mockery and ridicule of his miracles, the spitting, blows, scourges, and finally death itself, which he endured through the devil’s instigation of his members—all this was his being in the devil’s kingdom. He was also in the devil’s kingdom in this respect [Col. 0298A]: while he was seen and lived in this world for thirty years and more, none of his elect could, after laying aside the burden of the flesh, enter the kingdom of heaven. Thus John, his elect and beloved forerunner—of whom he himself testified, while John was still alive, that among those born of women none greater had arisen—descended to the underworld.

When Saul therefore persecuted holy David, David fled where he thought himself safe and came to Achish, who gave him the city of Ziklag to inhabit, as the Book of Kings testifies. Achish said to David: “I know that you are good in my sight, like an angel of God. Therefore rise early, you and your servants who came with you; when you have risen in the night and day begins to dawn, depart.” David therefore rose by night [Col. 0298B], he and his men, to set out in the morning and return to the land of the Philistines.

If all that was then being done was a figure of things to come, we find that our David—that is, Christ—fled to Achish in all his persecutions. Achish is interpreted “my brother, a man.” 408 In this brother, who is called “a man” with this addition, the mighty divinity of God the Father may be understood. He is appropriately called both brother and man. For divinity and humanity have, so to speak, a great kinship with one another: he who is true God is true man, and he who is true man is also true and perfect God. David therefore fled to Achish because the Son fled to God the Father, who always protected and aided him in everything through the power of his divine strength [Col. 0298C].

And he could truly say to his Son: “I know that you are good in my sight.” That Son of the Most High was good in the sight of God the Father, because from the day when he was born until the day when he was taken up, he never committed anything by will or deed that could offend the eyes of God the Father.

To him God the Father says: “Rise early, you and your servants.” God the Father commanded his Son—who appeared humble, was despised, and was scourged—to rise in the morning after overcoming all corruption; just as David long before, speaking in the person of God the Father raising the Son, says: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56:9). And the Son says: “I will arise at daybreak” (ibid.), that is, “I shall be impassible and immortal” [Col. 0298D]. This glory of the resurrection is immediately set forth when the following is added:

“And when David and his men came to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made an attack from the south; they had carried off captive the women from it, from the least to the greatest, and had killed no one, but had taken them with them and gone on their way.”

Do not these words point to the true and manifest resurrection of the Lord and of the other saints who rose with him? For just as David came with his men to Ziklag on the third day, so our true David, Christ, rising from the dead on the third day, came with his men—namely, his elect whom he had raised—and appeared in the holy city, Jerusalem. For by Ziklag, which is interpreted “cleansing,” Judaea or Jerusalem [Col. 0299A] may be understood, which Christ had cleansed—that is, purified—by his passion and death, washing it from the dregs of sins by his blood.

But when David came to Ziklag, the Amalekites had attacked from the south. Amalekites, interpreted “a people that licks,” 409 are evil spirits, consuming everything and reducing to nothing whatever they can. They attacked from the south when, after the Lord had suffered and died, they brought the apostles and Christ’s other faithful and elect into the mistrust of unbelief and doubt. And they carried off captive the women from it: that is, they made souls weak in faith which ought to have been strong in faith. And this was from least to greatest. Among the least, so to speak, were Mary Magdalene and those like her; among the great were the great apostles. [Col. 0299B] Great, I say, was Peter, and great were his other fellow-disciples; all of these the Amalekites carried off as though captive when, at the prompting of evil spirits, they doubted in faith.

Did Peter not endure a sufficiently harsh captivity when he denied the Lord three times? Was Thomas not carried captive by this people of Amalekites when, as his fellow-disciples told him that they had seen the Lord, he replied: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (John 20:25)? On the very day of the Lord’s resurrection, were not two of his disciples, going to the village of Emmaus and held in great captivity of heart, sorrowfully speaking to one another of what had happened to their Lord and Master, when they said: “We had hoped that he [Col. 0299C] was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21)?

Thus they had captured the women—that is, the weak souls among Christ’s elect—but had not killed them. For though they still doubted the resurrection of Christ, the ardour and affection of their inward love, with which they burned toward their Lord and Master, had not been extinguished. For that Mary Magdalene, who had bought spices for the very purpose of anointing his body, though she did not yet perfectly believe in him, nevertheless burned with an immense longing and ardour of love for him. Therefore the Amalekites—that is, evil spirits—although they did not kill all these persons, as we have said, nevertheless took them with them in unbelief. “And they went on their way.” They wished to lead them with them to the gates of hell, whither the whole human race [Col. 0299D] had descended, and to proceed by their accustomed road to the underworld. But lest his devout disciples should travel that road, our true David intervened, as follows:

“When David and his men came to the city and found it burned with fire, and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive, David and the people who were with him raised their voices and wept until their tears failed them.”

David, coming to his city—that is, Christ, rising from the dead with his elect—found his city set on fire by the Amalekite people: that is, he found that his people, dearly beloved to him, had been led by the hatred and prompting of evil spirits into doubting in faith. “And David and the people who were with him raised their voices and wept until [Col. 0300A] their tears failed them.” This lamentation in which David and his people weep signifies the grief and sorrow which the true David stirred up in the heart of each of his elect who bitterly repented. Because they had yielded somewhat through fear of death, he made them weep and mourn bitterly.

Thus the Gospel relates how Peter wept: after his threefold denial, he went out and wept bitterly. And what he did, there is no doubt that the others did as well. They wept until their tears failed them, because when their tears had washed away what they had sinned, then indeed their tears failed them.

Moreover, David’s two wives were taken captive, and David was greatly distressed. All these things belong to the glorious and mighty David, that is, Christ. He had taken [Col. 0300B] two wives, because he had joined to himself in faith and love two brides: the Church of the Jews and that of the Gentiles. The Amalekites, enemies of the human race, as we have said, seized them and carried them captive when they brought both peoples by one and the same road, under great domination, to the underworld.

When David’s wives had thus been taken away, did he bear it with equanimity? Not at all; he was greatly distressed. So also our David—God above us and man for our sake—was greatly distressed for his wives, sons, and daughters: first, because the devil had possessed the entire human race and held it liable to punishment by the written bond of sins; and also because his elect sons and disciples could not believe that the Son, glorified and raised by the Father, had risen. Hence the following is added:

[Col. 0300C] 411 “For the people wished to stone him, because the soul of each was bitter over his sons and daughters.” When, I ask, did the people wish to stone our sorrowing and grieving David, except when, remaining hardened in a stony heart, they continued to doubt the glory of the resurrection? Hence, as we read, while they were reclining at table he appeared and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen (Mark 16:14). Thus, when the enemies prevailed, our David, truly strong of hand, prepared himself to battle and overthrow them, as follows:

“But David was strengthened in the Lord his God.” For God the Father was the Son’s strength, because he aided him in everything. David himself—that is, the Son [Col. 0300D] of God—consulted God the Father whether he ought, by dying and descending into hell, to pursue the raiders, namely the evil spirits who had seized his noble creation and carried it down to the gates of hell. And he received from God the Father the command to follow and pursue those same enemies. For he says:

“Pursue them; for without doubt you shall overtake them and recover the spoil.” For our Redeemer, through the mystery of the cross, destroyed every dominion of the devil and won for himself a triumph of glory; he recovered their spoil, and, by driving every hostile power from the hearts of his faithful, brought back his captives. It follows:

[Col. 0301A] “So David went, he and the six hundred men who were with him, and came as far as the brook Besor; but the weary stayed behind. David himself and four hundred men pursued; for two hundred stopped, being too weary to cross the brook Besor.”

Those six hundred who go with David may signify all the saints who lived before the Law. They went with our David because, according to their measure, they strove to follow what was pleasing in his eyes. The four hundred men express the rank of the most perfect; for the number forty customarily holds a type of great perfection in Sacred Scripture. Four tens make forty. Who then are the most perfect, if not the apostles, martyrs, and those like them? Instructed by the perfection contained in the ten [Col. 0301B] commandments and the Gospel teaching contained in four books, 412 they were ready, strong, and fit to imitate the footsteps of the Lord God. All these, cleaving more familiarly as it were to David’s side, went out with him to battle and pursued and crushed invisible enemies.

By the number of the two hundred who stop exhausted, we may be understood: we who are so weak and so wretched that we cannot cross the brook Besor. Besor is said to mean “drive onward.” Understand evil desires by the brook Besor. Driven by this brook—that is, wearied by fleshly desires and vices which assail us daily—we stop. Therefore we are not among the perfect but, alas, among the imperfect. When we strive to go forward and pass farther on, we become dull and weak, and shamefully remain behind, unable to endure [Col. 0301C] labours and sufferings for the Lord.

Why are we designated by this double number, except because we hold the hope of the present life and of the life to come? And what hope of the present life and future life do I mean? In the present life we are encouraged by a good and holy hope: if we repent of past evils, we do not doubt that we shall receive forgiveness of sins from him who does not abandon those who hope in him. And from the expectation of future goods, we joyfully and confidently hope in God’s mercy that we shall someday be gathered into the number of the elect. Therefore, because we are wretched, imperfect, and without merit, because we stop as though weary when driven by vices and pleasures of the flesh and cannot go out to battle with our David, something remains in what follows that greatly consoles [Col. 0301D] us. It follows:

“And they found an Egyptian man in the field, brought him to David, and gave him bread to eat and water to drink, as well as a piece of a cake of figs and two bunches of raisins.”

This Egyptian man is that famous thief crucified with the Lord, who, at the very moment of death, knew and confessed the God of heaven and earth. Anyone finds him in the field of Sacred Scripture. For everywhere that memorable work of divine mercy, by which he was wonderfully saved, is read and proclaimed; everywhere it is announced for the consolation of the guilty and sinners. Although all the Lord’s works are wonderful, glorious, and worthy of praise, nevertheless 413 his mercies are above [Col. 0302A] all his works: by the grace of mercy with which he received the thief who repented late, he left, in the thief whom he mercifully received, an evident example of his clemency for all sinners.

Since we have found him, let us bring him with us to our David. What is it to bring him to David except to set before the embraces of our gracious Creator and Deliverer that same thief, and the wondrous manner in which he saved him; and to entreat him daily to deign to renew in us, whom the consciousness of our own guilt accuses, his ancient miracle? Hence comes the customary cry and prayer of penitents, who very frequently beseech God thus: “Lord, who hung innocent upon the cross for me, remember me, who am like the thief. I, unclean and defiled, with unclean lips, fear to name Mary, your mother, the Virgin of chastity and Virgin of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0302B]. For the present I pass over Peter, your key-bearer; Paul, your familiar instrument; and your other saints, as though declining to seek their assistance. I will remember only your mercy, by which you looked upon, received, and saved the thief hanging with you on the cross; and I humbly entreat you to accomplish the same works of your mercy in me, wretched and sinful as I am.”

In this manner, then, the Egyptian man is brought to David; and after this, the good things bestowed on him are enumerated.

“They gave him bread, and he ate; and he drank water, as well as pieces of a cake of figs and two bunches of raisins.” His eating bread and drinking water indicates his true and complete faith [Col. 0302C]. With the bodily eyes of the flesh he saw nothing but a crucified man; yet he believed that this same man was the bread of angels and men, by whom both the heavenly and the earthly are refreshed and satisfied. He also drank water when, after the Lord had delivered up his spirit into the Father’s hands, he, still living, saw that one of the soldiers pierced his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came forth. By that water and blood he did not doubt that he would receive forgiveness of all his sins.

He also ate a piece of a cake of figs. By the piece of a cake of figs may be understood those multitudes of sweetest souls who were awaiting the coming of the Lord their God in the underworld. That cake of figs is called a piece of a cake because, in descending to hell, the Lord did not take all from there, but only a piece—that is, that portion of his elect. But the other piece, namely the portion of the reprobate, he left there when he ascended in victory [Col. 0302D]. This man believed in Christ’s descent into hell and, enlightened from above, knew that it was written: “O death, I will be your death; I will be your sting, O hell” (Hos. 13:14). Animated by this faith, he ate, so to speak, the piece of the cake of figs.

He also ate two bunches of raisins. The two bunches of raisins express the two natures in Christ, namely the divine and the human. One was the nature of humanity, by which he was bound to endure the passion; the other, that of divinity, by which he was bound to the glory of the resurrection [Col. 0303A]. He ate these two bunches of raisins because he perfectly believed that Christ had two natures, divine and human.

“And when he had eaten, his spirit returned and he was refreshed.” For truly, animated by this faith, his spirit returned and was refreshed and strengthened in the Lord.

“For he had eaten no bread nor drunk water for three days and three nights.” For three days he had not eaten bread or drunk water, because he had never known or received faith in the Holy Trinity, which may be understood through the three days. He also remained fasting for three nights because he had spent the whole course of his life in the night of sins, and had grievously sinned before the Lord in three ways: in thought, speech, [Col. 0303B] and deed.

David said to him: “Whose are you? Or from where are you? And where are you going?” He replied: “I am an Egyptian boy, the servant of an Amalekite man; my master abandoned me because I began to fall ill three days ago.”

David’s asking and speaking here signifies that inquiry and word of the true David by which he led this thief inwardly to know himself 415, so that he might carefully consider and weigh whose servant he had been from the beginning. And he did so. For, drawing his final breath in inward repentance, he began to confess to the true Anointed One, the true High Priest Jesus Christ, who and what he had been, when he said to the other thief, who was reviling the Lord: “Do you not even fear God? We indeed receive the due reward of our deeds, but this man has done nothing wrong” (Luke [Col. 0303C] 23:40).

“I am,” he says, “an Egyptian boy, the servant of an Amalekite man. My master abandoned me.” This is to confess and say: “I was wicked; I was dark; I was the devil’s servant. But my master, whom I served and to whom I clung persistently, abandoned me and brought me to what I now suffer.”

David therefore said to him: “Can you lead me to this band?” This question by the Lord is in a sense an affirmation. He who seeks the salvation of all people does not deny, but indeed affirms, that through this thief he can and may well be led to this band of evil spirits. For, as we have said, sinners are not encouraged and consoled so greatly by all Christ’s works—by his birth or by his death—as by this deed, by this mercy which he showed the thief [Col. 0303D]: in that hour of death he received one who had never believed and never sought God, and promised him paradise. Through this hope, I say, which sinners derive from it, God is led against the band of evil spirits within sinners; and, stirred more and more to repentance by this hope, they are rescued from the band of evil spirits by the hand of mighty David. Therefore, when David asked whether he could be led to this band, let us hear his answer:

“Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will lead you.” When or how did this man adjure the true David not to kill him and not to deliver him into the hands of his master, [Col. 0304A] the prince of darkness? Certainly when, hanging upon the cross, he turned to Jesus and said: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (ibid., 42).

“And David swore.” What did he swear? “Truly I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise.” He who said this and swore this was true and faithful in all his words. Therefore he immediately fulfilled what he promised. He leads the thief, his sinner, first with himself into hell 416, and then at once leads him with the sweet company of souls into paradise. It follows:

“When he had led him there, behold, they were lying spread over the whole land, eating and drinking, and celebrating as though a festival day because of all the spoil and plunder which they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land [Col. 0304B] of Judah.”

Who were they who lay spread over the whole land, if not the evil spirits, who had violently oppressed and plundered the entire human race—eating the stronger, drinking the weaker—and for this reason celebrating as though a festival day?

“And David struck them from evening until the evening of the next day, and none of them escaped except four hundred young men, who mounted camels and fled.” After the Lord’s most victorious passion was completed on Friday at about the ninth hour, when the day was already declining toward evening, from that evening until the evening of the next day he struck down all his enemies: he overthrew the devil’s power, crushed the boldness of unclean spirits, broke the gates of hell. And none of them escaped [Col. 0304C] except four hundred young men: namely, all those elect and perfect persons who had mounted camels, that is, who had already taken up their bodies again and risen, as the Gospel relates: “Many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep arose, came into the city, and appeared to many” (Matt. 27:52). It follows:

“Therefore David rescued everything that the Amalekites had taken; he rescued his two wives; and no one was missing, from small to great, whether sons or daughters, nor any of the spoil. Whatever they had seized, David brought back and drove before him.”

Our true David rescued everything taken by the Amalekites, namely evil spirits. For he redeemed from hell not only those who had received the Law, circumcision, and baptism, but also brought back with himself those who had been holy and righteous before the Law: blessed Job and those like him, who were from the Gentile people and exceedingly pleasing to God in their life; Moses, Abraham, David, and all his other chief elect [Col. 0304D]. He also rescued his two wives, because he gathered the two peoples—the Jews and the Gentiles—whom he had lost, and made them new brides of God’s Only-Begotten Son. One of them was called Ahinoam the Jezreelite and the other Abigail.

These names suit the wives of the true David. Ahinoam is interpreted “the beauty of my brother”; Jezreelite, “seed of God”; and Abigail, “the Father’s rejoicing.” The Church is appropriately signified by Ahinoam, who is called the beauty of the brother. For the Church is the brother’s beauty: the beauty, I say, that is, the honour and kingdom, of Christ the Son of God [Col. 0305A]. She is also a Jezreelite—that is, the seed of God—when she strives to keep the seed of the Word of God in heart and deed, with faithful sincerity and unflagging diligence, so as to bring forth the fruit of good works. She is also Abigail, the Father’s rejoicing, because when the Synagogue deserves to be joined to the true David by believing in him, then there will in some sense be days of joy and exultation for God the Father.

Therefore he who is truly strong and truly desirable rescued everything from the hands of his enemies; he also took away his sons and daughters, whom that strong armed one was lawfully holding in hell by the victor’s right, when this stronger one came upon him. And he drove before him whatever the Amalekites had taken.

“And they said: ‘This is David’s spoil.’” Was this not the voice and praise of the beloved sons and daughters of our David, namely those souls which immediately followed their Father, the King of eternal glory, from hell with great joy of heart? “This,” they say, [Col. 0305B] “is David’s spoil.” As though they said: “To you alone, great David, must this victory and such a triumph be ascribed, because you despoiled hell and, by delivering us from hell, freed us from death’s hand by your death.”

The great and mighty David had already conquered his enemies, overcome death, and redeemed his perfect and elect saints. Let us now see what he does daily; let us now hear our consolation. It follows:

“David came to the two hundred men who had stopped exhausted and could not follow David, and whom he had ordered to remain by the brook Besor.”

Those two hundred who, as I said above, stop after failing are we imperfect and sluggish people: we who are not equal to enduring the labours of persecutions for the Lord, who cannot imitate the great works of outstanding saints. And I say that we cannot because, by David’s command, we sit beside the brook Besor. For the brook Besor—that is, evil desires and evil wills, which daily drive us onward—does not allow us to go out to battle with our David [Col. 0305C]. Yet he does not disdain to come to us through his manifold grace, if we prepare ourselves not sluggishly to imitate what follows.

“They,” it says, “went out to meet David and the people who were with him.” For we then go out to meet the true David and his people [Col. 0305D] when we rejoice at the magnificent and glorious manner of life of the saints and at the reward already appointed for them by the Lord, and when we praise and venerate him by whose gift and grace they conquered themselves and the world. There will also be a reward for our work if, by loving it in others, we make our own what we have less of in ourselves.

“But when he came up to the people, he greeted them peacefully.” Our Lord Jesus Christ came up to his people when, rising from the dead, he appeared to his apostles in whatever manner, at whatever time, and as often as he wished. He greeted them peacefully when, standing in their midst, he offered them the gifts and joys of his peace, not once but again and again, saying: “Peace be with you.”

Then one wicked and most evil man among the men [Col. 0306A] who were with David answered and said: “We shall give them nothing from the spoil which we recovered, because they did not come with us into battle.” By this wicked and most evil man, heretics may be understood, who strove to divide and injure God’s Church through their countless heresies and schisms. One of these, Novatian, with his followers falsely maintained that, after the first innocence of baptism had been lost, forgiveness was thereafter to be granted by God to no one, even if that person repented. David rightly appears to oppose this false and God-hating assertion, as the following makes clear.

But David said: “You shall not do so, my brothers, with what the Lord has given us, preserved us through, and delivered to us: the raiders who broke out against us. No one shall listen to you in this matter.” Our Lord Jesus Christ indeed wills rather to save all people than to destroy them; 419 he wills that through the true satisfaction of repentance we may obtain the full reward of eternal life. Nor does he will anyone to heed heretics in this matter, because just as he has a merciful will to forgive, so he does not lack the power to pardon; he does not deny forgiveness after repentance, he who calls and stirs humanity to seek the grace of his mercy.

“For the share of the one going down into battle shall be equal to that of the one remaining with the baggage, and they shall divide alike.” In the army of the great David, some go down into battle, while others remain with the baggage. Those went down to battle with their leader, Christ, [Col. 0306C] who long ago, following the example of the Son of God himself, offered their bodies to executioners to be killed for Christ; we marvel at and venerate their constancy of faith. But we who remain with the baggage are the least, the sinners, still groaning under the weight of the body of death. Yet, insofar as he grants it, we submit to him in faith and hope, that we may share in whatever reward he gives.

For although the merits of different persons differ, the share will be equal, because the glory of all in heaven will be the same, though it is apportioned to each according to merit. For although there are many and diverse dwelling-places in the Father’s house, all shall be rewarded with the price of one denarius, when he alone will be the reward of all, who alone suffices for all. Lest anyone should doubt this [Col. 0306D], he removes every scruple when the following is added:

“And this was established from that day onward, fixed and appointed as a law in Israel to this day.” For there is nothing that can overthrow this law, nothing that can impede forgiveness of sins, if a person does not neglect the time of repentance now granted him by God; there is nothing that can turn aside the good and merciful will of the Lord who divides equally and rewards his elect worthily. It follows:
