“David came to Ziklag and sent gifts from the spoil to the elders of Judah, his neighbours, saying: ‘Receive a blessing from the spoil of the enemies of the Lord’: to those who were in Bethel, and in Ramoth to the south, and in Gether, and in Aroer, and in Sephamoth, and [Col. 0307A] in Esthamo, and in Rachal, and in the cities of Jerameel, and in the cities of Ceni, and in Rama, and at the lake of Asan, and in Atach, and in Hebron, and to the rest who were in those places in which this David and his men had stayed.”

Our David, Christ the Lord, truly mighty of hand, after despoiling hell sent his gifts to the most noble elders when he conveyed himself—so to speak, coequal and consubstantial with God the Father and God the Holy Spirit—to the palace of heaven. He also commanded his neighbours, namely the angelic ranks, who are near and neighbouring because of their continual vision of him, to receive a blessing from the spoil of the enemies of the Lord. This occurred when he distributed and enrolled that chosen multitude of souls among the nine orders of heavenly spirits, which may be understood by the previously listed place-names [Col. 0307B]: so that one portion might join the choirs of angels and archangels; others might be admitted among the orders of virtues, principalities, and powers; others might rejoice in the companionship and fellowship of dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim; while others, as we said, might chiefly enjoy the perpetual vision of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

These precious gifts, these blessings, our King and Lord David gave as a gift to God the Father. And appropriately, after such an illustrious palm of victory, Saul’s death is described.

“It came to pass,” it says, “after Saul’s death, that David returned from the slaughter of Amalek and remained in Ziklag two days. But on the third day a man came from Saul’s camp, with his garment torn and dust sprinkled on his head.”

The two days may signify the time before the Law and under the Law. But the third day expresses the time of grace, in which the Maker of heaven and earth accomplished a great and memorable deed: when he suffered and died, rose on the third day, and thereby willed Saul’s death—that is, the devil’s death—to be proclaimed; which is indeed to proclaim God’s kingdom. The man coming from Saul’s camp 421, with torn garment and dust sprinkled on his head, signifies those soldiers appointed to guard the Lord’s tomb. Their garment, so to speak, was whole when they proclaimed that Christ had risen; but their garment was torn and their heads sprinkled with dust when, overcome by the dust of avarice and corrupted by money, they departed from the truth which [Col. 0307D] they had previously professed.

That man is subsequently killed at David’s command, as is explained in what follows:

“David,” it says, “called one of his servants and said: ‘Come near; fall upon him.’ He struck him, and he died.” This servant whom David calls is the apostolic order, sent throughout the world to preach. Coming upon that people which did not yet believe in Christ, it fell upon and struck them dead when, by the sword of God’s word, it happily caused to die within them whatever residue of unbelief and doubt remained in their hearts.

Therefore, after the resurrection of that most victorious king had been preached throughout the whole world, it is fittingly added as a type of this matter—on account of which we all rejoice—that [Col. 0308A] the men of Judah came and anointed David at Hebron to reign over the house of Judah. David reigned over Judah seven years. After this all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron, anointed him 422 king over Israel, and he reigned in Jerusalem over all the people of Israel and Judah.

These words commend the state of the present and future Church, in which our King and Lord Jesus Christ—who has received from the Father all power in heaven and on earth—rules. Our David is now anointed king by the men of Judah, that is, by those alone who believe in God and truly confess God. He reigns seven years in Hebron, which is interpreted “marriage,” because throughout the whole time of this life, which runs its course in the sevenfold number of days, our heavenly King and Lord celebrates a spiritual marriage and nuptials with his bride, the holy Church [Col. 0308B].

But after the completion of the number six—that is, when the age is ended and completed—he shall reign over all Israel and Judah in Jerusalem. Then, with all his elect gathered to himself, he, King and Lord of all, shall reign in all things and over all, and shall eternally satisfy them by his perpetual vision of himself. May our Lord Jesus Christ bring us to that satisfaction, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

423 HOMILY XLVI. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY IN WHITE.

“When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors [Col. 0308C] were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst and said to them: ‘Peace be with you’” (John 20).

The sacrament of the Lord’s Resurrection, which we recall once accomplished in the yearly solemnity because of our hope for the general resurrection that we await in the future, signifies for us that resurrection by which the almighty Lord, in his wondrous mercy, deigns daily to raise his elect from death to life, from sins and vices to a good and praiseworthy way of life. We are instructed and taught by the words of this Gospel reading in what order he works this resurrection within us. For the Evangelist says:

[Col. 0308D] “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered for fear of the Jews.”

Evening comes in a person when, through God’s prevenient grace, he is brought gradually to be able to arrive at knowledge of himself and to consider with the eye of his heart his useless and fruitless life. When he has carefully considered it, the pleasure and prosperity of the world begin to become bitter and dark to him. Hence it is said in Genesis: “And there was evening and there was morning, one day” (Gen. 1:5). In evening may be understood knowledge of oneself; in morning, knowledge of God. For when a person begins to attend to and consider with what great and inestimable mercy the Lord has borne with him in his sins and has not abandoned him while sinning, he begins to be displeased with himself in his iniquities and, for God’s sake, to scorn and despise the pleasures of the world which he formerly loved. For there are some whom God loves and embraces with such mercy and kindness that he patiently and long-sufferingly waits for them, until their desires and pleasures have passed and been fulfilled, to turn to him of their own accord.

424 After this evening follows the morning of which it is also said here, “on that day,” because the person comes from knowledge of himself to knowledge of God; on that day, in that illumination and knowledge, he begins to love God and to love him purely. The first day of the week appropriately follows that day—that illumination. By “the first day of the week” good works or virtues may be understood. For it does not say, “one Sabbath,” but “one of the Sabbaths,” because from that illumination not one virtue alone is acquired, but [Col. 0309B] virtues are heaped upon virtues; many good and holy works are added to and support one good work. After the first day of the week there fittingly follows:

“And the doors were shut for fear of the Jews.” For when evening has come in a person, when he has trampled underfoot the pleasure of the world by the mind’s contempt for it, when in the heart’s illumination he has knowledge of God and of himself, and when he has advanced from virtue to virtue through good works, then, with God’s help, he closes his doors for fear of the Jews. By the Jews we may understand evil spirits, who assail and attack us by their perverse and malicious suggestions. Therefore, for fear of the Jews—that is, of evil spirits—the doors of both the inner and outer person must be shut: the inner doors, lest evil desires and perverse wills find the heart’s entrance open; the outer doors, lest, at the prompting of evil spirits, they fall into carnal and wicked deeds.

“Where,” he says, “the disciples were gathered.” Where doors are shut in this manner, as we have said, there the disciples—that is, good and useful faculties—are gathered by God’s grace. Jesus comes into their midst, and, 425 standing in the midst, says to them: “Peace be with you.” Jesus’ coming is the visitation of his consolation. Jesus comes to some persons, yet does not stand in their midst: for a time he admonishes and rouses them to knowledge of their sins, but when the time of his visitation and their recognition has passed, they return to their sins as though they had never known or mourned them. But to those whom he foreknew as his own in his eternal [Col. 0309D] predestination, and whom he has advanced and glorified in their lives in the order already stated, he comes by his ordering and dispensation, and establishes in them a stable state of salvation. He stands in their midst when, resting in the inmost part of their hearts, he brings about in them a stable state of salvation; and he says to them, “Peace be with you.” Jesus’ speaking is his acting, when he gives peace from the world, so that a person is moved neither by this world’s prosperity nor by its adversities: that is, he scorns and despises human praises, while he does not fear adversities, mockeries, and reproaches for God’s sake. It follows:

“And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side.” To those to whom the Lord has said this, to whom he has bestowed this peace through his grace, he also shows his hands and side. By the hands, activity may be signified; by the side, the holy way of life which a person ought to attain and in which he ought to work. The Lord shows him his hands when he displays the good works in which he ought to exercise himself in the spiritual arena. He shows him his side—that is, the holy way of life in which he may be hidden from the tumult and noise of the world, and in which he should strive and serve as a soldier for God’s love. When, therefore, he has come to a holy way of life and has exercised himself in good works, the following is rightly added:

“Therefore the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.” Those who have experienced it know what joy, and how great a joy, those possess who have seen the Lord in their inward faculties. For they see the Lord [Col. 0310B] in themselves; they see the Lord in good prelates; they see the Lord in the holy conduct of the faithful dwelling with them; they also see the Lord in Holy Scripture. Seeing the Lord in all these things, they exult and dance with great joy. It follows:

426 “He said to them again: Peace be with you.” After seeing the Lord, a second peace is bestowed: peace from vices, peace from one’s own flesh, so that a person refreshed by the dew of the Holy Spirit may no longer fall into unlawful sins.

“As the Father has sent me, so I send you.” The Lord Jesus Christ, sent to us into this world by God the Father, suffered for us every tribulation and anguish, temptation and passion which a human being can suffer and endure in this life, except sins alone. For whatever a human being ought to have suffered for himself, Christ took so fully upon himself that he was tempted in every respect in human likeness, yet without sin. In this manner we too are sent by the Lord: that in the present life we may be worn down by tribulations, distresses, and diverse temptations, until, having passed through and overcome the labours and miseries of this life, we come to his kingdom. Although, following the Lord’s example, we cannot be without fault in our temptations, so as to be without sin as he was without sin in this world, nevertheless in his mercy he so works with us that we do not yield to the devil’s snares and deceits in our temptations, nor are altogether overwhelmed by them. It follows:

“When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: Receive [Col. 0310D] the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.” After the dangers of temptations and tribulations follows the grace of inward consolation and sweetness, which through his Holy Spirit he breathes and inspires into his elect, saying to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.” When the grace of divine visitation and sweetness overflows, such great benefits are granted by the Lord to the elect that the sins and offences which, in the time of pure prayer, they perfectly recognize in the bitterness of their hearts, mourn, and repent of, are forgiven them by divine mercy. They themselves first forgive them—that is, they bring it about that they are forgiven to themselves—when, with inward sorrow and contrition of heart, they offer themselves in tears as a sacrifice to the Lord for those sins. They are also forgiven them by the Lord when, after labour and true repentance, they obtain pardon.

427 “And whose sins you retain are retained.” But concerning the sins which they retain—that is, from which they have been unable to be perfectly released and cleansed—the Lord supplies them with such power and strength that they restrain and hold them within themselves in such a manner that the sins do not prevail over them. Rather, they are held beneath them, that is, beneath their power, so that they do not thereafter fall into open and unlawful wickedness. It follows:

“Now Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.” Thomas is interpreted “abyss”; by this name is signified the perfect person, strengthened in God, who has advanced in his life in the order already described. Of this abyss we rightly sing in the Psalm: “Deep calls to deep.” Deep calls to deep when the perfect person sets before the eyes of his mind the abyss of God’s mercy and judgment. He calls upon the abyss of mercy when, in subtle reflection, he considers how many people, entangled in grave sins, almighty God has turned, near the end of their lives, through his mercy from iniquity to righteousness and from love of the world to love of himself. He also calls upon the abyss of judgment when he weighs with an anxious mind that some appear adorned with innocence of life, yet are rejected at their end through the dispensation of a hidden judgment. When the perfect [Col. 0311C] person occupies himself day and night with this consideration, always returning to himself as he considers the end of others, he fears the abyss of divine judgments; in fearing he is humbled; and he no longer seeks outward glory from his works, but places his hope in the protection of heavenly help.

He indeed who lives in this way is called one of the twelve, as if one were saying, one of the perfect. In Holy Scripture, moreover, when “one” is used, the virtue of a single-minded disposition is frequently designated by it. Thus at the beginning of the Book of Kings we read: “There was one man.” One cannot be divided into many; therefore he is not inappropriately called one whose intention of mind is not diverted in different directions, who remains the same in adversity and prosperity, who is not lifted up in prosperity nor cast down in [Col. 0311D] adversity. He is not one whom pride now puffs up, anger disturbs, vain glory now delights, and hatred and envy now tear against his neighbour. Indeed, he may be called double—rather, triple, manifold—because he is divided in every direction while refusing not to submit to each and every vice. Therefore he who is Thomas, that is, “abyss,” through consideration of hidden judgments, and one through single-minded intention, is rightly described as being of the twelve because of his perfection of life. Hence the twelve apostles were chosen, so that the perfection of that very number might signify that they were endowed with the highest perfection above all mortals. This number has something in common with the number seven, which contains within itself the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. For the number seven consists of three and four; when these same parts are multiplied, they produce twelve. By this number the fullness of heavenly gifts and the true perfection of life can fittingly be expressed. It follows:

“Who is called Didymus.” The expression “is called” is in the present tense. Present time is rightly used with Didymus, because as long as one lives in this mortal flesh, the human mind is confused by a certain uncertainty: now it sighs for love of the Creator, now love of the world delays it as it sighs; now it begins steadfastly and fearlessly to do good deeds, now it fears that it may not be able to complete what it has begun well, saying within itself: “Undertake these and those works of virtue, and, labouring for God, persevere strongly in good works.” Yet, again overcome by the weakness of the flesh, it reflects: “Do not,” it says, “deceive yourself by beginning what you cannot finish.” The person’s outer faculties are also most harmful assistants to this same uncertainty, and very frequently hinder the inner faculties from divine knowledge. Hence it is rightly said: “Who was not with them,” that is, with the outer faculties, when Jesus came.

“Therefore the other disciples, rejoicing with him, said to him.” By the disciples we may understand the person’s inner faculties, 429 which the blessed person strives to make “other,” when they are impeded by obstacles of unstable thoughts, so that, gathered within himself and devoted to sacred meditations, they may be renewed unto heavenly desire. [Col. 0312C] At last, having tasted in advance the sweetness of the heavenly visitation, let us hear what the person’s faculties say: “We have seen the Lord.” These words are spoken by the invisible tongue of compunction and inward rejoicing, with which the person’s faculties are then filled when they deserve to taste the sweetness of inward joy. But because the sweetness of divine love, once tasted, does not suffice for one who tends toward perfection, the following is rightly added:

“Thomas answered: Unless I see in his hands the mark [Vulgate: fastening] of the nails.” By the nails may be understood the Lord’s commandments, as Solomon testifies when he says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven in deeply” (Eccl. 12:11). If, therefore, the words of the wise are compared to nails because they pierce and prick the hearts of hearers, how much more the words of him who is Wisdom itself? The mark of the nails, moreover, is the very understanding of the commandments. The Lord’s hands, in which these marks of the nails are seen, are divine operations. Therefore every blessed person desires to see in Christ’s hands the mark of the nails: to have a right understanding of the commandments and, understanding it profitably, to be able to imitate it after the example of our Saviour, of whom it is written: “Because [manuscript: ‘which’] Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

“And,” he says, “I shall put my hand into his side.” By Christ’s side we may understand the Church, which was joined to him on the cross when blood and water flowed [Col. 0313A] from his side. It does not suffice, therefore, for the perfect person to understand and perform the Lord’s commands unless he also puts his hand into the Lord’s side; that is, unless he is able to benefit other persons established in the Church by his works and example.

“And I shall put my finger into the place of the nails.” By the finger that is to be put into the place of the nails is signified the discernment of mind and reason. It ought so to distinguish and examine understanding and works that it makes a person’s heart the place of the nails—that is, of the Lord’s commandments—so prudently discerning all things that the person seeks glory neither from understanding, nor from good works, nor from the edification of neighbours, but attributes it not to vanity and pride but to him alone from whom it comes. Therefore let every blessed person tending toward true perfection say: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails”—that is, unless I have advanced so far that I understand God’s commandments and become an imitator of Christ in his works—“and put my hand into his side”—that is, unless I too strive to benefit others in God’s Church through the example of good works—and then attain this mean: “to put my finger into the place of the nails,” which is my heart, so that I distinguish between God’s works and my own works in such a way as to ascribe nothing to myself from understanding, from the result of work, or from others’ progress through my example, but attribute everything to him from whom all comes—unless, I say, I have experienced all these things in myself, I shall not believe; that is, I shall never be steadfast, never be able to render true faith to God my Creator. Since this perfection and power of blessedness can scarcely or never be acquired in this life, but is reserved for the life to come, where it is owed fully and perfectly to God’s elect, the following is rightly added:

“And after eight days the disciples were again within, and Thomas with them.” The whole span of the present life runs through six days. The seventh day signifies the rest of souls, in which God’s elect, having laid aside the burden of flesh, rejoice with Christ in the glory of eternal peace and security. But the eighth day signifies the general resurrection, in which the souls of the saints, having resumed their bodies, are rewarded with full and perfect blessedness. After eight days—after the day, that is, of resurrection—the disciples are truly within, when the inner and outer [Col. 0313D] faculties of the person, now truly established under God’s discipline and wholly freed from all these external matters by which they are now occupied, are so united to God and fixed and established in love of God alone that they are never separated from him even by the slightest movement of thought. Thomas too is there with them—that is, consideration of God’s hidden judgments—because there they will truly and perfectly begin to know the judgments of God which in this life they could never comprehend and whose depth they could never attain to behold amid the misery of this mortality. There will be perfectly fulfilled what follows:

The Evangelist says: “Jesus came, though the doors were shut, and stood in the midst, and said: Peace be with you.” The doors, which are the person’s inner and outer faculties, can never be perfectly shut in this life. Now they are shut, now opened. They are shut when, in order to seek God’s grace, persons sometimes gather themselves inwardly to themselves; they are opened again when, because of the oppressive burden of flesh, they relapse into external things. But when the eighth day has passed—that is, at the general resurrection—when they are so shut that they never relapse into the corruption of any changeability, Jesus truly comes and stands in the midst, because he so confirms the stable state of everlasting salvation in his elect that nothing can thereafter happen to them, in soul or body, that could disturb their blessedness. There he truly offers them the third peace: peace from the devil, which they could never have in this life as long as they lived, because no treachery or malice of his will thereafter be able [Col. 0314B] to harm or trouble them. After he has given this third peace, he says, as it were under the example of Thomas, to each of his elect made steadfast in eternal blessedness:

“Put your finger here.” By the finger is understood discernment. It is as though he said: “As long as you were clothed in frail flesh and laboured in the painful contest of the mortality now past, you were occupied here and there—for discernment was necessary to you—now with the body, now with the spirit, at one time with governing and arranging external things, at another with meditating upon and discerning inward and spiritual things. But because you are now freed and released from all these things, put your finger here: direct the power, discernment, and reason of your mind to contemplate and discern the greatness of my mercy. [Col. 0314C] Put your finger here, to me, where your spirit, strengthened in eternal blessedness, may rejoice and exult in my everlasting vision, and where your body, glorified by the splendour of eternal immortality, has need of nothing by which it might be sustained.

“And see my hands.” See, I say, and consider the wonderful works of my omnipotence and mercy which I have displayed in you. 432 For if you ever lived worthily in that life, if you ever pleased me by your works, your hands and my hands worked together, for they were your works and mine; yet what has now been accomplished in you is wholly from me. See my hands; see who I am. Consider what I have done in you: that you, from a mortal human being, have become an immortal human being; that from an infirm and frail human being you have been endowed and established in the blessed glory of eternal unchangeability and incorruption—these are my hands. You have nothing in common with me in this; it has been done in you by me without you. See, therefore, my hands; and bring your hand and put it into my side. You will no longer be wearied by any fatigue of labour, but turn all your activity toward the repose of contemplation; transfer your whole self into the joy and brightness of my eternal vision.

“And do not be unbelieving, but faithful.” While you were in the body, you were at times believing and at times unbelieving, because even when you were steadfast in devotion to good action, you often fell away from the inward fidelity which you ought to have had toward me, wandering through instability of mind and the unstable vanity of thoughts. [Col. 0315A] But because I have now advanced you to the brightness of my eternity, every inclination to unbelief and every inclination to instability will be removed from you. Henceforth you will be faithful, because, fixed in my love with all your faculties, you will cleave to me with all the desires and affections of soul and body, and dwell with me eternally. For, to speak boldly, Peter, Paul, and God’s other saints, although they now rejoice with Christ in eternal rest, have not yet perfectly attained this fidelity. For as long as they think of anything outside God, as long as they burn with the desire to recover their bodies, however slight it may be, that very desire partly delays and impedes in them the fullness of God’s love. But when, at the end of the world, having resumed their bodies, they are clothed in blessed immortality in flesh and soul together, there will be nothing by which they may thereafter be delayed from God’s love even by the slightest thought. Then what follows will truly be fulfilled: “Thomas answered and said to him: My Lord and my God.”

433 We may also understand these same words in another way: “Put your finger here, and see my hands, and bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but faithful.” In these three expressions—namely, “here,” “hands,” and “side”—we may understand the whole Holy Trinity together. “Put,” he says, “your finger here.” By the finger is understood discernment. It is as though he said: “While you were still living in the flesh, in the faith by which you laboured toward the glory of eternity that you have now attained, a certain distinction concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit was set before you: namely, that [Col. 0315C] you should believe in the Father, believe in the Son, and believe in the Holy Spirit. But bring this discernment of your faith, which then in some sense was there, here now; bring what was then outside you here now within you. Now know in reality and perfect truth the excellence and majesty of God the Father, which in that life you never knew except insofar as you could apprehend it by faith and hope.

“And see my hands”: know my works; now know in reality the indivisible union of my divinity and humanity which you could never know in that age. See now and consider with what merciful kindness I, coeternal with the Father in the essence of divinity, became for your sake a human being in the womb of my virgin Mother, and became your Redeemer in the humility of the humanity assumed for your sake. “And bring your hand and put it into my side.” By the side in which a person rests, the Holy Spirit, who is the rest of all his saints, may aptly be understood. “Bring,” he says, “your hand and put it into my side”: that is, turn all your activity into the rest of the Holy Spirit. For when you have passed from darkness to light, from image to sight, your activity will thereafter be nothing but everlasting rest and exultation in contemplation of the Father and the Son in the Holy Spirit. “And do not be unbelieving, but faithful.” No inclination to unbelief will thereafter remain in you, because your spirit, soul, and body will rejoice eternally in the vision of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Having heard this voice, Thomas then first truly answers and says: “My Lord [Col. 0316A] and my God.” Here Thomas “called Didymus” is not named, but only Thomas, because every doubt will cease there, where God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit reveal themselves truly and perfectly to their elect as they are.

434 We indeed now say, “My Lord and my God,” but as though in darkness. For we confess and believe our Creator and Redeemer, yet we do not perfectly know him as he is, because the shadow of mortality obstructs and hinders us. But when we see him eye to eye as he is, when we have been perfectly kindled by the inextinguishable flame of his love, so that we can be separated from the brightness of his vision neither by the slightest thought in spirit nor by any contrary action in body, then we shall truly proclaim eternally in body and spirit, in joy and exultation: “My Lord and my God.” For then we shall perfectly know with what omnipotence and magnificence of his divinity he created us, and with what mercy and sweetness of his humanity he delivered us. This vision and perfect knowledge of God is truly eternal life, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). There, in a truly ineffable manner of speaking, he says as though in these words to each of his elect:

“Because you have seen me, you have believed.” As if he said: “Because you have seen me, your Creator and Redeemer, as you have always desired, in the eternity and glory of my magnificence, you have believed; therefore you have deserved to attain this steadfastness, this firm stability of eternal blessedness which you will henceforth possess with me without pain or defect.” And because faith and hope alone lead God’s elect, labouring for God in the misery of this life, to the reward of this blessedness, he immediately makes this plain when he adds:

“Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” As if he said: “Blessed are those who, still placed in darkness and the shadow of death, laboured in hope for my vision and for the joys of eternal blessedness which they had not seen in reality.” For through this they believed; through this, I say, they attained the eternity of that steadfastness which they will now possess eternally with me.

435 After this state of future blessedness, which the Lord promised his elect in the life to come once the resurrection has been completed, [Col. 0316D] the Evangelist fittingly adds:

“Jesus indeed performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples which are not written in this book.” Although these words may, according to the common and simple sense, be understood to mean that the Lord performed many other signs before his disciples during the days of his flesh which are not written in this book of the Gospel, we may also note in the same words something else, still more sublime, which nevertheless does not appear discordant with true faith and sound understanding.

There are two matters around which the entire intention of Holy Scripture revolves: the works of creation and the works of restoration. The works of creation are many: they include the creation of heaven, earth, and sea; the creation of heaven with its ornaments—the sun, moon, and stars; the creation of earth with its ornaments—plants, trees, beasts, living creatures, and especially the rational creature, humanity, for whose sake all things were made; and the creation of the sea with everything created in it. All these things are truly “many” and “other” and “signs.” They are many because they were created in many ways; they are other than the works of restoration because they were not the truth itself but signs of truth: signs of the restoration of humanity which was to come through Christ.

Jesus performed these many other signs—the works of creation—in the sight of his disciples, as signs, because by suffering, dying, rising, ascending, and sending the Holy Spirit [Col. 0317B] from heaven, he opened those same signs, which had been removed from the sight of all people because they lay hidden from all knowledge, and made them manifest to the sight and understanding of his disciples. This is the book written within and without, sealed with seven seals, of which John says in the Apocalypse: “No one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth could open the book or look upon it” (Rev. 5:3). A little later the answer is given to him: “Do not weep. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, to open the book and its seven seals” (ibid., 5). And a little later: “You are worthy, Lord, to take the book and open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us to God by your blood” (ibid., 9).

For through his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit from heaven, [Col. 0317C] not only those perfect disciples themselves but also their imitators began fully and perfectly to recognize that those many preceding works of creation were, as it were, signs of the things accomplished in truth through him: the restoration of humanity. Those many other signs—the works of creation—are not written in this book of the New Testament, but in another book, the book of Moses, the book of the Old Testament. But these works of restoration, which are not many, not other, not signs, but are few, brief, and the truth itself, are written in this book of the Gospel, namely, in the book of the New Testament; and these few things suffice for the salvation of the entire human race. What are they? Surely these: “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that, believing, you may have life in his name.” This is the shortened Word of which the Prophet says: “The Lord will accomplish a shortened word upon the earth” (Rom. 9:28). In this shortened Word we shall be restored and made alive, if we believe that Jesus our Lord and Saviour is true God and true man, and that he who is our Saviour according to his humanity is our Creator according to his divinity.

“And that, believing,” he says, “you may have life in his name.” His name is faith in him. For just as a name is bestowed upon a human being or any thing so that it may be known by its name, so our Lord and Redeemer, since he is known in this world only through faith, has his faith rightly called his name. Truly, then, we shall have life in his name, in faith in him, if, believing him to be our Creator, we fear him as our Creator and Lord; if, believing him to be our deliverer and Saviour, we love him with the love due to our Redeemer; and if, because he is our Creator, we avoid evil through fear of him, and because he is our Saviour, do good through love of him.

437 May our Lord Jesus Christ, without whom nothing is perfect, grant us the perfection of this faith: that, believing and confessing him to be true God and true man, our true Creator and true Redeemer, we may so fear and love him that we may have life in his name. Thus, when after eight days he comes, when, after the resurrection has been completed, [Col. 0318B] he stands in the midst of his disciples—that is, all his elect—and we, with Thomas and the whole multitude of saints, hear from him in eternal glory: “Put your finger here, and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side,” may we rejoice and exult for endless ages of ages in the knowledge of God the Father, the contemplation of the Son himself, and the rest of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

438 HOMILY XLVII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EASTER.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10).

Because, according to the Apostle, the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14), the Word of God the Father became flesh and dwelt among us, so that, dwelling in flesh among human beings, he might awaken them to spiritual understanding through his bodily presence. Those unable to grasp spiritual things might hear bodily things and through them advance to spiritual things. Hence in the words of his teaching he often speaks of things which carnal people could indeed hear but could not understand; while spiritual people, to whom it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, might not merely hear but also understand what they heard for the salvation of their souls. The sacred reading of the present Gospel plainly demonstrates this to us, where the Lord names shepherd, hired hand, wolf, and sheep. These are all names of visible things known to carnal persons; but the outward ear receives one thing in these words, while spiritual understanding yields another fruit. In the shepherd of sheep is designated the good and true prelate of souls; in the hired hand, the false one; in the wolf, the adversary; and the sheep signify subjects. In the shepherd we may also understand every faithful person as the careful guardian of his own soul; in the hired hand, one who works while loving temporal things; in the wolf, the devil who lies in wait for a person; and in the sheep, simplicity of hearts and actions.

Having briefly set these matters before us from the Gospel reading, let us now proceed to elucidate its meaning more fully; and, with the help of him who uttered these holy words of the Gospel and of his Holy Spirit, let us set forth according to our ability what, by God’s grace—who gives all things freely—we have freely received from it for our own benefit or that of others. Thus the Lord says:

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” In calling himself shepherd and good, the Lord awakens hearts benumbed to love him by the novelty and sweetness of this name. For he is truly that shepherd who is good essentially: by his goodness alone he feeds in the flesh all people, good and evil, indeed everything that lives in the world; he feeds his faithful in mind by the word of sacred teaching; and he also daily supplies abundantly in the holy Church the delights of his most holy body and blood for the salvation of souls.

In imitation of this shepherd, whoever in the Church of God wishes to be a good shepherd gives his soul, withdrawn from carnal desires, for the sheep, 439 [Col. 0319B]: he gives it to God, subjects it to God’s service, and does this for the sheep entrusted to him, so that by faithfully serving God and firmly cleaving to him he may obtain through his devotion that God, in his mercy, may guard outwardly and inwardly those committed to him, where he himself is less able to do so. If necessary, moreover, in persecution he gives his soul even to its being shaken out, for the salvation of the souls entrusted to him: he would rather himself endure death for his sheep than leave them in danger and in the death of their souls. We read that many saints did this for their sheep in imitation of Christ; and for this reason we celebrate their memory gloriously and sweetly in the Church.

But the hireling, who is not a shepherd, thinks otherwise [Col. 0319C], and acts very differently from the good shepherd. For a hireling is one who occupies the position of rule more for temporal pay than for the salvation of souls; and therefore he is not a shepherd, because, as the Lord said three times to Peter, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), this man makes no effort either to preside over or to benefit the Lord’s sheep through that threefold feeding: the word of preaching, the example of good works, and the aid of holy prayer.

“The sheep are not his own.” What is a person’s own is loved by him more closely than what belongs to another. Thus the sheep are not called the hireling’s own because he does not love them unto salvation. Therefore he sees the wolf coming and flees. By the wolf he understands either some visible adversary coming from outside to disturb [Col. 0319D] the Lord’s flock or to plunder its goods, or the invisible adversary, the devil, roaring for the destruction of souls. In the battle of the Lord he ought to have stood against these by living well, preaching, and praying; but, seeking his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, he wretchedly abandons them. As blessed Gregory says, he leaves the sheep not by changing his place but by withdrawing his help; and he flees because he hides himself beneath the silence of his own perversity and uselessness.

[Note: [Col. 0319] St Gregory, *Forty Homilies on the Gospels*, book I, homily 14.2, vol. LXXVI of the *Patrologia*.]

“When he has fled, the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep.” The wolf snatches away the outward resources of the Lord’s servants, by which they ought to have ministered to the Lord, 440; and when these resources fail, it often happens that the sheep are scattered which had been gathered to serve the Lord [Col. 0320A].

“But the hireling flees, because he is a hireling, and he has no concern for the sheep.” The hireling flees by keeping silent: he neither dares, with freedom of speech, to oppose the outward adversary, nor can he resist the inward adversary by the word of preaching. And this is because he is a hireling—that is, because in his office of preeminence he loves the world more than God—and “he has no concern for the sheep”; that is, his heart does not draw near so as to be touched by concern for souls, but is occupied instead with concern for the pleasures of his flesh. Yet because the Lord is loving and merciful, and knows all who are his, the Lord does not forget his own even under prelates who live badly. Therefore he adds [Col. 0320B] what follows:

“I am the good shepherd; I know my own, and my own know me.” As though he said: “Although others who bear the name of shepherd do not carry out a shepherd’s office, I nevertheless will not forget what is mine, according to my inborn goodness. For I am a good shepherd not merely by name but essentially; and I know—that is, love—those whom I know will be mine, under whatever prelate they live. And my own know me”—that is, my own love me: those whom I shall know to be heirs of eternal blessedness. In the following words he appears to indicate a manner of love by which either God loves a human being or a human being ought to love God, when he says:

“As the Father knows me, and I know the Father; and [Col. 0320C] I lay down my life for my sheep.” For the Son to know the Father as the Father knows the Son is for the Son to be of the same power, the same wisdom, and the same goodness as the Father. And though the equality of divinity in the Son and the Father is one, the Son does not disdain, in obedience to the Father, to humble himself in humanity and lay down his life for his sheep. This, therefore, is the pattern of love which he set before us: just as he, equal to the Father in the form of God, did not disdain for the love and reverence of the Father to humble himself even to taking the form of a 441 servant, so every person, whatever his power, whatever his wisdom, if he is to be proved truly to love God, must not disdain to lay down his life in any abasement for the love of God [Col. 0320D].

For he laid down his life for us so that we too might lay down our lives for him. First, becoming flesh for us, he laid down his life in the flesh; then, to redeem us, he laid down that same life on the cross; finally, in order to redeem the souls of his own, he laid down his life in hell; and again he laid down that same life in the flesh by rising; and he laid down life and flesh by ascending into heaven. There, with flesh and soul, he stands daily before the countenance of God the Father, interceding for us. Therefore, because he loves his own and his own love him, whoever may be set over his sheep, whether hireling or shepherd, he alone and uniquely will be shepherd [Col. 0321A] of his own sheep in the life to come, whom he will make equal in blessedness to the holy angels. This is what he seems to say:

“And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd.” These other sheep may be understood as the multitudes of holy angels, whom he left in the mountains when he went to seek the one that was lost. They are not of this fold—that is, not of the visible and bodily congregation of holy Church—because they are spirits standing before the Lord in heaven. These, the Lord says, “I must bring; and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold and one shepherd.” For the Lord will bring them at the general resurrection, when he “will summon heaven from above, and the earth, to judge his people” (Ps. 49:4); and when, through the ministry [Col. 0321B] of the holy angels, the separation of the evil from the good has been completed, they will then hear his voice, by which he will say to his elect: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34). Then there will be one fold—that is, one fellowship, one blessedness, one glory, one joy of angels and human beings—and then there will be one shepherd, because then the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, will be shepherd 442 of all whom he will satisfy forever, by his presence and without any lack of misery, in the delight and exultation which he will store up over them.

Therefore, that we may one day deserve to be joined and rejoice securely under such a shepherd in the heavenly kingdom, let us take care meanwhile that in this present life we are found not sluggish shepherds of our own souls. For, as we touched upon above [Col. 0321C], by “shepherd” one may signify not only a prelate but every faithful person who is a solicitous guardian of his own soul. Such a person deserves rightly to be called a good shepherd by the Lord when he continually gives his soul to be fed in those good and blessed pastures of divine reading, sacred meditation, and pure prayer; and he does this for the preservation of sheep, if he has them, or for gathering them, if he does not.

By sheep we may understand gentleness and simplicity, which every faithful person who desires salvation must necessarily possess: gentleness—that is, patience—lest adversity break him; simplicity, lest prosperity exalt him; so that he simply awaits the reward of divine recompense for his good deeds and despises the praise of fleeting favor, even if it comes his way [Col. 0321D]. These are the seven thousand sheep which that Job, great among the Eastern peoples, worthy of imitation among spiritual people, rich in the world and richer in God, possessed: he took no care to be exalted by the good things bestowed on him by God, nor did he, worn down and broken by adversities, depart from God.

Therefore, in order to retain and guard these sheep, let every faithful person diligently feed his soul in the aforesaid pastures of reading, meditation, and prayer, so that he may truly be called before God a good shepherd, not a hireling. For one can be a hireling who indeed labors for God and considers eternal life the reward of his labor, yet, when temptation arises, is easily bent by adversity or prosperity, because he is not often refreshed by the pasture of reading and prayer. This is what the Lord seems to say [Col. 0322A]: “The hireling, who is not a shepherd, whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees.” For the hireling who labors outwardly for God, but who is not a shepherd 443 because he takes no pains to be fed inwardly according to God—he is the one whose sheep are not his own. These virtues, patience and simplicity, although they may sometimes seem to belong to those who labor, are not truly theirs; rather, they belong to those who feed themselves through reading and prayer. For they possess them as their own, and no force or deceit of the tempter can take them away.

But because the hireling does not possess these sheep as his own, he sees the wolf coming—that is, he understands that the devil intends either to corrupt him by flatteries or to overcome him by terrors [Col. 0322B]—and he leaves the sheep: in adversity he abandons gentleness, in prosperity humility; and he flees, that is, he turns his face—namely, the intention of his mind, by which he ought to look upon God—away from God. Hence follows:

“And the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep.” The wolf snatches one sheep, which we have called patience, amid adversities; and he so scatters the other, which we have called simplicity, that he turns the hireling’s simplicity into duplicity—that is, makes him desire for his works both God’s recompense and the world’s favor.

Certainly, then, the fact that the hireling flees because he is a hireling, 444 [Col. 0322C] happens entirely because he is not concerned for the spiritual pasture of the soul, of which we have often spoken. He has no concern for it; but the shepherd does have concern for the sheep, the virtues of patience and simplicity. The true shepherd can never lose them, because he is sweetly nourished every day by the pasture of reading and prayer in order to obtain them.

Therefore, beloved, that we may gather these sheep within ourselves and, by feeding them, preserve them firmly, let us humbly flee to him who is essentially the good shepherd and who laid down his life for his sheep. Let us beseech his mercy to drive away by his power the wolf that lies in wait for us, and to keep us, who are his people and the sheep of his pasture, so in his pastures that, aided by him, we may reach the place where, protected beneath that shepherd and set in the place of pasture, we shall thereafter fear no wolf [Col. 0322D], but rejoice with him in eternal and secure blessedness—he who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

445 HOMILY XLVIII. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE SAME SUNDAY.

“I am the good shepherd” (John 10).

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who is essentially good, calls himself the good shepherd by a most fitting comparison, because in his merciful goodness he rules and governs all that he created and made; and whatever he did or taught for human salvation, he did not thereby provide for his own honor or glory, but sought to benefit human salvation. For if no human being had been created or saved, he would nevertheless have remained, as he was from the beginning, almighty and eternal in his divinity [Col. 0323A]. Thus, in calling himself the good shepherd, he commends his goodness by which he created and redeemed us, so that every person may be admonished by these words as to how to answer his goodness with good works.

“I am,” he says, “the good shepherd.” It is the office of a good shepherd to care for the sheep entrusted to him by feeding them, watering them, and defending them from the bites of beasts. Therefore that supremely good shepherd does not cease daily to feed the sheep of his pasture—which we are—with spiritual and bodily nourishment, and at the same time protects and defends them from the bites of beasts, that is, from the harm of evil spirits, by the protection of his hand. How greatly he loved his sheep in free goodness he clearly indicates in the following words:

“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” He alone, truly good, laid down his life for the redemption of his sheep, not in order to gain or increase glory for himself, but in order to recall to the kingdom of heaven the human being who had been lost [Col. 0323B]. For though there were some good shepherds—Peter and Paul, for example, the other apostles, and imitators of the apostles—who diligently cared for their sheep, they nevertheless did not labor for those sheep without regard to their own 446 reward. If they had not expected recompense for their labor from the Lord, they would not have endured such great labors and persecutions without grievous weariness. What shepherd, however good and holy, could ever endure for his sheep as many injuries of suffering as he endured, when, though Lord of all, he appeared in the form of a servant [Col. 0323C], suffered spitting, blows, and scourges, and finally, condemned to a most shameful death, hung crucified and pierced by a lance between two thieves?

And because no one can imitate him in bearing all these things, he prescribes a pattern for good shepherds in Peter the apostle, the first shepherd of the Church. After rising from the dead, he asked Peter three times whether he loved him; and when Peter confessed his love in a threefold answer, he three times entrusted his sheep to him to be fed. Thus the Lord three times entrusted his sheep to the faithful shepherd of the Church to be fed, signifying the threefold feeding by which every good shepherd ought to feed the flock entrusted to him: preaching, action, and prayer [Col. 0323D]. Let every shepherd strive to feed the Lord’s sheep by this threefold nourishment, so that those whom he urges to act well by words he may instruct and form by good examples, and so that he may not cease to assist them in these things by continual prayer—which is most important. For there are some who cannot be formed to a better life either through preaching or through action; these must be aided before God by the assistance of prayers, so that they may advance toward what is better. But because the Lord foresaw that many in the Church would be not true shepherds but hirelings, possessing the shepherd’s position but not his merit, and laboring not for the gain of souls but solely for earthly advantages, he added:

[Col. 0324A] 447 “But the hireling, who is not a shepherd, whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming.” It often happens that hirelings, though they themselves do not live rightly, nonetheless set before their subjects the rule of right living. Their life is not to be imitated, but what they rightly say and command is not to be despised, as Truth itself admonished his disciples: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat. Do what they tell you; but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:2). The scribes and Pharisees proclaimed and taught in their synagogues the law which they themselves did not at all keep. Those are proved to be hirelings who imitate them, destroying by evil living what they have rightly preached and taught.

“He sees,” he says [Col. 0324B], “the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep and flees.” When the wolf comes, the hireling flees because, as blessed Gregory says, “he fears to oppose with the free voice of reason whatever powers act wickedly.”

[Note: [Col. 0323D] St Gregory, cited passage, note 32.]

Thus the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep, because, when the goods of spiritual people are squandered by the ungodly and the resources of life are taken away, the sheep are sometimes scattered. But now our Redeemer, the true and good shepherd, goes on to indicate by repeated reiteration the love through which he knows and loves his sheep:

“I am,” he says, “the good shepherd; I know my own, and my own know me.” As though he plainly said: “My sheep, for whom I laid down my life and whom I redeemed by my blood, I know and love with such an affection of fatherly love that, whether they are under a shepherd or under [Col. 0324C] a hireling, I never abandon them, either here or in the future, without the aid of my protection. And my own know me”: indeed, they know their shepherd and Redeemer, because, following not a hireling but me, the true shepherd, they hear my voice. Those who are truly the Lord’s sheep hear his voice speaking through inward inspiration; for many, if they are under a hireling, flee from him and humbly seek the Father and shepherd of their souls, under whom they may be saved. And lest it seem harsh and burdensome to the Lord’s sheep to follow his voice in imitation of true humility and obedience, setting before us a pattern in himself, he says:

448 “As the Father knows me, and I know the Father [Col. 0324D], and I lay down my life for my sheep.” This is the same as if he had said: “Just as I, although equal, coeternal, and co-omnipotent with the Father, humbled myself so greatly for love of him that, taking the form of a servant, I gave my life for the redemption of my sheep, so those who are and wish to be my sheep ought to return the same love to me: for love of me they should not shrink from humbling themselves under obedience, and, insofar as they can, should strive to benefit their neighbors in true charity.”

For one is known truly to love one’s neighbor who takes the greatest care to admit nothing by which one might offend or grieve that neighbor. We ought to love our Redeemer, who so loves us, in this manner: not to offend in anything the eyes of his majesty [Col. 0325A]. He loves us not for any benefit to himself, but solely through the goodness of his freely bestowed compassion. When a person loves another person, however, that person seeks his own benefit more than the other’s; and even the one who loves more, if he perceives that he is loved less, quickly turns his mind away from the person he loved. If, therefore, we love ourselves so greatly, how much more ought God to be loved in all things and above all things, since from him we have received what we ardently love: namely, soul and body. It follows:

“And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice.” The Jews were, as it were, Christ’s own sheep: among them he was born, nourished, and lived; by them also he suffered and was crucified. The other sheep, as the commentators say [Col. 0325B], are the faithful who came to faith from among the Gentiles. In a loftier sense, we may also understand Christ’s sheep to be the innocent, and the other sheep to be penitents, whom he graciously deigns to bring into his fold.

For there are some whom the Lord separates, while still of tender age, from the corruption of secular life, and preserves and keeps in spiritual conduct from grave sins. Such people are not undeservedly called Christ’s sheep because of the innocence of their life. Conversely, there are many who spend their whole life amid the vanities and seductions of the world. When, through the grace of his inward visitation, he has called them back from their evil way and brought them into the fold of holy conduct, they are called 449 Christ’s sheep through true repentance [Col. 0325C], just as those of whom we spoke above are called sheep through true innocence. They hear his voice because, as far as they are able with his help, they strive to fulfill in deeds what he commanded his disciples to learn from him: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). He did not say, “Learn from me that I hang on the cross for your salvation.” Rather, after setting aside all the labors of his passion, he proposed to them this one example of humility and patience, so that those who wish truly to be his disciples may be patient and humble of heart.

Of such persons, both innocent and penitent, there shall be one fold: united, that is, in the deep humility of the heart, because they think humbly of themselves and strive to outdo one another in showing honor. For the sheep [Col. 0325D] of the penitents, when they consider the labors, fasts, vigils, and other works of virtue in the sheep of the innocent, judge themselves truly sinners by comparison with them, and therefore humble themselves more and more. Conversely, the sheep of the innocent, when they observe the humility and worthy satisfaction in the sheep of the penitents, complain that they have done no good and have labored in vain; and they strive to imitate the penitents’ humility and perfection. As innocent and penitent people strive in this mutual contest of humility to outdo one another in showing honor, it may fittingly be said that there is one fold, because they agree with one another in unity of humility and submit and humble themselves to one another in unanimous charity.

[Col. 0326A] In this fold there will truly be one shepherd, the author of humility and innocence; and whatever the character of the prelate may be, he will nonetheless be the first and highest shepherd there, mercifully feeding and governing in soul and body the aforesaid sheep of innocence and repentance.

The apostle Peter notes these works of divine compassion in today’s reading. “You were once,” he says, “like straying sheep, but now you have returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” (1 Pet. 2:25). These words are aptly suited both to the innocent and to penitents. Penitents were straying sheep in that they had spent their whole life in the vanities of the world; the innocent likewise were straying sheep because they did not recognize the mercy 450 of God shown in them, nor did they render to God worthy thanks for their preserved innocence [Col. 0326B]. But after they have thus come together, as we said, into Christ’s fold, and have been united in true humility and charity, then, in a certain manner returned to the shepherd and bishop of their souls, they praise and love the mighty works God has done in them.

Our Redeemer is rightly called the bishop of our souls, since *episcopus* means “one who oversees.” Before a person is conceived and formed in the mother’s womb, God, by the hidden counsel of his providence, considers what he will do concerning and with that person, and how he intends to save the innocent and the penitent. As the knower of all, he knows the dispositions and qualities of each individual; and, according to what is beneficial for each, he orders their withdrawal [from the world] and their manner of life [Col. 0326C]. There are some who, if they were called pure and unstained from infancy to the spiritual profession, would exalt themselves above others by despising them. Therefore the Lord of knowledge sometimes mercifully calls such persons back through repentance after they have fallen grievously, so that, converted after the fall, they may become humbler and stronger. There are others who, if he permitted them to become entangled in the vanities of the world, would scarcely or never withdraw their minds from love of the world. Such people, by his prevenient mercy, he preserves in innocence from their earliest age to the end.

Thus the shepherd and bishop of our souls oversees each one who is to be saved: by what conversion and in what order both penitents and innocents ought to be called. And when he has brought them into his fold, fervent in charity and mutually obedient in humility, he feeds and refreshes us by the grace of his visible and invisible pasture [Col. 0326D].

And because we are the sheep of his pasture, whom he has deigned to bring into his fold, let us strive with the whole intention of our heart to hear his voice in such a way that, united in charity and subject in humility, we may deserve to be fed in the present upon the food of his sweetness and someday be led to the delights of eternal satisfaction. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

451 HOMILY XLIX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EASTER.

“A little while, and you shall not see me; and again a little while [Col. 0327A], and you shall see me, because I go to the Father” (John 16).

Because our Lord and Savior foresaw that the minds of the disciples would be greatly troubled by his bodily absence, he foretold and signified to them, in the words of this holy Gospel reading, his passion, resurrection, and ascension, so that those who would be troubled at his temporal death might, when they heard of the glory of his resurrection and ascension, have cause for consolation. Rightly, then, he said:

“A little while, and you shall not see me.” For from that hour—namely, his last supper, when he spoke these words to his disciples—the time was short until they began not to see him. Seized by the Jews that night, and on the following day crucified, dead [Col. 0327B], and buried, he was taken from their sight. But again, after a little while, they saw him when he rose on the third day; and during the forty days in which he remained in this world after his resurrection, he appeared to them when and as he wished. When he added, “Because I go to the Father,” he foretold by this the wondrous mystery of his ascension, by which, having completed the dispensation of mortality in the humanity he had assumed, he would reign eternally with the Father in heaven. But because they, still carnal and weak, could understand none of this, he added:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: you shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice; you shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” [Col. 0327C]. They indeed wept and lamented in inestimable grief when they saw him whom they loved above all the world, apart from whom they had no joy or gladness in this world, nor wished to have any, seized, bound, 452 scourged, and finally crucified, dying, and buried. But the world rejoiced, because the faithless Jews, who loved the world more than God, were delighted at his death, believing that they had extinguished his memory together with his life. Yet the sorrow of Christ’s lovers was turned into joy, because those who were afflicted and saddened by incredible grief at his death, upon recognizing his resurrection and seeing his most excellent ascension, were filled with unspeakable joy. Blessed Luke the Evangelist bears witness, saying [Col. 0327D]: “And they, worshipping, returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were always in the temple praising and blessing the Lord” (Luke 24:52).

Having briefly set forth these matters, he also offered for understanding another death and resurrection of his body: namely, holy Church, of which he is the head. In these same words he teaches us how those who desire to be called and to be his disciples and members ought to die and rise in this life.

“A little while,” he says, “and you shall not see me; and again a little while, and you shall see me, because I go to the Father.” Although these words seem indeed very obscure and difficult to understand, the eternal Wisdom of God rightly sets before us in them how those who have gone astray in sin ought by right living to return to the way of righteousness. For *modicum* (“a little”) is said from *modus* (“measure”). Therefore, when he says “a little,” he shows us, as I see it, a certain measure without which no human being can be saved. It is as though he says to all whom he desires in his mercy to save as predestined for life: “You who have hitherto been without measure, adding sin to sin without measure by living immoderately, now have some measure 453 in sinning: restrain yourselves from the vices which until now you have eagerly served without measure.” Yet God does not promise himself to be seen by a person at this first “little while,” which we may call the conversion of sinners, although it is the way and beginning of human salvation, until that person progresses to the second “little while,” by which he figuratively signifies a contrite and humbled heart [Col. 0328A].

“And again a little while,” he says, “and you shall see me.” This too seems to be suggested through the Psalmist when he says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27). A sinful person can turn away from evil, which is the first “little while,” but is not immediately sufficient for doing good until, through God’s mercy, he has attained again that “little while” which we called a contrite heart. For after the heart has truly been humbled through inward contrition, the formerly weak person grows strong for doing good; and, strengthened through true humility, advances to the vision of God. The Lord himself testifies: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). A humble heart is rightly called a pure heart. For it is written: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God” [Col. 0328B].

How a person may reach this purity of heart, in which God is truly seen, the Holy Spirit suggests through the Psalmist, though obscurely: “Myrrh and drop and cassia are from your garments” (Ps. 44:8). By myrrh may be understood the mortification of the flesh; by the drop, the humbling of the heart; by cassia, the contemplation of the mind. By God’s garments, however, sacred Scripture is understood, because just as a person is covered by garments lest he appear naked, so in a certain manner God and the divine meaning lie hidden beneath the covering of sacred Scripture. For from God’s garments proceed myrrh, drop, and cassia, because the converted person is instructed from the sacred Scriptures how diligently he ought to mortify his flesh by crucifying it with its vices and desires. This is truly myrrh, which gives life in Christ to the person truly cleansed from the corruption of vices. After myrrh comes the drop, which is humility of heart: the more the 454 mortified flesh is cast down, the more the humbled mind is kindled toward the pursuit of good works [Col. 0328C]. After myrrh and the drop comes cassia, because through mortification of the flesh and true humbling of the heart a person advances to the most sweet contemplation of the mind.

But because it is hard and difficult for a human being, by mortifying and humbling his flesh in this way, to despise himself, the Lord, who for our sake was willing to become both myrrh and drop, sets himself before us as an example, saying:

“Because I go to the Father.” For the Lord became a drop by being born for us as a little infant; he became myrrh by dying in the humanity assumed for us [Col. 0329A]. Nor is Christ’s coming in the flesh unjustly compared to a drop. As one drop is a very small thing in comparison with a great river, so Christ’s humanity was a very small thing in comparison with his incomprehensible divinity. Therefore whoever perfectly conforms himself in humbling himself to this drop—that is, to God’s Only-Begotten, made human for us—and whoever imitates this most choice myrrh by mortifying vices within himself: in that person the same God and man undoubtedly goes to the Father, when by the grace of his visitation he raises that person to the height of most sweet contemplation, signified by cassia. Nor is contemplation unjustly likened to cassia, an aromatic tree that grows only in moist places [Col. 0329B], because the noble moisture of tears, which contemplation of the mind draws from the soil of the heart, causes diverse trees—that is, diverse virtues—to grow in the human heart.

These three words of the Psalmist rightly correspond to the Lord’s three words mentioned above. For the first “little while,” like myrrh, signifies the mortification of the flesh; “again a little while,” like the drop, signifies humility of heart. And when he says, “Because I go to the Father,” he indicates contemplation of the mind, just as cassia does.

Through the same Gospel words today’s Collect is also rightly illuminated, in which we ask that the light 455 of truth may be shown to those who wander, so that they may be able to return to the way of righteousness [Col. 0329C]. For the way of righteousness is mortification of the flesh, and the light of truth is humility of heart. Through these two things the person to be saved is rightly illumined, so that, rejecting what is hostile to the Christian name, he may know how to turn from evil and, pursuing what is fitting, may be able to do good. Whoever is advanced by the hand of grace through these steps in the spiritual life may rightly say with him whose member he has become, “I go to the Father.” For with God and in God he goes to the Father, when, flying beyond all earthly and transitory things on the wing of contemplation, he attends only to heavenly things.

But because human mutability and misery have such alternation that one who is at one time sweetly delighted and refreshed with God through the hidden grace of heavenly visitation at another time, when the sweetness of God’s visitation is withdrawn, falls back into a kind of ignorance of God and of himself, there suitably follows:

“Then his disciples said to one another.” By the name of the disciples we may understand the human spirit, soul, and body. When these gather themselves under the Lord’s discipline by right living, yet cannot attain the desired sweetness of divine knowledge and love, they speak these words continually to one another:

What is this that he says to us: “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, and because I am going to the Father”? What is this that he says, “a little while”? Here he has posed two questions. The first question is the recognition of one’s own ignorance; the second question [Col. 0330A] is humble prayer, to be continually offered to God on account of the same blindness of one’s ignorance. For what else do the disciples of the true Lord do, when, as though abandoned by God, they see that by no bodily labor and no devotion of heart can they attain to the grace of divine sweetness, except to cry to the Lord in prayer with suppliant heart and voice: “What is this that he says to us, ‘a little while’?” As if they said: “O Lord, merciful and good in your very essence, what is this that is daily said to us concerning your ineffable sweetness? Teach us, Lord, in your accustomed goodness; grant that we may inwardly experience what is this ‘a little while, and again a little while,’ which we hear outwardly, without which we cannot attain to the grace of your vision.”

[Col. 0330B] “We do not know what he is saying.” It will profit us nothing to hear outwardly if your grace ceases to teach us inwardly. That the Lord gladly hears and answers prayer of this kind, the Evangelist accordingly shows in what follows.

“But Jesus,” he says, “knew that they wished to ask him, and said to them.” Jesus’ knowing is Jesus’ approving and loving. For he truly loves all who are concerned for their salvation, who are frequently distressed by the ignorance of God which they discover in themselves. A human being’s asking is a human being’s desiring. They truly ask God who desire, through prayers and tears and utterly tireless longings, that what they perceive to be inwardly lacking in themselves of the knowledge of spiritual perfection may be supplied in them through the mercy [Col. 0330C] of God. Jesus knows this desire because he approves and loves it in his elect.

He said to them: “Are you asking one another about this, because I said, ‘A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’?” God’s speaking is God’s stirring up; for the heart in which he finds some trace of good will, some longing for the heavenly homeland, he stirs and inflames to desire more and more. “You are asking one another about this,” he says. As if he said: “You seek and sigh for this with your whole heart’s desire: that you may know this ‘a little while, and again a little while’ of which I spoke to you—that is, that you may be able to know how to retain me as present to you through the sweetness of my visitation, and by what merits you may recall me when I depart and withdraw [Col. 0330D] my grace from you. Because I approve and love this inquiry of your desire, I show you the way by which you may attain it.”

“Amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice.” As if he said: “It belongs to the world and to those who love the world to exult and rejoice vainly; it belongs to you, by lamenting and weeping, to abstain from their empty joy.” The world’s joy chiefly rests upon two causes: the pleasure of the flesh and the will of the heart. And since few there are who have not sinned in these two matters—either by delightfully possessing bodily what belongs to pleasure, or by ardently desiring in heart, that is, in will, what they do not possess, and thereby straying from the way of truth—Christ, our true physician, has set before us two remedies by which we may heal [Col. 0331A] the crimes we committed through pleasure of the flesh and will of the heart. “Amen, amen,” he says, “I say to you: you will lament and weep.” Lamentation pertains to the body; weeping, to the heart. It is as if the Lord said to all who strive toward perfection: “Whatever you have committed bodily against the uprightness of my commands, you shall purge by bodily labor and affliction; whatever you have sinned in heart by unlawfully desiring the things of the world, you shall cleanse only by bitter weeping of heart.” Since lovers of this age do not readily accept counsel of this kind from the Lord, since they prefer and desire to rejoice and exult vainly rather than to lament and weep in this way, it is fittingly added:

“But the world will rejoice; but you will be sorrowful, [Col. 0331B] and your sorrow shall be turned into joy.” As if it were said: “The world indeed rejoices in a joy to which everlasting mourning succeeds. But you, who strive toward those joys to which no pain or sorrow succeeds, must always be sorrowful in this life, always humbled in heart and body. But your sorrow shall be turned into joy.” The sorrow of God’s elect which is truly according to God, which, as the Apostle says, “works repentance unto steadfast salvation” (II Cor. 7:10), is then truly turned into joy when, after the grief of true and humble repentance, God inwardly consoles a person with the sweetness of his visitation. Indeed, at the beginning of this reading he promises this joy to his humble ones, where, after “a little while, and again a little while,” he says, “and you will see me.” That joy [Col. 0331C] which is inwardly conceived from the inward vision of God surpasses every joy. For by it the sorrowful heart is not only consoled in the Lord, but even in that consolation it is enlightened and raised up to see and know many things that were previously unknown. Having attained such joy—namely, the joy of divine contemplation—the Lord seems, through the following comparison, to teach what and how great a watchfulness of heart and body must be applied, when he says:

“A woman, when she is giving birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come.” By “woman” we may understand the weak and infirm person, who is said, as it were, to give birth when, either by weeping over sins committed or by sighing for heavenly joys, he strives to bring forth from the womb of his heart something pleasing [Col. 0331D] and acceptable to God. While preparing himself for such a birth, he has sorrow.
