For unless humility and the affliction of repentance have gone before, a human being cannot bring forth from his heart anything that either pleases God or benefits himself. Yet since this sorrow is not lasting in weak people, the Lord fittingly adds: “because her hour has come.” Her hour—that is, the hour of such sorrow—comes from no one but the Lord himself, the giver of all good things. It is his gift that a person should know how to humble himself beneficially for his sins and, because of that very humility, deserve to be divinely consoled. It follows:

“But when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers the distress.” The weak soul, not yet founded in Christ, when the child has been born, in some fashion no longer remembers the distress—that is, the humility and affliction to which, in order to give birth to the child, namely the spirit of salvation, it had submitted itself for a time—when, after a time of prayer, forgetful of the inward sweetness it had briefly conceived, it returns to its former lightness and inconstancy of mind. But why is this?

“Because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.” It is therefore because he is human, and human born—that is, rooted not in heaven but in the world—that he no longer remembers the distress and forgets the visitation and heavenly sweetness. But why or how can one who has renounced the world be called a person rooted in the world? Indeed, one who is still inwardly ravaged by anger, hatred, or envy, who seeks not heavenly things according to his merits [Col. 0332B] but earthly things and delights in human praise, is rightly called a human being born into the world, rooted in the world, even if separated from the world.

Therefore blessed Peter teaches us in today’s reading how we should keep watch against these things, where he says: “I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (I Pet. 2:11). Not only those desires which entice a person into open deeds of the flesh are called fleshly desires, but also those which soften and cast down an unwary heart toward the craving for human praise, anger, or impatience. Whoever, then, knowing themselves to be strangers and pilgrims in this world, abstain from desires of this kind; whoever, in accordance with the Lord’s aforesaid [Col. 0332C] saying, through lamenting and weeping abase and humble themselves in this life in hope of future blessedness—the Lord himself, without whom there is no consolation, will be their comforter in the present and their rewarder in the future. Hence he added and said:

“And you therefore,” he says, “now indeed have sorrow. But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice.” As if he said: “You now have beneficial sorrow, namely the contrition of profound humility; but take care, with watchful guardianship of mind, that there may not be a human being born into the world—that after conceiving the grace of inward sweetness, you do not return in mind to the empty joys of this world, to the desires which wage war against the soul. Rather, persevering in the same humility and constancy of heart and body, attend only to heavenly things. But if this seems hard and difficult to you, consider how great is the joy promised to you as a reward after this happy perseverance: ‘But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice.’ For it does not suffice me to have seen you once; it does not suffice to have shown you once the grace of my sweetness. Rather, I will see you again and again, because as long as you labor in the exile of this life, I will raise you by the consolation of my fatherly visitation.”

“And your heart shall rejoice,” because the more harshly the flesh is troubled and worn down by the sufferings of tribulations, the more abundantly your heart is consoled by the grace of my desired sweetness. “And no one shall take your joy from you,” because that joy of my vision, begun here, [Col. 0333A] will be given to you more fully in the future, where it will be established for you with such security, with such secure possession, that, when every sorrow and every troublesome adversity has been removed, nothing will remain for you but the solemnity of eternal delight and the certain dignity of perpetual glorification, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

461. HOMILY L. FOR THE SAME SUNDAY, SECOND HOMILY

“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father” (John 16).

The present reading is part of that discourse which the Savior began at his last supper with his beloved and chosen disciples. By its dignity and excellence it surpasses all those discourses which the Son of God spoke in the flesh, so that none of the Evangelists was fit either rightly to comprehend or to record it except blessed John alone, who reclined meanwhile upon his breast and was worthy to draw from it the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in that breast of Jesus.

“A little while,” says the Lord, “and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.” In these words of the Lord are indicated those alternations and changes which every faithful soul suffers as long as it bears this corruptible body that weighs it down. Those who make it their practice to pray often, and whose concern it is to note with watchful attentiveness of mind the Lord’s departure and arrival in their heart, certainly do not fail to recognize these alternations: whenever he whom they love delights and refreshes them through the hidden grace of his inspiration, and whenever again he withdraws from them the same most longed-for sweetness of his visitation. Thus the bride speaks in the Song of Songs: “Flee, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” (Cant. 8:14). For these little beasts are so swift that, when they are thought already to have been caught and fixed, they slip from the hunters’ hands more quickly than a word can be spoken.

Christ, the Bridegroom of faithful souls, is not inaptly compared to them: while he encounters the soul that weeps and pursues him and allows himself to be grasped, suddenly he again flies away, as though from its hands, and returns anew if he is sought with whole-hearted desire. But when the bride says, “Flee, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of spices,” she does not say this as a request, but indicates these alternations which she must suffer while still surrounded by frail flesh. By the Lord’s saying, “a little while, and you will no longer see me,” we understand that he sometimes withdraws his presence from the soul that desires him; by “again a little while, and you will see me,” it is intimated that the soul thirsting for God again receives him, entering from heaven into its deepest affections and the very marrow of its heart.

And “a little while” is rightly said of both, because everything done amid the fleeting course of this present time is brief and little. It is a little while when the Lord comes to visit the soul by grace; again it is a little while when he withdraws in order to test it. The prophet Isaiah notes this “little while” where he records the complaint of those who longed for Christ’s presence in the flesh: “A little here, a little there” (Isa. 28:10).

Every soul devoted to God must therefore always observe carefully both when the visitation sent from the Most High comes and when, being withdrawn, it leaves the soul again; for if the mind neglects to observe this with vigilant care, it will doubtless be entirely deprived of inward sweetness. Hence, when Elisha asked that Elijah’s spirit might become double in him, Elijah answered:

“If,” he says, “you see me when I am taken from you, what you have asked will be yours; but if you do not see, it will not be” (IV Kings 2:10). Elijah bears the type of the Lord Savior. Elisha is portrayed as the soul thirsting for God. The soul asks that Elijah’s spirit may become double in it when it desires that the spirit of truth, the spirit of twofold love—of God, namely, and neighbor—may be given it by the Lord. The Lord promises that this cannot be bestowed on it by any other means unless it strives, as we have said, to seek out and foresee his departure and return with careful watchfulness. After the alternations which the soul suffers—of visitation, namely, and testing—have been described, there follows in due order:

“Because I am going to the Father.” The Son of God goes to the Father when he mercifully intercedes for those souls whom his visitation indeed gladdens but whose alternation nonetheless troubles, and presents himself to God the Father for their salvation. It follows:

“Therefore some of his disciples said to one another.” By the name of disciples we may understand the human spirit, soul, and body, which turn themselves inwardly and outwardly to this end: that they may learn the Lord’s commands, in accordance with that testimony of the Psalmist: “It is good for me, Lord, that you humbled me, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. 118:71). Those who are placed in the world cannot learn the Lord’s commands, because, excessively bent upon earthly pleasures and desires, they cannot attend to what concerns him and the salvation of the soul. But those are rightly called disciples of the Lord who have withdrawn within the bounds of the cloister, so that they may have heart and body free for learning the Lord’s precepts, and may live day and night under the Lord’s discipline and the strictness of the Rule. Certainly the human spirit, soul, and body which know how truly to adhere to the Lord’s discipline continually speak these words to one another:

“What is this that he says to us: ‘A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me; and because I am going to the Father’? What is this that he says, ‘a little while’?” These two questions are expressions of amazement, because amazement never arises except from excessive grief or excessive joy, nor does anyone wonder at anything except what appears new and rare. Amazement arising from the greatness of sorrow belongs to the exercise of temptation; but that which occurs from excessive joy concerns the time of consolation. A person wonders from sorrow when, under the force of temptation, he sighs from the depths of his heart that he is deprived of the sweetness of inward savor; he wonders again from excessive joy when, as the grace of heavenly visitation returns, he exults in the abundance of divine consolation.

Moreover, the fact that the Evangelist here says twice, first, “Therefore some of his disciples said to one another,” and again, “Therefore they said,” refers to the twofold amazement of which we have spoken, arising from excessive sorrow or joy. For this is the night-and-day discourse of the outward and inward senses of every elect person: either they grieve in the time of temptation when the sweetness of inward vision is withdrawn from them, or they rejoice when, all pressure of temptation at rest, they deserve to experience within themselves the aid of heavenly consolation. This amazement is also beautifully prefigured in the Old Testament, when manna descended together with dew at night, and the Israelites, wondering, said: “Manhu,” which means, “What is this?” (Exod. 16:15). By night we understand the present life; by dew, the chill of temptation; by manna, the savor of inward contemplation. Manna descends with the dew because, after the assault of temptation, the grace of inward savor comes to the elect person. Therefore, feeling these alternations in themselves, the inward and outward senses of a person say in amazement with the children of Israel, “What is this?”—whether they grieve or are sorrowful because of the trouble of temptation, or rejoice and are delighted because of the abundance of divine consolation. After the kinds of these alternations have been described, it is rightly added:

“We do not know what he is saying.” The disciples—that is, the spirit, soul, and body of the elect person—do not know what the Lord is saying, because, as long as they are in the body of this death, they can never discern and investigate for what merits the Lord consoles them; nor, when they are tempted, do they know whether he allows them to be tempted for testing or for destruction. Thus they say, as it were, “We do not know what he is saying,” when troubled and anxious over these alternations. That the Lord loves this concern in his elect is shown in the following words of the holy Gospel:

[Col. 0335D] “But Jesus knew that they wished to ask him.” Jesus’ knowing is Jesus’ approving and loving. Jesus knew that they wished to ask him. It belongs to one who does not know to ask, so that he may learn from one who knows what he does not know. The elect indeed wish to ask Jesus when they labor with every effort to investigate what he determines concerning them, while he either permits them to be distressed by temptations or raises them by his consolations. Jesus knows this inquiry because he approves and loves it in the elect.

He said to them: “Are you asking one another about this, because I said, ‘A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’?” That is, he makes and permits them sometimes, through withdrawal of the grace of his visitation, to be distressed by temptations, and again to be raised up by the consolation of his most blessed presence. “You are asking one another about this,” he says, “because I said, ‘A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.’” As if the Lord inwardly answered his elect concerning their aforesaid inquiry: “Since this is the day-and-night discourse of your inward and outward senses—that you may know and investigate what I signify in you by my departure and return—I set before you the pattern which you are meanwhile to follow, as long as you bear the body which weighs down the soul, in which you must suffer these alternations.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: you will lament and weep.” By these two words, “you will lament” and “you will weep,” which have a similar meaning, we may understand a twofold compunction: one produced by fear of punishment and by repentance and bitterness for sins; the other proceeding from love and desire for eternal life and heavenly goods. “Amen, amen, I say to you,” says the Lord, “in the institution of the Old and New Testaments; amen, amen, I say to you in love of God and neighbor; amen, amen, I say to you in the exercise of the active and contemplative life: you will lament and weep.” That is, as long as you live, you must be moved to compunction both by dread of my fear and by the sweetness of my love.

“But the world will rejoice,” he says. As if he said: “The world—that is, lovers of the world—neither wish nor are able to have a part in this lamentation and weeping. For, pursuing the empty happiness of this age, which must be made bitter by the mourning of eternal sorrow, they rightly do not know how to be moved to compunction for their sins and for the desire of eternal life.” The Lord restrains his elect from the blameworthy—indeed, damnable—joy of this age, when he immediately adds:

“But you will be sorrowful.” You, I say, whom I have devoted to my discipline, since I have separated you from the common way of life of humankind both in body and habit, must always, while you live in this life full of temptations, be sorrowful both because of your sins and because of love for me. Describing beneficial sorrow, the Apostle says: “The sorrow which is according to God works repentance unto steadfast salvation” (II Cor. 7:10). And he immediately adds: “See what earnestness this sorrow according to God has produced in you, but also defense, indignation, fear, desire, zeal, and vengeance” (ibid., 11). Beneficial sorrow produces defense in a person when he strives to defend himself before God by a worthy satisfaction of repentance for those things in which he remembers that he has sinned by thought, word, or deed. It produces indignation in him when he begins thereby to be indignant with and despise himself because he once admitted something capable of separating him from the love of eternity. It produces fear in him when he begins to fear God, and also to fear the punishment due for his sins. It gives rise to desire when he sighs with his whole heart’s affection for love of the heavenly homeland. It creates zeal in him when, armed with the zeal of piety, he strives vehemently to oppose his sins. It produces vengeance in him when, through the daily exercise of his labors—namely, persistence in fasts, vigils, and prayers—he persecutes within himself all that he remembers having done against God. But lest God’s elect shrink from being sorrowful in this way according to God, the Lord shows them in the following words of the holy Gospel what follows this sorrow:

“But your sorrow,” he says, “shall be turned into joy.” For not every sort of sorrow conceived from vain grief will be turned into joy, but this sorrow of which we have just spoken, because it will receive the reward of eternal recompense. To confirm this, the Lord sets before us a *paradigm* drawn from a woman, so that the mind may rise from what it knows to what it does not know, and infer spiritual things by comparison with bodily things.

“The woman,” says the Lord, “when she is giving birth has sorrow, because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers the distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.” The pain which oppresses a woman in childbirth exceeds every pain that a person can ever endure in his body. But when a child has been born to her and she sees that all its limbs are sound, she so rejoices in the fruit of her womb as though she had never been touched by any pain in giving birth. Eternal Wisdom therefore aptly applied the comparison of a woman to his preceding words, in which he says: “But you will be sorrowful, and your sorrow shall be turned into joy.” For as a woman in labor suffers and is tortured for a time, but afterwards, rejoicing in her offspring, forgets every pain and torment, so too the soul which brings forth works of virtue with labor and groaning will afterwards, when it has laid aside the body of this death which weighs it down, in the sight of recompense be forgetful of every groaning and labor.

“The woman,” he says, “when she is giving birth has sorrow, because her hour has come.” Since *woman* (*mulier*) is named from softness (*mollities*), the soul softened by God’s grace is very fittingly compared to a woman. As we have said, it gives birth when, by unceasing persistence in its labors and by abundant rain of tears, it strives to produce and bring forth from itself an offspring of virtues. In that birth it undoubtedly has sorrow because it does not see the fruit of its labors, namely, the reward of eternal joy which it will receive for its labors. For when a person has labored day and night and spent his strength in many fasts and vigils and continual prayers, he receives nothing for it in this world; no one addresses to him even a word of consolation for it. Indeed, when he is engaged in the spiritual life and subject to regular discipline, if he does anything inadequately, he is corrected by severe discipline. Thus it is rightly said: “because her hour has come.” The hour of the woman in labor—that is, of the soul laboring in the flesh—has come, because now is the hour of temptation, the hour of misery and pilgrimage.

“But when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers the distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.” But when she has given birth to the child—that is, when any faithful soul that has labored for God begins at the end of its life to behold the fruit of its labors and receives as its reward God himself, in whom is rest, forgetful of all its labors—it no longer remembers the distress, that is, all the pains it suffered while still bearing the burden of the flesh. It forgets because of that joy: because that person who had been born into the world has now become a citizen of the heavenly homeland and is fed by the vision of his Creator. Having thus set forth the comparison of the woman, the Lord added:

“And you therefore now indeed have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice.” You, I say, my elect, now indeed have sorrow while you groan over this death, your temptations, and your pilgrimage. “But I will see you again”: that is, when this corruptible thing has put on perpetual incorruption, I shall show myself to you as I am, in my divinity and humanity. “And your heart shall rejoice,” when, set at last in highest security, nothing from the devil, the world, or your flesh will ever again assail you to trouble you. Concerning this joy of heart the Lord also says through Isaiah the prophet, where he describes his elect as one day to be consoled in the heavenly Jerusalem: “And you shall see,” he says, “and rejoice, and your heart shall be glad” (Isa. 66:14). Who can explain what that joy is, when it cannot even be conceived? All the senses and all the members of the elect are raised into that joy of everlasting jubilation, in which they will be occupied without end in the praise of the Creator—a praise without weariness, because it is uttered without fatigue.

[Col. 0338C] This joy of the blessed can never be interrupted by any sorrow and will be terminated by no end, as the Lord promises in what follows:

“And no one shall take your joy from you.” May we too one day be made participants in this eternal joy through the abundance of his goodness—he who deigned to become human and undergo the sorrow of death in order to lead us to eternal joys—to whom belong honor, glory, and dominion unto ages of ages. Amen.

470. HOMILY LI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

“I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart” (John 16).

[Col. 0338D] This most holy Gospel reading which we have just heard, most beloved, is taken from that discourse which Jesus gave with his disciples at his last supper. And just as that discourse surpasses all the discourses he ever gave or spoke, so the dignity and excellence of the mysteries contained in it transcend the sense and understanding of all human beings. Nor is this surprising, because, just as on that same night he willed to perform a new and unheard-of work, never done before, so the discourse which he gave on that same night rightly had to be incomparable with all other discourses. All his disciples heard it together, but they could not all grasp it with equal understanding. This is sufficiently clear from the fact that those four eminent men who wrote the Gospel all kept silence concerning this discourse, except John alone, who alone was worthy to recline upon Jesus’ breast and from it deserved to draw the fountain of life, the streams of eternal wisdom. Matthew sat at the same supper with John; what John heard, Matthew heard also. Yet he said or wrote nothing of this discourse, because God did not wish to grant him what he wished to grant and reserve above all others for John alone, whom he loved above the rest because of the special prerogative of chastity.

What are we wretches to say of this? “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” Who is fit to see and know the mysteries of this discourse, if those could not grasp them who heard it from the Lord in his bodily presence? Yet I judge, insofar as mortal humanity can infer anything from it, that this was especially reserved for those who imitate John: namely, spiritual people who, after the example of John himself, having preserved their chastity and innocence from childhood, are both with the Lord at supper and recline at the same supper upon Jesus’ breast. Jesus’ breast is sacred Scripture, because, as the heart is in the breast and life in the heart, so in sacred Scripture there lies hidden that spiritual meaning by which a person is inwardly given life and revived.

There are some who rest their head—which is intention—upon this breast of Jesus and yet are not at supper: namely, those who labor to investigate and know the subtleties of the Scriptures not for God’s sake but for their own, so that, when they are known to know what escapes others, they may obtain greater honor and glory from people as more approved, that is, more eloquent, on account of their knowledge itself. This does not suit lovers of God, imitators of John, who ought to labor for knowledge of sacred Scripture only so that through it they may attain fuller knowledge of God and find in it the heart of God—that is, the meaning of God—by which they may be inwardly vivified, and by which they may be more strongly kindled and formed toward sweetness of heart, purity of body, purity of prayer, and longing for eternity. Whoever they are who recline in this manner upon Jesus’ breast, the Lord invisibly, amid the feasts and banquets of inward sweetness, addresses them ineffably with words of this kind:

“I am going to him who sent me; and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” In these words, as far as we can see, it seems to me that the Lord signifies certain alternations by which and through which God’s faithful are exercised in this life. There is an alternation that is sweet and dear to a person who loves God, and an alternation that is very sorrowful and bitter to him. They are in a good alternation when, visited by the grace of the Most High, they are sweetly refreshed with the Lord through inward sweetness. They are in a bitter alternation when God withdraws and inward grace fails, and they are afflicted in themselves with labors and sorrows. Therefore he says: “I am going to him who sent me.” He himself is the Word of God the Father who is sent. It is as though, present among his own children and faithful, he said: “I am he who was sent by God the Father into this world to visit and save you. Whenever, through my invisible presence, you have deserved to be filled with the dew of my sweetness and grace, and according to your heart’s desire to be inwardly consoled with me for a while, I tell you that you cannot remain long in this grace. For I am going to him who sent me, and you cannot retain me long in the sweetness in which you would wish to have me.”

“And none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” A human being’s asking is a human being’s desiring. “None of you asks me,” because, as I depart and withdraw my grace from you, you fall into such hardness of heart that none of you desires me; that is, you neither grieve over my departure as you ought, nor are you able to desire my return with the due ardor of love. By these laborious alternations the Lord exercises his faithful in this life; they are also noted in part in today’s reading, when it says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (Jas. 1:17). Almighty God, since he is always the same, always remains stable in himself; he is never changed and is never overshadowed by any alternation. With him is the light of wisdom and knowledge; with him is eternal sweetness; with him and in him is the delight of eternal exultation and joy.

[Col. 0340C] But we—we are those with and in whom there is change and the shadow of alteration. We do not remain even for an hour in ourselves, but are always changing; as various alternations follow one another, we are very often so overshadowed that we cannot desire or even think what is good. For what else do good people bewail in prayer and lament in confession, except that they feel in themselves that they lack God’s grace and are unable to have a longing for God or for the things which ought to be done for his sake? Yet, because he is, as we have said, the Word of God the Father—not only, I say, that word which sounds bodily in outward ears, but that which invisibly teaches the human being inwardly—he reveals what he accomplishes in a person by thus departing from the person, when he says:

But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. What is this sorrow which is produced in a person by his speaking—by his operation, I mean (for God’s speaking [Col. 0340D] is God’s working)? There is an evil sorrow, which offends God; there is also a good sorrow, which makes God, once offended, gracious again to a person. The Apostle defines this twofold sorrow when he says: “The sorrow of the world works death; but the sorrow which is according to God works repentance unto steadfast salvation” (2 Cor. 7:10). If a person is grieved over worldly loss, the death of friends, the inconvenience of temporal possessions, or even contempt or injury inflicted on him by his neighbors, this is the sorrow of the world which works death. But when a person, salutarily humbled within himself on account of the kingdom of heaven and the loss of God’s inward grace, begins to grieve all the more vehemently because, with him who is true [Col. 0341A] joy withdrawn, he finds within himself nothing by which he may be consoled—this is shown to be sorrow according to God; this works repentance unto steadfast salvation. Through it a person is so recalled to the grace and sweetness of God, which is truly the person’s steadfast salvation, that he deserves also to possess it steadfastly, as far as this is possible in this life. Or this is repentance unto steadfast salvation: that one repent, with such constancy, of the things one has committed by which one lost God’s grace, that one no longer admits them. This is the grace and benefit for which that supreme Word, Christ the Son of God—who is also Word by inwardly speaking to a person through his inspiration, Christ by anointing the heart with his invisible grace—withdraws himself beneficially from a person for a time, so that, when he departs, [Col. 0341B] the person may begin more humbly to recognize what he is by himself. For he himself reveals this benefit when he adds:

“But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go.” He who is true and supreme truth tells a person the truth when, after that salutary sorrow which is according to God, he grants the person to know himself truly, and in that very self-knowledge to see that it was wholly expedient for him that God should thus have forsaken him. For while he is humbled to the depths in this abandonment by almighty God, he is visited by the sweetest consolation of the Holy Spirit, which he could never attain unless he had been truly humbled. Thus he says: “Upon whom shall I rest, but upon one who is humble and quiet, and who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). [Col. 0341C] For if God were always present to a person in the grace of his sweetness, that person could never remain grounded within himself; rather, he would exalt himself above himself and would not fear to attribute to himself what belongs to God. Hence, according to these words of the Lord, it is expedient for a person that he go, so that, recognizing humbly in his withdrawal his own poverty and misery, he may learn through humility to submit himself to him from whom he has whatever he is and without whom he cannot subsist even for a moment. Therefore the Lord says:

“It is expedient for you that I go. For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.” A person may indeed possess the spirit of understanding, the spirit of counsel, or some other great spirit; but no one can deserve that Spirit who is the Paraclete, [Col. 0341D] the Spirit of consolation, who consoles sad and grieving hearts by his marvelous sweetness, unless he has been truly humbled within himself.

“But when that Spirit has come,” the Lord says, “he will convict the world concerning sin, and righteousness, and judgment.” The Holy Spirit convicts the world concerning sin because, through the visitation of his coming, he illumines a person so that he begins to convict himself concerning his sin. Being illumined by him, he convicts himself concerning the sin he has committed; he convicts himself concerning the righteousness he has neglected; he also convicts himself concerning judgment, when he grieves within himself because he has never judged himself, as he ought, either for the sin committed or for righteousness neglected. [Col. 0342A] Hence the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged by the Lord” (1 Cor. 2:31).

But that we may understand these same words more clearly in view of what follows, let us set before ourselves a certain comparison. Let there be a woman who has a husband. If it happens that her husband goes far away from her, let her, if she is faithful to him, show this by striving to preserve the same fidelity to him when absent as when present, and by fearing to offend him when absent in any of the ways in which she might offend him when present. This woman is any faithful soul; her husband is Christ. If this husband withdraws himself from his bride, that is, from the soul, then, if she has the faithfulness owed to God within herself, she ought to love him absent as present; she ought diligently to keep herself from every defilement of heart and body, [Col. 0342B] neglecting nothing and serving him in all things with the same discipline and constancy when absent as when present. For this is to preserve true fidelity toward him.

Yet we can understand something subtler in these words. For when he says, “He will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment,” and immediately, as though explaining the same words, adds: “Concerning sin indeed, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see me no more; concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has already been judged”—in these words, so far as seems to me, he marked out, or rather selected, three things: from among all sins, one sin, which is the greatest of all sins; from among all righteousnesses, one righteousness, which is the greatest of all righteousnesses; and from among all judgments, [Col. 0342C] one judgment, which is the greatest of all judgments.

The sum of all sins is unbelief. For a person’s not believing in God is a sin surpassing all sins; for no good can ever be done without faith, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). The sum of all righteousnesses is faith—not merely that faith by which a person believes in God, but that by which he keeps due faithfulness toward him in all things. This faith produces in a person contemplation of mind, which surpasses every work of righteousness. For when a person has come to such purity of heart that nothing in this world tastes sweet to him apart from God, and he directs toward heaven all the intention and devotion of his mind after him whom he cannot see with the bodily eyes, this is complete and perfect righteousness, in which all works of righteousness are fully comprehended and fulfilled. There God is truly fed and given drink, clothed and visited; there he is received as a guest; whatever belongs to righteousness is there wholly accomplished.

But the sum of all judgments is when a person weighs and considers what kind of judgment, how great and how terrible, that is by which the ruler of this world has already been judged together with all his followers. He is rightly called the ruler of the world because these two words signify two things by which the devil himself chiefly reigns in people and with which he is to be judged and condemned eternally: pride, [Col. 0343A] understood under the name “ruler,” and pleasure of the flesh, represented under the name “world.” When a person so weighs this judgment that he himself truly fears it with all his heart, and judges and condemns within himself those two things—namely pride of heart and pleasure of the flesh—with such strictness that he labors always to suppress pride through humility and extinguish pleasure within himself through self-restraint and chastity—this is judgment above every judgment. By this judgment a person escapes the punishment of eternal condemnation. It follows:

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” Concerning these words we briefly say, according to the interpreters, that the holy apostles [Col. 0343B] to whom the Lord was speaking, being still carnal and weak, were not yet able to receive spiritual things. This is clear from the fact that on that same night when he was saying these things to them—when, at that most holy supper, he instructed them with such sweetness concerning heavenly mysteries which he had never before told them, a sweetness such as they had never experienced from the time they began to remain with him until that hour—as soon as they left that house, all deserted him and fled. But when the Holy Spirit came down from above, he taught them all truth; for when he filled and taught them, they fully and perfectly knew the glory of the Godhead and preached it steadfastly to the world, though they had not been able to know it perfectly while Christ was present and teaching.

He did indeed open for them, as it were, [Col. 0343C] a certain door of truth when, taking Peter, James, and John up the mountain where he was transfigured before them, he showed them the splendor of his glory which the children of light will see after the resurrection. There they saw Moses and Elijah speaking with him. They also heard from heaven the Father of truth, when a voice came from the cloud saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 17:5). There they looked in, as it were, through the door of truth; but after the coming of the Holy Spirit they entered into truth itself. Enlightened and strengthened by the Holy Spirit, they proclaimed truth itself to the world steadfastly and without fear. For Peter himself, who denied Christ at the voice of the woman gatekeeper, [Col. 0343D] afterward said before kings and rulers, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29), and steadfastly accepted death for Christ. Hence the Lord rightly says: “But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth; for he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things to come.” The Holy Spirit does not speak from himself because he is not from himself, but from the Father and the Son. He speaks from those with whom he is known to be one essence. He announces to you the things to come because through the gift of his inspiration he reveals to you the joys of the heavenly homeland.

“He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” The Holy Spirit glorified [Col. 0344A] Christ when he perfectly enlightened the hearts of the apostles to know him. For the Lord himself proves that they had not yet known him perfectly when Philip said, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8), and he replied: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?” (ibid., 9). They knew him well indeed and did not doubt that he was their Lord and Teacher; but they did not yet fully know the glory of his divinity which was in him. Peter certainly knew him when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16); but he had not yet been so glorified in Peter [477] that Peter could die for the testimony of his divinity. But because the Holy Spirit was to work all these things in them, the Lord rightly said: [Col. 0344B] “He will glorify me”—that is, he will make me known to you—“because he will receive from what is mine,” from my essence, which is one substance with the Father in me, “and announce it to you,” so that you may fully and perfectly know what you do not yet know concerning me, that is, concerning my divinity.

Having briefly set these things down beforehand according to the sense of the interpreters, let us see whether, by the help of the Holy Spirit, we can find or understand anything subtler in these words.

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” I judge that these words are not to be understood altogether in this way: that he who is the Word of God the Father said them because he wished to teach his disciples, the holy apostles, things still greater and more sublime than he had taught. [Col. 0344C] For the excellence of his discourse does not permit this, since nothing more excellent can be found in all his teaching. But God’s saying is God’s doing, as it is written: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9). And because a person never advances so far in this life that he does not still have room to advance further—such is human nature that, just as it always has a way to descend, so it always has a way to ascend—he wished to advance his chosen and beloved disciples, whom he had raised above all other people, to still greater dignity. Thus, by the many things which he promised still to say to them, he signified the many graces, benefits, and advances which he was still to effect in them and through them. For although they had no need, [Col. 0344D] being after the coming of the Holy Spirit the most perfect of all people, to make higher progress within themselves, he still had much to add to them in the advancement of those who were to be saved through their word and teaching. For all that they labored for the salvation of their neighbors accrued to their advancement. Therefore he rightly says: “I still have many things to say to you,” that is, I still have many things to do for you. For he wished them always to go, in themselves and in their neighbors, from virtue to virtue, until they came to see the God of gods in Zion. These are those many things which he did with them for so long, until he reduced them to one thing. Yet one thing is necessary. They were troubled about many things while they were in this life, but those many things were reduced to one when they ascended so far [Col. 0345A] that they delivered themselves to death for God’s sake and received as their reward that one necessary thing, namely the kingdom of heaven.

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” As if he said: These many things which I am to do in you and through you in your neighbors, my faithful ones who are to be saved through you, cannot be done all at once; they cannot be completed in a short time. “But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” By “all truth” we may understand either knowledge of the Old or New Testament, or love of God and neighbor. But let us set these aside for the moment and see more subtly what all truth properly is.

All truth which the Spirit of truth truly teaches [Col. 0345B] is knowledge of oneself and knowledge of God, because whatever truth is contained in the sacred Scriptures is wholly fulfilled through these two things. Self-knowledge gives birth to fear in a person, and fear to humility. For the reason we do not fear is that we lack perfect knowledge of ourselves. If we knew ourselves rightly, we would find nothing in our whole life except what ought to be feared. That chosen servant of God, Job, whom the Lord extolled with such praise that none on earth was his equal, possessed this fear when he said: “I feared all my works” (Job 9:28). He was indeed praised by the Lord, but because he held the fear of God perfectly before his eyes, he feared all that he did. Of this fear it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:16).

[Col. 0345C] After humble self-knowledge, when a person has come to this fear, knowledge of God immediately follows, and this gives birth to the love of God; for whoever lacks knowledge of God cannot possess love of God either. Knowledge of God is present when a person, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, weighs and considers, in the sweetness of his heart, God’s marvelous and magnificent mercy toward the human race: that he took care to create from nothing a human being whom he made in his own image and likeness, whom he could have created as whatever he wished; a rational human being, that is, a human being capable of knowing and loving God. And finally—what is greatest and most precious of all—he made his own body and blood [Col. 0345D] the price of our salvation, so that, just as he once wished to be offered for us who were perishing upon the altar of the cross, so also, through the sacraments of that same body and blood, he makes us, dying daily, live again daily. Through this true knowledge of God a person proceeds to the sweetest love of God, of which it is written: “Love is the fulfillment of the law” (Rom. 13:10). In fear is the beginning of wisdom; in love is all wisdom, because whatever the law commands is wholly fulfilled through this love of God. And these are the words which he says: “He will teach you all truth,” that is, he will give you knowledge of God and of yourselves, which may truly be called all truth.

“For he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce [Col. 0346A] to you the things to come.” He who speaks from himself, as the Lord says elsewhere in the Gospel, seeks his own glory (John 7:18). The Holy Spirit does not speak from himself because he is not from himself, but from the Father and Son; nor does he seek his own glory but that of the Father and Son, from whom he proceeds. But, so that we may more easily arrive at the sense, let us distinguish this verse member by member. “For he will not speak from himself”: that is, he will make you despisers of your own glory. “But whatever he hears he will speak”: that is, he will make you true worshipers of God in spirit. “And he will announce to you the things to come”: that is, he will make you faithful proclaimers of eternal salvation and everlasting damnation. Now let us consider the meaning.

The speaking of the Holy Spirit is the visitation and inspiration [Col. 0346B] of the Holy Spirit. He does not speak from himself because, by his mercy, he humbles and enlightens the heart which he visits and inspires, so that in all its deeds and words it may seek not its own glory but that of God alone. Before all things every person must labor to obtain this mercy from the Lord: that in everything he is going to do, say, or teach, he may seek only the glory of him from whom he also expects recompense, lest he be among those of whom the Lord says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2). After this it is rightly added: “And whatever he hears he will speak,” because whomever this Spirit of truth makes a perfect despiser of his own glory, him he makes a true worshiper of God in spirit. And whatever that person says in that most sweet illumination of mind, in that most pure prayer, he surely hears who makes him speak inwardly through the touch of his grace. What he does not speak in a person, he is not shown to hear either, because he does not cause it to pass into the person’s advancement and benefit. It follows:

“And he will announce to you the things to come.” As if he said: while by the grace of the Holy Spirit you daily ascend these steps—truly despising your own glory, and in your prayer attending only to the will of him who speaks in you—you will be able profitably to announce the things to come. What are the things to come? Two: eternal salvation and eternal [Col. 0346D] damnation. He will announce to you the things to come when, through his mercy, he gives you fruitfully and salutarily to announce eternal salvation to the good who are to be saved, and perpetual damnation to the evil who are to be damned. But from where will he give you this? From where does he make you announce these future things profitably? I tell you:

“He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” In these two expressions, “me” and “from what is mine,” two things which are in God are expressed—namely, the divine and human natures. For he is God and man, Word and flesh: invisible God, visible man; Word according to divinity, flesh according to humanity. Therefore, by “me,” which is the Word in itself, divinity may be understood. But by “from what is mine,” which is, as it were, adjectival, the humanity assumed into God [Col. 0347A] may be understood. The former was in itself; the latter he assumed into himself. And as these two are in God—inner divinity and outer humanity—so too in sacred Scripture, which is likewise called God’s flesh, there are two things: letter and sense, flesh and spirit; the literal sense outwardly, the spiritual sense inwardly. Hence he says: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine.” As though he had said: The Spirit of truth will glorify me, who am God and man, Word and flesh; for he will announce to you my sense, the spiritual and divine sense, which he will receive from what is mine, from my flesh, which is my letter. He will make it known and explain it to you so that in all my Scripture there may be nothing that can remain hidden from you. “He will announce it to you”: he himself will give you power profitably and fruitfully to announce eternal salvation to those who will believe, [Col. 0347B] and eternal damnation to those who are to be damned. “He will announce it to you,” because whatever you labor for in the advancement of others, he will recompense to you in eternal life, when he gives himself to you—he who is eternal life—as your reward, so that he himself may be your recompense, everlasting praise, and inestimable glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LII. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1), etc.

In these two sayings, of which the first is called “every good gift” and the other “every perfect gift,” the twofold love of God and neighbor is not inappropriately understood. “Every good gift” aptly expresses love of neighbor. [Col. 0347C] For among all gifts, that gift is rightly called and is the best gift by which a person, casting aside all bitterness and deceit, can love his neighbor with a gentle heart and can also wish and desire for his neighbor, with a simple heart, the good which he loves to be done to himself. But “every perfect gift” fittingly signifies the love of God, which belongs only to the perfect; for all people can have love of neighbor, but only the perfect ascend to the love of God. Peter did indeed have the good gift, because, as no bitterness of hatred or envy reproached his holy conscience, he loved all people with a pure and simple heart. But he did not yet have the perfect gift, while he loved himself more than God and, at the voice of a single maidservant, denied Christ because he feared to die for him.

It is well said, moreover: “From above.” For the twofold gift of the love of God and neighbor is truly from above, because the holy angels and the blessed souls of the elect, who are above, who are in heaven, have received from God both these gifts. Loving God himself above all things and burning with mutual charity toward one another, they can admit nothing contrary either to the one love or to the other. And although it is from above, it is also said to be descending, because almighty God distributes this very gift also in this life to his chosen and beloved children, when by his sweet inspiration he advances and kindles them both toward love of himself and toward love of their neighbors. Therefore, when he says “descending,” he admonishes us [Col. 0348A] that, when we perceive in ourselves this gift of love of God or neighbor, we should humbly ascribe it not to our own merits but to the gratuitous goodness of him from whom it descends.

And note that he does not say, “Descending from God,” or “from the Creator,” or “from the Almighty,” but “descending from the Father.” For in this word there is great consolation: the marvelous and inestimable compassion of almighty God toward us sinners is shown. For he is our Father, that good and merciful Father who always has a fatherly affection for his children. Just as some good father is at times troubled and moved with greater concern and compassion for one weak and frail little child than for those who are healthy and can stand on their own, so almighty God, our sweet Father, stoops and has compassion, with a special sweetness of mercy, [Col. 0348B] upon his weak children—that is, sinners. For he is that Father who has many children: he has the healthy, and he has the weak. The sound children are the righteous and innocent; the weak and frail children are miserable sinners. And although he provides the protection of fatherly love for both, the righteous and sinners alike, still he watches with a more abundant regard of compassion over those who are weak, who have fallen from true health by sinning, in order to save them.

And he fittingly says, “descending from the Father of lights.” For in himself there is unfailing light, everlasting light; but in us there is effective light—light, I mean, that enlightens and enkindles—for it enlightens us unto knowledge and kindles us unto love. And that we may know more fully [Col. 0348C] and perfectly his manifold mercy toward us, the Apostle further adds and says:

“With whom there is no change, nor shadow of turning.” Although these words are to be understood in the sense that he, according to the excellence of his divinity, is never changed and is never overshadowed by that eternal brightness of splendor which he possesses not only according to divinity but also in his humanity, according to the Prophet’s words: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:28), they may also be understood thus: although we often change away from filial love and from the filial reverence which we owe him, he nevertheless never changes away from the sweetness of his fatherhood, from that inestimable mercy which he has toward us. For since he knows himself to be Father, he loves those who are his children, whom he predestined to become heirs of his kingdom, even when they lie in sins; for he does not regard them as they then are when they commit sins and serve vices, but as they will be when, after their fall, they rise stronger and more perfect. For, to speak boldly, when Peter denied him and when David committed the crimes of adultery and murder together, God, pious and merciful, was not changed by their offense away from that sweetness of his mercy by which he loved the former before his denial and the latter before the guilt of adultery and murder, when he said: “I have found for myself a man according to my heart.” For he looked upon them mercifully with the provident eye of his mercy, not as they then were but as they would be. [Col. 0349A] Therefore no human sin, however grave, can change that marvelous affection of his fatherhood toward us who are to be adopted as children of God by eternal predestination.

Rightly, moreover, after saying, “with whom there is no change,” he adds, “nor shadow of turning.” We miserable ones, we sinners, are overshadowed, as it were, by certain turnings arising from the misery of our mutability. Thus, according to the Prophet, who says: “He will praise you when you do him good” (Ps. 48:19), when prosperity comes we love God; when adversity follows, we withdraw from the love of God. When all things are available according to our wishes, we serve the Lord cheerfully and devoutly; when something is adverse, we grow weary in God’s service as though affected by a kind of tedium. [Col. 0349B] But the shadow of this turning does not fall upon God, because with one and the same fatherly affection and sweetness he loves all of us who are predestined to life: when we are unable to love, when we do good, and when we are unable to do good. For he knows those whom he has chosen; he knows what those now lying in sins and serving sin will afterward become through his grace.

No person’s feeling suffices to know and investigate such great kindness and mercy of almighty God toward us miserable creatures; no person’s understanding can comprehend it. For the effective cause of so great a mercy is God’s will alone, God’s inestimable and gratuitous goodness. [Col. 0349C] Seeing this, the blessed Apostle aptly adds: “For willingly,” he says, “he begot us by the word of truth, that we may be a certain beginning of his creation.” He says “willingly,” surely, because he begot us for himself as children not through any preceding merits of ours, but solely by his own will and his own merciful goodness. And how did he beget us? Certainly not by the generation through which earthly fathers beget children, but by the word of truth. The Word of truth is the Son of God; the word of truth is the word of his faith which he gave us, by which we believe him to be the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages; to have descended, at the end of time, to the depths of our mortality; to have suffered, died, and been buried in the humanity assumed for us; to have risen and ascended, and now to sit at the right hand of the Father; and to be coming at the end of the ages to judge the human race.

But since we have heard how he begot us, let us also see for what purpose he begot us: namely, “that we may be a certain beginning of his creation.” Heaven, earth, sea, and whatever is in them—all are God’s creation. Humankind is the beginning of this creation, for humankind stands above all these things and holds dominion over them all. For whatever was created was created for humanity. Thus, in the mutability of this life we are the beginning of God’s creation; in eternal life we shall be the consummation of God’s creation. For here, by the word of truth through which we are begotten as children of God, we are in some way initiated into that glory of blessedness in which, when consummated in the life to come [Col. 0350A] and transformed into perfect children of God, we shall glory eternally with Christ without failing.

But because blessed James addressed this epistle not universally to all people but to the tribes of Israel—that is, to the perfect, who strive by devout living to attain the vision of God into which they have been initiated—after this lofty presentation of his teaching he adds: “You know, my most beloved brethren.” As if he said: You yourselves know the things I write to you; yet I write them to you so that you may always be ready and diligent to do and preserve what you know. What it is that can help and stir them toward this observance, he immediately shows when he adds: “But let every person be swift to hear, [Col. 0350B] slow to speak, and slow to anger.” Although one may often hear what, once heard, not only does no good but even does harm, “let every person be swift to hear” signifies, as we judge, not every kind of hearing, but the hearing of the word of God, the word of truth through which we are begotten as children of God. For whoever does not know and believe this word of truth cannot in any way be saved. It is as if he said: Let every person who desires to be numbered among the children of God show himself eager and diligent to hear the teaching of God’s word, so that through continual hearing he may learn what he ought to know, believe, or teach concerning God. When, by the enlightening grace of God, he has learned this, let him labor and strive to remain humbly within himself, lest the desire for preeminence creep in.

For the Apostle teaches us this in the following words when he says: “But slow to speak.” One ought always to be swift to hear and to learn, through continual attention to the word of God, what one ought to know or believe concerning God; but one ought to be slow to speak—that is, to preach and teach—lest one ever presume to claim or even desire for oneself the place of preaching, that is, the place of preeminence. [Col. 0350C]

But if, by the ordering of almighty God and an ecclesiastical calling, he is raised to a place of governance, the Apostle immediately shows what manner of person he ought to show himself in the seat and office of Christ, when he adds: “And slow to anger.” Why, passing over other vices such as pride, avarice, [Col. 0350D] and the like, which sometimes creep even upon good prelates, did he name anger alone? Surely because he saw that this vice sometimes prevails most strongly among prelates. Anger is the love of revenge. Therefore, whoever desires worthily to preside in Christ’s place and stead should strive to be not hasty but slow to anger, and never presume in God’s judgment to avenge his own injury. For the eye of the mind is blinded by the love of revenge, so that it does not see God’s righteousness. Hence it follows:

“For the anger of a man does not work the righteousness of God.” There are three kinds of righteousness: the righteousness of God, the righteousness of man, and the righteousness of the devil—if, indeed, one may say that the devil can possess any righteousness. God’s righteousness is to return good for evil; human righteousness is to return good [Col. 0351A] for good and evil for evil; the devil’s righteousness is always to return evil for good. However greatly we provoke God’s anger against us by our evils, nevertheless, from his innate goodness and mercy by which he loves the human race, his righteousness always answers our evils with good. Always ready and prepared to spare and forgive, he overcomes our evils with his mercy. But human righteousness is not such: it returns good for good and evil for evil, loving those who love it and meeting those who do it good by doing good in return. But the devil’s righteousness is always to return evil for good, because he wearies by temptation all people whatsoever who labor for God by doing good and living justly, in order to hinder them; he pursues them in order to cast them down and overthrow them. [Col. 0351B] Therefore whoever, sitting in God’s seat, seeks not the things that are God’s but his own and willingly avenges his own injuries, not only does not work the righteousness of God, but is shown to be altogether contrary to God’s righteousness.

To enable us to avoid this vice, which makes us opposed to the righteousness of God, the Apostle again admonishes us in what follows: “Wherefore,” he says, “putting away all uncleanness and abundance of malice, receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.” Every uncleanness which defiles and stains the human heart is pride of mind, as Scripture testifies when it says: “Every one who exalts his heart is unclean before God.” But abundance of malice is the effect of an evil will. [Col. 0351C] Therefore, since anger—that is, the love of revenge—arises from the swelling of pride, the Apostle rightly says: “Wherefore, putting away all uncleanness.” It is as though he said: In order that you may practise the righteousness of God, which is contrary to the righteousness of man and contrary to the righteousness of the devil—that is, in order that, conformed to the righteousness of God, you may render not only good for good but also good for evil to those who sin against you—it is necessary that you cast away every pride which makes you unclean before God; lest perhaps, if anger, namely the love of revenge for injuries inflicted upon you, creep in, the abundance of malice should ever so overcome you that you fail to guard against bringing your will, opposed to God, into effect—which is truly an abundance of malice.

When you have done this, that is, when you have been perfectly humbled and made conformed to the righteousness of God, “receive,” [Col. 0351D] he says, “the word.” What word, or what kind of word? “The word implanted in you with meekness.” The Word implanted in us with meekness is the Word incarnate for us: the Word of the Father, the Son of the Father. But how or when was this Word implanted in us with meekness? Certainly in the Passion, where his meekness was truly made manifest. For although he was incarnate for us, although for thirty years and more he dwelt with us in the world, he was not yet perfectly implanted in us. But on that night on which he willed to be delivered up to death for us—namely, at his Last Supper, in which he consecrated and handed over to us the most precious mystery of his body and blood—he began in some manner to be implanted in us. Yet he was perfectly implanted in us with meekness [Col. 0352A] when, like a meek lamb led to sacrifice, he offered himself upon the altar of the cross to God the Father for us. For his meekness was his wondrous and immeasurable patience, because, in order to redeem us, he patiently endured for us insults, spitting, blows, scourges, and finally the ignominy of the cross.

Therefore, in order that anyone who bears Christ’s office in the Church may be able to receive this Word implanted in us with meekness, let him, having cast away, as we have said, every uncleanness and abundance of malice, continually strive to set Christ’s patience against his own impatience. When you have done this, he says, “receive the word implanted with meekness,” because God the Father, God the Spirit, and he himself who is the Word of God, the Son, will give you such a word [Col. 0352B] as can save your souls—I mean the souls of those entrusted to you—because whatever you then preach, whatever you teach concerning the incarnate Word of God for the edification of your neighbours and the salvation of the souls committed to you, you will be able to proclaim confidently, beneficially, and fruitfully. May that same Word, the Word of the Father, Jesus Christ our Lord, grant that we too may worthily receive the Word implanted in us with meekness, preserve it when received, and be able to imitate it—he who lives and reigns with the same Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

489. HOMILY LIII. FOR FRIDAY AFTER THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF THE FIRST PASCHAL SEASON.

[Col. 0352C] “My little children, yet a little while I am with you” (John 13).

Since these words—the words, I say, of that beloved disciple who reclined upon the Lord’s breast—are full of mystical mysteries, it seems by no means devoid of mystery that, in this discourse which the Saviour delivered to his disciples at the Last Supper before his Passion, he called them not sons but little children, as we find at the beginning of this Gospel reading: “My little children, yet a little while I am with you.” For when he calls them not sons, as though strong and steadfast, but little children, that is, as though weak and tender, he indicates the tenderness of the slight love with which they still loved him. For they were not yet sons, but little children. Although they loved him with filial love as a Father, [Col. 0352D] nevertheless this same love was in some sense tender and slight, because they were not yet able to suffer reproaches and insults for the Lord, and loved the world’s prosperity more than its adversity. But why they were not yet sons but little children, Truth itself, which speaks these things, openly indicates when it says:

“Yet a little while I am with you.” Therefore, I say, you are still little children, as though small and weak; therefore you do not yet love me, your Lord and Father, with the great and perfect love of strong sons, because I, without whom you can do nothing, am still with you not much but only a little—that is, I have not yet bestowed upon you much and great strength of my love; I have not yet strengthened you with the manifold [Col. 0353A] might of the Holy Spirit for enduring the adversities of this world.

“You will seek me; and, as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I go, you cannot come,’ so I say to you now.” You will seek, I say, me who am your salvation; you will seek me, the Saviour of your souls, by believing faithfully in me and living justly and piously. Yet you cannot come where I go so long as you flee contempt of the world, so long as you love prosperity more than adversity. Hence, as I said to the Jews—as to that carnal people who sought and loved me carnally, to whom I promised not eternal but temporal things, namely that they would triumph over their enemies and abound in temporal wealth—so I now say to you also: because, so long as you are carnal, so long as you love me not spiritually but carnally and seek temporal prosperity, [Col. 0353B] you will not be able to be strong and steadfast in enduring the ignominy of the Passion. “And where I go, you cannot come.” Behold, I now go to be seized and bound by the Jews; to suffer spitting, blows, scourges, reproaches, insults, and mockery; and finally to be condemned to a most shameful death. But when you see me about to suffer all these things, you cannot come with me, for you will leave me alone, because you are still weak and feeble for enduring Passion and ignominious death. But in order that you may attain steadfastness in enduring the Passion, I set before you lesser deeds to perform, through which you may eventually reach greater things.

“A new commandment,” he says, “I give to you, that you love one another as I have loved you.” First it must be noted why he called the commandment of love new, when in the Old Testament he had also given this same commandment to his faithful. Love is rightly called a new commandment, we believe, because there is no virtue at all through which the inward person is so renewed, through which the mind’s inner sweetness is so increased and restored; and conversely, there is no vice whatsoever which so darkens the eye of the heart by its importunity, or so obstructs the mind from every intent of pure prayer, as hatred. For if a person is proud or lustful, he often rebukes, laments, and repents of that same pride and lust within himself. But hatred alone, when it has possessed the human heart in conquest, so devastates, disturbs, and [Col. 0353D] unsettles it that it can offer God no sacrifices at all of fruitful prayer. But because, as has been said, love alone especially renews the human spirit and kindles and strengthens it for doing good, the kindly Master, in provident mercy, wished to set before his disciples, still weak, the new commandment of love, through which they might be renewed and stirred toward better things. “A new commandment,” he says, “I give to you, that you love one another as I have loved you.” It is as though he said: If you are not yet able patiently to bear evils and reproaches inflicted on you by others, nevertheless, by loving one another, inflict no evil upon anyone, hate no one, and take care, out of love, to do for others the good which you wish others to do for you. Thus from this slight love of neighbour you will attain that greatest love, so that you may even [Col. 0354A] rejoice to endure reproaches and insults for my name.

Nor should what he says be passed over: “That you love one another as I have loved you.” The Apostle Paul indicates more plainly how we ought to love one another as Christ loved us, saying: “Walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself for us” (Eph. 5:2). Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Because he laid down his life for us, we too ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (John 3:16). With the words that follow, he invites his disciples to this imitation of love, saying:

“By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” Since there are many works of virtue pleasing to the Lord and fitting for Christ’s disciples to observe and fulfil, why did eternal Wisdom establish love alone as a singular sign by which he wished his disciples especially to be known? Faith, hope, self-restraint, chastity, constancy in prayer, vigils, fasts, and the other observances of holy service are indeed good and necessary for all who are to be saved. Yet all these may commonly belong to bad persons as well as good. But love alone is a distinctive virtue, through which Christ’s disciples are recognized, so that they deserve to be not only disciples but even most chosen sons. And because the most blessed Peter was to be recognized not only among the disciples but also among the chosen sons, he is rightly believed to have responded, in the person of all who desire to attain the perfection of true love, as is immediately added.

“Simon Peter says to him.” Simon—that is, “obedient”—may be said of every faithful person when, according to the voice of the commanding Lord, he begins to have love, however slight, toward his neighbour, even though he cannot yet suffer hard and bitter things for the Lord. He also becomes Peter—that is, “knowing”—when he sees that he lacks the steadfastness required to endure the Passion, though he nevertheless strives, by God’s mercy, eventually to attain it. But although Peter did not yet possess this steadfastness, this strength of mind, he nevertheless believed that he possessed it. Therefore he confidently said to the Lord who was about to suffer:

“Lord, where are you going?” He desired to follow his Lord and Master as he went to the Passion and death, because he still did not know his own weakness. But the merciful Master sought to call him back from this ill-considered intention. Therefore, answering him with gentle admonition, he said:

“Where I go, you cannot follow me now; but you will follow afterwards.” Where I go—namely, to be bound, scourged, mocked, spat upon, struck with blows, crucified, and to die—your weak intention of mind seeks to follow me. But what you do not know, I who know all things know: you cannot follow me now, because I have not yet strengthened you with my power to endure all these things. “But you will follow afterwards.” Afterwards, I say, you will follow the footsteps of my Passion and death, when the grace of the Holy Spirit descending from above [Col. 0355A] fills and strengthens you. Then you will not only follow, that is, imitate, me, your Lord and Master, in the things which I am about to suffer; you too will suffer certain new and harsher things. For I, fastened to the cross, shall commend my soul into the Father’s hands by my own will and power, with my head raised upward and my feet turned toward the earth. But you, because of profound humility, choosing as it were a more difficult death, will ask that your head be bent downward and your feet raised upward; and so, consumed by a more prolonged torment, you will glorify me by your precious death. By this glorifying death the most blessed Peter truly followed his Lord and Master and truly showed the great steadfastness of perfect love. But because we, weak and frail, cannot attain such perfection, let us strive with all earnestness, aided by his merits and prayers, so to love our neighbours in truth that he who is true love may one day deign to recognize us among his chosen disciples: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

494. HOMILY LIV. FOR THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER THE FIRST PASCHAL SEASON.

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16).

That faithful witness and true witness, full of grace and truth, namely the true Only-begotten Son of God the Father, wishing to make us certain and assured concerning the Spirit and confidence of his promise, confirms this same promise as though by an oath with these words, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” For in repeating this affirmative expression twice at the beginning of this reading, he gives us the firmest certainty of his promise: that if we ask God the Father for anything in the name of his beloved Son, we should believe that we shall without delay receive the fruit of our petition from the generous hand of God the Father. For he says:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you.” We truly ask in the name of the Lord and Saviour if we know God the Father by loving and confessing him with the sincerity of true faith, as it is written: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). He is truly said to believe unto righteousness who, in the time of temptation, does not abandon by denying his faith that faith which he held by faithfully confessing it in time of peace. Again, in another way no less salutarily, we ask in the Saviour’s name if, after the example of that same Saviour, we strive to be truly humble amid prosperity and gentle and patient amid adversity. Holy David prayed to be saved by this sweet and saving name, saying: “O God, save me in thy name” (Ps. 53:3). Hence we too, desiring to be saved by this same name, daily pray in the Lord’s Prayer, saying: “Hallowed be thy name” (Matt. 6:9). The Saviour’s name is truly sanctified and honoured in us when we are not exalted by prosperity, not cast down by adversity; and if we ask anything in this manner, praying in humility and patience, we shall without delay receive it from the Father of lights, either here or in the future. But those who neglect to observe this manner of petition do not ask fruitfully or truly in the Saviour’s name. The same Saviour next addresses them with a gentle exhortation, saying:

“Until now you have asked nothing in my name.” You have not yet come to this manner of humility and patience; therefore you have not yet sought, by truly asking in my name, in my faith and love, the joys of eternal salvation.

495. “Ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.” Ask, I say, as those truly humble and patient; [Col. 0356B] ask, not raised up by prosperity nor embittered by adversity. And, asking thus, you shall receive—not something earthly or mutable, not something passing or corruptible, but that your joy may be full: namely, that ineffable and unending joy when you shall behold, in perpetual unchangeableness, the most longed-for glory of the highest Trinity; when among innumerable multitudes rejoicing you shall delight in unchangeable happiness. But because the inestimable joy of eternal gladness surpasses every human understanding, whatever incarnate Truth promises his chosen ones in this Gospel reading concerning the rewards of future joys, he declares that he speaks entirely in proverbs. For he says:

“These things I have spoken to you in proverbs.” For just as a proverb sounds one thing and signifies another, so very many exceedingly glorious and joyful things have been spoken and written concerning the splendour of the eternal vision and the unspeakable blessedness of the elect; yet the blessed eyes of all the blessed will see other things far greater and more joyful, they who deserve to be co-heirs and fellow-partakers with their Lord and Creator. Then truly no proverbs will be spoken to God’s elect, for all things will be naked and open to them. Hence follows:
