“The hour comes when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs.” That desirable hour, the hour of joy and exultation, comes when the eternal Son of God the Father will speak to his most beloved children not in proverbs—that is, not in the mystical utterances of Scripture—concerning the hope [Col. 0356D] and glory of eternal immortality; but, he says, “I shall openly declare to you concerning my Father.” He will openly declare God the Father to his elect when, perfectly refashioned into the likeness of God, they shall contemplate with unveiled face what, how great, and of what kind is the splendour and magnificence of the Father’s majesty.

“In that day,” he says, “you shall ask in my name.” What do the elect ask in the name of the Saviour on the day of eternity, on the day of peace and security, they who have already received the fruit of their petition and labour? Since they already possess that highest and true good without end, what do they labour to gain by further asking? Their petition is their fervent love and desire; for with most ardent charity they always desire to see their desirable Lord and King. There is also in this life for God’s elect a day exceedingly great and solemn: namely, the day of divine contemplation, when that gracious Spirit of truth, acting as a merciful mediator between beloved and beloved in the illuminated bridal chamber of the heart, suggests by sweet inspiration to the loving beloved what she ought most earnestly to ask from her beloved. For this same beloved, made as it were bold by a heavenly longing, opens to that beloved, as to a faithful physician and intimate friend, in this hour of contemplation, through true repentance and confession, every wound of her hidden sickness, every infection, I say, of the wounding sin by which she recognizes, with conscience as witness, that she has been wounded and hurt. When he lays the hand of healing grace, the hand of saving mercy, upon each wound, [Col. 0357B] he will make her safe from every deadly infection of sins. In that day indeed, in that illumination of the heart, the elect truly ask in the Saviour’s name; for whatever they ask thus enlightened and divinely inspired undoubtedly concerns the true salvation of the soul, and such a petition can never be ineffective or fruitless. Those who ask thus in the present and receive in the future, as has been said, the fruit of their petition need no further help of intercession, since they enjoy unchangeably the joy of full gladness. Hence follows:

“And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father concerning you.” It is as though he said: I, the chosen Only-begotten Son of the Father, do not further intervene by asking God the Father on your behalf—for you, I say, my co-heirs already joined to me and reigning with me in eternity—because I know that I have reconciled him to you through faithful intercession, when I endured for you many miseries of assumed humanity, and at last, nailed to the cross, offered prayers and tears with a loud cry and laid down my soul for you. And now, because you have full and everlasting peace and security, there will be no need at all to pray for you.

496. “For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came forth from God.” The order of the words should be noted. For when incarnate Wisdom had first set forth in a sweet account the innumerable benefits of his mercy—how, by suffering and dying for us, he had asked God [Col. 0357D] the Father, and how, by asking thus, he had reconciled us to that Father—he immediately declares that those who love him and believe in him are loved by God the Father. “For the Father himself,” he says, “loves you, because you have loved me and have believed.” By these words the Son of the Father plainly indicates that God the Father does not love those who believe in the humility, Passion, and death of his Son merely by confessing them with words, but those who, believing and loving them—that is, persevering in faith and charity—desire to imitate them. For neither faith without charity nor charity without faith avails, as the blessed Apostle James says: “Faith without works,” that is, without charity, “is dead” (Jas. 2:20). Likewise, that charity cannot please God without faith, the same Apostle indicates when he says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). Therefore let one who desires to be loved and made blessed by God the Father strive both to love by believing and to believe by loving. But what are the things which one who is to be saved ought to believe and love, except those which Truth itself goes on to enumerate?

“Because,” he says, “I came forth from God. I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.” “I came forth from God,” he says, existing eternally as consubstantial with the Father. “I came forth from the Father,” assuming flesh through obedience to the Father; “and I came into the world,” being born of the Virgin Mother. “Again I leave the world,” by dying; “and I go to the Father,” by ascending. When, before his Passion or death, he announced these mysteries of faith to his beloved disciples, the Evangelist briefly summarizes what they conceived in mind concerning them and what they said in common reply:

“His disciples say to him.” Throughout the whole course of this discourse, whenever we read the disciples’ answering words, we nowhere find them replying to their beloved Master with so unanimous a declaration. This shared utterance plainly indicates that, through his inspiration, their minds had come to a common agreement: that they lovingly recognized with devout heart the work of mercy, the work of human redemption, which was to be accomplished through his Passion and death, and that they no longer desired, through a certain carnal affection, that the cup of the Passion which he was about to drink should be removed from him. Hence, though troubled and saddened, they say to him:

[Col. 0358C] “Behold, now you speak openly and say no proverb.” Behold, now you, noble Word of the Father, speak plainly, because you declare that you are now to suffer and die for the salvation of humankind; “and you say no proverb,” because you, the almighty Word, the eternal Word dwelling with God the Father before the ages, are the one concerning whom and for whom all things which the oracles of patriarchs and prophets once foretold, and all things which the legal sacrifices prefigured, were spoken and done as certain proverbs. And behold, you, the Word, will make these same proverbs cease, because through you grace and truth were made.

“Now we know that you know all things.” As God’s not knowing is God’s rejecting, so God’s knowing is God’s loving. “Now,” they say, “we know; now we have truly recognized; recognizing, we love: because you, Lord, in whom goodness is natural, know—that is, love—all things: all races of humankind, namely not Jews only but Gentiles also; and you hate none of the things which you have made, but have ordained to save all through your Passion and death.

“And you have no need that anyone should question you.” The Lord’s questioning is his admonishing a human being concerning salvation; human questioning, however, is the seeking of one’s own salvation. By his questioning the Lord wished to call Adam, transgressor of the commandment, back to the way of salvation and repentance, when after the Fall he called to him with a question, saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). Although Adam, being questioned, refused to be admonished, nevertheless the very questioning of the calling Lord was a kind of admonition to salvation. And because, as we have said, human questioning is an inquiry into one’s own salvation, the disciples rightly say to the Lord who is now about to suffer: “And you have no need [Col. 0359A] that anyone should question you.” It is as though they said: Although it is necessary for a person always to inquire after his salvation and always to be solicitous for the redemption of his soul, yet now you, Lord Redeemer, have no need that anyone should question you—that is, that anyone should rouse you through entreaty and prayer to accomplish the salvation of humankind. For you came willingly to this work, and have now resolved to complete this work of salvation. You have no need—no such work, I say, has been imposed upon you by God the Father that, once it has been completed, anyone ought to despair of his salvation or doubt the hope of eternal happiness. For the work imposed upon you, most gracious lover of humankind, will be salvation and redemption for those who belong to eternal life.

“And you have no need that anyone should question you.” A mortal human being indeed has need, from you, most gracious Saviour and lover of humankind, to seek the remedy of salvation with tears and prayers; and you, who know all and acknowledge all, and behold the frailty of human mortality with the eye of your mercy, have no need that anyone should make you mindful, by warning and exhortation, as though you were an ignorant and inexperienced person, forgetful and unmindful of human misery and weakness. For such is the sweetness of your goodness toward us that you can never forget our need and tribulation.

“In this,” they say, “we have known that you came forth from God.” In this ineffable work of mercy we have known that you descended from the bosom of the Father in order to raise us up; that you assumed the frailties of our mortality in order to heal our pains. For this ineffable mercy and compassion, to you be praise and glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

500. HOMILY LV. A SECOND HOMILY FOR THE SAME SUNDAY.

“Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (Jas. 1).

The chosen and beloved Apostle of Christ, blessed James, made himself so especially familiar and close to God through the merit of holiness and righteousness that, alone among his fellow Apostles, he deserved to be called the Lord’s brother. For although the merciful Master so loved and honoured all his disciples because of the holiness and innocence of their lives that he called them brethren generally, as he says through the Psalmist, “I will declare thy name unto my brethren” (Ps. 21:23), this man alone is honoured and exalted with this singular dignity, that everywhere in Scripture he is called the Lord’s brother. That same brother of the Lord, namely blessed James, in today’s reading admonished and instructed the people still situated in Judaism, who understood and fulfilled the Law they had received carnally and, because of their knowledge of the Law, vainly exalted themselves above the Gentiles who did not know the Lord’s Law. He taught them not to believe that they would be saved merely as hearers of the word, hearers of the written Law, but rather, passing from Judaism to the faith of Christianity, to strive to understand and fulfil the Law spiritually. What he then admonished and taught to the carnal Jews, living carnally, he now admonishes and teaches in the same words to us, who are spiritual and ought to be so.

“Be,” he says, “doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.” By God’s mercy we are indeed the people whom the Lord chose from the world, that we might be hearers of the word, hearers of divine knowledge. Therefore we must strive to be not hearers only of the word but doers also, that we may labour most earnestly to fulfil by deeds the knowledge of the divine Law which we frequently hear, read, and understand, lest, by hearing only and not doing, we deceive ourselves. It is indeed good and necessary to know and hear what ought to be done. But one who neglects to do what he knows and hears undoubtedly deceives himself, because he cannot be saved by hearing alone or knowledge alone. “For if anyone,” he says, “is a hearer and not a doer, he shall be compared to a man considering the countenance of his birth in a mirror.” If we wish to take simply the observation made in a mirror, we know that it passes quickly and is speedily surrendered to forgetfulness. Thus that person may not unfittingly be compared to a man considering himself in a mirror but not retaining for long in memory what he is like, who hears and receives the word of God with joy but becomes a forgetful hearer in doing it. Yet it is incredible that that chosen and perfect disciple of Christ, whom almighty God filled with such great knowledge and wisdom, should have said these things so simply, as we have already noted, and should have intended no loftier meaning in these words. Therefore let us examine these same words according to the spiritual sense which we have begun to discuss.

By the man considering himself in a mirror, Adam the first-formed may fittingly be understood; by the countenance of his birth we may understand the excellence and beauty of his creation. For just as the human face is the more eminent and beautiful part of the body, and we possess almost all the external senses—sight, hearing, taste, and smell—in the face alone, so Adam himself, born not from a human being but created from the earth, possessed a singular excellence and beauty of immortality, wisdom, and understanding, and could have possessed them perpetually had he not become a transgressor of God’s commands. Nevertheless, before the Fall he saw and considered this same excellence of his creation in a mirror—that is, in the awareness of his own heart—because he could feel in himself no weakness, no desire for sin, no fear of death.

The woman whom the Lord fashioned from Adam’s own rib can also be understood by the mirror; in her he considered more fully and perfectly the state of his condition. Therefore, when the Lord brought this same woman to him, looking upon her he said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23). What is stronger than bone in the human body, what more fragile than flesh? In this mirror, that is, in the sight of the woman, he considered, we believe, the strength and immortality [Col. 0361A] which he possessed before the Fall; perhaps by a prophetic spirit he foresaw the frailty and misery that would come after the sin of disobedience upon both himself and the woman. Thus it is as though he said: This which is now bone in me—now, I say, in the state in which I presently am—is in some sense bone, because it is strong and firm in me and in the woman taken from my bones, because the power and strength of immortality and incorruption are still in us. But if afterward I should be changed through disobedience into another state, that which is now bone of my bones, that which is now strong and firm in me, will then be flesh of my flesh, because it will be weak and fragile; because frailty and corruption will be in me myself and in this woman who has received flesh from my flesh. And because Adam, still full of God’s wisdom, foresaw by rational understanding that this frailty and mutability would come not only upon himself but also upon the whole human race, he fittingly adds in what follows: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). “Therefore,” because it will be so: strength and frailty will both be in a human being; now bone from bones, then flesh from flesh will arise; now a person will be firm and strong and perform works of virtue and strength, then again return to weakness and frailty. Therefore, I say, because it is so, it will be necessary for a person to leave his father, which is the vanity of the world, and his mother, which is pleasure, from which weakness and frailty are born, so that he may lawfully cleave to his wife, that is, to his flesh. [Col. 0361C] Holy David rejoices and glories in the Lord that they have left him—this father and this mother—saying: “For my father and my mother have left me” (Ps. 26:10). For if the inward person neither seeks nor loves this father, that is, the vanity of the world, and the outward person despises and rejects that mother, that is, the pleasure of the flesh, then he will be able lawfully to cleave to his wife; then he will be able lawfully to supply his flesh with what is necessary. For whether he eats or drinks, or does anything else necessary for his body, all will turn to his salvation and all will have regard to God’s honour.

“And the two,” he says, “shall be one flesh.” What two shall be one flesh? The inward and outward person will be united in one flesh and will agree and consent with one another so harmoniously that rational understanding will tend toward the one thing necessary—that is, toward seeking God—and the flesh, cooperating well, will seek and desire the same. It follows:

“For he considered himself, and went away, and immediately forgot what manner of man he was.” What is considering if not investigating the truth? Adam considered himself and truly investigated by rational understanding that he was strong and immortal in the state in which he then was, but would be weak and mortal if he became a transgressor of God’s commands. Yet, alas, he went away—that is, he departed from obedience to God—and believed and consented to the serpent suggesting disobedience. “And immediately,” he says, “he forgot what manner of man he was.” What did miserable Adam forget when he had been deceived and made disobedient? Did he forget that he had been and ought to have remained in paradise? He forgot, indeed, the strength and incorruption which he had before the Fall—what he had been like, how strong, steadfast, and robust he had been. After he consigned to forgetfulness the command of the Lord commanding him, he immediately felt his own flesh to be disobedient and resistant, just as he himself had become disobedient to his Creator. Hence he and the woman at once, ashamed before one another, sewed together fig leaves with which they covered the nakedness of their bodies.

They also felt in heart and body the fear of death, pain, and toil—things they had not yet experienced before the sin of disobedience. For there are some to whom that great and grievous punishment which followed upon such disobedience seems [Col. 0362B] excessive, because they committed no evil, they say, except that they presumed merely to eat from the forbidden tree. Let us therefore see how great an evil, how great a punishment, proceeded from this upon all human beings; and then we may know what kind of disobedience it was, **504** and how grave. For no one is so rich or powerful, no one so wretched and needy, as to be able to live without toil and pain; no one so holy or innocent as not to feel in his members a law opposing his mind.

There are also some who, following the example of disobedient Adam, not only disdain to keep the commandments of God which they have received, but also make light of and despise the good things divinely bestowed upon them. Yet by God’s just judgment such temptation sometimes comes upon them that they lose and forfeit the good things [Col. 0362C] granted to them through God’s mercy, so that they can scarcely—or not at all—sweetly recall to mind those very goods which they have lost.

“But whoever has looked intently into the law of perfect freedom,” he says, “and has continued in it, being not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this person shall be blessed in what he does.” The law of perfect freedom may quite suitably be understood as the life and manner of life of Jesus Christ, who alone among human beings was so free from sin, so perfect in all his conduct, that he could incur not even the slightest stain of sin in thought, word, or deed, since he did not will even to be able to sin.

But ought we so to look into this law of such great freedom as to suppose that we can imitate [Col. 0362D] it in such a way that, in thinking, speaking, and acting, we commit no sin whatever? Has the Lord commanded this of us? Is there not something else which he commanded us, which each person, if willing, can fulfil? “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). The Lord showed himself meek and patient above all people when he endured spittle, blows, and scourges with wondrous gentleness and wondrous patience; he showed himself truly humble when, against so many insults and so many false witnesses, he never answered with a word of pride.

If anyone has thus looked into and read this law of Christ’s patience and humility, so as always to remember to imitate it and not to be a forgetful hearer, that person shall be blessed in what he does, because from the deed—not from hearing—of a good [Col. 0363A] work he shall obtain the fruit of eternal blessedness.

**505** But lest anyone should believe that, by merely abstaining from evil and attending to good works, he had done enough for perfection of life, while taking no care for guarding mouth and heart, he immediately adds this admonition: “If anyone thinks himself religious, and does not restrain his tongue but deceives his heart, that person’s religion is vain.” Let no one think that he has done enough for true religion if he diligently exercises himself outwardly in good works, unless he also restrains his tongue from words of impatience and pride, and does not allow his heart to be deceived and scattered by empty and useless thoughts. For if anyone presents himself as devout in good works but neglects to keep watch in speech and thought, that person’s religion is vain. It is vain, I say, [Col. 0363B] because it quickly vanishes; and no religion of good works can be firm and stable if it lacks solidity through the guarding of mouth and heart. What religion ought to be, he plainly indicates in what follows:

“Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from this world.” This religion is pleasing and acceptable before God and the Father—our most sweet Father, I say—which is inwardly pure in intention and outwardly unstained in action: so that a person may not swell inwardly through pride of heart, nor seek outwardly, in pride, human praise for good works.

But although this religion is pure and undefiled, [Col. 0363C] a person cannot possess it without affliction—that is, without temptation. Therefore one must visit orphans and widows in this affliction. Orphans are those without father and mother, and widows are those whose husbands have died. By orphans we may understand our inward faculties; by widows, the outward works of the flesh. Our faculties are in some manner orphans, and the works of the flesh in some manner **506** widows, when they have forsaken that father and mother of whom we spoke above: namely, the vanity of the world and the pleasure of the flesh.

We ought to visit these orphans and widows in the affliction of temptation in this manner: in temptation we must come to their aid and help them, lest the vanity of the world prevail within through exaltation of mind, or the pleasure of the flesh cast us outward [Col. 0363D] through evil action. Concerning these orphans and widows the prophet Jeremiah said, not in lamentation but as if in congratulation: “We have become orphans without a father; our mothers are like widows” (Lam. 5:3). This is as though the faculties and works of a perfectly converted person should say to the Lord in thanksgiving: “Lord, through your mercy we have become orphans, because, with your help, we have forsaken our father, the vanity of the world, and our mother, the pleasure of the flesh. Now we are your orphans: we have you alone as Father, and rejoice beneath your motherly protection.”

Whoever, therefore, takes care to visit and assist these orphans and widows in temptation will be able to keep himself unstained from this world. John clearly indicates in his Epistle what is to be understood by “the world,” when he says: [Col. 0364A] “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16). One keeps oneself unstained from this world who strives, as far as possible, to avoid and overcome the stain of pride. We must therefore take care that, since the Lord willed us to be continual hearers of his word, we may also strive to be doers of that same word; and that, firmly holding in our hearts the pattern of humility which we display in habit and clothing, we may show it in words and works. May he deign to grant this: he who is the Word of God the Father, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns through endless ages of ages. Amen.

**507 HOMILY LVI. FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY WITHIN THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD, WHICH IS ALSO THE SIXTH AFTER EASTER**

[Col. 0364B]

“When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me; and you too will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning” (John 15).

This most holy Gospel reading is part of the discourse which the Lord gave to his disciples at his Last Supper, namely on that night when he was betrayed. There, among many sweet teachings of heavenly life, he sought to console and ease beforehand the grief and pain which they would suffer from his passion and death, by promising the coming of the Holy Spirit; as we heard at the beginning of this Gospel, where he says:

[Col. 0364C] “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me; and you too will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” This promise of the Lord was truly fulfilled in them when, after his Ascension, they were so flooded and illumined by the unheard-of and ineffable grace of the Holy Spirit that they confessed and preached the Lord’s name without fear, and nothing remained able to resist them.

Yet in this paternal promise he did not forget us either; for what he then promised to those most holy disciples, he promised in them and with them also to us and to all persons who imitate and follow them as far as they can.

[Col. 0364D] Their true imitators are all those who have perfectly renounced in heart and body the pleasures of this world, and who have placed all their hope and consolation in the goodness and mercy of God alone. To such persons he promises and sends his holy Spirit, the Paraclete, that he may be both the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of consolation.

He sends them the Spirit of truth when he inwardly illumines them, so that they begin **508** rightly and perfectly to recognize their transgressions and negligences; and, in considering the evils they have committed, they despise and make light even of what they have done well and rightly. They set themselves above no one, but submit themselves to all people in true humility of heart. After this inward consideration or self-knowledge, the same [Col. 0365A] Spirit of truth advances them to the knowledge of God, when, aided by his grace, they humbly recognize within themselves and render most humble thanks to God that he so mercifully and fatherly endured them in their folly and impiety, and that, according to his forgiveness and kindness, he reserved for them for so long a time for repentance and satisfaction.

This Spirit of truth is also for them the Paraclete, that is, the Spirit of consolation. For although it is grievous and difficult for a person thus to despise and humble oneself, perpetually recalling in penitence and tears one’s years and times in the bitterness of one’s soul, yet this very sorrow is mingled with a certain exultation and joy. For this bitterness concerning oneself becomes, as it were, a certain assurance of pardon and remission, and a hope [Col. 0365B] and consolation of everlasting salvation.

But, with these matters briefly set forth, let us consider the order of the words. For in God’s words nothing is disorderly, nothing uncomposed or superfluous. Where we cannot understand them, the defect is our weakness and ignorance; but where, by his own gift and mercy, we are able to perceive anything in them, there we recognize what a right order and what a perfect way of salvation they lay out and show to us.

**509** “When the Paraclete comes,” he says, “whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.” Who is he who speaks these things? Surely he who is called and is the Word of God the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ. That Word of God the Father truly sends, truly begets in the human heart the Spirit [Col. 0365C] of truth. Therefore it is necessary for one leaving the world always to attend to the teaching of the Word of God, gladly to hear God’s word, and carefully to keep it. For from it and through it one is taught and admonished where one has lived contrary to the divine will and one’s own salvation, and how uselessly one has passed all one’s days and years.

Those who do this undoubtedly receive the Spirit of truth, who truly becomes their Paraclete because he begets in them heavenly hope and heavenly consolation. But those who do not hear God’s word, or neglect to keep what they have heard, have in place of the Spirit of truth a spirit of falsehood. Deceived through it, they are so deluded that they reckon their very evil works to be good and just, while judging what is good to be evil.

[Col. 0365D] Spiritual persons, however, whose joy and exultation is to be continually refreshed by God’s word—these are truly blessed; these can receive the Spirit of truth. But this Spirit of truth begets in them the spirit of fear. For, instructed and admonished by God’s word, the more they acknowledge their sins in true humility, the more they begin to fear God, whom they despised and offended by sinning.

The spirit of fear is followed by the spirit of love, which the Lord seems aptly to signify in the following words when he says:

“Who proceeds from the Father.” The name *Father* is a word of sweetness and love, for it belongs properly to a father to act kindly and fatherly toward his children. Nor is it unfitting that this word, which [Col. 0366A] sounds sweet and loving, should signify the truly sweet and loving spirit of love. The Spirit of truth proceeds, as it were, from the Father when a person grieves and groans from the depths, not in fear, or because of fear of the future punishment deserved, but in filial love: grieving that, against the love and honour of his most kind Father—who bore with him so long in the sweetness of his compassion and bestowed so many and such great benefits upon his unworthy and undeserving sinner—he could commit so many enormities and offend the eyes of that Fatherhood beyond number.

Concerning this Spirit of truth, who so works through fear and love in God’s elect, the Lord fittingly adds:

“He will bear witness concerning me.” As if he said: When, through my gift and help, you have come from the spirit [Col. 0366B] of fear to the spirit of love, he bears witness to you concerning the things you have unjustly done against me; he makes known to you how many good things, which ought to have been done, you have omitted, and how many evils, which ought to have been avoided, you have committed. Nor do I think it unreasonable to understand the Lord’s words in this way, since a person can never truly know oneself as in the hour when one has come to the spirit of love. There one begins truly and perfectly to know not only one’s words and works, but also the desires and thoughts by which one has offended God.

Thus—yes, thus—when the spirit of love bears witness to God inexpressibly within the human heart, it can finally come about that what follows is fulfilled:

“And you,” he says, “will bear witness, because you have been with me from [Col. 0366C] the beginning.” A person truly bears witness to the Word of God when, taught and illumined by the spirit of love, one rightly recognizes that God’s word is justice and truth, while one’s whole life is injustice and falsehood. Or one bears witness to God in this way: when one truly and humbly reveals to God, with a penitent heart and voice, in prayer and confession, one’s sins and crimes which, through the testimony of the Holy Spirit, one knows inwardly within oneself.

The Lord immediately explains how a person can bear such witness to God, saying: “Because you have been with me from the beginning.” If we understand these words of the Lord literally, as though his disciples had been with him from his beginning—that is, from the time when he who was without beginning in divinity began to have a beginning in assumed humanity—we do not understand rightly, since he first chose and received them in the thirtieth year of his age. If **511** we say that the apostles themselves had been with the Lord from their own beginning, that is, from the outset of their birth, we are likewise mistaken. Therefore, if truth is to be preserved, we must understand these words of the Lord spiritually.

By “beginning” may be understood, as it seems to me, that which is truly the beginning and governing principle in a person: namely, the human spirit, wherein lies humanity’s dignity and honour, because there a person was made in God’s image and likeness. This I may not inappropriately call the beginning, since, according to the assertion of certain wise persons who know how to think and expound more deeply concerning God’s word, God first created the human being invisibly in the spirit in his own image and likeness, and afterwards visibly formed him from the visible material of the earth. Hence what was first created in a person may rightly be called the person’s beginning.

[Col. 0367A] This is the more excellent part of a person, the only part capable of divinity, the only part worthy for God to dwell in. Since God is spirit, he dwells not in human flesh but in the human spirit. Whoever, therefore, having despised this world’s pleasures, is so united to God in this part of oneself that in one’s spirit one seeks and loves nothing of this world, insofar as that is possible for a human being, apart from God—such a person is proved to be with God from the beginning. In such a person almighty God does not disdain continually to have his dwelling.

But because the more any of the elect strive to rise to God through zeal for a good manner of life, the greater the snares of temptation they suffer from God’s enemies, namely evil spirits, the following words teach us what we ought to do amid these temptations.

“These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you, that you may not be scandalized.” As if he said: So long as you are held down by a mortal body in the wretched exile of this world, you will always endure temptations from evil spirits lying in wait for your salvation. But I have spoken these things to you that you may not be scandalized. What is it to be scandalized except to provide an occasion for sin? We provide an occasion of sin to evil spirits when we yield in consent to the suggestions through which they tempt us.

**512** There is no person on earth from whom evil spirits restrain their hand, whom they do not dare to assail and weary with their various deceits and assaults. But according to this most salutary teaching of the Lord, we must always strive not to be scandalized. It is indeed impossible that we should not be tempted; it is unavoidable that we should sometimes take pleasure even in the sins by which we are tempted. But we must take the greatest care that the pleasure of sin is not followed by consent to sin, since we ought always to hate within ourselves that very thing which gives evil pleasure.

Because the Lord has already warned us, as we have heard, to be wakeful and vigilant against our enemies and their temptations, he now also partly reveals to us in the words which he adds how they tempt us:

[Col. 0367D] “They will put you out of the synagogues.” We read that these words of the Lord were fulfilled literally in the apostles, when faithless Jews, at the prompting of evil spirits, drove and cast them from the synagogue—that is, from their fellowship—because of their confession of Christ’s name. But those visible enemies of the Lord are now dead for the most part; his invisible enemies, namely evil spirits, remain alive, and daily do these same things invisibly to his elect.

For whenever, gathered together to pray to and praise God, we appear bodily in the Lord’s presence while our minds wander amid the vanities of the world—thinking and discussing things which do not concern us, which benefit us in nothing and bring forth for us nothing but God’s wrath and offence—or when we set ourselves above other people, preferring ourselves to others either for knowledge or for merit of life, imagining ourselves to be what we never were, and sometimes even planning for ourselves what we cannot become and would not be worthy to be: what can be said of us wretches except that our invisible enemies, at whose prompting we do these things, have put us out of the synagogues—that they have miserably cast us from the Lord’s presence and from fellowship in that holy congregation in whose midst we stand?

[Col. 0368A] These are the temptations of the ancient enemy, by which he commonly seduces and leads away the unwary, captured minds of people. We must guard against them, lest, when they come, we receive them; or, if we have received them, lest we take pleasure in them. If pleasure has seized us, let us beware lest it draw us on to consent to sin. [Col. 0368B] Let us always remember the Lord’s words, by which he foretold these same things and taught and admonished us to watch against them: “I have spoken these things to you, that you may not be scandalized. They will put you out of the synagogues.”

But because he foretold the dangers of temptation, after this warning he adds consolation in the manner of a loving father, saying:

“But the hour is coming.” As if he said: Evil spirits will put you out of the synagogues by their temptations, but the hour is coming in which I shall gather you, in which I shall mercifully raise you by my paternal consolations. [Col. 0368C] Nor do we think this expression, “but the hour is coming,” has been spoken unfittingly in this way. For as God loves a person, so a person never knows how to love oneself; nor does anyone ever desire or long for one’s own salvation with such devotion as God desires to save that person with the affection of a father.

“But the hour,” he says, “is coming.” This desirable hour is an hour of joy and exultation: an hour, indeed, of compunction, an hour of prayer, or an hour of contemplation. John speaks of this same hour in the Apocalypse: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8:1). This heaven is the human heart; the silence made in this heaven for about half an hour signifies the quiet tranquillity or serenity of mind which that hour—namely the sweetness of compunction, the purity of prayer, the constancy of contemplation—produces.

[Col. 0368D] For where a person is perfectly inwardly pierced with compunction for one’s transgressions and negligences, and through the earnestness of most fervent prayer is raised to the height of compunction and becomes, as it were, one spirit with God, that ineffable sweetness which one merits there to taste with God is not unfittingly compared to an hour, precisely because it is short: even if it were long, it could not seem long. For everything sweet is brief; everything bitter seems long.

**514** Yet this same hour, although short and seeming short, wonderfully and magnificently eases and consoles all a person’s labours, distresses, and tribulations. In it, alone with God, a person confidently and familiarly pleads one’s cause; for the manifold and inexpressible compassion and grace which God has shown, one humbly submits oneself in thanksgiving; and one does not blush to offer all the wounds of the sick soul to his compassion for healing and cure. Thus the following saying of Christ is fulfilled:

[Col. 0369A] “And the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.” In these words the Lord shows us how great and irreparable a tribulation and pain this hour produces for evil spirits, and how wonderfully it affects and afflicts them. For by saying, “Everyone who kills you,” we may understand him to have indicated any evil spirit who in some manner kills Christ’s disciples invisibly when he ceaselessly wounds them with evil suggestions and temptations, like arrows of death, so that he may somehow take from them their life, which is God.

[Col. 0369B] But when they come to that most blessed hour, when they flee from the face of those arrows into the bosom of God’s most merciful compassion, whatever vice is that by which they have been most wounded, they entrust it to the healing grace of God to be treated and cured with the greatest lamentations of penitence. Every spirit of wickedness, that is, whether a spirit of pride or anger, of envy or lust, who is the inciter or instigator of that vice which the person mourns so deeply, sees and understands that the person has bowed to God in such humility, and that the arrow of death has become for that person a cause of life and salvation; and he thinks that he is offering service to God.

He sees, indeed, and grieves that in the person whom he so afflicted with temptations, in whom he thought to diminish God’s honour, he has served God against his expectation; and that the person whom he believed he could kill by his temptations he has instead made alive. He says, as it were, within himself: “What did it profit me to tempt and weary this person in such and such a way? Did not all my effort and labour come to this: that I see myself to have saved the one whom I thought I had destroyed?”

[Col. 0369C] And lest I seem to have understood or interpreted too little the Lord’s words, “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God,” let us see what great and praiseworthy service the devil rendered to the Lord in his chosen servant, blessed Job. He sought and obtained permission to tempt him; he killed his children, took away his possessions, and at last wonderfully struck and afflicted him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. Yet Job remained steadfastly and innocently with God through all these things, always praising and blessing God in all his afflictions; and from being most perfect in perfection, from being a man of proven worth, he became a man most fully tested.

[Col. 0369D] And what wonder is this? The devil, the ancient enemy, whether he wills it or not, is God’s servant and cannot escape the service of his Lord. Therefore, when he strives, either through himself or through the evil spirits subject to him, to oppose God in his elect, he is compelled, as we have heard, to render him service. The Lord therefore added:

“And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father or me.” As if he said: All these things which I have foretold that you will suffer from evil spirits they will do to you because they have not known—that is, have not loved—the Father [Col. 0370A] or me, who am the Father’s Word. Therefore they can neither know nor love anything belonging to the Father or to me. They do not know how great is the kindness of my Father toward you, who created you; nor do they know how mercifully I, who am the Father’s Word, keep watch over you, who redeemed you by my death and blood.

“But I have spoken these things to you so that, when the hour comes, you may remember them, because I told you.” This hour is the good hour mentioned above: the hour of compunction, the hour of prayer, which transfers a person to the height of contemplation. When this hour comes to a person, there one truly remembers these things—that is, all God’s benefits. For that hour recalls more fully and sweetly to one’s mind everything which the grace of divine compassion has wrought [Col. 0370B] with that person than the tongue of any teacher could ever teach or remind one.

But what does he mean by adding, “Because I told you”? It means, as I see it, as though he had said: “I, your Creator and liberator, I who love your salvation, have spoken to you, so that, turning away from evil, you may practise good; and, despising all things which pass with time, you may hasten toward those joys which remain eternally beyond time.”

We may also understand in another way these words of the Lord: “And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father or me.” In what precedes, as we heard, he said, “They will put you out of the synagogues,” foretelling and disclosing the temptations of unclean spirits by which the elect are tested. But after the tribulation of temptations he adds consolation when he says: “And the hour will come when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.”

[Col. 0370C] Yet lest Christ’s disciples should suppose, when they come into this hour—that is, when in the time of prayer they are deemed worthy to draw near to God through true compunction and contemplation of mind—that their enemies, namely evil spirits, have then ceased from them, and that they have so escaped their temptations and snares that those spirits will not thereafter dare to assail them again or renew against them the darts of their perversity, the Lord adds again: “And they will do these things to you.”

[Col. 0370D] This repetition of the Lord’s words signifies the repeated temptation of demons. For although they know and see what service they have rendered God by tempting his elect, since they have made those very elect more proven and more perfect by their temptations, they nevertheless do not cease from them: always tempting them, always lying in wait for their salvation. And why is this?

“Because,” says the Lord, “they have not known the Father or me.” As we have said, *Father* is a name of love and fittingly signifies love. Therefore what he said—“Because they have not known **517** the Father or me”—is as though he had said: “All these things which they did before, they will do to you again and again, because they have not known—that is, they have not loved, nor can they love—that love [Col. 0371A] by which you attend to the Word of God, by which you love me, who am the Word of God.”

“But I have spoken these things to you, so that, when the hour comes, you may remember them, because I told you.” I, who am Truth, have foretold to you all these temptations of evil spirits by which they continually lie in wait for you, so that, when that hour comes in which, through the sweetness of compunction, prayer, and inward contemplation, you begin to rest with me and in me from their assault, you may remember them because I told you.

How do I say, “Remember”? Namely, that you should never presume so much upon that hour that you guard less carefully against the devices of the devil’s coming temptation. Rather, amid prosperity smiling upon you, always be solicitous concerning the adversity [Col. 0371B] to follow, so that, if it should come upon you, you may again be seized by the hand of my compassion and brought into that hour, in which you may merit to be raised up more abundantly and perfectly by the sweetness of my consolation.

The present reading looks back to this sense of the Gospel, which we have run through in exposition according to our measure. In it the blessed apostle Peter exhorts us, in the same sense though not in the same words, to keep watch against the snares of the tempting enemy, saying: “Be prudent and watchful in prayers; above all, have continual mutual love among yourselves, because love covers a multitude of sins.”

These three things which he sets before us to pursue—first, that we should be prudent; second, that we should be watchful in prayers; third, that we should have continual mutual [Col. 0371C] love among ourselves—we judge altogether necessary both for avoiding the temptations of enemies lying in wait for us and for obtaining that blessed hour of which we have treated in the preceding words of the holy Gospel.

**518** At every time, but especially when we enter God’s service, we must act steadfastly and guard ourselves prudently, lest something creep in upon us by the devil’s deceit which can delay us from that hour in which God is beheld. We must also watch in prayers, so that the heart may watch with the body and the mind’s intention may accord with the body’s labours. But these two—prudence and watchfulness in prayers—must be adorned by the third, namely the virtue of love.

[Col. 0371D] For we ought to have continual mutual love among ourselves, harming our neighbour in nothing; and, if we are harmed, patiently enduring and bearing it for the love and honour of God, on the condition that he too may remember us in the great abundance of his sweetness and, in his mercy, bring us into that hour where in him and through him we may forget and be comforted concerning all injuries and all adversities that can befall us. Nothing so renews this hour as love does; nothing so hinders it as hatred and bitterness.

All these things which we have heard from the Gospel and the reading are read to us on this Sunday, which is near the solemnity of the Holy Spirit, so that at least during these few days we may prepare our hearts more vigilantly and diligently for the Holy Spirit in all humility, love, [Col. 0372A] and chastity. For it is written: “The Holy Spirit does not dwell in a body subject to sins.” And again: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon one who is humble and meek and trembles at my words?” But because chastity of the flesh is nothing without chastity and humility of mind, let us strive for chastity with humility and humility with love, so that, when the Holy Spirit comes, he may find us such that, by dwelling in us, he may perfect us as the temple of his glory. May he deign to grant this: he who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the same Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

**519 HOMILY LVII. THE FIRST, FOR THE SATURDAY OF THE EMBER DAYS OF PENTECOST**

[Col. 0372B]

“Jesus, rising from the synagogue, entered into Simon’s house. But Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a severe fever” (Luke 4).

The end of this holy and venerable solemnity of Easter, now at hand, fittingly suggests to us that end of all flesh, when, after the temporal festivals which we now observe have been completed, the festal joys of eternal gladness shall follow—joys which can never be ended by any termination, nor ever disturbed in their eternity by any affliction of adversity.

At the beginning of that blessed and never-ending festival, these two miracles of our Lord and Saviour will be truly and perfectly fulfilled in the salvation of all, which are now read in the divine offices at the end of this festival already completed.

For yesterday, as evangelical truth testifies, we heard how the loving and merciful Lord healed a paralytic man; today’s holy Gospel reading shows us how he restored a fevered woman to desired health by the command of his divinity alone. In these two persons, namely the man and the woman, we may not unfittingly understand our spirit and flesh. Although they are now often freed from their infirmities, they will by no means be restored to stable and perfect health until, when these festivals which pass with time have been removed, that day of perpetual solemnity and joy dawns, in which all the elect will be so delivered from every corruption that they will experience no further affliction of infirmity either in body or [Col. 0372D] spirit.

The present holy Gospel reading plainly indicates in what order, with the Lord cooperating, a person may attain such glory in this life.

“Rising,” says the Evangelist, “Jesus left the synagogue and entered Simon’s house.”

[Col. 0373A] By the synagogue in this place we may understand the multitude of the faithful, in which and with which our Lord Jesus Christ was, as it were, at that time when, clothed in human flesh, he bore for our sake all the sufferings of the flesh except sin alone. He rose from that synagogue when, after the glorious triumph of his Passion, he rose again, having overcome death; and when the common passibility of the human flesh which he bore had been transformed into the dignity of a new and singular life, he became, in his humanity as in his divinity, impassible and immortal, as the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9). Thus, by rising—thus, I say, by abolishing through the power of his divinity the mortality of the humanity he had assumed—he entered Simon’s house.

By Simon, whose name means “obedient,” although our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who became obedient to the Father for us even unto death, may fittingly be understood, the angelic host may nevertheless also be understood through the same Simon: that host which has always clung to God in unchangeable love, and has never deviated from the way of truth through any instability of disobedience.

[Col. 0373B] We may also fittingly understand, by the name of this same Simon, the blessed souls of the elect who have risen with Christ. With them he entered that house of his, namely the heavenly Jerusalem, which he purchased by the shedding of his precious blood for all who obey him. Although this house was always his own according to his divinity, yet according to his humanity our true Simon received it, as though as a gift from the Father, when, after the triumph of the Passion and the glory of the Resurrection, he sat down as a glorious victor at the right hand of that same Father.

“But Simon’s mother-in-law was held by severe fevers.” When someone has taken a wife, the mother of that wife is customarily called the man’s mother-in-law. But since we have said that our Lord and Savior is to be understood by Simon, what may we understand by his wife or mother-in-law?

[Col. 0373C] His bride and wife is that immortal Church which, now stripped of earthly things, rejoices immortally with Christ in heavenly things. Since the present Church is her mother—for all souls that have been, or are yet to be, received into the bridal chamber of the eternal King must first be born from this mother’s womb—this present Church itself may deservedly be called the mother-in-law of our Lord.

Yet this mother-in-law of the Lord, while he rose from this synagogue through the glory of immortality and entered his own house, the heavenly Jerusalem, with his bride, the multitude of the faithful, was held by severe fevers. For as long as she remains amid the misery of this mortality, she is unavoidably weighed down by the various bonds of sins, which are aptly compared to fevers.

[Col. 0373D] For although there may be some who appear sound in their works, few are found who do not offend in speech, who do not often lose inward well-being through carelessness of tongue. But if anyone were so steadfast and perfect a guardian of inward health that he never corrupted it either by deeds or by words, who then boasts that he has a pure heart? Who, I say, can be found who does not suffer, even unwillingly, from the various fevers of harmful thoughts?

Those who now rejoice, reigning with Christ in heaven, are not ignorant of the miseries of this human weakness. Therefore they intercede with continual prayers for the present condition of the Church, as the following words of the holy Gospel testify. For it continues:

[Col. 0374A] “And they entreated him for her.”

By those who are said, without their names being given, to have entreated the Lord for the sick woman, we may fittingly understand here, as we often do, the holy angels who are daily concerned for our salvation, and likewise the blessed souls of the righteous already reigning with Christ. Although these are now free from every misery, being placed in the glory of eternal blessedness, they nevertheless know how laboriously they once lived in the exile of this life, and how scarcely they escaped the sorrows of this mortality except by God’s aid alone.

[Col. 0374B] Therefore, together with the holy angels, they plead with Christ all the more earnestly for our miseries because they know that they too once labored in the sufferings we endure.

But we must know that they do not implore for us the mercy of almighty God by approaching in a human manner or by joining words to words; rather, their prayer is their fervent desire for our salvation. For with inestimable longing they desire that this present age may come to an end, so that they too, once their bodies have been received again, may attain full joy, and that those still weighed down by the burden of the flesh may be freed from the fevers of both body and soul and restored to eternal health.

[Col. 0374C] Nor is the desire of so great beings there ever in vain. For if the merciful and compassionate Lord does not despise the groans and tears of those who still journey in the exile of this mortality, how much more graciously does he grant the prayers of those who already reign with him and behold more intimately the brightness of his face. For it is written: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Ps. 10:17).

Although they already possess the true riches of eternal blessedness, yet because they are truly humble they are not unfittingly called poor. And since they always have a heart prepared toward God, continually sensing him, whenever they bring before Christ the miseries of their sick mother in this world’s exile, namely the holy Church, he by no means refuses their petition, but heals her from the impending fevers of sins, as the Evangelist says in what follows:

[Col. 0374D] “And standing over her, he commanded the fever, and it left her.”

The Lord indeed stands over her, in whose midst he was once present, when, having become man for humankind, he so shared the condition of human beings that he bore for us—not by necessity, but solely by his will—all the pains, miseries, and infirmities which we suffer by necessity. But since no infirmity now falls upon him, since, crowned with glory and honor, he reigns immortally in his house, he is rightly said now to stand and command the fever.

[Col. 0375A] For according both to his humanity and to his divinity, he has power to save his Church from the various sufferings of body and soul by command alone. Thus after his Resurrection, appearing to his disciples, he said: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). Whatever infirmity, then, whether of body or soul, may hold the holy Church, as soon as he commands, she is released from the fever, doing as is said in the following words of the holy Gospel:

“And immediately,” says the Evangelist, “rising, she ministered to them.”

[Col. 0375B] But what does it mean that she “ministered to them,” except that the soul which, weighed down by the torpor of its infirmity, could render no service of due obedience to God, as soon as it feels itself restored to the desired health by the aid of divine mercy, begins to minister with a ready heart and body not only to him by whose gift and grace it has been healed, but also to those through whose intercession it does not doubt that it has been healed?

For why do we on earth venerate with such devout service the feasts of the most holy Mary, Mother of God, the holy angels, and the other saints, except that we may deserve both to be delivered in time from the daily ailments which assail body and soul, and at some time to be restored to eternal health through the aid of their intercession?

But because, as long as we remain in this place of infirmity, we must suffer the various infirmities of both the outward and inward person, it is fitting that we minister to them until the time of perfect health arrives, concerning which the Evangelist next adds:

“When the sun had set, all who had those sick with various diseases brought them to him.”

[Col. 0375C] We may understand this thus: as long as anyone remains in this life, may that true sun, namely the Sun of righteousness, never so set in his heart through the gathering darkness of sins that he cannot and ought not to hope that, stirred by pious works, holy vows, and prayers, it will rise again for him through the brightness of grace visiting him inwardly. For he is the one to whom mercy is never entreated without hope.

Every prayer must be directed to God with hope and confidence, because labor in prayer is vain unless true hope of heart accompanies pure prayer. Hence we do not pray for those who, while still living in the flesh, were separated from the communion of the holy Church, because such prayer would fall in vain, since no hope of salvation would follow it.

[Col. 0375D] All, therefore, in whose hearts that true sun, Christ, has so set in this life that the final day of their lives finds them persevering in sins with a hardened and unrepentant heart—all hope of seeing with joy the brightness of the eternal Sun will perish from them together with life. In those same shadows of sins, which here they refused to put off through repentance and by drawing near through worthy satisfaction to the true light, which is Christ—in these, I say, after the end of this life they will be tormented without end and without consolation.

[Col. 0376A] But those who now grieve over the inward setting of the true Sun already mentioned, and who, as long as they live, continually endeavor by pious labors to raise him toward his rising, will at the end of the world, when this visible sun has set and the time of this changeableness has passed, confidently go forth to meet the majesty of God, as the present sequence of words figuratively indicates:

“All,” says the Evangelist, “who had those sick with various diseases brought them to him.”

[Col. 0376B] It is not said “who have,” but “who had,” because, although they once had sick persons—namely, each of the senses of both their outward and inward person—yet they will not then have them. For, bearing witness in their own conscience, they did not cease in this life, as far as they could and with the Lord’s help, to relieve those infirmities through the medicine of steadfast repentance and perfect satisfaction. Therefore, because they had them but will then no longer have them, they will bring themselves to God with great hope and confidence, rejoicing to be presented before the sight of his eternal majesty, where they may deserve to be restored by him eternally to eternal health.

“But he, laying his hands upon each one, healed them all.”

[Col. 0376C] He will indeed lay hands upon each one when, making them sharers in his divine power, which may be understood through his hands, he establishes them so firmly in the glory of eternal blessedness in body and soul that they will no longer be able to offend the eyes of the divine majesty either through wicked deeds in the body or unlawful desires in the soul. Where this desirable and truly joyful laying on of hands by the supreme High Priest has taken place, there will be wonderfully fulfilled what is added in the sequence of the Gospel reading:

“And demons came out from many, crying and saying: ‘You are the Son of God.’”

[Col. 0376D] As long as we journey in the exile of this world, this departure of demons cannot take place. For although, because the divine hand restrains them, they cannot exercise the tyranny of their malice upon Christ’s faithful according to their will and pleasure, they nevertheless dwell, as it were, among us and with us, day and night opposing and plotting against our salvation.

[Col. 0377A] But after the setting of the sun—that is, after the end of this present world—when that true High Priest has laid hands upon each one, when he has healed all his elect from every corruption of body and soul, then at last demons will come out from many, because they will no longer be able to approach God’s saints with any temptations. And he rightly says “from many,” because not all who will be presented on that day before the dreadful judgment of God will be saved.

When the demons already mentioned are compelled by the urging of the divine sentence to depart from many—that is, from all who are to be saved—they will confess, although unwillingly, the omnipotence of God, crying and saying: “You are the Son of God.” For then at last they will know that he alone is Lord of all, who alone ought justly to reign eternally over his own.

[Col. 0377B] But such a confession is followed not by reward but by punishment, as is shown by the following words of the holy Gospel:

“And rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak.”

That rebuke of the Lord is surely the eternal condemnation to eternal death in which those same demons will be involved in the judgment of that final examination, when the elect have been received into the glory of eternal blessedness and they themselves, with their followers, have been assigned to everlasting fires. The Lord will say to them: “Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

[Col. 0377C] When this sentence of the Lord has been pronounced against them, it may rightly be called a rebuke, because it “bursts within” (*increpat*), crushing and nullifying all their strength [the manuscript reads *formidinem*, “fear”] inwardly. Hence it is well added: “And he did not allow them to speak.”

The speech of demons is their malicious suggestion. For they now in some manner utter the perverse speech of their unbelief when they introduce into any person standing or sitting alone evil thoughts and perverse desires, causing the person to begin to deliberate with them how he may accomplish by deeds or words something that is not expedient.

[Col. 0377D] In this life the Lord permits them to speak in such a manner with his elect, so that he may see who they are that, opposing their deadly speech, do not consent to it, but cling unshakenly to him through the praiseworthy steadfastness of heart and body by which they have been made his own. But when the time of this changeableness has passed, when the rebuke of the Lord already mentioned is turned against them, when at his voice all their power and strength are crushed, then at last they will cease from this pestilential speech, because they will no longer be able to disturb the saints’ joys by any assault of temptation or suggestion, knowing that he is God who will reign without end in his own and with his own. Therefore it is fittingly added:

“When day came, Jesus went into a deserted place.”

[Col. 0378A] We should consider more carefully what this “made day” (*dies facta*) is, which the Evangelist here so distinctly mentions. There is indeed a day—Christ, namely, the day of eternal joy and sweetness, a pleasing and desirable day. Yet he is by no means called a made day, because, just as he is never enclosed by any end, so he was without beginning, equal to the Father in the majesty of divinity.

There is also another day, which may rightly be called a made day: namely, the gathered multitude of the elect. That uncreated day mercifully illumined it in this life with the brightness of his grace, and by his hidden predestination ordained it before the beginning of the world for that day of eternal joy, to which no shadow of darkness succeeds.

[Col. 0378B] This is truly that day of which Scripture says: “And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.”

When, therefore, this day blessed by God has come, whose brightness, once begun, will remain without end, there will undoubtedly be fulfilled what is figuratively indicated by the following sequence of words:

“Having gone out,” says the Evangelist, “he went into a deserted place.”

[Col. 0378C] As long as we remain in the exile of this mortality, our Lord Jesus Christ is, as it were, within us, because, weighed down by the mortal burden of the body, we cannot see him as he is in the brightness of his divinity. For just as no mortal, with unimpaired sight, could gaze long upon the rays of this present sun, so truly, if that true Sun were now to go forth—if it were possible for him to appear to us as he is—we could not endure for even a moment the brightness of his face amid the pitiable darkness of this mortality by which we are oppressed.

Therefore, when the day already mentioned, the day of perpetual solemnity and joy, has come, when the entire multitude of the faithful, united to Christ its head, has entered the heavenly kingdom, then this same Savior of ours, who is now hidden, who is now in some manner within, will make a desirable, great, and wonderful going forth. Then, I say, when every darkness of human infirmity has been wholly wiped away, he will so illumine all people in body and soul by the grace of his perpetual visitation that each of them will behold his most holy humanity with bodily eyes and his incomprehensible divinity with spiritual eyes.

[Col. 0378D] For this is what the Evangelist immediately adds: “He went,” he says, “into a deserted place.” Although the heavenly kingdom may be understood by the deserted place, on the testimony of that man who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, went away to seek the one that was lost, yet here the heart of each elect person may also fittingly be understood by the deserted place. It is rightly called a desert, since by the invisible grace of his visitation it now rejoices that the Lord is present to it, and now, when the sweetness of that presence is withdrawn, grieves that it has been deserted by him.

[Col. 0379A] But after the miseries of this life, when he has gone forth in the manner stated above, when he has shown himself to all his own as he is, then he will truly go, as it were, into a deserted place, because he will so possess and fill the heart of each with the presence of his divinity that he will no longer be able to leave them. Thus there follows immediately:

“And the crowds sought him, and came as far as him.”

[Col. 0379B] There not only the great and incomparable saints—Peter, James, and John, and the rest like them—but even the crowds will be satisfied by the insatiable vision of his eternal divinity. By the name “crowds” we may understand all the less perfect. Whatever they may have been in this life, those who by God’s favor are at last admitted to the glory of eternal blessedness are rightly said to seek him and to come as far as him.

But how or where will they seek the Lord in whose presence they will exult and rejoice? Their seeking is surely nothing other than loving and desiring above all things him who is above all; and coming as far as him is passing into him with all the affections of soul and body. What follows, however—

[Col. 0379C] “And they detained him, lest he depart from them”—I judge to mean nothing other than that, bound fast by the strongest arms of most ardent love, they will cling to him unshakenly, so that neither he can depart from them nor they from him for any reason whatever.

Since this is so, and since no one of the elect will then remain outside the gate of blessedness, what is the meaning of that which Truth himself adds at the end of this Gospel reading, saying:

“For I must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also”?

[Col. 0379D] These final words of the Lord may therefore, without injury to the Catholic faith and truth, fittingly be applied to what precedes. For when he says that he must preach the kingdom of God to other cities, it is as though, when the whole multitude of the elect has been gathered to him, he says to each of them, rewarding individually their labors, deeds, words, and thoughts:

[Col. 0380A] “You were once indeed my cities: chosen cities, sweet and exceedingly pleasing cities, while still weighed down by a mortal body you fought against the ancient enemy with a strong battle-line of virtues, and, bravely trampling his fiery darts under the feet of holy action, you strove, as far as possible, to preserve for me alone the clean dwelling-place of your heart and body. Yet now you are no less my cities, though far different from what you once were. Then you were weak cities because of the weakness of the flesh that weighed you down; now you are cities made strong and fortified by the everlasting immortality, of both body and soul, which will remain with you forever.

[Col. 0380B] “Therefore, because you have become other cities—that is, because by my gift and grace you have been changed for the better—I must preach the kingdom of God to you. I must, I say, because the fatherly mercy within me requires that I show you the everlasting glory of my everlasting Trinity in such a manner that you can never again be separated from the abiding joys of my kingdom.”

May the joy of the Father bring us to the attainment of these joys, where, amid the delights of the heavenly homeland, we may be so united to the eternal Trinity that, contemplating its everlasting brightness with unveiled face, we may deserve to praise it through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY LVIII. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY OF HOLY TRINITY, WHICH IS ALSO THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0379C]

“There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said to him: Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher” (John 3).

As we have learned from the words of the holy Fathers, this ruler of the Jews, instructed to some extent by divine miracles, believed that Jesus Christ had come from God and that God was with him, but he did not yet fully know that he himself was God. He calls him Teacher because he hoped, through his heavenly instruction, to arrive at the way of perfect truth. Thus the Teacher of truth himself, while instructing and teaching this Nicodemus alone, who had come to him, showed all the faithful by what way and in what order they ought to be saved.

[Col. 0379D] “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

By this brief sentence the Savior foretold the sacrament of baptism, which is daily administered in the Church. For one who is conceived and born in original sin must be regenerated and renewed by the grace of baptism, so that he may both become a child of God and see the kingdom of God. But he, since he came at night, that is, since he still remained in the darkness of ignorance, could not grasp the mystery of this saying. Therefore he next asked:

[Col. 0380A] “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”

He believed that the Lord had not without cause spoken the words he spoke about a repeated birth. Therefore he inquired more carefully how these things could take place. Revealing to him more plainly the manner of that birth, the Lord said:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. What is born of flesh is flesh; and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.”

[Col. 0380B] It is as though he said: “It is indeed impossible for an old man to be born bodily again from his mother’s womb; but it is not impossible—indeed, it is most necessary—to be invisibly regenerated and washed through the water of baptism and through the grace of the Holy Spirit. For what is born of flesh is flesh; that is, a person not yet reborn is wholly flesh, because nothing holy and spiritual is in him. But after he has been spiritually and invisibly reborn, he may be called not only spiritual but also spirit, because, just as the substance of the Holy Spirit is invisible, so too the person reborn in Christ has invisibly become a child of God.”

“Do not marvel,” he says, “that I said to you: You must be born again.”

Nicodemus, not yet fully instructed, could reasonably have marveled at this invisible birth. Therefore that good Teacher reveals and makes known to him more clearly the author of this birth:

[Col. 0380C] “The Spirit,” he says, “breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes.”

It is as though he said: “As soon as the Holy Spirit, by the invocation of God’s word, sanctifies the waters by breathing upon them with his power, he so cleanses and regenerates all who are baptized in them that he makes them from children of death and the devil into children of God and heirs of the heavenly kingdom.”

“And you hear his voice,” he says, “and do not know where he comes from or where he goes.” Where the voice of the Holy Spirit speaks, there heavenly rather than earthly things are heard, spiritual rather than carnal things; yet we cannot know from where, when, or how the grace of the Holy Spirit comes into the heart of the person to whom he speaks [the manuscript reads *qui*, “who”], or toward what end and fruit that same grace goes and proceeds.

[Col. 0380D] “So it is,” he says, “with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

Every person who has been invisibly reborn inwardly begins to be faithful and spiritual, which he was not before; yet he does not know whether he will receive eternal grace in the future.

“Nicodemus answered and said to him: How can these things be?”

He asks how these things can happen not as one faithless and unbelieving, but requests that the manner and order by which they can happen be explained to him.

“Jesus answered and said to him: Are you a teacher in Israel, and do not know these things?”

[Col. 0381A] These words of the Lord are not the words of one rebuking but of one admonishing; they summon not only him, but also all who wish to be called teachers, to the way of humility, lest anyone presume to be called or to be a teacher who does not know what ought to be said or done.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: what we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify, and you do not receive our testimony.”

Here he offers himself as a pattern and example to all teachers and prelates, that they should speak, through love, what they know, and bear witness, through action, to what they see through understanding. “And you do not receive our testimony,” he says. He does not say, in the singular, “you do not receive,” but “you do not receive,” in the plural, because this was not to be said to Nicodemus, who earnestly desired to hear such a Teacher; rather, he looks to those who boastfully utter the things they know and despise to do themselves the things they teach others. It follows:

[Col. 0381B] “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?”

How did that man who came from heaven and was heavenly speak earthly things to them? For, as we find elsewhere, he said to the scribes and Pharisees concerning his Passion and Resurrection: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). But they, who sought and understood only earthly things, did not know how to understand these things spiritually. Yet the merciful Teacher wished to summon and stir up this same disciple, Nicodemus, with whom he was then speaking, from a carnal and earthly understanding to an understanding of heavenly things. Therefore, instructing him concerning heavenly things, he said:

“And no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

[Col. 0381C] It is as though he said: “Whoever desires to ascend into heaven should strive to unite himself in the unity of true faith to the Son of Man—that is, to myself, the Son of the Virgin—because he cannot ascend to heaven otherwise than through me, who descended from heaven.”
