But because this ascent cannot occur without faith in and the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion, it is rightly said next:

“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

The lifting up of the bronze serpent prefigured the Passion of our Redeemer. Whoever believes in him by imitating his Passion, insofar as he is able, will not only be saved from the punishments of hell and from danger to the soul, but will also deserve to possess eternal life.

[Col. 0381D] We have now briefly set forth the Gospel reading according to allegory. Let us now turn the eye of our heart back upon ourselves and learn from it its moral sense.

“There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.”

The present reading of the holy Gospel secretly indicates to us five steps of salvation, by which the Lord mercifully raises and advances from vices to virtues his faithful whom he has predestined and called to life. The first step of salvation is the inspiration of good will; the second, the conversion of habits and deeds; the third, the inward compunction of a contrite heart; the fourth, continual meditation on heavenly things; the fifth, cautious and circumspect reflection of the mind. The following sequence of the Gospel narrative indicates how all these things ought to be begun and brought to completion in the elect.

[Col. 0382A] “There was,” he says, “a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.”

*Pharisee* means “divided”; *Nicodemus* means “victorious people” or “victory of the people.” Through these words the manifest grace by which a human being is saved is shown. For every faithful person begins to be a man “from the Pharisees,” that is, from the divided, when, recognizing himself to be human, he repents that he has hitherto lived in a human manner, and desires to associate himself with those who are spiritually Pharisees, who are divided in heart and body from sins and from the business of this world.

[Col. 0382B] Likewise, the name Nicodemus, said to mean “victorious people” or “victory of the people,” fittingly applies. For, in order that a victorious people—that is, a people of virtues—may grow and rise up within him, he desires to exercise in himself the victory of the people, the victory over sin and injustice.

In this way he also becomes a ruler of the Jews, that is, a ruler of those who confess God, because, although he cannot yet do so in deed and truth, he magnifies God by confessing him in words.

“He came,” he says, “to Jesus by night.”

For when, through the inspiration of good will, he has ascended, as it were, the first step of salvation, and has wished to be one of the spiritual Pharisees, then, as though breaking out from the midst of the darkness of vices, he attempts with the steps of repentance to approach the very author of light. In bitterness of heart he addresses him in words such as these:

[Col. 0382C] “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher.”

It is as though he said: “We know indeed, Teacher and Lord, that you were sent by God the Father and set before your faithful the example of heavenly teaching, so that whoever strives to follow the footsteps of your humility may one day see you as most merciful Father and Redeemer upon the throne of majesty. But I fear to see you not as Father or defender, but as advocate or protector; rather, as judge and teacher, as Lord and most severe avenger. For I have never bowed the neck of my heart to your teaching as I ought.”

[Col. 0382D] While he frequently murmurs these things to himself in silent thought, at last desiring to come to the effect of good work, he entreats the Lord in these words:

“No one can do these signs which you do unless God is with him.”

“No one,” he says, “except you, Lord, has stirred up in me these signs of your fear. Your inspiration, Lord, has stirred up in me fear of your judgment, dread of eternal condemnation, and good will. Yet I cannot accomplish by myself the good that I wish to do. For what can a wretched and weak person accomplish by himself unless God is with him?”

[Col. 0383A] No one doubts that God is everywhere with all people through the power of his majesty. Yet he is with the good in one way and with the evil in another. He is with the good by cooperating with and assisting their good will, which he himself has inspired in them; he is also with the evil by mercifully pitying and tolerating their wickedness.

He was with Saul the persecutor by mercifully tolerating his wickedness, until he worked in him the wondrous grace of his mercy. He was also with the blessed Virgin Mary, cooperating with her voluntary chastity. For because she refused to know a man in conceiving, she deserved to be both mother and virgin. Thus the angel said to her: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28).

[Col. 0383B] “The Lord is with you,” he says. For he to whom your virginal purpose was pleasing will be your helper in preserving virginity, because under the overshadowing power of the Most High you will conceive and bear the Son of God.

Thus, surely, he will be the helper in good action to every person in whom he has inspired good will. Hence he next says:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

Behold, the second step, that of good conversion, follows. It is fittingly understood through the birth which must be repeated in a human being. For when someone, perfectly converted, begins to walk in newness of life, it is as though he has been born anew. Then he will be able to see in his body the kingdom of God, the kingdom of truth and righteousness; for to see the kingdom of God is to abstain from vices and carnal desires.

[Col. 0383C] But because one grown old in evil days cannot easily be born again in this manner, he says, as it were marveling at and joyfully praising the goodness of God:

“Can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”

It is as though he said: “Can so great mercy, so great clemency, occur in a human being without you, Lord Creator—that one who has grown old through long persistence in sins may again, cleansed from sins, enter into the womb of his mother, the womb of regenerating grace?”

For the mother of all who are saved is, if this may be said without injury to faith, the regenerating grace of the Creator. The womb of this grace is the hidden predestination of that same Creator. For this same mother in some manner conceived within the womb of her secret those whom she was to save, when she predestined them before the ages for eternal life; and she daily bears them with maternal compassion when, mercifully justifying them, she reforms them to innocence of life.

And who, after going out from the womb of this blessed Mother, can enter again and be born, except one who has been perfectly humbled through true conversion? Therefore, after the second step of good conversion follows the third step, namely the compunction of the humbled heart, as the saying of Truth itself immediately adds:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” From water and the Spirit the inward person is then 536 in some manner [Col. 0383D] reborn when, in the hour of inward compunction, he becomes one spirit with the Lord, when the uncreated Spirit is united and joined to the created spirit. In this compunction of heart and union with the heavenly Spirit there takes place a certain regeneration, which so reforms and regenerates a person that he may enter the kingdom of God, which is within him. For to enter the kingdom of God is to return by continual meditation into one’s own heart, where the kingdom of God ought to be; so that, should that heavenly Bridegroom come to visit him in an abundance of sweetness, he may receive him as he comes with fitting honour. Yet because carnal people do not know how to enter the kingdom of God in this way, but spiritual people do, it is aptly said in what follows:

“What is born of the flesh is flesh; and what is born [Col. 0384A] of the Spirit is spirit.” That everything born of flesh is wholly carnal and corruptible is indicated by flesh itself, with its enticements. For, as the Apostle testifies, “the flesh always desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5:17). Hence those who are carnal seek and love carnal things alone. “And what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” What is more sublime than this spiritual birth, when God himself is spirit? And therefore, whatever the faithful soul conceives and brings forth from the Holy Spirit, what can it be except wholly spiritual, wholly heavenly? “But the natural person does not receive the things that are of the Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:14); and therefore he speaks still more plainly about spiritual birth:

“Do not wonder because I said to you: You must be born anew. The Spirit breathes where he wills; and you hear his voice, and [Col. 0384B] do not know whence he comes or whither he goes.” Do not wonder, I say—that is, you will not be able, by wondering, to investigate how through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit I shall bring about anew in my elect the spiritual birth of which I have spoken. For “the Spirit breathes where he wills”: that is, by a voluntary breathing he visits his faithful ones beforehand. Yet there are some who hear the voice of him who breathes, and nevertheless disdain to know when he comes or when he departs. It is indeed not dangerous not to know whence he comes or whither he goes; but it is very dangerous not to know 537 when he comes or when he goes. For whoever strives, with watchful concern, both to hear the voice of him who breathes and to observe the time of his coming or departure, will deserve, in the aforementioned order of birth, to be born through conversion and reborn through compunction.

[Col. 0384C] “So it is,” he says, “with everyone born of the Spirit.” As though he said: Thus everyone tends towards true being and arrives at true being who, after the inspiration of good will, has thus been born through conversion and thus reborn through compunction. But how one who has experienced none of these things can inwardly answer them, this Nicodemus declares by his response.

“How,” he says, “can these things happen?” How, he says, in what way, by what discipline can I so govern my thoughts, words, and deeds as to deserve to be born through conversion and reborn through compunction? Immediately the rules of a right life are set before him, when the following is at once added:

[Col. 0384D] “Are you a teacher in Israel, and do you not know these things?” You, I say, if you desire to be such a teacher in Israel that you yourself may be Israel—that is, a man seeing God—do you not know that you cannot attain such a teaching office unless you dispose your thoughts, words, and actions under right governance? For you must be subject in humility and, in love of neighbour, as it were a companion, if you would be a teacher in Israel, if you desire to see God in sweetness of heart. And because imperfect persons are wholly unable to attain these things, he speaks again, more plainly, in the person of the perfect:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: we speak what we know, and testify to what we have seen, and you do not receive our testimony.” It belongs to the perfect to know the things of God by the affection of the heart, to see them by the understanding of the mind, and to speak and testify of them [Col. 0385A] by the effect of deeds. But the imperfect do not receive their testimony, for they disdain to imitate what is testified.

Therefore the Lord again admonishes them as follows:

“If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” The three distinct stages mentioned above—of the inspiration of good will, conversion of character and deeds, and inward compunction of heart—seem in some manner earthly in comparison with what follows: namely, continual meditation upon heavenly realities and cautious, watchful reflection of the heart. Therefore, if anyone does not reach those things which are as it were earthly, how will he comprehend the heavenly? For now the fourth stage follows: meditation upon heavenly realities, which the Gospel reading expresses next.

[Col. 0385B] “No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.” To ascend into heaven is, through the desires of devout devotion, to be raised in thought and sighing from earthly to heavenly things. But no one can ascend to heavenly things in this way unless he descends from heaven: that is, unless he strives to bend himself down in profound humility from his whole heart, wherein heaven and the seat of God ought to be. And this man is truly, through unity in humility, the son of man who is in heaven: that man, I mean, who is the Son of the Virgin, whose heaven is in the humble and quiet heart. Thus the fifth stage follows: namely, the watchful reflection of the heart, which [Col. 0385C] the following sequence of Gospel truth indicates. For it continues:

“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.” If [Col. 0386A] anyone advances through the four stages mentioned above—namely, the inspiration of good will, conversion of character and works, compunction of a contrite heart, and holy and heavenly meditation—he will deserve also to be raised in the fifth stage, that is, by cautious and watchful reflection of heart. Thus, just as Moses is said, in a mystical sense, to have been taken from water, so this person too, taken from spiritual water—that is, from the grace of divine contemplation—may be inwardly instructed and taught, so that through a firm and watchful guarding of his heart he may begin to lift up within himself the Son of Man, the Son of the undefiled Virgin, by humility and gentleness, 539 just as formerly he lifted up the ancient serpent through pride, anger, and vain glory in the wilderness—that is, in his own heart. [Col. 0386B] For the sinner’s heart may rightly be called badly deserted and desolate when its heavenly inhabitant, excluded by the filth of sins, abandons it. It follows:

“That everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life.” A person who is not rightly provident and watchful is said to perish both to God and to himself when, wandering with the eye of his heart among diverse things, he is carried away; for he can neither see his own misery nor reverence the presence of the divine majesty.

540 But whoever believes in this way, as was said above, by lifting up the Son of Man, will be unable to perish either to God or to himself through wandering; rather, he begins in the present to have eternal life through the sweetness of inward contemplation, which in the future he will possess without end in unchangeable fullness. This is granted by [Col. 0386C] our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## PREFACE 541–542 TO THE SUMMER SUNDAY HOMILIES

[Col. 0385]

As we are about to begin the solemnities of the summer Sundays, let us humbly invoke the Lord to whom these Sundays belong and from whom they take their name, that he who is the way, the truth, and the life may deign to grant us the way for understanding what lies hidden in them, truth for writing, and, for their observance, everlasting life.

For, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, we intend to devote the labour of our work especially to those who mortify the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, that they may live for God in monasteries. From them we desire to receive this sole reward for our labour: that, if the work of our littleness is not pleasing, at least our devotion may not be displeasing. For although we cannot benefit everyone according to our desire, we believe that what we are about to do will harm no one. Let educated and wise persons therefore read the expositions of wise and learned men; and let the small and humble who live in monasteries, if they wish, read whatever discoveries our simplicity has made. And if in these they hear something differing from other expositions, let them not despise it, provided that they do not understand what they hear to depart from faith and sound doctrine. For the Holy Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills, is he from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift; and as he abundantly supplies the greater with that by which they are enriched, so he mercifully customarily gives the lesser that by which they may be consoled. Therefore, what by his gift we have received for our own consolation and that of others in the understanding of the Gospels, let us approach writing with his help, trusting not in ourselves but in him.

## 543 HOMILY LIX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0387A]

“There was a rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16).

Since the whole world consists of two orders, namely, the rich and the poor, in this parable the rich have their instruction and the poor their consolation. Here the rich have in this rich man what they may fear and dread; in this poor man the poor have that by which they may be consoled and strengthened in the hope of eternal life. For here the rich are warned to conduct themselves amid worldly riches and honours in such a way that, because of the brief and passing delights of this present life, they do not fall with this rich man, who was buried in hell, into the punishment of eternal damnation. [Col. 0387B] Here the poor are consoled, so that, if they act patiently, if in their poverty they remember God, set their hope in him, and seek and await from him consolation for their need, they ought, with this poor man who was taken from the present life and carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom, to hope after the grievous weariness of poverty for the sweet refreshment of eternal consolation.

We may also understand in these two, the rich man and the poor man, prelates and subjects. For those who, being endowed not only with rank but also with knowledge of God and the integrity of virtues and conduct, are called prelates in the Church of God, are rightly designated and honoured by the name of the rich. [Col. 0387C] But those who, despising and rejecting worldly riches, humbly submit for God’s sake to another’s will and command, are aptly represented by the name of poor Lazarus.

[Col. 0387D] In this rich man and poor man we may also understand the innocent and penitents. For those who by God’s mercy have preserved their innocence, and by mortification of the flesh and purity of heart have deserved to please God in holy conduct—these are indeed those who are deservedly honoured by the name of the rich and are said to be clothed in purple and fine linen. But those who have lived sinfully, 544 and, as though full of sores, have perfectly recognized the corruptions of their vices and truly submitted themselves to penitence, have taken upon themselves the name of the sore-covered poor man Lazarus. Having briefly set this forth, let us turn the eye of the mind to the understanding of the holy Gospel reading; and, leaving the spiritual rich man and poor man, let us behold the spiritual rich man and poor man, and carefully consider what we are warned and instructed by them. For the Lord says: “There was a certain rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day.” This rich man signifies the blessed person, one who has not fallen into or been stained by any criminal sins in his life, and who, whether dedicated to God by his parents from the days of childhood or voluntarily set apart from the common life of this age by the inspiration of almighty God, regards the transitory joys of the present life as of little worth and directs his mind to heavenly joys alone, which endure without end. [Col. 0388A] Since this person, serving God in his innocence and in the observance of the spiritual life, strives diligently to preserve in himself the image and likeness of God, he is rightly and fittingly called “a certain man”—a singular man, I mean. And because, advancing in the spiritual life, he is enriched and exalted through the overflowing gift of divine mercy by the desirable riches of virtues with which almighty God nourishes and sustains his chosen and beloved children in holy conduct, he is rightly called “a certain rich man.” But when, in that same innocence and holiness, he treats his body with the same humility, austerity, and severity with which the converted sinner treats his in penitence, and no less restrains himself by mortification of the flesh and purity of heart lest he admit sins [Col. 0388B] than the sinful person labours to erase and wipe away those already committed, it may rightly be said of him: 545 “And he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day.” Purple signifies the mortification of the flesh; fine linen, which grows from the earth and is brought to whiteness by labour, may express purity of heart. For unless mortification of the flesh is followed by purity of heart, so that one knows that he mortifies his flesh simply for God alone and does not seek outward praise for it, the undertaken mortification of the flesh will profit him little.

For many refrain from sins for the sake of a respectable life, lest they be put to shame before human eyes. Many also, after committing sins, are afflicted in penitence and mortify their flesh, yet desire to be praised and honoured before men [Col. 0388C] for their penitence and affliction. All these are clothed in purple insofar as, abstaining from sins, they mortify their flesh and afflict themselves by the labours of penitence. But they are not clothed in fine linen, because they lack purity of heart while mortifying their flesh for transitory praise. But whoever does both—mortifies his flesh by abstaining from vices and seeks no outward praise for it but inwardly the recompense of God alone—is rightly said to be clothed in purple and fine linen. Then follows appropriately the contemplation of the mind, understood in the words that follow:

[Col. 0388D] “And he feasted splendidly every day.” This feast, by which the blessed soul ought to feast in the Lord, is received through prayer, reading, and meditation. A person receives the feast of wisdom in prayer and takes the feast of knowledge from reading. But note that it says, “and he feasted splendidly every day.” For the perfect person who tends towards true life ought to strive with every effort to have this feast daily by God’s grace. Yet it is difficult for one to have each day the feast of wisdom, tasted and received in prayer, so as inwardly to taste God in compunction and to remain continually in this savour of prayer. Therefore, when the feast of wisdom is absent, so that one cannot beforehand taste God through prayer, let him take for himself the feast of knowledge arising from assiduous reading or meditation; and whichever of these feasts has satisfied him, he may be said to have feasted splendidly. 546 [Col. 0389A] And the word “splendidly” is well chosen. For it rarely happens that a person receives one of these three feasts without remaining fruitless, unless some brightness of mind comes to him thereby: so that he either tastes God in prayer, receives the light of knowledge in reading, or discovers in meditation what he did not previously know. Therefore, each day one ought to receive one of these feasts—prayer, reading, or meditation—if one strives perfectly to please the eyes of the supreme Majesty. It follows:

“And there was a certain beggar, named Lazarus.” Lazarus, whose name means “helped,” signifies any converted sinner, who needs to be helped by prayers, holy exhortations, and the holy examples and consolations of other holy persons. Of this [Col. 0389B] spiritual Lazarus it is fittingly added: “who lay at his gate, full of sores.” The sores are sins and vices. When he begins perfectly to recognize them, he does not stand but lies at the rich man’s gate, while, according to the instruction and holy way of life either of a superior or of any other holy person humbly serving God in holiness and innocence, he carefully considers what he ought to do and what avoid. And it rightly says, “at the rich man’s gate.” For through a gate there is exit from and entry into a house. The gate through which each rich person enters is watchfulness of heart, through which he enters into himself that he may recognize himself within; the gate through which he goes out is the performance of a good work, by which he seeks the salvation and benefit of his neighbours. [Col. 0389C] Of this going out and coming in the Apostle Peter says concerning the Lord Jesus: “During all the time in which the Lord Jesus came in and went out among us” (Acts 1:21). The Lord Jesus came in when, for our sake, he entered into himself to pray and intercede with the Father for us, as is written of him in the Gospel, how he went up alone upon the mountain to pray. And again: “When evening came, he was there alone” (Matt. 4:24). Having entered thus, he again went out when he spent the entire day in preaching, watched over the edification of his neighbours, and outwardly showed divine miracles to the needy and those who sought them. Each person ought to imitate such an entrance and exit: let him enter into watchfulness over himself and go out to the edification of his neighbour. 547 [Col. 0389D] At this rich man’s gate lies every poor person who sees himself full of sores, who knows himself entangled in great and grave crimes. He lies, I say, while he humbly considers how to enter into himself, when he turns himself to the practice of prayer, and how again to go out, when he extends himself to the exercise of good works and the edification of his neighbours. Therefore, just as one lying face-down upon the ground cannot quickly rise, so the humble poor person ought to lie at the rich man’s gate, that he may adhere to him firmly and steadfastly; he should not glance at his life hastily or fleetingly, but, carefully considering his entrance and exit, should strive to imitate his life.

“Desiring,” he says, “to be filled with the crumbs which fell from the rich man’s table.” The rich man’s table is Holy Scripture; the crumbs which fall from this table are the more subtle and [Col. 0390A] stricter precepts, which not all people can attain. For it is a great commandment not to commit adultery. But for one who humbly lies at the rich man’s gate, it is not enough to have observed this; rather, he undertakes to keep the narrower and more excellent path of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). Again, it is a great commandment not to commit homicide. But the person striving to enter through the narrow gate also attends to that subtle commandment: “whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). He desires to be filled with crumbs who strives to fulfil these lesser and more excellent observances in deeds, who has perfectly acquired the desire for a good and holy life. And the phrase “which fell from the table” is rightly used, because [Col. 0390B] these more subtle commands truly fall, since many cannot observe them. For few are those who guard themselves in the smallest things, who watch their wills and desires with such caution and diligence that they never lapse, even in thought, from true chastity. For who, in accordance with the Apostle’s judgment, will boast that he has a chaste heart? It follows:

“But dogs also came and licked his sores.” Whoever that beggar may be who truly knows himself to be a beggar—poor, I mean, and needy—who, lying at the rich man’s gate, humbly watches his entrance and exit and carefully considers his life in order to imitate it, to this person desiring, as we have said, to be filled from the rich man’s table, dogs beneficially come and lick his sores. That is, holy preachers, signified by dogs, [Col. 0390C] 548 come to the wounds of the sick soul with the tongue of exhortation and the tongue of consolation. For what else is it for dogs to lick sores than, after the example of the compassionate Samaritan, to pour now wine, now oil into wounds requiring healing, so that by the bitterness of penitence, which is wine, the corruptions of vices may be cut away, and by the sweetness of consolation, which is oil, the wounds of the stricken soul may be cherished and healed? After humble Lazarus, the true beggar for eternal salvation, has thus risen to true penitence and confession of sins—as though the corruption of his wounds had been drawn out by the tongues of dogs—at last, through the grace of God, [Col. 0390D] there occurs in this person the great and memorable event concerning which the only-begotten Son of God, who works all these things, testifies in what follows:

“And it came to pass,” he says, “that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom.” There is one death, a good death, called the death of the saints; there is another death, an evil death, called the death of sinners. Of the good death it is written: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). Of the evil death it is written: “The death of sinners is worst” (Ps. 33:22). Those die the worst death who, devoted to flesh and fleshly pleasures, follow their desires and, because they refuse to recognize in penitence what they do, fall into the punishment of eternal damnation. [Col. 0391A] But the humble beggar of Christ dies the good death—being, that is, a converted and perfect persecutor of his sins—the death that is truly precious in the sight of the Lord, when he dies to the world, dies to sins and vices, and dies to the pleasures and desires of the flesh. This is so insofar as lies in the person: he does not permit anything to rule in him that might offend the most merciful eyes of almighty God, whom alone he loves and desires. And when he is thus mortified in himself, he is more happily made alive in Christ, who is the life of those who see. Hence it is immediately added that he “was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom.” By Abraham, whose name means “exalted father,” God the Father is understood, to whose majesty’s height nothing can be compared. His bosom is that repose of inward sweetness by which the humble beggar of Christ is sweetly refreshed, when, after the long and enduring torments of penitence, he is restored and made alive by the most sweet savour of divine visitation and consolation, [Col. 0391B] 549 and wholly forgets his want and beggary. But by whom, or through whom, is the humble beggar carried into this bosom of Abraham? By angels. Through angels, who are called messengers, holy desires, holy thoughts, and holy wills are fittingly signified. Wonderfully raised by these and carried, as it were, into Abraham’s bosom, to the very sweetness of supreme repose, a person rests with God the more securely the less he admits or desires the things that are outside. It follows:

[Col. 0391C] “But the rich man also died and was buried in hell.” Who this rich man is, we have heard sufficiently in what precedes. But it remains to see by what death he dies who, as we have heard, is honoured and exalted by God through holiness and innocence of life and such excellence in diverse virtues. For it often happens that such a person, clothed in purple and fine linen and feasting splendidly each day with God in contemplation of mind, is sought out and raised through the choice of almighty God and of holy Church to a place of governance. But because, when a mind accustomed to heavenly sweetness begins to be dispersed among outward things, it necessarily becomes less able to gather itself to inward things, that very promotion becomes for him the occasion of a kind of harsh death. For he dies to that brightness and that sweetness which he formerly had by God’s mercy. [Col. 0391D] For when the affairs and anxieties of the world rush upon him from every side—anxieties in which he must be involved because of love for those whose bodily and spiritual needs he ought to provide for—the more external care increases, the more that divine brightness of heavenly illumination, which he once customarily received inwardly either from the sweetness of prayer, the assiduity of reading, or the persistence of meditation, decreases. And when he cannot have what he remembers once having had, life becomes burdensome, light itself becomes dreadful, and thus is fulfilled what follows: “And he was buried in hell.” Hell is a place of darkness and punishments. And “buried” is well said, for one who is buried is covered with earth. What is this burial except the care of earthly occupations and anxieties? Oppressed by it, because he cannot raise himself upward to heavenly things as he was accustomed to do, he lies as though buried in hell itself. [Col. 0392A] For the pain by which he tortures himself because of the unbearable lack of inward grace that he feels within himself is rightly compared to the pains of hell. For while he silently considers within himself how any one of the humble, in his repose, clings to God alone, unhindered by any earthly care, he would gladly, if he could, withdraw from his own prelacy. But because what he desires cannot be, he endures greater torments within himself. Hence it follows:

“But the rich man, lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, saw Abraham far off and Lazarus in his bosom.” For in torments—that is, in the excessive torture of his mind—he lifts up, as it were, eyes cast behind him and remembers his former life, when, having set aside all passing things, he clung alone to God alone, seeking and loving nothing outside God. [Col. 0392B] He sees Abraham from afar; he sees almighty God as distant from himself, because him whom he once had near through the continual grace of inward sweetness he can scarcely recognize from afar. And he sees Lazarus in his bosom. For while in the great bitterness of his heart he weighs and considers how any humble person, clinging to God alone in humility, is raised on high by the sweetness of inward repose and is pressed down by no burden of earthly occupation, while he himself, as though blinded by earthly occupations, perceives nothing of the inward light, he grieves for the tranquillity he has lost and fears lest he fall even into wicked deeds. Therefore he cries with the voice of the body and the voice of the heart to the ears of the compassionate Creator: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me.” As though he said: Father Abraham, who according to the excellence of your name once showed me the grace of paternal sweetness, have mercy on me; in the multitude of your mercies remember me.

[Col. 0392C] “And send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.” By Lazarus in this place we fittingly understand the spirit of the penitent; by the finger, the Holy Spirit; by the tip of the finger, the spirit of the fear of the Lord; by water, the grace of compunction. By the tongue, through which speech is uttered and a person’s will revealed, the will and desire of the heart are not unfittingly expressed. [Col. 0392D] The flame in which he is tormented aptly signifies the earthly care of occupation. It is as though he said: Lord, I am not worthy, because I do not deserve that my wretched soul should be consoled by the spirit of your love, by which I was once touched. 551 But send, I beg, Lazarus; send into me the spirit of a truly penitent person, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water: that is, that at least through the spirit of fear I may receive that water of compunction which may wash away the contagions of my sins, so that my tongue—that is, the will and desire of my soul, by which I burn and sigh towards you—may receive from this flame and burning of earthly occupation, in which I am tormented, some refreshing of your consolation. And because almighty God never permits such a person—a person, I mean, who loves and invokes him—to perish, even though he sometimes falls in some respects, he is warned and taught by the following words [Col. 0393A] to return within himself to himself, carefully weighing and considering what it was that most hindered for him the grace of the divine gift, namely the grace of inward sweetness. For it follows:

“And Abraham said to him: Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things.” As though he said: Remember, I beg you, that for the merit of your innocent life and for the diligent pursuit of good action, by which you ought to have pleased me alone, you received good things in your life; because, while you were more than rightly elated and raised above yourself by the favour of human praise, you sought outward things less cautiously, and you rightly lost inward good things. Lazarus, on the contrary—any humble penitent, humbly recognizing his sins—[Col. 0393B] although he has done evil, received evil things in his life, because amid all his labours he neither rejoiced nor delighted in the favour of any human praise.

“But now he is comforted here, and you are tormented.” For he recognizes himself as poor and needy, and therefore in the repose of his humility is cherished by divine consolations. But you, deprived through the occasion of earthly occupation of the sweetness of inward consolation which comes from God, torment yourself. Why he suffers these things is indicated in what follows, when it is immediately added:

“And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to here.” What are all these things? [Col. 0393C] Everything in this world is either good or evil, prosperous or adverse. For when a person loves good things too much, hates evil things too much, loves prosperity too much, and flees adversity too much, all these things establish a great chasm. For they create a great confusion between God and a person, preventing either the brightness of heavenly visitation and illumination from shining down from above or the disturbed mind from rising upward to God through the affection of holy desire.

Nor should these words be considered merely in passing. By those of whom it is said, “so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot,” I think, as far as I see, that angelic spirits, angelic blessednesses, and those inestimable delights of heavenly brightness and sweetness enjoyed by angels in heaven are fittingly understood. [Col. 0393D] But by the addition, “nor can they cross from there to here,” holy desires and affections of a person seem, as far as I understand it, to be signified. For it often happens that through the ministry of holy angels, grace of heavenly sweetness is sent down from heaven and comes beforehand to a person freely and without labour, from the sole and simple goodness of the most kindly Creator, so that he does not even know, when receiving it, whence comes what he receives. It also often happens that almighty God withdraws the hand of his gratuitous goodness, and a person can rise to what he desires only through his own labours. But when all these things of which we have spoken—prosperity and adversity, that is—are brought on by the unhappy mutability of human life and are not rejected, they establish between God and a person an impenetrable confusion, [Col. 0394A] so that neither God, always ready in the blessings of his sweetness to descend to the human heart in mercy, nor a person, through the affection or desire of holy devotion, can ascend to God. This is that cloud of which the prophet says: “You have set a cloud before yourself, so that prayer may not pass through to you” (Lam. 3:44). But because all things work together for good to those who love God, the righteous person does not fail amid these things, but advances; for the more humbly he recognizes his failure, the more he begins to advance in God. He therefore says:

“I beg you then, Father, that you send him to my father’s house—for I have five brothers—that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments.”

A person’s father is the person’s spirit; the father’s house [Col. 0394B] signifies the body, which the spirit inhabits and gives life to. By the five brothers we understand the five senses of the person. It is as though he said: I am unworthy, Lord, of that sweetness and 553 grace by which you, holy Father, who never fail in yourself, refresh Lazarus, any one of your humble servants, through yourself. But I beg you to send him to my father’s house; I beg, I say, that by the manifold compassion of your mercy I may be granted that humility and penitence which befit a truly penitent person. Thus, although I cannot be consoled from the abundance of sweetness which is in you because my inward senses are darkened from the light of your brightness, at least I may not allow through the outward senses of my body, on the occasion either of earthly prosperity or earthly adversity, [Col. 0394C] anything that might offend the eyes of your majesty. “Lest they too come into this place of torments”: that is, lest I endure after this, assigned to eternal punishments in both body and soul, those torments which I now suffer inwardly in my soul.

And Abraham said to him: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.” These words of Abraham are the words of almighty God speaking in the human heart, by which he admonishes and instructs a person how he may return to the grace of the lost sweetness above, and by what means he ought to escape the future torments that he fears. For in Moses, who was a lawgiver, continual meditation upon sacred Scripture is understood; in the prophets, who announce not only past things but also future ones, preaching is understood [Col. 0394D]. “They have Moses and the prophets,” he says; “let them listen to them.” As though he plainly said: If you seek to return to the inward joys of the mind’s sweetness that arise from contemplation, if you wish to keep yourself from sins and vices in your outward senses, you must apply yourself to reading; you must apply yourself to preaching. You ought to listen to Moses by frequently reading sacred Scripture; you ought to listen to the prophets by imitating the life of other people—whether those under your authority or those elsewhere—who, even if not by preaching, nevertheless by their heavenly manner of life suggest, as if by prophecy, both the future glory of everlasting life and the future punishment of eternal damnation.

For it often happens that, while one who presides over others preaches, he finds his own preacher among those to whom he preaches [Col. 0395A]. For one who, having cast aside and despised the pleasures of the world, lives humbly for God’s sake may rightly be called a prophet of God. In that he carefully avoids evil, he shows that the torments of Gehenna exist, which he desires to escape; and in that he humbly does good, he shows that the joys of the heavenly homeland exist, which he hastens to attain. But because sometimes neither diligence in reading nor the steadfastness of other people, in whom he observes zeal for holy conduct, can soften a mind occupied by outward cares toward inward sweetness, the rich man, rightly placed amid torments, added and said:

“No, father Abraham. But if someone should go to them from the dead, they will do penance.” As though he said: No, father, neither the study of reading nor the example of other people’s holy conduct helps me to escape the torments which my wretched soul, deprived of your grace, suffers within itself [Col. 0395B]. But if my miserable spirit, dead in itself, should somehow breathe again unto life through the grace of your most merciful visitation, then at last I could punish within myself by worthy penance those things which displease your fatherhood in me, and return to the grace of your lost sweetness.

But he said to him: “If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.” As though he said: If they do not give heed to reading, if they do not give heed to preaching—which is truly to listen to Moses and the prophets—neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead. For even if they are visited by God for a time and an hour through the grace of heavenly sweetness, and are inwardly brought to life from the death of the soul [Col. 0395C], this quickening or resurrection does not endure or remain effective for long unless it is assisted and strengthened by continual reading and diligent preaching.

With the help and gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit, we have thus far, as best we could, arranged these matters from the Gospel reading as an admonition and exhortation for the rich and poor who are in monasteries—that is, prelates and subjects—who strive to please God in the spiritual life. Those who are in subjection and quiet should hear of the death of the rich man of which we have spoken, be alarmed, and beware lest, desiring for themselves the burden of prelacy by their own will or desire, they come to the flame and torment of earthly anxieties, which those who preside cannot escape [Col. 0395D]. But those who, by the will and election of God—or even, as sometimes happens, through their sins and former desires—having not been content with their quiet, have deserved to be exposed to such great labours and to be raised to a position of government, should hear, attend to, imitate, and carry out the teaching and admonition of Abraham, who says: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.” Let them, I say, apply themselves to reading and persist in preaching, according to the Apostle, who, writing to Timothy, says among other things: “Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching” (1 Tim. 4:13). For if they do this, they truly listen to Moses and the prophets; and so it comes about that, both living rightly and teaching rightly according to sacred Scripture, they receive the fruit of their labours: the blessedness of eternal joys [Col. 0396A].

But since God alone is he who ought and is able to work these things in us, let us implore his help, that he who by his grace taught us these things in his holy words may also by that same grace assist us to carry them out, so that both you, for the humble devotion of your subjection, and we, for the grave labour of our occupation and administration, may attain those joys of eternal blessedness that are without labour. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

Having expounded, to the best of our ability, the words of this holy Gospel, it is pleasing to consider whether this first Sunday may have some agreement or suitability with that first day of the creation of the world [Col. 0396B]. For we should like, if by God’s gift we are able, to fit the works of the seven days by signification to these first seven Sundays, and to show how the work of each day agrees and corresponds in mystery with each Gospel.

We read in Genesis that light was created when the Lord said: “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. 1:3), and so forth. So far as it seems to me, in a simple and plain sense, by this light that just Lazarus may be understood who was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; and by the darkness, that rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted sumptuously every day, who died and was buried in hell. For God divided light from darkness [Col. 0396C] when, by the marvellous judgment of his justice, he willed that the one who had received evils in his life should be brought by the ministry of angels into Abraham’s bosom to be comforted and rewarded; but he permitted the other, who had abounded in every good thing in his life, to be buried in hell, tormented amid punishments, and not refreshed even by a drop of water. There he called the light day and the darkness night, because according to the merit of each he apportioned the recompense: upon this one he brought the day of eternal reward, but upon that one darkness—that is, the night of eternal damnation.

This we may understand simply in the division of light and darkness. But because we have surveyed the Gospel, as best we could, according to its moral sense, it is worthwhile to expound the work of the first day according to the mystical sense of the Gospel [Col. 0396D], and, so far as God grants, to indicate that there is some harmony between the day and the Gospel, both in this Sunday and in the following Sundays.

Therefore God said: “Let there be light.” And there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good; and he divided light from darkness. And he called the light day and the darkness night. And evening and morning came: one day. For whenever any rich man—one adorned by the riches of virtues and nourished by the feasts of sacred Scriptures—dies and is buried in hell, he dies, I say, to God while living for the world through vain exaltation of mind; and he is buried in hell when he is tormented and darkened by a shadowy and deadly conscience. It is necessary that God the Lord, God our Creator [Col. 0397A], command light to come into being and, as he once sent visible light, so also send down his invisible light, which may shine upon and illuminate the darkness of the heart; and that he divide light from darkness. This light which God commanded to be made is, good and pure, as it seems to me, the will through which, when first it is put into the heart, a person is enlightened and prepared to know, fear, and love God. Whenever, through the grace of divine inspiration, some beginning of good will has arisen in the human heart, this good will will be a great and splendid day before the Lord. This day—that is, good will and good consent—cannot come to be unless God speaks, whose speaking is his doing.

After good will has been received, what else remains, my brethren [Col. 0397B], except that one preserve in himself the consent of good and sincere will in such a manner that, with God’s help, he keeps it unstained and undefiled, to the best of his ability, from every vanity and emptiness of this world? When God gives and makes this light—that is, good will—and when we, according to our powers, remove and reject every surrounding occasion of vanity, it may rightly be said of us: “And there was light.” For, as I have said, God’s speaking is his doing. He makes his light shine in us; he enlightens us; and he supplies both willing and ability, not only to those who do not will the good, but also to those who will it yet are unable. When this light has been made, it fittingly follows:

“And God saw the light, that it was good, and divided light from darkness.” That will which is pure, which is not corrupted and stained by any vanity, is pleasing to God. He sees that it is good; and because it is good, he approves and loves it. In this loving gaze of almighty God, the division of light and darkness occurs. What are darknesses but evil desires, unlawful and confused pleasures, harmful and disgraceful thoughts? And these are rightly called darkness, because by them the heart is darkened if they are not rejected, if they are received with love [Col. 0397C]. Hence we must labour greatly that God may deign to divide light from darkness in us, lest evil and unlawful concupiscences and disordered thoughts so overwhelm and prevail that the light which shone in us begins to grow dark into the night of sins. For through this good and complete division we shall have in ourselves the light of a great day. That the entire sum of salvation or perdition consists in and depends upon the human will, so far as it seems to me, is taught us in the following words:

“And,” he says, “he called the light day and the darkness night.” For wherever a whole consent of good will, unmixed with any vanity, inwardly cooperates with divine inspiration, even if the outward effect of good works is lacking, the fruit of eternal recompense will by no means be taken away; indeed, it will be brought and given. For God himself calls the light day; he knows how greatly to value and reward the will of good action alone. And just as he calls light day, so he also calls darkness night, because just as good will [Col. 0398A] deserves from him rewards and the day of eternal joys, so evil and unjust will deserves from him the night of punishments, even if the acts of sins never follow.

And lest what we have said should seem unbelievable—that is, that good and evil will are reckoned before the Lord as deeds—listen to the Lord himself affirm the same thing in the Gospel, where he says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). Certainly we heard that a great day had been made in that rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted sumptuously every day: he had a purple garment because he devoted himself to the mortification of the flesh; he had fine linen because purity of body and soul pleased him. But because he did not divide light from darkness [Col. 0398B]—that is, because he did not preserve his holy and pure will from the vanity of boasting and empty glory, but, alas, defiled it through these things—God, who had previously called light day, that is, who had esteemed good will highly, himself called darkness night. For unjust desires, the wicked craving for human praise that he sought and loved, and also perverse thoughts—all of which were darkness—were turned before the Lord, because he failed to recognize [object unexpressed in the source], into a deep night of sins.

Meanwhile God must be invoked most earnestly, that whenever he creates in us the day of good will, he may also preserve it in us, making our will such that he may always call it day and never darkness. He is also prepared to do this with those who, after the manner of Lazarus, humble themselves; who truthfully behold their poverty and beggary; who live commendably indeed, yet do not desire to be praised; who, placed in great quietness of heart, often deserve in this life to enjoy the peaceful God [Col. 0398C]. Let these, then, rejoice in the day of true light which they have received, and give thanks to God. But those in whom the true day has set through the fall into sin should return to themselves and recognize what they have sinned in themselves and against their neighbour; and for this let them offer God the gift of worthy penance and satisfaction. John therefore admonishes us in today’s reading to come to the light, to know ourselves, and to hold fast the light of charity, saying: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20).

Therefore, whoever has perfectly known himself and does not forget the love which he owes his neighbour, in him without doubt evening and morning become one day. What is to be understood by evening except self-knowledge? From true self-knowledge one passes from evening into morning. And what is morning except the sweet and lovable knowledge of God? [Col. 0398D] These two forms of knowledge—our evening and God’s morning—make one day in us. And what is understood by the one day except the true God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who, having removed the darkness of hearts, creates and perfects in his elect the full and perfect day of his love? But that this day may come upon us, that such light may enlighten us at God’s command—that is, that such a will may be present as can be called light—we ask in today’s prayer for the help of his grace, that in carrying out his commandments we may please him both in will and in action [Col. 0399A]. For what is will but light? What is action but day? Therefore, because the elect are unable, through the hindrance of the devil and the world, through the weakness of their own flesh, or through the wickedness of evil people, to possess full and steadfast light, it is very necessary that these two persons, namely the rich man and the poor man—that is, every human being—cry out to God and commend themselves and all that is theirs to God.

Let the rich say and pray, trusting not in themselves but in the Lord: “O God, the strength of those who hope in you, graciously attend to our petitions, so that, if we have ever been rich in virtues and strong in our works, you may preserve these riches in us by your strength and power.” Let the poor—the humble and despised—say and pray: “And because mortal weakness can do nothing without you, grant the help of your grace to our weakness, that in carrying out your commandments we may please you in will, that is, in light, and in action, namely in the full day which you [the manuscript: ‘whom’] make in us” [Col. 0399B].

Today’s excellence of the Mass appears to me to refer to this meaning, where the enlightened person sings for exultation and sings in hope, expecting at some time to receive something great in reality, saying: “O Lord, I have hoped in your mercy; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation; I will sing to the Lord, who has bestowed good things upon me” (Ps. 12:6). “O Lord,” he says, “because I have been somewhat enlightened by your mercy, therefore I have hoped in your mercy; therefore you have granted me great confidence to hope in you, hoping that I shall one day come to that place where my light may arrive at full day. But meanwhile, until I am taken away from the midst [Note: [Col. 0399] Thus the manuscript. It is as though he said: “Meanwhile, until I am taken away from the midst,” that is, until this life is ended.], my heart shall rejoice in your salvation”—my heart which your salvation has filled and possessed with its light, that is, with good will and good consent, though not fully but in part [Col. 0399C].

And I rightly say, “in part,” because, having known this light in part, I desire and strive to advance and arrive from good will at the perfection of good works. But no perfection can exist or endure here. Why? Because “we now see through a mirror in obscurity; we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13:12); and then I shall sing to the Lord, who bestows good things upon me. What is “I shall sing”? To be there where I do not weep or pray, but where I praise you, knowing that nothing comes to me from myself, but every good thing from you. But meanwhile, since we are in evil days, when our invisible enemies rage against us, when sometimes darkness succeeds light immediately after light, after the Introit of hope and gladness of heart there follows in the Verse the prayer of the soul still groaning in the world and saying: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end? How long will you turn your face away from me?” (Ps. 12:1) [Col. 0399D].

Therefore in the Gradual the soul, labouring and endangered amid great crowds of temptations, sighs again, yet greatly hopes in God’s mercy, and says: “I said: O Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5). In my deeds, in my sins, I accuse before you, O Lord, not another but myself; I acknowledge myself to be a sinner. Therefore I say to you: “Have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.” “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor man; the Lord will deliver him in the evil day” (Ps. 40:2). Just as blessed is he who says, “Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you,” so he is no less blessed who understands concerning the needy and poor man, who faithfully beholds his own poverty and need, knowing and considering that Christ is all the good that he has, and that all that he has belongs to Christ. For that man is rich who is proud, who glories in his chastity and innocence, who flatters and exalts himself on account of his manner of life. And whoever does this will not be delivered in the evil day—in the day of death, in the day of judgment [Col. 0400A]. But he who understands himself to be poor and needy, and daily begs and knocks at the door of God as one needy and poor, him the Lord will deliver in the evil day; because, when God receives, aids, and leads him, he will be delivered from sins, from fear of death, judgment, and punishments.

After this the blessed soul sings, whose sole concern must be to avoid the devil’s snares, saying to the Lord God: “O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me from all those who persecute me, and deliver me” (Ps. 7:2). That he says in the plural, “Save me from all those who persecute me,” signifies prosperity and adversity, by which both rich man and poor man are tempted and tested. Hence comes Abraham’s saying to the rich man: “Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things. And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you” [Col. 0400B]. These two desires—to seek prosperity and to avoid adversity—make between us and God a chasm, that is, a great confusion, so that the light of the heart, which is God, is not seen, but rather darkness is loved and received as light. Whoever is not excessively elated in prosperity, and whoever is not excessively cast down in adversity, does not receive good and evil things in his life, because he despises alike both prosperity and adversity. And such a person ought to pray and invoke God, that, with God’s aid, he may so pass through the prosperity and adversity of this world as to arrive at him, saying: “Attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God, because to you, O Lord, will I pray.”

[Col. 0400D] Therefore, because we are between night and day, and each of us is compelled to endure days and nights in alternating succession, and, even when we sense and possess day, we decline into night more quickly than speech can tell, until every night has passed and the one day which has no evening arrives: he who endures these changes in such a way that he is not moved or wearied, when the Mass has ended and he has communicated—that is, when he has passed into the body of Christ—will sing with joyful heart and joyful body at the end of his life: “I will recount all your wonders; I will rejoice and exult in you; I will sing psalms to your name, O Most High” (Ps. 9:3).

For, seeing that invisible reward to which he is going to come, he begins in the gladness of his heart to recount all the wonders of God; he begins to remember and confess from the depth of his heart all his sins [Col. 0401A]. He begins to recount God’s wonders, considering that these are his wonders: wherever and from whatever sin he has kept himself. He recounts God’s wonders because God so long delayed and waited for the sinner, not in order to punish him, but to crown him when penitent and amended. Then, passing from visible things to invisible, he says: “I will rejoice and exult in you; I will sing psalms to your name, O Most High.” He gave two expressions—“I will rejoice” and “I will exult”—because of the twofold joy of body and soul.

“I will therefore rejoice,” he says, “and exult: I will rejoice in body, I will exult in spirit; and this comes from you, not from myself. I will sing psalms to your name, because as long as I am here I must sing psalms to my flesh and to my weak mind. But when I come to you, I shall sing psalms to you alone; I shall sing psalms to your most high and glorious name, because here there is groaning, here weeping; there, exultation without end.” My brethren, let us groan and pray now; let us weep here and humble ourselves, so that we may come to that most abundant and inexpressible joy which can never be uttered in words, can never be estimated, yet can be acquired. May he bring us to it, he who lives and is glorified with God the Father through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

563 HOMILY LX. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

“There was a certain man from Ramathaim-sophim, from Mount Ephraim,” etc. (1 Kings 1).

Since the Word of God, the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, says to the Jews: “Search the Scriptures, and they are those which bear witness concerning me” (John 5:39), it seems a great confirmation of truth if someone can interpret sacred Scripture in such a way that its mystery looks to the Lord himself, who established it [Col. 0401C]. A moral sense in sacred Scripture is indeed necessarily required, so that all the weak may have an example of how they ought to correct and order their life and conduct. But because Truth itself says that all Scriptures bear witness concerning him, it is a greater support of truth, as we have said, that the Scriptures which speak of him should also be mystically referred to him. Therefore, believing that he is marked here at the beginning of the book, we attempt, so far as he himself grants, to refer and interpret this text in the history of the first book of Kings with respect to him who is our head. For thus it is read at the beginning of the book of Kings:

“There was a certain man from Ramathaim-sophim, from Mount Ephraim; and his name was Elkanah, son of Jeroboam [Vulgate: Jeroham], son of Eliu, son of Thohu [Vulgate: Thohu], son of Suph, an Ephrathite.” By the name of this one man may be signified the Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, because apart from him alone no human being upon earth could ever truly be called, or will be called, by the name “man,” since all human beings, conceived and born in iniquities, are at times made effeminate by the defilement of sin. But our Lord Jesus Christ rightly ought to be called the one man, because he alone could live among people in this world in such a manner that he never admitted in thought, word, or deed anything except what was manly and virtuous [Col. 0402A]. David also identifies this man, Christ Jesus, in the psalm, and declares that apart from this one alone all people are enveloped in the contagion of sins: “All,” he says, “have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3). Behold this one, often already mentioned, and always to be spoken of and named, is our Lord Jesus Christ, who, because of his singular innocence, is often signified by the name of one in sacred Scripture.

But that he could live in this world as a true man without the guilt of human contagion did not come to him from his human nature, but from the fact that he was God, one in the holy Trinity, which we believe can be signified by these three names: Ramatha, Sophim, Ephraim. For Ramatha means “exalted,” by which name the Holy Spirit may fittingly be understood. Sophim means “watchtower,” by which the Son of God himself of whom we speak may be represented, since by assuming humanity he presented himself to people as God made visible. Ephraim means “fruitful,” by which God the Father may be designated, from whom whatever has ever produced good fruit receives its efficacy. Thus it was not human nature that bestowed on our Lord Jesus Christ the fact that his life and conduct were unlike the life and conduct of all the saints from the beginning to the end of the age; rather, he had this because he was God and man, and the entire holy Trinity worked with him and in him [Col. 0402B], with whom and in whom God is one without end or beginning.

“And his name,” he says, “was Elkanah.” Elkanah is interpreted “possession of God,” by whom this same man Christ Jesus is represented. We do not need much instruction concerning why he is called God’s possession, because we know that all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in him. And rightly the holy divinity, whose eyes are pure so as not to see iniquity, had claimed for its own special possession such a man, in whose thoughts, words, and deeds it never found anything that could displease it.

“Son of Jeroboam, son of Eliu, son of Thohu, son of Suph, an Ephrathite” [Col. 0402D]. Let us state the meanings of these names and briefly touch upon what seems to us to be contained in them. Jeroboam means “merciful”; Eliu, “this God.” Thohu means “a sign” or “below”; Suph, “watchtower”; Ephrathite, “fruitful.” For briefly and simply we may say of them that it was a work of gratuitous mercy that he who was God above us willed to be below—that is, to become man—for us; and that he who is the image and splendour of God’s substance offered himself to be seen by people. This is signified by the name Suph, because it means “watchtower”; and he then became Ephrathite, which means “fruit-bearing,” when by preaching and working miracles he turned human hearts to himself.

[Col. 0403A] “And he had two wives; the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah.” The two wives of our Lord Jesus Christ were his two natures, divine and human; these are also signified by the names of these two women. For Hannah means “grace,” whereas Peninnah means “conversion.” In Hannah’s name we may understand Christ’s human nature. For it was truly full of grace, and God was so well pleased in it that through it he willed to be reconciled to the whole human race which had provoked him to wrath. Nor is it without a certain cause of mystery that it is so notably said: “the name of one was Hannah.” One—that is, singular and incomparable—was the human nature in the Only-begotten of God, because he alone was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary without male seed [Col. 0403B]. From the beginning of time it has not been heard that any woman conceived or gave birth without the touch of a man. Hence Scripture, designating Christ’s human nature, rightly says: “the name of one was Hannah.”

By Peninnah, the divine nature in Christ may be understood, to which the interpretation of this name fittingly belongs. For Peninnah, as we have said, means “conversion.” It is indeed the operation of the divine nature whenever anyone is able to be converted from evil to good, and from the danger of misery to true blessedness. Therefore divine nature is rightly expressed through her who is called conversion, because by the power of the highest Divinity everything is converted that attains the gift of blessed conversion.

But it should be noted that he says, “the name of the second was Peninnah” [Col. 0403C]. This word “second” has the same meaning as if “prosperous” had been said. For we use “second things” to mean the same as prosperous things. If “second” here had been used to mean “later,” the name of Hannah would rightly have been called that of the first in the preceding words. But now it is said, “the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah,” in order that it may be understood that in this place the word “second” should be taken to mean “prosperous,” not “later.” The term expressing prosperity is properly applied to this woman through whom the divine nature is expressed. For whatever the human nature in Christ suffered, the divine nature in him nevertheless remained in the supreme tranquillity of prosperity; it could never suffer or admit in itself any trouble of adversity or disturbance, since it is joy to itself. It follows:

“And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no offspring.” Who were these children that Peninnah—that is, Christ’s divine nature—had, except the angelic spirits, whom from the time of their creation the sweetness of paternal love cherished in the most blessed contemplation of his countenance? But Hannah had no offspring. Notice that there they are described as “sons,” but here they are called “offspring,” a term derived from freedom. The children of Christ’s divine nature were sons because the angels clung to him with filial love; but the human nature had no free children, because through his death he had not yet led human beings to true freedom. For although the Son of God had assumed human nature, throughout all the days of his flesh people could not return from the captivity of the devil, but bore their necks bowed beneath the yoke of sin; and all alike, both just and unjust, descended into hell [Col. 0404A], until he took away the handwriting of the decree that was against us and nailed it to the cross.

“And that man went up from his city on the appointed days.” That man is the Only-begotten of God, who before becoming man—that is, human—for us in time, was man in eternity, in the divine dispensation; for divine eternity precedes all times, and no past or future thing is attributed to God, but all things are called present to him because he embraces all things in his eternity. For if the Apostle says of us, “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4), how much more was he himself man in eternity, in whom God chose us?

“And that man went up from his city on the appointed days.” The city of God is the angelic and human creation, with whom he purposed before temporal ages to build his city, the heavenly Jerusalem. That man, that is, the Only-begotten of God, went up from his city on the appointed days when he confirmed the holy angels, who can be signified by days, in that state of eternal blessedness, intending at some time to gather humanity there also, so that his city might be complete [Col. 0404B]. Let no one wonder that we say angels are designated by days, since at their creation God said, “Let there be light.” For they are called light and day because they partake of eternal light and day. But why did that man go up from his city on the appointed days?

“To worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts in Shiloh.” For this reason the holy angels received the firmness of eternal perseverance: that they might perpetually cling to the praise and vision of their Creator, for which they had been created—this is worshipping; and that they might be in the defence of the human race and be sent into ministry for those who receive the inheritance of salvation—this is sacrificing. This worshipping and sacrificing was done in Shiloh, which means “separation,” that is, in that separation in which God divided light from darkness and called the light day and the darkness night; where, that is, he separated and in some way tore away the elect angels, who are signified by light, from the apostate angels, who are represented by darkness [Col. 0404C]. He condemned the devil with his followers, who opposed him through pride, to hell for ever; and he confirmed those who remained with God in humility and obedience as destined to reign with him for ever.

And it is rightly ascribed to the Only-begotten of God that he himself worshipped and sacrificed to the Lord of hosts—that is, to God his Father and to himself in his divinity—because all the worship of the holy angels, that is, their perseverance in God’s praise, and their devotion and sacrifice, namely their service in the human race, are the operation of the Son of God in them. For if in this world a person who clings to the Lord becomes one spirit with him, how much more are he in the holy angels and they in him one [Col. 0405A], and may what they do rightly be said to be done by him? It follows:

“Now there were there two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests of the Lord.” Eli means “my God,” by whom he can be designated whose name is truly and substantially what this name possesses figurally. The two sons of Eli, that is, of almighty God, are angel and human being; this too is expressed by the meanings of the two names of Eli’s sons. Hophni means “barefoot,” while Phinehas means “sparing of speech.” By Hophni, angels are quite fittingly designated, in my judgment, for they are truly barefoot because they are known to have been created in such a way that they are burdened by no hindrance of mortality. By Phinehas human creation may not unjustly be represented, which, in the persons of the elect, is so sparing of speech [Col. 0405B] that it not only avoids unjust and harmful speech, for which punishment is rendered, but also anxiously guards against an idle word, for which account is given, lest through carelessness of the tongue it fall into the treachery of evil deeds. Therefore the two sons of Eli—that is, angel and human being, whom God had begotten for himself by creating them—are rightly called priests of the Lord, because they offer themselves to God in sacrifice: the angel in heaven by praising God and unceasingly clinging to him; the human being on earth by daily longing for his Creator in service.

Then the day came, and Elkanah sacrificed. The day came when the Word was made flesh and began to dwell among us. Before this day dawned—that is, before the incarnation of the Son of God—darkness was upon the face of the deep [Col. 0405C], because the blindness of sins and the profound darkness of ignorance covered human hearts. But after the day which the Lord made began to dawn, when, that is, the almighty Word came from the royal dwelling-place, the night of unbelief departed, and the light of faith and truth possessed human hearts. Therefore the day came, and Elkanah sacrificed.

And he gave portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters. The Son of God gave portions to his wife Peninnah—that is, to his divine nature—when he created angelic and human creatures for the praise and glory of his name. By Peninnah’s sons and daughters, that is, by those of the divine nature, we may understand angels and human beings: by the sons, indeed, who are of a stronger condition than daughters, we may believe angels to be meant; but by the daughters, human beings, since they are of a weaker nature than angels. To these sons and daughters, namely angels and human beings, the Son of God gave portions. To angels, from their first creation, he assigned heaven for possession, as though by hereditary right, that there they might continually devote themselves to the praises of their Creator; but he gave the earth to the children of men, where, labouring in the sweat of their face, they too might at last, in the portion of the elect, attain fellowship with the angels.

But to Hannah he gave one sorrowful portion, because he loved Hannah. To Hannah—that is, to his human nature—the Son of God gave one portion, when he imposed upon it this one necessary task: that human redemption should be accomplished through it and in it [Col. 0406A]. But how did he give this portion sorrowfully? We must not hastily conclude that any sorrow can approach the divinity, which is eternal joy to itself. Rather, this sorrow was compassion itself, by which he grieved with the human race in its destruction. Therefore he gave one portion to Hannah—that is, he entrusted the work of our redemption to his human nature, signified by Hannah—because he loved Hannah: for he had human nature as beloved, not only in himself, but also throughout the entire human race.

But the Lord had shut her womb. Bodily offspring is conceived in the womb. Hence, by the womb, as I think, the pleasure of the flesh may not unjustly be understood. Therefore the divinity in Christ’s human nature had in a certain manner so shut up every carnal pleasure [Col. 0406B] that, although he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, he never incurred any guilt of worldly pleasure in thought, word, or deed.
