And while by his preaching he taught that the delights and pleasures of this present age ought to be despised, he offered himself as an example, for he did not even wish to have a place in this world where he might lay his head. But what happened meanwhile?

Moreover, her rival afflicted her and sorely distressed her, so much that she reproached her because the Lord had shut her womb. According to the literal truth, there is no doubt that Peninnah was Hannah’s rival. But above we said that Peninnah could signify the divine nature in Christ [Col. 0406C]. Yet may something else be understood here by “rival” than was understood there by Peninnah—unless someone wishes to take it in this way: that the divine nature afflicted and severely distressed the human nature because it had mercifully ordained that she should endure the evils of the world and undergo death for the salvation of humankind.

But in this passage we may otherwise understand the Synagogue by the rival. When Christ appeared in the flesh, it burned with such jealous envy against him that it cruelly afflicted him with injuries, blasphemies, and mockeries. In return for the many good works which he performed among them by preaching and healing their sick, they gave him nothing but insults. Finally, it distressed him most severely [Col. 0406D] when, supposing that he could be brought to an end by death, they seized him, bound him, struck him with fists and scourges, covered him with spittle, crowned him with thorns, and killed him by hanging him on the wood. Yet amid all these things they could bring against him no reproach except that the Lord had shut his womb: that is, that he did not live according to the flesh, that he did not seek the pleasure of this present age by observing their carnal ceremonies. Did they not reproach him then that the Lord had shut his womb when they shouted that he was guilty of death because he had made himself the Son of God?

And thus she acted year by year. In this way the Jews reproached the Lord Jesus year by year—that is, at each act of perfection—which he displayed among them by working divine miracles [Col. 0407A]. Thus it was a great year, that is, a perfection, when he healed the man blind from birth. But hear the Synagogue’s reproach against this perfection: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16). Again, it was a great perfection when he called Lazarus, dead four days, out of the tomb, raised him, and made him go away free after being loosed. But the Gospel tells us how the Jews reproached him for this also: “The chief priests planned,” it says, “to kill Lazarus too, because many of the Jews were leaving on account of him and believing in Jesus” (John 12:10). Thus she acted year by year, when, at the returning season, they went up to the temple of the Lord; and thus she provoked her.

Time has this character: it does not possess an abiding state [Col. 0407B]. Therefore by time is not unjustly signified that movement of the Synagogue, by which it was stirred now by these, now by such hatreds against the Lord Jesus. At last its movement even brought it to this: that they went up to the temple of the Lord, that is, that they condemned the Lord Jesus to a most shameful death—he who, beyond all saints, was truly the temple of the Holy Spirit. This was the provocation by which the Synagogue provoked the human nature in Christ.

But she wept and did not take food. This weeping was that compassion of Christ’s human nature by which he grieved with the human race in its destruction. For while the Jews were already bringing death upon him, he burned with this weeping, because he considered neither their cruelty nor the pain of death, but only the liberation of humankind. Nor did he take food [Col. 0407C], because when the Jews gave him gall for food and wished to give him vinegar to drink in his thirst, he refused it, desiring and thirsting only that human salvation might be accomplished.

Then Elkanah, her husband, said to her: “Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? And why is your heart afflicted?” This question was a certain stirring-up of the human nature, by which the divinity urged it to have compassion upon humankind and, in this compassionate fellow-feeling, to be afflicted for it even to the acceptance of death. Therefore it is rightly said: “Then Elkanah, her husband, said to her.” God’s speaking is God’s acting. It was indeed an operation of divinity in Christ’s human nature that he wept—that is, grieved with our destruction [Col. 0407D]; that he did not eat—that is, sought no delight of human pleasure in this world; and that his heart was afflicted—that is, that he gave himself no rest until human redemption should be accomplished.

“Am I not better to you than ten sons?” By the ten sons we may understand the ten senses which Christ possessed in his human nature. For, as he was a true human being, so he existed, like other human beings, with ten senses in soul and body. “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” I, namely, the divinity that dwells bodily in you, O human nature of Christ, benefit you more than your ten senses, by which you exist in human flesh and in a rational soul, because I furnish you with the strength [Col. 0408A] by which you will accomplish the redemption of humankind.

Then Hannah rose after she had eaten and drunk at Shiloh. Hannah ate and drank when the God-man, on the very night when he was delivered up, held his supper with his chosen and beloved disciples, where he gave his flesh with his blood as food and drink for the soul. And it is well said, “at Shiloh,” which, as we have said, means “separation”; for there the angelic company was present, which, as we said before, was separated in the beginning from the fellowship of the reprobate angels. The apostolic order was also present, which may be signified by the same appropriateness as the angels through the Word, which is called “separation.” For the holy apostles themselves—through whom and with whom alone that supper was visibly performed—clung with such love to the sweetness of his humanity that they were in some measure separated from the love of the world [Col. 0408B]. After Hannah had eaten and drunk at Shiloh—that is, after Christ’s human nature had completed his supper with that apostolic company—she rose: that is, she girded herself for the triumphant contest of the Passion. He signified this very thing when, while still sitting at supper, he said to the disciples: “Rise, let us go from here” (Matt. 26:46), undoubtedly toward the Passion.

And Eli the priest was sitting upon a seat before the doors of the temple. As a man sitting on a seat rests, so the divinity, which may be signified by Eli, rested in the man Christ. By the temple mentioned here, Christ himself is very fittingly signified: in him God had made for himself, beyond all saints, a pleasing dwelling-place [Col. 0408C]. By the doors of the temple, moreover, God the Father and the Holy Spirit may be understood, for they so contained and sustained this temple that it could never be destroyed by even the slightest defilement of sin. This is said according to the human nature. For according to the divinity, the Son of God is known to possess equal power with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Eli the priest was sitting upon a seat before the doors of the temple.

When Hannah was bitter of soul. We have often said already that Hannah signifies the human nature in Christ. She was bitter of soul when, already at the point of the Passion, he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38). But should we believe that the Lord Jesus, who of his own will offered himself to the shame of Passion and death, was moved to bitterness by the Passion itself? No. Rather, he was bitter of soul because he grieved that the human race still remained in destruction and that souls descended to hell [Col. 0408D]. Christ’s human nature was also bitter of soul because it saw the Jews, from whom he had come, conspiring so cruelly for his death; and he knew that, because of this very crime which they committed against him, they lay exposed to the danger of eternal condemnation. But when he was thus bitter of soul, what did he do?

She prayed to the Lord, weeping abundantly. Does it not seem to you that the Lord Jesus prayed and wept abundantly when, being in agony, he prayed at greater length and “his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground” [Col. 0409A] (Luke 22:43–44)? O how great was that weeping, and that bloody sweat wholly unknown to human suffering, which the Son of God chose to flow from his body while in his Passion he poured out prayers to God the Father for human redemption!

While he thus prayed and wept abundantly, he made a vow to God the Father: that, if he should accomplish the work of human redemption for which the Father had sent him into the world, he would bring all the souls of the elect to the praise and glory of his name.

And she made a vow, saying: “Lord of hosts, if you will indeed look upon the affliction of your handmaid, and remember me, and not forget your maidservant, and give your servant a male child, I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life.” If we wish to consider carefully, we shall recognize that the Lord Jesus prayed in his Passion for the very cause signified here, even though not in these words [Col. 0409B]. Three terms of equal meaning occur here—handmaid, maidservant, servant—by which the whole Church of the elect may be signified, existing in three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. By the handmaid the Church which was in the patriarchs is rightly signified, for it faithfully served God in hope of the future redemption. By the maidservant may be represented those who, oppressed under the legal bond, served the Law as a mistress who was a slave-woman and could not attain the liberty of children. By the servant we may understand those established under grace, who knew how to keep the divine commandments, not compelled by servile fear but overcome by filial love.

For all these, then [Col. 0409C], the Son of God thus prayed to God the Father in his human nature: “Lord God, almighty Father, who ordained that I should be incarnate for the salvation of the world: if, looking upon the affliction of your handmaid, you turn the eyes of your mercy to those who served you faithfully before the Law, and free them from their long affliction because they are oppressed in hell; and if you do not forget your maidservant—that is, if you remember those who served you under the Law by granting them the true freedom of children; and if you give your servant a male child—if, that is, you now accomplish through me, in the time of grace, the redemption of humankind and completely free from the captivity of the devil both your elect who are held in hell and those still in the world; and if (as is inserted) you remember me—that is, if you do all this on account of me and my obedience—I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life: namely, I will entrust to you again the assembly of your elect, where there will be no days of death but all days of life, where you will be glorified in them and they will rejoice in you forever.”

“He shall drink neither wine nor strong drink, and no razor shall come upon his head.” Wine and strong drink are beverages of intoxication that alter the human mind. In that kingdom of blessedness, then, to which I bring your elect, O God the Father, through the mystery of my redemption, their minds will be so established in you that they will never be changed from the love of eternity by any intervening cause of instability or overthrow [Col. 0410A].

“And no razor shall come upon his head.” A razor is an exceedingly sharp blade, by which hair is shaved and by which a person is easily wounded. By the razor are figuratively understood the subtle suggestions of the devil, against which no human being except him alone who was God and man could or can guard with such watchful care as to avoid being wounded by them, in some respect—in thought, word, or deed, or in all three—with the wound of sin. Hence David also says in the psalm: “Like a sharp razor you have wrought deceit” (Ps. 51:4).

“No razor,” he says, “shall come upon his head.” By the head the mind may be understood, because as the members are governed from the head, so thoughts are arranged in the mind. Therefore, when in the glory of the future resurrection the whole assembly of the elect has attained to a perfect man [Col. 0410B] and advanced to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, no razor shall come upon its head, because there will then be such peace and security that the devil will never again be able, by his subtle suggestions, to inflict upon the minds of the saints even any wound of harmful thought. It follows:

And it came to pass, when she multiplied prayers before the Lord, that Eli watched her mouth. This occurrence is a great event and, that is, the wondrous work of human redemption, which is frequently commended to us in Holy Scripture where, as in this passage, the phrase “it came to pass” occurs. For “it came to pass” is properly prefixed where Scripture speaks in what follows of something great and memorable, whether according to the letter or according to mystery. Therefore human redemption was a great event [Col. 0410C], surpassing all God’s works, because “his mercies are over all his works.”

When Christ’s human nature was labouring to accomplish this work, it multiplied prayers, because his whole life—indeed, all his conduct in this world, all his works and words—was a multitude of prayers before the Lord; for in all these things he attended to and desired only that, through it, God should come to the aid of the human race in its destruction and be reconciled to it. In this multiplication of prayers, in his whole life and conduct, Eli watched her mouth, because the Lord God, the almighty Father, who may be signified by Eli, and the Son of God himself according to his divinity, so watched himself in his human nature [Col. 0410D] and held it under such guard that he never fell in word and could never be touched or corrupted by even the slightest defilement of sin in thought or deed.

But Hannah spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard at all. Therefore Eli thought her drunk. Christ’s human nature, signified by Hannah as we have often said, spoke in her heart because, from the time when he began to experience the necessities of our body, he bore in his heart this desire: to accomplish the work of human redemption, for the completion of which he had descended from heaven to earth. Only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard at all. By the lips, which appear outwardly upon a human being, we may understand the outward works of Christ’s humanity [Col. 0411A]. For during the continuous thirty-three years in which he chose to live as a man among men, only his lips moved, because only those outward works which he performed for the cause of our salvation were exercised by him. But, since he appeared and was regarded as a mere man, it could not be known whether in all these things he was working the redemption of humankind.

Why was this so, except because her voice was not heard at all? That is, he did not disclose the desire by which he burned to accomplish human redemption. This first appeared plainly when the Son of God himself chose to undergo the punishment of Passion and death. Therefore Eli thought her drunk.

And he said to her: “How long will you be drunk? Digest a little [Col. 0411B] of the wine with which you are saturated.” *Temulentus* means, as it were, “drunken,” and it is characteristic of a drunken person to have the mind altered and to be estranged from one’s senses. Thus, it says, Eli thought her *temulenta*—drunk. Whatever is held to be great and precious is properly said to be esteemed. God the Father held it in very high estimation; it was great and glorious in his eyes when he saw the human nature in his Only-begotten so estranged from every human impulse—namely, that impulse prone to evil—that it could never inwardly or outwardly perceive or admit, in thought, word, or deed, anything belonging to the defilement of sin.

And he said to her: “How long will you be drunk?” As though he said: “O human nature, in my Only-begotten I see that you are wholly estranged from every sense of sin by which other human beings are corrupted. But how long will you be drunk—that is, how long will you conceal your singular innocence, in which you lack every sense of human contagion, so that through it you do not come to the aid of the perishing human race in death? Digest a little of the wine with which you are saturated.” By wine, which gladdens the human heart, may be signified that delight and joy, perhaps also that desire, which Christ’s human nature had for completing the work of human redemption. Thus these were in some manner the words of God the almighty Father and of the divinity of the Son of God himself to his human nature: “Digest a little of the wine with which you are saturated”—that is, the desire you have for the redemption of humankind, in which you so abound [Col. 0411D] that it is the joy and gladness of your heart that through your Passion and death the human race itself should be redeemed. Therefore accomplish it by works, so that this digestion may pass into the faithful—the members, that is, of your body—in such a way that eternal salvation may come to all nations throughout the world when you openly accomplish what you have always desired in secret: namely, when you redeem at the price of your blood those who are to pass into your body through faith.

But this will be only “a little,” that is, for a short time. For through your redemption only the Gentiles are now to be enlightened; but the Jews, from whom you came and who cruelly conspire for your death, are to be blinded. This indeed was the judgment of divinity: that the Gentiles should be converted to faith through Christ’s death, while the Jews, guilty in his death, should be driven away from the knowledge of God [Col. 0412A].

Hannah answered: “By no means, my lord.” As our Lord Jesus Christ, the Only-begotten of God, existed from two natures, so likewise he had two wills: the human will, which belongs to the flesh, and the divine will, which belongs to the Godhead. The will of the divine nature was the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews; but the will of the human nature was that the enlightenment of the Gentiles should take place without the blinding of the Jews. Hence the response of the humanity was in some manner addressed to the words of divinity which announced only the redemption of the Gentiles: “By no means, my lord. It is not fitting,” he says, “my Father—whom I call Lord from the form of a servant, though in divinity I exist equal and consubstantial with you—that I, who came from your paternal bosom into the world through obedience to you, should now have so small a fruit from my death: that only the people of the Gentiles should be saved and redeemed, while the Jewish people, from whom I took this very body in which I come to the aid of humankind through death, should be excluded from your grace and eternal blessedness.”

Therefore, if we attend rightly, we shall see that, although not in the same words, the Lord Jesus Christ, already in the agony of the Passion, uttered this with the same sense and meaning: “My Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me” [Col. 0412B] (Mark 14:36). He asks that the cup be taken away from him, not from fear of suffering—for this was precisely why he deigned to come into the world, to undergo the shame of Passion and death for humankind’s salvation—but from the compassion which he had for the former people. He spoke these words to the Father because he found it grievous to drink the cup offered by those whom, on account of this very crime, he knew would incur the danger of eternal condemnation. But because the divine will had to be preferred to the human will, immediately returning to himself, he confirms by the power of the divine will what he had declined from the will of his human nature: “Nevertheless,” he says, “not my will, but yours be done” (ibid.). “Let not what I say from human affection be done, but that for which I descended to earth by your will.”

“For I am a woman exceedingly unhappy.” In these words, if anyone wishes to consider mystically, Christ’s human nature sets forth in itself all the miseries of human nature before the divinity. In saying this, it transfers us into itself and takes upon itself the affection of our body, its members. “For I am a woman exceedingly unhappy.” I, namely, human nature, from the first time of creation in the first man Adam, and after him in all human beings, am exceedingly unhappy, because all descend to the gates of hell, both righteous and unrighteous, and no one can attain the reward of eternal blessedness [Col. 0412D].

Therefore, O God the Father, because of my human nature—conceived and born without original sin, and having lived in this world without actual crime—turn the eyes of your mercy to all human nature, corrupted by both plagues, that is, impaired by original and actual sin. Have mercy in view of this: that I have not drunk wine or strong drink or anything that can intoxicate; that is, that I have now lived thirty-three years in this world, yet through my humanity I have not been able to bring it about that human beings should delight so in you, and that their minds should thus be changed from earthly desires and fleshly covetousness, that I might transfer them into my body [Col. 0413A].

But we may also understand differently the words, “I have not drunk wine or strong drink or anything that can intoxicate.” It is as though Christ’s human nature sets forth its singular innocence before God the Father and its own divinity, so that he may remember it and through it have mercy upon and be reconciled to all humankind, which had provoked him to anger. “I have not drunk wine,” he says, “or strong drink, or anything that can intoxicate.” As though he said: “Let this bend and move you, O highest divinity, to mercy: that you see me, the human nature of your Christ, so living in this world that I have never wished, like other human beings in whose likeness and appearance I am seen, to admit any delight of worldly pleasure by which my mind might be changed from you, whether in thought, word, or deed.” But what have I done?

“I have poured out my soul in the sight of the Lord.” That is, I have preserved the rational soul by which I exist in human flesh free from every corruption; and I am so free from every sin, not only in soul but also in body, both in manner of life and in the order of my birth, that it may be pleasing and delightful to the highest divinity to turn upon me the eyes of his majesty [Col. 0413C], which he has turned away from all humankind because of iniquity.

But the phrase “I have poured out my soul” must be examined more subtly. It is as though he said: “I, your Only-begotten, because I possess with you one divinity, equal glory, and coeternal majesty—when, through obedience to you, I decreed to come to the aid of humankind by my humanity—I myself poured out my soul. That is, I made myself in my mother’s womb; she did not pour me out, that is, give me my origin—she whom I created, in whom I chose to fit for myself a human body. And because I am God and man, and in the divinity there is humanity and in the humanity divinity works, therefore all that I lived was in the sight of the Lord, because in my entire life and conduct I never committed anything for which God could turn away his eyes [Col. 0413D].

“Do not account your maidservant as one of the daughters of Belial.” Belial means “without a yoke.” The children of Belial—that is, the children of disobedience—were Adam and Eve, who refused to submit themselves to the Lord’s yoke when, desiring to be like God, they transgressed the Lord’s commandment. Thus in them, and in all people up to the Son of God alone, there were children of Belial, because through the same disobedience of the first-created parents they were born in transgression and lived in transgression, adding actual sin to the original crime in which they were born.

Hence Christ’s human nature, which was neither conceived in iniquities nor lived in sin, could rightly say to God the Father: “Do not account your maidservant as one of the daughters of Belial” [Col. 0414A]. As though he said: “It belongs to your justice and mercy, O God the Father, that in reconciling the human race to yourself you consider this in me, your Only-begotten: you cannot account me among those who, from the first Adam until now, have been disobedient to you through original and actual sin. For I came into this world through obedience to you; in obedience to you I have lived as a human being among human beings for so long; and through obedience to you I now desire to undergo the punishment of Passion and death. When you consider this in me, it is just that through me you should be reconciled to humankind.”

“Because out of the multitude of my pain and sorrow I have spoken until now.” Christ’s human nature spoke amid a multitude of pain and sorrow when it set forth its complaint before the divinity: namely, that throughout his entire conduct in this world the devil exercised his tyranny over all human beings, just as before, and entrance into the kingdom of heaven was granted to no one, but all, righteous and unrighteous alike, descended to hell. “Out of the multitude,” he says, “of my pain and sorrow I have spoken until now” [Col. 0414B]. For according to what we have explained above, the hour of the Passion was then at hand when he said these things. “Out of the multitude of my pain and sorrow I have spoken until now.” That is, as though he said: “Ever since I became human, I have always borne this pain and sorrow: although I took humanity for the sake of human redemption, I nevertheless saw all held captive under the devil’s power and descending to hell. But this pain will now end, because through the Passion of the cross and my death I have determined to free my elect from the devil’s captivity and to extinguish with my blood that flaming sword which barred Paradise, so that free entrance there may lie open to all who either are joined or are yet to be joined to me through faith” [Col. 0414C].

Then Eli said to her: “Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant you your petition which you have asked of him.” Therefore God the Father, and the divinity of Christ’s human nature itself, assented to its prayer, stirred it up to accomplish human redemption, and said: “Go in peace. Gird yourself,” he says, “for the triumph of Passion and death, through which the things in heaven and the things on earth are to be made peaceful” (Eph. 1:10). “And may the Lord God grant you the petition which you have asked of him.” What was the petition of Christ’s human nature except that through his death the redemption should be accomplished not only of the Gentiles but also of the Jews, and that the one cornerstone should receive into itself the two walls coming from opposite directions [Col. 0414D]?

For, as we said before, according to his human nature the Son of God grieved at the destruction of the Jews, from whom he had come according to the flesh. And because the prayers which he poured out to God the Father for that people could not pass away fruitlessly, immediately after his ascension a great part of that same people believed, and from it the holy Church began to be established. Even if blindness happened to that people in part, the effect of the prayers of our Lord Jesus Christ will still be seen in fullest measure at the end of the world: “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25) [Col. 0415A]. Therefore Christ’s human nature wishes the blessedness of this salvation upon that same people in what follows, saying:

“Would that your maidservant might find grace in your eyes!” As though he said: “O God the Father, would that the time might someday come when your maidservant, that ancient Synagogue, should return to the freedom of your grace, from which she was cast out because of the obstinate persistence of her error!” Therefore the woman went on her way and ate. So that the redemption of Jews and Gentiles might be accomplished [Col. 0415B], this woman went on her way. What was her way? Her way was surely when he came from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, and from the Virgin’s womb into this world, and “worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12).

Again he went on his way when he chose for our sake to suffer, die, be buried, and rise from the tomb. But we may also understand something else by this way. After the fall of the first human being, this was the way of all human nature: to die in the body, and after the death of the flesh, to undergo also the death of the soul by descending to hell.

The Son of God went this same way, although not through the fault of transgression but for the sake of human salvation, because he chose both to be subjected in his body to the sentence of death [Col. 0415C] and to have his soul descend to the gates of hell in order to bring out all the souls of the elect.

Therefore, when he had both undergone the punishment of death in his body and descended to hell with his soul, he ate, because, rising from the dead by the power of his divinity, he transferred us into himself and conformed the body of our lowliness to the body of his glory. Or this eating signifies the joy in which he mercifully delighted when, through the triumph of his death and resurrection, the souls of his elect were delivered from the devil’s captivity.

The following words, mystically understood, show that the grace and blessedness which he acquired for his elect once for all through death and resurrection continue in all who are to be saved until the end of the age [Col. 0415D]:

“And her face,” it says, “was no longer changed in different directions.” For if now, as formerly, the righteous and unrighteous alike were led captive by the devil to death, her face would indeed be changed in different directions. But now her face is no longer thus changed, because for all who desire to enter through true innocence, or after lost innocence through worthy repentance, the entrance into the kingdom of heaven lies open immediately after the end of this flesh.

## HOMILY LXI. FIRST [HOMILY] FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

“A certain man made a great supper and invited many. And at the hour of the supper he sent his servant to tell those invited to come, because all things are now ready” [Col. 0416A] (Luke 14).

We fear to be accused of presumption because we dare to say or expound something concerning the words and judgments of the holy interpreters, and especially of blessed Gregory, who expounded this parable excellently. Yet we humbly excuse our smallness in this matter because we are chiefly concerned that what we do should arise not from presumption but from devotion, for the love of our neighbours whom we desire to benefit in these things. For although we, foolish and unlearned as we are, cannot at all attain the understanding and wisdom of blessed Gregory, nevertheless, because in his exposition of this parable he was then speaking, as place and time required, not to spiritual but to secular persons, we do not believe that we diminish anything from his honour and glory if, comparing spiritual things with spiritual [Col. 0416B], our humility ventures to say, for the edification of those who are in monasteries, what God may grant. Therefore the Lord says:

A certain man made a great supper and invited many. This man is the only-begotten Son of God, who is indeed God and man; and not merely man, but a certain man, a singular man, because he alone was conceived and born without sin, and he alone lived in this world without sin. He made a great supper when he gave himself to us, when, as the hour of his Passion approached, offering sacrifice, he prepared for us his most holy body and blood as a banquet of eternal salvation: “Take,” he says, “and eat: [Col. 0416C] this is my body” (Matt. 26:26). For unless this supper had come first—that is, unless he himself had consecrated and given us his most holy body and blood—no human being could have attained the banquet of eternal life. Hence he himself says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). And again: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (ibid., 55). He invited many because all who have received the sacrament of the Christian faith have been invited to the banquet of eternal life.

“And he sent his servant at the hour of supper to say to those invited that they should come, because now all things are ready.” The hour of supper [Col. 0416D] was the hour of the Passion. For, when his Passion and Resurrection had been accomplished, he sent his servant—that is, the apostolic company—when, ascending into heaven, he said to them: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Matt. 28:19; Mark 16:16). To say these things was in a sense to send his servant to tell the invited that they should come, because now all things are ready. For at the hour of that supper, when he who is the food of angels offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross for the redemption of humankind, all things were prepared: hell was shattered, paradise was opened, original sins were forgiven and wiped away on earth, and the rewards of life were restored in heaven. But after this preparation of eternal salvation, made [Col. 0417A] for us in the Son of God, after the preaching of the servant sent—that is, the apostolic company—let us hear what then occurred.

“And they all began at once,” says the Lord, “to make excuses.” Who are all these persons excusing themselves from God’s banquet? Surely those who have an estate, who have five yokes of oxen, who have a wife: that is, those who are rich in the substance of this world, which is the estate; those who, together with riches, have bodily health, which are the five yokes of oxen; and who, through these two things, freely indulge the third—that is, the pleasure of the flesh, represented by the wife—excuse themselves from coming to God’s banquet. For while they love earthly things more than heavenly, they themselves bar their own path to everlasting life. Thus, thus: while they refuse, through contempt for the present life, [Col. 0417B] to come to the Lord’s supper, the poor and weak are chosen; for the less they have in this world to delight them, the more readily they hear and follow the inward voice of the Lord who calls. Hence the Lord says: “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and weak, the blind and lame.” Thus it has happened: for the houses of God—that is, the monasteries—are full of the poor. The poor are those who use force against God, who, while the rich remain amid their pleasures, seize the kingdom of heaven through zeal for holy conduct. Therefore the Lord says: “I say to you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper.”

Having set forth these things according to the general sense, let us turn the eye of the mind upon ourselves and see how the words of this Gospel reading are fulfilled [Col. 0417C] particularly in every person being saved. For the Lord says:

“A certain man made a great supper and invited many.” So long as anyone is in the world, loving and committing the sins of the world, he is called merely a man; but once he begins to separate himself from the world and from the sins of the world, he is worthily called a certain man, a singular man. He truly makes a great supper when, through repentance and contrition of heart, he strives toward true forgiveness of sins. Hence it is written: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps. 50:19). This is the supper, and truly a great one, by which God is delighted [Col. 0417D] and fed, as he himself declares, saying: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I shall enter 588 to him and sup with him” (Rev. 3:20). He invites many when he begins humbly to confess and accuse before God himself, who was not one but, as it were, many and manifold, his own multiplicity. He invites many when, after perfect confession, he resolutely binds himself to perfect satisfaction for the many sins he has committed. After perfect confession and perfect satisfaction, he finally advances, through God’s mercy, to true compunction of heart or contemplation of mind, which is figuratively expressed by the hour of supper, concerning which the Lord immediately added and said:

[Col. 0418A] “And he sent his servant at the hour of supper, to tell those invited that they should come, because now all things are ready.” The servant who is sent is one and the same man who made the great supper in conversion, who invited many in confession and satisfaction, and who also sends in contemplation of mind. A person sends himself; he sends to himself; he sends on his own behalf. For this is what follows: “To tell those invited that they should come.” His telling is his desiring. For he desires that all those invited should come—that is, that body, soul, and spirit, which are the whole person, should strive continually to take part in that supper, in which now all things are ready. What are all these things except good and evil, prosperity and adversity? At the eternal banquet of everlasting life, these things are not found ready; for there good will be set forth eternally without evil, prosperity without adversity, in God’s everlasting banquets. Yet in eternal damnation, likewise, all these things will not be ready; for there evils without goods, adversities without prosperities, will eternally threaten the reprobate. But now all things are ready, because at that supper which is now—that is, in this present life—being made, concerning which the Lord says elsewhere: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I shall enter to him, and sup with him and he with me”—at this supper, I say, all things are ready: namely, good and evil, prosperity and adversity. For there, through God’s gift and mercy, a person begins rightly to know how to make satisfaction to God for evil deeds, and how he ought to preserve his good works, if they have been done in God and for God. When these matters have been diligently considered, let there be between spirit, soul, and body [Col. 0418C] what is said in what follows:

“And they all began,” he says, “to make excuses together.” By all these persons who began together to excuse themselves, all the faculties of the twofold human being may suitably be understood. For when, by the grace of heavenly visitation, a person begins to recognize what unlawful things he has committed in deeds, words, and thoughts, this humble acknowledgment of sins is before God a kind of excuse, which renders the person who repents perfectly excusable and innocent in God’s sight.

“The first said: I have bought an estate, and I must go out and see it.” By this first person the human spirit [Col. 0418D] may quite suitably be understood. When, through the breathing-in of the grace of heavenly visitation, it has perfectly recognized its own imperfection, it begins to excuse itself, not by contradicting, but by repenting from its inmost heart and confessing its negligences and transgressions, because it judges itself unworthy to be admitted even for a moment to this heavenly banquet or supper. “I have bought an estate,” he says. By this estate may suitably be understood love of the world, pride, avarice, and the like. But since no transaction of exchange can occur except between seller and buyer, who is he who brings this estate for sale except the ancient enemy, who craftily meets a person desiring to come to the Lord’s supper, in order, if possible, to turn him from the purpose and desire of good by love of the world, pride, or [Col. 0419A] avarice? Therefore the spirit, eager for the spiritual supper, laments that it bought this estate from him, by which it made itself unworthy of the banquet of spiritual feasts, and says: “I have bought an estate, and I must go out and see it.” As if it said: I and the devil met in one marketplace. My price, which I brought, was God, who was accustomed continually to visit me inwardly through his inspiring grace. This precious price of immortality that minister of death took from me, and put in its place within my wretched heart his own estate—that is, love of the world, pride, avarice, and the like. And because it then pleased me, wretchedly deceived by diabolical trickery, voluntarily to consent to this deadly 590 exchange, I must now go out and see [Col. 0419B] it. For my will has been turned into necessity. What was then voluntary has now become necessary to me. Having become wholly powerless over myself, I cannot remain within myself. Now I am compelled, even unwillingly and against my will, to sink into pride, now into malice, now into avarice, and into the other things that belong to the world. This is that estate of death and perdition which I bought; I am compelled not only to go out to it, but also—what is worse—to see it, that is, to love it. Such an outgoing was once abominable to me, but now it has become sweet and delightful, because I do not reject the unlawful thoughts of the world as they successively enter my heart; rather, I delightfully receive and admit them.

“Therefore, I ask you, hold me excused.” Who is this person to whom it is said, “hold me excused,” except the human spirit itself, which in a sense speaks to itself within itself? Its petition, indeed, is the continual exhortation by which it rouses itself to make satisfaction to God. It entreats itself to persevere in every way in labours for God’s sake, so that through true repentance and pure confession it may strive here to accuse itself, and thus deserve to be excused before the eyes of the divine majesty in the future. It follows:

“And another said: I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them.” By this other person, who uttered similar words of excuse, the human soul may quite suitably be understood. For as the first, who is the spirit, [Col. 0419D] begins to excuse itself before the Lord in the manner described, afflicting itself over the loss of the grace of inward sweetness, so likewise the soul is stirred to know and repent of the manifold excesses of its outward senses, as the foregoing words aptly show: “I have bought five yokes of oxen,” he says, “and I am going to test them.” As if he plainly said: I desire to come to the Lord’s supper, to which I have been called; I long somehow to experience in myself the grace of inward heavenly sweetness. But I have bought five yokes of oxen, because my five rational senses have now become bovine and 591 bestial: like beasts, they seek and love only what belongs to the flesh. And as an ox is yoked in order that it may be compelled to labour even against its will, so I, bowed down and miserably subjected to the dominion [Col. 0420A] of the flesh, cannot raise myself to do the good which I ought to do, even when I wish to do it.

This is sufficiently clear from the fact that I, who once wished to be a strong guardian of my outward senses, who wished steadfastly to sit in meditation, reading, and diligent application to other good works, now go because I cannot usefully keep myself fixed upon any of these things. I go to test now these, now those things. I go to test whether something from the vanities of this world may meet my eyes or ears; and while I am thus transferred, as it were, from place to place, I become abominable to God and wholly useless to myself. Thus, thus, when the soul which animates the flesh examines and scrutinizes before God, weeping and repenting, the excesses of its outward senses, it speaks inwardly to itself in the same manner as the spirit: “I ask you, hold me excused.” It asks itself to return to itself within itself, to repent perfectly of its excesses, so that through true repentance it may be able to return to true innocence. From this repentance and satisfaction of spirit and soul, the body also begins to lament the slothfulness of its torpor, as the Evangelist further adds, saying:

“And another said: I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.” In the wife we may understand the concupiscence and pleasure of the flesh. Nor should it be passed over that, whereas the first two seek to be excused, this third person, who signifies the body, does not ask to be held excused, but merely declares that he cannot come. But what is indicated to us by this, except what the chosen disciple of the Lord, the apostle Paul, [Col. 0420C] complains that he experienced in himself? “I know,” he says, “that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For willing is present to me, but I do not find the accomplishing of good” (Rom. 7:18). The human spirit rises upward in its desire for heavenly things, but the flesh, resisting the spirit, always pleads its own inability, 592 saying: “I cannot come.” As if it said to the spirit: You demand from me the labour through which you may attain with me the unfailing banquet of eternal sweetness; but I cannot meet your desire, because the wife whom I have taken—that is, the concupiscence and pleasure of the flesh, to which I am subject—draws me away from the banquet of this great supper. But what the mind stretching toward God ought finally to do in response is shown by the following sequence of words [Col. 0420D]. For it follows:

“And the servant returned and reported these things to his lord.” This servant, whom we have called the human spirit, truly returns to his lord when he humbly turns to God in order to make known to the clemency of divine compassion his sorrow and misery. What the merciful and compassionate Lord then does in response is shown by the Evangelist in mystical words:

“Then the master of the house, being angry, said to his servant: Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and weak, the blind and lame.” Although anger or change is wholly foreign to God, yet he is said, after our manner, to be angry when he stirs us against ourselves with a saving fury, so that the mind may begin sternly to rage over the guilt of its negligence and waste away in wholesome anger against itself. To one who is thus rightly angered and ardently takes vengeance upon the slothfulness of its own torpor, the Lord himself immediately speaks, as we have heard: “Go out quickly,” he says, “into the streets and lanes of the city.” By the streets we may understand the broad and spacious course of secular life; by the lanes of the city, the narrow and constricted purpose of spiritual life. Almighty God teaches a person to go out into the streets, that he may carefully consider the broad paths of his former way of life. There indeed he finds the poor, when he humbly recognizes his poverty, when he perceives that the time spent in the world has brought him nothing but need and misery, through which he sees that he has been stripped of the riches of eternal blessedness. There also he finds the weak, because if he remembers doing any good in the world, [Col. 0421B] he considers it weak and infirm, since it was done not humbly but proudly and arrogantly for the favour 593 of empty glory. After he has thus gone out into the streets, he must also go out into the lanes of the city, seeking there the blind and lame: that is, he must carefully consider how long, in undertaking the spiritual life, he has wandered from the knowledge of right truth like a blind man, and how often he has limped wrongly in those works of righteousness which ought to have been performed.

We may also understand in another way what he says: “Bring in here the poor and weak, the blind and lame.” These four must be set against the four preceding things: against the estate, the poor; against the yokes of oxen, the weak; against the wife, in whom we have said that concupiscence and pleasure of the flesh are to be understood, we must place the blind and lame [Col. 0421C]. But what is the blind person, and what the lame? The blind person is one who does not know; the lame person is one who errs. For love and habit of fleshly concupiscence and pleasure produce ignorance. What a person does not know to be his danger blinds him. He also begins to regard as good and just that which he formerly knew to be evil and unjust. Error, then, is born from this ignorance. For one who does not know his error rightly errs. This is what the prophet says: “Drunkenness and luxury take away the heart” (Hos. 4:11). Therefore, when the Lord says, “Bring in here the poor and weak, the blind and lame,” it is as if he said: Since you desire to return to the lost joys of my sweetness, you must humbly acknowledge the manifold guilt of your vanity. Remember in the humble conscience of your heart where you bought an estate, where you bought yokes of oxen—that is, how through immoderate pride you rashly raised yourself above yourself; how often, wandering outside yourself through curiosity of mind, you have formed exalted opinions of your own merits and low opinions of those of others. Thus bring in here the poor and weak, recognizing yourself poor in virtues and weak in acts of righteous virtue.

After the poor and weak, likewise bring in the blind and lame, humbly recognizing the blindness of your ignorance and humbly making satisfaction to God for the multiplicity of your error. The counsel of blessed John in today’s Reading accords with this most merciful counsel of the Lord, when he says: “My little children, let us love not in word only and tongue, but also in deed and truth” [Col. 0422A] (1 John 3:18). One loves not in deed but in word and tongue who confesses himself a sinner only in words, but after confession displays no work of repentance. But one loves not in word and tongue, but in deed and truth, who washes away by worthy satisfaction the sins that he confesses and strives to preserve that satisfaction in true humility.

Nor should it be passed over that he says, “Bring in here the poor and weak, the blind and lame.” It is the same as if he had said: Do not lead them out, but bring them in. Do not lead them out there, where you were before; but bring them in here—that is, to me, into your heart, where I now am, where I speak to you in an inexpressible manner. These words of the Lord are the works of his ineffable compassion, through which he works and brings about in a person the recognition that he is poor and weak, blind [Col. 0422B] and lame, so that he may be able worthily to make satisfaction to God for his sins. Yet because a person does all these things from fear and still in fear, desiring finally to pass from fear to love, he speaks to God, as it were, in this way:

“Lord, it has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.” This word, “you commanded,” sounds of fear and shows fear, and therefore fittingly expresses fear also. “Lord,” he says, “it has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.” As if he said: Lord, all that I have lived until now, I have lived under fear; whatever I have done that may be called good or right before you, I have done under fear, not from love. “And there is still room.” You sat and sit in me, Lord, upon the seat of fear; now, I beseech you, place within me also the seat of love. Let your love, Lord, fill that place [Col. 0422C] which is still empty in me; let your love, Lord, possess it, so that henceforth I may cling to you more from love than fear and may be able to do what ought to be done more for your love than from fear. The Collect for today directs us to understand and retain this sense when we say: “Lord, grant us to have perpetually both the fear and the love of your holy name.” For fear does not suffice for perfection unless love is also present; nor does love suffice unless fear accompanies it. The Lord mystically teaches us in the following words how a person may attain the desired sweetness of love. For it follows:

“And the lord said to the servant: Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them [Col. 0422D] to come in, that my house may be filled.” Although roads may sometimes signify human actions, in this place we may understand by roads a person’s thoughts, and by hedges the guarding of thoughts. It is as if the Lord said: If you ask me to establish within you the seat of my love, go out into the roads and hedges: hedge in and fortify your thoughts; do not allow them to flow away and wander about harmful and useless matters. But because this is hard and difficult for a person, he added: “and compel them to come in.” As if he said: You cannot otherwise attain that taste of my love and inward sweetness which you desire, unless you compel yourself to enter—that is, unless you exert a certain force upon your heart, so that it does not flow away through unlawful thoughts. For through this compulsion and force you must finally deserve that my house may be filled, which is your soul. It will then truly be filled when it is possessed by my perfect fear and love. That humility alone is the one for whom the wonderful sweetness of this great supper, of which we have spoken, is prepared, the Lord makes clear at the end of the Gospel when he says:

“But I say to you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper.” As if he said: I tell you—I who am truth, who can neither be deceived nor deceive—that those who seem to themselves to be men, who glory in their own virtue and judge themselves strong and perfect, although they have been invited and have laboured in spiritual life in whatever manner, can nevertheless never attain the most sweet taste of that inward sweetness which I am accustomed to prepare and preserve through myself in myself for [Col. 0423B] my humble ones. The tasting of this supper is the sweetness of prayer and contemplation of mind. The Holy Spirit teaches us, in today’s Collect, to desire and ask God altogether for frequent tastes of this kind, when we say: “Lord, grant us to have perpetually both the fear and love of your holy name; 596 for you never deprive of your governance those whom you establish in the firmness of your love.” What is the firmness of love except the taste of contemplation, through which a person is truly established in the will of God’s love? Whomever God establishes in this firmness of his love—that is, to whom he has granted a frequent taste of this supper—he never deprives of his governance. God’s governance is God’s kindly counsel, which he invisibly bestows upon his faithful, as [Col. 0423C] we heard in the Gospel where he said: “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and weak, the blind and lame.” For such persons, if at times they commit some fault, immediately flee, under God’s governance, to the familiar harbour of prayer; and through frequent tastes of the aforesaid sweetness they return to humble and perfect knowledge and repentance for their sins. This truly is God’s governance. But those whom he has not established in this firmness of his love of which we have heard, he often deprives of his governance. For they are governed not by good but by evil; they are governed by themselves, not by the Lord.

Moreover, it seems to me not unfitting that we may relate this second Sunday, according to the second day [Col. 0423D] of creation, to that day concerning which it is said:

“God also said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters. And God made the firmament, and divided the waters that were under the firmament from those that were above the firmament” (Gen. 1:6–7).

There are upper waters and lower waters, which, if we understand them mystically, we must distinguish from one another. The upper waters are, as we judge, good and spiritual desires; the lower waters, evil and fleshly desires. Behold waters and waters, which must necessarily be divided by provident discernment: namely, so that we distinguish each thing in such a way that we do not receive good things as evil or evil things as good, so that our mind may always attend to good and spiritual desires and resist evil and fleshly desires with all its strength.

[Col. 0424A] 597 There are also other waters which we must divide: namely, greater goods and lesser goods, greater evils and lesser evils. Greater and lesser evils must be divided in this manner: a person must judge and examine each one, repenting less for lesser evils, but washing away greater evils through greater repentance and satisfaction. What greater or lesser evils are, we have already heard in part in the Gospel reading. It is evil to buy an estate, that is, to incline toward the love and pride of the world; it is evil also to buy five yokes of oxen, that is, for a person to subject his five senses to curiosity and vanity. Yet it is a greater evil to take a wife, that is, to serve the concupiscence and pleasure of the flesh with such delight that one neither wishes nor is able to come to God’s banquet. Hence it is necessary that whoever has sinned in these several ways should so examine and distinguish greater and lesser sins that he may repent worthily for each and strive to cleanse each by due satisfaction.

There are also, as was said, greater and lesser goods which we ought to scrutinize and examine, and which we may likewise find in the Gospel reading. It is, so to speak, a lesser good to abstain from evil actions; but it is a greater good to keep the heart pure from evil thoughts. Hence, I think, it is in a sense a lesser good to go out into the streets and lanes of the city, but a greater good to go out into the roads and hedges. One who diligently examines within himself in meditation what sins he has committed in secular and spiritual life and, making satisfaction to God for them, resolves henceforth to guard himself from evil works, has indeed made a good going-out into the streets [Col. 0424C] and lanes of the city. But one who preserves in humility the works of virtue that he performs, and guards his heart with every vigilance against evil thoughts, has truly made a better going-out into the roads and hedges.

Therefore, as we have said above, let us so divide the waters from the waters that we prefer better things to good things and pass from good things to better things. Whoever thus divides waters from waters, discerning by judgment worse things from evils and better things from goods—to this person rightly applies what the Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 14:24). 598 How is he judged by no one? This spiritual person shall not be judged by that man who is God and man, the judge of the living and the dead, when he shall come; because the one who now distinguishes and judges all things, as we have said, leaves nothing unexamined for the strict Judge. Therefore, not to be judged, he will sit as judge of others with Christ the Judge, as the Lord himself promises his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

But for a person to attain this dignity of judging, God must make within him a strong and stable firmament: that is, he must so strengthen and establish that person’s mind that, as we observed on the previous Sunday in the rich man and the poor man, he does not wickedly lose the riches divinely bestowed upon him and then, as though buried in hell, begin again to beg; or if perhaps, as often [Col. 0425A] happens, he has fallen—if, stripped of purple and fine linen, he has come to poverty—he may again receive through God’s mercy the riches he has lost and, as the following text says, become the second day.

We may say that it was as it were the first day when, clothed in purple and fine linen, he feasted splendidly every day: that is, when, having mortified the flesh with its vices and concupiscences, he was generally able to ascend to the sweetness of prayer and the grace of contemplation. But because he “receives good things in his life”—that is, because he regarded as his own the gifts divinely bestowed upon him, and sought for them his own glory rather than God’s—he lost by boasting wickedly the same goods he had received. But when, through God’s mercy, he recognizes his poverty and begins humbly to beg, evening and [Col. 0425B] morning, the second day, came to be in him. What may be understood by evening except knowledge of oneself? What by morning except knowledge of God? He knows of himself that he can possess no good by his own powers; he knows God, from whom he had the goods that he vainly lost. Thus, through this humble knowledge of God and himself, the second day comes to be: that is, enlightened a second time by divine inspiration, he receives purple and fine linen again and is able once more 599 to feast splendidly with the Lord. May the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, bring us to this knowledge of himself and of ourselves—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXII. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0425C] “The boy Samuel ministered before the Lord in the presence of Eli, and the word of the Lord was precious” (1 Sam. 3), etc.

The readings from the Old Testament which we heard, when they were read by night, concerning Samuel’s calling, seem, through the ordering of the Holy Spirit—the author of both the Old and New Scriptures—to accord well with today’s Gospel reading. For as in the Gospel, so here we find three callings; both sets may fittingly be referred to three times: the time before the Law, the time under the Law, and the time under grace. Almighty God called his elect to the great supper of eternal sweetness first before the Law, second under the Law, and third under grace, because in each of these times there were always some who longed to taste the supper of eternal sweetness. Yet though they were called, none could come to that to which he was called so long as he had not come in the flesh through whose Passion the human race was to be redeemed—namely, the only-begotten Son of God. From eternity, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he had in his predestination this purpose: that, in order to aid fallen humanity, he would at last, at the end of the age, descend from the height of his eternity to the depths of our mortality. This most merciful predestination of God the Father and the Holy Spirit, to be fulfilled at the end of the world through the working of the Son of God, is, so far as I can conjecture, mystically and figuratively expressed at the beginning of these readings, where it is said:

[Col. 0426A] “The boy Samuel ministered before the Lord in the presence of Eli, and the word of the Lord was precious.” In these words we may observe the whole most holy Trinity together. In Eli, whose name is interpreted “my God,” God the Father; in “the Lord,” the Holy Spirit; in the boy Samuel, whose name is interpreted “his name is God,” God the Son, of whom it is said elsewhere: “And his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted “God with us” (Matt. 1:23). Since he is both God and man, each name suitably belongs to him: the name “boy,” on account of the innocence, simplicity, and purity which he possessed beyond all people in the humanity assumed for our sake; the name Samuel, on account of the excellence by which he was equal to God the Father in the eternity of divinity. From eternity he was God, but for our sake [Col. 0426B] he wished to become a boy, for our sake to become man.

But how did he minister before the Lord—that is, the Holy Spirit—in the presence of Eli, in the presence of God the Father, when he was neither less in essence nor inferior in power to them? Certainly this was not said on account of any lesser status or inequality, for none exists between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but on account of the dispensation of the human nature which he would assume in himself for the salvation of humankind. But because this most secret counsel of humanity’s restoration was still unknown to mortals, Scripture adds: “And the word of the Lord was precious.” It is called precious, as though rare. Whatever thing a person possesses in abundance, he sometimes values less highly; but what is rare, he judges precious and dear. [Col. 0426C] Therefore the word of the Lord is fittingly said to have been precious at that time, because—even though there were some who, through the Holy Spirit’s revelation, could know or understand something about God in themselves, and who knew how to say or teach something concerning God—they were exceedingly rare. The reason for this is indicated by the following Scripture, which says:

In those days there was no open vision. By “those days” we may simply understand the days of that time before Christ’s coming; or, in a higher sense, those holy persons who lived at that time, who could not unfittingly be called “days” because of the light of faith and the merit of their lives. For in those days there was no open vision, because God had not yet [Col. 0426D] become man, had not yet offered himself to be seen by mortals, through whom the night of human blindness was to be enlightened. Yet even when he came, when clothed in human flesh he began to live among human beings as a man, the vision was not open, because few recognized him or believed him to be their Creator and Redeemer. But why was this, except because, as is read in another Gospel, “the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 7:39)? But when he had been glorified through the death of his Passion, when after his resurrection he had been raised above the heavens, and had sent the Holy Spirit from above upon his disciples, enlightening in part the darkness of human blindness and ignorance, then open vision first began to come about. For not only the apostles, but also the imitators of the apostles, [Col. 0427A] began to know and understand many things concerning God which they had not known before. Yet this open vision still endures in the holy Church through God’s mercy, because by the illumination of that same Holy Spirit he still daily grants to his chosen and beloved children the same grace which he then gave his disciples—though not so fully as to the apostles, so that they might be able to speak in every tongue. Nevertheless, by his invisible visitation he reveals and opens many sweet secrets of sacred Scripture which had formerly been hidden. But before all these things came to pass:

“It came to pass on a certain day,” as follows, “that Eli lay in his own place, and his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished.” [Col. 0427B] 602 Often, where this expression *it came to pass* is read in sacred Scripture, it indicates something great, something precious and worthy of remembrance. So in this passage too we may say that it was indeed a great and glorious thing that Eli lay in his own place. If by Eli we understand God the Father, what should we understand by his place in which he lay? The place of Eli—the place, I say, of God the Father—in which he rested sweetly from eternity, was his only-begotten Son: in whom he rested in eternity according to divinity, and in whom he rested in time according to humanity. For apart from him alone, no human being has ever been found without sin. And Scripture fittingly says *he lay*, because before the ages were made, before angel or man began to exist, he was always at rest: nothing ever departed from him, nothing ever [Col. 0427C] came to him; he was never greater and never less. The honor of his divinity would not have been any less if man had not been created; nor was man created so that God might be made blessed by him. Rather, man was created that he might be made blessed by God. For he lay in his own place. When or how? “On a certain day”: that is, in the singular illumination of the Holy Spirit. For God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, just as they were always one, so they always rested together and in one.

But while God the Father thus rested eternally in his Son with the Holy Spirit, his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished. By his eyes we may understand our first parents, Adam [Col. 0427D] and Eve. Adam was, as it were, God’s right eye; Eve, as it were, his left, who, deceived by the serpent, looked not to the right but to the left. For Scripture says: “She saw the tree, that it was beautiful to look upon and pleasant for eating; she took and ate” (Gen. 3:6). Alas, those eyes of the Lord had miserably grown dim when, turning the eyes of their minds away from the true light—which they had been created to contemplate eternally—and looking toward the serpent, who urged what belonged to death and darkness, they swelled in pride against God.

603 We may also say that his eyes were the Law and the Prophets, by which, as by certain eyes of his mercy, he looked down from heaven upon earth when [Col. 0428A] through the Law and the Prophets he began to enlighten the darkness of human blindness and ignorance. Yet these eyes too had nevertheless grown dim, because very few were found who either believed, as was right, the things concerning Christ in the Law or the Prophets, even when he himself appeared and was seen; or who, believing, loved as was right. Hence it fittingly follows:

“And he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished.” A lamp is called that which contains light within itself. Therefore I judge that by the lamp we may not unfittingly understand human nature assumed into God. For just as light is within a lamp, so divinity lay hidden and concealed in the assumed form of humanity. But true Eli, almighty God, could not see this lamp before it was extinguished: that is, before [Col. 0428B] his Only-Begotten, made man for humankind, should die as a man for humankind. The statement, “He could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished,” must not be understood as though there were anything that almighty God, at whose will all things subsist, could not do. His inability was his justice. He could not see—that is, love—human nature, because he ought not to do so. For it was not just that humanity should be loved by God so long as it was held liable to the guilt of original sin. But after the lamp had been extinguished, after human disobedience had been destroyed and annulled through the obedience of the Son of God, then that former inability of God was changed into power. For, appeased through the death of his Son, he could love human nature because he rightly ought to do so—human nature which before [Col. 0428C] he neither could nor ought to love. For thirty years and more, he lived as a man among human beings. Yet this could in no way suffice for the perfect salvation of fallen humanity until he was extinguished, until he lay down in death. But before all these things were fulfilled in fact—which, as we have said, then existed in predestination—Samuel, as the following Scripture says,

604 “slept in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was.” At the beginning of the reading, where the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God was prefigured, he was called the boy Samuel. But here, where only the exalted height of his divinity is indicated, in which he is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, he is called not “boy,” but simply Samuel. “Samuel,” it says, “slept in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was.” By the ark of God is signified the divinity of God the Father; by Samuel, as has been said, the majesty of the Son of God, coessential with the Father; and by the temple of the Lord, the essence of the Holy Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son.

Samuel slept in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was, because in his eternity he rested eternally with the Father and the Holy Spirit. But because it was not the person of the Father, nor that of the Holy Spirit, but that of the Son which ought to undertake the dispensation of human redemption, the following Scripture shows how God the Father called and appointed God the Son from eternity and before times to accomplish this same dispensation of our redemption. It says:

“And the Lord called Samuel. He answered and said, ‘Here I am.’ And he ran to Eli and said, ‘Here I am, for you called [Col. 0429A] me.’ But he said, ‘I did not call; return and sleep.’ And he went away and slept. And so it came to pass three times.”

The first calling of the Lord was that predestination of Christ’s incarnation, made before times, by God the Father and the Holy Spirit. The second calling was temporal, made before the Law in the type of Abel, in Noah’s ark, and in the offering of Isaac, Abraham’s son. For what did Noah’s ark prefigure—an ark which could not be submerged by the floodwaters as they overflowed—except the holy flesh of Christ, which the wave of original and actual sin, overflowing upon the human race, did not touch? Or what were Abel’s slaying and Isaac’s offering except, so to speak, a calling and prefiguration of Christ’s future Passion? The third calling was made under [Col. 0429B] the Law, because whatever was done in the legal ceremonies was all, 605 as it were, a calling that foreshadowed Christ’s future incarnation and Passion.

Nor should it be passed over that, just as in the words set before us we have three callings of God the Father, so also in them we find three responses of the Son of God to the Father. In the first calling, made in eternity, we read that he answered, that he ran, that with utmost devotion he offered himself to obey the will of the calling Father. “Here I am,” he says, “for you called me.” So in the second and in the third calling he always gave the same answer, saying: “Here I am, because you called me; here I am, because you called me.” This response [Col. 0429C] and running were, I judge, nothing other than the ready will and fervent love which he always had—before times and in time, before the Law and under the Law—to obey God the Father for the redemption of the human race. But Eli’s saying to Samuel the first, second, and third time, “I did not call you, my son. Return and sleep,” expressed that delay which intervened in each of those periods, namely the time before the Law and the time under the Law, in which God’s Only-Begotten could not yet come for the redemption of the human race, because God the Father deferred this to the fitting time, the time appointed before times. For in each period the Son offered himself to God the Father for the redemption of the human race, saying, because of the great love [Col. 0429D] he had for humanity, “Here I am, because you called me.” But the Father, in a manner of speaking, said: “I did not call”—that is, what I arranged with you in my eternal predestination concerning the salvation of the human race will not yet be fulfilled in reality.

“Return and sleep.” He commanded him to return, though he did not yet wish him to become man for the salvation of human nature. But that this return, this delay of human restoration, in no way troubled the Son, and did not alter or lessen in anything the sweetness of his everlasting rest, which he eternally possessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God the Father showed in the following word when he said, “Sleep.” It is as though he said: “My Son, coeternal with me in my eternity, rest with me, 606 because the time has not yet come for your will [Col. 0430A] to be fulfilled, for human nature to be redeemed through you.” It follows:

“Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord, nor had the word of the Lord been revealed to him.” Everything which the Father knew and which the Holy Spirit knew, the Son also knew. He knew the Lord indeed according to the excellence of his divinity, but he did not yet know him through the experience of human nature. Nor had the word of the Lord been revealed to him. The word of the Lord, which had been spoken concerning the salvation of the human race in the most secret counsel of the Holy Trinity, had indeed been revealed to him in predestination; but it had not yet been revealed to him in the completion of the work, because he had not yet become man and had not yet redeemed humanity by his death. When the time before the Law had passed, [Col. 0430B] and the time under the Law had passed, the time of grace succeeded. In it God the Father at last willed, through his Son, to fulfill everything which in the predestination of his eternity he had conceived and ordained with that same Son and the Holy Spirit concerning the redemption of fallen humanity. Hence it follows:

“And the Lord came and stood; and he called, as he had called the second time: ‘Samuel, Samuel.’ And Samuel said: ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.’” It is as though he had said: “Speak, Lord. For your speaking is your acting: most merciful Father, let the working of your mercy at last be brought to completion through me, your Son—everything which the mercy of your compassion had ordained with me from the beginning concerning lost humanity. [Col. 0430C] Speak, Lord, for your Son according to divinity hears, that is, obeys your fatherly will to become your servant according to humanity.”

“And the Lord said to Samuel: ‘Behold, I am doing a thing in Israel, which whoever hears it, both his ears shall tingle.’” God the Father did a great thing in Israel when he sent his Only-Begotten into the world, when through the death of the Son he destroyed the death of the slave. “Whoever hears it, both his ears shall tingle.” By the tingling of both ears, I judge, the fear and love 607 of God may very fittingly be understood. For before the Word became flesh, before the immortal God took upon himself the miseries of our mortality, only one ear of humanity tingled, because humanity feared God only as Creator. [Col. 0430D] But after God became man, both ears—the ear of fear and that of love—began to tingle, because then humanity first learned both to fear and to love God: to fear him, I say, as Creator, and to love him as Redeemer, whom it had formerly only feared as Creator. For love was not principally connected with creation, but with redemption. Creation would have profited humanity nothing unless redemption had been added. Thus almighty God ought to have been loved more for re-creation than for creation. In creating man he did not labor; but in re-creating him he labored greatly. There he endured not only many abasements but also many humiliations; there at last [Col. 0431A] he willed to experience the punishment of a shameful death itself. Therefore Scripture next adds, as though in the person of the Son himself, and says:

“On that day I will raise up against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house.” We have said that God the Father is to be understood by Eli; we may also understand Eli as the Son himself according to his divinity. By Eli’s house let human nature be understood, which the Son of God was to assume into himself.
