By all those things which he said he had spoken in his eternal disposition concerning that same house of Eli, that same house of God the Father, he figuratively expressed, as it seems to me, all the needs and miseries of our mortality, which he willed to suffer in his flesh for the salvation of the human race. He raised all these things [Col. 0431B] up against himself, not on the day of eternity but on the day when he assumed humanity—for no capacity for suffering could come upon him in his divinity—because he so willed.

Nor should it be passed over that he said he would raise all these things up against Eli. By Eli may be understood, as we have said, the divinity of the Father, the divinity of the Son himself, and the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is well said: “I will raise up against 608 Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house.” For his becoming man, his living as a man among human beings, and everything that he suffered in assumed humanity, were all against Eli, because they were all contrary to divinity. But because he foresaw that human nature could not be saved without all these things, he added and said:

[Col. 0431C] “I will begin and I will complete.” It is as though he said: “I will begin by being born as a man for humanity; I will complete it by suffering and dying as a man for humanity.”

“For I foretold to him that I would judge his house forever because of its iniquity, since he knew that his sons acted unworthily, and he did not rebuke them.” As far as I can conjecture, it seems to me that in this place the house may be understood as human nature, which began in Adam and Eve, and which ought to have been and been called the dwelling-place of God Most High, if it had remained in the honor for which it was created. The iniquity committed in that house was their transgression and disobedience. Therefore the words, “For I foretold that I would judge his house forever because of its iniquity,” [Col. 0431D] mean the same as if he had said: “I foretold before times, I foretold in time; I promised through the Law, I promised through the Prophets, that I would visit the world through my incarnation, and would both judge Eli’s house—that is, human nature, condemned because of the iniquity of its father’s transgression—and myself bear its judgment.”

But how does this concern me? Namely, because he knew that his sons acted unworthily and did not rebuke them. We may say that the two true sons of Eli were our two first parents, who certainly acted unworthily when, seduced by the fraud of the evil one, they fell away from God through the evil of disobedience. God the Father knew beforehand of their unworthy action, before it took place, and did not rebuke them. He did not rebuke them because he allowed it to take place. [Col. 0432A] He would in some manner have rebuked it if he had not permitted it to happen. But because he did not rebuke it—that is, because in his hidden judgment he allowed it to take place—

609 “therefore I have sworn,” says the Lord, “to Eli’s house, that the iniquity of his house shall not be expiated by victims and offerings forever.” It is as though he said: “Because the evil of their transgression is so great that through it the whole human race descends with them into destruction, therefore I have sworn—therefore in the disposition of my eternity I established this with my Father and the Holy Spirit—that the iniquity of his house, which is human nature, shall not be expiated by victims and offerings, namely by legal ceremonies and observances, unless I myself become man for humanity and through my death destroy their death.”

[Col. 0432B] “But Samuel slept until morning, and opened the doors of the house of the Lord.” Samuel’s sleeping until morning prefigured, as was said a little earlier, that rest which our Samuel, namely the Son of God, possessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit in eternity. But then he awoke, as it were, in the morning, when, having become man, he descended from the utterly tranquil peace of eternity to the labors of our mortality. “He opened the doors of the house of the Lord.” By the doors of the Lord’s house may be understood the Old and New Testaments. Each is not unjustly called a door of the Lord’s house, because through their observance one enters the Lord’s house, which is the kingdom of heaven. He opened these two doors when, by legal and evangelical precepts, he taught humanity how it might merit, through the worthiness of a good life, [Col. 0432C] entry into the heavenly homeland, long shut off. But in the days of his flesh the Son of God also opened two other doors of the Lord’s house. He opened the door of innocence, and he opened the door of repentance: truly two doors which open to humanity access to the heavenly kingdom. He opened the door of innocence in baptism, where guilt is annulled and innocence restored. After the door of innocence, he opened the door of repentance, so that if the innocence received in baptism should be corrupted, it might be cleansed by the remedy of subsequent repentance and satisfaction. After this it follows:

“And Samuel feared to tell Eli the vision.” What was this vision? It was surely everything that he saw in [Col. 0432D] the human race. Finally, the pain and misery of human nature, which he had formerly seen through the power of divinity, he began to see through the experience of humanity when he took upon himself all our pains except sin alone. He saw the great and countless sins of the human race; he saw daily the souls of his elect descending into hell. Yet he feared to tell Eli the vision. From the time he became man, he was always in fear through the most merciful affection of compassion which he had for the ruin of the human race. Thus the prophet foretold of him, saying: “And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. 2:2). Therefore the Lord feared, not for himself but for us; he feared not for his sins, of which there were none, but for ours, which [Col. 0433A] were great and countless. He also feared this: he saw that the redemption of the human race would be prolonged and delayed because of the magnitude of its crimes. Thus he himself testifies concerning himself in a passage of the Gospel: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke 12:50). This baptism was Christ’s Passion, in which our baptism began. He was indeed constrained in fear until this baptism should be accomplished, until human nature should be redeemed through his cross and blood. But he had not yet told Eli. His telling was his dying. And because the time of his Passion and death had not yet come, when our sins were to be so set forth before God the Father as to be utterly erased, it is rightly said that he feared to tell Eli the vision. But when God the Father—or rather, [Col. 0433B] the Son himself—called himself to the Passion, then what Scripture adds shortly afterwards was truly fulfilled:

“Thus Samuel told him all the words, and hid nothing from him.” Samuel truly told Eli all the words when the Only-Begotten of God offered himself upon the altar of the cross to God the Father for the sins of all his faithful.

611 **HOMILY LXIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.**

“Now tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him” (Luke 15).

These seven Sundays which we now celebrate seem to me to correspond and agree quite fittingly in mystery [Col. 0433C] with those seven days in which God created heaven and earth. There we read what the Lord did or said on the third day; and that act of the third day can be applied quite suitably to this third Sunday and its Gospel. On the third day God said: “Let the waters which are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” And God called the dry land earth, and he called the gatherings of the waters seas. And God saw that it was good, and said: “Let the earth put forth green grass, bearing seed, and fruit-bearing trees whose seed is in themselves upon the earth.” And it was so. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening and morning, the third day (Gen. 1:9–13).

The waters, it seems to me, are gathered into one [Col. 0433D] place when a person predestined to eternal life gathers within one place—that is, within his own heart—his wandering and shifting thoughts, which may here be understood as waters; and when he begins, by rising up against himself, to be displeased with himself before the Lord for whatever sins he has committed. When the waters have been gathered—that is, when a person’s thoughts have been collected inwardly—what else does this signify but tax collectors and sinners drawing near to Jesus? But the waters are not gathered unless God’s speaking comes first. God’s speaking is his doing. For he is the one who works wondrously, enabling a person to recognize himself, and in true knowledge to weep for and punish himself. Then the dry land appears, because he already begins to wither and waste away from the sins in which he formerly [Col. 0434A] seemed to have great savor and delight. 612 “And God called the dry land earth.” For dry land is so called when a person, dried from sins in his flesh, knows how to crush his spirit by the lamentations of repentance and to discipline his body through the practice of outward satisfaction. For just as the earth is ploughed and broken up in order to bring forth abundant fruit, so the blessed person must be broken up and crushed in his own earth by the ploughshare of repentance and satisfaction, so that he may be able to offer God worthy fruit from himself.

“And he called the gatherings of the waters seas.” The person who has gathered the waters—that is, his flowing and wandering thoughts—so that they remain within him, and has truly recognized himself as a sinner, fittingly [Col. 0434B] calls the gatherings of the waters “seas.” For *sea* (*mare*) is so called from bitterness (*amaritudo*). And the heart made bitter by repentance may fittingly be understood through the sea. For when a person looks upon the former paths of his life and carefully considers all that he has done and whatever offenses he has committed, he turns it all into a kind of bitterness and pain for himself. When this has happened, let us see what follows:

“And God saw that it was good.” God’s seeing is God’s loving. For he sees such progress in a person because he approves and loves it, and says: “Let the earth put forth green grass.” The earth puts forth green grass when a person produces the fresh vigor and growth of good works. He bears seed when, inwardly enlightened, he shows others an example of good conduct, perfect humility, [Col. 0434C] and patience, so that one who had formerly been the destruction of others by living badly may now become their edification by living well. He will also be a fruit-bearing tree when one who was formerly weak in will and knowledge now stands strong and firm both in will and knowledge.

But amidst these things it is necessary that “the seed be in itself upon the earth.” What is it for seed to be in itself, except not to seek praise from the mouths of neighbors for good actions? For the one whose seed is not in himself upon the earth, but who seeks temporal favor, assuredly finds nothing of reward in the future life when he is taken hence from the earth in death; as the Lord himself says even of such persons: “Amen, I say to you, they have received [Col. 0434D] their reward” (Matt. 6:2). Hence, when the Lord comes to the wedding, the foolish virgins complain of their extinguished lamps and are shut out from the wedding, because while they sought human praise, they found extinguished the light of holy action by which they ought to have shone before the Lord.

I have said these things because, as I see it, they agree greatly with the Gospel reading; and all who make progress in this order properly draw near to Jesus—that is, to their Savior, Christ—or to Jesus, that is, to the salvation of their own soul. For this is why we now draw near to God through good conduct: that by drawing near to his eternity in heaven, we may deserve to receive from him eternal recompense.

But who are those drawing near to him, except the two peoples, [Col. 0435A] tax collectors and sinners? By tax collectors may be understood those who have sinned publicly in the world and whose sins have become known to others; by sinners, those who have not sinned openly and yet cannot excuse themselves from sin. For, as the Apostle says, “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). Whether we are tax collectors or sinners, we all need God’s mercy. Why, I ask, do these draw near to Jesus? Surely in order to hear him. For from the words they hear, they are admonished to begin to consider and recall how wickedly and ruinously they have lived. They also hear in his commandments what manner of repentance and satisfaction they ought to practice. There too they learn 614 what pleases or displeases their Creator. But because the more watchfully a person draws near to God, the more he is assailed by evil spirits, their temptations are fittingly indicated when it is immediately added:

“And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying: ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them.’” In this murmuring may be understood the hidden temptations which our adversaries send against us day and night. By these Pharisees and scribes, I judge, two temptations may be signified by which evil spirits sometimes ensnare converted persons. When a person comes to conversion, those invisible enemies murmur—that is, they introduce temptations—so that, in the Pharisees’ manner, he may separate himself from others and begin to live singularly and privately; may dare to undertake greater and holier observances than the common rule of the monastery requires; and on that account may judge himself holier and more acceptable to God than others.

On the other hand, there are others who, after the manner of scribes, wish to appear wiser than everyone else and therefore frequently scorn and despise others. Spiritual persons are sometimes attacked by these two temptations. For evil spirits judge it impossible that those who have wholly devoted themselves to God should depart from him through manifest crimes; and therefore they murmur such things. I say, they pursue them with these hidden barbs of temptation, and grieving invisibly say: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” For they resent and grieve that, through God’s mercy, they have lost those whom they possessed as their own servants. Yet, so to speak, they would endure this somewhat more mildly if they did not know that through his infinite mercy the following also happens with sinners. They grieve that he mercifully receives sinners; but when he does not disdain to eat with them, this is such a work and such mercy that they are utterly tormented and wounded inwardly. For he eats with his sinners when he graciously joins himself to them, granting and allowing them also to prepare a meal for him inwardly through pure and sincere thoughts, good and holy desires, frequent sweet prayer, and sometimes worthy penitential satisfaction. Thus he delights and rejoices in them, while they, in turn, deserve to be consoled and refreshed by his manifold grace. Hence it often happens [Col. 0436A] that they are so refreshed and encouraged by this inward sweetness that they even presume to approach the altar’s table to eat the most holy body of the Lord. This is truly a sign of that inward sweetness and grace which, if we were worthy, we ought to possess with God. While Pharisees and scribes murmur against us in these matters, the Lord teaches us in the following parable how we ought to resist them.

“Which of you,” he says, “is the man who has a hundred sheep?” This word *which* (*quis*) should perhaps not be thought superfluous or carelessly spoken. For everything which that eternal Wisdom said was great, everything was weighty. Whenever by his gift we understand his words, let us give thanks; but where they cannot be understood by us, we should nonetheless know that nothing is weightier and nothing [Col. 0436B] better than where he opened his mouth and taught. For everything Moses and the Prophets said was good; yet Moses, being human, though he spoke holy things, was not wholly clean but was defiled in his lips. “Which of you,” he says, “is the man?” So long as a person lives in sins, he is as though nonexistent, because he does not tend toward true being. Yet everything which God created in a human being is wholly good, as it is written: “And God saw all things which he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1:31). Therefore all is good. But what a person has from himself, namely sins, is nothing. For sin is nothing but the privation of good. When a person has recognized this and repents of sins, he becomes *which man* (*quis homo*), that is, some person—whereas before, while sinning, he was nothing, as we have said.

[Col. 0436C] Nor should it be passed over that he says, “Which of you.” It is the same as if he said: “From among you Pharisees and scribes—that is, evil spirits—that ‘which man’ is no longer one of you, because he has now become good and praiseworthy, 616 and has departed from you.” Or, “He is no longer from among you tax collectors and sinners, because he has ceased to be a sinner and has separated and alienated himself from you.” But that “which man” who has a hundred sheep—if he loses one of them, does he not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one which was lost? When a person is born, he does not have a hundred sheep—that is, perfect innocence, which may be understood by the hundred sheep—because he is conceived and born in sins. But when regenerated by baptism, he possesses a hundred sheep, because both original and actual sins are perfectly forgiven him and perfect innocence is bestowed upon him. But because there is almost no one who keeps the innocence received in baptism as spotless and whole as he ought, it is rightly said: “And if he loses one of them”—that is, if he falls into some mortal sin and loses his innocence—“does he not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness?” That is, if there are any good things in him, he ought to leave them, because he ought not to regard them as great; rather, he must leave them in the wilderness, that is, he should always regard himself as though God had abandoned him and as though he himself, by sinning shamefully, had abandoned and despised God. And he must go after the sheep that was lost until he finds it: that is, until through true repentance he returns to true innocence.

“And when he has found it, he lays it upon his shoulders [Col. 0437A] rejoicing.” Since burdens are carried on the shoulder, outward labors may fittingly be understood by the shoulders. Once innocence has been found and restored, it must be laid upon the shoulders, because our labor and satisfaction must never be interrupted. For it is not enough to have repented once or twice, or for a year; rather, throughout the whole period of our lives we must persevere in truly humble and perfect repentance.

And note that he says, “rejoicing,” because we must bear the labor of this bodily discipline with joy, not sorrow—that is, not because of fear of hell, nor under compulsion, as unwilling and constrained persons—but gladly and cheerfully. For, as the Apostle says, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). And the Psalmist says: “Willingly I will sacrifice to you” (Ps. 53:8). [Col. 0437B] 617 The blessed and spiritual persons to whom it has been granted to know the mystery of God’s kingdom are themselves ready to do this; for those who understand spiritual things are by no means sluggish or negligent in carrying them out. Hence we see that the repentance which secular people display outwardly is performed not joyfully, not truthfully, but rather from necessity: after completing public penance, they return again to their former ways and commit worse things than before. Therefore, because the repentance of the righteous ought to be continual and their labor unceasing, in today’s prayer they pray and beseech God, the protector of those who hope in him—without whom nothing is strong—to deign to send heavenly help to those who labor, being less strong in themselves.

[Col. 0437C] Accordingly, the person who truly repents, having found, as we have said, the sheep, returns home and calls together friends and neighbours, saying: “Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost.” To return home is to come back to one’s heart and conscience. Those are happy who long to possess the grace of inward sweetness: they frequently return home, because they wish to know what is hidden within, what is being done, what is stirring there; and the more searchingly they examine themselves, the more sweetly they find it to labour for the Lord. Conversely, those who wander out among external things and are reluctant to visit their own home—that is, their conscience—will bear their labours not with joy but with mourning and sadness. Appropriately, moreover, when one returns home, friends and neighbours are called together. Those are called friends who are bound to one another by mutual love; neighbours are those who are placed near us. [Col. 0437D] By these friends and neighbours bodily exercises may be understood. A person calls together these friends and neighbours when, inwardly moved at some time, he recalls so sweetly all his pains and labours which he has endured for the Lord that he begins in a marvellous way to rejoice with them, and counts those same labours or afflictions as dear friends, embraces them as neighbours close at hand, knowing that through outward exercises he is tending toward inward consolations. Thus he bursts forth into these words: “Rejoice with me.” These words are the words of a person exhorting himself to preserve his good works: namely, that he may preserve in humility those good things which he remembers having done, lest he lose them through some favour; for then they will rejoice with him in eternal life. [Col. 0438A] It is as though he said inwardly to himself: “If I do not seek human praise for good deeds, but preserve them in humility, I shall rejoice over them, and they themselves will rejoice with me in eternal life”—which is, as it were, to say, “Rejoice with me.” Then I have truly found my sheep, because, as I hope in God’s mercy, through repentance and satisfaction I have recovered my innocence.

After the outward person has in this manner found his sheep, placed it upon his shoulders, and come home, the Lord teaches us what joy such a sinner and penitent person produces. “I tell you,” he says, “that thus there shall be joy over one sinner doing penance.” “I tell you,” he says: I, who am unchangeable truth, tell you the truth. What do I tell you? I tell [Col. 0438B] you that thus—and not otherwise, but in this way and order—there shall be joy over one sinner returning through repentance to innocence, “than,” that is, and not over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need repentance. There, indeed, there will be joy over innocence restored through repentance; here there is joy over righteousness preserved, which needs no repentance. This word *quam* (“than”) is used in the sense of *et non* (“and not”), as in the Psalm: “It is good to hope in the Lord, than to hope in princes” (Ps. 117:9), that is, and not to hope in princes.

Therefore, because a human being consists of two things, body and soul, the Lord set forth two parables. And although the preceding parable is very prominent, nevertheless, as I see it, this following parable is more eminent and worthy, because it concerns the sweetness of the inward person. He presents it thus:

[Col. 0438C] “Or what woman, having ten drachmas [manuscript: *dragmas*].” By this woman understand the soul softened by God’s grace, which becomes a *quae*—that is, a certain woman—by following what is good, whereas formerly by sinning she was, as it were, nothing before the Lord. “Having ten drachmas,” he says. I would say that the ten drachmas can signify the Ten Commandments, if the loss of one did not stand in the way. Yet in the ten drachmas may be understood that which is also understood through Job’s seven sons and three daughters. The number ten, composed of seven and three, suggests something mystical. For what is understood by seven except the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and what by three except [Col. 0438D] faith, hope, and charity? The woman—that is, the soul softened by God—possesses these ten drachmas when she possesses the gifts of the Holy Spirit together with the three virtues, faith, hope, and charity.

But because it is difficult, and granted to few, to be able so to excel in the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the three virtues unless they are at some time withdrawn, one drachma, as it seems to me, is lost when, upon the arising of a slight adversity, love of God and neighbour is lost. Once it has been lost, the soul must light its lamp—that is, rekindle the extinguished light of twofold love through the illumination of instruction; overturn the house—that is, cast out the filth of sins through cleansing of the heart; and search diligently through contemplation of the mind.

[Col. 0439A] And it must truly search diligently, because such diligence must be exercised in the contemplation of the mind that every occasion not only of evil thoughts, but even of those thoughts which at another time are harmless, may be removed far away. The prayer of the day again leads us to this understanding, because, just as without Christ our protector and helper nothing is strong in bodily exercise, so without him nothing is holy in contemplation of the mind; for he must be our ruler in good works and our guide in good and holy desires.

Having found the drachma, therefore, she calls together her women friends and neighbours, saying: “Rejoice with me, for I have found my drachma.” These women friends and neighbours are, I think, the virtues of the soul, which this woman—that is, the blessed soul—[Col. 0439B] deserves to perceive as descending from heaven in that taste of the divine presence. She rejoices in their friendship and neighbourhood, saying, “Rejoice with me.”

It is as though the inward person exhorted himself to preserve the virtues and said: “If concerning my friends and neighbours—that is, the virtues joined and bound to me by a certain love—I desire to glory not in myself but in the Lord, I shall rejoice over them, and they themselves will rejoice with me in eternal recompense”; which is, as it were, to say, “Rejoice with me.” Then I have truly found my drachma, because, through God’s mercy, I have recovered the inward grace of my heart which I had lost.

[Col. 0439C] Thus, when the lamp has been lit, the house overturned, and the drachma diligently sought and found, the Lord again declares that joy occurs thus and not otherwise: “Thus, I tell you, there shall be joy before the angels of God over one sinner doing penance.”

Why is it that in the preceding parable joy is said to take place in heaven over one sinner doing penance, whereas here it is said to occur before the angels of God? In sacred speech heaven sometimes signifies the present Church; in this heaven joy takes place whenever a sinner is converted before the Church. But this joy of the soul, which occurs inwardly when the Lord himself deigns to come to the soul, takes place only before him and his angels. For the angels are aware of this mutual love and are faithful attendants of bridegroom and bride: they run between them, offering God the soul’s vows from this side, and bringing back splendid gifts from above from that side.

[Col. 0439D] When all these things have, with God’s help, been completed and perfected in his elect, there comes to be evening and morning, the third day. By morning is understood knowledge of God; by evening, knowledge of oneself. For a person can know what he is like, and from knowledge of himself can attain to true knowledge of the Creator. And in this evening and morning there will be a third day, because he is admitted to knowledge of the holy Trinity, insofar as this is permitted to mortals. The third day also comes about when a person knows how to measure and guard himself so in words, deeds, and thoughts that he does not wish to return to anything harmful or useless.

The reading bears upon these matters, in which Peter exhorts us, saying: [Col. 0440A] “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation” (1 Pet. 5:6). A person must first be humbled through satisfaction, which cannot occur except through true humility of heart; and the one thus humbled outwardly is, without doubt, exalted inwardly in the time of visitation. What greater exaltation could there be than that a human being, ashes and dust, should deserve to taste something of inward sweetness?

Therefore we rightly pray that he who is the protector of those who hope in him may multiply his mercy over us. For it is truly his mercy when a person can abandon sins and turn to God. But his mercy is manifold when that same sinner is admitted to that inward grace which is [Col. 0440B] ineffable.

He must also be our ruler and guide: ruler in outward things, guide in inward things, so that we may pass through temporal goods in such a manner that we do not lose eternal goods. The temporal goods through which we wish to pass are not gold, silver, precious stones, or any visible things. Rather, our temporal goods are the repentance of the outward person and the sweetness and grace of the inward person, for which we sigh, which, while we are on the way, we desire to have as our companion; and we wish to have it in such a way that we do not lose eternal things, because if we seek to receive temporal praise here in exchange for it, we shall lose what is everlasting.

May our Lord Jesus [Col. 0440C] Christ bring us to this humility and exaltation of which we have spoken, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

623. HOMILY LXIV. FIRST, ON THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

“Therefore be merciful, even as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke 6).

This fourth Sunday, on which the Lord taught his disciples not in parables, as on the three preceding Sundays, but in plain and lucid speech, is not unjustly compared with that fourth day on which God the Father first created the sun, moon, and stars, by which he illuminated and adorned the rest of his creation. For we read concerning that day: [Col. 0440D] “And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night; and let them be for signs, and seasons, and days, and years, that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth. And it was so. And God made two great lights: the greater light, to rule the day; and the lesser light, to rule the night; and the stars. And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine over the earth, and rule day and night, and divide light and darkness” (Gen. 1:14–18).

By the firmament of heaven we may understand the holy Church; by the lights of this firmament, the evangelical precepts by which that same holy Church is illumined. God placed these lights in his Church in order that they might divide—that is, distinguish—day and night: namely, prelates and subjects, good and evil, perfect and imperfect; and that they might be signs of direction, [Col. 0441A] seasons of conversion, days of perfection, and years of recompense. They are signs of direction for us because they teach us the way that leads to our homeland. And if, by living badly, we have strayed on this way and from it, they are seasons of conversion for us because they teach us how to move away from our evil life and how, by conversion, we ought to gird ourselves for running the path of life from which we have deviated. They are days of perfection for us because in them we find how we may attain the summit of perfection. They are years of recompense for us, for through them we are taught by what merits we may advance to the years of eternal reward. And this is what follows:

“That they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth.” In the preceding passage we understood the firmament of heaven as the holy [Col. 0441B] Church; here, however, we may take the firmament to mean the human mind made firm and stable in God. When the aforesaid lights begin to shine inwardly in it in the manner already described, they also illuminate the earth—that is, its outward works.

“And God made two great lights: the greater light, to rule the day; the lesser light, to rule the night.” By the two great lights we understand the two Testaments; by the greater light, the New Testament; by the lesser light, the Old Testament. And the greater light fittingly represents the likeness of new and evangelical teaching, whereas we may call the Old Testament, as it were, the lesser light. Evangelical perfection is much more excellent than legal perfection. [Col. 0441C] In the former it is said, “You shall love a friend; you shall hate an enemy”; in the latter it is said, “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you.” God made the greater light to rule the day, that is, the good and perfect; the lesser light to rule the night, that is, the worldly and less perfect. By adding “and the stars,” he also clearly indicated good teachers and prelates, of whom Scripture elsewhere says: “Those who instruct many unto righteousness [shall shine] like stars unto perpetual eternities” (Dan. 12:3).

[Col. 0441D] “And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine over the earth, and rule day and night, and divide light and darkness.” God placed the stars—that is, his teachers—in the firmament, in the holy Church, that they might shine over the earth: that is, illuminate earthly hearts with the brightness of their teaching; rule day and night, that is, the good and bad, perfect and imperfect, worldly and spiritual; and divide light and darkness, so that they may know what teaching they ought to employ in governing and benefiting the good and the despisers of the world, who are counted under the name of light, and likewise what teaching is appropriate for those who are night, upon whom the darkness of sins still lies. For a teacher makes little or no progress if he wishes to teach spiritual persons as though they were worldly, and worldly persons as though they were spiritual.

All these things which we have set forth concerning the fourth day may fittingly be applied to this fourth Sunday, in which certain lights of heavenly teaching shine forth, making a kind of division between [Col. 0442A] day and night. For here prelates, whom we said should be understood by day, find their teaching; and from it night—that is, the still less perfect subjects—can receive the light for right and humble living. God has distinguished and divided it thus: its earlier part concerns prelates and instructs them, while its latter part, beginning with the parable, can fittingly be referred to the instruction of subjects. For he says:

“Therefore be merciful, even as your heavenly Father is merciful.” How is our heavenly Father merciful? Our heavenly Father, almighty God, out of the great pity and mercy which he had toward the human race, sent his only-begotten Son into the world, that through him he might redeem us and, through his passion and death, relieve our miseries. We too shall be truly merciful in likeness of him if, after the example of the blessed patriarch Abraham, we give him our only-begotten one. Our only-begotten one is our spirit. We give our only-begotten one to God the Father for his Only-begotten if we dedicate our spirit and soul to him alone; [Col. 0442B] if, as far as lies in us, we keep and guard it inviolate and unstained for God, free from everything that can be desired against God or loved outwardly. This is in some measure for us to be merciful, as our heavenly Father is merciful.

[Col. 0442C] But because the first part of this Gospel reading specially concerns prelates, as has been said, the Lord particularly teaches them by these words to be merciful: to deal mercifully with matters requiring their attention among their subjects; always to exalt mercy over judgment, that they too may obtain mercy. Yet this cannot happen unless they live in their office of prelation as they ought; this is indicated to them by the Lord’s following words:

“Do not judge, and you shall not be judged. Do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned. Forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given to you.” When he says, “Do not judge,” he does not say it as though he were taking away the authority of just judgment from those whom, in the order of his dispensation, he has raised to judicial dignity. For he wishes them to have authority to judge justly, but he does not wish them to have the will to judge. He did not say, “Do not judge,” but “Do not be willing to judge.” He adds, “And you shall not be judged.” It is as though he said: “In order that you may be able to escape the sentence of my strict judgment, do not be willing to seek and desire, with an exalted mind and proud heart, the seat of judgment—that is, the seat of humility.”

[Col. 0442D] But how does he say, “And you shall not be judged,” when not even the slightest transgression of wicked thought passes before God unexamined? A person will undoubtedly be examined for every perverse and unlawful deed which subsequent penitential satisfaction has not cleansed; but he will not be judged for the disposition by which he is free from the vice of self-exaltation and from the desire to rule and judge. Yet just as he ought not to will or desire the seat of judgment, the place of governance, so also, when he has been appointed not by his own will but by God’s will and ordinance, if an occasion for condemning arises, he must indeed condemn, but he must not have the will to condemn. Hence he said: “Do not condemn, [Col. 0443A] and you shall not be condemned.” This word, *nolite* (“do not be willing”), which the Lord repeats, here as in the preceding statements concerns the inward will of the person. He must indeed condemn a subject in matters in which and for which that subject is to be condemned, but with sorrow in his heart and compassion, out of necessity rather than will. By condemning thus, he will not only not be condemned, but will also be rewarded with the eternal glory of recompense. It follows:

“Forgive, and you shall be forgiven.” These words must first be understood thus: if a person seeks to be forgiven by the Lord without punishment through the grace of remission for which he longs, he should be willing always to stand ready and prepared to forgive the neighbour who sins against him.

Yet it must be known that it is not sufficient for perfection to forgive outwardly the troubles caused by injuries, unless a person also forgives himself inwardly—that is, knows how perfectly to submit himself. For he rightly forgives himself who submits himself to all in humility and through humility. Thus, having forgiven himself, he is forgiven when, raised and lifted by the hand of heavenly visitation, he is mercifully admitted to the inexhaustible feast of inward sweetness. The word “you shall be forgiven” may also be referred to a person’s end. There he will truly be forgiven when, having laid aside the body by which he is held here, he is received into the joys of eternal life. It follows:

[Col. 0443C] “Give, and it shall be given to you.” It is as though he said: “Let not only whatever material resources you have be open to your neighbours’ need, but also whatever you have deserved, through my gift, to attain from the riches of inward wisdom and knowledge: dispense it generously to others with the hand of devotion. For thus, as you give, it shall be given to you; thus the grace of my gifts which you have received will be increased and multiplied for you from the abundant hand of my mercy.” What and how great is this increase of the divine gift, by which he promises to reward his own here and in the future, he shows more clearly when he says:

“They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.” We may quite fittingly adapt these four measures to those four words of the Lord of which [Col. 0443D] we have already spoken. The good measure, as I see it, pertains to his saying, “Do not be willing to judge”; the pressed-down measure to “Do not be willing to condemn”; the shaken-together measure to “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven”; the overflowing measure to “Give, and it shall be given to you.” Hence he immediately adds:

“[Col. 0444A] “For with the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you.” The good measure, I think, is the grace of God, by which he measures well to a person when he does not judge one whom he sees to be removed from the will to judge and the appetite for ruling. But because he bestows much more on a person when he is not condemned than when he is not judged, a measure, as it were, pressed down is given when the one who has not voluntarily condemned or sought to condemn is not condemned by God. And one who has escaped these two things—that is, one who, exercising the work of judging without the will to judge, has condemned a person who should be condemned, being compelled and grieving rather than rejoicing and willing—will be granted the shaken-together measure, when he receives that first robe: that is, when, having laid aside the burden of flesh, he is rewarded in soul. Nor is that reward of the soul inappropriately called a shaken-together measure, because all the human thoughts by which he was often scattered uselessly here will there in some manner be gathered and pressed together; there they are collected to one thing and into one thing; there they are united to the desire and love of that alone which God is, and to God alone. This can in no way occur in this life, for “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15).

[Col. 0444B] Yet even this same shaken-together measure, this same reward of the soul, is not yet full or perfect blessedness, nor can it be called such, as long as it thinks of the body to be raised, as long as it desires that what had been its companion in labour should also be its companion in reward. But when the general resurrection has come and the body, raised from the dust, has been united with the soul in glory, this is the fourth measure; this is the overflowing measure which surpasses all things, where one reward, one blessedness, one immortality, one dignity of everlasting glory will remain without end for soul and body.

[Col. 0444C] A person can attain this grace not by his own merits but solely through the sweetness of God’s prevenient and subsequent mercy, as the Lord mystically indicates to us by calling this grace of eternal reward not a flowing but an overflowing measure. For there is a grace of God which may be called flowing grace; there is also a grace of God which may be called effluent grace; and there is still a grace of God which may be called overflowing grace.

Flowing grace is visiting grace: descending from the inexhaustible sweetness of the eternal fountain, and, the more sweetly it kindles the heart it touches with love of eternity, the more perfectly it suspends it outwardly from weak action. Thus, flowing inwardly and spreading through all the marrow of the heart, it becomes in a wonderful manner effluent—that is, edifying—when the outward person begins to magnify with such effectiveness of holy activity the grace that works within that he can benefit not only himself but also all among whom he may happen to be, through words and example. To this there will undoubtedly be added overflowing grace—that is, rewarding grace—which is begun here and will be fully perfected in the future, [Col. 0444D] where God gives the Spirit not by measure, but the greatness of the rewards surpasses every human merit.

Nor should we pass over the words, “They shall give into your bosom.” Who are they who shall give? Or what is our bosom into which they shall give? These givers may be understood as angelic spirits, ministers of the supreme Trinity, through whose ministry the mystery of our salvation is dispensed.

[Col. 0445A] For just as our minds are affected by movements of uncleanness and levity through the suggestions and impulses of malicious spirits, so whatever is of equity and virtue is administered to a person from the bosom of God’s mercy through the office of the holy angels. “They shall give,” he says, not into the hand but into the bosom—that is, into a certain certainty of eternal blessedness, which is fittingly understood by the bosom. What is carried in the bosom is kept more securely than what is carried in the hand.

In fitting order, moreover, after the Lord had said, “They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing,” he added: “For with the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you.” It is as though he said: “If you do not have the will to judge, a good measure will be measured back to you, because you will not be judged.

“If you do not have the will to condemn, [Col. 0445B] a pressed-down measure will be measured back to you, because you too will not be condemned. If you forgive, a shaken-together measure will be measured back to you, because you will be forgiven—that is, when, with death intervening, you are released from the body which has always weighed you down, and your thoughts have been gathered and united to God and in God, you will be rewarded in soul, which truly is the shaken-together measure.

“If you give, an overflowing measure will be measured back to you, because at the resurrection a double robe will be given you, where the body together with the soul will be clothed and glorified in blessed immortality.” It follows:

“And he spoke also a parable to them.” To whom, “them”? Here there occurs what we set forth concerning the fourth day, on which the Lord said: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night” (Gen. 1:14).

[Col. 0445C] For these are the lights; these are the evangelical precepts and teachings which divide day and night. Day, as we said before, consists of good and perfect prelates; night, of subjects. Here God divided day from night through his lights—that is, prelates and subjects—because the preceding words of this Gospel, as we have already partly heard, concern prelates, whereas the following words concern subjects.

He taught those who are day, who ought to excel in understanding and knowledge as well as in rank and dignity, as it were in a pure and open manner, the truth. He taught them in plain speech how they should live in their office of prelation. But those who are still night, who as yet understand less perfectly, he taught by a parable how they should be subject.

[Col. 0445D] Therefore it is fittingly said: “And he spoke a parable to them.” For those who are less perfect, and understand the things of truth less by themselves, ought to hear and learn in parables and through parables those things which must be known and said. Hence our Lord too, when he spoke to crowds and imperfect people, as Scripture says, spoke nothing without parables. He says:

“Can the blind lead the blind? Will they not both fall into the pit?” Here he begins, as it were, to touch upon a vice which often prevails among less-perfect [Col. 0446A] subjects: namely, the vice of self-exaltation, by which they rashly criticize and judge the actions of prelates, think that, if they happened to preside, they would preside more profitably, and imagine and say that they would never do, were they to preside, the things in which they scorn their prelate as blameworthy. In this parable, as I see it, the Lord admonishes and instructs them to begin to recognize their blindness, so that they may be willing and strive to be subject in humility. “Can the blind,” he says, “lead the blind?” It is as though he said: “Why do you think evil in your heart? You are blind; you cannot lead the blind. You are blind in that respect in which you desire things not fitting for you, because you wish to be what God did not wish you to be; you exalt yourself above that which God ordained you to be.”

“Can the blind lead the blind? Will they not both fall into the pit?” By the pit may be understood a dark heart and dark conscience. The sense is: “You are blind; acknowledge your blindness. For if God allowed you to follow your own will, if, by his allowing it, you came to preside as you desire, you yourself, blind from your dark heart and dark conscience, would fall into something worse; and the one entrusted to you, who ought to be led by you to the light of truth, would remain in his blindness, in ignorance of his sins.”

[Col. 0446B] “A disciple is not above his master.” It belongs to the master to be above the disciple; it does not belong to the disciple to be above the master. You are a disciple; as a disciple you must be subject. For this is why you have been ordained by God: that you may be a disciple. Do not seek to raise yourself above the master; do not presume to attempt what has not been entrusted to you.

“But every one shall be perfect if he be as his master” [Col. 0446C]. The disciple’s perfection does not consist merely in imitating the praiseworthy life of his master in outward acts. Rather, he will be truly perfect if he is as his master is: that is, if he humbly remains that which God ordained him to be, just as his master remains that which God ordained him to be. For this is what God ordained the master to be: that he should preside; and this is what God ordained the disciple to be: that he should be subject to him with humility.

For often a prelate would gladly shake off the burden of governance and willingly be absent from the place of prelation. But because he neither dares nor can oppose God’s ordinance—for, as the Apostle says, “there is no authority except from God, and those that are, are ordained by God” (Rom. 13:1)—he humbly retains his being as something ordained for him by God.

[Col. 0446D] This is great perfection in a prelate. Thus every person will certainly be perfect if, following such a master’s example, he firmly and humbly retains his own appointed state. It follows:

“Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam which is in your own eye?” He does not say, “in the eye of your master,” or “in the eye of your father,” but “in the eye of your brother.” For he names him outwardly as he sees him regarded inwardly by the heart of the one who criticizes and despises him. By eye, and by what is in the eye, is understood the intention of the mind. The speck in the brother’s eye consists, I think, of those lighter and unavoidable sins which sometimes come upon a prelate, now from his own weakness, now from the laborious occupation of outward concerns. But the beam in [Col. 0447A] the subject’s eye may fittingly be understood as the swelling of pride.

For the one who, as we have said, has been raised to a place of governance not by his own will but by God’s will and ordinance, and who strives in his prelation to observe not his own will but God’s, if he happens at some time to sin, God—who considers the eye, that is, the intention, of his faithful heart with God—counts his sin as a speck, because he judges it venial. For he more readily and mercifully pardons the one whom he sees labouring under his burden, whom he perceives faithfully bearing his burden with him.

We have an evident example of this matter in Aaron, who, overcome by the madness of that tumultuous people over whom he presided, committed a great sin against the Lord by making the calf.

[Col. 0447B] But because he acted under compulsion, and if he had not done so the people would have departed from him, his sin was like a speck before God. For the Lord bore it mercifully, because he considered not the deed but the intention of the deed.

For he yielded to and complied with the people in casting the calf with this intention: that by it he might hold them back until Moses returned from the mountain, lest, wholly turned away from the Lord, they should return again to Egypt.

So also, even now, if a good prelate whose heart is with God should happen at some time to sin, whether from his own frailty, or from the necessity of an impending occupation, as has been said, or when he sometimes yields in condescension to the weaker in lesser matters in order thereby to hold them back from greater and more serious sins, he indeed sins against the Lord; yet that very sin of his, because it proceeds from a good intention, is in some sense a speck, because it is venial before God.

[Col. 0447C] But what is a speck in the prelate’s eye becomes in some sense a beam in the subject’s eye when, considering and judging his deeds not with a simple and humble eye of heart but with a double and proud one, he believes himself capable of presiding more rationally and profitably over the one to whom he ought humbly to be subject.

The Lord in some sense counters such thoughts with these words: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam which is in your own eye?” It is as though he said: “The one whom you ought to have regarded as a father, you scarcely regard even as a father.

[Col. 0447D] How do you not fear to criticize and condemn in outward acts one whose eye—that is, whose heart’s intention—you do not know? How do you despise and judge him in your heart for a speck, for even a lighter sin, when you do not consider the beam—that is, the great sin of pride—in your own eye, that is, in your own intention?

“The thing for which you criticize him is a speck, because it is slight and venial before me.” But because it is not sufficient for a subject blinded by pride to think these things which we have said concerning the prelate unless he also goes on to speak them, the Lord condemns and rebukes this too when he immediately adds and says:

[Col. 0448A] “Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, allow me to remove the speck from your eye,’ while you do not see the beam in your own eye?” It is as though he said: “How can you say this? How do you presume to open your mouth to criticize and rebuke your prelate for lesser faults, while you do not see the beam in your own eye—while you do not consider the pride and proud intention of your heart?”

“Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” A hypocrite is called a pretender. It is as though the Lord said: “I call you a hypocrite because I find you to be a pretender.

“You are not what you pretend to be. You pretend and show yourself outwardly as humble, as subject, as a disciple; but I see you not as humble [Col. 0448B] but exalted, not as a disciple or subject, but as though set over others.

“First remove the beam from your own eye”: that is, first cast out the pride which has blinded your heart’s eye, which has raised you above yourself. Then, when the eye of your mind has been cleansed by humility and illuminated, you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.

When you have perfectly humbled yourself and submitted yourself in humble subjection to the one to whom you ought to be subject, then you will see clearly; then you will truly begin to see the things in which you are now blind; then, if you see that your master should be admonished in anything, you will be able to admonish him profitably, both for yourself and for him.

[Col. 0448C] By this the Lord does not forbid a subject ever to admonish a prelate. But he ought not presume to do so except with the greatest humility, the greatest submission, and the greatest tranquillity of mind.

For if he acts proudly, his admonition will do no good. For the devil attaches himself to pride, and the superior cannot hear, or bear with equanimity, the words of the devil; nor, because of words of pride—which are truly the devil’s words—can he correct those matters in which he ought to be corrected.

But if he acts humbly, God attaches Himself to humility, so that the superior may humbly hear the words of God—namely, words of humility, which are truly God’s words—and may be willing and able to correct himself in those matters in which he needs correction.

That this peace and unanimity may flourish and remain between superiors and subjects, we ask of the Lord in today’s Prayer, when we say: “Grant us, O Lord, that the course of the world may be peacefully directed for us according to Thy ordering.”

God’s order consists of superiors and subjects. He ordained the former to preside; He ordained the latter to be subject. The course of the world is the present life, in which we labour. In eternal life there is no course. Here we run; there we shall stand. Here we labour; there we rest from our labours.

Therefore we ask the Lord—and we ought continually to ask—that, as long as we run here, our course may be peacefully directed for us by His ordering: that each estate may live according to its proper order; that, while the former preside in humility and the latter humbly submit themselves to those to whom they ought to be subject, His Church may rejoice here in tranquil devotion and, in the life to come, be rewarded by Him who lives and reigns unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXV. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“Now Samuel was dead, and all Israel mourned for him” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 28).

This Sunday, which is fourth in the number of the summer Sundays, has a fitting resemblance to the fourth day of creation, on which almighty God created the sun, moon, and stars, by whose brightness He illumined and adorned the works of the preceding three days. For just as, when the sun is darkened, there is no full and clear daylight, so in the preceding three Sundays there was a certain light of human instruction, yet not a clear one, because it was conveyed in parables. But on this Sunday, as though the sun had been created, a full and, in a manner, clear light shines forth. With the obscurity of parables removed, the eternal wisdom of God teaches us in plain and open speech what evils we ought to avoid and what goods we ought to do. For what could be more open and clear than His words: “Be merciful, even as your heavenly Father is merciful. Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned; forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6:36–38)?

This same fourth Sunday also has a not unsuitable resemblance to the fourth age of the world, in which almighty God began a certain excellence of new dignity which had not existed in the three ages then elapsed: namely, that He first exalted His people, the Israelite nation, with the magnificence of royal honour. The first of the kings whom He set over them was Saul. But because Saul displeased the Lord, Saul’s kingdom having been destroyed, God established David’s kingdom. David truly pleased the Lord, as the Lord Himself testifies when He says: “I have found for myself a man after my own heart.” These events, which occurred in the fourth age of the world, as we have said, are very fittingly read on this fourth Sunday: first, how Saul, good and chosen at the beginning of his reign, afterwards became reprobate and perished at the hands of his enemies; then, how David’s kingdom arose and was strengthened. All these things are set before us and read to us, not that we may know their wars, but that in the hidden mystery of these events we may seek the light of our instruction. For we are, as blessed Peter says, “a royal and priestly race” (1 Peter 2:9), signified by those kings and taught by their peril to watch against our own peril. It seems to me that Saul may be understood as any good Catholic, who profitably governs the kingdom received from God—that is, his body and soul—and who always keeps Christ’s death before his eyes, a death which, as we heard when the reading was read at night, is prefigured at the beginning of the lesson.

[Col. 0450A] “Now Samuel was dead, and all Israel mourned for him.” In Samuel, whose name is interpreted “His name is God,” our Lord Jesus Christ may fittingly be understood. The mourning by which all Israel lamented Samuel’s death prefigured that mourning by which the whole multitude of those believing in God grieved over Christ’s death, as His apostles and those holy women did, of whom it is written: “The women sitting by the tomb lamented, weeping for the Lord” (Luke 23:27), and the rest of the faithful multitude, who were overwhelmed with excessive grief at His Passion and death. As the Evangelist says: “And all the multitude of those who were present together at this sight, and saw the things that were done, returned striking their breasts” (ibid., 48).

[Col. 0450B] “And they buried him in Ramah, his own city.” This is the holy Church, which is truly His city, in which He has been so buried that, through the power of His divinity and the mercy of His unceasing protection, He can never depart from her. Therefore everyone who continually impresses this death of Christ upon his heart and memory can rise to the praiseworthy deed of Saul which follows.

“And Saul removed the magicians and diviners from the land, and put to death those who had python-spirits in their bellies.” Magicians are called, and are, those who deceive people by such frauds: by the tricks of their magic [perhaps *magiarum*, “sorceries”] they present something to human sight which appears plausible and yet is not true. So did those magicians in Egypt who, before Pharaoh, showed their rods as though they were serpents; yet they were not serpents, but actual rods. Diviners, however, were those accustomed to foretell from whatever things what safety would follow for people in doubtful affairs, or what prosperity would come to them. Those were called persons “having pythons in their bellies” who, through an unclean spirit, foresaw and foretold future events.

By the name of magicians, who show themselves to do what they do not do, may be understood, I think, those people who through a kind of hypocrisy show themselves to be what they are not; though wicked and imperfect, they desire to be thought good and perfect by others. Diviners, however, may be called those who indeed do good things, but seek, through those same good acts, to be glorified by people. Those having pythons in their bellies [Col. 0450D] may be called those who are both magicians and diviners, yet amid both vices are puffed up and swollen by the most wicked spirit of pride, which may be understood by the python. For whoever does not pretend to be what he is not, does not place his welfare and prosperity in the mouths of people, does not seek human praise for his deeds, and moreover always preserves humility in all his acts—such a person has, in a sense, removed magicians and diviners from the land, that is, has put to death those who had pythons in their bellies.

Magicians may also be understood as falsehood and diviners as prosperity. Or let us take both together: by magicians and diviners let us understand false prosperity, or false hope. To remove magicians and diviners from the land is for a person not to deceive himself through any hope of false prosperity.

When magicians and diviners have thus been removed from the land, it remains for him also to kill those who had pythons in their bellies. As we said above, persons having pythons in their bellies were those who prophesied in and through an unclean spirit. Just as to prophesy in the Holy Spirit is to announce beforehand, to oneself and to others, how great are the goods of the heavenly kingdom and how great are the evils of hell, so to prophesy in the python—that is, in the evil spirit—is to make little of the immeasurable goods of the future life and to reckon and declare the indescribable evils of hell lighter and more tolerable than they are. Therefore whoever, deceived by no false hope, labours steadfastly for eternal life; whoever, seized by no false fear, hopes courageously in God’s mercy, promising himself the joys of the heavenly kingdom if he acts well and foretelling to himself the punishment of hell if he lives wickedly—such a person praiseworthily kills within himself those who had pythons in their bellies.

Against such a person the ranks of evil spirits array themselves in fierce battle; against him they rage with astonishing fury, as is figuratively expressed in what follows: “And the Philistines assembled; they came and encamped at Shunem.” A camp is the gathering of soldiers; and the multitude of evil spirits is fittingly expressed through the camp of the Philistines. The Philistines assemble when evil spirits arm themselves with the weapons of their malice and wickedness to fight and wage war against the spiritual man. They come and encamp at Shunem, which is interpreted “cattle,” or “teeth,” or “pupil,” when, having covered and clouded the sight of the inner person with the dark mist of their suggestions, they assail him with brutish and carnal temptation, so that in his thoughts, understood by the teeth, he begins to entertain carnal desires and to feed delightfully upon those carnal desires within himself. But what the spiritual person sometimes does against such temptations is clearly indicated by the following sequence of words:

[Col. 0451D] “Then Saul assembled all Israel and came to Gilboa.” He assembles all Israel when, gathering his faculties together, he continues his vigils, fasts, and prayers, if somehow he may be able to resist the evil spirits assembled against him. But because it often happens that a weak person, struck down by the enormity of temptations, recoils from the labour he has undertaken all the more quickly as he sees God more slowly coming to his aid, the text fittingly adds: “And he came to Gilboa.” Gilboa is interpreted “rolling” or “running down.” To come to Gilboa is, in one’s thoughts, to roll oneself now here, now there; to flow away from thought to thought, from weak intention to weak action. Thus there comes about in him an abominable descent, when he runs down from the height of spiritual fervour and constancy to the depths of dullness and negligence. This daily descent becomes for him a cause of greater pain and failure. Hence it follows:

“And Saul saw the Philistines opposite him and was afraid, and his heart was greatly terrified.” Human life is in the heart; therefore the vital faculty of a human being may fittingly be understood by and in the heart. Saul—that is, the spiritual person—sees the Philistines opposite him and is afraid when, unable to endure the strong assault of evil spirits, he yields and succumbs to temptations. His heart is greatly terrified when the firmness of the faith and hope which he ought to have in God begins to weaken in his vital faculty, which is the heart: as though God’s hand were unable to help him, as though the greatness of temptation exceeded the greatness of divine mercy. Therefore a person must take care, when tempted, that his heart is not too greatly terrified, lest his faith and hope fall from their standing. For this is the true faith and hope of a person in God: that, however great the temptations and necessities which he suffers, he never despairs of God’s mercy, but, insofar as he can, confidently seeks and awaits the regard of divine mercy through good works. The man who said, “Though camps should stand against me, my heart shall not fear” (Psalm 26:3), possessed this true faith and hope. But the person whose heart has so feared the camps of enemies standing against him that he wavers in the faith and hope which he ought to have in God amid all his necessities is the one of whom the text next says:

“And he consulted the Lord, but He did not answer him, neither by dreams, nor by priests, nor by prophets, nor by sacrifices.” A person consults the Lord now by reading, now by praying, perhaps in the hope that something may occur to him from reading by which he may be awakened from the sleep of his sloth, or that through prayer, by God’s merciful visitation, he may receive some sweetness by which he may begin to be restored to the constancy of his lost fervour. But the Lord does not answer him, neither by dreams, nor by priests, nor by prophets, nor by sacrifices. By dreams, which come to a person without his knowing how they come, I think a good will, inspired in a person by God through His hidden mercy, may very fittingly be understood; by sacrifices, good and righteous works. Between dreams and sacrifices two things are placed—priests, namely, and prophets—by which we may understand the two movements of the soul: love and fear. These two ought to awaken in a person the two things which we have mentioned, namely good will and good works. Love produces good will; fear arouses a person to the pursuit of good action.

Therefore anyone who, as we have said, has either been deceived by false hope and fallen into negligence and sloth, or has been deceived by false fear and does not trust in God’s mercy amid tribulations and labours—if such a person at any time consults the Lord by reading or praying, the Lord does not answer him either by dreams, priests, prophets, or sacrifices: for He neither stirs him by love toward good will nor raises him by fear toward good and perfect action. But what that wretched person will finally do is shown by the following Scripture, which says:

[Col. 0453A] “And Saul said to his servants: Seek for me a woman having a python-spirit, and I shall go and inquire through her.” His servants are his senses. To tell his servants to seek for him a woman having a python-spirit is, with all his senses, to seek the softness of the flesh, flee his former labours, pursue frivolity, and delight in his own dullness and idleness; to despise the fact that he has been abandoned by God; and not to consider how or in what he has offended God, whether in himself, in his superiors, or in his other neighbours, so that by repentance and satisfaction he may strive to appease God in those same matters in which he had not feared to sin against God. It is as though he said: “I began to live harshly and austerely for God, but since the Lord has abandoned me and disdains to help me in the tribulations and necessities that have come upon me, why do I labour in vain? I shall live as other people do: they do not labour so greatly, yet they hope to be saved.” Thus, to incline from former constancy toward sloth and softness, yet to wish nevertheless to be saved in that same frivolity, is in a sense to say to his servants, his senses: “Seek for me a woman having a python-spirit; I shall go to her and inquire through her.”

“And his servants said: There is a woman having a python-spirit at Endor.”

This woman is the effeminate soul, swollen by the spirit of pride, which may be understood by the python: a soul that lives softly and enervatedly, yet desires to be held by people in the same honour and affection as before, when it lived praiseworthily. The answer of the servants, saying that there is a woman having a python-spirit at Endor, is the answer of good faculties that desire to call the person back from his begun softness and idleness. For Endor is interpreted “fountain of generation.” It is as though they said: “If you do this, if you allow this woman—that is, this softness, dullness, and idleness to which you have given yourself—to rule over you, many evils will come from you. For there is in Endor, in the fountain of generation, that which generates for you every kind of injustice and iniquity. It will surely result in your own destruction and in scandal and ruin for the other people who are with you.” But one who will not be saved scorns and rejects this answer of the servants, this counsel of his inward faculties, and falls into worse things, as the Scripture that follows shows:

[Col. 0453D] “So he changed his appearance, put on other garments, and went—he and two men with him—and they came to the woman by night.” He changes his appearance when he either wholly abandons, as sometimes happens, his purpose of spiritual life, or, though remaining in the community, begins to act and conduct himself very differently from before: he who had previously possessed the greatest constancy becomes utterly slothful and negligent; he who had formerly looked upon everything with a good and simple eye begins to turn all that he sees to an evil meaning with a malicious and perverse heart. He puts on other garments when, laying aside the adornment of virtues and abandoning, that is, works of righteousness, he falls into works of injustice and sin, which are like other garments.

“He went, and two men with him.” Who are these two men? We may say that one man is false hope and the other despair. The man called false hope accompanies him on one side when, through a false hope of heavenly reward, he begins to live shamefully and according to the softness of his flesh, yet thinks that he will be saved in this same softness and sloth. On the other side the man called despair accompanies him when, deceived by false fear, he despairs that he can be delivered from these temptations and passions by the help of God’s grace, or that he can in any way rise again to his former constancy and fervour of mind.

“And they came to the woman by night. And he said to her: Divinate for me by the python, and raise up for me whomever I shall name to you. And the woman said to him: Behold, you know what Saul has done, how he has eradicated magicians and diviners from the land. Why then do you lay snares for my life, that I should be killed?” These words of the woman are the words of the soul desiring to recall the person to his former state. “Behold, you know,” she says, “what Saul has done,” as though she said: “Recognize, wretched man, what you did at the beginning of your conversion, in what constancy of perfection you established your life; how you eradicated magicians and diviners from the land—that is, how, scorning every falsehood and worldly prosperity, you laboured for the reward of eternal life through fear and love of God alone. Why then do you lay snares for my life, that I should be killed? Why, having fallen into this misery, do you not heed your death? Moreover, by your evil actions, laying snares for my life and my salvation, do you hasten to kill me and perish with me?”

“And Saul swore to her by the Lord, saying: ‘As the Lord lives, no evil shall happen to you because of this matter.’” This oath is made between body and soul when a person brings his sloth to a kind of settled habit; when false hope of heavenly reward so weakens the perfect fear of future judgment which he formerly possessed that what he had once reproved and condemned in himself as a great crime he not only no longer fears, but even begins boldly to do with a certain freedom and security. He is therefore said to swear, as though to make something firm by law, because he establishes as lawful that he ought justly to be saved in the idleness of his dullness, since almighty God has withdrawn from him the aid of His mercy, so that he cannot rise again to his former constancy of heart and body.

“And the woman said to him: ‘Whom shall I raise up for you?’” These words are the words of a trembling soul desiring to call the person back from his ruin. It is as though she said: “Almighty God, who formerly lived for you, who was accustomed to give you inward life through the grace of His visitation, is now dead to you; His saints are dead to you. Whom shall I raise up for you? What can I now do for you, when I see you tending toward destruction?”

“He said: ‘Raise Samuel up for me.’” The words of the speaking woman and the answering Saul show us those astonishing struggles which a person endures within himself. At one moment the inner person grieves and groans, as has been said, because through the sloth of his dullness he has made himself unworthy of God’s grace; at another the outer person, as though deceiving himself with false hope, resists and in a sense says, “Raise Samuel up for me.” It is as though he said: “You think that I shall perish because you see that, after moderating my former labours, I live somewhat more laxly. But it shall by no means be so. Raise Samuel up for me—that is, invoke almighty God for me. For I can be saved like other people who live without great struggle of labour and yet are confident of salvation.” After this, the text adds:

[Col. 0455B] “But when the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice and said to Saul.” The woman—that is, the soul—sees Samuel when it is at times touched and pierced by fear or love of God. She cries out, as though with a loud voice, when, considering her frivolity and iniquity, she is so terrified that she is moved and kindled to tears of repentance, and in a sense addresses her body, understood by Saul, in these words: “Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul.” Saul is interpreted “desired” or “abusing.” It is as though she said: “You have brought all these evils upon me because you are Saul: you are one who abuses God’s mercy, who has forgotten the mercies of the Lord, who bore with you for so long, who made the kindness shown you by your Creator an increase of your ruin.”

Against this cry of the soul, Saul—that is, the body—again offers his false hope and false consolation, saying:

“The king said to her: ‘Do not fear. What have you seen?’ And the woman said to Saul: ‘I saw gods ascending from the earth.’” It is as though she said: “The holy inspirations by which I was formerly visited through the grace of heavenly sweetness I now behold, as it were, from afar; I recall the holy thoughts and affections that I once possessed, by which I was raised from earthly things to heavenly ones. Therefore I do not fear without cause, seeing that, after such great benefits from God, I have fallen back into weakness and am perishing with you.”

“And he said to her: ‘What is his appearance like?’” It is as though he said: “If you are afflicted with such great sorrow, why do you not order your life according to the form of your former way of life?”

“She replied: ‘An old man is ascending, and he is clothed in a mantle.’” It is as though she said: “Almighty God, with whom and in whom I flourished as in a kind of youth when I loved Him alone with the ardour of due charity, now ascends like an old man, because through the pride and wickedness of my dullness He has grown old to me: His love has grown cold within me.”

“And he is clothed in a mantle.” He is so covered and hidden from me by the mantle of your flesh and carnal life that no brightness of His accustomed visitation and consolation appears to me, because He sees that the light of His knowledge and love which was once within me is now extinguished. But while a person thus struggles with himself—while at one moment he strives through the heart’s desire to rise to God, and at another is thrust back and cast down through the sloth of the flesh—there sometimes occurs for a time in the person what follows:

[Col. 0456A] “Then Saul understood that it was Samuel; and he bowed with his face to the ground and worshipped.” He returns to his understanding and recognizes that God is within him.
