He bows his body with his face to the ground, humbling himself before God; he worships, invoking with all the prayers he can the mercy of divine compassion.

“But Samuel said to Saul: ‘Why have you disturbed me, that I should be raised up?’” This answer of Samuel is the answer of divine omnipotence, by which God sometimes answers one who thus bows with his face to the ground and worships—yet not with that sweetness of mercy with which He formerly used to answer him, but according to the weakness of faith and hope which He sees has now failed in him. “Why have you disturbed me,” He says, “that I should be raised up?” One is properly said to be raised up if he is sleeping or dead. But almighty God, who neither sleeps nor dies, is said to speak to a person as though raised from sleep or death by the same likeness by which a person, made sluggish by lukewarmness of soul, is said in some manner to sleep and die in an evil sleep. Thus, when He says, “Why have you disturbed me, that I should be raised up?” it is as though He said: “I once rested in you, when through the grace of My mercy I possessed you; but you disturbed Me, because you drove Me away from you. Yet now I speak to you as though dead, because I see that you are dead and find in you no sign of living action.”

“And Saul said: ‘I am greatly distressed, since the Philistines fight against me and God has departed from me; He has not been willing to hear me, neither by the hand of the prophets nor by dreams.’” It is as though he said: “Evil spirits and sins ruling me through the prompting of evil spirits have possessed me and prevailed against me. God has departed from me; He has abandoned me and has not been willing to hear me, neither by the hand of the prophets nor by dreams, because I neither have good will in my heart nor am able to rise bodily to good works.”

“Therefore I have called you, that you may show me what I ought to do.” These words show us the manifold and varied struggles a person undergoes and feels within himself: now utterly despairing, he says, “The Lord has departed from me”; then, in that very despair, he begins again to invoke God. But God indeed hears such an invocation, made without faith and hope, yet does not heed it; rather, He answers as though in these words:

“Why do you ask me, since the Lord has departed from you and passed over to your rival?” It is as though He said: “Why do you invoke me for your salvation when you despair of my mercy?”

We should note who this rival of Saul is, to whom the Lord testifies that He has passed after leaving Saul. Saul’s rival, who fell through pride and despair, was David, who in all his actions, all his thoughts, and all his tribulations and necessities always hoped in the Lord and always trusted in God’s mercy with the highest reverence of humility. He departed from Saul and passed to David, because nothing so offends God as the wickedness of despair, and nothing so pleases God as the integrity and sincerity of faith and hope. This is true and perfect faith and hope: that a person should never fall so far as not to believe that through God’s mercy he can rise again. We therefore have a clear example of this matter in these two kings. Saul sinned, and David also sinned. Saul sinned and perished in his sin because of despair; David sinned and deserved to be saved from his sin because of the faith and hope he had in God. Therefore whoever imitates Saul, so doubting God as to despair that he can or ought to be saved through God’s mercy, will without doubt find fulfilled in himself the following words of Samuel:

[Col. 0457B] “The Lord will do to you as He spoke by my hand; He will tear the kingdom from your hand and give it to your neighbour David, because you did not obey the voice of the Lord and did not execute the commanded wrath of His fury upon Amalek. Therefore the Lord has done to you today what you suffer.” By Amalek, which is interpreted “a licking people,” concerning whom the Lord commanded Saul: “Go and strike Amalek, destroy all that is his, and do not desire anything from his goods” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 15:3), I think we may not unsuitably understand either pride or the ugly and shameful sins and desires of the flesh, which truly provoke the wrath of the Lord’s fury. At the beginning of his kingdom—that is, at the beginning of his conversion—a person ought, at God’s command, so to kill these within himself that he destroys all of Amalek and, after killing the outward work of sin within himself, leaves nothing outwardly for himself to desire or inwardly to delight in.

But he does not execute the commanded wrath of the Lord’s fury upon Amalek who outwardly abandons the carnal works of sin but still inwardly feeds himself delightfully upon carnal desires and thoughts; who does not abandon the signs of pride—that is, who changes his clothing but not his mind, who bears an exalted heart beneath the garment of humility. It is as though God said: “I chose you indeed, that I might be and reign within you; but because you did not execute the commanded wrath of the Lord’s fury upon Amalek, I shall tear the kingdom from your hand, so that henceforth you may not be able to possess the power which you once had over your kingdom—that is, your body and soul—by My gift. Moreover, the Lord will give Israel with you into the hands of the Philistines.” For you will be so blinded by the evil spirits ruling over you that you yourself will even be wholly deprived of the light of My knowledge which still remains in you. Yet this evil would be tolerable if another, graver evil did not follow it after this life.

“For tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me.” Tomorrow, that is, when the time of this present life has passed and the day of My strict future judgment has come, you and your sons—that is, your works—shall be with Me, where you will sit before My dreadful judgment, not to be saved but to be condemned.

“And the Lord will also give the camp of Israel into the hands of the Philistines,” when, judgment having been completed, you will be subjected in body and soul alike to evil spirits, under whom you will lie eternally in the eternal punishment of hell. [Col. 0458A] But when or how does God speak these things to a person? Namely, when He rebukes him through a teacher’s tongue or threatens him through the voice of the Scriptures with eternal punishment unless he repents. But one who will not be saved is neither edified by a teacher’s tongue nor recalled from his iniquity by the denunciation of the Scriptures; instead, from correction he falls into despair, as is shown next when the text immediately adds:

“Immediately Saul fell stretched out upon the ground.” He falls stretched out upon the ground when he does not stretch himself toward God or heavenly things, but, as though wholly cast down to the earth and wholly devoted to earthly and carnal desires, begins daily to heap new sins upon the sin which he could cleanse by weeping and repentance. But why does this happen? Because of what Scripture adds, saying:

“For he had been terrified by Samuel’s words, and there was no strength in him, because he had eaten no bread all that day.” It is indeed good for a person to fear Samuel’s words, the words of almighty God, but in such a way that he does not fall into despair through fear. David sinned and indeed feared the Lord’s words which he heard through Nathan the prophet; but he was not terrified. Rather, by that very fear he escaped the punishment which he deserved, because he had the strength of faith: he hoped in the Lord and was saved. Saul heard Samuel’s words and not only feared but was terrified, because he did not have the strength of faith. For he despaired, and he was abandoned to despair. But let us return to ourselves and see what gives rise in the spiritual person to this fear that leads to despair.

[Col. 0458C] “And there was no strength in him,” Scripture says, “because he had eaten no bread all that day.” This bread is, I think, the teaching of sacred Scripture. That whole day in which Saul is shown not to have eaten this bread may not unsuitably signify the tranquillity of an enlightened mind which he once possessed with God at the beginning of his conversion. A person suffers all the things we have heard, by God’s permission, because while he still had day—while he was still with God in the prosperity of an enlightened mind—he made light of this bread of sacred Scripture, from which the strength of faith and long-suffering patience are acquired; nor did he strive, after the manner of one eating, continually to transfer it by the teeth of memory into food for his soul. The text continues:

[Col. 0458D] “Then that woman entered to Saul—for he was greatly troubled—and said to him: ‘I shall set before you a morsel of bread; eat, and regain strength, so that you may be able to make the journey.’” This woman is still, as we said above, the weak soul, which strives to set before Saul, that is, before its outer person, a morsel of bread by exhorting him to repentance and confession, fittingly signified by the morsel of bread, so that by eating he may gain strength to make the journey. That is, breaking and crushing his sins, as it were, with certain teeth of repentance, he may consider how deeply he lies cast down in wicked actions, in the hope that, having recovered hope, he may be able through repentance for his negligences and confession to rise again to complete the journey of spiritual life which he had abandoned by living wickedly and negligently.

“But he refused and said: ‘I will not eat.’” To say, “I will not eat,” is to refuse to return to pardon through repentance and confession.

“But his servants and the woman compelled him; and at last, having heard their voice, he rose from the ground and sat upon the bed.” This rising is not a good rising but an evil one. He rises from the ground when he falls so far that he even begins to take pride in his earthly and carnal life, and presumptuously dares to do irreverently and without fear those things for which he ought to humble himself and be afraid. He sits upon the bed when, with vices assailing him, he in no way resists but begins to make for himself a kind of rest in the delight of his flesh. For the flesh itself may fittingly be understood by the bed in which the flesh rests. The Scripture then fittingly adds:

But that woman had a stall-fed calf in her house; and she hurried and killed it; then, taking flour, she kneaded it and baked unleavened bread. And she set it before Saul and before his servants. By the stall-fed calf the wantonness of the flesh may very suitably be signified. Saul in some manner eats the calf set before him with his servants when a man in despair inclines, with all his senses, toward evil, and begins to serve his wanton pleasures and to feed himself delightfully upon them. By the flour, moreover, I think the subtlety of Holy Scripture is to be understood. To take the flour and knead it is to mingle a perverse [Col. 0459C] and unrighteous interpretation with the purity of Holy Scripture. When the flour has thus been kneaded—when, I say, Holy Scripture has been mingled with a perverse interpretation—it is rightly added: “and she baked unleavened bread,” that is, bread without leaven; for the bread, that is, the doctrine which proceeds from it, does not raise the human heart to God but casts it down, and seems rather to blind a person than to enlighten him. Hence it is fittingly added at once:

When they had eaten, they rose and went throughout all that night. To rise and to walk throughout the whole night is for a person, blinded in his pride and malice, to proceed so far that, by the just judgment of God, he is delivered body and soul into the hands of the Philistines—that is, into the hands of evil spirits—with whom, having lost the hope of eternal life, [Col. 0459D] he will be tormented without end. Behold Saul’s kingdom, the kingdom, indeed, of injustice and perdition. God willed it to be set before us and read, so that the more frequently we hear and read it, the more steadfastly we may keep watch against it; that, should it perhaps begin to rise against us, it may be repressed with the utmost effort, lest it grow and prevail, so that we may be found worthy to rise up to David’s kingdom, which is the kingdom of righteousness. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

655  
## HOMILY LXVI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“When the crowds pressed upon Jesus to hear the word of God, and he stood by the lake of Gennesaret” (Luke 5).

[Col. 0460A] The four preceding Sundays having passed, the fifth now follows in order; and it may not unjustly be fitted to that fifth day of the creation of the world. For whatever work the Lord is recorded to have done there agrees wholly, as it seems to me, with the Gospel reading and the prayer.

To speak first according to the letter, this present Gospel commends a great and evident work of divine mercy: after the disciples had laboured all night, he deigned to provide them with such abundant sustenance. For if, while they laboured during one night only, he graciously came to them by providing food, with what greatness of compassion, we may suppose, will he be present here and in the world to come to those who strive to watch and labour in his praises, not for one night but through unbroken days and nights? [Col. 0460B] Therefore the fifth beatitude, which the merciful Lord promises to the merciful, saying, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7), is not without reason assigned to this fifth Sunday. Hence Peter, in today’s reading, commends the same thing as the Gospel when he says: “Be all of one mind in prayer, lovers of the brotherhood, compassionate, merciful” (1 Pet. 3:8). Now let us speak of the fifth day, as we began.

On the fifth day God said: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of living soul, and birds above the earth under the firmament of heaven.” And God created great sea-creatures, and every living and moving creature which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good, and blessed them, saying: [Col. 0460C] “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth.” And evening and morning were the fifth day (Gen. 1:20–23).

656 In these waters which bring forth the creeping thing of living soul, the grace of compunction may be signified. For when a man first begins, through God’s mercy, to acknowledge his sins, and to acknowledge them, I say, in such a way that he can also weep and mourn for them before the Lord, this is in some sense for the waters to bring forth the creeping thing of living soul. This is what today’s Gospel calls the crowds’ pressing upon Jesus. And these waters rightly bring forth the creeping thing of living soul. For a dying soul is a person when he delights in sins and lives among sins. But when, aided by God, he turns away from sins, he truly becomes a living soul, so that it may fittingly be said of him what is read elsewhere: “And man became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7).

Having become a living soul, he now sees and carefully considers in what sins and vices he formerly crawled; and through this he becomes a bird above the earth under the firmament of heaven. By the creeping thing we may understand sins; by the bird, good works. A person who was formerly a creeping thing becomes a bird when he flies from repentance to the work of satisfaction, from the spirit of fear to the spirit of love. And through this he flies above the earth, when he begins so to overcome and tame his earth—that is, his flesh—by such mastery that he always keeps it pressed beneath himself, lest it seduce him, lest it at any time deceive the spirit. And he ought to perform good works beneath the firmament of heaven—that is, [Col. 0461A] beneath a mind made firm and thus established—so that he does not permit them to pass over his heart; that is, so that he does not seek human praise. For if he does not seek the glory of passing praise, his works will undoubtedly not pass over the heart, but will be preserved for God alone under the guard of a mind made firm.

And God created great sea-creatures and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth into 657 their kinds, and every bird according to its kind. It seems to me that by these three three orders may be denoted, which almighty God has ordered and established in the Church: by the great sea-creatures, the carnal; by the living and moving soul, the spiritual; by every bird, prelates. Since sea-creatures abound in flesh, the carnal and secular may fittingly be understood by the great sea-creatures; and the spiritual by the living and moving soul. That it says not *mobilis* (“moving”) but *motabilis* (“capable of being moved”) signifies for us a certain good motion which takes place in a person; for the word *mobilis* may be used in both a bad and a good sense, whereas *motabilis* is rarely found except here and may be understood in a good sense. Therefore God created the great sea-creatures because he wills secular and carnal people to be, and to be well, in the order in which they are. For not all can be spiritual. He wills spiritual persons to be begotten from carnal ones. He also created every living and moving soul—that is, the spiritual, whose soul is not “noble” but “capable of being moved”; for that soul is rightly called *motabilis* which God has moved wholly, so to speak, which he has mercifully advanced from sins to good and holy works, from the spirit of fear to the spirit of love. Of it it is rightly said, [Col. 0461C] “which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds,” because through the waters and streams of tears it is brought forth—or rather brought back—to its former kind, that is, to innocence and the soul’s earlier beauty, which it lost by sinning, so that through these it may again deserve to be refashioned after the image and likeness of God.

But because the guidance of prelates and teachers must not be lacking for the advancement of converts or secular persons, it is rightly added: “and every bird according to its kind.” In saying “according to its kind,” it shows that one sort of leadership ought to be over those who are spiritual, and another over those who are carnal. And this is to be a bird according to its kind. For one doctrine must be imparted to spiritual people, another to carnal people; nor should what is said to spiritual people be expounded to carnal people. Rather, every teacher ought in its proper time to teach and set forth what is suitable for each. A person himself too becomes, as it were, every bird when he is wholly lifted up to God, insofar as is possible here, through the sweet affections of the heart, and when he is granted by the Lord to fly over all the vanities of the present life with the wing of contemplation. It follows:

And God saw that it was good, and blessed them, saying: “Increase and 658 multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth.” God is said to see what he is proved to love. For he loves the advancement of his own people and gives them his blessing, saying, “Increase and multiply.” This is his blessing, by which he blesses the spiritual and the carnal: to the carnal, so to speak, he says simply, “Increase by being born and by begetting,” because it is not his will that all should be spiritual. For he wills spiritual persons to be begotten by carnal persons. Spiritual persons, however, are blessed by this blessing so that they may multiply; that is, so that they may make progress in good actions, ever advancing and excelling in the abundance of virtues. After this abundance of virtues, they are fittingly commanded to fill the waters of the sea. What are the waters of the sea but the profound knowledge of Holy Scripture? A person then fills—or rather fulfils—these waters of the sea when he does not fail diligently to carry out, according to his measure, in deeds the things he has learned or heard from Holy Scripture. Then also birds multiply upon the earth, because by the order of his merciful dispensation [Col. 0462B] the Lord commonly appoints and provides such teachers and doctors for such people as know how profitably to preside over them and benefit them. Or birds multiply in this way: when good works and good desires are added to the blessed person himself and increase in him daily. We read that all these things were made on the fifth day. These things, as I see it, may not unjustly be applied to the Gospel reading. For the Evangelist says:

“When the crowds pressed upon Jesus to hear the word of God, and he stood beside the lake of Gennesaret.” These crowds which press upon Jesus fittingly represent the senses of a person disturbed in repentance. For as long as a person loves sins and rejoices with sins, he has no senses disturbed unto repentance. But when, through the grace of heavenly mercy visiting him, he brings his past sins before the eyes of his mind and begins, through the spirit of fear, to be troubled and afflicted on account of those unlawful acts which he has committed, this is in some sense for crowds to press upon Jesus. Then also, as we said before, the waters bring forth the creeping thing of living soul. For to bring forth the creeping thing by the waters is to have crowds press upon Jesus. Why do they press upon Jesus? To hear the word of God; that is, to be taught by the word and commandments of God how they may attain him who is the Word of God the Father.

659 And it should be observed that they pressed upon him, because this intimates that, just as we were once inclined and swift toward sins, so now we ought to be equally eager and energetic hearers of God’s word. [Col. 0462D] But because a person has nothing of himself, nor can accomplish anything by himself, it is rightly added: “And he stood”—that is, the Lord began to stand—beside the lake of Gennesaret. A lake is called, as it were, “standing water.” Standing water comes to be in a person, as it seems to me, when the desire of carnal life, from the dissipation in which it flowed, begins through God’s mercy to stand—that is, to rest. For the Lord comes to the hearts of many people (“for there is none who hides himself from his heat”), but he does not establish his standing there where a person does not persevere both in good work and in perfect repentance. But beside all those who press upon him in such a way that they are steadfast both in good deeds and in repentance, he will stand, because he makes his dwelling in them. The Lord stands beside the lake of Gennesaret, which is interpreted [Col. 0463A] “generating for itself a breeze,” when, through this standing water of compunction, with the Lord himself assisting, a person generates for himself a breeze—that is, the hope of eternal salvation—because through this water of steadfast repentance he is given the hope of perpetual tranquillity and peace.

“And he saw two boats standing beside the lake of Gennesaret.” In these two boats our inward and outward person may be understood. These two boats stand beside the lake when a person establishes a certain steadiness for himself by knowing himself and persevering in repentance; for even if some acknowledge their sins, yet do not persevere in repentance, they in no way stand beside the lake. But those stand beside the lake who, as if in a lake or most clear water, look clearly upon themselves, recognize what sin they have contracted in body and in soul, [Col. 0463B] and resolve to make satisfaction by steadfast repentance for whatever it is that they have sinned. God is said to see this because God loves it; this is pleasing in his eyes. Standing thus beside the lake—that is, enduring in true repentance—they become those true and good fishers of whom it is added:

But the fishers had gone down and were washing their nets. These fishers are ourselves, who ought to labour in these two boats so that we may do and work something pleasing and acceptable to our Lord God, 660 and healthful and profitable to ourselves. Yet we can accomplish this fishing only by going down—that is, by humbling ourselves. For all our good works must be brought to completion in the depth of the heart’s humility. [Col. 0463C] After this, the nets must be washed; these are, as I see it, our senses. To wash the nets is to cleanse senses defiled by sins with tears. And when the nets have been washed—that is, when our senses have been cleansed from sins—the following is appropriately added as a figure of the things which the Lord does within us:

And, entering one boat, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. By the one boat which belonged to Simon, whose name means “obedient,” the soul of a person may be understood: a soul that has devoted itself to God and purposes to obey his commandments. It might seem to me that the Lord should rather have been said to descend than to ascend into this one boat. For all his grace descends to us from above; but by his descent to us he makes us ascend to him. For he does not ascend in his own person through himself, but he ascends in us when he makes us ascend. Therefore whatever he works in a person is wholly ascribed to him. “Entering one boat, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land.” A person puts out a little from the land—that is, from his earthly life—when, by God’s gift, he first begins to abandon sinful works. But this is little and slight if he still does not know how to despise the wills and desires of sinning. Thus it is little to abandon sins. But that little becomes in some way great when he begins also to abandon the wills and desires of sinning.

Nor should it be passed over that it says, “he asked.” The Lord asks some, as being pious and gentle; he compels others to come to himself strictly. He asks, as it were, those whom he brings to himself converted from the world by his visitation alone and loving sweetness, without any confusion of this world. But he compels, so to speak, those who resist for a long time and whom, through illness or some other adversity arising, he finally makes despisers of the world and lovers of himself. [Col. 0464A]

When this had been done, sitting down, he began to teach the crowds from the boat. This sitting signifies the rest of God which we make for him by resting from sins and humbling ourselves for sins. In this sitting or rest he teaches the crowds from the boat—that is, he teaches from the humbled soul the troubled senses of a person how they ought to know and bewail themselves, and make satisfaction to God. [Col. 0464B] All these things which we have just spoken of take place through the spirit of fear. But when the spirit of fear ceases, what follows is exaltedly brought about in a person:

But when he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: “Put out into the deep.” The Lord ceases speaking to the crowds when a person who has long been troubled for sins, and has also been cleansed by repentance, begins already to cease somewhat within himself from fear of eternal damnation. Thus, advanced to the hope of pardon, he is led from the degree of fear into the deep—that is, into that height which is truly high: namely, the spirit of love. Of this height the prophet David says: “Man shall draw near to a lofty heart” (Ps. 63:8 [Vulgate]). Behold: one who, by God’s bounty, thus leads his purified and enlightened soul into the deep becomes, as we said before, a bird above the earth under the firmament of heaven; because he truly flies upward from the spirit of fear—that is, to the spirit of love.

Or he puts out into the deep when he turns his whole understanding to the deep sense of Holy Scripture, so that he may see and understand what he ought to follow. But because God alone works through his mercy in a person both that crowds may press upon Jesus through the spirit of fear and that he may be able to lead his boat into the deep through the spirit of love, it is rightly in today’s Prayer—in which, as it seems to me, the sense of the Gospel is comprehended—that we pray and say: “O God, who hast prepared invisible good things for those who love thee, pour into our hearts the affection of thy love.” For all these things of which we have spoken at the beginning of the Gospel [Col. 0464D] are invisible good things, through which he prepares for his love the person whom he foreknew would become his lover; and thus, prepared through invisible good things, he leads him into the deep when he pours in the affection of his love. But once the boat has been led into the deep, the nets are fittingly commanded to be cast out for a catch.

“And cast out the nets for a catch.” We have said that the nets may signify a person’s senses. These nets were, as it were, bound as long as the person was under fear. For fear binds; love loosens. When fear has been softened, the nets—that is, the human senses—are freely and readily cast out through love for a catch: for a catch, I say, of good and righteous wills, or of holy desires, 662 and of an ample supply of useful perceptions. And because the spirit of love teaches a person more concerning the knowledge of sins [Col. 0465A] than the spirit of fear, Simon’s answer is rightly a salutary instruction for us.

“Master,” he says, “labouring throughout the whole night, we caught nothing; but at thy word I will cast out the net.” These words are the words of one who truthfully considers himself, deeply repents of the evils he has considered, and says: “O Lord, I acknowledge thee to be my master, for thou hast given me thy commandments. But I recall and see that I am a transgressor of all thy commandments. For I laboured throughout the whole night; that is, all that I have lived was in night, that is, in ignorance. And because both I and my senses were in night, we caught nothing: that is, we caught that which is nothing, namely sin and evil, which is nothing except the privation of good. This, I say, and nothing else have we attained. But at thy word—that is, strengthened more and more by thy promises, by which thou hast promised hope and pardon to sinners—I will cast out the net, because, turning to thee with all my senses, I flee for refuge to the infinite bosom of thy mercy.”

And when they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. It is rightly and fittingly said, “and when they had done this,” because whoever shall have fulfilled the things set forth before will, through God’s mercy, enclose and gather within themselves an abundant multitude of fish—that is, living perceptions. But because, as long as we are in this life, we cannot remain in these nets—that is, in these senses by which we ought to savour God—for “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15), the breaking of the boats [read: nets] which follows often occurs:

But their net was breaking. The net breaks when good thoughts and holy affections fall away from the heart and what is useless and harmful enters the heart.

But when the nets are broken we ought to signal to the partners who are in the other boat, so that they may come and help us. These partners in the other boat are, as we said before, the members of our body. We ought to signal to these partners that they may come and help us, because through the outward labours of the body we must return to that inward grace of the heart.

[Col. 0465D] 663 And they came and filled both little boats, so that they were sinking. When the labours of the body come upon us outwardly, both little boats are filled: the body with good actions and the soul with good perceptions. Observe that it does not say, “so that they sank,” but “so that they were sinking.” For the more the elect advance in God, the more deeply they immerse themselves before the Lord in the humility of the heart. And because one who has advanced in this order in the holy Church will be able to benefit not only himself but others also by word and example, it is sometimes brought about by divine prompting that he is taken up into prelacy even against his will. And this is what is added in the Gospel narrative.

When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.” By Jesus’ knees preachers and prelates are rightly understood. For as a person is raised and lowered by means of the knees, so prelates must admonish their subjects how greatly they ought to lower—that is, think humbly and meanly of—themselves, and must raise them from earthly love to heavenly love. Hence David, understanding by Jesus’ knees the first preachers of the holy Church, namely the apostles, says of them in the person of the Lord: “My knees are weakened through fasting” (Ps. 108:24 [Vulgate]). For they were fasting from the fear and love of God when, at the approach of the Passion, they all abandoned him and fled. Simon Peter therefore fell at Jesus’ knees when the one who was formerly Simon—that is, “obedient”—and Peter—that is, “acknowledging,” obedient to God and acknowledging himself—is taken up into [Col. 0466B] prelacy. He is rightly said to have fallen, because although outwardly he seems to have risen through the honour of prelacy, inwardly he suffers a grave dejection of mind when he is withdrawn from his accustomed rest and deprived of sweetness dear to him.

But when he sees and considers that he cannot oppose the ordinance of almighty God, he turns to him from whom every good gift, and all salvation and grace, are to be hoped for, praying that such activity, such a life, and such strength in preaching may be granted him, by which God’s name may be praised without end. “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.” As though he said: “Depart from me in preaching; depart from me in action. That is, depart from me in preaching so that thou teachest me what I should say; and thus depart from me in action so that I may be able [Col. 0466C] to do what is acceptable before thee at all times. For I am a sinful man; for if that which I am goes out from me, it is nothing but sin.”

For amazement had encompassed him and all who were with him at the catch of fish which they had taken. Amazement of mind is an estrangement by which a person is estranged from himself when he is turned into amazement. This amazement, namely the mind’s estrangement, encompasses him when he is distracted by outward cares and is made in some manner a stranger to the sweetness of accustomed contemplation. In this estrangement of mind, arising from the occupations of external affairs, he admits all who were with him—all, that is, the senses and motions which were with him at the catch of fish, namely those which he then possessed when, like a fisher, he used to draw subtle and noble perceptions and understandings from Holy Scripture—and he will no longer be able, as he once was, to rejoice in a catch of noble fish, namely noble perceptions.

Likewise James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon’s partners. By James, whose name is interpreted “supplanter,” good action is understood; by John, sweet prayer. These two are sons of Zebedee, which is interpreted “this one flowing”: that is, sons of the person who, by God’s grace, was once accustomed to flow abundantly in tears, and who abounded in the begetting of good sons—namely, advancement in worthy action and constancy in sweet prayer. These sons are rightly called Simon’s partners, because the excellence of good work and the constancy of inward sweetness have great partnership, so to speak, [Col. 0467A] with Simon, that is, with the person devoutly obedient to God.

And Jesus said to Simon: “Do not fear; from this time forth you shall catch people.” As though the Lord consoles the prelate excessively concerned for himself and says: “You fear, indeed, because you must preside over others and benefit yourself less. If you see a lesser fruit in yourself and a greater fruit in your subjects, do not fear; for from this time forth you shall catch people—that is, you shall lead many souls to the way of eternal life.”

Now follows, it seems to me, the reward both of subjects and of prelates: of those who strive piously to be subject, and, if it happens that they preside, to preside in humility.

665 And when the boats had been drawn up onto land, leaving all things, [Col. 0467B] they followed him. The boats are drawn up onto land when we arrive, body and soul, at the land of the living, where we shall truly be able, leaving all things, to follow the Lord perfectly. Today’s Prayer again leads and teaches us to obtain and seek these things, in which we pray that he who has prepared invisible good things for those who love him may pour into our hearts the affection of his love, so that, loving him in all things and above all things—that is, whether we are among all and with all in subjection, or above all in prelacy—we may attain his promises, which surpass every desire, when our boats have been drawn up onto land. May he himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

666  
## HOMILY LXVII. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0467C]

“And it came to pass, when the king sat in his house, and the Lord had given him rest on every side from all his enemies,” etc. (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 7).

Just as we said that this fourth Sunday has a certain fitting resemblance to the fourth age of the world, in which the Lord established kings over the Israelite people—of whom Saul was the first, and concerning whom it was then recounted how he displeased the Lord and, after his kingdom had been destroyed, he himself, rejected by God, perished at the hands of enemies—so on this fifth Sunday it is read, in a fitting and very beautiful order, how the kingdom of David, who truly pleased the Lord, arose and was strengthened in the Lord’s hand. [Col. 0467D] Saul’s kingdom signifies the kingdom of injustice and sin; unless it is utterly destroyed and perishes in a person, David’s kingdom, which is the kingdom of righteousness and godliness, cannot arise.

And because this fifth Sunday wholly concerns purity of thoughts and the guarding of the heart, all that is read concerning David’s kingdom seems to tend wholly toward that kingdom which we must establish for God within ourselves. For whoever, as we said before, has become a bird above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven; whoever’s soul the waters have brought forth according to its kind; and in whom the Lord Jesus has begun, as crowds press upon him, to stand beside the lake of Gennesaret: David’s kingdom has truly arisen in him. [Col. 0468A] It will one day be brought to completion in him, when, with the boats drawn up onto land and all things left behind, they follow the Lord. The second book of Kings relates of this kingdom of David:

“And it came to pass, when the king sat in his house, and the Lord had given him rest on every side from all his enemies, he said to Nathan the prophet: ‘Do you see that I dwell in a house of cedar, while the ark of God is set in the midst of skins?’” In King David you may understand any faithful person who is perfect in God, and who, by God’s mercy, having removed and cast away from himself the kingdom of injustice, has passed over and attained the kingdom of righteousness: that kingdom whose throne, as he says in what follows, shall be established for ever. When the kingdom of injustice has been destroyed in a person and the kingdom of righteousness established, then truly, as the text of the letter begins and sets forth, “it came to pass, when the king sat.” It is a great and memorable act of almighty God, a work of his infinite goodness, if ever the kingdom of iniquity falls in anyone and the praiseworthy kingdom of justice arises.

Nor should it be passed over that David himself is interpreted “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance.” For the faithful person, whom we said David may signify, if he wishes to possess a well-ordered kingdom of his heart, ought to be both strong of hand and desirable in appearance. He is strong of hand when he strives to be perfect in the active life; he is desirable in appearance when, in the contemplative life, he begins in some measure to see and desire those desirable joys of eternal life. He sits in his house when, in his body, which is a kind of house of the soul, he can, by God’s gift, possess a certain rest from carnal desires and vices. The Lord gives him rest on every side from all his enemies when, after outwardly quieting perverse motions and vices, he also removes inwardly [Col. 0468C] every will to sin.

When this great thing, as you have heard, has happened—that the king has sat in his house and that the Lord has given him rest on every side from all his enemies—he says to Nathan the prophet: “Do you see that I dwell in a house of cedar?” Nathan means “gift of God.” A person speaks to Nathan when he is visited by the gift of divine inspiration, and from this loving and sweet visitation rejoices and is made glad concerning the gifts bestowed on him by God; but he is sad, groans, and complains concerning impending evils and successively recurring temptations, saying: “Do you see that I dwell in a house of cedar, while the ark of God is set in the midst of skins?” Cedar possesses strength and fragrance. A person ought to possess these two things: strength, that he may resist sins bravely; fragrance, that he may emit to others from himself the perfume of a good reputation. “Do you see,” he says, “that I dwell in a house of cedar?” As though the blessed soul said: “It is from the gift of God and my Lord that my house is of cedar; that is, that I possess this strength by which I am able with a strong spirit to resist sins in the body of sin. But fragrance too is not lacking with strength; for even if I did not cease from sinning for the sweetness of thy love alone, at least, lest the odour of an evil reputation go forth from me and furnish others with an occasion for sinning, I would shrink from sins.” Behold the person who has become a bird above the earth, who has flown from the spirit of fear into the height of love, who has cast out his nets—that is, his senses—for a catch of good virtues, good affections, and holy desires: behold how he has built himself a house of cedar. [Col. 0469A]

But although his house is of cedar, so that he has both strength and fragrance, something remains on account of which he should always mourn and grieve in the present life. What is this? “And the ark of God,” he says, “is set in the midst of skins.” By the ark of God the human soul may be understood; it is then truly called and is the ark of God when it contains in itself the Son of God, when it bears and preserves in itself the manna of the sweetness of God’s word. This ark remains placed beneath skins as long as “the corruptible body weighs down the soul,” as long as we bear the skins of our mortality, by means of which skins we are assailed and attacked in the mind by sins. [Col. 0469B] Hence, as far as I can see, this meaning agrees with the Gospel’s meaning, and David’s words are Peter’s words, and Peter’s words are David’s words: the words of any person who now gives thanks for his advancement, now groans over his deficiency. The one says: “Do you see that I dwell in a house of cedar, while the ark of God is set in the midst of skins?” The other—one and the same person—says: “Master, labouring throughout the whole night, we caught nothing; but at thy word I will cast out the net”; and when they had done this, “they enclosed a great multitude of fish” (Luke 5:5–6). For however much our house may be of cedar, nevertheless, as long as the ark of God is placed beneath skins, we catch sin—that which is nothing—as though labouring throughout the whole night. But amid words of this kind Nathan answers the king, because that gift of God—that inward sweetness which refreshes the heart—strengthens and lifts a person upward to his Creator, lest he despair amid these alternations of temptations, saying:

And Nathan said to the king: “All that is in thy heart, go and do, because the Lord is with thee.” This, I think, means nothing else than that the Lord invisibly says, as it were, to the person’s good and holy desires: [Col. 0469D] “You have considered all things well in your mind; your will is good and perfect before me. Therefore go from good things to better, from virtue to virtue, because the Lord is with thee.” It follows:

And it came to pass in that night, and behold, the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: “Go and speak to my servant David: Thus says the Lord: Shall you build me a house for me to dwell in?” What is signified by the night but the ignorance of the present life, in which a person will always remain because he never attains in the present life to the full knowledge of God, however much he may be enlightened and visited by God? Hence today’s Gospel also says, “their net was breaking” (Luke 5:6); for the ignorance of the present life is a kind of rupture of the nets, so that we are in no way able, as we would wish, [Col. 0470A] to savour and retain God in our hearts. Yet in this night God works his work: he speaks to Nathan, 669 because, lest we be wholly enveloped in the darkness of ignorance, he enlightens and penetrates the hearts of his own by the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit, and grants them to know and understand the word of God. And what does God’s word say to us?

“Shall you build me a house for me to dwell in?” Your soul, he says, bears with difficulty the alternations of temptations and the troubles of rising vices. It would be your will that the ark of God should not be set in the midst of skins, that you should not dwell in the night of the present life, because you would wish to be where you might rejoice in the full day of my knowledge. But shall you build me a house for me to dwell in? That is: can you, in the body of death, [Col. 0470B] build for me a house in which I may dwell in you perpetually? This will not be, nor ought it to be, until after these things.

But the Lord speaks these words also to every good preacher and prelate whom He has raised to authority for the edification of others: “Will you, He says, build Me a house to dwell in?” You, whoever you are, whom I have taken up into a position of authority: if, distracted by external concerns, you cannot build Me a stable dwelling-place in yourself, do not be afraid, for that progress and edification of your neighbours will one day be for you a great fruit of rewards.

“For I have not dwelt in a house from the day when I brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt until this day.”

[Col. 0470C] By the children of Israel we may understand our first parents, Adam and Eve; by the land of Egypt, Paradise. “I,” says Almighty God, “created human nature in the beginning in such a way that My being would be in it, if it had not sinned. But because it was unwilling to obey and touched the forbidden fruit, and because of this I led them out from the land of Egypt and placed them before Paradise, from that day until this day I have not dwelt in a house. For every human being who ought to be My house, however perfect he may be, has experienced something of sins in himself; hence the house of My dwelling cannot be stable in him. Therefore, because what you seek will be not in this life but in the life to come, let it suffice you that I was with you in all things wherever you walked, and I slew your enemies and made for you a great name [Col. 0470D] like the name of the great ones who are on earth.” I certainly gave you a great name when I made you, from a carnal and worldly person, a spiritual person. And I bestowed this name upon you 670 alongside the name of the great—that is, of the perfect—who are on earth, so that you might belong not to the number of My imperfect ones, but to My perfect and great ones. These gifts, according to My magnificence and your benefit, I have granted you for the present; something great yet remains, something infinite, which I have prepared for you in the future and intend to bestow as a gift. It follows:

“And when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up the seed which shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom.” When you have completed the days and [Col. 0471A] years of your life, and have passed through this time full of miseries, tribulations, temptations, and labours, I will raise up your seed—I mean, your spirit—which has brought forth much fruit as good seed. When it goes forth from your womb, that is, when it has been released from the bonds of the body, and you sleep in the Lord with your fathers, I will raise it to eternal life and establish its kingdom.

“He shall build a house for My name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to Me a son.” That very spirit of a human being which I shall thus raise up shall build a house for My name; it shall itself be My house. It shall possess Me and be possessed by Me, and in My kingdom its kingdom shall be established for ever. There I shall show to My Son what belongs to the [Col. 0471B] Father, because I grant that he become a sharer and co-heir of My kingdom.

“If he commits any iniquity, I will rebuke him with the rod of men and with the stripes of the sons of men.”

“But I will not take My mercy away from him, as I took it away from Saul, whom I removed from before My face.” Since that heavenly court admits no stain, but all who arrive there are saints and perfect, we must consider what that “something” may be in which any of the elect can act wickedly there. It is indeed—so far as I can conjecture—nothing other than this: those holy spirits of souls, assumed into the eternal glory of brightness, still think of their body which lies in the dust of the earth, desiring that their fellow-combatant [Col. 0471C] may share in their crown and glory—the one who was once their companion and participant in labour and 671 hardship. Although such acting wickedly is slight and venial, it nevertheless turns aside, for a while and until they receive their body, the attention of holy souls—which ought to be wholly fixed upon God—from God. As far as I can understand it, the Lord confirms this interpretation by adding: “I will rebuke him with the rod of men,” as though He had said: If this “something” of acting wickedly is unavoidable for each of My elect, let him neither marvel nor be troubled. For I shall rebuke him with the rod of men; that is, let him truly know that this is a rod not of women but of men—of all My perfect and strong ones, I mean. For no one of such perfection and holiness has existed from the beginning, or will exist until the [Col. 0471D] end, who will not endure after death this rod of Mine, this sad sentence: that he lacks his body for so long, until in the general resurrection he receives the double robe of body and soul.

“But I will rebuke him with the stripes of the sons of men,” because he himself will endure those stripes which the iniquity of the sons of men deserved—namely, these stripes: that, just as every person, good or evil, returns at the appointed time to ashes and the dust of the earth, and ashes receive ashes, earth earth, so he too shall return to ashes and earth.

“But I will not take My mercy away from him, as I took it away from Saul, whom I removed from before My face.” What can we understand by Saul but that first cast-out one, namely the devil, [Col. 0472A] whom our Lord so removed from before His face that he can neither be able nor willing ever to rise again to the same glory which he lost? Therefore Almighty God, who is faithful and true in His promises, does not take His mercy away from the one whom He rebukes with the rod of men and with the stripes of the sons of men, as He took it away from that first cast-out one whom He removed from before His face.

“But your house and your kingdom,” He says, “shall be faithful for ever before My face.” Nathan spoke all these words to David. Then King David entered and sat before the Lord and said: “Who am I, 672 O Lord my God, and what is my house, that You have brought me thus far?” What is meant by the promise that Nathan spoke all these words [Col. 0472B] to David, followed immediately by, “Then the king entered and sat before the Lord,” except that each elect person, when Nathan speaks—that is, when the gift of God visits him and proclaims the hope of resurrection and the glory of immortality which he shall receive in soul and body—immediately enters into his heart and sits before the Lord? For to enter into one’s heart and sit before the Lord is to judge and acknowledge oneself in every way unworthy of such great goods and such great condescensions of Almighty God. In this blessed entrance and happy sitting a person uses these words, saying to the Lord: “Who am I, O Lord my God, and what is my house, that You have brought me thus far?” “This blessedness,” he says, “this grace surpasses all my merits; and they would be nothing if the gift [Col. 0472C] of Your mercy had not helped me.”

“And this also seemed too little in Your sight, O Lord my God, unless You also spoke concerning the house of Your servant for the distant future.” You spoke for the distant future because You made known what will one day happen to my soul and to my body. I do not ask that You take away from me the rod of men and the stripes of the sons of men.

“For this is the law of Adam, O Lord God.” Our first parent Adam earned this rod, to whom it was said: “When you work the ground, it shall not yield its fruits, but it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III, 18). He was the first to endure this stripe, in that he underwent the sentence of death, when it was said to him: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.” And therefore, because this is [Col. 0472D] the law of Adam and has thus been ordained before You, I ask only that You do not take Your mercy away from me; but, as You have spoken, when my days are fulfilled, raise up my seed—that is, my spirit—to life. Grant that it may contemplate Your glory for ever; and my body also, though it now decays, raise up and restore in incorruption and immortality on the day of judgment. Amen.

673 HOMILY LXVIII. FOR THE FIRST SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

“Amen I say to you: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

This present Sunday, which is sixth in the sequence of the Sundays [Col. 0473A] we have celebrated from the beginning, corresponds to the sixth day, on which God the Father, after creating heaven and earth and all things in them, created on the sixth day the noble creature—namely, man—in His own image and likeness. Of this sixth day Genesis writes as follows: “And God said: Let the earth bring forth the living creature according to its kind, cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds. And it was so,” etc. (Gen. I, 24). In the earth commanded by the Lord to bring forth a living creature, the sinful person may be understood. Such a person brings forth a living creature when, touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, he begins to recognize his iniquities and sins; and thus, by recognizing his sins, he is made into a living creature, because previously he was a dying soul while subject to sins [Col. 0473B] and vices. When he begins to recognize these sins, he brings them all forth according to their kind, while for each individual sin, according as he committed it, he makes worthy satisfaction to God by penitence for it. He brings forth cattle, creeping things of the earth, and beasts according to their kinds. By cattle, as it seems to me, we may understand ignorance; by creeping things, the lust or uncleanness of the flesh; by beasts of the earth, the malice of the heart. A person brings forth cattle when, in bitterness of heart, he calls to mind how many sins he committed while ignorant of God, how many he committed in ignorance of himself. He also brings forth creeping things when he begins to repent of whatever wrong he committed through uncleanness or lust of the flesh; and he brings forth beasts of the earth when he begins to recognize what he perpetrated through malice and pride of heart. And rightly these cattle, 674 creeping things, and beasts are commanded to be brought forth according to their kinds. For there are different kinds of sins. Some people commit graver sins; others fall into lighter sins. For those who sin deliberately, through obstinacy and pride of heart, offend more gravely than those who fall into sins through ignorance, the lust of the flesh, and weakness. Therefore, according to the kinds of wickedness and in proportion to the measure of the fault, the measure of penitence also ought to be assessed. Whoever has sinned maliciously through obstinacy and pride of heart needs greater penitence and satisfaction than one who has offended through ignorance and the frailty of the flesh.

[Col. 0473D] But because a human being can do nothing by himself, these words are rightly preceded by “God said,” because, for these things to be accomplished in a person, God Himself must speak and do this in his heart. Hence it follows: “And it was so.” God’s speaking is when He first implants in a person’s heart the will to repent and to recognize his sins. When He has spoken this in the human heart, it must be accomplished in deed what had first, by God’s gift, been in the will. It follows:

“And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and the cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind.” Although the order of sinning is such that a person first offends through ignorance and the lust of the flesh, nevertheless, because it is more serious to sin deliberately, to sin through pride, the sin committed through obstinacy and pride [Col. 0474A] is placed first here. For those sins committed either through ignorance or through weakness of the flesh are venial before God. And because, between ignorance and the lust of the flesh, the excess arising from ignorance is more serious 675 than that arising from carnal weakness—for, as the Apostle says, “he who does not know shall not be known” (I Cor. XIV, 38)—ignorance too is placed before the frailty of the flesh. Therefore God makes the beasts of the earth according to their kinds when, by the gift of His grace, He grants a person to recognize the individual kinds of sins, and, just as he sinned maliciously and perversely through deliberation and pride, so to make satisfaction to God for those same sins by heartfelt and steadfast repentance. He also makes the cattle and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind when He causes him to repent of the lesser and venial sins which he committed through ignorance or [Col. 0474B] weakness of the flesh, as it were according to their kind—that is, in proportion to the measure of the fault. It follows:

“And God saw that it was good, and said: Let Us make man in Our image and likeness.” When God sees in a person that he has corrected through humility the malice of heart which comes from deliberate action and pride, and has changed his ignorance through the knowledge received from Holy Scripture, from his teachers and masters, or from the holy manner of life of those among whom he dwells, God loves this, approves this in a person, and sees this as good in His eyes. Indeed, many who live in secular dress commit many sins through ignorance; when they return to God and receive the light of knowledge, they deeply grieve over what they have done, and groaning together in distress of spirit, say: “Oh, if I, while living in the world, had known beforehand that these things were so grievous before the Lord, I would never, God being my witness, have presumed to do these or such things.” God sees and loves this groaning, this grief which a person has acquired through knowledge; and thus by God’s power it comes about that what follows is fulfilled in him: “Let Us make man in Our image and likeness.” Although different people hold different views about the image and likeness of God, for the present passage it is enough for us that our outer person is formed, as it were, in God’s image when he imitates Christ through sanctification and the perfection of good works; and that our inner person receives God’s likeness [Col. 0474D] when, with God’s help, he has attained purity and cleanness of heart. It follows:

676 “And let him rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.” In the fish of the sea, as it seems to me, we may understand the vigorous faculties of a person, or the movement of fear; in the birds of heaven, the movement of love. By these two movements we ought to rule over the beasts, the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves on earth—that is, over malice, ignorance, and the lust of the flesh. To these fish of the sea and birds of heaven we may adapt the words of the Holy Gospel which we read today, on the sixth Sunday, in which the Lord speaks thus:

[Col. 0475A] “Amen I say to you: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.” And afterwards: “He who is angry with his brother”; “he who says *raca*”; “he who says, ‘Fool.’” In the fish of the sea we may understand the Scribes, who understood the sacred Scriptures through the keenness of their faculties; in the birds of heaven we may understand the Pharisees, because they were elevated above others by the righteousness of their lives, like birds of heaven. It is as though the Lord said: Let Us make a person such as rules over the fish of the sea, whose righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the Scribes; and who also rules over the birds of heaven, so that his righteousness surpasses the righteousness of the Pharisees. Let him also rule over the beasts, so that he is not angry with his brother in a beastlike manner; let him rule over the whole earth, so that he does not say *raca* to his brother; let him rule over every [Col. 0475B] creeping thing which moves upon the earth, so that he does not say “Fool” to his brother. Thus, by movements of fear and love, let him rule over all these things—let him rule, I say, so that they do not prevail—so that, when sins are subdued and brought under control, he may be able to do good and thus be conformed to Our image and likeness. Therefore all that has now been stated God first works in the human will; afterwards He brings it to effect. Hence it follows:

“And God created man in His image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.” God creates man in His image in the outer person when He causes him outwardly to live honourably and praiseworthily. He creates him in the image of God in the inner person 677 when He causes him, through cleanness and purity of heart, to please and cleave to God alone. He also creates them male and female. In the male may be expressed that understanding by which a person knows how to govern his spirit and searches into and understands those things above us, heavenly and eternal. In the female, however, is the lower faculty, by which he knows how to govern the flesh and the things of the flesh, to cut away what is useless and manage what is useful. Of this male and this female the Apostle Paul says: “A man ought not to cover his head, because he is the image and glory of God; but a woman ought to cover her head, because she is the glory of man” (I Cor. XI, 7). Therefore the man, through whom human reason is understood and in whom is the image of God, ought not to be covered: he ought not to be held down in lower and earthly things; he ought not to be prevented, so far as he can, from stretching upward and being raised to God and heavenly things. But the woman, the lower faculty which we have received for administering temporal [Col. 0475D] and external things, should be covered, lest she slip too far into useless matters and go on to things less necessary. It follows:

“And God blessed them and said: Increase and multiply; fill the earth and subdue it; and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every living thing that moves upon the earth.” It is as though the Lord said: Increase in good works; multiply in virtues. Or, increase in action and multiply in knowledge. And do not, because of that increase and multiplication, become proud; rather, subdue your earth through humility—the earth which you have filled by good action. “And rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every living thing that moves [Col. 0476A] upon the earth.” In the fish of the sea and the birds of heaven, as we mentioned above, the two movements of fear and love may be understood; in all living things, all good works and virtues. In these words there seems to be an effect of good works, when a person receives from God a certain dominion over the fish of the sea and birds of heaven, when he begins to employ to some extent according to his will those two movements, fear and love of the Lord. He also rules over every living thing that 678 moves upon the earth when, so far as is possible for a human being, he completes in deed the good works which he previously possessed in his will through God’s gift. This dominion, which a person receives from God in these words, is truly the Lord’s blessing; of this blessing it was written earlier: “And God blessed [Col. 0476B] them and said: Increase and multiply; fill the earth and subdue it.” It is as though He said: If this is in you, if you increase in good works and multiply in virtues, if you subdue your earth through humility lest you be exalted, I, the Lord of majesty, bless you. And immediately after these words of blessing He again adds, saying:

“Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and all trees which have in themselves the seed of their own kind, that they may be for you as food.” An herb is a weak thing; a tree is strong and solid. Through these two things given to human beings as food, two kinds, as it were, of weak and strong people in Holy Scripture are indicated, set before us for imitation. [Col. 0476C] And to provide examples of what we say, let us set before our eyes some saints who were not only strong but also weak, whose weaknesses at first multiplied, but afterwards, by the power of our God, changed their weakness into strength. At first David, king and prophet, was a frail herb when he saw Bathsheba and took her, and killed Uriah with the sword of the sons of Ammon, committing two crimes at once: adultery and murder. David was so frail an herb. But afterwards he became a strong tree, when Nathan came to him reproving him from the mouth of the Lord; Nathan’s words inflamed him with so great a fire of penitence that for seven days he lay on the ground, eating no bread [Col. 0476D] and drinking no water. See how great the strength of a tree he attained through penitence, after first being a frail herb!

Was not Peter also, chief of the apostles, a most weak herb when, on account of the word of a lowly maidservant, he denied the Lord of majesty—his Teacher, Creator, and Redeemer? But afterwards he became a strong tree when the Lord looked upon him and he went out and wept bitterly. The Lord has given us such herbs of the earth and such trees as food—that is, as an example—so that, when we see how the weaknesses of saints of old were multiplied, but afterwards they recovered from their weakness through God’s help, we too may hope, if we are weak—and even if we have not yet been so, since we can become so—that, with God’s [Col. 0477A] grace coming to our aid, we can be delivered from our frailty. It is as though God said: Let the herb of My saints, their weakness, bring you seed; let it bring you hope and confidence in your salvation. And when you see in any righteous and elect person that he was weak, and how by My grace and mercy he became a tree—that is, strong—then you too may be confident of your salvation, because I, who caused them to recover from weakness, shall also minister strength from heaven to you when you labour in weakness. Consider also that these trees had their seed in themselves, because they did not exalt themselves but ascribed everything to My name and honour. And you, by their example, should have your seed—that is, your good works—in yourselves, lest you be raised up by pride because of them; rather, turn all things to your food and salvation. It follows:

“And for all living things of the earth, every bird of heaven, and all things that move upon the earth in which there is a living soul, for food.” In these four things distinguished here may be understood the four stages of sin by which we advance toward sinning: in all living things of the earth, delight in sin; in the birds of heaven, consent to sin; in all things that move upon the earth, the act of sin; in those in which is a living soul, the habit of sin.

And delight in sin is quite fittingly denoted in the living things of the earth, because when a person delights in sin, he is, as it were, animated toward sinning. In the bird of heaven, however, consent to sin may rightly be expressed, because when [Col. 0477C] a person consents to sin, he already flies toward it, as it were, in mind, and can scarcely be held back or restrained. 680 And in all things which move upon the earth, the act of sin may likewise justly be understood, because when a person performs sin in the flesh, he moves the members of his body in order that the sin may be carried out. The habit of sin, moreover, can fittingly be prefigured in these words, “in which there is a living soul,” because when a sinful person has come into the habit of sin, he lives, as it were, wholly in sin. These are the four stages or processes of sins, which, with God’s help, we may also transform into the number and progression of virtues. For in these four we may understand the four cardinal virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. Yet these four may also be understood in a good sense in another way. For when a person is animated so as to delight in the good, his delight is good; if he adds to this consent to the good, action in the good, indeed perseverance in the good, then there follows quite justly and worthily:

[Col. 0477D] “And God saw all things that He had made, and they were very good.” For it is very good if one has delight in the good, consent to the good, action in the good, and preserves perseverance in the good in all these things. God sees this, loves this, and praises this. It follows:

“And evening and morning came: the sixth day.” In evening may be understood self-knowledge; in morning, knowledge of God. Thus evening and morning make the sixth day when a person has come, from self-knowledge and knowledge of God, to full and perfect [Col. 0478A] perfection. But why did I say “to full and perfect perfection”? Because on the first day of creation, where we read, “And evening and morning came: one day,” he had not yet attained full perfection; nor on the second, third, fourth, or fifth, but only on the sixth, on which he is conformed to God’s image. And this is full and perfect perfection: when a person offers his whole self to the Lord, as we also have at the end of the Gospel: “If you offer your gift before the altar.”

But that we may say a little about each of these days, let us see what is meant by the writing concerning the first day: “And evening and morning came: one day.” One day exists in a person when he has received from God the will to depart from evils and approach good things; that will is like one day. The second day is good action together with good will. The third day is when he begins to guard himself in thought, speech, and deed and takes care to govern his actions. To this third day the fourth is joined if, keeping diligent watch with attentive care over the guarding of his thoughts, words, and deeds, he preserves perseverance in them. The fifth day comes in a person when he not only turns the five outward senses of his body to God but also begins with his five inward senses to see, hear, bear, smell, and touch God. The sixth day, which corresponds to this present Sunday, comes in a person when he is formed in God’s image, in which he receives full and perfect perfection. The sixth day is followed by the seventh day, [Col. 0478C] which God blessed, on which He rested from every work that He had performed. By this seventh day eternal rest is signified to us: there we rest from the labours of this present life; there we shall rejoice in the eternal vision of God; there we shall always delight in Him. Having made these preliminary remarks, let us enter upon the text of the Holy Gospel:

“Amen I say to you: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.” The words of the Holy Gospel which we read today, on the sixth Sunday, are difficult and exalted words, taken from the Lord’s sermon which He delivered on the mountain, which only the perfect and chosen disciples of the Lord were fit to hear. For after He had taught and healed the crowds in the valley, while they remained below and were unable to follow Him up the mountain, He Himself went up the mountain with His disciples; and there, sitting, He showed them a more excellent way of spiritual and heavenly life, which the rest of the crowd could not ascend and was not capable of receiving.

The sublimity of this teaching is still proposed for observance by spiritual persons who have followed the Lord up the mountain and undertaken the spiritual life, who can say to God with the Apostle Peter: “Behold, we have left all things and followed You” (Matt. XIX, 27). We too can say these words, who under His guidance have left the world and entered upon the purpose of spiritual life. And if we cannot say them with the truth and perfection with which Peter spoke them, yet because we have done outwardly what we were able to do, may He Himself, in His goodness and mercy, accomplish in us that [Col. 0479A] which we still lack in truth. Therefore, as we follow Him upon the narrow way, He sets before us this perfect doctrine to be followed. For He now speaks these words not to Peter, Andrew, or John, but to us who still dwell in the flesh: “Amen I say to you: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.”

The righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees consisted in their observing with the greatest diligence the commandments of the Law and the other duties of righteousness set before them, so that by observing the Law they might be made more reputable and honourable than others. But what were the commandments set before them? Certainly the Ten Commandments, in which they were instructed thus: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal,” and other similar things. As we said before, the Scribes and Pharisees carefully observed these, not out of love for God, but lest they should be deprived of earthly honour, and so that they might be exalted by popular favour on account of the holiness of their lives.

The Lord wishes the righteousness of His children to exceed the righteousness of these people, so that whatever good they do in this present life, they may do it wholly for love of God alone and for the hope laid up in heaven. It is as though the Lord said to us: I speak to you, My chosen children, who have ascended with Me from the valley of this age to the mountain: unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of those established in clerical office, and also exceeds the righteousness of those [Col. 0479C] who live chastely in the world while joined in marriage, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. We believe the kingdom of heaven is not only that which we now await in the present by faith, and which we hope to receive from God after the end of the world in eternal life, 683 but also that kingdom which we ought to possess now with God in the sweetness of the heart, concerning which the Lord Himself says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21).

We cannot obtain this kingdom by our own powers, so as to deserve to possess it frequently in the sweetness of the heart, unless He Himself deigns to accomplish in us what He deigned to work on the sixth day, which corresponds to this sixth Sunday. Therefore this present Sunday summons us more than the preceding Sundays to the love of God and love of neighbour, although all of them proclaim and represent charity. Thus in today’s Collect, praying to God, we say: “God of virtues, to whom belongs everything that is best, implant in our breasts the love of Your name, and grant in us an increase of religion.”

We rightly call our Lord and Redeemer “God of virtues,” not “God of virtue,” invoking Him not for one virtue but for many. For it is not enough that by the gift of His grace we gain the virtue to do good, unless we also receive from Him the power to preserve our good works with great care. Thus indeed He is the God of virtues, to whom belongs, as follows immediately, everything that is [Col. 0480A] best. For it is always good that sins be avoided and guarded against, whether this is done because of a desire for passing praise and honour or through fear of eternal condemnation. But it is best if sins are avoided and restrained for love of God alone and for the sweetness and reward of the eternal homeland. Therefore, because this best thing belongs to Him alone, when in today’s Collect we ask, saying, “Implant in our breasts the love of Your name,” we do not say, “Give us,” or “Put Your love into our heart,” but “Implant in our breasts the love of Your name.” For we ask, Lord, that Your grace may act so that the love of Your name is implanted in the inward parts of our heart and cleaves so firmly to the marrow of our soul [Col. 0480B] that it is held more securely and not more easily lost. Thus, Lord, by implanting the love of Your name in our heart, grant in us an increase of religion, so that our righteousness may increase and exceed the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees.

The Apostle James teaches us in his Epistle what this religion is which we ask from God, saying: “Pure and undefiled religion before the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, and to keep oneself unspotted from this world” (James I, 27). Orphans are those deprived of a father; widows, those who have lost a husband. In the orphans whom we are commanded to visit may be understood good and righteous thoughts, which are begotten in us by the heavenly Father. They become as it were orphans when they lose the heavenly Father who begot them and are forsaken by Him in a kind of orphanhood. We ought to visit these orphans because we must strive with great care continually to gather and restore good and righteous thoughts within ourselves.

Widows also must be visited. By widows, as I judge, are meant holy and sweet affections, which ought to be brides of our husband, the everlasting King. These sweet affections become widows when they cannot enjoy their bridegroom and husband as their desire and will would have them do.
