We visit these widows, these holy and sweet affections, if, as far as we can, we aid their desire and gently and delightfully awaken them to the love of their husband. [Col. 0480D] And he rightly says that these widows are to be visited in their tribulation, since the tribulation of holy affections is precisely this: when they lose their husband, when, however much they desire to stretch themselves out in love for Him and enjoy Him whom they desire, they are not permitted to do so.

But if we have thus visited these orphans and widows, we shall be able to fulfil what follows: “And to keep oneself unspotted from this world.” A person acquires a stain before the Lord if he performs good works and thereby seeks passing praise and human friendships. But the one who keeps himself unspotted from this world is he who strives, as far as he can, to perform all good works for God’s love and seeks no human praises from them, but desires only eternal reward. This is pure and undefiled religion, [Col. 0481A] the increase of which in 685 us we ask in today’s Collect. It follows:

“You have heard that it was said to the men of old: ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.” What is anger? Anger is the desire for revenge. While it still creeps about in a person’s heart and has not yet shown itself outwardly either by words or by any sign through which it might be recognized, [Col. 0481B] a person can punish in himself, by inward judgment, the guilt of this anger hidden in the heart. Hence it is said here: “He shall be liable to judgment.” For he ought to ascend the tribunal of his mind, set himself before himself, and judge himself strictly for hidden anger, saying to the Lord in prayer: “Forgive us our debts.” And in such a judgment the fault contracted through anger will be expiated. It follows:

“But whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council.” In the preceding verse, anger that is hidden only in the heart is indicated; but in this verse anger that has emerged somewhat through the sound of the voice is shown. For *raca* is a vocal sound expressing the anger and indignation of the mind. Since this anger is such that, through the sound of the voice, the anger that lay hidden becomes somewhat apparent to others, it is not enough for a person to punish this guilt by his own judgment; rather, this anger must be referred to the council. The council is the assembly of the judging Church. For because the anger has proceeded somewhat and from it scandal has come to those who see it, it must be referred to the assembly of the judging Church, to the justice of teachers, so that the fault made known through the sound of the voice may also be punished and corrected through the words of teachers. [Col. 0481C] It follows:

“But whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” Who could observe these words of the Lord according to the letter? For if all who called their brother “fool” were liable to the fire of Gehenna, who could be saved? Since we often—if not habitually, still in jest—say, “Fool!” Therefore, far be it that every person should for this reason become liable to the fire of Gehenna if he says to his brother merely with outward words, as these words of the Lord appear to sound, “Fool!” But because the Lord himself, who speaks these things, is truth and wisdom, and has never uttered words that disagreed with truth or that could not be fulfilled by human beings, it is necessary that we understand the words of truth otherwise than they outwardly appear to sound, [Col. 0481D] so that the truth of the words may stand.

Therefore, wherever the Lord’s words sound with such strictness and severity that they can scarcely, or not at all, be fulfilled, the weight of his words must be moderated by sound reasoning. But where they abound in such gentleness and sweetness that the weak and idle, because of the gentleness of his words, become through moral lightness inclined to evil, there it is necessary for them to be seasoned with some moderation of strictness.

Let us therefore see what this means: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” What is a word? A word is a formed thought of the heart, which a person forms within and then expresses outwardly through the sound of words. We received words from the Creator so that [Col. 0482A] through outward words we might make the disposition of our heart known to others. For as long as we inhabit the misery of this mortality, we are in no way able to know and behold one another’s hearts unless we express in words the things hidden in the heart. For who, as the Apostle says, knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in that person? (1 Cor. 2:11.)

Thus, in my view, we may understand these words in a sound sense by saying: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool’”—I say, says it in such a way that, in his heart and in his thought, where the word is formed, he calls his brother foolish; and he judges him foolish not from a first impulsive movement (*propassio*), which is sudden delight, but from deliberation; and, holding this firmly in his heart, persists in this obstinacy until the end of his life—such a person is certainly liable to [Col. 0482B] the fire of Gehenna, because no proud person shall possess the kingdom of God. For whoever judges his brother foolish in his heart undoubtedly considers himself wiser. In this he is proud, and therefore liable to the fire of Gehenna unless through repentance he washes away this pride. We ought therefore to turn the right eye toward the simplicity of our neighbor, considering that our wisdom is foolishness before God, and that his simplicity is far more commendable and acceptable before the Lord than our wisdom. It follows:

“If therefore you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then, when you come, offer your gift.” [Col. 0482C] Behold, the merciful and compassionate Lord, employing his customary grace, after harsh words of address sets forth words of healing and exhortation. So also in another Gospel, when he was speaking about loving enemies—“Love your enemies” (Luke 6:27)—he immediately perceived that some people’s minds are so strong in obstinacy that they can never love their enemies from the heart, and he supplied a medicinal command, saying: “Do good to those who hate you; pray for those who persecute and slander you.” As though he said: If you cannot attain to loving your enemies, it remains at least that you do what you can: do good to them and include them in your prayers.

So also in the present passage he instructs us with a physician’s healing counsel, saying: “If you offer your gift [Col. 0482D] at the altar.” Our gift, which we offer to God, is our psalmody; it is our sighs, which proceed from the inward affection of the heart; it is our tears, which, if by God’s assent we can have them, offer him an acceptable gift. The altar upon which we ought to offer our gift is Christ, upon whom we sacrifice the incense of faith, hope, and charity. The altar is also our heart, which that supreme and true High Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ, consecrated by the anointing of the Holy Spirit, and in which it is exceedingly lovable and delightful for him to rest.

Therefore we offer our gift before the altar when we desire to partake of the flesh and blood of the Son of God. But when we remember that we have [Col. 0483A] injured our brother, we should in no way presume to approach this communion unless we first come to reconciliation with our brother. If he is bodily present, let us humbly prostrate ourselves before him, seeking pardon for what we have committed. But if he is bodily absent, let us humbly prostrate ourselves with the inmost affection of the heart before the Lord and before our neighbor whom we have provoked, as we ought to do if he were present. For if we do not humbly show this disposition of compassion and charity toward an absent neighbor, when would we assume this humility and compassion when he is present?

Therefore, in today’s Collect we ask the Lord’s help to obtain this disposition of charity, saying: “May you nourish what is good, and by the zeal of devotion preserve what you have nourished.” The Lord nourishes [Col. 0483B] good things in us when, by his mercy and goodness, he helps us to perform good works. He preserves the things nourished by the zeal of devotion when he himself—the lover and guardian of souls—keeps us from losing through pride or human favor all that we expend in love of God and neighbor, which is the zeal of devotion.

Therefore, because we can do nothing from ourselves or through ourselves, in today’s office we invoke him as helper and protector when we sing: “The Lord is the strength of his people and the protector of the saving acts of his Christ” (Ps. 27:8). But because a person cannot attain any of the things we have briefly considered unless he has the mortification of Jesus in himself, Paul says in today’s reading: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ [Col. 0483C] have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). Therefore may he in whom we have been baptized, through whom and in whom we have all things, grant that we may be worthy to put him on: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

689. HOMILY LXIX. THE FIRST, ON THE SEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

“When there was a great crowd with Jesus and they had nothing to eat, Jesus called his disciples and said: ‘I have compassion on the crowd, because behold, they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat’” (Matt. 8).

Today’s Sunday, which follows seventh in order from the beginning of the summer Sundays which we have celebrated, accords with and corresponds to the seventh day, [Col. 0483D] on which God the Father, after all things had been completed and created, rested from all the work that he had accomplished, as is written in the book of Genesis: “Thus the heavens and the earth and all their adornment were completed. And on the seventh day God completed his work which he had made, and rested from all the work which he had accomplished. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it God ceased from all his work which he had created in order to make it” (Gen. 2:1–3).

By heaven the angelic nature, and by earth human nature, may be designated. Each of these natures—that is, of angels and of human beings—was then perfect when it was created for eternity with the perfection suited to a nature at its beginning. But the entire adornment of the angelic creation was completed when, after the fall of the evil angels, [Col. 0484A] the good angels were confirmed; and, when the former had been cast down from God because of pride, the latter were granted as a gift never to be able to fall. This was the entire adornment of the angelic creation.

But likewise the whole adornment of human nature will be completed when all the elect and righteous attain to the perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ; when the Son delivers the kingdom to God the Father, and God shall be all in all. What is it to deliver the kingdom to God the Father? To deliver the kingdom to God the Father is to bring all the saints to the vision of God the Father. This will truly be a great and ineffable adornment, beyond every measure of human estimation. That adornment began with Christ and will be consummated in Christ. [Col. 0484B] Why do I say that this adornment began in Christ? Certainly because he first, he alone, among the entire human race appeared and lived without sin; and what he did and could do, he wills that a human being also may be able to do by his grace and help—namely, to be without sin—because he gave such remedies that the wounds of the sinful soul can be completely and wholly covered and healed.

Certainly, when each of us is regenerated in baptism, all sins are forgiven, and without doubt we are free from every sin. But if afterward we lose this adornment and become entangled in sins after baptism, then if we turn to God through a true acknowledgment and repentance for sins, no one doubts that we return to the true innocence which we lost, and our adornment will again be perfect, so far as is possible in this world. That entire adornment [Col. 0484C] will be completed when every one of the elect is consummated in Christ by a blessed end and departure, and comes to the true rest of the seventh day, which is Christ, where he will fear nothing from sins, because there will be absolutely no sin there.

Because the first human, prompted and persuaded by the devil, lost this adornment for himself and for us through his disobedience and pride, and could receive it again only through the incarnation of the Mediator of God and human beings, it fittingly follows:

“And on the seventh day God completed his work which he had made, and rested from all the work which he had accomplished.” This seventh day can signify that great and true day, our Lord Jesus Christ. In my view, he is rightly designated by the name of the seventh day because it pleased God the Father that in him all the fullness of divinity should dwell bodily, together with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, as the evangelist says in one place: “Jesus departed from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit” (Luke 4:1). [Col. 0484D] He was not full of the Holy Spirit only when he was baptized; from the time he was conceived and born, he was always the singular and special temple of the Holy Spirit.

In this seventh day God the Father completed his work, because the whole work of Christ’s conception and incarnation was accomplished in the blessed Virgin solely by the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon her. Since no human being worked anything there, but the whole work was divine, God the Father is truly and faithfully said to have completed in his Son the work which he had made.

[Col. 0485A] But because the human being who had perished could not be restored by Christ’s incarnation alone unless he also deigned to suffer and die for us, it fittingly follows, as I see it: “And he rested from all the work which he had accomplished.” For God the Father found rest only in him, whom alone he found free from every sin; and through him he gave us rest when through the blood of his cross he made peace with all things in heaven and on earth. Before his passion and death, so to speak, he did not rest, because his birth and his conversation among human beings did not confer complete and perfect salvation upon us, since while he lived the human race descended to hell as it had from the beginning. But in his passion and death he first began to have rest, when, as he gave up his spirit into [Col. 0485B] the Father’s hands, all the enemy’s power was taken away, and the gate of the kingdom, which had long been shut, was opened and unbarred.

Therefore, because his rest, and our rest in him, then began, it is well said: “And he rested from all the work which he had accomplished.” Paul agrees with this statement in today’s reading, saying: “But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:22). Hence, because the Lord willed to sanctify this seventh day not in any of his works but in his rest, which has no evening, there is a good fitness and harmony between the seventh day and this seventh Sunday, which signifies that rest of the saints now dying in Christ and resting with Christ in heaven.

[Col. 0485C] Yet this seventh day runs alongside the sixth, because as the sixth is the day of those who labor, so the seventh is that of those who rest and receive in heaven their reward after the labors and temptations of the present life. Here is labor; there is rest, the rest that is taken in God. And there our being shall not have death, where life will always be present. But did Christ labor in the work of his creation? By no means; for he spoke, and all things were made. And therefore he rested from all the work that he had accomplished. For he rested in himself, because in his divinity, which was never increased or diminished in him, all things that were to be created existed together.

He did not create this creation because there was any need in him or because he required the aid [Col. 0485D] of his creature, but so that the need and imperfection of that creature might be completed in Christ the Creator and reformed for the better through his death. Of this day it is further said: “And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he ceased from all the work which God created in order to make it.” By what blessing did God the Father bless his Son? By this blessing: he preserved him from every actual sin, and in this blessing of his Son he freed the whole human race from the first curse of our parents. And him whom he thus blessed, he also sanctified. In what did he sanctify him? In that he did not allow him, wholly holy and immaculate, to be touched by original sin.

And why did he bless and sanctify him thus? “Because on it he ceased from all the work [Col. 0486A] which God created in order to make it.” For he who, according to his divine nature, as God was sufficient for every good thing, could according to his human nature have had original sin. But he ceased in him, because both actual and original sin, which reigned in all, were utterly alien from him. Therefore, because now at this time we labor as though on the sixth day, and daily make our way and depart from the sixth to the seventh, from this world to the homeland where we may rest, let us hear the Gospel reading for this seventh Sunday, that we may know what we shall do or receive on that same seventh day.

693. “When there was a great crowd with Jesus and they had nothing to eat.” Because the indivisible omnipotence of the supreme Trinity, ordering all things from eternity by common operation, [Col. 0486B] sat down, as though wearied, in a most sweet repose when it rested on the seventh day from all the work it had accomplished, it prefigured, as we believe, the sweet joys of eternal rest. These too this seventh Sunday seems to signify in its order, when the blessed souls of the elect, laying aside the burdensome weight of corruptible flesh, rest in a blessed sabbath within the bosom of blessedness and henceforth rest from their labors.

But lest we suppose that those ignoble in life and character, degenerate in action and conduct, can attain so lofty a height of dignity, let us consider the words from the beginning of the Gospel reading. “When,” it says, “there was a great crowd with Jesus and they had nothing to eat.” [Col. 0486C] There is indeed a crowd made turbid by the disturbance of this world; and the less it labors in the pursuit of virtuous work, the less it is believed to possess praise. Thus it is neither called a great crowd nor said to be with Jesus. But a crowd is properly called great when it shines with the manifold glory of virtues, has set aside all earthly things, and by faith and hope alone attends to heavenly things. Sometimes, through God’s secret visitation, the heavy burden of this exile is lifted from it, when, prevented by him with blessings of sweetness, it has deserved to be made glad in the joy of his countenance.

Such a crowd is very fittingly said to be with Jesus, for it cannot be well without him. For it believes itself enveloped in countless miseries whenever it cannot share in the joys of such sweetness. Though it loves, seeks, and desires him alone and uniquely, it does not yet have what it may eat, [Col. 0486D] because mortal weakness can taste in this life the feast of eternal refreshment prepared by the Lord, but cannot yet eat it with a full mouth until it has laid aside this corruptible body. Then, eating and drinking above the Lord’s table, it will no longer fear exclusion from the banquet of eternity.

Thus, when the time predetermined by God the Father arrives—the limit which none of mortals can pass—when the spirits and souls of the righteous are to be transferred from this misery of mortality to the true joys of immutability, then, we believe, the following occurs in the heavenly court of the citizens above, as the evangelist presently adds:

“And Jesus, having called his disciples, said to them: ‘I have compassion on the crowd, because behold, they have now remained with me for three days [Col. 0487A] and have nothing to eat.’” Since there can be no doubt that those whom Jesus nourished and taught by special instruction during the days of his flesh are called and are his disciples, in this passage we may understand by the name of disciples the blessed spirits of angels, who, standing before the divine presence in perpetual immutability, have never been separated from his instruction. The Lord of knowledge in some manner calls to himself these disciples of eternal majesty, thus taught from the beginning in the secret place of divinity, when he communicates to them the hidden counsel of his dispensation.

The eternal wisdom of God also calls together those same ranks of heavenly spirits when he commands that, through their ministry, those whom he foreordained before the ages to be conformed to the image of his Son should be led out from the prison of this death. [Col. 0487B] Nor is it strange that the Creator of all things should communicate to administering spirits the things to be done concerning the salvation of human beings, since he has also revealed to his servants the prophets all that he will do upon earth, as one of them says in exultation: “The Lord will not do a word upon earth unless he has revealed it to his servants the prophets” (Hos. 3:7). If he does not disdain to reveal his word, which he will do upon earth, to his prophets while they are still enclosed in the prison of an earthly body, much more is the passage of any of the elect from death to life revealed to the heavenly citizens of the celestial homeland, so that, recognizing the compassion of their most gracious Creator for their fellow-heirs who have long been pilgrims, they may with greater rejoicing spread wide the bosom of their rest and go forth to meet [Col. 0487C] the crowd that has now remained with the Lord for three days.

For the crowd which, insofar as it can, abstains from sins in thought, word, and deed, has now worthily remained with the Lord for three days.

695. There is also another three-day period of laborious expectation: namely, the heavy yoke of all the children of humanity. Its first day is to be understood as the day of birth and the time of infancy; its second, the period of adolescence and youth; its third, the fearful day and hour of death. On the first day, a little child endures the Lord’s hidden judgment with such strictness that even amid the first cries of birth it cannot be free from guilt, although it has scarcely yet contracted any stain of contagion through personal guilt. [Col. 0487D] For every human being is so corrupted from the root of the first origin that not even an infant of one day is clean from sin; and the soul is entangled in the miseries of this world by such great ignorance that it does not know how to distinguish day from darkness.

When, reared with great care under guardians and stewards, it has passed the years of tender age, the second day—namely, the time of youth and adolescence—will now be at hand, in which it will remain with the Lord much more harshly and laboriously. For since youth and adolescence are vain, the desires of the flesh at once begin to wage a more grievous war against the soul. Now prosperity, smiling falsely, raises the mind up; now adversity, wounding it somewhat, casts down what has been raised up. These are indeed sharp arrows fixed in the human race; [Col. 0488A] this is the most grievous hand of the Lord. Hence holy David, groaning and troubled in the person of all flesh, cries out with tearful sighs: “For your arrows have been fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand upon me” (Ps. 37:3).

We have now heard how, on the two days mentioned above, we endure the Lord’s arrows firmly fixed within us; how the hand of the strict Judge has been heavily strengthened over the afflicted exiles of his kingdom. Let us now consider the third day, namely the final limit of life, when the departing soul endures the Lord in the greatest fear. There is then a very great and dreadful gathering of hostile power, a terrible and fearful conflict with the pestilential destroyer; there is the horrifying face of demons to terrify it, and the alien hand which, if permitted, might seize the departing soul.

But because the compassionate Lord knows what and how great are the things that a spirit in its death-agony suffers in the hour [Col. 0488B] of death, he makes the disposition of his most merciful compassion still more clearly known even to the inhabitants of heaven: “Behold, they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat.” Behold, he says, the three days having now elapsed; behold, the limit of temporal life having ended, which no mortal can transgress and which has been appointed for humankind by the just decree of my will: it is fitting for my omnipotence to anticipate with the help of my compassion the one who has now remained with me for three days, so that one who, by my will and command, has long endured the heavy burden of exile may at last, by my favor, deserve to be brought back to the homeland.

[Col. 0488C] “And if I send them away fasting to their home, they will fail on the way.” If, he says, I send my poor ones away fasting as they depart from the body; if I defer filling them with the desired sweetness of my delight until they return to their home, until they receive again the tent of the body that was laid down, they will undoubtedly fail on the way through their long expectation, because without me they have nothing to eat.

[Col. 0488D] “Some of them have come from afar.” Those come from afar to their Creator who serve their Creator from their very years of infancy; who bear the Lord’s sweet yoke from adolescence; who daily mortify the works of the flesh by the power of the spirit. Since, as was said, they have laboriously remained with the Lord for three days and have long sighed with tearful remembrance for the joys of the heavenly homeland, the divine mercy will be more abundant for them when they depart from the body, in proportion as they have lived longer in this misery of pilgrimage.

There are also certain others who come to the Lord from afar in this way: after many deeds of defiling sin, they return to him through repentance. Nevertheless, as they depart from the body, he places them within the bosom of mercy, lest they miserably perish and fail on the way of salvation for which they had hoped. Now, however, the truth of the Gospel indicates how greatly the angelic dignity rejoices in the salvation of the elect. For it follows:

“Whence will anyone be able to satisfy these [Col. 0489A] with bread in the wilderness?” These words are full of sweetest wonder and full of angelic rejoicing. The angelic spirits marvel with exceedingly great joy at the unsearchable riches of Christ’s goodness. “Whence,” they say, “O Lord Creator, comes the ineffable multitude of your mercy, which has been so magnified over the children of human beings that it surpasses all sense and understanding?” Since they cannot search it out more fully, they say to the same Creator in a suppliant question: “Who then, O Lord, can satisfy your hungry ones or console those afflicted for so long, except you, compassionate and merciful One, whose name is ineffable, whose name is unutterable and inconceivable? For it is yours, from the abundant fullness of your majesty, to satisfy these in the wilderness—that is, in the inward person—so that they may feel you alone in the inmost parts of the soul through an abundance of sweetness, where at times they built for you alone a house of solitude.”

[Col. 0489B] For the faithful crowd which remains with the Lord, as stated above, sometimes builds delightful solitudes for its Creator amid the varied storms of the present life, when it gathers all the intentions of its mind inward to itself so that it may deserve to become one spirit with the Lord. This is truly the solitude of exceptional sweetness, which in this passage is magnified in angelic praises.

There is another solitude, which must be understood here in a spiritual mystery: namely, the soul which has been led from the prison-keeping of the body and has not yet received the double robe of immortality, but enjoys, as though alone in some way, the rest of eternal blessedness, while the corruptible flesh is returned to the earth from which it was taken. [Col. 0489C] And who can console this solitude of the elect except him who alone is sufficient for the loving soul in all things? For there is a certain satisfaction by which God’s elect are satisfied when they are delivered from the evils and miseries of this laborious life: namely, the companionship of holy angels and of holy souls. Resting with them in the beauty of eternal light, they are consoled and refreshed. This satisfaction is certainly good, sweet, and delightful; yet it is not full satisfaction, because it is not from bread. For where the provision of bread is lacking, there cannot be complete refreshment.

698. [Col. 0489D] In the loaves we may understand the most joyful vision of the holy Trinity. God the Father is bread, because he is the full and perfect refreshment of the holy angels and holy souls. God the Son is bread, because he is the full and perfect refreshment of the holy angels and holy souls. God the Holy Spirit is bread, because he is the full and perfect refreshment of the holy angels and holy souls. Without these loaves there will not be full satisfaction, because in the most blessed vision of the eternal Trinity consists the entire happiness of the angels and of all the elect together. No one can give this satisfaction except God alone, who alone will be all in all to them.

Holy David believed that he alone sufficed for the desire of his soul; desiring nothing in heaven or on earth except him alone, he said: “[Col. 0490A] For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired upon earth apart from you?” (Ps. 72:25).

But while all the elect thus desire only the presence of divinity, the angelic powers agree with their desire in this voice, as has been said: “Whence will anyone be able to satisfy these with bread in the wilderness?” “Who,” they say, “can sufficiently satisfy those whom the sweetness of your divinity alone delights, for whom the brightness of your vision alone will be perpetual and unfailing satisfaction?” But to these things spoken by the blessed spirits of angels to God the Redeemer, acclaiming him with a voice of exultation, he immediately responds with words of mercy in questioning, as the evangelist relates:

“How many loaves do you have?” [Col. 0490B] Since the very fountain of knowledge can be ignorant of nothing, by asking he makes known to his angels the things which they do not know. For God’s questioning is his own making-known. The living bread asks how many loaves they have, so that he may make known to them what he desires to use to satisfy his poor ones: that he wills those long-pilgrim and exiled souls to become participants in the eternal banquet.

For it is as though he said: “Who distributed to you the bread of life and immortality? Who made you steadfast from the beginning in the glory of perpetuity? I, the living bread, have never ceased to satisfy you from the fullness of my divinity; so I have determined to fill these with the joy of my countenance.” When they learned that those formed from the parent clay were to be advanced to this glory, their ensuing answer plainly shows how greatly they rejoice in that advancement. For when, as we said above, the Lord of knowledge asks how many loaves they have, [Col. 0490C] they declare that they have seven.

“We have,” they say, “in some manner received seven loaves from you, Creator of all things, since the sevenfold grace of your Spirit has filled us, satisfying us with an insatiable desire, filling and inebriating us with inexplicable fullness. But this joy of new delight also comes to us: that it has pleased your omnipotence repeatedly to increase our number by the company of the elect. Nor is it surprising that the angelic spirits should have such great and abundant exultation concerning the salvation of the faithful, since, as Truth himself testifies, there is joy in heaven over one sinner doing repentance.”

[Col. 0490D] But the invincible goodness of eternal majesty, seeing this gracious rejoicing of the angels, immediately commands through their noble ministry that the souls of his poor ones be led out from this exile; he commands that those long wandering in the lake of misery be brought to himself with the joy of praise. Hence it follows:

“Jesus commanded the crowd to recline upon the ground.” He fittingly commands the crowd which has remained with him for three days to recline upon the ground when he makes it free from every disturbance as it passes from this world. In another sense, he commands it to recline upon the ground when he commands the soul to be raised above the body to heavenly things. What rewards of eternal blessedness immediately follow is plainly declared by the sentence that follows:

“And taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before them.” [Col. 0491A] As stated above, the seven loaves should be understood as the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. When the most gracious rewarder, receiving them in his own hands, mercifully distributes them to his fellow-heirs, he is said then to give the greatest thanks, because grace upon grace is multiplied for them by his gift: he grants them not only the grace of adopted pardon but also the grace of unchangeable glory, when God himself will be all in all and each of us will be given the complete manifestation of the sevenfold Spirit.

For what can we more fittingly perceive in the breaking of the seven loaves than that eternal Wisdom of God, signifying the seven seals, opens as though by breaking the hidden treasures of knowledge to those reigning with him and makes himself visible to the eyes of the elect as he is? And because this glory of blessed reward is believed to be distributed through administering spirits, the Gospel narrative adds more plainly: “And he gave them to his disciples to set before them.” [Col. 0491B] For power and knowledge are given by God the Father to these elect disciples—that is, to the administering spirits—concerning the place in which each elect soul is to be set, so that, according to the worthiness of its merit, it may be granted a seat and rest suitable to it in some rank among their nine orders. When it is set before them to be crowned forever, what follows immediately comes about:

[Col. 0491C] “And they had a few little fish, and he commanded that these too be set before them.” These few little fish may fittingly be understood as those saints whom the Lord has so blessed with every spiritual blessing that, like most choice fish, he drew them in the net of his charity from the waves of worldly tempest. Raising them from the region of the shadow of death, he has long since commanded them to be set before the blessed angels in the region of the living, where, not yet having received the double robe, they await with joyful expectation the completion of the number of their brethren.

But those who now pay the debt of the flesh and deserve to have as companions in the reward of blessedness those who have gone before them into life are delighted, as though fattened with fish of exceeding sweetness, by their most joyful presence. They shall deserve to behold many thousands of them truly rejoicing. Hence it follows:

And they ate and were satisfied. Those who eat will indeed be filled with complete sweetness, to whom such delights of sweetness as have been described are to be set forth; for them the presence of the unbounded Majesty will be a perpetual and unfailing refreshment without labour or weariness, and the sweet companionship of all the blessed will provide the delightful banquet-feast. And if the joy of the righteous will be so great before they have received the twofold robe of immortality, how much greater will it be when they receive an incorruptible body which will die no more, as the words which follow immediately indicate.

And they took up the fragments that remained. The bodies of those to be saved, now reduced to the dust of earth, may quite fittingly be called certain very small fragments. Yet these same bodies, now cast down and laid aside, are to be raised up in the glory of the resurrection, so that then they may possess their bodies incorruptibly for ever—bodies in which they now bravely overcome the very corrupter of souls and bodies. Then indeed, death having been utterly swallowed up in victory, the mysteries of the seven baskets will be fulfilled spiritually in them. For just as baskets are woven from many diverse twigs until the measure of that work is completed at its summit, so the bodies of the elect, perfected in every virtue, are made entirely free from every corruption. The grace of the sevenfold Spirit so inebriates them as it cleanses them that they perceive nothing, either in body or soul, except that highest Good. But who and what kind of persons attain this ineffable joy of eternity, and receive the inestimable feasts of heavenly delights, the text of the Gospel narrative immediately declares.

[Col. 0492B] Now those who had eaten were about four thousand. By the four thousand we understand all the perfect, who here, through a pure and perfect manner of life in innocence, with the cooperating grace of God, deserve to be admitted to the delights of eternal blessedness prepared in the vision of God. But since not only the perfect, but also the imperfect and sinners, were to feast with Christ in God amid the brightness of the eternal vision, it is rightly said here: *Now those who had eaten were about four thousand.* It does not say simply “four thousand,” but “about four thousand,” because not only the perfect will be crowned there, but also imperfect persons who lived wickedly but, after their evil deeds, turned to repentance, will be saved through the mercy of God in the number of the perfect. But what the end and consummation of all who are to be saved will be, and what their everlasting praise and jubilation, is indicated in these very few words:

And he sent them away. Having received their immortal flesh, he sends away those whom he has glorified for ever, admitting them into the deeper mysteries of his divinity in perpetual intimacy, so that they shall no longer depart, even in the slightest thought of the mind, from contemplating the glory of the divine greatness. They have before them the Lord himself of such great majesty; they have also the enduring, endless companionship of the citizens above. Then truly all the people of the elect celebrate the desirable sabbatism of supreme rest, which, as we noted at the beginning of this reading, this seventh Sunday prefigures. Then, as they repose in the safest tranquillity in the bosom of the highest peace, they will be able to see more clearly how great, what kind, and how sweet the Lord is.

Then, when all have been gathered into the heavenly temple, the Introit of today’s Mass, *All nations, clap your hands* (Ps. 46:2), will truly and with perfect joy be begun and sung at the entrance into the heavenly kingdom. For when all the corruption of this present life has been ended and laid aside, and we have come to the seventh day, where we keep the true sabbatism for the Lord, this song can be sung in truth. Then, because of the blessedness of eternal life received, all nations will clap their hands, will shout to God [Col. 0493A] with a voice of exultation, and, bearing a joyful triumph over the enemy, will fittingly add this verse in song: *He has subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet* (Ps. 46:4).

Who are these peoples, and what are these nations? These peoples, as I see it, are the evil spirits; when the saints have them subjected, they will no longer fear their snares and traps. The nations are vices and sins, which they will henceforth trample powerfully beneath their feet so that they may not rise up and rule them. There they will hear the voice of the Lord God sweetly inviting and calling them, saying: *Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord* (Ps. 33:12). For, having been made sons out of servants, they will serve and cleave to the Lord for ever, not with servile but with filial fear.

[Col. 0493B] There they will hear from the angels and from the whole multitude of saints: *Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded* (Ps. 33:6). For to draw near to him and to be enlightened by him will be such grace and blessedness as to remove every shame far from all God’s elect. Then they will solemnly sing Alleluia—that is, the praise of their devotion in celebration of their deliverance: *Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me* (Ps. 58:1). It is as though every elect soul said to God: “From those enemies of mine, once rising up and assaulting me, you will now deliver and free me, so that I may have perpetual peace with you and with your saints.” For there will be no battle or temptation there from visible or invisible enemies; these things will cease there, because after present temptations they will receive consolations that are eternal and endure without end.

The Offertory also concerns this very joy and rest: *As in a holocaust of rams and bulls.* A holocaust is called something wholly burned. And what will the souls of the saints be there except wholly burned offerings? For they continually burn and melt in their God with the fire of ever-new love. Established in such love and desire, truly offered to the Lord, they can sing: *And now we follow you with our whole heart, and fear you, and seek your face, O Lord.*

We would wish to follow the Lord in this world with our whole heart; but, alas, because the weakness of the flesh opposes us, we can in no way follow him and fear him with our whole heart. Yet in that blessed life we shall truly follow the Lord with our whole heart, because by doing nothing contrary to God we shall no longer depart from him; and, as we seek his face, he will never confound us, but will deal with us according to his gentleness and the multitude of his mercy.

When we have thus possessed eternal life, certainly, as Paul says in today’s reading, “we shall have our fruit in sanctification.” There too every harmful thing is removed, as we ask in today’s Collect when we say: “O God, whose providence is not deceived in its ordering, we humbly beseech you to remove all harmful things and grant us all things profitable.” For in this time of mortality all harmful things can never be removed, where harmful things of every kind arise daily. But there every harmful thing is perfectly removed; and, with all harmful things removed and taken away, all things profitable are granted through him whose providence is not deceived in its ordering. May he bring us to this life, in which every harmful thing is removed and every good and sweet thing is abundantly supplied—he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## 705. HOMILY LXX. A SECOND HOMILY ON THE SAME SUNDAY

When there was a great multitude with Jesus, and they had nothing to eat, Jesus called his disciples and said to them: “I have compassion on the multitude, because behold, they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat” (Mark 8).

We ought to know and investigate with spiritual understanding [Col. 0494B] what mystical dignity this seventh Sunday contains within itself. For, as the order of the Sunday narrative itself indicates, something new and eminent shines forth in the mystery. By this seventh Sunday this most joyful rest of sabbatism may quite fittingly be understood—the rest which the seventh day also prefigured at the beginning of creation, when the indivisible omnipotence of the Trinity rested, as though wearied, from every work which it had made.

At that time the rest of the supreme Trinity also prefigured in mystery that rest in which, at the end of the ages, God and man rested from his labours: when, having trodden the winepress of the Passion and triumphed over the prince of death upon the cross, he committed his soul, precious beyond estimation, into his Father’s hands, and the Lord’s very body rested in the heart of the earth for three days.

Thus, all things concerning him having truly been completed, he began to rest from every work which he had accomplished; and then the great multitude deserved to enter the banquet, long desired, of eternal refreshment, concerning which the present reading of the holy Gospel indicates:

When there was a great multitude with Jesus, and they had nothing to eat. By the great multitude—by a multitude, I say, of great dignity and great merit—that ancient people of the elect may most aptly be understood. The Evangelist fittingly indicates that it was with Jesus, because it waited for him who was to come at the end of the ages with faith and patience.

[Col. 0494D] And because it believed, on the testimony of the prophetic oracles, that it would be brought out of the lake of death and hell through the blood of Christ Jesus, it was with him in the lower world through believing and waiting. Yet there, through many thousands of years, it had nothing to eat, because it had not yet deserved to partake of the desired delights of paradise—until that same spotless Lamb, the Lamb of true innocence, offered upon the gibbet of the cross, prepared the food of redemption for that people.

But because this redemption itself was not to be accomplished without angelic ministry, he is rightly said to have called together his disciples—that is, the angelic spirits—as the Gospel narrative immediately adds:

And having called together his disciples. When, as has been said, the command of the Father had been fulfilled, the same King of glory and Lord of hosts called together those aforesaid disciples of his majesty, who had always from the beginning been instructed under the discipline of the supreme Trinity. He summoned them to precede him as he was about to overthrow the Tartarean bars of hell and to command the gates of death—the gates of hell—to be lifted up before the face of so great a king and so magnificent a conqueror. He called together, I say, these most chosen ranks of disciples, announcing that the mysteries of human redemption were now to be completed, saying:

[Col. 0495A] “I have compassion on the multitude, because behold, they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat.” “Behold,” he says, “the time has come to show compassion; the time in which, through my blood, that flaming sword must be quenched, so that the flowering garden of paradise may be opened to the co-heirs of my kingdom, long afflicted, who have remained with me, their Redeemer, in hell for three days. They have remained with me, I say, before the Law, under the Law, and under grace, as though for three days; and yet they have nothing to eat, because they have not yet been brought out of hell, nor transferred from darkness into light, nor deserved to taste amid the delights of sweetness me, the bread of life whom they hunger for, me, the fountain of life whom they thirst for.”

And if I send them away fasting to their home, they will fail on the way. For if, after the three days are completed, I send them away fasting—if I delay inviting them to the great supper prepared at the price of my blood until they return to their home, until they receive an incorruptible body in the glory of the resurrection—they will fail on the way that leads to life, because apart from me, who am the way, truth, and life, they will find no other. On the way, I say—that is, in the faith in which they have awaited me with laborious expectation—they will fail if, now that my death has intervened, they do not immediately receive the kingdom so long desired.

[Col. 0495C] But some of them came from afar. Did not righteous Abel come from afar, whose blood began to cry from the earth in the first age of the world? Did not many others before the Law and under the Law endure the long darkness of hell, until, in the fullness of time, mercy and truth came through Jesus Christ? How ineffable was the angels’ joy at their liberation, and what and how great the exultation of new expectation, is sufficiently manifest from this most sweet answer, by which they reply to the Lord as if with an uncertain question:

“Whence can anyone satisfy these with bread in the wilderness?” What or what kind of question this is from the citizens above, Paul, who knew the secrets of heaven, declares in sweet-sounding speech. He testifies that, through the Church, the manifold wisdom of God makes known to principalities and powers in the heavens the dispensation of the hidden mystery, so that they see and understand, in the Church’s daily-sacraments, certain things of the judgment of God’s secret counsel which they cannot comprehend by sense and intellect.

For although the angelic host saw that the opposing wall of enmity had long since been destroyed, although the compassionate Lord said that he had compassion on the multitude which had now waited three days, nevertheless, not knowing whether, now that all things had been completed, he would descend to hell in person, or whether perhaps he would prolong still further delays until, at the sounding of the last trumpet, he restored to each person the twofold robe of immortality, it desired more fully to search out the hidden treasury of secret mercy: whence, or who, could satisfy them in the wilderness of hell.

[Col. 0496A] “Compassionate Lord,” they say, “long indeed and laborious is the expectation by which this most chosen multitude awaits you in hell, where there is a place of horror and vast solitude as long as the brightness of your vision alone is lacking. And who, sovereign Lord, can satisfy this multitude in the infernal wilderness, when the presence of your majesty alone delights them? No delight, no table of new refreshment can any longer be prepared for your hungry ones if you, the spotless Lamb, now sacrificed, delay to fill them with the joy of your countenance.”

Thus, as the citizens of the heavenly country rejoice at the redemption of this multitude that had awaited the Lord for three days, and thus as they answer the most gracious Redeemer with a sweet question, the order of the Gospel narrative subsequently indicates what he himself, in turn, answered by a similarly questioning response with tender invitations of mercy:

And he asked them: “How many loaves have you?” And they said: “Seven.” Let us therefore consider what sweetness and delight this most gracious question contains, when no one doubts that the very fountain of knowledge is ignorant of nothing. He who knows all things asks how many loaves they have, making known to them by his questioning what he was about to do, because the angelic spirits could not yet perfectly know that those captives were to be recalled to the great supper—the supper of the spotless Lamb.

[Col. 0496C] It is as though he said: “Who refreshes you, eternally satisfied with the rich fatness of divine wheat? Who has enabled you to share in the everlasting delights of my sweetness? I indeed am the living bread, making you feast eternally at the unfailing banquet of my divinity; but I can no longer restrain the abundance of my compassion for these afflicted people. Now, then, when the time of promise is complete, I shall invite them to the feasts of eternal sweetness, which I have prepared for them at the great cost of my own blood.”

Thus the blessed ranks of angels, fully instructed concerning the redemption of this multitude which had awaited the Lord for three days, declare that they have seven loaves, with which they desire this same multitude to be satisfied in abundant sweetness. For what is this sevenfold number of loaves but that sevenfold Spirit? “We have received,” they say, “seven loaves from you, the giver of all things, when the sevenfold grace of your Spirit filled us, so that the everlasting brightness of your vision might be for us complete and unfailing satisfaction without weariness. But now, sovereign Lord, a new and singular joy comes upon us: that captive people of saints, now to be brought forth from the prison-house, will increase the number of our order, diminished for so long.”

[Col. 0497A] Seeing their rejoicing, the invincible goodness of that same Redeemer no longer delayed to visit in person those who were in darkness. The Gospel discourse subsequently indicates with clear reasoning in what bosom of repose, and in what delightful dwelling-place of tranquil rest, he immediately commanded his redeemed to be placed:

And he commanded the multitude to recline upon the ground. Jesus, it says, commanded the multitude to recline upon the ground. By this ground, upon which he commanded the most chosen multitude to recline, what worthier or more exalted thing can we discern here than the paradise of delight which the Lord planted in the beginning? This indeed is the flowering land, the habitable and spacious land, which the confession of the thief, repenting late, obtained to possess when the crucified and most gracious Redeemer said to him: “Amen I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

In this honey-sweet land of paradise, the people of saints, rescued from the dominion of death and hell, reclined in great joy. For it deserved to see the conqueror of death himself reclining with it. Then truly the goodness of eternal divinity was delightfully gladdened—a goodness which testifies that its delights are to dwell with the children of men. What rewards of blessedness, and how great, it then received from that wondrous generosity, the subsequent order of the Gospel narrative indicates.

[Col. 0497B] Taking, it says, the seven loaves, he gave thanks and broke them. Let us recall what has already been said: that the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit may be understood, in sound interpretation, through the seven loaves. When the same Redeemer took these in his own hands and distributed them to his redeemed, he truly gave the greatest thanks, because he multiplied grace upon grace for those to whom he bestowed not merely the adopted pardon of sins, but also the unchangeable glory of eternity.

But now the narrative expresses something new of hidden mystery: that it pleased such great Majesty to break the aforesaid loaves with his own hands. For the breaking of these loaves must be understood as the full manifestation of the sevenfold Spirit. Dissolving the seven seals, he opened to them every power hidden within, and disclosed in full knowledge that he and the Father are one in substance. The chosen Son of God the Father himself indicates that this knowledge of unbounded Majesty is undoubtedly everlasting life, where he addresses the Father thus: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). It follows:

[Col. 0497D] And he gave them to his disciples to set before them. And they set them before the multitude. The loaves are rightly said to have been given to the disciples—that is, to angelic spirits—to set before the multitude. For through their ministry a reward worthy of the labours of the saints will be repaid. And because it is certain that the cause of the entire judgment is likewise determined through their ministry, the same Son of Man declares plainly in these words: “The Son of Man,” he says, “will send his angels, that they may gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. 13:41).

For if the blessed ranks of angels are sent to gather out of the kingdom of God every scandal, then surely the ministering spirits, sent for the service of the elect, come and distribute to them rewards proportionate to their merits. Hence, when the captivity that had long been captive, brought out of hell, was about to receive the delightful feasts of paradise, authority and knowledge were given by the Mediator of God and men to the aforesaid disciples—that is, to the angelic spirits—concerning the place in which each elect soul should be set, so that a seat and rest might be given it among their nine orders in a rank suitable to its dignity. It follows:

[Col. 0498A] And they had a few little fishes; and he blessed them and commanded them to be set before them. The angelic spirits, whom we have above said should be understood spiritually by the disciples, may now again be perceived under the mystical signification of the little fishes. The blessing of the supreme Trinity, by the hand of mighty mercy, preserved these chosen little fishes—truly small and insignificant in their own eyes—when Lucifer, who rose in the morning, fell from heaven like lightning.

“He blessed them,” it says, “lest, consenting to iniquity, they should set their throne in the north and judge themselves equal to the Most High.” He also commanded them to be set before the unbounded light, in an eternal state of immutability, so that from him upon whom they desire to gaze they might always be satisfied with most abundant sweetness. How great an abundance of sweetness those aforesaid exiles of Christ received when they became sharers and fellow-partakers in the blessedness and glory of these angels, the Gospel’s subsequent statement declares:

[Col. 0498C] And they ate and were satisfied. Eating and feasting among so many thousands of angels, they were truly filled with wondrous sweetness. For he himself, who is the true and unfailing refreshment of all the blessed, became both their fellow-guest and their banquet.

## 713. HOMILY LXXI. A THIRD HOMILY ON THE SAME SUNDAY, PERHAPS THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

David, sitting in the chair, the wisest prince among the three, is like the tenderest little worm of wood (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 23).

By the name of this David we may not unfittingly understand Christ in his divinity. According to the interpretation of the name, he may rightly be called “strong of hand” or “beautiful in appearance,” since in his divine nature he possesses such strength that he encompasses heaven and earth by a psalm, and is so desirable in appearance that the vision of him is the refreshment of angels and of all the saints.

He is also said to sit in a chair, by which expression his incarnation is not absurdly understood; for just as one sitting in a chair rests, so divinity rested in humanity. Christ can also be understood through one sitting in a chair according to his human nature, because just as a chair is properly called the seat of teachers, so he likewise delivered, in the days of his flesh, all the teaching which he himself bestowed upon human beings. For we, entangled in the filth of earthly corruption, could not hear one speaking from heaven and were not fit to hear or comprehend the words of his divinity.

[Col. 0499A] No one of sound understanding is ignorant that the word *wisest* belongs to him most fittingly. What human being ever could or will be able to make himself equal to his wisdom—he who, throughout his whole life, throughout his entire way of life in this world, said and did all things in wisdom? The following word, *prince*, also aptly agrees with him, because he, the true man born of the Virgin, surpassed all human beings in wisdom, humility, and strength, and alone was able to live in this world without sin.

He was indeed prince among human beings because, as we have said, his life and manner of life surpassed the life and manner of life of all other people from the beginning of the world. Yet he was among, not alongside or above, the three, through whom we may understand the three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Our Lord Jesus Christ was among the three because, according to his human nature, he was beneath the substance of the holy Trinity.

He is like the tenderest little worm of wood. It is clear, therefore, that whatever is easily broken and quickly bent is called tender, just as an infant is said to have tender limbs because they can easily be broken. Thus this word *tenderest* can be most fittingly applied in mystery to the Lord God, because nowhere in heaven or on earth is there anything which can so easily be broken and bent from its hardness. How then do we say that he can be broken and bent, whose supreme strength is known?

[Col. 0499C] In this sense, certainly: no one is so wicked, no one so wrapped in the filth of sins, that his mercy does not, so to speak, break and bend him toward himself, if only that person repents and says from a truly repentant heart that he has sinned. Even if someone persists in contempt of him until the very end of life, if at the moment of death he seeks him without despair through repentance and confession, he is indeed broken and bent, because through mercy he is propitiated without any difficulty for the grave sins of a sinner grown old in sin. Therefore he is rightly and most consolingly called *as the tenderest* for wretched sinners, because he is most merciful.

[Col. 0499D] And it should be noted that it says, “He is *as* the tenderest,” as though it said: “In likeness to his divinity, in which through unbegotten goodness he is tenderest because most merciful, so also in his human nature, which he assumed for our sake, he is pre-eminent in mercy and compassion.” He is also not unjustly called a worm of wood, because just as a worm is born from earth without sexual union, so he was born without conception from noble earth—that is, from virginal flesh.

Nor is it without reason that he is called not a worm but a little worm; for although he alone was conceived, born, and lived in this world without sin, he is nevertheless humbler than all others. This is also why, when it says, “He is as the tenderest,” it immediately adds, “a worm of wood”: because that mercy proceeds from ineffable and incomparable humility. Though he is free from every sin both in the manner of his birth and in his life, he nevertheless does not disdain, as we have said, to be reconciled even with great and desperate sinners.

Again, in another manner we may understand our Lord Jesus Christ in his Passion to have been like the tenderest little worm of wood, because there, while the just one suffered for the unjust, the innocent one for sinners, he endured not only grievous but even unworthy things beyond all sinners, and appeared in human eyes as one most despised. But where he appeared tenderest—that is, most despised—there he was undoubtedly strongest. Let us therefore hear how great the strength of this tenderest one is, and how fittingly he can be compared to a worm of wood.

[Col. 0500B] For just as a worm in wood secretly consumes the wood, with no one knowing or seeing, so our Lord Jesus Christ in his Passion in some manner secretly consumed and destroyed the original sin which our first parents, Adam and Eve, committed in the wood. I say secretly, and consumed it with no one knowing; for amid so many and such great mockeries, amid so many humiliations of scourges, spittings, blows, the cross, and other sufferings, no one could know or investigate whether anything such as this was in him—that he could consume and blot out the sins of others—when he endured such unworthy and abject things in his own body. The strength of this tenderest little worm of wood is commended even more clearly in what follows:

[Col. 0500C] “He killed eight hundred,” it says, “in one onset.” In his Passion the Lord Jesus killed eight hundred, because he killed by the sword of his Passion the eight principal vices, the whole multitude of vices generated from them, and every power of evil spirits, who are the instigators of these same vices. I say that he killed them in such a way that they will never be able to exercise over believers such power as they had before his coming, both over the just and the unjust.

Before the incarnation of the Son of God, evil spirits held dominion generally over the entire human race and exercised their tyranny beyond measure, so that there was no person of such holiness, no one who practiced so strict a discipline of life in this world, for whom it was not certain that after death he would descend to hell like a sinner and evildoer. But when the Lord appeared in the flesh and, after the death of the cross, penetrated the bars of hell with great power and majesty, their power was taken away. They lost it not only over all the just and faithful, but also over every sinner and unrighteous person.

[Col. 0501A] Let us consider, then, that first thief hanging on the cross beside Jesus, who persisted in the obstinacy of his unbelief almost to his final breath. By one confession he deserved paradise in that same hour; and we may know that evil spirits lost the tyranny of their wicked power even over sinners themselves, provided that sinners are found at their death with true repentance.

The Lord Jesus did this in that one onset, when he committed his spirit into the Father’s hands and, crying with a loud voice, expired; and his soul descended to hell through the power of his divinity. Yet by this one onset we may also understand the coming of the Holy Spirit. Although the Lord killed all vices and the evil spirits themselves by descending to hell, rising, and ascending, he nevertheless extinguished them especially then, when, having sent the Holy Spirit from heaven like a certain onset, he enlightened the hearts of believers. These are the wondrous and magnificent works of this David sitting in the chair, namely Christ Jesus, God and man: works which divinity did in humanity and humanity in divinity. It follows:

[Col. 0501B] After him, Eleazar, the son of his uncle Aoy [Vulgate: Ahohite], among the three mighty men, who were with David when they reproached the Philistines. By Eleazar, whose name means “God’s helper,” the apostolic order may not unjustly be understood, because the apostles were Christ’s helpers and vicars. Hence, when in his Passion he was sought by the soldiers of the priests and Pharisees, knowing that his apostles would be his helpers, he forbade those seeking him to kill them, saying: “If therefore you seek me, let these go” (John 18:8).

And it should be noted that he is called the son of his uncle Aoy. The Jewish people was the paternal uncle of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh; it can be represented by the name Aoy because it could be called the brother of the Lord God almighty, namely of the Father—not according to merits, certainly, but according to the legal commandments which he had given it. For that people alone at that time possessed knowledge of the Scriptures and knowledge of God. Thus it was in some manner joined to him by kinship.

[Col. 0501C] And this name Aoy, which is interpreted “of thorns,” also fittingly belongs to the Jewish people because of that cruelty which it impiously and maliciously exercised against the Son of God—its kinsman according to the flesh—Christ the Lord. The apostolic order was the son of this people, because it was carnally descended from it.

“Prince,” it says, “among the three mighty men.” This apostolic order, because of the surpassing privilege that it deserved to follow and hear the prince of the living and the dead himself, openly living and teaching in this world, was indeed prince among all mortals. Yet it was among—that is, beneath—the three mighty ones: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For although, as has been said, the apostles were appointed princes over all the earth, they could by no means attain to the substance of the holy Trinity or to the power of its divinity.

“Who were with David,” it says, “when they reproached the Philistines.” We may understand this in two ways. In one sense, these words may be taken to mean that the three mighty ones—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in whose three persons there is one Godhead, equal glory, and coeternal majesty—were with the true David, the Lord Jesus Christ, when he descended into hell with the power of his divinity, which he has with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0502A] There he gave everlasting reproach to those Philistines—that is, the evil spirits—to whom he had appeared in this world weak and despised. Having taken their spoil, that is, the souls of all the righteous, he cast them down, so that they might never again dare to raise their head against God’s elect, so as to be able to lead them after death with themselves to hell as they had done before.

We may also not unfittingly understand by the Philistines, whose name means “falling through drink,” the Jews, who were so intoxicated by malice that they even broke forth into madness. When the Lord set heavenly things before them and performed many good works among them, they hurled countless reproaches at him. Finally, to the height of their misery, they increased their insults beyond measure. Amid all these many and great reproaches, which the Son of God made man endured from the impious for the human race, the three mighty ones were with him, because the divinity which subsists in three persons never departed from him.

Again, in another sense, we may understand the apostles here: that Scripture signifies in this place, when it says, “who were with David when they reproached the Philistines,” that they were present at all those insults which the Jews shamefully directed against our Redeemer. During the thirty years in which he was hidden in this world, he endured no insults from the impious, nor did he join his holy apostles to himself within those years. But after those years had passed, when he began to devote himself to the word of preaching, he chose the apostolic order; while they were present and lived with him, he endured from the Jews innumerable vexations from those who reproached him, even to the death of the cross.

And they were gathered there for battle. The adversaries of Christ, stirred up by evil spirits, were gathered “there,” that is, against his humanity, which may be understood by this word “there,” because it was localized; and against it, by plotting, reviling, and finally killing, they waged a very harsh war. Yet they could not reach “here,” that is, his divinity, which may be understood by “here,” because it is present everywhere. Therefore, since the holy apostles were present at all these reproaches, we rightly believe that they are signified here when it is said: “Those who were with David, when the Philistines reviled him and gathered for battle.”

In what follows we may perceive more clearly how rightly Eleazar, whose name means “God’s help,” may be understood as the apostolic order. For Scripture here more plainly suggests and expresses how, after the passion, resurrection, and ascension of Christ the Lord, he became his helper.

“And when the men of Israel had gone up,” it says, “he stood and struck down the Philistines, until his hand grew weary and stiffened upon the sword.” By the men of Israel, just as by the Philistines, we may not inappropriately understand the Jews. What then is meant by “when the men of Israel had gone up”? When a man goes up, he lifts himself on high. The Jews therefore went up because, after killing Christ the Lord by hanging him upon the wood, and after he had overcome that disgrace by the power of his resurrection, they still tried to raise themselves against him in pride, wishing to remove his memory from the earth. But when they had thus risen in pride and wished to blot out the name of Christ from beneath heaven, the apostolic order stood firm—confirmed and established in truth by the coming of the Holy Spirit. It stood firm, I say, because it defended Christ’s cause against those public enemies, the Jews, fighting strongly and manfully with the sword of God’s word; and, it says, “he struck down the Philistines.”

Indeed, the apostolic order struck the Philistines—that is, the Jews—with a grievous blow, when by its preaching it publicly and confidently affirmed that he whom they had killed because of their deadly hatred for him had risen and, ascending, had sat down at the right hand of God the Father. Nor did it cease to bear witness to the truth until its hand grew weary and stiffened upon the sword—that is, until life wholly failed within it, and it was killed because of its unconquerable constancy in preaching. Thus the hand—that is, the life—of the apostles failed, and stiffened upon the sword, while the cruelty of the rulers of this world raged against them; while, distressed by so many torments, crushed by so many persecutions, and finally delivered over to death, they fell. And “upon the sword” is well said, because they fell with the word of God, which is understood by the sword.

How do we say that they fell with the word of God? Surely in this way: they were unwilling first to be silent about God’s word, until, slain through the boundless cruelty of their persecutors, they lost their lives. Did not James’s hand fail and stiffen upon the sword when he fell, killed by Herod on account of that very word? But Scripture seems openly to declare here how great a fruit would follow from their death. For it says:

“And God wrought a great salvation on that day.” After the holy apostles had delivered their bodies to death to prove God’s truth, a great salvation was wrought on that day—that is, in the Church, which then began to be enlightened by their teaching. For countless peoples obtained salvation for their souls, because they no longer doubted that those things were true which the holy apostles proved even by their own death.

“And the people who had fled returned,” it says, “to strip the spoil from the slain.” The people of the Jews and the Gentiles had then fled through disobedience, when, while the apostles were still alive and earnestly preaching the word of God in order to convert and soften their hearts, they resisted by refusing to believe what was said by them. But when, as we have said, the apostles did not hesitate to prove by their death the very Truth which they preached in words, the people returned to strip the spoil from the slain—that is, to imitate the merits of Christ’s apostles, punished by death; and they became defenders of the right faith, though shortly before they had been its enemies and persecutors.

Or thus: the people who fled returned to strip the spoil from the slain, when all the faithful eagerly desired to carry away and venerate their dead bodies, and rejoiced even to touch something of the remains of those whom, while they lived, they had once despised.

But the order of martyrs rightly follows this apostolic order. For the text reads thus:

“And after him, Shammah son of Agee [Vulgate: Age] of Harar [Vulgate: Arari].” Nor without reason does this name Shammah, which means “where is?” or “hearing,” suit the order of martyrs. For in their time, while such madness of persecutions raged, the well-known cry among unbelieving peoples was “Where is he?” For those who were heard to be worshippers of the Christian religion were ordered to be sought everywhere, both in the caves of rocks and in the caverns of the earth, as well as in public places.

Let us hear the interpretations of the following names and consider how well these too fit this order of martyrs. Agga means “speaking” or “meditating,” while Merari means “mountainous”; for the holy martyrs themselves, meditating day and night upon the law of the Lord, always spoke of mountainous things—that is, things lofty and heavenly. In their time there was this station of the Philistines, of which we presently read:

“And the Philistines were gathered in a station.” A *statio* is properly called the gathering which takes place at solemn observances of distinguished persons, just as the *statio* of the lord pope is commonly called the place where he has gathered with leading persons to celebrate a solemnity. Thus in this passage we may understand the station of the Philistines as, so to speak, the solemn assembly which the demons, figured by the name Philistines, held among the rulers of this world. And because those rulers pursued worldly pleasures and avarice, almost the whole world was through them, as it were, in the station of demons, because it succumbed to the same vices, as the ensuing text makes clear:

“For there was there a field full of lentils.” By the field the world is understood; by lentils we may understand the pleasures and desires of this world. The field was full of lentils because the whole world was devoted to pleasures and carnal desire, so that all its concern was to be able freely to enjoy vain delights according to its desire. Hence also, as another ancient history relates, Esau sold his birthright for one dish of lentils (Gen. XXV, 33). And because the holy martyrs preached that these things should be despised and heavenly things desired, the Philistines—that is, the demons through their representatives, namely the rulers and lovers of the world—cruelly persecuted them. Thus, when the terror and dominion of evil spirits, who worked through and in the rulers, had seized almost the whole world, so that few dared publicly to profess that in Christian poverty they sought heavenly things, many fell away from the faith which is in Christ Jesus because of the cruelty of their persecution. Hence it is fittingly added:

“And when the people fled from before the Philistines.” Thus, while evil spirits raged through the rulers of this world against all believers by avarice and greed, the people fled; that is, as we have said, some, terrified by the enormity of their cruelty, fell away from the integrity of faith. But while the peoples fled from before the Philistines, what did the order of martyrs do? “He stood in the midst of the field”: strengthened by the power of God’s virtue, it refused to depart from the path of right faith and could never be moved either by the world’s prosperity or adversity. But what did it do? “He defended it”: that is, by his preaching he defended the Catholic faith, and, in defending it, fearlessly endured even a cruel death.

Then he also struck down the Philistines—that is, evil spirits or the rulers of this world—because, when he did not hesitate to die for the truth, he strengthened the faithful in Christ’s faith and caused many also to turn from the error of unbelief. Hence follows: “And the Lord wrought a great salvation.” Through the killing a great salvation was wrought, while many, pierced by their example, abandoned the vain superstitions of idols, and some likewise gave their own bodies over to tortures for God’s sake. It follows:

“And three had also previously gone down.” After Christ and the apostles, the order of martyrs is also followed by the order of patriarchs, prophets, and priests of ancient times—earlier indeed in time, but later in dignity.
