We therefore think that in the order of this text they were placed after those three, namely Christ, the apostles, and the martyrs, because they were certainly of lesser dignity, although in their own days they excelled all others then living in the merits of virtues. Scripture does not leave unspoken whom these three preceded, saying: “And three had also previously gone down.” And it should be noted that it says, “had gone down.” By this descent we may understand that, although they lived righteously, all nevertheless entered after death into the lower regions of the earth—that is, into hell. For the incarnation of the Son of God had not yet taken place, nor had Christ yet fastened to the cross that handwriting of the decree which was against them.

“Who were leaders among the thirty,” it says. The aforesaid fathers were leaders among the thirty—that is, among those who observed faith in the Holy Trinity and the Decalogue of the Law. And although the Law had not been given in the days of the patriarchs, some nevertheless, recognizing the Creator in created things, lived lawfully. Among these the patriarchs were leaders because they excelled in virtues.

“And they came at harvest-time to David in the cave of Adullam.” By the cave of Adullam, whose name means “their assembly” or “their testimony,” hell is fittingly signified. For before Christ’s coming all, both righteous and unrighteous, gathered there; and this was their testimony: however they had lived, after death all alike descended into that one place. The harvest-time mentioned here was when, in the fullness of time, that grain of wheat which had fallen into the earth was cut down—that is, when the Son of God, true man, born of the Virgin, fell in death.

When he had died upon the cross and his soul, with the power of his divinity, descended into hell, those of whom we have spoken came in the cave of Adullam to David, namely to the Lord Christ himself, who visited them in hell when he did not find them in the world, calling upon him with this tearful cry: “You have come, O Desirable One, whom we awaited in darkness.” This time, therefore, in which these things were to be fulfilled, had not yet arrived; yet it was present in predestination. Hence Scripture uses the past tense for the future: “They came at harvest-time to David in the cave of Adullam.” But before these things were done, the following words indicate what meanwhile was occurring in the world:

“Now the camp of the Philistines was stationed in the valley of the giants, and David was in the stronghold.” What does “the camp of the Philistines was stationed in the valley of the giants” mean, except that evil spirits ruled the whole world amid such blindness of sins and so deep a darkness of ignorance, and that depth of vices was so strong and, so to speak, so gigantic that no one could escape it? Some indeed at that time, like those of whom we have just spoken, abstained as far as possible from actual sin and lived devoutly and soberly in hope; but through original sin all were nevertheless placed under the dominion of those same evil spirits. For our David, the Lord Jesus, was still in the stronghold—that is, in heaven—resting in the bosom of the Father’s majesty, and had not yet, in assumed humanity, marked the world as his own possession by the ink of his blood upon the wood of the cross. It follows:

“Moreover, the station of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem.” Bethlehem was a city of the Jews, interpreted as “house of bread.” And it is rightly interpreted as “house of bread,” because God gave his Law and teaching to the Jewish people dwelling there. In this city of Bethlehem, therefore, was the station of the Philistines, because evil spirits held their solemn assembly among the Jewish people when, having received knowledge of the divine Law, that people itself performed deeds of wickedness and avarice. For each person prepares within himself a seat for evil spirits and heightens his guilt before the Lord all the more insofar as, by living perversely, he knows better what he ought to do or avoid. Thus the devil reigned more in that people which, after knowing God, served wickedness and worldly pleasures than among the Gentiles, who had been instructed neither by the Law nor by the prophets. But while all things held deep silence and night pursued its course, that began to be fulfilled which Scripture immediately adds.

“Therefore David desired water from the pool.” After man had deserved, by violating the divine commandments, to be excluded from eternal blessedness, the desire of the true David, namely the only-begotten Son of God, was always that such water might be brought to him as would quench his thirst; that is, that at some time, through his incarnate presence, the hearts of human beings—dark through ignorance and somehow muddy through sins—might gain true knowledge and purity. For, by the innate sweetness of his compassion and mercy, he thirsted for human salvation. Hence he found it delightful to take part in human miseries, as he says in the book of Wisdom: “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. VIII, 31).

From this same desire these words were also spoken: “O that someone would give me a drink of water from the cistern in Bethlehem, beside the gate!” A cistern has water from heaven. And the compunction born of love for God and desire for the heavenly kingdom is rightly understood by the water of the cistern. Therefore the Son of God desired that the time might someday come when God’s love would be so poured out in human hearts that they would be moved to compunction not only because of sins, but also through love for God and desire for the heavenly kingdom. For before he himself became man for human beings, no one could be thus moved to compunction for the heavenly kingdom—unless, as several other witnesses read, he knew very well that after death he would descend to hell.

> **[Note: Col. 0507D]** “Unless” (*nisi*) in place of “without/that not” (*quin*), as in several other witnesses.

After Christ fulfilled by his incarnation what he desired, all the elect are moved to compunction with this confidence of hope: that after this valley of tears they will enter the gate of life. The cistern also, which, as we have said, has water from above, may very fittingly signify baptism. For the sacrament of baptism is from above, not from below. Before becoming man, therefore, the Son of God knew in his predestination that this water of baptism would be drawn in Bethlehem—that is, in the Church. And it is rightly said to be “beside the gate,” as though to say, near the entrance of the heavenly kingdom, because unless one is reborn through this water, one shall not enter the gates of heaven.

But before he visited the world, it was unknown what these things were. Many indeed foresaw in faith and hope that they would come to pass, but did not yet possess them in actuality. Hence our true David, that is, the Son of God, desired that these things be fulfilled; and this was in some manner the expression of his compassion when he grieved over human misery: “O that someone would give me a drink of water from the cistern in Bethlehem, beside the gate!” That is: O that the time might at length come when, through the water of baptism which is to be in the Church, a drink might be given to my thirst, so that through this human salvation, for which I thirst, might be accomplished, and human beings might receive forgiveness of sins and deserve entrance into the heavenly kingdom! Did he not seek this drink when he said: “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John III, 5)?

“Therefore the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines, drew water from the cistern which was in Bethlehem beside the gate, and brought it to David.” By the name of these three mighty men, as above, we may understand the patriarchs, prophets, and priests. They were indeed mighty who at that time broke through the camp of the Philistines—that is, who were able by the merits of their virtues to resist the evil spirits under whose power the world then stood. And by the expression “broke through” (*irruperunt*), said as if “broke inwardly” (*intus ruperunt*), we may understand this: although outwardly they could not yet obtain in actuality the grace of which we have spoken, inwardly in spirit they fixed, as far as they could, all the intention of their hearts upon God’s grace to be received.

They drew water from the cistern which was in Bethlehem beside the gate, because they believed that the sacrament of baptism would come to be in the Church and that by it entrance into the heavenly kingdom should be opened. Did not that eminent patriarch Noah, who at God’s command made the ark into which he would enter when the flood-water overflowed, learn by God’s own revelation that the making of this ark signified the future Church, and the flood-water the water of baptism, through which all outside the ark—that is, outside the Church—would perish, while those within the ark—that is, within the Church—would be saved? Did not David, when he said, “Bless God the Lord in the churches, from the fountains of Israel” (Ps. LXVII, 27), foresee in spirit the future water of baptism? Was not this very thing revealed to that chief and eminent initiate of God, Isaiah, when in the joy of his heart he said: “Let the desert rejoice; let the wildernesses of Jordan rejoice”? Surely he was not ignorant when, that he might be established and confirmed, he prayed thus: “Let your ancient true counsel come to pass.” Do all these not seem to you to have drawn water from the cistern which was in Bethlehem beside the gate, in the manner we have described?

“And they brought it,” it says, “to David.” What does “they brought it to David” mean except that they offered their faith and hope to God, praying that what they possessed in faith and hope he would someday accomplish in actuality through himself? But what follows?

“But he would not drink it.” Although many perfect persons who could exist at that time clung to God in faith and hope, he nevertheless would not yet transfer them into his body—that is, he deferred transferring them to the fellowship of angels—because that original sin through which angel and man had become enemies of one another had not yet been removed in his blood. But what did he do? “He poured it out to the Lord.” Thus the Son of God poured out to the Lord, namely to his Father, the faith of the ancient Fathers who longed for his presence in the flesh: by his inspiration he taught them to offer God the sacrifice of their faith.

The words which follow are judgments expressing the compassion with which he grieved for those who clung to him in faith: “May God be gracious to me, that I should do this.” This is as if he said: May God, the omnipotent Father, who in his predestination disposed that I should be incarnate, hasten his propitiation, through which he decreed to show mercy to the human race through me, so that the time may at length come when, through his obedience, I must become man for human beings; “that I should do this,” that is, that I should leave outside my body those joined to me in faith because original sin requires it, rather than, having become Mediator of human beings unto God through human nature, being no longer able to despise them.

“Shall I drink the blood of these men who went forth, and the peril of their souls?” That is: I cannot now, nor ought I, receive into my body those whom original sin—that is, the disobedience through which they went forth from paradise—and actual sin, which is the peril of souls, defile. Therefore he would not drink. This is what we have said: the Son of God neither would nor ought to transfer into his body those who, though possessing faith in him, were enveloped in the guilt of original sin.

It follows: “These things the three most mighty men did.” Who are these three except the patriarchs, prophets, and priests of ancient times, so often mentioned already? What and how great were the things they did? Certainly these: as we have said, they broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water from the cistern which is in Bethlehem beside the gate. That is, through the faith and hope by which they clung to God, they withdrew themselves as far as they could from the common life of other mortals, and believed that one would someday come who would consecrate the water of baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and that through his blood the gates of heaven, long closed, would be opened by the font of regeneration. By this long-suffering of their faith and hope they did this: the Son of God could no longer restrain himself from being moved with mercy toward the human race and, as we have said, desiring to assume human nature for their salvation, so that he might transfer them into his body.

Having thus together indicated these three—the patriarchs, prophets, and priests—he now proceeds to commend specifically the dignity of the order of patriarchs. For he says:

“Abishai also, the brother of Joab, son of Zeruiah, was chief of the three.” Abishai means “father of sacrifice,” and by this name the order of patriarchs is not inappropriately signified. For of many of them it is specially recorded that they offered sacrifice to God. The first father of sacrifice was Abel, who offered God a lamb from the firstlings of his flock; then Noah, who built an altar to the Lord and sacrificed a burnt offering upon it. That supreme patriarch Abraham too proved a great father of sacrifice, for at God’s command he determined, had he been permitted, to sacrifice his only heir; and there were many others whom it would take too long to enumerate.

This order of patriarchs offered many sacrifices to God in its days, but it could not thereby be saved. Why? Because he was brother of Joab, which means “enemy,” and son of Zeruiah, which is said to mean “bound” or “constricted.” In this he was brother of the enemy and son of one bound or constricted: just as hell swallowed up after death this world which had become God’s enemy and was bound and confined beneath the devil’s yoke, so he too likewise descended to hell after this life. For the death of the Mediator had not yet intervened to remove that enmity which had arisen in the first parents through disobedience. This order was chief of the three because it excelled the prophets and priests.

“He is the one who raised his spear against three hundred, whom he killed.” A spear is longer than the other weapons soldiers usually carry; and by it long-suffering may rightly be figured. This long-suffering is well attributed to the patriarchs, for they remained in this world longer than other people and were wearied by a long expectation in faith and hope of their redemption. Let us bring forward the patriarch Noah and consider the steadfastness of his long-suffering. He remained in this life nine hundred and fifty years, yet, though overcome by no weariness of age, he did not cease to serve his God long-sufferingly and patiently.

And it is rightly said of this order that “he raised his spear against three hundred.” For by that long-suffering of which we have spoken, as far as was possible at that time, it strove to mortify in itself evil desires and every wicked work and word.

“Renowned among the three and more noble than the three, he was their chief.” This is the same point we made before: he was older in time and nobler in virtue than the prophets and priests. For he had not received through the Law the rule for living well, and yet knew how to live justly and lawfully. But he had not attained to the first three. It is as if he said: although the order of patriarchs possessed great excellence through the merits of virtue, it could not reach Christ and the apostles and the greater ones, who are rightly called first, not in time but in dignity. It follows:

“And Benaiah son of Jehoiada, a very mighty man, of great deeds, from Kabzeel.” Benaiah means “builder,” and this name rightly suits the order of prophets. For through the words and writings which they left in the world, the holy Church began to be built. This prophetic order is fittingly called the son of Jehoiada—that is, the son of the knowledge of God—for above all who had been in the world before it, it possessed divine knowledge and was aware of heavenly mysteries. For the Lord did nothing on earth without revealing it to his servants the prophets.

“Son,” it says, “of Jehoiada, a very mighty man.” When the order of prophets is called the son of God’s knowledge, it is also signified to be the son of him whose knowledge it possessed. And the words “a very mighty man, of great deeds” rightly suit him, because he is the mightiest of all spirits; and according to the Prophet: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. CX, 2). “From Kabzeel,” it says, that is, from the assembly of God. The angelic spirits may fittingly be called the assembly of God. He is of them, not as one among them, but as their Creator and ruler, as the maker of his creature. Since the prophetic order was the son of this very mighty man, it is fittingly added concerning it:

“He struck down the two lions of Moab, and he went down and struck down the lion in the midst of a cistern on snowy days.” By the two lions of Moab may be understood the kings of Judah and Israel, who, devoted to the avarice of this world, did not rule God’s people well. The prophetic order in some sense struck them down when in its prophecy it declared that God’s wrath threatened them because of their injustice.

Was it not a grievous blow when a certain man came to Bethel and, while Jeroboam stood over the altar offering incense, foretold that a king named Josiah would be born who would sacrifice the priests of the sacrifices upon that very altar? And when the king stretched out his hand so that the man of God might be seized for these words, his hand which he had stretched out against him withered, and he could not draw it back to himself (III Kings XIII). Thus also the prophet Elijah in some sense struck King Ahab when he met him going down to Naboth’s vineyard to possess it unjustly after Naboth had been killed, and said to him in the word of the Lord: “You have killed, and moreover taken possession. In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, they shall lick your blood also” (III Kings XXI, 19).

Another of them, namely Micaiah, also struck down that same king with a most grievous blow when he said that the Lord had revealed to him that, in order to deceive him, a lying spirit had been allowed by God into the mouths of all his prophets, so that, consoled by their deceitful promise of peace, he might go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead. By the third lion mentioned here, the priestly order may be understood. The prophetic order also in some sense struck this lion in the midst of the cistern on snowy days, when it rebuked him in prophetic speech because, in the temple of the Lord, where he ought to have offered lawful victims to God first for his own sins and then for those of the people, he directed his efforts instead toward satisfying his avarice.

It follows:

“He also struck down a man worthy of spectacle.” By this man we may understand the Jewish people, who are called worthy of spectacle because they were made an exalted people by God and offered a great spectacle to all nations of the earth because of the dignity they had received. “Having a spear in his hand,” it says. The Jewish people held a spear in its hand because it possessed the Law, the Temple, and the fatherland. The prophetic order struck this people too, because it did not use the laws of its God well, in the same manner in which, as we have said, it struck the aforesaid three lions, namely the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah.

Thus it says: “When he had gone down to him with a rod.” The rod was that correction by which prophetic speech rebuked injustice. “He forcibly wrested the spear from the hand of the Egyptian,” because in its preaching it foretold that the power and glory of the Jewish people—designated by the name Egyptian because of the blackness of its sins—by which it ruled many nations, would be removed and reduced to nothing; that vengeance would overtake it according to the deserts of its crimes; and that, by God’s power and by the power of rulers whom he allowed to come against them by his decree, it would suffer punishment. Such was Antiochus, who went up to Jerusalem, entered the sanctuary in pride, took everything away, carried out a great slaughter of the people, and returned to his own land; earlier Nebuchadnezzar; and after the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and ascension, the Roman rulers Titus and Vespasian, who, after burning the city, devastated the entire Jewish nation, killing some and leading others into captivity. The prophetic order foretold that all these things would come upon them. Hence it is rightly said here:

“These things Benaiah son of Jehoiada did, and he was renowned among the three mighty men,” because he too was great among those three orders of which we have spoken—namely the patriarchs, prophets, and priests—who were more noble among the thirty, that is, more excellent in virtue than those who possessed only faith in the Holy Trinity together with observance of the legal commandments. Yet he had not attained to the three, because he was far inferior to Christ, the apostles, and the martyrs.

But these same words, which we have referred to the order of prophets, may also fittingly be referred to Christ. By Benaiah, whose name means “builder,” our Lord Jesus Christ may be understood, because he is that builder who constructs the heavenly Jerusalem, composing its structure from living and elect stones. He struck down the two lions of Moab, namely original and actual sin, which may be understood by the two lions. And he went down and struck down the lion in the midst of the cistern on snowy days. By this third lion death may be understood, which Christ killed when he himself died. “In the midst of the cistern,” it says, because, according to the prophecy of the Psalmist, “he wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. LXXIII, 12).

“He also struck down a man worthy of spectacle, having a spear in his hand.” This man may signify the ancient enemy, who is called worthy of spectacle because his assaults must be guarded against by diligent vigilance of heart. Christ killed him, when he held a spear in his hand—that is, power and dominion over the whole human race—with the sword of his passion. Thus, “when he had gone down to him with a rod,” that is, when he had humbled himself unto the death of the cross, which may be understood by the rod, he forcibly wrested the spear from the hand of the Egyptian: by the power of his divinity he took away the power of the prince of darkness by which he ruled the whole world. “And he killed him with his own spear,” because the very power which he exercised over the righteous and the unrighteous became the cause of his death. These things Benaiah son of Jehoiada did: that true builder, the Son of God, who, himself being the cornerstone, joins all the living stones, each one in its proper order.

## HOMILY LXXII: FIRST HOMILY FOR THE EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. VII).

The words of this holy Gospel are part of the sermon which the Lord delivered on the mountain. The crowd remaining in the valleys could not hear it; only the disciples could hear it, for they were of such perfection that they deserved to fulfill in deeds the very things which their devout Master taught. They rightly heard upon the mountain, because this teaching is great and wonderful and belongs to the mountains—that is, to the elect and perfect—who, living under the discipline of divine instruction, can confidently say with Peter to their Lord and Master Christ: “Behold, we have left all things and followed thee” (Matt. XIX, 27).

He leaves all things who abandons not only the earthly goods possessed outwardly, but also, renouncing every unjust desire and will, despises whatever gave transitory delight and seemed sweet according to the flesh. To those who renounce the world in this way, the supreme perfection commended by the Gospel discourse is unquestionably to be imitated and followed.

“Beware,” says the Lord, “of false prophets.” By the name of false prophets we may understand evil spirits in another sense. They are not inappropriately called false prophets because they labor day and night for this one purpose: by their lying and falsehood to make a person depart from the true Truth, which is Christ, and to judge good as evil and evil as good. Therefore the Lord, desiring the salvation of his elect and at the same time considering the malice and snares of false prophets, says, “Beware”—that is, direct all your faculties and your whole desire upward, or direct them to this one end: do not consent; do not receive evil as good or falsehood as truth.

734 “For they come to you,” he says, “in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.” What does it mean that these false prophets are said to come in sheep’s clothing, when, as incorporeal and invisible spirits, [Col. 0513C] they never use garments? “The words,” the Lord says elsewhere, “which I speak to you are spirit and life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64). The flesh of the Lord’s words is their letter. “But the letter kills; the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Therefore let us follow the life-giving Spirit within the flesh of the words—that is, within the letter—and let us see spiritually how the aforesaid prophets come in sheep’s clothing.

Mystically, by the clothing of sheep are understood diabolical suggestions; by the sheep, simplicity or innocence, or rational perceptions. And rightly are the suggestions of malign spirits expressed by clothing. For just as a person is covered with garments so that the naked body may not be seen, so they too, displaying righteousness openly, [Col. 0513D] clothe and cloak themselves in such a way that one can hardly discern whether their suggestions are useless or good. For the thoughts which they introduce into the heart appear so innocent and simple that they are sometimes received with desire, and, once received, are believed to be just and holy. For they know that, if they attacked openly through disgraceful sins—if they assaulted spiritual persons with capital crimes, that is, murders, adulteries, and the like—some would be so steadfast and prudent that, although they would resist with labor and difficulty, nevertheless, with God’s help, they would reduce them to nothing. And therefore they come in sheep’s clothing, because they deceive a person by actions that seem highly reasonable and wholly harmless, as though under the appearance of holiness. To those who come, as we have said, in sheep’s clothing, 735 [Col. 0514A] the Lord indicates what they are and what they do in secret:

“But inwardly they are ravening wolves.” For malign spirits inwardly—that is, in their intention, which is wholly perverse and wicked—are savage wolves, ravening wolves. Paul makes clear that intention is one thing and thought another when he says: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning thoughts and intentions” (Heb. 4:12). These four terms which are set down—joints, marrow, thoughts, and intentions—show that there is a distinction between thoughts and intentions. By joints thoughts are signified, because, just as limbs are joined to limbs, [Col. 0514B] and bones to bones by joints, so thoughts likewise adhere to and are knit together with thoughts. By marrow, however, are signified those very intentions of thoughts which proceed from the depths of the heart.

It sometimes happens that a person supposes that he has conceived and thought good and praiseworthy things in his mind. But when, by reading or hearing the word of the Lord, he has been enlightened from above, then without doubt he sees that the whole intention of his thoughts was perverse and useless. These false prophets, therefore, against whom one must be on guard, are inwardly—that is, in their intention—ravening wolves. It is characteristic of a wolf to seize what belongs to another in order to devour it, always to pant after what belongs to another, and not to allow to live what it cannot devour, because of the innate fierceness of its wickedness. Thus too malign spirits are always ready to devour [Col. 0514C] the souls of the elect; and although it brings them no benefit and diminishes none of their punishments—indeed, although by hastening to destroy souls they acquire greater torments for themselves—nevertheless, because of the malice innate to them and the enormity of their hatred, they never wish to cease from the slaughter and assault of the righteous. Let us see why they are called ravening wolves.

For *rapax* (“ravening”) is so called as though *ad rapiendum audax*, “bold in seizing.” Now bold is he who dares both what ought to be dared and what ought not to be dared. This aptly applies to those invisible enemies of ours, who dare what ought to be dared 736 when they make little of leading headlong into whatever disgraceful sins they please those who are in the world and live worldly lives, and when they claim and subject to themselves hearts abandoned by God. [Col. 0514D] But they dare what ought not to be dared when they boldly hasten to assail and overthrow with the harsh goads of temptations those who have made praiseworthy progress in the spiritual life and in the growth of virtues. Therefore, just as Truth himself graciously taught us to beware of and guard against false prophets, so Solomon recommends the same thing in plain words when he says:

“Keep your heart with all vigilance, for life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4:23). For it is fitting that those who hasten in heart and mind toward the dwelling of everlasting blessedness should strive, insofar as they can, to guard the innermost part of their heart with every vigilance, and to resist watchfully those spiritual wickednesses which no weakness of the flesh, no necessity, ever hinders or delays. [Col. 0515A] They are present to those sleeping and do not leave those who rise; they anticipate us when we desire to watch in prayer, and under a covering of piety they promise and introduce such things as, later, when recognized through God’s inspiration, lead not to joy but to grief and mourning. Whoever neglects to observe this and does not guard against these false prophets remains in death; but whoever has a heart firm and fortified against their snares will inherit eternal life. Therefore, that their malice may be known and avoided more clearly, the Lord adds and says:

“You will know them by their fruits.” And he immediately indicates what their fruits are, saying: “Do men gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” Their fruits are useless fruits; their fruits are thorns and [Col. 0515B] thistles. By thorns and thistles two kinds of temptations may be understood, by which the ancient enemy is especially accustomed to assail spiritual people: by the thorn, which is strong and hard, pricks, tears, and draws blood, avarice; by the thistle, which is soft to the touch but likewise pricks, tears, and draws blood, the soft and unclean desire of lust.

737 We must understand by avarice not only the desire for temporal things, but also ambition for human favor and honor. This thorn—that is, the immoderate love of seeking what ought not to be sought—remains so fixed and inborn in us through the fault of our ancient parent that we can scarcely, or not at all, be freed from this plague. For when our first parents possessed great honor and surpassed every earthly creature both in dignity and [Col. 0515C] in knowledge, they desired to know more, and to know and seek what it was not expedient to know or seek. Thus we are always pricked by this thorn, that is, by the disease of avarice; we are always made to bleed. For we always seek honors, always praise; we always desire to be exalted, always to be regarded and honored above what we are. We are always driven by these thistles—that is, by the incentives of carnal desires—and are often wounded and torn. For as long as we bear this corruptible body, whose necessities of eating and drinking we cannot deny, so long are thistles of evil desires found in us; they are scarcely quieted, scarcely restrained from reigning in us. Let there be pride, anger, or envy [Col. 0515D] that devastates us: these, so to speak, are sometimes checked in us. Avarice alone, evil desire alone, awakens another law in our members, opposed to the law of our mind. For although the body is marvellously afflicted by abstinence over many years, still our enemy—that is, the flesh which we bear—hinders us, alas, with alluring desires.

From these two temptations that most holy man David, of whom the Lord says, “I have found a man after my own heart,” asks to be delivered when he says: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice” (Ps. 118:36). And immediately afterward: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (ibid., 37). For when vanities and outward appearances are taken in through the sight of the eyes, things badly seen are at once badly desired within. Solomon recalls us from this vanity when he says: “Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain” (Prov. 31:30). Whatever beauty appears outwardly in a human being is nothing but the putrefaction of worms and ashes. Solomon expresses these two kinds of temptation when he says: “The leech has two daughters, saying: ‘Bring, bring’” (Prov. 30:15). By the leech 738 [Col. 0516A] is understood the devil, who sucks the blood of the human heart in order to take away from human hearts the life of the soul, which is Christ. Its daughters are avarice and luxury, those two insatiable things always saying, “Bring, bring,” because these are the two vices by which the whole human race is most greatly tempted and assailed, from which all evils arise and streams of wickedness are spread over the whole earth. [Col. 0516B]

Therefore, when malign spirits have fixed these thorns and thistles in us, “Do they,” says the Lord, “gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” Certainly not. For a grape is far different from a thorn, and something far different is gathered from figs than from thistles. By grapes is expressed the ardor of fear; by figs, the sweetness of love. These are the two impulses by which we turn away from evil and delight in doing good. The ardor of fear causes a person to turn away from evils; the sweetness of love causes him to persist in good things. We ought to be so surrounded and fortified by the continual exercise of this fear and love that, if God at any time grants prosperity in carnal or spiritual matters, the urgency of fear may never slip from memory amid prosperity, nor the sweetness of divine love grow cold amid adversity.

[Col. 0516C] “Thus every good tree bears good fruits, but a bad tree bears bad fruits.” This addition to the saying, “thus every tree,” seems to me to be a recapitulating connection with what precedes. For it is as though he said: Thus, by being watchful, thus by guarding oneself from false prophets, every good tree—that is, every good person who has hope of one day rising to life—brings forth from himself good fruits, the sweet fruits of fear and love of God. But a bad tree—that is, a bad person who keeps no guard over himself—produces the bad fruits of thorns and thistles, that is, avarice and lust, to whose dominion he is shamefully enslaved because he has no hope of rising to life.

Moreover, in these three verses we may identify three [Col. 0516D] times. In the first, “thus every good tree,” is the present time, which consists in good action; in the second, “a good tree cannot,” is that time which is now the repose of souls; in the third, “every tree,” is the future time, which will be in eternal recompense. 739 Therefore every good tree should strive to offer fruit to God in good action, because, when stripped of the body, it will come to the other time which is now the repose of souls, where certainly what the Lord here says will hold true:

“A good tree cannot bear bad fruits, nor can a bad tree bear good fruits.” For the souls of the elect, established amid the wonderful and astonishing goods of their Creator, do not bear bad fruits, because they can sin no longer. Likewise, a bad tree—that is, a sinful soul—after the end of this life can neither perform good [Col. 0517A] fruits thereafter nor is ever permitted to make satisfaction to God for the evils it has committed in the past; rather, it will have eternal punishments to pay, because, as the day of death finds each one, so he will be judged before God, as follows:

“Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire.” Notice that he does not say every tree which did not bear, but every tree which does not bear good fruit, is to be cut down and cast into the fire. Every tree—that is, every person—who has committed few good things and many evil things, if at his end he recognizes himself and repents in true contrition of heart with the worthy tears of repentance, truly, so to speak, bears good fruit; and he is blessed here and is to be blessed, to be joined to the reward of heavenly fellowship. And [Col. 0517B] because no stain will enter that heavenly kingdom, whatever mark of sin he has brought with him may thereafter be purged in purgatorial fire and redeemed by alms or sacrificial offerings of prayers. Such a tree will not be cut down or cast into the fire.

But, on the other hand, there are some who throughout the whole time of their life struggled to devote themselves to pious labors and pious deeds, but who, alas, later fell into worse things and did not bring their works to completion in a blessed consummation in God. Thus, departing from this world, they will be cut off from the fellowship of the righteous and cast into the fire of eternal condemnation. And because it cannot easily be discerned and known here which is the portion of the saved and which the portion of the damned, it will without doubt appear at the time of recompense, when they rise not to life—indeed, to [Col. 0517C] life—so that, living, they may die more unhappily in death. 740 Then a joyful and ample outcome unto life will be opened to the righteous, when death has been swallowed up in victory and they are wholly transformed into a certain divine affection. And because what is hidden here in action is manifest there in recompense, therefore, he says, “You will know them by their fruits.”

He had first said, “By their fruits you will know them,” and again, “From their fruits you will know them.” For then the righteous see perfectly and plainly how useless and wicked were the fruits of the malign spirits whom they resisted and to whom they did not consent. They also see and know, though these things are now hidden, the fruits of the righteous and of sinners, how they were borne headlong toward every shameful act; and to the latter recompense will then also be rendered [Col. 0517D] according to the wickedness of their contrivances. Of them he immediately adds:

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven shall enter into the kingdom of heaven.” He truly and faithfully confesses the Lord, his Lord, not merely once but in repeated confession, who believes that the same one is both his Creator and Redeemer, and has adorned that faith by the witness of works. But not everyone who holds that same faith while contradicting it by works will enter the kingdom of heaven. Rather, he who does the will of my Father—that is, he who, by guarding himself from false prophets and keeping his heart with all vigilance, has, by the grape—that is, the ardor of fear—and the fig—that is, the sweetness of love—overcome [Col. 0518A] the thorn of avarice and the thistles of lusts, and has borne the good fruits of the good tree—he will one day be raised to the heights of heaven and rejoice in the everlasting vision of almighty God.

For this reason this Sunday is the eighth in number, signifying to us that eighth day of our future resurrection, when we shall rise with body and soul and must be led either to eternal joys for good deeds or to the punishments of Gehenna for evil deeds. For although the seven Sundays which we have celebrated are sufficiently festive and renowned, this eighth Sunday is the greatest and most celebrated, in which, so to speak, a certain prelude to our future resurrection is set forth: when God’s elect, stripped of every infirmity of the flesh, go wholly into God 741 and thereafter will be, as it were, one spirit with [Col. 0518B] the Lord.

The whole of today’s office looks toward the glory of this great dignity which the righteous will then receive from the hand of the Lord: after the general judgment, at the very entrance of heaven, so many thousands of saved monks, clerics, and virgins dedicated to God stand before the supreme Pontiff, Jesus Christ, and burst forth in great joy of heart, singing to the Lord in this way: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” (Ps. 47:10). As though, congratulating one another in the harmony of heavenly music, they say to the Lord: “O Lord God, whose greatness has no end, whose wisdom has no number, whose peace surpasses all understanding: that we have conquered the world and the devil, [Col. 0518C] that we have resisted our own flesh, that you have now made us sharers in your blessedness—this we have received solely from your free mercy; and this in the midst of your temple, that is, in Christ, who willed to become mediator of the temple—[the transmitted wording is corrupt or uncertain]—and by his death to reconcile God and humanity.”

“According to your name, O God, so also is your praise unto the ends of the earth” (ibid., 11). Every person is called by a proper and particular name in order that it may be known who he is. It is as though they say: “All that we once heard concerning you while dwelling on earth, through which we were found worthy to know and recognize you somewhat as through a mirror and in an enigma, we now see face to face. And we have received even greater and more magnificent things concerning you than were spoken to us, [Col. 0518D] because according to your name, so also is your praise—that is, in accordance with the magnificence of your name you have magnificently dealt with us, for you have wonderfully glorified not only our souls but also the ends of the earth, that is, our bodies, by raising them from the dust.” “Your right hand is full of righteousness” (ibid.). That Son of yours, who is understood by the right hand, alone is full of all righteousness; there are no merits of ours, no righteousness by which we could be admitted to the goods of so great a condescension on your part.

“Great,” they say, “is the Lord, and exceedingly to be praised.” You are great, O Lord, in your city, that is, in your elect; exceedingly praiseworthy on your holy mountain, that is, among your angels. Great in the city, because you have prepared the hearts of your elect so that you may be magnified in them as in your city 742; but exceedingly praiseworthy [Col. 0519A] on your holy mountain, because you are ever praised and adored with unceasing voice by all the orders of angels whom you have received into that ocean of sweetest contemplation and your divine brightness.

Very fittingly the Collect is also added for the Lord, in which this prayer is offered and spoken: “Graciously grant us, O Lord, always the spirit to think what is right and to do it, that we, who cannot exist without you, may be able to live according to you.” This is as though they said: “Once, surrounded by mortal flesh, we suffered manifold changes of vicissitude; and if at times it was granted us to cling to you, the body which decays immediately recalled us again and again to its accustomed changes. But now, O Lord, grant us not for a moment, or for the space of one day or one hour, but [Col. 0519B] always, continuously and perpetually, the spirit of thinking and doing what is right, that we who cannot exist without you may be able to live according to you.”

To live according to him is to be sharers in his eternal blessedness and glory: so that, just as he is supremely good and blessed, immortal, without sins, full and abounding in every good and delight, so they too, made exalted in every goodness, blessedness, and immortality, no longer hindered by any burdens of sins, may be rewarded with the highest and ineffable goods. This indeed is to live according to him. There God, who is without time, having become human in time, will be seen face to face by the whole multitude of the elect. There the words of the Apostle Paul, spoken in today’s reading, are truly fulfilled: [Col. 0519C] “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14). For then they are not restrained by servile fear or enticed by mercenary desire, but are always led by the Spirit of God, the Spirit of freedom, as sons of God.

The devout inhabitants of the heavenly homeland further raise in sweet melody the sonorous Alleluia: “A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall a vow be paid in Jerusalem” (Ps. 64:1). That whole city beloved of God, whose walls are living stones and whose foundations consist of companies of saints, is called Zion, that is, “watchtower,” because each person’s affections 743 lie open to every other. And since nothing is thought there except what is holy, [Col. 0519D], nothing desired except what is honorable, it offers, among other things, this great and wondrous joy: that they perceive nothing hidden from themselves in the secret places of a brother’s conscience. Nor is it surprising that such great increases of joy arise for them from knowing one another’s hearts, since even in this time of mortality it would be exceedingly pleasant and welcome if someone could know and see the holy thoughts and just desires of a good person, by which he delights and is refreshed with God and in God. Then all the righteous and elect will without doubt receive in reality what they now sing and seek in hope. Then, having received the double robe of bodies and souls, they resound in the harmony of heavenly symphony through the ages.

Therefore the verse that seems to indicate these same joys is immediately added by the singers: [Col. 0520A] “We shall be filled with the good things of your house; holy is your temple, wondrous in righteousness” (ibid., 5). Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and his fellow apostles, although distinguished by everlasting laurels, are not yet filled with the goods of God so long as they are concerned for the body which lies in the dust of the earth and is to be raised. But when death has been swallowed up in victory, and after the day of the general resurrection they are exalted with the two robes, as we have said, of body and soul, having obtained full joy they confess that they are filled with the good things of the Lord’s house, and they affirm forever that that temple is wondrous in righteousness. For truly that temple is wondrous in righteousness, where the wondrous righteousness of the Almighty has gathered not only all the holy and innocent, but also, by his wondrous [Col. 0520B] righteousness, has made unjust and sinful persons such through repentance that he willed them to become co-heirs of his kingdom, and foreordained and chose to dwell in them forever as in his temple. The long and well-articulated chant of musical notes seems not unfittingly to signify this wondrous righteousness, which will never end through the ages.

744 The Offertory and Communion suitably agree with these things, so that the jubilation of this Mass may be complete: “You will save the humble people, O Lord, and humble the eyes of the proud; for who is God besides you, O Lord?” (Ps. 17:28, 32). The Lord will save his people, his humble people, by placing them with himself in heavenly places; he will humble the eyes of the proud, whom he will condemn with their head—that is, the devil—to eternal [Col. 0520C] fires; and besides him there will be no God or Lord, he who alone is sufficient for all. But all these matters which we have touched upon are, so to speak, a song of gladness and exultation of holy souls proceeding after judgment with God and their Lord toward the palace of heaven. Let us now hear what is the reward of those who arrive, and what is offered or said to those already reigning with Christ: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9). Then, brought into the marriage feast of the Lamb, they are bidden to eat and drink at the Lord’s table in his kingdom; and the Lord himself, passing among them, will minister to them, because he will always provide in himself new joys and new delights, so that he himself may be the reward of those who love him—the eternal reward [Col. 0520D] of those who love eternally. That taste of eternal sweetness is unspeakable—indeed, inconceivable; it can be attained, but cannot be appraised. What will the wretched person do who then, excommunicated and cast outside, has received no place or communion among the celebrants of this festal Mass? It would have been better not to have been born for one whom, because his sins demand it, it has befallen not to share in this assembly. Therefore let us humbly beseech Jesus Christ, our advocate, that through his mediation and favor God the Father may one day deign to grant us peace and communion in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is our mother, where blessed and full joys are laid up, so that we may deserve to taste and see him who is desired without weariness and by whom we are satisfied without disgust. May he himself deign to grant this, [Col. 0521A] whose dominion endures for ages of ages. Amen.

745 HOMILY LXXIII. FOR THE SECOND EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

“The kingdom was therefore established in the hand of Solomon, and he was joined in affinity to Pharaoh, king of Egypt” (3 Kings 3).

This Sunday, which is the eighth in number among the seven Sundays which we have celebrated, signifies for us that eighth day of our future resurrection, when we shall rise with body and soul; likewise, wherever “the eighth” is written, the day of general judgment is signified. Both the nocturnal readings and today’s office indicate to us the distinguished proclamation of this eighth day. For we read tonight [Col. 0521B] how, after David’s death, the kingdom was established in the hand of his son Solomon. Accordingly, when David’s days drew near for him to die, and Adonijah his son, without his knowledge, attempted to succeed him in the kingdom, David summoned Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet and commanded that his son Solomon be anointed king; and he appointed him to reign after himself. But after King David’s death Scripture thus continues: “The kingdom was therefore established in the hand of Solomon, and he was joined in affinity to Pharaoh, king of Egypt.” By David may be understood God the Father; by Solomon, the Son of God the Father. The kingdom of Solomon is the eternity of the same Son of the eternal Father. That kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon, in the hand [Col. 0521C] of the Son of God the Father, when he himself, remaining for ever equal, coeternal, and co-omnipotent with that same Father, is eternally begotten of him as that which was from the beginning, and, set over all things both in heaven and living on earth, orders all things with the same Father and holds all things enclosed beneath the hand of his omnipotence.

But while in this co-presence of paternal majesty he lay, as it were, hidden in his divine co-essentiality, at last, having compassion upon human misery and providing for human salvation, he was joined in affinity to Pharaoh, 746 [Col. 0521D] king of Egypt. Pharaoh, interpreted as “one who destroys” or “scatters,” not inappropriately signifies the human race, which in our first parents, namely Adam and Eve, alas, wickedly squandered through disobedience the honor and glory of the heavenly dignity divinely bestowed upon it. This human race is called king of Egypt—Egypt meaning “darkness”—because before Christ’s coming every human being was in the region of the shadow of death: both because he governed himself badly amid the darknesses of the present life and because, after the darkness of this world, he descended to the darkness of hell. Therefore the true Solomon, that is, the true Son of God, was joined in affinity to this king of Egypt, to this human race. That affinity by which the Son of the eternal Father is joined to the aforesaid king of Egypt is the flesh which he assumed for us, and in which, though invisible, he presented himself as visible to human beings. And because affinity is customarily spoken of where persons become relatives through the parents of a wife, the nature of that affinity by which the Son of God was joined to the human race is made still more explicitly understood by the following text.

“For he took his daughter and brought her into the city of David.” The daughter of this aforesaid King Pharaoh is, as we have said, the flesh and nature of our race, which our true Solomon so took, so joined to the divine nature, that he can never be separated from it. “And he brought her into the city of David, until [Col. 0522A] he had finished building his own house, and the house of the Lord, and the wall of Jerusalem round about.” The city of King David is the homeland of eternal blessedness, the court of the heavenly kingdom—the city, I say, of the living God. Into this city, therefore, into this heavenly Jerusalem without doubt, the true Solomon, our Lord Jesus Christ, brought the nature of our mortal flesh which he had assumed, 747 [Col. 0522B] when, having performed and completed all for which he had come, after the disgrace of passion and death, after his descent into hell, after his resurrection from the dead, he placed this nature in heavenly places in himself above every angelic dignity.

“Until he had finished,” it says, “building his own house, and the house of the Lord, and the wall of Jerusalem round about.” What, then, is this house so illustrious which Solomon, the mighty king and lord, is still building on earth? We truly, who are still wandering amid the misery of this mortality, are that house which the heavenly Wisdom of the true Solomon is building and completing on earth. For he began, as it were, to build his own house—to make us a house of [Col. 0522C] sanctification—when through the sacrament of baptism he brought us to true faith. And as long as we are in the body, he does not cease to build, by inspiring good desires and increasing good works, until he completes it—that is, until, so far as is possible in this time of mutability, he makes us perfect in the merits of virtues. But when the burden of bodily dwelling has been removed and we have been brought into the joys of perfect security, then we shall truly be the house of the Lord, because, completely freed from the sins and vices which assailed us, we shall no longer be able to be touched by any stain, even lightly, either in thought or deed. In this blessedness of eternal glorification the souls of the elect now rest with the author of their redemption, until, when the general judgment has been completed, clothed with the double immortality [Col. 0522D] of bodies and souls together, they are perfectly conformed to the brightness of their Creator. Then that true Solomon, our Lord Jesus Christ, mediator of God and human beings, completes the wall of Jerusalem round about, when, as we have said, he will adorn his elect with such splendor of immortality that they may appear in glory with him without end, conformed to and made co-participants in that eternity, in body and soul.

That judgment which King Solomon rendered concerning the two women at the beginning of his reign also points to this day of final examination. For we read that [748] at the beginning of his reign two harlot women came to him, bringing their case before the king’s just judgment. One of them maintained that the other had taken her little child, [Col. 0523A], whom she had recently borne, in the silence of the dead of night, while sleeping indeed having crushed her own son. But when the other answered that this was not so and affirmed that her own son was alive, and they disputed before the king in this manner, the king ordered a sword to be brought to him and the child to be divided into two parts. Thus discovering the truth of the matter by this judgment, he commanded that the living infant be given back to its mother (3 Kings 3 [1 Kings 3]).

By these two women, as certain expositors wish, the prelates of holy Church may be understood. The woman who crushed her son while sleeping signifies those prelates who oppress their children—that is, their subjects—because they make no effort to preside over them and benefit them either by word or by example. But, on the contrary, those are called and are [Col. 0523B] most true mothers who preside over their subjects by living well and governing well, and who do not cease to spur them by the word of holy preaching toward advancement to a more eminent life. Thus, under the examination of the strict Judge, they are justly distinguished according to the quality of their merits. For good prelates will be exalted to the greatness of glorious recompense because of the praiseworthy fruit which they have gained in their subjects; but those who crushed their children by neglecting the life of their subjects will remain empty and without honor.

We may also, though it seems arduous and difficult for the unlearned, seek in these women a more subtle meaning. For by these two women may be understood two affections, namely good and bad, which [Col. 0523C] claim a dwelling for themselves in the chamber of the human heart and from which, so long as we are in this life, we can very rarely be wholly freed. A good affection exists when a person resolves to devote himself to the labors of a devout action; a bad affection exists when he seeks human praise for the good work which he has performed. For example, there is a person who has received this gift from God, that by the eloquence of saving teaching he may benefit others. When he is occupied in the labor of devout exhortation, this thought sometimes secretly enters into him: that in his teaching he may seek human praise more than the edification of his neighbors. [749] Thus he has, as it were, crushed his child while sleeping, because, vainly glorying in the reward of his work, he has deprived himself. But if, recognizing [Col. 0523D] this vanity in himself, he withdraws his mind from such an intention, he will deserve through God’s grace to receive his child alive. There is also a person who has this gift from God: that at the time of prayer he may wash away the stains of his former life in the fountain of tears. If he too, for the gift of compunction divinely bestowed upon him, desires more to be praised and loved by people than to please God alone, then, like the woman who crushed her son, he will remain devoid of the fruit of recompense. Yet if he makes satisfaction to God for these things by worthy repentance, he may, with God’s help, receive his child again.

These two women, therefore—these two affections—are joined to one another in the chamber of the human heart in such a way that the very person in whose heart these things take place can hardly recognize them. For as long as we are in this time of mutability, [Col. 0524A] we cannot fully know and discern who are those who serve the Lord in simplicity and who seek human praise for their labors. But when the day of judgment comes, when the true Solomon, our Lord Jesus Christ, sits upon the throne of his kingdom to judge the living and the dead, then in clear light it will be manifest to all which woman crushed her child and whose child lived; her living child will be given back to the true mother, while the other will be cast out empty and without honor. And who is fit to discern these things, who is fit to examine the works of all human beings, except him whose wisdom has no number?

750 Therefore, since the strict Judge and Lord will, in wholly just judgment, render to each the reward for his labours, [Col. 0524B] let us who are called by a spiritual name strive, by serving the Lord in truth, to bring our works living and entire before Christ’s tribunal, lest, though we seem in the present life to be engaged in pious labours, we be left without reward on the day of judgment. For just as in bodily generation both the woman who bears a living child and she who produces one dead suffer an equal torment of painful labour [cod.: “painful labour”], so it will be in the birth of spiritual children—that is, good works. For we who have professed the steadfastness of the spiritual life, if in our good works we desire to please the eyes of our Creator alone, shall be enriched with the recompense of eternal blessedness; but if we seek human praise for our labours, we indeed bear the burden of our labours, yet shall by no means attain the joy of the future reward. Let us therefore strive to persevere in works of righteousness in such a way that, in all we do, we seek solely the grace of divine mercy, seeking not our own praise but that of our Creator, so that he who is rich in mercy may himself become the reward of our labours, our honour and unfailing exultation and everlasting glory. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, he who lives and is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit through the infinite ages of ages. Amen.

751 HOMILY LXXIV. FOR THE FIRST [READING] ON THE NINTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST.

“There was a certain rich man who had a steward; and [Col. 0524D] this man was accused before him of having wasted his goods” (Luke 16).

Since our Lord and Redeemer has foreordained his chosen and faithful people as heirs of future goods, he has more fully declared in the present parable with what prudence their possession is to be sought. For he says:

“There was a certain rich man who had a steward.” In the name of this rich man the figure of the Redeemer is expressed, in whose house riches and glory truly abound. By his dispenser and steward is understood every human being endowed with rational understanding, who has undertaken, as it were, the governance of the household belonging to the Lord’s right: the substance of body and soul. A person is known to preside worthily and faithfully over this household if, with vigilant care, he prepares the senses of the soul [Col. 0525A] and the members of the body for the service of God alone. But a human being sold under sin often misuses his Creator’s good, when he governs the substance entrusted to him with insufficient care, seeking his own interests and neglecting those of the Lord. Hence the present passage immediately adds concerning that same steward:

“And this man was accused before him of having wasted his goods.” We waste the goods of the Lord entrusted to our faith when we bend to the use of wicked action whatever strength and ability we have received for carrying out the works of the divine will. Alas, because of the guilt of such imprudence we are badly accused before God, who is the Lord of vengeance; we are charged under witnesses altogether severe. For although it is certain that the eyes of the Godhead behold good and evil everywhere, [Col. 0525B] yet there are guardians and agents of ours, appointed by God the Father for this very purpose, so that we may know that through them all that we do is to be reported to the throne of justice. But although an evil report about us is often brought to the ears of the Lord of hosts, God, compassionate toward human misery, nevertheless does not withdraw the gifts of mercy granted to sinners.

752 For in his patience he delays punishing those whom he wishes to correct by repentance, rather than let perish through negligence. Therefore, when we spend the whole course of life in idleness and vanity, after he has long laboured in forbearance, he finally becomes zealous and avenging and truly does what is said in the present parable:

“And he called him to himself and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear of thee? Render an account of thy stewardship, for thou shalt no longer [Col. 0525C] be able to be steward.’” The Lord calls us to himself when, through the sentence of death, he sets a limit to life. He requires from us an account of our stewardship, because he examines and investigates most closely how much faith and how much diligence we have spent upon his goods. Since we are convicted of not having preserved these whole, but of having wickedly wasted them—alas!—we are no longer permitted to act as stewards, that is, to use those same goods in performing works of righteousness. But placed at such a turning-point of affairs, let us perceive what this steward did, not merely with the ear of the body, but also with the inward hearing of the heart. It follows:

“But the steward said within himself, ‘What shall I do, because my lord takes away the stewardship from me?’” By the example of this steward let us return to ourselves within ourselves, considering with anxious heart, while time is granted [Col. 0525D] us, that once the office of stewardship has been taken away there can be no performance of a good work. For when the use of life has been withdrawn, not even for a moment is the power to do good granted. Let each faithful person also ponder and observe what this steward says in what follows:

“I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg.” What more fittingly expresses, by the example of digging, a complete and worthy confession of sins? For just as one who digs covers over the outer things—or rather, brings forth what was hidden—so one who opens his heart by true and humble confession casts out whatever foul thing lay concealed in his breast; but if he remembers having done anything worthy of praise, he covers it more carefully in the hidden places of conscience. To dig, 753 therefore—that is, to confess sins—will not be lawful after death for one who, while it was permitted, had no zeal to do it. Then confession will be judged vain and fruitless; for “who shall confess to thee in hell?” (Psalm 6:6). It is also a mark of great shame to beg in that hour of necessity. Miserable and most unhappy is the person who happens to ask for help when the hand of God’s mercy has already been drawn in. Of such a beggar, rightly to be despised, Solomon says in Proverbs: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plough; therefore he shall beg in summer, and it shall not be given him” (Proverbs 20:4). For the person devoted to sloth and lethargy, who in the cold of this life does not persist in the labour of righteousness, shall beg needy and poor in the season of summer—that is, in the days of eternity—because with importunate cries he will seek the regard of pardon; but it shall not be given him, since the bowels of [Col. 0526B] God’s mercy will be closed against the wicked and idle. Yet this wise steward found a counsel altogether worthy of his prudence; by using it confidently he could escape the loss of the misery to come. For it follows:

“I know what I shall do, that, when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.” “While I am able,” he says, “I shall show favour to my lord’s debtors, so that when my strength has failed, I may deserve to obtain the benefits of their assistance.”

“Therefore, having summoned each of his lord’s debtors, he said to the first, ‘How much dost thou owe my lord?’” Here let us give ear to the inner person, that we may investigate more carefully why the Evangelist says, “having summoned each of the debtors,” as though he were about to relate matters concerning several persons, while he seems to mention no more than [Col. 0526C] two. By these words he teaches us more plainly what we ought to know and consider: we are debtors to our Creator in only two matters, namely, in perfect love of God and unfeigned love of neighbour. For on these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets. Therefore, that we may understand fully what we first owe the Lord, let us attend to the Evangelist’s words: “Having summoned,” he says, “each of his lord’s debtors, he said to the first, ‘How much dost thou owe my lord?’ And he said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’” By the name of oil, pure and sincere love of God is fittingly expressed; for as oil always rises above every liquid with which it is mixed, so the love of the Godhead, which never fails, surpasses and exceeds all things. Thus in the hundred measures [Col. 0526D] of oil is signified the completeness and perfection of divine charity. We are debtors to the Lord for this love, because we have received the command to love God in all things and above all things. But since, through the claims of sin, transgression of this command often occurs, let us give assent to the counsels of this steward, who counsels us piously and faithfully. For he says:

“Take thy bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.” What is sitting except presenting heart and body humbled before the sight of God? In this true humility, let us undertake the obligation of a more careful and upright life, showing the works of steadfast repentance that endures to the end. What is it to write fifty? For what we write remains more firmly than what we say. Thus every day, [Col. 0527A] throughout all the time we live, repentance must remain with us. And this must be written not sluggishly or slowly, but quickly and swiftly—that is, with a discerning and most fervent heart. For by such sacrifices of repentance God is won over. It follows:

“Then he said to another [Note: Thus the codex, [Col. 0527D]]: ‘And thou, how much dost thou owe?’ And he said: ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’” Since human life is fed and nourished by wheat, the full and perfect love of neighbour is rightly expressed by the hundred measures of wheat. For this same charity must be proved not in word and tongue, but by the performance of works in every need of a brother. Hence John says: “Whoever has the substance of this world, and sees his brother in need, and closes his bowels against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3:17). Therefore, that measures of oil, as [Col. 0527B] has been said, concern love of God, while measures of wheat concern love of neighbour, is rightly inferred from the fact that the first debtor is asked, “How much dost thou owe my lord?” but the second, “And thou, how much dost thou owe?”—the word “lord” being omitted. For in the enigma of oil we are admonished to render the Lord the debt of perfect love; but in the description of wheat we are commanded to extend the hand of assistance to our neighbour.

There is also another, more excellent way of this same love: to bear with gentleness and patience whatever annoyance or injury a neighbour inflicts upon us. For charity is patient 755 and kind; seeking vengeance from no one, it endures all things and bears all things. But because, under the compulsion of the frail flesh that we bear, we often stray from the path of this love, let us likewise hear [Col. 0527C] what this same steward judges must be done.

“He said to him, ‘Take thy bill, and write eighty.’” What is it to take the bill except to inscribe the meditation of heavenly words upon the tablets of the heart? For frequent meditation upon the Scriptures, if it is continually exercised in the mind, prevents whatever pain or annoyance comes from without from penetrating the depths of the breast. To write eighty also has great power for obtaining the merits of patience. This number, as is clearer than light, commonly presents everywhere the figure of resurrection, because the Lord’s resurrection is known to have occurred on the eighth day. Let us therefore write eighty: that is, without interruption let us keep the future resurrection in memory, and remember that we must all be manifested before Christ’s tribunal, so that each may receive according to what he has done [Col. 0527D] in the body. If we continually remember what trembling there will be in that examination, what terror of fear, we shall readily grant pardon to a brother who has injured us in whatever way. It follows:

“And the lord praised the unjust steward, because he had acted prudently; for the children of this world are more prudent in their generation than the children of light.” Truly—and it is grievous to lament—children of this world labour more earnestly for their business and affairs than children of light for the attainment of eternal salvation. For the rich of this world grieve to let an hour or moment pass in which they see that they have added nothing to their heaps of wealth. But who, I ask, can apply such zeal to spiritual business? O [Col. 0528A] how often we fail in our own affairs, we who commonly grow weary in gathering the works of virtues! This prudent steward, who provided well and profitably for his future, is truly worthy of praise and is accordingly set before all who are worthy of praise for imitation. Instructed by his example, let us so prudently provide for our future that we may one day deserve to be approved by the testimony of divine praise.

We have said these things briefly according to the sequence of the letter; but in a higher 756 sense, by “the children of this world” we may appropriately understand the children of this time, namely, the children of holy Church; and by “the children of light,” people of the ancient time, people of the Old Testament, whom almighty God illumined by the Law that he had given them. To them, indeed, it was commanded in the Law: “Thou shalt love thy friend and hate thine enemy.” And because they followed such a command, they were considered prudent in a certain way. But the children of this world, the children of the new grace, who according to the grace given in the New Testament love not only friends but even enemies for God’s sake, are truly more prudent than the children of light in their generation—that is, the generation of holy Church, which through baptism and repentance does not cease daily to beget spiritual children for God.

And because the whole of this parable tends to show how one who had wasted his lord’s goods may cleanse, through the love of God and neighbour, whatever he has sinned through his outward or inward senses, and thereby deserve to be praised by the Lord, we may also understand by [Col. 0528C] “the children of light” the evil spirits, whom almighty God created in such dignity and excellence that they ought to have remained children of light eternally, if they had humbly persisted in obedience and love of their Creator. But because through malice and pride they fell from that brightness of eternal light in such a way that they can never return to that genuine love of God and humanity, the children of this world—namely, the children of holy Church—are rightly more prudent than they and are so called, since even after a fall and transgression they can return through the love of God and neighbour.

And he rightly says, “in their generation.” This generation is a heavenly generation: the generation by which they are begotten of God, namely, by the grace of baptism, through which those who were children of wrath and children of the devil can be born again as children of grace and children of God. And in that heavenly generation they received what enables them to be more prudent than the children of light—that is, evil spirits—because after sin and transgression they know and are able to return and recover the salvation they lost through the twofold love, as [Col. 0528D] we have said, of God and neighbour. But since this most holy teaching of the Gospel reading concerns universally all who desire salvation, it is fitting that at the end of the parable it should set forth, as a special command, something for Christ’s special lovers, for whom these common things are insufficient, when it says:

[Col. 0529A] “And I say unto you: Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness, that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings.” As if he were saying: “I have spoken all these things in the parable generally to all who desire to be saved. For it is necessary that those who have wasted the Lord’s goods, as has been said, should endeavour to amend what they have sinned by loving God and neighbour and by showing that same love in deeds and words, so that, when they are thus reconciled to God, they may deserve praise and reward from him because they have acted prudently. Having spoken these things generally to all,” he says, “I say to you disciples, to you my special children, to you my imitators, who have left all things and followed me, that you should not only do these things but also add greater and higher things: [Col. 0529B] ‘Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness.’ That is, apply such vigilant and careful custody to your senses that there may be no dissension among them, but humbly subject your outward senses to the inward, and the inward senses to God the Creator. This is truly to make friends from the mammon of unrighteousness.”

Nor is it unjust that we understand the inward and outward senses of a human being by the “mammon of unrighteousness.” For since they are daily defiled by 758 sins, they are not inappropriately called riches of unrighteousness. However justly and however holily a person may ever have lived through outward or inward senses, so long as he remains in this life he cannot be without the blemish of unrighteousness. And he rightly says, “Make to yourselves friends.” For as long as spirit and flesh, opposing one another, are at variance with each other, our inward and outward senses are not our friends but our enemies. Therefore, as the Lord teaches us, we must make friends for ourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness: that is, without misusing the riches divinely granted us in our inward and outward senses, we must subject the flesh to the spirit and the spirit to its Creator, so that, when we fail—that is, when death intervenes and we are released from the miseries of this life—according to these joyful promises of the Lord, they themselves may receive us into everlasting dwellings.

These dwellings are our bodies, which are now fleshly, weak, and changeable, but shall be spiritual and eternal in the glory of eternal blessedness. There we shall enjoy them without misery and without any affliction of corruption; there flesh shall never oppose spirit; there the one who created us shall eternally preside and rule over our spirit, soul, and body: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

759 HOMILY LXXV. FOR THE SECOND [READING] ON THE NINTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST.

“There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and he was accused before him of having wasted his goods” (Luke 16).
