In this parable of the Lord, as also in the other parables of the Lord, the wise and learned can find manifold teaching for edification, if they hear externally the words [Col. 0530A] of the sounding parable in such a way that inwardly they seek the lessons of spiritual understanding. But for the foolish and negligent, who allow even what they have heard outwardly to pass by the deaf ear of the heart, there is only, as it were, the surface of the letter as a parable, since in it they seek no benefits of salvation and teaching. For they hear it for the moment as a parable, but neglect to fulfil in the effectiveness of good works what they have heard. But let us, insofar as we know and are able by God’s gift, hear the sounding letter of this present parable in such a way that from it we may take something for the use of our own edification.

“A certain man,” he says, “was rich and had a steward.” This rich man is truly that unique man, as we may perceive with sound understanding, who alone is singularly rich and powerful above all others, and who distributes the riches of his goodness to his faithful people in such a way that, although one receives more and another less from him, he nevertheless leaves none devoid of his riches. But the steward of this rich man is, as we judge, the spirit and soul of each human being, to whom this same rich man apportions many goods and many riches when he grants a sound body and upright, rational outward and inward senses. But if this steward does not use such great goods and riches well, and does not strive by good stewardship and governance to subject his body and senses to the service of his Lord, we must greatly fear what immediately follows:

760 “And he was accused before him of having wasted his goods.” Although the eyes of the Lord behold evil and good in every place, and not even the slightest movement of our thoughts can be hidden from him, there are nevertheless guardians assigned for this purpose—namely, angelic spirits—who report our works, whether good or evil, at every hour and moment to the divine sight. These guardians indeed rejoice and exult if they see in us anything good and right which they can report with joy and exultation to God our Creator; and although they sympathize and grieve over our evil works, which, alas, we commit very often, yet by the obligation of their office and ministry they nevertheless report them to the divine majesty. When they report concerning us those things for which we ought justly to be accused and rebuked, we are in a manner badly accused as having wasted the goods of our Lord. We surely waste the goods of our Lord by evil desires and wicked works, when we make no effort to accomplish through the senses of both aspects of the human being anything worthy of God or necessary for our salvation.

There are also other goods and other riches which every spiritual steward—that is, any good prelate—receives by God’s bounty. God often distributes to him teaching, knowledge, and many gifts of virtues, so that he may provide for his own salvation by living well and may benefit his neighbours by teaching and exhortation. When, by living rightly and teaching wisely, he has provided both for his own salvation and for fraternal charity, he begins to be spoken of before him as though he had wasted his Lord’s goods. But to be spoken of in this manner concerns not disgrace but good report, not dishonour but glory. [Col. 0531A] For he is indeed spoken of and praised by all, both for the merits and examples of holy conduct and for the wisdom and words of salutary exhortation. When he begins thus to be spoken of and praised among people, if he has not taken delight in human favour, he has indeed been spoken of, but not before the Lord, for whom he reserves the testimony of a good conscience alone. But if he vainly glories and exalts himself within himself in human praise, and does not fear presumptuously to ascribe to himself what belongs to God, he is said to have been accused not well but badly, because then the vain presumption of pride will be a sad and dishonourable accusation before God and his angels. For he wastes and scatters the goods of his Lord as though dissipating them, if from what he has done or taught well he seeks the glory of his own praise.

Hence it should also be noted why the text says not simply “having wasted,” but “as though he had wasted.” For when it says “as though he had wasted,” it secretly suggests that he has not made a complete dissipation. For the person who magnifies and exalts himself by boasting wickedly, and ascribes and attributes goods divinely bestowed upon him not to God but to his own merits, wastes the goods of his Lord not wholly but in part; nevertheless he does not cease to persist in pious works, and although in the meantime his right intention is diminished in the sight of the Judge, the exercise of his body is by no means diminished in human eyes. Yet, that he may at last turn from this vanity and come to his senses, the merciful Lord does not disdain to call him to himself, [Col. 0531C] as the Evangelist subsequently indicates:

“And he called him to himself and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear of thee?’” That this calling is one of compassion and grace can plainly be understood from the fact that he is said not merely to have called him, but to have called him to himself. He truly calls mercifully to himself the person whom he causes, through inward inspiration, to return to himself within himself; and he also indicates inwardly to him, through the language of compunction, how he ought to avoid the favours of vain glory, lest he receive the reward of his recompense here, rather than in the future. “What is this,” he says, “that I hear of thee?” Of thee, I say, to whom I committed the care of my stewardship, I hear something which by the just judgment of my equity I rebuke in thee. [Col. 0531D] For while thou showest and feignest thyself before people to be a good and perfect man, a steward administering well, thou appearest before me not such a person but another. I, whom not even the smallest thought escapes, know and consider what secretly murmurs in thy heart: namely, that thou dost not strive prudently or humbly to administer the stewardship entrusted to thee, and that from thy labours thou seekest not my glory but thine own.

“Render an account of thy stewardship.” I gave this account to thy soul: I mean rational understanding, by which, in governing thy stewardship rightly and profitably, thou oughtest to have fixed thy attention only upon heavenly things—not earthly, not passing things, but enduring ones—so that thou mightest administer the stewardship committed to thee not for the vanity of this world or empty boasting, but for the glory of my name alone. But thou hast taken this account away from me, and in the proud exaltation of thy mind hast not feared to give it to thine own will and thine own praise, since thou hast resolved, in administering the stewardship, to please not me but people.

“For thou shalt no longer be able to be steward.” Unless thou render and return to me alone this same rational understanding which thou hast taken away, unless thou strive with all thy might to devote all thy rational senses to the office of stewardship in such a way that thou seekest, in simplicity of heart, only the grace of my recompense, thou shalt no longer be able to be steward—that is, thou shalt not be able to administer thy stewardship profitably or fruitfully.

But when this steward, who is to be saved, has inwardly heard this from the Lord, he returns to himself, is salutarily pierced with compunction, and, speaking to himself, says:

“What shall I do, because my lord takes away the stewardship from me?” In this passage we may understand by stewardship the grace of heavenly visitation. When it is withdrawn from the aforesaid steward—that is, from a good prelate—he rightly laments that a great stewardship is being taken from him. For he immediately begins to diminish in spiritual sense and understanding when this blessed stewardship, this heavenly visitation, has been removed from him. Thus grieving and groaning over this same diminution, he expresses it in these words:

“I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg.” Just as a person who digs the earth turns over and casts out what lay hidden, so a person taught by divine inspiration searches out and brings forth, as if by digging, the spiritual meaning hidden in the letter. [Col. 0532C] But because, when stewardship has been removed and inward visitation withdrawn, as we have said, he cannot dig spiritually in this way, he sees his misery and poverty and rightly groans and grieves. “I cannot dig,” he says, “because I can see or find in the Scriptures, as I was accustomed, no spiritual understanding for my own edification or my neighbour’s benefit. I cannot dig because I cannot soften the earth of my heart, as I used to do, through the power of compunction. I cannot dig because I can bring forth from the earth of my heart no savour of the divine, no good thoughts.

“And because I do not deserve to be visited or comforted by the illumination of grace coming from above, I have come to such beggary and destitution of mind that I am ashamed to confess it before thee, O Lord, [Col. 0532D] and before people. But since, as has been said, I can no longer dig spiritually and am greatly ashamed to be a beggar, I must provide by prudent counsel for my beggary and weakness.”

“I know,” he says, “what I shall do, that, when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.” We have already said that this blessed stewardship is the visitation of an illumined mind. But one is in a certain sense suspended and removed from this stewardship when, in prayer, the customary grace of divine sweetness is lacking, and in reading no spiritual understanding shines forth. But in order that this grace and understanding may be recovered and renewed, he should prudently provide for himself so that his lord’s debtors may receive him into their houses. By the houses into which this man, removed from stewardship, desires to be received, we may fittingly understand, as we think, the practice of prayer and reading. For if the stewardship of spiritual goods has been removed, it cannot easily be recovered without continual devotion to prayer and reading. Therefore, wisely providing for himself, he indicates in these words what counsel he has found within himself: “I know what I shall do. I know how I shall provide in the future for my want and need: namely, I shall devote all diligence and all labour more carefully to prayer and reading, so that when I am removed from stewardship—that is, when I feel spiritual goods diminishing in me—then those things which I tasted in reading and prayer may return 764 to memory and, as though I had been received into the house of prayer and reading, may defend me against the poverty that comes upon me.” When a person has thus anticipated approaching evils and has taken care, by prayer and reading, to fortify and protect himself, then what the Evangelist subsequently says truly comes to pass:

“Having summoned each of his lord’s debtors, he said to the first, ‘How much dost thou owe my lord?’” Not without reason, we believe, is he said to have summoned each debtor, although no more than two appear to have come. For in these two debtors we may perceive with sound understanding the twofold love of God and neighbour. For in these two commandments, namely the love of God and neighbour, every human being is a debtor to his Creator. Thus this blessed steward, received into the aforesaid houses of prayer and reading, finds these two debtors within himself and asks with faithful inquiry how much the first owes his lord: “How much,” [Col. 0533C] he says, “dost thou owe my lord?”

“And he said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’” Just as oil rises above every liquid with which it is mixed, so God alone is to be loved above all things and before all things. Therefore perfect love of God may rightly be understood by the hundred measures of oil. Thus this steward arouses himself to better things by provident questioning, when with anxious mind he asks and examines how many things, or how much, he owes God his Creator. When he sees that he has sometimes transgressed the command of divine charity, he provokes and exhorts himself to repentance, saying:

“And he said, ‘Take thy bond, and sit down quickly, and write fifty.’” A repentant person takes his bond when, in truly repenting, he determines to undertake the purpose of a more cautious and stricter life. But for repentance to be true and fruitful, he must sit down quickly and write fifty. By the number fifty, repentance for sins is frequently signified in the Scriptures. A sinner who truly repents must sit down, lowering and inclining himself in the deep humility of the heart; and in this humility he must hasten to write fifty—which is true repentance—not slowly but quickly, not negligently but fervently. What we write is more settled and firm than what we say. 765 Therefore the manner of repentance must be written humbly, fervently, and firmly upon the tablets of the heart, so that it may never depart from memory until life’s end, because repentance must be humble, fervent, and steadfast. It follows:

[Col. 0534A] “Then he said to another [thus the codex], ‘And thou, how much dost thou owe?’ And he said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’” As we have said that love of God is to be understood through oil, so through wheat, by which human life is fed and nourished, we may understand love of neighbour. Therefore this prudent steward, because he remembers that he has transgressed against both loves, admonishes and instructs himself to perform worthy repentance for each transgression.

“Take,” he says, “thy bill and write eighty.” A transgressor against fraternal charity takes his bill when, instructed by continual meditation upon the Scriptures, he sees and understands how perfectly and faithfully our neighbour is to be loved in God. But because he sometimes sees that he has transgressed against this fraternal charity, he must write eighty. [Col. 0534B] Since the Lord’s resurrection occurred on the eighth day, our general resurrection is fittingly signified by the number eight. Therefore this steward, who is to be saved, ought always to have before his eyes, as if written, the time of the future resurrection, and never cease to consider with a fearful heart what he will answer the strict Judge on that dreadful day concerning the debt of fraternal love. If he considers this with vigilant mind, he not only loves his neighbours as himself, but also freely forgives those who sin against him; and so that he himself may deserve from the Lord forgiveness of many sins, he is always ready and prepared to remit to his neighbour whatever small and pardonable injuries there may be. When, as has been said, he strives to inscribe upon the tablets of his heart fifty—that is, true repentance—and eighty—that is, the time of the future resurrection—he will in some manner deserve to receive the upper watering and the lower watering. The upper watering is that God should be loved; the lower watering is that neighbour should be loved. The faithful soul receives the upper watering in the time of prayer; the practice of reading grants it the lower watering. It follows:

“And the lord praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently.” He who was previously an unjust steward because he had acted imprudently in wasting the goods of his lord, now deserved to be praised and magnified by the Lord because he acted prudently in repenting and making satisfaction for his transgression against the twofold love.

“For the children of this world are more prudent than the children of light [Col. 0534D] in their generation.” By the children of this world may fittingly be understood the hearers and doers of the New Testament; but by the children of light, the fathers who were founders of the Old Testament. He calls them children of light because the knowledge of the written Law which they had received illumined them; in accordance with the Law’s command, they knew only to punish and kill those who sinned and acted wickedly, and therefore they seemed to themselves to be prudent. But the children of this world—the children, I say, of grace and the Gospel—who not only love those who love them, but also, according to the Lord’s command, do good to those who hate and persecute them, are more prudent than the children of light in their generation: namely, in the generation of evangelical truth, the generation of faith and baptism. But because the Lord wishes to lead these same children of this world to perfection, [Col. 0535A] he deigned to set before them new commandments of charity.

And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tabernacles. By mammon, which is interpreted as riches, we may understand riches both spiritual and carnal. Hence within ourselves, so to speak, we can find these riches of iniquity, from which we may provide for ourselves most faithful friends. For the very faculty of perception and understanding of the inner person can sometimes, alas, be called mammon of iniquity, when it commonly meditates upon vain and empty things after the joys of inward delight. Yet this same faculty of perception and understanding often abounds in many spiritual riches, which it eagerly gathers by praying and reading, while in the sweetness of the heart it feeds and satisfies itself with the Lord. But because such riches are changeable and passing, they may rightly be called mammon of iniquity, because all changeableness of passing things is mystically called iniquity and vanity. Solomon, foreseeing this vanity or uncertainty in the Spirit, cries out, as though groaning and grieving, saying: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1:2). And because the souls of the elect and perfect are often disturbed by this uncertainty of vanity or changeableness, all spiritual stewards should make friends for themselves from the aforesaid mammon of iniquity—that is, from the foretaste of inward sweetness—which, when they fail, when they can have no inner experience of divine savor, may receive them into eternal tabernacles.

What we noted above should be understood by “houses,” we believe can again be understood here by “tabernacles”: namely, the practice of prayer and reading. For these are the best houses and the best tabernacles of those who serve God: the continual practices of prayer and reading. But so that they may be received into these houses and tabernacles in time of need, let them secure for themselves certain familiar friends in the hour of inward visitation. Therefore let them gather whatever they have inwardly tasted in prayer, whatever spiritual understanding they have discerned through reading, and preserve these things in the secret place of the heart, so that later, when they fail in this fervor, they may be refreshed and consoled from them.

There are also other friends whom we must secure for ourselves with every devotion and every intention of heart, whose mercy and help we especially need: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For no fellowship of friends can be greater or more delightful than that in which a mortal human being—earth and ashes—makes God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit his friend and neighbor.

There are also countless thousands of other friends: namely, the angelic powers and all the citizens of the heavenly homeland. Let us strive to be united and associated with them in joyful and blessed friendship, so that we may one day deserve to dwell with them in the eternal tabernacles, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

769. HOMILY LXXVI. FOR THE SAME THIRD SUNDAY.

“Let us not be desirous of evil things, as they also desired them” (1 Cor. 10).

In this day’s reading the blessed Apostle Paul sets before us five clauses, which, as we are given to understand from them, he arranged so orderly and distinctly not without the cause of a definite mystery. For he in whom and through whom God spoke could say or write nothing without cause, as he himself bears witness concerning himself: “Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). Therefore, in these words of his, in which he recalls certain things that once befell the fathers, we ought to seek something pertaining to our salvation; for, as he himself says a little later, “All these things happened to them in figure; but they were written for our correction.” For if they were written for our correction, when the blessed Apostle—who spoke by that Spirit which searches even the hidden things of God—recalls them in his Epistles, he wished us mystically to draw from them something by which we might amend and correct ourselves. “Let us not,” he says, “be desirous of evil things, as they also desired them.”

“Neither become idolaters, as some of them; as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and there fell in one day twenty-three thousand; neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and perished by serpents. Neither murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer.”

By these five matters, so expressly set forth, five stages in the growth of sin, through which a person makes himself guilty before God, are not unjustly signified: delight, consent, and the act of sin; habit; and the defence of sin. Let us explain why we think these five stages of sin are mystically signified in the five clauses set forth here.

Certain matters are found here which, according to the letter, sound more grievous, though punishment does not immediately follow them; while other matters are mentioned which, by human estimation, appear lighter and more pardonable, yet are described as having been punished with the severest retribution. Who would not think that the one who becomes an idolater is more guilty before God than one who tempts God or murmurs against the Lord? Yet these last two, which seem to be the least serious, are followed by the greatest punishment. In the first statement, “Let us not be desirous of evil things,” we understand that the delight of sin is indicated, against which the Apostle warns us to guard. For we are desirous of evil things when we begin to delight in those things which we have conceived in thought through the devil’s suggestion. Yet a suggestion—which a person can never lack in this present life—does not corrupt the soul if delight or consent does not follow; nevertheless, when sin comes into thought or memory, its beauty is in some manner dimmed.

For just as pallor sometimes stains a person’s face upon the skin, yet, if the flesh is not burdened by some other sickness, does not harm health, so, in order now to describe the face of the mind as well as of the body, and to fit the pattern of the proposed comparison, let us understand thought to be, in a sense, the skin of the soul. Its color of beauty is then changed and lost by a certain pallor, so to speak, when the suggestion of sin intrudes through thought. But just as, as we have said, it does not harm a person if his face is superficially overspread with pallor while his body is not wounded by the pain of any sickness, so the soul is not harmed by the suggestion of sin which comes into memory and thought, if it is not touched by the wound of sinful delight.

But if, after the suggestion by which the beauty of the soul is merely disfigured in thought, the delight of sin also follows, it is immediately wounded, because it is wounded by that in which it takes pleasure in its affection. If, overcome by our frailty, we cannot resist delight, we must at least take anxious care that, through the negligence of an unwatchful mind, the will or consent to sin does not steal in. For the soul is disfigured in thought by suggestion, wounded in delight, and killed in consent.

For just as in a wounded person the health of the body is indeed impaired, yet he still remains alive in vital spirit and the antidote of healing medicine may be applied to his wound, so likewise the soul which falls through delight is wounded by the wound of sin. Yet, since that sin, though contrary to the soul’s health, is not fatal, it can more quickly obtain the remedy of salvation through the regard of divine mercy, if it does not join to delight the consent of the will. Delight is therefore forbidden lest, while a person frequently meditates upon things contrary to God and to his own salvation, consent to sin should follow.

If, therefore, memory is, so to speak, discolored and defiled by suggestion, and the will is wounded and injured by delight, and if that third faculty—the person’s reason, by which good must be distinguished from evil, advantage from disadvantage, truth from falsehood—also inclines toward consent to sin, then without doubt, if we attend mystically, the soul incurs the crime of idolatry, by which it is put to death through the death of sin. Desiring us to be free from this death, the Apostle adds in what follows: “Neither become idolaters, as some of them; as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” A person becomes an idolater when he voluntarily subjects himself to sins and vices. For he was created for such great dignity that he ought to be subject to no one except God alone, his Creator. But when, in place of God his Maker—to whom alone all worship is due, as it is written, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4)—he enslaves himself to the shameful service of the body, to obey the flesh and satisfy its desires, he makes for himself, as it were, an idol before which he bows and prostrates himself.

And when he has thus bowed down through consent to sin and become an idolater, what follows is immediately fulfilled: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” The people sit down to eat and drink when the people of thoughts begins, with a certain sweetness, as it were to chew over and ruminate upon the things it conceived through consenting delight, and makes for itself in them a kind of seat—that is, repose—so that it no longer wishes to rise and shake itself free from the dust of earthly pleasure. After this eating and drinking there follows, as it were, a certain play: the dissolution of the spirit, by which a person reveals through wanton and insolent bodily movement the things he meditates and entertains in his heart.

If, then, a person does not draw himself back from this dissolution with every effort and care, he falls into the third stage, namely the very act of sin, which the blessed Apostle mystically describes for us in these words: “Neither let us commit fornication,” he says, “as some of them committed fornication.” Thus fornication is said to occur when that soul which ought to be united and adhere in the embraces of love to the heavenly Bridegroom alone, in whose image and likeness it was created, abandons him to whom it was betrothed in baptism, follows its corrupter, and becomes so entangled in gratifying the senses of its flesh that it does not fear to accomplish in deeds things which it was wicked even to conceive in the mind for an hour. Eternal destruction follows this fornication unless the person comes to his senses and returns, as the Psalmist declares in speaking to the Lord: “You have destroyed everyone who commits fornication apart from you” (Ps. 7:27).

Therefore we must guard ourselves from this fornication with every watchfulness and circumspection, lest through the devil’s suggestion we [not] fall into the delight of sin or even slip into that consent—God forbid!—such that, if opportunity were afforded, we would gladly fulfil in deed what we have conceived in mind. Yet during the interval in which we cannot obtain what our perverse will desires, let us strive to return inwardly to ourselves, lest, when an opportunity to accomplish sin occurs, we depart from God by perpetrating evil works.

For in the two preceding stages, in which sinful delight and consent are indicated, no punishment is prescribed; but punishment immediately follows the third, namely fornication, that is, the very act of sin: “And there fell,” he says, “in one day twenty-three thousand.” By this number twenty, which consists of twice ten, the outward and inward senses, which are likewise ten, may, I think, not inappropriately be understood. By the three thousand we may understand faith in the most holy Trinity, which we received in baptism. Or let us understand that three thousand signifies the perfection of thoughts, words, and works. For when a person, by committing fornication away from God, falls into the perpetration of evil works, twenty-three thousand fall, because he loses all the labor of his former good works, performed through the service of inward or outward senses. If he has ever rendered to God any service in faith which works through love, or in holy meditation, or in the usefulness of words, or in the perfection of good works, it will be reckoned as nothing before God when he so forgets his Creator and himself that he brings perverse consent to the effect of evil actions. We do not, however, say that he loses the good deeds done in the past in such a way that they cannot be recovered and restored [Note: Col. 0539D: That is, “so that not”], if, after a person has transgressed by sinning, he returns again to his own heart and strives, by strict and steadfast repentance, to erase before the face of his Creator what he remembers having unlawfully done.

After the act of sin follows habit, which the Apostle forbids us in the following words: “Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents.” To tempt, according to the letter, sounds lighter than to commit fornication. But according to the meaning we have proposed, one who tempts God sins much more grievously than one who commits fornication. He commits fornication, as we have said, who fulfils in action a perverse consent; he tempts God who turns sin into habit and, where he was not permitted to fall, takes pleasure even in lying there. Does not one tempt God, then, who adds sin to sin and, as it were, says to himself in his thoughts either that God does not see his evils, or that, seeing them, he cannot avenge them? God waits for him patiently and long-sufferingly precisely in order to lead him to repentance.

Therefore all who, infected and overcome by the habit of sinning, refuse to return from their evil way are surely followed by that dreadful punishment: they perish by serpents, which kill a person by injecting deadly venom with their biting mouths. The serpents are evil spirits, which always creep toward the soul through hidden suggestions and do not cease striking it with the poisonous bite of their contrivance until they bring it to destruction through the vice of an ingrained perverse habit. Hence we must take the greatest care that, if through the devil’s instigation we fall into consent and the act of sin, we do not in any way slip into the habit of sinning, lest we perish by serpents—that is, lest we be dragged by evil spirits into the snare of destruction. It follows:

“Neither murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer.” According to the letter, this seems to be extremely slight. Yet it is more serious than all those things we have mentioned, because by this murmuring is signified the defence of sin, which is truly unforgivable blasphemy and the greatest offence, left for vengeance only to the destroyer, that is, the devil. One who murmurs does not speak openly but mutters in secret. Thus everyone who prefers to defend his sin rather than correct it sets this purpose in his heart: even if his offence is exposed and he is rebuked, he chooses rather to persist in the wickedness of an obstinate mind than to confess and amend his guilt.

This is that fourth dead person whom the Lord Jesus heard was dead but was unwilling to raise, concerning whom he said: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke 9:60). For we read that the Lord raised three dead persons in the days of his flesh: the young girl, daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, in the house; the young man, son of the widow, outside the gate; and Lazarus, dead four days and already foul with deadly decay. Of these three dead, since the matter is known, we must briefly say this: the first dead person is one overcome by the delight of sin; the second is one led by full consent to the perpetration of evil works; the third is one bound also by the habit of sin. All these, though not with equal ease, can nevertheless be restored to life.

But that fourth dead person, by whom we understand the defence of sin, is not raised at all, because it is rare that one who rashly defends sin is converted from the stubbornness of his mind. This sin, therefore, belongs to no one except the destruction wrought by the devil, because it is itself diabolical. For the devil himself always wishes to persist in his wickedness, and prefers to be eternally condemned in the everlasting punishment of Gehenna rather than humbled and recalled from the state of his pride. These are the five stages in the growth of sin which the Apostle mystically indicates for us in the present reading that we have expounded. Then he adds and says:

“Now all these things happened to them in figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” For all things which then happened carnally and visibly to carnal Israel can be applied spiritually to us and serve for our correction—to us, I say, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, in whom the world has received its end; we who are designated by a spiritual name, and for whom the world ought to be crucified. Therefore the Apostle warns those upon whom the ends of the ages have come—that is, those who have renounced the world in deed and manner of life—not to boast of their state of uprightness, but to preserve themselves in true humility, in these words:

“Therefore let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.” Who are those who think themselves to stand, except those who, living in holy conduct, have preserved their innocence for God from childhood; or those who, having remained for a time in the world, abandoned the world in mature age, entered the fellowship of the spiritual life, and there recovered through true repentance the innocence they had lost in the world? Those who are in the world and devoted to worldly cares and activities do not think themselves to stand; rather, they publicly profess and affirm that they cannot be saved in their fallen state. Thus we are the ones who think ourselves to stand because we have assumed the habit of holy conversion. But let each of us take heed lest he fall: that is, let him carefully examine himself, continually return to the guarding of his mind, lest he fall through self-exaltation while he thinks himself to stand upon the summit of virtues.

Therefore, if he has laid the foundation of true humility beneath his heart, let him trust that he stands and can be saved. But if he detects in himself the vice of self-exaltation, let him immediately fear a fall. Again, then, the blessed Apostle restrains us from defending sin in mystical words, when he adds:

“Let no temptation take hold of you except what is human.” It is human, therefore, if a person overcome by the frailty of the flesh falls into delight and consent, or even into the very act of sin. It is likewise a human temptation if, having sinned, he becomes entangled in the habit of sin. But to defend sins and to desire to persist in them until life’s end rather than to be corrected is altogether diabolical. Against this temptation and diabolical sin he recalls to our minds the benefit of divine mercy, immediately adding:

“But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able [to bear].” Therefore whoever is borne into this mortal precipice and reaches this consummation of all wickedness—so that he defends his sin and, through despair, chooses rather to persist in it than to correct himself humbly, and wishes to be overcome by his tempter rather than to overcome him—is indeed tempted beyond what he can bear. Peter was not tempted beyond what he could bear: after his fall he immediately returned to the tears of repentance and overcame, in the power of God’s virtue, the tempter who had prevailed against him for an hour. Thus he who had previously feared at the voice of the servant-girl who kept the door and incurred the guilt of denial afterward stood undaunted before armed kings and governors and said with great constancy: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

David likewise was not tempted beyond his power, because after committing adultery and murder he did not fall into despair; rather, in a contrite and humbled heart he overcame the devil, the author of his fall. And because he was not ashamed to confess to the Lord that he had sinned, he deserved to receive from him the fruit of repentance, that is, pardon.

But Judas the betrayer was tempted beyond what he could bear, because when he committed that greatest sin—selling the most glorious price of the whole world—he did not fear immediately to cast himself into the abyss of despair. Yet he could have deserved to obtain the same grace of forgiveness which Peter and David received from the Lord, if he had been willing in a spirit of humility to change from the treachery of his obstinate mind. But God is faithful, who does not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able:

“But with the temptation he will also make the way out, that you may be able to endure it.” The Lord makes a way out with temptation when he helps those who love him so that not only good things, but even evil things, work together for good.

Therefore let us implore the faithful God in all his words, that he may not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear; that he may not allow us to be cast down into the depth of evils, which is the defence of sin and despair; but that with temptation he may also make the way out, so that we may be able to endure it. That is, may he make us such that not only the good things we have done, but also the evils we have committed, may turn to our salvation, while we humble ourselves more and more and make satisfaction to God for them by the worthy fruit of repentance. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself deign to grant this, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

778. HOMILY LXXVII. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY, THE TENTH AFTER PENTECOST.

“When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If only you too had known!’” (Luke 19).

Having completed the eight Sunday Gospels to which we assigned the eight beatitudes, through which one tends toward that eighth glory of the resurrection, we likewise noted and began the following Gospels in their series of eight, in the Sunday now past, in which the steward is read of. But the following Sundays, of which today’s Sunday is the first, may, it seems to me, be referred to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. They are, so to speak, certain draughts by which and through which a sick person—that is, any sinner—ought to be healed and saved.

And not inappropriately are the gifts of the Holy Spirit assigned to these seven following Sundays, since Paul, more in today’s reading than in another, recalls the manifold gifts of the Holy Spirit, saying: “There are diversities of graces, but the same Lord. To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit,” and the rest which he there enumerates.

But it should be known that the preceding Sunday, on which we began another series of eight, concerns prelates throughout, who are like physicians through whom the medicines of the Holy Spirit are to be dispensed and infused into those sick in sins. For just as a physician who possesses various medicines first gives a draught by which, after the stomach is cleansed, he prepares the sick person usefully to receive the other remedies that are to be administered, so a good prelate, who ought to be a faithful physician of the soul, must first instruct the sinner through the spirit of fear, so that he may recognize, fear, and repent of what he has done. Thus, once the stomach of the soul has been cleansed through the spirit of fear, which pertains to today’s Sunday, the Lord begins in a manner to draw near to the sick person, as the present Gospel relates, saying:

“When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it.” All these things which are read as having been done once visibly by the Lord, he still performs and works invisibly every day in the holy Church in saving his own. By Jerusalem, to which the Lord once drew near, any blessed soul may be signified. The Lord then in some manner draws near to it when, touched inwardly by the spirit of fear, he inspires from above the good will to turn away from its sins and pursue good things. And because a person has no power to do any good by himself, it is rightly said of the Lord: “Seeing the city, he wept over it.” The sight of God is the grace of God; his eyes are the gifts of that grace. When a person still lives in sins and is left to his own will, the eyes of the Lord are, so to speak, turned away from him. The Lord graciously looks upon and regards a person when he makes that person, who did not see himself, see and recognize what he has become through sinning.

After the Lord’s seeing follows his weeping; after his weeping follows his speaking. And I say *his* rightly, because all that he himself works in a person is deservedly ascribed and attributed to him as though he performs it. Therefore, whomever the Lord sees thus in his gifts—that he has freed him from sins and from the world and united him with the company of good people—he afterward makes to weep and mourn. For he grants that blessed soul a certain sweet and good weeping, which is wrought upon it when it is bitterly pierced with compunction for its sins and, kindled with desire for eternal life, is sweetly nourished and refreshed in tears.

There is a certain evil and useless weeping when a person, stirred by anger and bitterness or by any other inconveniences of the present life, laments. That useless weeping comes, so to speak, from the lower part of the heart; this weeping is that upper watering which truly rises from the upper part of our heart. In this happy weeping and mourning, the truly penitent person repeatedly says and meditates these words to himself:

“If only you too had known!” This is to say: O my wretched soul, if formerly, when you took delight in sins, you had known the things which you now know by God’s gift, you would rightly have wept, deservedly repented, and shuddered to commit the deeds you performed and committed. Thus, when a person is somewhat enlightened by the grace of God, a certain day comes to be, concerning which it follows:

“And indeed, in this your day, the things that are for your peace.” For a certain day then arises when one who was previously surrounded by the dark night of sins is mercifully illuminated and enlightened from above by God and courageously prepared to repent and make satisfaction to God for his sins. In this enlightenment of the heart, in this day of repentance and sorrow, he in some manner earns and obtains what will confer eternal peace upon him, whereas once, darkened by sins, he had acquired and accumulated for himself not things of peace but things of eternal unrest. Of such people Paul says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). But because a person cannot remain long in this day of enlightenment, the temptations that he will suffer seem to me immediately to be indicated when it follows:

“But now they are hidden from your eyes, because days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and surround you, and press you in on every side, and cast you and your children who are within you to the ground, and they will not leave in you one stone upon another.” By the four expressions set forth here—“they will surround you,” “press you in,” “cast you to the ground,” and “they will not leave in you one stone upon another”—we may understand four vices opposed to the four cardinal virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. For as all virtues, as it were, depend, move, and work upon the hinge of these four virtues, so in these four vices—imprudence, inconstancy, intemperance, and injustice—all vices and offences are contained and carried out.

And, as I see it, imprudence can fittingly be compared to a rampart, because in a rampart there are two things, depth and height: the deeper it is, the darker it is; and the deeper and darker it is, the higher the earth thrown out on either side rises. Thus through this darkness and shadow of the rampart may be figured the ignorance which imprudence produces in a person. And by the phrase “they will surround you,” twice repeated, he seems to me to signify that ignorance is twofold. There is ignorance of ourselves and ignorance of God. And the more a person becomes imprudent through these ignorances, the less he recognizes God as his maker and redeemer, and the less he can consider what he himself is. This twofold ignorance produces pride from itself, which, as I judge, may be signified by the height of the rampart. For if a person found himself in truth, rightly set himself before his own face, and from knowledge of himself extended toward knowledge of God, he would reckon himself less and lower than everyone; he would rarely be proud by exalting himself above others, but would always think humbly and lowly of himself.

It may also be understood in another way why “they will surround you” is said twice. When a person begins to be proud through this twofold ignorance of God and himself, enemies—namely evil spirits—surround him: inwardly, pride is in his heart; outwardly, they surround him with acts of pride in the body.

When pride, produced by imprudence and ignorance, thus prevails, another vice follows: inconstancy, the opposite of fortitude. It is indicated by the following words: “And they will press you in on every side.” And not unfittingly can the phrase “they will press you in” be applied to the vice of inconstancy. For just as perfect charity broadens and enlarges the heart so that it extends itself not only to friends and neighbors but also judges that its compassion must not be closed even against enemies, but does good to those who hate it, so inconstancy, which is lightness of mind, narrows and constricts the heart, so that it can neither retain social and brotherly charity nor, through instability of mind, have any steadfastness in good things. Thus one who had once, on hearing the word of God, resolved to be patient in adversities, strong in patience, and steadfast in humility becomes so narrow and cramped in heart that he cannot endure even the least onset of adversity.

From this inconstancy he slips into intemperance, the opposite of temperance, to which vice the following words suit well: “And they will cast you to the ground.” A person is cast to the ground when he begins to serve gluttony and luxury; he is cast to the ground when, by consenting without restraint, he yields to his flesh, which is understood by the earth.

And note that he says, “and your children who are within you.” What can be understood by children except evil wills and desires? There are some who are cast to the ground by sinning more through the weakness of the flesh than through the will of the mind. But when, by God’s mercy, they grieve and come to their senses, the children are by no means cast down there. On the other hand, there are others who sin with such will and desire that they find it sweet both to sin and to repeat their sins; and what they have not yet perpetrated in deed, they have in their will, so that they may at some time accomplish it and satisfy their desires. Such persons are cast to the ground with their children, because they refuse to restrain themselves both from evil willing and from evil action.

When a person has thus become imprudent, inconstant, and intemperate, he falls into the fourth vice, injustice, which is opposed to justice. To this vice we may apply the statement: “And they will not leave in you one stone upon another.” For even if there is in him some firm and good work, which we may understand by a stone, it will all be destroyed after the things we have mentioned, because he loses and forfeits everything before God.

These are the four vices which destroy four goods in a person: humility, charity, chastity, and perseverance. Imprudence, which produces pride, destroys humility; inconstancy, which makes a person light and unstable, destroys charity; intemperance, by which a person does not know how to restrain himself from sins, extinguishes chastity; injustice removes perseverance in every good. You now have the four vices opposed to the four cardinal virtues. Hear next by what preceding merits these vices come to rule over us.

“Because,” says the Lord, “you did not know the time of your visitation.” There are many and diverse visitations of the Lord, some lesser and some more eminent, by which he deigns to visit each of his elect. God visits a person when he chastises him with bodily scourging, so that the body which he once nourished uselessly for sins, girded with the divine lash, may no longer be allowed to rise up to its former crimes. He also visits one who loves him in another manner, when he permits some adversity or injury to occur where that person had hoped for an encounter with prosperity and joy. And this visitation is good and useful if it is recognized and not despised.

Again, a person is visited when he is hurt and troubled by the adversities of his friends or loved ones, whose worldly goods and prosperity had delighted him beyond measure. Likewise, there is another visitation by which a person is visited whenever he hears the word of preaching. For he rarely hears the word of the Lord without being admonished to see how much good he has neglected and how much evil he has committed. And this is his visitation if the good neglected is immediately restored by him, and the evil committed is washed away by repentance.

There is yet another visitation of the Lord, surpassing all the rest: that continual visitation by which he deigns to visit the hearts of his children in prayer, and in which he pours into those reborn and renewed therein the gifts of his virtues. In this visitation, if a person attributes anything to himself or to his own merits, he does not rightly recognize the time of his visitation. For this time of visitation everyone must take care to watch and guard himself. For if, before the time of prayer, he has not restrained himself from unlawful things, how will he share in this blessed visitation? There are, alas, those who remain dry and fruitless every day from morning until [Col. 0546B] evening, and take no concern for this visitation. And as such people are unhappy, so, conversely, blessed and to be blessed are those who continually seek their inward solitude, return within to the heart, and with all their desires long for the Lord to visit them.

We may turn those things which we have touched upon concerning the four vices toward four other goods, because it is sweet and delightful when, in the divine Scriptures, the Lord’s words can be interpreted in a good sense. “If only you too had known.” As the Lord approached Jerusalem—that is, as he had mercy on the sinful soul—and deigned, in the manner we have described, to behold it and weep over it, he addresses it with joyful promises, saying: “If only you too had known, indeed in this your day, the things that make for your peace” [Col. 0546C] (Luke 19:42). This is as if he said: Because, by my gift, you recognize yourself, a certain day has been made within you; yet greater goods, greater illuminations which will come to you, are still hidden from your eyes. He immediately adds what these goods are: “For days will come upon you.” By these days we may understand good impulses, good affections, holy virtues, or good works, which our Lord imparts to the blessed person by pouring them in, when that person begins to see and recognize himself and God.

**784.** In these days of chief and holy illumination, “your enemies will surround you with a rampart.” By “enemies,” as it seems to me, we may understand holy affections hostile to a person’s sin. For while a person is wholly moved inwardly by God’s illumination through good impulses, good affections, and virtues, he begins to become his own enemy: detesting himself, he hates and pursues his sins. Hence the Lord admonishes in the Gospel: “Be reconciled with your adversary while you are with him on the way” (Matt. 5:25). This adversary of ours is the word of God; we agree with it when we oppose and pursue in ourselves that which resists God’s word within us. These blessed enemies of ours work four goods in us, which may suitably be indicated by the four expressions: “they will surround,” “they will hem you in,” “they will cast you to the ground,” and “they will not leave in you one stone upon another.” In the rampart understand confession; in the words “they will hem you in,” contrition of heart; by “cast to the ground,” bodily [Col. 0547A] satisfaction; by “they will not leave in you one stone upon another,” the observance of humility.

And, as I see it, confession is rightly signified by a rampart [*vallum*], because the deeper the rampart, the more strong and secure it will be. This fittingly applies to confession. For the more deeply and perfectly a person, in confessing, casts out his own earth—that is, his sins and earthly deeds—as though digging them up and examining them carefully, the more firmly he rises against the temptations of evil spirits. Since confession ought to be twofold, the words “they will surround, they will surround” are, I think, repeated twice. A person must confess and disclose not only the sinful act, but also the will and consent belonging to the sin. But since perfection does not consist in a person’s confessing sins merely with his lips [Col. 0547B] unless he is inwardly pierced with grief of heart for those same sins, the words that follow are apt: “and they will hem you in on every side.” What does this constriction mean but contrition of heart? It is fitting that, after confession has been made, a person should be distressed in a contrite heart for his sins. And this “on every side,” because he ought to have a contrite spirit not at one moment, not on one day, nor in one place, but everywhere; as we read of Hannah, “her countenance was no longer changed in different ways” (1 Sam. 1:18). Our blessed father Benedict likewise teaches this in his twelve degrees: “Wherever we may be—sitting, walking, or standing—let us have our heads bowed and our eyes fixed upon the ground; at every hour let us regard ourselves as guilty because of our sins.”

[Col. 0547C] From this distress which the blessed person thus has for his sins will result what follows: “And they will cast you to the ground.” By this casting to the ground we may understand the satisfaction which, after confession and contrition of heart have been made, a person must render to God. For in a certain way he casts himself to the ground with his children when he turns all his will and all his desires toward making satisfaction to God.

After all this it is necessary that one stone not be left upon another. Then one stone is not left upon another when a person is not lifted up above others on account of his firm and strong works, but strives always to preserve them under the guard of humility. We may also understand [Col. 0547D] in “stone and stone” a twofold hardness of heart. Hardness of heart means that a person does not do good; and this is “one stone upon another.” These two stones are not left, but removed, because confession made, contrition of heart shown, and bodily satisfaction completed bring about in a person both the willing and the ability to do good—what formerly he neither wished nor was able to do. Why, then, a person ought so to confess, to have contrition of heart, and to make satisfaction in this manner, is indicated, I think, by the following words:

“Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” This is as though the Lord admonished each of his own, enumerating every occasion on which he proved ungrateful for God’s visitations, and saying: First I visited you when I regenerated you through baptism; secondly I visited you [Col. 0548A] when I gave you perception and understanding to discern good and evil. But you did not recognize this time of my visitation, because you turned that understanding toward worse things. A third time I visited you when, freed from the world, I led you into the repose of the spiritual life, where you saw and heard many useful things, many good things pleasing to me. But you did not recognize the time of my visitation, because you neglected much and became a transgressor of very many of my commandments. Therefore, since he has despised these visitations, it is truly fitting that he should confess, be contrite in spirit, make satisfaction in the body, and keep his goods in humility. Purified and cleansed by these things, and illuminated in part, he can come to the full and perfect days of which the following speaks:

[Col. 0548B] “And entering the temple, he began to drive out those selling and buying in it.” Who are these sellers and buyers but evil spirits? Let there be, so to speak, some elect person who has reached the summit of perfection with God’s help: will he not suffer these sellers and buyers? Indeed he will suffer them; he will endure their buying and selling. They put forward and offer what is theirs in order to take our goods from us; they wish to buy virtues from us, so as to bring in the dung of vices, and finally to remove from our hearts our best price, which is Christ. But if he enters the house of his heart, his enemies do not prevail to the extent they wish, for he begins powerfully to drive them out and expel them.

And “he began” is rightly said, because no one is at first at the summit; rather, by degrees and through the progress of time, with God’s gift, he begins to advance and go from virtue to virtue. Yet you may also understand “he began” in another sense. It belongs to the Lord to begin; it belongs to us, by a good will and the performance of good labours, to cooperate with and assist him. If we do this obediently and faithfully, he whose speaking is doing says:

“It is written.” For he writes—that is, he fixes within us so that we may remember and set before the eyes of the mind—that our heart ought to have been a house of prayer; but we, alas, made it a den of thieves. It is not enough for us that we have added sins to sins; moreover, we have made ourselves a den of thieves when we were not ashamed [Col. 0548D] to hide our sins and were never able to disclose them in confession as was fitting and useful for us. When the Lord speaks such things and writes such things in a person, then what is said will be fulfilled in a lofty manner:

**787.** “And he was teaching daily in the temple.” In the temple of the human heart, in which he deigns to dwell, he teaches daily, because he teaches his elect person to do good and shun evil. Wherever he thus teaches in the present life, there he will rest and reign in the future. To this evangelical sense the Collect of today is well suited, in which we pray: “O God, who chiefly manifestest thy omnipotence by sparing and showing mercy.” If some rich and very powerful king in this world, in proportion to the greatness of his wealth and power, should win a joyful triumph over enemies from a besieged city, [Col. 0549A] perhaps no one, considering his strength and power, would wonder at his victory. But if it happened that that same rich and powerful man, or his son, were struck in the face, injured, and subjected to insults by some inferior person, would not his power be more praised and proclaimed for the clemency of his forgiveness than for the cruelty of revenge, if he chose not to avenge it but mercifully forgave? If a mortal person especially manifests his power through such patience and mercy, much more does God—who is greater, better, and more powerful than all—declare his omnipotence by having mercy upon and sparing sinners. For his power is not called only his avenging himself upon evildoers or ruling in heaven and on earth; rather, this is more truly [Col. 0549B] his omnipotence and almighty mercy: that he endures the wicked, knows how to have mercy on sinners and spare them, and is thereby more abundantly praised, loved, and proclaimed.

Since this is so, multiply, O God, your mercy upon us, so that, as you have taught us, we may be able to confess to you, please you with a contrite heart, make satisfaction to you, and preserve our goods for you in humility. Thus, hastening toward your promises—that is, recognizing the time of your visitation—we may deserve your entry into the temple of our heart; and, when the sellers and buyers, namely evil spirits, have been expelled, may our house be a house of prayer. There may you now sit continually teaching us, so that we may deserve to become sharers in heavenly goods, where you may rest [Col. 0549C] and reign in us forever. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns unto infinite ages of ages. Amen.

**789. HOMILY LXXVIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST**

“Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (Luke 18).

As in the Gospel of the preceding Sunday, when Jesus approached and wept over the city of Jerusalem, we observed his gracious and merciful visitation toward every sinful soul, so the mystery of today’s reading prescribes the manner of good conversion which the gift of the Spirit of piety must truly effect in a person.

“Two men,” says the Evangelist, “went up into [Col. 0549D] the temple to pray.” Any temple made by hands rises high from a gathered diversity of stones; within it, affairs of no other kind ought to be conducted, but remembrance of continual peace and praise must be kept. By this handmade temple, as I see it, any good community may be understood: gathered and built from living and elect stones, namely blessed souls, it daily rises higher, progressing from virtue to virtue and preparing itself as a temple worthy of almighty God. For the hearts of the elect are the dwelling-place of God, as the Apostle Paul testifies when he says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). And the Lord himself says of each one who loves him: “We will come,” he says, “and make our dwelling with [Col. 0550A] him” (John 14:23). One certainly does not reach this temple except by an ascent that is difficult and very laborious, because for those who arrange ascents in their heart, the ascent to the virtues will then be more laborious than their former walking on the broad and spacious path of the world toward vices.

After the word “went up,” the phrase “to pray” is fittingly added, because these climbers ought by no means to be subject to sloth and idleness, but must labor with all their strength to bring forth the fruits of good works—which is indeed to pray. For prayer is not called only compunction of heart and frequent speech addressed to God; the whole life of a person is said to be, as it were, a prayer, **790** if he strives, as far as he can, to live holily and justly and to have an unstained heart [Col. 0550B]. Then the Apostle’s command to “pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17) is fulfilled, if a person’s life is such that the disposition of his life and conduct is before the Lord like an acceptable incense of prayer.

In these two men any one and the same person may be understood. Although he has no quality in his essence, yet, as it seems to me, he is not one but, as it were, two when he comes to the temple; for at the beginning of conversion the flesh always desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, and these two persons—the outward and the inward—suffer innumerable troubles of conflict with one another. Paul felt the opposition of these two persons within himself when, groaning, he said: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward man; but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive to the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:22–23). These two persons are shown when it is said: “One a Pharisee, and the other a tax collector.” “Pharisee” is interpreted “divided.” A person may fittingly be called divided, and divided from God, when merely because he has left the world he thinks that he has attained a certain perfection, and does not truly see how much imperfection he still has before the eyes of the supreme Inspector. Hence it is aptly added:

“But the Pharisee, standing, prayed these things by himself.” He is said to stand, although he does not stand in truth, because in his estimation of himself he thinks that he stands and expects the glory of recompense solely because he has renounced the pleasures of his former life. He is said, standing, to have prayed these things by himself:

“God, I thank you that I am not like other people: robbers, unjust persons, adulterers.” Since there are countless offences hateful and grievous to God, it seems to me that these three are singled out by name above the rest because all vices are found intertwined with and entirely connected to these three. For just as there are three principal goods in which the whole sum of our salvation consists—namely, to love God with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s mind—so, conversely, these three things, robbery, injustice, and adultery, bring death [Col. 0551A] and take away the life of the soul, which is Christ. Through the former three almighty God is honoured and loved; through the latter three, unless they are avoided, he is altogether held in contempt.

He loves with all his heart, that is, all his understanding, who separates himself from the love of carnal pleasures, recognizes what he ought to believe and understand concerning God his Creator and Redeemer, and strives to turn this whole good understanding of the heart toward the service of his Creator and Redeemer. He loves with all his soul, that is, all his will, who, in order to please the Lord to whom he has devoted himself, directs the whole will of his heart toward the devotion of good works. He loves with all his mind, that is, all his memory, who, remembering his Lord in all things, is not puffed up by prosperity nor cast down excessively by adversity. Whoever does not advance through these three goods, and does not love the Lord God in this way, is a robber and unjust. He is an evil and unworthy robber who does not love God with his whole understanding, but turns his good intellect and ability away from God and disdains to know what he owes to his Creator and Redeemer. He is unjust who, just as in understanding, so also in his will turns away from God and, lured by evil desires, slips daily toward worse things. He is an adulterer when—an impious thing to say—he abandons his bride, namely the eternal Wisdom of God, whose lover he ought to be, and joins himself in all his mind, that is, all his memory, to the adulterous embraces of the world, submitting himself wholly in love.

Therefore this Pharisee gives thanks because he is not [Col. 0551C] like other people—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers. It is as though he said: I do not bear the name of robber, because I have devoted my whole understanding, as far as I can, to loving God and my Lord. **792** I am not unjust, for I am prepared to serve and subject myself to him with all my soul, that is, all my will. I am not an adulterer, because I have expelled and cast away every worldly desire from my whole mind, that is, all my memory. Exalted by these goods, I am not like even this tax collector. “I am not,” he says, “that man who was once entangled in public business, who heaped up right and wrong together and considered permissible whatever pleased him, however disgraceful.”

“I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess.” By the twofold Sabbath fast, as it seems to me, the discipline of body and soul may be expressed. He boasts of this on the Sabbath, that is, in the rest of the spiritual life; and, since he thinks that he has attained the standard of perfection, he keeps a Sabbath as though fasting from vices. The tithes of all possessions are the duties owed to God by the senses. He says that he possesses these perfectly when he believes that he refers the sum and perfection of all that he does to God’s work. This Pharisee, then, because he proudly enumerates so many goods of his own, is first said to have stood badly; but, admonished by the invisible gift of the Holy Spirit, gradually laying aside the arrogance of his mind, he strives to stand in a better way and, as though exercised by the long discipline of labour, comes to profound humility of heart, as the Evangelist continues:

[Col. 0552A] “And the tax collector, standing at a distance, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but struck his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” The tax collector stands at a distance when a person begins to think no longer lofty but humble things of himself, and judges himself unworthy and blameworthy in a true knowledge of sin. Not wishing to lift his eyes to heaven is to humble oneself from the deep root of the heart. To bruise the breast with blows is to make worthy satisfaction to God for crimes committed. For the hidden inward parts of the heart, whence come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, and blasphemies, he would perhaps have made bloody with his own hands, if he could, so as even thus to satisfy God and overcome the contests of temptations.

**793.** And because after salutary knowledge of sin, true humility of heart, and worthy satisfaction he removes harmful shame, he at once opens the door of his mouth in penitential confession, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” He confesses all the more gravely that he has sinned against the Lord alone, as he beholds him purer and holier than all mortals. Hence the prophet David indicates how truly each person ought to humble himself in the knowledge of sin, and how fruitful satisfaction is if worthy confession is not lacking, saying: “For God loves mercy and truth; the Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 80:8 [Vulgate numbering]). The Lord loves mercy because he loves the sinner to be moved by a devout mercy toward his own soul in true knowledge of sin, lest he easily [Col. 0552C] despise the misery of his own heart, as it is written: “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24). He also loves truth when he approves the true and voluntary humility of the devout mind. He will give grace, because he finds grace before the eyes of the supreme Judge who has offered the Lord the gift of worthy satisfaction. Glory follows, because God’s purpose and sentence of peace will rest upon those who confess to him. And truly blessed is the person to whom sins are now no longer imputed: when God overlooks his evils and rewards his goods, even evils in a wondrous way work together for good.

Or thus: “God loves mercy and truth.” Mercy, that we may acknowledge our sins; truth, that we may confess our sins. “The Lord will give grace and glory”: grace in the remission of sin; glory in the sinner’s justification or the rewarding of a recompense. It follows:

“I tell you: this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.” He makes a truly good descent who submits himself from the root of profound humility. “To his house,” because he examines not another’s knowledge but that of his own heart. “Rather than the other”—rather than the one who had formerly been a proud and exalted Pharisee, but is now a tax collector humble in his own eyes.

**794.** “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted.” Everyone who exalts himself through pride, with God cooperating and assisting, shall be humbled through penitence; and whoever humbles himself through penitence [Col. 0553A] shall be exalted through true righteousness and innocence.

The Collect of today has great suitability to this evangelical sense. Divided into two parts, it looks toward the two men, the Pharisee and the tax collector. Its first part—“Almighty everlasting God, who by the abundance of thy loving-kindness exceedest both the merits and vows of thy suppliants”—looks toward the Pharisee, who boasted of his merits and thought his prayers pleasing to God. Its second part—“Pour out thy mercy upon us, that thou mayest forgive those things which the conscience fears, and grant what prayer does not presume to ask”—looks toward the tax collector, who, unwilling even to lift his eyes to heaven because his sinful conscience reproached him, begged only for the remission of sins.

[Col. 0553B] These two men, as we stated in discussing the Gospel reading, are one and the same person. At the beginning of his conversion he is a Pharisee; afterward, truly recognizing himself, he becomes a tax collector humble in his own eyes. Trusting greatly in the abundance of divine mercy, which exceeds both the merits and vows of suppliants, he humbly prays that the sins he has committed may be forgiven him through God’s mercy; and he asks that the reward of eternal things, which prayer does not yet presume to ask for, may be added to him. What, then, are our merits and vows? The merits of a sinful person, as it seems to me, are to renounce the world, leave sins behind, and turn to the Lord. His vows are made when, now established in a good manner of life, he promises under a holy profession always to serve God, and never in any way consents that these vows should become void. These merits and these vows come from God’s mercy, because no one can either turn from the world or offer vows to God except by God’s gift.

**795.** Moreover, we must inquire what his mercy is, and what the abundance of his mercy is. His mercy is when he calls a person and makes him come out of the world; and this mercy is great and worthy of proclamation. But the abundance of his mercy is when he leads and advances his elect person so far in a good way of life that he merits remission of sins and the working of virtues, and after these things receives, beyond what prayer presumes, the reward of eternal prizes. This is what we pray for and desire in today’s Collect: that he [Col. 0553D] by whose mercy our merits and vows exist may, through the overflowing abundance of his mercy, pour out his mercy upon us, so that in those things which conscience fears we may deserve remission and the working of virtues, and in the future the reward of eternal goods.

The Introit of the Mass bears upon these matters. One who has deservedly entered this temple—the spiritual life—sets it forth, invoking God suitably not with a clamor of words but from the affection of the heart, and saying: “God is in his holy place; God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house, will himself give power and strength to his people” (Ps. 67:6, 7, 36 [Vulgate numbering]). It is as though he said: I perceive and see that you, O God, are in this holy place, because concord and unity are in this house of yours; and therefore, you who give power and strength [Col. 0554A] to your people, grant also to me the strength and power I need.

Nor does today’s reading disagree with these things. In it Paul says something about himself that seems very fitting for a sinful but penitent person: “I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; that he was buried; that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures; and that he was seen by Cephas and afterward by the eleven. Then he was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once; then by all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he was seen also by me. For I am the least of the apostles and am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15:3–9). By Peter, who is Cephas, any good prelate may be understood; **796** by the eleven apostles and the other five hundred brethren, good and spiritual people, who have deserved to see and contemplate God in their hearts as far as is permitted in this life. Living among them, this person rejoices in their continual daily contemplation; but, judging himself abject and unworthy, he says: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, he was seen also by me. For I am the least,” because I am a useless and unworthy sinner; “but by the grace of God I am what I am” (ibid., 10), because I received from his singular gift both that I left the world and that I entered this haven of rest.

After this is added and sung: “My heart hoped in God, and I was helped, and my flesh blossomed anew” (Ps. 27 [Vulgate numbering]). This is indeed the voice of a converted sinner, saying [Col. 0554C]: While I was still in the world and in sins, I hoped in the Lord; and behold, I was helped, and my flesh blossomed anew—namely, my body toward the beginning of good works. “Blossomed anew” is well said, because as fruit is hoped for in a flower, so when he comes and leaves the world there is a kind of flower, and in that flower remains the hope of greater goods and future joys. And because he has thus been helped, and his flesh has thus blossomed anew, “behold,” he says, “I will confess to him from my will” (ibid., 7). What is, “I will confess to him from my will”? It means: I will praise and glorify him with my whole will, and while I live I will continually offer everlasting praises for all his goods. “To you, Lord,” he says, “I shall cry; O my God, do not be silent toward me; do not ever be silent toward me; [Col. 0554D] do not depart from me” (ibid., 1). I pray, he says, O Lord, because I cry to you: do not be silent toward me—that is, do not be hidden from me—but deign to grant and bestow the exercise of virtues. Or thus: I pray you, do not be silent toward me, so that you may now grant me remission of sins; do not ever be silent—that is, do not at some time be silent in your judgment by rejecting and condemning me, when you refuse to hear those who say, “Lord, Lord, open to us.”

The Alleluia is appointed, signifying praise: “O Lord, God of my salvation, by day I have cried out, and by night before you” (Ps. 87:2 [Vulgate numbering]). This is a voice of praise and thanksgiving from the sinner. It is as if he said: You are the God of my salvation; you have saved me; you have helped me. **797** And therefore I shall cry before you by day and night: by day, that is, in joyful and prosperous times; by night, that is, in adversities. I shall always [Col. 0555A] praise and magnify you; looking to you alone, I shall cry before you.
