The Offertory agrees with these things, in which he again bursts forth in praise, saying: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have taken me up, and have not made my enemies rejoice over me” (Ps. 28:2 [Vulgate numbering]); that is, you have not made my enemies, my invisible adversaries, rejoice in my destruction.

And rightly, after all these things, there is at the end of Mass, so to speak, an exhortation in the Communion concerning how one who advances in such an order ought to order his life before the Lord: “Honor the Lord from your substance” (Prov. 3:9). It seems to me that this substance can signify our body and soul; the first fruits of the crops, the guarding of the senses; and the storehouses, our five senses: sight, hearing, taste, [Col. 0555B] smell, and touch. We faithfully honor God in this our substance when, for love of him, we labor in good works and give him the first fruits of our crops, striving before all things to guard the outward senses and to maintain the purity of inward thoughts. Thus, when we first rise at night and in the morning, he alone may first be thought of, invoked, and received; and so we shall truly seem to have honored God with our first fruits.

We also honor him with our first fruits in another way, if we do not first attend to any earthly actions or works until we have rendered him the service that is due and customary. For then, with his help, the salvation and grace of greater prosperity meet us every day in all that must be done. Our storehouses too [Col. 0555C] are filled with abundance when we receive God’s teaching with all our senses in such a way that, filled from it, we gain richness and fruit for our souls. Whoever hears the word of God and hears it without fruit is certainly not filled or enriched by it, but wastes away from hunger like a fasting person.

“And the winepresses will overflow with wine.” Understand our hearts by the winepresses, and God’s sweetness by the wine. When our storehouses have been filled with abundance, our winepresses will overflow with wine: that is, our hearts, pressed and compressed by the fear and love of God, will overflow with the wine of compunction, the wine of inward sweetness, which, when drunk and tasted beforehand in this life, truly gladdens the human heart.

**799. HOMILY LXXIX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE TWELFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST**

[Col. 0555D]

“Jesus, going out from the borders of Tyre, came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, between the midst of the borders of the Decapolis” (Matt. 7).

In these seven Sundays we have assigned the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The first gift, the spirit of fear, belongs to the first Sunday, in which the overthrow and destruction of the city of Jerusalem are described. In that overthrow and destruction of the walls I think nothing else is signified to us except that a sinful person, aided by the spirit of fear, should see and reflect lest he suffer at death what the Lord threatened would befall that city. And the gift of the spirit of fear is rightly first among the gifts, because if a person did not fear hell and the sentence of eternal [Col. 0556A] damnation, he would late or never choose to leave the world and turn to God.

But, initiated and pierced with compunction by the spirit of fear, he passes to the spirit of piety. This gift of the Holy Spirit belongs to the following Sunday, when a person enters the temple—that is, the spiritual life—to worship there, so that he may obtain pardon for offences committed. And this is not unsuitable, as I see it: that Sunday belongs to the spirit of piety because it is great piety of almighty God when he deigns to hear a sinful person and be propitiated for his sins.

After these two gifts follows the third gift, the spirit of knowledge. This third gift is not unjustly ascribed to this third Sunday, on which the deaf and mute man was healed by the Lord. For it is truly a great gift of the Holy Spirit when a person begins to know what he formerly did not know: namely, to know that he did not know himself, that he did not see what he was like while sinning, that he did not recognize that he had been deaf and mute. As I have said, when one enlightened by the gift of the spirit of knowledge truly recognizes that he was deaf and mute, that he has uselessly spent the whole time of his life living contrary to God, and when he looks upon the lives of others who serve God in goodness and simplicity of heart, does he not seem to you rightly **800** to invoke God and, seeking the aid of heavenly help, sing from his heart the Introit of today’s office: “O God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. 69:2 [Vulgate numbering])? “I know,” he says, “O Lord, and [Col. 0556C] recognize that until now I have lived uselessly, and have spent my life in deeds, words, and thoughts very contrary to you and useless to myself. And now, O Lord, in this holy way of life, I do not know how to praise and honor you as would be fitting. Therefore attend to my help; hasten to help me, so that by your gift and grace I may render to you worthy satisfaction for my sins and offer praise worthy of your name.”

Today’s Collect does not disagree with these words, in which we pray: “Almighty and merciful God, from whose gift it comes that thy faithful serve thee worthily and laudably, grant, we beseech thee, that we may run without stumbling toward thy promises.” It is a wondrous condescension and mercy of almighty God when he works these things in a person through the spirit of fear, piety, and knowledge, and deigns to inspire worthy and praiseworthy service to him. What is it to serve him worthily and laudably? One serves God worthily who performs worthy and good works in the body. One serves laudably who preserves those same goods in humility of heart and does not seek earthly praise for those good actions. Whoever thus serves God worthily and laudably runs without stumbling toward his promises. What are his promises but the blessedness and glory of eternal life? He runs without stumbling toward these promises who attributes nothing to himself from his good deeds, but ascribes all to him from whom he received all that he has. For he stumbles greatly who takes from God what is God’s and attributes it to himself, though by himself he has no power and possesses nothing.

[Col. 0557A] Hence Paul likewise commends this in today’s Lesson—he who teaches us to run without stumbling—saying: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think or say anything as from ourselves, as though it came from us; rather, our sufficiency is from God. But if the ministry of death was in glory, how much more shall the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?” (2 Cor. 3).

The ministry of death existed when we performed those things through which we incurred the death of the soul. This ministry of death was in glory when we judged it fitting to rejoice and glory vainly in the evils we had done. If we were unashamed to exalt and glory ourselves in things hateful to God, what wonder is it that, at our tempter’s suggestion, we uselessly glory and exalt ourselves over our good deeds? Our first parent, Adam, was tempted and overcome by vainglory in Paradise. The second Adam, whose life and conduct surpassed those of all mortals, allowed himself to be tempted by vainglory. Therefore it is no wonder if even the most perfect are assailed by the same vice; yet, though assailed, following the example of their Lord, they are not overcome.

You have heard how the Prayer agrees with the Lesson and the Lesson with the Prayer; see now how the Gospel also does not disagree. There the Lord, having performed a miracle, commanded them not to tell anyone, as an example for us in fleeing vainglory.

Therefore, since all these things mutually answer and agree, hear how the Offertory may fittingly be referred to the man healed. Its words, it seems to me, are those of one who hears rightly and speaks rightly through God’s gift:

“[Col. 0557C] Moses prayed before the presence of the Lord his God, and said: Why, Lord, art thou angry with thy people? Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom thou didst swear to give a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exod. 32).

Moses is said to mean “drawn from water.” This name fittingly belongs to the man who has been drawn out and liberated from the waters—that is, from this world’s carnal desires. Yet the name Moses, “drawn from water,” is also justly given to him when, through God’s gift, he can by repentance and mourning wash away and cleanse his sins in the waters of tears; and, having thereby become clean before the Lord, he is rightly said to be drawn from water.

What does such a Moses pray for? What does he entreat? “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” In the three names of these Fathers understand three virtues: faith in Abraham, hope in Isaac, and charity in Jacob. “Remember,” he says, “Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” It is as if a man addressed these words to Christ the Lord, his Mediator: “Remember Abraham”—that is, “Lord, call to mind my faith, which I have shown and offered to thee. Although my faith is slight and unworthy, yet I wish to be found and reckoned faithful before thee in this: that I left the world and fled to thee; I came to thee.

“Remember also Isaac,” that is, “remember my immense hope, by which I trust in thee and concerning thee, hoping through thee to receive forgiveness of all my sins and, my sins at last forgiven, someday to become a participant in thy joys in eternal life.

“Remember also Jacob”—I mean, “[Col. 0558A]remember my love,” by which I shall strive, insofar as thou grantest, to love thee and my neighbour.

Again, in another way you may understand what he says: “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” For it is as if he said: “Just as Abraham, once thy chosen one, first of all men left his land and kindred for love of thee, so I too, though less perfectly, have become his imitator: I have left my land, my kindred, and the comfort of all my friends. Therefore, because I have done what I could by thy gift, let it, I pray, be acceptable in thy sight; and deign to remember me, thou who art known to approve even good intentions.

“Remember Isaac also. Isaac was once offered to thee to be slain and sacrificed; and unless his father had been divinely warned, he would have killed his son. Yet in this too I have something that I have imitated in part. I am thy Isaac: I who have offered and sacrificed to thee, Lord, my body and soul; daily I am immolated and sacrificed for thee. And although I sometimes suffer unwillingly, nevertheless, because the discipline of regular life is strict, I endure all things for thee. Let this, I pray, be pleasing and acceptable to thee, who graciously regardest the vows and sacrifices of the humble.

“Remember Jacob also, who served Laban a long time for Rachel and Leah, and was scorched night and day by frost and heat. I am thy Jacob, surely thy servant—if thou deignest to acknowledge it—for I have freely surrendered myself into thy service. And as Jacob served for Rachel and Leah, so I serve thee for the active and contemplative life: for the active life, I say, that I may be able in this life to exercise myself in the practice of virtues, in something pleasing to thee and necessary for me; but for the contemplative life, that I may meanwhile receive some small portion of thy sweetness, and after this sweetness obtain the fullness of eternal delight.

“Jacob was once scorched night and day by frost and heat; and I now fail, sometimes from frost, sometimes from excessive heat. Most severe frost threatens me whenever the ardour of thy love is extinguished in me; I am afflicted by excessive heat when I am consumed and tormented not only by the fires of evil desires, but also by anger, envy, vain joy, and immoderate sorrow. Remember all these things graciously, Lord; and as thou didst swear to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that thou wouldst give them a land [Col. 0558D]flowing with milk and honey, so give me meanwhile milk—that is, the teaching for little children. Give me also honey, that I may be able to grasp and imitate the teaching of the perfect.”

And what was the Lord about to do after so many prayers of Moses? Hear what follows: “And the Lord was appeased concerning the evil which he had said he would do to his people” (Exod. 32:14). The Lord will now do the same for his people, his nation, which commits itself wholly to him in devotion. He is appeased concerning his evil when he removes the punishment due to our sins; he is appeased concerning his evil when he makes quiet and still that which lives evilly in us.

When the Lord has thus been appeased, can not any person who was once deaf and dumb fittingly burst forth into a voice of praise and thanksgiving, saying: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth. My soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. 33:2–3)? Again he adds Alleluia, that he may render the Lord the reverence of greater praise: “Lord, thou hast become our refuge from generation to generation” (Ps. 89:1). This is to say: “Thou alone, Lord, art my refuge; thou hast delivered me from the generation of wicked and unrighteous people and led me to the offspring of righteous people. And, because thou hast graciously done this, I ask thee, Lord, to lead me from the temporal offspring of the righteous [Col. 0559A]to the immortal generation of thy saints.”

The Gospel reading has great agreement with all this, and in it we have great consolation and instruction. I call it consolation because he deigned to heal this man at the request of others, although the man himself sought no salvation. From this we may gather that the person whom the common prayer of holy Church assists never perishes, even though he seems, of himself, to implore the Lord less than he ought. If such a one is aided and delivered by the prayers of others, much more will he be saved who both prays for himself and is one for whom holy Church does not cease to pray.

The Lord’s teaching also shines forth from another side: we are instructed not only by his words, but are taught and built up by all his deeds. Hence, as it seems to me, the Evangelist did not describe so carefully where he went and where he arrived without the reason of a definite mystery; rather, as I have said, because all that he did was our instruction.

By that departure of the Lord, he shows the journey and departure which the Lord deigns to bring about in the blessed man whom he has predestined for life.

“Jesus,” he says, “going out from the borders of Tyre by Sidon came to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the borders of Decapolis.” A man dwells in Tyre, which is interpreted “narrowness,” when he still clings to, seeks, and loves the world. Yet amid the very joys of the world, he is sometimes, by God’s gift, distressed when he begins to remember that, if final death finds him thus, he will undergo the sentence of eternal damnation. Such distress especially makes people leave the world.

For if anyone knew that he would live only so long in this world and that, after present goods, he would possess the future joys of God’s kingdom, he would never turn to God, never leave the world; rather, even if everything did not come to hand according to his desire, he would still prefer above all things to have his own will. But when the Lord Jesus, who works all things in all, produces a departure in him, so that he makes him leave the world, then Jesus may rightly be said to have gone out from the borders of Tyre.

Two boundaries, namely the spirit of fear and the spirit of piety, produce this departure in a man, because through fear and piety a person begins to bring his distresses to an end. Hence there is the customary cry of converts, now resting in hope of attaining eternal life: “[Col. 0560A]Behold,” they say, “the Lord has put an end to my distresses.”

Once this departure has been made—that is, once the former distresses have been left behind—he must come through Sidon, when he pursues and persecutes within himself his past sins and his beastly life, repenting in heart and confessing with his mouth; and he must do so until, by God’s mercy, they are extinguished and mortified.

After this, he must come to the Sea of Galilee. By the sea made bitter through repentance, understand the human heart, which is rightly made bitter when it beholds its many vanities. For though it trusts greatly in the Lord’s boundless mercy, yet, when it begins to ponder and reconsider how just a Judge the Lord is—who never forgets, but wishes to know, though nothing is hidden from him, how many warnings, how many years, how many days in which he ought to have served God it has lived uselessly—it finds it sweet to weep, and in proportion as it sinned delightfully, it loves to repent and mourn bitterly. From this bitterness it makes a certain crossing, which is what Galilee signifies, because it passes from sins to virtues; and, when joys in the Lord succeed, it will overcome every sorrow.

“Through the midst,” he says, “of the borders of Decapolis.” By Decapolis may be understood the Ten Commandments, or the ten senses of the inner and outer person. But if we wish to refer both boundaries to the Ten Commandments, let us consider the first and the last.

And lest it seem absurd to you that I have called the first commandment a boundary, just as I called the last, hear that the first part of anything is called a boundary as properly as its last part. The first boundary of these commandments is: “Thou shalt have no strange gods before me”; the last: “Thou shalt not covet.” He makes strange gods for himself who loves anything besides God; whatever it is that a man prefers to God and loves is rightly called his god. He covets who receives consent to sin; and whoever delights in sin by consenting has, as it were, already committed the sinful act—as the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). But he does not covet who, even if suddenly impelled by a thought of sin, does not delight in bringing the sin to completion.

Therefore we hold Jesus in the midst of these boundaries if we do not make strange gods for ourselves—that is, if we prefer nothing in this world to the love of God. We also do not covet if we give no consent to evil pleasures. Since both commandments concern both aspects of the person—one the inner person, the other the outer—by loving God we preserve the soul, and by not coveting we keep the body from evil acts. Thus, by loving God above all things and by abstaining from evils, what follows comes to pass:

“And they bring to him one deaf and dumb, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him.” Who bring the deaf and dumb man except either the holy angels, by whose good and holy promptings a man is sometimes assisted, or good wills and holy desires, sent from above, by which he is led to God? He is rightly called deaf and dumb. When he first comes away from the world, he is still deaf in that he cannot profitably hear the word of the Lord. He is also dumb because he cannot speak anything good with God or about God. For when he turns to the time of prayer, the world comes and, hardened, does not allow him to speak or pray anything with God; hindered by countless crowds of thoughts, while others stand before God in great sweetness of heart, he is silent as though dumb. For that crowd which rebuked the blind man lest he cry out hinders and opposes this man lest he cry to God.

Since he has thus become deaf and pitiably dumb, it is necessary that good desires bring him by affection and plead for him by action, so that almighty God may lay his hand upon him—that is, that God may begin to work his work inwardly in the human heart. When he has graciously done this and begun to work good in the man, he takes him aside from the crowd. Behold the crowd of which we spoke; behold the disturbed faculties of the man, through whose disturbances he could neither speak good nor hear good. But, when he is taken by the Lord, he is led aside from the crowd, as he is set free from the troublesome tumult of thoughts.

After this, fingers are put into his ear. By the fingers of God may be understood the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or the words of the Lord. These fingers of the Lord are sent not into the ear, but into the little ear (*auricula*, a diminutive term), when the Lord’s words and sayings are heard with a humble heart and received in exceeding sweetness, as Solomon also says: “To a hungry soul bitter things are sweet; but a sated soul mocks the honeycomb” (Prov. 27:7). The hungry soul is one that truly hungers and thirsts for God. Whatever it hears concerning God tastes good and becomes truly sweet to it. It is sweet and pleasant to it whenever it is pierced by an admonition in the Lord’s word concerning its sins, because through that repentance which it has for its sins it truly deserves to attain that inward sweetness of heart. But the sated soul mocks the honeycomb, because surely the soul sated with the vanities of this age mocks the honeycombs of God’s word and disdains to hear.

When the fingers have been put into the little ear, the tongue is touched with spittle, as the Evangelist subsequently adds:

“And spitting, he touched his tongue.” By the spittle which flows from the head into the mouth may be signified that sweetness which descends to us from our head, Jesus Christ. The human tongue is indeed touched with this spittle when, touched inwardly by the divine savour, a person begins to have such a tongue that he can rightly confess his sins to God. Thus, one who formerly confessed his offences only through fear of Gehenna thereafter grieves all the more that he has offended almighty God, the more he sees in him what he may love; and he confesses his sins more from love than from fear.

With the tongue thus touched, hear further the manner of the cure. It follows:

“And looking up to heaven, he groaned and said: Epphetha,” [Col. 0562A]“that is, To open.”

By heaven may be understood the human heart or sacred Scripture. A person looks up to this heaven when he examines his own heart, wishing to know what is going on in it; and, sitting as a kind of judge in this heaven of his heart, he separates good things from bad, gathers good and useful thoughts to himself and keeps them within, and rejects useless and harmful thoughts from himself.

After looking up to heaven, it is fittingly said that “he groaned.” What is groaning? Groaning occurs when a person’s spirit is drawn from the innermost heart with pain. By this, it seems to me, is signified that the man who rightly examines his heaven—that is, his heart—by considering himself, as though groaning draws his spirit from the innermost heart with pain, when he draws spiritual understanding from within; and this pain of heart becomes a kind of enlivening of the heart.

Sacred Scripture too may be understood by heaven, which a person rightly examines when, by God’s gift, he finds in it something by which he may be taught. He also looks upon heaven in this way when, intent upon heavenly things, he becomes able to think and meditate upon heavenly things.

After this looking upward and groaning, it fittingly follows: “And he said: Epphetha, that is, To open.” God’s speaking is his doing. For he opens the inner heart to understanding, so that it may know and see what it ought, with humble and contrite heart, to disclose and confess to God in prayer—whatever sins it has ever committed. And, when it thus inwardly knows itself by God’s mercy, it follows that by good works it becomes known to others and discloses what it rightly understands within.

Once the heart has inwardly been opened to understanding, the following words are fittingly added, as I see it, in this sense:

“And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke rightly.” The ears of the heart, formerly shut against obedience to God, are opened; the bond of the tongue is loosed, so that it speaks rightly. For then it speaks rightly when it performs good works. But because it often happens that a person, while doing good works, glories in them as though they were from his own merits, he must hear and keep in his heart the Lord’s command which follows:

“And he commanded them to tell no one.” There is something which the Lord commands to be done; there is something else in which he gives counsel. It is within your choice whether you wish to assent to his counsel or not; and you are not thereby condemned if you do not assent. But if you do not fear to be a transgressor of his commands, there will be great danger to your soul unless you repent.

It is the Lord’s command that we flee vainglory. To form us by his own example, he commanded that the miracle he had performed should be told to no one. For he desires us, in doing our good works with humility, to hide them from human praise, lest we lose those good works through vainglory. Thus we rightly ask in today’s Prayer that we may run without stumbling toward the Lord’s promises; for we run without stumbling when we flee vainglory.

But we must ask why the Lord says elsewhere to the Apostles, “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16), while here he commands them to tell no one. The reason is this: for those who seek God with a perfect heart, it does no harm if their works are seen. What harm was it to the Apostles when they performed wonderful signs before the people? Strengthened by the Holy Spirit, they ascribed everything to the power of almighty God. Therefore to them it is said: “Let them see your good works.” But to these it is said: “Tell no one.”

> [Note: Col. 0563D: Some material is lacking in the manuscript.]

But what does the following mean—“For the more he commanded them, the more exceedingly they proclaimed it”—except that the more anyone seeks concealment and avoids human praises, the more, by God’s ordering, he is proclaimed and exalted even in this world? Conversely, whoever desires to be praised and exalted here receives far less of this world’s honours and favours than he wishes.

But even if a righteous person were never praised or magnified in this world, a better and surer praise is stored up and preserved for him by the Lord. At the end of life, when the holy angels arrive, his soul is led from this mortality to the joys of heaven amid a great triumph of praise and wonder; and there, raised amid the sweet songs of angels, it deserves to hear: “He has done all things well; he has made the deaf hear and the dumb speak.” Truly this is a great proclamation of praise: “He has done all things well,” for even the evils he once committed have, in a marvellous way through God’s gift, all worked together for his good; he has made his deaf faculties hear rightly and his dumb faculties speak good and useful things.

Thus brought out from the prison of this death and with its labours ended, it concludes, as it were, the praise of its Mass—for *missa* is said to mean “sent praise.” It has now sent to God all its works, in and through which it strove in this world to praise and honour God; and then it will truly be joined to the communion of all the saints, from which no intervening necessity will exclude it.

Therefore, that we may reach that communion of saints, let the chant of today’s Communion teach us: “The earth shall be satisfied from the fruit of thy works, that thou mayest bring bread out of the earth, and that wine may gladden the heart of man” (Ps. 103:13). By earth the soul may be signified; by bread, the teaching of God’s Word; by wine, spiritual joy; by oil, mercy; and by bread, eternal refreshment. The fruit of our works—which God works in us, and by which our earth, that is, our soul, ought to be satisfied and refreshed—is fourfold.

The Lord brings bread out of the earth when he daily causes the bread of his word to grow and increase in the hearts of his elect, and inwardly refreshes and nourishes them with the food of that saving bread. He also brings bread out of the earth when he sets over others, to form and feed them with the breads of teaching, the one whom he has already raised and strengthened by the bread of his word.

Wine too is brought forth, which gladdens the heart of man, when one satisfied by this bread can, through God’s gift, attain that spiritual joy of heart which truly gladdens and intoxicates the minds of God’s children. This wine is drunk in two ways: either when a person is pierced with double compunction for sins, or when, inflamed by the sweet remembrance of eternal things, he is intoxicated and filled with the sweet wine of tears. These first two are to be attained in the present life.

The other two—“that he may make the face cheerful with oil, and that bread may strengthen the heart of man” (ibid., 15)—are to be obtained in the life to come. For in the future life our face is made cheerful with oil, because there, knowing God’s mercy, we shall rejoice with everlasting gladness in the vision of the Lord’s countenance. And because there is full satiety from the bread of angels, that living bread which we now desire and hunger for will there satisfy and strengthen us. It will satisfy us, I say, and not satisfy us, because it is eaten and hungered for, drunk and thirsted for, yet never cloying. May he make us satisfied with that bread who lives and reigns for endless ages of ages. Amen.

812. HOMILY LXXX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE THIRTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0564B]

“Blessed are the eyes that see the things which you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings wished to see the things which you see, and did not see them; and to hear the things which you hear, and did not hear them” (Luke 10).

Since the preceding Sunday, on which the deaf and dumb man is read to have been healed by the Lord, pertains to the gift of the spirit of knowledge, today’s Sunday fittingly performs the work of the spirit of fortitude and follows the preceding one in a very suitable order. For when, aided by the spirit of knowledge, a person can know and recognize himself, it is then necessary that, strengthened by the spirit of fortitude, he rightly open and disclose in confession whatever things his sinful conscience accuses him of. Indeed, all who advance through the spirit of fear to the spirit of piety, from the spirit of piety to the spirit of knowledge, and from the spirit of knowledge to the gift of the spirit of fortitude, are shown to possess blessed eyes of the heart by which they may see God.

“Blessed,” he says, “are the eyes that see the things which you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings wished to see the things which you see, and did not see them; and to hear the things which you hear, and did not hear them.”

In the prophets and kings may be signified the two orders of prelates and subjects: prelates in the prophets, and subjects in the kings—subjects who know how to govern themselves by the teaching and instruction of good prophets, that is, their teachers. Their eyes would be blessed if they saw God through faith and heard through love. For there are some who see through faith because they believe in God, yet do not hear because they do not love God. There are also many prophets and many kings who desire both to see through faith and to hear through love, yet do not attain the effect of their desire. Therefore only those are blessed who deserve both to see through faith and to hear through love.

Because the eyes of such persons are blessed, it sometimes happens that the Lord chooses from among them persons such as these, whom he sets over his bride, the Church—that is, blessed souls—and establishes as teachers—as I see indicated by the following words, when it is added:

“And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing the Lord and saying: Master, what shall I do to possess eternal life?” In the lawyer may be signified some good prelate. He is rightly called skilled in the law because he ought to possess knowledge and understanding of sacred Scripture, in which, by God’s gift, he may see what sort of life and teaching he ought to have.

When this lawyer rises to a position of government, he speaks to the Lord in great humility of mind, saying: “Master, what shall I do to possess eternal life?” It is as if he said: “Because thou, Lord, who art Lord and Master of all things in heaven, hast taken and chosen me for this, that I may be thy vicar on earth, and because the more I am an object of fear to others, the more I ought to fear thee, teach me how I may live cautiously and holily in thy place, and how I may teach. For even if I neglect myself in order to provide for my subjects, I shall not thereby possess eternal life. But if I provide for myself and neglect their salvation, again I cannot be saved in this respect. Since this is so, I would wish, through thy instruction, to know what I ought to be in my life and teaching, and how through these things I may so provide for my subjects that both I with them and they with me may possess eternal life.”

After the lawyer’s question, hear the Lord’s answer.

“But he said to him: What is written in the law? How do you read?” By these words, after such a question, the Lord sends the prelate to sacred Scripture, so that, if he desires to know how he ought to live and teach, he may seek the truth of sacred Scripture. But once the truth is known—which is as though to say, “What is written in the law?”—it is most fitting that he hold the truth with humility—which is to say, “How do you read?” For the whole work of the divine page everywhere proclaims and commends these two goods: truth and humility. Therefore, when he is asked what is written and how he reads, he is taught by his own answer that he ought to hold truth in knowing and humility in uttering:

“You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and your neighbour as yourself.” When he says, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” truth is shown; when he says, “and your neighbour as yourself,” humility is shown. For it is the highest truth to love God, and true humility to love one’s neighbour. And, as I see, just as truth pertains to love of God, so humility pertains to love of one’s neighbour. For as the devil, falling from heaven through pride, will never be able to return to love of God and neighbour, so no person can love his neighbour as himself unless he is truly humble in heart. And where humility is absent, pride reigning there will always be enmities and hatreds.

Therefore, if the prelate preserves truth by loving God and preserves humility by loving his neighbour, he is shown to have answered rightly and taught himself rightly, as the Lord says: “You have answered rightly; do this and you shall live.” But because the prelate desires to know toward how great a perfection he ought still to strive, it is fittingly added:

“But he, wishing to justify himself.” What is it to wish to justify oneself? It is to have no will other than that of acting rightly and carrying out, according to one’s ability, the things pleasing to God. For it is not justice, even though it often seems just, that greater grace should be bestowed on one who needs less grace, while less grace is given to one for whom greater grace would be necessary. Considering this, the prelate earnestly asks God graciously to show him whom, among his subjects, he ought especially to love, saying:

“And who is my neighbour?” “Lord,” he says, “thou who willst me to be skilled in the law, thou who hast appointed me to be a teacher and prelate, show me which of my neighbours I ought especially to love according to thy justice, and to whom I ought to give greater help.”

That this will of the prelate is pleasing and acceptable to God is rightly indicated by the immediate statement:

“But Jesus, looking upon it.” He looks upon this justification because he loves and approves it; and he introduces and shows who ought to be regarded as the neighbour, saying: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers.” This certain man is the sinful person who, despising the vision of eternal peace, goes down into Jericho—that is, he comes into the failure and changeableness of crimes and sins. In this descent he falls among robbers: that is, evil spirits, who, assailing him in various ways, cause him to fall through diverse sins and vices.

They also stripped him, not of a visible garment but of an invisible one: the garment of innocence, which he received in baptism in order to preserve it unstained for God. Once stripped of the garment of innocence, it would be remarkable if he did not suffer the blows of these robbers.

“And having laid wounds upon him,” says the Evangelist, “they departed, leaving him half-dead.” Blows are one thing and wounds another; wounds are one thing and blows another. Blows are said to occur when flesh is worn down by lashings and beatings, and, as the flesh swells, putrefaction sometimes breaks out. What can we understand by this disfigurement of blows except the filth of evil and unclean desires, which the robbers—that is, our invisible enemies—lay upon and inject into a person? By these they presume to assail him against his will in the spiritual life, setting before and pressing upon him things that he once did with pleasure.

But having inflicted these blows, they depart, leaving him half-dead. He is aptly called half-dead. Insofar as he has some recognition of God, he lives; but insofar as he has fallen through sins, he is truly dead before God. Whoever he may be who falls among robbers in this manner, who is so stripped and suffers their blows, must be regarded as a neighbour. It is fitting that neither priest nor Levite should pass him by, of whom the Gospel subsequently says:

“Now it happened that a certain priest passed by; and, seeing him, he went on. Likewise also a Levite, when he was near the place, went on.” In the priest, the Levite, and the Samaritan may be signified one and the same prelate, who fittingly bears the name of priest and Levite: priest because he ought to pray, and Levite because he ought to read. Yet unless he is a Samaritan pouring in oil and wine, he does not fully or rightly discharge the obligation of his office. Therefore it seems to me that in the parable proposed to the lawyer the Lord, as it were, reveals to the prelate what he wills, saying:

“You are a priest, daily sacrificing and offering yourself to me upon the altar of your heart; your concern is how you may please me in prayers, vigils, and fasts. You are my Levite, constantly reciting and reading the divine pages. But none of these things is sufficient for me in you unless I see you imitate the work of the merciful Samaritan, so that his deeds may be yours.” These deeds are described by the Evangelist with such care:

“But a certain Samaritan, journeying, came near him; and seeing him, was moved with compassion. And approaching, he bound his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.” Behold the order; behold the kind of treatment that ought to be given. These are the Samaritan’s remedies, through which he must heal to its former health the soul wounded by sins.

He must journey from place to place, because he must pass from concern for himself to concern for the other, from care for himself to care for the other. He must also come near him, because with good and loving words, now with good examples, he must follow him until he sees him. What do I mean by “until he sees him,” except until he learns, through careful examination in confession, the miseries of his sins, and by his merciful admonitions makes him see himself more and more?

Once he has seen his misery, he must not have a hardened heart, but must be moved with great compassion for him, so great is the misery of the sinful soul.

In this mercy he must bestow two benefits upon him: namely, draw near to him and bind up his wounds. What is it to draw near to a man, except to present oneself to the sinner as though oneself a sinner, to confess oneself guilty in every way with humble words, and to make oneself like the sinner? For a good prelate to whom the care of souls has been entrusted is accustomed, when a sinful man is ashamed to confess his wrongs, to console him in this manner: “Do not be afraid; do not be dismayed. I too have fallen into such sins, [Col. 0567D] or even graver ones; and if I have not fallen, I may yet fall.” By this accusation of himself, through God’s mediation, he removes all fear and shame from confession. Thus, by drawing near and rendering such compassionate help, he must also bind up the man’s wounds through admonition, and for this purpose pour in oil and wine. See how fittingly oil pertains to drawing near and wine to binding up. For by the drawing near I have described, he pours in oil, signifying consolation; by binding up, he pours in wine, signifying fear. Both are necessary: one must draw near by pouring in the oil of consolation, and bind—that is, frighten—by pouring in the wine of fear. He must be comforted by hope of pardon, lest he despair; and frightened by the punishment of penalty, lest he presume to repeat the same sins. After consolation has been given [Col. 0568A] and fear set before him, he places him upon his own beast.

“And placing him,” he says, “upon his own beast, he brought him to an inn and took care of him.” Since the Gospel does not expressly say whose beast it was—whether the Samaritan’s or that of the man who fell among robbers—we may understand the words, “placing him upon his own beast,” in two ways, referring them both to the prelate and to the subject. By the beast may be understood the human body, upon which a man is placed when he makes strict and exact satisfaction to God in his body for whatever he has at any time committed before the Lord through the pursuit of evil action. But we may also understand it thus: the Samaritan, that is, the good prelate, places that wounded man upon his own beast [Col. 0568B] when, out of excessive compassion and pity, he offers and sets forth himself to make satisfaction for him and with him; and, so that the sinner may be encouraged by greater hope, he now multiplies vigils, now fasts, prayers, and scourges. And he truly brings him to an inn, that is, into his own heart—formerly proud, now foul-smelling and humbled in the recognition of sin—because through this condescension of the prelate the sinner begins more and more to recognize and abhor the stench of his own heart, to regard as great what he had formerly counted slight and insignificant, and, by God’s mercy, to lament it more abundantly. Thus healed, he proceeds to the second day, of which it is immediately said:

“And on the next day he brought out two denarii, and gave them to the innkeeper, saying: ‘Take care of him; and whatever [Col. 0568C] you spend beyond this, I, when I return, will repay you.’” The first day is self-knowledge; the second day, knowledge of God. For each person begins to be righteous when he recognizes himself as a sinner; and the more humbly he recognizes himself, the nearer he approaches divine knowledge. Or the first day is when he laments through worthy repentance the evil he has committed; the second day, when he laments that through negligence he did not do good. The two denarii are the two commandments: love of God and of neighbour. Or, in the two denarii may be signified the knowledge of Holy Scripture, possessed in its historical and moral senses.

These two denarii rightly pass to the use of the innkeeper—I mean the one who always strives to be an innkeeper, who always in humility sets the stench [Col. 0568D] of his crimes before the eyes of his heart—for he is commanded to observe the two commandments of charity, to love Holy Scripture, and to take care of that man. *Cura* (“care”) is so called from *urere cor*, “to burn the heart.” It is as though the prelate exhorts and admonishes his innkeeper, saying: “By continually reading Holy Scripture, burn your heart; and whenever any wantonness or frivolity of mind comes upon you, run to Scripture and consume yourself wholly there. For if you do this, you will have a heart not lukewarm or cold, but burning and fervent in God.”

“And whatever you spend beyond this, I, when I return, will repay you.” What does this mean: “I, when I return, will repay you”? Who will repay, and what will he repay? “I,” he says, “I, your teacher; I, your judge, appointed by God in this world—I shall repay you that ‘whatever,’ that is, that ineffable joy [Col. 0569A] which is above all things. You now expend it—meaning, as it were, you ask beyond what is due—because you do not yet possess it, you do not yet see it. That joy, I say, when I return—that is, when I rise in the general resurrection and return to the body and see you—I shall repay to you. And I promise this with such certainty as though I held it in my own power.” Lest perhaps we wonder at this and say that it may be incredible, let us hear what he says to Peter and the other apostles and their followers, whom, rooted and grounded in his charity and despising the world, he willed to set over others in this world: “Amen I say to you, that you who have left all things and followed me shall sit upon seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XXIV, 28). Therefore the words [Col. 0569B] of the prelate who says, “I, when I return, will repay you,” do not seem to me frivolous or absurd. For it is as though he said—and he can say this truly, without at all departing from the words of his Master Jesus Christ—“Because in the healing of your soul I bear Christ’s role, I shall be your judge with God; in judgment I shall carry out God’s work with God; and as I can condemn the wicked, so I can reward the righteous. If you repent rightly and live well, I shall give you eternal life, which is that ‘whatever.’”

The following words seem to me to agree sufficiently with these words of the prelate:

“Which of these three, do you think, was neighbour to the man who fell among robbers?” But he said: “The one who showed mercy to him.” “Go, and do likewise.” It is as though he said: “You asked and inquired who ought to be your neighbour; and you yourself judged that he is neighbour [Col. 0569C] who showed mercy. Go, therefore, and do likewise: that is, whoever you see to be most wretched, reckon him your neighbour.” Why do I say “most wretched,” and whom do I call most wretched? I call him most wretched whom you know to be most subject to sins; and the more you know someone to be subject to sins, the more you should reckon him your neighbour. If you do this, what you desire will come about. What do you desire? You desire to be righteous. And you will truly be righteous if you do these things.

The excellence of today’s office seems to me greatly to accord with all this. In it, he who is Christ’s vicar presents himself between God and the people entrusted to him, in order to plead with God the Father, saying: “Look upon thy covenant, O Lord, and do not forsake the souls of thy poor [Col. 0569D] unto the end. Arise, O Lord, and judge thy cause; and forget not the voices of those who seek thee” (Ps. LXXIII, 19–23). “The salvation,” he says, “of these souls whom you have entrusted to me is your cause, not mine. Therefore I beseech you to look upon your covenant—that is, to show me the way of truth in which I may walk, rightly loving and teaching you. And again I ask you to look upon your covenant—that is, that I may love you in humility and teach you in humility. And because both I and my subjects are your poor, do not forsake the souls of your poor unto the end; but arise and judge your cause, not mine. Remember the reproach of your servants, because great reproach will fall upon us if we love you and our neighbour less than we ought.”

[Col. 0570A] Nor does the Alleluia disagree with these words: “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us make joyful noise to God our saviour. Let us come before his face in confession, and in psalms let us make joyful noise to God” (Ps. XCIV, 1–2). This, as it seems to me, is the voice of subjects mutually exhorting one another to repentance and saying: “Come, let us rejoice”—that is, let us make a certain leap outward, turning ourselves from sins and vices to virtues; let us make joyful noise to God by repenting in the bitterness of heart; let us come before his face through confession; and in psalms let us make joyful noise to him by making satisfaction for our sins. After confession has been made and satisfaction rendered, they can now hope and place confidence in God’s mercy, as the prophet David says: “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. IV, 6). And immediately he adds: “And hope [Col. 0570B] in the Lord” (*ibid.*). That is, when through repentance and satisfaction you have offered to the Lord an acceptable sacrifice, after this hope in the Lord; and, relying upon his goodness, you may say: “In thee have I hoped, O Lord; I have said: Thou art my God; my times are in thy hands” (Ps. XXX, 15–16). That is: you alone, O Lord, are our hope, because our coming to you, our fleeing to you, and all our hope and confidence in you are from you, by whose singular gift we have received this. What will happen to us hereafter, we do not know. You alone know, because our times are in your hands.

Today’s Collect looks to these matters and embraces both the Gospel and the whole office of the Mass. In it we pray thus: “Almighty everlasting God, grant us [Col. 0570C] an increase of faith, hope, and charity; and, that we may deserve to attain what you promise, make us love what you command.”

For we must pray in faith that the Lord may look upon his covenant and not forget unto the end the souls of his poor. We must place our hope in him, in whose hands are our times. We must love with burning charity him in whose body and blood we communicate, who gives himself as bread from heaven, containing every delight and every savour of sweetness. And that we may deserve to attain that “whatever,” that ineffable joy which he promises through the mouths of prelates, may he make us love what he commands. For through his prelates he commands and teaches us to have a heart fervent and burning in him. [Col. 0570D] And if he grants this, we shall without doubt deserve to attain what he promises, which is nothing other than eternal life. May he lead us to it, whose dominion remains without end unto ages of ages. Amen.

821. HOMILY LXXXI. ON THE SAME SUNDAY, SECOND [HOMILY].

“A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers” (Luke X).

This certain man is God, the Son of God himself: truly “a certain man,” truly a particular and singular man. I call him singular because, alone among sinners, he lived in this world free and exempt from every stain of sin; in him, as the Apostle says, it pleased God the Father that all the fullness of divinity should dwell bodily (Col. I, 19).

[Col. 0571A] “Who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” Jerusalem means “vision of peace”; Jericho is interpreted “moon.” Clearly, the Lord Jesus Christ went down from Jerusalem to Jericho when he was sent by God the Father from the vision of peace, from the homeland and kingdom of his heavenly city, into the waning and mutability of this world.

And in going down—that is, in being wonderfully clothed with human nature—he fell among robbers, because that Jewish people from whom he proceeded according to the flesh began to persecute him as soon as he was born, and, in the manner of robbers, did not cease to pursue and plot against him until death. “They also stripped him.” That body of the Lord, the beautiful temple of divinity, lost its own garment through the hands of the Jews when the apostles—who the day before had clung to him as friends and members of his household—forsook him at the very point of death and fled. [Col. 0571B] For this reason we may call them the Lord’s garment. For as clothing surrounds and adorns a human body, so Christ, indeed, clothed and adorned himself as it were with his garments when he chose and united to himself apostles from the whole world.

“And having inflicted wounds,” he says. The wounds signify all Christ’s persecutions, which he suffered not unwillingly but, as one hungry, delighted in and was satisfied by them. For in the house of those who loved him he was wounded with wounds: namely, with most savage injuries and blasphemies, terrors, reproaches, scourges, spittings, and blows.

“And at last, when he had been brought to completion by the bitterness of death, they departed, leaving him half alive.” The Son of God is said to have been left as it were half alive when, in human nature, he willed to taste death for an hour; according to his divine nature he was impassible, immortal, and invisible, and could never suffer anything subject to suffering or misery.

[Col. 0571C] “Now it happened that a certain priest was going down the same road, and, seeing him, passed by.” By this priest, the Levite, and the Samaritan may be understood the three orders: those who were before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. The order of the patriarchs and other righteous persons who were before the Law is rightly signified by the priest. They were truly priests of the Lord because they had no other law than striving daily to sacrifice themselves as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, upon the altar of their heart; and by the sacrifices which they offered, they made God in some sense gentle and propitious toward themselves. It is well said of them that they went down the same road, because all were exiled from that road of Paradise by which our first parent Adam had gone down; and because our death had not yet been destroyed by Christ’s death, after the darkness of this mortality they went down to hell without reprieve. Seeing that deified man, [Col. 0571D] certainly by faith and not by sight, they passed by, because they did not await his coming in the flesh; and thus, without having attained salvation, they entered upon the way of all flesh and were held captive in hell for many thousands of years.

[Col. 0572A] “Likewise also the Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by.” In the Levite, so far as I can see, is not unfittingly figured the order of those righteous persons who were under the Law. The Levites are said to have been near the place because they were near the Law and had and read the Law, in which lay hidden all that was fittingly to be accomplished at the end of time through the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension. They too saw him only by faith; but without attaining the salvation which they sought and sighed for, they passed away after paying the debt of the flesh.

“But a Samaritan, making a journey, came near him; and seeing him left half alive, was moved with compassion.” By the Samaritan, I think, the Gentile peoples are signified. [Col. 0572B] For Samaritan is interpreted “keeper.” The people of the Gentiles are rightly figured by the Samaritan, for, having received the faith of baptism, they were being prepared to keep and observe every command of their Lord. This people stood still and did not hasten toward the Lord God by the steps of faith as it ought, while it was given over to the impurities of idolatry. Hence elsewhere, to those called into the Lord’s vineyard at the eleventh hour, it is said: “Why stand you here all the day idle?” (Matt. XX, 6). Because they had neglected to labour for their life and worshipped idols instead of God, they stood as it were idle all day. But that people, which had long stood still, in some sense made a journey when, helped and pierced with compunction by God, it began to come to God by the steps of the mind through faith. It also came near him because, eagerly and desirously, it received by hearing what great and ineffable goods he had bestowed on humankind. [Col. 0572C] It likewise saw him when it recognized and loved those same works of mercy and compassion, presumed nothing of itself, feared and repented of its past deeds, and began to be moved with mercy. For it was bent in compassionate mercy over its own soul: that mercy which Solomon commends and urges, saying, “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX, 24).

“And approaching, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.” By approaching through faith, it bound the wounds of Christ to its heart through hope. For Holy Church—or any blessed soul—must not merely glance in passing at and contemplate the wounds of her Lord and Redeemer for the hope of life [Col. 0572D]; rather, she must carefully bind them to her heart as though into a little bundle, because she must always consider and ponder how she may worthily answer for them. Thus Solomon again admonishes, saying: “Have you sat at a great table? Consider what is set before you, and know that you must prepare such things” [Note: [Col. 0571D] The Vulgate does not have precisely the same wording.] (Prov. XXIII, 1). For then we prepare like things, when we are not ungrateful to him for his innumerable benefits; when, admiring and embracing his surpassing charity, we strive according to our ability to render back the little that we are in return for such love and condescension.

“Pouring in,” he says, “oil and wine.” By oil and wine understand two impulses, fear and love, [Col. 0573A] through which evils are avoided and good deeds performed. The blessed soul then pours in oil and wine when, through God’s help, it pours love and fear into its heart: fearing God because he is its Creator, loving him because he is its Redeemer; pouring inward by doing good for love’s sake, and pouring outward by avoiding evil for fear’s sake.

“And placing him upon his own beast, he brought him to an inn and took care of him.” The beast rightly signifies the human body. Upon it that blessed soul places the wounded man—that is, its Lord, pierced with thorns, struck with blows, crucified, and pierced with a lance—when, mortifying its flesh with its vices and desires, it strives to follow and imitate the blessed passion of the Son of God, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying of himself: “But I bear the marks of Jesus in my body” (Gal. VI, 17). [Col. 0573B] It brings him also to an inn when it brings Christ into its humble and foul-smelling heart. That heart will then be foul-smelling when it begins in bitterness of soul to reflect and reflect again upon how it has defiled itself by most disgraceful and filthy deeds. Then, after the dung of sin has been expelled and cleansed away through repentance, it will rejoice in Christ, whom it has brought into the inn of its heart and body, as its possessor.

It also brings the Lord of angels himself into its inn when it communicates in the most holy body and blood of its Lord, which truly supplies our souls with a great and wonderful nourishment of eternal life. We communicate worthily and faithfully in his body and blood when, in order to imitate Christ’s passion and to commit to memory what he suffered for us, we offer our whole selves in most burning charity. There are some indeed who chastise and mortify their flesh, but do not bring Christ into the inn of their heart, because they do not preserve in humility the good works they perform. While they ascribe those works to themselves rather than to God, they miserably lose the fruit of their labour. [Col. 0573C] Therefore, those laudably bring Christ into the inn who, conformed to the likeness of his death, tame and mortify the flesh; and who, lest they be lifted up in pride and at some time lose the reward they hope to obtain from God, undertake to preserve the virtue of Christ, which is Christ’s humility. Blessed is she who is fortified with this virtue—that is, humility—as companion and helper [Col. 0573D]; for whatever soul is truly humbled in its own eyes, known only to the one Lord and to angelic spirits, can render worthy care to God and its Lord, so that it may rightly be said of her, “and he took care of him.” For she has great care and concern as to how she may keep Christ in her heart, how he may continually be cherished by her; she seeks what chiefly her beloved loves, what delights and gladdens him; and she expends upon him, as far as she can, all that she is and lives. This is indeed to take care of Christ.

“And on the next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying: ‘Take care of him; and whatever you spend beyond this, I, when I return, will repay you.’” We must ask what the first day is and what the second day is. The first day can be called the day of knowledge; the second, the day of illumination. The two denarii are the two commandments of love of God and neighbour, or the two Testaments. The first day, then, is the day of knowledge, on which a man begins to recognize himself in true humility of heart. From this knowledge of himself he advances to the second day, the day of illumination, on which, enlightened from above, he progresses to the knowledge and understanding of God. [Col. 0574A] On that day the two denarii are produced, because the two commandments of love of God and neighbour, or the words of the two Testaments, are set before us to be followed. The authority of all Holy Scripture tends to this one end and teaches this alone: that we should turn away from evil and do good. By turning away from evil, the image of the denarius—that is, the likeness of Christ [Col. 0574B], which we lost by sinning—is restored in us; by doing good, that same image of Christ is adorned in us.

These two denarii are rightly given to the innkeeper, to whom it is also said, “Take care of him; and whatever you spend beyond this, I, when I return, will repay you.” By the innkeeper is understood the humble man himself, the governor and keeper of his own heart, upon whom is laid the care of that wounded and crucified man, Jesus Christ the Son of God. “Take care of him,” he says. *Cura* is so called because it burns the heart. It is as though the human spirit inwardly exhorts itself and says: “Do not grow weak; do not become sluggish; do not dissolve in idleness, but keep your heart burning and inflamed in the love of God.” “And whatever you spend beyond this”: that is, however much labour you expend in attaining that reward of eternal blessedness [Col. 0574C] which is above all things and surpasses all, which is therefore called “whatever” because it is ineffable and boundless—“I, when I return at the final examination of judgment,” that is, when I have been raised with body and soul, “will repay you.” For then you will possess with me the same glory which, before the Day of Judgment, I shall possess in my soul with God’s help.

David speaks plainly of this return, saying: “His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return into his earth; in that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. CXLV, 4). The spirit goes forth when we lay down the body in death; but it returns into its earth when, in the resurrection, having resumed the flesh, it is rewarded with the glory of perpetual immortality. [Col. 0574D] On that day of resurrection all their thoughts shall perish, because whatever pious labour and striving, whatever holy and continual meditation and good desire, is expended and performed here in order to gain the glory of eternal life, will then perish in this sense: when that supreme gift has been received, which is bestowed above all things and beyond which nothing greater or more precious can be acquired, a human being will rest from all these things.

Having set forth this example, the Lord makes the Pharisee, who believed himself righteous, know by his question how much he lacks and how much imperfection he possesses. “Which,” he says, “of these three seems to you to have been neighbour to the man who fell among robbers?” But he said: “The one who showed mercy to him.” And Jesus said to him: “Go, and do likewise.” It is as though he said: [Col. 0575A] “If you assert that the priest and Levite are not my neighbours, but that those are neighbours who, receiving me by faith and love, know how to have compassion and sorrow with me, go and do likewise. That is, go and turn from your false righteousness to true righteousness; do likewise, so that your life may accord with that of my bride, my Church, which received me through faith, and great reward shall be yours for your work.”

HOMILY LXXXII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FOURTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

“While Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee” (Luke XVII).

On the preceding Sundays we have heard how God deigns to draw near to a man through the spirit of fear, piety, knowledge, and fortitude. On this Sunday [Col. 0575B] we are now taught by what way a man, aided by the spirit of counsel—which works on this Sunday—ought to come to him. For all that we heard in the preceding Gospels is the way of Jesus, by which he makes his journey to the human heart; and by his journey to us he brings us to Jerusalem, as the present Gospel says: “While Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee.”

By Jerusalem, interpreted “vision of peace,” may be signified that heavenly Jerusalem, or the repose of the spiritual life, in which a man must rest, insofar as God mercifully grants, from sins and from the world. But because we are still on the journey and have not yet reached our homeland, we must pass not only through Samaria but through the midst of Samaria [Col. 0575C] and Galilee. Samaria is interpreted “guardianship,” Galilee “migration.” Between us and the heavenly Jerusalem there must lie Samaria and Galilee, because as long as we are here we must keep ourselves with every vigilance from unlawful actions and make a passage from Samaria to Galilee—that is, from vices to virtues. By this way and journey of Jesus, by this guardianship of life and blessed passage, Jesus enters a certain little town, as is added:

“And as he entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him.” The certain village seems to me to signify man himself. By God’s fortification he becomes a particular little stronghold when he is somewhat fortified against the devil and vices; Jesus enters it when he deigns to visit the human soul [Col. 0575D] and gladden it by his presence. Yet although God has advanced his journey in man and done all these things in him, because he can in no way exist without attacks of temptations, it is well said: “Ten leprous men met him.” Who are the ten leprous men? The ten men are the whole human being, consisting in five inward and five outward senses. Since *vir* (“man”) is derived from *virtus* (“virtue”), the ten human senses are men and are called men when a person imagines himself to possess some virtue, and, because he hopes that he has done some good and made progress in God, begins vainly and heedlessly to exalt himself and glory. Such men are altogether leprous, because it is a great impurity of leprosy to presume upon oneself and glory without cause. And because this vice of self-exaltation is not hidden from God—for all things are naked and open to him—it is fittingly and appropriately said that these ten men met him.

[Col. 0576A] 829. Note that it says, “met.” It sometimes happens in good and tested people, after they have advanced in the order described, that a certain boasting of mind touches them on account of their good merits. Yet because this does not enter the human senses through deliberate intention or decision, but suddenly, as though by a kind of assault, the evangelist aptly uses this word: “Ten leprous men met him.” But although it is an encounter, the encounter itself, suggested by the devil, often becomes inwardly sweet and delightful to a person; and the more he delights in it, the farther he is removed from God.

Hence it is fittingly added [Col. 0576B]: “Who stood at a distance.” A person seems to himself to stand, but does not stand, when he considers that he has something from good merits; and therefore he stands at a distance. For an exalted heart is far from God, and cannot approach God unless it is a humble heart. When this encounter has occurred in a person, the voice must be raised, as the following Gospel text says of those men:

“And they raised their voice.” This voice is the desire of the heart, through which God is called upon and invited, and which he desires to hear. For he rarely deigns to hear the voice of the mouth without the desire of the heart. And it rightly says, “they raised,” because nothing placed on high or above is said to be raised; rather, what lies upon the earth is properly said to be lifted upward from lower things. Therefore the voice is raised when a man raises his desire from the things on earth and below which he had sought, and lifts and elevates himself from the lower regions to the heights. For it is low and most base to seek transitory things and to seek upon earth that reward which ought to be sought and hoped for from heaven. What then does this voice of desire, raised upward, say? What does it pray?

[Col. 0576C] “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” It is as though it says: “O Lord, I fittingly apply to you both names, Saviour and Master: Saviour, because through the ineffable grace of your mercy you came to save me by redeeming me from sins. You are my Saviour, I say, because you have wrought my salvation in me. And just as I embrace and love you as Saviour, so, because I know myself guilty and attribute to you what is yours, I therefore fear you as my master—that is, as it were my judge and condemner. [Col. 0576D] But because I know you as my Saviour, I cry: ‘Have mercy on me.’” After such an elevation of the heart, the evangelist adds:

“Whom, when he saw them, he said: ‘Go, show yourselves to the priests.’” Clearly, whenever a sinner raises the inward desires of his heart to God, God sees it. God’s seeing, as we have often said, is God’s loving. For he loves that a person recognizes him as Master and Saviour, and through the spirit of counsel he supplies him with salutary counsel. For just as on the preceding Sunday the spirit of fortitude, whose strength is necessary in confession, was at work, so on this Sunday the spirit of counsel works together with the spirit of fortitude. Just as there, strengthened by the spirit of fortitude, the man was not ashamed to confess his evil deeds, so here, aided by the spirit of counsel, he must not conceal in confession the encounter of leprosy which takes place in the heart, when the Lord commands and says: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” “Go,” he says, “in desire; show yourselves in good works.”

[Col. 0577A] “And it came to pass, as they were going, they were cleansed.” In another Gospel we read that the Lord said to a certain leper: “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer your gift which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them” (Matt. VIII, 4). In the leprosy of that man may be signified deeds actually committed; and without doubt forgiveness does not follow unless a true confession of the mouth first precedes it. But here, where only an encounter of leprosy occurs, so to speak—that is, vain glory from good works—it is said [Col. 0577B]: “And it came to pass, as they were going, they were cleansed.” This is a great lesson and a great aid to our consolation: these lepers are cleansed as they go. A man goes and is cleansed when he humbly recognizes himself in his heart; and while he has the will to confess, this humility removes the will of self-exaltation. If he truly and not falsely resolves, when the occasion arises, to confess the encounter of this leprosy, by God’s mercy, which deigns to regard a good will, it is immediately forgiven him and he is cleansed before God. David himself confirms this, saying: “I said: I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord; and thou hast forgiven the impiety of my sin” (Ps. XXXI, 5). [Col. 0577C] The impiety of sin is the swelling and arrogant self-exaltation which, when a man decides truly to confess it against himself, immediately receives from the Lord the grace of pardon. But if he falsely resolves in his heart to confess, and does not confess even when opportunity is available, the grace of forgiveness is far from him. It follows:

“But one of them, when he saw that he was cleansed, returned with a loud voice, glorifying God.” Behold, from those ten lepers one man is made: one, I say, when he returns wholly, with every intention, to God. That one returns to God who had as it were departed from God when the unclean leprosy of self-exaltation defiled him. For he returns through the repentance of a humbled heart, having as it were departed from God, as we have said, through the exaltation of a proud mind. The impurity of leprosy can fittingly be applied to the vice of pride, because it is written: “He who exalts his heart is unclean before God.” But when this one, abandoning the sins of pride, returns and is reconciled to God through repentance and satisfaction, he begins to glorify God. He glorifies God who judges himself humble, unworthy, and sinful. But he does not glorify God—rather, makes him as it were small in his own eyes—who considers himself exalted and possessed of some merit, when he is nothing and has nothing except what is supplied to him by God’s gift. Therefore this one praises and glorifies God with a loud voice [Col. 0577D] when, from deep humility of heart, he assigns glory to God alone and disgrace to himself. Of his devotion it is then figuratively added:

[Col. 0578A] “And he fell upon his face before the feet of Jesus, giving thanks. And he was a Samaritan.” The Lord’s feet, by which he walks through the devout minds of his elect, are, as you have heard in many passages of Scripture, mercy and judgment. A man falls before these feet when he always keeps before himself both God’s mercy and God’s judgment, hoping in God’s mercy and fearing his judgment. Now he embraces one foot, now the other: lest the remembrance of judgment alone bring despair, he embraces the foot of mercy; lest remembrance of mercy alone produce negligence and carelessness, he always sets the fear of judgment before the eyes of his mind. For he who lives in the self-exaltation of mind embraces neither foot, and does not keep the foot of mercy before his face, because he forgets the work of God’s mercy and in a sense detracts from it, appropriating to himself the few good things he seems to possess. But when he attributes nothing to his own merits and has glorified God by humbling himself, it follows afterward that he gives thanks. A person gives thanks when he shows in good works, for the edification of others, what he attributes to God in understanding and affection. Whoever advances in such an order is and will be a Samaritan, interpreted “keeper,” of whom the evangelist adds: “And he was a Samaritan.” For he will truly be a Samaritan, that is, a keeper of the mind, who, after receiving the grace of cleansing and repentance, does not abandon humility—the guardian of virtues—by living well unto the end.

[Col. 0578C] But Jesus answered and said: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” When a person is united to God alone with all his desires and has offered his satisfaction, the Lord Jesus, answering his inquiries, calls him inward, in order to make him marvel at His ineffable goods, saying: “Were not ten cleansed?” As though Truth plainly said: “That your ten senses have been cleansed from the leprosy of pride is not from yourself, but from Me. And where are the nine?” Three times three make nine; and by this triadic number words, deeds, and thoughts may be signified. It is as though the Lord said: “Formerly you exalted yourself over holy deeds, good words, and right desires; now where are those nine?” [Col. 0578D] They appear nowhere; they are nowhere with you, because they have been cleansed by Me.

833 “There was not found one who returned and gave glory to God, except this foreigner.” When you sought your own glory rather than Mine, you were not found to return and give glory to God; but since you have made foreign to yourself those things in you which displeased Me, now, having become a good foreigner, you seek in every way not your own glory but Mine. And since you ascribe nothing to yourself but attribute all that is yours to Me alone, “Arise and go, because your faith has made you whole.” Arise, I say, in presiding; go forth in edification, so that the good which you have tasted inwardly may become known to others. For that faith—by which you kept yourself from sins and attributed all your good works to God alone—has made you whole [Col. 0579A] and will join you to everlasting salvation in the life to come.

But these words may also be referred in another way to each elect person, to whom God says at the end of life, when cleansed from every leprosy of sins: “Arise, go, because your faith has made you whole.” “Arise,” He says, “from what is below you; leave the confines of the flesh; go to the dwellings prepared for you in the house of My Father. And because you kept faith with Me alone, attributing wholly to Me what you had from Me, you shall be saved forever; forever you shall behold My face in joy.”

The excellence of today’s office looks to this evangelical meaning, in which the person cleansed from leprosy is commended to Christ and admonished henceforth to strive to live under great watchfulness. Thus we sing: “Look upon us, O God our protector, and behold the face [Col. 0579B] of Thy Christ, for one day in Thy courts is better than thousands.” Christ is called “Anointed.” A person is called God’s anointed and God’s Christ when one previously dry, having no sap of God’s sweetness within, is anointed and filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, in the Introit of the Mass we ask that He who is our protector, by giving us His Christ, may always look upon us as His anointed ones, always preserve us in this: that we may give glory to His name, not to ours. For one day in His courts is better than thousands; that is, in our bodies and souls, which may be understood as the Lord’s courts, one day of His knowledge and illumination is better than thousands—it surpasses and excels all our works and merits. Those who meditate on and do these things [Col. 0579C] are the beloved tabernacles of the Lord, of whom it follows: “How beloved are Thy tabernacles, O Lord of 834 hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:1). For they are those tabernacles in which the Lord deigns to walk and dwell; and such are those whose heart and soul long and faint for the courts of the Lord.

To such persons Paul speaks in today’s Lesson, saying: “Walk in the Spirit, and do not fulfil the desires of the flesh. Now the works of the flesh are manifest: adulteries, fornications, uncleanness, lust, idolatry,” and such like (Gal. 5:16–19). They walk in the Spirit who, even though carnal desires assail them, do not seek to bring them into effect by deed. For as long as [Col. 0579D] we live, the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. But blessed are those who walk in the Spirit and do not fulfil the desires of the flesh.

Yet it must be known that carnal desires are not only adulteries and fornications, but that there is also said to be a certain spiritual fornication of the soul, when a person commits fornication away from God. When, I ask, does one commit fornication away from God?
