Certainly when he sins by anger, pride, or vainglory; when he pursues love of human praise and desires that the goods of God’s manifold grace, which God has bestowed upon him, should be referred to himself rather than to Him from whom he received everything. Of such persons David says: “Thou hast destroyed every one who commits fornication away from Thee” (Ps. 72:27). Hence it is added: “It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man” (Ps. 117:8); that [Col. 0580A] is, it is better—indeed, best—to trust in God’s power than to presume upon one’s own merits. “It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes” (ibid., v. 9). Who are these princes, and who are our servants? Our inward senses are princes; our outward senses are servants. We are not to hope in these princes or servants, but rather to hope and place confidence in the Lord our God. Why? “For God is a great Lord, and a great King over all the earth” (Ps. 94:3). He alone is great and most worthy of praise; He alone is the great King, who works all things in all, since He is He of whom the Offertory cries: “The angel of the Lord shall encamp round about those who fear Him, and shall deliver them. Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:8–9). This angel [Col. 0580B] whom God sends about those who fear Him is the gift of His grace, without whose gift a person can never see and taste that the Lord is sweet.

835 After all these things the Communion fittingly follows: “The bread which I shall give is My flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52). This suitably agrees with the end of the Gospel, where it is said, “Arise, go”; for this is to give bread, namely, after the end of this life eternally to satisfy all the elect with the sweetness of Christ’s divinity and humanity. “Keep Thy Church, O Lord, by perpetual propitiation; and because human 836 mortality without Thee falls through pride, may it always by Thy assistance be drawn away from the harmful things of pride and exaltation of mind, and, under Thy guidance, be directed toward the saving goods of true humility.” [Col. 0580C] May our Lord Jesus Christ Himself deign to grant this, He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXIII. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE FIFTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6).

In the present reading of this holy Gospel, our Lord Jesus Christ, speaking of the great summit of perfection, exhorts and instructs His disciples toward the same perfection, and admonishes them that every anxiety, both in spiritual and bodily matters, is to be removed from their hearts. For we must suppose that He did not so strongly admonish them not to be anxious about visible food, drink, or clothing [Col. 0580D], but rather that they ought not to be anxious for the invisible food, drink, and spiritual clothing of soul and spirit, since He says later: “Be not anxious for your soul, what you shall eat.” The elect and perfect, following the example of His apostles, are not anxious for these things if, as the Lord says at the end of this Gospel, they seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness—that is, if they preserve their heart, which ought always to be God’s kingdom, with every safeguard and purity. For then they can have ready and at hand, without anxiety, the spiritual food and drink of the soul, by which they are refreshed in God and with God, and the garment of righteousness, by which they are outwardly adorned through good works.

And fittingly, after the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit have been enumerated, the gift of the spirit of understanding [Col. 0581A] is assigned to this Sunday and Gospel from the second octave, because what is set forth to be followed is offered not to the imperfect or negligent, but only to Christ’s most perfect apostles and their imitators, who are enlightened by the eye of spiritual understanding. Therefore He says:

“No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and despise the other.” These two masters, greatly opposed to each other, are Christ and the devil, or the love of God and the love of the world. No one can serve both alike, because whoever hates him who ought rightly to be despised—that is, the devil—will cleave to the other, the true Lord Jesus Christ, who is to be loved above all. Nor can the love of God and the love of the world be possessed together for any reason, [Col. 0581B] because to despise the present world and not to love transient things belongs truly to the person who loves God purely. But to love the world and pursue transient things belongs to the perverse, who hate God and serve the devil by their disposition. Therefore, lest we be turned away from love of the Lord and drawn away by love of the world, He again admonishes us and says:

“You cannot serve God and mammon.” By mammon, which is interpreted “riches,” is understood not only love and desire for temporal things, but whatever it may be upon which a person sets his aim and which he loves more than God is rightly called mammon. For not to tend toward God, but to love and seek something other than God, is indeed to serve mammon.

[Col. 0581C] “Therefore I say to you: be not anxious for your soul, what you shall eat; nor for your body, what you shall put on.” As though Truth plainly said: “Just as no one can serve these two masters, love them equally, or equally hate or despise them, therefore I say to you that you, as My perfect disciples, should love the true master and hate the false. And you who ought first to seek the kingdom 837 of God and His righteousness—that is, who ought to turn your whole heart away from love of carnal things and keep it unstained for Me—for what you shall eat, that is, what taste of contemplation you may possess when raised by love, and with what you shall be clothed, that is, what good works you shall do, I do not wish you to be anxious. [Col. 0581D] For if you are such as you ought to be, and have withdrawn yourselves from worldly cares and the anxieties of this life, you can have the gift of My grace which you desire, and righteous works by which you may please Me.”

For there are some who in perverse order demand the reward before merit; having defiled themselves by certain wicked acts and followed their own desires, they nevertheless dare, with every urgency of prayer, to invite the Lord of all purity, and only then anxiously seek spiritual food and drink—in vain. By God’s just judgment, the taste of contemplation is not owed to such persons, since they are shown to seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness too little. It follows:

“Is not the soul more than food, and the body more [Col. 0582A] than clothing? Look at the birds of the sky: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.” By the birds of the sky the good angels may be understood. By considering them, a person dwelling on earth and clothed in flesh can perceive what he ought to do, and, insofar as is permitted to mortals, may be free from anxiety in comparison with them. They do not sow nor gather into barns: that is, they do not sow by reading, reap by receiving the fruit of reading, or gather into barns by collecting in memory what they have read. But the heavenly Father feeds them with incomparable nourishment: blessed and immortal, they will always and without any end see His face and be fed immortally upon that highest good with which they are full and with which they will remain full. It is as though [Col. 0582B] the Lord said: “If I am accustomed to refresh My holy angels with such pastures, shall I not also be ready to give you, whom I redeemed with My blood, an abundance of My sweetness if you devote yourselves to purity?”

“Are you not of much greater value than they?” Here a question arises. For if, as we have said, the good angels may be signified by the birds of the sky, it is not easy to understand how man, now dust and ashes, may be of greater value than they. But, with the Holy Spirit helping us, let us say what we can and what, by His revelation, we understand with sound faith and sound understanding. The angelic creature is worthier in creation, but man is of greater value than they in redemption, because God the Father gave His Son for our redemption—that great and inestimable price, the price [Col. 0582C] of our satisfaction. He gave Him to us, I say, to us: because He was incarnate for us, given to us, crucified and died for us. Nor did He come into the world to restore the angel who had not sinned, but to redeem and deliver the human being who, through sins demanding punishment, had made himself liable to death. It follows:

“But which of you by thinking can add one cubit to his stature?” Just as a person cannot add a cubit to his stature by thinking, so he cannot attain the summit of perfection, signified by the cubit, by thinking unless he also strives to enlarge and extend himself through good works. Hence, in praise of the bride who has conformed herself to her Bridegroom Christ by living well, it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your stature is like a palm tree” (Song 7:7). What is signified by the palm but Christ’s victory? Where was Christ’s victory accomplished? In His death. His victory was when, triumphing over the enemy, He conquered death by dying. No one, as we have said, can come to imitation of this victory merely by thinking, but by mortifying his flesh with its vices and desires.

“And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labour, neither do they spin.” In the preceding comparison the Lord gave us an example from the good angels concerning purity of heart; in the following comparison, concerning evil angels, who may be understood by the lilies, He gives us [Col. 0583A] an example concerning action, signified by clothing. And malignant spirits may not unfittingly be understood by the lilies, because they were created in such beauty of honour and splendour that they would have been an ornament not only of heaven but also of earth, signified by the field, had they remained in their glory and dignity by obeying God. Beholding their pride, David says: “The pride of those who hate Thee has risen continually” (Ps. 73:23). Hence that first angel, swollen with pride against God, said: “I will place my seat in the north; I will sit upon the mount of the covenant; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13). Hence Paul says: “He is lifted up above all that is called God or that is worshipped” (2 Thess. 2:4).

839 “They do not labour, neither do they spin.” For malignant [Col. 0583B] spirits do not labour in being proud, nor do they account it laborious that they are occupied and labour day and night in the seduction of the righteous. “Neither do they spin.” It is known that one who spins draws thread from left to right. And thus, rightly as I think, it is intimated that the elect tend toward this right hand throughout the whole of their present life, which is signified by the right hand. In this way malignant spirits do not spin, because they draw everything they do not to the right but to the left. For all their labour and effort tend only toward this: how they may cast the righteous from the right hand to the left, that is, from eternal life into eternal damnation. Concerning their strength the Lord further adds:

“But I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed as one of these.” By Solomon, [Col. 0583C] whose name means “peaceful,” Christ is understood; His glory is understood as His flesh or the holy Church; and by “one of these” is signified one—the head, I say, of all the wicked. Of this glory Paul says: “The man indeed is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man” (1 Cor. 11:7). This woman signifies the Church, whose husband and bridegroom is Christ. She may also not unfittingly be called His glory. Therefore our Solomon was not clothed in all His glory as one of these, because, just as through exceeding condescension and love He became weak for the weak, and in glory—that is, in the flesh which He assumed—endured hunger, thirst, and the other miseries of mortal life, sin excepted; so also in the whole holy Church [Col. 0583D] He did not will that any of His own should be equal in strength to this single enemy of whom we have spoken, namely the ancient enemy who raised the head of wickedness against God in heaven. Although this enemy lost the state of angelic dignity by pride, he did not lose the power of angelic subtlety, for he neither suffers thirst nor hunger, and neither sleeps nor slumbers. From this we may gather that the Lord set forth all these things for the consolation of His own: for if malicious spirits rejected by God have received such strength, how great a grace of consolation and strength, we think, will He bestow upon those who love and seek Him with their whole heart? Therefore it follows:

“But if God so clothes the grass which is today and [Col. 0584A] tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, O you of little faith?” As we said above that evil spirits can be signified by lilies because of the dignity of their creation, so they can also be called grass because of their pride and disobedience. This grass is today, that is, in the present; tomorrow, that is, in the future, it shall be cast into the oven, namely into the fire of eternal damnation, as the Lord says at the judgment: “Depart from Me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). It is as though the Lord, strengthening and consoling His faithful, said: “If God so clothes this grass—that is, if He has not denied to His adversaries such wonderful strength and subtlety—how much more will He strengthen you for good works, and, once all anxiety has been removed from you, abundantly provide food of reading, drink of prayer, and clothing of holy action.”

“Therefore do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat? or what shall we drink? or with what shall we be clothed? For the Gentiles seek all these things.” The elect ought so to preserve their kingdom—that is, their heart—once uncleannesses have been expelled, that, insofar as is permitted to mortals, they may always seek and meditate upon heavenly things; for then, according to the Lord’s precept, they need rarely be anxious about what they shall eat by reading, what they shall drink by praying, or with what they shall be clothed by doing good works. “For the Gentiles seek all these things.” The Gentiles seek and wish to have all these things—that is, food of reading, drink of prayer, and clothing of action—yet they do not wish to seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness. Rather, made foul by much filth of vices, they are Gentiles altogether [Col. 0584C] because they live according to the manner in which they were born. Although they seek all these things, nevertheless, because they are Gentiles and serve the flesh, that which is freely and abundantly bestowed from above upon those who seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness is rightly denied to them.

“For your Father knows that you need all these things.” Your heavenly Father, abundant in mercy, knowing that His own need all these things, also knows how, by opening His hand, to bestow the rich grace of His blessing upon those in need—if only they do not refuse to follow these words with which the Lord concludes this Gospel, saying:

“Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you.” The kingdom of God, as we have said, [Col. 0584D] is the human heart, which every blessed person ought always to seek and keep under guard, because he ought to consider what is done and what occurs within it, whether good or evil. The righteousness of that kingdom is to fortify its inner parts with such guarding and purity of heart that He alone, the King of kings and Lord of lords, may hold primacy and dominion in it. To those who thus seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness, all these things we have mentioned shall be added: food in reading, drink in prayer, and clothing in good action. Truly, whatever soul is diligent concerning the guarding of its heart, whatever soul wishes to be the kingdom of God, will easily find what it shall eat, drink, and wear. For such a soul, as we often see, refreshed by the feasts of divine Scripture, [Col. 0585A] if it ought to preside over others, will be able sweetly and fruitfully to bring forth what it understands through God’s revelation; after diligence in reading it will receive a sweet abundance in prayer; and after the sweetness of prayer, whatever good works it undertakes, it will prosper in them with God’s help. May He grant us, in order that all these things may be added to us, to seek before all things the kingdom of God and His righteousness—He who is the King of righteousness, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXIV. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE SIXTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“Jesus went into a city called Nain, and His disciples went with Him, and a great crowd” (Luke 7).

[Col. 0585B] Knowing that we walk in the midst of the shadow of death, we ought to consider how we may die to sins and live to righteousness, so that, translated from death to life, we may learn to glory not in ourselves but rather in the Lord. For the fact that He whose house holiness befits deigned to come to the city of Nain, accompanied by disciples and crowds, and restore the only son of his mother to life—all this, I say, venerable in its mysteries, commends to us the salvation of the soul as something to be desired and sought. Nain means “movement” or “wave.” The city of Nain not unfittingly, as I think, represents any spiritual manner of life, or specifically any blessed soul which, stirred by frequent sighs and groans for its sins or from desire for eternal life, does not cease to send forth continual [Col. 0585C] waves of tears; such a soul may aptly be called the city of Nain. Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ in a certain manner enters it when, by the grace of His mercy, He invisibly visits and enlightens it within. His disciples go with Him, by whom we may understand good, holy, and righteous affections, because He awakens and inflames with good wills and holy desires that soul which He enters to visit and enlighten. “And a great crowd.” By the great crowd may be understood the good and ordered habits of the soul, which, like a great crowd, follow the Lord when they are outwardly manifested through the exercise of good works.

[Col. 0585D] “And when He approached the gate of the city, behold, the dead man, the only son of his mother, was being carried out.” The Lord approaches the gates of our city when He graciously enlightens our heart. We open our gates to Him when, in confession of true humility, we lay open what we have done—for, as it is written, “The just man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17)—and, confessing with inconsolable groaning that through culpable negligence we have lost our one good.

But by the gate of the city a good prelate may also not unfittingly be represented, through whom entrance to the soul is prepared for God. For when holy preachers by their preaching and teaching instruct and inflame a faithful soul in the love of God, they become the gate of the city, because they introduce the bridegroom to the bride—that is, God [Col. 0586A] 843 to the blessed soul. Thus the Lord approaches the gate of the city when, through the grace of His inspiration, He mercifully supplies the teacher with a word of salvation by which he can fruitfully touch the human heart. Thus, yes thus, as the Lord approaches the gate of the city—thus, I say, while the teacher, prompted by divine inspiration, preaches the word of salvation, the word of truth—at last what follows is fulfilled:

“Behold,” says the Evangelist, “the dead man, the only son of his mother, was being carried out.” By this dead man, described as the only son of his mother, there is rightly represented the extinguished fervour of love and sweetness of God in the soul. For just as one who is an only son of his mother is cherished, embraced, and loved more tenderly, so the blessed soul seeks more eagerly, desires more ardently, and loves more intensely that one good of inward savour—the gift, I mean, of divine sweetness and love—[Col. 0586B] than all those goods which it can ever attain in this life. But because this only son, the desirable fervour of divine sweetness, is often extinguished in the elect, they carry him out as dead beyond the gate when, awakened at some point by the preacher’s voice, they lament miserably that they do not taste Him by the affection of inward sweetness, for love of whom they deem slight and despise the sweetness of this present world. It follows:

“And she was a widow, and a great crowd of the city was with her.” This widow is the same faithful soul represented by the city. Her husband is the word of God, from whose constancy and remembrance [Col. 0586C] that only son—the sweet fervour of God’s love—is conceived and born. But when the soul is hardened within itself, not touched or delighted by the word of God, it is accounted a widow, as though its husband were dead. For just as a dead husband remaining with a living wife does not multiply joy but pain and lament for the widowed woman, so the word of God lies as though dead in the soul when it hears it indeed but does not taste it, when it receives no inward fruit of spiritual delight and joy from it.

[Col. 0586D] Nevertheless, it is mystically indicated that because of a deficiency 844 of inward grace it ought not to cease from the pursuit of good works, when there immediately follows: “And a great crowd of the city was with her.” By the great crowd of the city are understood good and righteous works, because the soul tending toward God, although widowed of her husband, although bereft of her son, although, I say, the utterance of God’s word in no way tastes sweet to her, although with the fervour of divine love and sweetness extinguished within her she inwardly feels no refreshment of life—that is, of spiritual sweetness—nevertheless ought never to cease outwardly from good works. For that the grace of God’s mercy and consolation is not far from that soul is mystically indicated when it is added:

“When Jesus saw her, He was moved with compassion for her, saying: ‘Do not weep.’” Jesus’ seeing is Jesus’ loving. The words, “When Jesus saw her,” may be referred both to the widow and to the crowd. For He sees the grieving widow and [Col. 0587A] the following crowd: He willingly considers, mercifully loves, and approves both the pain by which, through withdrawal of inward sweetness, the soul is wounded within, and the pursuit of good works in which it does not cease to persist outwardly. Therefore, as the Evangelist says, moved with compassion for her, He at once brought words of consolation and grace, saying: “Do not weep.” God’s speaking is God’s doing. It is as though He said: “You would wish to weep; you would wish through the delight of inward savour to attain the desired fervour of My love. But do not weep—do not, I say, by showing outwardly the sorrow of your heart, making manifest for the display, I mean, of empty glory what you ought to hope for from Me, destroy the reward of your sorrow. For I am He who did these things in you, who for a time withdrew from you the grace of My sweetness, [Col. 0587B] not in anger, not in vengeance, but in My mercy, so that you may receive it more abundantly and preserve it more carefully in humility.”

Having held such familiar discourse with the blessed soul, He at last begins faithfully to fulfil, according to the sequence of the text set forth, what He mercifully promises. For it follows:

“And He came near and touched the bier.” He comes near when He first produces through inspired fear the affection of a penitent; He touches the bier when, in the humble and lowly place of the heart, enkindled by the touch of incoming grace in love for heavenly joys, He enters more lovingly and sweetly. Thus perfect compunction of fear gives the soul compunction of divine love. To the humbled heart, which true humility humbles, [Col. 0587C] the highest majesty inclines itself very readily to remain. “Upon whom,” He says, “shall I rest, unless upon the humble, quiet man, trembling at My words?” (Isa. 66:2). Therefore, when these two movements—the spur of fear and the fervour of love—have filled the mind, the narrative of the Gospel again reveals that a fuller grace of God’s gifts comes to the person.

“But those who carried him stood still.” Once the allurements of carnal desires have been laid aside, he consents to stand firmly in the Lord and no longer go after his desires; and what he was less able to do by nature, he now begins to possess by grace. For he remains immovable after the manner of one standing, because, no longer scattered outwardly by desire, he fixes the steps of his mind in the dwelling-place of true light.

[Col. 0587D] “And He said: ‘Young man, I say to you: arise.’” He decrees that he be neither a child nor an old man, but a young man, whose mind the burning fire of love vehemently kindles, by ascent in prayer, toward the inward security of deepest rest. For who does not know that a child and an old man made old are unfit for love? Who doubts that a young man burns in the affection of love? Let the Lord therefore speak; let Him command not a child or an old man, but a young man, to be a young man. This is as though He said: “I say to you that you should be a young man—that is, neither cold nor sluggish, but burning with the greatness of My love—so that, founded and rooted in charity, you may arise stronger, [Col. 0588A] prompt and prepared for every good thing.” “Arise,” He says. For, despising what is low, raise yourself to desire heavenly things; arise now living and strong, you who a little while ago lay lifeless and dead in sorrowful funeral. Therefore, when the Lord speaks to any elect person with such inspiration, what follows happens in a wonderful manner:

“And he who had been dead sat up and began to speak.” That he is said not simply to have sat but to have sat up again clearly indicates that he had at one time also sat worthily by doing works pleasing and acceptable to God; and he who is said to have been dead must be believed to have previously lived. For the name of death is not assigned to stone or wood, to which life is denied. He sits up again in worthy sitting who rests in his former contemplation; and he who was dead revives when he now begins, according to the wish and desire of his mind, to enjoy that very Life which is Christ. [Col. 0588B] “And he began to speak.” For when that torrent of delight has filled his mind with friendly sweetness, it is fitting indeed that streams should flow forth not only of good action but also of holy and fruitful preaching, so that by speaking and exhorting he may kindle those formerly sluggish, since divine fire has blazed in his meditation. It follows:

“And He gave him to his mother.” He gives him to his mother when the soul as mother recognizes that whatever good it possesses is held not from itself but from God who gives it, and humbly attributes it not to itself or its merits but to Him alone from whom it has it. And rightly after these things is added:

“And fear seized them all.” For after one has truly [Col. 0588C] recognized God’s gift within oneself, one begins to preserve in fear whatever one has from God, lest through any levity one lose what one considers to be God’s gift alone. Hence it follows:

“And they magnified God.” He also magnifies God who, so to speak, makes himself small. Thus, by humbling himself and exalting God, he begins humbly to give thanks to God, learning:

“Because a great prophet has arisen among us, and because God has visited His people.” In the two clauses of this verse we may understand those two movements of the soul, namely fear and love. A great prophet arises in a person when God visits the human heart through fear. For fear prophesies [Col. 0588D] concerning fear of future punishment. And because God is charity, God visits His people when He touches the human heart through love, so that both through fear of future punishment it may carefully guard itself from evils, and through love and hope of heavenly life it may strive without ceasing to devote itself to whatever good works it can.

847 May He who created and redeemed us awaken us to this fear and love, and not permit us, raised from the death of the soul, to perish in the course of this present life. But may He grant those whom childish understanding has made unfit and whom the long-standing age of crimes has rendered as though extinguished, to burn and flourish with the youthfulness of the spiritual soul; so that, trampling carnal desires beneath spiritual mastery, we may one day deserve joyfully to enter the house of the Lord, through our Lord Jesus [Col. 0589A] Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXV. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE SEVENTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“When Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching Him” (Luke 14).

As we said on some earlier occasion, if your charity remembers, concerning the three octaves into which we divided the order of the summer Sundays, the third octave begins on this Sunday. Continuing until the coming of the Lord, it teaches and instructs us with what zeal and exercise of labour we must keep watch against those things called the principal vices, by which a person, as long as he remains in this life, is assailed and troubled.

[Col. 0589B] And rightly indeed, in the beginning of this octave, the eternal wisdom of God speaks against the first and highest vice, as it may be called: pride. It is rightly called first and highest because it cast down the highest angel and deceived the first human being. And because this miracle of the Lord, displayed in the healing of the dropsical man, was performed on the Sabbath, the entire force of this reading tends toward the Sabbath, because it commends to us the rest of spiritual life, signified by the Sabbath, in which we ought to be free from vices and watchful in virtues.

The Alleluia of today’s office is fitting for this Sabbath, in which we sing, saying: “When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judah became his sanctification, Israel his dominion” (Ps. 113, [col. 0589C] 1–2). Egypt is the world; the barbarous people are the vices. Those go out from Egypt who, leaving the secular world behind, abandon the vices of the flesh. To them the verse is fitting:

“Judah became his sanctification,” when God grants them, after true confession, true sanctification. “Israel became his dominion,” when, cleansed by the mercy of God both from the 848 effect of evil deeds and from consent to evil thoughts, they attain the power whereby they can become Israel—that is, whereby they can see God in the sweetness of their hearts. This sanctification from vices, and this power of seeing God in the sweetness of an illuminated heart, we ask for in today’s prayer, in which we say: “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, that your people may avoid diabolical contagions and pursue you alone, God, with a pure mind.”

Having briefly set these matters forth, before we enter into the meaning of the Gospel, let us state a certain summary drawn from this same reading, which we believe useful not only to the simpler hearers, but also to those who are wise and seek higher things in the words of God.

This Sabbath, on which our Lord and Savior entered the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, where he also healed the man with dropsy, signifies for us every good and spiritual manner of life, in which we must keep Sabbath from servile works—works forbidden by the Law on the Sabbath—that is, from sins and vices, which are denoted by servile works. But because the Only-Begotten Son of God healed an infirm man on the Sabbath, [col. 0590A] and did not thereby violate the Sabbath, this indicates that the holier the day, the more suitable and fitting it is for doing good works.

That he asks the lawyers and Pharisees whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and, when they are silent, heals the man with dropsy whom he has taken hold of, mystically suggests to us that—even if there are Pharisees who, as though from a certain perfection and strictness of spiritual discipline, 849 say that a person established in Sabbath, a person professing the holiness of spiritual life, ought to be despised and cast away if, through the devil’s overthrow, he falls into some deadly crime—yet it is not his most merciful will (for he wills all human beings to be saved) that such a person perish or be despaired of, but that he be gathered up, treated, and healed. Certainly, even if this sacred Gospel reading contained no further [Col. 0590B] usefulness, this verse alone could suffice us for consolation and as an example of divine mercy. But because the word of God is manna, offering to those who read and ponder it a varied delight of sweetness, edification, and teaching, let us grind it, eat it, and chew it over, in case something may occur to us by God’s own gift from this sacred Gospel reading which may taste sweet, edify, and instruct.

“When Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they themselves were watching him.” The Pharisees, whose name is interpreted “the divided,” prefigure those who, leaving behind the common life of the world, have separated themselves from sins and vices. Any good prelate is their ruler. The house [col. 0590C] of this ruler is understood either generally as the holy Church, or as any holy congregation, or specifically as any good soul. Jesus enters the house of the ruler of the Pharisees when, through the grace of his visitation, he draws near either to the holy Church, to any holy congregation, or to any blessed soul.

But when, or why, does he enter? “On the Sabbath to eat bread.” The Sabbath, which was a day of rest, signifies tranquillity of mind. For when a person secures for himself a certain repose, not only from sins and vices but also from the disturbances that may arise in the spiritual life, he brings almighty God into his house. God gladly enters there in order to eat bread. [Col. 0590D] God’s food is our salvation. Therefore, when by living devoutly and holily we devote ourselves to our salvation, we are refreshed with God and we refresh God within ourselves.

After this mutual refreshment of God with the human being and the human being with God, there 850 finally occurs what follows: “they themselves were watching him.” The Jews watched him maliciously; they watched him in order to rebuke and repel him. These watch him lest they lose him. They watch for when he comes; they watch in what manner he comes—whether through the sweetness of love to soothe them, or through the spirit of fear to terrify them. They watch him lest they admit anything that would offend or delay him as he comes; they watch how, through purity of heart and zeal for holy action, they may cause him to remain with them. Such watchfulness [col. 0591A] pleases God.

But such is the changeableness of the present life that no human good can be so pure that evil is not mingled with it, either from the weakness of the person himself or from the malice of the ancient enemy; just as there is no evil which is not for the most part followed by some good. Therefore there is immediately added:

“And behold, a certain man with dropsy was before him.” For we are in a certain middle position between those above us and those below us. Above us are God with his angels and holy souls; there too is no evil. Below us is the devil with apostate spirits and lost souls; there too is no good. In the midst of these we are, as we have said, good mingled with evil and evil with good. Some of us strive and ascend to those above; some strive and descend to those below. Therefore, because this middle state of ours is such that, placed amid evil, we cannot escape evil, but often, the more discerning a person becomes in the practice of good through progress in virtues, the more easily pride—the pride which overthrew the first human being—steals in, there is appended after the good things mentioned above: “And behold, a certain man with dropsy.” A person becomes dropsical before the Lord when, because of virtues bestowed upon him by God or even because of his own good acts, he swells and is puffed up within himself, and thereby cheats himself of the reward which he had deserved. Yet almighty God, because he is merciful, does not permit him to perish, but teaches and admonishes him how he ought to return inwardly to himself and to God. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0591C] 851 “And Jesus answered and said to the lawyers and Pharisees.” Lawyers are those who, taught inwardly by God and outwardly through the knowledge of doctrine, know and recognize the good things which must be done. Pharisees are those who carry out in good works the good things which they know and recognize.

“Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” This question of the Lord is our instruction. For he asks in order to make us, who are ignorant, knowing; so that we may know, I say, that it is lawful for us to be healed on the Sabbath—that is, if we sin, we should hasten to return again to Sabbath, again to the tranquillity of our mind, and humbly acknowledging ourselves, should correct the vice which has wounded us. For then what follows is truly fulfilled in [col. 0591D] us:

“But they were silent.” Those who had been crying out are silent when, in that very quietness of mind, as the person humbly applies himself, the vices grow still.

“But he took him, healed him, and sent him away.” To take hold is, when a person draws to himself, as if by a certain force, that which is far from him. Thus God takes hold of the person who had withdrawn from him by sinning, when he binds him to himself in a certain intimate familiarity of inward sweetness. Thus is fulfilled that apostolic saying: “He who clings to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6:17). He heals him because, through this taking hold of him, he works the person’s true salvation. He sends him away when he truly humbles him. For *dimittere*, “to send away,” is said as though it meant “to send downward” [*demittere*]. [Col. 0592A] Thus a person is rightly sent away when, through true humility, he is submitted to God.

But because it is impossible for a person in this life ever to ascend to such perfection and such holiness of heart and body that he cannot fall, the Lord again teaches us how we ought to rise after a fall. For it follows:

“And answering them, he said: Which of you, if his ass or ox falls into a pit, does not immediately draw it out on the Sabbath day?” This second question of the Lord is again our perfect instruction. As the Law says, the ass is an unclean animal; the ox is a clean animal. Our ass is our faculty of perception when we incline toward thoughts that are unclean and contrary to chastity and sanctification of life. [Col. 0592B] 852 Our ox is our faculty of perception when we meditate upon things clean and rational. Our ass falls into a pit when we slip from the uncleanness of thoughts into the lust of the flesh. Our ox falls into a pit when, from clean thoughts and holy desires by which we believe ourselves superior to other people, we swell with pride. Therefore, when the Lord says, “Which of you, if his ass or ox falls into a pit, does not immediately draw it out on the Sabbath day?”, he teaches us that if some unclean thought casts us headlong into carnal lust—which is uncleanness of the flesh—or some clean thought into pride—which is uncleanness of the heart—we should not linger in these things, but immediately draw both our ass and our ox out of this pit of destruction, and do so on the day [col. 0592C] of Sabbath, that is, in the illumination of our heart.

But because this strength belongs to few, it is fittingly added:

“And they could not answer him in these matters.” Those are said to answer God who carry out this teaching of the Lord in deeds. But since there is no one who does this immediately, no one who can easily free himself in the very hour in which he feels these things in himself, whether from the lust of the flesh that arises from uncleanness of thoughts or from the uncleanness of heart produced by pride of mind, the Lord adds teaching so that, if they cannot avoid falling into this pit, they may have instruction in how they can rise. It follows, therefore:

“And he also spoke a parable to those who had been invited, observing how they chose the first places at table, saying to them: [Col. 0592D] When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place, lest perhaps one more honorable than you has been invited by him; and he who invited you and him may come and say to you, ‘Give this man your place,’ and then you will begin, with shame, to occupy the last place.” What, I ask, what are we taught by these words of the Lord except to flee pride and devote ourselves to humility? We too are those who entered the wedding as invited guests when, leaving the world behind, we undertook the purpose of spiritual life. The Lord therefore admonishes us not to recline in the first place but in the last—that is, 853 desiring for ourselves the honor of no dignity, we should not prefer ourselves to any person, but should call and believe ourselves, in our own estimation, the [Col. 0593A] lowest and last of all.

For there are some who sometimes call and confess themselves the lowest and last of all, and complain that they have no merit among the other emulators of spiritual life with whom they live. Yet if they were judged or regarded by others according to their own words, they would be afflicted and disturbed within themselves; they would grieve, groan, and object; and to those by whom they were despised and insulted they would loudly protest and declare that they were in no way inferior. But the one who rightly and truly occupies the last place is he who thinks humbly of himself and, if he is despised by others, bears it humbly and patiently; who reclines in the last place in such a way that through true humility he subjects himself to all who are humble for God’s sake. Such a one, even if not earlier, nevertheless at the last time of his life merits to hear from the Lord: “Friend, go up higher.” [Col. 0593B] He is commanded to go up higher when, removed from the miseries of this life, he is assigned to eternal blessedness. There what follows will be fulfilled:

“Then you will have glory before those reclining with you.” He will glory before those reclining with him when he is crowned with the blessedness of eternity before the holy angelic spirits and holy souls of the elect.

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” Everyone, he says, who exalts himself in conscience will be humbled in repentance; and whoever humbles himself in repentance will be exalted in glory. These are the words of the holy Gospel, through which we have run in exposition according to our measure. Now let us look more carefully into the parable, if by God’s gift we may find or perceive something more subtle in it.

[Col. 0593C] “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place.” There can neither be called nor be a wedding where those two principal persons, namely bridegroom and bride, are not present. A person is invited as if to a wedding when, by the grace of heavenly inspiration, he is called inwardly to that 854 nuptial sweetness of God’s love in which God gives himself to the soul. How he should comport himself and how he should sit at these weddings is shown by the following saying:

“Do not recline,” he says, “in the first place.” Here the Lord names only two places, the first and the last. By these two places may fittingly be understood two motions of the soul: the motion of fear and the motion of love. A person is touched by the motion of fear when he is pierced by the recollection of sins and the fear of punishments; he is touched by the motion of love when he is pierced by the sweetness alone of God’s love and the desire for the kingdom of heaven. But because there are some who think it enough if they can at least mourn their sins in the spirit of fear, and do not consider it possible that they can in any way attain that inward sweetness born of the love of God, the Lord rightly says: “Do not recline in the first place.” The first place is the place of fear, because first a person must fear God, mourn sins committed because of the fear of God, and guard against sins yet to be committed. But one must not recline or rest in this first place; rather, with every effort and haste of heart and body one must strive toward the last place, which is the motion of love. [Col. 0594A] For he who called him is neither so poor nor so powerless that he cannot advance and lead him to that to which he called him. Therefore he added and said:

“Lest perhaps one more honorable than you has been invited by him.” By this more honorable guest we may soundly understand the Holy Spirit, who is said to have been invited, as it were, by the Lord when he is sent by God to assist a person through the unexpected grace of his visitation—that is, suddenly and unlooked for. Nor should we pass over his saying, “more honorable than you.” For it is as though he said: If you consider yourself honorable and deserving of honor because of your good deeds and the virtues you have received, there is one more honorable than you, deserving of far greater honor, reverence, and veneration—he from whom you have all these things, without whose will and grace you can do nothing.

[Col. 0594B] But what follows: “And he who invited you and him, coming, may say to you, ‘Give this man your place’”? This one who comes, who invites the one and the other, is almighty God, who invites the human being by inspiring him and invites the Holy Spirit 855 by sending him to assist the human being; for whatever he works in a human being, he works through the grace of the Holy Spirit. He says, indeed, “Give this man your place,” when, having expelled the filth of sins, he makes the human heart an acceptable dwelling-place for the Holy Spirit. There what follows is truly fulfilled:

“And then you will begin, with shame, to occupy the last place.” This shame seems to signify the remembrance of Christ’s passion and blood. He begins to occupy the last place with shame when, set ablaze by the fire of divine love through the remembrance of Christ’s passion and blood, he transfers the whole [col. 0594C] affection of his heart to God. This is what follows: “But when you are invited to a wedding, go and recline in the last place.”

But why does he say, “Go”? Because there are some who sometimes feel themselves inwardly called through the grace of God, and yet do not go, because, lying in the slothful idleness of their dullness, they refuse to follow the grace that calls them. But that person goes who does not neglect to cooperate by good living with the grace of God that calls him. He reclines in the last place when, through the sweetness of divine love, he begins to rest in God. And God’s love is rightly expressed by the last place, because there a person is truly made new. In this most health-giving renewal of the human being, what follows is fulfilled:

[Col. 0594D] “So that he who invited you may say to you: ‘Friend, go up higher.’” It is as though he said: I call you friend because I recognize that you have dealt as a friend with me both by repenting of your sins and by carrying out my commandments in works. Go up higher. Ascend from knowledge of yourself to knowledge of me. But because the full and perfect knowledge of God is not given here, but is reserved for God’s elect in eternal life—for this, the Lord says, is eternal life: “that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3)—there is fittingly added: “Then you will have glory before those reclining with you.” This glory, by which you may know me as I am in the height of my divinity and humility, will not be yours now, that is, in the present life. But when you have passed beyond the 856 miseries of the present life and obtained the promised joys of the kingdom of heaven, [col. 0595A] then you will have glory before those reclining with you—namely, my holy angels and chosen human beings. For there you will truly glory, where by contemplating my face eternally you will be established with me in my glory through the unchangeableness of eternal blessedness.

This glory will not be in the present life, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted. By this “everyone who exalts himself” we may not inappropriately understand the first progenitor, our father Adam, who is rightly called “everyone,” because all human offspring was in him and proceeded from him. This “everyone” exalted himself when, in Paradise, the devil speaking through the serpent said, “You shall be as gods,” and he wished to become equal to God. But when he wished to be exalted above himself, he fell, humbled below himself. Therefore everyone who is an imitator of Adam, who exalts himself above himself, will be humbled after Adam’s example. What is this humiliation except the misery, affliction, and disturbance of the present life, to which they will always be subject, because in this life they will always suffer for Adam’s excessive self-exaltation?

[Col. 0595B] But as old Adam, by exalting himself, conveyed pains and groans to his imitators, so the new Adam, the Only-Begotten Son of God, by humbling himself bore our pains and, by bearing them, emptied them of their force. Therefore it follows: “And whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” Who is this one who humbles himself, except he himself who speaks these things, our Lord and Savior, who descended from the height of his divinity to the depths of our weakness? Therefore everyone who, in imitation of him, leaving lofty things and desiring lowly things, humbles himself in the present life, will be exalted in the life to come, where he will rejoice and exult without end with the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. May the Only-Begotten Son of God lead us to this exaltation—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

857 HOMILY LXXXVI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE EIGHTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

“The Pharisees came to Jesus, and one of them, a lawyer, asked him, testing him: ‘Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?’” (Matt. 22.)

Although all sacred Scripture is true teaching, through which the life of eternal blessedness is promised to believers and the righteous, yet the words of the most holy Gospel reading, [Col. 0595D] which the very Wisdom of God appearing in the flesh set forth and taught, surpass all others. For these are the way and the truth, through which a person striving to attain true perfection and eternal reward is never deceived or led astray. Even if the words of the letter sometimes seem somewhat harsh in sound, the mystical meaning hidden within is exceedingly sweet and pleasant.

For it would bring little benefit to read, at every revolution of the year, about this question in which the Jews ask Christ whose son he is, since it is known to all the faithful by God’s grace that he is the Son of the Blessed Mary, ever Virgin, according to his humanity, and the Son of the eternal Father according to his divinity. But in the great mystery of this reading there is commended to us a very lofty and eminent [Col. 0596A] perfection of our life which we must attain and possess. And if, by God’s gift, we perceive anything from this reading, we are by no means able to set forth, as we ought and would wish, that very thing which in some measure glimmers before the eyes of our heart. But because the Holy Spirit ought to be the guide and teacher of all our words and deeds, let us say what we can to God’s honor.

“The Pharisees came to Jesus.” Pharisees is interpreted “the divided.” It seems to me that a certain good division occurs in a person not yet converted from the world when he begins to think about the danger to his soul. From this thought and inspiration, by which he is made concerned for his soul, he begins to divide himself from the world and join himself to God. But so long as he remains joined to the world through his secular manner of life, not yet changed, 858 [Col. 0596B] in that respect he is separated from God. In this good and health-giving division he makes a certain approach to Jesus. Jesus is interpreted “Savior,” or “Saving.” From that division, by which he begins in mind and thought to separate himself from the world, he makes a certain approach to Jesus because he seeks the progress of his salvation and blessedness.

He rises after this approach when he leaves behind his former way of life. One rises from among them who was once one of many; he becomes that one man of Ramatha (1 Sam. 1:1), because he seeks that one thing which is necessary, which David the prophet desired when he said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Ps. 26:4). After this necessary rising, he must also be a teacher of the Law. The teaching of the Law is this: “Turn away [Col. 0596C] from evil and do good.” Let him learn and firmly hold this teaching of the Law, that he may vigilantly and circumspectly turn away from evil and prudently do good. When he has learned this Law and fulfilled it in action, he must be a teacher of the Law, so that, if he is a prelate, he may set before others under his governance, by word and example, what he has learned. But if he is not a prelate, he should nevertheless be a teacher of the Law in his life, so that all among whom he lives may read in his life what has not been entrusted to his tongue to preach.

The lawyer ought to test and question the Lord, saying: “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?” Just as there is evil testing, so there is good testing. Properly speaking, a person tests, whether the matter be good or evil, [Col. 0596D] when he proves himself, wishing to know whether he can do what he has resolved to do or cannot. Therefore a person rightly tests God when, established in the spiritual life, he tests himself to see whether in a frail body he can offer God some service and labor; 859 and if, because of weakness, he cannot yet accomplish what he would wish, he tests himself again and again. Such testing is surely good and praiseworthy. He also tests God when in prayer he entreats divine assistance; and if he does not deserve to be heard once, twice, or three times, patiently bearing his rebuff, he approaches again and knocks at the door of God’s mercy, waiting to see whether at last he may deserve to be heard. He tests and asks in reading; he tests in prayer; he tests in continual meditation. In this good and holy testing, such as the Evangelist describes, he employs this question: [Col. 0597A] “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?”

“Teacher” is a name of fear. It is as though he says: I do not dare call you my Father, because I have not shown you a son’s love; I call and name you only my Teacher, because I ought to fear you as my Teacher. Henceforth I desire to live under your instruction, because I have not learned from you the things I have done and committed until now; and because you are he who teaches a person knowledge, and “blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord,” as the Psalmist says (Ps. 93:12). Teach me to do what you will, and show me what is the great commandment in the Law. I have no need of a small and minimal penance, which suffices those who have pleased you in their innocence. Show me the great commandment of great penance, [Col. 0597B] and teach me how I may know and be able to make satisfaction to you for my great sins; and, to the extent you grant it, let me extend and offer the measure of my penance according to the number and gravity of my offenses.

The letter seems, and so sounds, to represent this question of the Pharisee testing the Lord as malicious. But if we attend at once to the words of our Lord answering and teaching him, we find plainly that the testing was not evil but good. It follows:

“Jesus said to him: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind.’” These words have been expounded in many holy and useful ways by holy teachers; therefore we think it less necessary to dwell long upon these same words. Yet, lest we leave them altogether untouched, [Col. 0597C] let us first see, if we can, what he says:

“This is the greatest and first commandment.” It is truly the greatest and first: first, by which we are initiated; greatest, by which we are perfected. “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind.” These are three things: heart, soul, and mind. To these three we may relate three others, of which John says in his Epistle: “Do not love the world or the things which are in the world, for all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:15–16). But what is the heart? The heart is flesh; the soul is spirit; the mind is the soul’s power and strength.

To give one example out of many: [Col. 0597D] Pharaoh saw a dream which, while his body slept, he truly saw in his soul; but when he awoke, he did not know what it signified. Afterwards Joseph came and, understanding with his mind the dream which Pharaoh did not know, clearly explained it. Thus the lust of the flesh concerns the heart, which is flesh; the lust of the eyes concerns the soul, which is spirit; and the pride of life concerns the mind, which is the soul’s power and strength.

To love God with one’s whole heart is, having despised and cast aside the lust of the flesh, to implant the sweet love of Christ in that heart in which the love of the world formerly reigned, so that, just as it previously served banqueting, drunkenness, and the other pleasurable things of this world in order to nourish and perfect in itself the pleasure of the flesh, so now it may strive vigorously to gird itself for the pursuit of chastity of life and for those [Col. 0598A] things that belong to holiness and righteousness. When a person has thus abandoned the sins of the world, rising gradually to greater things, he will then be able, through God’s mercy, to despise and overcome within himself even the will to sin. One thus initiated through God’s mercy loves the Lord his God with his whole heart.

But it remains that he must love God with his whole soul also. 861 To love God with one’s whole soul is to drive away the lust of the eyes. The lust of the eyes is worldly favor and empty glory, which the person who wishes to love God with his whole soul ought to drive away. He who formerly sought the applause of the world and sought through conduct and appearance to please people should not shrink from being despised and insulted for God’s sake in the spiritual life, [Col. 0598B] but should endure it patiently in hope of the life to come. Christ’s chosen disciple Paul also instructs us by his example when he says: “If I were still pleasing people, I should not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10). And the Psalmist says: “Those who please people have been put to shame, because God has rejected them” (Ps. 52:6).

After these two comes the third: that a person should love God with all his mind. To love God with all one’s mind is diligently to guard oneself against the third vice, the pride of life. Since we live by the soul, we rightly understand by the pride of life the pride of the soul. That person rightly and perfectly loves God with all his mind who, in that part by which he ought to live for God—that is, the soul—strives as far as he can to exclude the vice of self-exaltation: [Col. 0598C] so that if he has left the world, if he endures or has endured the contempt of people patiently for God’s sake, he may not be puffed up within himself—that is, in his soul—on that account; but may remain before God in the same humility, as though he had done or endured nothing great for God’s sake, desiring only to please by his works him alone whom he loves and desires. This is truly to love God with one’s whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind. To sum up briefly what we have more fully distinguished: by the first we are initiated, by the second we advance, by the third we are perfected.

“But the second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” What does “is like it” mean except that the love of neighbor [Col. 0598D] which follows ought to resemble the preceding love of God? For whatever a person has deserved to receive from the knowledge and love of God, he should disclose to his neighbor now by example, now by word; and in this way he is truly proved to love his neighbor as himself.

862 “In these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.” We may understand this simply: namely, that in these two commandments of the love of God and neighbor the whole Law and the Prophets are fulfilled and perfected.

But we should note why he did not say, “The whole Law is fulfilled,” but, “The Law and the Prophets hang.” The Law and the Prophets were, as it were, hanging because before Christ’s coming they were neither on earth nor in heaven. How do I say that they were neither on earth nor in heaven? I say that they were not [Col. 0599A] on earth because, raising human hearts from below, from earth—that is, from earthly things—they did not speak about earth, but, announcing Christ, spoke about Christ. I say also that they were not in heaven because no one, however holy and perfect, could enter the kingdom of heaven; rather, all descended to hell before the coming and death of Christ. Christ came and suspended the Law and the Prophets with the wood of the cross. Compelled by the hanging of the cross, the Law and the Prophets gave up the spirit, because they disclosed from themselves the spiritual meaning formerly unknown. When we say that the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments of the love of God and neighbor, we not inappropriately relate these two commandments to the two pieces of wood of Christ’s cross: one to the love of God, because Christ descended to earth for love of God [Col. 0599B] the Father; the other to the love of neighbor, because Christ did not disdain to die for humanity’s redemption. It follows:

“But when the Pharisees had gathered together, Jesus questioned them, saying: ‘What do you think of Christ? Whose son is he?’” By the Pharisees, as we mentioned above, we may understand the human faculties separated from the world. Although they are not always scattered harmfully, they are nevertheless often scattered and dispersed in vain; and they are in a sense truly gathered together when, through the grace of heavenly visitation coming upon them, they are united and collected to receive and taste the gifts of divine sweetness, unto him alone whom they love and desire. Thus, thus gathered together, as he advances and teaches them 863 toward higher and more divine joys of inward sweetness, the voice of divine mercy in some manner sweetly [Col. 0599C] thunders. For this is what follows:

“Jesus questioned them.” For almighty God to question is to arouse a person toward things unknown. “What do you think of Christ? Whose son is he?” By this “what,” that ineffable sweetness of heart can be received with which almighty God pours out and refreshes the chaste hearts of his children and beloved ones at the time of his visitation. This “what”—this sweetness, which can be felt in the heart and tasted but cannot be comprehended or explained in words—truly belongs to and proceeds from the anointed Spirit; it truly descends into the human heart from the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

But between these two words, “what” and “Christ,” there is a middle term: namely, “seems” [*videtur*]. For by that heavenly sweetness poured into the human heart from the anointing of the Holy Spirit, a person truly becomes one who sees: through the splendor of that divine light he comes to know things of which he was formerly ignorant; and he comes to understand not only inwardly, but also in outward things and concerning outward things, what he had previously not understood. God asks whose son is this sweetness [Col. 0599D] that works such things in a person—whence it is generated in the human heart and how it is acquired—in order through his inquiry to make a person know how he may deserve, through God’s mercy, to attain it. The following answer of the Pharisees seems figuratively to express how greatly this inquiry or questioning works in his children, his elect and beloved ones. For it follows:

[Col. 0600A] “They say to him: ‘David.’” By David, whose name is interpreted “desirable in appearance” or “strong in hand,” the knowledge of truth and the doing of good are not inappropriately signified. When the Lord asks—or rather, to put it better, when by his sweet inspiration he teaches the human being—whence this son is generated and by what merits a person may obtain this sweetness, the answer is: “David.” A person answers the God who questions when he begins humbly to obey God’s word. He says “David” when, through the prompting of divine inspiration, he begins to strive and yearn with his whole being both for the knowledge of truth and for cooperation in good. To this God invisibly responds in the words that follow:

“How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand’?” [Col. 0600B] The Lord does not deny that this son—this sweetness of divine anointing—can be acquired through knowledge of the truth and the practice of good; rather, he asks about a certain manner, namely, how David calls him Lord in the Spirit. He asks, indeed, whence this desire first arises in a human being—the calling of the Lord in the Spirit—and how that sweetness, which is the son, is afterwards acquired by the human being: not that he who knows all things might learn from us, but that by his questioning he might make us, who do not know, knowledgeable.

Accordingly, what he asks he at once expounds when he says: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.” It is as though he said: It is true, as you say, that this son is begotten through knowledge of the truth and the practice of good, that this inward sweetness of the heart is conceived. But there is an intermediary [Col. 0600C] that belongs to God alone: namely, humility of mind, which only God’s grace can confer upon a human being, and which is aptly expressed by that word “sit.” For to sit is to cleave to Christ in humility and in the peaceful tranquillity of the mind.

With God’s help and through the effort that he himself applies, a person may somehow attain knowledge of the truth and the practice of good; but by his own labours he can never ascend to true and perfect humility and quiet of heart, unless almighty God, out of his magnificent grace, causes it to descend into the human heart. Therefore it is rightly said: “The Lord said to my Lord,” that is, to my spirit. For when it says, “The Lord said,” almighty God is to be understood; when it adds, “to my Lord,” I judge that the human spirit [Col. 0600D] should suitably be understood.

A person’s spirit becomes that person’s lord when, united to its superior, who is God, it is associated with him through inward sweetness, and when it rules and governs its inferior, which is the body, through fear and love of God. But how sweet this humility is, how lovable this tranquillity of mind is—which descends into the human heart from God’s grace alone—true Truth itself indicates to us when it says: “Sit at my right hand.” 865 It says “at my right hand,” not “at my left.” It is as though it said: At the left hand—that is, amid the adversities of this world, whether from abuse or insults inflicted upon you by others—I do not wish you to be humbled; rather, I wish you to be gently humbled at my right hand, by the various gifts of my graces, and you will be able to be more sweetly inebriated by the torrent of my delight.

[Col. 0601A] “Until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” A footstool is placed beneath the feet so that the feet may be raised and supported. But what is signified by the feet? Certainly understanding and affection. Those enemies whom the Lord of ineffable mercy promises to make a footstool for these feet are good perceptions, good desires, holy thoughts, and whatever other goods lead and assist a human being toward that ineffable sweetness.

All these are, as it were, certain enemies of a person. For they oppose and resist him while they flee from him, while they refuse to approach or draw near to him. But when almighty God, through his mercy, has led a person to true humility and tranquillity of mind—in which and through which true sweetness of heart is acquired—[Col. 0601B] he makes his enemies a footstool for his feet, when he subjects all these things—namely, good desires, good perceptions, and holy thoughts—to him in such a way that they become, as it were, a support for his feet, by which he is raised to God both in his understanding and in his affection.

It is as though he said: I ask from you the manner in which these things come about; since you do not know it, I reveal it to you by my inquiry. This is the manner: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.” And rightly so, because a person can never descend to that special joy of inward sweetness, in which a pure mind contemplates God, unless he has been perfectly humbled by the grace of heavenly visitation. For it belongs to God himself to visit and humble the human heart by his grace, and, if I may so speak, to keep [Col. 0601C] and preserve it in that humility, until it reaches the point of beginning, through God’s mercy, to rule over its enemies. For this is what he says: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”

Until those enemies of yours—which are good perceptions and the other good things that previously in a certain way opposed and resisted you—are made a footstool for your feet; that is, until your understanding is enlightened by knowledge of the good, and until your affection is raised by the infusion of that very sweetness. This is the power and work of God alone. If he should cease, in his mercy, to perform it in a person, who could be fit to receive and attain it? Therefore, after all these things, the Evangelist adds:

[Col. 0601D] “And no one was able to answer him a word; nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him any further.” We wretches know and understand these words better in ourselves than we can explain them. Having heard this manner that eternal Wisdom has set before us, no one was able to answer him a word, because no human being can attain that ineffable mystery of divine sweetness by his own powers or merits. Nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him further, because no human being, however chaste or however righteous, ought to assume for himself such boldness as to desire to know, from that day—that heavenly illumination—when or how it is brought forth from the hidden treasures of divine mercy and infused into the inmost depths [Col. 0602A] of the human heart, when he ought not to know it.

For the Lord himself says: “The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know whence it comes or where it goes” (John 3:8). But may we deserve, through God’s mercy, to feel within ourselves what we cannot know, so that, rooted in true humility through the visitation of his grace, we may come so far that our aforesaid enemies are made a footstool for our feet: that is, that we may be enlightened in understanding through knowledge of the good, and raised in affection through the infusion of heavenly sweetness. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God through all ages of ages. Amen.

867 HOMILY LXXXVII. THE FIRST FOR THE NINETEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0602B]

“Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came into his own city. And behold, they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed. And Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you’” (Matthew 9).

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the salvation and strength of all who hope in him, first healed this man by forgiving sins in that part which is higher and more worthy, namely the soul; and afterwards restored him to the health he desired in that part which is lower, namely the body. By this he plainly wished to teach us that bodily infirmity is often born from infirmity of the soul. For when the soul is inwardly wasting away, worn down by the sickness of sins, [Col. 0602C] the body too is weakened by the just judgment of almighty God, so that it may be instructed outwardly through the torments of the flesh concerning what it suffers within.

But even if nothing else shone forth for us in this sacred Gospel reading, the magnificent compassion of almighty God would provide us with great consolation: he healed this wretched man, who did not ask for his own salvation, because of the faith of other people who offered him to the Lord in hope alone, without verbal petition. Our hope and our whole welfare depend upon God. For if he healed one who did not ask, because only of the hope, as we have said, of those who offered him, then much more willingly does he bestow the remedy of his mercy upon those who submit themselves to him alone with the complete devotion of heart and soul, and who day and night, both hoping and praying, tirelessly cast themselves at his feet for their salvation [Col. 0602D].

The prayer of such people truly never perishes. It never passes away without the effect of great fruit. For he who knows better what is beneficial and necessary for us, although he does not always hear us according to our desire, nevertheless always hears us for the advancement and fulfilment of our salvation. Faithful prayer is compared to an arrow. When an arrow is shot, it never falls without striking something. 868 So too prayer, which is sent toward God from a fervent spirit as from a certain bow, always strikes something, because grace and the remedy of salvation come either to the person who offers it, or to the person for whom it is offered, or indeed to both.

But that most holy Gospel also contains the mystery of Christ and of [Col. 0603A] the Church. For it sets before us that mercy which he showed to the human race through his holy humanity. It also sets before us that mercy and truth which he will exercise on the day of judgment toward good and evil, elect and reprobate alike.

The Evangelist says: “Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came into his own city.” In these few words all the mysteries of Christ are comprehended: namely, Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension. We ought to know that no one can be saved without faith in these mysteries. These are the four living creatures written as surrounding the majesty of the Lord: the man, the calf, the lion, and the eagle. Thus we are reminded, in the figure of the man, that the invisible God became visible man for us; in the calf, that he suffered for us on the cross; in the lion, that he rose again after conquering death; and in the eagle, that in ascending he carried his holy humanity into heaven.

“Jesus got into a boat,” he says. [Col. 0603B]

By the boat, the humbled flesh of Christ can be understood. By the boat, the humbled flesh, we may likewise understand the humbled conscience of the blessed Virgin Mary. Jesus entered the boat when he assumed the form of humanity from the immaculate womb of the most chaste Virgin Mary. And why does it say “he ascended,” 869 when it would more suitably say “he descended”? Rightly, because his descent to us was our ascent to him. For in descending to us in order to take upon himself the miseries of our infirmity, he made it possible that we too might one day ascend from the calamities and miseries to which we are subject to the joys of life which he has prepared for those who love him.

“Having entered the boat, he crossed over.” By the word “crossed over,” Christ’s whole life in this world can be understood. Christ’s passion and resurrection can likewise be understood in the same word. He crossed over when, in this great sea—that is, in this world—he laboured by suffering all the calamities and miseries of human infirmity, sin alone excepted. He properly crossed over when, by dying and rising again, he overcame all these things and, by his single death, which he underwent [Col. 0603C] [Col. 0603D] in the flesh, freed us from the twofold death of body and soul. He crossed over when, by the hope of rising again given us through his resurrection, he restored us to eternal life. Thus, by ascending and crossing over, he came into his own city.

He came into his own city when, together with all those elect persons who rose with him—whose multitude, as we may believe, was innumerable—he ascended into heaven, and raised and placed his most holy humanity, presented before the countenance of eternal majesty, above all the choirs of angels. And it is rightly said that he came into his own city, because he made the kingdom of heaven, which had always been his city according to his divinity, his city also according to his humanity. Therefore, as we have said, he ascended by being born, crossed over by dying and rising, and came into his own city by ascending.

[Col. 0604A] “And behold, they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed.” This paralytic signifies the whole human race, wounded and weakened by the sickness of sins. We wretches too are signified by the same paralytic: we lie in the flesh as though on a bed, while, loving and cherishing it more than is right, we grant it a repose which we ought not to grant beyond what is necessary, and sometimes even beyond what is necessary.

Those who are said to have brought the paralytic to the Lord, though they are not named, aptly signify either the holy angels; or all those blessed people who rose with the Lord and ascended into heaven; or again the blessed souls of the righteous who, from the time [Col. 0604B] when Christ rose and ascended, have been, or are daily, carried over to the joys of heaven.

Nor is “behold” added needlessly. For immediately after Christ ascended, when the holy angels saw that holy and glorified humanity of Christ, they were bound to him with such sweetness of love that through that love they began to love the whole human race, whose cause and nature he had assumed. So much so that from that hour they have not ceased to offer this paralytic—namely, the human race—to God. For they commended and continue without interruption to commend to his most holy humanity that humanity in which he deigned to become a participant and companion.
