Likewise, those saints who rose with Christ, and those blessed souls of the righteous who, after Christ’s resurrection [Col. 0604C] and ascension, have been withdrawn from human affairs and reign with Christ in heaven, offer us daily to God. For, interceding for us, they set before and make known to his mercy, day and night, the miseries of our mortality from which they escaped through God’s mercy. In compassion for such great pains and miseries of our humanity, and granting us such advocates and intercessors who might daily intercede with him for our sins, almighty Majesty has provided for us by his mercy. We have this specifically concerning our most blessed Lady, the Virgin Mary, in her prayer, by which we beseech the Lord through her and say: “For this reason you took her from this world, that she might intercede more confidently with you for [Col. 0604D] our sins.”

For how could we wretches, amid the diverse and innumerable sins and crimes of this world—whose greatest part, established in paganism and Judaism, opposes Christ and serves the devil, and in which, even among those who are called Christians, scarcely one person in ten preserves the faith owed to his Creator—how, I say, could we not merely be saved, but even continue for any time at all, if we did not have in heaven these who offer us: namely, our most blessed Lady, who prays especially and unceasingly for the human race; as well as the holy angels and the other elect of Christ of whom we have spoken, daily interceding before God for our sins? For they are of such worth before the Lord that their prayers and merits are the most secure supports of 871 our [Col. 0605A] life and misery. Hence it immediately follows:

“And Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic.” God’s seeing is God’s approving, God’s choosing, and God’s loving. “Seeing”—that is, approving and loving—“their faith”: either that of the holy angels, who always remained with the Lord in faith and truth and never departed from God; or that of those who, still placed in the flesh, had a faithful heart toward God—namely, the elect human beings and spirits who served God faithfully in this frail life.

“He said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.’” Faith is called not merely a person’s belief in God, but also the possession of a faithful heart toward God. Since it belongs to sons to love, [Col. 0605B] by these three words—“Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven”—the Lord wished to indicate three things to us: faith, love, and forgiveness of sins. Thus he teaches and warns us that, unless one has faith—I mean faith which works through love, for “faith without works is dead” (James 2:26)—one cannot attain forgiveness of sins.

Almighty God spoke these words in a certain manner when, because of the faith and merit of those offering the paralytic, he sent the Holy Spirit from heaven to his beloved disciples and wished, through his apostles, to have his faith preached throughout the world for the healing of the paralytic, that is, the human race: so that those who believed and were baptized might obtain forgiveness of sins; and that those who, [Col. 0605C] having corrupted the faith which they received and promised in baptism, were again defiled by sins might, through repentance and tears, be baptized again and healed.

After these gifts of divine mercy had been bestowed upon the human race, those who attacked and wished to destroy the faith of the holy Church immediately arose. Hence it follows:

“And behold, some of the scribes said among themselves: ‘This man blasphemes.’” By these scribes we may understand evil spirits, who, because they wished to be worshipped and regarded as gods, then hated—and now and always will hate—whatever service and honour the creature rendered, or still renders, to the Creator through faith and the working of faith. But by these scribes we may also understand heretics [Col. 0605D] who set themselves against God’s Church and sought to destroy the Catholic faith handed down to the holy Church by the apostles and their successors, attacking it with their perverse teaching. They said, “This man blasphemes,” in a sense asserting that the Catholic faith was a kind of blasphemy, and that through the regeneration of baptism a person could not attain pardon and forgiveness of sins.

There are also some among the very number of those to be saved who at times despair of God’s mercy, as though, because of the enormity of their crimes, they could not obtain forgiveness of sins. Within themselves they say: “I am defiled by such filth of sins, wrapped in such stains and wickednesses of heart and soul, [Col. 0606A] that I am unworthy even to be saved or able to be saved.” Of all these it is rightly said: “This man blasphemes.” For despair is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, who is called, and is, the forgiveness of sins.

But whether they are heretics attacking Christ’s faith, or those who, by despairing of God’s mercy, blaspheme God, those whom he who is the true hope and salvation of human beings has determined to save, he addresses, as it were, in these words and says: “And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’” He does not say, “Why did you think?” but “Why do you think?” showing that they will be eternally subject without end there to those punishments which here they deserved by their sins, whose forgiveness here they neither sought nor hoped for.

And because the unjust and sinners are not so much tormented by the punishments which they endure in the soul before the day of judgment as by fear of the future damnation in which, after the day of judgment, they will be eternally condemned both in soul and body, the following verse seems mystically to express this:

[Col. 0606B] “Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?” This question of the Lord is his own action. For, as we often say, God’s speaking is God’s doing. God says this, as it were, to wretched sinners when, placed amid their punishments, they are tortured within themselves by their own conscience, and, though too late, accuse and rebuke themselves because they did not wish, when they could, to avoid such great miseries. “Which is easier,” they say, “to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven [Col. 0606C] you,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?” It is as though they said: Easier—indeed, happier—it would have been for us wretched sinners to wash away through repentance and tears the sins for which we suffer these torments, than, through unbelief and despair of the mercy of the Most High, to have come to such miseries that it is said to us: “Rise and walk.”

For it will happen that we must rise. But this resurrection will be for us unto death, not unto life; not unto the refreshment of any consolation, but unto the accumulation of eternal condemnation, to which we shall be consigned in such a way that we can never rise from it. This everlasting condemnation of the ungodly is suitably expressed to us in the word “walk.” For just as one who walks is always weary and labouring, so these are as if always walking, because they continually pass from punishments to punishments. It follows:

[Col. 0606D] “But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic—“Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” He calls himself the Son of Man because he will appear to judge the whole human race in the human form alone, in which he willed to be judged, to suffer, and to die. There will truly be fulfilled what is said: “That you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins,” because there the good and the evil will know and see that the Son of Man, who is also the Son of God, alone was and is able to forgive sins; by whose mercy the righteous are saved, and by whose justice the ungodly are condemned. Hence it follows:

“Then he said to the paralytic: ‘Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.’” The paralytic is the human race, as we have said. It is then told, “Rise,” when every human creature is commanded to rise: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52). It takes up its bed when the soul of each person, united with the body, is raised again. It goes to its house when each enters the dwelling prepared for him by God. For this is what follows:

[Col. 0607A] “And he rose and went to his house.” For as soon as that heavenly trumpet has sounded, and each person has again put on his body raised from the dust of the earth, 874 [Col. 0607B] he goes to his house. The righteous go to the house of joy and rest; the unrighteous go to the house of destruction and the house of eternal damnation.

“But when the crowds saw it, they feared and glorified God, who had given such power to men.” These crowds are crowds of angels, crowds of all the redeemed, and crowds of all the damned. All these crowds, seeing how the godly are saved by God’s just judgment and how the ungodly are condemned by God’s just judgment, feared. The righteous will fear, and the unrighteous will fear also. The righteous will fear with holy fear, filial fear—namely, that fear of which the Psalm says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Psalm 18:10).

This fear is nothing other than that sweet and most humble submission by which angelic spirits and [Col. 0607C] the entire number of the elect will submit themselves to almighty God, when, having come to know his perfect and utterly just equity, they begin to love him with a greater love than they ever previously knew or could have known. The unrighteous too will fear, but not with an equal fear. Their fear is to lie eternally beneath the feet of almighty God: for they are there subjected, unwillingly and against their will, to him whom they despised here, so that they will lament without end in those torments prepared for the devil and his angels, which they deserved here.

When such judgment between good and evil, righteous and unrighteous, has been accomplished, there finally occurs what follows:

“And they glorified God, who gave such power to men.” The righteous glorify him, and [Col. 0607D] the unrighteous glorify him also, because, just as the most merciful salvation of the righteous is the glory of almighty God, so likewise the most just condemnation of the wicked is his glory. Yet the word “they glorified” applies especially to the redeemed, then placed eternally among the delights at the right hand. They glorify God without end, because they praise and worship him eternally, and attribute their salvation solely to his lordship and mercy.

“Who gave such power to men.” What kind? Certainly such as the redeemed of God then possess, who are able to do all things in Christ and through Christ. For they will have such great power that they can do all that they will. Wherever the soul wills, 875 there the body will be; the body will obey the soul in all things; and the soul [Col. 0608A] will desire or love nothing except what pleases God.

Thus comes about what Christ says in another Gospel: “If two or three of you agree on earth” (Matthew 18:19). Two or three agree on earth when, in spirit, soul, and body, all the elect are united and established in their Creator in such a way that they will never be separated from him; and just as they never will be separated from him, so they can never do anything that displeases the Almighty or offends the eyes of his majesty. May he who can do all things, Jesus Christ our Lord, bring us to this power—he who lives and reigns, God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY LXXXVIII. THE SECOND FOR THE SAME SUNDAY.

[Col. 0608B] “Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came into his own city” (Matthew 9).

Having passed through and expounded the allegorical sense, I should like to say something about the moral sense and, as the Lord grants, touch upon those things which touch us inwardly. For what is heard is more fruitful and eagerly received when one knows by experience how true what is said is of each of us. Where what is read can be referred to Christ and the Church, it is exceedingly sweet and pleasant to hear; but where the things said of Christ are referred to the soul, through them a person is stirred to know himself, warned how he ought to arm himself against temptations, and taught with what humility he ought to conduct himself regarding the good gifts of the Lord which he has received.

Thus, in the present [Col. 0608C] Gospel reading, we are instructed now concerning goods, now concerning evils: concerning the goods given by the Lord; and concerning the evils which rise against us as temptations, and how we ought to conduct ourselves amid these alternations.

“Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came into his own city.” By the boat may be understood the humbled human soul. The Lord Jesus enters this boat when, through his visitation and illumination, he deigns to come to it. He ought rather to be said to have descended than ascended into this boat. But because the Holy Spirit intends that his descent to us should be our ascent, it describes him as ascending into the boat in order to commend this point: that when he descends to us, he indeed causes us to ascend to him.

[Col. 0608D] And observe the order: ascending, he crosses over; by crossing over, he comes into his own city. Our Lord Jesus Christ crosses over in us by ascending when he represses and calms within us the burning desires that are hot like a sea. Once wicked desires are calmed and stilled, he comes into his own city. What is his city? His city is the human heart, which, when he visits it, he makes his own city, in which he may continually sit and reign.

When desires have been overcome and the Lord Jesus comes into his own city, that is, into the human heart, what follows will undoubtedly occur: “And behold, they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed.” This paralytic is, I think, the human spirit [Col. 0609A] weakened and broken by the paralysis of sins. Nor is sin unfittingly understood by paralysis, because just as paralysis breaks and makes weak every limb it attacks, so sin breaks and distracts the human spirit, making it feeble and powerless for every good work.

The spirit lies on a bed when, weighed down by the burden of the flesh, it is excessively given over to sloth and lethargy. This paralytic—that is, our spirit, broken and weakened through sin, unwilling and unable to rise from the bed of fleshly repose—must have those who offer him to the Lord. Who are these who offer him, if not holy desires, good wills, and harmless thoughts? For our spirit can be healed only when these offer it. But when we are set ablaze by desire for the good, [Col. 0609B] when we are stretched upward by holy thoughts, we shall not be far from our salvation; instead, he who is always present to righteous desires will grant us salvation.

We are subsequently taught this by the deed and faith of those who offer him. “And Jesus,” it says, “seeing their faith, said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.’” God’s seeing is God’s loving. He sees the faith of those who offer him because he loves and approves the desire and faith of his poor ones. He speaks to the paralytic when he satisfies the desire of our heart. For his speaking is his doing. “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” He warns him, as a son trusting, to have a faithful heart toward God, because this is the faith that works through love: that God is to be loved before all things and above all things, and then one’s neighbour, whom we ought to embrace and love so sincerely [Col. 0609C] that we harbour no bitterness or indignation against him, knowing that through this we may deserve forgiveness of sins.

But because the life of man upon earth is temptation and, as Solomon says, evil always rises against good and good against evil, the temptations rising against us are denoted when it adds: “And behold, some of the scribes said within themselves: ‘This man blasphemes.’” By the scribes may be understood those people to whom God has given his knowledge and whom he has instructed in his wisdom, making them wiser by his invisible teaching than any teacher can teach them outwardly through sounding letters. This is a great gift of almighty God, if it is preserved through the good of humility.

[Col. 0609D] But because many strive to turn the knowledge given them by God toward their own glory rather than God’s, it says “some,” that is, individuals, because such people suppose that they have from their own singularity what they received solely from God’s goodness. Yet amid these things, because God does not permit his own to perish, touched by a divine gift they return to themselves, inwardly saying with groaning: “This man blasphemes.” It is as though they said: This spirit and understanding of mine, which is thus lifted up, inflated, and vainly gloried in—this blasphemes, because it is truly blasphemy against God to make my own that which belongs to God, whereas through myself and from myself I am and can do nothing. 878 In this good thought and rebuke, because a person restrains and rebukes his own spirit, God presents himself by seeing this and questioning, as follows:

[Col. 0610A] “And when he saw their thoughts, he said.” He sees these thoughts because he loves such thoughts, by which a person inwardly judges himself severely for his blasphemy. And lest we consent to such thoughts if they happen to assault us, he warns us, saying:

“Why do you think evil in your hearts? Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?” When the Lord asks something, he does not ask because, being ignorant, he wishes to know, but in order that by his questioning he may make us know what we do not know. We think evil in our hearts when, through pride, we ascribe to ourselves a gift of God that is not ours.

For God speaks in a person when that person rebukes himself for his foolish and blasphemous thoughts, and inwardly sets before his mind that it is easier [Col. 0610B] for him to submit in humility than to lift himself up in pride: “Which is easier for you,” he says, “to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?” Although this “rising and walking” is elsewhere used in a good sense, here it is not understood in a good sense. To rise and walk, then, is to raise one’s heart boastfully and make from the very boastfulness of the heart a certain sweet delight in which one continually dwells.

Every soul hastening to the palace of heaven must beware of this evil rising and walking, imitating the example of him who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). It is certainly better that a person, recognizing himself as a sinner, humbly ask that his sins be forgiven, than that he rise upright and proud and walk in that very exaltation, pleasing himself sweetly. For those whose mind is humble and meek truly find rest for their souls.

[Col. 0610C] Considering this, the blessed soul says to itself inwardly: It is easier—indeed, happier—for you to recognize yourself as a sinner than to rise through exaltation of mind and walk, that is, to conceive from it a sweet delight in pride. For if, recognizing yourself as a sinner, you humble yourself, you will be exalted before God; if you rise by raising yourself up, you will be condemned.

“But that you may know that the Son of Man has power to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic—“Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.”

By saying “that you may know,” he wishes to make us know that, just as he himself, who is the Son of Man and Son of God, received from God the power to forgive sins through the humility of his humanity, so he wishes us to know this also: that through humility we ought to deserve forgiveness of sins. And because he alone can forgive sins by power and, as merciful, wishes to forgive them by mercy, he says to the paralytic—whose speaking is doing—“Rise, take up your bed.”

By this rising we may understand a certain good rising. The ruin and fall of the soul is pride; the exaltation of the soul is humility. And just as true lifting up of the heart toward God is humility, so the casting down of the heart is ruin and pride. A person rises from this ruin of pride when, in true humility, he raises his heart to God. He takes up his bed when, through the body, [Col. 0611A] he does what is right; he goes to his house when he conceals a good work within his conscience, which is his house, saying with the Apostle Paul: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12).

And he arose and went into his house. He mentions two things—“he arose” and “he went”—and omits the intervening point which another Evangelist records. For another Evangelist says that, rising, he took up the bed on which he had lain, and thus went into his house (Mark 2:12). By placing these two and leaving the middle unstated, I think this is signified: that the man who has risen from the downfall of pride, lifted his humble heart to God, and gone into his house—that is, who, by concealing good things within his conscience, seeks to please God alone—ought, in humility, to regard that intervening matter, namely his good works, as though they were nothing, and to keep silence concerning them. When a person has advanced in this way and proceeded in the order we have described, there comes about in that person a certain praise and glorification, of which the following is added:

The crowds, seeing it, were afraid, and glorified God, who gave such power to men. These crowds are the human faculties disturbed by humble repentance. Thereafter they begin to tremble and fear with holy fear, chaste fear, and to submit themselves with every reverence to their Creator, glorifying him who gave such power to men. What power? Certainly such power as we have heard of: for it is truly great power when, freed from sins, we are granted the remission of sins; when, rising through good and praiseworthy conduct of life, we judge in a humble conscience that we have accomplished no good or virtue, glorifying the Lord God with all devotion and humility—he who alone is glorious and exalted through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXIX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son.” (Matthew 22)

Although the kingdom of heaven has many meanings in the Holy Scriptures, in the present passage it may suitably signify any faithful soul, which is made like the king, namely the eternal Father governing all things, when in baptism it is washed through humble repentance from original sin, or after baptism from actual sin. Then indeed the everlasting King, God the Father, makes and prepares true nuptials for the supreme King, his Son, when, as we have already said, either through the grace of baptism or through true repentance he joins and associates with himself the souls of those to be saved. He also invites them to the heavenly wedding by a threefold calling: nature, teaching, and grace. What the first calling is, the present parable subsequently indicates.

“And he sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding.” By the servants sent in the first calling, we may suitably understand our natural faculties. For nature itself teaches every person how he ought to seek and know God his Maker. Every irrational creature walks with its face bent down and looks upon the earth; it knows nothing of heavenly things and cannot think of them. But a human being, walking with body upright, declares by posture, bearing, and gait that he ought to fix his heart and faculties on the things above; and, just as he stands and walks with body upright, so he ought to raise heart and mind from earthly things to heavenly ones. But because almost every person despises this first calling of nature and neglects to come to the heavenly wedding to which he is called by nature, Truth itself then adds:

“And they would not come.” This unwillingness is common to almost everyone, because very few, alas, are found who, after the remission of original sin which is wiped away in baptism, are not entangled in actual sins. Likewise, few are those who, after conversion and repentance for actual sins, guard themselves in such a way that they do not at any time return to the same sins either in deed or in will. Thus it may rightly be said of all these that, though called by nature, they would not come to the wedding. For as long as they seek, relish, and love the things of the flesh, they refuse to come to the heavenly wedding. But after they have neglected the first calling, which is nature, in the way stated above, this gracious and mighty King does not cease to invite by the second calling, which is teaching, those whom he predestined to life. Hence it follows:

“Again he sent other servants, saying: Tell those who have been invited: Behold, I have prepared my dinner.” By the servants sent again we may understand teachers and preachers, who proclaim by word and example to those invited to the wedding with what labour and zeal they ought to attain that wedding. And because preaching is chiefly exercised not by silence but by speaking, what is added—“tell those who have been invited”—seems very fitting for the preachers of truth. Tell them, that is, devote yourselves more diligently to preaching; stir the minds of hearers toward better things; announce to those whom I have invited the dinner which I have prepared, that is, the heavenly mysteries of the Scriptures.

“My oxen,” he says, “and fattened beasts are slaughtered, and all things are ready; come to the wedding.” By the oxen and fattened beasts we may suitably understand the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments. When we hear or read their praiseworthy manner of life while they lived in the body, we can receive, through imitation of them, spiritual banquets of virtues by which we are refreshed. For in the deeds and sayings of the saints all things are prepared, both good and evil: the good which we should love and seek, and the evil which we should avoid and beware of altogether.

Again, in another sense, by oxen and fattened beasts we may understand prelates and subjects who, when they mortify in themselves their flesh and its desires, prepare for the Lord worthy food in themselves and with themselves. For while he hungers and thirsts for their salvation, their holy and righteous works satisfy him, and the continual compunction of their tears provides him with a desirable drink. Therefore he will one day say to them in judgment: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” [the printed text reads *bitere*] (Matthew 25:35). Among such prelates and subjects, certainly, all things necessary for soul and body are prepared. There are prepared the good things which they should do and preserve in humility, receiving from the Lord a worthy reward for them. There are prepared the evils which, if they commit them or remember having committed them, they should duly atone for by repentance, so that they may escape the coming evils that have no end. And since all who desire to live devoutly find there all these things of which we have spoken, he again warns and exhorts them not to delay coming to the wedding. “Come,” he says, “to the wedding.” As if he said: Behold, there can be no excuse: you ought to come to the wedding without pretext and without delay, because in my goodness I have prepared for you all necessities and every useful thing.

[Col. 0613B] “But they neglected it and went away, one to his farm, another to his business. The rest seized his servants, mistreated them, and killed them.” They refuse to come to the wedding of the Lord who invites them because they are unwilling to set the step of their mind upon the path of humility. On the contrary, they seek and love their farm, which means honours; their business, which means favour; and mistreatment, which means pleasures. In order that all these may be understood more suitably, each must be explained in turn.

“And they went away,” he says, “one to his farm, another to his business.” An inherited possession, a farm, seems to its owner to be a great honour. Thus by the farm we may suitably understand the passing honours of this world. Someone is said, in a sense, to go away to his farm when he does not shrink from being puffed up and exalted by the honours of the present life. When, swollen by honours, he does not fear to go to his farm, he also begins to go to his business. For someone is said to go to his business when he seeks and desires human favour for the good works he has done. For it is a most dangerous business when someone exchanges the rewards of eternal recompense for the empty glory of human favour. It follows:

“But the rest seized his servants, mistreated them, and killed them.” After they have gone, as was said, to their farm and their business; after they have begun to delight beyond measure in honours and human favour, it commonly happens that they also seize their servants—that is, their own faculties—and, having subjected them to mistreatment, that is, pleasures, kill them. They seize their servants, meaning their faculties: that is, by consenting, they cause them to be held fast by pleasures; they subject them to mistreatment by submitting to pleasures; they kill them by persevering in pleasures. Pleasure is not unsuitably compared to mistreatment, for no insult can be more disgraceful than the unrestrained desire for carnal pleasure. Yet the merciful Lord does not abandon such people—those exalted by honours, delighted by favour, and subject to pleasures—but does not disdain to invite them by the third calling, namely the grace of inward visitation. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0614A] “But when the king heard, he was angry; and, sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city.” This king, the eternal King, who at the beginning of the Gospel is said to have made a wedding feast for his son, is mercifully angry not with the anger of vengeance but with good anger—with his own anger, that for which the prophet pleads, saying: “Arise, O Lord, in your anger” (Psalm 7:7). He is thus angry when, on account of sins and vices committed, he beneficially makes the sinner angry with himself: because he has despised, as we have noted, the first and second calling, namely nature and teaching; because, long entangled in many evils, he has not rightly and properly governed the kingdom of his body and soul. When he deserves through the third calling, namely the grace of inward inspiration, to hear the Psalmist’s voice: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5), he becomes beneficially and salutarily angry with himself and, whatever wicked deeds he remembers having committed, avenges them upon himself with salutary punishment.

“And, sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city.” That gracious and kindly King sends his armies into the heart of the person who is rightly angry with himself: that is, the various impulses of compunction and repentance. By them he destroys and puts to death those murderers, namely carnal pleasures and desires, which sometimes perpetrate deadly murder in the souls of those living voluptuously. “And he burned their city.” Once those murderers have been slain, their city, which is the human heart, is set ablaze by the fire of the Holy Spirit. Of this fire the Lord himself says elsewhere: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12:49). When the fire of the Holy Spirit is sent into the earth—that is, a heart that savours and loves earthly things—then, all earthly things being set aside, it is kindled by the ardour of divine love. Hence it follows:

“Then the king said to his servants.” The heavenly wedding has indeed been prepared, not only through the regeneration of baptism but also through the good conduct of the spiritual life. “But those who were invited”—my spirit, soul, and body—“we have made ourselves unworthy through our own negligence, so that we might not attain this wedding. But now this one counsel of salvation remains for me: to reflect, in the bitterness of my soul, on the time of my life consumed in vanity, according to that prophetic saying: ‘I shall review for you all my years in the bitterness of my soul’” (Isaiah 38:15).

“Go therefore to the exits of the roads, and invite to the wedding whomever you find.” Go, I say, my servants, all my faculties, who until now have not feared to serve me unto iniquity. Go now before the eyes of the mind, recalling the evils which you have committed, so that, considering not only the beginning of sins but also the exits and end of wicked paths, and reflecting in contrition of heart on days and years that passed without fruit, perhaps the guilt and negligence of time past may be blotted out before the eyes of the strict Judge.

“And his servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, bad and good; and the wedding was filled with those reclining at table.” Those often-mentioned servants go out through good action and gather together their deeds, bad and good: the bad, so that they may repent of them with worthy satisfaction; the good, so that they may humbly attribute them not to themselves but to God. Thus, when the multitude of both bad and good works has been gathered, the wedding will be filled with those reclining in humility. For we cannot otherwise fill the spiritual wedding except by repenting of the evils we have committed, and by attributing the good we have done not to ourselves but to God. It follows:

[Col. 0615B] “But the king entered to see those reclining at table, and he saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment.” The heavenly King enters through the presence of his majesty, sees and visits those reclining in humility, and teaches the inward person, still not clothed in a wedding garment, how he should obtain that garment. The holy Fathers and doctors have said that the wedding garment is to be understood as true and perfect charity; and we too believe and understand this. Yet in a subtler sense, we understand by the wedding garment not only that charity which is displayed outwardly either in divine service or in compassion for neighbours, but also the invisible charity of inward sweetness, which a faithful soul deserves to taste when it becomes one spirit with God.

[Col. 0615C] And inward sweetness may suitably be understood by the wedding garment, because, just as a wedding garment adorns and warms the human body, so the grace of divine sweetness outwardly adorns a person with good works and inwardly kindles him with the fire of twofold charity. Whoever therefore desires to obtain this wedding garment should heed the words of the inviting Lord that follow:

“And he said to him: Friend, how did you enter here without having a wedding garment?” Why does he call him friend, who was not clothed in a wedding garment? He is both friend and not friend. He is a friend through good conversion and holy conduct; he is not a friend through the sweetness of intimate savour. Thus it is as though he said: See and consider in what way, and in what order, you entered the wedding when I called you; how, with my help, you destroyed those murderers, namely carnal desires; how the city of your heart was kindled with the fire of the Holy Spirit. And when I have given you all these good things, do you not know why I have not clothed you in a wedding garment?

“But he was speechless.” These few words indicate that he lacked the wedding garment because he had not first become silent, as he ought, from the noise of tumultuous thoughts, nor had he been able truthfully to say with the Prophet: “I was dumb, and humbled myself, and kept silence” (Psalm 38:3). But now, because he was speechless, because he kept silence in humility, he therefore put on the wedding garment; that is, he deserved to taste a little of inward sweetness. The Evangelist next indicates to what great dignity he immediately attained:

“Then the king said to his ministers: Bind his feet and hands, and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” In accordance with the sense we have just expounded, we must understand these words not in anger but in mercy. For the ministers who are then commanded, when his feet—that is, his affections—and his hands—that is, his works—are bound, to cast him into outer darkness, may suitably be understood as angelic spirits. After the good soul has obtained the wedding garment, it is entrusted to them, so that by their faithful ministry it may be bound and guarded by the bond of charity inwardly from evil affections and outwardly from perverse works. Thus they cast it, in a sense, into outer darkness: so that it may scorn and despise all outward prosperity and adversity; so that all outward things, vain and passing, may grow dark and contemptible to the eyes of its heart; and so that the grace of inward visitation alone may please and delight it.

“There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” There, I say—where, through the ministry and assistance of angels, a person whose affections and works have been bound by the love of God is cast into outer darkness in the manner described—there appropriately follows weeping, which is continual compunction of tears, and gnashing of teeth, which is the strict guarding of thoughts. There, I say, a person pierced either by fear of punishment or by love of heavenly desire is cleansed and washed by tears; there the human heart is kept and restrained by close and strict vigilance against vain and unlawful thoughts.

Nor is it without reason that the guarding of thoughts is understood by gnashing of teeth. For just as a person gnashing his teeth in pain presses even his teeth more firmly together, so every perfect person who guards his heart with strong vigilance restrains himself, so that he may sometimes deserve to be gladdened and made joyful by divine visitation. It follows:

“For many are called, but few are chosen.” Many who are called are penitents; few who are chosen are contemplatives. For, through God’s mercy, many are those who bewail and wash away their sins with tears of repentance; who humbly render thanks to God for the pardon granted them for sins; and who thus strive to attain the wedding to which they were called. But few are those clothed in the wedding garment, worthy to be refreshed and gladdened by the grace of contemplative sweetness; few can bind their wills and actions with the bond of perfect charity, guard their hearts against the tumult of useless thoughts, and perfectly scorn and despise all external and visible things. But since we have not deserved to be numbered among the chosen or contemplatives, let us labour in every way at least to be found among the penitents, so that the joys of eternal blessedness, which we cannot obtain through perfection of life, we may attain through true and humble repentance. May he deign to grant this, who lives and is glorified in perfect Trinity through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XC. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE TWENTY-FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“There was a certain royal official whose son was sick at Capernaum.” (John 4)

This royal official represents any faithful person whom almighty God has purposed to save in his mercy. He is suitably called “a certain one,” that is, singular, when through the prompting of heavenly inspiration he receives the desire to forsake the world and serve God. Yet he must be called not a king but a royal official, because at the beginning of conversion he cannot yet govern himself perfectly. He would indeed be a great and mighty king if he could govern his thoughts, words, and actions. But because he is a royal official, having a good will but not yet advancing in good works or able to resist temptations, he is rightly called a royal official whose son is sick.

By the son of the royal official, the purpose of spiritual life may be understood. At the beginning of conversion, the blessed person sets before himself the purpose of serving God in humility and meekness, and of patiently enduring for God’s sake whatever adversity comes from the world, from the devil, or even from his own flesh. But because, when temptations press upon him, he commonly fails to keep this purpose, it is rightly said that his son was sick at Capernaum. Capernaum is interpreted “village of consolation,” or “most beautiful village,” or “field of abundance”; by it spiritual life is fittingly understood. It is a village of consolation because those suffering from various infirmities are consoled there in various ways. The sinner is consoled if he does true repentance for sins, because he will obtain true pardon, and, after pardon for sins, if he remains in humility, he deserves to attain everlasting life. It is also the most beautiful village, in which lost innocence is restored. It is also a field of abundance, in which souls grow rich through the abundant grace of divine sweetness.

But one should note why he uses the imperfect past tense, saying “was sick.” It seems to me that this is because the person who delights in temptation is, as it were, sick in that respect; while in the respect in which he does not consent to temptation, he seems to live and to draw near to his salvation. Hence there immediately follows:

“When he had heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, he went and begged him to come down and heal his son.” He hears, and hears rightly, when he is taught inwardly by the Lord; he hears when he is taught outwardly by his neighbour, that Jesus comes from Judea into Galilee. Judea is interpreted “confession”; Galilee, “passage”; Jesus, “Saviour” or “saving.” He hears through the words of teachers and through the authority of the Scriptures that the true salvation and medicine of the soul consists in true and pure confession. And, when he hears that Jesus—that is, the salvation of his soul—comes through this, he goes to make confession and to be cleansed of the harmful things by which he is held. Thus he makes passage from vices to virtues, from the weakness of temptations to the healing of his wounds. And when he has gone by making humble confession, he begs by pouring out to God a prayer of supplication for his sins, praying that he may come down—that is, that he may make him descend into true humility. For through humility of mind he can recover the health of his sick son. What indicates, as I see it, that this confession is humble and arouses in him a supplicatory prayer to God is what follows:

“For he was beginning to die.” There are three stages in the increase of sins, mystically denoted here. First it is said that his son “was sick”; second, that he “was beginning to die”; third, “before he dies.” The son—that is, the spirit or will—is sick when a person delights in sin; he begins to die when he consents to sin. He dies when he falls into the act of sin. He begins to die when, out of the very infirmities of temptations by which he is afflicted, he considers abandoning the spiritual purpose he has begun. But lest this death prevail in him, the Lord himself graciously intervenes with an admonition. It follows:

“Jesus therefore said to him: Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” For Jesus to speak is to put his word into the human heart, through which a person begins to recognize and rebuke himself, saying inwardly to himself: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” By these words, it seems to me, the source or cause of all the preceding weaknesses of temptation is disclosed. When Jesus puts his word into his heart, the person begins to reproach himself thus: “Wretched and sinful man that I am! Why do I not believe unless I see signs and wonders? Why, when I came to this spiritual life in simplicity of heart and proposed to be held in contempt, do I not love my own contempt and low esteem? Why do I judge the lives of others, and not believe unless I see signs and wonders of brotherly love and strictness in prelates and subjects? It was not the purpose of my resolve and will to seek my salvation from the sight and actions of others. If they were humble and good, I too would devote myself to goodness; if strict, I too would be strict; if lax and dissolute, I too would be lax and dissolute.” For such infirmities of temptation commonly steal upon the newly converted, in addition to others too numerous to enumerate: they think that they do not see signs and wonders in prelates and subjects, that is, that they do not possess the degree of perfection and strictness which they believed them to have. Therefore, when they see something burdensome imposed upon them by a prelate [lacuna: *[.....]uo*], they murmur, as though he himself does not do such things, and from this they take and generate scandal for themselves. When, by God’s gift, a person recognizes how very dangerous this temptation is, he no longer seeks signs and wonders. Concerned only for his own salvation, he will not judge another’s life, but, placing all his hope in the regard of heavenly mercy, earnestly asks, saying:

“Lord, come down, that you may heal my son before he dies.” As if he said: O Lord, fountain of all goodness and mercy, come down to me, and by your descent make me humble; lessen my pride before my son dies through pride. For if I have at any time delighted in sin, if I have consented to it, grant that my spirit may never die through the completed work of sin.

But we may also understand in another manner what the Lord says: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” There is a difference between signs and wonders. Wonders are called those miracles which appear terrible and fearful, such as lightning and storms; signs are those which are sweet and lovable, for example, where the sick recover health, the blind sight, and the lame their walking. Thus fear may be understood by wonders, love by signs. And although the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, yet because of its dignity the sign of love is set before the wonder of fear. It is as though the true physician were indicating true health to us by these words, saying: “Unless, terrified by the wonders of my fear, you set a guard over harmful thoughts, useless words, and deeds, and unless, touched inwardly by the sign of my love, you strive to desire holy things, think good thoughts, and advance in virtues, you do not believe.” That is, you cannot keep the faith which works through love, so as to be humble in prosperity and patient in adversity.

When he has heard these things inwardly through divine inspiration, he humbly entreats, saying: “Lord, come down, that you may heal my son.” I acknowledge, Lord, that I have not feared you with the due reverence with which I ought to have feared you as my Lord; that I did not turn away from evil through your fear; that I did not do the good things I ought through your love. Therefore come down: that is, make me humble before you in heart and body. That this contrition of heart and prayer will be acceptable to God, he immediately confirms by his answer:

“Go; your son lives.” Because you have thus recognized yourself, fearing that your son—that is, your spirit—would die through the pride which assails you, go: that is, press on from good things to better things; and your son shall live with life and shall not die.

“The man believed the word which Jesus had spoken to him, and went.” It does not say, “the royal official believed,” but “the man believed,” so that it may indicate that he who at the beginning of conversion was a royal official, weak and small in good action, is now by God’s mercy a human being, restored to the image and likeness of God, and ready, in order to preserve that same image in himself, to believe the word which Jesus spoke. Whatever God says to a person, whether through himself, through teachers, or through Holy Scripture, is wholly the word of the Lord. A person believes this word when, according to that word and insofar as he can, he orders his conduct and actions. He begins to go when he advances from virtue to virtue.

“But as he was now going down, his servants met him, saying that his son was alive.” As the man goes down—as, I say, he submits himself to almighty God through true humility—servants meet him. By them and through them may suitably be understood sweet affections, good faculties, and holy desires. These servants meet him with an exceedingly sweet and delightful encounter, because they furnish him with the sweetness of heavenly grace, which sometimes follows true humility. “Upon whom,” he says, “shall I rest, except upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2). They report that his son is alive, because through such affections his spirit is truly healed and given life.

“He therefore asked them the hour at which he had become better.” He asks the servants about the hour when he reflects within himself and recalls that hour, if ever he had been better, if he had ever deserved to be admitted, even for a moment, to the grace of heavenly sweetness. He gathers the hour within himself because, again and again, yearning and panting through God’s mercy, he desires somehow to reach it. And that heavenly sweetness, although brief, is fittingly denoted by an hour: it quickly passes; and even if it could be possessed for a long time in this life, it would seem brief and would be so because of the insatiable grace it generates in the human heart. John indicates to us the exceeding brevity of the sweetness of this hour: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Revelation 8:1). But a person can never attain this hour except through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. This is mystically indicated when the text immediately adds:

“And they said to him: Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.” Whoever deserves, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, to come to this hour is truly left by the fever, because, cleansed from the fever of vices and sins, he is made alive in Christ and restored to the desirable health of his soul. And why do they say “yesterday”? “Yesterday” belongs to past time. By this it is signified that they ought always to sigh for that hour, prepare themselves for what has passed, and desire and pray that it may return.

“The father therefore knew that it was the same hour in which Jesus said to him: Your son lives. And he himself believed, and his whole household.” He who was first called a royal official, then a man, is now thirdly called a father. For he ascends from the lowest things to the highest. He who at first could scarcely govern himself for some good work, gradually advancing became a human being restored to the image and likeness of God. But afterwards he rightly receives the name of father, because, if he has ever known that hour in which Jesus said to him, “Your son lives”—that is, if he has truly tasted, so far as is possible here, how sweet the Lord is—he may rightly be called and be the father of others, since he will be able to benefit not only himself but others as well. “And he himself believed, and his whole household.” He believes when he commits himself and all his faculties to God alone and serves him alone, praying and longing that he may sometime again be admitted to the sweetness of that hour, meanwhile until he arrives where no moment is imposed upon everlasting sweetness, nor does any hour pass without sweetness, but the eternal abiding of ineffable sweetness endures without end. May he lead us to it, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XCI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE TWENTY-SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0621A]

“The kingdom of heaven has been likened to a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants.” (Matthew 18)

The kingdom of heaven, which has various meanings in the divine Scriptures, may in this passage be taken figuratively as the inward person, in whom he from whom every good proceeds has decreed in his mercy to reign and dwell, as blessed James says in his Epistle: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

But this kingdom of heaven is said to be like a man who is king, namely Christ, the Son of God, the everlasting King, if only he who disposes all things from eternity deigns to work in us the things that follow.

“He wished,” he says, “to settle accounts with his servants.” Reason is the rational faculty of the soul, by the use of which a person can distinguish good and evil. Almighty God placed this reason in his servants when he created us in his own image and likeness. But not content with this benefit, the gracious Lord also wished to settle accounts with his servants, namely our faculties. He wished, I say, to unite his good and eternal will to the human will: united indeed already in predestination, but not yet perfected in deed and truth.

“And when he had begun to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents.” By this one who is said to have been brought to God, our spirit may be understood: formerly taken away through sins, but now described as brought. We rightly offer it to the Lord when, through watchful reason, we carefully consider the evils we have done. Therefore, considering ourselves in this manner and offering our spirit to the Lord, we are found debtors of ten thousand talents. But what is denoted by ten thousand talents except the commandments of the Decalogue, or justice in its entirety? When, therefore, a person looks inwardly upon himself with the gaze of the mind, he finds himself a transgressor of the ten commandments, because one who acts perversely violates the precepts of the Decalogue. But again, beholding himself in the clear light of truth, he discovers that he has despised every norm of justice and equity, and now has nothing with which or whereby to repay the most just Judge, whom he sees already seated in strict examination of himself. Hence it follows:

When he had nothing with which to repay, the master ordered him to be sold, together with his wife and children and all that he possessed, and repayment to be made. A human being, then, has nothing with which to repay the Lord; for although by the reasoning of his heart he sees how much he owes his Creator, he does not yet possess a contrite heart by which he may make restitution to his Maker, through penitence, for what he has done unjustly. On the one hand he perceives how repayment ought to be made; on the other, through the weakness of a feeble will, he finds himself unable to accomplish the good which he sees. [Col. 0622A] But if he desires to be freed from this misery, let him sell his wife according to the Lord’s command: that is, let him exchange carnal love for spiritual love; let him sell the pleasure of the world and buy the joy of eternity. Yet for one making his way toward the homeland of eternal brightness, it is not enough merely to have sold his wife; his children too must be sold—namely, the carnal works begotten from his own carnal life. Moreover, by the severity of divine justice he is commanded to sell all that he has: indeed, all the vices clinging to him, which he once possessed as his own; for by such a transaction repayment must be made to the Lord. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go, sell all that you have” (Matt. 19:21). But what is this wretched man to do, when such great and grievous things are commanded him by the Lord, while neither his heart has the will [Col. 0622B] to fulfil them nor his actions the capacity? Let him take the pattern of this servant, so that he may cease to be miserable, and let him do what that man did. For the Evangelist says:

**897** “And that servant, falling down, besought him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.” What is it to fall down except to humble oneself in truth? Let him therefore fall down; let him cast himself into profound humility, and by continual prayer bend the Judge’s wrath toward mercy. For true humility is true prayer, and in humility a person merits that his petition be heard by the Lord. Let him therefore say in his prayer, repeatedly using this servant’s words: “Have patience with me! You, fountain of surpassing compassion, who abundantly refresh all from your fullness, by the mercy of your goodness make me hold patience steadfastly. [Col. 0622C] Hold it within me by the strength of your arm; for unless you hold it in me, it quickly slips away from me.” And because “the prayer of the righteous pierces the heavens” (Ecclus. 35:21), so that it may most swiftly reach the ears of the Lord of hosts, let us see how much this humility and prayer avail before almighty God.

“The master of that servant,” he says, “had compassion; he released him and forgave him the debt.” Almighty God is accustomed graciously to have compassion upon his suppliants who humbly invoke him, because it belongs to him alone always to show mercy and to spare. Having compassion, therefore, he releases the person who had formerly been captive through sins, placed in the depths of vices, by making him free from sins. He also forgives the debt by granting the remission of all [Col. 0622D] sins. For “at whatever hour,” as the Lord himself says through the prophet, “the sinner shall turn from his evil way, I will remember his iniquities no more” (Ezek. 18:22). Yet in another way too he forgives a person’s debt: when he places that person’s sins before the eyes of his mind, so that he may know and recognize how or in what manner he has offended God. It follows:

“But that servant, having gone out, found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii.” Once the debt of sin has at last been forgiven, free and unburdened, he goes out from the world; he also goes out from the pleasure of the flesh, in which he had long lain in destructive delight. Having thus gone out, he finds one of his fellow servants: he finds his own body as though it were a fugitive servant. It began its flight [Col. 0623A] when it refused to serve its master, the spirit. He also finds his life, which he had lost when he had been utterly unable to rule it, when **898** the flesh, rising up against the spirit, rendered him no obedient service. But now let us see how much this fellow servant—truly, our body—owes its master, the spirit, so that our mind may become fit to demand repayment.

“A hundred denarii,” he says. The number one hundred is described as perfect in every place in Scripture; everywhere it is set down and taken as standing for perfection. But in this place the denarii mystically signify that obedience which the spirit is accustomed to require from the flesh, to which the flesh ought to be subject and obedient in servile ministry. And because the likeness of a king is found on a denarius, the likeness of God is expressed by the denarius. Retaining and preserving this likeness now in the spirit, [Col. 0623B] we shall one day merit it also in the body, when we have been called from darkness into his marvelous light. Finally, the Lord is impassible and immortal; we too shall receive his likeness in the body when, made glorious through the glory of the resurrection, we pass into incorruption, impassible and immortal. Therefore let everyone who now retains God’s likeness in the spirit demand the obedience owed by the body, and undertake to exercise graciously within himself the deed of this servant which Scripture records as having been done cruelly.

“And, laying hold of him, he was choking him.” Let him therefore hold his body with the bridle of continence, lest it abound in the pleasures of this world according to its own desire. Let him choke it by restricting gluttony, [Col. 0623C] lest he expend upon it as much as its enticement demands; rather, let him sustain the body only barely and sparingly. For just as a man attempting to choke another seizes his throat and presses it hard, so that his breathing is repeatedly interrupted, so the body must be kept by every perfect person under the measured tightening of a bridle at the throat, so that, although he remains in the flesh, he compels himself nevertheless to live beyond the flesh, saying to himself:

“Repay what you owe.” All things formerly sweet to you must be turned into bitterness. The body which delighted in the pleasurable use of food and drink must now be made parched and dry by fasts and much abstinence. You who were weakened by the vapor of sleep must now be exhausted by many vigils.

**899** “And his fellow servant, falling down, begged him, [Col. 0623D] saying: Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.” This is the thought of the weak person: when the flesh is worn down, it asks to be spared, as though the afflicted flesh were saying to the spirit: “Deal patiently with me by sparing me, lest I collapse under labors and, crushed by such great pains, give way. If you deal patiently with me, I will repay you everything: what I do not pay this year in worthy satisfaction, I will repay in the future; and so always, as long as I live, I shall not cease to repay what I owe.”

“But he would not; rather, he went away and put him into prison until he should repay the debt.” Certainly, the one for whom “to live is Christ,” who formerly, at the beginning of his conversion, maintained such strictness in his life that [Col. 0624A] at times he extended himself beyond what was right, weakening his body beyond its powers—that person is unwilling to heed the murmuring voice of the weak flesh. He will not depart from the rigor he has begun, but goes on by persevering in his resolve and stretching himself toward what lies ahead. “And he put him into prison.” Prison is a laborious and dark place. A person puts himself into prison when, laboring devoutly in the Lord, he shuts himself away from every pleasure and joy of this world as though in darkness. In this toil and darkness he keeps himself shut up until he repays the debt: until, purified through laborious penitence, he dares to have confidence in the forgiveness of sins.

“Now when his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly grieved.” These fellow servants, who are grieved at seeing such things, may fittingly be understood as the outward senses of the human being, which God has appointed beforehand to serve the inner person. They grieve together when they see these things, which we have mentioned, being performed within themselves. For he who once, with a cheerful face, used boldly to look about in every direction now walks sadly and mournfully, his head bent down and his eyes cast down. And he who formerly was accustomed to utter jesting words now strives, with his body thus afflicted, to conceal himself in silence. [Col. 0624B] They are rightly said to be “greatly grieved.” For powerful is this grief of one who thus repents and thus crushes himself, as the Apostle says: “Godly sorrow works a steadfast repentance unto salvation” (2 Cor. 7:10). It follows:

[Col. 0624C] **900** “And they came and reported to their master all that had happened.” At last they come in confession and prayer, reporting to the Lord what has been done: all that they have sinned from the beginning of life, every sin they committed in youth, omitting nothing, but recounting everything to the Lord in confession and prayer. After this narration, so wholesome and pleasing to God, almighty God bestows upon the person a wonderful and ineffable consolation, as is immediately added here:

“Then his master called him and said to him.” Then, that is, the Lord calls him to himself through inward inspiration, making him forget past bitterness, cherishing him in his own sweetness so that [Col. 0624D] the toil and pain that had arisen from his afflicted flesh are wholly moderated. But having been called so sweetly by the Lord, let us hear what reply he receives from him:

“Wicked servant, I forgave you your entire debt because you begged me. Should you not therefore also have had mercy upon your fellow servant, as I had mercy upon you?” The Lord’s words to us are our own words, which, inspired by him, we speak inwardly in prayer. He calls his body a wicked servant, because it always declares itself too weak for labor, as though saying: “You were assigned to me by the Lord to serve me, but until now you have refused to minister faithfully, always saying: ‘I cannot bear the weight of tribulations; I am not able to endure such hard labors.’ Therefore I forgave you everything which you ought to have paid me in obedience, sparing you beyond measure [Col. 0625A] because you begged me. For you did indeed beg me to spare you mercifully; and when you begged, I forgave you, not demanding what you owed. Should you not likewise have had mercy on your fellow servant—namely, me, your soul—so that you might not have deceived me in this manner and taken away from me so many devout labors, just as I had mercy on you by pitying your pains and remitting your labors?”

“And his master, being angry, handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt.” This anger is wholesome and lovable, by which a person laudably becomes angry with himself, lest he fall again into sins, but correct through penitence what he has wickedly committed, as the Psalmist says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). Thus, being benevolently angry with himself, he hands [Col. 0625B] his body over to torturers, always tormenting and punishing himself with bitter penitence, until he repays to the Lord all sins by a worthy fruit of penitence. But how we may attain the summit of this perfection the Lord himself declares to us in the conclusion of this Gospel reading, adding these words:

“So also will my heavenly Father do to you, if each one of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.” He is rightly called the heavenly Father, since everything that descends from heaven and from the heavenly Father can be nothing other than good, pleasant, and delightful. “He will do to you,” he says: he will bring you to this grace of perfection, if your spirit, united with God, **902** does not indulge its brother too greatly—if you do not forgive him from your hearts. [Col. 0625C] Our brother is our flesh, joined to the spirit by a certain kinship of brotherhood.

And note that he says, “from your hearts.” For a human being has, as it were, two hearts: one spiritual and the other carnal. If, therefore, we do not forgive our body from our hearts—in such a way, indeed, that while the carnal heart draws downward, the spiritual heart, bearing fruit, tends upward—then almighty Lord, the heavenly Father, will do for us according to the measure of perfection which we have described. May the heavenly Father bring us to that perfection, so that through his grace we may by merit tend there where he lives and reigns with the Son and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily XCII. First Homily for the Twenty-Third Sunday after Pentecost

[Col. 0625D]

“Therefore, when Jesus had lifted up his eyes and saw that a very great multitude was coming to him, he said to Philip: ‘Where shall we buy bread, that these may eat?’” (John 6).

When the children of Israel went forth from Egypt, from the land of exile and pilgrimage, in order to enter the land of promise at the Lord’s command, they received in the wilderness the help of heavenly nourishment. For forty years in the desert they were fed with the food of heavenly manna, concerning which Scripture testifies that it possessed every delight and every taste of sweetness (Wis. 16:20), and that it gave each person whatever taste he himself desired.

In accordance with this likeness the Lord still acts [Col. 0626A] with his elect, whom, having brought them out of the tumult of the world and taken them into his service, he has placed in the desert of the spiritual life. There he frequently refreshes them with the sweetness of the heavenly manna of his word, lest they fail on the journey of this life. For to those tending toward the homeland of eternal brightness, he supplies in his word the food of spiritual understanding according to the merit or desire of each. There are some who, because of the merit of a praiseworthy life, receive from God such great grace that, searching the depths of the Scriptures, they are nourished with a certain hidden sweetness in the Lord’s words. There are others less fit to grasp lofty things; yet, lest they remain empty and unfulfilled, according to the capacity of their understanding they find in the Lord’s words sufficient nourishment to refresh them.

[Col. 0626B] Thus in the words of today’s reading the eternal Wisdom of God has dispensed the seeds of his word so that he may grant profound knowledge in them to the perfect and wise, while to the unlearned and simpler he may grant as much spiritual food in them as will prevent them from remaining hungry.

It should be noted why the Holy Spirit, who has ordered the divine ministry in the holy Church, willed this Gospel to be read in the divine offices twice in the year, the Gospel in which we read how the Lord satisfied five thousand **903** people with five loaves and two fish. It is read now at the end of the Sundays, and again before the solemnities of the Sunday of the Passion and Resurrection. As we think, the Holy Spirit instituted and ordained this not without the cause of a definite mystery. [Col. 0626C] For the fact that this Gospel is read today at the end of the Sundays signifies to us the rest of holy souls, to which the Lord’s perfect and elect pass when they have laid aside the burden of the flesh. There they are refreshed with eternal satiety in the soul alone, while the body still lies in the dust of the earth. But the fact that this reading is repeated a second time in Lent before Resurrection Sunday signifies that the elect, in the general resurrection, having resumed the body, when “this mortal has put on immortality,” will eternally be made rich and satisfied in the sight of God with the blessed joy of both the inner and outer person. We are instructed by the Lord, in the words of today’s reading, how we may reach each of these satisfactions. For the Evangelist says:

[Col. 0626D] “When Jesus had lifted up his eyes.” By the eyes of Jesus we may understand the intention of the person to be saved, whom the Lord has anticipated by his mercy. The Lord lifts up that intention when, through the grace of his Spirit, he grants a person to begin raising and turning toward God the intention which he had immersed in the world and worldly desires. For everything in the present life is wholly temporal, passing, and beneath the human person. One is raised and lifted by the Lord above it when one’s intention is separated from these earthly and perishable things and lifted up toward God.

But we may understand the lifting up of Jesus’ eyes in another way as well. When he permits a person to enter the ways of the world according to the will [Col. 0627A] and desires of his heart, the Lord Jesus in some manner keeps his eyes within, hiding from human sight what good he has secretly foreordained and predestined concerning that person. But he lifts up those same eyes when that which was in the divine gaze and hidden from people outwardly is, by his help and cooperation, made manifest to human sight through the effect of that person’s work. Thus, when Jesus’ eyes have been lifted up, he sees that a very great multitude is coming to him.

**904** In the very great multitude which comes to Jesus, and this in a good sense, we may fittingly understand good dispositions and holy desires by which a person strives to attain the knowledge of God. When, therefore, the person to be saved, who in part has become a member of Christ by desiring good things, sees this very great multitude within himself by the inward light of the heart, Jesus too sees it: he sees because he loves, because he approves, and he says to Philip: “Where shall we buy bread, that these may eat?”

By Philip, whose name is interpreted “mouth of a lamp,” the enlightened heart of a person is signified: burning through fear and shining through love. To this heart, kindled with fear of the eternal Father and illumined by love, the Savior’s word is directed—to the person within the person: “Where,” he says, “shall we buy bread, that these may eat?” As though a person concerned for his salvation, bearing a heart somewhat enlightened through grace, were saying to the Lord: “O Lord, fountain of compassion and mercy, who long ago lifted up your eyes in me, when you turned toward yourself the intention of one unworthy and sinful, eagerly longing for earthly affairs, granting good dispositions and holy desires by which I might draw somewhat near to your knowledge and love. Since such grace has been bestowed and shown in me, how am I to buy or acquire what will enable these good dispositions and holy desires—which are a very great multitude before you—to receive from me such bread and food as they may eat and by which they may be refreshed? [Col. 0627C] For then they would be refreshed if I carried into the effect of good works what they suggest to me. I shall by no means be able to buy this bread unless I give over the price of my body for this exchange and despise myself and the sweetness of this present life for your love.” It follows:

[Col. 0627D] “But he said this, testing him; for he himself knew what he was going to do.” When a person is placed in such sorrow and inquiry, the Lord gives counsel and commands him to test whether he can practise in action what has been shown to him. For when food is often set before an ill person and he complains that he cannot take nourishment, the one who desires his health and recovery repeatedly says: “Try, beloved, whether you can take some of it for your benefit.”

The same is done when someone tries to lift a heavy weight beyond his strength. Unable to prevail by his own powers, he lies exhausted beneath the burden. Yet at last, when greater strength is added, he lifts a weight which he had previously [Col. 0628A] scarcely or not at all been able to move. By such an example God acts through inspiration upon the mind still situated in the whirlwinds of the world: it strives indeed to escape its evils and desires to leave the world and its worldly heart, but is hindered by worldly pleasures.

Although at the beginning of his illumination a person possesses less perfection, the Creator of all things nevertheless knows what he will accomplish in the end, and with what zeal and steadfastness of mind he will lay hold of eternal life. Therefore he urges the person to undertake experimentally the good work which he suspects to be so difficult. Hence it follows:

Philip answered him: “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not suffice for them, for each to receive a little.” In sacred Scripture the number one hundred is set down and received as representing perfection; that number one hundred is doubled and brought to two hundred. Thus, by two hundred denarii the perfection of good will and good work is expressed. For just as the image of a king was formerly stamped on a denarius, so the image of God the Father is imprinted upon a person’s perfect will and action. Philip therefore answers the Lord when a person enlightened by grace knows and abhors his sins and crimes, but, though still set amid the waves of the sea, has not yet completely abandoned the sins he has recognized. “Two hundred denarii,” he says, “would not suffice for them, for each to receive a little.” “But what are these among so many?” If, he says, with your help, Lord, nothing were lacking to the perfection of my will, and no weakness impeded my work, I would nevertheless not believe that this would suffice for each of my sins to receive even a little. [Col. 0628C] For a sin “to receive a little” is, once the debt of sin has been forgiven, merely to escape the fire and punishment of Gehenna. **906** For it is very little, with respect to the glory of true and everlasting immortality, where in your sweetness you will prepare yourself for your poor, that I should receive from you only forgiveness of my sins and escape the penalties of final vengeance, unless from your abundant blessing you add besides that I may merit to be granted some reward and joined to the fellowship of the saints.

“One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him: ‘There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish.’” Andrew means “manly,” [Col. 0628D] Simon “obedient,” and Peter “acknowledging.” In the significance of these names it is aptly made known how far one seeking the salvation of his soul ought to advance. At last, with God cooperating, he changes his worldly habit, goes forth from the storms of this world, becomes one of Jesus’ disciples, and, having subdued the dominion of the flesh, begins to be manly in the Lord. He becomes also a brother in the congregation of the faithful, who steadfastly bear the yoke of obedience in the knowledge of God and themselves. Having observed the purity of their perfect way of life among whom he dwells, and having seen their constancy of mind and labor, he immediately turns to words of lamentation: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?” As though he said: “O Lord! [Col. 0629A] Behold, I am your sole servant of mercy, who have lived childishly and have lived thus up to now. Though by your gift I have been freed from the tumult of the world, I am here only in body, while in my mind I still meditate upon the ways of the world. For my wretched spirit and soul are occupied with vain and useless things. I therefore have five barley loaves—that is, five carnal senses, living carnally and uselessly, sensing nothing of the sweetness of the spirit. For I do not know how to devote myself to the purity of mind through the practice of prayer, nor can I please you by a perfect confession of my sins. Sustaining my body only with food, drink, and sleep, I indulge the body’s needs more than is fitting.

“I also have two fish, that is, a twofold penitence: I grieve that I have committed so many evils against my Creator [Col. 0629B] and have so impiously offended the depths of your goodness. Again, I grieve that I have offered no fruits of good works to your majesty and have for so long neglected the righteousness pleasing to you. But what does this twofold **907** penitence avail among so many transgressions and such great crimes? What, I say, does this small penitence of mine avail among so many holy and innocent people whom I see flourishing before God—who, having led an unstained life in incorruption and abstained from every evil work, devote themselves more to prayer and afflict their bodies more by fasts, vigils, and scourges?” These are the words of the penitent, truly grieving for his sins, to whom the merciful Lord, according to the goodness of compassion innate to him, gives counsel. For it follows:

[Col. 0629C] “Make the people recline.” “Make,” he says, “each of your two persons, both inward and outward, lay himself down in profound humility. Let your outward person be the more abased and despised in humility, in proportion as he was once more exalted in contempt of God.
