And just as, in your worldly manner of life, you placed yourselves above all others through the pride of life, so in your spiritual purpose you ought, by serving all, to subject yourselves to the feet of all. Let the inward person too be established in the depth of humility, so that, the root of pride having been uprooted, you may reckon everyone superior to yourselves and, even in thought, prefer yourselves to none, however wicked. And if I find you in such a reclining of both persons, without doubt you will receive what you ask from me.” It follows:

[Col. 0629D] “Now there was much grass in the place.” After the Lord’s wholesome counsel, the person to be saved sees much grass in the place of his heart: namely, the many miseries of vices, formerly unknown to him. Setting them before the eyes of his mind, he draws from them abundant material for true humility. Hence it is added:

“Therefore the men reclined, in number about five thousand.” At last he reclines in profound humility both in heart and body. And he who, having first abandoned worldly business, was said to be manly in the Lord, now advances into a perfect man through the glory of profound humility. **908** And because the number one thousand signifies the perfect order of the elect and the perfect, he is marked by this number—the number of those who now stand before the Creator’s countenance, having laid aside [Col. 0630A] every stain of misery and corruption. But because, as long as we live in this tearful life, we cannot be perfect in our five senses, they are not said to be exactly five thousand but are described as “about five thousand.” Whoever, so far as lies in him, strives after perfection merits, through the mercy of his fellow-worker, to be numbered among those inscribed in the book of heavenly life. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matt. 10:30). Our head is Christ the Lord; all the hairs of that head are the elect, with whom the glorious King is adorned and crowned in the diadem of his kingdom. And just as the beauty of a person’s face consists greatly in the ornament of the hair, so the Son of God, the splendor of the eternal Father, receives a certain ornament from his elect, whom he has made co-heirs with himself in his kingdom. But let us now see what reward is obtained by one who has bowed himself to God through the humble reclining of both persons. For it follows:

“Therefore Jesus took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those reclining; likewise also of the fish, as much as they wished.” Jesus receives the loaves because the afflicted spirit becomes an acceptable sacrifice to him, as the Psalmist declares: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50:19). But in another manner too the Lord Jesus gives thanks when he has sprinkled a soul touched by a gift from above with the dew of his Spirit and filled all its inward parts with sweetness freely bestowed. [Col. 0630C] This, I say, is the surpassing grace which the mercy of the highest Giver supplies freely and not according to merits. Thus the person himself wonders, seeing such great grace in himself, by what labors he has earned it, knowing that he has done no such thing in deed as could suffice to obtain such grace. Therefore, in this grace, the Lord distributes loaves to the person reclining: namely, bringing to a person’s memory where and in what way he has offended divine grace, recalling now these sins in groaning of heart and considering other sins in sorrow of soul, so that in grieving for each one he may obtain from the Lord greater remedies. It follows:

“Likewise also of the fish, as much as they wished.” A fish [Col. 0630D] lives among the waves; and the thicker and deeper the water, the stronger and more vigorous the fish becomes. By the fish, as we said above, we understand a twofold penitence, which he often supplies to his faithful so abundantly that, dissolved in lamentation, they shed as many tears as the will of the mind suggests to them.

“And when they had been filled, he said to his disciples: ‘Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they perish.’” When the heart has been filled with the sweetness of heavenly inspiration and made bitter with the grief of penitence, the Lord commands the person to gather his former deeds, so that he may know even the smallest sins, which in his former life he could scarcely or not at all have known to be sins. For those renouncing this world, at the beginning of their conversion it is enough to confess and lament the greater crimes. When these have been fully purified by the fire of penitence and broken down by long exercise of labor, they at last turn their mind to lamenting lesser and lighter sins. But why must the fragments of bread—that is, the lesser sins—be gathered? Certainly, lest they perish. For we believe and confess that, under the sentence of the strict Judge, whatever has not been purged in this life by worthy penitential satisfaction will perish.

“Therefore they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves, which were left over after those had eaten.” By the baskets, in which worthless things are usually carried, the heart of the humble may aptly be understood: narrow through humility, enlarged through charity. But by the ten baskets the commandments of the Decalogue are signified; and when knowledge of the New and Old Testament, that is, the two commandments of charity, is joined to them, the twelve baskets are certainly filled.

[Col. 0631B] And it should be noted that these fragments of bread are said to have been gathered from the five barley loaves. For barley is fodder for beasts of burden, and therefore by barley is signified the life of carnal people, who live carnally in their life. The heart, then, which is bowed in the keeping of humility, enlarged in the breadth of charity, and moreover filled with the knowledge of the New and Old Testament, is commanded by the Lord also to be filled with the gathered fragments of bread—indeed, with small and light sins which had formerly remained over from those who ate, namely, from those washing away their greater sins with the bread of tears [Col. 0631C]—so that those lesser sins too may be forgiven, once recalled to memory.

“Those men, therefore, when they had seen the sign which he had done, said: ‘This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.’” Soldiers about to go to war set up in themselves a certain and evident sign by which it may be known to what king or ruler’s dominion they are subject, or under whose power they are to fight in battle. Thus truly the soldiers of Christ, who are to fight with him and for him, are now marked out as belonging to his rule by the noble sign of his inspired visitation and sweetness; and they are to reign with him one day in heaven. Whoever, therefore, sees the sign of this beloved visitation in himself certainly awaits the glory of eternal reward with a kind of confident hope and has grounds for confidence in the Lord.

For although the Lord’s elect can never be secure in the present life, they nevertheless receive in this heavenly gift a certain pledge of assurance. When they have laid aside the tabernacle of the body, left behind the deadly labors of the world, and flown toward God on the wing of desire, they will behold the most beloved Lord for whom they now labor; then they will joyfully say in the exultation of their hearts: “This is truly the prophet who, when we were placed in the lake of misery, often prophesied to us through his Spirit concerning these joys. This is indeed he who, so delightful and lovable, is to come into the world—into our heart and our body—so that, with him remaining in us, we too may remain continually in him.”

The whole of today’s office looks toward this end: that at the end of a person the words which we sing today in the Introit of the Mass may be fulfilled, words which the Lord himself commanded to his faithful through the prophet, saying: “The Lord says: I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction” (Jer. 29:11). [Col. 0632B] The thoughts of peace, which the mercy of God the Father secretly arranges concerning his elect, are now hidden and concealed in the present, but at their end they come forth and are made manifest, when, transferred from this valley of tears, they merit to attain true peace, which is Christ.

When, therefore, the Lord’s elect arrive there and have passed beyond the corruptions and miseries of this world, in great joy of heart they burst forth in thanksgiving to the Lord, singing thus: “You have delivered us, Lord, from those afflicting us, and you have confounded those who hate us.” Those afflicting and hating us are evil spirits, [Col. 0632C] who from the beginning of human creation afflict and persecute the whole human race with perverse and deadly hatred. From their hatred and affliction the Lord’s **912** elect will be delivered when, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, they are presented in joy and exultation before the countenance of their Creator. There indeed those hating and pursuing them—the evil spirits, that is—will be confounded with great confusion when they see weak and frail human beings, having trampled down and overcome their snares and traps, granted eternal freedom in the sight of God.

May the only-begotten Son of God himself deign to bring us to the glory of such great dignity and freedom, which the righteous are to receive from the Lord’s hand, so that where glory and riches are in his house, there we too may one day merit to reign with [Col. 0632D] him. He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0633]

## Homilies of the Venerable Godfrey, Abbot of Admont, for the Feasts of the Whole Year

**1. First Homily. First Homily for the Feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle**

[Col. 0633A]

“Jesus, walking by the Sea of Galilee, saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea” (Matt. 4).

Although the text of this sacred Gospel reading is comprised by the Evangelist in very few words, no small power of mystical subtlety shines forth in it. “Jesus,” he says, “walking by the Sea of Galilee.” To walk is to proceed delightfully. By the Sea of Galilee in this place we may fittingly understand the present world. Let us therefore consider through subtle inquiry how Jesus walked by the Sea of Galilee.

Source/review notes: The first listed edit is a no-op and should be disregarded; the intended correction is not representable without rewriting the sentence: its final clause reverses the source’s agency. It should read: “Therefore, he will one day be crowned with as many rewards of recompense as, here, he has drawn to salvation by his example, as though fishing.”

Ever since the world was truly created, he has not disdained to walk with pious steps beside the sea of Galilee [Col. 0633B]. For while he still remained invisible with the Father, he delighted, by an ineffable grace of kindness and an inestimable abundance of sweetness, in the salvation of the human race. Hence, too, how great a devotion—what longing, I say—he had to become man himself for the restoration of man, had long before his incarnation been prophesied, as though in his own person: “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. VIII, 31). And when the time of grace came, in which the invisible God appeared visibly by assuming flesh and began to dwell among men, he again walked beside the sea of Galilee. For, filled with the bowels of unconquerable loving-kindness and mercy, he showed himself gentle and approachable even to sinners.

[Col. 0633C] But the same merciful and compassionate Lord who then visibly walked beside the sea of Galilee in mercy and compassion does not disdain even now to walk invisibly beside every person whom, according to the multitude of his mercies, he purposes to save. For, in a moral sense, we may understand by the sea of Galilee every individual person who, although long tossed about by the waves of the sea—that is, of worldly life—is nevertheless ordained in the divine predestination for the haven of salvation, namely conversion to the spiritual life. As the Apostle Paul says: “Whom he foreknew, them he also predestined; and whom he predestined, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 29). For the omnipotent Lord will one day glorify by recompense those whom he calls here through conversion [Col. 0634A].

3 Therefore Jesus walks beside those whom, even as they lie in the filth of their sins and forsake him, he does not forsake. Rather, he guards them, concealing them beneath the shadow of his hand, so that, although inwardly defiled by many disgraceful vices, they nevertheless do not become subject to public shame. Therefore, whichever elect children of God the protection of the right hand of the Most High has thus overshadowingly concealed, let them humbly rejoice, placing all the confidence of their hope in him; and let them devote themselves with humble devotion to rendering thanks to God their protector, when they recall that, though they have fallen grievously, they have nevertheless not been publicly disgraced, while, on the other hand, they know that very many are ill spoken of in the world for committing [Col. 0634B] a lighter fault. Whoever, then, are those beside whom God has walked in this manner, concealing and guarding them beneath the shelter of his wings, even if the time of their conversion is not delayed, he nevertheless does not disdain to work in them what is added here below.

“He saw two brothers.” And shortly afterwards, indicating how he saw them and in what occupations he found them engaged, he says: “They were casting a net into the sea.” In these two brothers, therefore, we may fittingly understand the body and the soul. They truly cast a net into the sea when, wholly entangled in the things of the world, they attend to them with all their senses. Therefore, if they are to be torn away from these harmful anxieties of business, Jesus walking beside them must behold them with the eyes of heavenly compassion [Col. 0634C]. He sees them when, through the light of inward visitation, he illumines the eyes of the human heart, so that a person begins to see and attend to himself, and can, by subtle reflection, consider how ruinous is the path upon which he walks. Through this vision, namely inward visitation, when a person has now seen himself by watchfully considering himself and has begun to displease himself in his ways, the name Simon, which is interpreted “obedient,” fittingly comes to him.

A human being was in some sense made disobedient to his Creator when, by satisfying his own desires and the enticements of secular life, he obeyed them. But he becomes obedient when, utterly renouncing these things, he subjects himself to obedience to the living God and, for the sake of him who for his own sake became obedient unto death, humbly submits himself to another’s rule. When, in this purpose of subjection, he has made some progress through devout labour, and, considering the lives of others, has begun to humble himself before all, then, ascending to higher degrees of virtues, he will deserve to be called Peter, which is interpreted “recognizing.” For a person may then be called recognizing when he has come in some measure to the knowledge of God and of himself, recalling to the eyes of his mind by the gaze of subtle reflection how the mercy of his Creator has preserved him for life by gratuitous loving-kindness, and conversely how great a punishment of vengeance he has deserved by the works of his wicked action [Col. 0635A].

Having received this knowledge of God and of himself, and still tending upward with more exalted steps, he will deserve to receive the name Andrew, which is interpreted “manly” or “beautiful.” Thus, having recognized, as we have said, such benefits of his Creator [Col. 0635B], and having also recognized the countless contagions of his sins, he acts manfully in the Lord and does not cease to persist in pious works, so that by the labours of worthy satisfaction he may redeem the guilt of his wicked manner of life. Having thus become manly through good works, it follows that he also becomes beautiful through pure confession. For a person appears foul and, as it were, unclean in the eyes of the divine Majesty when he conceals his sins within the bosom of his conscience and trembles to confess his injustice against himself. But he will appear beautiful and, as it were, restored in the sight of the Lord when he has revealed his ways by humble confession and a penitent heart. Hence David also says: “Confession and beauty are before him” (Ps. XCXV, 6).

But a person can in no way accomplish all these things of which we have spoken so long as, casting a net into the sea, he is entangled in worldly vanities. Rather, when the Lord visiting him has visited him by seeing him through the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit, it comes about that he may be called by these three names: Simon, Peter, and Andrew [Col. 0635C]. He becomes Simon, that is, Obedient, through conversion; he becomes Peter, that is, Recognizing, through knowledge of God and himself; he becomes Andrew, that is, manly or beautiful—manly through good works, beautiful through pure confession. Why, however, a person still tossed amid earthly affairs cannot extend himself to these degrees of virtue, the Evangelist at once indicates in what follows.

“For they were fishermen.” What he says, “They were fishermen,” is as if he said, “They were sinners.” They were sinners, I say, body and soul wandering badly amid the emptiness of secular life. For as long as a person’s senses, both inward and outward, cling to the vanities of earthly things, what more fittingly can those senses be called than sinners? Yet since, as Scripture says, “All have sinned and need the glory of God” (Rom. III, 23), there are very few who do not first love, by desiring, the things of the world before they begin to live according to the will of their Creator. Hence, unless heavenly compassion mercifully anticipates a person by beholding him, he is unable of himself either to will what is good or to accomplish a good will. But whoever, through the prevenient mercy of heaven [Col. 0636A], has now left his nets, renounced all outward things, and, pierced by divine inspiration, has given himself to the discipline of the spiritual life, cannot thereby be free from the onrush of earthly thoughts; rather, he often casts his net into the sea by meditating on empty things, as the following course of the narrative declares.

“And he said to them: Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” God speaks when, through the voice of a preacher, he teaches a person how to withdraw his mind from the instability of temporal things. Yet, however much preaching may be carried on outwardly, the preacher’s discourse seems to labour in vain unless the Creator of the heart himself addresses the heart through the voice of inward inspiration. “Come after me,” he says, [Col. 0636B] “and I will make you become fishers of men.” As though he said: Come after me by restraining your minds from the instability of lowly thought, and by raising yourselves with all your strength to the things above. For if, with the whole intention of your minds, you continually stretch yourselves upward after me, I will make you fishers of men—that is, of body and soul. I will make you fishers of these persons, so that, just as formerly in fishing badly you presented yourselves as servants to uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now in body and soul you may present yourselves as servants to righteousness unto sanctification (Rom. VI, 19).

But it rarely happens that any elect person, who, suspended as it were upon the aforesaid degrees of virtue, strives to attend to heavenly things alone, advances by bearing fruit only for himself, without his life also benefiting others by the example of good conduct [Col. 0636C]. Therefore, he will one day be crowned with as many rewards of recompense as he has here, as though fishing, drawn to salvation by his example. Therefore, whoever they may be to whom almighty God speaks in this way by the hidden language of inspiration, with what zeal and what diligence they ought to offer listening ears to the voice of his pious admonition, the Evangelist fittingly indicates in the following words:

“But they immediately left their nets and followed him.” To continue means to restore again things divided from one another. Therefore, immediately to leave one’s nets and follow the Lord is to draw back from the vain intention of thoughts the senses divided from one another by evil wandering, and to gather them to the pursuit of pious meditation. Thus those immediately leave their nets [Col. 0636D] and follow the Lord who, as we have said, resist perverse thoughts as though contradicting them, and do not cease, through strict guard, to train their changeable mind in the discipline of spiritual meditation. But that a person ought by no means to be satisfied with these exercises and pursuits of pious labour [Note: [Col. 0635D] That is, content], unless he strives to extend himself to the height of a more exalted life, the following verse quite suitably indicates:

“And proceeding from there.” For, as the Psalmist says: “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII, 8), every elect person who, as we have said, has begun, forgetting what lies behind, to stretch himself toward what is before, ought with all the effort of body and mind to advance [Col. 0637A] from virtue to virtue. He ought, I say, to advance from the virtue of knowledge to the virtue of love; to proceed from the virtue of fear to the virtue of charity; and thus through each merit of the virtues always to seek difficult and higher things, until the God of gods is seen in Zion—that is, until by the grace of the contemplative mind he deserves to taste beforehand the abundance of divine sweetness. Thus advancing, thus proceeding in good works, the following words make known with what a gaze of compassion and with what gifts of merits the omnipotent Lord again anticipates him.

“He saw two other brothers.” As we said at the beginning of the Gospel reading, we may understand body and soul by the two brothers. For the two preceding brothers whom the Lord, walking beside the sea of Galilee [Col. 0637B], saw, he found casting a net into the sea; but here, as the Evangelist says, he saw two others. They have become others, I say, because, putting off the old man with his deeds, they strive to walk in newness of life. The names added here fittingly indicate this: James, son of Zebedee, and John his brother. For James is said to mean “supplanter”; John is interpreted “the grace of God,” or “in whom is the grace of God.”

Therefore a person may be called and may be James—that is, a supplanter—when, persisting in good works, he does not cease to uproot and tear out the roots of vices, as though supplanting them, and strives to plant the shoots of virtuous action in the place of vices. Thus, where formerly the root of the sin of pride, envy, and bitterness sprang up, there may afterwards begin to flower and germinate flowers of righteousness, humility, patience [Col. 0637C], and chastity. Whoever therefore labours in this manner to make continual progress for the better by supplanting vices in himself truly receives the name of a greater dignity, namely John, which is interpreted “the grace of God.” For when, walking the arduous path of virtues, he refuses to delight in lowly things, divine loving-kindness bestows upon him the desired grace of inward sweetness, so that, refreshed by frequent visitation, he may be made readier for the practice of pious labour. The words immediately following show where these virtues of spiritual exercise may be practised.

“In a boat with Zebedee their father.” By the boat, therefore, we may understand the spiritual life through a sound understanding of the Scriptures. For certain likenesses seem to exist in a boat which can, with fitting meaning, be referred to the spiritual life. Although a ship has good sailors and other helpers of the vessel, unless the skill of a good pilot provides diligently, it is quickly overwhelmed by waves. So also the spiritual life, although the advances of religious observance and the merits of virtuous conduct flourish in it, is gradually weakened from the state of uprightness by growing negligence unless it is frequently directed, as it were by propulsion, through the governance of a pious ruler [Col. 0637D].

There is also another likeness in a boat which rightly seems to suit the spiritual life. Just as one who is in a ship has hope of reaching the harbour, while one in danger in a river outside the ship is despaired of as able to escape the danger of death, so indeed one who remains in the spiritual life, like one now tending toward the harbour, should not doubt that he has laid hold of the way which leads to life. But one who is still tossed upon the sea of this age utterly does not know whether he will reach the harbour of eternal life. Yet although every converted person keeps watch with all his powers, always tending upward, as long as he remains in this time of mutability he cannot have the firmness of complete security. For the name Zebedee, which is interpreted “this one flowing,” shows that he cannot be free from the flowing vanity of the age. What, then, can we understand by Zebedee but the present world? And what is the world but man himself? For every human being is the whole world. As the world, always tending toward its end, incessantly flows away in a certain sense, so a person comes nearer to death from day [Col. 0638B] to day. Therefore we have the world in us and with us, because we endlessly endure the misery of human mortality.

Thus the elect remain in the boat—that is, in the spiritual life—with Zebedee their father, namely the world that is passing away. For as long as they live in this world, although they do not cease always to keep watch in good works, they nevertheless cannot retain the integrity of righteousness perfectly. For while at one moment, despising all earthly things, they strictly suppress within themselves the tumult of vainly wandering thoughts and delightfully devote themselves to pious labours, delighting in divine contemplation alone, suddenly, impeded by the frailty of mortal life, they lapse from the practice of pious action by meditating on the vanities of earthly occupation. Yet any who are to be saved, having now taken their stand in the boat [Col. 0638C] and resolved to reach the harbour, the more strictly they formerly held themselves in the guard of the mind, the more quickly they return to themselves within themselves, recognize their sins, and strive to correct their guilt before God through worthy fruits of repentance. The words that follow also clearly indicate this:

“Repairing their nets.” For what is it to repair nets except to correct faults by worthy repentance? Therefore the elect repair and correct their nets when, wherever they know that they have sinned in any way, they immediately have recourse to pure confession, do not fear strictly to accuse themselves, and do not cease to afflict themselves before God with frequent lamentation. And by repairing their nets in this manner—that is, by worthily repenting of their sins—they obtain pardon through the clemency of divine compassion [Col. 0638D]. Therefore those who repair their nets in this way, that is, who thus strive to make satisfaction to God with their gathered senses, are followed by the mercy of heavenly loving-kindness with what grace of consolation and what abundance of sweetness is openly declared to us in what follows:

“And he called them.” It should be noted that the Lord is read not to have called the preceding brothers whom he saw beside the sea of Galilee, but only to have spoken to them; here, however, where he saw two other brothers standing in the boat, the Evangelist expressly adds that he called them. For to call is to invite a friend to familiar conversation. We sometimes speak to a person, yet do not call him to a conversation of secret familiarity. Therefore, the omnipotent Lord in some sense calls to himself those whom he finds, as we have said, repairing their nets [Col. 0639A]; that is, he admits them to the familiarity of divine contemplation, so that the more frequently they are joined to his familiarity, the more powerfully they may despise and trample underfoot the vanities of the flowing world, as the following verse declares.

“But they immediately left their nets and father and followed him.” For the more frequently, as we have said, they are called to heavenly secrets, the more contemptuously they deal with the world and its desires; and although some earthly things may occasionally come to mind, they utterly refuse to delight in them, desiring only to follow the Lord, insofar as is possible amid the misery of this mortality, by thinking on heavenly things. Therefore, whoever they are who deserve to be called by the Lord in this present life and follow him who calls them with such diligence and such zeal as we have described, he will one day call them to himself when, putting off bodily corruption, he receives them to himself and makes them a worthy dwelling place for his eternal divinity. As the Bridegroom himself speaks in the Song of Songs to his bride, every elect soul, saying [Note: [Col. 0639D] The Church in the Office of the Holy Virgins]: “Come, my chosen one, and I will place my throne in you, because the king has desired your beauty.”—They immediately leave their nets and father and follow him who, free from every affliction of bodily infirmity, shall without end behold him who is true eternity and eternal joy, joined also to his eternal divinity, through him who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

10 HOMILY II. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD.

[Col. 0639C]

“When Mary, the mother of Jesus, was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to have conceived by the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I).

Just as in secular writings three things are customarily sought—subject matter, intention, and narrative—so in the sequence of this Gospel reading these three things may be found: a person’s calling, testing, and perfection. We must diligently inquire in what order these are fulfilled in a person. The Evangelist therefore says:

“When Mary, the mother of Jesus, was betrothed to Joseph.” By Joseph, whose name is said to mean “increaser,” almighty God may fittingly be represented; but by Mary [Col. 0639D], who is called “star of the sea,” any blessed soul may suitably be understood, which is betrothed to Joseph. And because betrothal is a sign of a future marriage, a person’s calling may be expressed by this betrothal; that calling is a sign of that person’s future union with God. For a woman not yet betrothed has free power to turn aside to whomever she wishes; but when she has been betrothed, she is so bound that she may no longer dissolve the bond or take anyone else in his place.

Thus indeed the true Joseph, the almighty Father, when he calls each blessed soul, a future mother of Jesus, away from the wicked world through inward inspiration, causing her to pass from harmful freedom to praiseworthy servitude, binds her to himself, or to his vicar, any prelate, in that calling and betrothal in such a way that she may no longer return from her spiritual purpose [Col. 0640A]. Yet, after she has been called, before she may attain this dignity and come together into one with God—as bridegroom and bride are customarily joined, so that the two are found in one flesh, and she likewise becomes one spirit with God—what follows must first be fulfilled in her:

“She was found,” he says, “to have conceived by the Holy Spirit.” By whom, then, is she found? She herself finds that she has conceived in her womb the spirit of the fear of the Lord. And note the word he uses: “Having in her womb.” For what we carry in our hands we sometimes lose by an accident; but what we have in the womb [Col. 0640B] we can scarcely lose. Therefore, for the same reason, the blessed soul ought to possess firmly and steadfastly in the womb of her heart the spirit of the fear of the Lord. Instructed by it, she should abstain from everything that she knows displeases the sight of the supreme Deity; and, conversely, she should strive to perform in deed, with all devotion, whatever she knows is pleasing and perfect before God. This, therefore, is a person’s calling—indeed, betrothal. But now we must come to the testing; hence what follows:

“But Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her publicly, wished to put her away secretly.” Therefore, the true Joseph is the husband of the blessed soul in hope, not yet in actuality; because he is righteous, his righteousness does not allow him to give greater rewards to the soul that has deserved lesser things. Rather, according to each person’s merit of life, he must give greater rewards of recompense to the greater, and lesser rewards to the lesser [Col. 0640C]. This his righteousness requires. For this reason he does not wish to bring home the less deserving soul; he does not wish to receive her into his own household. We call it “bringing home” when a husband takes his betrothed wife from her father’s house and her own relatives and introduces her into his own dwelling places.

Thus, plainly, the true Joseph, the heavenly Father, does not wish suddenly to bring the soul that has not yet deserved it from the carnal life to the spiritual, or rapidly to raise her from earthly to heavenly things. But what does he do? “He wished,” it says, “to put her away secretly.” Therefore, in his hidden will and thought he puts her away; and she who hoped to be anticipated by him with blessings of sweetness, having none of the things she hoped for [Col. 0640D], now anxiously laments that she has neither God nor the world. For if she should fall again into sins, this would be to put her away secretly; but it would be to have put her away openly. And therefore, thus secretly put away, she grieves and is sorrowful that she has been abandoned by God.

So too the blessed Joseph of old was troubled when he saw our Lady, the perpetual Virgin Mary, pregnant—she whom he knew to be most holy in body, most chaste in morals, and whose life was pleasing both to God and to men. What state of mind do we suppose he had when he saw these things and did not know what to do? So also the blessed soul, conscious of good works and remembering that she has never committed anything of the sort in her spiritual conduct for which she might rightly be shut out from the love of her bridegroom, sees herself deprived of grace and, with humble and contrite heart, grieves and groans that she has been so abandoned [Col. 0641A]. Thus, at last tested, the soul becomes worthy to deserve to arrive at perfection. Hence follows:

“As he was thinking these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying.” When the true Joseph frequently works these things which we have mentioned in the hidden will and thought of a person, immediately the angel of the Lord—that is, the grace of the Almighty—appears to him in a dream. And it is well said that it appears to him in a dream. For as the sleep of dreaming is rest for the body, so in the blessed sleep of this grace there is rest for the heart. Yet this grace truly occurs under a kind of appearance, because it swiftly passes and does not remain; nevertheless, in it a person rests sweetly [Col. 0641B]. In this rest the blessed soul sometimes customarily utters the words which follow. But even if she does not know how to use such words to the Lord, the inmost desires of her heart supply the place of these words.

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to receive Mary your wife; for what is born in her is of the Holy Spirit.” Since every perfect prayer is commonly directed to God in faith in the Holy Trinity, behold, we may find here three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. “Joseph, son of David”—as though a soul panting and sighing for the joys of the Lord’s nativity, and desiring to rejoice and be refreshed with him in that solemnity, should say in her prayer to the Lord: O Joseph, most desired son of David [Col. 0641C], who wished to assume the frailty of our flesh not only from righteous and holy parents, but also from wicked and sinful ones—of whom David was one, an adulterer and murderer. I, wretched woman, following him in this respect, am an adulteress and murderess, killing myself by sins. By this mercy I ask you: do not receive Mary your wife, namely my soul, in fear during this holy solemnity in which the whole world throughout the earth rejoices. It is enough, Lord, that I have lived in your fear until now. Remove fear now, I pray; add love. Deal with my soul in the manner of marriage, loving and cherishing her in your mercies. For the fact that I formerly left the world, and that by your gift I despised the delights of the world, was born in me from the spirit of your fear [Col. 0641D]; and this very thing now born in me is wholly from the spirit of your fear.

“But she shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins.” Therefore, if, fear having been removed, you impart your love in this venerable solemnity, my soul shall bear a son, not a daughter. She shall bear, I say, a son of contemplation; she shall bear a son of inward prayer, whom you shall call Jesus, calling him my salvation and saviour, granting him to me for salvation and to yourself for honour. Therefore you shall give him his name. For all will be reckoned to you, and whatever I shall bring forth by your inspiration will look wholly to your glory, not to mine [Col. 0642A], according to the Psalmist’s words: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name.” But this son of sweetness, thus begotten from me through you, shall save the people of my thoughts, the people of my words and works, from their sins. For whatever I may otherwise sin, whatever negligence may mark my life at another time, all will be saved through the begetting of this son.

HOMILY III. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD.

“A voice saying: Cry out. And I said: What shall I cry?” (Isa. XL.)

The pages of sacred Scripture testify, in both hidden and manifest words, what the ardour and greatness of the desire of the ancient Fathers were, as they sighed for Christ’s presence in the flesh [Col. 0642B]. The holy men of old clearly knew that the Lord of Majesty entertained thoughts of peace concerning the race of mortals. Therefore they most ardently desired him to appear in the flesh, so that, with death destroyed, they might be freed through him from the prisons of hell and recalled to the homeland of eternal life.

One of these, the outstanding prophet, Isaiah—God’s chosen fellow-initiate—unable to bear the Lord’s delay and not enduring the postponement of Christ’s birth, said: “Would that you might tear open the heavens and come down!” (Isa. LXIV, 1.) Therefore he who is “the desire of the eternal hills” (Gen. XLIX, 26), he who is “desired by all nations” (Hag. II, 8), kindled the burning desire and loving expectation of this prophet and the other saints by no slight promises [Col. 0642C]. Thus this outstanding prophet, sighing in sorrow of heart for Christ’s coming, had heard from the Lord: “A voice saying: Cry out.”

By the voice, which precedes the word, divine inspiration may be understood. By this inspiration this prophet and the other saints were inflamed to pray that the almighty Father might send into this valley of tears, clothed in flesh, the Word of the most high Father, which rested in the Father’s bosom, poured forth from the Father’s heart by their cry and desire, in order to free the elect [Note: [Col. 0641D] Thus the manuscript]. And because a cry commonly arises either from excessive grief or from immense joy, the Lord’s elect had altogether need of a great cry [Col. 0642D]: they who asked that the Son of God, truly unfailing joy, should be incarnate, and who in turn needed a great cry of sorrow because they knew that after the darkness of this mortality they would descend to hell. Therefore the prophet, commanded by the Lord to cry out, asks, saying:

“What shall I cry?” And the Lord says to him: “All flesh is grass.” Grass is fodder for an ox and other beasts. Hence the human race may be understood by grass, but by the ox the devil may be understood, of whom it is said through blessed Job: “He shall eat grass like an ox” (Job. IV, 10). Therefore all flesh, indeed the whole human race, had become grass, food for the most wicked ox, the devil, who had swallowed all the elect into the belly of his malice and held them captive [Col. 0643A] in hell. For the saints who, for nine hundred years and more, had served the Lord in the flesh justly and piously, descended to hell when the debt of the flesh was discharged. There, on account of the guilt of original sin, sitting in darkness, they awaited for a very long time—the five thousand years—the joys of the promised salvation. This was a great calamity, worthy of a mighty cry. He from whom every good flows inspired this cry in his saints, caused those inspired to cry, heard those who cried, and raised up those whom he heard with sure promises, as is immediately added below:

“And all its glory is as the flower of the field.” The flower of the field is Christ, the Son of God, who blossomed in his nativity and came forth like a flower from the virginal womb. Therefore all the glory of the human race, which before Christ’s coming had been the devil’s grass, was made in redemption like a flower of the field after the beginning of his nativity [Col. 0643B], because the flower of the field, as we have said, is Christ the Son of God. In likeness to this flower the elect were restored in Christ’s passion and will be restored in the future, when they shall indeed be heirs of God and co-heirs of Jesus Christ (Rom. VIII, 17). But for the accomplishment of this work a certain singular and noble grass was found, concerning which the Lord immediately added:

“The grass has dried up and the flower has fallen, because the Spirit of God has breathed upon it.” This noble grass, set in contrast to the former grass, was the blessed and undefiled Virgin Mary. Though she had been taken from the common mass [Note: [Col. 0643D] See the preliminary dissertation to the first volume of this work.] of human corruption [Col. 0643C], by God’s grace she had been dried of all moisture of carnal desire and carnal life. But after that noble grass—the body of our Lady, the perpetual Virgin Mary—had been dried, the flower fell into her: that eternal flower, that excellent flower, the most high Son of the living God. But whence, I ask, did it come about that this flower, descending from heaven like dew, fell into her, except because the Spirit of the Lord breathed upon it, and because the Holy Spirit came upon her and overshadowed her? The prophet therefore continues and says:

“Truly the people are grass.” After the signs of the Lord’s nativity, after the venerable joys of the new salvation, the prophet groans and grieves that the Lord’s elect are still the devil’s food [Col. 0643D], still held in the prisons of hell. For although the Saviour had appeared in the flesh, they could in no way be brought out from the lowest pit in which they were bound until blood and water flowed from the opened side of the crucified Lord, pierced by the soldier’s spear. Through this sacrament hell was shattered, and the gate of the heavenly kingdom was immediately opened to the elect. As if the prophet, lamenting with a wounded heart, said to the Lord: O Lord, now truly, as you formerly promised your servants, you have come down to earth through the mystery of your incarnation; but your people are still grass—the food, alas, of malignant spirits who rule insolently over them [Col. 0644A]—as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us and the name of Jesus Christ, your Son, was not invoked over us. Where is what you formerly promised: that you would bring the human race to the glory and honour of the flower, your Son, when your having become incarnate now profits us nothing, and we are all still the devil’s prey? To one thus complaining and grieving, the Lord declares the mysteries of human redemption more openly, saying:

“The grass has dried up and the flower has fallen; the word of the Lord remains for ever.” By this dried grass, now set in the third place, the Lord’s body must be understood, most pure from every corruption. That sacred little body [Note: [Col. 0643D] The Church in the Paschal hymn for the Sunday in White.] was dried upon the altar of the cross, for the redemption of the human race [Col. 0644B], by the bitterness of passion and the harshness of death. Thus, when this noble grass, namely our Saviour, hung upon the cross and withered for our salvation, at last the flower fell when he died upon the cross, bowing his head and giving up the spirit. And when he had given up the spirit, descending with his soul to hell, God appeared in hell and willed that his body be laid in the tomb. But when the flower fell, the word of the Lord remains for ever, because the divinity of the incarnate Word remained and remains for ever when the flesh died—never to die, never to see setting.

Having first set forth the two mysteries of incarnation and passion, he immediately adds the two others, resurrection and ascension, saying:

“Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion” [Col. 0644C]. By the high mountain the Lord’s resurrection may be understood; by Zion, which is called “a watchtower,” the Church gathered from the Jews may be understood. As though he said: You, Lord, who, having destroyed the dominion of death, overcame death, ascend victor over its setting, and appear to your faithful in the glory of the resurrection, so that the glory of your kingdom and resurrection may be announced to the Church gathered from the Jews.

Exalt your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem. The Lord exalted his voice with strength when, after the glory of the resurrection, he raised above all the heavens the body which he had assumed from the blessed Virgin, strengthened by the power and might of incorruption and immortality. “You,” he says, “who bring good news to Jerusalem.” Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace” [Col. 0644D], by which the Church gathered from the Gentiles is understood. In her, after the Ascension, the Lord exalted his voice with strength, because he commanded that the mystery of the incarnate Word be preached to the Gentiles. After the first exaltation, that of the Ascension, a second exaltation immediately follows, when it is said:

**17. Exalt your voice; do not fear.** This exaltation was accomplished on the day of Pentecost, when, seated at the Father’s right hand, he poured out the Holy Spirit upon the children of adoption. Through him he was so exalted in the hearts of the disciples that those who had previously been fearful and wholly unfit for any courageous act, after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit and casting off all fear, confidently preached before kings and rulers concerning the incarnate Word [Col. 0645A]. An example of this is described for us in the Acts of the Apostles: when the rulers of this world, after having the apostles beaten, ordered them no longer to speak in the name of Jesus, Peter, chief of the apostles, answered with the disciples: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

**Say to the cities of Judah: Behold your God.** Judah is interpreted “confession” or “praise.” By the cities of Judah, therefore, the present condition of the Church is described, to which it is now frequently said through the mouths of preachers: “Behold your God”; that is, he is shown as present through the word of exhortation.

Therefore let us celebrate with inward devotion the solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity, serving the Lord in joy [Col. 0645B], so that at the hour of the saving sacrifice, when we come to receive the immaculate body which was taken from the blessed Virgin through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, as we receive the Lord’s body in an affection of sweetness, the holy angels standing by—the messengers of our King—may say to us: “Behold your God, who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.”

## HOMILY IV: THIRD HOMILY FOR THE SAME VIGIL

“Today you shall know that the Lord will come, and in the morning you shall see his glory” (Exod. 16).

The Holy Spirit, desiring us to be ready to receive the proclamation of the Lord’s Incarnation—that is, the new joys of our salvation—addresses and exhorts us, saying: “Today you shall know that the Lord will come, and in the morning you shall see his glory” [Col. 0645C]. For what else does he suggest to us by saying that the glory of God is to be seen in the morning, except that our minds should be prepared all the more as we recognize that the birth of our Redeemer is nearer at hand? Indeed, if any powerful man were to invite his friend to this most holy solemnity, throughout the whole preceding period before his arrival that friend would prepare himself in every way, considering with what honor and reverence he ought to receive his guest. But if, having previously had some doubt about his arrival, he were to learn with certainty that he would come on this day, then, however little time remained, he would hasten to make himself presentable for his guest’s coming. Therefore, when mortal human beings strive to outdo one another with such honor [Col. 0645D], with what devotion of heart and preparation of actions ought this magnificent guest—our Redeemer—to be received by us on his feast, he with whom grace and salvation have come to us?

Forewarned, therefore, and repeatedly assured during these holy days of the coming of so great a guest, let us prepare our houses and cleanse our hearts, so that, with our inner eyes cleansed, in the morning we may behold the glory of our God—namely, that bride, the flesh assumed into God—and may worthily receive his sacrament at the most holy altar. But whoever recognizes, under the accusation of his conscience, that he has prepared himself too little beforehand, should not despair of the Lord’s mercy; rather, let him at least accomplish on this day what he previously neglected.

This is indeed the feast for which all the ancient Fathers, recognizing it to be most necessary, yearned with the whole desire of their hearts [Col. 0646A], and therefore prefigured it in all their deeds and writings. Thus we read concerning this solemnity in Exodus—something which, according to the letter, seems unsuitable to this day, but which, if we investigate its sense carefully, we see to be quite fitting:

When King Pharaoh, who held the people of Israel under his dominion, saw that the people themselves were increasing and growing daily, he commanded his servants to cast into the river every male child born among them. “After this, a man went forth from the house of Levi, having taken a wife from his own stock” (Exod. 2:1 ff.).

Whom, beloved brethren, does this king signify except the one who held the whole human race captive before the coming of Christ [Col. 0646B]? He also cast everyone into the river, because he led with himself into hell not only the wicked but even God’s elect after they had paid the debt of death. “After this, a man went forth from the house of Levi.” This man was the holy and righteous Joseph, who took a wife from his own stock—our most precious Lady Mary—not in order to defile her holy virginal body through human contamination, but in order to provide what was necessary for her and for the infant after his birth. She conceived and bore a son, not violated by the touch of any man, but overshadowed by the Holy Spirit coming down from above. She conceived him and bore him, not as other mothers conceive and give birth, but conceived him without contamination of the flesh and bore him without any pain.

“And, Scripture says, seeing him beautiful, she hid him for three months” [Col. 0646C]. Our Lady Mary truly saw her Son beautiful, because no human being has known, nor can know, as she herself perceived with the sight of heart and body, the beauty and loveliness of his unsearchable divinity. She hid this for three months because she did not wish to reveal it to human beings in his infancy, childhood, and youth.

“And when she could no longer hide him, she took a basket of reeds, coated it with pitch and bitumen, and placed the infant inside.” What is signified by the basket of reeds except that venerable manger, which was adorned and consecrated by Christ’s tender infant limbs? His mother, the glorious Mother [Col. 0646D], coated it with pitch and bitumen when she placed within it that same Redeemer of ours—God and man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh—incarnate from herself. For thus the Evangelist says: “The days of Mary were fulfilled, and she bore her firstborn son; and she wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for him in the lodging” (Luke 2:7).

And rightly by the name of pitch is signified the soul of our Redeemer, because pitch is by nature black and, as it were, despised. So his soul, although higher than all souls, was nevertheless humbler than all. But bitumen, which is part of the earth and clings to the earth, signifies his body: taken from our earthly body, it clung to our weaknesses and labors, yet without sin. This basket, then [Col. 0647A], coated with pitch and bitumen—that is, the venerable manger, consecrated by Christ’s soul and body—all now adore; and, if not bodily, they nevertheless bow to it reverently with devotion of heart. For if any altar consecrated by a bishop ought to be held in such reverence that no one dares touch it except honorably, how much honor, we think, is owed to this manger, which the Creator of the whole world, made little for our sake, deigned to touch with his little limbs?

“And she placed it in the reeds by the river, while his sister stood at a distance and awaited the outcome.” The sister of this heavenly child is that Church, the multitude of the angelic host, which on this night announced new joys on earth and peace to people of good will while this child lay in his basket, that is, in the manger [Col. 0647B]. This sister also awaits the outcome of our affair on the festival of this night, while she stands by us as we serve God in hymns and praises and reports our prayers to the throne of the divine majesty. For if angels appeared to shepherds tending animals, who as yet neither knew nor thought of this feast, much more should we believe that they stand by us, although we do not see them with bodily sight, while on this night we praise their Lord, born from the Virgin. It follows:

“And behold, Pharaoh’s daughter came down to wash herself in the river.” Pharaoh’s daughter may fittingly be understood as those Magi, the firstfruits of the Church, who, with sound understanding, came from the farthest regions of the East when the Lord was born. They came down in order to wash themselves in the river—that is, so that, once they had recognized the Savior and found the King of the Jews, they might be washed in the water of repentance [Col. 0647C]. How many tears, we may suppose, did they then shed when they saw him whom through the Holy Spirit they truly knew to be their Creator, tender and wrapped in such small cloths! Hence it is well added that, when she saw the little child crying, she had compassion on him, because he appeared exceedingly pitiable, when they saw him lying thus emptied and humbled.

Let us therefore hear what reward the mother of this child received because she bore him incorruptibly and nourished him. Her reward is truly incomparable: not only do human beings devoutly praise her, but even the angelic spirits rightly venerate and magnify her as their Lady and as the mother of their Maker [Col. 0647D].

After Moses had grown up, he went out to his brethren and saw their affliction, and an Egyptian striking one of his Hebrew brethren. Looking this way and that, and seeing no one present, he struck the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Our Redeemer undoubtedly saw the affliction of his brethren when, with a gaze of mercy and compassion, he looked upon the whole human race and grieved over its miseries. And when the Egyptian—that ancient adversary—struck one of his Hebrew brethren, that is, when he subjected all the sons of Adam to his dominion, the true Moses, namely Christ Jesus [Col. 0648A], looked this way and that and saw no one present. He looked this way, toward those living in the world, in order to teach them through his preaching the way of righteousness; and he looked that way, toward those held captive in hell, in order to rescue them through his death. And when he saw no one present who could help them, he himself attacked and struck the Egyptian, because he conquered the proud tyrant by the glorious trophy of his death. This stricken enemy is hidden by him in the sand, since he is permitted to reign only in the hearts of fools, who are understood by the sand, by the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth.

It should be noted that he is said to have hidden him in the sand, because he who once openly reigned before the Savior’s coming now does not dare openly to exercise his tyranny even among such persons, but does so secretly [Col. 0648B].

Therefore, as we splendidly celebrate the feast of this day, let us invite in prayer the sister of our Lord, the angelic multitude, so that, as she awaits the outcome of our affair and guards all that concerns us, our praise may become so acceptable to Christ that he himself, coming, may rest in the manger of our heart, make holy nights within us, and through these temporal feasts bring us to the eternal ones, where God is all in all. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY V: FOURTH HOMILY FOR THE SAME VIGIL

[Col. 0648C] “Sanctify yourselves today and be ready, for tomorrow you shall see the majesty of God within yourselves.”  
[Note: [Col. 0647D] The Church, in the office of the preceding day, responsory of the first lesson of the first nocturn.]

Though the splendid and joyful gladness of this solemnity shines festively throughout the whole world, the tongue of flesh cannot worthily speak of it. To celebrate these things worthily, every blessed soul has prepared itself throughout the whole period of this preceding Advent of the Lord, so that it may be consoled with special joy at the birth of its Redeemer. Therefore, that we may prepare ourselves more and more, on this preceding night the Holy Spirit thus admonishes and exhorts us: “Sanctify yourselves today and be ready, for tomorrow you shall see the majesty of God within yourselves.” We ought not indeed to be sanctified in such a way as to suppose ourselves equal to those saints who now rejoice with Christ in heaven; for they, having been taken from corruption to incorruption [Col. 0648D], can neither sin nor wish to sin. But we, so long as we are in this life, cannot be without sin. Rather, we are sanctified and prepared for these solemnities if we have neither hatred nor envy against our neighbors in our conscience.

Whoever strives to be sanctified in this way will undoubtedly see God’s majesty within himself on the following day. By God’s majesty, indeed, his fear may fittingly be understood; the holy soul will see that fear within itself on the following day, when, at the holy altar, receiving his most holy sacrament with cleansed heart and body, it merits inwardly to taste beforehand who and how great he is [Col. 0649A] whom it receives there. Yet there are some who, through slothfulness of heart and softness of flesh, are so frivolous that they neither wish nor are able to sanctify themselves. They approach the holy table of the altar with others, yet receive their Redeemer neither with heart prepared nor body sanctified. Such people, assuredly, see in themselves not God’s majesty but, so to speak, a kind of weakness of his, because they are neither pierced by his fear nor set aflame by his love.

The elect are also sanctified today and made ready when, in this age—which is understood by “today”—they sanctify their works and thoughts, so that, when the tomorrow dawns, when this same Savior of ours appears in his majesty at the last judgment, nothing may appear in them before the sight of the strict Judge for which they could justly be condemned [Col. 0649B].

And because our Lord Jesus Christ was promised especially and chiefly to these two Fathers, namely Abraham and David—promised to Abraham because he was to be born from his seed, and to David because David himself, a most mighty king, prefigured in his writings and deeds this same king who was to be born, our Lord Jesus Christ—we therefore read concerning him in a certain place where the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation is indicated in words that are plainly obscure. When the Lord had rejected Saul, whom he had appointed king over the Israelite people, he says to the prophet Samuel: “Fill your horn with oil, and come; I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite” (1 Sam. 16:1).

Thus, when God the Father had looked upon the misery and calamity of the whole human race [Col. 0649C], he spoke in the counsel of his eternity with God the Son: “Fill your horn with oil.” Throughout Scripture, a horn signifies power and honor; therefore in this place the horn may fittingly be understood as Christ’s divine power. “Fill your horn with oil”: that is, as though God the Father, eternally arranging with the Son coeternal with himself the mystery of human redemption, were saying: “Behold, in the regard of my clemency and mercy I see the whole human race which I created so subject to sins and death that it cannot be restored otherwise than if you descend and assume human flesh. Therefore fill your horn with oil; that is, join human nature to your divinity, so that, made man yourself [Col. 0649D], you may learn to have compassion on human miseries.”

For the nature of oil is that, mixed with other liquids, it always rises above them. And oil rightly signifies his mercy, because, according to the Psalmist, “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9). Indeed, it would not have sufficiently benefited humanity merely to know the power of his divinity, unless it had also received the oil of his mercy.

“And come,” he says, “that I may send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite.” It is the custom of every person who comes to move himself. Thus “come” is spoken here as though the Father had said to the Son, when he entrusted to him the salvation of human nature: “Humanity can neither return to the glory for which I created it nor be reconciled to me, its Maker, unless you move yourself, unless you yourself come and assume the humble form of man” [Col. 0650A].

“That I may send you,” he says, “to Jesse the Bethlehemite.” By Jesse, whose name is interpreted “sacrifice of the island,” both peoples may be understood: by the island, the people of the Gentiles, who, swallowed up by the water of unbelief and idolatry, were alienated from God; by sacrifice, the Jewish people, who, knowing God, appeared to serve him by lawful sacrifices. The eternal Father therefore says to the Son consubstantial with himself: “Come, that I may send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite,” that is, to both peoples: that you may assume flesh from the Jews and, recalling the people of the Gentiles from the worship of idols, convert them to yourself. Make yourself also a Bethlehemite—that is, the bread of all your faithful—so that all who are willing to believe in you may be satisfied through you and from you.

“For I have provided for myself a king among his sons” [Col. 0650B]. We see, indeed, how great a multitude from the Gentiles has been converted to faith; this multitude may rightly be called “a chosen and royal race” (1 Pet. 2:9). But at the end of the world, when the Jewish people comes to faith and the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then there will indeed be among the sons of Jesse the king whom the Lord has provided and predestined through his grace: namely, an innumerable people which will then come to the catholic faith. It follows:

And Samuel said: “How shall I go? For Saul will hear and kill me.” This answer of the Son of God is both teaching and consolation for us: it teaches us and makes known how he wished to come, namely, that on his very journey he was killed for us.

And the Lord said: “You shall take a calf from the herd in your hand” [Col. 0650C]. We should not understand this speaking of God the Father as though he spoke with a human tongue; rather, his speech was the predestination of human salvation. “You shall take,” he says, “a calf from the herd in your hand.” What can be understood more fittingly by the calf than the flesh of our Redeemer, which he offered on the altar of the cross for the salvation of the whole world? “You shall take a calf from the herd”: that is, take a body from the flesh of the patriarchs and prophets, whom we may rightly understand by the herd. Thus blessed Matthew, tracing his genealogy, says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac; Isaac begot Jacob” (Matt. 1:1–2), and so he descends to blessed Joseph and our blessed Lady Mary [Col. 0650D], “from whom,” he says, “Jesus was born, who is called Christ” (ibid., 16).

“You shall take,” he says, “the calf in your hand.” The hand of the Son of God, in which he was commanded by the Father to take the calf—that is, the flesh—is his power, because he had such power over his flesh that it was rightly subject to him as to its Maker. For no saint, not even his own mother, has been granted such power over his or her flesh as to be able to die or live according to personal will. He alone had his flesh in his own power, because when he wished, by dying he laid down his soul, and when he wished, by rising again he took it up. Thus, as he approached his passion, he says: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down and take it up again” (John 10:18). And immediately: “I have power to lay down my soul and power to take it up again” [Col. 0651A] (ibid.).

Therefore, exhorting the Son to the Passion, the Father says: “You shall take a calf from the herd in your hand, and you shall say: ‘I have come to sacrifice to God.’” As though he said: “Make all the faithful know what sort of sacrifice you offer, so that they too, following your example, may henceforth offer the same sacrifice through which they may receive forgiveness of sins.” For what victim has pleased the eternal Father from the beginning as did that which his Only-begotten offered, not for himself but for us? Abel, the first martyr, offered a lamb to God, and God looked upon his gifts; nevertheless, slain by his brother, he descended into hell. Likewise the aforesaid patriarch Abraham, commanded by the Lord to offer his only son, was ready to do so, but, again at God’s command, offered a ram in his place [Col. 0651B]. Yet this great patriarch, like the others, descending to hell after death, awaited there for a long time the coming of his Redeemer.

In this offering alone, which Christ made, there was such power that until the end of the age, as often as it is offered and received with right faith, all the sins of those who receive it are blotted out through it, by the aid and gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY VI: FIFTH HOMILY FOR THE SAME VIGIL

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim good news to the meek” (Isa. [Col. 0651C] 61), etc.

In the words of this holy prophecy, as it seems to me, the character, course, and order which the whole life and conduct of the elect ought to have in the present life are shown; and after their life’s course has been well completed, how great the glory and blessedness of eternal recompense that follow are mystically indicated [MS reads *quantae*]. For though the prophet spoke these words especially concerning Christ, nevertheless, because Christ is our head and we are his members, he speaks of the head in such a way that he appears prophetically to touch and exhort his members also—those whom Christ himself deigns to lead, as his members, to the knowledge of himself and to perfection in virtues.

“The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “is upon me.” We read in the Scriptures that the Spirit of the Lord deigns to come and visit the hearts of his elect in diverse ways. He comes to some in order to strengthen and confirm them; to others he comes in order to anoint and suffuse them with his sweet and lovable unction. He came upon Samson, that very strong man, as you know, as it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson” (Judg. 14:6), to make him mighty and strong, and, in that strength, to break the weak and feeble devices of that Delilah. As he is accustomed to come in order to strengthen and confirm some, so he also deigns to come to the hearts of others through the invisible sacrament of his anointing. Perceiving what kind of advent of the Holy Spirit this was, the prophet distinguishes it, saying [Col. 0652A]: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me.”

What and what kind of anointing is this? This anointing is the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit, by which hearts are inwardly enlightened to know God and instructed for preaching. Of this anointing John says: “His anointing teaches us concerning all things” (1 John 2:27).

This anointing is greatly necessary for the preacher and teacher, and necessary also for the hearer. For if a preacher is anointed with this anointing of the Holy Spirit, he is usefully sent to preach, because he is then gladly heard and obeyed. But if the covering of his heart is not anointed with this unction, he is sent to preach in vain. After this anointing there fittingly follows:

“To proclaim good news to the meek he has sent me” [Col. 0652B]. First they are anointed, and afterward sent to proclaim. To whom? To the meek. Who are the meek? The humble, gentle, patient in adversities, despisers of this world, poor in spirit, able to endure poverty and every extremity. To these meek and humble people the preacher ought to announce whatever he himself has received from the invisible anointing of the Holy Spirit. After this proclamation follows the healing owed to the contrite in heart:

“That I might heal,” he says, “the contrite in heart.” Who are the contrite in heart? The contrite in heart are truly penitent people, having contrition of heart and body for their sins; wherever they hardened their hearts by resisting God’s will, commandment, and knowledge [Col. 0652C], for that very reason they bruise and break their hearts through daily repentance. To those thus contrite in heart the preacher, because the Lord has anointed him, ought to offer the healing of counsel. For a teacher’s counsel is a great healing for the sinner: counsel concerning recognition of sins, counsel concerning repentance and satisfaction.

After the healing of counsel, forgiveness ought immediately to be preached. To whom? To captives: namely, to those who have given themselves over to captivity and the snare, who have voluntarily submitted themselves to the yoke of obedience, who glory in their captivity, saying with the Prophet: “You brought us into the snare; you laid tribulations upon our back; you set men over our heads” (Ps. 65:11). These too are captives and are held as captives when they confess their sins. They are held captive, I say, because they ought not to return to the sins they have already confessed; or they are held captive because they remain ashamed and covered with shame until what they have done is washed away and cleansed by the gift of satisfaction [Col. 0652D]. To these captives forgiveness must be preached, namely the grace of true remission, which the Lord is always ready to grant from his heart to those who repent.

Once forgiveness of sins has been given, opening must be preached to those who are shut in. Who are these shut in, except those who, by devoted and watchful enclosure, close and fortify both sorts of senses, of heart and body, against the vanities of this world? They guard and close their eyes, ears, mouth, and every member, with God’s help, lest these become gates of death. To such persons who are shut in it is fitting that there be opened—that is, that there be given an opening for understanding and wisdom: understanding in reading, wisdom in divine sweetness and prayer. Although they cannot always close their senses, they are nevertheless shut off from outward things when in reading they are led to understand hidden things, and in prayer are rapt to taste heavenly things [Col. 0653A]. But exceedingly blessed also are those who, just as they shut themselves in inwardly, so also outwardly: those who have made themselves strangers to all the joys of this world and have resolved to persevere until death within the circuit of walls; for to such people the joyful and spacious entrance of the heavenly court will one day stand open.

After this opening there is consequently preached “the year acceptable to the Lord and the day of vengeance to our God.” They will be pleasing and acceptable to the Lord in their actions who were once abominable to the Lord through perverse living. And in them there will be a day of vengeance to our God when they pass from the darkness of heart into the day of light. Since they are children of light and of day, they make a day of vengeance for our God when, for any very small and slight transgressions, they rise up in vengeance against themselves and provoke themselves against themselves. And because they know that “no living person shall be justified in the sight of God” (Ps. 142:2), they do not know how to spare themselves for small transgressions any more than for great ones [Col. 0653B]. Such people ought to have a double mourning, of which he immediately adds:

“That I might console all who mourn, that I might give strength to those mourning in Zion.” By twice using “mourn” and “those mourning,” he shows that the mourning which every one of the elect ought to have in the present life must be twofold. “All who mourn” are those who, although their past sins have long since been blotted out before the Lord by prolonged repentance, are pierced as if they had never repented, with a certain fresh grief and mourning; and they are so pierced because in this mourning they grieve both for the past and for daily defilements, and because they have not only sinned but also omitted the good they ought to have done. Such persons are indeed consoled, because they merit to receive from God the consolation of forgiveness. For it is a great consolation to have this certainty: that after the mourning of repentance comes forgiveness of sins from God [Col. 0653C].

Although this mourning is good and necessary, there is yet another mourning, far sweeter, more excellent, and more worthy, which is possessed by those mourning in Zion. Those mourning in Zion are those who mourn for the glory and sweetness of eternal glory, for love of the heavenly homeland; whom the exile of the present life burdens; who would be released from the body of death and be with Christ; who delight in the dwelling-place of that heavenly Zion, the city of the living God, whose architect and builder is God. To such mourners the Lord gives strength, because from this blessed mourning they receive such strength that they become strong against the devil, against vices, and against the world, and prevail against these things.

Whomever of his elect the Lord has advanced in this order, after the good contest which he has fought, when he comes to pay the debt of the human condition, the Lord will truly fulfill in him what is promised here [Col. 0654A]:

“And I shall give them a crown instead of ashes, oil of joy instead of mourning, a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.” What is signified by ashes except ourselves, who are earth and ashes? The Lord will give a crown instead of ashes when, at the hour of death of any blessed soul, he himself deigns to come with his angels and makes known to the whole multitude of angels what that blessed soul, placed in its ashes—that is, in its frail body—has done. [Note: [Col. 0653D] That is, “will make known.”] He will say: “This and this my beloved, my bride, has done; she did what I commanded, avoided what I forbade, accomplished so many and such great labors in her ashes, and defeated in this and that manner the manifold snares of the devil. Therefore, according to the worthiness of my name, I shall give her a crown instead of ashes”—that is, in return for the works which she performed in the body of death and frailty, a crown of everlasting recompense [Col. 0654B].

This, I think, is how the words “I shall give a crown instead of ashes” may be understood. For it is no wonder that an angelic creature, burdened by no weight of bodily frailty, should thus stand with the Lord. But it is very wonderful that a human being, in his ashes—that is, in a mortal and frail body—offers to God all that he can. And because he does not neglect what he can do, by God’s command he will receive in place of ashes the unfading crown of glory.

“Oil of joy instead of mourning,” because for the mourning with which he now frequently grieves, with which he now sighs for heavenly things, when he reaches that place he will receive in eternal life greater glory and grace than he could have imagined or known how to desire while he remained in this life [Col. 0654C].

But we should note what he means by “oil of joy.” By oil, which is of such a nature that it floats above every liquid with which it is mixed, charity may be signified. Of this Paul says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31). By this more excellent way the elect will walk in eternal life, because, when faith has passed away and hope has failed—since all things are possessed in reality—they will burn forever with perfect charity, which will never fail there. There all the elect are now anointed in soul with the oil of gladness and exultation.

But in the general resurrection also, what they receive, as I judge, is not left unmentioned in the words: “A garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow” [Col. 0654D]. By the garment the body may be signified, in which the soul is clothed and veiled. Each person will receive this garment when, in the general resurrection, he has obtained the twofold robe, of body and soul. This body can then rightly be called a garment of praise, because what was laid aside mortal will be received immortal and incorruptible.
