And “instead of a spirit of sorrow” is aptly added, because the souls of the saints now have a certain sorrow because they lack their body, their fellow combatant and co-athlete, which is not a participant in joy though it was once a companion in suffering and sorrow.

They will also receive a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow [Col. 0655A], because those who now refuse to live loosely and carelessly but waste away in grief and sadness, when they have one day received their body, will be suffused with and made joyful by the gladness of a new gift. Then, when they have been admitted into the joys of perfect freedom and liberated from every changeability, what follows will be fulfilled in them:

“And in her they shall be called strong in righteousness.” In that city, in that heavenly Zion, they shall be called strong in righteousness, because no weakness of sin will cling to them any longer; but they are strong in righteousness, because they are righteous in word, righteous in deed, righteous in thought. But lest it be thought that anyone is crowned there by personal virtue, rather than by God’s singular gift, it is immediately added:

“The planting of the Lord, for glorification.” For all is the Lord’s planting: he plants everything good in the work, everything glorious in the recompense, and he is able to bring what he has planted to its increase [Col. 0655B]. And because all is the Lord’s planting, that planting will be for glorification. For the glorification of whom? Of Jesus Christ our Lord, whose name is praised and glorified for all and in all the good things which he has done and rendered to us through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY VII: FIRST HOMILY FOR THE HOLY NIGHT OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” (Ps. 97).

By these words we receive and greet the only-begotten Son of God, our God and Savior, who in this most holy night deigned to be born for the salvation of the human race from the [Col. 0655C] undefiled Virgin. For he, who from eternity orders all things and was begotten by the Father in his eternity before Lucifer, having become a participant in our mortality, willed in this sacred night to be born of a virgin Mother. Therefore this night overflows with such sweetness and is so full of every delight and grace that all faithful people on this night obtain the effect of their prayers, and obtain on this night [codex: “will obtain”] what they cannot obtain through the whole course of the year, and become possessors of their desire [codex: “become”] through the abundant blessing of the Son of God who is born.

The pages of both Testaments speak of the excellence of this most holy night. Thus also, in the Book of Judges, it is written concerning Gideon in the person of the Son of God: “Therefore [Col. 0655D] Gideon rose by night, and, having wrung out the fleece, filled a bowl with dew” (Judg. 6:38). Gideon is interpreted “going about in the womb”; by him the Son of God is signified, who by the circuit of his majesty embraces all things at once, heavenly and earthly, and yet, according to the substance of human nature, is enclosed in the Virgin’s womb. This Gideon rose by night, when in the night hours he came forth from the virginal chamber like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. Of this night the holy prophet, illumined by the prophetic Spirit, joyfully said to the Lord: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” (Isa. 21:11). As though he said: “O Son of God, who are the guardian of the human race, for our sake take the form of a human being; and in the silence of the night come forth from your mother’s womb for the salvation of your people; and again, having conquered [Col. 0656A] the dominion of death, rise triumphantly from the tomb at midnight.” “Having wrung out,” he says, “the 34 fleece, he had filled a bowl with dew.” In the fleece the assumed humanity of the Son of God is expressed, as David testifies in the Book of Psalms: “He shall descend like rain upon a fleece” (Ps. 71:6). When this fleece was wrung out—that is, when the holy humanity of the Son of God was displayed—he filled his bowl with dew. In the bowl is understood our Lady, Mary ever-Virgin, star of the sea; she was so filled by the dew of the Holy Spirit through him who was born from her that, full of grace and overflowing in her womb with mercy, she is always ready to assist all the needs and distresses of the wretched. For after God she is the one hope of the afflicted who invoke her with their whole heart in their miseries.

Again, concerning this birth the holy prophet declares: [Col. 0656B] “A stone shall cry out from the wall, and the timber which is between the joints of the buildings shall answer” (Hab. 2:11). This stone is our Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whom the Apostle says: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). This stone cried out from the wall when the Son of God, in the assumed humanity signified by the wall, was born of the Virgin and immediately began, like other infants, to cry out; by the very wailing of his infant limbs he showed that he had taken upon himself the toil and pain of the human race. The timber between the joints of the buildings answered this crying stone, because the blessed Virgin Mary answered her Son by kissing him, cherishing him, soothing him with every comfort and tenderness that she could offer. And the blessed Virgin Mary is fittingly [Col. 0656C] compared to the timber between the joints of the buildings, because she, our Lady ever-Virgin, in her Son, whom she brought forth with her womb closed for the salvation of the world, made peace and joined together those things which are in heaven and those which are on earth.

Some material appears to be lacking in the codex.

## 35 HOMILY VIII. FIRST HOMILY ON THE THREE MASSES ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

Although the benefits of almighty God, which according to the fullness of his grace he has bestowed upon the human race, are innumerable, there are nevertheless three principal reasons for which he ought especially to be loved, venerated, and praised by every person who is to be saved. First, because he is our Creator; second, because he is [Col. 0656D] Redeemer; third, because he will one day be Rewarder.

The order and dignity of these three reasons are rightly commended to us on this present day by the solemn proclamation of three Masses: one of which we celebrated in the depth of night, another at first morning, while darkness still remained in part, and the third solemnly in full daylight. The Mass “The Lord said,” celebrated in the nighttime, seems not unjustly suited to our Creator, because as long as we remain in the night of this present age, we are so enveloped in the darkness of ignorance that no one—even if perfect and holy, nor indeed any prophet, apostle, or evangelist—has been able by the penetrating gaze of the heart to comprehend how almighty God [Col. 0657A] created the whole world from nothing, or how he ordained and disposed each person’s origin. But we may refer to our Redeemer the Mass “Light shall shine,” which we celebrated before full light, because the elect and those who are to be saved know and confess that he saved us by his passion and death; whereas Jews and pagans, enveloped in the darkness of ignorance—and, grievous to say, even some who are called by the Christian name—refuse to believe and acknowledge it.

The third Mass, however, which is customarily celebrated festively in clear day with more excellent worship, looks to our Rewarder, 36 because when that day of eternity comes, in which he will reward the righteous with eternal recompense according to their merits and assign the reprobate to eternal damnation, [Col. 0657B] then, with all darkness of ignorance entirely removed, we shall clearly and openly know those things now hidden from our eyes. On that day of eternity, in which no darkness can be present, when all who have been redeemed by the Lord begin to appear in glory with the author of their redemption, there they will resound with the joyful delights of their redemption in these words, in a most solemn [codex: “just now”] and most joyous harmony of heaven: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6).

It belongs to a child to fear, but to a son to love. This is as though all the elect, who have then been received into true freedom and the glory of the children of God, should say to their Redeemer with humble thanksgiving: “O Lord, once sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, [Col. 0657C] we were once subject to you in servile fear; but now, servile fear having been set aside, we fear you with the holy filial fear that remains for ever and ever, because, having been freed from the dominion and fear of death, there will no longer be any struggle against flesh and blood, nor any further conflict with the prince of darkness.” And how whatever honor and glory, whatever reward and grace they rejoice to have received in the kingdom of blessedness, they ascribe not to their own merits but to the praise of their Redeemer, is rightly declared by the following words: “Whose dominion is upon his shoulder” (ibid.). As though they said: “While dwelling in the deep valley of miseries, through your fear we turned away from evil; through love, however, we were able to persist in good works; and now, raised from the dust of the earth, we are heirs and coheirs of your kingdom and [Col. 0657D] glory. These joys, I say, of such great blessedness were not obtained for us by the merits of our own action, but we were redeemed solely by the price of your life-giving blood; for you, the author of eternal salvation, bearing the gibbet of the cross upon the shoulders of your humility in order to redeem us, deigned to undergo the punishment of passion and death.”

“And his name shall be called the Angel of great counsel.” Our Lord Jesus Christ is rightly called the Angel of great counsel, because no patriarch or prophet could give the counsel which he gave in the days of his flesh. For to leave the world, love poverty, and devote oneself to chastity were impossible and unheard of before [Col. 0658A] the counsel of this great Angel. Of this counsel the Apostle Paul says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:24). Blessed, then, and glorious is the assembly of the elect, knowing itself saved by such counsel; calling the author of its salvation the Angel of great counsel, it will praise him for ever with humble thanksgiving.

Moreover, recalling with the watchful memory of the heart the great deeds of almighty God performed in them—how he, though Lord of all, emptied himself by taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death; how he offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross for their redemption; how also they escaped innumerable experiences of calamity solely by his mercy—[Col. 0658B] they will resound, as it were, with new harmonies concerning the state of their blessedness. This the following Verse fittingly announces: “Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done wonderful things” (Ps. 97:1). To this jubilation of new wonder and praise the Gradual rightly corresponds, which the very host of the elect, having passed from death to life, immediately takes up in one voice: “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God” (Isa. 52:10). Although by “ends of the earth” the limits of the world may be understood, we may also rightly understand the limits of our body. These limits will see the salvation of our God when all that is earthly and perishable which now hinders the bodies of the elect is wholly purged through the grace of the Mediator of God 38 and humankind. For as long as we dwell in this earthly habitation [Col. 0658C], we cannot be without the manifold misery of calamities. But when we come to that day of eternity, we shall receive complete and secure salvation in soul and body, because the salvation then given to the elect as their reward will be possessed without end and without any fear.

That illustrious and joyful Alleluia also agrees and corresponds with this most delightful day, which then the instruments of the saints will resound in heavenly melody: “A sanctified day has shone upon us; come, nations, and worship the Lord, because today a great light has descended upon the earth.” Truly it is a sanctified day, truly a day which the Lord has made, never to be ended by any alternation of night; there the host of the redeemed, bearing the twofold robe of immortality, [Col. 0658D] will rightly be able now to sing: “Because today a great light has descended upon the earth.” As though it said: “That inaccessible light in which the glorified souls hitherto rejoiced alone, without bodies, has now through the ineffable grace of our Rewarder descended and shines upon the earth; because not souls only, but also the earth of our body, will enjoy without end the eternal brightness of the countenance of God.”

The Offertory looks to this, which the same assembly of the elect will then be able most truly to sing: “The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world and its fullness; righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne” (Ps. 88:12–15). By the heavens souls may be understood, and by the earth the bodies of the saints. This is as though all the elect, now standing in full security, [Col. 0659A] should say to their Redeemer: “Placed in the exile of earthly habitation, we could by no means cling to you with steady constancy; but now, fully conformed to the body of your glory, in soul and body we shall cleave eternally to you, our Redeemer, without any hindrance of obstacle.” “Righteousness,” they say, “and judgment are the preparation of your throne.” By righteousness may be understood the rewarding of the righteous; by judgment, the condemnation of the reprobate; and by God’s throne, his repose. 39 Although no distress of unrest can come upon our Lord and Redeemer in himself, yet while his members—that is, all the elect—are carried about amid the various storms of this present age, he who is true repose in himself cannot possess complete tranquility of rest.

> [Note: [Col. 0659D] “Quod” in place of “qui” or “quae,” as elsewhere frequently.]

[Col. 0659B] Hence the Head cried from heaven to Saul the persecutor, who was attacking and scattering his members on earth: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). Likewise his chosen athlete, the first martyr Stephen, amid all the blows of those stoning him, saw not him sitting, but standing at the right hand of the power of God (Acts 7:56), whose assistance he felt amid such danger of conflict. Therefore righteousness and judgment become the preparation of God’s throne, because, when the people of the elect have been admitted to the stability of complete security, and the reprobate have also been cast with their head—that is, the ancient enemy—into eternal fire, the throne is in some manner prepared for the Lord: then, with all his members gathered to himself, he rests and rejoices without end. Thus, through the power of the Mediator of God and humankind, the head [Note: [Col. 0660D] That is, removed.] of all the wicked having been removed, [Col. 0659C] the elect, in a voice of praise and thanksgiving, extol and magnify the might of their Rewarder in these 40 words: “You have humbled the proud one as though wounded” (Ps. 88:11). “That impious king of pride,” they say, “who did not cease to attack and assail us, placed in the pit of calamity and misery, with countless deceits—you, Lord of hosts and King of glory, having slain him with the breath of your mouth, reduced him to nothing by the strength of your arm.”

Then, again exalting the joyful delights of their salvation, they sing in a voice of exultation what the following Communion declares: “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, that we may deserve to attain the joys of which [Col. 0659D] we speak, let us strive in the present life so to acknowledge our Creator with true thanksgiving, and to be devoted to our Redeemer with worthy praises, that when he one day appears in his glory, we may experience him not as a terrible Judge but as a gracious Rewarder. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY IX. SECOND HOMILY ON THE THREE MASSES ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

“A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, whose [Col. 0660A] dominion is upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called the Angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9).

Although many and varied meanings may be understood concerning these three Masses which we celebrate today, we may nevertheless more particularly apply them mystically to the praise of the Savior who was born: namely, so that in the first Mass we understand the hidden mystery of divinity; in the second, the mystery of assumed humanity; and in the third, the glory of eternal recompense.

And fittingly in the first Mass, which is sung in the deep night, is understood that invisible and inaccessible light of divinity, which no mortal could see or approach. For, as John says: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4:12). But that God the Father ineffably begot before the ages the Son born on this present day from a virgin Mother is plainly indicated by the Introit of the first Mass, which begins: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). Since that eternal divinity admits no times of change, having neither yesterday nor tomorrow, but always today and always remaining without beginning or time, God the Father rightly says to his Son: “Today I have begotten you.” Today, I say—that is, in eternity—God the Father begot the Son consubstantial with himself, as has been said. And the entire present office, in its order, looks to this ineffable generation. The Gradual also proclaims it: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints; from the womb before Lucifer I have begotten you” (Ps. 109:3). The Alleluia likewise [Col. 0660C] commends it: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today he has begotten you.” The Communion agrees in affirming and resounding: “In the splendors of the saints, from the womb before Lucifer I have begotten you.” Yet it speaks of the coeternal substance of the Son in such a way that the whole Trinity is simultaneously included in these words. For by “beginning” God the Father is understood; by “the day of power,” God the Son; and by “the splendors of the saints,” God the Holy Spirit. And we rightly believe that the Holy Spirit is signified in the splendors of the saints, because he is the light and illuminator of all the saints.

But how did God the Father beget a Son equal to himself? “From the womb,” he says, “before Lucifer.” “From the womb,” that is, from my invisible substance. “Before Lucifer,” [Col. 0660D] that is, before every visible creature, I have begotten you. But because the Son of God could not be seen in the substance of his divinity, for the sake of our salvation he became human and willed to be seen on earth and to converse with human beings. And therefore, just as from the beginning divinity alone was always praised by angels, so now humanity assumed together with divinity is praised and adored. And the Introit of the second Mass looks quite plainly to this generation of the assumed human being: “Light shall shine today upon us, because the Lord is born to us.”

It should be noted why it says, as though of the future, “Light shall shine upon us,” when it immediately adds, “the Lord is born to us.” This voice, as we suppose, is the voice [Col. 0661A] of all the elect awaiting the true light in darkness and the shadow of death; yet as soon as the Lord was born, the light of redemption had not yet shone upon them in hell. Hence this Mass too is not unfittingly sung at twilight, when neither complete night nor full light is seen, because, though the Savior Lord had been born, redemption had not yet been fully accomplished, the gate of the heavenly kingdom had not yet been opened, and many even of the elect—of whom John the Baptist was foremost—had descended to hell after the Savior’s birth, until, the dispensation of assumed flesh having been completed, the side of the crucified Redeemer was opened by the soldier’s lance.

But we, who today adore and worship that same Savior who was born, receiving him as it were in a voice of exultation, consequently sing in the Gradual: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117:26). But because the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation is exceedingly marvelous and ineffable—namely, how the eternal divinity was united in the womb of the Virgin Mother to human nature—we add the Verse of the Gradual in wonder, as if overcome with joy: “This has been done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes” (ibid., 23). It is indeed marvelous in our eyes, for no one can fully perceive or search out how that supreme majesty, as said before, assumed human nature.

But because we cannot comprehend so great a mystery with sense and intellect, let us strive also to magnify it with worthy [Note: [Col. 0661D] “Quoque” for “saltem,” “at least,” as elsewhere.] reverence of faith, singing [Col. 0661C] with joy of heart the delightful Alleluia which follows: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on beauty; the Lord has put on strength and girded himself with power” (Ps. 92:1). In these words we find briefly comprehended four sacraments of the divine dispensation: the Lord put on beauty in the incarnation; he put on strength in the passion; he girded himself with power in the resurrection and ascension. And how did he put on beauty in the incarnation? Because he deigned to put on an immaculate body from the immaculate Virgin Mary. He also put on strength in his passion, because by suffering and dying he overcame that strong man armed. But in the resurrection and ascension he girded himself with power in this way: rising from the dead, he girded with such power of his divinity the cloak of his flesh, which he laid aside for a time in dying, and exalted it with such glorification by ascending to the Father’s right hand, that, being to live for ever, he neither wills nor can ever again lay aside or put off that same flesh. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

The entire multitude of the elect will one day attain this blessedness of immortality, when after the end of the world it receives the glory of eternal recompense. This may not unfittingly, as we have said, be understood by the third Mass, “A child is born.” 43 Therefore this Mass too is customarily sung more solemnly not in the night nor at twilight, [Col. 0662A] but in clear and full daylight, because in the enduring glory of blessedness both eternal divinity and assumed humanity are revealed to the eyes of all the elect. Then the saints and elect celebrate this Mass together in festal solemnity; then, united with Christ in body and spirit, they joyfully cry with harmonious voice: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us.” Since a child is accustomed to fear his lord and master, but a son loves his father with filial love, what is to be understood by the child except fear, and by the son except love? Hence it is as though they said: “To us once laboring in the land of pilgrimage there was born a [child], that is, the spirit of the fear of the Lord; and a son was given to us, namely, love of divine sweetness then began to exist in us in some small measure. But now, [Col. 0662B] the child of fear removed, we possess without end in complete sweetness the son of love, whom we then received only in part; and him whom we then feared as Judge and Lord, we now love with filial love as Father and most gracious Rewarder.”

The souls of the elect do not yet possess this son of love fully; not even the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, can yet sing with full joy, “A son is given to us,” because he has not yet put on again his incorruptible body; rather, love and desire for the resurrection of his body still draw him back somewhat from the inner sweetness of divine love. But when, in the glory of the resurrection, Peter himself and the whole number of the elect have received their incorruptible bodies, they pass into God with such complete sweetness and such unchangeable love [Col. 0662C] that they can love, think, or desire nothing except him alone. Then too will be truly fulfilled in them what immediately follows:

“Whose dominion is upon his shoulder.” The dominion of the Lord their Creator alone will be over them; then they will not follow a strange lord, and no vice at all will prevail over or rule them. And what is meant by “upon the shoulder”? By the shoulder we rightly believe the labor of this present life to be signified. Therefore that most lofty dominion is rightly said to be upon the shoulder, 44 because then the dominion of the eternal King will be of such joy that this joy will surpass all their labor and every merit, and make them utterly forgetful of all pain and misery.

[Col. 0662D] “And his name shall be called the Angel of great counsel.” In the future the Lord will indeed rightly be called by his elect the Angel of great counsel. For although he commands all the faithful to turn away from evil and do good, he nevertheless willed to give two counsels of great perfection to those who desire to follow Christ perfectly: one, that by denying themselves they should leave behind the world and the things of the world; the other, that by living chastely they should preserve uninjured the integrity of heart and body. Therefore those who now comply with these two counsels, one day receiving for this the reward of eternal recompense, will with great exultation and worthy thanksgiving call his name the Angel of great counsel. For they will recognize that they accomplished the good which they did by the counsel of his goodness [Col. 0663A], and therefore will humbly attribute it not to themselves but to his name. Hence, as though urging one another to a new praise of the Savior, they will sing in wonder the Verse that follows, saying: “Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done wonderful things” (Ps. 97:1). It will appear to them supremely wonderful that earth and ashes have attained such glory that they feel no corruption at all, and behold their Savior without end with unveiled face, as the Gradual with its Verse consequently declares.

“All the ends of the earth,” it says, “have seen the salvation of our God” (Isa. 52:10). “Let all the earth cry out joyfully to God” (Ps. 65:1). “The Lord has made known his salvation; before the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. [Col. 0663B] 97:2). What is it to see the ends of the earth see God’s salvation, and for all the earth to rejoice? For all earthliness will one day receive its end in the elect, and all corruption will pass into incorruption; and then all the earth—that is, their body and soul—will see and praise God the Creator in jubilation. And in the sight of the nations, that is, of all those reigning with him, God the Father will make known his salvation, namely his Son, and will reveal his righteousness, namely the grace of the Holy Spirit.

45 Contemplating this glory of the supreme Trinity, they joyfully proclaim the Alleluia, saying: “A sanctified day has shone upon us.” There indeed will be an everlasting day and an everlasting sanctification, where no darkness of sins will intervene at all. There too they will sing the desirable [Col. 0663C] Offertory, offering their body and soul to God their Maker. “The heavens are yours,” they say, “namely our souls, and the earth is yours, that is, our bodies. We belong to you alone, O Lord who rules; we serve you alone in body and spirit with inseparable love. You founded the world of the earth, that is, the perfection of our earthly body; by your fear and love you strengthened us in good works, and now from you, our most gracious Rewarder, we have received the fullness of eternal recompense.” 46 “Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne” (Ps. 88:12–15). “Your throne, O Lord, is prepared in righteousness and judgment, because by your gift we have come to this righteousness: that we love you alone and cling to you alone, our God. Judgment, moreover, is that we now know how to judge and discern what we owe to you, our Creator and Redeemer. For while placed in the land of pilgrimage, we often reckoned what was yours to be ours, and from the things you worked in us we sought not your glory but our own. But now your throne is so prepared in us that you will always remain in us and we with you without end, and we shall glorify you with ineffable voice through infinite ages. Amen.”

## HOMILY X. THIRD HOMILY ON THE THREE MASSES ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

Because this most celebrated day is honored, as it were, by new proclamations of joy with the three solemnities of Masses, [Col. 0664A] this threefold celebration of Masses is not believed to lack mystery.

For by the first Mass, celebrated at cockcrow, as it were at the birth of the infant Jesus, may fittingly be understood the infancy of the human race regenerated in Christ, when someone born again of water and Spirit deserves to become a son of God. Such a person, rejoicing and exulting in the Holy Spirit, can truly sing a new song to the Lord, saying: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” When, thus reborn, he has passed the time of infancy as if in the darkness of ignorance, he will come to the second Mass, customarily celebrated at the dawning of day, when in the years of adolescence the light of knowledge and truth has arisen for him through the word of preaching. Then he can truly sing to the Lord in a voice of exultation, [Col. 0664B] saying: “Light shall shine today upon us.”

Thus reborn and enlightened, he will assuredly attain the glory of youthful age signified by the third Mass, which is to be celebrated in clear light. Since it is customarily celebrated above the others with a special proclamation of praise, it also signifies a special grace of divine fear and love, as we can recognize from the plain indication of the words in the Introit beginning the Mass: “A child,” it says, “is born to us.” Since it is the practice of a child, still being nurtured under discipline, to fear the severity of lord and master, the fear of the Lord is fittingly understood by this noble child who is born in the heart of one thus reborn and enlightened. He is rightly said to be born, because fear arises from the natural concern of the human heart; [Col. 0664C] for it is natural for a human being to fear the day and hour of final judgment, to fear the worm that does not die and the unquenchable fire of the infernal conflagration. Such fear often draws the human mind back from committing evils and, as a kind of beginning of salvation, leads it toward obtaining higher and more sublime things. Hence follows:

“And a Son is given to us.” Since it belongs to sons not to fear but to love, who is this noble and lovable son except the inward love [Col. 0664D] of divine sweetness? Therefore this great and such a son is rightly said to be given, not born, to us, because, as was said above, fear is born from the natural consciousness of guilt incurred, whereas love of heavenly wisdom is poured down from above into the faithful soul. Hence the blessed Apostle James says: “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). Truly the sweetest love of Christ is the best gift and perfect gift. For it makes those whom it has filled with the ineffable grace of its visitation likewise good and perfect; and so it comes about that those who earlier could scarcely turn away from evil under compulsion of fear now sweetly burn with fervent love for doing good. Hence follows:

“Whose dominion is upon his shoulder.” What is to be understood by the shoulder except bodily labor in good works—every exercise, I say, of bodily labor? For in the sight of God a few things which affectionate devotion, moved by pious love, offers [Col. 0665A] with cheerfulness of heart are of greater worth than can be a manifold activity of the outward person undertaken solely with fear in view.

We have now briefly run through the dignity of this most noble Son. Let us now hear his great and glorious name. “And his name,” he says, “shall be called the Angel of great counsel.” For angel in Latin means “messenger.” One who has deserved to hear the inwardly speaking voice of heavenly love may rightly be called Angel of great counsel, not only by himself but also by others. For what he declares by the word of exhortation, he takes the utmost care to fulfill by the effect of his work. He may also be called Angel of great counsel who strives to obey not only the Lord’s commands but also his higher counsels. The rest appears to be lacking.

## HOMILY XI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT STEPHEN, PROTOMARTYR

[Col. 0665B]

Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews and to the chief priests: “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes” (Matt. 23).

Just as there is one generation of the upright and those who are to be saved, which will be eternally crowned with its head, namely Christ, so there is one generation of the reprobate and unbelieving, which will be condemned forever with its head, that is, the devil. Blessed indeed is the person found in the generation of the righteous, because he will receive not only a reward for the good things he himself has done, but will also share in all the blessedness which all the saints and elect are to receive for their labors. He sees the ineffable glory which the blessed Mother of God [Col. 0665C] Mary merited by her chastity and humility; he also sees the delight and joy which Peter, prince of the apostles, obtained when glorified by the martyrdom of the cross, and thus will rejoice in his glorification as though it were his own:

> [Note: [Col. 0665D] That is, his.]

He also sees the crown with which Stephen the first martyr, whose feast we celebrate today, triumphs crowned; and he rejoices and exults as though he himself had been crowned with that same crown. And because he has deserved to be a member of him who is the head and crown of all the blessed, he will share a common joy with all the blessed. Conversely, whoever has become a member of him who is the head of all the wicked will undoubtedly suffer everlasting punishment with all who are to be condemned; and he will endure eternal punishment not only for the evils which he himself [Col. 0665D] committed, but also whatever torments, punishments, and miseries Herod, Pilate, Decius, and those like them have earned by their tyranny—he will suffer these with them without end. Hence our Lord and Savior in this 49 Gospel reading indicates the evils which the generation of the reprobate will one day receive by the just sentence of condemnation:

Jesus, he says, was speaking to the crowds of the Jews and to the chief priests: “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city.” The Jews or chief priests to whom the Savior spoke these words in person, and who persecuted the same Savior unto death, inflicted the evils mentioned here upon the preachers of truth sent to them. For by killing they put some of them to death; they destroyed others by crucifying them; they inflicted most severe scourges upon others in their synagogues; and they drove many of them from their own city into the cities of the Gentiles. Therefore, under the name of these Jews or chief priests, the whole generation of the reprobate is represented: that generation which will be condemned with its prince, the devil, at the end of the age by a just judgment; which now kills and crucifies the prophets, wise men, and scribes—that is, the teachers of truth—sent to it, when by living wickedly it does not fear to kill in itself the word of life which it has heard from them. Furthermore, [Col. 0666B] it does not cease to scourge them in its synagogues—that is, with innumerable contaminations of vices—and to persecute them from city to city, while, adding sins to sins as scourges to scourges, it drives away the word of holy preaching from the city of its heart by neglecting and rejecting it. But with what vengeance of punishment visitation will come upon this generation, which thus kills and crucifies, scourges and persecutes, he indicates by plain reasoning in what follows:

“...that every righteous blood may come upon you, which has been shed upon the earth.” By righteous blood we may fittingly understand the whole tribulation of the righteous; by the earth, their earthly bodies—those who rejoiced and desired that the earth of their body should be afflicted and crushed for Jesus’ name through many tribulations and pressures [Col. 0666C]. But all this blood—that is, all the tribulation of the righteous—shall come in the wrath of vengeance not only upon those by whom they suffered, but also upon the entire generation of the wicked, which, as was said above, has deserved to be one body with its father.

**50.** “From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar.”

We believe that righteous Abel is fittingly placed first in the order of the righteous, since Scripture testifies that his was the first voice of blood to cry from the earth to the Lord (Gen. 4:10). Therefore, through Abel, whose name is interpreted “mourning,” we should not unfittingly understand that first people of the fathers who went before, who, longing for the Saviour’s coming through a long desire, descended mournfully to hell after the end of life [Col. 0666D]. After him, in a quite fitting order, Zechariah is placed; his name is interpreted “one mindful of the Lord.” Through him the people of the New Testament and the new grace are signified: they celebrate each mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and attend it with the remembrance of devout devotion. He is rightly called the son of Barachiah, a name rendered in our language as “Blessed of the Lord.” This name, certainly, is to be ascribed to the Son of God alone, who will come blessed in the name of the Lord at the end of the world, in order to join to himself in the kingdom of glory those blessed by his Father.

Again, in another mystical sense we may understand what, from the beginning of the Gospel reading, we have briefly expounded allegorically [Col. 0667A]. Jesus said to the crowds of Jews and to the chief priests: “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes.” By the crowds of Jews and the chief priests we may understand two orders in the Church, namely the spiritual and the secular. By the crowds of Jews, all secular persons may fittingly be understood: they are entangled and involved in the cares and disturbances of this present age, yet are Jews—that is, confessors—because they desire to please God through the confession of the true faith, and from the outward goods alone which they possess they serve God the Creator in his members. To them the Lord will say in the judgment: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). By the chief priests, moreover, spiritual persons may rightly be understood [Col. 0667B]: like good rulers, they strive to rule over vices and carnal desires, and, as true priests, offer themselves to God through the fire of compunction. To these crowds and chief priests the Lord promises that he will send prophets, wise men, and scribes.

For prophets are those who proclaim the joys of future blessedness not merely by the knowledge of words which they learned outwardly through another person, **51** but also teach and preach the word of truth from the abundance of the sweetness which they have deserved to taste inwardly. Such persons may deservedly be called wise men and scribes as well. For what they apprehend inwardly in the sweetness of the most intimate savour, they set forth before the eyes of their subjects, as it were in a living lesson, by worthy conduct and useful preaching [Col. 0667C]. Yet although they are such prophets, such wise men, and such scribes, the Lord sometimes permits them to be killed, crucified, and scourged by the aforesaid crowds of Jews and chief priests. Hence the following words are added:

“And some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues.” When ungrateful hearers, through perversity of morals and deeds, oppose the saving exhortation of teachers, they in some manner kill those teachers by an invisible killing. For the word of God, which is living and effective (Heb. 4:12) in the hearts of the elect, seems as though killed and dead in the hearts of the reprobate, since they refuse, through the word of life which they hear, to repent of dead works. There are also others [Col. 0667D] whose life and conduct are so perverse and evil that they seem a harsh crucifixion to those same preachers. For just as one fastened to a cross remains almost motionless, so ungrateful and unworthy hearers, as their sins demand, make the teacher’s tongue cling, as though motionless, to his palate when they oppose the word of holy exhortation in will and deed.

There are also some who do not fear to scourge them with the lash of detraction and hatred in their synagogues—that is, in the gatherings of slanderers assembled together. For they judge that such men ought rightly to be despised as reprobate and irreligious, since, setting aside the opinions of the ancient Fathers, they set forth not the teaching of sound faith but false doctrines of their own invention. Thus, scourged by wicked lips, they do not cease to persecute them [Col. 0668A] from city to city—that is, from one opinion to another. For, as though they were unlearned and foolish, they put various opinions before them to explain, with silent mockery. But after they have inflicted so many insults upon them, the words that follow clearly show how great evils will come upon those who kill, crucify, scourge, and persecute them.

“...that every righteous blood may come upon you, which has been shed upon the earth.” **52** By righteous blood we may understand spiritual understanding, or the inward contrition of the heart, or the sweetness of contemplation. Righteous blood is wrongly shed upon the earth when spiritual understanding is disclosed in preaching to those who savour only earthly things. Again [Col. 0668B], righteous blood is uselessly shed upon the earth when the earth of the human body is not humbled through contrition of heart. Again, righteous blood is shed upon the earth without fruit when, because of earthly joys, contemplative sweetness is withdrawn from the inner person. Hence it follows:

“From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar.” By the blood of righteous Abel, whose name is interpreted “mourning,” the mourning or contrition of the penitent soul is signified. Those who despise to hear, for the advancement of their salvation, the saving instruction of prophets, wise men, and scribes certainly do not know how to possess or taste it. By the blood of Zechariah, whose name in Latin means “mindful of the Lord,” the grace of contemplative sweetness is mystically prefigured [Col. 0668C]. It is taken from the mind so completely that it cannot even be recalled to memory, because that same Zechariah seems to have been killed between the temple and the altar.

By the temple and altar we may understand the ears of the twofold human being, or the twofold substance of body and soul. Between this temple and altar this spiritual Zechariah is in some manner killed when the memory of God’s word dies fruitlessly in the hearer’s mind. For although the sound of the words reaches the outward ears of the body, it cannot usefully and fruitfully reach and penetrate the inward ears of the heart. Thus it comes about that a person cannot possess the paternal blessing, which the father of that same Zechariah, Barachiah—that is, “Blessed of the Lord”—signifies by his name [Col. 0668D]. For where the memory of God’s word is taken from the human heart, there can be no doubt that the person will be deprived of the blessing of God the Father. Hence it follows:

“Amen, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation.” No other generation but this same generation of the reprobate may be understood here: upon it, as we said above, a just condemnation for sins will come on the day of judgment. Yet the merciful Creator of all things, desiring to call this same generation back to the way of salvation, exhorts it with these words:

**53.** “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you.” What he formerly prefigured by the temple and altar, namely body and soul, he here repeats as an admonition by repeating the name Jerusalem. For whoever desires to attain the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 0669A], to the vision of eternal peace, must strive to keep soul and body unstained for God and beware of killing or stoning the messengers of peace sent to him. We have mentioned above what the killing of prophets is. Let us now consider the stoning of those sent to us.

The stones with which we stone those sent to us are thoughts which accuse us inwardly—thoughts divinely inspired, warning and reproving us for the killing of prophets. But the depraved and perverse mind often stones these same thoughts, because it hardens itself, resisting strongly like stones lest it be softened to repentance. Yet the most gracious Creator does not disdain still to soften this same hardness; and he recalls and brings back to human remembrance, in these words [Col. 0669B], what he has done and endured for humankind:

“How often,” he says, “have I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” The words of this Gospel reading agree with the words of the Prophet—or rather, of the Lord speaking through the prophet: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2). Seeing these same children turned away and alienated from him, he imitated the nature of this small bird in order to call them back beneath the wings of his mercy. Its nature quite plainly indicates that the almighty Majesty did not compare himself with this bird without reason.

For it is the hen’s natural habit, through a special providence, to love and defend her chicks. Whenever she seeks to gather and summon them beneath the covering of her wings [Col. 0669C], the greatness of her love seems to alter her voice. If anyone wishes to snatch or harm them, she resists, striking back as much as she can with wings, beak, and claws, so that she exposes herself to the danger of death before she abandons their defence.

Therefore the nature of such a bird fittingly corresponds to the same Redeemer, who willed to compare himself, **54** so great and so immeasurable, to so tiny a thing. For when the Lord came in the flesh, he changed the voice of that stern sentence which he had formerly pronounced in his Law against sinners: “Whoever does this or that shall surely die.” But to his children, whom he foreknew and predestined to be gathered into the kingdom of his glory [Col. 0669D], he promised the kingdom of heaven if they were willing to repent and turn back, however unjustly they had lived and however wickedly they had acted: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2).

He also changed the voice of his omnipotence in the struggle of his passion, when he said in sorrow, not for himself but for us: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” What sorrow could have been in him for his own sake, since, as he himself says, “the ruler of this world finds nothing in me” (John 14:30)? For he willed to be sorrowful and distressed for us, in order to rescue us from the sorrow of eternal death and make us companions of eternal joys. Therefore, overcome as it were by maternal love, he offered himself to God the Father on the altar of the cross to redeem these same children; he underwent a hard and exceedingly mighty battle with death [Col. 0670A] and with the devil, the prince of death. Afterwards, returning to the Father as a glorious victor, he mercifully gathers and receives beneath the wings of his mercy those who flee to him.

There he frequently changes his voice, speaking now through prosperity, now through adversity, now through fear, now through love, to every faithful soul. Through the tongue of compunction he invisibly admonishes and instructs it how it ought to fear and love him. Therefore he warns and exhorts it to strive to gather its children—that is, its perceptions and thoughts—into one, beneath the wings of his protection, to meditate and think on the things of God, and not to allow them to wander everywhere after vain and unlawful things. But whoever despises to hear his voice and refuses to flee beneath the wings of his mercy will without doubt deserve to hear what is terrifyingly added next [Col. 0670B]:

“Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” This house—this house, I say—is that of body and soul. It is then left desolate and deprived of every good when he who created and made it does not deign to dwell in it; when the eye of the mind is darkened by such great shadows of sins that it cannot discern even the slightest ray of divine brightness. As follows:

“You will see me no more until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” So long as wretched humanity is enveloped in the darkness of vices and does not know or recognize its own darkness, it cannot see the true light, which is Christ. But when it returns to itself within itself [Col. 0670C], and begins to recognize, whether by inward inspiration or by the admonition of some teacher, in what great darkness and miseries it stands; and when it takes care to purify and cleanse the eyes of its heart through worthy repentance, then, by God’s mercy, it will receive again the light of truth which it had lost. Receiving with a voice of exultation him who returns to it—the one whom the negligent and proud soul had formerly rejected from itself and had despised to hear—it will cry: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

While he remains in us, we shall be able worthily to praise him in the present; and when he comes in the glory of the Father, we shall safely see him face to face in the future. May he deign to grant this—he from whom are all things and through whom are all things, who lives and reigns unto the endless ages of ages [Col. 0670D]. Amen.

## HOMILY XII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST JOHN THE EVANGELIST

Jesus said to Peter: “Follow me” (John 21).

Blessed John, the apostle and outstanding evangelist, begins his Gospel—“In the beginning was the Word”—with such height and depth that he seems in understanding to fly above the heavens and heavenly things. He is therefore fittingly compared, in the figure of the four living creatures, to a soaring eagle. Since he began his Gospel with such subtlety, we must believe that he concluded and determined it in today’s reading from the holy Gospel with no less depth and excellence of mystery. We would like to say something about today’s reading from the holy Gospel, yet nothing can be said worthily [Col. 0671A]. Nevertheless, let us say what we can, and as much as God may deign to grant.

In these two disciples, Peter and John, two lives may be signified: the active and the contemplative—active in Peter, contemplative in John. No one can rise to these two lives or perfectly comprehend them unless the customary and blessed “saying” of our Lord Jesus Christ comes first. God’s saying is his doing. It is his work; whatever progress each of his elect makes in this life through the praiseworthy exercise of virtues proceeds from his grace and gift.

And what does he say to his Peter—that is, to each of his elect? “Follow me.” That person follows the Lord who, through the zeal of good action, imitates the Lord according to his ability. After that health-giving saying, after this praiseworthy following, the words added are fitting [Col. 0671B]:

**56.** “Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following, who also reclined at supper upon his breast and said: ‘Lord, who is it that will betray you?’” Peter turns when each elect person is raised up by good works. But one who has turned and been fully proved in the active life advances to higher things, when from the condition of good conduct he comes to the height of divine contemplation. This is to see the other disciple whom Jesus loved following. That height of contemplation is received only at supper, where one reclines upon Jesus’ breast.

In the breast is the human heart; in the heart is wisdom. For one is imbued with and illumined by true wisdom when one deserves to receive something of the divine savour at the Lord’s supper [Col. 0671C]. But what and of what kind is this supper? Certainly, a sweet supper, abounding with rich dishes: that supper, I say, when God comes to the human heart and the human heart is illumined, and is either touched and pierced by fear of sins, or kindled and inflamed by love of God and eternal longings. Whether this supper is made ready through fear or through love of God, it is proved truly to be the Lord’s banquet, by which he himself is refreshed and delighted, because our salvation is indeed his food and nourishment.

At this supper a person reclines when one truly recognizes oneself in humility. And in this knowledge one can faithfully and intimately commend oneself and all that one has to God with the whole heart.

**57.** In this blessed reclining one often uses these words, saying to the Lord: “Lord, who is it that will betray you?” This is the same as saying: “Lord, who dwell in the human heart, show me myself, that I may know where, how, and how often I have betrayed you to the Jews—that is, to malignant spirits. For in every evil work, unjust thought, and useless word by which I have sinned before you, I betrayed you, who ought to have been the indweller of my heart. And because I have thus betrayed you, preserve me in the future through the repentance laid upon me for the past, so that there may be no longer in me anything that betrays you.”

It follows:

“When Peter had seen him, therefore, he said to Jesus: ‘But, Lord, what of this man?’” What is it for Peter to see this disciple, except for the one and same person who is represented by Peter to possess the spirit of divine contemplation [Col. 0672A]? When he has seen it—that is, when he has tasted beforehand what the savour of inward sweetness is like—he anxiously and sorrowfully asks within himself, because he does not yet hold in reality what he nevertheless holds in hope: “But, Lord, what of this man?”

By these words two things are indicated: the affection and the effect of contemplation. In “this,” the demonstrative word, may be understood what a person presently tastes and sees by affection; in “what,” what one cannot yet comprehend or see by effect. For one sometimes tastes something of God and sometimes does not; one is partly illumined and partly touched by blindness. Why is this—that one tastes something and does not taste something, sees something partly and partly does not see? It is, surely, because the disjunctive conjunction *autem* (“but”), placed between *hic* (“this”) and *quid* (“what”), delays this and obstructs it, as though by a certain impediment [Col. 0672B].

And what is that disjunctive conjunction? It is, of course, the body, which corrupts and weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15), always pressing the spirit that tends upward downwards. For as long as we exist in this mortal body, we are partly joined to God and partly separated from him; and we cannot see God fully as we would wish. Since the contemplative person is always grieved by this adversative conjunction, let that person hear what the Lord said to Peter:

“If I wish him to remain thus until I come, what is that to you? Follow me.” It is as though the Lord consoles each of his elect and says: “If I will it to be thus—that I partly reveal and partly conceal the light of my brightness in the present—then this alone remains for you: follow me; that is, walk humbly in my footsteps according to what is in you. For when you lay aside this corruptible thing and receive incorruption, you will attain the ‘what’ in full.”

That the person ought to serve the progress of others is indicated by the words that follow:

“So this saying went out among the brethren that this disciple does not die.” This saying is the saying of contemplation. It goes out among the brethren—among those, that is, who preserve brotherly love—when it reaches the progress and benefit of many. When this saying goes out, that disciple—that is, the savour of contemplation—does not die. What does “does not die” mean? What dies perishes and becomes fruitless. Thus, yes, this disciple would die and in some manner perish if he did not go out for the edification of others [Col. 0672C–D]. For God works this gift of contemplation in no person merely so that it may benefit that person inwardly alone, but so that it may benefit others outwardly.

But why does this disciple not die? Although the letter does not agree, the evangelist indicates it in hidden words. He did not say that Jesus said, “He does not die,” but: “If I wish him to remain thus until I come, what is that to you?” Jesus—that is, our Saviour—whose saying is doing, wills that the good which he works in the heart of a contemplative person should not die: that is, should not profit and work merely for the person in whom he works it, but should go out through that person for the benefit and fruit of others.

“But if I wish him to remain thus until I come, what is that to you?” My will, I say, is that my Spirit, which I have given you, remain in you; and that, remaining in you, it should not die, but go out and bear fruit. And let it go out from your heart until I come to you through *what*—that is, through the taste of my sweetness—to you, whoever you are who bear Peter’s form, and through you to those who have not yet deserved to receive this gift [Col. 0673A]. Or: I will it to remain thus, so that you may never fully attain the *what* until you receive an incorruptible body; for when you receive the immortal body, you will fully attain and perfectly comprehend that which is now “what” to you.

**59.** Therefore, whoever proceeds, as we have said, in both the active and contemplative life in this order, may rightly be described by the words that follow: “This is that disciple who bears testimony concerning these things and wrote these things; and we know that his testimony is true.” For anyone whom God the Father has thus illumined, as you have heard, and invisibly taught something of his secrets, knows how to bear faithful testimony of what he has learned. And whatever such a person attests by teaching and writing, there is no doubt that his testimony is true [Col. 0673B].

Therefore, beloved brethren, since we have not yet been able to please the Lord our God in the active or contemplative life, let us strive that we may still deserve to be ennobled through our actions, manner of life, and conduct; so that we may be made worthy to receive this disciple—that is, the spirit of divine knowledge and adoption—and attain the full *what*, namely full joy, through the true and only Son of God, who lives and reigns unto endless ages of ages [Col. 0673C]. Amen.

## HOMILY XIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE LORD’S CIRCUMCISION

“After eight days were completed, so that the child might be circumcised, his name was called Jesus” (Luke 2).

The order of the words should be observed. The evangelist says: “After eight days were completed, so that the child might be circumcised,” although the eight days had not yet been completed at all: rather, when seven days had been completed, the child Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day. Thus the holy evangelist noted here not only the circumcision of Jesus Christ visibly performed, but also, beholding with the eyes of the heart the circumcision which would at some time be accomplished in Christ’s body—that is, in his elect—expressed and prefigured it figuratively [Col. 0673D].

The seven days are those through which this present world revolves; in them everyone who is to be saved must be circumcised from sins. But the eighth day is the day of resurrection. When it has been accomplished, the elect will be circumcised from every misery of soul and body. In this time of mortality, they strive, as far as they can with God’s gift, to circumcise themselves from sins and vices by repentance. Yet no one, however holy or perfect, can be circumcised entirely from misery as long as one remains in a corruptible body. But when eight days are completed—after the general resurrection has taken place—when “this corruptible has put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:53), then the saints and elect will be truly and perfectly circumcised from every misery, which will never afterward approach them [Col. 0674A], neither in body nor in soul.

And it is well said, “when the child was circumcised.” By the child we should rightly understand the Christian people, who may fittingly be called a child because of the purity of faith by which they believe in God and through which they will be saved. Therefore, when this child, after the glory of the resurrection, is circumcised from every misery, as we have said, then what the evangelist adds will truly be fulfilled: “his name was called Jesus.” A name is given to a person so that one who was unknown may be known by the name.

This name Jesus, which means “Saviour” or “Saving,” seems well suited to that child—that is, to the Christian people—because after the resurrection has been accomplished they will receive full and perfect salvation in soul and body [Col. 0674B]. No one placed in this mortal flesh, however holy or justly one may have lived, can deserve to obtain it fully. For in the misery of this fragile life no one can attain the joys of perfect salvation. One who rejoices today in bodily health may perhaps tomorrow grieve, overtaken by sudden afflictions. Likewise, one who today glories and rejoices in the salvation of the soul may perhaps tomorrow groan and sorrow grievously and miserably that one has sinned.

But when the day of universal judgment has been accomplished and this child, namely the Christian people, has been perfectly circumcised from every misery of body and soul, then his name will rightly be called Jesus, because then he begins fully to know and experience what the good of true salvation is and of what kind it is. But lest anyone believe that one can attain this salvation through one’s own merits, the evangelist declares in the following words:

**61.** “Which,” he says, “was called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.” To say “was called” is the same as to say “was predestined.” Whoever has not been called and predestined by God, his Saviour, cannot at all attain this saving name. Therefore every person to be saved must know and consider in profound humility of heart that one can never arrive at true and eternal salvation through one’s own merits or the power of one’s good works. Rather, one was predestined to it by God before one was conceived in the womb of one’s fleshly mother or reborn in the womb of one’s spiritual mother, which is the Church [Col. 0674C].

Perhaps someone says in silent thought: “If no one will be saved except one predestined by God, why do I labour? Why afflict myself? Why should I not enjoy the joys and pleasures of this world? If I am predestined to life, I shall be saved; but if I am not predestined, I cannot be saved.” These are not the words of a wise person, but of one who presumptuously wishes to investigate God’s predestination. It is as though, in pride, one says: “Lord, if you wish, I can be saved; but if you do not wish, how shall I be saved?”

Whoever does not fear to entangle and occupy oneself with such utterly useless thoughts is altogether ungrateful and opposed to divine grace and mercy. On the contrary, for any person blessedly tending toward true salvation and desiring to place one’s hope in the Lord God, such vain and useless phantasms of thoughts ought to be wholly foreign and alien. One must not presume boldly to investigate or search out God’s predestination and the deep abyss of his judgments, which one cannot comprehend. Rather, one should devoutly and humbly subject one’s body and soul and all the faculties of the twofold human being to the service of him from whom one received them; one should strive vigorously to exercise oneself in every action pleasing to God; one should subject and bring one’s flesh under labours, as far as human frailty allows. And when one has done every good thing that one can in soul and body with God’s help, one ought to commit oneself to divine grace and, in humble conscience, pray to the inward judge [manuscript: *arbitri*, “judge”] that he may make one’s service and all one’s labours acceptable to himself, and in his freely bestowed mercy deign to number one among his predestined [Col. 0675A–B].

**62.** Although, as we have said, the hidden counsel of divine predestination is wholly unknown and concealed from human knowledge, we can conjecture a little as to who are predestined to life from the words of the blessed Apostle Paul: “Those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30). The two words placed in the middle—“called” and “justified”—show us to whom the first and last words, “predestined” and “glorified,” refer. For predestination and glorification concern those in whom calling and justification take place [Col. 0675C]. Those whom God deigns, through the prevenient grace of his mercy, to call from the vanity of this world to conversion and to justify by good conduct, we surely believe to be those whom by his wonderful dispensation he has predestined to be one day glorified with eternal glory.

Thus upon those eternally predestined, mercifully called and justified, and to be eternally glorified in the future, this saving name Jesus will be bestowed, as we have said. For not without the reason of a definite mystery did the evangelist call our Redeemer simply Jesus, while the prophet Isaiah mystically designated him by six names, saying: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6). The evangelist, as we may believe, foreseeing what would someday take place in the body of Jesus Christ—that is, in his Churches—figuratively called him Jesus alone. But the prophet, beholding with the spiritual gaze of his heart what was to be fulfilled in Christ’s person alone, called him by the six names mentioned above. For he was Wonderful in his incarnation, Counsellor in his preaching, God in the working of miracles, Mighty in dying, Father of the age to come in rising again, and will be Prince of Peace in rewarding [Col. 0675D].

He was Wonderful, I say, in his incarnation because he willed to work the mystery of his incarnation so wonderfully that no human being, however just or holy, however resplendent with any fullness of knowledge, could or can comprehend in one’s own thought or understanding how God became man and joined and united divine and human nature together in one person [Col. 0676A]. John the Baptist also, the friend of the Bridegroom, whom the Saviour himself testifies that none greater has arisen among those born of women, said as he beheld the wonderful mystery of his incarnation: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Luke 3:16). The strap of his sandal is the union of his divine and human natures. The elect friend of the Bridegroom says that he is not worthy to loosen—that is, to search out or know by the subtlety of his understanding—this wonderful and unsearchable union of divine and human nature.

He was also Wonderful in the incarnation because, conceived of the Holy Spirit, he was born without sin from a Virgin Mother and alone among sinners lived without sin.

He who was thus Wonderful in the incarnation was Counsellor by giving human beings the counsels of new salvation. For he gave counsels such as had previously been unheard and unknown in the world. Thus we read in one place in the Gospel that when a certain young man came to our same Saviour and asked him what he should do to possess eternal life, he said to him: “Keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17). When the man asked which commandments they were, he set before him the ten precepts of the Law. And when he said, “I have kept all these from my youth,” Jesus said to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, come and follow me, and you will have eternal life” (ibid., vv. 20–21) [Col. 0676B–C]. This, I say, is the new and unheard counsel, beneficially delivered by the Redeemer and most gracious lover of humankind: that a person, embracing voluntary poverty and devoutly following poor Christ, should possess nothing in this world, but cast away and despise absolutely everything in hope of the heavenly country.

In this manner, therefore, the mediator of God and human beings, Counsellor in preaching, is fittingly called God in performing miracles. For he worked wonders not as a prophet by praying, but as God by commanding. Elijah, Elisha, and many other prophets performed many miracles and even raised the dead; but to be able to do these things, they obtained them through prayers before God. Our Saviour alone, however, acted as God. By the power of his majesty alone he performed miracles; by his word alone he raised the dead, as when he said powerfully to Lazarus, dead four days: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43) [Col. 0676D]. And elsewhere: “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke 7:14). He also restored the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue to life by command alone (Mark 5:41).

Thus he who was God in performing miracles was surely Mighty in dying. For it was a virtue of great strength that he, who knew better and more perfectly than any mortal could know the pain and bitterness of death, did not refuse to taste and experience that same bitterness in himself. Rather, for the sake of our salvation, he willingly and unafraid underwent the cruel and dreadful death of the cross [Col. 0677A].

For he who, girded with such wondrous strength, was mighty in dying, triumphing over death and the prince of death, became the Father of the world to come by rising again. For, rising from the dead, he became the Father of all whom he predestined to become co-heirs of his paternal inheritance; by his resurrection he gave all his children hope of future glorification and immortality. And just as he himself, after his resurrection, having become immortal and incapable of suffering, appeared to whom he wished, was wherever he wished, and entered in to his disciples when the doors were shut, so in the world to come he will enrich and glorify all the elect with the eternal reward of blessed immortality and incorruption, so that wherever the spirit wishes to be, [Col. 0677B] there the body will immediately be also.

And he who thus became the Father of the world to come in the resurrection will be Prince of Peace in recompense. For when the eight days mentioned above have been completed, and the child Jesus—that is, the Christian people—has been exalted by the grace of eternal salvation and circumcised from every misery of body and soul, then our Redeemer will truly be Prince of Peace. For he will establish and strengthen his elect in so firm and stable a peace that the spirits and souls of the righteous will desire, seek, and love nothing but God alone; nor will the flesh any longer lust in opposition to the spirit. Rather, enjoying the tranquil calm of perpetual peace in the towers of the heavenly Jerusalem, and seeing face to face the Prince of Peace—their rewarder, I mean, and bestower of this peace—they will glory with him without end and delight and rejoice without weariness in his praise. May he himself bring us to this peace: Jesus Christ our Lord, who is true peace and who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

65 HOMILY XIV. FIRST HOMILY ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD.

“When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea, in the days of King Herod” (Matt. II).

Our Lord and Saviour, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who came into the world in order to destroy the kingdom of sin, is clearly described by the Evangelist as being still born in the hearts of the elect, whom he has ordained to become co-heirs of his kingdom:

“When Jesus,” he says, “had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea, in the days of King Herod.” These glorious and blessed Magi, who in royal magnificence rendered service to the newborn heavenly King, were the first-fruits of the Gentiles; and thus they fittingly represent those who once lived in the manner of the Gentiles, without God in the world, but, enlightened by the brightness of heavenly grace, came to the true knowledge of their Creator. But this Herod, in whose days Christ Jesus was born, represents the unique author of sin, namely the ancient enemy. The days in which he is said to reign may rightly be understood as the whole period of this mortal life, in which that wicked king is permitted to reign by tempting the elect—yet thereby making them more approved—[Col. 0678A] while by the goads of temptations he draws and deceives the reprobate into the abyss of eternal damnation. Nevertheless, in these days of this wicked tyrant Jesus is sometimes born in the hearts of his elect: namely, in that holy congregation in which there is truly fulfilled what the mystical name of Bethlehem and Juda signifies. For Bethlehem means “house of bread,” while Juda means “confession.” The Lord Jesus is born in Bethlehem of Juda because, although he is himself the King of glory, he especially chooses to be born where the loaves of sound doctrine abound, by which the faithful soul is nourished lest it perish of hunger; where a multitude of believers dwells, which by zeal for a praiseworthy life offers God a true confession of praise. The Evangelist seems to indicate in the following words how great is the grace that follows where such [Col. 0678B] a King and Lord of hosts is born:

“Behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying, ‘Where is he that is born King of the Jews?’” For as soon as this noble child—a child, I say, of singular innocence and purity—has arisen in the hearts of the elect, the Magi come to Jerusalem when converted sinners return to their own conscience, carefully and vigilantly considering all the filthy and perverse deeds of their past life. And when, with the keen gaze of the mind, they perceive how vile, miserable, and pitiable they have made themselves through sinning, they are moved by great compassion for themselves, according to the words of the most wise Solomon: “Have mercy,” he says, “on your soul, by pleasing God” (Ecclus. [Col. 0678C] XXX, 24). And because they remember that they have grievously offended their Creator, they earnestly strive truly to appease him. At times they ask, in the words of the Magi, where he is who is born King of the Jews, because they anxiously seek by what labour and what zeal of penitence they may obtain from the Father of lights the remedy of salvation and pardon.

“We have seen,” they say, “his star in the East, and have come to worship him.” This visible star invisibly represents the brightness of inward illumination. By its most sweet visitation they are brought back to themselves within themselves and truly worship their Maker, while they strive by continual labour to restore to its former beauty the image of the Creator, darkened and effaced by wicked deeds. They are also rightly said to have come from the East. For they can truly say with the prophetic voice: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke I, 78), because unless that true [Col. 0678D] Sun of righteousness had visited their hearts by the hidden inspiration of his grace, they could neither abandon their ingrained habit of vices nor raise themselves to a manner of life pleasing to God. Herod, that is, the ancient enemy, grieves greatly that this work of divine mercy occurs in his days. For just as he is greatly delighted when a perverse person persists in perversity to the end, so he is struck with severe grief when someone strives through penitence and tears to return from death to life. Hence it is rightly said in what follows:

“When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all [Col. 0679A] Jerusalem with him.” For when he sees that one who, as a slave of sin, had hitherto lain under his suggestions has shaken off the yoke of wicked domination and resolved to submit himself, in heart and body, to his Creator, he employs every artifice of his malice in order to turn that soul back from this purpose. Now setting before his eyes one hardship, now another, he makes him, in trembling anxiety, consider how harsh and difficult the purpose of the spiritual life is. Thus he brings it about in a remarkable way that all Jerusalem is troubled with him. For he causes every faithful soul, which, as it tends toward the joys of inward peace, could through the grace of divine visitation be called Jerusalem, to be agitated by such disturbances that, placed between love and fear, it sometimes does not know what it should choose above all: whether it ought to pursue the purpose [Col. 0679B] of the spiritual life or abandon it. But the enemy of humankind strives through his deceits to draw a person back from this purpose because he is grievously pained if ever a human being possesses by humble penitence the kingdom which he, though an angel, lost through pride. Hence the Evangelist indicates how great his envy of us is by the words that immediately follow:

“And gathering together,” he says, “all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born.” For the ancient enemy, although through the subtlety of his angelic nature he is accustomed to perceive many things, nevertheless cannot discover what is generated in a human heart unless he learns it through the movements or signs of the outward person. Therefore he gathers together the chief [Col. 0679C] priests and scribes of the people—that is, he carefully attends wherever he hears Holy Scripture recited by the mouths of preachers—if perhaps by these means he may learn with what intention a person has resolved to turn to God: whether he has determined to renounce the world and its desires because of lack of possessions, some occasion of adversity, or love of God alone. For he knows that a will is easily changed when it has been inspired not by the grace of divine sweetness but by the fickleness of sudden impulse. Thus, when he has perceived the sincere and simple character of the intention, he prepares new instruments of impiety, as the words of the Gospel make clear.
