“Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully learned [Col. 0679D] from them the time when the star had appeared to them.” For when he has recognized that the mind of any penitent, now inflamed with heavenly longing, is firmly grounded in good will, he turns to crafty arguments and prepares still harsher devices of ambush. For when he cannot turn a person away from good intention, he tries secretly to strike him with the vice of pride at the very beginning of conversion, as follows immediately:

“And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: ‘Go and inquire carefully concerning the child; and when you have found him, report back to me, so that I too may come and worship him.’” These are the words of the venomous serpent, by which, at the outset of conversion, he persuades anyone incautious and still insufficiently watchful—when he cannot turn him from good will—to seek human praise, so that, delighted with human applause, he may remain empty and void of eternal reward. It is as though he said: “Behold, you have begun to enter hard paths, in the observance of which you will suffer many struggles and labours. Yet your labour will by no means remain fruitless and empty. For when you have advanced through growth in merits and proved yourself in all things, you will become an outstanding teacher of others, and many, by the example of your imitation, will submit themselves to heavenly instruction.” The first-fruits of the Gentiles—the Magi [Col. 0680A] themselves—plainly indicate how the elect ought to resist these diabolical suggestions; concerning them the Gospel narrative relates:

“When they had heard the king, they departed.” The enemy of humankind has his conversation with [Col. 0680B] the elect when he persuades them to meditate upon vain things and think upon unlawful things. But because they do not receive the words of evil suggestion through consent of delight, they merely hear Herod speaking, but depart silent and without reply. For they despise the devil’s words more lightly the more frequently they employ themselves in converse with God. By contrast, the mind of the reprobate, because it savours nothing of heavenly words, whenever it is driven by wicked suggestions easily inclines to consent; for while it refuses to hear the exhortations of spiritual teaching, it gives diligent attention to the discourse of diabolical delusion. But how greatly those who despise the pleasures of the carnal life are illuminated by the grace of divine brightness is indicated by the words that follow:

[Col. 0680C] “And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them.” For, as blessed Gregory says: “If we cut off from the flesh what pleases it, we immediately find in the spirit what delights us.” As soon as Herod is despised with all the deceit of his subtle art, he who is the brightness of the eternal Father illumines and kindles, by the grace of his visitation, hearts previously made dark by temptation, so that they may see what is to be done and what avoided, and may be strengthened to accomplish what they see.

It should also be noted that, while the Magi were detained with Herod, they did not see the star which had appeared earlier; but as soon as they turned their backs upon him in contempt, they found again the star that guided their journey. So, indeed, when a powerful temptation comes upon us, the true Divinity hides from us the brightness of inward contemplation; but when, with its help, that temptation is driven a little from the mind, the brightness of the sweetness for which we long arises. The same grace of divine illumination, when it has so kindled the cold hearts of people with the flame of inward fervour, remains with some, [Col. 0680D] while in others it quickly grows cold: this is indicated by the sequence of the following narrative:

“Until it came and stood over the house where the child was.” For, as the Psalmist says: “There is none that can hide himself from his heat” (Ps. XVIII, 9). A visitation sent from the Most High sometimes penetrates certain hearts so deeply that they are moved even to tears. But because after their time of tears they return to the works of their habitual perversity, the star does not stand over them, since the power of compunction does not persevere in them. But among the elect, [Col. 0681A] who have fixed the whole intention of their heart upon love of the Creator alone, this star has firmly established its dwelling; for they hasten, by continual meditation, to return to the joys of eternity which they have tasted through the grace of contemplation. And the more often their mind is touched by remembrance of the heavenly homeland, the more strongly it is inflamed to acquire the brightness of that same homeland. In them, too, this child—the author, I mean, of singular innocence—has, insofar as is possible in this changeable time, a stable abiding; for as long as they live in exile, the consolations of his goodness will not fail them. The Evangelist then magnificently suggests, in the following words, what kind of joy it is, how ineffable, by which the hearts of the elect deserve to be made glad after the clouds of temptations:

[Col. 0681B] “And when they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.” For in saying not simply “with great joy,” but adding, as it were, “with exceedingly great joy,” he intended us to understand that this joy is ineffable and immeasurable, exceeding every mode of expression: the joy by which the elect, although only in a mirror and in an enigma, deserve to see in Sion the God of gods. They rejoice, indeed, with exceedingly great joy when, though confined in the prison of an earthly body, they deserve, however fleetingly, to contemplate that glory which the citizens of the heavenly homeland enjoy in fullness. This is that glory of surpassing dignity which the blessed Apostle Paul seems to indicate when he boasts that he was caught up to the [Col. 0681C] third heaven, where he heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter (II Cor. XII, 2). Blessed are these persons, who, though burdened by the exile of an earthly dwelling, deserve through contemplation of mind to draw near to the Lord of the universe! The Gospel’s words seem to indicate still more fully the magnificence of their excellence.

“And entering into the house, they found the child with Mary his mother.” Whenever they enter the house of the mind, what other inhabitant do they find there than the very author of purity and integrity? “With Mary,” he says, “his mother.” The mother of Jesus is the same as his faithful bride: truly, every soul. The mother and bride of the Lord is found with the child in the house of the mind when, in a wondrous condescension of loving-kindness, he alone, holding sweet converse with her alone, refreshes by the grace of divine visitation her who has been melted by the fire of most ardent [Col. 0681D] love. What the elect do amid words of such great intimacy is declared by the following narrative:

“And falling down, they worshipped him.” For the only true worship offered by the elect to God is then offered when they strive to submit themselves before his exalted majesty with all abasement of mind and body. Hence the Psalmist, indicating how one ought to worship the Most High, says: “Come, let us worship and fall down before God” (Ps. XCIV, 6). Therefore, the one who in worshipping God truly falls down is he who, knowing the greatness of his Creator, believes from his inmost heart that he is earth and ashes. To those who pray much, often fast, and sweat under great labour, the Lord will by no means grant such grace [Col. 0682A] as he grants to the humble alone, according to another Scripture, which says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (I Pet. V, 5).

“And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.” A treasure is called not the place where a small possession of gold and silver is kept, but the place where an inexhaustible store of whatever is precious and desirable is held. For *thesaurus* derives its name from the Greek *thesis* [θέσις], which in Latin is called *depositio*, “a depositing.” Therefore the elect open treasures to the glorious King Sabaoth when they attribute the merit of good conduct, zeal for holy meditation, and the practice of perfect integrity not to themselves but to the gifts of his grace. These gifts, indeed, to be offered to the divine majesty, are within the reach of every person, poor no less than rich, and suffice for the needy no less than for the abundant, [Col. 0682B] provided that, where means to give are lacking, good will is not lacking. For if good will is present, the outstanding possession of heaven is purchased with a small thing; because, as blessed Gregory says, the kingdom of heaven is worth as much as you have. For the two small coins of the widow were of greater value than the lavish gifts of the rich and powerful. “They offered,” he says, “gold, frankincense, and myrrh.” By gold is signified the brightness of heavenly wisdom, as is said through Solomon: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XX, 21). And because this wisdom is from above, it must surely be sought from him who dwells on high, as the Apostle James exhorts: “If anyone,” he says, “lacks wisdom, [Col. 0682C] let him ask God” (Jas. I, 6). By frankincense, which is burned upon divine altars, is signified the power of prayer, as the Psalmist testifies: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight” (Ps. CXL, 2). But myrrh, with which the bodies of the dead are customarily embalmed so that they may not readily be consumed by decay, signifies the mortification of the flesh, which is accustomed to restrain the consciences of believers from dead works. Therefore those strive to honour the countenance of the most mighty King with gold who offer to God a mind darkened by no evil intention. And if we desire truly to attain this before God, the incense of most pure prayers must continually be kindled upon the altar of the heart. But in order that the incense of prayer may give forth a sweet fragrance, continence of the flesh, by which the corruptions of vices are expelled, must be added without ceasing.

Gold, which shines and excels other metals, may also be understood as devotion of heart; frankincense, which yields a fragrant sweet odour, signifies the sweetness of good works; while myrrh, with which, as we have said, the bodies of the dead are embalmed so that they do not waste away in decay, prefigures true humility of heart. These are the three precious gifts altogether necessary to every person striving toward true salvation. [Col. 0682D] For to offer gold is to direct ourselves to God and to the things of God with the whole devotion of our heart. We join frankincense to gold when we show in good works the good will that we have toward God, so that we may be able to say with the Apostle: [Col. 0683A] “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Cor. II, 15). We join myrrh to gold and frankincense when we attribute nothing to ourselves either for our good devotion or our good works, but ascribe all simply to God alone in true humility of heart, saying with the Prophet: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to thy name” (Ps. CXIII, 1). For gold and frankincense do not suffice for God if myrrh is absent, because no action of ours is acceptable to God without humility. Hence the prophet says: “All shall come from Saba, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord” (Isa. LX, 6). What the Evangelist calls myrrh, the prophet calls praise, because whoever so mortifies his carnal senses within himself that he seeks, not his own glory for any merits of his, but [Col. 0683B] God’s glory, truly proclaims praise to the Lord. It follows:

“And having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way.” When the hearts of the elect deserve to be lulled into blessed sleep in the secret chamber of conscience, away from the tumult of the world, they receive faithful answers amid the very silences of inward rest: they must return to the homeland of blessedness by another path of actions. Thus they must exchange the step of pride for the foot of humility; they must cleanse the path of disobedience by the narrow track of submission, so that, humble and submissive, they may obtain the glory of the kingdom—those who, rebellious and proud, had deserved the misery of exile.

Since, therefore, we have in some measure learned by what path of actions we ought to return to the heavenly homeland, let us strive to enter upon the way of this present world with such steps of action that, when the body of this death has been changed, we may at last be permitted to rejoice with the immortal King of the ages in the land of immortality through endless ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY XV. SECOND HOMILY ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD.

The most holy solemnity which we celebrate today is called Epiphany, which in Latin is interpreted “manifestation” or “appearance.” For on this day we solemnly commemorate three manifestations or appearances of the Lord, by which, during the days of his flesh, he willed to be manifested and to appear to humankind.

[Col. 0683D] His first appearance or manifestation took place at the beginning of his birth, when the Magi, enlightened by the unfamiliar light of a new star, came under its guidance to the manger of the newborn Saviour; and, having worshipped him, they opened their treasures and offered him three precious gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The second manifestation or appearance took place at the waters of the Jordan in the thirtieth year of his Incarnation, when he, the Creator and Restorer of all things, alone free and clean from every stain of sins, came among other sinners to John to be baptized by him. There the heavens were opened to him; he saw the Spirit of God descending in the form of a dove and coming upon him; and a voice came from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). The third manifestation [Col. 0684A] we read to have taken place in Cana of Galilee, where at a wedding he changed water into wine and manifested his glory. Although these things are recorded as occurring at different times, they are nevertheless gathered into one day and reverently commemorated in Christian devotion.

Therefore, just as our Redeemer ordained to work all the mysteries of his Incarnation for the sake of our salvation, so he willed to show and fulfil in himself these three miracles of his threefold manifestation or appearance, not for his own sake but for ours. By them he willed not only then, when as a visible human being he appeared in visible flesh, to become known and manifest bodily and visibly to human beings; but by these bodily appearances or manifestations he mystically prefigured and foreshadowed [Col. 0684B] how every day he manifests himself spiritually and invisibly to every blessed person, appearing through the grace of his inward visitation, and also in what manner the blessed and elect person himself ought to appear in the sight of the divine majesty.

Let us therefore consider what this great and splendid day is, fittingly adorned and sanctified by the Saviour’s threefold appearance or manifestation. This splendid and sanctified day is every person who is to be saved, who, illuminated by the star of heavenly enlightenment and visitation, casts away the darkness of secular life and, led by that star—that is, preceded by divine grace—seeks and finds Christ’s manger. By the manger one may rightly understand the manner of life of the spiritual life, both because of its firm observance of discipline, its strict rigour of custody, and the enclosure of perpetual confinement, and also because of the many other instruments of spiritual arts by which their praiseworthy life is adorned with the utmost foresight and, so to speak, securely fenced about: those who strive to serve God in the deepest quiet of heart and body. Therefore all those blessed persons who, with the faithful Magi, are illumined not now by the transient light of a visible star, but by the incomprehensible and invisible grace of divine inspiration, and come to Christ’s manger—that is, to the rigour of spiritual warfare—undoubtedly find Jesus [Col. 0684D] sweetly lying and resting in the manger, that is, in the congregation of the faithful who live worthily and praiseworthily according to spiritual discipline. If, by God’s gift, some good teacher and ruler presided over the most worthy community of these blessed persons who desire to recline at the Lord’s manger, one could truly and quite fittingly say there what the Evangelist says: “They found the child with Mary his mother.”

Meanwhile, whoever knows himself to have been divinely enlightened, as has been said, should by no means think it sufficient that he has come to the Lord’s manger, that he has already passed over to the desired purpose of spiritual life, unless he also devoutly offers Christ three precious gifts after the example of the three Magi: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. By gold is fittingly understood knowledge of truth; by frankincense, devotion to good works; [Col. 0685A] by myrrh, the mortification of human praise. The converted person ought to offer God gold, which is knowledge of truth, so that, illumined by the brilliant splendour of exalted spiritual understanding, he may know to reject evil and choose good; may discern between truth and falsehood; may understand what must be done and what avoided; and may consider and weigh with the prudent eye of circumspection what pleases the sight of the divine majesty and what can displease him and offend his eyes. But because knowledge of truth by no means suffices for the person who is to be saved, it is necessary also that he freely offer to the Lord frankincense, which is devotion to good works, so that he may strive to practise and fulfil in good works the truth which he has deserved to know through the understanding of his inward sense. And whoever is devoted to Christ through zeal for good action frequently emits from himself the most sweet fragrance of a good odour, by which not only is God delighted, but also many people, sprinkled with the fragrance of his praiseworthy and virtuous manner of life, are beneficially edified and refreshed. By their example, despising earthly things, they are kindled more and more with love of the virtues and longing for the heavenly homeland.

Once these two gifts, gold—that is, knowledge of truth—and frankincense—that is, devotion to good works—have been rightly offered to God, it remains that he remember also to offer myrrh, by which the mortification of human praise is understood; without it he cannot ascend to the summit of perfection. For once he has exercised knowledge of truth [Col. 0685C] through devotion to good works, he ought utterly to mortify within himself the desire for human praise, lest the vice of pride steal upon him and cause him to seek to be praised and magnified by people for his good works.

The Lord’s chosen prophet Isaiah quite plainly recalls these same three gifts which the Evangelist narrates, saying: “All shall come from Saba, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord” (Isa. LX, 6). In this place the Evangelist and the prophet appear to agree well with each other: where the Evangelist names myrrh, there the prophet, suppressing the name of myrrh, mystically foreshadows “proclaiming praise to the Lord”; and by this mortification of human praise, thus signified, he in some manner explains it clearly, showing and, as it were, warning that the person devoted to good works, utterly mortifying his own praise, should attribute nothing to his own powers or merits, but, in proclaiming praise to the Lord, should humbly ascribe everything that he is to the grace of God alone. Hence he fittingly says: “All shall come from Saba.” Saba is interpreted “burning.” For a blessed person comes from the burning of divine love if he worthily offers God these three gifts of the threefold virtue. Unless he is set ablaze and inflamed by the fire of divine love, he will deserve neither to know truth, nor to please God through devotion to good works, nor to possess within himself the mortification of human praise.

Therefore, whoever is that blessed person in whom God so mercifully works the mystery [Col. 0686A] of his first manifestation or appearance—whom he deigns to lead, illumined by his star, that is, by the grace of his heavenly visitation, to the purpose of spiritual life, and whom he makes burn with the fire of his love so that he strives to appear before the sight of his Creator with the three aforesaid mystical gifts of the three Magi—in that happy and faithful person he will also reveal the glory of his second manifestation and appearance, which occurred at the waters of the Jordan. There, when the Lord was baptized, the heavens were opened to him; he saw the Holy Spirit of God descending in the form of a dove and coming upon him; and a voice came from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

[Col. 0686B] By the waters of the Jordan, whose name is interpreted “descent,” we may not improperly understand the final end of every person’s life: from birth each day one descends and flows away toward death. When each of the elect comes to this descent, that is, to the end of life—when he has paid the debt of the flesh and passed beyond the miseries of mortal life—then the heavens will truly be opened to him, and in the form of a dove he sees the Spirit of God coming upon him. For then, filled and made full with the everlasting and inestimable grace of wondrous sweetness and gentleness, he will be forever, like a dove, without gall and without all bitterness. Indeed, many saints and righteous persons often receive in this life many and diverse charisms of the Holy Spirit, according to what the Apostle Paul says: “To one indeed is given through the Spirit the word of knowledge; to another the word of wisdom according to the same Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 8). Yet they cannot possess the Holy Spirit fully in the form of a dove. However strongly they may inwardly burn when set on fire with divine love, however brightly they may outwardly shine, adorned with splendid merits of virtues, however abundantly God may anticipate them with blessings [Col. 0686C] of sweetness, still, as long as they carry the corruptible body which weighs down the soul, they are compelled often to be made bitter and to be angry with the vices and sins within themselves.

Some saints also, having zeal for righteousness, frequently inflict vengeance by severely pursuing the impious and rebellious, as is written concerning Moses and Elijah, the Lord’s elect and specially chosen prophets, who, inflamed and armed with zeal for righteousness, struck down by killing a very great multitude of wicked people in their days. But when the souls of the elect, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, are freed from the straits of this laborious struggle and, with the heavens opened, have been transferred to that most joyous vision of eternal peace, then at last they fully receive the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. For, sprinkled with the overflowing dew of divine sweetness and endowed with the grace of perpetual simplicity and gentleness, they will never again be able to be stirred by any gall of bitterness, either against themselves or against any other.

Therefore, for whomever the heavens are thus opened after death and the Holy Spirit is given in the form of a dove, that person will also deserve to hear this most sweet voice of the eternal Father: [Col. 0687A] “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” He does not say, “This is my servant,” or “my handmaid,” or “a hired labourer,” because a servant or hired labourer indeed receives a reward from his lord for service, but will never receive or possess an inheritance. For there are many in this world who serve God not for eternal but for temporal goods, and who receive the reward of servants and hired labourers, not the inheritance of sons, while they enjoy earthly pleasure and prosperity according to their will, and while, puffed up by riches, powers, and honours, they exalt themselves according to the desires of their heart. But this blessed and specially chosen person, whom God deigns, with such wondrous and inestimable condescension, to receive into the bosom of his incomprehensible and inexhaustible sweetness, he addresses, with the ineffable voice of paternal compassion, in these sweetest and most joyous words: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” This, I say, is my beloved Son, the everlasting co-heir of my kingdom, who has always cleaved to me and served me not with servile fear but with filial love and with the dear honour of humility beloved by me. “In whom I am well pleased”: whose life and conduct were pleasing in my sight, who in all his works sought not the honour of his own praise but the praise and glory of my name alone. Blessed and truly happy is the person for whom the heavens are thus opened, to whom the Holy Spirit is given in the form of a dove, and who is exalted and commended by so paternal and desirable a voice of the eternal Father.

To the glory of such dignity and blessedness that person can attain [Col. 0687C] who, while established in this pilgrimage, continually runs to the waters of the Jordan; who always brings the memory of his death back to mind; who always recalls that he is flowing away toward death; who, considering and weighing the innumerable calamities and miseries of this laborious life, brings forth continual streams of tears from a humble heart; and who strives to cleanse and purify himself by compunction flowing from the invisible sweetness of inward inspiration, so that he may utterly die to sins and vices. Therefore, in whatever elect and God-beloved person this second manifestation or appearance of the Lord is so gloriously fulfilled, in that person without doubt the glory of the third manifestation will be fulfilled still more gloriously—the manifestation that took place at the wedding, [Col. 0687D] where the power of divinity was made manifest when water was changed into wine.

This joyful and glorious miracle of divine manifestation will truly be fulfilled in a human being when, after the general resurrection has been completed, the multitude of the elect is invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb. Just as at the weddings of secular people two principal persons customarily come together—the bridegroom and the bride—so too at the heavenly wedding two come together: Christ the bridegroom and the Church the bride. There the souls of the saints, having received their bodies for which they have long yearned, will be crowned with the glory of blessed immortality and incorruption, and will be joined to the immortal bridegroom of perpetual incorruption by the pledge of eternal betrothal.

In these nuptials and in this delightful banquet of all the blessed [Col. 0688A], who partake of the heavenly table with Christ their head, water is truly changed into wine. Water is cold and tasteless matter, and gives scarcely any strength to the drinker; but wine, warm, ardent, and strong, strengthens and cheers the drinker. Thus the spirits and souls of the righteous, if they formerly entertained anything watery, so to speak, or weak, while they groaned that the tasteless and frail matter of the corruptible body was rotting in the dust of the earth, and sighed with all desire to receive it again, will then be changed into wine—that is, transferred into the most fervent savor of divine love and ineffable sweetness. And as one intoxicated by wine is alienated from his ordinary awareness, so the elect, intoxicated in that glory of eternity by the abundance of heavenly joys [Col. 0688B] and filled by the insatiable fullness of the divine vision, when their body, formerly corruptible and mortal, has been clothed in immortality and made spiritual, with every carnal sense emptied out, will no longer perceive or relish anything earthly or imaginary. Made one spirit with God, they transfer their whole understanding and affection to God.

In this everlasting banquet that commandment of love which the Lord himself commends is truly and perfectly fulfilled and discharged: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole mind” (Mark 12:30). For, with faith preserved and sound understanding, I believe I may say that the Lord’s chosen apostles Peter and Paul, and the other saints, whose blessed souls, although already resting in that heavenly vision [Col. 0688C] of perpetual peace, enjoy the delight of inexpressible gladness, nevertheless cannot fully and perfectly fulfill this command so long as they remember their bodies as separated from them and laid away in the bosom of the earth. For although, as I have said, they fix the keen sight of their eyes upon the ray of that unbounded brightness, and although they burn strongly in love for their Creator and Redeemer, nevertheless they cannot, with their whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind—with all thought, all intention, all memory—adhere in some manner wholly to his love. For they turn their thought somewhat away from him, the author, so to speak, of immortality and incorruption, when they think of receiving again their body, now reduced to dust [Col. 0688D], and desire with their whole affection that what shared in labors on earth should share in rewards in heaven.

But when these heavenly nuptials of which we have spoken are royally celebrated in the house of the Lord, and water has been changed into wine in the manner I have described—when flesh, cold and frail and formerly possessing no savor in itself, has been changed into wine, that is, into the vigor of eternal strength, has become spiritual and immortal, and has begun to possess in itself the savor and ardor of divine love—then our Creator is truly and perfectly loved by all his elect with their whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind. For they are joined and clung to him by so indissoluble a bond of charity that they can neither think nor wish to desire anything other than him whom they ardently [Col. 0689A] and insatiably behold and contemplate.

There too that saying is truly and fully accomplished: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” All the elect are neighbors to one another; but, in a special sense, each person’s own body will be his nearest neighbor. For when one has put on again that very body which, because of the misery of corruption innate to it, he sometimes hated in this world, and from whose weight and bond he often desired to be released and to be with Christ, now made heavenly, immortal, and incorruptible, he judges nothing to be so near to himself, so singularly his own; and he embraces, cherishes, and loves it with his whole affection.

Therefore we, who, as long as we are placed in this world, are pilgrims away from the Lord—even though sometimes, intent upon good deeds, we despise transitory things and strive through a taste of contemplation to touch the eternal [Col. 0689B] goods of our homeland—nevertheless, because, just as those Magi, having adored the Lord, returned to their own country, so we too often return to our own country, that is, to the country of our bodily frailty, when natural necessity compels us to provide for the body’s restoration by food or sleep, let us humbly beseech the Lord that the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, may deign to lead us to the eternal joys of the heavenly nuptials—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## 82. HOMILY XVI. THIRD HOMILY ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come [Col. 0689C], and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gloom the peoples; but the Lord shall rise upon you, and his glory shall be seen in you” (Isaiah 60).

Just as in many places of the holy Gospel we are most fully taught in what order and by what perfection of life we ought to enter into life, so also in certain sayings of the prophets an exhortation is addressed to us, which likewise instructs us by what path and sequence, our sins having at last been put away through satisfaction, we ought to strive toward the perfection of virtues. For there are certain words of sacred and evangelical reading which, as they are full of every perfection, suggest and signify nothing other than matters of perfection. [Col. 0689D] And, just as evangelical utterances do, so also, as I have said, prophetic utterances often seem to speak and exhort us of nothing other than correction of morals and perfection of life. Hence this prophetic reading is a salutary exhortation, prescribing the order of our whole manner of life; it addresses every soul that has long been defiled in sins, saying:

“Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem.” By the name Jerusalem may be denoted any chosen and saved soul, which God the Father foresaw and predestined one day to behold the peace above. To this soul it is said through the prophet—indeed, through the Lord of the prophets himself—“Arise and be enlightened.” As though he were plainly saying: “You have made for yourself a certain rest in the vices and pleasures [Col. 0690A] of this world. Arise, I pray; arise from evils. And when you have risen from evils, be enlightened in my good things.”

## 83

Paul urges the same thing, saying: “Arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14). See how prophet and apostle agree. See how each awakens those who sleep. The one says, “Arise and be enlightened”; the other says, “Arise, you who sleep, and Christ will enlighten you.” He sleeps—and sleeps most wickedly—who does not resist carnal desires; he is dead who, captured by the delights and enticements of the desirable things of this world, incurs death of the soul by persisting long and long in sins. Whoever he may be, summoned and roused by the trumpet of the Lord’s word, let him rise by abandoning former evils; let him be enlightened by doing good.

[Col. 0690B] And because among many things one is necessary, without which a person cannot arise or be enlightened, it is fittingly added: “because your light has come.” This light is the light of perfect self-knowledge, by which one begins truly to recognize and know as evil the evil things that one has done, recalling to memory both the kind and the number of one’s offenses. Unless this light of knowledge comes, one cannot arise or be enlightened. After receiving the light of knowledge, by which the quality and quantity of crimes are perfectly considered, it remains that one should faithfully confess, because confession of sins is that glory of which the text immediately adds:

“And the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.” Nor is confession of sin inappropriately understood by “glory,” because one who confesses sins in hope of pardon greatly glorifies the Lord—God in prayer and the confessor in confession. Thus Joshua, the leader of the Israelite people, exhorted Achan, who had taken from the accursed spoil by theft, to confess his sin, saying: “My son, give glory to God” (Joshua 7:19). By saying “give glory to God,” he signified confession of sin, because confession of sins is a great glory of the Lord, and after confession comes remission of sins. For if in this world the cure of the sick person is the physician’s glory, how much more are the honor and glory of the true and heavenly physician, Jesus Christ, displayed when he applies medicine to souls and grants perfect health to sinners?

Since confession of sins does not suffice unless satisfaction is added, [Col. 0690D] we are immediately admonished concerning satisfaction when it is added: “For behold, darkness shall cover the earth.” What is meant by darkness except bodily hardships? And what are bodily hardships except vigils, fasts, scourges, cold, nakedness, hunger, and thirst? All these are very necessary for the body. And these darknesses—that is, these hardships—ought to cover the earth, because after a person has confessed sins with a true heart and faithful speech, he ought to cover with harsh satisfactions before God whatever he committed amiss in his earth, that is, in his earthly body.

After these darknesses, namely bodily afflictions, “gloom must also cover the peoples.” By gloom may be understood the bitterness of penitence; by peoples, the rational faculties. Gloom covers the peoples when the rational faculties are made bitter in true penitence. [Col. 0691A] And why do I call them rational faculties? I call them rational because it is eminently rational to offer God not an unwilling or forced bitterness of penitence, but one that is due, voluntary, devout, and from the whole affection of the heart. For some people, both in secular and in spiritual life, do indeed perform penance, but with such ingratitude that it is done more from necessity than from good will. Such people do not grow dark rightly, because they are not rightly sad and do not rightly mourn in their penitence; for they perform their penitence without love of heart. But the elect always grow dark inwardly in a rational way, because for all that they have committed it is sweet to them to have frequent and devout bitterness of penitence. And the bitterness of penitence is aptly understood by gloom, because it is like a heavy darkness to renounce the delights and pleasures of the world, to disdain the joys of the present life, never to allow pride to rule in one’s thought or speech, but to persist in a humble and contrite heart and a mourning spirit. Whoever has thus risen from evils, been enlightened in good things, given glory to God in confession of sins, covered his earth with darknesses—that is, harsh satisfactions—and striven to grow dark by rational penitence for all that he has done, will experience what is added:

“But the Lord shall rise upon you, and his glory shall be seen in you.” “Lord” [Col. 0691B] is a name of fear. And not inappropriately, this word that sounds of fear signifies the spirit of fear. That spirit of fear will rise “upon,” that is, in the higher part of the heart, because the more they recognize their sins in true humility, the more they begin to fear God, whom they have offended by sinning. The spirit of fear is followed by the spirit of love, which the next phrase seems to designate when it says, “and his glory shall be seen in you.” By the glory of the Lord is understood the spirit of love, to which a person passes from the spirit of fear when he grieves and groans, not merely from fear but with filial love, over every occasion on which he remembers having offended God. Illuminated inwardly by the inexpressible touch of this spirit, he will burn with full love of God and neighbor. This glory of the Lord will be seen in you, whoever you are, because such love and sweetness of heart will be seen by God; it will be seen by angels, because [Col. 0691D] they rejoice with you; it will be seen by people, because it is welcome and lovable to good people. When the glory of the Lord is thus seen in the elect, although they cannot live without sins in this world, it may nevertheless happen that what follows is fulfilled in them:

“And the nations shall walk in your light.” The nations are vices. If nations are vices, how, I ask, are we to understand the statement that “the nations shall walk”? To walk is to proceed gently. Thus a pacing horse is called an *ambulatorius*, because it proceeds smoothly and slowly. Therefore, since we have said that nations are vices, the nations—that is, the vices—in the good and righteous will, as it were, walk: they will not prevail against them with the same force with which they formerly attacked and cast them down. And although, as long as they live, they cannot be entirely free of vices and are always assailed, they are nevertheless never conquered. To say it still more plainly: the nations will walk in the light when one who formerly could scarcely, or not at all, restrain the eyes from unlawful sight, the ears from useless hearing, and the tongue from evil speech, now, with all members restrained, can, by God’s help, measure and restrain himself from everything by which he may offend God.

“But kings also shall walk in the brightness of your rising.” By kings you may understand the outward senses, which are rightly ranked under the name of kings when through them the whole human body is ruled and directed to righteous, praiseworthy, and God-pleasing works. But lest anyone presume of himself, as if he possessed anything from himself, these words are added: “in the light, in the brightness [Col. 0692B] of your rising.” By these three words I think the work of the whole holy Trinity may be understood: by “light,” the Holy Spirit; by “brightness,” the Son of God; by “rising,” God the Father. The Holy Spirit is light, who enlightens us, because it is his gift and work that we live well. The Son of God, the Word of God the Father, is brightness, teaching us inwardly from the brightness of his Word what we ought to do and what we ought to avoid. God the Father is the rising, because he is the one from whom this light proceeds and from whom this brightness arises.

But because the whole time of our life is spent in temptations, and the more any of the elect are raised in virtues, the more keenly they are attacked by enemies, namely malignant spirits (for from the day on which we are born [Col. 0692C] until the day on which we die, we shall always suffer the temptations of invisible enemies lying in wait for us), the Holy Spirit teaches through the prophet that Jerusalem—that is, the blessed soul—what it ought to do amid those very temptations and how it ought to fortify itself against the enemies lying in wait. He says: “Lift up your eyes round about, Jerusalem, and see. All these have gathered together; they have come to you.” Who are those around us but those of whom the prophet says: “The wicked walk round about” (Psalm 11:9)? Those wicked adversaries of ours are always and everywhere around us, carefully observing our action and conduct: whether the sight is shameless, the tongue wanton, the hearing useless, so that through these outward things they may come to inward things. Though they cannot sit down above us, [Col. 0692D] they are nevertheless sitting around us, leaping upon us, lying in wait. Therefore, because they are thus around us, the eyes must be lifted up.

There are two eyes which the elect ought to possess and lift up. One eye is understanding in reading; the other is affection in prayer. These two eyes are very necessary: so that one may understand in reading what is good, and the affection of the heart may be drawn in prayer to relish God.

## 87

For if anyone has the eye of understanding, let him ask God in prayer that he may be able to fulfill through the practice of good works what he already understands. And these two eyes must be lifted up against those who are around us, because, lest they prevail against us, we must continually occupy ourselves in understanding through [Col. 0693A] reading and in relishing God, drawing near to God in contemplation and prayer of the mind. And he rightly says, “lift up and see,” because we must always have the watchful eyes of the heart, so that we never act carelessly. For security is the mother of negligence, and from negligence, unless one comes to one’s senses, the judicial sentence of eternal death follows.

The Holy Spirit further teaches why we ought thus to lift up our eyes all around and see, when he adds: “All these have gathered together; they have come to you.” “These” is a demonstrative pronoun. By this word our invisible enemies may be designated, because although they are invisible, they are always present to us, never departing, but always making themselves evident within by invisible attacks. And he fittingly places these two words, “all these,” because we ought to see, carefully and diligently consider, and guard against however many and however great are the spirits that weary us and assault us with their various incitements. And why are they called “gathered together”? Because they succeed one another in turn: when someone is freed from one vice, he is immediately attacked by another. Yet, if you, whoever you are, O Jerusalem, are not moved, do not yield, and are not conquered, all these gathered together have come to you. “For what,” you ask, “have they come to me?” For glory. Certainly, if Job had not been tested, he would not have attained such great glory; but because he endured evils and bore them patiently, he received testimony and praise from God that there was no man like him on earth. Thus every soul that has endured all these gathered together and refused to yield to their attacks will receive the very endurance of temptations not unto shame, but unto glory [Col. 0693C] and the crown of eternal reward. I think this is why this chapter is so frequently used in evening and morning praises: because this is more necessary than anything else contained in this reading—that we always remember to lift up our eyes and see these gathered foes, lest they deceive or lead us away, but so that their temptation may become glory and reward for us. But if we are to attain such glory, so that we may be found victorious in our temptations, we must seek with all our strength the two things which follow.

“Your sons,” he says, “shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise from [Col. 0693D] your side.” By sons, who are strong, may be understood the affections of contemplation; by daughters, who rise from the side, good bodily works. Those sons—that is, the affections of contemplation—are rightly said to come from afar, because heavenly sweetness comes only from afar, that is, from heaven. Or it comes from afar because it is attained only by prolonged labor. The daughters also rise from the side. Because Eve was fashioned from Adam’s side, flesh may fittingly be understood by the side, through which we ought to apply ourselves to good work. For whatever we render to God in vigils, fasts, and other labors, we offer all of it from our flesh. Therefore, because there are works both of spirit and of flesh, the affections of contemplation are rightly denoted by sons, and works of the flesh by daughters, who are weaker. Thus sons come from afar when the sublimity of contemplation is sent down from above to the elect; daughters rise from the side when, after contemplative sweetness, they are active and vigorous in the labors of good works.

Nor should it be passed over that in certain manuscripts one reads: “Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall suck milk.” Milk is the food of the weak; and the weak are not improperly signified by milk. The weak ought to suck milk, because, if they cannot rise to the perfection of contemplation, they can nevertheless perform good works. But solid food belongs to sons—that is, to the perfect—who receive from God and in God that food and taste of inward sweetness by which they become strong and vigorous for bearing all things. With eyes lifted up, sons gathered—that is, affections of contemplation—and daughters rising from the side, that is, holy works performed and completed with the body, they rise to a more eminent progress, as follows:

## 89

“Then you shall see and overflow, and your heart shall wonder and be enlarged.” What will it see, and how will it overflow? It will see through understanding; it will overflow through teaching. For even if one is never appointed to the office of teacher, one can nevertheless see through understanding and overflow through teaching. Every Christian who lives rightly and, as far as he can, instructs another who does not know, by life and word, rightly overflows through teaching. Then your heart shall wonder and be enlarged. It will wonder at the progress of others and be enlarged in its own affection; and the more it has labored for others’ progress, the more it will be enlarged, because it will be enriched by greater and more excellent gifts [Col. 0694C] from God.

“When the multitude of the sea shall be turned to you, the strength of the nations shall come to you; the flood of camels shall cover you.” By these three—the sea, the nations, and the camels—we may understand three things: by the sea, thoughts; by nations, words; by camels, works. Thoughts are aptly expressed by the sea because, just as the sea is always in motion, going out and returning, so thoughts too are always in motion, never at rest, now considering one thing and then another, reconsidering them. Hence it is fittingly said of the sea, “the multitude of the sea,” because just as the drops and waters of the sea are manifold and innumerable, so infinite are the things we think and carry about in the heart. This multitude of the sea—that is, the infinite crowd of thoughts—will be turned to you, O Jerusalem, when, having gathered all your senses, you truly consider, examine, and test yourself.

“But the strength of the nations also shall come to you.” We have said that thoughts may be signified by the sea, which is mute and without animal sense; but words may not inappropriately be signified by nations, which use reason. “Strength” is aptly added, because whether what is done is good or evil, strength is required, and whatever is afterward completed in action is always first worn through in speech. This strength of the nations shall come to you, whoever you are, blessed soul, so that you may rightly and perfectly confess your sins; for it is indeed a great gift of God to possess the strength [Col. 0695A] faithfully and truthfully to confess the ugliness of one’s sins. For many know their sins, but from a certain weakness and frailty they are ashamed to confess what they know.

After the multitude of the sea, after the strength of the nations, “the flood of camels shall cover you.” The camel is partly a clean animal and partly unclean: in the respect that it chews the cud, it is clean; in the respect that it does not have a cloven hoof, it is unclean. Works may be signified by camels: they are clean in the respect that we chew the cud—that is, mourn for our sins and confess them to God in prayer. They are unclean in the respect that we do not divide the hoof—that is, that we do not rightly divide things with God, but often love things of the world more than things of God and serve our own will more than the divine will. The flood ought to cover these camels, namely our works. What flood? Certainly, the abundance of tears, through whose flood the unclean part of works tends toward and arrives at true cleanness and innocence. But who, I ask, are those who can or ought to do this? Hear what follows.

“The dromedaries of Midian and Ephah.” Dromedaries are swift runners. Midian is interpreted “iniquity”; Ephah, “pouring out” or “loosened.” We, brothers, ought to be those dromedaries, namely swift runners, because not slowly or sluggishly but with all possible speed and haste we must pour out and cast away every iniquity and injustice that we have committed, both in confession and in [Col. 0695C] prayer.

But by these three—the multitude of the sea, the strength of the nations, and the flood of camels—may be denoted the three orders that belong to the profession of spiritual life: by the multitude of the sea, simple and unlearned people; by the strength of the nations, soldiers; by camels, canons and religious women. And not inappropriately: by the sea, which is mute and innumerable in its drops of water, is understood that innumerable multitude of converted people who were formerly bound to Christ, although [f. *quanquam*, “although”] defiled by the affairs of this world. Although their ability may be slight and they may not possess great knowledge of doctrine, in their very simplicity, greatly pleasing God, they show forth in quietness and silence, by obedience, all that they can [Col. 0695D] worthily offer. This multitude of the sea will be converted when a multitude of such persons is daily converted to God and offers God a life pleasing to him.

And the strength of the nations will come when the strong and mighty tyrants and soldiers of this world pass from the acts of warfare in which they had been defiled before God to the good warfare of Christ. The more notorious and distinguished they were in wicked deeds, the more eminent and praiseworthy they become afterward in virtues and good works when converted to God. By camels, partly clean and partly unclean, is understood the order of clerics and religious women: clean in the respect that they possess the teaching and knowledge [Col. 0696A] of sacred Scripture; unclean in the respect that they have sinned secretly and their sins have not come to human notice. A flood will cover these when, humbly recognizing themselves and joined to the fellowship of good converts, they cover with the continual flood of tears whatever unlawful deed they have committed. It follows:

“All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord.” Who are “all,” except those who, having overcome and conquered temptations, fought well to the end of their lives and ran without weariness? To them seems fitting what occurs also at the end of this reading: “All,” he says, “shall come from Sheba.” Sheba is interpreted “captivity.” And what is the whole time of this life except a certain mournful and harsh captivity? For we, once citizens of heavenly Jerusalem, are captive children of Babylon; but when the yoke of captivity is loosed after death, all who are predestined to life come from [Col. 0696B] Sheba, because free and secure they will pass to their homeland and their own land, from which they are now exiles. But will they hasten there empty-handed? By no means, for they bring gold and frankincense. What is meant by gold except pure devotion and the clean will of the heart? What by frankincense except the good odor of good works? With these gifts every soul, having laid aside the burden of flesh, enters to Christ its king, because it must bring either gold or frankincense: gold, that is, the diligence of pure devotion and clean will; frankincense, that is, the fragrance of good and perfect action. This will be a most sweet and acceptable odor before the Lord, so that it may deservedly be worthy to hear from the Lord: “Behold, the odor of my son is like the odor of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27).

Having offered these gifts, because they see that they could do nothing of themselves, they continually proclaim praise to the Lord, perpetually declaring him the giver of reward and the crowner of merit. For now we praise the Lord in part and do not praise him in part. We praise in part when, placed amid the pressure and frailty of flesh, we praise what we believe; we do not praise in part when, fixed upon worldly and perishable things, we depart from the love of God by satisfying desires of the flesh. But when we have come from Sheba, that is, when we have been transferred from this captivity, we shall proclaim to the Lord perfect [Col. 0696D] praise, which will know no weariness, because there we can always praise him whom we can always love. May the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, lead us to this praise that is ever to be proclaimed—he who lives and reigns through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## 93. HOMILY XVII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE OCTAVE OF THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior” (Isaiah 12).

Today’s feast, celebrated in honor of the baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ, ought to have been celebrated on the same day as the calling of the nations through the guidance of the star to the three Magi. But because the dignity of these mysteries is so great [Col. 0697A] that they cannot fittingly be celebrated on a single day, Mother Church, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, judged it good to give the first day to that miracle in which those three kings, coming from the East, offered their gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—to the little child seated in his mother’s lap; and to give this eighth day, with no less devotion, to that dignity by which he himself, the author of life, wholly clean and whole, willed to be baptized by John his servant in order to wash away our sins. A third miracle also, the change of water into wine, is recounted and commemorated in the Sunday Gospels.

These three great and memorable miracles of the Lord, which were visibly performed in him and through him, must be accomplished spiritually in every person who tends toward the kingdom of heaven.

The first sign of this mystery is accomplished in a person when, under the guidance of the star—that is, the light of divine grace—he leaves his land and kindred and, despising all things, hastens to the manger of his Lord, that is, to the purpose of spiritual life. He also leaves his land, namely his own body, in which he dwelt through desires and delights, when, aided by the divine gift, he does not consent thereafter to seek again the things he has left. Having passed beyond the departure from his own country, he must hasten to another mystery and seek saving baptism—namely, he must strive through inward compunction of heart to weep for sins committed. After those two, the third miracle remains: that water be changed [Col. 0697C] into wine, that is, that his tasteless and watery heart be changed by the sweetness of divine contemplation into the savor of wine.

All the prophets from the beginning foretold the mystery of this day, enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit and foreseeing all future things. Among them, the eminent prophet Isaiah did not pass over in silence the honor and magnificence of this day in his canticle, which we always sing when we begin the weekday night office: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior.” There are two fountains of our Savior: one, the fountain of baptism; the other, the fountain of compunction. In baptism remission is granted for all original and actual sins. But since very few preserve the dignity of this mystery with an unspotted heart and body, as would be fitting, that other fountain, the abundance of tears, is available to us; washed and cleansed in it, we receive anew remission of our sins. From these two fountains we ought to draw with joy, because no joy and exultation can be greater than when a sinful person is reconciled to his Creator through the laments of penitence. Of this fountain it is elsewhere written: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of Judah and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zechariah 13:1). One who wishes to draw water usually lowers a bucket on a rope into the fountain, then, having drawn out the water, offers a drink to the thirsty. The bucket with its rope is our soul surrounded by mortal flesh. This flesh, like a rope twisted here and there, ought to be restrained and twisted by manifold continence and chastening [Col. 0698A], and kept bowed down in profound humility; for then we can draw water springing up into eternal life. For whereas one whose grave conscience of sins does not accuse him sometimes becomes cheerful, those who recognize the greatness of their offenses ought to walk with sad and downcast countenance, and, with that evangelical publican, not lift their eyes to heaven but humbly implore pardon for their sins. The example of that impious king Ahab shows how much true humility obtains before God and what it deserves. For when his iniquity and malice had grown so great that the Lord wished to deprive him of life and kingdom, humbled by penitence, he obtained divine clemency, so that the Lord said concerning him to the prophet Elijah: “Have you not seen Ahab humbled before me? Therefore, because he has humbled himself on my account, I will not bring evil in his days” (3 Kings 21:29).

Again, by the fountains of the Savior may be understood the holy Trinity: in the fountains, God the Father and God the Holy Spirit; in the Savior, God the Son, eternally begotten from the Father, who, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, was temporally born of the blessed Virgin Mother. We ought to draw from these fountains with joy, because every sweetness flows and overflows from God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“And you shall say,” he says, “on that day: Confess to the Lord and call upon his name.” On that great and desirable day—namely, in the illumination of your hearts—confess to [Col. 0698C] the Lord, because whether it is confession of sins or commemoration of his praise, all will please your Savior. “And call upon his name,” as if he said: Call upon him in the hidden place of your hearts, so that the good which he has worked in you may remain hidden within and be manifest only to God’s knowledge, always remembering David’s saying: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Psalm 113:1).

But someone says: “Why should I hide my upright works from human sight, when the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven’” (Matthew 5:16)? This does not contradict that saying in any respect; but what especially pleases God is then added:

Make known among the peoples, he says, his discoveries [Col. 0698D]. Make known, he says, to those who are with you his discoveries, not your own. I say “his,” because he gave them; and whatever fruit of good works there is in you, he, not you, has discovered it in you. Among these discoveries you must always remember that his name is exalted, so that your good works may be visible to human beings only to the extent that you remain mindful that God’s name alone is exalted and glorious, and do not seek the craving for human praise on account of the progress of your good work. But someone says: Why should I exert myself so greatly in good things if I ought not to be praised and commended by any mortal for the honour of my life? The answer is that he should wait a little, knowing that all his works are reserved for a single hour [Col. 0699A] of recompense and praise, as the following words indicate:

Sing to the Lord, for he has acted magnificently; proclaim this throughout the whole earth. When, he says, shall I sing, and when shall I proclaim? Certainly, when you have completed the due end of life by a good course, then you will sing and will not be silent, because your works will be praised not by human beings but will be celebrated and magnified before the whole heavenly host by angelic spirits. Do not be puffed up by this glorification of praise, knowing truly and perfectly that God has acted magnificently with you. Then you too will proclaim throughout the whole earth. For when in the general resurrection you have obtained the twofold robe, all your members will proclaim praise to the Lord, and you will be in the everlasting praise of God and the angels [Col. 0699B] and of all blessed spirits. May our Lord Jesus Christ bring us to these goods, he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

97 HOMILY XVIII: SECOND HOMILY FOR THE OCTAVE OF THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, in order to be baptized by him (Matt. III).

Our Lord and Savior, the mediator between God and human beings, just as he was willing to become a human being for human beings, so also, for the sake of our salvation, did not disdain to be washed in the font of baptism—not in order to remove any stain of his own action, but in order to remove the flaming sword which had fastened shut the gates of Paradise.

But because the most blessed John the Baptist, who was also his herald, knew by the prophetic Spirit that he himself would one day be baptized in that water and blood [Col. 0699C] which flowed from the side of the crucified Redeemer, he devoutly declined, in humility, the office of so great a sublimity: “I ought to be baptized by you,” he says, “and do you come to me?” This is as though he had said: “I indeed, together with the rest who in the underworld await your coming in long expectation, am to be baptized and freed by the life-giving blood of your covenant; and do you, the author of unique innocence, come to me to be baptized?”

And because the redemption of the human race could not be accomplished except through the blood of our Redeemer, he seems, by confirming the testimony of his herald, to intimate this in mystical words: “Allow it now,” he says; “for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” As though he said: “Just as [Col. 0699D] I now receive from you the sacrament of baptism for the sake of humility, so I am prepared, for your redemption and that of the entire human race, to obey God the Father even to death on the cross. For if obedience were lacking to my humility, it could be called injustice rather than righteousness.” When he heard these promises of such great kindness from the mouth of Truth, he believed what he heard and, without delay, obeyed the commanding voice. But let us hear what the Lord did immediately after being baptized:

And Jesus, when he had been baptized, immediately came up out of the water. Just as he was willing humbly to be baptized for us, so by his ascent he taught and showed how we ought to arrange ascents in our heart. It follows:

And behold, the heavens were opened over him. It is fittingly related that the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord [Col. 0700A] when he had been baptized and the heavens were already open. For it must unquestionably be believed that we, who are his body, have received in the water of regeneration the Spirit of adoption.

And because “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19), it was fitting that the voice of the Father should be heard from the magnificent glory: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” For the coeternal Son of God ought worthily to be praised by the Father for his reverence, since in all that he did and taught in the days of his flesh he never sought or loved his own glory, but always the glory of the Father. And how greatly, we may suppose, did the eternal begetter glory in his coeternal Son when, looking down from the lofty dwelling-place of his glory, he recognized that he had made such a human being—one who, although appearing [Col. 0700B] in sinful flesh, nevertheless never offended the eyes of the Father’s majesty? Let it suffice to have said these things briefly in an allegorical sense. Now let the discourse return to the mystical moral sense.

Let us first see whence our Savior came to be baptized, where, and by whom he wished to be baptized. “Jesus came,” he says, “from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, in order to be baptized by him.” Galilee is said to mean “a migration accomplished”; Jordan, however, “descent”; and John is interpreted “God’s grace.” By John—who, as we have said, sounds in our language as “God’s grace”—any faithful soul may not unfittingly be understood: a soul which glories humbly not in itself but in the Lord, 99 and, as though in some sense not knowing itself, truthfully declares with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am” [Col. 0700C] (I Cor. XV, 10). Thus Jesus—that is, our Savior—is rightly described as having come from Galilee to the Jordan, because in every blessed soul in which a perfect migration away from vices has taken place, and in which the virtue of perfect humility is present, he chooses a dwelling worthy of his majesty. When that soul has been drenched, at the time of prayer, with the waters of most fervent love, the very author of salvation is said in some manner to be baptized by it—not because eternal holiness needs to be sanctified, but so that by sanctifying it he may make the soul chosen and beloved by him holier. But what every blessed soul will say to its beloved being baptized amid such joys of sweetness, the Evangelist indicates by evident reasoning:

But John restrained him, saying: “I ought [Col. 0700D] to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” What is it, then, not to consent, as it were by restraining the Savior, except to stand amazed in wonder at the abundant grace of heavenly sweetness? It is as though a truly humble soul, thinking humbly of itself and judging itself unworthy of such great benefits of God, should cry out already from the deepest humility of its heart: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me? I, in whom iniquity has long abounded, would count it a great benefit if the riches of your goodness so abounded in me that at last, through the baptism of repentance, I might obtain from you forgiveness of sins; and do you come to me, beyond what I desire, with so great an abundance of your sweetness? By what exertions of labor, by what merits of virtues have I attained this: that the sweetness of eternal majesty should [Col. 0701A] prepare for me such delights in your sweetness?” But because, so long as the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, it can never be so watchful and provident that it does not frequently exclude from itself, through unlawful thoughts, the joys of divine visitation [Note: [Col. 0701D], that is, “that it does not”], the author of mercy shows in the following words how it ought to be renewed in the font of baptism:

And Jesus answered and said to him: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” As though he said: “Allow me, I say—allow me to find in you a prepared place of sanctification, so that, when I have been sanctified in you by the tears of inward compunction, you may receive from me a more abundant fruit of sanctification.” Again, in another sense: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” There are some who, while desiring [Col. 0701B] to prepare a place worthy of God’s baptism, subject their body through too little caution in chastising it to such indiscriminate servitude that, with the flesh slain rather than the vices, virtue quickly fails, weakened, so that it cannot perform the due service of good action; and thus, their bodily strength exhausted, they are by no means able to prepare a lodging of the heart. But all who, by the just moderation of discretion, have so mortified the deeds of the flesh in themselves that both inner and outer human beings remain untiring for service to the living God—to these, through merciful and constant collaboration, the Mediator between God and human beings promises that he will be an ever-present fellow-worker. “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness”: thus, I say, we—indeed I and the human being, applying ourselves together to devout labors—will be able to fulfill all righteousness, provided that through the virtue of discretion [Col. 0701C] that person suitably prepares for me the bridal chamber of his heart. Therefore, beloved, let us prepare the house of our heart in the spirit of devout discretion, so that the Mediator between God and human beings may deign to undertake with us the shared labor. But with what affection of devotion and what reverence of submission this one who is to be baptized must be received, the obedience of most humble John plainly indicates. For it follows:

Then he let him. He is not inappropriately said to have been “let go” when someone free and unencumbered is permitted to enjoy his own will. We must therefore consider diligently how wondrous is our Creator’s merciful condescension toward us: he who bestowed true freedom upon us desires, in some sense, to be let go by us as free—not because he himself needs any freedom, but in order to make us, freed [Col. 0701D] from sins, truly free. For then we let our liberator himself go free when, as he wills, we permit him freely to act with us, so that a free entrance may lie open to him into the inmost places of our heart and he may find a spacious place always to dwell within us. What strength and grace the abiding presence of so great an indweller confers upon us, the Gospel reading now plainly testifies:

101 And Jesus, when he had been baptized, immediately came up out of the water. Although water can be understood in various ways, in this place it signifies the sweet tears of compunction. For this is the water through which, according to the Savior’s testimony, “there shall be in the soul of the one who drinks a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV), when, through the grace of compunction, [Col. 0702A] spiritual steps of ascent arise in the soul. Thus, lifted heavenward by the sweetness of heavenly desire, it will also receive another water, namely that of saving wisdom; and so, while it strives to ascend by the different steps of virtues, the Savior is said in some manner to have ascended, not to have descended.

And behold, the heavens were opened over him. What can more rightly be understood by the opened heavens than the clear exposition of the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments? Because through these Scriptures we recognize the mysteries of heavenly wisdom, we not inappropriately call them by the name of heavens. Hence holy preachers too, who examine those same Scriptures more diligently and, drawing from them, offer us the mystical waters of wisdom to drink, are proved by prophetic testimony to be called heavens from the very office of divine preaching: “The heavens,” he says, “declare the glory of God” [Col. 0702B] (Ps. XVIII, 1). For the heavens proclaim God’s glory when they make known to us the joys of eternal brightness beloved by those who love the heavenly homeland. Yet something else can also soundly be understood by the heavens: namely, our outer and inner senses, which the brightness of divine visitation makes enlightened and clear at the hour of compunction, so that human understanding may recognize more clearly than light what in itself pleases or displeases the eyes of the Creator. Hence he aptly adds:

And he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and remaining upon him. Therefore every faithful soul, instructed in heavenly disciplines, when it has been greatly kindled with zeal for righteousness, will see the Spirit [Col. 0702C] of God descending and remaining upon it in the form of a dove, because that same Spirit causes him to descend in true humility and simplicity of mind. It sees him, I say, remaining upon it because he not only instructs and forms the outer person for good and righteous works, but also kindles the inner person with desires for the heavenly homeland. Hence it will deserve to hear joyfully that voice of paternal praise which is added here:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am pleased.” This voice—the voice of exultation and gladness—will truly be heard when the coeternal Son of God hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when we all attain “to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ,” and God himself is all in [Col. 0702D] all. Then indeed God the almighty Father, as though glorying, will burst forth in this new praise of the Son: “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am pleased. This, I say, is my beloved Son, in whom, through the grace of adoption, I have become the Father of so many sons. For in him I am well pleased, because I sent him as a propitiation for sinners, so that, taking away from the midst the handwriting which was against them, he might fasten it to the cross and dissolve by his death the enmities between myself and the human being.” But is the chosen Son of the eternal King praised by the Father alone, without the co-heirs of his kingdom? His brothers and co-heirs are likewise praised by the proclamation of the Father’s praise [Col. 0703A]—those whom the Son himself redeemed at the life-giving price of his own blood. Every blessed soul too will deserve to hear this desirable voice of the eternal Father when, at his command, it is called from this valley of tears. Although it may once have displeased through depravity of character or perversity of works, so that it rightly was and was called a daughter of rejection, reconciled at last by the fruit and remedy of repentance, it will hear the voice of exultation and gladness: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am pleased.”

For there is no doubt—indeed it must be believed with every joy—that the Son of the eternal Father, bridegroom of every faithful soul, will be present to that soul as it leaves the prison of the flesh, in order to introduce his daughter—indeed, his bride adorned with necklaces—rejoicing with him [Col. 0703B] to the wedding feast.

But because one who has not yet been cleansed from sins by worthy repentance and clothed in the wedding garment cannot participate in these nuptials, 103 let us put off the old human being with its deeds, so that, clothed with the new human being, we may obtain by the worthy fruit of repentance the robe of immortality which we cannot have through innocence, and, as though surrounded with a golden garment, may deserve to enter with joy and exultation the wedding supper of the Lamb. May he grant and assist this, he who deigned to prepare these nuptials for us by his own blood and who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY XIX: THIRD HOMILY FOR THE SAME OCTAVE OF THE EPIPHANY

[Col. 0703C] “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters; the God of majesty thundered” (Ps. XXVIII), etc.

The solemnity of this day, dearest brothers, on which we observe the octave of the Epiphany with due praises, is chiefly recalled and celebrated in memory of the Lord’s baptism, although the same sacrament was performed and completed in the Lord on the one and same day of the holy Epiphany. For that day is celebrated for three miracles: on it he is visited and adored by kings, guided by a star, in a poor dwelling with his virgin Mother; he is baptized by John in the Jordan in his thirtieth year; and at a wedding, by changing water into wine, he becomes known and is manifested to the world through the glory of his divinity. Since these miracles are great and [Col. 0703D] principal, and works of divine condescension so outstanding cannot be celebrated with due veneration on one day, it pleased Mother Church, under the direction and ordering of the Holy Spirit, that the first day should be given to the Lord’s manifestation, and that the eighth day should be especially revered in honor of the baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as he did all that he did in the days of his flesh not for himself but to free us, so also he wished to be baptized for our sake—he who had neither original sin nor committed actual sin—in order to sanctify for us the streams of all waters, through which all who are predestined to eternal life must be born again and regenerated. It is established that this sacrament of the Lord’s baptism was prefigured in several places of Holy Scripture, just as David, that excellent psalmist, long beforehand, seeing the excellence of that baptism, sang in Psalm twenty-eight:

“The voice of the Lord is upon the waters; the God of majesty thundered; the Lord is upon many waters” [Col. 0704A].

In the three divisions of this verse shine forth the three persons of the Holy Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
