First, where it is said, “the voice of the Lord is upon the waters,” is the person of the Lord the Son; second, where it says, “the God of majesty thundered,” is the person of God the Father; third, “the Lord is upon many waters,” is the work and excellence of the Holy Spirit. And what was the voice of the Lord the Son upon the waters? Surely it was that voice of great and marvelous humility, when, to expiate the sins of all, he who was immaculate and holy came among other sinners to the baptism of John, his servant, [Col. 0704B] and answered him as he trembled, resisted, and said, “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?”: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” He did not say, “Thus it is fitting for me to fulfill all righteousness,” but, “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” What is all righteousness? All righteousness is the true and perfect grace of humility. It is as though he said: “In that I, who am the Creator and Lord of all, do not refuse to come to you, my servant, and to be baptized by you, I provide all my members an example and pattern of humility: they must thus fulfill all righteousness, by not refusing to follow the footsteps of my humility.” This was the voice of the Lord the Son upon the waters.

Now hear how the God of majesty thundered from heaven [Col. 0704C] when he had been baptized: “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” From the beginning God the Father could say these words of no mortal, because in no human being, except this one blessed and most holy Son of God the Father, was God the Father pleased. He alone, free from every contagion of sin, never offended the eyes of the Father’s majesty. God the Father had once chosen and adopted for himself a son and daughter—namely Adam and Eve. Yet he was not pleased in them; indeed, he was greatly displeased, because, disobedient and rebellious toward God, they corrupted and defiled the entire human race. Thus, when crimes had spread everywhere, God is recorded as having said that he repented of having made humankind [Col. 0704D] upon the earth (Gen. VI, 7). This grievous and mournful judgment was changed into new and wonderful joys when God the Father, reconciled with the entire human race in his Son, thundered from heaven, as we have said: “This,” he said, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

And the Lord, the Holy Spirit, is also upon many waters, because, as Luke says, when the heavens were opened he came upon the Lord in bodily form (Luke III, 22); and he not only came but also remained upon him, just as this had previously been indicated and revealed to John the Baptist by the Holy Spirit, who gave him this response: “He upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, [Col. 0705A] this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John I, 33). And what are the many waters except, as it is written, “many waters are many peoples” (Apoc. XVII)? The Holy Spirit fittingly comes upon these many waters, because, just as he then descended visibly upon the Lord, so now also until the end of the age he comes invisibly upon all who are to be baptized, works his sacrament invisibly, and through him, properly and especially, forgiveness of all original and actual sins is bestowed. For he is our propitiation; he is the remission of all sins; and except through him there is no remission of sins.

106 You have now heard the voice of the Lord the Son, the God of majesty thundering, and the Lord the Holy Spirit working [Col. 0705B] upon many waters. Hear still another voice of his, of which the text adds:

The voice of the Lord is in power. Truly the Lord’s voice was in power, because he by no means rendered void in his works whatever he taught, but adorned it with the great authority of his works, just as it is written of him that “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I).

The voice of the Lord is in magnificence. His magnificence is his mercy, which is indeed great, infinite, and ineffable, and surpasses all his works, as it is written: “His mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLI, 9). For what is marvelous or great about his creating, as the Almighty, heaven, earth, sea, and everything in them? [Col. 0705C] We do not marvel so much at the structure of the world; rather, there is something else at which we marvel: namely, his marvelous mercy, by which he bears with and endures the wretched and sinful so that, though he could plunge someone into the abyss by one word, he waits for him and supports him until he fulfills all his will.

Afterward he receives that unworthy person and makes him worthy of himself. Therefore his voice was truly in magnificence. For throughout the time he lived among us, he was unwilling to exercise any severity or punishment upon sinners; rather, in great gentleness and mercy he accommodated himself to sinners and could not be moved to any vengeance upon the guilty, even at the instigation of the Jews.

[Col. 0705D] Thus we read in the Gospel that, when the scribes and Pharisees brought to him a woman caught in adultery, he spoke as follows, answering those who wished to stone her according to the Law of Moses: “Let whichever of you is without sin cast the first stone at her” (John VIII, 7). Confounded by that judgment, all went out one after another, and the wretched woman alone remained with Mercy. And what did true Mercy say to that wretched woman? “Where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?” 107 “No one, Lord.” — “Neither will I condemn you. Go, and sin no more” (ibid.). Behold: this voice of the Lord was in magnificence, in great and exceedingly abundant mercy. And his voice is heard daily; daily this voice of his is in magnificence, because he does not seek the death of sinners but inspires and cooperates so that each may be converted and live.

We may also refer all these things to ourselves, because the incarnate Word worked all these things visibly for our sake, so that sinful humanity might be cleansed and, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, prepared for and joined to God. For by the fact that in this twenty-eighth Psalm the voice of the Lord is described seven times, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified; they worked and rested most fully in Christ and, through him, being distributed among his members, sanctify all the elect and fit the merits of virtues to the Lord. The voice of the Lord is upon the waters when a person despises the vain and transitory joys of the world and abandons wicked and diabolical works. But the God of majesty [Col. 0706B] thunders when, through fear and dread of God, that person returns and has recourse to tearful repentance. The Lord, the Holy Spirit, comes upon many waters when, inflamed with love of the Holy Spirit, one not only bewails evil works and unjust words but also pursues and punishes in oneself the many waters—that is, the many carnal desires and wicked wills—through which one has sinned. Therefore, after this voice of the Lord upon the waters, after the voice of power and the voice of the Lord’s magnificence which we have referred to Christ, the fourth voice, by which he addresses us inwardly, is added:

The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars, and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon. Cedars are trees surpassing other trees in size and height. What, then, is denoted by the cedars except those who surpass others [Col. 0706C] in this world in birth, wealth, and rank, who seek worldly honors and utterly reject the pattern of humility? The almighty Lord breaks these cedars by his voice when, through his gift, they set temporal things aside and choose to serve God in poverty of spirit, so that, fully sanctified at last, they may possess the kingdom of heaven. But by the cedars of Lebanon, a name meaning “whitening,” may be denoted those who are whitened before God by the brightness of modesty and chastity, endowed with learning or loftiness of understanding, and who therefore are especially exalted and glory in their own mind, as if they possessed these things from themselves. The Lord also breaks these cedars when they begin to consider that they can possess neither purity of heart or body nor any light of knowledge without him, and that whenever it pleases him [Col. 0706D] they may be deprived and emptied of all these things. After this kind of voice of the Lord, breaking cedars in these ways, another voice of the Lord follows:

The voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire; the voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness, and the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh. There is the fire of anger which inflames us; there is the fire of pride which consumes us; there is the fire of lust which ravages us and shamefully enslaves us to its domination. But the voice of the Lord cuts through these fires when, these wicked impulses being calmed, hearts are cleansed and cooled by the dew of the Holy Spirit. The wilderness too is shaken by the voice when the human heart, desert and forsaken by God, becomes heaven and God’s dwelling. And the wilderness of Kadesh, which is interpreted “holy,” will be shaken [Col. 0707A] when the soul, now free and cleansed from sins, becomes holy by God’s grace—pure, whitened, and unstained.

After these voices of the Lord is set down the seventh voice of the Holy Spirit, which accomplishes that great work which follows: The voice of the Lord prepares the stags, and he will reveal the thickets; and in his temple everyone will speak glory. What is it to prepare stags except to grant the forest-clearings of contemplation? In these clearings of contemplation the thickets will be revealed, because every chosen person can most rightly and truly perceive himself and recognize and understand the hidden mystery in the thickets of the Scriptures. Then in his temple everyone will speak glory, because the whole person is bound to God by eager and ardent desire: one always wishes to praise him and does not grow weary of always giving glory to his name [Col. 0707B]. The following words are suitably fitting for those who thus contend and run:

109 The Lord makes the flood to dwell, and the Lord will sit as king forever. A flood (*diluvium*) is so called from washing away (*diluere*). And what is denoted by the flood except an abundance of tears, which is well and properly called a flood? For just as long ago, in the flood of waters, all living things perished and were consumed, so in the flood of tears and repentance all things must likewise perish. What things? Certainly all vices and sins, which without doubt are washed away and perish; they will be as though they had not existed, if this flood of tears, by God’s gift, dwells in us. I think this is why worldly people who are sometimes pierced with compunction in tears later return to their former or even worse ways: [Col. 0707C] this flood does not dwell in them, nor has it a firm state with them. Just as they are unhappy because they do not recognize this flood, so, conversely, those in whom this flood dwells will be happy without end: those who strive to wash themselves in this flood not once, twice, or three times, or less often, in a year, but always at the fitting time, so that whatever clings in them from the dust of earthly defilement may perish. In them the Lord will sit as King forever, because, pouring them out with wonderful joy here and in the future, he will rule and possess them by eternal recompense.

But by this flood which the Lord makes to dwell, the water of baptism may also be signified, in which all sins are washed away and forgiven. The Lord fittingly makes this flood dwell, because the same sacrament will endure until the end of the age; and through it the Lord [Col. 0707D] will sit as king forever, because in his children reborn through the Spirit of adoption he himself will reign gloriously here and in the future.

And because we must be cleansed and washed in both floods, of baptism and compunction—for unless one is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, one cannot enter God’s kingdom (John III, 4)—the reward and glory of blessedness which those who live well after baptism, or who have lived badly but repent, obtain from the Lord is indicated in what follows:

[Col. 0708A] The Lord will give strength to his people; the Lord will bless his people in peace. His people are all the elect, to whom he will give in the present life the strength of good action; and after the strength of their completed action he will bless them in peace, giving them the eternity of recompense. He will bless his people in peace when, coming at judgment as the discerner of merits, he says to the good: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

In this blessing there will be great peace and perpetual tranquility, because then everlasting reward will be given to those who now work well, the prize to those who run tirelessly, and the crown to those who contend tirelessly. May Jesus Christ our Lord bring us to this blessing and peace, he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages [Col. 0708B]. Amen.

111 HOMILY XX: FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE PURIFICATION OF SAINT MARY THE VIRGIN

After the days of the purification of Jesus were fulfilled (Luke II).

The present reading from the holy Gospel commends to us the immense and inestimable riches of immortality which the eternal power and wisdom of God has prepared for the co-heirs of his kingdom: “After,” it says, “the days of the purification of Jesus were fulfilled.” Since our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ lived in this world as the only one among sinners free from every sin, it is astonishing what may be meant by his days of purification, on which he ought to be purified according to the Law of Moses. For the lawgiver owed nothing to the law, being a transgressor of no [Col. 0708C] ordinance.

But it must be understood that, since Christ is the head of the body of the Church and all the elect are its members, what Holy Scripture frequently says of him is not inappropriately understood of his members, that is, of the chosen human beings. Thus, by the days of Jesus’ purification may be understood the whole time of this passing age, during which every soul must necessarily be purified daily; and in the devotion of a devout mind it ought carefully to consider that, even if, with God’s help, some virtue or observance is found in speech or deed, it nevertheless cannot preserve inner purity of thoughts. For who, as the Apostle says, will boast of having a chaste heart? What in this life is ever accomplished without the contagion of sin, however slight? Therefore, in these days of Jesus’ purification, Jesus ought to be purified not in his own person but in his members, namely the elect—by the purification which occurs according to the Law of Moses, because, in the life-giving Spirit, the letter of the Law teaches with what diligence unlawful things must be avoided and, if they have been committed, how they must be purified. But after, in the glory of the future resurrection, the days of this sort of [Col. 0708D] purification have been fulfilled, there will take place in all those predestined to life what follows:

“They took him,” it says, “to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the Law of the Lord.” Notice that the Evangelist sets down three laws. The first is where he says: “After the days of the purification of Jesus were fulfilled according to the Law of Moses.” The second is where he says: “They took him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the Law of the Lord.” The third: “And to offer a sacrifice, according to what is said in the Law of the Lord.” We can therefore call the first law, namely the Law of Moses, the law of servitude, through which we are justified. But the written law of the Lord is the limit of death ordained and prescribed by God, which no living person in the lot of the children of humankind can pass over. This second law may be called the law of freedom, through which, having been justified, we shall be freed; for when we lay aside in death this body which is corrupted and weighs down the soul, freed from sin we shall be granted, as it were, a new and true freedom. This law of freedom is followed by the third law: the law of glorification or [Col. 0709B] recompense, when, having received an immortal body in the resurrection, we shall be glorified in body and soul alike by the twofold robe of immortality.

Let us see, then, who they are who, when the days of purification have been fulfilled and completed, take Jesus in order to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the Law of the Lord. They are, indeed, those blessed multitudes of heavenly hosts who attend with diligent ministry at the final examination of judgment in order to distinguish good and evil, as the Lord says in one place: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom all stumbling-blocks.”

113 These angels, princes of the heavenly city, stretch forth [Col. 0709C] arms of joy to take into Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace—the souls of the elect departing from this world, leading them to the prince of life. There they will truly and perfectly be presented to the Lord, never at all to fall into worse things; and just as, established in true blessedness, they never cease to be blessed, so they will never cease from everlasting praise, so that they may rightly say to the Lord: “You have brought your saints into the dwelling-place which your hands prepared.”

And whence come these goods, so great and incomparable? From God, certainly, because “every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” Every male—that is, every manly work—opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord. For the saints who pleased God by strong and manly works then open the womb when, freed from the straits and darkness of this [Col. 0709D] exile, they attain the light of the unfailing sun and deserve to be called holy to the Lord, because there they are made forever holy in conformity with the image of his Son.

And, he says, “that they might offer a sacrifice, according to what is said in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.” This third law, then, is the law of glorification, of which we spoke above: not written, but spoken, because, as Scripture says and teaches, we now hold the promise of heavenly rewards only in hope, not yet in possession. For many and exceedingly glorious things have been spoken to us concerning the city of God and His holy mountain; all these we embrace with the certainty of faith and hope, until we attain the very greatness of eternal blessedness [Col. 0710A]. In the resurrection, therefore, when the third law of glorification shall appear, the holy angels will offer to the Lord a pair of turtledoves—that is, contemplatives—or two young pigeons—that is, those active in life—as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God. By this offering of birds the two lives may indeed be signified: namely, the contemplative and the active. The contemplative life is denoted by the pair of turtledoves, and is greater than the active life, because the latter toils amid the employment of the present time, whereas the former already tastes, by an inward savor, the rest that is to come.

**114** But let us consider why He commanded not simply pigeons, but two young pigeons, to be offered; for individual words require individual mysteries. Although the whole Church together is one dove, “perfect, one of her mother, chosen of her that bore her” (Song of Songs 6), nevertheless diverse doves are found, gathered from differing religious observances into the one harmony of faith. There are, therefore, those who labor in the active life, like two young pigeons, while, laying aside the old man, they begin through good works to grow young into the new. There are also those whose conduct is dovelike: they possess none of the bitterness of gall; with their mouths they utter reproach or injury against no one; and with their claws—that is, their works—they do not injure their neighbor. By turtledoves, however, contemplatives are denoted, who, through the abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, deserve by a certain higher understanding to taste and investigate the mysteries of Christ.

Contemplatives are signified by turtledoves because, under the name of turtledoves, we may perceive, while preserving the faith, God as one in substance and three in persons [Col. 0710C], just as elsewhere we sometimes see the Holy Spirit signified by a dove. But the contemplative person will then be a pair of turtledoves—that is, equal to the Father, equal to the Son, equal to the Holy Spirit, so far as is lawful for mortals—who is now, through an ecstasy of mind enlarged in God, found worthy to receive within himself the divine presence and capable of grasping it. And lest this perhaps seem incredible to anyone—that we have called equal to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit one whom the wisdom of God the Father instructs and sweetly moves through love—let us hear the Apostle saying: “He that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Therefore, because such likeness of Him shines in the hearts of the elect, the likeness of eternity follows also in the resurrection, where, as He is one with the Father, so they too shall be one body with Him, as John says: “We know that, when He shall appear, we shall be like Him” (1 John 3:2). For as He is good, blessed, just, incapable of suffering, and immortal, so we too, in His likeness, shall be good, blessed, just, incapable of suffering, and immortal. Hence it fittingly follows:

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon.” Certainly it will be a joyful “behold” when this man, our mediator Jesus Christ, with all His members belonging to Him gathered into one, will dwell in Jerusalem as one man [manuscript: *dwells*]. And that we may understand this more clearly, let us hear the Lord’s own words: “No man hath ascended up to heaven, but the Son of man which is in heaven; He Himself who descended, He is the one who ascended” [cf. John 3:13]: one and the same Lord and bridegroom in the head, and bride in the body. This man, then, the head with His members, will be in Jerusalem, because what shall be there shall be firm and everlasting, altered by no external force or necessity.

“Whose name was Simeon.” Simeon means “hearing sorrow.” What then? If God is the highest good, what place, I ask, can sorrow have with Him? If joy and gladness are granted to their hearing, what sad or mournful thing will be heard there, to diminish their joys? It must be understood that the souls of the reprobate, bound in everlasting damnation, never pass into the lot of the elect. Yet before the day of judgment they behold the elect in the repose of eternal brightness [Col. 0711B]. The souls of the righteous, joined to the justice of their Creator, are moved by no compassion at their punishments: they see the penalties, but do not feel them; they hear, but do not suffer; and the very torments of the unjust become to them an occasion of joy, so that, while they behold the evils from which they have mercifully escaped, they may render fuller thanks to their Redeemer, because they too might have endured such things had they not been anticipated by the blessings of His sweetness.

But lest it seem harsh and cruel in the saints that they look upon the suffering of the miserable, let us propose an example that makes this highly probable and fitting. If good and perfectly righteous persons in this world, when people commit deeds worthy of wickedness and disgrace, are inflamed with good zeal and rejoice that they are struck with the fitting punishment of correction [Col. 0711C], what wonder is it if those who agree with the very Judge of justice, adhering to Him, bear the torments of the reprobate with equanimity? It follows:

“And this man was just and God-fearing.” For the elect are then just and God-fearing: just through the true love they render to their Creator; God-fearing through a certain filial fear, not servile fear—namely, that fear by which a good, faithful, and disciplined son now fears more to offend his Father out of the sweet affection of love than out of the impending necessity of fear. Of the reverence of this fear the Prophet says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18:10 [19:9]).

“Waiting,” he says, “for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him.” What power of consolation, I ask, will be needed there? It may truly be called great consolation to have passed from the glory of faith to the glory of sight: to wait—that is, to look outwardly, face to face, upon the glory of the assumed man; to adhere to Him and share in Him. And the addition, “the Holy Spirit was in him,” clearly shows that blessed souls possess such brightness of mind and understanding that they can contemplate and perceive spiritually the beauty of Wisdom, of the Word, and of Truth, and consider the ineffable nature of the Godhead itself. The same Holy Spirit, by whose gift and grace they merit to be raised thus high, graciously works in them what follows:

“And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit [Col. 0712A] that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.” Whoever, in this place of mortality and pilgrimage, send forth devout vows and desires toward the palace of heaven receive from the Holy Spirit a good and delightful answer. Although they groan in the body of this death and are held enclosed in the prison of this evil age, where it is wholly unavoidable not to touch sins, nevertheless, under God’s protection, they are never permitted to fall into the death of the soul before they are found worthy at some time to see the Lord’s Christ—that is, God and man.

“And he came in the Spirit into the temple.” Oh, how often we frequent the temple of God—the house, that is, of prayer—when we come there not in spirit but in body alone: with our feet, but not with our affections! But when we merit to enter the holy courts of our God [Col. 0712B], then we come in spirit into the temple, because we no longer seek mentally to go forth toward earthly thoughts.

“And when His parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for Him according to the custom of the law.” By the parents of Jesus those heavenly ministering spirits may fittingly be signified, because through holy and good promptings they beget and form the Lord Jesus in us: faithful companions of the bridegroom, aware of mutual love but in no way envious. They bring in the child Jesus when, at the end of the world, they hasten to unite and bind to its head—that is, to Christ—the whole multitude of the elect [manuscript: *gather*]; and, admiring the same Lord of glory with His members, they do for Him according to the custom of the law.

But let us hear what the parents of Jesus do according to the custom of the law. The holy angels, who always have present before them Him “whom they desire to look into,” and who are always ready to obey His most righteous will, are accustomed to praise and bless Him with unceasing voice. And when any person to be saved departs from the body, they present that person to their Lord with the rejoicing of new praise. Thus, by the custom of the law of angels we may most rightly understand the praise and devotion of their song. Therefore, to do according to the custom of the law for the child who has been offered is, as we have said, once the whole body of Christ has been gathered, to exalt and glorify the head of that body with infinite proclamations of praise. Then what the following narrative intimates is truly accomplished in the saints.

“And he himself received Him into his arms, and blessed God, and said.” For what they were least able to attain perfectly here, they then receive there into their arms, when they cling to Him, bound fast in the arms of inward love, so that thereafter they admit neither word, deed, nor thought by which they might offend the eye of eternal majesty.

Having therefore received gifts so great and so sublime, they bless God, attributing nothing to their own merits but ascribing wholly to the free goodness of God their salvation, saying: “Now Thou dismissest Thy servant, O Lord, according to Thy word, in peace.” As though the elect, inhabiting the city of the living God and beholding the multitude of many thousands of angels, were saying to the Maker and Founder of that city [Col. 0713A]: “Now Thou dost dismiss us”—that is, Thou makest us truly humble—because we, once burdened by the weight of flesh, were unable to render free service to Thee, Lord of all. And therefore, according to Thy word—that is, according to Thy promise, or according to Thy Son—having been released from the stumbling-block of sin, Thou dost console us with manifold peace: granting peace from the world, which attacked us; peace from the devil, who tempted us; peace from the flesh, which always resisted the spirit.

“And this because mine eyes have seen Thy salvation.” We rejoice that we shall see without end, with the eyes of the mind, what the Lord Jesus Christ is in His divinity, and with the eyes of the body, the humanity united to His divinity—He whom we formerly merited to embrace with the eyes of faith.

[Col. 0713B] “Which Thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples.” For Thou didst prepare this Thy salvation—that is, Thy Son, in whose eternal enjoyment we rejoice—before the face of all peoples, when Thou didst ordain that He should be incarnate for the salvation of the human race, so that, seeing Him, people from every nation might believe in Him and, believing, be saved. “A light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of Thy people Israel.” For He came as a light for revelation to the Gentiles, that minds living in darkness might be illumined, and that the people Israel—that is, the multitude of those who see God—might be glorified by a greater grace of His sweetness. Yet by the Gentiles those active in life, and by Israel contemplatives, may not unfittingly be understood. For when the Son shall at some time deliver the kingdom to God the Father, and God shall be all in all [Col. 0713C], there will be for the Gentiles—that is, for those laboring in the active life—a certain splendor and light, and for the people of Israel—those who contemplate God—a glory so great, so such, so ineffable, as “eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love Him” (1 Cor. 2).

Again, by the Gentiles may be understood the number of all the elect, and by Israel the angelic host. The Lord Jesus Christ will therefore be a light for the revelation of the Gentiles when all the elect, gathered from the darkness of this world to the joys of eternity, are so illumined by divine splendor that they contemplate eternally not merely the glory of the assumed man, but also the magnificence of the Godhead itself. He will also be the glory of His people Israel—that is, of the angelic powers, who have always contemplated God from the beginning—an admirable and immeasurable exultation, when the gathering in heaven of the whole multitude of the blessed brings the complete restoration of their number. For those who rejoice over the conversion of one sinner surely rejoice ineffably over the reward of so many righteous persons.

**119 HOMILY XXI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST. BLAISE, BISHOP AND MARTYR**

“If any man will come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow Me” (Luke 9).

Because blessed Gregory, the outstanding teacher of the Church, expounded this Gospel passage brightly and excellently, as one full of the Holy Spirit, we fear that some may be displeased—or that we may even be charged with presumption—if after the words of so great a man we should attempt to speak about it or expound anything from it. Yet because this same reading is read on this solemn celebration of our most holy lord, father, and patron Blaise, we do not think that we detract in this respect from the dignity or excellence of blessed Gregory if, out of the devotion and reverence which we owe to this our lord, blessed Blaise, both by the obligation of servants and by the affection of sons, we dare to say something to his glory and praise, according as the almighty Lord may deign, through his merits, to grant us. Let us therefore approach the exposition of the Gospel reading and set forth, according to our measure, what the Lord shall deign to grant us for the praise and glory of blessed Blaise.

[Col. 0714B] Since our Lord and Savior, who is the wisdom of God the Father, saw and foreknew that not all people could receive this saying, that they should come after Him by denying themselves and taking up their cross, He placed it within human choice when He said: “If any man will come after Me.” For in Sacred Scripture some things are commanded, some forbidden, some permitted, and some recommended. Good things are commanded; evil things are forbidden; intermediate things are permitted; difficult things are recommended. Thus when the law says, “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength; honor thy father and thy mother,” and so forth, good things are commanded. When it says, “Thou shalt not kill; thou shalt not commit adultery; thou shalt not steal,” and the like, evil things are forbidden.

By commandments a person is bound to obedience: good things are commanded to all people, and evil things are forbidden to all people. For whether one neglects the commandments or commits evils, one will be subject to the penalty of guilt. But intermediate things, which are permitted, and difficult things, which are recommended, are placed within human choice. Thus, if one not bound by a higher vow wishes to possess the world, worldly possessions, a wife, and children—those intermediate things which are permitted—let such a person have them in hope of a lesser reward. But one who wishes to come after Jesus—that is, one who resolves, leaving the world and its pleasures, to lead a celibate life after the example of Christ the martyr, which are the difficult things recommended—should undertake it in hope of a greater reward and more excellent glory [Col. 0714D]. The order by which one should attain this, so as to be able to come after Jesus, He immediately shows when He adds:

“Let him deny himself.” This denial is the renunciation of one’s own will. A person denies oneself when one renounces and casts away the life and will by which one lived according to oneself and not according to God, in order to live according to God and God’s will. But since it is not sufficient for a person to deny oneself and renounce one’s own will unless one strives, through repentance and satisfaction, to amend what one has sinned, He added and said:

“And let him take up his cross daily and follow Me.” Notice that He does not say, “Let him take up My cross,” but “Let him take up his own cross.” For Christ’s cross is one thing, the thieves’ cross another [Col. 0715A]. The cross of the thieves is the cross of sinners. A person ought first to take up one’s own cross, signified by the cross of the thieves who suffered for their own crimes, by first tormenting oneself for one’s own sins. And this must be done not for one or two days, but daily, so that by daily repentance and satisfaction, punishing in oneself what one has sinned, one may strive to amend it. Once one has thus borne one’s own cross, one can usefully take up Christ’s cross. For, as blessed Gregory says, Christ’s cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted by abstinence, or the mind is afflicted by compassion for one’s neighbor.

Where a person has denied oneself—where, by abstinence and worthy torments of repentance, one has made full satisfaction to God for one’s sins—one can also follow Christ, which is to take up Christ’s cross. One can, I say, after the example of Christ, who bore the cross for others’ sins, aid before God those who stray through one’s own sufferings: namely, fasts, prayers, and vigils. It follows:

“For whosoever will save his life shall lose it.” By *soul* is sometimes understood the human spirit by which the body is animated and governed; sometimes, a person’s animal life. Here we may indeed understand by *soul* a person’s animal life. Whoever wishes to save it—that is, to make it spiritual from animal, which truly is to save the soul—shall lose it: one shall lose, He says, that life by which one loved the world and the pleasures of the world, in order that one may live for Me alone. “But whosoever shall lose his life for My sake shall save it” [Col. 0715C]. He rightly says, “for My sake,” for there are some who abandon the world and the will by which they seemed attached to the world in order that, while renouncing the few possessions they have, they may thereby obtain and acquire greater goods of this world. Such people lose their souls not for God’s sake but for their own. But whoever loses one’s soul for God’s sake—that is, whoever, having cast away worldly desires, has wholly devoted oneself to the divine will—shall save it. For carrying out the divine will is the certain salvation of the soul that has been lost. It follows:

“For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and lose himself, and suffer loss of himself?” What may be understood by “the whole world” blessed John shows where he says: “All that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16). The gain of this world is pleasure of the flesh, vanity of heart, and pride of mind. A person seems to gain the whole world when, living voluptuously according to the concupiscence of the flesh, one delights in worldly allurements; one gains the world when one falls into the concupiscence of the eyes, that vanity of heart by which one loves and desires even to be praised for one’s voluptuous acts, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. 10:3 [9:24]). After vanity of heart one falls into pride of mind, even beginning to be proud because one sees all worldly things available according to one’s wish [Col. 0716A].

Thus, in gaining the whole world, a person not only gains nothing but suffers great loss, because by such gain one loses oneself and suffers loss of oneself. What is the human being? Let us hear what the supreme Trinity, ordering and disposing all things from eternity, said when It wished to create the human being: “Let Us make man in Our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Therefore, in that part in which one was made in God’s image and likeness, a human being is truly oneself. One loses oneself, then, when one effaces God’s image in oneself; for while following pleasure of the flesh, vanity of heart, and pride of mind, one imitates not God but the world and the devil.

After this follows something worse still: once one has thus lost oneself by abolishing God’s image within oneself, one also suffers loss of oneself. *Detrimentum* (“loss”) is, as it were, called the wearing-down of the mind. One then suffers loss of oneself when one produces a kind of wearing-down of one’s mind: that is, when one wears down and reduces almost to nothing what is most excellent in oneself, namely the reason of one’s mind, in which, through God’s likeness impressed upon it, one ought to know, understand, and love God. Consequently one will not easily be able to return either to knowledge or to the sweetness of divine love. Pride of mind especially produces this wearing-down of mind. For one person sins through pride, another through weakness. The person who sins through pride is in great danger if ever one is to rise to eternal life, which is granted only to the humble; but one who sins through weakness will easily be saved by the loving mercy of divine compassion. For He who willed to become weak for us mercifully considers the weakness of His weak one, in order to save that person. He immediately shows the order in which He does this, saying:

“For whosoever shall be ashamed of Me and of My words, of him shall the Son of man be ashamed when He shall come in His own majesty, and in His Father’s, and of the holy angels.” Although these words are to be understood thus: that the only-begotten Son of God, coming in His majesty on the last day, will be ashamed of and condemn those who are now ashamed of confessing His name; yet in accordance with the sense we have just given, we judge them to have been spoken not only terrifyingly concerning those to be condemned, but also mercifully concerning those to be saved [Col. 0716D]. For there are some in the world who would willingly sometimes do good and would readily despise the vanities of this age, but who in their weak-minded shame fear being despised or mocked by their neighbors if they do not share in their works; in this sense they are ashamed, as it were, of Christ and of Christ’s words.

Nor should we pass over what He says: “Whoever is ashamed of Me and of My words.” In these two expressions He conveys, as I see it, both the work of our creation and the work of our redemption. Thus one is ashamed of Christ and of Christ’s words who does not fear Him because He is one’s Creator, and who is ashamed to show by good living the love by which one ought to love Him because He is one’s Redeemer. But He who willed to become weak in order to condescend to the weak, mercifully considering that person’s weakness as we have said, “will be ashamed of” that person—that is, He will make one humbly ashamed—when He comes in His own majesty, and in the majesty of the Father and of the holy angels.

He comes in His own majesty when, through the visitation and illumination of His grace, a person is shaken and trembles in wholesome fear within oneself because, for one’s sake as an unworthy sinner, the Lord of such majesty willed in His most holy humanity to endure such miseries, insults, injuries, and finally the ignominy of the cross, in order to aid that person’s misery [Col. 0717A]. He comes in the majesty of the Father when a person, humbly considering the excellence and dignity of one’s creation—by which almighty God deigned to create one from nothing in His own image and likeness—is ashamed and groans because through love or fear of this world one ever admitted anything contrary to such great mercy and condescension of His.

He comes in the majesty of the holy angels when, after this humble consideration of the divine mercy which He showed in His humanity, and after recognition of the condescension by which He created one in His divinity, He further enlightens one to consider and dread the most just and unsearchable equity of God’s judgments, which He exercised in that most excellent angelic creature in heaven. Those who refused to remain with Him in obedience He eternally damned because of their pride; but those who remained with Him in the submission of humility He so established in the unchangeableness of eternal stability and confirmed in His love that, just as they do not wish to fall from Him, so they can never fall from Him [Col. 0717C]. The more subtly the person to be saved perceives this, the more strongly one burns in God’s love. For one marvels in oneself that He who did not spare even His angels in heaven has endured for so long, with such marvelous mercy and clemency, oneself, who is dust and ashes, in such madness of sin.

But lest anyone should suppose that these same words of the Lord refer only to the future judgment, when He will indeed come in His own majesty, and in the Father’s, and in that of the holy angels, to judge the human race, He added at the end of the Gospel and said:

“But I say unto you, There be some standing here, which shall not taste of death till they see the kingdom of God.” When He says, “There are some standing here,” He signifies the state of the present life. For those are rightly called “standing here” who, raising and strengthening themselves against sins and vices in this present life—that is, “here”—and striving to remain steadfast in Catholic faith and in constancy of good works, persevere. These indeed are they who shall not taste death: neither that death of the flesh by which the soul is separated from the body, nor that death of sin by which God is separated from the soul, until they see the kingdom of God.

Nor should we cursorily overlook that He says, “shall not taste death.” For the tasting of sins may fittingly be called the tasting of death, because the soul begins to die from tasting sin. But those who stand here shall not taste death until they see the kingdom of God. For as soon as they feel the taste of death—that is, the taste of sin, through which they fear to be separated from themselves and to lose the life of their soul, which is God—drawing near and approaching, they flee to the kingdom of God. They flee to the secret place of their heart, persisting in tears and prayers until they find the kingdom of God within themselves: that is, until they inwardly taste and understand the presence and mercy of Him who comes to them in His own majesty, and in the Father’s, and in that of the holy angels [Col. 0718A].

These are the words of the Gospel reading, which, aided by Christ’s grace, we have briefly run through in exposition for the praise and honor of our most blessed lord Blaise. The Holy Spirit rightly and fittingly appointed it to be read on this sacred solemnity of his. For he was truly one of those standing here whom the only-begotten Son of God foreknew and signified in these words; because, so long as he was here, so long as he was in this present life, he stood so firmly within himself both in the integrity of the Catholic faith and in perfect constancy of good works that he never willed to incline toward the fatal fall of any sin. From his infancy he adhered inviolably to the pure and innocent God, himself pure and innocent in holiness of heart and chastity of body. And because, set aflame by the unquenchable fire of Christ’s love, he loved or desired none of this world’s pleasures or honors, being wholly devoted in body and soul to God, he truly did not taste death. That is, he always strove, through the rigor of his life and through the fervor of a soul burning toward God, to drive away and avoid that death—the death, I say, of sin—by which he might lose almighty God, the life of his soul. Therefore he truly saw the kingdom of God, because he was filled with the grace and sweetness of almighty God reigning within him.

And lest anything might hinder the inward eye of his heart from the vision of this kingdom of God, under the pretext of avoiding persecution according to the Lord’s command, he fled human company—not to escape bodily death, but the death of the soul [Col. 0718C]; that is, so that, dead to the world, he might live more freely for God alone. Hence, when the time of his reward had now come, he was seized and dragged away and compelled toward idols; yet neither beatings, prisons, suspension on wood, the most cruel tearing by which his most holy body was ripped with iron combs, nor even the cutting off of his head could recall him from that unchangeable love in which he was fixed in God, until he passed into that kingdom of God. There he possesses, as the reward of his glorious contest, the joy of eternal blessedness with the angels of God; there, with Him for whose love he denied himself in this world and whose cross he bore on every day of his life, he can obtain grace and mercy for all who hope in him and all who invoke his name in faith and hope.

Let us also implore with humble heart and body the aid of his intercession. For when, placed in the final agony of his passion, he prayed and obtained from almighty God—as the book of his passion recounts—that all who faithfully invoke his name might merit to experience mercy and consolation in whatever necessities they have [Col. 0719A], we, although unworthy, are nevertheless his servants and sons. As we love him with special devotion and rejoice in his glory, so, placing special hope and confidence in the sweetness of his compassion, we ought humbly to submit ourselves to his grace, in order that, through his intercession and merits, we may so stand in this present life in right faith and holy conduct that we do not taste death until we see within ourselves the kingdom of God; and may pass from that kingdom to the kingdom in which we may rejoice eternally with him and all God’s saints. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

**127 HOMILY XXII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST. AGATHA, VIRGIN AND MARTYR**

[Col. 0719B]

“The kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; which when a man hath found, he hideth it; and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field” (Matt. 13).

Our Lord and Redeemer, who, existing in the form of God, willed to become like human beings so that the human being also might be made like God, has set before us in this parable four likenesses which must come to pass in every person striving to attain the likeness of his or her Creator. The first likeness is that of treasure hidden in a field; the second, that of a merchant seeking good pearls and finding one precious pearl; the third likeness is that of a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind; the fourth, that of a learned scribe bringing forth new things and old from his treasure.

In the first likeness is expressed the conversion of a person who, having sold all that one has, merits to find in that field of spiritual life the hidden treasure—namely, the desire for the kingdom of heaven. But because it is not enough for a person merely to be converted unless, after conversion, one also binds and girds oneself for good work pleasing to God, the second likeness is fittingly added, in which it is said: “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls.” By this second likeness, as I see it, the perfect conduct of the converted person may fittingly be understood. To establish and strengthen one in that conduct, the third likeness is altogether necessary, in which it is said: “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind.” The casting of the net into the sea is frequent meditation upon Sacred Scripture. When the person to be saved has perfectly submitted one’s heart to it and, drawing fish from it—that is, living meanings—knows how to choose those which are good and can direct and raise one toward perfect conduct of life, while casting out and rejecting the bad, one at last reaches the fourth likeness. There, made like a householder—that is, like the Son of God Himself—one can beneficially attend by word and example not only to one’s own advantage but also to the benefit and salvation of one’s neighbors.

This is the briefly summarized substance of the Gospel reading. Let us now consider more closely the order of its words, to see whether perhaps, under the guidance of the grace of the Holy Spirit, something may shine forth to us from them that may more sweetly and perfectly teach and inflame us inwardly to seek and find that hidden treasure of heavenly desire.

“It is like,” he says, “the kingdom of heaven unto treasure hidden in a field.” By the kingdom of heaven I judge that the human heart may not unfittingly be understood. The field is the place of any spiritual life which has such cultivators that, diligently cultivating it day and night, they labor to root from the hearts entrusted to them the thorns and briars of vices, and daily to sow within them the good seed—the seed of virtues—both by right living and right teaching. The treasure carefully guarded lest it perish fittingly represents the desire for everlasting life [Col. 0720B]. This treasure is rightly said to be hidden in a field, because it is especially concealed and abundant in such an exercise of spiritual life as has just been described.

Or, if we may put it so, the treasure of the desire for eternal life must especially be sought and found in a hidden field. For the hidden field fittingly represents spiritual people, who tirelessly and unceasingly exercise themselves day by day in spiritual life through manifold efforts of labor. They are rightly and fittingly called a hidden field because they are hidden from the world, hidden from the devil, and known and manifest to almighty God: “For the Lord knoweth them that are His” (2 Tim. 2:19). Thus the kingdom of heaven becomes like treasure hidden in a field when the person to be saved, anticipated by the gift of heavenly mercy, first conceives within oneself a desire for eternal life, considering where one may find such a place of spiritual life that one may deserve, according to the desire conceived in part, to attain eternal life. Thus one begins to moderate one’s former acts and vanities, and begins humbly to supplicate God, that by His assisting grace one may at length bring to fulfillment what one desires. But the devout and merciful Lord does not at all despise a supplication of this sort, as He Himself makes plain when He adds:

Whom, when a man has found it, he hides. A man finds the treasure he desires when, for bringing the longing of his good desire to fulfilment, he receives from God a perfect will; he hides it when he conceals within his mind the desire he has conceived, lest it perish—lest perhaps, if disclosed, it be hindered and delayed either by the devil’s malice or by other people who oppose him in this matter. For joy over it he goes away, when, because of the love by which he has now begun to love God, he abandons the world and its pleasures and submits himself to the labours of the spiritual life. He sells all that he has and buys that field, when he casts aside whatever worldly substance he may possess, whether by distributing it to the poor, transferring it to the place he has entered, or even leaving it for God’s sake, so that he may attain the fellowship of the spiritual life which he desires.

Once the field—that is, the resolution to live the spiritual life—has been purchased, the second parable is altogether necessary, by which, as we have said, perfect conduct is expressed. “Again,” he says, “the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls.” A person in some sense takes on the likeness of the merchant when, considering and pondering the labour and diligence of God’s merchants—that is, the holy people among whom he lives, who labour untiringly in hope of the heavenly homeland—he toils, as though conducting business, in manifold exercises of the spiritual life, so that with God’s help he may at last find fine pearls: namely, the precious ornaments of virtues, such as obedience, patience, chastity, humility, and the rest like these. To one seeking such pearls there is present the wonderful and gratuitous goodness of almighty God, [Col. 0721B] which sometimes advances him to loftier and more sublime gifts of its mercy than the man himself knows how to desire or dares to hope for. Hence it follows:

“But when he had found one precious pearl, he went away and sold all that he had and bought it.” This one precious pearl is the surpassing and pre-eminent inward sweetness of contemplation, by which almighty God refreshes the soul that labours and burns with longing for eternity at the time of prayer, so that it may blaze more strongly and sweetly with love for him. Having found this one precious pearl, he goes away, and having sold all that he has, buys it. He buys it not by trading any of the outward goods which he had long since sold, but at the price of his own body. For he goes away by leaving himself; he goes away by crucifying his flesh with its vices [Col. 0721C] and desires. He sells all that he still had in himself as though free and remaining—namely, his own will. Or if any sweetness remains in his heart in which he still takes carnal delight, he utterly casts it away, so that he may more frequently possess the sweetness of almighty God which he has deserved to taste beforehand. And because nothing so avails to nourish in oneself the grace of this sweetness as continual application to Holy Scripture, the third parable rightly follows, by which frequent meditation upon that same Holy Scripture is understood.

“Again,” he says, “the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind.” By the net, which is woven together in many ways, is fittingly understood the manifold connectedness of thoughts. [Col. 0721D] When a person has perfectly cast this multitude of his thoughts, linked and gathered into one, into the sea—that is, into the depth of the Old and New Scripture—by meditating and ruminating upon it, he gathers, as though from every kind of fish, a multitude of living senses. For from continual meditation upon it he begins to recognize where its meanings are good and useful, and where they are evil and useless. Hence it follows:

“When it was full, they drew it out; and sitting beside the shore, they put the good into their vessels, but cast the bad away.” This filling, by which the net cast into the sea—that is, a person’s thought intent upon the study of reading—is filled, is, as I understand it, the sweetness of God, which is often conceived in prayer after meditation on Holy Scripture. In some sense he draws out the full net when, at the time of prayer, he transfers his thought, drawn from the memory and meditation of Scripture, into what is sweeter and more excellent—namely, into love and desire for the Creator alone—where he then thinks of nothing else but him alone, whom above all things he then loves and desires. When the net has thus been drawn out, he is rightly said to sit beside the shore, by which the solidity and tranquil security of eternal life are fittingly expressed. He is well said to sit not on the shore but beside it, because, although weighed down by the burden of this mortality and not yet able to pass into that perfect abiding-place of eternal blessedness, he nevertheless sits beside the shore, beside [Col. 0722B] eternal life. For nothing in this life brings a person so near to that unchangeable solidity of eternity as the sweetness of prayer and the humility of mind conceived in prayer, signified by sitting. He fittingly adds:

“They put the good into their vessels, but cast the bad away,” because, when in that sweetness of prayer, in which he has perfectly humbled himself before God, he begins rightly to recognize his good and evil thoughts, he puts the good into his vessels when he gathers and stores in the inward receptacles of his heart the upright and perfect thoughts that raise and kindle him toward the love and sweetness of God. But he casts the bad away when he rejects and repels from his heart those thoughts which separate and delay him from God and from God’s sweetness. After all this, the eternal Wisdom of God fittingly adds:

“So shall it be at the consummation of the age.” By “the consummation of the age” may be understood the consumption and extinction in a person of delight in worldly life. It is as though he said: In whatever person the world must be brought to its end—that is, in one who, despising and rejecting the world’s pleasures and vices, desires to attain the perfect love of the heavenly homeland—it shall be thus. Without this order which I have set before you, I say, it can by no means come about. Once this order has preceded—that is, once harmful love of the world has been removed through conversion, good conduct, and continual meditation on Holy Scripture—then at last the Lord’s following sentence will be fulfilled, [Col. 0722D] where it is said:

“The angels will go forth and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire.” The angels go forth when righteous and holy thoughts, which are as it were a person’s messengers to God, effectively manifest themselves in that person. They separate the wicked from among the righteous when a person who has deserved thus to be inwardly illuminated by the mercy of heavenly visitation humbly acknowledges, by discerning them from the good, his perverse and wicked actions. He casts them into the furnace of fire when, with the most ardent fire of compunction, represented by the furnace, he fittingly purges and refines them through repentance.

“There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” For that burning furnace—the mighty fire of repentance, surely burning and kindling within—raises up that smoke which draws forth from the depths of the heart such weeping and tears as perfectly erase and wash away whatever a person has sinned against God by living wickedly. After weeping, gnashing of teeth is rightly placed, by which is understood a strong and rigorous guarding of thoughts and actions.

But because the understanding of all these matters which we have discussed is not granted to everyone in general, the merciful Teacher’s discourse turns particularly to the disciples, as is said in what follows: “Have you understood,” he says, “all these things?” There is no doubt that Christ’s chosen disciples, as the most perfect of all people, understood all these things; for the confidence of their answer indicates this, and the Evangelist fittingly adds: “They say to him: Yes.” They answer confidently that they have understood. And deservedly so. For what could be hidden from their minds, when Wisdom itself, the Lord of all knowledge, nourished and taught them? Yet any blessed person who, exercised in the spiritual life by voluntary conversion, conduct pleasing to God, and continual meditation on Holy Scripture, recognizes this evangelical teaching fulfilled in himself, may confidently answer the Lord with the holy apostles that he has understood all these things. Such a person will be able to be useful not only to himself but also to other people, as the Lord shows at the end of the Gospel, where he says:

“Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.” A person is rightly called an instructed scribe [Col. 0723C] when, by carrying out in good works what he has learned from knowledge of the Old and New Scripture to be done or avoided, he shows these things as though written within himself. Such a person indeed takes on in himself a certain likeness of the supreme householder, namely the only-begotten Son of God, when, after the example of our same Lord, who descended from the seat of his majesty into the depths of our mortality and misery and in a sense left himself in order to redeem us, he seeks not his own interests but those of his neighbours; he sometimes leaves himself in order to gain them, and despises what is his own so that he may watch more profitably over their salvation. He brings forth from his treasure things new and old when at one time, by promising the joys of everlasting life, he delights the hearts of those subject to him so as to kindle them toward love of the good; at another, by threatening the harsh punishments of hell, he terrifies them so as to restrain them from evil.

These are the words of the Gospel reading, which are read fittingly and suitably in praise and glory of the most blessed virgin and martyr of God, Agatha, whose feast we celebrate today. She truly found the hidden treasure. For from her infancy, burning within herself with heavenly desire, she innocently clung to the Lord through purity of mind and chastity of body. Therefore, for joy over it, she went away and sold all that she had, because, through the greatness of love for her heavenly Bridegroom, she despised worldly glory and distributed her riches and possessions to the poor and needy. This was truly to sell all that she had, so that by such a transaction she might become worthy [Col. 0724A] of fellowship in the heavenly kingdom. And because, after the example of the good merchant seeking fine pearls, she exercised herself in the manifold labours of holy and perfect conduct, she deserved, while still living in the body, to find so perfectly that one precious pearl—the grace of heavenly sweetness surpassing all the joys of this world—that nothing in this age could call her back from love of him whose sweetness she had tasted inwardly. Hence what is said fittingly applies to her: “But when he had found one precious pearl, he went away and sold all that he had and bought it.” For she went away by leaving herself; she bought it not only by the substance of outward possessions, which while still living in the body she faithfully distributed for Christ, but also [Col. 0724B] by the shedding of her own blood, whereby, after many kinds of torments, she courageously died for him. For unless she had been inwardly and strongly inflamed by the inextinguishable fire of divine love, she could never have endured in so frail a body those extraordinary and unheard-of tortures—blows, prison, the rack, tortures and cutting off of the breasts, and the other punishments which the book of her passion records. But because, despising all these things, she did not fear to die temporarily for Christ in order to live eternally in him, she has now received, she now possesses, that heavenly pearl: namely, the boundless sweetness and contemplation of almighty God. Adorned with it, she shall rejoice without end in the embraces of her Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0724C] May her most holy intercession with God help us to obtain the same grace of blessedness, so that almighty God may here increase and preserve within us that treasure, the desire for the heavenly kingdom, which by God’s grace we have found in part, and for whose joy and love we despise the passing delights of this present life. Thus, when we have been freed from the miseries of this present life, may we arrive there through the aid of her merits, where, together with her and all the saints, we may rejoice eternally in the full and perfect finding of that precious pearl—that is, in the most sweet vision of our Creator and Redeemer. May our Lord himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all [Col. 0724D] ages of ages. Amen.

135. HOMILY XXIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST AMAND, BISHOP.

“Take heed, watch, and pray; for you do not know when the time will be” (Mark 13).

Although the whole sequence of evangelical Scripture is full of mystical subtlety, the words of our Lord and Saviour, which the very author of sweetness uttered most sweetly with his own mouth to instruct the hearts of his disciples, are so weighted with the fullness of mystical meaning that the human mind can scarcely reach them by investigation. Thus the present reading of the holy Gospel shines in every word with mystical meaning, and the power of the mysteries discerned in it exceeds human eloquence. Yet, [Col. 0725A] so far as we can with his help, let us draw from the words of his exhortation edification and increase in salvation for ourselves.

“Take heed,” he says, “watch, and pray.” Our Lord and Saviour not only admonished by these words his disciples to whom he then spoke bodily, but also plainly made known through these same words what we must do and how we must keep watch. For this threefold division of words openly shows us how everyone to be saved, who desires, forgetting what lies behind, to stretch himself toward what lies ahead, may attain the summit of perfection toward which he strives. Therefore, whoever, pierced by divine inspiration, resolves to renounce the world and its desires, must, as the divine voice admonished at the beginning of the Gospel reading, keep the eyes open to see: that is, he must first wisely understand what he ought to do and what he ought to avoid. For just as a person deprived of the outward sight of the body walks as though in darkness and, setting down his foot uncertainly, sometimes suffers serious bodily injury, so likewise, if the eye of the heart is blunted while the blind mind rolls about in the darkness of ignorance, a person is sometimes miserably deceived by error. He thinks that he is doing works of righteousness, yet grievously offends his Creator by wicked conduct; likewise, he judges himself to be sinning when in fact he does what is right. Hence, as we have said, it is necessary that everyone, [Col. 0725C] at the beginning of conversion, should diligently strive with the vigilant gaze of the heart to discern what he ought to do and what he ought to avoid. But because for anyone coming to conversion it is not sufficient for perfection merely to understand what is right, unless, after receiving the understanding of right living, he also strives to watch through the practice of good works, the Lord fittingly added immediately after exhorting his disciples to see:

“Watch and pray.” A person is commanded to watch—that is, to strive to fulfil in action what he rightly understands, and to drive away from himself by the wakeful zeal of good action the sloth of the idle life in which he had formerly lain. For just as one weighed down by sleep takes the rest of sleep in order, through rest, to sustain and refresh the body—whereas one awake through labour denies himself the benefit of rest—so too one who does not fear to lie in sins and vices in a wicked security sleeps as though badly lulled to sleep. But one who, intent on works of righteousness, strives to be roused from them is rightly said to watch before the Lord. Whoever watches in this way through zeal for devout work, to him the Lord shows a still more eminent way, immediately adding in admonition, “and pray.”

Every elect person, therefore, is commanded to pray: that is, by desiring eternal things, he is to undertake the fruit of devout labour solely in hope of heavenly reward. For prayer is not only that which is performed by movement of the lips; the whole life of every person to be saved, who labours for eternal things, is prayer before God. The apostle Paul seems to have commanded his disciples to persevere in such prayer when he says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17). For we pray without ceasing if, when we do a good work, we seek no glory of earthly praise for it, but think only of what is eternal by desiring it.

This truly threefold order of the Lord’s command in some measure opens for us the way of perfection, so that a person desiring to go from virtue to virtue may learn from these words how he can attain perfection of life. For, as we said above, our Saviour not only admonished his disciples by these words when he spoke bodily to them then, but, speaking spiritually through the same words, he instructs us daily. “Take heed,” he says, “watch, and pray”: that is, take heed by understanding what is right; watch by doing what is good; pray by desiring eternal things. Why, however, we must so earnestly take heed, watch, and pray, he openly shows in the words that immediately follow.

“For you do not know,” he says, “when the time will be.” Our time is when, through some divine visitation, we are brought back to ourselves within ourselves, and either are pierced with remorse for the evil deeds we have committed or are delighted by the vision of eternity. Therefore, because we do not know when the time of so great a visitation will be, we must always watch and pray: that is, by vigilant effort prepare the inner chambers of the heart for the grace of such a visitation. And how we ought to watch and pray, he shows quite fittingly by proposing an example worthy of imitation in what follows:

“It is like a man going abroad who left his house.” This man, whose example of imitation the Lord sets before us in these words of the Gospel reading, is the Creator of all things, the mediator, that is, of God and human beings, God and man, who for the sake of human redemption deigned to become man. This man of such nobility, who was made for us by God the Father righteousness, exhorts us to follow his footsteps: namely, that we should strive, taught by his example, to imitate the virtues which he possessed in fullness. Who among mortals ever could or can become like him through the merit of a praiseworthy life? Who, I ask, could in this mortal life equal the author of holiness, purity, chastity, and patience with an equal pre-eminence of virtues? No one at all—truly, no human being born of woman—can be made like him, who was conceived and born without the contagion of sin. But we must follow the footsteps of our Redeemer in these exercises of virtue, so that, sanctified in truth after his example, we may strive to appear pure in heart and body in the eyes of the divine majesty, and after his example may strive to persevere in humility and patience.

“He,” he says, “who went abroad left his house.” What was the house of this most noble man, and what was that journey abroad upon which he went after leaving his house? This most glorious house—the house, I say, of eternal sanctification—was his body, [Col. 0727A] in which the fullness of all divinity dwelt. He truly left this house when, having completed all the sufferings of his passion, he gave up his spirit while lifted upon the altar of the cross. And then indeed he went in some sense upon a journey abroad, because with his soul alone he descended to hell in order to free souls. This house may also signify the Church, in which this heavenly man chose to dwell bodily during the days of his flesh, as the blessed apostle and evangelist John testifies concerning our same Redeemer and his body, namely the Church, saying: “He came unto his own, and his own received him not” (John 1:11). He likewise left this house when, after his resurrection, ascending to heaven, he left his Church, which is his body, bodily here. The kingdom of heaven is called a foreign country because it was in some sense foreign and alien to all who journeyed in the valley of tears, and before this man’s entrance into the kingdom of heaven no entrance into it was open to any human being. Therefore this man, the mediator indeed of God and human beings, Christ our Lord Jesus, being about to go abroad, commanded and assigned what duty to those whom he left bodily, his beloved ones, as may be understood from the following words.

“And he gave to his servants authority over every work.” The servants of this Lord may fittingly be understood as the holy apostles, to whom he gave authority over every work when he imposed upon them the office of saving doctrine and at the same time subjected to their jurisdiction the pontifical power of binding and loosing. Thus, by their preaching, they might open the entrance of the heavenly kingdom to those converted to faith by removing the burden of their sins; but close the entrance of that kingdom to those who did not believe and persevered in unbelief, as he promised when sending them to preach: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

The servants of this Lord may also be understood as the teachers of the holy Church, to whom authority over every work has been entrusted by the Lord, because in the place of the apostles they have in this world the power to forgive sins. But it must be more carefully noted that he says distinctly, in a sense, “authority over every work.” For our Lord and Saviour performed all his works—whatever he did in the midst of the earth—for our salvation. Hence every work in which provision is made for human salvation, and through which a person is led to fellowship in eternal salvation, is rightly called good. Thus, just as the Lord then gave the apostles, so now he gives the vicars of the apostles, namely the rulers of the holy Church, authority over every good work, because he raises them to the summit of governance in order that they may remember to benefit others. He gives them the power of binding and loosing, upon whom he lays this special duty: that they may be able to free those weighed down in sins from the burden of sins. It follows:

“And he commanded the doorkeeper to watch.” This doorkeeper may first be understood as Peter the apostle himself, the chief of the apostolic order; then his fellow apostles may fittingly be understood as doorkeepers, for they received from the Lord the key of the kingdom of heaven. The Lord commanded them to watch because he appointed them leaders for shutting and opening the gate of eternal life.

But all these things which we have now briefly touched upon according to the allegorical sense may be investigated with a more subtle inquiry according to the moral understanding, so that we may truly understand all that we have said to signify our Redeemer as applying fittingly to ourselves. “Take heed,” he says, “watch, and pray.” And shortly afterward he suitably shows by a clear example how we ought to watch and pray: “It is like a man who went abroad and left his house.” A human being (*homo*) is so called from soil (*humus*), because he was created from soil. Thus, a person may fittingly be understood here under the name “man”: one who is still devoted to earthly activities and knows only to seek the things that the appetite of mortal life urges. He goes abroad when, renouncing the world and its desires, he does not delay to pass from worldly life—like the homeland of an inherited estate—to spiritual conduct, as though to a sojourn in a far country.

He leaves his house when he strives wholly to alienate and cut off from himself earthly desires or the desires of his own flesh, in which he formerly delighted in the hidden place of his heart as though in the familiar privacy of his own house. We may also understand by this man who went abroad and left his house any spiritual person who, although he appears bodily free from worldly actions, yet allows his mind to range by wavering around the occupations of earthly vanity. When, pierced by divine inspiration, he strives to withdraw himself from these, he has in some sense gone abroad and left his house, in which he had formerly dwelt wickedly but sweetly.

“He gave,” he says, “to his servants authority over every work.” What more fittingly can we understand by the servants of this man than the faculties of the twofold human being, namely soul and body? A person gives his servants authority over every work when he not only restrains his outward senses to works of devotion, [Col. 0728D] but also, having gathered the faculties of the inward person, remains wholly, so to speak, attentively awake in the praises of his Creator. And this is rightly called a good work when, as we have said, a person devotes his whole self, soul and body, to the service of divine praise. But what diligence and what rigorously guarded watchfulness he must still employ in his soul while thus intent and thus devoted to good works may be plainly gathered from what the present reading immediately adds:

“And he commanded the doorkeeper [the codex here and above reads *praecipiat*, ‘that he command’] to watch.” What can we understand more fittingly here by the doorkeeper than the reason of the soul? Human reason is that power of the soul by which it contemplates God and heavenly things alone.
