This reason must keep watch as a vigilant guard over the inner chambers of the heart, so that it may hold fast, as though with certain keys of strict observance, the intention of the human heart, lest it seek the glory of human praise for works of righteousness.

And it should be noted that it says, “that he command him to watch.” For a person must restrain the inner things of the heart, as though under the rule of his own authority, by the custody of discipline, lest the mind go out through the desire for human favour; lest one who seems outwardly to excel in the virtue of good works inwardly take delight in the glory of favourable regard. But because a person cannot at all stand perpetually upright at such a height of virtues by his own power, nor keep such watch around the guarding of the mind that the merits of good works are not emptied by vain glory, divine mercy must come to his aid, and the protection of the right hand of the Most High itself must guard the works of his hands, as the Psalmist entreats, saying: “The Lord,” he says, “shall guard you; the Lord is your protection upon your right hand” (Ps. 120:5 [121:5]).

By the right hand good works are understood, just as, conversely, every wicked action is denoted by the left. Unless these works are guarded by divine protection, they are easily overthrown when the disturbance of temptation breaks in and are turned in another direction. Hence the same Psalmist immediately adds: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (ibid., 6). In sacred discourse, day is sometimes used to signify good action; the sun, prosperity; night, adversity; and the moon, good reputation. Good action is aptly signified by day, prosperity by the sun, and good reputation by the moon, because just as the moon has no brightness of radiance from itself unless it receives it from the sun’s ray, so good reputation arises only from the excellence of good action. But what does it mean that this sun is said to burn by day, while the moon burns by night? One is burned by the heat of the sun when one is lifted up in a time of prosperity; but one is burned in the night, as it were by the moon, when one is cast down through impatience in a time of adversity. The sun burns by day through the pride of prosperity; the moon burns through impatience in adversity. But lest the sun’s heat burn us by day or the moon by night—that is, lest we be puffed up and exalted by prosperity, or broken and cast down through impatience in a time of adversity—the Lord himself again commands us in words of admonition to watch, so that we who do not know when the master of the house will come may stand ready for his coming in anxious expectation. Hence it immediately follows:

“Watch therefore; for you do not know when the master of the house will come.” Who is this master whose coming we must await in watchfulness, and what is his house, which must always be ready to receive a master of such authority? This master is our Creator himself; and his house is our heart, which then truly becomes his house when a worthy dwelling is prepared for him in it, so that he may delight to dwell familiarly in the habitation of the heart, as though in the familiar privacy of a house. “For you do not know,” he says, “when the master of the house will come.” Here the Lord more clearly explains what that time is of which he said at the beginning of the Gospel reading, “You do not know when the time will be.” This time, as we said above, is the hour of divine visitation, in which this master of the house—the indweller, that is, of hearts—deigns through the grace of his innate goodness to visit the soul of any person to be saved. To receive into our house, that is, our heart, the author of our salvation, we must watch frequently and prepare the house of the heart with utmost care. For the following words plainly show how this master of the house comes and by what diverse modes of visitation he anticipates each of the elect: “In the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning.”

The Lord comes in the evening when, by hidden inspiration, he visits a person so that he begins to consider with himself how uselessly he has spent all the days of his life, how by living slothfully he has neglected to perform works of righteousness; and thereby, with the saving anxiety of sorrow, he afflicts himself before God. He comes at midnight when, by inward visitation, he opens the eyes of the human heart so that it can carefully weigh how, blinded by the darkness of sins, it has been wrapped as though in the dense gloom of night; and therefore, in bitterness of soul, does not cease to lament the guilt of its wicked conduct.

But some do not possess the grace of such subtle understanding that they are able by their own sense to consider the matters we have mentioned or to recognize for themselves with subtle discernment how many stains of sin they have acquired by wicked living. The Lord visits these people as though coming at cockcrow through the grace of his advent, when through the voice of any devout preacher he makes known to them the manifold ugliness of their sins. He also comes in the morning when, either by inward visitation or by the admonition of a devout teacher, a person recalls to the eyes of the heart that final morning in which we must all either be crowned eternally or condemned eternally, and frequently considers with anxious meditation of heart what answer he will give to the strict Judge when rendering an account. Of this morning—that is, the day of future judgment—the Psalmist says: “In the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Ps. 5:5). The Lord comes in the evening, that is, in remembrance of neglected righteousness; he comes at midnight in remembrance of sins; he comes in the morning in remembrance of the future judgment; and this by means of cockcrow, that is, preaching, because nothing so rouses the human heart to think of and retain these things in memory as the frequent admonition of a devout preacher. In these four ways, as we have said, the Lord visits all whom he intends to save; but those whom he has not predestined to fellowship in eternal salvation he admits to the grace of none of them.

“Lest, coming suddenly,” he says, “he find you sleeping.” The Lord, when he comes, finds a person as though sleeping if a heavy sleep of mind so oppresses that person that no remembrance of any of the things mentioned above can rouse him to watchfulness. Hence the apostle Paul speaks thus of those who, so badly lulled to sleep, roll about in the darkness of ignorance: “Those who sleep sleep at night” (1 Thess. 5:7). It follows:

“But what I say to you I say to all: Watch.” By these words the Lord plainly declares to us that the admonitions of salvation which he set before his disciples in the days of his flesh were proposed not only for their imitation but that he also wished these same words of most saving admonition to be prescribed for our edification. It should be noted, moreover, that in the present reading of the holy Gospel the Lord has now for the third time commanded his disciples to watch. It is as though he said: Watch by doing good; watch by guarding good things; watch by persevering in good things. The Psalmist seems to express this in a brief formulation: “Turn away,” he says, “from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27 [37:27]).

[Col. 0731B] Therefore, whoever strives to attain the summit of perfection has great need, if he watches by doing good, also to strive to watch by guarding good things and to persevere until the end of life in those things which he does and guards well, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY XXIV. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE CHAIR OF ST PETER AT ANTIOCH.

“Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi and questioned his disciples, saying: ‘Who do people say that the Son of Man is?’” (Matthew 16.)

The most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, whose solemn feast we celebrate today, is truly that man whom God exalted above all his companions; for just as he himself honored God’s Son with the marvelous and unheard-of glory of a new confession, wholly unknown to all people before him—“You are,” he said, “the Christ, the Son of the living God”—so the Only-begotten Son of God exalted this most steadfast confessor of His divine and human nature with the marvelous and unheard-of grace of a new praise and reward, in heaven and on earth: “Blessed are you,” He says, “Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon [Col. 0731D] earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

Behold, we have heard the steadfastness of blessed Peter’s confession; behold, we have heard the glory of blessed Peter’s reward. From this it is clear how great is his glory in heaven, since God raised him, while he was still living on earth, to such an excellence of dignity that, at his nod and command, the kingdom of heaven should be shut and opened. For his glory and power have neither been altered nor diminished, because he lives with Him in whom he believed, whom he confessed, whom he served, in whom he possesses all things, and through whom he is able to do all things.

Having briefly set forth these things concerning the glory of blessed Peter, if we consider more closely, we shall find at the beginning of this evangelical [Col. 0732A] reading a great lesson in humility and steadfastness in him. “Jesus,” says the Evangelist, “came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, and questioned His disciples, saying: Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” That our Lord and Savior, who was truly the Son of God, calls Himself the Son of Man—He who became for us the Way—sets before us the way of true humility, so that no one may exalt himself either because of nobility of birth or because of the distinction in wisdom or knowledge divinely bestowed upon him; rather, judging humbly and lowly concerning himself, he should always submit himself to humility. For He who was truly the Son of God could have called Himself the Son of God; but suppressing that which belonged to the strength of His divinity, He spoke of that which He possessed through the weakness of His humanity. If He did this in order to give us an example of humility, how much more [Col. 0732B] ought we, who are mere human beings, both to think and to speak humbly and lowly of ourselves? For, as the Apostle says, “the weakness of God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1:25). God’s weakness is God’s humanity. What was weak in Him was stronger than all our strength. For we human beings are conceived and born from human beings in sins; but He, as was never heard before Him and never shall be after Him, the Son indeed of one human being only—the most chaste Virgin—was conceived and born without sin. Therefore, whoever carries out humility in word and deed truly imitates God, who became humble for our sake; but whoever walks with a proud heart is an imitator of him who, exalting himself above himself, wished to be like the Most High.

[Col. 0732C] Nor should we cursorily pass over why He wished to come into the region of Caesarea Philippi in order to inquire into the opinion and judgment concerning Himself, whether of His disciples or of outsiders—a place where, because of fear of the rulers to whose jurisdiction the city was subject, it was dangerous even to think of the name of God. Thus the Lord wished, in the region of this city, where fear and trembling before rulers prevailed, to hear, after the common opinion of the crowd, also His disciples’ estimation of Himself, in order thereby to teach us that, if we desire to share their rewards, we should follow the steadfastness of their faith and confession. And just as blessed Peter—and in him the whole apostolic company—did not fear to confess with an undaunted heart the truth which, by God’s revelation, he knew [Col. 0732D] in Christ, so neither should we withdraw ourselves from truth because of fear or love; but, if we are questioned, we should not fall away from truth, even on account of the danger of death.

But if we consider more subtly, the eternal Son of God, who did all things in wisdom, nothing without cause and a definite purpose, and whose deeds, no less than His words, were sometimes prophecies of future things, prefigured in this action of His—namely, His care to come, not elsewhere but into the region of Caesarea Philippi, in order to ask and learn from His disciples both what people said of Him and what the disciples believed concerning Him—something that He was still to do in His Church for the manifestation and propagation of the excellence of His divinity. Caesarea [Col. 0733A] Philippi, which is called from Caesar, interpreted as “chief possession,” and from Philip, interpreted as “mouth of a lamp,” plainly signifies the magnificence of Caesarean dignity and honor. For at that time this was a mark of Caesarean dignity: Caesars or kings were never seen without the finest royal apparel that could be obtained upon earth; nor were they greeted by anyone, however great his dignity or nobility, unless adoration and the kissing of their feet had first been offered.

From the excellence of this Caesarean dignity, therefore, because our Lord and Savior decreed to assume certain features for Himself in His vicar—that is, in the man who is head of the Church, namely the Roman bishop—for the exaltation of His holy Church, He fittingly came not into Caesarea Philippi itself but into the region [Col. 0733B] of Caesarea Philippi. In the imperial dress and in all the honors paid to him—in adoration and in the kissing of feet—He took for Himself an elevation of honor; He left to them the cruelty of imperial government by which they punish people. For, after the manner of Caesar, he is never seen in public without purple or without the honor of imperial garments; and he is seldom greeted by anyone unless adoration and the kissing of his feet have first been offered.

But what does the name Philip signify? Christ came into the region of Caesarea Philippi because He wished both names, Caesar’s and Philip’s, to be fulfilled in this same vicar of His. Philip is interpreted “mouth of a lamp.” He whose duty it is both to proclaim in words and prove by deeds Christ’s truth ought to be the mouth of the true lamp, that is, of Christ. And although he is to be revered, honored, and magnified in Christ’s place and stead by all Christ’s members—that is, the children of holy mother Church—yet, after the example of Him who, though Lord of all, became for our sake the lowliest of all human beings, he should preserve humility and should set forth and teach the way of humility in word and deed.

The Lord and Savior indeed then foreshadowed this dignity now bestowed upon His Church, but He did not bring it to completion immediately in the times of the apostles. For the age of the martyrs followed the age of the apostles; and while impious persecutors of the Christian name reigned, all who confessed Christ [Col. 0733D] were killed like sheep, as though of no account. But after the persecution of the martyrs subsided in the reign of the Emperor Constantine—who, baptized by blessed Pope Sylvester and cleansed of leprosy, became a magnificent worshipper of Christ and bestowed upon that same blessed Sylvester the honor and power of his imperial dignity, for the honor of God and holy Church, obeying him as a son obeys a father and serving him as a servant serves his lord—this was, in a manner of speaking, as I said, Jesus’ coming into the region of Caesarea Philippi. From that time holy God’s Church began to flourish with the excellence of Caesarean dignity.

That He questioned the disciples whom men said the Son of Man was not before, but after, He came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, mystically prefigured that time [Col. 0734A] in which, after the persecution of the martyrs had been stilled, a graver and more intolerable evil welled up from the very entrails of holy Church: namely, the Arian heresy. It penetrated and devastated the whole body of the Church so thoroughly that almost the whole world followed Arius, apart from a few servants of Christ, such as Athanasius, Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine, who then stood with Christ and began most steadfastly to defend Christ’s faith. Thus, to ask His disciples whom men said the Son of Man was meant to test His disciples in that most savage storm, to see what either those who were of the earth—that is, human beings—or those who were of heaven and loved heavenly things, believed concerning the Son of Man. “For there must be heresies,” says the Apostle, “so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19). For all who held Christ’s perfect faith then truly began to be made manifest as Christ’s disciples.

And because there were diverse heresies—some erring concerning the Father, some concerning the Son, some concerning the Holy Spirit, and rashly asserting that the Son was less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than the Son—the disciples rightly answered: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah.” And because they held their greatest heresy in Christ’s humanity and concerning His humanity, they rightly added: “or one of the prophets.” They said that He was one of the prophets because they utterly denied that He was the true and eternal Son of God. But because those who were approved had to become manifest, [Col. 0734C] Jesus says to them: “But whom do you say that I am?”

[148] Simon Peter answered and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Here Peter did what he was always accustomed to do whenever an opportunity offered itself for showing the steadfastness of his most fervent love for God. Among Christ’s disciples he was always first; he was always the one to break forth; and he loved more than all the rest, as the Lord Himself attests when He says: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15). As though snatching the word from the mouth of all the others, Peter alone answered before all and for all: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Jesus answered and said to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but [Col. 0734D] my Father who is in heaven.” What, I ask, was such power and such marvelous merit in Peter’s words that, after words so simple, he should deserve such gifts of blessedness and such proclamations of praise from the Lord? At times he spoke greater words, but never deserved to be thus praised by the Lord: “Even if all are scandalized in you,” he says, “I shall never be scandalized” (Matt. 26:33); “I lay down my life for you” (John 13:37); and again: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke 22:33). These words were indeed great, and the purpose of his heart agreed with the words of his mouth, for as he spoke with his mouth, so he held in his heart—although he did not persist in these words when, accused by the maid who kept the door, he denied Christ.

Yet, according to the dignity of the mystery, this confession—“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”—was greater because it was more excellent. For it is as though he had said: No, Lord, I do not call You John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets; rather, I know that You are Christ, the true Son of God. For You are that anointed King who must save the whole world through Your most holy humanity; You are the Son of the living God, equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with God the Father in the excellence of Your divinity.

In this marvelous confession and faith of blessed Peter, previously unknown to all people, we who are reckoned, in the person of blessed Peter, within the womb of holy mother Church are taught what we ought to believe concerning our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. We ought [Col. 0735B] to believe Him to be our Creator; we ought to believe Him to be our Redeemer. For by the power and might of His divinity He created us; by the mercy and sweetness of His humanity He delivered us. He created us that we might exist; He delivered us that we might exist well. And because redemption bestowed more upon us than creation—for we should have been created to our misery unless we had been redeemed—blessed Peter rightly placed the work of redemption before the work of creation, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

From these two facts—namely, that He who is our Creator is also our Redeemer—arise two movements of the soul: the fear and love of God. For it is not enough for our salvation that we believe Him to be our Creator and believe Him to be [Col. 0735C] our Redeemer, unless we love Him as our Redeemer and fear Him as our Creator. We ought to love Him because He redeemed us; we ought to fear Him lest perhaps He who created us from nothing reduce us to nothing. We ought to love Him in order that, for love of Him, we may do good things; we ought to fear Him in order that, for love of Him, we may endeavor to avoid evil things. This is the right and perfect confession of true faith, which is truly praised and rewarded by the Lord: “Blessed,” He says, “is Simon Bar-Jonah.” Simon is interpreted “obedient,” and Bar-Jonah, “son of the dove.” For he who fears God because He is his Creator, and obediently observes God’s commandments in the fear of God, is rightly called Simon. But he who loves God because He is his Redeemer, and, like a son of the dove, without the gall of bitterness, in the sweetness of dovelike simplicity does whatever good he can for the love of God alone, may rightly be called Bar-Jonah, that is, son of the dove. Such a person is truly blessed, because he shall both be made blessed by the Lord in this present age and be rewarded in the future with the imperishable prize of eternal glory.

That this blessedness should be attributed not to human endeavor but to the ineffable grace of God alone, the Lord teaches us in the following words when He says: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah.” It is as if He said: You are blessed, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. What are flesh and blood? In flesh we may understand the operation of the body; in blood, wherein the soul has its seat, [Col. 0736A] the consideration of the heart. And it is as though He said: That you believed Me, Christ, to be the Son of the living God; that you knew Me as your Creator and Redeemer as you ought to know Me—believe that this is to be attributed not to the merit of your own action, nor to the knowledge of your wisdom or understanding. For you received it not from yourself but from the mercy and sweetness alone of my Father who is in heaven.

And because my Father, who is in heaven, has wrought these things in you, I also say to you—for my works are inseparable from the works of my Father. Whatever my Father has wrought in you, I have indeed wrought with the Father; and whatever I shall do with you, my Father will do in you with Me. I indeed say to you, whose speaking is doing, that you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build [Col. 0736B] my Church. It is as though He said: Because, by the revelation of my Father who is in heaven, you have deserved to know what fear and honor you owe to my divinity, by which I created you, and what sweetness and love you owe to my humanity, by which I redeemed you, therefore I also say to you that you are Peter: giving you grace for grace; that is, endowing you with a greater gift of knowledge of Me, and exalting you with a greater steadfastness in my love and fear.

“And upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” The Church of God is called the whole assembly of believers throughout the world; any good congregation is called the Church of God; any good and faithful soul may also be called the Church of God. Whether it be the whole Catholic Church together, any good congregation, or [Col. 0736C] any holy soul, founded upon this rock—that is, upon the foundation of apostolic faith and love—the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; for although sins and vices, which are truly the gates of hell, assault it, they cannot prevail against it.

How can they not prevail against it? Certainly in this way: when a righteous person falls, even if he has slipped down to the very gates of hell, the love, hope, and consolation of God which he has toward God will draw him out from the very jaws of hell.

This chosen disciple of the Lord, blessed Peter the apostle, of whom we speak, came as it were even to the gates of hell when he denied Christ. But because he had first laid beneath his heart the foundation of true love, by which he loved Christ above himself, [Col. 0736D] although the gates of hell had drawn him somewhat, they nevertheless did not prevail against him. For he immediately acknowledged his guilt, went out, and wept bitterly.

Let us consider also blessed David, king and prophet, who likewise in some measure came to the gates of hell when he committed adultery and murder together. But because before his fall he had possessed a heart most devout in the love of God, after committing the crime the gates of hell did not prevail against him. For with as great a sweetness of delight as he committed sin, with so great a bitterness of repentance he afterward sought to punish it in himself. For as soon as he learned from the mouth of Nathan the prophet that he had offended God in the crime he had committed, he answered from a truly humble and penitent heart: “I have sinned [Col. 0737A] against the Lord.”

Judas, one of the Twelve, after betraying the Lord, seeing, as Scripture says, that He was condemned, threw down the silver coins and said: “I have sinned, betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:6). David and Judas alike uttered the word of confession, for each said, “I have sinned.” But because in a similar confession their intention was not similar, a similar fruit of repentance and confession did not follow. The gates of hell could not prevail against Peter and David; they did prevail against Judas. For as soon as, as we have said, they sinned and recognized that they had sinned, they could not despair of God’s mercy and compassion, from the most faithful heart by which they had always loved God. But Judas, because he had not first possessed the foundation of divine love—for he always walked with our Lord Jesus Christ with a treacherous [Col. 0737B] and wicked heart, and never loved Him—could have no hope in God, but went away and hanged himself with a noose.

Therefore, because one who truly loves God can never perish, but always, as we have said, receives grace for grace, the Lord adds:

“And I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” These words, indeed, were spoken by the Lord not to Peter alone but also to his other fellow apostles. For as they stood with Peter as true confessors of the one and same divinity and humanity of Christ, so beyond any doubt they received with Peter the same keys that were entrusted to Peter, namely the same power of binding and [Col. 0737C] loosing. Yet they were given in a special manner above all others to blessed Peter himself, who, being foreordained by God as the future shepherd of the Church, alone answered for all.

Every prelate and teacher of truth still in holy Church likewise has this power from God; but above all others, in a special manner, he has it who presides and rules over all in the office and place of blessed Peter, and who alone, above all mortals, can loose what others have bound and bind what others have loosed.

But we may understand these same words in another way. The kingdom of heaven is the human body and soul, as the Lord testifies when He says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). The keys by which this kingdom [Col. 0737D] of heaven is opened and entered are knowledge and power. Peter had one key, the key of knowledge, because he both believed and confessed Christ to be the true Son of God when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” But he did not have the other key, the key of power, because he was not yet able to die for Him. For if he had possessed the key of power together with the key of knowledge, he could not have denied Christ out of fear of the maid who kept the door. Nor had the Lord said to him, “I give you,” but “I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” He did not give them immediately when He promised them; rather, only after the coming of the Holy Spirit did Peter himself, together with his fellow apostles, receive from God these two keys of perfect knowledge and perfect power, so that they might know all things [Col. 0738A] that had to be known concerning Christ and might be able to endure and do all things that had to be endured and done for Christ. Then for the first time they confidently and boldly preached Christ’s glory before kings and rulers, confirming what they said by the mighty testimony of works and miracles.

The Lord manifests the power of this knowledge and authority when He says in what follows: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” These words were perfectly fulfilled in blessed Peter and his fellow apostles: for those to whom they shut the kingdom of heaven shall find it shut, and those to whom they open the kingdom of heaven shall find it open. But these same words also apply generally to the universal holy Church, [Col. 0738B] because whoever are called prelates in holy Church must necessarily be endowed by God with these two keys. For if they do not possess the key of knowledge, they cannot possess the key of power.

Hence the Lord commanded in the Law: “If there is a plague of leprosy in a man, he shall be brought to the priest, and he shall look at him; and the priest shall shut him up again for seven days, and shall consider him on the seventh day; and if the leprosy has not increased further nor spread in the skin beyond its former limits, he shall shut him up again for another seven days” (Lev. 13:9 ff.). The key of knowledge must indeed be possessed and continually exercised, which is signified by the confinement of seven and seven days. For if he sees that during the first seven days, by which the present time is understood, the leprosy has not spread beyond its former limits in the skin—that is, if the sinner [Col. 0738C] is unwilling to turn from his sin, which is leprosy—then the second key, the key of authority, must be applied, so that he may be shut up again for another seven days; that is, so that, because the leprosy persists, he may without delay be consigned to everlasting condemnation.

But we may apply these same words, which we have said pertain generally to the prelates who are in holy Church, specifically to every person. The key of knowledge is necessary to a person, so that he may know the good he should do and the evil he ought to avoid. Yet since many know what should be done but lack the strength and power to do what they know ought to be done, one key is of no avail without the other. For knowledge is of no avail without power, nor power without knowledge.

After these two keys have been received, the grace which follows is immediately declared in the words that follow: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” By earth we understand the body; by heaven, the faculties of the inner person. There are some indeed who bind and restrain themselves from sins and vices in the body, and yet cannot avoid sins in the inner person. But while they do [154] what they can, through God’s mercy there is added to them also what they cannot do. This is what He means when He says, “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven.” It is as though He said: If in your outward person you endeavor to restrain and bind yourself from sins in sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, by the gift of my compassion you shall also be kept in your inner person from harmful desires and thoughts.

A person ought indeed to be bound against sin and loosed for good. Therefore the Lord added and said: “Whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” It is as though He said: If by the outward action of your body you labor to be loosed for doing good works, by my gift you shall also be able inwardly to have a heart loosed unto the sweetness of my true love. But why did He say this, except because there are some who diligently do for God the good works which they are able to do bodily, but their mind does not concur with their outward acts through inward sweetness? This is, as it were, to be loosed upon earth but not loosed in heaven. Yet while they render the endeavor of good works outwardly with diligence and watchfulness, they receive from God what they do not yet possess: namely, that in heart as well as in body they may discern, love, will, and be able to do what is good. Thus at last is fulfilled what is said: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

This is the teaching of today’s Gospel reading, by which the eternal wisdom of God instructs us. But because we can neither be bound against evils nor loosed for good things without His gift and grace, may He, with whom nothing is impossible, deign to give and help us, so that, bound against evils and loosed for good things, we may so please Him in the present life that the gates of hell may not prevail against us in the hour of our departure, lest at any time our enemy say: “I have prevailed against them” [Col. 0739C] (Ps. 12:5); but, led and helped by Him, may we arrive where, seeing and praising Him without end, we may rejoice eternally with Him. May He Himself deign to grant this, He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[155] HOMILY XXV. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST. MATTHIAS THE APOSTLE.

Jesus answered and said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11).

At the beginning of this reading, as we have already heard, we read that the Only-begotten Son of God rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and answered. But we do not read why He rejoiced, or what and how ineffable were the words to which He answered. He answered, indeed, Himself—that is, His own divinity, by which He was God and by which He eternally possessed all things with the Father. And just as the conversation by which the Father spoke with the Son is ineffable and incomprehensible to human understanding, so the Only-begotten Son’s answer to the Father is unspeakable and inexplicable to human speech. But since the soul raised up to God always seeks and desires in the Lord’s words something that may nourish and refresh it, let us see whether, by the gift of His grace, we can find in these words of the Lord anything suitable for us.

“I confess to you,” He says, “Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, [Col. 0740A] and revealed them to little ones.” What are these things which God the Father hid from the wise and prudent? Namely, the glory and exaltedness of the humanity and divinity of His Son. The wise from whom these things were hidden were the scribes and Pharisees, who had indeed received from God wisdom and knowledge of the Law; but seeking in their wisdom not God’s glory but their own, they did not recognize the glory of God’s Son. They saw Him as a human being, but neither recognized nor wished to recognize what kind of a human being He was: namely, a human being above all human beings, conceived and born without sin, and living in the world without sin. Therefore, because pride blinded their hearts, when they heard Him preaching and saw Him performing, by divine power, signs and wonders which no one else could do, [Col. 0740B] they despised Him and accounted Him as nothing. These were the wise.

But the prudent, from whom the glory of the humanity and divinity of the Son of God was likewise hidden, were all those who among the Gentile peoples received from God prudence and knowledge for knowing many mysteries unknown to other people, yet did not recognize God in these things. But God the Father revealed to little ones—that is, to the humble—what He had hidden from the wise and prudent. These little ones are the apostles, who, on account of the outstanding splendor of humility, recognized and loved Christ, the Son of God, beyond all human beings, both in the excellence of His humanity and in the power of His divinity.

But why almighty God blinded the wise and prudent to knowledge of His Son; why He revealed His Son to little ones, that is, to the humble apostles; or why, as it were by His judgment, He still daily gathers and saves one person in His mercy and compassion while rejecting and condemning another in His judgment and justice—we cannot know. Yet we do not fail to know that whatever the true, just, and holy God does is true, just, and holy. The Son of God, coeternal with God, also declares this when He says in what follows:

“Yes, Father, for so it was pleasing before you.” It is as though He said: Yes, Lord Father, it pleased Your merciful goodness and Your most just equity that You should reveal Me, Your Son—consubstantial and coeternal with You in Your majesty—not to the wise and prudent but to Your humble ones. It follows:

“All things have been handed over to me by my Father.” Behold, the incomprehensible glory of the humanity of the Son of God is comprehended and indicated in few words, because He possesses, governs, and sustains all things with the Father. “And no one knows the Son except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son may will to reveal Him”: behold the glory of the divinity of the Son of God. For in these few words is indicated and set forth the boundless and invincible substance of the whole holy Trinity, by which the Son is one God with the Father, and the Holy Spirit is one God with the Father and the Son. For how the Father is unbegotten, how [Col. 0741A] the Son is Only-begotten, neither later than the Father in time nor inferior to Him in power, no one knows except the Father and the Son, and the one to whom the Son may will to reveal it (Luke 10:22)—namely the Holy Spirit, one perfect God with the Father and the Son. It follows:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I shall refresh you.” Just as, when the Only-begotten Son of God was in the bosom of the Father, where He could neither be seen nor heard by human beings, He emptied Himself by taking the form of a servant in order to aid servants, so here too, after the high and sublime words which we have heard, to which a human being cannot ascend and which he cannot comprehend by his own understanding, He emptied Himself, descending below Himself and in some manner taking the form of a servant, in order to condescend to servants. Thus we, who are little ones in understanding and insufficient to grasp and understand the sublimity of the foregoing words, may have in these following words something by which we are instructed and consoled: “Come,” He says, “to me, all you who labor and are burdened.”

If we understand spiritually, this labor seems to me not to be of the body but of the soul. For it is the labor by which the soul labors through evil desires and evil longings, which, when they reach the effect of action, become certain harsh burdens of soul and body. It is as though the Lord said: You who, exhausted beneath the laborious weight of evil desires, have fallen under the burden of sins and have failed in the strength and health of your souls, do not despair, but come to me through repentance and conversion, laying aside the burdensome and laborious oppression of vices. [Col. 0741C] “And I shall refresh you.”

To refresh (*reficere*) is, as it were, to restore (*reparare*). We ourselves have destroyed and in some sense broken ourselves when, under the evil pressure of the burdens of sin, we subjected our bodies and souls. But the Lord refreshes and restores us when we turn to Him, mercifully reviving us in spiritual life when we are weary and failing through His refreshment. For just as a person exhausted by much labor is refreshed by the sweetness of food, drink, and sleep, and, as though his strength had been restored, returns to his former vigor, so in the spiritual life there is food by which the Lord restores His weary and failing sinners who come to Him; there is also drink, by which He intoxicates them so that they may forget their poverty and miseries; and there is sleep, by which He calls them back to true rest.

This food is sacred Scripture, by which a person is truly refreshed and revived; the drink is the sweetness of prayer, by which a person is truly encouraged in God as though strength were restored; sleep is tranquility of mind, by which a person is truly united and joined with God. By what merits, however, a person may deserve this grace of divine refreshment, the Lord teaches us in the words that follow, when He says:

“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.” If we wish to understand the Lord’s yoke simply, it is obedience to the Lord. We take the Lord’s yoke upon ourselves if, in true humility of heart, we subject ourselves in every respect to obedience for God’s sake. [Col. 0742A] But in a higher sense there is something else that may not inappropriately be understood by the yoke. A yoke is so called from joining. For it always joins two things together—an ox, that is, with an ox—so that they cannot be separated from one another, may work together, and may go together. Therefore, by the yoke, which always joins two, a human being’s consent may fittingly be understood. For a person’s consent always joins two. If the consent is evil, two are joined through it: the human being and the devil; if it is good, God is joined through it to the human being. For when a person consents to good, that person’s consent becomes God’s consent; and thus, under one consent as under one yoke, God and the human being are joined.

Therefore the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you.” That is, as though he said: “So long as you are clothed in a mortal body, [Col. 0742B] you cannot live without sin. But if the pleasures of carnal vices assail you, take my yoke upon yourselves, in that which is higher within you, so that you do not consent to enticing vices; but, by resisting and struggling against them, make your consent my consent.” For it sometimes happens that a person sins, but through weakness, not through consent, because he hates in himself what he sins, and would wish not to sin, but cannot. Whoever is such a person truly has the Lord’s yoke upon him, because in that which is higher within himself he truly consents to God. For although he sometimes falls into sin through the weakness either of body or even of mind, yet, because he does not consent to sin 159 [Note: [Col. 0741D] That is, he does not maliciously persist in a sin he recognizes. See the middle of the preceding homily.], but grieves for his sin, he is joined and bound to God under one consent, as under one yoke, saying with the Psalmist: [Col. 0742C] “I became as a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. XXVII, 23).

Thus Peter sinned; thus David also sinned. Peter sinned by denying Christ; David sinned by committing the crimes alike of adultery and murder. The former sinned through sudden fear, because he feared losing his life; the latter sinned through the impulse of sudden desire, for he saw a woman and desired her. But since there was no consent in sin [Note: [Col. 0742D] That is, stubborn approval and obstinacy.], and their sin displeased them both, each at once returned through penitential satisfaction and obtained pardon.

Moreover, since there are three things that assail a human being—flesh, the world, and the devil: the devil by suggestions, the world by prosperity and adversity, and the flesh by pleasures—the Lord here teaches us how we ought to meet and resist these three by three other things. [Col. 0742D] “Take,” he says, “my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.” That is, as though he said: “Against the devil take my yoke, so that you do not consent to his suggestions; against the world learn from me that I am meek and humble of heart. Learn from me, I say, to be meek by overcoming the adversities of the world through patience; learn from me to be humble by guarding yourselves humbly amid the world’s prosperities, so that you are neither cast down too greatly by adversities nor lifted up too greatly by prosperity. If you take my yoke upon yourselves in this way, if you labor to learn from me, because [Col. 0743A] I am meek and humble of heart, in this way, then at last, through my grace, you shall come to the third thing, where you shall truly find rest for your souls: namely, so that, having overcome the pleasures of the flesh, you may be able through the tranquil sweetness of the mind to cling to me alone. This truly is the soul’s rest.

“For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light.” He rightly says, “My yoke is sweet.” For it is exceedingly sweet and delightful where there is one consent of God and human being. Just as in that consent which belongs to sin there is a certain sweetness which comes from sin and entices the flesh toward sin, so in that consent which belongs to good—the consent of the human being and God—there is generated a certain sweetness 160 without sin, through which God truly delights with the human being, and the human being with God, despising the sweetness of the flesh. [Col. 0743B] But what does he mean when he adds, “and my burden light”? What is the Lord’s burden? The burden of sinful humanity becomes the burden of God the Redeemer—not, indeed, a heavy burden, but a light one. For when a person turns to God, breaking the chains of vices and casting from himself the yoke—that is, the consent—of sins, in accordance with the Psalmist who says, “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Ps. II, 3), God takes upon himself the burden of the sinful soul. And God’s burden becomes light when, through God’s mercy, the person, made light from sins and vices by which formerly he was weighed down, is raised up to contemplate God by the vision of a pure mind.

This is the sacred Gospel reading, which, by the ordering of the Holy Spirit, is fittingly read in praise and glory of the blessed [Col. 0743C] apostle Matthias, whose feast we celebrate today. According to the meaning of his name—for *Mathias* is interpreted “God’s little one”—he was truly one of God’s little ones, one of God’s humble ones, to whom God the Father revealed what was hidden from the wise and prudent. For, to preach and proclaim the mysteries of the incarnate Word, he deserved, by divine dispensation and apostolic election, to be called into the number twelve of the apostles, which had been diminished when Judas fell and paid the penalty of his crime, because of the outstanding beauty of humility by which he shone among the other distinctions of his virtues.

How this same election was made, blessed Peter shows us in today’s reading, where he says: “Men and brethren, it was necessary that the Scripture be fulfilled, [Col. 0743D] which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who was guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and received a share in this ministry. And he indeed acquired a field with the reward of iniquity, and, having hanged himself, burst open in the middle, and all his entrails were poured out; and it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. For it is written in the Book of Psalms: ‘Let his dwelling be desolate,’ and ‘Let another take his episcopate.’ Therefore, of these men who have been gathered with us throughout all the time [when] the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, 161 beginning from John’s baptism until the day when he was taken up from us, one of these must become a witness with us of his resurrection. And they put forward two: Joseph, called Barsabbas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias; [Col. 0744A] and, after prayer, they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles” (Acts I, 16–26).

In this election of this most holy apostle, therefore, the greatness of God’s mercy must be considered and weighed. For when he rejected the one who was righteous in the mouths of men and chose one who was humble and little, he taught and admonished all of us never to presume upon our own righteousness or merits. Rather, if we wish to attain election to eternal life, we should imitate and follow the humility and meekness of this little one of God. He truly took the Lord’s yoke upon himself, because, joined and bound to God under one consent, as under one yoke, he neither yielded to flattering flesh, nor consented to the devil suggesting sins, nor gave way to the world raging through prosperity [Col. 0744B] and adversity. He truly found rest for his soul, because from that rest in which he rested here with God through the grace of inward sweetness, he was transferred into that rest which is never disturbed and never changed.

But let us, who in whatever measure bear the Lord’s yoke, strive to imitate his humility and meekness, so that, in the final examination of strict judgment, where the wise and prudent of this age are cast aside, through the intercession of his merits we may find that rest for our souls in which, with God’s little and humble ones, we may rejoice without end in the eternal vision of God. May our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages, deign to grant this. Amen.

162. HOMILY XXVI. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST MATTHIAS THE APOSTLE.

[Col. 0744C]

“On the tenth day Ahira, son of Enan, prince of the sons of Naphtali, offered a silver dish weighing one hundred and thirty shekels” (Num. VII).

Blessed Matthias the apostle, whose feast we celebrate today, who advanced by the lot of election to the summit of apostolic dignity, is not thought inferior to his fellow apostles in eminence of glory or authority because he was not chosen with them by Christ while Christ still remained in the flesh. For the eternal wisdom of God the Father, which in the days of his flesh drew his apostles to himself by the sweet calling of his election, seated at the Father’s right hand received blessed Matthias, through the ministry of the apostles, into their fellowship. [Col. 0744D]

And the apostle’s name fittingly corresponds to his perfect humility. For *Mathias* is interpreted “God’s little one”: little not in bodily size but in humility of heart, because he was truly humble in spirit and truly despised in his own eyes. For just as someone destroys and loses whatever good he has done through pride, so, if he has committed some offence, he may return through humility to the grace of pardon.

This eminent leader and prince, one of the distinguished princes of heaven and earth, is mystically signified in a passage of the Old Testament where, after the sacrifices of eleven princes of the children of Israel have been enumerated, it is added concerning the twelfth:

“On the tenth [twelfth] day Ahira, son of Enan, prince of the sons of Naphtali, [Col. 0745A] offered a silver dish weighing one hundred and thirty shekels.” By Ahira, whose name is interpreted “friend of my brother,” this blessed apostle is signified as the truly beloved and chosen friend of our brother Jesus Christ; through the most outstanding merit of humility he obtained with him a place of friendship and love. He is written to be Ahira, son of Enan, a name said to mean “cloud.” For by the name of cloud the Holy Spirit is understood, who through the grace of his election made him a worthy son of adoption.

It should be noted that the sacrifice of the twelve princes of the children of Israel was equal: none offered more or less 163 than another. So too our twelve leaders, namely the holy apostles, [Col. 0745B] received equal grace of the Holy Spirit, possessed an equal prerogative of merits, and an equal excellence of holiness and devotion.

The present text shows what their sacrifices were. Each of them offered a silver dish weighing one hundred and thirty shekels; a silver bowl weighing seventy shekels by the weight of the sanctuary; both full of fine flour mingled with oil for a sacrifice; and a golden little mortar weighing ten shekels, full of incense. These three sacrifices, indeed, blessed Paul seems to commend in the words of his Epistle: “May the God of peace sanctify you in every way, so that your whole spirit and soul and body may be kept blameless on the day of our Lord” (I Thess. V, 23).

Our spirit is the understanding [Col. 0745C] by which we recognize good and evil. By the name of the dish, however, we may fittingly understand the apostles’ body: it was not softened by any sweetness of luxury, but was grievously afflicted and worn down by every bitterness of labors and miseries. This dish is fittingly described as silver. Silver, first of all, is a stone; but for it to acquire its customary brightness and whiteness, the craftsman’s skill applies continual labor through the heat of fire. Thus the apostles’ body too was at first in a sense irrational and ignorant; but when the fire of the Holy Spirit kindled them with such heat, it made from stone silver that had been tested and become most precious. Hence blessed Job says: “Iron is taken from the earth, and stone, melted, is turned into bronze” [Col. 0745D] (Job XXVIII, 2). Iron was taken from the earth when fragile and earthly people became most vigorous and unyielding fighters. Stone, moreover, melted, was turned into bronze, because through the heat of the Holy Spirit they became resonant preachers, though before they had been lowly and ignorant people. But the following text indicates the value of this silver dish.

“It weighed,” he says, “one hundred and thirty shekels.” By this number, one hundred and thirty, we may understand the very great merits of apostolic perfection, because their thoughts, words, and works were certainly endowed with zeal for great perfection. For after they were kindled by the wondrous fire of the Holy Spirit, so filled were they with the overflowing grace 164 of divinity that they could think [Col. 0746A] or do nothing but spiritual things, speak nothing but divine things. It follows:

“A silver bowl weighing seventy shekels.” By the silver bowl we may understand their spirit or their most precious soul, in which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit rested with a most abundant fullness of its sweetness. Let us now see for what purpose this silver bowl had seventy shekels: “by the weight of the sanctuary.” They did not possess the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit according to the weight of the world, because they expended it wholly for God’s honor. Therefore the following words reveal with what acceptable offering the silver dish and the bowl were filled:

“Both full of fine flour mingled with oil for a sacrifice.” [Col. 0746B] What can we understand in this place by the fine flour except the purity of their souls and bodies? For when the grace of the same Holy Spirit came, it not only filled their souls ineffably, but also their bodies, so that both were white, both most pure receptacles of such majesty. And because it would not be enough for the fine flour merely to be pure, it is rightly said to have been mingled with oil. By the name of oil, pure and sincere love of God and neighbor is fittingly expressed: by it they loved God above all things and embraced all people with the sweet affection of the heart. All these things were “for a sacrifice,” that is, for God’s honor and the neighbors’ benefit, because the more perfectly they knew how to love God, the more abundantly they were able to administer to others the grace received from him. [Col. 0746C] It follows:

“A golden little mortar weighing ten shekels.” Because the Lawgiver did not write “mortar” but “little mortar,” the apostles’ contrite and most humble heart is rightly understood. For they possessed such a privilege of humility that, apart from Christ and his mother, no humbler human being could ever be found. We may also understand by the golden little mortar their most excellent understanding, by which they crushed into the finest powder everything that they found in Holy Scripture. It was truly golden, that is, adorned with every brilliance of knowledge and wisdom; for as gold surpasses other metal, so their understanding surpassed in wisdom the understanding of all mortals.

“It weighed,” [Col. 0746D] he says, “ten shekels.” As is clearer than light, the number ten commonly signifies throughout Scripture 165 the form of the Ten Commandments. Because the holy apostles perfectly knew the commandments of the Decalogue, they strove to devote all their understanding to performing them in deed. And rightly this little mortar is described as full of incense. What was the incense but the sweetly fragrant perfume of apostolic prayer? Their hearts, filled most abundantly with divine sweetness, at the time of prayer gave forth such fragrant perfume that, ascending to the highest throne, it there diffused a most welcome sweetness. Of this fragrant incense of prayer the Psalm says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL, 2). Hence the following words show how great their preaching was [Col. 0747A] and what testimonies they bore concerning the good Jesus.

“A bull from the herd, a ram, and a yearling lamb for a holocaust, and a goat for sin.” This bull taken from the herd was Christ, sprung from the flesh of the patriarchs and prophets. Our most illustrious leaders offered him when they taught that he was a true man, born from the race of the patriarchs, and sacrificed for the salvation of the whole world. They also offered a ram when they proclaimed that same Redeemer of ours to be the leader of his Church. For the ram goes before the rest of the flock. So too Christ, going before all his faithful into the kingdom of heaven, opened its entrance to all.

“And a yearling lamb,” he says, “for a holocaust, 166 [Col. 0747B] and a goat for sin.” This yearling lamb is the immaculate Christ, who, for the salvation of all the elect, became the sweetest holocaust upon the altar of the cross. Therefore the holy apostles proclaimed this yearling lamb also to be a goat for sin, because he who was in himself immaculate and most pure was offered as a goat, not for his own sins but for ours.

“And peace-offerings: two bulls, five rams, five goats, five yearling lambs.” By the two bulls we understand the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles. The apostles offered them as peace-offerings because, through him who is our peace, making the two one, they formed the holy Church from these two peoples. And because the Church is constituted and governed by three orders, it is consequently added: “and five rams, [Col. 0747C] five goats, five yearling lambs.” By the rams, prelates are expressed; by the goats, penitents; and by the yearling lambs, the innocent. Through these two peoples and these three orders, the holy Church was founded by its leaders, and from them all a most pleasing offering is made to almighty God.

This is the threefold offering excellently presented to Christ by our leaders. For they offered the dish, bowl, and little mortar in the perfection of their own life; the bull from the herd, the yearling lamb, and the goat for sin in preaching Christ; and the two bulls, five rams, five goats, and five yearling lambs in establishing the Church.

HOMILY XXVII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.

[Col. 0747D]

“The angel Gabriel was sent by God into a city of Galilee, called Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary” (Luke I).

Although the splendid day of today’s feast is exalted by joys of solemn celebrations in many ways, it is especially renowned because on it the beginning of our redemption commenced through the incarnation of the Son of God, and on this same day, through the sacrament of his passion, the same Son of God willed to complete the work of our salvation. For on this day the Son of the eternal Father took human nature for the liberation of humankind; and, when time had run its course, on this same day [Col. 0748A] he surrendered this same humanity to passion and death for the salvation of the whole human race. This is that desirable and joyful day for which all those who had pleased the Lord from the beginning of the world sighed, which all desired and longed for; concerning it those who foresaw the redemption of humankind with the eye of a prophetic heart spoke beforehand in obscure utterances. Thus one of them, namely the prophet Isaiah, who foresaw that he would be incarnate, ardently longed for him now to come to earth: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One” (Isa. XLV, 8).

167. These words of the Lord’s chosen prophet seem to accord with today’s Gospel reading, in which we find openly declared what the prophet had foretold in obscure and mystical words. Although various things may be understood by heaven, [Col. 0748B] yet in this place that archangel Gabriel may fittingly be signified, who then dropped dew from above when, as the Gospel relates today, he was sent by God to bring to earth that great and ineffable mystery of divine counsel which God the Father had undertaken for humankind’s liberation. And this announcement of the Lord’s incarnation is rightly compared to dew, because, just as dew waters dry earth and moderates heat, so the Lord’s incarnation watered the dry world, so to speak, by extinguishing the toil of sin in the world and cooling the fire of hell.

What salvation and grace the whole world received while the heavens were thus dropping dew may be understood from the following words: “And let the clouds rain down the Just One.” Although prophets are signified in some passages by clouds, [Col. 0748C] nevertheless, in keeping with the sense we have begun to expound, we may understand by the clouds the Father and the Holy Spirit, and by the Just One the Son of that same Father. For when a cloud covers heaven, no one doubts that a flood of rain will follow. Therefore, while the heavens dropped dew, the clouds began to rain down the Just One: for while the archangel spoke to the blessed Virgin Mary, the Father sent the Son, whom the Virgin Mother conceived through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit.

Nor should we pass over the fact that the heavens are said to drop dew and the clouds truly to rain. We know that when rain pours down the earth is made fruitful with greater abundance than when it is watered with dew. So too those words of the archangel were in a sense dew, because they only announced beforehand the grace of the salvation to come. But the clouds are said to rain [Col. 0748D] because, as they rained—that is, as the Father and the Holy Spirit sent the Son into this world—a great fruitfulness, I mean a great fruit of salvation and grace, followed throughout the whole world.

And the same Son of God is rightly called the Just One, because he, conceived and born without sin, he who justifies all, the just for the unjust, the innocent for the guilty, willed to suffer. “Let the earth be opened,” he says, “and let it bring forth 168 the Savior” (ibid.). What earth is this but our perpetual lady, the Virgin Mary? Let this earth, I say, be opened: opened, namely, by conceiving without pleasure; opened by giving birth without pain, as we sing in praise of this Virgin: “She bore without pain the Savior of the ages.” “And let it bring forth [Col. 0749A] the Savior,” that is, let it bring forth from itself the author of eternal salvation. The words of the Gospel reading seem to agree with these words of the prophet, showing that what the prophet long ago announced obscurely and mystically was fulfilled in truth.

The evangelist says: “Gabriel the angel was sent by God into a city of Galilee, called Nazareth.” Almighty God performed all his works—creating heaven, earth, sea, and all things in them—using, so to speak, no exertion of strength, for he merely spoke the word and they were made (Ps. XXXII, 9). But that he deigned to become human, and in that humanity overthrew the strong man armed, who had subjected the whole world to his dominion, and liberated the whole human race from his unjust rule, was an act of his greatest strength. It was truly great strength that he who was invisible in divinity and incomprehensible in majesty made himself so small that he could be contained in the womb of a tender Virgin, and in that humanity freed the whole world from the condemnation of eternal death. [Col. 0749B]

That archangel Gabriel, whose name means “God’s strength,” had been ordained from the beginning to announce this work to the world; for it was fitting that he who is called God’s strength should announce that this strong Son of God would be incarnate. Therefore he was sent by God into a city of Galilee called Nazareth. *Nazareth* is interpreted “flower of purity.” How fittingly is our lady, the perpetual Virgin Mary, described as having her home in a city distinguished by such a name! For she first displayed in herself the flower of virginity and chastity; first among all women, prompted by no one’s example, she vowed her virginity to God. After her, this flower breathed such sweetness throughout the whole world that an innumerable multitude of both sexes followed, and still follow, the example of her virginity. Even if they cannot preserve complete integrity 169 of mind, they nevertheless strive, so far as they can with her help, to avoid bodily corruption. [Col. 0749C]

Or Nazareth, which is called “flower of purity,” rightly suits the blessed Virgin because, without injury to the integrity of her body, she bore the Son of God, that ever-blooming flower, the incomparable glory of virginity. For just as, when we observe trees putting forth flowers, we hope for the fruit that will follow, so, when this blessed Virgin conceived and bore this flower, namely the Son of God, the entire world obtained the fruit of eternal salvation. The evangelist indicates in the following words to whom, or to what person, this mighty messenger was sent:

“To a virgin,” he says, “betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David.” Blessed Joseph and the blessed Virgin Mary herself were not wealthy by worldly standards; they lived a poor life in this world, yet shone brilliantly, fully surrounded by the riches of virtues. Nevertheless, they were descended from the royal stock of King David. Blessed Mary had sprung from that line to which the Lord swore that one born from the fruit of his womb would come. For, as we read, he promised Abraham only that all nations would be blessed in his seed; but to blessed David God pledged his own Son by oath, as David himself testifies: [Col. 0750A] “The Lord swore to David, and he will not deceive him: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne’” (Ps. CXXXI, 11). Hence the blessed Mother of God and Joseph himself are rightly described as belonging to the house of David, not because of an abundance of royal wealth, but according to genealogy. Having set forth all these things—the name of the city in which the blessed Virgin lived and the name of the man to whom she was betrothed—the evangelist now at last declares the Virgin’s illustrious name.

“And the virgin’s name,” he says, “was Mary.” *Maria*, as is well known, is interpreted “star of the sea.” This interpretation of her name grants great confidence of hope and a great grace of consolation to both the just and sinners. Sailors desiring to sail to some land customarily choose for themselves, when the darkness of night comes on, some star by whose light and sign they may reach unharmed 170 the harbor toward which they are bound. The ray of such a star is rightly compared to the name of our queen. For she is that excellent star which shines upon us who are endangered on the sea of this age and desire to reach the harbor of eternal life, both through the example of her life and through the help of her mercy and compassion. [Col. 0750B]

Let us therefore set this guiding star of the sea before our eyes; and if anyone is puffed up by the wind of prosperity, or cast down into despair by the wind of adversity, let that person look to this star and unceasingly seek the light of her maternal compassion. If anyone, oppressed by the burden of sins, is anxiously distressed because of the countless stains of offences, let that person look to this star and confidently fix in her the anchor of hope. Likewise, if the just and innocent person is anxious to preserve innocence, let that person fix the whole attention of the mind upon the brightness of that star. For if that person faithfully seeks the help of her grace, without doubt that star of the sea will grant to the sinner pardon, and to the just the assistance and grace of her mercy according to the desire of that person’s heart.

These are the festal joys of the present day; this, I say, is that celebrated and joyful day on which, for the redemption of the human race, God the Father decreed that his Son, coeternal with himself, should be incarnate.

[Col. 0750D] But where, or engaged in what pursuits, do we believe that the archangel Gabriel, sent to the blessed Virgin, found her? Certainly not wandering outside, but within, devoting herself to some great work of devout concern. For although Scripture does not at all report how that heavenly messenger found her, we may nevertheless judge that she had in her hands that magnificent work than which nothing can be more precious, more worthy, or more acceptable to God. This excellent work, acceptable to the Lord and most beneficial to human beings, is surely this: when a person, gathering all the senses together, either entreats the Lord for forgiveness of sins, or humbly gives thanks for the benefits of his gifts and reverently prostrates himself in supplication.

As we may believe, our lady the Virgin Mary had wholly gathered herself for such a work. We therefore believe that the angel found her within; this may also be inferred from the very words of the holy Gospel: “The angel,” it says, “entered in to her and said.” As we have said, blessed Mary had strictly recollected herself in order to pray to the Lord for the salvation of the whole [Col. 0751A] human race and had directed the entire attention of her mind to the one thing she asked. Thus she deserved to obtain so unheard-of a greeting and so ineffable a grace of salvation from God that she was found worthy to bring forth the salvation of the whole world.

Indeed, we may believe without doubt that any blessed person who, following the example of this Virgin, endeavors to gather the senses of both the outer and inner person and to direct the gaze of the mind upon God and heavenly things alone, allowing nothing besides that one thing which is sought to dwell in the mind at the time of prayer—although that person does not receive from the Lord the same, or such complete, grace of visitation, which is altogether impossible—nevertheless spiritually conceives and gives birth in the womb of the mind to him whom the blessed Virgin bore bodily.

But whoever refuses to imitate this example, and instead follows Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, when she went out to see the women of another land, cannot at all attain these joys of divine visitation. This Dinah, daughter of Jacob, is our soul, daughter of the true Jacob, namely the eternal Father. It goes out to see the women of another land when, wandering wrongly, it willingly lends the hearing of heart and body to the vain reports of this world, turns these vanities over in itself and entertains them; and so it happens that, seized by the wicked man Shechem, by whom the devil is understood, it is violated when it is defiled by voluntarily consenting to perverse pleasures. [Col. 0751C]

Let us hear, then, what the angel said when he entered in to blessed Mary and how he greeted her:

“Hail,” he said, “full of grace; the Lord is with you.” These words of greeting he did not utter from himself, but received them from God the Father, composed and ordained in the heavenly court. “Hail,” he says, “full of grace.” That is, as though he said: “You are full of grace, because he who is incomprehensible in divinity, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, has resolved to be contained in you, and to be conceived in you as perfect God and human being, with soul and body.” For all human nature consists of soul and body; and the Son of God took this human nature from the blessed Virgin in such a way that, at the angel’s word, she immediately conceived him as perfect God and complete human being, with body and soul. [Col. 0751D]

Or we may call her full of grace in this sense: that in some manner she is indebted both to the just and to sinners. To the just she ought by right to bestow grace because they strive, after her example, to retain the purity of an innocent life; to sinners, however, she ought to show herself abundant in mercy and compassion because she was chosen as Mother of God for their sake. For if sinners did not exist, the Son of God would not have descended to earth to be incarnate, nor would she have borne him.

“The Lord,” he says, “is with you; blessed are you among women.” This is the same as if he had said: “You are full of grace because the time is now at hand when you will conceive the Lord in your virginal womb.” “Blessed are you among women.” Why “blessed among women,” and not among men? Certainly because she was altogether free from that curse pronounced upon Eve, to whom it was said: “In pain you shall bear children.” For all women conceive with pleasure, but bear children in pain. Blessed Mary, as we said before, was free from this curse because she conceived without pleasure and gave birth without pain. Or she is blessed among women because, by bringing down blessing from above, she dispelled the curse which Eve had brought upon all. [Col. 0752B]

We may also understand otherwise what he said, “Blessed are you among women.” It is as though he said: “I call you blessed among women because, although there are many women who please God through good devotion, none can be free from original and actual sin. But you are blessed among women because, just as you are almost [Note: [Col. 0751D] Thus the manuscript; but it seems one should read *plene* (‘fully’) or *penitus* (‘entirely’).] free from actual sin, so you will also be wholly freed from original [Note: [Col. 0752D] See the preliminary dissertation in vol. I.] sin. And why do I call you more blessed among women than among men? There are also some blessed among men through the merit of praiseworthy life, yet no one is without original and actual sin. But I see a singular man now to be born from you, alone free from original and actual sin. And just as he alone will be blessed [Col. 0752C] above all men, so you too will be blessed above all women.” It follows:

When she heard this, she was troubled at his saying. How are we to believe that the blessed Virgin was troubled? What was that disturbance? Are we to suppose that she trembled at the presence of a man because she feared for her virginity? By no means. For it was not fitting that the mind of one so illustrious in merits, so precious in virtues, should decline into any despair. For she herself, as we said above, supplicating the Lord for the salvation of the whole human race, had raised the whole intention of her mind from lower things to those above; and in that most serene state of mind, in which she fixed her attention upon heavenly things alone, she had transcended all that appeared outwardly. Therefore, in that very hour of divine contemplation, [Col. 0752D] her heart was so strengthened by confidence of hope from the Lord and in the Lord that it could be touched by no despair. She was troubled, then, at the angel’s speech, not because she wavered in any despair, but because she had gathered her whole self for meditation upon heavenly things; and when she bent toward the things spoken outwardly the mind which she had raised on high, that serenity was somewhat disturbed, and her mind no longer remained fixed upon heavenly meditation as fully as before. This commonly happens when any blessed person is wholly absorbed in attention to the things above: if perhaps something sounds externally, the mind recoils somewhat from its concentration and cannot remain wholly gathered to what it had begun [Col. 0753A]. That the blessed Mary was troubled by such a disturbance seems to be indicated by the words that follow:

And she considered what manner of greeting this might be. For when she reflected within herself upon the angel’s greeting, she drew her mind somewhat back from the concentration in which she had previously gathered herself. The messenger of God’s secrets, finding her thus troubled and reflecting, admonishes and exhorts her not to fear by the words of his unheard-of greeting, as follows:

And the angel said to her: Fear not, Mary; for thou hast found grace with God. What, we may ask, was that fear which occupied the virginal breast of so mighty a queen? Are we to believe that she was frightened by some phantom of diabolical deception? [Col. 0753B] It seems unfitting to the dignity of blessed Mary that she should have feared a diabolical illusion, she who had made herself near to God through such singular and incomparable excellence of virtues. For she feared not for herself alone or for the salvation of her parents, but for the deliverance of the whole human race. She feared, I say, lest, because sins demanded it, this redemption should either not take place at all or should be deferred so long that a very great multitude might be condemned to the destruction of everlasting death. That this was the cause of her fear seems to be insinuated by the angel himself when, calling her by her own name, he says, “Fear not, Mary.” Mary, as is known, means “Lady” in our language. This is as though the angel had said: “You fear for human redemption; you fear lest the human race be condemned forever. Behold, I say to you, Mary, [Col. 0753C] do not fear or be alarmed, because you have been chosen for this: that you may become Lady of the whole world; that you may bear the salvation of the whole world—your Redeemer and Savior and that of all people. You have found grace with God.
