That grace which the whole human race had lost through the pride of the first parent, you have found by seeking in profound humility; for you have deserved to conceive and bear him through whom the whole world must be saved.”

He is said to find who seeks and finds something which he has lost. Thus the whole human race had lost the grace of its Creator—that grace, namely, by which no one, however just and holy, merited entrance into the heavenly kingdom, but after the exile of this life all descended into hell. Our blessed Lady [Col. 0753D] grieved deeply over the calamity of this misery, not for herself alone but for the whole human race. She sought this lost grace with tears and prayers, persevering day and night before God the Father; and because she sought with a contrite heart and profound humility, she at last deserved to find it. By the importunate voice of her cry she so prevailed with God that, as it were doing violence to him, she drew him down from the heights to the depths, from heaven to earth.

Therefore the most mighty messenger of heavenly secrets, after sufficiently addressing the most beloved Virgin with words of unprecedented greeting, when he foretold that the Son of the most high Father would be born from her while the seal of virginal modesty remained closed, immediately announced to the same Virgin in due order all the mysteries of his humanity, as he had learned them in that heavenly assembly:

“Behold,” he says, “thou shalt conceive in thy womb and bear a son.” In this brief utterance he comprehends the great and immeasurable work of the human nature of the Son of God: namely, conception and then birth, and thus all the mysteries which the Son of God deigned to accomplish in his humanity for the restoration of human salvation. For in the angel’s first words, “Behold, [Col. 0754A] thou shalt conceive in thy womb,” he who according to divinity is of incomprehensible nature, taking an animate body, perfect God and perfect man, was conceived in the virginal chamber. And just as this same blessed Virgin and mother, by the angel’s word alone, conceived from herself the Word of God who was ineffably to be incarnate, so she was also to bear him from herself ineffably and wonderfully [Col. 0754B]. Accordingly, immediately after the mystery of conception, the angel adds the mystery of his birth in these words: “and thou shalt bear.”

Moreover, the only-begotten of the eternal Father, the only son of the undefiled Virgin, because he came not to dissolve the law but to fulfill it, would observe the commandment of the law even at the beginning of his birth through the mystery of circumcision; and the angel openly announces this in these words: “And thou shalt call his name Jesus.” For by saying, “Thou shalt call his name Jesus,” he foreshadowed the mystery of his circumcision. For, as the Evangelist testifies, on the very day of his circumcision his name was called Jesus.

This splendor and image of the Father’s majesty, who was thus made a little lower than the angels—this [Col. 0754C] cornerstone, I say, who lay hidden beneath the covering of humanity—what and how great he would afterwards be, the messenger of his birth himself testifies. Not only when, having become a young man, he showed the power of true divinity by signs and wonders, but even while he was still a little child under his mother’s care, he says: “He shall be great.” He was indeed made great as King and Lord in the eyes of the three Magi. Recognizing at the very beginning of his birth the sign of the great King, they reverently strove to honor magnificently with gold, frankincense, and myrrh, in accordance with the magnificence of royal majesty, [Col. 0754D] the little one still sucking at his mother’s breast, wrapped in swaddling clothes, crying in the cradle—him whom the attesting signs had made known to them as the King of the ages, true God and man. This same one, having afterwards become a young man and appearing openly to the world by signs and wonders—raising the dead, restoring sight to the blind, cleansing lepers, and displaying other miracles of divine power—was called by some “a great prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people” (Luke 24:19).

“And he shall be called the Son of the Most High,” namely at his baptism, when the Father’s voice came upon him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). Peter confessed him to be the Son of God, saying: “Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). Martha also affirmed that he was the Son of God, saying: “I have believed that [Col. 0755A] thou art Christ, the Son of God, who hast come into this world” (John 11:27). He was also called the Son of the Most High in the Passion, when that centurion, seeing the earthquake and all the other elements shaken at his death, proclaimed in a voice of devout faith, confessing him to be God’s Son: “Truly,” he said, “this man was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54).

And because, after all these things which he was to suffer in the most humble nature of his humanity, he was one day to rise from the dead by the power of his divinity and ascend into heaven, and to be set over all the works of the Father, the same mysteries of his glorious resurrection and ascension may rightly be understood through the words immediately following:

“And the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father, [Col. 0755B] and he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever.” What is said here, “the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father,” may be understood in two ways. First, as David’s royal throne was in Jerusalem, so the Son of God—called according to his humanity the son of David—after his resurrection had the beginning of his kingdom in Jerusalem, when there began there, in the primitive Church, as it were a noble kingdom of the true David. The Father also figuratively indicated this throne of David, which had been specially promised to him, in the Psalm, “The Lord said unto my Lord” (Psalm 109), which he composed concerning Christ’s resurrection and ascension. For just as in the preceding psalm he foreshadowed Christ’s Passion, so likewise in this following one he prefigured his resurrection and ascension. For he says in that psalm: [Col. 0755C] “The Lord said unto my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” Although this was said particularly of his ascension, when he sat down at the right hand of God the Father, it is nevertheless not unjustly believed to have been said of his resurrection as well. How almighty God gave the throne of David to his consubstantial Son, he himself indicated after his resurrection when he appeared to his disciples and said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18).

And how not only the Jews but also the Gentiles, who may be understood by the name Jacob, which is interpreted “supplanter,” were to be gathered into his kingdom after his resurrection and ascension; and how that kingdom was to remain stable and firm after the rejection of the Jews—is rightly added immediately: “And he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever.” Thus the eternal Father gave his Son the throne of David in the resurrection; in the ascension he began to reign eternally over the house of Jacob.

“And of his kingdom,” he says, “there shall be no end,” both in the present Church and in that Church which after the Judgment is to be gathered in true eternity. Therefore, when that angel, the messenger of future things, foretold that the Son of God would one day come in the flesh and reign over the house of Jacob forever, blessed Mary understood—being truly the daughter of most wise Solomon, who had already conceived within herself the wisdom of the eternal Father—that what long before had been prefigured figuratively and in enigma was one day to be fulfilled in reality: namely, that just as Jacob of old became the supplanter of his brother Esau, [Col. 0756A] so indeed, by the calling of the Gentiles, the Jewish people ought to be supplanted.

Therefore, although in her spirit she exulted at the angel’s unheard-of greeting and so salutary promise, knowing without doubt that he desired by all nations was to be born from her for the redemption of the human race, yet, recognizing from the angel’s words that her own nation, the Jewish people, was to be cast out from God’s mercy, she began, being ever full of the bowels of piety and mercy, in some manner to grieve and become as though more sorrowful. Wishing to know more fully how this could be, she immediately asked; whence follows:

But Mary said to the angel: How shall this be, since I know not a man? As though she said: “How—[Col. 0756B] that is, in what manner—can it happen that the only-begotten of the eternal Father, who, as you have said, is to be born from me for the salvation of men, though he is ready to save the whole world, should exclude his own nation, his own inheritance, namely the Jewish people, from the fellowship of eternal salvation, and make dear to himself and near to salvation a foreign nation wholly estranged from the knowledge of the divine name?”

To this the angel, being privy to divine secrets, first announces in fitting order the great works of God which were to be accomplished in her and with her; and then, by a clear judgment of events, explains to her by what hidden judgment of God salvation was to be removed from the Jewish people, as the sacred reading [Col. 0756C] continues:

But the angel said to her: The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee. This is as though he said: “When the grace of the Holy Spirit comes upon that which is higher—namely, your soul—whatever ignorance or concupiscence of the flesh now seems to lie hidden in you will be wholly removed and extinguished, so that, alone with your only Son, you may become entirely free and unencumbered both from actual fault and from original sin. Therefore also that holy thing which shall be born from thee shall be called the Son of God. That holy one, I say, who sanctifies all things and shall be born from thee, shall be called and proclaimed throughout the whole world not only thy son but also the Son of God.”

And it should be noted what the two conjunctions [Col. 0756D] which seem to have been placed here signify, where it is thus said: “therefore also that which shall be born.” Conjunctions are fittingly placed there where the union of both natures, divine and human, was made. It follows:

“And behold, Elizabeth thy kinswoman, she also hath conceived a son in her old age.” “Behold,” he says, “Elizabeth thy kinswoman”—that is, thy race and kindred, namely the Jewish people, for whom thou art so solicitous with an affection of devout piety—“has conceived a son in her old age.” That is, through faith and love it once conceived the Son in the patriarchs and prophets, when, believing the divine promises, they awaited with great longing and the affection of great devotion the only-begotten, then hidden in the bosom of the Father, who would one day come to earth for human redemption.

“And this is the sixth month with her who is called barren, because no word shall be impossible with God.” The sixth month may be understood as the sixth age, [Col. 0757A] in which the invisible God appeared visible in the flesh and dwelt upon earth. It is as though he said: “Because the sixth age has come—that is, because the fullness of time has now arrived, in which the almighty Father decreed, by sending his Son to earth, to fulfill the oath which he had given to his faithful ones—this aforesaid Jewish people is barren and shall remain so, because with a reprobate and obstinate mind it insolently refuses and disdains to believe, until the end of the age, that he whom thou shalt bear is true God and man. But because no word shall be impossible [Col. 0757B] with God, this same Jewish people shall be converted to the faith at the end of the age,” as the grace of divine promise once deigned to testify of them in the prophets: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Rom. 9:27).

After blessed Mary learned from the angel’s words of the rejection of the Jews, touched inwardly by sorrow, she began, as we said, to grieve for her people. But now, when she heard of their conversion, strengthened by such consolation, she burst forth in a voice of exultation, humbly offering herself to obey God. The words of her most humble answer seem well to indicate this: But Mary said to the angel: “Behold the handmaid [Col. 0757C] of the Lord; be it done unto me according to thy word.” As though she said: “Now I confess myself the Lord’s devoted handmaid; now I am ready to obey God; now I offer myself devoutly to receive the Son of God. For in carrying, bathing, and nursing him I shall gladly perform the office of a handmaid; I shall gladly supply all things necessary to human frailty, so that he who is to be born from me may become salvation and redemption not only of the Gentiles but also of the Jews. Be it done unto me according to thy word. I do not say this so that I, the queen of heaven, may become Lady of the whole world, but so that I may conceive and bear that Word of the eternal Father through whom the whole world may obtain the grace of eternal salvation. Let it be done, I say, to me and to my people according to thy word: that he who is the salvation and redemption of the whole world may be born from my [Col. 0757D] womb, and that the Jewish people now rejected may at least at the end of the age be numbered among the lot of the elect.”

O blessed Mary, by thy grace cause it to be done to us according to this Word, which thou didst ask might be done to thee: namely, that we may worthily deserve, through the aid of thy merits, to conceive and bear in the womb of our mind that Word of the eternal Father whom, Virgin, thou didst deserve to bear incarnate from thee; and that, where hitherto the kingdom of sin has reigned in our mortal body, this wicked kingdom of vices being destroyed, he himself, the King of righteousness, may establish in us his kingdom, the kingdom, namely, of virtues; and thus may place in our soul and body, in the present life, the seat of his kingdom, so that in the future he may make us co-heirs of the heavenly kingdom. May he deign to grant this, [Col. 0758A] whose kingdom and dominion endure without end unto ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVIII. A SECOND HOMILY FOR THE SAME FEAST

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the diadem” (Song of Songs 3), etc.

The venerable solemnity of this day, [Col. 0758B] as it surpasses all other festivals in the dignity of its mystery, so from the beginning of the world it was desirable and longed for by all the faithful. For this is the day on which our salvation was begun and consummated; on which God, having become man, willed to become a participant in our nature, our mortality, and our misery in the womb of the most blessed Virgin Mary; on which he offered to God the Father upon the cross, for our redemption, that same humanity which he assumed. Beholding the ineffable mystery of this day with the prophetic eye of his heart, Solomon cried out, seeing it as future yet as though already past, and said: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousals and on the day of the joy of his heart” (Song 3:11).

It is characteristic of daughters to hold, to love, and to be loved. Therefore by the daughters of Zion—which is interpreted “watchtower”—are suitably understood those souls which, striving toward the watchfulness of divine contemplation, love to hold God and are loved by God to be held. The Holy Spirit accordingly admonishes these daughters of Zion to go forth to see King Solomon. By Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” is signified our Lord Jesus Christ, to see whom we must go forth in three ways. [Col. 0758C] Hence God says to Abraham: “Go forth from thy land, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house” (Gen. 12:1). He goes forth from his land who extends himself from earthly and evil actions toward the pursuit of a better life. But because it does not suffice merely to leave evil works if one does not also advance to leave and cast away evil desires, he adds: “and from thy kindred.” It is in some way easy to leave one’s land—that is, evil works—but very difficult to cast away with contempt evil desires, which cling and adhere to us as if by a certain kinship [Col. 0758D] and affinity.

Yet whoever has been able, by God’s mercy, to make these two departures must not stand still or delay as though he had arrived at perfection; rather, he must still manfully gird himself for the third departure, which is mystically indicated to us when it is immediately added: “and from thy father’s house.” This father, from whose house we must go forth, may be understood as the devil, who, through the pride by which he deceived and cast down the first man, began to be the father and prince of the whole human race. Since by nature we were children of wrath, it is not unfitting to understand by this father’s house the human heart which he inhabited through pride, and which he still makes, as though by ancient right, his own house while he deceives through the arrogance of exaltation and pride. Therefore a person must strive, if he has gone forth from his land by abandoning evil works, if he has gone forth from his kindred by repressing evil desires in himself, nevertheless to go forth from his father’s house by departing from pride of heart [Col. 0759A] and carefully preserving himself in true humility. For whatever a person gains by rejecting evil actions and resisting evil desires is lost if it is not guarded by the gentleness of humility.

Let us therefore go forth from our land, from our kindred, and from our father’s house, that we may deserve to see King Solomon. By these two words, “King Solomon,” we understand fear and love. Fear pertains to a king; love is fitting for Solomon, whose name means “peaceful.” And because there are some who see the King but not Solomon—namely, those who fear God as King because of their sins, but in their very trembling fail in hope—and, conversely, there are others who, casting aside reverence for fear and presuming more upon God’s mercy than they ought, [Col. 0759B] neglect themselves, it is right that after saying, “Behold the King,” he added “Solomon.” We must see God as King by fearing him as our Creator and turning aside from sins because of that fear; we must see God as Solomon by loving him as our Redeemer and, because of that love, humbly persevering in good works in hope of reward.

Judas, who betrayed the Lord, saw the King but not Solomon: he feared his sin and, despairing because he did not love, went away and hanged himself with a noose. Peter, who denied the Lord, saw both the King and Solomon: he feared the guilt of his denial, yet did not despair because he loved; instead, he went out and wept bitterly, and deserved to be saved. Therefore, as we have said, we must see God as King by fearing him; we must see [Col. 0759C] God as Solomon by loving him. What awakens these two things in us—namely, fear and love of him—is suggested in the following words when it adds:

“In the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” This noble and inestimable diadem, I think, was human nature, with which his mother, the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, crowned him, and in whose most chaste womb God became man on this day. And it is well said, “with which she crowned him.” Before this day the Son of God was, in a sense, not crowned: for although nothing has ever been added to or taken away from him in the ineffable and boundless excellence of his divinity, and he has always remained the same, yet he had not been crowned with that crown which accrued to him from human nature. On this day his mother gloriously crowned him with this crown; and on this same day the Son of God brought this crown to its perfect beauty and adorned it with the price of his blood. Therefore he willed to be crowned on this day with a twofold diadem: one of incarnation, with which his mother, the Virgin Mary, crowned him by wonderfully supplying flesh from her own flesh; the other, with which his mother, Judea and the Synagogue, crowned him by cruelly condemning him to death with a crown of thorns placed upon his head.

Let us therefore go forth, that in this twofold diadem we may behold King Solomon crowned by his mother. For he is the King who searches and examines our departure from the land, from kindred, and from the father’s house [Col. 0760A]; he is Solomon, who reconciles us to God the Father and rewards us with the Father. Nor without cause did he permit his most holy head to be lacerated and bloodied by thorns. There is something by which it is fitting for us to answer those thorns with thorns. We must set thorns against thorns. Rising up, we must pierce within ourselves the stings of vices and temptations with the sharpness of God’s commandments, so that thorns may be rooted out by thorns—that is, so that the assaults of vices may be suppressed by constant meditation on God’s commandments. Hence the Psalmist says: “And they are mindful of the commandments of God to do them” (Ps. 102:18). And Solomon: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep” (Eccles. 12:11).

“Behold King Solomon in the diadem with which [Col. 0760B] his mother crowned him on the day of his espousals and on the day of the joy of his heart.” By the day of his espousals and the day of the joy of his heart, we see that one and the same festival of the present day was indicated beforehand. For this day of the Lord’s incarnation was truly the day of espousals, because in that bridal chamber, the womb of the most blessed Virgin, the same Son of God became both bridegroom and bride: bridegroom according to divinity, bride according to humanity. Therefore the Psalmist says: “He hath set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself as a bridegroom proceeding from his chamber” (Ps. 18:6). The tabernacle of the Son of God was his holy humanity, in which he served God the Father for the salvation of the human race. The sun in which he placed this tabernacle was his most blessed mother, the Virgin Mary, who, bright and radiant in body and soul after the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, like the sun, could feel [Col. 0760C] in herself no clouds or stains of sins. In this sun, in this most blessed Virgin who possessed no portion of darkness, the Son of God placed his tabernacle when, taking an animate body from her, wholly God and wholly man, he rested bodily in her. He proceeded as a bridegroom from his chamber when he was born from the most holy womb of that same Lady, our Virgin Mary.

After the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation had been set forth and foreshadowed by the Holy Spirit—a mystery by which the only-begotten Son of God made this present day at once honorable and lovable to all the faithful throughout the earth—the mystery of the Lord’s Passion [Col. 0760D], completed on this same day, is added when it says: “and on the day of the joy of his heart.” Without doubt the day of the Passion was the day of the joy of his heart, on which, by dying on the cross for love of his bride, human nature, which he had espoused by assuming flesh in the Virgin’s womb, he joined her to himself. Before he assumed human form he was not a bridegroom, because he rejoiced in heaven with angels alone. But when by being born he united human nature to his divinity, and in that humanity died asleep upon the cross, Eve was fashioned from Adam’s side: for from Christ’s side, opened by the soldier’s lance, came forth blood and water, with which he washed, endowed, cleansed, and justified his bride, which is the holy Church.

How greatly he desired this day, and what joy he had looked forward to it from the beginning [Col. 0761A], he himself showed long before it came to pass when he said: “I shall play in the circle of the earth, and my delights shall be with the children of men” (Prov. 8:31). But when, having assumed humanity, he came to this day—when he willed by death to accomplish all for which he had come—he showed in other words that that day was truly the day of the joy of his heart, when he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Mark 14:34). He did not say, “My soul is sorrowful because of death,” but “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” He was sorrowful indeed not in death or because of death, but until death. From the moment when he first assumed human feeling in himself, he was in sorrow for us; he suffered with his chosen and beloved faithful who were in the world; [Col. 0761B] he suffered with the beloved souls of his faithful, who were held captive in hell under the power of death; and he suffered also with the holy angels in heaven, who nevertheless were in a certain sorrow because they did not see the diminished number of their company restored by the elect among humankind.

But because this sorrow was to end in his death, when, as the Apostle testifies, “making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth,” he offered himself to God the Father for the redemption of the world in the joy of his heart, he rightly said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” Thus that day, as we have said, was truly the day of the joy of his heart.

[Col. 0761C] No joy can be compared with that joy which the Son of God had within himself at that approaching hour, when his most holy soul was about to descend and visit and deliver the souls of his saints, who had awaited him through many thousands of years in darkness and in the shadow of death. With what joy, we may suppose, did he see Abel, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and many thousands of his elect coming to meet him, applauding him as their Creator and Deliverer with an ineffable and inconceivable festival of exultation and joy? Therefore, that his joy and that of his own in heaven, on earth, and in hell might be fulfilled, at the very point of death he cried to his Father: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). These words were not words of bitterness proceeding from fear of death, but the words of one exulting with intense desire [Col. 0761D] and eagerly longing for the visitation and deliverance of his own who were in hell.

And because he was God on earth without a father, and in heaven without a mother, he alone could say twice, “My God, my God.” As though he said: “Thou art my Father in heaven according to divinity, by which thou begottest me coeternal and consubstantial with thee; thou art my Father on earth according to humanity, because thou didst will that I should be assumed for the human race from a Virgin mother without a father. My Father according to divinity, my Father according to humanity, why hast thou forsaken me?” This “why,” I think, signifies and indicates for us that act of thanksgiving by which he gave thanks to God the Father for the redemption of the human race, for which he had sent him into this world and which was to be accomplished at that same hour through his Passion, death, [Col. 0762A] and descent into hell. “Why hast thou forsaken me?” he says. As though he said: “Behold the hour for which thou didst send me, thine only-begotten, and for which thou didst leave me without the aid of divinity, that through my Passion thou mightest work the salvation of the human race. I pray therefore that through thy compassion it may be accomplished: that through my cross and blood thy creature may be restored and reconciled to thee.”

These are the mysteries of our redemption, ordained from the beginning and accomplished on this day through the mediation of our most blessed Lady, the Virgin Mary. As she grieved more than all others over the perdition of the human race, so on this day she deserved to be comforted ineffably above all human beings, when, the angel announcing and the Holy Spirit overshadowing, she deserved to be made pregnant [Col. 0762B] with him who on this same day destroyed death and by mighty power brought his chosen ones back from hell to the joys of paradise. Whatever joy, exultation, and gladness existed in heaven, the supreme divinity poured it all into her today. Today she received in such abundance and fullness of sweetness that sweet kiss of the Father and the Holy Spirit which was the Son of God, for whom the ancient Fathers had sighed from the beginning of the world, Solomon saying in their person: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1); so that not only spiritually in her most holy soul but also bodily in her most holy womb, wholly God and wholly man rested.

What shall we wretched people say on this day of so great a joy of hers, we who are placed amid pains and miseries? How can we rejoice with her blessedness, exalting her with worthy praises [Col. 0762C], when in the body of this death nothing meets us but pain and groaning? Yet, because she is the mother of mercy and does not despise the praise of the humble or the devotion of sinners, let us flee from this valley of tears in which we sigh, with heart and mind, to her mercy; so that, through her intercession, going forth from our land, kindred, and father’s house, we may imitate her humility in such a way that we may deserve to behold without end with her the true King Solomon, her Son, our Creator and Redeemer, in the diadem with which she crowned him on the day of his espousals and on the day of the joy of his heart—he who lives and [Col. 0762D] reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIX. THIRD HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

“He hath set his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm 18).

There are three things in the sun: first, that it gives light; second, that through heat it rises; third, that it dries things saturated with moisture. By the sun is understood the blessed Virgin Mary, in whom the true Sun, the Lord, effected these three things which are found in the sun. He illumined her indeed through knowledge of himself, when the Holy Spirit, coming upon her, freed her soul from ignorance, so that, knowing herself, she might truly know him also by whom she had most graciously been known. He also kindled her in the love of God the Father, so that, entirely estranged from the joys of the present world, she might burn wholly in God [Col. 0763A] and be wholly drawn to the love of God, whom alone above all things she loved. And he dried her through the grace of his Spirit of every carnal moisture and carnal concupiscence, so that, perfectly cleansed in her from every corruption, he might place in her his tabernacle: namely, an immaculate body, conceived of the Holy Spirit, in which he might serve the eternal Father for us.

And because in these words which we have set forth beforehand the Lord’s conception is prefigured, in the following verses the mysteries of his birth, Passion, resurrection, and ascension—indeed, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, the whole order of ecclesiastical religion—are excellently expressed. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0763B] “And he himself as a bridegroom proceeding from his chamber.” When the bridegroom goes forth from his chamber, it is certainly clear that, joined to his bride, he has become one flesh with her. So Christ Jesus, when at the beginning of his birth he proceeded from the virginal chamber, was united through the flesh which he had assumed to his bride, which is the Church. It follows:

He exulted like a giant to run his course: his going forth is from the highest heaven. Thus, through the Incarnation, as we have said, joined to his bride, he exulted like a giant—190 he exulted, I say, with great exultation of heart and great devotion of mind—to run the course which he had undertaken to complete out of obedience to the Father; and, despising shame, he endured the cross for the joy [Col. 0763C] set before him. Therefore, when he was consummated through the Passion, his going forth from the highest heaven took place, because, though he went forth alive from the tomb, he was to rise not through the weakness of the flesh but from the highest heaven, that is, from the supreme Godhead.

And his meeting is unto its height, and there is none that can hide himself from his heat. Therefore, glorified by the glory of the Resurrection, his meeting through the Ascension was made unto its height, because, ascending above all the heavens, he returned in encounter to the supreme Godhead whence he had come. But after he returned there, he abundantly filled and intoxicated his chosen disciples by sending the Holy Spirit from heaven, as is openly understood from these words: And there is none that can hide himself from his heat.

[Col. 0763D] The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, bestowing wisdom upon little ones. Before the glorification of the Saviour and the grace of the Holy Spirit, the Law had a certain stain, because, understood carnally and observed carnally, it conferred upon its observers no goal of perfection, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “For the law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19). Therefore, after the Ascension of the Lord Jesus and the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Law lost the stain which it had, when, understood spiritually and fulfilled spiritually, it promised the joys of eternal life. Thus, when the legal ceremonies were transferred to spiritual understanding, the law of the Lord appeared spotless; and through it a great conversion [Col. 0764A] afterward took place in the Church. For by converting the souls of the elect, it directed them spiritually to seek and find the Lord their God.

The faithful 191 testimony of the Lord, bestowing wisdom upon little ones. By the faithful testimony of the Lord the holy Gospel may be designated, which, after the transfer of the Law, was revealed in the time of grace and preached in the world; through it the almighty Father bore witness that the works of the Lord were done in truth and equity. And it is rightly called a faithful testimony. For whatever the holy Gospel promises, the faithful—indeed, the true—Lord will faithfully fulfil. It also bestows wisdom upon little ones: that is, upon persons made little through true humility, to whom it imparts the great savour of divine sweetness.

[Col. 0764B] The just ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts. After the age of the apostles and after the sacred writings of the evangelists, interpreters of Scripture appeared in the Church, through whom the righteous ordinances of the Lord—which had lain hidden in the words of preachers and in the writings of prophets and evangelists—were openly set forth and revealed. As these interpreters proclaimed the righteous ordinances of the Lord to the world, many human hearts were gladdened thereby, and are gladdened to the present day; for nowhere do we find the righteous ordinances of the Lord more clearly than in the books of the interpreters.

The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes. By the clear commandment of the Lord the holy apostles are designated, to whom he himself, present in the flesh, had said: [Col. 0764C] “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15:12). They not only preached this commandment of charity to others, but in a certain manner they themselves 192 were this commandment, for in their life these precepts—this love, through which eyes are enlightened—were displayed more clearly than light.

The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever. This fear is not servile fear but holy love, which begins in fear but ends in love. The blessed martyrs indeed possessed this fear and holy love; for unless they had been perfectly inflamed by this love, they could never have endured for the Lord so many torments of suffering, so many punishments of wounds, and such dreadful tortures of the body. But because this holy love had perfectly possessed them, they not only despised the things that were in the world for love’s sake, but, transcending even themselves through the sweetness of divine love, they scorned the bitter rackings of their own bodies.

[Col. 0764D] After the illustrious victory of the martyrs, the splendid order of confessors immediately followed, concerning whom it is rightly added: The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves. By these words the holy confessors are rightly prefigured. For they made the righteous judgments of the Lord known to the people of the faithful by the word of their preaching; and by their life and example—indeed, by their exhortation—they instructed them to enact the judgments of the Lord in themselves. And because “the thoughts of the righteous are judgments,” they judged themselves strictly and anticipated the Lord’s judgment [Col. 0765A]; and so, by vigorously enacting in their own life the judgments of the Lord which they preached to others, they in a manner justified them.

193  
## HOMILY XXX. FOURTH HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE ANNUNCIATION OF SAINT MARY THE VIRGIN

The Lord spoke to Ahaz, saying: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, whether in the depths of hell or in the height above” (Isa. 7).

Whatever things have been written have been written for our instruction, so that through the practice of right faith we may obtain divine mercy. For divine Scripture contains within itself that by which every little one may be fed and from which every perfect person may be abundantly refreshed. [Col. 0765B] Whatever we read or understand, we can apply wholly to the use of the inner person. Therefore, if we wish to search out more carefully the entire sequence of the Old and New Testaments, we find everywhere a mystical moral sense implanted within it.

Accordingly, it pleases us to examine with all the intention of the mind the words of the prophet Isaiah, who says: “The Lord spoke to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, whether in the depths of hell or in the height above.” This man had been exhorted to pray with devout mind that he might devoutly pray that he who would free his elect might deign to come, plunged into the depths of hell, and place them in the height above. Since the holy man had long desired this with much longing, he wished by equal earnestness in prayer to obtain from him that very remedy of salvation. But let us hear what reply the wicked man gave to the prophet’s pious exhortation.

“I will not ask,” he says, “and I will not tempt the Lord.” For since he had not lived such a life, nor yet desired to live it, he despaired of being heard by the Lord. Since he had not set God before his eyes, but preferred to remain in sins, he did not seek the sign of salvation, which he was not worthy to find. Therefore, seeing that the king’s mind was estranged from God, the holy prophet immediately turned his words to the entire lineage of David, saying:

[Col. 0765C] Hear therefore, house of David: Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God? This Ahaz, and nearly all those dwelling under his rule, had, because of their sins, become troublesome [Col. 0765D] both to God and to 194 men. Hence the prophet rightly said: “Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God?” As though he openly said: Is it not enough for you that you have become detestable to men, unless you are also found abominable before God?

Therefore he himself will give you a sign: the Lord himself will give a sign, and, though unwilling and ungrateful, he will show you the clemency of his mercy. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.” Behold, the Son of God will be conceived in a virgin’s womb and, like a bridegroom, will go forth from his chamber. And his name will be called Emmanuel, because he will deign to dwell openly with us upon earth. Let these brief remarks according to the letter suffice. Now let the words be turned to their mystical moral sense and more sweetly expounded for the soul’s advancement.

[Col. 0766A] We ought to understand how this king Ahaz, who ruled the people of God by temporal authority, may be understood as representing ourselves. For every one of us has received for governance his thoughts, all his actions, and every sense of his body; whoever governs these well may truly be called and be a king. Moreover, we are shown to be not only kings but also priests of the Lord, if we endeavour faithfully to fulfil both offices in ourselves, so that it may not unfittingly be said of us what Peter, prince of the apostles, says in his epistle: “You are a royal and priestly race, a holy nation, a people of acquisition” (1 Pet. 2:9).

Let us therefore carefully consider how we may fulfil within ourselves the office of priest. [Col. 0766B] For it is the office of a priest to offer sacrifices and sweet-smelling incense upon the altar. Thus we too ought, in a contrite heart and a spirit of humility, to offer ourselves to God as a sweet savour; to cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, that we may be a living, spotless sacrifice pleasing to God; and that we may be able to obtain the sign mentioned below, not by tempting God but by asking faithfully.

195 We must, by a continual fountain of tears, ask the Lord for the sign of salvation as though from the depths of hell, so that the wounds of the sick soul may be laid open, and that we may understand what deeds we have done on that side which have led us into the pit of destruction. When, therefore, the eyes have been enlightened by such compunction of heart, then at last we must ask for a sign in the height above: namely, the virtues by which the kingdom of heaven may be attained.

[Col. 0766C] It should be noted, moreover, that nothing is signified by the name “sign” except something proved to be new and unheard of. Truly worthy of miracle is this: that man, dust and ashes, who is always subject to lowly actions, should suddenly be lifted through the heights of virtues to God at the summit of contemplation, and, according to the Apostle, should become one spirit with the Lord (1 Cor. 6:17). Let us seek this sign with unfeigned faith and every purity of heart from him who is near to all who call upon him in truth.

For if lovers of this world were instructed to ask the Lord for such a sign, they would immediately answer with proud mouth and uplifted neck of heart: “I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord.” For those subject to the vice of pride disdain to seek the sign of humility and submission. But when they do not receive counsels of salvation, holy teachers add through words of preaching:

[Col. 0766D] Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God? We should know that some are troublesome to God but are still beloved by men: namely, those whom the enemy injures by deadly persuasion, though their wickedness has not yet come to human notice. There are also others who are indeed adverse to men but are not yet troublesome to God: truly, those who live wickedly but intend to change their life for the better. To these the Lord himself will give a sign, when, freeing them from the depths of sins, he illumines them by the grace of his sweetness. For it immediately follows:

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.” Behold, when that soul, long prostituted to many lovers, begins, at the Lord’s summons, to renounce her 196 corrupter—that is, the unclean spirit—and to preserve whole and undefiled faith for her bridegroom, she suddenly becomes a virgin and is taken into the bridal chamber of the immortal Bridegroom. She will conceive and bear a son: namely, virtues, adorned by which she may fittingly proceed to the banquet of the eternal King.

[Col. 0767A] Therefore, when that soul beloved by God is impregnated with the sweetness of the Word of God, and has deserved to conceive the desire of eternal life and to bring it forth by working, then she may truly and joyfully proclaim and say: “God is with us.” But when a son of such nobility has been conceived and born, we must especially consider with what food he ought to be nourished, lest he perish, consumed by the want of hunger. For it immediately follows:

He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good. What is expressed through butter except the less profound knowledge of the Scriptures, by which every little one is refreshed as if with a draught of milk? And what can be understood by the sweetness of honey except the subtle and spiritual sense in the letter, which is the food of the perfect? This son, then, must be nourished with these foods until he becomes fit to reject evil and choose good.

[Col. 0767B] He must reject evil—that is, the devil, who is the head and beginning of all evils. For at every hour and moment he goes about roaring like a lion, seeking whom he may devour; this noble son must reject his thousand arts with every effort. [Col. 0767C] Therefore, when he and his works have been rejected, the supreme and only good must be chosen: namely, Christ, who is the true hope and rest of the saints. Let us love him; let us desire him with our whole heart; let us hasten to please him alone with greater attentiveness. Let us search and examine our ways, and return to him, praying that he may deign to be the end of our desires—he who in eternal life will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without fatigue. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

97  
## HOMILY XXXI. FIFTH HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE ANNUNCIATION OF BLESSED MARY THE VIRGIN

[Col. 0767D]

“My soul melted when my beloved spoke,” etc. (Song of Songs 5).

When the flesh, from the root of its first origin, had been sold under sin, so that the eternal Wisdom of God found almost no one with whom to mingle the sweet conversations of its secret, the Holy Spirit found the Shunammite bride, a peerless virgin. God the Father took care more intimately to impress upon her the sweetest kiss of his mouth, and to instil into her ears words sweet and altogether ineffable to humankind, more sweetly than into those of other mortals. Therefore the most wise Solomon, in the Song of Songs, expresses how sweetly she, chosen and pre-chosen, melted at the voice of the beloved speaking to her, melted by the fire of inward love. Amid the sweetest mutual conversations of bridegroom and bride, he introduces words of this kind: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke.”

[Col. 0768A] Although she said this, indeed, in the person of the Church, it is more particularly attributed to that unique and most noble bride who knows not man—our Lady, Mary ever-virgin—into whose embraces that same beloved wholly rushed, and to whom he made himself known, by an ineffable mode of speech, as such and so great as no saint from the beginning of the world could or will be able to know him. Therefore, loved above all, she loved more than all, so that she alone can truthfully say: “My soul melted; my beloved spoke.”

For the ecstasy of her fore-illumined mind, passing wholly into God, had from tender age learned to transcend herself in the affections of both the inner and outer person, so that, removed from every human tumult not less in body than in heart, she could rightly say with the Prophet: “I will hear what the Lord speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9). For her whole intention looked to this alone: that of all the things which God the Father had set before his heirs to be accomplished, she should pass over none with a deaf ear, but should endeavour most fully to perform by works whatever she received by hearing.

[Col. 0768B] Indeed, she heard and, alone beyond other mortals, fulfilled more perfectly what the Lord commanded through Moses to all who wish to enter the way of life: 198 [Col. 0768C] “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and your neighbour as yourself.” The love by which she was accustomed to love God surpasses every measure of human narration. For, dead to the world, she rejoiced to live for God alone; nor did she know how to admit in deed or thought anything that could, even for a moment, draw her back from the intimate fellowship of him who, as the author of purity and integrity, had made her near to himself.

Moreover, the following words make more evident the unquenchable ardour of charity with which her most holy soul was inflamed toward her neighbours. For after she says that she melted from the conversation of beloved with beloved, she immediately adds:

“I sought him, and did not find him.” What, then, does this most beloved of beloved women mean by asserting that she sought and did not find her beloved, whom she had always present, dwelling between her breasts through the sweetness of inward inspiration? Truly, this was her incomparable seeking: compassion, by which she condescended to human miseries.

[Col. 0768D] Whenever it came to the memory of the most holy Virgin how man, created in paradise for the honour of so great a dignity, experienced neither trouble nor want, and how by his own free choice he had changed such glory into the disgrace of such calamity and misery, she mourned his utterly irrecoverable fall so deeply that, through the affection of her most merciful compassion, she shared not only the miseries of those then living but also of all who would be born until the end of the world.

[Col. 0769A] What every person placed in hell suffered, the blessed Virgin believed that she herself endured; for she bewailed their punishments as much as the peril of her own soul, a peril which she knew she could not escape in any way unless the Only-Begotten of the Father, consubstantial with the Father in all things, should be clothed in human flesh, open the gates of paradise barred by the bolts of original sin, and, having destroyed the wall of enmity, 199 restore the seal of peace and grace between God and man.

Therefore, because she had heard that such a mediator of God and men, so mighty, had been promised through the Law and the prophets to her fathers, so that at last he might come forth for the salvation of his people, heal the contrite in heart, and heal those who were in the flesh and outside the flesh, she sought him with desires altogether untiring. But because the fullness of time had not yet come for that same beloved to depart from the hiddenness of his dwelling, he did not deign to show the beloved woman, however exceedingly anxious in her search, the beauty of his form in bodily presence. What then did she do? Did she cease to seek, she whom the whole love of the beloved had wholly possessed and occupied? Certainly not. Rather, the power of love stirred the desire for human salvation and multiplied in her the intensity of seeking. It follows:

[Col. 0769B] “I called, and he did not answer me.” How then did our Lady, mother of everlasting salvation [manuscript: *materia*, “matter”], add that she called the beloved whom, though sought for so long, she had not deserved to find? She called, indeed, when after long desires for the restoration of humankind she turned to the practice of unconquered prayer. [Col. 0769C] There, carried above herself in a fiery flood of tears and with spirit greatly contrite, she set before God the Father the various calamities and miseries not only of those who lived justly and piously, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of his Only-Begotten in the flesh, but also of those who, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, sighed inconsolably for the same grace of redemption.

Her calling, therefore, was earnest supplication to God day and night, that, mindful of the oath by which he had freely bound himself to humanity—by which, according to gratuitous goodness, God had willed to make himself, the Lord, debtor to man his servant—he might send his Only-Begotten into the world, to redeem humankind from hostile dominion by the mystery of his Incarnation.

[Col. 0769D] Yet in this most anxious seeking of him and this most steadfast invocation of him, the ever-virgin did not seek that which God the Father had nevertheless decreed before the foundation of the world should be done through her—and for which, as soon as she was born, the Holy Spirit took her into his protection, so that, shaded by the safeguard of his protection, she might grow high as a blooming rose among thorns, unharmed by their thorns, and so that in its own time the sweetest little flower of all sweetness, all purity, and all chastity might emerge powerfully from her.

200 This most beloved of beloved women, as we have said, did not seek this—indeed, so to speak, she did not know how to seek it. For although she flourished in an incomparable strength of holiness, innocence, and chastity, the profound and inexpressible humility of her most holy heart, by which she made herself lower than all those superior to her, allowed her not only not to desire this but not even to think of it.

[Col. 0770A] Thirsting ardently only for the beloved’s presence in the flesh, amid tears and groans she joined prayers to prayers, daily crying to heaven with the most holy Moses, her spirit deeply afflicted: “I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou art going to send” (Exod. 4:13). Also, to kindle more strongly the flame of her desire, she had, as we believe, that familiar saying of the Psalmist, by which, longing to see this same beloved, she spoke with a groaning voice: “Show us thy face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:4).

But although with the most welcome humility of so great a calling she penetrated all the secrets of heaven; although by the importunity of this desirable cry day and night she disturbed the beloved himself, established in the rest of his eternity, that same beloved, who rejoiced to have this force done to him, as though he did not hear what he desired to hear, neither gladdened the seeker with the desired presence of his face nor took care to satisfy her cry with any word of answer as to when it would come to pass.

[Col. 0770B] Yet how could he, to whom sweetness is familiar and goodness consubstantial—how, I say, could he to whom the cry of the humble ascends—contain himself so long in the face of the great cries of so great a beloved? Did he not hear the groaning of her whom, before the times of the world, he chose and foresaw as his bride and mother? The desire of her most holy heart could not be hidden from him, since by his inspiration she had conceived that very fervour of mind.

[Col. 0770C] For from the beginning, ardently desiring the salvation of humankind, he made and created this same beloved for himself; preserving her without sin in the place of sin, he formed and trained her, so that he might have her in due time as a helper, both a sharer in the desire and fit for accomplishing that which he desired. But because the acceptable time and the day of salvation had not yet come, in which that same brightness of the Father’s glory would deem it fitting to assist human misery, the long waiting for his coming was in some manner a hard and unbearable denial of the long-sought answer.

201 Yet the blessed Virgin, whose mind was founded upon the rock, clung immovably by the unchangeable affection of love to him who does not know how to change; wholly secure in his ineffable goodness, she could be recalled from the constancy of her begun invocation neither by delay nor by any injury of difficulty.

[Col. 0770D] For, mindful of Scripture saying, “In the day of evils do not be forgetful of good things,” she strove to raise the voice of her heart all the more strongly as she had deserved, by the grace of inward savour, to taste more sweetly the inexhaustible sweetness of him whom she sought. Therefore, for this constancy and such perseverance in untiring labour, the grace of heavenly consolation which she obtained is plainly expressed in the following words: “The watchmen of the city found me,” she says; “they struck me and wounded me; they took away my cloak.”

By the watchmen of the city we may fittingly understand the angelic spirits. The glorious Virgin deserved their special care in guarding and protecting her all the more because, living in the flesh beyond the flesh through the innocence of her singular life, she was the first of all to imitate the excellence of angelic life. Therefore, since virginity is always akin to angels, they rejoiced always and everywhere to be with this Virgin in grateful familiarity and familiar kinship, but especially at the time of prayer; and they offered to the beloved whom she sought her holy desires, prayers, tears, and sighs.

[Col. 0771A] By such guardians, never absent from her through the invisible grace of their protection, she was found in visible presence when the counsel of the undivided Trinity, hidden from the beginning, was made known to her by angelic address, [Col. 0771B], as the text of evangelical Scripture openly declares: “The angel,” says the evangelist, “entered to Mary and said: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee” (Luke 1:28).

Although Gabriel the archangel alone is named there, we nevertheless do not believe that he entered alone and without a great retinue of the heavenly host to so great a bride of so great a Lord, bringing to her—not to her alone but to the whole human race—the announcement of eternal salvation. For if the ancient enemy, as is certain, oppresses any 202 wretched and unhappy soul by so great a multitude of his like-minded followers when, by authority granted from above, he begins to enslave her to his dominion, what wonder if we rightly believe that so great an ambassador of so great a King was honoured by no small company of blessed spirits? This befitted the excellence both of the one sent and of the sender, and the reverence due in every respect to the Virgin who was to be greeted—indeed, betrothed.

[Col. 0771C] Further, lest this be less certain, the preceding words of this same beloved woman provide testimony: “The watchmen of the city found me.” In saying this, she expresses not only the throng of holy angels visiting her, but also the special prerogative of her merits: namely, that she alone, blessed among all and above all, was alone most justly and worthily chosen above all the elect, from whom the eternal Father willed that his coeternal Son should be incarnate.

It is as though she said: Having trampled under the strong foot of contemplation all that the present world desired; having diligently locked all the entrances of heart and body with the virginal key of modesty, they found me wholly within myself, because I knew how to admit nothing through thoughts and seek nothing through desires except the sole desirable face of the desirable beloved, in whom I did not doubt that I and the whole human race would be saved.

[Col. 0771D] Because they found me thus, therefore, they struck me and moreover wounded me. But what kind of blows, I ask, were these wounds? Fear and love, undoubtedly. By fear she is shaken as though with a hard lash, when, mindful that the angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, she is disturbed by the angelic splendour. For unless that special guardian had seen her fearful and trembling, he would never immediately have added, consoling her with such sweet blandishments: “Do not fear, Mary” (Luke 1:30).

But while he endeavoured, by such a gentle hand of consolation, familiarly to touch, soothe, and heal the bruises of her blows, he suddenly shot an exceedingly sharp arrow. With a sweetness exceedingly delightful, it reached even to the division of soul and spirit, delightfully wounding the beloved soul of the beloved Virgin with the sweetest wound of love: “Behold,” he says, “you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1:31).

[Col. 0772A] “Do not fear,” I say, “nor be afraid,” you whom eternal majesty has deigned to visit in regard for so great a dignity. Behold, you shall conceive: behold, he who was long desired, sought, and called is not only presented 203 for you to see, but will also be clothed in human flesh from you. O wound more delightful than every sweetness, for to be wounded thus is to be healed entirely from every pain! [Col. 0772B] It follows:

“The watchmen of the walls took away my cloak.” By the cloak that was taken away, original sin may be understood. Original sin is the concupiscence of the flesh and the ignorance of the soul. Since this blessed Virgin, as one conceived and born in sins, was not without this cloak, she believed what she had heard, but was utterly ignorant how these things could happen.

> **[Note: Col. 0771]** See the preliminary dissertation in volume I of this work concerning this now obsolete opinion of Godefrid.

She therefore says: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” But, as though to remove the cloak both of this ignorance and of all ignorance, the angel immediately extended his hand, adding an explanation of the manner and order of conceiving and also of giving birth: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.”

[Col. 0772C] When the Holy Spirit came upon her, ignorance was entirely put to flight, because none of the treasures of heavenly wisdom could thereafter remain hidden from her, since she was worthy to receive and bear in her virginal body, as well as in her heart, the very Wisdom of the eternal Father bodily. Moreover, at the very same hour in which she deserved to be overshadowed by the power of the Most High, every stain of concupiscence, implanted by original sin, utterly vanished, 204 because although from the beginning of her birth she was incomparable with all virgins, nevertheless, from the angelic service of that new and unheard-of greeting, she was in every respect conformed to him whom she conceived, becoming holier in merits and loftier in virtues, as is plainly declared by her following words:

“Daughters of Jerusalem,” she says, “tell the beloved that I am sick with love.” By the daughters of Jerusalem in this place we may understand the same angelic spirits of whom we spoke above. As witnesses and messengers of this mutual love, she sent back to her beloved, namely God the Father, this message:

[Col. 0772D] “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell the beloved—tell him, I beseech you, whom from my earliest age I have loved with an unchangeable and steadfast love—that I am sick with love. By love and desire for him, I have until now appeared languishing and weak toward all that the present world loves, because my soul, thirsting for everything that was not God, despised it as though in disgust. [Col. 0773A] Therefore I sought him alone, I called him alone; and hence I alone, above all others, have deserved most rightly to be consoled by so great an answer of divine favour: by conceiving and bearing him who is the true consolation, hope, and redemption of the whole human race, to whom be honour, power, and glory through the infinite ages of ages. Amen.”

205  
## HOMILY XXXII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT RUPERT, BISHOP

“A certain nobleman went into a far country, to receive for himself a kingdom and to return” (Luke 19).

This man, so glorious and so noble, is the Firstborn Son of the Virgin Mary, nobler and more excellent than all mortals by as much as he contracted not the slightest sin in deeds, words, or thoughts. For all, by sinning in Adam, degenerated into the ignoble disgrace of vices. But not even the faintest contagion of sin ever came upon this blessed Son of the Father. Therefore he is called “a certain man,” that is, singular among all human beings: singular in conception and birth, singular in teaching, having conducted himself reverently in miracles according to God the Father; and after the disgrace of Passion and death, he showed the singular power of his Resurrection.

[Col. 0773B] He went into a far country when, as a faithful advocate who was to be heard because of his reverence, he presented before the sight of the Father’s majesty the manhood which he had assumed, reconciled to the Father. For when we fell from the eternity for which we had been created in paradise [Col. 0773C] by our own free choice, the kingdom of heaven became for us, cast down as we were, a very distant country. For the first man was so created that, if he freely chose to obey his Creator, he should pass without death into the fellowship of angels.

Moreover, he received a kingdom because, though he was King of kings and Lord of lords, he received by the gift of divinity the power which human nature did not possess, as the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2:9).

He will return at the final assize of judgment to render to each according to his works. Yet he also returns daily to restore peace and tranquillity to the Church that cries to him, and to give gifts from the treasures of the kingdom of heaven to his servants. For it follows:

[Col. 0773D] Having called his ten servants, he gave them minas, and said to them: “Trade until I come.” By the number ten of the servants is expressed the order of all who have received from the Lord the commandments of the Decalogue and, exercised in them like most faithful traders, have more diligently subjected themselves to divine work.

Indeed, the Holy Spirit, who apportions to each as he wills, has left no one wholly without a divine gift. Though he may not bestow upon some great merits of perfection, he nevertheless always grants them some gifts by which, if they are willing, they may attain the joys of eternal blessedness. Therefore, through the practice of continual work, each of the elect denies himself idleness, lest he ever grow sluggish, and scarcely permits any moments of time to pass without hope and fruit of eternal recompense.

[Col. 0774A] But let us hear what immediately follows:

“His citizens, however, hated him, and sent an embassy after him, saying: ‘We do not wish this man to reign over us.’” What do we understand by the citizens of this most noble prince except malicious and unclean spirits? On account of the dignity of their angelic nature, they are rightly called citizens of the Lord, who created them exceedingly beautiful and exalted for the praise of his eternity, as the prophet Ezekiel says to their prince: “You were the outstretched and protecting Cherub; you were the seal of the likeness of God; you were in the delights of paradise” (Ezek. 28:14).

Therefore, although they fell with their prince through pride, they did not lose the sublimity of their angelic nature; and from this point, because they do not repent unto life through hope, they do not cease to pursue and hate the Son of God, who loves and defends the children of adoption. [Col. 0774B]. “They sent,” says the evangelist, “an embassy after him.” For malicious spirits, after the grace of divine mercy which goes before us, after the regard of inward love, form a plan against us and importunately put before our ears manifold embassies of carnal desires, saying:

“Nolumus hunc regnare super nos—We do not want this man to reign over us.” For when they see, through the generosity of the divine gift, that sins are being avoided and the kingdom of virtues is being increased, they immediately oppress the hearts of the good with a harsher conflict; and the more vigorously they are cast down, the more strongly they strive to rise again. The kingdom of chastity and purity these unjust rulers strive to defile with the stench of lust; the kingdom of humility and gentleness they assail with the arrogance of pride and the zeal of bitterness. Concerning this kingdom blessed Paul gives this warning: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI.12). What kind of kingdom he means, he indicates when he adds: “That you should obey its desires.” For sin then reigns in us when, in will and desire, we obey the lusts of carnal pleasures. Therefore, since we perceive that the adversary fights against us in many ways, we must be all the more vigilant as soldiers of God, armed with the virtues. For as long as we endure this wretched exile, we shall by no means escape the wars and snares of our enemies. Of this conflict John says: “There was,” he says, “a great battle in heaven” (Apoc. XII.7).

[Col. 0774D] In the kingdom of heaven, where there is highest peace and highest tranquillity, where there is the unity of true peace, the savagery of combatants has never risen. Therefore “heaven” here is more rightly understood as the universal Church, or every soul devoted to God, which here suffers without interruption so many and such great battles from the ancient enemy. Yet the one who trusts in the protection of God, the heaven, will not lack the assistance of blessed and angelic powers; they fight valiantly for their fellow-soldiers against invisible enemies, lest they yield feebly. It follows:

“And it came to pass that he returned, having received the kingdom.” This return is the advent of the strict Judge, exceedingly great and fearful: he surveys everything, penetrates everything, examines the hidden things of hearts with the discriminating scales of equity, and strictly smites the one whom he finds not to have employed for gain the talents entrusted to him. It is rightly said that he returns “having received the kingdom,” so that the exile which still remains in part may be ended, and the heavenly dwelling which has already begun in part may be completed. For he has not yet received the kingdom wholly, because, until the number of the elect is complete, he cannot be praised and glorified amid the joy of his people with the jubilation of perfect exultation. But when he has delivered the kingdom to God the Father—that is, when he has brought all believers to the contemplation of God, which is to deliver the kingdom to God the Father—then those in whom he now reigns will themselves indeed reign with him by grace in glory.

“And he commanded his servants to be summoned, that he might know how much [Col. 0775B] each had gained by trading.” Let us now direct the gaze of our minds and inquire why several are summoned in number, yet only two are rewarded, while the third is condemned. These two, specially set forth in this way, undoubtedly signify something; if we attend to their merits in their figurative meaning, we shall find in them something by which to advance through imitation. By these two, therefore, are represented the great merits of the twofold life, namely the contemplative and the active: one consists in the height of contemplation, the other in the work of action; one by which attention is devoted to the knowledge of God, the other by which service is rendered to the advantage or love of neighbours.

Accordingly, those are rightly signified by the first servant who comes to the Lord who, setting aside every care, merit to taste and see how sweet the Lord is; who already have a spirit united with God; and who, as it were, through a certain familiarity with his sweetness, frequently recalling it, now by thinking on divine things, now by praying, now by reading, prepare for the Lord a banquet of inward sweetness surpassing honey and the honeycomb. These people, although held here in body, are nevertheless sometimes raised in mind to the joys of the heavenly dwelling-place. They grieve that the kingdom is delayed, where he himself will give himself as the everlasting reward to those who love him. Therefore, seeking and longing for his presence, they sometimes come with joy, confidently claim the reward of their labour, and declare by saying how they have guarded, with a pure heart and a good conscience, the senses of the twofold human being:

“Lord, your mina has gained ten minas.” It is as if the happy soul bursts forth into praise of its Creator by recounting the great things done in itself. “Lord,” it says, “your grace and gift, going before and following your elect, bestowed upon me these undeserved benefits—not because of any merits of mine which preceded them, but through the helping grace of yours: I have preserved unstained, to the praise of your name, the ten minas, namely the outward and inward senses of the human being.” Nor should it seem incongruous to anyone that we have said ten minas ought to be understood as the ten senses of a human being. For just as there are five bodily senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—so likewise, as sacred Scripture testifies, we have learned that there are as many senses of the soul, a fact unknown to some. For if there were no spiritual sight in one who loves God, the Lord would never have said in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V.8). If the most sweet sound of heavenly and ineffable words did not penetrate the hearing of the heart, the Prophet would certainly not cry: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. LXXXIV.9). Likewise, if the happy soul were not nourished by the taste of inward sweetness, the Psalmist would not declare: “Taste,” he says, “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII.9).

If the fragrance of virtues did not emit the odour of a good reputation, Paul could in no way say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Cor. II.15). Perhaps Paul, in flesh that at some time would decay, had no odour other than other human beings; and therefore he uttered these words not concerning the flesh but concerning the more sweetly fragrant scent [Col. 0776B] of virtues. Likewise, if there were not a happy and sweet touch of the soul touching God and handling from its depths the Word of life, John would not add: “And our hands have handled the Word of life” (I John I.1). Whoever, according to his ability, presents these senses uncorrupted to the Bridegroom of incorruption, cries out that God is their Creator and giver, confesses him, and by confessing truly loves him; such a one is surely most readily admitted into the joy of his Lord, when the proclamation of praise is offered to him not by a human voice but by the wisdom of eternal majesty, in the words:

“Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful in a little thing, you shall have authority over ten cities.” He is rightly called faithful “in a little,” because, when he possesses everything in him who is the highest and best good, he will consider everything passing to be very slight and little. But what is it to be set over ten cities except to rule with authority over the senses wholly subjected to the spirit? For, as blessed Augustine says, a city consists not of any sort of animals but of rational beings living under the same law. There will then be no allurement of animal sense; rather, the mind, wholly transformed into the light of God, will be wholly spiritual, where those who are ruled by one King of peace live under the same law of repose.

But in another way the saints of God are set over ten cities when, having at some time received the second robe of the body, they are borne wholly into the love of God. For as long as they still think of the body that is to be raised, they are turned somewhat away from God, though only by a slight attention. Peter, prince of the apostles, already buried in the earth, awaits the resurrection of his body, so that the flesh which was the good and faithful companion of holy desire and labour may share in joy and exultation. Having seen how those placed in the surpassing sweetness of the contemplative life are thus rewarded, let us see what reward those who sweat in the labour of the active life may expect. It follows:

“And another came, saying: Lord, your mina has made five minas.” There are some who, through the grace of the active life granted them, despise worldly things, diligently guard the five outward senses in good deeds, and pour themselves out in compassion for their neighbour’s benefit; yet they never raise themselves to higher things through the grace of contemplation, nor even sometimes establish within themselves a solemn day for the Lord, because they do not know how to refresh their mind with the desire of holy love. The less, then, that these persons now enter into inward joys, the less they have to offer the Lord when they say: “Lord, your mina has made five minas.” It is as though any such person, in receiving the reward of labour, should say to the Lord: “Lord, who gives abundantly to all and reproaches no one, you did not grant me greater merits; you did not admit me to the secret places of your inward sweetness. I would often have poured forth the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness, if you had given yourself to me; I would have drunk you with a thirsty breast, if you had opened yourself, the fountain of life, to me.”

“And he said to him: And you, be over five cities.” The five cities are the five bodily senses, which anyone of this kind, when he has laid aside this mortal corruption, freely and tranquilly subjects to himself, so that, now that the term of present labour has ended, his mind may not be disturbed about many things. Yet it should also be noted that, although he is set over five cities, he does not deserve to hear the joyful “Well done” of the good and faithful servant, though he is crowned by the Lord with a sufficiently worthy recompense. This occurs because not all are to be rewarded with equal blessedness; rather, as there are divisions of graces, so there are differences of glories; and as there are distinctions of works, so there are many dwelling-places in the Father’s house. Some will have more than others according to the measure of their merits; for as star differs from star in brightness, so also will be the resurrection of the dead. Yet, as someone says, by whatever path each reaches any of the dwelling-places, he will not be excluded from the one house.

It is fitting that, after the reward of the two who contain in themselves the figure of all the righteous, the condemnation of the reprobate follows, as is immediately added:

“And another came, saying: Lord, behold your mina, which I kept laid away in a napkin.” By the napkin is understood the present age, which is not undeservedly compared to a napkin, because the whole course of the present life is indeed labour and affliction. Of this napkin it was said to the first man, cast down into this misery of exile: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III.19). For lovers of the world, while they labour with all their efforts for earthly desires, labour in vain and think the present life not a road but a homeland; and in order to gain the joys of transitory happiness, they turn the whole understanding of their mind away from God. Such people, in accordance with the statement of this servant, confess that they have laid away in a napkin the mina—that is, the knowledge granted them by God—and, lying dead in sin, fear lest they should at some point be drawn away, through the operation of the divine gift, from delight in work and pleasure of the flesh. And because they trembled with fear where there was no fear, they add, with great shame of heart, words such as these: “For I feared you, because you are an austere man: you take up what you did not lay down, and reap what you did not sow.”

Let us see what sort of fear theirs is; let us examine how the Lord takes up what he did not lay down and reaps what he did not sow.
