Every reprobate person, rejoicing in temporal goods, fears the Lord not with the chaste fear that endures for ever, but with a most wicked fear; and him whom they ought to have loved as Father they fear as an austere master. They also wickedly assert that he takes up what he did not lay down and reaps what he did not sow. What, then, is it that the Lord did not lay down and yet takes up? It is surely sins, which he himself did not place in a human being, yet removes through the regard of inward mercy. And he reaps not what he himself but the hostile man—that is, the devil—has sown, when he more sternly cuts down with the sickle of severity our vices, which he long bore with patience; and sometimes he mingles bitter things with sweet, so that even in this way the mind may recollect itself to him.

Therefore the Lord takes up what he did not lay down when, in the hearts of those whom he has destined for salvation, he crushes and breaks down, through a contrite and humble spirit, the swelling pride and arrogance. For to those truly converted to himself he customarily gives such contrition of heart that, in view of the dignity above, they utterly lay aside whatever pride and haughtiness seemed to stand in them.

It is also said that he reaps what he plainly did not sow: “You reap what you did not sow.” One who reaps gathers fruit. So too God Almighty, for the fruit and benefit both of himself and of the human being, reaps what he does not sow, when he turns to good that which is evil in a human being—that is, human sin. For that person who would never turn to God and to the purpose of the spiritual life unless, bound by the grave consciousness of his crimes, he recognized himself as guilty before God and feared that he was to be condemned to eternal torments—when this person humbly and patiently subjects himself to God in the purpose of the spiritual life, and to those to whom he ought for God’s sake, then God Almighty truly reaps what he did not sow; because he has changed into good fruit the evil of a human being, that is, human sin, which he himself did not make in the human being. The perverse fear this taking-up and reaping of the Lord, although they know with complete certainty that they will perish unless the Lord does this in them. Therefore the following words are immediately added:

“Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant.” “You ought rightly to be condemned from your own words,” he says, “for you yourself bear witness that you feared to be saved by me, knowing that I am such an austere Lord that I shall by no means spare wicked works: taking up what I did not lay down, namely sins which I have always hated; reaping with bitterness the pleasures of the flesh, which I long endured with gentleness. Since, therefore, you knew all this to proceed from my gift and power, tell me, I ask you, wicked servant, why did you not give my money to the table—that is, to the measure? If you had begun even the least good according to your ability and measure, and thus advanced from good things to better, I would have come by helping grace and exacted it with interest. I, I say—I who thirst for the salvation of all, who regard a human being’s willing of the good as a great thing—I would indeed have come and kindled whatever little spark of holy desire there was into a great flame of my love.”

Since every condemned person trembles, while there is time, to hear this, let us hear with how great a punishment he strikes such a one in the future. It follows:

“And he said to those standing by: Take the mina from him and give it to him who has ten minas.” Who are these standing by except angelic spirits, who so stand present before the face of their Creator that, through unchangeable love, they attend him who always stands in eternity? Through their ministry every judgment is carried out, as we have fitting testimony from Scripture, which says: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks” (Matt. XIII.41); and again: “Gather the tares and bind them in bundles to burn” (Matt. XIII.30). Thus in the present passage he commands the standing-by angels to take away the mina from every person justly condemned and to give it to the one who was unwilling to be idle in acquiring eternal things.

“Take the mina from him”—take away, that is, all knowledge, all confidence of hope; let the one who, while it was permitted, refused to serve me as Father and Lord be deprived of every aid of my goodness. Then the unhappy soul thus abandoned by its Creator, wholly losing through despair the light of knowledge and understanding, will never be able to rise to the joys promised to the righteous. That there is no knowledge of truth in the hearts of the condemned is also indicated by the words of Solomon, who, wishing to make every faithful person diligent in works of righteousness, says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do earnestly; for there will be neither work nor reasoning in hell, to which you are hastening” (Eccl. IX.10).

It should be noted, moreover, that the talent taken from this man is deservedly given not to the one who had less but to the one who had received more, although to some who do not know the hidden things of divine understanding it seems much more fitting that it should be given to the one who had less. But if we observe that the one who had ten minas bears the figure, as we said before, of those who, trampling down every care, seek the repose of contemplation and sometimes, raised beyond the constraints of the flesh, merit to be one spirit with the Lord, we see that those who loved more than others most fittingly receive greater rewards. The angels standing by affirm that this is worthy and just, replying to the righteous Judge:

“Lord, he has ten minas.” “Lord,” they say, “you are just and your judgment is right. Holy Lord, we declare that you have judged justly: he possessed more because he loved you with his whole soul, whole heart, and whole mind. Lord, he has ten minas. Under your favour he preserved pure and undefiled the senses of the twofold human being; from the depths of his heart he hungered and thirsted for righteousness and truth. Open now the fountain of your sweetness; let the longed-for form of your vision be manifested, that the hunger for your satiety—which is not to be despised—may be sustained, indeed renewed, in him. For nothing could suffice for the satisfaction of this hungry servant of yours as long as he was not permitted to see you.”

Happy then is the soul, endowed with every fullness of perfect knowledge: it will enter the treasures of Wisdom hidden from the ages; and it will contemplate face to face all the sublime things concerning Christ’s divinity and the Trinity and Unity of the whole Godhead. It will be openly made manifest that he alone is true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. This will be so great, so splendid, and so exalted a reality that nothing can be compared with it. And that these words are most faithful and true, he himself who promised these things affirms again when he says:

“I say to you that to everyone who has, more shall be given; but from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away from him.” Truly, to everyone who has shall be given, because whatever is devoutly believed, whatever is holily thought, whatever is justly loved, is there wholly comprehended in perfection. But from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away—from the person, I mean, whose conscience supplies not even the least desire of good will. It is fitting that one alienated in mind from God should lose every grace of everlasting life.

[Col. 0780B] Therefore let us strive, with God’s help, to keep our inward and outward senses pure and undefiled; let us strive to love our Creator with our whole soul and all our strength, so that we may merit to attain that glory of blessedness in which the elect of God now behold the King of glory in his beauty. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIII. FIRST HOMILY ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

“Before the feast-day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own, loved them unto the end” (John XIII).

This most holy Gospel reading, in which the evangelist makes, as it were, a certain entrance into the Passion of the Lord that he is about to recount, sets forth for us, as it seems to me, the entrance into our own passion—the passion in which we must suffer with Christ if we desire to become participants in the glory of his resurrection. For thus the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. VIII.17). If in the present life we suffer with Christ by crucifying our flesh with its vices and lusts, we shall reign with him in the glory of the future resurrection.

The evangelist figuratively marks the entrance, so to speak, of this our passion in the beginning of this holy Gospel, when he says:

“Before the feast-day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come.” By the feast-day of Passover we may fittingly understand the conversion of every person who is to be saved. For what could Passover, which means “passing over,” signify more fittingly than that most saving passage when a person, God inspiring and helping, despises the passing joys of this present life and passes from the world to God, from vices to virtues, from an evil life to a good life? The day of such a passage may rightly be called a feast-day. For it is truly festive and joyful to God and his angels when a sinner converted from former pleasures begins to subdue the flesh and, through heavenly desire, to draw near to his Creator. Of this feast-day the Lord says through the Prophet in the psalm: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. XLV.11).

And it fittingly accords with the majesty of his omnipotence that it is said: “Before the feast-day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come,” because before this passage takes place in a human being, he himself—the true and merciful maker of our salvation—knows when his hour comes, for him to pass from this world to the Father. How do we say that he passes from this world to the Father, when we confess and believe that he reigns in heaven with the Father? It is not in his own person, certainly, but in the person of his elect that he passes to the Father, when he causes them to pass from the world to God, from the manner of life of secular wickedness to the warfare of the spiritual life. The hour of this most saving passage is rightly called his hour. For he himself foreknew and foreordained this hour in the ordering of his eternity: the hour in which he predestined that his sinner, straying from the path of truth, should be recalled to himself through repentance and conversion.

And this expression, “that he should pass from this world to the Father,” greatly befits his immeasurable goodness and mercy. For it is a great consolation and a wondrous condescension toward us that, although he is Lord and Creator of all, he is not ashamed to be called, and to be, the Father of sinners. He is indeed our Father: we are his creation, we have our being from him, and from him and through him we live. And because he recognizes himself as Father, he loves his wretched and despairing children even when they are submerged in the deadly abyss of sins, as the evangelist subsequently adds:

“Having loved,” he says, “his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end.” All whom he decreed to save in the order of his wondrous providence, even while they are still in the world—that is, while they still serve sins and vices—he embraces and loves as a Father loves children, although they are wholly unworthy of the name of children: he loves them not as they are, but as he foresees they will be. And lest they pass away and perish with the passing world, he holds and guards them with a fatherly hand. For he himself knows what he will do with them and in them.

For he often permits his elect and beloved servants to be cast down by a grave fall into sin, so that they may rise stronger after their fall, and so that with greater steadfastness of humility they may subject themselves not only to God but also to all people for the name of God. It was not [the manuscript reads *nonne* for *non*] because he did not love his chosen disciple Peter that he permitted him to fall. Indeed, he truly loved him; but he allowed him to fall so that he might rise stronger and, humbled and instructed in his own weakness, might know how to condescend to the weakness of his neighbours. So too, loving those who are still devoted to the world and flesh, he in a sense feigns not to know and see what they are, because he mercifully considers their end. Therefore, after the evangelist said, “Having loved his own who were in the world,” he immediately added, “he loved them unto the end.”

The Apostle teaches us what this end is when he says: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X.4). Christ indeed becomes the end for righteousness to every believer when, through the inward grace of his inspiration, he mercifully gathers his elect to himself after the love of the world and sins has ended in them; and inwardly and invisibly kindles them to desire and seek that end which is without end—namely, the end of eternal blessedness. For he loves them while they are still placed in the world in order to bring them to this end. But what a storm of temptations commonly rises against a person beginning to tend toward this end the evangelist makes known by adding these mystical words:

“And supper,” he says, “having taken place, when the devil had already put it into the heart that Judas, Simon Iscariot’s son, should betray him.” By the supper may be understood the holy way of life of any spiritual persons, who by their good works daily look toward God and offer him, with the highest devotion and humility, the sweet draught of continual compunction. This supper is rightly said to have been made and prepared, as it were, for the converted sinner when, admitted into the fellowship and way of life of spiritual persons who thus refresh God and drink of him, he has sat with them at one table of spiritual refreshment and has begun, by imitating their holy and praiseworthy life, to advance in the fear and love of God. Such a one may also not unfittingly be called Judas, Simon Iscariot’s son. For Judas means “confessing,” Simon “obedient,” and Iscariot “memory of death.” A person becomes Judas by humbly confessing and repenting of the crimes of his past life before God. He becomes Simon Iscariot by subjecting himself to God and people with every obedience and humility, solely on account of the remembrance of death and the attainment of the glory of eternal blessedness.

But because the more humbly a person strives through zeal for good conduct to draw near to God his Creator, the greater are the dangers of temptation which he endures from the malice of the ancient enemy lying in wait for him, it is rightly said: “When the devil had already put it into the heart that Judas, Simon Iscariot’s son, should betray him.” Note that it is not said, “when the devil had already put it into Judas’s heart,” but simply, “into the heart.” For here, as we may believe, the holy evangelist foresaw not only the betrayal of the Lord once accomplished through Judas, but also that betrayal which is still often invisibly carried out in the hearts even of God’s elect servants through the devil’s injected suggestion.

For Judas, having entered into counsel with the Jews and received money from them, betrayed the Lord. The evil spirits, signified by the Jews, invisibly carry on this same counsel and business with us, in order that, allured and deceived by their money—that is, their suggestions—we may abandon the Lord and subject ourselves to their dominion. The following text indicates what the perfectly converted person does, and ought to do, against these contrivances of the ancient enemy:

“Knowing,” it says, “that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and goes to God, he rises from supper and lays aside his garments.” What can we understand in the phrase, “the Father had given all things into his hands,” except prosperity and adversity? Whether favourable things smile or adverse things threaten, he receives everything from God and bears and endures everything with equanimity, knowing that the Father has given all things into his hands. In what sense “into his hands”? What better meaning can “hands” have here than power? He knows, then, that God the Father has granted to him, and to every human being, this power: that, with God’s grace cooperating, it lies within his own choice whether he wishes to receive or not receive the devil’s promptings and suggestions.

Considering this within himself, he receives and endures with such steadfast humility all those things—both favourable and adverse—which occur by God’s will or permission, that through them he is crowned rather than perishes. For this is what the Apostle says: “All things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. VIII.28).

But what especially awakens and kindles in him this steadfastness of humility and endurance is his knowledge that he came from God and goes to God. He clearly recognizes that it is the work and mercy of God alone that he has left the world and merited to pass into the warfare of the spiritual life. And because he goes to God—that is, because he desires at last, by living rightly, to return to his Creator and Redeemer, from whom he had long departed through sin—“he rises from supper and lays aside his garments.” How does he rise from supper? Does he leave the supper, that is, the holy fellowship of spiritual persons to which he has been joined? Far from it. Rather, from the supper—that is, by the merit of the supper—he receives that whereby he can rise.

How by the merit of the supper? Helped by the merit of the good people among whom he lives, and stirred by their example, he rises with a certain manly steadfastness, lifting himself up from the torpor of body and soul in which he previously lay. He also lays aside his garments when he subdues and humbles his body, which may be understood by the garments, with various labours, so that he may be able to attain true purity of the flesh. Accordingly it is immediately added:

“And when he had taken a linen cloth, he girded himself.” By the linen cloth may fittingly be understood purity of the flesh. For just as linen is brought to whiteness through great labour, so purity of the flesh is not attained without great bodily affliction. Many indeed take this linen cloth but do not gird themselves with it: they receive purity of the flesh but do not preserve it to the end; or, even if they preserve it, they do so not for love of God or the reward of the life to come, but because of shame in the present life, which they fear to incur. But the person who, having taken the linen cloth, girds himself is one who perseveringly restrains within himself the wantonness of the flesh by manifold labours, and in the holiness of chastity desires to please him alone whom no stain of defilement has ever touched. The following order of words mystically shows how great a grace of divine condescension comes to, and grows in, one who thus girds himself.

“Then,” it says, “he puts water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet.” By the basin we may understand the earthly heart of a human being; by the water which the hand of divine mercy puts into that basin, either knowledge of sacred Scripture or the grace of continual compunction; by the feet, thoughts or affections; and by the disciples, the human being’s own senses. Almighty God puts water into the basin when he mercifully illumines with the knowledge of sacred Scripture a human heart which had previously been earthly. For we often see that even unlearned persons sometimes receive from God such knowledge of the Scriptures in the spiritual life as more learned persons can rarely or never attain in the world.

He puts water into the basin when he grants a person so great a grace of compunction and such power of tears that, by weeping and repentance, the person can steadfastly wash away not only the stains of evil works but also the defilements of his deeds, thoughts, and senses. God comes to a person through such things. For when a person, with God cooperating, begins so to act inwardly, he makes a way for the Lord who comes to him. Hence it follows:

“He came, therefore, to Simon Peter.” By the grace of his visitation he comes to the obedient; he comes to the one who recognizes. When a human being begins to feel in himself this power and grace, he speaks to him, as it were, in these words and says: “Lord, do you wash my feet?” These words properly suit the person who has become Simon by humbly obeying God, and who has become Peter by humbly recognizing both the misery of his own weakness and God’s manifold mercy toward him.

For when he rightly recalls God’s mercies—how mercifully God bore with him amid so many and such great wicked deeds; how he restored hope of life and eternal salvation to one despairing and, so to speak, dead in sins; and how far the grace of his mercy advanced him, so that he can bewail not only his acts but also his affections—he says in wonder within himself: “Lord, do you wash my feet?” That is: “Lord, how wondrous and magnificent is the abundance of your sweetness over me! You wash me: that is, by the grace of your visitation you raise me to wash away the defilements of my affections and thoughts. It would be enough for me if I could ever wash away before you the crimes of my sins.” Jesus answered and said to him:

“What I do, you do not know now; but you shall know afterwards.” It is as though he said: “What I do in you through the unsearchable grace of my mercy, washing and cleansing you in your affections, you do not know now. For since you are still at the beginning of conversion, you do not yet perceive or understand what I intend by this work, since you have not yet merited to be wholly washed and cleansed in your deeds. But you shall know afterwards.” Your knowing is your loving. Later, when you have overcome your sins in part and washed and cleansed them by repentance, then you shall know; then you shall begin to love what I do; then indeed you shall first understand what benefit this work of mine brings you and how greatly it advances your salvation.

Peter says to him: “You shall never wash my feet.” This saying of Peter is the saying of a person truly repentant and recognizing himself in true humility. For, not to mention his acts, when he rightly looks upon himself in his thoughts and affections, he judges it altogether impossible that he should ever be cleansed from them or be capable of being cleansed. Therefore, grieving and groaning, he cries to God, as it were, in these words: “You shall never wash my feet.” He says this not in despair, since he knows and believes that all things are possible to God, but because he fears lest, on account of his sins, it ought not to happen. While he is in this fear, Jesus answers him inwardly in an ineffable manner, saying:

“If I do not wash you, you will have no share with me.” To be cleansed in your affections and thoughts is not within your own power or possibility. This belongs to me alone, who am able by my will alone to cleanse you. For unless I wash and cleanse you, you will have no share with me. I see nothing more fittingly understood here by this share which the blessed person has with God than that grace of inward sweetness [Col. 0785B] through which God invisibly visits and consoles his children in the time of prayer, when the blessed soul truly participates in God as far as is permitted in this mortal life. This sweetness is rightly understood as a share, because however much a person may deserve to taste of it in this life, it is nevertheless only a share: no one surrounded by a mortal body can attain its fullness in this life. Here it is given to the elect in part, as it were; its true fullness is reserved for eternal life. Thus he rightly says: “You will have no share with me.” That is: you will not deserve to attain and possess with me a share of my sweetness unless you have been washed and cleansed inwardly by me; and unless you have a share with me here, you cannot pass after this life [Col. 0785C] to its fullness.

After this inward speech of the Lord, which is perceived not by the hearing of the ear but by the understanding of the heart, a person is more and more enlightened toward the knowledge of God and of himself. Therefore it follows:

Simon Peter says to him: “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.” By the hands we understand works; by the feet, as has been said, affections or thoughts; and by the head, the intentions of thoughts. It is as though he said: Lord, unfailing fountain of mercy and grace, I see myself, in my works and thoughts and even in the intentions of my thoughts, wonderfully and miserably defiled before you; and unless you wash me, unless I deserve to be cleansed by you in all these things, I know and judge myself altogether unworthy [Col. 0785D] to have a share with you, or ever to taste, even in the slightest draught, the grace of your sweetness.

Jesus says to him: “He who has been washed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.” How does he say, “He who has been washed has no need except to wash his feet”? If he has been washed, how does he need to wash his feet? Thus a person perfectly converted, bound to God by the bond of obedience, is rightly said to be washed. For he is washed through conversion; he is washed through true and perfect confession. And he has no need except to wash his feet—that is, to labour to present himself to God unstained in his affections and thoughts. If indeed he does this by the helping and cooperating grace of God, it may rightly be said of him: “and he is wholly clean.” But because our Lord [Col. 0786A] and Saviour foresaw that this was impossible for a human being, he added accordingly and said:

“And you are clean, but not all.” For he knew who it was who would betray him. He knew, indeed, that our wretched and frail mind would often betray him. For we betray him when we receive that evil money of the Jews—that is, the suggestions of malignant spirits—and wretchedly fall away, weak and feeble as we are, from the fervour of that love by which we ought to love him before all things and above all things. Therefore, after the Evangelist had first said, “he knew who it was who would betray him,” he added: “therefore he said, ‘You are not all clean.’” And he rightly said, “You are not all clean,” because although a person may sometimes become clean in body [Col. 0786B] from evil action, one can rarely be found clean in heart from evil and useless thought. Although this grace is sometimes given here for a time to God’s chosen and beloved children, its perfect fullness will be possessed only in eternal life, where they will be established in such purity and cleanness of both body and spirit that not even the slightest thought will draw them away from beholding the ineffable brightness of God. This glorification of the righteous, as it seems to me, is accordingly expressed in the following words, when it is said:

“After he had washed their feet and taken his garments, and reclined again, he said to them: ‘Do you know what I have done to you?’” Earlier it was said, “and he began to wash the disciples’ feet”; but here it is said, [Col. 0786C] “after he had washed their feet.” In this present life the Lord begins to wash his elect, showing by example and foreshadowing in them that endless incorruption of cleanness and purity which they shall possess when the term of the present life has run its course. But after he has lifted them from the mire of this mortality and transferred them into the kingdom of his glory, there he more fully completes his washing, begun here; there, established in body and soul in the everlasting state of immutability, they think of nothing outside God, seek nothing apart from God, and desire nothing apart from God. Thus it is rightly now said: “After he had washed their feet and taken his garments, and reclined again, he said to them.” Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ takes his garments [Col. 0786D] when he has gathered all his members to himself, when at the end of the age he has brought all his elect, redeemed with the twofold robe of immortality, into his body. There indeed occurs a certain marvellous and glorious reclining which no mind can conceive and no tongue explain.

Even now the Lord sometimes reclines in the hearts of his elect. But this reclining is brief. Hindered by the obstacle of this mortality, it cannot be stable and enduring. But when he reclines again—when, after the resurrection has taken place, he begins to rest and reign in all his elect—this reclining will be everlasting. It will be bounded by no end and troubled by no unrest; and reclining among them, he will speak to them, as it were, these words [Col. 0787A]: “Do you know what I have done to you?” That is: You know, my most beloved fellow-partakers and co-heirs of my kingdom, that this your glorification is the work of my mercy. For whatever I did with you in the past life, I did in order to bring you to this glory that will remain without end.

“You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for I am.” You call me Lord because you acknowledge me as your Creator and Saviour. You call me Teacher because you rejoice that through the discipline and instruction of my teaching you have attained this unchangeable glorification of soul and body. And you speak rightly, because you speak truly: “For I am.” I am, because I created you; I am, because I delivered and saved you. I chose you from the world; [Col. 0787B] I trained you through the instruction of my teaching, in order to make you worthy and bring you to the great glory which you now possess with me. It follows:

“If therefore I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” What does it mean to say: If I—or rather, because I, your Lord and Teacher, your Creator and deliverer—in the misery and calamity of that past life washed your feet, cleansing you not only from evil deeds but also from evil affections, as much as was necessary and beneficial, “you also ought to wash one another’s feet”? How does he say, “you also ought to wash one another’s feet”? Who are this “one” and “another,” unless they express the glorified spirit and body of each of the elect? [Col. 0787C] For in this life we cannot be, nor be called, “one another,” because even if we are sometimes renewed in our inward person by the cooperating grace of God, we always relapse into what we are, oppressed by the burden of the body which we bear. But after we have laid aside this body which weighs down the soul and have passed into immortality, then our inward person will truly be another, and our outward person will be another: another indeed in glory, yet the same in nature. For we shall be marvellously and gloriously made other when, with body united to spirit, we are transformed into that state of perpetual immutability and incorruption, where we shall feel none of the contagion of the old person and where the new joys of eternal life are always renewed in us. There [Col. 0787D] we shall hear the most sweet voice of our Lord and King Jesus Christ reigning in our midst, saying: “If therefore I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” That is: the purity and chastity of body and mind which, while still surrounded by mortal flesh, you deserved to possess only for a time, when I washed and cleansed you—you will now possess not temporarily, but eternally.

For what you then could not do except through me, I now will to be within your power: that in your inward and outward person (each of which has now become “another,” because each is crowned with an equal glory of incorruption and immortality), there may be such purity and sincerity of thoughts, such harmony of wills [Col. 0788A] and affections, that the body may neither will nor be able to think or desire anything except what the spirit does, nor the spirit anything except what the body does; and that through unchangeable love you may always cleave to me, who am your head, so that you seek nothing outside me and can love nothing further apart from me.

“For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do.” By this—that while you were still in the flesh I sometimes lifted you invisibly and ineffably beyond the flesh through longing for my love and vision, so that in that hour of my visitation you sought and loved nothing but me and the joys of the heavenly homeland—I gave you an example and hope of that power and immutability which you have now received, in which you shall reign with me for ever, [Col. 0788B] and in which not even by the slightest thought will you ever again be hindered from beholding the glory of my majesty. This indeed is the reward for which we wait. May he make us worthy of it, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily XXXIV. First Homily for Good Friday

“Jesus went out with his disciples across the torrent of Cedron, where there was a garden” (John 18).

These are lofty and sublime words—the words, I say, of the soaring eagle—wrapped in a manifold depth of mysteries. How can a weak human being, scarcely, so to speak, creeping upon the earth, suffice to expound what the flying eagle, penetrating the secrets of heaven in its flight, published in noble writing? Eminent teachers too, whose sense and understanding have touched heaven somewhat, have passed briefly over certain mystical meanings in the words of this soaring eagle; yet they have left this present reading almost untouched. But though we scarcely creep upon the earth and are by no means fit to investigate these matters more subtly, we may nevertheless judge this: just as the Only-Begotten of the eternal Father willed all that he did and taught while living among human beings to be a pattern of right living for the elect, co-heirs of his kingdom, so likewise through the things which he said, did, and endured in his passion he set before his faithful an example of the passion to come. For what he then visibly endured [Col. 0788D] in his own body, he will also endure invisibly in his members daily until the end of the age. Hence, whoever wishes to be a companion in Christ’s passion should attend to and understand what he, about to suffer, said while questioning and answering his persecutors, and should endeavour to confront his malignant tempter with this same questioning and answer.

“Jesus,” he says, “went out with his disciples across the torrent of Cedron, where there was a garden.” Whence, why, or whither Jesus went out with his disciples, the Saviour himself, who went out, clearly indicates in this: that he willed to go out not elsewhere, but across the torrent of Cedron. For Cedron, which is interpreted as “hardness,” signifies the grievous and cruel hardness of the Jews, which returned upon God [Col. 0789A] the Saviour with such great and perverse cruelty that it laboured by every means to remove his memory from the earth. Although he loved the Jewish people as a people chosen especially for himself, and, appearing in the flesh, was always among and with them, teaching, preaching, and healing their sick, at last, as their hardness grew strong, he was compelled through the torrent of passion and death to depart from them. And David, foreseeing long before in the Holy Spirit that he would one day drink from this torrent of passion, said: “He will drink from the torrent on the way” (Psalm 109 [Vulgate 110]:7).

When this prophetic saying had been fulfilled—when he had crossed the torrent of passion and the glory of resurrection had been accomplished—he went out with his disciples, where there was a garden. By the garden the holy Church may fittingly be understood: either the congregation of those living well, gathered together in Christ; or any faithful soul beloved of God. For just as a garden well planted and watered generally seems more fruitful than the rest of a field, so the spiritual garden of the Church, and also the garden of the chosen multitude gathered in Christ, or the garden of each blessed soul, is always made fruitful with new shoots of virtues. This garden, producing the fruits of holiness and righteousness, is thus commended by the Bridegroom himself in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed,” he says, “my sister, my bride, a garden enclosed” (Song 4:12). It is rightly said to be enclosed not once but twice, since it is guarded outwardly from wicked acts and inwardly from evil desires.

Such a garden is truly a paradise of delight, [Col. 0789C] planted by the Lord in the beginning, in which tender and delightful souls are joined to their heavenly Bridegroom in the inestimable sweetness of love. This garden—that is, the garden of holy Church—began to be established and planted when one of the soldiers pierced with a lance the side of the Saviour hanging upon the cross. For just as Eve was formed from the side of Adam sleeping in paradise, so the Church was built from the side of Christ dying upon the cross. Therefore, rising from the dead, he immediately entered joyfully with his disciples into the garden of that same Church, as the Evangelist subsequently says:

“Into which he entered, he and his disciples.” This happy and desirable entrance truly occurred when, after his resurrection, he commanded his chosen disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 28:19). Thus, yes, thus, leaving the Jewish people and going out with his disciples for the salvation of the nations, and while they went and taught entering with them and through them into the garden of holy Church, he also prefigured another invisible going-out and entrance: that by the hidden steps of mercy he often deigns to go out and enter in the hearts of the elect. He goes out in this way in the minds of the faithful, in order that, softened inwardly by the touch of coming grace, he may cause them to leave the hardness of their heart. This hardness can fittingly be understood by the torrent of Cedron. For when this torrent—the torrent, I say, of evil lusts and carnal desires—begins to overflow beyond measure in the human heart [Col. 0790A] and by this flood overturns the mind from the state of uprightness, such hardness of heart often follows that the inward person cannot taste any divine sweetness. But when the Saviour, going out across this badly overflowing torrent, deigns to calm the motion of its waves, immediately the inward person goes out free—or rather, freed, so to say—from every hardness of heart. Thus the heart formerly wickedly hardened is sweetly softened by this health-giving departure and becomes a garden of spiritual delights, into which the same Saviour enters with his disciples—that is, with holy and virtuous desires and with spiritual pursuits of heavenly instruction—so as to cause new plantations of virtues there to sprout and bear fruit.

[Col. 0790B] “But Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with his disciples.” By Judas, who in mystical interpretation is said to mean “confessing,” that ancient enemy who confesses the Lord with a malicious heart is not unfittingly understood. Nor is it surprising if we have said that the devil is to be understood by Judas who confesses wickedly. For according to the Gospel, demons often confessed the Lord: “You are,” they say, “the Son of God” (Mark 3:11). And again: “Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matthew 8:29). Likewise elsewhere: “What have I to do with you, Son of God?” (Matthew 8:29). They also confess that God, the Creator of heaven, is their God and Lord, and that they can prevail in nothing against his power and dominion. And how did this aforesaid confessor betray [Col. 0790C] the Lord? In this way, certainly: because he incited the Lord’s betrayer to betray him, and stirred up the Jews to mock and crucify him. From the beginning this ancient confessor and betrayer knew that the place of the divine dwelling was in the spiritual garden of the Church, and that he had often met there, nor does he cease to come daily with his disciples, not disdaining to visit and console his bride with diverse pursuits and advances in virtue—his universal Church, that is, or the beloved multitude of those who love him, or, more particularly, any faithful soul closely joined to him. Hence he himself promises to be present among his faithful everywhere, saying: “Where two or three are gathered [Col. 0790D] in my name, I am in their midst” (Matthew 18:20). Therefore, when that ill-named Judas knows and understands very well, as has been said, what benefit, virtue, and grace the coming presence of the Saviour confers upon his faithful, he too seeks, through the attendants of his hidden malice, auxiliaries with whom, arriving at once, he may as far as lies within him nullify the mighty works of divine mercy. Thus it follows:

“But Judas, having received a cohort and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns and torches and weapons.” A cohort consists of three hundred soldiers. Since the soldiers of the cohort were Roman, secular rulers are fittingly understood by the cohort; by the chief priests, who were teachers of the people, spiritual governors of the Church are understood; and by the Pharisees, priests and presbyters, who seem to be spiritually subject to those governors. From these, alas, this Judas takes some servants and fellow-workers devoted and obedient to himself, so that through them and with them, as soldiers subject to him, he may fulfil the devices of his malice. For he himself could in some sense do nothing against the children of the Church if he did not possess ministers and soldiers of such great perversity.

There is also, according to the mystical moral sense, another cohort and other chief priests and Pharisees which it is pleasing to consider in a deeper interpretation. By the cohort are to be understood the outward works of the flesh; by the chief priests, the spiritual and inward senses of a person; and by the Pharisees, the hidden [Col. 0791B] thoughts of the heart. From all these—works, senses, and thoughts, that is—when they often turn toward worse things, this Judas, the author of all wickedness, alas, sometimes gains for himself many ministers and soldiers through whom he can strike down and overthrow the less watchful person more severely. For if one were watchful and observed one’s works, senses, and thoughts more diligently, that malignant one could find scarcely any entrance for tempting him. But when he finds in human work, sense, and thought some excesses, so to speak, and has taken these as ministers of iniquity and temptation cooperating wickedly with himself, he immediately comes there, as is added, with lanterns and torches and weapons.

By these three—lanterns, torches, and weapons—we are to understand the whole perfection of consummated wickedness: namely, consent, action, and defence. Since suggestion and pleasure are, as it were, a certain beginning of sin, why, omitting these two, did he foreshadow these three already named—consent, action, and defence? Certainly for this reason: a person is often tempted by suggestion and yet does not fall through delight in sin; sometimes the mind is assailed unwillingly by delight, yet no consent to sin arises. Thus too the Saviour of humankind endured the tempter’s suggestion, yet could not be moved by any delight in sin. Therefore, because in suggestion and delight there is often, as it were, no fault, omitting these two he wished to foreshadow these three—consent, action, and defence—by which and in which the fullness of all wickedness may be understood. “He came,” it says, “there with lanterns and torches and weapons.” By lanterns, in which there is fire indeed but hidden and concealed, consent to sin is rightly understood, because when a person falls merely by consent without the effect of an act, the fire is still, as it were, hidden in the lantern of the heart. But if this Judas discovers that consent is present—God forbid!—he immediately supplies torches of manifest action and weapons of perverse defence to one who wickedly consents (*consentienti*; manuscript *consentientem*, “one who consents”). And blazing torches, which both shine and smoke, fittingly signify the openly wicked works of action. For if a person is entangled in the filth of sins, he emits from himself a most foul smoke before God and human beings. And lest this smoke, once raised, should vanish, Judas hastens to furnish weapons of wicked defence. Defence is fittingly understood by weapons: weapons are called those things by which a person defends and protects himself from injury; missiles, however, are those by which he strikes an enemy down with force. When this often-mentioned Judas has acquired such a cohort and such servants, and has thus come armed with lanterns, torches, and weapons, as though to fight, into the garden mentioned above, the words of the same Saviour which follow indicate what every person who is to be saved ought to answer him with whom he attempts to enter into battle.

“But Jesus,” it says, “knowing all the things that were to come upon him, went forward and said to them: ‘Whom do you seek?’” By the name Jesus, which means “Saviour,” every person to be saved is fittingly understood. For the passion of the Saviour is the passion of the person to be saved; and whatever the person to be saved suffers, the most gracious Saviour does not disdain to suffer in him and with him. By prevenient grace, he who is Lord of all knowledge causes him to know all that is to come upon him and how great it is. He knows truly, by the Lord’s inspiration, [Col. 0792B] that if he consents to the malignant enemy through consent, action, and defence, eternal condemnation will come upon him. Therefore, advancing more and more in good and virtuous works, he answers the temptations of the devil who wickedly confesses and unjustly betrays, saying: “Whom do you seek?” This answer of the Lord, now about to suffer, seems most rightly suited to the faithful person suffering diabolical temptations. By these words the supremely good Teacher wished to teach us that we should strive always to be cautious and vigilant against the devil’s snares, so that with wakeful watchfulness we may wisely see and attend to what the ancient enemy seeks from us and in us. For it follows:

“They answered him: ‘Jesus the Nazarene.’” The Jewish answer now clearly declares what the diabolical assault seeks in us. For Jesus, as has been said, means “Saviour,” while Nazarene means “clean.” The malignant plotter always aims, labours, and watches toward this: that he may take away from us the salvation of our soul, which is Christ, and the purity of heart and body. [Col. 0792D] For this deceiver of souls often suggests to us things which a person considers entirely holy and just, so that even under the false appearance of good he may draw one into the snare of destruction. For example, when, at his suggestion, someone destroys his body by excessive, severe, and immoderate labours, or begins to practise immoderate abstinence in food and vigils beyond his strength, it follows that, being exhausted in strength and rendered weak and useless for everything that must be done, he is then compelled to indulge the body’s necessities beyond due measure. There are also some who, falsely thinking that they possess zeal for righteousness, become through his instigation judges and despisers of their teachers, puffed up by the spirit of pride. When he insinuates these and similar things into us by the counsel of hidden deception, he who suffers and is tempted in us subsequently indicates by his answer what we ought to answer in contradiction.

Jesus says to them: “I am.” “I am,” I say, one who seeks my salvation and my Saviour, one who will take care always to preserve my heart and body unstained for God my Creator. Having heard such an answer, let us see what the assault of the malignant tempter does in response. “Judas,” it says, “who betrayed him, was standing with them.” What is this standing of Judas the betrayer—that is, the devil—except his pressing more strongly upon the person who gives such an answer, by wicked temptation and deceitful ambush? And what does it mean to stand with them? He surely stands with all those things mentioned above, namely the various conflicts of vices and temptations, in order to draw him (*pertrahat*; manuscript *protrahat*, “drive him forward”), as has been said, into consent, action, [Col. 0793B] and defence of sin, and to take away from him the salvation of soul and the purity of heart and body. But will he always stand in this way and persist in fighting? Let us hear what the Evangelist says:

“But when Jesus said, ‘I am,’ they went backward and fell to the ground.” Therefore, when Jesus—that is, the person to be saved—has continually endeavoured to be cautious and watchful about what that fraudulent investigator seeks and investigates in him, the temptations and assaults of the malignant one undoubtedly go backward, because they cannot impel him to the crimes and offences which they intend. For what else is it for malignant spirits to go backward than to be unable to find a person compliant with them in sins and vices? When they cannot tempt the hearts of the perfect as much as they wish, they fall with cruel temptation to the ground—that is, into earthly hearts. For they readily find those who serve earthly cares and desires compliant and obedient to themselves, and make them fall with themselves, by a miserable fall, into the pit of destruction. When they have been repelled in this way and, by such a fall, have fallen into earthly hearts, let us see what the compassionate Lord says again by questioning—or rather, by teaching.

“Whom do you seek?” This second question of the Lord is a salutary teaching and admonition of the same Saviour, by which he mercifully wished us to be taught and warned to attend and consider carefully that, if they cannot draw us into consent and the accomplishment of wicked action, they seek deceitfully to ensnare and cast us down through our own victory, as we glory in it less cautiously. Thus it follows:

“They said therefore, ‘Jesus the Nazarene.’” Now, by the malignant answer of unclean spirits, it is clearly indicated with how great zeal of their malice they desire to wound inwardly with the vice of pride and render alien from salvation the person whom they cannot bend outwardly to works of wickedness. But the prudent words of the Lord answering show what one providing for one’s own salvation ought to answer: “If you seek me,” he says, “let these go away.” That is, answering those same malignant spirits in contradiction, he says: If you seek me—or rather, because you seek me for this purpose, [Col. 0794A] to destroy my salvation by the vice of pride and to violate the purity of both my inward and outward person—let these go away. Let, I say, my deeds and labours reach God the rewarder whole and unharmed, lest, while you press upon me and, God forbid, prevail through the desire of human praise, they perish; so that if I am inwardly touched and impelled by vain glory, I may nevertheless never be overcome by you through voluntary and consenting pride.

“That the word of Jesus which he spoke might be fulfilled: ‘Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none of them.’” The word of Jesus—the word, I say, of the Saviour—which is daily directed through the mouths of teachers to the hearts of hearers, whereby we are admonished to oppose vain glory and to glory not in ourselves but in the Lord, is then truly fulfilled in us if nothing of those things which the Lord has given us—that is, of good and virtuous deeds—perishes through pride, but we take care to ascribe and assign them in humble contrition to him alone, without whom we can neither do nor possess anything good. Let us therefore see with how great and lofty a dignity of name one who, as has been said, fulfils the words of the commanding Lord by resisting vain glory and humbly acknowledges that the good things he has done were given from above is to be honoured. It follows:

“Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the chief priest.” Simon means “obedient,” while Peter means “acknowledging”; and the sword of this obedient and acknowledging person is the Word of God. For the one who strives to possess the sword [Col. 0794C] of the Word of God—the two-edged sword, the sword that cuts away vices on both sides—will be able to obey the words of Jesus and humbly acknowledge the grace given to him by God. Above all, one must possess the double-sharpened sword, namely the sword of fear and love: the sword of fear, so that through fear of Gehenna and punishment, through fear of the dreadful and strict judgment, a person may turn aside from evils; and the sword of love, so that through hope of eternal reward one may always strive to be watchful in good works. Whoever deserves to possess this double-sharpened sword strikes the servant of the chief priest with a health-giving blow. This servant of the chief priest is fittingly understood as the spirit of the spiritual person himself, who, alas, through excessive desire for human praise sometimes loses his dignity and must be called a servant rather than a lord. [Col. 0794D] But in order that he may return to his former freedom, he must be struck in this way by the two-edged sword already mentioned: he must always fear being puffed up in vain glory over his good deeds, and attribute the good things he has done to God alone in the deep humility of his mind. Therefore it immediately follows:

“And he cut off,” it says, “his right ear.” The ear of this servant must above all be cut off, not the left but the right. For by the right ear is understood the desire for human praise and the love of earthly prosperity. It is rightly called not an ear but an *auricula*, an “earlet,” because praise and prosperity in the present life are not great but brief and slight. Whoever cuts off this earlet with the double-sharpened sword of fear and love will nobly restore in himself the name of lost nobility. For it follows:

[Col. 0795A] “For the servant’s name was Malchus.” The servant’s name, Malchus, means mystically “ruler”; and he will deserve rightly and praiseworthily to be called and to be such when he has reduced the outward person into servitude under powerful dominion, when, after cutting off the right ear—that is, the praise of vain glory—he begins to serve not human favour but God his Creator in simplicity of heart. But because this salutary cutting-off of the ear must above all be performed with the two-edged sword, as has been said, of divine fear and love, let us hear what the Gospel reading further adds concerning this sword. It follows:

“But Jesus said to Peter: ‘Put the sword into its sheath.’” Peter—that is, each person who acknowledges the time of temptation and warfare—is rightly commanded to put the sword of God’s Word into the memory of the heart, so that he may know [Col. 0795B] at what hour and season he ought to draw it, and not delay repeatedly to cut off the ear already mentioned when it wickedly arises again. Thus, now armed with the sword of fear and now with that of love, he may resist the ambushing adversary bravely and manfully, because in this misery of mortality victory can never be stable and perfect. Hence the Father of mercies himself indicates in the following words how greatly he daily suffers in compassion with his members.

“The cup,” he says, “which the Father has given me—shall I not drink it?” What did he wish to be understood mystically by the cup which he declares that he will drink, except the cup of our passion, which we drink daily unwillingly and reluctantly as long as we remain exiles and pilgrims separated from the fountain of eternal life? Yet he himself, in a manner of speaking, mercifully drinks this cup of our passion in us when he bends down in gracious compassion to our suffering and temptation. And he rightly says that this same cup was given him by God the Father, because the compassion of Father and Son toward us is one and alike; and God the Father loves in marvellous condescension those whom he created, whom he willed to redeem with the precious blood of his Son.

## Homily XXXV. First Homily for the Holy Day of Easter

“Mary Magdalene, and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might come and anoint Jesus. And very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb, when the sun had already risen” (Mark 16).

[Col. 0795D] It was not without reason that, on this celebration, the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, the present Gospel is read—namely, that according to Mark—while the Gospels of the other evangelists are passed over. For Mark, Scripture testifies, represents the figure of a lion; and the Holy Spirit, author and arranger of the divine office, ordained this. For on this day that mighty Lion of the tribe of Judah conquered and cast down by his strength that fierce lion who prowls about seeking someone to devour, when by the invincible power of his divinity he snatched the souls of his faithful from the prisons of hell—those whom that cruel lion had wickedly held captive and possessed from the beginning of the world. For just as this noble Lion, our Redeemer, rose from the dead in the spirit of his strength, so he deigned to give his faithful the hope of a blessed resurrection: that in the present life they may rise from the death of the soul through true repentance, and in the eternal glory of the resurrection to come may receive the twofold robe of immortality, never again to die.

Likewise, at the beginning of this Gospel reading, great hope and consolation for obtaining salvation are shown to us wretched sinners: the Lord deigned to comfort these blessed women, grieving and mourning over Christ’s passion and still doubting his resurrection, not only by an angelic vision but also by his own appearance and speech. If, then, he appeared to those who loved him, as it were, carnally, and showed himself alive and visible to those who sought him as though dead, how much more will he now be present, by the invisible grace of his visitation, to those who seek and love him in truth—those who honor, observe, and preach the glory of the Lord’s resurrection in this faith and hope—so that they too may one day rise to reign eternally with him?

Great confidence in divine mercy is granted to us sinners on this most holy day, when Mary Magdalene, who was a sinner and was cleansed and purified of sins by the Savior himself, is named and read at the beginning of the holy Gospel. She, together with the other women mentioned above, wished to anoint with the visible ointment of spices which they had prepared the Lord’s body, [239] which shortly before they had seen scourged, wounded, and pierced with a lance. And if such devotion of a kindly will so pleased the Lord that, as was said, he chose visibly to appear to them and mercifully to greet and address them, how much more does he reward with a worthy recompense the faith and devotion of those who, as it were, anoint his wounds with the invisible ointment of inward compunction and continually recall his passion and death to mind.

For those blessed women, whom he so magnificently comforted by the presence of his vision, had for only a short time been anxiously watching around his tomb and seeking him. But those who throughout all the days and nights of this holy Lent did not cease to apply themselves to vigils, fasts, and many labors, so that they might now deserve to receive some consolation from him in this solemnity—he will by no means leave them desolate; he will by no means turn from them the eyes of his mercy. For even if they do not receive according to their wish what they ask or desire, nevertheless that gracious Creator does not withhold from those who love and seek him the grace of his visitation, insofar as he knows it will benefit each person.

It often happens that, while many sit together in darkness, one among them asks that a light be brought; then not that person alone, but all who are present rejoice in seeing by this light. So indeed, when in a great multitude only one faithful soul deserves to be visited and comforted by the Lord, salvation and blessing will come even to many through the merit of one.

Therefore let us rejoice and exult if any among us deserves to be enlightened by divine inspiration, hoping in God’s mercy that the merit of one will bring salvation to all of us who devoutly believe. For just as this day is the most celebrated of all the days of the year, so divine mercy may more easily be obtained and implored on it for all who are to be saved. Hence, too, from this Gospel reading shine forth the mystical first principles of all that perfection by which one comes to the resurrection to come. For these three women, most devout toward God, seem mystically to prefigure it both by their service and by their names.

[240] “Mary,” it says, “Magdalene, and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might come and anoint Jesus.” Magdalen, from which Magdalene is named, is called “tower” in our language; James means “supplanter”; and Salome is interpreted “peaceful.” If anyone drives back and conquers fleshly desires and evil longings through the constant practice of virtues, that person builds for himself within himself an impregnable tower; such a one can be called Mary Magdalene and can be a well-fortified tower.

Yet no one should suppose that this alone suffices for salvation, if he persists in good and upright works, unless he also strives to restrain his tongue from evil and idle words, so that whatever sin he remembers having committed with his tongue, he may not cease to supplant or abolish through good, holy, and saving speech. Thus, with Mary of James, he may become a praiseworthy supplanter in his words.

But in order to reach the summit of perfection, he must by every means labor to calm and restrain the tumultuous thoughts of a restless heart, so that, tranquil and peaceful in himself, he may obtain with Salome, “the peaceful one,” the joys of inward peace. Whoever, then, as has been said, has become Mary Magdalene—that is, a tower—in action; Mary of James—that is, a supplanter—in speech; and Salome—that is, peaceful—in thought, can procure spices of diverse virtues, worthy of and pleasing to God.

For whatever vanity, whatever evil delight, enticing flesh formerly suggested, he labors, insofar as possible, wholly to cast away and cut off. Distributing the desires of the flesh and the wishes of the world, as it were, in exchange for virtues, he gathers different kinds of spices from which to prepare ointments precious and acceptable to God. The more valuable the spices, the better and more precious the ointments prepared from them. For it does not suffice for a soul that loves God to prepare one ointment; it strives most earnestly to prepare three ointments.

The first ointment may be called the ointment of contrition; the second, of devotion; the third, of love. The first ointment, that of contrition, is when, through true repentance and steadfast satisfaction, a person does not cease to lament and abolish whatever sins against God or against the soul’s salvation he remembers having committed in thought, word, and deed. By such an ointment of contrition, the wrath and vengeance of the strict Judge are appeased.

But lest this ointment of contrition perish through vain glory, let him not neglect to apply the second ointment, that of devotion. The second ointment of devotion is this: if he sees anything upright or just in himself, he should ascribe and attribute it not to his own powers or merits but to God alone, and with complete devotion render him worthy thanksgivings because he left many worthier and better persons amid the vanities of this world, yet by his free goodness called him back, though unworthy, from the error of his life. But for this ointment of devotion to please God, it is necessary to add the third ointment, that of love.

The third ointment of love is to love God alone, before all things and above all things, with the whole intent of the mind. For there are some who, though they lament their sins and give thanks to God for the good things they have received, nevertheless love God less than they ought. Therefore, as we have said, let the faithful soul apply the third ointment, so that it may prefer or set absolutely nothing before the love of God.

For this ointment of divine love is not otherwise to be prepared [codex: *confitendum est*, “must be confessed,” apparently for *conficiendum est*, “must be prepared”] except in that hour of inward contemplation. Therefore the soul beloved by God should guard and protect the bridal chamber of its heart with all diligence, so that, admitted by the grace of inward contemplation into heavenly mysteries as far as possible, it may learn and know how to prepare the ointment of true and perfect love with which the Lord is to be anointed.

These three precious ointments which we have noted are greatly necessary for a person striving toward the salvation of the soul and the perfection of life. For by the first ointment the Lord’s feet are to be anointed in asking pardon; by the second, his hands are to be anointed in giving thanks for pardon granted; by the third, his head is to be anointed in contemplating the glory of his divinity with the eye of contemplation. But no one is fit for these things unless what follows first takes place.

[242] “And very early, on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb, the sun having already risen.” It should be noted why he says not merely “early,” but “very early,” since “very early” is the beginning of the rising dawn, when, the darkness of night scarcely passing away, the faintest ray of the sun has begun to shine. It is not merely early but very early in a person’s heart when, enlightened by the grace of divine visitation, he has in some measure recognized the darkness of ignorance of God and of himself, yet has not at all begun to strive to perform works of light and righteousness.

But in order to be strengthened to perform works of righteousness and light, it is necessary that “one of the Sabbaths” should come to be in him. The “one day of the Sabbaths” is when any faithful person desires to rest from evil works, so that he may be freer to devote himself to the one Lord. Again, the one day of the Sabbaths is when they have received such grace from the Lord that they deserve to become one spirit with him. Then indeed, walking in the path of the upright, they come to the tomb of their heart, where they perceive the sun of divine brightness already risen.

For when this visible sun rises in the morning, it gives the world both brightness and warmth. So too, when that invisible Sun of righteousness touches the minds of his faithful with the light of grace coming from above, he makes them shining and burning: shining, I say, in action; burning in love. Yet it often happens that, while they desire to celebrate a joyful and solemn Passover with the Lord, they feel in themselves nothing of Paschal joy, nothing of Paschal gladness. Accordingly, the Evangelist next reports what, groaning and sighing within themselves, they say to themselves:

“And they said to one another: Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” As if they said: Behold, Lord, the Paschal joys are at hand; behold, Paschal gladness presses upon us; yet no grace of your visitation softens the hardness of my stony heart. Behold, Lord, as you yourself bear witness, I have labored as much as I could during this holy season of fasting; in these holy days of your passion and death I have striven to obtain from you, by tears and prayers, this one thing only: that in these Paschal feasts your consolation might not be lacking to me. And behold, I do not know what Paschal joy is, because I feel you, Lord, who are the true Passover, to be far from me.

Who will roll away for us the stone from the entrance of the tomb—that is, the stone of hardness laid at the entrance of my heart? Who, Lord, I ask, but your fear or your love? If you, Lord, lay upon it the hand of your fear or of your love, you will swiftly remove the heavy, hard stone. And who, as Scripture says, has called upon the Lord and been forsaken by him? For he will mercifully be present at once to those who call upon and seek him, and with the hand of his mercy will roll away and remove the stone of hardness that has been laid there. Hence it follows:

“And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away; for it was very great.” Before the sight of divine mercy, great hardness of heart is easily removed; and then the blessed soul enters the invisible tomb of its heart with all its desires and all its faculties, and by God’s mercy deserves to find what it sought.

“And entering,” says the Evangelist, “into the tomb, they found a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe; and they were astonished.” This young man—that is, the visitation sent from the Most High—announces the joys of the Paschal feast. He is rightly called young, because by this visitation the inward person is renewed in holy youth. He is rightly described as sitting at the right hand, because through this visitation the rest of true humility is found. Or he is said to sit at the right because, for the faithful soul, all things then work together for good: even works that are left-handed and perverse become, as it were, right-handed. For by the white robe, which is innocence, all that soul’s sins are covered, as though they did not exist.

After this white robe, after innocence has been restored in this illumination, comes an astonishment wholly unknown to us who are weak and negligent. Very few know it: only those who have deserved to know it even once by experience. Astonishment is said to occur when someone sees or hears something of such a kind that, through an ecstasy of mind, he becomes forgetful of himself. The blessed soul suffers this astonishment when, passing swiftly into God, it is led outside itself and above itself; and in this astonishment the inward person is humbled more and more.

For it fears the corruptible body that weighs it down; it fears lest perhaps fleshly desire or worldly allure prevail. While it fears and trembles with this good and praiseworthy fear, it hears within itself the young man mentioned above, comforting and exhorting it not to fear or be dismayed.

“Do not be dismayed,” he says. “You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified; he has risen; he is not here.” “Do not be dismayed,” he says, as though saying: Put aside the dread and fear you have. Fear no discomfort of corruption, no enticement of mortal life. For the glory of future blessedness, which you have known in some measure in a mirror and an enigma, you will one day see as it is, face to face, if you seek Jesus of Nazareth, who has risen, as you ought, to the end of life.

Jesus is called “the Nazarene” from Nazareth, which is interpreted “flower of purity” [codex: *Nazareth*]. Why “crucified” is added is unknown to none of the faithful. Jesus the Nazarene must first be sought through the flower of purity—that is, through true and humble confession. Then he must be sought as crucified: that is, we must labor in every way, through mortification of the flesh, to imitate the passion and death of Jesus crucified. If anyone earnestly seeks Jesus the Nazarene in this way, as has been said, then, with God’s help, he will be able to attain what is added:

“He has risen; he is not here.” What is it to rise after humble confession and continual mortification of the flesh, except to strive toward the perfection of life by uninterrupted steps of virtue, and to despise alike prosperity and adversity? Yet lest the wind of self-exaltation cast down those who thus rise on high, all who are wise in vain glory should answer in these words: “He is not here.” The reward and glory we seek are not here; we wish to be praised and magnified not here but in the world to come.

“Behold the place where they laid him.” Behold the place of testimony: namely, the conscience of our heart, where Jesus the Nazarene crucified is laid as witness and rewarder of our works. As they answer inwardly in this way and thus repel from themselves the spirit of self-exaltation, he further exhorts and stirs them to higher things, so that they may provide not only for their own salvation but also for the benefit of their neighbors.

[245] “Go,” he says, “tell his disciples and Peter that he will go before you into Galilee.” Go, as you have begun, by the path of the right way; and take care to benefit not only yourselves but others also. Tell the disciples—that is, the innocent—and tell Peter—that is, the fallen and sinners. Tell each group what is suitable for it, how each should see Jesus, who goes before them in Galilee.

Tell the disciples, those who have been instructed for some time under the discipline of the Holy Spirit, to follow and see the Lord Jesus who goes before them in Galilee in this way: that, as far as they can, they may effect in themselves a migration even from the smallest sins, and preserve their innocence by humility of heart. Tell Peter too—that is, sinners who have fallen by the threefold fault of thoughts, words, and deeds, just as Peter fell by denying the Lord three times—tell them, I say, to come to their senses from their sins and repent of the evils they have committed by humbly confessing them.

But amid these things it should be observed and retained with great joy that not the other disciples but Peter alone, who in this passage represents the person of sinners, was called by name. Hence great hope of divine mercy is given to sinners, so that they may not despair or lose confidence concerning their salvation. Indeed, let them not fear to follow the Lord who goes before them in Galilee, which means “migration,” striving to migrate from vices to virtues and from death to life.

“There you will see him, as he told you.” There—that is, in eternal life—he will be seen with face unveiled, as he now promises both to the innocent and the penitent, whether through the words of teachers, in the hour of contemplation, or through the language of inward compunction. There we shall truly celebrate the Paschal feasts, where we shall see our true Passover, Christ, face to face. May he himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[246] HOMILY XXXVI. FOR THE SECOND DAY OF HOLY EASTER.

“He also sent out a dove after him, to see whether the waters had already ceased from upon the earth” (Gen. 8), etc.

Just as the festival of this holy and venerable day surpasses all solemnities, so it is celebrated throughout the whole world by all Christ’s faithful with the rejoicing and exultant gladness of a greater triumph. Nor without reason. For on this day God Almighty completed and perfected his work—the work, indeed, of our redemption—for which he deigned to descend from the height of his divinity to the depths of our mortality.

For his being born, living in this world, suffering, dying, and being buried would not have been our full and perfect redemption unless, in his resurrection, he had given us the hope of rising again. Joy would not be complete if souls alone were saved after this life, while bodies reduced to dust did not deserve to be raised to life.

But because, made alive through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, we hope and await the twofold robe of immortality, it is not unjust that on each of these days, as though consoling ourselves and in some manner calling to our own remembrance what we await, we sing at Mass: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.” The Lord made all days; the Lord created all days. But above all days—indeed, more excellent than all—he made this day, which he consecrated and honored beyond all others by the unheard-of glory of his most glorious resurrection.

There were indeed some before and after him who, by his gift and cooperation, raised the dead; but no human being ever raised himself from death except this man alone, our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as he was able to die when he wished and as he wished, so he was able to rise when he wished and as he wished; and he rose not only for himself but also for us. For by his resurrection he gave us hope and confidence that we shall one day come to the same glory of resurrection and immortality.

But since joy is twofold—one joy which, after the misery of this present life has run its course, will be in the rest of souls; the other which will be in the resurrection of bodies—after the words, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” there immediately follows, “Let us exult and rejoice in it.” The word “let us exult” may refer to the joy given after this life in the rest of souls. But the words immediately following, “and let us rejoice in it,” express that ineffable and unending joy which, when the world’s end has come, will belong to all God’s elect in the resurrection of bodies.

This is that true day which the Lord has made, the one day deservedly to be preferred to all former days. This will truly be the day of exultation and gladness, where, when soul and body are united, no place for grief or sadness will remain. Before this day comes, though the souls of the saints are at rest—and in such rest as no mind can conceive and no tongue can explain—they do not yet possess full and perfect joy. For they are troubled in part because they are still concerned and think about their body’s resurrection: what they had as a companion in labor, they desire also to have as a companion in glory and recompense.

For no love can be compared to that love which exists between body and soul. Hence comes the deadly pain and torment a human being suffers at the end; for it is harsh and difficult to leave the familiar dwelling of the body. But after it has left, although it is received into the joys of eternal blessedness, it is nevertheless always desiring and longing to receive again that through whose labor it has deserved so great an honor.

For just as a mother who has a beloved son, or anyone else who has a friend whom he loves as himself, makes little of—or counts as nothing—the honor shown to himself unless the one whom he loves as himself is also held in equal honor and love, so the soul’s own honor and blessedness do not suffice for it as long as the body, which it loves as itself, cannot share in that honor and blessedness.

But lest this seem strange and unbelievable, let us look to our Head; let us behold our Lord and Savior. By his own example he confirmed what we say.
