When his most holy body had been laid in death for us, he could not remain away from it long: he willed it to be absent only for the very brief interval from the ninth hour on Friday, when he died on the cross, until the third day, when he powerfully raised it from death.

This also was nobly prefigured long before it occurred in the Scripture of the Old Testament, where we read of that dove which Noah sent from the ark to see whether the waters had already ceased upon the face of the earth. When it found no place for its foot to rest, it returned to him into the ark.

By Noah, Christ’s divinity may be understood; by the ark, the humanity assumed into God; and by the dove, I judge that the soul of Christ is rightly understood. For it truly was a dove, and a most beautiful dove, which alone lacked every gall of duplicity and sin. Thus the true Noah, namely God Almighty, who according to the Apostle was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, in a certain manner sent out this dove when, for the salvation of humankind, lifted up on the cross, he allowed it to be separated from the body.

But why did he send it out? “To see whether the waters had already ceased from upon the face of the earth.” By the waters, which are used in various senses in the Scriptures, I think that in this passage original sin or fleshly desires may fittingly be signified. Through the guilt of original sin these had grown to a remarkable degree over the whole human race. By the flood, however, actual sins may aptly be understood—the sins added to original sin—which had engulfed the whole human race in the precipice of eternal death.

For this reason the only-begotten Son of God, equal to the Father in the substance of divinity, became mortal man for us and sent out his dove. For this reason he allowed his beloved soul to be separated for an hour from that ark of human nature into which he had entered at the Father’s command, so that he might see whether the waters had already ceased upon the earth: namely, the waters of original and actual sin—not upon the accursed earth producing the thorns and thistles of sinners, but upon the blessed, fruitful earth, daily bringing forth to God the fruit of good works.

For in paying the debt of death, though he owed nothing to death, and in willing to descend into hell to see and visit his elect who were held captive in death, he caused the waters of the flood to cease and erased the crimes of original and actual sin.

The following text clearly indicates how greatly that chosen dove, that is, Christ’s beloved soul, desired to resume, in the glory of immortality, the body it had laid aside as mortal. For it follows: “And when she had found no place where her foot might rest, she returned to him into the ark.” It did indeed find the souls of his saints placed in hell; but among all of them it found no place where its foot might rest, because among all of them there was no resting-place so pleasing and so beloved as that most holy body of its own, which it had put on spotless and undefiled, without sin, and had laid aside likewise spotless, undefiled, and without sin.

Therefore it returned to him into the ark. To whom, “to him”? Certainly it returned to Almighty God into the ark—that is, into its own flesh. For God was with the soul in hell; God was with the body in the tomb. Why did it return to him into the ark? Namely because it found no dwelling such as that from which it had departed.

“For the waters,” as is added, “were over the whole earth.” And it is rightly said, “over the whole earth,” because over all human beings, however fruitful they may have been, however much they may have labored for God, that water of original and actual sin stood above them. For all were conceived and born in sins; all lived in sins. But Noah’s ark alone was borne upon the waters, because that incomparably chaste and pure dwelling-place of the indivisible and everlasting Trinity alone could in no way be touched by that water of original and actual sin.

Therefore that most blessed dove, Christ’s most elect soul of dovelike purity and sweetness, after flying down to hell with the power of divinity, binding the tyrant and opening paradise to his elect whom it brought away from there, returned without delay to him—that is, to Almighty God—into the ark.

“And he stretched out his hand, took her, and brought her into the ark.” What was this stretching forth of the hand of the true Noah? By his hand, his power is understood. His hand was, as it were, restrained and enclosed when he allowed himself to be seized, scourged, struck with fists, crowned with thorns, and finally condemned to the most shameful death while hanging between two thieves. But he nobly stretched out that same hand when, having overcome all these things, he gently took his dove, which he had sent forth in dying, and powerfully brought it into the ark by rising from death.

Nor should the phrase “having taken her, he brought her into the ark” be passed over. A person draws to himself with a certain force what he takes hold of. So too our Lord Jesus Christ brought his dove—namely, his holy soul—into the ark, having taken it hold in the strength and power of his divinity, in such a way that neither divinity can thereafter be separated from humanity nor humanity from divinity.

“And having waited yet seven days, he again sent the dove out of the ark.” These seven days were, I think, the joyful and glad days after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, during which he gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples for the forgiveness of sins. On account of the sevenfold grace of gifts, I think the Spirit is rightly to be understood here by the number seven: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:22).

These days were truly days awaited. For all who had existed from the beginning of the world awaited and desired these days. Nor is it without mystery that it says, “having waited yet seven other days.” By this we are taught that there were days before these days, though altogether unlike these days. Were not Noah, Abraham, Isaac, David, and the rest like them in their day—who all had the Spirit of God? They did indeed have God’s Spirit, yet it was given to none of them for forgiveness of sins. For, as Scripture says, “the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

But after Christ had suffered and died, after he descended to hell and rose again, then truly the awaited days came: days above all days, seven other days above all days, in no respect comparable with the preceding days, in which forgiveness of sins was given through the Holy Spirit.

When these awaited days had passed, he again sent the dove out of the ark. The repeated sending of the dove from the ark may fittingly be understood as Christ’s glorious ascension. For just as in the preceding passage we understood Christ’s flesh by the ark, so in this passage likewise his flesh is aptly understood by the same ark—not, indeed, that flesh which, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, he took from the blessed Virgin Mary, but his other flesh, which is the holy Church.

For because of love for this flesh he exposed that flesh which he took from blessed Mary to reproaches and torments. He gave that flesh so as to free this; he allowed it to be scourged so that this might be healed; he willed it to undergo the punishment of the cross so that this might deserve to return to the joys of paradise from which it had fallen; he allowed it to die so that this might be made alive.

Therefore our Noah again sent his dove out of the ark when, on the fortieth day after his resurrection, he transferred it from the present Church into heaven. How delightful, lovable, and glorious was the manner in which it came before the face of the Father’s majesty is plainly explained by the following text, when it says:

“But she came to him at evening, carrying in her mouth a branch of green olive with green leaves.” She is rightly said to have come to him at evening, because Christ is read to have ascended about the ninth hour, when the day begins to incline toward evening. She came to him—that is, to God the Father—carrying in her mouth a branch of green olive with green leaves.

There are three things in a branch which, if we consider them rightly, show that the man who was in Christ was justly prefigured by the branch. A branch proceeds from a tree; the strength of the tree is in the branch; a branch bears the fragrance of a good odor. So too Christ, who according to his divinity was consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal with the Father, proceeded according to the substance of his humanity from the tree and stock of human nature. And just as the branch is the strength of the tree, so he was and is the strength and power of the entire human race.

From him also a good and sweet fragrance, greatly pleasing to God the Father, rose into heaven, because by the glorious price of his blood he himself wiped away and banished that evil stench of sins which had arisen from the whole offspring of the human race.

The branch is also fittingly called that of a green olive. For oil proceeds from the olive, and by oil peace and mercy are signified. For he made peace between God and humanity; he brought mercy—that is, forgiveness of sins—by destroying the dominion of death. Why, moreover, is that most noble flesh of Christ called not merely a branch of olive but a branch of green olive? Very fittingly and appropriately: having been, as it were, parched and dried by the fire of passion in death, it was enlivened by the sap of divinity and, in the resurrection, wonderfully became green and flowered anew, so that it can never again lose its freshness. For, as the Apostle says, “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

The green leaves produced by the same branch were the enlivened bodies of his elect, whom, rescued from Tartarus and raised in his mouth—that is, in the power of his divinity—he brought with himself to the throne of paternal glory. For he is the mouth of God; he is the wisdom of God, as Scripture testifies, saying: “O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High.” After all these things, it rightly follows:

“Therefore Noah understood that the waters had ceased from upon the face of the earth.” For when, after accomplishing his passion and resurrection, our Lord and Savior, having given the Holy Spirit, sent his disciples into the whole world to preach and to give baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and himself ascended into heaven in such a triumph of glory, then for the first time the true Noah understood that the waters had ceased upon the earth.

For as soon as baptism began through the apostles’ preaching—a baptism in which, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, forgiveness of sins takes place—that water, namely the water of original and actual sin, immediately ceased upon the earth: upon the fruitful earth, I mean, upon the souls and bodies of the faithful, which bring forth to God the delightful fruit of good works.

253 Yet he waited another seven days, [Col. 0806C] and sent out the dove. By these other seven days we may understand the whole time from the Lord’s Ascension until the end of the age, during which the pious and merciful Lord, who desires all people to be saved, mercifully awaits the repentance and conversion of sinners. Nor should we pass over his saying, “yet he waited another seven days.” For by this, it seems to me, is signified that the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are now distributed through Christ’s fellow-workers—that is, good bishops and priests—are nevertheless, that is, no less efficacious now than then; for the grace of the Holy Spirit now works no less in the holy Church through Christ’s ministers than it worked after his Ascension through the holy apostles. For the same baptism is still administered in the holy Church, in which, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, the same remission of sins is still without doubt granted to every believer. After these seven days have been mentioned, it is again said:

“And he sent out the dove.” First he sent her out, as we have heard, in the Passion; the second time he sent her forth at the Ascension; her third sending will be at the future Judgment. When this third sending has at last taken place, what follows will be fulfilled:

“She did not return to him again.” For no return will be needed there, where there will be no further departure. For when, the Judgment having been completed, he has gathered his whole body to himself, she will not return to him again, because she will never again depart from him. And not only that human nature which is in Christ, but also the whole human nature redeemed and saved through him, will reign forever in him with God. May our Lord Jesus Christ bring us to this glory of perpetual immortality, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

254 HOMILY XXXVII. FOR THE FIRST MONDAY OF EASTER.

“Two of Jesus’ disciples were going that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem” (Luke 24).

Because, as blessed Gregory says, on a daily feast, when we are engaged in work, few things should be said, and perhaps they will prove more useful, we cannot run through the words of the Gospel reading word by word. Yet for the sake of those for whom the letter of the historical account alone is insufficient, we shall say a few things concerning its moral meaning, insofar as the Lord himself may deign to grant us.

These two disciples signify the body and soul of each of Christ’s faithful people, who, having left behind the world and worldly desires, live under God’s discipline and regulate their conduct and life according to his discipline. For what else did righteous and good people do during these most holy days of Lent, except that, restraining themselves as though under God’s discipline by vigils, fasts, scourges, and other pious bodily labours, they laboured to be found worthy on the day of his Resurrection to deserve to have joy and gladness with him? Yet however much a person may at times have laboured, however much he may have toiled in guarding heart and body, it often happens that he cannot possess with God, according to his wish and desire, that grace of heavenly sweetness for which he laboured and after which he longed. Therefore, saddened and groaning within himself, he begins, as it were, on that very day to go to the village named Emmaus. That day is the present day, the day of joy and exultation—the day, indeed, of the Lord’s Resurrection—on which the person who remembers having lived under God’s discipline, yet sees himself deprived of the hoped-for and desired grace for which he laboured, begins to go to the village of Emmaus, which is interpreted “an abject people.” For when he judges himself to be, as it were, cast off and despised before the Lord, and on account of this very self-abjection humbles himself before God as one of no merit, this is to go on that very day to the village of Emmaus.

Nor should we pass over what was added: that it was sixty stadia from Jerusalem. The distance of sixty stadia is the perfection either of good works or of the divine commandments. For in this very self-abjection he sees himself as being at a distance from Jerusalem, as though by sixty stadia, when, because of the imperfection of his works and his neglect of the divine precepts, he laments that he is far from the vision of peace: either the inward sweetness of the heart in which God is beheld, or the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, which is reserved in eternal life for God’s elect. Hence, returning to himself, he humbly recalls within himself what and how great things the omnipotent Majesty, coming in the flesh, did and endured for him. Therefore the Evangelist says:

“And they were speaking with one another about all these things that had happened.” All those things that happened fittingly signify the Incarnation, Passion, and Resurrection of the only-begotten Son of God. These two disciples—namely, that person who is willingly subject in body and spirit to Christ’s discipline—speak of all these things when, with a humble heart, he continually reviews and reflects upon them within himself, so that he may be more powerfully kindled in love for him who endured such great things for him. He also speaks of all these things when he laments and groans within himself that he remembers having answered such great goodness with none of his own labours or merits, and therefore recognizes that, by God’s just judgment, he has been deprived, during the time of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, of the grace of the sweetness he desired. While they thus speak of themselves, the merciful Lord draws near, as is mystically suggested in what follows:

“And it came to pass,” says the Evangelist, “while they were conversing and discussing together, that Jesus himself, drawing near, went with them.” For when a person converses within himself by recalling the Lord’s mercies, when he examines and laments with himself in humility his ingratitude and negligences, Jesus himself—the true salvation of the humble, who beholds the hidden things of hearts—begins to draw near to the person through the invisible grace of his visitation, while through his fear he awakens him more and more to knowledge of himself. But because in this self-knowledge a person is seized by fear and is not yet refreshed by love, the Evangelist rightly continues:

“But their eyes were held, so that they did not recognize him.” The eyes of the heart, by which the invisible God must be seen, are held fast by fear, so that a person cannot recognize God through love. Yet with all those to whom he draws near through fear, he in a sense goes with them; for through the progress of virtues and good works, love carries them from the bitterness of fear to sweetness. Hence it follows:

“And he said to them, ‘What are these words that you are exchanging with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?’” This questioning by God is his invisible awakening. For he asks in order to make the one who does not know, through his question, know; and it is as though he said: You are indeed walking—that is, making progress and not falling away—but in the very course of your progress you are sad, being without the grace of my desired sweetness. But recognize what it is that has hindered you from this grace. Awakened by this invisible questioning of God—or, more truly, by this most merciful awakening of God—a person inwardly grows stronger and stronger; gathering himself within himself, he burns more intensely in love for God. Hence it follows:

“And one of them, whose name was Cleophas, answered and said to him.” A person becomes one when, gathering his senses to himself within himself, he begins through holy desires to be united with God. He is also rightly called Cleophas, which is interpreted “investigating” or “keen-sighted,” when he carefully investigates what within himself pleases or displeases God, and when he becomes keen in doing good and avoiding evil. After this most salutary investigation or discernment, when he begins to be united to God, from the very love by which he burns toward God he bursts forth, as it were, into these words:

“Are you alone a stranger in Jerusalem?” By Jerusalem, which is interpreted “vision of peace,” the soul of a person striving toward the vision of eternal peace is aptly figured. It is as though he said: You alone, whom alone I desire, for whose love I despise all the pleasures of the passing world; you alone, the joy of those who seek you, the salvation of those who find you; you alone, I say, who suffice for all and never fail in yourself; you alone, for whom alone I sigh, whom alone I seek—are a stranger in Jerusalem, in my soul, which you disdain to visit and vivify with the longed-for grace of your sweetness. “And have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?” For, my labours by which I sought you and by which I thought I pleased you being rejected and despised, you have become alien to me. But the merciful and compassionate Lord, from whom nothing is hidden and to whom not only human action but also thought lies open, questions the person again in order to kindle him more strongly toward his own desire and love. For it follows:

“He said to them, ‘What things?’” As though he said: What are those things which you assert have happened in Jerusalem, on account of which you are afflicted with such sorrow? “And they said, ‘The things concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people.’” As though he plainly said: Do you ask, Lord, consolation and redemption of my soul, what those things are by which my soul is so greatly disturbed? All my disturbance concerns Jesus of Nazareth—concerning you, who are the flower of purity, the salvation and redemption of my soul; who were once a man within me, when you caused me to act manfully; a prophet mighty in deed and word, when you made me powerful both in the exercise of good action and in the sweetness of continual prayer; before God and all the people, when I deserved to find grace before you in the secret of my heart and, in my outward actions, gave no occasion of stumbling to those who looked upon me. But behold, I appear rejected and despised before you because, at the time of your Passion—when you were handed over by our chief priests and rulers to the condemnation of death, and crucified for me—I deserve to find no grace of your desired sweetness.

“We, however, hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” I hoped, Lord, that you yourself, apart from whom I have no hope of joy, would redeem me from the hardness and torpor of my soul, so that I might see you in the multitude of your mercy.

“And now, besides all these things, today is the third day since these things happened.” After the days of your Passion have passed for me in the bitterness of my soul, behold, today is the third day, the day of your most holy Resurrection, on which heaven and earth rejoice; yet from me, who groan and have no consolation because of you, nor seek any, the grace of your desired visitation is withheld.

“Moreover, some women from among us terrified us. They were at the tomb before dawn, and, not finding his body, came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who say that he lives.” O compassionate Lord, I am tormented by the bitterness of my own abjection, desolation, and hardness in proportion as I see you visit with more abundant sweetness those of yours whom you love. For certain women from among us—that is, the softened and tender souls of some whom I see among us—having been flooded with the light of your brightness, went before dawn, that is, in the time of vigils before today’s light had dawned, to the tomb, to the secret place of their hearts, under the guidance of your mercy; and, though they had not found the body, not yet refreshed by the sacrament of your life-giving body and blood, they deserved to have infused from heaven the grace of your sweetness, which truly may be compared to a vision of angels and which testifies that you live in them. But why should I wonder at tender souls, whom you are accustomed to soften by your grace and nourish in the abundance of your mercy?

“Some also of our number went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said.” For they received from you that same grace of sweetness both in the secret of their hearts in prayer and in the preaching of your word, though they had not yet found you yourself, though they had not yet communicated in your body and blood. But I, alone cast away from your eyes and repulsed, find nothing that delights, nothing that gladdens, since I see myself deprived of the grace of your long-awaited and greatly desired visitation. While he thus inquires and, with a contrite heart, humbly groans over the miseries of his desolation, the one who is the fountain of mercy makes more clearly known through a secret inspiration what it is that has hindered him from the desired grace of inward sweetness. Hence it follows:

“And he said to them, ‘O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!’” God’s speaking is God’s doing; for he himself causes and works in a person what enables him perfectly to recognize the foolishness and slowness of his heart and humbly begin to rebuke it within himself. It is as though he said: I do not fail to know what you have done for my sake, what labour you have expended for me in the pursuit of good works during these holy days; but I confess that you were slower than you ought to have been in good works, and foolish in not preserving what you had done. You were slow in doing, foolish and readily inclined to losing. “All that the prophets have spoken”: that is, the holy Scriptures, resounding day and night in your ears, or your teachers proclaiming to you the joys of eternal life and the eternal perils of condemnation.

“Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” Must not a person, through the observance of humility and endurance of the labours that arise in the present life, attain the excellence of eternal blessedness?

“And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them the Scriptures concerning all the things about himself.” By Moses, whose name is interpreted “taken from water,” we may fittingly understand the grace of compunction. All the prophets are all the pages of the sacred Scriptures. The Lord begins with Moses when he grants a person the desired compunction of heart; he interprets the Scriptures to him when, by the grace of his inspiration, he illumines him to understand and follow the mystery of sacred Scripture—concerning all things that may either benefit or harm that person with regard to eternal life.

“And they drew near to the village to which they were going.” The village to which they go may fittingly in this place be understood as the human heart, to which God and the person alike draw near: God when, through his visitation, he illumines it; the person when, through true love, he draws near to God.

“And he made as though he would go farther.” These words are not to be understood as though the true and simple God, who always subsists in himself, is one thing and pretends to be another. Rather, he who is always the same in himself is rightly said, in accordance with the changes of our mutability and instability—since we cannot remain long with God on that height of mind of which we speak—to have “made as though he would go farther.” For however much God draws near to a person through the grace of his visitation, he nevertheless seems in some way to be farther away, because the more a person tastes of his inward sweetness, the more ardently he thirsts and longs to taste it. Hence it follows:

“And they constrained him, saying, ‘Stay with us, for it is toward evening, and the day is now declining.’” A person constrains God to remain with him when he gathers himself inwardly, when he collects every faculty of his soul within himself so that, applying heart and body to divine service, he begins to cleave to God alone, saying with mouth and mind: “Stay with us, establishing your dwelling in us; for if you withdraw, if you do not remain with us by the grace you breathe into us, that evening of temptation, that evening of adversity and tribulation, draws near; the day of joy and prosperity, the day of spiritual gladness and exultation, declines and departs.” This is a certain force and constraint which the mercy of heavenly condescension cannot resist: it holds and compels him, so that he can neither be able nor willing to depart from the person. Hence it follows:

“And he entered in with them.” He enters in with them when, by his visitation, he illuminates the human heart. After this entrance of almighty God, a wonderful event follows.

“And it came to pass,” says the Evangelist, “as he reclined with them, he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them.” Truly great and wonderful is the event in which almighty Majesty stoops so low that he does not disdain, through the condescension of his visitation, to join himself to the soul that seeks him. In this most desired union of God and the faithful soul is fulfilled what follows: “He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them.” The bread which strengthens the human heart signifies heavenly sweetness, by which the soul failing in its longing for God is refreshed and strengthened. A person is said to receive the desirable bread when he desires . . . [The remainder is missing in the manuscript.]

261 HOMILY XXXVIII. FOR THE FIRST TUESDAY OF EASTER.

“Jesus stood in the midst of the disciples and said to them: ‘Peace be to you. It is I; do not be afraid’” (Luke 24).

[Col. 0812A] Since disciples are so called from learning, all those are rightly called disciples of Jesus who, constraining body, soul, and spirit by the rigor of spiritual discipline, delight in living always under his teaching. Our same Lord Jesus Christ loves to stand in their midst, because by his mercy he makes them stand, so that, strengthened in him and through him, they cannot be cast down either by prosperity or adversity, but whatever may occur, according to the saying, “Cast your thought upon the Lord” (Ps. 54:23; Ecclus. 6:37), may strive always to have recourse in mind to him who is their hope and consolation. He also stands in their midst, offering them his customary assistance in all their needs. Thus Stephen saw the Lord standing amid the assaults of those stoning him, so that by this it might be signified to us that he is always prompt and ready to aid his own. Standing thus for them, he says to them:

“Peace be to you; do not be afraid.” At the beginning of conversion, the Lord offers his own a threefold peace: peace from the devil, peace from vices, and peace from death. “It is I,” he says, “do not be afraid. I am your Creator; I am your Liberator. By the same loving-kindness by which I created you and redeemed you, I have determined to preserve you to the end.” But since no one can live upon earth without temptation, the Evangelist accordingly adds:

“But they, disturbed and terrified, thought that they saw a spirit.” Disturbed by fear of sin, terrified by fear of death, Gehenna, and the future Judgment, they thought that they saw a spirit, because at the beginning of conversion they hope that they can possess here the grace which will only come at some future time.

“And he said to them, ‘Why are you troubled?’” This second speaking of God, which we have here, is that great consolation by which he mercifully aids his own in tribulations. “Why are you troubled,” he says, “and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” Good thoughts concerning the good God descend from heaven, but evil thoughts ascend to the human heart from the earth and earthly things. There are, indeed, four things by which a person is troubled: unsuitable joy, excessive sadness, evil desires, and wicked fear. From these four vices manifold and various thoughts ascend into the human heart, bringing it so many and such great temptations that no human being, except God and the one who suffers them, can know them. The Lord then adds in his following consoling words how a person may be freed from these temptations:

“See my hands and my feet.” As though he said: In all your tribulations and distresses, flee to my hands—that is, to the work of my divinity, by which I made and formed you—and look trustfully to my feet—that is, to my Incarnation, by which I redeemed you—for I myself am he. I am who I am; I am the same unchangeable God, always present for you.

“Handle me and see.” As long as you are in the darkness of this world, handle me by labouring in the active life, and see by the contemplative life. “For a spirit does not have flesh and bones.” When you have arrived there too, where you see me face to face, a spirit does not have flesh and bones, because it will suffer no weakness or frailty there; it does not have flesh and bones, because there will be no need there to resist temptations and vices, as you see me have flesh and bones, who suffered much in the flesh for you.

“And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet.” By the hands we may understand the power of his divinity; by the feet, the mercy of the Incarnation. But because, as long as a person lives here, he cannot be entirely free from temptations, the Evangelist consequently adds:

“But while they still did not believe and wondered for joy, he said, ‘Have you anything here to eat?’” There is a faith by which worldly people confess God in words and not in deeds; it is, as it were, no faith at all, according to the testimony of the apostle James, who says, “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:26). There is also a small faith, such as Peter had when, as the storm at sea arose, he doubted and began to sink. Those therefore have this small faith who, when storms of temptation rise, become so faint-hearted that they think they can scarcely, or not at all, be freed from them. But those have great faith who cleave so firmly to God in body, soul, and spirit that in every event they know and consider him to be their helper and deliverer. Yet because, while this age endures, temptation follows temptation, and this often makes the Lord’s disciples more perfect and more proven, he is rightly described as having said to them:

“Have you anything here to eat?” This third speaking of God in this place signifies that perfection to which the merciful God mercifully leads his own after the dangers of temptations: “Have you,” he says, “anything here to eat?” As though he said: If you are refreshed by that “something,” namely my inward sweetness, which is as though a small thing, you will at last be able, with my help, to escape the storms of temptations. For nothing is more effective for repelling temptations than for the soul to be continually nourished by inward sweetness and by the assiduity of his most sweet word.

“But they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb.” He himself is that sweet fish, caught in the waves of this age and broiled on the gridiron of the holy cross in the fire of his Passion for our sins. He is also fittingly called a honeycomb because, just as honey surpasses all things in sweetness, so he fills and satisfies all things with the inestimable sweetness of his divinity.

“And when he had eaten before them.” The Lord is therefore rightly described as having eaten before them, because everything that he did in the days of his flesh—namely, that he was born, suffered, and rose again—he did entirely [the manuscript reads: “entirely, which”] for the redemption of the human race; and his true food and delight was the human being alone, as he himself testifies elsewhere: “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:3). When this dispensation for us had been fulfilled, the Evangelist immediately adds what joys of the future life he has prepared for his elect:

“Taking,” he says, “the remains, he gave them to them.” He takes the remains when he will one day grant his elect the rewards of eternal life; then he has a fourth time to speak to them, when he will make them rejoice with himself in his kingdom concerning eternal recompense:

“These,” he says, “are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that all things written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled.” As though he said: This is the grace of the vision of me which I promised you; this is the grace which I obtained for you by my death and blood. All things written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms had, I say, to be fulfilled. For whatever sacred Scripture taught about me in the law of Moses—that is, in the letter—or in the prophets—that is, in allegories—or in the psalms—that is, in the mystical and moral sense—all these things had to be fulfilled. It follows:

“Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures.” Then—that is, in that eternal beholding of God—they are illumined with so great a light of divine Wisdom that they plainly understand all things once hidden and concealed and, so to speak, read in the book of Wisdom, where, as the prophet says, “they shall all be taught by God” (Isa. 54:13; John 6:45). Therefore, as the Holy Spirit opens their understanding and distributes the gifts of perfect understanding, the Lord is rightly described as speaking to his disciples in a fifth manner:

“For thus,” he says, “it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations.” This final speaking is in this place the everlasting and infinite jubilation by which the righteous will never cease to praise God. Speaking in their person, David says: “I will sing forever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. 88:2). It is as though they say: Thus and thus it is written; thus it was once promised us through the sacred Scriptures: that the Son of God was willing to suffer and rise from the dead in order to grant repentance and remission of sins to all predestined for eternal life.

This is the Gospel reading which, according to our measure and insofar as God has deigned to grant, we have run through in exposition. Now let us turn the gaze of our mind to him who is the true and incomprehensible light, humbly imploring him that, after the darkness of this mortality has been overcome, he may deign to bring us there where, illumined in that eternal beholding of him by the light of divine Wisdom, we may know those things now hidden from our eyes; and, knowing them, may rejoice eternally in the eternal fellowship of him and all his saints. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

266 HOMILY XXXIX. FOR THE FIRST WEDNESDAY OF EASTER.

[Col. 0815A]

“Jesus manifested himself to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. And he manifested himself in this way” (John 21).

In many sayings of holy and evangelical teaching, certain Gospel passages have, by the ordering of the Holy Spirit, been so arranged that in them may be found the beginning and end of human life: namely, the beginning of conversion, and the end of life and recompense. Thus in the present Gospel we may find both the beginning of conversion for every spiritual person striving toward perfection, and also the end of that person’s life, in which, with God’s help, he will obtain eternal reward. Therefore the Evangelist says:

“Jesus manifested himself to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias.” By the Sea of Tiberias may be understood the embittered human heart, to which heart, made bitter through repentance, the Lord Jesus then indeed manifests himself when, by his hidden visitation, he inspires the person to recognize himself in true humility. But how can a sinful and unrighteous person recognize his sins and transgression except because Jesus has deigned to manifest himself to him at the Sea of Tiberias? For Tiberias is interpreted “the vision of his goodness.” Since the Lord saw him in his goodness and mercy, he began thereby to recognize himself. And because two manifestations are set forth here, we must carefully observe that almighty God also deigns to manifest himself to a person in two ways in saving him.

The first manifestation of the Lord takes place inwardly in a person, when, graciously and mercifully preceding him in his blessing, he grants him a good will. He manifests himself a second time when, by his loving-kindness, he assists him so that he may also bring to completion in the performance of good works the good will he had received invisibly within. Many, indeed, conceive a good will in their minds from God’s prevenient gift, but do not rise to accomplish good works. Thus the second manifestation is more expressly indicated by the phrase set down here, “and he manifested himself in this way,” when that which lay hidden in good will is brought outwardly into the effect of good works before God and people. Therefore, if the Lord manifests himself to anyone in these two ways, both preceding him in good will and assisting him in the completion of good actions, he leads that person onward to higher progress. Of him the text immediately adds:

“Simon Peter and Thomas, who is called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.” In these seven disciples we may understand the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, because by sevenfold grace he illuminates and inflames the elect person predestined to eternal life so as to obtain the perfect life, and afterward leads him through progress in good works to eternal blessedness. Certainly, the person whom the Holy Spirit has visited with this sevenfold grace will indeed fulfill what follows:

“Simon Peter said to them, ‘I am going fishing.’” By the living fish, which are unseen when submerged in the waters, we may, it seems to me, understand the living faculties of a person, which, like fish immersed in water, lie hidden in the concealed heart. But a person draws out these living faculties of his as though from waters when he strives to turn and withdraw them from the love and delight of the present age, to which they had clung and in which they lived. A person therefore fishes well when he draws his faculties out of the world and turns them from the pleasure and love of this life, in which they had been immersed, toward love of God and conversion to the spiritual life. For what else is it to say, “I am going fishing,” than to say: “With God’s help, I wish to leave the world and enter upon the way of life of the spirit”?

“The disciples said to him, ‘We also are coming with you.’” In these disciples may be understood the spiritual faculties of the inner person, who, inwardly touched and forewarned by God toward spiritual conversion and perfection of life, strive to follow him. It follows:

“They went out, got into the boat, and caught nothing that night.” This blessed departure, of which we have just heard, is then truly accomplished in a person when he departs from the world and worldly conduct, when he afterward manifests in good and holy works what he had first conceived in his mind through God’s inspiration. But, departing from the world, he gets into a boat when he reaches a good and spiritual way of life. He is rightly said to get into a boat, for the ascent is difficult and laborious: indeed, one strives toward a good spiritual way of life with toil and difficulty, with great labour of heart and body. What adversities and temptations he must experience and suffer in this spiritual life is fittingly added when it is said:

“And they caught nothing that night.” The night in which a person can catch nothing may, it seems to me, signify ignorance and adversity, which often confront him in his holy resolve and which, by God’s permission, he suffers either from the devil, from wicked and perverse people, or from his own flesh. When this night, this ignorance, confronts him, the mind of the converted person is sometimes so disturbed that it nearly falls into despair. At one moment he reflects that he cannot possibly endure in his spiritual resolve, nor bear the labours and afflictions that he will suffer.

When these adversities arise, when these storms of ignorance rush upon him, he thinks for a time of abandoning his spiritual purpose and returning once more to the world. But then, with God’s help, he reflects again on how he may cleave to God alone and remain in holy conduct. Caught in this affliction and tribulation, he can lay hold of none of the good thoughts or holy and righteous works for which he had left the world: he had gone out only in order, by living holily and piously and abounding in good and salutary thoughts, to attain eternal life; but hindered by the storms of temptations, he cannot attain that toward whose seeking and obtaining alone he had directed the gaze of his mind. Yet almighty God, who is a helper in times of trouble and neither deserts nor forsakes his own, afterward comes to the aid of the wretched person placed in straits and necessities through the help of his loving-kindness. Hence it follows:

When morning had come, Jesus stood on the shore. Yet they did not know that it was Jesus. Morning comes in the human heart when, after temptations and adversities, by God’s favor a person returns somewhat to self-knowledge; illumined inwardly by God’s grace, he begins to recognize that the sufferings he undergoes are proportionate to his deserts, yet he has not received what his deeds deserve, although he is worn down by many tribulations. [Col. 0817B] And he begins to quarrel and struggle with himself, saying to himself: “O wretched and miserable man, what is wrong with you? What, I ask, has happened, that you strive with so obstinate a mind to resist God, without considering that what you suffer is far less, vastly lighter, than what you have deserved from God by your perverse and wicked life? Why do you destroy your soul by impatience, you who receive tribulations and afflictions far smaller than you have deserved?”

Raised up against himself by this struggle, when morning has now come within him through this conflict, he sees Jesus standing on the shore of the sea. The shore may fittingly signify the human heart made firm, which had previously been unstable amid temptations and adversities. Once this morning has come—namely, once some measure of self-knowledge has arisen in his mind—the Lord makes him firm through his fear. In this shore, in this firmness, the Lord Jesus then indeed stands, when the spiritual person is strengthened and made firm in the Lord and in the power of his might, and thus receives his salvation securely, so that he will never again wish to depart from God. It follows:

Yet they did not know that it was Jesus. For although he has attained some degree of self-knowledge, he is not yet able to reach full salvation and perfect knowledge of God. But why does he not yet advance to the knowledge of God, unless because he has not yet merited to possess the relish of food mentioned below? Thus it is immediately added:

Jesus said to them: “Children, have you any food?” God’s speaking is his acting. Therefore the Lord Jesus calls every person living in the state described above a child, so that he may recognize himself as foolish and weak: foolish in evil works, weak in good deeds, and also weak in offering God worthy satisfaction for his sins. He also asks whether he has food, not because any ignorance can befall God, who knows all things, but because he asks the person in order to make him know the deficiency of which he had previously been unaware. By this food of which he is asked we may fittingly understand the sweetness of God, or the inward delight of the heart. Refreshed and illumined inwardly by this sweetness, a person begins to labor vigorously for love of God and for the sweetness of the heavenly homeland; he regards the labors of his body as nothing, whereas before tasting this sweetness from God he could scarcely, or not at all, suffer or endure bodily labors for the Lord. It follows:

They answered him, “No.” God’s question, as we said above, is addressed to a person so that he may know how much he lacks of what he ought to have; a person’s answer to God occurs when he humbly recognizes and laments that he does not possess what he ought to have through God’s grace. Once this question and answer have taken place, the Lord Jesus gives saving counsel concerning how the grace not possessed is to be found and sought. Hence it follows:

Jesus said to them: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find.” By the net we may fittingly understand the human heart; by the boat, the holy manner of life to which one has come. Thus one casts the net on the right side of the boat when, established in the spiritual life, one patiently endures for God’s sake all things harsh, adverse, and contrary; one is not broken or cast down by adversities. And if prosperity follows, one is not exalted by it, but humbly ascribes everything to God and makes both adversity and prosperity work together for the acquisition of eternal life.

Previously, indeed, he had cast his net on the left side of the boat, when, placed in the night of temptations, he had been unable to grasp anything good: in adversity he became impatient and was scattered from the rectitude of his state; in prosperous circumstances he was vainly and uselessly puffed up. But after he has cast his net on the right side of the boat in the way described above, it immediately comes about, according to the Lord’s promise, that he finds what he lacks. For what a person is often unable to attain and find through devout and strenuous bodily labors, he sometimes receives from the Lord when his heart is touched inwardly with sweetness and delight. It follows:

Therefore they cast it, and now they were not able to draw it because of the multitude of fish. Every elect person casts the net on the right side of the boat at the Lord’s counsel—that is, his heart—when, so far as lies in him, he resolves patiently to endure everything for God; and then, by God’s permission, he will be unable to draw his heart away from the multitude of fish. By fish, which live among the waves, we have already said above that a person’s living senses may be expressed.

These words are exceedingly lofty and difficult, words belonging only to the perfect, who love God perfectly. When they have advanced in this holy manner of life in the order we have described, they finally arrive, through God’s mercy and aid, at the point where they cannot draw their heart back from the multitude of living thoughts and reflections—for they do not wish to do so. And that we may see this more fully and clearly, let us set forth what we have said by an example, so that these words may be made more manifest to us.

It is plainly evident to us all that a weak and fragile person, who loves this present world more than God, when he has passed from secular life to a spiritual purpose, may hear or read much about God in Holy Scripture and have many good and holy thoughts about God; nevertheless, his mind remains so entangled and occupied by worldly thoughts that he cannot at all withdraw his heart from the tumult of secular thoughts. For, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel, “Where your treasure is, there also will your heart be” (Matt. 6:21).

If, therefore, a fragile person cannot tear his heart away from worldly thoughts, how much more is the good and perfect person, who faithfully relies on almighty God, his beloved, who has fixed the marrow of his heart in love for the Creator, unable—because unwilling—to withdraw his heart from good thoughts, Holy Scripture, and heavenly meditations? Never, while established in a secular habit of life, did he cling so ardently and sweetly to secular thoughts as he then clings to divine and heavenly meditations. It follows:

Therefore the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord.” The disciple whom Jesus loved was John; and, as Holy Scripture records, John is interpreted “the grace of God.” This is the grace which he had previously been urged and stirred to seek through the Lord’s words, when the Lord said to him: “Children, have you any food?” When this grace comes into a person’s heart, it clearly reveals and declares in that heart that the Lord is: for his being—that he himself is God—is now also present in that person’s heart. Of this being the patriarch Jacob prophesied long before when he said: “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” (Gen. 28:11). It follows:

[Col. 0819C] Simon Peter, when he heard that it was the Lord, girded himself with his tunic—for he was naked—and cast himself into the sea; but the other disciples came by boat. On hearing that by his very being the Lord is within him, the good and perfect person—who has become Simon by obeying God in good and holy works, and Peter by knowing God in good and righteous thoughts—at last girds himself with a tunic, following the example of blessed Peter. By the tunic may be understood the pleasures of the flesh and fleshly desires, which he must then gird up; for he must strongly bind to labors his weak flesh, which had flowed loosely and in which he had still lived delicately, constraining himself, with God’s help, to good and perfect works.

But why this blessed person should gird himself with the tunic in this manner is made clear by the following words:

For he was naked. For then, for the first time, he truly recognizes how miserable he was, how stripped of all divine grace and good deeds in his former life. This is the tunic of which the chosen bride of God declares herself stripped in the Song of Songs, speaking thus to her bridegroom: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” (Song 5:3). It follows:

And he cast himself into the sea. Once the perfect and blessed person has so strictly and strongly girded his flesh, he then casts himself into the sea: into the deep and bitter penitence of the heart. In that penitence he bewails not only his evil works, but also washes away with inward tears of his heart his thoughts, wills, and desires, and makes worthy satisfaction to God for them. This, indeed, is that food of which we spoke above, which, when the Lord asked whether he had it, he had long ago lamented that he did not possess. It follows:

But the other disciples came by boat. Thus, once he has plunged himself into the sea, once he has given his heart to sweet bitterness, once he has obtained that food of heavenly sweetness, it immediately comes about that his other disciples too come to him by boat. By the other disciples we may not unfittingly understand his outward senses and outward deeds, acquired through bodily and external exercises. They come, as it were, by boat when they prosperously approach and succeed him in the holy manner of life which, as we have said, may be understood by the boat.

Indeed, one who formerly had been disordered in all his actions, who spoke jesting words freely and without restraint with his tongue, who frequently turned his ears to vain and harmful hearing, and conformed his eyes and other limbs to this world—after receiving the grace of divine sweetness, all his members, his eyes, ears, steps, bearing, and actions are ordered, seemly, and reverent according to the fear of the Lord, so that he becomes acceptable both to God and to human beings.

For they were not far from land, but about two hundred cubits away, drawing the net of fish. For when, as we have said, a person had turned his tongue, eyes, hearing, hands, and other members toward conformity with the world, he was not far from land—that is, from earthly life. Indeed, he was not merely near earthly life, but was himself in a certain sense earthly and was earth. But after turning to God and ceasing to be conformed to this world, he is separated from this land—that is, earthly life—and, drawing near to God, reaches a certain goal of perfection. Of this it is here said: “but about two hundred cubits away, drawing the net of fish.”

By two hundred cubits a double perfection may be expressed: one perfection in good will, the other in good action. And since, as long as we live in this misery of mortality, we cannot attain this double and full perfection, it is said here, “about two hundred cubits,” to show us that in this unstable and uncertain life we can rise to a certain likeness of perfection, but that absolutely no one can attain perfection itself in this life. This double perfection is reserved for us in eternal life, where we shall arrive not at an approximate, but without qualification at this full and perfect number of two hundred, in which the perfection of life consists.

But because we are now imperfect, we are always drawing the net of fish—which signifies our heart or the thoughts of our heart—rather than possessing it. For we always ascend here to the virtues with labor and difficulty, until we arrive there, where without labor we shall find God, whom we now seek. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0821A] Therefore, when they came down to land, they saw coals laid out, and a fish laid upon them, and bread. This descent to land occurs at a person’s death, when, released from the flesh, the soul lays down its lifeless body in the earth and the spirit returns to God its maker. Therefore, when the Lord’s elect have arrived there, they shall find fully all that they desired in the present life. Returning to their homeland, they shall see coals laid out, and a fish laid upon them, and bread. By the coals we may understand the ardor of unquenchable love, which is the Holy Spirit; by the fish laid upon the coals, the only-begotten Son of God, God and man; and by the bread, God the Father.

Therefore, when the faithful arrive at this blessed vision of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Jesus will plainly say to them there:

[Col. 0821B] “Bring some of the fish which you have now caught.” By these words almighty God seems to intimate to us that he rewards his elect not only from his grace, but that they also receive the gift of reward according to their merits—the merit which they truly gained in the present time, signified by the word “now,” by laboring for God. But let us see what the fish are which the Lord commands to be brought. By these fish may be expressed good wills, holy desires, and righteous works, which the Lord’s elect caught amid the storms of this life.

It is as if almighty God were saying to his elect, who glorified him in their life while still in the present world and have now reached eternity: “My prevenient grace stirred you up to do good; my following grace strengthened you to complete good works; and, saved by this grace, you have finally reached me, your Savior and Redeemer, whom you always desired. And because, between my grace preceding you and my grace following you, there are whatever merits of yours, however small, which you obtained by your own labors, I say: bring some of the fish which you have now caught. Bring your good wills and desires; bring also your good and holy works, which you performed for love of me amid the changeability and instability of the present life, so that you may be crowned not only from my grace but also from your merits.” It follows:

Simon Peter went up and drew the net to land, full of great fish, one hundred and fifty-three. Therefore, after the Lord’s voice commanding and wishing to reward, Simon Peter—the good and perfect person, who by obeying God came to know him—goes up and draws the net to land. Truly, he draws his heart into the land of the living, so that he may be there with all his thoughts and desires; and once he has arrived there, he will never again draw his heart back from God, because he no longer returns to thinking and meditating on outward things.

But from the perfection of this number we may aptly gather why a person has merited to become worthy of arriving at so great an excellence and glory. For the Evangelist says: “The net was full of great fish, one hundred and fifty-three.” In the hundred, then, may be understood the perfection of life acquired in the present life through good works; in the fifty may be expressed true and perfect penitence, which is accompanied, through the working of the Holy Spirit, by the saving remission of sins; and in the three may be understood knowledge of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Thus the heart of every perfect and blessed person established in eternity becomes full of great fish when it is filled by God with great and sublime works: it is filled with a hundred through perfection of life; it is filled with fifty through the working of the Holy Spirit; it is filled with three when it reaches the full and eternal vision of God, or perfect knowledge of the holy Trinity. Of the blessedness which they will obtain there, the text further adds:

And although there were so many, the net was not torn. The sense of these words must be understood differently from what the words seem to say. For what is said here—“and although there were so many, the net was not torn”—may be understood as if it said: “And because the merits of the elect are so great, because they are a hundred in perfection of life, fifty in the anointing of the Holy Spirit, and three by attaining the full vision of God and knowledge of the holy Trinity, therefore their net is no longer torn.”

For, established in eternity, they will always have a firm and stable heart in the Lord; since they enjoy the vision of God according to their will and desire, they will no longer be torn away from God even by the least thought. There, as is immediately added, Jesus says to them:

“Come, dine.” As if he said: “Come, that you may dine with me. For this is the joyful and delightful meal: that you may see me in my divinity face to face, and, remaining with me in the brightness and fullness of the vision of me, may rejoice eternally.”

And none of those at table dared ask him, “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord. Here, while established in the present life, we all question concerning God, because—alas!—we do not know him whom we do not see. But in eternal life no one will dare to question, because no one will need to question. For there all will be taught by God; there, from the least to the greatest, all will know that he is the Lord.

And Jesus came, took the bread, and gave it to them, and likewise the fish. The Lord Jesus gives bread to his elect established in eternity when inwardly he grants them the essence and power of his divinity to contemplate. By this contemplation and vision the inward person is glorified, satisfied, and made blessed: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Likewise he gives the fish when outwardly he grants their bodily eyes the glory of the humanity he assumed, by which we were redeemed, to behold. By that vision the outward person rejoices and is made blessed, so that both persons, inward and outward alike, may have in his divinity and humanity that by which they are glorified, rejoice, and are made blessed. It follows:

This was now the third time Jesus was manifested to his disciples after he had risen from the dead. As we stated at the beginning of this Gospel reading, there are two manifestations by which the Lord deigns to manifest himself to the person being saved. But now, at the end of this Gospel, a third manifestation is added, which must be fulfilled after the end of this mortality in each elect person, when it says: “This was now the third time Jesus was manifested to his disciples.”

First, the Lord manifests himself to a person at the beginning of conversion; second, he manifests himself in the perfection of good conduct; third, he manifests himself in the reward of eternal recompense. But this third manifestation, which will occur in the state of everlasting retribution, does not first take place in a person until he rises from the dead: that is, until, dead to sins, he utterly abandons and casts away sins. But when he has left sins behind and risen from sins and vices, then the third manifestation will be perfectly and fully fulfilled in him in eternal recompense.

[Col. 0823B] May he who deigned to die and rise again for us, Jesus Christ our Lord, bring us to this third manifestation, which will occur in the resurrection after the labors of this life have been completed; he lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## 278. HOMILY XL. FOR THE THURSDAY IN THE FIRST WEEK AFTER EASTER

Mary stood weeping at the tomb. Therefore, while she was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been laid (John 20).

Mary, who was a sinful woman, not unfittingly signifies every converted sinner. When such a person begins, through penitence and conversion and by God’s grace, to raise himself from the sins and vices in which he had formerly lain in evil, it may fittingly be said of him: “Mary stood.”

And it should be observed that it is not said, “she stood,” but “she was standing.” For “she was standing” is said as though she was beginning to stand. But how or where was she beginning to stand? At the tomb, weeping outside. By the tomb, which is so called as though “admonishing the mind” (*monens mentem*), the human heart may fittingly be understood. A person begins, as it were, to stand at this tomb when, admonished by God’s prevenient grace, he recognizes how ruinously he has lived and how opposed he has been to the divine will in all his actions.

What is added—“weeping outside”—mystically suggests to us that there is one kind of weeping which takes place only outwardly through the body, and another weeping, far more exalted than this, which takes place inwardly in and from the heart. A person at the beginning of conversion stands at the tomb as if weeping outside, when, reminded of his sins and considering the manifold guilt of his fall, he weeps indeed with his body—which is as if to weep outside—but has not yet been able or merited to know what is the touch of divine fear and love, which invisibly melts the inmost heart into inward and burning tears.

Yet this weeping, although it takes place outside, is from God and leads to God, because it finally leads the person elected by God to that more noble and sweeter weeping which comes from the touch of God’s fear and love. Hence it follows:

Therefore, while she was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been laid. This bending down is true humility of heart. For a person bends himself well when he begins to humble himself before God for the sins he committed against God with proud heart and body. Humbled, he finally looks into the tomb, because this bending of humility gradually admonishes and illumines him inwardly, enabling him to recognize his sins more and more.

Nor should we pass over the word “looked.” “She looked” is said as though “she looked forward” (*porro aspexit*). He looks into the tomb of his heart not from close at hand but as though from afar, who knows only his evil deeds, but has not yet learned to know or weigh the excesses of his evil wills and evil desires, which are not far away but, as it were, close at hand. Nevertheless, from recollection and consideration of outward faults he gradually advances and is led toward knowledge of inward faults. For this, I think, is mystically suggested to us when the Evangelist immediately adds:

And she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been laid. By the two angels we may understand two forms of knowledge: one of God, the other of oneself. The angel who is found sitting at the head not unfittingly signifies knowledge of God, who is indeed our head. The angel described as sitting at the feet very aptly displays knowledge of the person himself.

Although the angel sitting at the head, expressing knowledge of God, is placed first in the sequence of Gospel truth, as being more worthy, nevertheless the angel sitting at the feet, who figures self-knowledge, must come first. For unless a person first recognizes himself, he cannot at all come to knowledge of God. The twofold character which this self-knowledge ought to have is mystically indicated by the pair of feet. In the head a person is single; in the feet, double. So too the knowledge of God signified by the head is in a sense single and is called so, because by it only the one, simple, and undivided God is known. But, conversely, just as there is doubleness in the feet, so self-knowledge must also be twofold. The right foot may signify omitted good; the left foot, committed evil. Therefore, when a person begins carefully to consider and remember with himself how much good he has neglected and how much evil he has committed, this is, as it were, to see the angel at the feet.

While these two angels continually sit and preside over the tomb of his heart, he sees, as follows, where the body of Jesus had been laid. A body, so called from corruption (*a corruptione*), may fittingly signify corruption as well. But how can we say—or dare to say—that the body of Jesus is named from corruption or signifies corruption, when it was wholly whole, wholly holy, pure and undefiled, indeed utterly foreign to every corruption?

We say this while preserving Catholic faith and Catholic truth: not of that particular pure body of Christ which he assumed for us, but of that body of his which the person to be saved becomes when he begins perfectly to recognize where he corrupted and laid down through his sins his salvation, which may be understood by the name Jesus. For he cannot otherwise pass into the body of Christ unless he truly, humbly, and perfectly recognizes the body of Jesus—that is, the corruption of his salvation. The two angels mentioned above seem mystically to awaken and urge the blessed soul toward this recognition of corrupted salvation by their address, as is immediately stated concerning them:

[Col. 0825B] They said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?” This question of the angels is like a saving awakening. For *mulier* (“woman”) is said from softness (*mollitie*). It is as though they said: “Woman, recognize yourself as a woman; recognize how softly you have lived according to the pleasures and desires of your flesh; recognize how unjustly you have acted until now against God your Creator. You indeed weep, and you weep justly and worthily; for you will always weep, you will always grieve.

“You weep for these two things, and rightly weep: first, because you are a woman and have lived womanishly; second, because you have never known your Lord and Creator as worthily as you ought, nor loved him by knowing him.” Knowledge of God may fittingly be understood by this word “what” (*quid*). For it is ineffable. It can be partly grasped and inwardly perceived, but cannot be named or explained in words.

Thus, when she has been inwardly illumined and instructed in part by outward knowledge of God and self, as though by an angelic address, she breaks forth in these words with a penitent and humble heart:

“Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.” As if she said: “I am indeed what I am called, a woman; I recognize myself as a woman; and because I have lived womanishly and have passed my days without the firmness of all manly—that is, good—works, my soft, evil, and wicked deeds have taken away my Lord. They have removed my Savior from me, and I do not know where they have laid him. I feel that he has been taken and removed from me, but I do not know where they have laid him, because I do not recognize him through due fear or due love. I do not know where he has been laid, because I do not find from myself or in myself where or how I ought to seek him.” It follows:

When she had said this, she turned backward and saw the Lord standing, and did not know that it was Jesus. A person to be saved turns backward when, turning the eyes behind his back, he begins to see and recognize more perfectly the crimes of the past. Thus, turned backward in body but not in heart, he sees Jesus standing. Jesus stands when he begins in some measure to have a standing-place in that person’s heart, and through his standing makes him more steady and constant in seeking his own salvation.

But although he has already received in part knowledge of God and of himself, because he has not yet merited to love God perfectly, the Evangelist rightly adds: “and did not know that it was Jesus.” To know God is to love God; not to know God is not to love God. So too, to know a person is to love a person. “She did not know,” he says, “that it was Jesus,” signifying that she cannot yet love God perfectly, as we have said. Yet though she is not yet able to do so, because she desires to love God, the highest and almighty One inwardly instructs and forms her toward his love, saying:

“Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?” As if he said: “You were a woman; you have recognized yourself as a woman; you have recognized yourself as soft in your actions. Recognize now also that you were soft in your desires and wills. It is not enough for you merely to recognize and repent of sinful actions, unless you add recognition and lamentation for your unjust desires, wicked thoughts, and wills.

“Whom do you seek? Me, surely, whose name is ‘Who’ (*Quis*). For I am beyond estimation and beyond speech. You seek me among outward and visible things, in which and through which, since I am invisible, you cannot find me. Seek, therefore, the invisible One among invisible things: that is, in a pure heart, pure desires, and pure thoughts.”

When the Lord inwardly calls, teaches, and illumines the human heart in such words, through the unspeakable and indescribable language of his inspiration, he more and more raises, kindles, and lifts it toward his love. Hence it follows:

But she, thinking that he was the gardener, said to him. This word “thinking” (*existimans*) must not be understood as though it were the word of one who errs or doubts. It is the word of one affirming, the word of a soul desiring God from its inmost marrow. For “thinking” is said as though reconsidering inwardly with herself. Thus the blessed soul judges within herself that this highest and almighty God, whose voice she has now merited to hear inwardly, is the one true and most mighty gardener. He knows how to cultivate the human heart—which may fittingly be understood by a garden, more fertile than the rest of the field—by pouring in and irrigating it with the grace of his mercy. By the hand of his divine power, he knows and is able to uproot what is harmful and useless, and to plant and graft what is good and useful.

While she so judges, she also comes to desire and long more for that same gardener: that he may deign to visit, inhabit, and cultivate the garden of her heart with the grace of his mercy, so that through him, who possesses such knowledge and such power, the evil shoots of vices may be uprooted and wither, and the noble shoots of virtues may be grafted and grow. Thus, when she begins to judge and consider the excellence of his wisdom and power, she says to him, as the Evangelist immediately adds:

“Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him up.” These words are deep words. Nor is this surprising, for they are the words of the flying eagle: that is, of John, who even while still remaining bodily in this life reached in his understanding to the very mysteries of divinity. “Lord,” she says, “if you have taken him away, tell me.” What, I ask, or what kind of question is this which the blessed soul asks God?

We surely know that when someone desires to learn something from a neighbor, he seeks and asks in order that what he cannot know by himself, he may know from the other’s words and answers. So too the good soul understands that the Lord has been taken from it; but because it cannot know or recognize from itself and by itself why, or by whom, he has been taken away, it cries out, as it were, to God the Father in these most humble words: “Lord, if you have taken him away.”

It asks whether God himself has taken away his Son from it in order to increase or multiply his mercy toward it, or whether it has lost and destroyed him solely through its own sins, by God’s just judgment allowing it. For the merciful and compassionate Lord often withdraws himself even from his elect, not on account of sin but on account of their merit: he withdraws the grace of his sweetness in order to increase and establish more firmly in them the constancy of his love. At times he also removes himself from those less perfect, not to increase merit but to punish sin.

These, then, are the things the blessed soul seeks and asks of the Lord when it says: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me.” As if it said: “Tell me, I beg you, Lord, in that ineffable manner of your mercy; speak there where you are accustomed to speak, and in the manner in which you are accustomed to speak. Speak to me, Lord, in a humble and contrite heart; for there you speak, where you wonderfully instruct and form the person whom you take care to save.

“Tell me, Lord, whether you have taken away my Savior, your Son, my one hope, my one refuge and joy. Tell me also why you took him away; you who know all things, who are acquainted with all things, speak, so that by your speaking you may make me, who do not know, know; so that I may know that he has been taken from me as I ought to know it, and grieve for his removal as I ought to grieve.

“For if you speak to me in a humble and contrite heart, there indeed is that place where you placed him from the beginning. For you willed and ordained from the beginning that he should be and remain, not in a proud and unrepentant heart, but in a heart truly humble and penitent. Therefore, if you speak to me there, I will take him up—him whom I laid down through my sins. Indeed, I will lift him up in my inward thoughts through due fear and love; I will lift him up also in my outward faculties through good action, so that if by my sins, desires, and negligences I have been an occasion of scandal or ruin to anyone, I may through the good conduct and example of a perfect life become an occasion of edification.”

But we may also understand differently what he says: “if you have taken him away.” “You have taken away” is said as though, “you have borne him upward.” It is as though she said: “Holy, just, and merciful Lord, I do indeed acknowledge that you have taken your Son, my Lord and Savior, from that which is above within me—from my spirit and heart, namely, where he alone, since you created me in his image and likeness, ought to have his dwelling—and that by your just judgment; for such is what I have deserved before your equity. But tell me, Lord—since your speaking is your doing—tell me, I beg you, where you have placed him. Speak within me, that is, work within me,

[Col. 0828A] accomplish within me the accustomed work of your mercy, so that by your grace I may be able to know where you have placed him. Grant that I may recognize to what lofty excellence of dignity I was first created by you, when the image of this same your Son was impressed upon me; and into what misery I have now fallen, as my sins have deserved.

All that I hear concerning you indeed passes entirely beyond me, because it does not touch me inwardly. But if you speak to me—if, by restoring and renewing your image in me to that higher state of mine from which he was taken away, you cause your Son to be restored—then I shall take him up. I shall take him up for myself, because then I shall begin to know, understand, relish, and love him as my Lord, my Creator, and my Savior. While the blessed soul thus diligently cries out through these prayers, through such great cries of a contrite heart, to the ears
