[Col. 0828B] of God’s mercy, what at last the merciful Lord does is mystically indicated when the Evangelist immediately adds:

Jesus said to her, “Mary.” Turning, she said to him, “Rabboni”—which means, “Teacher.” Jesus’ speaking is, as we often say, Jesus’ doing; for, according to the ineffable work of his mercy which he performs inwardly in the blessed soul, he also gives her a name outwardly. “Mary,” he says. He calls her Mary, a name which in our language signifies “star of the sea” or “illuminatrix,” an enlightener. For through his calling and working she becomes a shining star of the sea—that is, of her heart made bitter through penitence—when, illumined by the light of perfect repentance, she begins rightly to penetrate the darkness of her sins by discerning it. Likewise, she becomes, as it were, the enlightener

[Col. 0828C] of her own self, when, with holy desires and daily advances in virtue, and with God’s grace cooperating, she daily renews and illumines herself. Hence it is fittingly added concerning such a soul: “Turning, she said to him, ‘Rabboni’—which means, ‘Teacher.’” This second turning of the blessed soul differs greatly from that turning which the Evangelist mentioned earlier. There she turned backward, to call to mind her time spent in sins; here she turns much more worthily and sweetly, because with all her affections she gathers her whole self to love God, saying to him: “Rabboni”—which means, “Teacher.” “Teacher” is certainly a name of fear. Nor is it without significance or reason that we find these two words, having one and the same sound and meaning, placed together.

[Col. 0828D] For when the Evangelist, not ignorant of God’s mysteries, says in the person of the woman, “Rabboni,” and immediately adds in his own words, “which means, Teacher,” he expresses for us, as I think, two fears: one called servile fear, which is also initial fear; the other called filial fear. Servile and initial fear is when one fears God because of the future punishment deserved for sins. Filial fear, however, is when one, inflamed with filial affection toward God, fears to offend him; and, through this fear alone—lest one offend him whom one recognizes as Father—avoids sins as far as possible, and in every way, as far as lies in one’s power, labors earnestly in virtuous deeds. The merciful Lord instructs and forms such a person still more deeply, so as to bring him to that for which he longs and sighs: the love of God himself.

[Col. 0829A] Hence follows:

“Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” As blessed Augustine says, touch brings movement to an end. For when a person has advanced in God in the order already described, he has been well moved—indeed, greatly advanced. Yet God, the supremely good and supremely perfect teacher of the soul, the faithful God, desiring to advance that soul still further, speaks invisibly in these words: “Do not touch me.” Do not, I say, set the end of your mind’s movement there, so as to believe that I, who am invisible, am to be found only by the visible labors of external works, or are to be seen in this life with outward and bodily eyes. It remains for you, then, to advance still further;

[Col. 0829B] it remains, indeed, for you to stretch forth toward invisible things, and to rise from your visible things to my invisible things. For I am spirit, and cannot be seen except in spirit. Therefore, unless you keep yourself among invisible things—that is, in your spirit and inward faculties—through cleanness and purity of heart, and thus pass from your invisible things to my invisible things, I have not yet ascended within you to my Father. For I cannot, because I ought not, admit you, as you desire, to that sweetness of my charity which is understood under the name Father, the name of love.

“But go to my brothers and say to them: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.’” What, I ask, may we understand by these brothers to whom he then sends the blessed soul,

[Col. 0829C] except the spiritual faculties of that same soul? Those are brothers, and are called brothers, who are begotten of one father and one mother; who also gladly dwell together and agree and live in harmony with one another in brotherly love. So too the pure and spiritual faculties of a human being, which God the Father generates in the human heart through the most noble seed of his aspiration and inspiration, as the Holy Spirit makes it fruitful—when they begin to agree and remain, as far as this may be done in a mortal body, in unity of will in and with him whom he ineffably and without limit begot from himself, Jesus Christ our Lord—may fittingly be called his brothers. To this end the Lord admonishes and exhorts the soul that loves and desires him, saying: “Go to my brothers and tell them.”

[Col. 0829D] It is as though he said: “Go to yourself within yourself through the guarding and purity of your heart; gather your faculties inwardly, and tell them”—that is, make them such that they may be called and may be my brothers, so that they may agree, consent, and obey my will as brother agrees with brother. Make them spiritual, so that I, who am spirit, may be able to dwell and remain in them as with my brothers.

Finally, if you say this to them—that is, if you make them such—then indeed “I ascend to my Father and your Father.” Father, as we have said, is a name of love, through which the perfect love of God may fittingly be understood. Therefore, when the Lord says, “I ascend to my Father and your Father,” it must be understood as though he said: “I ascend to the Father, not in my own person,

[Col. 0830A] but in yours; indeed, I ascend within you, because I shall cause you to ascend through me and in me to the long-desired sweetness of my love.”

But how do I say, “my Father and your Father”? My charity, which I have purposed to pour into you and into my brothers—that is, your faculties, when they have become spiritual—is mine, because no one can possess it except through me. It is certainly mine by power; it will also be yours by my gift and grace. And if in this present life I ascend in you and in your faculties in this manner, after the end of this life I shall ascend also in you and to my God, and to your God. I shall bring you to full and perfect knowledge, to the joyful and everlasting vision of my Father, which indeed is mine;

[Col. 0830B] for no one can attain it except with my help and by my granting it. He is my God by nature, because I am one God with him; but he will also be your God through me, who with him can give all things. For if in this life I continually ascend to him through love within you, that same charity of my Father which I give you and pour into you in the present life will be yours and all people’s in the life to come, where you will be so blessed in eternal reward that no cloud of adversity will ever again hinder you from contemplating the glory of the everlasting Trinity.

These are the words of the Gospel reading. Since we have expounded them according to our measure, insofar as God in his grace has deigned to grant us, let us give thanks to him, humbly imploring his mercy,

[Col. 0830C] that he may so ascend within us to his Father and our Father, so kindle us in this present life through the grace of the Holy Spirit with love for himself and for the Father, that, after the end of this life, we may attain that place where with him and in him we may rejoice eternally in the eternal vision of the Father. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the same Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

289. HOMILY XLI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST GEORGE THE MARTYR.

“I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman” (John 15).

The splendid and sublime words of this Gospel reading form part of that outstanding discourse which the Lord delivered to his disciples at the Last Supper, when he was freely offering himself for his Passion.

[Col. 0830D] This discourse so surpasses and excels all his teaching in dignity and loftiness that the three Evangelists, although holy, chosen, and filled with the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, regarding this discourse as beyond their understanding, made no mention of it. But John the Evangelist, that chosen and beloved disciple who reclined upon his breast at supper and, while reclining, drank deep wisdom from the breast of Jesus, alone deserved the grace of being able to retain this discourse in memory and commit it to writing in faithful testimony. And what wonder is it that the Lord Jesus, when leaving his disciples in bodily presence,

[Col. 0831A] spoke more excellent and divine words, since we see something comparable even among mortals? When a faithful friend leaves a friend whom he believes he shall never see again, then, in order to demonstrate the affection he has held for him, he pours forth from the inmost feeling of his heart many words that he had never previously spoken. How much more fitting was it that the only-begotten Son of God, who is the power of God and wisdom, should utter words more profound and wiser as he passed from this world to the Father and left his familiar friends? Thus, in so excellent and preeminent a discourse are also contained these Gospel words now before us, in which he set forth his divinity and humanity, saying:

[Col. 0831B] “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.” A vine is planted in the earth, sends its root into the earth, and springs and proceeds from the earth. Accordingly, by the vine, which springs and grows from the earth, the holy humanity of the Son of God may fittingly be signified; for, as a vine springs from the earth, so it proceeded from that noble earth, the blessed and undefiled Virgin, and came into this world. Notice that he says, with an addition, “the true vine.” For the Lord had also planted another vine in Paradise, when he formed the first man, Adam. Yet he was not truly a true vine, but a false vine, an alien vine. God the Father created this first vine, this first human being, in order that, faithfully serving his Creator, he might inherit the glory and honor of eternal blessedness and continually enjoy the joy and delight of the heavenly homeland,

[Col. 0831C] if he were willing to render to his Creator the service of due subjection and obedience. The serpent, the ancient enemy of the human race, envying his honor and splendor, enticed him into deceit when it persuaded him through disobedience to raise himself against his Creator. Adam, therefore, was false when he presumed to do what he ought not to do: resisting his Creator, to whom he ought to have rendered obedience, he rendered disobedience instead.

291. Thus corrupted by the devil’s falsehood, he transmitted the guilt of this falsehood to all his posterity, and the guilt of his falsehood became hereditary for the entire human race. For no human being, except the mediator between God and humankind, the man Jesus Christ, could be or will be free from this falsehood unless, washed in the laver of regeneration and renewed, he has been freed from this falsehood through Christ. David the prophet, groaning sorrowfully over all human nature corrupted by this falsehood, said: “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:11). In short, no human being from the beginning of the world has responded to God in truth without being found corrupted by this falsehood—not even our Lady, the ever-virgin Mary,

> [Note: [Col. 0831D] See our dissertation prefixed to the first volume of this work.]

although holy, immaculate, and untouched, could be without the blemish of this deception; for she, like other human beings, was conceived and born in this falsehood, that is, in original sin. But her only-begotten Son, the mediator between God and humankind, the man Christ Jesus,

[Col. 0832A] alone was found free from this falsehood. Therefore he speaks of himself most justly and fittingly when he says: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.” It is as though he said: “I, who am God and human being and remain in two substances, am in my humanity the true vine, because I have never degenerated from the nobility innate to me by committing sin; I have never fallen into that falsehood in which the whole human race is held. And therefore, because I am so true a vine, my Father is the husbandman of this vine.” Plainly, my Father is the husbandman because the divinity of my Father—and my own divinity—planted my vine. For the divinity of my Father is my divinity, since I am one God with him. That very divinity cultivates my vine, this human nature which I assumed.

[Col. 0832B] For it befitted my divinity diligently to cultivate and guard this vine. Therefore, because the Father himself—that very divinity—was the cultivator of this vine, this vine was deservedly true, since it never fell into falsehood. It follows:

“Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he takes away; and every one that bears fruit he cleanses, that it may bear more fruit.” A branch grows and buds from a vine; therefore every human being may be represented by the branches, for one is truly grafted and planted together with Christ the Lord, the vine, through the laver of regeneration, and renewed from this vine grows into eternal life. For before we are reborn through Christ in baptism, we are all by nature children of wrath and, as though alienated from God, are reckoned among the Gentiles, until, regenerated by the saving laver,

[Col. 0832C] we put on Christ. As a branch grows from a vine, so a person grows in Christ according to Christianity and grows into Christ. For when one is immersed in baptism, one is buried with Christ; when one is raised from the font, one is conformed to Christ’s resurrection. This is to grow in Christ and grow into Christ. Whoever, therefore, is planted together with the true vine, the Lord Jesus; buried with Christ in baptism and raised in him; and yet does not bear saving fruit in him—the heavenly Father will surely take that person away from the fellowship of the righteous in the future.

Let us see what kind of fruit is to be borne in the Lord, of which this passage speaks. A vine does not produce apples or pears, wheat or similar things; rather, it sprouts grapes and bears a cluster from itself. By the cluster the fervor of charity may be expressed, as we also have in another Gospel, where the Lord says: “Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” (Matthew 7:16). Whoever, then, reborn in Christ does not have this fruit, this fervor of charity, but proceeds in this spiritual life with a lukewarm and

[Col. 0832D] barren heart—let us see what John the Evangelist thinks of such a person. When he set forth words of life and wrote down the commandments of life to the seven angels, that is, the seven Churches represented by angels, he wrote to one angel among the rest from the Lord’s own mouth: “Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 5:15 [sc. 3:15–16]).

[Col. 0833A] A person is cold when wholly dependent on this world and wholly immersed in the abyss of sin. A person is lukewarm when he has neither God nor the world: he is neither united and joined to God in true love, nor lawfully enjoys this world with any delight. How greatly one who lives in this spiritual profession so lukewarmly displeases God, and with what punishment God will punish him in the future, is made clear by the words that follow: “I shall begin,” he says, “to vomit you out of my mouth.”

293. If a person were wholly cold, lying entirely and completely in sins, he could, with God’s assent, be converted more easily than one who remains in a spiritual profession yet bears toward God a dry and lukewarm heart. The Lord sometimes permits this wretch, proceeding with such a lukewarm heart, to continue in the congregation of the faithful in the present life—that is,

[Col. 0833B] to remain in his body until the end of his life; but at death he begins to vomit him out, and at the universal judgment completes that vomiting out. There, according to these Gospel words, “he takes him away,” when, removing him from the company and exultation of the good, he sends him, body and soul, into eternal condemnation. But what glory is to come to those who, with God’s help, know how to bear this fruit, this fervor of charity of which we have spoken, is shown by the following words:

“And every one who bears fruit, he will cleanse, that he may bear more fruit.” The one who has inward fervor of charity toward God and neighbor, the heavenly Father, the true husbandman, will indeed cleanse him. Even if such a person has less perfection in other actions,

[Col. 0833C] and even if, hindered by the frailty of the flesh, he cannot through strenuous bodily labors outwardly show in works that same fervor of charity as he wishes, the heavenly Father, who sees that fervor within him, nevertheless cleanses such a person through repentance in the present age. And if his sins have not been wholly cleansed by repentance in this present life, the Lord will cleanse him after his departure from this life by the fire of purgatory in justice. Once the sins have been cleansed in justice, in the life to come he will reward him, cleansed, eternally in mercy through mercy and justice. Thus, thus is cleansed by God the person who, planted together with the true vine, bears fruit—that is, who brings forth inward fervor of charity

[Col. 0833D] in the Lord Jesus.

But he is cleansed by God in this manner in order that he may bear more fruit. This fuller fruit, of which the Lord speaks in the present passage, cannot be attained by believers in this life, because, while they remain in this wretched and changeable life, they can never reach the full and perfect fervor of charity. But in the life to come they deserve to attain this fuller and greater fruit, where the testimony of the apostle Paul will be fulfilled. Speaking of himself and those like him, he says: “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Here we all have shaded and veiled faces, while we cannot see God, whom we desire to see, though to see him is the salvation of the one who sees. This veil and shadow now exist in us because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wisdom 9:15).

[Col. 0834A] When this veil has been taken away and this corruptible body laid aside, when we have reached the very fountain of life, the King of glory, there with unveiled face we shall behold the glory of the Lord; there we shall be transformed into the same image as by the Spirit of the Lord.

But let us see what this image is, into whose likeness we must be transformed. The only-begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, is the invisible image of God the Father. He is now, in his own image and in himself, immortal and impassible, just, good, and holy—and not merely just, good, and holy, but justice itself, goodness itself, and holiness itself.

[Col. 0834B] We too shall someday be transformed into that same image, when, having received our bodies again in the resurrection, we have been made immortal, impassible, just, good, and holy by him. We shall also be transformed from glory to glory: from glory, that is, from the fervor of transitory and temporal charity, into glory, that is, to the ardor and vision of everlasting charity. It follows:

“You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.” The Lord Jesus was an eminent and most wise teacher, and as he himself willed—for he was the Word of the Father—so his word ran its course. For some, hearing the word did no good, indeed did greater harm, because he who spoke outwardly did not inwardly soften them by saving grace to hear words of salvation, as he himself said to the Jews: “My word has no place in you.” But when he returned to his chosen and beloved disciples and addressed them sweetly, while speaking outwardly he addressed them more sweetly inwardly; by the delightful attraction of his divinity, he cleansed their hearts, so that he could fittingly say to them:

[Col. 0834C] “You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.” Yet what the Lord then did in person, he still deigns to do through his teachers, who are his members. For any teacher who speaks for God alone, who seeks in his teaching not his own glory but the glory of him from whom comes what he speaks—“for without me,” says the Lord, “you can do nothing” [John 15:5]—and who therefore, speaking for God, seeks in God the salvation of those subject to him: that teacher’s discourse, proceeding from the gift of the Holy Spirit, often cleanses the hearts of hearers. When hearers have been admonished by the Lord’s word, they hear something from the words of their teacher and master which recalls to them their sins and negligences; and immediately they are inwardly touched by a certain sorrow of repentance, a sorrow of heart which often cleanses them amid the teacher’s words.

296. Concerning this sorrow of repentance David the prophet said: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Psalm 31:5). It is as though he said: “Admonished by the words of preaching concerning my sins and negligences, and inwardly touched by sorrow of heart,

[Col. 0835A] I formed a saving resolve with my soul: that I wished to confess my sins to the Lord.” He did not say, “I confessed my sins,” but said, “I agreed with my soul that I wished to confess my sins. And you forgave the impiety of my sin.” The impiety of sin is an unlawful thought of sin,

> [Note: [Col. 0835D] That is, sinfully so in a venial sense.]

and this impiety of sin may be cleansed by the Lord through inward sorrow of heart, which a person perceives amid the words of preaching, without confession. But if unlawful consent to sin has joined the unlawful thought of sin, it cannot be cleansed except through confession. And if an unlawful act of sin has joined unlawful thought of sin and unlawful consent to sin, it must be cleansed not by sorrow of heart and oral confession alone, but by bodily labor and satisfaction. It follows:

[Col. 0835B] “Remain in me, and I in you.” We remain in God in two ways, and the Lord himself remains in us in two ways. For he subsists in two natures: he is God and human being, Word and flesh; for “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). According to his divine nature he is Word; according to his human nature he is flesh. Therefore, according to each nature, divine and human, we remain in him, and he according to each nature remains in us. We remain in God according to his human nature if we remain unanimously in the unity of Catholic faith and in the unity of the holy Church, which is his flesh, and do not rend the faith of the Catholic Church by any schism. We also remain in him in this way if, in the unanimity of the holy

[Col. 0835C] congregation in which we live, we live without murmuring and detraction and do not disturb that congregation by our evil conduct. According to his divine nature, in which he is Word, we remain in him if we take continual delight in his word and, inwardly meditating on his word, are frequently occupied with the sweetness of his word. If in these two ways, insofar as is permitted to mortals, we remain in God, then, as he promised us, he too remains in us. He remains in us outwardly according to his human nature, in which he became flesh for us, guarding us outwardly from wicked action; he remains in us inwardly according to his divine nature, guarding us inwardly from evil will. It is as though the Lord says to us:

[Col. 0835D] “Remain in me, so that you may persist in the faith of the Catholic Church, and may not make divisions by murmuring, detraction, and evil conduct within the congregation to which I have brought you through my mercy. If you do this, I shall guard you outwardly from wicked action and protect you inwardly from evil will.” It follows:

“As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.” A branch which proceeds from a vine has no sap in itself; rather, the vine sends the sap of its greenness into the branches, so that from its sap the branches may grow green and flower. As we recalled above, Christ is the vine; we are the branches, having been planted together in baptism with the vine himself, the Lord Jesus.

[Col. 0836A] From him, as branches from the vine, we receive sap: the sap of life, that we may be and live; the sap of life, that we may be well and live well. In that respect in which he is our Creator, when we are born from our mother and receive body and soul, we receive from his divinity the sap of life, that we may be and live. But in that respect in which he is our Redeemer, we receive from his humanity the sap of life, that we may be well and live well. For we would be ill if we had not been redeemed. But because we have been redeemed, we are well, so that we may live blessedly. For, that we might be well, he gained this for us in redemption: dying for us and shedding the blood of his side, he made it possible for us to live well and blessedly. It follows:

[Col. 0836B] “I am the vine; you are the branches.” In this passage, where the Lord Jesus calls himself the vine for the second time, he seems to indicate to us the simple essence of his divinity, since without any addition he declares himself to be the vine. In the earlier verse, where he said with an addition, “I am the true vine,” he wished to signify his holy humanity united to divinity; in that human nature he had nothing through itself or from itself, but everything from God the Father and his divinity. But in the divine nature, in which he is simple God, the word “vine” is used simply and without any addition, because through himself and in himself he is good, just, and holy—indeed, goodness itself, justice itself, holiness itself. What he added, “and you are the branches,” he said to his disciples and says also to us, admonishing us to be grafted into the vine himself, the Lord Jesus Christ,

[Col. 0836C] to grow in him and unto him, and to receive from him the sap of life.

“He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing.” In these three verses that follow, I think, we may find the work of the holy Trinity, which works invisibly and incomprehensibly in the elect and the reprobate, often rewarding the good not only in eternal life but also in the present, while rejecting the evil here and condemning them eternally in the future. Thus, in the first verse may be expressed the consolation and reward of the righteous, with which the Lord consoles them in the present life. In the second verse may be understood the rejection of the wicked which occurs in the present, and their condemnation which will occur in the future. In the third likewise may be understood the reward of the righteous which will be in eternal life. “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing.” It is as though he says: Whoever remains in me according to my divine and human nature; meditates and ruminates upon my word inwardly in the heart; and lives without murmuring and dissension in the unity of Catholic faith and the unanimity of the holy congregation in which he lives, without rupturing that unanimity through strange and disorderly conduct—in that person I too shall remain, guarding the body from wicked action and the soul from evil will.

[Col. 0837A] If anyone remains in God in this manner, steadfastly cleaving to him, and God remains in that person by guarding him, then, according to the Lord’s word, that person bears much fruit. In the earlier fruit, of which we have written above, we said that the fervor of charity may be understood, where “fruit” alone was used. Here, however, we find the addition “much fruit.” In this much fruit we may understand manifold virtues, because one who remains in God as described above, and in whom God has made his dwelling, will by no means remain at one level of perfection. Rather, according to the Psalmist’s words, he will “go from strength to strength” (Psalm 38:8), always advancing and always seeking better and more perfect things. The apostle Paul explains to us the nature of this fruit: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering,

[Col. 0837B] goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Galatians 5:22).

“If anyone does not remain in me, he shall be cast out like a branch and shall wither; and they shall gather him and cast him into the fire, and he burns.” If anyone does not remain in God in the manner described above, that person will be cast out at the Lord’s command. The sinner will be cast out when, at the future judgment, the Lord rejects him from his society and familiarity. He will be cast out when the Lord separates him from the fellowship of his elect. Although in the present Church he may seem bodily to remain with the elect, nevertheless at the future judgment he will be separated from them, as the Lord says: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). And it is well said, “like a branch.” For although he has not stood in truth, nevertheless he has had here some likeness to the elect; but he has never truly been grafted into the true vine, the body of Christ. Therefore there he will be cast out and wither.

[Col. 0837C] There he will wither from the fatness of the Holy Spirit, of which David said: “May my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Psalm 62:6). He will lack that fatness of the Holy Spirit for eternity and will always be a stranger to the richness of spiritual joy. “And they shall gather him,” he says, “and cast him into the fire, and he burns.” We may understand malicious spirits here, or good angels, to whom the Lord will say at the future judgment: “Gather the bundles for burning” (Matthew 13:30). Once this judgment has been made, they will be cast into eternal fire, and there they burn.

[Col. 0837D]

300. Notice that he uses the present tense here: “and he burns.” For the fire and punishment which the reprobate will suffer are always present to them. They are future for them now, but then they will always possess them as present. For without interval, without a moment’s respite, they burn in the fire. And because these words have a double meaning, those things which, we said, are fulfilled in the eternal punishment of the condemned are also frequently fulfilled in the reprobate in the present life. Thus the Lord Jesus says: “If anyone does not remain in me, he shall be cast out like a branch and shall wither; and they shall gather him, cast him into the fire, and he burns.”

When we refuse to remain in God as described above, it happens by his just judgment that, our heart being abandoned, we are often cast out even against our will and unwillingly. What this casting out is like we wretches

[Col. 0838A] know well and experience frequently: when we abandon our heart and God, who ought to be the inhabitant of our heart, and go forth to think of secular and outward things, often considering and turning over in our minds things which we have never seen or experienced. From that useless wandering we become so dry within that we cannot raise our heart upward toward God through any richness of heart or sweetness of mind. When we see other people, remaining in Christ and bearing God in heart and mouth, enjoying great sweetness with God, we persist in our dryness and are joined to God by no love. Hence, alas, what immediately follows here is fulfilled in us: “and they shall gather him, cast him into the fire, and he burns.” When, as our sins deserve,

[Col. 0838B] we become so dry within, malicious spirits are immediately present, carefully investigating and gathering whether, according to the casting-out by which we have sent our heart outside ourselves, they can see us living uselessly in any respect. They mark our words, signs, bearing, and deeds, to see whether, following the perverse thoughts through which we have dried up within, they catch us outwardly changing our bearing. Thus, while drying up and wandering outside ourselves, we are often cast by malicious spirits into the fire: plainly, into the fire of envy, anger, lust, and the other vices. Cast into that fire, we undoubtedly burn.

301. Of this fire the Psalmist said: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Psalm 57:9). Therefore, when the fire of anger, envy, pride, and other vices falls upon our

[Col. 0838C] higher part, we are so darkened and clouded by this fire that we are in no condition to see the true sun, the Lord Jesus Christ; and therefore we burn, quite justly and fittingly, in this fire of vices. It follows:

If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you shall ask whatever you will, and it shall be done for you. In these words, as was stated above, the reward of the righteous which is to come in eternity may be understood. It is as though the Lord were saying: If you remain in me—that is, in my flesh and body, which is the Church—do not divide by murmuring or detraction the unity of faith, morals, and the holy congregation in which you live; and if you diligently keep within the inward person the words of my commandments, then you shall ask whatever you will, and it shall be done for you.

The Lord himself has deigned to instruct us concerning what we ought to ask of God. For he does not allow us to pray excessively for transitory and temporal things; rather, he wills that we continually entreat God with prayers for eternal and heavenly things. But since our body ought to serve the spirit and cannot do without the comfort and use of temporal things, we should pray for these briefly and moderately, so that we may not be deprived of temporal aids, and so that, supported by the assistance of temporal goods, we may be able to render the service due to our Creator. But for the obtaining of eternal and heavenly things we ought, as it were, to press God, and earnestly beseech him that his good and perfect will may be fulfilled in us, just as we say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Matt. VI, 10). The will of the Lord is that we should become sharers and fellow-heirs of his kingdom and enjoy his delightful vision in eternal life. If we pray faithfully for this, it will without doubt be done for us in eternal life.

May he therefore, the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends, who teaches knowledge to humankind, teach us how we ought to remain in him, so that after the miseries and labours of this exile he may at length fulfil our desire with good things in our homeland—he who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE VIGIL OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PHILIP AND JAMES

[Col. 0839B]

“Joseph commanded the steward of his house,” etc. (Gen. XLIII).

The feasts of all the saints, whose sacred solemnities we celebrate throughout the year, ought to be recalled by us with great reverence. For they have now reached the harbour of eternal security, while we still toss amid the perils of this present life; they do not cease to help us by the aid of their intercession and continually sustain us by the hand of their protection. But the most sacred feasts of the apostles ought to be celebrated by us with so much greater devotion and with so much more excellent a service of veneration, as they have been exalted above the other saints in the heavenly court by a greater glory of honour and dignity from our Lord Jesus Christ himself.

For we may firmly believe that those whom divine predestination chose from the whole world for this purpose—that they might be deemed worthy, more intimately than all other mortals, to enjoy the bodily presence of the incarnate Son of God—were also exalted above the other saints with a fuller glory of dignity in heaven. If, therefore, the feasts of other saints, who are indeed to be judged along with us, must be remembered by us in solemn veneration, then with far more excellent proclamation of praise should we venerate the most sacred feasts of the apostles, who are to judge us on that dreadful day of the Last Judgment.

[Col. 0839D]

For these are they through whom the salvation of the whole world was accomplished. All the works which the Lord performed in the midst of the earth would in some fashion have remained dead and buried, had the redemption of humankind not been proclaimed to the world through the voice of their preaching. Hence it was necessary that, when our Lord Jesus Christ passed from the world through the disgrace of his passion and death and was assumed into glory, they themselves should be preserved in the body. Thus, in his passion, he answered the persecutors who sought him: “If you seek me, let these go” (John XVIII, 8). Without doubt he was taking thought beforehand, lest, if these preachers of eternal life had died with him, the seed-bed of faith and the true knowledge of the divine name should never have been made known to human minds.

[Col. 0840A]

And because they were such and so great—those through whom the almighty Lord had purposed to summon the whole world into fellowship in eternal salvation—it was truly fitting that in all the Scripture of the patriarchs and prophets which concerned him, their inestimable glory and dignity, their incomparable holiness, should be prefigured. Thus Scripture mystically prefigured them in the Old Testament, where Joseph commanded a banquet to be prepared for his brothers, at which banquet he made himself known to them as the brother whom they had sold into Egypt. For Scripture relates thus: “Joseph commanded the steward of his house, saying: Bring the men into the house; kill a victim; and prepare a banquet, because they are to eat with me at noon.”

[Col. 0840B]

This Joseph bears the type of the true Joseph, our Lord Jesus Christ. His brothers are to be understood as the holy apostles. That banquet which Joseph made for his brothers—that is, for his disciples—was that last most sacred supper, at which he offered them the cups of eternal life and treated them with such merciful intimacy as never before in all his life. For then too he spoke that discourse which he had never previously spoken in the days of his flesh, and revealed those heavenly secrets which had never been heard before the ages.

They drank and were made drunk when, on the fiftieth day, at the coming of the Holy Spirit, they were so strengthened by the fullness of heavenly grace and so intoxicated by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit that, wholly renewed in the Holy Spirit, they transcended all visible things in the height of their minds. They no longer feared any adversities of the world, but, as though joy had been set before them, willingly accepted the insults inflicted upon them; indeed, with all the devotion of their minds they desired and longed to die for Christ’s name, as is written of them: “The apostles departed rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus” (Acts V, 41).

Again, the history of the Books of Kings prefigured their praise and glory, when, after recounting the Philistines whom King David and his servants—David two, and his servants three—had slain in praiseworthy victory, Scripture adds:

[Col. 0840D]

“These five fell by the hand of David and his servants” (II Kings I, 22). By David, whose name means “strong of hand,” is signified our Lord Jesus Christ, truly strong of hand and strongest among spirits; his servants are to be understood as the holy apostles.

By the two Philistines whom the true David, our Lord Jesus Christ, slew, we may understand, so to speak, two deaths: the death of the body and the death of the soul. He killed bodily death in himself, because, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall have no further dominion over him. No one among the elect ever could or will be able to do this. He killed the death of the soul in those holy souls whom he rescued from the infernal prisons by the triumph of his passion. In certain elect persons he also killed at once the death of body and soul: having made their souls alive, he caused them also to rise in body with himself.

[Col. 0841A]

The three Philistines who fell by the hand of David’s servants—that is, Christ’s apostles—are the Jews, pagans, and heretics. The apostles so put them to death with the sword of God’s word that, when they could not convert them to the faith by the word of preaching, they cast them down with such force of eloquence that they could in no way resist their words.

But in another sense also three Philistines fell by the hand of David’s servants. Since every sin is committed in three ways—namely, by thought, speech, and deed—there are said to be, as it were, three deaths, when a person is in some manner made dead through wicked thought, perverse speech, and unrighteous action.

[Col. 0841B]

These three Philistines fell by the hand of David’s servants because, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, the holy apostles put to death with such steadfast zeal whatever vices had previously lived in them, whether in thought or deed, that apart from our Lord Jesus Christ himself and his most holy Mother, no mortal has ever been able to equal them in the same prerogative of holiness.

From among these chosen disciples of Christ, today we anticipate the glorious solemnities of two apostles: blessed Philip and blessed James. This is the blessed James of whom the prophets spoke, who is called the brother of the Lord, not only according to the flesh but also through imitation of virtues and holiness. For if one were to be called greater among Christ’s disciples, we could say that blessed James attained a greater prerogative of holiness than all the rest, he who so pleased the eyes of divine mercy that alone among the apostles he was raised to pontifical honour in that place where the Mediator of God and humankind himself wrought salvation for the whole human race. At his command and counsel not only did the whole multitude of the people gather, but the eyes of all the apostles also looked to him.

[Col. 0841C]

And his fellow apostle blessed Philip—of how great merit and holiness he was—the island called Scythia shall bear witness for ever. He won it for Christ by the overflowing eloquence of his teaching and by the help of continual intercession.

[Col. 0841D]

Therefore today we anticipate the sacred solemnities of these disciples of Christ, whose glorious merits we shall celebrate on this night. If, then, at the feasts of other saints we desire to please Christ by worthy service and fitting honours, how much more must we keep watch in divine praises with all our strength, all devotion, and all intention of mind on this most sacred solemnity of these apostles? If it were the feast of one apostle, it would be fitting that it be received with the highest praises, as far as human capacity could prevail. But now, because the festive solemnities of two apostles are to be celebrated together, it is most fitting that all human strength and intention should rouse itself and keep watch for their worthy veneration and solemn observance.

[Col. 0842A]

For they are our judges; they are the counsellors of the eternal King; and according to their counsel and will, almighty goodness thus comes generously to the aid of human miseries with compassion. Therefore, as each of us desires and longs to obtain the protection of their intercession, so should each strive to keep watch in their praise with mind and body.

But our praise of rejoicing will then be pleasing and acceptable to the blessed apostles if, while the tongue exalts their praise, the attention and devotion of the mind also keep watch, lest, while we seem outwardly to persist in their praises, we be deprived of reward inwardly by wandering about vainly. But because mortal weakness can do nothing without the help of divine mercy, let us beseech the blessed apostles, our patrons and judges, that their glorious intercession may go before and follow us, so that we may deserve their patronage; and that we may be able so to persevere in their praises in this present age that, when they themselves come at last with Christ as judges, they may cause us to be numbered among the lot of the elect. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this, he who is the exultation, praise, and glory of his saints through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PHILIP AND JAMES

“Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. LX), etc.

Because today we celebrate the festive solemnities of two apostles, two disciples of Christ—Philip and James—we find that the holiness of their lives and the special prerogative of their merits were foretold by the prophets long before them. For although the holy prophets were great before God and surpassed the lives of others by the excellence of their virtues, nevertheless, beholding the blessed apostles with the foreseeing eye of the heart, they held them in such high esteem and considered their lives to surpass others with such excellence that they could not speak of them without great admiration. And sometimes, while mystically prophesying of the incarnation of the Son of God, they exalted the praise and glory of the apostles by celebrating them beforehand in obscure sayings.

Thus one of them, the prophet Isaiah, beholding them in the prophetic Spirit, spoke of them with a kind of wonder, saying: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” Although these prophetic words were spoken of all the apostles, yet because today we celebrate the feasts of the two apostles Philip and James, we may apply these same words especially to them and fittingly understand that the prophet indicated them in particular by these words.

“Who are they,” he says, “who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” By the flying cloud we may understand blessed Philip; by the dove at its windows we may quite fittingly understand blessed James. Let us read their lives, and it will immediately become clearer than light how blessed Philip was a flying cloud and in what manner blessed James was a dove at its windows.

[Col. 0843A]

Scripture relates of blessed Philip that for twenty years he diligently preached the Gospel of Christ to the nations throughout Scythia. There, after displaying many notable miracles—restoring health to the sick and raising the dead—he converted almost all Scythia to Christ’s faith. Having ordained there a bishop, priests, and deacons, and having established many churches, he rescued many thousands of people from the worship of idols and committed them to the service of almighty God. Thus he is not unfittingly compared to a flying cloud: he traversed so many expanses of land on bare feet, and in preaching flew through a region so distant that it lies almost near the furthest bounds of the earth.

[Col. 0843B]

Two things are observed in a cloud: it flies, and it contains water. Blessed Philip, therefore, was both a flying cloud and a cloud containing water. He flew, as we have said, through so many expanses of land; he poured forth water when he sent the streams of saving teaching upon dry ground.

We may also understand in another way that blessed Philip was in himself a flying cloud, when, lifted above earthly things in the height of contemplation, he was intimately present at heavenly mysteries. When that flying cloud lowered itself somewhat from this height, it poured out such streams of saving doctrine that it watered the dry hearts of unbelievers and continually urged them to bring forth the fruits of good works. Thus blessed Philip may be understood by the flying cloud.

Blessed James, however, may quite fittingly be understood by the dove at its windows.

[Col. 0843C]

If we wish to understand this sense simply, we may simply say that blessed James was like a dove at its windows because, when the apostles were dispersed throughout the whole world, he received the place which is Jerusalem to govern; while they travelled through the entire world, he alone presided over that place where the sacrifice of our salvation was offered, holding in some manner a special primacy and authority above all the rest.

But blessed James was also like a dove at its windows in another sense. Since the dove is a simple creature, and since “windows” in sacred discourse sometimes signify human faculties, he is quite fittingly designated by the dove who shone with such purity of holiness and innocence that Scripture reports of him that he was holy from his mother’s womb; he drank neither wine nor strong drink; he was not anointed with oil; he did not use baths; he alone was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies; he did not use a woollen garment, but only linen; and, entering the temple alone, he lay upon his knees, praying for the people’s forgiveness.

[Col. 0843D]

So continually did he bend his knees and never cease from prayer that he formed calluses upon his knees like those of camels. Therefore, because he guarded his windows—that is, his inward and outward faculties—with such strict discipline that, on account of his incredible continence and supreme justice, he was called “the Just” by everyone, it may rightly be said of him that he was like a dove at its windows.

[Col. 0844A]

For we may firmly believe that he was endowed with a special prerogative of holiness, since he received the summit of governance in that place where, as we said above, the Author of salvation himself completed by his passion and death the work of human restoration. The eyes of all looked to him; they had great regard for his holiness; in doubtful matters they fled to his help and counsel, as to one whose holiness no one—even one unbelieving and perverse—could doubt. All alike, both believers and those who entertained some doubt concerning our Lord Jesus Christ himself, nevertheless bore witness to him.

[Col. 0844B]

We too may follow the blessed apostles in these advances of virtue, as the Lord deigns to grant. For any elect person is a flying cloud when he diligently strives to be able frequently to fly in mind from low things to heavenly things through the grace of contemplation. And one who has thus become a flying cloud sometimes sends forth from himself rivers of living water when, moved to compunction either over his pleasures (*deliciae*) or by love of the heavenly homeland, he produces continual fountains of tears. By them the dry soil of the heart is sweetly watered and made fruitful for producing the fruits of worthy action.

Our windows are the inward and outward faculties. If, therefore, we strive to guard our inward and outward faculties with such careful discrimination that we do nothing through them except what may please the eyes of our Creator, it may rightly be said of us that we are like doves at our windows.

[Col. 0844C]

The blessed apostles were so fully endowed with this excellence of virtues and magnificence of holiness, and they so incomparably surpassed all others, that, apart from our Lord Jesus Christ himself and his most blessed Mother, no mortal has ever been able to equal them in the height of divine contemplation or in holiness of mind and body.

Today we celebrate the feasts of two apostles among these chosen disciples of Christ, namely blessed Philip and blessed James, whose glorious merits, as we have mentioned above, were proclaimed by the prophets long before them. Blessed Philip is commemorated for us in today’s reading from the holy Gospel, and blessed James is quite fittingly signified in the reading, “The righteous shall stand” (Wis. V).

[Col. 0844D]

For when, as today’s Gospel relates, our Lord Jesus Christ was admonishing his disciples at his Last Supper not to let their hearts be troubled because he was about to pass from the world to the Father, and when, desiring to relieve their sorrow by manifold consolation, he foretold to them that there were many dwelling-places in his Father’s house, blessed Philip plainly declared by his words the great flame of love and burning desire with which he was kindled in divine love: “Lord,” he said, “show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV, 8).

[Col. 0845A]

It is as if he said: Everything seen in the world produces weariness in us; nothing can be delightful or pleasant if we may not enjoy your presence. Therefore show us the Father; show us your divinity, for then it will be enough for us when, with unveiled face, we begin to contemplate the glory of your divinity.

In these words blessed Philip gave clear proof of how truly he was a flying cloud penetrating the heights of heaven. For when he spoke these words, he had been wholly lifted from earthly things to God and to heaven; he had excluded from the intention of his mind all visible things and everything commonly loved in the world; he had been wholly inflamed by the ardour of heavenly desire. He was not like us, weak and frail persons, who sometimes, through the help of divine mercy, are raised swiftly and, as it were, in the twinkling of an eye into contemplation of mind, yet cannot wholly remove from the mind’s attention what we love according to the flesh.

[Col. 0845B]

But what Philip prayed for, James and his other fellow apostles also prayed for—not with their lips, but in their hearts. For they had such desire for Christ’s bodily presence that they believed themselves already perishing if they could not have him bodily.

In today’s reading, however—“The righteous shall stand in great steadfastness”—we make special mention of blessed James. Let us read his passion, and we shall clearly see with how great constancy of mind he stood in his suffering. When at one time heresy had arisen in Jerusalem, all came together to James, so that, since he was considered by all most righteous on account of the merits of his devout and most continent life, he might satisfy the people by the testimony of his exhortation.

[Col. 0845C]

The scribes and Pharisees set him on the pinnacle of the temple and asked him, since the people were going astray after Christ who was crucified, to declare to them what was the *ostium Jesu*, “door of Jesus.”

> [Note: [Col. 0845D] Thus the manuscript; it appears to read *hostis Jesu*, “enemy of Jesus.”]

When that most invincible witness of truth bore testimony with great steadfastness concerning the Son of Man—that he sat in heaven at the right hand of the highest Power and would come in the clouds of heaven—many believed, and, praising God, said: “Hosanna to the Son of David.” But again the scribes and Pharisees, blinded by the enormity of their malice, turned to kill him, saying: “O, o, even the just man has gone astray!” As though mockingly they said: This man, who was held in esteem as most just, has been corrupted by the wickedness of error and is guilty of death.

[Col. 0845D]

Immediately, after casting him down from the highest steps, they began relentlessly to press him with stones. Cast down from the pinnacle of the temple, he turned to the Lord and, according to his customary practice, falling upon his knees, besought the Lord for the ignorance of those who stoned him in these words: “I beseech thee, Lord God the Father, forgive them their sin; for they do not know what they do.” Thus he undoubtedly stood in great steadfastness: amid the most dreadful bitterness of suffering, amid the hard blows of stones falling like hail, he could not be removed from the love of Christ or from testimony to the truth.

Blessed James was not compelled to sacrifice to idols; he received the sentence of death solely for the testimony which he bore to truth. Had he not borne this testimony alone—for he was considered just by everyone—no cause could have been found for consigning him to death.

[Col. 0846A]

Blessed Philip also stood in great steadfastness against those who afflicted him. For, as we read, he was brought bound before a statue of Mars and shut up in prison; yet he could not be overcome. Rather, with great steadfastness he preached Christ’s name and converted many to Christ’s faith, as we recalled above.

How great was the holiness of blessed James, and with what special dignity and excellence of merits he was endowed, may be clearly seen in this: our Lord Jesus Christ himself bore witness to his holiness in a passage of the Gospel, not only praising his glorious life but also attesting his precious death by the authority of his own words.

[Col. 0846B]

For when, as the authority of a certain Gospel narrative relates, the Lord rebuked the faithlessness and cruelty of the Jews and foretold the dangers of condemnation awaiting them on account of the blood of the righteous which not only they but also their fathers had shed, he added among other things: “That there may come upon you all the blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. XXIII, 35).

Zechariah means “one mindful of the Lord,” while Barachiah is interpreted “blessed of the Lord.” And who is more rightly understood as the Blessed One of the Lord than he of whom it is sung: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 24)? By Zechariah, who is interpreted “mindful of the Lord,” blessed James is not unfittingly signified. For he demonstrated by the witness of good works how deeply he retained the remembrance of almighty God implanted in his heart, so that, on account of the merits of his praiseworthy life, as we have often said, he was most certainly considered righteous in the estimation and sight of all people.

[Col. 0846C]

Therefore he is rightly called the son of Barachiah, which is interpreted “blessed of the Lord,” a name which, as we have said, is understood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed James was truly the blessed son of the blessed Father, both through the purity of his innocent life and through the inestimable holiness of his conduct.

[Col. 0846D]

The blood of righteous Abel, therefore, is the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. It possesses such power and is held to be of such weight that it cannot be repaid by the price of the whole world. The Jews are to be punished with a harsher penalty of condemnation for vengeance upon this blood than for all the blood of the righteous shed upon earth from the beginning of the age. Thus the Jews were to suffer the punishment of vengeance from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, who was killed between the temple and the altar.

[Col. 0847A]

For after they fastened our Lord Jesus Christ himself to the cross, they began to incur vengeance; but after the death of blessed James they were so devastated by the retribution of persecution that they could exercise no power, as formerly they had been accustomed to do, in persecuting the saints.

“He whom you killed,” he says, “between the temple and the altar.” Blessed James was killed between the temple and the altar. For, as the narrative of his passion relates, after he had been thrown down from the pinnacle of the temple and while the Jews cruelly and relentlessly assailed him with stones, one of them ran up, seized a club, and struck his most holy head with it. Thus, completed in glorious martyrdom, he was buried in the same place where he ended his life.

These are the festive joys of the present day: the most sacred solemnities of the apostles Philip and James. For the Lord fulfilled for them and their fellow apostles the grace of the most excellent promise which, as today’s Gospel relates, he promised them at his Last Supper: “Amen, I say to you: he who believes in me shall himself do the works which I do, and shall do greater than these, because I go to the Father; and whatever you ask in my name, this I will do” (John XIV, 12, 13).

[Col. 0847B]

The only-begotten Son of God, Christ Jesus the man, as he was the power and wisdom of the eternal Father, displayed exceedingly great signs of miracles in the days of his flesh: raising the dead, restoring sight to the blind, and working innumerable other wonders of his divinity. Yet his holy apostles, though he himself worked in them and through them, did some greater works; greater signs and prodigies were wrought through them by the cooperation of his divine grace. Truly, to heal the sick by the shadow of the body was greater than to raise the dead. These, therefore, were the greater works which he himself could have done had he willed, but which he did not will to do because he reserved the glory of such sublimity for his apostles.

[Col. 0847C]

But we too, weak and frail though we are, may through Christ’s cooperating grace be imitators of these works. “He who believes in me,” he says, “shall himself do the works which I do, and shall do greater than these.” One may rightly be said to believe in God who, pierced by divine inspiration, has renounced the world and all earthly things. These indeed are Christ’s works, because what a human being appears outwardly to perform, God himself works invisibly in the human being and through the human being.

[Col. 0847D]

But what are those greater works which that highest goodness promised that his elect would perform? He himself created heaven and earth and all that is in them: what mortal could ever perform works greater than these? We cannot, nor ought we to think that we can, equal Christ in the creation of heaven and earth by an equal power of works. Yet there is a magnificence of worthy action in which human frailty in some manner performs works greater than Christ’s.

[Col. 0848A]

When, as we have said, a person renounces the world and submits himself to another’s rule, he performs Christ’s works. But when with all his strength he strives to put to death within himself vices and the desires of the flesh, to cut away from himself the pleasures of his own will and the delights of his former life—this diligent labour, I say, these works of such virtue, will be so precious and magnificent in the sight of divine mercy that, in comparison with his own works, God judges them to be greater.

For when almighty God created heaven and earth, he endured, so to speak, no burden of labour, because he merely spoke and they were made. But when a mortal person, to whom frailty is inborn, strives by the condition of his very nature, through such labours and exercises of virtue, to please the eyes of his Creator, this, I say, is of such great value in the Creator’s estimation that he judges human works even greater than his own works.

“Because I go to the Father,” he says, “and whatever you ask in my name, this I will do.” It is as though he said: I, who am both God and man, raise to the highest throne of paternal glory, to intercede in myself for the whole human race, that human nature which I united to myself for the restoration of human salvation.

[Col. 0848B]

Through this, I say, it will come about that whatever you ask in my name shall be done for you; that is, whatever prayers and supplications you pour out for the salvation of your souls, you shall without doubt receive the fruit of your petition from my generous hand.

The elect also sometimes ask for bodily necessities; and because they ask not so much from greed for earthly convenience as from love and desire for heavenly goods—namely, so that, when the prosperity of this present life smiles upon them, they may more freely persevere in the praises of their Creator with mind and body—they are not deprived of the effect of their petition, because they appear to ask in such a manner and with such happy purpose.

[Col. 0848C]

The holy apostles were endowed so incomparably with the grace of this outstanding power, even while they were still in the present life, that they obtained swiftly whatever they wished. Therefore, if the Son of God himself deigned in this present life to embrace them with such a special privilege of love that he judged them worthy above all mortals to be continually present to his bodily presence by day and night, to behold his actions and demeanour more intimately, and to receive the sweetest eloquence of his words with the ears of heart and body, we may firmly believe that in heaven he associated them with himself above the other elect and righteous in a special sweetness of love.

[Col. 0848D]

Whenever they wish, concerning any matter, they may approach the throne of grace more confidently than the other saints and obtain more quickly, because, as we have said, as they are loved by Christ in a special manner, so they are also heard in a special manner.

Let us therefore, with all intention and devotion of mind, implore the grace of their intercession: moved by mercy for the desolation of our pilgrimage, under which we groan while burdened in this frail body, may they deign somewhat to relieve our poverty from the full and most abundant table of heavenly delights, in which they themselves glory and rejoice with ineffable and inestimable fullness.

[Col. 0849A]

And when at last they come with Christ as judges on the day of final judgment, may they exalt mercy above judgment, so that, if we are not worthy to be fellow-heirs and fellow-partakers of their glory, we may at least, beholding their glory, rejoice eternally with their splendour and dignity in the heights above. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIV. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PHILIP AND JAMES

“Thy perfection and thy teaching [belong] to thy holy man, whom thou didst prove in temptations at the waters of contradiction” (Deut. XXX), etc.

The glorious and joyful feast of the most blessed apostles Philip and James compels us to say something of their glory; but the tongue of flesh is insufficient to speak of it worthily. For as they and their fellow apostles surpassed all people in the eminence of holiness, so they surpass all saints in heaven in the greatness of glory. Therefore it exceeds human understanding and eloquence for anyone worthily to speak or think of those whom no saint, apart from the Mother of the Lord herself, ever could or will be able to equal.

For the very Wisdom of God the Father, dwelling bodily with them in the days of his flesh, commended by many testimonies how far they surpassed all the ancient Fathers. In particular, she commended the greatness of their blessedness when, among other sayings, she said:

[Col. 0849B]

“Blessed are the eyes which see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings wished to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke X, 25).

All the patriarchs and prophets, with the entire desire of heart and soul, longed to see God coming in the flesh; yet they did not at all merit to receive what they so ardently desired. Hence Moses, whom the Lord sent to deliver His people, considering the immensity of so great a task to be beyond him, said: “I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou wilt send” (Exod. IV, 13). This is as if he had said: “I, Lord—I see myself to be weak and unequal to so great a burden; I beseech Thee, at last send Him whom Thou hast purposed should someday come to save the whole human race.” Thus too the prophet Isaiah, [Col. 0849D] unable to endure Christ’s advent being postponed for so long, cried out to Him in impatient longing: “Oh that Thou wouldest rend the heavens and come down!” (Isa. LXIV, 1). Certainly all the saints desired this advent with ardent affection of heart, since they knew that without it they could by no means be redeemed.

Blessed therefore were the eyes of the apostles alone; the apostles alone, I say, were most blessed above all people, since they both saw and heard Him desired by the ancient Fathers, and merited to enjoy the most sweet presence of Him, and to behold His coming in and His going out. Hence elsewhere He Himself, proclaiming their glory, says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14). Surely, if these words had been spoken to the Son of God Himself, no one could wonder; but it is exceedingly glorious and magnificent [Col. 0850A] that such an eminence of dignity is bestowed upon mortal men, that they should be called the light of the world. David, foreseeing in the Holy Spirit how great their dignity and power would be, foretells this when he says: “Thou shalt make them princes over all the earth” (Ps. XLIV, 17).

For although the patriarchs and prophets were great in their own lives, none of them attained this glory: to rule over all the earth. To Abraham, the chief patriarch, God promised, saying: “Blessing, I will bless thee” (Gen. XXII, 16); yet He did not say: “I shall appoint thee prince over all the earth.” To Moses also He spoke with the sweet intimacy of a friend to a friend; nevertheless, He did not give him dominion over the whole earth. But from among all, and above [Col. 0850B] all, the apostles chosen by the Lord were appointed princes over all the earth. They alone were worthy to hear from the Lord: “You are they who have continued with me in my temptations; and I appoint unto you, as my Father hath appointed unto me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXII, 30). And because in this world they were companions in Christ’s sufferings and temptations, they now reign with Him in heaven as sharers in His glory, and at the final judgment they will be judges of the world together with Him.

But that we may demonstrate by a clear proclamation of glory that they are sharers in the glory of their Lord, let us mention one thing by which, in the present life, we see the eminence of their dignity quite plainly commended. For the holy [Col. 0850C] Church grants them this privilege of honor: only on their feast days are brides of Christ joined to Him through the pledge of betrothal. This is not permitted on any solemnity of Saint Mary or of the other saints, except on the two solemnities of the Lord Himself, namely Epiphany and Easter. And because all souls that are worthy to be called brides of Christ signify His universal bride, the holy Church, they are offered to Him in fitting order on the holy feast days of such princes, whom the heavenly Bridegroom made His vicars for winning this bride to Himself.

Among these glorious chiefs of heaven and illustrious fathers of the Church, these two excellent princes stand forth: blessed Philip and James, whose [Col. 0850D] splendid feast shines forth today. They are not inferior to the others in dignity or glory, since the same Lord exalted them by an equal glory of election.

Nor do we think it without purpose that we celebrate on one day the feast of two apostles together; rather, we believe that it was ordered and established by the disposition of the Holy Spirit. For we are accustomed to do this three times a year: today, namely, and on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, and likewise of Simon and Jude. Philip, whose name is said to mean “mouth of a lamp,” signifies the knowledge of God; James, however, whose name is interpreted “supplanter,” signifies the fear of God. For through the knowledge of God a person begins to shine and burn in His love; through His fear, he learns to supplant vices and sins. Peter also, whose name means “recognizing,” and Paul, 319 who is called [Col. 0851A] “quiet,” signify this: that by recognizing God a person orders his life in all things peacefully and tranquilly. Likewise, through Simon, whose name is interpreted “obedient,” and Jude, whose name is interpreted “confession,” the same knowledge and fear of God are signified: for to know the Lord is to obey His will; and through fear a person is compelled to confess and believe in his Creator.

And because these most glorious apostles Philip and James were most perfect in the knowledge of God’s love and in His fear, we rightly celebrate their solemnities together. For they were companions in Christ’s sufferings in this world, and now, as sharers in His glory, reign with Him in heaven. Blessed James, indeed, by continuing with Christ in temptations, seems by a certain special likeness of suffering to have imitated His temptations. For when our Lord Jesus Christ was tempted by the devil and had not been overcome by him in the first temptation, the tempter took Him into the holy city and set Him upon the pinnacle of the temple, urging Him to cast Himself down and thereby gain the favor of human praise.

Just as Christ was tempted by the devil through vainglory and was not overcome, so James was tempted by the devil’s members. For the Jews, seeing that some believed in Jesus, set James upon the pinnacle of the temple, asking him to call Christ’s faith a heresy and to recall the people from error. For he was of such great sanctity that no one, though unbelieving and perverse, could doubt him; rather, all bore witness to his holiness. Therefore, just as the devil [Col. 0851C] tempted Christ so that, for vainglory, He might cast Himself from the pinnacle, so his members urged James, standing on the pinnacle, to seek empty glory by preaching that belief in Christ was error. Accordingly, just as the devil was overcome by Christ, so in his members—that is, the Jews—he was confounded and defeated by James. What they urged him to do for empty glory resulted in the crown of eternal glory for him, when, cast down from the pinnacle for his confession of the truth, he attained through a precious death the palm of praiseworthy victory.

Since, therefore, he was endowed with so wonderful a prerogative of holiness, Scripture seems in many places to foretell the excellence of his merits. Let us mention one place in which, in obscure words, testimony is given to his most perfect righteousness. Moses, at his death, blessing the individual tribes of the children of Israel with separate blessings, exalted the tribe of Levi in a glorious blessing with these words: “Thy perfection and thy doctrine [belong] to thy holy man, whom Thou hast proved in temptations and judged at the waters of contradiction.” These words of this illustrious blessing, which were then spoken to the carnal Levites, prefigured in mystery those spiritual Levites who were someday to be chosen and assumed by Christ for the ministry of the true priesthood, as most perfect imitators of Christ’s perfection and doctrine.

Among these outstanding Levites of the Lord, blessed James was the beloved and chosen devotee and priest of Christ; the testimony of his holiness and perfection [Col. 0852A] is confirmed by the proclamation of this blessing: “Thy perfection and thy doctrine [belong] to thy holy man,” whom Thou didst sanctify not only by the singular holiness of his life, but didst consecrate in his mother’s womb; whom Thou didst prove in temptations as an imitator of Thy perfection and doctrine. Thou didst prove him in Thy temptations, in which he perseveringly remained with Thee; Thou didst prove him in the temptations by which the devil tempted him through his members, namely the Jews; Thou didst prove him by making him approved, and through victory in temptations Thou didst make him praiseworthy.

“And Thou didst judge [him] at the waters of contradiction.” “The many waters,” as blessed John says, “are many peoples” (Apoc. XVII, 15). And fittingly in this place the Jewish people are designated by “the waters of contradiction,” always hostile to the truth, [Col. 0852B] and deservedly called the waters of contradiction, because they always contradicted and resisted the preaching of their Redeemer. But how did the Lord judge James at these waters of contradiction? By a most just judgment He declared him to be an unconquerable preacher of the truth, who did not fear to undergo death for the testimony of truth.

Therefore, that the perfection of blessed James and the other apostles may be further glorified, the testimony of the blessing rightly still says of them: “He who said to his father and to his mother, ‘I do not know you’; and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them’—these are they who have kept Thy testimonies, O Jacob, and Thy commandments, O Israel” (Deut. XXXIII, 9). Do we suppose that these words were spoken of those Levites who certainly had wives, by whom they fathered sons to succeed them in their priesthood? Did they then not know father and mother, and did they not recognize their own children? Since, therefore, spiritual Levites were someday to exist, surpassing the priests of the ancient law far in the prerogative of holiness and perfection, the mystery of the blessing quite openly says concerning them: “He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you’; and to his sons, ‘I do not recognize them.’”

Those, certainly, did not know father and mother and did not recognize children whom they despised for Christ’s love; and—what is greater than this—counting their own body as nothing, they freely offered themselves to death for the Lord. Truly blessed Peter was a genuine despiser of the world and of himself, who said to the Lord with great confidence of hope: [Col. 0852D] “Behold, we have left all things and followed thee” (Matt. XIX, 27).

There are also now innumerable imitators of apostolic perfection who, despising the delights of the world and setting aside the consolations of friends, desire only to cleave to the Lord, for whose love they submit themselves to another’s authority. Spiritual persons, followers of the apostles’ perfection and doctrine, learn from their example not to recognize father, mother, and brothers—that is, to estrange themselves from this world in heart and body. The following words also declare what the prayer of these most perfect Levites, namely the apostles, can obtain. For it follows:

“They shall place incense in Thy wrath, and 322 a whole burnt offering upon Thy altar.” Just as God’s anger is spoken of [Col. 0853A] when He is mildly moved against a person, so His fury is when He is grievously indignant against sinners. When we provoke God so greatly that we deserve even the punishments of eternal condemnation, these most glorious priests offer the sweetest incense of their intercession, whose most acceptable fragrance delights the Lord and reconciles Him to sinners through His freely given mercy. Since they were a sacrifice most acceptable to God, more than other saints they are able by their intercessions to appease the Lord’s anger and fury; and the grace of His inexhaustible mercy is more quickly turned toward reconciliation through the intercession of friends beloved by Him.

Let us therefore earnestly implore these most sweet Fathers and advocates with continual praise of devotion, so that, when we have departed from the exile of this present life, we may be led forth by their help and, under their guidance, may attain the table of the eternal banquet, where with them we may enjoy the inexhaustible vision of our Creator. May He deign to grant this, whose kingdom and dominion remain without end unto ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLV. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE FINDING OF THE HOLY CROSS

“An angel stood beside the altar of the temple” (Apoc. VIII).
