The sacred festival of this day, which the Church of God observes and venerates with pious devotion, is that on which the precious wood of the Lord’s cross is remembered to have been found. For when the Jews had put Christ the Lord, our Redeemer, to death by the punishment of the cross, they hid from human sight the wood upon which the Author of life Himself died for us, adding this to the heap of their unbelief, so that by this deed they might utterly remove the memory of His name from the earth. So long as it lay hidden and the holy Church lacked the protection of this saving sign, it endured such apparitions and assaults of demons that, wherever there was a gathering of God’s servants, they did not dare to rest together because of the terror the demons brought upon them while they slept. Rather, while one part of the community gave itself to rest, the other persisted in vigils and divine praises to restrain their attack.

But after that glorious cross itself was found by the Lord’s revelation, the sign of the same cross began to be honored and adored in the Church. Thus the devil’s power was broken and excluded from humankind, so that evil spirits, terrified at the sight of this sign, flee; nor can they any longer disturb at their will believers marked with the sacred sign.

Nor is help through the holy cross granted only to those who are acceptable to God through right faith and the merit of their life; it also often defends and aids those whom neither faith nor any good action commends. Thus blessed Gregory tells of a certain Jew who, seeing a multitude of evil spirits standing about him, terrified by fear of them, fortified himself with the sign of the holy cross although he was an unbeliever. When those enemies sought to harm him, they immediately turned to flight, crying: “Woe, woe—an empty vessel, yet sealed!”

This most holy cross of Christ, through which the salvation of the human race was accomplished, was extensively prefigured in the holy Scriptures, although in obscure mysteries. Saint John the Evangelist also, in his Apocalypse, in which, by the Lord’s revelation, he discussed the past, present, and future condition of the Church, commends the grace of this same holy cross where he says: “An angel stood beside the altar of the temple, holding a golden censer in his hand; and much incense was given to him, and the smoke of the spices rose from the hand of the angel before God.”

This angel is the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, whom the prophet calls the Angel of great counsel. For *angelus* means “messenger.” And He is truly a messenger, who, sent by God the Father to save the human race, came into this world announcing salvation through the mystery of His Incarnation. Many messengers indeed were sent before His advent to announce to the world a redemption that would someday come, but their announcement passed away without effect; for by it lost humanity could not be liberated. But this Angel of great counsel, the Son of the eternal Father, alone brought the glorious, sweet, and singular message: the Savior came to redeem humanity through Himself.

For the whole world was made for humanity. But when humanity perished by sinning, every creature was in a sense reduced to nothing. Indeed, it would have been better for humanity never to have been created by God than, unredeemed, to lie subject to eternal condemnation. But in order that humanity might be liberated, the Mediator between God and men, made redemption for us by God, stood beside the altar of the temple. The temple spoken of here is the holy [Col. 0854C] universal Church; the altar of this temple is the Lord’s cross. The temple in which the Lord’s name is continually praised by those who worthily serve Him is holy and honorable; but the altar of the temple surpasses it in greater holiness and magnificence, because upon it is offered to God the pure offering of Christ’s body and blood, a pure and immaculate victim. Just as in a temple made with hands the visible altar surpasses everything else in dignity, so in the Church the cross of Christ is loftier and holier than all things because of that great price which hung upon it: namely, through the offering of the body of Christ Jesus, sacrificed upon it for the salvation of the whole human race.

All the sacrifices of ancient times offered to God to obtain His propitiation, and all which pleased Him from the beginning of the world, prefigured that noble sacrifice of future redemption, Christ Jesus. Thus the lamb which righteous Abel offered to God prefigured that the true and immaculate Lamb, Christ, was to be sacrificed for our salvation on the altar of the cross. Thus the patriarch Abraham, by the sacrifice of Isaac, his only heir, foreshadowed the same Redeemer, the only-begotten Son of God, who offered Himself to the eternal Father for us upon the altar of the cross.

Therefore the Savior of the world Himself stood beside the altar of the temple when, having become man, He gave Himself upon the cross, as has been said, as the price for our redemption. For it was fitting that humanity, which incurred the loss of destruction through wood, should also be redeemed through wood and attain the grace of salvation, according to what we say today in praise of the holy cross: “Christ bore our sins in His body upon the wood, that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness; by whose wound we have been healed” (II Peter II, 24).

And it is rightly written that He stood beside the altar; for sitting belongs to one at rest, but standing to one who fights. He truly stood, because when upon the cross He gave up His soul to death, He entered into a very hard battle with that strong ancient adversary, who unjustly possessed as his own noble handiwork, humanity, violently taken away; and who, from the fall of the first human being until that time, held the entire race of mortals captive under his dominion, so that there was none so holy and righteous [Col. 0855B] as to escape his hand. Rather, he carried all alike—the elect with the reprobate—into his kingdom, namely hell. This wicked strong man, confident in his strength, the mightiest warrior defeated and overthrew by the passion of the cross, rescuing His elect from his power. And not only the righteous: even the thief hanging beside Him on the wood, whom the devil believed he had already swallowed up, He snatched in the very moment of death from the devil’s jaws. Thus He deprived him of his own power, so that he can no longer, as before, exercise the force of his unjust domination against humanity.

It should be noted that our Redeemer Himself stood beside the altar of the temple, because the temple, as we mentioned above, is the holy Church still laboring on earth. By this temple we may also understand the Church which already reigns with God in the heights in blessed immortality. Standing beside the altar of both temples—the present Church, that is, and the heavenly—God accomplished salvation, as Paul testifies when he says: “Making peace through the blood of His cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth” (Col. I, 20). The Church of heaven consists of the souls of the saints, whom the same gracious Savior rescued from the infernal prisons by the triumph of His Passion; many of them also rose with Him; and of the spirits of all the elect who, laying down the burden of flesh, daily pass from death to life. The present Church is called a temple because of the elect, whose mother she is, who are God’s temple, whom He Himself inhabits and possesses by His grace, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (I Cor. III, 17).

It is certainly plain with how great a crime one is held guilty before this world who violates a material temple by some shameful act. But how great a criminal, do we suppose, is one who does not fear to defile the temple of God—the temple, I mean, of his own body and soul—by filthy deeds? Let us hear the Apostle thunder terribly about such a person: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III, 17). This sentence is exceedingly terrible. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God. If that person were condemned to punishment for his guilt by an angel or by someone else, surely one might hope for the mercy of absolution. But if God Himself destroys one by condemning him, will there be any hope of recovering salvation? Therefore let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, that we may deserve to become the immaculate temple of the immaculate King and Lord. For it is fitting that nothing unclean should either touch or be looked upon by the very author of all purity; and no place is believed to be foul or abominable to Him except the sinners’ heart, polluted with filth. It follows:

“Having a golden censer in his hand.” By the censer, which is vigorously struck so that the smoke of incense placed upon it may emerge through its many open holes, we may understand the most holy body of Christ, which for our salvation He assumed from the mass of the human race. Throughout all the days in which He chose to live on earth, it was beaten by many and diverse pressures of tribulations and labors, and, so to speak, pierced through with unbearable pains. For throughout His life He never granted Himself anything of sweetness, comfort, or rest; rather, He always served God the Father in labors for us. He did not even choose in this world to possess a place where He could recline His head for a single night; but passing from place to place as an exile and pilgrim, He always lived in great poverty.

When He began to persevere in preaching—O how many reproaches, how many snares, contradictions, and mockeries He endured from the ungodly Jews! And in His Passion, no one can be ignorant what He endured: seized and bound by the Jews, then brought before Pilate the judge, He was cruelly scourged by him as though He were a most wicked thief and robber. Then He was handed over to Pilate’s soldiers to be mocked and shamefully treated by them. He suffered spitting, blows, and many other insulting injuries; and at last, nailed to the cross, given gall and vinegar to drink, and pierced by a soldier’s lance, He hung between two thieves in sight of all the people.

Yet He suffered all these things innocently, “having a golden censer”: that is, a body most pure, entirely immune and free from every stain of sin. We are all conceived and born in iniquities and live in sins. But He alone, conceived in His mother’s womb by the divine operation of the Holy Spirit and born from the virginal and undefiled flesh of blessed Mary, was wholly immaculate, because He never contracted any sin in thought, word, or deed. Humanity was so created by God that, had it not sinned, it would never have had to die; but when it fell through sinning, by God’s just judgment it was made subject also to sin’s penalty, namely death.

But the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, because alone among humankind He was free from sin, owed nothing to death. Yet He underwent death—not demanded by justice—solely from love and of His own free will, for us. This merciful and compassionate will is demonstrated by the words, “having a golden censer in his hand,” because He endured death for our redemption not from debt or necessity, but from generous and gracious will, according to what He says of Himself: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again” (John X, 18). If then He so loved us, unworthy though we were and owing Him nothing but evil for evil, that He did not disdain freely to die for us, let us have great hope and confidence in Him, trusting that, redeemed by His precious blood, He will never abandon us. Paul affirms: “God commends His love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more now, justified in His blood, shall we be saved from wrath through Him” (Rom. V, 8).

The following text declares, therefore, how Christ’s blessed Passion bore fruit and what salvation and grace it conferred upon the Church:

[Col. 0857B] “And much incense was given to him.” This abundant incense is the manifold service of believers worthily serving Christ, which they render to Him continually by day and night, mindful of the multitude of His mercy and of His love, in that He gave His beloved soul over to death. Before Christ’s Passion there were indeed many who, recognizing God their Creator, glorified Him; yet they did not know, nor were they able, to praise Him with so great sweetness of love as believers now serve Him, because they had not yet received from Him the grace of redemption. But once redemption was accomplished through His Passion, the earth was filled with the sweetness of His praise, so that no place in the whole world is now concealed where there are not some who, knowing the Lord’s name, faithfully serve Him.

For this reason the Lord’s servants spend the long watches of the night in His praises and labor so greatly every day in His service: that in some small measure they may answer for the great labors He endured for us, and that, as He gave His body to the torments of the Passion, so they may make return to Him by subjecting their bodies to slavery under another’s authority. And truly blessed are those whose hearts do not disagree with the voice of praise, but who strive, as far as ability permits, to devote themselves to the divine work not only outwardly in body but also with the intention of the mind. For these certainly receive the grace indicated in what follows:

“And the smoke of the spices rose from the hand of the angel before God.” The smoke of the spices is the tearful prayer of the faithful when, pierced by divine inspiration, they weep for their sins. Nor are they moved to compunction only for sins; sometimes, from longing for the heavenly homeland, they are sweetly stirred to tears. The smoke of spices also arises when a person, sweetly pondering in memory the work of human redemption, breaks into tears from love of the Redeemer; and when he calls to mind not only the common grace of redemption by which Christ saved the whole human race, but also the particular sweetness of mercy which God has worked with him. In fervent compunction of heart, he laments with bitter tears that he has not only proved ungrateful for God’s benefits but has even repaid Him evil for good.

This smoke of spices—that is, the most sweet affection of holy prayers—rises before God, because the prayer which is directed to God in the sweetness of tears indeed penetrates heaven and reaches the very presence of the highest Majesty.

But lest a person boast that he possesses such grace through his own merits, the smoke of spices is aptly said to have risen from the hand of the angel. For the Angel of great counsel, our Redeemer, works all these things in the hearts of His elect by His prevenient and subsequent grace. He is the One who kindles this smoke of spices on earth; He is also the One who receives it as it rises in heaven. Thus it is truly fitting that a person should not deceitfully claim for himself anything of the good he sees in himself, but humbly ascribe all to God alone, from whom all good things proceed.

We have offered these preliminary remarks, with God’s help and as we were able, concerning the solemnity of this day, which has dawned illustrious in the Finding of the Holy Cross. We ought therefore to honor and love the Lord’s glorious cross with a special devotion, because through it we have been released from the ancient curse of the first transgression. But those rightly venerate and commemorate the life-giving cross who, through continence of life, are imitators of Him, having crucified their flesh with its vices and desires, bearing in their bodies the marks of the crucified Lord and continually carrying His very cross in their members.

Let us also strive, according to our measure, to be imitators of Him, purifying ourselves in the fear of the Lord and fastening our bodies to that ever-memorable cross. The piercings of the nails are spiritual disciplines by which we ought vigorously to fasten our bodily senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—and indeed all our members, lest they yield to sins.

Therefore all who have thus imitated the Lord’s cross, when they come to the end of life and are now set in the struggle, have the same holy cross placed before their eyes. They behold it joyfully and, without doubt, are fortified by the help of its protection against the snares of the evil spirits standing there; they are rescued from their power, and so, free and unencumbered, stripped of the misery of this mortality, pass over to the joys of eternal blessedness. May He lead us to these joys—Jesus Christ our Lord, who through His cross and Passion restored us from death to life—to whom be honor and glory unto infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## 329 HOMILY XLVI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT BONIFACE, BISHOP AND MARTYR

“Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. Therefore be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X).

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, against the rage of visible wolves—against, I say, the persecution of visible enemies to whom they were sent and among whom they lived—armed and strengthened His disciples then, present among them, just as we have now heard when the Gospel was read. By those same words He warned and taught us with what zeal and care we ought to keep watch against the rage of invisible wolves, namely evil spirits. For though the persecutors who then harassed and attacked Christ’s elect martyrs have been removed from their midst, wolves fiercer and more wicked than these still live and cannot die: the evil spirits who incited them to persecute and kill the saints.

That we may be able to beware of and escape their cruel bites, let us hear the Lord as though He were present among us, daily crying out: “Behold,” He says, “I send you,” plainly showing that although according to the substance of His humanity He sits at the Father’s right hand in heaven, according to the excellence of His divinity He remains with us on earth, as He Himself testifies: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). He is our sender; we are His messengers. For we are sent by Him; and wherever we are sent, we are always observed by Him.

A person sent by another person may conduct himself faithfully or unfaithfully in the business of the one who sent him, because he does not fear being seen by him. But our Lord and sender is not such: wherever He is present with His servants whom He sends, He carefully observes how faithfully and diligently each shows himself in His mission.

There are three missions upon which the elect are sent by the Lord. The first mission is when a person, preceded by God’s grace, is sent from secular life to the spiritual life. The second is when, through the exercise of holy conduct, he is admitted to the sweetness of prayer. The third is when he stands for the work of God. In each of these missions we ought to show ourselves cautious and provident, considering the most savage strength of those who always and everywhere persecute and attack us, and fearing our own weakness. Therefore the Lord says: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves.” A sheep is a powerless and weak animal. It is as if He said: “I send you as sheep—as unstable, powerless, feeble beings—into the midst of wolves, into the midst of evil spirits, [Col. 0859D] so that, always considering your weakness, you may humble yourselves beneath my hand; for you are able to resist their strength not by your own power, but by mine.”

The Lord also directs us to consider this powerlessness of our weakness when He speaks to blessed Job: “Remember the battle, and add no more to speak” (Job XL, 27). Who is this one with whom we wage war? The twisting serpent, the ancient enemy. The Lord figuratively expresses how great are his pride and strength—namely, that he knows how not to spare even the elect and perfect themselves—when shortly afterward He adds: “He shall strew gold beneath himself as mud.” It follows:

“Therefore be prudent as serpents.” The highest prudence is to seek and love, before all things, that which is above all things: the kingdom of heaven. Thus the Lord says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness” (Matt. VI, 35). And He fittingly adds, “as serpents.” The serpent’s prudence consists in guarding its head with exceeding cunning and care; it does not greatly mind if another part of its body is injured, provided only that its head remains unharmed. Therefore, imitating the serpent’s prudence, we ought to guard our head, which is Christ, with utmost care, lest by our sins He be so wounded that He utterly dies to us. Or we may guard our head in this way: by keeping our heart and the faculties of our heart unharmed—that is, undefiled by wicked thoughts and harmful delights.

And innocent as doves. The dove has no gall; it tears no one with its beak and stains no one with its claws with blood. So we too, after the likeness of the dove, ought to be innocent, without the gall of bitterness: holding no duplicity in our heart; injuring no neighbor with our beak—that is, with our words; grieving no one with our claws—that is, by our deeds. This teaching is the teaching of God, belonging only to the perfect, according to which we who are spiritual must be judged, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “On the day when the Lord shall judge the secrets of hearts” (Rom. II, 16). For the spiritual are judged and rewarded in one way, the worldly in another; “for one is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon; for star differs from star in brightness” (I Cor. XV, 41). It follows:

“Beware of men.” In the preceding verse we are admonished concerning the inward guarding of the heart; but by these words the Lord admonishes us how we must guard ourselves also in the outward person. For those ravening wolves, the evil spirits, labour day and night to cast us down both inwardly before God in our thoughts and outwardly before men by wicked actions. Hence it follows:

“For they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you.” A council is called an assembly of judges; but synagogue is interpreted “congregation.” By the name congregation, which derives from “flocking together,” flockish and beastlike thoughts are fittingly signified. But why does he say, “They will hand you over”? The handing over by evil spirits is their suggestion. And he fittingly says: “They will hand you over into their councils.” For this is why they hold their assembly: that they may determine among themselves how to deceive a human being, by what snares of suggestions they may overthrow him. They also assemble to determine among themselves whether a person will receive or reject their suggestions. They scourge us in their synagogues—that is, in their congregations—when they thrust flockish and beastlike thoughts upon us. For just as the outward body is wounded by a visible scourge, so wicked thoughts are a kind of scourge of the soul, by which, pitiably torn, it is defiled. It follows:

332 “And you will be led before kings and governors for my name’s sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.” By kings we may understand the outward senses, through which the body is governed; by governors, the inward senses, which preside over the outward senses. [Col. 0861A] And it should be noted that he says, “You will be led.” Their scourging pertains to consent to sin, which occurs in thoughts; their leading pertains to the act of sin, which is committed through the body. We are led before kings and governors when, through the suggestions of evil spirits, we are bent by outward and inward senses toward the act of sin. But why do they do all these things to us? “For my name’s sake,” says the Lord. In the name Jesus, which is interpreted “Saviour,” our salvation is signified. Therefore they pursue us for his name’s sake—that is, on account of our salvation—in order to draw us with themselves into the destruction of eternal damnation. But that we may be able both to discern and avoid their suggestions, the Lord admonishes us in what follows:

[Col. 0861B] “But when they hand you over,” he says, “do not consider how or what you are to say.” As if he said: When they hand you over—that is, when they first begin to assail you by their suggestion—do not consider; that is, do not admit into your thought what they suggest. “For in that hour there will be given to you what you are to say.” If you keep your heart pure and whole, and do not receive what they suggest to you, it will be given you what you are to answer them; it will be given you, I say, that you may be able to resist them. “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” The speaking of the Holy Spirit is the working of the Holy Spirit. And it is as though he said: If you are not speaking according to them, the Spirit of your Father, who speaks in you—that is, who works in you—will give [Col. 0861C] and teach you what you are to say against them. That this is indeed the working of the Holy Spirit he expresses figuratively when he says:

“But brother will hand brother over to death, and father son; and children will rise up against parents and put them to death.” By this brother who hands his brother over to death may, I think, be fittingly understood the human spirit, which hands over its brother, the body, to death when, through the Holy Spirit working in it, it puts to death in its flesh whatever sin and injustice it sees living within itself. “And father [will hand over] son.” In the father, as I judge, consent to good or evil may fittingly be understood; in the son, the act of good or evil. [Note: [Col. 0861D] Thus the manuscript.] When brother hands brother over to death—that is, when spirit puts flesh to death—[Col. 0861D] the Father also will hand over the son. For that good consent which a person then begins, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, to have toward good, begins within him to punish and suppress the son—that is, the sinful act—which it once produced from itself.

The remainder is lacking in the manuscript.

## HOMILY XLVII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE VIGIL OF THE LORD’S ASCENSION

“Father, I have made known your name to the people whom you gave me” (John XVII).

These words are the words of the only-begotten Son of God, who in the majesty of his divinity is consubstantial and coeternal with the same Father, and who descended from the height of his divinity to [Col. 0862A] the lowest depths of our mortality, so as to reveal and make known in the world the name of God the Father to his elect. But what sort of name is his? It is, to be sure, the name Father. The name father is applied from sons; for one who has no sons cannot be called father. But did Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others who were before Christ neither know nor believe in God? They certainly knew and believed. They knew, I say, the name of God the Creator, who created all things; but they did not know the name of God the Father, who through his Son coeternal with himself, whom he was to send into the world, was to recreate and restore all things.

Thus the Son of God, eternally begotten of the eternal Father, and temporally born into the world as a man from a Virgin mother, made known the name of the Father to human beings. And [Col. 0862B] this very revelation was so necessary that, had it not been made, no human being could have been saved. For this, says the Lord, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only God, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” This indeed is that most sweet and saving name which we ask to be hallowed in us in the Lord’s Prayer, when we say: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name” (Matt. VI, 9). Almighty God, whose majesty is incomprehensible and whose power is without limit, is the Father of his coeternal Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. Since we are and ought to be 334 his members, by his own institution and teaching we dare to call his Father by nature our Father with him by his grace. If we strive to hallow this name in ourselves as we ought, we can be not ungrateful or degenerate, but chosen, beloved, and noble sons. We truly hallow worthily and rightly the name of our Father who is in heaven if we fear and love him perfectly: if, because he is our Lord and God, we avoid evils through fear of him, and because he is our Father, strive to do good through love of him. Therefore, since we subsist from him and in him, and can do nothing without him—that is, without his gift and grace—we ask him to hallow his name in us: that is, to grant us the will and ability to avoid evils in his fear and to do good in his love, when we say, “Hallowed be thy name.”

After this first petition follows the second, [Col. 0862D] in which we ask for the coming of the kingdom of God (ibid., 10), where he himself may reign in us, and we may be able to reign with him and in him. This petition will be fulfilled not in this world but, after the misery of the present life has run its course, in the glorification of souls. For as long as, weighed down by a mortal body, we live in the kingdom of sin and cannot avoid sin’s stain, we cannot be the kingdom of God. For although God sometimes reigns in us by the grace of his visitation, the contagions of sins variously succeeding one another dissipate his kingdom in us, so that he does not reign steadily in us. But once we have laid aside the burden of the flesh and have arrived where we can never be stained by any blot of sin, there we shall truly be the kingdom of God. For there he will reign in us in such a way that he will never be taken from us.

But because in this glorification of souls the joy of the elect is not yet complete, a third petition is joined to this one, which will be perfectly fulfilled after the resurrection of the dead. For we say: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (ibid.). By heaven we understand the spirit; by earth we understand our body. Therefore we ask that God’s will may be done in our body as in our spirit: that is, that our will may be so united and conformed to God’s will that neither in body nor spirit may we think, desire, or seek anything by which we dissent in any respect from God’s will. But when will this be? [Col. 0863B] Not in the present life, nor even in the repose of souls which the elect possess after this life, but in that glorification of souls and bodies together with which God’s saints and elect will be rewarded after the universal resurrection. For those holy spirits of the elect who already rejoice with Christ in heaven are still in that desire to receive the bodies in which they laboured. [Note: [Col. 0863D] Something appears to be missing.] But after the resurrection has been accomplished, when glorified together in body and soul they are transferred into eternal rest, there God’s will is, as it were, done in heaven and on earth: because in spirit, soul, and body they will be so united to and established in God that they will not be separated from God—not merely by their will, but not even by the least thought.

Having explained, according to our measure, the first three petitions, [Col. 0863C] let us see how the remaining three which follow correspond to them. For we say: “Give us this day our daily bread” (ibid.). In these words we ask for that heavenly sweetness of divine visitation with which our Father who is in heaven customarily nourishes his beloved children amid this hunger of mortality. It is rightly compared to bread, because just as the outward person is sustained by bodily bread lest he fail, so indeed the soul is refreshed and strengthened by this spiritual bread so that it may advance. And this fourth petition rightly corresponds to the first, in which we say, “Hallowed be thy name,” because one who receives this bread daily from the most merciful visitation of God will truly be able to hallow the name of his Father who is in heaven. From the sweetness of that heavenly 336 [Col. 0863D] nourishment, by which he is daily refreshed inwardly, he is renewed, formed, and strengthened, so that he may fear and love God, avoid evil because of his fear, and strive to persist in good works because of the sweetness of his love. This is truly to hallow the name of God.

And the fifth petition corresponds to the second petition, in which we say, “Thy kingdom come”; in it we entreat God, saying: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (ibid., 12). For as long as we subsist in this life, we always offend and always seek remission of our offenses and debts; yet we can never attain it perfectly in this life, as John testifies when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8). If so great a man as this, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper, could not, by his own testimony, be without sin, what shall we say, who are daily subject to sins? Therefore this petition, in which we ask that our debts be forgiven us, cannot at all be fulfilled in the present life. But when the kingdom of God comes—that is, when, having laid aside the body of this death, we cease to be the kingdom of sin and begin to be the kingdom of God—then all our debts will be perfectly forgiven us. For just as we will never be able to sin there, so we will never cease to be the kingdom of God.

There the sixth petition will truly be fulfilled, in which it is said: “And [Col. 0864B] lead us not into temptation” (Matt. VI, 13). And this sixth petition fittingly corresponds to the third petition, in which we say, “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” For as long as we remain in this life, no human being, however just or holy, can live without temptations. But what shall we say of those who are in the place of temptation, when those who already rejoice with God in the repose of heaven are not yet completely freed from evil? For what they do not suffer in themselves through the affliction of pain, they suffer in their members—namely, in those elect who are still everywhere sojourning on earth—through most gracious compassion. For just as, when one member of the body suffers, all the members suffer together, so that part of the body [Col. 0864C] of Christ which now in itself is with God in 337 eternal blessedness suffers with that part which is still tossed upon the waves of this exile and misery. But after the judgment has been accomplished, when the devil, the head of all the wicked, has been cast down into hell with his members, and Christ has entered his kingdom with his body—that is, with the multitude of his elect—then he will truly deliver them from evil (ibid.), where he will give himself to them as their reward, and they will be one in him, because they will rejoice with him without end. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, that he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them” (Luke XII, 37).

## HOMILY XLVIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE LORD’S ASCENSION

[Col. 0864D]

“While the eleven disciples were reclining, Jesus appeared to them and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen from the dead” (Mark XVI).

Because we celebrate the festal joys of the Lord’s Ascension, it is fitting that we speak by more subtle consideration of the mystery of so great a solemnity. Our Lord and Saviour, the Redeemer of the human race, just as he did everything in the days of his flesh not for himself but certainly for us, so likewise after the glorious triumph over conquered death he ascended into heaven on this day not for himself but for us. For as by dying he taught us not to fear death, and by rising taught us to hope for life, so by ascending he taught us to rejoice in the inheritance [of] our heavenly homeland, so that the members of the faithful might not doubt that they would follow whither the head had gone before. Hence not undeservedly is the mind of the elect, despising lower things, lifted up to contemplate things above, where that singular man, “beautiful in form beyond the children of men,” dwells (Ps. XLIV, 3). In comparison with him all earthly things grow cheap, and whatever they possess in his absence does not suffice, until they find him alone, whom alone they uniquely seek and love. Finally, just as it is the custom of those journeying in this world often to recall, with groaning and sorrow, the land and homeland of their birth, so the just are daily kindled with new desires to see and receive their homeland, the land of the living, [Col. 0865B] longing that, when this world’s miseries are ended, they may deserve to be joined forever to their head, that is, Christ. Therefore, by the words of the present holy Gospel we are instructed and strengthened concerning how, made one with him, we may deserve one day to ascend to the heights of heaven and become citizens of the heavenly homeland. Therefore the Evangelist says:

“While the eleven disciples were reclining.” Whoever, through God’s prevenient grace, despise the deceits of this world, take upon themselves the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden, and submit themselves to spiritual teaching, to be trained and instructed in the knowledge of God, are deservedly found worthy to be numbered under the name of Christ’s disciples. When they consider in their minds how far they have departed from God through unlawful deeds, kindled with zeal for justice [Col. 0865C] they devoutly submit themselves to the judgment of another ruling over them; and, as far as lies in them, rising against themselves, they diligently pursue their sins by repentance. Since they are found to be transgressors of God’s ten commandments, they are described as belonging not to the perfect number ten, but to the number eleven of Christ’s disciples. For by ten, which is a perfect number, perfect observance of the Decalogue can be signified; but by eleven, which does not have perfection, transgression of God’s commandments may be represented.

Thus, as we have said, those still imperfect are as it were of the number eleven, whose conscience is vehemently reproved by transgression of God’s commandments. 339 [Col. 0865D] If they wish to render to God the debt of that transgression by worthy satisfaction, they must beyond doubt conform themselves with all zeal and all strength to the reclining disciples. For to recline properly means to lie down; thus in ancient times people at banquets were accustomed not merely to sit but also to recline. And thus by reclining the true virtue of humility may be expressed, which is wont to bestow inward quiet upon the mind. Therefore, that the fault of their transgression may be washed away, let the disciples recline—that is, let them truly humble themselves. For grace from the merciful Creator will at once come to those whose hearts are wholly contrite and humbled, as follows:

“He appeared to them,” he says. God’s appearing is his inwardly visiting with sweetness those who desire to be comforted by absolutely nothing except himself alone. The farther they are driven from human prosperities, the more sweetly they deserve to rejoice in divine consolations. And it should be noted that he is said to have appeared because—alas!—they know the sweetness of inward delight by tasting it beforehand, not as something enduring, but as a sudden flash, swiftly passing away. Thus blessed Paul says: “We now see through a mirror and in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII, 12). Therefore, because they see the immensity of so great a sweetness furtively, as it were, and in passing, it can rightly be called a kind of appearance. And the more this appearance—the grace, that is, of inward sweetness—is desired after it has once been tasted, the more it increases when poured into the hungering soul. Conversely, the slothful and negligent, who neither strive to receive with love the Lord coming to them nor to recall him, as he turns away from them, through inward desires, become altogether strangers to this blessing. For they are not led to contemplate inward things unless they are diligently withdrawn from the tumult of earthly matters. Of such people the Psalmist says: “He did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him” (Ps. CVIII, 17). To refuse God’s blessing is, after tasting heavenly gifts, to be estranged from God by wicked deeds.

But the more the elect show themselves approved in good actions, the more closely they approach the taste of this appearance, as blessed James says: “Draw near to God with good desires, and he will draw near to you” (James IV, 8), through the manifold grace of his blessing. Whoever therefore has received even the smallest ray of this appearance [Col. 0866C] surely finds his whole self in true knowledge; and, carefully considering and examining his sins, is constrained by fear. From this he is carried away into the knowledge of God and nourished by a certain inward love, reflecting on what good things he has received from God and how great evils he repays for his benefits by living perversely; how patiently God has borne one whom he ought by his just judgment to have punished; how he has rejected another better and stronger than himself, while mercifully drawing him inwardly to himself. When they gather up these things within the bosom of reflection, they vehemently reprove themselves, as follows:

“He reproached their unbelief and hardness [Col. 0866D] of heart.” For God, compassionate and merciful, then reproaches a person when he makes that person reproach and be angry with himself for his former unbelief. A person’s former life in sins may fittingly be called a kind of unbelief. For while by wicked works one contradicts faith, though one be called believing and faithful in word alone, one does not possess the reward of faith which could have been received as the recompense of good action. Hence James says of such people: “They profess to know God, but by their works deny him” (Titus I, 16). Therefore, when a soul is stirred by compunction and remembers the shameful deeds it has done, piercing itself with the sword-point of repentance, it persecutes itself by reproach and rebuke; and sweetness and bitterness meet together in this affliction of mind. It grieves that it has committed deeds deserving mourning, yet the very bitterness of repentance, while afflicting the mind, inwardly refreshes it sweetly. Angry with itself, it observes how it has come to such hardness of heart after the grace of conversion; it observes how the outward person, which ought to have been exercised daily through contests of labours, has enslaved itself to negligence or torpor. And when it considers with what holiness every soul in which God dwells by inspiration shines, and what solemn feast it keeps for the Lord in its heart, it begins, by reckoning the loss caused by its negligence and sluggishness, strongly to rebuke itself. But whence this hardness of heart arises is fittingly shown by the following words, when it is added:

“Because they did not believe those who had seen him risen from the dead.” [Col. 0867B] Since there is no mortal person still living in the flesh who confesses to have seen with witnessing eyes the signs of Christ’s resurrection, or who has seen any of those to whom he is read to have appeared truly after his resurrection, it is necessary that what we cannot establish according to the literal appearance be mystically turned, through the understanding of mortality, toward the advancement of our profit. Almighty God is especially seen by his elect in four ways; by these ways he invisibly draws to himself those whom he has predestined through the spirit of adoption to come one day into the inheritance of his sons. Some see the Lord as though born and clothed in tender limbs, wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger; some hanging on the cross; others rising from the dead; still others ascending into heaven. These are the four mysteries which, when he once dwelt on earth, he displayed to the whole human race. Yet he does not cease spiritually to work these same mysteries in his elect until the end of the age.

For in some God-man appears, as it were, to be conceived and born, when by his gift they conceive a desire for good will. But as long as good will has not yet arrived at the perfection of a completed work, God is as it were a child and tender son in the human heart. At times they wish to escape from the desires of this world, but contrariwise judge it utterly impossible to leave all earthly things. At times they excuse themselves on the ground that their bodily strength is insufficient to bear labours. But when at last, leaving all things, they begin to deny themselves and carry the Lord’s cross, [Col. 0867D] they see the Lord as though hanging on the cross. Filled with devotion to him, they prepare themselves to endure every evil for his name’s sake; for crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires, they long to die with Christ and, as far as lies in them, to be conformed in all things to the likeness of his death.

Thus, dead to sins and living to righteousness, they see as it were the glory of the Lord’s resurrection. For that person has truly risen in Christ who, putting off the old man with his deeds, walks not in the flesh but in the spirit, not in oldness but in newness of life. We have heard how eminent and praiseworthy all these are before the Lord. But still more eminent and exalted are those in whom Christ deigns to ascend, so that they themselves, ascending upward through the grace of contemplation, pass with God to God, continually directing their hearts where he ascended bodily. Whoever, therefore, refuse to believe such persons who have deserved to see God in this way, as we have said, will undoubtedly remain cold and hard of heart. But how do they fail to believe, except by scorning to imitate the praiseworthy conversion of saints already reigning with Christ, or of those still living praiseworthily in the flesh? Indeed, this word “to believe” is fittingly used for imitation. For example: whatever a truthful and exceedingly trustworthy person declares seems altogether fitting to follow and imitate; and therefore people are rightly said not to believe such a person because they by no means imitate, by following them, the good deeds they see in others.

But since very few of the elect experience the manner of this appearance and such reproach, imitating those who rise or ascend, nevertheless, because there is no one “who hides himself from his heat,” God does not forget to have mercy on his poor, but mercifully makes known what must be done. It follows:

“And he said to them: Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature.” To go into the whole world is to know oneself in every respect: how one has offended God not in one bodily member only, but with all one’s members—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. And because, as blessed Gregory says, a human being is signified by the name “every creature,” that person rightly preaches the Gospel to every creature [Col. 0868C] who offers to those same members by which he sinned against God’s commandments a pattern of good living according to the Lord’s commandment, so that those which formerly departed from God through unlawful deeds may now proceed with right governance. Concerning those who carefully examine and investigate their actions, it is rightly added:

“He who believes and is baptized will be saved.” Above we said that unbelief is a person’s former life in sins; but this believing may be understood in a good sense. For those truly believe who, bound by the observance of God’s commandments, persist in works of virtue pleasing to God. Touched by a higher knowledge of truth, they approach baptism by tears so as to see the inward light; there, by daily weeping, they are renewed and healed in the inward person. Not only graver crimes, but also hay and straw—that is, works of lighter transgression—are consumed by the fire of this compunction. But because the grace of this baptism is not administered to all, though the discipline of good living is nevertheless enjoined on them, it fittingly follows at once:

343 “But he who does not believe will be condemned.” For he did not say, “He who is not baptized will be condemned,” but omitted that which he foresaw belonged to few, and set down that which applies to every human being: namely, believing, which is to live blessedly. There are indeed some who do not deserve to be baptized in the saving font of compunction and are not thereby condemned. But those who do not believe—that is, those who by living badly contradict faith through wicked works—will undergo the sentence of just condemnation. For those who have scorned to live blessedly and have persisted in the depths of vices until the end of life, however much they may be comforted by the grace of consolation from any persons whatever, should know that they can by no means attain the entrance to the heavenly kingdom unless they are truly converted through the lamentations of repentance. But amid these matters, perhaps each of us looks upon himself, desiring to know whether he will arrive, to be saved, in the inheritance of God’s elect, or whether he ought to be condemned by the vengeance of God, the just Judge, among the reprobate. To those considering these things with fear, what will become of them is immediately taught in the following words:

“But these signs will follow those who believe in me: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak [Col. 0869B] with new tongues; they will take up serpents.” If the three following signs have been spiritually fulfilled in them, they ought in no way to doubt that they will one day pass into the glory of God’s sons. Let us therefore see what these signs are: not bodily but spiritual signs, performed in the mind, by which not bodies but souls are healed. Those who live rightly renounce the pomp and works of the ancient enemy, so that those who were vessels of wrath fitted for destruction may now be vessels of mercy through the merit of praiseworthy conduct. They speak with new tongues when they leave behind the worldly words of the old life and now, insofar as they can, strive to utter heavenly mysteries and recount the praises and power of their Creator. They take up serpents when, having abandoned evil works, useless words, and unlawful desires, they remove them from their hearts; even if they cannot preserve inward purity of thoughts, they nevertheless strive to chastise within themselves the very desires of sin.

“And if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them.” We should observe why they are said to drink deadly poison rather than eat it, for an antidote to death is sometimes taken not only in drink but also in food. But if we observe that food affords those who eat it a certain labour, so to speak, through the repeated chewing of the teeth, whereas drink has a smooth and easy passage through the human throat, we may rightly understand by the draught of poison the slippery suggestions of the serpent. These penetrate inward hearts so easily that they are not felt, and under the appearance of good sometimes draw people toward vices as though toward virtues. [Col. 0869D] Therefore that person drinks what is deadly who is incautiously deceived by the pestilent suggestions of the devil. But though he insinuate himself into the minds of the elect through tempting suggestions, it will not harm them, because, according to the words that follow: “They will lay hands upon the sick, and they will be well.” And what can be expressed by hands except the power of good action? Therefore, when the elect return inwardly to their hearts, whatever transgressions they find, they cover with the hand of holy action, and they will be well.

Whoever is one of the reclining disciples, and under the presence of the Lord’s appearance diligently reproves himself by examining his deeds; whoever washes away his unbelief by good conversion; whoever gathers before his eyes in repentance the negligences of his life by which he deserved hardness [Col. 0870A] of heart; whoever does not cease to gather in his heart the examples of the Fathers who have gone before and of others living praiseworthily in the flesh; whoever is renewed from his oldness by the baptism of tears, is not bound by unbelief, since, seeing the works of the saints, he is stirred to imitate them; and whoever has been cautious and restrained in the three following signs—that is, in his deeds, words, and desires—deserves to be exalted by God, as follows:

“And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, ascended into heaven and sits at the right hands of God.” After our Creator has completed by inspiration and aid all the things we have spoken of, he ascends into heaven, placing his ascent in those elect themselves, so that, ascending upward in mind through him, they may enjoy inward sweetness. Yet they also ascend into heaven in another way, when he deigns to open to their understanding and intellect the mysteries of Scripture.

345 But the source of all this and the one to whom they must ascribe it is added when it is said, “and sits at the right hands of God.” Since elsewhere it is read that our Lord sat at the right hand of the Father, we must ask why here he is written to have sat not *at* the right hand but *from* the right hands of God. The right hands of God are his graces or works of mercy; but to sit from the right hands of God is to be humble concerning the gifts of God received. For whatever the godly can do, possess, or desire, they ought to acknowledge that they have received it not from their own merits but from the right hands of God—that is, from God’s help and work alone. [Col. 0870C] From this sitting—that is, from true humility of heart, by which they humble themselves because of God’s benefits received and ascribe them to his glorious name—he also deigns to make his seat and dwelling in them, and causes them to pass from virtue to virtue by great stages of progress, as follows:

“But they, going forth, preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.” 346 Exercising themselves, indeed, in great advances of virtue, they preach everywhere, because the holy examples of their conduct are like proclamations of a living voice. For even if they do not enter upon the public office of preaching, yet by furnishing an example through their own character and zeal for holy conduct, they always and everywhere form and teach their neighbours, through God’s prevenient and subsequent grace, as follows: “the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.” Finally, as a fellow-worker in all their works, the Lord Jesus Christ himself will confirm the word which we have spoken concerning his ineffable appearance—an appearance that awakens in one judging oneself a praiseworthy reproach for unbelief and hardness of heart—and the other matters which, by God’s gift, we have briefly set forth, by the signs that follow, which are spiritually performed in the minds of his elect. He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIX. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE LORD’S ASCENSION

[Col. 0871A]

“Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII).

The festival of this day is to be celebrated and revered by us and by all the faithful with the more devoted earnestness, inasmuch as on this day the very Son of God, who consecrated it by his Ascension, was pleased by a greater grace to exalt human nature, transferring it today in himself above that for which it had been created. For man was so created that, had he remained with God in humility and obedience, he ought to have passed into the fellowship of the angels. But let us consider how great was the condescension of almighty God, how beyond measure his mercy toward us: after sin [Col. 0871B] he bestowed a greater grace, in that he not only restored human nature after its fall, but also bore it upward in himself above all the choirs of angels—to a place it would never have reached had it not fallen. Hence Scripture says:

> Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.

The captivity which, ascending on high, he led captive on this present day was the multitude of his elect, whom, rising from the underworld, he brought back. Yet, according to the words of blessed Augustine, by this captivity we also understand the prince of death himself, who had made the whole world captive, because he had subjected the entire human race to his dominion. The Only-Begotten Son of God led captivity captive when, by his death, having destroyed the dominion of death, he so crushed and bound beneath his feet [Col. 0871C] the enemy of the human race by the power of his strength that he can exercise no authority, no cruel violence of his malice—not, I say, over the good and righteous alone, but even over sinners and the unrighteous—unless insofar as he is permitted by him who holds him bound in the chain of his own strength and power. Hence the Apostle says: “The Lord is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (1 Cor. 10:13). He who, before the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, powerfully swallowed up good and bad, righteous and unrighteous alike, can now possess no power even over sinners themselves, if they should have repentance, even for a single instant, before death.

What is added—“he gave gifts to men”—we rightly understand as the gifts [Col. 0871D] of the Holy Spirit which he distributed to the faithful after his Ascension. Through these gifts, faithful persons of both sexes, men and women alike, instructed and inspired, began to devote themselves to the various pursuits of spiritual life in God’s service; nor will they cease to serve until the end of the age.

But these same words, spoken of the head, may likewise be applied to the members. Christ ascends on high when, by the grace of his visitation and inspiration, he raises and kindles the heart of a person whom he has resolved to save: from the lower regions to those above, from carnal desires to heavenly desires. He leads captivity captive when, through God’s mercy, that person overcomes and crushes within himself the sins and vices beneath which he had served the devil as though carried off and deceived in captivity [Col. 0872A]. After captivity has been taken captive—after the enormity of vices has been abandoned and overcome—there follows:

> He gave gifts to men.

These gifts are the diverse endowments of grace which the almighty Lord grants his faithful: when he makes a sinful and vicious person righteous and virtuous; when he makes one foolish and ignorant of truth wise and knowledgeable in righteousness and equity; when, through the illumination of sacred Scripture, he brings that person to the knowledge of God and of himself.

Luke the Evangelist mystically indicated such persons—emulators, surely, of spiritual life—in whom God thus ascends on high, whose captivity he has led captive by his power, and to whom he has given his gifts [Col. 0872B], when he said in today’s reading: “Therefore those who had assembled asked him, saying, ‘Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?’” It is well said of “those who had assembled”: those who, having abandoned the world, serve God in holy conduct with body, soul, and spirit, in the unity of fraternal charity and sweetness. Since their delight and thought are set upon the Most High, and since they seek and love nothing in this world except God, it is rightly said of them: “they asked him.” Their asking is their desiring. “Lord,” they say, “will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” As if they said: “Lord, unfailing fountain of eternal sweetness and grace, behold, all the desire of my soul is before you. In the abundance of your mercy, show me [Col. 0872C] whether, at this time of your most holy Ascension, having destroyed within me the kingdom of vices, you will establish your kingdom in me; whether you alone—whom alone I desire, seek, and love—will reign in me; whether, by some grace of your condescension, you will deign at this time to visit me.”

But because this grace of inward sweetness lies not in human choice, but in the power and mercy of almighty God, who gives and withdraws it from his elect when and how he wills, he rightly answered: “It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power.” Since a person cannot attend to eternal good at every moment, there are times set apart from other times, such as this present day and the other festivals, on which he who is loved—namely, almighty God—is sought more earnestly and desired more ardently by the blessed soul. Those times, indeed, are indicated here when it is said: “It is not for you to know the times.” What is added—“or moments”—may fittingly be understood to mean the very hour of heavenly visitation. It is as though he said: “It is not within your capacity to know, or to possess according to your wish, the times or moments of my visitation.” And he added: “which the Father has placed in his own power.” “Father” is a relative name with respect to the Son; for unless he had a Son, he could not be called Father. It is as though he said: “Rejoice that what you cannot possess through yourselves has been placed in the power of him whose children you are; and because he is Father, when he sees that it is timely and beneficial for you, he can grant it to you with paternal sweetness” [Col. 0873A]. “It is not for you,” he says, “to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power.”

> But you shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.

The power of the Holy Spirit is the power of humility. This is indeed that power which the Apostle calls the power of Christ when he says: “That the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9). And truly, what is the power of Christ is the power of the Holy Spirit. “Therefore,” he says, “it is not for you to know the times or seasons, so that you may receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you”: that is, so that you may submit yourselves in true humility to him from whom alone, and through whom alone, you can obtain what you desire. Nor does it seem idle to me that he says, “You shall receive [Col. 0873B] the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you.” The power of the Holy Spirit comes upon us when that which is higher in us—namely, the human heart—is touched by humility, which is truly the power of the Holy Spirit. And after you have received this power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, you will be able to be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in true self-recognition; in all Judaea, in true confession of heart and mouth; and in Samaria, in the observance of life; and unto the uttermost part of the earth, in the complete mortification of the flesh.

Nor is it without reason that Jerusalem, whose name means “vision of peace,” expresses a person’s recognition of himself. Whoever truly recognizes himself is not at discord with himself; rather, remaining humble and gentle within himself, he rests as though placed in a vision of peace. For whence do we dissent within ourselves? Whence are we subject [Col. 0873C] to such storms of impatience, except because we do not possess true self-recognition? If we knew ourselves perfectly, we should not be disturbed by even the smallest injuries; indeed, at times we should consider great evils light. Thus a person becomes a witness of Christ’s works, as though in Jerusalem, when he recognizes himself in true humility; he becomes Christ’s witness in all Judaea when, after true knowledge of himself, he rises to true confession; he becomes his witness in Samaria—interpreted “guarding”—when, after true confession, he undertakes perfect observance of life; and he becomes his witness unto the uttermost part of the earth when, through careful observance of life, he attains complete mortification of the flesh. It follows:

> And when he had said these things, he was lifted up into heaven.

God’s speaking is God’s doing. And it is well said, “when he had said these things,” because in whatever persons God has performed these things through his mercy, in them he is undoubtedly lifted up into heaven: by heavenly sweetness he raises them so to himself that they pass beyond all that is low through the desire of the mind, panting and burning only for the embraces of their Creator and Redeemer. After this, the following is rightly added:

> And while they looked into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, and said—

These two men may be understood as the two Testaments, which then truly stand beside that person in whom [Col. 0874A] God has performed these things, because whatever he hears or reads from the sacred Scripture of the Old and New Testaments is entirely sweet to him and wholly stirs and kindles him toward the love of God.

> “This Jesus,” they said, “who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same manner as you saw him going into heaven.”

As though it were said: “This Jesus, this author of eternal salvation and sweetness, who has been taken up from you, who is joined to you in heavenly sweetness, will come in the same manner as you saw him going into heaven.” For although for a time he withdraws as though abandoning you, yet if he is sought again in the same gentleness of humility, he will come to visit you in the same abundance of his mercy.

These are the joys of this day; these are the festivals of the Lord’s Ascension, in which all the mysteries of our redemption have been accomplished and completed [Col. 0874B], as the Psalmist says: “The Lord will save me at evening, in the morning, and at noon” (Ps. 54:18). By evening Christ’s Passion is signified; by morning, Christ’s Resurrection; by noon, Christ’s Ascension. But why did he omit the mystery of his Incarnation? For this reason, I think: in Christ’s Incarnation the salvation of humankind was indeed begun, but not completed, since, while Christ was being born and living in this world, souls, just as before, descended to hell; no one, however righteous or holy, could merit the kingdom of heaven. But when that evening came in which eternal Life, by the grace of our salvation, willed to taste death, hell was despoiled and paradise opened; and thus was fulfilled the saying: “The Lord will save me at evening [Col. 0874C] and in the morning.” After “evening and morning” he added “and at noon,” because human nature, saved through the death and Passion of Christ, was fully glorified in Christ’s Ascension, when, in our Lord Jesus Christ himself, it was placed above all choirs of angels at the right hand of God the Father.

These are the mysteries of our redemption, without faith in which no one can be saved, as the Psalmist mystically indicates in the words that follow: “At evening and in the morning and at noon I will recount and proclaim, and he will hear my voice.” “I will recount,” he says, “that it may be known; I will proclaim, that it may be believed.” For everyone who faithfully believes these mysteries of Christ and follows them by living rightly, God hears that person’s voice; that person’s prayer will be fruitful and acceptable to God [Col. 0874D].

Nor without reason do we believe that Christ’s Ascension was accomplished at noon. Mark testifies to this in today’s reading from the holy Gospel, where he says: “As the eleven disciples reclined at table, Jesus appeared to them and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen from the dead.” They reclined when they were taking refreshment; and that hour of refreshment, when the Bridegroom was taken from them, was always the ninth hour, as that same Bridegroom foretold to John’s disciples before his Passion: “The sons of the Bridegroom cannot mourn while the Bridegroom is with them; but the time will come when the Bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then they will fast” (Matt. 9:15).

The Scripture of the Old Testament likewise indicates this noon to us, where we read of Joseph and his brothers coming to him, though not recognizing that he was their brother. When he wished to admit them to recognition of himself, he commanded the steward of his house, saying: “Bring the men into the house; slaughter victims and prepare a banquet, for they shall eat with me at noon” (Gen. 43:16) [Col. 0875A]. By Joseph, God the Father is figured; by the steward of his house, his only-begotten Son is signified, whom he commanded to prepare the banquet when he sent him into this world as Redeemer of humankind. This banquet of human redemption, this banquet of eternal salvation—to which all are called who have received, or will receive, faith in God—began to be prepared when he willed, incarnate of the Holy Spirit, to be conceived in the Virgin’s womb. He prepared it by being born; he prepared it by dying; he prepared it by rising; he prepared it—indeed, completed it—today by ascending into heaven. Thus he is rightly called the steward of God’s house, which is the holy Church, whose redemption he effected through the dispensation of his Incarnation.

He therefore says: “For they shall eat with me at noon.” For when today, at the noonday hour, about the ninth hour, the Victor ascended into heaven, he set before his elect, snatched from darkness and the shadow of death and brought with him, that banquet which he had prepared. There, with the firstborn seated according to his birthright and the youngest according to his age, he distributed to each, according to his merits, the joys of eternal blessedness [Col. 0875B].

[Col. 0875C] Nor is it devoid of mystery that, after the banquet was completed, that carnal Joseph ordered his silver cup, in which he used to practise divination, to be placed in the mouth of his youngest brother’s sack. The elder brothers signified the Jewish people; the younger brother Benjamin, whose name is interpreted “son of the right hand,” figured the Christian people. The true Joseph ordered his silver cup to be placed in that people’s sack when, having sent the Holy Spirit from above, he began to reveal the mysteries of sacred Scripture to the Christian people gathered in the unity of faith. For just as Joseph’s brothers were then brought back, on account of that cup, to intimate recognition of him, so through the mystery of the sacred utterance, now laid up in the heart of the Christian people through the illumination of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0875D], it will come about that the Jewish people, signified by the elder brothers, together with the people of the Gentiles who shall then be found, will at the end of the world attain intimate knowledge and love of the true Joseph.

It is rightly said of this silver cup that Joseph used to practise divination in it, because sacred Scripture sets before us diverse divinations: namely, how those who live rightly attain the reward of eternal life through the pursuit of good works; and how those who, by living badly, neglect their salvation incur the peril of everlasting condemnation. We find these very divinations in today’s Gospel reading: “He who believes,” says the Lord, “and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned.” [Col. 0876A] Behold one divination leading to eternal salvation and the kingdom of heaven! Behold another divination threatening the fire of infernal punishments!

Having briefly tasted these joys of the present day, let us rejoice today with the angels. For it is fitting that on this day of the Lord’s Ascension we should raise our hearts to a special joy, since it is certain that, because of the exaltation of human nature in Christ, deadly sorrow arose for the devil, the enemy of our salvation and blessedness. For when God willed to become man and to be born, he wasted away indeed with inexpressible grief; when Christ suffered, died, and rose again, he was struck numb with immense and deadly pain, because then he utterly lost the power of his tyranny, by which he had raged against the souls both of believers and unbelievers [Col. 0876B]. Yet these things were in some way more tolerable to him in comparison with the pain he conceived today at the sight of the glory of the Lord’s Ascension. In it he saw the man whom he had despised with such deadly hatred not only restored to the former state of blessedness, in which he ought to have been equal to angels, but even exalted in Christ the Lord above every angelic creature; and he himself was so trampled down that he never again dares raise his head against God’s elect. Therefore it is just that the feasts of this present day, which are the cause of greatest pain to our enemy, should be for us a perpetual matter of rejoicing; and that we should celebrate them in such a manner as to deserve one day to reach that place where we shall possess those joys not annually, but eternally and ever-presently. [Col. 0876C] May our Lord himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY L. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE VIGIL OF PENTECOST

> While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having travelled through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples; and he said to them: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” (Acts 19).

This most holy feast of the Holy Spirit is to be celebrated and revered in a special way by those who derive their name from him: that is, those who, because they profess to live not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit, are called spiritual. Other festivals of the Lord—such as Christ’s Nativity, his Resurrection [Col. 0876D], and his Ascension—are in some sense common even to secular persons. But this feast, consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit, is rightly celebrated by spiritual persons not only in figure but also in truth.

Secular people do indeed celebrate it by playing, feasting, and needlessly and vainly adorning their clothing, as persons ignorant of what sweetness from above the feast of the Holy Spirit contains in itself. Those, indeed, who are situated in the world and devoted to worldly activities can truly say what is read in today’s lesson from the Acts of the Apostles: “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.” No secular person bound by the profession of the Christian name fails to have heard the Holy Spirit named or to know that his feast—that is, Pentecost—is celebrated in the Church. Yet those devoted to this world have not heard that there is a Holy Spirit in such a way that, knowing nothing but what is carnal, they are strangers to spiritual grace and sweetness [Col. 0877A]. And would that we, who are designated by the spiritual name, were not touched by the reproach of these words! For we too can sometimes say, “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit,” when, having the ears of our hearts hardened, although we appear in spiritual dress, we nevertheless involve ourselves in worldly cares and, savouring the things of the flesh, make ourselves deprived of and unworthy of spiritual gifts.

[Col. 0877B] And because in discussing today’s reading we have touched on something of this matter, let us now begin from its opening and see, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant, whether we can find in it anything suitable to our profession. For the Holy Spirit, who dictated and arranged the service of God, would not have appointed that this passage be read on his feast unless it also indicated something that could be applied to spiritual persons. Thus Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles:

> While Apollos was at Corinth, and Paul, having travelled through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples, he said to them: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?”

In these two preachers of God’s Word may be understood any person composed of soul and body. The name *Apollos* may be interpreted as “disciple”; *Paul* is interpreted as “little” or “quiet” [Col. 0877C]. Every person represents within himself the name Apollos when, leaving the world, he begins to be a disciple of Christ and of his superiors in the spiritual life, and resolves to live under the Lord’s discipline until death. The word “at Corinth” is rightly added; it is interpreted as their way of life or the administration of the commonwealth. The interpretations of this name are fulfilled in a person when, having entered the spiritual life, he begins to live well and honourably, and carries out the administration of the commonwealth: that is, he strives to be a vigorous fellow-worker in the labours incumbent upon him and, in observing every order under the spiritual habit, himself takes bodily part in it. All this may be called administration of the commonwealth.

[Col. 0877D] But whoever diligently carries this out at the beginning of conversion gradually advances from day to day, through the accompanying mercy of God, to greater things, so that he may also be called Paul—interpreted, as we said, “little” or “quiet.” He begins, that is, to restrain himself from all unlawful things and, in true humility, subjects himself, insofar as he can, to God and to all who see him. Thus, made little—that is, humble—he advances also so that he may be quiet: namely, that he judges no one in his heart, speaks ill of no one, and is moved by no bitterness, hatred, or envy, all of which are recognized as great unrest of heart [Col. 0878A]. Whoever can thus become quiet arrives at this through striving to be little, because nothing produces such quiet in a person as true humility, which judges itself lower than all others. He is also quiet in this way: having turned outwardly from the pleasures of the age in his manner of life, inwardly too he strives to rest in mind from the uproar of carnal desires.

Taught through this true humility and quiet of mind, he begins to travel through the upper regions, as Scripture says in what follows: “And Paul, having travelled through the upper regions.” By the upper regions may be understood the inner person, who, created in God’s likeness, surpasses the body in greater dignity. Any blessed person travels through the upper regions when, with diligent care, he strives to search and examine within the inward senses of his soul how he has offended God, what sins and how grievous—how deadly—he has committed against his Creator. He is also understood to travel through the upper regions when, despising all earthly things, he relies with his whole heart and all his desires upon heavenly things.

Having thus travelled through the upper regions, one comes to Ephesus, which is interpreted, “My will is in him.” When any blessed person examines himself so strictly in all the things in which he remembers that he sinned against God, or when, drawn away from earthly desires, he has devoted his whole mind to pursuing heavenly things, it may rightly be said that the will of the Lord is in him [Col. 0878B]. A person’s will also comes to be in God when he turns all his own will to the direction of the divine will and abhors, as though it were a deadly evil, whatever he knows resists the will of his Creator.
