[Col. 0878C] He then delights, for God’s sake, to labour in spiritual life at whatever good works he can, just as formerly, while in the world, it had been sweet and delightful to occupy himself against God with wicked deeds and worldly pleasures.

Therefore, having travelled through the upper regions, when he has thus come to Ephesus, he will be able to find certain disciples: that is, when he has forgotten all that lies behind, stretched himself toward what is before and above, and become a fellow-worker with the will of God through his own good will, then through God’s grace he will find within himself not, as before, carnal perceptions concerned with the things of the flesh, but distinct and spiritual perceptions, which may be understood by “certain disciples.” Thus he will be able to know and investigate many things in the holy Scriptures that were formerly unknown to him [Col. 0878D]. Having acquired these special perceptions, he begins to know himself in many respects; and for this reason he humbles his conscience more and more, and, confessing his negligences before God, accuses himself. This is what we understand from the words that follow in this reading. We do not undertake to interpret each individually, but attempt briefly and in summary to indicate here a kind of accusation made before God by a blessed person who knows himself in truth and confesses himself guilty.

[Col. 0879A] For after the statement, “Paul, having travelled through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples,” it is immediately added: “And he said to them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said to him: ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ And he said: ‘Then into what were you baptized?’ They said: ‘Into John’s baptism.’ But Paul said: ‘John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance, telling them to believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.’” These exchanges of question and answer constitute that rebuke by which the person who has found certain disciples—that is, the distinct perceptions of which we have spoken—does not cease in many ways to accuse himself within himself.

“Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” As though he said: “Alas, wretched person, you who received in baptism the pledge of the Holy Spirit—that is, faith—where you promised that you would renounce the devil and his pomps! Alas, you rendered void all that you vowed by living wickedly in the world and contrary to God!” [Col. 0879B] “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.” “I have thus far borne the false name of a Christian person who received the Holy Spirit in baptism; but because by wicked and carnal living I have opposed the Holy Spirit, I have never deserved inwardly to hear through life and experience what the gifts of spiritual charisms are.” “Then into what were you baptized?” “Into John’s baptism.” “God’s grace indeed worked with and in me when it willed to bring me, through faith, to knowledge of his name; but his same grace has remained empty in me until the present time, because I proved ungrateful to it by living badly and disdained to adorn in myself by good works the Christian name which I received through faith.”

[Col. 0879C] By these words any blessed person reproves and accuses himself for all the things in which he sinned in the world. In the words that follow, if we attend mystically, he laments the negligences he remembers having committed after he assumed the spiritual habit. It follows:

> But Paul said: “John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance, telling them to believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.”

“I,” he says, “an unhappy person, lived foolishly and wantonly in the world. But, intending to put an end to all these things, I assumed the habit of humility and separated my body from the tumult of the world so that I might rest in God. And John indeed baptized with a baptism of repentance: that is, God’s grace, which the name John expresses, worked with me in such a way that at some time it granted me to wash myself in the flood of my tears—which is the baptism of repentance—telling them to believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus [Col. 0879D].” That is, it sought to effect in me this: that, keeping right faith in God my Creator and Saviour—which is believing—I might obtain eternal salvation. “But now I know that I have shown myself unworthy of God’s freely given grace because I performed, more negligently than I ought, the good things I could and should have performed.”

These are words of confession by which a person accuses himself before God in the spirit of true humility. But the following text shows us both that the Lord, whose proper work is to give grace to the humble, hears the voice of the confession of one who, in true self-knowledge, knows himself; and that the person recognizes the words of humility as God speaking within him.

> “When they heard this,” it says, “they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.”

God indeed, as we have said, hears a person speaking to him in the desire of his soul and in delight in virtues, as the Psalmist declares from his own experience: “Lord, you have heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Ps. 9:22) [Col. 0880A]. A person also hears God speaking within him when, through grace following upon him, he begins to experience that God has spoken in him words of true humility, desiring to prepare for himself a way into the human heart by giving that person, through prevenient grace, the ability perfectly to humble his conscience. [Col. 0880B] Between God’s hearing the person and the person’s hearing God, he is sometimes baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus: that is, such compunction is born in him as may truly be said to work eternal salvation within him. It follows:

> And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them.

For when that person who expresses in himself the name Paul—who is little through humility and quiet through gentleness of mind—hears God speaking within him, is heard by God speaking words of humility to him, and demonstrates in himself this reality through the testimony of humble works (which is Paul’s laying hands upon them), then indeed the Holy Spirit comes, as he himself promised through the prophet to those who humble themselves in truth: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2) [Col. 0880C]. What the Holy Spirit, coming upon elect persons who have attained all the things we have described, accomplishes is testified by the words that follow:

> “And they spoke,” it says, “with tongues and prophesied.”

In hearts in which the Holy Spirit has prepared a dwelling for himself, there is no doubt that they can speak in various tongues. What are these tongues? They speak one tongue when through repentance they accuse and condemn whatever evil they remember having done: they rebuke themselves for their thoughts, pursue themselves for their words, and punish themselves with tears for their deeds. Again they sound forth with another tongue when they lament that they have neglected the good things which they ought and were able to do. Thus, in the hour of the Holy Spirit’s visitation, the elect speak with tongues when they mourn and lament having lain so long under temporal things and having separated themselves from the homeland for which they were created; and when, yearning to behold the countenance of their Creator, they cry strongly to God through their desires [Col. 0880D]. Then they also begin to prophesy, because, just as it belongs to prophets to foretell future things, so they prophesy to themselves concerning the future punishments of the wicked and the glory and reward of the good: striving to escape the condemnation of the wicked, and desiring with their whole longing the joys of the heavenly kingdom. It follows:

> Now all the men were about twelve.

By twelve, which is recognized as a perfect number in many places of Scripture, perfection is signified. For all the men who have become, as we have said, speakers with tongues and prophets are about twelve, because they stand perfect in the vigorous virtues which may be figured by men [Col. 0881A]. The fact that the word “about” is added indicates to us that, however great the height of virtues to which any elect person may rise, he can nevertheless never attain in this world to full perfection, in which nothing would oppose or be lacking to him. Rather, the blessedness of full perfection is reserved for the future life, where there shall be such freedom of bodies and souls that a person will neither wish nor be able ever to contract any stain in thought, word, deed, or desire.

That one who has attained such a grace of virtues as we have described is sometimes, by divine dispensation, taken up for the word of teaching may also be inferred from the words that follow:

> [Col. 0881B] “And entering into the synagogue, he spoke boldly for three months, disputing and persuading concerning the kingdom of God.”

He enters the synagogue when he is placed over God’s Church or some holy congregation. There he speaks boldly if he does not destroy by his deeds what he teaches in words. He truly speaks God’s word boldly who does not fear that it may be objected against him that he himself does the very things he teaches must be avoided. Rather, he watches over himself so carefully in all things that his life can accord with his word. But that person cannot speak boldly whom his own teaching rebukes, whose conscience accuses him because, by living badly, he himself contradicts what he preaches in words [Col. 0881C].

“He spoke boldly,” it says, “for three months.” In the three months we may understand these three: faith, hope, and charity; or thoughts, words, and deeds. For every superior directs his charge to instructing those subject to him in faith, hope, and charity, or to teaching them to strive to be cautious and watchful in their thoughts, words, and deeds. “Disputing,” it says, “and persuading concerning the kingdom of God.” He disputes when he persists in the word of preaching; he persuades when he confirms what he teaches by the testimony of works. But whether he disputes or persuades—that is, teaches by word or example—let him do both concerning the kingdom of God: let him not attribute these things to his own merits or seek from them the favour of human praise, but refer everything to God, from whom he has both the ability to speak God’s word well and the capacity, in speaking, to set before those subject to him in himself a pattern of right living [Col. 0881D].

This same little verse, which we have already applied to any prelate, may also be adapted to every individual who is to be saved. For every blessed person himself, with whom and in whom God has worked all the things mentioned above, enters the synagogue—that is, he walks within; both in mind and body he lives in the congregation. He does not set the steps of his mind outside, that is, he does not roam through the world by fleshly desires. He considers that, according to his profession, he ought to be crucified to this world; [Col. 0882A] he takes no care inwardly or outwardly to deal with any of the things that are in the world, but is one who has no concern for worldly matters. What does such a person practise in the congregation? “He spoke,” it says, “with confidence for three months.”

For whoever thus enters the synagogue—that is, thus remains in the Church or in some holy community—being within both in body and in mind, and having entirely removed the steps of his thought from delight in the present age, can speak with confidence and rebuke whatever he sees committed against God in the congregation. For a person can rebuke every evildoer with all the more confidence and freedom to the extent that he knows himself to have a life such that no one can throw in his face that he himself yields to the fault which he reproves in others. He speaks for [Col. 0882B] three months when he rebukes the evil will, wicked words, and perverse deeds of others living in the congregation in such a way that he himself vigilantly and carefully guards himself in these three respects. “Disputing,” it says, “and persuading concerning the kingdom of God.”

He disputes when, as we have said, he rebukes the vices of his neighbours with the zeal of charity and exhorts them to whatever good he can; he persuades when he so corrects and admonishes them that, by his own example, he teaches in himself what ought to be done or avoided. “Concerning the kingdom of God,” it says—that is, concerning a good and humble heart. For the kingdom of God, as the Apostle says, is within us [Note: [Col. 0881] These words are found almost thus in Luke, chapter XVII, verse 21, but not in the Apostle Paul, nor elsewhere]; and this truly is a good and humble heart, very pleasant and delightful for God to dwell in. Every blessed person disputes and persuades concerning the kingdom of God when all his correction and exhortation, and also the testimony of [Col. 0882C] his works, proceed from a humble heart and true love of God and neighbour; when he is stirred against no one by the zeal of bitterness; and when he does not fall into the fault of boasting because he lives blamelessly among the rest.

361 Since these things which we have expounded from today’s Lesson are brought about in no human being except through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, it is fitting that on the feast which we celebrate there should be read: Therefore, turning to the Holy Spirit himself, our Lord and Creator, let us implore his goodness, that on his feast he may not permit us to be without his visitation and consolation, but may so cleanse our hearts for himself to dwell in them that we may inwardly experience what we outwardly celebrate. The Holy Spirit himself, our God and Creator, [Col. 0882D] who is called by many names suited to his dignity, is also called both stable and moving.

Why he should rightly be called stable, we do not fail to understand, since we know him to be unchangeable. But how can he be called moving, who lacks every change and motion? He is rightly called moving as well as stable according to what we shall now say. There are certain merits of virtues without which no one can be saved, such as faith, hope, and charity; and in these the Holy Spirit is stable in his elect—that is, in these he never abandons them, because those who tend toward the heavenly homeland must always be endowed with [Col. 0883A] faith, hope, and charity. Behold, we have heard how the Holy Spirit is stable; now let us learn how he is also called moving.

Again, there are other gifts, such as kinds of tongues, prophecy, and many others, which, although holy persons may sometimes lack them, do not thereby have to be excluded from eternal salvation or entry into the kingdom of heaven. In these the Holy Spirit is moving, because when he wills he gives them, and again, when he wills, he takes them away. Elisha was certainly a holy man and often foretold the future, yet he did not possess the gift of prophecy at every hour. This was plainly shown when that Shunammite woman came to him on Mount Carmel to ask concerning her dead son: he did not know why she had come. And when [Col. 0883B] Jehoshaphat inquired about future events, he had a psalmist brought to him, so that through the praise of psalmody the Holy Spirit might descend and fill his mind concerning what was to come. Such also are the other spiritual gifts of charisms, which a person cannot always possess in this age, such as the sweetness of blessed contemplation.

Let us therefore implore our Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, that he may deign to be both stable and moving in us: stable, that is, by these virtues he may continually persevere in us, without which we cannot be saved; and that he may sometimes confer on us those gifts in which he is moving—that is, that he may, if only for an hour, pour into us the grace of his sweetness, so that through his momentary visitation here we may be able to attain there, where we shall continually cling to his love and sweetness. May he deign to grant this, [Col. 0883C] the Holy Spirit, our God and Creator, who with the Father and the Son lives and reigns as one God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE HOLY DAY OF PENTECOST

“Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord your God in the place which he shall choose: at the feast of unleavened bread, at the feast of weeks, and at the feast of tabernacles,” etc. (Deut. XVI).

The holy and venerable solemnity which we observe is the feast of the Holy Spirit. By his coming he wonderfully consecrated and adorned it; long ago in the Old Testament it was shown and prefigured by many figures. [Col. 0883D] Thus in one place the Lord commanded the children of Israel through Moses the lawgiver concerning this sacred solemnity, saying: “Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord your God in the place which he shall choose: at the feast of unleavened bread, at the feast of weeks, and at the feast of tabernacles.”

These three solemnities, which excel all the feasts we celebrate throughout the year in preeminence and dignity, had been commended by the Lord’s command through the lawgiver to the children of Israel in such a manner that every year, on these three occasions, everything among them that was of the male sex was to appear before the Lord—that is, in the holy Temple at Jerusalem. When they had presented themselves at Jerusalem, in the place which [Col. 0884A] the Lord had chosen, 363 no one was to come there empty before the Lord; rather, each was required to offer saving sacrifices to the Lord according to what his hand was able to find.

“All these things happened to them in a figure,” as the Apostle says, “but they were written for our instruction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. X, 11). They understood and celebrated everything carnally; but we, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, in whom this world has reached its end, who have renounced the age and the deeds of the age—even if we cannot be wholly absolved from sins—nevertheless, with God’s help, shall no longer turn aside through capital crimes into the path of stumbling.

Therefore, according to the Lord’s command, all that is male in us appears before the Lord when, laying aside [Col. 0884B] all womanish frivolity, we perform manly, strong, and virtuous deeds by which we may please the sight of the supreme Deity and be found such that the Lord may deign to set his eyes upon us. For, as we see in the present world, any powerful lord disdains to look upon a servant who has offended his eyes, but takes pleasure in looking often upon one whom he truly loves. So indeed those whom he judges worthy of his love are before the Lord; but from those who do not merit the regard of his grace, he turns his eyes away. We also appear before the Lord in another way when we approach the holy altar, where from the innermost affection of the heart we receive, with due reverence, the sacraments of the body and blood of the Son of God.

[Col. 0884C] We are also commanded not to come empty before the Lord, lest we be found unprepared at these three solemnities; rather, let each offer to God such devotion as he can. Let one of greater merit offer splendid and greater things to God; but one of lesser merit should strive, according to what he can in his poverty, not to appear empty before the Lord.

“At the feast,” it says, “of unleavened bread.” The feast of unleavened bread is the Paschal feast, in which Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed. He was prefigured by that lamb which the children of Israel dwelling in Egypt sacrificed at evening on the fourteenth day of the moon. He commanded that this lamb’s blood be put upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses, so that when the destroyer came—sent by God in punishment of that nation to kill all the firstborn of Egypt—[Col. 0884D] he should by no means enter their houses, but, seeing the blood, should pass over.

We truly observe the figure of this thing in our solemnity when, with pure heart and body, we receive as a remedy for our souls the flesh and blood of our Lamb, who was sacrificed for us upon the altar of the cross. We place the blood of this Lamb upon both doorposts and the lintel when we fortify our body and soul with the blood of the Son of God, so that the destroying devil—namely, God’s servant and messenger—may not presume to harm us in any respect [MS: “lest he not harm us”]. But why have we called the devil God’s servant? For this reason: the devil, together with his members, wicked people, greatly [Col. 0885A] serves and has served God; even though he does so wickedly and with a perverse will, nevertheless the almighty Lord, who makes good use of evil persons, turns it all to the praise and glory of his name and to the salvation of his elect.

After the days of unleavened bread follows the feast of weeks, which we call Pentecost. By the Lord’s command it was celebrated on the fiftieth day after Passover, and in it was prefigured the coming of the Holy Spirit, who on this present day came upon the apostles with a sudden sound. Luke says concerning this sacred solemnity in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place; and suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind approaching, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting” (Acts II, 1–2). [Col. 0885B] Let us therefore see how this sacred solemnity was prefigured also in the Old Testament.

“In the third month,” Moses says, “after Israel’s departure from the land of Egypt, on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai, and there Israel pitched its tents opposite the mountain. But Moses went up to God; and the Lord called to him from the mountain and said: ‘Thus shall you say to the house of Jacob, and announce to the children of Israel: You yourselves have seen how I carried you upon eagles’ wings, and took you for my own possession from among all peoples; and you shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation’” (Exod. XIX, 1–6).

When Moses had expounded these words to the elders, all the people answered: “All that the Lord has spoken we will do” (ibid., 8). When Moses had reported the words of the people to the Lord, the Lord said: “Now [Col. 0885C] I shall come to you in darkness, so that the people may hear me speaking with you, and may believe you forever” (ibid., 9). Moses therefore came and announced to the children of Israel all that the Lord had spoken. But they worshipped. And Moses reported the words of the people to the Lord. He said to him: “Go to the people, and sanctify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day, for on the third day the Lord will descend before all the people upon Mount Sinai.” Moses went down to the people and sanctified them. When they had washed their garments, he said to them: “Be ready for the third day; do not approach your wives.” The third day had now arrived and morning had grown bright; and behold, thunder began to be heard, lightning to flash, [Col. 0885D] a very thick cloud to cover the mountain, and the blast of a trumpet sounded with ever greater force; and the people who were in the camp were afraid (ibid., 10–16).

In these three days we may understand the time before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. In the three days we may also understand the Lord’s annunciation, his incarnation, passion, and resurrection. And the Lord’s resurrection can fittingly be understood in the morning, because, as the end of night comes with dawn and darkness is separated from light, so, when Christ rose after destroying the dominion of death, that morning shone forth by which the darkness of sins was driven away through Christ’s mercy.

Before his passion and resurrection the whole world was set in darkness, because all the saints, whoever they were before Christ’s coming, having paid the debt of death, descended to the underworld, where they awaited the salvation of the world with great longing. When his passion had been accomplished, he shone brightly among those in the underworld and, rising from the dead, led them with himself, with the thief going before, into the pleasant places of Paradise. [Col. 0886A]

But we may also understand Christ’s incarnation in the morning, when the Only-Begotten of God chose by his birth to be joined to human substance, when the time of grace arrived. Thus, at the birth of our Saviour, a splendid morning shone forth, by which the darkness of the unbelief and ignorance of this age was driven away. For his manner of life among sinners in this life, and his preaching by which he called sinners to repentance, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV, 17), [Col. 0886B] illuminated the darkness of the whole world.

Therefore it is immediately added concerning his preaching: “And behold, thunder began to be heard and lightning to flash.” In thunder are found two things which we may apply to Christ’s preaching: first, that people are terrified with great fear when thunder is heard; second, that those struck by thunder often die. For this reason Christ’s preaching may fittingly be understood in thunder. He thundered with great terror to the Jews, lovers of the world, when he lived humbly and poorly in this world and preached contempt for the world and poverty of spirit, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3).

But the Lord, through Moses, had commanded the Jewish people [Col. 0886C] and had confirmed by his promises that, if they carefully kept his commandments and legal ceremonies, he would grant them without any lack abundance of all things, a multitude of children, fertility of fields and vineyards, and whatever pertains to transitory happiness. Yet after our Lord Jesus Christ came into this world and taught that all these things should be despised for love of the heavenly homeland, the wicked Jews, struck by the thunder of this preaching and inflamed with the torches of envy against the Son of God, persecuted him even to death. That death of his body truly became the death of their souls.

Thus it is written in the Gospel concerning a certain young man who came to the Lord, asking what he should do to possess [Col. 0886D] eternal life. The Lord answered: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness.” When he replied, “All these things I have kept from my youth” (Matt. XIX, 20), the Lord said to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give it to the poor, and you shall have treasures in heaven; and come, follow me” (ibid., 21). Having heard this word—that he ought to leave possessions and riches for God—the young man departed from him sorrowful, because the thunder of God’s word shook him inwardly with the great terror of grief.

Oh, with what terror did the thunder strike the wicked Jews when, coming to Jerusalem, he found people selling and buying doves in the Temple! Having made a whip of cords, he drove the buyers and sellers from the Temple, overturned the money and the tables of the money-changers, and said: [Col. 0887A] “It is written: ‘My house is a house of prayer for all nations’; but you have made it a den of thieves” (Matt. XXI, 13). Others, healthfully terrified by the fear of this thunder, such as the apostles, imitated the poor Lord, left all things, and followed him.

367 After the Son of God had thus thundered in his preaching, lightning then began to flash. By this may be understood the wonderful and astonishing miracles which he worked on earth by the power of his divinity. Before his coming, however, there were good and holy persons who displayed signs and wonders before the people. Yet they did not perform these miracles by their own power or strength, but obtained from God by prayers the ability to do wonders. Elijah and Elisha, for example, raised the dead by praying. But the almighty Lord, needing no assistance of prayer, raised the dead by the mighty power of his words. So we read in the Gospel concerning the son of that widow, who was being carried outside the gate and was restored to life by the Lord’s word alone: “Young man, I say to you: Arise” (Luke VII, 14). [Col. 0887B] So too, by a powerful word he called Lazarus, four days in the tomb, from the grave, saying: “Lazarus, come forth” (John XI, 43).

Having thus lived among men by preaching and displaying miracles, at last, when the dispensation of the flesh had been completed, he was brought to completion upon the cross through the ignominy of his passion; glorified by God the Father in the triumph of the resurrection, he returned to heaven. There, sitting at the right hand of the Father, he truly fulfilled in his apostles what follows:

[Col. 0887C] “And a very thick cloud covered the mountain.” The very thick cloud is the grace of the Holy Spirit: thick in the patriarchs, thicker in the prophets, and very thick in the apostles. This very thick cloud began to cover those eternal mountains—the apostles—after Christ’s ascension to heaven, because the grace of the Holy Spirit by which the apostles were enlightened surpasses all the gifts of the Holy Spirit which the Lord’s elect have received from the beginning of the world. For although Moses, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets were full of the knowledge of God, nevertheless the knowledge of the apostles—received on this day as the gift of the Holy Spirit appeared over them in tongues of fire—surpassed the knowledge of all the ancient Fathers. [Col. 0887D]

And because, when a thick cloud is seen, rain by which the earth may be watered is expected, so surely, when the apostles were filled with the abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, so great a shower of spiritual grace descended from their teaching that the whole Church throughout the world could be watered by it. It follows:

“And the blast of the trumpet sounded with ever greater force.” In the trumpet blast we may understand the sound of apostolic teaching. After receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, this teaching was made so strong and forceful that, by the word of their preaching, they bore greater fruit for the Lord than Christ himself had borne by preaching to the people. For while he preached and taught on earth, very few Jews believed. But the apostles, enlightened when the Holy Spirit had been sent from heaven, [Col. 0888A] converted three thousand persons to the Lord in one day and five thousand on the following day when they addressed words of exhortation to the people.

Luke writes concerning their perfection in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; and, bringing their prices, they laid them at the apostles’ feet, and all things were common to them” (Acts IV, 32). The blast of this trumpet now sounds more powerfully, because the conversion and unanimity of the common life, which began under the apostles in the primitive Church with a small number, has now spread throughout the whole world so greatly that, from the beginning of the world, there has not been as great a multitude of people serving God as is now, by God’s grace, in the holy Church. Men now leave wives for God; women leave husbands; they despise their dear pledges, that is, their children, for love of eternal life. [Col. 0888B] Others, persevering in virginity, subject themselves with all obedience to their prelates and willingly and patiently endure all adversities for the Lord.

It must be noted that when the trumpet sounds, soldiers are armed and prepared for battle: some to gain victory, others to fall in death. By the sound of this trumpet, the blast of apostolic teaching, you also, dearest women, have been stirred to despise all the world’s allurements and riches and to place yourselves under obedience in the most strict cloister, where, bound for God, you are separated from all the joys possessed by the world. Your weapons, by which you ought to fight against the enemy, are [Col. 0888C] your chastity and continence, your veil, and your other garments, signifying renunciation of the world. With these you are armed in order to gain victory over the tyrant.

But alas, a grievous thing! Many are in the spiritual vocation who, although they have gone out of Egypt with the children of Israel, nevertheless fall in the wilderness and by no means enter the land 369 of promise. These are those who do not endure in spiritual life until the end of their lives, but return to the world and its pleasures.

There are others who persevere bodily in the spiritual vocation until their end, but remain cold in heart and die in it miserably and without profit. [Col. 0888D] It follows:

“And the people who were in the camp were afraid.” That people in the camp was the Jewish nation. While they remained at Jerusalem and occupied themselves with the Law and legal ceremonies, they heard that the apostles, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, spoke the languages of all nations. They were struck with great amazement and fear, and, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, said in wonder: “Behold, are not all these who speak Galileans? And how have we each heard our own language in which we were born?” (Acts II, 7). And again: “These men are full of new wine” (ibid., 13). Then they said to Peter and the other apostles: “What shall we do, brethren?” And Peter said to them: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord [Col. 0889A] so that your sins may be forgiven” (Acts II, 38). It follows:

“When Moses had brought them out from the place of the camp to meet the Lord, they stood at the foot of the mountain.” When the Jews who believed in the Son of God through the apostles’ preaching had been struck with holy and chaste fear, Moses began to bring them out to meet the Lord, when they began to understand that the things written in the Law, which they had understood carnally, were Moses’ bringing-out to meet the Lord. For whatever Moses concealed beneath the veil of the Law, they saw fulfilled wholly in the Lord Jesus Christ. Then they truly recognized that Moses had intended only to bring them out from the place of the camp—that is, from the legal ceremonies—to meet the Lord, that they might believe in the Son of God clothed in flesh, whom all things in the Law prefigured.

“They stood,” it says, “at the roots of the mountain.” That mountain is the apostolic assembly. The roots of this mountain were their faith, upon the foundation of which faith the Church is established and founded. And because “roots of the mountain” is put in the plural, we may observe here two roots of faith upon which all believers rest and are made firm. We believe, namely, that the Lord Jesus is our Creator and Redeemer: our Creator according to his divinity, our Redeemer according to his humanity, in which he offered himself to God the Father for us. We rest upon these roots in such a manner that we confess that no one can be saved without both these beliefs. [Col. 0889C] Those recently converted through the apostles’ teaching stood at the roots of this mountain when they believed the Lord Jesus Christ to be their Creator and Redeemer and placed all their hope in the steadfastness of this faith.

“But all Mount Sinai was smoking, because the Lord had descended upon it in fire, and smoke ascended as from a furnace.” In Mount Sinai, which is interpreted “commandment,” the Jewish people may be signified, since they had received above the other nations the precepts of the Law to observe and keep. In the smoke, which commonly causes tears, we may understand their tearful sighs. For they, having heard Gospel teaching concerning the observances of the Law, were wholly smoking, because when they recognized how perversely and maliciously [Col. 0889D] they had acted toward their Creator and Redeemer, they uttered tearful sighs from the inmost affection of their hearts and said to the apostles: “What shall we do, brethren?”

“Because the Lord had descended upon it in fire.” Seeing the signs and miracles, and seeing that the Holy Spirit had descended upon the apostles in tongues of fire, they too were inwardly inflamed with the fire of the Holy Spirit and were converted to the love of the Son of God, whom they had previously persecuted.

“And smoke ascended as from a furnace.” When a furnace is kindled with fire, we hope that bread will be prepared in it, by which the corruptible body that we bear may be refreshed and sustained. So, when the apostles were inflamed with the Holy Spirit, the bread of God’s word [Col. 0890A] was prepared in them, by which all believers are fed and refreshed.

371 “And the whole mountain was terrible, and the sound of the trumpet gradually increased and was prolonged.” In this mountain, as we have said, the apostolic assembly may be understood. It was made terrible when, after the Most High had sent down the Holy Spirit, they were so inflamed in love for their Creator that, setting aside all fear, they preached God’s word with confidence. Thus Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “But none of the rest dared join them; rather, the people magnified them, and they were unanimously praying in the Temple” (Acts V, 13).

The apostolic assembly was therefore made terrible to the unbelieving Jews, just as we frequently see now how secular [Col. 0890B] persons, devoted to the vanity and greed of this age, revere spiritual and good men and are afraid in their presence.

“And the sound of the trumpet increased.” The sound of apostolic teaching increased when the apostle Paul was joined to the apostolic order. In preaching the word of God, as he himself asserted, he laboured more than all the others. For by his preaching he converted the whole world to faith in and knowledge of the Son of God, so that from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum he filled everything with the Gospel. “And it was prolonged,” it says. The trumpet of God’s word is prolonged when the mystery of the incarnate Word advances even to foreign nations.

Who in former times could have believed that the faith of the Lord [Col. 0890C] would extend as far as Ascalon, where the power of the nations was located and which always rebelled against God’s people? But now, many thousands of God’s servants are gathered there, and the worship of demons has been eradicated. May the Spirit grant us that, by the Holy Spirit’s ordering, he may also cause us to attain in Persia, Babylonia, and the other nations still deceived by Gentile error to knowledge of his holy name.

Therefore, since we celebrate the coming of the Holy Spirit, strive, dearly beloved women, to show yourselves worthy of the Spirit of grace, so that as of old he abundantly poured out the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, upon those assembled in the upper room of Zion and shut in for fear of the Jews, so he may deign to send heavenly consolation to you also, [Col. 0890D] who likewise are shut in for fear of Jews—not carnal, but spiritual Jews.

For you feared that, if you made lawful use of this world, malignant spirits would kill you in soul through sins. Therefore, separated bodily from the world, you despised for God’s sake whatever delights the world possesses.

Accordingly, it befits his majesty and goodness that Jesus Christ our Lord may deign to grant to you also, his bound and desolate ones, the consolation and joy of the Holy Spirit—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the same Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## 373 HOMILY LII. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE HOLY DAY OF PENTECOST

[Col. 0891A]

“If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV).

Because this most holy solemnity which we celebrate is the solemnity of the Holy Spirit, it is fitting, through the providence and ordering of that same Holy Spirit, that the reading from the holy Gospel which we have heard—wholly directed to making manifest and commending the divine and human nature of the only-begotten Son of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ—has been appointed for this first day of the Holy Spirit. For on this day, when the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven upon the apostles, they began to know both his divine and human nature more fully and perfectly [Col. 0891B] than they had ever known it before.

And if we consider more subtly, that special gift of the Holy Spirit, namely the spirit of wisdom, rightly belongs to this day. For truly the spirit of wisdom worked on this day in the apostles and in the other faithful of Christ gathered with them, on which day it poured into their hearts in fullest measure, by the immeasurable and ineffable gift of its anointing, whatever was necessary to know and believe concerning our Lord Jesus Christ.

For this is full and perfect knowledge: that a person be enlightened unto knowledge and inflamed unto love; that we may know the things that ought to be known and love the things that ought to be loved. What are the things that ought to be known, and what are the things that ought to be loved? That we may know, in our Lord Jesus [Col. 0891C] Christ, that according to his divinity he is our Creator; and love him because, according to his humanity, he is our Saviour and Redeemer. Since on this day he chose to reveal this knowledge and love of his divinity and humanity to his holy disciples, and through them to the whole world, by the wonderful coming of the Holy Spirit, the Gospel of this day rightly takes its beginning from love. For the Saviour says:

“If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.” There are three members of this verse, because love is also threefold, by which one reaches the rewards of eternal blessedness. The first love is beginning love, the second progressing love, the third perfecting love. The first arises in conversion, the second in the middle stage, the third in perfection.

When it is said, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word,” beginning love is signified, by which a person is first initiated. For one who, leaving the world, has begun to love God must learn through many words of the Lord in the spiritual life how he ought to reach the one word of the Lord which signifies perfection. And because he does not say, “If anyone loves me, he keeps my word,” but “he will keep it,” he has mystically taught us that at this stage of beginning love a person should not remain fixed, but should always stretch himself forward through observance of the words—that is, the commandments—of God. Hence he also says:

[Col. 0892A] “And my Father will love him.” By the loving Father we understand progressing love. For in this the God and Father displays his love to one who loves and keeps his word, as a father does to a son: he makes the person progress in spiritual life through virtues and virtuous acts, so that he may know and understand what he did not previously know, and may be willing and able to accomplish the good things which before he neither wished nor was able to accomplish.

By these two stages, of beginning and progressing love, a person ascends to the third stage, of perfecting love. In it he is in some manner happily brought to completion, when he is frequently visited through the grace of heavenly visitation, as the Lord indicates in the following mystical words:

“And we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.” [Col. 0892B] In these words the operation of the whole holy Trinity is shown to us. Although the person of the Holy Spirit is not here specially named, nevertheless whatever is said of the Father and whatever is said of the Son is also said of the Holy Spirit. For the work of the holy Trinity is inseparable: whatever the Father does, whatever the Son does, the Holy Spirit does with the Father and the Son; for everything is accomplished and brought to completion through the Holy Spirit.

“We shall come to him,” he says. The Word of the most high Father, the only-begotten Son of God, comes through the illumination of his visitation; God the Father comes through the compassion of his consolation; the Holy Spirit comes through the outpouring of his anointing. For in this indivisible coming of the holy Trinity, a person is truly enlightened to know, to repent, and to make satisfaction to God—not only for the evils he has committed, but also for the good things he has neglected and omitted. There, by the gift of divine consolation, he is encouraged to hope for pardon; there he is truly perfected and brought to completion in the love of God; there he receives a certain pledge of eternal life. Explaining this, the Saviour adds:

“And we shall make our dwelling with him.” The almighty Trinity comes here to its elect, whom it visits by the grace of its sweetness, but does not remain with them, because this grace occurs as though in a certain rapture and does not last. But in the life to come it will make its dwelling with them [MS: “with him”], whom it will never abandon; rather, they will always be in eternal sweetness, where without end they shall see the Father in the Son, the Son [Col. 0892D] in the Father, together with the Holy Spirit.

Behold, we have heard both the manner and the reward of one who loves. But what follows for one who does not love, he immediately makes known when he says:

He who does not love me does not keep my words. In what precedes he said, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word”; but here he said, “He who does not love me does not keep my words.” And rightly so: for there are many words of God which the person who desires to come to that one word, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend, must strive to keep. It is as though he said: He who does not love—that is, who lacks even the beginning of love for God—does not keep the many words through which one comes to the one Word, but is wholly in evil; for without the beginning love which is directed toward God, and the advancing love which pertains to one’s neighbour, he cannot be saved. [Col. 0893A]

But because the Lord’s chosen disciples possessed not only beginning and advancing love, but had also arrived at perfecting love, they deserved to hear from the Lord: And the word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.

Nor should we pass over without notice what he says: “the word which you have heard.” Those to whom the Lord said, “My word has no place in you” (John 8:37), did not hear the Lord’s word. He hears God’s word for whom God’s word is savoury. Therefore, because the Lord’s chosen disciples—the holy apostles—found inwardly savoury in the sweetness of their hearts the Lord’s word which they heard outwardly, they rightly deserved to hear from the Lord: “And the word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.” It is as if he had said: That you were able to hear my word in such a way that what you heard externally became savoury inwardly to you is not due to my humanity, but to the divinity by whose gift this was granted to you. [Col. 0893B]

These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you. These things, I say, I have worked in you when I remained with you by that indwelling which belongs to God; when, by the invisible anointing of my divinity, I enlightened and enlarged your hearts so that they might receive and find savoury my word. And the word which you heard I spoke not only to you but to every human being; for whoever hears my word in such a way that what he hears is savoury to him, receives this by the gift of my divinity. For unless I dwell wondrously within, the teacher’s word labours in vain by preaching outwardly. But should a person therefore withdraw himself from hearing God’s word if he is unable to grasp it through inward savour? Far be it! Let him listen; let him attend as much as he can. For if he is attentive and perseveres in that very attentiveness, the grace of the Holy Spirit will not be lacking; it makes the diligent hearer wise. For this is indicated to us by him who is Truth, when he adds:

But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and will bring to your remembrance whatever I have said to you. And it should be noted that he does not simply say, “the Holy Spirit,” but “the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name.” The Holy Spirit is always sent by the Father, but he is not always Paraclete. He was sent to the prophets, that they might foreknow and foretell things to come. He was also sent to Balaam, who, brought out to curse God’s people, not only did not curse them but even, as though blessing them, foresaw and foretold in the Holy Spirit things that were to come. He is still sent to holy preachers, that they may know and be able usefully to admonish God’s people in the word of God. Yet in all these instances the Holy Spirit is indeed present, but not Paraclete. But wherever he sees a humble heart—a heart, I say, grieving either in remembrance of sins or in love of heavenly goods, and diligently seeking in God’s word the consolation by which it may breathe again—there the grace flowing abundantly from the Father’s sweetness is sent, so that he may be Paraclete to it in every tribulation of both soul and body. [Col. 0893C–0894A] Hence he rightly says: “Whom the Father will send in my name.” What is his name? Jesus, which is interpreted “Saviour.” For this sending never occurs without the remedy of salvation. Therefore he added and said:

He will teach you all things and will bring to your remembrance whatever I have said to you. It is as though he said: The Paraclete Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send to you in my name so that he may be your Consoler and Saviour, will teach you by knowledge and bring things to your remembrance by love. He will teach you those things which you need to know, illuminating you inwardly; he will bring to your remembrance those things which you need to love, by giving love. What are these things? “Whatever I have said to you”: I, who am the Word of God the Father; for whatever is spoken to you in my word, I, the Father’s Word, speak to you. [Col. 0894A–B]

Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you. This threefold peace must be discerned by careful consideration. The first peace is peace from vices; the second, peace from the world; the third, peace from the devil. Thus to leave peace is to give peace from vices. The Lord gives peace from vices when, in the abundance of his power, he grants his faithful people that, by resisting flesh and blood, they become superior to vices; they restrain and cast away from themselves whatever they know can displease God within them. This is the first peace, to which the second must succeed; the only-begotten Son of God calls this his own peace. “My peace,” he says, “I give to you.” This is peace from the world.

What is peace from the world? The world offers us joys and sorrows, prosperity and adversity, through which it often makes one who is tending toward heavenly things divided within himself. At one time it raises him by prosperous and joyful things; at another it casts him down by sad and adverse things. But because it lies in the power of the Creator alone to suppress this evil of unrest, he rightly says: “My peace I give to you.” It is as though he said: This is my peace, which I specially give to my own, so that those to whom I give it may have peace from the world: I make them stand so firmly in themselves that neither prosperity raises them above themselves nor adversity makes them fall beneath themselves. But because there still remains one peace, higher than both peace from vices and peace from the world, the Saviour further added: “Not as the world gives do I give to you.” This is peace from the devil, which will not be given in this world but is reserved for eternal life. For who can be safe from the devil in this world? Therefore, the higher that peace will be, where no saint will fear the devil, the more specially he took care to commend it when he said: “Not as the world gives do I give to you.” But how?

Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. It is as though he said: The peace which I shall give in eternal life will not be such as the first peace or the second peace was; rather, I give you such peace that your heart may not be troubled or afraid—that is, that you may be there with me, free and at rest from every assault of the devil, so that you are neither troubled in heart by any evil thought nor afraid in body of the dread of any evil act that may befall you. And because our Saviour had two natures within himself—one which they saw, and another which they were not yet able perfectly to know; one of humanity, in which he ate and drank with them, and another of divinity, in which and through which he promised that he would do all these things in them—he added and said: [Col. 0894B–0895A]

You have heard that I said to you: I go, and I come to you. It is as if he said: You have heard that I, made man for your sake, said to you: “I go, and I come to you.” I go where I shall be known by you not as I am known here; where, I say, I shall be known in the magnificence of another dignity, that is, in the excellence of my divinity. I go to that glory which my Father has, to whom I am consubstantial and coeternal—a glory which, since you are still carnal, you cannot know here in me. Therefore I go by withdrawing my bodily presence from you; I come to you by the coming of the Holy Spirit, showing you the excellence of my divinity. And unless I bestow this grace upon you—that is, unless I send you the Holy Spirit—I cannot be known by you in the substance of my divinity. [Col. 0895A–B]

If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I. Why does he say, “If you loved me”? Did they not love him, for whose love they left the whole world? Indeed they loved him, but not with the love with which they afterwards began to love him. They had beginning love for God, and they also had advancing love; but they did not have perfecting love. Therefore they heard from the mouth of Truth: “If you loved me.” It is as though he had said: If you loved me as you will love me later, when you receive the grace of the Holy Spirit who is coming, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father. You would rejoice, I say, in the joy of my divinity, by which I am coequal and consubstantial with the Father. You would surely rejoice because I, who now eat and drink with you, am true God and true man. But because you rejoice only in my human nature, which you see, and have no joy in the visible and incomprehensible nature of my divinity, I therefore say to you: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.”

He is greater than I in humanity; he is not greater than I in divinity. Yet I myself am greater than myself: for I am greater in the substance of divinity than I appear to your eyes in the substance of humanity. But all these things concerning the excellence of my divinity, which are now hidden from you, will be made known to you through the coming of the Holy Spirit whom I shall send. [Col. 0895B–D]

And now I have told you before it happens, so that, when it has happened, you may believe. For after I send you the Holy Spirit, at whose coming I shall fill you with the inestimable knowledge of my divinity, then you will first believe; then you will first know and love the things which I now have told you.

I will no longer speak much with you. For the prince of this world is coming. Although, according to the opinion of the commentators, the prince of this world is understood to be the devil, nevertheless, because in the sacred Scriptures one and the same expression is often understood both in an evil and in a good sense, I would say—if I dared; indeed, I dare, because I do not consider myself in this to think contrary to sound understanding—that the Holy Spirit may be understood as the prince of the world. Nor is it unjust that we call him through whom the world was formed the Prince of the world; for whatever things were created received their form from him. Thus indeed, at the beginning of creation, it is written concerning him: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth. But the earth was formless and empty, and the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:1–2).

He therefore says: “I will no longer speak much with you, for the Prince of this world is coming.” It is as though he said: I have spoken many things to you in my human nature; but after the Prince of this world, the Holy Spirit, comes, he will make few things out of many, because while he enlightens you by the overflowing gift of divinity, he will disclose to you in few words all the things that you need to know. [Col. 0896A–B] But if the Prince of the world is the Holy Spirit—or rather, because he is—how can what he says be understood:

And he has nothing in me? Shall we say that the Holy Spirit has nothing in him? Far be such a thought from the minds of the faithful: that the Holy Spirit, with whom he is one God, should be said to have nothing in him. It is as though he had said: As I and the Father, so the Holy Spirit, who is one God with us, is Prince of the world, and he has nothing in me—that is, he does not have merely something in me, but he has the whole of what I am, the whole of what is divine and human in me; he has it in me and with me. That I am God, he has with me; that I am man, he has with me, because in the divine nature I am true God with him, and in the human nature I was conceived as true man from him. [Col. 0896B–C]

But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father has commanded me, so I do. Therefore, I say, the Prince of this world, the Holy Spirit, comes in order to make both you and, through you, the world know that I am God and man: God, because I love the Father—that is, because in my divine nature, in which I am consubstantial with God the Father, as the Father loves me, so I too love the Father with that love which no one knows except the Father and the Son; but man, because in my human nature, as the Father gave me commandment, so I do—that is, for the Father’s command and obedience I became man, and for the redemption of human beings I am prepared to give the human nature which I assumed over to death. [Col. 0896C–D]

These are the words of the Gospel reading, which, according to our measure and under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, we have arranged as best we could. Let us now implore his help, that he who is called Paraclete may deign to be Paraclete to us, so that by his grace we may both be enlightened unto knowledge and inflamed unto love; that we may so know what the Father’s love for the Son is, and what the Son’s love for the Father is, that we may also imitate in this present age his obedience by which he obeyed God the Father for the redemption of humankind. Thus may we ourselves at some time be redeemed by his grace and, with all the redeemed, be admitted to the joys of eternal blessedness, where we may deserve to see without end the Father in the Son, and the Son in the Father, with the Holy Spirit. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0896D–0897A]

## HOMILY LIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE NATIVITY OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST

The time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son (Luke 1).

Although all Scripture divinely inspired seems to indicate the joys of everlasting life both through words and through enigmas, the authority of Gospel truth nevertheless declares more fully and plainly what the brightness of the heavenly homeland itself is and of what kind. So too, if the meaning of the present holy Gospel is examined carefully, it mystically declares what honour and glory, what peace and concord, are in the court of the heavenly King, in the city of the living God. For the Evangelist says:

The time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. Since blessed John, whose feast we celebrate today, was the unique herald of the highest blessedness, we may not unfittingly understand by his parents all those who pertain to the joys of eternal felicity: by Zachariah, the human spirit; by Elizabeth, the flesh, which alone bears labour and pain in the present life. Every faithful person, then, has a time of giving birth when, in the time of this mortality, he multiplies—as though a glorious number of children—the praiseworthy fruits of good works, through which he may possess the joys of the heavenly kingdom and the glory of the eternal inheritance. The time of this birth is fulfilled when that end arrives which no mortal can pass beyond. Therefore, if anyone in this time of giving birth strives earnestly in good work to be found not barren but fruitful, then, when this time has been fulfilled—that is, when he has come from the body of death to the state of immortality—it may not unfittingly be said of him that he has borne a son. And it is rightly said that he bore not a daughter but a son, because, once every weakness of the carnal life has then been removed, he will advance into the perfect man, into the fullness of the age of Christ, into the stability of unchangeable righteousness. What joy is made in the heavenly court over the glory of such a birth is rightly indicated by the words that follow:

And her neighbours and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy with her, and they rejoiced with her. The angelic spirits may not unfittingly be understood as the neighbours of every blessed soul; in every battle which it has against flesh and blood, against spiritual wickedness, they always offer it kindly support as true neighbours and those near at hand. For how could fragile man—man who is earth and ashes—ever engage or resist evil spirits, who are burdened by no weight of flesh, unless the host of the heavenly camp unceasingly brought him the aid of its protection? These angelic spirits are also called relatives of that same soul, as having been begotten by one Father, the Lord Jesus Christ. For he who is the author of the angelic condition both wonderfully created human nature and reformed it by wonders. [Col. 0897B–0898A]

Therefore, when any blessed soul has been brought forth from the labours and misery of the present life; when, I say, the report of such a birth—namely, the report of its virtues and praiseworthy merit—begins to be spread abroad in the heavenly court, its neighbours and relatives are rightly said to rejoice kindly with it. For if, according to the testimony of Truth’s own declaration, our fellow-citizens, the angels, rejoice so greatly over the repentance of one sinner, how much greater joy do they have when they know that he has been snatched from the dominion of death and has passed into true freedom, into the glory of the children of God, into the kingdom of immortality, where he cleaves in such union to the author of righteousness that he can no longer contract even the slightest stain of sin? How greatly they rejoice in human blessedness, and with what admiration they display and exalt their assessment of human merit, the further course of the Gospel narrative seems still more fully to show us.

And it came to pass on the eighth day that they came to circumcise the child, and they called him by the name of his father, Zachariah. Since the glory of the Lord’s resurrection is celebrated on the eighth day, the general resurrection of the dead is rightly expressed through the eighth day. But who are those who come on the eighth day to circumcise the child? They are the ministering spirits, through whose ministry every judgment of living and dead will be concluded, as the Lord of judgments himself more plainly testifies in the Gospel: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals” [Matt. 13:41]. The ministering spirits therefore come on the eighth day to circumcise the child, that they may render every chosen person, wholly cleansed from all the misery of corruption, fit to drink from the fountain of eternal purity.

When they see the lowly nature of the human race not only made equal to their own dignity but also marvellously exalted above themselves in its head, the mediator between God and humankind, Jesus Christ, and even in certain members, namely the mother of that same mediator, they greatly wonder that fragile clay gave so great a price of suffering in order to acquire the kingdom of glory—a price for which they know that they themselves never expended even the least labour. Therefore, seeing the incomparable merit of the elect, they rightly judge that they should be called by the name of their father Zachariah, because, according to the magnificent works which they performed in the body, they judge them worthy to be crowned with everlasting honour and glory.

They rightly judge John, the intimate friend of the Bridegroom and illustrious senator of heaven, most worthy through the merits of exceptional innocence for the senate of everlasting glory, since, in order more familiarly to deserve to participate in heavenly secrets, while still in the very time of tender age he utterly withdrew himself from human companionship. They rightly judge Lawrence, roasted upon the fiery gridiron, worthy to be crowned with the laurel of heavenly dignity. They rightly judge George and the other unconquered witnesses of truth, who won a noble triumph over their enemies, worthy, for the shedding of their own blood, of the robe of everlasting glory and immortality. [Col. 0898B–0899A] But that blessed company of the elect, when they see that the angels bring them so much honour of reverence and praise for the merits of their praiseworthy life, thinking not lofty but humble things of themselves, openly declare by the following words to whom the magnificence of their merits should be ascribed:

By no means; but he shall be called John. For when they recall to mind how great calamities and what miseries they endured in exile; when, I say, they remember what temptations they suffered from the assembly of the wicked, and that in all these things they proved glorious victors in the frail body, they ascribe the palm of victory not to their own merits but to the gift and grace of God Almighty alone. They therefore say to their fellow-citizens, those angelic spirits so greatly wondering at the glory of their reward: “By no means; but he shall be called John.” That is: By no means have we been raised to this glory of heavenly dignity by our works or merits; rather, both the merit of our good action and the splendid joy of so great a reward must wholly be ascribed to the grace of him from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift.

Thus too Paul the apostle, outstanding teacher of the Gentiles, ascribed the labour of his teaching and preaching not to himself but to the gift of Christ’s manifold grace: “I laboured more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of Christ with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). Therefore, while the company of the elect attributes nothing concerning the state of its blessedness to its own merits, but ascribes everything to divine gifts, those heavenly ranks of angels magnify and approve their humility more and more, as the following words declare:

And they said to her: There is no one in your family who is called by this name. This is as though they said: You think worthily of the Creator’s majesty when you ascribe the joys of the reward you have received not to your own strength but to the gift of the merciful Redeemer. For there is no one among the children of humankind whom the nature of the human condition does not draw toward seeking his own praise and preferring to glory in himself rather than in the Lord. It follows:

But they made signs to his father, what he wished him to be called. As long as we inhabit the dreadful prison of this mortality, we suffer such great darkness of blindness and are bound by such great mists of ignorance that the consciousness of our own heart is scarcely sometimes known even to ourselves; but another’s remains altogether unknown to us unless it has been disclosed by the gestures or signs of the outward person. The brightness of the heavenly homeland is wholly ignorant of the shadows of such darkness; there the hearts of all who reign with God are illumined by so great a glory of divine light that each person’s affection lies open to every other. And this is why they are said to make signs to one another: there will be no need there to express anything by the movement of the outward person, where the consciences of all are manifest to all. Thus the spirits of the heavenly ranks make signs—that is, through the subtlety of angelic nature they understand what the souls of the elect ask and desire from the Lord: namely, that they long and desire most earnestly to receive their bodies, as the following words declare in fitting order. [Col. 0899B–0900A]

And asking for a writing tablet. A *pugillaris* is properly called that which can be held in the fist of the hand. And what can we understand more fittingly by the writing tablet than the flesh and body of the elect, which in the present life they strove to cleanse from dead works for service to the living God, crucifying it by the strong hand of contrition together with its vices and desires? The spirits and souls of the elect, therefore, seem to ask God with a great cry of longing that they may receive their own flesh, the immortal and incorruptible fellow-combatant of their faithful struggle; for they are unable to have complete joy in the vision of almighty God so long as they cannot have as a companion in the joy of attainment that flesh which they had as their faithful companion in every harshness of the present age.

This too is the power of the mighty cry with which the souls of the elect are reported in the Apocalypse to cry to God in a loud voice: “How long, holy and true one, do you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Rev. 6:10). But when this power of the mighty cry has entered the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth, and the Redeemer himself has satisfied their desire by the resurrection of their bodies, then what is recalled in what follows will truly be fulfilled:

He wrote, saying: John is his name. Therefore, when all the elect who are predestined to eternal life have from the beginning of the world been clothed at once with the twofold immortality of bodies and souls, and recall that they escaped all the labours and miseries of the present life and every temptation and snare of the ancient enemy solely under the protection of the God of heaven, they declare in truth—not merely in passing words but in permanent writing—that they were saved not by their own strength but by the grace of God alone. Accordingly, in profound humility of body and mind, and in truest self-knowledge, they submit themselves forever to the Redeemer by whom they were mercifully redeemed from the condemnation of eternal death. With this praise and glory of all the elect there will also arise among the highest citizens no small wonder at the indescribable mercy of the merciful Creator, as the following words plainly show:

And all marvelled. Although all the works of our Creator are very great and inexpressible, there is nevertheless one chief work, one surpassing all others: that ancient counsel—that the blessed Son of the blessed God once considered his delights to be with the children of humankind. The whole dignity of the heavenly ranks therefore marvels, and in marvelling magnifies, that God, who was without time, willed to become man under time; that he whom the vastness of heaven and earth cannot contain willed to be conceived and enclosed in the womb of a tender Virgin. [Col. 0900B–D]

But will the very company of the elect, ungrateful for so great a condescension, thereafter cease from the praises of its Redeemer? Certainly not; for immediately his mouth was opened, and his tongue, and he spoke, blessing God. By the mouth, which is outward, every visible aspect of a human being is expressed; by the tongue, which is inward, that which lies hidden invisibly in a person’s conscience may not unfittingly be understood. Both together, the outward and inward parts of the elect, are opened in the Creator’s praise in such a way that they shall never again be closed through the ages. Rather, giving thanks to their Creator, they will resound forever with the pleasant joys of their redemption in the most joyful harmony of heavenly music.

And fear came upon all her neighbours. It was said above that the heavenly citizens are neighbours. When they see these same persons, all the affliction of corruption overcome, conformed in every respect to the body of Christ’s glory, holy fear will arise in them—a fear that will remain for age upon age. For they fear with reverent fear; they will revere and praise throughout the ages not only the power of the divine majesty but also the ineffable mercy of the same Redeemer, who loved those whom he created with such weight of love that, having no one greater than himself, he gave himself as their ransom. [Col. 0901A–B]

And all these words were spread abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea. Judaea, which signifies confession, denotes the heavenly city, in which the name of the eternal Creator is continually praised and magnified with the voice of exultation and confession. The hill country of this Judaea is called those ranks of angels which are joined in such proximity to the unbounded light that nothing stands between them and God. Above these hills all the words concerning human redemption are spread abroad, because the angelic spirits themselves never cease to reverence and marvel that the mighty Lord of heaven deigned to become a humble man for human beings.

It will also be a cause for supreme wonder that human nature, brought forth from the clay of earth, has been exalted in its head, the Mediator between God and humankind, above every principality and power, above every virtue and dominion, in such a way that the humanity assumed into God seems to reign in the same brightness in which eternal divinity reigns. Therefore, when all those redeemed by the Lord begin to appear in glory with the author of their redemption, those ministering spirits will do nothing other than what the following words of this Gospel declare:

And all laid these things up in their heart, saying: “What, do you suppose, will this child be?” The only-begotten Son of God, together with his whole body, which is the Church, is in some manner called one child; he will adorn that beloved body with such beauty of immortality that it will be deemed worthy of the proclamation of admiration even by angelic spirits, whose nature is brightness and glory. “What,” they say, “will this child be?”—that is, what will be this exalted assembly of the children of God, so perfect in beauty, so fittingly crowned with glory and honour? For the hand of the Lord was with him. Therefore, they say, man, earth and ashes, deserved such an adornment of brightness because his Creator so deeply sympathized with his miseries and frailty that the Son of the Most High became man. For the Son of God is properly called the hand of the Lord, as the Psalmist says to him: “Your hands, Lord, made me and formed me” (Ps. 118 [119]:73). [Col. 0901B–0902A]

And Zachariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people. The company of God’s elect, prefigured by Zachariah, so long as it bears the body which weighs down the soul, cannot fully know the things of the Spirit. But when this corruptible has put on incorruption, when it has passed into the joys of complete security, there with unveiled face it will perfectly know the fullness of divine wisdom and knowledge. There it declares the joys of its redemption not as future, but as truly already accomplished through the Mediator’s blood; and with the inmost offerings of thanksgiving it blesses and magnifies forever the name of that same Redeemer.

“Blessed,” it says, “be the Lord God of Israel.” It is as though it said: Blessed is he who, in order to make many co-heirs of his kingdom, did not refuse to endure the injury of cursing and the shame of the cross; who visited us amid the manifold misery of our mortality with abundant compassion and mercy; who abolished all that either flattering flesh or raging world used to bring against us through the revelation of his glory, accomplishing the everlasting redemption of his people. To him be honour and dominion through infinite ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0902A–C]

## HOMILY LIV. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE VIGIL OF THE FEAST OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

Jesus said to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” (John 21).

The most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, because he had such great faith and such most ardent love toward his Lord and master, as we heard from the Gospel reading, deservedly received from the Lord, as a faithful steward, the charge of feeding his sheep. He indeed glorified him who is wondrous in his saints by his death, when he devoutly and gloriously died raised up upon the wood of the cross for his sake. But what profit will there be for us in knowing or hearing the merits of so great a man unless we are willing somehow to imitate in deed what we hear? For just as he then asked Peter whether he loved him more than all these, so every day in the holy Church—that is, in chosen souls—after the time of conversion he seeks a greater and more ardent work of faith and love. The Evangelist therefore says:

Jesus said to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” Simon means “obedient”; John is interpreted “the grace of God.” By Simon, who means obedient, any faithful person may be understood who, abandoning the world, seeks to renounce his own wills and, submitting himself to another’s rule for the sake of the divine command and the hope of eternal recompense, strives to obey the Lord’s commands in every respect; and from this good of obedience he deserves to receive abundantly the grace of God, which is figured by John. [Col. 0902C–0903A]

Here the Lord himself, by his teaching, indicates how, at the beginning of conversion, such a person ought to prefer God and his Lord to every pleasure of the world, how ardently he ought to thirst for him, and how vehemently to love him: “Simon,” he says, “son of John, do you love me more than these?” What is meant by saying “more than these,” except that the Lord must be loved more than all earthly and passing things? For “these” is a demonstrative word through which is indicated whatever is visible and transitory in this world.
