It is fitting for those who humbly submit their devout necks to the yoke of obedience and thereby receive greater gifts of graces from God the Father to embrace and love God and their Lord, the Creator and Redeemer of all, more than these—that is, above all visible things and all the world’s riches—not father or mother, not brothers or sisters, but God alone, blessed above all, with all the depths of their soul.

Whoever in the changeableness of this mortality so burns in love for his Creator that he loves God alone above everything that exists, rightly calls upon him as witness to his sincere love, saying with Peter: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.” When a person has advanced in God’s love through true humility of heart, the Lord indicates in the following words with what strict scrutiny he ought afterwards, during the time of good conduct, to punish in himself whatever he has sinned against God:

Feed my lambs. By the lamb is signified repentance, which must first be sought and desired, because unless the sins of one’s former life are washed away by the fitting satisfaction of repentance, the soul is by no means admitted to the mystery of heavenly purity. But when we wipe away the faults of our past life through repentance, released from former sins, we return to true innocence. And observe that he says: “Feed my lambs.” For just as the devil’s feeding is the foul wallowing in vices and sins, so in a certain sense true purity and innocence of heart, acquired through true repentance, is a praiseworthy and delightful refreshment of the Almighty.

Yet while God forgives the penitent person that for which he has wept, and while the sins which he once committed are no longer imputed to him by God, he is commanded to feed God’s lambs not only once but a second and third time, as the Lord says to Peter a second time: [Col. 0903A–D]

Simon son of John, do you love me? He said to him: “Yes, Lord.” He said to him: “Feed my lambs.” As lambs above signify repentance, so here lambs signify simplicity, gentleness, or patience. Therefore whoever, enlightened by the touch of the true light, has risen up against himself and through bitter repentance has returned to true innocence, must henceforth devote himself earnestly to simplicity and not seek human praise for his good deeds. Thus let him be simple in evil, while remembering to be prudent in good. For he does not possess a simple but a double heart who here, proud because of the merit of his good action, feeds upon human favor, [Col. 0904A] yet glories in the future recompense of eternal life.

He also cultivates gentleness, because he wholly prepares rest for himself—rest which he immediately finds in the secret place of his heart—when, living according to the command laid upon him, he now avoids what is forbidden and now courageously and diligently performs whatever is enjoined. He is patient and strong under injuries inflicted, measuring himself so that he is neither unduly exalted by prosperity nor excessively cast down by adversity. It follows:

He said to him a third time: “Simon son of John, do you love me?” Why, after progress in so many virtues, must he now confess his love a third time, unless it is because one who has advanced in such an order is called to the advancement of many others, so that he ought to preside over others who lives more worthily than they? [Col. 0904B] For almighty God wills that the fervent grace of love which he bears toward Him in his heart should also become known to others, and that by the power of teaching he should make others burn and glow for the highest things, remembering to announce and preach to his hearers what he has learned through divine inspiration. Yet that he must utterly fear this office, and be more saddened than delighted by it, the following words properly indicate.

“Peter was grieved,” it says, “because he said to him a third time, ‘Do you love me?’ And he says to him: ‘Lord, you know all things; you 393 know that I love you.’” At the first stage of conversion, it is sweet and pleasant to obey God’s commands devoutly in all things and to prefer nothing to His love. Likewise, in the period of good conduct, when a person sees the number of such virtues increasing in himself, he is rightly made glad. [Col. 0904C] But when he is compelled to be promoted to the summit of prelacy, where he must serve the characters of many people, he rightly has cause for disturbance and grief.

For he knows that it is exceedingly dangerous to examine and judge another’s life when he is scarcely sufficient to govern and direct his own. Therefore he rightly says to the Lord with Peter: “Lord, you know all things. You know that I love you.” As though he said: “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, know whether I am worthy to preside over your people. I perceive in myself no merit, no virtue, no knowledge. Yet I commit everything to your will and cast my whole self before your mercy.”

Hence blessed Martin, who had long desired “to depart and be with Christ,” placing nothing in his own wish [manuscript: *your*], leaving nothing to his own will, said: “Lord, if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor; let your will be done.” When, following the example of this most blessed man, every prelate humbly offers himself to God and his Lord in obedience, he immediately hears how he ought to care for those same sheep:

“Feed,” he says, “my sheep.” As though he said: “Feed my sheep—namely, those of mine who are simple and innocent; and not only the simple and innocent, but also my sinners, made mine indeed through repentance—those over whom I have willed you to preside and whom I have entrusted to your faith and love. Feed them with the utmost diligence of your own; feed them, I say, by preaching, action, and prayer.”

[Col. 0905A] By this threefold nourishment every spiritual preacher ought to feed the Lord’s sheep: by preaching, action, and prayer. He must first exercise himself in lofty deeds, and then admonish others to act rightly. For if life is at variance with speech, he feeds indeed by preaching, but he does not feed by action. Therefore what he thunders forth with his voice he must adorn with the brightness of his character and deeds; and, what is most important, he must commend to the Lord by the continual sacrificial offerings of his prayers the souls entrusted to him, so that they may one day be found in Christ. But how great a labor and how great an anxiety await him in prelacy, the Lord affirms by an oath, as follows:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where [Col. 0905B] you do not wish.” We should observe what youth is, in which a person girds himself and walks according to his own will; and what old age is, in which he stretches out his hands and is led where he does not wish.

Let us hear David speaking of this youth and old age: “I was young, and indeed I have grown old” (Ps. 36 [37]:25). And again: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102 [103]:5). Let us see why a human being should be renewed after the manner of an eagle rather than another bird. For a closer consideration of the eagle’s nature supplies certain things that may be drawn into an example. When it has grown old and its eyes have become dim, it goes up to the very fire of the sun, burns its wings, and then, falling into a fountain, immerses itself three times in the waters; from this it is restored to its former youth.

[Col. 0905C] By the eagle is understood the sinner, weighed down as though by old age and covered, as it were, by a certain darkness, when he loses the youth of his soul and is unable, as formerly, to see the inward light. In order to lay aside the burden of this old age, he seeks higher things in the manner of the eagle, stretching himself with all desire and all intention toward heavenly things. Reaching even to the splendor of the eternal Sun itself, he is more powerfully inflamed and kindled by it. Thus, growing warm with the fire of compunction, he is immersed as though in a fountain when he is drenched by the sweet stream of tears; washed and made white by it, he is renewed in the youth long desired.

The Lord therefore teaches his pastor and preacher that, impeded by innumerable occupations and cares, he cannot possess the grace of such youth according to his wish and desire. Formerly, resting from outward matters, [Col. 0905D] he deserved to be renewed all the more in spirit, the more diligently he trampled in his mind those dreadful things that clamor outside. In that youth he in a sense girded himself, because by the discipline of watchfulness, with God’s help, he vigorously restrained himself from every superfluous desire for visible things.

For as garments are girded so that, hanging down, they do not hinder one on the ground, so he restrained himself by the strict guarding of his life lest he slip into vain and useless things. He also walked where he wished, for, living in abundant tranquility and sweetness of mind, he was permitted now to meditate on sweet things, now to contemplate lofty matters in rapture of mind, [Col. 0906A] and now to give himself to prayer as much as he pleased.

But that in the administration of governance, where many cares enter in, he can have these things less fully and less often is made clear when it is added: “But when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” As though he said: “You who were once wholly inward and clung to the one thing necessary, after you have grown old—that is, after you no longer deserve to be renewed as often as you formerly were by the greatness of my sweetness—you will stretch out your hands: you will extend yourself outward to external tasks. For because of the necessary resources for expenses which must be bestowed upon your children, you must be troubled and anxious about many things. Another, too, [396] will gird you—that is, another labor will bind you—and will lead you where you do not wish, because it is not the purpose of your will that you should be compelled [Col. 0906B] to enter into worldly cares.”

Now he said this—that is, he showed beforehand that it must happen so—signifying that he would glorify God not only in a praiseworthy life but also in his death, by which he dies to God for God. For first he dies to the world through repentance and innocence; second, he dies to sin through patience, gentleness, and simplicity; third, as we have said, in prelacy he dies to God for God, when he begins to die to inward sweetness in order to provide for the salvation of many.

For if precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of those who, living for God alone, die to the world through repentance and innocence, and likewise die to sin through patience and simplicity, then this too is a praiseworthy and glorious death: when, for the gain of many, they begin to die to inward sweetness, so that others also, through their prompting and example, may learn to glorify God in their lives—He who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

397 HOMILY LV. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE COMMEMORATION OF ST PAUL THE APOSTLE.

“Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?” (Matt. 19.)

Because the blessed apostles of Christ were the most perfect of all human beings, they rightly dared to say to Him who searches hearts that they had left all things, and rightly and deservedly professed that they had followed Him himself. Although they had left few visible possessions, [Col. 0906D] they nevertheless left everything, because they had lost every will and every desire to possess. After this degree of such great perfection, they also strove to follow the Lord by the merit of a praiseworthy life along a yet more exalted way. By the Lord’s gift they, above all other people, were able to do these things; and they deserved to hear in what reward they would receive for them.

But we wretched people also, if we wish to be their imitators and sharers in their reward, ought, following their example, to leave all things and follow the Lord according to our ability. For what is it for any blessed and faithful person to leave everything, except to turn away from evil with his whole will? What is it to follow the Lord, except, after the beginning of good will has been undertaken, by which one turns away from evil, to devote oneself [Col. 0907A] to virtuous action? It is indeed praiseworthy to leave everything—that is, to turn away from evil. But because perfection does not consist in this, it is a praiseworthy good to follow the Lord—that is, to do good; for the former merely escapes punishment, while the latter increases and confers the reward of merit. Therefore, leaving all things—that is, turning away perfectly from evils according to their strength—and following the Lord—that is, pleasing the Lord by good action—they rightly say with the apostles to the Lord: “What then will there be for us?” “We desire,” they say, “to know and understand, Lord, what reward you grant us not only in the future but also in the present, [398] because we have left everything and followed you.”

But Jesus said to them: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit [Col. 0907B].” In this regeneration, which the blessed Son of God promises to those who carry out His commands, renewal of the mind may fittingly be understood, a renewal worked by true compunction of heart. For when a person is perfectly and humbly pierced inwardly by compunction, he is invisibly regenerated before the Lord: stripped, by grace working with him, of the oldness of sins, he is cleansed and renewed by Him as though wholly another person. Such and so great is this regeneration that it makes him who is dust and ashes, according to the Lord’s present saying, a seat of supreme and eternal majesty. “In the regeneration,” he says, “when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty.” But what is it for the Son of Man to sit on the throne of his majesty?

A human being who is to be saved, who has good will toward God and toward the things [Col. 0907C] of God, but is not yet able to bring good will into good action, is indeed a seat of God, but a seat of weakness. But when he has put off the old man and, regenerated and renewed through continual compunction of heart, has begun to apply himself vigorously to good works, he is rightly called not a seat of weakness but a throne of God’s majesty, in which the almighty Son of God does not disdain to sit and reign.

And truly blessed are those who have been regenerated and cleansed in this way. For, since the Lord sits and rests in them through the presence of his divinity, they too will nevertheless be established upon twelve thrones, because they deserve to possess with authority their body and soul, their inward and outward senses, [399] which are to be understood as twelve thrones. Therefore, when the Lord had first said, “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty,” he immediately added: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” They become powerful possessors of themselves when, with God’s grace aiding and cooperating, they so subject the body to the spirit that the senses of both their inner and outer human being taste, seek, or love nothing but God. They also judge the twelve tribes of Israel when they examine and scrutinize with the greatest care individual words, thoughts, and deeds—which are, as it were, the twelve tribes of Israel, namely of the soul that sees and desires to see God—to discover whether even in their good deeds there is anything that might offend, however slightly, the eyes of the inward Judge. [Col. 0908A]

But because the merciful and compassionate Lord so refreshes and consoles His elect and perfect children with the sweetness of His word that He nevertheless neither rejects nor despises the weaker and less perfect, the eternal wisdom of God rightly foresaw that the earlier part of the Gospel reading should concern only the perfect, while the latter part should invite and teach those still weak and infirm to attain the summit of perfection. Hence it follows:

“And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life.” This house, which one who desires to attain the height of perfection must first leave, fittingly signifies the earthly heart and the evil will or conscience of a person. There, truly, the work of goodness, truth, and grace begins: first of all, a person must cast away the evil will—that is, the will to sin—and leave the earthly heart; as long as it remains subject to sins, it may rightly be called the house of the devil. Therefore the Lord says to Abraham: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. 12:1). [Col. 0908B]

After leaving the house, brothers must be left as well. For after a person has rejected the evil will of the earthly heart, he can, with God’s help, also abandon the works of the flesh, which may be understood by brothers. But because some reject the works of the flesh while not abandoning its desires, the eternal wisdom of God rightly taught, after the house and brothers have been left, that sisters too must be left. For it is not enough to reject the works of the flesh unless one strives in every way to oppose carnal desires, which we may understand by sisters. The father too must be left, by whom the devil is signified. For he is the one who gladly inhabits this house, that is, the earthly heart; he is the one who produces in a person’s heart these execrable brothers and sisters, namely evil works and evil desires, and hastens by various temptations to resist their abandonment and rejection. He perfectly leaves this father of evil offspring who strongly and courageously resists his temptations and oppositions.

But opposition of this kind cannot be perfect, stable, and firm [Col. 0908D] unless the mother is left as well—that is, unless a person utterly opposes worldly conduct. Since it nourishes and cherishes the evil children of whom we have spoken, it can fittingly be understood under the name of mother. After leaving his mother, as soon, I say, as he has passed from worldly conduct to the warfare of the spiritual life, it remains for him also to leave his wife: that is, to reject and despise in every way the pleasure of the flesh, which may be understood by the wife. For one who does not fear to live according to fleshly pleasure in the spiritual life cannot please God. Once the wife has been put away, children too must be left; these are worldly senses. For one must take the greatest care not to dare to treat or judge spiritual matters and causes according to secular perceptions, but, in all simplicity, humbly submitting to the commands and judgments of elders, should strive to avoid evil and embrace and love good. [Col. 0909A]

After all these things, fields too must be left for the Lord’s name. A person is recognized by a name; therefore the Lord’s name may fittingly be understood as the knowledge and recognition of the Lord, to which purity of mind and sincerity of heart alone lead a person. By fields, however, good works may fittingly be understood. But how do we say that good works must be left? They must not be left; yet they must sometimes be interrupted for the sake of the Lord’s name, which is the knowledge of the Lord. For as soon as, through God’s prevenient grace, a person senses that it is fitting to devote himself to the study of reading and prayer, the fields must be left: outward good works must for a time be interrupted, so that he may pass to inward goods. The goods by which the outward person is exercised must be interrupted, so that the inward person may be admitted more sweetly and freely to that pleasant name which is the knowledge of God, revealed in the contemplation of the mind. [Col. 0909B]

Everyone, therefore, who in this way has left not only all evil and harmful things, but has also, when fitting, interrupted outward goods in order to receive and attain inward goods, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life. This hundredfold which he receives is the abundant fullness of the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which he is invisibly filled and enriched inwardly. Eternal life, however, may be understood as the understanding of Holy Scripture, through which, by God’s gift, a person is enlightened and made alive in this life, so that he may more happily deserve to live with Him in the life to come—He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

402 HOMILY LVI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE OCTAVE OF THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL.

“Jesus commanded his disciples to get into the boat” (Matt. 14).

If we wish to examine the words of this Gospel reading with subtle consideration, we find in it a great manifestation of divine mercy toward His elect: namely, that He never abandons them in temptations, nor allows them ever to be tempted beyond what they can bear. For just as of old He did not delay mercifully to aid His disciples, endangered amid the waves of the sea, so now every day He mercifully and invisibly comes to meet the dangers of His elect laboring in this great and wide sea, rescuing them from the storm of heavily pressing temptations and bringing them to the harbor of rest and tranquility. But those deserve to experience the Lord’s consolation and help in temptations who strive to obey Him in those things which, in this Gospel reading, He commands and counsels.

“Jesus commanded his disciples to get into the boat and go before him across the sea.” By the Lord’s disciples in this place we may understand ourselves and all who bear the Christian name; [Col. 0910A] by the boat may be understood the congregation of the present Church, or any good and spiritual manner of life. Therefore the Lord commands His disciples—those, I mean, who have resolved to live under His discipline—to enter this boat, that is, a good and spiritual life, and to go before Him across the sea: to despise all transitory things and to pass beyond, through the desire for immortality, the straits of mortality by which they are oppressed in this world. But how long every person who is to be saved must go before the Lord across the sea in this manner is shown by the following text.

“Until he had dismissed the crowds,” it says. The Lord undoubtedly dismisses the crowds when every disturbance of the elect ceases. But when will this be, unless when the present life ends and a person is brought to the height of heavenly glory? Therefore, as long as one lives in this mortal flesh, the Lord is said in a sense to be with the crowd. For He who deigns to dwell in the hearts of His elect does not disdain to be disturbed in them also; and if any adversity or trouble is perhaps inflicted on them in this world by the wicked, He certainly reckons it as an injury to Himself and, as the head, suffers with them as with His members. Thus He says to Saul, while Saul was still persecuting His members: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). [Col. 0910B] For He had already passed, by the power of His resurrection and ascension, beyond all the misery of this mortality; already crowned with glory and honor, He had taken His seat at the Father’s right hand. Yet He said that Saul was persecuting Him, though Saul could not approach Him at all. This is what we have said: He suffers daily whatever His members suffer from the reprobate. And although He, the head of this body—which consists, namely, of all the elect—now manifests Himself free above all things, He nevertheless still feels the disturbances of the reprobate through the body which He retains below. It follows:

“And when he had dismissed the crowd, he went up the mountain alone to pray.” Therefore, when the crowd has been dismissed, that is, when every disturbance of His members has been stilled—which will never happen until the present life comes to an end—then, according to the Evangelist’s words, He goes up the mountain alone to pray. What can the mountain more fittingly signify here than the height of the heavenly court? Jesus ascends this mountain alone with His whole body after the general judgment has been completed. He is said to ascend alone because Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and human beings, after gathering all His members, becomes one body with the assembly of the righteous. [Col. 0910D] For He is the head of the body, while all the elect are members of this head; just as the ancient enemy is one body with the company of the reprobate, because in this world he held precedence over them in wickedness, while they, in serving wickedness, clung to him like a body joined beneath its head.

The Evangelist says: “He went up the mountain alone.” But what did He ascend for, or why? To pray, certainly. Here a question presses upon the mind: why is He said to pray, since where all the elect, united to their head and freed from the bonds of their corruption, have attained those joys of freedom, there is no need to seek mercy by prayer, because there is no misery there. But this question is quickly resolved if we recall that before God everything which the elect, still established in this world, do for the praise and glory of their Creator is prayer. For often, when we stand at God’s service, we sing a hymn to the Lord in sweet melody, in which often no words of prayer sound; yet it will be reckoned as prayer because it belongs to the Creator’s praise. For if everything which we do in the valley of tears for the glory of our Creator may in some way be called prayer, how much more is this so in that blessed homeland, where there will be no evil and no good will remain hidden? [Col. 0911A]

Therefore the elect are said to pray in that heavenly court; and this is nothing other than that they will praise, without weariness, in the joy of everlasting jubilation, God their Creator and Redeemer, whom they will love without satiety. They delight to sing forever of the Lord’s mercies, through whose blood they deserved to attain the glory of so great a blessedness. Saint David, beholding by the spirit of prophecy the ineffable joy of their blessedness, said to the Lord: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83 [84]:5).

“But when evening had come, he was there alone.” By this evening may be signified the end of the present life. When this evening has come, Jesus will remain alone upon the mountain, that is, in the height of the heavenly kingdom; alone, I say, because, as was said above, head with members—that is, Christ with the faithful—will be one body with the whole multitude of the faithful. But the ordered sequence of the following text expresses what meanwhile often happens in this world to those whom that eternal rest will receive in the future:

“But the boat was being tossed by waves in the midst of the sea, for the wind was contrary.” By the boat, in a sound interpretation, may be understood either the present Church, any spiritual congregation, or any faithful soul. Whichever of these we wish to understand by the boat, what the Evangelist says is certainly, indeed most certainly, true: “But the boat was being tossed by waves in the midst of the sea.” Whether it is the Church, any holy congregation, or any blessed soul, as long as it remains in the midst of the sea—that is, in this world—it is tossed by waves, oppressed and distressed by various temptations. Whoever thinks rightly understands how true this is. For when a soul thinks that everything about it is proceeding rightly, in less time than it takes to speak the waves of the great sea rise up—that is, the various troubles of temptations come upon it—troubles whose source or root one is not even permitted to investigate. [Col. 0911D]

There are three things contained in this Gospel passage: the sea, the waves, and the contrary wind; for the stormy disturbance of temptations arises from these three—namely, from the world, from one’s own flesh, and from the devil. The sea, by which the world is figured in the manner of divine speech, troubles the soul by prosperity and adversity. The waves, by which carnal necessities may be understood, burden it with vices and desires. And even if these two sometimes grow quiet, behold, the contrary wind threatens—the devil, who does not cease by day and night to unsettle the soul with his suggestions. Therefore, when we are assailed in this way and afflicted on every side, we must flee sluggishness of mind and strive with every diligence to be watchful in good actions. For if we do this, we shall experience the Lord’s help and consolation in so critical a situation, as we find in what follows:

“But in the fourth watch of the night he came to them.” In ancient custom those on campaign divided the night into four watches; and the end was always about the fourth watch of the night, when dawn began to break. By the four watches may be understood the four principal virtues: temperance, prudence, fortitude, and justice. Many call these cardinal virtues, because just as a door hangs on its hinge (*cardo*), so the other virtues subsist in and from these. Let us therefore inquire a little more carefully how each person ought to possess these virtues.

Temperance arises in a person when, moved beforehand by fear of almighty God, he desires to restrain himself from unlawful things. If he has committed capital crimes in the world, he withdraws from them utterly; or if he has not committed graver offenses but has nevertheless lived childishly in this life—by “childishly” I mean that he lay foolishly and wantonly in a certain negligent sluggishness—he endeavors to restrain and correct himself in all these things. [Col. 0912C] But what benefit will temperance bring if the virtue of prudence is lacking? For it is little to turn away from evil if one does not know how to be diligently watchful in good. There are some who do not know how great is the difference between light and darkness and who often reckon evil good and good evil. If they wish to escape this fault of ignorance, they should strive to acquire the virtue of prudence in this manner: if they themselves have understanding, they should devote their whole mind to the study of sacred reading, so that among the Lord’s words they may learn what they ought to do; or, if they are not themselves fit to understand Holy Scripture, they should not cease diligently to seek its truth from those who know it.

When a person has thus received the gift of prudence, he has now completed not only the first but also the second watch. But many seem indeed endowed with prudence, while their mind, still confused by its own weakness, does not carry out even what it can understand prudently. Therefore it is necessary that the third watch, called fortitude, be added, so that one who prudently understands what he should do may strongly and courageously carry out what he has understood. Yet after these three watches have been completed, Jesus still does not come—that is, He does not make Himself present through the grace of inward sweetness—unless the fourth watch too is completed, which is called justice. [Col. 0912D]

What is justice, which surpasses the other virtues, except profound humility of heart? For true justice is said to be giving each person what is his due. What else does true humility of heart do but give to each one—that is, to God, oneself, and one’s neighbor—what is his own? It gives God what is His in this manner: whatever progress one has made in good actions, one ascribes it wholly to God alone; one diligently considers one’s own weakness, and does not exalt oneself on account of goods received through grace. Thus, when one ascribes to God all that one is and does, one also gives oneself what is one’s own, since whatever wickedness, sluggishness, or negligence one finds in oneself, one humbly acknowledges to be one’s own fault. One then gives a neighbor his proper right as well, because one does not rebuke him within oneself by silent judgment. And when one knows oneself to possess some virtue which one sees lacking in a neighbor, one nevertheless does not suppose oneself righteous by comparison with him, because one who truly humbles oneself immediately considers, with the eye of reflection, by what filth of vices one is oneself surrounded. [Col. 0913A]

One also carefully reflects that one does not know one’s own condition: for example, the virtue in which one boasts today may perhaps tomorrow be possessed by one’s neighbor, while one oneself is deprived of it by God’s hidden judgment.

Before anyone completes this fourth watch, which is humility, the Lord Jesus does not come—I mean, He does not come in such a way that a person can have present the sweetness of heavenly contemplation. Let those who have experienced this return to themselves, and then they can recognize in themselves that what we say is true: namely, that a person can never taste beforehand in prayer how sweet the Lord is unless, before the time of prayer, one possesses the gift of true and perfect humility. But those who have not experienced what we say should be watchful with every effort to obtain this from God’s mercy: that He may yet cause them to experience it. Therefore, especially commending humility, the Lord speaks through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). “It is not,” He says, “in the temperate, the prudent, or the strong that I can rest; rather, I have prepared a seat for myself only in the humble.” And David, who had learned this in the book of experience, said thus to the Lord: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50 [51]:18). [Col. 0913D]

And it should be noted that, according to what we said above, the end of the night was about the fourth watch and morning was beginning to dawn. For when a person becomes truly humble, night—that is, sins and vices—comes to an end in him, and that desirable morning, which is the grace of God, rises in his heart. “In the fourth watch of the night,” says the Evangelist, “he came to them.” And how did he come? “Walking upon the sea.” To walk is said of moving gently onward. Thus the walking of Jesus is His sweetly bringing about progress in those who submit themselves to Him so devoutly in humility. He walks above the sea when He grants His elect to trample all transitory things underfoot through love of His most sweet contemplation and to pant for heavenly things with the whole intention of their mind.

“But when they saw him walking upon the sea …” [Col. 0914A] What can we understand by this vision except illumination of the mind? For the more the elect humble themselves, the more they are enlightened to consider the regard of divine mercy toward them. They see the Lord Jesus walking upon the sea because, established in profound humility of heart, they truly consider how, through the sweetness of His inspiration, He has made them pass beyond all temporal things in hope of heavenly things. After such consideration of an enlightened mind, there follows what the Evangelist adds: “They were troubled.” This is a good and salutary disturbance, of which it is also said elsewhere in the Gospel: “Mary was troubled at the angel’s saying” (Luke 1:29). For they are troubled because they utterly despise their own life. Then, truly and perfectly humbled, they recognize that they have never glorified God in their lives as was fitting—God who has granted them such great benefits and, by His free mercy, has often and repeatedly rescued them from many dangers of temptation.

For this reason, disturbed as they are, they often say: “It is a phantom.” What is a phantom except deception? It is as though any blessed person, enlightened by the spirit of humility, said: “Alas, useless sinner! Until now, deceived by false hope, you thought that you were something; but now, when carefully examined, your life is nothing but deception. You hoped that your vigils, fasts, and the other exercises of your labors could be acceptable to God; but alas, wretched one, you have been deceived! For whatever is in your life is either feigned, imperfect, or corrupted by something, such that it is able not only to fail to please but even greatly to displease God, who searches the heart.”

And out of fear, he says, they cried out. Therefore, when each of the blessed is thus humbled, and, in their humility, is so beneficially troubled by recognizing themselves, as we have said, what else do they then do but cry out in fear of the eternal Judge and of that strict examination? They cry out, indeed, to God with the voice of prayer; they cry out also to those entrusted with the care of souls through the words of confession. For each cries out all the more loudly insofar as he more truthfully confesses to God in prayer, and to the confessor in confession, his sins and negligences. When this powerful cry of prayer and confession reaches the ears of almighty [Col. 0914D] God, then without doubt there will truly happen to them what the letter of the Gospel here contains.

And immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying. For immediately, while each elect person thus weighs his life inwardly, Jesus begins to speak to him; because whatever he understands or hears from sacred Scripture then first becomes fruitful for him, and he delights to draw all of it toward his salvation, since he thinks that he himself is marked by everything that it says. For example, when he hears discussion of pride, anger, the sluggishness of negligence, or any other vices, he reproves each vice within himself; and, silently rebuking himself in thought, says: “Alas, wretch! You have committed all these things; in all these things you know yourself to be guilty. For pride puffs you up, anger disturbs you, and besides this you find in yourself an infinite negligence of life.” [Col. 0915A] When each of the blessed thus thinks such lowly and contemptible things of himself, he sometimes hears inwardly within himself this sweet and fatherly admonition of the Lord:

“Take courage,” he says. For confidence is so called from faith. That the Lord admonishes His elect to have confidence is as though, through the voice of inward visitation, He says to them: “Now, conscious of your weakness, you humbly despise your life; it remains for you henceforth to have firm, steadfast, and constant faith in the humility you have begun, considering that I am He from whom comes everything that you possess, and whatever progress you have made in good works; and that it must likewise be through My gift that you are able to persevere in them. If you consider and humbly acknowledge this, do not [Col. 0915B] fear”—that is, let the disposition of fear be transformed into the disposition of love.

This may also be understood thus: that the Lord speaks these words for the consolation of those who truly humble themselves: “Do not fear,” He says. “If, in the spirit of humility, as you have begun, you have now resolved to serve Me, do not fear that your former sins will be imputed to you; for they have already been covered and forgiven through My grace.” It follows:

But Peter answered and said to Him: “Lord, if it is You, command me to come to You upon the waters.” This name *Peter* is interpreted “one who recognizes.” For he who truly recognizes—that is, who knows in himself all these things which we have mentioned—often answers such consolation from the Lord with the rejoicing voice of his heart: [Col. 0915C] “Lord, if it is You, command me to come to You upon the waters.” “Lord,” he says, “if it is You—indeed, because it is You—Yours is the power, Yours is the strength, to command me to come to You upon the waters: that is, to bring it about that, in hope of attaining Your love, I may be able to trample underfoot all the desires of this world.”

And He said: “Come.” For God’s speaking is His doing. What He says—“Come”—is this: He grants fulfillment to the devout desire of His elect who so humble themselves, so that they may be able to tread beneath the steps of His love the pleasures of the age, and, desiring Him and loving Him, may cling to Him alone and only to Him. But after someone has attained the inward quiet of the mind, he will also be able to experience in himself what follows.

[Col. 0915D] And Peter, descending from the little boat, walked upon the water in order to come to Jesus. The aptness of the words should be noted; then it will become clear what sweetness and grace they contain. “And Peter,” he says, “descending from the little boat.” For when each elect person, who may rightly be called and be one who recognizes, perceives so wondrous and ineffable a grace of divine mercy overflowing within him, he descends from the little boat: that is, from a humbled heart he advances more and more into humility. Thus it comes about that, at the hour when the soul is made so near to God through the gift of humility, it embraces all people, enemies as well as friends, with the affection of sweet love. It no longer delights in rendering evil to anyone for evil, but resolves within itself that, should harm be inflicted upon it, it will willingly [Col. 0916A] embrace it, bear it patiently—indeed, render good in return for the evil inflicted.

Then it also walks upon the waters, because it now truly and perfectly tramples all earthly desires. It walks, surely, because it sweetly advances from virtue to virtue, until the God of gods is seen in Zion. It despises every prosperity and patiently accepts adversity, provided only that it may come to Jesus: that is, through the sweetness of inward contemplation, may become ever nearer to God. But because, however much the happy soul advances in God and however exalted it becomes in contemplation, it will nevertheless never be free from temptations as long as it is weighed down by earthly habitation, the following is fittingly added:

But seeing the strong wind, he was afraid. By the wind in this place may be understood the favor of human praise. [Col. 0916B] Nor without reason is human favor received under the figure of wind. For what is the word by which one person praises another except wind? A person sees the strong wind when a weak mind, receiving the breeze of human favor for its good actions, is drawn away toward outward joys, so that it sets aside what it desires inwardly and gladly lies dissolved in what it hears outwardly. It rejoices to be called blessed, thirsts after the sounds of its own praise, and now judges itself to possess some great merit.

For while such a wind puffs it up from one side, another wind sometimes threatens from the other, by which the weak mind is no less shaken and somewhat moved from its state of uprightness. This wind, indeed, is human reproach and false accusation. For the very person who is made exceedingly cheerful by delight in the love of his own praise [Col. 0916C] and secretly swells within himself is again pierced by immoderate grief, if perchance the dart of reproach and false accusation is shot from a neighbor’s mouth—for example, if someone says: “This man, who appears to advance thus from virtue to virtue, does not strive to do everything in God or in simplicity of heart. His every action is a kind of pretense; he lives less praiseworthily and greatly desires to be praised.”

All these things are not without reason called a strong wind, because they prevail over the weak mind and violently shake it by their force. Seeing himself by no means fit to endure these things, holy David prayed to the Lord, saying: “Redeem me from the calumnies of men” (Ps. 118:134). For calumny is a false accusation. [Col. 0916D] Hence Solomon says: “Calumny disturbs the wise man and destroys the strength of his heart” (Eccl. 7:8).

Therefore, when the mind feels the opposition of these winds—that is, when it is raised up by prosperity and easily cast down by adversity—it begins again to fear. Though it had already been released from the chains of carnal desire and knew how to direct the free step of love toward its Creator, now, just as it had formerly, sweetly intoxicated by love of its Redeemer, continually panted after contemplating the beauty of His exaltation, so again, when the force of temptation comes upon it, laying love aside, it trembles before the examination of the strict Judge.

And when he began to sink, he cried out, saying: “Lord, save me.” Each blessed person certainly begins to sink when, in the deep humility of the heart, [Col. 0917A] he casts himself down before God; when he humbly sets his faults before the eyes of his heart and, on their account, turns his whole self to the laments of penitence. Then he also begins to cry out; by this cry may be understood the inward desire of the heart. There Judah and Tamar meet: undoubtedly confession and bitterness. For in the bitterness of his soul [the manuscript: “my soul”] he confesses the troubles of his temptations; and the more he trembles under assault, the more strongly he desires to plant the foot of hope in the help of his Creator alone, and day and night he does not cease to entreat Him for his deliverance: “Lord,” he says, “save me.” As though he were saying: “Lord, who are eternal salvation, I perceive that the supreme consolation of my now troubled mind is this: that, assaulted by temptations, I should flee to the hope of [Col. 0917B] Your mercy alone. Save me by mercifully delivering me and granting me tranquillity from the vices which attack me.”

But does the Lord, by whose grace and gift a person is anticipated so that he begins to know and lament his sins, turn away the ear of His mercy from the cries and sobs of one who thus invokes Him? No. Rather, just as He once stretched out His hand to Peter when he faltered amid the waves of the sea, so now every day He will be present to help the soul that seeks Him amid all temptations. Therefore the Evangelist adds:

And immediately Jesus stretched out His hand. For by saying “immediately,” he means the same thing that the Lord promises to His elect through the prophet when He says: “Before you call upon Me, I shall say: Behold, I am here.” “And immediately,” he says, “stretching out His hand, He caught him and said to him: ‘O you of little [Col. 0917C] faith, why did you doubt?’” Therefore for Jesus to stretch out His hand is to exert the force of His power against the vices attacking a person—so to exert it that He expels them and restores the mind to quiet and tranquillity.

“He caught him,” he says. To catch is said when a person suddenly draws something to himself. Thus the Lord catches each blessed person when, by the sudden fervor of His inspiration, He draws him, so to speak, almost against his will away from dissipation of spirit, anger, hatred, and every other unlawful thing; so that the mind, immediately raised by His gifts, becomes vigorous, though only a little before it was being weighed down by contending vices. Then He also says to him: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?”

For we find a threefold faith in the sacred Gospels: namely, the least, little, and great faith. [Col. 0917D] The least faith is said to be when a person is anxious about the body and bodily matters. But he has little faith who is lifted up by prosperity and broken by adversity; and it is this little faith that is reproved here. The Lord in a certain manner speaks in a person when the person, speaking with himself in the bitterness of his soul and thinking nothing of himself except what is lowly, rebukes himself inwardly, saying: “Behold, wretch assaulted by vices, it is clearer than light what you are: that your faith until now has been little. For when the prosperity of this world smiled upon you, you were exalted in empty joy; again, when adversities threatened, you uselessly hurled yourself into the abyss of immoderate sadness. [Col. 0918A] Hence all that you have lived has been, as it were, doubtful, precisely because you have never walked before God in truth, never with a perfect heart.”

If a person has thus conducted himself and strives to persevere in such knowledge of his own weakness until the end of his life, then the reward of eternal exaltation will follow this abasement of true humility. Therefore it is immediately added:

And when He had entered into the little boat, the wind ceased. In this place the little boat may signify the repose of eternal life. When Jesus enters into it with His whole body, the wind will doubtless cease, because there every onset of temptations will surely be stilled. There will also sometimes be a moment in this life when the Lord enters the little boat [Col. 0918B]—that is, joins Himself to the humility of the soul—and the wind ceases: that is, every temptation comes to rest, and the mind, longing only for contemplation of its Creator, established in the greatest tranquillity, despises all present things without conflict of thought. But in eternal life temptation will cease fully and perpetually, where no affliction opposes us and where we suffer nothing from the devil, the world, or our own flesh that could disturb the joys of our everlasting tranquillity.

But those who were in the little boat came and worshiped Him, saying: “Truly, You are the Son of God.” By those who were in the little boat we may understand the inward and outward senses, through which and in which a person subsists inwardly and outwardly. All these come in that blessed repose [Col. 0918C] and worship: that is, they exult in the living God by giving thanks, attributing the joys of their blessedness to His grace alone, then truly confessing Him to be the Son of God, because through the power—indeed, the mercy—of His divine majesty He has brought them to the glory of perpetual immortality: He who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

### HOMILY LVII. THE SECOND FOR THE SAME OCTAVE

Jesus commanded His disciples to enter into the little boat (Matt. 14).

The disciples of the Lord in this passage represent all worshipers of the Christian religion, and signify especially those who, after the example of those who then bodily [Col. 0918D] adhered to His discipleship, resolve to leave everything and follow the Lord. The Lord confidently commands these to enter the little boat in their blessed resolve: namely, a good and spiritual life; and to go before Him across the strait—that is, to pass beyond the burning heat of carnal desire.

And one should note what He says: “to go before Him across the strait.” For that person is said to go before who waits for another following after him. The Lord wishes us to go before Him across the strait in this way: by manfully leaping over the heat of carnal desires, to wait for Him to follow us, consoling us here and rewarding us perpetually hereafter. “Until,” [Col. 0919A] says the Evangelist, “He had dismissed the crowds.” Since *crowd* (*turba*) is named from disturbance (*turbatio*), we may quite suitably understand disturbed senses by the crowd. We must indeed go before the Lord until He dismisses the crowd within us: that is, drives away disturbed senses and admits and bestows pure and quiet senses. We have disturbed senses when, wearied by the trouble of temptations, we are not permitted to do the good we would wish, and are bound under sin’s yoke to things we do not wish.

“And, having dismissed the crowd,” he says, “He went up alone into the mountain to pray.” The crowd is indeed dismissed when the stings of temptations have become quiet and, through God’s grace, free choice is granted us for the performance of good works. Therefore, with the crowd dismissed—that is, with disturbed senses somewhat calmed through God’s cooperation—each blessed person goes up the mountain: namely, he will be able to reach the height of inward contemplation. [Col. 0919B] He goes up the mountain when he is touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, is summoned to heavenly desires, and, raised inwardly beyond the narrow confines of the flesh by love of his Creator, is granted to know how to contemplate His beauty. He goes up alone because, when the mind is suspended in divine contemplation, so that it already rejoices in perceiving through a certain image something of that eternal freedom which eye has not seen nor ear heard, at that hour the created spirit doubtless becomes one with the Creator Spirit.

“He went up,” he says, “alone into the mountain to pray.”

[Col. 0919C] For prayer does not always mean that someone entreats God concerning one or another of his needs; it is sometimes also understood as praise of God. Therefore, when someone has thus, as we have said, gone up the mountain alone, he surely prays, because whatever he does or thinks in such illumination of mind belongs wholly to the praise and glory of almighty God, with whom he has now, through inward sweetness, as we said before, become one spirit.

But when evening had come, He was there alone. By this evening we may understand knowledge of ourselves. For evening comes about in the human heart when a person truly recognizes the darkness of his blindness; and in this true and perfect knowledge he is sometimes so pierced by God’s inspiration that, in the compunction by which he weeps for his sins, [Col. 0919D] he is also deemed worthy to taste how sweet the Lord is. In a certain manner morning comes about in a person when he has attained the knowledge of God. Hence Moses the lawgiver, describing the creation of the world, says so often: “Evening came, and morning, one day.” Evening and morning came when a person can possess knowledge of himself and knowledge of God. From this evening and this morning one day is made, because knowledge of oneself and of God makes a person perfect.

“When evening had come,” he says, “He was there alone.” Therefore, when this evening of which we have spoken has come, a person is alone because, when he is suffused with the light of that inward sweetness which he has gained through the humility of self-knowledge, he thinks of nothing apart from God and is wholly suspended upon Him. The tumult of earthly deeds falls silent in his thoughts, so that the mind may more intimately incline its ear toward the inward secret [Col. 0920A] and may be able to sigh, burn, and pant from its inmost marrow for Him whom it loves.

But these words which we have examined morally may also be understood otherwise. For there is no obstacle if, by the evening mentioned here, the end of a person is understood. Evening indeed comes when, at God’s call, the soul must leave the enclosure of the flesh. It is well said, therefore, that “He was there alone,” because in that evening God alone has His being with that person who has conducted himself, as we have said, during the course of the present life. But because, however deeply the mind of each elect person may be rooted in the love of eternity in this world, it is nevertheless violently shaken by great terror at the very point of death, it is fittingly now said:

But the little boat was tossed by waves in the midst of the sea. [Col. 0920B] In this place the little boat is the humbled soul. When it sees that its last day has now come upon it and considers that the terror of strict examination is at hand, it is then tossed by waves: that is, dread and fear rush over it. Note what he says: “it was tossed by waves in the midst of the sea,” because [the manuscript: *qui*, “who”] even if in the present age it had advanced so far as to be moved neither by prosperity nor adversity, it will not then be free from fear, because it now sees that the inward Judge is at hand, before whom not even the smallest thought is hidden, and who must examine the secrets of its heart.

“For,” he says, “the wind was contrary.” What could be understood more fittingly by the contrary wind than the ancient enemy of the human race? Although he lies in wait for a person throughout all the days of his life and does not cease to oppose him, he will nevertheless be more contrary than usual at that hour. Then, like a roaring lion, he circles about, seeking to devour the soul and draw it with himself to the destruction of eternal damnation. [Col. 0920C] But does the Lord despise His own at such a crisis and fail to defend them from the deadly ravager? Far be it! Rather, He does what follows:

But in the fourth watch of the night He came to them. By these four watches we may suitably understand faith, hope, charity, and perseverance. Therefore whoever has kept these four watches in this world—that is, has possessed right faith, firm hope, perfect charity, and perseverance in these until the end of life—to him Jesus will come in the hour of final need, giving some sign of His mercy so that he may not despair. “In the fourth watch of the night,” he says, “He came to them.” According to those who in ancient times were on military service and divided the night into four watches, dawn always began to break about the fourth watch. The fourth watch is when a person is called to leave this night—that is, the present life—and to arrive at that bright morning of eternal blessedness. [Col. 0920D]

“He came,” he says, “to them, walking upon the sea.” The Lord walks upon the sea when He has decreed to free the soul from the enticing misery of this life. “But when they saw Him walking upon the sea, they were troubled, saying: ‘It is a phantom.’” They see the Lord walking upon the sea when, at the very point of death, they consider that just as no one [Col. 0921A], whether righteous or unrighteous, can pass beyond this limit, so they too are now to be called out of the present age and set before the terrible examination of the strict Judge.

When the elect consider this at that hour, although they are conscious that, insofar as was possible in this world, they have walked before God in truth and with a perfect heart, they are nevertheless troubled, fearing that before the inward Judge they may not be found such as they were considered here by human beings to be. Then, troubled, they break forth into these words: “It is a phantom.” In the spirit of humility they sharply reproach themselves and truly recognize that their whole life, if the Lord’s mercy be set aside and it be examined, is nothing but a kind of deception, [Col. 0921B] because they have either committed evil or sinned through lack of caution even while doing what was right.

And out of fear, he says, they cried out. By this cry of which he speaks here, confession and prayer are expressed. When those who are to be saved set their lives before the eyes of their hearts in that dangerous hour of death, they sometimes cry out, truthfully confessing their sins in the bitterness of their souls; they also cry out by inwardly entreating God concerning them. But that the Lord extends the hand of fatherly consolation to the soul laboring at its end and placed in such affliction, the Evangelist well shows in what follows. For he says: “And immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying.” This speech, therefore, is the Lord’s consolation, heard then not outwardly but inwardly. But let us hear what the Lord says in consoling His elect:

“Take courage. Have confidence,” He says, “in eternal salvation; place great trust in My mercy. I am eternal salvation. Therefore do not fear the peril of damnation, but rather hope for the joys of everlasting reward.” [Col. 0921C]

But Peter answered and said. For by Peter may be figured the blessed soul which was recognizing in this world: namely, which had true knowledge of God and itself. When it hears inwardly the words of the Lord’s consolation, this soul, which a little before greatly feared to depart from the body, desires sooner to be dissolved and to be with Christ; it now longs to be without the darkness of the present life, so that it may know what is the joy of eternal recompense. [Col. 0921D] But what does it say when so moved by desire? “Lord,” it says, “if it is You, command me to come to You upon the waters.” “Lord,” it says, “if it is You. I know indeed that You are the One whom I desire, for whom I sigh. But I speak as though doubtfully, saying, ‘if it is You,’ because I have not yet received in reality what I possess in hope. For I am still shut out and do not openly enjoy the joy of contemplating You. Command me, therefore, to come to You upon the waters: that is, make me pass beyond the misery of this pilgrimage, and, with You as my guide, arrive there where Your true being is.”

And He said to him: “Come.” This is the same as what He says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned.” “Come,” He says: that is, lay aside this mortal body which weighs you down and enjoy the presence of the longed-for vision of Me.

[Col. 0922A] And Peter, descending from the little boat, walked upon the water in order to come to Jesus. Therefore, at God’s call, every faithful soul descends from the little boat: that is, it leaves the dwelling of the flesh, is led out from the present Church, and begins to walk upon the waters—that is, in migrating to heavenly things, it passes beyond all the enticements of this world. Note that the Evangelist says “was walking,” which is as though he said, “he began to walk upon the waters.” For at that time the soul begins to be separated from the body, when, being in its final agony, it feels nothing in this world and nothing of those things which surround the body, but attends only to the invisible things of the age to come, to which it is now about to pass.

For this reason the happy soul is led out from the midst of the shadow of death: that it may come to Jesus—that is, be consoled in the embraces of its heavenly Bridegroom—and [Col. 0922B] after the misery of this pilgrimage, may always see Him in the joy of everlasting jubilation. But because the ancient serpent, like a highwayman lying in ambush, besets the road by which it journeys to its homeland, the Evangelist fittingly adds:

But seeing the strong wind, he was afraid. By the strong wind we may understand the devil. This adversary, who did not prevail against the soul departing from the body, trusts that he may prevail against it once it has departed; and he will stand ready before it as it journeys by the narrow way toward its homeland, casting in its face some evils which it did, or good things which it ought to have done but neglected. He also casts before it many things which it never did—or, if it did them, which it nevertheless washed away by penitence—so that by such an accusation he may prevent it from entering upon the way of blessedness. Thus he set himself before Martin, but discovered that he could find nothing of his own in him. [Col. 0922C] When it sees this strong wind—that is, the devil—thus reproaching it and casting such things before it, it rightly trembles and fears.

This may also be understood thus: that the soul sees the strong wind when, led out of the prison-house of the flesh and set before the presence of the strict Judge, many things suddenly come forth which it had not thought evil even here, and therefore had delayed to blot out by satisfaction worthy of penitence; there also things which it had judged to be good appear as blackest sins. When the soul sees these things, it indeed fears before the face of the Judge and His strict examination.

[Col. 0922D] “And when he began to sink”: that is, when, because of its sins which it did not wash away here through the sorrow of penitence, it fears that it must now undergo the sentence of damnation—then that soul which is nevertheless to be saved, trusting in the mercy of Him whom it remembers to be not only its Judge but also its Redeemer, cries out in such distress, imploring the help of His mercy: “Lord, save me.” As though it says: “Lord, I now truly see that whatever good I have ever done is not worthy of Your appeasement. I am now set where there is no place for penitence, where I can neither appease Your face by confession nor labor in good works. By Your free mercy save me; receive me to Yourself, delivering me from the hand of the stranger and from the present anguish by which I am constrained.”

But does the compassionate and merciful Lord despise there, for small things, the soul which in this flesh has done great things for His sake? [Col. 0923A] By no means. Rather, He is prepared to help the one who prays, as we have in what follows.

And immediately, stretching out His hand, He caught him. For as long as the soul was enclosed in the prison-house of the flesh, the Lord had His hand, so to speak, as though held out: because even when He came to help and gave rest from the attacking vices, He withdrew His help more swiftly than words can say and allowed its quiet to be disturbed by something. But there, then, as Lord of hosts and King of glory, He will in a certain manner stretch out His hand, because He will so perfectly free the soul from every corruption that it will never again be subject to the dominion of vices or to any danger.

“He caught him,” he says. We say that to catch is when a person suddenly draws something to [Col. 0923B] himself. Thus the Lord catches the blessed soul in the future so that it can never be separated from Him, but may itself rest forever in the embrace of love, in the vision of its heavenly Bridegroom.

And He said to him: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” These words sound as though the Lord Himself speaks them in rebuke. But, according to the interpretation we have given, it should rather be understood that the soul itself addresses these same words to itself; for it would be quite unfitting that words of the Lord’s rebuke should follow after it has attained the joys of such great blessedness. [Col. 0923C] As we have said, when that soul has been thus made blessed in the Lord and beholds there the joys of angelic and human blessedness, when it contemplates what is their unending festival of the vision of God and their unfailing joy, it rightly says to itself: “O you of little faith,” because there it truly knows that what it now possesses in reality was little in faith and hope in this world. Thus, now enjoying the vision of the true Peacemaker, it can use the words of the queen of the south: “Your works are greater,” she says, “than the report that I heard” (3 Kings 10:7).

And when it considers there how great were the benefits of God overflowing toward the human race—so great that He did not spare even His own Son, but gave Him up for the redemption of that same human race—and when, in that heavenly court, it beholds very many who, once placed in this world, were oppressed by the heavy weight of sins, yet whom He mercifully received after opening to them the bosom of His mercy, and thus exalted upon the lofty throne of His glory: then, because of ineffable joy, [Col. 0923D] it rebukes itself, saying, “Why did you doubt? Since you knew all these things in faith, although you did not see them in reality, why did you ever doubt concerning the salvation of body or soul?” This rebuke is a full and ineffable exultation of the heart.

“And when He had entered,” he says, “into the little boat, the wind ceased.” Here, by the little boat, we may understand the joyful and desirable hall of the heavenly kingdom. When the happy soul has been introduced into it, the wind will cease: that is, every disturbance; no temptation will assail it any longer. It follows:

But those who were in the little boat came and worshiped Him, saying: “Truly, You are the Son of God.” Who are those who stand in the little boat except the blessed ranks of angels and the elect? If, then, as Truth itself [Col. 0924A] testifies, there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance, how greatly, we ask, do they rejoice at the assumption of one whose conversion they so kindly celebrated? “They came,” he says, “and worshiped Him, saying: ‘Truly, You are the Son of God.’” Therefore all the elect, seeing such grace bestowed by God upon the soul, come and worship: that is, they rise up in thanksgiving, praise the power of His divinity, by and through which He protected it from the hostile power and brought it forward to contemplate the beauty of His exaltation. He lives and reigns as God with His coeternal Son and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

### HOMILY LVIII. FIRST FOR THE FEAST OF THE TRANSLATION OF ST. BENEDICT

[Col. 0924B] “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light” (Luke 11).

By this lamp is understood the most sacred humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, which God the Father truly kindled and illuminated with the light and flame of His divinity. For the light in the lamp is divinity in human nature; it so shone forth and so radiated in this world that it alone, above all human beings, was free from every stain of sin. This lamp was placed neither in a hidden place nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light.

What are the hidden place and the bushel? So far as we can understand, by these two may be signified two peoples: the Gentiles and the Jews—by the hidden place, the Gentiles [Col. 0924C]; by the bushel, the Jews. And Gentile life is not incongruously signified by the hidden place, because, by persisting in its unbelief, it is in a certain manner hidden from God, and God Himself is hidden from it. Yet I do not call it hidden from God as though God does not know it or does not see its perversity—for God knows and sees all things—but it is said to be hidden from Him because He has excluded and removed it from all His love until it comes to its senses.

But by the bushel, which is a certain measure, is understood that Jewish people measured by the Law, for whom all the commandments of the Law were so measured and ordered that, according to the quality of each person’s offense, the measure of punishment had to be exacted—for example, one had to render eye for eye, tooth for tooth, fracture for fracture. [Col. 0924D]

But this lamp, namely the illuminated humanity of Christ, ought not to dwell or be placed either in the hidden place or under the bushel—that is, either among the Gentile people or among the Jews—but upon the lampstand. And what is signified by the lampstand except the holy Church? The Church is aptly expressed by the lampstand, because just as a lampstand is brought into its form and nature now by fire, now by the repeated and various hammerings of the smith, so the holy Church has from the beginning been formed, and is formed and polished until the end, through the hand of the supreme Craftsman by the varied and countless hammerings of persecutions, labors, and sorrows, so that it may be found worthy even to suffer punishment while holding the light of this lamp—that is, faith in the Son of God. [Col. 0925A]

But why was this lamp placed upon the lampstand—that is, Christ upon the Church—except so that those who enter, namely all Catholics, whether Gentiles or Jews, who enter through faith, may see the light, hold the faith of Christ’s humanity, and be saved? These things may thus be understood concerning Christ and the Church.

Nevertheless, these same words of this holy Gospel touch us, concern us, instruct and edify us. “No one,” says the Lord, “lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but on a lampstand.” God in some manner lights and illumines every faithful person predestined to eternal life, when from his gratuitous goodness he grants from above the light of some good knowledge and good will, and deigns to inspire it in him from heaven [Col. 0925B]. These two things, namely good knowledge and good will, are a kind of lamp of the soul. Enlightened and kindled by them, the soul ought to prepare and offer its whole self so that the light of God’s grace may not be made ineffectual in it; for it will then be useless and unfruitful if it refuses to cooperate with God’s grace.

For a person puts his lamp in a hidden place if he does not bring to the fullness of perfect action the light of good will, good knowledge, and good dispositions with which God has filled him. He will be an imitator 425 of that wicked servant who, having received his lord’s money, went away, dug into the earth, and hid his lord’s money (Matt. 25:18). That hiding-place of the money corresponds mystically to this hiding-place of the lamp. For just as one is figuratively said to hide God’s money when he is unwilling to invest the gift of God which he has received for the gain of good action [Col. 0925C], so he too puts his lamp in a hidden place who does not put into practice what he sees through knowledge, what he possesses through good will, what he understands, and thus makes it unfruitful and useless both for himself and for others.

But if someone performs works which may be called good, yet performs them for human praise, he undoubtedly puts them under a bushel. What does the bushel signify but temporal recompense? If anyone eagerly seeks this and always desires to receive transitory praise for his good deeds, he will lose the exalted reward of eternity. Yet amid these matters one must know what it means to lose one’s good works altogether and what it means not to lose them. A person does not lose his good works [Col. 0925D] if he began them with a good and simple intention rather than an evil one. Since the beginning of his intention was good and sound, although vainglory may steal in—if some frivolity intervenes—when this is recognized and, with God’s help, washed away by the gift of repentance, the good of the past work is not lost. But one who is corrupted at the beginning of his thought, and seeks through these deeds to please not God but human beings alone, loses everything he does, however just and upright it may seem, because an evil intention went before it. He will belong to the number of those of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2).

Therefore our lamp must not be put in a hidden place, because we must by no means be sluggish and dull in doing good; nor under a bushel [Col. 0926A], so that, if we do works worthy of praise, temporal recompense may not please or delight us through them; but upon a lampstand—that is, upon our body—because we must place the honor of God and the welfare of our soul above all the earthly conveniences of our body, so that we establish the Lord above and ourselves below, humbly submit ourselves to his grace, and submit to him who reigns above us and governs us.

Certainly that blessed David had placed his lamp upon a lampstand when he said: “If I remembered you upon my bed, 426 in the early mornings I shall meditate upon you” (Ps. 62:2). It is as though he said: “Because above all things and in all things which were sweet and pleasant to me according to the flesh, I loved you alone, O Lord my God; I possessed you and remembered you, therefore in the early mornings I shall meditate upon you. For when your serene morning shall come, when the heavenly kingdom shall shine upon all your elect, you will lead me there, where I shall always meditate upon you, never departing from you.”

By “bed” may be understood the same thing as by “lampstand,” namely our body, in which the wretched soul lies back and rests as upon its bed. The remembrance of God, however, which ought to be upon that bed, is the honor and praise of God: those holy words which we use in God’s service. Yet we are not mindful of them but, alas, forgetful, while there, where our meditation ought to be fixed upon God alone, we are stung by injuries inflicted upon us and ponder and consider what just retort we may make against wrongs unjustly done to us. Hence, because the remembrance of God is not upon [Col. 0926C] the bed of our body, but we place the remembrance of our bed above the remembrance of God, it often happens by his just judgment that we do not meditate upon him in the early mornings. For when the bright morning of his sweetness shines upon those meditating upon him, we remain in the darkness of our heart and are unable to perceive or see anything of that morning.

But why ought our lamp to be so kindled, and why ought it to be placed not in a hidden place nor under a bushel but upon a lampstand, except because of what follows: “that those who enter may see the light”? There are good persons and evil persons who enter. Where? Into our heart, surely. Good affections, good desires, and holy thoughts enter the heart; but evil thoughts and unjust desires also come to the heart, and enter it in order to commit and work some evil there. Since this is so—indeed, since nothing is truer—let us raise the lamp, kindle the light, and always retain within us the light of God’s grace and remembrance. For if we keep this light continually, when good and holy thoughts enter, they rejoice and delight in this light; when evil and useless thoughts come, they are terrified at the sight of this light and are driven out.

Elsewhere the Lord confirms this teaching when he says: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved” (John 3:20). 427 Everyone who does evil is every perverse thought that comes either from the devil, from the flesh, or from the world. Every such perverse thought hates this light [Col. 0927A] and does not come to this light, lest its works be reproved. But every wicked thought reproved by this light is immediately put to flight and expelled. With regard to such great and such perfection as you have heard, our Lord Jesus Christ took care to admonish his children, in whom he wished his own dwelling to be stable.

This grace of perfection was faithfully attained by our blessed father Benedict, one of his children, whose feast we celebrate today. He truly placed his lamp neither in a hidden place nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand. For while still of tender and youthful age, he strove so to cooperate with the divine will inspired by God that, abandoning everything he might have possessed in this world, naked and unencumbered [Col. 0927B] he sought the wildernesses of the forests. There, having deprived himself of every bodily comfort and repose, he set the honor and remembrance of God above every bodily sweetness and prosperity. For the lamp of God’s grace burned inwardly, and therefore he made little of what he suffered outwardly.

But let us now return and see what the Lord adds:

“The lamp of your body is your eye.” By these words, as we think, the Lord explained the preceding words—he who knew how, and was able, to contain and utter great and profound mysteries in brief and few words. And those blessed apostles to whom he spoke these things, taught as they were by the eternal wisdom of God, could know in very few words what these things meant. But for us, foolish and slow of heart, who scarcely understand a few things even if many are said [Col. 0927C], it is necessary that they be explained more plainly, with God’s help.

By the eye, intention may be understood; by the body, a person’s work. If the intention of the heart is good and pure, it is the lamp and light of the whole work.
