Let an example therefore be set forth, and let us see how an evil intention makes a good work perverse. There is someone who speaks sweet and loving words to his neighbor, not, I say, from the affection of sincere love, but for the sake of cunning deception. He displays indeed a good work; but because his intention was evil, that eye was not the lamp of the body. There is someone who prays much and does a good work; but if he prays with the intention of being seen, this eye of perverse intention is not the lamp of the body [Col. 0927D], that is, of the work. There is someone who gives much to the needy; but if he does it in order that people may call him blessed and praise him for the generosity of his almsgiving, his eye—that is, his intention—is not the lamp of his body. Yet because we do not readily know how to distinguish duplicity from simplicity, the Lord teaches us in what follows what true simplicity is.

“If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light.” True simplicity has two eyes, by which it sees clearly. One eye is knowledge of the good; the other is love of the good. If a person does not know this knowledge of the good, let him learn it and ask someone wiser and better than himself what knowledge of the good is; and, having received knowledge of the good, let him ask the Lord that love of the good may be given him [Col. 0928A]. For if he knows but does not love, he sees indeed and does not see: he sees with one eye but does not see with the other. But if he both knows the good and loves it, this single eye makes the whole work full of light.

“But if it is evil, your whole body also will be dark.” Just as the single eye has two goods, knowledge of the good and love of the good, by which it is enlightened and guided, so the evil eye has, conversely, two points of vision: ignorance and malice. Ignorance is when one does not recognize what is good. This ignorance must not be called or named simplicity, but great foolishness and stupidity. This ignorance produces malice from itself, so that one envies others the good which one does not know; or, if one perhaps knows it, one can never, because of the malice pressing upon the heart, love it either in oneself or in one’s neighbor [Col. 0928B]. This evil eye makes the whole body dark, because where ignorance and malice have taken possession of the heart, a person’s entire work is in the night and darkness of sins.

Therefore, that we may avoid these things and carefully attend to ourselves, the Lord warns us, saying: “See therefore that the light which is in you is not darkness.” What is it to say, “See,” except: Carefully beware lest the light of God’s grace which is in you should become the darkness of ignorance and malice? “If therefore your whole body is full of light, having no part of darkness, it will be wholly full of light.” This is as if he had said: If your whole work is so full of light that it has no portion of darkness—neither a portion of the darkness [Col. 0928C] 429 of ignorance nor a portion of the darkness of malice—it will be wholly full of light here and in the future; it will be wholly full of light before me when, at the judgment, I come to examine words, deeds, and thoughts. There, if your eye is now single, if you have also loved the good which you recognized, if you have avoided malice and ignorance, you will be wholly full of light. You will pass through and arrive at that brightness of eternal life, where no part of darkness will ever meet you.

That we may deserve to become wholly full of light there, it is necessary that he who said nothing superfluous or foolish in his Gospels may deign to fulfill in us what he added at the end:

“And as a lamp of brightness shall give you light.” The lamp of brightness is, as I have said, the grace of divine and inward splendor. By it, while a person is inwardly illumined for knowing the good [Col. 0928D], he is also outwardly illumined for accomplishing it. And while he strives to labor outwardly, by his outward works he merits that he may be more and more inwardly enlightened, as the Lord says in another Gospel: “Every one that bears fruit, he will prune it, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2).

Truly our blessed father Benedict, whose feast we celebrate today, possessed a single eye in every respect, because he knew the good and loved the good. He did not possess an evil eye, because he diligently avoided ignorance 430 and malice. He was a lamp placed upon a lampstand, burning and shining, so that he might shine upon all who are in the house of God. Let us look to this gleaming lamp and see in it where we ought to direct the step of our work, hoping that, as soldiers under his leadership [Col. 0929A], we may be admitted to the palace of the heavenly King; and let us trust that, what we do not presume upon our own merits, we may attain through the intercession of this same leader of ours.

Certainly, when he rises in the general resurrection, all ranks of both sexes and every age, who now have fought bravely beneath the banner of his holy rule, will then, gathered into one, follow his banner. And truly blessed are those who will not be absent there, who are found worthy to be present in such an army! Let us therefore earnestly implore our most blessed father Benedict not to forget the name of father in his children. Let him remember that, although less courageously and less gloriously than we ought, we have fought the Lord’s battles, yet for the love of our King we have never laid down the standards of our service [Col. 0929B], but have always stood by him according to our measure. May he not reject us on the day of the last examination, but grant us a place among the innumerable multitude of saints whom he acquired for the Lord, through him who lives and reigns through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LIX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST. PATERNIAN, BISHOP OF BOLOGNA

“A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and entrusted his goods to them” (Matt. 25).

Because the words of our Lord and Savior taste more sweetly and draw the human mind more delightfully to the love of God when they can be gently interpreted for the instruction of human life, let us see whether, by the gift and grace of the Holy Spirit, something may occur to us from the hidden meaning of this Gospel reading which may inwardly draw and kindle us toward our own profit, instruction, and salvation [Col. 0929C].

“A certain man,” says the Lord, “going abroad called his servants.” This certain man who goes abroad may fittingly be understood as any person who is to be saved. He remains “man” so long as he loves and follows that which he is and that from which he is—namely, earth, that is, his flesh and the pleasures and desires of the flesh. This man, this certain man, becomes a single or distinct man when he begins somewhat to separate and restrain himself from his fleshly pleasures. He goes abroad when he makes a blessed passage from the world to God, from the carnal life to the spiritual, from earthly and perishable things to the seeking and obtaining of heavenly and eternal blessedness [Col. 0929D]. And rightly it is said, “going abroad.” For it is an exceedingly arduous 431 pilgrimage for a person to depart from himself, to leave himself behind, and to stretch himself toward that which is opposed to himself: so that one who formerly, by loving the world and the things that belonged to the world, was a carnal man, may begin to be a spiritual man and to live spiritually through chaste and sober living.

When he thus at last goes abroad, thus forgets the things which are behind, what he must then do in order to arrive is mystically shown by the following order of the Lord’s words.

“He called,” it says, “his servants and entrusted his goods to them.” These servants may be understood as the human senses. He calls his servants when he gathers and recalls his senses to himself, within himself, in order to subject them to himself and make them serve his own benefit and salvation [Col. 0930A]. “And he entrusted his goods to them.” These goods, insofar as it is granted us to understand, are all the works of divine mercy and compassion. When a person begins humbly to recognize, weigh, and magnify them within himself, and thereby gathers himself to fear and love God, this is truly to entrust his goods to his servants.

“And to one he gave five talents, but to another two, and to another one.” According to the sequence of the letter, this man seems to have given five talents to one of the servants. But we, as we suppose by the generosity of the Holy Spirit, who gives to each as he wills, considering something else in these words, leave it to the reader’s judgment whether he wishes to receive our interpretation—although different from others, yet, as we think, not discordant with truth [Col. 0930B]—provided only that he understands us to devote such effort as we can, not to the display of those who praise us, but to the edification of those who hear.

Through this threefold distribution of talents we may understand the inseparable operation of the supreme and undivided Trinity. For by the one to whom five talents are given, God the Father is understood, whose work is our creation; by the other to whom two are given, God the Son, whose work is our creation and redemption; by the other to whom one is given, God the Holy Spirit, whose work is our illumination. Observe how appropriately and significantly the Evangelist, in these words which we refer to the Trinity, says “one,” “another,” and “another,” not “first,” “second,” and “third.” For in the holy Trinity the Father is one God, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; yet in this Trinity nothing is earlier or later, but these three are coeternal and coequal with one another. 432 [Col. 0930C].

Therefore, we give as it were five talents to the one when we honor and praise God the Father, who created us and enriched us in soul and body with five senses, as though with five talents. We assign as it were two to another when we humbly praise and love God the Son, who created and delivered us, for our redemption. We give one to another when we glorify and praise God the Holy Spirit, who, by the infusion of his light, illumined the darkness of our ignorance both for the knowledge of God the Father, who created us, and for the knowledge of God the Son, who delivered us. For neither our creation nor our redemption would have profited us [Col. 0930D] unless the illumination of the Holy Spirit had been added, so that we might know our Creator and Redeemer.

This threefold yet inseparable operation of the holy Trinity is expressed still more clearly when it is added: “To each according to his own ability.” The Father’s own power is to create us; the Son’s own power is to deliver us; the Holy Spirit’s own power is to illumine us—yet we call each one’s power “his own” in such a way that we do not doubt that their operation in our salvation was shared. Therefore, when the person to be saved thus ascribes to each according to his own power—that is, when he begins to recognize and love the work of his creation in God the Father, the work of his redemption in God the Son, and the work of his illumination [Col. 0931A] in God the Holy Spirit—it may rightly be said of him: “And immediately he went away.”

This departure is the departure of the soul, when through humble remembrance of God’s benefits a person advances so far toward God that, for his love, he despises and makes little of every perishable and earthly thing. From this inward progress there likewise comes a sound and saving progress in the outward person, when he does not cease to exercise himself in holy and righteous labors even in his external senses. Therefore the Lord says:

“He who had received five talents went away, traded with them, and gained another five.” Whom, I ask, does this one who had received five talents signify, except the one and same person? He who gave is himself he who received. He gives God the five talents which he received from him when, by keeping his body and bodily senses from sins and vices, he begins steadfastly and diligently to serve God. While thus he labors tirelessly for God with the five talents received from God, he gains another five. 433 For the gifts of the five senses, expressed by the five talents, become other gifts and yet remain the same. They are transformed and changed for the better when, after long labor and prolonged zeal and effort in bodily discipline, those things which formerly were carnal and insensible become spiritual and intellectual [Col. 0931B].

“Likewise, he who had received two gained another two.” By the two, understanding and action are signified. The person who had received two gains another two when he directs wholly toward God and the things of God both his understanding, formerly carnal and carnally minded, and does not neglect to carry out and show by right action the things which he rightly understands concerning God.

“But he who had received one went away, dug into the earth, and hid his lord’s money.” This one talent which the third servant had received prefigures only the understanding of the person to be saved. He goes away and digs into the earth when, by unceasing meditation, he digs, splits, and searches that earth which bears the fruit of salvation and grace—the earth, namely, of Holy Scripture—to see whether he may find there something that inwardly awakens and kindles him to the desire for eternal things [Col. 0931C]. He hides his lord’s money when he does not cast forth the gift of spiritual knowledge and understanding in the boasting of pride, but stores and conceals it within himself through humility, lest it be seized and stolen by wicked robbers, namely evil spirits. Instead, alone with the One from whom he received it, he rejoices and delights in the secret of his humility.

Whoever is the person who, by meditating, understanding, and acting in this manner, displays in himself the form of these three servants, Almighty God never abandons him. Rather, he draws near to him when, after the weariness of long bodily labors, he comforts and relieves him by the remedy of his hidden visitation and consolation. Therefore he added and said:

“After a long time the lord of those servants came and settled accounts with them.” He rightly says, “after a long time,” because this person’s time is not short or small, but very long and great in the sight of the divine majesty. For just as those who lived wickedly and uselessly are before God and in his reckoning persons of no time or moment, so those who live according to God are esteemed before him as persons of much time. Therefore, after a long time 434 [Col. 0932A] the lord of those servants comes, when, after much labor, he bestows upon them great consolation in his visitation. There he settles accounts with them when he grants to a person that he may lay himself down, that he may truly submit himself to his Creator, Deliverer, and Enlightener—to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—in true humility of heart. For this humility gives a person a certain approach to God, as is mystically suggested when he immediately adds:

“And he who had received five talents came forward and offered another five talents, saying: ‘Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained another five.’” What do this reckoning and this offering of talents express for us except humble thanksgiving, through which a person humbly submits himself to God when, whatever strength or good action he perceives to be present and active in his inward or outward senses, he humbly attributes and ascribes it not to himself but to him from whom he received it? To him the Lord says: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful in a few things, I shall set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.”

Then he who had received two talents came and said: “Lord, you entrusted two talents to me; behold, I have gained another two” [Col. 0932C]. His lord said to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful in a few things, I shall set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.” The person who had received two talents presents another two gained when, both for the spiritual understanding which he possesses inwardly and for the good action which he performs outwardly, he submits his entire self to God and ascribes it, in humble thanksgiving, to him alone from whom he has it.

But because both he who brings back five talents with gain and he who brings back two signify one and the same person, each is rightly honored by the lord with one and the same response: “Well done,” he says, “good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful in a few things, I shall set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.”

Observe why he says, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” A good servant is one who diligently performs whatever good works he can. But if from his good deeds he seeks not God’s praise but his own, he cannot in any way be called a faithful servant. Therefore the one who is good and faithful—that is, who willingly performs good works and seeks from these good deeds not his own glory but God’s—will hear that true “Well done” from the Lord, because he will inherit eternal 435 salvation with the Lord: “Well done,” he says, “good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful in a few things, I shall set you over many things” [Col. 0932D].

As Blessed Gregory says, all the goods of the present life are few things. But the good and faithful servant will be set over many things when, in that eternal blessedness, in exchange for these few goods which pass with time, he will enjoy without end those many goods of the heavenly homeland which are neither numbered nor bounded [Col. 0933A].

But because after this joyful promise of eternal goods he repeats not once but a second time, “Enter into the joy of your lord, enter into the joy of your lord,” a certain twofold joy is set before us. By the grace of heavenly visitation, a person conceives it in the present life, and is sustained here for the time being by it until he reaches that joy which is never disturbed and is limited by no end. We may interpret this twofold joy as “the lower watering-place” and “the upper watering-place” (Judg. 1:15). The lower watering-place is when a person is humbly pierced by compunction through remembrance of the sins which he recalls having committed through either his outward or inward senses. The upper watering-place is when, through the humble thanksgiving which he offers God, either for his spiritual understanding inwardly or for his good action outwardly, he is carried forward so far that he is invisibly touched within by the grace of God’s sweetness. This is truly joy, and the joy of the Lord. By it, as we have said, the good and faithful servant is meanwhile comforted and sustained here, until he reaches that place where he is set over many things, where he may rejoice eternally in him who is the joy of all his saints, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

436 ## HOMILY LX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST. MARY MAGDALENE

[Col. 0933C]

“A certain one of the Pharisees asked Jesus to eat with him” (Luke 7).

Our Lord and Redeemer, who descended from the bosom of the Father into the womb of his virgin mother in order to save the human race, often deigned in the days of his flesh both to be invited and to come to a banquet—not that he might delight in the outward provision of food, but that he might display there some great work of mercy, by which he might summon and kindle human hearts toward the desirable and inexhaustible feasts of eternity.

With the same compassion and mercy he entered the house of this Pharisee, not so much in order to eat with him as to invite this blessed woman, whose feast we commemorate today, cleansed from the filth of sins, to the banquet [Col. 0933D] of his own feast. Thus even now, whenever he deigns to come daily to the house—that is, the heart—of any person who is to be saved, according to the grace of his ancient compassion he works some great and memorable work of salvation. What could be greater than, according to the multitude of his mercies, to forgive sins and form a person in virtues? But how this comes about, or from where it begins, the present reading of the holy Gospel mystically suggests to us.

“The Evangelist says, ‘A certain one of the Pharisees asked Jesus to eat with him.’” A Pharisee, which is interpreted “separated,” may aptly be the name of any person when, anticipated by the grace of heavenly mercy, he begins to separate himself from the world and the sins of the world [Col. 0934A]. For such a name by no means suits him so long as he embraces and loves in body and heart, with desire and affection, the world and those things which are of the world. But as soon as, having cast these aside and despised them, he has entered upon the warfare of holy conduct, he must, after the example of this Pharisee, ask the Lord to eat with him. God’s eating with a person is his working the person’s salvation within that person. For our salvation is God’s food.

With what diligence and steadfastness of mind he ought to be asked and invited to the banquet of this food, Paul, the excellent teacher of the Gentiles, more plainly suggests to us in his words: “Pray,” he says, “without ceasing” (Acts 12:5). A person prays without ceasing who every hour and every 437 moment implores the aid of divine compassion, not only by words [Col. 0934B] and tears—which cannot be done at every moment—but by vows and desires.

It is rightly shown that a certain Pharisee asks Jesus to eat with him when every convert, at the beginning of his conversion, now by prayers, now with all the desires and affections of both the inward and outward person, humbly entreats the Lord: just as through his great mercy he willed to separate him from the world and unite him to the company of his own people, so may he also deign through his assisting grace to cooperate with him in the spiritual life, so that by the convert’s good manner of life both the person may be refreshed and rejoice in God, and God in him. For a person can do nothing of himself unless it is given him from above, as the Lord himself shows elsewhere when he says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). It follows:

“And having entered the Pharisee’s house, he reclined.” By the Pharisee’s house is signified the conscience of the converted person. The Lord mercifully enters it in a manner of speaking when, by the grace of his visitation, that person is divinely brought back to himself within himself—that is, into the conscience of his own heart—in order to know himself [Col. 0934C]. He also reclines in the same house when he mercifully causes that person, who until then stood through evil pride, to recline through humility. In that praiseworthy and desirable reclining, what follows immediately takes place:

“And behold,” says the Evangelist, “a woman who was a sinner in the city, when she learned that he had reclined in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster vessel of ointment; and standing behind beside his feet, she began with tears to wet his feet, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, and kissed his feet and anointed them with ointment.” By the woman—so called from *mollitia*, “softness”—the soul softened by God’s grace may suitably be understood. The city in which that woman dwells rightly signifies the human body. It is well said: “And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city,” because so long as the soul rouses, moves, and directs the outward members of the body to works of iniquity, it dwells like a sinful woman in the city of the body. Thus whatever good or evil the outward person does is reserved either for the soul’s reward or its judgment.

But the woman—that is, the blessed soul [Col. 0935A] 438 predestined to eternal life—who was at one time like a sinful woman while she lay subject to sin in the senses of both aspects of herself, as soon as, softened by God’s grace as we have said, she begins to know—that is, to love—that Jesus, the author of eternal salvation, reclined in the Pharisee’s house, that is, that through the entrance of his inward visitation he has somewhat inwardly humbled her after separating her from the world and the world’s sins, brings an alabaster vessel of ointment. This is a contrite heart, strengthened and made firm by true humility for receiving the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

“And standing behind beside his feet.” A person is rightly said to stand when, lifted from the depth of the vices in which he lay while living in a worldly manner, he is raised aloft into the height of virtues by conversion, contrition of heart, and humility [Col. 0935B]. For the Prophet shows that virtue always follows humility when he says: “Rise up after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126:2).

But what does it mean when it says: “Standing behind beside the Lord’s feet”? One who stands behind a person always looks upon, as it were set before his eyes, the one behind whom he stands. He stands behind beside the Lord’s feet who frequently considers, with fearful and humble heart, his mercy and judgment; who, turning his eyes behind him, carefully considers how ungratefully he has behaved toward divine goodness and mercy, and by how many and how great crimes of sin he has provoked God’s strict judgment. With these two feet—his mercy and his judgment or truth—God walks through the whole world over the entire human race. For every human creature is either saved by the foot of mercy or judged and condemned by the foot of his truth.

But that one of many may be an example to us, let us see how David, God’s chosen prophet, placed himself behind beside these feet of the Lord when he said: “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50:1). But for what cause, on what ground? “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (ibid., v. 4). To obtain the grace of divine mercy, he offered not himself, not half his goods, but only the continual remembrance of sin, which true and perfect repentance daily renewed within him [Col. 0935D]. But that we too may be able to efface past crimes and more cautiously avoid future ones, 439 let us hear what elsewhere the Lord said to this same David, and how he instructed him to fight against his enemies.

We read in the book of Kings that, when David had been anointed king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to seek David; and that David himself consulted the Lord whether he should go up against them or not; and the Lord answered and said: “Go up, for I will certainly deliver the Philistines into your hand.” And when the Philistines again went up, David once more consulted the Lord: “Shall I go up against the Philistines, and will you deliver them into my hands?” He answered:

[Col. 0936A] “Do not go up to meet them, but circle around behind them, and come upon them opposite the pear trees. And when you hear the sound of one walking at the top of the pear trees in the dawn, then you shall begin battle against the Philistines; for then the Lord will go out before your face to strike the camp of the Philistines” (II Kings [= II Samuel] 5:19–24, etc.).

By the Philistines we may understand malignant spirits, or any sins whatsoever, which, as though going up to seek David, first strive to seize the heart of every strong-handed athlete of God—who is represented by David—either through an evil thought or an evil will. When these rise against us in this way, we too are nevertheless commanded to rise, since we must set the shield of most unconquerable prayer against the darts of evil thoughts.

[Col. 0936B] For we shall overcome them more easily if we hasten to uproot and drive them away at their very beginning, from the root of the heart. But if they rise again against us—that is, if by their importunity they attempt to bend us toward delight and consent—we are forbidden to go up to meet them, but are divinely taught to circle behind them. Just as persons who walk together along one and the same road are said to meet one another, so in a sense those hasten to meet the Philistines—that is, the malignant spirits suggesting sins—who associate themselves with their path by committing sin.

The Lord calls us back from this path when he says: “Do not go up to meet them, but circle behind them.” As though he said: Whenever malignant spirits meet you by suggesting sin, never go forth to meet them in such a way that, walking the same road with them, you accomplish the deeds they suggest; rather, circle behind them. That is, remember always to stand behind sins, to surround them on every side from beginning to end, so that

[Col. 0936C] you may be able, with the eye of prudent watchfulness, to discern and avoid both their beginning, which arises from thought or evil will, and their end, which is completed through the act of sin. He immediately reveals whence and how a person may advance to this virtue when he says: “And you shall come opposite the pear trees.” Since the first human being sinned through fruit, we may rightly understand by the name of pear trees, which offer a pleasant taste to those who eat them, the delight of sin.

To come opposite the pear trees is to oppose, contradict, and resist delights. Whoever advances in this way, whoever thus raises himself against vices, receives the aid of the pious and merciful Lord through the invisible help of his compassion, as the following wording mystically indicates when it says: “And when you hear the sound of one walking at the top of the pear trees in the dawn, then you shall begin battle against the Philistines.”

By the one walking at the top of the pear trees the only-begotten Son of God is fittingly signified: he lived without sin in the likeness of sin, because whatever is called sin or delight of sin he had so placed beneath and trampled under his feet by the power of his divinity that not even the slightest stain of evil thought could ever approach his most holy

[Col. 0937A] soul. His sound is his inward and invisible visitation. When this sound has sweetly resounded in the inward ears of a human being, that person will be able confidently to enter battle against the Philistines. Then the Lord will go out before him through the power of his divinity to strike the camps of the Philistines: that is, having quieted the greater warfare of vices, he will make his soldier, strengthened by constancy, advance more and more from virtue to virtue.

Thus strengthened by the Lord and in the Lord, a person may, following the example of this blessed woman whose feast we celebrate, water Jesus’ feet with tears, wipe them with the hair of her head, kiss them, and anoint them with ointment. By tears we may understand sorrow of heart and repentance for the past; by hair, the superfluities of the flesh and continence for the future; by the kiss, confession; by ointment, satisfaction for sin. A person waters the Savior’s feet with tears when, through the daily repentance of a grieving and groaning heart, he labors to bend to the grace of mercy the harsh and strict sentence of God’s future judgment that he has deserved. He wipes them with the hair of his head when, diligently restraining and guarding himself against future sins, he hastens to cut away whatever superfluity—that is, whatever sin and iniquity—has reigned either in the mind through an evil intention or in the flesh through evil action.

[Col. 0937B] He kisses them when he strives through true and humble confession to be reconciled to God his Creator. He anoints them with ointment when he begins to mitigate and soften the anger of the heavenly Judge by good works.

How great and powerful the fragrance of this ointment is before God, another evangelist makes known to us when he says: “And the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12:3). This house is the heavenly and earthly Church. For the fragrance of this ointment penetrates even the heavenly dwellings of the blessed, because not only the spirits and souls of the righteous, but also the heavenly company of angels, rejoice and congratulate a person who is perfectly repentant and produces fruits worthy of repentance, as the Lord testifies in another Gospel when he says: “I tell you, there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing repentance” (Luke 15:7).

But the earthly Church too is sweetly sprinkled with the fragrance of the same ointment when all who live with that person

[Col. 0937C] rejoice and are edified by his progress and constancy. After such ointment, after such great works of repentance, when at last the darkness of sins has been removed through God’s grace, the person begins to open a little the eyes of the mind to the light of the knowledge and love of God, as the evangelist subsequently makes clear when he says:

“The Pharisee who had invited him, seeing this, said within himself.” The Pharisee—that is, a person perfectly converted—is rightly said to see him whom he has invited by repenting for the past, restraining himself from the future, and now in some measure reconciling to himself through confession of sin and satisfaction. This happens when love of God somewhat moderates fear, and confidence in hope, renewed by consideration of the divine mercy,

[Col. 0937D] lifts the whole human heart toward God through desire. There, indeed, amid groans and sighs, he often bursts forth in these words:

“If this man were a prophet, he would surely know what sort of woman this is who touches him, because she is a sinner.”

Although every blessed soul may in some sense be believed to touch God whenever it is caught up and raised by contemplation of the mind to the throne of God’s glory through the fervor of most ardent love, yet it truly and especially touches him when, with a chaste body and a pure and humble heart, it faithfully approaches to partake of his most holy body and blood. In that invisible touching of eternal majesty, in that true and inexhaustible tasting of eternal sweetness, mindful of its own miseries and also of the multitude of God’s mercies, it humbly and suppliantly addresses and appeals to him whom it touches and with whom it communicates in words of this kind:

[Col. 0938A] “If this man were a prophet.” As though it said: “If this Lord of angels, merciful Creator and Redeemer, were a prophet—that is, merely a human being and not God—he would certainly know by what and how great contagions of sins this woman, this wretched soul of mine, is defiled and fouled; this soul which burns, thirsts, and pants to touch him, to partake, that is, of his flesh and blood, so that inwardly it may soften and come to life again. But now, because he is God and man, because he is naturally kind, essentially good and merciful, he knows my sins through the power of his divinity; yet he does not know them, because he does not will to know them, through the clemency of his mercy and kindness, which are coessential with him.”

But in another sense, by the name “prophet” one may understand any good prelate or any other person who has learned profitably to prophesy, for himself and others, concerning the future recompense of everlasting life and the condemnation of eternal death. Thus when a blessed person, encouraged by hope in divine mercy, begins at any time to reconsider and recollect the Lord’s mercies within himself, he consoles himself with words like these and says: “If this man were a prophet.” As though he said:

[Col. 0938B] “O Lord, unfailing fountain of compassion, source and fulfillment of eternal sweetness: if any of my neighbors knew, as you do, the hidden wickednesses of my heart; if he found me liable to himself, as I am to you, for so many and such great evils, he would surely know—that is, as I suppose, he would never consign my guilt to oblivion, but would repay my soul with the punishment it deserves in reproaches and injuries. But you, who are in no way like other human beings, who are shown to be the supreme God and likewise supreme goodness: I know indeed that you know my sins through the foreknowledge of your divinity, but I trust that you do not know them because of the inexpressible greatness of your compassion.”

Whoever hopes in the Lord’s mercy in this way, and makes good works accord with good hope, will receive blessing and consolation from the Lord, as the evangelist subsequently adds when he says:

“And Jesus answered and said to him: Simon,

[Col. 0939A] I have something to say to you.” As though he said: “You who until now have lived contrary to the righteousness of my commands: because you have now become Simon—that is, because through repentance for the past, continence for the future, true confession, and worthy satisfaction you have subjected yourself to my obedience—I too have something great, something magnificent, to answer you, something which I ought justly to render in return for your great labors.”

And he said: “Master, speak.” As though he said: “Although, merciful Lord, your mercies abound in my soul, since you have drawn me out of the pit of misery and mercifully rescued me from the depth of vices, nevertheless I call you Master; for, though I desire to love you because of the inexpressible clemency of your compassion which you have shown in me,

[Col. 0939B] I am still compelled to fear you as Master and Judge because of awareness of my past crimes.” The pious and merciful Lord does not despise such humility in a human being, but, in order to make one who humbly fears perfectly loving, he speaks to him inwardly in ineffable words.

“Two debtors,” he says, “owed a certain moneylender: one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty.” In these two debtors we may understand Adam and Eve. Adam was a debtor to a certain moneylender, namely Almighty God, as it were for five hundred denarii, because both by the dignity of his creation and by the perfection of all wisdom and knowledge he excelled every irrational creature. But Eve owed fifty denarii, because, placed under the power of her husband, she received a lesser grace of heavenly gifts.

[Col. 0939C] And God, the creator of all, may indeed fittingly be called a moneylender: for he created us and raised us above his other creatures by sense and intellect so that, both in spirit through holy desires and in flesh through good and righteous works, we might make gain in the present which we may bring back for the praise and glory of his name in the future.

For we are two debtors, who must discharge a debt of five hundred denarii in spirit and fifty in flesh. Five times one hundred make five hundred. This number, and rightly so, because it is perfect and consists of a perfect number, mystically shows us the perfection of the five senses, over which that one element—the spirit in a human being—ought so to preside that in all perfection,

[Col. 0939D] in all holiness and righteousness, it might preserve them clean and unstained for the Lord, without contagion of sin. But a debt of fifty denarii is also demanded from the flesh, which was created as though to assist the spirit, so that it might innocently consent to the spirit in everything and, through the external works of justice and equity, which are fittingly understood by fifty, serve the one Lord humbly and simply, with one vow and desire.

But through the disobedience and transgression of the first human being, that perfect fullness of heavenly gifts was turned into the ill-perfect fullness of sins. Thus the human spirit became debtor for five hundred, and the flesh for fifty denarii, because the transgressions of the flesh are in some manner fewer and less numerous than those of the spirit: the spirit now commits many inward sins through evil will and harmful thoughts, now through unlawful desires and harmful delights, from which the flesh is free because it does not share in them through the performance of sin.

[Col. 0940A] Moreover, by the fifty denarii is expressed the true and perfect repentance for inward and outward transgressions which is demanded from the flesh. When a person to be saved begins humbly, with a repentant heart, to consider within himself these changes of human misery which he suffers now in spirit, now in flesh, the pious and merciful Lord immediately speaks to him inwardly and invisibly: “Two debtors owed a certain moneylender.” These words of the Lord mystically signify the grace of his wondrous visitation, by which he mercifully makes known and intimates to the one whom he visits what he was through himself and what he received from God: how he was conceived and born in iniquities; how after his birth he lived in sins; and how, though he was liable to God’s justice in spirit and flesh as one who had committed many crimes, he was released from the debt of both and restored in baptism to his former innocence through God’s grace. This is what follows:

[Col. 0940B] “But since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave them both.” He forgave both when, as has already been said, he cleansed by his free goodness in baptism both the contaminations of spirit and flesh. By this humble consideration of God’s benefits, a person finally advances more and more from fear to love, as the Lord reveals in the words that follow: “Which of them, therefore, loves him more?”

When a human being asks, he asks in order that he may know what he still does not know. But when God, the Lord of knowledge, asks, he does not ask because something is hidden from him, but in order that through his questioning he may cause us to know what we do not know. Thus also through this question, which is inwardly and invisibly put to a person, he intimates in ineffable words how much love the person owes God when he says: “Which of them, therefore, loves him more?” The Lord speaks these words when he makes the person speak inwardly, when the person himself cries out within himself from the deep humility of his heart: “Which of them, therefore,

[Col. 0940C] loves him more?” As though he said: “It would be fitting that I should love wholly, with my whole self, him who created me from nothing in his image and likeness; who, though nobly created, was wonderfully corrupted, and cleansed me through the grace of baptism. It would be fitting that I should expend all that I am and all that I can do upon the praise and glory of his name.”

And again, as though answering himself, amid groans and sighs he immediately bursts forth in these words: “I suppose it is he to whom he forgave more.” As though he said: “I know, merciful Lord, hope and refuge of my soul, that I ought deservedly to love before all and above all things you, whose mercy toward me has until now been so great, in my spirit which you cleansed and to which you pardoned such great crimes of sins. Yet, already anticipated by your mercy, I love you, as I suppose; nevertheless I do not dare affirm that I love you perfectly, because, since my love is as nothing in comparison with your love,

[Col. 0940D] I do not know how it may please you, or whether it can be called love before you.”

And he answered: “You have judged rightly.” He fittingly says, “You have judged rightly,” because God loves and approves such a judgment: that a person, because of true humility of heart, should consider his love—by which he loves and embraces God—not to be perfect love but merely, as it were, an opinion of love; since no human being, even if he gathered his whole self to return love, can render anything worthy in return for God’s love.

“And turning toward the woman, he said to Simon: ‘Do you see this woman?’” The Lord turns toward the woman when he returns wholly through the grace of his compassion to that softened and humbled soul from which he had once turned away.

[Col. 0941A] “Do you see this woman?” he says. As though he said: “Because not by your merits but by my free compassion I have made you worthy for me to turn the eyes of my mercy toward you, I wish—because it is beneficial for you—that you too should, by repentance, look upon yourself as you formerly were, and should always strive, with joy and humble thanksgiving, to attend to this woman which you have now become through my grace.”

“I entered your house; you gave no water for my feet. But she watered my feet with tears. You gave me no kiss; but she, from the time she entered, has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil; but she anointed my feet with ointment.”

In these three things—water, kiss,

[Col. 0941B] and oil—I judge that three virtues, namely faith, hope, and love, without which no one can be saved, are fittingly to be understood. Faith, which is received in water—that is, in baptism—is appropriately understood by water. The kiss, which takes place among people in the hope of greater love, not unjustly expresses hope, through which a person is raised toward God. And in oil, which surpasses all liquids, we fittingly understand love.

Therefore God admonishes a person through his inward inspiration to know what he has committed and how contrary to these three virtues he has lived. “I entered your house,” he says, “when, having driven out the ancient possessor, the devil, I cleansed your heart and soul through the sacrament of baptism and invisibly consecrated it, so that it might be my house, through the invisible anointing of my Spirit.

[Col. 0941C] But you gave no water to my feet, because you neglected to live according to the sacraments of the faith received and promised in baptism. But she, whom I have now made out of you by changing you from your former manner of life, watered my feet with tears and wiped them with the hair of her head, because through steadfast repentance for past crimes and continence for the future, having softened the strict foot of my justice and truth, you have at length deserved, by my gift, to attain the foot of my mercy and compassion.

“You gave me no kiss, because until now you have not had that hope in me—who am truly compassionate and truly merciful—which you ought to have had, and by which you ought to have stirred yourself up to a greater sincerity of love for me. But she—she, I say, your soul, now softened by my grace—from the time she entered, that is, from the time she was granted humbly to return within herself and recognize her own misery and my mercy, has not ceased to kiss my feet, because through true faith and firm, steadfast hope, faithfully clinging to me,

[Col. 0941D] she has learned both perfectly to love my mercy and humbly and profitably to fear my judgment.

“You did not anoint my head with oil; but she anointed my feet with ointment.” In this place we may understand by Christ’s head his divinity, and by his feet his most holy humanity. “You did not anoint my head with oil,” he says, “because, although I am your Creator, you have until now not loved me as worthily as you ought. But now you have in some manner anointed my feet with ointment, because by worthy works of repentance you have worthily responded, according to your ability, to the passions, humiliations, miseries, and wounds which I endured in the humanity I assumed for you.”

“Therefore I say to you: Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much. But to whom less is forgiven, he loves less.” These words of the Lord seem to mean that love is the cause of forgiveness, and forgiveness the cause of love. And indeed no one can doubt that this is so: the God who is loved cleanses and purifies from every defilement of sins the heart which overflows with perfect love of God; and the purer it is from sins, the more capable it becomes of divine love.

[Col. 0942A] But the person to whom less is forgiven is shown to love less; and where love is less, there is less forgiveness of sins. Yet, that we may distinguish these same words of the Lord somewhat more subtly, let us see how they are often fulfilled through hidden operation in a single person. It sometimes happens that someone, as we have said, is able to love God greatly and, in that great love, receives great forgiveness of sins. But if, perhaps, pride secretly enters the mind and he becomes inwardly proud of God’s gift, attributing to his own powers more than is right what he was granted to have solely by God’s grace, then by God’s just judgment it happens that, when he has recognized his error and returned within himself, he finds a lesser grace of forgiveness. At once that lesser forgiveness begins to be the cause of lesser love, and thus is fulfilled what is said: “But to whom less is forgiven, he loves less.”

“And he said to the woman: ‘Your sins are forgiven.’” What is mystically given us to understand in these words of the Lord, who now says concerning the woman to Simon, “Her many sins are forgiven,” and now says to the woman herself, “Your sins are forgiven,”

[Col. 0942B] except that God speaks to a person in two ways and grants forgiveness of sins in two ways? First, he speaks outwardly through the teaching of his word by his teachers; second, he speaks inwardly through the invisible and inexpressible language of his inspiration. So too forgiveness of sins is first given to a person in hope, and secondly given in actuality.

When a person has been perfectly converted and has deserved, as it were, to apply to the Lord’s feet the sweet-smelling ointments of works worthy of worthy repentance, as soon as he hears the word of God here and begins to keep it within himself by carrying it out in deeds insofar as he can, he is encouraged by hope of forgiveness through confidence in God’s mercy and is inflamed with the constancy of a more ardent love. Thus, in a wonderful manner, he who had first sounded in the outward ears by the voice of his word speaks inwardly in person to the woman—that is, to the softened soul—“Your sins are forgiven.”

[Col. 0942C] And this is the true and perfect forgiveness of sins, which takes place in actuality and which the very author of pardon grants in person, when he has poured his whole self into the loving soul; when, through the ineffable grace of his visitation, having at last removed the bitterness of fear, he has brought it to the perfect sweetness of perfect love. Through this love he so claims the whole human heart for himself that it thinks of, seeks, and desires nothing except God. Therefore it is rightly added at once:

“And those who reclined together began to say within themselves: ‘Who is this, who also forgives sins?’” Those reclining together are all the human senses, humbly agreeing together in the love of God alone. They are rightly said to recline together when they agree with and delight in the spirit in all things as far as possible.

“Who is this,” they say, “who also forgives sins?” This voice is the voice of the soul loving God from its inmost marrow and ardently sighing to contemplate the height of his majesty; a soul which now in heart, now in body, now in voice, now in desire, humbly cries out to the Lord:

[Col. 0942D] “Who is this?” As though it said: “O merciful Lord, when—when will it be permitted me to pass to you from the prison of this laborious exile, where, casting off the heavy burden of the body, I may behold you in the glory of your majesty? I find nothing delightful in this life as long as I cannot see you, who have forgiven me so many and such great sins and bestowed upon me benefits so many and innumerable.”

Blessed and truly beatifiable is the soul which, in the exile of this life, is afflicted with such a desire for eternity. For when the time of its release comes, he whom it has always desired, sought, and loved will meet and assist it, strengthening and defending it by the consolation of his most merciful compassion against fear of diabolical attack.

“Your faith,” he says, “has made you whole; go in peace.” As though he said: “Because until now you have clung to me through true faith and love, because in this life you have glorified me through perfect works of faith, healed from the wounds of sins you have contracted, you will depart from this life in peace; you will be received in peace into the joys of eternal rest, where you will be harmed by no wound of sins and no assault of enemies, but will rejoice without end in the tranquility of perpetual peace.”

May he who lives and reigns without end through all ages of ages bring us to these joys of inward rest, to this tranquility of perpetual peace. Amen.

450. HOMILY LXI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST JAMES THE APOSTLE.

[Col. 0944A]

“The mother of the sons of Zebedee came to Jesus with her sons, worshipping him and asking something of him” (Matthew 20).

The blessed apostle James, whose feast we celebrate today, was one of the Twelve—one, I say, whom the Lord loved among his other disciples with a certain special love and wished to have more familiarly present at his secrets. For although he loved them all as most blessed and holier than all other people, and had made known to them all that he had heard from the Father, nevertheless, as we read in the Gospels, he deigned in some special manner and more frequently to show the sweetness of his love to those three—Peter, James, and John—not in order to single out these three by loving them with some exclusive preference, but because he knew that more compassion, more inward and divine sweetness, resided in their hearts; and thus he made them worthy of a fuller measure of his love. What this principal holiness was, and what singular sweetness of heart they possessed, he alone who gave it knows; we neither know, nor are worthy to know.

We read in the Gospel concerning these three men that, when our Lord Jesus Christ had ascended a high mountain with them, he chose to make the brightness of his glory visible there. Peter, filled with joy at the whole vision and desiring to dwell there always with Jesus, where he rejoiced in his glory made manifest, said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah”

[Col. 0944B] (Matthew 17:4). And when the hour of his passion was imminent, again taking only Peter, James, and John, he began, as the evangelist says, to be sorrowful and troubled, saying: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Mark 14:34).

What is the reason that the Gospel of this blessed John overflows with such sweetness beyond the other Gospels, unless it is because he burned in the inward person with a certain unheard-of sweetness which he could not conceal in speech? Hence the present Gospel also, which is read today concerning blessed James, seems to touch upon a certain singular sweetness of God, with which his heart and soul are undoubtedly believed to have been most fully suffused.

[Col. 0944C] The evangelist says: “The mother of the sons of Zebedee came to Jesus with her sons, worshipping him and asking something of him.” This mother who comes to Jesus with her sons is the holy Church, which is mother and yet virgin; her sons through grace are all the elect and holy, predestined to eternal life. Nor is she without definite mystical reason described as the mother of the sons of Zebedee. For Zebedee is interpreted “this one flowing.” And who is this “one flowing” except the present world?

“This” is a demonstrative pronoun, and by this word the present world is not incongruously understood, because everything that is in the world is visible and demonstrable, whereas what is not of the world is invisible. It is also flowing because daily, like water, it slips away, fails, and passes on, and never remains in the same state. For if the things which happen are good, prosperous, or pleasant, they flow away more swiftly than speech because they do not endure; if evils or adversities threaten, these too flow away because they likewise fail.

[Col. 0944D] Each one of us flows daily because, passing from youth to old age, we draw near to death; and our very living and growing is, so to speak, a miserable flowing away and failing.

We were sons of this Zebedee, that is, of this world, until we were regenerated in baptism. In baptism, cleansed from original and actual sin, we were changed from sons of the world into sons of mother Church. And now we are those who have the first fruits of the Spirit, as Paul says: “We were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest; but now, justified, we have been made children of God through his death” (Ephesians 2:3). Thus, when the children of the Church have been reborn in baptism, holy mother Church comes with her sons to Jesus when she strives to draw near to their salvation by right faith, good will, and holy works.

[Col. 0945A] But once she has thus come to Jesus, by striving to be concerned for the salvation of her soul, she must be worshipping him and asking something from him. What is worshipping except humbling oneself? Since we frequently read, in both the New and Old Testaments, about human worship by which people wished to worship angels or human beings, the virtue of humility is fittingly understood by this worshipping. One truly worships who humbles himself, who approaches prayer with a contrite and humble heart, and who wishes to have no bitterness toward his neighbor at the time of prayer.

Conversely, the person who comes to worship not with a humbled but a proud heart—who, making light of injuries inflicted upon a brother, wishes to offer to the Lord the sacrifices of his prayers with bitterness of heart—is by no means humble. Such a person is undoubtedly shown to be arrogant and proud, because he is found to be a transgressor of the Lord’s command, by which he is first admonished concerning reconciliation with his brother and then commanded to offer his gift at the altar.

[Col. 0945B] If someone were given an order by his teacher and disdained to obey it, then immediately came boldly to ask or say to him whatever he wished, he would be judged very proud and arrogant. But much more does the person provoke the wrath of divine indignation who transgresses the Lord’s command by failing to love his neighbor and yet, coming proudly and boldly before God, thinks that he will be heard by him in his prayers—the God whom he has despised.

Therefore we must first worship—that is, cast ourselves down in true humility—and then we may ask something from the Lord. What is it, my brothers, to ask something? Someone prays and asks for temporal and perishable things; that person does not ask for something, but asks for nothing. The person who presses the Lord with prayers for the salvation of his soul and the attainment of the glory of eternal life truly asks for something—something great, something ineffable. Yet, even if we sometimes entreat God for the necessities of this life, without which we cannot do, the intention of eternal life must nevertheless come first and be joined to the petition, for the sake of which alone we seek these outward things in the meantime, lest we fail.

[Col. 0945C] Thus holy mother Church irreproachably worships and petitions the Lord for her sons. And because her worship is good and humble, her just petition is not disregarded; rather, she who worships and asks is told:

“What do you wish?” God’s speaking is his acting; his questioning is our stirring-up, by which he stirs us to ask for his will, not our own. And what does holy mother Church ask for her sons?

She says: “Command that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” It should be noted why the mother of the sons of Zebedee is neither repelled nor rebuked by the Lord in her petition, while the sons, from whom this petition arose, are rebuked and reproved when the Lord says to them:

[Col. 0945D] “You do not know what you are asking.” Since we have said that holy Church is represented by this mother, we believe the reason is this: the petitioning mother is not rejected because the general petition of holy Church, which she makes to God for all her children, is just and necessary. But the sons, who, still carnal, sought a greater glory and seat in heaven above their fellow apostles, are corrected by the Lord so that we may learn from this that none of us ought to pray that God grant the kingdom of God, or a glory and seat in heaven more excellent than those of others, to himself alone. Rather, each should desire for all Christians the same merits and the same rewards according to merits that he desires for himself.

For this reason, even in our daily prayers, we ask for nothing individually but say everything generally: “Give to us, Lord; give to all of us,” not “Give to me alone,” because the person who prays only for himself and not for his neighbor prays wrongly.

“Say,” she said, “that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” By the right hand the future life may be understood; by the left, present prosperity; and by the kingdom of heaven, which has various meanings, the Church both present and future may be signified. The mother of Zebedee’s sons speaks; and so too the Church, mother of God’s children, speaks to Christ: “Say, O Lord, that my sons, whom I have regenerated and brought forth for you through the grace of motherhood, may sit in your kingdom—that is, in the present Church—at your left hand: namely, that they may have the prosperity and glory of this present life; and, departing from the left hand, [Col. 0946D] that is, from this temporal joy and glory, make them sit at your right hand, that is, grant them a share and fellowship in eternal life in your kingdom.” This interpretation agrees with the prayer in which we ask both to abound in temporal advantages—that is, the left hand—and to be sustained by eternal things—that is, the right hand.

Blessed are those who are thus transferred from the left hand to the right; but far more blessed and more worthy of God are those who refuse to sit at the left hand—that is, who refuse to have rest in the present life—and who choose to be disciplined by labours and hardships and voluntary poverty, according to the Lord’s command; for by this means they will one day sit more gloriously and more exaltedly at God’s right hand.

That blessed Job at one time sat at the left hand, when, like a mighty and wealthy king, he abounded in every good thing. [Col. 0947A] Even if he had remained as he was before the Lord’s scourge, so that it was said of him that there was no man like him on earth, he could have obtained a sufficient reward from the Lord in the kingdom of heaven. But because he was afterwards tested and proved—his children taken away, his possessions lost, and he himself wounded from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head—and was found most faithful by the Lord, a greater crown was given at God’s right hand to one who conquered than would have been given to one who did not conquer. 454 The Lord took away a lesser thing in order to give a greater; for if he had sat at the left hand amid glory and prosperity, he would have received a lesser reward at Christ’s right hand in the kingdom of heaven.

We may also understand, in a loftier sense, by the right and left hands the two natures of God and man in Jesus Christ: the divine nature in the right hand, the human nature in the left. [Col. 0947B] Of both natures the bride speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs 2:6). It is as though she said: “If, with my whole intention—which is my head—I consider the deeds of my Lord Jesus Christ which he performed in his human nature, and hold them fast with a faithful heart, then his right hand, namely his holy divinity, will one day so embrace me that it will never allow me to be separated from him.”

Of this right and left hand Solomon says: “Length of days is in his right hand, and riches and glory in his left” (Prov. 3:16). Length of days is in his right hand because in his divine nature he admits no changeability, but possesses an unchanging being forever. Or again, length of days is in his right hand because from the light of his divinity [Col. 0947C] he enlightens his faithful with good understandings, holy desires, wills, and praiseworthy works. Although he now distributes these gifts to his elect in portions, as he wills, when the darkness of this mortality has departed he will grant them more fully and perfectly. For the body that is corruptible weighs down the soul; and no one can be of such holiness as to gather his senses, keep watch over his thoughts, and perform good works as he ought. But when we come to length of days—that is, to contemplate the light of his divinity—we shall be so enlightened that all our life will be lived in the light of holiness.

If length of days is thus in his right hand, tell me, I ask, how are riches [Col. 0947D] and glory in his left hand, when he did not possess even a foot’s breadth of ground, nor had a place where to lay his head, and for thirty years and more lived in this world like a poor man and beggar? If you consider what kind of riches and glory these are, you will understand that what you hear is altogether true. We have said that Christ’s humanity is figured by the left hand. In that sacred humanity there were riches and glory, 455 because every richness of all holy virtues was implanted in his holy soul and in that holy man whom he had assumed; so that it may rightly be said of him: “Glory and riches are in his house” (Ps. 112:3 [Vulgate numbering]).

Glory is rightly added to riches, because, although he laboured in preaching and endured many wearinesses in vigils, fasts, temptations, and tears, all these things were of no avail, because while he still lived souls nevertheless descended to hell, [Col. 0948A] until, raised upon the cross, he triumphed most gloriously over the devil. Of this glory Paul says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Gal. 6:14). This, then, may be understood concerning Christ’s right and left hands.

Therefore the holy Church, or each individual soul, prays that it may deserve to sit at this right and left hand: that it may be found worthy more keenly to consider and investigate both the divine and the human nature; or, as we have said, that it may possess prosperity and rest at the left hand and may deserve to receive eternal blessedness at God’s right hand, which is the future life. It follows:

Jesus answered and said: “You do not know what you ask. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?” These words seem to convey some rebuke. But [Col. 0948B] they are not words of rebuke; they are words of salvation, full of sweetness and exhortation for us. “You do not know,” he says, “what you ask.” Nothing is truer. For when we come to prayer, where we ought to ask for what is necessary to our salvation, we are often led into such wandering and error that we ourselves do not know what we ask. For there is nothing by which we are more assailed—whether by the world, the devil, or our own flesh—than this: that our mind, which ought to be wholly serene at the hour of prayer, is so estranged from itself by phantasms of useless thoughts that at times it does not even know or understand the words of its own petition.

The Lord therefore wishes his children to ask knowingly, because if they ask knowingly, they also become able to drink the Lord’s cup. “If you know,” he says, “what you ask, you are able to drink the cup [Col. 0948C] that I am about to drink.” By the cup is understood Christ’s passion. Why did Christ suffer? He suffered in order to reconcile us to God the Father. And not inappropriately, 456 by Christ’s passion, through which he restored us to God’s grace, love of neighbour is understood, because through the mediation of love of neighbour one reaches the love of God.

But by the cup, in which the figure of wine is offered at the altar, the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is also understood; by it the holy Church, or each individual soul, is given drink and refreshed for the remission of its sins. It approaches this cup worthily only if it has laboured to possess love of God and of neighbour.

When the elect are questioned—that is, stirred up—to love of God and neighbour, which is to drink the Lord’s cup, they rightly [Col. 0948D] say, “We are able,” because he is the one who gives them the ability to bring into effect the good disposition which they have toward God and neighbour. If they approach in humility and worship, if they ask knowingly, if they are able to drink the Lord’s cup—that is, if they have love of God and neighbour—they hear a good answer from the good master:

“You shall drink,” he says, “my cup; but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give to you, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” It is as though he said: “Because you have come for your salvation, worship me in true humility, ask knowingly, and, having love of God and neighbour, have washed away before me by worthy satisfaction what you sinned against in your neighbour, you shall now drink my cup. You may freely [Col. 0949A] communicate in my body and blood; by my enabling power you may bring your good disposition into effect. But it is not mine to give you to sit at my right or left hand.

“To sit at my right hand is to consider the greatness of my divinity; to sit at my left hand is to consider the infant needs of my humanity: how I, who am immeasurable and incomprehensible, the Creator of all things in my divinity, chose to experience being laid in a manger, cherished in my mother’s bosom, nourished with milk, bathed, carried, and all the other things which assumed humanity required, even unto death. To consider all these things, to the degree that you ask and wish, is not mine to give you unless you prepare yourselves by a great preparation of your hearts sent down from my Father. Yet even though [Col. 0949B] you seek with great equipment of heart, 457 to weigh and behold all that is mine and all that concerns me, and to delight sweetly in it in the sweetness of your souls, this cannot be perfectly accomplished here. My sweetness, for which you sigh and which you desire, cannot be possessed here perfectly and fully. But that here, insofar as is permitted, and in the future life with fullness, we may possess what we seek, we must prepare ourselves with the many ornaments of virtues, as Solomon warns us, saying: ‘My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation’” (Ecclus. 2:1).

That whole outward preparation of the priest for the altar is an exhortation to us, showing with what preparations we ought to adorn our hearts. For every [Col. 0949C] soul performs the office of a priest if it invisibly imitates what is visibly done there. The priest is clothed in an alb. We too must clothe ourselves in the white garment of purity and chastity of body and soul, putting away the blackness of sins and vices. The priest is girded with a belt. We too must be bound under the yoke of obedience, so that we may not desire to be loosed by evil freedom, but may desire to be firmly bound and held under the purpose which we have professed, even unto death. The priest puts on the chasuble over the other garments. We too must put on above all virtues, as something loftier and more excellent, that exceedingly broad commandment: the twofold love of God and neighbour.

Again, in another way, what he says may be understood: “You shall indeed drink my [Col. 0949D] cup; but to sit at my right hand or left hand is not mine to give to you, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” “You,” he says, “my apostles, who have followed me by leaving all things, shall drink my cup—that is, you shall be imitators of my passion. But to sit at my right and left hands is not mine to give you, because you cannot, and ought not, possess together the prosperities of this present life, 458 which are the left hand, and future goods, which are the right hand. There will come those for whom this has been prepared by my Father; for after you have been killed by the hands of persecutors and transferred to my right hand, namely to everlasting rest, there will be faithful people in my Church who will sit at my right and left hands, possessing present and future goods in my kingdom.”

[Col. 0950A] Certainly blessed Sylvester, Gregory, Martin, and other confessors sat, as it were, at the Lord’s right and left hands; for although they daily offered themselves to the Lord in hidden martyrdom, their times were times of peace and prosperity, unlike the times of the apostles and martyrs, when persecution was such that no one could openly confess Christ’s name without immediately being handed over to death. Those blessed confessors passed from the left hand, that is, temporal repose, to the right hand, that is, future blessedness, because this had been prepared for them by the Father. The apostles and martyrs, however, endured many evils in God’s kingdom—that is, in the present life—and found future goods that endure without end.

These matters from the Gospel reading we have briefly touched upon, insofar as [Col. 0950B] God has enabled us. They are appropriately read concerning so great a man, in whose heart there was such sweetness. Through them may we also, being admonished, strive to advance, earnestly imploring the holy apostle of God, James, that through Jesus Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages, we may deserve to share here and in the future that supreme good, the sweetness of Christ, which he began to taste here and now receives in fullness. Amen.

459 HOMILY LXII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST LAURENCE THE MARTYR.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains by itself alone” (John 12).

[Col. 0950C] The words of this holy Gospel reading were spoken in that discourse which the Lord Jesus delivered to the crowds before his passion, when certain Gentiles who had come to Jerusalem to worship on the feast day approached holy Philip and asked him, saying, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” And Philip told Andrew; and again Philip and Andrew told Jesus. Then he began this very discourse in these words: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” And immediately he added: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains by itself alone.”

In the words of this sacred Gospel reading the Lord Jesus mystically prefigured the glory of his passion and death; he also foretold [Col. 0950D] what fruit would follow from his passion throughout the whole world. In this same Gospel he was also pleased to reveal what glory, what reward of great dignity, those should obtain who wished, with right faith and worthy conduct, to become imitators of his passion.

“Unless,” he says, “a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains by itself alone.” By the grain of wheat the Son of God himself may be understood, for he is the food by which the angels in heaven are fed and by which the souls of saints, still established in this pilgrimage, are sustained. And as in the sweetness of his divinity he is the invisible food of holy souls, so likewise through the power of that same divine majesty he is the restorer and sustainer of bodies. For from what else, if not from the power of his divinity, does the earth produce fruit, without [Col. 0951A] 460 which bodies cannot live?

Therefore, if he had remained in his sweetness and had not himself, by falling into the earth, come to the aid of us who had miserably fallen, his divinity would have been of no benefit to us, since through original sin, with the wall of enmity set between us, we could not reach it. And because it was not consonant with the justice of the Son of God merely to restore us, who had voluntarily fallen, by the power of his divinity, he condescended to us, humbled himself unto the assumption of our body, and fell into the earth—that is, into the womb of the undefiled and perpetual Virgin.

But because his being born would have profited us nothing unless our redemption had profited us, it is rightly added, “dies.” Just as before the Son’s incarnation, for five thousand years [Col. 0951B] [Note: [Col. 0951D] Thus the manuscript.] no entrance into life lay open to any human being, so likewise throughout all those thirty-three years in which God and man lived on earth among human beings, it was permitted to no soul to enter through the gate of life. Therefore, that the work of our redemption might be complete, he who assumed human form for our sake died in that same humanity through his passion. Then indeed, when upon the cross he entrusted his soul into the hands of the Father and a soldier opened his side with a lance, the gate of life was immediately opened; and it remains open so that from that day until the end of the age it receives all who wish to enter through it with worthy conduct.

Unless this grain of wheat, as we have said, had fallen into the earth and died, it would certainly have remained alone: [Col. 0951C] that is, unless the Son of God had become the Son of Man and delivered his soul unto death, no human being would have had access to him; he alone would inhabit inaccessible light.

461 But why is he said to remain alone, he who has no need of human companionship and is eternal joy to himself? Therefore, if he had not created us, and had not afterwards become man to redeem us anew when we were exiles from him, this would have caused no loss to his glory, which he possesses not from communion with us but from his own eternity. For in creating and redeeming us, he did not will us to be his co-heirs because he would gain any increase of blessedness or glory from our fellowship, but so that we, joined to him, might be blessed and glorious through him. Nor, through the sweetness of his uncreated [Col. 0951D] compassion, could he endure to be joy unto himself alone without also having those whom he might make participants in his joy and who could rejoice in that joy which he himself is.

Therefore, that this might happen, this noble grain of wheat fell into the earth: that is, the Son of God, who feeds angels in heaven and refreshes the faithful on earth, emptied himself by assuming flesh. But what then? Was this enough? By no means. He would still have remained alone unless he had also died for us. For in not refusing to undergo death, he fulfilled the things that follow.

“But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” How great a fruit has grown throughout the whole breadth of the world through his death [Col. 0952A] we can now, by God’s grace, behold more clearly than light. Let us first consider the apostles and the primitive Church founded through them: how great was the fruit in them. Then let us consider how much this grain bore fruit in the martyrs and afterwards in the confessors. Even now, until the end of the age, it does not cease to bear manifold fruit. For from the beginning of the Church, never at any time, as in our own days, has so innumerable a multitude of both sexes endeavoured to enter by the narrow gate.

This Gospel is not inappropriately read for blessed Laurence, whose birthday into heaven we celebrate today. For he too was that grain which, dying, brought forth much fruit, because in suffering bodily death [Col. 0952B] for Christ he restored to his Creator very many who had been delivered from the death of the soul.
