For he, one of the great arch-senators of the heavenly court, attained the glory of eternal dignity by a noble triumph. Just as some mighty prince enters the king’s court with some bearing his arms before him and others following as 462 soldiers, so blessed Laurence is known to have entered the palace of the eternal emperor. The soldier who preceded him to the heavenly court was Romanus; the soldiers following their leader were Hippolytus and his companions. We have said this by way of digression; now let us see how the very words of the holy Gospel, which we referred to the head—that is, to Christ—may also be applied to the members.

“Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, [Col. 0952C] it remains by itself alone.” By comparison, a human being may be understood by the grain of wheat, because before the grain reaches maturity, before it is prepared to become the substance of bread, it is cultivated with much toil. In the same way, immense labours are expended before a person who remains for so long in this present age conquers the necessities of childhood and advances to mature age.

Let us now describe in detail how the nature of a grain reaches its full use. First, a field is cultivated with much labour so that it may be fitted for receiving seed. Then seed is scattered upon ploughed ground, in which it lies and decays throughout the long winter, enduring the onset of storms and winter frost. Afterwards, in springtime, it barely puts forth the tiniest shoot and begins as the tenderest grass alone; then, little by little, it grows from day to day; [Col. 0952D] later it ripens in summer and produces ears. Then, when it has reached full maturity, it is reaped with no small labour, gathered into the granary, laid upon the threshing-floor for threshing, then crushed in the mill, and finally put into the oven, in which at times all the labour expended is rendered vain.

Likewise, in the mother’s womb a human being is gradually formed member by member. Afterwards, when born into the world, much time and immense labour are spent before one conquers the necessities of childhood and is taught [Col. 0953A] to speak and to walk. Then, when one has advanced to mature age, how great are the distressing trials and temptations one endures! A person himself can know more by experience than by instruction how great are the straits of tribulations and temptations which he endures, just as grain endures storms and tempests.

But alas! Just as a grain, after it has been formed and perfected for the use of bread, is at times placed in the oven and all the preceding human labour is frustrated, 463 so too, in the case of a person nourished and instructed with so many labours from the day of birth, if that person turns in the contrary direction, every care bestowed is lost and brought to nothing. But if, with God’s help, one strives not to let the days of life granted pass uselessly and to live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age, nothing in all God’s creation on earth can be compared to that person’s nobility and [Col. 0953B] glory.

And because no person who has lived for any length of time in this world can be free from some fall into sin, it is rightly added: “falling into the earth.” That person falls into the earth who falls into the fault of an earthly will or action. As we have said, no one can be without a fall of this kind unless the Lord upholds that person by the arm of his power. But when anyone has fallen into the precipice of sin, the further phrase, “dies,” must follow for the salvation of each person. For every person dies salutarily if he utterly removes and mortifies from his soul the causes of his fall, namely earthly allurements and carnal desires.

We know that the apostle Paul spoke of this blessed death: “He who has died [Col. 0953C] has been justified from sins” (Rom. 6:7). For if he had said this about the common death of the flesh, by what testimony of truth could he prove it, since many ungodly people die and are nevertheless not justified after death, but rather are condemned for the sins they committed, for which they neglected to make satisfaction to God in this world? The blessed Apostle instead signified that death by which the elect, after their fall, desire to die to the sins into which they have fallen, in order that they may live to God and righteousness. But whoever neglects to undergo this blessed death will without doubt experience what follows:

“It remains by itself alone.” Therefore, one who refuses to die to sins will remain alone, because the grace of divine visitation [Col. 0953D] will not accompany that person here, having been excluded by that person’s own negligence. Such a one will also remain alone in the world to come if death suddenly finds him living thus in sins, because he will not be a participant in eternal life, having refused in this world to die the death precious in the Lord’s sight. But what grace follows one who strives to die to sins and live to righteousness 464 is plainly shown here:

“But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” The apostle Paul indicates what fruit one who happily dies to sins brings forth: “The fruit,” he says, “of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering” (Gal. 5:22). Such a person displays this fruit in himself and also bears fruit for God in other people, because one who is of this kind is sometimes placed by divine dispensation [Col. 0954A] in authority so that others too may be built up by that person’s word and example. It follows:

“He who loves his soul will lose it.” If we wish to understand this simply, it means that if necessity presses, each person ought even to give his soul unto death for God. If one loves it wrongly, so that when persecution comes one would rather deny God than give the soul for him, one will certainly lose it, because one will expose it to the danger of eternal death.

According to the earlier moral sense which we have set forth, however, one is said to love one’s soul who neglects to withdraw it from carnal pleasure and every unlawful thought, but when harmful things creep in, does not refuse to receive them with lax security and slothful delight. Such a person will indeed lose it, [Col. 0954B] because, having spent much time uselessly in the things we have mentioned and later returned to oneself, one begins to shudder at one’s wickedness and negligences. Looking also at others nearby who have remained vigilant in guarding their heart, one sees how great is their fervour of spirit and how in their prayers they deserve to experience how sweet the Lord is. One then strives to banish the languor of the withered soul and the dullness of the foolish mind; but the previous negligence stands in the way, and one is granted to feel nothing of the Spirit’s sweetness. It follows:

“And he who hates his soul in this world preserves it unto eternal life.” Who is said to hate his own soul but one who is harsh with oneself in all evil pleasures and never permits harmful [Col. 0954C] thoughts to remain within? “In this world,” he says. John indicates what the world is in his Epistle, where he says: “All that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16). Therefore, whoever so hates the soul 465 as to cut from it the evils of this threefold pleasure—namely, avoiding the lust of the flesh, turning away the eyes lest they see something that disturbs the mind’s purity, and guarding against all pride within and without—preserves it so that one may sweetly contemplate eternal life, that is, Christ, through an ecstasy of the mind at the time of prayer.

And it should be noted that in the preceding verse [Col. 0954D] the future tense is used—“will lose”—whereas here it says “preserves,” which is in the present tense. For one who occupies the soul all night or day with vain matters will lose it later, when, having returned to oneself, one wishes to have it prepared for the sweetness of divine contemplation. But one who remains constantly in the watchfulness of the heart and does not allow the soul to wander through the empty pleasures of present things always has before one the means by which to obtain the grace of inward sweetness.

So that it may not seem difficult or harsh to anyone to maintain oneself constantly in such vigilance, let one always extend the gentle charity of one’s heart to imitate Christ, whose example he sets before us in what follows. For he says:

[Col. 0955A] “He who serves me, let him follow me.” It is as though he said: “Whoever resolves to serve me by the wakeful vigilance of the heart should not shrink back as though unable to accomplish it. Let such a one follow me—that is, set me, the Saviour, before the eyes of the heart, and strive, according to one’s ability, to live as I lived in this world.” But perhaps someone may say: “I am earth and ashes, carrying flesh which I always feel resisting the spirit. How can I advance to the point of imitating him who is God and man?”

Let one who is thus anxious yet devoted to the good hear words of consolation from the Lord: “It is indeed laborious, as you say, always to remain, according to my example, in the guarding of life; but hear the reward of immense dignity which I offer, so that in [Col. 0955B] considering and receiving its recompense you may not shrink even from my example, however arduous and difficult it may be:

“And where I am,” he says, “there also my servant shall be.” By the word “I,” which is demonstrative, Christ’s humanity, 466 which was local and tangible, may be understood; by “am,” which is in the present tense, his divinity may be signified, for which nothing is future or past, but to which all things are present, whether they have been or are yet to come. Thus he indicated his divinity to Moses when Moses asked his name, saying: “I am who am. And thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14).

O what a reward, and of what great sweetness, does the Lord promise! “And where I am,” he says, “there also [Col. 0955C] my servant shall be.” It is as though he said: “I shall so recompense the service of each imitator of mine that I will make that person taste the sweetness of my divinity and humanity; and the one whom I visit here by the grace of inward inspiration I shall also satisfy in the future with the glory of that same divinity and humanity.” It follows:

“If anyone serves me, my Father who is in heaven will honour him.” When, then, will God the Father honour the servant of his Son, except when at the general resurrection he will glorify wonderfully and ineffably the body which now decays in the earth? “If anyone,” he says, “serves me”—that is, whoever perseveres in my service until the end of life—“my Father who is in heaven will honour him.” It is rightly said, “will honour,” [Col. 0955D] because the body which is now corruptible will put on eternal incorruption in the future and will receive from the soul such a condition that it will never, as it does now, desire against it, but the firm bond of perpetual peace will remain between them forever.

For if the Lord restored to us a body such as we now bear, its recovery could bring us no joy, but rather grief. But now we believe, and know truly, that he will conform the body of our lowliness to the body of his glory; and for this reason souls sigh for its resumption, because they know that it is to be so honoured. We think that blessed Paul signified this honour when he said: “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication, that each one of you may know how to possess his [Col. 0956A] vessel in sanctification and honour” (1 Thess. 4:3–4). Our vessel is our body. We shall indeed one day possess it in sanctification and honour if in this world we strive to preserve holiness of life and purity of body and soul. 467

Thus far, as the Lord has granted, we have treated the Gospel. Now let us take care briefly to note in a few words what we have explained.

This Gospel is divided into four parts. Two verses together seem to belong to each part, up to the final verse which remains. The first part is: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains by itself alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit”; in this may be noted the mortification of the flesh. The second is: “He who loves his [Col. 0956B] soul will lose it, and he who hates his soul in this world preserves it unto eternal life”; in this the vigilance of the heart may be understood. The third is: “He who serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also my servant shall be”; in this is signified the reward of souls. The fourth part follows: “If anyone serves me, my Father who is in heaven will honour him”; in this is figuratively understood the glorification of bodies.

Let us now turn in prayers to him who, falling into the earth as a grain of wheat—that is, the Son of God made Son of Man—willed to die in order to bear much fruit: namely, that by his body he might acquire those to whom he could grant glorification of the body. May he, through the abundance of his compassion, grant us so to mortify the flesh with its vices and desires in this present age, and so always to remain in the guarding of the heart, [Col. 0956C] 468 that at our end we too may confidently say the words which, on the present feast of blessed Laurence, we sing in his person: “On the gridiron I did not deny you, O God; and laid upon the fire, I confessed you, O Christ.”

The gridiron is our body, upon which the wretched soul suffers diverse fires of temptations. For though Decius, who caused Laurence to be burned on a material gridiron with an illusory fire, is dead, the devil lives, who stirred the tyrant’s mind to this wickedness. Through his executioners, that is, unclean spirits, he does not cease to supply beneath our gridiron—namely our body [Col. 0956D]—the coals of diverse passions and tribulations. If a person takes care constantly to extinguish them in the heart with the dew of compunction, one may sing at one’s departure in complete security: “On the gridiron I did not deny you, O God.”

One does not deny God on the gridiron and confesses the Lord Jesus Christ when, at the devil’s suggestion, one does not consent to be burned by the fire of wicked pleasure; and if one has at some time consented, one does not neglect before death to amend this before God by the worthy satisfaction of repentance. Such a person, I say, will sing these words joyfully at the end of the struggle. That we too may then be able to say them, may he grant it who is the author of all our salvation, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0957A] lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY LXIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE VIGIL OF THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.

“Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9).

Since we are about to celebrate the glorious Assumption of the most blessed Virgin Mary, it is fitting that we should endeavour to say something, insofar as we are able, in praise of her. For Holy Scripture foretold in many places that this same Virgin would surpass all human beings in the merit of holiness and dignity; before she was born, it often made known in advance what she would be like and how exalted she would become. Hence Solomon also, the wisest of men, from whose line she was to be born, as he extolled her by many testimonies, so in his Proverbs [Col. 0957B] he set forth in these words the grace which God wrought with her and through her for the whole world: “Wisdom has built herself a house.”

The Eternal Wisdom of God the Father, sweetly ordering all things, built herself a house when she consecrated the virginal chamber of blessed Mary as her dwelling. For when someone wishes to build a house, he first cuts away and planes down whatever he sees in wood or stone to be superfluous or less suitable, so that it may be fitted in due order within the joined structure. Thus indeed that most wise architect, the eternal Father, together with his Son prepared this most eminent house, cutting away from her utterly every contagion of original [Note: [Col. 0957D] See the preliminary Dissertation.] and actual sin, so that she had not even the slightest stain in herself, [Col. 0957C] but was wholly clean, wholly holy, and most fit for the King of heaven to dwell in. What eminence of virtues supported this house, so greatly prepared, is indicated by the words that follow:

“She hewed out her seven pillars.”

The number seven, which consists of four and three, here commends to us certain special excellences of virtue, with which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit had fortified our Lady Mary on every side: namely, because faith in the Holy Trinity was fully active in her, together with the four cardinal virtues—fortitude, temperance, prudence, and justice. Blessed Mary was truly strong in her resolve of chastity: she never allowed her body [Col. 0957D] or soul to be defiled by the stain of sin. Let us also see how temperate she was in silence. For surely, when the archangel Gabriel brought her that embassy divinely dictated in the secret places of heaven—“Hail,” he said, “full of grace, the Lord is with thee” (Luke 1:28)—she was not bold or hasty in replying at once; rather, pondering long in her heart, she considered what this greeting might mean (ibid., 29). And because she was strong in her resolve of chastity and temperate in silence, she was also prudent in her reply. Finally, when the same angel disclosed the order and reason of that unprecedented greeting—“Behold,” he said, “thou shalt conceive and bear a son”—she wisely asks how and by what means this can happen: “How,” she says, “shall this be, since I know not a man?” [Col. 0958A] For she knew that her resolve of integrity was most steadfast, and therefore wondered at the outcome of this conception. Therefore, because in silence she possessed temperance and in her reply prudence, in true humility she displayed perfect justice.

For when she heard that she would bear the Son of the Most High through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit coming from above, the most humble Virgin humbly answered: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done unto me according to thy word” (ibid., 38). And elsewhere: “Because he hath regarded the humility of his handmaid” (ibid., 48). As though she said: “I am conscious of no merit in myself for so great a condescension, except that God has regarded the humility of his handmaid.” Hence it is said also in the Song of Songs: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave [Col. 0958B] forth its fragrance” (Song 1:11). Nard is a lowly but sweet-smelling herb, to which the humility of the holy Virgin is suitably compared. She diffused in the heavenly palace so lovely a fragrance of sweetness that the very Son of God, delighted with such a scent, descended from the bosom of the Father into her womb and took from her the substance of human flesh. This is the house of Wisdom, divinely built, supported by seven pillars, and splendidly adorned.

If we refer the seven pillars also to Christ himself, we rightly recognize in them the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, who rested bodily in him: gifts which he hewed from the mountain of eternity, from the height of the Trinity, and distributed to his humanity. For Isaiah the prophet thus foretold concerning that noble flower which sprang from the rod of Jesse: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:2). The spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him, because no one ever saw him except in holy fear, by which he humbly subjected himself to God the Father in his humanity. The spirit of piety rested upon him, because whatever he did, whatever he taught, was all directed to piety, all to the grace of sweetness. Why should I mention that the spirit of wisdom and knowledge dwelt in him, when he himself was the Lord of all knowledge, in whom all treasures of wisdom are hidden? By the spirit of fortitude he overcame the temptations [Col. 0958D] which he endured for our sake; and finally he bravely conquered the very ignominy of the Passion by the glorious trophy of his death. By the spirit of counsel he called sinners to repentance, giving them counsel in a judgment of piety and mercy, when he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 4:17). He powerfully made known that he possessed the spirit of understanding in his resurrection, when he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures. It follows:

“She slew her victims, mingled her wine, and set forth her table.”

Christ surely slew his victims when, upon the altar of the cross, he offered himself as a saving victim, a living sacrifice pleasing to God the Father, [Col. 0959A] as an odor of sweetness. From the immolation of that victim such great power truly grew that, as often as it is now offered at the most holy altar, it grants forgiveness of sins and opens the kingdom of heaven. He mingled the wine when he transformed the severity of the old law into the gentleness of evangelical grace. For just as wine is sometimes mixed with water so that it may be easier to drink, so he who formerly commanded in the old law that eye be returned for eye, hand for hand, and tooth for tooth, commanded in the Gospel that debts be forgiven to debtors. He also mingled the wine because, rising from the dead, he sent his disciples to all nations, whereas previously he had forbidden them to go into the way of the Gentiles. “Going,” he said, “into all nations, baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). [Col. 0959B] But when did he set forth his table, except when, at his ascension, he carried with himself into heaven the bodies raised when he rose? For one who eats standing or walking is less filled; but one seated at table is refreshed fully and abundantly. Thus indeed, when the Lord ascended, their refreshment became full and abundant, because they sat with him at the feast of the heavenly banquet, to reign with him likewise forever. Therefore, when Christ had ascended into heaven and sent the promised Holy Spirit to the apostles, then what follows took place:

“She sent her maidservants to call to the walls and to the citadel of the city.”

By the maidservants, the holy apostles may here be understood, who before the coming of the Holy Spirit were frail and fearful. Was not blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, soft and frail, whom the voice of a single serving-woman moved to deny the Lord? But after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, he and his fellow apostles received such confidence that they did not fear openly to confess the name of Jesus before kings and governors, and indeed even surrendered their bodies to death for his sake. “To call to the walls,” he says, “and to the citadel of the city.” By the walls the active life is signified; by the citadel of the city, the summit of contemplative life. Therefore the holy apostles called us to the walls and to the citadel of the city, because they founded the holy Church upon the stability of the active and contemplative life.

## HOMILY LXIV. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

“Jesus entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house” (Luke 10).

Entering the village of this present age, the Son of God possessed two natures in himself, namely the human and the divine, which are also rightly signified by these two sisters, Martha and Mary. By Martha, who is described as busy with much serving, the assumed humanity of almighty God may fittingly be represented; but by Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and heard his word, his divine nature may be signified.

But it should be noted why, when this Gospel reading has spoken of two sisters, the evangelist, in describing the name of one—Martha—immediately and distinctly adds “a certain woman,” whereas he introduces the name of the other—Mary—merely in simple speech. For *woman* is a name of weakness, because our Redeemer, in the human nature which he assumed for us, bore our weakness. But his divine nature could never be touched, even slightly, by any affliction of weakness or misery of human frailty. Yet this woman—that is, the human nature of almighty God—was not just any woman but “a certain” woman, that is, a unique one; for every human nature, which began to grow weak in Adam, is weak and will always be sinful, except this alone, which truly, as we have said, was a certain one: namely, immune from all sins, [Col. 0960B] altogether free from every human contagion.

This certain woman therefore received him into her house, namely into the house of weakness and misery, because, having become man for our sake, he did not disdain to endure every frailty of human mortality except sins alone. And this same woman is appropriately named Martha, which is interpreted “irritating” or “provoking,” because our Redeemer, as we have said, clothed in the members of human frailty, by the much serving which he rendered to God the Father for human redemption, powerfully provoked against himself the wrath of the ancient enemy; and, provoking him even unto death, afterwards overthrew him by his own death.

“And he had a sister named Mary.” They are called sisters, and are sisters, who are born of one father or one mother. Therefore the human and divine natures of almighty God were in a certain manner sisters to one another, because both natures are from God the Father: human nature was created by God the Father; divine nature was begotten from God the Father in Christ [Note: [Col. 0959] That is, Christ, as God, is from God the Father—namely, God from God, etc.]. His divine nature is also rightly to be understood through Mary, whose name in our language means “ruling” or “lady,” because although, appearing in flesh, he humbled himself unto death and endured all manner of unworthy things belonging to human frailty and misery, nevertheless in that divinity by which he always was and remains coeternal with the Father, he ruled both heavenly and earthly things. It follows:

“She also, sitting at the Lord’s feet, heard his word.” To sit belongs to one judging; to stand, to one fighting. By the Lord’s feet, moreover, as the authority of Holy Scripture frequently teaches, all the ways of the Lord are to be understood—namely mercy and truth. Beside these feet of the Lord [Col. 0960D] the divine nature then sat, when the Son of the eternal Father, equal, coeternal, and co-omnipotent with that same Father, judged all things in mercy and truth; for all who are to be saved are saved through mercy, and all who are to be condemned are judged through truth. Seated in this rest of eternity, in this majesty of coequal substance, she heard the word of the Lord; that is, she heard and obeyed God the Father. But the word of that same Father was the counsel concerning human restoration, which true and eternal divinity deliberated from the beginning of the world: namely, that God-man, destined to suffer much for the restoration of man, should appear in the flesh. This word, this counsel of the paternal will, she heard, embracing and desiring it with the delightful affection of devotion, so that God, taking the form of a servant, might empty himself and bring aid to fallen man through the ignominy of Passion and death.

But amid these matters we must return to ourselves, entering within ourselves, and with anxious reflection recall to the eyes of the mind how great is the danger of condemnation in that we, who are indeed earth and ashes, disdain to obey the divine commands for the advantage and benefit of our own salvation, when he who was in the bosom of the Father, equal in omnipotence and of undivided majesty, having no need and requiring no grace from anyone, did not disdain to obey the eternal Father out of love for our salvation. But since we have heard how eternal divinity humbled itself and inclined to come to our aid, it is fitting that we should devoutly consider how solicitous his humanity was, by a grace of kindness, for our salvation. For the sacred reading continues:

“But Martha was busy with much serving.” Martha was busy with much serving because the humanity afterwards assumed voluntarily accomplished everything which the divine will had ordained to be done for the restoration of man. She was also busy with much serving when, serving God the Father humbly in his body, he rendered the service of due satisfaction which man owed for himself. I would further seek a subtler understanding in this word, “was busy” (*satagebat*).

For in saying *satagebat*, we may understand the phrase as though it said *satis agebat*, “he did enough.” For if our Lord and Redeemer had only been born for us—if, I say, he had only lived well in the world and taught well; if, moreover, enduring death itself, he had not descended to hell to free souls; or if, after his resurrection and ascension, he had not sent the Holy Spirit, the Father’s promise, into the hearts of believers—he certainly would not have done enough. But after he had completed in the humanity he assumed all these things which the misery of human destruction required, when, I say, he had finished the work which the Father gave him to do, then it could rightly be said that Martha had been busy with much serving, that is, had done enough.

Martha was also busy with much serving when, at the Last Supper, he delivered his body, a holy and living sacrifice, to his disciples: “This,” he said, “is my body; do this in remembrance of me, as often as you receive it” (Luke 22:19). This service is rightly called frequent, because as often as the commemoration of this sacrifice is celebrated, the work of our redemption is performed.

For not only did that service which he rendered to God the Father in the days of his flesh then intercede for the sins of the world, but this same service is made frequent until the consummation of the age; that is, it does not cease to intercede for the sins of humankind. For this is why the same Son of God offered himself as a living sacrifice to God the Father: that that service might in some manner be frequent for those liberated and to be liberated; that is, just as at that time it was the quickening to true immortality for those dead in death of soul, so, as long as the present age remains, those dead in sins may be quickened through this service. That is, as often as a person has strayed from the way of truth by sinning, so often he may find reconciliation through this service. Thus, how Martha, being busy with much serving, labored in serving for us, and what and how great things she endured for us, the reasoning that follows immediately declares plainly. For it says:

“She stood and said.” As we said above, sitting belongs to one judging, but standing to one fighting. The Son of God came into this world not to sit or rest, but to stand: namely, to attack that strong man armed who guarded his courtyard, and whose possessions were in peace. He therefore stood, not for the sake of resting, but having undertaken the battles of arduous conflict. He stood laboriously when he steadfastly endured spittle, blows, scourges, and every misery of human mortality. Hence, when he had labored standing even unto death, and, wearied by the immense weight of the struggle, had sweated drops of blood, his holy humanity—which alone suffered—complained as though abandoned: “Lord,” he says to the Father, “dost thou not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?” Dost thou not care that I alone, without sin, author of innocence, endure such abject [Col. 0962C] misery and such manifold ignominy of Passion? Hanging also upon the cross, placed at the very moment of death, crying out with a loud voice, he said to the Father: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). For just as here he spoke as though asking: “Dost thou not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?” so there too he speaks to the Father in a certain manner by asking: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”—“Dost thou not care,” he says, “that my sister has left me to serve alone?” My sister, that is, my divinity, since she is impassible and immortal, has as it were left me alone to serve. She has left me, I say, to serve alone, because with humanity alone I have endured and endure all the labor of the conflict and all the pain of the Passion.

“Tell her therefore that she may help me.” Then the Son of the eternal Father sought the aid of divinity when, as we said above, being in agony he prayed to the Father: “Father,” he said, “if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39). If it be possible, I say, for the redemption of the human race to be accomplished without the price of my Passion and death, tell her, namely divinity, to help me; that is, by the power of divine majesty, remove from me the imminent misery of the Passion.

“And the Lord answered and said to her: ‘Martha, Martha, thou art anxious and troubled about many things.’” This is as though the paternal voice answered the Son now about to suffer in these words: “I know that thou art anxious with an affection of merciful compassion, that fallen man may be restored to the dignity of his uncreated inheritance; I know that thou art troubled about many things, because weak flesh fears to suffer the pains of so many passions. But one thing is necessary. This one necessary thing is the saving remedy of thy Passion and death. For it is necessary that thou, the just, suffer for the unjust; thou, alone free from sins, for slaves of sin; thou, the innocent and spotless Lamb, for the lost sheep. It is necessary, I say, that by thy death the dominion of death be destroyed and dissolved.”

It is fitting also to seek an understanding of a still deeper sense in these words of the Lord. For we should not leave unexamined the fact that, answering Martha, the Lord did not name her once only, but, repeating it as it were, called her twice by her name: “Martha,” he says, “Martha, thou art anxious and troubled about many things.” But since every human being consists of two things, namely soul and body, he also possesses within himself two wills: one according to the soul, the other according to the body. Thus the incarnate Son of the eternal Father, possessing two natures within himself, namely human and divine, is known likewise to have had two wills: one according to humanity, the other according to divinity; according to humanity, indeed, a will of obedience; according to divinity, a will of justice. But when human nature, constrained by the will to obey yet weak through the frailty of flesh to bear the force of the Passion, sought the assistance of her sister, as though complaining that she was abandoned, God himself, remaining in divine nature, answered his humanity in these words: “Martha,” he says, “Martha, thou art anxious and troubled about many things.” As though he said: “O human nature, composed of soul and body, thou art anxious according to the soul that fallen man may be redeemed; but thou art troubled according to the body, because weak flesh trembles to suffer the labors of so many struggles and the pains of so many passions. But behold, thy anxiety will be exceedingly useful and thy trouble exceedingly profitable, because thou art troubled about many good things—namely, about the salvation of many. But one thing is necessary. This one necessary thing is my divinity, by which thou art one with me and remainest forever consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal with me. Yet this one thing is necessary—that is, it must always exist—because my divinity, just as it receives no changeability, so admits no weakness and can suffer no Passion. Therefore it is altogether necessary that, while it remains unchangeable, thou be troubled about many things; that is, that the trouble of thy Passion may bring to many the salvation of eternal redemption. For unless thou, becoming obedient unto death (Phil. 2), destroyest the prince of death, the human race, dead in the death of the soul, can in no way be quickened.”

“Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her.” The best part of Mary was the work of human redemption. The work of human redemption was best because it was a work of mercy. For God performed all his works through power; but he performed this work of human redemption through mercy. And the Holy Trinity apportioned this work of mercy among itself in such a way that the divine nature in the Father should be propitiated, the divine nature in the Son should make propitiation, and the divine nature in the Holy Spirit should kindle and overshadow the blessed Virgin Mary, through which overshadowing she should conceive the Son of God: “Which shall not be taken away from her,” until it is completed, until man is redeemed.

And the present Gospel is not read unfittingly on this most holy Assumption of the blessed Virgin, because this same blessed Virgin Mary was the singular material of human redemption, since she bore incarnate from herself the Son of God, through whom this entire work of mercy, the work of our redemption, was to be accomplished. Therefore, turning now to her, let us pray that she, full of grace, piety, and mercy, may obtain for us by her venerable intercession that we may be made participants in this best part and may deserve to behold her upon the throne of glory, to which on this day she merited gloriously to be exalted above the choirs of angels, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXV. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE SAME FEAST

“Jesus entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house” (Luke 10).

Since we celebrate the solemnity of the glorious Virgin Mary, let us contemplate the magnificence of the glory of her holiness in the heading of the Gospel reading, as in a mirror of virginal composition. Although the subtle and lofty intellects of many great interpreters, both modern and ancient, have labored hard in the field of this reading, nevertheless countless mysteries, fragrant and hidden beneath the chaff of the letter, still give forth their fragrance—mysteries both of the glorious Virgin Mother and of the most high royal Son. For the Holy Spirit, author and writer of this reading, has wonderfully opened the storehouse of his treasure to whom he wished and as he wished; and this same reading, overflowing with an inexhaustible abundance of mysteries, he still mercifully discloses to whom he wills and as he wills. Therefore the evangelist says:

“Jesus entered into a certain village.” A fortress, where it is built for protection, is surrounded on every side by the fortification of a wall; and, with a tower rising in its midst, the structure of the wall is protected from above, so that in turn the wall is defended by the tower and the tower is fortified by the wall. Accordingly, by the name of this village the undefiled virginity of blessed Mary is suitably represented: her life, established under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, is wonderfully strengthened by the entire defense of continence, and is humbly defended against every missile of diabolical suggestion by the incomparable and impregnable citadel of humility. Jesus entered into this village when the Son of God, King of angels and Creator of heaven, delighted alike by the incomparable chastity and humility of the most blessed Virgin Mary, visited the palace of her womb and, like the sun striking a glass window with its ray without breaking it, made her virginity fruitful without violating it; and by his entrance and exit he wonderfully adorned, glorified, and exalted her.

Concerning this glorious and wonderful entrance and exit of the eternal King, Ezekiel the prophet spoke magnificently when, beholding the eastern gate in the structure of the mountain, he described it thus: “And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it; and it shall be shut for the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord. By the way of the vestibule of the gate he shall enter, and by its way he shall go out’” (Ezek. 44:2–3). The shut gate was blessed Mary, ever-Virgin, who lay open to the Prince alone, when the Holy Spirit, by the overshadowing of his power, opened her womb to the Son of God alone for the redemption of the world. The Prince himself sat in her and ate bread before the Lord when the King of kings and Lord of lords himself chose, in the bosom of her humility and chastity, the most sweet and most desired shade of his rest, like a young hart, as he himself foretold through Isaiah the prophet: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon one humble and quiet, and trembling at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). The blessed Virgin herself also testifies to this in reality in her canticle, when she rejoices that through her profound humility she has been regarded from heaven by the Son of God: “For,” she says, “the Lord hath regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). Therefore, when the Prince sat in her and ate his bread before the Lord, the Son of God, with the majesty of the Father and Holy Spirit cooperating, assumed flesh in her womb, which he offered to God upon the cross for the redemption of the whole world. Concerning this bread the ungodly said in the book of Wisdom: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. 11:19). “By the way of the vestibule of the gate he enters, and by its way he goes out,” when the Son of God is conceived through the faith of the most blessed Virgin and is wonderfully born from the Virgin’s womb through her faith for the redemption of the world. For the vestibule of the gate signifies the virginity and humility of blessed Mary; the way of the vestibule signifies her faith, through which she spoke thus to Gabriel, the heavenly bridegroom’s friend: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done unto me according to thy word” (Luke 1:38). Hence the Gospel reading appropriately continues:

“And a certain woman, named Martha, received him into her house.” The certain woman described here by the evangelist is surely she of whom the Creator speaks to the serpent in paradise: “I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed” (Gen. 3:14). The serpent signifies the ancient enemy; the woman signifies the blessed Virgin Mary. The seed of the serpent was that death which entered the world through the devil’s envy; the seed of the woman was Christ the Lord, who by his death put death and the author of death to death upon the cross. Of this most blessed woman Jeremiah the prophet also says: “Behold, the Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). Since *mulier* (“woman”) is named from softness, the most blessed Virgin is rightly expressed by this name: her heart, melted by the fire of the Holy Spirit into love of her Creator, was so dissolved that she merited bodily to conceive him in her womb and to bear the true God and true man whom, before all mortals, her soul spiritually embraces with incomparable and ineffable love.

She is also rightly described by the name of woman, since by a singular affection of mercy she is moved to compassion for the human race, so that she may pour out continual sighs of prayer for the redemption of the world to him whom she herself loves especially above all others, the Son of God. The intensity of this mercy and compassion in the most blessed Virgin Mary is indicated in the Book of Kings, where the third captain of fifty, after the first two had been consumed by heavenly fire, humbly bends his knees and suppliantly begs Elijah to come down from the mountain (4 Kings 1:13). Elijah, whose name means “the Lord God,” signifies Christ the Lord; the third captain of fifty signifies the human race, which is established in the third age of this world, namely after the natural law and after the written law, under grace. This captain of fifty bends his knees before Elijah when the human race sets the most blessed Virgin, fulfilling its embassy, before the Son of God, so that she may overcome him by her tears and prayers and bring him, thus overcome, down from heaven to earth—him whom not even the intolerable cry of patriarchs or prophets could overcome. The blessed Virgin Mary is rightly expressed through the captain’s knees, because in her God is joined to man and heavenly things are allied with earthly, just as the upper and lower parts of the body are connected at the knees. Of this blessed and glorious woman the evangelist says: “And a certain woman, named Martha, received him into her house.”

Because Martha is interpreted “irritating,” “provoking,” or, in the Syrian language, “ruling,” the etymology of this name rightly represents the body of the most blessed Virgin. By the abundance of fasts, vigils, and all continence it irritates the ancient enemy; by the abundance of tears, by the contrition of fasts and vigils, and by bending of knees, it provokes the Son of God to come down from heaven to earth, that the blessed Virgin herself may merit to rule over heaven and earth. This Martha therefore receives Jesus into her house when the most blessed Virgin Mary, by her humility, chastity, and love, brings the Son of God down from heaven to earth; and receives him, made poor for us, an exile and pilgrim for us, into the lodging of her own body, when she gives him from the substance of her flesh the material of flesh which he may offer to God the Father on the cross for us. Finally, she makes him a little tunic, as Hannah made one for Samuel, by which he may hide the power of his majesty from the ancient enemy. For Samuel’s little tunic is the humble humanity of Christ the Redeemer, which the Holy Spirit wove in the Virgin’s womb, and in which the Virgin Mother clothed him from her own flesh, so that his divinity might not be recognized by the enemy and the redemption of the cross might not be impeded. “For,” says the Apostle, “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). For it would have profited us nothing to be born unless redemption had come about. It follows:

“And he had a sister named Mary.” Mary is interpreted “star of the sea,” or, in the Syrian language, “lady.” Accordingly, as Martha represents the flesh of the blessed Virgin, Mary signifies her most holy soul. She is rightly called the star of the sea because she becomes, through her protection, deliverance, and propitiation, a star to all believers tossed upon the sea of this age, through whom they may escape the darkness of sins and the abyss of death and reach the harbor of eternal salvation, [Col. 0967B] where she, exalted above the choirs of angels by her Son, is appointed mediatrix and lady of the whole world. Mary is therefore described as Martha’s sister because the soul of the blessed Virgin Mary, while it is bound to her body in the present life, is expressed as being indeed an heir of Christ and a coheir of God to come, just as the Holy Spirit speaks to her in the Song of Songs: “Arise, make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come; for now winter has passed, the rain has gone and withdrawn.”

“She also, sitting at the Lord’s feet, heard his word. But Martha was busy with much serving.” Mary sits at the Lord’s feet when the soul of the blessed Virgin, placed in the flesh, clings inseparably to the love of her Creator. She sits at the Lord’s feet when she directs all the attention of her heart to consideration of divine mercy or judgment: namely, the mercy by which man, formed from earth, was placed in paradise, and the judgment by which he was exiled from paradise. Therefore, while she sits at the Lord’s feet, she hears his word, because the soul of the blessed Virgin, placed in the flesh, while constantly attending to the mercy or judgment of God the Creator, recognizes in the Holy Spirit the dispensation of the Son of God for the redemption of the world.

The soul of the blessed Virgin therefore hears that word of God by which Moses, at the beginning of Genesis, describes light as made. For light is made through the word of God when the Son of God himself, with the Father and Holy Spirit cooperating, personally unites a rational soul and flesh to his divinity in the Virgin’s womb; he who says of himself in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Concerning him the evangelist likewise says: “He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world” (John 1:9). Moses also describes the word of God when, after the making of light, he says: “And God said: ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters’” (Gen. 1:6). A firmament is made through the word of God in the midst of the waters when the true Son of the Virgin, by the operation of the Holy Spirit, is temporally born for the salvation of believers. The waters are divided from the waters when believers are separated from unbelievers, through the mystery of his birth, at the future judgment. The word of God is repeated when, after the interposition of the firmament, Moses adds: “Let the waters which are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear” (ibid. 1:9). The waters which are under heaven are gathered into one place when, through the Redeemer’s baptism, all believers emerging from the laver of baptism and abiding in the unity of Mother Church are at some time gathered together in the heavenly kingdom. There, indeed, the dry land appears, because in the heavenly kingdom the land of the living abounds, concerning which the Psalmist proclaims: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13).

When the waters under heaven had been gathered together, Moses adds that God said: “Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed” (Gen. 1:11). The earth brings forth green grass when, after the baptism of the Saviour, as he himself preaches the word of salvation, the earth multiplies the offspring of believers. It bears seed when, through faith, hope, and charity, in pure thoughts, upright words, and devout works, it sends forth the succession of eternal life. Of this sending forth the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruits of fruit-trees” (Cant. 4:13).

After the earth’s germination Moses adds that God said: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night” (Gen. 1:14). Lights are made in the firmament of heaven when, through the Passion of the Redeemer, the wounds of redemption shine in his body. They divide day and night when the mysteries of his Passion separate Judas from the apostles, one thief from the other thief, and the faithful from the faithless in hell.

After the lights had been made in the firmament of heaven, Scripture adds that God said: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of living being, and fowl above the earth” (ibid., v. 20). The creeping thing of living being is brought forth from the waters when the Redeemer’s soul returns in triumphal procession from the prisons of hell with innumerable companies of believers. A bird above the earth is brought forth when the body of the Redeemer, dead and laid in the tomb, is brought forth from the bosom of the sepulchre by gloriously rising on the third day, as the soul returns. Here God is described as having blessed creeping things, swimming things, and flying things, because in Christ’s resurrection God the Father is understood to have multiplied the orders of the holy Church among married believers, among the continent, and among prelates.

After all this Moses adds that God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (ibid., v. 26). Man is formed in the image and likeness of God when, through the Redeemer’s Ascension, the human race is re-formed in the image and likeness of its Creator. This re-formation indeed begins in the mystery of his Ascension, but is fully consummated at the future judgment, when he himself, the head of all believers, will graciously address his elect, set at his right hand as members joined to him: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34). For then, says the Apostle, we shall be like him, when we see him, established in the kingdom of his Father, as he is, face to face (1 John 3:2): so that we may truly live in him who is life living in himself; that in him who is supremely blessed we may be able to share true blessedness; and finally, that in him who is the joy of all the elect we may rejoice eternally, and in him who is the unchangeable God may ourselves always remain unchangeable.

Therefore Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, hears his word, when the soul of the blessed Virgin, while placed in the flesh and intent upon the mercy and judgment of God the Creator, fully apprehends in the Holy Spirit the dispensation of the only-begotten Son of God concerning the redemption of the world—a dispensation which the Only-Begotten of God, and her own first-born and only-begotten son, mercifully and wonderfully accomplishes in the mystery of his incarnation, birth, baptism, Passion, resurrection, Ascension, and future judgment. It follows:

“But Martha was busy with much serving.” [Col. 0969B] While Mary hears the Lord’s word, Martha is busy with much serving; for while the soul of the blessed Virgin, placed in the flesh, apprehends in the Holy Spirit the mystery of redemption, her body, made pregnant by the Holy Spirit, wonderfully accomplishes that same mystery of redemption by conceiving and bearing the true Son of God, true man. Accordingly Martha is described as being busy with much serving, because this Lady of the world, after the only-begotten Son of God the Father—her own first-born and only-begotten—was born of her, renders him many services: she wraps him in swaddling clothes; binds his hands and legs with bands; places him in a cradle; lays him in a manger; carefully gives him the nourishment of milk; gently offers him kisses; receives the gifts of the Magi; brings him to the temple with offerings; leads him, fleeing from Herod, into Egypt and brings him back; and, finally, most diligently performs for him every office of maternal tenderness and compassion in the weakness of humanity assumed by her and in her.

Therefore the Evangelist consequently adds: “She stood and said: ‘Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her therefore to help me.’” The blessed Virgin stands while she stands by her son set upon the cross, with untiring maternal compassion, all her inward parts and bones resounding, beyond remedy, from the excess of sorrow, while streams of tears flow incomparably from her most holy eyes day and night. The blessed Virgin speaks when, gazing on the bitter wounds of her beloved first-born and only-begotten son and contemplating his bloodied limbs, she expresses also the bitter wounds of her own heart for him through continual floods of tears.

“Lord,” she says, “Son of God, Creator of heaven, who formed the first man from earth; who, by the command of God the Father, assumed true manhood from me, a Virgin-mother, for the redemption of the human race: do you not care—something unfitting to your mercy, you who are the mercy of God the Father—while you hang upon the cross for the salvation of the whole human race? You who care for all who love you, believe in you, desire you under the natural law, desire you under the written law, await you in hell, and serve you through the succession of ages until the end of the world.

“Lord, my only-begotten, do you not care for me, a poor woman, though a Virgin-mother, that my sister has left me to serve you alone? Do you not deign to consider that my soul—which once exulted in my most holy impregnation, in your most sweet and most desired conception, and magnified God the Creator—that soul, I say, now pierced by the sword of your Passion, as that Simeon prophesied to me, who carried you as an infant in his arms—that soul, I say, surrounded by the darkness of death, has now drawn near to the gates of hell as grief overwhelms it?

Therefore my sister has left me to serve you alone, because, as my soul fails in the pain and sorrow of death, my body, as though lifeless, can no longer bear—indeed is scarcely able still to bear—the weight of vigils, the wasting of fasts, and the showers of tears. Therefore tell her—you who are the Word of God the Father, who have the words of eternal life—tell her, tell my desolate and embittered soul words of eternal consolation. Let me hear your voice; let your voice sound in my ears. Tell her therefore to help me, so that my soul, raised up by your filial consolation, may raise, sustain, and revive my lifeless body, now nearly dead and about to fall.” It follows:

“And the Lord answered and said to her: ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things.’” Christ, in his Passion, answers his most holy mother: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26), who in the flesh taken from you has become on the cross the sacrifice for the whole human race. In his resurrection Christ says to his most holy mother, gladdening her by his vision and appearance: “Mother, behold, your son lives, who had died on the cross for the salvation of the world.” The holy Evangelists were silent about this vision and appearance, judging that the most holy Mother of the Lord was not to be compared with the other persons who merited to see him after his resurrection; and therefore they perhaps considered that the appearance of her son made to her should be suppressed in silence.

Thus the son, set upon the cross, says to his mother: “Martha, Martha, beloved and chosen mother! Martha, who cherished, cared for, and brought me up, incarnate from you, with maternal affection; Martha, who do not abandon me in my Passion, who suffer with me in maternal affection: you are anxious [perhaps *pro fuisti*, “you have been”] who strove to attend upon me, born from you, with the tenderness of maternal devotion—washing me when born, clothing me when naked, feeding me when hungry, giving me drink when thirsty, consoling me when crying, laying me in the manger, carrying me to the temple, migrating into Egypt, bringing me back from Egypt, taking me at twelve years old to the temple, seeking me when lost, receiving me again when found, and diligently fulfilling in me every office of maternal affection and care.

“But now in my Passion you are troubled about many things, seeing so many bloody wounds of my body and grieving at the many and great streams of my blood. You are troubled about many things, burning with maternal concern over how, and by whom, my body, once I have yielded up the spirit, may be taken down from the cross; how it is to be buried, wrapped in linen cloths; and how, where, or by whom it is to be committed to burial.

[Col. 0971A] “Yet one thing is necessary. It is fitting that I, one man—I, innocent God and man, who alone shall be free among the dead—it is fitting that I alone should die for the whole people of my elect, and that not the whole nation should perish, lest the whole multitude of my faithful, from the beginning to the end of the world, fall into the depth of the abyss. Everything written of me in the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets must be fulfilled: since by my blood, which shall be poured out from my side, the flaming sword shall be quenched, paradise shall be opened to my faithful thief, by my descent into hell the people of the saints shall be delivered, and by my resurrection and Ascension the kingdom of heaven shall be opened to my elect.

“Therefore Mary has chosen the best part, because your most holy soul, O most beloved mother, lady of the souls of all the faithful, has chosen for itself the best part: while placed in the flesh, it set all earthly things after the love of God the Creator alone, and by the integrity of its love earned for itself and for all its children the kingdom of heaven. For when you, most holy Virgin, bore me, king, prince, and head of all the elect, you yourself merited to be called and to be the mother of all my elect, as of my members, from the beginning to the end of the world. And indeed, for all of them together with you, O worthiest mother, this best part shall be the unfailing and eternal vision of God the Creator, overflowing with everlasting satisfaction, as the Psalmist says: ‘They shall be filled with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight’ (Ps. 35:9). This shall not be taken from her, because from you, my most holy, sweetest, and most loving mother, and from the whole household of all my elect joined to you, my vision, full of delight and joy, shall not be taken away; through it every misery of the present life shall be blotted out in forgetfulness for endless ages of ages. Amen.”

489 HOMILY LXVI. THIRD HOMILY FOR THE SAME FEAST.

“Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall” (Cant. 2).

The splendid feast of the present day, on which we venerate and celebrate the Assumption of the holy Mother of God, is to be reverenced and commemorated by all the faithful with so much the greater solemnity and celebration because it is certain that the Lord wished to remove her from this present world for this purpose: that, raised above the choirs of angels, she might intercede more confidently for our sins, as the universal Church humbly entreats him on this feast, saying: “Great, Lord, before your mercy is the prayer of the Mother of God, whom for this reason you have removed from the present world, that she may intercede more confidently before you for our sins.”

So that this same blessed Virgin, whose prayer is truly of great weight in the ears of the supreme Majesty, might be able to intercede more confidently with God for us sinners, the Holy Spirit, inviting her in the Song of Songs to be raised from this vale of tears above the throne of glory, says through the mouth of most wise Solomon: “Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.” Although these words, and indeed the individual mysteries of the book, are most aptly applicable to the universal Church or to each faithful soul, and spiritually express in mystical understanding the love of bridegroom and bride, they nevertheless seem to apply more particularly to the blessed Virgin Mary, who above all others was singularly full of special love and merited to be specially loved above all by her bridegroom himself. And because she is able to obtain more than all others from the same bridegroom through her prayers, she is now, as we have said, invited to arise and come, so that she may intercede unceasingly with greater confidence for those who sin.

“Arise,” he says, “my friend, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.” What do these different names mean—that she is called friend, beautiful one, and dove? Since she was adorned with many and diverse virtues, the Holy Spirit also wished to honour her with many and diverse names. For each of these distinctive names displays singular marks of virtue, with which divine grace wonderfully adorned her. She is called friend because of faith, beautiful because of hope, and dove because of charity. For how great was the constancy of faith in the blessed Virgin is clearly shown by this: she believed without hesitation the angel’s wondrous and unheard-of announcement; she did not doubt that, with her virginity preserved, she would conceive and bear a son; and thus, believing well the words of the announcing angel, she became a special and singular friend of God. She was likewise beautiful through hope, because she placed all the confidence of her hope in God and most certainly hoped that everything said or promised to her through the angel would truly be fulfilled in her. She was also a dove through charity, because no one at all could or will be comparable to that Virgin in charity toward God and neighbour. For who ever loved the Lord so greatly? Who knew how to grieve and suffer with such feeling for the miseries and afflictions of neighbours?

The names already mentioned—friend, beautiful one, and dove—may also be understood otherwise: she is to be called friend through humility, beautiful through chastity, and dove through simplicity. And she may fittingly be called God’s friend through humility, since true and perfect humility makes the faithful soul near and most friendly to God; and just as pride often separates a person, even a holy and devout one, from God, so humility mercifully reconciles a person, even a sinful and impious one. Where the true and profound virtue of humility exists, there undoubtedly will not be lacking true and fruitful repentance, which by humble satisfaction destroys and wipes away a multitude of sins. Just as by pride an angel became the devil, and that first parent was driven and cast out of paradise, so by the humility of the blessed and immaculate Virgin, after the wall of enmity had been destroyed, the reconciliation of the human race was accomplished.

For the words of the same Virgin plainly indicate how humility alone, among all the virtues with which she was adorned, pleased the Lord above all others: “For he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). Although she surpassed all mortals in holiness, chastity, humility, and every moral excellence, nevertheless in the deep humility of her heart she judged herself inferior and more contemptible than all. And therefore she deserved, not incongruously, to be called and to be the friend of God, who knows how to give grace only to the humble.

She was also made beautiful before the Lord by complete chastity of heart and body, never stained by carnal desires; for she not only strove to preserve the integrity of her limbs and senses, but kept wholly unstained every inclination of her thoughts. And while she was thus beautiful in the Lord’s eyes through chastity, she was nevertheless a dove through simplicity. But how can we call simple one whom eternal Wisdom itself, God, inhabited? In many persons of little shrewdness there is a certain simplicity that is not praiseworthy and is more usually called blameworthy foolishness. But who would suppose that such foolish simplicity existed in the blessed Virgin, who merited to be the mother of eternal Wisdom and was wiser than all the wise?

That good and praiseworthy simplicity is believed to have existed in her by which most holy Job is praised, of whom it is said: “A man simple and upright” (Job 1:1). Although the whole conduct of this wisest Virgin was upright, holy, and just, and although every inclination and thought of her virginal heart was chaste and pure, she nevertheless weighed all things with such a measure of simplicity that she ascribed nothing whatever to her merits, nothing to her own merits, but everything to divine loving-kindness and mercy.

Therefore the Holy Spirit calls back with joyful voice this humble friend, this beautiful one, most chaste in heart and body, and this dove truly simple, exhorting her to arise and come. Whither, or for what purpose, does he exhort her to arise? Surely not to some praiseworthy work, she who never ceased from good works. Rather, he exhorts her to arise from this exile, from the misery of this life, and reach the royal throne of the kingdom, where without labour or weariness she may, as said above, aid us wretched and afflicted persons. “In the clefts of the rock,” he says, “in the hollow of the wall.” What is to be understood by the rock except Christ? “The rock,” says the Apostle, “was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). By the clefts of this most firm rock we may not unfittingly understand the heavenly companies of blessed spirits. For just as holes are prepared in precious stones, into which gold must be inserted so that each receives ornament from the other, so those blessed angelic spirits possess the splendour of eternal brightness from the precious stone, Christ, to whom they cling inseparably. They are likewise in a certain manner an ornament to their Creator, because they were created by him for his glory; and not only angelic spirits are the beauty and ornament of their Creator, but also the blessed souls of the elect, who seem not unfittingly to be designated by the hollows of the wall.

The conclusion appears to be missing.

HOMILY LXVII. FOURTH HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE ASSUMPTION OF ST MARY THE VIRGIN.

[Col. 0974A]

“You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no stain in you” (Cant. 4).

Since the chosen and pre-chosen Mother of the Redeemer alone became the material cause of our redemption by the sole Redeemer, it is rightly recognized as the common duty of all the saints to render to the Mother of the Creator—who is to be preferred before all creatures—an homage of praise as devout as it is due. The praiseworthy knowledge of patriarchs and prophets everywhere published testimonies to the most excellent renown of her merits, as they awaited and desired the only son of this unique woman, whose coming in the flesh would become the necessary and longed-for end of bondage to captivity. Hence most wise Solomon adds a new jewel of nobility to the bright gold of his wisdom, when, among the other things that he wonderfully declared in praise of the Creator, he desires to bring forth a song of singular elegance in glory of the Mother. In one particular passage among the many things worthy of remembrance in this song, he marks her with special praise, to be admired through all ages: “You are wholly beautiful,” he says, “my friend, and there is no stain in you.”

The blessed Mary, Lady of the world, Queen of heaven, Empress of angels, and singular material of all sacraments, is worthily and fittingly described as wholly beautiful and wholly fair. As befitted the Mother of the supreme King, by the beauty and loveliness of virginal flesh she clothed the Father’s Only-Begotten himself, who, being ineffable, willed to work ineffable things in his Virgin-mother, so that no sin might cling to her in the place of sin, whether in word, thought, or deed.

The words of Solomon, again spoken in praise of the Mother of the Saviour, show how vigilantly she guarded her mind against unlawful thoughts: “She has considered the paths of her house, and has not eaten her bread in idleness” (Prov. 31:27). Clearly a path is narrower than a broad and spacious way. What then do we understand by the paths of the house but subtle and minute thoughts? She considered these paths—that is, the inclinations of her thoughts—with so watchful an inspection of mind that she remembered to investigate and guard even the roots of thoughts themselves, so that her entire intention might look to him to whom she adapted herself in every way. Nor did she eat her bread in idleness, because she turned all the fruit she received from spiritual teaching toward the practice of praiseworthy life. For everyone eats bread idly who neglects to fulfil in works the words of life received by hearing.

Hence it is immediately added how great was the sweetness of the blessed Mary’s words and how beautiful their gravity: “And the law of clemency,” he says, “is on her tongue” (ibid., v. 28). For the praise and honour of her son, she uttered with honeyed throat the sweet testimonies of the Law which she pondered in her most holy heart; and him whom she had conceived not only in her womb but also in her mind, through the Gospel believed in the heart unto righteousness, she in some manner also bore in the hearts of believers by announcing and preaching the grace of that same son. Since she had enlarged the dwelling-place of her breast so as to confer and retain all the words which she had eagerly drawn by hearing from her son’s mouth, she deserved rightly to be called and to be the special and intimate friend of God: namely, the faithful and whole keeper of his mind.

But it should be noted: when she is called wholly beautiful in mind and most chaste in body, why is it immediately added, “and there is no stain in you”? Since she is the complete pattern of holiness, what stain of sin, I ask, could touch her? The mother of innocence therefore had a stain: none other, namely, than the guilt of original sin, which she did not lack at her birth, because, like the other children of Adam, she could not come forth into the world without sin.

In pleasures conceived and born, she shared with other sinners, through the usage of nature, this condition: that she lay subject to original sin until her own Only-Begotten, through himself, from his Mother and through his Mother, should remove and blot out from all persons the stain of that same original sin.

> **Note:** [Col. 0975D] On this opinion of Godfrey, see our preliminary Dissertation.

The teaching of the Fathers plainly explains what original sin is: namely, ignorance of the soul and concupiscence of the flesh, which all human beings have contracted from Adam’s fault as by hereditary right, and which, we do not doubt, adhered also to our Lady, the perpetual Virgin Mary, alone. But when the manifold fullness of the grace of the Holy Spirit inundated and suffused her, it so diminished and expelled every ignorance and every concupiscence of the flesh in her that, not ignorant of all divine secrets, she alone knew all things knowingly, and, under the overshadowing power of the Most High, felt no concupiscence of the flesh.

For so the angel’s speech promises the Virgin who is to bear Christ: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). When the Holy Spirit comes upon your higher part—that is, your soul—all ignorance will be removed from you, and every concupiscence of the flesh in you will be diminished and extinguished, so that, just as no actual sins adhere to you, neither may any original sins adhere to you. It follows:

“Your lips are a dripping honeycomb.” Her lips are rightly compared with a dripping honeycomb, because the honey-flowing utterances of her mouth overflowed with such grace that, however she gave forth a voice of exhortation, they never sent away the hearts of hearers empty and without fruit. For, according to the Apostle, she was accustomed to drip nothing except honeycombs of exhortation, edification, or consolation, by whose drops she could profitably pour refreshment into and restore the hearts of her neighbours.

Indeed, it is fitting for every teacher to maintain this pattern of instruction: to set before those advancing from good things to better words of exhortation; not to neglect to edify the slow and ungrateful; and to remember to support the faint-hearted and wavering by a word of consolation. Our Lady the Virgin Mary fulfilled all these things all the more perfectly because she merited to love and acknowledge the Father’s Only-Begotten more sweetly and pleasantly than all others, not partly but wholly; and from him she had received in fullest measure what she could sweetly dispense to others. Therefore it fittingly follows:

“Honey and milk are under your tongue.” For while through lips dripping the honeycomb of honey-sweet grace she served the benefit of her neighbours, in the time of prayer she entered the repose of inward contemplation, and found honey and milk stored not upon but beneath her tongue, because she was permitted to taste as much as she wished of the ineffable sweetness of Christ’s humanity and divinity. And it was beneath the tongue because human eloquence is not adequate to them. For eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the human heart how much sweetness that most sweet son of the Virgin poured into the Virgin’s heart.

“The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” What are meant by the ointments of spices except the sweetly fragrant perfumes of virtues, with which our Lady Mary was so anointed inwardly and outwardly that she imparted a fragrance not only to earth but also to heaven? But although the spices of every virtue were fragrant in her, she nevertheless merited especially to possess two chief virtues, which surpassed all spices—that is, all the distinguished marks of merits. But what, I ask, are these two, from which so wonderful a greatness of fragrance is exhaled? Surely the beauty of chastity and the weight of humility. Her guardian, the Holy Spirit, had so surrounded her with these and rendered her so eminent by them that even the angelic spirits marvelled and stood astonished at how she immersed herself in such great and profound humility, she who surpassed the excellence of angels and the holiness of human beings by the immensity of her merits: so that the more chaste and pure she was, the humbler she was in her own eyes; and the more exalted she was above all mortals, the lower she considered herself.

Her most noble praises of virtue are further and more broadly expressed when it is added:

“For now winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed.” What is designated by winter except the hearts of the whole human race frozen by the cold of unbelief? This wintry freezing wholly passed away in the blessed Virgin, because, from the time that she was born and taken into the discipline of the Holy Spirit, she began always to burn with an unquenchable ardour of love. For she alone, though still clothed in flesh, most fully discerned and acknowledged—indeed, tasted in truth—what would be the reward of future blessedness, by which the author of recompense will give himself as a reward to those who love him. What could she have failed to know when the Father with the Son, and the Son with the Holy Spirit, continually made her rejoice in joy with his countenance?

Therefore, because winter has passed, the rain also has gone and departed. By rain is understood the flow of unclean seed by which all human beings are begotten and conceived in their mother’s womb. That rain indeed departed when our Lady, proceeding from the sin of unclean seed, lived without sin and became a virgin of the Holy Spirit.

> **Note:** [Col. 0976D] On this opinion of Godfrey, see what I noted a little above in note 66.

Nothing of carnal concupiscence flowed into this Virgin; though she proceeded from carnal intercourse, she did not know carnal pleasure. It departed completely when that noble man, the one man, deigned to be conceived not from seed in the womb of the same Virgin. Therefore, because the winter of sin passed, because the rain of unclean seed departed, because it withdrew by the power of the Most High, manifold flowers appeared—flowers which could bring forth nothing but the most splendid gems of virtues. For she flowered in every bodily sense so completely that she alone, from the flower of virtues, brought forth the flower—her Son, the fruit of all grace.

“The flowering vines gave forth their fragrance.” By the vines are understood her body and soul, from which the vine-dresser, the supreme Father and husbandman, pressed new wine, wine of delight and joy, by which he intoxicated angels, gladdened human beings, and scattered fragrance through heaven and earth.
