497 HOMILY LXVIII. FIFTH HOMILY FOR THE SAME FEAST.

> **Note:** [Col. 0977D] Perhaps because the manuscript does not expressly contain this.

“There shall be a firmament in the earth upon the tops of the mountains; its fruit shall be exalted above Lebanon, and they shall flourish from the city like the grass of the earth” (Ps. 71).

The holy prophet David, beholding in prophetic spirit the Lord who was to come in the flesh, sang of that incarnation, filled with the Holy Spirit, saying: “There shall be a firmament in the earth.” Our Lord Jesus Christ may fittingly be understood by the firmament, because just as the sun, moon, and stars are contained in the firmament of heaven, so all these things are truly found in Christ Jesus. The sun in the Lord Jesus was divinity, which dwelt bodily in Christ; the moon was assumed humanity; and the stars were the virtues with which he, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, was filled.

The Prophet therefore rejoiced in the Holy Spirit because this firmament, although it was in heaven, would nevertheless come to be on earth; that is, although he was God above all things, the Son of God nevertheless willed to assume flesh among all things from that noble earth, the blessed Virgin Mary.

But someone says: “Therefore, if this firmament is to be on earth, if the Word is to assume flesh, what will happen in heaven?” The Prophet answers such a questioner thus, saying: “Upon the tops of the mountains.” The highest mountains are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; as though he said: Although this firmament is to be on earth, although the Son clothes himself with the substance of flesh from an incorrupt Virgin, nevertheless the Son, who is one person in the Trinity, will not depart from the highest mountains—from the Father and the Holy Spirit—but will remain in them and with them in the glory of his divinity. He then adds what is to become of the assumed humanity of the Son of God:

“Its fruit shall be exalted above Lebanon.” In Lebanon, which is interpreted “whiteness,” the angelic creation may be expressed, which has remained with God in the brightness of everlasting life. Therefore his fruit, namely the Son of God and man, whom the blessed Virgin Mary bore fruitfully in the Holy Spirit, after completing the dispensation of the flesh which he undertook for our salvation, will not remain here in his assumed humanity; rather, he will exalt that flesh, in which he will live forever, above all the choirs of angels.

What fruit has arisen, or will arise, in the holy Church from the fact that our Lord Jesus Christ, incarnate for us, has now been exalted in that flesh above every angelic creature, is immediately added in what follows, when it is said:

“And they shall flourish from the city like the grass of the earth.” The city is the holy Church, in which holy souls now, after Christ’s incarnation and Ascension, flourish with the little flower of virginity and chastity like the grass of the earth. The grass of the earth is Christ the Lord made man; blessed souls now fashion themselves after the likeness of this grass, following his purity and integrity, because the flesh of the Lamb too is virgin.

Before the Saviour’s incarnation, indeed, few vowed and consecrated their virginity to God. But after the Son of God became man, many of both sexes, following and imitating the Spouse of incorruption in virginal body, have flourished in the holy Church through chastity and integrity.

Having foretold these things concerning Christ’s incarnation and the exaltation above the angelic creation of the human substance which he took from the womb of the immaculate Virgin, the Prophet had first said in the preceding psalm concerning the power of his divinity and the judicial authority which he received from God the Father according to his human nature:

“I will proclaim your arm to every generation that is to come” [Col. 0978C].

By the Lord’s arm may be understood the strength of his divinity. For the greatest strength of a human being is vigorous in the arms, and all strong and praiseworthy deeds are performed and accomplished through the arms.

Accordingly, his divine strength is rightly understood by the arm: by that strength he performed and performs strong and praiseworthy works, doing whatever he willed in heaven and on earth. The Prophet said that he would proclaim this arm, this strength of divine majesty, to every generation that is to come. The generation that is to come is the generation of the righteous, which tends toward true being, which the Lord chose for his inheritance, and which throughout succeeding ages until the end of the world is to come to faith in and love of the Son of God. For whoever does not tend toward true being is nothing and is counted as nothing before God, because without God a human being is nothing. It follows:

“Your power and your righteousness, O God, reach unto the highest things—you who have accomplished great deeds. O God, who is like you?” God the Father gave to the Son, under our Lord Jesus Christ’s human nature, authority and judgment to execute judgment, so that in the form of a servant, in which he was judged, he might be judge of the living and the dead, as the Son himself says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

Therefore the power and righteousness that he exercises in judgment are so great and so strict that he exercises this judicial power not only among human beings but extends in this severity of justice even to angels, as is said here: “Unto the highest things, which have accomplished great deeds.” In the words “the highest things” and “great deeds,” apostate angels may be understood. Although they degenerated by apostatizing from God, they were nevertheless created in great honour and, as the prophet testifies, were “the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40:14).

His power, therefore, which according to his human nature he received from God the Father, and his justice, which he employs in judgment, extend from human beings even to the apostate angels, whom he eternally condemns in hell because they sinned against the Lord.

## HOMILY LXIX. FOR THE FEAST OF THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, SIXTH.

[Col. 0979B]

“I sought rest in all things, and I shall abide in the inheritance of the Lord” (Ecclus. XXI).

The words of this sacred reading, taken from the book of Wisdom [Ecclesiasticus], would reveal within themselves the whole work of human redemption, if anyone were able worthily and adequately to perceive, understand, or set them forth. These words are aptly taken from the book of Wisdom, because the salvation of human redemption was truly a book of Wisdom and a work of Wisdom. For although eternal Wisdom made all his works with great and wonderful wisdom, the work of redemption surpasses all his works. And because the blessed Mother of God, Mary, was the cause of that redemption, since it was to be accomplished and completed through her and through her Son, the Holy Spirit rightly and fittingly appointed this reading in the present feast in her honour.

“I sought rest in all things.” These are the words of the holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. “I sought rest in all things.” God created all things that exist; yet he did not seek rest in all of them. There were certain things in which he sought rest. These were rational creatures, namely angelic and human beings, for whose sake he created all things. And because all other things were created for rational creatures, when the eternal wisdom of God rests in that creature to which all things are subject, he is not improperly said to have sought rest in all things. Yet he sought and seeks rest in this way, not because any rest was necessary for him—he to whom, in respect of divinity, nothing has ever been added or taken away—but so that angels and human beings might find in him everlasting rest and blessedness, becoming sharers in his knowledge and love. But in all these beings he did not find the rest he sought, because the highest angel fell, and man fell.

Nevertheless, that rest did not perish altogether. When the apostate angel fell with his followers, a certain part of the angels remained, among whom he dwelt and rested, as he says: “And I shall abide in the inheritance of the Lord.” For they became the Lord’s inheritance, in which he might dwell, since through the fall of the wicked angels they were so confirmed that they could never fall. Nor did humankind fall in such a way that it could not rise again and, redeemed, someday attain the same inheritance of the Lord—that is, the fellowship of angels. Since the holy Trinity foresaw and ordained this from eternity, the future tense is rightly used: “I shall abide.” For God the Father always held this in his purpose: that the rest which had been lost should be restored and renewed. Yet because this restoration and renewal could not take place except through the incarnation and passion of his Son, he then commanded and spoke, so that through Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension this rest might be restored, and through the coming of the Holy Spirit might be preached throughout the whole world.

In the three expressions, “commanded,” “spoke,” and “Creator of all,” the whole holy Trinity may be understood together: in “commanded,” God the Father; in “spoke,” God the Son; in “Creator of all,” God the Holy Spirit. By the command of God the Father, God the Son came into this world for the redemption of humankind; by the command of God the Father, the Holy Spirit was sent for illumination and preaching. But since the work of redemption belonged to the Son alone, he does not say, “He commanded me,” but “He spoke to me.” For he is the ineffable Word of the Father, through whom all things were made, as it is written: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII [33]:9). He spoke, I say, to me, his Son, so that through me, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, the redemption of humankind might be accomplished.

And while I obey the Father’s command through the mediation of the Holy Spirit, he who created me rested in my tabernacle [Col. 0980C], and said to me: “Dwell in Jacob, and take Israel as your inheritance.” Here all Christ’s mysteries are indicated: in “he created me,” the incarnation; in “he rested in my tabernacle,” the passion. God the Father in a certain manner created the Son, equal and coeternal with himself, when he decreed that he should become incarnate; and he rested in his tabernacle when he sent him to his passion. For a tabernacle, which belongs to soldiers, rightly signifies his most holy body, in which he faithfully and courageously served under God the Father for the salvation of humankind.

Before this tabernacle, which he had put on from the undefiled Virgin, blessed Mary, was rent through the passion on the cross, God the Father rested in no human being; for after Christ’s incarnation, as before it, all descended to hell after completing the course of this present life. But when this tabernacle was rent upon the altar of the cross, God the Father then first found the rest he had sought. For through the passion of his Son, the long-closed gate of the heavenly kingdom was opened to those who believe in him. Immediately after the trophy of the passion follows the glory of the resurrection.

“And he said to me: ‘Dwell in Jacob.’” By Jacob, whose name means “supplanter,” Christ’s resurrection is signified, because through his passion and resurrection he overthrew the devil and conquered death and the dominion of death. The word “dwell” aptly belongs to the resurrection, because where a person dwells, there he desires to possess a stable abiding-place. Christ, according to his human nature, was mortal and willed to die. But, rising from the dead, [Col. 0981A] he so established himself that he would die no more; dwelling in the stability of eternal incorruption, he rules and reigns over heaven and earth. And after the instability of this life, once the resurrection of body and soul has been accomplished, he promised us mortal beings immutability.

But because neither in his incarnation, nor in his passion, nor in his resurrection would we have full hope of the eternal vision unless he placed at the Father’s right hand that same human nature which he assumed, he added and said:

“And take Israel as your inheritance.” By Israel, interpreted as “the man seeing God,” the ascension is rightly signified. For the Son of God, who descended from the Father’s bosom, brought the humanity that he assumed to the vision of God the Father; and thereby gave us hope that we too must someday arrive where he ascended, there to possess with him the rest of eternal blessedness. The word “inherit” aptly belongs to the ascension, because what belongs to a man by hereditary right can neither be nor ought to be taken from him by any mortal. Thus, indeed, the Son of God inherited heaven when God the Father—whose every possession he shared according to divinity—delivered all things to him according to humanity, as he himself says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII:18).

But for all these things to be confirmed and made known to the whole world, the Holy Spirit had to be sent to the apostles. Thus it immediately follows:

“And send roots among my chosen ones.” God’s chosen ones were the holy apostles, whom he chose for himself from the whole world. Into them he sent his roots—that is, all the mysteries of his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension—when he entrusted to them the task of preaching and proclaiming these mysteries everywhere, saying: “Go, teach all nations” (ibid., 19). Why are these mysteries signified by roots? Where there is a root, fruit is hoped for, whether good or bad; but if the root is uprooted, there is no hope of fruit. So all who believe the Lord’s mysteries, confess them, and carry them out in good works, certainly bear such fruit as saves them eternally.

It follows:

“And thus I was established in Zion; likewise I rested in the sanctified city; and my power is in Jerusalem.” [Col. 0981D] These three—city, Zion, and Jerusalem—may signify the three orders in the Church: Zion, interpreted “watchtower,” those engaged in contemplation; the sanctified city, those who do good works; Jerusalem, called “vision of peace,” prelates who preach well. After the passion, resurrection, and ascension, it is aptly added: “And thus I was established in Zion,” because thus—that is, in this faith of the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension—that rest was established among those engaged in contemplation, those who do good works, and those who preach well. Without these mysteries, a human being could attain neither the sweetness of prayer, nor contemplation of the mind, nor knowledge of holy Scripture. These mysteries sweetly inflame a person inwardly and open holy Scripture, which is wholly [Col. 0982A] full and suffused with the price and splendour of our redemption.

But because the power of contemplation belongs to few and to the perfect, we are consoled by what follows:

“And likewise I rested in the sanctified city.” By the city, in which there is a multitude of people, are signified, as I said, those who act well in the active life. God likewise establishes his rest in them, because as the former are saved and sanctified through contemplation of the mind, so the latter are saved and sanctified through the action of a good life. But because pastoral concern must not be lacking to these two orders, he added: “And my power is in Jerusalem.” By the name Jerusalem, interpreted “vision of peace,” prelates are designated because they ought to show and make known the way by which one proceeds toward the vision of eternal peace—by teaching to contemplatives and by good works to those who act well. They are aptly admonished by the words:

“And my power is in Jerusalem.” For their pre-eminence over others and their greater power than other people do not come from themselves but from God’s power. Therefore he says, “my power”: “my power,” so that they may be admonished to exercise the lordship and authority they wield over their subjects in such a way that it may be called not their power but God’s power. And because this rest was established not only in those now present, but also in those who were before the Law and under the Law, it aptly follows:

“And I took root among an honoured people, and in the portion of my God is his inheritance.” [Col. 0982C] The honoured people were the patriarchs, whom God truly honoured and in whom he rooted his faith, though they did not deserve to see and await what they believed. That pious and great patriarch Noah was greatly honoured by God when, as the world perished in the flood, he alone with a few was saved in the ark. Abraham, the outstanding and chief patriarch, deserved to be greatly honoured by the Lord: at the Lord’s command he left his country and his kindred; he did not shrink from offering his only son to the Lord; and through this he deserved to be called teacher and prophet among God’s people. Having thus shown that this rest was established in them and in the other saints before the Law, he immediately adds how it was established also in those under the Law:

“And in the portion of my God is his inheritance.” The Jewish people were the portion of God’s inheritance: he chose them as his own possession and gave them his Law. For he allowed all nations to go their own way, but took these alone as his inheritance, as it is written: “But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the cord of his inheritance” (Deut. XXXII:9).

Having indicated those who were before the Law and under the Law, he also introduces those under grace when he says: “And my possession is in the fullness of the saints.” For although he rooted his rest among the honoured people, and although from many he took a certain part into his inheritance, yet his possession is in the fullness of the saints. For those whom he chose and redeemed under grace, admitting them to the fullness of his grace, he holds so firmly [Col. 0983A] and binds so closely to himself that neither they can nor he will—or can—be separated from the other forever. What this fullness of the saints ought to be in merit, and what it will receive in reward, eternal Wisdom of God, who here speaks, mystically reveals, saying:

“I was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon, and like a cypress on Mount Zion; I was exalted like a palm tree in Cades, and like a planting of roses in Jericho; like a beautiful olive tree in the plains, and like a plane tree exalted beside water in the streets; like cinnamon and balsam giving forth fragrance I gave an odour; like chosen myrrh I gave the sweetness of fragrance.”

Here four things are set forth: a cedar exalted in Lebanon, a cypress on Mount Zion, a palm tree exalted in Cades, and a planting of roses in Jericho. By these four is expressed the life of all who have been or are to be saved, as follows. By Lebanon, interpreted “whitening,” may be understood those whitened or cleansed through baptism; by the cypress on Mount [Col. 0983B] Zion, penitents enlightened through teaching; by the palm tree exalted in Cades, those sanctified by a good life; and by the planting of roses in Jericho, those perfected through martyrdom.

Those first persons, whitened through baptism, are aptly compared to the cedar, whose scent drives away serpents: when they are whitened and cleansed in baptism, evil spirits are driven and put to flight far from them. Likewise, by Mount Zion are fittingly understood penitents enlightened through teaching. For Mount Zion signifies the height of doctrine; taught and enlightened by it, they do not cease, through the endeavour of inward satisfaction and repentance, to cleanse themselves of their sins. Such persons, converted through repentance to true innocence, resemble the cypress, whose scent, like that of the cedar, drives away serpents. For those who truly repent flee and detest those evil serpents—the invisible enemies—who have no power over them.

After the cypress on Mount Zion—that is, after that height of penitents—follows the palm tree exalted in Cades. Cades is interpreted “holy”; it signifies those sanctified through a good life. Like a palm tree exalted in virtues, advancing beyond those whitened through baptism and rising above those cleansed through repentance, they have deserved to be sanctified by God through a good life: such as blessed Gregory, Martin, Nicholas, Benedict, and those like them. Like a palm tree, they were exalted as they strove [Col. 0983D] to go from virtue to virtue, conquering what lived in them according to the flesh and living holy and righteous lives according to the Spirit.

After the palm tree exalted in Cades follows the planting of roses in Jericho. By the rose, which is red, are aptly understood those perfected through martyrdom. They came to Jericho—that is, to the failing of their flesh—when they unhesitatingly shed their blood for the confirmation of the truth, and thereby planted Christ’s faith in the hearts of others. Such was blessed Stephen, who at that time strengthened faith in Christ in the hearts of believers more by his blood than the apostles, still teaching, either did or could have done. Therefore those whom we have called whitened through baptism, enlightened through [Col. 0984A] repentance, sanctified through a good life, and perfected through martyrdom, we may call in another way the innocent, penitents, those advancing or conquering, and those being perfected or dying.

The other four members which follow—beautiful olive tree, exalted plane tree, cinnamon and balsam, chosen myrrh—rightly correspond to these four members which we have distinguished. The preceding have great correspondence with the following, and the following with the preceding. To the cedar exalted in Lebanon rightly corresponds the beautiful olive tree, that is, mercy; to the cypress on Mount Zion rightly corresponds the plane tree exalted beside water in the streets, that is, forgiveness of sins; to the palm tree exalted in Cades rightly correspond cinnamon and balsam, that is, chastity of the flesh and purity of heart; to the planting of roses in Jericho rightly corresponds chosen myrrh, that is, perfect mortification. Why and by what property we have thus assigned these virtues to each expression, let us now examine, God granting.

By the olive tree mercy is rightly understood, because as oil surpasses all liquids with which it is mixed, so God’s mercy is above all his works. By the field, which is neither ploughed nor cut, are understood the innocent. Thus he rightly says, “a beautiful olive tree in the plains,” for the beautiful olive tree in the plains is indeed God’s gratuitous mercy toward the innocent: by it he rewards and crowns those who, not furrowed or cut by the plough of labour or the share of discipline, immediately pass over and arrive at the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

By the plane tree, which has broad leaves, forgiveness of sins due to penitents is not unfittingly understood, because according to the multitude of sins almighty God ought to extend the breadth of his forgiveness: “For all have sinned and need the glory of God” (Rom. III:23). “Beside water in the streets” means among those who walk, according to carnal [Col. 0984C] desire, on the broad and spacious way of the world.

By cinnamon, which is ash-coloured, and balsam, which has a pleasant scent, may most fittingly be signified chastity of body, purity of heart, or the glory of righteousness. Some attain these so perfectly that they never feel any unlawful movement in their flesh; thus we read of blessed Benedict that after he had once overcome temptation, he thereafter suffered no such trouble in his flesh. They also attain purity of heart when they are so justified and glorified that, as they are not moved outwardly toward unlawful things, so neither do they inwardly admit a perverse delight of the heart. Like cinnamon and balsam giving fragrance, they yield to others a good fragrance from themselves while preserving chastity of body and purity of heart.

After all these things, chosen myrrh fittingly follows: this is perfect mortification, which will be given in the future. To summarize and repeat these same words: to the innocent, beautiful olive tree—that is, gratuitous mercy—is given as their reward; to penitents, forgiveness of sins is given as their reward; to those who conquer, chastity of body and purity of heart are given as their reward; to those being perfected or dying, perfect mortification is given as their reward. This perfect mortification, as we have said, will be given in the future, because although there are persons who mortify themselves in the present, they nevertheless receive chosen myrrh, that is, perfect mortification, only in that eternal life. For where there will be no death, there will be neither sin nor any pain or weakness, nor will anything subject to corruption thereafter approach; there our Lord Jesus Christ will be the fragrance of sweetness, and he will satisfy and fill his elect with every good thing through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXX. FOR THE SAME FEAST, SEVENTH.

[Col. 0985B]

“Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a little column of smoke, from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Cant. III).

In these words, which the Holy Spirit, as though in wonder, utters through the mouth of wisest Solomon, he plainly indicates the glory and blessedness of the undefiled Virgin whose feast we celebrate today. For, briefly comprehending that her chaste and immaculate life on earth, and her venerable assumption into heaven, celebrated today, were objects of wonder not only to human beings but also to angels, he says: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a little column of smoke?”

This same blessed Virgin Mary passed and ascended through the wilderness of this present age by an immaculate path, while with all the intention of her heart and all the devotion of her soul she attended solely to heavenly things and, through contemplation of the mind, transcended all visible and earthly things. Hence her ascent or assumption today was wonderful and venerable to all angelic spirits when her only-begotten Son received her with ineffable joy, to reign with him forever.

Yet while she still remained in this mortal body, she ascended daily in heart and mind; she ascended not like a rod, but like a little rod—not as something great, but as something small—because she did not consider herself great, lofty, or exalted, but judged herself little and humble, inferior to all others. For as a little rod is straight and tender, easily bent and inclined, and as a person is often corrected and restrained by it for discipline, so the blessed Mother of God, walking the straight paths of righteousness, always had a mind tender and pliant toward every good and perfect work. Making herself a little rod of discipline, she guarded and restrained all her senses so that she preserved both soul and body from every sin.

She is aptly said to have ascended “like a little column of smoke.” [Col. 0985D] For by smoke, which rises on high and is bitter, producing bitter tears, may fittingly be understood her tearful and afflicted spirit, which daily offered bitter tears to God for the salvation and redemption of humankind. Her tearful prayer, like a little column of most sweet smoke rising on high, ascended before the Lord from the humble and contrite heart of that Virgin.

And from where did such a little column of smoke arise? “From the perfumes,” he says, “of myrrh and frankincense.” By perfumes we may fittingly understand the works of good virtues; by myrrh, mortification of the flesh; by frankincense, contemplation of the mind. What human tongue could sufficiently describe or recount the virtues of the most holy Mother of God, in whom the very power and wisdom of God dwelt bodily? Every adornment of virtue which the Holy Spirit distributes to his elect as he wills, God-made-man bestowed all together upon his Mother. Although holy Scripture says almost nothing about the mortification of her virgin flesh, no one can doubt that she always mortified her flesh and the things of the flesh in herself by a firm and strict discipline. And what can I say of the contemplation by which she attended to God alone, when the entire abundance of divine sweetness undoubtedly filled her?

“And every powder of the perfumer.” Although the perfumer of every powder—that is, the magnificent worker of all virtues—must most fittingly be understood as the Holy Spirit, nevertheless we may understand something else in these words. Just as any skilled perfumer strives to grind and prepare every kind of spice into the finest powder so that he may heal the various troubles of illnesses, so that aforementioned true perfumer, the Holy Spirit, bestowed and gathered in the heart of the undefiled Virgin Mary every powder of healing grace, namely all gifts of mercy and grace, so that because there are many diverse ailments in humankind, she might have many diverse remedies by which she is able to heal and cure the sick souls of sinners. For even if a sinful person were utterly hopeless or dead in sins, if that Mother of Mercy lays the hand of her intercession upon the sick person, no infirmity whatever, no iniquity at all, can prevail against the sinful soul.

We have briefly run through these matters, as best we could, in praise and glory of today’s feast. Let us now endeavour to apply the same words to ourselves. For although they belong especially to our most noble Queen, they may nevertheless be applied mystically to every faithful soul, because they express for us both the beginning of good conversion, the pursuit of holy conduct, and the contrition of humbled heart and body.

Therefore those angelic spirits, who always rejoice and exult in human progress, praise and magnify, as though in wonder, every person to be saved who desires to ascend through the wilderness of this present age. “Who is this,” they say, “who comes up through the wilderness?” By the wilderness, in which there are cruel beasts and innumerable animals, may aptly be understood the present age or the heart of a sinful person. A person to be saved desires to ascend through this wilderness by good conversion and holy conduct, when, preceded by divine mercy, he begins to recognize and fear spiritual beasts and harmful animals—that is, his own iniquities and sins. And lest he be slain and perish through these beasts and animals, he resolves in his heart to ascend through the aforesaid wilderness, that is, to flee to God through good conversion. But the following words plainly indicate what the beginning or the first impulse of this conversion is like.

“Like a little rod,” he says, “of smoke.” In the little rod, which, as I said, is straight and tender and by which a person is restrained through fear of discipline, is rightly understood the will for good conversion, born either from fear of punishment or from fear of strict judgment. For as the little rod has straightness and tenderness, so the will of a new conversion likewise possesses straightness and tenderness. It has straightness because it is a right will when an animal-like human being desires to turn to good things. It has tenderness because he cannot yet fulfil in action the good which he wills. Accordingly, this will is called not only a little rod but also a little rod of smoke: just as smoke is seen but cannot be touched or handled, so a right will, though still weak and tender, is seen by the Lord and by the holy angels, but is not touched or handled by hands, because it is not yet proved by good works.

Moreover, just as smoke is bitter and dark, so a person then suffers bitterness and darkness within himself, because it is very bitter for him to despise the sweet pleasures of the world and mortify and cut away within himself the sweet desires of the flesh. Therefore he walks, in a sense, in darkness, for he does not know what he ought to choose or reject. But when, with the Lord’s help, he has fulfilled his good will by a conversion pleasing to God and has begun to labour in holy conduct, then what follows is surely realized:

“From the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.” In myrrh is understood mortification of the flesh; in frankincense, contemplation of the mind or the fragrance of good reputation; in every powder of the perfumer, contrition of humbled heart and body. Once the flesh has been mortified with its vices and desires by the myrrh of continence, by the myrrh of continual and untiring labour, there follows the frankincense of contemplation or the frankincense of good reputation. For after a person has conquered, by mortifying them through vigils, fasts, and other labours, the vices and desires of the flesh, and has deserved to taste beforehand the grace of divine contemplation, insofar as this is possible in the present life, it frequently happens that the fragrance of good reputation and the fame of his holy conduct reaches the ears of many. Thus the wind of self-exaltation begins incautiously to buffet a mind insufficiently on guard. There it is certainly necessary that every powder of the perfumer be applied against rising self-exaltation.

For “every powder” is rightly understood in a twofold manner as contrition of humbled heart and body: namely, so that a person may neither seek nor desire outwardly human praise for good works, nor inwardly become proud or puffed up because of illumination of mind. For if he avoided being praised by human beings for good works but did not fear being vainly exalted by the invisible grace of contemplation, he would indeed be powder, but not every powder. Therefore let the faithful soul strive to possess every powder: namely, most profound humility of heart both for good action and for divine contemplation. It must also possess every powder in this way: if it has fallen through the vice of self-exaltation, it should displease itself for this in its own eyes and, repenting sincerely, have recourse to humble satisfaction.

But because no one can possess this whole powder of which we have spoken without the gift and grace of that true perfumer, the Holy Spirit, let us humbly entreat the Mother of Mercy, whose feast we celebrate today. Through her intercession—she who, holier than all saints and most chosen of all the elect, testifies that by humility alone she especially pleased the Lord—may we so humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God in the present life that we may deserve, with joy and exultation, to see her in the glory in which on this day she was exalted above all choirs of angels. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXI. FOR THE FIRST DAY OF THE OCTAVE OF THE FEAST OF THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.

“I, like a vine, brought forth the sweetness of fragrance” (Ecclus. XXIV). [Col. 0988C]

Today, on the eighth day, we conclude the joyful feast of the Assumption of our precious Lady and Queen, which we have celebrated with solemn devotion during these seven days. For by the octaves of the saints, which we celebrate with worthy proclamation of praise, there is signified the future resurrection of bodies and the twofold reward of bodies and souls together. During six days we continually work and labour in this present life; on the seventh day we cease from all labour. This seventh day signifies for us the time in which the souls of the elect, having received the rewards of their labours, enjoy the eternal vision of their Creator, while their bodies, as though released from the excess of their labours, rest safely in their graves from all work and pain. But when the desirable brightness of the eighth day shines forth—that is, when the future resurrection comes—then body and soul alike, having received the twofold robe of immortality, will triumph in the joy of complete security.

Therefore, although the octaves of all saints are festive and joyful in view of the ineffable glory of that eighth day, the octave of the most glorious Virgin Mary is to be venerated with a more excellent honour of dignity. Through her alone all the saints were sanctified and predestined and called by her Son to this glory. And just as the dignity of her life surpasses the merits of all the saints, so she likewise avails more than all of them; therefore, before all others, her grace must be sought, through which alone the intercessions of all saints are directed to her Son.

The reading appointed for today commends to us the excellence of merits and the greatness of sanctity through which she attained such glory. In it the Holy Spirit enumerates her glorious merits, speaking as if in her person: “I, like a vine, brought forth the sweetness of fragrance.” Though these words apply generally to the holy Church, they are most fittingly suited to the dignity of blessed Mary, for whose praise they were selected and arranged. She was truly a noble vine, in whom the Holy Spirit planted most delightful gardens. Well cultivated and protected on every side by him, she brought forth the sweetness of fragrance.

A vine, indeed, is a contemptible and unattractive wood among other trees, yet the fruit it bears abundantly nourishes people with sweetness. Thus the humble Virgin fittingly compared herself to a vine: she humbled herself so greatly that in her own eyes she appeared lower than all human beings. This fruitful vine, therefore, sets forth to us the praises of her humility in these words: “I, like a vine, brought forth the sweetness of fragrance.” This is as though she said: “I, who in the estimation of my most humble heart subjected myself to all, brought forth the sweetness of fragrance, because my humility itself diffused a most sweet fragrance in the court of the heavenly kingdom.” Thus also in the Song of Songs: “While the king was at his repose, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Cant. I:11). Nard is indeed a lowly herb, but exceedingly fragrant. Blessed Mary’s humility is rightly compared to it, for the King of kings delights lovingly in its most pleasing sweetness.

“While the king,” she says, “was at his repose”—while he lay hidden in the secret place of his divinity—my profound humility exhaled before him a fragrance of such sweetness that it drew him from the bosom of God the Father and from the height of heaven into my virgin womb. Thus she also says elsewhere: “When I was little, I pleased the Most High, and from my own womb I bore God and man.”

Since, therefore, I brought forth such sweetness of fragrance, “my flowers are fruits of honour and dignity.” When flowers appear, fruit is soon expected to follow. In this place, the flowers aptly signify the heavenly embassy and the glorious words brought to the Virgin by Gabriel, prince of the heavenly court. “When these flowers of mine appeared,” she says, “when the words of the supreme embassy sounded in my ears through the archangel, that noble fruit immediately followed—the fruit of honour and dignity—because at once I conceived the Son of God by the power of the Holy Spirit coming down from above.”

And he rightly calls him the fruit of honour, because he is truly the honour of God the Father, whom in the eternity of his divinity he begot as coeternal, coequal, and consubstantial with himself. He was also his honour in his humanity, because through him God the Father was recognized [Col. 0990A] and made manifest, though previously hidden and unknown. For before his coming in the flesh, it was unknown to the world that the Holy Trinity existed—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and scarcely a few could attain recognition of this faith. But when Christ appeared in the flesh and began to preach, faith in the Holy Trinity was made known through him to the whole world. [Note: Col. 0989D: So the manuscript.] Hence he himself says to the Father in the Gospel: “Father, I have made your name known to the people whom you gave me” (John 17:6).

He was also made the fruit of honourableness; for the honourableness, or holiness, of all the saints cannot be compared with his. They indeed were conceived and born in sins, and, as long as they lived, were never entirely free from the stain of sin. But this most honourable man [Col. 0990B] was conceived and born without sins, and never contracted the stain of sin in word, deed, or thought. Since, then, the fruitful vine, the virgin and most humble mother, brought forth this noble fruit, she rightly says further of herself:

“I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope.”

That is to say: I am the mother of that man whose love alone was truly fair, because it flowed solely from the fountain of his most merciful compassion. For one person loves another for personal advantage, hoping to receive some benefit in return; and this love is not fair, but may rather be called necessary. The love of the Son of God alone, by which he loved us, was fair love, since it arose not from any necessity, but from the greatness of his incomprehensible [Col. 0990C] goodness.

Some material appears to be missing.

517  
## HOMILY LXXII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW THE APOSTLE

“A dispute arose among the disciples of Jesus as to which of them seemed to be greater” (Luke 22).

We must raise the attention of the inner person and consider what moral sweetness this Gospel reading contains within itself. And lest we believe that the dispute which arose among Jesus’ disciples is to be imitated by us, let us hear how the Master of humility himself recalled them from this contention:

“The kings,” he says, “of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them.” These kings are our carnal senses, under whose power our body [Col. 0990D] and soul are governed with too little caution in opposing directions. For they are rightly called, and indeed are, kings of the Gentiles: that is, of all who live after the manner of the Gentiles, who, while subjecting the things of the spirit to carnal desires, bear the yoke with unbelievers under a Christian name. But when sin begins to reign in their mortal body, and the flesh, lusting against the spirit, wholly prevails, then what is said later suddenly comes to pass: “And those who have power over them are called benefactors.” For then our carnal senses are called, as it were, benefactors, while, as they wage war against the soul, we supply them with every incentive to vice, so that the fattened corruption of the flesh [Col. 0991A] spreads abroad, and the soul’s strength, dissolved like a spider’s web, grows thin.

“But not so with you,” he says. You, my most chosen disciples in humility, strive after the better gifts, so that whoever is greater among you may become like the lesser. These words indeed present on the surface a great pattern of humility; 518 yet they indicate something loftier through spiritual understanding. For who can more rightly be called greater than the human spirit that is within a person? This spirit is greater and more sublime than every creature, provided, as has been said, that it is always like the younger—that is, that it always strives to renew in its soul by works of righteousness and truth the youth it received through newness of life at the font of baptism, [Col. 0991B] lest that old person at some time again envelop the soul, now aging badly, in those deeds from which it was once stripped through the regeneration of water and Spirit. David had experienced both this praiseworthy youth of which we have spoken and the old age which all good people must avoid, when he said: “I have been young, and indeed have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken” (Ps. 36:25).

He flourished in great beauty of youth when he judged it best to cling to God alone and place all his hope in him; and, in the flower of youth, he foresaw with the eye of spiritual contemplation that the righteous person would never be forsaken by the Lord. But afterwards, weighed down by the old age of sins, his soul began to slumber from weariness. Hence Truth at once shows how this perilous old age of the slumbering [Col. 0991C] soul must be guarded against.

“And let the one who goes before be as one who serves.” Let every wise person carefully observe who this one who goes before may be. The forerunner of each of our actions is the very spirit dwelling within us. For whenever we desire to do either good or evil, it is the forerunner in all things, inwardly disposing all things by hidden inspiration. It serves each of the individual members by faithful administration, while bodily activity is through it worthily ordered beforehand within. When it performs well the office of its administration, all our action is approved before God. Then that Mediator between God and human beings, who came not to be served but to serve, will be as one who serves in our midst [Col. 0991D]. Hence he immediately says:

“I am in your midst as one who serves.” For the kindly minister will then deign to be in the midst of our soul, when that overflowing sweetness of divinity, pouring itself into our hearts through the grace of the Holy Spirit, has filled at once the whole substance of the inner person. Dwelling delightfully in its midst, he claims for himself the place of ministry, piously gathering there the various gems of virtues by administering them. But that we may know in whom so great and such a minister of majesty deigns to dwell, let us hear what is immediately added:

“For you are those who have remained with me in my temptations.” There are some who, at the first onset of temptation, do not give place to the devil, but for a while resist the deceits of the tempter with a strong mind; yet as soon as a more grievous storm-blast strikes, the weak mind suddenly abandons its state of firmness [Col. 0992A].

Since these do not run well in the racecourse, they cannot remain long in temptations with the Lord. But there are many who not only reject unlawful words or deeds, but also keep their hearts with every vigilance. These, surely, he who was tempted for us will at times not permit to be tempted beyond what they are able to bear; rather, with the temptation he will also provide the means of endurance. To them he immediately promises, saying:

“And I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, [Col. 0992B] a kingdom.” By the kingdom appointed for him by the Father, in which the eternal Son of God glories, we understand nothing more fitting than the kingdom of virtues. Since he is the radiance of the Father’s glory, bearing all things by the word of his power, it is beyond doubt that all the glory of virtues has been delivered to him as an everlasting kingdom by the Father’s appointment. This kingdom, which he alone possesses by the power of divinity, he wonderfully works by grace in the children of adoption, so that, distinguished by uprightness of character, they may have the kingdom of God within themselves and may sweetly eat and drink from his table among Jesus’ fellow guests. Thus what follows says:

“That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.” By the Lord’s table, upon which varied feasts of delights abound, the pages of the divine Scriptures are to be understood. Some merely skim and swallow them in their brief historical sense, refreshing the thirsty soul as though by drinking, without the sweetness of mystery. But those who search out every depth and hidden thing through laborious inquiry are filled with overflowing refreshment, receiving sweet food with the Lord [Col. 0992C].

Concerning this table the Psalmist says joyfully to the Lord: “You have prepared before me a table against those who afflict me.” The banquets of this table are prepared before the sight of our soul. For those who are daily pressed into combat against afflicters must surely be nourished by the refreshing abundance of this table’s sweetness, [Col. 0992D] lest, weighed down by the burden of their toil, they fail in the contest; rather, after overcoming their enemies, they may at last hold the throne of glory with the princes. Hence it also follows:

“That you may sit upon thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” When every faithful soul has happily triumphed over the enemy and gained the joys of inner peace, it is said to sit upon thrones like a mighty queen, exercising powerful judgment over the senses of the flesh. When it has reached the glory of such dignity, it will be able to judge the twelve tribes justly.

521 Yet perhaps we should consider more deeply what is to be understood by the twelve tribes. By the number twelve let us understand the entirety of our [Col. 0993A] actions, which we commit in three ways: in thoughts, words, and deeds. When the mind cleaving to Christ strives to order these with prudent discernment, it is said, as it were, to judge or govern the twelve tribes.

Therefore, that we may be able to attain so sublime a rule of judgment, let us diligently attend to the things set before us upon the Lord’s table; so that, feasting sweetly from it in the sight of God, we may become strong and steadfast against those who afflict us—he himself granting and aiding this, to whom be praise, power, and glory through the endless ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXIII. FOR THE FEAST OF THE BEHEADING OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST

“Herod sent and seized John, and bound him in [Col. 0993B] prison because of Herodias, the wife of Philip his brother, because he had married her” (Mark 6).

This outstanding forerunner of the Lord, just as by the holiness of his birth he prefigured our same Lord in a new and singular manner of life, so likewise in his death—which he suffered in the depths of prison for bearing witness to the truth—he fittingly represents that hidden and invisible death of Christ, by which Christ daily dies miserably in the human heart. The words of this present reading plainly suggest that very lamentable and miserable death, which even many of the perfect can scarcely sometimes escape, or cannot escape at all.

“Herod,” says the Evangelist, “sent and seized John, and bound him in prison.” By King Herod we believe that any spiritual prelate may quite fittingly be denoted: one who, in order to govern himself and all entrusted to him according to God, must wholly free himself from all worldly cares. Yet by the same king are likewise fittingly signified all who, having utterly left the world for love of their heavenly homeland, strive to empty themselves and, by habit and profession, show themselves worthy of God. Such persons indeed are in God’s sight and are called chosen kings when, judging themselves and their deeds strictly, [Col. 0993C] they do not cease to cut away with manifold contrition of heart and body whatever less worthy thing they discover in themselves.

The apostle Peter exalts these with a still greater proclamation of praise when, without distinction of sex, he says: “You are a royal and priestly race” (1 Pet. 2:9). But we may wonder how those constituted in the frailer sex ought to be called priests of the Lord. Yet this wonder is quickly removed by the testimony of sacred Scripture, which says: “Whether male or female, we are all one in Christ” (Gal. 3:28). In either sex, therefore, those are called kings and priests before the Lord who burn with longing for the heavenly homeland, kindle the fire of divine love upon the altar of their hearts, and through continual inward compunction offer themselves to the Lord as a living, holy, and spotless sacrifice.

But just as we have heard that all who fulfill not only so lofty a title but also that of priest are represented in Herod, so in his brother Philip [Col. 0994A] we may likewise understand secular rulers, and also all lovers of the world. Since these do not walk according to God, nor order or govern their life, conduct, and actions by God’s commands, they are called neither kings nor priests by the testimony of sacred Scripture, but only our brothers, because, created by one Father—namely Christ—they share with us the name of Christianity.

Their wife is Herodias, by whom is signified the concupiscence of this world. Embracing her freely and, as it were, permissibly, they shamelessly pursue her in heart and body, because the more truly they conform themselves to this world, the happier they judge themselves to be. [Col. 0994B] But it must be understood that worldly concupiscence is called not only the lust of the flesh, but also everything possessed or desired in the world: namely pride and sloth, vain glory, and other things like these. And the concupiscence of the age is well said to be represented by Herodias; for just as she then strove to bend Herod’s incautious heart toward unlawful love, so this concupiscence invisibly insinuates itself daily into all denoted by Herod, and labours, by the various illusions of its imaginings, to turn them aside from the path of uprightness. Thus it often happens that those who had once rejected the broad ways of the world, and had begun, through zeal for holy conduct, to pursue heavenly things alone, deceived by love of this spiritual Herodias—that is, worldly concupiscence—take her as wife. Placing her delightfully in the chamber [Col. 0994C] of their hearts, they unlawfully enter upon unlawful marriage with her. This is certainly not accomplished only when someone falls into the vice of the flesh; it happens as often as the inner person is corrupted by pride, avarice, or other such things. For when one who has resolved to serve God in a spirit of humility and gentleness delightfully subjects his heart to vices of this kind, he is, as it were, joined to another’s wife and commits the detestable crime of adultery before God’s eyes.

John—that is, the voice of the Word, the voice of Wisdom—strongly resists this person, and urgently addresses such forceful words to him, that he may return to his heart: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” As though saying: It is not expedient for you, whom a life of perfection begun had freed from the present world, to be defiled again by the desire [Col. 0994D] for earthly things, and, scorning the sweetness of Christ, to presume to direct your mind’s steps after the lusts of the flesh. But this voice of rebuke, alas, is sometimes made without the fruit of correction; for wherever the mind, subdued by the vices mentioned above, is held inwardly in evil captivity, what appears at the beginning of this Gospel reading takes place in a wondrous manner: “Herod sent, and seized John, and bound him in prison.” These three words plainly show that every stain of sin is committed in three ways: by consent, by deed, and by habitual sin. This is also aptly demonstrated in the three dead persons whom the Lord is remembered to have raised miraculously. But we must now examine more carefully [Col. 0995A] when and how Herod sends, by what bonds, and in what sort of prison he holds John bound.

Herod’s sending is the spiritual suggestion of sins. A person is said to send when, yielding by consent to vices which assail him, he opens [Col. 0995B] the door of the heart and delightfully consents to them within; yet he cannot carry them out outwardly, or is ashamed to do so. This is the first death of the soul, fittingly represented by the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, whom the Lord, with very few witnesses, raised within the shelter of her father’s house.

Whoever desires to escape this death should, at its very beginning, hasten as quickly as possible to the Lord with the steps of a contrite heart. For one swallowed inwardly by consent of heart in the abyss of harmful pleasure will undoubtedly suffer still greater losses. Therefore, after “he sent” has been said, “and he seized” is immediately added. For it is clear that, for everything we hold, we especially need the service of the hands. But in holy Scripture, what is indicated by the name “hands” except good or evil action? Thus one extends a hand to seize John who, cast down by consent to wicked pleasure, abandons the paths of virtues and descends to the depths of perverse action. If he seeks to rise from this deadly pit of destruction, he will undoubtedly need a greater remedy: that is, through the fruitful consideration of repentance, he must be carried out to meet the Lord beyond the gate of his foul [Col. 0995C] conscience. Unless the noisy crowd of carnal desires and deeds is repressed through the hidden grace of heavenly visitation, the dead person not only does not rise, but will also be subject to the sentence of a still worse death, as is aptly declared in what follows:

“And he bound him in prison.” By the chains with which a person is customarily bound may be understood the hard habit of sinning; by the prison, a dark place defiled by many uncleannesses, is fittingly understood a perverse heart made foul and dark by the filth of manifold vices. John is then said to be held bound amid the squalor of such a prison when a perverse person falls so far that one who formerly sinned, as it were, in fear and dreaded rebuke from human eyes for evil deeds, blinded by a long habit of sinning, is not ashamed, as though he had gained a certain liberty, to add worse evils to bad ones day by day [Col. 0995D].

But since by the Herod mentioned above we have heard signified not only those who do not walk spiritually in the spiritual life, but also all who, set over others, occupy Christ’s place in the Church, let us examine more carefully how they too—that is, preachers—become imitators of that most proud Herod. The person truly imitates him who, abandoning humility, is inflamed by the harsh torches of pride. Once pride has stormed the wall of the heart and prepared in it a place for its own dwelling, it introduces all its retinue along with itself and assigns to each vice its particular place and mastery. [Col. 0996A] There, without doubt, the word of the Lord, the voice of Wisdom, is held captive as though in chains, because one who has subjected himself through levity of mind to vices cannot usefully rebuke or correct them in another. For how can one admonish and urge others toward the good of humility and gentleness when he is himself raised above himself by anger or swelling pride? How can one restrain others by the word of preaching from the desire for earthly things when, even if not openly, he is not ashamed to yearn with the whole desire of his heart after worldly gain? The Apostle rejoiced that he was free from chains of this kind; fearing no accusation of blameworthy life, he confidently said: “I discharge an embassy in chains, but the word of God is not bound” (Eph. 6:20). For the word of God was not bound in his heart: although his body was held fast in iron, his spirit was free, unimpeded by any vice of a reproaching conscience; no circumstance could turn him from the path of truth [Col. 0996B]. But if we attend more carefully to the subsequent words of the holy Gospel, we shall see that all these things of which we have spoken are accomplished more by hidden contrivances of snares than by manifest defilements of action. It follows:

“But Herodias lay in wait for him.” It would indeed be abominable and altogether horrible if one who had ever deserved, even for a moment, to taste how great is the condescension of divine visitation, overcome by the wickedness of diabolical deceit, were suddenly bent toward manifest crimes of the flesh. Since the ancient enemy knows this, he meets a person through the unavoidable snares of his deceit, [Col. 0996C] introducing now arrogance of mind, now pride, and the favour of vain glory. When these vices have been laid, as it were, as a foundation in the human heart, and the inward gaze of the mind is turned away from the sight of the true light, the evils which immediately follow are more clearly shown in the Evangelist’s next words.

“She wished,” he says, “to kill him.” The life of the flesh is the soul; the life of the soul is God. Herodias wishes to kill John because the concupiscence of this world tends to nothing else than to remove, through the seductively sweet enticements of the carnal life, the soul’s life, which is God. Yet because this wicked desire of Herodias cannot suddenly be fulfilled in one who had once been a king, who had at least once deserved to taste, however faintly, the inward sweetness of Christ, the Evangelist sufficiently indicates in the following verse that Herodias had the desire to kill John but lacked the power to accomplish what she wished. “She wished,” he says, “to kill him, but could not” [Col. 0996D].

But he immediately reveals the cause of this inability when he says: “For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just and holy man, and he protected him.” Herod fears John because, when he hears or reads the word of God represented by John, he begins to fear his sins. “Knowing that he was a just and holy man, and he protected him.” He knows, I say, that all which holy Scripture sets forth tends toward virtues, righteousness, and holiness, and therefore begins to observe it insofar as his capacity allows.

527 [Col. 0997A] “And when he heard him, he did many things, and heard him gladly.” Having heard John, having heard the word of sacred Scripture in which the grace of God lies hidden, he begins to do many things which he had previously neglected to do; and he listens to it gladly, although he knows that all it says is against him. “And when a suitable day came, Herod made a supper on his birthday for the chief men, the tribunes, and the foremost men of Galilee.” This suitable day, which the Evangelist so emphatically notes as having come, fittingly expresses the suitable grace of heavenly visitation, which often presents itself appropriately and opportunely not only to those who live perfectly but also to those who walk before God less perfectly.

[Col. 0997B] This day is rightly said to come to Herod when a faithful prelate, or any blessed person, raised above himself by the sweetness of inward contemplation, is permitted to approach—not bodily but spiritually—the table of that supreme and ineffable sweetness. There, refreshed by spiritual delights, he is spiritually born anew in God. Thus, thus enriched by the heavenly banquet and, so to speak, happily regenerated within himself, he begins through the office of preaching to serve to the chief men, tribunes, and foremost men of Galilee that heavenly supper which he himself deserved to taste inwardly.

The Psalmist shows more plainly who these chief men, tribunes, and foremost men of Galilee are, for whom such a supper is fitting: “The princes,” he says, “of Judah, [Col. 0997C] their leaders; the princes of Zebulun; the princes of Naphtali” (Ps. 67:28). Judah is interpreted “confession.” The chief men of Judah are fittingly called those who, having utterly left the world, strictly judge themselves for their former transgressions. They do not make excuses for sins, but uncover the wound of their own weakness through the bitterness of pure and perfect confession.

When they proceed armed against themselves with such zeal of fervour, they may, through the helping grace of God, also become tribunes—that is, princes of Zebulun. Zebulun is interpreted “dwelling of strength.” They may be called princes of Zebulun when, prompted by divine inspiration, they arrive at that strength whereby, walking in the Spirit and consenting in mind to the law of God, they cut away the vices of the flesh, as far as they can, with the sword of continence, and guard themselves diligently no less in thought than in word and deed.

Through this threefold guard, as they advance praiseworthily in their tribunate, they become the foremost men of Galilee—that is, princes of Naphtali, which is interpreted “a hind let loose.” This truly occurs when, running in hope of the heavenly homeland, they manfully pass through whatever obstacles confront them from the hindrance of this mutability, and ascend to things above in heart and mind with the lofty leaps of contemplation [Col. 0997D].

But in another way we may understand this suitable day, and in another way these chief men, tribunes, and foremost men of Galilee. By the suitable day we may fittingly understand worldly prosperity and temporal goods. When this comes to the person who embraces Herodias—to the person, I mean, who cherishes the concupiscence, love, or avarice of this world—it supplies a great opportunity for sin, in which he begins to prepare a delightful supper for the chief men, tribunes, and foremost men of Galilee.

By Galilee, which is said to mean “wheel” or “rolling,” we may fittingly understand this world, which never stands still but is always carried about and turned like a wheel. The chief men, tribunes, and foremost men of this Galilee may fittingly be called evil spirits, as we find in the testimony of Truth himself in the Gospel: “For,” he says, “the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

[Col. 0998B] But we should note why they are called chief men, why tribunes, why foremost men of Galilee. We believe they appropriately bear these three titles because there are three realms in which all people are tempted and attacked by these demons: they are tempted in the flesh, tempted in the spirit, and tempted in the mind. Thus those demons are rightly called chief men who tempt a person in the flesh—that is, who present carnal vices to carnal people by their malicious suggestion. Those demons may fittingly be called tribunes who attack spiritual and more perfect persons by their deceit in the spirit. 529 For a tribune is one set over a hundred soldiers; and by this number, which is perfect, every spiritual and perfect person may fittingly be understood. They are tempted in the spirit when they are inwardly deceived by images of things brought before them by demons. Images of things are spoken of when one thing is seen through which another is signified; for example, where “God” or “human being” is written, this is not God or a human being, but an image and a certain sign that God is, and that a human being is. One who is deceived in this—that is, who embraces the image in place of the truth—is badly tempted in the spirit by demons [Col. 0998C]. There are other spirits, more wicked than these and subtler in tempting humankind: namely those who attack a person in the mind, that is, in the intellect. But since mind or intellect is the first and chief thing in a human being, these can rightly be called not chief men, not tribunes, but the foremost men of Galilee. Yet so that this threefold temptation of chief men, tribunes, and foremost men may become clearer, [Col. 0998D] let us not be reluctant to discuss this same matter a little more subtly.

There are three visions: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual. We call bodily vision that which we see bodily with bodily eyes. Spiritual vision, however, is when we see something in the spirit but cannot discern with the intellect what it is. Thus we read of Pharaoh that he saw seven beautiful and fat cows, and as many ugly and lean ones. He also saw seven full and handsome ears of grain, and seven thin ones struck by blight. These visions were certainly certain images of events to follow, which Pharaoh foresaw in a dream and in the spirit, but he could not grasp with the understanding [Col. 0999A] of his mind what they foretold. But Joseph deserved to see in the intellect of the mind when he sublimely explained to Pharaoh the truth of the future events that had been prefigured in images.

By this intellectual vision, through which the truth of things itself is perceived, that third heaven is fittingly represented to which the apostle Paul says that he was caught up, where he deserved to hear secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak. For just as vision is threefold—of body, spirit, and mind—so also in the holy Scriptures meaning is threefold: literal, spiritual, and intellectual. That outstanding teacher of the Gentiles had then transcended literal and spiritual meanings and had gloriously ascended as far as the third heaven—that is, the intellectual meaning—when he was so joined to heavenly things with the whole understanding of his heart that he declared he did not know whether he was in the body or outside the body [Col. 0999B]. Therefore there are demons who, as we have said, attack us in bodily matters; demons who attack us in spiritual matters; and demons who attack us in intellectual matters.

A person makes for all these a plentiful and delightful supper when he does not fear to sin against God in body, spirit, or mind. This supper, so sweet and pleasing to unclean spirits, can seldom be prepared unless that aforementioned day—which we called worldly prosperity—begins to smile upon the person. For that day is very fit, very favourable for sins, because exceedingly rare is the person who, when all things prosper, can so maintain his state that he does not often prepare this deadly supper for the chief men, tribunes, and foremost men of Galilee mentioned above, whether by disordered thought, superfluous speech, or unlawful action [Col. 0999C]. For one who is continually oppressed by illness, some other affliction, or adversity is not easily drawn into sins. Blessed Job seems to suggest more plainly in his own words that the state of uprightness is more easily preserved in adversity than in prosperity: “Let the day perish in which I was born” (Job 3:3). Job cursed the day of his birth because he saw that all the prosperity of this world, in which a person is, as it were, delightfully born anew within himself, tends toward the destruction of the soul. Hence, as has been said, even a perfect person is more easily bent toward sins by prosperity than by adversity; [Col. 0999D] but a fool is cast down by both prosperity and adversity, as Solomon testifies when he says: “The turning away of the simple will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. 1:32). Therefore a person begins to prepare for the princes of this world a deadly supper from diverse kinds of sins when, through the smiling prosperity of temporal things, he turns wholly away from God and turns toward the world with the entire desire of his heart. Thus what the Evangelist then visibly relates is invisibly accomplished in him:

“And when the daughter of Herodias herself entered,” he says, “and danced, and pleased Herod and those reclining with him.” By the daughter of Herodias may fittingly be understood pleasure of heart and body [Col. 1000A]. She is rightly said to enter among the dining chief men, tribunes, and foremost men of Galilee, whom we called evil spirits, when a person begins, under their malicious suggestion, to sin sweetly, pleasurably, and delightfully. As sins grow sweet inwardly, this miserable daughter adds the same dance-steps, making a person leap from vice to vice and from sin to sin. Thus one who now seems to seek one place and now another rightly imitates a dancer, as diverse wickednesses succeed one another in turn. Such and so perverse dances of Herodias please Herod when a person begins to take pleasure in himself in sins. They also please those reclining with him—that is, all his senses, as they consent to sins. Thus what follows comes to pass:

“And the king said to the girl: Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” Thus [Col. 1000B] the person who had once been a king, who had resolved to govern his kingdom—that is, his body and soul—according to God’s will, promises to satisfy in all things the perverse request of this girl, by whom, as we have said, pleasure is signified. Pleasure is not unfittingly denoted by the name of a girl: for as a girl is tender and soft, weak and fragile, so pleasure makes every heart it possesses soft and pliant in consenting, weak and fragile in resisting sins. Hence it is aptly added: “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” To ask is the work of pleasure in enticing a person toward manifest crimes of wickedness. But for a person to say to it, “Ask of me,” is to submit himself with devoted heart and body to the carnal enticements proceeding from it [Col. 1000C]. “Ask of me,” he says, “whatever you wish.” As if to say: I shall be ready for everything you ask, for whatever crimes you wish to bend me toward; for I shall strive to satisfy you with unlawful words, superfluous thoughts, and evil deeds.

“And he swore to her: Whatever you ask, I will give you, even half my kingdom.” By this oath may be understood that strong and firm consent by which a person, prompted by the perniciously sweet pleasure of sins, binds himself to destructive pleasure. Bound by this deadly oath, blinded by this ruinous consent to sins, when he is inwardly overcome by love of carnal things, [Col. 1000D] he promises even half his kingdom if it should be asked. But since the whole kingdom is the person’s soul and body, half the kingdom may fittingly be understood as the body. The wretched person promises it to Herodias when, in obeying and gratifying the flesh and its desires, he submits himself wholly to pleasure. After making this miserable promise, however, he grows worse day by day, as the Evangelist subsequently relates:

When she had gone out, he says, she said to her mother: “What shall I ask for?” We believe it is not without reason that the Evangelist so particularly notes that the aforesaid daughter of Herodias now entered, now went out. The daughter of Herodias is said, in a sense, to enter when pleasure begins by various sinful delights to soften the prudently watchful heart of a man toward wrongdoing. She is said to go out, however, when, by repeating sins, he strives continually to renew himself in fresh crimes. “What shall I ask for?” he says. The daughter, as it were, asks her mother what she ought to request when a man given over to pleasure now runs after the lust of the flesh, now returns to pride of mind, carefully seeking and investigating by which vices he may most of all delight his wretched soul. “What shall I ask for?” he says.

And she said: “The head of John the Baptist.” By the name John, which is interpreted “in whom is the grace of God,” the Old and New Law may suitably be understood, in which the grace of God is truly said to be present, because from it a man is perfectly instructed how he may please God and by what merits obtain both forgiveness of sins and the fullness of eternal joys. Although Christ is the head of this John—of this, I say, Old and New Law—yet in John, and in John’s head, we may also understand a man’s intention. John therefore has his head when a man who is to be saved directs his whole intention toward God and Holy Scripture, and reads and hears the word of God with such devotion that he may find in it that grace by which he can perfectly know both God and himself. Herodias with her daughter always lies in wait for this head of John—for this, I say, most health-giving intention of man—because the concupiscence and pleasure of the world aim at nothing else than to turn a man’s whole intention away from God and from God’s teaching, and to put in its place within the human heart the love and delight of the carnal life. This is aptly shown by the counsel of Herodias herself, by which she urges and exhorts her daughter to request the head of John the Baptist.

But it must be noted why, when she said “the head of John,” she added “the Baptist.” In the word of God, which is understood through John, there is a baptizing grace, and there is a grace that does not baptize. The grace is called baptizing when a man, softened by the word of God, is moved to compunctious lamentation; for that sweet stream of tears, bursting forth from the depths of the heart through remembrance of sins and love of heavenly things, is a kind of baptism of the man, in which he is in some sense blessedly baptized, in which, the oldness of sins having been abolished, he is blessedly regenerated in Christ. There is also another grace conceived from the word of God, indeed quite good and useful, yet in no way like this: namely, the grace by which a man willingly and delightfully receives the word of God. Yet this cannot be called John the Baptist—that is, baptizing grace—for although he delights to hear God’s word, he is not baptized by it because the power of tears is lacking; for a man is not cleansed from the stain of sins without compunction and humble contrition of heart. Therefore, since the ancient enemy is not unaware of such power in God’s word, by which a man is thus baptized and renewed, he now through concupiscence, now through pleasure, concupiscence’s daughter, importunately presses upon the man that he may request the head of John the Baptist: that is, that he may turn his whole intention utterly away from that baptizing grace which he once deserved to conceive from the word of God. When wretched man has in this consented to the devil, when conquered by concupiscence and pleasure he has preferred carnal things to spiritual, he suddenly slips into worse things, as the Evangelist subsequently relates:

And when she had entered, he says, immediately with haste she asked the king, saying: “I want you at once to give me on a dish the head of John the Baptist.” The daughter of Herodias enters the king with haste when pleasure so subjects a spiritual man in heart and body to itself that he wholly burns for crimes and hastens to accomplish whatever the flesh seems to entice him to do. “I want,” she says, “you at once to give me on a dish the head of John the Baptist.” Pleasure, which formerly flattered, now in a sense commands, when a man has become altogether powerless over himself and cannot resist sins, but turns heart and body to the dish—that is, to gluttony—so that he takes pleasure in doing, saying, or thinking nothing except what the flesh suggests or desires.

And the king was grieved. He who had once been king is grieved at first, while he sees himself thus conquered by the flesh and so miserably deprived of that grace which he once possessed as God’s gift. But because of the oath and because of those reclining with him, he was unwilling to grieve her. By the oath, as we have said above, we understand a firm and stable, lethal and accursed consent to sin; those reclining together are the senses of the inner and outer man consenting to sin. When firm consent to sins has taken possession of the heart within, it makes all a person’s senses think, love, and seek the same thing. And so it comes about that he is unwilling, by resisting sins, to grieve the pleasure ruling over him; instead, at its command, he strives in every way to satisfy the desires of his flesh, saying to himself inwardly: “What does this sorrow profit me? What good will it do me now to abandon sins, when, since I cannot resist the flesh, I shall repeat the same things again?” And thus he plunges wholly into ruin, as the Evangelist subsequently adds:

And having sent, he says, an executioner, he commanded that his head be brought on a dish. Since the executioner bears his lord’s weapons, he suitably signifies man’s understanding, which used frequently to gather and carry within itself those darts—namely, the testimonies of Holy Scripture—by which it might strike the ancient enemy and by which it formerly strove to fortify itself against his invisible assault.
