A man sends his executioner to behead John when he turns his whole intention away from God and Holy Scripture, and directs all his understanding and perception toward the dish—that is, toward satisfying the desires of his own gluttony. Thus what follows comes to pass:

And he beheaded him in prison, brought his head on a dish, gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. By the prison, as we said above, we understand the dark heart of man. John is beheaded in prison when a man is inwardly emptied of every spiritual grace. When his disciples heard this, they came, took his body, and laid it in a tomb. They came by affection; they took by action; they laid it down by contemplation of the mind. Let us also come through obedience of mind, take through the effectiveness of our work, and lay it down in perseverance in good work, so that we may one day deserve to attain joys that endure without end. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

535  
## HOMILY LXXV. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE NATIVITY OF THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY

“Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah; and she entered the house of Zacharias and greeted Elizabeth” (Luke II [OCR; Luke 1]).

Because the Nativity of Mary, perpetual Virgin, which we commemorate with due veneration, announced the joy of everlasting life to all who groan in this pilgrimage, we ought carefully to consider how the splendid birth of this glorious Virgin is expressed in the words of the Gospel reading. For many, remaining without spiritual understanding, are accustomed to ask how these Gospel words are fitting for the Nativity of the glorious Virgin. But to those to whom the Spirit speaks inwardly it is plainly given to understand that not only the beginnings of her birth, but also the merits of her praiseworthy manner of life, are excellently set forth in them. For the Evangelist says:

“Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country.” Therefore our Lady, Mary the perpetual Virgin, first arose when, born of royal lineage—the rod from the root of Jesse, the Virgin of the flower—she came forth into the light of the world. But let us see where this Queen of Heaven, thus arising, ascended; to what place she went, turning aside; and to what work of virtue she there applied herself.

“She went,” he says, “into the hill country with haste.” Therefore our Lady Mary went into the hill country as soon as she was born, because, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit receiving her into his care, she was separated from all earthly things in such a way that with her whole heart she passed over to love of God the Father, according to the precept of the Lord’s Law, which thus commands: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Deut. VI, 5): that is, with all understanding, all will, and all memory. She plainly loved the Lord with all her understanding—him whom, as she merited beyond all others to receive into her virginal bridal chamber, there to be embodied from her, so she alone loved the sole Lord, the unique Virgin loved the unique Lord of unique majesty, above all mortals. To love him, she strove with all her strength to devote everything that she was, everything by which she lived, everything that she could grasp with her understanding. She did not hold this love sluggishly, but took the greatest care to exercise it in work “with haste,” that is, with good will. For nothing makes a person so swift, ready, and eager as the devotion of a good will.

To complete this love, the blessed Mother of God Mary added above all the earnest fulfillment of the fourth commandment of the Law: to love God with all one’s strength—which is to go into the city of Judah. For Judah is interpreted “confession” or “praise,” and this praise and confession are most justly and fittingly attributed to our Lady Mary. In a voice of exultation and confession, with all her strength she sought the glory of her Creator, continually confessing and praising him both in heart and body, through whom she knew that she was to be saved and blessed forever. It follows:

“And she entered the house of Zacharias.” By Zacharias, whose name is interpreted “mindful of the Lord,” is figured the love of her chaste heart and pure mind, by which she loved God with all her memory. To him alone she so clung that she did not allow the memory of her beloved, the eternal King, to be removed even for an hour from the ruling part of her heart. Thus burning in love of her Creator, the mediatrix of God and men watched over the salvation of her neighbours with no lesser affection of charity, as we may aptly gather from the following words. For he says:

“And she greeted Elizabeth.” By holy Elizabeth, whom this glorious Virgin greeted in love, is indicated the love of neighbours, which she held so unwaveringly that she desired with every longing that the salvation which she asked for herself day and night with such great tears might, by no lesser affection of charity, benefit the whole human race. And therefore, according to the commandment of the Law, she loved her neighbour as herself. Nor did she announce this salvation only to the ancient Fathers; in truth, she announces it daily also to the co-heirs of the New Testament. And although, having paid the debt of the flesh, she has passed into the kingdom of her beloved Son, she still speaks to us by her wonderful life and still greets her own people by her inestimable example.

Since we have briefly sampled these matters concerning the glorious and undefiled Virgin, let us now see how these words may be fulfilled in every faithful and elect soul which wishes, insofar as is lawful for mortals, to follow and imitate the blessed Mother of God. The Evangelist therefore says:

“Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, and entered the house of Zacharias, and greeted Elizabeth.” The blessed and faithful soul arises when it lifts itself from earthly desires and pleasures; when it abandons vices and sins; when, renewed in the spirit of its mind, it puts on the new man and resists earthly and harmful acts in body and soul alike. And when it has thus arisen, it should, following the example of our Lady Mary, go into the hill country, that it too may love the Lord its God with all its heart, all its soul, all its mind, and all its strength. It ought, then, so to go into the hill country that it may transfer all its love to that mountain of God—God Almighty, that is—and love him with sweet affection above all things and among all things, insofar as it can grasp him with its understanding.

But this going, this loving, must not be done with a lukewarm and slothful heart; rather, it must hasten with good and devout will toward this: to love God with all one’s mind. In loving God thus, in hastening to him thus, it befits the blessed soul also to go into the city of Judah, so that it may effectively fulfill that fourth component of love which the lawgiver has set forth in the love of God. It indeed proceeds into the city of Judah if it loves God with all its strength. For, as we said above, Judah is interpreted “confession” or “praise.” It will be able truly to offer God this praise and confession if, praising and confessing the heavenly Father in heart and body, it ascribes nothing of this to its own merits, but seeks only the praise and honour of its Creator.

Let it join to this praise and confession that memorial love mentioned in the following words, when it is said, “and she entered the house of Zacharias.” Zacharias is interpreted “mindful of the Lord.” The faithful soul enters the house of Zacharias when, burning in the love of God, the mind strives day and night to pour forth and meditate upon the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness. It follows:

“And she greeted Elizabeth.” In blessed Mary, mother of the Lord Jesus, who bore the Saviour for us, prelates and teachers are designated in many passages of Scripture; for truly, just as she brought God forth for us in incorrupt flesh, so prelates and preachers in a certain way bring God to birth in their subjects by the word of their exhortation. Thus, in the present passage, blessed Mary may figure those prelates who, established and exalted in the love of God in the order we have described, finally deserve to be called by God to the care and governance of souls. By Elizabeth, however, whose name is interpreted “the fullness of my God,” good subjects may be understood: those who can neither be satisfied, nor wish to be satisfied, by any delight in transient things, but have placed their satisfaction in the vision of God alone, so that they can confidently say with the Psalmist: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.” Good prelates, designated by the Mother of Jesus, frequently greet these good subjects, designated by Elizabeth, when they address them with the word of sweetest exhortation; when they set before them the commandments and precepts of life; and when, by salutary words which they have themselves received from the Lord’s mouth, they make them concerned for their salvation. Thus, when good prelates greet their subjects in this way, great profit commonly results therefrom through God’s help, as is plainly made known in the words that follow. For it follows:

“And it came to pass, when Elizabeth heard the voice of Mary, that the child leaped for joy in her womb.” This great and memorable event, of which we have just heard, God frequently works among subjects through the words of preaching by good prelates. When they hear words of divine sweetness, which inwardly touch and kindle them by the grace of the Holy Spirit [manuscript: “touching and kindling”], such exultation commonly arises in their hearts as may rightly be expressed by the name *infans*, “infant.” For *infans* is said as though *non fans*, “not speaking.” Truly, this exultation which they receive from the Lord in the jubilation of the heart amid the words of preaching is such that a man cannot speak it; it is so ineffable that no one can adequately express or explain it in human words.

## HOMILY LXXV. SECOND HOMILY ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

“Your Nativity, holy Virgin Mother of God, announced joy to the whole world; for from you arose the Sun of righteousness, Christ our God” (Liturgy).

The most blessed Virgin Mary, who was to bear the Sun of righteousness, illumined and gladdened the whole world on this present day by her Nativity. For the whole human race was so enveloped in the darkness of sins and in the darkness of eternal damnation that none of the ancient Fathers, however holily, devoutly, and justly he lived, failed, after the long miseries of this life and the long darkness of this world, to descend sorrowfully into the underworld—until, at the end of the ages, the Sun of righteousness himself arose from that blessed Virgin. Having accomplished the dispensation of his assumed flesh, he deigned to lead back to the homeland of eternal brightness those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death. And now the dignity of human nature has been restored so wonderfully and mercifully that every elect person who has lived well and blessedly in this life will immediately, at the hour of departure from the body, possess the joys of perpetual blessedness. But an ungodly person and sinner, even if he repents perfectly in his last hour, will doubtless obtain forgiveness which he did not deserve, after the example of the thief who repented late. For while he spent his life in robbery and persistence in many evils, he at last repented late upon the cross and obtained by grace the good things of Paradise which he had not deserved by innocence.

And because the blessed Mother of God Mary became, so to speak, the material of human restoration, nearly all Scripture which recalls the work of human creation and restoration commends this same Virgin, as the restorer of the human race, with special praise. For if we had not been restored, it would have been better not to have been created. Hence that first lawgiver of God, Moses, everywhere making mention in his writings of this glorious Virgin, at the very beginning of the Old Testament almost announces by these words that she was to be born and that the human race was mercifully to be restored through her: “For the Lord God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was no man to cultivate it. But a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” (Gen. II, 5–6).

Although according to the letter the truth of the matter is indeed such that, at the beginning, when all things were created, rain did not fall upon the earth, nevertheless the Spirit of truth mystically indicates something that looks very fittingly to the praise and glory of the blessed Mother of God. For visible rain, descending from above and soaking and drenching the earth, aptly signifies the rain of heavenly discipline: namely, the teaching of chastity and humility which was one day to come by the example of this most chaste Virgin. For while the earth of the human heart is watered and soaked by this health-giving rain, it is made fruitful with abundant good works. The Lord had not yet rained this rain upon the earth—that is, upon any wholly earthly human being—but God the Father especially reserved it above all for the Mother of his beloved Son, who was one day to be born, that he might above all mortals drench and make her fruitful with this saving rain of chastity and humility, and thus, by her example, with God’s gift, convey it into the hearts of many.

“And there was no man,” he says, “to cultivate it.” Because, as was said, the Lord God had not yet rained upon the earth, there was no man to cultivate it: that is, no one who knew how to cultivate the earth of heart and body in such a way as both to live chastely and preserve that chastity in such great humility of heart; or who knew how so to cultivate his earth as to return after the end of life to the joys of Paradise.

There is another truly heavenly rain: namely, the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which, in the fullness of time, that same Virgin Mary was to be overshadowed and made pregnant. But this rain had not fallen from above upon the earth, because the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon this Virgin. Hence also that eminent prophet Isaiah, who foretold in the prophetic Spirit, saying, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 14), invites this very Virgin, who was to come for the work of human redemption and be made pregnant by the Holy Spirit, and says: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” (Isa. XLV, 8). Since in Scripture the name “heavens” is commonly used to designate holy and righteous persons, why should the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit not most rightly be understood also through these same heavens? For who is so truly holy and righteous as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? It is therefore as though this elect prophet, who, as was said, foresaw the Virgin’s conception and birth of God’s Son, were humbly interceding with the omnipotence of the supreme Trinity on behalf of this Virgin, asking that God the Father might provide such a Virgin Mother for his beloved Son as would conceive and bear him, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, for the redemption of the human race.

“Drop down, heavens,” he says, “from above.” You, O heaven of heavens—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—send down the dew of mercy; hasten the time of mercy for which we wait. Therefore let God the Father bedew [send down] the Son by sending him, as he has spoken; let the Son bedew the Father who sends him by obeying; let the Holy Spirit bedew the Virgin, who is to be consecrated for divine childbirth, by coming upon her. “And let the clouds rain the Just One.” Therefore let the clouds rain this Just One—he who alone is just and who will mercifully make the unjust righteous. Let the angelic powers, coming down from above, announce to the Virgin Mother that he is to be conceived and born. Let Gabriel, that supreme messenger of the heavens, come and say to the blessed Virgin: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” (Luke I, 35). Let that earth to which the Lord has given blessing—the earth, I say, of the virginal bridal chamber—be opened without violation of modesty to the only Son of God. Let it be opened, I beseech you, for the eternal Prince, so as to conceive and bear the Saviour of the whole world. Let it be opened, I say, so that, as the same Virgin resolved in her mind, it may always remain closed and untouched, and, made a Mother, may not lose the glory of virginity. “And bring forth the Saviour.” What is meant by “bring forth the Saviour,” when it might rather have been said “bear” or “beget the Saviour”? The shoot of anything, whether herbs or trees, is at first very small, weak, and fragile; yet in the shoot itself the hope of its future fruit is in some way already displayed. So too that little Son of the Virgin, while clothed in tender limbs and crying amid the narrow manger, nevertheless displayed by many signs of power the hope of the future salvation which he would effect for the human race through the omnipotence of the divinity dwelling within him. And now the fruit of that virginal shoot—the faith, I say, of that tiny infant—has filled the whole expanse of the world. Therefore the aforesaid Moses, beholding still more deeply the praise and glory both of Mother and Son, says:

“A spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.” This earth is that truly blessed, truly benedicted earth of which we spoke above; the spring proceeding from it is her little Son. He is quite fittingly said to have watered the entire surface of the earth, because through faith in his Incarnation and Passion he alone, Creator and Redeemer, is adored and worshipped throughout the earth. And behold, from that small spring innumerable rivers of heavenly wisdom have flowed through the ends of the world.

And because, without impairing the true sense, we may apply to the praise of the Virgin Mother almost everything that Scripture teaches us to understand mystically concerning the Son of that Virgin, behold: by the spring rising from the earth, which we said pertains to the person of the Son, the same Mother and Virgin may also fittingly be understood. Born from the earth—that is, from earthly parents—she watered the whole surface of the earth—that is, she illumined all the Churches by the example of her chastity and humility. Behold, that virginal spring has so watered the entire earth and spread streams of chastity and humility through the ends of the world, that now an innumerable multitude of both sexes does not cease, by living chastely, to put to death its members which are upon the earth; and it desires to preserve not only the chastity of the outward person, which is bodily integrity, but also chastity of spirit, which is true humility of heart. This, I say, is the saving irrigation of this spring, now poured out and spread throughout the world. Solomon, the wisest of men, foreseeing it in the Holy Spirit, bears witness concerning this same spring: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters” (Cant. IV, 15).

A spring is water rising from the earth and visibly flowing over the earth; a well, however, is high and deep, and the water it contains cannot be plainly seen. These two things appear well suited to the blessed Virgin. For to some she is as a fountain of gardens; to others, as a well of living waters: a fountain, I say, to the simpler and less intelligent; a deep and profound well to those wise in high matters. For some people, like very fruitful gardens, strive to bring forth outwardly the fruit of good works and inwardly the fruit of true love; yet they do not know how to speak or think of this Virgin in lofty and sublime terms through the mystical understanding of Scripture. They know only that she, the Mother of mercy, gently intercedes for sinners; that many almost despairing people have been saved by her most merciful prayers; and that she is so honoured by her Son that nothing can be denied her when she asks him. Therefore they offer her prayers and tears with a simple heart, humbly entreat her for their sins, and do not doubt that through her intercession they will obtain forgiveness of offences. To those who think of her thus simply and invoke her thus humbly, she is as a fountain of gardens. For they draw waters of salvation from this spring when they find, through the aid of her merits, the mercy for which they ask.

But as she is, in the manner stated, a fountain to the simpler, so she is a well of living waters to the more perfect, who are wise in deep and difficult matters. They understand in a mystical sense many things pertaining to the Virgin’s praise; after long lamentations of repentance, as though cleansed by worthy satisfaction, they rejoice in the hope of pardon received, and now count almost sweet only the desire and love of the heavenly homeland. To such persons she is in this way a well of living waters, because if at any time they are less able to rise to mystical understanding or less able to taste the inward sweetness of the mind, they come to this well—to the blessed Virgin, that is—by prayer and supplication, and draw from this well of mercy living waters: waters of wisdom and understanding, waters of inward compunction.

“Whence do these waters flow? They flow,” he says, “with force from Lebanon.” By Lebanon, which is said to mean “whitening,” may fittingly be understood the white and spotless Son of the Virgin herself. Although he appeared in flesh of sin, he was in truth wholly white, because he was touched by not even the slightest contagion of sin. For from this Lebanon—that is, from the Son of the Virgin, our Lord Jesus Christ—flows and truly proceeds everything whatever of consolation and grace which the same Virgin Mother bestows upon humankind.

And it should be noted that it is not said simply, “which flow from Lebanon”; rather, “with force” is added. For what is it for living waters to flow with force except powerfully and sweetly to seek the human mind inwardly? Therefore they flow with great force when they raise the heart from low things and lift the mind to love of invisible things, because whatever is granted from above to a supplicating human being through the prayers of the Virgin Mother cannot be without great fruit of salvation.

545  
## HOMILY LXXVI. THIRD HOMILY FOR THE SAME FEAST

“Jacob saw a ladder. Its summit touched the heavens,” etc. (Gen. XXVIII).

The solemnity of this day, just as it brought the world a special cause for salvation, is likewise celebrated by holy Church with special rejoicing and exultation. For Mary, perpetual Virgin and Lady of the whole world, ineffably exalted this day, she who by the brightness of her birth illumined the entire globe. When the feasts of other saints are celebrated, what is recalled is that they departed from this world and received the worthy rewards of their labours. But holy Mother Church attributes this prerogative of honour only to her—one which none of the saints has or can have, except him alone who is the Holy One of saints, whom she herself, his incorrupt Mother, bore. The Nativity of John, the Baptist and forerunner of the Lord, is also honourably commemorated; this, however, regards not so much the dignity of his own merits as the honour of him whom he preceded and prefigured by his birth.

Indeed, this festival day gives us, as it were, an occasion to praise blessed Mary, because through her that curse was removed which Eve, the first mother, brought upon her posterity; and that pain which Eve merited through her pride is mitigated for us. For when we are born into the miseries of this life, we indicate, if not by words, then by our pitiable and tearful cry at our first beginning, what our first-formed parents deserved and what we ourselves are to suffer. Rightly, therefore, ought this Mother—worthy to be praised by the common acclaim of all—to be exalted by women with a special prerogative of love and thanksgiving, because she took away the reproach which the first woman brought upon them. For if this Woman and Virgin had not been born, perhaps men would say that woman was the cause of guilt and death. But now the charge of this reproach has no validity, since our Lady, the Virgin Mary, brought forth the life of all men and women. That first parent long ago, excusing his fault, said to God: “The woman whom you gave me as companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. III, 12). But now both men and women can say in thanksgiving to their Creator: “The woman whom you gave us as the author and restorer of salvation brought forth for us the tree of life, by which our souls are restored.” For the life-giving fruit is that living bread which descended from heaven and daily restores holy souls in the sacrament of the altar.

The birth of this Virgin, therefore, necessary to the whole world, was remarkably foretold in many ways by the holy Fathers, both in writings and in figures. Hence what is read concerning the patriarch Jacob may fittingly be applied to her praise. He was one of those three fathers of whom Almighty God especially customarily calls himself the God, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III, 6). Thus we read concerning him: “Jacob saw a ladder—its summit touched the heavens—and angels descending; and he said: ‘Truly this place is holy.’” What can we more fittingly understand by this ladder than the blessed Virgin Mary, whose life was ever *creata* [perhaps *erecta*, “raised”] from the depths to the heavens? This ladder had three things which may deservedly be called its summit: namely, the summit of chastity, the summit of charity, and the summit of humility.

And truly its summit touched the heavens, so greatly that the immense devotion of her charity, by which she was concerned for the human race, reached the throne of the divine majesty and was preferred to the prayers of all saints; and she deserved fully to obtain what they had desired. The prayer of Moses and of the other saints indeed had great power before God; but her prayer so surpassed their prayers that it drew to itself the whole magnitude of divine power, and the Creator of heaven himself descended into her womb.

It should be noted that it does not say “heaven” in the singular, but “it touched the heavens,” because it touched the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who are designated by the heavens. The sides of this noble ladder were her body and soul, in which God placed three rungs—those of humility, chastity, and charity—by which he wished to descend from the heavens to earth through her. Hence it immediately follows:

“And angels descending; and he said: ‘Truly this place is holy.’” If we consider in what way angels descended through her, we may understand that the eminent archangel Saint Gabriel, sent to her from heaven, is mystically denoted by these words. He came, as we suppose, not alone to greet so excellent a Virgin and announce to her the magnificent work, but came to her like a mighty prince with the other innumerable angels subject to him. The holy angels also descended through her on the night when she bore our Redeemer, because, as the Evangelist relates, when one angel appeared to the shepherds and announced to them the work of our salvation, suddenly there was with him a multitude of the heavenly host, praising and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 13–14).

We may also refer these words to every blessed soul that, by loving and praising God, leans upon this ladder. So long as it lives in this world, the angels often deign to descend to visit it, and they do not cease to relieve with their consolations its labours, by which it is oppressed in the present life. But when it has been commanded to depart from the body, if it has held a fixed hope in the firm foundation of this ladder, then without doubt the entire host of angels will descend to receive it and will lead it, with praise and exultation, into the presence of the eternal King. Rightly, therefore, did the holy patriarch, when through the Holy Spirit he had foreseen this ladder, say: “Truly, this place is holy.”

[Col. 1012A] Therefore, as we celebrate her Nativity with solemn devotion, whatever thanksgiving and whatever praise there is, we ought to devote it all to her veneration. In this feast let us fulfil the words of the prophet Isaiah. For he says: “You who remember the Lord, do not be silent; and give him no silence” (Isa. 62:6). Let us therefore not be silent in the praise of the Mother of our Creator—for her praise is the honour of her Son. May he himself make our heart silent from the clamour of vices, so that we may freely praise him and cry to him with mouth and heart. And that he may not be silent within us, but may speak words of forgiveness and peace, may he deign to say to us the words which he said to Mary Magdalene, who washed his feet: “Many sins are forgiven you; go in peace” (Luke 7:48). May he forgive us our sins here, and at our end say: [Col. 1012B] “Go in peace”; and may he transfer us to eternal peace, that we may see him face to face. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself deign to grant this, he who lives and is glorified as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

549 HOMILY LXXVII. FOURTH HOMILY FOR THE SAME FEAST.

“The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways; before he made anything from the beginning, I was ordained from eternity,” etc. (Prov. 8).

What cause or rationale is there for this lesson to be read today, on the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, when it seems wholly to proclaim and commend the eternity of the divinity of her only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, by which he is coequal and coeternal with the Father? I judge [Col. 1012C] that this is the cause and rationale: on the feast of the temporal Mother of God, the Holy Spirit arranged for this lesson to be read in order that it might thereby be signified and affirmed that, because of the humanity assumed from a temporal mother, he neither lost the divinity by which he is equal to the Father nor diminished his power. The Word of the Father himself affirms this at the beginning of this lesson when he says: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways; before he made anything from the beginning, I was ordained from eternity, and from ancient times, before the earth was made.” Here he set forth three things through which he mystically expounded the inseparable and undivided substance of the Trinity. What are these three? Beginning, origin, eternity. By “beginning” God the Father, by “origin” [Col. 1012D] God the Son, and by “eternity” God the Holy Spirit are fittingly understood.

He rightly assigned and adapted to each person a word proper and suitable to it. To “beginning,” which is the Father, he attached “The Lord possessed me”; to “origin,” which is the Son, “before he made anything”; to “eternity,” which is the Holy Spirit, “I was ordained.” In the word “possessed” two things are indicated, namely power and sitting, and these two properly belong to the Father. Sitting signifies rest. Those who are powerful in this age often succumb to great unrest because of the power they have undertaken. But the power of God the Father is not such: his power is both power and rest; he is always powerful and always at rest. Eternal Wisdom distinguishes this by these words: “The Lord,” [Col. 1013A] it says, “possessed me,” 550 and adds, “at the beginning of his ways.” The ways of the Lord are, as we have often heard, the Lord’s truth and mercy.

In these two ways of the Lord the Son and the Holy Spirit may likewise be understood. For truth is the Son; mercy is the Holy Spirit. The Father himself is he who is from no one; and since the Son and the Holy Spirit are from him, he is rightly called “the beginning of his ways,” that is, the beginning of the Son and the beginning of the Holy Spirit. For through these ways he proceeds, since he works all things through the Son and all things through the Holy Spirit. Yet this beginning, which the Son and Holy Spirit have from the Father, is without beginning, because the Son is coeternal with the Father, and the Holy Spirit is coeternal with the Father and the Son. Nor is it without reason that in the expression “from the beginning” we recognize the Son as coeternal [Col. 1013B] with the Father. For in the Gospel we find that he called himself “the Beginning.” When the Jews asked him who he was, he answered: “I am the Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25).

And what is said, “Before he made anything,” rightly suits that person. For as possession belongs to God the Father, so making belongs to God the Son. “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). And because it is proper to the Holy Spirit to order all things made by God the Father through God the Son, it is rightly said there, “I was ordained from eternity.” For the Holy Spirit disposes all things and orders all things; he gives form to the formlessness of things. Thus we read that when God created heaven and earth, all things were confused; but when the Holy Spirit came, he formed and ordered all [Col. 1013C] the formlessness of all things. Thus possession belongs to the Father, making to the Son, ordering to the Holy Spirit.

And lest anyone suppose that there is some singularity or division between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he immediately comprehends together what he has just said separately concerning the distinction of the persons, adding:

551 “And from ancient times, before the earth was made.” By this one expression he fittingly demonstrates the coessential substance of the Holy Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are all ancient; all are coeternal, because all are coequal and consubstantial. But why did he add, “before the earth [Col. 1013D] was made”? In this place, by “earth” we understand the humanity of the Son of God assumed for our sake. “Before the earth was made,” he says—as though to say: Before I, who am the Father’s Wisdom, became earth; before I assumed human nature from the Virgin Mother—I existed from ancient times; I existed, as it were, in the Trinity; I existed in the Father and in the Holy Spirit in equality of divinity.

“The abysses were not yet, and I was already conceived.” By the abysses we understand the angelic creation, which may not unfittingly be called and compared to an abyss because of the depth of wisdom in which it was created. This is also indicated elsewhere in Holy Scripture, where it is said: “Wisdom was created before all things” (Ecclus. 1:4). The eternal Wisdom of the Father is not to be understood there, but rather the angelic nature created in wisdom and through wisdom. Thus, “The abysses were not yet, and I was already conceived.” I was conceived by God the Father in eternity, and yet that conception was coeternal with God the Father. Or again: I was conceived in the ordinance of God the Father, to be conceived and born in time from the flesh of a virgin mother.

[Col. 1014A] “The springs of waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet stood in their heavy mass.” By the springs we may understand our first parents, Adam and Eve; by the waters, humankind. Nor is it unfitting that our first parents should be called springs of waters. They were indeed the springs and origin of the whole human race. After these springs he appropriately places mountains, by which the patriarchs are suitably signified; because of the height of their life and character, they are rightly compared with mountains. [Col. 1014B] This expression is certainly aptly set against them: “The mountains had not yet stood in their heavy mass.” That heavy mass may be understood as original sin, which flowed from the corrupted springs—from the first parents deceived through the serpent’s malice—into them and into the whole human race. This original sin, indeed, lay upon them as a heavy and intolerable mass and grievously weighed them down; for although they lived faithfully in God’s service amid the afflictions and miseries of this mortality for so long a time, after the present life they all descended to hell.

After the mountains he places hills, because by the hills he signifies the prophets who succeeded the patriarchs signified by the mountains, saying: “Before the hills I was brought forth.” [Col. 1014C] How does he say, “I was brought forth”? *Parturire* means, as it were, “to be eager to give birth.” Thus the expression “I was brought forth” indicates that ineffable desire which the Son, coeternal with the Father, had to be born for humankind. “Before the hills,” he says—as though to say: Before the patriarchs and before the prophets, this was always my desire in eternity: that I should be born in time.

“He had not yet made the earth, and the rivers, and the poles of the earth’s circle.” By the earth in this place we may fittingly understand the Church. How do I mean the Church? I call it the Church because the Church did not begin only when, at the birth, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of the Lord Jesus [Col. 1014D] Christ, the multitude of believers grew in faith and began to multiply. It began also in the first man who was predestined to life. For from the foundation of the world there was no time in which God did not have someone belonging to his Church. Hence, concerning this same Church, the eternal Wisdom of the Father—the same one who speaks here—says in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one” (Song 6:8), because, although times were different and sacraments different, nevertheless before God the Church was and is one in the simplicity of faith. “He had not yet made,” he says, “the earth, the rivers, and the poles of the earth’s circle.” If we understand the Church by earth, what are the rivers except the legal and prophetic teaching by which this same holy Church of God was to be filled and watered? By the poles [Col. 1015A] of the earth we may understand the holy apostles. Nor was the apostolic order unjustly prefigured by poles; for upon it the door of the whole holy Church turned.

“I was before all these things,” says the eternal Wisdom of the Father: I was before the abysses, before the angelic creation; before the springs of waters, before humankind; before the mountains and hills, before the patriarchs and prophets. God 553 the Father, making all things through the Son and ordering all things through the Holy Spirit, had not yet made the earth, that is, the Church; he had not yet sent forth the rivers of the legal and prophetic Scriptures. Yet I was in the Father, possessing all things with the Father, making all things with the Father, and disposing all things with the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1015B] “When he prepared the heavens, I was present”: that is, when he created the rational creation in angelic and human spirits, which are his heavens, in which he sits and rests, I was present with him; with him and in him I made all things.

“When by a fixed law and circle he enclosed the abysses; when he strengthened the upper airs, and balanced the springs of waters.” In these words we may understand the casting down of the evil angels, the confirmation of the good angels, and the restoration of fallen humanity. By the abysses here we understand evil angels cast down by God because of pride; by the upper airs, good angels strengthened with God so that they could fall no further; by the balancing of the springs of waters, God’s most merciful ordering concerning the restoration of fallen [Col. 1015C] humanity. And he fittingly says, “When by a fixed law and circle he enclosed the abysses.” For by this fixed law and circle we may aptly understand that sentence of everlasting damnation by which, through the just judgment of God, apostate spirits have been so enclosed and surrounded on every side that by no means can they ever escape it. In proper order he continues: “When he strengthened the upper airs,” since the confirmation of the good angels took place after the fall of the evil angels. But what follows—“and balanced the springs of waters”? If we attend to and weigh this expression rightly, it has a most sweet resonance. For it nobly denotes God’s sweet and wondrous compassion toward the human race. Almighty God did not enclose those springs of waters, [Col. 1015D] Adam and Eve, from whom the whole human race was propagated, by the fixed law and circle of eternal damnation as he did the abysses, the devil and his angels; rather, he balanced them. He balanced them, so to speak, on the scale of equity and mercy, because according to the multitude of his mercies he compassionately weighed what they were: he considered that they were ash and dust; he considered that they had fallen at the devil’s prompting. Those who fell through pride alone 554 and through their own malice caused human beings to fall, he justly enclosed by the fixed law and circle of everlasting damnation, so that they could not rise again. But those who fell not of themselves but when deceived through the devil’s malice, he balanced on the scale of compassion. He condemned the deceivers eternally; he mercifully saved the deceived. And because there were two peoples—one to be assumed, the other to be left—he mystically marked them both in what follows:

[Col. 1016A] “When he set its boundary around the sea, and laid down a law for the waters, that they should not pass their boundaries.” By the sea the people of the Gentiles may be understood; by the waters, the Jewish people. That boundary which God the Father set around the sea, that is, the Gentile people, fittingly prefigured the time in which he intended, through the incarnation of his Son, to visit them and lead them from the bitterness of unbelief to the sweetness of divine knowledge. But the law which he laid down for the waters prefigured the just judgment of God by which the Jews, rejecting the Son of God who came to them in the flesh, were rejected by God and left within the bounds of their [Col. 1016B] unbelief. For these he laid down a law so that they would not pass their bounds—that is, that they should remain in their faithlessness and malice. Around the Gentiles he set a boundary within which they were to be saved and delivered from the folly of their unbelief. But this boundary of the Gentiles’ salvation was extended until the Son, coeternal with the Father, became man from the most blessed Virgin Mary. In this present prophecy too, God’s Wisdom did not pass her over in silence, but nobly and fittingly announced and prefigured her in the following words:

“When he suspended the foundations of the earth, I was with him, composing all things.” By that earth we believe the blessed earth, the blessed Virgin Mary, to have been signified beforehand. The foundations of this earth may be called her wondrous chastity and incomparable [Col. 1016C] humility. But how was she founded upon these foundations? How did God the Father suspend these foundations in her, when she had not yet been born? Certainly, though she was not yet born into the world, she was such in God’s foreknowledge and ordering; Almighty God foresaw her to be such as she would afterwards be born and live in the world. But because God foreknew and foresaw that this Virgin would surpass not only all other women but absolutely all human beings in wondrous chastity and incomparable humility, this was in a manner the suspending of her foundations. For the virtue of chastity and humility, which he foresaw would be in [Col. 1016D] that same blessed Virgin Mary, was so weighty and so gracious before God that he judged her alone among all women worthy to receive his only-begotten Son, to be clothed in human flesh. But when God the Father first set these foundations in her by predestination, the same Son, remaining in the Father, together with the Father composed them. He himself shows this here when he says: “When he suspended the foundations of the earth, I was with him, composing all things”—as though to say: I was composing with the Father in the future Virgin Mother all these marks of chastity and humility.

“And I delighted day by day.” What is meant by “day by day”? One day was the day of chastity; the second day was the day of humility. Because the Son of God foresaw that these individual days would be found uniquely and especially in the blessed Virgin Mary, [Col. 1017A] he therefore said: “And I delighted day by day.” By this delighting of his was prefigured that great desire which he had to be incarnate from so precious a Virgin for the salvation of humankind. He desired her to be born, since he foreknew that she would be so unlike other women. But when this desire of his was fulfilled, when this most noble queen of heaven and earth was born into the world, he looked upon her from the height of his heavenly dwelling, surpassing all other human beings in a virtue of chastity and humility unheard of and wholly unknown to people of earlier times; he rejoiced over her and desired to come to her. This is proved for us by that twofold play of which the same only-begotten Son of God immediately speaks:

[Col. 1017B] “And I delighted,” he says, “day by day, playing before him at all times, playing in the circle of the earth.” He was playing before him—that is, before God the Father—at all times, that is, in eternity; he was playing in the circle of the earth, that is, according to his humanity, in having such a mother on earth. Christ’s joy was twofold. His joy was to be the Son of God; his joy was to be the Son of Man. The former joy was for his own sake; the latter was for our sake. How it was for our sake he himself shows in what follows:

556 “And my delights,” he says, “were to be with the children of men.” Why does he say “delights”? What delights did he have with the children of men? Delights are said to be where sweet and varied things are set upon a dish. The delights of the only-begotten [Col. 1017C] God—the things that drew him from the bosom of God the Father into the womb of the Virgin Mother to live and share life with the children of men—were the diverse holy ways of life which he foresaw would be found in the holy Church, and the diversity of holy souls. These are set before God each day and at every moment, because they are renewed, multiplied, and varied each day. Such delights could in some manner not exist among the multitude of holy angels, because, always remaining in the state in which they were created, they could neither multiply, be renewed, nor vary; nor did they need to do so. But the delights which God has in good human beings living holy and just lives in this world, and which he has in holy souls passing daily from this life to God, [Col. 1017D] are multiplied and renewed at every moment. For every day people are converted to God; every day people are born; every day people die; every day holy souls are transferred to the palace of heaven and set upon God’s table.

These are the delights of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, and leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5). By this woman who ascends in the wilderness, the human nature assumed into God may not unfittingly be understood, leaning upon her beloved—that is, upon God, upon its own divinity. When the only-begotten Son of God, after his death and resurrection, ascended to heaven with the holy humanity which he had assumed for our sake, [Col. 1018A] and showed it to God the Father and the holy angels, we may believe that this voice was the voice of the angelic multitude, wondrously praising, glorifying, and at once admiring the human nature united to divinity, together with the harvest of holy souls which the same only-begotten Son of God acquired for God the Father through his death. At that time their abundant multitude, rescued from hell, entered heaven with him and was thereafter to follow him there each day until the end of the age. 557 “Who is this,” they say, “that comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights?” What does “from the wilderness” mean? May we call the world a wilderness? Why a wilderness? Because of a fitting analogy. So long as someone greatly loved, whose presence is most pleasing and dear to those living with him, remains in a house, [Col. 1018B] the whole house seems full through his dwelling with them. But if he departs, the whole house seems to them deserted and empty. So too this world: while that noble and beloved man Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was in it and with it, it was in some manner wholly full. But when Christ left the world and ascended to heaven, the whole world was like a wilderness, because true fullness was and is nowhere but where he is—in heaven. But how and what is that same holy humanity of Christ in heaven? “Leaning upon her beloved,” leaning upon God, leaning upon its own divinity. For humanity is so united to divinity that they can never be separated from one another. It is also always “abounding in delights.” These delights are the delightful souls of the just, which daily flow to it [Col. 1018C] as they pass from the misery of this mortality to eternal life. These delights did not flow to it when he was born, nor when he died; but when he rose and ascended to heaven, it then first began to abound in these delights, because from that hour there was no day or moment in which blessed souls, which are truly his delights, did not flow to it.

Notice that he says “abounding.” No one can come to God unless he flows to God. There are rivers which carry souls from this world to heaven and into heaven. There is the river of baptism; after baptism has been received and violated, there is the river of tears, the river of compunction; there is also the river of martyrdom. For the kingdom of heaven receives absolutely no one unless that person has flowed there through one of these rivers. The holy martyrs who shed their blood for God flowed to him through the river of martyrdom. Those who preserved the innocence received in baptism and kept the faith owed to God flowed to him through the river of baptism. Those who had lost the innocence [Col. 1018D] received in 558 baptism, or had corrupted the faith which they vowed to almighty God in baptism, flowed to him through the river of tears and compunction, renewing and restoring in this life, by the daily stream of compunction and tears, that innocence and faith. Through whichever of these rivers they flowed to God, they were his great and delightful delights. These delights of his are continually renewed and multiplied each day until the end of the age. For even if they do not flow through the river of martyrdom, they nevertheless flow daily to him through the river of baptism or through the river of compunction and tears—whether the innocence received in baptism has been preserved after baptism, or, when not preserved, has been restored by the power of tears. Each day they pass into his delights.

[Col. 1019A] To summarize this same verse briefly: its first part, “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness?” indicates, as we have said, Christ’s ascension; its second part, “abounding in delights,” indicates the congregation of the saints already gathered to him and to be gathered to him until the end of the age; its third part, “and leaning upon her beloved,” indicates the confirmation of those same saints. This beloved is almighty God, upon whom they now lean, as it were, with only one foot. For they are not yet so confirmed in God that they lean upon him with both feet—that is, so that they seem to desire nothing except God alone. [Col. 1019B] They still think of the resurrection of the body. But later, when at the end of the world, having recovered their bodies, they are clothed in the blessed immortality of flesh and soul together, they will then be united and lean always upon God alone with both feet, that is, with all the faculties of body and soul, in such a way that nothing further can turn their minds away from him even for an instant. There indeed God’s delights will be fully brought to perfection. For there he will always delight in his saints; there he will be glorified without end in his saints.

While the Son of God still rested in the Father’s bosom, he foresaw these delights; in foreseeing them, he desired them, when he said, “And my delights were to be with the children of men.” Because he desired [Col. 1019C] them, he descended from the Father’s bosom for their sake; he sought them; for their sake he became man. He descended to us in order to make us ascend to him. Therefore he adds and says:

559 “Now, therefore, my children, hear me.” As though he said: Because it was always my delight to come to you and make you my delights, now that I am present, now that I have become man for you, therefore, my children, hear me. Before my coming, before my incarnation, you were servants; you served as servants; you had [neither] share nor inheritance in the Lord’s house, because you were servants, as it is written: “The Son remains in the house; the servant does not remain for ever” (John 8:35–36). But now, because I have been born for you and by my death have changed the name of servants, I have made you inherit the sweet name of children. Through this name you have received a dwelling and inheritance in the house, that is, in the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, my children, hear me. What are you to hear from me? What do I say to you?

“Blessed are those who keep my ways.” To understand this simply, by the ways of the Only-begotten of God we understand his meekness and humility, or his works in the flesh, or his teaching. We truly keep these ways if we imitate his humility and meekness. Hence he himself says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). And again: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). But if we wish to understand something more subtle in his ways, we may say that he has, as it were, [Col. 1020A] two ways in divinity and four in humanity. His two ways in divinity are his mercy and truth. His four ways in humanity are the four mysteries of his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension. These are the ways by which God came to human beings; by these same ways human beings ought to come to God. For no one can come to God unless he faithfully believes his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension, and imitates them in good works as far as he can. All who keep these ways, whether those of his divinity or those of his humanity—that is, those who frequently set before their eyes the ways of his divinity, which we have called his mercy and truth, attentively considering that, though he is merciful, he does not abandon equity, and who therefore do good in view of his mercy and forsake evil out of fear of his truth and justice; or those who faithfully believe and, so far as they can, imitate the ways of his humanity [Col. 1020B] as we have said—are beyond doubt blessed in this life and will be blessed in eternal life. He continues and says:

“Hear discipline, and be wise, and do not cast it away.” What is discipline? Discipline is both knowledge of things and the ordering of character. A disciplined person is called not merely one who knows what ought to be known; a person is also disciplined and called disciplined who strives to adorn his knowledge with ordered—that is, good and honourable—conduct. Here the Lord exhorts us to this discipline when he says: “Hear discipline, [Col. 1020C] and be wise, and do not cast it away.” Hear by understanding; be wise by the affection of the mind; do not cast it away by the effect of action. These three rightly suit one another, because when a person often hears what is good, he also begins thereby to understand the good. But since it does not greatly profit a person to hear and understand the good unless he also begins to love the good, he rightly adds, “Be wise.” This word “wise” aptly accords with love: a person finds savour in what he loves; what he does not love, he finds no savour in. But since there are some who hear, understand, and love the good, yet do not do it, he continues: “And do not cast it away.” As though he said: If you hear discipline by understanding it, if you are wise by loving it, [Col. 1020D] do not cast it away by failing to fulfil it in action.

“Blessed is the person who hears me, who watches daily at my doors and keeps watch at the posts of my doorway.” Blessed is whoever hears me as has now been said, and, after hearing me, also watches daily at my doors and keeps watch at the posts of my doorway. Doors are the outer entrances of a house. The legal and prophetic Scriptures, or the teachers of the Old Testament, may fittingly be understood by doors, since they were, as it were, doors: they could introduce neither themselves nor others into that house of the kingdom of heaven. They showed a certain path by which one must go there, but they could not open its entrance. By the door, however, which is inner and nearer to the house, [Col. 1021A] Christ and faith in Christ, through whom entrance into the kingdom 561 of heaven is made, may very fittingly be understood. By the two posts of this door, hope and charity may be understood; or, by the door, the preachers of the New Testament, and by the two posts, evangelical and apostolic teaching. All those things which we said were prefigured by the doors, although they were outside, as was said, taught some approach to the kingdom of heaven. But the door, which is Christ, together with faith, hope, and charity, which he taught and gave to the coheirs of his kingdom—or else evangelical and apostolic teaching—opened, and daily opens, the very gate of the kingdom of heaven to those who love and keep these things.

Nor should we pass over his saying: “Who watches daily at my doors, and keeps watch at the posts of my doorway.” [Col. 1021B] For the legal and prophetic Scriptures, being difficult and obscure, require watchfulness and understanding; evangelical and apostolic Scripture requires observance. There were many observers of the Old Testament, and yet they were not thereby saved. But all who were or will be worshippers and observers of the New Testament have obtained or will obtain everlasting salvation from the Lord. The Lord mercifully demonstrates and affirms this in what follows.

“Whoever finds me,” he says, “finds life and draws salvation from the Lord.” As though he said: Whoever, by thus watching at my doors and keeping watch at the posts of my doorway, finds me, finds life—that is, [Col. 1021C] in the present life he finds rest for the soul, through which he is continually consoled with God and mercifully given life by God; after this present life, he will find life enduring without end. “And he will draw salvation from the Lord.” What does “draw” mean? This word indicates the ineffable and inexhaustible blessedness of the life to come, with the fullness of everlasting joy that after the general resurrection will be given to all predestined to life. Water is drawn from a spring or well. Though it is always drawn, the spring or well is never diminished from the abundance of its fullness: it provides a like abundance of water to all who draw from it, yet suffers no lack in itself. This spring or well, which is always drawn upon but never exhausted, is almighty God, sufficient for the salvation of all and never [Col. 1021D] deficient in himself. Those who draw from this spring may be understood as all who are predestined to life. What will they draw from it? Salvation. In the present life they draw from it forgiveness of sins; after the misery of this present life has run its course, they will draw from it the salvation of their souls; after the resurrection, they will draw from it the double robe of immortality for soul and body and that inexhaustible fullness of eternal blessedness which never comes to an end. That fullness will be without any weariness. There will be no deficiency in the giver; in those who receive there will always be a fresh desire to receive. The desire to receive will never fail there; weariness in drawing will never succeed it. Though it is always drawn upon, there will be no want in that spring; [Col. 1022A] rather, in it there will be full and eternal sufficiency of every good thing for all.

This is the lesson which the Holy Spirit has appointed to be read annually, on the present feast of the Nativity of the most blessed Mother of God, Mary, for the praise and glory of her name. It rightly accords with her excellence, for none of all these things would happen unless through her, unless she had become our mediatrix between God and humankind, unless she had borne into this world him through whom we are saved and delivered, our Lord Jesus Christ. No mortal would have attained, or would attain, the glory of eternal blessedness of which we have spoken. Therefore she can never be praised and glorified worthily enough by the human race, through whom such great salvation has come to us and [Col. 1022B] will come. And since, by her gift and help, we have briefly set forth, according to our measure, what and how this holy lesson pertains to her, let us also seek and see whether anything occurs in the Gospel that may have prefigured this same most blessed Lady, our Lady, and may be referred to her praise and honour. For the Evangelist says:

The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham (Matt. 1:1). And thus, enumerating forty-two generations, he descends as far as Jacob, through whom he begins, as it were, to close the same book of Christ’s generation, when he says: “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ” (ibid. 1:16). Let us first consider what cause or reason there is that we read this most holy Gospel every year on this sacred solemnity of Mary, the most exalted Mother of God. It seems greatly suited to her excellence. For although we cannot survey the whole Gospel, nor are we worthy to do so, we nevertheless find in it something which, with her own help, may suitably enough be referred to her.

We find there four women interwoven and numbered in the genealogy of our Lord Jesus Christ, women notable in some respect and possessing something in themselves injurious to feminine modesty. One was Tamar, another Rahab, the third Ruth; the fourth, whose name the Evangelist suppresses, was Bathsheba, mother of King Solomon. But why is this: that Christ, passing over Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Leah, and the other noble and praiseworthy women of Israelite stock, wished these four notable women to be entered in his genealogy? If we wish to understand it simply, great consolation and hope are here given to sinners: namely, that no one is so wicked or so desperate that he may not deserve to be inscribed in the book of life, if only he strives to return to God through true repentance and satisfaction.

But in a loftier sense we may understand our most blessed Lady and Queen, Mary the Mother of God, through these four women. Nor do we think this unworthy of her mercy or injurious to her excellence, since her only-begotten Son deigned, as we often find in the Scriptures, to compare himself with a worm and other lowly things. [Col. 1023A] But first let us consider the names of these women, to see whether in their interpretation we may find anything that pertains to her. Tamar is interpreted “bitter,” Rahab “breadth,” Ruth “hastening,” Bathsheba “well of satiety.” But how does the name Tamar, said to mean “bitter,” suit or apply to the sweetest Virgin Mary?

Was she bitter toward human beings? Far be it from us to think or say this! No human being has been born into the world, apart from him alone whom she bore, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was of such gentleness and such sweetness toward all people. She was not bitter toward people, but bitter on account of people. She was bitter, daily sighing and weeping most bitterly over the bitter death of the whole human race; [Col. 1023B] she was bitter because Almighty God endured such loss in his creation: the whole human race being under the power of the devil, all people—even though living holily and justly in this world—would hasten together to hell as soon as they departed from this life. Thus she bore the name Tamar within herself. Let us see also whether anything in the things done with Tamar, or done by Tamar herself, may in mystery be referred to this same most blessed Lady of ours.

The history says of Tamar (Gen. 38) that Judah, one of the twelve sons of the patriarch Jacob, gave her as wife to his firstborn son, named Er. But because he died childless, and this custom was observed as lawful in Israel—as it was later confirmed by the Law—namely, that whenever one among them died childless, the brother of the deceased should take his widow as wife and give the first son whom he had by her the name of the deceased brother, to renew and preserve his memory in Israel, [Col. 1023C] Judah joined her to his other son, named Onan. When he too died childless, Judah would not give her to his third son, whose name was Shelah; for, as Scripture says, he feared that he too might die.

But after many days had passed and Judah’s wife had died, Tamar was told that Judah was going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. Grieving because she was childless—for in Israel that woman who had no offspring was accursed—she changed her clothing and sat at the crossroads; and, with her face covered, she pretended before Judah to be what she was not. Having received from him his ring, bracelet, and staff which he held in his hand, she conceived by him and departed. Three months later Tamar was accused of having committed fornication. When, after a sentence of death had been pronounced against her, she was being led to punishment, she produced the ring, bracelet, and staff, saying: “By the man whose these things are I conceived” (ibid., v. 25); and thus she was saved. When the time of birth arrived, she bore twins, and called one Perez and the other Zerah.

In Judah we may understand God the Father; in Tamar, as we have said, the blessed Virgin Mary; in Judah’s two sons, Er—whose name means “skin-clad”—and Onan, whose name means “their sorrow,” the infancy and [Col. 1024A] childhood of this same blessed Virgin may not unsuitably be understood. Nor is it unjust to refer Er, said to mean “skin-clad,” to the infancy of the Virgin Mary. For although, as we truly believe, she passed through this age innocently, nevertheless, while she was an infant, she was subject like an infant to the senses of the flesh. Onan, however, whose name means “their sorrow,” is quite fittingly referred to her childhood, because after she had passed through infancy and was able to feel and understand more deeply, her life was always in sorrow over the destruction of the human race.

In a sense she did not bear children by these two sons, because neither in infancy nor in childhood was she fit to bear him through whose blood the whole succession of those predestined to life was to be revived and restored. Thus, when those two sons, Er and [Col. 1024B] Onan, had been removed without offspring—that is, when those two periods of her infancy and childhood had at last passed without the fruit of humanity’s restoration—she long awaited the third son, Shelah, whose name means “shadow.” That is, she longed with an excessively great desire for forgiveness of sins, which may be understood through “shadow,” both for those still living and also for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, for whom “shadow” means refreshment. Yet, as the time for mercy had not yet drawn near, she could no longer endure to wait. Following Tamar’s example, she sat at the crossroads and offered herself to God the Father. First receiving from him a ring, bracelet, and staff, she submitted herself to him.

For sitting at the crossroads—that is, between the way of life, which she desired to be opened to herself and all people, and the way [Col. 1024C] of death, which she desired to be closed to all—sitting, I say, at this crossroads, she approached God the Father. At his feet, with the persistence of faith, hope, and charity, which are as it were the ring, bracelet, and staff, she lay prostrate and submitted herself amid sighs and tears, prayers, vigils, and fasts, until, having conceived a child by him, twins appeared in her womb. That is, until the fullness of time should come, [p. 566] so that she might become pregnant with him who was a giant of twofold substance, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who was true God and true man.

“And the name of one was called Perez, and the name of the other Zerah” (Gen. 38). Perez means “divided,” Zerah “rising.” These twin names suited exceedingly well that giant’s twofold substance. In that aspect in which he was to be human, he could rightly be called Perez, that is, “divided.” How divided? From himself. For, as the Apostle says, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:2). But in that aspect in which he was God, he was deservedly called Zerah, that is, “rising”: one and the same God with the Father, one and the same God abiding in the Father without end. In this manner this most blessed Queen of heaven and earth displayed Tamar’s likeness in herself. Let us see also whether there was anything in Rahab that may be referred to her excellence.

Rahab, as Scripture says (Josh. 2), was a prostitute in Jericho. She received the spies sent by Joshua to spy out the land and city of Jericho; [Col. 1025A] she hid them in the upper room of her house from the king’s messengers, who sought them in order to destroy them. Having received from the spies an assurance that, when Jericho was delivered by God into their hands, she and her father’s household would be saved, she let them down by a rope from the window. Therefore, when Jericho was destroyed, she and her father’s household were saved, and they dwelt among Israel.

If Rahab was a prostitute—indeed, because she was—how did she prefigure her to whom, in innocence and chastity and in all uprightness of life and character, no mortal being could or can be likened, except him alone whom she bore, our Lord Jesus Christ? We say, with due regard for her grace and holiness, that she was quite suitably foreshadowed by Rahab. [Col. 1025B] Rahab, then, means “breadth,” a name fittingly suited to the blessed Virgin Mary. For if she could be called Tamar because of the bitterness she bore over the destruction of the human race, she may also be called Rahab because of the ineffable love by which her most holy heart was enlarged beyond that of all people toward God and neighbor.

But in that respect in which Rahab was a prostitute, what correspondence could she have with the most chaste Virgin Mary? Absolutely none. For under the overshadowing and preserving power of the Holy Spirit, nothing could ever befall her to corrupt in any way the most perfect chastity of her heart or body. Therefore we do not compare her to Rahab in any notable action of her life, but in the praiseworthy significance which may be found in certain actions of this same Rahab. [Col. 1025C] Rahab was a prostitute; and rightly so. For a prostitute is so called from earning, because she earns payment from her lovers with her own body. Rahab had lovers like herself, unjust people and sinners, to whom she prostituted her body. Mary too had lovers: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to whom she consecrated the integrity of her virginal body, and for whom she preserved inviolably throughout her life the virginal chastity of her spirit and soul.

Therefore, just as Rahab earned from her lovers, by the corruption of her body, the payment due to her, so the blessed Virgin Mary earned from her lovers—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—through the incorruption of her body that payment by which the human race, sold [Col. 1025D] under sin, was to be restored to life. That most noble payment was the only-begotten Son of God, whom she alone was worthy to bear and bring forth into this world; for by the price of his blood the salvation of the human race was accomplished.

Rahab received spies sent by Joshua; Mary also received spies sent by God the Father, the first of whom was the archangel Gabriel. He could rightly be called a spy of God Most High, for he had come to search out and betroth this most blessed Virgin. But how did she receive them? She received them faithfully, believing everything said to her by the angel. She also received God’s spies, namely the shepherds, who came to her at the very birth in order to discover whether what they had learned concerning the newborn Savior, as attested by the multitude of angels, was true. [Col. 1026A] For they said: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this thing which the Lord has shown us” (Luke 2:15). Could not those who said these things rightly be called spies?

She also received other spies of God: namely, those three kings who came from the East, guided by a star, to investigate, venerate, and adore the mysteries of Christ’s birth. The blessed Virgin Mary not only received all these spies, but also caused them to ascend to the upper room of her house. She received them by faithfully hearing all their words; she hid them in the upper room of her house, that is, by carefully gathering everything in the higher part of her heart. Thus the Gospel says of her: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (ibid., v. 19). Thus she was Tamar; thus she was also Rahab.

But in Ruth also we may find something which, we believe, may quite suitably be referred to this same Mother of God. Ruth was very praiseworthy in herself and notable in her lineage. For she was born of the shameful and accursed race of the Moabites. Leaving her parents and the land in which she had been born, she chose to live as a stranger in a land not her own; and because of the great uprightness of life and character within her, she was joined in marriage to a noble man of the Israelite race, named Boaz. By him she bore a son named Obed, the father of the father of King David, from whose seed Christ, the Son of God, was born.

Ruth means “hastening.” We believe this name fittingly applies to the blessed Mary, Mother of God, [Col. 1026C] who was always hastening—that is, fervent—in holy and just works. Ruth was born from the shameful and accursed race of the Moabites; Mary likewise came forth from that people whom the sins of original sin had made ignoble and accursed. Ruth left country and parents in order to preserve faithfulness to her mother-in-law, and lived as a stranger in a land not her own; Mary too left her country and her parents when, in order to preserve faithfulness to God the Father and her chastity, she separated herself from the common manner of life of the world. She regarded herself as an exile and stranger in this world, because, despising all that the present world loves, she hastened toward the sole and unending glory of the heavenly homeland.

From Ruth’s seed King David was born; from the virginal flesh of the Virgin Mary was born our true [Col. 1026D] David, truly mighty of hand and desirable in appearance, our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the whole world was saved.

The fourth woman, Bathsheba, whom David took from her husband and joined to himself in marriage, and by whom he begot King Solomon, likewise prefigured the blessed Mother of God. For God the Father, as we may say, in some manner took her too from her husband, namely Joseph, who had betrothed her, because he preserved her immaculate. Thus, thus separated from her husband and joined to Almighty God, she conceived by the Holy Spirit and bore that true Solomon, that true Peaceful One, our Lord Jesus Christ, who through his blood made peace between God and humankind. This is also signified by the name Bathsheba, for Bathsheba, interpreted, means “well of satiety.”

Thus the blessed Mary, Mother of God, mystically bore in herself the names of these four women. To summarize briefly: she was Tamar in contrition of heart; she was Rahab in true love of God and neighbor; she was Ruth in perfect action; she was Bathsheba in full reception of the Holy Spirit.

We may also quite suitably refer all these things, which with her own help we have applied to our Lady, the blessed Virgin Mary, in part to any individual who is to be saved. First, such a person becomes Tamar, bitterly repenting of sins and humbly laboring to conceive from God offspring of virtues; [Col. 1027B] then becomes Rahab by loving God and neighbor, eagerly receiving and gladly preserving in the upper part of the house—that is, the higher part of the heart—the spies, namely God’s preachers and their teaching; then becomes Ruth, that is, hastening and fervent in doing good; and becomes Bathsheba through mental contemplation.

Judah, through whom Almighty God is figured, first gives a person his two sons, Er and Onan, through whom we may understand the human body and soul. Nor is this unjust. For Er means “skin-clad,” and this name may fittingly be applied to the body, which consists of flesh and skin. Onan, however, means [p. 570] “their sorrow,” and this name rightly pertains to the soul, which mourns and laments the sins committed by the body.

[Col. 1027C] When these two sons die, as alas commonly happens, in sins, Tamar—that is, the repentant person—at length awaits and desires to receive the third son, who is called Shelah, that is, “shadow,” through whom forgiveness of sins is very suitably understood. Such a person certainly awaits and desires forgiveness of sins. But when that person considers that it cannot be obtained by any merits or powers of one’s own, one burns inwardly and is troubled lest, if one dies childless—that is, without the fruit of good works—one’s memory be removed in the future life from the midst of Israel, from the midst of those who see God.

When this person begins to consider these matters anxiously, at last hearing that Judah was going up to Timnah, which [Col. 1027D] means “defect,” to shear sheep—that is, that Almighty God deigned to come to the decline of this world to relieve souls of sins, and that for this reason, having become human, he took upon himself every misery of our weakness except sin alone, so that by his death he might strip us of the old human being and clothe us with the new—then Tamar fittingly changes her clothing, following the example, and comes and sits at the crossroads.

A crossroads is called the place where two ways divide. Nor do I think it unfitting that every spiritual way of life should be understood by this crossroads, since it distinguishes, as it were, two paths: one leading to death, the other to life. Spiritual persons sit, as it were, at the crossroads. For they utterly despise the one road which leads to hell; and they cannot reach the other road, which leads to the kingdom of heaven, before [Col. 1028A] death. Tamar—that is, the repentant person—changes clothing when one leaves sins and the world; one places oneself at the crossroads when one joins oneself to the fellowship of just people in some spiritual way of life.
