But when Judah comes—that is, when God visits with the grace of heavenly mercy—and Tamar receives his ring, bracelet, and staff, that is, faith, hope, and charity, the person joins oneself to God in order to conceive from him the long-desired offspring of virtues. Pregnant with his mercy, one at last advances to birth, [p. 571] and twins appear in one’s womb, through whom we may understand the knowledge of God and of oneself. “And the name of one was called Perez, and the name of the other Zerah.” Nor is it unfitting that by Perez, whose name means “divided,” self-knowledge should be understood; while by Zerah, whose name means “rising,” the knowledge of God is signified. For when one begins rightly to know by how many and how great sins one has divided oneself from God and from the kingdom of God, how mercifully divine compassion has borne with one amid so many sins and delivered one from so many evils, then through this knowledge of God and oneself one gradually advances to the love of God, which is always rising. It begins here; in the life to come it will be fulfilled more fully.

But behold: after three months Tamar was accused of fornication. In these three months we may not unsuitably understand the time before the Law, the time under the Law, and the time under grace. After these three months Tamar will be accused—will be accused, I say, after these three periods have passed, that is, after the course of the present life, when the devil comes [Col. 1028C] and begins to object against that person all transgressions and sins. But what will that soul do at last, placed in so great a crisis of necessity? From the face of the wicked accuser it will flee to the mercy of the merciful Savior. “By the man whose these things are I conceived. Recognize whose ring, bracelet, and staff these are” (Gen. 38:25). “Recognize, most merciful Judge, your faith, hope, and charity in me. These are your gifts, which you gave me; these I have preserved, so far as I could by your gift, and have returned them to you as testimony to my salvation.”

When Judah—that is, God the Father—has recognized these gifts, the devil will be confounded, and the soul will be received into the joys of eternal blessedness through him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXVIII. FIFTH HOMILY ON THE SAME FEAST, AS IT APPEARS

[Col. 1028D]

“And he built his sanctuary like that of the unicorn upon the earth” (Ps. 77 [78]).

The most blessed Mary, Mother of God, because she alone among all women was a blessed virgin, alone, I say, among the whole human race deserved to be worthy for the only-begotten Son of God—intending to come to the aid of fallen humanity—to will to become human from her virginal body: all who deserved to foresee this grace in the Holy Spirit did not remain silent concerning her as the mediatrix of that grace, but mystically foreshadowed and extolled in many places, in speech and writing, the excellence of her dignity.

Among these, one chosen in a special way, namely the prophet of the Lord David, foreseeing in the Holy Spirit what this blessed Virgin would be like long before she was born, foreshadowed her in a passage of the seventy-seventh Psalm, saying: “And he built his sanctuary like that of the unicorn upon the earth, which he founded for ever.”

In saying, “and he built,” he very suitably expressed the person and work of God the Father, which he wondrously and ineffably accomplished in this blessed Virgin. For she was that earth, noble and blessed earth, in which God the Father truly built his sanctuary. That sanctuary was her spirit and soul, which from the beginning of her birth God the Father wondrously formed into a dwelling-place for himself by a marvelous structure of virtues and holiness of inestimable chastity and purity; he fittingly adorned [Col. 1029B] and sanctified it.

But how did he build it? “Like that of the unicorn,” that is, adorned with the singular glory of dignity. For as she alone was without example, singular in the new and unheard-of vow of chastity by which she consecrated herself to God, so she possesses a singular dignity in this present age and in that to come. Indeed, she received a singular dignity, because after God there was not and will not be such a human being: namely, one who should be both virgin and mother, mother not merely of a human being but of God and man; who should bring forth a son as a virgin and remain a virgin as a mother. Thus, with a sound understanding of faith, we may understand what was said: “And he built his sanctuary like that of the unicorn upon the earth, which he founded for ever.”

Let us now see how he founded for ever that earth, namely blessed [Col. 1029C] Mary. A foundation is commonly called that which strengthens and supports the mass of a building rising on high. This surely is most fittingly suited to the excellence of this Lady of ours. For she is that foundation which God the Father laid, upon which he wondrously built the house of his holy Church. She is the foundation of our faith. For from her we take the beginning of belief, because we confess and believe her to be the Mother of our Creator and Redeemer, Jesus Christ. God the Father so founded her for ever that without this foundation, without the sacrament of faith which is in her and in him whom she bore, our Savior, no one could be or can be saved.

After the aforesaid prophet of the Lord, in foretelling, had exalted the Virgin Mother with so great a proclamation of praise, he adds concerning him whom she was to bear for the salvation of the human race, saying:

“And he chose David his servant.” This David bore the figure of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to the assumed form of humanity is fittingly called the servant of God the Father. No human being ever served the Father with such faith and truth, because he never allowed even the least thought that might offend the eyes of his Fatherhood. How he chose him, he makes clear in what follows, saying:

“And he took him from the flocks of sheep.” The flocks of sheep were the multitude of all the elect who preceded Christ. He took him from those flocks of sheep because he exalted him above them, so that among all [Col. 1030A] people he alone might be one to whom no stain of sin, original or actual, could attach. But from where he chose him—that is, from whose lineage he had ordained that he would be born—is then expressed when it is said:

“From behind the ewes with young he took him.” By the ewes with young we may understand the holy patriarchs, who could fittingly be called fruitful either because they possessed the seed of God’s word or because they had received in promise that Christ would be born from their seed. And because after the fruitful ones, that is, the patriarchs, there arose prophets, from whose lineage Christ was born, it is rightly said, “from behind the ewes with young he took him”; that is, he appointed that he should be born from the seed of the holy prophets who came after the fruitful ones. For Christ came into the world after the times of the patriarchs [Col. 1030B] and prophets. And why did he take him from behind the ewes with young?

“To shepherd Jacob his servant, and Israel his inheritance.” Jacob bears the figure of all who, trampling down vices and sins in themselves, steadfastly serve God in the active life. By Israel, however, whose name is interpreted “the man who sees God,” are fittingly signified those who, established in the contemplative life, continually contemplate God in the inward sweetness of the heart. And the Lord speaking in the prophet rightly called Jacob his servant, but Israel his inheritance. For although by his mercy he feeds all who labor faithfully for God in the active life, yet with a certain special sweetness he feeds more intimately those whom he sees devoting themselves to him alone in the contemplative life. For they are his inheritance, and they in turn will sometime possess his inheritance with him more intimately. Hence it follows:

“And he fed them in the innocence of his heart, and guided them in the understandings of his hands.” It might seem to us that it would sound more correct if he assigned understanding to the heart and innocence to the hands. But according to the mystery of the spiritual sense this arrangement is reasonable: those whom the grace of his compassion has preserved in innocence of heart he also brings to the understanding of their hands, so that they may do all their works intelligently and prudently, seeking nothing in them except the honor of God and the salvation of their souls. May our Lord Jesus Christ lead us to this understanding of our hands, [Col. 1030D] he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXIX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE EXALTATION OF THE HOLY CROSS

“If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12).

These evangelical words are the words of anyone who despises all earthly things, who, pierced by divine inspiration, rejects what is upon the earth and desires to raise the gaze of the mind to seek the things above.

“I,” he says, “if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” That person desires to be lifted up from the earth who resolves in mind and body to be separated from earthly activity, so that, withdrawn from the works of the world, one may more freely devote oneself to the advancement of one’s salvation. It is as if one openly said: “If, through the prevenient mercy of God, my life is lifted up from the actions of the world, I will draw all things to myself”—all things, that is, not only good deeds but also every work of evil perpetration, through worthy fruits of repentance, to the advancement of my salvation.

For in this, that one does not simply say, “I will draw all things to me,” but distinctly, as it were, “to myself,” something more subtle must be considered. For sometimes a person draws something to oneself from which, nevertheless, one cannot obtain any effect of benefit. But that person draws everything to oneself who, as we have said, considers in repentance with vigilant inward attention all evil deeds performed, and by this means, becoming more and more contemptible in one’s own eyes, humbles oneself more deeply; and the more lowly one becomes to oneself by humbling oneself, the more precious one becomes before the eyes of God. It follows:

“But this he said, signifying by what death he was to die.” Therefore, while such a person is still silently pondering within how one may be withdrawn [Col. 1031B] from temporal things, one begins to signify by certain works how one may mortify vices and desires in one’s flesh. For one already abstains from unlawful things, restrains oneself by resisting carnal desires, and thereby gives some sign concerning oneself that one desires to carry about in one’s body the mortification of Jesus. The following sequence of thought declares what conflicts of mutually accusing or even defending thoughts every person arranging these steps of ascent in the heart will find within oneself.

[Col. 1031C] “The crowd answered him.” What can we more rightly understand by the name of this crowd than the disordered faculties of the human being? They are aptly compared to a crowd, for in their discord they stir up certain tumults in the heart and disturb the tranquility of the mind, agitated on every side by the whirlwind of temptations. A person suffers diverse disturbances in the heart while desiring to forget the things behind and stretch forward to those before. The sweet but evil pleasure of the flesh, ingrained by habitual vices, draws the mind back; the person desires to undertake the arduous discipline of spiritual life, but fears that strength will not suffice to accomplish what has been well begun. The crowd mentioned above produces such wavering in a person when it secretly suggests the following objections. For it says:

[Col. 1031D] “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains for ever.” In this place, by “Law” we may fittingly understand the testimony of the Scriptures. Christ, moreover, means “anointed.” But the anointed one of the Lord is called that person whom divine grace has anointed with spiritual anointing and rendered, as it were, alien to the passing world. This is as if that tumultuous crowd itself answers in these words to a person tending toward the harbor of salvation and rest: “The testimony of Scripture teaches that Christ remains for ever.” That is, one who has once resolved to live anointed by divine anointing must, under the discipline of the spiritual life, take fervent care not to decline from it at some point through the sluggishness of life, [Col. 1032A] but by diligent perseverance in preserving one’s purpose, remain for ever in what one has well begun.

“And how do you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up?” How—that is, in what manner, firmly or changeably—have you resolved to undertake a rigor of such strictness? Do you wish to remain perseveringly in the labor you have determined to undertake, or to stay in these things for a time and then relapse once more into the customary delights of the present life? “Who is this Son of Man?” Who are you, and what are you like, that you undertake a burden of such gravity? Let the concern of your mind therefore weigh the fact that you are a child of man, a human being born of a woman, to whom frailty is innate through the very condition of nature. You are, I say, a child of man, lacking the nature and sublimity of angels; therefore you will by no means be able to live an angelic life in this world [Col. 1032B] and lack the goods of the world. This is the reply of the tumultuous crowd, which everyone to be saved must overcome by manly constancy, through the prevenient mercy of God, as the words of the Gospel immediately indicate.

Therefore Jesus said to them. God’s “saying” is to invite a person by secret inspiration to the effect of good work. “Yet a little while,” he says, “the light is in you.” By this little light may be understood the human heart enlightened by good will. But because it does not yet possess perfection in works, it is still as it were a little light. Hence it follows: [p. 578] “Walk while you have the light.” Walk in the disposition of the heart while you have the light of good will. To walk is to proceed with a pleasant step; that is, to do what must be done delightfully, so that through the good works one performs, one may desire to please the eyes of the Creator alone, and not seek to be exalted by human favor. “Lest darkness overtake you.” By this darkness are understood ignorance and desire, not only of the flesh but also of human favor. Therefore the desire of good will must be carried out not slowly but with a kind of delightful devotion, lest the heart be clouded as by darkness through ignorance, or desire seek the glory of earthly praise.

“The one who walks in darkness does not know where he is going.” That person is said to walk in darkness who performs the good things one does ignorantly and without the sweetness of inward savor. Such a person certainly does not know where one is going, because one is utterly ignorant toward what end one tends, or what grace of reward one will obtain. Hence it follows: “While you have the light, believe in the light.” While you have the light—that is, while you have good will—believe in the light, that is, pass by believing into good action. “That you may be children of light.” By the name of light, the Father of lights himself is understood. Children of light are those who, setting aside servile fear, perform works of light, as John says in his Epistle [Note: The following text is read in the Gospel, not in the Epistles of John]: “The servant does not remain in the house for ever; but the son remains for ever” (John 8:35). All who, as we have said, obey God the Father in all things by faith and devotion as sons, [Col. 1033A] he will assuredly one day make co-heirs of his kingdom and sharers in paternal glory. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with that same Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXX. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST MATTHEW, APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST

“Jesus saw a man sitting at the tax office, Matthew by name, and said to him: Follow me” (Matt. 9).

The blessed apostle and evangelist Matthew, whose venerable festal solemnity we celebrate today with joy, affords all sinners a great example for hoping in the divine mercy, both through the instruction of his preaching and through the conversion of his life. For at no feast of Christ’s apostles is such confidence of hope and assurance granted to sinners, nor can they look to the grace of any other with such consolation as to his—the one whom they know was converted from a tax collector and raised by the Lord to such a height of dignity and glory. For no disciple of Christ is so plainly recorded either as a friend of tax collectors or as one who pursued worldly gain with such ardour. Philip, James the Lord’s brother, Peter, John, Andrew, James, and their fellow apostles were chosen by the Lord as though innocent; but this man, since he was raised from public practices of vice to the dignity of apostleship, ought to condescend to sinners with a greater compassion than those who incurred no grave liabilities of sin, because a sinner ought to have compassion upon sinners.

This blessed Matthew, therefore, although by living perversely he long thirsted after earthly profits, was nevertheless, in the divine predestination, ordained before the foundation of the world not only to be an apostle, but also to write, as the first among the evangelists, the Gospel book concerning Christ’s incarnation. Hence also, in the description of the four living creatures, he appears to have the face of a man, because he too, as we have said, disclosed to the world more fully and perfectly, by writing, the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation. How he was called by the Lord to this grace of election, he himself openly declares in today’s reading from the holy Gospel, [Col. 1033D] and thus sets down the course of his own conversion, so that by his example every sinner may learn how he ought to turn to God and how he ought to persevere in the perfection of a good way of life until the end of his life.

“Jesus,” he says, “saw a man sitting at the tax office, Matthew by name.” Our Lord and Saviour then saw His chosen apostle and evangelist with the eyes of heavenly mercy when He decreed to remove and draw him away from the harmful worldly business after which he thirsted. With these same eyes He still looks upon every sinner whom He purposes to separate from preoccupation with worldly things. For His seeing is His having mercy. Just as we cannot sufficiently gaze with loving attention upon those things which we love most dearly, while we more quickly turn our eyes away from one whom we hold less dear, so almighty God beholds with the eyes of divine mercy the person whom He intends to save; but from the one whom He has not foreordained to eternal life He in some manner turns away the eyes of His compassion.

“Sitting,” he says, “at the tax office.” The custom of one who sits at the tax office is to take others’ property and assign it to his own use. What, therefore, can more fittingly be denoted by the name “tax office” than the greed of this world? Whoever devotes himself to worldly avarice, whoever does not fear miserably entangling himself in temporal affairs, receives others’ property in the manner of a tax collector: for he takes, as though by plunder, sins and vices which properly belong to the devil, and by wickedly possessing them he shamefully joins them to his own body and soul. [Col. 1034B]

And notice that it says, “sitting at the tax office.” There are some who remain in secular life as though unwillingly, so that, if they could, they would gladly renounce the world and its desires. Conversely, there are some who delight with all their desires and all their devotion in the vanities of this present life, so that they never grow weary of worldly pleasures but find it sweet to persist in them until the end of life. Whoever, then, delights in using earthly things in this way is rightly said to be sitting at the tax office. But when almighty God sees a person sitting thus wrongly at ease in the tax office—that is, when, having mercy upon him, He decrees to call him back from this wretched manner of life—He addresses him through the hidden grace of inspiration and makes him consider how vainly he has spent all the time of his life, as follows:

“And He said to him: ‘Follow me.’” God’s speaking is His inspiring: when, as we have said, He addresses the human heart inwardly and invisibly teaches and exhorts it concerning what it must do and how it may attain eternal life. It is as though He said: “Rise from this disgraceful way of life in which you have lived until now; withdraw your mind from this harmful pursuit of earthly things. Follow me—that is, imitate me.” And indeed, whoever has thus been called inwardly by divine grace and invisibly drawn within will at once be able fittingly to fulfil what follows here.

[Col. 1034D] “And rising, he followed Him.” When, pierced by divine inspiration, a person begins to consider the punishments of eternal condemnation, he speaks to himself within himself with the groaning voice of his heart: “O wretched and miserable man! What hope of salvation can remain for you if you are found in this state? With how great torments of eternal condemnation will your wretched soul be tortured if the end of life finds you thus!” And, pierced by this fear, he rises from the perverse deeds of his former life and follows the Lord by taking up the habit of spiritual life.

Yet all these things which we have mentioned, although almighty God works them in us and with us through His inspiring grace, are in some way shown to be small in comparison with the grace which follows, as the following text seems at once to suggest. For that we have left the world and entered spiritual life is indeed His work; but that memorable event of which we are now to speak is greater than all these things.

“And it came to pass,” says the evangelist, “as He reclined in the house.” Often in Holy Scripture, where the expression “it came to pass” occurs, something great is thereby indicated to us. Thus in the present place we may understand by this event a memorable work of divine mercy. This is the work of divine mercy: when almighty God graciously deigns, according to the multitude of His mercies, to visit a person whom He has called from the common life of the world to a spiritual way of life. All His works are great and praiseworthy; but this work of mercy is greater than all the works of His power, because Scripture testifies: “His mercies are over all His works” (Ps. 144 [145]:9).

Luke the evangelist seems to indicate more plainly in yesterday’s reading from the holy Gospel what this great event is, which we have called a work of divine mercy. Describing the same glorious conversion of this tax collector, he says: “He made Him a great banquet in his house” (Luke 5:29). By the banquet which this converted tax collector is described as making for the Lord in his house, we must understand not only what he visibly offered Him outwardly, but rather what he invisibly prepared for Him in the house of his breast. For Christ’s food and refreshment are, so to speak, our good desires and our continual meditation upon our salvation, as He Himself says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). He is truly fed in us when, through good desires, we continually direct ourselves toward heavenly things by considering our salvation. If, therefore, we desire to prepare in the house of our breast a banquet pleasing to the author of our salvation, in which He Himself may delight, we must always keep our minds ready for this. For if we are going to receive some friend of ours into an outward house, we cannot suddenly find what is necessary unless we have first prepared services for his arrival. So we must always be ready to receive in the house of our heart the author of eternal salvation.

But, in order to say something about what is usually done outwardly, let us see with what labour the refreshment of bodily food is customarily prepared, and let us draw to ourselves spiritually, as an example, what we see done among visible things. Worldly people commonly invite their friends into their homes and prepare various foods for their banquet. At such a feast boiled meats are first set out, and then roasted meats are offered. This preparation of meat is usually done as follows: an animal is slaughtered; its flesh, cut into pieces, is put into a pot or cauldron; then water is poured in, and after this a fire is placed beneath it. When this preparation has been completed, the meat is taken from it, arranged upon dishes, and brought to the table. If it has been well prepared, it delights, refreshes, and strengthens those who eat it; but if anything remains raw in it, it causes sickness in those who eat it. [Col. 1036A] After this dish, roasted meats are customarily brought in, which we ordinarily call a roast.

Let us therefore endeavour to carry out spiritually what we see done carnally. Our sacrificial victim is our carnal life; the pot, made from clay, signifies our earthly heart. By the water customarily poured in from above, the water of tears may be understood; by the fire placed under the pot, compunction may be understood. Therefore, in order to prepare for the Lord within us a pleasing banquet, we must slaughter our victim—that is, our carnal life. I do not say this so that anyone should wish to kill himself—far be it!—but so that we should strive with all our might to mortify whatever we discover living carnally within us.

[Col. 1036B] Having slaughtered the victim, we must put its flesh into the pot and supply fire and water for cooking, because we must boil in our heart, through the fire of compunction and the water of tears, the carnal deeds which we have done, until our very life, which was formerly as it were raw, becomes, after the blood of vices has been wholly drained away, food desirable to the Lord. And truly, if we prepare ourselves with such diligence, we shall be choice and delicate food on the Lord’s table; the heavenly King Himself will delightfully take us into His body, and, incorporated into Him, we shall remain in Him without end. But whoever has less zeal for such preparation, whoever, being as it were raw, does not strive to dry up the blood of vices within himself, is not desirable food but, as though producing sickness, is to be avoided and abhorred. He is abominable, I say, and produces sickness, because such a person’s conduct breeds grave illness when he does not cease to stir up anger, envy, and dissension in the community by his perverse habits.

It sometimes happens that, when the fire’s heat prevails, the boiling pot causes the water to bubble over. But as soon as it is removed from the fire, the excessive heat is moderated; and when a fork is put into the pot, the meat is held down within, because the more fat runs off, the less flavour the meat will afterward have. Therefore, if ever we perceive our heart, signified by the pot, swelling through our good deeds, let us strictly restrain it within, lest, while it is lifted outward through the desire for human praise, it be emptied inwardly of the richness of divine sweetness. [Col. 1036D]

After these meats boiled in water, we must bring to the Lord’s banquet meat roasted over fire. Flesh which is roasted over fire is fastened to a piece of wood—that is, a spit. A spit, as is known, is a piece of wood not curved but extended forward and sharp; once flesh has been fixed upon it, it cannot turn aside in either direction. What can be understood more fittingly by this piece of wood than the strictness of spiritual discipline? It is extended and sharp because it always stretches toward what lies ahead. When any person is subjected to it, he is held fast by its sharp strictness, so to speak, so that, whether willing or unwilling, he can wander no further. If our life is fastened to this wood in such a manner and roasted by the fire of compunction, it can offer the Lord, as we have said, the taste of the sweetest flavour.

How well and strongly was the flesh of blessed Lawrence roasted, when the judge Decius had him placed alive upon a gridiron and roasted! Taken from the gridiron and brought to the Lord’s table, the Lord received him into His body as choice and desirable food, joining him both to the congregation of holy Church and to the angelic spirits in heaven. [Col. 1037A]

We have said these things so that we may draw spiritual examples from what we see done outwardly. This, then, is the work of mercy; this is the visitation of divine compassion: when a person is inwardly prepared in such a way that the very author of sweetness, in the mercy of wondrous condescension, deigns to recline in the house of his heart.

[Col. 1037B] Nor should we pass over the fact that it says “to recline”: that is, when He finds the dwelling-place of the heart so prepared that He may rest there and deign worthily to make His abode in that habitation. For just as a house seems almost desolate when its master is absent, but is cheerful and, as it were, full through his presence when he is there, so when that supreme master of the household leaves the house of the human heart, it is empty and besieged by many miseries. And just as any abandoned house is sometimes full of filth and surrounded by spiders’ webs, so the house of the heart in which Christ the indwelling resident does not remain is polluted by foul thoughts and exposed to manifold calamities of misery. But where the Creator of the heart deigns to recline—that is, to rest—in the human heart, there surely comes about what the sequence of the narrative declares.

“Behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and His disciples.” By tax collectors we may understand grave sins, but by sinners lighter offences. At that hour, therefore, as we have said, when Jesus deigns to rest familiarly in the human heart, these tax collectors and sinners come and recline with Jesus and His disciples. That is, a person then gathers his inward senses, which are signified by Jesus’ disciples, and is so brought back into himself within himself that he is able not only to repent worthily through considering his graver sins, but also to repent and weep through perfectly recognizing every lighter offence of thought or intention. It follows:

“And the Pharisees, seeing, said to His disciples.” By the Pharisees, whose name means “the separated,” evil spirits may be understood in this place. For these perverse enemies and foes of human salvation, when they perceive such saving progress in a person, inflamed by the torches of envy, labour by every crafty device to call him back from the begun fruit of compunction and repentance.

The Pharisees may also signify those thoughts which evil spirits themselves customarily send into the human heart in order to pervert a person. When any person, blessed in the bitterness of his soul, recalls and examines the guilt of his wicked way of life, this thought sometimes comes upon him: that his repentance is useless, that his compunction can obtain no grace of salvation. In the sorrow of his heart he speaks to himself the words which the following text seems to indicate: “Why,” he says, “does your Master eat with tax collectors and sinners?” That is: “Why must I repent my sins so greatly? What benefit is it to me to be frequently pierced with compunction for my sins? For although I now weep over them, I return to doing the same things again. Can I obtain forgiveness through such repentance?”

But these perverse thoughts are, so to speak, diabolical promptings. They send them into the human heart in order to take away the fruit of repentance and compunction and to lead it into the abyss of despair, so that the person may begin to despair that he can obtain forgiveness, as though God had consigned his earlier repentance to oblivion. Against these thoughts our Lord and Saviour, in the following three verses, gives us great consolation through His mercy; and, lest a person ever despair of the compassion of divine goodness or neglect the time granted for repentance, He confirms and strengthens us by a clear example of His mercy.

But Jesus said to them: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill.” And again and again, consoling us and commending the riches of His mercy and compassion, He says: “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” [Col. 1038C]

In these three verses we may observe three stages, which blessed Gregory also seems to have expounded in the *Morals*, where he says: “God works all these things three times for each person.” In the first verse, therefore, where the Lord says, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill,” the beginning—that is, a person’s conversion—may be denoted. In the following verse, where He says, “Go and learn,” the middle stage is denoted; and in the final verse the end may fittingly be figured.

At the beginning, that is, in conversion, a person is still as though ill and therefore needs a physician. He is ill because he has not yet recognized his sins, repented, confessed, or made satisfaction. But in order that he may attain perfect health, he needs a physician to help him—that is, some good teacher to take care of him, never ceasing to assist him by gentle consolation and stern rebuke until he recovers perfect health. He may truly be called sound and strong when he has learned from the mouth of a good teacher to recognize the sins which he committed and, after recognizing them, does not cease to amend them by worthy repentance, confession, and satisfaction.

Thus, healed and helped at the beginning—that is, in conversion—he needs, in the middle stage, continually to strive to ascend to higher degrees. This is rightly declared by the following verse: “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’” He must always tend upward, go, I say, from virtue to virtue; and so long as he remains in this time of mortality, he must always lend the ear of his heart to sound teaching, striving with all his might to learn and fulfil that which the Lord here declares almost as a command: “Learn,” He says, “what this means: ‘I desire mercy.’”

He must strive to learn this: to know and be able to have mercy—that is, to have a wretched heart—so that, if he feels any virtue within himself, he may ascribe it not to his own merits but to divine mercy. “And not sacrifice,” He says: that is, he must not wish, as though boasting, to glory in having offered himself as a sacrifice to God, nor seek the glory of human praise because he strives to bear the mortification of Jesus in his body. Whoever has thus been healed at the beginning and instructed in the middle stage may now confidently hope in the Lord that He will mercifully be present for him at his end, as He Himself subsequently promises in this final verse:

“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” By these righteous persons the holy angels may be understood; by sinners human beings may fittingly be signified. Justice or injustice is attributed to no creature of God except the angelic and human creatures alone. For the holy angels, who remained with the Lord in their righteousness when the apostate angels fell, have always been righteous before the eyes of the divine majesty. But when our first parent Adam, through disobedience, departed from the path of righteousness, he left to all his posterity the guilt of injustice as though an inborn inheritance. For we are all conceived and born in sins, and there is no one born of a woman who can be free from the contagion of sins, as the apostle Paul says: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23).

But the Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, conceived and born without sin, came entirely free from all sins. He came, I say, not to restore the angel who did not sin, but to help the human being who lay held in the bonds of sins in the pit of misery. And this is what He says: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” That is: “I entered the world as a human being not for the angels’ sake, but for human beings’ sake I united human nature to myself.” Therefore, because our Redeemer declares that He came not for angels but to call sinners, He truly gives all people great confidence for hope, lest any converted sinner should ever lose hope of obtaining forgiveness.

It is as though He were consoling with these words a person almost already despairing because of the enormity of his sins, and saying: “Since I have been so generous toward you through such great benefits—since at your beginning my medicine helped your weakness, and in your middle stage I gave you sound teaching—why are you anxious, as though about your end, and distrustful through despair of my mercy? Why do you not rather place your hope confidently in me? For I am He who holds your beginning and your middle stage in my hand. I too, if you firmly place your hope in me and do not depart from righteousness, will grant you at your end the reward—that prize of eternal life which I myself am, I who alone am the eternal blessedness of all the saints reigning with me through infinite ages of ages. Amen.”

## 589. HOMILY LXXXI. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ST MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL

“The disciples came to Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?’” (Matt. 9.)

Because the Gospel reading contains, in a mystical sense, the marks of true humility, it is quite suitably read at the feast of the angels, because they recognized themselves as little and humble in God’s estimation. Therefore, on account of this humility, they were enriched with the glory of so great a reward, so that, while apostate spirits were cast down, they perpetually enjoy the vision of the unbounded majesty. And because the dignity of this great reward is believed to have been granted not only to angels alone, but also to all who strive to follow in the footsteps of the Lord who goes before them—those who become both disciples and sons by adoption—the evangelist declares at the beginning of this reading with what disposition of intention they ought to cling to God:

“The disciples,” he says, “came to Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?’” Those who diligently undertake virtuous works and strive to erase the stain of inveterate sin endeavour, presuming to approach the throne of grace, to submit themselves to the discipline of heavenly teaching. When, therefore, many are placed under this discipline of Christ’s love but are not yet able to attain the summit of perfection, the thought easily steals into the secret recesses of the mind which is expressed in these words: “Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?”

Although in Holy Scripture “the kingdom of heaven” is understood in various senses, here it may fittingly be understood as the warfare of spiritual life. Those who are truly repentant and have turned somewhat from the error of their path profess this warfare; but, not sufficiently armed with prudent watchfulness, they are assailed by this hidden thought: how much wealth and glory they once possessed, how much abundance they supplied for the need of their brethren, and how, for the benefit of such generosity, they desire to be preferred before the community of their companions with a greater magnificence of rank. If the windy exaltation of such persons prevails, and they do not cease to be proud by exalting themselves above themselves, the silent tongue of pride boldly presumes to break forth in these words: “Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?”

The kingdom of heaven is, indeed, what is called life living in itself, enclosed by no end. Those puffed up by the spirit of pride imagine themselves to be rewarded in that life with an incomparable prize; nor, because of the greatness of their unjust desire, can it enter their hearts that God does not accept a person’s status, but the one who perseveres in righteousness will receive the delights of the eternal dwelling prepared by God. But, desiring mercy, He does not permit those who think so wrongly to fall into the precipice of eternal condemnation, but applies such a remedy:

“And Jesus, calling a little child, set him in their midst.” Who this little child is, whom sweet and righteous Jesus calls, it is pleasing to inquire with the discerning gaze of the mind and to follow the purity of that innocence. For true and tested humility, which restrains the proud minds of the carnal, is what Jesus calls by the regard of His compassion, when He visits hearts long hardened in evils by hidden inspiration. But since the abyss of the human condition is tossed about by diverse movements, occupying itself with innumerable tumultuous affairs, it neglects, through forgetfulness, the grace of humility once given to it. Jesus, however, whose works are in faithfulness, sets the aforesaid little child in their midst, making the spirit of humility stable and immovable in their hearts, so that the foot of pride may no longer move those whom He also admonishes in what follows:

“Amen I say to you: unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” No one fully apprehends the singular excellence of such great humility unless he has deserved in this life to taste beforehand from the abundance of divine sweetness. Hence it is clear that the blessed—indeed, most happy—soul, when in the hour of compunction it has been united with its bridegroom, namely Christ, judges itself, by humbling itself, inferior to all mortals, and desires in mutual love to embrace those who afflict it with the hardships of injuries. When the faithful are frequently fortified inwardly and outwardly with these virtues according to the admonition of Truth, they become little children; with no obstacle of vices standing in the way, the gate of the heavenly kingdom is opened to them.

But there are some devoted to an unyielding hardness of mind, who taste nothing of the sweetness of inward savour but greedily consume with all eagerness the things that are upon the earth. Such persons are altogether unable by their own powers to attain the surpassing gift of perfect humility. But He who raises the poor from the dung heap provides, with the eye of mercy, to all who are predestined for the rest of eternal blessedness the grace of perfect conversion even when they are in their final agony. For at the very point of death, with God’s assent, an incredible bitterness of repentance shakes them, so that in that very bitterness of a contrite heart they attain the virtue of profound humility. That this is not contrary to reason, Truth itself indicates by these words:

“Whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven.” For those who have cast away the exaltation of a proud heart and have believed themselves little in their own eyes with their whole affection, when they lay aside the dwelling of this body, are gloriously raised to the throne of eternal rest. But because the gift of humility granted to many does not result in the advancement of salvation, what follows indicates this more plainly:

“And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.” Many indeed receive such a little child—that is, the grace of humility—but do not know how to preserve it in the Saviour’s name. For the virtue of humility bestowed by God is emptied by human favour when they desire to appear holier than the holy merely for the sake of the reverence of honour and glory. But those receive the aforesaid little child in the Saviour’s name who ascribe nothing of their virtuous works to their own merits, but attribute everything solely to the Father of lights, from whom is every good gift. [Col. 1042A]

“But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble.” Those may be called and may be little ones who, by loving, believe in the power of His majesty. Whoever gives them a stumbling-block, which is called an occasion of sin, ought to be subject to the satisfaction which the Lord commends in the present passage. He says, therefore: “It is expedient for him that a millstone turned by an ass be hung around his neck.” What, then, is signified by the millstone turned round through the weariness of great labour, except the irrational faculty, defiled with countless filthy thoughts, after the likeness of an ass, which is burdened with a diversity of loads more than other beasts of burden?

It is expedient that this faculty be hung upon the neck and plunged into the depths of the sea. For by the neck, through which every utterance is sent forth to the instrument of the tongue, the confession of the truly penitent is fittingly indicated. The millstone is rightly hung around the neck when those who have sinned strive humbly to confess to the physicians of souls everything done by the irrational faculty; and thus, by confessing their crimes, they are plunged into the depths of the sea. Although the sea, which is salt and bitter, is taken in the testimonies of Scripture in various senses, in this place it seems to express the bitterness of contrition and repentance, into which those who afflict themselves for sins immerse themselves when, through an abundant fountain of tears, they wash away the vices formerly committed. With God’s help, such persons illumine the darkness of their ignorance with the ray of virtues, and the following curse will be far removed from them:

“Woe,” He says, “to the world because of stumbling-blocks.” John the theologian indicates what this world is: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16). From this threefold snare of deception all destructive stumbling-blocks take their beginning. For whoever transgresses by violating the Lord’s law is bound in the harmful fetter of these three. That the state of this present life cannot pass without stumbling-blocks of diverse kinds is shown by the Gospel words:

“It is necessary,” He says, “that stumbling-blocks come; yet woe to the person through whom stumbling-blocks come!” What a woe will come upon the person who does not fear to cause Christ’s little ones to stumble! Either it is fitting that he render to God the worthy fruit of repentance while life remains with him, or, taken from this light, he will endure the grave punishment of condemnation. Therefore every wise and blessed person, fittingly adorned with the disciplines of God’s commandments, should not delay too long in attaining, according to his measure, the counsel of the Lord which remains for ever.

“If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you.” Just as a person’s deed is understood by the hand, so by the foot is understood the inclination of human intention. Whoever senses that he is being caused to stumble by these should not receive with a deaf ear of the heart the words of Truth, which healthfully admonishes: “Cut it off and cast it from you.” It will not profit anyone greatly merely to cut off vices unless he also removes what has been cut off far from himself and, cleansed by the sword of a worthy excision, strives by the steps of virtues to receive the reward of promised blessedness. Therefore it follows: “It is better for you to enter into life maimed or lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be sent into eternal fire.”

What the Lord says—“It is better for you to enter life maimed and lame”—plainly declares that it is judged a singular and lasting good if the marks of good works, performed with pure affection and a simple heart, are referred to the glory and honour of God alone, who knows how abundantly to grant His own the benefits of eternal reward. For those who, thus clinging to the good, cut away vices from both the inner and outer human being, beneficially make themselves weak and will at last overcome the devouring flames of fires. For that weakness is blessed—indeed, most happy—which lifts the simple and upright in heart to the gates of paradise. [Col. 1043B]

“If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you.” What can more fittingly be expressed by the eye, which directs all a person’s steps, than the understanding of the twofold human being, in which the reason of prudent discernment is strong? But if this eye—that is, the understanding—makes anyone stray through a reprobate perception, let him, cleansing his conscience, pluck it out, and with a simple and sound understan—

[Note: [Col. 1043D] The remainder, together with three leaves, has been cut out at this place from the manuscript.]

## 594. HOMILY LXXXII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

“I saw a great multitude, which no one could number,” etc. (Rev. 7.)

[Col. 1043C] Today’s feast, celebrated in honour of all the saints, differs from the other solemnities of saints which we observe throughout the course of the year, in which we recall either the triumph of their passion or their passage from death to life. But we venerate together, under one celebration, the merits of all the saints in order that, aided by their merits and intercessions, we may deserve to be reconciled to the Lord; and that, if at another time we have been slower or more negligent in their service than we ought to have been, we may wash this away by repentance through the devotion which we display in today’s celebration.

This present chapter also appears rightly suited to this illustrious feast; and in all Holy Scripture [Col. 1043D] nothing could have been found more fitting to be read at the solemnity of such great princes. Hence blessed John, soaring above every creature in the exalted vision of his mind, and beholding the multitude of all who are predestined to life, says: “After these things I saw a great multitude.” And why does he say, “after these things”? Because before this he had seen a numbered and sealed multitude, one hundred and forty-four thousand. By this number of those sealed may be understood all the saints and elect who lived before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. For many perfect and righteous persons lived before the Law, who were truly full of the grace of the Holy Spirit: Abel the proto-martyr, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and some others, who were so lofty and eminent in virtues [Col. 1044A] that almighty God even chose to be called their God, as he himself says to Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6). Under the Law also there were found persons of great perfection: Moses, with whom, as Scripture says, the Lord deigned to speak as familiarly as a friend is accustomed to speak with his friend (Exod. 33:11); David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and those like them. And under grace there were the holy apostles, all of whom are marked and distinguished by a fixed and definite number because few and rare are those able to imitate their perfection.

They are fittingly signified by the number one thousand, which is perfect, because they were found perfect in faith and conduct. And the composition of this number with forty, [Col. 1044B] completed by seven times twelve, signifies the perfection of the Holy Spirit, who had filled their hearts. Their pre-eminence is magnificently recalled in what follows:

“These are those who have not been defiled with women; for they are virgins, who follow the Lamb wherever he goes.”

By “women” softness and weakness of spirit are customarily signified. Therefore they were not defiled with women, because they repressed within themselves the soft and feeble works of sin. And for this reason they are virgins following the Lamb wherever he goes: for although not all are virgins in body, they are nevertheless virgins in mind and soul, because they were penitent and humble. Therefore they follow the Lamb wherever he goes, because whatever is best that God possesses in his gifts, he will not deny them; and that reward which is common to all, [Col. 1044C] he will sufficiently give to all—namely, himself. For many are called virgins and are incorrupt in body, yet are not counted among the virgins, because they preserve virginity of the flesh without virginity of heart. And many who possess integrity of heart have lost bodily virginity. Such persons follow the Lamb wherever he goes because, when through true repentance they have returned to true innocence, they truly follow the Lamb wherever he goes, when at last they are crowned. But those who are virgins in body yet are not humble in mind do not follow the Lamb at all, when they are condemned for pride and self-confidence.

Having determined and completed the number of the sealed—that is, [Col. 1044D] of the perfect—he turns to the innumerable number which cannot be estimated, concerning which he adds: “I saw a great multitude, which no one could number.” By the great multitude which no one could number are signified those who cannot attain the perfection of those of whom we spoke above, and yet are saved through God’s mercy. He distinguishes and describes them thus: “From all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues.” There are nations; and those people are aptly called nations who lived according to the condition in which they were born, 596 who, conceived and born in sins, added sins to sins. For all are conceived and born in sins. But those live according to the condition in which they were born who do not oppose or resist the desires of their flesh, but live pleasurably in them. When they are visited by God’s mercy [and] recognize their sins, they begin, as it were, to be tribes.

How do they begin to be tribes? Certainly when, for these three things—evil wills, useless words, and wicked deeds—they offer repentance to God: now disclosing their sins in confession to their confessor, now presenting and committing themselves to God in prayer. They also begin to be tribes when, by believing and living well, they submit themselves to their Creator—that is, to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

After this they become peoples. By “peoples” subjects are understood. Those who, from nations, have become tribes also become peoples when they take from themselves the evil freedom to sin which [Col. 1045B] they formerly possessed and humbly submit themselves, for God’s sake, to the obedience of others. After nations, tribes, and peoples follow tongues. They become tongues when they begin to teach others not only by words but also by examples.

In these four terms—nations, peoples, tribes, and tongues—we may also understand the four orders in the Church: penitents in the nations, the innocent in the tribes, the obedient in the peoples, and rulers in the tongues. To these four correspond the four things which follow: “standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, and palms in their hands.” “Standing before the throne” concerns the nations, inasmuch as they are penitents. For the throne, which properly is and is called the seat of kings, signifies the final judgment of the dreadful [Col. 1045C] Judge. They stand before the throne when they carefully consider that condition in which, at the dreadful examination of the final judgment, they must stand and be examined before the face of dreadful Majesty. They prepare within themselves the throne of the Judge, punishing with strict repentance what they have sinned, and by the sentence of their own strictness forestalling the terrible judgment of the eternal Judge which they have deserved. For here are mercy and truth; there is justice alone, without mercy. And as each person is found at the hour of death, so shall he be judged on the day of judgment. Therefore, one who judges himself here while there is time removes his judgment from almighty God, so that he need not be judged by him in the dreadful judgment.

After saying “standing before the throne,” he rightly added [Col. 1045D] “in the sight of the Lamb,” which can suitably be referred to the tribes, by which we understand the innocent. For those are truly innocent and are rightly called innocent who are conformed in their innocence to the innocent Lamb, our Lord Jesus Christ; who guard their innocence so that it may be in the sight of the Lamb—that is, so that they may please him who, innocent, died on the cross for us who were guilty. For he was the humblest of all in his innocence. Therefore, unless one who is innocent is also humble, his innocence cannot be in the sight of the Lamb—that is, acceptable to the innocent and humble Lamb. For there are some who, because they recognize themselves as innocent, swell with the vice of pride; grieving to be despised, they desire to be regarded above other people [Col. 1046A] as though they had lived more holy lives than the rest. Although these are innocent, such innocence is not in the sight of the Lamb, because it does not please him who was slain innocent for us. But those who are innocent and preserve their innocence in such humility that they exalt themselves above no person, however sinful, have innocence in the sight of the Lamb, because they imitate the Lamb’s singular innocence, from whom and with whom they will receive the reward of their innocence and humility.

After nations and tribes, peoples are also added; by these, as we have said, we understand the obedient, to whom “clothed in white robes” fittingly corresponds. For by the white robe we understand innocence, which is acquired through humble obedience. They are indeed clothed in white robes [Col. 1046B] because, however much they have sinned in the world and however greatly they have fallen, through the obedience which they offer to God and, for God’s sake, to their prelates with a good and willing heart, they are numbered among the peoples—the innocent themselves—because through humble obedience, if only they persevere, they arrive at true innocence. It follows:

“And palms in their hands.” “Palms in their hands” concerns the rulers, namely the holy teachers, who may be understood by the tongues and who know how to preside in holy Church over penitents, innocents, and obedient persons. The palm, which signifies victory, signifies the reward and glory of those who conquer vices within themselves. But why is it said only of the persons of prelates, “and palms in their hands”? There will indeed be palms in the hands of penitents, in the hands of innocents, and in the hands of the obedient. Yet, because, according to the words of blessed Jerome, this book—namely, the Apocalypse of John, from which this reading is taken—contains as many mysteries as words, it is not without a definite mystical reason that it is said of the persons of prelates, “and palms in their hands.” For hands customarily signify works. Therefore, not inappropriately, the hands of prelates signify their subjects, in whom and upon whom they ought to work for almighty God. Good prelates work for God in their subjects when they strive by words and examples to bring them to perfection. For when they conquer vices in themselves and teach those whom they govern to conquer vices in themselves by their example, this is to bear palms in their hands. Thus it is written: “Therefore God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, that he might work” (Gen. 2:15)—that is, that he might fashion that man, who was still imperfect, into a perfect man.

Of this multitude of penitents, innocents, obedient persons, and rulers it is rightly said: “I saw a great multitude, which no one could number.” Why does he say, “which no one could number”? Where there is no number, there is confusion; but where there is number, there are beauty and adornment. This multitude of penitents, innocents, obedient persons, and rulers is so great and so immense before God that no one—that is, no human being, not even the blessed Virgin Mary herself, who bore for us the eternal Savior, nor even her only-begotten Son himself, insofar as he is man—can fully adorn, that is, fully reward, this multitude. For whatever is below God is insufficient for this multitude, because no human being attains the full satisfaction of his desire in this life. Those who seek and love the world and its honors and riches never attain such fullness 599 that there is nothing more they desire or wish to add to their riches and honors. So also those who perfectly love God are never drawn into such a force of divine love and sweetness that there is not still something they long for, by which they may burn ever more and more in the love of their desire. But there, [Col. 1047B] where God will be given to us, where, when our bodies are restored at the end of the world, we shall attain that fullness of our desire beyond which there is nothing, because we shall see God himself face to face—there this multitude will truly be numbered, there rewarded, there fully adorned; there it will seek nothing further, because he who is above all will be its beauty and adornment.

There will truly be fulfilled what is said: “You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight” (Wis. 11:21). He is measure, because he measures and bounds all things; he is number, because he forms all things; he is weight, because he orders all things. In the glory of eternal blessedness all things shall be established in measure, number, and weight, where he who is the full desire and the full joy of all his saints [Col. 1047C] numbers and grants the joys of rewards according to the measure of their merits; where, in that weight of eternal stability, they will be made so steadfast with God in God that, as they need nothing further, so they will never again be able to desire anything further.

Let us therefore implore the help of all the saints whose feasts we celebrate today, that as they have been gathered from all classes—that is, from sinners or penitents, from the obedient, or from rulers—and made citizens of heaven, so they may make us from sinners into penitents, from penitents into obedient persons, and from obedient persons into rulers, so that we may rule our own souls in such a way as to deserve to obtain the palm of victory. Then, united and joined to their company, may we behold face to face the God of gods, who lives and [Col. 1047D] reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

600 HOMILY LXXXIII. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE HOLY BISHOPS MARTIN AND UDALRIC.

“These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands shining before the Lord” (Rev. 11).

Since we celebrate the venerable solemnity of the holy confessors of Christ, blessed Martin and blessed Udalric, we venture, according to our ability, to speak of their praises. We can surely apply to them without incongruity those words which the Church is accustomed to sing from memory concerning other saints: “These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands.” For the olive produces a life-giving fruit, since oil shines, refreshes, and heals. These two noble olive trees produced from themselves such oil [Col. 1048A] as shone quite clearly, refreshed, and healed. Their most holy teaching supplied the light of faith and refreshed their hearers with the wondrous sweetness of God’s word. And because, in accordance with the excellence of their episcopal dignity, they were eminent in the world through the greatness of their wealth, they not only refreshed all poor and needy persons with bodily food, but also did not cease to provide them with spiritual things. How many sick persons they healed need not now be rehearsed, because all who have read the Life of Saint Martin know that he healed not merely countless sick persons but also raised three dead persons.

“And two lampstands,” he says, “shining before the Lord.” A lampstand is battered and bruised by many blows before it is fitted and formed into its customary beautiful shape. And indeed these splendid lampstands of the heavenly light were in this world variously beaten and worn down by great and countless pressures of blows from the supreme Craftsman. Blessed Udalric, indeed, he began to wear down at the very, so to speak, beginning of 601 his birth with a great blow: after only a few days from his birth, by the prophetic utterance of a certain messenger of his, he commanded him to abstain from the milk by which that infant age still had to be fed and nourished. Later, when he had become bishop, he was again worn down by new blows. For, as is also read among other things, the invading Hungarians devastated that entire region and led away many captives from the people under his charge.

[Col. 1048C] As for blessed Martin, we know with what austerity of affliction he chastised himself throughout his life. Even after receiving the episcopate, he diminished in no respect the humility and austerity which he had possessed as a monk. Thus these two lampstands, sufficiently polished by so many and such great blows, shone before the Lord. They shone among human beings indeed with the distinguished light of life and teaching, but that would not have been enough unless they had also shone before the Lord in merits and holiness.

And because they thus shone before the Lord, they have power to shut heaven against clouds and to open its gates. If we wish to understand this according to the letter, they truly have power to shut heaven against those who offend God by evil living; but they open its gates to all who devoutly seek their patronage. There is also another heaven in which Christ truly rests, concerning which Scripture says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” For whatever soul has made itself a clean dwelling-place truly becomes for the Son of God a most pleasant and delightful seat. For there is no place in which he deigns to dwell more lovingly than in a soul which, adorned by the merits of virtues, offers itself worthily as his dwelling.

But there are certain clouds that overshadow this heaven and seek to obscure its light with the darkness of ignorance. By the name of clouds, in this place, we may quite fittingly understand evil spirits. Heaven is in a manner 602 shut against clouds when a holy soul, fortifying itself with good works, seals itself [Col. 1049A] so that entrance to it may not lie open to evil spirits. When they have been excluded and the soul is well fortified, its gates are truly opened. The gates of our soul are its senses; these are opened to receive the grace of heavenly dew when our heaven is shut against these harmful clouds. The following words indicate how these saints have received the power by their prayers to shut heaven for us or to open its gates: because their tongues have been made the keys of heaven. Since their tongues were the keys of heaven, they are worthy to shut and open the heavens.

Therefore the feast of such intercessors, whose power and dignity gloriously excel in heaven and on earth, must be celebrated with fitting reverence. Today we honor the birthday of blessed Udalric—that is, the day on which, stripped of the earthly dwelling of the body, he was born into eternal life. But today we celebrate blessed Martin’s ordination or translation, or even the dedication of his basilica, when the supreme Pontiff consecrated his church by a glorious dedication. It fittingly accorded with his dignity that the heavenly Pontiff should deign to come to consecrate his basilica, since he himself, while he lived, constructed so many beautiful temples, both from stones and from holy souls. May they, therefore, by the aid of their intercession so shut our heaven against harmful clouds, so, I say, fortify our soul against evil spirits at our end, that, safely led out from the present prison-house, it may be brought by their aid to eternal rest. May our Lord [Col. 1049C] Jesus Christ grant this, he who lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

603 HOMILY LXXXIV. SECOND HOMILY FOR THE SAME SAINTS.

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle” (Song 4).

Today shines forth the festive solemnity of the exalted Fathers of the Church, namely blessed Martin and blessed Udalric. We ought to celebrate it with all the greater devotion because we recognize that these same chosen ones of God have been exalted to a more eminent dignity in heaven. For on this day the holy confessor and bishop of Christ, Udalric, released from the bonds of this life, rejoices in eternal life with his King, crowned by him with glorious rewards; he who, adorned inwardly with the excellence of every virtue, also shone by worldly rank through descent from a most noble family. [Col. 1049D] Yet, turning all this nobility to the love of Christ, when he intended to imitate Christ, who was poor, in poverty and to join the fellowship of monks, he was warned by divine revelation to turn his mind from this intention, and it was intimated to him that he would become a bishop. And so it happened. For afterward, raised to the episcopal chair in the city of Augsburg, how great and how eminent he was in the Lord’s eyes is more fully declared by the history of his deeds.

We celebrate Saint Martin’s birthday—that is, the day when he departed from this world to God—not today but [Col. 1050A] at another time; today’s feast, however, recalls his translation, the dedication of his episcopate, or the dedication of his basilica. Therefore, how glorious his life was in the eyes of the supreme Judge he deigned to show in this: that he wished his basilica to be dedicated by no one other than himself. For when the day of its dedication arrived, and no small multitude of bishops, clergy, and other faithful of Christ had assembled, night came; and after all had gone out according to custom, the basilica stood inside bare and, as it were, deserted. A leper, having nowhere to rest, remained in it alone. As he lay awake at midnight, he saw someone adorned with episcopal mitres consecrating that church with an innumerable multitude. When the rite of consecration was completed, the one who appeared to be a bishop came up to him and asked whether he recognized him. When the man said that he did not recognize him at all, he replied: “I am Jesus Christ, who myself have dedicated this temple to my name in honor of my beloved Martin. Therefore, when morning comes, rise and announce to everyone that no one is to lay a hand upon this temple to dedicate it, because I myself have dedicated it.” Again, when the leper declared that people would not believe him, unworthy as he was of such a message, he stripped away his leprous skin from his head to the soles of his feet and healed him. Placing the skin before his feet, he said: “If they do not believe your words, show them this sign.” Then, when morning came, the man rose quickly and related to the bishops and the rest of the multitude everything [Col. 1050C] he had seen. On hearing it, all glorified God and did not dare consecrate the church, knowing it had been dedicated in so remarkable a manner. It is also reported that no one presumes to enter that basilica on this night to serve God, because it has been revealed to some that the supreme Pontiff who consecrated it is openly present there with his angels.

Since this day shines with special eminence, exalted by these three feasts of his, all Christ’s faithful ought deservedly to extol it with the highest proclamation of praise—those who embrace and love with special affection of heart the man of special glory, blessed Martin. His praise and glory are rightly special, because his life was special and wondrous. For when he had ascended to the summit of ecclesiastical [Col. 1050D] dignity, he sought no glory of earthly rank, but remained with the utmost constancy what he had previously been: for the humility of his person and the plainness of his clothing remained the same. Thus he fulfilled the dignity 605 of a bishop without abandoning the purpose and virtue of a monk.

Truly, to these two Fathers of the Church, the splendid foremost men of the heavenly court, blessed Martin and blessed Udalric, fittingly belongs that praise with which the heavenly Bridegroom, praising each individual member of his bride, says among other things: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.” If we wish to understand these breasts simply, what usefulness, I ask, or what excellence suitable to these blessed men can we find in them? But if we pursue this meaning by subtle inquiry, we recognize that two breasts of rejoicing and compassion, by which these saints nourished all the children of the Church whom they themselves begot for Christ through words of teaching and examples of life, may fittingly be compared with two fawns of a gazelle. Those whom they saw steadfast in the Catholic faith and intent on good works they nourished with the left breast of rejoicing, encouraging them; but to those who suffered some tribulation or distress, they offered the milk of consolation from the right breast of compassion.

Every prelate chosen by God ought likewise to feed his subjects with these two breasts: namely, as the life of each individual requires, he should administer to each the nourishment of his teaching. Hence Paul says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15). He rejoices with those who rejoice when he congratulates those whom he sees cheerful in good works and encourages them to advance to better things. He is said to weep with those who weep when he compassionately consoles someone made fainthearted and crushed by some temptation.

There are also two other breasts by which every blessed soul ought to nourish itself: the left, of good action, and the right, of continual contemplation. But what are these breasts said to be like? “Like two,” he says, “twin fawns of a gazelle.” The fawn is swift, while the gazelle is keen-sighted; for every elect person ought to possess these two things: swiftness in good action and keenness of sight in guarding good action. For while doing good works, one must examine and attend with the keen gaze of the heart, lest there be anything impure in one’s action that might offend the eyes of the supreme Inspector. These two fawns of a gazelle are also twins, because good action is not without interior contemplation of the heart, nor is contemplation without the outward good action of the body. By the twins we may also understand the twofold love of God and neighbor. For these are called twins because they are born together in one birth; likewise the twofold love of God and neighbor is mutually joined by the indissoluble bond of kinship. But where, or what kind of pasture, do these two fawns seek?

“They feed,” he says, “among the lilies.” By the lilies among which the fawns feed, manifold virtues may be understood. Note that he calls them not one lily but, as it were, many lilies, because a single virtue is insufficient for the faithful soul: it always advances from virtue to virtue, seeking nourishment for itself. We observe three things in the lily that provide delightful nourishment for these two fawns: it does not grow tall; it is very white; but the little flower standing in its midst has a golden color. In the lily’s low growth is understood perfect humility; in its whiteness, true chastity; and in its little flower, which displays a golden color, pure and eminent charity. These three are indeed very necessary for good action and continual contemplation: through humility one guards oneself lest one lose, through the glory of human favor or through pride, the good one has done; through chastity one fortifies the heart in which one desires to contemplate the supreme Author; and one displays the purity of charity in all words and deeds. Whoever, being a blessed person, possesses all these things offers from himself a sweet fragrance like a lily; those who see it are delighted and begin to imitate his example. And indeed with blessed Paul he can say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15). It follows:

“Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” There are two days in which and through which the whole span of our life passes; a third has not yet come but is still to come: namely, the day that inspires and the day that gives breathing-space; the third, not yet come, is called the day that breathes forth. For when a visitation sent from the Most High has illuminated the human heart, then it may truly be called the day that inspires, because the person, recognizing the darkness of ignorance, begins to turn to the true light. But because after conversion one is often overwhelmed by various temptations, it is necessary that the day that gives breathing-space should arise in the heart, lest, wholly blinded by the darkness of temptations, one be plunged into the abyss of despair. Therefore, if these two days have shone upon anyone, the third day that breathes forth—that is, the day of eternity—will without doubt shine upon that person, in which he will see God face to face. Thus the prophet says: “After two days he will revive us” (Hos. 6:3)—that is, after the day that inspires and [Col. 1052C] the day that gives breathing-space, on the third day, namely the day that breathes forth, he will raise us, and we shall live in his sight; we shall know and follow on, in order to know the Lord.

These saints have already reached that day, having blossomed in this world like a lily through humility, chastity, and charity. Was not blessed Martin a white lily, he who never stained his actions with fleshly pleasure? At his death God made known by certain signs how great the purity of chastity was in which he had lived. For all his flesh shone brighter than glass and whiter than milk, so that the grace of a seven-year-old boy appeared to be visible in him. May blessed Martin, our patron, and blessed Udalric, by the aid of their intercession, bring us [Col. 1052D] to that third day of eternity, that rejoicing with them we may behold the beauty of the supreme Creator. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this, he who lives and is glorified as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

608 HOMILY LXXXV. FIRST HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH.

“Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them—I will show you to whom he is like” (Luke 6).

Since the Only-Begotten of God the Father, taking flesh for our redemption, provided for our salvation in all that he did or taught in the body, we must carefully consider what he has comprehended in a brief saying in the Gospel reading: how each person to be saved ought to come to him through affection, hear through understanding the good things that must be done, [Col. 1053A] and put into effect through works what he has heard.

“Everyone,” he says, “who comes to me.” The beginning of good and holy conduct is that every faithful person, abandoning the appetite for fleshly desires and wholly withdrawing from the tumult of earthly affairs, should come to the Lord through affection; and, recognizing what is the perfect and well-pleasing will of God, should submit the freedom of his own will to the divine will.
