But because it does not suffice for true salvation that a person abandon evils unless he also endeavors, through the hearing of spiritual understanding, to perceive the good works which must be done, he appropriately adds:

“And hears my words and does them.” To hear is, as it were, to obey. For everyone who has turned must diligently incline the ear of the heart to hear the law of God’s commandments; he must devote every care to discover therein how he ought to please God by worthy actions; and, when fully instructed he has learned what good things he ought to do, he must not delay to practice them through the endeavors of holy action. Hence the Apostle says: “For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified” (Rom. 2:13). David the prophet also, beholding in the Spirit the life of the perfect, says: “They are mindful of his commandments, to do them” (Ps. 102:18). “They are mindful of his commandments,” he says, not in order to excel others by greater knowledge through them, but in order always to be ready to do them. But the person who has advanced in the spiritual life in such an order—coming through affection, hearing through understanding, [Col. 1053C] doing through effect—will be exalted one day to what glory of eternal recompense is plainly declared in what follows. For it is added:

“I will show you to whom he is like.” The very Truth who speaks these things fittingly utters words manifest with pure truth: “I will show you,” he says, using the future tense, not the present, as though he said, “I show you.” For all things are reserved uncertain for the future (Eccl. 9:2). For as long as we live in this corruptible flesh, we are so enveloped in the darkness of our mortality that we cannot at all penetrate with the eye of the mind the hidden things of another’s life. Hence it is said through blessed Paul: “For who knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being which is in him?” (1 Cor. 2:11). But when [Col. 1053D] this corruptible body has put on incorruption and this mortal body has put on immortality; when, I say, in that heavenly homeland we are numbered among the glorious lot of God’s children, where in the joyful fellowship of blessed citizens the splendor of eternal vision reveals in turn the hearts of each to all—then indeed it is shown what each person’s life in this world was. For the reward assigned to each by the good Rewarder distinguishes each person’s merit. But to whom is the blessed soul, established then in supreme blessedness, said to be like?

“He is like,” he says, “a man building a house, who dug deep and laid foundations upon the rock.” This man building a house—this singular man, I say—is Christ Jesus, the man who is the one Mediator of God and human beings, the coeternal Wisdom of God the Father, of whom it is said through Solomon: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1). Wisdom built herself a house when the only-begotten Son of God, for the salvation of the human race, prepared for himself a human body within the womb of the undefiled Virgin. Therefore the person who, by Christ’s help, is brought to the joys of everlasting life is made like this man Jesus Christ, the one and the same Son of God and of man, as it is written: “When he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2).

But let us examine more carefully this very saying, “Wisdom has built herself a house,” and strive to understand how it has a special reference to our Lady, the perpetual Virgin Mary, mother of that same Jesus. [Col. 1054B] She indeed was the chosen house, the most noble house, adorned with every beauty, which the eternal Wisdom of God deigned to build and consecrate for itself, so that it might have in her a dwelling perpetually worthy of its majesty. Nor is she inappropriately called that most blessed house. For what is ordinarily done in the construction of any house, the supreme Craftsman performed spiritually in her. First of all, a foundation is laid in a building; afterwards, with two walls on either side, a front is raised above and an end below; finally, when tiles are laid over it, the entire house is roofed.

Thus indeed, thus was the most precious house, namely blessed Mary, built by the supreme Builder—not with a material structure, but a spiritual one; not liable to fall, but firm and stable for ever. [Col. 1054C] If we consider it, she contains all these things fully within herself according to the mystical sense. The foundation which almighty God laid in her was plainly the singular glory of obedience. By this the same Lord of hosts founded and made her stable, suitably adorned; and this obedience she herself—the practiser and teacher of virtues, the mother of the Obedient One who was obedient for us even unto the death of the cross, and mistress of all holy religion—endeavoured to preserve throughout every day of her life, always obeying the divine commandments and showing humble submission in obedience also to her parents and to Joseph her spouse.

Nor should we pass over without examination the statement that he “laid the foundation upon a rock,” since the rock is Christ, upon whom all her works were firmly founded. [Col. 1054D] Hence the Evangelist’s carefully expressed words also apply to her very fittingly: “He dug deep.” And how or when did the everlasting Wisdom of God dig deep in her? Clearly when she, the most chosen of the chosen, was to be consecrated by divine childbirth, and deserved to hear from the archangel Gabriel, sent to her from above, among the sweet words of his angelic greeting—or rather, heavenly embassy—these words: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

For immediately the Holy Spirit came upon her; illumining her by the wondrous manner of his coming, he prepared the bridal chamber of her virginal womb to receive the splendour of the most high Father by overshadowing it with his power. And, rendering her free from every stain of original or actual sin, if any trace even of the faintest blemish adhered to her from the root of natural sin, the spade of that same Holy Spirit cast it out [Col. 1055A] so powerfully that she was wholly holy in body and spirit, wholly clean and chaste, and, so to speak, wholly passing over into God; no contagion of sin whatever remained in her.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] See the preliminary dissertation.]

By the conjunction of the two walls we may understand the outstanding glory of virginity and the special merit of her humility. In these two degrees of virtue the Mother of the Lord of hosts stood far above all mortals. In her shone incomparable beauty of mind and integrity of flesh: her womb was accessible to no carnal intercourse, and [Col. 1055B] her mind could never be penetrated by any spiritual wickedness. Thus she alone, without example, pleased the Most High by the special prerogative of her chastity.

Surpassing all virgins in the purity of innocence, she is the Virgin of virgins. To her praise especially applies what Scripture says, in commendation of the other holy virgins: “No lie was found in their mouth” (Rev. 14:5). Yet although by the singular purity of her life she surpassed all the children of men, she held herself in such low esteem, through most profound humility, that no sinner conscious of many crimes could possibly equal the greatness of her humility by humbling himself for his sins. Therefore, as she was higher than all others, so she was humbler than all others. She thought loftier things of almost everyone else; and she whom none even of the holiest could equal in the magnificence of holiness judged herself, because of her excessive humility, to be lower even than unworthy sinners. [Col. 1055C]

Moreover, adorned with every virtue, she excelled all especially in faith, hope, and charity. These three marks of virtue are to be understood mystically by these three parts: faith by the upper part of the house, hope by the lower part, and charity by the roof. Great indeed, praiseworthy, and admirable was her faith: she believed the angel who announced the new and unheard-of miracle—that, while the glory of virginity remained intact, she would conceive and bear a son without intercourse with a man. [Col. 1055D]

Because she was so strong in firmness of faith, she also remained steady in the perseverance of hope. With her whole being she leaned upon Christ, whom alone she had made the foundation of her hope. And who was such in love for God and neighbour as this singular beloved of the Beloved? The eternal love of the eternal God wholly flooded and possessed her, so that apart from the ineffable sweetness of this inward charity she neither knew nor could desire or love anything in this world. She was likewise most full of love for her neighbour. Always, from the most ardent affection of charity, she desired her neighbours’ salvation; so much so that the most burning desire of her impatient love surpassed the longing of the ancient Fathers, who desired with their whole heart the redemption of the human race. [Col. 1056A]

She continually lamented and afflicted herself with frequent tears and sighs; she grieved so deeply at humankind’s ruin as though she herself had been the cause of that ruin. How unshaken she remained in true and perfect charity is plainly indicated in the Gospel words. For it continues:

“But when a flood arose, the stream dashed against that house, and could not move it.” What, I ask, was this flood? Surely it was those flooding persecutions of diverse sufferings which her most noble Son, her singular Beloved—ever remaining impassible in his divinity—innocently endured in the flesh, without the debt of sin, in the flesh assumed from her virginal body. Therefore, when this flood occurred, the stream dashed against that house: that is, the stream of the tribulations of her only Son struck powerfully against the house of her heart. Whatever adversity or hardship he bore in this misery of mortality inflicted an incurable wound of pain upon the virginal breast of his compassionate mother. [Col. 1056B]

This flood of troubles began from the very beginning, when this Son of singular innocence wailed in the cradle. For while he was still of tender age, she fled with him into Egypt from the face of Herod, who sought to kill him; and with the same little child she returned again to her own land after Herod’s death. When, however, he reached manhood and began to undertake the office of preaching, she suffered daily with her Son and in her Son, seeing how many reproaches of the envious, [Col. 1056C] how many blasphemies of the impious he endured, and how he bore Jewish slanders, plots, and accusations.

But then the greatest flood of pain inundated her, when such a Son was seized and maltreated by wicked Jews: mocked, spat upon by them, struck with blows, crowned with thorns, scourged, and led through the streets of Jerusalem as a spectacle and object of public derision, like a most wicked thief and robber. At last a sword pierced her soul when, as the hour of his Passion approached, she saw that same Son and her Redeemer undergo the torture of the cross, be fastened with nails, be given gall and vinegar at the point of death, [Col. 1056D] be pierced with a soldier’s lance, be reckoned among criminals, and thus, according to human estimation, miserably end his life in the most shameful death.

She was present as a spectator of such great evils, standing beside his cross, upon which he hung dead before her eyes. Yet none of these things could move her so that she should be stirred to anger against those who perpetrated so great a crime upon her innocent Son, seek vengeance from them, or fall into hatred or envy of them. It was indeed the desire of maternal compassion that, if it were possible, such a Son should not die. But she preferred the divine will to this maternal feeling, choosing rather to desire the salvation of the human race and unwilling that the purpose of God [Col. 1057A] the Father should be turned aside—he who had ordained that the whole world should be saved through Christ’s death.

For when, standing beside the cross of her most beloved Son, she heard his words—when he was dying and, as it were, drawing his final breath: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34)—she too prayed with him as he prayed, that God might not charge the sin against them but might instead, in merciful kindness, pardon those who had gone astray. And whence came such kindness in her, such ineffable compassion? For she was founded upon the rock. Truly she was founded upon the firm rock, that is, Christ, so that so great a flood of tribulations could in no way move her or bend her to impatience of heart or enmity.

Let us also imitate this most compassionate Lady of ours. Assisted by her glorious merits and by the virtues already described, through which we have learned that she was especially pleasing to the Lord, let us endeavour to imitate her according to our measure, as far as we can. [Col. 1057B] Let us lay the foundation upon the rock, remembering to place whatever good we do upon the rock which is Christ, so that the whole intention of our action may proceed from love of God alone and, rooted and founded in that love, may always remain stable and unshaken.

The foundation, as we said above, is obedience to the heavenly commands and to those under whose rule we have undertaken service for Christ’s sake. We ought to observe this approved obedience with devout care, so that, always mindful of all that God has commanded, we may always obey his commands as is fitting. We must also lay ourselves beneath our superiors in devoted submission [Col. 1057C] and obey their commands not slowly or grudgingly, but with a cheerful and willing mind. For, according to the teaching of our father Benedict, the obedience which is pleasing to men and acceptable to God is that which is performed in a good spirit, without contradiction or murmuring. If we find that we have observed the commitment of this obedience with any less than due reverence, let us hasten to wipe it away before the eyes of the divine majesty by worthy penitence and satisfaction.

Having laid such a firm foundation of worthy obedience, let us also dig deep. And what, I ask, can the image of digging express more fittingly than a worthy and perfect confession of sins? For one who digs deep opens the ground from above by repeated blows and throws out by digging the earth lying beneath. Let us likewise dig deep, scrutinising the depths of our thoughts by careful examination and digging out from the bottom of our heart whatever hidden defilement has been heaped up in it, so that we may disclose by humble confession whatever foul thing lies concealed within our conscience. [Col. 1057D]

Let us also dig deep in another way: continually piercing the ground of our mind with the sharp goad of compunction, that we may taste a little how sweet the Lord is and daily strive, in the illumination of our spirit, to attain something—however briefly—of his sweetness; so that, having in some measure received that grace, we may be somehow refreshed amid the frailty of the present life.

[Col. 1058A] Therefore, in order that we may raise within ourselves the two walls, namely chastity and humility, let us strive to fulfil spiritually the office of a builder. Anyone who builds or constructs a wall does not cease to smooth wood or stone by cutting away every superfluity until he renders it fit for the structure of the building. So let us, in building the house of our body and soul, cut away every superfluity from our flesh and spirit, so that we may find, without reproach, a place suited to our merits in the building of the eternal city, where stones polished by hammering and pressure are fitted into their places. [Col. 1058B]

For here the souls of the elect are beaten and polished by many tribulations, in order that in that heavenly building they may be fitted together without any blow. Therefore, when unlawful delight strikes within the mind, let us restrain the tongue with every care, lest what defiles the mind inwardly through wicked desires break out externally in speech. For if almighty God sees that we guard ourselves outwardly with such watchful circumspection, he himself, being compassionate, will be present as a helper to our efforts and will grant us to overcome the evil desire to which we inwardly yield through weakness.

Likewise, when our heart swells with the vice of pride, let us set a guard upon our mouth, lest proud speech come forth from it; for by this means, divine grace following us, we shall overcome inwardly the vice that attacks us, namely pride.

Thus fortified, as it were, by the two walls of chastity and humility, let us diligently ensure that we have within ourselves faith, hope, and charity, the three most eminent virtues. [Col. 1058C] We may understand them by these three parts: faith by the front part of the house, hope by the lower part, and charity by the roof. Let us therefore build the front part, so that we may steadfastly preserve until death the sacrament of the Catholic faith which we received in baptism. Confessing our Lord Jesus Christ as true God and true man, namely our Creator and Redeemer, let us faithfully believe without any doubt all that has been told us concerning him.

Let us also strive to fulfil the vow of faith which, having entered upon the path of spiritual life, we pledged to God in holy conduct; and let us exercise ourselves in the good works which we have rightly vowed. [Col. 1058D] Let us build the lower part, so that we may place the certainty of our hope in confidence in divine mercy, and, lest we ever fall into the danger of despair, let us always trust in that mercy itself.

When these two parts have been built, let us place the roof above them, by which we appropriately understand the virtue of charity. For just as the roof by which a house is normally covered is twofold, so charity must be twofold: love of God and love of neighbour. Let us strive above all to possess this twofold love within ourselves, according to the Apostle’s admonition: “Above all, maintaining continual mutual charity among yourselves” (1 Pet. 4:8), so that we may love God and our neighbour with all the affections of our heart, [Col. 1059A] preferring divine love to all earthly and transitory things, and preserving among ourselves the sweetness of brotherly charity.

When we are adorned with such great and splendid merits of virtue, the words of the Gospel reading are truly fulfilled in us: “But when a flood arose, the stream dashed against that house, and could not move it, for it was founded upon the rock.” This flood is the manifold tribulations which often meet us in the misery of this pilgrimage. When the storm of this flood arises, the stream dashes against that house [Col. 1060A], because some adversity of the present life, or an injury inflicted by a neighbour, often strikes the house of our heart with such a heavy onset of temptation that we think we cannot bear it with equanimity.

But because our mind is founded upon the rock, that is, Christ, no flood of tribulation will be able to move us from the state of our uprightness, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1059]

HOMILIES OF THE VENERABLE GODEFRID, ABBOT OF ADMONT, ON VARIOUS PASSAGES OF SCRIPTURE.

617 HOMILY I. FIRST HOMILY ON GENESIS, CHAPTER 24.

[Col. 1059B]

“Abraham said to the elder servant of his household, who was in charge of all that he possessed: ‘Put your hand under my thigh, that I may adjure you,’” etc. (Gen. 24).

The present narrative concerning Rebecca which is set forth for us in Holy Scripture, if it could be investigated with subtle understanding, would be found full of the mystical moral sense. But even if in this narrative nothing else could be found than what the bare letter states, it ought nevertheless to be loved and embraced by us with inward affection. For this Rebecca of whom the narrative speaks was, so to say, a certain line or material of that blessed [Col. 1059C] seed from which the Lord Jesus willed to assume the nature of our mortality. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel, “Salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). The Psalmist also declares concerning the same matter: “From Zion is the splendour of his beauty” (Ps. 49:2).

Therefore, by assuming flesh from this people, the Son of God worked salvation in the midst of the earth. For this reason that race is worthy of reverence and love: because he chose to assume flesh from them, to live among them, to be born in their land, to die and be buried there, and finally to ascend into heaven. But let us see what mystery this reading itself contains; and, if we cannot comprehend everything in a mystical sense, let us at least endeavour to turn some things to our edification, attending to the Lord’s command spoken thus in the Law: [Col. 1059D] “If you enter your friend’s field of grain, you may pluck ears and rub them in your hand, but you shall not reap with a sickle” (Deut. 23:25).

Our friend is almighty God, whose crop is Holy Scripture. He himself, the Word of the eternal Father, cultivated and sowed it. Having entered this crop, this Holy Scripture, we ought to rub in our hands the ears of this crop: that is, by mystical understanding to draw out the sense hidden within it. But where we cannot rub in our hands the sacred meaning covered by the letter, there too we are forbidden by the Lord to reap with a sickle, but must leave what is covered to the Holy Spirit. To reap with a sickle is to judge rashly that Holy Scripture, divinely promulgated, is vile and worthless, and to savour it carnally; the Law of the Lord forbids us to do all these things. [Col. 1060B]

Therefore, entering the crop of our friend according to the command, namely this reading, let us break off for ourselves the ears which we can rub; but let us not judge or regard as worthless the remaining things to which our understanding does not reach. Thus Holy Scripture says:

“Abraham said to the elder servant of his household, who was in charge of all that he possessed.” In the figure of the patriarch Abraham, God the Father can be signified; his house is the holy Church. The elder servant of that house is any prelate called by God’s ordering to the summit of governance: especially the pope, established in the highest place, whom other bishops, archbishops, and other eminent teachers appointed by God over the holy Church support. But in this servant we may more fittingly understand the faithful superior of any holy and spiritual community. He is well said to preside over all that his Lord possesses when he presides over good and blessed persons. To this faithful servant, appointed over all that his Lord possesses, the true Abraham, the almighty Father, says: [Col. 1060C]

“Put your hand under my thigh, that I may adjure you by the God of heaven and earth, that you do not take a wife for my son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell.” In Abraham’s thigh the Lord Jesus Christ is to be understood. For just as the seed of generation proceeds from a man’s thigh, from which children are born, so the Son of God is begotten from the heart of God the Father, as he himself says through the Psalmist: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3). What he says, “From the womb I begot you,” is the same as if he had said, “From the thigh I begot you.” [Col. 1060D] For just as he said, “From the womb I begot you,” so, if he had wished to say it, he could certainly have said fittingly, “From my thigh I begot you.”

By the hand placed beneath Abraham’s thigh is expressed the activity of the good prelate, which God the Father commands to be placed beneath Christ. Why is this? “That I may adjure you,” he says, “by the God of heaven and earth.” What is this adjuration by which a faithful servant, appointed over all that his Lord possesses, is adjured by God, except the very prelacy to which he is assumed? It is a great adjuration for him, a prelacy in which he is commanded to live in such a way that he does not destroy by the example of his life what he teaches in words. It follows:

“That you do not take a wife for my son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell.” Because in this world good and evil are together, corrupt Christians are rightly understood by the daughters of Canaan. The Lord says that he dwells among them, not in them, precisely because they have received the Christian faith and name, though they contradict it by their morals and works. [Col. 1061A] In the good and blessed, predestined to eternal life, the Lord says that he dwells. Among those persons—that is, among the corrupt—he dwells as if unwillingly; but in these, namely the blessed souls, he dwells, feeds, and delights himself joyfully.

Therefore, the good prelate is commanded by God the Father as he adjures him not to take for his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, a lawful wife from the daughters of Canaan—that is, from corrupt and worldly people. A concubine or a handmaid may indeed be taken from such persons, but a lawful wife, who passes into the lawful marriage of the Son of God, is not to be sought among them. But let us now see where that blessed soul is to be sought which deserves the indissoluble union of the Son of God, and in what place it is to be found.

“But you shall go to my land and my kindred, and from there take a wife for my son Isaac.” The land and kindred of the Lord are those blessed people who, living the spiritual life, daily or on certain appointed days feed upon the body and blood of the crucified Lord. By communicating in his body, they pass into Christ and become his blood-relations. Good prelates ought to go to these people, who are thus the Lord’s land and kindred, and from there invite blessed souls to the marriage of the true [Col. 1061D] Isaac, the Son of God.

And the Son of God is rightly understood by Isaac, whose name means “laughter,” because he is the true and eternal laughter, who grants full and perfect joy to blessed souls, both to those now abiding in eternity and to those still dwelling in exile. It follows:

621 “The servant answered: ‘If the woman should not be willing to come with me into this land, must I bring your son back to the place from which you departed?’” By the place from which Abraham departed are signified the hearts of sinners, the hearts of evil persons, from which the Lord has departed. It is as if the good prelate, consulting God concerning what he has heard, were to say: “If those to whose salvation you sent me do not wish to come through the word of my exhortation to the marriage of your Son, must I bring [Col. 1062A] your Son—namely the sweetness of your Word—back to the hearts of those who have despised you, from whom you have departed, who do not follow you, who do not receive the word of God?” This is the prelate’s question, to which the Lord then answers, as follows.

Abraham answered him: “Take care never to bring my son back there.” This is as though he said: “Take diligent care that you do not at any time bring my Son, the sweetness of my word, back to those who are there, who are far from my salvation and love. But if once you lead him there—as it often happens through habit—that you insert the sweetness of my word into your sermons, take care that you do not wish to bring him there again and again. For you will not find in them the spirit of love, the spirit of freedom, because I have departed from them.” It follows:

“So he took ten camels from the herd of his lord and departed, carrying with him some of all his lord’s goods.” By the ten camels may be understood the ten inner and outer senses of a person, which the prelate takes from his lord’s herd when he gathers all his inward and outward senses to himself. He also takes with him the ten commandments of the Law, and he departed carrying with him some of all his lord’s goods. What, I ask, are all his lord’s goods? All his lord’s goods are all Scripture; and because he cannot carry all of it with him—for human understanding is insufficient for this—he carries at least some things from all these goods, perhaps useful for the benefit of those to whom he goes. [Col. 1062B]

“And he came to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.” Mesopotamia means “exalted calling.” What is signified by this city called an exalted calling, if not the practice of spiritual life? It is very fittingly called an exalted calling, because those who live in it, called by God and lifted from earthly to heavenly things, are separated from the common life of secular people. [Col. 1062C]

“And he made the camels lie down outside the town beside a well of water in the evening, at the time when women usually go out to draw water.” By the camels, as we said above, are to be understood the senses of a person; by the well of water, Holy Scripture or the power of inward compunction may be understood. Therefore, when the faithful servant—any good prelate—begins, in the order we have described, to go to Mesopotamia, that is, to reach the congregation of the faithful called to eternal life, it is necessary that he make his camels, namely his inward and outward senses, rest beside the well of Holy Scripture or beside the well of inward compunction.

But this lying down must take place outside the town in the evening. For if he wishes to serve his neighbours’ good, so that he may be able to bring forth matters conducive to his subjects’ advancement, he must do so outside the town, that is, outside the advantage of his own flesh; and in the evening, in the deep humility of his heart. “At the time,” it says, “when women usually go out to draw water.” The time when women usually go out to draw water is that time when souls, softened by grace, have begun to prepare their hearts to receive the word of God with sweetness and to draw from the water of the word of God that by which they may be refreshed and renewed. [Col. 1062D]

Of this time Solomon says: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3:7). The time for silence is clearly when the prelate perceives and judges that it would be fruitless to go out to his subjects with words of exhortation. But the time for speaking returns when he is convinced and judges it fruitful to dispense the streams of teaching to his subjects. Knowing that at this time the teacher is expected by the disciples, he is greatly concerned and anxiously reflects, so that, his own senses restored by inward repose, he may receive from God something with which he may sweetly and fruitfully refresh those who desire and await him. In such concern he often breaks forth in his prayer into the words of this servant, saying: [Col. 1063A]

“Lord God of my lord Abraham, meet me, I pray, today, and show mercy to my lord Abraham.” It is as though he says: “Lord my God, meet me, I pray, today, because I am now acting as your envoy for you. Meet me, that in the dispensing of your word entrusted to me I may be able to offer you some fruit of salvation. Show mercy to me also, going before me with blessings of sweetness, by preparing their hearts for yourself and for your words.

“Behold, I stand near the fountain of water, and the daughters of the inhabitants of this city will come out to draw water.” The good prelate stands near the fountain of water when he offers the streams of teaching to his hearers. But the daughters of the inhabitants of that city come out to draw water when blessed souls, daughters of that congregation, receive with eager and most longing hearts the counsels pertaining to their salvation. [Col. 1063B]

“Therefore let the maiden to whom I say, ‘Lower your jar that I may drink,’ and who answers, ‘Drink, and I will give your camels drink also,’ be the one whom you have prepared for your servant Isaac; and by this I shall understand that you have shown mercy to my lord.”

At this point it should briefly be noted, according to the letter, how kindly Rebecca answered this servant when he asked her to give him a drink. He prayed only to hear such an answer: “Drink.” But she graciously added: “Drink, my lord.” Therefore in this maiden may be understood the blessed soul from whom the good prelate asks for drink when, in the time of preaching, he addresses her with heavenly words. But what, I ask, is the thirst which prelates have, that they ask to be given drink? [Col. 1063C]

Their thirst is truly like the thirst of our Redeemer, hanging on the cross for our salvation, when, as death drew near, he said upon the cross: “I thirst.” Do we suppose that this thirst was bodily? No: standing at the point of death, he thirsted for the salvation of the human race. So too good prelates thirst for the salvation of their subjects; and their subjects refresh them with wholesome drink when they find in them the spirit of love.

“And I will give your camels drink.” By the camels, as we said above, the senses of a person can be understood. Thus it is as though the blessed soul, with kindly heart giving thanks in the secrecy of her heart to her teacher and master, answers in these words: “Since, through your teaching, I have received counsels of everlasting salvation, from this time I will give drink to your camels—that is, I will give the drink of joy to your senses—so that by my words and deeds I may make you understand what fruit my soul has received from the words of your teaching.” [Col. 1063D]

But if we wish to apply these words to Christ, so that the blessed soul may use these words to the Lord, we may rightly say: “These camels, namely my senses, once deformed and twisted through sins, I will now make yours, O Lord, by this means: I will wash away my past sins by the lamentations of tears and penitence.” Therefore whatever soul, with God’s help, has advanced in its life according to such an order, that soul, I say, is the one of whom it may be said to God: “For this is she whom you have prepared for your servant Isaac”: “whom you, O Lord, have so adorned and prepared by the merit of her life that she might be worthy to be joined perpetually in marriage to your Son.” [Col. 1064A]

625 HOMILY II. FIRST HOMILY ON THE FIVE BOOKS OF MOSES, AND THE BOOKS OF JOSHUA AND JUDGES.

On the holy days of fasting, bodily delights are therefore withdrawn from the body, so that while the flesh is worn down by fasts and other labours, the mind may be raised more ardently in love and desire for God and enlarged in heavenly and spiritual goods. Hence on these sacred days the five books of Moses, with the two additional books of Joshua and Judges, are read throughout the whole Church, so that the spiritual understanding and spiritual delights hidden in these books may pass into the nourishment and strengthening of every blessed soul. [Col. 1064B]

Therefore, if a diligent and watchful investigator knows how to examine the order of these books, the order and progress of our life are most rightly expressed in them. First in order is placed the book of Genesis; second, Exodus; third, Leviticus; fourth, the book of Numbers; fifth, Deuteronomy; sixth, Joshua; seventh, Judges. If these seven books are properly examined according to the mystical understanding, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are most suitably fitted to them.

In the book of Genesis, whose name means “generation,” is fittingly figured that first generation of our salvation which divine mercy wonderfully and mercifully works, through the spirit of fear, in the heart of the person whom it intends to save. [Col. 1064C] But let us now see how a person is spiritually generated by God. When someone living in a carnal manner begins to consider beforehand what punishment and what judgement awaits him if he is found in so carnal a life, the spirit of the fear of the Lord inwardly impelling and working upon him causes him to resolve to leave this most wretched and unstable life as quickly as possible.

Thus, inwardly generated through the spirit of the fear of the Lord, he finally comes to Exodus, which is placed second and also means “departure.” He rightly arrives there when, departing from sins and vices, putting an end to worldly desires, he passes to a spiritual way of life. Therefore it is fitting that Exodus writes of the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, of their passage through the Red Sea, and of the manna which the Lord rained down from heaven for them to eat. [Col. 1064D]

Every person who leaves the world should therefore have a passage through the Red Sea, so that by bitter repentance and the blessed flood of tears the enemies of his soul, namely sins, may be utterly drowned. Then, once those enemies have been overwhelmed in the penitence and pain of the embittered heart, it remains for them to await from God the manna of sweetness, by whose taste they may be inwardly renewed, fed, and sweetly refreshed in the inner person.

Yet it must not be passed over that the Lord Himself went before those same Israelites by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire. Thus also the Lord goes before those who are under cloistered discipline: by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire. He goes before them in a pillar of cloud because, while excessive heat and the sun beat upon all lovers of this world, the Lord graciously protects those dwelling in the monastery, as though they rested beneath the shade of a pillar of cloud. And He goes before them in a pillar of fire by night because, while all who make use of this world—even the mightiest rulers—sleep, a lamp of light shines in the darkness in every dwelling occupied by God’s servants, whether in the oratory or in the dormitory. Thus the Lord is the guide of their journey not only in spiritual matters but also in bodily and outward things.

Therefore, in such an exodus from Egypt as we have described, what else does a person recognize as at work in himself than the Spirit of God’s mercy, when he begins to recall with how great a mercy the Lord has borne with his sins, and again with how great a mercy He has brought him forth—after patiently enduring him for a long time in those same sins. [Col. 1065B–C]

A person, as it were made inwardly one with the Lord by consideration of this mercy, at last ascends to the book of Leviticus, when he is chosen and taken up for God’s service. For *Levi* means “taken up”; by this name are understood all who, by God’s grace, are taken up out of the common life of secular people. For them too this book of Leviticus is written, in which due provision is made concerning sacrifices to be offered to God. In it are distinguished victims offered to the Lord for sins; likewise, certain whole burnt offerings sacrificed in thanksgiving; and certain peace offerings consecrated to God when offered for peace—so that each person may find the sacrifice appointed for whatever need he has, provided that he has deserved to be enlightened by God with the Spirit of knowledge.

For in this book the Spirit of knowledge is necessary, through whose knowledge, with God’s mercy helping, one may know how to make satisfaction to God for one’s sins. This book, therefore, as we have said, chiefly concerns those who have passed from the tumult of secular life to the quiet of monastic discipline, serving God night and day in the tabernacle—that is, in the monastery—as true Levites. For the Lawgiver—or rather God through the Lawgiver—perceiving that those who are thus taken up and separated from secular noise, although subject to the strictness of monastic life, nevertheless cannot pass beyond the boundary of this fleeting life without the contagion of sin—for in this body of mortality, not to sin is altogether impossible even for the Lord’s most chosen people—instituted in this book of Leviticus sacrifices fit for washing away daily sins.

We therefore, who formerly were in Genesis while we lived according to earthly and carnal generation, and who afterwards passed to Exodus when we departed from sins and from the tumult of worldly affairs, are now in Leviticus. [Col. 1065C–1066A]

We must therefore pass beyond Leviticus, in which we now are, so as to arrive at the book of Numbers. In the book of Numbers those who are to fight in battle are arranged and numbered: who and what manner of men they are who are to advance equipped for combat; in what place they are to pitch their tents according to their companies; who are to fight in the first rank and who in the last. What else is indicated to us by these companies of combatants numbered for war than that unending battle which will endure in the elect until the end of the age, in which they must fight both against the devil and against the vices of the flesh resisting the spirit?

In this struggle the Spirit of fortitude is necessary, by whose strengthening they may be able to resist the vices propagated by the flesh, so that, having at last conquered their enemies, they may deserve to be numbered in the lot of God’s children, both in heaven and on earth.

But after they have been counted among God’s children and their lot has fallen among the saints and elect, then they rightly arrive at the book of Deuteronomy, which is placed fifth. For *Deuteronomy* means “second law.” The first law is the law of fear; the second law is the law of love and liberty. By the law of fear people are restrained from sins and vices and exercised in virtues through the performance of the commandment. But in the second law, which is the law of love, counsel is added to the commandment, so that one who has already fulfilled the commandment may be helped by the Spirit of counsel and advance to a higher degree of merit. [Col. 1066B–C]

But let us see what a commandment is and what counsel is. A commandment is that which is commanded to a person without any qualification whatever, and which it is altogether unlawful to transgress, such as that commandment of the Law: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22:37). This must be fulfilled precisely as it is commanded.

Counsel, however, is that by which a person is truly advised in such a way that, if he does not act upon it, it is not imputed to him; but if he follows the counsel, he is more magnificently praised and crowned. Such are virginity preserved undefiled for God’s sake and contempt for the world. These are not commanded, but are proposed by way of counsel only to those who can receive them. Hence the Apostle Paul said: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord; but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:25).

These things, then, and things like them, are wrought in a person by the Spirit of counsel. Ascending through it from the law of fear to the law of love, he arrives at the point where he lives no longer by the restraint of commandment, but by the guidance of the Spirit of counsel through the devotion of his mind. [Col. 1066D–1067A]

Thus, living for a time in Deuteronomy—that is, in the second law of love and liberty—he will come to the sixth book, Joshua. *Joshua* means “Saviour.” And rightly, through the book of Joshua the true salvation of a person is prefigured. In this book of Joshua, that is, of true salvation, the Spirit of understanding is at work. For in true salvation true understanding is received from God.

Understanding, however, is not acquired except through true purity of heart, because the light of the heart is perfect purity of mind, through which one attains understanding, as the Lord Himself declares in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). And purity of heart is fittingly signified in the book of Joshua, who, as is read in that same book, is said to have circumcised the children of Israel a second time. The first circumcision occurs when a person is outwardly cut off from perverse and dead works. The second circumcision occurs inwardly, when the heart is cleansed from impure and harmful thoughts. [Col. 1067A–B]

After the book of Joshua, the book of Judges follows very suitably, because after true salvation and true understanding acquired through purity of heart, a person will doubtless be able to exercise just judgment within himself. And if, by God’s ordinance, it should happen that he is raised higher and assumed to leadership, he will be able, through purity of heart, to execute the judgment of justice and equity not only in himself but also among those subject to him.

For it is exceedingly dangerous for anyone to be promoted and taken up to a position of government before he has deserved to be exalted by God through true purity of heart. But one who has advanced in his life in the order described, and has ascended through purity of heart to understanding, may quite worthily become a superior and judge of souls. In such leadership and judgment he needs to be filled by God with the Spirit of wisdom, through which, inwardly affected and enlightened, he knows wisely how to discern just judgment. [Col. 1067B–C]

Having briefly set forth this order of the books, let us return to our Leviticus, written for us; and whatever we can investigate concerning sacrifices offered to God, let us turn it to the use of our edification. Thus the Lawgiver says among other things:

> “If a ruler shall sin and shall do one thing out of many through ignorance, which is forbidden by the law of the Lord, and afterwards understand it, he shall offer to the Lord as a victim an unblemished he-goat from the goats, and shall lay his hand upon its head” (Lev. 4:22).

In this ruler may be understood every superior, who, living as a ruler, knows how to preside over both his own people and his subjects by word and example. Yet every faithful person may also be signified by this ruler. Although he may be poor and obscure by the standards of worldly birth, if he has stood nobly on the summit of virtues, he may without doubt truly be numbered among the princes of God in heaven. For who are the princes of God except the apostles, martyrs, and other saints? Among them everyone will deserve to be numbered who has followed God in a spiritual life, however lowly and contemptible he may appear in this world. [Col. 1067D–1068A]

But, alas, it sometimes happens that one who is such a prince before the Lord falls headlong into sin; for, as the Psalmist declares, “No living person shall be justified in the sight of God” (Ps. 142:2). What, then, or what kind of sin is this which is committed by such a ruler? “And he shall do,” it says, “one thing out of many.”

What is this “one” except the human heart united to God through charity? For the heart, joined and bound to God in the sweet union of love, is God’s bridal chamber, in which bridegroom and bride—those two beloved ones—meet in one love. In this one thing, which is the human heart, those two, God and the soul, ought to delight one another so amicably and intimately that no stranger should be allowed to share in this mutual knowledge and no alien love be mingled with this affection. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “He who is joined to God is made one spirit with Him” (1 Cor. 6:17).

But, alas, the grievous thing frequently happens that a person makes this one thing into many. This indeed occurs when he divides into many things his heart, which ought to be one and united and bound to the love of God alone, and causes it to sin in many ways. When that heart, which ought to be one, begins to entertain many things, now admitting an unrighteous love, now introducing from another source an unprofitable sorrow, now considering how to escape by prudent circumspection whatever troubles may arise, now exerting great effort to establish an unrighteous love—and thus divided amid prosperity and adversity, at one time accompanying hatred, at another pursuing envy. [Col. 1068A–C]

But whence comes this committing of such a sin and this division in what is one? “Through ignorance,” it says. Here we understand ignorance as weakness. For some sin knowingly and yet, as it were, do not know that they sin, while their minds are darkened by such great delight in sin and obscured by such great desire for sin that for the time being they cannot know what they have done against God. Although they know in their understanding, they are unable to know through the will and desire of sin; and in such ignorance they often sin grievously. It follows:

> “Which is forbidden by the law of the Lord.”

What, then, is the law of the Lord? Or what does that law forbid? The law of the Lord is the law of charity, of which the Psalmist says: “The law of the Lord is undefiled” (Ps. 18:8). Concerning this charity the Lord again says in the Gospel: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:11).

Therefore, since the law of the Lord is the law of charity, that law commands good and righteous love and forbids unrighteous love. Whoever, then, acts against this law of charity, so that he divides through unrighteous love and other sins that one thing which ought to exist in one love, making many out of one, has committed the sin forbidden by the law of the Lord. But how one who commits such a sin should make satisfaction to the Lord is immediately added:

> “And afterwards,” it says, “when he has understood his sin, he shall offer to the Lord as a victim an unblemished he-goat from the goats.” [Col. 1068C–1069A]

After committing sin, a person commonly understands his sin when, after sin, he returns to conscience and, inwardly inspired through God’s mercy, recognizes his iniquity. He also understands his sin when, inwardly admonished through the words of outward teaching, he begins to recognize his iniquity. But after he has thus understood his sin, what must he do? Let him offer an unblemished he-goat from the goats.

In the he-goat, which is a foul-smelling animal, we may understand our spirit; but sins are signified by the she-goats, as the Lord Himself testifies in the Gospel, saying: “He shall place the sheep on His right hand, but the goats on His left” (Matt. 25:33), signifying sinners by the kids, which are from the goats. We therefore offer the Lord a he-goat from the goats when we acknowledge that our spirit stinks with sins. For nothing is as foul-smelling before the Lord as sins. But this he-goat is commanded to be offered unblemished; we remove its blemish when we wash away our sins by inward repentance. [Col. 1069A–B]

> “And he shall lay his hand upon its head.”

By the hand, action is signified; by the head, intention. We therefore place our hand upon the head of our victim when we establish good works upon the foundation of good intention. It follows:

> “And when he has sacrificed it in the place where the whole burnt offering is customarily slain before the Lord, because it is for sin, the priest shall dip his finger in the blood of the victim for sin, touching the horns of the altar of whole burnt offering, and pouring the rest upon its base. But he shall burn the fat above, as is customary in peace offerings; and he shall pray for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.”

The place where the whole burnt offering is customarily slain is the human heart, in which he sacrifices the he-goat—that is, his spirit—to God when, as we have said, he recognizes that his spirit stinks with sins. When the he-goat has thus been sacrificed, the priest—that is, his spirit—shall dip his finger in the blood of the victim. For then a person’s spirit takes up its discernment, signified by the finger, and dips this discernment in the blood of the victim, which is his sins.

For he distinguishes between greater and lesser sins; between will and consent; between desires and deeds; between the chance onset of a thought and pleasure. He further distinguishes, among greater sins, whether he has committed them rarely or often. He distinguishes between will and consent: whether the will was of such a sort that, were an opportunity for sin given, it would, with consent plunging headlong, lapse into sinful deeds. He distinguishes between thoughts and pleasures: whether pleasure followed the thought of sin, or whether the thought alone, without pleasure, merely touched the heart with a light and wandering incursion.

Therefore, after he has dipped his finger in the blood of the victim—after he has discerned his sins as we have said—he shall at last touch the horns of the altar. The horns of the altar are the two extremities on the altar, and by these two extremities may be signified knowledge of God and knowledge of oneself. [Col. 1069B–D]

In knowledge of God, each person touches one horn of the altar when he devoutly recalls in his heart how many blessings he has received from the hand of his Creator; how patiently the Almighty has borne his sins when He might have punished them; and how graciously He has brought him from the whirlpool of this world, without the disgrace of sin, to the haven of monastic quiet, while leaving in the world many others better than himself and of greater merit. By this recollection of God’s most gracious mercy, having inwardly touched the knowledge of God, he bursts into tears, sweetly afflicts himself with weeping, and steadfastly raises himself to render thanksgiving and proclamations of praise to his Creator.

He then touches the other horn of the altar in knowledge of himself, when he remembers the burden of his sins—what and how great were the sins he committed, how grievously he offended against God—and in this recollection begins to weep most bitterly. [Col. 1070A–B]

Having touched the horns of the altar through this twofold knowledge, of God and of himself, he shall pour the remainder upon its base. By the base of the altar, upon which the altar stands, are signified preachers and superiors. For as the structure of a house is sustained by its foundations, so the Church is sustained by the word and example of preachers and superiors. Since, therefore, we have said that a superior is signified by the base, the sinner fittingly pours out his crimes and offences upon this base when he opens his heart to the superior in humble confession.

For when he has confessed lesser sins and the intention to sin to God in prayer, afterwards he ought to pour out the remainder—that is, his greater crimes—upon the base, which is the confessor.

> “But he shall burn its fat above, as is customary in peace offerings.”

By the fat may be understood the pleasant sins of a person, which he committed with the appetite of perverse pleasure. This fat, this richness, he ought to burn in his higher fire of inward compunction. If he does so, he will obtain peace and forgiveness from God; and immediately there will be fulfilled in him what is next added here:

> “He shall pray for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.”

Whoever, as we have said, burns his pleasant sins before the Lord in that higher fire, and has deserved peace from God through such a victim, will have the true Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, pray for him and for his sin. His confessor also prays for him, the one to whom he opened his heart in confession. The person himself likewise prays for himself and for his sin. And with all these praying for him, he will obtain pardon. [Col. 1070B–D]

## HOMILY III. FIRST HOMILY ON CHAPTER VII OF THE BOOK OF NUMBERS

> “And it came to pass on the day when Moses completed the tabernacle, and set it up, and anointed and sanctified it with all its vessels, etc.” (Num. 7).

This great and wonderful event is the marvellous and magnificent work of our redemption, which that true Moses of ours completed not in night but in day, when He set His tabernacle in the sun; when, free from every stain of original sin, He took the tabernacle of an animate body from the Virgin Mother. He truly raised that tabernacle, then completed and brought to perfection, when, after the many miseries of this life—after reproaches, spitting, blows, and scourges—He willed to be lifted up upon the altar of the cross. [Col. 1070D–1071A]

And because in that tabernacle of the Lord’s body all the fullness of divinity dwelt, it may rightly be said to have been anointed and sanctified with all its vessels: its thoughts, words, and works. When that tabernacle had been raised—not only, as stated, in the exaltation of the cross, but also in the resurrection and ascension—the twelve apostolic leaders who clung to that tabernacle in faith and love offered their oblation, as is subsequently stated, on each successive day.

They offered an oblation pleasing to God on each day because, with equal zeal, they laboured in preaching and prayer for each of the souls entrusted to them. And so that this same offering might be more and more acceptable to the Lord, let us hear what the following text further adds concerning the offering they presented:

> “A silver dish weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, a silver bowl.”

Vinegar, from which the word *acetabulum* (“vinegar dish”) is derived, is a sour and bitter drink. Therefore, by vinegar may rightly be understood the bitterness of repentance, because the apostolic leaders mortified their bodies through harsh and bitter contrition, offering to their Lord and Master a silver dish—that is, their body, tested by the bitterness of repentance as silver is customarily tested by fire.

But because repentance and harsh mortification of the flesh are of little worth if either true confession of faith or perfection of good works is lacking, this is shown in what follows, where the weight of the dish is described: “weighing one hundred and thirty shekels.” By one hundred, unquestionably a full and perfect number, we may understand the perfection of holy and good action which they offered to God. But to this perfection they added thirty—that is, faith in the Holy Trinity—because they knew that nothing pleases God without faith. It follows:

> “A silver bowl,” it says, “containing seventy shekels.”

Having offered the above-mentioned dish of the body, embittered and tested by long and harsh repentance, they also offered a silver bowl—that is, a soul capable of Holy Scripture, enkindled and purified by the fire of divine love. “Containing,” it says, “seventy shekels.” Seven times ten, and ten times seven, make seventy. Therefore, by this number may rightly be understood the Ten Commandments, written and ordered by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

And how did the silver bowls of the apostles—that is, their divinely enlightened souls—contain these commandments? They possessed, I say, not the letter that kills but the spirit that gives life. They possessed them because they understood them spiritually, strove to fulfil them spiritually, and laboured by teaching and preaching to bring others to spiritual understanding. And in all this they looked not for temporal praise but for the glory of eternal recompense. [Col. 1071B–1072A]

> “According to the weight of the sanctuary.”

By the weight of the sanctuary may fittingly be understood the hope or measure of eternal reward. For although they lived holily and justly, they nevertheless weighed these works of holiness in the balance of humility: they sought not their own glory but God’s glory, and expected only the reward of future blessedness. It follows:

> “Both full of fine flour, mixed with oil for sacrifice.”

What does “both full of fine flour” mean? Both the above-mentioned dish and the bowl—that is, the body and soul of the apostles—were full of fine flour, full of purity and innocence. For they were pure and simple, clean in intention and innocent in action.

“Mixed,” it says, “with oil for sacrifice.” The fine flour, I say, of purity and innocence, or of good action and devout intention, was sprinkled and mingled with the oil of twofold love. For although inwardly fervent and ardent in love for God, outwardly they were not idle or withdrawn from love of neighbour. Therefore, because they lacked no oil of twofold charity, they offered to the Lord a pleasing and acceptable sacrifice. [Col. 1072A–B]

> “A little golden mortar, of ten shekels, full of incense.”

By the little mortar we may understand their humble and contrite spirit, which was always full of ten golden shekels—that is, the Ten Commandments shining with spiritual understanding—and of the incense of pure prayer and the incense of contemplation. For after perfect observance of the Ten Commandments, they lacked neither continual sweetness in prayer nor the grace of heavenly visitation in the contemplation of the mind. It follows:

> “A bullock from the herd, and a ram, and a lamb of a year old for a whole burnt offering, and a he-goat for sin.”

That bullock from the herd—the Mediator of God and men, born according to the flesh from the noble stock of patriarchs and prophets, slain and sacrificed for us upon the altar of the cross—the first leaders of the Churches in a certain sense offered by their preaching, because they announced to the faithful that the mystery of His incarnation, passion, and death must be believed and confessed.

“And a ram and a lamb of a year old for a whole burnt offering, and a he-goat for sin.” The ram, lamb, and he-goat are figuratively the same Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. He is called a ram because, as a ram customarily goes before the flock that follows it, so the Son of God Himself, returning as the guiding leader to the Father’s right hand, went before the whole multitude of His elect. He also formed and instructed them by the example of His humility, showing how every faithful person may follow His footsteps by living well. [Col. 1072B–D]

He is indeed the Lamb: altogether innocent, altogether spotless, offered to God the Father as a whole burnt offering—that is, as wholly consumed. For whatever He chose to suffer for the redemption of the human race was wholly consumed; the fire of paternal love so inflamed and burned it all that He never sought His own glory, but the glory of the Father alone.

He is also the he-goat for sin. For although He contracted no stain of sin in Himself, nevertheless, in order to redeem us from sin, He appeared as a man in the likeness of sinful flesh, and by suffering and dying bore our sins. And because He thus deigned to become for us bullock, ram, lamb, and he-goat, and thus offered Himself through the Holy Spirit for the salvation of the world, behold, the discourse turns to His members and subsequently states what must be offered by all the orders generally existing in the Church.

> “And in the sacrifice of peace offerings: two bullocks, five rams, five he-goats, five lambs of a year old.”

By the two bullocks we may understand our body and soul. For we offer them as two bullocks when we subject an unblemished body to His service in humility, and when we keep a clean and unstained soul in His love.

“And five rams.” By rams, which lead the flocks, may fittingly be signified the leaders and teachers of the Church. They offer the Lord the customary sacrifice of peace offerings when, searching the five books of Moses with mystical understanding, they gather from them such knowledge as enables them both to advance by living well and to bring their hearers, through preaching and exhortation, to the joys of eternity. [Col. 1073A–B]

“And five he-goats.” Since the law frequently commands that a he-goat be offered for sins, married life is rightly expressed by the he-goats. Those who seek and love the things of the world through their five senses cannot live their lives without even grave sins. Nevertheless, some of them, being anticipated by divine mercy, worthily wash away their sins through repentance and in a sense offer God a sacrifice of peace offerings, because through humble repentance they make peace between themselves and God.

“And five lambs of a year old.” By lambs, which are certainly clean and simple animals, is fittingly signified the life of those who are continent and desire to live chastely and innocently, guarding their five senses from sins as far as possible. As they desire thus to please God alone through purity of chastity and innocence, they offer Him a most welcome sacrifice of peace and charity. [Col. 1073B–C]

## HOMILY IV. FIRST HOMILY ON CHAPTER XX OF JOSHUA

### On the Six Cities of Refuge

We read that six cities of refuge were established by the Lord, to which one who had unwittingly struck down a soul might flee and escape. Three were beyond the Jordan and three on this side of the Jordan.

The first of those cities beyond the Jordan was called Bosor; the second, Ramoth; the third, Gaulon. Bosor is interpreted “narrowness,” Ramoth “vision of death,” and Gaulon “rolling.” These three cities fittingly represent secular people living in the pleasures of the world, because everything loved in the world is possessed with narrowness and lost with pain and distress.

They are also in the vision of death, as the second city, Ramoth, signifies by its interpretation, because they behold the death in which they live; yet they do not turn aside from it. Rather, willingly lying in it, they daily make their way to the third city, Gaulon, because they do not fear to roll from sin into sin and thus make for themselves a certain rest in the very sins they love. [Col. 1073D–1074A]

By this first city, Bosor, we may also understand secular rulers, who live amid the straits of this world, as the following words make clear when they state that the same city was situated in the wilderness of the plain. The wilderness of the plain is the rustic conduct of those who live in a secular manner and without God.

By Ramoth, however, which was situated in Gilead, of the tribe of Dan, are very suitably signified those who possess knowledge of the Scriptures. This knowledge may be represented by Gilead, which is called “a heap of witness,” but they do not at all live according to Scripture. It is appropriately added that it was of the tribe of Dan. Dan means “thief.” And because *latrunculus* (“thief”) is said to derive from *latere* (“to lie hidden”), hidden love of the world may fittingly be understood by Dan.

They are plainly in Ramoth, which, as we have said, means “vision of death” and is situated in Gilead, because the heap of testimony—that is, Holy Scripture, which they read and hear—daily sets before their eyes the death in which they lie. But Gad—that is, hidden—love of the world, concealed in their hearts, does not allow them to rise to life, because they do not fear to practise secretly the pleasures and desires of the flesh which openly they cannot and dare not practise. They come from Ramoth to Gaulon, which means “rolling,” when they slip from sin to sin, from evil thought to harmful words, and roll from harmful words to wicked deeds. [Col. 1074A–C]

And Gaulon is rightly described as situated in Bashan, of the tribe of Manasseh, whose name means “forgetfulness,” because those who live in this way forget God their Creator and are indeed often excluded from the memory and mercy of God.

But because these cities are called cities of refuge, everyone who has unwittingly struck down a soul—that is, everyone who, through the ignorance of this mortality, which arises either from unrighteous love or unjust anger or fury, kills either his own soul or another’s, whether by living badly in himself or by setting a bad example to others—if he desires to escape the wrath of his neighbour, that is, the wrath of the Son of God, who became our neighbour by assuming for our sake human nature, must flee spiritually to these same cities.

Let him flee to Bosor through the narrowness of the present life, abandoning and lamenting the broad excesses of sins. Let him flee to Ramoth by dying to sins and vices. Let him flee to Gaulon by humbly wrapping himself in the squalor of repentance. [Col. 1074C–D]

If he lives in this way in these cities situated beyond the Jordan, then, God being propitious, he will at last be able to reach the remaining cities on this side of the Jordan. The first of these is Cedes, interpreted “holy” or “changed”; the second, Sichem, “shoulder” or “labour”; the third, Hebron, called “union” or “marriage.”

He comes to Cedes when, changing his secular habit, he begins to live holily and justly in spiritual life. He comes to Sichem when he willingly and patiently puts forward the shoulder of body and heart to bear for God’s sake all the labours encountered in spiritual life. He comes to Hebron when, after leaving the world and undergoing the laborious exercise of spiritual life, he is divinely advanced to that ineffable marriage in which God joins Himself to the blessed soul through the grace of His inward visitation and consolation. [Col. 1074D–1075A]

But we do not doubt that, from the additional words, these matters which we have referred to one individual apply more broadly. For it is not without reason that Scripture notes so particularly in what regions and within what boundaries each city was established. Cedes, as the same Scripture says, was situated in Galilee of Mount Naphtali; Sichem on Mount Ephraim; and Kiriath-arba, which is also Hebron, on Mount Judah.

Cades or Cedes is interpreted “holy” or “changed”; Galilee, “made migration”; Naphtali, “sent-out stag.” Accordingly, Cedes signifies the change from secular life; Galilee, contempt for passing things; and Naphtali, contemplation of mind. Cedes, situated in Galilee of Mount Naphtali, especially represents spiritual people who, scorning and rejecting the pleasures of the present life, have changed what they were, and who know how frequently to ascend, by migrating in desire for the heavenly homeland beyond all that belongs to this world, to the height of contemplative sweetness.

By Sichem, interpreted “number,” situated on Mount Ephraim, interpreted “fruitful,” may be understood those who pass from secular life to Christ’s service and, most devoutly placing their shoulders beneath the great and excessive burdens of outward labours for the service and support of those devoted to the Lord, offer a fruit pleasing and acceptable to God. [Col. 1075A–C]

But Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, situated on Mount Judah, bears the figure of good, just, and spiritual prelates. They are, as it were, set upon Mount Judah because they preside over those who strive for the prize of the heavenly calling: those who on Mount Naphtali contemplate God in mind; on Mount Ephraim bear fruit for God through outward labours; and on Mount Judah continually confess and praise God.

Nor is the name Kiriath-arba, interpreted “city of letters,” unsuitably applied to good prelates, who have both received from God knowledge of the Scriptures and learned to preside, live, and teach according to the instruction of Scripture. Their second name, Hebron, meaning “marriage,” also fittingly accords with them, because, spiritually united in a chaste and spiritual bond to the chaste and spiritual souls of their subjects, they beget children beloved by God as they daily form and instruct them in spiritual virtues by words and examples. [Col. 1075C–D]

These are the cities established through God’s mercy in the holy Church as places of refuge and salvation for sinners, set apart from the midst of the world, so that those who desire salvation may flee to them faithfully in heart and body. Therefore the Lord says: “Set apart the cities of fugitives, of which I spoke to you through the hand of Moses, so that anyone who has struck a person unwittingly may flee to them, and may escape the wrath of his neighbor, who is the avenger of blood.” He strikes a person unwittingly who, through ignorance and the blindness of this mortality which we endure, or enticed by an evil love, as we said above, or even inflamed by unjust hatred and rage, kills either his own soul by living badly, or another’s soul by infecting it with his evil example. Our neighbor—the Son of God, certainly—is provoked to avenge this invisible killing of souls by the wrath of due indignation. In order to become our neighbor and bring us into the inheritance and glory of the children of God, he took upon himself the miseries of our humanity; and through his cross and blood he made us, who were far off, his neighbors. Not without reason is he called both neighbor and avenger of blood, because he himself demands from us in the present life a fitting vengeance of repentance 643 and satisfaction for all the transgressions of our sins, lest anything remain for the future that might at some time separate us from his eternal brightness. Therefore, the Lord clearly teaches us in what order one who desires to escape the wrath of this neighbor should flee to one of the aforesaid cities which he chooses, and with what humility he ought to enter and dwell there, when he says in what follows:

“And when he has fled to one of these cities, he shall stand before the gate of that city, and speak to the elders of that city [Col. 1076C] the things that prove him innocent; and so they shall receive him and give him a place to dwell.” By a city, any spiritual congregation may be understood; by the gate of the city, the good prelate of that same congregation, who is fittingly called the city’s gate, for through him one enters and through him admission to the city is granted. He stands before the gate of the city when, with steadfast constancy, he asks that he may deserve to be received. He speaks to the elders of that city the things that prove him innocent when, by deeds and words, he truly shows himself repentant. For these are the things that prove a person innocent, because through true repentance one returns to true innocence. Thus they receive him and give him a place to dwell when they open to one who knocks humbly and, having received him [Col. 1076D] into the congregation, instruct him by words and examples how he ought to live.

“And when the avenger of blood has pursued him, they shall not deliver him into his hands.” The avenger of blood is the devil, the enemy of the human race, of whom it is said in the Psalm: “That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger” (Ps. VIII, 3). He is the enemy of the good and the avenger of the wicked. He avenges and punishes whatever a person commits against God; he continually pursues the sinner who flees and desires to live devoutly, in case he might turn him from his purpose and entangle him again in his former crimes, so that he may perish. But they do not deliver him into his hands when, on the one hand, they kindle him by their admonitions and counsels to resist the devil and serve [Col. 1077A] the Lord; and, on the other, defend and fortify him by their merits and prayers.

“Because he struck his neighbor unwittingly, nor was he proved his enemy before two or three days.” By the two or three days may be understood either the reception of baptism or the confession of the Holy Trinity. Therefore everyone 644 who is found outside this twofold or threefold reality is delivered into the hands of him who is the avenger of blood, because he is shown to be an enemy of God. But one who has deserved, through receiving baptism and confessing the Holy Trinity, to be counted among the friends of God and the children of holy Church—although he has struck his neighbor unwittingly, if he has fallen into some mortal sin not from malice but from ignorance and weakness—is not therefore given into the hands of the ancient enemy pursuing [Col. 1077B] him, whom we have called the avenger of blood. Rather, he is freed and saved by his own prayers and merits and by those of others who serve God with him in the spiritual life, provided that he does not depart from the path of spiritual life which he has undertaken and perseveres steadfastly in repentance and humility until the end of his life. Hence the text immediately adds:

“And he shall dwell in that city until he stands before judgment, rendering an account of his deed.” By the words, “until he stands before judgment, rendering an account of his deed,” I think the final day of a human being—that is, the day of death—is signified, on which he shall stand before judgment and render an account of his deed, so that either he may be punished for his evil deeds or receive the joys of eternal blessedness for his good actions.

[Col. 1077C] But in what follows, “and the high priest who shall be in that time shall die,” I judge that the final day of judgment may be understood: when that true and supreme priest, our Lord Jesus Christ, who offered himself upon the cross to God the Father for the salvation of the human race, dies not in his own person—for “Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI, 9)—but in the person of his elect; and in his body, which is the multitude of the elect, he is brought into the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

“Then the manslayer shall return and enter into the city, and into the city, and into the house from which he fled.” The manslayer who has cleansed in this life the guilt of his homicide through the tears [Col. 1077D] of daily repentance and satisfaction shall then—that is, at that time of the final judgment—return from the exile of this mortality and enter into the city of blessed immortality, and into the house from which he fled: namely, the house of eternity, from which through the fault of disobedience he had fallen and perished in the first man. There he shall not fear the face of the pursuing enemy, but shall rejoice in the vision of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

645 HOMILY V. FIRST HOMILY ON CHAPTER XVII OF JUDGES.

“There was at that time a man from Mount Ephraim, named Micah,” etc. (Judg. XVII).

Because, according to the Apostle, “the letter kills,” and because we desire to seek the life-giving spirit in the killing letter, [Col. 1078A] let us examine the course of this narrative. Even if we cannot unfold its mystery word by word, let us at least gather its general meaning, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant it. The Jewish people may fittingly be signified by the name of this Micah. *Michas* is interpreted, “Who is here?” “Who?” is the word of those who doubt. This name, “Who is here?” may fittingly be applied to the Jewish people, because there is great doubt concerning their salvation: glorying only in the law they had received, they could not know the author of the law.

This Micah is said to have been from Mount Ephraim because the Jewish people derived their origin from the stock of the patriarchs and prophets. These may fittingly be signified by the name Ephraim, which is interpreted “fruitful,” [Col. 1078B] because in the good works of toil and patience they were truly fruitful. We should note the words: “There was at that time a certain man.” The preceding narrative concerns Samson, who in his entire life and all his actions bears the type of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus the narrative of Samson, who signifies Christ, is fittingly followed by the narrative of Micah, who bears the figure of the Jewish people, because in the time of Christ there existed that Jewish people whose words are remembered as having this mystical interpretation, as follows:

He says to his mother: “The eleven hundred pieces of silver which you had set apart for yourself, and concerning which you had sworn in my hearing—behold, I have them, and they are with me.” By these two numbers, one thousand and one hundred, two things may be understood: namely, the Law and the Prophets. By the greater number, the teaching of the Law; by the lesser, prophetic speech.
