In these two, namely Law and Prophets, consisted the whole teaching of the Jewish people, nor was any other Scripture besides these two handed down to them. Therefore the Jewish people told their mother—that is, the Synagogue, which was in some manner their mother—that they possessed and kept with themselves the eleven hundred pieces of silver when they professed that, with the greatest zeal and observance, they kept the letter of the Law and the Prophets handed down to them by her [variant: “by him”]. And it is rightly said: “which you had set apart for yourself.” The Synagogue, mother of the Jewish people, had in a sense set apart for herself the eleven hundred pieces of silver, because she boasted proudly that, above all the peoples of the earth, she had been so loved by God and held in such honor that he had handed down to her the instruction of his Scriptures through the Law and the Prophets. She had also sworn concerning those eleven hundred pieces of silver when, with the whole multitude present and hearing, the Lord gave his commandments and she said: “All that the Lord has spoken we will do” (Exod. XXIV, 3). Let us hear what his mother—the Synagogue—answers to the Jewish people professing that they diligently observe the carnal ceremonies of the Law.

“Blessed,” she says, “is my son by the Lord.” The Synagogue declares that her son is blessed by the Lord because she thinks that the Jewish people, who endeavor to observe only the killing letter without the life-giving spirit, will inherit the reward [Col. 1079A] of eternal blessing. Or she asserts that her son is blessed in this respect: that he alone among the other nations received the Law from God. The following words plainly indicate that the Jewish people attributed this not to God’s freely bestowed mercy but to their own merits and those of their fathers: “Therefore he restored them to his mother.” Thus the Jewish people restored the eleven hundred pieces of silver to their mother because they think that they received the writings of the Law and the Prophets not by grace but by right, since their fathers had been of such and so great merit that this special honor was rightly owed them by God above the other nations. It follows:

647 She answered: “I have consecrated and vowed this silver to the Lord.” For whatever is contained in the letter of the Law and the Prophets seems consecrated, according to the carnal understanding, to that proud Synagogue. And she vows this vow to the Lord: that she will observe and understand carnally, not spiritually, the Scripture entrusted to her, which, as we have often said, consists in the Law and the Prophets. It should be noted that she draws this to her own person when she says: “I have consecrated and vowed this silver to the Lord.” This is as though she said: “My own merit and the worthiness of my fathers demand that this sacred Scripture of the Law and Prophets should rightly have been given to me by God; for they were certainly such and so great that, through the received knowledge of divine Scripture, they alone excelled all the nations of the earth.”

“So that my son,” she says, “may receive it from my hand and make a carved image and a molten image.” By the carved image we may understand the interpretation of the Law and the Prophets; by the molten image, [Col. 1079C] that satisfaction by which every observer of the killing letter, should he commit anything forbidden by the Law, is commanded to melt away—that is, cleanse—his sin, just as we often find in the letter of the Law: one person is commanded to offer a she-goat, another a he-goat, another a sheep; and such and such burnt offerings are prescribed for each according to the character of his crimes. Therefore the Synagogue says: “I have consecrated and vowed this silver to the Lord”; that is, “For this reason I and my fathers have handed down this utterance of the divine Law as consecrated and to be observed, so that my son may receive it from my hand and make a carved image and a molten image.” That is: from my merits, through which I deserved to receive from the Lord the Scripture of the Law and the Prophets, every one of my sons—namely, one who wishes to observe it according to [Col. 1079D] the letter—may be able to understand and find in it how he ought to melt away, that is, repent of, the sin of his transgression.

“And now I give it to you.” As though she said: “So long as you enjoy the present life, which is understood by ‘now,’ know that this utterance of the Scriptures, entrusted by me to you, must be observed and understood carnally.” “Therefore he restored [it] 648 to his mother.” Scripture here again emphasizes and repeats the vain boasting of the Jewish people, by which they gloried in their own merits and those of their fathers on account of the Law they had received. It follows:

“He took two hundred pieces of silver and gave them to a silversmith, that he might make from them a carved image and a molten image.” By this silversmith may be understood every prelate and preacher in Judaism. The Synagogue gives him two hundred pieces of silver—that is, the jewel of the Scriptures, namely the Law and the Prophets—so that he may make a carved image and a molten image. This is because she commands every teacher of Judaism to endeavor to open and unfold for all his subjects the interpretation of the letter—not, I say, a spiritual but a carnal interpretation—so that every person under the Law, if perhaps he has transgressed any commandment, may know how to make the very purification for his offense which the Law prescribes.

It fittingly follows that it “was in the house of Micah,” because only the proud and carnal interpretation remains in the Jewish people, who seek to please God solely through outward sacrifices and who set apart therein a small shrine for God. By the small shrine, the Temple at Jerusalem [Col. 1080B] may be understood: the one place set apart for the offering to God of victims and sacrifices commanded in the Law; for it was not permitted to celebrate the rite of their carnal sacrifices elsewhere.

“And he made an ephod and teraphim,” that is, a priestly garment and idols; “and he filled the hand of one of his sons, and he became his priest.” The ephod, which is a shoulder-garment, may signify the laborious works of the Law. The Jewish nation indeed toils greatly to fulfill the carnal works of the Law. By the teraphim, that is, the priestly garment, there is no objection to understanding the killing letter, because just as the body is wrapped in a garment, so the killing letter appears to have been laid over the life-giving spirit. For the Jewish people make a priestly garment because they attend outwardly to the killing letter and, blinded by the darkness of their ignorance, neither can nor seek to perceive the inwardly hidden sweetness of the life-giving spirit.

649 It is fittingly added after the ephod and teraphim that he also made idols. For an idol, as the Apostle Paul testifies, “is nothing” (I Cor. VIII, 4), though it bears some carved likeness of God when no indication of divine truth exists in it. This signifies that the Jews, through their outward observance of ceremonies and the carnal command of the Law, put forward a certain likeness as though they worshipped and honored God. But there is no truth in them, because they do not understand the true Redeemer of humankind, whom the entire Scripture of the Law and the Prophets proclaims. “And he filled,” it says, “the hand of one of his sons, [Col. 1080D] and he became his priest.” Here every preacher in the Synagogue is indicated, because he is appointed for the purpose of setting forth the outward works of the Law for observance and carrying out the carnal rite of sacrifices.

“In those days there was no king in Israel, but everyone did what seemed right to himself.” Throughout all the days in which the vain superstition of legal and carnal ceremonies persists among the Jewish people, the true king, our Lord Jesus Christ, does not rule; nor does he have his own dwelling among them. Rather, everyone does what seems right to himself, not what seems right to God, because they live not according to God’s good pleasure but according to the desire of their own pleasure.

650 HOMILY VI. FIRST HOMILY ON THIS AND THE FOLLOWING CHAPTER OF THE BOOK OF JUDGES.

[Col. 1081A]

“There was also another young man from Bethlehem of Judah and of its kindred; and he was a Levite and dwelt there” (Judg. XVII).

Who can more fittingly be understood by this young man than the new man, our Lord Jesus Christ? For our first parent Adam, the old man, cannot be called a young man; but our Lord Jesus Christ, who, as we have said, is the new man, ought rightly to be signified by the name of a young man, since he never contracted any harmful oldness of sin in thought, word, or deed. “From Bethlehem,” it says. Bethlehem is interpreted “house of bread,” by which Christ’s divinity is not unjustly figured. Our Lord Jesus Christ is rightly said to be from Bethlehem because he is true God from true God. Judah, however, which is interpreted “confessor” or “praiser,” may figure the company of angels, who always praise and confess God in the joy of perpetual jubilation. The kindred of this Judah is ourselves, who are kin to the angels because we have one Father and Creator, God, together with them.

“And he was a Levite and dwelt there.” *Levite* is said to mean “one assumed.” How fittingly this name belongs to Christ the Lord, who, though he was the Lord of majesty, assumed human form for our sake! Yet although he fitted to himself in the womb of the blessed Virgin a body subject to our mutability, he nevertheless dwelt there—that is, he remained unchangeable in his divinity, assuming what he was not while remaining what he was.

“And he went out from Bethlehem.” By these words the same humanity of Christ is again commended. For he went out from Bethlehem when he came from the bosom of the Father into this world and, mercifully incarnate for us, made himself visible. But for what reason did he go out? “To sojourn wherever he found it convenient”: that is, so that he who, by assuming an earthly body, had, so to speak, become a sojourner from heaven, might invite foreign nations to his faith. We call them foreign because through unbelief they had gone into exile far from God. In body indeed, as long as he chose to remain on earth, he lived among the Jews, lest he give their unbelief an occasion [Col. 1081D] to say that, leaving them, he had turned aside to the Gentiles. Yet in heart, thought, and the regard of mercy he was with the Gentiles, in whose hearts he foreknew and predestined that he would someday find rest through faith—a rest which the proud Jewish people refused to receive.

“And when he came to Mount Ephraim, journeying on his way, he turned aside briefly into the house of Micah; and Micah asked him: ‘Where do you come from?’” The only-begotten Son of God came to Mount Ephraim when he appeared incarnate among the Jews. He journeyed because, though he is unchangeable in his divinity and not confined by place, he deigned through assumed humanity to become changeable and local. He turned aside briefly into the house of Micah because, as we have said, during the short time in which he chose to appear upon earth he lived only among the Jewish people. From them, if we heed the Gospel, he was asked—as this young man was asked by Micah—“Where do you come from?” Was it not the same when, after he said that unless they believed that he was, they would die in their sins, they answered him: “Who are you?” “I am a Levite,” he says, “from Bethlehem of Judah.” Thus, although not in the same words, the Lord Jesus gave the same answer to the Jews who asked who he was when he said: “The beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII, 25). Therefore, when he called himself the beginning, he undoubtedly declared himself to be from Bethlehem—that is, God from God. “I am a Levite,” he says, “from Bethlehem of Judah”: I have assumed human nature among you and from you, though according to divinity I am God the Son from God the Father, without beginning [Col. 1082B] and without end.

“And I am going,” he says, “to dwell where I can and where I see it will be useful to me.” It is as though the Son of God said to the Jews who did not believe in him: “Among you indeed I became human, and I minister to you the word of preaching so that you may be saved. But because my word finds no place in you, I shall go through my preachers, whom I will send to the Gentiles, where I can obtain a pleasant dwelling in faithful hearts; where my preaching shall bear fruit through the faith of the Gentiles who will receive it.” Hence after his resurrection he commands the apostles: “Go, teach all nations; baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). It follows:

[Col. 1082C] And Micah said: “Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest.” Hearing these things, that old Synagogue suffered a great torment of envy—for she was always envious of the salvation of the Gentiles—and in some manner used these words to the Lord Christ: “Stay with me,” that is, “Let your dwelling be with me; do not go far away from your own kindred in order to preach to the Gentiles. Be to me a father and priest”; that is, “Do not neglect whatever good you may be able to bring forth here among us by teaching the ceremonies of our Law, which was given us from heaven. Fulfil also my carnal priesthood by carrying out the rite of legal sacrifices. And I will give you ten pieces of silver every year, a double garment, and things necessary for food.” This is as though she said: [Col. 1082D] “As long as you live with me, I place before you the Ten Commandments, signified by the ten pieces of silver, and the Law and Prophets, signified by the double garment, that you may live in these and teach them. For if you do and teach these things, they are enough for you to obtain whatever necessity demands for soul or body.” Such, in some sense, were the words of that proud Synagogue, because, as we have said, she took it grievously that this salvation should come to the Gentiles, so that anyone by the word of teaching might make them capable of divine knowledge. Since our Lord Jesus Christ knew that the Jewish people had the eye of their heart darkened by the beam of envy, lest, through the occasion that he preferred the Gentiles to them in teaching, they should break forth into hatred of him, he acted according to their words: throughout all the days of his flesh [Col. 1083A] he lived among them, as the following text indicates.

“He consented and remained with the man, and was to him as one of the sons.” The Jewish people did not indeed regard the Lord Jesus as the true Son of God and Savior of the world, but as one of the sons—that is, as another wise man born of their stock and kindred.

“And Micah filled his hand.” Therefore the Jewish people—whom we have said may be figured by Micah—filled the hand of our true Levite, the Lord Jesus Christ: that is, they completed the work for which he came into the world when, after the many good works which he showed among them while living with them, they finally hung him on the cross. Placed there, [Col. 1083B] he said: “It is finished” (John XIX, 30). It fittingly follows: “and he had with him the young man as priest,” 653 because he, the supreme high priest, who is the propitiation for our sins, was crucified, died, and was buried among them for us. He is also rightly called a young man because he alone was pure and innocent, the only human being to live among humans without the stain of sin. We may understand the following words as spoken on the part of the elect, namely the apostles and the other faithful who were found among the Jewish people.

“Now,” he says, “I know that God will do me good, since I have a priest of the Levitical tribe.” It is as though they said: “At last, after so many cycles of time during which we were ill because we had no redemption, now it will be well with us, because God, having become human, has deigned to become priest and sacrifice for us upon the altar of the cross.” But if we wish to understand these same words also on the part of the reprobate, they indicate that boastfulness of the Jews by which they rejoiced that they had removed from the earth the memory of him whom they regarded as a deceiver, supposing that once he had been removed they would thereafter be secure in the joy [Col. 1083C] of worldly prosperity.

“In those days there was no king in Israel.” Certainly, when the Jewish people were doing these things, the true King, our Lord Jesus Christ, was not among them through the presence of his grace. Rather, the Jews having been expelled from grace through the deserts of their unbelief, the tribe of Dan sought a possession in which it might dwell: that is, the Gentile people desired to come to faith in their Redeemer, through which they might someday attain the land of promise. This name Dan, which means “judgment,” is rightly applied figuratively to the Gentile people, because it was the true judgment of God that, when the Jewish people refused to believe in him, he should call the Gentile peoples.

“Until that day they had not received a lot among the other tribes.” Until the day of Christ’s death, the Gentile people had no lot among the Jews, because they had not received the knowledge of God and the learning of the Scriptures, namely the Law and the Prophets, nor could they have fellowship with those whose fathers, covenant, and legislation these were.

[Col. 1084A] “Therefore the children of Dan, from their tribe and family, sent five very valiant men from Zorah and Eshtaol to explore the land and inspect it carefully. And they said to them: ‘Go and consider the land.’” Although here we cannot investigate every word as would be useful, let us at least gather the general meaning, as God grants. It seems to me that by these five men are figuratively expressed the five persons only whom we read to have been from the Gentile people and to whom our Lord Jesus Christ, in the days of his flesh, communicated himself and deigned to impart grace. For apart from these five we find no other Gentiles to whom, while he lived in this world, he showed works of his divinity as great as those shown to these five. During his infancy those Magi from the East, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, came to worship him; but we do not count among these those who worshipped only the silent child, whereas these worshipped him openly while he was speaking and saw him work miracles.

Of these five whom we have mentioned, the first was that blessed centurion whose incomparable faith the Lord commended to his disciples, saying: “I have not found so great faith in Israel” (Matt. VIII, 10). The second was the other centurion whose mind’s eyes God had so enlightened that, seeing all that happened when the Lord was crucified, he cried out: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark XV, 39). The third was the thief who hung beside him on the cross and interceded with him for himself, saying: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII, 42). In the fourth and fifth places come two women, who, though they were not men in sex, were nevertheless men in mind and understanding. One was that Canaanite woman who came out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon and asked the Lord for her daughter’s deliverance, and who deserved to hear from him: “O woman, great is your faith” (Matt. XV, 28). The other was the Samaritan woman, whose understanding God opened so that she said: “I know that the Messiah is coming” (John IV, 25). Even if she was not of wholly Gentile stock, nevertheless, as she herself testified, Jews do not associate with Samaritans. These five, of whom we have just spoken, were in some manner sent beforehand by the Gentiles to explore, through whom hope was given to them of possessing the land of promise. For example, if Christ had never communicated with any Gentile in the days of his flesh, no confidence of hope for conversion to him would have remained for the other Gentiles, to whom the sacrament of faith was afterward preached through the apostles. But because they had the example of those whom he kindly received in person and made participants in his grace, they themselves had greater confidence in the mercy of his loving-kindness: that he too would receive them mercifully and make them companions in the eternal inheritance.

“When they came, as they went on, to Mount Ephraim, they entered Micah’s house.” They entered, in some sense, the house of Micah, whom we have said signifies the Jewish people, because they first began to live among the Jews, among and through whom they received knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. [Col. 1085A] “And they rested there,” because, instructed by the testimonies of Scripture, they found rest for their souls. “And recognizing the voice of the young Levite, they made use of his lodging.” The Gentiles recognized the voice of the young Levite—that is, of the new man Jesus Christ—through the words of the preachers in whom and through whom he himself spoke. They made use of his lodging, namely his flesh, which he assumed for their salvation. We believe it is signified by a lodging because in it he could undergo now good things, now evil things. We do not say “evil things” because he, who was free from every evil, ever did evil to anyone in all his life; rather, because he endured harsh and bitter things in that same flesh. It follows:

“And they said to him: ‘Who brought you here? What [Col. 1085B] are you doing here? For what reason did you wish to come here?’” Let us touch only upon the main point here, and say what we have been given to understand through these three interrogative words—who, what, why. It seems to me that this threefold question expresses that the Gentiles, converted to Christ, then confessed him to be one person in the Holy Trinity. To these three questions three other words are attached: “here,” “here,” and again “here”—that is, he came into this world for their salvation. Confessing in this way the assumption of humanity into God in Christ, he answered them in some manner by the words that follow: “Micah has provided me with these and these things.” This is as though he said: “I received from the Jewish people this human nature, consisting of soul and flesh, through which you were saved.” It fittingly follows:

“And he hired me for wages, that I might be his priest.” For this reason the Son of God assumed the clothing of human flesh from the Jews: that he might offer himself to God the Father as a sacrifice for them and take their sins upon himself without sin on the cross. “And they asked him to consult the Lord.” If, then, we consider carefully, we find that all those of whom we have spoken—the persons we said had been sent beforehand, as it were, to explore the grace of God’s condescension toward the Gentiles—poured out their prayers to the Son of God: namely, the centurion and the thief, the Canaanite woman and the Samaritan woman. What do we believe they mystically desired in their petitions but that he should consult [Col. 1085D] the Lord—that is, that he who was the supreme high priest, God above us and human for us, should approach as mediator between God and humanity? Why? So that they might know whether they were proceeding on a prosperous way and whether the matter would have its effect: that is, so that, with the Son of God as mediator before the Father, they might have this assurance, that he would not reject them from his grace, but that their devotion, by which they desired to draw near to God, would attain the effect of eternal salvation. But let us hear what our true Levite and priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, answers to those seeking the grace of divine mercy:

“Go in peace.” Let us set before our eyes those of whom we have spoken, and we shall be able to see that, when each of them made petition, the Son of God answered what belongs to peace. Does it not seem to you that he answered the Canaanite woman and the thief, to pass over the others, in some manner with “Go in peace,” when he said to the one, who persistently implored him for her daughter’s health: “Let it be done for you as you wish” (Matt. XV, 28); and answered the other, hanging beside him on the cross and imploring his grace: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43)? It follows:

“May the Lord regard your way and the journey on which you go.” It is as though the Lord had said to those inquiring about their state of salvation: “God the Father, who willed me to be incarnate and suffer for you, has now resolved, for those who desire to walk in the way of his commandments, to open through me the gate of the kingdom of heaven. For God did not, in some sense, regard the way of the fathers who went before, although they desired to draw near to him through good works, [Col. 1086B] because, with original sin standing in the way, he neither willed nor could open the entrance of heavenly life to any of them. For I had not yet assumed human form for your sake, 657 nor had I yet, by the payment of my blood, quenched that flaming sword which had barred the entrance to paradise.” It follows:

Then the men went and came to Laish, and saw the people dwelling there without any fear, after the manner of the Sidonians—secure and quiet, with absolutely no one opposing them. By Laish, which is interpreted “lion,” the people of the Gentiles may fittingly be signified; for, since the knowledge of God was lacking to their hearts, they were placed under the dominion of that lion, namely the devil, who goes about seeking whom he may devour. The second interpretation of the same name also seems aptly to suit them, because Laish is also interpreted “a man for himself.” The Gentile people was, in a sense, a man for itself, because they lived not for God but for themselves, being devoted not to divine works but to the pleasure of carnal desire.

But by these five men we believe those preachers to be mystically signified who, under the five books of Moses, were then instructed by the grace of the new law and were sent after the Lord’s ascension to minister the word of preaching to the Gentiles. But when they came to Laish—that is, to the Gentiles—what did they find among them? “They saw,” he says, “a people dwelling without any fear.” The Gentile people dwelt without any fear, because, swelling outwardly with carnal glory and enslaved to the worship of idols, it had not learned to keep before its eyes either the fire of Gehenna or the dread of the coming judgment. “After the manner of the Sidonians,” he says. The Gentiles indeed dwelt after the manner of the Sidonians because, according to the interpretation of that name, they were useless hunters of irrational desires, pursuing unlawful things in themselves and loving transitory things without ceasing, and committing iniquity without any restraint. “Secure,” he says, “and quiet.” Before the Gentiles became capable of divine knowledge, they lived in evil security: hoping in no way for abiding things, they placed their whole hope in transitory matters and knew how to possess or desire nothing except what passes away. In these things they had in some fashion made rest for themselves, judging that all things which had to be left behind were to be possessed as though forever.

[Col. 1087A] But whence did this evil security and harmful quietness arise in them, except because, as is stated in what follows, no one at all opposed them? For those to whom the commandments of the law were given were opposed even by the law itself, which inspired great trembling of fear because, without the seasoning of grace, it commanded every sin of transgression to be punished rather harshly and strictly. But no one at all opposed the Gentiles, because the law was not given to them—a law which, although it did not remove guilt through grace, nevertheless made it known by its commandment and sternly punished the deeds of offenders by severe judgment.

But, according to the mystical foretelling of the subsequent text, when preachers of the divine word came to them, they became possessed of great riches and were separated far from Sidon and from all men. For they abounded in great and praiseworthy wealth when they began to be adorned with the great beauty of precious virtues; when they adopted the word of sacred utterance—which may also rightly be signified by riches—for the use of their adornment; and when they laboured with the greatest zeal to grasp the mysteries of Holy Scripture. They also became far from Sidon, that is, from that useless hunting of which we have spoken, because they now knew how to restrain the heart under the divine law and did not permit it to wander among the irrational motions of the flesh. “And separated from all men,” he says. It is clear how true these words are, and how truly they have been fulfilled and are daily fulfilled in the Church which has come from the Gentiles. For the people of the Church is in a sense separated from all men, because from those who think merely human thoughts and things upon the earth, if it cannot meanwhile separate itself in body, it nevertheless strives to segregate and estrange itself in heart through love of the heavenly homeland; it disdains subjection to temporal things and ardently longs for eternal things.

We may also, under another interpretation, understand by the five men—whom we said could signify preachers—those same five persons mentioned above, of whom alone among the Gentiles we read, as was said earlier, that our Lord Jesus Christ, in the days of his flesh, made them participants in his grace and showed them works of his divinity. These five men came, in a sense, to Laish [Col. 1087D] when it became known to the Gentile people, which may be signified by Laish, through the apostles and the other faithful who received ministry to them, what great and what kind of things the Lord Jesus had done with them in person; how kindly he had received them; and how graciously he had shown himself toward them. Encouraged by this hope, they returned all the more confidently from darkness to light and from stains to purity through the mystery of the sacred washing, because they had received with greater certainty in the reception of these persons a pledge of their hope.

“And they returned to their brethren in Zorah and Eshtaol.” These five men returned to their brethren when, as we have said, it became known to the other Gentiles with what condescension the Lord Jesus had shared in the flesh with these persons. Therefore, having heard the works of divine mercy [Col. 1088A] which he had deigned to work among sinners, they surely became such that the interpretations of these names—Zorah and Eshtaol—could suit them. For Zorah is interpreted “coals” or “straits,” while Eshtaol is interpreted “fire bringing forth.” Thus they began to be distressed and anxious because they had so long been extinguished—that is, had so long lacked the light of divine knowledge. And so it came about that, according to the interpretation of the second name, namely Eshtaol, they became “fire bringing forth”: kindled by the ardour of divine love, they searched out the mystery of Holy Scripture and learned how they might bring forth to God from themselves the offspring of good virtues.

“And having returned to their brethren in Zorah and Eshtaol, when they asked what they had done, they answered: Come, and let us go up.” What had the five men mentioned above done except reveal their case to the Son of God, who was living among them in the flesh, and seek grace from him? Since, then, they found this grace, as the Gospel testifies, this exhortation to the other Gentiles followed. We do not speak of their exhortation as though they themselves had been sent to preach to the Gentiles. Rather, because their deed and their reception became known among the Gentiles, by the hope which they gave them through their example, it was in a sense their saying to them: “Arise, and let us go up to them”—that is to say: arise by abandoning sins and idolatry, seek the height of true conversion, and let us go up to them; that is, by setting our minds on the things above, not on things upon the earth, let us hasten to attain fellowship with our heavenly fellow-citizens, namely the angels.

[Col. 1088C] “We have seen,” they say, “a land very rich and fertile.” By this land the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, may be understood because of his assumption of an earthly body. Scripture mystically and very fittingly declares this land rich and fertile, because in the man Christ Jesus all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily. This land is also rich and full of sweetest truth [perhaps “fertility”] in this sense: our Lord Jesus Christ is rich in mercy, rich indeed toward all who call upon him. The abundance of this incomparable land—that is, the abundance of the loving-kindness and mercy of Jesus Christ, God and man—was long ago promised to the Gentiles who desired to receive the sacrament of faith, through the examples of those to whom he himself, while living as a man among men, deigned to grant the aid of his compassion.

“They say: Do not be negligent; do not cease.” As though it were said: Do not despise the grace of our salvation, appointed for you by God’s free mercy; do not cease, but hasten to obtain it with heart and body—with the heart by believing, and with the body by receiving the mystery of sacred baptism. Must you now remain in unbelief when you possess so many examples of mercy as a pledge? “Let us go and possess it.” To go and possess the land of which we have just spoken is, by hoping in God’s mercy, to advance from virtue to virtue, and through faith proved by works to have Christ abide in the human being and the human being in Christ.

[Col. 1089A] It fittingly follows:

“There will be no toil,” because Christ’s yoke is sweet and his burden light. For when toil has been endured so long that Christ is possessed, thereafter there will in some sense be no toil; because, although the continual exercises of labour are hard for bodily weakness, yet through love of him who reigns in the heart they are reckoned light. It follows: “We entered among the secure, into a very broad land.” What is more fittingly understood by “the secure” than the angels, whose security no anxiety can ever disturb? By the very broad land, however, either charity or the heavenly homeland acquired by charity may be understood. Let the preachers of the holy Church therefore say: “We entered among the secure”—that is, we who preach to you the word of truth, though we are pilgrims in body in this world, yet in faith and hope our citizenship is in heaven among our heavenly fellow-citizens, namely the angels. We trust that after laying aside our tabernacle we shall one day depart in reality and truth to their fellowship.

The words that follow are pleasant and exceedingly joyful to hear—for those, I mean, who, because of the abundance of future goods, have chosen to endure temporal poverty in this land of pilgrimage.

“They say: And the Lord will give the place in which there is no lack [of any] of the things that are produced in the earth.” By this place may be mystically signified that unique homeland for which all those sigh who know themselves to be sojourners upon the earth. Of this place it is well said that there is in it no lack of anything. For in the heavenly kingdom the fullness of every good overflows. Nor is this surprising: for there he is visibly present, from whom, in whom, and through whom are all things; and in the most desirable vision of him such goods overflow as surpass all merits and all desires of all people.

[Col. 1089C] “In which there is no lack,” he says, “of the things that are produced in the earth.” What are the things produced in the earth? Surely wealth and riches, which thieves dig up and steal, which rust and moth destroy. Yet there will be no lack of these in the heavenly kingdom, for the treasures stored there are corrupted by no age and can be lost through no circumstance.

## Homily VII: First Homily on Chapter XIX of the Third Book of Kings, Concerning Elijah

[Col. 1089D] “When Elijah the prophet came to Horeb, the mountain of God, he remained in a cave,” and so forth. (III Kings XIX.)

By Mount Horeb, which is interpreted “dryness,” the height and excellence of divinity may be understood; in Elijah, the Lord the Son of God. This Elijah, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, came to Mount Horeb: he was eternally begotten from God the Father, and was always consubstantial, co-omnipotent, and co-eternal with him before the ages and is before the ages. But how does the meaning “dryness” suit his most excellent divinity, in which the perpetual abundance and fertility of all good things essentially was and is inherent? It does indeed suit it. For just as the eminence of all virtues naturally overflowed in him, so he was in some sense dry, because not even the slightest sin ever approached him.

But he “remained in a cave” when he was in the hiddenness of his divinity. And the hiddenness of his divinity is rightly understood through the cave: just as what is in a cave is concealed, so he himself, abiding with the Father in eternity, was an incomprehensible God, a hidden God. And he who was thus in heaven with the Father, lofty God, eternal and immeasurable God, later appeared upon earth as a visible and manifest human being. Since all things which were someday to be accomplished by the Son of God in the glorious manifestation of his works were in the predestination of God the Father, it fittingly follows:

[Col. 1090A] “And behold, a voice came to him and said to him: What are you doing here, Elijah? But he answered: I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have forsaken the covenant of the Lord.”

What the Father’s speaking to the Son and the Son’s answer to the Father may be, and how it occurs, we do not know. Therefore, because we cannot know it, Scripture speaks to us in a human manner and fashion, opening up what we may in some way grasp in words and understanding. Expositors who have understood this more deeply say that God the Father’s speaking to the Son is the will and predestination of God the Father; while the Son’s answer is the obedience which he renders to God the Father. Therefore, when it says, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” it is as though God the Father, before all ages, imposed upon his Son the predestined work of our salvation which ought to be accomplished through him, saying: “What are you doing here, O my Son? Why do you not accomplish your work, to which I eternally preordained and chose you? You rest safely and quietly in my kingdom as my only-begotten Son, and appear to do nothing while you do not work the salvation of the human race.”

[Col. 1090C] In answer to this, the Son indicates that he has worked gloriously and sublimely not only on earth but also in heaven:

“I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have forsaken the covenant of the Lord.” The zeal of the Son of God, by which he was zealous for the Lord God of hosts, was that vengeance which he exercised in the ruin of the apostate angel. He removed and cast him down from heaven and from among the fiery stones because that angel wished to be like the Son of God, who is the image and likeness of God the Father, saying in his heart: “I will set my throne in the north; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV.13–14). Therefore, because God made all things through the Word of God, it was fitting that this work should be accomplished through the Son of God, who is the Word of the Father: that the one cast out of heaven should be so condemned that he might never return and might never be restored to his former dignity.

Why, then, was he thus zealous? “Because the children of Israel have forsaken the covenant of the Lord.” By the children of Israel, the angelic creature fashioned through God’s wisdom may be understood. It is not unfittingly understood through Israel, which is interpreted “a man seeing God,” because through the merit of angelic nature it had received as a gift always to see God and always to contemplate his face in joy. But because they forsook the covenant of the Lord—that covenant which he established, namely that the creature should be subject to the Creator and should not be proud of the dignity it had received from God—therefore those apostate angels who forsook this covenant were rejected in heaven and cast down to earth. They can no longer be called or named children of Israel, because they will never rise again to the vision of eternal brightness.

[Col. 1091A] Concerning their fall, and also the destruction of humanity which occurred through their malicious suggestion, the Son of God continues to speak:

“They have destroyed your altars, killed your prophets with the sword, and I alone am left; and they seek my life to take it away.” That highest archangel was a kind of principal altar of God; but the altars were that multitude of reprobate angels, followers of the devil. They are called altars because they had been created for this purpose: that on them nothing but the sacrifice of praise and rejoicing should be offered and immolated to God the Creator. These altars were destroyed and reduced to nothing in the sight of the Lord when they raised themselves against God on the horns of pride and thereby irrecoverably lost the state of their ancient and former glory. But that apostate angel, cast down from heaven to earth with his followers, immediately overthrew and killed the first human being through envy, as the words immediately following show.

“And they have killed your prophets with the sword.” For Adam and Eve were prophets, because they themselves, first among all, received from the Prophet of prophets the spirit of every grace and prophecy. Hence Adam, as soon as he had been formed, prophesied quite notably concerning Christ and the Church, saying: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. Therefore a man shall leave father and mother, shall cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II.23). What was the sword by which they were killed except the deception of the devil’s suggestion? Certainly he killed them mortally when he said: “Why has God commanded you not to eat from every tree of paradise? On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes shall be opened and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III.1, 5).

[Col. 1091C] Therefore, when the altars had been destroyed and the prophets killed—that is, when angel and human being had sinned—the merciful and compassionate Son of God besought God the Father to deign to remember mercy in wrath, and offered himself as Mediator between God and humanity, saying:

“And I alone am left, and they seek my life to take it away.” “My angels,” he says, “whom I created for the praise of my name, have forsaken me because they sinned. My human beings, Adam and Eve, whom I made in my image and likeness and placed in the paradise of delight without death and without sin, have forsaken me because they were unwilling to render me the good of obedience. Therefore I alone am left. And because I am thus as one alone in my kingdom, they seek my life: all my elect, my saints, my friends seek my life—that is, with all their heart and all their affections they desire that, having become human, I should take a human soul. And they do not merely seek it; they seek it so as to take it away—namely, that I may descend from the highest seats of my kingdom to those places where they fell miserably, and raise them up to that from which they fell. And if this is pleasing to your majesty, behold, send me.”

All these things were in predestination. Now, in the words which follow, what was someday to happen in the accomplishment of the divine work is prefigured.

[Col. 1092A] “And he said to him: Go out, and stand on the mountain before the Lord.” What is “go out” except: come from the hiddenness of divinity and appear visibly to the world? What is “stand on the mountain” except: rest in the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary, who is rightly called a mountain because in her the gifts of every merit stood preeminent by a special prerogative? Or, “stand on the mountain,” that is, remain at such a height of virtues that you alone may be free from every original and actual sin. Or, “stand on the mountain,” that is, in the holy Church, so that you may be the bridegroom of the Church and she may be your bride and wife. It follows:

“And behold, the Lord passes by. And a great spirit overthrowing mountains and breaking rocks before the Lord; but the Lord was not in the spirit. And after the spirit, an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake.” The Lord passes by when he abandoned the evil angels in their pride. They are rightly called mountains because of their exaltation and rocks because of the hardness of their hearts. The Lord overthrew these mountains and shattered these rocks in such a way that those who had been wholly created for glory were wholly consigned to punishment and possess no hope of salvation, since they can never lay aside—and never will to lay aside—their pride and hardness of heart. Nor should we pass over what it says: “before the Lord,” because everywhere they are under the Lord’s scourge. Indeed, it is entirely fitting [Col. 1092C] that those who fell from the glory of such blessedness, not through any necessity but by their will, should always and everywhere be punished by God’s just judgment.

That the whole holy Trinity together overthrew these mountains and shattered these rocks is indicated by these three words: “spirit,” “great,” and “strong.” In the word “great” is great God the Father; in the word “strong” is strong God the Son; and in the word “spirit” is God the Holy Spirit, who together worked in the casting down of the evil angels. But what does the phrase, “the Lord was not in the spirit,” mean except that after the angel’s fall the Son of God did not immediately choose to assume human nature, although it was in the predestination of God the Father?

“And after the spirit, an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake.” What is “after the spirit, an earthquake” except that after the angel’s fall an earthquake occurred in paradise—an exceedingly lamentable earthquake, namely the fall and transgression of the first human being? For it was a great earthquake when humanity touched the forbidden fruit and thereafter slipped from the state of immortality into mortality and sin. But the Lord was not in the earthquake, because, although the human being had been miserably shaken, God still delayed becoming human.

[Col. 1092D] “And after the earthquake, fire; the Lord was not in the fire.” After the angel was moved in heaven and removed from it because of pride, and after humanity was moved in paradise and removed from it because of the guilt of disobedience, fire is described as following in fitting order. By this fire may be signified the punishment of eternal condemnation, prepared for the apostatizing angel and the transgressing human being. But “the Lord was not in the fire,” because although the fire of eternal condemnation punished miserable sinners, and not only the ungodly and sinners but also the righteous—though free from that fire—descended into hell, redemption was still delayed, through which that fire was to be extinguished and entirely removed from the elect.

Fire may also signify the law of Moses, because the law was given in fire. After that disturbance which occurred in paradise over the whole human race, fire followed, because the law was given, by which God began to care for humanity and restrain it somewhat from sins. But when fire came—that is, when the law was given and received—the Lord was not in the fire; because, although he knew and heard the groans and longing of his people awaiting him, the Creator did not yet choose to become creature, nor did the eternal one yet choose to assume temporality.

[Col. 1093B] “And after the fire, a whisper of a gentle breeze; and the Lord was there.” After the first age, which was before the law, and after that age which was under the law, the age of grace came, in which this whisper of a gentle breeze was made. The whisper of a gentle breeze was the Lord’s annunciation, when that highest archangel Gabriel, messenger of the most glorious birth, was sent to the blessed Virgin Mary. Then he uttered a sweet whisper when he said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women. Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (Luke I.28, 31). Truly the Lord was there; there was the Son long desired and awaited by all the nations, because through the angel’s word the blessed Virgin Mary conceived the Son of God and felt in her womb the most sweet weight of him whom heaven and earth cannot contain. Hence what follows is fitting:

“When Elijah heard it, he covered his face and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave.” When the Son of God in heaven heard the whisper of this gentle breeze—that is, the Word of God the Father sent through the angel to the Virgin who was to give birth—he covered the face of his divinity with the mantle of humanity; and having gone out, that is, having been born into this world, he stood at the entrance of the cave. By the entrance you may understand humanity, and by the cave divinity. Nor is humanity unfittingly understood by the entrance and divinity by the cave. For as one enters a house through its entrance and the inner parts of the house are opened through the entrance, so through the open entrance of humanity we come and press forward to the knowledge of divinity.

[Col. 1093D] Because he went out—that is, because he became human, so that the same one might be Redeemer who was also Creator—he therefore stood at the entrance of the cave, so that the nature created by him, having considered and recognized his humanity, might learn to love the excellence of divinity that was hidden from it.

When he had thus gone out and was thus standing at the entrance of the cave, behold, again a voice said to him: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” This voice is the voice of God the Father and of the Son himself in his divinity, speaking to assumed humanity: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” That is to say: “O Son equal to me, of the same substance and the same glory, attend and consider why you have gone out from the Father’s bosom. See that the hatred of ancient time which was between God and human beings may be destroyed, and that the peace long desired may be restored through the noble price of your blood, which you will shed to liberate my children and yours.”

[Col. 1094A] And he—the Son, without doubt—answered the Father: “I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant.” Zeal does not always signify hatred, but love. And just as above we understood by zeal the vengeance and retribution which the Son of God exercised in heaven, so in this place we may understand divine love by zeal. It is as though the Son of God says to the Father: “Your love and affection, by which I have loved and love you, and not love for you only but also love for the human race, made me become incarnate; made me, immutable and immortal, become mutable and mortal. But I have been zealous because the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant: the covenant of obedience which you established for the children of Israel, namely the children of human beings enjoying your vision in paradise. Therefore, overcome by excessive love, I have come to bring them a remedy; I have come to give aid.

“They have destroyed your altars, killed your prophets with the sword, and I alone am left; and they seek my life to take it away.” Above we said that apostate angels may be signified by the altars, and Adam and Eve by the prophets. Here, however, by the altars we may understand the body and soul of the human being; by the sword, the word of the Lord; and by the prophets, the preachers of God’s word. “Humanity,” says the Son of God, “has destroyed these your altars, because it did not preserve its body and soul, which ought to have been your altar, in which the sacrifice of praise ought to have been offered to you alone. It killed your prophets with the sword because it did not show faith in good works to the heralds of your word.

[Col. 1094C] “And I alone am left, who have not destroyed your altars. For I alone am whole and spotless both in body and in soul. I have not killed your prophets, because I kept your word and fulfilled it in deed. And they seek my life to take it away. For all my elect, who descended to hell because of the guilt of the first transgression, mournfully request and seek the descent of my soul into hell. And they seek it in such a way as to take it away—that is, that, separated by the bitterness of death from the midst of my heart and body, it may be drawn to them and come to them, so that with it and through it they may have a free and joyful exit from the prisons of hell.”

“And the Lord said to him: Go, and return by your way through the wilderness to Damascus.” What is “go” except: just as you became human by obeying me, so also go, by obeying me, to Damascus, which is interpreted “drinking blood”; that is, drink the cup of suffering. And when you have drunk the cup of suffering, go through the wilderness: descend, I say, into hell, and make it a wilderness, because, having despoiled it, you will permit none of my people to remain there. And when you have risen from the dead, you shall return by your way. For your way was your descent from heaven to liberate humanity on earth; but when you have accomplished the dispensation for which you came to liberate, you shall return to me by the same way by which you came. For just as you descended to liberate, so you shall return to glorify; and as conqueror you shall sit at my right hand [Col. 1095A], where you shall wonderfully glorify the human nature which you assumed, exalting it above every creature.

“And when you have arrived there, you shall anoint Hazael king over Syria; and you shall anoint Jehu son of Nimshi king over Israel; and Elisha son of Shaphat, who is of Abel-meholah, you shall anoint prophet in your place.” “When you have arrived there,” that is, when, ascending to heaven, you have gloriously accomplished the works for which you came, you ought to anoint and pour out the anointing of the Holy Spirit upon the children of my Church. The names of the three men—Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha—indicate who should be anointed with this anointing. For by these three men may be understood the three orders within the Church, through which the Church endures: the married, the continent, and the prelates.

By Hazael, which is interpreted “seen by the Lord,” good and holy married persons are rightly understood. For those who have lived well and lawfully in married life and have done the good works they could truly are seen by the Lord and are found worthy of God and known to him. Such persons are kings over Syria, which is interpreted “lofty,” because, undoubtedly, governing themselves well, they are kings lofty and exalted before the Lord; and their life is by no means to be despised or scorned. For from such persons is generated that innumerable multitude of saints through which the kingdom of heaven daily grows and increases.

[Col. 1095C] By Jehu, however, which is interpreted “this one” or “is,” continent persons may be understood. The interpretation of “this one” or “is” accords with their merits and dignity, because these are they who tend toward true being, who seek eternal life with all the affections of their hearts; whereas, conversely, those who despise eternal and never-ending goods for the sake of brief and temporal things are as though nothing. These continent, true, and perfect despisers of the deceitful world are sons of Nimshi, which is interpreted “touching,” “feeling,” or “handling,” because, living an angelic life on earth, they are always feeling about to see whether amid the darkness of this world they can touch and discern anything of heavenly things; they are always handling, because they are devoted and ready, so far as they are able, to pass in mind from visible things to invisible things.

For though good married persons are lofty and blessed, these are loftier still: they are pleased, with God’s help, to abstain and guard themselves for love of God not only from unlawful acts but even from lawful ones. Such persons are kings over Israel, which is interpreted “a man seeing God,” because from that lofty vision of the mind, by which they now merit to see God, they strive toward the full and perfect vision of him.

By Elisha, whose name means “salvation of the Lord,” good prelates may be understood, who are called the salvation of the Lord because they ought to announce and preach the salvation of souls. They are those who ought rather to save than destroy the souls of those subject to them. They ought indeed to weigh and consider that they are sons of Shaphat, which is interpreted “judging,” namely, sons of him who is Judge of the living and the dead. And because they have this Judge over them [Col. 1096A], they must administer and judge the matters entrusted to their care in such a way as always to remember that they themselves must be judged before the Lord concerning all their judgments and must answer to God.

They are sons of Shaphat, of Abel, which is interpreted “mourning,” and of Meholah, which echoes “choir.” Of Abel, I say, because they ought always to be in mourning both for themselves and for those subject to them; and of Meholah because they ought to admonish and teach their subjects to belong to the choir of mourners, lamenting their past sins and daily transgressions, and persistently raising frequent laments out of desire for eternal life.

Note that it says, “You shall anoint a prophet in your place,” because in truth every prelate holds in this world the office and place of Christ. They are therefore designated by the name of prophets, because it belongs to them at an opportune time to teach and set forth what is appropriate to each person: how one in married life ought to live, and how one who has vowed to God the purpose of continence ought to keep oneself, so as to please him to whom one has devoted oneself. It follows:

[Col. 1096B] “And it shall be that whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall slay.” One escapes the sword of Hazael who begins to abhor and detest worldly life. And one who so escapes the sword of Hazael that he perfectly abandons the things he detests in the world and takes up the purpose of a higher life—Jehu shall kill him; because, long exercised and tested in spiritual life through the good of continence, he so dies to sins and desires that he no longer lives to sins according to the flesh but lives and walks according to the Spirit. And whoever thus escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall slay him: that is, one who has thus conquered the world and sins is often taken up into a place of governance, so that one who has learned well how to be subject may know how to preside over and benefit others.

[Col. 1096C] But in what follows—“And I shall leave for myself in Israel seven thousand men whose knees have not bent before Baal, and every mouth that has not worshipped him by kissing the hand”—a general consolation is offered to all. By Baal, an idol of shamefulness, the impurity and lust of the flesh may be signified. Those bend their knees before and worship this idol by kissing the hand who have an evil will to sin and do not resist that wicked will, but willingly consent to it and carry it out. Those, however, who are of such perfection that they have never had a will to do wicked and shameful things—though such persons are very few and rare—are in some sense like the seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal. And because they belong to the thousandfold number of men, that is, of the perfect and strong, the Lord leaves them for himself, because he makes such persons co-heirs of his kingdom.

“And every mouth which has not worshipped Baal by kissing the hand”: that is, the Lord leaves for himself not only those who have never had the will to commit shamefulness, but also those who have sinned in will yet have neither loved nor consented [Col. 1097A] **[Note: That is, they did not cling to the will to sin stubbornly and obstinately, nor indulge themselves so much as to proceed to an outward act.]**; rather, they have cleansed themselves through repentance. The Lord leaves these also for himself, because he will not deprive them of the crown of eternal glory.

## Homily VII: First Homily on Chapter XX of the Third Book of Kings

“A certain man of the sons of the prophets said to his companion by the word of the Lord: Strike me,” and so forth. (III Kings XX.)

In this man we may understand any converted and spiritual person, who is said to be one of the sons of the prophets when he begins to be a good subordinate, a good son of the prophets—that is, of good teachers and prelates. This certain man addresses his companion, saying: “Strike me.” The inward and the outward man are two companions. That inward man of ours—namely, the spirit pierced and humbled by God—sometimes addresses his outward companion, that is, his body, saying: “Strike me.” As though he said: “Strike down and kill the pride and arrogance of my mind by your just and unwearied labours. Strike me, because your striking is my striking; and strike me in such a way that what has hitherto lived in me contrary to God may not rise again, but may fall altogether.” But because our outward man, resisting the spirit, always seeks his own softness and whatever outwardly flatters him, he refuses to suffer this blessed striking, as may be observed in what follows.

673 “But he,” it says, “was unwilling to strike him.” To whom he said: “Because you were unwilling to obey the voice of the Lord, behold, you shall depart from [Col. 1097C] me, and a lion shall strike you.” Who is this one unwilling to obey the voice of the Lord speaking inwardly in the human heart, if not the outward man, unwilling to consent to the spirit in doing good? And what is meant by the lion that strikes the man, if not our adversary the devil, who goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour?

Since the flesh resists and is unwilling to yield to the spirit, refusing the striking of blessed mortification, the spirit rightly groans and grieves for its destruction and responds in these words: “Because you, my outward man, were unwilling to obey the voice of the Lord—that is, because you were unwilling to obey the command of one who rightly enjoins and rightly commands—behold, you shall depart from me, unwilling to consent to the spirit, and a lion shall strike you”; that is, the devil will burden you with many sins. Thus, when he departed through disobedience, the lion—namely the malignant spirit—found him consenting to himself, and struck him through evil action, as follows:

“And when he had departed a little way from him, a lion found him and struck him.” It often happens that one departing in this manner is so struck and killed by this lion, namely the devil, that he does not fear even to commit more serious and deadly crimes. Or, if perhaps he does not fall into greater sins, he is nevertheless sometimes inwardly wounded by anger, impatience, drowsiness, or negligence. But when, through the regard of divine mercy, he sees himself wounded and struck in this way and begins at last to know himself, what follows will be salutary:

“But he said to another suitable man: ‘Strike me.’ And he struck and wounded him.” A man is said to encounter another man when he is no longer such as he formerly was, but, made another through God’s mercy, he keeps watch with anxious care over how he may worthily make satisfaction to God. He immediately addresses his companion—namely, the outward man—again, saying: “Strike me”; which is as though he said: “Because you have grievously offended God, because you have grievously sinned before him, now consider how, by killing and mortifying yourself 674 with your vices and desires, you may worthily make satisfaction to the Lord your God, your Creator and Redeemer.” When a man consents to do this and gives all his members over to the perfect measure of penitence and labour, what follows immediately takes place: “He struck and wounded him.” For he inflicts and makes upon himself a good wound: a wound by which he is salutarily wounded—the wound, I mean, of penitence—by which he is wounded, healed, and cured.

“Thus struck, thus wounded, he went away and met the king on the road, changing his mouth and his eyes by a sprinkling of dust.” For a man to go away is to leave all earthly things; to meet the king on the road is, in spiritual life, to please God the King through good conduct. This king signifies God, the highest and best King of angels and men. What is meant by dust, except evil action? By the mouth, except useless speech? By the eyes, except perverse intention?

Therefore, when a man meets this king—that is, when he has committed and prepared his whole self for service to God the King—he is changed by a sprinkling of dust, because whatever filthy dustiness he possessed through evil action, he will, through the aid of divine power, change into good. His mouth too is changed by a sprinkling of dust when he resolves henceforth profitably to change and correct whatever sins he committed through idle and vain speech. And his eyes are changed because he turns the effort of perverse intention toward a will worthy of and pleasing to God. But because we are in great changeableness and live amid the great misery of mutability, it sometimes happens, when a man is thus wounded and thus changed by God’s gift through the sprinkling of dust, that the king passes by, as is added:

“And when the king was passing by, he cried out to the king and said: [Col. 1098D] ‘Your servant went out to fight at close quarters.’” Our heavenly King in a certain sense passes by when, despite a person’s wish and desire, he appears not to hear him. But the good and blessed person ought all the more, with that blind man, to call upon the passing king, that he may deign to stand a little, and cry out that the heavenly King may grant the necessary aid to his soldier, saying: “Your servant went out to fight at close quarters.” 675 That is, he should pray and say: “O Lord, I your servant left the world in order to serve you and to undertake battle and conflict against vices and sins. And because I have gone out to fight, hasten to my help.” The following words aptly correspond to these:

“And when,” he says, “one man had fled, someone brought him to me and said: ‘Guard this man.’” As though he said: “I was one man fleeing from you and from myself. And now someone—that is, my singular spirit—has brought me back to myself and said: ‘Guard this man; for if he slips away, your life shall be for his life, or you shall pay a talent of silver.’”

In the talent, which consists of a full and perfect number, perfect penitence may be signified. This man—that is, every person fleeing from the Lord, withdrawing from himself by sinning, and now brought back by the Spirit of the Lord into the way of upright and holy conduct—rightly hears and diligently obeys the Lord commanding and saying: “Guard this man.” That is to say: “Guard that man which you have now become, and keep yourself under your own guard. For if henceforth you are inclined and liable to sin, your life shall be, not like that of a spiritual man, but for the life of that man—that is, the sinful and worldly man you formerly were—or you shall pay a talent of silver.” That is, you must render the full measure of perfect penitence—not such as you have invented for yourself, but that established for you by the authority of Holy Scripture, which is signified by silver.

Again, by the talent of silver we may understand the two natures in Christ, namely the divine and the human: in the talent, which is made perfect by number, his humanity; in the silver, his divinity. Humanity is fittingly signified in the talent, which is counted and weighed, because he who according to his divine nature receives neither number nor measure, according to his human nature willed first to be a child and then, as age and number of days increased, to become older.

Again, because the utterances of God’s words are understood by silver, we may understand by silver the Son of God, who is the Word of God the Father. A person pays that talent of silver whenever he presumes to receive, for the salvation of his soul and remission of all his sins, the price of the world—the great and inestimable price, namely the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—and trusts that all the burdens of his sins are loosed by the weight of that incomparable price, praying and saying within himself: “I pray, Lord, that this price of your body and blood may continually intercede with you for me.” What fruit and what grace follow upon the reception of this divine sacrament and the penitence of a contrite and humbled heart is aptly added:

“While,” he says, “I was troubled and turned myself this way and that, suddenly he did not appear.” This disturbance signifies the sorrow of penitence, in which a person turns this way and that, anxiously examining and considering what he has sinned against in spiritual life, and, troubled and distressed in heart, diligently reflecting on what sins he committed while living in the world. Thus, by God’s gift, after turning this way and that, he suddenly does not appear, because he is no longer such as he was before in sinning, but has become good and praiseworthy, cleansed before God through penitence and satisfaction.

“And the king of Israel said to him: ‘This is your judgment, which you yourself have decreed.’” These are words of divine consolation and mercy, by which he deigns to encourage and raise up every sinner to hope for and obtain pardon. “This,” he says, “is your judgment, which you yourself have decreed,” as though he said: “Because you have judged yourself and have never wished to spare yourself in making satisfaction, you shall by no means be judged by me as a sinful and fallen person; but you shall be held before me as a just and innocent person, and you shall be rewarded with my goods in eternal life.” After these consoling words of the Lord, there fittingly follows:

“But he immediately wiped the dust from his face, and the king of Israel recognized that he was one of the prophets.” By dust may be signified the activity of this present life; by face, knowledge—that is, love—of God. A man whom God predestined for eternal life is known by God—that is, loved—while he still remains in the world and in sins. But when he has departed from the world and its desires, he is known more fully, because through good works he is loved more and more by the Lord his God. Having wiped away, in death, the activity of this present life, he proceeds to another activity, which will by no means be laborious, but forever delightful, pleasant, gracious, and without weariness. The Psalmist commends this praiseworthy activity when he says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you for ever and ever” (Ps. 83:5).

[Col. 1100C] In that pleasant activity of praise, every elect person is known and loved more specially and intimately, because then he has laid aside the body in which he could not avoid the works of sin; for the corruptible body weighs down the soul. But then, when every corruption has been taken away in death, it is recognized that he was one of the prophets. For he was himself a useful and good prophet to himself when he always strove to prophesy to himself concerning the future joys of life and the impending torments of Gehenna. And therefore he is then recognized, because, loved and acknowledged by the Lord, he is not deprived of the reward of eternal blessedness for which he laboured. It follows:

“Who said to him: ‘Thus says the Lord: Because you have released a man worthy of death, your life shall be for [Col. 1100D] his life, and your people for his people.’” To say this is God’s saying is the saying and thanksgiving of a person who gives thanks to God, his Creator and Deliverer, at the hour of death for all his benefits, saying: “Because you have released a man worthy of death”—that is, “I, a sinner, I, an unjust man, was worthy to be punished by your hand, that is, by your power, with everlasting death. But because you released me—that is, forgave me my sins—your life shall be for my life: your holy soul, which you gave for me in death, shall be for all my sins, not only those which by your gift I have known and confessed, but also those which I have not yet been able to know and recognize. And your people—that is, your holy angels, your servants—shall intercede and aid for his people, namely for the multitude of [Col. 1101A] my sins.”

And because, at the death of every person, malignant spirits are present, casting before him the sins that he has committed, and also alleging many things he never did—or, if he did perform them in deed, things he nevertheless washed away by the tears of penitence—the following is rightly and suitably added:

“Therefore the king of Israel returned, disdaining to listen.” When the malignant spirits come, the compassionate and merciful Lord is also present, hearing their criminal accusations with which they abuse and ensnare the elect person, in order to drag him by their false charges with themselves into the abyss of despair and delay and hinder him from the path of the heavenly homeland. Thus, when the Lord’s chosen bishop Martin was departing from this world, a malignant spirit came with his own to meet him and tried to detain him with the wicked angels; finding nothing of his own in Martin, he finally departed in confusion. Thus, at the departure of every elect soul, the malignant enemy seeks what is his in it and, finding nothing, makes many false and criminal accusations. But the kindly Lord disdains to hear these false and unjust charges and returns, together with the elect soul to be crowned forever, to his own house—namely, the heavenly Jerusalem, the vision of peace.

The following words show what kind of judge he will be for the reprobate, having become so good and faithful a rewarder of the elect:

“And,” Scripture says, “he came in a rage to Samaria.” By Samaria, which is interpreted “she-ass,” may be signified those who live carnally. Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ, the heavenly King, will come in fury to Samaria when, in his severe judgment, he comes for the condemnation of those who now live animal-like and carnally in the manner of asses. To them he appears as though enraged, when rebuking them in his wrath he commands them to go into the fire of eternal damnation. May Jesus Christ our Lord, the Bridegroom of the Church, who is blessed for ever, deliver us from that curse. Amen.

679 HOMILY VIII. FIRST HOMILY ON CHAPTER VI OF THE BOOK OF TOBIT.

“Tobias went out to wash his feet; and behold, a huge fish came out to devour him,” etc. (Tobit 4).

[Col. 1101D] By Tobias we may understand the only-begotten Son of God the Father; by his feet, the teachers of Holy Church. He went out when he went out from the Father and came into the world, in order to wash his feet: namely, those feet by which he walks and goes, of which Habakkuk says: “The devil shall go forth before his feet” (Hab. 3:5). As we have said, by the Lord’s feet may chiefly be understood the holy apostles and the other teachers of truth, who preached and announced the word of God throughout the ends of the earth. For this purpose, therefore, he went out; for this purpose he assumed human nature: that he might wash those feet, that he might cleanse the teachers of his faith from all original sin through baptism. When the Son of God made such an exit, what the text immediately adds came to pass:

[Col. 1102A] “And behold, a huge fish came out to devour him.” A fish is often understood both in a good and in an evil sense. For sometimes Christ, sometimes the devil, is understood by the fish. Hence concerning this same fish, namely the devil, the Lord says to blessed Job: “Those who are ready to rouse Leviathan” (Job 3:8), signifying the devil by Leviathan; for Leviathan is a certain kind of fish. Therefore, in this place too the devil may fittingly be understood by the huge fish. He came out to devour the Son of God when he saw him clothed in tender limbs and surrounded by mortal weakness; and, because he did not at all recognize the power of his divine majesty, he thought that he could devour him, just as before his coming he had drawn and swallowed nearly the entire river of the human race into his belly.

[Col. 1102B] He also came out to devour him through Herod, his member, who at the beginning of Christ’s birth began to persecute him, wishing to kill him. For when 680 he saw that he had been mocked by the Magi, he sent to Bethlehem and killed all boys of the suspected age (Matt. 2), hoping that among the boys of the same age he might also kill the very author of life.

“Terrified, Tobias cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Lord, it is attacking me.’” How did the Son of God fear this huge fish, namely Herod, a member of the devil? He in a certain way showed himself afraid when he fled from Herod’s face into Egypt, though, had he wished, he could have remained hidden beneath Herod’s eyes and escaped unharmed. He was also afraid in this way: just as he possessed human nature, so he willed also to possess human fear. For the Lord’s fear was a sign of the future fear which his elect would suffer in time of persecution. He fled also as an example to his faithful, whom he later openly taught, saying: “When they persecute you in this city, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23).

“And he cried out,” it says, “with a loud voice, saying: ‘Lord, it is attacking me.’” It was a kind of great cry and outcry that, when he saw the Jews plotting against him and desiring to inflict death upon him, he avoided their plots by hiding himself, as the Evangelist John says: “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (John 8:59). And again: “But Jesus, passing through their midst, went away” (Luke 4:30). And what he said, “Lord, it is attacking me,” means that his divinity did not will that his humanity should be attacked and killed, because, although his hour was coming, it was not yet time for him to accomplish, through his passion and death, the work of human redemption for which he had come.

“And the angel said: ‘Take hold of its gill [manuscript: *branciam*], and draw it to yourself.’” These words are in a certain sense the words of Christ’s divinity speaking to his humanity: “Take hold of the gill of that huge fish, namely the devil, who wishes to devour you, who wishes to attack you, by piercing his jaw through your cross and passion and by drawing your elect, whom he has swallowed from the beginning, out of his mouth.”

And because a fish expels outward through its gill all the water it has taken into its mouth, we may fittingly understand penitence by the gill.
