For many who entered the mouths of Leviathan by sinning have deserved, through God’s mercy, to come out through penitence. Hence it is written: “Leviathan’s jaw is pierced by a ring” (Job 40:21). Through the opening in this jaw Mary Magdalene and countless others have been drawn out, and are daily drawn out—those who, through penitence after sins committed, deserve to return to innocence.

But, since so many are saved through penitence, as has been said, why is it called his gill—that is, his penitence—when he envies the salvation of all people who desire to be saved through penitence? It is called his penitence because, when by his persuasion he causes a person to be subject to sins and vices, he in a certain manner causes that person to repent and to need penitence. For if a person did not sin, he would have no need at all of penitence.

When the true Tobias, namely the only-begotten Son of God the Father, thus takes hold of the gill of this huge fish—when, by the ring piercing Leviathan’s jaw, he has snatched all who are to be saved from his jaws—Scripture consequently adds:

“And draw it to yourself.” To draw penitents to himself is, by the sweetness of inward love, to make more devoted and ready for himself those whom he deigned, through penitence, to draw out of Leviathan’s mouth after they had been wickedly swallowed by sinning. For the more gravely a person recognizes that he has sinned against God, the more ardently, after penitence has been performed and the grace of forgiveness received, he burns with love for him. And the more carefully he considers in his mind what he has escaped through God’s mercy, the more truly he understands himself to be indebted to his Deliverer.

Mary Magdalene burned strongly with the fire of this love, and in her was fulfilled that word of Truth: “Many sins have been forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:46). So too Paul, after through God’s mercy he was changed from a persecutor into a chosen vessel, became so devoted to God and so inflamed with the fire of divine love that, as he himself says of himself, he laboured more than all the apostles in the word of preaching. It follows:

“When he had done this, he drew it onto dry land, and it began to flop before his feet.” When a fish is in a river, it swims vigorously here and there through the depths of the water; but when it comes onto dry land, it lies upon the ground as though without strength and flops about. By this dry land may fittingly be signified first the dry and clean hearts of the holy apostles, then those of all the elect. The Lord Jesus dried them by the fire of his Spirit from every flow of carnal desire, so that that fish, the ancient serpent, was unable to exercise any power in them. Rather, in them was rightly fulfilled what is immediately added: “And it began to flop before his feet.”

The devil begins in a certain sense to flop before the Lord’s feet—that is, before the elect who are his feet—when, through subtle suggestions, he seeks to instil carnal impulses into them, by which he does not cease to assault and attack them as long as they remain in this mortal body. But because he finds their hearts dry and barren of carnal desires, he will be unable to live and swim vigorously in them—that is, to exercise those powers of his malice by which he might incline them to deadly sins.

“And the angel said: ‘Gut this fish, and keep for yourself its heart, gall, and liver.’” By the devil’s heart may rightly be understood his cunning; by his gall, his malice; by his liver, his impurity. For his cunning, which is understood by the heart, is so manifold, subtle, and countless that no person, however wise or prudent, can know or be able in any way to guard himself against it. For the devil secretly and subtly creeps into the hearts of the elect and so craftily insinuates himself into their thoughts that he is scarcely, or not at all, recognized unless the grace of divine protection deigns to be present with them. Concerning this manifold cunning the Lord says, speaking to blessed Job: “The archer shall not put him to flight” (Job 41:19). And again: “He will laugh at the brandished spear” (ibid., 20). And shortly afterward: “He will treat gold as mud beneath him” (ibid., 21).

To this cunning of the devil succeeds his infinite and perpetual malice, by which he persecutes all people, good and evil, created in God’s image and likeness, and strives by every means to prevent them from reaching the kingdom of heaven, from which he himself was cast out. For he rages against all people with such envy and hatred that he can never be sated with their destruction. If he casts someone down by a thousand crimes, it does not satisfy him unless he persuades that person to sins yet greater and more serious, through which he may, if God permits, make him subject to eternal damnation. Through this cunning and malice the devil attempts to drive a person to impurity. And although he gains many for himself through various sins and vices and makes them companions in his destruction, he nevertheless causes the greatest part of those who perish to go to destruction through the impurity of the flesh.

And he fittingly says: “Keep [these] for yourself,” because every faithful person ought to store all these things which we have mentioned in his heart, so that with every care and vigilance he may always strive to defend himself against these wickednesses and temptations of the devil. Hence there appropriately follows at once:

“For these are usefully necessary for medicine.” It is indeed a great medicine for the soul, very useful and necessary, if a person so stores within himself the things mentioned above that, as far as possible by God’s gift, he keeps himself from them. Therefore, when a person thus guards against the devil’s cunning, malice, and impurity, what the ensuing text immediately indicates takes place in him: “And he roasted its flesh, and they took it with them on the journey; they salted the rest, enough to suffice them until they reached Rages, the city of the Medes.”

[Note: [Col. 1103D] Thus the homily ends in the manuscript.]

684 HOMILY IX. FIRST HOMILY ON CHAPTER XXX OF PROVERBS.

“There are three things that are insatiable, and a fourth that never says: ‘Enough’: hell, and the mouth of the womb, and earth, which is not [Col. 1105A] satisfied with water; but fire never says: ‘Enough’” (Prov. 30).

The eternal goodness of God, beholding with the eye of his mercy the misery of human mortality, has set before us in this place three insatiable things, and a fourth that never says: “Enough”: namely hell, the mouth of the womb, earth that is not satisfied with water, and fire that never says: “Enough.” And because the first insatiable thing, namely hell, is never filled with evils, while the second, third, and fourth are never perfectly filled with goods in the present life, he has set these three insatiable things, which cannot here be filled with good things, in opposition to that first insatiable thing which always insatiably desires evil; but in the future they shall rejoice in full satisfaction from the Lord’s good things.

[Col. 1105B] By insatiable hell we may fittingly understand him who goes about like a roaring lion, seeking those whom he may devour and torment eternally with himself in hell. In the present life he is not sated with harassing people; in the future he will not be sated with their destruction. The devil is fittingly compared to insatiable hell, because, just as in hell there is everlasting horror and everlasting darkness, so the devil too is always and everywhere wholly dark, wholly horrible and terrifying. And just as hell is never perfectly filled by the multitude of the damned, so the devil’s insatiable greed can never be fully satisfied by the deception and destruction of souls. Since he is not only insatiable but also very strong and unconquerable, who could escape his bloody jaws unharmed, unless divine goodness had set against him the second insatiable thing that follows?

“And,” he says, “the mouth of the womb.” By this womb, then, we may fittingly understand the womb of Holy Mother Church, in which we who believe in Christ are conceived through faith and regenerated to eternal life through the sacrament of baptism. By the mouth of this womb may fittingly be expressed the mouth of every good preacher, which cannot easily be sated with teaching, preaching, and exhorting. For every good preacher, hungering and thirsting for the salvation of souls, strives through the word of constant exhortation to carry into the womb of this mother those alienated from the womb of the aforesaid Mother Church, whom that insatiable devil seeks to devour and destroy, so that the same mother may spiritually conceive and bring forth through penitence those who had been alienated and rejected from her through sin. Thus, while that mouth—the mouth, I mean, of the good teacher—cannot be satisfied with preaching, the third insatiable thing follows, concerning which he immediately says:

“And earth, which is not satisfied with waters.” By the earth that is not satisfied with waters may fittingly be understood the truly penitent person, who humbly recognizes himself as earth and ashes. When admonished by the preacher’s voice, he has recognized that, by despising God and loving only earthly and transitory things, he has wickedly and fruitlessly spent the time of his life. He cannot in a certain sense be satisfied with waters, because, in order to blot out the sins he has committed, he strives to have not momentary but continual tears of penitence. Hence the fourth insatiable thing follows, of which he immediately says:

“But fire never says: ‘Enough.’” By the fire that never says “Enough” we rightly believe that the fire of divine love is understood, which kindles and illumines the heart of the truly penitent. Yet this fire never says “Enough” in the present life, because a person, however perfect, will never attain in this life to the full sufficiency of divine love. This insatiable fire begins to burn a little in the hearts of the elect here, and when they see him whom they love, it shall burn with full sufficiency without end.

686 HOMILY X. SECOND HOMILY ON THE SAME CHAPTER OF PROVERBS.

[Col. 1106B]

“There are three things difficult to me, and a fourth I utterly do not know: the way of an eagle in the sky; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; the way of a man in youth” (Prov. 30).

Because the way that leads to true joys is exceedingly narrow and steep, Solomon the wisest—or rather, through Solomon, the eternal wisdom of God—describes for us in this place three difficult things through which this same narrow and confined way must be traversed: the way of an eagle in the sky, that is, the life of a person in conversion; the way of a serpent upon a rock, that is, the life of a person in mortification of the flesh; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea, that is, the life of a person in the practice of virtues. The fourth thing, however, which is wholly unknown, is the life of a person in contemplation of mind or in eternal reward.

The way of an eagle in the sky occurs when a converted person, loving heavenly things and despising earthly things, begins, as it were, to fly by good thoughts and holy desires toward that place which he strives at last to reach by just labours and upright works. Nor is the life of the well-converted person unfittingly prefigured by the way of an eagle flying upward, because, while he is lifted up on high through the flight of heavenly desires, despising all things, renewed in the spirit of his mind he will be renewed in Christ after the likeness of the eagle. For, putting off the old man with his deeds, through the grace of good conversion he grows young in the new man. When he has thus become an imitator of the eagle through conversion, it remains for him also to traverse the way of the serpent through mortification of the flesh. Hence follows:

“The way of a serpent upon a rock.” By the way of the serpent moving upon a rock may fittingly be understood the life of the truly penitent person, who humbly lays the foundation of himself upon the rock, which is Christ, and vigorously dashes against that same rock the sins now past through mortification of the flesh—vigorously, I say, in such a way that he makes worthy satisfaction to God by penitence for them, so that on the day of final judgment he may experience not this most severe judge but the most kindly defender. Therefore, when he has traversed the way of the serpent in this manner through mortification of the flesh, he must also traverse the way of the ship through the practice of virtues.

687 “The way,” he says, “of a ship in the midst of the sea.” The way of a ship is spiritual conduct. Nor do we believe that spiritual conduct is unfittingly understood by the ship. For just as sailors customarily make their way more safely toward the shore of the sea in a material ship, so spiritual sailors, labouring in the vessel of holy conduct, strive through the practice of good and virtuous works toward the grace of true perfection.

“In the midst,” he says, “of the sea”: in the midst of the sea, namely amid the waves of temptations and amid adversity as well as prosperity, the life and conduct of the converted person fluctuates. Therefore he must humbly keep himself in the middle between prosperity and adversity, lest he rejoice excessively in prosperity or, excessively fearful, be gravely terrified by adversity. When he has securely passed the way of the ship in the midst of the sea through the practice of virtues, it remains for him to enter the way of a man in youth through contemplation of mind.

“And,” he says, “the way of a man in youth.” By the way of a man in youth are to be understood the joys not only of inward contemplation but also of eternal reward. And each—the contemplation of the mind and the reward of heavenly life—is fittingly a kind of youth that, so to speak, never grows old. For in the hour of divine contemplation the inward person, previously grown old in sins, receives the youth of holy newness; but in eternal reward no old age ever comes upon the inward person.

It should be noted, moreover, that when he first marked out three difficult things—the way of the eagle, the way of the serpent, and the way of the ship—he immediately added the fourth, namely the way of a man in youth, which nevertheless he said he utterly did not know. These three difficult things are not altogether unknown to all truly penitent persons; but the fourth, namely what and of what kind is the way of a man in youth, is known by the experience of few. For although some feel the joys of inward sweetness in the secret place of the heart, they nevertheless cannot clearly express in words how great and how vast they are. And what shall I say of the ineffable glory of eternal reward, which no eye has seen and which no one can know except the one who receives it? It follows:

[Col. 1107D] Such also is the way of the adulterous woman, who eats and, wiping her mouth, says: “I have done no evil.” Such is—or rather, such ought to be—the way, that is, the life, of the adulterous woman: the life of the sinful soul which, by living wickedly, has committed adultery against the Lord. It should strive, through good conversion, mortification of the flesh, and the practice of virtues, to fulfil those three difficult things of which we spoke, and thus attain that fourth thing: contemplation of the mind or eternal recompense. “Who eats,” he says, “and, wiping her mouth, says: ‘I have done no evil.’” This blessed and chosen woman, when she remembers that she was once adulterous, wretched, and sinful, eats the food of sweetness and salvation amid bitterness of heart.

[Col. 1108A] For at times she refreshes herself with the bread of tears, the bread of sorrow and repentance. Thus, eating happily and restoring herself wholesomely, she wipes her mouth—her mouth, that is, of heart and body—with the continual tears of repentance. Whatever she has sinned through will and deed, she blots out and wipes away before the eyes of the supreme Judge by worthy satisfaction. Therefore, on the day of her departure from the body, when those malignant spirits press upon her with fierce cruelty by accusing, terrifying, and threatening her, and seek forcibly to drag her with them to torments as though she were adulterous, unclean, and defiled, she answers boldly in a free and confident voice: “I have done no evil.” “The evil,” she says, “which I did at your prompting and evil persuasion is no longer evil,

[Col. 1108B] because God has turned it to good; and what I did not deserve to possess through innocence, his surpassing grace has now deigned to confer on me through repentance. Therefore you will not carry me away as an adulterous woman to be tormented with you forever, because, through God’s mercy and his merciful forgiveness of the sins I committed, you will find nothing true in me.”

689  
## HOMILY XI. THIRD HOMILY ON THE SAME CHAPTER OF PROVERBS

“By three things the earth is moved, and by a fourth which it cannot bear: by a slave when he becomes king; by a fool when he is filled with food; by a hateful woman when she is taken in marriage; by a handmaid when she becomes heir to her mistress” (Prov. 30).

The eternal Wisdom of God, which alone knows and is able to have mercy upon human miseries,

[Col. 1108C] sets before us in this passage three great works of its mercy, which it also accomplishes in this life through the hidden grace of its visitation in saving its own people; and a fourth which it will accomplish in them in the glory of eternal blessedness.

“By three,” he says, “the earth is moved.” By “earth” one may fittingly understand the earthly human being who loves earthly things, who, through God’s mercy, is moved from earthly to heavenly things in three ways: first, by a slave when he becomes king; second, by a fool when he is filled with food; third, by a hateful woman when she is taken in marriage; fourth, by a handmaid when she becomes heir to her mistress. By this slave we rightly believe that our spirit is signified,

[Col. 1108D] which is deservedly called a bad and ungrateful slave when it does not shrink from being the slave of many vices. Yet, through God’s mercy, it begins to reign well and happily when it passes from the kingdom of sin to the kingdom of righteousness. When this happy inward passage has taken place through the spirit, the earthly human being—the outward human being—then resolves to be moved in this way, namely, to strive to turn away from the evils in which he had long lain, as though motionless. Having first been moved, through the slave now reigning well, to turn aside from evils, as has been said, it remains that he must also be moved a second time, through the fool to be filled with food, to do good things. Hence follows:

“By a fool, when he is filled with food.” By this fool nothing is more rightly understood than the aforesaid

[Col. 1109A] spirit of ours, which must truly be called foolish when it serves the creature rather than the 690 Creator, when, despising God its maker, it loves only passing and perishable things. Once it has recognized this folly through God’s mercy, it must be filled with a twofold food: namely, repentance and instruction, so that through repentance it may make worthy satisfaction to God for the evils it has committed, and through instruction may learn to guard itself against future evils. Notice that it is not merely to be refreshed but filled with such food. For only those are refreshed who hear the word with sweetness and gladness of heart, yet neglect to fulfil in deeds what they have heard; and those who are for an hour contrite for their sins, yet disdain to mourn and weep for them perfectly.

[Col. 1109B] But if the spirit, reigning well and truly recognizing its folly, has been filled with this twofold food of repentance and instruction, then the outward human being begins again to be moved a third time through the hateful woman, of whom he consequently says:

“By a hateful woman, when she is taken in marriage.” By this hateful woman we may understand the true virtue of humility. Yet it is quite remarkable why the virtue of humility should be compared to a hateful woman, when this same virtue seems to be, as it were, the mother of all virtues. This is easily understood, however, if we consider what we said above: that by the slave and by the fool our spirit is to be understood. As long as this spirit does not refuse to be a slave of vices, and as long as it has not recognized

[Col. 1109C] its folly, it will also regard this woman of such great nobility—that is, humility—as hateful. But after it has passed into the kingdom of righteousness, ceased to be foolish, and been filled with the twofold food of repentance and instruction, it eagerly desires to unite itself, in hope of begetting offspring, with this 691 most noble woman—that is, humility—whom it formerly hated.

When she is taken in marriage in faithful wedlock, held and loved with steadfast mind, a manifold and noble progeny of heavenly desires and good thoughts is born from so noble a mother. Thus the outward human being also, displaying the sign of humility in bearing and gait, words and deeds, begins to be moved toward that fourth thing, of which he immediately says:

[Col. 1109D] “By a handmaid when she becomes heir to her mistress.” By the handmaid who becomes heir to her mistress may here be understood any happy and faithful soul, which now labours, sighs, and longs in its due service that it may one day possess the inheritance of its mistress: that is, the heavenly Jerusalem. Then indeed, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words, “the eyes of the handmaid” (Ps. 123:2)—that is, of every chosen soul—will be so fixed “upon the hands of her mistress” (ibid.) that she may behold and see without end the splendour of the eternal vision and the joys of the heavenly peace; nor will the gaze of her inward mind ever again turn back to see or experience the miseries of this mortality.

Therefore it should be observed that, after first naming these three things

692  
through which the earth—that is, the slave, the fool, and

[Col. 1110A] the hateful woman—is to be moved, he immediately adds and says, declaring that fourth thing, namely the handmaid:

“And by a fourth which it cannot bear.” That fourth thing is the ineffable and inexpressible joy in which the faithful handmaid—that is, the blessed and chosen soul—rejoices, where it can endure no affliction or adversity. For what can it endure there, where no pain, adversity, tribulation, or distress is ever present? Once it has received the glory of blessed immortality and the inheritance of the heavenly homeland, there will be a perpetual inability to endure evils, a perpetual omnipotence to do nothing evil, and an inability to suffer anything harsh, rough, or adverse.

But in the present life, whether he wishes it or not, wretched man always has the opportunity to endure evils. For what can he endure in this valley of tears, this place of misery,

[Col. 1110B] except evil and misery, where no evil, adversity, pain, or distress is lacking? May the very Author of all good grant that we may deserve to come there, where there is no pain, misery, or distress, but everlasting joy, everlasting glory, and gladness—he who lives and reigns without end. Amen.

## HOMILY XII. FIRST HOMILY ON CHAPTER I OF ECCLESIASTICUS

“All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him, and is before him” (Ecclus. 1).

Having read through the books of Kings, we now read the Sunday lessons from those books which we call the books of Wisdom. These are rightly called the books of Wisdom because the most wise Solomon, than whom no human being before him was wiser,

[Col. 1110C] composed them under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. They are also rightly called books of Wisdom because, although all sacred Scripture instructs and teaches human conduct and life, in these books it has especially set forth a certain rule of uprightness, through which it has fully taught each person what to do and what to avoid.

For this reason, the book which we now read, although it was not composed by the most wise Solomon as the preceding three were, is nevertheless most rightly called a book of Wisdom, as is plainly shown in the opening of that book. For the first verse declares the faith of the holy Trinity; the second clearly sets forth the three periods through which the present world runs its course; and the third plainly indicates the three orders within the Church: the continent, the married, and the prelates.

“Every,” he says, “wisdom is from the Lord God.” By the phrase “every wisdom,” our Lord Jesus 693

[Col. 1110D] Christ may fittingly be understood. In saying not simply “wisdom,” but in a manner of speaking distinctly “every wisdom,” he intended it to be understood that all fullness of wisdom dwelt in him not only according to his divinity but also according to his human nature. This same every wisdom is from the Lord God: from the Lord, namely the eternal Father; and from God, that is, the Holy Spirit. For according to his divinity he is eternally begotten from the Lord the Father; but according to his humanity he was temporally conceived by God the Holy Spirit, as we, instructed in the Catholic faith, sing daily:

[Col. 1111A] “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit.”

Moreover, in the following words, “and has always been with him,” we may understand the eternity of his divinity, in which he was always coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father, in which nothing was ever added to him and nothing ever departed from him. For he was never greater and never lesser.

But in the words, “and is before the age,” Christ’s humanity may fittingly be understood, in which he began to possess the course of temporality and, advancing in age, willed to pass from childhood to youth and from youth to mature age. This is the Catholic faith which we must preserve whole and inviolate: that we should faithfully

[Col. 1111B] and firmly believe in Christ’s divinity and humanity. For if anyone should give his body to be burned but did not have this faith, it would profit him nothing (1 Cor. 13). For this is the foundation of which the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11).

Whatever any faithful person builds upon this foundation by good works will be acceptable and pleasing to the Lord. But if he also builds upon it wood, hay, and stubble, which are venial sins, these will either be cleansed here by the fire of repentance or consumed hereafter in purgatorial fire; and he himself, by virtue of the foundation, will be saved, yet as through fire (ibid. XIV, 15). We have briefly surveyed these matters concerning the glory of the supreme Trinity and the profession of the Catholic faith in the first verse.

[Col. 1111C] Now let us consider, in the following verse, the three periods of this age:

“Who has counted the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age?”

694  
By the sand of the sea, which is indeed abundant but unfruitful, the people who existed before the Law may fittingly be understood: they were numerous indeed, but brought forth no fruit of righteousness worthy of God. For we may clearly perceive how few in that period pleased God by right faith or good works from the fact that, when the Lord willed to destroy all flesh upon the earth by the flood, he found in the whole world no righteous persons except the eight souls who were saved in the ark. Yet not all those saved in the ark were perfect before God.

[Col. 1111D] For one of them, namely Ham, by mocking his father, deserved from his own father the curse that made him a servant of his brothers. Thus he himself could not undeservedly be counted among the sand.

What the ancient fathers under the Law were like is clearly indicated in the following words: “and the drops,” he says, “of rain.” Drops of rain are small and scanty, but they water the earth and make it germinate. So too, those who served God under the Law were few in comparison with those who now serve God.

Therefore, when the period of the Law that had been received had passed, and the time of the new Law arrived—that is, of grace and truth—there succeeded in the Church persons so eminent and outstanding in faith and merit

[Col. 1112A] that it may rightly be said of it: “And who has counted the days of the age?” By “the days of the age” the holy apostles are especially to be understood; by their faith, miracles, and teaching the whole Church was enlightened. Although the patriarchs and prophets did much and taught much, the creed of faith alone, which the holy apostles taught, is of greater value than all these things and more necessary to human salvation.

Having briefly expounded the first and second verses, he encompasses in the third verse the three orders through whom and in whom the holy Church consists.

“Who has measured the height of heaven, the breadth of earth, and the depth of the abyss?” By the height of heaven the life of the continent, by the breadth of earth the life of the married, and by the depth of the abyss the order of prelates may rightly be understood.

[Col. 1112B] The life of the continent may rightly be taken through the height of 695 heaven, because as far as heaven in its height is from earth, so far is the life of the continent from the common life of secular people. Their manner of life is, in a sense, in heaven: though placed in the flesh, they live apart from the flesh, and amid the allurements of this age they strive to lead an angelic life. What wonder is it for angels to live chastely, since no corruptible body weighs them down and no fleshly allurement or fleshly desire attacks them? But it is a great and admirable thing, very hard and difficult, that a mortal and fragile human being—indeed, flesh and blood—whom earthly dwelling weighs down and fleshly pleasure assails, can so rule his body that he tames and restrains every fleshly desire by strength of mind.

[Col. 1112C] Therefore, the more great labour and sweat are required to accomplish this, the more gloriously and splendidly the one who accomplishes it will be crowned and rewarded by the Lord. But since not everyone can attain this perfection, the words that follow clearly express the life of secular people.

“And the breadth,” he says, “of the earth.” By the breadth of the earth the life of married people may be expressed, because they have increased and multiplied beyond number. For although the continent and those who have renounced this world appear numerous, they are considered few in comparison with those who lead a secular life. Although these also love the things of the world, because they live lawfully and make use of lawful marriage, they will at the end be saved through God’s mercy.

[Col. 1112D] But because neither the continent nor the married can know what they ought to do without prelates and teachers of truth, the words which follow indicate the dignity of prelates:

“And the depth,” he says, “of the abyss—who has measured it?” By the abyss we may understand sacred Scripture. In this abyss holy teachers, searching and investigating, discover how they ought to preside over both orders—the continent and the married—and how by their life and teaching they may lead them with themselves to eternal life.

696  
He indicates these three orders of which we have spoken when the Lord speaks through the prophet: “Though Noah, Daniel,

[Col. 1113A] and Job should be in the midst of my people, they by their righteousness shall give life to their own souls” (Ezek. 14:14). Noah, who presided over the steering of the ark in the flood, represents the figure of prelates. For every prelate must strive to govern the souls of those subject to him so that they do not perish in the flood of this age.

Daniel, who by living chastely and leading a celibate life deserved such dignity from the Lord that, being made privy to God’s secrets, he could even foresee and foretell future things, fittingly signifies those who, pursuing chastity and virginal life and despising the pleasures of the age, merit from the Lord very many gifts of virtues. Job, however, although by his righteousness he so pleased the Lord that God said there was none like him on earth, nevertheless, because he had a wife and children,

[Col. 1113B] suitably represents the life of those who, living praiseworthily, make use of lawful marriage in the world and thus at last deserve to be saved through God’s mercy.

Who has measured, then, the blessedness and glory of all these—that is, of the continent, the married, and the prelates? Who, I say, can know the measure of the rewards prepared for those found in these orders, except him alone who will be their reward and crown?

Therefore, we who are in that habit and profession by which we seem to have renounced this world and its pleasures should labour in every way to be found one day in our proper place and order, and deserve to be counted among those who are worthily called the height of heaven; through the help of our Lord

[Col. 1113C] Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

697  
## HOMILY XIII. FIRST HOMILY ON CHAPTER VI OF THE PROPHET ISAIAH

“I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the whole earth was full of his majesty, and the things that were beneath him filled the temple,” etc. (Isa. 4).

The holy and chosen prophet of the Lord, Isaiah, to whom the Holy Spirit deigned to reveal very many mysteries of divine secrets, relates, among the other things he sets forth concerning Christ and the Church, in what great glory he saw the Lord, saying: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne.” This vision was a great and exalted vision.

[Col. 1113D] Yet he saw this vision not for himself alone but for us also. For today, and until the end of the age, all who are to attain the future vision of Almighty God ought to behold this vision within themselves by the spiritual gaze of the mind. “I saw,” he says, “the Lord sitting upon a high throne.” By the high throne the human spirit may be understood, which is rightly taken as a high throne because of the excellence of its creation: it was created with great nobility and fashioned and formed in exceeding loftiness.

But what great thing is it that we are a high throne by creation, if we do not also strive to be an exalted throne by divine inspiration? Every rational spirit is indeed a high throne by creation; but not every spirit is an exalted throne through contemplation of the mind.

[Col. 1114A] Therefore every one of the elect who is a high throne by creation must also be an exalted throne through contemplation of the mind. Once made an exalted throne through inward inspiration, he now begins to see the Lord sitting—sitting, that is, within him, remaining and dwelling in his heart. After this splendid exaltation, after this good sitting, what follows comes about in a sublime manner:

698  
“And the whole earth was full of his majesty.” Majesty properly belongs to the power of divinity. And by majesty we may fittingly understand the fear of the Lord. The whole earth becomes full of majesty when the human being is touched inwardly by the fear of God and, by fear of his Creator and Judge, wipes away and cleanses whatever earthly activity he has contracted in heart and body. Thus he trembles with this holy fear, grieving over past things and, insofar as God grants, guarding against future things.

[Col. 1114B] When in this way the whole earth—that is, the earthly heart and body, which once sought nothing other than earthly works—begins through fear of its Creator to withdraw itself from earthly things, it passes from fear to love, as follows:

“And the things that were beneath him filled the temple.” What is this that he says: “And the things that were beneath him filled the temple”? What are the things that were beneath the Lord whom he saw? God the Father himself, who is above all and in all, had certain things in his Son according to his humanity which were beneath him.

[Col. 1114C] For all the works of his humanity were beneath the excellence of his divinity; and all that he did and suffered for humankind fills the temple, because the work of our redemption makes Jesus Christ supremely lovable to us. For when any blessed soul begins to consider and meditate how great was the humility and condescension by which he was willing to be carried nine months in the womb of the blessed Virgin, to be born from her, cherished in her lap, laid in a manger, to endure other infant necessities,

699  
and to become a participant in all our miseries except sin, is not this what more gently draws our devotion, binds it more closely, and more vehemently arouses it to the sweetness of love? Are not these the things which fill the temple

[Col. 1114D] of the heart through the inward affection of love? Are not these the things that blunt our pride, teach humility, and commend humility? For when we have considered the lowliness and humility of our Redeemer, what is fitting except that we should despise ourselves and humble ourselves from the heart, and show outwardly to all people that humility and submission which we hold in the heart?

Understand the same thing by “temple” as by “throne.” For the heart, which is the throne of God through contemplation of the mind, will also be the temple of God if nothing is done in the inward human being except what is customarily done in temples made by hands. There people devote themselves to the praises of God and to prayers. Certainly, according to this likeness, when a human being has become the temple

[Col. 1115A] of God, he will devote himself only to praises, while he regulates and guards everything he does in such a way that everything may be called praise and prayer before God. Thus, elevated by God’s inspiration, touched by fear, moved by sweet love of heart toward the things God accomplished in humankind, and made a temple by the sweetness of prayer—the following words indicate what further grace of God comes to such a person:

“Seraphim,” he says, “stood above it; six wings to one, and six wings to the other.” By the seraphim the two Testaments, Old and New, may be understood. These Testaments stand above that temple because the commandments and ordinances of God, which the Old and New Testament proclaim and teach, establish their place in the higher part of the human being. The words of God and the meditations that were formerly driven away from him begin to remain with him,

[Col. 1115B] so that after the sweetness of prayer he hears nothing more willingly, meditates on nothing more earnestly, reflects upon nothing more sweetly, nor desires to speak of anything more than those things which recall the words of both Testaments and proclaim Christ.

“Six wings to one, and six wings to the other.” What do the six wings signify except faith, hope, and charity; thoughts, works, and words? These six wings belong to the one Testament and six to the other, because each Testament commends these six wings:

700  
faith, hope, and charity, and how we ought to exercise ourselves in good works, be cautious in words, and diligent in thoughts, that by these we may strive not to displease God but rather to please him. But what do these six wings do?

[Col. 1115C] “With two,” he says, “they covered his face; with two they covered his feet; and with two they flew.” Blessed Jerome says that by the face may be understood the beginning of creation, and by the feet the end of that same creation. The beginning of creation was covered because what existed before the beginning is unknown. Its end also is covered because what will occur after the judgment is unknown. But we see the things that now lie between, and cannot fail to know what we see.

Yet in a deeper sense we may refer all these things to ourselves. The two wings which cover the face are the two virtues faith and hope. Since the face is the beginning in a human being, the face rightly signifies human intention, because intention is always the beginning of either good or evil work. Therefore he covers his face with two wings, that is, faith and hope, who resolves no longer to be unfaithful but faithful to the Lord; who faithfully makes satisfaction to the Lord for those things which he committed by evil and unjust intention,

[Col. 1115D] though he did not carry them through to complete consent; and who in prayer supplicates the Lord, now hoping in God’s great mercy that, just as he himself has resolved to turn to God in all faith, so God may preserve faith and mercy for him and mercifully forgive him whenever and wherever he has been found unfaithful through evil thoughts and unlawful desires.

These two wings very well and fittingly cover the face, because, just as the things we think and commit in unlawful pleasures are countless and infinite, so no one can worthily disclose or lay them open in confession. Therefore they must be covered with these two wings—that is,

[Col. 1116A] faith and hope—so that the person who formerly lived unfaithfully in his intention may henceforth live faithfully.

Likewise, the feet must be covered with two wings. By the feet, which are the ends of the body, we may understand the completed act of sin. These feet—that is, the completed work of sin—must be covered with two wings, because after the deed of 701 sin has been committed, speech in confession is necessary, and after confession, action in satisfaction. We must also fly with two wings. The two feathers by which we must fly are charity and full resolve. We fly with the feather of charity when we burn with full and perfect love of God and neighbour; we fly with the feather of full and good resolve when we are joined to God in will, love what belongs to God, and, just as we went astray through evil will by flying away and departing from God, so return through good will by consenting to and obeying his will.

[Col. 1116B]  
## HOMILY XIV. FIRST HOMILY ON CHAPTER II OF DANIEL, CONCERNING THE STATUE OF NEBUCHADNEZZAR

“In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream,” etc. (Dan. 2).

Because all the authority of Scripture prepares the delights of eternal life for the soul seeking God, let all the children of promise eagerly gather within themselves new and old fruits, lest they fail on the way in this time of hunger and famine. Therefore let them mark closely in their hearts what the Saviour has set forth for his co-heirs to carry out in deeds. Let them diligently search out the dark waters in the clouds of the sky—that is, the obscure meanings in prophetic words—which abundantly provide nourishment for the inward human being.

[Col. 1116C] Therefore let us now, insofar as understanding is presently available to us, strive to examine those matters recounted in Daniel’s mystical narrative.

“In the second year,” says Scripture, “of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream.” It should be observed that Nebuchadnezzar sees a vision, yet has closed eyes in the vision; he dreams things full of mysteries, yet does not awaken to recognize in truth the things he sees while sleeping. So all the wicked and reprobate, over whom the king of Babylon—the devil, the author of inward confusion—presides, hear indeed how manifold is the wisdom of Christ. But because they refuse to follow Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, by imitation of virtues, they never deserve inwardly to grasp in understanding that very thing which they seem to know faintly and see as in a dream.

[Col. 1116D] But Daniel,

702  
who, because of his immense desire for the heavenly homeland and everlasting salvation, is rightly called “a man of desires,” and who chose rather to be sustained by modest vegetables than to be excessively filled with royal foods, profoundly recounts what was seen in the dream and more profoundly weighs what things are to be discerned through the narration of mystery in the dream. Thus surely all who, not considering the kingdom of God to be food and drink, have become devoted imitators of Daniel’s continence, behold with the clear sight of understanding whatever heavenly mystery is forbidden to be seen by dogs—that is, by consciences defiled with sin. Therefore, as Nebuchadnezzar did not understand the dream,

[Col. 1117A] let us strive with the wise Daniel to seek its mystical meaning.

“You, O king,” he says, “were looking, and behold, as it were a great statue.” By the statue which is seen as great and terrifying is expressed the state of wickedness and perdition, which rises at the very beginning of birth in almost all descendants of Adam, growing and increasing in those who do not labour to add themselves to the heavenly building by the merit of good works.

But the qualities of the works by which this structure of perdition rises are found to be as distinct as the diverse parts of this statue are various. For its head is said to be of gold, its breast and arms of silver, its belly and thigh of bronze, and its legs of iron. By the head of the statue, which is described as having been golden, the human will is fittingly expressed.

703  
[Col. 1117B] For it is clear that those who possess gold use it less frequently, but strive more carefully than with other metals to conceal it. Therefore the human will is aptly compared to a thing guarded with such care: it is hidden in the heart as gold in a chest, and cannot be known by anyone unless the person himself wishes to reveal it.

But the breast and arms were formed of silver. Let the quality of silver itself teach us what ought to be understood by the silver breast and arms. Almost the whole human race, deceived by the appearance of silver, hastens toward destruction. For there is nothing under the sun sought with greater ambition, because the children of this age, as long as they remain in the body of sin, never cease labouring to obtain it,

[Col. 1117C] because they judge money alone to be the whole sum of wealth and happiness. Therefore nothing is said to exist for the sake of which so great a crime of wickedness is committed.

> **Note:** [Col. 1117D] The passage is obscure.

For this reason, consent to and execution of evil deeds are fittingly expressed by that metal. But the belly and thigh are of bronze. By bronze, which is very hard and unbreakable, is to be understood the pleasure of sin, which reigns especially in the belly and thigh. For among the many kinds of vices none is found that seems to adhere to the nature of the human condition with such great and stubborn indissolubility.

[Col. 1117D] For where it is received with delight and granted a place of rule, it is by no means overcome without severe labour and great contrition of heart and body. The same statue is also said to be supported by iron legs. Iron, which subdues and crushes everything, fittingly expresses the habit and defence of sin, which weakens all strength of mind. For just as the whole human body is supported by two legs, so the entire structure of spiritual wickedness rests chiefly upon these two things: the habit of sinning and the defence of sin. From long habit of sin the mind of every reprobate is so darkened that the longer he remains in the depths of sins, the more difficult it is to call him back from his evil way, believing that nothing is sweeter than always to be entangled

[Col. 1118A] in crimes. For, owing to the very sweetness which fleshly pleasure imparts,

704  
unable to bear correction and desiring to justify himself in his works, he always strives to fortify himself with the shield of self-defence. The following words plainly testify what evils still attend such a person:

“But part of the feet by which the statue was supported appeared to be partly iron and partly earthenware.” Therefore let the eye of the inward human being look more carefully at when and how clay is mixed with earthenware. We believe this happens when the sinner’s heart, burning in crimes, is so hardened that, should it ever need to return to its senses or be able to do penance for its offences, it becomes wholly incapable of knowing how. From such hardness, the deadly wickedness of crimes grows and increases more and more from day to day,

[Col. 1118B] because then at last—as is signified by the partly iron and partly earthenware feet—nothing can be so earthly, nothing imagined so shameful, that a child of such perdition would be ashamed to undertake it boldly and without blushes.

Once this structure of wickedness has thus grown up, it can never be crushed by any means unless that stone cut from the mountain without hands strikes the statue on its feet: that cornerstone, namely, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, begotten from the inviolate Virgin without a man’s embrace, who is able to raise up children of Abraham from stones. He alone can save such a person.

[Col. 1118C] Looking down from the lofty dwelling-place of heaven with the eye of his customary mercy, he will strike one foot of the statue with repentance and the other with fear, so that bitter repentance may restore to life the person whom long habit of sinning had made as though already dead. And he who formerly was accustomed to set the shield of pride and self-defence against the sins he had committed will strive, by closely examining his guilt, greatly fearing it when examined, and mourning it with worthy fruits of repentance. Once the state of perversity has been cast down by such blows, when it has thus fallen and been broken, that stone will begin to grow and increase, as is stated in what follows.

705. But the stone became a great mountain and filled the whole earth. That living stone, namely our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1118D], becomes a mountain of wondrous greatness when the knowledge of his greatness has so grown within a human heart that the person who had formerly been accustomed to despise him beholds him as the most mighty God of majesty, Lord of all nature, and can say abundantly: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. XLVII, 1). By this very greatness the whole earth of that person is filled, when, together with body and soul and all the senses, he is so subjected to almighty God that, knowing nothing except God, desiring nothing except the things that are God’s, he becomes one spirit with him.

## HOMILY XV. FIRST HOMILY ON CHAPTER VII OF DANIEL, CONCERNING THE DREAM OF KING BELSHAZZAR.

[Col. 1119A]

“In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream,” etc. (Dan. VII).

This chosen and beloved prophet of the Lord, Daniel, though holy and righteous, though enlightened by the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, because he was a fleshly man, because he was mortal and burdened by the weight of the body, was still laboring and groaning in the night of this exile. He saw the great and marvelous vision which he testifies that he saw by night in such a way, as we may believe, that he had experienced in himself in part those things which that same vision mystically intimates. For no one in this life is so righteous, no one so holy, as not to sin; since not even the apostles themselves [Col. 1119B], the most perfect of all human beings, were able to avoid sins as long as they were in the flesh. But if—an incredible supposition—he did not perceive in himself this conflict of winds and this rising of beasts, nevertheless in the Holy Spirit he foresaw those who would come after him, who would both see the winds fighting in the sea and the beasts rising from the sea, and, enduring them and seeing them, would overcome with God’s help. For Daniel himself fittingly signifies these by his name; for *Daniel* means “judgment.”

But let us first see who Belshazzar, that king of Babylon, is, or what his first year is, in which Daniel was worthy to behold this marvelous vision. Belshazzar, indeed, whose name is interpreted “hair of the head,” and Daniel, who, as we have said, is called “judgment,” mystically represent one and the same person predestined to eternal salvation [Col. 1119C], who receives different names according to different actions. For as long as he is in the world and gladly and willingly serves the sins of the world, he may fittingly be called Belshazzar, king of Babylon, king of confusion. But when, through the visitation and assistance of God’s grace, the time of oldness—the time, I mean, of an old and guilty life—has passed, and through devotion to a new life he begins to be a new person, then in a certain manner the first year of Belshazzar, king of Babylon, begins. In that year, while he strives, by that same power with which he had formerly lived among vices, also to restrain vices, judge them within himself, and condemn them, he is not inappropriately called Daniel.

Of this person it is fittingly said: “I was looking in my vision by night.” For although he is held in the night—that is, the darkness—of this ignorance [Col. 1119D], yet, desiring in spirit to attain the brightness of the heavenly light, he is always in a kind of vision, because he never, or rarely, neglects to see what is happening within him, and by what winds his sea—that is, his heart—is driven about.

Yet this vision takes place as though by night. For the ignorance belonging to the misery of this mortality does not permit him clearly to see what he desires. Still, that little which he sees is his vision: a vision, I say, useful [manuscript: “useless”] and good for him. Therefore he rightly says, “I was looking in my vision by night,” and immediately reveals what he had seen when he adds:

707. “And behold, the four winds of heaven were fighting upon the great sea, and four great beasts, different from one another, were coming up” [Col. 1120A]. By the great sea we may fittingly understand the embittered heart of a human being; by the four beasts, the four cardinal vices opposed to the four cardinal virtues. The four winds signify either the four holy angels who preside over the four cardinal virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—or the four evil angels who stir up and nourish in the human heart the four cardinal vices: imprudence, intemperance, incontinence, and injustice. For every virtue has its spirit, and every vice has its spirit. The virtues have their angels, who fight against and drive vices from the heart of a good person; and the vices likewise have their angels, always opposing the virtues and desiring to stir up a great conflict in the great sea [Col. 1120B].

The great sea, as we have said, is the embittered human heart. In what sense do I call it embittered? A blessed person is embittered in this world in three ways. He is embittered by remembering and repenting of the sins he has committed; he is embittered because he cannot escape and avoid sins; he is embittered because, while so long placed in this pilgrimage, he cannot see and possess the God whom he loves before all things and desires above all things. In this great sea, in this heart, I say, so healthfully embittered, he often feels and understands the conflict of the winds mentioned above and the detestable ascent of the beasts we have described. Since these beasts were different from one another, Daniel immediately distinguishes their differences, adding:

[Col. 1120C] “The first was like a lioness, and it had the wings of an eagle.” The first beast, which is imprudence, opposed to the first virtue, prudence, is not inappropriately compared to a lioness, which, insofar as its nature may be understood, possesses a certain imprudence. When she has given birth to cubs and some robber, watching for her departure, has secretly carried off those cubs, knowing her nature he craftily places in the road behind him a glass sphere bearing the likeness of a cub, so that by this he may delay the lioness pursuing him. When, therefore, she has returned to her den and realizes that the cubs are gone, she immediately pursues the robber’s tracks. But when she comes to the place where the sphere has been set before her with the likeness of a cub, she examines the cub more closely and is diverted from her pursuit; at last [Col. 1120D], recognizing that she has been deceived, she sadly returns to her place. Because of this foolishness, then, this first beast, which we have called imprudence, is not unjustly compared to a lioness. It follows:

“And it had the wings of an eagle.” Imprudence has two wings, one of which may be called ignorance and the other forgetfulness. But we must see what ignorance is. Ignorance is when a person neglects to learn what ought to be learned and understand what ought to be understood; or, if he has learned it, through the vice of imprudence ruling him he forgets it as though he had not learned it. Nor should we pass over the fact that this beast of which we speak is described as having the wings of an eagle. In the eagle, which rises higher in flight than other birds, pride is not inappropriately expressed. “It had the wings of an eagle,” mystically intimating [Col. 1121A] by this that forgetful and ignorant persons are sometimes prouder than the learned and wise.

But the person to be saved does not permit this beast to reign long within him. Following the example of the good Daniel, he gazes upon it until, with God’s help, it is broken down and overcome. Thus it is rightly added:

“I was looking until its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the earth.” To look upon the beast is to direct the whole gaze of one’s heart diligently toward learning carefully both what should be done and what should be avoided; and, once one has learned, to commit these things to a deep memory and strive wisely to fulfill them in deeds. Thus, when those two wings—ignorance and forgetfulness—have at last been plucked out through knowledge and remembrance of the good, the beast itself, imprudence itself, is lifted up and overcome by prudence. Then at last comes what follows:

“And it stood upon its feet like a human being.” In this place we may understand the feet as a person’s thoughts. As long as the sense of the heart is veiled and darkened by those two wings which we called ignorance and forgetfulness, a person does not stand upon his own feet like a human being, because he has no power over his thoughts and neither knows nor discerns what he is thinking. But once the vice of ignorance and forgetfulness has been overcome and the good of prudence has been attained in some measure, he at last [Col. 1121B] stands upon his feet like a human being, when he begins to think wisely as a human being—that is, when he recognizes himself as human, a human being, I say, made in the image and likeness of God. After this it is fittingly added:

[Col. 1121C] “And a human heart was given to it.” By the heart we may understand human reason. A person is rightly said to have been given his heart when he begins wisely to direct the whole rational capacity of his soul to distinguishing and discerning good and evil.

Since this first beast has in this manner been lifted up from the earth, that is, from the earthly heart, the marvelous difference of the second beast is mystically set before us, because one must watch against it with no less zeal and effort. Daniel describes it wonderfully when he immediately adds:

“And behold another beast, like a bear; it stood on one side, and there were three rows in its mouth and in its teeth; and they said to it thus: ‘Arise, eat much flesh.’” In the other beast, which is noted as resembling a bear [Col. 1121D], the second vice, intemperance, opposed to the second virtue called temperance, is not unjustly represented. Nor without cause do we read that this beast stood not “in the parts,” but “on one side.” For by the two parts we understand a person’s soul and body. This beast stands chiefly in that part called the body, because, as imprudence is attributed to the soul, so intemperance is attributed to the body.

The words which follow—“There were three rows in its mouth and in its teeth”—express the three ways in which intemperance especially reveals and exercises itself in a person. We may call these three ways gluttony, drunkenness, and lust. For gluttony and drunkenness occur through the mouth and teeth; and one who does not know, or neglects, to restrain himself from these two quickly falls into the third, which is lust. This is more plainly suggested to us when, after the three rows already mentioned, there immediately follows:

“And they said to it thus: ‘Arise, eat much flesh.’” Who are these speaking and making such suggestions? Certainly either evil desires, which are stirred up and nourished in a person through gluttony [Col. 1122A], drunkenness, and lust, or those four winds, namely the evil angels mentioned above, who always incite and entice a person to wrongdoing. They exhort him to rise and eat—that is, by exercising himself in the evil desires of fleshly life, to answer them with fleshly deeds. But if a person rejects their suggestion and at last, with God’s help, begins to be temperate [Col. 1122B], he must nevertheless watch against the third beast, concerning which Daniel immediately adds:

“After this,” says Daniel, “I was looking, and behold another beast like a leopard; it had four wings upon it like a bird, and the beast had four heads, and power was given to it.” In this third beast, which was like a leopard, we fittingly understand the third vice, inconstancy, opposed to the third virtue which we call fortitude. It has as though four wings upon itself, which we may call wantonness of sight, curiosity of hearing, frivolity in speech, and falsehood. A person may properly be called inconstant when he is unsteady in sight, curious in hearing, and neglects to restrain and guard himself from frivolous speech. For through this negligent frivolity he is sometimes drawn, unknowingly or unwillingly, into the fault of falsehood [Col. 1122C].

For some are entangled in these vices only in body and not in heart, because they fall into them not through love or desire but through a certain lightness or negligence of mind. And some admit them into their inward senses through wantonness, curiosity, frivolity of speech, or falsehood. These are the four wings and the four heads which were in the beast, when the outward senses, understood through the wings, and the inward senses, understood through the heads, agree with one another from both sides in vices. It is therefore rightly added:

“And power was given to it.” This beast—that is, incontinence—is of such power and strength [Col. 1122D] that it lasts a long time even over good and perfect people. For even if they sometimes keep themselves in the outward person, in the inward person they scarcely sometimes restrain themselves—scarcely, I say, and not without great labor—from keeping their eyes from unlawful sight, their ears from curious hearing, and their tongue from frivolous and harmful speech. Therefore, unless the third beast is manfully repressed and crushed, the fourth beast at length rises up terribly. Daniel mystically identifies it in what follows when he says:

“After this I was looking in the vision of the night, and behold a fourth beast, terrible and marvelous and exceedingly strong.” By the fourth beast we understand injustice, the fourth vice, opposed to the fourth virtue, which we call justice. Injustice is and is called that state in which a person, prone and headlong toward evil, is subjected in heart and body to iniquity and sin [Col. 1123A]. This beast is rightly described as terrible, marvelous, and exceedingly strong. It is terrible in suggestion, marvelous in pleasure, and strong in action. And we rightly call it terrible in suggestion, for by the things it suggests it shakes a good person, a person to be saved, with great terror and trembling. But if it is received, it becomes marvelous in pleasure, because, as it entices and presses itself upon him, the person begins to experience in his flesh things previously unknown and untried. It also becomes strong in action, because the person whom it has subjected to its dominion through suggestion and pleasure it can powerfully bend toward whatever shameful acts it chooses. Hence follows:

“It had great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the remainder beneath its feet” [Col. 1123B]. By the great iron teeth we may fittingly understand those thoughts which injustice suggests; they are indeed very hard and strong. Whatever good or virtue exists in a person, they consume it, as though by eating; and what they cannot utterly consume, they diminish, as though crushed by certain teeth. The words which follow—“and trampling the remainder beneath its feet”—suggest nothing else to us than that, by the evil affections which injustice itself introduces, as by certain feet, it reduces to nothing by trampling whatever residue of good or virtue it finds in the person. Hence follows:

“But it was unlike the other beasts which I had seen before.” This fourth beast, injustice, is rightly said to be unlike the other three beasts already discussed [Col. 1123C]. For it is stronger than all of them, because it contains every vice within itself, as is more plainly declared in the following words:

“And,” Scripture says, “it had ten horns.” These horns are the seven principal vices: pride, sloth, anger, envy, avarice, gluttony, and lust. When the three vices mentioned above—imprudence, intemperance, and inconstancy—are added to these, injustice has, as it were, ten horns. Whoever desires to be freed from these horns should strive wisely to imitate the righteous Daniel.

“I was considering,” he says, “the horns.” He considered them so that he might be freed from them, plainly intimating to us that anyone who still neglects spiritually to consider these horns cannot be freed from them. To consider the horns is continually to watch against vices with deliberate and vigilant guarding of heart and body. But after the blessed person’s consideration and watchfulness, because the appetite for human praise sometimes creeps in, Daniel rightly adds, after saying, “I was considering the horns”:

“And behold, another little horn came up from among them” [Col. 1123D]. By the other little horn we may not unjustly understand vainglory. It is fittingly called a little horn because, at the very beginning of its rise, so to speak—when it first begins to claim a person’s heart for itself—it is a horn, because through the appetite for empty favor it already attacks the mind in some measure; yet it is a little horn, because it has not yet become fully strong in the person. Nevertheless, if it is allowed to grow, it becomes greater and stronger than all the horns mentioned above. “I was considering the horns, and behold, another little horn came up from among them.” What does “from among them” mean? One who stands in the middle seems to touch neither one side nor the other.

713. Thus this horn, the vice of empty glory, is not inappropriately said to arise from the midst of the vices already mentioned, because it does not seem to touch vices, and yet it comes from vices. It certainly is a vice, but is sometimes not regarded as a vice, because, since this vainglory arises not from vices but from virtues, wishing to glory and to be praised for virtues is often thought to be a virtue. Hence it is immediately added [Col. 1124B]:

“And three of the first horns were plucked up before it.” When three of the first horns have been plucked up—that is, when the vices of imprudence, intemperance, and inconstancy have been subdued and overcome—this other horn of which we have spoken arises, when a person, insufficiently cautiously glorying within himself in virtues attained, is inwardly lifted up and begins also outwardly to seek glory from other people, as the following text immediately mystically intimates:

“And behold, in this horn were eyes like human eyes, and a mouth speaking great things.” In vainglory there are eyes like human eyes because, while the person who glories not in God but in himself begins inwardly, with a lifted-up heart, to behold and weigh his own merits, it seems reasonable and just to him [Col. 1124C] that he should also outwardly possess glory among people for his good life. It also has its mouth, namely a mouth speaking great things, because it commonly leads a person so far that he himself begins to speak of, magnify, and boast of his virtues and merits.

Alternatively, by the four beasts mentioned above we may understand the four ages of a human being. The first is infancy or childhood; because of the foolishness or imprudence which, as we said, belongs to the lioness, we fittingly compare it to a lioness. For as long as a child is a child, he acts childishly and has little or no understanding of the first virtue, which we called prudence. Therefore imprudence, signified by the lioness with its two wings, which we called ignorance and forgetfulness, fittingly belongs to this age [Col. 1124D].

When childhood has passed, adolescence follows. It is aptly represented by the second beast, 714. which was like a bear and had three rows in its mouth and teeth. For a bear is strong; and so is an adolescent. Since he sometimes cannot, and sometimes does not even know how to, moderate and restrain within himself those three rows which we called gluttony, drunkenness, and lust, the second vice, intemperance, may not unjustly be assigned to this age.

After adolescence follows youth, which we may fittingly liken to that third beast, which was like a leopard and had four wings upon it like a bird. For the leopard is an unstable and incontinent wild beast [Col. 1125A]. So also youth scarcely, or sometimes not at all, tolerates the restraints of stability and constancy. And since it does not lack those four wings which we interpreted as wantonness of sight, curiosity of hearing, frivolity of speech, and falsehood, the third vice, inconstancy, is not undeservedly attributed to this age.

In any person in whom these three beasts have grown strong and endured until the fourth age, called old age, that fourth beast, terrible and exceedingly strong—that is, injustice—will rule terribly, marvelously, and very strongly over him. For with its ten horns, that is, the ten principal vices which we noted a little earlier [manuscript: “knew”], it so subjects and prostrates him before itself that he cannot rise effectively to any works of justice [Col. 1125B]. But since we have already heard in part with what vigilance the righteous and spiritual person watches against these beasts, and with what zeal and constancy he strives to repress and restrain them, let us now examine what follows. It continues:

“I was looking until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat.” A throne is a king’s seat. Thus by the thrones we may not inappropriately understand a human being’s soul and body, which ought to be the throne and seat of the highest and eternal King, almighty God; and by the Ancient of Days, the grave and mature understanding of a human being. This looking of the good and righteous person is nothing other than the continual and steadfast endeavor of a devoutly watchful heart, 715. by which he arms himself manfully against the beasts already mentioned and against those ten horns [Col. 1125C], especially against the vice of empty glory, mystically figured by the other little horn rising from among them. He does not withdraw the eye of his mind from this looking until thrones are set in place: that is, until, having become superior to those vices and king and ruler of himself, he begins to sit for himself; until, that is, by commanding and ruling his body and soul, he knows, wills, and is able to govern himself according to God’s will. Thus, being perfectly subdued and humbled in body and spirit, he becomes worthy for that highest King of kings to wish and be able to possess his throne and seat in him. After this it continues:

“And the Ancient of Days sat.” By the Ancient of Days we said that the grave and mature understanding of a human being should be understood. He may worthily be called not simply Ancient, but Ancient of Days, when, after vices have been cut off, he begins happily to grow old and mature among the brightest days of heavenly visitation. Nor is it without reason said, “And the Ancient of Days sat.” For he sits in a kind of desirable and pleasant repose [Col. 1125D], when he begins to rest and delight in the Lord through both knowledge and devotion. It follows:

“His garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool.” In the garment of this Ancient One the body may not inappropriately be understood; it becomes white as snow when it passes from vices to purity. And it is well said, “white as snow.” For snow, which cools and washes, fittingly signifies repentance: it makes a person’s body cold toward the heat of fleshly pleasure and worthily washes and cleanses away whatever sin and stain it contained. Thus, according to the mystical understanding of the following words, with God’s help a person advances from purity of body to purity of heart. Hence is added: “and the hair of his head like clean wool.” By the hair of the head we understand the holy and pure thoughts of the heart. Nor is it without reason that snow is used for the whiteness of the garment, but wool for the whiteness of the hair. Snow is cold, as we have said [Col. 1126A], but wool is warm. Thus outer purity, which arises from coldness—that is, the rigor of repentance—is indeed good, but is in some sense cold in comparison with inner purity, represented by clean wool, because the pure thoughts of a pure heart warm a person and kindle him toward the love of God. Hence follows:

“His throne was flames of fire, its wheels burning fire; a fiery and swift river went forth from before him.” Previously we understood the soul and body of a human being through the thrones. Here, however, where “throne” is singular, it is fitting to understand the human spirit, in which that Ancient of Days—that is, grave and mature understanding—has established his seat. Notice what is said: “His throne was flames of fire.” Flame shines; fire burns. This is fitting, because the throne—that is, the spirit over which God presides—shines with the knowledge of sin and burns with the ardor of repentance and satisfaction. By the wheels of this throne we may fittingly understand the thoughts of a shining and burning spirit [Col. 1126C], which indeed become as burning [fire] when a good person, after the fashion of a wheel, is turned and revolves now by reading, now by hearing those things that concern God, carefully seeking and investigating whether anything may perhaps meet his outward eyes or ears by which he may be kindled more and more inwardly to repentance and satisfaction. There follows in due order:

“A fiery and swift river went forth from before him.” By the fiery and swift river we may fittingly understand the fervent prayer of a fervent heart. When it arises through the pain of repentance and the flooding of tears, it may be called a river not only fiery but swift, because it is truly swift to obtain whatever it asks of God [Col. 1126D]. For the devout and merciful Lord will be present to it, as is mystically declared in the following words, which immediately add:

“Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand and hundred thousands stood before him.” But in order that we may understand more subtly the mystery of this number, let us strive to distinguish and discern the individual words one by one. First it says “thousands,” then “of thousands”; third, it adds “ten thousand”; finally, “hundred thousands.” By the first thousands we may understand perfect divine promptings; by the following thousands, perfect human acts of will or consent; by the final thousands, perfect human actions. In the two words “ten thousand times,” which we left untouched in the middle [Col. 1127A], we may recognize legal and evangelical perfection. And perfect divine promptings are not unjustly called “thousands of thousands,” because the first thousands are, in a certain manner, the cause of the subsequent thousands. For where the gracious prompting of almighty God comes first, a perfect will and the perfect action of a perfect life immediately follow.

This is more plainly suggested when it is said: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him.” For God’s perfect inspirations minister to a human being perfect desires and perfect wills. A will is perfect, and is called perfect, when a person strives, to the extent of his ability, to agree and cooperate through the good consent of a good heart with God’s prevenient inspiration. After God’s prevenient prompting and the following good human will come the perfect works of a perfect life [Col. 1127B], which, as we have said, are fittingly represented by “ten thousand and hundred thousands,” when they are supported and adorned by legal and evangelical perfection. That is, when a person has advanced so far as to begin to order and regulate his life, character, and deeds according to the Law, indicated by “ten,” and according to the Gospel, indicated by “thousand.”

And it is rightly said above, “Thousands of thousands ministered to him,” but here, “and ten thousand and hundred thousands stood before him.” For such works truly stand by a person in such a way that they depart from him neither here nor in the future. But because the more a righteous person advances in God, the more he subjects himself to God in the fear of greater humility and reverence, it is rightly added:

[Col. 1127C] “The judgment sat, and the books were opened.” But what is judgment? Judgment is that by which either a guilty person is condemned to punishment or an innocent person is freed from punishment. A person becomes for himself not merely a judge but also a judgment by which he is both condemned and freed. For when he judges himself worthy of punishment by strictly accusing and humbly condemning himself for his sins, he in a certain manner frees himself from punishment. For while he is condemned by his own judgment as guilty to punishment, he is freed by God’s judgment as innocent from punishment. And because this judgment ought not to be sudden or only temporary, but something a perfect person continually keeps with himself in the secret of his heart, it is aptly intimated when it says, “The judgment sat.” For this word expresses a certain continuance and persistent constancy, which it is fitting for the blessed person to maintain in the judgment already described [Col. 1127D]. It follows:

“And the books were opened.” The books are opened when a person reveals and opens, both to God in prayer and humbly to his superior in confession, the secrets of consciences—the secrets, I say, of his own heart—which may be understood through books. “And another book was opened, which is the book of life.” By this other book, called the book of life, the hope of everlasting life is fittingly signified. The hand of divine mercy, opening this book, in a certain manner mercifully opens his books to the person when, strengthened in the Lord and setting aside all transitory things, he rises with firmer hope to obtain the joys of promised blessedness.
