But because it is impossible that, after so great a grace of God’s gifts, the vice of empty glory should not insert itself, it is rightly added: “I was looking because of the sound of the great words which that horn was speaking.” Since this horn is great, it especially exalts itself against great and perfect people, as Daniel, mentioned shortly afterward, more plainly shows when he says: “I was looking, and behold, this horn was making war against the saints and prevailed against them.” Indeed, this horn—the vice of empty glory—especially attacks those who are more perfect, because one who serves sins and lies under vices plainly has nothing in which to glory. But those who are perfect and strive toward advancement frequently discover within themselves the sound of these great words. Thus it is rightly said here: “I was looking because of the sound of the great words [Col. 1128B] which that horn was speaking”; and immediately it adds: “And I saw that the beast had been slain, and its body had perished and had been given to be burned with fire.”

To look upon this horn is, as we have said, diligently to direct the whole affection of one’s heart toward crushing and repressing within oneself the appetite for empty glory. For this horn gives forth its utterances when it inwardly provokes and impels a person to boast of and magnify the merits of his virtues.

But why is its voice allowed to reach the ears of the human heart, except because it sees the beast slain—that is, because it understands that injustice within itself has perished through the grace of divine mercy? The beast is also slain and its body given to be burned with fire when every will toward injustice is driven out inwardly from the heart and every work of injustice outwardly from the body through the fire of repentance and confession. “And I saw,” he says, “that the beast had been slain, and its body had perished and had been given to be burned with fire [Col. 1128C], and that the power of the other beasts also had been taken away, and periods of life had been assigned to them until a time and times.”

By the other beasts we understand the remaining vices, described above under the figures of the preceding three beasts. Since they cannot be utterly slain—for no one in this life can become perfectly prudent, wholly temperate, or wholly constant—their power is nevertheless taken away and they are repressed. For after the destruction of the fourth beast, which is injustice, they are not permitted to rule over a righteous person and subject him to themselves as much as they wish. They indeed live in a person, yet as though under fixed periods. For, as Daniel says, periods of life had been assigned to them “until a time and times,” because they rejoice to enjoy their life only as long as they dare to rule and prevail over a good and righteous person by a power received, as it were, for an hour.

But when “a time and times” comes—that is, when the time for repenting and the time for making satisfaction have forestalled the assigned periods of their life—they fall as though dying, because they cannot have a place of life in a soul perfectly repenting and worthily making satisfaction to God. This time and times acceptable and desirable to God—the time of repentance [Col. 1129A] and the time of satisfaction—makes a person worthy of heavenly visitation, as is subsequently intimated when it immediately adds:

“I was looking in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven the Son of Man was coming; and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him; and he gave him power and honor and kingdom, and all tribes and tongues shall serve him.” In the Holy Scriptures the Holy Spirit is often signified by a cloud; where clouds are found in the plural, the gifts of that same Holy Spirit are sometimes understood. Thus also in this place, where the Son of Man is described as coming with the clouds of heaven, the whole Holy Trinity—namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is fittingly denoted.

The Son of Man, coming with the clouds of heaven, comes even to the Ancient of Days when almighty God, who is God and human, begins inwardly to touch a person’s mature understanding sweetly through the invisible and inexpressible contemplation of his divinity, illuminating it with the gifts of his Spirit [Col. 1129B]. After so great a grace of heavenly condescension, what follows immediately takes place:

“And they presented him before him.” Those who then present the person before the Most High are either holy angels or the holy desires of the person; they lift and kindle him more and more to desire and contemplate the ineffable splendor of unbounded light. Yet he beholds that splendor as though in a vision of the night. For the darkness of corruption hinders and overshadows him, so that he cannot see clearly and perfectly the little that he does see [Col. 1129C]. What that supreme Majesty bestows in mercy and grace upon the blessed person is mystically intimated by the text that follows:

And he gave him, he says, power, honor, and a kingdom. He gives power when he mercifully grants him the ability to resist vices. 721 After power he grants him a kingdom, because, after vices have been subdued, he bestows the dominion of reigning among the virtues. Honor is rightly placed between power and kingdom, for the highest and perfect honor is when merciful God, by his gift, has raised a person to such grace of perfection that, both for conquered vices and for virtues obtained, that person humbly attributes honor and glory not to himself but to God alone, subjecting his whole [Col. 1129D] self to him alone, as the following text teaches when it says:

“And all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him.” In the Holy Scriptures, *people* is seldom used except where a multitude of human beings is indicated and expressed. But since the human being is a rational creature—for no creature apart from angel and human being possesses reason—we may not unfittingly understand here, by *peoples*, the multitude of rational actions and rational affections; and by *tribes*, that noble offspring which proceeded from God, namely the human spirit, soul, and body. As it were, all peoples and tribes serve the Lord when the gifts of divine mercy are so multiplied in a person that he begins to serve God alone laudably and rationally with spirit, soul, and body—[Col. 1130A] in the soul, that is, through the many good actions which are made rational by the spirit that presides and governs.

But since there is no one who can be found always steadfast and always perfect in this service of spirit, soul, and body, Daniel rightly added, after saying “all peoples and tribes,” “and tongues shall serve him.” By the service of tongues we may understand the true and perfect confession of sins, by which whatever stain or imperfection may be found in this threefold service of spirit, soul, and body ought to be cleansed 722 and justified. And it should be noted that he did not say, “a tongue,” but “tongues shall serve him.” A human being ought certainly to possess two tongues in confession: the tongue of the heart, which speaks sorrow; and the tongue of the body, which speaks the act. But with what [Col. 1130B] worthiness of reward, with what everlasting stability of eternal blessedness, this service of peoples, tribes, and tongues is rewarded in the future, the oft-mentioned Daniel seems elegantly to comprehend and conclude in the following words:

“His power,” he says, “is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.” That power—that is, the power of resisting vices—which, as was said above, the merciful Lord gives a person in this life, is not eternal power. For a human being cannot always resist sin in the place of sin; moreover, the kingdom of virtues received from God is often corrupted here, for it is very often interrupted by creeping-in vices. But his power, which after the end of this life he will give in his kingdom to all [Col. 1130C] his elect, is eternal power.

For in that place, to all who are gathered and are yet to be gathered, the will and ability to turn aside from evil are eternally subject. Likewise, his kingdom—that is, the kingdom of virtues—will not be destroyed there, because the virtue of doing good will never be lost there. May he who lives and reigns without end through ages of ages lead us to this power and this kingdom. Amen.

## 723 HOMILY XVI. ON THE FIRST CHAPTER OF THE FIRST BOOK OF MACCABEES

“And it came to pass, after Alexander, the Macedonian son of Philip, who first reigned in Greece, had gone forth from the land of Kittim and slain Darius king of the Persians, etc.” (1 Maccabees).

[Col. 1130D] This book, which is read at the end of the year when the summer Sundays have ended, is called the Book of Maccabees. And it is rightly called the Book of Maccabees. For *Maccabees* means “warriors,” by which name are designated those true and strong warriors who, continually waging the harshest war day and night against those invisible enemies, never rest until they arrive where they receive the reward of all their labors and contests. In this book three things seem to be prefigured: first, those things done at the beginning of human creation; second, those now done in the Church; third, those that will occur at the end of the world in the time of Antichrist. Let us therefore see what we find at the beginning of this book.

“And it came to pass,” he says, “after Alexander [Col. 1131A] the Macedonian son of Philip, who first reigned in Greece, had gone forth from the land of Kittim, that he slew Darius king of the Persians and Medes, waged many battles, and seized many strongholds.” By this name Alexander, which means “lifting distress,” we may fittingly understand that dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan. From the time when he first deceived the human being in paradise through disobedience, he initiated and raised such [MS: *tantas*, “so many,” rather than *tam*] inextricable distresses and labors that daily distresses and labors never were and are not lacking to all Adam’s posterity so long as a human being lives upon the earth. He is also called the Macedonian son of Philip. For *Philip* means “mouth of a lamp,” and *Macedonian*, “eastern.” Why “mouth of a lamp,” and why “eastern”? He is called Philip, [Col. 1131B] 724 that is, “mouth of a lamp,” because he ought to have been the mouth of the true lamp, that is, Christ Jesus, who illuminates earthly and heavenly things, had he remained in the state of angelic dignity; with mouth and heart he ought to have uttered what pleased his Creator. He was also an eastern man, because the Lord God created him in great glory and splendor and set him above the whole multitude of angels.

“He first reigned in Greece.” Greece means wisdom or eloquence. In this Lucifer reigned, because for this purpose he had been created: that he might reign in eternal wisdom, delight in the wondrous sweetness of divinity, and speak or do nothing except what pertained to the praise of his Creator. “He went forth from the land of Kittim.” Kittim is called “fear.” [Col. 1131C] Alas, he went forth from Kittim when, despising the fear of God, he was lifted into such pride of mind that he chose rather to be under his own rule than under the Lord’s, saying in his heart: “I will set my seat to the north; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XXIV, 13–14).

Having gone forth from there, he slew Darius, king of the Persians and Medes. Darius means “generation of counsel,” by which name our first parent Adam is expressed. Eternal divine wisdom created him with this purpose: that, if the host of angels were diminished through proud angels, their number might be made complete through elect human beings. This Darius is described as king of the Persians, which means “those who tempt,” because the Lord God had bestowed on that first human being such a gift of wisdom that he knew how by wondrous and powerful government to restrain and tame temptations which came upon him, so completely [Col. 1131D] that none of them could have harmed him, if he himself had willed it. He was also king of the Medes, which means “those who measure.” For such grace of power was bestowed on him by God that he knew how to direct all his works according to God’s will and assign a fitting measure to every matter.

This king Darius Alexander, having gone forth from the land of Kittim—that is, the evil angel fallen from heaven—slew when, through envy, he persuaded him to eat the forbidden fruit and thereby miserably cast him into death. We, all Adam’s children, alas, have become participants in this lamentable slaying; bearing the punishment of this guilt and placed amid the labors, miseries, [Col. 1132A] and temptations of the present life, deprived of the gift of eternal wisdom, we cannot at all maintain the proper measure even in those necessities by which we sustain this frail and mortal body. Concerning this ancient enemy it is further said:

“And he waged many battles.” What sort [MS: *quales* rather than *qualia*] of battles these are which this most wicked Alexander wages day and night, each one of us knows better than they can be explained by the power of speech. For everywhere he lies in wait for the salvation of our soul; everywhere he endeavors to drag us with himself into destruction.

“And he seized many strongholds.” He seized many strongholds because before the coming of the Lord no one was so fortified by Christ’s name as to dare, or be able, to oppose or resist the magnificence of his power. [Col. 1132B] “And he slew the kings of the earth.” He slew the kings of the earth because he so slew all the elect who lived before the Law and under the Law—called kings of the earth because they governed their own earth, that is, their bodies, by the discipline of good government—that after the end of life they descended to the barriers of hell. He also passed through even to the ends of the earth, because he did not cease to assail them until the end of all things came. It follows:

“After these things he fell upon his bed and knew that he was dying.” By this bed we may understand the cross of Christ, or the mystery of his humanity, in which, in his most holy humanity, all the fullness 726 of divinity rested bodily. Upon this bed this Alexander, namely our enemy, fell, because, when Christ the Lord slept upon the bed of the cross, he was cast down and crushed so completely [Col. 1132C] that he was deprived of the dominion of all his former power. There he knew that he was dying, because through Christ’s death he foresaw that he would utterly lose the power by which he had raged against Christ’s elect. “And he called his boys who had been reared with him, and divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive.” His boys, the evil angels reared with him, are the host of apostate angels. While still alive, he divided his kingdom among them because, imparting to them his wickedness of harming and raging against human beings, he granted them equal power over all Adam’s children. Hence it is aptly added at once: “And his boys obtained the kingdom, each in his own place, and all put crowns upon themselves after his death.” Deceiving spirits obtain a kingdom and put crowns upon themselves while, throughout [Col. 1132D] the whole world, they boast that they have conquered this person and that person, while they shake the hearts of the just through various battles of temptations.

“And from them came forth a root of sin, Antiochus the Illustrious, son of King Antiochus.” Antiochus means “silence of poverty.” And who more fittingly comes under this name than that crafty enemy of the human race? For he who once cried out and clamored throughout the whole breadth of the world, by whose command all descended into hell, has become so silent before God that he can accomplish nothing openly except insofar as he accomplishes it by foolish and hidden suggestion. For he prevails to rule over no soul unless it voluntarily subjects itself to his power.

But by the name Antiochus may also be understood that man of sin, the son of perdition, Antichrist, [Col. 1133A] who is truly called the root of sin because he is raised and exalted above everything called God or worshiped. The devil will enter him fully, possessing him with all vices and sins not only invisibly but visibly also. Concerning him it is further said:

727 “And he entered proudly into the sanctuary, and took away the golden altar, the lampstand of light, the table of the offering, the golden mortars, and also the veil that hung before the face of the temple.” The sanctuary of the Lord is every faithful soul, or a congregation of spiritual persons. The devil enters it with pride and destroys its golden altar, because when the soul is vainly raised and exalted, the purity and cleanness of good thoughts—which is the golden altar—is lost. [Col. 1133B] The lampstand of light is also removed when, through the suggestion of evil things, it loses contemplation of heavenly brightness. The table of the offering is destroyed when, through unlawful delight, it loses the sweet refreshment of Sacred Scripture. The censers and all ornaments are taken away when, through consent to sin, all the instruments of virtue are reduced to nothing. The veil of the temple is destroyed when, after even the good of modesty has been set aside, what it once blushed to think it is not ashamed through evil habit to practice repeatedly.

[Col. 1134A] When this lamentable destruction has occurred in us, it is necessary that Mattathias come—his name means “gift of God”—that Judas come—his name means “confessing”—and that his brothers also come to cleanse and dedicate the temple. For if we wish perfectly to rebuild and restore in ourselves the good things that have been destroyed, it is altogether necessary that Mattathias come, that is, that the grace of God come, which makes us weep for the evils we have committed. After this it is necessary that Judas, meaning “confessing,” come, that is, that through pure confession, the stain of sins having been driven away, we return to a perfect cleansing of mind. Judas’s brothers also come when humility, chastity, patience, self-restraint, obedience, sobriety, and the other virtues come and begin to cleanse the temple of the heart and grant us [Col. 1134B] good progress.

When the temple has been cleansed, the altar dedicated, and new vessels brought in, great joy arises among the people. For when a person has been visited by God’s grace, cleansed and dedicated through confession, and adorned by the bringing in of new vessels—that is, virtues—great joy arises among the people, because the inward and outward faculties of the human being begin to rejoice with perfect joy in the Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1133]

# THE VENERABLE GODEFRID’S LITTLE WORK ON THE BLESSINGS OF JACOB THE PATRIARCH, ON GENESIS CHAPTER XLIX

## 729 CHAPTER ONE. On the Blessing of Reuben, Jacob’s Firstborn Son

[Col. 1133C]

The patriarch Jacob, foreseeing in the Holy Spirit the condition of the present Church, expressed this same condition in blessing his sons in these words: “Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow, first in gifts, greater in authority; you are poured out like water” (Gen. XLIX). He begins prophesying with Reuben the firstborn, and thus, enumerating each one, proceeds downward as far as Benjamin, who is the last. Since the entire order of the Church consists of prelates and subjects, prelates may be understood through Reuben the firstborn, and all good and perfect subjects through Benjamin the last.

Every good prelate may fittingly [Col. 1133D] be called Reuben, which means “seeing a son,” when he strives, with the prudent eye of circumspection and according to his ability and knowledge, to provide in [Col. 1134C] everything both for himself and for his son—that is, his good subject. He is also not undeservedly called God’s firstborn, because just as of old royalty and priesthood belonged by hereditary right to firstborn sons, so now every good prelate, by spiritual dignity, is king and priest. They are indeed most powerful kings, who know how to govern themselves by good living and to govern those subject to them by salutary admonition. They are likewise priests, because every day they offer gifts and sacrifices for themselves 730 and for the people subject to them.

Our true Jacob, almighty God, addresses such kings and priests, as it were gently, saying: “You are my strength.” They deserve well to be called the Lord’s strength when, strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power, they resist carnal desires bravely and manfully, and do not cease to uphold and strengthen all weak persons subject to them, not only by the word of preaching but by zeal for holy prayer as well.

[Col. 1135A] How such praiseworthy strength is acquired is mystically indicated in the following words, when he immediately adds: “And the beginning of my sorrow.” There is an evil sorrow, through which a human being is separated from God; and there is a good sorrow, which the merciful Lord acknowledges as his own sorrow. A good prelate has good sorrow when, continually imploring God for his own sins and transgressions and those of his subjects, he groans and grieves. He has good sorrow when he is afflicted and saddened because, entangled in the bonds of this mortality, he remains so long a pilgrim from the Lord. Thus, thus, by mourning himself before the Lord, he becomes the beginning of God’s sorrow, humbly stirring up his subjects by word and example to the sorrow of repentance and satisfaction and to the desire for everlasting life. Such [Col. 1135B] sorrow of prelates and subjects is rightly called the sorrow 731 of God the Father, because he approves such sorrow and counts the sorrow of his own as his own sorrow.

Therefore he says, “You are my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow.” As though he said: You ought deservedly to govern yourself and your subjects according to my will; you ought to support my weak ones; you ought to stir up in the hearts of my own my sorrow—that sorrow, I say, which is pleasing to me—because you are first in gifts and greater in authority. You are first in gifts because, above others, I have endowed you with greater prudence and wisdom, greater understanding, and the grace of other virtues. You are greater in authority because I have set you over other people as lord, master, and teacher.

But you too have answered my gifts in part. For you are poured out [Col. 1135C] like water. By water is denoted the grace of preaching and spiritual teaching, as elsewhere the Lord testifies in the Gospel when he says: “Whoever drinks the water that I give shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV, 14). For just as water extinguishes, washes, and refreshes, so the preaching of good persons washes the hearts of subjects, drawing forth from the abyss of the heart the water of compunction, through which cleansing from sins takes place; it extinguishes the burning of thirst; it refreshes—or rather, arouses hunger and thirst for heavenly joys.

When a good prelate has attained this grace, the following word fittingly indicates in how great humility he ought to keep himself, when it says: “Do not grow.” There is a kind of good growth, and there is [Col. 1135D] a kind of evil growth. He grows well who increases in virtues; he grows badly who, from an increase of virtues, is lifted into swelling pride of mind. 732 Therefore, “Do not grow,” he says—that is, do not be lifted into haughtiness of heart, pride, or grossness of mind, and by attributing to yourself what is mine, appear ungrateful to me. For whatever you have, you have received from me. I am he who gave it; I, when I will, can take away what is mine: “For I have mercy on whom I will, and I will be gracious to him with whom I am pleased” (Exod. XXXIII, 19). Therefore, the more exalted you are through my gift, the more humble you ought to be in your own eyes, attributing all that you have to me alone.

“For you ascended your father’s bed.” By the father’s bed we may understand the innocent and chaste, clean and spotless souls of subjects. They may suitably be called the bed of God the Father, because they make within themselves a pleasant and desirable resting-place for him whom not even the heavens can contain. “You ascended your [Col. 1136A] father’s bed,” because you received power and dominion over the bodies and souls of my humble ones in my place and stead. Therefore, if you grow inwardly from so great a gift of mine—that is, if you do not keep yourself in true humility—“you have defiled my bed.” God’s bed signifies the heart of every good prelate. Since it ought always to be laid low before God in humility, it is in a sense badly defiled when it is sprinkled and fouled with the harmful dust of pride and self-exaltation.

[Col. 1136B] But since we have said that through Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, the order, life, and manner of living of prelates are suitably to be understood, we must now see also how, in his last son Benjamin, we may recognize the order of perfect subjects.

## CHAPTER II. On the Blessing of Benjamin

“Benjamin,” he says, “is a ravening wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Gen. XLIX). Benjamin means “son of the right hand.” Therefore, all who desire to become and be sons of God’s right hand must strive to imitate the nature of the wolf. It is characteristic of the wolf always to seize what belongs to another, always to pant after what belongs to another in order to devour it. So indeed the person to be saved, to be numbered among the children [Col. 1136C] of God’s right hand, ought always to desire what belongs to another—that is, he should continually strive to satisfy his hungry soul with those things which are not his own. By things that are not ours but are in a sense alien to us, spiritual and heavenly things may suitably be understood. For since a human being is earthly and carnal, whatever belongs to earth and flesh may in some sense be called his own; but whatever can be thought or desired concerning spiritual or heavenly things is not his own. Thus Benjamin becomes like a ravening wolf when a good subject begins to desire with all the longing of his heart those non-his-own things, namely heavenly and spiritual things. For he is called ravening as one bold in seizing; and bold is one who dares things to be dared [Col. 1136D] and things not to be dared.

From the desire for heavenly and spiritual goods there is inwardly born in a person a certain salutary and praiseworthy boldness. For, from the confidence that he has in the Lord, he endeavors with a kind of violent constancy in daily labor to seize—that is, to obtain from God—things above himself: namely, the grace of heavenly sweetness reserved for God’s elect and beloved children alone. That this good boldness, this blameless seizure, does not displease God is mystically indicated by the sequence of the following words:

“In the morning,” he says, “he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils.” By morning may suitably be understood heavenly illumination or knowledge of God; by evening, knowledge of oneself. For when a person has been inwardly illuminated by the grace of heavenly visitation, this is a certain sweet and desirable [Col. 1137A] morning, by whose brightness he advances toward the desired knowledge of God. In this light-bearing morning he eats the prey when he has deserved to be inwardly refreshed by the long-desired grace of heavenly sweetness. After that desirable morning comes evening, when he begins rightly and perfectly, humbly and subtly, to recognize himself. In this evening—in that, I say, perfect knowledge of himself—he divides the spoils when he labors to turn to Christ’s service all the members of his body which, withdrawn from God, he had subjected to the devil’s dominion; when he seeks neither to see with his eyes, nor hear with his ears, nor work with his hands, anything except what he believes pertains to the praise and honor of God’s name.

## 734 CHAPTER III. On the Blessing of the Brothers Simeon and Levi

[Col. 1137B] But since the order of prelates and subjects, expressed through Reuben and Benjamin, consists of penitents and innocents, of active and contemplative persons, in the remaining ten sons of Jacob, whom we left untouched between Reuben and Benjamin, we may not unfittingly understand the two spiritual lives. In Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, and Issachar, the active; through Dan, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, and Joseph, the contemplative. And the active life is suitably designated through Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, and Issachar. For Simeon means “being heard,” Levi “added,” Judah “confessing,” Zebulun “dwelling of strength,” and Issachar “reward.” Since the active life is difficult and laborious, penitents are rightly understood in Simeon, converts in Levi, confessors in Judah, those fighting against the devil [Col. 1137C] and vices in Zebulun, and those worthily making satisfaction to God in Issachar.

A person who perfectly repents may fittingly be called both Simeon and Levi when, moved by worthy repentance for sins, he is heard by the Lord and, added to the congregation of the just, is united to his head, Christ, through holy works and righteous desires. Of such a person it is rightly said:

“Simeon and Levi are brothers, vessels of iniquity waging war” (Gen. XLIX). The blessed patriarch, illumined by the Holy Spirit, foresaw in his sons that the true sons of Jacob—all, that is, predestined to eternal life—although they had been vessels of iniquity through the daily increase of sins, ought, by returning to the Lord through repentance and conversion, to become vessels vigorously waging war against that same iniquity. Simeon and Levi—that is, penitents and converts—are rightly called brothers, because neither repentance without conversion nor conversion without repentance can suffice for salvation. Yet that repentance and conversion cannot please almighty God unless adorned with the good of discernment. [Col. 1137D] 735 Therefore it is aptly added at once:

“Let not my soul enter into their counsel, and let not my glory be in their assembly, because in their fury they slew a man, and in their will they undermined a wall.” It is the habit of certain penitents who pass over to spiritual warfare to prostrate themselves, by indiscreet labor, at the very beginning of their conversion. But because the Almighty does not approve such fervor in them, [Col. 1138A] it is rightly said, “Let not my soul enter into their counsel.” As though he said: My soul takes no delight in their counsel, because my heart is in no way gladdened by their indiscreet and insufficiently prudent affliction of the flesh, through which they make themselves useless both to me and to themselves. And because whatever a person indiscreetly begins without the counsel of God and of prelates holding God’s place, he also generally attributes not to God but to his own strength, the Lord consequently adds:

“And let not my glory be in their assembly.” As though he said: My glory shall not be in their assembly—that is, in the multitude of their labors—because in what they do without the moderation of discernment, they seek not my praise and glory but their own. I shall not glory in such persons, because “in their fury they slew a man, and in [Col. 1138B] their will they undermined a wall.” In the man is strength and vigor of body; in the wall may be understood hardness of heart. They slay the man in their fury when, through indiscreet fervor, they afflict themselves by excessive mortification of the flesh. They undermine the wall in their will when, after the hardness of heart has been softened through voluntary labors, they finally attain some illumination and tranquility of mind.

“But their fury is cursed, because it is stubborn; and their indignation, because it is harsh.” That fervor of penitents and converts by which, at the beginning of conversion, they destroy the strength of their bodies by unjust labors, become enfeebled within themselves, and afterward become fit for no pursuit of good work, may rightly be called cursed fury. Since it is stubborn—that is, [Col. 1138C] since it occurs without obedience to God 736 and teachers—it lacks God’s blessing. Their indignation too is rightly called harsh, that is, inflexible, when no command or admonition of teachers can call them back from their unadvised rigor.

But shall those who are to be saved perish through such stubborn fury and such harsh indignation against themselves? By no means. “I will divide them,” says the Lord, “in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.” By Jacob, whose name means “supplanter,” the supplanting of vices and the praiseworthy work of the active life are very fittingly designated. By Israel, however, who is called “a man seeing God,” contemplation of heart and the good work of the contemplative life are suitably expressed. Almighty God [Col. 1138D] divides a person in Jacob when, by his mercy, he inwardly teaches him how, after vices have been overthrown by the successes of virtues, he ought to separate and reject from the good acts performed in the active life what is harmful and useless. This salutary division takes place in a person when he endeavors, with prudent discernment and discriminating caution, to perform what he does in God and for God. After this praiseworthy division, he is scattered in Israel—that is, into contemplation of mind.

And it should be noted that it says, “I will scatter.” What is scattered, divided into tiny particles, gradually fails and is reduced to nothing. Thus when, through God’s mercy, a person has come to the sweet contemplation of mind, illumined by rays of heavenly splendor, he scatters and rejects from himself little by little, through God’s helping and cooperating grace, whatever he knows has remained in his body from less discerning acts, or in his heart from wicked thoughts or affections, [Col. 1139A] down to that point. He also fittingly receives the noble name of Judah when, having exercised himself somewhat in the active and contemplative life, he turns to humble, true, and perfect confession; and after true confession of sins receives from God the Father the very sweet blessing which follows.

## 737 CHAPTER IV. On the Blessing of Judah

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. XLIX). Whom, I ask, do these brothers more fittingly signify than the angelic hosts of the heavenly army? They stand ready for Judah—that is, the person truly and humbly confessing—even at the very [Col. 1139B] hour of his confession; receiving the true humility of the penitent and the humble repentance of the confessor, they raise him up, as the chosen son of the beloved Father and their brother, with no slight praises before the eyes of the highest Majesty. For the spiritual progress of a person still wandering on earth produces joy and gladness in the angelic virtues of heaven.

“Judah,” says the Lord, “your brothers shall praise you.” As though he said: Because you have truly humbled yourself before me, you have deservedly earned praise from your brothers, the angelic spirits. “For when you were little in your own eyes, I made you head over the tribes of Israel.” And what wonder if we call the holy angels brothers of elect human beings, since the Creator and Lord of angels himself deigned to call himself their brother, saying [Col. 1139C] through the Prophet: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you” (Ps. XXI, 23). And again after his resurrection: “Go,” he says, “announce it to my brothers” (Matt. XXVIII, 10). Those confessors too, who receive the confession of one confessing in God’s place and stead, are called that person’s brothers; praising the wondrous mercy of almighty God in him and for him, they rejoice in all things at his progress.

But whoever has deserved to be raised before God by such great praises of angels and human beings who behold the perfection of his life, to him the gracious and merciful Lord indicates in the following words with what prudent eye of circumspection he ought to guard himself, lest through praise or vain glory God’s gift perish within him.

[Col. 1139D] “Your hand,” he says, “shall be on the necks of your enemies, and the sons of your father shall adore you.” By the hand may be understood good action; by the necks of enemies, the hidden temptation of malignant spirits that secretly suggest pride of mind. For pride is expressed by necks, as it is said through the Prophet in the psalm: “The Lord, being just, has cut down the necks of sinners” (Ps. CXXVIII, 14). Apostate spirits, ever envious of human salvation, rise against a person all the more importunately the more they see him advance spiritually in God; and, when they cannot overthrow him through outward acts, they endeavor to overthrow him by lofty thoughts in the secrecy of the heart.

Therefore, the Lord says, “Your hand [Col. 1140A] shall be on the necks of your enemies.” As though he said: When you have acted well and praiseworthily, remember always to keep yourself in humility, lest you be exalted in the secret of your heart. If you do this, “the sons of your father shall adore you.” In this place, by father may be understood either the devil or this present world; by sons, the works of the world, which are works of sin. Of this father it was said to Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. XII, 1). And again, through the Prophet, the Lord admonishes every blessed soul, saying: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XLIV, 11). He rightly says, “your father.” For we were once children of the devil; we were also children of the world. We were children of the devil through the fault of the first human being, but reborn through baptism we became children of God by grace. After this, by the deliberation [Col. 1140B] of our own will, we were also children of the world, when we yielded more to worldly than to heavenly desires.

But every person converted from the vanity of the world and perfectly returned to God through true repentance and confession, if he keeps himself in true humility, shall be adored by the sons of his father. For, having received through God’s mercy the pardon of sins, he shall be mercifully cleansed from dead works contracted through diabolical suggestion and love of the world. And it is well said, “the sons of your father shall adore you,” because, just as one who wishes to adore someone prostrates himself upon the ground, so every iniquity falls and melts away from the soul of one truly confessing and, after confession, persisting in humility, while God cleanses that person inwardly. But our true Jacob, after this noble counsel and consolation of mercy, sets forth an example of humility to be learned, when he immediately adds and says:

The lion’s whelp of Judah. The lion is by nature the strongest of beasts. It also sleeps, as we read, with open eyes; and when it gives forth its roar, the remaining multitude of beasts trembles at its voice. Quite fittingly, therefore, by the lion we may understand any good and righteous superior and teacher, who ought to be most strong in holy conduct, most strong in restraining vices and carnal desires. He sleeps with open eyes when he strives so to withdraw himself from the tumults of the world that nevertheless he does not neglect to keep watch over the spiritual and bodily needs of those subject to him. When such a man sends forth the roar of preaching, all the beasts—that is, all people who acknowledge that they have at some time lived beast-like lives—on hearing of the joys of everlasting life and the perils of perpetual damnation, begin to tremble with salutary fear at his voice [Col. 1140D]. Almighty God therefore wills that everyone who desires to be His son should always strive to remain subject in humility. Thus He says, “The lion’s whelp of Judah,” as though saying: “Be a lion’s whelp; be, I say, the humble subject of that superior and teacher whom I have set over you. Be an imitator of his strength; be a provident follower of his teaching. Remember why you have come and to what end you have resolved at last to arrive.”

“You have gone up for prey, my son.” From the valley of this world you have ascended to the height of this holy conversion [Col. 1141A], in order to seize what is not your own—that is, in order that you may deserve to be filled with spiritual sweetness and the gift of heavenly virtues. You have likewise gone up to make prey of the devil, so that, having recognized that you were once his willing slave, you may snatch yourself from his power and dominion and, by living holily, righteously, and soberly, restore yourself, body and soul together, to Me, your Creator and Liberator.

But by the aid of My preceding and following grace you have by no means been deprived of your desire. “Resting, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness.” Resting from evils, you lay down in good things, after the example of the lion—that is, of the good superior, the good teacher whom I gave you—and of the lioness, namely this holy congregation [Col. 1141B] which has received you. Blessed is the person who, resting from sins and lying down in good things, deserves to be praised by the Lord. For how great a grace still follows upon him, the next phrase mystically indicates to us. For it continues:

“Who shall rouse him?” As though it said: He alone to whom alone belongs this name, “Who”—whose name no one knows—raises him in this present life from the death of sins, from the death of the soul, so that after the death of the flesh He may restore him, raised in body and soul together, to eternal salvation. Such a person will indeed be able to please God in his life, as the following text immediately adds:

“The sceptre,” it says, “shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until He comes who is to be sent” [Col. 1141C]. In the sceptre, which kings alone are accustomed to hold forth, we may fittingly understand that royal rod by which the person truly raised from the death of the soul to life governs himself in good things and strikes himself away from evils. In the ruler of his thighs, moreover, we believe that the sense and understanding of the heart are rightly to be understood. It should be noted that it says, “from his thighs.” There is, indeed, as it were one thigh of the heart and another thigh of the body. A person has in the thigh of the flesh good works by which he lifts himself toward God; he has in the thigh of the heart understanding, through which he continually flies from the narrowness of this mortality to God and to the spacious freedom of the heavenly country. Upon these two thighs the blessed person must be supported until He comes who is to be sent: until that sweet love of God, which is the Holy Spirit, who is sent from above into human hearts, scatters the darkness of the mind by the brightness of His wondrous visitation and pours Himself desirably into the longing heart through the grace of eternal sweetness innate to Him [Col. 1141D]. “And He shall be the expectation of the nations.” For in Him and through Him forgiveness of all sins comes about. When He comes, He kindles the human heart with the invisible fire of His love to a greater constancy of spiritual fervour. Hence the words that immediately follow are apt:

“Binding his foal to the vine, and his ass, O my son, to the vine-stock.” By the foal may be denoted the small and humble spirit of a person; by the vineyard, the spiritual dwelling-place of religious life. The Holy Spirit binds His foal to the vineyard [Col. 1142A] when, by the sweetness of His love, He so confirms in spiritual life the spirit of a person made small through humility that, if anything in the austerity of spiritual life had until then seemed hard or difficult to him, or if he still suffered any uncertainty or instability in mind, it all vanishes; and he begins, so far as humanly possible, to embrace and love bitter things as sweet for God’s sake. He also binds His ass to the vine-stock when He strives to bend the body, which is represented by the ass, and every bodily sense to the service, praise, and honour of our Lord Jesus Christ. For He is that vine from which the wine of eternal sweetness springs forth, as He Himself testifies of Himself in the Gospel: “I am the true vine, and My Father is the husbandman” [Col. 1142B] (John 15:1). Everyone, therefore, who is so grafted into this vine that he gladly occupies himself often, with all his senses and with the whole frame of his outward members, in the service, praise, and honour of God, deserves inwardly to hear from the most sweet voice of the Lord, speaking invisibly to him: “O my son!” For he is a son of God, because he deserves continually to be made drunk with paternal sweetness by Him. Hence it follows:

“He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes.” By wine may fittingly be understood the abundant grace of the Holy Spirit; by the robe, the soul adorned with humility and the other virtues. The robe is washed in wine when the humble soul, cleansed and purified in compunction proceeding from the invisible fountain of eternal sweetness, strives to die utterly to sins and vices [Col. 1142C], so that it may deserve to be clothed with Christ, its heavenly Bridegroom. He also washes his cloak in the blood of grapes when, in conformity to Christ’s Passion, he daily washes and renews his body, signified by the cloak, from the oldness of sins. But because the more a person grows strong outwardly in virtues and virtuous actions, the more spiritual sense and understanding increase inwardly in him, the following is rightly added:

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.” Here wine signifies either the severity of the Law or the pleasure of the present world; the eyes, understanding; the teeth, spiritual senses. When a person begins to understand spiritually the severity of the Law, and has spiritually turned his senses away from the milk of the letter so as to draw forth the hidden sweetness of spiritual grace [Col. 1142D], his eyes are rightly proved more beautiful than wine, because that spiritual understanding which then arises from Holy Scripture may deservedly be called more beautiful, purer, and more delightful than every worldly pleasure. He also has teeth whiter than milk when, strengthened in spiritual understanding and having set aside the milk of the simple letter, he begins, with the strong teeth of constant meditation, not only to chew and break up lighter matters but also the stronger mysteries of Holy Scripture.

## CHAPTER V. On the blessing of Zebulun

After Judah comes Zebulun, whose name is interpreted “dwelling-place of strength,” in fitting order, because it does not suffice to confess sins if, after confession, one ceases to resist sins and enemies in a certain strong struggle. Thus he says:

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the haven of ships, reaching as far as Sidon” (Gen. 49). By the shore of the sea we rightly understand the steadfastness of a heart made bitter through repentance. Those who fight well against the devil are aptly said to dwell on the shore of the sea, because demons are overcome and vices are driven out by the stable bitterness of the penitent heart. Therefore, whoever wishes to be found superior to his enemy in this most strenuous encounter of battle should not delay to flee to the haven of ships. A haven is a port in which ships are placed after the dangerous waves of the waters have been traversed. And by this haven is aptly figured the most peaceful harbour of eternal rest [Col. 1143B], in which the multitude of the elect is established when the labours and miseries of the present life have ended. Yet no one can reach this haven if he is found outside the ships built by the hand of the Most High for human salvation. By the name of ships, by whose conveyance the stormy dangers of the waters are avoided, may be understood the different orders in the holy Church which suffice for salvation, which lift a person from the deepest whirlpool of vices and restore him to the harbour of eternal salvation.

There is also another haven of ships in this life: namely, the steadfast love of God and love of neighbour. When a person has been established in holy life by this love, Zebulun may rightly be said to dwell—that is, to rest—at the haven of ships. For if the heart inwardly burns with true love of God and neighbour, then, even if outward things attack it, it is nevertheless in true rest; because, though not yet in possession, it is in hope, as though established in the harbour of everlasting salvation, and happily rests with the Lord. The shore restrains him from admitting evil; the haven guards him so that he may delight in doing good [Col. 1143C]. Hence there immediately follows:

“Reaching as far as Sidon.” Sidon is said to mean “useless hunting.” One reaches as far as Sidon who diligently pursues, as though by a certain subtle hunting, everything useless and less praiseworthy that he finds in his body or soul, in order to reduce it to nothing.

## CHAPTER VI. On the blessing of Issachar

After such hunting, Zebulun becomes Issachar when he willingly embraces for God’s sake whatever labour or difficulty there may be. It follows, therefore:

“Issachar, a strong ass lying down between the boundaries, saw rest, that it was good, and the land, that it was very good; and he put his shoulder to bear, and became a servant paying tribute” (Gen. 49). In Issachar, whose name is interpreted “there is reward,” we may understand, as we said much above, those who worthily make satisfaction to God for their sins. But one who seeks so to make satisfaction for past offences that his satisfaction may please almighty God must strive to be a strong ass. An ass is indeed a beast of burden, and patiently bears and carries whatever is placed upon it [Col. 1144A]. Thus—yes, thus—Issachar, that is, the person who strives to repay to God by the recompense of pious labour what he wickedly stole away through sight, must be a beast of burden; and, in bearing whatever may arise from the weakness of his own flesh, from the malice of the ancient enemy, or even from those dwelling with him, he must show himself humble, strong, and gentle. Let him be strong in body for endurance, strong in heart for patience. The order of the following words mystically indicates how he may advance to such strength:

“Lying down,” it says, “between the boundaries.” Note that it sets, as it were, two boundaries here. In the one boundary may be understood the eternal life which we await; in the other, the eternal death which we desire to escape [Col. 1144B]. To lie down is to rest in humility of heart. For when he considers on one side the joy of everlasting life, and on the other carefully reckons the dangers and miseries of eternal death, he becomes in a manner a strong ass lying down between the boundaries; because, encouraged to bodily endurance by the prospect of eternal blessedness and to patience in heart by fear of eternal damnation, he happily advances through true humility to true tranquillity of heart.

But whence does this come? For, as follows, “he saw that rest was good, and the land that it was very good, and he put his shoulder to bear.” He sees how health-giving, sweet, and delightful it is in the present life to rest in true humility. For true humility is true tranquillity of heart and body. It is deservedly declared to be good, because through it a person deserves finally to reach the land which is very good, namely the land of the living. This land is good in hope, but will be very good in eternal recompense, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” [Col. 1144C] (Ps. 26:15). Therefore, through love and desire for this most excellent land, he puts his shoulder to bear, when he firmly restrains himself beneath himself and devoutly girds the shoulder of the heart, as we have said, for patience, and the shoulder of the body for endurance.

“And he became a servant paying tribute.” He serves in paying tribute when he does not refuse devoutly to render from the flesh the labour of the flesh and from the heart the sorrow of the heart [Col. 1144D]. Thus the prophet David paid tribute perfectly when he said: “For Thou alone considerest labour and sorrow” (Ps. 10:14). We must continually pay these tributes to God, so that we may serve Him at all times with the body, as far as we can, and may always strive with the heart to return to the desire for heavenly goods. This is the active life, not unfittingly expressed through Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, and Issachar: it is so exercised in active labour that it is nevertheless not deprived of contemplative sweetness.

## CHAPTER VII. On the blessing of Dan

After the labours of the active life have been traversed, the contemplative life follows. It is rightly expressed by the five remaining brothers—namely Dan, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, and Joseph [Col. 1145A]. It shines with the splendour of contemplative sweetness, yet does not lack active labour. Neither life can be practised perfectly or profitably without the other. Hence there fittingly follows:

“Dan shall judge his people, as also another tribe in Israel” (Gen. 49). Dan, whose name is interpreted “judgment,” signifies the spiritual person who, lifting himself above low and earthly actions, insofar as this is possible for a human being, by contemplation and delight in the heavenly country, carefully weighs and judges not only his deeds and words but even each of his smallest thoughts, which are as it were his people, according to what Scripture says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15). But because it is necessary for him wisely to provide for himself in both the active and contemplative life, the following blessing or prophecy of the patriarch Jacob mystically indicates this: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the hoofs of the horse, so that its rider may fall backward.” The snake, which is also a serpent, has by nature such gentleness in its movement that it often shows itself to be seen before it can be perceived to be moving. A *cerastes*, however, is said to be a horned serpent, which is not found at all in these regions. The serpent signifies prudence, as Wisdom itself, of the eternal Father, testifies elsewhere in the Gospel: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). In the horns of the *cerastes* we may understand power [Col. 1145C].

It is indeed necessary for the spiritual person to imitate the serpent in the way; that is, in all things which must be done in the active life, signified by the way, he should endeavour to act not through a sudden or importunate assault, but through a pleasing, prudent, and provident deliberation of mind. Let him also be a *cerastes* on the path: powerful, that is, and prudent in the contemplative life. Let him be prudent in prayer and powerful in contemplation of mind. He is prudent who can drive from the sight of his heart the useless phantasms of thoughts that arise during prayer, by the prudent hand of heavenly desire, and who has learned wisely to discern what should be prayed for and how. Through this prudent prayer he is lifted to powerful contemplation of mind [Col. 1145D], where he becomes so powerful in contemplating many things previously unknown that, despising transitory things, he is sweetly kindled to seek and desire only those things which remain. Thus he will be able effectively to fulfil what follows:

“Biting the hoofs of the horse, so that its rider may fall backward.” Our flesh, upon which our spirit rides, may be signified by the horse; and by the horse’s hoof, which is as it were a kind of dead flesh, whatever dead work may be found in the flesh. He is said to bite the hoof of the horse who strives to crush and cast away with the harsh bites of repentance whatever subject to death he discovers lodging in his flesh, so that the ancient enemy, who is understood by the rider of the horse, may fall backward and find no place in him where he can sit.

It should be noted why it says, “that he may fall backward” [Col. 1146A]. What is behind a person cannot be seen by him. He makes the rider fall backward who, when he perceives that the devil—the instigator of all evils—is preparing to mount his flesh through the seductive suggestion of sin, does not consent to these promptings but, by biting the horse’s hoof in the manner already described, crushes him, dashed down by a mighty fall: backward, that is, before his sins come before his face; before they begin to be known by God or by people; before the consent becomes known to God, who searches the secrets of the heart, or a disgraceful deed becomes widely reported in human ears. Once the enemy has been crushed in this manner, let him confidently cry out and say to the Lord:

“I shall await Thy salvation, O Lord.” As though he said: “Because, in view of the eternal vision of Thee, I appear estranged from all the joys of this world; because, with heart and mind eagerly fixed upon Thee alone, who alone sufficest me for all things, I await Thy salvation by desiring it and desire it by awaiting it. Nor, Lord, do I await only that salvation of Thine which is reserved as a reward for Thy elect unto eternal life, but also that salvation which in this life is daily prepared, through the visiting grace of Thy inspiration, in the blessings of Thy sweetness for those who love Thee.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On the blessing of Gad

But because the higher a person is raised above himself by desire to contemplate heavenly things, the more subtly he is inwardly assailed by the enemy’s stings of temptations, the patriarch, filled with the Holy Spirit, added in a fitting order:

“Gad, girded, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be girded backward” [Col. 1146C] (Gen. 49). Under the name Gad, interpreted “temptation” or “robber,” is fittingly figured the hidden and secret temptation by which the malicious enemy attempts to overthrow even the most perfect. A hidden temptation is one that occurs so inwardly that even the person who suffers it cannot discern or recognize it. As it gently and secretly pours itself into the human heart, it shakes and confounds with a sudden disturbance even the mind which seemed to stand on high, so that, as though placed in a cloud of anxiety, it does not know what it suffers; reckoning good to be evil and evil good, it begins to find sad and bitter all the things that previously seemed sweet and desirable [Col. 1146D].

Against this plague of temptation, which especially attacks spiritual persons, let a person gird himself with manly strength of mind, always return to the bosom of inward self-examination, and diligently fortify himself with the shield of continual prayer. Let him permit nothing to enter his mind whereby the eye of the mind may be struck back from the love of inward light. When he has thus girded himself to fight the Lord’s battle, it may fittingly be said of him:

“Gad, girded, shall fight before him,” because the Most High Searcher of hearts sees and approves his struggle and conflict [Col. 1147A], and grants him not merely victory with Himself but mercifully rewards him as victor both here and in the future, as is mystically shown by the words that follow:

“And he himself shall be girded backward.” What is it to be girded backward? What is conveyed by these words except that almighty God, preserving him mercifully, girds that person who by vigilant custody of the heart restrains himself inwardly, as far as he can, from harmful thoughts, against harmful action backward—that is, in the body? Thus girded or made ready, the more he is lifted above earthly things by the love of heavenly desire, the more richly he deserves inward refreshment through the savour of heavenly sweetness, as the following blessing or prophecy seems mystically to signify.

## CHAPTER IX. On the blessing of Asher and Naphtali

“Asher,” he says, “his bread is rich, and he shall provide delights for kings” [Col. 1147B] (Gen. 49). Asher is interpreted “blessed,” and fittingly signifies the one and same person who deserved to be called both Dan by strictly judging himself and Gad by stoutly resisting his temptations. What and how great his blessedness is becomes more clearly evident when it says, “his bread is rich.” By bread may be understood heavenly refreshment, which is continual compunction of heart; by the richness of bread, abundance of compunction proceeding from heavenly sweetness. The prophet David desired to be satisfied with this richness of bread when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise Thee with lips of exultation” [Col. 1147C] (Ps. 62:6). His bread is therefore rightly called rich who is frequently refreshed in himself by the sweetness of this heavenly refreshment; and, should necessity require it, he will also be able sweetly and profitably to refresh others. Hence there immediately and fittingly follows:

“And he shall provide delights for kings.” In Holy Scripture those are called kings who, holding forth in the hands of their hearts the sceptre of justice, leave nothing uncorrected in themselves, but know how to rule and order their dispositions, speech, actions, and thoughts in accordance with the will of God. To such kings the administration of heavenly teaching is like a sweet and abundant preparation of delights. But those who are not kings, who lack the governance of this power [Col. 1147D], regard God’s word not as delight or sweetness, but as bitterness. Asher’s bread is therefore rightly said to be rich, and he is said to provide delights for kings, because, filled in himself with the marrow and fatness of inward sweetness, he is rendered fit and able, with lips [the manuscript reads *labia*, “lips”] of exultation, to praise and, that is, to proclaim the words of heavenly instruction to kings—that is, to those who rule themselves.

After so great a grace of heavenly condescension, he also becomes Naphtali, whose name is interpreted “breadth.” Though narrow toward all that the present world possesses, he is expanded more and more, with all the depths of heart and soul, toward Him alone whom he beholds in mind. Hence follows:

“Naphtali, a stag sent forth, giving words of beauty.” He indeed becomes a stag when he begins to make the lovely and desirable leaps of prayer and contemplation [Col. 1148A]. For unless the leap of prayer comes first, the leap of contemplation is very weak. Therefore, when he has passed from the leap of pure prayer to the strongest leap, namely the leap of contemplation, he is deservedly called not merely a stag but, with a sweet addition, “a released stag,” because neither the flesh, nor the world, nor even the devil himself can hold him back from being continually sent forth, lifted above all things lying below, to Him whom he worships and loves before all and above all, whom alone he hungers and thirsts for. If he should at any time be recalled from this state for the edification of his neighbours, he will be able to give words of beauty—that is, to put forth such teaching as makes a human heart beautiful. And thus finally he becomes Joseph, whose name is interpreted “one who increases,” and may deservedly be so called.

Thus, yes, thus, one perfectly spiritual person mystically takes upon himself the five names of five brothers: when, as we have said, he is Dan by diligently judging his people; Gad by strongly girding himself against hidden temptations; Asher—that is, blessed—in his life; Naphtali, enlarged in the love of God; and Joseph, increased in the love or edification of his neighbours [Col. 1148B]. He advances so far that he deserves to be called the true son of the true Jacob and, in accordance with the fitting meaning of the text that follows, to be blessed by him with the fatherly blessing. It follows:

## CHAPTER X. On the blessing of Joseph and its allegorical meaning

“Joseph, an increasing son; an increasing son and beautiful in appearance” [Col. 1148C] (Gen. 49). These words may first be referred most fittingly in a special sense to the special and only-begotten Son of the eternal Father, who is rightly called Joseph because He is our Creator and Re-creator. He is the author and increaser of all our salvation; and, being both God and man, He ought in prophetic foresight to be called not once but twice “an increasing son, an increasing son.” For He is the increasing Son of God the Father in heaven according to divinity; He is also the increasing son of His virgin Mother on earth according to humanity. How the Son of God, eternally and without beginning begotten from the same Father, could increase to God the Father, eternally and without beginning unbegotten, no one ought or is able to investigate [Col. 1148D]. For in all things He is equal, co-omnipotent, and co-eternal with Him by whom He was begotten. But He who according to the nature of divinity could become neither greater nor less deigned to increase for humankind through the form of humanity which He assumed. Yet that growth was so clean, so pure, and so holy that it could never be stained by any defilement. Hence it fittingly adds, “and beautiful in appearance.” In the very weakness of humanity which He assumed, He remained wholly chaste, wholly clean, wholly sound; and therefore He was always lovely, delightful, and desirable to behold for God the Father and the angelic host. He is “beautiful in form,” whose appearance and beauty the eminent prophet David, foreseeing in the Holy Spirit, extolled with due praises, saying: “Beautiful in form above the sons of men” [Col. 1149A] (Ps. 44:3). For He was beautiful because He alone was conceived and born without sin, alone lived among sinners without sin, and remained in the beauty of His own loveliness. For He did not come to be defiled by our sins, but to cleanse those who were defiled and to call back to the light and glory of everlasting life those enveloped in the shadow of eternal death. Hence the next words are aptly added:

“The daughters ran about upon the wall. But those possessing arrows provoked Him, quarrelled with Him, and envied Him.” By the wall is understood Christ’s divinity: He is truly the wall of His Church, which He guards by protecting with the defence of His mercy and protects by guarding, as the prophet testifies when he says: “Sion, our city of strength: the Saviour shall be set therein as wall and outer wall” [Col. 1149B] (Isa. 26:1). By the daughters, a term denoting weakness, we rightly understand human weaknesses, which He took upon Himself from no necessity but solely from love. The running about of the daughters signifies human affections, which made Him—who in His divinity was stable, unchangeable, and impassible—mutable and passible in the humanity assumed for us, moving from insult to insult and from place to place.

In this running about, “those possessing arrows provoked Him, quarrelled with Him, and envied Him.” In those who possessed arrows and embittered the Lord may be understood the perverse hosts of malicious spirits, abounding in the diverse arrows of diverse temptations with which they continually assail good and evil, righteous and unrighteous alike [Col. 1149C]. Nor did they withhold these their arrows from their own Creator and Lord of all, but in accordance with this present prophecy first provoked Him, then quarrelled with Him, and finally envied Him. They provoked Him when, at the very beginning, so to speak, of His birth, they stirred up against Him the fury of wicked Herod. Because of Herod’s cruelty, He, so small, so crying, so tender, fled into Egypt at an angel’s warning and there remained hidden until Herod’s death. But when they had been unable to destroy Him in infancy through these and similar afflictions, they were not afraid thereafter to assail Him with quarrels, saying: “If Thou art the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” [Col. 1149D] (Matt. 4:3); and again, “If Thou art the Son of God, cast Thyself down” (ibid., 6); and again, “All these things will I give Thee if, falling down, Thou wilt worship me” (ibid., 9). But when they had not prevailed even thus, and saw at last that the venomous arrows of their malice had recoiled upon themselves contrary to their hope, kindled by greater fires of wickedness, they continued to envy Him until through their members they killed Him by the hanging of the cross.

In another sense, by those possessing arrows we understand the Jews themselves, who had indeed the Law and the prophets, with which, as with certain strong arrows, they ought to have struck back and overcome the ancient enemy. Yet, not receiving the Lord who came in the flesh for their salvation, they provoked Him by their unbelief and evil life. Then, to increase the measure of their iniquity [Col. 1150A], they quarrelled with Him, blaspheming His name and maliciously contradicting in every respect His sayings and deeds. Finally, they envied Him. For He was grievous for them even to behold, and they did not rest from this same envy or hatred until they condemned Him, suspended between two thieves, to the punishment of an ignominious death. Yet in the very thing in which He seemed to be conquered, He conquered, because by the glorious triumph of His death He abolished the dominion of death. Hence follows:

“His bow sat in strength, and the bonds of His arms and hands were loosed by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob.” The bow, composed of wood and string, or of horn and string, nobly signifies the same Lord and our Redeemer. For by the string may be signified His most holy flesh, wondrously drawn and stretched by the manifold straits of tribulations; while by the wood or horn may be signified His omnipotent divinity, which remained in a manner rigid and unyielding in compassion for human miseries until this noble string—the most sacred flesh of Christ—began for the sake of our salvation to be twisted by reproaches and mockeries, drawn, and stretched by the fastenings of the cross [Col. 1150B]. When the string was drawn through the Passion of His humanity, His divinity was at once bent to compassion; because the more harshly the only-begotten Son of God suffered in the flesh, the more benignly God the Father was inclined toward the reconciliation of humankind. This is that bow which the same Father long ago promised, saying: “I will set My bow in the clouds of heaven” [Col. 1150C] (Gen. 9:13).

This bow “sat in strength”—that is, it was drawn with great and grievous force—when, after accomplishing all for which He had come, He was at last raised upon the wood of the cross, given gall and vinegar to drink, and said: “It is finished” (John 19:30). Immediately, in a wondrous manner, He sent forth a noble and chosen arrow, exceedingly strong and sharp—namely, His most sacred soul—with such power and strength that it even mightily penetrated the lowest regions of hell and, having overthrown the dominion of death, powerfully bound the strong prince of death. Without delay, as follows, “the bonds of His arms and hands were loosed by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob.” By His arms and hands are not unfittingly signified the patriarchs, prophets, and His other elect [Col. 1150D], who, bound by original sin, were held captive for many thousands of years in darkness and the shadow of death. Their bonds were at last loosed by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob when, suddenly illumined by the brightness of His divinity and with the record of sins abolished, they deserved to be called back to their former freedom. Then was fulfilled what had long before been nobly prefigured in the patriarch’s following words:

“From there,” he says, “the Shepherd went forth, the Stone of Israel.” By Israel, interpreted “the man seeing God,” we rightly understand the holy and elect angelic spirits, who from the day of their creation see without interruption the desirable face of their Creator, because no instability of changefulness could ever separate or turn them away, even for a moment, from beholding the brightness of His divinity [Col. 1151A]. The same almighty God was and is their stone, because He sustained them so that they should not fall, and established and strengthened them by His own might and power so that they could no longer fall. Therefore He who is in heaven the Stone of angels went forth from hell as the Shepherd and Redeemer of human beings. Those whom He found wandering in the cavernous winding passages of the Tartarean city, sorely afflicted amid the jaws of the wolf—that is, the ancient enemy—by their long waiting for His coming, He at last led up victoriously and mercifully brought back to the pleasant pastures of heavenly life. Thus, finally, was fulfilled the patriarch’s following prophecy, in which he said:

God of your father shall be your helper, and the Almighty shall bless you with blessings of heaven above, with blessings of the deep that lies beneath, with blessings of breasts [Col. 1151B] and womb. The God of the Father of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ is the divinity of Almighty God, which always and in all things aided him, which performed all his works in him and with him; for just as, after assuming humanity, he always remained true man, so too he never ceased to be true God. And the Almighty—that is, the Holy Spirit—blessed him when, by an unheard-of and ineffable gift, he filled the hearts of the disciples and made them strong, fearless, and steadfast in glorifying, blessing, and magnifying his name.

Therefore God the Father and God the Holy Spirit blessed God the Son with blessings of heaven above and blessings of the deep lying beneath, because “in him,” as the Apostle says, “it pleased all fullness to dwell, and through him to reconcile [Col. 1151C] all things unto him, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth” (Col. 1:19–20). He made peace with things in heaven and things on earth because he began to restore and make whole the diminished number of holy angels by the glorious price of his blood—that is, by the number of his redeemed. Thus, with the wall of hostilities, which stood not only between God and humankind but also between angel and humankind, dissolved in his flesh, humanity rejoices, restored to blessed intercourse and one day to be admitted to the rejoicing fellowship of angels.

The Almighty also blessed him in another way with blessings of heaven above when the heavens—that is, the heavenly choirs of angels—applauded him, clothed in flesh, with the new song of praise [Col. 1151D], saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). He blessed him with blessings of the deep lying beneath when, as he descended to hell after his glorious triumph over death, the people of the saints, held captive in death, cried out with joyful voices:

> 756 You have come, O Desired One, whom we awaited in darkness,  
> that on this night you might lead the bound from their prisons.  
> Our sighs called for you; abundant lamentations sought you.  
> You have become hope for the despairing, great consolation amid torments.

He blessed him with blessings of breasts when the breasts of that first Church, which began in the apostles and had already been divinely prepared for the milk of heavenly faith and teaching, began through the wondrous coming of the Holy Spirit to be filled with a new and unheard-of abundance of the heavenly gift [Col. 1152A]. He blessed him with blessings of the womb when the nations, which had not yet received his faith, were gathered into the womb of their mother, the holy Church; gradually nourished with the food of spiritual grace, they were granted, in the womb of their own heart, to conceive by faith and bring forth the same Lord and our Redeemer.

Yet these blessings of the increasing Son, the Son of Almighty God, did not come to an end when he died, rose, and ascended. They remain now, and will always remain until the end of the age. This is fittingly represented in the following words:

“The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the everlasting hills should come.” The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, as [Col. 1152B] we have said before, is Almighty God. The fathers of this Father were not only the patriarchs and prophets, from whose seed he was begotten according to the flesh, but also his most holy apostles and the other righteous and elect persons, who begot him in the hearts of believers through the teaching of their preaching.

“The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers.” It is as though he said: The blessings which you received from God the Father, which you brought about through the grace of baptism and forgiveness of sins—by being born, dying, and rising again—in order to annul the curse of the first human being, are strengthened daily by the blessings of his fathers: not only the apostles and other holy teachers who have already departed, but also those who daily beget him in the holy Church by teaching and baptizing. [Col. 1152C] For they are renewed daily until the desire of the everlasting hills comes—757 that is, the desire of the angels established in the height of eternity. Their desire is that the course of this present age may run its course, so that their choir may be completed by the number of elect human beings. At the end of his blessings, the faithful patriarch admonishes and exhorts us to seek and desire the same things.

“May they be upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers.” It is as though he said: May these blessings flourish in the mind of prelates, and flourish also in the intention of subjects, so that in all their actions and affections they may be found to possess a mind so pure and an intention so holy that they may one day deserve to be numbered among their brothers—the holy [Col. 1152D] angels [758].

Having set forth these matters according to allegory, to the extent of our capacity, let us turn back the eye of the heart to the mystical moral sense and consider more closely how these same words apply spiritually to every perfect prelate.

## CHAPTER XI. On the same blessing of Joseph and its moral meaning

Joseph, as we began to say, bears the figure of every elect and perfect prelate, who through the daily increase of good works makes daily progress toward the distinguishing marks of spiritual virtues. When he thus increases before his Father—that is, the true Jacob—he deserves to be called once and again by the most sweet name of son: “Joseph, an increasing son; a son,” he says, “increasing” [Col. 1153A] (Gen. 49). By this twofold repetition we may understand the twofold love of God and neighbour.
