When the one who must preside over others has perfectly attained this love, he may rightly be called “an increasing son, an increasing son.” For he is the son of the one whom he imitates, whom he honours, and to whom he strives to become conformed: an increasing son in the love of God, an increasing son in the edification of his neighbour. For the more he inwardly increases toward his heavenly Father through true and perfect love, the more, by that Father’s help, he is inwardly strengthened for the edification of neighbours.

He is also called “beautiful in appearance” when he strives, insofar as this is possible for a human being, to present himself as beautiful and pleasing before the divine gaze: inwardly free from consent to sin and outwardly free from sinful action [Col. 1153B]; and when in all that he does he aims either at divine honour or at the edification of neighbours. To such a person, without doubt, the desirable blessing that follows is added:

“The daughters,” he says, “ran about upon the wall.” As we have said above, *daughter* is a name for weakness. We may fittingly understand by the name of daughters the weak souls of converts, who in a certain manner begin to run about upon the wall when they delight to set beneath their heart as its chief foundation that living stone, Christ the cornerstone, which Jacob placed beneath his head. They direct all their will in accordance with him and desire, in character and life, to please him alone who is above all things.

And it should be noted that it says, “they ran about.” Everyone [Col. 1153C] who runs neither stands still nor lingers, but strives speedily to reach the place toward which he is moving. Therefore, in the running about of the daughters running upon the wall, we may not unfittingly understand, in accordance with this sense, the constant and vigorous zeal of novices. They are said, as it were, to run about upon the wall when, not sluggish or lukewarm, but with a certain strenuous zeal and fervent energy, they strive to pass over to God and into God. The prophet David foresaw in the Holy Spirit that this running would occur among God’s children when he said: “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:8). But because, so long as we are in this life, we must be worn down by labours and tempted by vices, the following is consequently added:

[Col. 1153D] “But they provoked him bitterly, and quarrelled with him, and those having arrows envied him.” By “those having arrows,” as we said above, we understand the bands of evil spirits, who possess the arrows of temptations. Armed with these, they advance against Joseph and his sons; by them they now cast unwary souls down from the state of their uprightness by wounding them, and now kill them utterly once wounded. But what do “they provoked bitterly,” “they quarrelled,” and “they envied” mean? By these three words are indicated three successive periods of temptations: the first, of conversion; the second, of progress; the third, of perfection, or the completion of life. They provoke beginners; they contend against those making progress; with arrows of envy they attack those being perfected. They provoke a person bitterly at the beginning, when they commonly inflict upon [Col. 1154A] the heart a certain anxious bitterness, so that, while what is heard or seen outwardly has little savour, the soul may more easily be hindered or recalled from longing for the heavenly homeland.

But when someone has broken within himself the shackles of this diabolical bitterness and has resolved to walk steadfastly through the narrow way of spiritual conversion in hope of a better life, they quarrel against him as one standing, as it were, in the onward course of virtues. For now by the world, now by his own flesh, sometimes by prosperity and sometimes by adversity, they seek to hold him back. When provocations and quarrels have at last been overcome, envy follows. Although they cannot harm those placed on the summit of perfection, they nevertheless always desire to harm them. They provoke bitterly at the beginning, quarrel during progress, and envy at the completion of life, because even the very hour [Col. 1154B] when the final lot comes cannot be safe from their envy. For against one whom they then cannot truly harm, they boldly display the arrows of their deceit.

But whoever does not yield in the present to those who provoke bitterly, quarrel, and envy will not be able to be terrified at the end by the malicious objections of their falsehood, because, as is said in what follows, “His bow sat in strength.” This bow, consisting of wood and string, fittingly signifies the human being, composed of soul and body.

The bow, that is, the human being, whose string—that is, the flesh—is dried out from the moistness of vices, and is here vigorously stretched by frequent bending and mortification through vigils, fasts, and other devout labours, shall sit in strength after the end of this life. For he shall rest eternally in Christ and with Christ, who is denoted by “the strong one” [Col. 1154C]. In that resting-place of perpetual repose, what is figuratively expressed in the subsequent wording will be perfectly fulfilled:

“And the bonds of his arms and hands were loosened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob.” We understand here by Jacob the one and same Lord and our Redeemer whom we understood by “the strong one” above. Therefore everyone who receives a place of eternal rest in this Strong One deserves to be mercifully freed, through his hand—that is, through his almighty working, through his wonderful and magnificent compassion—from all the bonds of his arms and hands: from all sins, I say, contracted inwardly or outwardly.

[Col. 1154D] But in another interpretation, as regards the state of the present life, by the bow let Almighty God be understood, while by “the strong one,” in whom this noble bow deigns to sit, let a truly humble person be understood. For no one is truly strong who is not truly humble, since the one who is truly humble can stand firm strongly in all things and through all things. The bow sits in the strong one because the Lord delights, through the invisible grace of his visitation, to dwell and rest in a truly humble heart.

Blessed, and truly blessed, is that strong person, that humble person, in whom the bow—that is, Christ—sits. For by his abiding and dwelling with him, that person deserves even in this life forgiveness for his sins. Hence there follows: “And the bonds of his arms [Col. 1155A] and hands were loosened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob.” By the arms, which are joined to the body in a closer connection, are fittingly expressed the inward faculties of the human being; by the hands, the activity of the outward faculties is understood. The bonds of arms and hands are the enticements of the devil and of fleshly desires. A person is said to be bound in arms and hands when, at the devil’s suggestion, he is ensnared inwardly by enticing desires and outwardly by enticing actions. But if he is truly strong—that is, if, persevering in humility, he offers himself to God as a welcome seat—then the bonds of his arms and hands are loosed, because the inward restraints of fleshly desires are so broken by God’s help that, although they attack through the devil’s suggestion, they nevertheless cannot bend him to consent to sin [Col. 1155B] or to commit it.

But whence does this come, except through the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob? By the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob may be understood both, as stated above, the working of divine compassion and the vigorous exercise of the person himself in good actions. For a person is not unfittingly called a mighty Jacob—a mighty, that is, supplanter—when he steadfastly performs with a certain power and strength the virtuous works by which vices are overthrown and perish. The following sequence of words mystically bears witness to what and how great is the grace of heavenly blessing which immediately follows such a person.

762 “From there,” he says, “came forth the shepherd, the stone of Israel.” What is “from there”? “From there,” he says—that is, from that person who was first a daughter running about upon the wall; who, knowing not how to yield to evil spirits who provoked bitterly, quarrelled, and envied, at length deserved to be called Jacob through the overthrow of vices. From that person, I say, there often comes forth such a shepherd as strives daily to fulfil in himself the name and office of shepherd.

For someone may rightly be called a shepherd when he always delights to feed himself by constancy in reading and sweetness in prayer [Col. 1155C]. Nourished by this pasture, he is nobly strengthened in virtues and virtuous works; for whatever good seed may have sprung up in a human heart quickly dries up if it is not watered by the moisture of prayer and reading. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Some fell upon the rock, and when it sprang up it withered, because it had [Col. 1155D] no moisture” (Luke 8:6). Therefore one who gladly and frequently remains in these pastures, if it is God’s will that he should go forth as appointed shepherd of others, will be able sweetly and profitably to provide his sheep with the pleasant pasture of heavenly teaching. For though he must go forth to care for others, he nevertheless does not cease to be within himself the stone of Israel. Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God.” He is in some sense like the stone of Israel when he so performs outwardly the offices of pastoral care that he nevertheless hastens always to return within himself to the familiar grace of contemplative sweetness. And when in this way he often turns back with heart and soul to God and into God, he deserves to be established by the Lord through the mercy and blessing which the following words [Col. 1156A] spiritually set forth. It follows:

“God of your father shall be your helper, and the Almighty shall bless you with blessings of heaven above, with blessings of the deep lying beneath, with blessings of breasts and womb.” 763 It is as though he said: Almighty God, whose son you have made yourself, whose faithful servant you have shown yourself in all things, shall be your helper; for in all things, wherever you go and whatever you undertake, he will gladly stand by you with fatherly assistance. And when you attempt to lead the sheep entrusted to you into the pleasant and verdant pastures of spiritual teaching, he will accompany you and help you; for by the prevenient grace of his visitation he will prepare for you the hearts of your subjects [Col. 1156B] to receive from your mouth the seeds of eternal salvation.

And this blessing is truly magnificent, because for the one whose voice Almighty God has gone before in the hearts of hearers, the doorkeeper undoubtedly opens; for that person the Holy Spirit makes the hearts of disciples fit and capable, by his invisible blessing, to receive with sweetness the word of the eternal Father. He therefore says:

“He shall bless you with blessings of heaven above, with blessings of the deep lying beneath, with blessings of breasts and womb.” In the blessings of heaven above we may fittingly understand an abundance of heavenly sweetness; in the blessings of the deep lying beneath, the bitterness of eternal damnation. When, through God’s prevenient mercy, the hearts of hearers have been opened, the Almighty also blesses the teacher himself when, filling him with the grace of his blessing and inspiration, he makes him speak blessing and profitably utter words of life. Thus, whether his blessing begins by soothing the souls of the righteous with the delight and glory of eternal blessedness and blessed immortality, or by terrifying sinners and stirring them to greater constancy in repentance through the pain and misery of the infernal deep, it brings forth the sweet and pleasant fruit of eternal salvation in the hearts of subjects [Col. 1156C].

He is also blessed with blessings of breasts when those who strive somehow to carry out in deeds the milk of heavenly teaching conceived in the breasts of their heart are, through his preaching and teaching, more and more delightfully expanded in longing for the heavenly homeland. He is blessed with blessings of the womb when those also who have not yet prepared themselves through love to receive the streams of spiritual milk delightfully open the womb of their heart to the noble seed of God’s word [Col. 1156D].

Therefore every prelate divinely honoured with blessings of this kind ought always to desire and pray that these blessings may not diminish either in himself or in the people subject to him, but may day by day grow and increase in strength. The oft-mentioned patriarch shows this in the blessing that immediately follows when he says:

“The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the everlasting hills should come.” The Father of every good prelate is God; and by the fathers of this Father, as we have said above, we understand the patriarchs, prophets, and holy apostles.

By the everlasting hills, however, are fittingly represented the holy souls of the elect, who, having shaken off the burdens of earthly occupation and been lifted up by holy prayers and righteous meditations, are sometimes carried from the valley of this mortality to the hill of everlasting eternity, in their longing for him himself [Col. 1157A].

By the desire of these hills he is rightly signified—the one whom angels desire to look upon—because he alone is sought and desired by them above all things and in all things. This same blessing also fittingly indicates, though covertly, what every faithful congregation ought to ask the Lord in humble prayer for its beloved teacher [Col. 1157B]. Let it therefore say, in prayer and longing, what the blessed patriarch said by way of affirmation:

> 765 May the blessings of your father be strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the everlasting hills comes.

It is as though it said: May the blessings by which you deserved to be blessed by your heavenly Father as a beloved son be so strengthened by the deeds and words, prayers and merits of his fathers—the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all the elect now reigning with Christ—that your blessing, that is, your teaching and preaching, may never come to an end, until the blessed Son of the eternal Father comes, desired and longed for, through the visiting and consoling sweetness of his blessing, to those everlasting hills—that is, to souls seeking the glory of eternity alone [Col. 1157C].

“May they be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers.” By Joseph’s head is understood the will of the teacher; by the crown, the intention of that will.

Therefore it is to be desired and prayed that he may always have the good will to edify his neighbour, and may diligently guard the intention of his will against the desire for human favour. For if in his blessings he seeks to please the eyes of God alone, he may rightly be called a Nazirite—that is, one who is pure—among his brothers [Col. 1158A].

But because it comes solely from the mercy and compassion of God alone that he can proclaim God’s word both humbly and profitably, let the faithful congregation strive humbly to direct to God the words of this prayer, to him “who gives generously to all and does not reproach”: 766

“May the God of your father be your helper, and may the Almighty bless you with blessings of heaven above, with blessings of the deep lying beneath,” so that, under your teaching, the more perfect may burn and be inflamed with a greater longing for heavenly sweetness, and the slower may be awakened by the terrors of the infernal deep and stirred to spiritual steadfastness.

“May he bless you with blessings of breasts and womb” [Col. 1158B], so that those who desire to receive the milk of heavenly teaching within the breasts of their heart may find in your words what may refresh and fill them; and so that those who have not yet deserved to receive God’s word through love may at last begin sweetly to conceive it in the womb of their heart.

“May the blessings of your father be strengthened by the blessings of his fathers”—the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all the righteous—“until the desire of the everlasting hills comes”: until those holy souls tending toward the height of eternity receive, in and with your blessings, him whom they thirstily desire before all and above all things.

“May they be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the Nazirite among [Col. 1158C] his brothers.” Grant, merciful Lord, by the manifold gift of your mercy, that whenever he sits down to proclaim your word among his brothers, his will 767 and the intention of his will may be such that in his teaching he may think, seek, or desire nothing except that in himself and in the people subject to him you alone may be 768 honoured and glorified, whose honour and glory endure through endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1157]

# THE BOOK OF THE VENERABLE GODEFRID, ABBOT OF ADMONT, ON THE TEN BURDENS OF ISAIAH

From an Admont manuscript codex.

(This short work was first published by the Reverend Father Bernard Pez under the name of the Venerable Irembert, Abbot of Admont, in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, p. 428. But when he afterwards discovered with complete certainty that it was the work of our Godefrid, he advised that it should be restored to him in the preliminary dissertation to Godefrid’s works, no. XVII. See above, col. 19.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1157D]

Every human being, because he possesses ten senses—five, namely, in the soul and five in the body—by and through which, alas, he sometimes stands opposed to the ten commandments of the Lord and grievously burdens and loads his wretched soul, [Col. 1158D] receives from Isaiah, the Lord’s chosen prophet, ten burdens set forth in his book. Those who desire to have the burdens of sins contracted through the ten senses of the inner and outer person smoothed away and removed by the hand of divine mercy ought courageously to place beneath them the shoulder of heart and body [Col. 1159A]. Moreover, in order to distinguish these same burdens, he assigns them, as it were, to the places and peoples of ten regions; and, figuratively assigning to each place and people its appropriate burden, he begins thus:

## CHAPTER ONE. The burden of Babylon, or of those truly repenting

ISAIAH 13, VERSE 1. By “the burden of Babylon,” which is interpreted “confusion,” may be understood either the present world or all people who, cast down by the confusion of sins, acknowledge themselves to be unrighteous and sinful. The prophet just mentioned [Col. 1159B] imposes upon such persons a certain burden—the burden, namely, of conversion, which is the beginning of salvation. Under this burden he immediately shows how they ought to live:

VERSE 2. “Raise the banner upon a dark mountain; exalt the voice; raise the hand; and let the leaders enter the gates.” By the name of the dark mountain we may rightly understand the ancient enemy, the prince of darkness. Because of the height of his pride he is rightly called not merely a mountain, but a dark mountain, since he wraps all those who consent to him in the darkness of sins in the present life and, after this life, will drag them down with himself into the gloom of death and the darkness of eternal punishments. Upon this dark mountain we must raise the banner of conversion, exalt the voice of confession, and raise [Col. 1159C] the hand of good works. For conversion alone is insufficient to conquer and overcome him unless true confession of sins follows. After the banner of conversion has been raised and the voice of confession exalted, it remains that the hand also be raised—that is, that a person should strive energetically to exercise himself in every action pleasing to God.

But since even this is not enough for a person tending toward perfection unless he humbly subjects heart and body to all heavenly teaching, it is rightly added: “And let the leaders enter the gates.” Leaders are those who lead an army. By leaders we may fittingly understand all good prelates, who go before the army of the Lord in teaching and example and diligently instruct, arm, and fortify it against the arrows of the ancient enemy [Col. 1159D]. These leaders enter the gates, as it were, when the inner and outer senses of subjects, which we understand by the gates, are graciously opened through their admonitions and teachings.

But because the prophet foresaw in the Holy Spirit that these matters concerning the raising of the banner of conversion, the exalting of the voice of confession, and the raising of the hand of good and perfect action are very difficult and laborious for a human being, he rightly prefaced, before breaking forth into the words of the exhortation and heavenly teaching just mentioned: “The burden of Babylon.” It is as though he said: This burden of laborious yet fruitful, difficult yet health-giving spiritual perfection, which I am about to speak of and teach, is fitting for those to receive and bear [Col. 1160A] who recognize that they have been defiled in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of sins; who grieve and groan that they have stood contrary to the divine will, grievously oppressed under the dark mountain, namely the proud and dark devil. It is indeed a burden; but so that it may willingly be received and vigorously borne, the merciful Lord deigns, in the following words, to lighten and commend it to us.

VERSE 3. “I,” he says, “have commanded my sanctified ones; I have called my strong ones in my wrath, those exulting in my glory.” It is as though he said: Not some stranger or outsider, but I, your Lord, Creator, and Liberator—I, the lover of your salvation—have commanded my sanctified ones, those, namely, whom by the wondrous grace of my dispensation I predestined for this purpose: that they should one day become my sanctified ones [Col. 1160B]. I commanded them to lift themselves up upon the dark mountain through the banner of conversion, to exalt the voice of confession, and with the hand of good works to wipe away and cleanse the crimes of their past life.

“I have commanded my sanctified ones; I have called my strong ones in my wrath,” because all who are my sanctified ones in predestination will also be my strong ones in the calling of election. They will indeed be my strong ones, because they will receive and possess strength to resist the devil and vices not from themselves but from me. I have called them my strong ones in my wrath—in a lovable, desirable wrath—which I shall mercifully exercise in them when, through the prevenient grace of my mercy, I beneficially stir them up against themselves, so that they begin to be strongly angry with themselves for their evil deeds and show themselves strong and vigorous in every good action [Col. 1160C]. This is my wrath—the wrath pleasing to me—of which the Psalmist says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5).

Moreover, after saying, “I have called my strong ones in my wrath,” he fittingly added, “those exulting in my glory.” For just as it is his wrath, and may be called his wrath, when he makes his elect angry with themselves because of their evil and sinful life; and just as it is his strength when he grants them to resist vices strongly and to persist vigorously and manfully in virtuous deeds; so likewise it is his glory, and may be called his glory, when, after subduing vices and applying themselves to a praiseworthy life, they begin humbly to exult and glory in the Lord because of the good testimony of conscience. For while they humbly attribute nothing to their own strength and merits, but attribute all that they are to God alone, they may be said to exult in the glory not of themselves but of the Lord. Of this glory of the elect the Apostle says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12) [Col. 1160D].

Because the eternal wisdom of God foresaw that such persons would exist in his Church, he prophesied and foretold through this Prophet, as it were long before it happened, concerning their praiseworthy conduct, saying: “I have commanded my sanctified ones; I have called my strong ones in my wrath, those exulting in my glory.” It is as though he had said: Those whom I foresaw as my sanctified ones in predestination, I shall also call my strong ones in conversion or good conduct; and those whom I shall strengthen by my wondrous and ineffable calling [Col. 1161A] in good conduct, I shall also make to exult in my glory—that is, in the perfection of spiritual life. When the Lord’s prophet mentioned above deserved inwardly to hear this prophecy of the Lord in an inexpressible manner, he looked upon future things as though already past and consequently continued:

VERSE 4. “The voice of a multitude upon the mountains, like that of many peoples; the voice of the sound of kings, of nations gathered together.” In these words he mystically foreshadowed two callings: one of the Jews, the other of the nations. For he foresaw that from both peoples there would be persons by whose voice the Lord’s name would be exalted, by whose confession of faith God would be magnified and glorified until the consummation of the age. For when he said, “the voice of a multitude upon the mountains, like that of many peoples,” he foresaw those who were to be gathered from the Jewish people into the fullness of perfect faith [Col. 1161B]. But when he added, “the voice of the sound of kings, of nations gathered together,” he foreshadowed the multitude of all who were to be received from the Gentile people into the same unity of faith.

And not unfittingly was the prophet bound to express under the name of a multitude of many peoples the calling of the Jews, which was to be earlier but smaller. To indicate the calling of the nations, however, he rightly had to say, “the voice of the sound of kings, of nations gathered together,” because those whom he prophetically foresaw as to be received from the Jewish people, although he saw them as great and rightly comparable to mountains by reason of their holiness, he nevertheless foresaw would be fewer and smaller than those who were to be gathered to Christ from the nations [Col. 1161C]. Therefore he not unfittingly called the former “many peoples” and the latter “mighty kings.” For noble and strong kings came forth from the nations who began to rule both themselves and others royally and powerfully according to the Lord’s command and will. The voice of the sound of these kings went forth into all the earth because their preaching and teaching resounded powerfully throughout the whole circuit of the world to win souls for God.

These same words of the prophet may also be understood differently. When he said, “the voice of a multitude upon the mountains, like that of many peoples; the voice of the sound of kings, of nations gathered together,” he foresaw that there would be in the holy Church many lofty and holy forms of life, which we understand by mountains. In them the voice and praise of a multitude like that of many peoples would be heard: peoples, that is, frequently serving God in heart and body. Among them would be found those noble kings who could and knew how not only to rule themselves but also to instruct others, by teaching and example, in the norm of uprightness with a sound like a great voice [Col. 1161D].

But through whom or from whom was this multitude of peoples to be gathered? Through whom or from whom was this voice, this sound of kings, to be raised, if not through the command of the unbegotten Father, the cooperation of the only-begotten Son, and the infusion and illumination of the Holy Spirit? For we may understand that the mystery of the holy and indivisible Trinity is covertly indicated in the following words: “The Lord of hosts has commanded the army of battle.”

[Col. 1162A] VERSE 5. “Those coming from a distant land, from the summit of heaven: the Lord and the instruments of his wrath, to destroy the whole earth.” By the Lord of hosts may be understood God the Father, who sent his Only-Begotten into the world. By “the Lord from the summit of heaven” may be understood God the Son of God, who descended from heaven’s summit to the lowest parts of the world for our salvation. By “the instruments of his wrath” may be understood God the Holy Spirit, who, after the resurrection and ascension of this same our Lord, wondrously illuminated with the wondrous light of his coming those whom the Only-Begotten Son of God had cleansed from sins through the passion of his death.

And not absurdly do we understand the Holy Spirit by the wrath of the Lord, and the gifts of that same Holy Spirit by the instruments of his wrath. For that is rightly called an instrument which mercifully works in a human being through its gifts [Col. 1162B]. When he came and began to pour out and infuse his instruments—that is, his gifts—into human hearts, he aroused in them a new wrath, previously unknown. For then they first learned to rise up against themselves; then they first began to rage against the devil and against vices. He still daily arouses and kindles this same wrath in the hearts of the elect by the sweetness of his infusion, making them happily rage well in the present life and fiercely act against vices, and through this wrath overcoming and casting down within them the devil, who rages wickedly.

But since, according to our capacity, we have touched upon the mystical meaning of the works of the holy and undivided Trinity as indicated in these words, let us now hear what this warfare is, who those are who “come from a distant land” [Col. 1162C], and to whom the command of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit is directed through the prophet. “The Lord of hosts,” he says, “has commanded the army for battle, those who come from a distant land: the Lord from the height of heaven, and the instruments of his wrath, to destroy the whole earth.” By the army for battle he indicated all people whom, having abandoned the world, he foresaw would serve as soldiers against vices and would fight powerfully against the devil with the weapons of spiritual virtues. To such an army for battle the Lord of hosts, God the Father, has given command; the Lord from the height of heaven—that is, God the Son—has given command; and the instruments of his wrath—that is, God the Holy Spirit—have given command: that it may come from far away from the earth, that is, may remove all earthly things far from itself, and may destroy all [Col. 1162D] the earth—that is, may strive to destroy and vigorously cast away from itself everything earthly and weak which it discovers within itself. But because this can occur only through true repentance, he immediately makes this clear when he adds:

**VERSE 6.** “Wail, because the day of the Lord is near; it shall come as devastation from the Lord.” Wailing, which takes place in the body and through the body, rightly expresses manifest repentance. “Wail,” he says, “because, if you wail—that is, if you perform perfect repentance—the day of the Lord is near”: namely, the illumination of heavenly visitation, which will come as devastation from the Lord, because whatever weak thing and whatever subject to sin it finds in you, it will powerfully lay waste and remove. It follows:

**VERSE 7.** “Therefore all hands shall be weakened, and [Col. 1163A] every human heart shall melt away and be crushed.” Here we may understand evil works by the name “hands.” Hands are certainly weakened when, upon the coming of the day of heavenly visitation, wicked and perverse deeds are abandoned and cast away. Every human heart likewise melts away and is crushed when, by the grace of God, it gradually fails and turns back from that evil strength by which it used to be active in committing vices. For as long as a person sins pleasantly and delightfully, he is shown to possess a heart as though unshaken and strong in evil. But when, through the prevenient and softening grace of God, the will and desire to sin are somewhat diminished, and that former ardor by which he burned for crimes is somewhat cooled by the dew and grace of the Holy Spirit, then the human heart, as though broken, beneficially melts away [Col. 1163B] in contrition. It follows:

**VERSE 8.** “Twistings and pains shall seize them; they shall suffer as a woman in labor.” To be seized by twistings and pains is to punish and erase past crimes through bodily afflictions, sighs, and pains of heart. But what does the addition mean: “They shall suffer as a woman in labor”? A woman in labor is so called as one eager, as it were, to give birth. He suffers as a woman in labor who is always eager to bring forth within himself and from himself new desires every day, a new zeal of repentance, and a new love for the heavenly homeland. But how, or by what means, a person may advance to bring such offspring forth from himself, the often-mentioned prophet teaches when he immediately adds:

“Each one shall be astonished at his neighbor; their faces are faces burned.” Astonishment is called an alienation of the mind, [Col. 1163C] by which a person, shaken by sudden and unexpected terror, not yet knowing what has happened, is in some way estranged from himself. This neighbor, at whom each is commanded to be astonished, may fittingly be understood as a person’s own body. The one to be saved must estrange himself from it and, in some manner, not know it in those things in which he formerly knew and recognized it. He must indeed not know it in the sins which he had previously committed knowingly and willingly with it. But whoever, with God’s favor, has thus estranged himself from himself must thereafter strive to live according to the form of teaching set forth, if he desires perfectly to please God. It follows:

“Their faces are faces burned.” In the face, through which a person is known, we may rightly understand the knowledge of God and the knowledge of the person himself [Col. 1163D]. Their countenances are like burned faces when, in true humility, they continually acknowledge themselves to be sinners, and are constantly burned by the fire of repentance in their wills and desires—which we may understand through “countenances”—so that, burning humbly in self-knowledge, they may deserve both to know God and to be known by God.

## CHAPTER II. The burden of Moab, that is, of those who live carnally while holding office and dignity.

**ISAIAH XV, VERSES 1–2.** “The burden of Moab. Because Ar of Moab has been laid waste by night, it is silent; because the wall of Moab has been laid waste by night, it is silent. The house has gone up, and Dibon [another reading: *Edibon*] to the high places for mourning; over Nebo and [Col. 1164A] over Medeba Moab has wailed.”

In the former burden, inscribed “Babylon,” is marked an exhortation to conversion and repentance, by which almighty God calls to himself the sinful person lying in the confusion of vices. But this second burden—the burden of Moab—looks especially toward those who are set over others but live carnally in their office. Such persons may not unfittingly be understood by the name Moab. For *Moab* is interpreted “from the father.” Those are from the Father who have received authority from God the Father. For, as Scripture says, “all authority is from God” (Rom. 13:1). They are indeed from the Father in what they are, but they do not live according to the Father in what they do, because they do not savor the things of God. The divine voice rebukes such people in this burden and calls them back to acknowledgment [Col. 1164B] and repentance, when it says:

“Because Ar of Moab has been laid waste by night, it is silent; because the wall of Moab has been laid waste by night, it is silent.” By the name *Ar*, which is interpreted “he raised up” or “watchfulness,” we may fittingly understand both the souls of prelates and the souls of subjects; by the wall, the body; and by night, ignorance. “Because Ar of Moab has been laid waste by night,” he says. As though he were saying: Because you who have received from God the Father the authority of governance have yourselves been silent through evil living and through failing to rebuke evils in your subjects, therefore Ar has been laid waste by night. Therefore your souls, which you ought continually to rouse toward heavenly desires, and the souls of your subjects, over whose salvation you ought to have watched with the greatest diligence, have been devastated by the night of ignorance. And from that inward [Col. 1164C] devastation—namely, ignorance of truth—the wall also has been laid waste: that is, the body which surrounds the soul has been devastated by the night of sin and iniquity. The body is devastated by the night of sin when it is handed over and subjected to impurity. He expresses this devastation of the inward and outward person more clearly in what follows, where again and again he exhorts them to repentance and mourning, and suggests what they ought to mourn, adding:

**VERSE 2.** “The house and Dibon have gone up to the high places for mourning; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab has wailed.” By Dibon, which is interpreted “their flowing,” we may fittingly understand lascivious and unstable people, whose house in some way ascends to high places when they exalt the house of the flesh—that is, the body—above the spirit [Col. 1164D]: when they subject the spirit, which ought to preside over and rule the flesh, to the flesh through slippery and wanton movements of heart and body. Nebo, however, which is interpreted “their sitting,” or “prophecy,” suitably signifies the dignity of teaching and the office of preaching. Medeba, said to mean “from the forest,” denotes the bestial—that is, sinful—life of prelates and likewise of subjects. “Over Nebo and over Medeba Moab has wailed.” As though he were saying: All you who are such teachers, because through your evil life you do not know—or do not dare—to rebuke iniquity in your subjects, wail over Nebo and Medeba. Wail, indeed, because you have received the seat and place of governance. You must weep and groan [Col. 1165A] because you yourselves have lived bestially and have not rebuked those living bestially. These words, then, belong to almighty God mercifully exhorting prelates and subjects to repentance. He now immediately makes clear in the following words what the manner of repentance ought to be:

“In all its heads there is baldness; every beard shall be shaved.” Baldness is where hair is plucked out or falls of its own accord. By all the heads we may understand all the intentions of the mind, in which those who desire to be reconciled to God through true repentance ought in some way to become bald and bare. For the perfect measure of perfect repentance is to draw out and pluck from the head—that is, from the repenting heart—all evil wills and all intentions of the will that are not good. After the inward person has thus been made bald of those harmful hairs, namely perverse wills and intentions, it remains that every beard also should be shaved. In the beard and through the beard we understand virtuous and manly works. Every beard must be shaved because the perfectly repentant person ought also to regard lightly, in view and comparison of the evils he has committed, whatever he has done well and manfully, and whatever virtue he believes to be in himself, and count it as though nothing and useless. Let him bind himself firmly to repentance and satisfaction alone, as the mystical order of the following words teaches, where it says:

**VERSE 3.** “In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth; upon [Col. 1165C] its roofs and in its streets every one wails [another reading: all wailing descends into weeping].”

By the crossroads we may understand our spirit, soul, and body; or again our thoughts, speech, and deeds. For these are, as it were, three ways by which we either approach God or withdraw from God. One girds himself with sackcloth at his crossroads when he binds himself to the mourning of threefold repentance. But everyone wails upon its roofs and in its streets when, upon the flesh and in his flesh—which may be understood by the roofs—he punishes and exacts, by the judgment of worthy correction, the threefold failings of spirit, soul, and body, and all, so to speak, the wanderings of a broad and criminal life, which we understand by the streets. But since bodily affliction is of little value unless humility [Col. 1165D] of mind is also present, it is rightly added: “He descends into weeping.”

**VERSE 4.** “Heshbon and Elealeh cried out; its voice [another reading: their voice] was heard as far as Jahaz.” Heshbon is interpreted “thoughts,” Elealeh “ascent,” and Jahaz “deed” or “command.” A person descends into weeping when he both mortifies the flesh through repentance and approaches God in heart through the descent of true humility. Heshbon and Elealeh cry out when he accuses and condemns, with worthy groaning of heart and body, in prayer and confession, his ascending—that is, proud—thoughts. His voice is said to be heard as far as Jahaz when he strives to fulfill and observe the Lord’s command in deeds and words. But because this virtue belongs not to all but only [Col. 1166A] to spiritual persons, this is suitably shown when it says:

“Therefore the unencumbered of Moab shall wail; his soul shall wail for itself.” As though it said: Not those who are in the world and are weighed down by worldly sins, but those who by God’s grace have abandoned the world, who have estranged and freed themselves from works of sin through repentance and conversion—whether prelates, understood by Moab, or subjects, called as it were the unencumbered of Moab—shall wail over this. They shall wail over what we have most recently mentioned: that is, they can worthily repent over their lofty thoughts and, so to speak, know how worthily to bewail themselves for the inward excesses of the mind. And it is rightly added: “His soul shall wail for itself.” For whoever in this manner makes satisfaction to God not only for evil deeds but also for his proud thoughts, that person truly wails for himself because he wails to good purpose. Through such fruit of repentance he secures for himself the joys of eternal salvation. But God alone works this repentance in a person, by the grace of his mercy alone, as is immediately added in his person, when it says:

**VERSE 5.** “My heart shall cry out to Moab; its bars shall reach as far as Zoar, a three-year-old heifer.” The heart of the Lord is the will of the Lord. It is as though he said: If anyone receives the repentance of which we have now spoken, and is found constant and perfect in it and perseveres, let him humbly attribute it not to his own powers but to my mercies. For unless my heart cries out to him—that is, unless my merciful will, my voluntary mercy, goes before [Col. 1166C] and follows him—he will be unable either to repent worthily in his soul or to bring forth worthy fruits of repentance in or through his body. It follows:

“Its bars shall reach as far as Zoar, a three-year-old heifer.” Zoar is interpreted “small.” Not unfittingly, through Zoar and the three-year-old heifer—which blessed Jerome calls a three-year-old cow—we may understand humble and perfect repentance. Just as a human being is strongest in bodily power and mental capacities in the thirtieth year, so this kind of animal possesses its greatest strength in its third year. Humble repentance is therefore suitably compared with a three-year-old heifer. For that repentance has the greatest power to obtain [Col. 1166D] from God the grace of forgiveness which is accompanied by true humility and adorned by firm and strong keeping of life, understood through the bars.

There is another reason why true and humble repentance is rightly likened to a three-year-old heifer, which, as we have said, is strongest in its third year: unless the mourning of our repentance is threefold, it is neither perfect nor can it be called perfect. Repentance is threefold: repentance in the soul, repentance in the spirit, and repentance in the body. This threefold repentance is shown more plainly in what follows:

“For by the ascent of Luhith he shall go up weeping; and on the way of Horonaim they shall raise a cry of contrition.” Luhith is interpreted “cheeks,” Horonaim “an opening of sorrow.” But what is signified by the ascent of Luhith—the ascent, I say, of the cheeks—except a stream of tears ascending from the depths of the heart? Or what is figured by the ascent of tears, which flow down the cheeks and are seen upon them, except the repentance of the outward person, namely the body? He goes up weeping, as it were by Luhith, who shows repentance in the body through the signs of tears and other good works.

After he has thus gone up weeping by the ascent of Luhith, he at last begins to raise the cry of contrition on the way of Horonaim. By Horonaim, which we have said is interpreted “an opening of sorrow,” we may understand the heart of each elect person. It is not wrongly called an opening of sorrow when, through the grace of the Holy Spirit coming and breathing upon it, it is pierced and softened from its former hardness by fear and love of God, and is broken in itself with healing sorrow. For the Holy Spirit himself is as it were a way, under whose guidance—indeed, through whose inspiration—the human heart becomes an opening of sorrow and begins to raise a cry of contrition. To raise a cry of contrition on the way of Horonaim is, when the soul repents and the heart suffers and grieves, continually to lament the old contagions of sins. After this it is rightly added:

**VERSE 6.** “For the waters of Nimrim shall be deserted, because the grass has withered, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished.” Nimrim is interpreted “leopards” or “transgressors.” Not unfittingly, through the waters of Nimrim, the waters of leopards or transgressors, we understand evil and iniquitous desires, which incline a person, designated by the leopard—an uncontrolled and unstable beast—toward transgression of the divine will. These waters of Nimrim shall be deserted because, after the cry and contrition of the heart pierced by the sorrow of repentance have been raised, the evil desires of the flesh, through the Holy Spirit’s coming and working, are so restrained and held back in a person that they cannot flow out and run on in their accustomed manner. That is, they cannot sweep away and separate from God the human heart, now made an opening of sorrow, by the familiar current of instability and transgression.

After the waters of Nimrim have been deserted, after evil desires have been subdued and restrained, it suitably follows: “The grass has withered, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished.” By grass may be signified the will to sin; by the shoot, the work of sin; by greenness, perseverance in sin. The grass is rightly said to have withered when the perverse will, as though deprived of the moisture of the waters mentioned above, has been dried up—indeed, overcome. The shoot fails when, through God’s mercy, the evil will has been removed from the heart and the work of sin is also cut off from the body. When the shoot of evil work has been cut off, all greenness has perished, because in that person in whom the will and work of sin have ceased, insofar as is possible in this life, perseverance in sin happily dies away. This is the perfect measure of perfect repentance which the merciful Lord has shown and prescribed to all who desire salvation. To commend it more attentively, he immediately added and said:

[Col. 1168A] **VERSE 7.** “According to the greatness of the work, also is their visitation.” We may understand these words thus: that the measure of repentance and satisfaction ought to be extended according to the greatness of the sin; and thus, according to the greatness of good action and perfect satisfaction, the grace and sweetness of heavenly visitation will be present to a person. But, as is said in Job, “God works all these things three times with each person” (Job 33:29). In these three occasions by which almighty God works a person’s salvation, the exhortation, method, and perfection of repentance are mystically indicated. He has set forth the exhortation; he has shown the method. Now he also declares what the perfection of repentance is, saying: “They shall lead them to the torrent of the willows.”

**VERSE 8.** “For the cry has gone around [another reading: went around] [Col. 1168B] the border of Moab; its wailing reaches as far as Gallim, and its cry as far as the well of Elim, because the waters of Dibon are filled with blood.”

Willows are unfruitful trees, because they produce no fruit fit for human use. What he says, “They shall lead them to the torrent of the willows,” is as though he said: Those who have received the prescribed exhortation and have made worthy satisfaction to God for their sins according to the manner of repentance set forth will bring those deadly fruits of sins which they once used to produce to a certain blessed barrenness, because they vigorously uproot them from their heart and body, lest they be able to rise up or prevail over them in their accustomed way.

And why is this so? Because “the cry has gone around [Col. 1168C] the border of Moab; its wailing reaches as far as Gallim.” The border of Moab fittingly signifies the end of the repentant person. Gallim, interpreted “calves” or “mounds of sand,” may signify the person’s very death. The cry goes around the border of Moab and its wailing reaches Gallim when a righteous person perseveres and remains, until the end of his life, both in repentance of heart, understood through the cry, and in repentance of body, understood through the wailing. It is rightly further said of such a person:

“And his cry reaches as far as the well of Elim, because the waters of Dibon are filled with blood.” The word *Elim*, interpreted “rams” or “strong ones,” fittingly signifies almighty God [Col. 1168D], who is the fountain and origin of all good things, the strength of the strong and the one who strengthens all his rams—that is, all his teachers. But by Dibon, interpreted “sufficient sorrow,” is aptly figured a sufficient lament of repentance, which then truly suffices for God when it is filled with blood—that is, when it has been consummated through death, which in this place may be understood by blood. The cry of one thus repenting, who ends his repentance together with death, will be heard at the well of Elim, because he will be established by the one who, as we have said, is the fountain and origin, the strength and consummation of his people: established in the stability of eternal strength and rewarded with the stable and unchangeable delight of everlasting blessedness. Hence it is further added:

[Col. 1169A] “For I shall place additions upon Dibon: a lion upon those who flee from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land.” As though the Lord said: Upon that person who has sufficient sorrow and perseveres in it until the completion of life, I shall place these additions; I shall add this grace of my loving-kindness and mercy: that I shall save him not only in the soul, by which he was accustomed to flee the pleasure of sin, after the end of this present life, but also shall glorify, together with the soul, on the last day the remnant of the earth—namely, the body—by which, as far as he could, he fled the practice of sin. I shall give him as his reward that noble lion, the great lion who rose from the tribe of Judah: namely, my only-begotten Son, who shall be the crown, praise, and [Col. 1169B] infinite glory of all his saints for ages of ages. Amen.

Behold the burden of Moab: the burden, that is, of those who hold the name and place of governance but do not live in accordance with the dignity of that name. Behold the lofty and sublime teaching of the Most High, in which he so rebukes prelates that, in correcting them, he also calls back and reforms the life of their subjects from the twisting of your perversity [perhaps “their perversity”]. In it, after the zeal of just denunciation, he returns to the gentleness of fatherly exhortation; after the gentleness of exhortation, he shows the method of repentance and satisfaction. He also teaches what is the perfection of repentance; and finally, what and how great is the eternal reward of blessedness which follows that repentance. Whoever takes upon himself this burden, which is second in number, whoever takes care to order his life, actions, and conduct according to the prescribed [Col. 1169C] and set-forth teaching of the eternal Father contained in it, may, with God’s favor, attain the third burden, which is inscribed “Damascus.”

## CHAPTER III. The burden of Damascus, or of those who perfectly repent of evil deeds committed.

**ISAIAH XVII, VERSES 1–2.** “The burden of Damascus. Behold, Damascus shall cease to be a city and shall become like a heap of stones in ruin. The cities of Aroer are abandoned; they shall belong to flocks, which shall rest there, and there shall be none to frighten them.”

Damascus, interpreted “drinking blood,” or “kiss of blood,” or “blood of sackcloth,” signifies the person who repents perfectly and lives according to the things taught by the eternal wisdom of God in the burden already set forth [Col. 1169D]. He becomes as it were “blood of sackcloth” when, mortified and bloodied through the harshness of true and perfect repentance, he begins to be reconciled to God. He also becomes “drinking blood” when he is sweetly nourished and given drink by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and, through utter self-abasement of mind and good and righteous bodily action, vigorously imitates, insofar as he can, the passion of that same Lord.

He may also fittingly be called “a kiss of blood” when he begins to love and venerate sweetly and humbly, with sincere affection of heart, the blood—that is, the passion—of Christ. For the kiss of blood is love and imitation of Christ’s passion. It is rightly said of such [Col. 1170A] a person: “Behold, Damascus shall cease to be a city,” because, purified by the sackcloth of repentance, strengthened by glorious participation in Christ’s body and blood, and made partly conformed to Christ through love and imitation of Christ’s passion, he ceases to be what he was and begins to be what he was not. He ceases to be a city of the devil and begins to be a city of God; he ceases to be a city of sins and begins to be a city of virtues. This is mystically shown in the following words, which are immediately added:

“And it shall become like a heap of stones in ruin.” In a heap of stones, made from the gathering of many rocks, we may understand a multitude of diverse virtues. It will indeed be like a heap of stones in ruin when evil things begin to fall and good things to rise in it. As the contrivance of vices, heaped together from different sins, falls, there rises and grows on high a diversity of good virtues and a multitude of praiseworthy deeds. Hence follows:

“The abandoned cities of Aroer shall belong to flocks; they shall rest there, and there shall be none to frighten them.” Aroer means tamarisks—that is, unfruitful trees—whose juice, when mixed with human food or taken in drink, is said to extinguish the bonds of charity and stir up enmities and hatreds. By the cities of Aroer—cities, so to speak, of barrenness—we may understand the inner and outer senses of the person, which are like unfruitful trees as long as they serve iniquity unto iniquity. But the abandoned cities of Aroer shall belong to flocks when those senses which were cities of vices begin to be receptacles and dwellings [Col. 1170C] of flocks—that is, of good virtues. And it is well added, “They shall rest there, and there shall be none to frighten them,” because, once the vices have been driven out and overcome, the person will rest and reign in the virtues, and the virtues in the person, so that there will be none to frighten them: that is, not even the devil himself will be able to disturb, drive away, or take them from the person.

**VERSE 3.** “And help shall cease from Ephraim, and kingship from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria shall be like the glory of the children of Israel, says the Lord of hosts.” Ephraim is interpreted “fruitful,” Syria “lofty,” Israel “a man seeing God.” Help shall cease from Ephraim when, through God’s inspiration, the outward person, whom we believe to be understood through Ephraim, ceases to seek and produce from himself such fruit [Col. 1170D] as he used to seek and produce by sinning and consenting to sins. When such help has been removed from Ephraim, kingship also shall cease from Damascus, because the kingdom of virtues, succeeding and increasing, will pluck out and overthrow the kingdom of vices from that person who has now, as we have said, become Damascus. When the kingdom of vices has been overthrown, the remnant of Syria shall be like the glory of the children of Israel, because that soul, now become Syria—that is, lofty—being freed and cleansed from sins, is conformed to the example of the glory of the children of Israel, that is, the glory of children who love God and desire to see God. By their righteous deeds and pure thoughts, which we understand through the remnant of Syria, it diligently labors to be numbered among the children of Israel [Col. 1171A], so that, with his help, it may deserve to attain the vision of God. It follows:

**VERSE 4.** “And it shall be in that day: the glory of Jacob shall be diminished, and his fat flesh shall waste away [another reading: and the fatness of his flesh shall waste away].” By Jacob, interpreted “supplanter,” is figured the same person who is also fittingly represented by Damascus. That day in which Jacob’s glory is diminished suitably figures the grace of heavenly visitation. For when a person is first illumined by it and begins to know himself and renounce himself, the glory of Jacob is in some way diminished. Whatever glory or favor had arisen inwardly either from supplanting vices or from praiseworthy conduct, he empties through humility, attributing nothing to his own powers or merits but humbly attributing to God alone all that he is and all that [Col. 1171B] he has. And it is well added: “His fat flesh shall waste away,” because when, with God’s illumination, he begins perfectly to know his own weakness, all the rich and powerful strength of carnal senses, as though dried up through humility, wastes away.

**VERSE 5.** “And it shall be like one gathering in harvest what has remained, and his arm shall gather ears of grain.” It sometimes happens that a person abandons the world yet, at the very entrance of his conversion, does not know or is not able rightly and perfectly to accuse himself to God in confession for the sins he committed in the world. Yet as time passes he learns this more fully, when he becomes like one gathering in harvest what has remained. For he carefully gathers, examines, and scrutinizes his whole life and all his actions, as though preparing for himself a harvest of eternal salvation. If he finds anything left behind which he has not yet mourned or confessed, he hastens to cut it off with the keen sickle of true and perfect confession. And his arm shall gather ears of grain when, after confession, he begins to make satisfaction to God strongly and manfully. By the arm may be designated strength; by ears of grain, a multitude of good works.

“And it shall be like one seeking ears of grain in the valley of Rephaim.” Rephaim is said to mean “giants.” In the valley of Rephaim we may understand any spiritual community in which persons are gathered, and are gathered still, who because of the strength of their perfect life are deservedly compared with giants.

[Col. 1171D] Alternatively, by the name Rephaim we may understand malignant spirits; by the valley, any humble righteous persons. They may be called the valley of Rephaim—that is, the valley of those same malignant spirits—because they are contemptible in those spirits’ sight. For the more humble they are in their own estimation, the more contemptible they are to malignant spirits. A good person will be like one seeking ears of grain in the valley of Rephaim, because among those who serve God in humility, whom malignant spirits despise on account of their humility and gentleness, he humbly seeks whether he may be able to see or hear in them something to imitate, through which he may be more and more kindled toward love of the heavenly homeland. To seek ears of grain in the valley of Rephaim is to take, in a spiritual community, from one an example of humility; from another an example [Col. 1172A] of obedience, patience, and charity; from one an example of good conduct; from another an example of seriousness, spiritual steadfastness, and zeal. From this excellent gathering of ears, from this humble imitation of those who live humbly, there arise in the soul those two movements—fear of God and love—of which he immediately adds:

**VERSE 6.** “And there shall remain in him as a cluster of grapes, and as the shaking of an olive tree: two or three olives on the top of a branch.” By the cluster of grapes may be understood love of God; by the olive tree, the human soul itself. The soul may fittingly be compared to an olive tree, or even called an olive tree, when it has been drenched with the oil of God’s mercy, divinely softened from its former hardness, and touched by perfect fear and love of God. It is well said, “There shall remain in him as a cluster of grapes, and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives,” because while on one side he is possessed by the love of God and on the other touched by fear of God, from these two movements comes a certain healing shaking: namely, the shaking of two or three olives. By the two olives we may understand twofold repentance. Twofold repentance is strictly repenting and mourning both neglected goods and evils committed. The shaking of three olives is the prudent and careful examination of words, deeds, and thoughts, which that olive tree—that is, the soul anointed with the oil of God’s mercy—in some way shakes out, while it not only investigates and examines where it has admitted anything unlawful in deeds or words, but also refuses to let pass without examination any point at which it may have departed from the path of uprightness even through the slightest thoughts [Col. 1172C].

Nor should we pass over what is added: “On the top of a branch.” The branch fittingly signifies the fragrance of a good odor which, proceeding from the shaking or examination of the two or three olives already mentioned, rises before God. For the highest and sweetly fragrant odor before the Lord is that repentance which, after words, thoughts, and deeds have been shaken out and examined, now punishes neglected goods and now consumes committed evils with the zeal of worthy correction. Cleansed and illumined through this twofold repentance, the person gradually advances to an understanding of sacred Scripture, as is shown by the typical signification immediately appended:

“Or four or five of its fruits on its topmost branches, says the Lord of hosts.” What do we understand by the topmost branches but the lofty faculties of the soul? Or by its four or five fruits except the fruit of the Gospel and of the Law? A person has, as it were, four or five fruits on his topmost branches when he begins profitably and fruitfully to hear, grasp, and understand with the lofty faculties of his soul the Scripture of the New Testament, understood through the four, and the Scripture of the Old Testament, understood through the five; and when he begins wisely to carry them out and keep them in his deeds. It follows:

**VERSES 7–8.** “In that day a person shall bow toward his Maker, and his eyes shall look toward the Holy One of Israel. [Col. 1173A] And he shall not bow toward the altars which his hands have made, nor toward what his fingers have fashioned.” On that day of heavenly visitation a person bows toward his Maker. To bow is to be humbled, because the more he approaches God through love and knowledge, the more truly and perfectly he humbles himself before him. “And his eyes shall look toward the Holy One of Israel.” The Holy One of Israel signifies the holy human mind, which may truly be called holy when it has been made stable and sanctified in the Lord, so that nothing outward gives pleasure to it, but it rejoices always to look toward God with all its desires and affections.

“And he shall not bow toward the altars which his hands have made, nor toward what his fingers have fashioned.” By the altars made by his hands we may understand good works; by the fingers [Col. 1173B], discernment in good works. A person does not bow toward the altars which his hands have made and which his fingers have fashioned when, even in those deeds which he has performed discerningly and simply for the Lord, he judges himself unworthy and, as it were, impious, and in true humility attributes everything to him from whom he received it.

He will not look back to groves and shrines. By groves, in which sacrifices to demons used formerly to be prepared and offered, we may understand male lovers [MS: *to love*] living according to the shamefulness of the world and daily sacrificing themselves to the devil by evil works. By shrines, however, in which idols were kept and worshipped, women who pursue the vanities of the world and the desires of the flesh, and who are temples of demons [Col. 1173C], are not incongruously signified. Assuredly, that man who has advanced in the order described above does not look back upon these groves and shrines in any way, because, in hope of the heavenly homeland, he utterly rejects and despises their pleasures and everything that can be desired or possessed in this world.

VERSE 9. On that day the cities of his strength shall be deserted like crops and ploughs, which were deserted before the children of Israel, and it shall be [variant: “you shall be”] desolate. By “the cities of his strength” we may understand all his senses, in which he was strong for evil when he vigorously and sweetly served vices. The spiritual man certainly leaves these senses of his, which are like certain cities of his strength, in one respect and does not leave them in another. He leaves them, not in order to lose them, but in order to begin to possess them better [Col. 1173D]. He leaves them like crops and ploughlands which were deserted before the children of Israel, when he powerfully draws them back from that evil strength by which they were strengthened for sins and vices. He does not leave them when, like certain ploughs for producing harvests of good works, he vigorously carries and turns them toward the daily exercises of the spiritual life after the example of the children of Israel—that is, children who see God, children who love God. Therefore, whatever the blessed soul thus leaves without leaving itself shall be desolate. It shall be deserted by the devil; it shall be deserted by the world; it shall be deserted by sin. For neither the world, nor sin, nor the devil himself, the author of sin, will dare on that day, in that light of the heavenly visitation, to approach it [Col. 1174A].

But because this day cannot be constant in this life, and because a person sees that, through the ensuing night of temptations, his progress is now often delayed and hindered outwardly while in the body, and because, seeing the progress of others, he grieves that he himself advances little or not at all, he speaks to himself in the groaning voice of his heart, saying inwardly:

VERSE 10. Because you have forgotten God your Savior and have not remembered your mighty helper, therefore you shall plant an unfaithful planting and sow a foreign shoot. By an unfaithful planting we denote evil thoughts; by a foreign shoot, less perfect actions. “Because you have forgotten,” he says, “God your Savior.” As though he said: Divine justice indeed requires this, because your injustice has so deserved it: since you have forgotten God [Col. 1174B], your Savior, and have not remembered your mighty helper when you ought to have remembered him, you now unwillingly and against your will are subject to the importunity of useless and evil thoughts; and because you neglected to do the good that you ought to have done, now, even when you do not wish it, you cannot escape the stumbling-block of imperfect action.

VERSE 11. On the day of your planting, a wild vine. Because the day of your former planting—the day, that is, of your past manner of life—brought again before your eyes presents to you nothing but a wild vine, namely an intolerable hardness of heart; nevertheless, if, trusting in the goodness and mercy of God, you steadfastly and perseveringly devote yourself to such labors as you can, your seed shall flower in the morning. For when the morning of heavenly visitation and mercy shines upon you, almighty God will at last make your seed—that is, the labor of your works—rise into good fruit [Col. 1174C].

Thus, thus, humbly bewailing his failure, he again takes up from God’s mercy the hope of consolation, exhorts himself to greater steadfastness in labor, and says: The harvest has been taken away on the day of inheritance, and you shall grieve grievously. By inheritance, holy manner of life may be signified; by harvest, good action. It is as though the faithful soul laments and declares within itself: Because in this holy manner of life, in which and through which you ought to obtain the inheritance of the heavenly homeland and render service, you alone proceed without the fruit of good action, it is fitting for you to grieve grievously. It is fitting, I say, that while others rejoice and exult, you should be saddened by the unceasing remembrance of your sins; [Col. 1174D] that while others eat, sleep, and lawfully use other lawful things, you should humble yourself continually before God through frequent fasts, persistent vigils, and self-discipline, judging even lawful things not to be permitted to you.

## CHAPTER IV. The Burden of Egypt, or Perfect Repentance, Which God Mercifully and Wondrously Works in a Human Being by the Power of His Divinity

ISAIAH XIX, VERSES 1–3. The burden of Egypt. Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt; and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt within it. And I shall set Egyptians against Egyptians, and man shall fight against [Col. 1175A] his brother, and man against his friend, city against city, kingdom against kingdom. And the spirit of Egypt shall be broken within it, and I shall cast down its counsel.

This whole burden seems to treat of the perfect repentance which almighty God, by the power of his divinity, mercifully and wondrously works in a human being. Yet this burden befits, and only he can bear it profitably, the person who has been humbled by his preceding burden, which is entitled “of Damascus,” and, as we have said, exercised and instructed by it. “Behold,” says the prophet, “the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt.” In the light cloud may be understood the life of a human being made light and relieved of sins and vices. In Egypt, however—which is interpreted as “pursuing,” or “darkness,” or “oppressing tribulation” [Col. 1175B]—the human heart is not inappropriately figured. The Lord in some manner ascends upon a light cloud when he makes the person whom he has lightened of the heavy burden of sins to ascend and advance in virtues. He also enters Egypt when he penetrates and illumines with the ray of his visitation that heart which had formerly been dark.

“And the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence.” By idols—which are called *simulacra* because they imitate holiness and divinity yet do not possess them—we may very suitably understand those human works which resemble good works but tend toward an evil end. Idols are moved when evil works are changed. But whence comes this movement of idols—whence, I say, this change of evil works? From his presence [Col. 1175C], that is, from the knowledge of almighty God. For when a person begins inwardly to be irradiated by the presence of the visiting heavenly majesty, he finds even his works, which he believed good and just, to be evil and unjust.

But because it frequently happens that a person leaves sins in bodily act and yet still feels them in the will, it is fittingly added:

“And the heart of Egypt shall melt within it.” In the heart of Egypt we may understand the human will. The heart of Egypt melts within it when, touched by the grace of heavenly mercy, it begins to grow weak in every harmful will and keeps itself in a certain praiseworthy mean, so that it neither loves prosperity too greatly nor fears adversity too greatly. Let us hear what the Lord further adds concerning such a person standing in so praiseworthy a mean:

“And,” he says, “I shall set Egyptians against Egyptians.” By Egyptians rushing against Egyptians we may suitably understand one and the same person. The Lord sets Egyptians against Egyptians when he arouses, in a blessed conflict, persecuting persons against sinful persons—that is, repentant persons against sinning persons. Certainly, a good and happily discordant encounter of Egyptians against Egyptians occurs when one who was Egyptian in sinning begins, by the sentence of strict judgment, to be Egyptian in himself by pursuing and punishing sins within himself. Therefore it is immediately added:

[Col. 1176A] “And man shall fight against his brother, and man against his friend, city against city, kingdom against kingdom.” By brother and friend we may suitably understand the spirit and body of a human being. A man fights against his brother when he begins manfully to resist those very inclinations which arise in the spirit. He fights against his friend when he regards as an enemy for God’s sake the body which he had formerly loved against God; when he crushes it as an enemy and tames and breaks it by diverse adversities and labors. City also fights against city when the city of good works rises against the city of evil works. Kingdom fights against kingdom when, by the strong and manly constancy of good action, the kingdom of vices [Col. 1176B] is destroyed and the kingdom of virtues is established and strengthened in a human being through God’s grace. The following words mystically show what grace and virtue follow this praiseworthy battle:

“And the spirit of Egypt shall be broken within them, and I shall cast down its counsel.” In this place Egypt may signify the world; the spirit of Egypt, the desire of the world; and the inward parts, the vital faculties of the human being. So long as a person is in the world and possesses the world pleasurably, he has the spirit of the world. For, as the apostle John says, “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16). But when he has been perfectly converted from this age to God [Col. 1176C] and begins in his conversion to live according to the prescribed order, the spirit of Egypt is in some manner broken within him. For when the spirit of pride—which is indeed the spirit of Egypt, the spirit, that is, of the world—has been expelled, the spirit of humility is divinely poured out in his inward parts, that is, in his vital faculties.

The Lord fittingly added, moreover, and said: “And I shall cast down its counsel.” For he casts down the counsel of its spirit and makes useless in a human being the counsel of the spirit of Egypt. The counsel of the spirit of Egypt is that a person should live according to the desires of the world. The counsel of the Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit, is that, despising and rejecting the desires of the world, he should always submit himself to God through true humility. All, moreover, [Col. 1176D] who, after the counsel of the spirit of Egypt has thus been cast down, consent to this counsel of the Holy Spirit should take from the following words an example of how they ought thereafter to live. It follows:

“And they shall consult their idols, their diviners, their pythons, and their soothsayers.” *Diviners* were those who foretold the future as if by a prophetic spirit. *Pythons* were those possessed by an evil spirit, who prophesied as if in a kind of madness. *Soothsayers* were those accustomed to foresee the future either in the stars or in the entrails of animals. By idols, as we have said, we may understand human works; by diviners, the inward faculties of a human being; and by pythons and soothsayers, two kinds of sins. One kind is when, at the instigation of an evil spirit, a person sins deliberately—that is, willingly and knowingly. The other is when, without the mind’s pleasure and deliberation, he sins by chance and by a certain sudden precipitancy [Col. 1177A].

He in some manner consults his idols who strictly and carefully examines and tests what and how much he has committed by evil acts in the outward person. He consults his diviners when he subtly and humbly recalls to memory what and how much he has sinned in the inward person by unjust desires against God. Yet even this does not suffice for a person unless he also consults pythons and soothsayers. For one who wishes to repent perfectly must not only know when or how much he has sinned, but must also rightly distinguish and carefully consider where or how he has sinned: whether by deliberate intent or by occurrence—that is, whether he incurred the guilt of sin through purpose and love and long deliberation of mind, or only through the precipitancy of an unguarded and weak mind. After this consultation, after this most strict, so to speak, examination of himself, what follows at last takes place.

VERSE 4. “And I shall hand Egypt over to the power of cruel masters, and a strong king shall rule them,” says the Lord of hosts. These masters are good masters, who cruelly yet healthfully exact from a person what he has sinned; who arouse and urge him to rage against himself in repentance with as much cruelty and bitterness as was the love and sweetness of heart and body with which he sinned. Thus a strong king comes to rule them when the ruling spirit, which we understand by the strong king, governs the senses of the flesh with strength and lofty direction, and powerfully restrains and restricts all their looseness so that the flesh cannot serve the former impulses of its lust [Col. 1177C].

VERSES 5–6. “And the water shall dry up from the sea, and the river shall be desolated and dried up. And the streams shall fail, and the channels of embankments shall become thin and dry up. Reed and rush shall wither.” Water dries up from the sea when the concupiscence of the flesh, denoted by water, is overcome as though drained from the heart made bitter through repentance. The river too is desolated and dried up when carnal action, through which a person had been accustomed to flow and run out to his death, is strongly checked, as though its support had been removed [Col. 1177D]. Support is withdrawn from the river when the turbid river of carnal activity, which proceeded from excess of food, drink, sleep, and the abundance of other pleasurable things, is vigorously crushed by thirst, hunger, vigils, scourges, and other pious labors.
