After this, “the streams shall fail, and become thin, and the channels of embankments shall dry up.” By streams we may understand great temptations, which often strike a person advancing in virtue through the malice of the devil; by channels of embankments, lesser temptations, which in some manner arise and proceed from the fostering of the flesh. For just as embankments are made from heaps of earth, so, while a person treats his earth—that is, his flesh—softly and pleasurably, he accumulates, as it were, certain embankments from which harmful channels of temptations arise. But when the flesh is reckoned an enemy and is, so to speak, treated hostilely for God’s sake, those temptations which it formerly bore from itself perish like dried-up channels [Col. 1178A]. Great and severe temptations also—that is, streams by which he was struck through the devil’s importunity as by a strong rush of rivers—when checked by God’s power and mercy either wholly fail or are so diminished and moderated that they can no longer prevail against him. The mystical sequence of words indicates whence this diminution of rivers and drying up of channels comes. For it follows:

“Reed and rush shall wither.” What may be understood by the reed, which is hollow, except the human heart now emptied of love for the world? And what by the rush, which is fragile, except the frail and weak human body? How the heart and body of a human being ought to wither, however, the prophet immediately explains more plainly in other words, when he says:

VERSE 7. “The bed of the stream shall be laid bare from its source, and every irrigated seed-field shall dry up and wither and be no more.” As by the rush, so also by the stream-bed we understand the human body. The bed of the stream is laid bare from its source when a person truly and humbly opens in confession what, how much, and how shamefully he has sinned in his body. There truly, when a person thus lays himself bare, every irrigated seed-field shall dry up, wither, and be no more. For that soul or flesh which was irrigated in sins, dried out through repentance and cleansed through confession, shall rejoice in perfect remission of sins [Col. 1178C].

VERSE 8. “And fishermen shall mourn, and all who cast a hook into the river and spread a net over the face of the water [variant: ‘waters shall wither’] shall lament.” There are certain fishermen who are good, namely holy angels, who draw a person from the sea of this age and restore him to his Creator. There are also fishermen who are evil, namely opposing spirits, who continually strive by their stormy suggestions and promptings to plunge a person beneath the waves of sins. For when they see that the man whom they had formerly caught, into whose heart they had firmly driven the hook of their deceptions, over whom they had spread their net—that is, their violent compulsion—thus advances in the Lord, they shall mourn and lament, because human salvation is an intolerable grief and affliction to them [Col. 1178D]. Therefore he further adds:

VERSES 9–10. “Those who worked flax, braiding [variant: *pectentes*, ‘combing’] and weaving fine things, shall wither and be put to shame. And its irrigated places shall become weak: all who made pools to catch fish.” By flax, which grows from the earth, we may rightly understand the person who was formerly earthly and carnal. Evil spirits may rightly be called workers of flax, because this is their work: to make an earthly person think earthly things and live carnally. How are they “braiding and weaving fine things”? They braid in action [Col. 1179A]; they weave in thought. They are said to braid in action because they always link sins to sins. They are said to weave in thought because, by their evil suggestions and promptings, they weave harmful and unlawful thoughts together with thoughts in the human heart, so that from these they may make for themselves pools—that is, carnal human hearts and bodies—in which they may gather and preserve their fish, namely sins and vices, which serve them as bait.

But they shall wither and be put to shame: they shall wither in the person’s conversion and be put to shame in his perfect manner of life. “And its irrigated places shall become weak,” when both the abundance of evil desires which overflowed inwardly in the soul and the abundance of the flesh which flowed outwardly through evil deeds have been so drained by God’s grace [Col. 1179B] that no place remains, either in his soul or in his body, for evil spirits to make pools and catch fish.

## CHAPTER V. The Burden of the Desert Sea, or Concerning the Grace of Threefold Compunction

ISAIAH XXI, VERSES 1–2. The burden of the desert sea. “As whirlwinds come from the south-west wind, it comes from the desert, from a dreadful land. A harsh vision has been announced to me: the unbeliever acts unbelievingly, and the despoiler devastates. Go up, Elam; besiege, Mede; I have made all its groaning cease.”

In this fifth burden is set forth and shown to us the threefold grace of compunction, by which a person who has now become a desert sea—that is, who, having deserted and left the world, has begun to make satisfaction to God in bitterness of body and soul [Col. 1179C]—is often mercifully touched and visited. For he is sometimes pierced by compunction through the grace of the Holy Spirit alone, acting beforehand; sometimes through remembrance of evil desires and evil inclinations by which he offended God in his heart; and sometimes through remembrance of evil deeds which he committed against God in the body.

This is nobly expressed at the beginning of this burden when, in the person of one perfectly repentant and truly recognizing himself in humility, it is said through the prophet: “As whirlwinds come from the south-west wind, it comes from the desert, from a dreadful land; a harsh vision has been announced to me.” Here, by an appropriate comparison, we may understand the Holy Spirit by the south-west wind, because just as great and diverse storms commonly arise when the south-west wind blows, so, when the Holy Spirit breathes and inspires, hearts once hardened by sins are moved and stirred, as by certain great and good whirlwinds, and are wondrously and mercifully dissolved into tears of repentance [Col. 1179D].

By the desert, however, we understand the heart of a person now perfectly deserting the world and deserted by the world; by the dreadful land, the human body itself, by which he sinned dreadfully against the Lord. For just as good whirlwinds—namely, sweet and just tribulations—come from the south-west wind, that is, from the visiting and inspiring Holy Spirit, and sweetly affect a person inwardly, so another whirlwind, though not equally sweet, is nevertheless equally healthful, comes from that desert, which we have said is the human heart [Col. 1180A], when, humbly remembering the many inclinations and desires by which he often offended, unseen by anyone but observed by God alone, in the heart denoted by the desert, he is pierced to the marrow by compunction. Another whirlwind also comes from the dreadful land when, humbly recalling the many dreadful contaminations of sin which he committed in the body, he shudders and is terrified; shaken, as it were, by a mighty whirlwind through the overpowering pain of repentance, he groans in compunction.

From these diverse whirlwinds, now coming from the south-west wind, now from the desert, now from the dreadful land, a harsh vision is announced to the person. This harsh vision is the true and perfect recognition of sins. For before these whirlwinds come, a person cannot see, cannot know himself, cannot know or understand how much evil he has deserved before God. But when these whirlwinds have come, and he has perfectly recognized himself, he often says to himself in the groaning voice of his heart, with spirit and mind contrite: “The unbeliever acts unbelievingly, and the despoiler devastates.” A person is in some manner unbelieving when he is inwardly corrupted by an evil will; he acts unbelievingly when he pursues an evil will by evil works. The just person, happily aroused by the whirlwinds mentioned above, often rebukes, accuses, and punishes these two things in himself, saying: “The unbeliever acts unbelievingly, and the despoiler devastates.” As though he said: Wretched and lamentable one [Col. 1180C], recognize yourself as unbelieving. For by every kind of wickedness of the worst will you have inwardly defiled yourself before God; by the enormity of criminal action you have until now lived unfaithfully against God, like an unbeliever. But now too—and this is more grievous—after you had turned to the Lord and ought by the humility of subsequent repentance and satisfaction to amend and blot out former transgressions, you have become like a despoiler who lays waste. For you have taken from God his honor, and you have wasted the goods and virtues received from his gift, by foolishly attributing them to yourself as though they came from you—though by them you might have deserved the grace of God and pardon and remission for your former unbelief and unfaithfulness.

Thus, thus, while he calls to mind God’s goods and anxiously examines the evils which he has rendered in return for them, the more truly he considers what he has deserved, the more he crushes and afflicts himself with the laments of stricter repentance, again saying inwardly to himself:

“Go up, Elam; besiege, Mede; I have made all its groaning cease.” By Elam, which is interpreted “his ascent,” we not inappropriately understand pride of heart; by the Medes, said to mean “those who tempt,” we rightly signify diverse temptations of the flesh. The perfect person rebukes first the ascent—that is, the pride of his heart—through which, while he did not fear heedlessly to rise up against God by exalting himself, he deserved miserably to descend into the abyss of sins. He also rebukes the wickedly tempting impulses of his flesh, by which and through which, overcome and cast down, he offended God his Creator and Redeemer time after time [Col. 1181A].

“Go up, Elam,” he says. This is to say: You pride of my heart, rising wickedly, who so often blinded my inward eyes from the sight of the true light, who removed and drove God from me and me from God my Savior—go up, go up, I say, into the conscience of my heart; go up before the eyes of my heart, where I may always look upon you, always repent in confession, and in repenting bitterly lament you. Thus, after he has mourned his pride of mind, he likewise bewails with equal humility the temptations of the flesh by which and through which he slipped into works of iniquity, and adds:

“Besiege, Mede.” As though he said: You my wretched temptation, who cast me down as weak and powerless, who made me before God an accused person defiled with so many, such great, and such criminal contaminations of sins—besiege me. I mean: like one besieging, always stand before me, so that by your unyielding siege, by the sad and bitter recollection of you, you may always oppress and humble me; so that I may always look upon you and always find in you something by which I may be inflamed to the laments of repentance [Col. 1181B]. “I have made all its groaning cease.” Those things over which I ought to have groaned I did not groan over as I should have done; rather, while groaning ceased, I exulted and rejoiced in the things for which I ought to have wept and been sorrowful.

VERSES 4, 3. “Therefore my loins are filled with pain; anguish has seized me like the anguish of a woman in labor; I collapsed when I heard; I was troubled when I saw. My heart withered; darkness stupefied me.”

[Col. 1181C] These words, which true humility forms in the heart of one perfectly repentant, are so distinguished and carefully differentiated that some may be quite suitably referred to the inward person and others to the outward person. When he says, “My loins are filled with pain; I collapsed when I heard; I was troubled when I saw; my heart withered,” he signifies the contrition of the inward person. But when he adds, “Anguish has seized me like the anguish of a woman in labor; darkness stupefied me,” he indicates the affliction of the outward person. The loins are filled with pain when all the inward parts of a person are stirred to repentance. This inward pain, the pain indeed of deepest repentance, makes a person hear, makes him see, makes him wither. For when he is touched and filled within by perfect pain of repentance, he begins to hear God his Creator; he begins inwardly to hear what God commands and what he forbids; through love he begins to see God, whom he had formerly neglected to see and love. At this inward hearing he collapses; at this inward vision he is troubled and withers [Col. 1181D]. He collapses from his former pride of mind, is troubled by the excessive pain of repentance, and withers from every pleasure and love of the world.

But when he has thus been touched inwardly by pain, when, thus troubled, he has happily withered away from all things belonging to the world, through the help of heavenly mercy’s grace, his outward acts correspond to his inward progress. This we may suitably gather from those words which we left untouched in the middle and at the end of this present verse [Col. 1182A]. For after he said, “Therefore my loins are filled with pain,” he added, “Anguish has seized me like the anguish of a woman in labor.” Again, when he said, “I collapsed when I heard; I was troubled when I saw; my heart withered,” he added, “Darkness stupefied me.”

But what is this anguish by which, after so great a perfection of the inward person, he is seized outwardly? Or what is that darkness by which he says that he is stupefied in the outward person? A person lives as if in a certain spaciousness when he treats his body indulgently, when, according to his own pleasure and the desire of the flesh, he indulges beyond measure in food and drink, sleep, amusements, and other things which the flesh desires. But this spacious breadth passes into a certain praiseworthy and blessed narrowness when, in the things in which he had formerly relaxed himself, he so constrains and restricts himself for God’s sake that he steadfastly rejects, casts away, and despises for God not only unlawful things but also lawful things and, so to speak, every thing sweet and pleasurable to the flesh [Col. 1182B].

Such a person can rightly say before the Lord, “Anguish has seized me like the anguish of a woman in labor.” As though he said: I have made this anguish—under which, having cast away and despised the wickedly expansive sweetness of carnal pleasure, I have now subjected myself for God’s sake—my possessor, so that, constrained and confined under it, I may no longer flow out into the vanities of the flesh. It has become for me like the anguish of one in labor, like the anguish of one desiring to give birth, because not only in order to escape the punishment of hell, but also from love and desire to bring forth from my heart and from my body something pleasing to God, something worthy of God, everything broad and pleasant in this world has become sad and narrow to me. After such anguish there is fittingly placed:

“Darkness stupefied me.” By darkness we understand adversities of the flesh. For when he increases for himself vigils, fasts, silence, and scourges, all these are like a kind of darkness which, withdrawing him from the light of worldly pleasure, makes him insensible to the world. Stupefaction is said to occur when a person, shaken by sudden and unforeseen terror, is carried outside himself. A perfect person is rightly said to be as if stupefied by darkness when, shattered by the narrownesses and adversities of the flesh, he is changed from himself—from the person, that is, whom he had formerly been—and even if the world is present, he no longer feels it [Col. 1182D], because, dead to the world, he loves to live for God alone. Therefore he fittingly adds:

“My beloved Babylon has become a wonder to me.” For he marvels, and in marveling weeps and laments that he spent his days so foolishly and senselessly, lost such great goods, and deserved such great evils for the brief and unstable delight and love of this world. “My beloved Babylon,” he says, “has become a wonder to me.” Babylon is interpreted “confusion.” It is as though he said: The confused and confounding delight of earthly love, which, as beloved, had possessed me as its beloved and subjugated me to itself, has now become a wonder to me. What was formerly beloved has now become detestable and despised to me. For I judge it marvelous and utterly miserable that any person should desire and possess with such love and longing that which confounds its possessor and, when lost, adds such great bitterness and pain [Col. 1183A].

While he humbly considers and marvels at his own folly, he is mystically instructed by the following words to turn his sense and understanding to consider and weigh also the works of divine mercy:

VERSE 5. “Set the table; look out from the watchtower.” By the table may be understood Sacred Scripture, in which the food of the faithful soul is truly laid up and stored, as the prophet testifies when he says: “You have prepared before me a table against those who afflict me” (Psalm 22:5). By the watchtower, from which and in which a person looks upon things near and far, a pure heart and pure soul are aptly figured. He is commanded, when the table has been set, to look out from the watchtower, because he is taught to set before the pure eyes of a pure and cleansed heart the dishes of Sacred Scripture divinely served, so that from them he may discern and understand what he owes to his Creator and Redeemer [Col. 1183B]. Therefore it is further added:

“Rise up, you who eat and drink, you princes; seize the shield.” By the shield with which a person is fortified against the blows and darts of enemies, we suitably understand the glorious wood of the holy cross, through which the arrows of invisible enemies are invisibly struck down and turned aside. The wood of the Lord’s cross both signifies and teaches the mortification of the flesh. “Rise up,” he says, “you who eat and drink, you princes.” As though he said: You who have already become princes, who, leaving the world, have begun to rule and govern vices—while eating the harder matters of Sacred Scripture, that is, breaking and crushing them with the tooth of continual meditation, and drinking the lighter matters, that is, transferring them into food and refreshment for the soul—rise up; always lift yourselves by desire and love from low things to high, from earthly things to heavenly. Seize the shield: love the mortification of the flesh, humbly imitating my passion. But if, O human being, it seems hard to you to seize the righteous shield, if you refuse to become an imitator of my passion and death:

VERSE 6. “Go and set a watchman, and whatever he sees he shall announce to you.” This watchman, whom we are commanded to set, is our understanding, through which, as though placed on a high watchtower, we ought to consider and humbly weigh what and how great things almighty God, Creator of heaven and earth, has endured for us unworthy persons and sinners [Col. 1183D]. For if we look frequently upon our Author, if we continually recall the manifold humiliations of his passion, whatever may befall us will all be light and bearable to us for love of him. Therefore, “Go,” he says, “and set a watchman.” As though he said: Go by understanding; set by affection. Go, worthily considering and weighing in the understanding of your heart the gifts of my mercy and compassion; set in your affection how much I have labored for you and how much I have endured for the sake of your love and salvation.

When, at this voice of the Lord’s inward exhortation and instruction, a person has inwardly awakened and been illumined, and has turned his whole understanding toward God, then at last what is said comes about: “And whatever he sees he shall announce to you.” He sees in some manner when he begins prudently to understand all the works of God’s mercy. Whatever he sees, he announces when he reverences and loves, with the affectionate devotion of his heart, those things which he knows and understands concerning God. But let us hear what he sees and, seeing, loves. It follows.

### Verses 7, 8, 9

“And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel; and he looked attentively with a long gaze. And the lion cried: ‘Upon the Lord’s watchtower I stand continually by day, and upon my guard I stand through all the nights. Behold, this rider comes, a man in a chariot of horsemen; and he answered and said: “Babylon has fallen, [Col. 1184B] and all the carved images of her gods are shattered upon the ground.”’”

[The Vulgate omits *alis*, “with wings.”]

In these words, if they are examined closely, all the mysteries of Christ are found contained and signified. There are his incarnation; his singular and distinctive manner of life in this world; his passion and death; his resurrection; his ascension; the promised and accomplished descent of the Holy Spirit; his second coming; the reward of the elect; and the condemnation of the reprobate.

By the chariot we may quite suitably understand his holy incarnation. For he who, in the substance of his divinity, could neither be seen nor moved, by assuming our humanity became in some manner a chariot for us, upon whom we miserable and weak people might be placed, and through whom, and by whom, we might mercifully be carried back to the joys of the heavenly homeland, from which we had been expelled. And this chariot is rightly called a chariot of two horsemen. For by these two horsemen God the Father and God the Holy Spirit are worthily represented. These most noble horsemen, in shared divinity and indivisible unity, always presided over this most noble chariot, always, so to speak, rode upon it; because Christ Jesus, our Creator and Redeemer, who appeared as visible man in visible flesh, nevertheless always remained God, coeternal and consubstantial with the invisible Father and the Holy Spirit.

And rightly, after it has been said, “And he saw a chariot of two horsemen,” there follows:

“A rider on an ass and a rider on a camel.”

By the ass we understand the Jewish people; by the camel, the Gentile people. God incarnate for our sake first became [Col. 1184D] a rider on an ass when, from the Jewish people, he mercifully drew to knowledge and love of himself his chosen disciples, the holy apostles, and all other followers and imitators of their faith and teaching. Afterwards he also became a rider on a camel when he drew that crooked and misshapen people of the Gentiles away from the filth of idols and to the mysteries of his faith, and made them worthy for him to sit upon—that is, worthy for him to dwell, through faith and love, in their hearts.

How this noble rider on an ass and rider on a camel lived in this world, and how unlike the rest of humankind his life and conduct were, the prophet declares in the following words:

“And he looked attentively with a long gaze.”

This is the life of Jesus. He “looked attentively with a long gaze,” always abstaining from every evil and always performing many good things. Or, he looked attentively with a long gaze upon the life of the good for eternal reward, and upon the life of the wicked for eternal condemnation.

“And the lion cried.”

In these two words the mystery of Christ’s passion and resurrection is briefly contained. He who cried out in his passion became a lion in his resurrection. He cried out humbly while dying on the cross; he became a lion powerfully when rising from death. But what grace and blessedness that cry of one thus dying on the cross bestowed upon the Church, and what the strength of this lion, rising with such power, bestowed: let him who cried speak; let him who rose again speak.

“Upon the Lord’s watchtower,” he says, “I stand continually by day, and upon my guard I stand through all the nights.”

In this short verse are contained the glorious ascension of our same Lord Jesus Christ and the promised and accomplished descent of the Holy Spirit to earth. By the watchtower may quite fittingly be understood the beautiful and glorious multitude of blessed angels and holy souls already reigning with Christ in heaven. By the guard which he calls his own guard, over which he declares that he stands through all the nights, he mystically signifies the present Church, still labouring in the night of this mortality.

He began indeed to stand upon the Lord’s watchtower when, after conquering death and after the glory of the resurrection, exalted and raised above all the choirs of angels, true God and true man, he sat powerfully at the right hand [Col. 1185C] of the Father. But he was also standing over his guard through all the nights when, after his ascension, he protected by the power of his divinity that primitive Church which he had left in the night of ignorance and the night of human adversity, amid the world’s adversities, until he made them—illuminated by the new and unheard-of radiance of the Holy Spirit, and flooded and filled with the gift of overflowing divinity—strong and unconquerable against every adversity.

This is the glory of his ascension briefly expressed: in it he is honoured, adored, and venerated, standing continually by day upon that lofty and sublime watchtower of holy angels and blessed souls, where there is no night but unceasing day; no ignorance, but all knowledge; no sorrow, but perpetual joy; no adversity, but continual prosperity. This is the grace of his fatherly consolation briefly expressed, by which he then consoled that primitive Church through the Holy Spirit given from above, prefiguring, demonstrating, indeed also confirming, that mercy and compassion by which he still watches daily with fatherly concern over his guard—namely, the whole holy Church which he redeemed and undertook to protect.

“Upon my guard I stand continually by day, and upon my guard I stand through all the nights.”

As though he said: Although, in the assumed form of my humanity, I have been raised above the heavens and heavenly dignity [Col. 1186A], and I, the coeternal Son, have been placed at the right hand of the coeternal Father, nevertheless I neither forget nor can forget my guard, my Church, which I must protect; standing over it through all the nights—that is, in all its adversities, distresses, and tribulations—always and everywhere sustaining it with the unfailing consolations of my mercies.

After the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension have been set forth and signified, the prophet immediately declares in the following words what kind of judge Christ will be, and how stern, when he returns:

“Behold,” he says, “this rider comes, a man in a chariot of horsemen; and he answered and said: ‘Babylon has fallen, has fallen, and all the carved images of her gods are shattered upon the ground.’”

[Col. 1186B] “Behold,” he says, “this one who cried out in death, who became a lion in the resurrection, who as a rider with wings—that is, through the power of his divinity—or with wings—that is, through the ministry of the holy angels—has been raised above the stars and reigns in heaven with the Father and the Holy Spirit: behold, he comes as a man in a chariot of horsemen,” that is, as true God and true man. He comes indeed as a man—that is, in that same humanity in which he was a man, in which he was judged by human beings—about to judge the whole human race.

And the words of the angels fittingly agree with the prophetic words. When this same Lord ascended, they said to the disciples standing by: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Nor should what is said, “a man in a chariot of horsemen,” be passed over. [Col. 1166C] There are two kinds of horsemen. Almighty God has his horsemen in this world—namely, all his elect, upon whom he himself rides, whom he rules. The devil also has his horsemen—all the wicked, upon whom he rides, in whom he reigns, over whom he presides. The Lord will one day come as a man in a chariot of horsemen, the judge of good and evil, and will answer and say: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen.” He will answer the good with good and the wicked with evil. He will answer by eternally rewarding the good for their good deeds; he will answer by eternally condemning the wicked for their evil deeds.

And he says, “Babylon has fallen.” This fall of Babylon is the confusion of eternal condemnation. Babylon will fall when, after the elect have been gathered to the joys of eternal blessedness and the general judgment has been completed, the assembly of the wicked—which may be understood through Babylon—will be assigned to the punishment of eternal damnation.

In this fall, all the carved images of her gods will be shattered upon the ground, because all the desires of the reprobate, which in this place may be understood by the carved images of gods, will there be reduced to nothing. For Babylon’s fall will be such and so great that, even if the desires of those who are to be condemned could be called and could be right, they nevertheless cannot be heard by God, the just judge, because they ought not to be heard. They will cry out and not be heard; they will grieve and not be consoled.

When the dread and fearful severity of the final judgment has thus been prefigured and foretold through the prophet in these mystical words, he who is to come—the Son of God himself—confirms and concludes the discourse of his prophecy, speaking to the evil and the good, the reprobate and the elect:

### Verse 10

“My threshing, and daughter of my threshing-floor: what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you.”

By “threshing” the evil and reprobate are not unsuitably denoted. By the “daughter of the Lord’s threshing-floor” all God’s elect are worthily named. For evil and perverse people are, as it were, a certain threshing of the good. By the many tribulations and adversities which the elect suffer from the impious upon the threshing-floor of the present life, they are cleansed and purified after the manner of wheat, so that they may one day be found worthy to be stored in heavenly granaries.

Cain was Abel’s threshing, because he purified him. Blessed Job’s wife was his threshing, because, when he could not be overcome by pain or moved to impatience, he was threshed by the words of his wife, who gave evil counsel, and thus in some fashion purified; and he deserved ever more and more to be praised and crowned by the Lord.

Nor should what is said be passed over: “What I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you.” “Lord” is a name of fear; “God” is a name of love. The almighty Creator is called the Lord of hosts; he is called the God of Israel. He is Lord to very many through fear, but God to few through love. For he is feared as Lord by more people with servile fear, but he is loved as God by fewer—namely, by Israelites alone, by those alone, I mean, who see God and desire to see him with a pure mind.

Those whose Lord he is through fear he calls his threshing; but those whose God he is through love he calls the daughter [Col. 1187C] of his threshing-floor. “My threshing,” he says, “and daughter of my threshing-floor: what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you.”

As though he said: You portion of the wicked, appointed for this purpose, that through you my children may be purified; and you portion of the elect, who upon my threshing-floor—upon the threshing-floor, I mean, of this present age—must for my sake be threshed and purified by the adversities of the impious: what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you. I, I say—I who, as God with God, know and hear all things with him and in him—announce these things to you and say these things to you, so that you who are wicked and resist God’s will may, fearing the Lord, turn back from evil; and so that you who are good may, progressing from good to better, love God as God. Thus, when you have been taken from the threshing-floor of the present life [Col. 1187D], by his help you may at last be found worthy to be brought into the heavenly granaries, through him, in him, to be crowned at the end.

This voice of almighty God, invisibly calling and admonishing within, unto the grace of salvation, not only the good but also the wicked, is surely so powerful and resonant that it not only lifts and kindles the righteous toward a more perfect norm of righteousness, but also mercifully raises and revives the sinner himself, asleep in iniquities and despairing. Thus he begins humbly to apply the ear of his heart to the Lord crying out to him, as the prophet shows in the type of the following burden, as if speaking in the sinner’s own person:

## Chapter VI. The burden of Dumah, or of those whom God awakens from the sleep of sins to amendment of life and morals

[Col. 1188A]

### Isaiah 21, verses 11–12

“The burden of Dumah. One cries to me from Seir: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’ [Alternative reading: ‘what concerning the night?’] The watchman said: ‘Morning comes, and also night. If you seek, seek; turn back, and come.’”

By these words, the burden of Dumah, which means “silence,” is fittingly prescribed to the sinner awakening [manuscript: “of the awakening sinner”] from the sleep of sin. For unless sin is silenced and stilled in a person by the calming and restraining hand of the Most High, he cannot receive with the inner ear of the heart the voice of the Lord’s cry.

Once the tumult of vices has been calmed, he hears and understands the voice of the Lord and his Creator; and, watchfully observing and discerning what or why it cries out to him [Col. 1188B], he humbly cries out within himself:

“One cries to me from Seir: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’”

By the name Seir, which means “rough” or “hairy,” we may understand the rough and hairy course of a sinful life. When the sinner, awakened by God’s cry, begins somewhat to recognize this, moved at last by repentance he breaks forth tearfully into these words: “One cries to me from Seir.” As though he said inwardly to himself: “Through the grace of his compassion and inspiration, I hear the Lord crying out to me within; from Seir—that is, from my rough and evil life—I perceive that he mercifully calls me back.”

But what further remains for you, wretched soul? If you complain of impossibility, if you assert that you are weak and unable to resist vices, consider the strength and power of him who calls. And who is he? “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” He is the Watchman who always watches over his own with the guardianship of his protection, lest the night of evil pleasure prevail against them. He is the Watchman who protects and preserves them by the power of his virtue from the night of perverse and wicked action.

When the sinner has thus been awakened and enlightened, the voice of God’s inspiring grace resounds more powerfully in him and raises him more and more to repentance. Hence follows:

“The watchman said: ‘Morning comes, and also night.’”

The Lord says: “Morning comes”—that is, the time of my grace, by which, awakened and enlightened, you have finally begun to recognize how harmfully and ruinously you have until now been defiled in Seir, that is, in [Col. 1188D] the dreadful and lamentable blindness of carnal life. But if you neglect to walk in and according to this morning of my visitation and illumination, by returning from evils, night will come: indeed, the night of your former ignorance and blindness, in which you will again be wrapped. The night of future damnation will also come, under which, all hope of the heavenly day having been removed, you will lie forever.”

All who desire to escape this night and attain the joys of eternal light should strive to regulate and order their life, morals, and actions according to the following teaching of this same Lord and our Redeemer.

“If you seek,” he says, “seek; turn back and come.”

As though he said: “If you seek to pass from the night and ignorance of the present life to me, who am the splendour of unchangeable and unfailing light, seek more attentively; seek more earnestly. Turn back by abandoning the vain conduct of this world; come by drawing near to me through good works. Seek in this temporal life, by the merits of good conduct, that for which in that life which is without time you may acquire eternal rewards.”

## Chapter VII. The burden of Arabia, by which the manner of returning to God is signified

### Isaiah 21, verses 13–14

“The burden in Arabia. In the forest at evening you shall sleep on the paths of the Dodanim [alternative reading: Dedanim]. Meet the thirsty; bring water, you who inhabit the land of the south; meet the fugitive with bread.”

After the burden of Dumah, the burden in Arabia is set in fitting order. For the person who in that burden is commanded to seek, turn back, and come, is mystically taught in this burden how he should seek, how he should turn back, and how he should come.

“In the forest,” says the prophet—or rather, the Lord through the prophet—“at evening you shall sleep on the paths of the Dodanim.” As we know, beasts dwell in a forest. Therefore I judge that the present age, and the bestial conduct of worldly life, are not unjustly understood by the forest.

Dodanim, however, interpreted as “judgment” or “kinsman,” fittingly signifies our Lord Jesus Christ. He is our kinsman and our Lord. He is not without reason called our kinsman, because his father—that is, the Jewish people, from whose seed according to the flesh he deigned to be born—and the Gentile people, from whose stock we have sprung, were in some manner brothers, because according to the dignity of their creation they had one Father, God almighty.

“On the paths of the Dodanim.” Everyone walks on the paths of this our kinsman who imitates his ways as far as possible.

Nor should what is said be passed over: “In the forest at evening you shall sleep on the paths of the Dodanim.” We may understand these words in two ways: either that a person should make evening—that is, an end—of bestial life within himself; or that he should always turn the eye of his heart toward that evening of which it is written: “At evening, and morning, and noon, I will speak and declare” (Psalm 54:18), namely, the evening in which this aforementioned kinsman of ours, Jesus Christ the Son of God, set [Col. 1189D]; considering what he endured for him, though unworthy, and striving also to respond in some measure to his passion.

Whoever abandons the world with this will and desire, the compassionate and merciful Lord sends such teachers to meet, through whom the desire of his good will may be helped, strengthened, and made firm. Hence follows:

“Meet the thirsty; bring water, you who inhabit the land of the south; meet the fugitive with bread.”

To bring water to the thirsty is to refresh and instruct the one thirsting and panting for life with the gentler or clearer streams of sacred Scripture [manuscript: *recitare*, “recite,” in place of *recreare*, “refresh”].

And the addition, “You who inhabit the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread,” is as though he said: “You whom that most sweet south wind—that is, the Holy Spirit—has gently breathed upon and beneficially watered with the breath and dew of his grace: meet and aid this fugitive with bread, that is, with the stronger food of heavenly teaching.”

### Verse 15

“For they fled from before swords, from before the threatening sword, from before the drawn bow, and from before grievous battle.”

These four things suggest four causes that make a person flee the world and what belongs to the world: namely, fear and love of God, which are not unjustly understood under the name of “swords”; fear of death, which, because it certainly awaits all people, is fittingly understood by the threatening sword; fear of the future judgment, which is rightly represented by the drawn bow, because above the entire human race it will be terribly stretched, like a bow striking forcefully; and the recollection and dread of the everlasting condemnation which will follow judgment, a dread that will be raised like a grievous and intolerable battle against the impious, when everyone found there to be reprobate will be assigned to eternal punishments.

That we may not succumb to enemies in this battle or incur the punishment of eternal death, let us pursue this in the present time with utmost zeal and concern. For now is the time of grace, as is mystically shown when the text immediately adds:

### Verses 16–17

“Yet within one year, as the year of a hired labourer, all the glory of Kedar shall be removed. And the remnant of the number of the mighty archers among the sons of Kedar shall diminish.”

This one year fittingly signifies the time of the present life. It is and is called like a hired labourer’s year because, through the temporal labours of life, a person to be saved acquires for himself, as by a kind of fortunate transaction, the means by which he may live eternally with God.

Therefore, if in this year we have laboured faithfully in the manner of a prudent hired labourer, we shall be relieved through God’s grace of the grievous burden of sins, as is promised to us in mystical words in the following statement:

“And the burden of the glory of Kedar shall be removed.”

By the name Kedar, which means “darkness,” we may understand the dark enemy of the human race. His burden and glory are sins and vices, through which and in which he glories against God. For it is his joy and glory when he has so crushed a person beneath the burden of vices that the person cannot rise in body to God his Maker even through good works.

But when, at last through God’s pity and help, the person has returned through repentance and begun, like a hired labourer eager for eternal reward, diligently to exercise himself in good deeds, the burden of the glory of Kedar will be removed. For one who, crushed beneath the weight of sins, was the devil’s glory becomes, by repenting and making satisfaction, the same devil’s shame, but God’s glory and exultation.

There also “the remnant of the number of the mighty archers among the sons of Kedar shall diminish,” because the evil suggestions and harmful pleasures by which those mighty archers—the evil spirits—strongly shoot at the unwary human heart, in order to inflict upon it the wound of wicked action, become like “the remnant of the number of the mighty archers” when a person carefully and diligently considers, and by considering reckons, what, how much, and in what way he has sinned; how long and how often he has stood opposed to God, now through wicked pleasures, now through perverse actions.

Thus, thus the numbered remnants will finally diminish among the sons of Kedar—among those, that is, who from sons of the devil and sons of darkness have become sons of light and righteousness. For although in this life they cannot be wholly removed or guarded against, they will nevertheless diminish, and by God’s grace will be so restrained that they can no longer prevail.

“For the Lord, the God of Israel, has spoken.”

As though it were said: The almighty Creator, the God of Israel—the helper and protector of those who see and love him—is he who speaks these things. His speaking is his working. For it is he who, by the ineffable grace of his compassion, works these things in those whom he saves. The work is his; let the glory also be his, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## Chapter VIII. The burden of the Valley of Vision, which those take upon themselves who exercise themselves in the labours of religious life

### Isaiah 22, verses 1–2

“The burden of the Valley of Vision. What ails you also, that you have all gone up upon the housetops? [Alternative reading: ‘because.’] Full of shouting, a populous city, an exulting city: your slain are not slain by the sword, nor dead in battle.”

After the burden in Arabia, the burden of the Valley of Vision is placed in fitting order. For the person who was once in Arabia, while he lived beastially in the forest of worldly conduct, level-ground dwelling and estranged from God—for Arabia is said to be “level country”—in some manner takes on the burden of the Valley of Vision when, having left the world, he begins humbly and meekly to bear all the labours of spiritual life, understood through the Valley of Vision.

But even in this Valley of Vision there is, alas, such changeableness that one who now advances in virtues now falls short in progress in virtues; and one who now rejoices, as it were, in the inward vision of God is now hindered from contemplating inward light, disturbed either by the devil’s malice, by his own weakness, or by the harassment of other people.

Yet one who is truly a Valley of Vision—that is, one who tends toward the vision of the Almighty through true humility of mind—when he does not see, is seen. That is, when he judges himself abandoned and rejected by God, the unexpected grace of the merciful God again illuminates him, and he is shown to himself, when he deserves inwardly to hear from God in unutterable words:

“What ails you also, that you have all gone up upon the housetops?”

By the housetops, which rise above houses, we may understand spiritual conduct. And it is as though he said: “You wholly—you, I say, who in heart and body, desire and will, have ascended from the low valley of this age to the height of spiritual life—what ails you also?”

This questioning by the Lord is his merciful illumination, by which he mercifully enlightens a person so that he begins to know himself perfectly. He asks what it is that the person suffers, and then himself answers for the person, making known to him the cause of his sufferings, when he immediately adds:

“Full of shouting, a populous city, an exulting city.”

As though he said: “This is what you suffer; this is the cause by which you are vainly tossed about.” [Note: “[Col. 1191A] Thus the manuscript.”] You are full of shouting, because you are disturbed by the tumult of a badly sounding shout: now by anger, now by impatience, now by troublesome importunity, through which, while troubling your neighbour, you are troubled yourself.

And for a greater accumulation of wickedness you are a populous city, and rightly so called, because this shouting frequently resounds in your heart and soul, which ought to have been God’s city and dwelling-place. You are also called an exulting city—a city, I mean, leaping outside—because the things by which you are inwardly ill-tossed you carry out in evil bodily act and habit, as though leaping outside. Or you are called an exulting city because, over things for which you ought to weep and groan, you are lifted up, rejoice, and are glad.

“Your slain are not slain by the sword, nor dead in battle.”

Your perceptions, holy desires, and righteous wills—in which and through which you ought to live for me alone—have indeed been slain, but not slain by the sword: that sword, namely, which is the Word of God (Ephesians 6:17), by which they ought to have been slain to all things which are of the world. Nor have they died in battle, for you neglect to fight against vices and grow numb in idleness and sloth.

### Verse 3

“All your princes have fled together; they have been grievously bound.”

All your innocent, chaste, and holy thoughts, and your inward perceptions—by which you ought to oppose and resist the surreptitious tumults of vicious thoughts, governing and ruling over them—have fled together and perished; and they have been grievously bound, because, ensnared and entangled in the cords of sins, they have become weak and powerless in virtues.

“All who have been found have been bound together,” because even when, as though your perceptions had been found, you desire to rise toward God, you cannot free yourself as you wish, held back and delayed by the bonds in which you voluntarily entangled yourself.

“They fled far away,” because, scattered and dispersed among outward things, they are less able to receive inward goods.

But when, or how, does the invisible God speak these words to a visible human being, except when the mercy of his inspiring and visiting loving-kindness rightly shows the person to himself, and by the touch of his grace coming upon him makes him truly repentant and humbly self-knowing? For the following words figuratively suggest this; they are spoken as though in the person of the human being himself, rejecting every consolation of carnal life. For the text continues:

### Verse 4

“Therefore I said: ‘Depart from me; I will weep bitterly.’”

It sometimes happens that, attentively examining and considering the miseries of his weakness because of his many transgressions, a person now humbly condemns and accuses himself in conscience, and now, as if over less serious matters, excuses himself inwardly by consoling himself. Yet the truly perfect person steadfastly repels the consolations of flattering thoughts that come upon him, and forcefully drives and compels both heart and body toward the tears of repentance alone, saying within himself:

“Because I know that I have grievously sinned against God and unbelievably offended God, my Redeemer, therefore I said: ‘Depart from me; I will weep bitterly.’ Depart from me, consoling thoughts. I will weep bitterly; I admit no empty blandishment of consolation.”

“Do not press upon me to console me over the devastation of the daughter of my people.”

My soul, which was once the daughter of a people—the daughter, that is, of holy kindreds and of holy desires among which it was accustomed to exercise itself—now devastated and stripped, indeed almost stripped, of virtues, denies me the sweetness of every passing consolation.

### Verse 5

“For it is a day of slaughter, trampling, and weeping to the Lord God of hosts in the Valley of Vision.”

This day of slaughter is the day of heavenly visitation, which may not unjustly be called a day of slaughter. For it slays evil wills and harmful desires in the heart of one humbly repenting. It is also a day of trampling, because it at once strengthens and enlightens the person so that he can despise and trample underfoot whatever he formerly loved against God. It also becomes a day of weeping to the Lord God of hosts in the Valley of Vision, when, through the weeping of repentance, he begins humbly to make satisfaction to the Lord in holy conduct for those things in which he remembers that he has offended God.

And it is as though the blessed and truly repentant soul said within itself: “This day—that is, the visitation and illumination of heavenly mercy and grace, which has shown me to myself, which has made me see and know the miseries of my weakness—will be to me a day of slaughter, slaying from my body that which until now has lived wickedly; it will be to me a day of trampling, trampling down and rooting out from my heart that in which I formerly took evil delight; it will also be a day of weeping to the Lord God of hosts in the Valley of Vision. For always weeping, always repenting, and always making satisfaction to God, I shall be lowly and despised in the humility of this holy manner of life.”

He immediately reveals what it is that the soul should weep for, when he adds:

### Verse 6

“And Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of a horseman, and the shield uncovered the wall.”

By Elam, which means “his ascent,” pride ascending wrongly may quite fittingly be understood. The human soul is appropriately represented by the quiver, and the human body by the chariot.

“Elam,” he says, “took up the quiver.” As though he said: “Elam took up my soul, which ought to have been God’s quiver, in which God’s arrows ought to have been gathered, stored, and kept: the arrows of the Scriptures, holy thoughts, and good desires, by which the devil’s weapons and arrows ought to have been repelled and shattered. Elam took it up because my pride, ascending against God, corrupted it and consumed all the strength of its virtue.”

“And the chariot of a horseman”: that is, my body, upon which that noble horseman—God and man alone—ought to sit and rule, pride has claimed as its seat. “Therefore the shield uncovered the wall,” because the strong protection of God uncovered—or rather, abandoned—the hardness of my heart, and it became like an intervening wall, because it so separated me from God that nothing of his inward sweetness and grace now tastes sweet to me.

Thus, thus, the more a person humbly recognizes and mourns himself, and is troubled from his inmost thoughts, the more sweetly he deserves to be consoled by the regard of divine mercy. Hence the text immediately adds, as though in the person of the Lord himself:

### Verses 7–9

“And your chosen valleys shall be full of chariots, and horsemen shall set their seats in the gate. And they shall uncover [alternative reading: ‘it shall be uncovered’] the covering of Judah; and in that day you shall see the armoury of the house of the forest. And you shall see the breaches of the city of David, because they have multiplied.”

It is as though he said: “Because I now see you perfectly humbled before me, the perceptions of your body and soul, which formerly savoured nothing but lofty things, will now, like chosen valleys made worthy of my visitation and indwelling, be full of chariots. For they will be filled, as I teach and impart, with understanding and knowledge of evangelical doctrine.”

“And horsemen shall set their seats in the gate.” Under the name “horsemen” he mystically signifies holy preachers. Since they bear in their hearts the sayings of the four Gospels and imitate them in deed, approaching one person by the teaching of preaching and another by the example of good conduct, they may rightly be called the Lord’s horsemen.

“The horsemen,” he says, “shall set their seats in the gate.” As though he said: “As I administer to you understanding and love of the Word of God, the horsemen—that is, my preachers—will establish their seats in the gate of your heart, because whatever you hear from them will settle within you. Everything will remain with you for the advancement and profit of your soul.”

“And they shall uncover the covering of Judah.”

Judah means “confession.” Holy preachers uncover the covering of Judah, the covering, so to speak, of confession, when by their preaching and teaching they make a person known to himself. Thus he enters beneath that covering under which he was in some manner covered and hidden from himself, and, with the covering of ignorance as it were uncovered through their words, he comes to know and understand sins which he had known by experience but not by understanding; and he begins perfectly to uncover them through confession.

When the covering of Judah has thus been uncovered, what follows at last comes about:

“And in that day you shall see the armoury of the house of the forest. And you shall see the breaches of the city of David, because they have multiplied.”

That time and hour is aptly called “day” when a person is divinely enlightened, through the words of teachers, to know himself. For on that day he sees the armoury of the house of the forest. An armoury is a place where weapons are stored. Not unfittingly, in this place, different kinds of sins are understood by weapons.

He sees, indeed, and in seeing grieves, that the whole time of his life has been nothing but a kind of armoury of the house of the forest: that is, by living beastially he has laboriously borne the devil’s armour—namely, sins and vices. Through this he has made the city of David, that is, his own soul, broken and corrupted by breaches multiplied through different sins, hateful and uninhabitable to that true David: the one truly strong of hand and truly desirable in appearance.

Yet it often happens that a spiritual person humbly recognizes himself to be a sinner, yet, with the grace of compunction withdrawn, is unable to weep for himself as a sinner or to wash himself through tears as he desires. But the merciful and compassionate Lord, in order more deeply to form and instruct His soldier, reveals him to himself still more subtly: He begins invisibly and ineffably to admonish him, so that he may not merely remember and grieve over his evil deeds, but also consider where he has performed good deeds with insufficient caution—that is, where, through the creeping vice of vainglory, he has exalted himself beyond measure in his good deeds and has humbled himself before God less than was fitting in his evil ones. [Col. 1195B] For this is aptly suggested by the mystery of the following chapter, when, in the very person of the Lord, as though He were addressing—indeed rebuking—the person present, it is said:

**VERS. 9–11.** “And you gathered the waters of the lower pool. And you counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you destroyed houses to fortify the wall. And you made a reservoir between the two walls, with the water of the old pool; and you did not look to Him who made it, nor did you see its maker from afar.”

The waters of the lower pool signify the desires of the flesh; the houses of Jerusalem, a person’s good works. “You gathered,” He says, “the waters of the lower pool”: that is, you piled desire upon desire. “You counted the houses of Jerusalem,” because, though you sinned without number, you counted your good works, and by counting [Col. 1195C] and magnifying them you foolishly boasted. “You destroyed houses to fortify the wall,” because, with your senses scattered, wandering and dissolving around unlawful things, you hardened against yourselves, as it were, the austerity which you endure, like a wall. “And you made a reservoir between the two walls, with the water of the old pool.” The water of old desire, of old pleasure, ought to have been drawn out and dried up by the water of new and daily compunction. But this water of compunction has become like a reservoir between two walls, because, just as a reservoir has muddy, turbid water, so you too, surrounded by the two walls—that is, hardness of heart and hardness of body—sometimes have water not clear from a spring but turbid as though from a reservoir, because you have not yet deserved to attain, according to your desire, that pure and sweet grace of compunction for which you long. [Col. 1195D]

But why has this happened to you? Clearly because “you did not look to Him who made it, nor did you see its maker from afar.” You did not look to God, your Creator and Maker, so as to turn away from evil through fear of Him. You did not see from afar the Redeemer and worker of your salvation, because you preferred to His love and sweetness the love and sweetness of sins. Therefore, after the almighty Lord has thus mercifully rebuked and gently enlightened within the person whom He has determined to save, He teaches, as it were through the prophet Himself, how that person ought thereafter to live, when He adds:

**VERS. 12–13.** “And the Lord of hosts will call in [Col. 1196A] that day to weeping and mourning, to baldness and the girding of sackcloth. And behold: joy and gladness, killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine.”

God’s call is God’s inspiration. Through the grace of His inspiration He first calls a person to weeping of heart, then to bodily mourning, so that the person may both weep in penitence with the heart and answer the heart’s weeping in the body by works worthy of repentance. He calls also to baldness and the girding of sackcloth, because He wills that one should gradually pluck out and cast away the vices of mind and body; and, girded firmly with the strong guard of life, signified by the girdle, should diligently beware the future snares of creeping vices. Thus—yes, thus—when the person has been made bald and girded, what follows finally comes to pass:

“And behold: joy and gladness, killing calves and slaughtering [Col. 1196B] rams.” By calves we understand the wantonness of the flesh; by rams, the pride of the mind. Or the calves may signify the senses of the outer person, which, like a frolicking calf, are always carried headlong; and the rams, the inner senses, which, like a ram leading the flock, are accustomed to go before the outward senses, whether toward good or toward evil.

And one should note that it says, “joy and gladness.” Joy belongs to the outer person; gladness, to the inner person. The perfect person, who has been made bald and girded in the manner described above, counts it all bodily joy and considers it the supreme gladness of the heart to kill the wanton motions of the outward senses by continence of the flesh—this is to kill the calves; [Col. 1196C] and wholly to subject the proud senses of the inner person, through true humility of mind, to God’s will and service—this is to slaughter the rams. Such a person’s joy and gladness also consist in eating flesh and drinking wine. For he rejoices to break and crush, by continual handling and reconsideration, as though with teeth, the more obscure and difficult mysteries of Holy Scripture—which we may understand by “flesh”—and to turn them into the desired savor of understanding. He rejoices also to drink wine: that is, continually to be intoxicated by the wine of spiritual perception, which gladdens the human heart, and thus, intoxicated, to become wholly estranged from all that belongs to the world.

For this purpose he exhorts and urges all his senses, saying within himself to himself: “Let us eat and drink, [Col. 1196D] for tomorrow we shall die.” It is as though he said: If we make Holy Scripture our food through understanding of heart and imitation in deed; if we love continually, while we are in this life, to be refreshed and made drunk by the wine of spiritual perception and understanding, then that serene morning of the heavenly visitation will rise upon us. Illuminated by its splendor, we shall die to the world and to the world’s vice, and shall begin to live to the virtues. Or again, when the today of this present life has passed, and that final morning—the morning, namely, of the future resurrection—has arrived, we shall die with a blessed death to the corruption which we now endure, so that we shall experience no further stain of corruption.

Blessed, and truly blessed, is the person who has borne the burden of the Valley of Vision [Col. 1197A] in this manner; who, through the aforesaid weeping of heart and mourning of body, having been made bald of vices and girded with the guard of mind and body, has thus advanced in the perfection of spiritual life. The following burden most fittingly applies to such a person, since he mourns and laments not only himself and his own sins, but also the perils of other people still tossed upon the salt sea of this age. The prophet mystically indicates this when, as though in the person of such people, he adds and says:

## CHAPTER IX. The burden of Tyre: concerning those who weep for both their own sins and those of others, and exhort all to repentance.

**ISA. XXIII, VERS. 1–2.** “The burden of Tyre. Howl, ships of the sea, because the house from which they used to come has been laid waste; it has been revealed to them from the land of Kittim. Be silent, you who dwell on the island; the trade [variant: *traders*] of Sidon, crossing the sea, filled you in many waters.”  
[Note: [Col. 1197] The words “in many waters” are assigned in the Vulgate editions to the following verse.]

Tyre is interpreted as “narrowness.” Tyre fittingly represents the person who, despising for God’s sake the broad expanse of the whole world, has given himself to the straits of this present life, so that, God being gracious, he may deserve to reach the breadth of the heavenly homeland. By the ships of the sea any form of spiritual life may not inappropriately be understood: just as one crosses the stormy tempest of the sea and escapes the danger of death, so every spiritual form of life is like a ship which carries a person across the dangerous rivers of sins and safely brings him to the haven of everlasting blessedness, where there will be no danger of death. The ships may also signify persons themselves, living spiritually in the spiritual life and tirelessly pressing toward the one and same harbor of eternal salvation with one and the same love and desire.

The house from which these ships usually come rightly signifies the world. For in this house the ships are built, since all who pass into spiritual soldiery are born and brought forth from this world and in this world. “Howl,” he says, “ships of the sea, because the house from which you used to come has been laid waste.” As if he said: All you who have already crossed the sea of this age, who, with the sails of holy conduct raised, make for the place of the heavenly homeland, look with merciful regard and compassionate affection upon those whom you left behind you in the world; howl over their destruction. [Col. 1197D] For the house from which you used to come has been laid waste, because the conduct and life of those who live wickedly in this house—that is, in the present age—and persevere in that wickedness, though not yet so condemned in actuality, are already condemned before God in predestination. The prophet in some measure confirms this judgment of the elect concerning the destruction of the reprobate when he adds:

“From the land of Kittim it has been revealed to them.” Kittim is interpreted as “a freezing sea” or “a broken sea.” And, just as it has two interpretations, so it contains two mystical meanings. Insofar as it means “broken,” it aptly represents the heart and body of the elect, broken through repentance and humbled. But insofar as it is called “a freezing sea,” it fittingly denotes the world frozen in sins. The sense is: Do not doubt, wretched people, concerning your devastation and condemnation, over which the saints and elect of God howl and mourn. For it has been revealed to them from the land of Kittim. They too were once in the land of the freezing world, in which there is no warmth of fear or love of God; and from the miseries to which they themselves were subject, they cannot fail to know your miseries and the perils to which you are subject. If you remain in these, you will undoubtedly be laid waste, because you will be eternally condemned to the punishments of everlasting death, where devastation means the absence of every good and the abundance of every evil. [Col. 1198B] After this, the person of the elect, exhorting them with devout affection of heart to repentance and conversion, is again introduced.

“Be silent,” they say, “you who dwell on the island: the trade of Sidon.” You who are surrounded on every side by the waves of the sea—that is, by diabolical temptations—and battered by diverse passions of the flesh, cease from the loudly seething tumult of carnal desires; consider what threatens you. For your whole life and conduct are the trade of Sidon: the trade of the wicked hunter, the devil, who hunts you so that you may carry on his business on the island, the island of this present age—that is, so that, serving in the present life the vices and desires which are his business, you may receive from him in the future the reward of your trade: the punishment of everlasting death. Therefore, whoever you are who desire to be saved, flee the business of this useless hunting, or of this hunter. For you cannot be saved unless, when the tumult of vices has grown quiet and ceased, you depart from the island of the age and from worldly conduct.

“Crossing the sea, they filled you in many waters.” The malignant spirits, who have spread the net of their malice and wickedness over the sea of this age, have filled you with many waters—that is, with diverse desires and vices. From this flooding of waters everything in the world tends toward destruction. Nor is this surprising: there is no one who conducts God’s business; no one who, by the hand of holy preaching and the example of upright conduct, removes the rush of these waters. [Col. 1198D] For even if there is someone who bears the name of teacher, yet loves earthly things more than heavenly ones, he is deservedly without a teacher’s merit. Therefore what follows aptly applies to him:

**VERS. 3.** “The seed of the Nile, the harvest of the river, is its produce; and it became the trade of the nations.” By the river Nile, which, as Blessed Jerome writes, receives its water not from heaven but from earth, we may fittingly understand such a teacher as loves earthly things more than heavenly, seeking transient rather than enduring goods. His seed is his preaching; its fruits, which arise in the hearts of his subjects from the seed of his preaching and teaching, are rightly compared to the river’s harvest. For, in the manner of a harvest, they soon wither and quickly fail. Thus [Col. 1199A] what follows comes about: “And it became the trade of the nations.” His preaching becomes in the hearts of his hearers the trade of the nations—that is, the trade of sinners—when, by the example of his evil life, he withholds from God and leads away from the path of truth the bodies and souls which, after the manner of a faithful merchant, he ought to gain for God through his teaching. But as the devil rejoices and is glad over such persons, so he is saddened and confounded by perfect despisers of the world, as the prophet subsequently indicates when, either in his own person or that of these same elect, he adds:

**VERS. 4.** “Blush, Sidon; for the sea says—the strength of the sea, saying: ‘I have not labored in birth, nor have I borne; I have not nourished young men, nor brought virgins to maturity.’”

By Sidon here, as in the preceding passages, we understand the devil, the malignant hunter and deceiver of souls. By the sea and the strength of the sea we understand strong emulators of spiritual life. They are called both sea and strength of the sea because they were in a sense sea when, given over to secular life, they seethed with crimes; they became the strength of the sea when, having crossed and trampled underfoot the waves of the sea—that is, sins and vices—they began to live strongly and manfully for God. Such persons indeed speak to Sidon, so that he may blush, when they perform deeds at which the devil is ashamed and confounded. For when they humbly acknowledge themselves sinners, they greatly confound him who suggested their sins.

“I have not labored in birth,” they say, “nor have I borne; I have not nourished young men, nor brought virgins to maturity.” [Col. 1199C] By young men we may understand strong works of virtue; by virgins, integrity of mind. It is as though they said: I have not labored in birth by desiring good things; and, if I have at any time labored by desiring what was good, I have not brought forth in good works what that good desire suggested. And even if I have brought forth by applying myself for a time to a good work, I have not nourished the tender offspring of a work begun through the constancy of subsequent good works; rather, overcome by weariness, I quickly abandoned what I had well begun. Nor have I brought virgins to maturity, because, even if I at some time devoted the integrity and incorruption of my mind to Christ, the incorrupt author of integrity, I did not preserve it. Instead, since it was not fostered by any growth in virtues or led on to perfection, I soon recalled my mind from it. [Col. 1199D] When the person who has now become the strength of the sea begins to say these words of true repentance to God and before God, whether inwardly in heart or outwardly in body, he brings great shame and sorrow upon the malignant spirits, as is mystically shown when it is immediately added:

**VERS. 5.** “When it is heard in Egypt, they will grieve when they hear concerning Tyre.” Egypt, as we have often said, is interpreted as “darkness”; here it represents the malignant spirits. When they hear of the perfect conversion and praiseworthy conduct of the elect, they grieve when they hear concerning Tyre: that is, when they understand that the person whom they formerly possessed as a slave of their own right has withdrawn himself from their jurisdiction and dominion through the straits of this present life, to which he submitted himself for God’s sake in the spiritual life. This is their crushing, their sorrow, and their affliction. But because the elect, the more they love and know God, the more ardently desire the salvation of all people, the following is rightly still added, as though in their person:

**VERS. 6.** “Cross the seas; howl, you who dwell on the island.” As if they said: Wretched people, battered by the temptations of the age and the diverse passions of the flesh, cross the seas by leaving the world. Howl, you who dwell on the island, by humbly recognizing and repenting of your ignorance, blindness, and danger.

**VERS. 7.** “Is not this your city, which gloried from ancient days in its antiquity?” This world which you love, to which you cling as though it were your own, is an island surrounded and flooded on every side by waves of the sea—that is, by inundations of sins. From ancient days, from the time it was first created, it gloried in its antiquity, because it has wickedly rejoiced until now in the oldness of sins which it ought to weep and mourn. Therefore any soul that shares in the glory of this island, glorying in its antiquity by loving and pursuing the oldness of vices rather than the newness of virtues, can scarcely—or not at all—be saved unless, having crossed the river of sins, it wholly withdraws itself from the world. Hence it is immediately added:

“Its own feet will carry it far away for sojourning.” It is necessary that a person of this kind should make himself alien to the desires and pleasures of this age with all the affections of both the inward and outward person, and be Christ’s stranger and pilgrim on earth, if he wishes one day to become His co-heir in heaven. But because some scarcely, or not at all, accept this counsel of salvation and continually plead their own impossibility, they are in a sense admonished by the following words to look to and flee to God’s mercy, through which He has saved many:

**VERS. 8.** “Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned, whose merchants were princes, whose founders were the renowned of the earth?” As though it were said: If it seems hard and impossible to you to leave for God’s sake the joys of this present age, look to Tyre; look to the many thousands of people who have despised the broad ways of the age for God’s sake and have willingly given themselves to the straits of this present life for the breadth of the kingdom of heaven. “Who has devised this against Tyre?” Who, I ask, could have conceived or hoped that this or that person could be so cast down and humbled, whose crown or glory was an incredible and unheard-of pride? “Whose merchants were princes, whose founders renowned of the earth”: that is, whose outward senses sought only vanity and the empty glory of this present life, and whose inward senses were renowned of the earth because they loved not the glorious and incomprehensible dignity of heaven, but the joys of earthly and passing prosperity.

**VERS. 9.** “The Lord of hosts devised this, to bring down the pride of all glory and lead into dishonor all the renowned of the earth.” The Lord of hosts—the Lord, I say, of angels and human beings, whose thought is itself His action—devised this. This was the work of His mercy and compassion: to cast down into the depths of humility the pride of a person glorying wickedly, and to bring all that person’s senses—which, as we have said, were renowned of the earth, knowing and loving only earthly things—to the dishonor of good and praiseworthy shame which repentance produces. He accomplishes this: the blessed person, designated by Tyre once crowned, ashamed in himself and humbled for his sins, counts as the greatest dishonor what he had previously believed to be supreme glory. It follows:

**VERS. 10.** “Pass through your land like a river, daughter of the sea.” As though it were said: Whoever you are who, because of the weakness and instability of your sea-like—that is, sinful and slippery—life, are and are called a daughter of the sea, despise by passing through them the fleeting and perishable joys of the age; seek the stability of eternity. For all that is loved in this world is like a river, because it quickly passes and ends.

“You have no longer a girdle.” If you wish to change your life yet remain in the world, you will have no girdle, because among sins there will be no guard, no security, no ability to avoid and turn away from sins.

**VERS. 11.** “He stretched out his hand over the sea; he troubled kingdoms.” Who is this that stretches out his hand over the sea but the malignant enemy, who draws almost every class of people to destruction? He also troubled kingdoms, because he is accustomed inwardly to disturb and blind through the wickedness of his deceit those who reign in sins and vices, lest they should wish or be able to look toward the true light. But the Lord’s hand is not powerless to break this outstretched hand of the devil and turn the kingdoms troubled by him toward seeking and desiring the joys of everlasting serenity. Hence it is further added:

“The Lord commanded against Canaan, that He should crush its strong ones.” Canaan, interpreted as “movement,” signifies a certain good and praiseworthy movement occurring in a person when he begins to move himself from evil to good, from vices to virtues. It is as though He said: If you, who have hitherto stood in the place not of life but of evil death—mobile toward vices, immovable toward virtues and virtuous works—now wish to move yourself against yourself, that is, if you wish, leaving the world and worldly conduct, to pass into the soldiery of spiritual life, the Lord rich in mercy has commanded—that is, promised—to crush your strong ones, so that by the mighty hand of His divinity He may reduce to nothing the malignant spirits who hold you under the most grievous bond of sins.

**VERS. 12.** “And He said: You shall no longer continue to glory, enduring reproach, virgin daughter of Sidon.” You who are called virgin—that is, barren and fruitless—daughter of Sidon, daughter of the wicked hunter, the devil, not because you merit chastity but because of the barrenness of good works and good virtues, shall no longer continue to glory in sins. For unless you are humbled through true repentance and conversion, you will endure the reproach of everlasting damnation.

“Arise; cross over to Kittim; there too you shall have no rest.” Kittim, as we said above, is called “the freezing sea,” signifying a world frozen, without the fire of the fear and love of God. “Arise; cross over to Kittim.” As though He said: Suppose that, while remaining in the world, you begin to rise to good works, to cross over and avoid vices, and to beware sins. “There too you shall have no rest.” There will be no rest for you there from sins. For since you live amid sins, it is impossible and utterly unavoidable that, whether willing or unwilling, you should not be entangled in the snares of sins. But what remains beyond this?
