[Col. 1202B] **VERS. 13.** “Behold the land of the Chaldeans: such a people was not; Assyria founded it.” By the land of the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as “fierce,” we may fittingly understand the community of any spiritual persons. They were once fierce and untamed in sinning, but afterward they are no less fierce in the spiritual life, fiercely punishing sins in themselves. “Behold,” he says, “the land of the Chaldeans; behold before you the holy and spiritual way of life and community of those who fear God, who rage fiercely against themselves. Flee to this land; live by their example. If you are frightened by the enormity of your crimes, take comfort in them and through them; imitate their constancy and humility.” “Such a people was not”: that is, it was formerly distinguished by pride and exaltation of mind, headlong and slippery toward sins. “Assyria founded it,” because the malignant enemy, whom they set beneath their hearts as a foundation and in place of a foundation, moved them powerfully wherever he wished.

“But now, strengthened in the Lord, they led its mighty ones into captivity; they undermined its houses; they made it a ruin.” They undermined its houses because they so prepared and subjected to virtues the secrets of their hearts—where Assyria formerly dwelt as though in a familiar home of its own right, through suggestions and injections of evil wills and through the delights of fleshly pleasures—by undermining and digging out vices and vicious wills and desires through true repentance, that no place of the former habitation is open in them to the ancient enemy.

[Col. 1202D] They also led its mighty ones into captivity because they have now overthrown and extinguished the sins and sinful works of the flesh, which are the devil’s mighty ones—for through them and with them he prevails over human beings. Those which they cannot wholly extinguish while the frail substance of the flesh remains, they rule as though led into captivity, so that, even if they rise against them and make an assault, they cannot prevail over them. Hence it is fittingly further added:

“They made it a ruin.” For when the perfect person holds captive and restrains within himself those vices which he cannot utterly extinguish, from this captivity comes the ruin of sins, while the structure of virtues rises and grows on high. But because, under the first chapter of this burden, the holy prophet of the Lord mourned in howling and groaning, under the person and voice of the elect, the devastation—indeed, the condemnation—of those who, as stated, still stand in peril in the world; foreseeing also the devastation which often occurs to these elect and perfect persons themselves in spiritual life, he exhorts them in this second chapter to repentance, saying:

**VERS. 14–15.** “Howl, ships of the sea, because your strength has been laid waste. And it shall come to pass in that day: You, O Tyre, shall be forgotten for seventy years, according to the days of one king; but after seventy years Tyre shall be like the song of a harlot.”

These words of the prophet—or rather, of almighty God speaking through the prophet—to any chosen and beloved soul occur when, by His inspiration, the person begins carefully to recognize, upon considering his own devastation, his former progress and his now-imminent failure. “Howl,” He says, “ships of the sea, because your strength has been laid waste.” As if He said: You who, having crossed the river of the great sea, established as though in ships in the conduct of spiritual life, were accustomed to make for the harbor of the heavenly homeland with the greatest strength and constancy: howl now, because, with the torpor of negligence and sloth of mind creeping in and increasing, you exercise not at all your customary strength; but, as though stripped of former virtues and emptied under the oppressive weight of the flesh, you lie subject as weak and feeble persons. After God has in this manner inwardly stirred and enlightened a person, He immediately indicates in the following words how that person ought to return to lost strength:

[Col. 1203C] “And it shall come to pass in that day: You, O Tyre, shall be forgotten for seventy years, according to the days of one king.” The number seventy signifies perfect and complete repentance. He rightly says, “You, O Tyre, shall be forgotten for seventy years.” We know, indeed, that those undergoing public repentance are excluded from the entrance of the church and from communion with Holy Mother Church, and are regarded during the appointed time of penitence not merely as forgotten but almost as dead. So too, when the spiritual person represented by Tyre, as stated, seeks through the exercise of spiritual labors to recover the devastation of spiritual riches—which are virtues—he is in a sense forgotten for seventy years. In his repentance he submits himself to God with such humility that he counts himself forgotten by God and before God; withdrawing himself from everything sweet and pleasurable to the flesh, he judges himself unworthy for almighty God to remember in His mercies. Yet in this forgetfulness he is “according to the days of one king,” because the bright and illuminating guardianship and protection of the highest and best King, almighty God—understood in this passage by the day—remains over him, invisibly enlightening him within and mercifully protecting and preserving him outwardly from sin. It follows:

“After seventy years Tyre shall be like the song of a harlot.” What, I ask, are these words of the prophet—or rather, of the Lord speaking in the prophet—but a teaching by which Tyre, that is, the person to whom the whole world is narrow for love of the heavenly kingdom, is instructed in humility? “After seventy years,” He says, “Tyre shall be like the song of a harlot.” As if He said: It is not enough for you to complete the number of seventy years by perfect repentance, unless, after repentance has been accomplished, you persist in the same humility and constancy of mind and endeavor to sing and repeat, as it were, the song of a harlot. To sing the song of a harlot is continually to reflect in contrition of heart and, as it were, to sing beforehand to oneself how shamefully and how often one has many times played the harlot against Christ, one’s true Bridegroom. Yet this too is not sufficient for a person’s progress unless he answers the mournful song of the heart by continual mortification of the flesh. Therefore it is aptly added at once:

[Col. 1204B] **VERS. 16.** “Take a harp; go about the city, harlot given over to forgetfulness.” As if He said: Because, by transgressing My commandments, you have not kept the fidelity due to Me, always consider yourself a harlot given over to forgetfulness. Take a harp: mortify your flesh by crucifying it with its vices and desires. Go about the city, seeking the aid of intercession from the holy and righteous persons who are with you, who have deserved to be called and to be the city of God; take from them the example of holy conduct.

“Sing well, repeat the song, that you may be remembered.” You sang badly when, despising and forsaking Me, you rejoiced in sins. But now sing well; repeat the song. Change, as though by a reversed harp, the voice of your former singing, which sounded evil in My ears, into the voice of continual contrition and compunction, so that you may be remembered by Me: that is, so that I may gather you, once given over to forgetfulness, back to Myself in My many and great mercies. It follows:

**VERS. 17.** “And it shall be after seventy years: the Lord will visit Tyre, and will bring her back to her wages.” This visitation, by which after seventy years the Lord visits Tyre, is the inestimable abundance of His inexhaustible sweetness, by which He ineffably refreshes and gladdens the soul wounded by the bitterness of repentance. He brings her back to her wages when, amid the grace of His very sweetness, He grants her as the desired reward of her labor the forgiveness of sins. But however much a person advances by God’s grace and gift, because one cannot live without sin as long as one remains in the body of sin, it is aptly added:

“And she will again commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the earth upon the face of the earth.” By the earth we understand the human body itself; by the kingdoms of the earth, the inner senses of the person. Because of the dignity of the spirit, which ought, like a king and ruler of the earth—that is, of the outer person—to preside and rule, they are deservedly called kingdoms of the earth. The soul which, after long forgetfulness and rejection, rejoiced that it had at last been received back to the long-desired and long-awaited embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom, again commits fornication with all the kingdoms of the earth when it delights in sin in its inner senses, whether through evil thoughts, evil wills, or unlawful desires. It commits fornication upon [Col. 1205A] the face of the earth whenever it admits through the bodily senses—namely sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—anything contrary or unworthy of the love of the heavenly Bridegroom.

And it should be noted that, first indicating the fornication occurring in the spirit and then that occurring in the body, he says, “And she will again commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the earth,” and immediately adds, “upon the face of the earth.” For even if there were anyone who did not incline to sin in body or in the body’s senses, there is scarcely anyone—or perhaps no one—able to preserve the chastity and integrity of his inner person in such a way that no stain of corruption should accrue and adhere to him from diverse movements of the soul. Yet because the spiritual person often suffers unwillingly, but by compulsion, this intolerable divorce which arises between God and the soul from the fornication of heart and body already described, he hastens quickly to return through repentance and tears to the grace of his Bridegroom and Beloved, and to mitigate the offense. Thus what follows is fulfilled:

**VERS. 18.** “And her trade and her wages shall be sanctified to the Lord.” By her trade we may understand transgressions and sins by which God is offended; by her wages, the forgiveness of sins, by which almighty God graciously rewards her repentance and satisfaction. “Her trade and her wages shall be sanctified to the Lord,” because as soon as she has repented and groaned from a humble heart, both the evils which she unlawfully committed and the good works which she performed in amendment and satisfaction for those unlawful acts are sanctified to the Lord, because they are reckoned to God’s praise and honor.

“They shall not be stored up or laid aside, because her trade shall belong to those who dwell before the Lord, that they may eat to fullness and be clothed even unto old age.” What is signified by those things which, as the Lord testifies, “shall not be stored up or laid aside,” if not the excesses and sins of the elect serving God in the spiritual life? These are by no means stored up in this life. They accuse themselves, judge themselves, condemn themselves; afflicting themselves by the daily laments of repentance, submitting themselves to the discipline of a strict spiritual life and practice, they disclose their faults to God in prayer. They also humbly reveal them to their confessors in confession. And since they thus daily reveal what is hidden in them, they leave nothing for themselves to be laid aside [Col. 1205D] in the future—that is, nothing to be made public and reserved for punishment in the stern severity of the final judgment. Hence concerning such persons it is fittingly further added:

Because for those who dwell before the Lord his gain shall be, that they may eat to satiety and be clothed even unto old age. They are said to dwell before the Lord because, through the laborious exercises of the spiritual life and through holy, daily longings for the heavenly country, they stand daily, as though present, before the gaze of the divine majesty. And the merciful and compassionate Lord himself dwells with those who thus dwell before him, because with a gaze of loving mercy he watches over them: he himself considers their labors; he himself counts them. Their gain shall be that they may eat to satiety and be clothed [Col. 1206A] even unto old age, because wherever they remember that they have gathered and amassed anything by unjust gain, they in a manner eat it: lest it appear before the Lord, by bitter recollection, vigorous repentance, and punishment they make it their food, because daily they feed themselves with tears. They eat to satiety by repenting inwardly fully, perfectly, and sufficiently. They are clothed even unto old age, in order to cover and conceal those things for which they repent, by manfully persevering until the end of life in the works of righteous beauty.

After the burden of Tyre, which we have now passed over in expounding according to our measure, in fitting order is set down the burden of the beasts of the south, which is tenth in number. For spiritual persons, perfect despisers of this world, who truly dwell before the Lord, whose gain is, as we have said, that they may eat to satiety and be clothed unto old age—these are truly the beasts of the south, the beasts of the Holy Spirit, who is signified by the south wind. For he himself, by the strong impulse of his inspiration, has driven them from the broad and spacious field of the world into Tyre—that is, into the narrow path of spiritual life—not that they may rest there, but that under diverse burdens, amid innumerable labors and temptations, they may learn to be tamed from their former fierceness. The prophet accordingly proceeds to enumerate these temptations in mystical words, saying:

## CHAPTER X. The burden of the beasts of the South; that is, of those who embrace the narrow way to heaven.

[Col. 1206C] **Isaiah 30, verses 6–7.** The burden of the beasts of the south. In a land of tribulation and distress are the lioness and lion, the viper and flying basilisk, carrying their riches upon the shoulders of beasts and their treasures upon the hump of camels, to a people that cannot profit them. For Egypt shall help vainly and to no purpose; therefore I cried concerning this: “It is pride only; be still.”

By the land of tribulation and distress may fittingly be understood the land and place of every spiritual and perfect manner of life, inhabited by those beasts of the south—namely, the beasts of the Holy Spirit, subjected beneath the yoke of obedience—which, through the tribulations and straits of this present life, make their way toward the most spacious pastures of eternal delight. By the lioness, lion, viper, and flying basilisk we may understand four stages in the growth of sins. The first is delight in sin, signified by the lioness. The second is consent to sin, which is rightly compared to the lion because of the strength by which it sometimes overthrows even the robust. The third is the performance of sin, which, like the sudden bite of a viper, kills the soul. The fourth is the scandal caused by sin, which is aptly likened to the flying basilisk: the more swiftly it ranges abroad, the more ruinously it causes scandal and corrupts the souls of many.

These four beasts in the land of tribulation and distress are, as it were, carrying their riches upon the shoulders of beasts and their treasures upon the hump of camels. By the hump of camels we may understand the heart [Col. 1207A] of sinners, swollen in a crooked manner with an abundance of vices. When, having taken upon themselves the yoke of obedience in order to receive and bear the burdens of spiritual discipline in the land of tribulation and distress, they willingly begin to humble themselves, they may rightly be called beasts of the south—beasts, as we have said, of the Holy Spirit—crying to the Lord with the prophet and saying: “I have become like a beast before thee, and I am always with thee” (Psalm 72:22).

The lioness and lion, the viper and flying basilisk, in a manner carry their riches—that is, their diverse sins and vices—upon the shoulders of these beasts, when these perfect persons daily set before and oppose to their own eyes with anxious attention whatever they have committed through the delight, consent, or act of sin, or wherever they have become a scandal to their neighbors. Through this hard [Col. 1207B] and difficult burden of daily labor they humble and afflict themselves. They are also said to carry their treasures upon the hump of camels when these same elect persons carefully heap together in their hearts, for recollection, the treasures of evil thoughts, wicked wills, and desires collected and accumulated from those same four stages of sin—not that they may delight in them, but that they may be punished for them by fitting tears of repentance.

Nor should it be overlooked that, after saying, “carrying their riches upon the shoulders of beasts and their treasures upon the hump of camels,” he added: “to a people that cannot profit them.” These words plainly make it understood that these vices, which we have denoted under the names of lioness, lion, viper, and flying basilisk, can indeed be restrained so that they do not prevail over a person according to their accustomed manner; but they cannot be extinguished so completely that they do not rise again and again against the person. For they always strive to turn the beast of the Holy Spirit away from the way of truth and righteousness and, with sudden and unforeseen violence, to divert it toward a people that cannot profit them—that is, toward the people of wicked spirits. But this people cannot profit them while a person, governed and guarded by the Holy Spirit, walks in the path once begun, despising and rejecting whatever is set against him by diabolical contrivance. Hence it continues:

“For Egypt shall help vainly and to no purpose.” For, when the grace of the Holy Spirit breathes upon and assists him, the crafty and dark suggestion of wicked spirits—[Col. 1207D] who are signified by Egypt, whose name is interpreted “darkness”—is rejected by him as vain and useless. Hence it is fittingly said shortly afterward, in the person of that same man: “Therefore I cried concerning this: ‘It is pride only; be still.’” As though he said: Whatever this people puts forward tends wholly toward wickedness. “Therefore I cried concerning this: ‘It is pride only; be still.’” Be still from consenting inwardly, through delight and consent, to their turbulent assaults. Be still from evil works, abstaining from deeds that bring both peril of death upon you and scandal to your neighbors. But because this rest is possessed only through continual mortification of the flesh, this is fittingly shown in what follows, when it is immediately added:

[Col. 1208A] **Verse 8.** Now go in; write it for him upon boxwood, and carefully inscribe it in a book. By the boxwood we may understand flesh chastened through repentance; by the book, a person’s memory or conscience. It is as though the merciful and compassionate Lord says inwardly to a person: “Having entered into yourself, always recognize yourself as a sinner. Write it upon boxwood: do not cease to chasten your flesh with steadfast and perfect repentance; and whatever it is by which you have offended the eyes of my majesty, carefully inscribe that in the book; continually recall it with humble repentance in your heart and conscience.”

“And it shall be, on that last day, as a testimony for ever.” On the last day, when you have passed from darkness to light and from death to life, this temporal repentance shall be for you a testimony for ever against the threatening assault [Col. 1208B] of your enemies.

**Verses 9–11.** For it is a people provoking to anger, and lying children, children unwilling to hear the law of God; who say to those who see: “Do not see”; and to those who behold: “Do not behold for us the things that are right. Speak to us pleasing things; behold errors for us. Take away the way from before me; turn aside the path from before me; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face.”

In these few words the eternal wisdom of God briefly comprehends and distinguishes all the incitements of wicked spirits by which they raise themselves against God’s elect; these indeed need no exposition. For we know them better within ourselves than we can express them in speech or writing.

They are a provoking people because they always provoke men to stir up and arouse against themselves God’s anger and indignation by acting unjustly against God. They are lying children because they love falsehood. They are children unwilling to hear the law of God because they themselves abhor it and try to overthrow those who are willing to hear and keep it. They say to those who see, “Do not see”; and to those who behold, “Do not behold for us the things that are right,” because by the manifold wickedness of their deceit they habitually blind people, lest they see what is right, and lest they be able to carry out in right works what they have rightly seen and understood. Whomever they can withdraw from the ways of truth by dulling the edge of the mind, upon them they persistently press, as it were with a commanding voice, saying: “Speak to us pleasing things; behold errors for us. Take away [Col. 1208D] the way from before me; turn aside the path from before me; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face.” These words of wicked spirits certainly mean and suggest nothing other than how, by the many forms of their instigation, they may make men subject and enslaved to their error.

But because the merciful and compassionate Creator and Instructor of humankind has shown and uncovered, as was said above, these most subtle and inescapable devices of demons, in order to make his elect more watchful and circumspect against their deceit and malice, now also, in order to suggest the ineffable sweetness of his compassion, whereby he daily observes and weighs their conflict, he rises up as though with a mighty denunciation against these same demons and adds:

[Col. 1209A] **Verses 12–13.** Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel: “Because you have rejected this word, and have hoped in calumny and tumult, and have relied upon it, therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a falling breach, sought out in a high wall.”

As though he said: “O wicked spirits, fraudulent deceivers of souls, who have rejected the word of truth from the beginning, and have hoped in calumny and tumult, and have relied upon it: this iniquity, through which you have captured the souls of those whom I save, shall be to you like a falling breach, sought out in a high wall. For I, strong and mighty, merciful and gracious, shall powerfully break in; I shall, as a wall is broken down, shatter and destroy by the hand of my power every fortification—indeed, every security—by which you hoped to dwell in them and possess them; because suddenly, when it is not expected, its destruction shall come.”

**Verse 14.** “And it shall be crushed as the potter’s vessel is crushed by a very violent [or: prevailing] breaking.” By the name “potter,” the one speaking—our Creator and Redeemer—wishes himself to be understood. The vessel of this potter is, in a manner, every creature. For he is our potter; we are his clay-work. He is our maker; we are his handiwork. The potter’s vessel is crushed, as it were, by a very violent breaking when that clayey mass—that is, the human being—which has hardened under the harmful heat of vices, is moistened and softened by the dew of the Holy Spirit and dissolved to its depths in the laments of contrition [Col. 1209C] and repentance. This is that prevailing breaking by which our excellent potter mercifully crushes the vessel—that is, the despairing sinner—by which he casts down and scatters, with the strong hand of his mercy, the accumulated engine of sins, broken apart on every side. Thus comes about what follows:

[Col. 1210A] “And among its fragments there shall not be found a potsherd with which a little fire may be carried from the blaze, or a little water drawn from the pit.” For when the muddy moisture of carnal desire—which may be understood by the water—has been drained from the pit of the heart, the flame of harmful delight is also lulled and extinguished in the flesh, which is understood by the potsherd, through the intervening and cooling Holy Spirit; but only in such a way that the fire of repentance, burning strongly within the heart, does not allow the little spark of fleshly potsherd—that is, of perverse delight—to approach.

But as for his addition:

**Verse 15.** “For thus says the Lord of hosts”: by this he in some measure confirms his preceding words, so that no one may despair of God’s mercy because of the enormity of his crimes, if he finally takes care, having abandoned sin, to return to him who is truly merciful. Hence he fittingly adds:

“If you return and rest, you shall be saved.” As though he plainly said: “If, leaving your vices, you return to me, your God and Savior, and, putting aside the tumultuous cares of carnal desires and pleasures, are willing to rest in me and upon me, who am true rest, I shall restore you to eternal salvation: saving and cleansing you from past crimes, and mercifully strengthening you by the power of my might against the violent assault of the wicked spirits that persecute you.”

“In silence and in hope shall be your strength.” If, when vices creep in and make a clamour, you do not answer them by consenting thoughts inwardly or by perverse actions [Col. 1210C] outwardly; and if, moreover, with firm hope and most whole faith you adhere perfectly to me alone—for I stand by as an unfailing helper to those who hope in me and trust in my mercy—then the most powerful devices of the most wicked enemy shall grow weak and perish before you.

[Col. 1209]

## LETTER OF THE VENERABLE GODEFRID, ABBOT OF ADMONT, TO O., FORMERLY HIS MONK

That he should send him books of Josephus and other authors to be copied. (Year 1153.)

(R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, part III, col. 364, in the *Codex diplomatico-historico-epistolaris*, from a Tegernsee manuscript.)

[Col. 1209D] G., by the grace of God what he is, to his beloved son in Christ O.: imitate Noah’s dove, which, when sent forth, brought back to the ark a branch of green olive.

Those who have studied and know the natures of wild beasts write and say that, by a certain natural sweetness, they frequently return to the places from which they first received the beginning of life. Thus you also, brother, so that your shoots may be a paradise of pomegranates, ought frequently to return, if not in body, at least in mind, to the bosom of your mother, the Church of Admont, from whose fountain you are known to have received whatever discipline and learning are in you by God’s grace. I should therefore wish, most beloved one, that from that renowned book-chest of your church you would send us something not available among us, either to be copied or copied by yourself, so that our want might be supplied from your abundance and, through it, the memory of your affection for us might grow warm again.

If Josephus’s work, *The Destruction of Jerusalem*, and the celebrated *Triumph of Vespasian and Titus at Rome* are among you, I ask that you inquire carefully and truthfully, and do not delay, in true charity, to send it to us through someone to be copied. For it is a long time since I truly heard that this same work was among you, but I have never been able to see it. Labor, therefore, so that what has not been done by others may be done by you, so that thanksgiving may be rendered to you by your brethren and recompense by God. Farewell. Greet very warmly on our behalf the lord abbot, your brother; and take care, as a good son, to obey and serve him devoutly.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1142: HARIULF, ABBOT OF ALDENBURG

[Col. 1211]

## HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 191.)

Hariulf, formerly a monk of Saint-Riquier at Centula, was abbot of Saint Peter’s at Aldenburg, not far from Bruges in Flanders, of the Benedictine Order, from 1104 to 1142. He was the author of a chronicle of the monastery of Centula in four books, extending from the middle of the sixth century to the year 1088. It was edited by D’Achery in the *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, p. 419 (new edition, vol. II, pp. 291–356), where it is presented much more fully and accurately through the services of Ursin Durant, from the Centula manuscript. Mabillon had published the verses with which the work closes in vol. I of the *Analecta*, p. 431 (new edition, p. 378). In Book III, p. 310, there is a notable catalogue of 256 manuscript volumes preserved among the cloister’s treasures of this monastery.

As in Book I he narrates the Life of Saint Riquier the abbot, so in Book II he treats, among other matters, the Life of Saint Angilbert, the seventh abbot. Mabillon also cites this from the Chronicle in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century IV, p. 91; and he discusses Riquier’s miracles in century V, p. 585; concerning these see Book III, chapter 18, and Book IV, chapter 9. Hariulf discusses the confessor Madelgisil in Book III, chapter 29, but he wrote his Life in a separate book, which he dedicated to Gervin, bishop of the see of Amiens. Papebroch reprinted this Life from Mabillon’s edition, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century IV, part II, p. 537, with notes added in vol. VII for May, 30 May, pp. 265–269.

Hariulf treats the Life of Abbot Gervin in Book IV, chapter 13 and following; there, likewise, in chapter 32, one should note the catalogue of thirty-six manuscript volumes which Gervin bestowed on the monastery. Upon the death of this Gervin in 1071, Gervin, second abbot of that name, succeeded him; concerning him see Book IV, chapter 34 and following, where his epitaph also occurs in chapter 36; he died in 1074. Hariulf also wrote the Life of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, who died in 1087, addressed to Lambert, bishop of Tournai; it is manuscript in the Cistercian monastery of Ourscamp in France, diocese of Noyon. Lisiard, likewise bishop of Soissons from 1108, added an appendix on Saint Arnulf’s miracles. Thereupon Surius published the Life, interpolated in a bad fashion and under the false name of Lisiard, on 14 August, omitting its threefold preface. Oudinus, vol. II, p. 926, testifies that, after Vossius, he saw it in the manuscript of Ourscamp and another manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Mabillon published it complete and uncorrupted in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century VI, part II, p. 522.

In Sanderus’s *Catalogue of Belgian Manuscripts*, p. 235, one may find mention of Hariulf, abbot of Altenburg, on the miracles of Saint Peter the Apostle at Aldenbrock. I do not doubt that he is not different from our author, and that Cange has wrongly divided one Hariulf into three.

[Col. 1211]

# CHRONICLE OF CENTULA, BY HARIULF

(D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, De La Barre edition, vol. II, p. 291.)

## NOTICE

Since the Chronicle of Centula, in its earlier edition, had been made public disfigured by various errors and mutilated not merely through the loss of several short sections but even of chapters, we now publish it complete, through the kindness of the Reverend Father and Lord [Col. 1213] Ursin Durant, who compared the manuscript of the abbey of Centula with the printed editions with the greatest care and restored all the chapters that were missing.

“All,” I say; for Acherius seems to me to have erred in suspecting that chapter 14 was missing from Book I, and therefore calling the chapter to which we have assigned the number 14 “the fifteenth.” For in the table of chapters prefixed to this book twenty-six are counted, but the copyist omitted to state what was contained in the fourteenth. Thus it is evident that the same thing happened here as in Book II, where seventeen chapters are numbered in the table although only seven are found in the book itself, because someone made five chapters out of the second chapter: namely, “On the eminence of Lord Angilbert,” chapters 3 and 4; “Bertha, the king’s daughter, joined to him in marriage,” chapter 5; “That he left the world and became a monk,” chapter 6; and they also divided the sixth chapter into several chapters, to which they were not even able to prefix titles.

Moreover, in the manuscript of Centula, besides these four books and the items published in the appendix to volume V of the *Annals of the Benedictines*, the same Lord Ursin Durant found the Life of Saint Madelgisil written by Hariulf; the Life of Saint Angilbert the abbot; and a little book of miracles of the same saint, by the same author, dedicated to Radulf, archbishop of Rheims, in 1110.

In volume II of the *History of France by Ancient Writers*, edited by André Duchesne, there appears an engraved representation of the churches constructed by Angilbert at Centula in the year 809.

## HARIULF’S PREFACE TO HIS DESCRIPTION OF THE DEEDS OF THE CHURCH OF CENTULA

[Col. 1213]

[Col. 1213A] After humankind, cast down from the blessedness of paradise by the sin of the first man, began to be divinely admonished, by the display of divine compassion, to amend itself and to seek by upright living the homeland from which it had fallen, we believe that nothing more useful can be found in human pursuits—provided only that love of God and neighbor and the performance of divine commandments are preserved—than that righteous and faithful persons have transmitted to the knowledge of posterity in writing what they rightly did or said.

For in this way a kind of image, and as it were a presence, of good deeds is set before the minds of rational persons, by which they may form themselves: when at one time it is told how a righteous person lived and with what reward he was endowed, and at another how an impious person, despising the good, was burdened with so many evils, the human mind is beneficially drawn by the righteous person’s reward to do good, and terrified by the impious person’s ruin lest it do evil. It is surely for this reason that we think not only the legal and prophetic Scripture, but also the Gospel Scripture, was composed: so that man, glorious to God—concerning whose creation God the Creator, as though taking counsel, said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness”—man, I say, of such excellence and such worth, may plainly see what he should eagerly reject and what above all he should embrace; and, when he has observed how greatly God is concerned for him . . . , may at last learn himself to be concerned for himself.

Therefore all the signs or admonitions of divine goodness by which we are instructed are found inserted in the pages of ancient Scriptures. Strengthened by this undertaking, I, Hariulf, monk of Saint Riquier, and likewise stirred by the encouragement of honorable brethren, have resolved to bring together into one whole what I had gathered in scattered fashion concerning the antiquity and nobility of the Church of Centula; and, lest these scattered things perish utterly, to preserve them more earnestly for the knowledge of posterity, protected by the unity of one body. We now offer our tongue to the highest Majesty, that he who granted the misshapen she-ass words to utter [Col. 1214A] may deem worthy also to pour into me the spirit of his grace, whereby I may be able to bring my purpose to fulfillment.

The preface ends.

O you, whoever you are, able to ponder spiritual things,

behold, I set before you those whom Christ’s [Note: [Col. 1213C] “Christ’s.” We have emended thus, following the Centula manuscript; the earlier edition read “to you.”] grace bestowed as a gift;

to whom it granted life and enriched with virtues,

whom Centula counts as fathers, whom the assembly of heaven counts as brothers,

whom, in increasing its holy companies, it counts as its companions.

They rejoice eternally who rightly applaud them.

The illustrious first and prince of these men

you are known plainly enough to be, Riquier:

for, made glorious by God, through whom the world became bitter to you,

you rightly smile upon the heavenly choirs.

Hence also the written company of the elder saints

illuminates minds that do not walk by devious paths.

### Names of the same abbots

[Col. 1214B] 1. Saint Riquier, abbot and first founder. 2. Ociolald, abbot. 3. Coschin, abbot. 4. Saint Guitmar, abbot. 5. Aldric, abbot. 6. Symphorian, abbot. 7. Saint Angilbert, abbot and rebuilder. 8. Nithard, abbot and count. 9. Heric, abbot. 10. Helizachar, abbot. 11. Ribbodo, abbot. 12. Louis, abbot. 13. Hruodulf, abbot and count. 14. Helgaud, abbot and count. [Col. 1214C] 15. Guelfo, abbot. 16. Carloman, abbot. 17. Hertbert, abbot. 18. Hedenold, abbot. 19. Girbert, cleric and abbot. 20. Fulcheric, abbot. 21. Ingelard, abbot. [Col. 1215A] 22. Angelrann, abbot. 23. Gervin, abbot. 24. Gervin, abbot.

Those which follow were written in another hand in the manuscript codex.

25. Anscher, abbot. 26. John, abbot. 27. Gelduin, abbot. [Col. 1216A] 28. Peter, abbot. 29. Guifred, abbot. 30. Richer, abbot. 31. Lawrence, abbot. 32. Ursus, abbot. 33. Richer, abbot.

O how many tombs of holy disciples

the spacious hall covers, under its fatherly prince Riquier.

# IN THE NAME OF THE HOLY AND INDIVISIBLE TRINITY BEGINS THE TEXT OF THE DEEDS OF THE CHURCH OF CENTULA. BOOK I.

[Col. 1215]

## CHAPTER I. On the deeds of the Franks.

With God as author, as I am about to describe the deeds of the Church of Centula, I judge it most fitting—because this same church has often been enriched by the benefactions of the kings of the Franks—to set forth here something concerning their deeds. For it is indeed just that I should commemorate the advancement of that kingdom by which nothing was taken away from Mother Church but much was bestowed upon her.

Therefore, since, as we are taught by ancient histories, the citizens of Troy, when the Greeks were attacking, abandoned their native place, and some went into Italy while others began to inhabit regions adjacent to Pannonia; and since there a portion of the same people, namely twelve thousand, increased into a mighty population, they retained their native fierceness and [Col. 1215C] would not allow themselves to be designated by a name shared indiscriminately with other nations. Instead, appointing a head from among themselves, they founded a city, which they called Sicambria; and from it they themselves were named Sicambrians. For that people always had—indeed, still has—such power that, wherever it comes, it presents more the appearance of rulers than the misery of captives.

But when almighty God, whose will is power, foreknew that this people would one day receive most devoutly the knowledge of his divinity, he allowed it to be exalted in the name and honor of a kingdom. They are said first to have had as king Merovech, and because of his mighty deeds and marvelous triumphs, they were called Merovingians, abandoning the name Sicambrians. Likewise, by the Attic tongue, they were called Franks—that is, “fierce”—by the Romans, whose yoke they had cast off from their necks.

When Merovech had passed away, he left as successor his son Childeric, who by Basina, queen of the Thuringians, begot Clovis. This king Clovis, succeeding his father, possessed the height of royal power as a most fierce warrior, sparing no one. Through the preceding abundant goodness of God, he received the ordinances of the divine law from the blessed Remigius, archbishop of Rheims; and, baptized by that bishop, he was beneficially taught to adore what he had burned and to burn what he had adored. Since the king devoutly heard these things and observed them still more devoutly, thereafter such favor of divine power followed him that he who had formerly been victorious on several occasions was then made most victorious, and magnificently enlarged the borders of the kingdom he had received. For divine mercy was not content merely to deliver unbelievers to his sword, but was pleased also to exercise the miracles of its majesty against his enemies.

Finally, when the king, having defeated Alaric, king of the Goths, near the city of Poitiers, had resolved on his return journey to take those cities that remained opposed to him, the walls of the city of Angoulême, which he intended to besiege, collapsed divinely before his eyes. But although, by God’s gift, he was held superior to all enemies, after reigning thirty years he died at the royal city of Paris and was buried there. When, as is believed, he had been joined to the saints above, his eldest son, Chlothar, after the deaths of his brothers, ruled the kingdom most vigorously for nearly fifty-one years.

## CHAPTER II. On the time when Saint Riquier was born, and on the kings.

In the time of this king, our blessed and God-chosen shepherd Riquier, born of most noble parents in the illustrious district of Ponthieu, poured forth the joyful blessings of his birth upon a world lacking the knowledge of salvation. When Chlothar, king of the Franks, died, his four sons divided his kingdom in equal shares. The first, Charibert, established his seat at Paris; the second, Guntram, at Orléans; the third, Chilperic, at Soissons; and the fourth, Sigebert, at Metz, also called Mediomatricum.

The youngest of these brothers, Sigebert, married Brunhild, brought from Spain, and she bore him a son, Childebert. While these men reigned, several ministers of the divine word, natives of the island of Ireland, came to visit the soil of France. Two of them, as we shall narrate later, were initiators of the blessed Riquier, then already a young man, into the Lord’s service [Note: [Col. 1217D] “Service.” Thus the Centula manuscript; the earlier edition reads “salvation.”]. But while still a boy, Childebert assumed the government of the kingdom with his mother, after his father was killed through the fortune of war. For Sigebert himself, at the estate of Vitry, situated in the suburb of the city of Arras, was treacherously killed by his brother Chilperic, who was then at the town of Tournai and whom Sigebert had been pursuing unto destruction.

After Childebert’s death—he is said to have been killed within his adolescent years, together with his own wife, by poison—they reigned: his two sons, Theuderic and Theudebert, assisted by their grandmother Brunhild. Childebert reigned twenty-two years. Guntram, Childebert’s paternal uncle and king of Orléans, on approaching the end of his life, left to Brunhild the kingdom which he held; it afterward fell to Theudebert’s share. Thus Theuderic received the kingdom of Burgundy, and Theudebert that of Austrasia. Chilperic, too, who had killed Sigebert, begot a son named Chlothar, a most shrewd and wise man, who retained the portion of the kingdom held by his father.

While Chlothar lived in Neustria, a quarrel arose between Theuderic and Theudebert. As they disputed concerning the boundary of the kingdom, each sent envoys to Chlothar, and each sought his help against the other. He refused this, being forbidden by the most holy man Columbanus, who had been driven from the monastery of Luxeuil through the wickedness of Brunhild and Theuderic, and who divinely foretold to Chlothar himself that, within three years, the whole kingdom would come under his rule. Theuderic therefore challenged his brother Theudebert to war and fought cruelly with him near the city of Toul, putting him to flight from the battle.

## CHAPTER III. How, after the destruction of the impious kings, Chlothar obtained all France.

While these men were thus fighting one another, the blessed confessor of the Lord, Riquier, now having attained mature age, was devoted to divine works. His chief concern was to snatch the vessels of the devil—that is, the souls of sinners—and assign them to his heavenly Lord. How devoutly and how earnestly he accomplished this will shortly be shown, not in our own words but in those of Lord Albinus.

Let us return to the history of the kings. Theudebert, grieved that his brother had driven him from battle, gathered the strength of an army and came against Theuderic, who thirsted for his brother’s blood, to fight at the fortress of Tolbiac. But, betrayed by his own men, he was captured and sent to Theuderic’s grandmother Brunhild. Because she favored Theuderic more, Brunhild, in fury, ordered Theudebert to be made a cleric and afterward had him impiously killed. Theuderic, greatly exalted by this unhappy victory, returned to Metz and there, struck by God, perished amid a burning fever.

[Col. 1218A] Brunhild then installed Sigebert, Theuderic’s son, in the kingdom. But Chlothar, remembering the prophecy of blessed Columbanus, sought with a strong hand to recover the boundaries of the kingdom which ought to belong to his rule. Sigebert advanced against him with hostile troops, was captured, and killed; his five brothers were captured together with their great-grandmother Brunhild. The boys were killed separately. She, however, like a second Jezebel, was first set upon a camel and displayed as she was led around before the whole army; then, tied to the tails of untamed horses, she was miserably deprived of life, as was fitting.

When these things had taken place, Chlothar, with no one opposing him, alone obtained sovereignty over the three kingdoms. Having attained the dignity established by his forebears, and having accomplished many things with vigor, he left posterity especially this memorable example of his power: when the Saxons rebelled against him, he subdued them so completely by arms that he killed every male inhabitant of that land who exceeded the length of the sword which he happened then to be wearing, so that remembrance of that life-giving—or death-dealing—sword might cut off in the younger generation any venture of rebellious pride.

By Queen Bertrude he had a son named Dagobert, worthy to succeed his father in ability and character. While still a child, Dagobert was entrusted by his father to the venerable Arnulf, afterward bishop of Metz, that he might rear him according to his wisdom, show him the path of Christian religion, and be his guardian and tutor. Chlothar, therefore, the fourth in rightful succession from Clovis, while still living and unharmed handed over to his son Dagobert the kingdom of Austrasia [Note: [Col. 1218D] “Of Austrasia.” Thus the Centula manuscript, in accord with history; the earlier reading, “his kingdom,” is wrong.]. After Chlothar’s death, Dagobert shrewdly took possession of his entire father’s kingdom and governed it peacefully, in some measure representing another Solomon.

## CHAPTER IV. The words of Lord Albinus concerning the life of Saint Riquier.

Therefore, in the times of Dagobert, the most glorious king of the Franks, who shone forth both eminent in secular power and ennobled by Christian religion—for he raised his nobles to dignities and honored the servants of God with offices—very many monasteries began to be built by holy fathers, and many religious men were found who had left secular dress. Among them, a certain Riquier, born in the village of Centula in the province of Ponthieu, shone forth like the morning star rising among shadows. He was born not so much of parents noble according to the world as distinguished by honorable morals and most devoted in every virtue, so that even in secular life he bore certain signs of future holiness.

## CHAPTER V. Explanation concerning the same.

What we noted in the preface we now likewise point out: no one should take it amiss if we attempt, for clearer understanding, to unravel these words of Lord Albinus concerning the life of the most holy confessor, expressed rhetorically and intricately. For behold, he seems to have said [Col. 1219A] that the saint was born in the time of Dagobert; whereas it plainly could not have happened that, during the reign of a single king who ruled for so short a time, a man should be born, grow up, be educated, and reach either the summit of perfect holiness or the old age of extreme senility.

[Note: [Col. 1219] “Holiness.” Here too we follow the Centula manuscript; for the reading *old age* printed by Acherius is not satisfactory.]

“What then,” you ask, “are you contradicting the author of his Life?” I do not contradict him, nor do I maintain anything different; rather, I wish to make clear what that most eloquent man expressed in few and closely linked words. Listen, then. He says that, in Dagobert’s time, many monasteries began to be built and many religious men were found who had come from secular life. Then he adds: “Among these, a certain Richarius.” Observe that he does not say that they were born in Dagobert’s time, but that religious men were found—men whom one must certainly understand to have been born long before and then to have been of advanced age [Col. 1219B].

It is as though you said: “Look, worthy man, you have said that many religious men were found, and I thank God that I have been granted one of them as a patron. But when you begin to proclaim the good of his holiness, I should like you also to state the place where he was born.” Immediately the excellent man, complying with your counsel and returning to what preceded, inserted rhetorically and with excessive brevity: “Born in the village of Centula in the district of Ponthieu.” And then, as though you were still asking whether his birth itself came from a humbler stock of parents, he thunders in indignant emphasis against this absurd question, saying: “He shone forth like the morning star rising amid shadows.”

Then, indeed, as though you were still pressing the point—lest perhaps that most splendid birth and the saint’s distinguished lineage had harmed his virtues, so that one who might have presumed so much from worldly rank had, as it were, humbled himself less—the modest teacher, drawing you away from this thought, wholesomely adds: “Born not so much of parents noble according to the world as honorable in character and most devoted in every excellence”; as though saying: His outstanding nobility was so vigorous that, just as the morning star is amid shadows, so he too was regarded among his countrymen by the splendor of his lineage. Yet, lest you suppose that, born to such lofty blood, he took up the arms of heavenly warfare with greater difficulty, know that he despised the pride of ancestry and obeyed the divine commands so humbly and submissively that the greatness of religious devotion overcame the greatness of nobility; and, with sweetness preserved in all things, integrity claimed the whole man and arrogance possessed nothing [Col. 1219C].

These matters being so, let us recount something concerning the times of his life. For it seems incongruous that he should be thought to have been born in Dagobert’s time, when the account of his deeds, after describing how he was converted by the preaching of God’s servants, how he conducted himself after conversion, how zealously he proclaimed God’s word after his most austere way of life, how, visiting his holy co-mother Richtrudis, he blessed her son—the holy Maurontus—and finally overcame the enemy who tempted him, clearly teaches that King Dagobert himself, stirred by the saint’s renown, visited this man of God [Col. 1220A] and requested the favor of his blessing or prayer.

Indeed, the blessed Maurontus, just mentioned, served at the court of that same king and, as a nobleman, was the bearer of the royal *bulla* or seal [was]; this was the one whom Christ’s priest Richarius had long before regenerated in baptism while still an infant. Therefore this sequence of events must wholly be maintained: Chaydocus converted this young man by holy preaching, but King Dagobert visited the priest of God when he was already almost decrepit with age. The evident logic of the deeds themselves shows that all this is so, provided that the diligence of readers examines it with discerning understanding. We have set these points forth in advance so that, once the chronology has been established, we may proceed more confidently with the rest [Col. 1220B]. Yet may brotherly charity kindly pardon us for presuming to speak after the eloquent utterances of the venerable Albinus.

Accordingly, this region which produced the birth of the blessed patron, washed around on every side by converging waters, planted with woods, extremely suitable for the pasture of flocks, exceedingly fertile in wheat and other seeds, prosperous through the traffic of merchandise and revenues, very healthful in the moderation of its climate, and quite suited to every bodily convenience and enjoyment—though it lacks cities and fortified strongholds except for camps—possesses wealthy towns comparable to cities. Moreover, it is exceedingly warlike and troublesome, famous for men distinguished in military service.

The blessed Richarius, a native of this land, possessed the noble character of a splendid lineage; even then [Col. 1220C], bearing signs of future holiness, he showed in his secular purpose what the later accomplishment of holy works made manifest.

## CHAPTER VI. On the arrival and preaching of the holy Irishmen

At the time when the most distinguished youth of the blessed Richarius, not yet stripped of secular dress, was already, by Christ’s will, to be formed by divine commands—at the time, namely, when King Sigibert, together with Queen Brunhild, having established the throne of his kingdom at the city of Metz, governed eastern Francia—it happened that two priests, flourishing in holiness and resplendent with the merits of virtues, arrived in the regions of Ponthieu from Ireland. The first was named Chaydocus. The second, because his name seemed unsuitable in the pronunciation of a barbarian tongue, was changed by earlier writers and is called and written Adrianus.

At the very time when these men left their own country and followed Christ, Ireland is known to have produced companies of many saints. Among them also flourished the blessed Columbanus, a man of the Scottish people, whose praiseworthy way of life and exceptional virtue spread over all regions of Gaul. It is reported that they too crossed the seas in haste with him. We relate that they turned aside to our parts. Thus the chronological argument noted a little above is especially confirmed, because, since it is well known to all that blessed Columbanus came into Francia in the time of King Sigibert [Col. 1221A] and his consort Brunhild, it must be believed that the most blessed Richarius was born in the time of the earlier King Clothar; the holy men found him already a young man in Sigibert’s days. Yet I call him “young” in such a way that the freedom of his spirit and the vigor of his capacity, flourishing in him, admitted nothing youthful. [But let us come to the history.]

The holy priests of the Lord therefore began to preach the word of God in the village of Centula, fighting as excellent soldiers in the wars of Christ our Lord. But the rustic people, unaccustomed to hear such things and unable to endure being urged to entertain new thoughts in minds corrupted by the devil’s wickedness, were inflamed with zeal and, moved by the onset of anger and fury, resolved to drive them contemptuously from those dwellings [Col. 1221B]. They did not perceive that the Lord was sending them rays of the true sun from the direction of Ocean, perhaps because they were not yet worthy to be saved.

When Richarius, still a layman but of good hope, learned this, he set himself against the rebellious crowd on behalf of God’s servants. Forcibly snatching the nobleman from their blows, as was proper, he brought him into his house with acts of service. From this a discerning reader may clearly understand that, after the king’s authority, no one in those parts was then more powerful, since he possessed such influence for rescuing God’s servants. Treating them humanely, he begged them to recline; he set a table, refreshed them, and was himself refreshed. For amid the dishes of bodily feasting these devout spiritual heroes did not cease to provide spiritual food in return.

Without delay Richarius—on whose account the heavenly Lord had truly sent His ministers there to make a gain—was pierced with compunction and dissolved into tears. And, as Scripture says that the righteous man is at the beginning his own accuser, he confessed that he had gone astray through the impulsiveness of youth. The seed of God’s word had not fallen, I say, upon stony ground, where it would wither, nor beside the path, where it would be trampled or eaten by birds; rather, it fell into excellent soil, inwardly and invisibly cultivated by the true husbandman himself. As will appear in what follows, this soil, made fruitful with a hundredfold crop, afterward enriched innumerable persons by its abundant fertility [Col. 1221C].

From that time he assumed the religious habit and eagerly strove day by day to ascend from virtue to virtue. The aforementioned men of God, moreover, after completing the course of this present life and attaining the prize of immortality, gladdened the heavenly dwellings by their entrance. They ennobled with their bodies the church of Centula, founded by their own care, and sustained it by their prayers when it was already nearly ruined.

[Note: [Col. 1221] “Founded by their own care.” A foolish reading represented by the Centula manuscript; for the earlier edition has a lacuna here. Read: “founded by their care.”]

Nevertheless, although we have now described their passing, the reader should know that they lived at Centula in divine works until they grew old.

## CHAPTER VII. On the austerity of life of the most holy Richarius

Setting aside digressions, since the narrative requires the course of the composition, let the page now tell how Saint Richarius thereafter lived. He who is touched by the divine Spirit and suddenly transformed in all things denies himself as he had been before and suddenly becomes what he was not. I shall speak of wonderful things, which a carnal man could scarcely endure unless God truly dwelt in him. For he inflicted such austerity upon himself and bound himself by such harsh discipline that he utterly despised whatever things are customarily pleasant for human bodily nourishment.

From the beginning of his conversion to the end of his life he never admitted the taste of wheaten bread, the relief of oil, the eating of legumes, not to mention meat or fish, nor even wine or any other prepared drink. But because bodily substance cannot survive without food, after long and prolonged fasts he restored his little body, wearied by fasting, with barley bread mixed with ashes and water tempered with tears [Col. 1222A]. To impose upon himself a more severe affliction of fasting, he was not content with plain barley—which is known to have an extremely harsh taste—but, because he knew himself to be ashes through the sin of the first-formed man, he mixed ashes with the barley. Nor was pure water fit for him to drink unless he first increased it with most abundant tears. His pale features showed his continual vigils.

I confidently say that he would not have shrunk from Neronian or Trajanic tortures for the faith of Christ in a time of persecution, since he voluntarily subjected himself to such affliction. For the passion of those who in that time were compelled to deny Christ’s name scarcely occupied a week—indeed, scarcely extended to three days—whereas this man endured a long martyrdom through the prolonged span of his life. And if any faithful person judges the merit of the matter rightly, it is no lesser thing to wear down the flesh by continual mortification for God’s love than to expose it to the swords of unbelievers for the faith [Col. 1222C].

## CHAPTER VIII. On his ordination

As he thus increased in the growth of virtues and offered his venerable body as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, he was assigned to a ministry worthy of him. He became an executor of apostolic preaching, a participant in divine mysteries, and a priest, so that he who had offered his whole self unstained to Christ in holy deeds might himself handle the unstained body of Christ with undefiled hands; and so that the dignity of office might not be lacking to one in whom the devotion of preaching was present [Col. 1222D].

The servant of God adorned this honor with great humility, cultivated it in true charity, enlarged it by preaching the word of God, and, like a good farmer, uprooted the thorns of sins from the Lord’s field with the Gospel ploughshare. He watered dry hearts with the heavenly dew of everlasting salvation. Divine mercy also granted very great growth in faith among the people of Ponthieu through his preaching. Therefore the aforementioned man of God, Richarius, became honored and beloved by all, because he showed by example what he preached with his mouth, and he himself first ran ahead in action along the way of life which he showed others in speech.

Whatever the people offered him as payment for preaching, he hastened to distribute entirely among the poor [Col. 1223A]. It was unworthy of one who longed to receive the riches of eternal life to think about the morrow of the present life. Therefore he distributed what people offered, that he might receive what God promised. Blessed exchange: having cheerfully distributed small and passing things, he was to receive happily great and eternal ones.

For he was a most diligent comforter of the poor, receiver of pilgrims, defender of widows, and father of wards and orphans, so that the testimony of most holy Job may most truly be spoken of him: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the orphan; and I searched out most diligently the cause which I did not know” (Job 29). Hence the sick flocked to him from every side. Receiving them with a joyful mind, he furnished them healing through holy prayers. For, on making the sign of the cross, he gave sight to the blind more swiftly than speech; he raised paralytics by the power of prayer and the laying on of hands. He cast demons out of possessed bodies, now by prayer poured out to God and now by command alone; indeed, very often he put them to flight by his presence alone [Col. 1223B].

## CHAPTER IX. On the miracle involving lepers

He did not recoil from lepers or those suffering from elephantiasis, but embraced them as brothers, soothed their wounded limbs in baths, and entered the same baths after them. On account of such unheard-of humility and ineffable compassion, a great and unheard-of miracle occurred: when he humbled himself so far as to wash his own body in waters infected by poisonous discharge, he not only drew no evil into himself, but the lepers themselves [Col. 1223C], who had previously been washed, were immediately cleansed of every affliction, through the healing hand of God and the merit of the saint.

Nor was he a deaf hearer of the prophetic saying: “Bring the needy and wandering into your house; cover the naked with your garments; and do not despise your own flesh” (Isaiah 58). He not only sustained those who came to him with bodily refreshment, but also did not cease to refresh them with the spiritual consolation of holy preaching. And just as he was everywhere a fitting comforter of the wretched, so he did not fear to be a stern rebuker of the proud. The gentleness of compassion raised up the former; the censure of severe rebuke brought down the latter. He did not outwardly fear the anger of earthly power, because fear of divine power inwardly strengthened him wholly. He made little of the threats of the rich, that he might be a herald of truth.

Nor was he a reed shaken by the wind, such that the breeze of human praise or detraction might move him. Standing in the stronghold of solid truth, he despised being judged by a human mouth, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 4) [Col. 1223D]. Walking the royal way, he turned neither to the right because of the terrors of the powerful nor to the left because of flatterers’ blandishments. Therefore he won a great people for the Lord his God in this district of Ponthieu and gained for himself everlasting honor.

## CHAPTER X. On his compassion toward captives, and on his journey to Britain

Accordingly, when the people saw his religious devotion in Christ, they began to honor him more attentively and to bring him many things for the distribution of alms. Being full of love for God and neighbor, he bestowed them all as relief for the poor, and especially spent them on the redemption of captives. Some, bound by the hidden snares of sins through diabolical fraud, he released through the exhortations of diligent preaching; others, oppressed by worldly captivity, he redeemed through gifts of money. Thus the former, spiritually released, might rejoice in the Lord, and the latter, freed from bodily servitude, might turn to God [Col. 1224A].

The aforesaid man of God, Richarius, shone gloriously not only in these regions of Gaul through works of compassion and the light of preaching, but also, like the morning star crossing the watery expanses of Ocean, which by its rising scatters the night’s shadows as herald of daylight, he spread the light of truth by his arrival into the overseas regions of Britain. There he expelled the darkness of ignorance [Col. 1224B], so that, as in these regions, he might free some from diabolical slavery and others from bodily captivity. To the former he imparted God’s word; for the latter he paid the price of charity, that through temporal redemption they might receive eternal freedom.

## CHAPTER XI. On his arrival at Sigetrudis and the miracle of snow

There was a village in the district of Ponthieu called Sigetrudis, where the often-mentioned—indeed, ever-to-be-mentioned—venerable Father Richarius customarily had a lodging-place whenever he was intent on crossing the watery expanses of Ocean, partly applying himself to the life-giving preaching of the British region and partly to redeeming captives [Col. 1224C]. The lady of that village was named Sigetrudis, from whom the estate itself received its name.

But let the pen briefly relate what happened when the blessed confessor of the Lord came there on one occasion. It happened in winter that the holy Richarius, returning from Britain, arrived at that place; night overtook him there with those whom he was leading away after redeeming them. The blessed man asked the aforementioned noblewoman to receive himself and his companions as guests. But she altogether refused him this hospitality, not yet fully knowing the virtue or merit he possessed and, as is reported, prompted by some malicious rumor; she lightly despised his request.

When the man of God saw that no one wished to provide him a dwelling, and that the hour prevented him from proceeding elsewhere, he went about the site of the same village with his redeemed people, of whom he then had a great multitude with him. He found a large ditch in which quite a few people could gather secretly [Col. 1224D]. There he withdrew with his companions and passed the whole night.

But what is wiser than God? Certainly the woman was not allowed to furnish him lodging for one night, so that divine power might have occasion to act; when she learned how great his merit was before God, she would surrender to him not only her house but her whole estate. That same night, while the saint and his companions slept in the ditch, so great a mass of snow happened to fall from the clouds that the whole countryside could scarcely bear its depth. Everything was covered and all things suddenly changed to whiteness. Only that space of the ditch in which the saint and his companions were sheltered was not invaded by snow. The snow which, whether driven by the winds or through its own fineness, penetrated even the interiors of houses, held itself back from injuring him who, lacking a human dwelling, was covered by heavenly protection [Col. 1225A].

When morning came, the inhabitants of the place rose and were forced to cut a path through the snow for themselves and their livestock. When the sun shone and everything became visible, the holy Father Richarius was found to have remained untouched by the melting snow. At this deed all were astonished and amazed, and declared that the man thus defended was a worshipper and friend of God. When that noble woman perceived in the ear of her heart this power of the holy man with God, she was greatly terrified that she had denied him lodging; and thereafter she loved him with such a bond of charity that she transferred the village itself to him for perpetual possession. Truly God is wonderful in His saints, truly faithful in His promises: He did not abandon His faithful servant once deprived of human help, but where He did not allow him to have lodging for an hour, He caused him to receive an inheritance in its entirety [Col. 1225B].

## CHAPTER XII. On the spring brought forth there through his prayer

While blessed Richarius still lived a life of warfare on earth for the crown of the heavenly homeland, he often lodged on the aforementioned estate with the aforesaid handmaid of God when he was travelling to Britain or returning thence to his own country. Since she was on very intimate terms with him, as one who saw his life continually occupied in God’s work, she asked him to obtain by his holy prayers from the mercy of the Almighty that she might be favored with an abundance of water, for it was very necessary there [Col. 1225C].

Compelled by her request, he prayed. After the prayer he thrust his staff into the ground; and immediately a spring burst forth, which endures there to the present day. It provides what the prayers of God’s servant originally sought. Although it never ceases to flow in any drought, it never passes beyond the fields of that village; rising there, it runs a short course and then fails and disappears there. Much could be said about the spring and the village; but we omit it, so that we may more quickly dispatch other matters.

## CHAPTER XIII. On his prophecy

[Col. 1225D]

But amid so many and such great miracles which Christ the Lord performed through His servant, the Holy Spirit—who is truly the artificer of all things, foreseeing all things—also filled him with so great a grace that he effectively attained not merely signs of healing but announcements of future events. This will be clear from the following example.

While he was staying for a long time in Britain for the purpose of preaching, it suddenly came to his mind, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, that he had left some persons belonging to his household in servitude in Gaul. Struck by grief, he said to his companions: “Alas! We left our own people in servitude in our homeland while we came here to free others—especially because I know that they will soon die. But go quickly, board a ship, and make them free before they die.”

They followed their father’s command without delay, came to their homeland, found the aforementioned servants of the man of God sound and well, and, as they had been ordered, formally manumitted them and made them free. Not long afterward, as the holy man had foretold, they died. O how great is the mercy of God Christ, who implanted in His servant an affection of compassion and showed him the future death of his servants, so that the reward of mercy in respect of his own might not perish for him, and so that the yoke of servitude might not weigh upon them in death [Col. 1226A].

From that time he was unwilling to retain under the yoke of servitude anyone belonging to him, but everywhere granted freedom outright to all dependent upon him, lest perhaps he should seem harsher toward his own people when he wished to appear most gentle toward others, and so that he might add to the reward he had gathered from others a reward from his own people [Col. 1226B].

## CHAPTER XIV. On the construction of the monastery at Centula

After Richarius, servant of Christ, had put the darkness of ignorance and error to flight, filled many regions with Christ’s name, instructed innumerable converted pagans in the holy faith, and trained many in monastic religious life, he established churches and appointed clerics. When he felt that he could no longer sustain the circuit of preaching, though his unfailing desire for holy exercise remained, he withdrew to his native soil and paternal inheritance—what our people call an *allodium* or patrimony—intending to spend there what remained of his life in God’s service.

He had long before offered this possession together with himself to Christ and had built a monastery on paternal soil, so that where he himself had been brought forth for the world, he might by God’s grace bring forth many, and so that sons of the heavenly inheritance might be born in the place of his own birth [Col. 1226C]. That place, preserved by God, still remains renowned in the village of Centula and to this day retains a community serving Christ the Lord.

Having accomplished this in accordance with his most holy desire—which sought not the size of buildings or the beauty of roofs, but the salvation of souls and holiness of upright conduct—he established there as brothers certain men of the district and some of those whom he had redeemed and made free, namely those who more surely emulated his holiness. Examining their lives and correcting their conduct, he thoroughly taught them, more by example than by word, to strive from the depths to the heights and from earthly things to heavenly, presiding over them by the right of an abbot [Col. 1226D].

Many nobles of the Franks also, adhering to his goodness, continually pursued the paths of life. As he observed that his disciples’ minds were fixed upon heavenly things and raised above the world, he rejoiced, and, stretching himself eagerly toward higher things, said: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41). And again: “But I shall appear in your sight with righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Psalm 16).

For, always illuminated by the Holy Spirit and aided by Christ’s grace, he subjected himself to God’s service all the more ardently as he perceived the day of reward drawing nearer. He wore himself down with daily fasts, restrained himself by mortification of the flesh, afflicted himself with vigils, fortified himself with prayers, confirmed himself by charity, strengthened himself by hope, and armed himself with faith. He repaid evil to no one for evil, flattered no one, and despised no one, so that he himself might first walk in the way of truth which he had shown others by preaching [Col. 1227A].

Thus the man of God, clothed with the helmet of salvation, girded with the sword of God’s word, surrounded on every side by the breastplate of righteousness, armed with the shield of faith, and shod with readiness for the Gospel of peace, went forth to battle against the ancient enemy. With the most powerful boss of faith he repelled all that enemy’s burning darts; and by daily victories, having overcome the foe, he carried much spoil into Christ’s Church. He was as formidable to the enemy of humankind as he was greatly necessary to humankind, since he sought the salvation not only of himself but of many. Therefore it is fitting that he should be praised in Christ by the mouths of many: through Christ, redeemer of many.

So great a zeal for gathering souls to God inflamed him that, while presiding over the monastery, he travelled continually through churches, military camps, villages, and also throughout the houses of individual believers, everywhere kindling his hearers’ hearts with love for the heavenly homeland [Col. 1227B].

[It is not so great a matter to relate the miracles performed by him as to recognize his miraculous virtue, because in his days he won much people for the heavenly King. For there is no doubt that the office of preaching is greater than every display of signs, although, according to the opportunity of the times or the suitability of circumstances, the performance of signs was not lacking, wrought through him by divine mercy [Col. 1227C].]

## CHAPTER XV. On his holy co-mother Hrictrude

A certain distinguished matron, named Hrictrude, now blessed in the heavenly dwelling, had once entrusted her son Maurontus to the holy abbot. The saint washed him in the water of baptism and marked him with Christ’s branding-iron. When the boy, now reborn, had been restored to his mother, temptation by the malignant spirit befell the man of God on the following occasion.

He visited on horseback the aforementioned woman devoted to God, Hrictrude. Then, after sweet feasting upon heavenly life and beneficial conversation, the man of God mounted his horse and intended to return home. The aforementioned matron, according to custom, followed the departing rider’s track, carrying her little son in her arms so that the child also might be strengthened by the blessing of the man of God—the very one whom, as was indicated a little above, he had regenerated to God by holy baptism [Col. 1227D].

When the venerable rider had taken the child, either to bless or to kiss him, the ancient enemy, foe of all good, envying both the glory and virtue of the holy man and the future religious devotion of the holy child, made the horse savage. Gnashing its teeth here and there, kicking with its hooves, and raging in its whole body, it began to race across the field in a strange frenzy. When the frightened mother saw this, she turned away her eyes lest she see her son die, held in the hand of God’s servant while the horse raged [Col. 1228A]. The household did not cease from raising an outcry, lamenting, and wailing for the death of the child or disaster to the man of God.

But the right hand of Christ, which lifted up trembling Peter lest he sink in the waves, lifted up the falling child lest he be dashed upon the ground. For when God’s servant had prayed, the child came safely to the earth like a little bird, the horse was restored to its gentleness, and the mother received her son from the ground, healthy and smiling, into her arms.

Yet the priest of God thereafter chose to travel not by horse but by a most gentle donkey, mindful, of course, that when the Lord Christ hastened to redeem the human race, He travelled on a donkey, not on a horse. Thus, thereafter, when he hurried daily through many places for the preaching of salvation, he considered a donkey sufficient to carry him. Thus, by God’s mercy, the temptation of the malignant enemy was turned for him into an occasion of honor and praise, and the horse’s pride became his teacher in humility [Col. 1228B].

## CHAPTER XVI. On the blind man given sight

On one occasion, wishing to cross the water at the shore of the Altea and waiting for the arrival of a boat, he sat down. And behold, a native of Ponthieu, a blind man who gloried with his fellow countrymen in so great a patron, learned that he was staying there. Led by the sight of others, he came to meet him and, extolling the dearest Father and Lord of his homeland with countless cries, begged that his own sight might be granted him.

The holy man, compassionating his need with the most merciful heart that he always possessed, called him closer [Col. 1228C]. When he had approached, Richarius placed his fingers upon his most holy lips, then took saliva from them and anointed the deprived eyes.
