Immediately, the same power following the Lord’s example restored him to sight after long darkness. At that place there remains a village and church which, from love of him, is called Lord Richarius.

No antiquity has ever been able to erase from the mouths of descendants the report which our fellow countrymen repeat daily among his other great miracles: when this same most blessed shepherd was occupied in Britain with redeeming captives, if it happened that a vessel was late in arriving to carry him back across the rivers Altea or Quentia, he crossed it without wetting his feet and without assistance from any human aid [Col. 1228D].

[It happened once that Lord Richarius, returning from Britain, was leading a great multitude of redeemed persons. Suddenly looking back, he saw crowds of wicked people wishing to inflict harm upon those whom he was leading. Fearing more for them than for himself, he invoked the Divinity that he might be delivered from the hands of his pursuers. Heavenly power swiftly came near in answer to his prayer and carried him with his companions across the River Altea to the nearby wood. Thus, when the pursuers had been frustrated, the place where he settled received the name Moxultrum,

[Note: [Col. 1227D] “Moxultrum.” The reader understands for himself that all enclosed in brackets has been added from the Centula manuscript. Yet it is necessary to note that what is printed in italics has been supplied by us conjecturally, because several words had been erased by a scribe’s knife. Moxultrum, now Maisoutre, on the southern bank of the Altea.]

because, that is, by the power which had immediately carried him [lacuna] across.] [Col. 1229A]

But we have not undertaken to recount every virtue of the saint of God reported in the sayings of the faithful. Therefore let us come to the more certain matters which the discerning industry of the ancients, with a higher purpose to be imitated, inserted into the little book of his Life. Wherever he travelled, either psalms resounded from his mouth or preaching of salvation was heard. Nor is it surprising that he always preached Christ with his tongue, since he always bore Him in his heart. Through Christ he was a compassionate comforter to the wretched and a stern reprover of the powerful: he relieved the need of the former with gentle compassion and restrained the pride of the latter with severe correction.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the arrival of King Dagobert to him
[Col. 1229B]

So great a reputation for his blessings did not remain hidden; rather, by God’s will—who glorifies those who glorify him—the sweet fragrance of his holiness spread through all the neighboring regions, so that it did not escape even the nobles and magnates of the kingdom, and remarkable reports moved King Dagobert himself to visit him. For at one time King Dagobert himself, most powerful as he was, came at the request of the illustrious man Giselmar into the district of Ponthieu to visit the man of God and commend himself to his most holy prayers. The servant of God strengthened him with the blessing of his holiness, but also freely rebuked him with priestly authority, warning him not to take pride in secular power, not to place hope in fleeting riches, not to be exalted by the empty acclaim of flatterers, and not to rejoice in perishable honors; but rather to fear God’s power [Col. 1229C] and praise his immeasurable glory. He should count human power or glory as nothing, since it suddenly recedes like a flying shadow and, like foam upon water, vanishes when the wind of temptation blows. Above all, he should consider this with fear: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom V), and: “To whom more is given, from him more shall be required” (Luke XII). And how will one who can scarcely render an account to God for himself alone on the day of judgment be able to render an account for so many thousands of people entrusted to him? Therefore anyone may more rightly fear to rule than to be subject; for one who is subject will render account to God for himself alone, whereas one who rules will render account for all those placed under his authority.

The king, being wise, accepted this rebuke graciously [Col. 1229D] and rejoiced in his frank confidence in the truth. He asked the priest of Christ to come with him to the banquets. Strengthened by Christ’s example, he did not reject secular feasts, since he might thereby gain an opportunity for preaching; he came to table with the king and, throughout that day and night amid the festivities, served his fellow diners the saving fare of God’s word. Delighted by his steadiness of character and persistence in preaching, the aforesaid king began to love him in his heart and honor him so greatly that on that very day he granted him some part of his own revenue for the lamps of the house of God. [Col. 1230A]

[Judging it fitting [Note: [Col. 1229D] “Judging it fitting.” In the same codex of Centula from which these passages were copied, it is written in the margin of the book: “This Dagobert reigned sixteen years.”] that, just as he himself had been illuminated by the light of preaching, so the house of the Lord might be lit through him by visible light; and that what shone within him in faith might shine forth in the Church. Mindful of the precept which says: “So let your light shine before men” (Matthew V). Likewise in the Psalm: “In your light we shall see light,” that is, in the light of faith, which shines . . . outwardly, that which gleams.]

But after first making confession of his sins and receiving absolution, he assigned to him a certain territory in the district of Ponthieu called Campania. There are three estates there, which from that day served the holy man and, after his passing, still serve the monastery of Centula today: the first is called Altvillaris, the second Rebellismons, and the third Valerias. [Col. 1230A]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the appointment of Abbot Ocioald, and how the saint sought the wilderness.

[Col. 1230B]

Thereafter the servant of God, because he was venerated by people, planned to flee from people, so that, by declining temporal honors, he might receive everlasting honors. The leaders of every rank, following the royal example, were accustomed eagerly to seek the blessings of holy men. Since he now desired to be joined to heavenly things, he bore it with considerable difficulty that he should continue to be surrounded by the attentions of so many men who honored him. He desired the wilderness, so that he might devote himself more freely to God alone and gather contemplative fruits, though he had labored untiringly in active works.

But since the church built at [Col. 1230C] Centula neither ought nor could be without an abbot, he relieved himself of this office and set over the aforesaid monastery as abbot one of his disciples, Ocioald by name, a man of perfect and proven holiness. Having duly arranged this, [namely, recalling what the Lord said concerning Mary, seated at [Note: [Col. 1230D] “Seated at.” The manuscript read *sedis pedes*, plainly incorrectly.] his feet and listening more intently to the word of life: “Mary has chosen for herself the best part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X), mindful of this saying], he gave himself wholly to divine contemplation (*theoriae*). He sought the eremitic life, that in greater seclusion he might investigate heavenly things alone in his mind and consecrate his whole self in God, by whom he was soon to be received.

Giselmar, an illustrious man and devoted lover of the Christian religion, together with Mauronius, son of holy Hrictrudis [Col. 1230D]—who, because of his outstanding nobility, possessed much influence with King Dagobert and was then regarded as administrator and guardian of lands or woods belonging to the king—provided him a place to live in the forest of Crisciacum, at the place now called Forestis-Cella, ten Roman miles from Centula. No one, indeed, had lived there in former ages. In that place he began to build for Christ a monastery in honor of our Lady Saint Mary.

We also wish the reader to know that this Maurontus of whom we speak later trampled underfoot secular pomp and dress, became a monk and father of monks, and now, by the merit of his holy life, shares in the heavenly company. For that most sacred blessing of the great Father Richarius, which he had obtained as a boy through his mother’s intercession, could not be annulled. [Col. 1230D–1231A]

## CHAPTER XIX. By what mortification he wore down his own body in the wilderness.

Thus the great confessor of God and eminent father Richarius entered the aforesaid dwelling with one companion only, Sygobard by name, illustrious in the height of his nobility. He was content with a small hut constructed in the meanest fashion, so that his dwelling might suit his manner of life, judging it superfluous for one who despised the world to seem to possess any of the world’s riches.

There he bound himself by such mortification of the flesh and wore himself away by such constancy in fasting and vigils that his dry bones scarcely held together, their joints having come apart. With trembling footsteps, supported by a staff, he moved only with difficulty. Yet his mind, greater than the world, always considered heavenly things alone; and the more alien he was from the world, the nearer he was to God. Daily in the wilderness he overcame him by whom Adam was once overcome in Paradise; walking upon the asp and basilisk, he daily crushed the head of the ancient serpent. Despising all temporal things and longing only for eternal ones, he fortified his journey along the narrow way that leads to life with unceasing prayers. [Col. 1231A–B]

Yet the column of light could not remain hidden within the confines of the enclosed wilderness, but became known far and wide through the great rays of its splendor. Therefore from every side the blind, deaf, mute, lame, leprous, paralytic, and those afflicted by every kind of illness came or were brought to the man of God. He healed them with the remedies of holy prayers, and caused all who came to him afflicted by any disease, or distressed by the bitterness of any sorrow, to return home healthy and cheerful.

Nor is it surprising that a man dear to God was thronged by people, when even animals entirely lacking reason were most ready to serve God’s servant. For if, on some rare occasion, bodily need compelled him to obtain something to eat, [Note: [Col. 1231] *Conquirere*, “to procure.” I have judged this should be read by conjecture; for the printed text had *concurrere*, “to run together.”] the birds with which the woods were filled descended before his face so fearlessly and perched upon his knees or shoulders, that from the very nature of the scene you would have thought them not senseless animals, but children affectionately clinging to their father. Some crumbs were offered them from the holy man’s hands; and things unfit for human use because of their hardness or austerity seemed most pleasing to the birds themselves, now coaxing with their voices, now with their wings. [Col. 1231C–D]

[It is not my purpose to recount individually every kind of his virtues, but to sketch the holiness of his life in a few words, lest the reputation of the many signs wrought through him be obscured rather than praised by the slowness of my uneloquence. Leaving these matters to more learned persons, it will suffice for me to say only by what end that holy soul departed the present world.]

## CHAPTER XX. On his passage to Christ.

[Col. 1232A]

So long as the account treated of the saint’s life, my mind rejoiced and was glad as though in a living patron, while it recounted what he had done in life. Thus far we seemed to be sailing under favorable winds and, in calmly reading through the deeds of our beloved Father, to be singing a sweet rowing-song. But now, soul, what do you choose? Will you fall silent, or will you tell of the righteous man’s death? Yet do not call it death, which made the saint’s birthday. For when he died to the world, then he was truly born to Christ in heaven. It is wretched to love the places of death willingly and, after dangers have at least been experienced, to refuse to behold the harbor. You must also rejoice with the Father, who, saved from the shipwreck of the world, lives joyfully crowned with Christ in a secure dwelling. Secure, I say, because heavenly; secure because eternal; secure because it cannot be taken away by any assaults of enemies.

Therefore, having eased the grief of our hearts through an abundance of tears, let us call it not the Father’s death but his passage, for he was truly blessed precisely because, despising the world, he had always desired this passage. But now let us unknit our brows, so that the Father’s glory may be freely proclaimed. [Col. 1232A–B]

Foreknowing the day of his summons, on which he was to receive the happiness long desired and to be forever joined to God whom he had always loved, he called to him his aforementioned companion Sygobard and said:

“I know, my son, I know that my end does not delay, and that I shall soon see my King, whom I have long desired—if only as gracious to me his servant as he is desirable to his saints. But you, my son, prepare a vessel for my little body in which it may be laid, not with superfluous care but for necessary use, so that it may be preserved there until that day when this corruption shall be changed into incorruption and this mortal thing shall put on immortality. And prepare yourself with all diligence, my son, so that when that day, now drawing near to me, shall also come to you, it may find you ready. As for me, I go the way of all the world. Only may the Savior of the world be merciful to me, defend me now from the enemy, who once redeemed me from the enemy; and may I find him, whom I had as the comforter of this present life, to be the giver of eternal life.”

Hearing these words from his Father, the disciple was bathed in tears. At last, obeying the command, he found timber, split it, hollowed it out, and fitted it to the Father’s body. He watered with weeping the work he made, and almost filled it first with bitter tears rather than with the Father’s limbs. Having arranged the sarcophagus as best he could, he placed it in the spot appointed beforehand by the Father. [Col. 1232B–D]

Meanwhile, while the son prepared these sorrowful services for his Father, illness consumed the Father ever more severely. In his cold little body scarcely a final breath remained, yet he did not cease from the office of prayer or the service of divine praise. And when he had fortified his journey with the saving provision of Christ’s body and blood, he gave up his spirit amid thanksgiving and words of prayer on the sixth day before the Kalends of May [26 April]. He was placed in the tomb by his disciple, [in the place] where he himself had commanded.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the heavenly glory shown to Sygobard.

[Col. 1233A]

But, wonderful to relate! During the Father’s funeral rites, the disciple was suddenly overcome by sleep and saw in a vision that he had been caught up into a most splendid hall, beautiful in every adornment—indeed, brighter than the light of the sun. There he saw blessed Richarius dwelling with a radiant and cheerful countenance and saying to him:

“Behold, brother Sygobard, what a dwelling God has prepared for me: in heaven, most beautiful in exchange for the mean one I had on earth; glorious for the contemptible; most radiant for the dark; and shining with every sweetness in exchange for the smoky.”

(Indeed, this must not be passed over: among the other torments he inflicted upon himself, the holy man of God also imposed this affliction. If at any time he was cold, the fire was removed; if warm breezes prevailed, they were employed not to warm him, but green wood was placed on the fire so that his sight might be filled with smoke.) [Col. 1233A–B]

When the disciple awoke, happier than before, he completed the funeral work. God thus provided both that the son should be consoled and that the Father’s glory should be shown. He was buried, as I have said, the soldier of Christ where he had most fully performed service for his King.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the transfer of his body to Centula.

Blessed Richarius, being very renowned among our peoples both for his most distinguished lineage and for his exceptional holiness, was not permitted to rest long in the place to which he had withdrawn because of its rarely traveled route and more secluded life. Yet the venerable jewel of his holy body lay in that wooden sarcophagus for five months and twelve days, that is, from the sixth day before the Kalends of May [26 April] to the seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October]. At that time the brothers came from the monastery of Centula, which, as said above, the saint himself had built, with their abbot Ocioald, a religious man and successor of the saint. They raised the beloved Father’s venerable body, entirely free from the decay of corruption, just as his heart had remained pure from every love of the world. [Col. 1233B–C]

With the reverence due to so great a confessor, they most devoutly laid upon their shoulders that clod, dearer than all gold. Preceded and followed by a multitude of religious persons and common people, they bore it to Centula, so that the place which rejoiced in the holy man’s birth might in turn be adorned by his burial. Thus Richarius, Christ’s friend and glorious confessor, was buried in his own church, which he had long before built in honor of our Lady, Saint Mary, Mother of God, on the seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October]. At the head of his burial place there is now an altar of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.

There he rested for a long time in another tomb, until after one hundred and fifty years and more he was honored with every distinction of veneration by the holy men who governed this our monastery, and especially by Abbot Angilbert of holy memory. How this was accomplished will, with God’s help, be explained elsewhere. But there, by God’s granting—he who knows how to glorify his faithful—new miracles are often known to have occurred. The almighty Lord is clearly understood to have wished to perform them for two reasons: that the faith of those praying might be made manifest and the merits of his servant shown, so that Christ’s praise might always be celebrated in his servant, as it is said: “Praise the Lord in his saints” (Psalm 150). [Of these, it pleases us to recall those which the diligence of the ancients committed to writing, so that posterity might know them.] [Col. 1233C–1234A]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On miracles performed at his tomb.

[A certain crippled man, weak in body but strong in faith, regularly visited in prayer the tomb of the saint of God. Suddenly receiving the health he had desired, he gave glory to God, for he had come sick and departed well. In memory of this miracle, the supports of his infirmity hung in the church of Saint Richarius for a long time.

Often, too, demoniacs and those possessed by demons, when brought there by the assistance of relatives, were immediately freed, by divine mercy, from the torment of the evil spirit. On one occasion certain bound and chained persons were being led along the public road which lies near the church of blessed Richarius. When from a distance they saw the temple of the man of God, they cried in a loud voice: “Saint Richarius, release us!” At once their bonds broke, and all were set free.

Likewise, a great affliction called *pamicula*, or “poisonous lizard,” struck one of the brothers of Saint Richarius’s monastery. Although he feared death because of the affliction, he did not despair of life because of his patron. Therefore, as though running to certain aid, he ran with the other brothers to the tomb of God’s servant. When prayer had been made there, he himself was immediately healed, and all the others were thereafter protected from the plague.] [Col. 1234A–C]

## MYCON, DEACON AND MONK.

Today the annual festival is celebrated in honor  
Of kindly Richarius, who dwells among the stars of heaven.

For Christ’s name he led a life of poverty,  
That he might become an angelic companion in heaven.

For he strove to be a most generous redeemer of captives,  
Protector of the needy and father of the poor.

I confess: I neither need nor am able to compress into brief form  
All that he accomplished in life, and all the greatness of his teaching.

For what and how great he was, the miracles reveal  
Often performed in his holy place.

Born within the territory in which he himself rests,  
The place stands unharmed through his merits.

[Col. 1234D] Through his intercession, and Christ’s favor besides,  
We servants at last stand unharmed.

Therefore today, rejoicing, let us sing jubilant praises to Christ  
For the merits of Saint Richarius.

So that our hymns may please all who are present,  
And no less the Lord—I therefore exhort this:

Let us ask with a pure heart our holy patron,  
That he may be our spearhead and likewise our shield,

So that, armed with prayers, we may overcome  
Those excessively hostile to the Catholic Church.

Do this, Ruler of the world, for you have power to do it;  
We ask only that it be your will, O Lord.

And to you, teacher, on your joyful feast day through the years,  
Behold: these few verses in number make this request.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the succession of the kings of the Franks.

[Col. 1235A]

Since something concerning the deeds of the Franks was mentioned at the beginning of this work, we think it necessary—and most fitting—to report something again about them. After acquiring the kingdom in its entirety following his father’s death, Dagobert is found to have lived only a few years. He had two sons, Sigibert and Clovis. He sent Sigibert, with Duke Pippin, to rule the Austrasians; but he retained Clovis with himself. After him Clovis received the kingdom of the Franks.

This Clovis married a wise and very beautiful girl, Balthild, by whom he had sons: Chlothar, Childeric, and Theuderic. During his reign Pippin, duke of the Austrasians, died, and Grimoald, son of that duke, was appointed mayor and duke by King Sigibert. Sigibert too died, leaving as heir a son named Dagobert. Grimoald tonsured him and, through Dido, the profaner of Poitiers—I do not call him a bishop—sent him into exile; he installed his own son as king. When the Franks learned this, they took it indignantly. Seizing Grimoald by treachery, they sent him to Clovis, king of the Franks. Clovis treated him as he deserved, threw him into prison [at] Paris, and finally punished him with a fitting death. [Col. 1235A–B]

Then Childeric, son of Clovis, received the kingdom of the Austrasians and ruled it most honorably. But after Clovis, son of the great Dagobert, departed this life, Chlothar attained the height of royal power and ruled the people of the western Franks for fourteen years, while Ebroin administered the dukedom and the affairs of the palace. When Chlothar died, his brother Childeric was elevated over the whole kingdom, through the agency of Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, who at that time was regarded among the kingdom’s great men as outstanding in energy of mind and merit of life.

Ebroin, who had been mayor of the palace, wished Theuderic, Childeric’s brother, to become king. But because the Franks hated him for his ferocity, they utterly rejected his plan. Seeing himself abandoned and his design rendered futile, he asked the king to allow him, after leaving everything behind, to become a monk. When Childeric consented, he immediately went to Luxeuil; and with feigned devotion he lived there for some time as though a monk, in order more freely to contrive what he might someday do against those who had rejected his choice in establishing a king. [Col. 1235B–D]

King Childeric, therefore, once established in the kingdom, destroyed whatever decrees of tyrants he found contrary to the laws of earlier kings and restored to their former condition of justice those things which had been foolishly enacted. He also entrusted his brother Theuderic to a servant of God for education and upbringing. While he was governing the monarchy most excellently, he was rashly murdered by plotters, though he had held the kingdom for only three years.

His venerable mother, likewise perfect in every holiness and pursuit of virtue, after the honor of temporal royalty—which she had abandoned in taking the habit of the monastic life—received the glory of eternity, happily departing this world on the eighth day before the Kalends of February [25 January]. Theuderic, surviving his mother Balthild, then took up the reins of the kingdom. When that true dissembler and false monk, namely the utterly wicked Ebroin, heard this, he left the monastery, cast off the habit, and was restored by that king as mayor of the royal household. He inflicted many evils upon those who had formerly opposed his counsel in the choice of a king. [Col. 1235D–1236A]

Among all the unspeakable deeds of his most savage cruelty, this is judged the most detestable: he subjected the most reverend bishop Leodegarius to such injuries and such manifold torments that, in devising punishments, he may rightly be said to have equaled or even surpassed the cruelty of the pagan rulers of old.

These, then, were the kings who had ruled from the beginning of the kingdom of the Franks down to this time: Merovech, Childeric, Louis, Chlothar, Aripert, Guntram, Chilperic, Sigibert, Chlothar, Hildebert, Theuderic, Theudebert, Sigibert, Dagobert, Sigibert, Clovis, Dagobert, Chlothar, Childeric, and Theuderic. [Col. 1236A–B]

## CHAPTER XXV. On Abbot Ocioald and four other abbots.

But now it is fitting to state that, when the most holy Abbot Richarius died, Ocioald, an honorable man, presided over the monastery of Centula. As has been set forth above, the saint himself had honored him with this office. Having faithfully completed the course of a holy life, he received from Christ the prize of immortal glory. But after he was released from the debt of our mortality, it is not clear to us who immediately succeeded him in this ministry.

There were indeed other not undistinguished men who served as abbots of this our monastery. Although their deeds have been hidden from humankind, the merits of their lives are believed to be great before God. Among them flourished Abbot Coschinus, a man of venerable life and supreme simplicity. They say that he was one of the disciples of Saint Philibert and that, on account of his upright character and abundance of learning, he presided over the monastery of Jumièges. [Col. 1236B–C]

For when our most sacred Father Richarius, having conquered the world in the struggle of this life, was already regarded as a veteran soldier close to death, blessed Philibert was spending his youthful years in God’s service, undergoing the apprenticeship of a most strict servitude at the monastery of Rebais under the holy Abbot Agilus. Hence it is said to have occurred that, when Philibert as an old man founded the monastery of Jumièges, this Coschinus was trained in divine observances and, by merit of his life, presided over that monastery after certain others.

And thus, while he enriched its monks with words and examples of worthy conduct, our monks chose him as their abbot—not because there had been lacking among them anyone able worthily to carry out this task, but because the highest charity and loftiness of humility compelled them to do so. For by that time all who could have seen the most holy Father Richarius had already departed the world. Therefore the brothers of this place were moved by great affection toward Coschinus, because he had seen with his own eyes blessed Philibert, the most fervent lover, as they said, of most blessed Richarius. Thus, while he was already governing the monastery of Jumièges, he was also set over our monastery by the brothers’ election. [Col. 1236C–1237A]

To encourage virtue and provide an edifying example for the souls entrusted to him, he ordered the life of blessed Philibert to be written in a truthful but not highly polished style. For he wished to speak in such a way that even the simpler sort could draw the fruit of understanding from a very plain reading. From the time of this abbot, therefore, the monasteries of Centula and Jumièges have embraced each other with such great charity that, apart from being separated by their locations, they seem united by the greatest love.

In those days holy and good believers did not care much to commit their deeds to writing, since they strove only to deserve to be inscribed in the book of life. Consequently, we would have been completely ignorant of the abbots of that time had not the venerable Abbot Angelrannus made some provision for this. While briefly listing the catalogue of the earlier abbots, he indicated that one of them was Guitmarus, whom he also called a most holy man. And because such a great man deserved such testimony, it is fitting that he be remembered by us insignificant people, since the mouth of a truly holy man marked him as “most holy.” He rests buried in the land of Neustria, and there is a church dedicated in his name. How great his holiness and righteousness were, we are not prepared to say; we entrust their proclamation to the canons who serve his holy body. We place him fourth, therefore, in the order of our account. [Col. 1237A–C]

After these reverend abbots, Aldric is said to have governed the congregation of Centula in fifth place. We find among ourselves no evidence of his deeds, and indeed we would not even have known his name, had the diligence of the venerable Abbot Angelrannus not revealed it.

When Aldric too had been taken away, Symphorianus presided over the monastery of Centula: a good, chaste man, fearing God, separating himself from sinners, and made higher than heaven in purity of mind. [Col. 1237C–1238A]

In the time of these abbots, divine marvels of such magnitude and frequency were performed at the tomb of the most sacred body of blessed Richarius that the immensity and greatness of the events altogether took from writers of that age the desire to write. They considered it superfluous to record what they saw each day, or were prevented by slowness of ability or lack of means from describing things which they thought could never be erased from memory.

Nor were mighty miracles shown only in this place, where the saint rested in body. They were also displayed very frequently at Forestis, where he had dwelt for some time. Let the reader know that from the day of the most holy death of blessed Richarius, this cell at Forestis was suitably maintained by the brothers; and it had the same abbot as this place, since both had from the beginning one and the same most sacred founder. [Col. 1238A–B]

Now that we have set forth in some measure the life of blessed Father Richarius, who became the foundation of our faith and religious life—and have made that life both the support and adornment of this work—let our exercises have this portion as a little book, so that our spirit, now falling silent after its long discourse, may through a brief rest return stronger to speech. But now, giving thanks to God the Father and the Son for benefits bestowed, and seeking the grace of the Holy Spirit for what remains to be said, let us conclude this little composition. Let us pray that in word and deed we may be guided by the power of the Holy Trinity, whose confession may make us glorious unto ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 1238B–C]

# BOOK II

[Col. 1237]

## CHAPTER I. On the genealogy of the princes of the Franks.

[Col. 1237D]

The preceding little book made known how great and what kind of a founder this monastery of Centula received as the source and beginning of its holiness; how our first shepherd lived in the world; and how he was admitted into heaven. Thus our discourse was carried in sequence down to the sixth abbot of our place. Let us therefore finally designate the seventh, to whom the number seven is rightly assigned in return for the grace of the Holy Spirit, whose gracious dwelling was the man whom we are to discuss.

This is Angilbert, dear to God and men, distinguished by birth, outstanding in virtue, foster-child of kings and magnates, and now blessed far more abundantly through the company of angels. But since we have undertaken to describe in some measure the nobility of our place, which we have shown to have been ennobled by the holiness of its first founder, it is fitting that we explain, as far as we can, the nobility of the man through whose work and diligence our place deserved to be greatly enlarged. [Col. 1238D]

Therefore, in the year 754 of the Lord’s Incarnation, when Pippin, together with his sons Charles and Carloman, ruled the realm of the Franks—always to be exalted by praise of every good thing—Angilbert, by the natural quality of his nobility, had so won these aforementioned kings’ love that they loved him wonderfully and deeply; and, conversely, kings to whom others usually sought to be pleasing strove, through affection, to please him.

We judge this little book would be further honored if we briefly noted the genealogy of these kings as well. The fourth king of the Franks, Chlothar, son of the Louis whom Saint Remigius baptized, begot a daughter named Blithild. Ansbert, a man of senatorial rank, obtained her as wife, and by her begot the brothers Arnulf, Feriolus, and Modericus. Arnulf begot Flodulf, Ansegisus, and Gualchisus, father of Saint Wandrille. Ansegisus, after his father mayor and prefect, begot Pippin the Elder and duke, who in turn begot Charles, likewise elder and duke. [Col. 1239A]

When Ansegisus and his son Pippin departed this human life, Charles seized the leadership of the entire Frankish people from the hand of the tyrant Ragenfrid, though only after many wars and struggles, and brought it under his own authority. Persisting most energetically in military affairs, he crushed throughout all Francia the tyrants claiming lordship for themselves. On that account, taking much property away from ecclesiastical right, he joined estates to the fisc and then distributed them among his own soldiers.

Moreover, in two very great battles he so defeated the Saracens attempting to occupy Gaul—one in Aquitaine near Poitiers, the other near Narbonne by the river Birra—that he compelled them to return to Spain. Since he knew no yielding to opponents and spared no one, he acquired from posterity the harsh byname *Tudites*. For *tudites* are the hammers of smiths, by whose blows every hardness is worn down. [Col. 1239A–B]

He made an alliance with Liutprand, king of the Lombards, and sent him his son Pippin, so that, according to the custom of faithful Christians, Liutprand might be the first to cut his hair and become his spiritual father. Liutprand most gladly fulfilled this and sent the boy back to his father enriched with many gifts.

After Charles was removed from human affairs following a long administration, his two sons, Pippin and Carloman, divided the supreme power of the kingdom in harmonious partnership and governed it for several years under Childeric, king in name only. For at that time, royal glory having declined, the royal household was governed by the prefects of the palace. Nothing was left to the king except that, content with the royal name alone, he should sit upon the throne and present the appearance of a ruler; hear envoys coming from every direction; and, when they departed, give them replies which he had been taught—or rather commanded—to give, as though from his own authority. But the prefect of the court managed the government of the kingdom and everything needing to be done or arranged at home or abroad. [Col. 1239B–C]

## CHAPTER II. How Carloman, having yielded his share of the dukedom to his brother, became a monk.

[Col. 1239D]

After some time had passed, Carloman left to his brother Pippin the share of the kingdom that he had undertaken to govern. Inflamed with love for the contemplative life, he went to Rome and lived for some time quite religiously in the monastery of Saint Sylvester, situated on Mount Soracte. But because Frankish people who came to Rome under the patronage of blessed Peter the apostle turned aside there and visited him frequently, he saw that this hindered his purpose. He withdrew from there and afterward entered the monastery of Monte Cassino, then being restored by a most religious man named Petronax.

Pippin, having obtained the supreme power of the Frankish kingdom, at the command of Stephen, bishop of Rome, who was then staying at Paris after being driven from Italy by the wickedness of the Lombards, deposed and tonsured the utterly incompetent King Childeric and compelled him to live as a private person. Pippin himself had by his wife Bertrada two sons, Carloman and Charles. [Col. 1239D–1240A]

While the aforesaid pope remained in Paris for a long time, he happened to fall very seriously ill. But the holy apostles Peter and Paul and Saint Dionysius appeared to him, and he heard that he would be healed and would return in peace to his own see. Having recovered his health, while celebrating the divine offices at the blessed martyr Dionysius on the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity itself, he anointed Pippin, his wife Bertrada, and their two sons as kings of the Franks amid the most holy mysteries of the Mass.

Pippin then survived for twelve years and left the succession of the kingdom to his two sons. Of these, Charles, on his brother’s death, alone obtained the monarchy. The most illustrious man Angilbert was dearer to him than all others by reason of nobility and wisdom, so that he was considered his closest intimate. Their friendship grew so strong that Angilbert took the king’s daughter, Berta by name, in marriage and by her begot two sons, Harnid and Nithard. To increase his palatine honor, the dukedom of the whole maritime region was also entrusted to him. [Col. 1240B]

At that time the monastery of Centula, long before founded by Saint Richarius, had until then been inhabited by monks who served God with sufficient honour. [Col. 1240C] They led a life rich indeed in virtues, but not very wealthy in worldly resources—not because the abundance of estates, revenues, and villages bestowed on them by Saint Richarius was lacking, but because they devoted all the expenditure of their income to the benefit of the poor rather than to their own uses. When Angilbert, therefore, having received the duchy, visited Ponthieu, he heard from the people of the province of the signs and miracles which almighty Christ continually worked at the tomb of his most holy confessor Richarius. These deeds inspired in his heart a great love for this place.

Accordingly, the manifestation of a deed—which is the proof of love—immediately followed. Having obtained from Emperor Charles permission to fulfil his vow, and having at the same time disclosed [Col. 1240D] the desire of his heart, namely, his ambition to restore Saint Richarius’s church, he received from that king a most gracious reply, Charles promising that his support and assistance would never fail him. At the king’s command vast treasuries were opened for him; and he was asked to take from them whatever, and as much as, he wished, so that the intention of this most beloved man might be fulfilled with the greatest care.

Thus, after the kisses exchanged in sweet friendship, the venerable Angilbert returned to Ponthieu and Centula, and at the monastery of the most holy father Richarius assumed the monk’s garment and true humility. Not long afterwards the abbot of the place died, and, both at the brothers’ request and by the king’s command, Angilbert—truly a monk in continence and humility—was raised to that office. After this [Col. 1241A] had taken place, royal authority sent to Angilbert highly skilled craftsmen in wood and stone, glass and marble. Then, because Charles desired to exalt the monastery of Centula with every honour, both for love of Saint Richarius and for his beloved Angilbert, he sent many strong wagons to the city of Rome to carry back marble and columns for the adornment of the aforesaid church. Not content with this, he sent envoys through kingdoms and cities, commanding his subjects and requesting non-subjects to send him relics of the saints possessed by their various localities. If anyone wishes to know what relics of the saints, and of what sort, were brought here, it will be shown not by our own words but by the writing of Lord Angilbert himself, which will be inserted a little later.

## CHAPTER III. On the rebuilding of the monastery of Centula

[Col. 1241B]

Angilbert, therefore, relying on God’s aid and on Lord Charles’s consent and unlimited generosity, first demolished that ancient church built by Saint Richarius, and with great and remarkable wisdom laid the foundations of a new one. He removed the old structure because the venerable body of Saint Richarius lay there in a tomb, and it was his desire to construct an elegant basilica above those holy remains. The most devout King Charles, from his treasuries, as has been said, assigned to him such a vast and immense sum of money that, for every necessary work, the labourers and the work itself would fail before there was any lack of funds with which to pay the labourer.

[Col. 1241C] When marble columns were being raised in the *buticum*,[Note: [Col. 1241D] *Buticum*. I conjecture that *buticum* is the same as *ciborium*, a structure consisting of four or eight columns, customarily erected above altars and the tombs of saints. MABILLON.] one of them slipped from the hands of those raising it and broke into two pieces. At once such grief seized all who were present that they completed no work that day. When morning came, and the craftsmen returned to consider how they might repair the break, they saw the column standing upon its base, wholly undamaged. For an angel of the Lord came, touched the fissure with his finger, and restored it completely more swiftly than words can tell. The imprint of the angelic hand is still shown: to those looking upon it, the column seems to remain divided, although the place itself has become stronger.

Accordingly, with much equipment, the greatest diligence, and exceptional beauty, the monastery was begun and built; [Col. 1241D] and a most splendid church, superior to all the churches of that age, was completed in honour of the Saviour and Saint Richarius. On its eastern side it has a huge tower beyond the chancel; and, with a vestibule lying between, another tower stands toward the west, equal to the first. The eastern tower is situated near the place in which Saint Richarius had his burial. The burial itself is arranged so that an altar stands in a higher place at the saint’s feet, while at his head there remains an altar of Saint Peter the Apostle. Thus the eastern tower, together with the chancel and the *buticum*, was dedicated to Saint Richarius; and the western tower was especially dedicated in honour of the Holy Saviour. [Col. 1242A] Around its interior, too, the memorable Angilbert caused these verses to be written:

> Almighty Lord, who rulest heights and depths,  
> God mighty in majesty, ever present everywhere,  
> Look down from the lofty throne of the saints’ glory,  
> And grant thy servants aid, good King.  
> Add peace to rulers and salvation to subjects;  
> Drive away the enemy’s threats and subdue savage wars.  
> These shining heights of the temple which I have established—  
> I, Angilbert—may they be pleasing to thee, O God.  
> Grant to Augustus Charles, by whose strength I completed them,  
> The great joys of thine empire.  
> And whoever here strikes upon thy highest ears with prayers,  
> Grant, O God, that he may always obtain their effect.

To this day there can be seen in the pavement of the choir such beautiful [Col. 1242B] and carefully ordered marble work that everyone who inspects it declares it an incomparable work. Before the altar of Saint Richarius, he caused certain verses to be painted on the pavement itself; we must also set them down here.

> This pavement I, Angilbert, a humble abbot,  
> Caused to be made, led by the love of God,  
> So that after my death Christ, my life and salvation,  
> May deign to grant me holy rest.

Moreover, because that ancient church of Saint Richarius had been consecrated in honour of Saint Mary, and lest the venerable man of God should seem to have dishonoured the Mother, he built another church for her; it still stands on this side of the little river Scardon. He also built one for Saint Benedict the abbot, which he placed on the bank of the aforesaid [Col. 1242C] stream. Thus, if the layout of the place is considered, the larger church, that of Saint Richarius, is seen to occupy the north; the second and lower church, dedicated to our Lady Saint Mary and situated on this side of the river Scardon, the south; and the third, which is the smallest, the east.

The monks’ cloister was made triangular: that is, there was one covered walk from Saint Richarius to Saint Mary; one from Saint Mary to Saint Benedict; and likewise one from Saint Benedict to Saint Richarius. Thus, as the walls meet one another from different directions, a triangular open space is formed in the middle. The monastery was arranged according to the decree of the Rule of the most holy Benedict, so that every [Col. 1242D] craft and every necessary work might be carried on within the enclosure. The water of the torrent Scardon flows past the cloister itself and there turns the brothers’ mill. But since we have said these things briefly concerning the site, let us now discuss the dedication of the monastery. This, however, must be shown not in our words but in the writing of Lord Angilbert, which still survives today, and is as follows.

## CHAPTER IV. The writing of Lord Angilbert on the completion and dedication of the church of Centula

“I, therefore, the aforesaid Angilbert, considering and examining with the most diligent inquiry and with the affection [Col. 1243A] of my mind how, with the consent of my brothers and of all the faithful of holy Church and other good men, I might, with the Lord’s help, rebuild for the better this holy place entrusted to my governance—though I am unworthy—by almighty God and my most excellent lord Charles, most serene Augustus: so that the monks and other servants dwelling there, and also our successors who shall come after us through the successive periods of time, might serve God and more earnestly implore the mercy of that same God for me and for my aforesaid lord; so that these works might bring them perpetual consolation, and might bring us, who have laboured for God’s love, everlasting reward through their prayers—I took care to labour, as reason allowed [Col. 1243B] and our resources administered: not, however, as much as we wished, but as much as we were able, as is declared below.

“Since, therefore, all the body of the faithful must firmly confess, venerate, and honour in mind, and firmly believe in, the most holy and inseparable Trinity, in accordance with the meaning of this faith, with the Lord’s assistance and the aid of the aforesaid lord Augustus, we have endeavoured to found in this holy place three principal churches with their dependent parts, in the name of almighty God. The greater and first is in honour of the Holy Saviour and Saint Richarius; another is in honour of Saint Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of the holy apostles; the third, in the brothers’ cloister, [Col. 1243C] is in honour of Saint Benedict the abbot and the other holy abbots who observed the Rule.

“These also were dedicated in a wonderful order by twelve venerable holy bishops. In reverence and remembrance of them, we have judged that their names should be attached to this little work. They are: Megimhard, venerable archbishop of the see of the church of Rouen; George, Absalon, Gerfrid, Pleon, Hildiguard, Theudoin, Ydelmar, Benedict, and Kellan, most distinguished bishops; and John and Passivus, most noble bishops and legates of the holy Roman Church of God.

“For the altar of the Holy Saviour, in which are placed his relics and those of the Holy Innocents who suffered for him; and the altar of Saint Richarius, in which are relics [Col. 1243D] of holy Mary the Mother of God and of Saint Richarius himself; the altar of Saint Peter, in which are his relics and those of Saint Paul and Saint Clement; the altar of Saint John the Baptist, in which are his relics and those of Zechariah, his father; the altar of Saint Stephen, in which are his relics and those of Simeon, who received the Lord in his arms; the altar of Saint Quentin, in which are his relics and those of Saints Crispin and Crispinian; the altar of the Holy Cross, in which are relics of its wood; the altar of Saint Denis, in which are relics of him, Rusticus, and Eleutherius; the altar of Saint Maurice, in which are relics of him, Exuperius, and Candidus; the altar of Saint Lawrence, in which are relics of him, Sebastian, and Valerian; and the altar of Saint Martin, in which are relics of him and of Remigius, Vedast, Medard, Walaric, Lupus, Servatius, Germanus, and Eligius—in the church of Saint Benedict, [Col. 1244A] the altar of Benedict himself, in which are his relics and those of Antony and Columbanus; the altar of Saint Jerome, in which are his relics and those of Ephrem and Equitius; and the altar of Saint Gregory, in which are his relics and those of Eusebius and Isidore—all these were worthily and most carefully consecrated to the Lord, with great joy, on the Kalends of January, by those same excellent men already named.

“In the church of the blessed Virgin Mary, moreover, the altar of Mary herself, in which are deposited relics of her and of the holy women Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Agnes, Lucy, Cecilia, Anastasia, Gertrude, and Petronilla; the altar of Saint Paul, in which are his relics and those of Barnabas and Timothy; the altar of Saint Thomas, in which are his relics and those of Ambrose and Sulpicius; the altar of Saint Philip, in which are his relics and those of Sylvester and Leo; the altar of Saint Andrew, in which are his relics and those of George and [Col. 1244B] Alexander; the altar of Saint James, in which are his relics and those of Sixtus and Apollinaris; the altar of the blessed John the Evangelist, in which are his relics and those of Linus and Cletus; the altar of Saint Bartholomew, in which are his relics and those of Ignatius and Polycarp; the altar of Saint Simon, in which are his relics and those of Cosmas and Damian; the altar of Saint Matthew, in which are his relics and those of Mark and Luke; the altar of Saint Thaddaeus, in which are his relics and those of Nazarius and Vitalis; the altar of Saint James, the brother of the Lord, in which are his relics and those of Gervasius and Protasius; and the altar of Saint Matthias, in which are his relics and those of Hilary and Augustine—were dedicated with the highest honour on the sixth day before the Ides of September, on her most sacred Nativity, by the venerable bishops George, Absalon, Pleon, and Gerfrid.

“Further, the altar of the blessed archangel Gabriel, situated in [Col. 1244C] the southern gate, was consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the Annunciation of Saint Mary; that of Michael, in the western gate, on the third day before the Kalends of October, by the venerable bishop Hildewald; and that of Raphael, in the northern gate, on the second day before the Nones of September, in honour of these archangels and all the powers of heaven, was most fittingly consecrated by Jesse, a devout bishop.

“With the same Lord assisting us, we have endeavoured to rebuild from the foundations all the remaining walls of this monastery which are now seen to have been built, just as they are seen; and, with his aid, we took care to surround them firmly with a wall, so that their inhabitants might celebrate the solemnities of Mass in it and delight in serving almighty God.”

## CHAPTER V. On the relics which he gathered in this holy place from different provinces, and on the reliquaries in which they are deposited

[Col. 1244D]

Since we perceived that the aforesaid churches had been founded by prudent counsel, as written above, in honour of our Lord Jesus Christ, of his glorious Mother, and of all his saints, we were inflamed with great desire and with the excessive love of zeal, that, according to our means and by the mercy of that same Lord, we might merit to obtain a portion of the relics of those saints for adorning these holy churches of God. Therefore we strove with all our strength and the entire intention of our mind to obtain, through the assistance of almighty God and the aid of my glorious [Col. 1245A] lord, the great emperor, as many relics as we could from all parts of Christendom, of whatever kind and from whatever places brought, and to deposit them in this holy place, as appears below.

That is: first, relics brought to us from the holy Roman Church through the generosity of Hadrian, pope of blessed memory, and after him of the venerable Leo, Roman pope; from Constantinople or Jerusalem, through envoys dispatched there by my lord; then relics sent to us from Italy, Germany, Aquitaine, Burgundy, and Gaul by the most holy Fathers—namely patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and abbots; and also those which had been gathered in the sacred palace over time by earlier kings and thereafter in the greatest quantity by the lord just named. By his almsgiving, we merited to receive a portion of all of these and fittingly to deposit them in this holy place.

Of those relics concerning which we were certain, and for which we received written lists from the aforesaid most holy men, we have not neglected to insert all their names in this little work, so that by us and by all our successors who shall in time succeed to this holy place and wish to know these things, the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—through whom these and all other good things have been bestowed upon us, though unworthy—may in all things and always be glorified, he who is blessed for ever. But concerning the other relics, received from those same holy Fathers, whose names are uncertain to us, we have written nothing. The names of the remaining relics, however, we have taken care to record in the following order. [Col. 1245C] First we have listed relics of our Lord and Saviour, of his glorious Mother, of the holy apostles, and of the other martyrs; afterwards those of confessors and likewise of holy virgins and women of continence.

### RELICS OF THE LORD AND SAVIOUR

Of the wood of the Lord’s Cross. Of his garment. Of his sandals. Of his manger. Of his sponge. Of the Jordan, where he was baptized. Of the rock on which he sat when he fed five thousand men. Of the bread from which he distributed to his disciples. [Col. 1245D] Of the Lord’s temple. Of the candle that was lit at his birth. Of the Mount of Olives, where he prayed. Of his table. Of the mountain on which he was transfigured. Of the column at which he was scourged. Of the bonds with which he was bound. Of the rock from which he ascended the Cross. Of the nails with which he was crucified. Of the place of Calvary. Of the morsel in which gall and vinegar were mixed. Of the rock upon which blood from his side trickled. Of the Lord’s sepulchre. Of the stone rolled away from the entrance of the tomb, and also of the sepulchre of the Innocents who suffered for him. [Col. 1246A] Of Mount Horeb, and likewise of the wood of the three tabernacles. Of Saint Mary’s milk. Of her hair. Of her garment. Of her mantle. Of Saint Peter’s beard. Of his sandals. Of his chasuble and his table. Of Saint Paul’s table. Of his *orarium* [liturgical cloth]. Of the pillar to which he was sent. Of Saint Andrew’s cross. Of the manna of Saint John the Evangelist. Of relics of the apostles James, Philip, Thomas, [Col. 1246B] Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon, Thaddaeus, Matthias, Barnabas, and Timothy. Of the bones of Zechariah, father of Saint John the Baptist. Relics of blessed Simeon, who received the Lord in his arms. Of the hair of blessed John the Baptist. Of his blood. Of his garment. Of the ribs of Saint Stephen. Of the stone by which he was stoned. Of Saint Lawrence’s gridiron. A finger of Saint Apollinaris. Of Saint Symphorian’s sponge and of his mother’s garment.

### RELICS OF MARTYRS

[Col. 1246C] Vigilius. Sisinnius. Martyrius. Pamphilus. The holy Geminus [or: the holy twins]. Fabian. Valerius. Pergentinus. Cosmas. Damian. Anastasius. George. [Col. 1246D] Alexander. Cassian. Magnus. Vitalis. Nazarius. Nabor. Celsus. Gervasius. Protasius. Innocent. Lawrence. Tributius. Valerian. Hippolytus. Christopher. Felix. Maurice. Candidus. Exuperius. Victor. Innocentius. Benignus. Denis. Rusticus. Eleutherius. Cornelius. Leodegar. Sixtus. Firmin. Saturninus. Quentin. Valentine. Marcellus. Lucian. Crispin. Crispinian. And bones of forty martyrs, and blood of many others.

### RELICS OF CONFESSORS

[Col. 1247A] Saint Hilary. Martin. Germanus. Medard. Audoen. Eligius. Amandus. Lupus. Aventinus. Sulpicius. Remigius. Maurilio. Albinus. Servatius. [Col. 1247B] Jerome. Equitius. Ephrem. Gregory. Augustine. Leo. Sylvester. Felix. Isidore. Donatus. Benedict. Columbanus. Isaac. Vincent. Antony. Paulinus. Fortunatus. Simplicianus. Walaric. Vedast. Relics from the bodies of saints which Pope Paulinus enclosed. Relics of Saint Megimbold. Priscus. Eugenius. Fronto. Fidelis. Asterius. Simplicianus. Faxidus. Astogius. Gislarius. Speratus. Robert. Galemer. Oswald.

### RELICS OF VIRGINS

Felicity. [Col. 1247C] Perpetua. Agatha. Eugenia. Thecla. Cecilia. Petronilla. Euphemia. Fausta. Euphrasia. Aldegund. Columba. Felicula and Scholastica.

Thus far we have separately recorded the martyrs and confessors among the certain relics of saints, whose certain names we received from the holy Fathers who bestowed them on us. Hereafter, because we did not discover the distinct names of other saints, whether martyrs or confessors, we have written nothing of them.

When these things had been honourably and fittingly deposited, as was written a little above, in the name of the holy [Col. 1247D] Trinity we prepared with great care a larger reliquary, ornamented with gold and gems. In it we placed a portion of the relics written above, and, out of veneration for those saints whose relics appear to be deposited in it, we took care to place it beneath the crypt of the Holy Saviour. We divided the relics of the other saints listed above among thirteen smaller reliquaries, most honourably furnished with gold, silver, and precious gems, which, by the Lord’s gift, we merited to acquire from the venerable Fathers often mentioned together with the same relics. We took care to place them upon the beam which we established in the arch before the altar of Blessed Richarius, so that in all things, as is fitting, the praise of God and [Col. 1248A] the veneration of all his saints might always be adored, honoured, and revered in this holy place.

## CHAPTER VI. On the altars and the adornment of the altars and of Saint [Richarius]

When altars had been appointed for the veneration of the aforesaid saints and reverently adorned with their relics, as has been related above, we began carefully to consider how we might also adorn them, by the craftsman’s work in gold, silver, and gems, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ and in veneration of all the saints in whose honour they were consecrated, from the gifts of God and the generosity of my great lord and his most noble offspring, as well as of other free and good men who had made gifts to me; and how, where suitable places existed, we might place *ciboria* above them. Accordingly, with that Lord assisting, we endeavoured to do as much as we could.

That is: in the church of the Holy Saviour and Saint Richarius, eleven constructed altars, two *ciboria*, and two lecterns furnished with gold, silver, and marble; [Col. 1248B] in the church of Saint Mary Mother of God and of the holy apostles, thirteen constructed altars, one *ciborium*, and one very finely furnished lectern; in the church of Saint Benedict, three furnished altars; and in the churches of the holy angels Gabriel, Michael, and Raphael, three altars. Thus there are in all thirty altars, three *ciboria*, and three lecterns.

Of other vessels and furnishings, the same churches possess seventeen crosses made of gold and silver; two golden crowns; [Col. 1248C] six silver lamps; twelve bronze lamps adorned with gold and silver; three golden apples; two gold chalices with patens; one large gold chalice with images and a paten; twelve other silver chalices with their patens; ten silver offertory vessels; one panel made of gold and silver at Saint Richarius’s head; two larger doors made of gold and silver, two smaller ones, and two other small doors similarly furnished; one golden belt; one excellent silver inkstand adorned with gold; one knife furnished with gold and pearls; one ivory codex most finely furnished with gold, silver, and pearls; one purse furnished with gold; four silver censers adorned with gold; thirteen gilded silver drinking-cups; one larger silver basin with silver images; [Col. 1248D] one silver drinking-vessel; two silver ewers with their aquamaniles; one silver reed [or tube], one ivory one; two silver holy-water buckets [two silver *sivones*, uncertain term]; one golden key; one silver bell; thirteen crowns with lights; six columns before the altar of Saint Richarius furnished with gold and silver; three smaller beams with their arches, furnished with silver; three bell-turrets furnished with gold; fifteen excellent bells with their fifteen rings; three *skillae* [bells]; six bronze images and one ivory image; two candlesticks furnished with gold; seven doors furnished with gold.

In addition, we bestowed there seventy-eight excellent hangings, two hundred copes, twenty-four dalmatics, six white Roman silk albs with their gold-furnished amices, two hundred and sixty linen albs, thirty chasubles of *pallium* fabric, ten of purple, six of *storax* fabric, one of *piscis* fabric, fifteen of *platta* fabric, and five of *cendatus* fabric; five gold-furnished stoles; ten gold-furnished *fanones* of *pallium* [Col. 1249A] fabric; five cushions of *pallium* fabric; and five cloaks of *pallium* fabric.

Of books: one Gospel-book written in gold, wonderfully furnished with silver covers, gold, and precious stones; one other complete Gospel-book; and two hundred volumes of other books. There were also very many additional ornaments for construction and various uses—in lead, glass, marble, and other implements—which would take too long to enumerate and describe at length. Yet at that time the faithful servants of God and Saint Richarius, who had laboured with us in God’s service, appraised all these things as having a value of fifteen thousand pounds, or more.

Thus far extends the account composed by the most holy man Angilbert concerning the construction, dedication, and adornment of the church [Col. 1249B] of Centula. It has become very old through three hundred years and more from that venerable man’s own time down to ours, and not without labour has been inserted by us into this work for the instruction of posterity. Certainly there are many other things which he is found to have honourably established, together with those above, for the splendour of the divine office. But because, after so long a time, they are not observed among us, both because of changes in the place and because of abbots’ preferences, we avoid recounting all of them here. Nevertheless, we shall still cite some things in order to convey the greatness of our house.

After he had said that the ornaments of the church and the expenditure from its treasury might have been valued at fifteen thousand pounds and more, he added the following words:

## CHAPTER VII. On his establishment concerning the divine offices

[Col. 1249C]

“When these and other things had, by the Lord’s gift and so far as we were able, been elegantly arranged, and the churches adorned with the aforesaid relics of the saints collected from various places, we began to consider with diligent affection of mind how, with the Lord’s gift, we might attain this end: that, just as they shine honourably before human eyes in marble buildings and other ornaments, so too we might be able to please Christ almighty in the praises of God, in diverse learning, and in spiritual songs.

“Therefore, with God’s assistance, we have established three hundred monks to live according to the Rule in this holy place, desiring and ordaining that this number of the community, if not a greater number, should be maintained forever. We have also established one hundred [Col. 1249D] boys to be trained in the schools, under the same habit and sustenance, to assist the brothers in psalmody and singing, divided among three choirs. Thus the choir of the Holy Saviour shall have one hundred monks and thirty-four boys; the choir of Saint Richarius shall continually have one hundred monks and thirty-three boys; and the choir singing before the Holy Passion shall likewise have one hundred monks with thirty-three boys added.

“These three choirs shall resound in divine praises according to this arrangement: all of them together shall chant all the canonical Hours in common; and, when these have been duly completed, one third of each choir shall leave the church and for a time attend to bodily necessities or other useful tasks, [Col. 1250A] returning after a fixed interval of time to celebrate anew the offices of divine praise. In every choir, too, it shall continually be observed that there be an equal number of priests, levites, and members of the other sacred orders. An equal division of singers and readers shall likewise be arranged, so that no choir is burdened by another. Rather, all with one accord shall continually offer to the Lord almighty the sacrifice of praise, with unceasing devotion, for the salvation of my glorious lord Augustus Charles and for the stability of his kingdom.

“When the Matins or Vespers office has been completed, all the choirs shall immediately assemble in proper order before the Holy Passion, with only ten psalm-singers remaining from each choir. Then, passing through the gate of Saint Gabriel [Col. 1250B] and through the abbot’s hall, they shall proceed singing through the western side of the cloister to Saint Mary. Having there offered the prayer appropriate to the time, they shall return to Saint Benedict, situated in the eastern part of the cloister. From there they shall enter by the steps of the arches to Saint Maurice, and thus, entering the basilica of Saint Richarius, return to their choirs.

“We also command, with especial devotion, that no day pass without the chanting of holy Masses: that is, if no more, at least thirty Masses shall each day be celebrated by brothers of the different choirs at the different altars, apart from the two conventual Masses which are celebrated with the greatest solemnity in the morning and at midday. At these, every day, commemoration shall be made of the most holy Pope Hadrian and of my glorious lord Augustus [Col. 1250C] Charles, his wife, and his offspring; so that, according to the Apostle’s word, we may continually offer to God our Saviour thanksgivings of supplications and prayers for kings and for all who are established in high station (1 Tim. 2).”

“Charles, by God’s grace king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to his most beloved master and to us lovingly named Albinus the abbot, eternal salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ. It has come to our attention …” [Note: [Col. 1249] Published in the Works of Alcuin, p. 1147. We have omitted it because it does not pertain to this history.]

[Note: [Col. 1249] Published thus far.] “But concerning your letter, which continued by saying that much might be said on this matter, but that you did not wish to extend the length of the letter, especially because one must use few words with a wise man: so [Col. 1250D] in return we too write briefly. As for your appropriating the words of the queen of Sheba to Solomon concerning the blessedness of the servants who stand before us and hear the words of our wisdom: if you know this will be true, come, stand before us, and listen, so that together we may delight in the Lord amid verdant meadows, rejoicing in the variety of the flowers of Scripture.”

Here ends the letter of Charles the Great to Albinus the master.

This same Albinus, summoned to Centula by the venerable Angilbert, composed in elegant language the Life of Saint Richarius, which had been arranged rather carelessly in ancient simplicity. He prefixed to the work a preface addressed to the same [Col. 1251A] glorious Augustus Charles, in which it is plainly shown that Blessed Father Richarius had wrought great and more numerous miracles than the brief text of his Life recounted. He also composed antiphons, responsories, and hymns concerning the same saint, so that the festival of the great Father might seem to lack no fitting office. It should be noted that in a certain hymn, praising Saint Richarius himself, he addresses him thus: “You built a monastery in a place near Argubium, and another at Centula, both by everlasting merit.”

## EPITAPH OF SAINT RICHARIUS

*On the front of the tomb:*

> A golden urn received the heavenly treasure,  
> A worshipper of the Lord, named Richarius;  
> Of exalted lineage, whom this Centula brought forth,  
> [Col. 1251B] And who flourished as the outstanding shepherd of this place.

*On the right side:*

> Setting aside the world’s honour, in which he shone greatly,  
> He despised abundant wealth for love of God.  
> Here, breaking his own body in harsh struggle,  
> The pious and great man is ever renowned throughout the world.

*Above, on the summit of the shrine:*

> Here he restored life to the dead and sight to the blind,  
> And, through his aid, health returns to lepers.  
> Full of apostolic powers and utterances,  
> He ever held the food of heaven in his mouth.

*On the left side:*

> Prince Charles, with gracious mind,  
> Completing a fitting church for him, also built a tomb,  
> After about one hundred and sixty years,  
> [Col. 1251C] While he still remains whole among the Lord’s servants.

*At the feet:*

> So that through his merits he may obtain the heavenly kingdom  
> And may govern the kingdom of the Franks in peaceful rest.

Amen.

*Elsewhere:*

> Ever, holy Richarius, protect thy servants,  
> That the heavenly hall may receive those withdrawn from earth.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June died Albinus—also called Alcuin—abbot, levite, monk, and author of the Life of Saint Richarius.

In these same times flourished Saint Adalard, abbot of Corbie, who was honoured throughout all Gaul for the renown of noble birth and holy religion. Ratbert shone forth as his distinguished admirer and pupil. [Col. 1251D] He was moved by such fervent charity toward our monks that in the very things he sent or wrote to our people one discerns not words of love but love itself and pure affection throughout. When he composed the Life of that same Saint Adalard, he said: “Rejoice, Corbie, because, while other holy places have sent forth their own patrons—Arras, Vedast; and Centula, most holy Richarius—you too shall send forth your Adalard.” In this one should carefully observe with what great reverence he exalted our magnificent shepherd and patron: he named him with a superlative addition, whereas he was content to designate that eminent bishop Vedast by his bare name. He did this because of the continual greatness of the miracles performed among us, and because of that [Col. 1252A] truly most holy life of Richarius, which is proved to be not so much holy as a mirror of holiness itself.

This man wrote for Gollandus, a monk of our monastery, an exposition on the Gospel of Matthew. He valued the men of Centula so highly that he sent them his writings, so that they might be circulated everywhere with authority according to their judgment.

## EPITAPH OF SAINT CHAIDOCUS, CONFESSOR

> Beneath this mound lies Chaidocus, rightly a priest;  
> Scotland gave him birth; the land of Gaul covers him.  
> Joyfully following the commands of Christ the Lord,  
> Blessed in mind, he despised his native wealth.  
> From this there grew for him an abundance of a hundredfold fruit,  
> And he reaps rich rewards from the heavenly soil.  
> Angilbert, trusting in piety as his teacher,  
> [Col. 1252B] Made both a poem for his tomb and the tomb itself.

## ANOTHER

> He who is seen buried in an earthly body  
> Joyfully possesses heavenly delights according to his merits.  
> This was Fricorus, joined in fellowship with Chaidocus,  
> Whom exultant Centula rejoices was granted to her.  
> Strong in virtue, he despised the world’s prosperity,  
> And now great glory lies open to one who lives.  
> When it pleased God, he sought the kingdom of heaven.  
> Now he shines in Angilbert’s poem. Amen.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the death and burial of Saint Angilbert, and on his son and successor Nithard
In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 814, in the sixth indiction, Charles the Great, Augustus of most excellent memory, [Col. 1252C] after most victoriously triumphing over his enemies with God’s favor, while he held in the greatest peace the empire of the Romans and the kingdoms of the Franks and Lombards, departed this world on the fifth day before the Kalends of February. For the services and honors diligently rendered to God and His saints, he was, as we hope, graciously to receive the blessed and immortal kingdoms. The venerable Angilbert, although his body, worn down by old age and by the austerity of fasts and vigils, could not—or would not—go anywhere, nevertheless attended the disposition by which, as ever the beloved of the Lord, he assigned treasures for almsgiving to the bishops of the churches; and he obtained from Charles, before his death, the elevation of the church of Centula by great honors and benefactions. There were twenty-one [Col. 1252D] metropolitan cities to which he ordered a large portion of his wealth to be distributed. Their names are these: Rome, Ravenna, Milan, Forum Julii, Grado, Cologne, Mainz, Juvavum—that is, Salzburg—Trier, Rheims, Sens, Besançon, Lyons, Rouen, Arles, Vienne, Tarentaise, Embrun, Bordeaux, Tours, and Bourges. Only four abbots are recorded as having been present at this distribution: Fridigius, Adalongus, Angilbert, and Irmino. The king himself had honored and exalted the place to such an extent that the records of that time sometimes report him as having held his royal court there on Christmas Day or on Easter Day. This too was lovingly maintained for a long time by his successors—namely, those who held our Gaul as their allotted kingdom. [Col. 1253A]

When, therefore, after the death of Charles the Great, Louis succeeded him and assumed the summit of the kingdoms acquired by his father, as the first year of his reign began, the most holy Abbot Angilbert, afflicted by bodily illness, was approaching heavenly joys; and, by the disposition of the heavenly Father, the son who was shortly to be received was scourged, that he might become worthy to receive a happy inheritance that would not perish. As his illness grew worse and he seemed already about to be removed from human affairs, employing great humility—as one who had been its steadfast guardian—he ordered that he should be buried before the doors of the church. Certainly, the sighs and tears poured out when he approached death [Col. 1253B] are not a subject we undertake to narrate, lest renewed sorrow after so great an interval of time should call us also back to mourning. Having survived by twenty days after the death of the great Augustus Charles in the same year, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 814, the sixth indiction, in February, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, after the ecclesiastical mysteries had been celebrated around him, the glorious soul of Angilbert, truly a lover of Christ, filled with exercises of good works and acts of piety, left the vessel of its earthly body and was joined to the citizens above. Presently he is gladdened by the sight of Christ, seeing Him as He is, having attained by works what he had sought in his prayers. This is affirmed by the truthful and unassailable declaration of Christ, who declares that those who love Him are loved by His Father and by Himself, and reveals the outcome of so great a love—[Col. 1253C] the vision of Himself: “And I will manifest myself to him” (John 14), that is, to one who loves Him and carries out the proof of love, namely the performance of works.

Then the venerable body of the most loving father was prepared by the tender service of his sons and honorably buried, with all veneration due to a holy abbot, before the gate of the greater church. The place of his burial is so near the entrance of the church that no one can enter the basilica without stepping upon the holy tomb of his body. There, as was said [Col. 1254A] a little above, he had requested to be placed for humility’s sake. Around the burial were set out these little verses on stone tablets: the first at the head, the second on the left, the third at the feet, and the fourth on the right:

> King, O Father and gracious King, grant Angilbert rest.  
> Law, grant him eternal life according to the laws, for you are the Law.  
> Light, grant him light forever, for you are the good Light.  
> Peace, give him everlasting peace, because you are Peace.

There are many great and notable things which we had to say concerning this venerable man; but because we have been unable to comprehend everything found in the histories of the Franks concerning him and his excellence, we ask that these few things may for the present suffice our own people, to the praise of Almighty God and the honor of the blessed man. Moreover, [Col. 1254B] we lacked the capacity to relate everything concerning him; yet we also exercised caution, lest by discoursing at excessive length we bring weariness upon the listener. He rested in the place written above for twenty-eight years, while the Augustus Louis reigned for twenty-six years; but the reign of Christ our Lord reaches no end throughout all ages. Amen.

Thus, after making known the seventh abbot of the monastery of Centula and showing his zeal and goodness, let our tongue now be granted a brief rest, so that the sorrow conceived at his loss—which, since we are mortal, we cannot help admitting for a little while—may more swiftly be relinquished when it has found satisfaction in sighs. At the same time, it seems fitting that he who showed singular love toward us should also be singularly praised in this little account of his deeds. [Col. 1254C]

Yet we necessarily record at the end of this book that, after his holy departure, his son Nithard—whom he had begotten by Bertha, the king’s daughter—was placed over the people of Centula by right of abbacy. After he had spent only a few days in office, he was killed in battle and lost the sight of this present light. Buried beside his own father, he rested in peace, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1253]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning Abbot Hericus

[Col. 1253D]
