In the year 814 of the sacred Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the seventh indiction, while blessed Francia flourished in every splendor under the rule of the most glorious Caesar Louis, Hericus the abbot obtained, through the favor of that prince, the government of the monastery of Blessed Richarius. The chronology should be noted: although Hericus was placed over the abbey of Centula in the same year in which the most holy Abbot Angilbert died, it was not in the same indiction, since the indictions change on the twenty-fourth day of September. Nothing memorable concerning his deeds is preserved among us, except what is found in [Col. 1254D] the book of the miracles of the blessed father Richarius: namely, that he granted to one of his vassals, named Heuto, the estate of Sidruda, which had formerly been assigned for the brothers’ footwear. This small estate had been given to the saint himself during his life in this world, as is clearly evident in the account of his life. But now it pleases us to recall what miraculous event happened there after it had been subjected to Heuto’s lordship.

Nearby there was a wood, in which the inhabitants of the place handed down, from the testimony of their fathers and forefathers, that Saint Richarius had rested his bodily weariness and offered holy prayers beside a certain beech tree, both while making his journey to Britain and on his return. When the aforesaid Heuto had received [Col. 1255A] the estate, he began to use it with unrestricted power. One day, while he was inspecting its fields, he came upon the beech already mentioned; seeing its great size, he ordered it cut down, so that it might furnish him firewood. His servants refused to obey, saying that it was a consecrated tree and that Blessed Richarius had been accustomed to pray there. But he scorned this in his proud mind and compelled them to cut it down. When the tree had been felled and divided into sections, the upper parts could indeed be split, but the two lower sections, being thicker, were split only with great difficulty. Nevertheless, the peasants persisted with great effort and broke apart the next-to-last piece, in which there were found remains resembling hair and clippings of a beard. The peasants held these in honor, as things deposited there by the saint; but miserable Heuto, an evil lord of the estate, [Col. 1255B] reckoning them worthless, ordered them scattered. Then he commanded that the final remaining trunk of the beech be split; but it remained unbreakable under every blow. Seeing this, he ordered it carried into the courtyard of his house—what the common people call a *curtis*—and, as is customary, thrown down before the doorway.

That same day, a certain tenant of the estate lightly struck the wood with an axe he had taken up, as if merely testing it; at that blow it immediately split, and a certain cross was found embedded in one of the pieces. The outline of the same sign appeared inscribed upon the other piece. When those present saw this, they were struck with extreme terror; and, after taking counsel, they brought the pieces with the cross into a storehouse for safekeeping. Then, on the following night, after the doors of the storehouse had been secured, they went to sleep. In the morning, when they awoke from sleep, [Col. 1255C] neither the cross nor the pieces could be found anywhere. The aforesaid Heuto, who had violated holy things, lost his life on the fifth day, God acting as avenger. Hericus too, after completing several years in office, closed his final day.

## CHAPTER II. Privilege of Emperor Louis

At this time, when the glorious Augustus Louis happened to enter the province of Ponthieu, he sought the venerable church of Saint Richarius for the sake of prayer. The brothers of the monastery, fearing that someone of the family of the aforesaid Heuto might seize the estate of Sidruda, entreated and persuaded the royal majesty to confirm by a charter of his authority both this estate and all those estates which they feared they might lose by some occurrence, and which Charles the Great, Louis’s father, had bestowed by royal gift. Thus the estate already mentioned and the other possessions might freely serve the monastery without anyone’s objection, and no future abbot might remove any of them from the lordship of the place and grant it to another. He therefore graciously complied with these requests and drew up the authority of his decree concerning these matters in this manner:

> “In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ: Louis, by the ordering of divine providence Emperor Augustus. We wish it to be known to all faithful members of the holy Church of God and to our own faithful, both present and future, that when we came for the sake of prayer to the basilica [Col. 1256A] of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Richarius, the monks of that monastery approached our exalted person, asking that we order our authority to be issued, for the sake of confirmation, concerning the property which they presently hold for their food and clothing in various districts and territories under the jurisdiction of our empire. By this authority we should decree that neither abbots residing there in successive times, nor administrators, nor any other person of the aforesaid higher or lower rank [Note: [Col. 1255D] “Aforesaid.” Read: “rank.”], may presume to remove or diminish anything from those properties, or divert it to other uses.
>
> “Judging their petition just and reasonable, we have ordered these our imperial letters to be drawn up for the sake of confirmation on behalf of the servants of God dwelling there as time passes. By them we decree [Col. 1256B] and in every way establish that no superior of the aforesaid monastery, nor any of its administrators, may presume to remove or diminish anything, divert it to other uses, or demand or exact provisions, *lidimonium*, military service, or any other exactions, from the properties which they presently hold in various districts and territories under the jurisdiction of our empire for their use, food, and clothing. Their names are these: Cininicurt with Bronoil, Aldulf’s estate, Valles, Drusciacum, Novavilla, Mount of the Angels, Wiberentium, Bagardas, Curticella, Crux, Langoratum, Altegium, Sidruda, Niviella, Verculf, Concilium, Mount of Rocco, Maris, together with whatever at the present time appears justly and lawfully to belong to the aforesaid places.
>
> “Rather, they shall hold and possess them in the manner and under the terms which we now establish, and shall have and enjoy them securely and peacefully in our time and in future times, so that the servants of God serving in the aforesaid monastery may delight to implore continually God’s mercy for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our whole empire. And that this authority may retain inviolable and unshaken force in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.”

The sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

> “Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the seventeenth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the eighth indiction.
>
> [Col. 1256D] “Done at the monastery of Saint Walaricus, happily. Amen.
>
> “I, Durandus the deacon, acting in place of Fridusi, have reviewed and subscribed.”

Of the estates mentioned in this charter, our most holy father Richarius had held some in peace; but because the brothers were harassed concerning them by the insolence of wicked and depraved men, they obtained confirmation of them by a royal decree. The estates which had been held from the time of Saint Richarius and concerning which no harm was feared—including Centula, Abbatis-villa, Altvillaris, Rebellis-mons, Valerias, and many others—were not thought necessary to be written here.

## CHAPTER III. Inventory of the treasure, possessions, and vassals of Saint Richarius

[Col. 1257A]

After Emperor Louis had issued his decree concerning the possessions of the monastery, he summoned the monks and asked them to write down and show him everything that could be possessed, both in the treasure of the church and among its external goods. Therefore, in the year 831 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the ninth indiction, an inventory was made of the abbey of Saint Richarius at the request of the most serene Augustus, in the eighteenth year of his reign. First came the ecclesiastical goods; then the estates and possessions; and also the vassals who held benefices from the same abbey.

There are three principal churches there: one greater church [Col. 1257B] in honor of the Holy Savior and Saint Richarius; another in honor of Saint Mary; and a third in honor of Saint Benedict. In these are three principal altars, namely those of the Holy Savior, Saint Richarius, and Saint Mary, fashioned from marble, gold, silver, gems, and various stones. Above these three altars are three canopies made of silver and gold, from which hang three crowns, each separately fashioned from gold and gems, with small golden crosses and other various ornaments. In the same churches are three lecterns made of marble, silver, and gold. There are thirty reliquary chests, fashioned in gold, silver, or ivory; five larger crosses and eight smaller ones; and twenty-one altar ornaments in the form of apples, of which three are of gold and the rest silver. Likewise, there are seven banner-finials made from silver [Col. 1257C] and gold; fifteen large and seven small iron candlesticks adorned with silver and gold; seven silver crowns and seven gilded copper crowns; six silver lamps and six gilded copper lamps; thirteen hanging silver cups and two hanging silver basins; three larger and three smaller chests; eight gilded silver censers and one of copper; one silver fan; a screen at the head of Saint Richarius, and two small doors fashioned of silver, gold, and gems; at his feet, six doors made of silver and gold. There are also four others similarly made. Before the altar of the same saint stand six great columns of copper, ornamented with silver and gold, supporting one beam likewise of copper and ornamented with silver and gold. There are three other smaller beams [Col. 1257D] of copper, silver, and gold around the altar or choir, supporting seventeen arches made of copper, silver, and gold. Among them stand seven images of beasts, birds, and human beings, made of bronze. Five circular ornaments from which signs hang are silver; the rest are of brass.

One Gospel-book written in gold, with a silver case fashioned with gems and stones. Two other Gospel-book cases made of gold and silver, with one silver *faldene* [uncertain object] made for their use. Four gold chalices; two larger and thirteen smaller silver chalices; two gold patens; four larger and thirteen smaller silver patens; and one of brass. Four gold offertory vessels; sixty silver ones; one ivory vessel; and one large vessel made of silver and gold. One large silver cup; [Col. 1258A] four smaller silver cups; and one of brass. Four silver *tutelli* [uncertain vessels]; two silver ewers with hand-washing vessels; one silver drinking cup; one silver bucket; two of copper and bronze; and one ornamented with silver. One silver reed or tube; one of tin. One ivory tablet ornamented with gold and silver; two larger and two smaller tablets; one of cypress wood ornamented with silver. Two silver keys; one gilded brass key. One staff ornamented with gold, silver, and crystal; and one crystal fitting for a staff. Forty chestnut-colored chasubles; ten black silk chasubles; three purple silk chasubles; one of *plata*; and twenty of cloth. Five silk *galnae*; three silk *melnae*; one of *piscis* fabric; and four of *cendal*. One chestnut-colored cope ornamented with gold; one silk cope. Thirty-one dalmatics; fifteen silk *hrocci*; eleven woolen ones; one white silk garment; two purple silk garments; one breast *roccus*. Fourteen gold-ornamented offertory *fanones*; [Col. 1258B] three of *brandeum*; fifteen of cloth; four coverings for carrying patens; seventy-eight cloths; forty-nine vestments; twenty other vestments; one furnished with cloth; one linen vestment furnished with cloth in the sacristy for covering the altar-table; six tapestries; three curtains; four silk bench-coverings; six other cushions, two silk and four cloth; one linen vestment for the Lord’s service; two gold-ornamented *nastolae*; two chestnut-colored gloves ornamented with gold; two linen gloves; two gold-ornamented hand-*fanones*; one gold-ornamented cap; one of cloth; two *facitercula* [uncertain objects]; and 377 copes.

Concerning books: canonical books; a complete Bible, containing seventy-two books in one volume; likewise, a Bible divided among fourteen volumes.

Of the books of Saint Jerome: on Isaiah; likewise, on Isaiah; on the Psalms; an exposition of Leviticus; his shorter works [Col. 1258C] on Jeremiah, the Twelve Prophets, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, and Ezekiel; the Episcopal Book; a commentary on Matthew; an exposition on Mark; “On Illustrious Men”; on the whole Psalter; on two Epistles of Saint Paul, namely Galatians and Ephesians; on the Epistles to Titus and Philemon; a complete book of his letters; the Psalter according to the Hebrew truth; Against the heretic Jovinian; and the Apology to Pammachius; Questions on Genesis and the Book of Places; the book called *Antiomenon*; On the Seven Vengeances of Cain; On the Departure of the Children of Israel from Egypt; On Isaac; On Hosanna; On the Seraphim and the Coal; On the Death of King Uzziah; On the Prodigal Son; On the Nature of Things; On Rhetoric. [Col. 1258D] All these are in one volume. A Gospel written in Greek and Latin. These are twenty-two books.

Of the books of Saint Augustine: his Hexaemeron against the Manichaeans and other heretics; Decades of Psalms; his letters; a complete exposition on the Gospel of John; another exposition by the younger Augustine; On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount; On the Ten Plagues; On the Ten Commandments, in one volume; on the Epistle of the Apostle John; Harmony of the Gospels; On the City of God; Enchiridion; On the Nature and Origin of the Soul; On Christian Doctrine; Augustine’s Mirror; Confessions; Hypomnesticon; On the Ten Strings and the Good of Marriage; On the Art of Music; On the Preservation of Virginity; and his sermons; On the Twelve Abuses; the Questions of Orosius; and Augustine’s Answers, in one [Col. 1259A] volume; Against Heretics; On the Christian Contest; On Blasphemy against the Spirit; Rufinus’s Explanation; On the Twelve Blessings of the Patriarchs, in one volume; On the Trinity; On Seeing God; On the Formation of the First Human Being; On Definitions of Ecclesiastical Doctrines; and the letters of Saint Fulgentius, in one volume; On the Teacher; On Holy Virginity; and the Academics, in one volume; Augustine’s shorter works and letters to Pelagius and Valentinus, and Prosper’s replies, in one volume; an explanation by Augustine, Julian, and Paul, On the Parts of Speech, in one volume. These are twenty-nine books.

Of the books of Saint Gregory: exposition on Ezekiel, three volumes; *Moralia*, five volumes; forty homilies, two volumes; the Pastoral Rule; Dialogues; Register; Ecclesiastical Order; the Book of Parterius; On His Sayings. [Col. 1259B] These are fifteen books.

Of the books of Isidore: Etymologies; On the Wheels; Prologues; On the Wheels and Offices; likewise Prologues; likewise On the Wheels; treatise on the Pentateuch, on Kings, on Ruth, and on Ezra, in one volume; two volumes of Sentences; Synonyms. These are nine books.

Of the books of Origen: sixteen homilies on Genesis, in two volumes; on the Song of Songs, in two volumes. These are four books.

Of Hilary: On Faith in the Holy Trinity; questions of Hilary, Cyprian, Alcimus Avitus, Jerome, and Augustine on the Pentateuch, in one volume. These are two books.

Of John Chrysostom: thirty-three homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews; On Compunction of Heart against the Novatians; [Col. 1259C] On Fasting; his sixty-two sermons; and the Life of Saint Ambrose, in one volume. These are seven books.

Of Cassiodorus: on the whole Psalter.

Of Fulgentius: fourteen books, each of which omits one letter in succession.

Of Bede: On Solomon’s Temple; his Thirty Questions on Kings, with Justus’s exposition on the Song of Songs, in one volume; on the Proverbs of Solomon; on the Book of Tobit; on Mark; on Luke; on the Acts of the Apostles; on the Catholic Epistles; on the five books of Moses; on Revelation; on Habakkuk, with glosses on the Pentateuch; On the Nature of Things; On Times. These are sixteen books.

Of various authors: Julius, On Divine Authority; [Col. 1259D] Eugippius, an extract from the books of Saint Augustine; Paschasius, On the Holy Spirit; Primasius, on Revelation; four books of Timothy, together with Peregrinus’s treatise against heretics and the letters of Theophilus to the bishops of all Egypt, in one volume; Arnobius’s exposition on the whole Psalter; eight books of Gregory Nazianzen; and Augustine’s homilies on joy and grace, in one volume; Athanasius on Leviticus. These are eight books.

Of the canons: the Canons of the Apostles and of the Council of Nicaea; the Twelve Councils and the Decretals of the Apostles, in one volume; canons collected from various councils, two volumes; Caecilius Cyprian, On the Canons and Institutions of Churchmen, eighty-seven [chapters], in one volume; Pope Gelasius, On Books to Be Received and Not Received; fifty-five letters of various persons, in one [Col. 1260A] volume; a homiliary of the holy Fathers for the yearly cycle—Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, Origen, Leo, John, Fulgentius, and Bede—in one volume; likewise homilies of the holy Fathers for the yearly cycle, in three volumes; homilies of Saint Agnes; Boethius, On the Consolation of Philosophy; Gregory, bishop of Tours, On the Generation of Adam and On the Deeds of the Franks; Philip’s exposition on Job; glosses of the holy Fathers on the Psalms, three volumes; Cassian, On the Incarnation of the Lord; Justus’s exposition on the Song of Songs and Bishop Eucherius’s book On the Eclipse of the Sun and Moon; Lives or Passions of holy apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins; and conferences of various Fathers in eighteen volumes; Julianus Pomerius’s exposition and the *Prognosticon*, in two volumes; Pelagius’s exposition on the thirteen Epistles of Paul; [Col. 1260B] an exposition by an unnamed author on the Epistle to the Romans; glosses from the sayings of the Fathers, in three volumes; likewise glosses of the Fathers, three volumes; the book of Pope Martin; the Rule of Saint Benedict, six copies; the Rules of Saint Augustine, Fructuosus, and Isidore, one volume; homilies of Caesarius, bishop of Arles; Saint Jerome’s exposition of the Catholic faith; sayings of Isidore On the Heresies of Jews and Christians and On Philosophers and Poets; letters of Cyril, Leo, Dionysius, and others On the Reckoning of Easter; and Easter cycles, in one volume; the Debate on the Law between Simon the Jew and Theophilus the Christian; Ephrem, On the Day of Judgment; Alcuin to Charles, On Faith in the Trinity and On the Incarnation of the Lord; letters of Charles to the emperor of the Greeks; seven Psalters; Questions on the Seven Liberal Arts; a collection by an unnamed author on Matthew; a [Col. 1260C] Scottish collection, whose first item is on charity and whose final item begins, “Run; do not spare”; the Book of Sparks. These are seventy books.

All the codices of the cloister’s theological books total 195.

Of the books of grammarians: Donatus; Pompeius; Probus, On Feet and Syllables; Priscian; Comminianus; Servius; Victorinus Mar . . .; Diomedes; Verus Longinus; Taduivus; Marcus Tullius Cicero, two books of rhetoric—all in four volumes; Prosper; Aratus; Sedulius; Juvencus; the Epigrams of Prosper; the verses of Proba; and half of Fortunatus, in one volume; Quintus Serenus, On Medicines; the Fables of Avienus; Virgil; his Eclogues with glosses; Aldhelm; the verse work of an unnamed author on the Old and New Testament, together with the metrical Life of Cosmas and Damian [Col. 1260D] in one volume. These are twenty-six books.

Of books by ancient authors who wrote on the deeds of kings or the situation of lands: the complete Josephus; Pliny the Second, On the Customs and Life of the Emperors; the Epitome of Pompeius; Aethicus, On the Description of the World; the history of Homer, containing Dictys [Note: [Col. 1259D] “Containing Dictys.” Thus Baluze emended it; the printed text had “where he says.”] and Dares the Phrygian; the histories of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret; the books of Philo the Jew, one volume; Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History; Jerome’s Chronicles, two volumes; the History of Jordanes; On the Sum of Times and On the Origin and Deeds of the Romans, one volume; Roman Law; the Pact of Salic Law. These are fifteen books. Likewise, one volume containing sermons for the Nativity of the Lord, Stephen, and the Innocents; [Col. 1261A] *Bodanicum*; the glossed Parts of Donatus; the Book of *Logoi* (Λογῶν), that is, Greek or Latin Discourses; the Genealogy of the Bible; the Passion of the Lord in Theodisc [Germanic] and Latin. These are six books.

Of the books of the sacristy, which serve the ministry of the altar: three Gregorian missals; one Gregorian and Gelasian missal arranged in modern times by Alcuin; five lectionaries of Epistles and Gospels, arranged partly in mixture and partly in order; nineteen Gelasian missals; four Gospel texts; one written entirely in golden letters; one complete lectionary arranged by the aforesaid Alcuin; six antiphonaries. These are thirty-five books.

Thus all the codices together total 256, provided that books are not counted individually [Col. 1261B] but as codices, since, as noted above, diverse books are often contained in one codex. If we counted these separately, they would exceed five hundred in number. Such are the riches of the cloister; such are the treasures of heavenly life, nourishing the soul with sweetness. Through them, that salutary saying was fulfilled among the people of Centula: “Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love vices.”

But now let us also set down here a list of the external goods and briefly note the estates which at that time served the monastery of Christ’s outstanding soldier Richarius. Whoever wishes to know the revenues of the estates should consult the codex written on this subject, for it cannot all be set down here because of its size. These, therefore, are the estates of Saint Richarius: Buniacum, Valles, Drusiacum, [Col. 1261C] Novavilla, Gaspannae, Guibrentium, Bagardas, Curticella, Crux, Civinocurtis, Haidulficurtis, Maris, Nialla, Langradus, Alteia, Rochonis-mons, Sidrunis, Concilio, Buxudis, and Ingoaldicurtis. Among these were some, though few, in which certain military men held some benefit of Saint Richarius. But these are the estates in the direct lordship of the same saint, without any admixture of benefice or other authority: Pontias, Altisgnico, Tulino, Durcaptum, Abbatis-villa, Forest-monastery, Majocch, Saint Medard, Alliacus, Longavilla, Altvillaris, Rebellis-mons, and Valerias. These were regarded not so much as estates as towns—or, so to speak, cities—since no force of injustice was inflicted upon them.

In the forest cell there are three churches: the first of Saint [Col. 1261D] Mary, the second of Saint Peter, and the third of Saint Richarius. There are five altars ornamented with gold and silver; one silver crown; one gold-ornamented reliquary; three gold-ornamented crosses; one reliquary fashioned of gold and gems; one small silver cross ornamented with gold; six other gilded crosses; five gilded altar ornaments; one canopy ornamented with gold and silver; six candlesticks ornamented with gold and silver; one gilded fan; one gilded *fuscellum* [uncertain object]; one silver cup; two gilded ivory tablets; three large gold-ornamented chalices; four smaller silver chalices; eight silver and three gilded offertory vessels; one silver ewer; one silver Gospel-book case; fifteen rather precious chasubles; five dalmatics; two small silk chasubles; three *hrocci* of cloth; four woolen *hrocci*; twenty-seven white garments; nine stoles; fourteen *fanones*; [Col. 1262A] two *boculares*; two basins; six pairs of sandals with stockings; fifty-one books. The estate of Dulciana-vallis belongs to the lighting of the church. There are thirty canons there, who have for their stipends four estates—namely Eghod, Saint Vigilius, and two *mansioniles*—and the church of Saint Martin; they also receive certain revenues in other estates of Saint Richarius.

There is also a cell called Botritium in the district of the people of Thérouanne. It contains one furnished altar; three crosses, two gilded and one silvered; eighteen furnished reliquaries; one censer; two ornamented candlesticks; two bronze vessels; four silver chalices; two silver patens, one gilded; one silver cup; one offertory vessel; one covering-cloth; one chasuble; one dalmatic; one missal; one lectionary; one antiphonary; one homiliary; one passionary; [Col. 1262B] one Psalter. There are ten canons there, holding the estate of Teones, the estate of Neudum, two churches, the estate of Albitrium, the estate of Guadannia, and many other revenues from the benefice of Saint Richarius, whom they serve.

There is another cell in the district of Amiens, called Incra, where there are ten furnished reliquaries, three furnished crosses, two chasubles, two dalmatics, two ornamented candlesticks, the books of Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Kings, the Prophets, and the Proverbs of Solomon, one missal, one lectionary, and one antiphonary. There are twelve canons there, who have a tenth and a ninth part, and one mill, for their food. The estate itself serves the monastery of Centula and has 180 occupied holdings. The estate of Flamiriaca, Catiacus-villa, Montes, Vadimiacus, and Loacas—all these [Col. 1262C] were subject to Saint Richarius.

But let us now recite the names of those who held benefices from Saint Richarius, and who, with the soldiers subject to them, served our abbot and the ministers of the church quite nobly by land and sea, or wherever any of the brethren of the holy place needed their company:

Heligaudus, Mainfridus, Itherus, Hubertus, Bertuinus, Alguala, Berlandus, Ratuinus, Gisloldus, Lantgerus, Hardradus, Algodus, Geroldus, Israhel, Harbertus, Amalbertus, Droptulfus, Milo, Hrodinus, Gutheus, Grinarius, Helmericus, Beringarius, Adalelmus, Aldricus, Heriulfus, Godeardus, Teutsinus, Sigefridus, Hildegarinus, Helmericus, Otlaricus, Hildelandus, Landricus, Regueguardus, Gualcerdeos, Rohingus, Gualterus, Ingelbertus, Fredenertus, [Col. 1262D] Ombertus, Gualbertus, Madelguarius, Egfridus, Tredico, Eremboldus, Odelricus, Guandelmarus, Leodricus, Ermenardus, Framericus, Boso, Guntselmus, Zacharias, Gosbertus, Hatto, Harfridus, Flodeneus, Guandelmarus, Regemfridus, Gualcarius, Odilo, Godefridus, Herembordus, Restrudus, Adico, Amalfridus, Adelfridus, Ingrannus, Deodatus, Fronulfus, Regembertus, Aschelo, Berharius, Framericus, Odfulcus, Ermengarius, Eginboldus, Cuaringandus, Bonothus, Gondacher, Odo, Amalricus, Altmarus, Lambertus, Raimbertus, Fulchramnus, Hysail, Onulfus, Emlinus, Bero, Regemlandus, Alguinus, Rogherus, Leutbrandus, Berlaicus, Salomon, Meginarius, Guilgeradus, Donatianus.

These are the names of the soldiers serving the monastery of the most blessed [Col. 1263A] Richarius. The abbot or provosts took them everywhere with them; and, according to custom, they were always present at the monastery on the feast day of Saint Richarius, at the Nativity of the Lord, at the Resurrection, and at Pentecost. Each was carefully equipped according to his means, and by their gathering they made our church almost into a royal court.

It would be long and excessively burdensome for us to recount here the estates, lands, various possessions, and revenues which they held from the benefice of Saint Richarius, especially since a volume fully treating these matters is preserved among us. Whoever wishes to know them may obtain his knowledge from that volume.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning Abbot Helisachar

[Col. 1263B]

After Abbot Hericus had been removed from human affairs, Helisachar, a man of distinguished renown, succeeded to the rank of abbot. They say that he was also a *nector* [one who joined or linked] of the monastery of Jumièges, because of the brotherhood of mutual love which we commended much earlier. He was distinguished by the pursuit of great holiness and advanced to such strictness of the highest religious observance that he entirely forbade women access from the entrance of the monastery. By the merit of his great holiness he pleased the Lord, and, as may be discerned from the event itself, he remained dear to the holy confessor, because in his time, through God’s grace, many great miracles occurred at the tomb of the saint’s most sacred body. Some of these must here be set down to the praise [Col. 1263C] of our Lord God.

And so that it may be known that Almighty God, in granting the benefits of miracles, does not always regard only the merits of His saints or the faith of those who ask, but sometimes also considers the worthiness of those who see them—worthiness, I mean, not the lofty rank of earthly honor but the sincerity of minds—for miracles not occurring before our eyes is prevented not only by the weakness of faith in those who ask, but our own wickedness also stands in the way. By it we are sometimes foul in God’s sight and are judged unworthy to behold great things. Great, therefore, was this venerable abbot in the merit of his life, to whom the almighty and merciful Lord granted, through the glorious merits of His most faithful servant Richarius, the sight of great things. These matters stand thus.

A certain head of a household in Burgundy, very eminent for wealth but deprived of children, had an only daughter, his sole child [Col. 1263D], afflicted with paralysis. After carrying her through many shrines of saints in hope of receiving the grace of health, he was warned in a vision and brought her, with a large retinue, to the venerable shrine of Saint Riquier. There he stayed for the saint’s feast, celebrated on the seventh Ides of October, awaiting the salvation promised from heaven to his daughter. Since, under the regulation instituted at that time by the aforesaid Abbot Helisachar, women were not allowed even to approach the thresholds of the monastery, she could not be brought inside but remained outside beneath tents that had been spread.

On that day, after the solemn celebration of the Masses, the brothers, out of charity and in token of honour, sent the woman a blessing from Saint Riquier’s wine. Though she was held by dreadful paralysis and had never [Col. 1264A] spoken or taken food into her mouth, as soon as she drank that wine she at once received such complete health that she immediately sprang up and, in her joy, herself served the others. Proclaiming to all the saint’s love and praise, she returned home on horseback, not as an infirm woman but as one truly restored to health.

In the little village of Villare there was a certain prostitute, Olgia, a snare for souls. God gave her the recompense she deserved: she suffered a contraction and twisting of all her limbs, so that her face itself, in an unnatural manner, looked backward. Her relatives, pitying her, brought her to Riquier, the skilled chief physician, and there she was wholly healed. Yet though her body was healed, her mind remained sick in its will, as she again wallowed in her former crimes. This deed of hers did not escape the divine eye; her wickedness having returned, [Col. 1264B] the judgment also returned. She was therefore contracted again in the likeness of her earlier affliction and—what was worse—deprived of the power of speech. Then her relatives, not despairing of the physician’s power, brought her back to seek the patron’s aid. Thus she was healed and reformed, lest, if she sinned further, she should thereafter be punished more hopelessly. There are indeed many other great things which we might recount; but since a little book worthily setting them forth is kept in our archives, let these suffice here: elsewhere other things will be told.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Abbot Ribbodo and the translation of Saint Angilbert

When the venerable Helisachar, after serving not many years in office, had been taken from this wicked world, the distinguished Abbot Ribbodo adorned the community of Centula with his pastoral care. While he administered the affairs of the monastery, Emperor Louis of blessed memory, having reigned for twenty-six years, died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 840, in the third indiction. Among his great and royal works, he is said to have gone to Constantinople and brought back from there great and wondrous relics. Distributing them among holy places, he entrusted them to posterity for veneration. Since the church of Saint Riquier was then considered inferior to no church in Gaul in honour, glory, or religious observance, he bestowed upon this place a great portion of those relics: namely, a sandal of the Lord Christ; the tip of the spear by which the side of the same Lord was opened; ten stones of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, stained with blood, by which that martyr was killed; and [Col. 1264D] an ampulla filled with that saint’s blood.

This Augustus had by Queen Ermengard three sons: Lothair, Pippin, and Louis; and by the Empress Judith he had the glorious King Charles. After their father’s death disputes arose among the brothers, as each desired the empire for himself. While these matters were in progress and events tended toward conflict, it was decided that they should enter battle, and that he to whom fortune granted victory should be regarded as king or emperor. Accordingly Lothair, having joined Pippin to himself, led an army against his brothers Charles and Louis in the district of Auxerre, at the place called Fontenoy. There the Franks and the nations subject to them struck one another down in mutual slaughter, until at last [Col. 1265A] Louis and Charles, having put Lothair to flight, gained the victory.

As has been said, Ribbodo was then abbot over the monastery of Centula. Seeing that the holy body of the most holy Abbot Angilbert rested in a place through which those entering the church necessarily walked, he was deeply grieved that so great and such a man should be trodden upon by the daily passage of people. Judging it right that a man of God should rest within God’s house, he raised his holy remains and translated them into the basilica of Saint Riquier on the Nones of November. He had rested in the former place for twenty-eight years; yet, by God’s action, who displayed the merit of His servant, his holy body was found so whole and free from decay as though the soul had left it that very hour. A fragrance of wondrous sweetness is also affirmed to have abounded there. The histories of the Franks—those, that is, which record the events of that period—bear witness to this certain fact.

For when a certain little book had at some time come into the hands of our brethren, after some other matters concerning Saint Angilbert they noted these words written there:

> “After the death of Emperor Louis, son of Charles the Great, his three sons, Lothair, Louis, and Charles, disputed among themselves concerning the kingdom, as each strove to secure it for himself. [lacuna] At last a day was fixed on which judgment was to be made concerning these matters, and it was thought this could be done on the Nones of November. On that day a great earthquake occurred throughout nearly all this Gaul; and on that day Angilbert, a man of memorable worth, was translated at Centula, and in the twenty-eighth year after his death [Col. 1265C] was found with his body undecayed, without aromatic substances.”

The same book, repeating something said above, adds a few words concerning his nobility:

> “He was born at that time from a family not unknown. Madhelgaud, Richard, and he were of one lineage and were deservedly held in high esteem by Charles the Great. Angilbert by the king’s daughter, named Bertha, begot Harnid, my brother, and me, Nithard. At Centula he built a wondrous work in honour of almighty God and Saint Riquier; he governed wonderfully the household entrusted to him; and after a life ended in every happiness he rested in peace at Centula.”

The same Nithard, son of Lord Angilbert, is said to have presided over this monastery after his father’s death. Having governed only a very few days, he was killed in battle and was granted burial beside his father. After he had rested there for several years, and long after the body of Saint Angilbert had been translated into the church, certain devout persons placed Nithard’s body in his father’s sarcophagus.

At the place where Lord Ribbodo placed Saint Angilbert, the following epitaph was set up:

> In this tomb rests the ever-memorable Abbot  
> Angilbert; rejoicing in spirit, he dwells among the stars.  
> He died on the twenty-second day before the Kalends of March.  
> He built the church in which his tomb is kept.  
>
> [Col. 1266A] He flourished in the time of the great Emperor Charles,  
> Renowned for learning, companion of princes.  
> He commanded that he be buried before the church doors;  
> Abbot Ribbodo brought him here and placed him here.  
> Twenty-eight years after his death,  
> His body was found whole in an extraordinary manner.

## CHAPTER VI. The privilege of Lothair

After that most bloody battle mentioned above, peace having been made among the brothers, they divided the empire of the Franks between themselves. Lothair received the kingdom of the Romans, all Italy, the eastern part of Francia—which, borrowing its name from him, is called Lotharingia—and the whole of Provence. This Lothair had been anointed emperor eighteen years before his father’s death. Louis, besides Norica which he already held, possessed Alemannia, Thuringia, Austrasia, Saxony, and the kingdom of the Huns. Charles possessed the western half of Francia and all Neustria, Brittany, most of Burgundy, Gothia, Gascony, and Aquitaine. Since the monastery of Saint Riquier lay within his dominion, he honoured it with the greatest privileges and enlarged it with gifts, as will be shown in what follows, with God’s help.

At that time a certain duke named Hugh gave Saint Riquier several estates of his own property for the salvation of his soul. After the gift had been made, he approached King Lothair, asking him to confirm by the authority of his precept the estates of Rollenicurt and [Col. 1266C] Botritium, so that in future they might remain subject to the saint’s service without legal challenge. Yet in the description partially quoted above it is found that these same estates had served the monastery of the saint, and it is clear that someone had taken them away, since this duke was now restoring them.

> **Note:** [Col. 1265D] “Lothair” is mistaken and misleads others. For the privilege published here belongs neither to Emperor Lothair nor to his namesake son, but to Lothair, king of the Franks, to whom was born Louis, the last king of the Franks from the line of Charles [Col. 1266D]. The Duke Hugh mentioned in that privilege is the same man who reigned after Louis, ancestor of the illustrious line which happily reigns to this day.

Lothair therefore treated him most favourably, for he had married his daughter Ermengard. He confirmed the authority of his grant over the requested estates in these very words:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Lothair, by the mercy of divine providence king of the Franks. If we grant the assent of our kindness to the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we perform works befitting royal majesty; and by this means we confidently believe that we shall more easily attain the glory of eternal blessedness.
>
> “Therefore let the diligence of all faithful people of the holy Church of God and of ours, present as well as future, know that Duke Hugh, wholly faithful to us, together with the religious monks of the monastery of Centula, of the most illustrious confessor of Christ Riquier, having approached the serenity of our highness, asked that we should fully confirm by an imperial precept certain estates of the abbey of Saint Riquier which Duke Hugh himself had added for the maintenance and use of the monks, for the remedy of his soul, so that they might never be removed from them through any diminution by any abbot or any person whatsoever.
>
> “We have graciously heard their petitions for the love of God and of His aforesaid soldier Saint Riquier, and also for love of our dearest kinsman Duke Hugh; and we wish it to be known that we have granted them everything accordingly. Indeed, we have ordered this document of our authority to be made under this special condition: that we grant and confirm for the maintenance and use of the monks serving Christ in the aforesaid [Col. 1267B] place the aforesaid estates situated in the district of Targonne—namely Botritium with all its entirety, and also the estate of Rolleni in the said district with all its appurtenances, and whatever appears justly and lawfully to belong to the aforesaid places—as has been established by the aforesaid duke and the abbot of the same place.
>
> “That is to say, no one may ever take away anything from those estates from their possession, diminish it, or convert it to other uses; nor may anyone in any way presume to exact *paratae*, *lidimonium*, *hostilicium*, or any other payments. Rather, as has been stated, they shall hold them securely and possess them peacefully in our time and that of our successors, in the manner and under the terms established by us and the aforesaid duke, so that those servants of God serving the Lord in the aforesaid monastery may delight to implore without ceasing the mercy of the most merciful Judge for the salvation of our father, the prosperity of ourselves, our consort and offspring, and the stability of our kingdom.
>
> “And that this authority may retain inviolable and unshaken force in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.
>
> “Done at the royal palace of Compiègne, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 843, in the sixth indiction, in the twenty-first year of the reign of the most glorious King Lothair.
>
> “The sign of Lord Lothair, most glorious king.
>
> “I, Adalbero, royal notary acting in place of Lord Adalbero, archbishop of Reims and chief chancellor, have examined it.”

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Abbot Louis

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 844, the fourth year of Charles’s reign, the sixth indiction, and the pontificate of Sergius, pope of the Roman Church, after Ribbodo, abbot of Centula, had died, the glorious man Louis assumed charge of that monastery. He was endowed with both divine and secular wisdom. [Col. 1267D] He was descended from royal stock and transferred the nobility of his illustrious lineage into the nobility of religious life, so that, just as his parents, relatives, and brothers shone in purple and diadems, he might shine in God’s sight through the virtue of his soul.

Before he became abbot, however, the brothers of our monastery had approached the royal clemency and shown it the precept of the divine Augustus Louis, which he had issued concerning the estates of this holy place, asking that he too should do the same and issue an authoritative precept of his power concerning those estates. Charles, king of western Francia, whose assent they respectfully requested, therefore agreed and, favouring God’s servants, granted them the authority of his precept, drawn up in these words:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by God’s grace king. If we grant the assent of our kindness to the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we perform works befitting royal majesty, and thereby confidently believe that we shall more easily attain the glory of eternal blessedness.
>
> “Therefore let the diligence of all faithful people of the holy Church of God and of ours, present as well as future, know that the religious monks of the monastery of Centula, of the most illustrious confessor of Christ Riquier, having approached the serenity of our highness, laid before our excellence the authorization of the Lord Caesar Augustus Louis, our father of glorious memory. It records how that same lord and father of ours granted to them certain estates of the abbey of Saint Riquier assigned for the use and maintenance of those monks, and fully confirmed them by an imperial precept so that they might never be taken from them through diminution by any abbot or any person whatsoever.
>
> “Accordingly, the same monks begged our Magnitude that we should deign to confirm anew or renew through an instrument of our excellence the imperial authorization of our lord and father. We have graciously heard their requests and wish all to know that we have granted everything to them accordingly. Indeed, we have ordered this document of our authority to be made under this special condition: that we grant and confirm for the maintenance and use of the monks serving Christ in the aforesaid place the estates named Civinocurt with Bronoil, Aldulficurt, Valles, Drussiacum, Novavilla, [Col. 1268C] Mont-des-Anges, Guibrentium, Bagardas, Curticella, Crux, Langoratum, Altegium, Sidrude, Nivielle, Verculf, Concilium, Roconis-mons, and Maris, together with whatever appears at the present time justly and lawfully to belong to the aforesaid places, as established by our lord and father.
>
> “No one may ever take anything from those estates out of their possession, diminish it, convert it to other uses, or in any way presume to demand *paratae*, *lidimonium*, *hostilicium*, or any other payments. Rather, as stated above, they shall hold them securely in our time and that of our successors, and possess them peacefully in the manner and under the terms established by our most pious father, the emperor, so that those servants of God serving the Lord in the aforesaid monastery may delight to implore unceasingly the mercy of the most merciful Judge for the salvation of that same father of ours, the prosperity of ourselves, our consort and offspring, and the stability of our kingdom.
>
> “And that this authority may retain inviolable and unshaken force in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.
>
> “The sign of Charles, most glorious king.
>
> “I, Meginarius, notary acting in place of Louis, have examined and subscribed it.
>
> “Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth year of the reign of the most serene Lord King Charles, in the sixth indiction.
>
> [Col. 1269A] “Done at the royal palace of Compiègne, happily in God’s name. Amen.”

At the beginning of the fifth year of Charles’s reign, Abbot Louis sent his monks, over whom he had recently been placed, to the king so that he might again confirm by an authoritative precept those estates which Louis had acquired and received by royal gift. They obediently carried out their abbot’s command and again entreated King Charles to reconfirm the authority of royal power, as his father and the king himself had done shortly before. Charles willingly and graciously granted the request. In this privilege he recorded the estates which he had already confirmed in the preceding one, adding those which the industry of the most illustrious abbot sought to have confirmed: namely, the cell of Forestis and all belonging to it, together with certain other properties, which the charter itself clearly sets out as follows:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by God’s grace king. If [we grant the requests] of God’s servants, etc., as in the preceding [charter].
>
> “At the will and with the permission of our beloved kinsman Louis, abbot of the same sacred monastery, the religious monks of the monastery of Centula, of the most illustrious confessor of Christ Riquier, having approached the serenity of our highness, etc., as above.
>
> “We have graciously heard their petitions in view of God, and at the request of the aforesaid venerable and beloved kinsman Abbot Louis, and wish all to know that we have granted them everything accordingly. Indeed, we have ordered this document of our authority to be made under this special condition: that we grant and confirm the aforesaid estates—Civinicurt with Bronoil and Argovillare; Adulficurt; Valles; Drusciacum; Novavilla; Mont-des-Anges; Guibrentium; Bagardas; Curticella; Crux; Langaratum; Alteia, called Abbatisam; Concilium; Verculf with the *seticae* at Ragineri’s enclosure and the lands belonging to it; Roconis-mons with the *seticae* and lands situated at Asflariae, Sacrocampus, and Petronutius; the precarial holding of Hegfrid, to pass after his death; Nigella; Sidrude; the chapel in the estate of Maris with the *mansi* belonging to it; and also the cell called Forestis with the estates belonging to it, which the venerable Abbot Louis has added for the monks’ maintenance.
>
> “Their names are as follows: Argubius with the settlement called Romamgilis, and the small benefices of Nortbert and Guicbald situated in the same settlement; Bonella with the benefices of Angaltius and Godolard; likewise the estate called Saint-Vigilius, with Berniacus, Accinicurt, and Euholt. In the district of Beauvais, at the place called Gellis, six *seticae* and eight *aripennes* of vineyard; at Rivirtsicurt, two *seticae* and six *aripennes* of vineyard; at Quentovic, two *seticae*; at Mosultre, one *mansus*; at Asco, three *seticae*; and at Avisnis, one *mansus*.
>
> [Col. 1270A] “On this condition: those who now hold benefices from the aforesaid properties shall retain them until they either obtain elsewhere other properties in exchange for those benefices, or die; unless, perhaps, the abbot has first taken them from them because of their fault. Thereafter the brothers shall receive them without any claim being raised. The monks shall also, under their care and direction, devoutly provide for twelve canons in that same cell, supplying their due and necessary maintenance. From the woodland which appears to belong to that cell called Forestis, they shall provide, according to the abbot’s judgment and direction, whatever is needed for the needs of the greater monastery.
>
> “All these things, and whatever at the present time justly and lawfully belongs to the aforesaid places, etc.
>
> “The sign of Charles, most glorious king.
>
> “I, Jonas, deacon acting in place of Louis, have examined and subscribed it.
>
> “Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the fifth year, the seventh indiction, of the reign of Charles, most glorious king.
>
> [Col. 1270B] “Done at the royal palace of Compiègne, happily in God’s name. Amen.”

## CHAPTER VIII. The removal and return of Saint Riquier

While Louis presided over the monastery of Centula, many monasteries near the sea and prosperous estates lost their former splendour through fear of the wicked Danes, whom the Seine nourished in those times. This report also shook the monastery, so greatly that it was necessary for not only the church’s property but even its incorruptible treasure—the body of Saint Riquier himself—to take flight. The brothers took it, left a few guards of the place behind, [Col. 1270C] and departed. Scattered abroad, they remained away from the monastery for about three weeks.

But when, by God’s will, the Danes departed and sought other kingdoms, the brothers brought the saint of the Lord back to his own place. The people of Ponthieu came out to meet their returning patron and rejoiced beyond expression at his restored presence. Almighty God, to kindle a still greater love for His saint in the hearts of the people of Ponthieu, worked two great miracles during this return.

A certain nobleman, Gotselm, was held by paralysis and deprived of the use of all his limbs. Carried by the help of his people, he came out to meet the returning holy confessor; and as soon as he saw the saint’s bier, he was immediately freed from every affliction and received the health he had desired, perfectly and completely.

Another man, of low birth, named Magimbert, suffered from dropsy. Useless for every task, unless someone else moved him he always sat in one place like a log. Others urged him to go out to meet the returning saint and seek his health from him. When he refused and pleaded impossibility, they took him and carried him to meet the saint. As the procession of brothers bringing back the saint approached from the opposite direction, the sick man cried out that someone was trampling on him. Afterwards it seemed to him that hot water was being poured over him; and so he was wholly healed.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Abbot-Count Hruodulf

After several years, when Abbot [Col. 1271A] Louis had died, the abbey of Centula had as its ruler the distinguished Hruodulf, an imperial man, most highly endowed both with divine philosophy and secular wisdom. Although he was uncle to the most glorious King Charles, he despised worldly glory in order to serve the Lord nobly, as one most noble. He was elected abbot by the brothers of Centula, among whom he was a companion in their religious purpose. Having undertaken this office at the king’s request, he received, by the gift and request of the same King Charles—his nephew—the county of the maritime province, for, as we have said, he was highly skilled not only in spiritual pursuits but also in practical judgment. Thus our monastery was adorned by Hruodulf as abbot; the commonwealth in turn shone through Hruodulf as count.

By his generosity our church then acquired six excellent estates, named below. Like the preceding abbots, he also sent monks to the king, so that the king might again confirm by an authoritative instrument of his power those estates and others concerning which future legal challenge was feared. This was done. The brothers approached the royal majesty bearing their uncle’s request; and he, as was his custom, graciously complied and confirmed for them the following precept:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by God’s grace king. If [we grant the requests] of God’s servants, etc., as above.
>
> “Since, with the will and permission of our beloved uncle Hruodulf, ruler of the sacred monastery of Centula, the monks of the same monastery of the most illustrious [confessor of Christ Riquier], etc.
>
> “Moved by divine prompting and by the request of our aforesaid uncle, Abbot Hruodulf, we have graciously heard their petitions and wish all to know that we have granted everything accordingly. Indeed, we have ordered this document of our authority to be made under this special condition: that we grant and confirm the aforesaid estates—Civinicurt with Broniol and Arcovillare; Hardulficurt; Valles; Drusciacum with the church of Cardordensis and its appurtenances; Novavilla; Mont-des-Anges; Guibrentium; Bagardas; Curticella; Crux; Langoratum; Alteia, called Abbatisam; Verculf; Concilium, with the *mansus* at Vertunno which Teutrad gave Saint Riquier in exchange for a certain property; Nialla with the small holding of Filcarii; Roconis-mons with *seticae* and lands situated at Masfiariae, [Col. 1271D] Sacrocampus, and Petronutius; and Sidrude with a full complement of all property.
>
> “Moreover, [we grant] that which a man named Ragembert held by beneficial right in exchange for the cell of Forestis, which they have hitherto held under the authority of our precept: in accordance with need, their petition, and the consent of our aforesaid uncle Hruodulf, namely Argubium with its appurtenances; Upper Longum; Spania; Hadardivillare; Habacurt; at Hambiaca-villa, one church with two *mansi*; one small holding called Ponticulis; and at Buxide one *mansus* with its full entirety; together with whatever now justly and lawfully belongs to these additions, exchanges, and aforesaid places, as established by our lord and father, etc.
>
> “The sign of Charles, most glorious king.
>
> “I, Aeneas, notary acting in place of Louis, have examined and subscribed it.
>
> “Given on the second day before the Kalends of March, in the third indiction, in the sixteenth year of the reign of Charles, most glorious king.
>
> “Done at the royal palace of Germigny, happily in God’s name. Amen.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1269] “After several years.” Acherius found the following in the margin of his manuscript: “After Lord Louis, Lord Nithard is said to have presided [Col. 1271D]; and because a severe persecution by the pagans then pressed upon them, he also took up the county of the maritime [Col. 1272D] coast.” The same words are read in the Centula manuscript.

Thus the venerable Abbot and Count Hruodulf, after governing the monastery and the maritime provinces for some years, departed from the mockery of this world when God called him, to receive the sweet things of paradise in return for his faithful administration. The brothers, deeply saddened by his death, prepared a mortuary roll and sent it through churches and holy places, announcing the death of their beloved father and asking that prayers be offered for him. It pleased us to mention this because the letter of that very roll, still surviving in our own age among the ancient records of the holy place, gives the brothers a welcome reading. The letter of his roll is as follows:

> “The brothers of the monastery of Saint Riquier of glorious memory earnestly ask all soldiers of Christ: deal fraternally with our deceased brethren, and likewise send us the names of your dead. Let the day of arrival of the present messenger coming to you be made known through the records of the calendar, lest he be able to deceive us through the tricks of his deceit. Let him also know to announce together those who appear to hold the office of abbot, provost, or dean.
>
> “Lord Hruodulf, our count and at the same time our abbot, died among us on the eighth Ides of January. Therefore strive before the Lord for him, so that you may receive your reward and he may be gathered into the assembly of the righteous, supported by your most holy assistance. We judge it right that, since we had him as a most loving father, we should continually ask the merciful Lord for him with the tender love of sons.”

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Abbot-Count Heligaud

When Hruodulf had entered upon the way of all flesh, Count Heligaud assumed the governance of the people of Centula. [Col. 1272D] He passed from a secular countship to leadership of souls. Before he became either abbot or monk, he had served the world; he had even been married and left a son of his own flesh, Herluin by name, likewise a count—an heir indeed to worldly power, but not to monastic service.

If anyone asks why our ruler was at once abbot and count, we give the reason transmitted by our elders. At that time, with God permitting it and the sin of the Christian people demanding it, the savage peoples of the Danes and the barbarism of other nations frequently invaded the borders of the Franks and tried to drive the kings and nobles themselves from the kingdom and utterly destroy them. Ponthieu and the Vimeu then had few, if any, castles or fortifications; therefore through these regions the enemy had open access into Francia. This may be observed in this little work from two examples: when we related that Lord Nithard, son of Saint Angilbert, was killed in battle, and when we showed that in the time of Abbot Louis the holy Father Riquier had been removed from here for fear of them. Our elders have indeed affirmed that Nithard himself held both offices and, while serving on campaign without abandoning the regular rule, was killed by enemies.

Since the dog-like fury of these peoples inflicted grave evils upon the Frankish world through its repeated invasions, the kings and nobles of the Franks judged that the abbot of Centula, who possessed great glory and a great name, ought to take up the burden of calming this storm. For men of very high birth lived in this holy place, and, through the greatness of their resources and the number of their military relatives, could undertake great and difficult enterprises. Indeed, no one speaking of the noble ever sought anything nobler, if he had been told of the nobility of Saint Riquier’s monks. In this monastery were brought up dukes, counts, sons of dukes, sons of counts, and even sons of kings. Every higher dignity established anywhere throughout the kingdom of the Franks rejoiced to have the monastery of Saint Riquier as its parent.

For the reason stated, some of our abbots were at once counts and abbots. They shone with the distinction of noble descent and were observers of the sacred rule, being deemed before God to do so even in the ranks of armies.

Abbot and Count Heligaud, while governing this monastery, granted Rollenicurt and certain other properties—alas, properties which our place had only recently recovered from Duke Hugh—to a military man as a benefice for a specified period. We possess the precarial charter of this transaction.

> **Note:** [Col. 1273D] In the twentieth year of Charles.

But we set down none of those matters here, since they would furnish no increase of honour but rather material for grief. After administering the abbacy and countship for some years, he departed from human affairs.

> **Note:** [Col. 1274D] He died on the third Nones of November.

He left to abbots no longer the administration of the county, for his son Herluin took it up. Nevertheless, the laws of this Count Heligaud which he established in secular affairs are still maintained, known, and observed by the people of the province.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Lord Abbot Guelfo and the translation of Saint Riquier’s head

After Heligaud was removed by the event of death, we had as abbot—and truly as father—a man of royal descent named Guelfo. His vigour and excellence can be made clear from no few accounts. Yet anyone may plainly grasp the goodness implanted in his mind from this: as what follows will show, he was faithful and devoted toward Saint Riquier, kind toward those subject to him, and always beloved by princes. Because of his proven prudence and devotion to religious life, he remained abbot, as our own abbot was, of Saint Columba, virgin and martyr, located at Sens. The matters found to have occurred under his rule should be recounted, so that the nobility of the man may be clearly perceived in these also.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 864, in the twelfth indiction, in October, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, that abbot and the brothers translated the glorious head of Saint Riquier from a wooden shrine into a silver shrine adorned with gold and gems. For when, as stated above, the country was ravaged by barbarian attack and the brothers were forced to flee, [Col. 1274B] they had made a wooden shrine in which they placed the blessed head of Saint Riquier, so that they might carry it with them easily and lightly wherever they went.

When peace was granted and the enemies put to flight, the venerable monk Odulf was keeper of this saint. Since he pursued the most sacred Father with ardent devotion and every honour, he had made from the church’s treasures a shrine exceedingly rich in gold, silver, and precious stones, into which, as we have said, the head of their beloved patron was transferred from the wooden shrine. While this was taking place, one of the monastery’s servants, named Gerald, happened to be present. By God’s permission he had been deprived of the sight of his eyes for a year and a half. As the saint was translated, he lay praying upon the ground; while the saint’s head was reverently placed anew, a strange light returned to this man’s eyes.

The aforesaid keeper also placed in the shrine which we have mentioned many relics of saints together with the saint’s head; of these we shall shortly say a little. But since the piety of kings is found to have bestowed many things upon us, let the pen return briefly to their deeds.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning kings and the relics which Odulf the keeper obtained from every quarter
The reader will recall that above we said that Louis, son of the Emperor Louis, after engaging in conflict with his brothers, received the kingdoms of the Noricans and Alemanni, as also of the Austrasians, Saxons, and Huns. After he had vigorously governed them for forty-three years, and had begun to consider his burial, he divided his kingdom among his three sons. To Carloman he gave Noricum—that is, Bavaria—and the Marches against the Slavs and Lombards. To Louis he left Thuringia, Austrasia, the Franks, and Saxony. To Charles he left Alemannia and Curguala, that is, the county of Cornouaille. In the year of Christ’s Incarnation 865, indiction XII, after the Paschal feast, this partition of the kingdoms was made. Louis himself nevertheless happily retained supremacy over his sons for a further eleven years; and so he died.

In the year, therefore, in which he bestowed the kingdoms upon his sons, Odulf, keeper of the church of St. Riquier, asked the venerable Hilmerad, bishop of Amiens, to give him some portion of relics for the honour of God and out of love for his brethren. Enlightened by divine grace, the bishop willingly assented, and fixed the day on which he would send them. The aforesaid keeper sent his disciple, the priest Samuel, to Amiens. Having received the relics from the bishop, he brought them to Centula on the Ides of June: namely, material from the chasuble of St. Firmin, which he had worn when he was killed for Christ; bones from the knees of the blessed martyrs Fuscian, Victoricus, and Gentian; and also part of the forefinger of a most renowned and honoured confessor of Christ. Then the most devout brethren came forth from the monastery to meet them; prostrating themselves on the ground, they received them with immense joy and highest honour, and placed them in the casket in which the blessed head of St. Riquier was kept.

In the same year this same sacristan asked the brethren of St. Josse that, out of charity, they might grant him something from the body of that saint. They rejoiced that they possessed something for which the men of Centula could ask them; they very promptly complied with the keeper’s request and gave him half a finger of that saint. As was customary, our monks honourably received it and, on the Ides of December, placed it in the aforesaid casket together with the head of St. Riquier.

In the following year the same monk asked the brethren of the monastery of Fontenelle, which had very recently been newly populated, to grant to him and to our community some small portion from the bodies of the blessed Wandrille [Guandregisilus] and Ansbert. The envoy of the sacristan therefore brought the received holy relics—that is, bones and ashes—to Centula on the second Ides of February. The brethren received them with honour and placed them in the often-mentioned casket.

The aforesaid keeper Odulf asked a certain abbess, who was travelling to Valenciennes for an assembly of King Charles, to obtain for him by her intercession some gift from the relics of the venerable martyr Salvius, from the keepers of that saint. When she arrived at the place, mindful of the request she had received, she obtained from the members of that community—whose head was her son, named Hugh—a portion of the relics of the aforesaid martyr: namely, some of his blood together with hair, and also a portion of the sleeve which he wore during the sacrifice of the Lord. These were brought to Centula on 4 Non. May, reverently received by the brethren, and honourably deposited in the prescribed casket.

In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 866, indiction XIII, the aforesaid keeper obtained, through the intervention of Hilmerad, provost of St. Lucian the martyr, from Hudo, bishop of the Belgians, that he might deign to grant him something from his relics. The envoy accordingly went there and received from the aforesaid bishop relics from the hair and garment of St. Lucian, and also a certain bone from the little body of St. Justus. He brought them to the monastery of Centula on the second Ides of June. The brethren received them with hymns and praises, prostrating themselves in worship, and deposited them with the head of St. Riquier, Father of Ponthieu.

## CHAPTER XIII. Louis’s Privilege concerning Civinocourt

After this, in the following year (867), indiction XV, while the most honourable Abbot Guelfo was governing the monastery of Centula modestly and devoutly, it happened that the estate of the most holy Father Riquier, called Civinicourt, was excessively burdened by the frequent passage of foot-soldiers and horsemen. The pious ruler perceived this and reflected that, if the matter became habitual, the estate would be ruined by the excessive number of travellers. He approached King Louis, who nearly three years earlier had been established king by his father, and asked him, by an ordinance of his own authority, to forbid any travelling foot-soldier or horseman to enter the aforesaid estate for lodging.

The king assented to this venerable abbot as to a beloved kinsman, and at his request confirmed the following decree:

> “In the name of the Lord God eternal, and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, Louis, by the mercy of God king. Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own faithful, present and future, that the venerable Abbot Guelfo, our dearest kinsman, coming before our serenity, requested that, because of oppression by guests, we should order a decree of our authority to be made concerning the estate of the brethren of St. Riquier called Civinocourt: so that no one should make a lodging there, whether going against the enemy or travelling onward, but that the aforesaid estate should be free from every oppression by guests and might freely serve its lords.
>
> “We, therefore, assenting to his petitions for the love of God, the reverence of the aforesaid place, the remedy of our soul, and love for the aforesaid Abbot Guelfo, our dearest kinsman, have done so. By this decree of our authority we command and order that no one from all our kingdom may enter the aforesaid estate for any lodging without the consent of the aforesaid brethren, but that it remain free from the oppression of all guests, without any objection. If anyone, violating this our decree, should do anything of the aforesaid without permission of the brethren, he shall be compelled to pay thirty pounds of silver.
>
> “And in order that the authority of this our grant may be preserved inviolate by all for all time, we have ordered it to be sealed below with the impression of our ring.
>
> “Audacher, notary in place of Gauzlin, examined and subscribed it.
>
> “Given on the third Kalends of January, indiction XV, in the second year of the reign of the most glorious King Louis.
>
> “Done at the palace of Compiègne, happily in the name of God. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Again concerning Odulf and relics

In this same year and the same indiction, Odulf, doorkeeper of the holy shrine of the venerable Riquier, asked the brethren of Sens, from the monastery of St. Columba the virgin, in the presence of Guelfo, by God’s grace abbot of both places, that by his assent and command they might grant him something from the body of the aforesaid virgin; for some of those brethren were then residing at Centula. They most willingly favoured the petition and said that they would fulfil it if, under Christ’s protection, they could return safely to their own place. When they had returned and communicated the requests of the men of Centula to their other brethren, the latter replied with great devotion that, if anything from their place could go forth for the honour of that renowned community, they wished to give it with every generosity.

They therefore took from the sacred body of the virgin and martyr a bone from the shoulder, attached to the shoulder-blade, and sent it to the monastery of blessed Riquier. The monks of that place received the welcome gift, rendered a melody glorifying God, and placed it within the casket adorned with gold and jewels, where other relics were also deposited together with the glorious head of the most blessed Riquier.

In the same year the venerable Abbess Hruodum, chaste lover of the men of Centula, brought to the monastery of St. Riquier relics of the holy Fathers—namely, Arator, St. Paul, St. Maurus, and St. Salvius, confessor and bishop. The brethren of that place placed them, on the second Kalends of April, in the casket in which the other relics of saints had been deposited.

In the same year of Christ’s Incarnation, one of our brethren, named Samuel, happened to visit the thresholds of St. Denis. There he obtained from a priest of the city of Paris a small bone from the body of St. Vitus the martyr. He sent this also to Centula, where it was received by the brethren on the fifteenth Kalends of May and fittingly placed in the upper casket.

While Nicholas presided as pope of the Roman Church, a monk of the venerable Riquier, a prudent man named Ansegisus, carried an embassy from the most glorious King Charles to that supreme pontiff, for the common good of the holy universal Catholic Church. Ansegisus was honourably received through the generosity of so great a man. After he had set forth the matters for which he had been sent, he obtained from a certain Roman, partly by request and partly by payment, relics of saints: nearly the whole body of St. John the Martyr; the arm of St. Urban, pope; the arm of St. Alexander the Fifth, successor of the Apostolic See; the head of blessed Felicity, together with relics of her four sons; and relics of a great many saints whose names we do not list because of their number. Bringing these treasures back with him, he brought them into the treasuries of his own monastery. At last, a company of monks went out to meet them and, lying prostrate on the ground in the form of a cross, received them on the Kalends of December and honourably placed them with the head of the most holy Riquier.

The venerable Odulf again obtained from a certain servant of St. Maurice, who happened to be in Ponthieu at that time, that he might be worthy to receive something from the sacred body of the aforesaid saint. In due return for Odulf’s integrity, that man gave him a small portion from the most sacred head of the glorious martyr Maurice and a fragment of St. Exuperius’s shirt, stained with blood, which he wore when he was martyred for Christ. When these had been reverently received, the portion of St. Maurice’s head and the aforesaid portion of St. Exuperius’s undershirt were made fellow-contents of the casket with the head of blessed Riquier.

## CHAPTER XV. Charles’s Privilege concerning Hasloas

In the twenty-eighth year of the reign of the glorious King Charles, son of the earlier Louis, indiction I—that is, the year 868 of the Lord’s Incarnation—the venerable Guelfo, Father of the men of Centula, entreated the majesty of that king to authorize by his decree the perpetual possession of the estate called Hasloas, situated on the river Somme, on the condition that no abbot or any other person should remove anything from it or assign it to purposes other than the use of the brethren. The glorious king assented and issued the following decree for this purpose:

> “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Charles, by the grace of God king. If we grant assent to the just and reasonable petitions of our faithful, which they make known to our wisdom for the sacred places entrusted to them, and bring them into effect, we do not doubt that this will benefit us in passing more happily through the course of the present life and in attaining more readily the rewards of future blessedness.
>
> “Let, therefore, the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and our own faithful, present and future, know that our beloved Guelfo, venerable abbot of the monastery of Centula, where the eminent confessor St. Riquier rests in the body and where a company of monks is known to serve God continually, petitioned our exalted majesty. He asked that we should assign certain possessions of that abbey, namely the estate called Hasloas in the district of Amiens on the river Somme, with its mills, fisheries, and all that pertains to it, to the use and support of those monks and to their own refuge, and should confirm their perpetual possession by a decree of our authority. He further requested that we should again confirm by the authority of our majesty other possessions assigned to the use and support of the same monks and confirmed by decrees of our father Louis, the most serene Emperor of pious memory, and by our own decrees.
>
> “Favouring his just and reasonable petitions, we have ordered this decree of our majesty to be made and given to the same monks. By it we command and confirm that they shall firmly hold, administer, and possess, without contradiction or diminution by any abbot, all possessions assigned to them and confirmed by the authorities of our father and ourselves, as is contained in those decrees. We assign the aforesaid estate called Hasloas, with houses, buildings, lands, woods, meadows, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, male and female dependants residing thereon or rightfully belonging to the same estate, and its complete integrity, to their own refuge, and confirm this by the decree of our authority. No ruler of the same monastery may remove or diminish anything from these possessions, or divert them to uses other than those we have established, so that the monks may serve God more freely and may continually implore God’s mercy for us, our wife, our offspring, and the stability of our whole kingdom.
>
> “That this decree of our authority may possess inviolable force, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.
>
> “Sign of Charles, most glorious king.
>
> “I, Frogtarius, notary in place of Gozlin, have examined and subscribed it.
>
> “Given on the seventh Ides of December, indiction I, in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of the most glorious King Charles.
>
> “Done at the royal palace of Quierzy, happily in the name of God. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XVI. Charles’s Donation of Vallis-Villa

God prompting him, and the religious devotion of the brethren meriting it, it was not enough for this most powerful king to grant what had been requested concerning the confirmation of estates and lands. Of his own accord, out of love for the sustenance of that place, he granted also things which no one had ever asked of him: both because, amid abundant income, there was no need, and because it was not proper to ask so eminent a man for many other things. Therefore, for the remedy of his soul, he gave the monastery of Centula an estate called Vallis, situated in the district of Beauvais. Concerning its grant, he confirmed the following decree:

> “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Charles, by the grace of God king.
