Whatever we grant and bestow upon places devoted to divine worship, we do not doubt will benefit us in passing more happily through the course of this present life and in attaining more readily the rewards of eternal blessedness.
>
> “Let, therefore, the prudence of all faithful of the holy Church of God and our own faithful, present and future, know that, for the love and honour of God and of St. Riquier, eminent confessor, and for the absolution of our sins, it has pleased our majesty to grant and assign for the use and support of the monks serving God in the monastery of that same St. Riquier, where the holy confessor rests in the body and where Guelfo is known to be abbot, certain possessions and dependants of our own property: namely, in the district of Beauvais, in the estate called Vallis, a demesne holding 130 quadrelli; of vineyards, 30 bonuaria; of arable land, 21 bonuaria; of meadow, 2 bonuaria and 48 quadrelli; of woodland, 20 bonuaria; of cleared land, 5 bonuaria and 2 quadrelli; of marshland, 110 quadrelli; of alder-grove, 1 bonuarium; 1 mill; and 4 manses, each holding 3 bonuaria, and 2 other small holdings, each holding 3½ bonuaria.
>
> “We have therefore ordered this decree of our majesty to be made and given to the same monks. By it we grant and bestow the aforesaid possessions and dependants, with houses, buildings, vineyards, lands, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, male and female dependants residing thereon or rightfully belonging to those same possessions, mills, and all their integrity. No ruler of the same monastery may remove anything from these possessions, etc., as above. We have ordered it to be sealed.
>
> “Sign of Charles, most glorious king.
>
> “I, Frotgarius, notary in place of Gozlin, have examined and subscribed it.
>
> “Given on the sixth Kalends of April, indiction I, in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of the most glorious King Charles.
>
> “Done at the city of Senlis, happily in the name of God. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XVII. His Donation of Bersaccas, with Privilege

When the venerable Guelfo—worthy of God and beloved by all—learned of the royal generosity toward the holy place, and also that, as has already appeared, he was the king’s kinsman, he took from affection boldness and confidence. He repeatedly urged the aforesaid King Charles, for the praise and love of God and the veneration of St. Riquier, whose friendship with God frequent miracles testified, to grant something further to the brethren of Centula. By this the king might make God favourable to himself through the saint’s merits and might in some degree increase the honour of that place. The advice, beneficially offered, was fulfilled still more beneficially. Yielding to the exhortation of his beloved kinsman, he again gave St. Riquier an estate situated near the monastery, called Bersaccas, and drew up the following testimony of his authority concerning this grant:

> “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Charles, by the grace of God king. If we provide places devoted to divine worship with suitable assistance, we confidently believe beyond doubt that this benefits us in obtaining the aid of those saints and, through their prayers, in attaining the clemency of God’s most merciful loving-kindness.
>
> “Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and our own faithful, present and future, know that, for the benefit of our salvation, at the request of Guelfo, abbot of the monastery of the chief confessor St. Riquier, we assign by decree of our authority a certain place called Bersaccas in the district of Ponthieu, not far from the monastery of that confessor, for the perpetual provision of lamps for the aforesaid church; and also certain possessions known to belong by right to that church. The condition is that henceforth the lamps before that eminent confessor and the relics of the saints dwelling there shall be supplied under the charge of the ministers.
>
> “We have therefore ordered this decree of our excellence to be made and given to the appointed minister. By it we grant to the aforesaid holy place all the aforesaid possessions, with the church founded there, woods, meadows, pastures, mills, waters and watercourses, and everything which appears justly and lawfully to belong to the place called Bersaccas. We decree that, by means of this assistance, three lamps shall continually burn before the head of the aforesaid eminent confessor and the relics of saints; and that, on the annual translation of the holy relics deposited there, which occurs on 4 Non. December, suitable and ample provision of food and drink shall be supplied to the brethren serving God there, in commemoration of the saints and in participation in their rewards, by those who have received these possessions to administer and order in the aforesaid monastery.
>
> “And lest anyone from this day onward should attempt by any device to withdraw the aforesaid estate Bersaccas from the service of divine worship, or presume to extort gifts or any exactions from it, but should strive that it remain inviolate as established, we pray before the divine presence, with the aforesaid patron and his companions standing around. Let the ministers of that place, enjoying the tranquillity of this perpetual stability, continually maintain the aforesaid lamps and annually administer the brethren’s refreshment. And let them unceasingly ask the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife, our offspring, and the stability of the kingdom.
>
> “That this authority of our confirmation and grant may obtain fuller force of stability in the name of our God, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.
>
> “Sign of Charles, most glorious king.
>
> “I, Hildebold, chancellor in place of Gozlem, have examined and subscribed it.
>
> “Given on the fourth Kalends of June, indiction I, in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of the most glorious King Charles.
>
> “Done at the palace of Quierzy, happily in the name of God. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Miracles of St. Riquier

But now we must return to the deeds of our holy Father, so that from them a kind of divine seasoning may be imparted to our little works, which are in themselves altogether insipid.

At that time a poor woman brought to the aid of our patron her son, born four years earlier and wholly contracted in every limb for two years. When she entrusted his condition to the compassionate physician, he immediately recovered his lost health through the power of the saint’s merits.

In the district of Vexin there was an elderly and poor man in the estate of Floriacum. From the day of his birth, the faculty of all speech had been denied him for the rest of his life. Divine mercy persuaded him in a vision to seek St. Riquier, assuring him that the saint could grant him the use of speech. Believing the words, he sought the physician of whom he had been told. On finding him, he at once experienced the heavenly remedy. At the feast of the holy Father, his congenital condemned silence was removed, and he received the functions of a speaking tongue.

A boy named Dodigerus, whose condition at birth had been altered, entered this light contracted and twisted, with the order of his limbs disarranged; he was a native of the territory of Rouen. But his father, learning through many reports of the power and compassion of Riquier, patron of Ponthieu, and not despairing that he might benefit from him, carried the boy to our monastery at the saint’s great feast. Because he had faith, the hope he had ventured upon did not deceive him: while he stood in the church holding his son in his arms, the child was healed by heavenly regard.

It happened at that time that a band of Danes, returning from the palace of Lord Charles and making again for the English shores, passed through this monastery. Let no one think that these were the people by whose violence our country was devastated both before and afterward. For these men had perhaps gone to the royal court on a peaceful embassy, led by Ansleicus. On their return journey, having this holy monastery on their route, those whom Christian faith had enlightened entered the basilica to pray; with them entered one still possessed by the error of paganism. He showed no reverence to almighty God or his saints, but, acting from curiosity, began to inspect the chambers of the sacred buildings, wishing to find something with which he might insult the worshippers of our faith.

Divine judgment immediately followed his malicious presumption, by which he was compelled, for his own good, to become a Christian, lest the devil continue to rule him to his ruin. For after he had searched the basilica and departed, and had reached the point at which he was about to entrust himself to a ship for passage across the sea, all his strength began to fail; he was also severely afflicted with bodily illness and great anguish. As he was already closing his eyes in death, his companions sought by divinatory inquiry the reason for his grievous torment. They discovered that the cause was that, as a pagan, he had entered the basilica of St. Riquier; he himself had already confessed that this seemed to be so. He therefore promised, if health were restored, that he would never again seek the death of Christians and would adopt their rite.

He also had four silver threads and one gold thread made, equal in length to his own height, and asked that they be sent as a devotional offering to blessed Riquier, together with as many candles as he had seen altars there. As soon as he resolved that this should be done, he immediately received relief from all his affliction through God’s favour, and afterward suffered no further distress from it.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Abbot Carloman, and the Donation of Durcaptum

Thus, when the most holy Abbot Guelfo had happily surpassed all mortal things in a blessed departure, our most fortunate monks received as their royal abbot a man named Carloman, a good successor to a good man. He was the son of the most glorious King Charles, and in the practice of holiness and piety he happily surpassed the nobility of imperial birth. From the time he embraced the holy order, he so shone with every humility that even his supreme and eminent birth produced in him no baseness of mind. Rather, as he was great in birth, so he was chosen great in virtue as a shepherd; indeed, by his own brilliance he had drawn dignity to himself.

Let no one consider it unworthy that, as we say, the son of a king was our abbot, because at that time the abbey of St. Riquier, through abundance in every kind of possession, the distinction of its lordship, and certainly the services of military men, surpassed the dignity of any bishop.

After he was established abbot, it pleased him to approach his father Charles and ask him, for love of himself, to increase the possessions of St. Riquier. The sweetest son therefore went to the court of his beloved father and disclosed his intention. The father embraced his son, understood his wishes, and, contrary to the custom of secular power, rejoiced to see his son a monk and abbot, though he could easily have been adorned with the insignia of a duchy or kingdom. Charles rejoiced in his son because he had despised transient things; and the son rejoiced because he saw that his father not only did not oppose his purpose but wholly favoured it.

In the enumeration of soldiers inserted above, there is found a soldier named Hungarius who had held the estate of Durcaptum as a benefice from Hericus, abbot of Centula. Since he had died and left no heir able to hold it against them—so great was the authority, fear, and reverence enjoyed by our people—Abbot Carloman asked his pious father to establish the aforesaid estate Durcaptum by his decree, so that it might not be withdrawn from the brethren’s lordship by a grant in benefice or by any other means, but should henceforth serve the holy monastery as its own possession.

His reason for making this request was as follows. While Lord Guelfo was still alive, the same king had given the estate Bersaccas to St. Riquier and had decreed in writing that, from its income, three lamps should burn forever before the glorious head of St. Riquier. This venerable Abbot Carloman considered that the following should be added: that three lamps, likewise from his father’s gift, should always burn at the feet of the eminent patron, and that every night one lamp should be placed before each altar. This was done. The glorious father, assenting to the requests of his beloved son, quickly ordered all that he had asked to be carried out, confirming the following decree concerning these matters:

> “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Charles, by the grace of God king. Since we duly favour the requests of our faithful, it seems all the more proper, beyond doubt, that we should not refuse, to excellent effect, to assent to the pious counsels of our children.
>
> “Therefore let the diligence of all faithful of the holy Church of God and our own faithful, present and future, know that our most beloved son Carloman, abbot of the monastery of St. Riquier, came before our magnificence and humbly requested that by decree of our authority we should deign to grant and consent that a certain estate of that church, called Durcaptum, which Hungarius is known formerly to have held by right of benefice, should in its entire integrity serve God continually for the lamp of that most holy confessor of Christ, Riquier.
>
> “Assenting to his sound and reasonable requests, we have ordered this decree of our majesty to be made and given to the altar of the aforesaid church. By it we grant that the aforesaid possessions, with their most complete integrity—with cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, meadows, pastures, mills, waters and watercourses, and all legal boundaries and appurtenances—shall serve perpetually under this condition: that at the feet of the most holy confessor three oil lamps shall continually burn for us, for the soul of our once most beloved wife Yrmindrude, for our aforesaid most beloved son Carloman, and for his brothers.
>
> “Moreover, to this pious arrangement, so that each altar of that church may have its own lamp every night, we add in the estate of Encra one holding and one mill, to serve perpetually for the use of these lamps. We also grant for the use of the brethren two mills in the estate of Hasloas, which the notary is known to have held as a benefice; we had already bestowed that estate in its complete integrity upon these same brethren by our decree. We likewise bestow, at the gate of the monastery itself, the estate of Anisceias, and at Hamingi-mont that which Atto and Otger held, at the request of our supplicating son Carloman, that they may serve perpetually; and, in bestowing, we grant them.
>
> “Therefore we command, and in commanding earnestly ask, that no one in the succession of abbots and rulers of this abbey should dare or attempt to divert the aforesaid possessions to any other uses, but that they allow and consent, without opposition from anyone, that they serve with proper stability those purposes for which we have established them: so that by this arrangement and the prayer of the holy confessor of Christ Riquier, we may find the Lord’s mercy favourable; the soul of our wife Yrmindrude may obtain eternal rest; and our son may obtain perpetual and steadfast salvation.
>
> “That the authority of this our assent and confirmation may obtain firmer force of stability for future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.
>
> “Sign of Charles, most glorious king.
>
> “I, Hildebold, notary in place of Gozlen, have examined and subscribed it.
>
> “Given on the eighteenth Kalends of February, indiction III, in the thirtieth year of the reign of King Charles, and in the first year after the succession to Lothar’s kingdom.
>
> “Done at the palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XX. On the Kings of the Franks and the pagan Guaramund  
*[Note: “Pagan” [Col. 1283D], that is, Norman.], under whom our church was burned.*

Since, as is already clear, many great benefits of King Charles have been bestowed upon this place, it seems right to recount briefly his temporal good fortune. Having shown by the example of our community how generous he was toward places of saints, let us relate how greatly he was exalted by God.

In the thirty-sixth year of his reign he travelled to Italy and came to the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul to pray. There he was chosen emperor by the whole Roman people and was consecrated emperor by Pope John on the eighth Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 875. From there he returned prosperously to Gaul. Besides enlarging works constructed long before, he restored certain holy places in which Christ’s praise and glory still fittingly flourish today.

In the thirty-eighth year of his reign and at the beginning of the third year of his empire, he again went to Italy. As he returned from there, after crossing Mount Cenis, he lost the sight of this present light on the third Non. October, indiction X, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 877. His son Louis succeeded him in the kingdom.

Moreover, Carloman, son of the same Charles and abbot of the men of Centula, having completed the course of this present life, happily departed from the world.

> Golden sceptres destiny was preparing for you, Carloman,  
> renowned alike for excellence of character and of birth.  
> But, scorning all things that will one day become nothing,  
> you rejoice, bearing the insignia of an eternal kingdom.  
> These are the rewards, Christ, which you give to your saints:  
> that they may possess you, who seek you above all things.

*[Note: “Carloman” [Col. 1285D]. Acherius records that he found the following in the margin of his manuscript: “To the reader. We have learned with certainty that what is related concerning this venerable Carloman is true, because he offended his father’s favour so greatly that he was afterward blinded by that same father. But because we do not know on what occasion this was done, we urge that the occasion be sought out and, once discovered, written.”]*

His brother, King Louis, died at the palace of Compiègne on the fifth Ides of April, before the completion of the second year of his reign.

Certainly, no reliable narrative tells us who presided over this holy place after the venerable Carloman. Yet around this time Herebert and Hedenolbus, both distinguished men, were abbots of our community; likewise Hugh and Gerard, men of great sanctity. But no memorials of the ancients instruct us how long they continued in government or at what end of their lives they departed this life.

But after the death of Louis, his sons Louis and Carloman divided the kingdom between themselves. While they were reigning, it happened, by God’s judgment, that an innumerable multitude of barbarians [Col. 1285C] overran the borders of Francia, led by their king Guaramund. Having, as is reported, subdued many kingdoms beneath his most cruel rule, he wished also to rule Francia. He was persuaded to undertake this by a certain Esimbard, a noble Frank, who had offended King Louis and who, betraying the land of his birth, urged the barbarian peoples to visit our borders. But since the manner in which this happened is remembered and sung every day not only in histories but also in the memory of the people of the country, let us mention a few things and omit the rest, so that anyone eager to know everything may be instructed not by our writing but by the authority of the ancients.

When, indeed, the aforesaid peoples were already approaching our shores and threatening all with destructive devastation, the monk Jeremiah, treasurer [Col. 1285D] of Saint Riquier, a noble man distinguished not only by monastic but also by worldly prudence, resolved to preserve his life by flight, lest, if found by those whom he heard were coming, he should be cruelly killed or compelled to see others dying. He therefore made a chest of some size and, lest it should be easily opened by anyone, firmly bound it with iron bands. Then, since no one opposed him—for the abbot of the place himself wished this, and the other brethren were likewise preparing for flight—he took from the church treasury [Col. 1286A] and its ornaments whatever precious objects he could, and placed them in the aforesaid chest.

For from the time of the lord and holy abbot Angilbert this place had continually grown greater and better, and had been exceedingly enriched both in external goods and in the treasures of the Church. Thus many things were removed from here because of [this] fear, which our account does not set out, because to enumerate everything would be as lengthy as it would be burdensome. Yet these are the things, dearer than all gold and to be preferred to kingdoms, which were carried away from this place by the aforesaid Jeremiah: the sandal of the Lord and Savior, which he used during his holy childhood—for it is one cubit long; the point of the spear by which the side of that same Lord, already dead, was opened by a soldier’s hand for our salvation, [Col. 1286B] whence also the sacraments of the Church flowed; two ampoules containing the blood of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, together with ten blood-stained stones by which he was stoned by the Jews. He also carried away such a quantity of relics of the Innocents, the apostles, and the martyrs that, apart from the beloved body of most blessed Riquier, what remained would be thought few or very small things in comparison with those many objects.

The aforesaid guardian carried all these things away with the church’s outstanding ornaments and deposited them in the monastery of Saint Columba the Virgin at Sens, because of the union of the two houses which had taken place in the time of Lord Welfo. Received there with due honor, both because of the friendship [Col. 1286C] of their ancient affection and because he had brought so great a treasure, and being a good man who had determined to live there henceforth, he was elected by the brethren upon the death of the abbot of the place and appointed ruler of that monastery. Since he administered this office very fittingly, after the bishop of Sens had been taken by death, he was elected by all the clergy and people and ordained archbishop of that city. Moreover, when he possessed so great a dignity, at the clergy’s urging he judged it right to transfer the aforesaid glorious relics to his own church, so that the church by which he had been exalted might be eternally honored by the reception of such great pledges. But, setting aside these sad matters, let us proceed to what remains.

When the invading peoples first arrived upon our borders, they disembarked from their ships and ravaged the districts of Vimeu and Ponthieu. They destroyed churches, slaughtered [Col. 1286D] Christians, and filled everything with death and blood. Finally, they set fire to the most splendid church of blessed Riquier, which could not be demolished because of its size and solidity, after first carrying off everything from the church furnishings that had remained when the brethren departed.

The aforesaid King Louis, waging war against these peoples in the district of Vimeu, gained a victory, having killed their king Guaramund. When the soldiers of the unbelieving people had been slain, the rest [Col. 1287A] were put to flight. It is said, however, that in that battle, through excessive exertion in striking, his internal organs burst and he afterward died. He reigned two years, three months, and twenty-four days. His brother Carloman succeeded him in the kingdom; he too possessed the kingdom for three and a half years, and then died after being struck by a solitary wild beast in the forest of Euvelina, on Mount Aeric. He died in the year of the Lord 884, indiction 2, on 6 December.

Then King Charles, son of the second Louis—whom we mentioned much above as king of the Alemanni and of Cornwall—assumed the monarchy of the whole empire of the Franks and Romans, in the year of our Lord 885, indiction 3. We have learned that he was zealous in the service of God and gave something from his revenues for rebuilding [Col. 1287B] the churches which had been destroyed by the pagan incursion.

But the almighty Lord, who has never withheld the reward of any service rendered to him, chastened this King Charles, so that, purified from the contagion of crimes, he might become a vessel fit for mercy. For, God willing—who has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills—the torments of punishments by which sinners’ souls are chastised under God’s judgment were shown to him. After he saw them, we suppose that he was very greatly corrected, since he feared to suffer the same things. The matter itself, described by earlier writers, seems worthy of narration, since it truly strikes fear into the hearer when read and perhaps thereby contributes to purification. Let no one judge it foolish that [Col. 1287C] we set down the vision itself here, because two considerations draw us to do so: first, that we may show how a royal man was terrified by the merciful judgment of God, lest he perish; and second, that those who read this, fearing to incur such things, may shape themselves toward penitential lamentation. The account of this matter is as follows:

## CHAPTER XXI. The Vision of Charles

The vision which Emperor Charles saw concerning his own name:

> “In the name of God, the highest King of kings. I, Charles, by the freely given gift of God king of the Germans, patrician of the Romans, and emperor of the Franks, on the holy night of the Lord’s Day, after the divine office of the nocturnal Hours had been celebrated, as I went to the bed of rest and wished to take the sleep of slumber, [Col. 1287D] a terrible voice came to me, saying: ‘Charles, your spirit will now depart from you, and you will see God’s just judgments and certain signs concerning yourself; yet your spirit will return to you again after no small interval.’
>
> “Immediately I was caught up in the spirit. He who lifted me up was most radiant, and in his hand he held a ball of thread emitting the brilliant gleam of light, as comets are accustomed to do when they appear. He began to unwind it and said to me: ‘Take the thread from the shining ball, and bind and knot it firmly around the thumb of your right hand, because by it you will be led through the labyrinthine punishments of hell.’ Having said this, he went swiftly before me, unwinding the light-bearing ball, and led me into valleys most deep and fiery, which were full of pits burning with pitch, sulphur, [Col. 1288A] lead, wax, and fat. There I found bishops of my father and of my uncles.
>
> “When in fear I asked them why they suffered such grievous torments, they answered me: ‘We were bishops of your father and your uncles, and we ought then to have admonished and preached peace and concord to them and to their people. Instead, we sowed discord and were instigators of evils. Therefore we, together with other lovers of murder and plunder, are now burned in these Tartarean punishments. Your bishops and the followers among your people who now likewise love to do such things will also come here.’
>
> “As I listened to this trembling, behold, blackest demons flew toward me with iron hooks, intending to seize the thread of the ball which I held in my hand and draw it to themselves; but, repelled by its rays, they could not touch the thread. [Col. 1288B] Then, running behind my back, they wished to hook me and hurl me into the sulphurous pits. But my guide, who carried the ball, threw the thread from the ball over my shoulders and doubled it; he pulled me strongly behind him, and so we climbed over very high fiery mountains, from which marshes and boiling rivers arose, with every kind of molten metal.
>
> “There I found innumerable souls of the men and princes of my father and of my brothers cast down: some up to the hair, others up to the chin, others up to the navel. Wailing, they cried to me: ‘While we lived, we loved, together with you and with your father and your brothers and your uncles, to wage wars, commit murders, and carry out plunder for earthly greed. Therefore we endure torments in these boiling rivers and diverse kinds of metals.’ As I looked fearfully upon these things, I heard souls behind me crying: ‘The mighty suffer mighty torments’ [Wisdom 6].
>
> “I looked and saw on the banks of the boiling river furnaces of pitch and sulphur, full of huge dragons, scorpions, and serpents of various kinds. There I also saw certain princes of my father, my uncles, my brothers, and my own, [Col. 1288C] saying to me: ‘Alas for us, Charles! You see how grievous are the torments we suffer for our wickedness, pride, and evil counsels which we gave to our kings and to you for the sake of greedy gain.’
>
> “As they groaned in sorrow, dragons ran against me with open mouths full of fire, sulphur, and pitch, wishing to swallow me. But my guide more closely tripled the thread from the ball over me; by the rays of its brightness their fiery mouths were overcome, and he drew me onward more powerfully.
>
> “We descended into a valley which on one side was dark, burning like a fiery furnace, and on the other side so delightful and splendid that I cannot express it in any way. I turned toward the dark, flame-spewing side and saw certain kings of my lineage there in great punishments. Then, oppressed by extreme anguish, I thought that I was at once to be plunged into those very torments by gigantic black beings who were setting the whole valley aflame with every kind of fire.
>
> “Trembling greatly, while the thread of the ball illumined [Col. 1289A] my eyes, I saw at one side of the valley a little light beginning to whiten, and there two springs flowing: one exceedingly hot, the other clear and lukewarm. There were also two tubs. As I went there, the thread of the ball directing my steps, I looked into one tub containing boiling water and saw my father Louis standing there up to his thighs. Struck by severe pain and oppressed by anguish, he said to me: ‘My lord Charles, do not fear. I know that your spirit will return again to your body, and God has permitted you to come here so that you may see for what sins I, and all those whom you have seen, suffer these torments. For one day I am in this tub of the boiling bath, and on another day I am transferred into that other tub of most pleasant water. This occurs [Col. 1289B] through the prayers of Saint Peter and Saint Remigius, by whose protection our royal race has hitherto reigned.
>
> “‘But if you, my faithful bishops and abbots, and every ecclesiastical order quickly aid me by sending offerings, psalmody, vigils, and alms, I shall swiftly be freed from that tub of boiling water. For my brother Lothair and his son Louis have been delivered from these punishments through the prayers of Saint Peter and Saint Remigius and have already been led into the joy of God’s paradise.’
>
> “Then he said to me: ‘Look to the left.’ When I looked, I saw two very high boiling tubs. ‘These,’ he said, ‘have been prepared for you unless you amend yourself and do penance for your abominable crimes.’ Then I began to be grievously horrified.
>
> “When my companion saw my spirit in such great fear, [Col. 1289C] he said to me: ‘Follow me to the right side of the most splendid valley of paradise.’ As we walked, I beheld, amid immense brightness, my uncle Lothair seated with glorious kings upon a topaz stone of marvelous size, crowned with a precious diadem; beside him was his son Louis, likewise adorned with a crown. Seeing me near at hand, he called me to himself in a loud, gentle voice, saying: ‘Charles, my successor, now more secure in the empire of the Romans, come to me. I know that you have come through the penal place where your father and my brother has been placed in the baths appointed for him. But through God’s mercy he will very swiftly be freed from those punishments, just as we were freed by the merits of Saint Peter and the prayers of Saint Remigius, to whom God gave great apostolic authority over kings and over the whole people of the Franks.
>
> “‘Unless he comes to the aid and assistance of the remnants of our line, our genealogy will now fail in its kingship and empire. Therefore know that the power of the empire will quickly be taken from your hand, and afterward you will live for a very short time.’
>
> “Then Louis, turning toward me, said: ‘The Roman empire, which you have hitherto held, ought by hereditary right to be received by Louis, the son of my daughter.’ At these words, it seemed to me that the infant Louis was present. Then Lothair, his grandfather, looking upon him, said to me: ‘Let this child be seen to be such as that boy was whom the Lord set in the midst of the disciples and said: “Of such is the kingdom [Col. 1290A] of heaven. I tell you that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven”’ [Matthew 19].
>
> “‘But you, through that thread of the ball which you hold in your hand, restore to him the authority of the empire.’ Unknotting the thread from my right thumb, I bestowed upon him the entire monarchy of the empire by means of that thread. Immediately the shining ball, gathered together like a ray of the sun, passed wholly into his hand. After this marvelous sight, my spirit returned to my body, greatly wearied and terrified.
>
> “Therefore let all know, whether they wish it or not, that, according to God’s ordinance, the whole Roman empire will return into his hand; and that I am unable to act against him, since the moment of my calling by the Lord forestalls me. God, who rules over living and dead, [Col. 1290B] will accomplish and confirm this—he whose eternal kingdom and everlasting dominion remain without end unto ages of ages.”

The vision ends. Thus Charles, according to the prediction of the vision, survived only a short time and so ended his last day.

But while these matters stood thus, let us return to the course of our history of this holy place.

The Christian people who had been able to survive the slaughter of the heathen, and all faithful persons who deeply mourned the destruction of this place’s distinction, sought by every means to ensure that the sacred place should not be utterly wiped out, but that, as far as possible and as time allowed, the life-giving praise of Christ and the memory of the saints might begin again to be celebrated there. Although the workshops, cloister, and all the former dwellings of the monks had been destroyed, [Col. 1290C] the altars and the walls of the church remained unshaken; hence there was readier hope of restoring the place. Moreover, whoever served the Lord there would possess great abundance of revenues and estates. For this reason, and through the pious concern and industry of the faithful, the place began in some measure to be restored. Its roofs were covered, as they could be, not with lead as formerly but with wooden planks; and a body of clerics, together with certain monks, daily offered there vows of praise to God and the saints, with a cleric named Gerbert presiding over them by right of abbot.

After he had governed the place for some time, having sold [Col. 1290D] given away, or allowed many estates, properties, and revenues to be occupied, he died at Buxude, an estate of our church assigned to him for his own support. During the whole time that he presided, the monks who were present always prevailed in every matter. Both because of regard for their religious life and because of their proven faithfulness toward the place, the lay people accorded them especial honor; consequently the resources and free action of the clerics were altogether diminished. Finally, since the control of the place was chiefly entrusted to the monks, whether the clerics wished it or not, they endeavored to compel Gerbert to abandon worldly frivolity and take on an equal manner of life and dress. But he preferred to surrender the honor of preeminence rather than cease to serve worldly enticements. The monks, showing him great kindness, granted him the aforesaid estate of Buxude, [Col. 1291A] where he lived a private life, keeping away from himself, as far as he could, both the monks’ diligence and the clerics’ company; and he would consent by no means to become a monk.

After his death, the monk Fulcheric assumed leadership over the clerics and monks of Centula, because by then the monks had advanced so far through the Lord’s grace that, disregarding the arrogance of the clerics, they were both able and willing to set one of their own over themselves.

## CHAPTER XXII. The Removal of Saint Riquier by Arnulf of Flanders

After, therefore, divine justice, demanding this because of sins, had been pleased that Francia should be afflicted through the hands of the pagans whose leader had been Guaramund, and after the dignity and glory of the church of Centula [Col. 1291B] had likewise been largely destroyed, together with many holy places, very confused events took place throughout Gaul. For with royal authority failing, the other magnates and peoples exercised the perversities of their ways like sons of Belial. Indeed, any dukes or counts who were more powerful did not cease to lay hands everywhere, devastate neighboring districts, and subject them to themselves; they also sought to usurp the kingdom.

Among these, Arnulf, count of Flanders, began to commit many improper acts. Having seized the royal fortress of Montreuil, he brought the district of Ponthieu under his own dominion. Having acquired it by fraud, as he was accustomed to do in most things, he removed Saint Father Riquier from there, wishing to possess so noble a treasure together with certain saints of his own region. At that time [Col. 1291C] he also took away the holy body of blessed Walaric and ordered it to be kept at the fortress of Montreuil together with the holy body of most blessed Riquier.

After the passage of some years, the monk Fulcheric, who after Gerbert the cleric and abbot of the clerics was ruler of the monastery of Centula, went to the said fortress. Speaking with the custodian who guarded the bodies of the saints, he secretly obtained, with very great gifts and endless prayers, the return of his beloved patron. On the appointed night Fulcheric mounted a horse and, while all the people were asleep, stood waiting at the church doors. But that guardian, greatly fearing the wrath of his lords and the fury of the people—for this saint of ours was revered and loved by all beyond belief—[Col. 1291D] came out of the church and addressed Fulcheric in these words:

> “I shall indeed yield Saint Riquier to you, in response to your prayers and from fear of the judgment of the Lord. But if it becomes known that I have handed him over, I shall without doubt incur danger to my life. Therefore, as the saint departs with you, I must cry out as if there had been a theft, so that by such a device I may feign ignorance. But you must quickly take flight with the saint of God. Thus, by restoring the saint to his place, you will save yourself as well.”

After arranging matters thus, he entered the church and took up the glorious bier of the saint’s body. When he wished to hand it over to Fulcheric, the horse on which Fulcheric sat immediately lowered its knees to the ground and, bowing its head to the very earth, adored the Lord’s confessor with all the reverence it could show. Fulcheric, rejoicing in such a miracle, [Col. 1292A] received the most blessed Father with ineffable joy and immediately turned back, coming as swiftly as he could.

But when the custodian learned that he was already a league away, he rose as if for some necessity, lit lamps, cried out, made a tumult, and loudly complained that Saint Riquier had secretly been stolen from him. At once the church was disturbed, the people were inflamed, and the princes were struck by the news. Immediately soldiers and people pursued the fugitive; and because the horse on which Fulcheric rode was pure white, he was more easily recognized in the black night while fleeing. Yet when he was already almost weary, much road still remained, and they were drawing near to him. Then it pleased the Creator Lord to perform something marvelous, by which it might be known [Col. 1292B] that he favored the return of this saint.

For when Fulcheric reached the estate which was anciently called Mount of the Angels, but from this event is called Cloud-Mount, such density of air and darkness of mist enclosed the pursuers that they could see not only neither the fugitive, but not even one another. The difficulty of the journey was likewise extraordinary for them, so that they plainly recognized that they had truly been impeded by God’s will. Seeing that they accomplished nothing—for the people of Centula were already running to meet him—they withdrew with ineffable sorrow.

But this return of the saint availed little, since the people of Centula were not permitted to possess him for long. For the same Arnulf who had first taken him again claimed the saint for himself; and, having become more cautious, he placed him not in the land of Ponthieu, which he feared he might someday lose, but in a safer place [Col. 1292C] near himself, namely in the monastery of Saint Bertin, together with Saint Walaric, where they remained for a longer time than at Montreuil. Thus the monastery of Centula was deprived for a long time of the presence of so great a Father through the power of the aforesaid Count Arnulf.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Abbot Ingelard

At last the Godhead, appeased and moved by the prayers of his own people, decreed by the glorious return of the fathers to relieve the hearts of the children, which were burdened by long-lasting groans over their removal. But the Arnulf of Flanders mentioned above had long since been taken by death, and his son and heir, also named Arnulf, had succeeded to his power. Hugh, the illustrious duke, son of Hugh the Great, administered the governance of the Franks without the title of king. [Col. 1292D] Deeply grieved that the country had been destroyed by hostile cruelty, and no less indignant because the bodies of saints and other objects adorning churches had been fraudulently removed from their proper places, he diligently prepared his mind to remedy these matters. One night, as he rested, a vision came to him by heavenly command. Dispelling the hindrances of doubt, it encouraged him to accomplish what he had planned with a pious but nevertheless fearful heart.

Blessed Walaric appeared to him in a vision and, by God’s command, spoke these words:

> “What are you doing here?” he said.

At hearing these words, Hugh began to ask who he was. And the saint said:

> “I am Walaric [Col. 1293A], formerly abbot of the monastery of Leuconay, and by God’s command I have come to bring these things to your mind. The venerable confessor Riquier, a priest glorious before God, and I have for years been captives together; through Arnulf’s deceit we have long remained driven far from our own seats. It now pleases God that our return should be obtained through you as agent and at your command, so that the sorrowful hearts of servants may be refreshed by the sight and presence of our bodies, and those may rejoice at our return who, after God, delight in possessing us as pious patrons.
>
> “Do this most swiftly: remove the clerics from our places, and strive to unite monks there under the Rule, as they formerly were. If you fulfill these things, I promise you, by God’s command, through the pious merits of Saint Riquier and by my prayer, that you shall be king, and that your offspring, your Frankish descendants, and your line shall hold the kingdom for seven successions.”

The illustrious duke [Col. 1293B], desiring swiftly to fulfill the command of God thus communicated through the saint’s voice, summoned his counselors and inquired how he could find a suitable man to whom the monastery of Centula might be entrusted for restoration. During this inquiry, certain persons who knew the inhabitants of that district well intervened and are said to have given Hugh this counsel:

> “Behold, Corbie possesses a man most distinguished by nobility, to whom we think the work you speak of may fittingly be entrusted. For he is strongly supported by noble parents and illustrious military kin; since they live near that place and in the same district, they will not refuse assistance to their kinsman laboring in God’s work.”

Hearing this, the illustrious duke [Col. 1293C] rejoiced at so beneficial a counsel and immediately sent honorable men to request from the abbot of Corbie that the election of the aforesaid monk should not be delayed. With the abbot’s consent, the accomplished young man Ingelard was summoned. At that time, it is said, he was still engaged in the schools and was performing the ministry of the subdiaconate that very day or hour. Brought into the duke’s presence, he received the charge and labor of restoring this abbey, with the duke’s support, as far as he was able. Thereupon, according to custom, he was consecrated abbot, and with a company of brethren and soldiers he came to Centula.

Now Fulcheric [Col. 1293D], the abbot who had brought back Saint Riquier, had departed this world on 6 November; through his persuasion and encouragement some of the clerics had adopted the monastic order. Thus Abbot Ingelard, coming to Centula, improved everything as far as he could and repaired the cloisters—not indeed as they had been of old, but in the form in which they are still seen to stand. Then, applying himself to religious observance by day and night and increasing the community of monks, he soberly pursued the advancement of the place entrusted to him. For to one who had the will, no difficulty could stand in the way, because the place, rich in extensive estates, towns, and revenues, gave easy fulfillment to his undertakings.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Return of Saint Riquier

When the monastery had therefore been partly restored with dwellings suitable for religious life, the aforesaid duke began to inquire how what still remained might be accomplished: namely, that Saint Riquier, God’s confessor, should be restored to his own place. Employing wise counsel, he sent envoys into Flanders, commanding Count Arnulf to return the holy bodies of the saints to their proper seats. Hearing this, and finding it exceedingly hard to part with such treasures, Arnulf first refused, saying that he ought not to return saints whom he had not himself taken away. The messengers returned and informed the duke that the count was unwilling to obey.

Then Hugh gathered a very powerful force of soldiers and resolved to go where the saints were, intending himself to take them away and bring them back to their own places. Arnulf, however, perceiving that it would not turn out well for him if he, being unjust, entered into conflict against the just Franks, was moved to tears. He sent envoys to Duke Hugh, begging him to inflict no devastation upon the country but merely to send the best men, who might receive the saints of God and go in peace.

Count Arnulf had made silver biers [Col. 1294B] for the most blessed confessors, in which he had honorably deposited their holy bodies. Upon the bier of our most glorious patron Riquier, he ordered these verses to be inscribed:

> Know everywhere the deeds of Count Arnulf,  
> Which he himself was accustomed to perform for the pious Lord.  
> He who made this bier for kindly Riquier  
> Has placed within it his chaste limbs.

Distinguished men were therefore sent. The saints were received by our rejoicing people, who magnified God with pious tears and praises; they were followed by those who grieved and, raising their voices on high in excessive sorrow, wailed. When they could now be seen by Duke Hugh [Col. 1294C] and all who waited at some distance, who could adequately describe the cries uttered for joy or the abundant outpouring of sweet tears? The greatness of joy removed all measure from their shouting, while the gladness conceived at the saints’ return burned in the heart of each and could scarcely contain itself.

Having received the most beloved shrines of the blessed bodies, our people paused briefly. After this, the leading men of the people and those thought to be of good conscience were asked to swear to the duke that nothing had been removed or altered from the saints’ bodies. When they had done so with free minds and cheerful hearts, they took up the saints’ bodies and began to hasten modestly toward their own places.

The report of this most happy return stirred the hearts of the inhabitants of the district, and immediately all came forth: both sexes, every social condition, young men with the aged, monks with clerics, and every profession rushed to meet them. Each considered himself guilty of a crime if he had not gone out to meet them. In June, on the second day, blessed Walaric was restored to his own place; but the return of our native Father was postponed until the following day.

On the third day of the aforesaid month, the illustrious Hugh received the saint and carried our blessed Father upon his own shoulders for one league. Barefoot and drenched with tears, he came to the church and placed Christ’s friend upon the seat of his altar, while meanwhile the choirs and the whole people cried out thanks to God and praises to Christ.

In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1295A] 981, indiction 9, on 3 June, this return of the most blessed Father Riquier took place. Yet we think it worthwhile to relate what miracle occurred during the journey of that return. For at this season the yellowing fields and ripened ears promise the farmers an abundant harvest. When blessed Walaric had been restored to his own seat, and the return of Saint Riquier, as has been said, had been arranged for the next day, Duke Hugh with his army and people spent that night in the midst of fields laden with flourishing and already fruitful grain.

Thus, while cooking was carried on here and feasts celebrated there, while rest was provided there both for human bodies and stabling for beasts of burden, while the crop was beaten down by the prolonged pressure of those standing or lying upon it, and while it was crushed under grazing livestock and trampling feet, all hope of harvest was denied to the reaper. Yet the cultivator [Col. 1295B] did not grieve over the crop so bruised and ruined by such trampling, because, through regard for the patron, he accounted it as nothing. Later, when harvest time came, the ruined and despaired-of crop was cut so luxuriant and fruitful that fields protected and enclosed with hedges seemed of little account in richness of grain by comparison.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Letters of Pope John

By hearing and sight Abbot Ingelard learned from his predecessors, namely Gerbert and Fulcheric, who had presided over the clerics, that many lands of Saint Riquier had been given away and sold; some also, while they kept silent and did not object, had been occupied by more powerful men. [Col. 1295C] He began with all diligence to labor for the restoration of the saint’s property. This was accomplished in part with God’s aid. Yet some, more arrogant, took pleasure in the goods which they had taken from the saint and either very unwillingly restored something, or certainly never restored anything at all.

Therefore the shrewd abbot appealed not only to the royal favor of Duke Hugh, but personally sought the authority of the pope of Rome. For, after constructing a dwelling suitable for the religious order, and seeing that the hard hearts of the inhabitants refused to restore to the saint what they had taken, he went to Rome. He informed the supreme pontiff how the famous monastery of Saint Riquier had been devastated by the pagan incursion, and how, by the counsel of Frankish magnates, he had been appointed to restore the place. He prayed [Col. 1295D] that, since excommunication was the only aid that the pope could provide, the pope’s authority might be directed against those who refused to restore the saint’s goods unjustly taken.

The apostolic pontiff, deeply sympathizing with him and grieving that a church of so great a name had been destroyed, very kindly agreed, granting him letters of apostolic authority to be shown to the invaders.

### To the Counts

> “John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Count Arnulf, Count Baldwin together with his mother, Viscount Gozbert, and Ildiard, our most beloved spiritual sons: complete greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “We admonish you to withdraw from evil works [Col. 1296A] and cleave to good works, so that you may deserve to obtain the mercy of almighty God and be able to acquire eternal life. Therefore, beloved ones, we command you, for the love of almighty God, to take care to restore every inheritance which you have taken from the monastery of Saint Riquier the confessor. For if you restore it, you shall have the blessing of Saint Peter and ours; but if you do not obey our admonitions, know that, by the authority of almighty God and ours, you are excommunicated and accursed, separated from the Church of God and from the communion of all Christians, unless you make satisfaction.”

### Likewise, to the Bishops
«John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Guy, venerable bishop [Note: [Col. 1295D] Bishop of Soissons.], Fulk, venerable bishop of the city of Amiens, Baldwin, bishop of the city of Thérouanne, our most beloved spiritual sons: most cordial greeting and apostolic blessing.

“If we know that you enjoy an abundance of well-being and fullness of cheerfulness, we rejoice no otherwise than over yourselves. Moreover, we command you, for the love of almighty God and in reverence for Saint Peter, with our intervention, to assist this abbot named Ingilard, so that the monastery of Saint Riquier the confessor may be restored through our and your help. Nor should you fail to send each of those knights who have taken away the monastery’s inheritance letters of excommunication, so that they may take care to restore everything which they have taken from the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1296C]. In this it will appear that you love the holy Roman Church: when our petition comes before you, if you fulfill it.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the prudence of Abbot Ingelard

Strengthened by these apostolic letters and fortified with the blessing, Abbot Ingelard returned to Gaul. He delivered the mandates of the apostolic see specifically to the designated counts; and, employing the bishops’ commands toward their subordinates, he managed the matter excellently. For they excommunicated, by the authority of the Roman Church, those unwilling to restore what they had taken from the holy place.

Accordingly, this resourcefulness of the abbot [Col. 1296D] was very effective: taking away many estates and many revenues from usurpers, he vigorously restored them to the Church of Centula. Thus, in the territory of Thérouanne, he restored the estate of Rolleni and Botritium, which, as is recorded above, had been granted by Abbot and Count Heligaud to a certain person; likewise Guatenaas in the aforesaid territory, and Buxudum in the district of Ponthieu, which had been taken away because it had been assigned to Abbot Girbert while he was living privately. He also succeeded in having many other things restored to himself—things which, if recounted, would cause weariness.

He likewise took many churches, which in former times had served our holy place and which clerics had recently seized, from the power of their unjust lords and restored them to the abbey. Among these, he caused the church of Berella to be restored; but this had happened previously [Col. 1297A]. Therefore, on account of all these exertions and labours, he was esteemed by all good people, as may be understood from the letter sent to him by the archbishop of Rheims. We insert it here for the benefit of his praiseworthy deeds:

“Arnulf [Note: [Col. 1297D] Arnulf. Acherius found the following in the margin of his manuscript, and it is also read in the manuscript of Centula: this Arnulf, archbishop of Rheims, was the son of King Lothair; and because he wished to betray the kingdom of the Franks to the Lotharingians, he was deposed, after a council had been held, by order of Hugh, then king and formerly duke. Godismannus, bishop of Amiens, and Ingelard, abbot of Centula, were also present at this council.], by the grace of God archbishop of Rheims, to the most beloved lord Abbot Ingilard: an abundance of every blessing.

“It has reached our ears how faithfully you have laboured in Christ’s vineyard from your youth. Take care, therefore, lest, after you have borne the burden and heat of the day, the reward of your labour—the glorious denarius—be denied you. For the restoration by you, from its foundations, of your place, once deserted by the assault of pagans and wisely cultivated through your fruitful perseverance, is manifest to us.

“It is therefore necessary for you [Col. 1297B] always to retain, for the benefit of your monastery, the church of the place called Berella, lest any person by any pretext be able to take it away from you and your brethren—a church which God has restored to your charity. Therefore, always keeping watch with the eye of your providence, firmly preserve for your benefit what God has placed in your power. God willing, our authority will not fail you if your inheritance proves distinguished. Farewell.”

Supported by so many and such favourable attentions from honourable persons, he grew daily in good repute: by great energy, with God’s help, he brought a desperate matter into good order.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the abbot’s estate, Incra, and Lord Medard

[Col. 1297C]

Yet because nothing is wholly blessed in every respect, in these very times—when everything was corrupted and all things changed for the worse—the abbot of whom we speak, just as he strove to recover what had been lost, did not refuse to grant away, alienate, or pawn many things that had been freely possessed. Sometimes he was compelled by kinship or services rendered to bestow something upon those to whom he gave; sometimes it was necessary to allot many deserted lands to people who could make them habitable or fruitful. Moreover, around this time the kings of the Franks took from us great estates, surrounding them with ditches and enclosing them with walls, and made them into castles.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The coming of the most blessed Bishop Vigor from Neustria into Ponthieu

[Col. 1297D]

The grace of God began to be powerfully active toward this holy place, so that through the merciful merits of Saint Riquier much desired salvation was often granted to many. In these times, too, the bodies of saints, venerable to us and to our descendants for the perpetual protection of the place, were bestowed upon us at God’s command. Their presence and intercession remain a shelter of safety and protection against the adversities of the world.

Among these stands out the illustrious bishop Vigor [Col. 1298A], who, preceded by God’s power, has made our seat renowned from then until now. Since, therefore, by God’s authorship we have deserved to be enriched with the most holy body of blessed Vigor, it is fitting that, to the praise of God—the giver of all good things—and of our Lord Jesus Christ, we briefly set forth how the venerable body of this most blessed bishop came to us.

It happened that, while the venerable body of the most blessed Vigor was still resting within the territory of his former bishopric, the homeland of Neustria was so devastated by a barbarian incursion that not only worldly splendour but even ecclesiastical beauty was defiled. At that time a certain cleric named Avitianus was a *matricularius* at the church of Bayeux. Seeing that his homeland no longer abounded, as formerly, in material resources, and that the services of churches customarily devoutly rendered to God’s saints had entirely failed, he began to consider within himself how he might escape the poverty of the present life. He reflected that, in his age, a homeland devastated by hostile savagery could not be restored.

Surrounded by this whirl of thoughts, he judged it resolved and advantageous to his own interest if he carried off the sole remaining treasure of the most holy body of blessed Vigor. For he knew indeed that, wherever he brought it, good things would be provided to him through its grace. But the devotion of the faithful ought rather to know that this thought had been instilled in his mind by God, because the heavenly plan was to be fulfilled—a plan which had determined to strengthen the people of Ponthieu with this patron also. He therefore secretly took away the body of the most holy bishop [Col. 1298C], wishing to carry it wherever it might be worthily sold—perhaps to Arras, as some say.

Pursuing these plans, he entered Ponthieu alone and lodged in the estate of Centula, anciently noble and famous above all the district. Blessed Father and outstanding confessor Saint Riquier had once adorned it by his origin, distinguished it by his example, and now protects it by his patronage and gladdens and blesses it by the presence of his body. Arriving there by chance in the course of his journey, he was received as a guest by a man named Bernard, known to be a kinsman of that cleric.

But the cleric, conscious of his treasure, earnestly entreated his host with endless pleading to entrust the bag (*zaberna*) laden with holy bones to the most diligent and faithful custody, since after a short time he intended to continue his journey wherever he should see fit. Bernard, receiving the bag, sought to place it where thieves could not reach it, though he knew nothing at all of what or how great a thing it contained. In the monastery of Saint Riquier he had a chest for the safeguarding of precious objects of every kind, so that articles which he did not dare keep at home might be preserved in that dwelling-place of peace as securely as faithfully. This trustworthy guard was considered suitable for the cleric’s treasure.

But when the bag had been placed within the chest [Col. 1299A], the goodness of divine mercy—which had foreseen before the ages what was to happen—began at once to act. For on one occasion, when Bernard opened his little chest, wishing, I know not what, to take something out of it, he saw the entire interior of the chest shine with wonderful brightness, as though it were filled with flame-bearing fires. Terrified by the sight, he withdrew far away, thinking that something divine had been entrusted to him by his guest. Then he called the cleric and asked what that was which had been committed to his care. The latter, afraid because he saw himself being exposed, yet unable to conceal what almighty God had revealed, answered that he had left there relics of great price and merit. Saying this, he begged that these matters be disclosed to no one.

But though neither of them made anyone aware of so great a secret, heavenly power brought it about that what was hidden became known to all. It is reported that many religious persons, while praying more privately in that basilica, saw lamps there kindled by God. But, omitting doubtful matters, let us rather pursue those things which have been reliably learned.

One day, while the divine office was being performed, a certain woman came there, unaware of what the chest contained. After standing for a long time, she weariedly threw her limbs upon it. Although no fault arose from her consciousness, since she did not even think there was a fault, nevertheless it pleased divine justice to work a certain wonder, so that, while it seemingly avenged the injury done to its saint, it might reveal his merits and dignity to all. The garment of the woman leaning upon the chest began to burn from the region of her buttocks [Col. 1299C]. Suddenly, before the watching people, the woman, compelled by the burning fire, sprang back from the chest and was forced to yield to the blaze from the place to which she had indecorously clung. At once there arose a cry with trembling, and it was disclosed beyond doubt that something great was in the chest.

In those days the noble man Ingelard held the government of the monastery of Centula. When the deeds wrought by the wonderful God had been reported to him, he immediately, without delay, ordered inquiry to be made swiftly into whose chest it was concerning which such things occurred. Those who knew named the owner, and he at once summoned him by messenger. Asking him the cause of the miraculous event, he heard at once that the chest indeed was Bernard’s, but that what had wrought the miracle was not his; it had been entrusted to him, and from it had proceeded an operation of such power. “But because,” he said, “the divine condescension has shown this to others, let what it has also revealed to me be heard.” He then added the foregoing account, which he had sufficiently concealed: namely, that when he had opened the little chest, heavenly power had presented a wondrous radiance to his eyes.

Inflamed by so great marvels, Abbot Ingelard resolved absolutely not to leave these matters unexamined, but to investigate them more diligently. He asked the man promptly to bring before him the bearer of so great a thing. The cleric was then absent; but when he returned, he was brought before the abbot with the utmost speed. The abbot soothed him with a very gentle address and urged him to confess what he held in his mind. He said that he knew the contents of the bag were holy, and asked only that he disclose to him the saint’s name and rank. The abbot further asserted [Col. 1300A] that he would provide everything the cleric requested, provided that he revealed the secret of such power. He also urged him to consider in this matter the divine will: “Surely,” he said, “if it had not wished that this sacred object should be possessed by us, it would by no means have shown such a sign of power beforehand.”

Thus encouraged by promises and overcome by sound reasoning, he consented and disclosed that he had brought the body of Saint Vigor, bishop of the city of Bayeux. The abbot then allured his mind with many gifts and at last obtained the most holy bones for an agreed price. The brethren were assembled, splendidly arrayed in suitable vestments, and the choir proceeded thither with a numerous crowd of people, immense joy, and great honour. The most holy remains of blessed Vigor were brought forth and carefully deposited, as a heavenly treasure, in a more fitting place within the basilica of Saint Riquier.

But the divine command, which had adorned the people of Ponthieu and the community of Centula with so great a confessor, did not permit time to pass idly without showing how great was, in God’s sight, the merit of him whom by gratuitous goodness He had chosen to bring to our dwelling-place. Indeed, although when invoked in any danger he is a swift hearer, in the very dangers of fires he displays a power so effective and so conspicuous to human sight that, whenever a fire strengthened and driven by winds cannot be extinguished by human hands and the flame spreads through everything nearby, as soon as Saint Vigor is brought forward, it is seen to recoil and at once, by divine will and the saint’s merit, to leave what it had already begun to consume [Col. 1300C]. This has happened not once, twice, or even three times, but very often, before the eyes of the people of Centula, in their homes. These things occur when necessity demands them; and through Christ our Lord they are hoped for always, until the end of the age. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Translation of Saint Madelgisil the confessor

While Ingelard still held the government of the monastery of Centula, among the other good things which heavenly mercy bestowed on him, he deserved also to possess the bodily presence of Saint Madelgisil the confessor. There is a village in the district of Ponthieu called Monasteriolus, where this saint had rested continuously from the day of his death [Col. 1300D]. But when his body, through the curiosity of the faithful, had been brought to Centula, to the monastery of the most holy Riquier, some of the monks, stirred by a certain foolishness, began to say that it was unworthy to venerate the little bones of a man whose deeds and life they did not know.

When they repeatedly disputed on this ground—or rather, without reason—there was an ancient little church at the boundary of Centula, dedicated in the saint’s own name. They decided that he should be carried there, so that he might enjoy the dwelling-place of his own church and they would not be compelled to honour him in this manner. And so it was done.

When he had been placed there, God, who looks upon the lowly, and who of old, seeing Leah despised because of her ugliness, gave her fertility so that she might at least be loved for the number of her offspring, though she was repulsive because of the unattractiveness of her face—this God, I say, when He saw that His servant was not sufficiently loved because the deeds of his life were wholly unknown, wished in His mercy to work many great miracles in the place to which his remains had been carried not without contempt, in order to show the people how highly his merit ought to be valued.

[“For He granted sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, and such remedy for other infirmities that, if the things done could have been written down in sequence, their burdensome multitude would altogether have taken away the desire to hear them. So greatly did heavenly power work there that two beams could scarcely bear the tokens of cures: namely, the crutches of the crippled; wax models made for infirmities of eyes [Col. 1301B] or other limbs, offered to the saint himself; the chains of prisoners; and also the diverse signs of manifold diseases which we cannot describe.”]

When, therefore, it had become so evident that he was truly great before God, Abbot Ingelard and his monks began to be moved to repentance because they had cast away so bright a pearl of God as though it were something vile. Him whom they had earlier despised because the obscurity of his sanctity was unknown, they resolved to bring back with devout humility of heart and solemn honour, being invited to love and honour him by God’s magnificent power.

Then, having gathered the brethren, he went with much honour and great reverence in the fear of God to the aforementioned little church. After repentance for their error had first been expressed, and after they had adored the Lord, who is wonderful and glorious in His saints, he received the holy body and restored it with praises to the church of the most holy Riquier [as to one who had softened the hardness of minds by the power of his merits]; it is preserved there even to this day.

These things occurred in the time of Lord Ingelard. But since we have now undertaken to speak of this saint, let us add here also those things which happened long afterward, lest they wholly fall from memory and posterity be deprived of knowledge of them. It subsequently became the custom that, every year on his feast day, the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May], a multitude of faithful would process with him to the place where he had once rested in burial. A crowd of people gathered from neighbouring villages and towns [Col. 1301D], and celebrated the saint’s feast with great joy.

On one occasion, after he had been carried there and the solemn rites completed, when the time and hour had come for bringing him back, such a storm of rain and winds arose as the brethren were leaving the church that the day itself seemed uglier than night. As was customary, two silver candleholders were carried before the holy body. Although their lights were struck by winds and drenched by rains, they could not be extinguished until he had passed through the parish in which he had lived—thus, as it were, marking by a miracle and consecrating what had been his own.

At one time a certain piece of land was taken from that church by the force of injustice by a more powerful man. When the saint was customarily being brought there, after the honour had been celebrated [Col. 1302A], the brethren wished to carry him back to Centula; but by divine will their strength failed. For, on the return journey, when he had reached the very land remembered as having been his own, accompanied by the people, he stopped immovably with the most grievous weight. Some then said that he had been moved by the taking away of his possession, and that this heaviness showed the sign of his indignation. The event itself later proved this true. The deceiver was summoned, and the brethren begged him to restore his property to the saint. Struck by fear of heavenly vengeance, he willingly yielded to the brethren’s prayers and granted that the saint’s property should remain free. When this was done, they returned to the saint; the bier was carried, and no weight was felt.

These, then, are the glorious pledges of saints with which noble Centula is adorned, in addition to those [glorious relics] described much earlier. It joyfully honours as its chief native son Saint Riquier, its abbot and most beloved father. After him, blessed Bishop Vigor is venerated among us in second place of honour; then Caydoch, fruitful in divine commands, is held in esteem; after him Saint Madelgisil, of whom we have just spoken, is loved beyond expression. With these is venerated the companion of Saint Caydoch, whom some call Adrian. Amid the merits of so many, we are protected by the relics of the blessed and holy Abbot Angilbert, and sustained by the patronage of the blessed martyrs of Christ and virgins Elevara and Sponsara. These most blessed virgins, as we have learned from our predecessors, were companions and fellow-virgins of the blessed martyr Macra [Col. 1302C], and were martyred with her by the persecutor Rictiovarus for Christ’s name.

Fortified by these patrons and protected by these advocates, Abbot Ingelard deserved, God ministering, an abundance of good things. Under him also there were in this holy place a number of very good men, both observers of the regular rule and helpers to him in his labours. We mention some of them out of reverence:

Angelrannus, surnamed the Wise, afterward our abbot; Guy, abbot of Forest Cell; Arnulf, abbot of Saint-Josse; Hubert, abbot of Forest Cell; Walter, surnamed Grimutio, abbot of Saint-Saulve.

## CHAPTER XXX. On estates pawned to Notger, bishop of Liège, in Lothair’s kingdom

[Col. 1302D]

There were some estates in Lothair’s kingdom which, because they lay far away, could not easily be inspected. It pleased the lord abbot to entrust them to the bishop of Liège, then Notger, upon receipt of thirty-three pounds of denarii, on the condition that the bishop should enjoy their revenues for twenty years; and that, once this money had been restored to him or to his church, the Church of Centula should recover its property. The following instrument was drawn up concerning this agreement:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Notger, by the providence of the grace of God alone somewhat watchful bishop of the Church of Liège. To the sons of the Catholic mother Church, both present and future [Col. 1303A], who are known to be bound always by the profession of piety which must be maintained: we wish it to be made known what agreement Abbot Ingelard and I have made with one another.

“The aforesaid abbot of Saint Riquier had certain estates situated in our bishopric: namely, five *mansi* in the estate of Hair, five in the estate of Farmala, one in Bursis, and one in Gledela. He pawned them to us, receiving from us thirty-three pounds of denarii from the treasury of Saint Lambert, on the condition that we or our successors should hold them for twenty years without challenge, taking only the usufruct together with the other revenues, without any other usurious gain. But after the said years had ended, on whatever day he or any of his successors should restore the stated weight of silver to us or likewise to our successors, he should recover his estates without obstruction from any contradiction.

“Therefore, so that our descendants might know that the matter had been carried out in this way, we ordered this little charter of testimony to be written and, as the prudent abbot requested, decreed that it be confirmed by our seal and by the marks of our faithful men, clerical and lay, who were present with us at that time.

“Mark of Bishop Notger. Mark of Provost Godescalc. Mark of Nitho. Mark of Sico. Mark of Ecbert. Mark of Frederick. Mark of the knight Walter. Mark of the knight Hiserelm. Mark of the knight Norbert. Mark of the knight Odelm. Mark of the knight Butso. Of his own men: mark of Abbot Ingelard. Mark of the monk Angelrannus. Mark of the monk Duodelin. Mark of the knight Senard. Mark of the knight Heribert. Mark of the knight Ruethelin.

“These things were publicly enacted at Liège on the fifth day before the Kalends of November [28 October], in the year 989 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twelfth indiction, in the first year of Emperor Henry [Col. 1303C].”

Once this condition had been established, Abbot Ingelard, having returned, sent letters to the bishop asking that the agreement be ratified again and that, lest any future bishop break it, he forbid this under anathema, so that it might remain inviolable not merely by the testimony of a charter but also through fear of the pronounced excommunication. He wrote as follows:

“To Notger, most eminent of bishops, Ingelard, abbot, together with the whole company of the brethren of Centula: perseverance in very many virtues and good works.

“Since the vast extent of your benevolence has spread far and wide to us—namely, through your compassion for us as we repeatedly expend useless labour in going and returning while striving to inspect the estates of Saint Riquier which are in this land—we give thanks; and for your and your people’s welfare we offer the vows of our prayers to divine ears, being prepared also, should there be need, to render manifold bodily services.

“And since you deign to bear so great a burden with us, we ask you to be diligent concerning this affair, cultivating the uncultivated, rebuilding what has been destroyed, so that, when the loan received from you has been repaid, our Church may receive back through your industry its goods increased. We further urge that, by the authority entrusted to you, you forbid anyone to presume to alter the arrangement otherwise than has been established, so that if any of your successors—may God forbid—should make evil use of matters well arranged by you, we may not suffer loss in recovering our property when the silver is repaid [Col. 1304A].

“Nor do we say these things because we are at all unprepared to restore what has been received; rather, because we hold from the testimony of Holy Scripture that God permits the wicked to reign because of sin, we desire to bar every door of opposition.

“May the right hand of Christ Almighty,
who, pitying our frailty,
sent from on high,
came down to the depths,
and by his precious death redeemed
the harmful sins of our life,
protect you, gracious shepherd,
through every age of the world;
and thus grant you chastely
to lead your entire life,
