so that, stripped of the covering of flesh,
you may deserve to be a co-heir
of the inhabitants of heaven.”

The venerable bishop accepted these requests [Col. 1304C], and, wishing the agreement to remain wholly inviolable among his successors, wrote the following in reply to the often-mentioned abbot:

“Notger, bishop of Liège, to his most beloved Abbot Ingelard.

“Since until now, my most beloved, we have wished to possess nothing through sacrilege, and do not wish it now, lest anything—which God forbid—be left to our Church after our death from sacrilege, overcome by the exceeding greatness of your love and favouring your petition, we have thought it worthy to do what you prudently requested: namely, that none of my successors should presume to alter for the worse the agreement which we have made with one another.

“Accordingly, we wish it to be known to all faithful of the Church, future as well as present, that on whatever day you, or any of your successors, restore thirty-three pounds of denarii to us or likewise to our successors, the church of Saint Riquier shall recover its estates without the impediment of any contradiction. Whoever presumes to violate this shall, by the authority of God, of holy Mary the Mother of our Lord, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of blessed Lambert, martyr of Christ, be condemned and bound in the bonds of anathema [Col. 1304D].”

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the estate called Matermortua

There is in the district of Liège an estate of Saint Riquier named Matermortua. The oft-mentioned abbot granted it to a certain petitioner to possess so long as he lived, and after his death one of his heirs likewise to hold it during his lifetime [Col. 1305A]. In consideration of the labour occasioned by the long journey, he allowed this upon receiving one hundred silver solidi from the aforesaid knight, provided that an annual rent of twenty-five solidi should be paid. The following little charter was drawn up to confirm this:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Ingelard, by divine disposition abbot of the monastery of Centula. Let it come to the knowledge of the faithful of the holy Church of God, future as well as present, that a certain knight named Hubert came into our presence, earnestly asking us to grant him, by right of sale, a certain land situated in Lothair’s kingdom, called Matermortua. Favouring his petition, we thought it worthy to do so.

“We therefore granted to him, to his wife named Alguidis, and to their one heir, the land which he had requested, receiving from him one hundred silver solidi, on this condition: that whichever of them survives shall possess it without any contradiction, and every year in the season of Lent shall pay twenty-five solidi in denarii. But because he was not yet certain of the heir’s name, he requested a delay of two years, which he obtained from us. This is because the parchment is left blank for writing that name: indeed, he will be called [Note: [Col. 1305C] In the margin of the manuscript used by Acherius is written: Alguidis.] . . . , lest by a difference of handwriting a false addition be subscribed to the charter. And so that this may remain firmly established through succeeding times, it is ratified by the hands of all of us.

“Mark of Abbot Ingelard. Mark of Adier, dean and monk. Mark of the monk Ingelrannus. Mark of Otbert, archdeacon of Liège. Mark of Albold, archdeacon. Mark of John, archdeacon.

“Done at the monastery of Saint Riquier on the fourth day before the Ides of March [12 March], in the eleventh year of King Robert [Col. 1305C].”

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the mill granted; and his death

[Col. 1306A]

On the bank of the little river Scarduo is, among other properties, a certain mill called Mirumdolium. The same abbot granted it for some time to a relative of his named Raginier as a means of support, together with the revenue from the public oven. There are many other things which he did—sometimes in redeeming, sometimes in pawning the lands and estates of the holy place—which we refrain from recounting, because we do not expect all of them to be useful.

But we must fittingly make known this: after establishing the brethren’s workshops and also establishing the community of monks, over which he presided for a very long time, he died on the Nones of June [5 June] and deserved burial in the church of our holy Father Riquier, where his tomb is still visible [Col. 1306B].

> Here, Abbot Ingelard, your material body rests,  
> until the heavenly trumpet recalls the dead.  
> A distinguished lineage of heroes begot you for the world;  
> baptism begot you for Christ through the word, font, and water.  
> First a monk, then ruler of monks,  
> you zealously restored from its foundations  
> the sacred church of holy Riquier,  
> which the barbarian enemy had filled with briars.  
> But June was turning through its fifth course  
> when harsh death brought you the common lot.

One of his own monks succeeded him, Angelrannus by name, surnamed the Wise. Since the third book of this work has become rather long, we now refrain from recounting his history, especially since his distinguished life, written before this time by a certain brother, is to be found [Col. 1306C]. Therefore, when our spirit has been renewed, we shall begin a fourth little book in order to relate some things about him, so that, in evangelical fashion, we may seem to lead forth the four-horse team of the righteous, aided by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the eternal Father and the coeternal Spirit, be praise, honour, and power unto ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1305]

## CHAPTER I. On the birth and education of Lord Angelrannus

[Col. 1305D]

Although the whole world rejoices that it has been redeemed by the descent of God’s Only-Begotten Son through the assumption of flesh, and although the common liberation is a universal exultation, yet certain places are known to have a particular joy in having possessed men who, by the prerogative of holiness and learning, are rightly called fathers and shepherds.

Endowed with this privilege both in location and in name, sweet Ponthieu has often rejoiced in the birth of exalted men. It once produced that most radiant star, blessed Riquier, in whose patronage and bodily presence Centula rejoices that it is blessed. After those whom it is recorded above to have deserved such distinction, it is also known to have produced Angelrannus, a man of glorious memory, who, because he surpassed all the praise of his age [Col. 1306C], has spread the remembrance of his name everywhere.

Angelrannus, a bearer of God, was born of parents not especially noble in worldly magnificence, though entirely freeborn, but plainly most distinguished in the fear of God. Before his birth it was divinely foreshown how great would be his renown and how sweet his savour. One night, while asleep, his mother saw what seemed like a garland gently coming forth from herself, encircling all the walls of Centula and causing every mouth to break forth in its praise and admiration. When she disclosed this to her devout husband, he, inspired by the grace of a heavenly gift, said that it was certainly a presage of the excellent offspring which, by the Lord’s gift, they were soon to receive, and which would fill all people with the fragrance of good works.

Thus, beginning to show good natural qualities and vigorous in keen profundity of understanding, he was found while still a boy to burn with the greatest zeal for learning letters [Col. 1307A]. For, God inspiring him, the boy already showed by a certain foretoken what he was to become. Since it is written, “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom,” and the wisdom of God is Christ, he signified that he would become a temple of the highest Wisdom, in that he could not be satisfied with knowledge of letters.

And because he chose not to embrace worldly licence but to devote himself perpetually to God’s service, he was clothed in the monastic habit within the enclosure of Saint Riquier’s monastery. Then, as divine gifts increased with his age, he adorned with manifold forms of holiness the habit which he preferred to human gaze. Humility, the mother and nurse of virtues, was in him; he excelled in an inexpressible quality of obedience; and he maintained that charity which knows how to hate no one.

Indeed, because, as was said above, he was greatly eager in learning, he received from the father of the house, named Ingelard, permission worthy of no small reverence. He sought out schools at a great distance, in the manner of the most prudent bee, which flies around the growths of diverse flowers so that it may fill its storehouses with the sweetness of honey. He obtained as teacher and instructor the venerable Bishop Fulbert of the city of Chartres, proved by the experience of many and most richly endowed with liberal learning, and spoken of with great honour. Fulbert was his adviser and instructor alike in morals and letters. The venerable bishop rejoiced in the support of so great a pupil and was refreshed by the zeal and intelligence of so capable a listener [Col. 1307C].

At length, having trained this most beloved novice excellently in grammar, music, and dialectic, and having already adorned him with the priesthood, he sent him back to Centula. The devout congregation of Centula received him as a great treasure. Thereupon, what had been sought with immense zeal was brought forth as a precious pearl of great learning: books were repaired, books not yet written were copied, boys were educated, treasures of wisdom were distributed to very many, the homeland was enlightened, and Centula was called happy by all around because it was foreseen to be blessed by so great a father. And happy fulfillment attended the will and desire of the people who eagerly sought this result.

## CHAPTER II. How he became known to the king, and how he became abbot

[Col. 1307D]

At that time King Robert, illustrious in the light of prudence, was invested with the royal authority of the Franks after his father Hugh. By divine direction, as we believe, the aforesaid man was brought to his notice in the following manner. While he was still detained in the regions of Francia by his scholarly studies, the aforesaid king was compelled by devout goodwill to undertake a journey to Rome. And while, by the king’s command, men thoroughly instructed in the offices of divine service were being sought in various places, the venerable Angelrannus was commended by all as especially capable in this matter.

Accordingly, when the expedition had been prepared, the king set out upon the road, and Angelrannus, distinguished by a most honourable life, joined him as companion. Meanwhile, as they journeyed, treasures hitherto concealed were more widely disclosed [Col. 1308A]; words of preaching issued forth and were poured into the hearts of the travellers. The king marvelled at his speech; he delighted in the purity of his restrained life; all were astonished at the brilliance of his language and revered the purity of his soul. Yet what is reported to have occurred upon that journey seems worthy of insertion into the history. For he is said, on abundant testimony, to have served God and king in divine worship throughout the whole journey in such a way that he never needed the aid of books. Whether this could have occurred, let not the idle judge, but let the diligent investigate. Thus Rome was reached, and they returned thence safely.

By the outcome of this journey, therefore, the man of God Angelrannus came to the king’s notice. Hence the king earnestly desired not to leave him among the lowly [Col. 1308B]. Meanwhile, while the king considered with what honour he might support him, the ever-venerable Angelrannus exalted Centula by his residence there. And, by God’s ordering, it came about that the abbey of Centula was deprived of its fatherly care. By the unanimous election of the brethren of sounder counsel, Angelrannus was compelled to undertake that office—he whom the foreknowledge of the Lord had prepared for this before all ages.

Then the king rejoiced that, as he had wished, he had found a place in which to honour him, and hastened with rapid step to the oft-mentioned Centula for this purpose. Indeed, the swiftness of Angelrannus’s fame struck his ears and at once filled his heart with wholesome fear. He did not know what to do. The unanimous election of the brethren compelled him to accept the pastoral office, although there was a very slight opposition from certain men puffed up by their own nobility [Col. 1308C]; and royal authority, ready to urge the same thing, was also approaching. But he, who preferred to be subject rather than to rule, judged himself wholly unworthy to receive such a charge.

Therefore, gathering courage, he sought the woodland thickets and hid himself in certain secret retreats lest he be found. When the king arrived and asked for the man, the crowd of monks declared that he had slipped away secretly. The king marvelled at his intention, praised his humility, and ordered that they go quickly and bring the Lord’s chosen one back to him. The royal attendants therefore went out in search of the illustrious soldier of God; they asked everyone whom they met whether the most renowned man had been seen anywhere. At length, after much searching, he was discovered to be hiding in the forest of Olnodiolum. [Col. 1308D] They went swiftly, sought him out, found him, brought him back, and set him before King Robert.

The king, rejoicing, entered the church basilica and, before the assembled throng of noble and humble alike, entrusted him with dominion over the whole place by hanging the ropes upon the bells. Then, at the king’s command, the worthy consecration of his blessing was hastened as quickly as possible. Truly, then, this man was a member of the heavenly Head: mindful that his Lord, when the people wished to make Him king, fled to the mountain, he chose to enter a cave rather than be exalted by the pride of prelation.

## CHAPTER III. Renewal of the agreement between Abbot Ingelardus and Nother, Bishop of Liège

Now that he had assumed the office of abbot, who could adequately explain his good qualities [Col. 1309A]? His constant concern was to be free of the blemishes of his own life; always to provide what was good before God and men; to cut away the unprofitable habits of those entrusted to him; to increase their good qualities both by example and by word; always to pursue whatever was good and always to avoid whatever was wicked. Nor was it enough for his benevolence to secure the salvation of souls: he also took care to honour with earthly buildings the place entrusted to him. Thus he built walls, adorned sacred altars with gold and silver, and increased, as far as he could, the holy vessels of Christ. His holy intellect delighted in good work; his devout mind was nourished by holy exercise.

Meanwhile Notker, bishop of Liège, to whom certain estates of Saint Riquier had been mortgaged by Lord Abbot Ingelardus, had died, and after two others Durandus had assumed the episcopate of that see [Col. 1309B]. Abbot Angelrannus therefore approached him and asked him to renew in writing the agreement made by his predecessor and Angelrannus’s own predecessor, lest it lose force. The bishop, yielding to the prayers of the venerable man—for Lord Ebalus, archbishop of Rheims, had also requested him to do this—issued anew the following instrument:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Durandus, by the favouring mercy of God bishop of the holy Church of Liège, wishes all the faithful of the Christian religion, present and future, to know that Angelrannus, abbot of Saint Riquier, confessor of Christ, has asked us [Col. 1309C] to renew in writing the agreement which his predecessor had made with Notker, bishop of this holy see.
>
> “For that predecessor had taken from the treasury of Saint Lambert thirty-three pounds of denarii, mortgaging to us certain estates of Saint Riquier: namely, five manses in the village of Hair, five in the village of Farmala, one in Bursis, and one in Glemdena. This was on the condition that, on whatever day he, or any successor of his, restored what was owed to us, he should receive back his own property without contradiction.
>
> “We have therefore done what he requested, and by the writing of this present charter have renewed what our predecessors had established.
>
> “These things were enacted publicly at Liège, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1022, and in the nineteenth year of the empire of Henry.
>
> [Col. 1309D] “The mark of Count Hezelo. The mark of Humbert, cleric. The mark of Guatho, cleric. The mark of Hildrad, cleric. The mark of Adelard, layman. The mark of Libuin, layman.”

## CHAPTER IV. How he acquired the church in the village of Scabellum

When this agreement had thus been beneficially renewed, he returned to the monastery. On another occasion he went to Neustria and, having obtained an interview with Margrave Richard, asked the same duke to make some gift to Saint Riquier for the salvation of his soul. Richard, knowing him to be a prudent man and a lover of the monastic way, graciously complied, granting through his hand to Saint Riquier a chasuble of precious purple and the church of Scabellivilla. Concerning this gift he drew up the following charter.

> [Col. 1310A] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Richard, by the grace granted by God duke of the Northmen, wish all diligent faithful of God’s holy Church to know that Angelrannus, abbot of the monastery of Centula, where the venerable confessor Saint Riquier rests, has entreated our clemency to confer something upon that saint through the gift of our alms.
>
> “Accordingly, by the counsel and urging of our faithful men, we have decreed to grant in perpetuity to the aforesaid saint and his servants the church situated in Scabellivilla. The aforesaid abbot and brethren have promised, under the testimony of this present charter, that for the love of our father, ourselves, our mother, wife, and offspring, the number of monks in that community shall be increased by one person, on condition [Col. 1310B] that, when he departs this world, the succession of another shall follow in perpetuity.
>
> “Furthermore, from this day forward, we and our sons, being called associates of the aforesaid community, shall be held participants in all the good works carried out there. Therefore, that this gift may remain firm in future times, we ordered it to be confirmed under a grave anathema pronounced by the archbishop in my presence, or by certain bishops with their priests who happened then to be present at our court. We also ordered this charter to be made and wished it to be authenticated by the mark of our own hand.
>
> “The mark of Richard, margrave. The mark of Robert, archbishop. The mark of Gonnor, their mother. The mark of Judith. The mark of Richard the boy. The mark of Robert the boy. The mark of William [Col. 1310C] the boy. The mark of Malger.
>
> “Done at Rouen, on the second day before the Ides of March.”

Robert himself, archbishop of Rouen, recognizing Lord Angelrannus as a good man, also gave him a fine hanging, with which our church is adorned even today.

## CHAPTER V. An affirmation concerning Saint Vigor

Since we have now entered Normandy, it is pleasing to pause briefly in order to explain a necessary matter. We have related that under Lord Ingelardus the venerable body of Bishop Saint Vigor was brought from Neustria to Centula. Since we have deserved this, let us render heartfelt thanks to almighty God. Confident, therefore, in God’s gift and in the blessing bestowed upon us through the saint’s body, we must now take action against those who strive to obscure so great a blessing of ours.

Something has indeed been brought to our attention which, with God’s help, will be refuted by abundant reasoning, provided that no biased listener be present through envy. Yet we attack no one in particular, answering all at once. Whenever one of our people happens to discuss the saint’s body with the Neustrian or Sylvanectian people, the former say, “He was our bishop; he rests with us”; while the latter likewise declare that they possess him. Thus our treasure, given to us by God, seems to be darkened, as it were, among the uncertain. We therefore set forth this argument very necessarily, in order to prove that he is truly with us [Col. 1311A]. And if anyone maintains that he has the saint by appealing to manifest miracles, we too have experienced the same things much more magnificently.

For Christian faith truly confesses that all those joined to God can display divine wonders not merely in the place where they are possessed bodily, but wherever they are faithfully invoked. But now let the discourse proceed, in the Lord’s name, toward its appointed end, and let us establish that we possess this saint, even though elsewhere he appears to work great deeds. Christ, the Truth, supports our case; the blessed soul of the holy man, forever united to its heavenly inheritance, bears witness; indeed, testimony for our assertion will arise from his own words.

The Neustrians, who are also Northmen, seemed deserving of blame for not keeping their bishop well. Yet conscience reproves us, because “unless the Lord guards the city, he watches in vain who guards it” (Ps. 126 [127]) [Col. 1311B]. Leaving them aside, therefore, let us explain other matters, since they have plainly been sufficiently punished by the loss of a treasure once possessed and now lost. Let us now silence the mouths of the citizens of Senlis, who boast vainly concerning the saint’s body.

When Centula was first blessed by the arrival of the saint’s body, it remained for some time without any supporting accounts of his deeds. The informant had reported the saint’s name, rank, and episcopal city, but had kept silence about the rest. But when Abbot Ingelardus had been removed from the midst, and this venerable Angelrannus, surnamed “the Wise,” had taken his place, necessity compelled him to go to Normandy, as was explained above. When he had discussed or settled the matters for which he had gone, he began to ask the clerics of that province [Col. 1311C] and the monks of Saint-Ouen whether they knew any saint called Vigor.

They knew him very well; they wondered only that the abbot himself did not know so great a confessor, and they related his origin, life, and dignity. Then the abbot asked them to show him the written Life of the saint and to grant him leave to copy it. When they consented, they were struck by what they heard him say: “The body of this saint is kept at the monastery of Centula, in the monastery of my lord Saint Riquier.”

Then the monks of Saint-Ouen said to him: “Know this, honourable Father: you truly possess him if, upon examining the very bones, you do not find the chin with you. You will not find that bone there, because, thanks be to God, we possess it.” When he had returned to our country with the little book containing the saint’s Life, he hastened to verify what had been reported. He examined the sacred remains and, finding the whole collection of bones, discovered that the chin was missing. But because the reading of the Life itself taught on what day the saint had departed from the world, he hesitated somewhat about what to do: the feast of All Saints, by a recent institution of the Fathers, claimed that day. He therefore decreed that the saint’s feast should be celebrated on the following day. And so it was done, though not in a manner worthy of so great a confessor.

Having profitably inserted these matters, as we hope, let us return to the Life of Lord Angelrannus. Elsewhere we shall state more certain proofs concerning Saint Vigor, proofs which cannot be gainsaid.

## CHAPTER VI. On the steadfastness of Lord Angelrannus, and the donation of Comitisvilla

[Col. 1312A]

With much labour and ingenuity this venerable man constantly endeavoured to restore to the use of the monastery whatever had been fraudulently removed, either during the time of desolation or in the time of his predecessor. The steadfastness of inward strength that dwelt in his mind subdued much of the pride of the powerful, because, fortified by confidence in holiness, he feared no one’s power.

Count Angelrannus of Ponthieu, son of the advocate Hugh, had become his spiritual kinsman because of the holiness proved in him; and he acted toward him with great fear, knowing that no wickedness of human ingenuity succeeded in the presence of this man [Col. 1312B]. An ancient custom had been preserved: on the feast of Saint Riquier the whole military force of Ponthieu came to Centula and held a solemn court, as before the lord of their native land and the guardian and advocate of their salvation.

Whenever the aforesaid count inevitably entered the monastery for the feast of the holy Father, or on any other day, the venerable abbot immediately rebuked him with such authority of denunciation for anything he had taken from the place that one would marvelously think not that a monk was rebuking a count, but that a lord was reproving a servant. If he sometimes failed to obey the rebuke, the abbot, a lover of the place, who could say, “Zeal for the house of God has consumed me” (Ps. 68 [69]), immediately intensified his words and, calling him faithless and a robber, excommunicated him at once unless he promised to make restitution.

This strength of his spirit contributed greatly, and secured that nothing was taken from the place in his time [Col. 1312C]. We say this because, in our age, when benefactors are lacking, it would seem to us that things were going well if we did not suffer the most grievous plunderers. Yet the venerable Angelrannus achieved not only that nothing be taken from him, but also that, by God’s grace, many things be given and restored to him.

Count Angelrannus, therefore, encouraged by his admonitions, granted a certain village to Saint Riquier. In drawing up a charter concerning this grant, he wished it confirmed by royal authority, in the following terms:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Angelrannus, wish all diligent faithful of God’s holy Church to know that, while the most excellent King Robert was staying in the palace at Compiègne, I presented before him for confirmation a charter of donation which I had made to Saint Riquier.
>
> “For I had given to that saint, in the district of Ponthieu, the village called Comitisvilla, upon this condition: that I myself should hold it while I live, and after me one heir, whom I shall designate during my life; and that, on the feast of Saint Riquier, celebrated on the seventh day before the Ides of October, he should pay twelve denarii in rent. If the heir designated by me should neglect to pay, he shall either make lawful amends or lose the holding. I presented this grant in the presence of the king and the nobles of the realm, and judged that it should be confirmed by royal authority.
>
> [Col. 1313A] “The mark of King Robert. The mark of Queen Constance. The mark of Duke Henry. The mark of Robert. The mark of Odo. The mark of Count Angelrannus.
>
> “Done at the palace of Compiègne, on the Nones of April.”

## CHAPTER VII. On his love for those subject to him, and the restoration of Nogueriae

A certain knight named Hucbertus, who held a benefice under oath of service to our abbot, was on several occasions a cause of trial to the venerable Angelrannus. Some of Hucbertus’s relatives had held, for a stipulated period, a village of Saint Riquier called Nogueriae, and under this pretext he claimed it for himself as though it were hereditary property. The abbot resisted, and Hucbertus raged; by his attacks the venerable Angelrannus suffered many hardships [Col. 1313B].

Here it became clear how strong a bond of love he bore toward his people, since he did not cease to contend against Hucbertus and against all who attempted to seize the brethren’s possessions, using the authority both of divine and human laws. Instructed by the example and inflamed by the love of God and our Lord, who laid down His life for His sheep, he too did not fear to endure many dangers and many ambushes of wicked men for the villages and estates of the Church of Centula. Certainly, he would have laid down his life for those entrusted to him, if necessity had demanded it, since, when necessary, he did not refuse to suffer many injuries for their temporal property. In order to save the souls of those subject to him, he was never known to spare his own temporal safety [Col. 1313C].

The savagery of tyrants had not yet grown so great that, by killing bodies, they drove souls away; rather, their greed had proceeded so far that, by despoiling people of their possessions, they made them wretched. And because that great man stood as a constant opponent of their cruelty, he suffered much from them, and the lover of God even endured a blow from the sword. But since we may truly confess that “the righteous is bold as a lion,” this man, relying on a good conscience for those entrusted to him, feared no suffering. For charity held the first place in him, and charity surely casts out fear.

He persisted against Hucbertus until, by the judgment of the nobles in the king’s presence, he recovered by legal right the village of which we have spoken. But what human hearts does greed not seize when opportunity is present? King Henry, indeed, enticed by avarice, after it had been determined that Hucbertus possessed no rightful claim, took the village and enjoyed its revenues for five years. But when he was frequently reproved by the abbot, at last compelled by fear of God’s judgments and overcome by the venerable Angelrannus’s persistent threats, he surrendered it to us and made a charter concerning its restoration, which we also appropriately record here:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by God’s grace king of the Franks, to all children of the catholic Church who have care for soul and body. We wish all present and future to know what restoration we have granted to Saint Riquier for our souls and those of our successors [Col. 1314A].
>
> “A certain knight named Hucbertus held Noguenaria, a village of Saint Riquier with its appurtenances, by the wrongful violence of his own seizure. All his predecessors who had held it had taken it from Saint Riquier under the pretext of a temporary grant. But he, wishing to seize it as his own, was resisted for some time by the complaint of the abbot and brethren. When he had been completely repulsed, it fell by the judgment of our court into our command. I held it for five years, possessing it wholly and peacefully. Afterwards, mindful of my soul and thinking, though only a little, of its redemption, and also persuaded by the abbot and the community of monks, I gave it to Saint Riquier.
>
> “Count Angelrannus, advocate of the same place, also added his petition. I consented on this condition: that he should never receive from it any customary due. And lest any of my successors dare to violate this, I have struck them with the anathema of Hezelin, bishop of Paris, and of all the Franks who were with me. Nor did I exempt the abbot himself, lest he transfer it to anyone under any pretext, so that no further error may endanger our soul [Col. 1314B].
>
> “Therefore, again and again, by our royal command and by the warning of all our bishops, we forbid any evildoer in any manner to dare to usurp it, lest condemnation become necessary for me in that matter where my merits will be unable to help me. Let no one whatsoever doubt this command: let him see the edict of the ruler written down.
>
> “Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1035, in the third year of the reign of King Henry.
>
> [Col. 1314C] “Abbot Angelrannus subscribed. The monk Rollandus subscribed. Gualterus subscribed. Algisus subscribed. Count Ingelrannus and his son Hugh subscribed. Viscount Godefridus subscribed. Oylardus subscribed. Robertus subscribed. These also are witnesses of the excommunication pronounced by all the bishops, especially by Hezelin of Paris. Whoever henceforth violates these terms, let him be anathema maranatha with Dathan and Abiram. Amen.”

It has been mentioned above that, in his time, Lord Ingelardus had permitted a knight named Raginerus, partly for friendship and partly on account of kinship, to hold for some time a mill below Montigniacum called Mirumdoleum. After the abbot’s death, when Lord Angelrannus wished to restore that mill to the use of our Church [Col. 1314D], Raginerus tried to retain it but was defeated by him. Seeing that he would gain nothing by contention, he asked that it be permitted to him, then after him to his son, and after his son to his grandson, so that the Church might finally recover what was its own.

The abbot agreed to do this and confirmed the following written instrument concerning the arrangement:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Angelrannus, abbot of the people of Centula, wishes all the faithful of God’s holy Church, present and future, to know that a certain knight named Raginerus made a claim against us that he ought to hold from us a certain mill situated below Montigniacum [Col. 1315A].
>
> “Having, for just cause, set aside his claim, and at his request for something else, we consented and granted to him and to two heirs—namely, Gualterus his son, and another whom Gualterus himself may have by a lawful wife—the mill at issue, subject to the payment of rent. This is only on the condition that, if Gualterus dies without leaving offspring, the Church shall receive what is its own. But if, as stated above, one heir born of lawful marriage succeeds, he too may hold it during his lifetime and shall pay four solidi of denarii on the feast of Saint Riquier, celebrated on the seventh day before the Ides of October. When this third heir has died, it shall thus return to us again. And that this agreement may remain unshaken, we have caused it to be subscribed with the marks of our brethren and faithful men.
>
> [Col. 1315B] “The mark of Abbot Angelrannus. The mark of Advocate Angelrannus. The mark of his son Hugh. The mark of Odelgerus. The mark of Urso. The mark of Robertus. The mark of Herbertus. The mark of Guerno. The mark of Rodulfus. The mark of Godefridus. The mark of Arnulfus. The mark of Oylardus.
>
> “Done in the monastery of Centula, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, in the twelfth year of the reign of King Henry.”

## CHAPTER VIII. How merciful he was toward the poor

Although Abbot Angelrannus’s provident care was always shown in every matter affecting this holy place, his benevolence was not lacking in relieving the need of the poor. Compassion was therefore his inseparable companion, and, through it, with God’s grace aiding him, he shone as an exceptional comforter of the wretched. He often went out from the cloister in order to find some opportunity to show mercy. And though he was thought to be going out to arrange some useful matter, he, hungering for righteousness, desired to be satisfied by works of mercy.

Indeed, this devout “robber” sometimes carried a purse filled with the treasures of mercy [Col. 1315C]. When he saw from one side or another any poor person approaching, before the person reached him he would cast coins onto the ground. The Father of mercies would call to himself the person who wished to pass by, and, as though not knowing what the thing lying on the ground might be, he would ask. The man, unaware of the act, would say, “Lord, I see coins lying upon the ground.” Then he, beneficently deceptive and piously misleading, ordered him to go and pick them up, saying that they had been prepared for him by the Lord.

O man truly worthy of God! O spirit ever to be exalted with every praise! Lest his life should remain without action, he continually devoted himself to devout works; and lest fleeting praise should strike him, he concealed those very good works. It is pleasing to look briefly at our own depravity and the crookedness of our minds. Even when we do no good, we wish to be praised; and if it happens that we do some small good, we want to be commended by all. We shine neither in deed nor in any virtue, yet we extort honour as though holier merely because of our outward dress. It is altogether a misery deserving condemnation: not to be holy and yet to demand the honour due to holiness.

Thus Angelrannus, a true worshipper of God, illustrious in the practice of good works, devoted lover of hospitality, constant guardian of humility [Col. 1316A], and perpetual servant of charity, remained such to the end. Yet I consider it a most impious error not to mention the keenness of his intellect. For, at the command of his venerable former master, that is, Lord Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, he rendered more pleasing in heroic verse the Life of the grace-filled confessor of Christ, Riquier, which had been briefly written by the ancients. He added almost nothing from outside, but represented the same meaning in every respect.

Moreover, gathering into a single little book the miracles which our Lord and Saviour displayed in his own time through the merits of the same saint, he joined them to the saint’s ancient miracles. At the beginning of these, after the matters set out above, he began to speak thus:

> Now I shall recount more particularly what my own eye saw.

Thereafter he incorporated the account of Saint Riquier which we set forth more fully in the preceding book. [But from the miracles divinely performed after the saint’s restoration, which he testifies that he himself saw, we place some here, so that, as was said much earlier, this man of God may be recognized as great in judgment, since it was divinely granted to him to see such things.]

## CHAPTER IX. On the miracles of most holy Riquier which occurred in his time

When a great multitude of people was again gathering for the annual feast of our most holy patron Riquier, there happened to be near the monastery a well, immensely deep but entirely dry [Col. 1316C]. On its edge, because no one went there, bushes had grown up and covered its mouth, preparing an unforeseen destruction for strangers. A man and a woman, walking above without knowing, fell into its great depth.

When this was heard, the men of Centula grieved that the feast of the principal advocate of the wretched should be darkened by the death of these unfortunates. They therefore sent down a man to raise the bodies of those killed from the deep well. And—O wondrous thing!—those thought to have been broken apart and completely scattered were brought out sound, uninjured, and unharmed; and they offered the people a great spectacle of their restored lives. For it was the saint’s merit that obtained their preservation, since they had sought his shrine with votive devotion.

Palm Sunday, which the common people call Flowering Easter, was being observed according to ecclesiastical tradition. On that day a certain cleric, eating with our monks in the refectory, swallowed a fishbone [Col. 1316D]. When evening came and it began to trouble him, he tried to eject it by vomiting but could not. The following day he was in torment; on the third day the illness became worse. On the fourth, already contemplating death, he asked to be visited by the abbot and requested that he be considered worthy to be buried in the cemetery of the brethren.

On the fifth day—the day which Christian custom calls the Supper of the Lord—seeing that he was now on the point of death, he asked to be carried to the altar of the most blessed Saint Riquier, so that through the saint’s great merits his soul might be commended to the Lord. His household servants carried him there from either side, and certain books were placed upon the altar as an offering from his hand. But when those who had carried him wished to return, divine medicine was immediately present. For he felt himself as though warmed by hot water, and thereby deserved immediately to receive complete health.

There was a certain carpenter named Engelguinus who served our church by repairing collapsing roofs through his craft, or, if need required, by fitting new work neatly in place [Col. 1317A]. During the days of Easter he climbed up to the bells, wishing to retie a broken bell-rope. When the work was done, he was returning when, behold, as he closed the opening in the roof, every support by which he thought to brace or hold himself failed. He fell, and as he rushed toward the ground he would have been received by black death, had not divine power, which did not wish the house of its saint to be bloodied by a man’s death, caught him up.

For, to explain it to one unfamiliar with the place: the very construction of the church, with stones projecting forward, forms an interior passage; ancient workmanship strengthened it with the safeguard of parapets so that one might walk there safely. The man fell upon these stones and, through the Lord’s mercy shown by the saint’s merit, received the joy of his preservation.

The feast of Saint Riquier was being celebrated in its yearly course, but continuous floods of rain prevented people of the district from visiting our walls. One day, when the monks were sitting together, one of them began to complain that the saint’s solemnity was not being observed by the people of the province because, with rain hindering them, no one could come there. Then another monk, trusting in God, answered his despairing brother: “Holy Scripture proclaims that our Lord granted His servants the power to open heaven when they wish and likewise to close it when they wish. I do not believe that our patron is deprived of this power, so that he could not indeed provide a bright road, under a clear sky, for the people coming here in devotion.”

When the vigil of the feast was to be observed, the clouds were removed and such a broad serenity of sky appeared that, wonderfully, what yesterday seemed wholly to dissolve into water, today, shining beyond speech, produced joy in our world by its appearance [Col. 1317C]. The people gathered; the feast was observed; and, as though the tribute of devotion had been rendered, they returned to their homes. Hardly had each person reached his own roof when, behold, such a density of clouds appeared that it signified a flood like a universal deluge. Thus it might be more plainly known that the serenity had been granted not by chance but by the saint’s merit: after the three days during which the solemnity lasted had been completed, the storm returned.

On one occasion some robbers entered Civinocurt, a village of Saint Riquier, and forcibly carried off two of our people. To exact from them what they did not possess, they put iron chains upon them and delivered them to a cruel captivity. Yet while these men were in chains, they did not cease to implore the Lord and His saints with supplicating prayer for aid, especially their patron, Saint Riquier. While they did this, the yearly course of the sun brought round the saint’s feast; and in its night, as they lay exhausted by great suffering in chains and called again upon the same saint [Col. 1318A], all their bonds were immediately released. Thus afterward our men enjoyed complete freedom.

It must also now be related what was divinely brought about in connection with the aforesaid Hucbertus. As he tried, in a proud and rapacious spirit, to seize the villages of Saint Riquier, and was vigorously repelled by Lord Angelrannus, he plotted many evils against him. On one occasion he seized one of the faithful men of Saint Riquier and, both because of the wickedness of his own heart and because of hatred and injury toward the abbot, cast him into a most harsh prison. He afflicted him with such chains and blows that death might reasonably have been thought not merely to threaten him but actually to be inflicted.

Since no earthly power acting in the abbot’s place was at hand to rescue him [Col. 1318B], the chained man prayed that the power of God might come to his aid through the merits of his lord, Saint Riquier. As he persevered in these prayers, the bonds loosened and fell away of their own accord, and, freed from the chains, he began to hold in his hand those by which he had previously been held.

Yet another difficulty remained: shut up in an inner place and secured by locks, bars, and guards, he could not easily conceive hope of escape. But He who saved the apostle Peter from Herod’s prison under angelic guidance now opened the barriers by the command of His own power and overwhelmed the guards with deepest sleep so that they might not hinder the fugitive. Thus, by God’s action, our man was saved. He came to the church of the holy Father, offered his fetters to the saint, and fulfilled the vows of all the brethren in praises of God.

Although the venerable Angelrannus ascribes this miracle to the merits of most holy Riquier [Col. 1318C], we reasonably believe that so great a miracle was performed on behalf of that same blessed man himself, since he made himself such in the eyes of God that great things ought indeed to be done for his sake.

Now let us recount certain things that are known, without any embellishment, to have been wrought by God on account of his goodness. Compelled by some necessity, he had sent two brothers on a rather distant journey. As they hurried along far from our territory, they were attacked by robbers, thrown from their horses, and, with insult, made foot-travellers instead of riders. But when those wretches tried to drive away the animals taken from the monks, immediately—as though they had been cast statues—they could not be moved forward either by blows or by the urging of spurs. Thus, recognizing [Col. 1318D] their sin, they restored to our men what was theirs. On another occasion he likewise sent brothers to the royal court. A horse of considerable value was stolen from them through the daring of a robber; but when the thief, secretly leading away the stolen animal, had been pointed out to the brothers, and our men followed him, the horse at once became rigid and could proceed no farther anywhere. Then the wicked thief, seized by fear of death, unwillingly released the horse and took flight; when our men came up, the horse was caught and again went on without difficulty. Moreover, the pestilential Hucbert, through whose agency this blessed man endured many harsh things, afterward perished with all his lineage by the judgment of the king, because, truly, as the persecutor of a good man, he ought not to have met a peaceful death.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Lord Odelger, a Monk

[Col. 1319A]

The eminent life of this man, so renowned before God, had kindled many people’s zeal toward the love of heavenly things. Therefore we now judge it entirely fitting to show, in the deeds of his disciples, how greatly God’s grace was active, so that he whom we have already shown to be truly holy and thus near to God may shine forth still more in his goodness, being proved great not only by his own attainments but also by the advancement of those entrusted to him.

There was in this holy monastery a man of venerable life named Odelger. He displayed, by God’s grace, a great light of religious life: remarkable in abstinence, supreme in obedience, and watchful over his own mouth. From childhood [Col. 1319B] he had indeed been trained in sacred disciplines under Lord Abbot Ingelard; but under the most reverend Angelrannus he held the office of dean or prior. Applying himself continually to reading and prayer, and striving also for simplicity and purity of heart, he flourished in the pursuits of a great life. He was likewise sufficiently worthy and very capable in the administration of external affairs.

It was his constant custom that, whenever the brothers, by the indulgence of a less strict life, discussed together some secular or even religious matter, he would withdraw into the church. There, diligently intent upon psalmody and compunction, he joined himself to the Lord. And lest he be impeded by any disturbance or by anyone’s coming, he took care to ascend to the upper parts of the church; there, free and secluded, as though from nearby and close at hand, [Col. 1319C] he offered to the divine gaze holocausts of praise and prayer.

After spending a long life in this holy purpose, he came to his end. When he was near death and surrounded by brothers and servants of the church, he suddenly cried out and said: “Behold, the choir of angels is present.” For the almighty and merciful God, wishing to show how devoutly he had served him, chose to send the ministers of his divinity to him at his death, so that in their sight and presence he might depart from the body without severe fear and pain. At this utterance, while all who were present were astonished, he immediately added again: “Behold, the choir of prophets.” After a brief silence he continued: “Behold, the choir of apostles.” Then: “Behold,” he said, “the choir of martyrs.” And after he had been silent a little while: “Behold,” he said, [Col. 1319D] “the choir of confessors.” Finally, when he had announced, saying, “Behold, the choir of virgins,” at that same moment he gave up his spirit. And because he had truly seen the citizens of the heavenly homeland come to receive him, he testified to it by following them.

The most reverend Abbot Angelrannus buried him with veneration, as befitted one truly holy, in the little church of Saint Vincent the Martyr, which stood adjacent to the cloister. Over his tomb he composed this epitaph:

> A cultivator of justice and a lover of piety  
> Was Odelger, who rests in this tomb.  
> Scarce had the ninth day of February taken him from life;  
> As hope has it, it sent him to the heavenly kingdom.

## CHAPTER XI. How He Was Corrected by the Lord

[Col. 1320A]

The venerable Angelrannus, among the memorials of his great learning in honor of Saint Richarius—although ancient compositions abounded—composed certain chants with sweeter melody. He also adapted proper chants for the honor of Saint Walaric, abbot, and Wlfrannus, archbishop. He composed the Passion of Blessed Vincent the Martyr in verse, and rendered the Life of the holy virgin Austreberta into metre.

Because so great a brilliance of learning could not easily remain concealed, many nobles submitted themselves to his instruction. Among them were two distinguished men: Guido, bishop of Amiens, and Drogo, bishop of Thérouanne. They called themselves his disciples and, so long as they lived, always rejoiced that they had been enlightened by his wisdom. [Col. 1320B] Indeed, the excellence of his teaching had spread so widely that Angelrannus was everywhere and by everyone, quite deservedly, especially called “the Wise.”

Since, then, he flourished in such and so great a reputation for goodness, and the apostolic saying was fulfilled in him, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” [2 Cor. 2], that Searcher of hearts, God, seeing that this his servant wished to be joined to him with unwearied longing, determined to refine him further by the file of temptation, so that he might receive him at last more pure—or rather, so that he might heap up an abundance of merits for him. He placed him upon the anvil of bodily weakness and tested him with the hammer of his own striking.

At length paralysis struck him with such severity that he could neither bring his hand to his mouth nor thereafter move himself in bed. [Col. 1320C] His innocent hands were bound by the bond of heavenly severity: hands that had always exercised themselves in good works and had most diligently avoided evil were constrained so that neither these things nor those—good, I mean, or evil—might be touched. Yet he always gave thanks to his Creator; and he who had previously shown himself devoted to God in every good work, now, oppressed by illness, offered a sacrifice of praise with heart and tongue.

Though he was so bound by this illness that he remained wholly unable to control himself, his authority was nevertheless feared everywhere and his name revered everywhere. Often, while sitting somewhere, he would weep most abundantly; and when those attending him asked the cause of his tears, he replied that he was considering in fear the punishments for sins, which were endured within the enclosures of Tartarus through the devil’s ministrations, and that therefore he could not refrain [Col. 1320D] from weeping. Likewise, when at other times he appeared exceedingly joyful, and his attendants asked what it was that made him seem cheerful, he said that this exultation had flowed into him from the heavenly joys of the angels and the everlasting blessedness of the saints.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Fulco’s Usurpation and Lord Angelrannus’s Prophecy

As he grew old, many thought it beneficial that a successor should be appointed to him. A certain man noble according to the flesh, Fulco by name, son of Angelrannus, count of Ponthieu, and himself reared in that place, attempted, with his parents’ assistance, to usurp for himself the government of the aforesaid place at Centula. [Col. 1321A] When Henry, king of the Franks, happened—I do not know by what circumstance—to come to Ponthieu, this Fulco, through the intervention of the aforesaid count, his father, sought to obtain from that king lordship over the entire place. And this was done, wholly without the knowledge of Lord Abbot Angelrannus.

The aforementioned Fulco, anticipating that the royal grant would make him abbot, boldly and shamelessly gave a lavish banquet to certain military men in the brothers’ refectory, a wholly improper practice, in order to make them more faithful to himself and readier to procure the office for him. When this was reported to Father Angelrannus, he called his attendants and immediately ordered himself to be carried there. Thus he was borne in the hands of servants as far as the door of the refectory; there he took his stand and, [Col. 1321B] by the authority of almighty God, anathematized those who had assembled. From that point their entire faction began to dissolve. For one could see all the better men among them, in whom some little fear of God still remained, trembling before the face of the righteous man as defendants before a judge, and being wonderfully terrified by the fire of excommunication which he had pronounced.

The man of God then withdrew and summoned Fulco. In threatening words he asked whether he wished to become abbot. When Fulco, through shame, answered nothing, he pronounced sentence upon him, saying that he could not become abbot so long as he himself remained in the body. And although Fulco received from his father the grant of another abbey as well, he could in no way become an abbot for as long as the blessed man survived, because the word of the man of God prevailed. In this matter it may be observed [Col. 1321C] that the holy man was moved by a prophetic spirit, for not without divine prompting had he foretold that Fulco could not become abbot as long as he himself remained in the body.

For after the venerable Father Angelrannus departed to the heavenly dwellings, Fulco received the office of abbot on the first day after his burial and was placed over the monastery of Forest. From ancient times, as is clearly shown in this work, it had been a cell of the brothers of Saint Richarius; but, having shortly before been taken away by the counts of Ponthieu, it claimed for itself the title of an abbey.

Since we have reached this point, it is pleasing to record, in order to impart knowledge of events to posterity, how that place was taken from us. From the day when the blessed and holy Father Richarius there received the end of his mortal life until the time of Abbot Ingelard, it remained under our jurisdiction. [Col. 1321D] But Hugh, first duke and afterward king, at the time when, to guard against barbarian attacks, he took from us the abbot’s estate and made it into a castle, placing over it a knight named Hugh, took Forest-cell from our jurisdiction and granted it to that same Hugh to possess in perpetuity, because he had married the duke’s daughter, named Gela.

Previously clerics had served the Lord in that cell. But at Hugh’s request, some of our monks were placed there; and they received as abbot, likewise a monk of ours, Guido by name, the brother of Lord Angelrannus. After he had ministered there for some years in the governance of souls, [Col. 1322A] he had as his successor in office a monk of ours named Hucbert. Although that place was taken away from us, it was nevertheless established, out of love and honor for blessed Richarius, that abbots there should always be chosen from among our monks. After Hucbert’s death, its government was assumed by this Fulco, whom we have noted to have wished to usurp lordship over our monastery.

It is pleasing also to speak of Lord Abbot Guido. Although he shone with excellent manners pleasing to God, he was deprived of the light of his eyes, as was holy Tobias; nevertheless, the brightness of divine contemplation endured entirely in his mind. As soon as he received this scourge with thanksgiving from God, the merciful Father, he asked that a successor be appointed to him. Returning to Centula, he fulfilled the remainder of his life there in holy service. [Col. 1322B] He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of May [24 April] and was buried by his venerable brother Angelrannus beside the body of that holy monk Odelger, and was marked by the following inscription:

> Here a carved stone, inscribed with letters, shows  
> That the tomb holds Father Guido, worthy of remembrance.  
> The grace of his excellent life raised him from the world;  
> May the world raise him on high through its prayers.

It is also worth reporting that the Hugh of whom we spoke above was called not count but advocate. That was the title by which he was known, because King Hugh had appointed him defender of the church of Saint Richarius. His son Angelrannus, father of this Fulco, was likewise content with that title until, by God’s permission, he acquired the count of Boulogne in war [Col. 1322C] and married his most noble widow, Adelvia by name. Because he took a countess as his wife, he thereafter assumed the name of count, a name which his successors have continued to hold consistently through established custom. But let us return to our Angelrannus and now begin to tell how the good man had a good successor.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Lord Gervin, Abbot

When Angelrannus, as has been said above, learned that Fulco had sought, by parental intervention and the payment of money, to seize the administration of government, he wished to approach the royal majesty to pray that the care of souls should not be sold. Since he could not do this otherwise because of his illness, he accomplished it while being carried in a cart. He laid before the king’s ears [Col. 1322D] sufficiently harsh words, threatening him with the torments of hell for the sale of grace. The king, who was regarded as well-disposed, repented; having asked forgiveness for his guilt, he promised that he would make amends.

Not many days later, Abbot Richard of Verdun, as we maintain, came to the royal audience by divine will. With him he had as chaplain the most reverend monk Gervin, uniquely beloved for the merit of his goodness. Since this is the Gervin in whose succession Centula rejoiced after Angelrannus, we consider it most fitting to relate from the beginning who he was, so that a man deserving of love may be loved the better as he is known the better.

Gervin was born in the territory of Laon, to a father named Guillencus and a mother named Romild. [Col. 1323A] From his earliest years he was entrusted for instruction in letters to the church of Saint Mary, the metropolitan church of our Gaul, where at that time a clergy truly renowned served the Lord. But, as often happens, when as a young man he applied himself to grammar and with an open mind was already weighing the force of the poems themselves, he observed among them certain works whose entire purpose was either to describe gratified lusts or to recount how someone wished, or was able, to gratify them. While the chaste mind of the youth was defiled by continual meditation upon such things—through youthful ardor, through hearing shameful words, and especially through the devil’s instigation—he began to be impelled toward doing those things which he thought were celebrated in the narratives of such great poets.

Thus, led on by the urging of companions, [Col. 1323B] he came to seek ill-fated embraces, having learned from the pronouncements of poets and the suggestions of already corrupted young men that the ardor of the flesh could not otherwise be restrained. Matters therefore came to the point at which the laws of chastity were to be broken. But almighty God, who had appointed him as a vessel suited to his grace, suddenly flooded him with such shame that he not only did not carry out his evil thoughts, but also repented deeply that he had wished such things. He sprang away from the embrace of the concubine who was kissing him and enticing him to sin—indeed, from the very jaws of the devil—and with such authority suppressed within himself the force of wicked pleasure that from then on he ceased even to listen to the poems of the ancients, lest, as had nearly happened, he should slaughter his soul while learning letters.

We do not tell this [Col. 1323C] because it is unusual for a person to have been tempted by fleshly desire, but because by such an occasion a mind was to be tested which had already resolved to become a dwelling-place of chastity. This, then, was the reason why he abandoned secular studies. Consequently he did not acquire great mastery of those arts; yet because he had tasted them in part, he entered more readily into divine learning, in which he was afterward regarded as skilled both in word and deed.

## CHAPTER XIV. How He Left the World and Became a Monk

After his father and mother died, Gervin was regarded as the manager and lord of the entire household, which was large; he was also a canon of the mother church of Rheims. He considered setting aside the tumults of the world and serving God more strictly. [Col. 1323D] But the care of perhaps two sisters stood against his desire. Among the many vassals whom he held under him by the law of benefice was a good and capable man, a knight of the greatest courage, named Haymo. Gervin, unburdening himself of the weight of earthly affairs, entrusted to this man the chief part of his patrimony and gave him in marriage his sister Rotsellina. The other sister, who refused a husband’s bed, deserved to be betrothed to Christ and devoutly lived out a religious life as a nun in a monastery of holy women.

At this time the venerable Abbot Richard flourished in the virtue of moderation; his great reputation for goodness made him beloved and venerable to all. Gervin sought him out and begged him to grant him the monastic habit and rule. That man of God, filled with the fountain of teaching and an observer of the holy Rule (ch. 9), deferred [and delayed] him, according to the warning of Father Benedict: he set forth hard things, foretold rough things, taught arduous things, and showed the narrow path that leads to the kingdom of life. But while the teacher spoke of great things, the hearer professed greater. He said that he wished to be ready for everything at once: though things be hard or unheard of, and though nature were unaccustomed to them, he promised to endure all, provided only that entry into the cloister not be delayed for him. Moved by such promises, Richard said: “Behold, the holy Rule is here before you. See whether you are able to obey what this book will command you. If you find that you can endure these things continually, you will be received. But if you do not wish, or are unable, to observe them, you came free; depart free.”

[Col. 1324B]

Almost a whole year passed under such delay.

Then, after the man had been duly tested, he was given the sacred garment of the Rule and joined to the holy congregation serving Saint Vitonus, confessor and bishop. Having become a pledged servant of holy religious life, obedient to all, devoted to all, and kind to all, he was therefore dear to all. But so that the constancy of his humility might be more certainly known, he was made guardian of the boys, so that he who was to be chosen by God’s judgment as shepherd of souls might foreshadow pastoral office in such a task.

When he appeared most fit even in this, Father Richard began to embrace him with more fervent affection, so much so that he appointed him both his own chaplain and a provider of many benefits for others. Thereupon Gervin, stirred by holy desire, wished to visit the holy places [Col. 1324C] in which the birth and earthly life, death and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ are known to have been celebrated. But while he feared to reveal his vow to the Father, lest he gain not permission but rebuke, the desire came to the father’s heart through the same divine prompting that fulfills the will of those who fear him.

Thus, while Gervin prayed to God to grant him the fulfillment of his vow, the aforesaid abbot disclosed to his dear companion that he himself wished to go and see the holy places of Jerusalem. He asked Gervin to be his companion, so that, through Gervin’s assistance, the necessities of life might quickly be prepared. Gervin rejoiced that the abbot spoke what he himself desired, and immediately hastened to prepare the things that were to be carried on that journey. Since he was already a priest, he set out with Abbot Richard [Col. 1324D] and other excellent men for the walls of the aforesaid city. When he arrived there, he pressed kisses upon the holy places, shed tears, offered prayers, praying for the holy and universal mother Church.

## CHAPTER XV. How He Was Chosen and Became Abbot

When they had fulfilled the solemn observances of their vows and prayers, they returned home. But not long afterward, compelled by some necessity, they went, as noted above, to the royal court. Then King Henry, mindful of the threat laid upon him by Lord Angelrannus, humbly addressed Abbot Richard in these words:

> Within the bounds of our kingdom stands a monastery generously endowed by the ancient kings. Although in former times [Col. 1325A] it was destroyed by pagans, its name is nevertheless not held least among holy places. It has as shepherd a man prudent in deed and name, Angelrannus, who, having completed the most faithful course of his life, now wishes to put off the garments of the flesh, and therefore asks that a successor be appointed to him in the governance of souls. I beseech the goodness of your holiness to permit Brother Gervin to receive the pastoral charge of that place.

The venerable man, although he bore with difficulty the loss of so great a companion, consented and ordered Brother Gervin to receive the royal gift. Then the reverend prince gave orders; at a quick pace, with certain courtly men … [lacuna] … they arrived. They were received most gladly; afterward they arranged to set out promptly for Centula.

Then Gervin objected, saying that he would not see the place until the unanimous election of the brothers [Col. 1325B] had been reported to his ears. Accordingly prudent men of the clergy were sent to announce these matters to the community at Centula. The venerable Angelrannus was approached and informed that the king had chosen a man who ought worthily to be called shepherd of Christ’s fold, but that he did not wish to come there hastily until he knew Angelrannus’s own wish and the election of all the brothers. And the venerable Angelrannus rejoiced at this and confessed that he desired such a man to succeed him, one who knew how to feed Christ’s flock.

Then, when the assembly of brothers had gathered, he gladly announced the king’s action: that, providing kindly for their care, the king had selected a friend of the good, steadfast in governance, to preside over them by the right of an abbot. “Come,” he said, “and tell us what your mind wishes concerning this man, so that your flock may soon be adorned with so great a shepherd.” [Col. 1325C] Hearing this, all praised and approved the action. Then the consent to the election was written down. The holy man surrendered the pastoral care, in which he very humbly confessed that he had not ministered worthily.

The envoys of the bishop received these documents and returned in swift course to Amiens, reporting to the bishop and the abbot the gracious election of the brothers and the consent of the holy old man. Accordingly, on the day when the birth to come of the Lord Jesus was announced by the angel Gabriel to the undefiled Virgin, Gervin was consecrated abbot; and on the following day the desired shepherd was brought into our house.

Raised to the honor of government, he took up the weapons of continual humility: he did not use fine clothing, more delicate food, or the haughtiness of authority, but by common fare and humility equal to that of the brothers and sons he inspired their love for himself. [Col. 1325D] Some honorable men from the monks of his own monastery immediately followed him, drawn by affection of charity and especially distinguished both for learning and secular prudence. He made one of them, named Guarin, provost; he appointed another, named Regneguard, dean. But since we have briefly related the birth and arrival of glorious Gervin, granted to us by divine favor, let us now take courage to narrate the honorable death of Lord Angelrannus.

## CHAPTER XVI. The Venerable Death of Lord Angelrannus

God, the Creator of all things, had now determined to soothe the desire of his servant with the delight of the heavenly kingdom; [Col. 1326A] and, having made him fit for himself through a most prolonged purifying illness, he made the health of this servant still more grievous, by the inward counsel of his wisdom whereby he chastises every son whom he receives. To him, to whom he was soon to give incomparably sweet things, he multiplied the intensity of pain long endured. Yet, to show that this chastisement proceeded not from anger but from the highest mercy, he displayed over him signs of most evident kindness.

For although this most blessed man had always been most attentively occupied in the study of sacred Scripture, even when he was burdened with the most grievous illness, his disposition and will could never be restrained from divine works. At one time he devoted himself tirelessly to psalmody; at another he clung to sacred meditations on the divine commandments; [Col. 1326B] at another, lying in bed, he himself sang the solemn offices of Mass as though standing at the altar. Consequently, some marveled that a man known for such great wisdom should perform what seemed the act of a madman; yet he judged all those whom he heard wondering at it to be foolish and ignorant of every good.

It happened once that, after he had sung Mass while lying in bed with outstretched hands, almighty God wished to reveal to the ignorant what was being done for him. When the Mass had ended, he indicated that he was thirsty. He therefore ordered an attendant to bring him a cup of wine. The attendant hastily brought wine, but the saint indicated that he did not wish to drink from it. Returning, the attendant brought another wine, but at the first taste the blessed man rejected this also. When the servant saw that he had rejected wine once and twice, [Col. 1326C] and that the old man indicated he wanted another, he excused himself by saying that he had no other wines. Then the holy man said—the very words must be given—“Bring me some of that from which I had at Mass just now.”

Upon hearing this, those standing by froze in trembling and replied to their sweetest Father with tears: “Father, you will have no more of that unless he gives it to you who gave it before.” For while he was celebrating Mass he was believed to be outside himself, and, when the point had been reached at which the most holy offering of the Lord’s body is customarily made, he was refreshed by heavenly food sent by a gift from above. Thus, perceiving that his own attendants had discovered the secret, and wishing by every means to conceal the goodness God had wrought in him, he ordered them, as if disturbed, to leave quickly. [Col. 1326D] For holy men have this characteristic: when they do good, they wish it to be hidden, lest, by receiving the applause of passing praise, they diminish before God the reward of their work.

While these things were occurring, and the blessed man was thought to be on the point of being released from the body by the great severity of his illness, and was therefore carefully watched by those whom he had nurtured, a necessity arose for which it was necessary to send someone to the royal court. Lord Gervin, who now held the government of the place, ordered one of the brothers to carry out that business. But the brother, who wished to be illuminated by the excellent Father’s death in person and to take part in the funeral rites, replied with every excuse that he would not do it.

Then the venerable [Col. 1327A] Gervin, compelled by this response, went to the holy man of God Angelrannus where he lay and told him of the monk’s disobedience. Angelrannus had the monk summoned to him and asked why he had not fulfilled the command; then he ordered him to fulfill it. When the monk still refused, the holy abbot, enlightened by the grace of a prophetic spirit, made this promise: “Go and do what you are commanded, and know that this body will not enter the earth until you return.”

Cheered by this promise, the brother set out and presented most effectively before the royal ears the matters for which he had been sent. But when the heavenly summons came, through which Angelrannus, seeking the things of heaven, left earthly things, that holy soul departed the enclosure of the flesh on the fifth day before the Ides of December [9 December], to be presented before the gaze of God through the ministry of angels.

[Col. 1327B]

Now the stone that had been polished by manifold discipline was placed in the heavenly building. Now the flower of the lily, which had grown in the valley of humility watered by heavenly dew, adorns the heavenly garland. Now the gem that had shone amid diverse cuttings completes the divine diadem.

The monk, having completed the matters for which he had been sent, was returning when, suddenly, in the city of Amiens, where he had turned aside to lodge, dire news of the Father’s death struck him. He then left the lodging and the preparation of food—for it was evening and supper was being prepared—and, mounting horses in haste, rode back to Centula. He found the holy body, now lifeless, laid in the monastery and reverently surrounded by the vigil of the brothers, about to be entrusted to burial at the next hour. Thus he was present and performed his duty; and, once his desire had been fulfilled, [Col. 1327C] the Father’s prophecy was fulfilled as well: he had promised that his body would not enter the earth until that monk returned from the king’s court.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Burial of Lord Angelrannus

The body of the holy man was buried within the venerable church of the most holy Richarius, soldier of Christ, at the place where the martyrdom of blessed Lawrence is venerated. His venerable successor, Abbot Gervin, bestowed such honor upon his burial that one might think an honor of so great a sepulcher sufficient for the sanctity of any of the ancient Fathers. He judged it altogether fitting that the earthly substance of his body should be kept with fitting honor, since, crowned with everlasting laurel, he hymns praises to Christ forever with the inhabitants of heaven. Amen.

These things were done [Col. 1327D] in the year 1045 of the Incarnation of the Son of God, indiction 13. But Christ the Lord, whom this blessed man had faithfully served, deigned to reveal to human knowledge by clear signs how greatly he valued his servant’s service and with what reward from heaven he exalted him.

In the district of Vimeu there was a woman who had a daughter struck by paralysis. Incapable of every task, the daughter lay at the point of death upon a pallet. When the mother learned of the holiness of blessed Abbot Angelrannus, she was inflamed with zeal of faith and, desiring her daughter’s health, brought her with a candle to his tomb. After the sick woman had devoutly offered the candle at the sepulcher of the man of God, she sat beside the tomb and yielded a little to sleep. Then she awoke entirely well and, while the brothers [Col. 1328A] of the monastery looked on and praised God, returned briskly and joyfully to the village from which she had come, called Filcharias, to her own home, proclaiming to everyone how great were the things God had done for her through Blessed Abbot Angelrannus.

Guido, then archdeacon of the church of Amiens and afterward bishop of the same see, who had been Angelrannus’s disciple in the study of letters, adorned his tomb with this epitaph:

> The most choice Angelrannus, whom this tomb covers,  
> Was shepherd and abbot of this monastery.  
> Leader of the Church’s flock, a monk, the noble hope of life,  
> He lived in the world unstained, and in the Lord.

Whoever wishes to know more fully how greatly this holy place profited through him should examine the verses that were written concerning him so that later generations might know and imitate them. [Col. 1328B] They read as follows:

> The written record visible here retains what few things  
> Abbot Angelrannus bestowed upon our shrine.  
> He built the church of Saint Vincent and also that of Saint Benedict,  
> And prepared a cell for the sick.  
> He rebuilt the cloister-garden from its foundations;  
> He had an altar frontal made for Peter’s altar,  
> And also had a pair of silver censers cast.  
> His own zeal adorned in pure silver  
> A Gospel-book and the Life of Saint Richarius.  
> There is also a book of Epistles and Gospels,  
> Which his industry likewise prepared in silver.  
> Through his zeal there is also seen a splendid chalice,  
> With a fitting paten joined to it;  
> Besides this, another which he always used at Mass.  
>
> [Col. 1328C] One hanging and three very precious cloths.  
> He preserved and redeemed lands that had been seized:  
> Namely Noguerias, Gaspannas, and Drusiacum;  
> The church of Guibrent, Froocort, and Mont-Rochon;  
> The church of Sacri-Campus. Amid grievous contention,  
> While many strove for the opposing side to prevail,  
> He was deprived of much and suffered many wrongs.  
> He accomplished what I have recounted above, and very much besides;  
> The Lord’s knowledge knows how it was done.  
> The books which he made new exceed counting;  
> Those which he restored also exceed counting.  
> By these and other such things he earned, as hope has it,  
> The rewards of the heavenly kingdom. Reader, we urge what you can do.
>
> [Col. 1328D] This was the final object of his efforts:  
> In dying, he restored the church of Saint Mary;  
> May her intercessions avail for us before the Lord.  
> Therefore let there be the rewards of life for the restorer of these things.  
> Let him be condemned through whose neglect these things perish.

That same honorable man, providing for posterity, wrote a rhythmic catalogue of the Fathers of this holy place.
