He did not identify all of them, but mentioned only those whose names seemed to be indicated by charters or by any little written slips, or whom the Life of Saint Richarius specifically made known. [He wrote as follows:]

> The names of the abbots  
> Of the monastery at Centula  
> That come to mind,  
> Though not in order, I write.
>
> [Col. 1329A] Before all stands our outstanding  
> Shepherd Richarius,  
> Born in this estate,  
> First entered on the list.
>
> Ocioaldus follows;  
> Magnificent Angelbert,  
> Who built the present church  
> By the power of King Charles;
>
> The most holy man Guitmar;  
> Helysachar and Aldricus,  
> To whom Hericus is added;  
> Hludogvicus and royal  
> Herbert, Symphorianus,
>
> [Col. 1329B] Ruodulfus and Carlomannus,  
> With Guelfo and Hedenold,  
> Gerbert and Fulchericus.
>
> After Ingelard, therefore,  
> Angelrannus is entered,  
> An imitator of the holy order  
> And devoted to letters.

Indeed, the venerable Angelrannus [wrote] these things. Yet we are greatly astonished how it could have happened that so learned a man did not know the deeds of Lord Helgaud, count and abbot; or, if he knew them, why he omitted to mention his name, since the deeds of that same Helgaud were not found somewhere only recently, but had, unless we are mistaken, been kept and preserved from ancient times in the archive of this place. Nevertheless, it must be believed possible that, after the death of [Col. 1329C] Lord Angelrannus, these accounts concerning that count and abbot were brought here from some place; since, as the preface to this work testifies, at the time of devastation, when the monks fled, not only were relics and ornaments carried off, but also the writings composed concerning the holy place were conveyed and scattered to various places.

For the venerable Gervin once went to the monastery of Gorze, and brought back from there a codex concerning the deeds of this holy place. There was discovered what had previously lain hidden for a very long time: namely, that when Lord Abbot Angilbert passed to heaven, his son Nithard succeeded him, after several others, in governing the holy place; along with the other matters which we have taken care to note above in their proper places. [Col. 1329D] There too was set forth concerning Abbot Ribbodo that he translated the body of Saint Angilbert; and many other records of this place were found in the same volume, which the venerable Angelrannus is known to have been ignorant of.

These four names of abbots, therefore, which occur less fully in Lord Angelrannus’s writing but more fully in ours—namely Lord Nithard, Lord Ribbodo, Helgaud also, and Coschin—were found as follows: the first two in the codex brought from Gorze; the third in the parchments of our school. For more writings concerning Lord Coschin are kept at the monastery of Jumièges; from these it is proved [Col. 1330A] that this same man was abbot both of our place and of that one. Since these matters stand thus, let the mind now turn back with pen in hand to setting forth the life of Lord Gervin.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the praiseworthy deeds of Lord Gervin, and the construction of the crypt.

Gervin, then, attending to the care of those entrusted to him and reproving offenders, planted seedlings of virtues in their hearts by the words of his preaching and the examples of his deeds. Receiving also the confessions of wicked people, and restoring their wounded souls by the healing applications of the holy Scriptures, he recalled them to God’s mercy. If he perceived that any of them were wealthier, he urged them to build houses of prayer [Col. 1330B] in order to obtain pardon. His pious purpose brought much beauty and improvement to our native land, while things that had not existed were erected, and those constructed of timber were rebuilt in mortar and stone.

He himself, very solicitous for the place committed to him, strove to renew what had grown old, repair what had fallen apart, and construct what had never been made. Thus he built a very remarkable crypt, which endures to this day, and obtained its consecration in honour of our Lady, Saint Mary the Mother of God. In this crypt, at the four altars that are there, he placed relics of the Lord Christ and His saints so numerous and so glorious that, even if there were no others, our little homeland would truly be adorned by these more than sufficiently and fittingly.

[Col. 1330C] We therefore append an inventory of these sacred relics, so that posterity may know with what glory that holy place flourishes. The relics presently designated are those by whose multitude the principal altar of the crypt at Centula is adorned. It is dedicated in honour of the Annunciation and Nativity of the Lord, of the holy and most victorious Cross, of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist, of the most illustrious confessor of Christ Richarius, of the blessed virgin Cecilia, and of all holy virgins. These are the relics of the saints named:

Of the wood of the holy Cross; of the Lord’s tomb; wax from the holy Resurrection. [Note: [Col. 1329] That is, unless I am mistaken, from the Paschal candle, or from that lamp which was lit at Jerusalem every year on the vigil of Easter. MAB.] Of the column at which the Lord was bound; of the stone on which He stood when He mounted the Cross; of the linen cloth with which He girded Himself when He washed the disciples’ feet; of the Lord’s manger; [Col. 1330D] of the rod of Moses; of manna; of the garments of Saint Mary the Mother of God; of her hair; of the thread which she herself spun; of her tomb; [of the pallium of Saint Michael the Archangel]; of Saint John the Baptist; of the body of Isaiah the prophet; of Saint John the Evangelist; of the Holy Innocents; of Saint Stephen the protomartyr; of the holy martyrs Pope Stephen, Pope Felix, Eusebius bishop of Vercelli, Florentius, Blasius, Crispin, Crispinian, Paternus; a tooth of Saint Livinus the martyr; of the holy martyrs Hermes, Praejectus, and Romanus.

Relics of the holy confessors Martin, Remigius, Nicholas, Vedastus, Medard, Cassian, [Col. 1331A] Amandus, Cadoc, Salvius, Paul, Machutus, Gaugeric, Autbert, Ranulf, Acharius, Otbert, Wandrille, Bertin, Philibert, Bavo, Walaric, Maurontus, Guingualoeus, Judoc, and Cuthbert.

Relics of the virgins Petronilla, Anastasia, Justina, Prisca, Praxedes, Gertrude, and Augusta.

Likewise, on the southern side of the crypt an altar is dedicated in honour of the coming of the Holy Spirit, of the most blessed apostles Bartholomew and Matthew, and Luke the Evangelist; of the holy martyrs Maurice, Nicasius, and Leodegar; and of the holy virgins Agatha and Lucy. The relics there are: hair of Saint Bartholomew; the head of Saint Matthew; the head of Saint Nicasius; relics of the holy martyrs Maurice, Leodegar, Firmin, Cyriacus, Agapitus, Crispin, Crispinian, and Anthimus; [Col. 1331B] likewise of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian, of Saint Agatha, of Saint Sabina, and of the Lord’s tomb.

Likewise, on the northern side of the crypt an altar is dedicated in honour of the glorious Resurrection and Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ; of the holy apostles James, Simon, and Jude; of the saints Quentin, Lucian, Fuscian, Victoric, Gentian, and Lambert; and of the holy virgins Agnes and Scholastica. These are the relics: garments of the apostles Peter and Paul, together with dust from Saint James; a tooth of Saint Simon the Apostle; relics of Saints Christopher, George, Crispin, and Crispinian; hair of Saint Quentin, and relics of his body, and of the nail by which he was pierced; of Saint Lambert’s chasuble; of Saint Hilary; and of the holy virgins Agnes and Scholastica.

[Col. 1331C] Likewise, an altar beneath the altar of Saint Richarius is dedicated in honour of the holy and undivided Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, Eleutherius, Gervasius, and Protasius; of the holy confessors Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and Athanasius; and of All Saints. These are the relics: of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, Eleutherius, Gervasius, and Protasius; and of the holy confessors Satyrus, Ambrose, and Augustine.

Gervin, that most discerning shepherd, sought these many and most precious pledges of our Lord Jesus Christ and His saints with great diligence through different parts of Gaul; some he also found at Saint Richarius’s [shrine]. He honourably placed them in the altars which he erected in the crypt, [Col. 1331D] on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November [19 October], dedicating that same building reverently to God Almighty and Saint Mary.

There are also many other things which this good man undertook in caring for the place, whether in acquiring vestments, making tapestries, or redeeming lands. Although many proofs of these things are before our eyes, some indications must nevertheless be set down here.

## CHAPTER XIX. How he obtained the restoration of the church of Scabelli-villa, which was being claimed against it.

In this little work of ours we have related that the venerable Angelrannus went to Neustria and received, for the use of our place, the church of Scabelli-villa through the grant of Duke Richard. But when Richard the marquis, who had bestowed this benefit upon us, died, his son [Col. 1332A] Richard surrendered the duchy—which he had held for a short time—to his brother Robert; and after this Robert, William arose. The aforesaid church was then obstructed against us by a certain abbess, who by some means unknown to me was attempting to convert it to her own right.

On this occasion the memorable Gervin went to Neustria, carrying with him the chirograph which Marquis Richard had drawn up concerning the surrender of that church. He wished to vindicate it for us by truthful assertion and documentary proof, and also to entreat the aforesaid Duke William not to permit that which his predecessors had given to be taken from Saint Richarius. But the said count, greatly loving and honouring him for his holiness, favoured him in every respect, enlarged the church’s lands, and ordered the following charter of confirmation concerning its perpetual security [Col. 1332B] to be made.

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. William, by the grace of God duke of the Northmen, to all children of the Catholic Church who have concern for soul and body.
>
> “We wish it to be known to all future posterity how, for the salvation of my soul, I have confirmed by the authority of our judgment that the church of Scabelli-villa is to belong to Saint Richarius in perpetuity. When it was claimed by the abbess of the Monastery of Villaris, and when I had been summoned by Gervin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Richarius, that same man set forth the case of this dispute before the chief men of my court: namely, that it belonged to him by right through the gift of my predecessors. Their judgment having so decreed, I restored it on the following terms. I further gave him the assurance of my pledge that thereafter [Col. 1332C] he should hold it freely under my protection, just as he had received it from my grandfather and father. For, from the report of those who knew the case, I had learned that it was properly incumbent upon them to maintain a prebendary in remembrance of us for this benefice. Therefore, lest our confirmation should be annulled by the rashness of any future person, and lest we should lose the merit [thereof], we caused the letters of this charter to be written.
>
> “Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1048, at Argentulum, on the third day before the Kalends of November [30 October].
>
> “Fit witnesses of this matter are Storinstingus, Richard his son, Ivo of Bellême, Arnulf his nephew, and Rodulf Taxo.”

When Count William had been approached by Lord Gervin concerning this [Col. 1332D] matter, he earnestly requested the abbot to grant him some portion of the body of Saint Vigor the bishop, which had formerly been brought to our dwelling places under God’s gracious guidance. Unless the abbot had promised that he would do this, he would truly, as the saying is, have lost the aforesaid church; for the count would rather have yielded it to his kinswoman and relative than granted it to anyone else, since that same abbess was related to the duke’s family.

## CHAPTER XX. A further account concerning Saint Vigor.

But since mention has now arisen of the body of that most holy bishop, we think it worthwhile here to relate the true attestation which that blessed [Col. 1333A] prelate himself accomplished, the Lord acting on our behalf. In the deeds of Lord and Saint Angelrannus, indeed, it is found how that distinguished abbot became certain concerning the body of this saint; and how, bringing a little book of his life from Neustria and learning from it the day of his glorious passing, he established the observance of his feast-day.

This ordinance remained in force down to the time of the glorious Gervin, of whom we are speaking. Flourishing in the fear of the Lord and love of the saints, he improved many things among us in divine worship. It happened, then, that the annual cycle brought around the feast of Saint Vigor, which the brethren observed according to the custom formerly established by Lord Angelrannus. By chance Abbot Gervin was absent at that time, and the prior, named Regneguardus, was overseeing the brethren’s care.

That same Regneguardus, [Col. 1333B] on the night when the brethren were celebrating the holy solemnities, was detained by a slight bodily illness. He was absent from the solemnities and, lying in bed, slept rather heavily. (Otherwise he was a good man, chaste and God-fearing.) Behold, as he slept, there stood before him a person of venerable stature and supreme beauty, displaying episcopal attire, who said very gently to Regneguardus: “Why do you lie here and not take part in my solemnities?”

Terrified by the majesty of the figure, he nevertheless replied when questioned: “Lord,” he said, “because I am ill.”

Then he added: “Who are you, lord?”

“I,” he said, “am Vigor, bishop of the Church of Bayeux. Rise, be well, and hasten to take part in my solemnities. Tell your abbot and brethren that, since the goodness of our Lord has granted that my body should be kept here, [Col. 1333C] and since I myself desire this, my feast ought to be made more splendid than it is.”

Having perceived these things by sight and hearing, the monk rose up healthy, went to the choir, and with the others sent forth, as best he could, loud chants in praise of the saint. The brethren were astonished; and, because at that hour he refused the courage to speak, they asked in the morning for the order of events. He related the vision, declared his recovery, and recounted the command. All rejoiced and were inwardly kindled with love for the saint. When the abbot returned, all was reported to him in order. He, who even without any such occasion had exalted the feasts of many other saints, ordered that henceforth the feast of Saint Vigor should be observed with the greatest solemnity.

### Fulcard

The festal day of Father Vigor shines forth, worthy of celebration—  
[Col. 1333D] Bayeux calls him father; Arras rejoices to call him brother.

His mother, pleasing to God, a noble woman,  
receives from so great a pledge a heavenly defender.  
The divine power blessed the son whom she bore,  
consecrated him to itself, and consecrated him to the whole world.

Thus the boy is born beautiful in form, and becomes  
another Samuel, worthy of the Lord from tender childhood.  
Soon he gently bows his neck beneath the Lord’s yoke  
and, a boy monk, is brought into the flock at Arras.

Advancing beyond all the Fathers, he advanced through them—  
that illustrious boy, joyfully subject to all.  
Already the blessed novice meditates something greater:  
that, with the patriarch, he may become an exile from his homeland.

Therefore this exile, a sower of the word, goes far into exile,  
making his way to the people revealed to him from heaven.

[Col. 1334A] Bayeux is the city which ancient Neustria points out.  
He goes to it to teach those whom impious error possessed,  
with Christ’s grace of miracles accompanying its foster-child.  
What he teaches and enjoins, he proves by signs and fulfills by deeds.

He restored those drained of strength, drove out serpents,  
and by poured-out prayer drew one whose life had ended up to the world above.  
Seeing these things, the people devote themselves to the sacred waters;  
and, through the honour of the sacred font, you beget this offspring for God,  
holy Vigor, to whom we offer sacred songs—

you who subdue flames and crush the fires of the world:  
restrain the flames of Gehenna, lest they burn us.

But Marquis William, by sending to us a monk named Guarin from the monastery of Cerisy, obtained a bone from the right arm of the holy bishop. That bone is worshipped at the same monastery of Cerisy with boundless [Col. 1334B] veneration. This place lies in the territory of Bayeux, and there Vigor, the man of God and bishop, as is read in his Life, while he still lived in the exile of this pilgrimage, drove away a monstrous serpent. On account of this miracle, the place was granted to the holy man; and there is now still a congregation of servants of Christ there.

When the monks living there had joyfully received with ineffable gladness the relics of their most holy patron, they wished to test whether that bone was truly from Saint Vigor’s body. They knew that among the other gifts of miracles by which he had always shone—indeed, by which he still shone—he also possessed this especially outstanding one: that he could in no way be harmed or burned by the heat of fire.

They therefore made a pile of flax, a material which catches fire very readily, [Col. 1334C] and laid that arm of the most holy bishop upon it. They then heaped flax over it and set fire beneath the dry and delicate material. Although almighty God ought not to have been tested concerning the merit of His servant, the event of the miracle and power nevertheless did not disappoint those brethren, who did this not from any vice but in order to gain certainty. For not only did the fire not harm the saint’s right arm, but the flax placed upon it also remained untouched by fire. Thus those brethren became certain of the Father’s relic.

Not yet eight days had passed after this event when, behold, a man possessed by a demon received, through the compassion of those brethren, water in which that blessed bone had perhaps been washed. Having drunk it, [Col. 1334D] he received bodily health and freedom, and thereafter suffered no assault from the Enemy. These two miracles Christ the Lord performed at the monastery of Cerisy through the relics of Saint Vigor which we had conveyed there.

After some years, Gervin the Father summoned honourable men, namely bishops and abbots, removed the most sacred limbs from the shrine in which they had rested since the time of Abbot Ingelard, and displayed them to the faithful people through the hands of the assembled bishops. Then he honourably placed them, as befitted so great a confessor of God, in another shrine prepared with gold and silver. This translation of the blessed body took place on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [21 March]. This day is observed each year with the devotion of the Lenten fast. We believe this was done by divine [Col. 1335A] providence, so that faithful people might deserve to see the bones of the most holy bishop when they had offered God the sacrifice of a stricter, and therefore purer, life.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the counts of Ponthieu, and the estates of Portes and Nogueries.

After this necessary account concerning Saint Vigor, let us return to the deeds of our Gervin and briefly explain how our place came to possess the estate called Portes. First, since we acquired it through the gift of the counts of Ponthieu, it is considered fitting briefly to set forth their succession.

When the little country of Ponthieu was first strengthened with castle fortifications, three towns—Abbot’s Estate, Saint-Medard, and Incra—were taken from the monastery [Col. 1335B] of Centula and made into castles. Many other estates and revenues of Saint Richarius were assigned by King Hugh for their maintenance. At that time our province was not governed by a count, but was protected by royal soldiers stationed here and there. In an earlier period, however, it had often been defended by many of our abbots who bore the title of count. But because those appointed in the later period were not all inhabitants or lords of castles, Hugh the Abbot became stronger than his peers: protected by a castle’s fortification, he could do whatever he wished without fear, while the others, if they attempted anything, had no refuge and easily succumbed.

[Col. 1335C] Yet he never received the title of count; his distinction was that he was called advocate of Saint Richarius. This likewise greatly contributed to his power, since under the pretext of his advocacy he used the revenues of Saint Richarius’s estates and the labour of peasants. When he died without the title or dignity of count, he was succeeded by his son Angelrannus. This man too was content with the title of advocate, until he killed the count of Boulogne in battle and married the latter’s widow; from his countess wife he claimed the title of count.

Angelrannus thus transmitted the title of count which he had acquired to his descendants. Dying after a long life, he left an heir to his rank and title named Hugh. When Hugh had completed his span of life and [Col. 1335D] saw himself near death, he assigned to Saint Richarius the aforesaid estate called Portes, wishing that it should serve the uses of our monastery for the remedy of his soul.

He had begotten four sons. The first, named Angelrannus, a man of remarkable appearance, succeeded his father. On the day of his father’s burial, he gave the aforesaid estate to the saint and confirmed the surrender by the following charter of testimony:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Angelrannus, count by the grace of God, wish it to be known to all children of God’s Church, present and future, that my father, Count Hugh, while still living but drawing near the final day of death, gave, for the remedy of his soul, the estate which he possessed in full ownership, [Col. 1336A] named Portes, to Saint Richarius, to be held in perpetuity. This was on the condition that none of his successors should ever again demand from it any payments or small or great customary dues, so that it might serve wholly, with its revenues, the saint and the brethren dwelling there. At the request of Abbot Gervin, therefore, we caused this small charter of donation to be written and confirmed it with our mark and those of our faithful men.
>
> “Mark of Count Angelrannus. Mark of Godefrey. Mark of Oylard. Mark of Robert. Mark of Bernard. Mark of Walter. Mark of Gerard. Mark of Ingelrannus.
>
> “This transfer was made upon the altar of Saint Richarius, on the day of Count Hugh’s burial, the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [20 November], by his son Ingelrannus with his magnates, in the presence [Col. 1336B] of Lord Bishop Fulco. Immediately entreated by the brethren, and at the count’s own request, he forbade under excommunication anyone thereafter to demand in that estate anything further of the relinquished customs, whether by force, entreaty, or advocacy.”

Thus far the charter.

Furthermore, a certain knight named Walter, whom the common people called Tirel, wished to claim for himself Saint Richarius’s estate called Nogueries. After all the events written above, which took place in the time of Lord Angelrannus, he maintained that this same estate was owed to him by some alleged right of succession, through a certain semblance of legal right derived from King Henry and the treacherous Hubert. Colouring his greed with such a pretext, [Col. 1336C] he invaded the estate, held it, and for some time usurped it while the brethren excommunicated him.

But when his friends urged that enduring this excommunication would bring death to his soul, he at last, God looking upon him, yielded somewhat. During the life of himself or his wife he retained one half for himself and restored one half to the saint, establishing that after his death the whole estate should return intact into the saint’s right. For this reason the venerable shepherd placed in our archives a written chirograph, which reads as follows:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Brother Gervin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Richarius, wish it to be known to all faithful of the holy Church of God, whom Christ adopted as brethren in the adoption of children through His blood [Col. 1336D] and through the sanctification of baptism, that a certain knight, Walter by name, whom many of us call by the vain surname Tirel, maliciously invaded the estate of Saint Richarius called Nogueries, long possessed by our predecessors and handed down to us by hereditary right. By invading, he stole it away; and by stealing it, he held it for some time under the bond of anathema.
>
> “But at last, his friends opposing him and repeatedly representing this injury as the ruin of his soul, he was overcome and ashamed. Abandoning the wickedness of his mad covetousness, he asked forgiveness from Saint Richarius and from the brethren. Having restored the estate and granted to us a chapel founded long ago, he received absolution from excommunication, prostrate upon the ground with his wife Ermina present. In settling the matter, [Col. 1337A] he said that the aforesaid chapel, just as it had hitherto remained in service to himself or his people without any synodal exaction, should likewise continue for future ages in the same liberty.
>
> “These things were done on the seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October], in the year of the Lord 1103, indiction 6; the same knight, together with the witnesses recorded below, confirmed the anathema, so that from that day no one, for any occasion, either from their descendants or at the instigation of any of them, should rashly dare again to usurp this estate for himself.
>
> “I, Gervin, together with the priests of our religious community, the deacons, and the monks of this foundation, by the authority of God the Almighty Father, of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, and of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, [Col. 1337B] condemn and anathematize forever all who from this day shall wish by any boldness to annul, remove, or oppose this restoration of the estate and the gift and liberty of the chapel. Amen.
>
> “Witnesses of this matter were Odo, Alulf, Hugh Boquels, Boso, Oylard, Hugh of Saint Mary, Boselin, Alelmus, another Odo; in the twenty-first year of the reign of Henry, king of the Franks.”

In the deeds of our most holy Father and patron Richarius it is recorded that the glorious King Dagobert, commending himself to the prayers of that saint, gave him a tract of land called Campania. Gervin’s predecessors had granted this to a certain Agenard, that he might possess it securely for as long as he lived. [Col. 1337C] He came to Lord Abbot Gervin and asked that, after his death, his two sons might be permitted to hold the land which he himself held; after their deaths, the Church was to recover worthily what was its own.

The venerable abbot granted his request and, for the legal security of the matter, drew up the following charter:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Gervin, by the favour of divine grace abbot of the monastery of Centula, wishes it to be known to all Christian people that a faithful man named Agenard has asked us to grant him, his wife Hildesend, and their two sons, namely Guenerannus and Anscher, the right to hold: all the land of the small property called Rebellis Mons, which he held only for his lifetime under secure tenure [Col. 1337D] and subject to the payment of rent; the whole land of Valeries with its adjoining small wood; and, in addition, one quarter of the enclosed homestead at Floherimans.
>
> “We therefore granted him what he had asked, having received from him the most reliable witnesses, but only on this condition: that they should hold it only for their own lifetimes, and should pay a rent of four solidi at the feast of Saint Richarius, celebrated on the seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October]. After their death, the land shall return to us improved. Therefore we wrote this charter for them and confirmed it with our mark and those of our faithful men.
>
> “Mark of Abbot Gervin. Mark of Algis. Mark of Heribert. [Col. 1338A] Mark of Ingelrannus. Mark of Dominic. Mark of Oylard, a layman. Mark of Boso. Mark of Odo. Mark of Rodulf. Mark of Guido, archdeacon.
>
> “Done at the monastery of Saint Richarius, on the eighth day before the Ides of December [6 December], in the sixteenth year of the reign of King Henry.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On estates redeemed and altars given by Bishop Guido.

Meanwhile, King Henry of the Franks died after twenty-eight years of his reign. Philip, still a boy, had already received from his father the summit of royal dignity, but had not yet the ability or knowledge to rule. He was entrusted, together with the kingdom, to Count Baldwin of Flanders to be his guardian. While Baldwin governed the kingdom, a knight named Walter, [Col. 1338B] son of Hugh the king’s butler, wished to take from us a certain tract of land situated in the district of Vimeu.

Since he was powerful and no ready means existed to resist him, the anxious shepherd Gervin, wishing that the Church should not lose the estate, preferred to appease the man with money rather than suffer so great a loss. But he granted the requested favour not so much enticed by money as compelled by reverence for the holy man’s prayer. In order that neither he nor anyone else might thereafter take the same land from the holy place, he requested that a charter be made in the following words:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Gervin, by God’s grace abbot of the monastery of Centula, wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that a certain knight named [Col. 1338C] Walter, son of Hugh the king’s cupbearer, brought a claim against us concerning a certain tract of land in the district of Vimeu, called Filcarias. We answered his claim with just legal argument and refuted his wrongful allegation. Having received from us one hundred solidi, he restored the aforesaid land, free from claim, to Saint Richarius, to be held forever for the brethren’s use. And in order that this agreement may remain unshaken, we decreed that the marks of our brethren and faithful men should be recorded.
>
> “Mark of Abbot Gervin. Mark of Incelerius. Mark of Algis. Mark of Anscheric. Mark of Frameric. Mark of Anscher the knight. Mark of Odo. Mark of another Odo. Mark of Adelelm. Mark of Ilgerius.
>
> [Col. 1338D] “Done at the monastery of Centula, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September [29 August], in the fourth year of the reign of King Philip.”

Not much time had passed when Gervin, the vigilant and solicitous steward, who was always a true lover and guardian of the Church’s children, approached Count Guido with prayers. He asked him not to refuse some merciful regard for the holy place concerning a certain estate which had formerly served our monastery, but had some years before been taken from us by that count himself or by other military men.

What he did at the prompting of love for the Lord could not fail, by God’s own divinity. For the count gave his consent after some delay, appeased not only by the holy man’s prayer but also by the Church’s gift. Accordingly, the following document was drawn up concerning the properties which he [Col. 1339A] then restored to Saint Richarius:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Guido, count of the land of Ponthieu, at the request of Lord Abbot Gervin, and with the assent of the chief men of my province, in the presence of King Philip, Margrave Baldwin, and also the princes of the royal palace, restore to Saint Richarius one quarter of the estate called Ultrabaiz. I likewise hand over to Saint Richarius, the abbot, and the monks, to possess forever, all the revenues of my advocacy which I received in the aforesaid estate, receiving from them a little money: namely, twenty pounds of denarii and fifty oxen.
>
> “Concerning Robert also, who formerly held the advocacy of that same estate from [Col. 1339B] me, and concerning anyone who on any pretext should attempt to claim anything in the aforesaid estate, I pledge that I shall make peace for the holy Church.
>
> “That the agreement of this present charter may remain firmly in force, it is strengthened by the authoritative mark of the royal right hand, +. The suitable witnesses who were present at this declaration are listed in order:
>
> “Mark of Baldwin the young Count. Mark of Frederick. Mark of Baldric. Mark of Rodulf. Mark of Roric. Mark of Anscher. Mark of Oylard. Mark of Godefrey. Mark of Richoguard. Mark of Abbot Gervin. Mark of Ingeler, then dean. Mark of Saxogual. Mark of Walter. Mark of Odo the knight. Mark of Dudilo. Mark of Boso.
>
> “This was done in the sixth year of King Philip’s rule, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1067, indiction 6, epact 3, [Col. 1339C] concurrent 7.
>
> “Whoever shall wish to undo the things which we have set forth above, let him be cursed and excommunicated by God the Almighty Father, the holy Mother of God Mary, and all the saints. Amen. So be it, so be it.”

Thus far the charter.

Gervin was always dear and venerable to King Edward of the English, and when he entered the king’s territories he was received with remarkable honour. If that king learned that Gervin was in difficulty through, or for the sake of, any need of our place, he was most generous in coming to his aid, putting aside every excuse. The queen, his wife Edith, also loved and revered Gervin more than enough for the merit of his holiness; and, following her husband’s example, was very [Col. 1339D] liberal, gladly granting whatever he requested.

On one occasion, however, when the abbot had newly entered that land, the queen offered him the kiss of greeting and peace. He refused to receive it, shrinking from it in order to preserve his purity. She, angry at seeing herself, a queen, spurned by a monk, took this very badly and angrily withdrew certain things which she had intended to give him so that he might pray for her.

But her husband reproached her for wishing to persecute with hatred so religious an abbot because he had not relaxed his strict rule. Other honourable men likewise advised her that a man ought not to be hated who had devoted himself to God so completely that he would not allow even a queen’s kiss to caress him contrary to the rule. The queen was appeased. Not only did she [Col. 1340A] not blame this conduct in him, but, extolling it with great praise, she required that such a custom should thereafter remain among the bishops and abbots of her realm.

Therefore she sent him away, enriched with many honours and gifts, asking only this of him: that at the time of prayer she might deserve to be numbered among his benefactors. The king’s wife also gave him a very precious amice, wonderfully adorned with gold and precious stones, which the abbot brought into the treasury of our church.

Later, when it happened that Guido, bishop of Amiens, saw this amice, captivated by its excessive beauty and preciousness, he asked the abbot to transfer it to the mother church of Amiens. In exchange for it, he declared himself willing to give the church of Saint [Col. 1340B] Richarius two altars to possess in perpetuity. Judging it right to yield to the entreaties of this most loving man, the abbot gave the aforesaid amice to the bishop and to the church of Saint Mary, holy Mother of God and ever-virgin; and, with the consent and grant of the whole Church of Amiens, he received into his own legal possession two altars. One is in our estate of Argubium; the other in the estate called Monshelisi.

But lest the abbots succeeding in posterity should lose these same altars, the most prudent Gervin obtained from the bishop that testamentary instruments should be made concerning them, which read as follows:

“Guido, by the grace of God bishop of Amiens, to the faithful of the present and future: a peaceful pilgrimage in this worldly life, and the joy of the heavenly reward. [Col. 1340C] Since the deeds of those now living are made better known to posterity through written accounts, we have thought fit to make known to your charity how we have enlarged the church of St. Riquier by the gift of certain altars. At the petition of Abbot Gervin, we grant the altars of the villages of Argœuves and Mont-Élisy, over which Ratbod and Hugh are held as persons, on the condition that, for as long as they live, they shall render the church-revenue due to St. Riquier at the appointed times, with the consent of the archdeacons John and Baldwin. The arrangement is that, after their deaths, clerics who pay the ecclesiastical dues to us and to our successors shall be personally installed there by the abbot; and when they die, others shall be substituted in their place. [Col. 1340D] We confirm this in the presence of our clerics and request that it remain valid with our successors.”

But, these matters having thus been settled, let us turn briefly to Count Guy. He was the son of Count Hugh; and after the killing by Norman treachery of his brother Enguerrand—of whom we related above that, in his father’s stead, he had made a gift concerning the estate of Portes—he received the county of Ponthieu. Thus he also became our hereditary advocate. Yet he excessively oppressed the estates of St. Riquier and their tenants, extorting and taking away their money and small possessions.

The pious father Gervin confronted his injustice and impiety, exhorting and beseeching him not to remain so harsh toward the servants of St. Riquier. He admonished him not, while holding the emoluments and title of an advocate [Col. 1341A], to become so evil a plunderer. But a just petition had little force with a savage mind, lifted up by the height of power or wounded by the passion for rapacity, unless perhaps a sum of money opposed its hardness—for earthly hearts are readily softened by that means.

At one time the substance of this Father’s request was that he should somewhat remit, for the love of St. Riquier, a very burdensome payment imposed upon the tenants of the village of Majoch. The count agreed for the present and drew up the following testimony concerning the remission or moderation of the customary due of his advocacy.

“I, Guy, by the grace of God Count of Ponthieu, wish it to be known to those present and future that Gervin, abbot of St. Riquier, approached our presence [Col. 1341B] and earnestly requested that I lighten, for the love of God and St. Riquier, the due of twenty pigs which I held in the village called Majoch, because it was very burdensome to the tenants of that village. Having therefore received one hundred solidi from him, we have granted that the aforesaid pigs shall never again be demanded from those peasants; rather, in their place, forty solidi shall be paid annually on the feast of St. Remigius.

“Nevertheless, none of our officials or servants shall enter the aforesaid village to collect those solidi; instead, the monk to whom this obedience has been assigned shall take care to deliver them, on the aforesaid feast, to our provost established at St. Riquier. And so that the monks themselves may more earnestly implore the Lord’s mercy for our condition and safety, and likewise for those of our wife and offspring, we have decreed to confirm this [Col. 1341C] in the presence of our nobles.”

## Chapter XXIII. On King Edward and King William of the English, and how Gervin crossed the sea

Edward [Note: [Col. 1341D] This is St. Edward the Confessor, who held the kingdom of England from 1043 until the beginning of 1066. After his death Harold, son of Count Godwin, seized the kingdom; but William the Bastard, duke of Normandy, having defeated and slain Harold in battle, was soon afterwards acknowledged by all as king of England. MAB.] king of the English, having happily completed the course of his mortal life, passed, as is believed, to eternal glory.

While he was still living and flourishing in his earthly kingdom, a certain nobleman, a Briton by nation, named Ralph, powerful and honoured at the king’s court, gave to the holy confessor of Christ, Riquier, through the hand of the memorable Gervin, certain estates and revenues as alms. Their total will shortly be recorded.

After King Edward’s death [Col. 1341D], a certain Count Harold unlawfully took the kingdom for himself, contrary to right and contrary to the faith of the oath which he had sworn to the aforesaid king, promising that he would yield the kingdom without any impediment to that king’s great-nephew, named Edgar. But when he unjustly exercised royal power and its insignia, having expelled Edward’s great-nephew Edgar, the supreme and all-powerful God—at whose command the kingdoms of the earth stand, and who gives them to whom He wills—showed a miraculous sign from heaven and appointed William, duke of the Normans, to become king of the English. And because William truly sought this by God’s will, the successful outcome proved it.

But since the memory of his deeds is still recent, leaving them aside, let us pursue our own subject.

In the second year of his reign, the venerable Gervin, wishing to inspect the estates mentioned above, hurried to the sea-crossing which the common people call Wissant. With him were more than a hundred abbots and monks, besides a very great multitude of soldiers and merchants, all of whom wished to embark and cross the sea into England.

It was then the month of February, known always to be troublesome because of the conflict of the elements, the violence of winds, the flooding of rains, and the abundance of snow. At that season the sea also roars more fiercely, as the violence of storms is prolonged by excessive winds. Therefore, after fifteen days had passed [Col. 1342B], while the sea ceased not from its raging and a crossing was despaired of, it was decided that they should return home. Since passage was refused and their supply of funds was failing, they could remain there no longer.

Indeed, they did not think it right to depart without Gervin’s consent and permission, for he had filled all with the fragrance of holiness. Gathering together, they asked him as a heavenly counsellor and one knowledgeable in divine law what they should do, since after so long a wait they had been unable to secure passage. They maintained that it was best to return, saying that the barrenness of the place could not provide food for so great a crowd.

Then Gervin kindly strengthened those overwhelmed by such despair. He urged them not to distrust God’s mercy, but to come early the next morning to the church, and, when the service of the divine [Col. 1342C] office had been completed, humbly ask God mercifully for a journey. Then, barefoot, they were to seek the nearby church of St. Peter the Apostle, asking through the merits of that apostle for grace from Christ.

The counsel pleased all. They came to the basilica of the Archangel Michael; after the morning hymns had been offered, they made their prayers, and each person desiring to cross offered a denarius in thanksgiving. Gervin, by the decree of the others, took this money under his own direction, seeming almost to preside over all who were present. Having bought wax, he made two very large candles. One he offered to the Archangel Michael and to St. Nicholas the Confessor; the other he kept, vowing it to Christ’s virgin [Col. 1342D] and martyr Margaret, who possessed a church across the sea.

Then, with the company already arranged, he appointed one of his monks, named Saxogualus, as precentor. Proceeding barefoot and leading chants such as might implore God’s mercy, they went to the aforesaid church of the blessed Apostle Peter. When prayer had been completed there, and the most honourable Gervin had celebrated the solemn rites of Mass, they returned, having implored and urgently entreated the mercy of Christ the Lord.

After resting during the following night, they gathered again at dawn and returned to Gervin. Behold: they saw by God’s power that the sea had become calm; every storm had withdrawn, and it appeared tranquil [Col. 1343A]. Thus, with Christ as their agent, they embarked and crossed the sea without being struck by any roar of winds. So great indeed was the stillness of the quiet sea that sails spread today could scarcely carry them across, whereas yesterday no remedy of any kind had sufficed.

At last, leaving the ships, they returned to the church of the virgin named above. Having given thanks and offered the candle, they separated, each swiftly going where he wished. Yet all believed and proclaimed with great praise that this speed of crossing had been granted through Gervin’s mind.

## Chapter XXIV. On the honour bestowed upon him by the king, and on the lands given by Ralph

[Col. 1343B] Thus Gervin, having crossed successfully in this fashion, went to the royal court. He proclaimed Christ and His commandments; he urged the confession of sins, exhorted repentance, advised the keeping of peace, and counselled imitation of all things known to please God.

King William was informed that he was present. The king valued him so highly that he granted to this man what he had denied to bishops and abbots: immediate audience and unimpeded access to himself. The abbot therefore asked the king to assent to the estates which had been given to St. Riquier in Edward’s days, and to confirm them for perpetual possession by a decree of royal authority. Ralph, who had granted the same lands, was present with his son of the same name; they too asked the royal majesty to do this.

Accordingly, granting the requests of the abbot and his friends, the king ordered the following edict to be drawn up concerning them.

[Col. 1343C] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, William, by God’s grant king of the English, moved by my own advancement in the Lord and compelled by the prayer of Lord Abbot Gervin of the monastery of St. Riquier, situated in the district of the county of Ponthieu, and likewise by the urging of my friends—namely Count Ralph and his son Ralph—with the unanimous assent also of the chief men of my court, grant by royal custom whatsoever these two, father and son, have devoutly granted for the use of the brothers of the aforesaid saint.

“In order that knowledge of these churches and holdings may be evident to all, we have considered it fitting to set them forth by name in this present document. This is the land of St. Riquier situated within the bounds of England, delivered to that saint by Count Ralph.

“The village called Esperlais, where there are thirty-seven tenants, each of whom annually pays at the Nativity of the Lord two horse-loads of malt. From the feast of St. John the Baptist until the feast of St. Michael, they shall perform every labour for their lord on three days; during the remainder of the year, they shall be available once a week for every task imposed upon them. There are there six ploughlands, excellent woodland, arable and uncultivated land, and meadows most suitable for every kind of fodder.

“There is another village called Acre, where there are two tenants and three mills, which pay thirty-five oras [Note: [Col. 1343D] “Thirty-five oras.” At this place the following is noted in the manuscript used by Acherius: “Just as among the Franks twelve denarii make one solidus, so the English make sixteen denarii a solidus, and call it an ora.”] of denarii. Furthermore, all the men of the village shall reap the crops [Col. 1344A] three days each week, and all the plough-teams shall plough three days for wheat and oats.

“There is a third village, called Culesthorpe, which pays five oras of denarii, and with its plough-teams tills the land three days for wheat and oats. A fourth village follows, called Achotes; and another called Apicheneam, where all the aforesaid customary obligations of the plough-teams apply. Merefort is joined to these; from it the lord of the village shall customarily have eight plough-teams for two days for wheat and oats, and in August twenty-five men for two days to reap the harvest.

“The next village is called Assuafam in their language; from it is received the entire tithe both of grain and of other things. There is another called Guenite, where there is one mill, woodland, and excellent fishing.

“I affirm this again and again with the prohibition of a binding decree: henceforth let it not be usurped in any manner through the invasion of any tyrant. Therefore, so that this charter may endure unchanged for our descendants, we confirm it by our royal authority.”

## Chapter XXV. On the places where he kept solitary watch before the Lord

The modest Father and diligent provider Gervin beneficially administered these and very many other matters. For these merits, with the help of Him for whose love he performed them and whose vicar he was—the great priest and splendid abbot Riquier—we believe that he has been joined to the citizens above.

Nevertheless, though oppressed by the anxiety of many cares, he always had recourse to prayer and the practice of compunction [Col. 1344C], like a sailor to a most secure harbour. Thus, if amid the cares of the world, like waves of the sea, he had been disturbed by any stealthy temptation, he might again be made firm by inward contemplation, like a strong anchor, cleaving to God.

For this reason he sought wooded and secluded places. Whenever he was agitated by the care of affairs, he fled to them and was refreshed as though by the delightfulness of paradise. In the territory of Amiens he possessed a cell at the place where the body of the martyr Gratian is said to rest. In the same territory he acquired another, called Luliacum, where there is a church in honour of the blessed martyr Lucian and the most holy Riquier. In Neustria also, namely in the forest of Auge, he had a third cell containing a church in honour of the blessed Martin [Col. 1344D]. He loved it more than the others, visited it more often, and tirelessly continued there spiritual rejoicings of psalms and praises to the Lord.

## Chapter XXVI. On the holiness of his life

Since we have shown in part what he was, by God’s working, in enlarging the Church’s possessions, it is especially worthwhile to unfold the holiness of the good man. In seeking to do so, we seem to undertake a necessary task. For we have shown him to have been a good and diligent steward of the Church’s earthly affairs—a quality which the wicked sometimes imitate—but he will be considered far more worthy of imitation if we recount the greatness of his holiness [Col. 1345A], in which alone he is in some measure known to be imitable by truly good people.

Throughout the whole time of his life during which he remained strong without infirmity, after taking little sleep, he would rise from his bed and enter the house of prayer. Praying, weeping, and bending his knees, he went around all the altars of every saint. He multiplied his petitions for himself and for those entrusted to him, for his friends, for those united with him in prayer or confession, and for the repose of the dead. For the condition and increase of the holy universal Church, and for peace among rulers, he repeatedly offered to the Lord God the Father, His Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit sacrifices of praise and prayer—rich through contrition of heart and commendable through abundance of tears.

When the frail material of his flesh was exhausted and wearied by this exercise, he cast himself for a little while upon his bed [Col. 1345B], preparing himself to repeat his labours. Once he felt himself refreshed by brief rest, he sprang up again and resumed his vigils.

Besides the offices of prayer and the sweetest singing of psalms, he most diligently observed the following: every day he rendered to the Lord the nocturnal and diurnal office concerning the Holy Trinity, then concerning the Holy Spirit, then concerning the Resurrection of the Lord, and concerning the holy Mother Mary; afterwards concerning the angels, St. Peter, all the apostles, and all the saints—apart from the monastic office, from which he was almost never absent. Then, visiting again the altars of the saints, he sang to each an appropriate and fitting votive psalm.

After worthily completing these duties toward God, if he perceived that the hour had come when the brothers would rise, he immediately withdrew, lest any sacristan or doorkeeper see him, and returned to bed, so that the good things related of him might be possessed all the more firmly the more hidden they were.

When the signal of the church announced the hour of the nocturnal office [Col. 1345C], he rose and behaved as though he had been filled with sleep and had enjoyed the rest of the whole night. He observed, in the cockcrow of his mighty voice, the command of the most blessed Benedict (chapter 19): “Thus let us stand to sing the psalms, that our mind may be in harmony with our voice.”

If anyone reproaches us for calling this most excellent man a cock, let him turn to the exposition by St. Gregory, pope of Rome, upon the words of holy Job: “Who gave understanding to the cock?” (Job 38). When he has understood it according to the capacity of his mind, he will surely recognize that the parable of the cock belongs not to any lowly person, but to one adorned with the virtues of a holy life [Col. 1345D].

Intent upon divine service, Gervin—never wearied by travel or detained by illness unless it was severe—never failed, in accordance with the Rule’s command (chapter 11), to read the Gospel lesson himself after the twelve lessons on Sundays or feasts of saints. Thus present at every office, he gave the brothers an example of sobriety and holy zeal.

When the nocturnal praises had ended and most of the brothers, indeed often all of them, had returned to their beds, Gervin did not seek bodily rest. Rather, beginning anew what he had done before the nocturnal synaxis, he occupied the interval of dawning light and departing darkness with the continuation of prayers [Col. 1346A] and persevering genuflections. And because the inward day truly shone upon him, according to the teaching of our doctor, the Apostle Paul—“We who belong to the day, let us be watchful and sober” (1 Thess. 5)—he declared this through unceasing practice.

While he was intent upon these exercises, when day shone with the ray of the sun, he withdrew to the cloister and, reading through a book, gathered for himself the honeycombs of the divine word. Reflecting upon them in the assembly of the brethren, he shaped them toward the pursuits of devout action and a more disciplined life.

But after he had refreshed his mind, as though exhausted by insistence in prayer, with the holy food of reading, he immediately returned to the church and celebrated the solemn rites of Mass: shining with the gold of understanding, eminent in the purple of fortitude, glowing in twice-dyed scarlet—that is, aflame with the double fire of love—and resplendent in fine linen, that is, the mortification of the flesh.

During the forty days sanctified by the fast of our Lord, he imposed greater austerity upon himself. He subdued his devoted limbs wrapped in haircloth; he very rarely ate bread made from wheat; he allotted himself only a small quantity of water for drink; and with such refreshment of food he restored himself only after every third day [Col. 1346B]. Far from him was the piled luxury of a bed: he lay upon a cheap mat. Thus sleep did not easily overtake one lying so hard, whose tongue the psalms scarcely permitted to rest.

Certainly neither care of the place, nor necessary business, nor the occasion of travel, nor any bodily illness except the greatest, could obtain from him any diminution of psalms, praises, or the canons mentioned above. If he travelled anywhere, following the custom of our holy and most blessed [Col. 1346C] father Riquier, either psalms sounded from his mouth, or salutary preaching or admonition toward correction was heard.

When received as a guest, he did not seek the efforts or inventions of cooks. He was not a participant in, but a despiser of, that one who destroys the walls of Jerusalem. When his travelling companions saw to the purchasing and preparation of provisions, he rested on a bench while keeping vigil for the Lord. When supper had been set out, if he reclined to eat, he strove to occupy himself with hearing a reading or meditating upon the divine law.

If there was a church nearby, he went there to render the customary tribute of vows required of himself. If no church building was available, he was quickly put to bed as though to rest, and with covered head weighed the life-giving words. When his companions had completed what was necessary and gone to bed [Col. 1346D], Gervin rose swiftly and without sound. Placing beside himself the little pouch which he always carried, full of saints’ relics, he performed the prayers and genuflections which, as mentioned above, he performed in the monastery.

Thus the truthful saying was fulfilled in him: “Where the faithful soul is, there also is the temple of God.”

Among his other exercises of virtue, this observance remained unaltered for as long as he enjoyed health: on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, the vigil of holy Easter, Good Friday, the vigil of the Ascension, the vigil of Pentecost, the feasts of St. John the Baptist, the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, the vigils of the holy martyr Lawrence, the Assumption of St. Mary, All Saints, and the blessed Apostle Andrew, he abstained entirely from food [Col. 1347A] and chanted the whole Psalter to the Lord without omission.

Although he so greatly subdued his own flesh, he displayed such cheerfulness that from the brightness of his face you would have thought the renowned abbot not hungry but overflowing with rich food. Yet he preserved that cheerfulness so that no levity appeared in it, maintaining the gravity of propriety in all things.

## Chapter XXVII. How diligent he was in healing sick souls, and how he was accused for this before the apostolic pontiff

Moreover, he was so urgently concerned with converting and saving the souls of sinners that, wonderfully sympathizing with and coming to the aid of those oppressed by the burden of sins, he seemed to be governed by the spirit of him who [Col. 1347B] said: “My little children, with whom I am again in labour” (Gal. 4).

He corrected not only wicked men of this region whenever he knew them, but also travelled through Neustria, Flanders, Gaul, Aquitaine, and Hungary with devout diligence. Receiving the confessions of offenders and changing their lives for the better by most salutary admonitions, he fulfilled the work of evangelist and apostle without the name, displaying in himself to all the Lord’s declaration: “I have set you as a light to the nations, that you may be for salvation” (Isa. 49).

We often saw him at Centula, beside the glorious confessor Riquier, spend the whole day in a chamber without any bodily food, while some departed and others came who needed care for their souls. He delighted, as a heavenly physician, to heal their sick souls [Col. 1347C], whose salvation he sought.

For this office a cell had been assigned to him, which the brothers called the “confession.” In it, through God’s grace dwelling in him, that blessed man restored to divine mercy the souls of many people who had gone astray through the enormity of their crimes, by the humility of confession and the intervention of his prayer. Thus he truly deserved to become the person to whom the divine word fittingly says: “If you bring forth the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 15).

But what good has ever not been followed and envied by envy? Many clerics, whose occupation—alas!—was to envy better men, did not consider that the gift of the Holy Spirit is not bound by law. With poisonous words they attacked our horseman, asking why a man who was not a bishop dared preach without apostolic permission, and why this presumptuous intruder upon an office not his own heard sinners’ confessions and investigated their conversions.

Corrupting some minds with this wicked report, they finally brought these deeds of the man of God to the ears of the pope of Rome. Since he was ignorant of Gervin’s goodness and could not judge the voices of detractors, he issued an order by his authority that the man whom rumour called rash should be summoned to the Apostolic See, to give the pope, as they said, an account of his presumption.

Thus Gervin, summoned by the pope’s decree, joyfully set out for Rome, trusting that help from above would not fail him [Col. 1348A]. As soon as the pope saw him, he discerned from the very appearance of his countenance the man’s most reverend life, and magnificently venerated the presence of the Godhead dwelling in him.

He rose to meet the visitor and very humbly gave him the kiss of peace; then he ordered him to sit with him and, as was Gervin’s custom, to expound heavenly words before him. When the pope informed him of the aforesaid accusation and asked him to disclose whether he had undertaken the things alleged, Gervin set forth examples from Scripture which command: “Do not cease to rescue those who are being led to death.” Likewise the Apostle James says: “To one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin.”

“Since, therefore,” he said, “merciful God has granted to my lowliness knowledge of the good [Col. 1348B], do you command me to withhold the knowledge of the word entrusted to me and, like the idle servant, incur condemnation because I have not administered the money? One must also consider what the Apostle James likewise says: ‘If anyone causes a sinner to turn from the error of his way, he will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins’” (James 5).

“If, therefore, by converting sinners I save not only their souls but also, through the love I expend, wipe away my own sins, consider, I pray, whether such a work should be restrained by the supreme Shepherd—so that no devout person may have opportunity to perform works of love.”

That truly apostolic pontiff Leo, who desired not to restrain good things but always to increase them, became more joyful when he heard so useful and fruitful an account of Gervin’s purpose. Since he had learned that Fulco, then bishop of Amiens [Col. 1348C], devoted himself not to the salvation of souls but to catching birds and hunting wild beasts, he strengthened the venerable abbot with this authority, confirming him in these words:

“By no means, most beloved brother, shall you henceforth shrink, because of the whispering or detractions of the envious, from providing so great a consolation to perishing souls. Thus the fruit of the Lord’s vineyard shall increase through you as its cultivator, and the grace of Christ the Lord shall accompany you for the labours you have undertaken, undoubtedly to reward you one day with eternal recompense.

“Behold, by the authority of our Lord, of the blessed Apostle Peter, and by our own authority—and not only by authority but also by entreaty—we grant and command that, in receiving the confessions of the guilty and imposing penance, you shall hold a share in our office. Thus what you bind shall be bound by the authority of Christ the Lord [Col. 1348D], and what you loose shall be loosed by the mercy of that same Lord.”

Having said this, the holy pope also offered sandals and ordered Gervin to use them, so that he who practised the task of preaching might be adorned with the insignia of a preacher. But the venerable abbot, guardian of true humility, refused these ornaments, saying that the authority of apostolic permission alone was sufficient for him to exercise the ministry of the divine word among sick souls. Thus enlarged by the pontiff’s manifold favour, he returned and resumed the work of the Lord which he had begun, exercising it more freely, more fully, and more widely.

Since the occasion has presented itself, we consider it very proper briefly to write here what sort of man and how great was he of whom mention has been made. Pope Leo, a German by nation [Col. 1349A], resplendent through the most excellent nobility of his parents and foretold by a heavenly vision before his birth, came forth into the world in Lorraine. Most keenly educated in sacred letters and liberal studies, he preserved the honourableness of a God-fearing mind throughout childhood, youth, and adolescence. By election of clergy and people he was ordained bishop of the Church of Toul, even while his imperial kinsmen were discussing the conferral upon him of the Roman apostolate.

Since the most holy brightness of character was not lacking to him along with nobility of birth, that illustrious man did not refuse to take charge of a poor little city; indeed, in order to avoid a greater honour, he readily accepted this one. While bishop of the town of Toul, he was raised, by election of the pontiffs with the emperor’s assent [Col. 1349B], to be Roman pontiff. Formerly called Bruno, he deserved to be called Leo because of the papacy.

He flourished in such purity and strength of mind that, through his merits, it pleased almighty God to perform great miracles. When he came to dedicate the church of the most blessed Remigius, bishop of Reims, he selected the venerable Gervin, together with three other men equally holy, to bear the body of that confessor.

## Chapter XXVIII. A miracle which the Lord deigned to perform on his account

Thus Gervin, with God’s help, continued diligently in the praiseworthy work of his life. Unfolding the seeds of the divine word to Christian peoples, he made known what was to be avoided [Col. 1349C] and taught what was to be embraced. His good manner of life so pleased God that God deemed it worthy to declare his devotion even by miracles.

For once, as he was travelling, he came to a certain place. Hearing the fame of the holy abbot—for so he was called by the people—a sick woman came forward and publicly began to tell everyone what had been divinely revealed to her: if she obtained the blessing of this venerable man, she would immediately receive health.

But the man of God was absent, having been led away by the faithful at that same hour to minister in a remote place to the ailments of souls. The woman, afflicted by a grievous calamity, asked in God’s name that his pastoral staff—which the common people call a *crocia* and which, according to custom, was bent at its upper end [Col. 1349D]—be washed in water and that she be given a drink from it.

Then the monk who was the keeper and bearer of that staff, named Ralph—who still survives as we write this and attests these very things—marvelling at her faith, granted her request. The *crocia* was washed; and when she drank the water of its washing, by God’s will, who makes His servants wonderful, she was healed of every illness.

## Chapter XXIX. Another miracle concerning Odelric, sick with fever

In the castle of Auge also, situated at the very entrance to Neustria, Christ the Lord performed another great wonder on his account. For when Gervin once arrived there, a certain boy named Odelric was present, diligently studying letters. [Col. 1350A] He was gripped by the force of fevers and did not know what he could do for himself.

When he learned that the holy abbot had arrived, supported by hope of a sure remedy, he approached Gervin’s attendants and begged and entreated them to give him to drink water in which the holy man’s hands had been washed. Moved by compassion, they complied with his request. The abbot washed his hands, and they set aside the water for him. When the sick boy received and drank it, without any delay he was wholly freed from fever.

This Odelric is still alive today and at Corbie holds the habit and rank of monk and abbot.

## Chapter XXX. The vision of the monk Hugh
Saint Richarius also, lord of our monastery, wished in those days to show great miracles, [Col. 1350B] thereby indicating that the abbot was pleasing to him, since in his time he revealed knowledge of his power. For a certain brother, converted from secular knighthood, named Hugh, conducted himself honourably in the monastic habit. One night, having anticipated the nocturnal hymns, after prolonged prayer he sat on a bench in the choir, when suddenly he heard from the western side of the basilica—from the tower where the altar of the Holy Saviour stands—sweet voices singing on high. As he afterwards related, the voices of men and boys could readily be distinguished by the different quality of their sound. Startled by the hearing of this, he turned his eyes in that direction, thinking that some persons were there singing the heavenly hymns so sweetly. In truth, the presences of the holy angels and of the holy Innocents had solemnly visited the most holy memorial of the Saviour which is there, [Col. 1350C] and the relics of those same Innocents formerly placed there by Lord Angilbert; but the aforesaid brother was unable to see their forms. Yet, while he listened with the greatest attentiveness to their songs and was ineffably delighted, he saw a diffused light fill the whole tower; spreading outward, it began to fill the entire nave of the basilica. The monk, seeing with his eyes the heavenly light moving toward the place where the body of the most blessed Richarius rests, and deeply moved by this sight, rose swiftly. Wishing to have a witness to so great a glory, he hurried to the dormitory and summoned the first brother he encountered, indicating that he should rise quickly and follow him. When both had returned to the entrance of the church, they saw [Col. 1350D] the whole basilica filled with divine light and heard voices singing most sweetly. Shaken by great fear, they did not dare enter; but, standing outside, their frightened hearts were refreshed by the sweet-flowing melody.

The venerable Gervinus experienced the same thing. For when, according to his usual custom, he was going round the altars in prayer, he came to that same memorial of the Holy Saviour and there offered the sacrifice of praise. Suddenly a light sent forth from heaven flooded the entire tower. Shaken by the terror of so new a vision, he fled; and, going as far as the Memorial of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, he began to halt, wondering what God intended to do. Behold, he saw the same light gathering at the honourable Memorial of Saint Richarius. When the sacred place in which the body of the most blessed [Col. 1351A] Richarius rests had been filled with heavenly light, and the celestial radiance was already spreading through the other parts of the basilica, the venerable Gervinus, overwhelmed with fear, went quickly and awakened one of the *matricularii*, who was then living religiously. He wished him to behold with him the brightness of so great a glory, and himself to recover from the extreme terror that had seized him through that man’s companionship.

Thus both came; and the abbot, kneeling before blessed Richarius’s altar and stretching out his hands, prayed with tears, while the church-keeper, standing in the lower part of the choir, drank in with his eyes the ineffable glory. As they beheld this great magnificence of the Lord, they afterwards perceived such a fragrance that, in comparison with such sweetness, every perfume compounded by human art [Col. 1351B] seemed a stench. Certain forms of heavenly bodies were also seen, most lovingly joining themselves to the body of Saint Richarius. But we decline to set forth everything, lest, by recounting things unfamiliar, we produce weariness in the unbelieving.

This is truly established: after the heavenly watch had paid the honours due to the Memorial of the Saviour and the relics of the holy Innocents, they hastened to blessed Richarius, bringing joy and honour concerning the glory of the soul already present and the future immortality of the body. But, setting aside these hidden and, as it were, mystical matters, let us proceed to more manifest things.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Certain miracles of Saint Richarius

Once, when a very great fire arose on the north side of the monastery of that confessor, [Col. 1351C] Lord Richarius, the brothers, terrified and labouring amid the destruction threatened by so great a conflagration, concentrated solely on carrying out the most sacred pledges and the treasure of the Church. For already—marvellous to relate—the fire had spread over more than a hundred places upon the church; the lead, overcome by the fire, was melting and running down; and, with nearly all the ornaments removed except the shrine containing the sacred body of blessed Vigour, nothing remained to be expected but the desolation of the place and the conflagration already visible before their eyes.

When the solace of human frailty had failed, God’s mercy gave a visible sign of its helping clemency. One of the church ministers, who had climbed up to beat down the fire if he could, [Col. 1351D] hanging by a hand that did not hold securely, slipped and fell headlong to the ground. At that very hour, when he wondered that he was not injured—indeed, that he had not rather died—he sprang to his feet through God’s grace and the merits of blessed Richarius. The fire, moreover, like a blaze checked in straw where it has no strength, was extinguished through God’s grace, with the confessor Richarius acting as intermediary, and without human aid.

A certain man from the district of Tournai, blind in his eyes, was staying at Corbie, where at that time the Lord bestowed much grace of healing through the merits of the saints who protected that place. In a vision, as he reported, he was instructed by a handsome old man to go as quickly as possible to the monastery of Saint Richarius, because there he would receive restoration of sight. Obeying his adviser, he came, led by his sister, who was already of marriageable age, to the monastery of Saint Richarius. [Col. 1352A] What rarely happens to anyone occurred: when he arrived at evening, no one offered him the hospitality of human lodging. Thus he was compelled to lodge under the roof of paradise, where, lying through the night on a hard bed, he cried out to the mercy of the most holy confessor.

In the morning, when the doors of the church had been opened, he entered and sat down; and, with the people present for the divine offices—for it was then the season of Lent—he too stood devoutly. Meanwhile, as it seemed to him, the gracious guide, the handsome old man whom he had seen at Corbie, appeared. With both hands he pulled his eyebrows, and by the powerful word of the healer’s command drew harmful blood from the sufferer’s mouth, restoring and renewing sight in the man who had long prayed for it and obeyed him. Rising as the healing was performed, he cried out loudly and satisfied those who ran up with the joyful account of the event; while the company of brothers sang praises to God and to Richarius, their holy patron. [Col. 1352B]

After being detained for some time, he at last returned with his sister, though not with his guide, and by a path not equally fortunate. For he was stripped and tortured by robbers, and the sister whom he had been leading was also carried off. When they departed, he became mad and rushed headlong wherever the force of his flight carried him. At length, in a wretched condition, he was brought again to the monastery of his healer, to be healed anew. In a vision the kindly father again laid his healing hand upon him, restored him to his senses, and brought him back to his own home.

Another man, whose sight had been impaired by an illness, became wholly blind. While he was making his way elsewhere, to the place where he had learned that divine mercy worked, he was warned in a dream to seek blessed Richarius for the recovery of his sight. He came; after his face had been anointed with water touched to the shrine of the saint, [Col. 1352C] he stood seeing. But, excessively hasty, he departed before taking leave; at the doors of the church he again fell into darkness. What was the wretched man to do? He returned to him whom he had found merciful; importunately praying, he sought again the light which had been removed through his own frivolity—or rather by God’s providence.

One night as he lay asleep, he saw the sanctuary of the church, clothed in an entire company of certain white-robed persons; and the whole precinct of the monastery was illuminated by their splendour, as if by festal light. Then it became clear with how many and how great saintly protections this place consecrated to God was upheld. By this blessed vision he received his light, and joyfully prepared once more—though still in poor health—to return home; but darkness met him, and he was compelled, blind once again, to return to the physician. [Col. 1352D] After binding himself by a vow that, if he deserved to be healed, he would annually render to the saint throughout the remainder of his life an offering in recognition of his head, he departed healthy and seeing clearly, amid the joy and blessing of all the brothers. Nor did darkness meet him a third time, whom the blessed Father, worshipper of the Holy Trinity, had entrusted to perfect health.

A certain boy, devoted to study in order to learn letters, ran away from school and fell asleep in a field through childish foolishness; he contracted an illness. He also lost his hearing and languished in bed for three continuous years. For a further six years he remained with trembling head and incomplete hearing. Warned three times to go to the monastery of Saint Richarius and there, upon invoking him, to receive healing, he came. Having offered in fulfilment of a vow of faith a candle, and having prayed before the altar of the Saviour, blood [Col. 1353A] burst from his nostrils and ears and caused him to cry out. The brothers and the faithful people, roused by this, ran together, and heard the event in order from the man now healed. Rejoicing in so great a visitation of God through their merciful patron, they raised praises on high.

At one time, on account of some occasion, the sacred body of our blessed patron Saint Richarius was being carried to the village of Asliacum, accompanied by the brothers. As the route passed through our village of Buxudum, it happened that in a small house there lay a woman at the point of death, whose whole body had been paralysed for many years. While the saint of the Lord was being carried past that same house and came opposite the bed on which she lay, the woman immediately sprang up and began to cry out and say: “I praise and bless the Lord [Col. 1353B] Almighty, who through the presence of my lord, Saint Richarius, has restored me to complete health.”

This miracle seems comparable to that of the most blessed Benedict—except that it is more astonishing that a man already united with God should have had such compassion for human infirmity that by the mere presence of his bones he raised a sick woman, than that man who, though most holy, was still a prisoner of the flesh and was drawn by the very urgency of circumstances to assist human miseries.
