Yet, in saying this, we do not diminish the outstanding merits of blessed Benedict, but proclaim as best we can the admirable deed of this our Father.

Who, moreover, could enumerate how many men, bound and chained, have been freed when they invoked him? For the present, let it suffice [Col. 1353C] to have said this: those things which are to be done without end as long as the world shall stand cannot be enclosed by our literary capacity.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Of the books which he bestowed, and how zealously he sought the body of Saint Angilbert the abbot

Therefore the good abbot, keeping watch with diligent concern over the restoration and preservation of the good place, striving to rebuild what had fallen down, preserve what had been built, and protect it with suitable covering, and most devoutly providing also for the salvation of souls, was preparing for himself entry into the kingdom of heaven. Among the other things that he bestowed upon our house, he supplied an abundance of books for the edification of those serving God there. Since the matters which [Col. 1353D] we record are written to incite future generations by their examples, we think it useful to add a catalogue of the volumes which the venerable Gervinus bestowed upon us.

The Letters of Ignatius; the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius of Caesarea; Ambrose’s apologies *On David*, *On Joseph*, *On Noah*, and *On Abraham*; Ambrose’s *On the Trinity*, addressed to the Emperor Gratian; likewise his *On the Holy Spirit*, addressed to the same; Ambrose’s *Pastoral*; Ambrose’s *On the Sacraments*; *On the Death of Theodosius*; *Against Auxentius*; *On the Surrendering of Basilicas*; *On the Holy Martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, Deposited and Found*; Ambrose’s *On the Death of Satyrus*; *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, and certain other works by the same author.

Gregory Nazianzen’s *Apologeticus*; by the same, *On the Epiphanies*, *On Pentecost*, *On Himself, after Returning from the Country*; *On the Sayings of Jeremiah*; *On the Devastation Caused by Hail*. [Col. 1354A]

Jerome’s *On Illustrious Men*; the Letters of Jerome; Jerome on Zechariah; Jerome on Isaiah; Augustine on John, volume I; Augustine, *Against Five Classes of Enemies*; *On Holy Virginity*, I; *On the Good of Marriage*; *On Various Questions*, addressed to Bishop Simplicianus; addressed to a certain count; addressed to Paulinus of Nola; *On Care for the Dead*; Augustine on the Psalter, volume III; Augustine, *On the Nature and Origin of the Soul*; Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*; Augustine, *On Fasting on the Sabbath*; Augustine, *On the Creed*; Augustine, *On the Four Virtues of Charity*; *On the New Song*; *On the Last Fourth Day*; *On the Flood*; [Col. 1354B] *Against Felicianus*; *On the Time of the Barbarians*; *On the Trinity*; *On the Ten Strings*; *On the Greatness of the Soul*; *To Januarius’s Inquiries*; *On the Paschal Solemnity*; *On Shepherds*; *On Sheep*; *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*; *Against Lying*. Likewise Augustine, *On Lying*. Likewise Augustine, *On Avarice and Luxury*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, *On Christian Doctrine*, *On Christian Combat*, *On Christian Life*, *On Christian Discipline*, *On the Grace of the New Testament*. Thirteen books of his *Confessions*; *Retractions*; *On Heresies*, addressed to Bishop Quodvultdeus; *On Charity*, on the Epistle of the Apostle John; *Enchiridion against the Jews*; his sermons.

John Chrysostom’s *On Compunction of Heart*; by the same, *That No One Can Be Harmed by Another unless He Has First Harmed Himself*; *On the Restoration of One Who Has Fallen*; *On Penance*; Laurentius’s book *On the Three Times of Penance*. Likewise John Chrysostom, *On the Conduct of Life*; *On the Lord’s Prayer*; *On Psalm 50*. [Col. 1354C]

The Register of blessed Pope Gregory; the fifth and sixth parts of his *Morals on Job*; his homilies on the final part of the prophet Ezekiel; a codex *On the Canons*; Paschasius, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*; the *Tripartite History*.

A large codex *On the Passions and Deeds of the Holy Apostles and of Very Many Martyrs*, together with the *Life of Saint Maurus*; the *Lives of the Holy Desert Fathers*; the Lives of Saints Basil, Remigius, Vedastus, Fursey, Ambrose, Lupus, Saint Mary, Germanus of Auxerre, Romaric, [Col. 1354D] Augustine, Jerome, Amandus, Wandrille, Audoin, Ansbert, and Mary of Egypt, together with the Translation of the most blessed Benedict, in one volume. Likewise, the Lives of Saints Richarius, Augustine, Hilary, Columbanus, Fulgentius, Medard, Firmin, Salvius, Bertin, Bavo, Vedast, Martial, Severinus, and Felix; together with the Passions of Saints Hermagoras the bishop, George, Blaise, Menas, Theodore, Lambert, Timothy, and Apollinaris, Perpetua and Felicity, Anastasia, and Sabina, with the Life of Saint Geneviève, in one volume.

The venerable Gervinus, compiling all these in thirty-six volumes, condemned with a grave and irrevocable anathema whoever should dare to remove them from the holy place or withdraw them on any pretext. He perpetually excommunicated not only the thief of the books, but also the thief of the cloths and the other ornaments which he himself had amassed or found amassed by his predecessors. [Col. 1355A]

Now, because at that time the tomb of Lord and Saint Angilbert the abbot was not known with certainty, and therefore enjoyed no earthly honour, although his most celebrated memory shone in the mouths of all the French and Ponthieu people, and in the sight of the splendid church once founded by him, the venerable Gervinus endeavoured by every means in his power to seek out the body of the same holy man, so that, if the Lord granted his prayers, he might exalt it with fitting honour.

Accordingly, at one time he went to the monastery of Gorze, situated on the border [Col. 1355B] of the city of Metz. There he found and borrowed from the brothers a codex that preserved some material concerning the deeds of that holy man and of other abbots of our house; he brought it to Centula. In it was found how Saint Angilbert the abbot, leaving the burden of his earthly body, passed to glory on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [18 February]. Since, from the time when the monastery was burned under the pagan Guaramund until this discovery, the monks of Centula had not known the day of his passing, the brothers rejoiced greatly because they had learned the day on which so great a man ought to be honoured for the merit of his life and virtues.

Gervinus, therefore, who deserves to be called a man of desires, wishing, as has been said, to honour the same saint more worthily, began to seek near the doors of the church, where he had learned that the saint had first been buried, the sacred earth containing his body. He did not find his body there; but in the sarcophagus in which he had rested he found a leather-covered wooden bier containing the salt-preserved body of Lord Nithard, his son, abbot and count. On his head could be seen the wound by which he had been killed in battle. Closing that tomb again, Gervinus wished to seek him elsewhere, but did not know where to search, until the power of divine majesty guided him through a monk in this matter. For a brother named Teudoaldus repeatedly urged that the oft-mentioned saint should be sought at the western entrance of the choir, where, on the surface of the pavement, [Col. 1355D] was written: **REX. LEX. LUX. PAX.**—“King. Law. Light. Peace.” These four parts were the first and last words in his ancient epitaph. Teudoaldus maintained that consideration should be given to the significance of these monosyllabic elements: the man who had buried him had ordered these syllables of his epitaph to be inscribed above him so that their resemblance might indicate to a searcher where the body of Saint Angilbert rested.

Hearing this, the venerable Gervinus assented, and found what he eagerly desired: the body of Saint Angilbert the abbot. At the very hour in which it was found and uncovered, a scent of wondrous sweetness issued forth. Not only were those present touched by the most delightful odour, but all who were anywhere in the church perceived the marvellous fragrance. [Col. 1356A] Indeed, Lord Radulfus, surnamed Benignus, still testifies that, while sitting and writing above the doors of the crypt at that very hour of the discovery, he was refreshed by the sweet-flowing scent.

The holy bones themselves lay heaped together in disordered arrangement and wrapped in a green cloth. It is therefore certain that, after Abbot Ribbodo, who had translated him intact, others of the faithful had thus reinterred him for fear of the pagans. Yet the joy at finding the holy treasure was darkened by the fact that no written or documentary evidence was found to attest that it was Angilbert’s body. Divine providence quickly supplied for the pious concern of the abbot and brothers: it inspired the heart of the above-named brother Teudoaldus to take the saint’s head and examine it carefully. [Col. 1356B] As he did so, he found in the fold of the nostrils a small piece of parchment, which removed every anxiety of doubt. For that little page clearly revealed the truth, saying: **THIS IS THE BODY OF SAINT ANGILBERT THE ABBOT.** Thus obtaining what he had desired, the venerable shepherd reinterred the same saint with honour and ordained that his commemoration should thereafter always be celebrated. He also raised from the earth the bodies of the holy confessor Cadoc and his companion; placing their relics more fittingly, he judged them worthy of veneration by the faithful people.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How he was chastised by the Lord

After the venerable Gervinus had illuminated the world, which lies in evil, by [many] examples of his holy life, [Col. 1356C] after he had drawn many souls of sinners away from perversity to amendment through holy admonitions and, rescuing them from the jaws of the devil, had restored them to the grace of Christ Almighty; after he had adorned and enlarged the church of Richarius, Christ’s sweetly fragrant confessor, with a multitude and religious quality of brothers, buildings, books, cloths, gold and silver, and various ornaments; and while he was being extolled by the praises and acclaim of all peoples, and his sacred and spotless celibacy appeared wonderful to all members of the holy Church—God the merciful Father, wishing to render him wholly fit for himself, struck him with leprosy, so that, according to the prophet’s voice, all his dross might be purified. Thus, if he had performed anything inadequately in God’s service, [Col. 1356D] he might receive its recompense in this life; or, if any desire for human praise because of his good deeds had wounded him, he might likewise be purified.

As soon as he could perceive the first onset of this evil, not thinking the illness incurable, he sought to employ the skill of physicians, so that, with God’s approval, he might not be prevented from still helping the infirmities of souls. But when he recognized that he had been irrevocably struck in the flesh by the kindly Father, he poured out his whole heart to God and continually returned great thanks to the one who scourged him, unceasingly asking God’s mercy that this bodily affliction might contribute to the eternal salvation of his soul.

Although, as everyone knows, such a disease deprived him of the faculty of speech, he nevertheless did not fail to perform all those things which we have noted above [Col. 1357A] as done by him: the lengthiness of his prayers, the continuance of his genuflections, his circuit of the sacred buildings, and the recitation of the holy offices concerning the Holy Trinity, the Holy Spirit, Holy Mary, and All Saints. Though because of illness he was unable to take food or rest, he did not know how to fail in any of these acts of divine service. He remained the same in assiduous prayer, in reciting psalms, and in offering admonition to the brothers, except insofar as the nature of the illness sometimes compelled him to be separated from the community of brothers. Yet although he deliberately kept himself apart for that reason, he was surrounded by the sweet affection and devoted care of those whom he had trained, as a good father.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Where he asked the king for a successor, and how diligently he entrusted his death to the brothers

[Col. 1357B]

As the illness grew more and more severe, and he recognized that his health prevented him from maintaining the care of souls, he presented the case of his illness to Philip, then a young man and king of the Franks, who happened to arrive. He prayed that a shepherd and guardian might be given to the monastery which he had enlarged with such benefits to the extent of his ability: one who would not disperse what had been gathered, but would know how to unite what had been scattered. He asked the pious prince to yield the government to his nephew, whom he declared sufficiently trained for such a task: a monk of Saint Remigius named Gervinus. Since all who knew him could not think it other than sacrilegious to refuse obedience to so holy a man, [Col. 1357C] the aforesaid king agreed and granted that his nephew should hold the government after him.

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1071, at the end of October, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November [23 October], in the ninth indiction, the second Gervinus was ordained abbot of the monastery of Centula. The most reverend uncle, seeing that he was increasingly failing in bodily strength and oppressed by the burden of grave sickness, and accordingly sensing that the day of death was not far off, tirelessly prayed that the Lord’s mercy might come to him as swiftly as possible.

In the fourth year of his illness, when the often-recurring evil became exceedingly violent, he was so distressed that, with his nostrils and lips split apart and the rest of his skin turned into a bristly face, he could scarcely form a word. Yet since untiring meditation on the divine word remained in him, he ordered two brothers, or often one, to perform before him all that we have recalled him formerly performing while strong. It happened, at the beginning of the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1074, in the eleventh indiction, that on the second day of February—the day on which the offering of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Temple by his undefiled Virgin Mother is celebrated, and the expectation of the righteous Simeon was fulfilled—he celebrated Mass, in the devotion which had never grown cold within him, in the crypt of our Lady Saint Mary. There, more cruelly afflicted than usual by pain, he could scarcely complete the mysteries he had begun. [Col. 1358A] Yet, by the grace of God which remained in him, having duly performed them, the brothers supported him on right and left and led him back to bed, exhausted by extreme anguish. Suddenly, amid the conversations of his grieving sons, he inserted these words: “Know, O sweet sons, that today I have received from our Lady Saint Mary permission to depart.”

When they asked where he must go, he said: “Where I have always desired, and for which I have always prayed to God’s mercy.”

When the brothers said that he could still live and that sacrifices would be offered to the Lord Almighty by his hands, he added: “Brother Gervinus will never again sing Mass.”

Thereafter, as the pain daily increased, he took to his bed completely. When the Lenten observance came, on the very fourth weekday which the custom of the Church calls the Head of the Fast, he summoned the older brothers and those adorned with the rank of priesthood. Rising and sitting up with whatever effort he could, he finally opened his mouth before them in these words: [Col. 1358B] “As blessed Germanus said to his fellow bishops, so I too say to you, my sons: I entrust to you, dearest ones, my passing; for I feel the hour approaching in which the salvation long sought from the Lord will come to me. This has always been the purpose of my prayer: that my merciful God might ordain my death to occur during these holy days which are now approaching. But because, as I trust, he will favour my desires, I wish to confess before you in the sight of the Lord the evils I have done and those things on account of which I fear for my soul, believing that this confession, with the Lord’s mercy going before and your intercession assisting, will cleanse me.”

After he had said these things and the brothers had abundantly shed tears, he recounted before them certain grave matters which none had ever known him to have done. Finally, declaring himself burdened with the eight principal vices, he reduced the brothers to extraordinary amazement, for they knew well his celibacy from childhood and the innocence of his life.

> **Note:** [Col. 1357D] We commonly enumerate only seven sins called “capital”; nevertheless, many of the ancients, especially [Col. 1358D] among the Greeks, enumerated eight. On this matter see Cassian in the books of the *Institutes*. MAB.

They said: “Why, good Father, do you accuse yourself in this way, when it is clear that you have not done what you assert? Certainly you have not committed murder or adultery.”

He replied: “Spare me, brothers, spare me, I beg, and do not burden my soul. For if any have perished under my care—which perhaps could not be avoided—I shall assuredly be held answerable for their souls at God’s judgment. But concerning adultery, hear what Christ, the Truth, says: ‘Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’ [Matt. 5].” [Col. 1358D]

“It could not have happened that I was never at some time enticed by the desire of this lust; and for that reason I am as guilty because I willed it as if I had accomplished it in deed.” In accusing and reproaching himself with these and other matters, he entrusted the safeguarding of his departure to God and to their prayers.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How he ordered himself to be buried, and his death

When the customary observance of the sacred fast had begun, he lay confined to bed, deprived of every ability either to sing psalms or to say anything at all. Yet the spiritual offices were recited before him without ceasing. For he did not fail to have the entire Psalter sung every day of Lent by one of the brothers, because he could not do so himself, as he had been accustomed to do while well. [Col. 1359A]

The brothers, seeing that he was now on the point of dissolution in death, anointed him with blessed oil according to the command of Saint James the Apostle, and made him very joyful by this service. When asked where he wished his body to be buried, he refused to designate any place, leaving this to their judgment. But when the brothers more urgently pressed him to designate the place of his burial, he said: “I would tell you what I wish in this matter, but you would not carry it out.”

Then the brothers, truly ready to bury him in whatever place he commanded, even though it might be a holy place, promised that they would altogether fulfil his directions. He said: “I know that you will not do it. Yet if you did, great remedy would come to me from it, sinful man that I am. Tie a rope to my foot, drag me, and throw me upon a dungheap in the middle of the streets, for I believe myself worthy of no better tomb.” Hearing this, the brothers continued their repeated lamentations.

He prayed that, at whatever hour his death should come, they would immediately carry him into the basilica of Saint Richarius, for there he would yield up his spirit to God. The first week of the sacred fast had now passed and the second was under way, when the saving passage of venerable Gervinus—indeed, now to be called blessed—was at hand. For on the third weekday of the second week, which fell on the fifth day before the Nones of March [3 March], after Matins had ended, the anxious brothers visited him and found him drawing his last breath. They signalled to one another that he was dying. Perceiving this still, [Col. 1359C] he himself signalled with his hand that they should carry him into the church.

The brothers took him up and placed him upon a haircloth spread before the nearby altar of Saint John the Baptist. Then, setting before his eyes the image of the crucified Lord and placing upon his breast the pouch of relics as he had directed, the entire community began the litany of supplication, invoking the saints of God to help him. When they said, “Holy Mary, pray for him,” he, who had already lain still as if in death, stretched out his hands and prayed also: “Holy Mary, pray for me.” But when they came to say, “Saint Richarius, pray for him,” contrary to all expectation he wondrously raised himself, stretched his hands higher, and cried out through tears: “Saint Richarius, pray for me.”

After this he became more quiet. When the brothers, with the litany ended [Col. 1359D] and the commendation of the faithful begun, had reached the words, “May Christ receive you,” he breathed out his spirit at those words. When this became known, unspeakable and boundless grief suddenly seized all Centula. Men wept for the death of so great a shepherd; matrons, wailing and tearing out their hair, lamented the death of the holy abbot, the man of God. Without delay the whole district of Ponthieu rushed to the funeral rites of the man of God, and every ordinary need was immediately set aside in view of so great a ceremony. They assembled in the basilica and mourned the truly desolated house with loud voices.

“O Saint Richarius,” they said, “why did you allow such a lover of your honour to die so soon? Good confessor, why did you not preserve for yourself and your servants so good a protector?” [Col. 1360A] Thus men and women, nobles and common people, mourned the death of that excellent man.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. His burial and epitaph

When his body had been stripped for washing, such grace shone from his limbs that no one would have thought any disease had ever disfigured his skin. In his genitals there appeared such a beauty of virginal integrity that they resembled not so much those of a male as those of a venerable seven-year-old boy. From the constancy of his genuflections, hardened skin was found to have grown on his knees and elbows; and anyone who had not known his practices and life could plainly have recognized from this observation that his mind had always clung to divine contemplation.

Arranging those holy bones—for his flesh had wasted away both through abstinence and through illness—they carried him to the more honourable part of the church, commending his soul to God with devout vigils, as is customary. [Col. 1360B] When the solemnities of Mass had been abundantly performed by the abbots and all the priests present, Gervinus, the venerable abbot and servant of God, was buried before the altar of blessed Mary in the eastern crypt, amid the lamentation and grief of all—that is, Count Guy, the abbots, nobles, knights, and the populace at large.

Count Guy of Ponthieu, moreover, in indulgence remitted for love of him all the customary exactions owed to himself at Novavilla, saying: “I place this gift upon the holy tomb of Saint Gervinus.” These things were done at Centula in the year 1074 from the Incarnation of the Word, in the eleventh indiction, in the fourteenth year of the reign of Philip, king of the Franks.

## EPITAPH

[Col. 1360C]

This illustrious Father, through whom the dark demon fell,  
lies sleeping in this tomb, merciful toward these peoples.

Climbing rightly the steep paths of upright ways,  
he was an unceasing martyr-maker of his body.

A rule of virtues, a light to monastic rulers,  
from boyhood he remained a virgin in body.

Then Mars’s third day took him away, while thus he flourished  
and zealously taught what was right; yet he returns.

In the same year died Guy, bishop of Amiens, a most devoted friend of our house. When the venerable Abbot Gervin was removed from this present life, another Gervin succeeded to the government of the monastery of Centula, greatly inferior to his predecessor, although he was his sister’s son, reared and educated in the distinguished monastery of St. Remigius. [Col. 1360D] His speech was learned, but his conduct impaired; for he turned the care of government toward worldly glory, and reduced the gain of souls to secular gratification. Nevertheless, at that time this holy monastery still abounded in religious persons and weighty monks of steadfast uprightness, whose life and conduct shone in honourable renown throughout all the land of the Franks.

For some of them belonged to the time of the venerable Angilram, good disciples of a good master; and many more belonged to the recent memory of the praiseworthy Gervin. Their life and character seemed to the second Gervin heavier than sand, harder than iron, and sharper than steel. By their continence and integrity his unrestrained frivolity was greatly curbed. [Col. 1361A] He could not wholly reject their admonitions and verbal corrections, yielding often to their wisdom not so much through fear of God as through regard for worldly opinion. Thus he was honoured, tolerated, and awaited with settled affection by the elders of the monastery, in hope that God might at some time put into his heart a spirit of amendment. For this reason Masses and psalms were repeatedly offered to God for him, while they waited for him someday to be converted and become an imitator of his holy uncle.

Yet cunning and dissimulation so overflowed in him that anyone who did not know him would, from the abundance of his speech, judge him a man of complete integrity. He glittered in eloquence, with words arranged for every grace; but in deed he showed nothing upright. A painter of words, he stole the minds of his listeners by flattery, [Col. 1361B] so that they did not know how to escape from the artful subtlety of his speech.

He himself finally made a monk of me, among many others, and upon my tender heart, as upon soft wax, pressed an image of his deeds—not to be imitated, but rejected. Three years after my admission, compelled by the unanimous resolve of the monks, he took into the monastery, though groaning, the most elegant boy Anscher, who later succeeded him. Even then he feared that the outstanding boy might someday oppose his madness; and therefore, not as a father but as a pirate, he caused the boy to be reared laxly and negligently, so that, enticed by youthful ease, he might absorb no share of honourableness through which, or for which, he could be advanced to the height of honour.

But the aforesaid boy, [Col. 1361C] observing his deceits both himself and through the friends and retainers of his parents, cultivated the gentlest manners, so as to be loved by all. Lord Gervin had a certain nephew named Caesarius, made a monk at St. Remigius, for whom he intended to procure succession in the government. But woe to you, mad cunning! You yourself would never have been abbot had not the holy life of your blessed uncle deserved it. If you wished to install one of your own as heir, why did you not make yourself such a man that, through your merit, your nephew ought to have risen to honour? I often saw, and more often heard, that a considerable multitude of the older monks bitterly lamented his madness; and, as it is written, “With their mouth they blessed, but in their heart they cursed” (Ps. 61).

But let this brief account of the man’s unhappiness now suffice, so that posterity may have an example of what to avoid, and may take from good men an incentive to virtue. Let us say what good he did. [Col. 1361D] He began to demolish the tower of St. Saviour, which, because of an ancient fire, appeared split apart with gaping, cracking openings, in order, after its destruction, to restore it better and stronger. Immediately a great ruin of the basilica followed, inflicting heavy grief upon all the people of Ponthieu; for it was never believed that a basilica of such dignity could be restored, even in the fourth generation.

Why say more? It was resolved that, because they thought the work beyond recovery, the beloved body of our father Richarius should be carried through neighbouring castles, so that, through the offerings of the devout [Col. 1362A] people, the new work on the basilica might be funded. The day for this undertaking came. Guy, count of Ponthieu, was present with many nobles; a very great multitude from the surrounding region had gathered for this unfamiliar spectacle. Crosses and banners having been prepared, candles borne before, the saint was raised from his own altar with due honour.

> That greatest grief, the monks’ most dreadful horror,  
> Burst forth in voices, and the voice of joy withdrew.  
> Song fell silent; soon lamentation began to rise.  
> The monks cast themselves down, remembering the time of Dacius,  
> Who burned what they could burn, who thought it better  
> That what had not been burned should belong to them  
> Than that anyone should remove the saint elsewhere.  
> The populace too cast themselves down, and at last a great cry arose.  
> Alas! What are we doing? Through how great a crime do we pass?  
> This our lord, our chaste, kindly, bountiful father,  
> [Col. 1362B] Who has always been so rich and never a wanderer,  
> Will leave his seat, make the cloister and church bereft,  
> And become a beggar, dwelling among others’ possessions?  
> This land stands as his own; for us he remains a new,  
> Dear and gracious patron who protects all things;  
> And shall we let him go by giving nothing of what we possess?  
> Stay your step, Father; do not suffer any departure.  
> We would sooner die than be deprived of you, our shepherd.  
> The nobles lament you; the hearts of the people resound for you.  
> Holy Father, remain. The time will not come  
> When this mason will lack all that the work requires.  
> The homeland shall rejoice; this your flock shall be glad.  
> Thus speaking, and holding the shrine and the saint,  
> They wept greatly at the altars here left bereft.  
> Singing chants, weeping everywhere with psalms,  
> [Col. 1362C] They restored the pledges in which they placed all their joy.

Only through great prayers and much persuasion was the heart of the people with difficulty brought to allow the beloved body of their blessed patron to be carried as far as the abbot’s estate, so that the devotion of the people dwelling there might be desirably renewed by the blessing of the blessed body, and that the saint himself, honoured with many gifts, might be brought back the following day. All the people of Ponthieu flocked together, considering it an eternal disgrace if the saint were carried farther away.

For on the following morning the saint was brought back, accompanied by such rejoicing and such songs that no mortal voice could express the greatness of the joy. When he had been restored to his own place, the people of Centula assembled as one, and with a common will and ready spirit [Col. 1362D] each gave gifts to the saint for the restoration of the church and of the tower formerly dedicated to the name of the Saviour.

> They bestowed cows and oxen, horses and sheep;  
> Cloaks, mantles, rings, bands, and tiaras;  
> They gave belts, knives, sleeves, and leggings;  
> Maidens give necklaces hanging from their ears,  
> And our people weigh out the weight of silver.  
> They give from every side many pounds’ worth of coins.  
> The peasant gives barley; a gathering of many gives oats;  
> More give malt; many give wine.  
> From these goods one treasure is made greater,  
> Which none can count, even if he knows accounts.

With the Lord’s help, a new basilica was begun from the foundations; and, through the contributions of good people, [Col. 1363A] the building rose day by day. The inhabitants of Centula too, pursuing the matter with greater zeal, urged one another on with daily offerings, striving with their utmost effort beyond their means so that no one might seem inferior in furnishing assistance. Thanks be to God: we mourned it cast down; we rejoice together in it renewed and raised up. We see it elevated upon a stronger foundation and to a loftier summit.

Moreover, when this same Gervin saw himself placed in great glory and surrounded by much favour from courtiers and common people, imagining the honour and glory of the patron Richarius to be due to his own merit, he began to be inflated by the empty reports of flatterers. He regarded it as nothing that he was an abbot, and with burning heart longed to become a bishop:

> [Col. 1363B] What more should we relate, except now to tell the truth?  
> By gifts already given, by daily promises,  
> He seeks the see that we call Amiens,  
> Thinking himself to reign through pontifical honour.  
> By harshly stripping the church of its holy patron,  
> He exalts himself anew and leaps from the monks’ flock;  
> Making himself great, he brings harm upon the brethren on every side.  
> Christ stood against him; the enemy was overthrown.  
> All that he seized he justly left, with loss.  
> And, as you all know, he was an enemy to many everywhere:  
> Those whom he had raised up, he afterward cast down.  
> He squandered many possessions of St. Richarius,  
> Hated by the monks, hated by all his friends,  
> A most wretched man, unwilling to wish to cure himself,  
> [Col. 1363C] Until at last he strove toward a reprobate end.

The brethren, wearied by long waiting and seeing that he was always carried toward worse things, endeavoured by various means to call him back from the destruction and spoliation of the house. They approached him through Guy, count of Ponthieu, through noble palatines, through Rainald, archbishop of Reims, and through other noble persons; and they cried aloud, not without groaning, over the downfall of the once-blessed monastery. To their faces he flattered them, promising that he would soon amend himself in every respect; but in his heart he raged fiercely against those who lodged complaint against him.

When no hope of his correction remained, the Church of Reims advised that our brethren should reveal, either personally or through faithful envoys, the desolation and ruin of their house to Pope Urban, who was shortly to hold a council [Col. 1363D] at Clermont, and should implore the clemency of his majesty to restore, in the kindness appropriate to his office, the monastery now almost emptied, to some appearance of resurrection.

This was done, and a remedy immediately followed. For Pope Urban, sitting in council, pronounced canonical sentence against him, deprived him of the abbot’s staff and of the care of the monks, adding these severe words:

“You have treated the abbey of St. Richarius, once noble and rich, so wretchedly that you have stripped the church of its ornaments and made many monks, who resisted your vices, into exiles. Therefore you deserved wholly to lose every grace of ecclesiastical dignity, as a slaughterer of Christ’s sheep and a scatterer of the holy Church. But lest we seem to strike you with a double punishment, be content with the bishopric of Amiens, which you acquired so harshly. Let the monks of St. Richarius have freedom to elect an abbot, whom you must in no manner presume to oppose. This we command you to observe by the power of the Holy Spirit.”

Thus, by such a decision and such a Roman command, the power of the perverter was destroyed; the rod of the smiter ceased from us; the heavy yoke was removed from our necks, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, indiction IV. [Col. 1364A] This mercy of God was granted to Centula.

But that most cunning man was not so subdued from his deceit. Returning from the council, he urged with prayers and promises [Col. 1364B] all travellers present from these regions not to inform us of his fall. Thus for a whole year he deceived us, using a false title over our possessions, until it was again disclosed to us by the Church of Reims how he had been stripped of the abbey at the Council of Clermont. When this became known openly to the brethren, they summoned him, greatly resisting, into chapter and plainly renounced him and his obedience, declaring that they would immediately appeal to the pope unless he left the place altogether.

Seeing that his deceits were now exposed and guarding against the danger of greater disgrace, he rose, laid down the staff, fell prostrate, sought pardon, and begged with groans that he might be forgiven for his offence. But the monks, deeply embittered, did not heed his voice; spurred by the excess [Col. 1364C] of past and present evils, they assailed him with sharp reproaches until, leaving the place, he went to Abbot’s-villa. When he departed from Centula, not one person pitied him; all cursed him, rejoicing in his downfall.

> Thus he who was piously exalted was afterward disgraced;  
> Hostile to us, he became exceedingly troublesome to himself.  
> The plague he had inflicted, he drew upon himself.  
> Thus, through Richarius’s prayers, this Gervin fell.

I therefore beg all who come to know these events to remember how illustrious and honourable were the things related above, and to know that we should have preferred to report good and venerable things concerning Lord Gervin rather than what has been said above. But this has been written so that posterity may know with fullest certainty that the lovers of holy Father Richarius [Col. 1364D] and faithful guardians of his place receive a reward from God and retain the praise of good repute among humankind. For this reason we have taken care to recall Lord Gervin’s fall, so that his successors may know that those who cleave to Richarius are glorified, while those who despise and desert him are subject to everlasting reproach.

Moreover, the brethren could certainly, though with difficulty, have granted some pardon to the same Lord Gervin if, persisting in repentance, he had acknowledged that he had acted wrongly. But, as if to show himself unconquered, he did not cease to stir up disturbances against us and our house. Hence there soon arose that contentious lawsuit by which he wished to make our abbey, for himself and his successors, as though legally subject to him—an abbey which he himself had held free for twenty-four years [Col. 1365A] and had known to have enjoyed noble liberty throughout all the time of his predecessors.

He knew that Fulco, bishop of Amiens, had been greatly indebted for many services to Abbot Angilram and, after him, to Gervin; and that the abbots of Centula had not been regarded as subjects but as patrons. Indeed, the aforesaid Fulco would have been excommunicated at the Council of Reims by the blessed Pope Leo IX, had not the most reverend man, Abbot Gervin, diligently and prudently endeavoured to intervene for him. He knew that Guy, Fulco’s successor, born the son of a count, brother of Count Hugh and uncle of Count Guy, had been devoted in much service to the abbot of Centula—that is, to Gervin himself. Yet, under the pressure of malice, he showed himself forgetful of all this, attacking with new snares the noble young Anscher, chosen abbot, and diligently seeking how he might resist him or obstruct his promotion.

It would be far too long and tedious to set out the varieties of his machinations. Therefore, omitting these, let us say briefly how he ended.

His resources failed, and, as all the clergy sided with the reproach directed against him, he was compelled to leave his see. Without the knowledge of clergy or people, he succeeded at Tours, at Marmoutier, where Abbot Helgaud received him honourably and brought him to confess his error. In the assembly of the brethren, Helgaud heard from him with how great perversity and cruelty he had destroyed the monastery of St. Richarius and weakened it in its morals and possessions. After recounting these things with excessive lamentation, he survived [Col. 1365C] only a few months, and departed this life on the fourth day before the Ides of January [10 January].

> Let there be no vengeance upon him; but let the light of rest remain.

Amen.

There are also certain useful things which he is known, from the evidence of charters, to have accomplished; but they are so few that it does not please us to spend time explaining them. Yet, since we have set forth such sad matters concerning this abbot, by the mercy of Christ now bestowed we shall narrate prosperous things concerning his successor, so that Christ’s Church may rejoice thereby forever. Amen.

I, Brother Hariulf, humble monk of the monastery of Blessed Richarius, completing with God’s help this work on the nobility and benefits of our holy place, begun many years ago by Lord Saxowal, [Col. 1365D] beseech all who are to serve in this holy place—indeed, I adjure them by the power of God and by Christ the Wisdom—that they carefully preserve these materials for whose gathering we have laboured, [Col. 1366A] and do not permit them in any way to perish.

This work on the humanity of the Son of God was completed in the year 1088, indiction X, in the twenty-eighth year of King Philip, Guy having been count of Ponthieu for thirty-six years.

Here ends Book IV of the Deeds of the Church of Centula.

[Note: [Col. 1365] These are Hariulf’s words about himself, in the manner of an epilogue addressed to Centula, his monastery.]

> With all my heart I have loved you, Mother Centula.  
> Given to you as a boy, I bound my neck beneath you.  
> I swore the bonds by which I dedicated vows to you.  
> Holding faith’s pledge, I carefully avoided what was contrary to you.  
> Then I brought joy to the brethren and lords;  
> Writing the deeds of the fathers, I prepared these things according to my strength;  
> And upon them I multiplied the praises of God.  
> You are a noble palm, because I have borne fruit from you.  
> See how greatly I have magnified your sons with praise;  
> [Col. 1366B] And how I have compared your treasures with none before them.  
> By praising holy Richarius, I have made him illustrious.  
> Behold with kindly eyes how great a work I have made for you.  
> If there is one more noble than you, I have joined you to none.  
> By recording your fathers, I have made you greatly noble.  
> Mother, receive the servant who has made you thus marvellous;  
> Now free me from the sins by which I have stained myself.  
> And join me to those of yours whom I have rightly pronounced blessed.  
> May I be among the brethren, the lords whom I have desired.  
> May I not be cast out from those to whom I was formerly joined.  
> May Richarius cherish me, under whom I was sanctified,  
> So that I may please Christ, to whom I have offered myself in sacrifice.

The names of those whom I recall as expelled by the second Gervin are these: Walter, surnamed Ambrose; Walter, surnamed Samuel; Walter; Germanus; [Col. 1366C] Teudold; Guy; Bernard; William; Erluin; Hildemar.

## Epitaph of the Writer

> Hariulf, born in Ponthieu and inclined to study,  
> Entered as a boy the cloister of gracious Richarius.  
> There, instructed in what it befits a master to know,  
> He became the third abbot of Aldenburg.  
> He increased according to his strength the charge committed to him,  
> Ever desiring, Peter, that your wealth should grow.  
> Offering the brethren an example of fellow-feeling,  
> He kept silent about many things which it would have been fitting to tell.  
> He honoured the elder brethren whom Centula retains,  
> Ever desiring to see them held in honour.  
> [Col. 1366D] Centula, I love you, captivated by love for my teacher;  
> As I give you these final small gifts, farewell, mother.  
> And, returning the favour, fare well on the day known by birth [reading uncertain].

[Col. 1367]

# Life of St. Arnulf, Bishop of Soissons, by Hariulf, a Contemporary Author

And revised, as it appears, by Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, likewise a contemporary.

(Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century VI, part II, p. 502, from a manuscript codex of the abbey of Longpont, collated with others.)

## Preliminary Notice

1. In this century the distinguished monastery of St. Medard at Soissons was made illustrious by the merits and virtues of Blessed Arnulf. Surius published the Life of this blessed man for 15 August under the name of Lisiard, bishop of Soissons. At its beginning stands an epistle of the same Lisiard to Radulf, archbishop of Reims, in which he submits this Life, which he professes to have written, to Radulf’s judgement. Various other manuscript codices likewise bear the same letter under Lisiard’s name; consequently nearly all writers have cited the same Life under Lisiard’s name.

But if one examines the matter more carefully, one will discover that this Life itself, or its first two books, is the genuine offspring of Hariulf, third abbot of Aldenburg. This will not be very difficult to prove, both from the authority of manuscript codices and from certain other arguments drawn from the context of the work itself. Among the various manuscript codices containing this Life, one exists in the library of the Cistercian monastery of Ourscamp near Noyon, where this very Life, with three letters prefixed to it, is found under Hariulf’s name. The first is addressed to Lambert, bishop of Tournai; the second to Lisiard himself, bishop of Soissons; and the third, finally, to Radulf, metropolitan of Reims. This last is the same letter, with only very few alterations, which in some other codices and in Surius’s edition is addressed to the same archbishop under Lisiard’s name.

Moreover, Aubertus Miraeus had seen this same Life, as he himself testifies in his little work *On Benedictine Origins in Belgium*. Yet in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 362, he asserts that Surius and his followers wrongly attributed it to Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, since it is certain that it was in fact written by Hariulf. Vossius agrees in Book II of *On Latin Historians*. Indeed, the Life as published by Surius itself shows that it is Hariulf’s work. For near its conclusion these words occur:

> “At the end of my little book my apology must be set down, so that it may be clear to all from whose account I learned these things and at whose urging I dared undertake to write them. The first was the Everolph whom we have often mentioned, continuing in his service. Since he had more certainly known the events by being present, he stayed with me for several days at Aldenburg and recounted in order all that he knew while I wrote upon wax tablets. The second was Arnulf, the holy man’s sister’s son and first abbot of Aldenburg; what I had impressed upon wax tablets was of assistance to me in writing it down in ink on parchment. Finally, his sister Adzela, who had been more intimate with him, told us many things about him.”

It is difficult to see how these words could be attributed to Lisiard, who never resided at Aldenburg. Further, Lisiard would have written not only what others had seen, but also—and especially—what he had seen himself, since in the preface to the book *On Miracles* he declares that he had been ordained subdeacon by Blessed Arnulf and calls himself the blessed man’s fellow-dweller. Indeed, in the same little work he repeatedly narrates miracles seen by himself.

2. Yet I would not say that this work must be wholly taken away from Lisiard, since he himself in some way claims it for his own. In the already cited book *On Miracles*, speaking of this Life at the Council of Beauvais, he says:

> “Among the others, the abbot of Aldenburg was also present, carrying in his hands a little book concerning the life, character, and miraculous deeds of St. Arnulf himself. Taking this little book from his hands, I opened it, and having opened it offered it to the bishops, saying: ‘Behold, lords, this little book was written concerning his life with my knowledge and under my authority; and I bear faithful testimony that all that it recounts is true,’ etc.”

From these words it appears that, whether the work be attributed to Hariulf or Lisiard, nothing is taken from its authority. For Lisiard adopted the book of Hariulf, then abbot of Aldenburg, since it had been written with Lisiard’s knowledge and under his authority.

Surius published this Life in one book, frequently changing its style, as was his custom, and also omitting certain verses which, according to the practice of those times, had been interspersed at various places in the narrative. The manuscript codex of Ourscamp likewise contains it in a single book, divided into forty chapters, with the three letters just mentioned. But we present it, from a manuscript codex of the Cistercian monastery of Longpont, divided into two books, with a third book concerning the miracles and canonization of the same saint. All these are found in that codex under Lisiard’s name, although a separate letter is prefixed to the third book, in which the same Lisiard dedicates his work to Radulf, archbishop of Reims.

From all this one may infer that, after Blessed Arnulf’s canonization, Lisiard joined Hariulf’s work together with his own book *On the Miracles and Canonization of the Same Saint*. Thus it happened that this Life was subsequently copied by some under Hariulf’s name and by others under that of Lisiard. But, that we may leave everyone free judgement on this matter, we shall prefix to the Life itself the three letters of Hariulf contained in the manuscript codex of Ourscamp.

3. Lisiard, formerly provost of Soissons, became bishop of the same church in 1108, as is clear both from Alberic’s Chronicle and from the manuscript cartulary of St. Martin of the Fields, where the year 1123 is called the fifteenth of his episcopate. He attended several councils of the province of Reims; and Guibert, abbot of Nogent, dedicated to him the *History of the Deeds of God through the Franks*, with a prefixed letter in which he is celebrated with many praises.

[Col. 1369] Hariulf is the very author of the Chronicle of Centula, who, having been a monk of Centula, became abbot of Aldenburg about the year 1105, when Gervin relinquished the staff. He was present at the Council of Beauvais held in the year 1020 [probably an erroneous date], at which the elevation of Blessed Arnulf was approved by the judgement of all the bishops. The same abbot vigorously defended his monastery against the monks of St. Medard at Soissons, who maintained that it ought to be subject to them. He also obtained various diplomas from the counts of Flanders confirming the possessions of his monastery; some of these appear in Miraeus’s *Notitia Ecclesiarum Belgii*. Two are of Count Theodoric, and the third of Simon, bishop of Tournai, issued in 1130.

Besides the Chronicle of Centula and the Life of Blessed Arnulf, he also wrote the Life of Blessed Gervin, second abbot of Aldenburg, and a little book on miracles of St. Peter performed in the church entrusted to him. I would further warn the reader that this Hariulf is called Arnulf by some. We think this happened through an error of copyists, who carelessly read *Arnulfus* for *Ariulfus*; indeed Sanderus in *Flanders Illustrated* calls him now Arnulf and now Hariulf within a few lines. But let the narrative now return to Blessed Arnulf.

4. At the beginning of his Life, Arnulf is said to have been born of parents distinguished not only by nobility but by very great wealth. All writers on Belgian affairs agree that he sprang from the most noble family of the lords of Pamele in Belgium; the Sammarthani followed them in the *Gallia Christiana*. The author of the Life testifies that Arnulf had as paternal uncle Arnulf of Oudenaarde, and there affirms that his mother descended from the illustrious lineage of the counts of Louvain, Namur, Loon, and Mons.

This great nobility of lineage may be confirmed from an ancient manuscript codex of the Cistercian monastery of Clairmarais in Belgium, where, after the Life of Blessed Arnulf, his maternal genealogy is described thus:

> Albert, count of Namur, had three full sisters: Lutgarda, Goda, and Ermengarda. Albert begot Godfrey, father of Godfrey of Namur. Lutgarda bore Emmo and his brother Otto. Emmo begot Arnulf, count of Loon, and Sophia, duchess of Hungary. This Sophia bore the king of Hungary and the duchess of Huy. Otto, Emmo’s brother, begot Gilbert of Duras. Goda, sister of Count Albert, bore Meinsinda, mother of St. Arnulf, bishop of the city of Soissons in France.

In the summary of the Life of the same St. Arnulf, which we shall give at the end of Book III from the Longpont codex and which is also found in the Clairmarais manuscript, his father is called Fulbert Godelef, while his mother is said to have been born from the stock of German nobles.

5. Arnulf had already spent several years in secular military service when, upon his father’s death, he embraced monastic life under the rule of Rainald, abbot of St. Medard at Soissons. There he lived enclosed in a cell, until Pons, who had intruded himself into the abbacy after Rainald’s death, was removed because he was squandering the entire substance of the monastery. Arnulf himself, with the assent of King Philip, was appointed in his place.

Dormasius, author of a history of Soissons, thinks this occurred at the Synod of Soissons at which the foundation of the abbey of St. John was confirmed by Metropolitan Manasses and the other bishops of the province of Reims. But no trace of the matter appears in ancient records; and the author of the Life, who fully described the circumstances of Arnulf’s election, would certainly not have omitted it. In any event, Arnulf seems to have been placed over this monastery about the year 1077. We infer this because Gerald, who was substituted by the brethren after Arnulf had been compelled two years later to relinquish the government of the monastery, was immediately expelled by the queen in 1079. In that same year Gerald withdrew to Aquitaine, where toward the end of the year he laid the foundations of the monastery of La Sauve-Majeure. How piously and prudently Arnulf administered the monastery of St. Medard entrusted to him may be learned from his Life.

6. Having relinquished the government of the monastery, Arnulf had scarcely begun to enjoy the solitude he desired when he was again recalled to other and greater responsibilities. After the death of Theobald, bishop of Soissons, a certain Ursio had seized that see. At the command of Pope Gregory VII, Arnulf was appointed to this church at the Synod of Meaux in 1080. But while, because Ursio occupied the city of Soissons, he devoted himself wholly to episcopal duties at the castle of Oulchy, Pope Gregory sent him to Flanders to restore the magnates of that region to concord with Count Robert, who was most hostile to them.

Arnulf accomplished this, and many other things narrated in his Life. Among them the foundation of the renowned monastery of St. Peter at Aldenburg must occupy a prominent place, and it will be useful to note several matters concerning it here.

7. They report that the town of Aldenburg (Oudenburg) was once a most prosperous city, wholly ruined and overthrown when Attila devastated Gaul. They also think that it suffered the same calamity from the Northmen in the ninth century, when the renowned Flemish city of Bruges arose from its ruins, encircled and fortified with walls by Baldwin the Bald, count of Flanders.

They trace the origin of the church of Aldenburg to Blessed Ursmar, bishop and abbot of Lobbes, who toward the end of the seventh century spread the teaching of the Gospel in that region. For Aldo, lord of the district, converted to faith in Christ, gave to the same holy man, as is recorded in his Life, the village called Aldeburch after his own name; there he built and consecrated a church in honour of Blessed Peter the Apostle, together with a thousand paces in every direction around it, with which he afterward endowed the church of Lobbes, etc.

Though very small and built only of wooden boards, that church remained so for a long time, namely until 1056. Then the inhabitants of the town, stirred by the frequency of miracles occurring there, destroyed the former church and constructed another of stone, as these familiar verses state:

> In the thousandth year, and in the fifty-sixth besides,  
> The work of this temple is known to have begun,  
> Where first a wooden basilica had been founded.

Four years later it was consecrated by Radbod, bishop of Tournai, as these two further verses indicate:

> In Christ’s one thousand and seventieth year together,  
> This church of St. Peter was consecrated by Radbod.

But the same church, which at its first foundation had been given to the monks of Lobbes, had for many years passed into lay control. Conon, chamberlain of Count Robert, gave it to Radbod, bishop of Tournai, and Radbod in turn gave it to Blessed Arnulf, who, as we have said, was then staying in Flanders to settle disputes. There the blessed man immediately established a community of monks.

This is reported by the author of the Life of St. Arnulf in the Chronicle of Aldenburg, cited by Sanderus in *Flanders Illustrated*, in these words:

> “The nobleman Conon, chamberlain of Flanders, possessed it as a castle-fief; at the urging of his wife Hasecca, he gave it to Count Robert; Robert gave it to Bishop Radbod; and the bishop, with the approval of Walter the archdeacon and the clergy, granted it free and unencumbered to Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, and made canonical investiture to him of it. Arnulf endowed it as an abbey and a congregation of monks of the Order of St. Benedict in the year 1084, and governed it for three years.”

The first abbot established there was Arnulf, sister’s son of the blessed man, who died in 1095. In that monastery, besides Blessed Gervin and Hariulf, other illustrious men flourished later. Among them were the celebrated twenty-fifth abbot Henry and his successor Anianus, who [Col. 1371] restored the church in the fifteenth century. George Cabellian continued the annals of his monastery to the year 1574, when he was still alive.

At the same time two distinguished men, worthy members of the Benedictine order, flourished in that monastery: James Byns and Arnold Wion. In 1578, when the monastery of Aldenburg had been completely destroyed by Calvinist heretics, they were compelled to depart for other provinces. James went to Spain, where at Seville he built a hospice to receive and support his compatriots. Arnold withdrew to Italy, where he wrote a book on the beginnings, development, and other matters concerning our order, entitled *Lignum Vitae* (“The Tree of Life”); having long lived among our Cassinese brethren, he died in that region.

These events occurred under Abbot Melchior Everaert, during whose time the monks were scattered in various directions. Meanwhile, a very few monks preserved at Bruges the sacred relics and other things rescued from the fury of the heretics. When the disturbances had been calmed, they later returned to the monastery, which was finally restored through the care and diligence of Abbot Maximilian. But let us return to Blessed Arnulf.

8. Once monks had been established in the monastery of Aldenburg and concord confirmed among the magnates of Flanders, Arnulf returned to his see. But, since amid the disturbed affairs of his Church he could accomplish nothing, and since no aid could be hoped for from the metropolitan see of Rheims—for that Church, after the deposition of Manasses, was without a pastor, while Elinand of Laon, under the authority of King Philip, was devastating rather than governing it—the blessed bishop withdrew to the monastery of Saint-Médard, where he again undertook the life of a recluse. These events must be assigned to the year 1084, when he returned from Flanders; for in the following year Hilgot was substituted for Arnulf, and no one disputes that he was the lawful bishop. Indeed, under that title he attended the Council of Compiègne in that same year, 1085; and in a charter for the canons of Château-Thierry he himself calls 1087 the second year of his episcopate.

9. But when disturbances again arose in Belgium, Arnulf was compelled to visit that region anew. There, after reconciling the minds of the dissidents, he departed this life on the very day of the Assumption of Saint Mary, the fifteenth of August, in the year 1087; and there is no disagreement among authors on this point. He was buried before the altar of Blessed Mary, on the left side of the choir, and remained there until the year 1121, when, on the Kalends of May [1 May], his sacred body was raised from the earth and placed in a shrine. In 1457 Anianus, abbot of Aldenburg, caused a richer casket than the former one to be made, into which the body of Saint Arnulf was translated with the utmost solemnity. His name is entered in the Roman, Benedictine, Gallican, and other Martyrologies. Molanus, in his *Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium*, and Arnold Wion, in his notes on the Martyrology, composed summaries of his life. His encomium also occurs in Dormasius, historian of Soissons; in Marlot, in the *Metropolis of Rheims*; in Meyer, Miraeus, Sanderus, and others, especially Belgian writers.

Sigebert, who lived at that time, writes the following concerning this bishop under the year 1080:

> At this same time, in the monastery of Saint-Médard, the most blessed man Arnulf flourished in signs and virtues. Because of his wondrous fervour for holiness, he chose the purpose of reclusion; and, afflicting himself with excessively severe abstinence, he received from God the grace of prophecy. Having become abbot of this monastery from being a recluse, he later returned to that same reclusion out of contempt for the world and desire for inward rest. When the bishop of Soissons died, he was elected to the episcopate; and by order of Pope Gregory he was consecrated bishop by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, legate of the Apostolic See.

Concerning his death, Sigebert speaks thus under the year 1087:

> Saint Arnulf, formerly abbot of Saint-Médard and afterwards promoted to the episcopate of the city of Soissons, came into Flanders to restore peace among the Flemings. In a village named Aldenburg, he made the church of Saint Peter—already distinguished by divine miracles—into a monastery of monks, established the order of regular life, and at last in that same monastery received both the end of his life and burial, as he himself had foretold.

This is Sigebert’s account. It is not found in Miraeus’s edition; but there, under the year 1086, the following is printed in a different typeface:

> Arnulf, bishop of the city of Soissons, illustrious through the spirit of prophecy, purity of life, and miracles, is buried by God’s providence at Aldenbort, in the church of Saint Peter.

Trithemius likewise praises this holy man in the *Hirsau Chronicle* under the year 1084. But now his Life itself must be presented. As promised, it seemed fitting first to prefix to it three letters of Hariulf from the Ursicamp manuscript, which the Reverend Father Dom Nicolaus Perempertus, monk of the same Cistercian monastery, most courteously sent to us in the year 1687.

# THREE LETTERS OF HARIULF, ABBOT OF ALDENBURG, PREFIXED TO THE LIFE OF SAINT ARNULF, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

[Col. 1371]

## I. Letter to Lambert, Bishop of Tournai

[Col. 1371A]

To Lord LAMBERT, by God’s grace bishop of the people of Tournai, HARIULF, least of sons, greetings.

Royal dishes, though they shine with gold and silver, though they exhale the fragrance of exotic flavours and aromatic scents, become objects of contempt rather than pleasure unless they are seasoned with salt. So too the skill of an architect: if in his buildings he exceeds proper limits or fails to preserve the course of the lines in due balance, he will later vainly repent of his labour, having lost both the prize of skill and, to his grief, suffered the loss of his structure.

Considering these things, and fearing an outcome of like danger, I offer to you, venerable bishop, most gracious Father Lambert, this little work as a gift of hospitality. To you, as to a faithful shepherd, I entrust the fruitful little fleece of my small talent, [Col. 1372A] that your episcopal authority may give strength and confidence to these matters, to be read, known, and imitated for the benefit of Holy Church; lest, because of the lowly unworthiness of the farmer, fastidious citizens trample down the fertility of the young crop.

For such a density of thorns and harshness of briars—that is, the utterly foolish malice of my assailants—has hitherto so battered and shackled me that my mind has found pleasure in contemplating nothing but mournful flight. But after heavenly grace raised your fatherhood to the episcopal rank in the twofold see of Tournai and Noyon, the thorns and briars by which I was sharply goaded immediately began to wither and be cut down. At once a new peace arose for me, grievously afflicted as I was, and I give immense thanks to Christ and to you, because, just as frogs fall silent at the sound of thunder, so those who afflicted me at the beginning of your episcopate were soon subdued and left inactive by fear of your mercy.

Therefore, since through you I have received a certain liberty of life, in these days of peace, in which by your authority the yoke of the enemy has decayed away, I have composed this little book concerning the Life and virtues of the chosen man, Lord Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, granted to us by the wondrous mercy of God and buried in our place by divine disposition. Trembling, yet supported by complete certainty of its truth, I first entrust it to you, as is proper, for publication, so that by the judgment of your authority it may either become known to the holy children of the Church or else be kept within domestic bounds, pressed down beneath the weight of silence.

If, then, the light of God’s grace shall make this little work [Col. 1373B] worthy of notice, may it receive through you and from you the means of going forth. And when by your merciful judgment you judge it worthy of praise, we beg you not to be reluctant to pass it on to our lord, your brother and fellow bishop Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, so that through your office and his it may be spread before the noble eyes of the citadel of Rheims. Farewell.

## II. Here begins the same author’s letter to Lisiard, Bishop of Soissons

To LISIARD, bishop of the holy Church of Soissons, resplendent with the flowers of every virtue, H., servant of Saint Peter the Apostle under the title of abbot, greetings and the brothers’ continual remembrance in prayer.

Two fitting reasons have moved us to address the reverence of your fatherhood in these words. The first is that you are supported by no slight knowledge of the present matter: namely, of the life, virtue, and merits of our lord Arnulf, bishop and your predecessor. The other is that, even if he had never been known to you, nevertheless, since God made him wonderful through the practice of righteousness, whatever holy and authentic matter can be spoken or written about him ought to be confirmed by your testimony.

We rightly judge authentic whatever does not depart from the deeds and virtues of the saints of old according to a reasonable likeness. Wishing, therefore, to bring to the knowledge of holy Mother Church this little book concerning the Life and miracles of the grace-bearing man Arnulf, bishop of the same Church over which, by God’s appointment, you preside; and striving to convey it by the lawful path, through the hand of Lord Lambert, bishop [Col. 1373D] of Noyon and Tournai, to the hearing of the metropolitan; we have judged it proper first to submit it to your examination. For we know assuredly that whatever pleases you according to the balance of truth will in no way displease the judgment of the holy Church of Rheims.

Let the truth of these matters, which is not unknown to you, be more freely disclosed under the protection of your authority; and let a fuller confidence in believing arise in the hearts of those who receive this account, in view of your experience. For this little page will not sound forth empty trifles, but works of power that belong to God alone, and which, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, are able to urge every faithful soul toward the exercise of virtue.

Therefore faithfully take care to make more widely known the gift which we commit with pious boldness to the examination of your discernment, so that knowledge of the godliness which once shone upon your mind may be diffused through your ministry into the hearts of others. Farewell.

## III. Likewise, the same author’s letter to Lord Radulf, Archbishop of Rheims

To the venerable and most beloved Father and Lord Radulf, by God’s grace archbishop of the holy Church of Rheims, Hariulf, the offscouring of all abbots, greetings and the fullness of every good.

Frequent opportunities of seeing and hearing you have revealed to me the boundless sea of your learning, your prudent heart’s discernment in all things, your love for the advancement of Holy Church, and the rule of discipline in those matters which need correction. Therefore, strengthened by so many supports from your virtues, I have ventured upon a small work deservedly reserved for skilled writers—not from the swelling pride of self-exaltation, Christ knows, [Col. 1374B] but for the sake of usefulness—so that by the service of my littleness the works of God, which wise and learned men have hitherto neglected to raise from the depths of silence, might somehow be made public.

As I turned my mind to writing these things, my heart trembled with fear. But when I reflected that this fear of mine would be an obstacle to fraternal benefit, I raised my heart again to the lofty gaze of your discernment, knowing without doubt that ready pardon is open to the rashness which arises in serving fraternal charity. May your fatherhood, therefore, pardon one who has presumed, who in attempting such things has in every respect sought your honour. May your authority grant favour and strength to one who publishes these things, lest he be subject to shame because of his own worthlessness.

Moreover, let no one’s mind be turned into uncertainty concerning their truth; for they have been so carefully investigated by those who were present and so clearly ascertained that in all things the firmness of truth is certain. And because I hold it settled that above all else you pursue the advancement of the Churches, I entrust to your wisdom and that of your people whatever in these matters has been expressed with insufficient elegance, so that through the noble sharpness of Rheims eloquence what sounds uncouth through my dullness may be polished.

As I am about to relate in some measure the holiness of life and works of power which Christ the Lord bestowed in recent times upon his soldier Arnulf, I desire the Holy Spirit, maker of every good, to be present with me, that he may graciously fill my mouth with his praise in recounting these things—he who illuminated the inmost heart of this same servant with his light, that he might perform such deeds.

Let those skilled in most eloquent writings admit this uncultivated utterance into the building of Holy Church under the rule concerning woodland timbers, so that in the house of the Lord goats’ hair may have its place, and the diverse vessels of a great house may not, as is fitting, be deprived of their proper functions. May our God preserve your life and your primacy, sound in body and spirit, for a long time. Amen.

# HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE OF SAINT ARNULF, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

[Col. 1375A]

To the venerable and most beloved Father and Lord RADULF, by God’s grace archbishop of the holy Church of Rheims, LISIARD, least of all bishops, greetings and [Note: [Col. 1375] In the other manuscript and in Surius it reads: “and the fullness of every good.”] the fullness of all holy obedience.

Frequent and celebrated opportunities of seeing and hearing you have revealed to many, among whom I too am numbered, the immense weight of your learning, your prudent heart’s discernment in all things, your love for the advancement of Holy Church, and the rule of discipline in correcting matters. Therefore, strengthened by the endeavours of so many of your virtues, informed also by the manifold testimony of truthful witnesses, and moreover impelled by the greatness of the events, I have ventured upon a small work deservedly reserved for learned writers—not from the swelling pride of self-exaltation, but for the sake of [Col. 1375B] usefulness—so that through the service of my insignificance the great works of God, which wise and learned persons have hitherto neglected to raise from the depths of silence, might somehow be made public.

As I directed my mind to write these matters, my heart trembled with fear. But when I reflected more carefully that this fear of mine would obstruct fraternal benefit, I raised my heart again [Col. 1376A] to the regard of your discernment, knowing beyond doubt that ready pardon is open to the rashness which arises in serving fraternal charity. May your fatherhood, therefore, pardon one who has presumed, who in undertaking such things has in every respect sought the honour of your Church. May your authority grant favour and strength to one who publishes these things, lest because of his own worthlessness he be subject to shame.

Moreover, let no one’s mind be turned into uncertainty concerning their truth, because they have been so carefully investigated by those who were present and clearly ascertained that in every respect the firmness of truth is certain. Whatever in them has been set forth with insufficient elegance, I entrust to your wisdom and that of yours [variant: “ours”], so that by the noble sharpness of the Rheims intellect what is seen to be uncouth through my dullness may be polished. [Col. 1376B] As I am about to relate in part the holiness of life and works of power which Christ the Lord bestowed almost in our own times upon his soldier Arnulf, I call upon the Holy Spirit, maker of every good, that he may graciously fill our mouths with his praise in recounting these matters—he who illumined the inmost heart of this same servant with his light, so that he might accomplish such deeds.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK BEGIN

[Col. 1375]

I. On the place and country of the man of God Arnulf.  
II. On the forewarnings of his birth.  
III. On the name found on a brick, and the prophecy of the pilgrim.  
IV. On his illustrious youth and prowess in arms.  
V. On his conversion from soldier to monk.  
VI. On his obedience and severity of life.  
VII. On the recluse monk who appeared to Arnulf himself after death.  
VIII. On his silence for forty-two months, that is, three years and six months.  
IX. On the flight he undertook at night, so that he might not become abbot.  
X. On the wolf that led him back at night while he was unaware.  
XI. On the disabled ass which he restored.  
XII. On the man suffering from epilepsy whom he healed.  
XIII. On the sick man who loathed food, whom he healed by the taste of his bread.  
XIV. On the woman blind for ten years, who was given sight through water touched by his hands.  
XV. On the turbot (*rumbo*) suddenly found at the dedication of the crypt.  
XVI. On the French king’s expedition which he rejected.  
XVII. On Abbot Gerard, appointed in his place.  
XVIII. On his manifold practice of holy life.  
XIX. On the foreseen death of Israel, once his companion.  
XX. On the fish recognized by the Spirit as spoiled, and on the obedience of the raven.  
XXI. On the foreknown death of his nephew.  
XXII. On the thirteen-year-old mute to whom he gave speech.  
XXIII. On the man possessed by a legion, whom he cleansed as soon as he saw him.  
XXIV. On the reported arrival of barbarians, which he rejected by divine action.  
XXV. On the death of the once-glorious Count Simon, which he immediately recognized.  
XXVI. On the nobleman Guy, long sick.  
XXVII. On the endangered wife of this same Guy.  
XXVIII. On the child born blind, to whom he gave eyes by means of saliva.  
XXIX. On the sister of that same child.  
XXX. On the king and queen of France asking Saint Arnulf for a son.  
XXXI. On the soldier Geric, whom he healed in body and heart.  
XXXII. On his wife Judith, to whom he prophesied a future son.

# THE LIFE BEGINS. BOOK ONE

[Col. 1377]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1377A]

I. At the time when the region of Flanders was adorned by the government of Count Baldwin [Note: [Col. 1377D] Called Baldwin of Lille; he was guardian of King Philip while Philip was still a boy. His wife Adela, daughter of Robert, king of France, founded the Benedictine monastery of noble virgins at Messines, near Ypres; she received the veil from Alexander II and finally died piously in the said convent in 1079. She is frequently praised by authors of her age.] and his wife Adela, while Henry son of King Robert ruled the kingdom of France and the pious King Edward reigned over the English, there was a man named Folbert in the district of Brabant near the river Scheldt. He was distinguished among all his fellow countrymen, not only by the conspicuous nobility of his lineage but also by an abundance of worldly possessions, and in every respect he was illustrious both in mind and body.

According to the honourable custom of nobles, he was joined in marriage; and by his most noble wife, named Meinsinde, he begot a handsome son. When this son had grown up and was especially fitted for bearing arms, he was taken from the present light. His death brought most grievous sorrow upon his father, mother, and all the household dependants, so that at the anniversary season [Col. 1377B] they wept for him and mourned unceasingly.

## CHAPTER II

Several months had now passed in this grief, when behold, in a dream a man fair in appearance and radiant with shining light appeared to that same lady and said to her:

> Why do you afflict yourself with sorrow and depress yourself with useless grief over a son who died to so good an end? If you knew that he had received from you the spirit of life, you would indeed have reason to lament and mourn one made or formed by you. But since the heavenly Creator removed him from this life according to the incomprehensible judgment of his justice, how have you presumed to grieve? Henceforth admit no sorrow into your heart for his death; rather rejoice with great joy, because you carry in your womb [Col. 1377C] a child whom heavenly election has foreordained to become great. When you bring him into the light, you shall wish him to be called Christopher, because this child has indeed been appointed to bear Christ in his heart by his works and words. And that you may know for certain that these things have thus been divinely ordained, go to the church; in the place where you are accustomed to pray, have the ground dug up, and in the excavated earth you will find a brick engraved with large letters. Those letters will reveal to you the name and merit of your offspring.

## CHAPTER III

Having received this oracle of such great praise, the lady awoke from sleep and, with immense astonishment and wonderful joy, told the vision to her husband. At last, to prove the truth of the heavenly words, she took servants with a digger [Col. 1377D] and went to the church. In the place where she was accustomed to pray, she had them dig; and she found a square brick, inscribed in large letters thus: [Col. 1378A] **Christopher**.
