When this was found, she was filled with greater joy; and, now confident of the holiness of her child—since she had not previously known that she had conceived—she eagerly awaited so honourable a gift of divine activity. At the fitting time, therefore, she gave birth to the promised son, to the great joy of his father and relatives. According to custom, they brought him to Arnulf of Aldenarde (Oudenaarde), then a man illustrious in wealth and power, that he might receive him from the sacred font.

Gladly receiving the child, he at once hastened to administer to him the washing of sacred regeneration. But, through excessive affection as a relative and through boastful pride, he did not allow him to be named Christopher; rather, he had him named Arnulf, after himself. Although he lacked the name Christopher, the power of bearing Christ nevertheless continually grew in him day by day.

For while he was being reared with great care and attention, a certain pilgrim came by, sprinkled with the whiteness of age. Blessing the same infant, he said playfully, as if with a stammering utterance, to the nurse:

> Raise this little one with great diligence and utmost cleanliness, for Christ the Lord, dwelling in his heart, has determined through him to proclaim to his people the power of his works.

By such great and significant signs, God augmenting his merit, his future glory was made manifest; and before he performed the Lord’s works, he who was to perform them was already anticipated by the praise of divine favour.

## CHAPTER IV

At length, when he had grown up, he became gracious in speech, keen in intelligence, ready in service, energetic in work, vigorous and most strong in bodily power. He was so outstanding in excellence of strength and agility of body that he surpassed the power of four or five men of his own age; and everyone called him Arnulf the Strong.

His father and mother wished to commit him to the study of letters, but the other relatives strongly resisted, especially the aforementioned Arnulf of Aldenarde, his kinsman by paternal blood. For on his mother’s side his lineage was drawn from the stock [variant: “race”] of counts: namely, that of the duke of Louvain and the counts of Namur, Looz, Duras, and Mons.

Arnulf-Christopher—for so his mother preferred to call him, mindful of the divine promise—adorned with such great nobility, desired to turn everything excellent and pleasing that he possessed toward the Lord’s service. His relatives therefore wished rather to have him as a novice in military affairs than to devote him to the fellowship of ecclesiastical ranks. Thus it came about that, amid the great rejoicing of his loved ones, he took up the belt of secular knighthood, though later he would manfully assume spiritual arms.

Having received, in accordance with the wishes of his friends and the custom of nobles, the insignia of knighthood, he strove to maintain the bonds of piety: kind toward dependants; generous in aid to the needy; mercifully just in judgment; most eager in attending divine offices; wonderfully pleasing in love toward his companions; grounded in the fear of the Lord; diligent in honouring his parents; and supported by the heartfelt affection of all who knew him.

[Supplement: Note: [Col. 1379D] The material enclosed here in brackets has been copied from Surius.]

Although many things could be offered to show his bodily strength, we shall set forth only two briefly. For since all the works of the Lord are exceedingly good, knowledge of his strength and power will likewise provide matter for the praise of God, who bestowed it on him. At the same time it will add to the sum of this saint’s glory that, though he could have misused such strength for worldly vanity and false madness, he did not do so; rather, despising the world and the worldly glory acquired by it, he turned wholly toward the Lord.

Indeed, even bodily gifts of God are proclaimed in the saints: nobility is commended and wealth extolled, not because these gave them blessedness, but because by despising things which they might powerfully have used for evil, yet refused to use, they became more glorious and illustrious.

At the emperor’s court at Maastricht there was a frequent gathering of secular men swollen with worldly pomp, and among them the count of Flanders was foremost and greatest. When he found an opportune hour free from certain matters, youthful ardour, as is customary in seeking empty favour, readily set itself in motion. On either side a company of knights rose up; hurling lances and expending no small amount of strength, each eagerly strove to surpass another. In these bold and audacious attempts, bows were broken; and, since the emperor’s soldiers were almost superior in this contest, while the Flemings achieved nothing remarkable that might serve as a proof or demonstration of their celebrated valour, they were not far from reproach and disgrace.

At that time, among the Flemish company was the distinguished Arnulf. Young in years but endowed with the wisdom and gravity of old age, he was stirred by none of the frivolity of the others. Certain men, aware of his strength—equal to which none could be found in the German kingdom—approached him and not so much asked as compelled him to take part in the sportive contest. To their requests were added the commands of elders and seniors. Since he judged it foolish stubbornly to refuse obedience in a matter which, though of no benefit to himself, would harm no one, he ordered that the timber be brought which, placed at the top of a mast, holds the sail.

When the timber was brought—much longer and thicker than lances—he rose, while all marvelled, and hurled that mass, that weight rather than lance, far away with many a shaking movement. Immediately the noise and shouting of all arose in praise of the man, and the Flemings won victory in that game without danger. For, as the poet says:

> For sport has bred anxious contest and anger;  
> anger, savage enmities and deadly war.  
> (*Horace, Epistles*, Book I, Epistle 19, verses 48–49.)

Such contests took place in royal courts: begun indeed as sport, but very often ending in sorrow and killing. This could easily have happened also to those frivolous men, swollen with mutual pride, had Arnulf, a man of valour, not ended the game.

On one occasion, travelling as he often did with his elder, Arnulf of Aldenarde, he came to a very narrow passage, where a cart laden with hay, occupying the narrowness of the road, blocked all passage. While his companions went elsewhere, he remained there alone with his squire. Throwing part of the hay upon the ground and lifting the rest together with the cart by hand, he moved it some distance into a place occupied by brambles and thorns, which made the way narrow. Thus he removed the obstruction from the road for travellers, no less easily than kindly.

## CHAPTER V

At length he passed through every pursuit of military life, took part in imperial and royal wars, and distinguished himself everywhere in princes’ courts as an eloquent advocate. He repeatedly ended the quarrels and seditions of Brabant and Flanders by the barrier of his prudence, and restrained them by the terror of his incomparable strength; for there was no one who dared oppose his power or his arguments, strong in reason.

He always refused extensive estates, administrative charges, and most illustrious marriages offered him by the emperor of the Romans, the king of the English, and his kinsmen who were counts, remembering, surely, that he had deserved to be called Christopher not for worldly use but for the praise of God’s grace. And because so many and such great shoots of virtue, which divine grace had sown within him, could not bear fruit abundantly while mortal soldiery held them back, he conceived the noble plan that the labour and care of warfare should be turned to a better use, and that he should seek the wages which would know no end of life and praise.

Therefore, summoning his two squires, he ordered them to prepare all his weapons as quickly as possible, so that he might be able to go to the court of the king of France with exceptional splendour and fitting pomp. The squires obeyed their commander: they prepared the horses, arranged the arms, and took up all things worthy of a valiant knight.

Then Arnulf, bidding farewell to his mother—for his father had already died—set out toward France. Passing by the court of King Philip, he hurried to the church of the blessed confessor Médard, situated near the walls of the city of Soissons. At that time there was in that monastery a distinguished congregation of monks, whose honourable discipline shone forth as they offered sacrifices of praise worthy of God under Abbot Renald.

The prudent brothers of this congregation, skilled in the wisdom both of God and of the world and provident of good things before God and human beings—for men could not be uncultivated in manners when they were supported by intercourse with the whole courtly world of France and of Rome or Rheims—devoutly received, as was fitting, this aforementioned man hastening toward Christ in special devotion. Rejecting the belt of knighthood, he presented to the church his arms and the most elegant clothes he had brought; and they cut his hair and clothed him, now tonsured, in the regular habit, the mortification of Christ’s cross.

Having made him a monk and truly crucified him to this world, they instructed him in letters, formed him by the laws and precepts of the Lord, and adorned him with every ordinance. He stored all these things so deeply in the inner chamber of his inward person that his subsequent life showed that the seeds of God’s word had fallen neither beside the way, nor on rocky ground, nor among thorns.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1381B]

He had now completed a year’s course on the path of the Rule, and, for a greater test of his devotion and obedience, he was assigned responsibility for almsgiving and the care of feeding the poor. It was indeed a fitting duty to entrust the care of the poor to one who abounded in merciful compassion and was held to be generous in every respect.

For this reason, on a certain day, while he was visiting alone an estate assigned for the *agape* [Note: [Col. 1381D] That is, meals given for the sake of charity.]—that is, charitable meals—all the dogs of the adjacent village suddenly sprang upon him, wishing to tear him apart with rabid teeth. Extending his hand, he signalled them to follow him. Thus changing their rage into obedience, they went on with gentle disposition; and for as long as he remained there, they remained with him. At last, when he returned, they returned with him together, nor did they attack anyone in his presence with bite or bark.

Meanwhile he began to bind himself with vigorous mortification of the flesh, applying himself to vigils and fasts, persisting in lengthy prayers with tears, and showing himself approved to all. And, that he might utterly extinguish laughter and every movement of temporal joy within himself, he girded his body beneath his clothing with a very harsh, knotted, thorny branch of thistle, manfully mortifying his limbs and directing his mind heavenward, while nevertheless presenting to everyone a cheerful and pleasant countenance.

One day, however, when he wished to say something in the assembly of the brothers, he was unable to pronounce a word with the exactness customary among the French. The abbot therefore told him to be silent for a while, lest the usefulness of the matter be delayed by a more extended discussion. Arnulf kept this command to be silent for several months with a simple heart and zeal for true obedience, giving speech to no one and answering no one, until the brothers told the abbot that he was altogether mute.

The abbot summoned him and asked why he was silent. He learned that the abbot’s own injunction to silence was the cause of the prolonged silence. Marveling at the renewed simplicity of Paul [Note: [Col. 1381D] Paul, surnamed the Simple, after Saint Antony had commanded him to be silent, did not speak for seven years. He is famous among ancient writers; his Life was written by Palladius in the *Lausiac History* and by Rufinus in the *Lives of the Fathers*. See the Bollandists, 7 March.] in him, and rejoicing in his ardour for obedience, he ordered him meanwhile, for the sake of edification, to offer the brothers the service of conversation.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 1382A]

At that time there was in the same monastery a monk named Erembold, a recluse for the love of God. Born among the Flemish people, he led a hard and austere life, continually longing for divine contemplation. Arnulf served him attentively, not because he lacked an abundance of attendants, but in order to draw more deeply from him proofs of holy fervour.

After many struggles of continence, when he was now approaching the end of his mortal life, his bodily strength began to fail and he was pressed by severe distress. Then he asked the beloved Arnulf, who ministered to him tirelessly, to procure a little milk with which his weak body might be refreshed, if only for a moment. Hastening to fulfil this request, Arnulf took one loaf from those assigned to the poor [Col. 1382B] and offered the servant of God milk purchased with that bread.

The latter took it, but profited little from it, for illness and age weighed him down heavily. Or rather, heavenly providence, which scourges every son whom it receives, was fitting him by divine chastisement to merit rest. Therefore Arnulf, Christ’s soldier, asked him to show, after his death, the condition of his recompense and the state of his soul. The other, recognizing that this request had been made out of the fervour of faith and the desire for progress, faithfully promised that he would do so.

When he had departed from the world, he often, according to his promise, granted to Arnulf, servant of God, a glorious vision of himself: cheerful and rejoicing, and showing that he had been joined to luminous blessed rest. Arnulf said to him:

> Father, how do you fare? What is your condition? Did you undergo any punishment for any offence?

He answered:

> Because of the milk which you procured for me and which I drank in a small quantity, I endured some punishments, because you bought that milk from the resources of the poor. But both this and all my sins have been forgiven, and the joys of the blessed have been granted to me.

## CHAPTER VIII
By this vision the venerable Arnulf was indeed greatly inflamed; he grew exceedingly fervent in the practice of divine service, and thereafter did not cease from prayers, importuning the abbot’s will, until he obtained what he desired: namely, that he might enter into the same enclosure of a secluded life. Having attained this desire, he became [Col. 1382D] “the good fragrance of Christ in every place”; and many, following his example, eagerly sought the monastic life from far and near. At the same time Theobald, a noble young man, secretly fleeing the company of his peers, served the Lord as an exile and a poor man; and, having by example attained the crown of rewards, he planted in the minds of many the victory in which he now shines.

[Note: [Col. 1382D] This is undoubtedly St. Theobald, born of the family of the counts of Champagne; we have given his Life above under the year 1066.]

For who, hearing that Arnulf had rejected the splendor of knighthood and the world, would not immediately be released from love of the world? Who, I say, could fail to marvel at a man noble by birth [Col. 1383A], supported by powerful friends, tall in stature, handsome in face, favored by the world, attended by all the glory of the age, so suddenly converted that, through love of Christ, he cast himself down from the highest riches into the lowest poverty? From the region of Flanders and Brabant also many, both clerics and laymen, sought the sacred monastery of blessed Medard, because monastic order then flourished in that place and because the love of Arnulf, the venerable disciple now enclosed, especially drew them.

But he himself, advancing daily from virtue to virtue and accounting as nothing what he had hitherto been, considered the enclosure of his cell the delights of paradise, and reckoned continual bodily affliction not pain or misery but glory and pleasure. Accordingly, leaving the church [variant: cell] [Col. 1383B], he dug a ditch outside in the open air and sat there, so that the dripping from the church roof fell upon his head and neck. Whenever rain or snow fell, he did not change his place in the ditch or avoid frost and cold; rather, enduring every discomfort of the weather, he remained there, praying and chanting psalms, groaning and weeping, and at times giving himself to reading.

For three years and six months he spoke no word to mortals, bound in continual silence and delighting in heavenly contemplation and unceasing meditation upon the word of God, which, reading alone, he abundantly drew from the rich store of sacred books. As his persistence bore fruit, and as the help of God’s grace went before him and abounded greatly, he became by no means slightly wise, prudently understanding and effectively [Col. 1383C] grasping the meanings of divine utterances—so much nearer to God as he was farther removed from human affairs. He also devoted himself to acquiring the art of writing, and gained no contemptible skill in dictation.

What shall I say of his food and drink, when long fasts pleased him more than delicious dishes? Bread of barley mixed with a third part [of another grain] was taken rarely and sparingly; no other bread was ever taken. Foul water was his drink, and it was neither set before him daily nor, when set before him, taken to satisfaction.

## CHAPTER IX

Meanwhile Abbot Renald died; and a certain Pontius, a false monk, prompted by the spirit of ambition, obtained from Philip, king of the Franks, the title and seat of abbot by a comparative degree—not according to grammar, but [Col. 1383D] according to simony. This Pontius, living with excessive extravagance and lavishness, quickly exhausted all the property of the place. He spent the church’s principal ornaments upon the uses of the soldiers surrounding him, and in his madness dissipated nearly everything belonging to the adornment of God’s house. Why say more? When famine came, the office of divine praise failed in the church; and that basilica of blessed Medard, once famous, became for a time a reproach to its neighbors.

Then the brethren of sounder [variant: elder] counsel, gathered together [Col. 1384A], deliberated upon what remedy was needed for so great a disaster. They found it best that, taking with them the bishop of the see of Soissons and the principal persons of the place, they should appeal to the royal majesty: that it might mercifully have pity upon a monastery founded in ancient nobility and now destroyed by Pontius; that it might reverence the bodies of precious martyrs and confessors resting there; and that, Pontius being expelled—not an abbot but a tyrant—a worthy father might be provided for the Lord’s sheepfold. Having done so and swiftly bent the king’s mind toward mercy, they elected as abbot the servant of Christ Arnulf, by the common counsel of the brethren and the church’s *casati*, with clergy and people in agreement.

[Note: [Col. 1383D] The *casati* were the church’s feudal dependents, or those who had received benefices from church property. See Du Cange’s Glossary.]

Then Bishop Theobald [Note: [Col. 1383D] Theobald, called “of Pierrefonds,” governed the church of Soissons from the year 1072 to 1080. During his episcopate the celebrated monastery of St. John of the Vines was founded, in which regular canons were established.] went with a company of brethren to the recluse; and, after a solemn prayer had first been offered, [Col. 1384B] the bishop addressed him, asking, entreating, exhorting, and commanding him to yield to the brethren’s wishes and to exercise, in Christ’s name, the care and office of abbot.

But he, who had now been silent for three years and six months, was greatly alarmed. He took up a writing-tablet and wrote upon it this reply:

> I beg you, dearest brethren, spare me; allow me, weighed down by the burden of my sins, to offer God some fruit of repentance. Do not compel me, an unworthy man, in any way to undertake such a burden. But if you will not now grant my request, at least give me a reprieve until morning, so that I may ascertain the Lord’s will concerning this matter.

When the bishop, together with the clergy and choir of monks, received this written answer, he perceived that some stratagem was turning in Arnulf’s mind. Yet they granted the reprieve and stationed guards around the cell lest he should flee by night [Col. 1384C]. But Arnulf, passing the night awake amid deep groans and frequent sighs, perceived that the guards had sunk into welcome sleep. He climbed a ladder and escaped over the wall; wandering in flight and not knowing where to flee, he eventually came to a certain village below the hill of Laon. Entering the lodging of a poor man, he rested there.

When supper-time came, water was lacking. Unbidden, he took up a pitcher, went to the well, drew water, brought it into the house, served everyone, and waited upon everyone—yet remained wholly silent.

## CHAPTER X

Toward evening the man returned from the city of Soissons, and while eating supper he began to relate what he had learned from common report [Col. 1384D]:

> A great rumor and great commotion have stirred the people over the departure of a certain servant of God, who, they say, has fled lest he become abbot of St. Medard. And behold, many envoys are being sent throughout the regions to seek the holy man through woods and mountains, with an edict issued that no one is to be refreshed until the man of God, who must be brought back, is found.

Hearing this report, the venerable hero, earnestly striving by every means to avoid the hands of those seeking him, rose from his bed in the first hour of the night and went to the church of that village. There, outside the door, prostrate on the ground, he cried to the Lord, with great weeping [Col. 1385A] entreating the Majesty that the burden of governance, for which he felt himself wholly unworthy, might by no means be laid upon him.

After praying thus much and long, when he believed that his prayers had been heard by the Lord, he resolved to flee into remoter wilderness. And suddenly a great wolf came and began to go with him. Believing that the wolf’s companionship would more readily bring him to trackless places, Arnulf allowed it to go ahead and tried to follow close behind. Thus, with the wolf as guide—or rather with God as author—he returned by night to Soissons. Sitting above a slope adjoining the city, he recognized where he was when the sun rose.

Then he was distressed in spirit and consumed with grief. Looking from afar, he immediately saw a pit in a rock where stones were being squared, and descended into it to hide. But when peasants and stonecutters arrived and saw [Col. 1385B] a man in humble clothing and without speech, they reported it to the city. What joy and celebration at once arose in the city, we believe impossible for any human being to describe. Young men and virgins, old men with the young, praised the Lord’s name because He had not deprived them of the discovery of their desired father. Monks went out with clerics, nobles with those from the suburbs; and they drew their bound fugitive to the church of blessed Medard, imposing upon him against his will the place and office of abbot.

At last, scarcely opening his mouth, he said: “Truly, unless I feared to resist divine promptings, I would wholly refuse what you impose.” Thus set over the monastery, he became an excellent restorer of holy order. He labored to correct what was wrong, root out vices utterly, [Col. 1385C] continually reform the brethren’s conduct by gentle speech and a leading example, and almost entirely destroy whatever opposed the sacred Rule.

Wonderful to say, with what swiftness the state of the whole monastery returned to the pattern of its former dignity! The church’s ornaments were restored; cloistered order was renewed; whatever was useful was repaired; whatever was useless was dispersed. All the nobility in those places rejoiced that the renowned and royal foundation would not long lack the observances of its former honor. The country too exulted because that great senator of heaven, the eminent martyr Sebastian, resting there with many others, was no longer deprived of the offices of praise due to him.

[Note: [Col. 1385D] We have given in its proper place the history of the translation of St. Sebastian to the monastery of St. Medard: fourth century, part I, p. 383.]

## CHAPTER XI

But since the order of the narrative has reached the point of showing that he was father of the monastery, it is fitting that we remember the labors and fatigues he endured in governing it, so that this also may offer most useful instruction to rulers. For Godfrey of Florennes, a powerful and strong man, and the prouder in proportion as he was more powerful, fearing neither man nor God, had for many years withheld from the use of the brethren of blessed Medard a great estate called Hancenias [Note: [Col. 1386D] There still exists at this place, commonly called Hensiennes, a provostship in honor of St. George, subject to the monastery of St. Medard.], situated in the district of the Sambre, and had appropriated it to the advantage of his own pride. Since his harsh power terrified everyone, none of the bishops dared confront him to his face; and, seeing [Col. 1386A] his intolerable wickedness, they did not dare proceed canonically against him in any way.

Therefore the united body of the brethren entreated the servant of Christ Arnulf, their abbot, for charity’s sake to undertake the labor of meeting that powerful man and, by coercive admonition, to compel him to restore the property he had taken from the church. The blessed man, burning with zeal for God’s house, assented to the brethren’s wishes and ordered the necessities for the journey to be prepared, among them an ass capable of carrying him.

Although he avoided worldly glory with all his strength, as one who had founded his whole mind in Christ’s love, the weak minds of certain of his retainers, caring little for the things of God, desired him to proceed in pomp and travel in luxury. Following the example of many abbots of France, they wished him [Col. 1386B] to ride ambitiously and live luxuriously, considering the humility practiced by the man of God a disgrace. Finally, they secretly maimed the little ass which he had chosen to ride, so that, with the ass removed, he would begin to use the mount of a foaming horse. They told the servant of God to order a riding-horse sought which should carry him.

Hearing this, Christ’s servant, abhorring horseback riding because of the firmness of his settled humility, went with a few disciples to the stable where the sick ass lay. Laying his hand upon the injury, he began to speak in a gentle voice and with still gentler affection:

> Almighty God well knows with what intention I desire to undertake the journey at hand. I seek to make this journey not in the manner of self-display, but by the obligation of divine office and the concern of brotherly usefulness. And because, since laying aside the warfare of the world, I have resolved never to sit upon a horse’s back—not from vanity, but in imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ—now, if it pleases Him that I should go, may it please Him that the shin or foot of this little ass be healed, so that, borne in a humble conveyance, I may gladly fulfill His service and the Church’s work.

Having spoken thus, he made the sign of the holy cross over it and departed. But the ass was immediately restored; shaking itself, it rose, and, wholly healed and cheerful, both received and completed the transport of God’s servant.

When Arnulf came before the aforesaid exceedingly arrogant rich man Godfrey, it is wonderful to say with what kindness Godfrey received him and with what ready humility he obeyed him. For as soon as Arnulf addressed him, his arrogance immediately subsided; immediately [Col. 1386D] that fierce stiff-neckedness collapsed; and at once the church’s former inheritance was restored. He who had hitherto been a ravager of churches became henceforth their devout protector.

## CHAPTER XII

After he had spent some days with Godfrey, Arnulf resolved to inspect the recovered estates with the brethren. While he was there and had greatly delighted the tenants by his presence, a noblewoman named Hesplendis came to him, honorable among her people in possessions and conduct. She presented to the man of God a plea on behalf of a servant, as the Gospel centurion had done [Col. 1387A]:

> A faithful steward and servant of my household is grievously tormented by monthly attacks. I ask that your prayer may be sent for him, so that, through God’s mercy, he may deserve to be healed.

Then he blessed a morsel of the bread from which he himself ate and ordered it given to the honorable woman, saying: “As soon as you return home, make him eat some of this bread before any other food; and, by God’s command, the suffering by which he is tormented will cease.”

She did as she was instructed. But the malignant invader did not allow him to touch any of that bread. He feared to touch it as though it were a fire, until compelled by prolonged hunger to eat of it; and immediately he received the freedom of perfect health.

## CHAPTER XIII

On the aforesaid estate there lived a man who, because of the excessive severity of an illness, had completely lost the ability to eat bread. Leading a miserable life on foul food, he wasted away daily in suffering. He made this request to the aforementioned woman:

> I beg you, my lady, when you approach the man of God, endeavor to tell him that a sure vision has frequently been brought to me: if I should deserve to receive some of the bread that sustains him, I shall immediately regain the ability to eat bread. Entreat his kindness to grant me this mercy and send me the desired blessing of his bread.

When the reverend man heard this from the woman’s report, he was immediately moved by abundant compassion. He poured forth tearful prayers to the divine goodness; and at the hour of his meal he blessed more abundantly a portion of the bread set especially before him, and assigned a monk to carry it through the aforesaid woman to the sick man [Col. 1387C]. As soon as the sick man put that bread to his lips, not only did the power of eating return, but an appetite for devouring immediately followed, so that his bodily strength, seemingly worn away by the hunger of a long time, was restored day by day.

## CHAPTER XIV

Thereafter he was pleased to visit another monastic estate, called Junciredium [Note: [Col. 1387D] Perhaps Dunciredium should be read. Here, it seems, the town called Donchery is indicated, situated in the diocese of Rheims, not far from the city of Sedan, where there still exists a distinguished provostship of the monastery of St. Medard.], situated wholly upon the Meuse. While he remained there for a few days, a woman living on the estate, blind now for ten years, approached the monks who were companions on his journey and said:

> Many days ago, as I lamented my affliction, a vision appeared to me in sleep, most certainly promising [Col. 1387D] that, if this man of God should deign to lend me water in which he had washed his hands, to bathe my eyes, the Lord would immediately restore by his merits the light of my eyes, long lost. Therefore I beg you, when he washes his hands, reserve for me the water by which I may be stripped of the darkness of long blindness.

Accordingly, the first time after this that the servant of God washed his hands, they gave the water to the blind woman. At once, applying it to her eyes and receiving sight were one and the same act. But when the man of God learned of this, he did not take it calmly; rather, he hastened his journey and departed quickly [Col. 1388A], clearly taking care lest popular applause for so great a sign should rebound upon him.

## CHAPTER XV

In the monastery of St. Medard there was a crypt in the eastern part, whose annual feast of dedication was solemnly celebrated every year. For the banquet of that day, the ancient refinement of the place, as they said, required the eating of turbot. The new abbot, however, did not know this custom until the festival itself, now close at hand, suddenly pressed this matter upon the abbot, who had not considered it and was occupied with other concerns.

For, when the first hour of the day had been chanted, the brethren assembled in chapter and asked their cellarer whether the turbot due for the day was ready. When he denied it and rather wondered at their words, they began to be angry [Col. 1388B] and insist contentiously that they would not celebrate the solemnity of the Mass unless a turbot were brought into their kitchen. Hearing this, some of the elders went to the abbot, who suspected no such thing, and disclosed the brethren’s decision.

The man, wise in every respect, heard this childish sentiment of the brethren. After reflecting in silence for a little, he sent forth the voice of his heart to Christ and at length answered:

> If we had known this custom long ago, we could have sought that fish in good time. But since we have learned of it suddenly, God’s omnipotence is able to grant this very thing, so that we may remove scandal from the brethren and the holy celebration may be completed cheerfully. Let the servant go at once with money to the bridge of the Aisne; finding a turbot, let him buy it quickly and present it to the brethren’s kitchen to be prepared.

Turning to the elders [Col. 1388C], he said: “Go, beloved ones, and tell the brethren that the turbot will not be lacking; let them joyfully celebrate the Lord’s solemnities. But tell them this also: whether I live or die, let them know that it is determined that from today for twenty years they shall not have dishes of turbot upon this day.”

Having spoken thus, a turbot, unexpectedly found in accordance with his word, was bought and brought in, still flapping, for preparation for the brethren’s table; and the solemnities of the dedication were celebrated more cheerfully than usual. The brethren who were present at this event testified under invocation of the divine name that, from that time onward for twenty years, such a fish could not be found for the same solemnity. It is very wonderful that the spirit of truth was so immediately present to him, and that whatever he uttered with his mouth was always established by the constancy of truth [Col. 1388D].

## CHAPTER XVI

Indeed, since among mortals nothing wholly blessed remains firm in every respect, at that time there was in the same monastery a certain man named Odo, an usurper of respectability and pretender to virtue. He greatly envied Arnulf, the servant of God and abbot, and judged himself worthier and more useful for the governance of the place. He also continually turned over in his mind by what pretext he might remove Christ’s servant from the office of governance which he had undertaken [Col. 1389A].

While engaged in external affairs, Odo sought through intermediaries, whom he blinded with frequent gifts, to persuade Philip, king of the Franks, that when he was setting out somewhere against an enemy, he should order the abbot of St. Medard to accompany him. The king consented to Odo’s counsel; and, when he had set his army in motion, he sent envoys to instruct Lord Arnulf to depart with him on campaign with an armed troop.

Arnulf was astonished at this and devoutly answered the king’s messengers:

> It is certain that I, a sinner, was once defiled by the deeds of military life; it is known that, from fear of the Lord, I abandoned military service and sought the fellowship of monks. We read the Lord saying: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 24). And shall I, miserable man that I am, who for God’s sake rejected military service, again be surrounded [Col. 1389B] by soldiers? Shall I again bear arms? A great crime! The Psalm rightly says of me and of men like me: “I cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72). For I, who thought myself raised to the care of an abbey, behold, am compelled to fall into the pit of apostasy. I would certainly have preferred never to receive this name and office of abbot than, under the pretext of this dignity, to serve the world so shamefully.

When Philip learned this, he again sent envoys to say that it had been an ancient custom for the abbey’s soldiers, led by their abbot, to serve in the royal expedition. Either Arnulf must act according to the ancient custom, or make way for the king’s command to be carried out.

Arnulf, taking this opportunity, promptly obeyed the king’s command and gladly withdrew into the corner of his enclosure. He accounted the height of so great an honor as nothing, provided that he might preserve the Savior’s word, desiring to exert himself far better and far more fervently in the service of the divine Majesty [Col. 1389C].

But all the monks, greatly distressed by this act, came together and, as though besieging Arnulf with excessive lamentation, thus assailed him with sorrowful devotion:

> O beloved Father! What did you intend to do? To abandon so thoughtlessly the flock committed to you? To expose Christ’s sheep entrusted to you to wolves, and again hand over to ravagers the holy house which you governed so honorably? If it was burdensome for you to join the king’s army, you might have remained quietly in your own place; we, with our soldiers, would have obeyed the king’s command. Behold, Pontius, once our ravager, laden with the purses of our house, will again become its purchaser; and, having received authority [Col. 1389D], he will become an even harsher despoiler. Have mercy, we beg, on your sons; have mercy on your suppliants; do not cast us off, who rejoice to be subject to your commands. We admonish you by the martyrdom of Sebastian, by the confession of Medard, by the papacy of Gregory, and by the multitude of saints whose relics and memorials, as you know, are present in this place.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] The bodies of these saints remain in the monastery of St. Medard; the rest were scattered by Calvinist heretics.]

## CHAPTER XVII

Hearing these words, Arnulf was torn by conflicting feelings. Weeping most abundantly, he answered them:

> O sweetest brethren, I beg you, do not so greatly impute to me the desolation of our community or place. Rather, carefully understand that one dwells among you and has come forth from among you who is attempting to bring about all this evil. But now, thanks be to God, I have been stripped of the abbacy—which my soul had long desired, for it was more a burden than an honor to me—I exhort your united body never to seek to have me drawn again into presiding over you. If you wish to follow my counsel, I am ready to offer you good and useful advice. Summon your bishop and all the prelates of the churches of the city; quickly elect a father acceptable to God and necessary for your affairs.

The monks replied: “We would most gladly do this, but our election would immediately be annulled by the oppression of the greedy king. Therefore we have judged it better that our election should rest in your hand; and whomever we see elected by you, we will faithfully obey. For whoever you elect, we believe that the king’s madness will not resist him.”

Then, all the prelates of the churches having been summoned and counsel having been taken together, a man of great learning and outstanding piety named Gerald was elected abbot.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] You have his Life below under the year 1095; see there, in the preliminary observations, what is to be thought concerning this election of Gerald.]

Not long after he had been installed, that aforementioned Pontius, enemy of all piety, suddenly rushed in, bringing with him Bertha, queen of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1390D] Other manuscripts read Bertrada, but our reading is better, as appears from the following note.], so that by royal force she might expel Gerald and unlawfully introduce Pontius himself into the prelateship of the holy place.

When he learned this, the servant of Christ Arnulf came out of his cell and approached the enraged queen. In gentle speech he humbly begged her that, [Col. 1390C] although she was accounted a queen, she should nevertheless remember the condition of womanhood and the divine judgments; that she should fear to oppose ecclesiastical laws and modestly restrain herself from injury to so great a man.

When, swollen with royal pride, she refused to listen to these warnings, the servant of God said to her prophetically:

> O queen, if you please, believe Brother Arnulf—or rather, believe the Holy Spirit: if you violently expel Lord Abbot Gerald from this place, then by God’s vengeance you also, before the day of your death, will be driven from sovereignty over the whole kingdom, and will die deprived of the kingdom, in misery and contempt.

This prophecy of the man of God was made clearer than daylight. For it is known to all that the same queen, after some years, irreparably incurred the king’s displeasure, on account of which she was rejected from participation in the whole kingdom, removed in disgrace to the district of Ponthieu [Col. 1390D], detained there in prolonged misfortune, and died and was buried in the manner of a commoner.

[Note: [Col. 1390D] The event proved the truth of this prophecy: Philip, bringing in Bertrada, wife of Fulk, count of Anjou, expelled Bertha.]

Gerald, expelled by her, gave place to wrath and withdrew into Aquitaine. There he was graciously received by the duke of that land and founded the distinguished monastery of La Sauve-Majeure, where he worthily served God and rested in the Lord with a blessed end. Both his life and his death shone with signs of virtues and the glory of miracles.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 1391A]

At last Arnulf, withdrawn into his beloved enclosure, as though he were beginning only then, steadily mortified himself with daily fasts, afflicted himself with vigils, gave himself continually to prayer, and exerted all his strength in divine contemplation. Living thus and daily increasing in such exercises of virtue, he obtained great grace from the Lord and acquired glorious renown in the land of France. So great was this renown that all the nobility of the kingdom rejoiced to receive his blessings, and persons of every rank eagerly sought conversation with him, asking counsel both concerning the peace of the Church and the salvation of souls. Whoever could hear even a word from his lips believed himself exceedingly fortunate.

Thus whatever he said [Col. 1391B] seemed healthful and pleasing to every hearer, seasoned with spiritual salt, so that it was plainly evident that he was inwardly inspired by the presence of the Holy Spirit. The fame of his holiness spread through every province and summoned to speak with him persons of every age and rank from all directions. But we judge it fitting now to begin recounting what signs or gifts of prophecy the Lord bestowed upon him.

## CHAPTER XIX

In these days his sister’s husband, named Trudbert, came to him. After they had conversed concerning the salvation of the soul, Arnulf asked him: “Our former fellow-soldier and companion Israel—do you think he lives, or how do you believe he fares?”

Trudbert replied: “He is safe and well, and prospers in everything.”

Then the man of God, filled with a prophetic spirit, said [Col. 1391C]:

> It is not at all as you say. Israel, whom you report safe and well, is dead in body and spirit. Yesterday he seized much plunder, and while returning home with it, he reclined upon a bench by the fire in his concubine’s lap. There, about evening, he underwent sudden death and utterly lost both this life and eternal life. O dreadful funeral rites! O terrible exacters! His unhappy soul, accompanied by the curses of so many widows and orphans and tormented by so many pains, was dragged to eternal fire.

Hearing this, the aforementioned man was exceedingly terrified; and when he returned home, he found every part of Israel’s story to have occurred as the man of God Arnulf had announced.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 1391D]

On another occasion a sister of Arnulf’s, named Adsela, came to see him. While she sat with certain others before the window of his cell, discussing how the life of the soul could be preserved amid so many storms of the world, at the noon hour a servant came carrying fish cooked by frying; for it was a most celebrated feast day, and he set it before Arnulf at the window. In order wholly to repel from himself the spirit of vanity and the impulse toward self-display, Arnulf used to taste a little of the cloister’s food on Sundays and principal feast days, lest he seem to despise the brethren’s tables.

In this matter he had guides and counsellors, men endowed with the highest discernment: Gregory VII, pope of Rome [Col. 1392A]; the venerable Hugh, abbot of Cluny, leader in divine instruction and learned teacher; and Gerald, most holy abbot of La Sauve-Majeure. By letters frequently sent to him, they instructed him not to think more highly than he ought, nor, under the appearance of virtues, to exceed the measure approved by the Fathers.

When the fish had thus been placed before him, his sister said: “Now, holy brother, I must leave you, for it is time and food has been set before you, that you may eat something.”

The man of God replied: “No, dear sister; I shall not permit you to leave because of this food, since this fish, brought to me in this manner, must not be eaten. It is infected with the plague of poison, prepared for us by the hostile enemy, so that it might bring about my death. But thanks be to God, thanks be [Col. 1392B] to the Holy Spirit, who by His prompting disclosed to our heart that, by taking the poison, we should give joy to the enemy.”

[Note: [Col. 1391] Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 8, relates a similar miracle concerning the blessed father Benedict.]

Then he raised his voice and called for the raven to come, which he customarily fed at the window with gathered crumbs. Immediately the raven came. The servant of God commanded it: “In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, take this fish in your beak and cast it into such a place that it can never be found by a human being.”

The raven hesitated for a little, but at last took it in its beak, lifted it, and departed. Having cast it away, it returned and received its accustomed food from its feeder’s hand. Arnulf then forbade his sister and all who were present to disclose this to anyone during his lifetime.

## CHAPTER XXI

This same woman had committed her young son to a certain powerful man so that he might receive arms from him. The servant of God asked her [Col. 1392C]: “Where is your son, and how does he fare?”

She replied: “I sent him safe and sound to a powerful kinsman of ours, that he might live with him until he becomes a knight.”

Then the man of God said:

> At the beginning of the recently passed Lent you performed a vain omen—indeed, a wicked divination—concerning him: that he might, as it were, be unable to die if his shoe, thrown upward, flew over a beam. The sin remains with you, and your son’s life has departed. For he fell ill in that place and died and was buried on such-and-such a day, at such-and-such an hour of the day. Therefore I strongly exhort your charity to do penance and make satisfaction according to the ordinances of the Catholic Church, lest your last day overtake you bound by so grievous a beloved attachment. For those who do such things wholly resist the Holy Spirit and are proved to injure sacred Christianity.

Then she departed, amazed beyond belief and greatly terrified. Before she returned home, a messenger met her with news of her son’s death, reporting that he had died and been buried in that place on that day and at that hour, just as the man of God Arnulf had foretold through the Spirit’s revelation [Col. 1392D].

Before the door of his cell he had a space like a small garden, where he worked beds with his own hands and avoided idleness and sloth. He also had certain little trees; whenever they bore fruit, sick persons who tasted of them by his command were immediately raised from their illnesses. He frequently sent, at the request of persons lying farther away, bread or wine seasoned with his blessing; when they tasted it, they at once became better [Col. 1393A].

## CHAPTER XXII

The annual celebration of the solemn martyrdom of the glorious deacon Lawrence was being festively observed, as was fitting. A multitude of people had filled from every side the fields and open spaces around the monastery of blessed Medard, when a woman whose son had been mute from birth for thirteen years burst in at the window of the servant of God’s cell. With heavy sorrow she began to entreat the holy man to have mercy on her son:

> Servant of God, do not reject my prayers; do not disdain to attend to my calamities. Behold, the almighty Lord took away my only husband and left me my only son, by whose help I might be sustained; and behold, he is mute and deaf, unable to hear a word or give anyone an answer.

At this Christ’s servant, pierced by compassion and moved to mercy, poured forth tears and, from the sweetness of charity, directed an earnest prayer to the Lord. By signs and gestures he called the mute boy to himself. Having brought him before the window, he signed him with the sign of the holy cross, invoking the divine name; he impressed the sign of the life-giving cross upon his lips, touched his tongue with his fingers, and asked him: “What is your name?”

Immediately his speech was released, and he said clearly and distinctly: “John.” Having spoken this, he thereafter formed words without impediment and enjoyed the full gift of speech.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 1393C]

A certain young man, seized by a most violent invasion of demons and bound with fetters and chains, could not be subdued; rather, he tore with his teeth all whom he might touch. At last, overcome and restrained somehow by many persons, he was dragged with great force to the church of Saint Medard, and the man of God was informed about him. Taking pity on the wretched captive, he ordered him to be brought to him. When he had been dragged near, as soon as the servant of God could see him, he made the sign of the cross and said to those dragging him: “Release him.” They said: “Lord, we do not dare release him at all, lest perhaps he rise against us and kill us.” And the man of God said: “I have already told you—release him, fearing nothing.” [Col. 1393D]

Then, with the greatest reluctance, putting their hands to him, they began to release him. Once released, he immediately fell face-down upon the ground and worshipped. For after he had seen the servant of Christ and been signed by him, the whole hostile power within him had been lulled and fallen still. The man of the Lord ordered him to rise from the ground and come near the window of the cell. As he stood nearby, the servant of Christ began to question him:

“Tell me, son: when and how did this hostile affliction which held you come upon you?”

He narrated what had happened, saying:

“My dearest father, I had a kinsman, a friend related to me by blood, very handsome in appearance and strong in body. Some insignificant men from a certain little village had grievously offended him, so that my kinsman, gathering bands of companions and friends, attempted to attack that same village, intending, after breaking into it and slaughtering its inhabitants, cruelly to avenge the injury done to him. But because the village was surrounded on every side by woodland and enclosed by a rising rampart, the men found there also resisted bravely. My aforesaid kinsman obtained none of what he wished; rather, he was wounded by a spear, his entrails laid open, and he died there immediately.

“I, wretched man, took hold of the dead body and placed his ankles upon each of my shoulders; thus dragging him, I was bringing him through the middle of the forest away from the place of slaughter. It was then a dark night, and behold, countless throngs of evil spirits stood round me before and behind, howling and hissing, and at times laughing loudly. Then dreadful fear and trembling seized me, and the hostile power shook me to my very marrow. Not knowing what to do, I finally threw the corpse that I was dragging into some place or other—I do not know where. Immediately, having lost my senses and with my mind altered, I became such as your Blessedness saw.”

Then the servant of the Lord said to him: “Behold, thanks be to God: you have confessed wisely. It remains for you to appease God by penance, because you wished to take part in so great a crime.”

He said: “For this evil, and for all the offenses by which I have offended God, I wish, holy Father, to offer penance worthy of God and henceforth, as far as I can, to refrain from every evil.”

Thus the servant of Christ, having imposed a measure of penance, sent him back to his own home sound and unharmed, vigorous in a right mind, cleansed not only of the demonic legion but also of an inborn cruelty for drinking human blood. For had he not been hindered in this manner, he would have killed all the inhabitants of the village in vengeance for his slain friend. [Col. 1394A–C]

## CHAPTER XXIV

At the same time, a cruel report had filled the city of Soissons, its suburbs, and the neighboring villages, spread by certain rumor-mongers, concerning a hostile invasion of barbarians. Some said that the Danish people, emerging from their own land, were soon to occupy and destroy all France and would spare neither old men nor children nor churches in any way. This seemed credible because the histories of various chronicles reported that the Danes had often committed similar deeds.

This disastrous rumor grew so strong that Theobald, bishop of Soissons, earnestly sought the counsel of the man of God Arnulf—as, plainly, one initiated into divine mysteries—and anxiously begged him to inquire of God’s mercy whether this would indeed happen soon. But the servant of the Lord, as soon as he heard the report, recognized it as wholly empty and groundless. Yet, lest he be accused of rash levity, he asked for a delay until the next day, so that in the deep silence of the night he might pray more abundantly to the heavenly Majesty for some clear sign concerning this matter to be revealed to him.

Arnulf, spending the time in psalms, covered with ashes and clothed in haircloth, sent prayers to Christ, poured out a river of tears upon the ground, and implored the Majesty to reveal the truth of this secret. At the following dawn the bishop anxiously returned to this present spiritual ark of the covenant and asked for a heavenly oracle regarding what had been entrusted to him the day before. The servant of Christ, strengthening him with consolation received from God, said: “Do not fear, reverend bishop; for as long as you or I bear a mortal body, the Danish nation, or any other barbarian people, shall not lay waste the kingdom of France.” [Col. 1394D–1395A]

Theobald, wealthy shepherd and bishop of the people of Soissons,  
heard the report, flying abroad through the fickleness of the crowd,  
that the Danish people, laying waste every region,  
would seek to destroy the chiefs whom France possesses,  
and thus restrain the arms of French men.

What was heard repeatedly, or repeatedly repeated,  
shook the peoples and made the mighty grow pale.  
Moved by this popular murmur, the bishop,  
consults Arnulf, sustained by the divine Spirit,  
earnestly begging him to ask Christ to reveal  
whether it will come to pass, or whether the kingdom will fall.

Arnulf, God’s initiate into the mysteries, seeks the quiet of the night.  
He prostrates himself upon the ground and lets streams of tears fall,  
praying concerning this matter: “Almighty God, have mercy;  
spare your own; have mercy on the guilty, sole hope of the world,  
steadfast, unconquered, fashioned after the image of none;  
before whom kings bend and the heavens revolve;  
by the death of the Son, who by life broke the abyss:  
let not your power of mercy hand us over to unspeakable enemies.

“Let the vain not say that France serves an empty god;  
let the wretched not mock: ‘This God cannot show mercy.’  
Behold the fierce Danes, as the popular report declares.  
Protect now the people who rightly acknowledge you as Lord.  
Those who seek to destroy all things rise against your people—  
the French nation, given over to you and especially serving you,  
full of companies of monks,  
a people devoted to holy churches,  
who glorify you and always honor your saints.

“Remember them; be the protector of your servants.  
Let not the enemy behold deaths among them; let your people beware death.  
Through the Son, almighty together with you,  
and through the Holy Spirit, through whom your glory is established.”

While he was thus intent, a heavenly messenger stood by,  
shining like the dawn and clothed in splendid raiment,  
saying: “Servant of God, end these tears.  
For God Christ, moved by the voice of your tears,  
has determined to grant the prayer you have made.

“Know therefore with certainty that the hostile people  
shall not come into this kingdom during the time that you live;  
and after your end, for a long time  
France shall remain secure [or: securely], overcoming hostile claims.  
Peace be with you, servant of God; may Christ’s glory be with you.”

Then the servant of the Lord raised his face from the pavement  
and gave thanks to the Lord for such a revelation.

In the morning the bishop returned, very anxious, seeking hidden things,  
and tremblingly inquired what the decree of heaven might be.  
The servant of the Lord comforted him with gentle speech, saying:

“Do not fear, venerable father and bishop;  
for until we both leave the life of this world,  
France shall reign; no barbarian shall violate her.  
God taught me this; the judgment of heaven has ordained it.  
May his unconquered kingdom now be blessed.”

At this the bishop rejoiced, applauding with happy heart;  
he offered the gifts and accumulated those which he had vowed. [Col. 1395A–1396A]

## CHAPTER XXV

Christ was making his Church fruitful with gifts of grace. Inflamed by these, very many noble and illustrious men abandoned the empty prosperity of the world and, mortifying themselves, strove to acquire divine nobility. Among them, like a golden star, was the glorious count of Amiens and Vermandois, the most handsome Simon, son of Count Ralph. [Note: [Col. 1395D] See above, under the year 1082, the Life of this Simon.] Inflamed by divine love, he cast aside the honor and power of the countship, left cities and very wealthy castles, left a most beautiful bride, and, burning to follow Christ, emerged naked from such great riches. Leaving the entire French people, over whom he had ruled among thousands of servants, he made his way to Italy, especially in order to have the opportunity to see and pray before the most sacred presence of the glorious apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1396B]

As, divinely inspired, he frequently visited their holy memorials with devout devotion, the devotion of so great a man became known to Pope Gregory VII. Finally, after serving God [variant: “in diverse ways”] for a few years in simplicity and humility of heart, in continual bodily contrition, and stretching himself manfully in the exercise of holy virtues, he was, by God’s favor, perfected in a short time. Since his soul was pleasing to God, it was led forth from the prison of the world, to shine among the living stones in the diadem of heaven.

At that same hour when, released from the flesh, he deserved to pass into blessed rest, Saint Arnulf, shut up in his cell, was raised in ecstasy of mind and, by God’s gift, saw all that was taking place concerning the venerable man Simon, once a count and now a monk. When he had returned to himself after the vision, he hastened to summon the brothers, in order to tell them of the grace of so great a vision.

The brothers came, and he announced to them: “Go quickly, brothers, and tell the abbot and the brethren that Lord Simon, once count of Vermandois, has departed this life today. Let the abbot order the office for the departure of so great a man to be celebrated without delay.”

They went to the abbot and reported what they had heard. He was astonished and wondered all the more. Rising, he hurried to the recluse and inquired, testing him, who had informed him—or, according to another manuscript, what he had eaten. [Note: [Col. 1396D] Another manuscript reads: “what he had eaten.”]

Then the man of God said: “If I had previously told you anything false or uncertain, it would be right for you to believe us with greater difficulty. But since you have not yet found falsehood in my words, why are you so obstinate in believing that you think me almost mad concerning matters unknown? Mark the day; mark the hour; and you will find that it is, or has been, as has been revealed to me.”

Then the abbot and the community of brothers hurried into the church. The bells were rung, the psalms were sung, and the office of the dead was celebrated in its order. Meanwhile their minds were in suspense, wondering whether they were being deceived and would be mocked. But behold: before a month of days had passed, a messenger flew in, saying that Lord Simon had died on that day and at that same hour at which it had been revealed to Arnulf, the man of God. [Col. 1396C–D]

## CHAPTER XXVI

Not far from the city of Soissons there lived a nobleman, occupied in the pursuits of knighthood, named Guy. [Note: [Col. 1397D] Dormasius, *History of Soissons*, book V, chapter 15, considers this Guy to have been lord of the town of Châtillon-sur-Marne, whose wife Ermengard was the sister of Alberic, count of Coucy; they too are discussed here.] He had a wife devoted to piety, named Ermengard. Both flourished in the abundance of riches and abounded in works of mercy.

At a certain time Guy lay ill, oppressed by a severe sickness; having lost the ability to sleep or eat, he was despaired of by his household and mourned by his friends as though already dead. About these same days his wife was distressed by the pain and anxiety of an imminent childbirth. Worn down by a double fear, she dreaded her own death on the one hand and her husband’s on the other. Entangled in such torments, she believed that she had one remedy: to commend her own plight and her husband’s to the prayers of Saint Arnulf.

Sending a messenger, a faithful household cleric, she tearfully laid before him the danger both of herself and of her husband. The servant of Christ, as he was by God’s gift greatly foreknowing of future events, first prayed and then sent word to the woman:

“Go, brother, and carefully and quickly carry this message to our sweetest sister. Two grave distresses hang over her; by God’s favor she will overcome them with a good outcome. But a third distress is impending, of which she herself is unaware; it will therefore be more grievous, because it is less recoverable. Her husband, though he is now ill, will later recover and be granted lasting health. She herself also shall undoubtedly be saved from the danger of childbirth and, during this night, before the signal for the nocturnal office is heard, will bear a son in whom she will rejoice.

“But the third anxiety, which she does not now consider and which will torment her more persistently, is this: her brother Alberic, lord of Coucy, has been so ruined through the counsel of his wife Aveline that tomorrow he will be seized in his bed by his enemies and, once captured, carried off. When carried off, he will be bound; once bound, he will be subjected to harsh tortures and compelled to ransom himself. In ransoming his life, already near death, he will spend treasures; moreover, he shall neither see nor recover his castle. But let our sister send quickly and warn him both of his wife’s malice and of the enemies’ snares now impending.”

The messenger left him and quickly returned to the lady, reporting the holy man’s words. The mind of the noblewoman conceived joy mingled with fear. She sent a hasty messenger to her brother and expressly informed him what his wife had contrived and what his enemies, led by his wife, were plotting. Alberic believed his sister, but gave more credence to his wife, who denied these things. He made no preparations, fortified neither his tower nor his castle or town; and therefore, while still resting at dawn, he was attacked, captured, dragged away, bound, and led off, and was stripped forever of his dwelling and lordship of Coucy. [Col. 1397A–D]

## CHAPTERS XXVII–XXVIII

That same night, Guy’s wife, Alberic’s sister, being in labor, bore a son before the bell summoning the nocturnal assembly was rung in the church of Saint Medard. [Col. 1398A] But at the following dawn, when they examined the child more carefully, they discovered that he had been born without eyes. The places of the eyes were covered with skin and flesh, like the forehead or the cheek. What then were the midwives to do? Overwhelmed by excessive anguish, they wept and murmured in sorrow; and they labored by every means to prevent the mother, exhausted by childbirth, from learning of her son’s blindness.

Thus six days passed, and the mother did not know of the child’s blindness, until the time came when the child was to be taken to church for baptism. Then a greater agitation seized the maidservants, and they devised every possible means to prevent the blindness, so long concealed, from becoming known publicly. They approached the mother, still ill from her recent childbirth, and persuaded her to send the son first to Arnulf, the holy man of God, before he was brought to baptism. The mother favored the servants’ advice and, sending a messenger to the man of God, begged that he would deem her worthy for the little child to be touched and blessed by his hands.

The holy man replied: “It is truly necessary that we see the infant; therefore let him be brought quickly. Just as the mother has been saved from the distress and pain of childbirth by God’s great gift, so the merciful Lord will deign to save the imperfect son in his wholeness.”

These words showed that the servant of God already knew of the infant’s infirmity.

Accordingly, the servant of Christ brought the infant who had been brought to him inside the window, laid him upon a little bed of ashes, and himself prostrated upon the pavement, devoting himself to prayer. When the prayer was ended, he gathered the infant into his lap and anointed the places of the eyes with the saliva of his mouth. Immediately, by divine gift, the eyes opened, and new light entered the new little eyes.

When the child was brought back to his mother, there was immense rejoicing. Only then did the mother learn that she had borne a blind child, when she learned that through Christ’s servant her son had received new eyes. [Note: [Col. 1398D] This child, named Peter, later became archdeacon of the Church of Soissons; Lisiard speaks of him below in the preface to book III.] [Col. 1398B–C]

## CHAPTER XXIX

It also seems fitting and useful to relate that by which it may be known how subtle a prerogative of foreknowledge the holy man of the Lord Arnulf is found to have possessed.

The aforesaid nobles had earlier begotten a daughter of beautiful countenance. By this time she had reached marriageable age, and her parents had betrothed her to a certain knight, not inferior in wealth or birth. But she, as is the way of girlish inconstancy, loved another man, inferior in wealth and lineage, more dearly. She rejected the bridegroom chosen for her by her parents, affirming with many oaths that she would kill herself unless she obtained the embraces she desired.

Afflicted by the misfortune of this situation, the girl’s parents consulted Arnulf, the man of God, asking whether perhaps the Lord might deign to disclose to his mind what course they ought rather to take in such a conflict. The man of the Lord, after briefly hearing the parents’ complaints, gave a timely and salutary response:

“Canonical authority forbids that a girl be joined to one whom she never wishes to marry. Therefore I lay this command upon you: give the girl to the man she herself loves, lest you compel her to some improper act. But it is known to God, and shown to us on account of the merit of your piety, that after a short time you shall see your daughter eagerly seek the bridegroom from whose marriage she now so gladly desires to withdraw. Yield to her will now, and it will happen that she returns to your honorable purpose.”

Trusting his words greatly, they granted their daughter the marriage she desired and allowed her to enjoy union with the man she loved. But this man, married to the girl, was striving to appear a famous knight. As he was carried too eagerly into battle in order to make a name for himself, he was suddenly killed by armed men, and from a new bride made a very new widow all too quickly.

Thus, according to the word of the man of God, the girl returned to love for that bridegroom whom her parents had first chosen. Joined to him, she bore with equanimity the loss of her former husband. Although this may seem foreign to the order of our narrative, it should be heard because it displays in Saint Arnulf a special foretoken of prophetic power. [Col. 1398D–1399B]

## CHAPTER XXX

Philip, king of the Franks, having for several years already been joined in marriage, saw that his queen remained barren. He repeatedly begged Saint Arnulf, the servant of the Lord—both personally and through other very illustrious men—to implore the Lord’s mercy, that he might deign to grant him a son to succeed him for the protection of the kingdom and defense of the holy Church.

At first the faithful servant of the Lord recoiled from doing this, guarding himself against human favor arising from it and fearing that it might relax the severity of his mind. But when he learned from the venerable Theobald, bishop of Soissons, and from many other religious men that this would be good and acceptable before God—according to the teaching of the blessed Apostle that prayers should be made for kings and all who are established in high office, and that this should be done before all things—he was persuaded alike by the counsel of good men and the apostolic admonition, and promised that he would pray.

When the queen learned of this promise, she rejoiced greatly and, as though already assured, sent suitable envoys to the servant of God, urgently asking him to deign to tell her when it would now happen. But he, perceiving steadfastness of faith in the queen’s heart, sent her word that she should diligently care for the poor, declaring that their voice would exert force upon divine ears, so that the Lord might grant her the offspring she desired. The queen obeyed and provided daily meals for the poor, firmly persuaded that the prayer of the servant of God could not be frustrated. [Col. 1399B–D]

## CHAPTER XXXI

While Saint Arnulf, the man of the Lord, was still involved in worldly knighthood, he had a fellow knight especially dear to him, named Geric. After Arnulf withdrew from secular life, Geric devoted himself more diligently to robbery and plunder; fearing neither God nor man, he continually oppressed widows and orphans.

The servant of God learned of this blameworthy life through reports from arrivals and repeatedly prayed to the goodness and omnipotence of Christ the Lord that he might send Geric an occasion and compunction for repentance, through which he might abandon his wicked habits and begin to consider fear of eternal judgment. Through faithful men and women returning home from him, he also sent Geric admonitions to salvation; Geric heard them with the ear of the body but did not keep them by faith and works.

Meanwhile Geric, enjoying worldly prosperity, married a wife named Judith, of equal nobility; he begot several children and for many years was sustained in pleasant good fortune with his whole household. Afterwards his children began to die, and within a few years not a single son survived. He himself too fell into a severe illness and lay bedridden for forty-two months—that is, three and a half years—despairing of life and beholding the point of death before his eyes.

His nephews, born of his brothers or sisters, were already seeking to claim his lands and every possession as their own. They were already attempting to deprive his wife Judith of her dowry and alienate her from every inheritance of her husband. What was she to do? No protector, no comforter, offered himself to her.

Then, turning to God, she wept as she prayed that divine help might deign to be present where human help had failed. Remembering Arnulf, the servant of God, she approached her dying husband with many complaints:

“My dearest husband, behold, your children are dead; behold, your nephews, desiring your death, strive to claim all your goods as their own. Behold, they have prepared an evil pretext, so that, when you are buried, they may disgracefully cast me out and refuse to recognize that I was your wife. Why does your whole trust not assent to the counsels of your wife, who loves your life and safety above all things? Speak within your heart and make a vow to Jesus Christ our Lord: be carried in a litter to visit his servant Arnulf, once your companion and friend, and submit yourself and all that is yours to his counsel. Then the Father of mercies will look upon your pains and my griefs.”

He reflected a little, as though weighing the force of her words within himself, and replied: “You have dealt wisely and found the best counsel. I gladly embrace it, and both wish and vow that it be done quickly.”

Accordingly, carried in a litter borne by horses, he was brought to Soissons and taken to the man of God, who was laboring in his spiritual exercise. Rejoicing that the man had arrived—one formerly joined to him in faithful friendship—the holy man asked, indeed commanded, that he be brought to him.

On the next day Geric was brought before the window and heard from the man of God a friendly rebuke:

“Brother Geric, an excellent knight for your own men, but a most wretched one for yourself: how long did you provoke the Lord God by giving yourself to the works of robbery? Believe me: destruction was near you; you had almost fallen into the jaws of the dragon. But I give thanks to Christ the Lord, who, as I see, did not despise my tears: he hindered you by sending illness, lest, fattened utterly upon robberies, you should become food for the enemy’s teeth.

“Know without doubt that the infirmity which held you was obtained from the Lord through my long prayers, so that, even unwillingly, you might cease from oppressing widows and greedily devouring by robbery. Consider how great a benefit God has bestowed upon you in his immeasurable mercy, so that you may recognize that you have acted wickedly: inflamed by so many evil acts, you were nevertheless able to escape the lion’s bite. But you will ask: ‘What lion?’ Hear blessed Peter speaking with the divine voice: ‘Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour’ (1 Peter 5).

“By God’s mercy alone you escaped the jaws of this lion. Now take care to strip yourself completely of his will.”

Geric said: “Most holy and beloved Father, I hastened to your counsel with this vow and intention: that henceforth my life may be ordered according to the tenor of the Lord’s will and in accordance with the command of your holiness, and that I may do nothing further except what the judgment of your counsel directs. Only offer prayers to our God for my recovery, and I affirm and confirm by an everlasting covenant that henceforth I will do nothing which I know to be contrary to the divine laws.” [Col. 1399D–1401B]

## CHAPTER XXXII

As these words came to an end, the wife of Geric, named Judith, broke out in tearful speech:

“Holy servant of God, I beg you, consider my plight also, and bring help to one wretched and forsaken.”

The man of God answered her: “As I hear your voice, I immediately recognize your condition and need; and I promise you in God’s name that the arrival of either you or your husband will not be fruitless for you. Know therefore with certainty that joy will be given you in place of grief, because you faithfully attended to your husband in his sickness. Since this husband of yours rejects wickedness, he shall be completely healed. You will receive from him a son, to be named Lambert, who, by God’s command, shall be born on this very day when a year has elapsed. He will succeed his father; he will support your old age; nor shall you die until you rejoice in the lawful offspring of your Lambert.

“Therefore I wish and exhort you, sweetest brother Geric, that from now on you walk in the way of righteousness; honor the Church of God and the sacred clergy; take nothing from the poor—indeed, restore what has been taken; give alms continually and abundantly, for the holy Apostle thus commands that the rich be instructed. Never withhold your tithes, nor give them to anyone except the person whom the bishop orders. Cultivate your fields; strive to live from the fruits of your produce and from just profit; deal mercifully with your tenants, remitting at least part of what they cannot pay.

“Show faith and truth from the heart to your lord and your equals; give thanks to almighty God for the benefices conferred upon you; and strive to attend more frequently the divine offices being celebrated. If you do these things, God’s grace will be with you, give peace to your affairs, and bring you to a good end. And you, who were brought here ill, shall leave here healthy and riding.”

O how great was the mercy of heavenly goodness, which adorned its blessed servant Arnulf with such gifts of virtues, so that both his conversation might continually be in heaven and the merit of his life on earth might benefit others! For, as may be understood from his own words, this knight Geric would deservedly have been dead before God on account of his perversity, had Arnulf’s prayer not continually accompanied him.

Finally, by God’s favor, Geric left the man of God healthy, and, once settled at home, promptly begot a son. As foretold, he was born on the appointed day; after his father’s death, he became his successor and remained a loving support to his mother. Judith herself lived bodily until her son Lambert, lawfully married, had begotten children. [Col. 1401B–1402C]

## BOOK TWO BEGINS

[Col. 1403]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1403A]

Meanwhile, by divine command, Theobald, bishop of the august city of Soissons, was taken from this life. A certain nobleman, named Gervase, obtained his see and place for his own brother by way of recompense for court service. This brother, named Ursio, was indeed a monk in habit and educated in letters from childhood, but was in no way suited in character or disposition to the episcopal office.

The unworthiness of his life and his non-canonical accession soon came to the ears of the Roman pontiff Gregory.
