He immediately sent letters to Hugh, bishop of Die and then legate of Gaul, directing that Ursio’s life and promotion be canonically examined and that whatever in them was contrary to the sacred laws be corrected by synodal judgment. [Col. 1403B]

It happened accordingly that the aforesaid Hugh held a council in the city of Meaux, on the river Marne, with Count Theobald of Champagne supporting him. There, in accordance with the pope’s decree, Ursio was granted an opportunity to clear himself; but after he had been lawfully summoned, he disdained to appear when canonically called. He therefore incurred the judgment of the bishops and, being condemned, opened the way for an election to the clergy of Soissons, who were waiting there.

Then, by counsel of the council, the sounder part of the clergy and the householders of the Church of Soissons chose as their bishop Lord Arnulf, a cultivator of holy religion, who was at that time a recluse. They urgently acclaimed that he should be given to them without delay.

When this unanimous election had been made and put in writing, the legate Hugh immediately sent venerable persons from the council to the monastery of Saint Medard, directing and admonishing by letters, indeed commanding by the authority of the Roman Church, that Lord Arnulf should leave his cell and come swiftly to the council at Meaux; otherwise, as disobedient, he would incur anathema.

Terrified by the thunder of so great a command, Arnulf—a true son of the Catholic Church—though reluctantly obeyed the legate’s orders and came to the council. When it was in session, the petition of the clergy and noble people of Soissons, electing Lord Arnulf as their bishop, was immediately read aloud. Then the bishops spoke, asking that Arnulf, adorned with every holiness, should become their colleague. Thus he was immediately brought forward, invested with the episcopal insignia, not permitted even briefly to excuse himself, and at once seated in the assembly of bishops.

To him, afflicted and sorrowful, Hugh the legate imposed by sacred command, in the force of holy obedience, the duty henceforth to labor in the ministry of Christ’s Church in the episcopal office. Thus constrained, Arnulf yielded to the decree. Once the day and place of consecration had been appointed, he returned to the monastery of Saint Medard to prepare the necessities for his coming journey.

When these had been abundantly prepared, he set out—not according to his own inclination but in response to the wish of the faithful—with four monks and selected clergy. He came into Champagne, to the castle of Count Theobald called Vertus. [Note: [Col. 1403D] A town of Champagne in the diocese of Châlons, where there are two monasteries: one of monks of our order, the other of nuns of the order of Saint Augustine.] [Col. 1403C–1404A]

## CHAPTER II
Count Theobald, learning of his arrival, joyfully received him with a great retinue of soldiers and nobles, and ushered him indoors with due attendance. Now at the evening hour the man of God was sitting more privately in a somewhat secluded dining-room; the aforesaid count sat beside him with a very few nobles and was inquiring about spiritual salvation, when suddenly, his expression altered and as if stirred by the Spirit, he said: “Let those two brothers, Everolf and Ostermar, be summoned to us; for I have something to say to them.” Without delay they were called and came. As they stood before him, he said to Ostermar: “Since, by the Lord’s mercy, I abandoned the pride of secular soldiery [Col. 1404B], I have striven, as far as I could, not to inflict any injury or insult upon any brother; and what I carefully observed myself, I have zealously endeavored to have observed by all who adhered to me. For I know the punishment decreed by the divine mouth against one who causes one of the little ones to stumble. Since these things are most certainly true, how, brother Ostermar, did you dare to utter so grievous an insult against this our fellow-brother Everolf, sparing neither fear of God nor shame before us? Go, return and make your way back to the monastery, for after such an outpouring of folly I will not permit you to share this journey with us. For I want our companions on the road to be agreeable, gentle, kindly, serving one another, and guarded in speech [Col. 1404C], not rebellious or unsubmissive.”

Utterly dismayed, he answered in a trembling voice: “Lord Father, where, I beg you, have I been rebellious, or to whom have I given insult? Certainly nowhere.” Christ’s servant replied: “Were not my ears at your mouth when you said to brother Everolf that you would rather have his head plunged into a latrine than that your horse should have a larger-than-usual ration of fodder? Believe us: you would have shuddered to say such a thing, had you had any regard for our favor.”

When Count Theobald and all who were present heard this, they were exceedingly astonished at how he could have learned so distinctly of a thing uttered secretly and almost furtively. For the chamber in which the man of God sat was far removed from the horses’ stable, where this foolish saying had been spoken during the distribution of fodder [Col. 1404D]. At length the guilty speaker threw himself at the holy man’s feet; the other brothers too prostrated themselves, humbly imploring pardon for him. God’s servant said to them: “May the Lord forgive you; nevertheless, from now on you shall not be our companion on this journey.”

Then he, weeping and deeply sorrowful, said: “Alas, holy man of God! How shall I depart from you alone, or how shall I bear the disgrace of so great a rejection? Everyone will think that I have committed some abominable crime, and that for this reason [Col. 1405A] I have been expelled by you. Spare, I pray, my good name; grant forgiveness, lest I be subjected to perpetual grief.” At this Count Theobald rose, and with him all the nobility present; they became suppliants for the monk and asked that some remedy be found for his case, lest he be driven to a worse ruin.

## CHAPTER III

Then the man of God, taking pity on his distress and yielding to the entreaties of the brothers for him and to the requests of the count and nobles, took him aside and said: “Because of your excessive foolishness, you must indeed return entirely; but by God’s grace we shall lay upon you so honorable a charge that you will never suffer disgrace from this departure. But keep secret the command I entrust to you, and tell no one, except him to whom we wish it to be announced [Col. 1405B].

“Accordingly, when you depart from us, you shall go to the city of Paris, visit Queen Bertha [variant: Bertrada] on our behalf, and announce to her the welcome joy that she truly bears in her womb a son whom she will call Louis at the sacred font [Note: [Col. 1405D] Lisiard also relates this prophecy again below, in Book III.], and who, after his father’s death, will hold the kingdom of the Franks. She will scarcely believe you because the child does not yet have living movement. But tell her to believe confidently, because after a short time she will feel what she carries.”

Thus the monk, greatly delighted, set out for the city of Paris and disclosed the welcome message to the queen, saying:

> Our lord the king, now your husband, O queen,  
> And you, queen, desiring with equal mind to beget offspring,  
> Have often asked Arnulf, then enclosed in seclusion, [Col. 1405C]  
> To pray that God might grant you a child.  
> Through the highest nobles and also through great bishops  
> You earnestly sought what you could not attain by yourselves:  
> That the Creator of the world might give the churches a protector.  
> Persons devoted to the Catholic faith have urged him  
> To seek from the Lord of heaven, through prayer and faithful vow,  
> An offspring destined by lot to reign,  
> To be given by divine right to you and to the kingdom.  
> What you have jointly desired, I announce to you as fulfilled:  
> For the Lord of heaven, moved by faithful intention,  
> Has granted this to you, that the grace of offspring may be bestowed.  
> You carry a boy in your womb; you must believe this true.  
> That boy will be great; while he lives, gentle as a lamb,  
> He will reign over the Franks and will not tremble before enemies;  
> [Col. 1405D] He will destroy the worst evils and will bear the name Louis.  
> Yet he does not yet live, nor has a living spirit animated him;  
> But by the Lord’s gift it will soon enter into him.  
> By Arnulf’s prayers this son is brought into being.

She grew pale with astonishment and quickly sent messengers to summon King Philip, who was engaged in hunting. He came in haste; eagerly receiving the welcome embassy and learning that the offspring he had long desired had been granted him by the Lord, he began to rejoice [Col. 1406A] and to fear, wavering greatly between fear and joy. He would certainly have rejoiced had he been wholly certain; he feared lest such a promise should prove empty. At last confidence in faith prevailed in the royal heart, and he prudently judged that a prophecy uttered through such a servant of God could not be superfluous. For from manifold experience he knew the holiness and truth of the man through whom such a prediction had come.

> Five days after this, the child begins to show living movement,  
> And the mother’s heaviness increases in her womb.  
> Yet he declared that the child’s gladness should be such  
> That no pain or fear should burden the queen.  
> At the fitting time the king is born—this Louis  
> The Peaceful—who, bearing the scepter, governs the laws well.

Therefore, in the foreknown—indeed, obtained—birth [Col. 1406B] of this great prince, the devoted zeal of Christ’s servant Arnulf is worthy of praise and admiration: he deserved both to obtain the secret of so great a mystery through the prerogative of his merits and to conceal it in profound humility. For he never became burdensome to king or queen by asking any special favor from those upon whom he had conferred the benefit of such great joy. Though the king and queen eagerly wished to bestow something magnificent upon him, he never asked anything of them except that they should devote themselves to the care of the poor and the defense of churches, so that peace and truth might prevail in their days and the tranquility of the churches remain undisturbed.

In the year [Note: [Col. 1405D] The following material is not found in Surius, who instead gives a brief eulogy of King Louis: “And this is Louis, who now governs the reins of the kingdom of the Franks, restrains civil wars as far as he can, vigorously presses hostile enterprises; insofar as lies in him, he is devoted to peace, valiant in arms, cautious in speech, prudent in counsel, unafraid in war, a lover of good men, and a cultivator of the probity and integrity appropriate to the matter at hand. Yet if anything is lacking to royal perfection in him, it must be ascribed not so much to him as to the nobles of the kingdom.”] of the Lord’s Incarnation 1081, in the fourth indiction, the future King Louis was born, [Col. 1406C] obtained through the prayers and merits of this holy Arnulf. May he, by that same saint’s intercession, attain a good end!

## CHAPTER IV

When the journey was completed, he came to Hugh of Die. Hugh was at once delighted and troubled by his unexpected arrival: delighted that he had received so praiseworthy a man, troubled because he had invited no bishops to consecrate him. But entrusting all to God, he was gladdened by sudden news, and all his anxiety was removed. For on the following day three bishops presented themselves to him. No necessity had brought them then from their own places, but they openly declared that they had been inwardly moved by a silent prompting to visit the legate at that time. Thus the manifest secret of the divine counsel [Col. 1406D] became clear to all, and it was evident that by heavenly judgment this man had indeed been appointed to be consecrated bishop.

Everything that appeared useful for his consecration was so prepared and occurred without confusion, as though arranged by divine direction. When the sacred book of the Gospels had been placed upon his head, the bishops looked and found, in Matthew, the Savior’s words: “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children thou hast perfected praise” (Matt. 21). On the Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord, which fell on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December], he was consecrated bishop to the great joy of all, and, with every favor of divine providence, was happily sent to the see of Soissons [Col. 1407A].

Nor did his distinguished fame escape the Viennese people. Rather, gathering together, they encouraged one another to seize him by force and enthrone him as archbishop of their city. For at that time the city of Vienne lacked a bishop’s administration. When this report spread more widely, the man of God hastened to leave their territory, eager to exercise the care of souls especially entrusted to him and to cultivate the vineyard for which he had been appointed laborer and guardian.

## CHAPTER V

As he was passing through Cluny—glorious for its host of monks—and intended to avoid notice, as it were secretly, fame, the companion of virtues, did not allow him to remain hidden [Col. 1407B]. For Hugh, abbot of outstanding religious devotion, having learned of his journey and its purpose, swiftly sent his monks to meet him. He commanded him, and adjured him by the love of holy brotherhood, by no means to turn aside from the route to the sacred monastery of Cluny, but to hasten, accompanied by the monks sent to meet him, to see brothers rejoicing and eagerly longing to enjoy his blessing.

The man of God feared to refuse such an expression of profound humility; obeying the command, he turned his way toward the venerable monastery of Cluny. Then Hugh came out to meet him, with a great assembly of monks gathered and adorned in splendid array, and received the blessed bishop with exceptional reverence—not so much on account of his episcopate as because of the merit of his former life, known to him and pleasing to God [Col. 1407C]. For earlier this holy man Arnulf had constantly enjoyed the instruction and governance of the abbot of Cluny himself; hence there had also spread a report that, in his election, the Church of Soissons had been strengthened by the counsel of that same abbot.

After receiving and treating him honorably and kindly, this diligent examiner pressed him—not from a habit of curiosity, but from the fervor of holy love—putting questions from the Scriptures and drawing their solutions from his lips. By such inquiry he wished to discover whether Arnulf was ready to bring forth things new and old, lest the church entrusted to him should be inadequately nourished by sound spiritual teaching. In short, it happened that Lord Hugh, the pious abbot, who had supposed him to be unlearned and rustic [Col. 1407D], joyfully discovered that he overflowed with the zeal of charity in a stream of learning and possessed no slight strength in eloquence.

Yet the mind longs to linger here even briefly on the memory of the aforesaid Hugh. He was most chaste in body and heart; a perfect founder and guardian of monastic discipline and regular life; an unceasing nurturer of approved monks and persons of the greatest integrity; and a fervent champion [perhaps “guardian”] and defender of Holy Church.

## CHAPTER VI

A bishop named Ursio occupied the see of Soissons, not by right of the Church but through courtly favor. He was the brother of Gervasius, the royal steward, and therefore enjoyed the revenues of the bishopric because royal favor attended him on account of his brother. Accordingly, when Lord Arnulf [Col. 1408A], the bishop, was approaching and preparing to enter the city of Soissons, Gervasius himself met him with a crowd of armed men and strongly warned him not to enter the city if he wished ever to remain alive.

The man of God answered him steadfastly: “It is written, as the Apostle says, that ‘perfect love casts out fear’ (1 John 4). And because ‘for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain’ (Phil. 1), I shall endeavor to fulfill the obedience laid upon me by the apostolic command, lest by disobedience I deserve to be rejected. It is fitting that I should hear [perhaps: ‘approach’] what the pope commanded me to undertake:

> Christ’s shepherd is not broken by a hostile troop;  
> May my Lord God possess me either as a martyr, if I am killed,  
> Or as a confessor, if I escape.

‘For the love of Christ constrains us’ (2 Cor. 5).”

So saying, he urged on with spurs the animal he rode, that he might swiftly enter the city [Col. 1408B]. But Gervasius seized the beast’s bridle and, turning the animal, compelled both it and its rider to go elsewhere. The man of God immediately yielded to the one resisting him, mindful of the Lord’s words: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26). He also kept in mind that the Lord does not save by spear or sword. Thus he fulfilled, as far as he could, the command of obedience, and meanwhile calmly relinquished the see which he had not desired; yet he cultivated in compassion what he seemed to have abandoned in bodily presence.

## CHAPTER VII

But because it is not the see that makes the bishop, but the bishop the see, and because the power of majesty is not divided by places, he established a residence and a substitute seat for himself in a castle of that diocese called [Col. 1408C] Ulciacum (Oulchy), with the support of Count Theobald. There, as prelates of churches and senior clergy assembled, and mixed crowds of people also gathered, he vigorously and faithfully provided penance for those who confessed and restoration for the fallen.

> The bishop’s zeal cultivates every flock of peoples;  
> The clergy of the churches thirst for the prelate’s office.  
> He consecrates churches, instructs clergy, strengthens companies;  
> He preaches, absolves, baptizes, anoints with chrism.  
> To assemblies not foolish he pours forth words of salvation;  
> To the fallen he gives pardon, to the contrite in heart healing.  
> He gave himself as bridegroom to widows and father to the little ones;  
> Yet he also endeavored to provide aid for virgins.  
> He showed himself dear to all and despised bitterness;  
> [Col. 1408D] Above all he greatly cultivated the worship of the Church—  
> Wakeful, praying, weeping for the sins of the world.  
> Nor did he deem it unworthy to show himself kind toward his servants,  
> A pious and cheerful man, sustained by most sweet speech,  
> Becoming all things to all, strongly resisting the wicked.  
> Offering life, he did not permit himself to bring destruction.  
> Thus he appeared pleasing to the Lord, thus blessed in mind,  
> That praise and glory might be made in Christ, free from defilement.

## CHAPTER VIII

While the man of God was staying in that same place, a monk and priest named Everolf, wholly devoted to the bishop and greatly loved by him for his usefulness, fell seriously ill. Because of the severity of his burning sickness, he believed himself about to die [Col. 1409A], and therefore asked the bishop to anoint him with holy oil and fortify his departure with prayers.

Illuminated by the light of prophecy, the bishop said to him: “What you ask is untimely; I therefore do not grant it, because I know it to be contrary to the divine ordering. For it is not I who am to anoint or bury you; rather, at another time and in another place, you will attend me in the sacred offices of anointing and burial when I die.”

He replied: “How can I, so insignificant a person, come to attend upon your departure, when bishops or abbots ought to celebrate it?” The prelate said to him: “Know most certainly that no bishop or abbot will come to the funeral rites of my anointing or burial. But through the service of your love all things concerning me will be accomplished. But now arise; go to the church and, celebrating Mass, give thanks to our Savior.”

He said: “Lord Father, I have not eaten for twenty-one days; how do you command me to rise or go to church, when I have no bodily strength?” Then the bishop, taking his hand, said: “Behold, I say to you: in the name of Jesus Christ, rise quickly and gladly perform what I have commanded.” He rose, stronger than himself, and went to church [Col. 1409B]; he prayed and sang Mass. When he returned from the church, the man of God himself set food before him and served him a cup. Thus restored to complete health, Everolf accompanied him on his journey that same day.

## CHAPTER IX

When the same holy man of God was once asked by this brother when, how, or where his departure would occur [Col. 1409C], he answered: “Not long after I had, by the counsel of the divine will, been ordained bishop, though unworthy, I perceived that the monks of Saint-Médard and the clerics of the church [Note: [Col. 1409D] This is the cathedral church of Soissons, dedicated to God under the title of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.] of Saint Gervasius wished to contend with one another for the future remains of my body. With all my heart I implored the King to whom all things live that he might deign to reveal to me when and where my passage from the mortal body had been appointed, and what place had been designated for my burial.

“One night, while I was intent upon these prayers, a vision of the blessed Apostle Peter stood before me, instructing and strengthening me with these words: ‘In the region of Flanders is a place consecrated to our Lord Jesus Christ under the title of my name, where, by Christ’s will, many signs have been performed. For the renewal of its honor or advancement [Col. 1409D], I have obtained from the Lord that you must be buried in that same place, so that, when Christ glorifies you, the place may be made illustrious by the splendor of your merits and, through your beginning it, may be restored to the light of holy religion.’

“I said to him: ‘Lord, since that place is wholly unknown to me and lies outside the diocese entrusted to me, by what means can I come there to be buried?’ He replied: ‘You have heard repeatedly that “no word will be impossible with God” (Luke 1); therefore do not concern yourself about this, for as soon as the time comes, the Lord’s work is ready. The Roman pontiff will lay upon you a command through which your arrival in Flanders will have its cause. May Christ’s peace be with you; may our peace likewise accompany you for ever’ [Col. 1410A].

“Strengthened by such admonitions, I believe that what the first of the Apostles deigned to promise will not be void. And you, dearest brother, take care diligently not to dare reveal such things to anyone while I breathe.”

## CHAPTER X

As crowds of people hurried to him from every direction, and he labored diligently to cure their ailments, one day he stood in a hall and looked outside through a window. He saw in the street below a man walking breathlessly and carrying a plank upon his neck. Immediately he said to the clergy and soldiers standing around him: “That plank being carried at a distance is stolen property.”

Those around him replied: “And how, lord, could you know this?” God’s servant answered: “I know most certainly that it is stolen, because at this very hour the devil, author of the theft, is treacherously pressing upon the man’s neck [Col. 1410B].” They said to him: “Can we inquire whether this is so?” The saint said: “Do as you wish.”

Immediately one of them, acting for all, quickly ran off and addressed the bearer of the plank: “Hey, man! I ask you, where did this plank that you carry so breathlessly come from?” He answered: “I took part in a raid at the village of Nantolium, and there I acquired this plank by seizing it.” Hearing this, the questioner returned swiftly to those who had sent him and, to their amazement, reported that the testimony of the man of God had proved wholly true.

In this there is some resemblance to a miracle of blessed Martin, who, when he once came to the proud Count Avitianus [Note: [Col. 1410D] Sulpicius treats of Count Avitianus in Dialogue 3, *On the Miracles of St Martin*.], saw the devil crouching upon his head [Col. 1410C].

## CHAPTER XI

At one time, when he was about to dedicate the parish church of a certain village, he said to his attendants and prospective companions on the road: “I ask you to lead us to that church by such a path that the gathering people may not know by what route we are to arrive there; and bring some food with you, so that after the fatigue of the journey we may restore our bodies, if only a little.”

Accordingly, a more distant and out-of-the-way path was taken. Yet the fervor of the people who thirsted for him was not checked by this device; with all haste a great multitude gathered before and behind him. Seeing this, God’s servant broke into praise of the Creator and said to those serving him: “Bring out whatever food you have here, so that after the labor [Col. 1410D] of the road we may restore our bodily strength.” Without delay, five monastic loaves were brought out and five small vessels of wine poured forth, according to the measure of monastic provision. Carpets having been spread upon the grass, the man of God sat down, surrounded in groups by the overflowing crowd.

Then, blessing the loaves—few in number, yet many in the mystery of their number—he ordered that all those seated around on every side should receive portions of the same bread, and that wine too should be offered them in sufficiency. This event then appeared worthy of a great miracle because that bread and wine sufficed so abundantly for all that they said they had been well refreshed and richly filled. Indeed, some of them carried away small portions of that bread in believing hope [Col. 1411A]; when these were later applied to the sick, their taste provided a healing remedy. The company of those eating and rejoicing, apart from the bishop’s own retinue, exceeded seven hundred persons.

## CHAPTER XII

Count Roger of Porcien built a church in the town called Bald Mountain [Calvus-Mons; Chaumont] [Note: [Col. 1411D] Calvus-Mons, commonly Chaumont, is a town in the province of Reims near Château-Porcien. The church mentioned here, now honored with the rank of an abbey, is possessed by the Premonstratensians, as Marlot notes in *Metropolis Remensis*, vol. II.]. He earnestly invited holy Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, to perform its dedication.

They had reached the point where, after the basilica had been consecrated, the altar was to be consecrated. While the bishop sat and rested a little, the countess approached, leading by the hand a woman who had been blind for fifteen years. Kneeling before him, she said: “Merciful lord [Col. 1411B], take pity on this poor woman and, through your holy prayer and the laying on of your hand, graciously restore to her the light of her eyes.”

When he refused and protested that he was unworthy, the blind woman said: “Bishop of God, do not delay, for it has been promised to me from heaven that by the touch of your hand I shall receive the light of my eyes.” At once he was filled with tears, prayed, and laid his right hand, with the sign of the cross, upon the woman’s eyes. Immediately the woman received clear sight.

Witnesses of this miracle were Algelrannus, an eloquent man, then archdeacon of the blessed man and later bishop of Laon; Radulfus Viridis, later archbishop of Reims, to whom indeed the preface of this work is addressed; several abbots and provosts [Col. 1411C] of churches who had assembled; Count Roger himself and his countess; a great body of clergy and an innumerable people. Their voices celebrated the praise of our God loudly, all crying out in honor of the deed: “We praise thee, O God.”

## CHAPTER XIII

The proper order of the narrative now requires an account of how he came to seek the land of the Flemings and what cause drew him to those regions. Robert [Note: [Col. 1412D] Robert, commonly called the Frisian, who seized the county of Flanders after expelling Richildis, widow of Count Baldwin, and her sons.] was then count of the Flemings and was hostile to certain noble and wealthier men of his people. They formed a plan that, after the fierce Count Robert had been deposed, they might provide themselves with a milder ruler, as they thought—namely, Baldwin, count of Mons-en-Pévèle [Montis-Castrorum].

After their plan [Col. 1411D] became known to Count Robert, he exerted every effort to seize his traitors: he killed some, outlawed others, and compelled some, stripped of possessions and honors, to live in exile outside their homeland. Among them was Arnulf, archdeacon of Thérouanne and provost of the church of Saint Audomar (Saint-Omer). Expelled from every resource of his property and office, he lived as a fugitive for many days and endured intolerable persecution.

At last recovering himself, he sought the Roman pope, named Gregory, and tearfully complained of the persecution by which he had lost the honor of his rank and the resources of his property [Col. 1412A]. Moved by compassion for this great calamity of Arnulf and of men like him, the lord pope determined by his letters to call the agitated and fierce mind of Count Robert back to moderation, so that he might either grant full pardon to those he suspected or at least allow them an opportunity to clear themselves. But because no one could be found who dared carry the apostolic letters into the presence of so offended a count, the matter was long delayed.

At length remembrance arose of the steadfast holiness and fervent charity of this holy man Arnulf, bishop of Soissons. In the court of the lord pope he was well known as the one who could undoubtedly present the apostolic commands to Count Robert without delay. Encouraged by this counsel, Pope Gregory at last [Col. 1412B] sent written and sealed letters to the most reverend bishop Arnulf, ordering and commanding him to bring the intercessory letters and the persons concerned under his safe-conduct into the presence of Count Robert, and to obtain for them either pardon or an opportunity to clear themselves, for the honor of the Apostolic See.

Bound, therefore, by this twofold justice—namely, primary obedience and brotherly compassion—the man strong in mercy, not forgetful of the apostolic promise previously shown to him, came with some of these men to the town called Insula [Note: [Col. 1412D] Today a distinguished city of Flanders—indeed its capital—commonly called Lille.]. There, having found Count Robert, he presented the papal letters. While they were being read, the accused men secretly threw themselves at Robert’s feet. O fury! O madness! O bitter stirring of gall [Col. 1412C], which then boiled in the count’s brow, eyes, and whole face when he perceived that his hated enemies had touched his feet! But what could that ferocity do before a righteous man? He was present who “looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. 103), and, both through Arnulf’s attained holiness and through reverence for the Apostolic See, safety, life, and the resources of their property were granted them.

Behold how true and wondrous are God’s counsels! Who could have imagined that the wickedness of traitors would be turned into an occasion for saving peoples? Who could have known or conceived that the great fury of an angry count would result in great honor for a renowned bishop? But meanwhile let all flesh be silent, so that it may become apparent what the Lord Jesus has decreed to work through his servant.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 1412D]

For at that time daily murders and insatiable outpourings of human blood had disturbed the peace and quiet of the entire region in certain—indeed, in all—parts of Flanders. Therefore, with great entreaties, a very large multitude of nobles obtained that the Lord’s bishop should visit the places where savage cruelty raged most violently and in some measure admonish the unruly and bloodthirsty minds of the Flemings concerning the good of peace and concord.

Sensing in the Spirit [Col. 1413A] that this was pleasing before God and knowing, as has been stated, that he had to come there by divine command and through the intervention of the blessed Apostle Peter, he consented to their request all the more quickly because he saw more certainly that all these things were being arranged by divine action. Accompanied by a throng of nobles and magnates, he came to the town of Bruges, and from there into inland Flanders, to the village of Aldeburg.

In these places there was such a madness for killing and such a fury for revenge that they delighted in being continually stained with human blood, and judged it cowardly and shameful to abstain from slaughter even for a single day. A father scarcely spared his son, a son scarcely his father; a brother gave his own brother, a nephew his maternal or paternal uncle, and indeed an uncle his nephew, to death for a trivial cause.

Arnulf, the man of God, wonderfully tamed this diabolical frenzy and the insane ruin of the people of Bruges, Furnes, and Aldeburg by the word of his honeyed preaching and examples of exceptional holiness [Col. 1413B]. He brought the hearts of the cruel, though with very great labor, to a settled concord. For by urgently preaching to them, in season and out of season, and repeatedly prostrating himself at their feet, he finally stilled their enmity; from most bitter enemies they were bound together more closely as steadfast friends.

## CHAPTER XV

While laboring most earnestly in this work, he came to the village called Turhold; for there too the ancient enemy had breathed the fire of lawsuits and the flames of quarrels. As he addressed the close kin of those whose blood had been shed, urging them to enter into covenants of peace [Col. 1413C] and extinguish the diabolical fires, there was present a certain Herrad, son of the priest Herrad [variant, manuscript: Eraldus, son of Eraldus]. He preferred to reject the counsels of peace with a deaf ear rather than form himself and his neighbors toward the pursuit of peace.

He was seen to leave the churchyard in which the bishop stood, so that by being absent he might more readily evade the admonitions of justice. The bishop was told: “Look, one is leaving in whom the matter especially rests.” Immediately the bishop followed in his tracks and, pursuing him, came to the count’s lodging. There, prostrating himself on the ground at the man’s feet, he humbly begged that he should return to the concord of peace.

But the other, swollen with the manner of youthful arrogance, refused to stop; fearing [Col. 1413D] that others might detain him, he swiftly gave himself to flight. As he fled, an evil spirit leapt upon him and, turning him to madness, compelled him to tear himself with teeth and nails. When this became known, his friends and kinsmen came, bound the madman possessed by a demon, and dragged him, shrieking and struggling in his movements, into his father’s house.

Then they went to the holy bishop, urgently begging him to forgive the proud fool and not remember the injury done to him. The servant of the Lord said to them: “I welcome an injury suffered for truth; but I am more troubled by the folly of his heart. Therefore, if you wish me to pray to the Lord for his deliverance, give us assurance that all of you, whether he wishes it or not, will maintain firm peace; and if he stirs up a quarrel or sedition, none of you [Col. 1414A] is to offer him assistance.”

All said with one voice: “Let whoever gives him help be accursed among us, unless it be in order to keep your words.” Then the bishop, as though soothed by their promises, prepared blessed water mixed with an exorcism. When the young man was sprinkled with it, he immediately escaped the devil’s invasion; restored to sober use of his senses, he maintained peace and concord with special devotion.

## CHAPTER XVI
In the same village of Turhold another event, no less remarkable, took place. A certain knight, a native of Aldenborg, named William, tall in stature and surnamed Long, had a son already grown and bound to military service, but more devoted to thefts and robberies. Once, while this son was attempting in broad daylight to steal in the house of a certain Siger [Col. 1414B], he was struck by Siger with a sword and quickly died. When Siger perceived that he had sinned in the death of the young man, though he had been justly slain, he went to the venerable and holy man Bishop Arnulf, asking him to apply a remedy of words to heal the wound of so great a crime.

But the holy man, who had offered himself for the preparation of the Gospel of peace, promptly went out into Siger’s field, prepared to undertake combat against the powers of the devil; armed with the shield of faith, he fought manfully to seize the goods of the strong evil one. When the relatives of the slain youth had gathered together with his slayer, he sowed the word of righteousness, the word of truth and peace; and, God being the author of it, he reconciled Siger with William Long, namely the father of the slain man.

Afterward William, [Col. 1414C] rebuked by certain malicious persons because he had so lightly forgiven his son’s death, began to repent of his good deed and again began to seek an opportunity to take vengeance upon Siger. Nor was an occasion for revenge yielded to him until, in the course of time, around the feast of Saint John, at the fair of Turhold. Siger happened to arrive in order to buy cloth; William struck him with a very sharp sword as far as the neck, and, having made him bloodless but not dead, threw him into the basket in which the cloth lay.

Immediately the whole fair was thrown into confusion. There was shouting and indignation among the people: how had he dared violate the count’s peace? They ran to the count, who was then staying at his residence in Turhold. He was reproachfully told that he was now worth nothing [Col. 1414D], since he had been unable to defend his celebrated fair. Count Robert sprang up in furious anger and immediately ordered both the wounded man and his assailant to be brought before him. Meanwhile he learned from his knights that William Long had been the author of this audacious deed and had disturbed the fair in revenge for his slain son.

The count, now somewhat calmed, replied: “I love William Long, a valiant knight, as a son; but I condemn this: that he has renewed in vengeance the death of his son, which had been forgiven and settled in peace through the holy Bishop Arnulf.”

Meanwhile the wounded man was led before him, trembling indeed, but unharmed. His neck appeared not to have been struck by a sword, but rather encircled as though by a red thread. Then the count said to William: “I marvel at your rashness, but I am more appalled at such great weakness in you. Since [Col. 1415A] you were unwilling to spare him, why were you not ashamed to strike so childishly, so that in this neck one sees the hand of a woman rather than a man’s right hand? Know, therefore, that neither the sword nor your right hand was the cause; it was done by the command of the most high God, who did not permit the neck to be wounded which, through the teaching of so holy a man, had willingly embraced peace.”

Thus the count, the count’s nobles, and the knights proclaimed that whatever Saint Arnulf had reconciled would remain fixed and inviolable by God’s will.

## CHAPTER XVII

Within the boundaries of the parish of Gestel, which lies under the diocese of Tournai, there is a certain vein of black earth, somewhat reddish in appearance, which, being broken up by frequent marshes, cannot easily be crossed. In these places there dwells [Col. 1415B] a race of men ever desiring violence, like the common rabble of Scythians. The man of God was brought to these places in order to sow among such people the word of peace.

He was met by a certain old woman, crying out amid tearful lamentations: “Holy servant of God, have mercy on me, and deign to enter the hovel of my poverty; then you will see the manifold and prolonged punishment of my affliction.”

But he, gentle and humble, always mindful of the name Christopher divinely bestowed upon him, entered the shelter of the poor widow in order to see the causes of her loudly proclaimed distress. For her five sons lay in little beds, all confined by one and the same illness; none could assist another or support him in any way.

Then the woman said: “See, servant of God, how great [Col. 1415C] is my misery, how great the pain that torments me, how great the sorrow that afflicts me. Alone I serve five men; I run and hurry from this one to that one, from the former to the latter, and by serving I satisfy no one at all.”

Then the man of God, groaning with the deepest compassion, prayed silently. Next he prepared holy water, sprinkled the whole house and the sick persons, and thus commanded them: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let this illness depart from you, so that you may immediately recover, and may not need to wear out your mother, given over to so many sorrows, by requiring her service.”

The power of the Lord was immediately present: at once they rose together and eagerly took food which they had long loathed. On the following day they underwent bathing, and thereafter flourished in complete health.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 1415D] A certain Folcard, an inhabitant of Gestel, lively and robust, yet not so useful as rash, thought that the blessed bishop, while speaking of the grace of peace, ought to be treated with contempt. As he fled the face of the man of God, he was suddenly handed over to an evil spirit. Torn and miserably mangled by it, he could scarcely be restrained by friends or relatives. Thereupon, purified from the demon by the blessed pontiff—not through his own faith, but through the prayers of others—he learned from suffering how much love and reverence he ought to have shown to the blessed man.

## CHAPTER XIX

In the neighborhood of the castle of Furnes there lived a widow, supported by nobility and wealth, named Evergerda. Her husband and son together had been slain by cruel enemies, and grievous hostilities [Col. 1416A] pressed on every side against their killers because of their deaths. For on account of the death of the two men the whole region had been disturbed, while some devised vengeance and others the defense of the murderers.

To curb this evil, the holy bishop of the Lord, Saint Arnulf, freely and readily hastened wherever peace and concord were to be pursued. He came riding upon an ass to the house of that wealthy widow, against whom the Apostle’s saying resounds: “She who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5). Such as she was, she utterly refused the blessed man entry; instead, she ordered a drawbridge raised before her gate, lest access be open and the wishes of the man of God be fulfilled.

Yet he did not cease to preach, rebuke, and entreat her to pardon the slayers of her son and husband for the repose of their souls [Col. 1416B], and to consent that those whom she cruelly hated should become allies and friends. But she would receive neither his prayers nor his admonitions. Persisting in the swelling pride of her spirit, she mocked the servant of Christ, making sport of his seat upon an ass and the humility of his clothing, and drove him away—but not with impunity.

For after the grieving bishop departed from her, the heavy vengeance of divine judgment struck her. A short time afterward, though the sky remained clear, a light whirlwind arose, shook and shattered her house; caught in that ruin, she perished by sudden death. A very remarkable thing occurred there: although in that same house there were many male and female servants, pigs and dogs, hens, geese, doves [Col. 1416C], and swallows, nothing then perished there except the irreverent woman, nor was any animal or anything else harmed.

Utterly destroyed, she showed that the teachings were not feigned,  
Which so great a saint had taught under the weight of vengeance;  
Thus the woman, strong in wickedness, justly became a daughter of death.

Certainly, the flying report of this vengeance terrified the hearts of the hard-hearted Flemings, so that no one dared oppose the man of God or disobey his holy admonitions.

At that time in the village of Aldenborg there were two opponents of mad violence, one Conon and the other Robalin. Robalin had treacherously slain Conon’s father, named Hido; each butchered the other’s friends and household members, and each inflicted upon the other every evil he could, privately and publicly. The minds of these men also, [Col. 1416D] filled with demons, Arnulf summoned to the grace of peace by the teaching of his preaching and the terror of frequent signs.

Count Robert rejoiced at this, and all the nobility of the people swelled with great joy that Christ the Lord had granted in their time such a minister—one who bore concern for all with paternal affection and showed to everyone the way of life by the examples of his own actions. At the count’s command, Erembold the magistrate, taking prudent men with him, calculated in the palace of Bruges the names of those slain from the community of Bruges and other places, wherever they could obtain knowledge of persons. They found and recorded in writing that an expenditure of ten thousand marks of pure silver could not have paid for what the grace of God had deigned to bring under control through this minister of truth [Col. 1417A].

Hence it came about that every person, powerful and powerless alike, loved the holy man from the depths of the heart and most ardently wished him to live among them. Therefore they began with all their might to seek out a place in which the sacred bishop could reside usefully and honorably.

## CHAPTER XX

There was in the town of Aldenborg a church, anciently founded in honor of Saint Peter the Apostle and of all the holy apostles, renowned and abundant in divine miracles. A certain nobleman, very wealthy, named Conon, brother of Everard of Tournai, held it from the count of Flanders as a benefice; the count, however, held that same church from the bishop of Tournai [Col. 1417B].

The fear of God, prompted by his most faithful wife, named Huzecca [otherwise Zazecca], inflamed this Conon to make the church of Saint Peter the Apostle—which divine miracles had made awe-inspiring—free from his own legal claim, and to establish there, for the praise of God, an abbey of monks. For the previously recorded promise of blessed Peter, which we have reported as made to the bishop himself, had to be fulfilled, both concerning the construction of the place and the death and burial of the holy man himself.

By God’s ordering it came to pass that, when Conon restored to the count the church which he held, the count restored the same church to the bishop of Tournai, named Radbod. Bishop Radbod, with Walter the archdeacon, amid the approval of the clergy and rejoicing of the people, freely and unencumbered bestowed it [Col. 1417C] upon Bishop Arnulf, and made him a canonical investiture in it.

## CHAPTER XXI

The tradition of the elders records that this church was built in the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks, by Abbot Ursmar.

> [Note: [Col. 1417D] We have given the Life of Saint Ursmar, abbot of Lobbes, under the year 713, Century III, Part I, p. 246, with an Appendix containing some material concerning this church of Aldenborg, constructed by Ursmar himself.]

The majesty of the Lord made it marvelous many times through diverse revelations and manifestations of signs. The blind received sight, the deaf hearing, the mute speech; paralytics and those bent double were restored, and every sickness or disease there received the desired healing.

In the year of the Lord 1081 [otherwise, erroneously, 1091], on the holy night of the Nativity of the Lord, there arose a violent and powerful wind, which shook, broke, and cast down towers of cities, roofs of houses, and many church buildings. On that same [Col. 1417D] night, in the whirlwind of that same wind, the bell-tower of the church of Saint Peter was torn from its supports and thrown eastward over the roof of the tower on which it had stood. For six days and nights it could be seen hanging there, as though it must fall at any moment.

In the morning the inhabitants of the place assembled and hastily summoned builders, setting rewards to be given if they restored it. They made many promises, prepared ropes, set up crossbows or hoists, stitched together bindings, and devised various technical contrivances. While the people awaited the machines invented by the craftsmen [Col. 1418A], through which the bell-tower was expected to be restored, before midnight, on the day before the Kalends of January, power came from heaven in the appearance of fire. It set the bell-tower most firmly back in its place and clothed the church, within and without, in fiery light.

I would be ashamed to report these things in this manner, had not a thousand witnesses declared that they saw them.

> [Note: [Col. 1418D] Sigebert, a contemporary author, relates this miracle in the same way in his Chronicle under the year 1081.]

## CHAPTER XXII

This defender of the Catholic faith had the practice that, whenever a sick person approached him for healing, he would immediately make the sign of the cross, lay his hand upon that person, and chant three times the words of the Gospel: “They shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall recover” (Mark 16). When these words had thus been spoken three times, illnesses departed and health followed.

A woman native to the town of Aldenborg, knowing these things, [Col. 1418B] came to him where he was then dwelling at Saint Peter’s and prayed: “I beg you, holy bishop, touch and bless my head, that I may be healed from the affliction of such severe pains.”

The bishop said to her: “Tell me, sister, what trouble you suffer, and for what reason you have come to us.”

She replied: “For a long time I have endured very severe pains of the head, which torment me so greatly that people think I suffer madness, and neither by day nor by night can any rest find a place in me. I can never sleep, eat, or do any work. A certain divine adviser appeared to me when I was oppressed by so many evils, saying: ‘Go to Bishop Arnulf and ask him, by touching and blessing your head, to heal you; and immediately you shall be cured.’ Compelled [Col. 1418C] by these reasons, I have come and seek the healing that was promised.”

Then the bishop immediately said to her: “According to your faith, let it be done to you.” Likewise he touched and blessed her, and at once the pain in her head, together with the excessive heat, was removed.

## CHAPTER XXIII

While the holy man was still staying in the same place, a pilgrim came from Jerusalem and announced to him: “Lord, your sister Lady Oda, speaking to me in Jerusalem, earnestly entreated me to tell you that, with all the strength she has, she labors and hastens to see you in the flesh before your departure, to speak with you, and to seek and receive from you in person remission of sins, a rule for the life she is to lead hereafter, and counsel. The chief point of her requests is that your prayer to the Lord [Col. 1418D] should obtain that you do not depart until she arrives, and that she does not die until she sees your face, so beloved to her.”

Then the righteous man said: “Oda, our sister and sister in the Lord, though she hurries and eagerly makes haste, strives in vain, labors in vain, and contends in vain to obtain what the Lord has disposed otherwise. Let her see and contemplate our actions and our zeal in fearing the Lord.”

Thus that most chaste woman, hurrying and making haste, allowing herself no rest, quickly entered Aldenborg and found her brother already buried in the tomb for eight days.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 1419A]

But to return to the proper order: the blessed holy soldier of Christ, Arnulf, as the month of June approached, began carefully to inquire whether there might be a memorial of Saint Medard, wishing to celebrate his feast, which falls on the sixth day before the Ides of June, in a church dedicated in that saint’s name. While he was thus concerned, he was informed that on an estate called Ervingahem there stood a church distinguished by the name of Blessed Medard, not far from Aldenborg, to the south. The holy bishop of God came there in order to perform the due offices in honor of so great a confessor.

The people of that estate witnessed the holy celebration and, pierced in heart, gave to the church of Saint Peter in Aldenborg two thirds of the tithes from all their freehold lands, cultivated and to be cultivated, [Col. 1419B] marshy or dry, woodland or meadow; and from whatever their free land seemed to possess, they freely bestowed two thirds of the tithe of the entire yield of grain, flax, and reed.

The chief donors of this gift—the noble and freeborn men of that place—Bertulf son of Ermenar, with his wife Ingelborg; Erembold and Malger, sons of Almar; Leggiva, widow of another Ermenar, with her sons Ingran, Fredebold, and Lambert; together with all their kindred, required of the holy man that they or their descendants should be condemned by everlasting anathema if at any time they attempted to withdraw, diminish, or in any manner inflict any loss upon anything from the aforesaid tithe.

## CHAPTER XXV

Therefore, when the place had been assigned and lawfully conveyed to him by the canonical transfer already mentioned [Col. 1419C], he appointed some of his own men there to clear the site and prepare dwellings suitable for those serving God. The neighboring people, and also those settled far around, eagerly assisted by giving money, animals, and varied aid.

They rejoiced that the lamp of God had begun to shine among them. For high above the church of Saint Peter at Aldenborg, precisely at the place where this blessed man had stood or sat while laboring for peace and concord, a column of fire was seen rising from above and remaining there. From the beginning of the night until about dawn, by its exceedingly great brightness, it changed the darkness of night into light and brightly illuminated all the surrounding expanse.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 1419D]

Returning himself to the see of Soissons, he was sought by the prayers of all and celebrated amid the rejoicing of all. But he learned of King Philip’s blameworthy conduct in many respects, his continual neglect of restraining wrongdoers, and the indiscriminate appointment of bishops and abbots. Therefore he began to be wearied by the evils committed everywhere, since no governor was directing the commonwealth.

His soul therefore sank into slumber from weariness at the evils which grew daily, because that noble discipline of the Church of Reims had grown so cold [Note: [Col. 1419D] The Church of Reims suffered some loss through the evil conduct of Archbishop Manasses. Yet shortly afterward, under the government of Reginald, Ralph, Samson [Col. 1420D], and other distinguished bishops, it regained its splendor.], the right of metropolitan dignity having been cast down [Col. 1420A], so that neither councils of bishops nor ecclesiastical judgments were exercised there.

Therefore he resumed the path of his first seclusion: that nourisher of compunction, guardian of silence, companion of vigils and psalmody, friend of quiet and divine contemplation. He chose to be lowly in the house of the Lord rather than to go, stand, or sit in any transgression of divine law. For he knew that the mighty would suffer mighty torments; therefore he turned away from evils in order to do good with all his strength, desiring to be ready and watchful, so that whenever the Lord knocked he might immediately open to him.

He kept that path of seclusion by a steep course and adorned it with holy virtues, living in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness; always stretching forth his mind in the knowledge of God, in [Col. 1420B] unfeigned charity, in the word of truth, in the power of God, in patience, in gentleness, and in the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXVII

However, more pressing matters arose concerning the place and the neighboring region. The leading men of the settlement of Aldenborg, together with the monk Everolf, assembled and resolved to come to the man of God and compel him by every effort to return to Flanders and bring measure and an end to these urgent affairs.

But he, aware of the future—as one more frequently instructed by divine revelations—readily consented to the wishes of those seeking him, since he truly knew that he could not be dissolved in order to be with Christ except in the place of Aldenborg. Coming with them, he often admonished them, saying: “My children, know that my present journey to Flanders is not so much by your wish as by divine appointment.”

And while they traversed the clods of that region, he came to Arras,  
Where broad fields bear thickets over a spreading space.  
Wishing to sleep, he lay down beside his beast of burden;  
Praying, he addressed words to the flowering grasses,  
That he might take a little sleep—this he eagerly sought.  
Happy was this rest which summons the hosts of heaven.  
Then, while weariness pressed the man in sleep for a time,  
A vision was shown him, by which he was immediately made blessed.  
A messenger greeted him, whose message the bishop heard more joyfully:

“You will come to Aldenborg and will not live much longer.  
You will pass beyond the ages and enter blessed kingdoms,  
Which have no end and possess everlasting light.  
[Col. 1420D] The house of Peter will receive you when you are brought for burial;  
You will not endure many days while buried in the flesh.  
You will be raised from the earth and enjoy the praise of your merits.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

The man of God arose and strongly urged on his companions in the road,  
And spoke thus to his servants: “Rise now; it is enough  
That we have slept here in this fashion or have seen pleasing dreams—  
Dreams not false, which reveal exalted rewards.  
Conceal them well for the present, you who will know them from my telling.  
I foretell to you that sorrow awaits the enemy,  
And that I shall soon climb into heaven and become a citizen  
Among angelic companies—what I seek in daily prayers.

[Col. 1421A] Therefore rejoice, keep hearts most glad,  
And so honor Christ, so love him in your deeds,  
That he may receive you when this flesh becomes ashes.  
At the same time this is shown, which the mind strives to know:  
I shall be buried in the church and tomb of Peter.  
But now let us proceed; let us tread the road to our homeland.  
When the appointed time is completed, this will come through joyful grace.”

At this, astonishment and grief tore the hearts of his servants. Yet no one in his company was permitted either to be troubled by grief beyond measure or to break out in foolish joy. So great was his authority and grace, and so vigorous the discipline around him, that it was delightful to every soul to see and hear him, although the expression of his face guarded against offense as against a great crime.

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 1421B] In July, on the eighteenth day of the month, he entered Aldenborg with a prosperous journey and the happy renown of his virtues. Preaching the kingdom of God there, he remained well for seven days. But on the day of Saint James the Apostle, after the holy solemnities of the Mass had been completed, he began to fall ill and suffered from sickness for twenty-one days.

When he was believed to be at the point of death, the brothers urged him to fortify himself with the holy offices, lest perhaps he leave this life without them. He answered them in a most gentle voice: “Dearest sons, do not be troubled at all about this, for through God’s mercy I know well what is fitting for me and when. I know the time and I know the hour; and I shall remind you of these things when the opportunity comes.”

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 1421C]

On the twentieth day after he had taken to his bed, when it was Friday, before midnight the cell in which he lay was shaken three times by a marvelous trembling and dreadful crash, and was almost thrown down from its foundations. The monks and servants keeping vigil before him shook with unbearable terror and, fearing the collapse of the cell, wished to flee outside.

The man of God soothed them with words of consolation and urged them to lie down to sleep, promising that no harm would follow. Then the priest and monk Everolf said to him weeping: “Lord, the earth trembles, the cell is shaken, the door which I have carefully locked for the third time is open again, the murmur of crowds resounds here and there; [Col. 1421D] how can we sleep amid so many terrors?”

The man of God replied: “Dear brother, do not be afraid, and let none of you be frightened, for all these things are signs of the heavenly Majesty. Later it will be revealed to you what power has caused this earthquake and the shaking of this cell.”

On the following Saturday, when the man of God felt the approach of death, after the customary morning hymns had been completed, he said to the brothers: “Now prepare the things necessary for our funeral, because around the beginning of the night I shall pass from this life. For the Lord, whom I have labored to serve according to my strength, disclosed this to me last night—although I had long known it before, when the crash of the cell was made dreadful by the earthquake and the disturbance of the air.

“At the first shaking the blessed Apostle Peter came, saying that all my sins were forgiven and that the gate [Col. 1422A] of life stood open to me. A multitude of the blessed accompanied him, singing divine praises in a loud voice:

The companies then sang the highest praises;  
The doors perceived it, which opened with so great a force.

“Such was the first spiritual procession. At the second shaking, Saint Michael the Archangel arrived with the company of blessed angels and promised that at the present hour I would enter the happy life under his guidance.

He spoke intently: ‘You shall suddenly receive the heavenly kingdoms with me as guide; you shall become a citizen of paradise.’  
When this had been said, they rejoice and form heavenly songs;  
The hearts even of the devout scarcely contain the force of such words.  
The mind was terrified by such things, though heavenly power overwhelmed it.

“At the third movement our Lady came, the true Mother [Col. 1422B] of mercy, with a company of holy virgins. Under the joy of her Assumption she promised, in a most gracious voice, that my soul would be assumed. But I adjure all of you, brothers, by the mercy of God, that while I yet live you tell no one these things.”

While, on the Ides of August, the funeral rites of the righteous man hasten,  
On Friday, dyed by Christ’s blood,  
At midnight signs come to those who understand:  
Shouting, singing, fragrance, tumult, and the voices of men;  
The voice of the people resounded with hymns and psalms,  
And the doors of the cell were thrown open as by a storm.  
From these singers worship is perceived; tumult is rightly felt.  
They praise in song, they rejoice, and they cry aloud.

The monks tremble with their servants at the vehement sound;  
They believe that they themselves are dying, giving their hearts to fear.  
[Col. 1422C] Praises burst forth, as though they said everywhere, “Applaud!”  
The songs of the psalms are uttered by the voices of men;  
Lest the performance fail, women supply the response.  
The monk is shaken by these things; the troop of servants is put to sleep.  
Here a strong man falls, believing the perils of death are present.  
This flesh is powerless while it serves the greedy world  
And lacks these gifts under the burden of its condition.  
This heavenly choir, sounding with divine praise,  
Resounds here and there; the people of heaven offer songs.  
The monk quakes, fears, burns, is troubled, and breathes heavily.  
That house echoes with praise and melodious choirs;  
Fragrance fills the cell, signifying that the maiden has entered—  
To visit the servant, she who deserved to give birth to the stag,  
Bearing horns and sanctifying by leaping.

[Col. 1422D] She herself is the Mother of God, through whom black Behemoth falls;  
She herself is the God-bearer, ever the lover of the righteous.  
She rightly cherishes the devout, whose names she already knows.  
She herself, speaking thus to Arnulf in her own voice,  
Addressed him: “Adorn yourself with many virtues, blessed one.  
When my Son raised me from the vale,  
Then, taking you up, he will raise you to the kingdoms of heaven.  
Uttering devout words, you shall celebrate my solemnities;  
And I shall lead for you at your feast a song of love with choirs.  
The virgin company rejoiced gladly with me as its leader;  
All the companies shall lead you onward with united joys.”

Afterward the monk Everolf, already frightened, arose,  
Pale and trembling, stunned by so great a sound.  
He approached the saint, giving utterance to grief from his whole heart:

“Thus, Father and bishop, for whom I am far from home,  
[Col. 1423A] Tell me and do not conceal; reveal what was done in the night.  
With sorrowful affection I urge you in Christ’s name:  
Tell me all things, since you weary me in body.  
Alas, most unhappy that I am! Your great praise is veiled by so many coverings,  
And the world, deep in dark death, does not know  
Who you are or what you are—how radiant and singular.”

As he said many such things or repeated such words,  
The bishop in gentle speech ordered them dismissed,  
Commanding rather that a matter so like the truth be kept silent.

“But if you, Father, love me, dearest brother,  
As a father, take care not to betray me as a prophet.  
Keep silent from the companion of my life until you know  
That I have passed through death; then afterward  
You may disclose the hidden causes or reveal them by true signs.  
I more strongly adjure you, brother, with Christ as judge,  
[Col. 1423B] That you keep silent concerning what I entrust to you until I depart from the light.

“First there came with Peter, the bishop of heaven,  
A company declaring that he was absolving my sins.  
The pious Peter himself uttered these words, saying:  
‘Those things entrusted to me stand wholly open to you;  
Fear no harm: through me the gate of the kingdom stands open.’

“I always enjoyed the friendly faces of angels,  
Who strengthened me by delaying my holy end;  
They made joy and sang a hymn to God.

“The third order was the company of the gracious Mother,  
Who visits us and has sent joys into the world—  
The one full of God’s grace, which remains with this Mother.  
She conceals nothing from us, but reveals all things to come.

“This Mother of the Lord did these things, sweetest brother.  
[Col. 1423C] In the accustomed manner the cell then underwent a crash;  
The doors are opened, pressed by such power.  
Then mighty singing resounds with a heavenly song.  
Your mind thus failed because it could not bear the weight.  
That greatest day arose which the sacred author sets forth:  
It is exceedingly festive, because on it God rises from the depths;  
The Virgin Mary, assumed into heaven, makes this day blessed.  
A third cause is given by which the feast is increased.

“Therefore I ask you: guard what I tell you.  
Receive the commands of the Lord: on that holy day,  
Take care that the rites of burial are not performed;  
Let a clean grave be prepared for me on the second day.  
Let these my commands be ready in your heart.”

The brother replied: “All that you command, pious Father,  
I shall observe; I shall prepare to omit none of it.  
[Col. 1423D] But, Father, I beg you to make these feasts known to us.  
What place is worthy in which to lay so great a pledge,  
When we can then do so, when the heavenly hymn  
Shall receive you above and a heavier grief shall burn us?”

The bishop replied and checked those anxious thoughts:  
“Before the burial, do not direct your care to this.  
A messenger will come, showing where for me  
The grave of the holy tomb is to be made and the entire order of burial.”

## CHAPTER XXXI

Accordingly, on the twenty-first day of his illness, a Saturday and the vigil of the Assumption of our glorious Lady, Mary the Mother of God and ever-Virgin, he summoned his disciples and also assembled the clergy of the neighboring [Col. 1424A] church. With psalms and litanies he caused himself to be anointed with holy oil, made confession before them all, and humbly asked the prayers of all:

And so he made confession, as though burdened by crime:  
“I have utterly gone astray; I have multiplied the enormity of my crimes.  
Monk and knight, I pursued youthful things;  
Keeping folly in my heart, I did not live as proper conduct requires.  
A great sinner, burdening myself by sinning against myself,  
I offended the King who gives the law above all things,  
By which whoever reveres God may be saved.  
Behold, as I die, I confess my unpunished fault;  
I beg that you remove it by your dear prayers.”

He taught those same brothers, saying: “Tomorrow there will be joy in heaven over the resurrection of the Lord, and joy among the holy angels will be doubled by the coming [Col. 1424B] of the Queen of Heaven. Through Christ’s gift, a third cause will be added, for which joy may be tripled. Therefore I forbid you to open the earth tomorrow for the work of my burial; reserve this for the second day of the week. For it has been appointed from heaven that, on the day of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, the little body of this sinner Arnulf shall be given back to the earth.”

> [Note: [Col. 1423D] You have his Life in Century II, under the year 640, p. 157.]

He foretold many things, both concerning the future condition of the kingdom and of that place, and concerning the future fates of princes and bishops; all of them came to pass as he prophesied. As evening was now approaching, he received with supreme devotion the body and blood of the Redeemer. Blessed by all, he asked to be blessed by all; then, longing for rest, he more devoutly adored the sign of the holy cross [Col. 1424C] and marked his whole body with it.

Then, laying himself on the floor strewn with ashes and haircloth, praying and blessing the name of the Lord, he received a happy sleep and entered the land of the living, to be united with the Lord. He died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord 1087.

## CHAPTER XXXII

When his death became known to the people, it is marvelous to say with what eagerness and devotion the crowds flowing in from every side filled the whole surrounding area. Clerics continued the psalms; some laymen provided refreshment for the poor who came running; and a very great multitude of nobles and knights exerted themselves greatly that the funeral rites of the holy bishop might be celebrated with exceptional splendor.

Such a multitude of clergy and people rushed together that not merely the basilica, but the court itself and the grounds adjoining it, could not contain so abundant a gathering. Some brought in lights; very many rejoiced that they had been worthy to attend such great obsequies.

When the blessed man’s body had been prepared according to custom, adorned with pontifical insignia, and brought into the church, Brother Everolf feared lest amid so mixed a crowd someone, desiring the golden ring on his hand, might snatch it away. He therefore took it and put it aside. But when the hour of burial arrived, he wished to place that same ring on the dead man’s finger. His cold hand and bent fingers were so stiff and hardened that they could not possibly be extended.

[Col. 1425A] Then the love of the faithful present was grieved by this difficulty, and with groaning they implored the Lord to grant that that holy body might not lack its proper honors. Bernard, provost of Guasten, was present at these obsequies, together with Ricoard the dean.

> [Note: [Col. 1425D] Another manuscript, Gitaleniensis, reads: “with Richard.”]

There was also a very great crowd of priests and clerics. At their urging and with their leading voice, psalms were sung, the litany followed, and the assembly of laypeople wept. Suddenly the wonderful God made his saint wonderful in the eyes of those present. Truly, marvelous to say: while they lamented, the dead man’s right hand raised itself from his breast, separated the fingers by lifting them, and made room for the insertion of the ring. Once it had been inserted, that same hand returned to its former position and bent its fingers beneath the palm as before.

[Col. 1425B]

The people’s voice is borne forth; at once all things are given to praise,  
And they weep the more because they ever honor the saint.  
He retains the rewards of virtues, he who was their seeker.  
When the bishop has been translated and set in a dwelling away from earth,  
His lordly body is conveyed to the church of Peter.  
The flock of people and monks prepares the funeral service;  
The priests come, the clergy goes forth, and the companies hasten.

Bearing lights for the saints, of every sort of people;

Meals are given to the poor, gifts likewise to the clergy;

The duties of Mass are here celebrated abundantly and beyond measure;

And the festal day of Christ or of his Mother

Is observed with lofty solemnity, awaiting the following Monday.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

And now the bright morning of Monday had come.

[Col. 1425C] An angel descending from heaven points out openly,

With speech, the place where they should duly make the tomb;

He shows it to the brethren, then hastens back to ascend to heaven;

And they make the tomb on Monday,

The table shown from heaven by a heavenly gift:

For Peter’s church becomes the coffin of the holy body;

And beside the cloisters which are on the left side,

A grave is prepared in which the holy man may be laid;

In the month of August the holy man gave his funeral rites to the grave,

He is placed in the tomb, leaving to the world pledges of his limbs.

Lamentation and groaning, sighs from the depths of the heart—

Oh, how many are uttered! how often then repeated!

The heart’s love cries out; love’s ardour bellows and wails;

To him is given a staff as the sign of his episcopate;

[Col. 1425D] A pewter staff and chalice become witnesses of his celebrating sacrifice.

Lead tablets are inscribed, to be read when later found;

And a tablet of suitable size is placed in the cavity of his breast;

The bishop’s mitre is displayed with the appropriate vestments;

Golden sandals are placed upon the saint’s feet;

Such adornments that blessed man took with him,

By which it might be evident with what worthy splendour

His spirit, happy in heaven and living through the ages, shone.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Now, therefore, it must be considered and held in faithful remembrance through what great labours and what kinds of afflictions this servant of Christ deserved such efficacy of power [Col. 1426A] that even the limbs of the dead man should flourish in the renown of miracles. For he did not receive such a gift from Christ by serving throat and belly and pursuing human desires, but by mortifying his body, keeping watch over God’s commandments, adhering to true charity, and increasing and persevering day by day in the way of righteousness. And because the chamber of his heart, after the body had been subdued, had rightly been purified, the Holy Spirit was pleased to glorify the one who glorified him, and to make the one who served him purely lovable and praiseworthy in the sight of all people.

Let those who read these things, then, consider them attentively and gather into prudent memory this man’s prophecy: for many days beforehand, while living at the castle of Ulciacum in the district of Soissons, he had foretold that no bishop or abbot would come together to celebrate the rites [Col. 1426B] of his funeral, but that everything concerning him would be supplied by his monk and priest. For such and so great an occupation hindered the neighbouring abbots—two of Ghent and one of Bergues—so that, although earnestly invited and willing to come, they were in no way able to do so.

Therefore, after the solemnities of the Masses had been celebrated by many priests who had assembled from all sides, and most generous alms had been distributed for the use of the poor, on the day upon which the anniversary of holy Arnulf, bishop of Metz, is remembered, the body of this holy man was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter at Aldenborg, and was marked by the following epitaph.

> [Note: The author of this epitaph is said by Surius to have been Regemarus, a monk of Saint-Bertin.]

[Col. 1426C] A knight in this world, now dust in this tomb,

He despised the warfare of the world for love of God.

By whose protection one lives free from complaint,

First, devoutly, a monk of Soissons;

And soon, a yet more devout inhabitant of a narrow cell,

Through poverty, cold, and hunger,

And through sleepless nights spent in tears and prayer,

He raised himself through the pursuit and merits of virtues.

Then made abbot and bishop—both against his will—

What he worthily underwent, he cultivated still more worthily.

At last, coming here by the Lord’s gift,

Closing his final day in death, he passed into rest.

His passing befell him at the close of the day

Followed by that famous day which the whole world observes,

On which the heavenly company bore Mary,

Mistress of heaven, from the valley of the world

[Col. 1426D] into the star-bearing choirs of heaven;

On the festal day of Bishop Arnulf,

The body of Bishop Arnulf is covered with earth.

This little work was completed in the twenty-eighth year after his passing, in the seventh indiction, which we believe to be the year 1114 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Louis, son of King Philip—whose reign this man of God had prophesied before his birth—held the kingdom of the Franks, in the seventh year of his reign; while blessed Pope Paschal II presided over the Roman Church; while Lord Ralph, archbishop, governed the metropolitan see of Reims; and while [Col. 1427A] our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ reigns, to whom, with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, be all honour and [Col. 1428A] glory, praise and dominion through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

> [Note: In Surius’s edition these words occur: “At the end of my little book my apologetic is to be fashioned,” etc., as in the preliminary Observations, no. 1.]

## PREFACE OF BISHOP LISIARD TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS, IN THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 1427]

[Col. 1427A] To the lord Ralph, deservedly and rightly beloved, venerable archbishop of the Church of Reims by God’s grace: Lisiard, his son, would-be worthy minister of the holy Church of Soissons, greeting and the victorious palm of the godly.

While your fatherhood sat in that great council, attended by an unheard-of multitude of bishops, which was celebrated at Reims under the authority of Lord Pope Calixtus—

> [Note: This council was held in 1119 on the question of investitures, at which Emperor Henry was excommunicated. Five canons were issued there. Louis VI, king of the Franks, was present and complained much before the Fathers concerning the king of the English.]
