—and while I too, humble as I was, remained at your side, your brother and fellow bishop Lambert, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, complained publicly to us that it seemed unjust and grievous to him—and not to him alone but to many—that the holy bishop Arnulf, my predecessor, who had lived a holy life pleasing to God, and whose holiness had been strongly confirmed by the Lord through many [Col. 1427B] miracles, should still lie in the bosom of moist earth.

The royal majesty was present as witness to his miracles, having been granted pardon through the tears and prayers of Saint Arnulf himself. Peter, archdeacon of Soissons, was present, who confessed, with the testimony of many, that he had been born blind and had received sight through the saliva from the mouth of Arnulf, the man of God. I too was present, though less worthy: I rejoiced greatly that he had consecrated me to the order of subdeacon; and, having once lived with him, I had come to know more fully his abstinence [Col. 1428A] and rule of life. I had heard many prophecies and had personally witnessed no few miracles.

When many persons bore witness to these and many similar matters, your fatherhood was pleased to say: “Why do you burden me with your reports, when I myself know his works of holiness better than you? I saw him perform a dedication at Mont Calvus, where a woman from the village called Caviniacum,

> For three periods of five years afflicted by injuries to her eyes,  
> threw herself before the saint’s face with a pleading voice.  
> There was no delay once the bishop had blessed her:  
> her eyelid opened, the light appeared, and the woman saw.

“But let that be. He may have performed wonders; he may have lived righteously. I do not say that he should be raised up unless God’s grace gives heavenly testimony through very clear signs. The Roman Church is present; the lord pope himself is present. Let the matter be brought before their consideration, and let their examination follow from it.”

This was done, and with one harmonious voice they adopted your judgment. Therefore we have resolved, in this present little book, to inform you and Mother Church what and how great miracles the Lord and Saviour has deigned to show around his dead bones after he was buried, so that your prior knowledge, by its authority, may make the reading of it safer and more useful for others.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD BOOK BEGIN

[Col. 1427]

I. On the fiery radiance and the crucifix leaping forth.  
II. On the dust gathered around his tomb.  
III. On the terror sent from heaven against those who sought to steal him.  
IV. On a contracted woman healed there.  
V. On candles there lit from heaven.  
VI. On the multitude of sick persons restored there.  
VII. On a dropsical man healed.  
VIII. On a whale overcome through his name.  
IX. On a paralysed woman healed.  
X. On two old men improved there.  
XI. On a cripple restored there.  
XII. On a man healed on the night of Saint John the Baptist, the eighth day before the Kalends of July [24 June].  
XIII. On the relics of Saint Arnulf not being burned in a burned church.  
XIV. On a man who fell ill because he did not fulfil a vow.  
XV. On the elevation of his body.  
XVI. On three miracles then performed.  
XVII. On a sphere appearing in heaven.  
XVIII. On a man weakened for rejecting peace.  
XIX. On Bishop Belgoto, who succeeded him against his will and soon perished.

> [Note: Nothing whatever concerning that bishop occurs in this book. Indeed, Bishop Hilgot of Soissons—of whom this heading seems intended to speak—did not perish quickly, but, after about twelve years of rule, withdrew in 1088 to Marmoutier near Tours, where he later became abbot. His defence was written by Ivo, bishop of Chartres, in a letter to Pope Paschal II.]

## THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1429]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1429A]

After this blessed servant of God had happily been removed from human affairs, various miracles were performed by the Lord around his remains, and very many cures were granted to the sick. Not far from his tomb stood an altar, with a great cross placed beneath it, bearing an image of the crucified Lord. Two spiritual brothers saw a fiery globe or flash burst from the face and breast of that image and swiftly leap into his tomb around his breast. This sign makes it understood that he who bore our sins in his body upon the tree bestowed upon this servant of his the joys of the true light.

At a later time, though in the same year, the tomb itself was split from its head-end beyond its feet and divided in a straight line, [Col. 1429B] as though it had been cut along a ruler. This division or fissure, a preceding omen of his imminent elevation, made its meaning known to all minds.

## CHAPTER II

From the very first time of his burial, such ardour of faith and devotion shone forth around him that whoever came, either in person or by messengers, to the tomb of Saint Arnulf, and gathered the dust that was blowing about its circuit, carried it away as though it were a sure medicine. By mixing that dust into their food or drink, or by licking and swallowing the dry dust, they escaped every illness and obtained a most certain remedy with greater speed. This happened not four, seven, or ten times, but, as is well known, a thousand times.

We saw a demoniac [Col. 1429C] grievously tormented. When that dust was put into his mouth against his will, he immediately escaped the enemy and recovered his mind. This celebrated dust carried the knowledge of its great benefit not only through our France but to every neighbouring region. England, Gaul, Scotland, and Frisia: foreign peoples thus possessed and at the same time carried off the ashes to their homelands.

## CHAPTER III

After these and many similar things became widely known, and this praiseworthy report spread through France, while a pleasing fragrance continually issued from his tomb, the monks of Saint-Médard, deeply grieved that they lacked the remains of so great a man, made a plan with their abbot Odo: under the pretext of a visit, they would go to Aldenborg, [Col. 1429D] secretly open his tomb, remove the bones, and carry them with all speed to their monastery at Soissons.

They came there and, having prepared the instruments for this undertaking, began by night to open his tomb from the right side. At once a huge crash thundered from heaven, shaking the diggers and deterring them, in extreme consternation, from their enterprise. A little later, recovering themselves and supposing the event to have arisen from some hidden disturbance of the air, they returned to the tomb to complete what they had begun. But as soon as they started to dig, the crash sounded again in terrible rebuke.

They were struck senseless and fell to the ground. At last, when they had recovered breath, they fled in great terror. While standing at a distance and muttering in subdued tones, the thought came upon them to repeat their rashness a third time and try once again whether any result might follow. They came trembling; they put forth fearful hands; but immediately, for the third time, intolerable terror struck them down. They were dashed upon the pavement, lay gasping and senseless, and, almost dead, did not know what had happened to them. When three hours had passed, they returned to consciousness and, in their great distress, vowed never again to attempt rashly to violate the holy body or its tomb.

Arnulf, nephew of the holy bishop himself and first abbot of Aldenborg, attempted this deed with two monks: Godebert, an Aldenborg man by birth, and Balrad of Bruges. Their report made known that these events happened in this manner.

## CHAPTER IV

At a later time, a most miserable woman, hideously twisted by a contraction, was brought there. Her knees were fixed against her breast; the palms of her hands were bound under her hams; and her buttocks were likewise joined, skin against skin, to those same limbs. Through the efforts of a compassionate crowd she was laid before the tomb of Saint Arnulf. There she seemed to rest a little, and by a divine gift, to the honour of God’s servant, she was healed and raised upright. Walking straight through the church and part of the church, she showed the places on her limbs, dreadful with blood, where [Col. 1430C] one part had formerly adhered to and been folded and joined with another.

## CHAPTER V

It often happened that lights there appeared to be kindled from heaven. But lest we seem to report something fictitious or contrived by any device, what we narrate is supported by a thousand witnesses. The chief feast was being celebrated on the first day of May, and a multitude of people had filled the place from every side. Behold: at the third hour of the day, as the solemn procession took place, two candles being carried were extinguished by the wind at the church door. But when they reached the tomb of Saint Arnulf, those very candles were immediately lit—and so lit that they could not be extinguished by the gust of wind.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1430D] In the year 1115 from the Lord’s Incarnation, a plague of raging diseases arose throughout the whole neighbouring region among persons of both sexes and every age. Then bearers of the sick hurried there in companies, striving to lay their patients around the tomb of Arnulf, Christ’s servant. So abundant was the grace poured out in restoring the afflicted that from mid-April to the middle of August, when his passing is celebrated, there were sixty [Col. 1431A] cures of persons known to us, besides those healed in such a manner that they did not come to our knowledge. Likewise, in the following year, from May until August, restoration was granted there to fifty persons of both sexes and various ages.

## CHAPTER VII

Among them there came a dropsical man, greatly swollen by distension of his belly and veins. He sprinkled into water dust taken from the low turf adjoining the tomb, drank the water, and immediately received health.

## CHAPTER VIII

At the same time, fishermen leaving this part of Flanders surrounded an enormous whale, [Col. 1431B] wounding it with lances and javelins in order to bring it, once subdued, to land and enrich themselves from the beast’s death. But the monstrous animal, though it had been severely wounded with javelins and lances, could neither be captured nor calmed. More maddened by pain, now it cast waters up to heaven, now it plunged itself into the deep, now it rose again from the deep and, by the force of its tail and fins, shattered the ships’ rigging.

In this great difficulty, one said to his companions: “Let us invoke Saint Arnulf of Aldenborg and vow him a share of the fish. I trust that through his aid we shall quickly overcome this beast.” They did so. Immediately the whale ceased raging and afforded the calmest opportunity for being captured and bound with ropes.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1431C]

On the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension, during the chanting of the holy Gospel in the evening synaxis, a paralysed woman was healed.

> [Note: This seems to refer to the canticle *Magnificat*, since no other portion of the holy Gospel appears to have been sung at that time in the evening synaxis.]

## CHAPTER X

On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, while we were holding vigils at night, a man was healed there.

## CHAPTER XI

Two elderly men, also advanced in age, violently afflicted by a severe and similar disorder, regretted being alive. For intestines that had descended into the genitals of each inflicted upon them intense suffering and difficulty in living. Having heard of the graces of [Col. 1431D] Blessed Arnulf, they came with great labour to the tomb, and their distress was changed by God’s providence into saving joy. Through the merits and prayers of Saint Arnulf their intestines were drawn upward and restored to their natural position. Those who had come there with the greatest difficulty returned free and cheerful, with the joy of health.

## CHAPTER XII

On the Friday of Pentecost week, a young man grieving that he had a withered hand came and threw himself before the shrine-tomb of Saint Arnulf, repeatedly invoking the saint’s compassion with much weeping. While the Gospel lesson [Col. 1432A] was being recited, his hand was healed and perfectly restored.

## CHAPTER XIII

Before the bones of Saint Arnulf were raised from the ground, the church of Saint Peter possessed many relics of that saint: namely, the whole furnishing of his private chapel. From these relics the brethren gave a certain portion to some men from the island of Scolda, that they might build a church in Christ’s name under the title of Saint Arnulf. When that church had been built and an altar erected, they placed a reliquary of these relics in the altar.

It happened through negligence that the church caught fire and was burned to its foundations. Yet the reliquary of Saint Arnulf’s relics remained untouched and wholly unharmed by the flames upon the altar. [Col. 1432B] Moreover, the altar-cloth remained unburned wherever it touched or lay beneath the reliquary.

## CHAPTER XIV

On the island called Bevelauda—that is, “Trembling Land”—certain nobles, headed by Alvisus son of Landrada and his brother Ellicus, were engaged in strife and litigation against their peers, men equally noble. It happened that one man, named Wido, was wounded in the hand before Ellicus’s gate and lost two fingers, the middle and the index finger, remaining disabled and maimed in two fingers. On this account great enmity prevailed between Wido and his friends on the one side, and Alvisus, Ellicus, and their friends or accomplices on the other, until the shrine of Saint Arnulf was brought into those regions to make [Col. 1432C] peace among peoples who did not know God.

The man disfigured by the loss of two fingers was found in the church by monks and clerics, prostrate before him. As the relics of Saint Arnulf lay on the ground before him, he was compelled to promise that he would make peace with Alvisus and Ellicus, formerly his enemies. As a pledge of that undertaking, they made him place the glove of his hand upon the bier of the relics. Out of reverence for the saints present, he complied for the moment. But on returning home, reproachfully rebuked by his kinsmen and retainers, he turned away from good and neglected to fulfil what he had promised Saint Arnulf.

Immediately a severe illness seized him. Held by it, he lay sick [Col. 1432D] for twenty-one days, taking neither sleep nor food and wasting away more grievously day by day, until he was reduced to sending for a priest and considering his funeral. Then the priest said to him: “All this illness, which you have endured for so long, is justly inflicted because you lied to Saint Arnulf. But if you trust me and do not refuse in good heart to grant the peace you promised and forgiveness for the wrong done to your maimed fingers, I hope in the living God that you will recover and find your life restored to prosperity.”

Without any deliberation, he said: “Bring me that holy cross.” When it had been brought before his hands, he said: “Behold, I know with complete certainty that I incurred this illness because of [Col. 1433A] my falsehood. But if Saint Arnulf now intercedes for me, so that I may live, I vow and swear upon this cross that I will wholly fulfil whatever I formerly promised concerning peace and forgiveness for my fingers.”

Having said this and, by a new gift, completed a new vow upon the cross, he immediately added: “If I have a friend or faithful servant, let him see that I eat quickly; for fear of death is leaving me, and the whole hope of life is succeeding to me.” Why say more? Restored immediately by food and drink, he recovered. On the third day afterwards he mounted horses, entered Flanders, sought Aldenborg, and did penance before the brethren. Returning to his home, he completely fulfilled everything that had been demanded of him and everything that he himself had first vowed, and he remained steadfast in the peace he had promised.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 1433B]

After these and other proofs of heavenly grace had become widely known to Lord Bishop Lambert and the faithful people, that bishop took counsel at the Council of Beauvais, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October], with certain of his fellow bishops, as to what ought to be done in response to so great a manifestation of God.

> [Note: We infer that this synod was held in 1120 because chapter 17 below says that the elevation took place in May 1121.]

There were present the bishops of France: William [of Champeaux], bishop of Châlons, pillar of the teachers; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; Delbert [Dambert], archbishop of Sens; [Henry], bishop of Orléans; [Gilbert], bishop of Paris; Clarembald, bishop of Senlis; Peter, bishop of Beauvais; Angilram, bishop of Amiens; Robert, bishop of Arras; [Col. 1433C] John, bishop of the Morini; Lambert, bishop of Tournai; Borgard [Burchard], bishop of Cambrai; Bartholomew of Laon; I, Lisiard, unworthy bishop of Soissons; and a great multitude of abbots, archdeacons, provosts, and clergy.

> [Note: That is, William of Champeaux, as he is commonly called, from his birthplace in the diocese of Paris.]

Among the others the abbot of Aldenborg himself was present, carrying in his hands a little book concerning the life, conduct, and miraculous acts of Saint Arnulf. Taking the book from his hands, I opened it and, opened, presented it to the bishops, saying: “Behold, lords: this little book concerning his life was written, with my knowledge and at my instigation. I testify in faith that everything it relates is true, and I produce truthful witnesses to his miracles, some here and very many more at home. I ask you to consider this book carefully, so that from knowledge of it you may be better informed what ought to be done concerning him. But let your holiness hear my judgment: if he rested in the diocese entrusted to me, he would not have lain long in the earth.”

Then William, bishop of Châlons, took the book. Looking through its beginning, he saw the number of chapters and said to the bishop of Tournai: “Lord, what more do you seek? Even without this book, the testimony of the lord bishop of Soissons and his clergy is sufficient for you. Such an abbot should inspire great confidence in you: his age commands respect, and his prudence is pleasing. As for this little book, we have no leisure to run through it because we are occupied with synodal business.”

Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, said: “Lord bishop of Tournai, I tell you truly: if the Lord had done such things even once around any of my predecessors, I would consult neither pope, legate, nor even archbishop; with complete confidence I would exalt God’s saint as he deserves.”

Meanwhile, while the bishops deliberated these matters, certain noble masters of the schools had taken the little book and quickly read some chapters of its deeds. Returning to where the bishops were, some of them declared with great confidence: “Truly, whoever opposes the exaltation of this saint is not of God.”

Then William, bishop of Châlons, said: “By God, it is shameful that we doubt concerning a matter so manifest. Therefore, lord bishop of Tournai, by the Lord’s grace, put uncertainty aside; appoint a day on which you may gather at the place and honourably reinter the Lord’s holy servant when he has been raised from the earth.”

Lambert, bishop of Tournai, said: “Behold, the legate is sitting at a distance in this very basilica with our archbishop of Reims, or of Tours [perhaps Sens]. I ask you: may it please you to go before them and conform your judgment to their decision.”

The bishops said: “Let it be done in the name of the Lord.” When they came, Bishop Lambert said to the bishop of Châlons: “I ask you: plead my cause.” When he had briefly and eloquently presented the matter before the legate and the archbishops, both the legate Conon and the archbishop of Reims replied with one voice: [Col. 1434C] “We fully accept the judgment of your authority and confirm the decree of your consensus.”

Accordingly Bishop Lambert summoned the abbot and appointed the day on which he should come to Aldenborg—namely, the Kalends of May [1 May]—and should raise the holy body of the man of God from the earth and reinter it, according to the custom of the Gallican Church, as one truly holy. He also gave letters sealed with his seal, summoning all the people of the diocese of Tournai to so holy an office.

Swift-flying report, racing on its rapid course,

Caused diverse peoples to visit these places.

Let us say nothing of Flanders. The people of Walcheren, Scolda, Beveland, Antwerp, Texandria, Waas, Brabant, Menapia, the Morini, Boulogne, and other regions were present in abundance. At the appointed time the bishop arrived with the honourable Robert, archdeacon of Tournai, and a great company of clergy. The trophy of the cross was borne before them; the holy Gospel-book was also brought. Amid candles and perfumes, with the clergy singing, the tomb of the holy man was opened and the blessed bones were raised from their dusty resting-place.

A chalice buried with him stood over his breast; a lead tablet also lay beneath the chalice before his breast. The inscribed tablet contained his name, homeland, lineage, military service, conversion, promotion to the abbacy, the day of his ordination as bishop, and the day of [Col. 1435A] his passage from this world to Christ. When this tablet was raised from the saint’s breast and left with the bishop standing by, it gave him great joy. He had feared that, misled by some error, the brethren might raise under a saint’s name not Saint Arnulf but some unworthy person. Likewise, when they showed the bishop the pastoral slip of parchment, he rejoiced greatly.

> [Note: That is, a little written document (*schedula*), as we have already noted elsewhere.]

Finally, when he saw the sandals embroidered with gold taken out, he dissolved into tears. Three men who had received priestly ordination were chosen to receive the bones and raise them from the tomb: Abbot Ariulf [elsewhere, erroneously, Arnulf], the monk Godwin, and the monk Hagaming. When the abbot raised the skull from the earth and placed it in a chest prepared for the purpose, behold: his hands were found plump and soaked with the liquid of oil, [Col. 1435B] as though he had dipped them into a vessel full of oil.

Behold, before God, it is true—and what is said is true—that a fragrance of great sweetness was also spread there. Nor was this without reason. For one who strove during mortal life in every place to be Christ’s good fragrance deserved, now crowned by God through the bounty of him whom he served, to be honoured with a heavenly fragrance. Meanwhile the enclosure of the church resounded with praises of the blessed Trinity. Until the blessed bones, clothed with worthy honour, were placed in the shrine, both bishop and clergy devoted themselves to divine words. When the bones had been brought into the shrine, the bishop immediately began the hymn: “We praise thee, O God; we acknowledge thee to be the Lord.”

After this hymn had been sung with rejoicing as many as a thousand times, the saint was carried outside the church to the appointed station, indeed by the hand of soldiers. [Col. 1435C] So great a multitude rushed upon the saint that they trampled, shoved, and bruised one another excessively; and through love for the saint no one spared either himself or another. Devotion and longing for the saint had so cast aside all bounds of reason that neither abbot nor monks could by any means approach the saint.

## CHAPTER XVI

Divine miracles were not lacking. The one true God in Trinity, whom Arnulf had served purely, displayed there a threefold miracle. For a young man possessed by hostile force, and for that reason long driven into madness, was there freed from the enemy and granted both bodily health and freedom of mind. Two women likewise, struck by paralysis and wholly deprived of the use of their limbs, were restored to complete health. These three signs were performed inside the church, but did not become sufficiently public knowledge among the people dispersed through streets and fields, because the dense multitude of people packed the basilica so closely that no one there could speak openly, no one could turn in any direction, and no one could hear anything except the roar of the tumultuous crowd.

## CHAPTER XVII

God in heaven, taking pleasure in his Saint Arnulf, then gave a sign from heaven as well. From the first hour until the full sixth hour, there appeared in [Col. 1436A] heaven a burning sphere like a flame of fire, which hung over the holy body of the blessed man. Across the sphere shone the sign of the holy cross, like the purest gold tested in a furnace. This cross surpassed all the sun’s splendour by its brightness; by its length it also exceeded the breadth of the said sphere, extending beyond it by its four ends and glowing with intense brilliance like gold.

This sign seen in heaven certainly seems to signify a heavenly mystery. For what does the sphere represent, except the breadth of the world? And what does the vision of the cross denote, except the mortification of the earthly body? What do gold and golden brightness indicate, except the clarity of eternal wisdom and inward contemplation of the divine light? A flame appeared in the sphere [Col. 1436B] because throughout the world it is known—indeed, it shall be known—that the charity of God was poured out in Arnulf’s heart through the Holy Spirit given to him. If it was given, it was given by the God of heaven. Rightly, therefore, a sign glorifying Arnulf appeared in heaven.

And let no one say, “Who knew Arnulf?” We say that he is very well known, who rightly deserves to be known by heaven. For the Prophet does not deceive when he says: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psalm 111 [112]). The sphere which appeared in heaven, therefore, represented the extent of his good fame; its fiery appearance, the ardour of inward charity. The cross signifies martyrdom; the golden brightness, the mystical understanding of divine charity; the length of the cross surpassing the sphere indicates the holy perseverance of blessed mortification.

Blessed and holy Arnulf could say: [Col. 1436C] “My citizenship is in heaven”; he could say: “All the lovable or delightful things of the world that I have left behind I reckon as dung.” Such a man deserved to be revealed by such signs.

## CHAPTER XVIII

This translation of Saint Arnulf took place on the first day of May, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the fourteenth year of Louis, son of Philip, as holder of the sceptres of the Franks; while Charles, son of the king of the Danes—whose mother had been the daughter of Count Robert—held the county of Flanders; and while Abbot Hariulf had already ruled the monastery of Aldenborg for sixteen years.

It was observed that, with the elevation of the blessed man, abundance of crops, health of bodies, and wholesome weather came to the region of Flanders. Before this, for seven years it had suffered grievously from inundations of rain, barrenness of the fields, plague among animals, and frequent mortality among human beings.

> [Note: The table of chapters makes no mention of the matters contained in this chapter, but instead gives the subject of the following chapter.]

## CHAPTER XIX
On the third Sunday after Easter, when the Introit of the Mass is sung, “Make a joyful noise unto God, all the earth, alleluia,” the blessed bodily elevation of Saint Arnulf took place. Eighteen days after that Sunday came the splendid solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension, the fortieth day from the holy day of the Resurrection. This solemnity of the Ascension is observed in the town of Aldenburg with a greater concourse than other feasts, because solemn fairs are held there on that day; and therefore the people, free from their labours, gather in greater numbers than usual. On this occasion, when mixed crowds were rushing in from every side, it happened that three knightly brothers from one neighbourhood met two other brothers, also knights and separate from them, who were enemies of those three, because the three had recently killed the two brothers’ brother.

Now the three killers of the other brothers’ brother came to the abbot and monks of that place and most humbly begged them to bring assistance by working for their reconciliation. The abbot and monks, readily asking where the two bereaved brothers were, took with them the bier of blessed Arnulf and suddenly came to where they were sitting and had begun to dine. When the elder brother saw the monks and the holy bier, he understood that they had come to compel him. At once, throwing aside the dishes and cups, he wished to rise and flee; but by the power of the Lord and the merits of Saint Arnulf, his buttocks adhered to the bench and his feet to the footstool, and thus shackled and restrained he sat down again against his will. When the monks asked him for forgiveness, he answered with foolish words.

[Col. 1438A] Why delay with many words? His insolent tongue, fierce eyes, and the disordered movements of his whole body showed that he was out of his mind; and his friends wept for him as one already given over to death. Then the younger brother made a vow, saying: “Saint Arnulf, have mercy on me, and restore to me the life of my brother. Behold, I vow and promise that, if my brother escapes, I shall become a friend to these enemies for love of you; and I shall draw him himself, willing or unwilling, to make with them a covenant of perpetual peace.”

The monks present, hearing this, rejoiced; and, taking water, they moistened the feet of the bier, then took up that water and poured it into his mouth and over all his face. Then he, as if awakened from a heavy sleep, recovered himself; afterwards, calling to his loudly lamenting brother, he said: “Rejoice, brother, for I have come back to life. Through the prayers of Saint Arnulf, God has allowed me to live.” Rising, he worshipped with [Col. 1438B] great devotion. Then he received his brother’s killers as friends with great affection, and, under the guarantee of an oath, promised them that he would keep a lasting peace. Thus to enemies came favour, to those who hated came goodwill, to blessed Arnulf came the reverence of honour, and to Christ our God came praise and glory for his name, unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1437]

## A COMPENDIUM OF THE LIFE OF THE SAME SAINT ARNULF

(From the same manuscript codices.)

[Col. 1437C] 1. Although Brabant was once the nurse and mistress of disputes and robberies, and although it has been said in a truthful poem:

> As many vines as France possesses, so many lawsuits has Brabant,

yet in the time of Count Baldwin and Countess Adela it deserved to be illumined by a heavenly gift, when it deserved to bring forth in its bosom Arnulf, a man of holy memory and a future bishop, begotten for the enlightenment of not a few people; or rather, a ray made radiant by the Sun of righteousness. His father, Fulbert, cousin of Godelef’s mother, shone with illustrious nobility; and his mother, named Mainsindis, born from the stock of Teutonic nobles, was distinguished by notable free birth.

These illustrious parents, flourishing in carnal and spiritual offspring, had a son already grown, outstanding in elegance of appearance and military deeds. Suddenly untimely death carried him off and crushed his parents’ hearts with the agony of irremediable sorrow. Yet the mother’s affection mourned more urgently for the loss of her child [Col. 1437D] and prolonged her days and nights in weeping. As she slept under excessive anxiety, a beautiful man appeared to her, resplendent in shining light, and said:

“Why do you afflict yourself with grief for a son who has died so profitably? If he had lived longer, he would indeed have become dissolute, a robber, and a companion of wicked men. Rather rejoice with great joy, because you carry in your womb a son whom heavenly election has predestined to become great. When you bring him into the light, you will wish him to be called Christopher, for this child will truly bear Christ in his breast by his deeds and words. And that you may know with certainty that these things have been divinely ordained, go to the church and have digging done in the place where you are accustomed to pray. When the earth is dug up, you will find a stone inscribed with large letters; those letters will disclose to you the name and merit of your offspring.”

The venerable matron, having received this oracle of so great a promise, awoke from sleep and [Col. 1438C] related the vision to her husband with immense joy. Finally, to test the truth of the matter, she took servants and a digger; having them dig as she had been instructed, she found a square tile inscribed with large letters, reading:

> CHRISTOPHER.

Having found it, she was filled with greater joy; now certain of the holiness of the offspring whom she had not previously known herself to have conceived, she joyfully awaited the promised gift of divine operation.

At length, when he grew up, he began to be gentle in speech, keen in intellect, ready in obedience, eager in work, effective and very strong in bodily power. Then, having cheerfully completed his period of training, he received the military belt and was superior in military affairs to every human excellence.

2. After his father’s death, however, he entered the monastic order; and in the church of Saint Medard at Soissons he showed himself a proven monk, fervently not only in the fellowship of the cloister but also in solitary enclosure. Thereafter, when Abbot Rainald died, [Col. 1438D] Arnulf was chosen as abbot; judging himself unequal to this office, he attempted to evade it by fleeing at night.

Thus, after escaping for one day, while he sought a more remote hiding-place on the following night, he was led back to the city by the companionship of wolves. In the morning he was seized and, unwillingly, installed by episcopal authority in the seat from which he had fled. Then he ended the long silence which he had maintained for three years and six months; and, appointed a herald of the Lord, he strove to benefit all by word and deed.

Toiling in the office of governance, he performed many miracles: he subdued the rebellious and unbelieving; he healed the sick by the gift of God’s grace; he restored sight to the blind; he flourished in the spirit of prophecy. It became known to all that he was truly holy and pleasing to God. At that time Philip, king of the Franks, wished him to come to the royal court in order to take part in arranging the affairs of the kingdom; he also wished him to take part in an armed expedition. Since the servant of Christ perceived that both [Col. 1439A] were contrary to his earlier profession, he refused; and, lest he offend God, he did not fear to offend the earthly king in this matter. He preferred not only to incur the king’s displeasure but also to abandon entirely the care of the abbey, fearing, of course, that after putting his hand to the plough, if he looked back, he would not be fit for the kingdom of God.

3. Thus, he who remained faithful in little things was set over many, so that—without prejudice to the higher meaning—he restrained within himself the crowds of all vices and the limits of every sin, and, enriched by an abundance of virtues, pleased God and good men. For the Lord glorified him in the sight of the kings and nobles of the realm, in the esteem of the lord Pope Gregory of Rome, and of the whole clergy; so much so that, when the church of Soissons languished through the negligence of Ursio, no remedy could be found except that this blessed servant of Christ should, by the pope’s counsel, assume pastoral charge of that church.

Therefore, while the court of the Franks refused [alternative reading: assented] to this decision, but the apostolic authority of the Roman pontiff compelled it, he was consecrated bishop, after a canonical election had preceded, so that the lamp of God’s grace might no longer be hidden in a corner but, set upon a lampstand, might shine for all.

Certainly, when he was going to Hugh, bishop of Die and then legate of the Roman See, for consecration, he sent a message to the queen of the Franks, most sorrowful because of her long barrenness, declaring to her that she bore in the womb a son not yet alive with vital breath, but who after a few days would receive the spirit of life from the Lord. He foretold both his name—Louis—and openly prophesied that, after his father’s death, he would become king and enjoy a more abundant peace.

In December, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, he received the sacred episcopal blessing; and, on his return, barely escaped the devoted violence of the clergy and people of Vienne, who would have carried him off to be their bishop if they could have captured him. Finally, when he came to the see of Soissons, [Col. 1439C] the armed force of the royal household came out against him and strove to kill the blessed bishop, but feared lest the earth should swallow them alive. The man of God yielded to those standing against him and, with Count Theobald’s support, took up his residence in the castle of Ulcy; there, with prelates and nobles of the people assembled, ecclesiastical business was carefully conducted, the welfare of clergy and people was settled to the last detail, and the salvation of souls was pursued.

4. On one occasion, when he was going to dedicate the parish church of a certain village, he said to his attendants: “Lead us, I beg you, to that church by such a path that the people may not know by which road we must come; and bring some provisions with you, so that we may at least somewhat relieve bodily fatigue.”

Accordingly, they took a more remote and winding path; yet the people’s zeal was not cooled by this device, but with all speed a great company of travellers gathered from every side. Seeing this, the servant of God burst forth in praise of the Creator and then said to his household: “Bring out whatever provisions you have here, that after our labour we may restore our strength.”

Without delay five biscuits were brought out and five half-measures of wine were poured. Then carpets were spread upon the ground, and the man of God sat down, while a flowing multitude surrounded him in groups. Blessing them, he ordered the few loaves in number—but many in the mystery of their number—to be distributed to all who were seated round about, and likewise that wine should be served in sufficient quantity. The servants marvelled that the bread did not fail; they marvelled also that so little wine should abound for so many drinkers. For, apart from the bishop and his company, the crowd of those eating numbered seven hundred [Col. 1440B].

5. In that same castle, the holy man of God Arnulf healed his monk and priest Everolf, worn down by fevers and dysentery, by the laying on of his hand; he saw the devil, bearer of plunder; and there, through God’s revelation, he learned a prophecy concerning his death or burial.

The cause of his coming was brotherly charity and obedience: the lord pope, by his command, had compelled him to reconcile to their count clerics accused of betraying that count, and not to permit anything to be extorted from them contrary to the sacred canons. Obeying the holy commands imposed upon him by apostolic authority, he returned to Flanders and, a true minister of peace, made peace. He not only restored the clerics shaken by calumny, but brought the whole region of Flanders, raging against itself with diabolical fury, back to a peaceful and tranquil confederation.

Then, by the counsel and will of Lord Radbod, bishop of Tournai, [Col. 1440C] at the request of Count Robert and the urgent petition of the nobleman Cono, he undertook to build and adapt for the use of an abbey the church of Saint Peter the Apostle and All the Apostles, situated in the village of Aldenburg. There, by God’s ordinance, he received the sleep of rest; there he underwent the burial divinely provided for him beforehand; and there, in the thirty-fourth year after his holy death, he furnished joyful solemnities for the translation of his sacred body, through the favour of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1439]

## THE LIFE OF SAINT MADELGISILUS, CONFESSOR AND HERMIT IN PONTHIEU, BY HARIULF

(Mabillon, *Acta SS. Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century IV, part II, p. 537, from the manuscript codex of Centula.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

[Col. 1439]

Hariulf, who arranged the Chronicle of Centula in four books, also wrote a short work, *On the Deeds of Saint Madelgisilus* (Saint Mauguille), confessor. Madelgisilus was first under the discipline of Saint Fursey, then a monk at Centula; from there he sought retirement at Monasteriolum (Monstrelet), on the river Alteia, where he completed the final days of his life. Hariulf dedicated the following little work to Gervin, the second abbot of Centula bearing that name. This second Gervin was the nephew of the other, but very unlike him in character; he was also bishop of Amiens. Pope Urban II deprived him of the abbey of Centula at the Council of Clermont. These facts are established from Hariulf’s Chronicle, to which, under Abbot Anscher, Hariulf added certain material to this Life from chapter 16 onward—or at least someone else did. A metrical eulogy of Anscher was prefixed to the beginning of that Life, which we extracted from a manuscript codex of Centula containing Hariulf’s Chronicle. In the manuscript codex, the Life of Saint Madelgisilus bears this title:

> IN THE NAME OF CHRIST THE SAVIOUR BEGINS THE PREFACE TO THE LIFE OF THE HOLY CONFESSOR MADELGISILUS.

[Col. 1441A] To the most beloved lord and father, to be embraced with spiritual love, GERVIN, bishop of the holy see of Amiens and likewise ruler of the life-giving monastery of Centula: HARIULF, a little sheep of your flock—would that he were worthy!—sends greeting and sincere obedience.

From the manifold reports of elders who have survived from the time of the venerable Abbot Angelramn to our own day, I learned certain things worthy of narration. [Note: [Col. 1441D] Ingelramnus, surnamed the Wise, governed the people of Centula during the reign of King Robert; Hariulf praises him in book I, chapter 1 and following chapters, of the Chronicle.] I have diligently entrusted these things to memory for the knowledge of posterity: namely, those things reported to have been done by the saints resting among us, whose series of deeds the equally diligent account of the ancients had transmitted to the knowledge of posterity.

Among all these matters, the brethren took pleasure in hearing and knowing concerning the blessed confessor Madelgisilus, who had rested among us since ancient times: who he was, how he served the Lord Almighty [Col. 1441B], and how or when his holy body was brought to the place of Centula and placed there; and by how many and how great signs of miracles he was glorified by the Lord.

[Col. 1442A] We have acquired certain knowledge of these signs not so much by report as by sight, since we ourselves have clearly known some of his miracles and have learned innumerable others through witnesses who testified that they had received knowledge not by hearsay but directly by their own sight and presence. Therefore, wishing at least in part to satisfy the holy desires of our dearest brethren, for the honour of God and reverence for this saint, and also for the benefit of posterity, we set down in writing what the frequent testimony of elders has conveyed to us concerning the same saint, lest through our idleness the diligence of those to come should seem deprived of knowledge of so great a matter [Col. 1442B].

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF SAINT MADELGISILUS, CONFESSOR

[Col. 1441B]

### Chapter I. Fursey comes from Ireland into Gaul. He founds a monastery.

While the kingdom of the Franks was ruled by Louis, son of Dagobert, and Austrasia by Sigibert, likewise a son of Dagobert, the holy man of God Fursey, born in Ireland and there made wondrous by signs of powers [Col. 1441C] and knowledge of revelations, left his native land by divine command. Passing through Britain, which is called England, he came to the regions of Germany, where the aforesaid King Sigibert received the same holy man with great honour and joy. Eager to retain him with great affection, the king offered him whatever places were suitable for monastic life, so that Fursey might be pleased to remain in the lands of his kingdom.

[Note: Hariulf is mistaken through an ambiguity of name. Fursey was not received by Sigibert, king of Austrasia, but by Sigibert, king of the Saxons in the island of Britain, as is evident from the Acts of Saint Fursey included in Century II, where the origin of the monastery built by Fursey with Sigibert’s assistance is discussed. Cols. 1441D, 1442D.]

But Saint Fursey, perceiving in the spirit that he ought by no means to remain in those places, yet desiring in some measure to comply with the king’s requests, travelled around the estates offered him and everywhere fervently devoted himself to preaching God’s word. At length he found a pleasing place, where, with God’s grace [Col. 1441D] and the aid of the aforesaid king, he founded a distinguished monastery and adequately filled it with a multitude of God’s servants. For through the preaching of this holy man many from that same kingdom were almost kindled toward faith and worthy [Col. 1442B] fruits of repentance. Some of them, supported by greater devotion, hastened in rivalry toward better endeavours of divine service, fleeing every worldly impediment so that they might become monks.

[Col. 1442C]

### Chapter II. Madelgisilus is instructed by Fursey and accompanies him on his journey.

Among them was a certain man named Madelgisilus, born of a lofty family, and, what is greater and more blessed, inscribed by the grace of election in divine foreknowledge. Clinging to blessed Fursey’s preaching and rejoicing in the examples of his holiness, he resolved to be the inseparable companion of his deeds and journeys, that he might deserve to share in Fursey’s merits and rewards.

Thus, Saint Fursey, after fully establishing and ordering the aforesaid monastery and entrusting the government of the place to his beloved brother, the blessed Abbot Ultan, and after seeking and receiving King Sigibert’s permission, decided to set out with disciples for western Gaul [Col. 1442D], later called Francia. It had already been fixed by heaven that there he would be released from his earthly body and that Francia itself, by divine decree, must be illumined by his examples and merits.

[Col. 1443A] The man of God Madelgisilus was his inseparable companion on this journey. With blessed Fursey he travelled through cities and regions, endured hunger, thirst, vigils, and other labours; he practised prayers and psalm-singing with him as a good disciple with his master, and proved himself a most patient imitator of Fursey’s preaching and abstinence.

### Chapter III. After Fursey’s death, Madelgisilus withdraws to Centula.

After the holy man of God Fursey, as had been ordained from heaven, laid aside the burden of earth in the district of Ponthieu at the place called Macerias and rendered his spirit to his Creator; and after his sacred body was brought to Péronne and buried by the illustrious men Duke Haymo and Prefect Archenold, blessed Madelgisilus began to be greatly afflicted by sorrow for the loss of his dearest master. Being a stranger and ignorant of the country, [Col. 1443B] he began with eager effort to seek whether there might be some place established for the pursuits of monastic life, where he could cling to the Lord and gather contemplative fruits.

While he sought such a place, the celebrated name of the monastery of Centula, long before founded in all holiness and righteousness by blessed Father Richarius and to that time wondrously and most divinely adorned by the most sacred remains of Richarius’s body, immediately became known to him. There a congregation of monks pleasing to God laboured vigorously in the path of the Rule and exerted every effort, in poverty of spirit, to obey the divine command.

Therefore the aforesaid servant of God hastened to that place with all eagerness and devoutly sought admission to the blessed assembly of the holy brethren; even more devoutly he obtained it. [Col. 1443C] There indeed he found true Israelites, fleeing with their whole heart from spiritual Egypt and seeking with all desire the heavenly manna: monks of pure life, armed with the strength of every abstinence and humility. The servant of God Madelgisilus fervently joined their most blessed fellowship and, stretching himself day by day toward better things, made great progress in the fear of God and continually strove to go from strength to strength.

### Chapter IV. Under Chlodovech and Balthild, miracles occur at Centula.

At that time the commonwealth of the Franks flourished under King Louis, son of Dagobert, and the venerable Queen Balthild. After the death of her husband, the aforesaid Louis, she built the monastery of Corbie. At Saint Philibert’s urging she also built the monastery of Jumièges [Col. 1443D] in the territory of Rouen, and in other places lavishly employed royal munificence in building monasteries.

The monastery of Centula therefore surpassed the other holy places in antiquity and religious observance, and every day shone through signs of miracles divinely performed at the tomb of blessed Richarius. As the brothers continually beheld these, they were inflamed to their inmost marrow as if by rays of divine love. They knew that by manfully following the narrow and strait way and cheerfully fighting against the ancient enemy, the blessed confessor Richarius had grown to such grace of merits that Christ the Lord displayed so many and such great miracles to demonstrate his merits. While these were performed, they abounded in manifold praise: they rendered honour and glory to Christ the Lord, reverent praise to his confessor, [Col. 1444A] the desire to imitate him to those who saw, and the joy of healing to the weak.

### Chapter V. Madelgisilus withdraws into the wilderness.

These divine miracles, I say, inspired in blessed Madelgisilus great ardour for the worship of God, kindled in his heart a great flame of divine love, and produced in his inmost being great power for despising the world. After spending some time in divine exercises and performing spiritual warfare in this monastery of Centula, he was held venerable by the other brethren because of the honour of his holiness. Yet, seeing that the reverence bestowed upon him by the brethren hindered him, and wishing to adopt a stricter and more secluded rule of life, he humbly asked permission to seek a remote and quiet place, [Col. 1444B] where he might apply himself more safely and abundantly to divine praises, attend without disturbance to prayers and tears, and, by continually mortifying himself, present himself ever more purified before the divine gaze.

The brothers’ freely given kindness granted with great sweetness what he devoutly asked, since they did not know how to envy the spiritual advancement of their brethren but rather rejoiced in it. Having obtained his desire—that is, permission to go into the wilderness—he began with most earnest prayers and tears to beseech more intensely that Christ’s immeasurable mercy would deign to show him such a place where, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, he could continually offer before the divine gaze a sacrifice of praise.

### Chapter VI. Heaven reveals to him the wilderness into which he should withdraw.

[Col. 1444C] To obtain this, he undertook the labour of greater fasting, the practice of prolonged prayer, and continual singing of psalms. He also sought the prayers of spiritual elders, that heavenly grace might deign to reveal to him in what place he should receive the solitary station of the Lord’s service.

While he persisted in these practices, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in sleep, led him out, and said: “Follow me, and carefully observe the place which I shall show you, where you shall henceforth fulfil the Lord’s service.” Having said this, the angel went before him and led him through various places until he came to the dwelling ordained from heaven. There he stopped and said to the servant of God: “Here is your rest for the appointed time; here you shall dwell, and here you shall make the due passage [Col. 1444D] from the body.”

After speaking thus, the angel disappeared. The servant of God returned to himself, understood what he had seen, and, prostrating himself with tears, gave thanks to God for his inexpressible gift.

### Chapter VII.

At the following dawn, after the offices of the hymns had been completed, he called together the senior brethren and related the vision in order. They, as servants of God truly without guile, rejoiced and gave immense thanks to the Creator. Then they hastened to complete the work, lest any delay obstruct so great a token of divine goodness. At the abbot’s command, brethren were chosen to guide him, and the things necessary for Christ’s soldier were prepared.

When these things had been duly prepared, the strong athlete set out for his solitary contest. Led through various places, when he arrived at the place shown him, [Col. 1445A] he immediately knew by an inward savour that this was the place divinely chosen for him; he loved it and took possession of it. First of all he fell down in prayer and, wet with tears, at once began the task for which he had come. The brothers who had led him remained with him until a cell and an oratory were erected, where Christ’s soldier might render his King the service due to him. When these were properly arranged according to the law of the wilderness, they returned to the camp of heavenly exercise.

### Chapter VIII. The site of the wilderness. There he obtains a spring.

The servant of Christ Madelgisilus thus remained alone and secluded. With all fervour he devoted himself to divine praises and hymns, attended more earnestly to prayers and vigils, and expiated the evils of the world by continual tears as though they were his own, desiring that all might be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth.

This place lies in the district of Ponthieu [le Ponthieu], around the river Alteia [l’Auchie], enclosed by flowing water and the shade of woods, very free and quiet for serving God, and called Monstroledus [Monstrelet].

[Note: In Hariulf, book III, chapter 20, it is called *Monasteriolus*, commonly Monstrelet. Col. 1445D.]

But the water of the same riverbed was inaccessible because of intervening marshy ground; consequently drawing water caused the servant of God unbearable labour. Therefore, turning with all his strength to the Lord, he prayed to the heavenly Majesty to remove from him this great difficulty of drawing water. Prostrate upon the ground, he shed tears with prayers that almighty God might grant him a supply of water.

Sensing in the spirit that he was swiftly heard by the Lord, he rose after praying [Col. 1445C] and made the sign of the cross upon a very hard turf. Immediately a vein of the clearest water opened there and poured forth a bright spring. Bubbling in a small sloping flat below the descending hillside, it runs back to the channel of the Alteia, or its parent bosom, but in its course supplies all with abundant water for drawing.

This same little spring, filled with heavenly medicine, has banished diverse illnesses by its draught; and no one should doubt that this is still done, unless the unbelief of the person seeking it prevents it.

### Chapter IX. The monks of Centula help him in illness.

Thus serving God without interruption in all holiness and great simplicity, and remaining steadfast in the austerity of the difficult undertaking he had assumed, after the course of some years he became bodily ill with a severe sickness [Col. 1445D]. Yet he was not hindered from divine service; thinking that he was already about to be released, he began to be even more fervent in God’s work, the closer the hoped-for blessedness seemed to be.

Immediately an angel of God appeared to the abbot of Centula, admonishing and commanding him to visit God’s servant in the wilderness and provide him comfort, lest he fail in Christ’s service. The abbot rose quickly and, taking with him such brethren as he chose, earnestly hastened to visit the servant of God, whom he learned was not without heavenly watchfulness.

They came to the aforesaid wilderness and the man’s dwelling; they found him ill, [Col. 1446A] prayed, and sang psalms. Then, having first given the blessing, they greeted him with a holy kiss and brought forth what they had carried for his use at the heavenly command. The servant of God was so greatly cheered by joy at their arrival that he at once forgot the whole burden of his illness. Leaving with him a brother who might give comfort to his solitude and weakness, they returned to the cloister, outside which it was in no way profitable for them to remain longer.

### Chapter X. Saint Wlganius heals him.

At about the same time there was in Greater Britain a man pleasing to God, distinguished by birth and learning, named Wlganius.

[Note: You will look in vain for Wlganius in the catalogue of the bishops of Canterbury; yet I have also read this in the manuscript Acts of Saint Wlganius. Cols. 1445D, 1446D.]

When he had been chosen for the episcopal seat of the city of Dorovernia, now called Canterbury, he perceived that the summit of such honour hindered him, since he preferred to serve God [Col. 1446B] in poverty and lowliness. He prayed to the Lord that he might provide him such counsel as would enable him to be freed from the bonds of so great a pre-eminence and to be involved as fully as possible in the office of divine service.

As he prayed these things and frequently persisted in such prayer, he who gives grace to the humble looked upon him—of whom it is written, “Lord, thou hast heard the desire of the poor” [Psalm 10]—and a heavenly messenger standing beside him disclosed the counsel he sought, saying:

“Cross the sea quickly toward Gaul. You will land on the Alteia, above which a certain servant of God lives. Go swiftly to him, heal him of his infirmity by God’s command, and thereafter remain with him in fellowship in God’s service.”

Having received this oracle, blessed Wlganius immediately went out to the city and took the road leading to the sea. By God’s will he found a little boat, entered it at once, invoked Christ, and did not distrust God’s presence. Immediately the boat, raised on the waves, ran straight across the seas without human rowing, and, guided by angels, swiftly reached the harbour of the Alteia. From there, following the shore, he sailed against the river’s current until he reached the dwelling of God’s servant [Col. 1446C].

### Chapter XI. They live together.

Leaving the boat and entering to the servant of God, the fellow servant of God Wlganius at once gave himself to prayer. When this was completed, he laid his hands upon the sick man; immediately the illness was driven away, and health began to return. Blessed Madelgisilus too, rising with slow effort, rushed into his embrace. They embraced one another in mutual love as though they were brothers born of the same womb, meeting again after long distances of lands or places.

These two venerable men were joined in faith and devotion, strengthened by spiritual grace, unanimously animated for the persistence of divine praise, strong in trampling down vices, joyful in contempt of the world, eager for the acquisition of virtues, and ready to bestow benefits. Since neither thought can conceive nor tongue express their virtues, let us now undertake to reveal how, with God as author, these pearls of such great price, polished in the exile of this world, [Col. 1447A] were transferred to the heavenly crown.

### Chapter XII. Wlganius, struck by illness, dies strengthened by anointing and viaticum. Madelgisilus also dies.

In the following period, as heavenly providence pleased, when the course of this frail life was now completed, bodily sickness befell the servant of God Wlganius. As he lay ill, blessed Madelgisilus bore his companion’s suffering with great distress; standing by him, he lamented with sobs:

“Then, my brother, have you come to this: that, leaving me in the valley of tears, you hasten to the fellowship of rejoicing souls? I certainly hoped that you would commend me, body to the earth and spirit to Christ; but now you desire to depart swiftly from here, so that before me you should enter heaven in spirit and earth in body?”

Saint Wlganius said to him: “Bear it patiently, I beg you, most blessed brother, and willingly submit to God’s will in us. For what profit would there be in having laboured our whole life in obedience to God’s commandments, if at our end he who watches for the heel should be able to find us rebellious and murmuring? Nor should you think it harsh that I leave you for a time, for as soon as I see the face of God, I shall not cease to pray that you may be removed from here.”

Thus blessed Madelgisilus was somewhat comforted. He quickly sent to the same monastery his servant, who had long before been assigned to him by the abbot, instructing the brethren to visit his sick fellow-dweller as soon as possible and to administer to him whatever belongs to the viaticum of one departing.

As soon as they heard this command, the monks of Centula—effective and ready for every good work—[Col. 1447C] came with all speed. They anointed God’s servant with holy oil, gave him communion of the Lord’s mysteries, and then, when that holy soul left the body on the fourth day before the Nones of November, they accompanied it with psalms and readings, and finally committed the body to fitting burial in the oratory.

[Note: The body of Saint Wlganius was later translated to the castle of Lens, in the diocese of Arras. Baldric, *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 22: “Near the castle of Lens there is also a monastery of canons, where Saint Volganius rests, who is said to have been a Scot.” Col. 1447D.]

Not long afterwards Saint Madelgisilus also survived only a short time; rather, full of days and good works, he passed over to the joys of the saints, receiving the crown from the Lord’s hand and restoring his little body to the earth beside the burial of his former companion Wlganius, in the same compartment of his oratory. The ancient tradition assigns the heavenly birthday of this man of God to the third day before the Kalends of June, for the praise and glory of Christ’s name.

[Col. 1447D] **CHAPTER XIII. His body is transferred to Centula. Doubt concerning his cult dispelled by miracles.**—After many cycles of years had subsequently passed, the body of blessed Madelgisilus was transferred to the monastery of Centula, to the church of Blessed Richarius, and rests there, namely where the sound of divine praise does not cease, and where are contained many bodies whose souls live in heaven. [Note: Namely, the *laus perennis* (“perpetual praise”) formerly instituted by Saint Angilbert, as we have said; whether it was still flourishing at that time I do not know.]

When, in the time of Abbot Ingelard, [Note: Abbot Ingelard, toward the close of the tenth century, had as successor Ingelramnus, mentioned above. Read Hariulf’s *Chronicle*, book III, chapter 29, where these matters are related in precisely the same words.] this confessor of Christ had been honorably placed among them, some monks, moved by a certain foolishness, began to say that it was unworthy to venerate the little bones of a man whose life and deeds they did not know. For his glorious works had not yet been committed to writing, nor had they yet been commended to the memory of the faithful.

While the aforesaid brethren were disputing this matter repeatedly, there was from ancient times a certain small church on the boundary of Centula itself, named after this same saint. They resolved that he ought to be carried there, provided that he might possess a dwelling in a church of his own and that they should not be obliged to honor him thus from afar. When therefore he had been placed there, that God who looks upon the lowly, and who does not cease to exalt even His saints, though hidden, resolved to perform many miracles in that place, so that in this way the merits of the aforesaid saint might be recognized and the folly of those who had rejected him might be subdued.

For he granted there to the blind sight, to the deaf hearing, to the lame the power of walking, to the mute speech, and to other infirmities such and so great a remedy that no one could either proclaim with the tongue or retain in memory the abundant multitude of such works. When, therefore, this grace of God had shone forth there for a considerable time, and it became so evident to all that this man possessed precious merit before God, Abbot Ingelard and his monks began to be moved by great repentance because they had cast aside, as though it were something worthless, a pearl of such value. Him whom they had formerly despised through ignorance of his deeds or because of the obscurity of his sanctity, they resolved to bring back with devout humility of heart and public honor, being drawn to love and honor him by the magnificent power of God.

Then, the brethren having assembled and the people having been summoned, with crosses, candles, incense, and every ecclesiastical ornament preceding them, they proceeded in procession to the aforesaid small church with honor and with great reverence in the fear of God. After pardon for their error had first been sought, they received the holy body with hymns and brought it back with praises to the church of Saint Richarius—as was fitting for him who, by the power of his merits, had subdued the hardness of their minds. There it is likewise kept in honor and venerated with love.

**CHAPTER XIV. The annual carrying of the body.**—It thereafter became a devout custom of the people of Centula and of the inhabitants of the Ponthieu district that every year, on the day of his heavenly birthday, which is 30 May, they should carry his sacred body with joy and fitting honor to the place where he had formerly been buried. A great crowd of people would assemble from the neighboring villages and towns, and with much rejoicing they celebrated the saint’s feast.

On one occasion, therefore, when according to the solemn custom it had been carried there, and the ceremonies had been completed, and the time had come to bring it back, such a tumult of rain and wind arose as the brethren were leaving the church with the saint’s body [Col. 1449A] that, because of the excessive density of the stormy air, that day appeared more dismal than night. As was customary, two silver candelabra were carried before the holy body. Although their lights were struck by the winds and heavily drenched by the rain, they nevertheless could not be extinguished until it had passed through the parish in which he had lived. Thus, as though marking out what had been his own, he hallowed it by the miracle.

**CHAPTER XV. A miracle.**—A neighboring landholder, pricked by the dart of avarice, violently seized a certain piece of land formerly granted to the church of Blessed Madelgisilus and converted it to his own uses. Meanwhile, when the saint’s annual solemnity returned, it happened that his bier passed through the land taken from him. But when those carrying it began to tread upon that land, his bier was suddenly made so heavy by an excessive weight that it stopped motionless and, like a mountain, could not be moved from its place.

Then those who knew that the land had long ago been unjustly taken from the aforesaid saint complained, saying: “See: Saint Madelgisilus, angered on account of his land, has made himself heavy and does not permit himself to be carried from here. Let us go to the robber; let us beg and urge him to restore what is his to the saint.”

Thus the wrongdoer, exceedingly terrified and fearing that the earth might swallow him alive, came trembling. Humbly begging pardon, he restored his field to Saint Madelgisilus and declared it free and undisturbed forever. When this had been done, they returned to the saint; the bier was carried, and no heaviness was felt.

**CHAPTER XVI. In the year 1113 he is transferred to a new shrine.**—In the year 1113 of the divine manifestation in the flesh, in the fifth indiction, while Louis son of Philip was ruling the kingdom of the Franks in the fifth year of his reign, and while Anscherus had already held for sixteen years the once noble monastery of the most holy Richarius as abbot, it pleased the abbot and the other brethren to uncover and inspect the beloved body of Saint Madelgisilus, and, because the old chest was very fragile, to place it with diligent care in a new shrine.

Accordingly, when those things that appeared suitable for so great a work had been prepared, and they came to the point of relocating the sacred limbs, the little bag of deer-hide [Col. 1450A] in which they were to be received proved shorter and less capacious than the size and height of the bones required. For that reason, some of the same bones remained in their former covering until the matter could be more suitably arranged at a more convenient time. Nevertheless, all were placed in the new shrine with psalms and fitting honor.

Not many days after this, the custodian of the church, who cherished this same saint with ardent love, was overcome by illness and could not sleep. Throughout the night he had been considering how and when the transfer of the saint’s body could be completed. Then, as dawn was rising, the weary custodian fell lightly asleep; and in that very brief sleep he was thinking inwardly about arranging the saint’s relics when suddenly there stood before him [Col. 1450B] a tall and handsome man in glorious attire, who said: “Provide for this more carefully, and do it so that all my bones may be placed together.”

The custodian, who was held in the slightest sleep and inspired by fervent love for that saint, immediately understood clearly, upon hearing him say “all my bones,” that he was blessed Madelgisilus himself. Fixing his gaze upon him, he desired to ask his name and rank. But before he could be questioned, that great and glorious man vanished. Yet he left behind an exceedingly sweet fragrance and left footprints as though of gold.

The custodian grieved at his departure but rejoiced in the fragrance. Eager to retain some token of this vision, he said within himself, as he supposed: “At once I shall seize these golden footprints of his and carry them to the brethren as testimony.” Awakening, he leapt up; but when he stretched out his arms and was shaken by that movement, he no longer saw the golden footprints which he had thought he beheld. Thus he immediately cast off both the vision and the whole illness by which he had been oppressed, aided through the merit of the saint by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever. Amen.

**EPIGRAM ON HIS BIER**

This bier holds the bones of blessed Madelgisilus,  
Whom Christ duly made blessed as His confessor;  
And Anscherus rightly prepared a new shrine for him.

## APPENDIX TO HARIULF

[Col. 1451]

# SHORT CHRONICLE OF THE MONASTERY OF OUDENBURG

Edited by the Very Reverend J.-B. MALOU, Honorary Canon, Professor of Theology and Librarian of the Catholic University of Louvain.

(*Collection of chronicles, charters, and other documents concerning the history and antiquities of West Flanders, published by the Society of Emulation of Bruges.—First Series. Chronicle of the Monasteries of Flanders.—Bruges, 1840, quarto.*)

# PREFACE

## SITUATION OF OUDENBURG; ATTILA BESIEGES IT IN 453; SAINT URSMAR FOUNDS CHURCHES THERE

[Col. 1451] Oudenburg, now a mere village in West Flanders, situated between Bruges, Ostend, and Nieuwpoort, near the junction of the canals connecting these three towns, was in remote times a stronghold considered the capital of that country. The chronicle whose unpublished text we now publish informs us that it was besieged by Attila, king of the Huns, during the invasion which, according to our most respected historians, took place about the year 453 of the Christian era. This disaster deprived Oudenburg of its former splendor, without depriving it of its preeminence over the boroughs of the region; for, toward the end of the seventh century, Saint Ursmar, who traversed all Flanders as an apostle, founded there two celebrated churches.

Toward the middle of the ninth century, the ruins of its ancient fortifications were still visible. Baldwin the Bald, count of Flanders, gave them about this period to the inhabitants of Bruges to build and fortify their town. We owe these recollections to the pious cenobites of Oudenburg; they alone preserved the history of these times obscured by the ages.

## SAINT ARNOULD, APOSTLE OF FLANDERS, FOUNDS THE MONASTERY IN 1083

Saint Arnould, a Fleming by origin, raised to the episcopal see of Soissons by his virtues and merits, was sent into Flanders by Gregory VII, toward the middle of the eleventh century, to pacify that province. By his apostolic labors, prudence, and gentleness, he revived faith and restored peace among populations troubled by civil dissensions. As early as 1056, he had replaced the wooden churches built by Saint Ursmar with a stone church, whose materials were drawn from the ancient ruins of the town. In 1083 he had the happiness of founding [Note: Guided by the great manuscript chronicle of Oudenburg, we have assigned the foundation of the monastery to the year 1083. The account of the foundation appears under the heading of that year, but the catalogue of abbots assigns it to the following year, 1084. We have no reason to prefer one date to the other; the monuments known to us provide no means of discerning the truth.

The first abbot governed the monastery for eight years and died in 1095, eight years after his uncle Saint Arnould, bishop of Soissons, whose death is fixed in the year 1087. It is therefore impossible to calculate by how many years the monastery’s foundation preceded Saint Arnould’s death, since the succession of abbots began only after his death. Unable to remove this chronological contradiction, we have followed it. In this preface and the notes to the chronicle, we regard the first date as certain; in the catalogue of abbots, we have adhered to the text. In adopting either date, the reader should take account of the contrary date and always understand our assertions with the qualification just indicated.] an abbey of monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, entrusted with serving the church and maintaining in the town of Oudenburg and its vicinity the spirit of faith and fervor which he had revived by his zeal.

The first community consisted of six monks from the Abbey of Afflighem in Brabant and four monks from the Abbey of Flurs, situated in France. Despite the vicissitudes of the times, which sometimes obliged the monks to flee the walls of their monastery, this foundation endured until 1797. It was then swept up in the general suppression of Belgium’s religious establishments.

## HISTORICAL MONUMENTS OF THIS HOUSE

The monastery of Oudenburg formerly possessed three principal historical monuments of which knowledge has come down to us: first, the anonymous short chronicle which we publish here, written in the eleventh century; second, a Great Chronicle, composed in 1458 under the direction of Anianus, the twenty-sixth abbot of the monastery, of which we possess the original; third, the Annals of Oudenburg, written by George Cabiliauw, a monk of the convent, toward the middle of the fifteenth century.

## ANNALS OF G. CABILIAUW

Until now, it has been impossible for us to discover George Cabiliauw’s writings. Perhaps they passed into England with so many other precious monuments; perhaps they are buried in archives still unexplored; perhaps they perished in the revolutionary upheaval. Here, however, are the testimonies certifying their existence.

Sanderus, in his *Flandria Illustrata*, vol. I, p. 5, col. 1641, after citing the opinion of several authors who seek the etymology of the word *Flandria* in the name of Prince Flandbert, who ruled our country, immediately adds: “GEORGIUS CABELLAVIUS, author of the Annals of Oudenburg, which are preserved in manuscript in the same monastery, is wholly of the same opinion, and supports it with arguments that are not without solidity.”

The same author, in his description of the Franc of Bruges, p. 318 of the cited edition, says that the memory of George Cabiliauw was still recent. His words are: “He lived within the memory of the fathers, and composed the Annals for the monastery in the Latin language.”

Valerius Andreas knew these *Annals*, and speaks of their contents and author as follows: “Georgius Cabilliau, monk of Oudenburg in Flanders, of the Order of Saint Benedict, wrote a history of the town and abbots of Oudenburg, which is read there in manuscript. He begins with the first building of that town and its destruction by Attila and the Northmen, and carries the narrative down to the year 1470.”

By chance, on a loose sheet that formerly served as a draft in preparing the catalogue of the abbots of Oudenburg, we discovered the precise period in which George Cabiliauw lived. Among notes relating to the administration of Gaspar de Bovincourt, the thirty-seventh abbot, who governed the monastery from 1569 to 1577, we read: “At that time these religious were here: Adrianus de Gruytere, prior; Aegidius Sauvin, GEORGIUS CABILIAUW, Adrianus David, Melchior Everaert, priests; and Petrus Wilsoets, subdeacon.” This period agrees perfectly with Sanderus’s more general statement, written before 1641, that George Cabiliauw “lived within the memory of the fathers.”

If the volume of these *Annals* has been destroyed, its loss is deeply regrettable. Drawn from the archives of the monastery, it doubtless contained historical facts and details whose memory is now perhaps lost forever. Yet we should count ourselves fortunate to have snatched from the gnawing torrent of years the two chronicles that escaped, as if by miracle, an almost inevitable destruction.

## FATE OF THE TWO CHRONICLES

A fortunate chance made it possible, at the dispersal of the monks in 1797, to remove these two precious volumes. After the death of his brethren, Father Bouten received them as his share. Through excess of zeal, this religious entered the schism of the Stévenists and lived outside communion with his bishop, going from village to village in support of his adherents, until death struck him at a farm near Ypres, where he had deposited his books and papers.

An ecclesiastic called to the place was kind enough to examine the collection after his death. The books judged bad were destroyed, while the others were sold. The farmer who inherited from Father Bouten disposed of the original Great Chronicle—210 parchment folios with several fairly careful miniatures—for three francs.
