But because the *Life of Saint Arnould*, followed by the chronicle whose text we publish here, had lost half of its age-old cover, half an inch thick, and had suffered the teeth of rats, it found no buyer. It was deposited at Ypres in the house of an honest coppersmith, from whom I was able to acquire it for a rather modest sum. I later learned that smaller paper manuscripts had been destroyed as insignificant; it has been impossible for me to discover their remains.

## GREAT CHRONICLE COMPILED BY ANIANUS

The Great Chronicle composed—or rather compiled—by Anianus is preceded by a chronological and geographical introduction and followed by a catalogue of the sovereign pontiffs, the principal rulers of Europe, the bishops of the country, and the abbots of the monastery. This list provides a historical outline of the house; it is not without interest after the loss of the Annals of G. Cabiliauw, which doubtless entered into more extensive detail.

The celebrated Charles de Visch, monk of the Abbey of the Dunes, rightly observed on p. 145 of his manuscript notes, now preserved in the archives of the Bruges seminary, that Anianus owed much to [Col. 1455] Brandon, a monk of the Dunes, whose still unpublished chronicle will, we hope, be published by the Royal Historical Commission.

It cannot be denied that Anianus followed Brandon’s traces almost step by step. Nevertheless, comparison of several narratives has led me to believe that the compiler of Oudenburg had before him several historians whom Brandon copied slavishly; for he sometimes adds details that Brandon omitted. We shall speak more fully of this Chronicle when we send it to press with the other monuments relating to Oudenburg Abbey which we shall assemble either through our own researches or through the efforts of our friends.

We shall observe only that Sanderus, p. 318 of the cited edition, and Valerius Andreas, p. 59 of the works cited above, are mistaken when they assert that Abbot Anianus composed a universal chronicle from the origin of the world to 1457. For this chronicle begins with the birth of the Savior and ends in the year 1400. The heading of the table of contents at the beginning of the chronicle expressly states that the volume was written in 1458.

The Great Chronicle contains almost the whole of the Short Chronicle we publish here, but divided up and distributed among the various periods to which it pertains. This copy was useful to us in establishing several doubtful readings.

## THE SHORT CHRONICLE: IT WAS KNOWN TO OUR HISTORIANS

The Short Chronicle whose text we here publish for the first time is unquestionably one of the most curious monuments of our history, and perhaps the oldest work composed in historical form. Its contents make it seem indubitable that it was written in 1083, or very shortly afterward. The author repeatedly states that he witnessed the events which he recounts. He still saw standing the old wooden church built by Saint Ursmar; he saw the new stone church, begun by Saint Arnould in 1056, being built; he attended the dedication of that church in 1070; in 1081 he feared the effects of a terrible storm which nearly overthrew the church tower; he recounts the foundation of the monastery, which occurred in 1083, and this is the most recent event in the chronicle. It contains none later than 1083.

It is easy to be persuaded that the author could scarcely have delayed beyond that year in writing his chronicle, given his great age. In 1056, about thirty years before the monastery’s foundation, he had doubtless already reached or passed maturity, since he had noticed and retained in memory minute details which a young man does not notice. I would add that, in no. VIII of his chronicle, he states that he received the testimony of faithful persons who had lived under the reign of Arnould the Younger. That prince died in 989. It is therefore evident that in 1083 our author had reached an advanced age and could not have long deferred composing his Chronicle.

This monument was not unknown to our principal historians. Olivier Vredius speaks of it in his *Flandria Ethnica*, p. 491, Bruges ed., 1650, and in his *Flandria Christiana*, p. 161; Meyer in his *Annales Flandriae*, under the year 453; L’Espinoy in his *Recherches des Antiquités et noblesse de Flandres*, ch. V; and D’Oudegherst in his *Annales*, pp. 3 and 13, Lesbroussart ed., 1789. Yet, except for Vredius and Meyer, one may believe that these writers cited our chronicle without having read it and on the authority of others, as seems further indicated by the mistake of Sanderus and Valerius Andreas noted above. In any event, the short extracts they give are insufficient to make it known.

## ON THE MANUSCRIPT OF THE SHORT CHRONICLE

Let us say a word about the manuscript upon which we publish the text of this precious monument. Our Chronicle does not form a separate volume. It was copied on several blank parchment leaves between the *Life of Saint Arnould*, founder of Oudenburg monastery, and the work of Hugh, prior of Saint-Laurent, entitled *On the Cloister of the Soul*. On this author, widely read in the Middle Ages, see OUDIN, *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, vol. II, col. 1107, Leipzig ed., 1722.

The *Life of Saint Arnould* was written by Lisiard, one of his successors in the see of Soissons, in 1114, and published, with considerable omissions, by Surius under 15 August. These two works together form a large folio volume in the most beautiful handwriting, formerly used as a lectionary for the office of the holy founder. Between the two works our chronicle is inserted, [lacuna] in very small handwriting which seems to belong to the first years of the fourteenth century.

## ON THE AGE OF THIS MANUSCRIPT

It appears almost certain that the *Life of Saint Arnould* and Hugh’s work were copied at Oudenburg before 1278 by Jean de Biervliet, the fourteenth abbot of the monastery, of whom the catalogue of abbots published below speaks in these terms: “John de Biervliet, a monk of this monastery, whose handwriting is still in use, governed for twenty-nine years and died in the year of the Lord 1307.”

Here we have three important points: this abbot’s native place; the renown he acquired through his fine handwriting; and, finally, the esteem and use made of [Col. 1457] his manuscripts, indicated by the word *viget* (“is still in use”). These three characteristics are found in the manuscript at issue. First, his native place, for the copyist ends the volume with this epigraph:

> He who wrote me thus was a monk and a levite,  
> Born at Biervliet; may he be blessed as his reward.

Next, the art of writing: for the handwriting is remarkably beautiful and regular. Finally, the manuscript’s frequent use in the monastery is attested by inscriptions written at various chapters or in the margin: “First reading,” “second,” “third.” I could further cite the damage and color of certain leaves, which obviously result from frequent handling.

Jean de Biervliet governed the monastery from 1278 until his death in 1307. It is highly probable that, once invested with this office and fully occupied with its duties, he no longer had much time to devote to copying books, and therefore wrote this volume before 1278. The epigraph cited supports this assertion, for Jean de Biervliet was only a levite—that is, a deacon—when he completed this manuscript. The volume was consequently a work of his youth.

One may safely affirm that the Short Chronicle was added to the volume after 1278, perhaps at the beginning of the fourteenth century, after Jean de Biervliet’s death. For the cursive and compressed hand of our manuscript bears a striking resemblance to the script of the charters of Guy of Dampierre, found in large numbers in the archives of the Bruges seminary.

## ON THE EDITION OF THE SHORT CHRONICLE

To preserve the antique character of our chronicle, we shall follow the manuscript’s spelling, except with respect to punctuation and capital letters, for it is very defective in both regards. The notes and elucidations we have added are intended to facilitate reading or confirm its accounts.

We shall examine separately, in a dissertation to be added to the volume, whether Vredius’s and De Bast’s doubts concerning Attila’s devastations in Flanders are well founded. We believe that we can demonstrate that the contradiction which these great men gave to our chronicle is not based upon solid proofs.

## ABRIDGED LIFE OF SAINT ARNOULD; CATALOGUE OF ABBOTS

Our Chronicle is followed by a shorter chronicle, containing a simple summary of the life of Saint Arnould and the foundation of the monastery. We found it in the Great Chronicle, placed at the head of the catalogue of abbots, of which it forms a kind of preface. Since the catalogue of abbots contains an abridged history of the monastery from its establishment to our own day, we did not hesitate to include it in this volume, so that these three pieces together might offer a sequence of the historical events concerning Oudenburg from 453, when it was ravaged by Attila, to the death of the last abbot in 1803.

## CHARTERS FOUND BY M. VAN DE PUTTE

M. Van De Putte, a member of the Society of Emulation for the History and Antiquities of West Flanders, through his active research assembled a fairly large number of charters concerning the former Abbey of Oudenburg. He was kind enough to offer me a copy of them. But since these documents are of some length and have greater affinity with the extracts we shall give from the Great Chronicle, we shall reserve them for that second publication. To complete the history of this celebrated abbey, we shall add the documents already published by Miraeus in the third volume of his *Opera diplomatica*.

## GENERAL SUMMARY OF THE CHRONICLE

The chronological order is not scrupulously observed in our Chronicle. We shall give here a general summary that may serve as a table of contents.

| No. | Subject | Year |
|---|---|---:|
| I | Recapitulation of the principal epochs of the world, down to the year | 1056 |
| II | Conduct of Saint Leo IX at the Council of Reims | 1049 |
| III | Death of Saint Leo IX | 1054 |
| IV | Sovereigns reigning in | 1056 |
| XIX | Splendor and site of Oudenburg; its destruction; its misfortunes from | 453 |
| V | Apostolate of Saint Ursmar in Flanders, about | 690 |
| VI | Offerings of the faithful to Saint Ursmar | |
| VII | The first church built in honor of Saint Peter | |
| VIII | The church of the Holy Virgin built at the same time; plundering of the church and encroachment upon its property after | 989 |
| IX | Revenues of these two churches | |
| X | Church of Saint Peter rebuilt by Saint Arnould, bishop of Soissons | 1056 |
| XI–XV | Miracles occurring during or shortly after construction of this church | |
| XVI | Solemn dedication of this church by Ratbodonus, bishop of Noyon and Tournai | 1070 |
| XVIII | Storm which nearly overthrew the tower | 1081 |
| XVII | Conon, who held Saint Peter’s church as a temporal benefice, restores it to the count of Flanders; the count returns it to the bishop of Noyon and Tournai, who gives it to Saint Arnould, bishop of Soissons and apostle of Flanders, who founds a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict | 1083 |

Saint Arnould died in 1087.

I consider myself fortunate to be able to join this publication to the collection of monuments which the Society of Emulation for the History and Antiquities of West Flanders has begun to publish, thereby recognizing, at least through this modest cooperation, the honor it has done me by associating me with its labors.

Louvain, 4 February 1840.  
J.-B. MALOU.

# CHRONICLE OF OUDENBURG, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

[Note: The manuscript of this chronicle bears no title. We have not hesitated to give it the title which its wholly historical subject seems to require. In nos. X and XIX the author calls it a *Tractatus* (“treatise”); but this was a generic term in the Middle Ages and meant a chronicle just as readily as a sermon, a letter, an agreement, or a treaty of peace. On this point see Du Cange’s *Glossary*.

It appears that the author’s name had long been unknown even within the monastery, for Valerius Andreas—who could easily have learned it—after mentioning the Annals of G. Cabiliauw, adds: “There is also in the same place another Chronicle of the same church and abbey, written in a most ancient script, but by an uncertain author” (*Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 259). There can scarcely be doubt that he is speaking of our Chronicle.]

[Col. 1459]

## I

[Col. 1459A]

From Adam to the Flood: 2,242 years. From the Flood to Abraham: 942 years. From Abraham to the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ: 2,015 years. Thus, from Adam to the Lord Christ there were 5,199 years. [Note: Here the author follows the chronology of the Septuagint, adopted by Eusebius of Caesarea in his *Chronicle* and generally followed by the Eastern and Western Church, as Baronius observes under 25 December in his notes to the Roman Martyrology.]

And thus, from the beginning of the world to the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, there are 5,216 years. From the Passion of the Lord to the beginning of the construction of the church of Saint Peter the Apostle at Oudenburg: 1,056 years.

The work of the aforesaid church was begun on the eastern side of the aforesaid town, on 25 April, Thursday, in the ninth indiction, with epact 1 and concurrent 1, while Pope Leo was exercising the pontificate of the Roman Church. [Note: Here our author is in error. Saint Leo IX, of whom he speaks, was no longer alive in 1056, when construction of the church at Oudenburg began. All contemporary historians agree in fixing Saint Leo IX’s death in 1054. We may cite Hermannus Contractus in Usserman, *Prodromus Germaniae sacrae*, vol. I, p. 134, St. Blasien, 1790, and the *Annales Beneventani*, under 1054, in Pertz’s *Monumenta Germaniae*, vol. V, p. 180, Hanover, 1839. Among modern writers one may cite, in support of this generally recognized fact, Cardinal Stephen Borgia, *Memorie istoriche della pontificia città di Benevento*, etc., vol. II, p. 39, Rome, 1764. In 1056 Victor II occupied Saint Peter’s see.]

In whose time, about seven years earlier, the holy Synod of Reims had taken place. [Note: The Council of Reims did indeed occur seven years before 1056, that is, in 1049. The acts of this Council are printed in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, vol. IX, col. 1028 ff., Paris, 1671. It was directed against simony. Theodoric, in his history *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*, printed in D’Achery’s *Spicilege*, vol. II, p. 243, Paris, 1723, gives several details on this subject and expands what our author recounts in few words in the following section.]

At this council, while he presided, the Holy Spirit revealing it, he plainly disclosed to all the conduct, morals, and life of the bishops and abbots seated there.

## II

First, therefore, humbly correcting each one privately, according to the Lord’s command; then before two or three suitable witnesses; and afterward, when they persisted, he did not neglect publicly to rebuke them before the whole council. Thus, at that holy council, by apostolically commanding and confirming them, he established very many decrees pleasing to the Lord, which remain beneficial to the universal Church to this day.

## III

[Col. 1461A]

The most blessed pontiff Leo, after the beginning of construction of the aforesaid church of Saint Peter, happily departed this world in the following year, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, a Monday, about noon.

[Note: [Col. 1461C] Our author therefore places the death of Leo IX in the year following the beginning of the building of Saint Peter’s church at Oudenburg—that is, in 1057. This view conflicts with the account of contemporary writers and cannot be reconciled with other certain facts of the period. Historians do not agree on the day of this holy pontiff’s death. Our manuscript places it on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, that is, 14 April; Hermannus Contractus on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May (16 April); Cardinal Borgia on 19 April (the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May); and the great manuscript Chronicle of Oudenburg, correcting our old manuscript, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May (25 April).]

And at the very hour when his soul departed from his body, not only at Rome, where his body lay, but throughout the whole world, a circle of extraordinary brightness appeared in the sky to men for almost half an hour—perhaps the Lord thereby showing that he was worthy to receive in heaven the crown among those who love him.

IV.

In the last year of the Emperor Henry,

[Note: [Col. 1461D] Emperor Henry III, called the Black, died in 1056. See *The Art of Verifying the Dates of Historical Events*, etc., p. 440. Paris, 1770.]

the work on the aforesaid church of Saint Peter the Apostle was begun, while another Henry was reigning as king of the Franks,

[Note: [Col. 1461D] Henry I, who reigned from 1031 until 1060. Ibid., p. 544.]

and likewise Edward,

[Col. 1461B]

the most blessed king of the English,

[Note: [Col. 1461D] Saint Edward III, the Confessor, reigned from 1042 until 1066. Ibid., p. 775.]

while Baldwin of Lille

[Note: [Col. 1461D] Baldwin V of Lille reigned from 1034 to 1067. Ibid., p. 631, and in our historians. In 1060 he was entrusted with the guardianship of Philip I, son of Henry I, who was only eight years old at his father’s death.]

was at that time worthily governing the whole region of Flanders and the greater part of Gaul.

V.

Thus Bishop Ursmar, illustrious in holiness, travelled throughout Flanders, which was given over to idolatry,

[Note: [Col. 1461D] The manuscript has *ydolatrie* rather than the customary *idololatriae*.]

preaching the grace of baptism. Inflamed with zeal for the true faith, he sowed in many places the word of truth and planted the shoot of everlasting verdure.

[Note: [Col. 1461D] Saint Ursmar was born at Fleon, now Floyon, near Avesnes, in what is now the province of Hainaut, on 23 July 644 or 645 according to Henschenius, in vol. II for April of the *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 557 ff., and in the *Acta SS. Belgii selecta*, vol. VI, p. 247 ff., where there is a learned dissertation by Isfridus Thisius on the date when Saint Ursmar was made abbot of Lobbes and consecrated bishop. The writers differ on this question, and it is difficult to settle upon an opinion. Trithemius, in his treatise *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book III, ch. 157, says that Saint Ursmar flourished about the year 700. He died in 713. The author of the great Chronicle of Oudenburg places the account of Saint Ursmar’s apostolate in the year 650; but if, as Henschenius holds, the great saint was born in 644, he could not have evangelized Flanders in 650 at the age of sixteen. Thus this narrative can have been placed under the year 650 only because it mentions the time when Flanders was still given over to idolatry, before Saint Ursmar called it to the grace of baptism.]

While residing in the city once noble, but at that time mournful, Aldenburgh, he preached continually the name and glory of Jesus Christ our Lord, his coming, and his kingdom. By a heavenly admonition he was commanded to consecrate at Aldenburgh a church built in Christ’s name, under the dedication of the blessed Apostle Peter

[Col. 1461C]

and of all the Apostles. Joyfully obeying the heavenly vision, he consecrated most solemnly, under Saint Peter’s patronage, a wooden basilica erected in the place shown to him, on the outskirts of the city of Aldenburgh.

[Col. 1462A]

The power of the Most High repeatedly honoured it by miracles of signs and benefits of healing, to the praise of his name and to the honour of his chosen Apostle Peter. Finally, as has been said, Saint Ursmar, instructed by a heavenly admonition, first visited this city, Aldenburgh, in reverence for its dignity; enlightened its inhabitants with the word of holy exhortation; and specially chose the place where the aforesaid church of Saint Peter the Apostle now stands. There, with the aid of almighty Jesus Christ our Lord, he built a church and, as we have learned from very many faithful and trustworthy men, dedicated that same place. Therefore, out of reverence for his holiness and because of the blessing,

[Col. 1462B]

that place is regarded by many as holy and sacred. Those who come there may, even to this day, behold this beyond doubt with the eyes of faith. There he himself, diligently presiding over the people, travelled throughout all the surrounding country with his fellow-workers,

[Note: [Col. 1462D] In the Middle Ages, *patria* could mean village, region, or province. Du Cange provides evidence for this in his *Glossary*. Here the word seems to be used in the second sense.]

and throughout Flanders converted no small number of people to the true faith of Christ, by word and example, and brought them to the true mother Church.

VI.

Accordingly, the leading men of this most noble city and the remaining multitude of the faithful of this district

[Note: [Col. 1462D] *Parrochie*, more commonly *parochie*, generally meant a territory or district, and specifically a diocese or what we call a parish. The author of this chronicle uses the word in different senses, as will be observed below.]

resolved gladly to offer him a very great quantity of land,

[Note: [Col. 1462D] *Decretabatur*, a barbarous word, for which I find no example as a deponent verb. The context leaves no doubt as to its meaning.]

so that he might gather together a venerable multitude of clerics in two places, to serve the Lord perpetually,

[Col. 1462C]

by day and by night; and so that there should not fail those who, living regularly and soberly, might guard in sober chastity the Bride of the Lord—that is, the Church. And so it was done.

VII.

[Col. 1463A]

On the eastern side of this city, as we have said, he consecrated a wooden church in honour of Saint Peter the Apostle, and appointed there a suitable community of clerics. For the high altar and presbytery, and a certain part of Saint Peter’s church, have now been built on the very site of the court where the wooden church was erected in ancient times by Blessed Ursmar and was sanctified and blessed by him. Therefore, as I have said, from the presbytery on both sides of the church, and thereafter as far as the eastern boundary of the same court, that place always remains green and pleasant, adorned with grass, although it seems constantly trodden by the footsteps of those who walk upon it; while the remaining part towards the west continually remains dry and covered with dust.

VIII.

Blessed Ursmar also built another church on the northern side of this city, in honour of Saint Mary, holy and ever-virgin, and likewise established there a fitting body of clerics. That this is true is still testified by the land which stretches broadly and widely along the northern side of Saint Peter the Apostle’s church and still belongs to the church, although it has been violently taken away from both clerics and poor people and is wholly subjected to laymen of secular knighthood, who are not heirs.

If, however, any should doubt the existence of the other church of the most holy and ever-virgin Mary, which, as I have said, was built on the northern side of this city, because houses and dwellings of many people are now seen established on that side,

[Col. 1463C]

let them know certainly that, in the days of Count Arnulf,

[Note: [Col. 1463C] Arnulf II, called the Younger, reigned from 965 to 989. *The Art of Verifying Dates*, p. 630.]

father of Baldwin the Bearded, no house or dwelling of anyone stood in the other part, except those of two brothers, namely Wlinemar the priest and Erembald the layman

[Note: [Col. 1463C] These words are underlined in the manuscript.]

One of them, Erembald, built his house on the east of that side, and his brother Wlinemar on the west; and in the middle there stood the court of the aforementioned church of Saint Mary, as the ancient faithful without doubt attest. Where that oft-mentioned church had stood, Ingelbert the cleric afterwards undoubtedly built his house.

IX.

[Col. 1464A]

Not only had spacious and pleasant lands around this city been granted at that time by the faithful to Saint Ursmar and to the aforesaid guardians of the churches,

[Note: [Col. 1463C] *Cernitores* means protectors of the Church, those who, by their counsel, provide for its interests. The origin of this word may be assigned as that which Du Cange attributes to *cernita*, meaning deliberation or public consultation; it appears to derive from the Italian *cernire*, “to discern.” The word *cernita* occurs in the Acts of Saint Juvenal, vol. I for May, p. 404, of Bollandus’s *Acta Sanctorum*. I find the word *cernitor* nowhere else.]

but also in many places of this district and throughout the borders of Flanders. For it is most truly established by many men of this province that a rent and land-payment of twenty-five pounds

[Note: [Col. 1463C] According to the probable calculations of Abbé Ghesquière, in his *Memoir on Three Points of Interest in the Monetary History of the Netherlands*, octavo, Brussels, 1786, pp. 67 and 183, the sum of 25 pounds in the eleventh century may be estimated at 1,814 francs of our currency—a considerable sum at that time. The manuscript has *libra*; the final syllable appears erased.]

in denarii was paid to Saint Ursmar at this place by many persons, apart from

[Note: [Col. 1464C] The manuscript has *abque*.]

the aforementioned land which, as we have said, was made subject to laymen of secular knighthood. Moreover, the charter in which these matters were recorded retained the names of many who formerly used to pay the due. In the court of the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary, many saw the cartulary officer

[Note: [Col. 1464C] The *cartularius* was ordinarily responsible for preserving the church archives and collecting its revenues.]

sitting, who received the aforesaid

[Col. 1464B]

payment.

X.

The wooden basilica, built in the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks,

[Note: [Col. 1464C] Dagobert III is meant here; he succeeded his father Childebert III in 711. This date is probably mistaken, since Saint Ursmar’s apostolate in Flanders preceded 711. The holy bishop died in 713; it is not likely that in roughly two years he built the two churches of Oudenburg and received all the gifts mentioned in no. IX of this Chronicle.]

and with his permission erected by Blessed Ursmar in honour of the blessed Apostle Peter, as has been said above, remained strong for a long time, grew old with great age, fell through prolonged antiquity, and finally, after the passage of many years, the citizens of Aldenburgh began to build a new church in honour of the blessed Apostle Peter and all the Apostles.

In the year of the Lord 1056, work began on the aforesaid church of Saint Peter the Apostle, as is more fully stated at the beginning of this treatise. It was begun on the same site as before, built of stone, as is made evident

[Note: [Col. 1464C] The meaning is clearer if the word *est* is supplied, apparently omitted through the copyist’s negligence. The historian intends to prove, through the account of several miracles, that the new church was built on a site already sanctified by worship extending over many centuries.]

by the miracles which occurred while the church was being built,

[Col. 1464C]

which we shall undertake briefly to recount.

XI.

About the fifth year after construction of the church began, when the presbytery had been completed and roofed with thatch, and bells had been hung between beams before the high altar, the clerics arranged, before winter, to enclose with rods an arch before the presbytery, from the ground to its summit, and to cover it with hanging thatch, in order to repel rain, hail, and snow.

One day a young cleric, very simple and devout, named Lisger, devoted himself very earnestly, carefully, and cheerfully to this work, assisting with his hands.

[Col. 1465A]

When scaffolding had been erected on both sides in the upper parts of this same arch, Lisger stood inside and another man outside opposite him upon the aforesaid scaffold. The latter was trying to bind the roof to the wall with twisted rods—the structure which, as I said before, had been enclosed with rods—while he hurried to pass the rods inward through the wall. Lisger strove skilfully to fasten them to the inner side of the wall. As they had been doing this for a long time, Lisger carelessly pulled out one of the wands and fell backwards, together with the scaffold, down to the ground, as the other man, standing outside and having passed the rod inward, thought in great terror. But Lisger slipped lightly onto one side, between the second and third beam,

[Col. 1465B]

above the ridge-beam of the great bell, without any bodily injury. Since, as I have said, he had been working there in the service of the blessed Apostle Peter with a devout mind and simple heart, he could not be hurt; and in his fall he was borne by the most holy intercession of the Apostle.

XII.

Later, while the walls of the church were being built on the northern side, a worker in mortar was at work with his assistants on the southern side. One day, the boy who handed him stones and mortar placed so heavy a load upon the scaffold on which they stood that it could not bear the force of such a weight. The entire scaffold broke, and the stones and mortar fell to the ground with a great crash.

[Col. 1465C]

But the man and the boy unexpectedly found themselves in a window of the same wall, without bodily injury. It was not nearby, but so far away that, had they been standing upon the ground, they could scarcely have reached such a distance by jumping. This is understood to have occurred at the command of almighty God, through the merits of Saint Peter the Apostle, by one who faithfully believes that all things are ordered by divine providence.

XIII.

After this, when five or six years had passed, on a certain day Syger, the custodian of that church, was confidently sounding the last bell in the early morning in order to rouse the multitude of faithful in the neighbourhood. The rope

[Note: [Col. 1465D] *Corda*, used to mean a rope or cable, was very common in the Middle Ages. The word *planca*, which immediately follows, is cited by Festus: “*Plancae*: flat boards,” etc.; see Du Cange.]

with which he moved the bell accidentally struck a great and very heavy plank

[Col. 1465D]

of the high floor of the same tower, above which the bells hung. It immediately fell between his shoulders with a horrible crash, so that those standing there in the choir thought all his limbs were broken. Immediately, as they later related, Erembald the priest and Remger the cleric carried him in their arms and without delay placed him upon his bed.

[Col. 1466A]

But when they had sung the morning psalms that same day, he at once rose from his bed as sound and unharmed as though he had suffered no bodily injury at all.

XIV.

At another time, on the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle, while the same Syger was ringing the second signal for Matins, the nail from which the bell hung slipped out by accident. The bell itself fell with a great crash upon the roof of the tower, which was covered with fir beams, so that he and some bystanders did not doubt that the roof had been broken and the bell shattered into pieces. That same day he had a certain boy climb up and asked him to collect the broken fragments of the bell. The boy therefore climbed onto the roof of the aforesaid

[Col. 1466B]

tower and found the bell standing there so sound and whole that no trace whatsoever of a fracture could be found in it.

XV.

While this city was being reduced to nothing, though the mound of earth on which its wall was being demolished remained, the basilica of Blessed Mary, under whose patronage

[Note: [Col. 1465D] The manuscript has *matricinio* in place of *patrocinio*, probably because the church was dedicated to the Virgin Mary, who is Mother of God.]

it was venerated, was honoured with such reverence by the inhabitants that nobles in worldly rank were buried in its cemetery, while persons of low rank were committed to burial in the court of the aforesaid oratory of Saint Peter.

Meanwhile, the people of Flanders were endangered by the severity of famine,

[Note: [Col. 1465D] The historians of France mention this cruel famine in the reign of Henry I, who reigned from 1031 to 1060.]

and wandered everywhere seeking food. Very many of them flocked to this place and, despite their great number, lacking both lodging and food,

[Col. 1466C]

lay in the streets by the hedges and died miserably. It happened that one day a dead man was found in the street. The inhabitants, wearied by the repetition of such occurrences, supplied him with no human kindness in the matter of funeral rites. At last certain devout persons carried him to a lodging-place and, rendering what was due to the dead, approached the priest of the church, named Godebert, and according to custom requested permission to bury him and to ring the bells.

He is said to have granted permission for burial but not for bells to be rung for the man, because he did not know that the man had, in part, bought those bells.

[Note: [Col. 1466D] The manuscript has *emisisse*, but the sense requires *empsisse*, as Anianus rightly corrected it in the great manuscript Chronicle.]

Distressed by this prohibition, they carried the body to the church but did not dare force the forbidden bells.

[Col. 1466D]

Immediately, before they had arrived at the church with the body, the bells began to ring with no earthly person ringing them, and continued until they committed that body to burial.

XVI.

The church of Saint Peter the Apostle and of all the Apostles was consecrated on the first day of May, a Thursday, by Ratbod,

[Note: [Col. 1466D] Ratbod, or Rabdodus II, held the see of Tournai and Noyon from 1068 until 1098, when he died miserably at Bruges. See [Col. 1467C] *Summa statutorum synodalium cum praevia synopsi vitae episcoporum Tornacensium*, octavo, Lille, 1726, p. LVII.]

bishop of Noyon and Tournai,

[Col. 1467A]

in the year of the Lord 1070, in the eighth indiction, in the tenth year of the reign of Philip, king of the Franks,

[Note: [Col. 1467C] Philip I.]

and the seventh year of William, king of the English.

[Note: [Col. 1467C] William the Conqueror occupied the throne of England from 1066 to 1087. The year 1070 was therefore the fourth of his reign, rather than the seventh, as our two manuscripts indicate. The great Chronicle of Oudenburg adds: “And likewise in the third year of Baldwin, Count of Flanders; in the twelfth year of Flanders; Arnulf with his mother Richilde for two years.”]

This church, founded in the place of Aldenburgh under the dedication of Saint Peter the Apostle and all the Apostles, was renowned and rich in divine miracles. A certain nobleman, very wealthy, named Conon, brother of Everard of Tournai, held it as a benefice from the Count of Flanders.

[Note: [Col. 1467D] Robert the Frisian, who reigned from 1072 to 1093.]

The count himself held this same church from the bishop of Tournai.

[Note: [Col. 1467D] Ratbod had therefore surrendered the revenues of this church to the Count of Flanders. He was later accused of simony; and it was to clear himself of this accusation before the apostolic legate that he went to Bruges, where he died.]

Fear of the Lord, prompted by his most faithful wife Hasecca, inflamed Conon to make Saint Peter the Apostle’s church—rendered awesome by divine miracles—free from his own legal claim, and to establish, to God’s praise, an abbey of monks.

[Col. 1467B]

XVII.

By God’s ordering it came about that, when Conon restored to the count the church which he held, the count restored that same church to Ratbod, bishop of Noyon and Tournai. Bishop Ratbod, together with Walter the archdeacon, while clergy and people rejoiced, granted it free and unencumbered to Bishop Arnulf and made canonical investiture of it to him. This Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, first established a community of monks.

[Note: [Col. 1467D] The great manuscript Chronicle, fol. 64r, places this account in the year 1083 and adds: “of the Order of Saint Benedict, as may still be seen.” It is here that the little Chronicle beginning with the words *Clarissimus praesul Arnulphus* should be placed; we publish it after this Chronicle of Oudenburg. It contains an abridged history of Saint Arnulf’s life and the foundation of the monastery, and informs us that Saint Arnulf first obtained six monks from Afflighem in Brabant and four from the monastery of Flours in France, to establish the first community: “Six monks from the monastery of Afflighem, together with the four whom he procured for himself from the French monastery of Flours.” Under Olivier Van der Hulst, the thirty-sixth abbot of Oudenburg monastery, who had been prior of Saint Andrew near Bruges, the house abandoned the usages of Cluny and affiliated itself with the celebrated congregation of Bursfeld, whose rites it adopted. This change occurred in 1550. See the great manuscript Chronicle, fol. 202v, and below in the catalogue [Col. 1468D] of abbots. The monastery was suppressed in 1797, as we have said in the preface.]

XVIII.

In the year of the Lord 1081, on the holy night of the Lord’s Nativity, there arose a violent storm,

[Col. 1467C]

which forced the bell-tower of the aforesaid church of Saint Peter to lean from its position and threatened it with sudden collapse so greatly towards the east that any observer would have thought it could not remain standing for an hour unless divine providence delayed its fall. At dawn the inhabitants

[Col. 1468A]

began to gather for this spectacle. They feared to approach because of the horrible threat of its fall, but, seeing only the sudden shaking of the altar beneath it, they implored divine mercy for help in this danger, knowing that human assistance could offer no benefit.

Such was the height of their distress. While these miserable things were occurring, about cockcrow on the night preceding the Circumcision of the Lord, a little before Matins were rung, the west wind suddenly arose in a tempestuous whirlwind and, by divine grant, restored the bell-tower sound and unharmed to its former position. Hearing this exceedingly horrible noise of restoration, the neighbours, fearful that some customary disaster might perhaps have occurred, rose swiftly in great terror

[Col. 1468B]

and hurried in crowds to the aforesaid church. They found the restored bell-tower so completely renewed that nothing in it was broken or damaged. Feeling the generosity of the divine action, they immediately began to ring the bells and praised God in the highest.

[Note: [Col. 1468D] These details, to which everyone is free to give or withhold belief, are valuable because they reveal a contemporary author and eyewitness.]

XIX.

The northern gulf of Gaul encloses a certain fertile region called Flanders; on the north side of this region lies the Ocean.

[Note: [Col. 1468D] This final part of the Chronicle is also its most remarkable: it contains an abridged history of Oudenburg and covers all the time from Attila’s devastations in the fifth century to the eleventh century, when the author lived.]

Those who go down to the sea in ships and conduct voyages upon great waters testify that this Ocean is boundless towards the north and extends everywhere from the furthest shores of France to the limits of heaven. Flanders is said to derive its name from its condition, as though from enduring winds or waves.

[Col. 1468C]

[Note: [Col. 1468D] Most of our historians mention this etymology of the Oudenburg chronicler: Meyer, l’Espinoy, Vredius, Oudegherst, Sanderus, etc.]

In this Flanders, the industry of the ancients established a fortified and strong city, as circumstances required, since, situated near the seashore, it was frequently attacked by barbarians from the islands. This city, once long besieged and at length conquered by King Athalo,

[Note: [Col. 1468D] The manuscript spells the name in full, *Athalo*; the great manuscript Chronicle, which inserts this account under the year 650, fol. 35v, beneath the rubric “Destruction of the town of Oudenburg,” does the same. But Meyer, in his *Annals of Flanders*, under the year 453, where he recounts these disasters, writes *Atthila* and adds: “In our Belgium I read that Tournai, Thérouanne, and Aldenburgh were destroyed …”]

lost its splendour, strength, and urban population, cut down by the hostile sword; and from what was left of it scarcely restored a small town.

[Col. 1469A]

Those, then, who had escaped the slaughter began to erect huts in the town. In memory of their former glory they called their place Aldenborgh, and

[Note: [Col. 1469C] Both the manuscript and the great manuscript Chronicle read *et* (“and”); the sense would be clearer if one read *ut* (“as”).]

it was called in the ancient Teutonic tongue because it was known to have been the oldest and first in all Flanders: for *Aldenburgh* in Teutonic means in Latin *vetus urbs*, “old city.”

Yet at that time this city of Aldenborgh was the capital of all Flanders and, as I have said, most celebrated from its beginnings, very strongly fortified with walls and defensive works. For on its eastern, southern, western, and northern sides it had been constructed of black and extremely hard stones. Stones of this colour and exceeding strength cannot be found naturally anywhere in the province of Flanders, but only in Gaul, in the district of Tournai. On the northern side, an ancient hand had laid foundations of large squared stones, firmly fixed with iron and lead. This kind of stone is said to be found only in the district of Boulogne. Some dwellings within the defences of the walls were built of lighter and less hard stones. These stones are naturally found in the east, in the region of Cologne.

[Col. 1469B]

Beautiful and most elegant vessels, cups, bowls, and very many other utensils, ingeniously fashioned and carved by the ancients in that age, have been found in our time. Skilled craftsmen now could scarcely fashion and carve them as elegantly, even in gold

[Col. 1469C]

and silver.

And so that the aforesaid city might be more admirable and worthy, it was founded almost in the centre of all Flanders, as though in its very heart: eastward it seemed to lie at almost equal distance from the district of Ghent and, westward, from that of Thérouanne. Towards the south,

[Col. 1470A]

at a distance of two leagues, lies sandy ground, bounded there by a pleasant and very shady forest. To the north, the best land in Flanders stretches almost two leagues to the seashore.

This city, very secure in its fortifications of towers and walls and most famous also for every abundance of wealth, exercised lordship over the surrounding districts

[Note: [Col. 1469C] Here *patria* appears to mean a borough or village.]

and cities far and wide, for Bishop Ursmar,

[Note: [Col. 1469C] “The city … exercised lordship [over] Bishop Ursmar”: an obscure phrase whose meaning is difficult to grasp. Since it is immediately said that the prerogative expressed in these words was provided by royal munificence, and since in no. IX the author speaks of property granted to Saint Ursmar throughout Flanders, perhaps the reference is to a payment regularly made to the churches founded by this holy apostle.]

as has been said, because royal excellence so provided for him. The wall was so strong and firm that it could not be destroyed by battering-rams unless the stones of its foundations were first completely extracted and removed.

To remove entirely from readers any doubt concerning the exceptionally strong construction of the aforesaid city, I myself, who composed and first wrote this treatise,

[Col. 1470B]

saw with my own eyes the wall being demolished, and without doubt had the privilege of seeing the aforesaid church of Saint Peter the Apostle built from those very stones. Its columns and walls, however, are constructed of stones from Tournai, while the capitals of the columns are ornamented with inserted stones from Boulogne.

For in earlier times, during the reign of Baldwin of Lille, count of all Flanders, a great part of the building of Bruges is known to have been constructed from these stones. For after Count Ernald the Bearded had begun to build Bruges, he had the walls of this city demolished and the stones given to the people of Bruges for the building of their city,

[Note: [Col. 1469D] The author relied too much on memory when he attributed the building of Bruges to Count Arnulf the Bearded. No such person ever existed. The great manuscript Chronicle, fol. 36r, reproduces this error, but a sixteenth-century hand wrote the name *Balduinus* above *Ernaldus*, while leaving the word *barbatus* (“bearded”) intact. The great manuscript Chronicle, fol. 51v, under the year 881, corrects the error by telling us that Baldwin the Bald gave the stones of Oudenburg to the people of Bruges to build their city. The cited passage reads: “Baldwin the Bald, Count of Flanders, built the town of Bruges in Flanders; and, taking stones from the town of Oudenburg, which King Attila of the Huns had formerly destroyed, fortified the town of Bruges with them.” It should be noted that the name Oudenburg was written in various ways by the chroniclers. Baldwin the Bald reigned from 879 to 918.]

so that, when this city was destroyed, that one might be enlarged. Hence

[Col. 1470C]

this city was almost reduced to nothing, only the mound of earth upon which the wall was destroyed remaining.

If witnesses or testimony are perhaps demanded from me for the matters I have related, I acknowledge that almost all who dwell in the district of Aldenburgh will readily concur with me as credible witnesses.

[Col. 1471]

## NOTICE

[MONITUM.]

This little chronicle is drawn partly from the Life of Saint Arnulf by Lisiard, bishop of Soissons—though others attribute it to Hariulf, third abbot of Oudenburg—and partly from the great manuscript chronicle and other unknown documents. It contains facts which I find nowhere else and departs in no respect from historical truth. Its author has remained unknown. It was copied onto a sheet of parchment in the sixteenth century, if I am not mistaken, or at the earliest towards the end of the fifteenth, and was fixed into the great manuscript chronicle at the head of the Catalogue of Abbots. It is indeed the natural prelude to that catalogue, just as it forms the conclusion of the preceding chronicle.

[Col. 1471A] The most illustrious bishop Arnulf, a Fleming by birth, was born of Fulbert and Mainsind. [The following phrase is textually uncertain: *eis scaldam in loco cui nomen Tydeghem, in agro ac decharchia Aldernardensi, nobilissimo equite*—apparently referring to Tydeghem, in the district and deanery of Oudenaarde, and to a most noble knight.] He was afterward endowed with a belt by the pious Count Baldwin, called of Lille, and chose to serve Christ the Saviour. Shut up in the monastery of Saint Medard, he shone forth in admirable holiness and incomparable silence, having spoken to no mortal person for three whole years and six months. He was first made abbot, then bishop of Soissons. But while Robert the Frisian was waging war against his nephew Baldwin of Lille, the rightful count and heir of Flanders, whom at that time, besides others, many ecclesiastical magnates supported, Frisian persecuted them in every way, punishing some by exile, [Col. 1471B] others by death or confiscation of goods. Among these was Arnulf, archdeacon of the Morini and bishop of Saint-Omer, who, stripped of all his goods and expelled from his homeland, fled to Rome to Gregory VII. Pope Gregory then sent to Flanders the most holy man Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, who, restraining the disputes, made peace between the count and the clergy. Then, at the request of the count and leading men—[Col. 1472A] especially Everard of Tournai, his brother Conon, and Baldwin of Ghent—Blessed Arnulf travelled through many places in Flanders and, by unceasing holy sermons, pious examples, and holiness of life, largely calmed the people agitated by domestic strife and rendered the region much more peaceful. In the year 1084 the aforesaid Conon, chamberlain of Robert the Frisian, held the hereditary priesthood of the church of Oudenburg. Moreover, his wife Hasecca, a religious woman, feared to retain any longer a church distinguished by such great miracles. Therefore, at his wife’s urging, Conon handed over the church to Count Robert; Robert the tenth count [handed it] to Bishop Radbod; and Radbod to Arnulf, bishop of Soissons. At last Saint Arnulf, with the assent of Count Robert, [Col. 1472B] immediately converted it into a monastery of Benedictine monks, hoping that the monks there would lead a holy life for a long age. He obtained six monks from the monastery of Affligem, together with four whom he secured from France, from the monastery of Flore. After his death in 1087, he appointed his nephew as the first abbot.

[Col. 1471]

NOTICE.

The magnificent manuscript into which the little chronicle of Oudenburg, published at the head of this volume, was inserted contains, as we have said, the Life of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons and founder of the abbey of Oudenburg. This Life, as we find it in our manuscript, was published by the Bollandist Fathers under 15 August (*Acta Sanctorum*, vol. III for August, p. 230 ff.). Father G. Cuper, its editor, regretted that he had been unable to obtain the office and Mass celebrated in honour of Saint Arnulf. Father Papebroch had had them in his hands in 1672; but when publication was contemplated in 1737, they could not be found in the library of the Charterhouse of Bruges, where they had been deposited. Following the Life published by Father Cuper, we find in our manuscript the eight lessons of the office of Saint Arnulf, as it was celebrated at Oudenburg; we therefore hasten to publish them as a complement to his history.

The Life itself, which on the basis of the manuscript title and a brief examination we attributed to Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, appears to have been written by Hariulf, third abbot of Oudenburg. Such, at least, is Father Mabillon’s opinion in his *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, founded upon the authority of several manuscripts and fairly strong internal reasons. He believes that Lisiard merely composed the preface and in some sense adopted the work. Father Cuper shares this opinion.

[Col. 1473]

THE SOLEMNITY OF BISHOP ARNULF, CELEBRATED ON THE KALENDS OF MAY. A SERMON ON HIS LIFE.

FIRST LESSON.

[Col. 1473A]

Although Brabant was formerly the nurse and mistress of lawsuits and robberies, and though it was said in a truthful verse:

> As many vines as France possesses, so many lawsuits does Brabant possess,

nevertheless, in the time of Count Baldwin and Countess Adela, it deserved to be irradiated by a gift from above, when it was granted to bring forth from its bosom the man of holy memory Arnulf, the future bishop, born for the enlightenment of no few people and shining like a ray illumined by the Sun of Justice. His father Fulbert, cousin of Godelef the martyr, shone in distinguished nobility; and his mother, named Mainsid, descended from a stock of Teutonic magnates, was notable for her high birth. These illustrious parents, flourishing in both carnal and spiritual offspring, [Col. 1473B] had an already grown son, outstanding in elegance of appearance and deeds of arms, whom untimely death suddenly snatched away and crushed his parents’ hearts with the anguish of inconsolable grief. Yet the mother’s affection grieved more intensely for the loss of her child, and she wore away night and day in tears.

SECOND LESSON.

As she slept under this excessive anxiety, a handsome man, resplendent with flashing light, appeared to her and said: “Why do you afflict yourself with sorrow for a son who died so profitably? Had he lived longer, he would indeed have been dissolute, a robber, and the companion of wicked men. Therefore do not grieve that death has taken him from you; rather, rejoice with great joy, for you carry in your womb a son whom heavenly election has predestined to become great. When you bring him into the light, you will wish him to be called Christopher; for truly this child will bear Christ in his breast by his deeds and words. And, that you may know with certainty that these things have thus been divinely foreordained, go to the church in the place where you are accustomed to pray; have digging done there, and in the dug earth you will find a stone carved with great letters. Those letters will reveal to you the name and merit of your offspring.”

THIRD LESSON.

The venerable matron, having received this oracle of such great praise, awoke from sleep and with immense joy related the vision to her husband. Finally, in order to prove the truth of the matter, she took servants with a digger and, having ordered them to dig as she had been instructed, found a square stone engraved with large letters, bearing this: *Christoforus*—“Christopher.” Having found it, she was filled with greater joy; and now assured of the holiness of the child, though she had not previously known that she had conceived, she joyfully awaited the promised gift of divine action. At length, when he had grown up, [Col. 1474A] he became gracious in speech, keen in intellect, ready in obedience, energetic in work, effective and most strong in bodily vigour. Thereupon, having cheerfully passed through the period of military training, he took the soldier’s belt and surpassed all others in every human excellence in military affairs. When his father died, however, he entered the monastic order and, in the church of Saint Medard at Soissons, proved himself an approved monk, fervently practising not only fellowship in the cloister but also solitary enclosure.

FOURTH LESSON.

Thereafter, when Abbot Rainald died, he was elected abbot. Considering himself unequal to this office, he attempted to avoid it by fleeing at night. Having thus escaped for one day, while on the following night he sought a more remote hiding place, he was escorted back to the city by a wolf; in the morning he was seized and, against his will, installed in the see from which he had fled by episcopal authority. Then he broke the prolonged silences which he had kept for three years and six months, and, made a herald of the Lord, he endeavoured to benefit all by word and deed. Labouring in the office of governance, he accordingly performed many miracles; he subdued the rebellious and unbelieving and restored the sick. He flourished with the spirit of prophecy, and it became known to all that he was truly holy and pleasing to God. At that time Philip, king of the Franks, wished him to come to the royal court to take part in arranging the affairs of the kingdom; he also wished him to take part in an armed expedition. The servant of Christ perceived that both were contrary to the obligation of his former profession, and refused them; lest he offend the Lord, he did not fear to offend the earthly king in this matter. Rather than merely incur the king’s displeasure, he preferred to abandon altogether the care of the abbey, fearing, of course, that, after putting his hand to the plough, if he looked back, he would not be fit for the kingdom of God.

FIFTH LESSON.

Thus he who remained faithful in a few things was set over many, so that, without prejudice to a higher understanding, he might restrain in himself the hosts of all vices and the bounds of all sins, and, enriched by an abundance of virtues, please God and good people. For the Lord glorified him in the sight of the kings and magnates of the realm, with the knowledge of Gregory, lord pope of Rome, and of the whole clergy, to such a degree that, because of Ursio’s negligence, no remedy could be found for the languishing church of Soissons [Col. 1474D] except that this blessed servant of Christ should, by the pope’s counsel, undertake pastoral care of that church. Accordingly, while the public judgment of the court of France opposed it, but the apostolic authority of the Roman pontiff compelled it, he was consecrated [Col. 1475A] bishop, after a canonical election had gone before, so that the lamp of God’s grace might no longer lie hidden in a corner but, set upon a lampstand, might shine upon all.

SIXTH LESSON.

Indeed, while he was going to Hugh, bishop of Die and then legate of the Roman See, to be consecrated, he sent a messenger to the queen of the Franks, who was most sorrowful because of her long sterility. He announced to her that she carried in her womb a son not yet living with the breath of life, but who would receive the spirit of life from the Lord after a few days. He also foretold his name, Louis, and openly prophesied that, after his father’s death, he would become king and enjoy more abundant peace. In December, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, he received the sacred episcopal blessing; and, on his return, he scarcely escaped the devout violence of the clergy and people of Vienne, who would have carried him off to be their bishop had they been able to seize him. Finally, when he approached the see of Soissons, the soldiery of the royal household came out against him and attempted to kill the blessed bishop. But they feared that the earth might swallow them alive. The man of God nevertheless yielded to those resisting him and, with Count Theobald’s assistance, took up residence in the castle of Urcy. There, bishops and nobles of the people assembling, the ecclesiastical case was carefully discussed, the welfare of clergy and people was determined precisely, and the salvation of souls was pursued.

SEVENTH LESSON.

At one time, when he was about to dedicate the parish church of a certain village, he said to his attendants: [Col. 1475C] “I ask you, lead us to that church by such a path that the people may not know by what way we are to come; and bring some food with you, so that we may at least somewhat relieve the weariness of our bodies.” Accordingly a more remote and out-of-the-way path was taken. Yet the fervour of the people was not diminished by this device; rather, with all speed, a great crowd of travellers gathered from every side. Seeing this, the servant of God burst forth in praise of the Creator, and then said to his attendants: “Bring out whatever food you have here, [Col. 1476A] so that after the labour we may restore our strength.” Without delay, five biscuits were brought out, and five measures of wine were poured. Then carpets having been spread on the ground, the man of God sat down, while the flowing crowd surrounded him in groups. Blessing the loaves—few indeed in number, but many through the mystery of their number—he ordered them distributed to all who were seated on every side, and wine likewise to be served in abundance. The attendants marvelled that the bread did not fail; they marvelled also that that very little wine sufficed for so many drinkers.

EIGHTH LESSON.

In that same castle, the holy man of God Arnulf healed his monk and priest Everolf, worn out by fevers and dysentery, by the laying on of his hand. In him he saw that he bore the devil, the carrier of plunder; [Col. 1476B] in him, with God revealing it, he learned a prophecy concerning his own death or burial. The cause of his coming, however, was brotherly charity and obedience: the lord pope had compelled him by his command to reconcile to their count those clerics who had been accused of betraying him, and to allow nothing to be extorted from them contrary to the sacred canons. He obeyed the holy commands imposed on him by apostolic authority, returned to Flanders, and, as a true minister of peace, made peace. He not only restored the clerics shaken by calumny, but also brought the whole region of Flanders, raging against itself with diabolical fury, back to a gentle union of peace and tranquillity. Then, by the counsel and will of Lord Radbod, bishop of Tournai, at the request of Count Robert and the urgent entreaty of the nobleman Conon, he undertook to build and adapt for the uses of an abbey the church of Saint Peter the Apostle and of All the Apostles, situated in the village [Col. 1476C] of Oudenburg. There, by God’s appointment, he received the sleep of rest; there he underwent the burial divinely foreseen for him beforehand; and there, in the thirty-fourth year after his death, he provided joyful solemnities for the translation of his sacred body, through the favour of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1475]

NOTICE.

We observed in the preface to this volume that the sequence of documents which we publish forms a complete history of Oudenburg and its monastery. Indeed, in the little Chronicle we read of the vicissitudes of this town down to the year 1804, including the apostolate of Saint Ursmar and Saint Arnulf, who founded the monastery. The life of the holy founder belongs to the history of Oudenburg; we have given a brief unpublished summary of it, composed in the monastery itself, and, to complete that document, have added the lessons recited in the office of this saint. These unpublished lessons deserved all the more to appear here because they constitute one of the authentic monuments of the cult of Saint Arnulf and because, on that ground, the Bollandists had regretted being unable to publish them. By inserting them here, we fill a gap and gain the advantage of completing the documents concerning this saint’s life.

The catalogue of abbots offers us the history of Saint Arnulf’s successors at Oudenburg, beginning with his nephew. The earlier lives are very short; they have been interpolated. Since the notes added later contain dates that are not without importance, we have preserved them, carefully distinguishing them from the original text. Some, apparently added at the end of the fifteenth century or the beginning of the [Col. 1477] sixteenth, are placed in parentheses `( )`; others, in small fine handwriting, dating from the middle or end of the sixteenth century, are enclosed in square brackets `[ ]`. They may easily be recognized by these marks.

In the manuscript, the arms of the abbots are placed in the margin of their history. Most of these arms are missing.

Despite its brevity, this catalogue is not without interest, for it recounts the chief events of the monastery: the periods when the different parts of the buildings and church were constructed; the year in which the Cluniac rite was abandoned in favour of that of Bursfeld; and the decline and temporal prosperity of the house, down to the time of its final suppression.

Here is the synoptic table of the abbots of Oudenburg, according to the catalogue:

[Col. 1479]

CATALOGUE OF THE ABBOTS OF THE MONASTERY OF OUDENBURG, FROM THE YEAR 1084 TO 1797.

[Col. 1479A] In the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks, whose reign began in the year 614 of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Note: [Col. 1479B] The little chronicle, p. 25, mentions permission granted by Dagobert to Saint Ursmar to build a church at Oudenburg. Comparing the dates, we believed that this concession should be attributed to Dagobert III, who reigned from 711 to 715. The author of this catalogue attributes it to Dagobert II, who died in 638, some years before the birth of Saint Ursmar, which Henschenius places between 644 and 645. We have no means of reconciling these dates or explaining these errors. It should further be observed that the beginning of Dagobert’s reign is fixed in the year 614, whereas it should be fixed in 628, or rather in 622, when Clotaire II gave his still very young son to the Austrasians to govern them.] the church of Saint Peter at Oudenburg was first built with the permission of that king, and was dedicated and consecrated by Saint Ursmar, bishop. It flourished in enduring stability, grew old through a long age, and collapsed through extended antiquity. But after the passage of many years, namely in the year 1056 of the Lord’s Incarnation, it was begun anew and repaired, and reconsecrated by Lord Radbod, bishop of Tournai and Noyon. This took place in the year 1070 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the first day of May.

And because the nobleman Conon, chamberlain of Flanders, [Col. 1479B] and his wife Hasecca possessed this church as a castle-benefice, they handed it over to Count Robert. Count Robert in turn handed it over to the aforesaid Radbod, bishop of Tournai and Noyon. The bishop, with Walter the archdeacon and with the clergy approving, granted it free and unencumbered to the holy man Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, and made him canonical investiture of it. The aforesaid Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, founded it as an abbey and a community of monks of the Order of Saint Benedict. This occurred in the year [Col. 1480A] 1084 of the Lord, and he presided over it for three years. He closed his final day in the year 1087 of the Lord (18 Kalends of September). [Note: [Col. 1479B] The author of the catalogue placed Saint Arnulf’s arms here. A fifteenth-century hand added these [Col. 1480B] words: “These are the arms of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, who was the first founder of the monastery of Oudenburg.” See the general table.]

He was succeeded by Lord ARNULF, son of the sister of the aforesaid holy man, the first abbot of this monastery. He ruled for eight years and died in the year 1095 of the Lord.

Abbot GERVINUS, the second, [consecrated at Ghent, at Saint Peter’s]. Formerly a religious of Saint Winnoc at Bergues, a man of honourable life and holy conduct, as appears more fully in our books. [Note: [Col. 1480B] Here one sees that the catalogue of abbots is merely an extract from more extensive annals preserved in the monastery library, whose loss we must doubtless lament.] He ruled for ten years and resigned in the year 1105 of the Lord. (He survived two years; buried in Brabant, 17 April.)

[Col. 1480B] Abbot HARIULF, the third, [Note: [Col. 1480B] The manuscript reads *Hariulphus*; Sanderus reads *Arnulphus*; Fathers Mabillon and Cuper read *Hariulphus*, like the manuscript.] formerly a religious of Saint-Riquier in Ponthieu. A man of complete prudence and remarkable discernment. Through his diligence, in the sixteenth year of his rule, the body of the most holy bishop Arnulf was raised from the earth, in the thirty-fourth year after the death of that same first founder of this aforesaid monastery. [Note: [Col. 1480B] This was indeed thirty-four years after the death of the holy founder—that is, in 1121—that the elevation of his body took place, according to the Life published by Father Cuper in the *Acta Sanctorum*, of which we have before us an excellent manuscript.] Moreover, he stoutly and lawfully defended the church entrusted to him against the abbot and religious of Saint Medard at Soissons, who endeavoured to reduce it to a priory subject to themselves, as appears more clearly in other writings. [Note: [Col. 1480B] The large manuscript Chronicle contains the documents of this dispute under the year 1141.] He ruled worthily and praiseworthily for thirty-eight [Col. 1481A] years and died in the year 1143 of the Lord’s Incarnation (16 August). May his soul obtain a share in the blessed resurrection.

Abbot BALDRANNUS, [Note: [Col. 1481D] Sanderus writes *Balderamus*.] the fourth. Formerly prior of the church of Lobbes [in the regions of Hainaut], he ruled for two years and died in 1145 (17 May).

Abbot MARCILIUS, the fifth. Formerly a religious of Saint-Bertin at Saint-Omer. He ruled for twenty-five years and died in the year 1170 of the Lord (18 July).

Abbot HERMANNUS, the sixth. Formerly a religious of Saint Nicasius of Reims, he established a confraternity between the church of Saint Peter at Oudenburg and [Col. 1481B] Saint Nicasius at Reims. He ruled for seventeen years and died in 1187 (1 October).

Abbot BALDWIN, the seventh. Formerly a religious of Saint Winnoc at Bergues, he ruled for thirteen years and died at Cologne in the year 1200 of the Lord (10 November).

Abbot WITTUS, the eighth. Formerly a religious of Saint Peter at Ghent, he ruled for eleven years and died in the year 1200 of the Lord (27 November).

Abbot HENRY, the ninth. He ruled praiseworthily for twenty-five years and died in the year 1236 of the Lord (27 July).

EPITAPH OF THE AFORESAID.

Here lies Henry, an abbot devout and chaste,

[Col. 1481C] An exemplar of justice’s law, and a pattern for the flock.

Abbot GERARD, the tenth, one of our own, in whose time our estate of Boomburch was burned, a fire having been secretly set [in the year 1243, on the night of the holy Apostles Simon and Jude], and the community was dispersed [for two years]. He ruled for ten years and died in 1246 (4 December).

Abbot ROBERT, the eleventh. Formerly a religious and cellarer of Saint Martin at Tournai; afterward a monk of Thosan. He ruled for four years and died in the year 1250 of the Lord. [In this same year, weighed down by a mass of debts, our community was dispersed for three years.]

[Col. 1481D] Abbot JOHN, the twelfth. Formerly a religious and almoner of Saint Peter at Ghent, a man greatly to be preferred in temporal as well as spiritual affairs, he ruled for twenty years. He conferred many benefits upon this monastery. Moreover, he built the dormitory anew, as may still be seen, and closed his final day in the year 1270 of the Lord’s Incarnation (12 October). May his soul rest in the land of the living.

EPITAPH OF THE AFORESAID.

In the year twelve hundred and seventy,

This father passed away on the twelfth day of October.

Alas, dust covers the father who guided us well

For twice ten years. Jesus, have mercy on John!

[Col. 1482A] The brothers added:

May the devout and faithful abbot rejoice in heaven. (Buried in the middle of the choir.)

Abbot RASO, the thirteenth, (one of our own), ruled for eight years and died in 1278 (3 October).

Abbot JOHN OF BIERVLIET, the fourteenth, a religious of this monastery, whose writing still survives, ruled for twenty-nine years and died in the year 1307 of the Lord (17 January).

Abbot JOHN OF DONSA, the fifteenth (one of our own), ruled for a short time and resigned. He died in the year 1329 of the Lord (24 February).

EPITAPH OF THE AFORESAID ABBOT.

John, born of Donsa, lies buried here,

[Col. 1482B] An abbot, a humble prelate, gracious also to all.

He was such in life; afterward, becoming a monk,

He did not act against what was undertaken, but performed the rites well.

In the thousandth year, full with the wound of death,

Joined with twice ten, and likewise nine and thirty,

He passed away upon the then manifest feast of Matthew.

Whoever stands here, be ready with prayers for him.

Moreover, he was full eighty years old;

May delightful Paradise preserve this faithful race. Amen.

Likewise, upon the same stone:

Here rest together two brothers born of the same mother,

Born of Donsa; may they be united with the saints.

One was James, reckoned here a good monk;

And worthy John, beloved curate of Slijpe.

He had ordained that four Masses should be celebrated

Each week; the brother gave us sufficient provision for this.

Now, for these three named, grant aid, good Christ,

To afflicted hearts; we pray that it may be so. Amen.

[Col. 1482C] Abbot ROGER WEVEL, the sixteenth, formerly a religious of Saint Andrew near Bruges. He ruled together with his predecessor for twenty-seven years, and died in 1334 (18 October; buried beside the bell and the chapel of the Cross).

Abbot JAMES TINTORIS, [Note: [Col. 1482D] Sanderus writes *Tinctoris*.] the seventeenth, one of our own, ruled for twenty years and died in 1354 (25 August; buried in the chapel of Mary).

Abbot ZEGARDUS KARLIN, the eighteenth, one of our own, ruled for twenty-eight years and died in 1382 of the Lord (27 December; buried at the end of the church on the south side).

Abbot NICHOLAS ALOUT, the nineteenth, one of our own, ruled [Col. 1482D] for eleven years and died in 1393 (25 June; native of Bruges; buried in the chapel of the Virgin Mary).

Abbot GEORGE, the twentieth, formerly a religious of Saint Winnoc at Bergues, ruled for one year, then resigned the abbey and went to govern the aforesaid monastery of Saint Winnoc.

Abbot WITTUS TALLET, the twenty-first, formerly a religious of Saint-Bertin at Saint-Omer. He ruled for nineteen years and died in 1413 (11 January).

Abbot JAMES, called Coc, the twenty-second, (of Mechelen), repaired and rebuilt from its foundations the cloister court in the year 1421. He ruled [Col. 1483A] for twenty years and died in 1433 (13 August; buried in the chapel of Blessed Mary).

Abbot JOHN DURYNC, the twenty-third, ruled for ten years and died at Paris. He was buried in the collegiate church of Saint Benedict before Saint Christopher, in the year 1443 of the Lord (8 May; one of our own).

Abbot ANTHONY CLERICI, the twenty-fourth, ruled for two years and died in 1445 of the Lord (23 December; he lies in the nave of the church; adviser to the count; one of our own).

Abbot HENRY ONDERMARCK, the twenty-fifth, who laid the foundations of the present choir, raised its walls to a height, and left very many preparations suitable for this work (having great concern for souls), [Col. 1483B] also conferred many other benefits upon the church. He ruled for five years and resigned in 1451 of the Lord. (This Abbot Henry died in 1456 and was buried at Louvain, 5 June.)

(Through the diligence and care of the following Lord Anianus, all the foregoing were preserved in memory.)

Abbot ANIANUS, called Coussere, a native of the district of Cassel, formerly a religious and provost in the monastery of Saint Winnoc at Bergues, succeeded as the twenty-sixth ruler and received the blessing of office in the year 1451 of the Lord, on 12 Kalends of July, which was the feast of the Most Holy Trinity. Labouring in the Lord’s field and attentive to spiritual and temporal matters, he quickly completed and brought to perfection, with new seats, the choir which his predecessor had begun. In the year 1455, on 5 Kalends of May, the same abbot, with the consent of the reverend prince Lord John, bishop of Tournai, caused the said new choir and two new chapels to be dedicated, and two altars to be consecrated: namely, the high altar in honour of the Holy Trinity [and the Apostles], and the altar on the south side of the choir in honour of the Holy Cross and Saint Benedict. He also caused the nave of the church, the courtyard, refectory, chapter-house, dormitory, and entire cloister to be reconciled by the reverend lord William, bishop of Sarepta, in the presence of James, abbot of Saint Andrew near Bruges; James, abbot of Thosan de la Chapelle; [Col. 1483D] Abbot Anianus himself; and very many other ecclesiastical persons.

Furthermore, seeing that the body of our glorious patron Arnulf rested in an old wooden chest which, owing to its extreme age, was so modest in appearance and so poorly furnished that reverence for the saint was thereby neglected, he caused a new shrine to be made at Bruges, adorned with gold and silver as the eyes of beholders may see. Into it he had the most holy body of our father Arnulf translated in the year 1457, on the first day of May, which was then Sunday. Present were many abbots, provosts, doctors, curates, chaplains, and nobles, together with an immense multitude of persons of both sexes: namely, people of Ghent, Bruges, Oudenburg, Diksmuide, Nieuwpoort, [Col. 1484A] Veurne, Ostend, Bergues, Gistel, Ettelgem, and Leffinge. All marvellously adorned this place, going before the clergy in procession with innumerable torches and a great number of well-sounding trumpets, with devotion, joy, and gladness. These things I saw.

Copy of the letter of the lord bishop of Tournai consenting to the translation of the body of Saint Arnulf, bishop.

“JOHN, by divine mercy bishop of Tournai, to the reverend father in Christ Lord WILLIAM, by the same mercy bishop of Sarepta, greeting in the Lord. Recently the venerable father, the abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Oudenburg in our diocese, explained to us that the shrine in which the most glorious body [Col. 1484B] of Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor, rests in the same monastery is enclosed in a wooden chest which, owing to extreme age, is so modest in appearance and so poorly furnished that veneration of this saint is therefore omitted and neglected by Christ’s faithful. So that the said saint may be venerated by the said faithful of Christ and praises and encomia may be heaped upon him, the same abbot has caused a new honourably adorned shrine to be made, for transferring the said most glorious body from the said old shrine and placing it within the new one. He therefore petitions and humbly requests that we might deign and wish to grant our consent and assent to such a translation.

“Accordingly, favourably assenting to this so just request, [Col. 1484C] by these presents sealed with the seal of our chamber we grant and impart to you permission and authority to open the said old shrine; to take and raise from it the said most glorious body with the prayers, solemnities, and ceremonies necessary and requisite for this purpose; to transfer it to the said new shrine; and reverently to place it therein, with the grant of thirty days’ indulgence in the customary form. Given at Lille, in our said diocese, in the year 1456 of the Lord, on the twenty-fifth day of October.

“Thus signed: HULAND.”

Copy of the writing placed in the shrine beside the body of the aforesaid Saint Arnulf.

[Col. 1484D] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Here rests the glorious body of our most holy father and protector Arnulf, bishop and confessor, translated by the reverend father in Christ and lord, William, Bishop of Sarepta, suffragan of the most reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord John, Bishop of Tournai, in the fifth indiction, while Callistus III occupied the Roman See, John governed the metropolitan see of Reims, Charles VI reigned as King of the French, Louis, most noble Dauphin of France, was residing at Bruges, Philip, Count of Flanders, was beginning the thirty-eighth year of his rule, and Anianus, by God’s authorship, was administering the care of the monastery of Oudenburg; with many abbots, provosts, and other faithful of Christ besides standing by in joy and devotion. It was solemnly performed in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation one thousand. So that our descendants may believe it without doubt, honour it diligently, and celebrate it forever, it has been decreed that the names and seals of those present at this translation be recorded. Seal of Lord William, Bishop of Sarepta. Seal of Anianus, Abbot of St Peter’s, Oudenburg. Seal of James, Abbot of St Andrew’s near Bruges. Seal of Nicasius, Abbot of St Adrian the Martyr. Seal of Everard, Abbot of the Dunes. Seal of James, Abbot of the Chapel of Thosan. Seal of Peter, Abbot of Blessed Mary’s, Middelburg. Seal of Lyman, Abbot of St Nicholas’s, Veurne. Seal of Hector, Provost of Eversam. Seal of James, Abbot of Blessed Mary’s, Zonnebeke. Seal of Anthony, Abbot of St Bartholomew’s, Eekhout. Seal of Walter, Provost of the Churches of Blessed Mary at Bruges and St Peter at Cassel.”
