Copy of the letter given to the parishioners of Tiegem upon the donation of a relic of the same saint.

“William, by divine mercy Bishop of Sarepta, and Anianus, by the same permission humble abbot of the monastery of St Peter at Oudenburg, of the Order of St Benedict in the diocese of Tournai, to all Christ’s faithful who shall inspect these present letters: everlasting salvation in the Lord. We make known that, in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1461, on the first day of May, after we and very many prelates of various churches had, as was fitting, inspected the glorious body of our most holy father Arnulf, bishop and confessor, resting in the aforesaid monastery in a certain old chest, the same most holy confessor of the Lord, Arnulf, was solemnly translated and deposited in a new shrine honourably adorned with silver and gold. This was done by the said abbot under a special mandate obtained from the reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord John, by the same divine mercy Bishop of Tournai.

“To the humble petition, therefore, of the honourable men, the parish priest and the wardens of the fabric of the parish church of Tiegem in the said diocese of Tournai—whence the same glorious Saint Arnulf was native—we granted and gave one relic of the same most holy and most glorious confessor to the aforesaid parish priest and wardens, who humbly and devoutly requested it, so that he might be venerated and honoured more fervently and devoutly in that church and the places adjoining it. In testimony of all the foregoing, we have caused these present letters to be confirmed with our seals, in the year, month, and day written above.”

[Col. 1486A] When all the aforesaid had been duly performed, the same Abbot Anianus had the aforesaid altar in the chapel of our manor at Boomburck consecrated by William, Bishop of Sarepta, in the year of the Lord 1458, on the Kalends of August—that is, the day after the feast of St James the Apostle. In the same year he carried out many repairs there in the houses and in the ditches round about.

In the same year, the said abbot redeemed from the hands of the sons of Giles de la Chapelle our manor of Hemelghem, which they held for life together with all its houses and appurtenances. For this he expended one thousand Paris pounds and more. At this time the ditch of our manor commonly called St Arnulf’s Estate was repaired.

Anianus caused me to be cast and called consecrated Peter, in honour of St Peter, with Peter as maker, in the year of the Lord 1460.

And the same Anianus caused me likewise, at the same time, to be cast by the hands of the same Peter, and to be called Paula.

Thus [Note: [Col. 1485D] This paragraph was written after Anianus’s death by a fifteenth- or sixteenth-century hand.] the aforesaid ANIANUS, twenty-sixth abbot of this place, whose arms appear in this form [Note: [Col. 1485D] We have assembled in a single table, found below, the arms of the abbots of Oudenburg which we find scattered through the manuscript. All those mentioned hereafter must be sought there.], after he had bestowed many pious works upon our church and had laboured not sluggishly in the Lord’s vineyard, departed this world in the eleventh year of his rule, in the year 1462, on the penultimate day of May. He was buried in the middle of the choir of our monastery.

Since [Note: [Col. 1486D] This paragraph, and everything following down to the words “were fashioned and adopted, who …,” under Olivier Van Der Hulst, appears to have been composed under that abbot, between 1547 and 1550. What follows was added after his death, for the Life of Gaspar de Bovincour is written in another hand.] we see that the catalogue of our abbots has been interrupted through the negligence of copyists, we now judge it worthwhile to complete the number, so that [Col. 1486C] posterity may know in what order each fulfilled his office. Therefore, as we have received from our elders, we intend to set forth individually the abbots who are to be written of.

After the death of Abbot Anianus, namely CLEMENS EGIDII, a monk of this monastery, became the twenty-seventh abbot of this house, and counsellor to the most illustrious Duke of Burgundy and Count of Flanders. This abbot bore arms as the following figure shows. He presided for only one year and died on 14 June 1463; he was buried in the chapel of the Holy Cross in our church.

RAPHAEL DE MARCHATELLIS, son of Philip the Great, Duke of Burgundy, nevertheless retained the surname of his mother’s husband. A Doctor of Paris and monk of St Peter’s, Ghent, he was the twenty-eighth Abbot of Oudenburg. He bought the manor of Erninghem and obtained mortmain rights from the Duke, on condition that, during Charles’s lifetime, on St Martin’s Day—because he said that he had been born on that day—the first Mass in the monastery should be sung of the Holy Spirit; after Charles’s death, however, a perpetual Requiem. This abbot rebuilt on the south side our dormitory, which had collapsed with its roof, after shortening it in his time, and roofed it with artesian slate. At last, after presiding for fifteen years, in the year of the Lord 1478, he resigned and became Abbot of St Bavo’s, Ghent. He was escorted with distinction by fifty horsemen and obtained the bishopric of Rhosus, though he did not administer it. His arms appear in this form. He died and was buried in the monastery at Ghent on the fourth day of August.

WALTER DE LACU, a religious of St Peter’s, Blandinium, and its second prior, was the twenty-ninth abbot of our monastery of Oudenburg for eleven years. His arms appear here. He died in the year of the Lord 1489, on 16 September, and was buried in the chapel of Blessed Mary in our monastery.

[Col. 1487B] JAMES, SON OF JAMES, native of Bruges, monk and wine-steward of this place, became the thirtieth Abbot of Oudenburg, elected at Bruges in the sacristy of St Saviour’s. He presided for about eleven years. He was counsellor to the most illustrious prince and Duke of Burgundy and Brabant and Count of Flanders, Lord Philip. Under this abbot our community was dispersed because of the soldiers from Sluis, ravagers of Flanders, whose war was called the *garde*. He appointed as coadjutor a monk of Vlierbeek near Louvain, named James Courteville, and died in 1500, on the fifth day of August. He was buried before the altar of the Holy Cross, as is evident from the stone, on which his arms shine in this form.

JAMES DE COURTEVILLE, monk of the monastery of Vlierbeek, of the Order of St Benedict, was the thirty-first Abbot of Oudenburg, consecrated on the feast of the Beheading of St John the Baptist. His arms were depicted under this sign. In 1518, the eighteenth year of his government, having resigned, he transferred himself, on the vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul, to govern the monastery of St Winoc at Bergues, not without great obstacles. He died there in the year of the Lord 1524, on 19 November.

ANTHONY DE COURTEVILLE, brother of the aforesaid Lord James, formerly a Premonstratensian canon of the monastery of St Andrew in the Wood, in the diocese of Amiens, was the thirty-second abbot of this place, upon his brother’s resignation, consecrated on the feast of James and Christopher. He caused the place of the venerable sanctuary in the choir to be built of white stone, as is evident. He gave the church splendid ornaments of crimson velvet, where his arms shine in the form set down above. After presiding for nineteen years, he died in the year of the Lord 1636, on the sixth day of October, and was buried without memorial on the left side of the presbytery by the wall. Through the intervention of the Countess of Flanders, he put in his place a certain Augustinian brother from Ghent, named Gideon; but after obtaining the suffragan bishopric, Gideon refused the abbacy, content with an annual pension of fifty Flemish pounds from the successor.

JOHN DE GREBOUAL, native of Steenwerck, monk of St Saviour’s at Ham, but then titular prior of Beuvry in Artois, was requested by the brothers in Gideon’s place as above and consecrated [Col. 1488A] at Bruges, in the house of St Bertin, on 18 February, as Abbot of Oudenburg, of pious memory. I have seen his insignia painted in various places in our monastery, with this ornament. He governed worthily and laudably for four years and died in 1540, on 25 August, namely the day after St Bartholomew’s. He lies buried in the chapel of Blessed Mary. One of his subject monks, James Michiels, composed and wrote his epitaph:

Here lies the glory of abbots, here a most illustrious abbot.  
John, the great glory of this house.

The celebrated and spacious house of Grebouval brought him forth;  
Flanders gave him birth; Artois nurtured him.

Ham received him as a youth; Benedict’s rule refashioned him,  
which he entered at eight years old, aflame with religious zeal.

Thus Beuvry received him as its own prior, Christina;  
once made prior, he shone more highly.

But Almighty God, and all the holy powers together,  
suffer no adverse storm to overthrow the man.

Hence, by His holy will, He grants that he hasten to another place:  
Oudenburg is given to him, a house sought before,

which thirty-two renowned and pious fathers had governed;  
he was its most illustrious thirty-third.

He gave great comforts of life to the wretched;  
he was, by right, a great protection to those oppressed by evil.

Envious fates snatched the true man from us.  
Untimely death bore him away far too soon.

What he had contracted from the realm of death is consumed by disease;  
the earth covers the body, but the spirit holds the stars.

Grant, Almighty Father, the prepared heavenly kingdom,  
which that Thy Son restored by the cross!

And you also, loving reader, lest flame burn the departed spirit,  
relieve him by your devout prayers.

CHRISTIAN VAN BASSEVELDE, born in this town of Oudenburg, a religious of this monastery and its cellarer, receiver, and prior, became [Col. 1488C] the thirty-fourth abbot of this place, consecrated on the Sunday before the feast of St Martin in November. His arms were represented in this manner. He presided for one year and three months and died in the year of the Lord 1541, on 22 January, in the Reims style of dating. He was buried in the chapel of the Holy Cross of our monastery. Lord Francis Kempe composed his epitaph:

Here lies an abbot called from Christ’s name,  
his name suited to his devout life.

He was of holy character and a lovable cultivator of letters,  
the honour of religion and glory of the monastery.

While solemn Vincentian rites were being celebrated,  
he left the mortal remains of his body.

May Christ place Bassevelde, after the raging pest of Cocytus has been conquered,  
upon the Elysian height of the sun!

[Col. 1488D] JOHN VAN DER WEERDE, monk and receiver of the monastery of St Andrew at Straten, was the thirty-fifth abbot of this place, consecrated on the first day of May 1542. Having governed for about five years, he resigned to the imperial majesty and commended the abbey to Lord Oliver, formerly his prior. He returned to the aforesaid monastery, namely St Andrew’s near Bruges, in 1561, on 12 December. He was buried in the choir of his monastery, and we performed his funeral rites with a thirty-day observance.

OLIVER VAN DER HULST, monk and prior of the monastery of St Andrew at Straten near Bruges, became the thirty-sixth abbot of St Peter’s, Oudenburg, consecrated on St Benedict’s own day in March 1547. His arms were fashioned and adopted according to his surname, [Col. 1489A] which [Note: [Col. 1489D] Olivier Van der Hulst had the catalogue of abbots continued from Anianus, the twenty-sixth abbot, down to the words “were fashioned and adopted, which …”] in 1550, the fourth year of his prelacy, reformed the monastery from the old Cluniac custom to the new rite of Bursfeld; both the ceremonies and the customary forms for conducting the divine office were then changed. Among his other distinguished achievements, he also adorned the church with various kinds of ornaments, of which there was then the greatest scarcity there; he ordered five bells to be cast in due harmony of tones; he began to have the pavement of the nave of the church, hitherto laid with tiles, paved with stone; and he separated it from the choir of the religious by carefully fashioned openwork screens. He further raised anew from the foundations the eastern and southern parts of our cloister, twelve courses of stone higher than they had previously been. He acquired much temporal property for the monastery, relieved it of the immense burden of debts under which he had found it bound, and at his death left his successor, besides this, an inestimable treasure of money. He governed with great praise for twenty-two years, eight months, and one week, and died in the seventy-fifth year of his age, in the year of the restored world 1568, on the Nones of December, buried beneath the bell tower before the entrance to the high choir, beneath a new sarcophagus which he had placed there for himself before his death.

In this tomb lies he to whom Olive gave his name,  
and the sharp yew itself, his father, gave his surname.

He who flourished as the first glory of the reformed cloister  
and august honour of holy religion.

His name, as though equal to his virtues, meant  
to be gentle toward the harmless, fierce toward springs.

The rough yew marks the pricking goads of anger;  
the olive gives proof of a devout mind.

Wetteren deserved to behold him born from the womb;  
Ganda’s Iris deserved to nourish him with its gifts.

Then Andrew of the Cross made him monk and prior;  
then Aldenburg possessed him as its abbot.

He was added as the sixth after thirty abbots,  
nor was he inferior to any among them all.

Whatever shone as an image of virtue in the ancients  
this man surpassed by countless good endowments.

He had presided as abbot through four full five-year periods,  
and then a second year was added;

a third came on—alas, to be completed under an adverse  
omen; I wish it had never hastened so.

He was snatched away by death on the Nones of December,  
a death surely unworthy of him—alas, what rewards does it return for his merits!

For the rest, accompany the father’s merit with prayers  
and always hold the man in remembering heart;

and whenever you do so, let it not be burdensome, I pray, to say:  
“May Father Oliver’s bones rest gently!”

[Col. 1489D] LORD GASPAR DE BOVINCOURT [Note: [Col. 1489D] This Life is written in a hand which wrote no others. Gothic script ceases here with the thirty-eighth abbot.], Knight of Jerusalem, native of Bapaume, a town of Artois, religious and steward of the monastery of St Saviour at Anchin near Douai, was appointed to us by the court at Brussels as the thirty-seventh abbot of this monastery and the second after the reform, on 6 April 1569, in the fortieth year of his age. He received the office and grace of benediction in his aforesaid monastery of Anchin from the Bishop of Arras, Francis Richardot, on 8 May of the same year, the Sunday *Cantate*, while [Col. 1490A] the See of Bruges was then vacant because of the death of Lord Peter Curtius, its first bishop. Finding a considerable sum of money accumulated by his predecessor, he immediately, at the beginning of his prelacy, raised the entire abbatial house anew from the foundations, demolishing the old buildings he had found. Having erected chambers much more splendid and magnificent, he decorated the whole abbatial house, contrary to the monastery’s former custom, in a short time with furniture no less abundant than costly and magnificent. He clad the walls in tapestries, various pictures, and Spanish hangings, so that, through its sudden transformation, it might have appeared not so much an abbatial house as a royal court. In the convent likewise, he completed in glass two wings of the cloister which his predecessor had raised, adorning them by placing his own arms and those of the community upon them. He paved the remaining part of the nave of the church with Ordonnant stone, and from the bell tower to the porch, on the northern side, erected remarkable screens made of white stone for the greater adornment of the church. He was a man distinguished in appearance, eloquent in speech, adorned with excellent morals, delighting in magnificent display, greatly beloved by the nobles of the Low Countries and joined to them in the closest intimacy. Thus, in the fourth year of his prelacy, namely 1572, he was sent by the four Estates of Flanders, on account of the difficult circumstances of the state at that time, to lay their necessity before Philip II, King of Spain and Count of Flanders. He performed this embassy with the highest praise, made his name famous, obtained, by the voice of all who had accompanied the embassy, distinguished glory, and finally left to his monastery an immortal memory of himself. He presided seven years and, after a long bodily infirmity, died on 11 February in the year of the Lord 1577, at St Michael’s near Bruges, in the castle called Craneburg, to which he had retired for a change of air and recovery of health. Afterwards he was brought back to the monastery and buried in the high choir, beside the wall at the choir of the left-hand altar.

Thirty-eighth. In the abbatial dignity he was succeeded by the Reverend Lord MELCHIOR WUERAERT [Note: [Col. 1490D] The history of this abbot and of his successors down to and including Charles Gheleyns is in a very careless seventeenth-century hand. The sentence ending the life of Charles Gheleyns—“He left the monastery mortgaged with immense debts, so that scarcely any hope remains”—leads me to believe that this portion of the catalogue was written immediately after that abbot’s death, and conveys the very sad impression left by his bad administration. He died in 1667. Yet the histories of the following two abbots are written in the same hand.], appointed by John of Austria in 1577. He scarcely took up residence in the abbey because of the sectarians; indeed, on 24 September 1578 he was compelled, with his religious, to abandon his own monastery. [Col. 1490D] He was carried off by plague and buried at Nieuwpoort in October 1583, in the parish church.

Thirty-ninth. He was succeeded by the venerable Lord JOHN BOURRIER in 1584. He lived amid civil wars and was never able to reside there. This abbot also administered the abbey of St Andrew near Bruges. The divine office was entirely forbidden by the Geuzen for forty years; thereafter the monastery was converted into a fortress until 21 January 1616, the feast of St Agnes. On that day he died at Bruges and was buried at St Saviour’s, in the chapel of Blessed Mary of Loreto, in a free burial-place, with an epitaph still visible today on the wall between the two lateral windows of that chapel.

Fortieth. In the same year, namely 1616, the Reverend Lord JOHN MAXIMILIAN D’ENGHIEN succeeded him, appointed by the Most Serene Princes Albert and Isabella, Archdukes. Born from a noble Brabantine family, he was a religious of St Vaast’s, licentiate in sacred theology, and president of St Gregory’s College at Douai. He was frequently deputed by the clergy to the Estates of Flanders, and recovered in large part the possessions of the monastery which had been occupied and ruined by the Geuzen for forty years. He completely restored the monastery, which had been turned into a royal fortress. He died at Bruges, in his refuge, on 20 August 1662, in the seventy-ninth year of his age and the forty-seventh of his prelacy, and was buried in the monastery of Aldenburg in the middle of the presbytery. His epitaph is inscribed upon stone.

Meanwhile the see remained vacant until 1664, when the Reverend Lord CHARLES GHELEYNS of Bergues-Saint-Winoc, religious and cantor, was appointed by Philip IV, King of Spain, as the forty-first abbot of this monastery. He obtained the mitre and pontifical insignia from Pope Alexander VII, and was invested with the mitre on the Kalends of January 1665 in the choir of St Donatian’s by the Right Reverend and Illustrious Robert de Haynin, Bishop of Bruges, assisted by the Very Reverend and Most Honourable Lords de Wignacourt, Abbot of St Winoc’s, and Benedict van den Berghe, Abbot of St Andrew’s, in the presence of the Marquess de Castel Rodrigo, then Governor of the Low Countries, and the entire court.

[Col. 1491C] This abbot was deputed by the clergy to the Estates of Flanders. He died at Bruges, in the refuge, in 1677 and was buried in the monastery in the middle of the presbytery. He left the monastery mortgaged with immense debts, so that scarcely any hope remains. May he rest in peace.

Forty-second. He was immediately succeeded, appointed by the Most Excellent Duke of Villa Hermosa, Governor of the Low Countries for King Charles II, by the Reverend Lord PHILIP GHUERARD [Note: [Col. 1491D] The lives of the forty-second and forty-third abbots are written in the same hand, though different from the others.], native of Ghent, prior of the monastery of Aldenburg and professed religious of the same. He was mitred and blessed in the chapel of the Holy Blood by the illustrious Lord Francis de Baillencourt, Bishop of Bruges, in 1698. He died at Bruges, in the refuge, [Col. 1491D] on 14 March 1679 and was buried at Aldenburg in the middle of the presbytery.

In the year of the Lord 1676, when the monastery of Aldenburg had been vacant for two months, the venerable Lord ALBERT [Col. 1492A] FREDERICK TAYE, of the Barons of Wemmel, a religious of the monastery of St Saviour at Ename, was appointed by the Most Excellent Duke de Villa Hermosa, Governor of the Low Countries for King Charles II. He was installed, blessed, and mitred by the illustrious Lord Francis de Baillencourt, Bishop of Bruges, at the monastery of Aldenburg, on 24 June of the same year, and was the forty-third abbot of this monastery.

In 1687, in the month of …, on the day of …, the Reverend Lord AUGUSTINE VERMEULEN [Note: [Col. 1492D] The dates omitted on this line are lacking in the manuscript. The life of this abbot was written immediately after his death; the same is true of the following one.], a native of Bruges, religious and formerly prior and provost of Blandinium, his predecessor having died, was appointed by the Most Excellent Lord Marquess de Castagna, Governor of the Low Countries for the Catholic King Charles II. Not long afterwards he was confirmed and mitred as abbot of this monastery, the forty-fourth, by the Illustrious and Right Reverend Lord Humbert William van Precipiano, Bishop of Bruges, in the chapel [Col. 1492B] of his episcopal palace at Bruges. He found the monastery terribly mortgaged and exceedingly burdened with debts. Then followed those great wars waged by the King of France, after peace had repeatedly been broken and the twenty-year truce ended, against the Emperor, the Catholic King, and all the confederates of Germany, Holland, and England.

(Forty-fifth.) He was succeeded by MARTIN GEERTS. He received letters patent signed at Brussels on 2 April 1698 from Charles II. He was a religious of St Peter’s at Ghent and was installed at Ghent by Philip van der Noot on 24 June 1698, in his own abbey. The Abbots of Ghent and Ename assisted. He had taken possession on 13 April 1698 and died on 11 October [Col. 1492C] 1700. His motto was: “I do not refuse labour.”

In his place GREGORY LAMBERTI succeeded [Note: [Col. 1492D] The history of this abbot and all those following was composed after 1803 through the care of Father Bouten, who had received the great chronicle as his share. I found in the volume the notes used for its composition; they seem to have been taken from the convent archives. The handwriting of this final portion of the catalogue is that of a child.], a religious and prior of this abbey, the forty-sixth abbot. He received letters patent signed at Brussels by M. Barde under the order of Philip, King of Castile, dated 25 January 1701. He was instituted on 1 March of that year by Peter Boury, canon of the cathedral and official, and Andrew Mendez, canon of the same church, under the mandate of William Basser, Bishop of Bruges; and at Bruges, in the episcopal chapel, was solemnly invested with the mitre by that bishop on 17 April 1701. He died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, that is, 16 April 1713.

AMANDUS NEIRYNCK, forty-seventh abbot of this house, a religious of St Peter’s on Mount Blandin, was appointed at Brussels by Emperor Charles on 14 January 1716. The appointment was signed by A. Bollaert. On the eighth day of the month of … 1716 he was confirmed; he died on 9 March 1721.

The Reverend Lord JODOCUS GRAMON [Note: [Col. 1492D] The author of this catalogue forgot the ordinal number of this abbot, which he assigned to the following one; hence an error that continues to the end of the catalogue. We have corrected it in the synoptic table at the end of the prefatory notice, p. 50.], a religious [Col. 1493A] and for ten years professor at Bergues-Saint-Winoc, governed our abbey in the capacity of prior for approximately thirteen years, because of the lack of money and subjects. For the abbey, it is said, was terribly burdened by debts, contained only three religious, and they scarcely had the means to live. He worked with all his strength to bring relief, but a death far too early took him away on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July 1732.

He was succeeded in the abbatial dignity by the Reverend Lord FOLQUINUS GRAMON, forty-eighth abbot, brother of the deceased prior, a professed religious of St Bertin’s, where he was great in piety, zeal, and learning, and was a professor. The religious asked such a man to deign to undertake that burden. He became a great prior, professor, and pastor by merit, but greater in the abbatial dignity and greatest when he was made chief assessor among the illustrious Estates of Flanders. He was appointed at Brussels by Emperor Charles VI on 16 August 1734; the Abbots of St Winoc’s and St Andrew’s assisted. He died on 31 December 1736, in the forty-second year of his age.

GODEFRIDUS COLLIER, religious of Affligem, forty-ninth abbot of this abbey, not installed [*impilatus*, perhaps “invested/enthroned”], a devout and lovable man, constant in prayer and regarded by all as a saint, ruled the abbey for about a year and, full of merits, fell asleep in the Lord on 17 October 1739.

MAURUS ELOY, a religious from the monastery of St Adrian at Geraardsbergen, fiftieth abbot of this house, after building the cloister and recovering for the monastery by lawsuits many lost estates, died on 15 June 1760, [Col. 1493C] in the sixty-fourth year of his age and the twenty-first of his government. Strengthened by faith, he restored, supported, and renewed this almost collapsed house, hoping against hope: prudent in difficult matters, always steadfast in adversity, devout toward God, indefatigable in labour. May he endure in the memory of posterity.

PAULUS DIERIEXEN, a professed religious of this place, fifty-first abbot, received letters patent at Brussels signed by A. de Ferrari, while Maria Theresa reigned as Queen of Hungary, dated 20 August 1760. He was instituted on 11 September, and on the fourteenth day of the same month and year received abbatial blessing from John Robert Caimo, Bishop of Bruges, in the episcopal chapel. He was a very gentle man, beloved by all the religious. He took great care to restore [Col. 1494A] the buildings on the estates. He died on 13 March 1773, in the sixty-fourth year of his age.

PETER COUDELIER, of Nieuwpoort, a religious of this house and fifty-second abbot, finding the reserve of money which his predecessor had saved, began to build a new abbey. When he had built one-third of it from the foundations up to the windows, he saw that the treasury was wholly exhausted and desisted from the undertaking. But before his death, elsewhere he built a very celebrated guest quarter, and demolished the first work begun. Sparing toward his community and himself, he administered the abbatial charge for fifteen years. That religious, a cultivator [of the land], did not abandon the pastoral care which he had held for thirty-one years when he became abbot, until at last, in a good old age, he suddenly yielded up his spirit on 17 June 1788, having lived seventy-eight years. He was buried in the parish cemetery [Col. 1494B] in a stone tomb before the cross, because Emperor Joseph II had forbidden burial in churches.

PAUL DE BROUWERE, likewise of Nieuwpoort, a religious of this abbey and fifty-third abbot, nephew of the deceased, was called from the pastorate of Zandvoorde and received letters signed by Joseph II, Roman Emperor, dated January 1789. He was instituted by Secretary de Gryse and by a canon of the cathedral …, and was invested with the mitre by the illustrious Lord Felix William Brenaert, Bishop of Bruges, in the abbey church with solemn pomp, on 19 April of the same year. This magnanimous man, having received his uncle’s treasury, began to build, paint, and seek elegance for the house; to travel about in a carriage; and to invite people to many lavish entertainments. By these and similar expenses he burdened the house with debts to such an extent that [Col. 1494C] the French Republic, in the general suppression of 16 February 1797, expelled the religious together with their leader, with hands almost empty. He himself returned to the pastoral charge he had left and lived there for a time with an assistant priest. But, seeing that he could not maintain himself because the revenues promised by the peasants were not paid, he sold what belonged to him and left his charge. Afterwards, led astray, he swore the French oath and began to wander. Since he found no place where his foot could rest, having squandered the little he possessed, he fell into madness. Confined at Bruges in a house prepared for such persons, he lived until, finally restored to his right mind, having received all the sacraments of the Church and overcome by fevers, he died on 22 May 1803 and was buried there, in the house where he was kept, by order of his brother on the twenty-fourth [day; the month is not stated].

[Col. 1495]

[Col. 1497]

# Dissertation on Attila’s Devastations in Flanders

[Col. 1497A] Our historians generally agree that Attila, king of the Huns, during his famous crossing of the Rhine and the devastations which he extended over the greater part of northern Gaul, entered Flanders proper with part of his army and left there enduring marks of his ferocity.

Meyer, whose profound learning, curious researches, and authority are disputed by no one, accepts this fact and attests that he read it in most of the chronicles and historical monuments that he had consulted. “At that time,” he says, speaking of Attila’s invasion of Gaul, “scarcely any city throughout Gaul escaped the Hunnic fury. I read that in our Belgium Tournai, Thérouanne, and Oudenburg were destroyed, [Col. 1497B] as were Cologne and Tongeren …” [Note: [Col. 1497C] “At that time scarcely any city throughout Gaul escaped the Hunnic fury. In this our Belgium I read that Tournai, Thérouanne, and Aldenburg were destroyed … Then Cologne Agrippina … the town of the Tungri, etc.” *Annals of Flanders*, under the year 453.]

Our chronicle, at no. XIX, attests the same fact with respect to Oudenburg. “This city,” says the chronicler, “once besieged for a long time by King Attila and finally conquered, struck by the enemy sword, lost its splendour, strength, and urban population, so that from what was left of it it scarcely restored a small town.” [Note: [Col. 1497C] “This city, once long besieged and finally conquered by King Attila, lost its beauty, strength, and crowded urban population, cut down by the enemy sword; and from what was left to it scarcely restored a small town.” p. 34.]

Despite these positive assertions, Vredius, unquestionably one of our historians most learned in the study of our annals, maintains in his *Flandria Ethnica* [Note: [Col. 1498C] P. 87 ff.] that Attila never came into Flanders, and he regards in particular the assertion of our chronicle—which he seems to have in view—as a fable without any historical basis. Canon [Col. 1497C] De Bast, known for his works on Roman and Gallic antiquities [Note: [Col. 1498C] *Collection of Roman and Gallic Antiquities*, vols. I and II, quarto, Ghent, 1808.], follows in Vredius’s footsteps and attempts to confirm that writer’s opinion.

Having weighed the reasons of these serious writers, we believed that their opinion was not sufficiently grounded to compel our assent or to charge our chronicler with an almost unpardonable error.

Vredius first observes that Attila’s itinerary, as contemporary writers have traced it, makes no mention of Oudenburg; and De Bast, who [Col. 1498A] wishes to outdo his predecessor, maintains that Attila’s itinerary excludes the possibility of his coming into Flanders. “This monster,” he says, “thirsting for blood, after crossing the Rhine with innumerable armies, sacked Metz, Trier, Tongeren, Arras, and put to fire and sword all the towns lying in his path. Paris was delivered by the prayers of Saint Geneviève, and Troyes through the intervention of Saint Lupus, its bishop. He attacked Orléans when Merovech, king of the Franks, Aetius, general of the Romans, and Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, having united their armies, fell upon him unexpectedly. They gave him battle on the plain of Châlons and, it is said, slew more than two hundred thousand of his men, in 451. Attila, trembling with fury and rage, was [Col. 1498B] obliged to withdraw with the remnants of his army [Note: [Col. 1498C] *Collection of Roman and Gallic Antiquities*, vol. I, p. 324.].” Jordanes, in his history of the Gothic war, supplies the fullest account of this battle; after him, Saint Gregory of Tours is the author who enters into the greatest detail.

I reply, first, that it is scarcely surprising that foreign writers—some Greek, others Latin—cited by Vredius, omitted Oudenburg from their enumeration of the towns Attila ravaged in this invasion. First, they did not name every town: they confined themselves to enumerating the chief provincial capitals toward which Attila directed the main body of his army, because he expected to encounter greater resistance there. The cities cited were famous throughout all Gaul. To name only a few, Metz, Troyes, Orléans, and Paris—whose conquest seemed most important to the savage conqueror—could not be omitted; but it was necessarily requisite to omit a multitude of secondary towns, especially those which, by their remoteness and their less Gallic name, would less naturally present themselves to the pens of the historians who have left us accounts of these events.

Moreover, the generality of their expressions plainly includes Oudenburg. All unanimously attest that the devastation spread throughout all Gaul. Saint Prosper, in his chronicle, [Col. 1499A] speaks in these terms: “When Attila had crossed the Rhine, and many Gallic cities were already experiencing the most savage assaults of his army, it quickly pleased both our side—that is, the Romans—and the Goths to unite their armies, so that resistance might be made to the fury of the proud enemy [Note: [Col. 1499D] *Cum transito Rheno, saevissimos ejus impetus multae gallicanae urbes experirentur, cito et nostris et Gothis placuit, ut furori superborum hostium, consociatis exercitibus repugnaretur*: ‘When the Rhine had been crossed, and many Gallic cities were experiencing his most savage attacks, it quickly pleased both our people and the Goths that, with their armies united, resistance should be made to the fury of the proud enemies.’ P. 405, *Opera*, Venice edition, 1782.].”

Sidonius Apollinaris likewise relates that this barbarian king spread through Belgica. “The Hercynian forest,” he says, “felled by the axe, was used to make rafts, and covered the Rhine with alder; and already, O Belgian, Attila, followed by his dreadful squadrons, had spread himself across your plains [Note: [Col. 1499D]

. . . Quickly, felled by the double-edged axe,

Hercynia fell into rafts and covered the Rhine with alder;

and now Attila, with his terrifying squadrons,

had spread himself over your plains, O Belgian . . . .

*Carm.* VII, v. 331, p. 96, Paris edition, 1609.]!”

Saint Gregory of Tours, in his *History of the Franks*, also says: “When Attila had ravaged many cities in Gaul, he also attacked [Col. 1499B] Orléans [Note: [Col. 1499D] *Attila . . . cum multas Galliarum civitates opprimeret, Aureliam aggreditur*: ‘Attila … while crushing many cities of Gaul, attacks Orléans.’ *History of the Franks*, bk. II, ch. 7.].”

The author of the Life of Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes, affirms that the Huns, spread throughout all Gaul, sometimes attempted to take cities by the artifice of a feigned peace, and sometimes carried them by force [Note: [Col. 1499D] *Hunni per omnem Galliam diffusi, partim simulatae* [Col. 1500D] *pacis arte tentabant urbes, partim vi expugnabant*: “The Huns, spread throughout all Gaul, partly attempted cities by the device of a simulated peace, partly captured them by force.” *Life of St. Lupus*, in Bucherius, *Belgica Romana*, bk. XVII, ch. 3, no. 1, p. 512.].

Finally, Sigebert of Gembloux, one of our best chroniclers, writes “that at the outset divine wrath blazed so fiercely throughout all Gaul through the Huns that no fortification was able to protect from their fury even a single city, castle, or town [Note: [Col. 1500D] *Et primo per totas Gallias, per eos (Hunnos) tanta efferbuit Dei indignatio, ut nullam omnino civitatem, castellum vel oppidum aliqua a furore eorum potuerit tutari munitio*: ‘And first, throughout all Gaul, divine wrath blazed so fiercely through them—the Huns—that no defensive work was able at all to protect any city, castle, or town from their fury.’ *Chronicle*, under the year 453.].”

Hence Meyer’s expression, already cited: scarcely a single town was able to escape the rage of the Huns throughout the whole extent of Gaul.

[Col. 1499C] These testimonies show that Attila’s army spread throughout all Gaul, and principally in Belgica, which then comprised Champagne and other provinces now French. It is clear that the ravages were so general that no city, castle, or fortified town was preserved. Now Oudenburg belonged to the Belgica and Gaul of that time, and consequently may legitimately be included among the towns that were the objects of Hun fury. It should further be noted that Attila’s army, which Jordanes puts at three hundred thousand men, could not have crossed the Rhine at a single point. The river was doubtless crossed in part near Mainz, in part near Cologne, and still farther downstream, since a portion of [Col. 1499D] the army moved upon Tongeren, which was destroyed. It was impossible, as Bucherius also observes, for so great a multitude to cross so great a river [Col. 1500A] at one place [Note: [Col. 1500D] *Ut tanta hominum colluvies simul incedere non potuit, ita nec unum Rheni trajectum tenere*: “Just as so great a mass of men could not march together, so neither could it occupy a single crossing of the Rhine.” *Belgica Romana*, cited passage.]; and therefore it is reasonable to believe that part of the army moved toward Holland and the mouths of the Scheldt, where the Romans had their colonies, in order to plunder those regions, while the commander of the army plundered central Gaul.

It cannot be said that the itinerary outlined by Vredius and De Bast excludes Oudenburg from the towns that fell beneath the Hun sword. On the contrary, in the absence of positive monuments, it would be permissible to form highly probable conjectures in the opposite direction from the data supplied by these two writers alone. A portion of Attila’s army successively ravaged Tongeren, Tournai, and Arras. Now, in passing from Tongeren to Tournai, [Col. 1500B] troops obliged to follow the principal roads through the forests then covering the country must have passed not far from Flanders, where Oudenburg was situated. If we add, with Meyer—who always worked from sound monuments—that Thérouanne suffered the fate of the other cities of Gaul, we naturally picture a detachment of the Hun army crossing the Rhine sufficiently far downstream to attack the Roman colonies at the extremity of Batavia, then falling upon Oudenburg and proceeding thence to Thérouanne, either by following the sea coast to reach Morinia, or by passing through Tournai. It is certain that in that age, when almost all Flanders was covered with forests, armies seeking nothing but booty would move [Col. 1500C] even great distances toward centres of population where wealth was accumulated. Oudenburg must have tempted their greed if, as our chronicle assures us, it was the capital of the district and a town important enough to be furnished with strong walls. Everything, therefore, leads one to believe that the Hun army extended its ravages into Flanders proper; and nothing in the accounts of foreign writers obliges us to believe that this army never appeared there.

Vredius’s second reason is that in Francia Prima, where Oudenburg was situated, there were no cities, but only villages [Note: [Col. 1500D] *At verum id non apparet tum ex itinere Atthilae, superius demonstrato, tum ex eo quod Aldenburgum situm sit in prima Francia, ubi non in urbibus sed pagatim habitabatur*: “But this does not appear either from Attila’s itinerary, demonstrated above, or from the fact that Aldenburg was situated in Francia Prima, where people lived not in cities but in villages.” *Flandria Ethnica*, p. 87.]; from which it follows that Attila could not have destroyed a city that did not exist.

[Col. 1500D] That Oudenburg was a city, whatever Vredius may say, is so clearly attested by our chronicler, an eyewitness, that Vredius’s general reason ought not to prevail against his testimony. It may generally be true that people did not live in cities in this part of Gaul—that is, that there were not many cities—and that the population generally dwelt in boroughs and villages. This assertion may perhaps be strictly true for the seventh and eighth centuries; but it will not readily be admitted that Oudenburg was never a city and that this city could not have been destroyed by the king of the Huns.

Our chronicler attests that he saw the remains of ancient walls, so solid that great efforts were required to detach the stones from one another. It was discovered that the stones had been brought at great expense from the region of Boulogne [Col. 1501B] and from Cologne. They were used to build a church; vessels of admirable workmanship, of which no conception remained in the eleventh century, were discovered in these ruins—certain signs of the great antiquity of these structures. Facts of this kind scarcely lend themselves to illusion, and it is impossible to believe that a writer, having neither interest nor intention deliberately to distort the truth and fabricate falsehoods, invented such accounts in order to deceive future ages. The chronicler is an eyewitness: he saw the stones removed, he saw two churches built, and he calls the entire population of Oudenburg to witness his truthfulness.

I might add the relatively recent tradition recorded by our author. He says that part of the stones extracted from the ruins was given to the inhabitants of Bruges to build and fortify their town. This grant took place, as we noted in a note at the end of the chronicle, about the year 881—that is, about two centuries before the Oudenburg Chronicle was written, and a century and a half before the construction of the two churches at Oudenburg. The fact is reported in the Great Chronicle, whose account confirms our author’s assertion, since it comes from another source, doubtless a very ancient one. But I shall not insist further on this tradition, which here supports my argument. I ask only: these facts being assumed, how is it possible to explain them if Attila’s ravages in Flanders are denied?

Oudenburg was formerly a fortified city: this cannot reasonably be doubted. Its ruins—seen, demolished, and used amid a numerous population—attest too clearly to its former splendour. But through what vicissitudes was this city reduced to ashes? By what conqueror were its walls overthrown? I answer: by the Hun army, as our old chronicles relate; and the problem is solved.

If, with Vredius and De Bast, one disputes the ravages of Attila’s army, the problem remains insoluble. The latter, unwilling to deny that Oudenburg [Col. 1502A] was formerly a fortified city, says that it may have been destroyed in another manner; but truly this way of evading the difficulty is not a happy one. One must invoke here an historical monument and demonstrate that the positive assertion of our chronicle is false. It explains Oudenburg’s destruction; it attributes it to Attila’s army; it possesses the fact. It can be deprived of that possession only by other facts and other authentic testimonies which entirely remove its credibility. To oppose to it a negative conjecture is to admit that its account remains standing, and that the fact of Oudenburg’s ruins remains inexplicable to authors who deny that an army of Attila came into these regions. For I do not think it can be explained historically [Col. 1502B] by later times. No war fierce enough to have caused Oudenburg’s ruin in recent times is known; and if such wars had occurred between the fifth and eleventh centuries, when our chronicler was writing, there is no doubt that he would readily have gathered the tradition of those events and confirmed them in the city’s history. It must be presumed that at the time he wrote no events subsequent to Attila were known that could have caused the city’s ruin; and therefore it does not seem possible today gratuitously to suppose such events.

The third argument opposed to our chronicle is likewise negative. “I challenge anyone,” says De Bast, “to [Col. 1502C] show traces of Attila in the interior of Flanders proper.” I reply that traces of Attila in Flanders cannot be numerous. There may have been no cities except Oudenburg; the country was covered with forests and inhabited by populations little civilized; it was little known to foreign writers and possessed no native writers. Nevertheless, traces of Attila’s ravages exist, and they are easy to show: first, in the ruins of Oudenburg, which cannot be historically explained once those ravages are denied; second, in the unanimous testimony of our oldest monuments, reported by the previously cited Meyer, and which Vredius himself cannot disavow [Note: [Col. 1501D] *His temporibus Chronica nostratia volunt eversum ab Hunnis Aldenburgum, vetus oppidum tertio* [Col. 1502D] *ab urbe Brugensi lapide. At verum id non apparet tum ex itinere Atthilae, etc.*: “Our chronicles maintain that in these times Aldenburg, an ancient town three miles from Bruges, was destroyed by the Huns. But this does not appear either from Attila’s itinerary, etc.” *Flandria Ethnica*, p. 87.].

[Col. 1502D] The agreement of these chronicles, composed by different authors, would not exist if Attila’s ravages were merely a fable invented at will. Since Vredius opposes only conjectures and negative arguments to the more general opinion contrary to his own, it seems to us that the authority of the Oudenburg Chronicle alone suffices to refute his. Indeed, it was written on the spot by an educated man who could easily gather ancient monuments and traditions. These traditions had readily been preserved among the clergy whom Saint Ursmar had established at Oudenburg about two centuries after [Col. 1503A] the city had been ravaged by the Huns; and about two and a half centuries after Saint Ursmar’s death, our author lived at Oudenburg and was thoroughly acquainted with the affairs of this town. He therefore possessed every means of knowing the truth; he wished to know it, for his good faith and candour shine through the whole course of his chronicle. He has judgment; he avoids the dull and insignificant details with which many writings of this age are defiled. He observes serious and notable events: he speaks of the council of Reims, the death of Saint Leo IX, the first preaching of the Gospel in Flanders, the revenues of the Church, and finally the vicissitudes of the town. It is not fair to suppose historical fictions, frivolity, or credulity [Col. 1503B] in a man of this character. The marvellous events belonging to the building of the church of Oudenburg are not narrated as unheard-of prodigies, but as effects of divine providence, which watches over everything, and of the protection of the holy apostles in whose honour that building was erected. We therefore find here not childish credulity, discovering prodigies in the simplest things, but the sincerity of a writer recounting extraordinary events—indeed—but not impossible ones.

In order to evade the argument drawn from the etymology of Oudenburg to prove its antiquity, Vredius disputes it and sets against us the author of the Life of Saint Ursmar. We have seen that our chronicler, followed [Col. 1503C] by most of our historians, assures us that the name Oudenburg is formed from two words: *oud*, “old,” and *burg*, “borough” or “village.” By these words it was intended to express the antiquity of this city, whose origin was lost in the night of time. Admitting this etymology, one understands that Oudenburg could have been fortified by the Romans and destroyed by Attila. But Vredius evades this conclusion by denying the etymology proposed by our author. “Let no one imagine,” he says, “that Oudenburg was such an ancient city; for the author of the Life of Saint Ursmar expressly attests the contrary when he says that Oudenburg was the village of a local lord named Aldo or Aldus. Molanus extracted these words from the archives of Lobbes Abbey: ‘Aldo himself, lord of the province, gave [Col. 1503D] his name to the village called Aldenburg, in which he built a church in honour of Saint Peter, so that the blessed Apostle might be the protector of the Flemings and Menapians’ [Note: [Col. 1503D] *Et nemo credat Aldenburgum urbem adeo antiquam fuisse; secus enim attestatur aperte Vita S. Ursmari, ubi Aldenburgum dicitur cujusdam Toparchae cui nomen erat Aldo sive Aldus, vicus fuisse. Molanus ex archivis Lobiensibus: Ipse etiam provinciae dominus Aldo donavit, a suo vocabulo dictum Aldenburg, vicum in quo in honorem B. Petri ecclesiam constravit, quatenus B. Apostolus Flandrensibus et* [Col. 1504D] *Menapibus patrocinaretur*: “And let no one believe Aldenburg to have been so ancient a city; for the Life of Saint Ursmar expressly attests otherwise, where Aldenburg is said to have been the village of a certain local lord named Aldo or Aldus. Molanus, from the archives of Lobbes: Aldo himself, lord of the province, gave [his name to] the village called Aldenburg; in it he built a church in honour of Blessed Peter, so that the blessed Apostle might protect the Flemings and Menapians.” *Flandria Ethnica*, cited passage.].”

The passage published by Molanus was taken from the catalogue of the abbots of Lobbes, written toward the end of the [Col. 1504A] ninth century by Fulcuin, abbot of that monastery, who died in 890 [Note: [Col. 1504D] See *Acta Sanctorum Belgii*, vol. VI, p. 237.].

Henschenius published it in the Bollandist collection, and G. Thysius reproduced it in the sixth volume of the *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* [Note: [Col. 1504D] P. 252.].

We have no reason to prefer Fulcuin’s authority to that of our chronicler. The abbot of Lobbes was a stranger to Oudenburg; our historian had spent his whole life there. The etymology proposed by the former has no support in history; that of the latter rests upon the usage of the language itself and the natural meaning of its roots. Were there formerly proper names such as those Fulcuin supposes? We do not know. Has the language always possessed the word *oud* to signify an old thing? Of that [Col. 1504B] we cannot doubt. Thus Henschenius, so skilled in medieval history, observes in a note [Note: [Col. 1504D] *Acta Sanctorum Belgii*, vol. V, p. 253.] that Fulcuin’s etymology is much less probable than that of our chronicler, who knew the local history and saw with his own eyes the surest monuments of this town’s high antiquity.

A final conjecture of Vredius, which De Bast decides to copy, scarcely deserves an answer. He supposes that the belief in Attila’s ravages in Flanders arose because certain people, perceiving an analogy between the name Ettelghem, a village near Oudenburg, and the name of the king of the Huns, sincerely believed that this conqueror had appeared in our regions [Note: [Col. 1504D] *Origo hujus fabulae videtur profluxisse ex nuncupatione pagi vicini, qui Ettelghem cum dicatur, Atthilae domum, sive templum videtur sonare*: “The origin of this fable seems to have arisen from the name of a neighbouring village, which, since it is called Ettelghem, seems to mean Attila’s house or temple.” Cited work, p. 88.]. Vredius advances this hypothesis only hesitantly: *videtur profluxisse*, “it seems to have arisen”; and rightly so, for he attributes to those simple times a subtlety belonging to our own age. In the ninth and tenth centuries people scarcely indulged in refinements upon letters and syllables as they have done since the sixteenth. Besides, the conjecture lacks even plausibility here: Attila and Ettel are words whose pronunciation is so different that they do not appear sufficiently akin to give rise to a fable as complete as the one attributed to our author. Had the fact he advances rested upon the arbitrary foundation Vredius imagines, he would not have failed to cite the name Ettelghem. But this comparison never occurred to him; it could have been noticed only by [Col. 1504D] an author systematically determined to contradict the very simple and natural account of our historian.

We believe we have said enough to prove that there is no sound reason to depart from the account of our old chronicles concerning Attila’s ravages in Flanders, and that the Oudenburg Chronicle in particular retains all its authority. [Col. 1505A] It is opposed with the incomplete account of this conquering king’s itinerary and with the country’s custom of not dwelling in cities; but the first argument proves nothing, and the second is contradicted by a witness who saw the remains of this ancient city. De Bast’s challenge falls through by the same contradiction; for if traces of Attila’s ravages in Flanders are no longer found today, one is not therefore permitted to affirm and maintain that they did not exist in the [Col. 1506A] eleventh century, when our author could have recognized them. Let us therefore adhere to the account of our ancient monuments when more certain and more authoritative monuments do not contradict them. In departing from this rule, so consonant with the precepts of sound criticism, one casts oneself into hypotheses and conjectures, which are useful only for shaking the most constant facts and casting darkness upon the best-attested histories.

[Col. 1505]

# Greater Chronicle of the Monastery of Aldenburg

Edited by the Rev. F. Van de Putte, Rector of the Episcopal College of Bruges.

(*Collection of Chronicles, Charters, and Other Documents Concerning the History and Antiquities of West Flanders, published by the Society of Emulation of Bruges. Ghent, 1843.—First series: Chronicles of the Monasteries of Flanders.*)

## Introduction

[Col. 1505] Our ancient abbeys and other religious institutions customarily composed the history of their houses in annalistic form, interspersing contemporary facts from secular history. Such is the form of the oldest chronicles of our monasteries: those of Saint Bavo and of the Friars Minor at Ghent, those of Tronchiennes, Saint-Bertin, and many others. Several centuries later, Brandon, De But, and other monks compiled the ancient chroniclers, both sacred and secular, and wrote new and much more extensive chronicles, to which they ordinarily gave the names of their monasteries. Sigebert of Gembloux had the honour of being incorporated in part into all these diverse productions, which were very often carried back to the creation of the world.

Brandon, a monk of the Dunes, wrote the most extensive chronicle. It extended from the creation of the world to the year 1414 and was divided into three parts, entitled *Chronodromus seu Cursus Temporum*—“Chronodrome, or Course of Times.” It is especially the third part, beginning in the year 800, that is of interest for our history; and Meyer does not hesitate to say that he used it in composing his chronicle. A good copy of this third part is now in the Burgundian Library. It comes from the Abbey of Saint Peter at Ghent and was acquired at the sale of the Lammens library. Other copies were made from it, but they are often defective through the negligence of copyists. Already in 1659 Charles De Visch, author of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, had occupied himself with Brandon and used the Saint Peter manuscript, as is shown by an autograph manuscript of De Visch in which he says: “The most reverend lord abbot of Saint Peter on Mount Blandin near Ghent lent me the third part of the *Chronodromus* in the year 1659.”

De Visch’s purpose in borrowing the Saint Peter manuscript was to compare it with the Chronicle of Oudenburg, which seemed to contain a portion of Brandon. Indeed, he had borrowed that chronicle at the same time, as the following words drawn from the autograph manuscript just mentioned prove: “Extracts from a most ancient chronicle, a manuscript on parchment of Aldenburg Abbey, written by an anonymous author; lent to me by the most reverend Abbot Maximilian d’Engien in the year 1659.” De Visch copied several passages from this manuscript, showing that it is the same one we publish here in part. He maintained, against the monks of Oudenburg, that the writer of their chronicle was a plagiarist who had copied Brandon. On this subject he wrote as follows:

> It should be noted that in the monastery of Aldenburg they still possess the first part of our Brandon’s *Chronodromus*, copied by a monk of that same place. When he came to the second part, omitting many things here and there, he inserted in their place the entire chronicle of his own monastery, and condensed both the second and third parts into one volume. Thus it came about that, in the course of time, the monks of Aldenburg believed, and still believe, that the whole work was written by one of their own; for that reason they call it the Chronicle of their monastery. But the genuine third part of Brandon’s *Chronodromus*, preserved at Ghent in Blandin and at Louvain in the College of Arras, will reveal the plagiarism to the curious reader; indeed, so too will this Prologue, which I have therefore copied here word for word from the Aldenburg codex itself, which I kept with me for a long time.

After nearly two centuries, following De Visch’s example, I compared the Chronicle of Oudenburg with a copy of Brandon’s chronicle belonging to the Bollandists, and found true what that author asserts in the lines just cited. The compiler of Oudenburg indeed says in his prologue—which is word for word the same as Brandon’s—things that can belong only to that author. The phrases, “Carry on to the end the COURSE OF TIMES begun hitherto,” and “From the first year of the Lord’s Incarnation, I have attempted to begin this part of the CHRONODROME,” plainly indicate Brandon’s title, which we reported above. Exact comparison of the two manuscripts confirmed my opinion. The greater part of the Chronicle of Oudenburg resembles Brandon’s text, especially from the fourteenth century onward. Until that period, the Oudenburg writer consulted several works; but, whether from weariness or because he found few works more or less contemporary with the fourteenth century, he then ceased to scruple and copied Brandon verbatim down to 1400, though omitting the greater part of what that writer says.

The prologue found in the Chronicle of Oudenburg is that of the second part of the *Chronodrome*; that of the third part is not found there. The reason for the author’s preference for the one rather than the other is sufficiently natural. He began his chronicle at the birth of the Saviour, where Brandon’s second part also begins, and copied that preface as an introduction to his entire work, setting aside that of Brandon’s third part, in which Brandon explains the whole plan of what he had previously written. The monk of Oudenburg could not have copied that plan without committing an imprudence much greater than that of speaking, in his Prologue, of the *Chronodrome* and the *Cursus temporum*.

We publish the Prologue of the third part so that readers may be in a position to judge what we assert, and to complete the third part, of which this Prologue is the beginning.

Brandon’s *Chronodrome* is a compilation from other chronicles, both national and foreign, for his work deals with the history of the country and of the other regions of Europe. Among the sources from which he drew he cites Sigebert of Gembloux, Paul of Constantinople, Vincent of Beauvais, Martin of Poland, William of Malmesbury, Giovanni Boccaccio, the Chronicle of Cluny, Rabanus Maurus, and two works, one named *Gesta* and the other *Imago speculi Flandriae*—“Image of the Mirror of Flanders.” He also consulted many other works, as he states in his Prologue. The Oudenburg chronicler sometimes drew from sources other than Brandon. I have taken care to note the variants and the various sources from which the two authors almost always copied verbatim what they set forth.

We lack no chronicles dealing with our country, but, as I have said above, nearly all copied one another; and the variants introduced into them have occasioned the difficulties encountered there. To speak only of the history of Flanders, we have Meyer, who succeeded best in giving us an accurate chronicle. Yet Meyer copied Brandon, Sigebert of Gembloux, and several later writers verbatim. What did Despars do? He translated Meyer from the first Nuremberg edition. Custis copied Despars half a century ago, and in turn our historians have come to serve up warmed-over versions of one another. All nevertheless contain something proper to themselves, which they have sometimes drawn from sources unknown before their time. Meyer had access to archival repositories; Despars enjoyed the singular privilege of entering the libraries of monasteries and searching their ancient parchments. It is therefore not surprising to read in these authors things that would be sought elsewhere in vain. The Flemish chronicle edited by André Wyats is perhaps, in every respect, the fullest and most accurate of all these works: it is written from the works just enumerated.

The contemporary portion of each chronicler is always the part deserving the greatest attention. There the writer recounts what he saw, which would be difficult to challenge on grounds of truthfulness. M. Lambin very rightly observes in the preface to the Chronicle of Jean Van Dixmude that extracts from the contemporary portion of every chronicler would make an accurate chronicle written by contemporaries. Whoever undertook such a publication would make a very considerable contribution toward the making of a national history.

A work concerning Flanders, reproduced in many monastic chronicles and used also by Brandon and the Oudenburg chronicler, is the *Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders* [Col. 1509], otherwise known under the name *Generous Flanders* (*Flandria generosa*). The Oudenburg Chronicle is followed by a copy of this work, which we intend to publish later.

The history of the Crusades, in which the Belgians took a very great part, has been treated by a great number of writers. The *Deeds of God through the Franks* (*Gesta Dei per Francos*) supplies us with some of them; others are found in the *Treasury of Anecdotes* (*Thesaurus anecdotorum*). The chroniclers found an abundant harvest there, and Brandon did not fail to transcribe material once he reached the year 1096. The Oudenburg writer says little about the Crusades, but on page 150 he added a history of those distant wars entitled *Deeds of the Franks Who Conquered Jerusalem* (*Gesta Francorum Jherusalem expugnantium*).

The author of our chronicle does not identify himself. Sanderus informs us that it is by Abbot Anianus: “Anianus, a native of Cassel, first a monk at Bergues-Saint-Winoc, wrote a universal chronicle from the beginning of the world down to his own times, namely to the year of Christ 1457 [Note: [Col. 1509] *Flandria illustrata*, Cologne edition, vol. I, p. 318.].” Sanderus is mistaken here: the chronicle extends only to the year 1400. That writer would have done better to say that it was written in 1458, as Anianus tells us at the beginning of his table of contents.

The manuscript that we publish consists of 210 folio leaves of vellum, in two columns of 45 lines, not counting four leaves containing the Prologue and the table of contents, which the author did not paginate. Twenty-three unpaginated leaves, in the same hand, precede the Chronicle. These leaves contain a mixture of elementary material on the sphere and of sacred and secular history from the earliest ages of the world.

Two large miniatures, fairly well executed, adorn this volume. One, in grisaille, represents Saint Arnould and Saint Godelieve, who is said to have been his relative. This miniature appears before the calendar; the other is on page 64 and represents Conon [Note: [Col. 1509] This is what Sanderus says of this Conon on page 317 of the work cited: “The said Conon was the chamberlain of that count; and by that same title and prerogative of dignity all the ancient magistrates of the town of Aldenburg enjoyed their office. For the counts of Flanders are reported, in the manner of kings, from the beginning to have had four principal officers: namely, a chancellor, a master of the horse, a chamberlain, and a cup-bearer; these were commonly called the household officials. The chancellor was the provost of Saint Donatian at Bruges; the master of the horse, the governor of Lille; the cup-bearer, the governor of Torhout; and the chamberlain, the governor or magistrate of Aldenburg.” Sanderus drew this passage from the chronicle of George Cabillau, who had himself copied it from the archives of Bergues-Saint-Winoc.], chamberlain of Robert the Frisian, restoring the church of Oudenbourg to Rabodo, bishop of Tournai. This small picture is painted in colours: the church stands in the centre; on the right is Conon, with the features and costume of Philip the Good; on the left appear Saint Arnould and Bishop Rabodo, followed by a monk. Might not the painter, who took pleasure in representing Philip the Good here, have painted Abbot Anianus in the costume of Rabodo?—Two other, smaller miniatures, depicting religious subjects, are painted on folio 9.

A sixteenth-century hand has written on several lower margins verses relating to the events mentioned in the folios on which they occur. Sanderus cites some of these verses, which leads us to suppose that he consulted our chronicle at the same time as that of Cabillau, from which he reports several passages [Note: [Col. 1509] *Flandria illustrata*, cited edition, p. 317 ff.].

The chronicler of Oudenbourg, following Brandon’s example, wrote in chronological order, placing before each item the year to which it relates. We have followed that order in this publication, both for conformity with the author and for ease in locating events. This natural order is followed by almost all our chroniclers.

We have reproduced a portion of the Life of Saint Arnould found in the Bollandists, vol. III for August, which our chronicler gives with some variants. For their publication of this Life, the hagiographers used a manuscript from the abbey of Ter Doest, written from the Life of Saint Arnould composed by Abbot Hariulf. This abbot wrote the Life from the testimony of the monk Everolf, who had been bound in friendship with Saint Arnould, and from that of Adzela and Arnould, respectively the saint’s sister and nephew. This Life, found almost entire in Surius under 15 August, is wrongly attributed by that writer to Liziard, bishop of Soissons, as Mabillon proves in his *Annales Ordinis S. Benedicti* [Note: [Col. 1509] Vol. V, pp. 242 and 551, Paris edition.], saying that the first two parts of the Life of Saint Arnould are Hariulf’s and that the third, dealing with the saint’s miracles, came from Liziard’s pen. Our chronicle clearly states, under the year 1120, that Abbot Hariulf presented the Life of Saint Arnould to the bishops gathered in council at Beauvais. The abbot had completed it in 1114, says Mabillon, and dedicated it to Rodulf, archbishop of Reims.

Since the Royal Historical Commission proposed to publish Brandon in its *Corpus chronicorum Belgii*, we have omitted from the present publication everything in our chronicle copied from that writer, so as not to publish the same work twice.

The charters and diplomas which we give at the end of the work have in part been copied from charters reproduced [Col. 1511] in a *Factum* published in the seventeenth century, entitled: *Brief Deduction of the Rights of the Abbey of Oudenbourg over the Parish Church of the Said Place*. Aubert le Mire published four other diplomas in his *Notitia ecclesiarum Belgii* and in his *Corpus diplomaticum*.

This *Brief Deduction* states that around the year 700, in the time of Childebert, king of France, Saint Ursmar, second abbot of Lobbes and apostle of Flanders, preached the Gospel at Oudenbourg and built there two churches, that of Saint Peter and that of Our Lady. These churches were destroyed by the Normans, and their possessions and tithes were given by the popes to the count of Flanders, to defend the maritime coast against barbarian incursions. The counts ceded these properties to the lords of Oudenbourg, hereditary chamberlains of the counts of Flanders.

This account, drawn from the little Chronicle published by Dr Malou, is supported by no authentic document. The oldest charters mentioning Oudenbourg are those of Saint Arnould: one dated the fifth day before the Nones of March, 1084; the other, the eighth day before the Kalends of August, 1087. It is known that Saint Arnould was sent into Flanders by the pope to settle disputes that had arisen between Count Robert the Frisian and ecclesiastics and other subjects. Wautier and Conon, the count’s chamberlain and cup-bearer respectively, were then lords of Oudenbourg. They ceded the churches of the place to the saintly missionary, who installed religious there. These charters are therefore the foundation documents of the abbey.

As regards the great antiquity which some assign to Oudenbourg, historians have argued both sides of the question. According to Gramaye [Note: [Col. 1511A] *Antiquitates Flandriae*, p. 88.], fragments of vessels containing Roman coins were found in remains of ancient walls demolished at Oudenbourg, which would prove the presence of Romans there. Several old maps [Note: [Col. 1511A] Malbranq, Vredius, etc.] depict Oudenbourg as a *castrum*, and even carry a Roman road through it. All this serves to give the place a great antiquity; and it is probable that what the Normans demolished was merely the remains of an ancient *castrum*, notwithstanding what Lernatius says:

> There are those who assert that, when Aldburg had been devastated  
> By Norman arms, Bruges was walled  
> Against the Danes with its stone. They are mistaken: in those days  
> No such use was made of stones;  
> For towns were enclosed by a piled-up rampart,  
> And trusty earth ran about them, heaped in turf.

If what I have just advanced concerning the *castrum* that stood at Oudenbourg has any appearance of truth, one will be less astonished to see the Huns seize this fortress in the middle of the fifth century, when those barbarians made themselves masters of all the strongholds of Belgium.

> Into your plains, O Belgium:  
>   
> And now Attila had spread himself over the fearsome fields,  
> First laying low the Frank, then the German, and next the Belgian.  
> [Note: [Col. 1511A] Sidonius Apollinaris.]

The reader will find curious information on Attila’s ravages in Flanders in the Dissertation appended to the *Chronicon Aldenburgense* published by Dr Malou, who was prevented by his many occupations from editing this Chronicle himself. I have undertaken that task and have given the work the title *Chronicon monasterii Aldenburgensis majus*, in contrast with the little Chronicle. May my labours be of some use to scholarship, and my pains will be repaid!

## PROLOGUE

[Note: [Col. 1512A] This is the prologue to the second part of Brandon’s *Chronodromon*, placed before the Aldenburg Chronicle.]

[Col. 1511]

[Col. 1511A] 1 Now, growing squalid in the grim shadow of antiquity, and wearied by slow labour, drowsing in the bed of sloth, I had almost shut away in its chest the blunted pen of the writing-room, used for noting things down. Sunk in deep sleep, lying conquered and enervated, I said: “Why, madman, do you torment yourself with sweat in so vast a task? Why do you trouble yourself with such excessive labour over the monuments of the ancients? In vain, from the ruins of antiquity, do you desire by new little letters to surpass in acquired renown, when one already exists who, stripping you from mortal things, will turn your little body into ashes.” Pressed down, then, by many such persuasions of idleness, I laid back upon the pillow the head which I had raised, intending to rise upon my elbow.

And behold, I perceived as though suddenly standing behind me two men worthy of the highest reverence, modest in appearance and bearing. One was distinguished by the mitre of pontifical rank; the other by the diadem of imperial power. As, my eyes opened and sleep wholly banished, I looked at them more intently, there seemed to stand before me Saint Peter the Apostle, first pontiff of the Romans and vicar of Christ, together with Octavian, the first Augustus. With the sternness of just rebuke they reproved my drowsiness and addressed me in sharper words:

“What! Do you lie there, professor of idleness? Why are you numbed by the false persuasion of inertia? Have you forgotten that man is born for labour? You began the *Course of Time* and to review a few memorials of the ancients, in which paganism, wandering far from the way of truth, moved in shadow. And when you had arrived at the final boundary, where a plain road lay open for you into the light, you stop, deceived by foolish opinion! Is it enough for your labour merely to have committed to writing, as hitherto, a very few deeds of ancient men, darkened beneath the gloom of the old sin? Should you not rather, under the grace of the New Testament, now that the world has been made serene and divine light shines forth, unfold the illustrious times of Christians, in which, the truth of the Gospel having been proclaimed, that new Jerusalem, the Church, bride of Christ, stands firmly rooted, and the emblems of faith of our own soldiery, of every soldiery, and of our successors shine in the light?

“By divine authority we receive the name of Christ, the testament of the supreme God bequeathed to us and to our descendants as true heirs, divided in an equal balance: dominion over spiritual affairs falling to one, dominion over temporal affairs to the other. We are commanded to govern this whole world, renewed by the new sprinkling of Christ’s blood. So great a power has been granted us from heaven that whatever, by decree of our authority, we determine to bind or loose upon earth is neither loosed nor bound in heaven.

“Do the sanctioned ordinances of Roman pontiffs, the most holy shepherds of the Church, their decrees and synodal counsels, by which faith is defended, heresy confounded, [Col. 1513C] and the minds of the faithful everywhere governed in happy order, not seem to you worthy of narration, as examples for gathering virtue? And when the entire duty of pastoral care is fulfilled, do not the shepherds with their flock rejoice together for ever in the court of the supreme King?

“Likewise, are not the deeds, just enactments, laws, and legal ordinances of the illustrious Roman and Greek emperors, the kings of the Franks and English, and other nobles, deemed worthy of equal praise and report? By these concord is maintained, the discord of transgressors is restrained, each person is given what is his by the weighing balance of equity, and the whole polity of civil rule is ordered; thus prince and peoples rejoice happily in their eternal homeland.

“Would you think that the glorious contests of martyrs, the examples of virtue of holy fathers, and the continence of virginal chastity—[Col. 1514A] whereby all these are known in this mortal pilgrimage to have served God and not vices—should be trodden under blind forgetfulness? Far from it. Rather, you should strive with all your might to exalt them, so that, while you endeavour to magnify divine grace in them, you will find God himself a generous enlarger of grace toward you; and you will obtain, through their intercession as suppliants whose happy deeds you unfold, favour before the Judge at the hearing of the final examination. Even if among mortals the appearance of reward should wholly perish, your labour for God’s grace cannot perish before God and his immortal saints. He bestows—what is more desirable—a perishable gift upon the labourer who labours. Moreover, even if no recompense of reward were expected from anyone, you should still prefer to have kept watch empty-handed rather than to have been glutted with idle torpor.

“Therefore drive away this darkness, crush sloth, rise fervently, and carry through to the end of time the course you have thus far begun. Show posterity the glorious, noble, and splendid men of time past, so that, reviewing their fame won by diverse paths of virtue as though it were fresh, they may bear witness to honours deserved by the dead. Further, provide readers with another antidote of usefulness: for the matters which the style of your compilation enlarges, they would otherwise have to seek with laborious inquiry through the volumes of many authors and historians in order to obtain evident knowledge; what they would search for scattered and wandering through diverse books, they may find in orderly sequence in your compendium.”

Persuaded by these most truthful rebukes and by the charm of their words, awakened from the death-bearing weight of the body, and condemning the judgment of my folly, I embraced with grateful mind the commands of men of such reverence, intending to implore their mercy: that, having removed the cloud of deserved indignation, they might grant pardon for my purified sloth and recall into my breast the spirits dispersed in a gasp. But behold, just as they had come, as though by appointment, I know not at what hour, so, their office fulfilled, they departed—as I supposed—from heaven.

Therefore, gathering a little strength within myself, and perceiving the ways in which God awakens the foolish, I took up anew the pen for my old task.
