Inscribing the titles of kingdoms and the numbers of years, as hitherto, in the order of their arrangement, as the form of the work requires, I attempt to begin this part of the *Chronodromon* from the first year of the Lord’s Incarnation, and, supported by the aid of divine grace, to traverse the varied events of affairs, distinguishing them under their several years, as far as the one thousand four-hundredth year of the Lord’s Incarnation inclusive.

**Here ends the Prologue.**

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF THE THIRD BOOK OF THE *CHRONODROMON*, THAT IS, THE COURSE OF TIME, ABOVE THE FOURTH PART

[Note: [Col. 1521C] I copied this prologue from Brandon.]

[Col. 1521]

[Col. 1521A] 14–15 It is the way of the weak to be oppressed by the slightest burden; and they bear it the more easily as the boundary and end of their labour smile more nearly upon them. Those who undertake a long and laborious journey are accustomed, when they have completed more than half of it, not merely sometimes to halt, wipe away their sweat, lighten their bodies, catch a gentle breeze, and quench their thirst with drink; they also turn their faces backwards and measure the distance already travelled, and, reckoning all that remains of the journey a slight labour in view of the joy of the destination, complete it without weariness.

Reflecting a little upon this within myself, after finishing the labour of a compilation of three parts, inadequate and, I fear, of little usefulness, in which I had concluded the *Course of Time*—distinguishing in their respective years, from the beginning of the world through four thousand seven hundred and sixty-three years to the eight hundred and first year of the Word made flesh, the sequence of events and deeds of illustrious or learned men—I sat down intending to set my pen upon the plan of a fourth and final preliminary continuation.

And behold: the tedious excess of the labour already sampled, the deficient weakness of my powers, the forceful variety of frequent impediments distracting me because of the condition of the times, and also the discordant and scanty poverty of the manuscripts from which material especially for compilation had to be extracted, would scarcely have kept my pen from further progress in the work begun and kept my mind inactive, unless I had at once recognized that bodily rest is an enemy, the mother of torpor and foe of talent; and that I could indeed attain nearby the goal and conclusion of the proposed work—if the grace of the nourishing Spirit were granted—provided diligence drove away weariness of labour, grace relieved want of strength, steadfastness of mind governed the varied troubles of time, and above all the completion of the intended work and the usefulness of its contents benefited readers and hearers.

For I should seem to have done almost nothing, and rightly be blamed, if I had recounted in annual calculation the undertakings, deeds, and achievements of the ancients up to this point, together with what happened in their times, but then, setting my foot almost halfway in my study and becoming an apostate from labour, should think to trample in blind oblivion the illustrious times and deeds of the kings of France, England, Jerusalem, and especially of the Roman emperors—those, that is, who sprang from the noble blood of the Franks, through the great founder Charles—as well as of dukes, counts, and other illustrious men, and especially the events near to the present time in England, France, and above all Flanders, of which I am accounted an inhabitant. For the sake of recording very many of these I had taken up my pen. Instead, I should continue the task of compilation and set them down in writing down to the present age.

And if not all of them, at least those for which I have seen manuscripts, from which, if I wished, I could draw forth ample material concerning events: such as the works of distinguished men—Sigebert of Gembloux, Paul of Constantinople, Vincent, Martin, William of Malmesbury, John Boccaccio, and the author who published a certain new compilation called the *Image of the Mirror*—and whatever others there may be. Thus consoling my folly with these considerations, I gladly set my pen to the joining of the fourth and final part, intending, with divine grace assisting, to bring it down through more than six hundred years to the present age.

**Here ends the Prologue.**

## CHRONICLE

[Col. 1523]

[Col. 1523A] 18–19. In the year of the Lord 800, and in the thirty-third year of Charles, king of the Franks, the Romans—who had long since revolted in spirit from the emperor of Constantinople—now, seizing the opportunity provided when a woman ruled them in place of her blinded son, Emperor Constantine, unanimously acclaimed imperial honours for King Charles. Crowned by the hands of Pope Leo, they called him Caesar and Augustus. They also approved the appointment of his son Pippin as king of Italy. Amymurlin, king of the Persians, sent Emperor Charles an elephant and many gifts. Barcelona was taken. In Italy also, the city of Chieti was taken by the Franks. Saint Salvius, archbishop, travelling from Aquitaine to the royal estate of Valenciennes, was martyred by Winigard, son of Gerard, the administrator of that estate. [Col. 1523B] Emperor Charlemagne, divinely warned three times to seek his body, found it and buried it honourably. He punished the murderers severely; yet even so God’s vengeance against them did not cease.

Charles, emperor and king of the Franks, sent envoys throughout his empire to administer judicial proceedings and justice, and established twenty-three chapters of law. At Mainz, a bridge five hundred paces long across the Rhine, which Emperor Charles had built of timber over ten years with immense labour, so that it seemed capable of enduring for ever, was burned in three hours so completely that not one splinter remained upon the water. Emperor Charles placed the imperial crown upon his son Louis. [Col. 1523C] Emperor Charles ordered councils concerning the state of the churches to be held throughout all Gaul by the bishops. One was at Mainz, another at Rheims, a third at Tours, a fourth at Chalon, and a fifth at Arles.

### On the death of Charles, in the forty-sixth year

The glorious Emperor Charles, having enlarged and pacified his kingdom and empire and having established the condition of the Church in a holy and religious order, died in the forty-sixth year of his reign and the thirteenth of his empire, and was buried at Aachen, in the seventy-second year of his age. Because of the greatness of his deeds he was surnamed “the Great.” After him his son Louis ruled as emperor for twenty-six years. In the archives of Saint Medard at Soissons, when I was young, I read something concerning his burial, but I retained the sense rather than the Latin wording. Pope Leo was present there with Roman magnates, as were many [Col. 1523D] bishops and archbishops, dukes and counts, abbots also, and countless others. Clothing the dead emperor’s body in imperial and festal garments, they placed a golden crown upon his head. Then they seated him on a throne as though living and judging, and placed upon his knees the text of the four Evangelists, written in golden letters, which he held in his right hand; in his left, a sceptre. [Col. 1524A] They fastened a golden chain from the diadem to the golden throne on which he sat, lest the dead man’s head should fall; they set before his face the golden shield which the Romans had made for him; filled the stone arch in which he was buried with precious spices; and, sealing the monument securely, closed it. He died in the year of the Lord 813, on 19 January.

### 807

Emperor Charles diligently renewed at Aachen the baths whose water was tempered hot and cold; and he fittingly adorned with gold and silver and every ecclesiastical ornament the round church of Blessed Mary which he had built there. He caused the history of the Old and New Testaments to be painted in it, and likewise adorned the palace which he had built there. He also caused to be painted there, in a remarkable manner, all the wars which he had waged in Spain and the seven liberal arts. [Col. 1524B]

### 809

Pippin, son of Charlemagne and king of Italy, subdued Venice by war; not long afterwards he died at Milan, and Emperor Charles restored Venice to Nicephorus, emperor of the Constantinopolitans.

### 817

Turpin, archbishop of Rheims, died. Saint Folquin became bishop of Tournai.

### 819

Emperor Louis subjected the Bretons to himself.

### 823

The elevation of Saint Ursmar, confessor, was celebrated.

### 825

[Col. 1524C] When Ingelram, count of Flanders, died and was buried at Harlebeke, his son Audacer succeeded him and governed for thirteen years.

### 827

Baldwin, abbot of Saint-Denis and archchaplain of the sacred palace, sent to Rome and received from Pope Eugenius the body of Saint Sebastian the martyr; he placed it at Soissons in the basilica of Saint Medard.

### 828

22. The bodies of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, taken from Rome and conveyed into Francia, were glorified by many signs. The body of Saint Gregory, pope, is also said to have been brought to the city of Soissons.

### 832

Emperor Louis deprived some of those opposing him of office, others of their goods, and banished others; thereby he made his sons and magnates more hostile toward him. [Col. 1524D]

### 833

Emperor Louis, abandoned and betrayed by his own men and delivered into the power of his sons, laid down his arms by judgment of the bishops and was confined to do penance.

### 835

[Col. 1525A] Emperor Louis decreed, at the urging of Pope Gregory and with all the bishops present, that in Gaul and Germany the feast of All Saints should be celebrated on the Kalends of November [1 November]. The relics of Vitus the martyr were transferred from Paris to Corvey in Saxony. The Franks themselves testified that from that time the favour of the Franks was transferred.

### 837

The Northmen grievously harassed Gaul. They ravaged Dordrecht and burned Antwerp and Witla, a trading-place situated by the mouth of the river Meuse. They exacted tribute from the Frisians. These Northmen were Danish by origin and were called Northmen, as it were “men of the north.” Audacer III, count of Flanders, died [Col. 1525B] and was buried at Harlebeke. His son Baldwin, surnamed Iron Arm, succeeded him. He governed Flanders for forty years.

### 862

Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, was carried off from Senlis by Baldwin Iron Arm, count of Flanders.

### 864

At this time flourished Saint Odo, founder of the monastery of Cluny.

### 878

Louis, son of Charles surnamed the Bald, died at the palace of Compiègne. His sons Louis and Carloman divided his kingdom between themselves. More than five thousand Northmen were slain in Gaul by Louis and the Franks.

### 879

[Col. 1525C] Baldwin, son of Audacer, surnamed Iron Arm, son-in-law of the aforementioned Charles the Bald and count of Flanders, died. His son Baldwin, surnamed the Bald, succeeded him. He married Eltrude, daughter of King Elger of England, by whom he begot Arnulf the Great, restorer of Blandinium.

### 880

The Danes, or Northmen, burned the renowned palace at Aachen, and burned Cologne with the monasteries, royal palaces, and villages, having killed their inhabitants. For in the preceding year they had destroyed and burned the city of Arras, Cambrai, Tournai, and all monasteries around the river Scheldt and the river Yser; [Col. 1525D] they either carried the inhabitants of the land into captivity or killed them.

### 881

[Col. 1526A] Baldwin the Bald, count of Flanders, built the town of Bruges in Flanders. Taking stones from the village of Oudenburg, which Attila, king of the Huns, had once destroyed, he fortified the town of Bruges with them. He also transferred the body of Saint Donatian from the city of Rheims to the village of Bruges, where it is now preserved and venerated with honour.

### 882

Godfrid and Sigfrid, kings of the Northmen, encamped with an immeasurable multitude beside the Meuse, at a place called Haslon. They burned Liège, Maastricht, Tongeren, Cologne, and Huy with the adjacent castles. Stabling horses in the palace at Aachen, they set fire to the town and palace. Ministers of the sacred order, [Col. 1526B] both men and women, hid wherever they could most conveniently, and concealed the bodies and relics of the saints in safer places.

### 887

Charles, emperor and king of the Franks, unable to expel the Northmen from Francia, finally made a treaty and conceded to them the regions beyond the Seine, whose inhabitants had rebelled against him. What had formerly been Francia was called Normandy from the Normans.

### 888

The monastery of Saint-Bertin was thrown down by a storm.

### 889

25. Ralph, count of the district of Cambrai, brother of [Col. 1526C] Baldwin, count of Flanders, angered over the castles taken from him by King Odo, did not cease to plunder Saint-Quentin and Péronne. He was killed in battle by Count Herbert at the abbey of Saint-Quentin. Baldwin, count of Flanders, invaded the city of Arras and the fortress of Saint-Vaast, but lost it during the festival. Afterwards King Odo came to a certain castle on the river Yser called Fère, and there began to fall gravely ill. He urged them to receive Charles as king, and died there on the Kalends of January [1 January]. His body was carried to Saint-Denis and honourably buried there.

### 892

The Northmen, unable to take Paris by assault, attacked Burgundy [Col. 1527A]

and besieged the city of Sens, but did not take it. The Northmen returned from Sens toward Paris; repulsed from there, they crossed the river Marne, burned the city of Troyes, and laid waste everything as far as Verdun and the town of Toul. The fortress of Saint-Omer was consumed by fire.

### 894

In Burgundy flourished Berno, formerly a count and then abbot of the monastery of Gigny, which he founded. From the gift of Countess Awa he also built the monastery of Cluny as a cell of Gigny. The survivors of the Northmen, having crossed the Meuse, ranged through and ravaged Ripuarian territory and the Ardennes, and departed across the sea.

### 899

[Col. 1527B] In summer King Charles stayed upon the Yser with an assembled army, intending to deliberate what he should do about his enemies. Baldwin, however, went to that assembly and was able to ingratiate himself with the king, so that he might restore Arras, which he had taken from him. When Fulk, archbishop of Rheims, and Herbert opposed this, Winethmar suddenly arrived and, with his accomplices, wickedly killed Archbishop Fulk by many wounds, on 16 July. His body was brought to Rheims and laid in the church of Blessed Remigius. Afterwards, under the direction of Bishop Hereneus at Rheims, and after a synod had been held, all the bishop’s murderers were condemned and cast out from the thresholds of Holy Mother Church.

### 901

[Col. 1527C] The glorious translation of the body of Saint Winoc, abbot and confessor and most mighty protector of Flanders, from Sithiu to Bergues. This translation was carried out by Count Baldwin the Bald, who caused a church to be built in the lower part of that same borough. He completed it under the distinguished title of Christ’s confessors Martin and Winoc, and devoutly established there a body of canons to apply themselves most faithfully, day and night, to divine worship.

### 903

When Francon, bishop of Liège, died, Stephen was appointed bishop in his place: a man distinguished for holiness and learning. He composed in verse, for Archbishop Herimann, the life and passion of Saint Lambert, and also a nocturnal office in verse for the same saint; he composed in sweet and regular melody an office [Col. 1527D] on the Holy Trinity and on the finding of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr.

### 905

Charles, surnamed the Simple, king of the Franks, married as his wife Edgiva, daughter of Edward, king of England. By her he begot Louis, who reigned in Francia after him.

### 915

[Col. 1528A] 27. Charles, king of the Franks, recovered the kingdom of Lotharingia.

### 916

Baldwin the Bald, count of Flanders, died and was buried at Blandinium. His sons divided his march between them: Arnulf, the elder, received Flanders; Adulf received the city of Boulogne and the region of Thérouanne. But when Adulf died first, Arnulf held his county together with Flanders. Arnulf ruled Flanders for forty-six years.

### 925

Charles, king of the Franks, was captured by Count Herbert and thrown into custody at Péronne because of the killing of Duke Robert, whom he had slain.

### 928

[Col. 1528B] Louis, son of King Charles, fleeing those who lay in wait for him, crossed the sea into England, for his mother had been the daughter of the king of the English. He reigned in Francia, amid disturbances, for thirty-seven years. For thereafter the magnates of the Franks rebelled against him, above all Hugh the Great, count of Paris.

### 931

A certain Evrard, who founded the city of Bergues, gave Werhem to Saint Winoc. In the time of Adulf, the illustrious margrave, there was a certain distinguished man named Everard, who founded the city of Bergues because of the violence of robbers, as a protection for Christians. For the honour of Saint Winoc and in hope of the life to come, he granted to that saint a certain church on his hereditary estate, [Col. 1528C] which he had bought, together with its allod, from a man named Hemfrid, with the consent of Hemfrid’s sons, for thirty pounds of silver.

### 932

Hubald, monk and philosopher of the monastery of Saint-Amand at Elnone, who composed chants in sweet melody concerning many saints, died.

### 933

Adulf, count of Boulogne, died. His brother Arnulf received the county. Arnulf married a daughter of Herbert, count of Vermandois, named Adala, by whom he begot Baldwin, who died young of smallpox. This Baldwin had married a daughter of Hermann, duke of the Saxons, named Matilda, by whom he begot Arnulf. [Col. 1528D] Matilda, left a widow, married Godfrey, duke of Heyam, and bore him three sons: Duke Gezelon, Godfrey, and Heselon. Arnulf, her son by her former husband Baldwin, married a daughter of Berengar, king of the Lombards, [named] Rasela, and Susanna, by whom he begot Baldwin the Bearded. [The construction and names here are materially uncertain.]

### 961

Count Baldwin died and was buried at Sithiu.

### 966

> [Note: Col. 1529D]
>
> **Year 966.** Brando has almost the same account under 967.
>
> **Year 988.** The Chronicle of Saint-Bertin, or of Ypres, reports the same event.

[Col. 1529A] When Arnulf, the old count of the Flemings, died, King Lothair of the Franks grievously harassed and ravaged the march which he had governed most honourably and gloriously for forty-eight years. After his long and mournful death, Baldwin the Bearded, son of Arnulf the Younger, succeeded him in the county; he was called a strong and most handsome margrave. He married Ogiva, daughter of Count Giselbert, by whom he begot Baldwin of Lille.

### 970

29. Hugh the Great, count of Paris and duke of the Franks, died, and his son Hugh, surnamed Capet, was made duke of the Franks under King Lothair.

### 973

[Col. 1529B] The rebuilding of the monastery of Saint-Bertin was begun after its burning.

### 978

After Frederick, the duchy of Brabant and Lotharingia was given to Charles, brother of Lothair, king of the Franks, with many benefits besides, so that he too might desist from acts of insolence and resist the agitations of his brother King Lothair.

### How the bodies of Saints Richarius and Walericus were brought back to their monasteries

### 988

In the *Deeds* of Saints Richarius and Walericus we read that their bodies were transferred from their churches into Flanders and deposited in the church of Saint-Bertin. [Col. 1529C] I found the reason for the translation written obscurely, but it is clear that they were deposited there for safety, through fear of the Northmen and Danes. For the fortress of Saint-Omer, in which the church of Saint-Bertin stands, was then distinguished and sufficiently fortified against enemies. When, in the time of King Charles surnamed the Simple, the Northmen had been converted to the faith of Christ, the bodies of saints which had been moved into very strong places through fear of them were brought back by their own people to their own churches. But when the monks of Saint-Riquier and Saint-Valery sought back the bodies of their saints, the monks of Saint-Bertin retained them by the violence of Count Arnulf the Old.

Then Saint Walericus appeared in a dream to Hugh, count of Paris, and said: “Go to Arnulf, [Col. 1529D] count of the Flemings, and tell him to restore to our churches our bodies which are in the church of Saint-Bertin. For we love our own places more than those of others.”

“Lord,” he said, “who are you, and who is your companion?”

“I,” he said, “am called Walericus, and my companion is Richarius of Ponthieu. Do swiftly what God commands you through me, and do not delay.”

To conclude in brief: Hugh went to Arnulf and reported what had been commanded him. Arnulf, however, in a proud spirit refused to return the bodies of the saints. Then Hugh, count of Paris, said firmly to Count Arnulf: [Col. 1530A] “See to it that on that day and in that place you bring me the bodies of the saints honourably and of your own will; if you do not do so willingly, you will later do it unwillingly.”

Then Count Arnulf, constrained by fear of Hugh and by his forbearance, adorned two reliquaries with silver and gold and placed the relics of the saints in them. On the appointed day Hugh came with an armed and numerous army to the little monastery which is the fortress of the king of the Franks. When Count Arnulf heard of his arrival, he came to meet him with a great army, but unarmed and humble. He duly delivered the bodies of Saints Richarius and Walericus, properly prepared, to Hugh, who restored each to its own place.

On the following night Saint Walericus appeared in a dream to Hugh and said: “Because you zealously performed what was commanded you [Col. 1530B] and returned us to our own places, you and your successors shall reign in the kingdom of the Franks down to the seventh generation.” This revelation clearly shows that the transfer of the kingdom took place by the will of the Lord.

### 995

In the fourth year of Emperor Henry and the tenth of Robert, king of the Franks, Baldwin, count of Flanders, seized the imperial fortress called Valenciennes, situated in the march between Francia and Lotharingia. On hearing this, Emperor Henry summoned King Robert of Francia and Richard, count of the Northmen, to his aid and besieged the fortress. Since the emperor returned from that siege without success, he marched against Baldwin and attacked the fortress of Ghent. [Col. 1530C] Having ravaged the land, he captured some of the leading Flemings. Thereupon Baldwin, alarmed, made satisfaction to the emperor at the palace of Aachen. He restored Valenciennes and, giving hostages and swearing fealty, placed his hands in the emperor’s. Afterwards, compelled by a revolt of his own men, the emperor granted Valenciennes to Baldwin as a benefice, so that he might assist him against the disturbances of his men. Later he added Walcheren to him.

### 1016

Otto, duke of Brabant, died; and since he left no heir, in him ended the line of dukes of Lotharingia or Brabant descended from the stock of the Carolingians and Charlemagne. Emperor Henry gave the duchy of Brabant to Count Godfrey, son of Godfrey of Ardennes. His brothers were [Col. 1530D] Gozelo, who later held this duchy of Brabant after Godfrey, and Etzelo. Their mother was Matilda, formerly countess of Flanders and wife of Baldwin the Younger. After Baldwin’s death she married the aforesaid Godfrey, count of Ardennes and Ename, and bore him these sons: Godfrey, Gozelo, and Hetzelon.

Godfrey the Younger, eldest son of Godfrey and Matilda, was made duke of Brabant by the emperor’s gift. He held Brabant, the Ardennes, and the land of Ename, which is now an integral part of the county of Flanders, although it lies beyond the Scheldt. There then stood in it the castle of Brachant; there now stand Geraardsbergen, Ninove, and many other towns. [Col. 1531A] It lies between Ghent, Brussels, and Ath. A war was fought over this land between Emperor Henry III and Baldwin the Pious, or Baldwin of Lille, count of Flanders, because Baldwin invaded it. But afterwards, peace having intervened, the emperor gave it to Baldwin, adding also the land of Aalst, the land of the Four Offices, and likewise Walcheren in Zeeland, which at that time belonged by right to the emperor.

Lambert, count of Louvain, hearing that Godfrey had occupied Brabant after Duke Otto’s death, wished to acquire it by hereditary right with his wife Gerberga, Otto’s sister. Thus a long war arose between them. At last they met in battle at Florennes, where Lambert was killed. Yet the descendants of this Lambert afterwards possessed by hereditary succession, for a long time, the counties of Louvain and Brussels. [Col. 1531B] Godfrey held Brabant for fourteen years and was always faithful to Emperor Henry. Therefore he was sent by the emperor to assist Dirk, count of Holland, against the Frisians; he was captured by the Frisians and released not long afterwards, and died.

His brother Gozelo succeeded him. Gozelo’s children were Pope Stephen IX, who became pope after Victor II; Godfrey the Bold; and one daughter, countess of Brussels, otherwise called Reynel, countess of Namur. After Gozelo, his son Godfrey surnamed the Bold held the duchy of Brabant. He begot Godfrey the Hunchback and a daughter Ida, who married Eustace, count of Boulogne. Their sons were Godfrey of Bouillon, Baldwin—kings [of] Jerusalem—and Eustace, count of Boulogne. Godfrey the Hunchback, son of Duke Godfrey the Bold, succeeded his father in the duchy of Brabant. [Col. 1531C] He was killed in the city of Utrecht, leaving no heir; consequently Godfrey of Bouillon, son of his sister Ida, succeeded him in the duchy of Brabant. When he had been raised to the kingship of Jerusalem and died there, the duchy of Brabant was given by the emperor to Godfrey with the Beard, son of Henry, count of Brussels and Louvain. This Henry was son of Henry of Louvain, who was strangled in his own house by a certain captive. He was son of Lambert, count of Louvain, who was killed near Tournai. This Lambert was son of Henry, count of Louvain; that Henry was son of Lambert and Gerberga, [Col. 1531D] sister of Otto, already mentioned as dead, who was the son of the illustrious Duke Charles, brother of Lothair, king of the Franks.

Thus, when this Godfrey the Bearded had become duke of Brabant, it is evident that the duchy of Brabant returned to dukes descended from the Carolingian and Charlemagne’s line. This Godfrey the Bearded expelled Henry of Limburg from Lotharingia and begot Duke Godfrey, who married Luthgarde, sister of the emperor. By her this Duke Godfrey begot Godfrey III, duke of Brabant, who married a daughter of Henry of Limburg, by whom he begot Henry the Elder and Albert, bishop of Liège. Henry, made duke of Brabant, married Matilda, daughter of Matthew, count of Boulogne, brother [Col. 1532A] of Philip, count of Flanders; [and begot] Henry II, the Empress Mary, wife of Otto IV, Matilda, countess palatine of the Rhine, who later became countess of Holland, a countess of Guelders, and countess of Auvergne. This same Henry the Elder married secondly Mary, daughter of Philip the One-Eyed, king of France, who bore him a daughter whom Dirk, count of Cleves, married; from her was born the lady of Durbuy, and from her came the lady of Voorne and the lady of Gistel.

Henry’s son Henry succeeded Henry the Elder in the duchy. By a niece of Frederick II he begot Henry III; and by another wife, daughter of Saint Elizabeth, duchess of Thuringia, he begot another son also named Henry, landgrave of Thuringia, who fought manfully against the heretical Stedinger. [Col. 1532B] Henry III, receiving the duchy of Brabant, married Adelaide, daughter of the duke of Burgundy, who bore him a son named John. This John became *tutor* at Aachen. In the year of the Lord 1268 he married the daughter of Guy, count of Flanders, by whom he had several children, but all died in youth except one, who was also called John.

This John I, made duke of Brabant, fought at Worringen against the count of Guelders, the count of Luxembourg, and their allies, and won the victory. As stated, he begot John II and a daughter, later married by the count of Luxembourg, by whom he begot Henry, count of Luxembourg and later emperor, father of the king of Bohemia. John II, made duke of Brabant, married the daughter of the king of England. [Col. 1532C] Her sister married the count of Bar. John, the aforesaid duke, was called there for the wedding, was wounded in a tournament, carried back to his country, and died. He was buried at Brussels beside his wife.

In the year of the Lord 1294, his son John III, born of the daughter of the king of England, succeeded him. He married a daughter of Louis, king of France, and by her begot three sons and as many daughters. But all the sons were taken by premature death. Of the daughters, one, Joanna, married William, count of Holland; after he was killed by the Frisians, she married Wenceslas, son of the king of Bohemia and emperor. Widowed by him, she still rules Brabant today in venerable old age, more than ninety years old. Another daughter, Margaret, married the count of Flanders, namely Louis. Their daughter [Col. 1532D] Margaret married Philip, duke of Burgundy, whose distinguished sons are John, duke of Burgundy and count of Flanders; Anthony, duke of Limburg and also to become duke of Brabant after the death of Duchess Joanna; and Philip, count of Nevers. The third daughter of John, duke of Brabant, married the count of Guelders; widowed by him, she remained lady of Turnhout and died in a good old age. This is the genealogy of the dukes of Brabant brought down to the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1405.

### 1025

Baldwin, surnamed Fair Beard, associated his son Baldwin—afterwards called the Pious—with Adela, daughter of Robert, king of the Franks, as his wife. By her [Col. 1533A]

were born Baldwin of Mons, Robert the Frisian, and one daughter, Matilda, who later married William, son of Robert, duke of Normandy. This William acquired England and was the first of the Normans to reign there, as will be evident in its proper time.

### 1027

In the year 1027, Baldwin the Bearded, having taken up the sovereignty of the Flemings, built in the upper part of the borough of Bergues, namely on the hill which until then had been called Mount Bahal, a castle and beside it a church of greater magnificence. In the opinion of some, he is thought to have done this both in order to reside farther from the common intercourse of the townspeople and to visit more frequently and venerate more devoutly the most holy members of the body, transferred to the adjoining church. [Col. 1533B] Although he carried out with pious devotion what he had intended in his mind, nevertheless, as we have set down in the preface to this little volume, the result turned out contrary to expectation, and divine worship entirely grew cold through the negligence of the clergy. But when this became known to the illustrious margrave, he did not delay to correct, by sounder counsel, what his forebears had established well but the indolence of the wicked had ruined. Perceiving that clerics pre-eminent in rank of nobility and accustomed to pleasures could not easily be bent toward better things, he divided the possessions of that church—its clerics scarcely consenting even in this way, because no other way was possible—and expelled them, entrusting the place to the venerable Roderic, abbot of Saint-Bertin, to govern.

### 1028

[Col. 1533C] Since the aforesaid Margrave Baldwin devoted himself in every respect to religion and grieved that the monks of Saint-Bertin lived less according to rule and very secularly, he summoned this Roderic, a man most capable in every respect, from the monastery of Saint-Vaast, where religious fervour then flourished, and appointed him abbot of the church of Blessed Bertin. Roderic had commendably presided over the monastery of Sithiu for twenty-one years, and for almost seven of those years had supplied the church at Bergues with pastoral care. Perceiving that he could not bear the burden in both places, he had a certain brother appointed abbot over the monks of Bergues.

### 1029

The canons were expelled from Bergues, and the place was given [Col. 1533D] to Lord Abbot Roderic.

### 1030

When Robert, king of the Franks, died, his son Henry reigned in Francia for thirty years. Baldwin, count of Flanders, surnamed Fair Beard, died and was buried at Ghent in the monastery of Saint Peter. Baldwin the Pious, or Baldwin of Lille, succeeded him in the county. [Col. 1534A] He was called “of Lille” because he founded the fortress called Lille and built in it the church of Saint Peter. He married Adela, daughter of Robert, king of the Franks, and held the county for thirty-four years.

### 1034

The monastery of Saint-Omer was burned down.

### 1036

The monastery of Saint Peter and that of Saint-Bertin were consumed by fire.

### 1050

Baldwin the Younger, count, married Richilde, widow of Herman, count of Mons, and by her begot two sons, Arnulf and Baldwin. The body of Saint Bertin was discovered.

### 1051

[Col. 1534B] The elevation of Saint Bertin, 2 May.

### 1052

Emperor Henry came to the Ditch. Count Baldwin, invading the county of Hainaut, rebelled against the emperor.

### 1054

In this year Henry, emperor of the Romans, having elevated his five-year-old son Henry as king at Aachen, marched against Baldwin the Pious, count of Flanders. Baldwin fled; the emperor crossed the river Scheldt and ravaged everything. The gates of the enclosure were opened to him, and he made a great slaughter of the enemy. Advancing farther, he killed Count Lambert, Baldwin’s follower, with many others; [Col. 1534C] he also shut up within the city of Tournai many leading Flemings following his army and captured them while besieged.

### 1056

In the thousandth year and likewise the fifty-sixth,

the work of this church is known to have been begun,

where first a wooden basilica had been built.

### 1066

Alexander became pope.

### 1067

37. Glorious Baldwin died and was buried at Lille. His son Baldwin succeeded him.

### 1069

Baldwin, who lies buried at Hainaut, whose brother Robert was called the Frisian, married Gertrude, daughter of Bernard, count of the Saxons, widow of Florence, count of the Frisians. [Col. 1534D] With her he held her realm. Having received a very great sum of money from her father, he renounced Flanders by oath, conceding it by hereditary right to his brother Baldwin and his successors. For during the lifetime of his brother Robert he remained silent; but after Robert’s death, with the help of traitors, he killed his nephew Arnulf, count of [Col. 1535A]

### 1070

In the thousandth year of Christ together with the seventieth,

this church of Saint Peter was consecrated by Radbod.

In this year the blessed virgin Godelieve was martyred near Gistel on 6 July by the servants of her husband.

### 1072

The place of Watten in Flanders was founded. Robert the Frisian, the thirteenth [count] of Flanders, ruled for five years.

### 1080
At this same time, in the monastery of Saint Medard [Col. 1535B] at Soissons, blessed Arnulf flourished in signs and virtues. Because of his remarkable zeal for holiness, he chose the vocation of a recluse and afflicted himself with exceedingly strict abstinence. He received from God the grace of prophecy; and, having been made abbot of that same monastery from his reclusion, he afterward returned to that reclusion out of contempt for the world and desire for inward repose. When the bishop of Soissons died, Arnulf was elected to the episcopate and, by order of Pope Gregory through Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, was consecrated bishop.

### 1083

This year the monastery of Affligem began to be built, and the body of blessed Livinus was translated at Ghent. Flanders too was disturbed by wars and civil dissensions, which [Col. 1535C] seditions blessed Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, sent by Pope Gregory VII, checked and pacified by holy sermons, pious examples, and the holiness of his life.

### 1084

In the year of the Lord 1084, the body of blessed Godelieve was raised at Ghistelle by Lord Radbod, bishop of Noyon, on the third day before the Kalends of August [30 July]. She had been martyred in 1070, on the sixth day of July.

### 1087

The year one thousand and eighty-seven had come,

When the earth received the body of kindly Arnulf,

He through whom monks were first then established here.

Saint Arnulf, formerly abbot of Saint Medard at Soissons and afterward bishop, illustrious through divine miracles at Oudenburg in the church of Saint Peter, happily passed to the Lord this year.

### 1091

[Col. 1536A]

After our patron, blessed Arnulf, servant of God, had happily been removed from human affairs, diverse miracles were performed by the Lord around his remains, and health was granted to very many sick persons. For from the very time of his burial such ardour of faith and devotion shone forth around him that, whoever came in person, or sent representatives, to the tomb of this same Saint Arnulf, gathered up the drifting dust from around it and carried it home as a sure medicine. Mixing this dust into their food or drink, or taking it by licking and swallowing the dry powder, they escaped every infirmity and obtained a most certain remedy, or rather a cure. This happened not four, seven, or ten times, but, as is very well known, thousands of times.

[Col. 1536B]

We saw a demoniac most grievously tormented. When this dust was put into his mouth against his will, he immediately escaped the enemy and recovered his mind. This celebrated dust brought knowledge of its great benefit not only to our Flanders but to all neighbouring regions. England, France, Scotland, and Frisia—thus foreign peoples held it in esteem and likewise carried away the ash to their homelands.

After these and many similar occurrences had thus become more widely known, and this praiseworthy report had reached France—as a pleasing fragrance also continually issued from his tomb—the monks of Saint Medard, deeply grieving that they lacked the remains of so great a man, took counsel with their abbot Odo. Under the pretext of a visit, they would go to Oudenburg and secretly open his tomb,

[Col. 1536C]

so that, having taken out the bones, they might carry them with all speed to their monastery at Soissons. They went so far as this; and, having prepared the instruments for the undertaking, they began by night to open his tomb on the right side. Immediately a huge crash thundered from heaven, shaking the diggers and terrifying them so greatly that it deterred them from their purpose. A little later, having recovered and supposing that this had happened through some hidden disturbance of the air, they returned to the grave to complete what they had begun. But as soon as they began to dig, the crash sounded again in terrible rebuke. They fell to the ground as though lifeless and, at last recovering their breath, fled in extreme fear. While standing at a distance and muttering in subdued voices, the thought came upon them

[Col. 1536D]

that they should repeat their rashness for a third time and again test whether any result would follow. They came trembling, put forth fearful hands, but were immediately struck a third time by intolerable terror.

[Note: Col. 1537D]

In the year 1096, Brandon gives a fuller account, copied from the *Deeds of the Franks*.

[Col. 1538D] In the year 1099, the verses were written by another hand.

In the year 1119, Aldenb[urg] places the count’s death in this year and repeats the death in the following year, namely 1120, from Brandon.

[Col. 1537A]

They were dashed to the pavement, lay palpitating as though lifeless and nearly dead, and did not know what to do. After the space of three hours had passed, they returned to consciousness and, in great distress, made a vow never again rashly to attempt anything against the saint’s body or tomb. Arnulf, nephew of the holy bishop himself and first abbot of Oudenburg, attempted this deed with two monks, Godebert, an Oudenburg native, and Boldrad, a man of Bruges; and by their own outcry these events became known.

### 1096

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, the thirty-sixth of Philip, king of the Franks, the expedition to Jerusalem

[Col. 1537B]

was undertaken at Clermont in Auvergne through the authority of Pope Urban and the exhortation of Aimar, bishop of Le Puy. Dukes, counts, powerful men, nobles and commoners, rich and poor, free persons and slaves, bishops, clerics, monks, old men and young, even boys and girls, all with one purpose and constrained by none, assembled from every side: from Spain, Provence, Aquitaine, Brittany, Scotland, England, Normandy, France, Lorraine, Burgundy, Germany, Lombardy, Apulia, and other kingdoms. In this host of God stood out Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, and his brothers Eustace and Baldwin; Anselm of Ribemont; Baldwin, count of Mons; Robert, count of Flanders;

[Col. 1537C]

his kinsman Stephen, count of Blois; Hugh, brother of the king of France; Robert, count of Normandy; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; Bohemond, duke of Apulia; and Tancred. The army of God boldly entered the territories of the pagans. Its first battle against them was at the bridge over the river Pharphar, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March [21 February], where many Turks were killed. Its second battle against them was at Nicaea, on the third day before the Nones of March [5 March], in which the pagans also were defeated. Nicaea having been taken, and Laodicea likewise taken, there were more than three hundred thousand armed men in the Christian army. Such abundance of all provisions was available to them that a ram was sold for one coin and an ox scarcely for twelve coins, as is related at length above in the *Deeds of the Franks*

[Col. 1537D]

who captured Jerusalem, down to the year 1100.

### 1099

The monks of Affligem first entered the monastery of Saint Andrew near Bruges on the eighth day before the Kalends of March [22 February], and a flock of monks was formed.

In the year one less than eleven hundred,

When the Ides of July had been completed, under Godfrey

The Franks took Jerusalem by mighty valour.

After this, eight times twenty-four years passed,

When Saladin, king of Damascus, took it;

Then the first year took up the cross and the second the arms.

### 1111

[Col. 1538A]

Robert II, count of Flanders, while riding across the bridge of Melun with a multitude of knights, fell by accident and there ended his life beneath the trampling feet of horses. His body was carried to Arras and buried in the church of Saint Vaast. He was succeeded by his son Baldwin, surnamed Hapkin, born of Clementia, daughter of the duke of Burgundy. This Baldwin took as wife the daughter of Alan, count of Nantes, or Brittany; but, when kinship between them was discovered, they were separated by order of Pope Paschal. This kinship was set forth before the pope by Cono, bishop of Palestrina, in this manner: Constance, queen of the Franks and wife of King Robert, and Ermengard, countess of Auvergne,

[Col. 1538B]

were sisters. Adela, countess of Flanders, was born from Constance; from Ermengard came another Ermengard, countess. From Adela came Robert the Frisian, count of Flanders; from Ermengard, Countess Bertha. From Robert came another Robert; from Bertha, Hawise, countess of Nantes. From Robert came this Baldwin, and from Hawise Count Alan, from whom came this young woman. Thus Count Baldwin, powerful above all the princes of France in his day, governed the county of Flanders so nobly amid frequent wars that he inspired terror in neighbouring tyrants on every side. He held the county of Flanders for nine years.

Flanders and Burgundy, though separated by a long extent of land, conspire in the apostasy of the traitor Judas. Certain Flemish traitors, fearing condemnation for

[Col. 1538C]

their crime, cut down their lord Count Charles at Bruges in the church of Saint Donatian before the altar, while he was chanting psalms and giving alms. One and the same Satan, on one and the same day, dared a like crime in Burgundy. Certain condemned men, despairing of their salvation because they were guilty of treason, stabbed with swords their lord William, count of the Sedunenses, in a certain church before the altar while he prayed. The deed was done in the second week of Lent, on Tuesday. The murderers fled here and there, but through the agency of Louis, king of France, perished by various punishments and an end entirely deserved.

### 1112

In the twenty-eighth year of Louis, king of the Franks, the monastery of Saint Vaast at Arras

[Col. 1538D]

was burned, together with its cloister, workshops, and a great part of the town. No one in our age remembers so many villages and cities, castles, towns, or boroughs being burned by accidental fire as are reported to have burned within the space of this year. At Mons, the church of Saint Waudru, together with two other smaller churches, burned with nearly the whole town. The church of Saint Michael “of the Peril of the Sea” also, struck by lightning, burned together with all the buildings belonging to it.

### 1120

Baldwin, count of Flanders, died and was buried at Saint

[Col. 1539A]

Bertin. He was succeeded by Charles, nephew of Count Robert through Robert’s sister, and son of Canute, king of the Danes.

[Note: Col. 1539D]

In the year 1121. Although these matters are recounted in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. III for August, p. 257 and following, we judged that they should be reproduced here, both because certain words differ and because some matters are added here that were unknown to Father Cuper. Cuper used a manuscript copy from the monastery of Thosan, probably transcribed from some Oudenburg manuscript. From this it may be seen that the Bollandists did not use this our larger chronicle. At least our text will therefore serve to resolve certain doubts set out by the hagiographers in their notes.

### On the elevation of the body of Saint Arnulf, bishop, confessor, and our patron

After many and various proofs of heavenly grace concerning the life and miracles of our most holy father and defender Arnulf had more widely reached the ears of Lord Lambert, bishop of Tournai, and the knowledge of the faithful people, that bishop convened a council at Beauvais on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October], with certain fellow bishops, to decide what ought to be done in response to so great a manifestation of God. Present were bishops of France: William of Châlons, a pillar among teachers; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres;

[Col. 1539B]

Deibert,

[Note: Col. 1539D]

In the Bollandists: Delbert.

archbishop of Sens; the bishop of Orléans; the bishop of Paris; Clarembald, bishop of Senlis; Peter, bishop of Beauvais; Angelran, bishop of Amiens; Robert, bishop of Arras; John, bishop of Thérouanne; Lambert, bishop of Tournai; Burchard, bishop of Cambrai; Bartholomew, bishop of Laon; and Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, author of this treatise.

[Note: Col. 1539D]

In the Bollandists: “I, Liziard, unworthy [etc.].”

There was also a great multitude of abbots, archdeacons, provosts, and clergy. Among the others was present Hariulf, abbot of Oudenburg,

[Note: Col. 1539D]

Hariulf is omitted in the Bollandists.

holding in his hands a little book concerning the life, character, and miraculous deeds of this holy man

[Note: Col. 1539D]

In the Bollandists, *viri* (“man”) is omitted.

Arnulf. The aforesaid Lisiard,

[Note: Col. 1539D]

Where this text has *Lisiardus*, the Bollandists have *ego* (“I”).

bishop of Soissons, received the book from his hands,

[Col. 1539C]

opened it, and offered it open to the bishops, saying: “Behold, lords, this little book was written concerning his life with my knowledge and under my authorship. I testify in faith that all that it narrates is true; and concerning his miracles I can produce very truthful witnesses, some here and many more at home. I therefore ask you to consider this book carefully, so that from knowledge of it you may be better informed as to what should be done concerning him. Let your holiness hear my judgment: if he rested in the diocese entrusted to me, it would be a long time since he had lain in the earth.”

Then William, bishop of Châlons, took the book; looking through it from the beginning, he saw the number of its chapters and said to the bishop of

[Col. 1539D]

Tournai: “Lord, what more do you seek? Apart from this book, the testimony

[Note: Col. 1539D]

The Bollandists: “our” rather than “your.”

of the bishop of Soissons and his clerics is enough for you.

[Col. 1540A]

Such an abbot ought to give you great confidence, for both his age deserves respect and his prudence is pleasing. As for this book, since we are occupied with synodal business, there is no time to read through it.”

[Note: Col. 1540D]

The Bollandists: *percurrere*, “read through.”

Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, said: “Lord bishop of Tournai, I tell you truly: if the Lord had done such things even once for any of my predecessors, I would consult neither pope nor legate nor even archbishop; rather, with complete resolve, I would exalt the saint of God as he deserves.”

Meanwhile, while the bishops were deciding these matters, certain noble schoolmasters had taken the book and rapidly read some chapters of the deeds. Some of them then returned to where the bishops were and declared with great assurance:

[Col. 1540B]

“Truly, whoever opposes the exaltation of this saint is not of God.”

Then William, bishop of Châlons, said: “By God, it is shameful that we doubt a matter so plain. Therefore, lord bishop of Tournai, with the Lord’s grace and setting aside every uncertainty, appoint a day on which you may assemble at the place and, raising the holy servant of the Lord from the earth, honourably reinter him.”

Lambert, bishop of Tournai, said: “Behold, the legate is sitting at a distance in this very basilica with our archbishop of Reims or Tours. I ask that you be willing to come before them and have your judgment confirmed by their decision.” The bishops said: “Let it be done in the name of the Lord.”

When they arrived, Bishop Lambert said to the lord bishop of Châlons:

[Col. 1540C]

“I ask you, plead my cause.” And when he had set out the case before the legate and archbishops with brief eloquence, both the legate Cono and the archbishop of Reims answered with one voice: “We fully accept the judgment of your authority and confirm the decree of your agreement.”

Accordingly Bishop Lambert summoned the abbot and appointed the day on which he was to assemble at Oudenburg, namely the Kalends of May [1 May], and to raise the holy body of the man of God from the ground and reinter it as truly holy, according to the custom of the Gallican church. He also gave sealed letters summoning all the people of the diocese of Tournai to so holy an office.

A copy of the letter of the bishop of Tournai, found in an old chest.

[Note: Col. 1540D]

This letter is reproduced in the work of the hagiographers, in the Preliminary Commentary on the Life of Saint Arnulf, p. 223, third part of August. Lisiard does not reproduce this letter.

[Col. 1540D]

Lambert, by God’s grace bishop of Tournai and Noyon,

[Col. 1541A]

to all the deans and priests of our diocese, greeting and blessing. With the grace of the Spirit cooperating, we have decreed that the sacred body of Saint Arnulf, bishop, be raised from the earth. For the performance of this sacred office on the first day of May, Christ leading the way, we command that the people committed to you be admonished by your charity in each church, that they may assemble devoutly and obtain the Lord’s blessing at Oudenburg in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle. Given in the year of the Lord 1120, indiction 13.

Flying fame, speeding on its swift course, caused diverse peoples to visit these places. Let us say nothing of Flanders: the people of Walcheren, the Scheldt district, Beveland, Antwerp, Texandria, Waasland, Brabant, the Menapii,

[Col. 1541B]

the Morini, Boulogne, and other regions came in abundance. At the appointed time the bishop arrived with the honourable Robert, archdeacon of Tournai, and a great company of clergy. The trophy of the cross was borne before them; the sacred Gospel-book was also carried, with candles and incense. While the clergy sang in harmony, the tomb of the holy man was opened, and the blessed bones were selected from their dusty resting place. A chalice, buried with him, stood upon his breast; beneath the chalice, before his breast, lay a lead tablet. This tablet bore in writing his name, homeland, lineage, military career, conversion, promotion to the abbacy, the day of his ordination as bishop, and the day of his passage from this world to Christ. When this tablet had been raised from the saint’s breast and read aloud in the presence of the bishop,

[Note: Col. 1541D]

In the Bollandists: *astante*, “being present.”

it brought him great joy,

[Col. 1541C]

because he feared that, through some error, the brethren might raise not Saint Arnulf but some unworthy person under the saint’s name. Likewise, when they showed the bishop the pastoral staff, he rejoiced exceedingly. Finally, when he saw the sandals embroidered with gold drawn out,

[Note: Col. 1541D]

The Bollandists: *exstructa* (“constructed”) for *extracta* (“drawn out”).

he dissolved into tears.

Three men in priestly orders were chosen to receive and lift the bones from the grave: Abbot Hariulf, the monk Godewin, and the monk Haghaningh. When the abbot raised the skull from the earth and placed it in a chest prepared for that purpose, behold, his hands were found greasy and soaked with an oily liquid, as if he had dipped his hands in a vessel full of oil. Behold before God: what is said is true, and it was true.

[Col. 1541D]

A fragrance of great sweetness likewise spread there; nor was this undeserved. For since he had endeavoured in his mortal life to be in every place the good fragrance of Christ, it is not surprising that he, now crowned by God who bestowed the gift and whom he served, deserved to be honoured with a heavenly fragrance. Meanwhile the church’s enclosure rang with praises to the gracious Trinity; and until the blessed bones, clothed with fitting reverence, were placed in a shrine, both bishop and clergy devoted themselves to divine offices. When they had been placed in the shrine, the bishop immediately began the hymn: “We praise thee, O God; we acknowledge thee to be the Lord.” When this hymn had been joyfully sung to the clouds,

[Col. 1542A]

the saint was carried outside the holy church to the appointed station, indeed by a military hand. For such a multitude of people rushed upon the saint that they certainly

[Note: Col. 1541D]

The Bollandists: *nimium*, “excessively.”

trampled, shoved, and crushed one another, and through love of the saint no one spared either himself or another. Thus devotion and longing for the saint had cast aside the bounds of reason, so that neither abbot nor monks could in any way get near the saint.

Divine miracles were certainly not lacking. The true God, one in Trinity, whom Saint Arnulf had served purely, displayed there a threefold miracle. For a certain young man, possessed by an hostile power and because of this long driven into madness, was freed there from the enemy and granted bodily health and freedom of his mind.

[Col. 1542B]

Two women likewise, struck by paralysis and wholly deprived of the use of their limbs, were restored to complete health. These three signs, performed inside the church, did not become sufficiently known among the people dispersed through streets and fields, because the dense multitude of common people so closely filled the basilica that no one could speak openly there, no one could turn in any direction, and no one could hear anything except the roar of the turbulent crowd.

God in heaven, taking pleasure in his Saint Arnulf, then gave a sign also from heaven. From the first hour until the full sixth hour, there was seen in the sky a burning sphere,

[Note: Col. 1541D]

“Sphere.”

like a flame of fire, hanging over the holy body of the blessed man. Across the sphere there shone

[Note: Col. 1542D]

The Bollandists: “across that sphere itself.”

the sign of the holy cross, like purest gold tested in a furnace.

[Col. 1542C]

This cross surpassed every beauty of the sun by its brightness, and its length exceeded the extent of the aforementioned sphere, stretching beyond it by three arms and gleaming in one

[Note: Col. 1542D]

The Bollandists: *nimio fulgere*, “shining with excessive brightness.”

radiance like flashing gold.

This sign seen in heaven surely seems to signify a heavenly mystery. For what does the sphere represent except the breadth of the world? And what does the vision of the cross signify except the mortification of the earthly

[Note: Col. 1542D]

The Bollandists: *terrenam*, “earthly.”

body? What, moreover, does the splendour of gold indicate except the brightness of eternal wisdom and the inward contemplation of the divine light? A flame appeared in the sphere because throughout the world it is known—indeed, it shall be known—how greatly the love of God has been poured into the heart of Saint

[Col. 1542D]

Arnulf through the Holy Spirit given to him. Rightly, therefore, did the sign glorifying Saint Arnulf appear in heaven. Let no one say: “Who has known Saint Arnulf?” We say that he is very well known, since he is rightly worthy of being known by heaven; for the prophet does not deceive when he says: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.” The sphere which appeared in heaven, therefore, represented the breadth of his good fame; the fiery appearance, the ardour of inward charity; the cross, martyrdom; and the golden splendour, the mystical understanding of divine charity. The length of the cross surpassing the sphere signifies the holy perseverance

[Col. 1543A]

of blessed mortification.

[Note: Col. 1543]

In the year 1127, Brando gives a fuller account of these matters.

In the year 1126, Brando contains much concerning the visitation of blessed Bernard.

Blessed and holy Arnulf could say: “My conversion is in the heavens.” He could say: “All the things of the world that are lovable or delightful, which I have left behind, I count as dung.” Such a man ought indeed to have been manifested by such signs.

A writing found in the ancient shrine concerning the elevation of the body of Saint Arnulf.

[Note: Col. 1543D]

This writing is found in vol. III, August, *Acts of the Saints*, p. 223.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121, indiction 14, in the fourteenth year of Louis, king of the Franks, in the second year of Pope Calixtus’s holding the Roman see, and likewise in the second year of Charles, count of the Flemings: the sacred body of blessed Arnulf, bishop,

[Col. 1543B]

was raised and translated on the Kalends of May [1 May] by Lambert, bishop of Tournai, while the Roman cardinal-priest Peter de Leone was lodging at Saint Bertin during his visitation of these regions. This was accomplished while Abbot Hariulf had laboured at the monastery of Oudenburg for fifteen years and six months, less nine days.

The alb, lying separately in a linen sack, had belonged to the saint himself. He wore it when he was consecrated bishop and sang Mass in it until the end of his life.

The tibia placed in the alb was from his sacred body; but, out of love, we had thought to retain it separately, until the excessive importunity of those asking compelled us to place it in the reliquary. It is now in the sacristy, honourably adorned with gold and silver, and is called “the arm of Saint Arnulf.”

### 1121

This translation took place on the first day of May,

[Col. 1543C]

indiction 14, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121, when Louis, son of Philip, had ruled the sceptres of the Franks for fourteen years; under Pope Calixtus; and while Ralph held the see of Reims as archbishop. Charles, son of the king of the Danes, whose mother had been the daughter of Count Robert, governed the county of Flanders. Abbot Hariulf had ruled the monastery of Oudenburg for sixteen years. It was observed that, with the elevation of the blessed man, fruitfulness of crops, health of bodies, and salubrity of the air came to the region of the Flemings, which had previously suffered grievously for seven years from floods of rain and sterility of fields, as well as pestilence among animals and frequent mortality among human beings.

[Note: Col. 1543D]

These things were written by the compiler of the chronicle from Liziard.

In this one-thousand, one-hundred, and also eleventh year,

The translation of Bishop Arnulf is established to have occurred.

[Note: Col. 1544D]

These verses were written by another hand.

### 1124

The church of Saint Winnoc, with all its appurtenances and nearly the entire town, was again burned on the Nones of September [5 September].

### 1127

Charles, count of Flanders, in the eighth year of his rule,

[Col. 1544A]

was killed at Bruges by his servant Burchard before the holy altar during Lent, while he knelt in prayer with the Psalter and a priest before the same prince chanted the sacred canon at the altar. Also killed with him were Themard, castellan of Broborgh, and his two sons Gilbert and Walter, together with the count’s steward, Walter of Lokeren. When this became known, Louis, king of the Franks, came to Flanders to avenge him; he had many of the traitors thrown from a tower and appointed as Charles’s successor William, son of Robert, count of the Normans, surnamed Curthose, a most valiant knight.

### 1128

William, count of Flanders, was wounded during the siege of Aalst,

[Col. 1544B]

fell ill, became a monk of Saint Bertin, died, and was buried in the church at the head of his kinsman Count Baldwin. He was succeeded by Thierry, son of Thierry, duke of Alsace, whom he had begotten by Gertrude, daughter of Robert, count of Frisia and widow of Count Henry of Brussels. This year the monastery of the Dunes began to be built.

Here begin the deeds of Hariulf, abbot of Saint Peter at Oudenburg, against the abbot of Saint Medard at Soissons, at Rome in the presence of the pope and cardinals.

### 1141

Hariulf, abbot of Oudenburg, coming to Rome, on the first day visited and repeatedly attended the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. On the second day he went to the Lateran palace and, according to the instruction received from the bishop of

[Col. 1544C]

Noyon, first sought an audience with Lord Aimeric, chief chancellor, a man most distinguished and thoroughly learned in ecclesiastical law and the institutions of the papal court. He asked his counsel and aid, saying:

“Reverend lord, our lord the bishop of Tournai and Noyon, rightly well disposed toward you, sends me to your noble excellence, that before all else I may offer you such service as is within my ability, and that I may proceed by your counsel before the lord pope to set forth the whole reason for my coming. For although examination of every case pertains to the lord pope, you rightly bear the burden and drive the chariot of Israel. Your industry orders all things, arranging lesser matters and directing greater. Therefore, having come, I desire and ask to obtain the goodwill of your counsel, that I may in the end obtain the effect of truth and justice.”

[Col. 1544D]

The chancellor said: “Brother, or rather Father, it is fitting not that you should serve us, but that we should serve you, since your countenance and honourable grey hair present you as a man resembling the good. Therefore, I ask that you take care lest the darts of shame strike either you, or us through you.”

The abbot, alarmed, said: “How could shame come to you through me, for God’s sake? I have arrived only recently, am unknown to all of you,

[Col. 1545A]

and have done nothing among you from which shame could arise for you—or rather, even for me.”

He answered: “Since your old age is honourable to all and your speech mild and eloquent, we are greatly pleased with you. Therefore we take care and most earnestly desire to deal wholly with you so that through you a good reputation may be spread everywhere, and that wicked report, which circulates everywhere, may begin through you to be extinguished: so that, as it has hitherto been said, ‘Everything is for sale at Rome,’ it may henceforth be said, ‘Everything is most just at Rome.’ This is what I previously meant when I said that shame would await us, if we were to secure justice for you by gifts given, or fail to obtain it for you because gifts were not given. Therefore I earnestly warn you not to give or promise anything to any person in the Roman court; for if I learn that you have done so,

[Col. 1545B]

you will lack both our counsel and the lord pope’s aid. We strive urgently to suppress this poisonous hiss among ourselves.”

The abbot said: “I should be excessively foolish if, acting against your command, I deprived myself of your counsel. Yet, when I come to the feet of the lord pope, what, or how much, ought I to offer?”

The chancellor said: “Far be it from you that you should have to offer anything there.”

Hearing this, the abbot rejoiced greatly, because he did not have the means to make a gift. Then Chancellor Aimeric, taking the abbot’s hand, led him to the consistory of the palace, where the lord pope sat on a tribunal and the cardinals at his right hand. The more noble Romans, with curled hair and clothed in silk, stood or sat about his feet. When they saw the chancellor coming,

[Col. 1545C]

they immediately rose and made room for him. At once the abbot threw himself at the feet of the lord pope and, fastening his lips or eyes upon them, kissed his feet. Perceiving the devout and pious feeling with which the abbot conducted himself, the pontiff stretched out his hand, raised him up, gave him a kiss, and asked:

“Brother, who are you, and whence, or for what reason, have you been brought to us? For it seems unseemly that a man so advanced in years should be compelled to come to Rome.”

The abbot answered: “Lord, it would indeed be very unseemly, unless the weight of the case had compelled me. But the very grave burden of the case has made the sea-voyage bearable to us. I am that Flemish abbot whom the lord abbot of Saint Medard at Soissons harshly persecutes, wishing to subject our house to himself, indeed most unjustly.”

[Col. 1545D]

The pope said: “Can you show that it is unjust?”

The abbot said: “With God’s help, I trust and am confident that I can show it.”

Then the abbot offered the pontiff letters from the bishop of Noyon and letters from the abbot of Clairvaux. The pope then said: “And is that dearest brother well?”

Not fully understanding about whom the pope was asking, the abbot said: “We left them safe and well.”

The pope said: “Thanks be to God.” Then the pope said to the abbot: “Go now and find lodging for yourself; come to us tomorrow or the day after, and we shall hear you.”

The bishops then present said: “He is truly worthy of a hearing.” Those bishops were the archbishop of Santa Rufina, the bishop of Ostia, the bishop of Segni, the bishop of Ferentino, the bishop of Tuscania, and several abbots, all of whom with one voice

[Col. 1546A]

urged that the lord pope treat the abbot mercifully. The Roman nobles too said: “By the Lord God, he who compelled such an old man to be harassed has committed a great sin.”

The abbot, having bowed before the pope, withdrew and went to lodging not far from the palace. During the following days he assiduously attended the palace, going in and out and presenting himself before the eyes of the pontiff and gatherings of cardinals, in order that by this very persistence he might urge the pope to hear the case. The pope often said to the abbot with cheerful and kindly expression: “Lord abbot, how are you doing?” He answered briskly: “Lord, well; and it shall be better if your generosity looks upon me.”

The pope said: “Wait and do not weary yourself, for as far as we can, you shall have what you desire. It is not the custom of our court

[Col. 1546B]

that a venerable person coming here should be sent away too quickly. Rather, by staying and moving among our people, he learns what he does not know and comes to understand how to endure the rule of the Romans with equanimity.”

The abbot said: “Lord, if you delay me with such an intention, I shall rejoice in it; but I fear that an empty purse will deny sustenance to one who remains so long.”

The pope said: “Save provisions for your return; for as long as you remain here, you may dine with us.”

The abbot, lowering his face, said: “I give thanks for so great a promise.”

The cardinals—Chancellor Aimeric, Gerard of Santa Croce, Ivo of Saint Lawrence, Guy of Pisa, Gregory Centu [reading uncertain], and the other leading men—often spoke with the abbot. He especially begged them to suggest his case to the lord pope and, having suggested it, to press him, so that, taking pity on the abbot, he would appoint a place and day.

[Col. 1546C]

They also said publicly: “Truly, lord, if it please you, we consider it most fitting to hear and settle his case.”

At last, on the ninth day after his arrival, the lord pope assigned him a day and place, namely his own chamber. When the cardinals had been summoned, the abbot was admitted to the chamber and ordered to sit on a footstool before the pontiff’s feet, where the chancellor also sat. Then the lord pope said to the abbot: “Truly, brother, we sympathize and grieve with you over how greatly you have laboured beyond the strength of your age, and how extremely weary you are. And behold, for your sake we have summoned our brethren, before whom you shall state the reasons for your coming. We shall listen willingly and, after counsel, determine what ought to be done.”

The abbot, bowing before the pope, said:

[Col. 1546D]

“Lord father, I give thanks to almighty God because he has sent into your heart this graciousness, that you deign to extend to me so kind a mercy. But, so that you may understand my grief more suitably, do not think it unworthy to hear a speech of mine which I set forth in parabolic form.

“A man, young in age, took for himself a bride entirely manifest in her freedom. He cherished and possessed her in that same freedom for thirty-five years and five months. And behold, suddenly a certain fierce adversary rose up and said to the bridegroom, now old: ‘You shall be my servant, because your bride belongs to me as a handmaid.’ The bridegroom, once young but now aged, cries out to him: ‘Since none of your fathers was ever lord over me, whence have you the right to lord it over me?’ The other haughtily says: ‘By my own exertion I acquired you, and you cannot resist, because the Roman pope has placed your neck beneath

[Col. 1547A]

my yoke.’ He replies: ‘If the lord pope has placed your yoke upon my neck, that is still only in hope, not in fact; for I am certain that he did it in ignorance. It remains, therefore, for me to hasten to the lord pope and investigate whether this is so.’ Angered, the other says: ‘Will you investigate, dying man? You are already drawing your last breath, and do you seek the court of Rome?’ He says: ‘I shall plainly convict you of your lies and set your contrived deceits before your face in the presence of the Romans.’

“So far the parable; what follows is its most plausible explanation.”

The young man who takes a bride signifies the abbot of Aldenburgh, who, though promoted while still comparatively young, was canonically appointed to the office of abbot, freely and absolutely—that is, without the stain or blemish of any opposition. Finally, in the thirty-fifth year of his ordination, [Col. 1547B] the lord abbot of Saint-Médard at Soissons, prompted alike by his own zeal and by the treacherous scheme of two clerics, Ralph and Godwin, procured from the Roman pope misleading letters ordering the abbot of Aldenburgh to leave his place. The pope, however, perceiving no deceit in this matter and not imagining that the abbot of Saint-Médard wished to lie to him, granted the requested letters. They were delivered to the abbot of Aldenburgh on the first day of August.

Perceiving and recognizing the untimeliness and malice of so great a fraud, he hastened to the presence of Pope Innocent and, with eloquent truth, exposed the carefully devised machinations of the abbot of Soissons against him. Having heard these things, the merciful pope felt compassion for both parties, but differently: for the man of Aldenburgh, because of his unjust harassment; for the man of Soissons, [Col. 1547C] because the ancient enemy had been able to bind his heart in so great an excess of fraud. When these matters had been concluded, the pope said: “We have heard your parable; we have heard the explanation of the parable; and we see that your purpose tends to this—that no divorce should be made before us from the bride whom you have long preserved.”

The abbot said: “If I am proved to be in the wrong, I do not refuse a divorce; but if I am in the right, who shall separate us? It lies more upon you to cut away what is perverse than to destroy what has been founded in Christ.”

The pope said: “On the first day of your arrival, you promised to show us that the abbot of Saint-Médard unjustly opposed you. Proceed, then, before us, and say under what saint’s name your oratory has been consecrated.”

The abbot said: “Our oratory was consecrated in honour of two of your—indeed, of our—[Col. 1547D] blessed ones, namely the Apostles Peter and Paul. The estate and the church founded there belonged by right to the church of Tournai and were held in fief from Count Robert; they never in any way belonged to the church of Saint-Médard. Behold, I have come; behold, I have laboured. Therefore I ask that Your Serenity hear me and have compassion on me. The most holy Roman pontiffs who ended their lives by martyrdom established in their decrees that no one should be condemned while absent. Where, then, was the sincere provision of the holy Roman Church, when, contrary to the earliest decrees, you condemned me in my absence?”

The pope said: “We have not condemned you; rather, we gladly and honourably receive and hear you.”

The abbot said: “When, without summoning or hearing me, you despoiled me of the church canonically entrusted to me and granted it to another [Col. 1548A] without examination, you treated me as though I had been condemned.”

The lord pope said: “If anything has hitherto been done wrongly concerning you through ignorance, we wholly reject it—and you too must reject it. Spare us also; and henceforth, as we ascertain the truth, we shall gladly render you the justice of truth.”

The abbot said: “Thanks be to God and to you for benefits granted and yet to be granted. Yet I do not wish you to be ignorant of this: when I came from Flanders to Rome, whatever grievous or impossible hardships I endured were brought upon me by the majesty of your eminence. In all the land of the French there was no power or lordship that could compel me to come to Rome; but the authority of your apostolic office, to which every person ought to be subject, drew me here.”

The pope, astonished and [Col. 1548B] almost indignant, raised his right hand and made the sign of the cross upon himself, saying: “Brother, for God’s sake, what are you saying?”

The chancellor, seated on the same bench, said: “Lord abbot, take care that you speak cautiously.”

The abbot said: “Lord father, when your letters—not yours because false, but yours because authenticated with your seal—were brought to me, I was filled with exceeding zeal for the injury done to the holy Roman Church and to your name, under which those letters had been signed; for they were wholly full of deceit, lies, and fraud. And I was the more scandalized and troubled because the letters lacked all truth and nevertheless bore the bull of the Apostolic Lord. Yet although I admit this, I attribute absolutely no fraud to Roman integrity; rather, I grievously endure it as an outrage that any person should have been so shameless [Col. 1548C] as not to shrink from defiling your ears with such open lies, deceiving you and hastening to make me a party to them.”

To this the lord pope said: “Read us the letters themselves, that we may know whether you were troubled with good reason.”

Then the abbot read:

> Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Hariulf, abbot of Aldenburgh: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> It is not praiseworthy that you have raised altar against altar and, dissenting from a faithful servant, have endeavoured not to increase the talent entrusted to you but to bury it in the earth. Therefore, since you were formerly a monk of Saint-Médard at Soissons and, withdrawing from your profession, have by your cunning turned into an abbey for yourself the cell entrusted to you as a priory; since you have despoiled the monastery of Saint-Médard of your obedience and of its ecclesiastical [Col. 1548D] possession: we command you, by apostolic authority, to lay aside the staff, restore yourself without delay to the abbot of Saint-Médard as his monk and one rightfully obedient to him, and restore to the chapter of the brothers of Saint-Médard the church which you have taken away.

“Behold the letter—indeed, behold grave lies, for it is clearer than daylight that this never was so. I was never a monk of Saint-Médard; I never received a cell or priory from the chapter or abbots of Saint-Médard; I never held or possessed from the monastery of Saint-Médard even a quarter of a penny. I loved and revered the greeting and blessing which sounded in the first line of the letter, and prized them above gold and topaz, because through them my soul rejoiced exceedingly. But how could I endure [Col. 1549A] so immense a reproach and so unbearable an injury—that I should see or know that the sacred ears of the supreme pontiff had been so infected by the hissing of falsehood that letters were sent from the summit of the Roman see to the farthest bounds of the land of Flanders? Letters, I say, empty of truth, full of falsehood, and everywhere resounding with disgrace to their sender.”

Then the lord pope said: “Come now, brother: if you deny having been a monk of Saint-Médard for so long a time, you must say from what monastery we are to believe that you were chosen to be abbot.”

The abbot said: “From a monastery very well known to you and long attached in every devotion to the holy Roman Church through close familiarity: namely Saint-Riquier in Ponthieu. There, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth indiction, it happened that you came with the lord Peter [Col. 1549B] the priest of Leo, and stayed in that place for thirteen days. There both you and he, with your attendants, were generously supplied; and there Abbot Anscerus invited me into your service, when I had already spent seventeen years in the care of an abbey.
