“From that monastery, under Pope Paschal II, I was requested through Baldwin, bishop of Tournai, and also through Lambert, his archdeacon; I was released by Abbot A. and granted to the holy church of Tournai. After the election of the brethren had first taken place, I canonically entered upon the order of the abbacy. Before me, moreover, two abbots had presided in the same place, Arnulf and Gervin; in their appointments the church of Saint-Médard gave neither counsel nor aid, since nothing there belonged to it.”

Then the pope added: “And who was the founder or builder of that place of yours?”

The abbot answered: “Lord, [Col. 1549C] as regards the cultivation of religious life, a servant of God named Arnulf founded that place.”

The pope said: “And who was this Arnulf?”

The abbot said: “He was bishop of Soissons.”

The pope said: “What sort of man was he before becoming bishop?”

The abbot said: “He had been a monk of Saint-Médard.”

The pope said: “Since you say that he was a monk of Saint-Médard and the founder of your place, it follows that you must acknowledge Saint-Médard as the possessor of your place.”

The abbot answered: “Not at all, my lord, for the course of events runs otherwise. We beg that you may be pleased to hear us and permit us to relate the continuation of the matter.”

The pope said: “We willingly [Col. 1549D] grant you leave to pursue the truth, so that we too may learn the truth from your account.”

The abbot answered: “The man of God, Saint Arnulf, noble by birth and nobler in character, after leaving secular military service became a monk at Saint-Médard. Full of holiness and virtue, he passed from the cloistered life to the arduous life of a recluse; thence he was made abbot, and promptly restored the entire place with abundant resources and laws. But when summoned—or rather commanded—by King Philip to go out with armed troops on an expedition against the king’s enemies, he preferred to withdraw into a recluse’s cell.

“In the following period, Gervase, the king’s steward, set up his own carnal brother as bishop in the church of Soissons, without election by clergy or people and without the counsel [Col. 1550A] of the Roman or Rheims church. The uncanonical character of his entry and the excessive indecency of his life soon became known to Pope Gregory VII, who did not delay to depose Ursio and to substitute as bishop of the aforesaid church the man of God Arnulf, then a recluse.”

The pope said: “Behold, you have shown that this Arnulf was a holy bishop; but you have not shown how he came to found your place.”

The abbot said: “The demonstration is ready, if the hearing is at hand.”

The pontiff said: “Proceed.”

Then the abbot said: “Count Robert, betrayed by his own men and embittered by the resentment of their treachery, turned the charge of his own death against certain noble clerics. He expelled them from Flanders and, stripping them of offices and honours, compelled them to flee to the holy Roman Church. [Col. 1550B] Taking compassion on their affliction, the lord pope sent the man of God Arnulf, bishop, to Count Robert to reconcile those clerics.

“Once they had been fittingly reconciled, it entered the mind of the count and certain leading men—namely Everard of Tournai, his brother Conan, and Baldwin of Ghent—to establish for that man of God a suitable dwelling near the church of Saint Peter the Apostle at Aldenburgh. But the man of God, upright and simple, wholly refused that gift from the count’s hand. Therefore Radbod, the bishop of Tournai at that time, was summoned by the count; he entered into consultation with his clergy and decided, after deliberation, that he would not give a church belonging to his jurisdiction to anyone save on this condition: that an abbey [Col. 1550C] of monks should immediately begin to be established in that place. An abbey, certainly—not a cell. For already then he took precautions lest any claim should be raised because Saint Arnulf had formerly been a monk of Saint-Médard.”

Having said this, the abbot was silent for a little while; then, resuming, he said to the lord pope: “Behold, most reverend father, our place was founded on such a principle. It does not belong to Saint-Médard, nor has it ever up to the present been claimed by the abbots of Saint-Médard. For this abbot of Soissons had no confidence whatsoever in justice, but, instigated by two treacherous clerics of ours, rashly presumed upon this. They said to him: ‘Why do you delay? Why are you afraid? This abbot is half-dead and will not oppose you. Cry out, and you shall receive everything. There are no forces, no resources with which resistance can be made to you. Act courageously, and you will see their hearts shaken by strong fear.’

“Inflamed by such incitements, the lord abbot of Saint-Médard, hoping that our poverty of resources and strength would ensure his victory, clothed himself in the arms of falsehood. He did not fear to deceive the supreme pontiff, provided that he might thereby gain a thing not owed to him and earn for himself the reputation of having done what no one had done before. That you may see this more closely, I beg that the charter of the bishop of Tournai, decreed at the beginning, together with that of Arnulf himself, be ordered read aloud before us.”

The records of the two bishops, Radbod and Arnulf, were read. When they had been recited and carefully considered, the abbot said to the pope: “Behold, lord, your eyes see and your ears [Col. 1551A] hear; and the lord cardinals also plainly perceive that the document now read assigns absolutely nothing to Saint-Médard or its abbots.”

The pope said: “Truly, nothing.”

The bishops then present, together with Chancellor Aymeric, said: “These documents very strongly forbid the abbot of Saint-Médard ever again to speak against him.”

Then the abbot, greatly rejoicing, bowed in reverence to the pope and the assembly, and afterward said: “Lords, it is written of you after the apostles: ‘Their dominion has been greatly strengthened.’ Therefore those letters so terrified me that my soul could find rest by no means unless I, a very insignificant man, came to you in person and set before you the proofs of falsehood and the tenor of truth. In all the world I knew no person [Col. 1551B] before whom I could make my case clear except the Roman pontiff, Christ’s vicar, Peter’s successor, and patron of all churches. For if, considering my weakness, I had not come to the present court, the claimant to our place might perhaps have represented me as contemptuous and might have contrived to lay upon me the bond of excommunication.”

Then the lord pope said: “Behold: though you have laboured beyond your strength, though you have expended your goods against your inclination, you did very well to seek the Roman Church. Therefore you shall have our favour and shall find your cause prosperously resolved. Without hesitation, but proceeding learnedly, you have reasonably set before us the truth of events; and in your words you have shown no ambiguity. Henceforth rest in complete security, and we will [Col. 1551C] that no one shall afterward compel you to come to Rome.”

The abbot said: “Honoured father, since your magnificence is so great toward me, I ask that you confirm to me and to my successors the liberty in which I was ordained, so that our place, now unjustly oppressed, may no longer be able to waver once fortified by your privilege.”

The pope said: “Two things stand against both you and us: the church entrusted to you is oppressed by the present lawsuit, and your bishop’s petition has not been received. We gladly assent to your liberty and that of your place; but it is necessary to settle your cause in such a way that you may enjoy our peace and that the pressing adversary may be unable to find a ground for just complaint. Therefore it is necessary that, after you withdraw, we enter upon counsel with our prayers and establish both your tranquillity and our defence. And because we feel great compassion for you, we shall dispatch this promptly.”

These matters having thus been fully discussed, they departed.

On the following day the lord pope ordered the abbot to be summoned and directed the chancellor to communicate to him the counsel which had been devised. The chancellor said [Col. 1551D] to the abbot: “Lord brother, our Apostolic Lord and the whole court are concerned for you and your cause. If you are willing to agree, it has been arranged that, with your status wholly preserved, three religious persons be chosen from the land of the French. The lord pope will entrust your affair to them on such terms that, if your harasser refuses to be silent, he may bring his complaint before those persons and they shall judge between you; and their judgment shall be [Col. 1552A] binding and beyond challenge. We devised this arrangement for your advantage and take great care that you should not need to return to Rome. For the lord pope and the whole court together have shown you extraordinary condescension; indeed, you please us all both in manner and in speech. Your sitting at our lord’s feet is a mark of honour, and the choice of the persons to be elected is placed in your discretion.”

Bowing his head, the abbot replied: “Giving thanks in all things, I would prefer and desire that the lord pope or his court should make this selection, provided only that it does not appoint known adversaries.”

The pope said: “And who are opposed to you?”

The abbot answered: “The lord bishop of Châlons and the lord bishop of Arras.”

The pope, smiling, said: “We have great confidence in these men and trust in their truthfulness and religious character, that they will never do you any injustice.”

The abbot said: “Although very good men, they are nevertheless suspect to me: the bishop of Châlons, because he was formerly abbot of Saint-Médard; the bishop of Arras, because he himself stirred up all this harassment. And, as Jerome says: ‘What need is there to abandon certainties and pursue uncertainties?’ France has other men of no lesser merit whose judgment I do not fear.”

The pope said: “If you reject these, whom do you accept?”

The abbot answered: “If permitted, I accept the lord bishop of Thérouanne, the lord bishop of Chartres, and either the bishop of Laon or of Soissons.”

The chancellor said: “The lord bishop of Chartres will not be given to you, because he is far from you and extremely occupied with Roman affairs; nor the bishop of Laon, since he has obtained that no cause except his own be imposed upon him; nor do we give the bishop of Soissons, lest we be thought to have sown litigation or discord between him and the abbot of Saint-Médard. Find worthy men—bishops or abbots—who will be judges without pretence and against whom no suspicion can be brought by either side, and let them be judges of this affair.”

More cheerfully, the abbot said: “I gladly accept the lord abbot of Clairvaux, the abbot of Saint-Remi of Rheims, and the abbot of [Col. 1552C] Cîteaux.”

The chancellor said: “The lord pope does not permit the abbot of Clairvaux to be troubled because he is ill; the abbot of Cîteaux because he is far away; and the abbot of Saint-Remi is too near, and he would incur resentment if he favoured you. If he aided the other party, it would be said that he had done so because of an abundance of gifts. But let it be: accept the lord bishop of Thérouanne, together with the bishop of Arras and the abbot of Prémontré.”

The abbot said: “I approve two; if I can, I refuse the third—that is, the bishop of Arras.”

The pope said: “What do you fear from him, when we know him to be a religious man and a man of sound counsel?”

The abbot said: “I fear him because he is obstinate in his zeal, and the instigation of this trouble of mine is imputed to him.”

The pope said: “Accept him, and we promise that he will inflict no harm upon you. When you return in peace to Flanders, since the route lies open, visit him and convey my greeting to him; add also: ‘Lord, the Roman pontiff directs you, in the confidence which he has in you, not in any way to harm me.’”

Then the abbot said to the pope: “Lord father and pastor of all, since [Col. 1553A] it thus pleases you, I accept him, though he will do me great harm, so that you may understand that I obey you as a devoted son.”

The pope said: “You speak rightly and act more rightly; therefore we all favour you.”

Accordingly, after this had been said and done, the pope ordered the chancellor to write letters to be given to the abbot. Turning his face toward the cardinals, the pope said to them in a clear voice: “On my faith, this man has a noble heart.”

The cardinals said: “Truly, he has conducted his cause steadfastly, honourably, and with courtly propriety.”

The abbot said: “Lord, if you perceive me to be a man of good heart, you ought all the more promptly to do me good.”

The pope said: “Truly, we shall do for you whatever we can consistently with Roman justice.”

On another day, when the abbot came before the presence [Col. 1553B] of the lord pope, the pope said to him with a smile: “Well now, brother: have you seen the letters drawn up for you?”

The abbot answered: “Lord, I have not.”

“Behold,” he said, “they are with the chancellor. If you wish, go, look at them, and tell us whether they please you.”

He went, saw, read, and reported, saying: “They would please me well if the lord bishop of Arras had been removed; for that fear which once seized me never leaves my breast.”

The pope said: “By our concession you have been granted the choice of two; it is not fitting that we should be given less than the choice of one.”

The abbot said: “The choice both of one and of all rests in your discretion.”

The pope said: “You speak well. But first, out of affection, we ask and admonish you: since you are going to die, do not lose your soul over this cause. If you know that anything in truth and justice ought to belong to Saint-Médard, confess it openly to us. If you wish to do so more secretly, we shall arrange a good settlement for you with that abbot, and shall not on any account permit your grey hair to be treated dishonourably.”

Then the abbot rose and stood, saying: “Lord father and shepherd of the whole world, hear me, I beseech you, and attend to me. By that solidity of true faith upon which Peter was founded when he said, ‘You are the Christ, Son of the living God,’ I have never known or acknowledged in this matter any right of the church of Saint-Médard. Since I hold it most certain that blessed Medard is a precious confessor of the Lord, why should I diminish or deny his possessions, knowing that condemnation would thereby come upon me? Far be this from me; far be it from every Christian to suppose that I could be occupied by such madness.”

The chancellor said to the pope: “Truly, lord, though he had not prepared beforehand, he has answered you and your entire court most honourably. Therefore we judge that his cause ought to be held true and just, since he has expounded the grounds of his case before you and in your presence not obscurely but clearly. He has stumbled into no entanglement of words; all his speeches have run along a straight path.”

The pope said: “Let him be blessed by God and by us.”

The abbot said to the lord pope: “As I am about to depart, I ask that you deign to hear the confession of my sins, so that, having come as a sinner, I may depart cleansed through your absolution.”

The chancellor said: “On my faith, he asks for a just thing.”

The pope added: “We willingly do it.”

The abbot said: “If you will do it, do not delay.”

The pope said: “Let it be done; [Col. 1554A] behold, follow me.”

Immediately he rose and withdrew to a very private place. The abbot followed him, made confession, received absolution and blessing, and wished to depart. The pope, pausing, said: “Brother, I wish and ask that you greet our most dear brothers for me and gladden them with news of our welfare.”

The abbot said: “Most willingly, if I knew who they are and if their places lay on my route.”

The pope said: “I do not ask you to leave your route; but if they should perhaps meet you, even within the year, remember my request.”

The abbot said: “If it please you, say who they are.”

And the pope said: “The lords of Langres, Auxerre, Chartres, Châlons, Arras, Thérouanne, Soissons, and Laon.”

The abbot said: “And why do you pass over the lord bishop of Noyon, when his noble life is more useful than that of the rest?”

The pope said: “I do not pass him over, but I send him affectionate greetings.”

The abbot said: “You care for bishops; you wholly disregard abbots.”

The pope said: “I desire in the Lord salvation for abbots and all religious men, especially those of Clairvaux and men like them.”

The abbot said: “The abbot of Saint-Remi is very worthy to be greeted by you, since he has improved that place as much as he was able.”

The pope said earnestly: “Greet him too, and respectfully, for he has acquitted himself excellently in the house of the Lord. Above all, I ask that you greet loftily and solicitously our venerable brother and friend Hugh, abbot of Prémontré, and in our name return him great thanks for the benefits which he has diligently bestowed upon us.”

The abbot said: “Lord, if it pleases you that he should be greeted so earnestly by me on your behalf, then it will be suitable for me to return by that place and deliver to him, in person, your paternal message.”

The pope said: “You act excellently, and you could render us nothing more pleasing.”

The abbot said: “Perhaps he will doubt that such things were enjoined on me by Your Highness unless I bring him some fitting sign spoken from your own mouth.”

The pope said: “For the book of Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, which he sent us, well written, beautifully bound, and decorated, we return many thanks. Among them we seek to be neither lord nor pontiff, but desire to be and remain one of the brethren. Yet if we can benefit them in anything through our office, we shall indeed be found diligent and eager [Col. 1554D] to do so. Moreover, we desire and ask that they keep watch before God in prayer for us and for the Roman Church. Peace be with you.”

1159.

Theodore, count of Flanders, returns from Jerusalem for the third time. His wife, Countess Sibyl, remained there and, with her husband’s consent, assumed the religious habit at Saint Lazarus, where she rested in a holy end.

1160.

Matthew, son of Theodore, count of Flanders, takes as his wife the daughter of Stephen, former king of England—the sister of the aforesaid deceased count of Boulogne—an abbess carried off from the monastery where she had been consecrated to God by the violence of Henry, king of the English; [Col. 1555A] and through her obtains the county of Boulogne.

[Note: [Col. 1555D]

In the year 1179, Brando narrates this coronation of the king differently.

In the year 1187, Aldenb. relates the death of Philip, count of Flanders, which Brando relates under the year 1191.

In the year 1193, Aldenb. reports the rebellion of Theodore of Beverne; Brando, however, places it under the year 1192.]

For this reason he was excommunicated by Samson, archbishop of Rheims, and all his suffragans; and he was grievously injured by his father, Count Theodore, and his brother Philip because of the castle of Lens, which he claimed from them by hereditary right.

1178.

Philip, count of Flanders, returned in the month of October and was favourably received by his Flemings. Among them, the townsmen of Bruges presented a monstrous fish, long before caught by fishermen and preserved in salt. It had, in the likeness of a bird, an enormous beak and, above its head, a cartilage very like a sword.

1179.

[Col. 1555B] A famous council was held at Rome by Pope Alexander. Philip, son of Louis, the pious and religious king of France, having married the daughter of Baldwin, count of Hainaut—niece, through his sister, of Philip, count of Flanders—was crowned king at Rheims on the feast of All Saints by his uncle William, archbishop of Rheims.

1180.

The bridge of Oudenaarde was made by Gerard’s skill,

And by the double assistance of Libertus, through a sure gift;

The year one thousand one hundred and eighty was a year of joy.

[Note: [Col. 1555D] These verses were written in a different hand.]

1181.

Saint Folquin, bishop of Thérouanne, illustrious in holiness, whose body rests in the church of Saint-Bertin, was translated for the third time by two bishops—namely [Col. 1555C] Lord Desiderius of Thérouanne and Peter of Thérouanne—from the old shrine in which he had lain for many years. He was placed in a new reliquary honourably made by Lord Simon, abbot of the aforesaid place, in the 326th year after the saint’s death, on 6 June. Pope Alexander died and was succeeded by Lucius. In this year great discord arose between Philip, king of France, and Philip, count of Flanders.

1185.

Philip, count of Flanders, having sent envoys into Spain, married Matilda, daughter of the king of Portugal. Philip, king of the Franks, at the instigation of Baldwin, count of Mons, again rose against Philip, count of Flanders. On this account the latter Philip, relying on the aid of Philip, archbishop of Cologne, entered the land of the count of Mons and devastated much of it by plundering and fire. When this became known, the king of France entered Vermandois with his army and, approaching the castle called Mons-desir, burned its suburbs. Then, through the mediation of Henry, king of England—or rather because of the harshness of the winter, which was already pressing—each returned home.

[Col. 1556A] Philip, king of the Franks, a young man of no contemptible worth, entered Vermandois with his army. Philip, count of Flanders, met him with his army as far as Amiens; but the count, yielding no less to royal majesty than to his own honour, and fearing that the slaughter of peoples would be laid to his charge before God and humankind, conceded part of Vermandois to the king, that the remainder might be confirmed to him for peaceful possession. Henry, king and son of Emperor Frederick, who was expected to become emperor, married the aunt of the king of Sicily.

1188.

Philip, king of the Franks, Henry, king of England, and Philip, count of Flanders, took the cross after the Lord’s Nativity, at the exhortation of Henry, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1556B] After this bishop had armed all Germany and Gaul for vengeance for the destruction of Jerusalem and had issued for observance in all churches the public prayers instituted by Pope Gregory, he at last came into Flanders, died at Marœuil in the territory of Arras, and was transferred to Clairvaux through the aid of Queen Margaret, widow of Philip, count of Flanders. On Mid-Lent Sunday, at Mainz, a general court having assembled, Emperor Frederick, with many bishops, all the princes of his realm, and an innumerable multitude of Germans, took the cross.

1189.

Philip, king of the Franks, taking with him Philip, [Col. 1556C] count of Flanders, and Richard of Aquitaine, burned and destroyed the castles and towns of the realm of Henry, king of England. The king of England, unable to withstand their assault and fleeing from place to place to avoid their approach, finally reached Le Mans. The aforesaid princes pursued him there; overwhelmed with grief, he fell ill and, having proceeded as far as Chinon, closed his last day. Carried thence to Fontevraud, he, once rich and exceedingly powerful, scarcely had the necessary expenses for burial and was buried there in the monastery of nuns.

1198.

Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, besieged the castle of Saint-Omer for five weeks and, since King Philip brought no assistance, captured and held it. The people of Aire had already surrendered themselves voluntarily into his hands.

1200.

Philip, king of the Franks, John, king of the English, Baldwin, count of Flanders, and many other princes of both kingdoms met for a mutual conference on the borders of France and Normandy. There [Col. 1557A] Louis, the boy, son of the king of the Franks, married the daughter of the king of Spain, who was the daughter of the sister of John, king of the English. There a firm peace was confirmed between the kings and princes.

[Note: [Col. 1557D]

In the year 1205, there are a few differences here from Brando. Compare the Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders, from which Brando drew [Col. 1558D].

In the years 1213 and 1214, Brando is fuller.]

1201.

After the death of Philip, count of Flanders, war continued for several years in the territory of Veurne between the Blavotins and the Ingrikins. Murders, burnings, and plunder took place, and there was no one to apply the hand of justice. On 16 November, a certain knight named Herbert of Wulveringhem, who was regarded as foremost among the Blavotins, gathered a small band of his men and burned the count’s castle in the town of Veurne itself. Because of the boldness of this deed, both he and the supporters of his faction were, by the ban of Count Baldwin and the queen of Portugal, [Col. 1557B] expelled from the land for some time, and their goods were confiscated.

1202.

Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, on his way to Jerusalem wintered at Venice. He first delivered to the Venetians the conquered city of Zara, their enemy; and thus, trusting in God’s help, he came with few men to attack that noble, most strongly fortified, most wealthy, and almost impregnable city of Constantinople. After it had been captured for the second time, he was elected and crowned emperor there.

1203.

Mary, wife of the aforesaid Count Baldwin and niece of the illustrious Philip, king of France, followed her husband. After enduring many great perils of the sea, [Col. 1557C] she finally arrived at Acre; there, wasted by a long illness, she gave up her spirit.

1205.

Baldwin, emperor of Constantinople, was captured in battle by John, surnamed Blak. The emperor, however, having been led into captivity, was never afterwards seen by our people. Some, indeed, tell tales that after many years and much hardship he returned, but was not recognized by his daughters; and because he did not know the time of his betrothal, either he himself or another man who falsely claimed to be him was hanged at Lille. In the following year his brother Henry, count of Alençon, succeeded him in the empire. In the counties [Col. 1557D] of Flanders and Hainaut, however, his eldest daughter Joan succeeded; King Philip of France held her in his custody and guardianship until he married her to Fernando, son of the king of Portugal. Thus Flanders, as touching Joan’s share, and Hainaut were governed by the king of France for six years, until Fernando’s arrival. Matilda, queen of Portugal and widow of Philip, the former count, held by her testamentary right part of Flanders from his death onward: namely Bergues, Cassel, Broekburg [Col. 1558A] with their adjoining territories, as well as Lille, Douai, and many other towns lying here and there.

1213.

Philip, king of the Franks, having assembled an army and a great fleet, was thought by many to be about to cross to England. But, changing his plan as it seemed, he led all his army into Flanders and, having received hostages from the principal towns—namely Ypres, Ghent, and Bruges—returned to France. After his departure, Fernando, count of Flanders, recovered his towns. Afterwards Lord Louis, eldest son of the king of France, burned and devastated for the most part the town on the sea called Newport and certain others, namely Bailleul and Steenvoorde; innumerable people of both sexes were captured there. [Col. 1558B] Then, after a few days had passed, the count of Flanders captured the city of Tournai and partly demolished its walls. The town of Lille surrendered to him, but shortly afterward was again burned by the lord king of France.

1214.

John, king of England, came into Poitou with a great army. When the Poitevins made an alliance with him and the castles were surrendered, the lord king of France, greatly angered, sent there his eldest son Louis and the marshal with many knights to resist him. The lord king of France recalled his paid troops from the castles of Flanders. Those who had been staying at Cassel withdrew after setting the castle on fire.

[Col. 1558C] In the Lord’s year twelve hundred and fourteen,  
Philip, king of the French, at the bridge of Bouvines  
Captured Ferdinand, count of Flanders, and Otto’s host  
Collapsed, on the feast of Pantaleon.  
[Note: [Col. 1557D] These verses were written in another hand.]

1215.

After this, a few days having intervened, Ferdinand, count of Flanders, entered with a great army the territory of Arnold, count of Guînes. At Guînes the countess was captured with some of her people and taken into Flanders; the castles of Guînes, Colewide, and Sangatte were for the most part destroyed. Bonham also, the castle of that same countess, was surrendered after the tenth day of siege to Hugh of Boves, a knight who was assisting the count of Flanders on behalf of the king of England; and he himself utterly razed that castle. Then, fearing the arrival of the lord king of France, the Flemings abandoned the castle of Aire, which they had besieged for some time.

Soon afterwards, on hearing of the arrival of Emperor Otto, they met the lord Philip, king of the Franks, in Flanders with a great army, near the bridge of Bouvines, not far from the castle called Lille; and there, rashly engaging him in battle, they were defeated. But by the justice of the Lord, glorious victory was granted to the most unconquered king of France, lord Philip. Otto, who was called emperor, having been put to flight, the strongest and bravest in arms on the Flemish side were captured: namely Ferdinand, count of Flanders; the count of Salisbury, William Longsword; and Renaud, count of Boulogne, with many others among the chief men of Flanders. Few, however, were killed, because they escaped by flight. [Col. 1559A]

In the year twelve hundred joined with three fives,  
The land of Flanders lay submerged beneath the sea.  
[Note: [Col. 1559D] Written in another hand. The same event is reported under the years 1225 and 1227.]

1219.

Matilda, queen of Portugal, formerly the wife of Philip, count of Flanders, dies and is buried in the monastery of Dunes; later, however, she is transferred to Clairvaux and placed beside her husband.

1223.

[Col. 1559B]

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord 1223, the glorious translation of Saint Lewinna, virgin and martyr, was performed by Lord Adam, bishop of Thérouanne, upon the hill called Groneberch. Her glorious relics were placed in a shrine suitably fashioned of gold and silver; many venerable and religious persons attended this glorious translation.

1225.

In twelve hundred, the fifth year and twice ten besides,  
Lille grieved in the year when Bertrand was hanged.

1227.

The town of Bruges is miserably consumed by fire.

1228.

[Col. 1559C] Ferdinand, count of Flanders, who had been held at Paris as the captive of the king of France for twelve years and six months, was released for a great ransom around the Epiphany of the Lord.

1233.

Add thirty-three years of Jesus to twelve hundred:  
Then Flanders defeats five thousand men  
Of the Stedinger people; Brabant despoils them all,  
Whose lands enraged Holland had laid waste.  
[Note: [Col. 1559D] All these things were written in another hand. The same is to be said of the entries under [Col. 1560D] the years 1246 and 1253.]

1237.

The glorious translation of Blessed Bertin, abbot, was carried out by Lord Peter, bishop of Thérouanne, in the time of Lord James, then abbot of the same church. Many ecclesiastical and secular persons attended this translation: namely, the bishop of Arras, [Col. 1559D] Abbot William of Saint-Winoc, Abbot John of Alchiac, the count of Guînes, and many others.

1246.

In the twelve-hundredth year plus forty-six,  
At Paris, on Friday after the feast of Nabor,  
The king and the legate, dividing the counties,  
Gave Flanders to one and Hainaut to the other.

1253.

In twelve hundred and fifty-three,  
The convent was scattered because of debts.

The year was twelve hundred and fifty-three when, subdued,  
[Col. 1560A] Flanders, taken by treachery, came under the Hollanders.

In twelve hundred and fifty-three,  
Flanders attacked the Zeelanders by arms and fleet,

With an innumerable multitude, stout men, and strong soldiers,  
Whom fortune in part gave to cruel death—  
Not the force of arms, nor the enemy’s right hand, but their own  
Division, the tossing of the sea, and the wrath of the gods.  
[Note: [Col. 1560D] All these verses were written in another hand. The same is to be said of the verses recorded under the following years.]

1259.

In twelve hundred and fifty-nine,  
On the octave jointly of Peter and Paul, the lords  
First entered the dormitory of the convent.

1263.

In twelve hundred and sixty-three, England captured the king  
With the aid of Simon de Montfort;  
By his own courage he freed himself, Simon having been slain.  
[Col. 1560B] Then a mixed multitude assembled together at Bruges.

A little earlier, a comet-star had been seen.

1274.

In twelve hundred and seventy-four,  
Gregory the tenth summons every rank  
At Lyons, convening such a general council.  
He wishes to mark the people with the cross and summon the Greeks,  
And to reform the clergy, abolish the sack-clad friars,  
Levy a tithe for six years, and dishonour bigamists.

1276.

In twelve hundred and seventy-six,  
Flanders ravages the territory around Liège.

In twelve hundred and seventy-six,  
There was an earthquake on the night of the vigil of Matthew.

In twelve hundred and seventy-six,  
[Col. 1560C] Polrus is called Boomburch, Hem is so called;  
Thereafter another *polrus* is joined after twice ten.  
[The meaning of *polrus* is uncertain.]

Letter of Peter, king of Aragon, to Lord Charles, king of Sicily, in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1282.

1282.

To the magnificent prince Lord Charles, illustrious king of Jerusalem: Peter, by God’s grace king of Aragon and Sicily.

When we had come to the regions of Barbary to attack the Saracens, we sent our envoys to the Roman Church with certain petitions of ours, none of which we were able to obtain. Afterwards we came into Sicily, hearing the people complain that you had oppressed them and were attacking them as enemies. Therefore they sought our counsel, [Col. 1560D] and, because we neither wish nor can fail them, on account of our wife and children, to whom that kingdom is known to belong by hereditary right, we ask you to desist from injuries and oppressions of this kind. And give credence to the bearers of this letter in those matters which they shall tell you on our behalf.

Reply of Lord Charles, king of Sicily, to Peter, king of Aragon, in the year 1282.

1283.

To Peter, king of Aragon and Sicily in name alone, as he styles himself: Charles, by God’s grace king of Jerusalem and Sicily, duke of Apulia, prince of Capua, [Col. 1561A] count of Anjou, Provence, Forcalquier, and Piedmont, senator of the holy city.

If you wish to preserve the name you have acquired at great cost, you ought to come forth from the cave which you now inhabit. If your youth takes courage to test how much valour is customarily found in our knights, they will tell you that they await you with the utmost eagerness. Yet, lest any delay in your strength—God forbid—prevent the trial, I shall shortly, with the Lord’s authority, visit the place which you now inhabit.

Letter of Pope Martin IV to Lord Charles, king of Sicily, in the year of the Lord 1283.

To the illustrious king of Sicily. For mortals whom the zeal of sincere love moves, it is usually more grievous to be troubled by the disorder of those dear to them, more bitter to rebuke their errors, and more prolonged to reprove them. We therefore follow this practice toward you, dearest son, as the nature of the deed requires—especially now, when, though through insufficient merits, we bear the place of Him who rebukes and chastens those whom He loves, and not unworthily observe that duty.

For what report is this which we have heard—that, without our knowledge and, at least in this respect, against the judgment of law, you have so rashly assented to something that must be censured with reluctant mind? Namely, that you have promised to enter into a private combat with P., king of Aragon: you with one hundred knights and he likewise to meet opposite you there and fight together; and that, in a sudden impulse of spirit, you have confirmed this beforehand by oath, by common agreement, with the penalty alike imposed upon the defeated party. It was further added that whichever of you [Col. 1561B] should happen to be defeated in that combat, if he escaped from it alive, should thereafter call himself neither king of Sicily nor lord of any land, but should go alone for the whole period of his life; and the plain of Bordeaux was assigned as the place and the Kalends of June as the date for this, as has been said.

Do you not know that you hold the kingdom of Sicily from the Roman Church? And that you are bound to us and to that Church in many respects concerning it, under the bond of a bodily oath repeatedly taken? From this you ought sufficiently to have perceived that the business of that kingdom, both against the said king of Aragon and against any others attacking that Church and you within it, belongs no less to that Church than to you.

Whence, then, such presumption? What does this readiness mean for you? What reason persuades you to set a limit upon yourself, and likewise upon the Church’s own power, in defending the kingdom? Indeed, the Son of the living God, of immeasurable power, who promised the same Church perpetual supporting power when He said to His disciples—whom He made, that is, the chief foundations of that Church—“Behold, I am with you unto the end of the world,” has given no basis for this. Certainly, dearest son, this is not a saying to call forth mercy, but one to stir up anger and kindle wrath.

Was this, then, done without counsel? Are these acts of your customary prudence? Do not think it should be imputed to prudence, but rather to imprudence, that you have made equal to yourself, by the judgment of a warlike and accursed lot, the aforesaid king of Aragon, wholly unequal to you in strength—not to speak of the rest—who, like a man in despair, is judged to act thus because, despairing with reason that he can withstand the power of God’s justice, of that Church, of you, and of your people, [Col. 1561C] he has undertaken this course.

How could the provocation of so crafty and deceitful an enemy, who fraudulently entered your land, so inflame you that you proceeded to such disorder and leapt into such error, as though, without our consent, you could at your own will free yourself from those obligations to which you are so solemnly bound to that Church, to us, and to our successors for that kingdom, and by which you are so strictly held—or else, should the law deny it, lose the authority entrusted to you therein by thus renouncing it?

Do you not perceive into what acts, as indiscreet as they are rash and ruinous, the wicked craft and crafty malice of the said king of Aragon have drawn you? You have placed the kingdom at hazard with one who has no right in it, upon an issue which, so far as lay in you, was equal for both; and, with your consent, in a matter belonging to you, there is to be equal judgment, equal outcome, and equal result for you and him. Thus he, whose grave and enormous offences committed against that same Church and against your majesty bind him to more serious guilt, might redeem weightier penalties by the bargain of a brief and equal combat, although he has suffered injuries no more equal than the judgment he is to undergo for having inflicted such and so great injuries. Thus you, whose strength the world does not doubt to be greater, would willingly restrict your own strength and make his equal to it in an outburst of a certain unpraiseworthy boldness; and the prospect of this future conflict would withdraw you from recovering Sicily—which he occupied not by the strength of his own arm, but through the rebellion of the Sicilian people; or rather, which, as a secret plotter and usurper, he received from the hands of those rebels who had already seized and held it. And both he and others, who perhaps do not sleep in pursuing you, might more freely prosecute their plots while you are absent, chiefly because of this conflict.

O dearest son, if there were an opportunity of being present before you, if an hour were granted for mutual conversation, how more fully would speech than writing set forth the rash acts committed in the foregoing matters; how more bitterly would it rebuke, how more deeply would it reprove, how more plainly would living speech than written show the just grounds of rebuke. [Col. 1562D] But since paternal rebuke alone does not suffice in these matters unless correction follows, we turn to the remedy of swift correction and long for it with full desire.

Therefore, declaring your promise wholly unlawful and the oath sworn upon it rash, and decreeing that they lack force and that you are not bound to observe them, while nevertheless absolving you from them, we earnestly admonish, ask, and exhort you, for the remission of sins, that the rash acts undertaken in fact may be undone. We likewise strictly command you, under the obligation of the oath, vassalage, and homage rendered to us and to that Church, to refrain altogether and in every way desist from pursuing the aforesaid arrangements and oaths. [Col. 1563A]

[Note: [Col. 1563D]

In the year 1303 Aldenburg erroneously relates in that year the battle of Mons-en-Pévèle; Brando relates it more correctly in the following year.

[Col. 1564D] In the year 1326 Aldenburg appears to have abridged Brando.]

For we strictly prohibit each and every one of Christ’s faithful from approaching you in any manner in order to pursue those matters, and from assisting you in their pursuit by counsel, aid, favour, or any other means. Moreover, upon all who presume otherwise in any way, whatever their pre-eminence, condition, or rank—even if they shine with the honour of royal, imperial, or any other secular dignity—we hereby pronounce a sentence of excommunication, notwithstanding any indulgence granted to them or to any of them by the Apostolic See under whatever form or expression of words, even if full and express, or word-for-word, mention of it ought to be made in our letters. And unless you precisely obey our aforesaid admonitions and commands, [Col. 1563B] we decree that you yourself incur the same sentence automatically. No privilege of that See shall aid you in this matter; all such privileges, of whatever tenor or formulation, we entirely annul for this purpose.

1326.

In this year the peace which had been proclaimed between the count and the communes began to be disturbed. For while, according to the terms of the peace, arbitrators were investigating the wrongs committed by each side and were justly making reparation in each case, the common people pursued the aforesaid arbitrators in an armed crowd and, with insulting words, sought to gain their purpose, especially concerning the punishment of a certain homicide committed near the sea by nobles upon their enemies. The common people represented this as an injury done to the community and wished it to be redressed according to their will. Therefore, on the appointed day at the monastery of Dunes, when they were to assemble there peacefully and without arms, the common people immediately came in so great a multitude with their captains Nicholas Zannekin and Siger John’s-son, and the arbitrators appointed for reconciliation, though armed, did not dare to appear. For it seemed to them that the people were beginning once again to rage madly, and so it proved.

Count Louis was afterwards captured by the common people at Courtrai. After this, the army of Bruges came to Courtrai, and the count was immediately handed over to them as a captive with certain knights. They put the count on a small horse and had him conducted to Bruges, where [Col. 1563D] he was held firmly and under the strictest confinement. At last, after a great slaughter of the common people by those of Ghent, who supported the count, the men of Bruges, at the people’s demand, released and set free the count. The count, having promised impunity to the common people and forgiven what had been done against him, came alone from captivity to Ghent, and thence went to the king of France at Paris.

[Col. 1564A] 79 Genealogy of Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor

Albert, count of Namur, had three full sisters: Ludgarda, Goda, and Ermengarda. Albert begot Godfrey, father of Godfrey of Namur. Ludgard bore Emmo and his brother Otto. Emmo begot Arnulf, count of Loo, and Sophia, duchess of Hungary. This Sophia bore the king of Hungary and the duchess of Huy. Otto, Emmo’s brother, begot Giselbert of Duzas. Goda, sister of Count Albert, bore Meinsinda, mother of the most holy Arnulf, bishop of the city of Soissons in France.

Epitaph of Abbot Hariulf

Born in Ponthieu, Hariulf, inclined to studies,  
Entered as a boy the cloisters of blessed Richarius.  
[Col. 1564B] There, trained as befits one who would know a master,  
He became the third abbot of Aldenburg.  
According to his strength he enlarged the charge entrusted to him,  
Ever thirsting, Peter, that your wealth might increase.  
Offering his brethren the example of one who suffers with them,  
He kept very much silence where it was fitting to speak.  
He wrote the life of holy Bishop Arnulf,  
Bringing such honour to the citizens of Aldenburg.  
By his effort, too, the remains of that same bishop  
Were raised from the earth, with God’s help.  
May a crown be duly granted him by the Lord for these things,  
God being gracious to this Hariulf.

80 Life of Abbot Hariulf  
[Note: [Col. 1563D] Taken from the *Amphitheatre of Illustrious Men of Bruges*, a manuscript by P. J. Van Male, preserved in the museum of the most noble Lord Van Huerne de Puyenbeke at Bruges. Foppens reports many further curious details concerning Hariulf in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, vol. I, p. 432.]

Hariulf, abbot of the Benedictine monastery of Aldenburg, wrote and dedicated to William, bishop of Canterbury in [Col. 1564C] England, the life of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, as it is still read among the *Lives of the Saints* collected by Surius, volume V, under 15 August. There are omitted, however, the three prefaces found in the manuscript preserved among the Cistercians near Noyon, the first beginning: “To Lord Lambert, by God’s grace bishop of Tournai,” etc. He also wrote the life of Blessed Gervin, second abbot of the monastery of Aldenburg, whom he himself succeeded in the prelacy; from this it may readily be inferred that this Hariulf flourished in the twelfth century. According to Molanus, the aforesaid lives, together with the missal and pontifical of Saint Arnulf, were long preserved in the said abbey; but I do not know whether they still survive, [Col. 1564D] for, when that ancient monastery was destroyed in 1578 by the fury of heretics and traitors, the religious were scattered to various places. They returned afterwards, however, and now, at the beginning of the eighteenth century, that monastery, which for some time had almost perished, is beginning in some measure to flourish again through the care and diligence of its present prelate.

Life of Gaspar de Bovincourt  
[Note: [Col. 1564D] From the same manuscript in the museum of the most noble Lord Van Huerne de Puyenbeke.]

Gaspar de Bovincourt, an Artois nobleman, made religious vows in his youth [Col. 1565A] at the Abbey of Anchin. Subsequently, endowed with exceptional character and prudence, he was found worthy to be chosen abbot of the most ancient monastery of Saint Peter at Aldenburg, three miles from the city of Bruges. He was in every respect a grave and distinguished man, handsome in appearance, praiseworthy in morals, and welcome to the leading men of our country; indeed, he was so worthy that he was admitted to the assembly of the Estates of Flanders. In their name, in the fourth year of his prelacy—that is, in 1372—he was sent to Spain to the most powerful King Philip II, in order to set forth the condition then prevailing. With great skill and prudence he carried out his commission and brought back to the Estates a successful outcome to his mission.

He wrote various works, among which the authors especially list [Col. 1565B] an *Itinerary to Jerusalem and Mount Sinai*, in which he carefully described all the memorable things that befell him during that long journey; a *Treatise on Arithmetic*; *Spiritual Exhortations to the Brethren*; and finally, in French verse, [Col. 1566A] one book on divine providence and another on self-knowledge. These had indeed been prepared for the press and had already been approved by our most learned James Pamelius, then canon of Saint Donatian and censor of books; but the death of that great man prevented their publication. For while suffering from consumption, he sought a milder climate and moved to the village of Craneburg near Bruges; there he met the end of his life on 11 February 1577, after having governed the abbey for seven years, ten months, and seven days. His body was conveyed to the monastery and buried there in the choir, beside the high altar, on the left side.

Possevino, moreover, makes honourable mention of this man in his *Apparatus*, and not undeservedly; for, besides nobility of birth, the title of knight of Jerusalem, abbatial dignity, knowledge of many languages, and skill in the greatest affairs, he was commended by unfeigned piety, modest character, and learning far from ordinary. [Col. 1566B]

[Col. 1565]

## DIPLOMATIC CODEX

### I. 82–83. Charter of Saint Arnulf, Bishop of Soissons, concerning the donation of the tithes of the town of Aldenburg to Aldenburg Abbey. 1087.

[Col. 1565C]

In the name of God Most High, who in eternal foreknowledge disposes all things before the ages and accomplishes all things in their time. I, a sinner—Arnulf by name, not by merit, bishop by the consent and will of the venerable prelate Radbod, bishop of Tournai and Noyon—having undertaken to restore the buildings of a future abbey in the place of Aldenburg, that is, in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle and of all the Apostles, wish it to be known what and how great support Christ the Lord has supplied to that work through faithful Christians, and what gifts have been conferred upon that place during my lifetime and through my care.

For, after the place had been delivered to me by the hand of the aforesaid bishop, by canonical grant, in full liberty, Lord Conon granted a third part of the tithe of all the grain of the whole parish of Aldenburg, to be held and possessed forever, with the consent of the illustrious Count Robert, son of Baldwin. [Col. 1565D] Likewise, Godescalc the dean promised that he would give all that he possessed. Stirred by his example, five noble men from the village of Erneghem—Bertulf and his wife Ingelburch, with their sons and daughters; Cremold and Malger, sons of Almar; Ledgina, widow of Ermenar, with her sons Ingram, Fredebold, and Lambert; indeed their entire kindred—gave two parts of the tithe of all the grain, flax, and hemp from all their freehold lands, wherever situated, whether cultivated or to be cultivated. They offered this upon the altar of Saint Peter [Col. 1566B] the Apostle at Aldenborgh, to be possessed with perpetual security, asking and demanding that we condemn under the bond of anathema all their descendants or strangers whatsoever who might endeavour to cause hindrance or loss in the annual rendering of that tithe. This was done on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord 1084.

A few days later, the noble and wealthier men of the neighbourhood of Aldenburg assembled together and voluntarily gave to Saint Peter the Apostle, as alms for the support of the monks, portions of their inheritances: Walter, three measures; Trudbald, three measures; Walter, son of this Trudbald, one measure; Sigerd, three measures; Robalis, two measures; Fluitard, son of Goman, two measures; Bertelinus and his mother, two measures; Hermatus, two; Landrada, widow of Folcard, with her sons, two; Themard Rufus, one; [Col. 1566D] Reifrid, son of Ramger Canno, two; Evergerd, widow of Offrid, one and a half; Remilinus Calvus, two; Remelinus Longus, one; Bertof, son of Erembold, one; Seger, son of Olfrid, and his brothers, three measures; Anna, widow of Fredebold; Leccard and his mother, four measures; Remelinus and his brother, two; Oslif, three measures; Radlef, three measures and ten cows; Lebild and Ubuum and their sisters, twelve measures. At the place called Hem and Werf, and at Lissewege, twelve measures; Erenbold, son of Bono, fourteen measures; Hatewidis, sister of Bertolf, five measures; and from the territory of Bredene, Esuvedus and his wife Gilgorg, two measures called Wermbolbelc.

We have judged it proper to attest by the present charter these and several other gifts which the faithful, fearing the Lord, bestowed from love of God and for the honour of Saint Peter toward the foundation of a monastery of sacred life, [Col. 1567A] so that all posterity may know that our humility laboured for this end: that after my death an abbey might be regularly established in this place, whose abbot should canonically govern the brethren and, according to his strength, suitably seek the advantages of the place. Therefore, whoever shall endeavour to act against these provisions, by the authority of Almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul; and also of Pope Gregory VII, by whose counsel and command I do these things, let them be condemned to perpetual anathema and punished with the eternal penalty of Gehenna. Amen. So be it, so be it. Done at Aldenborch, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1087, indiction 10, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of Lord King Philip.

### II. Charter of Radbod, Bishop of Tournai, concerning the liberty of the Church of Saint Peter the Apostle. 1090.

[Col. 1567B]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I, Radbod, by God’s grace bishop of Noyon and Tournai, [wish] to all worshippers of holy religion the inheritance of perfect blessedness which God has promised to those who love Him.

Since the desire of a pious will and the purpose of praiseworthy devotion must always be assisted by priestly efforts, care must be taken that no presumption may disturb those things which any faithful person wishes to establish for the peace of religious conversion, nor violate them by injury to the increase of Holy Mother Church. Let the diligence of all, both future and present, know [Col. 1567C] therefore that my nephew Chuno and his wife Hazecca, knowing the dominion of laymen over a sanctuary to be unjust, have most devoutly entreated us to grant freedom to the church founded at Aldenburg in honour of Saint Peter the Apostle, which they had hitherto held from the count of Flanders, and to confirm under perpetual liberty the benefices granted for the use of the monks whom they wished to establish in that place for the service of Almighty God.

Having considered their good intention, and taken counsel from our archdeacon W. and our clerics, we granted this in such manner: that whomever the monks of that place shall canonically elect as abbot shall receive blessing and the care of souls from the bishop of Noyon or Tournai, and render him due subjection; and thus, freely under holy religion, shall endeavour to serve the Lord with the flock of monks entrusted to him. Therefore, lest any of our successors dare to violate this liberty which we have declared, we have strengthened this privilege by the authority of our office and sealed it with the impression of our seal in the presence of suitable witnesses. [Col. 1567D]

Sign of Lord Radbod, bishop. Sign of Walter, archdeacon. Sign of Henry, dean. Sign of Hermann, provost. Sign of Siger. Sign of Rudolph. Sign of Tanchmar. Sign of Bertulf. Sign of Godescalc. Signs of the laymen Conon, Everard, Adelard, Ricvard, Robert, Walter, Rodulf, Hiddon, Lidelm, Lambert, Louis, and Embald.

Done at Tournai [Col. 1568A] on the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, indiction 13, in the thirtieth year of King Philip I’s reign, and the twenty-second year of the lord bishop’s episcopate. I, Guido the chancellor, dictated, reread, and subscribed it below.

### III. Charter of Charles, Count of Flanders, concerning the donation of tithes and of all the grain of the whole parish of Aldenburg. 1119.

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Charles, by God’s grace count of the Flemings, to future and present alike, forever.

Because things done are erased by the forgetfulness of age unless they are committed to writing, we have decreed to enter in the present document, for the memory of successors, the revenues conferred during our rule upon Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and upon the church of Aldenburg. Let all defenders of truth, present and future, know therefore that Walter the Butler and his brother Conon have devoutly and lawfully granted to the brethren serving God there, for their perpetual use and for the remedy of their own sins and those of all their parents, a third part of the tithe of all the grain of the whole parish of Aldenburg, free from every exaction and from all disturbance or reclamation by themselves or their successors. [Col. 1568B]

Assuredly, confirming this donation with our hand as the highest authority, we have added whatever right in it belonged to us or to our successors. Since we wish them to be participants with us in so holy a donation, they have further lawfully granted to the aforesaid brethren, for the perpetual use of the brethren of that church, Saint Mary’s Church situated at Aldenburg, with all its appurtenances: namely another third part of the tithe, the whole small tithe of the entire parish, and every endowment of the church, that is, eight measures of land, together with any greater increase that may arise, or anything added by the gift of the faithful, under a hereditary and perpetual rent. [Col. 1568C]

This was upon the condition that the abbot of Saint Peter of Aldenburg and the brethren of the aforesaid church shall yearly pay to the brethren or their successors nine pounds of Flemish coinage, divided into three portions according to the aforesaid seasons—Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—while retaining nine shillings out of the nine pounds, with which the abbot and his brethren shall annually pay the synodal due. For this second donation also, that it may remain firm forever, we have added our hand, as we did to the first.

Furthermore, once this hereditary and perpetual rent has been paid yearly at the aforesaid times in the presence of two ecclesiastical persons as witnesses, there shall be no matter for which the aforesaid abbot or his brethren are bound to stand to justice in the court of the aforesaid brethren or their successors, nor shall an ecclesiastical person be subject to the judgment of secular persons for any cause. But that all these things may remain unshaken and forever valid, we have confirmed this present document containing the aforesaid donations by the authority of our seal and have caused the witnesses who were present to subscribe. [Col. 1568D]

Sign of Count Charles, [Col. 1569A] son of the king of the Danes. Sign of Walter the Butler and his brother Conon. Sign of Bertulf, provost of Bruges. Sign of William Malet. Sign of Robert, brother of William. Sign of Gorum. Sign of Desiderius Haket, castellan. Sign of Lambert Nappin. Sign of Tancmar of Straten. Sign of Theodoric of Diksmuide. Sign of Berennold of Straten.

Done at Bruges, in the house of the provost, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, indiction 12, in the twelfth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, son of Philip; in which year Lord Guido, archbishop of Vienne, was raised to the Roman pontificate.

### IV. Charter of Theodoric, Count of Flanders, confirming the donations of Conon and Walter. 1129.

[Col. 1569B]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Theodoric, by God’s grace count of the Flemings, make known to all sons of Holy Mother Church, future as well as present, that a certain noble and powerful man of ours, Conon by name, son of Adelard and brother of Walter, formerly the Butler, has appealed to our clemency, asking that we should confirm by recognition of our authority a certain gift long ago made both by Conon himself and by the aforesaid Walter, and command by our precept that it remain valid so as to obtain perpetual stability. We willingly assent to his requests.

For we desire to preserve, not enlarge, those things which have been bestowed upon churches by the gifts of our predecessors and other faithful persons. We now therefore establish by recital what gift the aforesaid Conon renewed in our presence and confirmed through us to the church of Saint Peter of Aldenburg: namely, a third part of the tithe of all the grain of the whole parish of Aldenburg. [Col. 1569C] Moreover, Conon lawfully granted, as he had previously done, for the perpetual use of the brethren of the said church, Saint Mary’s Church situated at Aldenburg with all its appurtenances: namely another third part of the tithe, the entire small tithe, every endowment of the church, that is, eight measures of land, and any greater increase that might accrue, or anything added by the gifts of the faithful, under a hereditary and perpetual rent.

This was upon the condition that the abbot of Saint Peter of Aldenburg, or the brethren of the church, should pay yearly to him and his successors nine pounds of Flemish coinage, divided into three portions according to the three seasons—Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—retaining, however, nine shillings out of the nine pounds, with which the abbot or his brethren should yearly pay the synodal due to the bishop. Moreover, after this hereditary and perpetual rent has been paid yearly at the aforesaid seasons in the presence of two ecclesiastical persons as witnesses, there shall be no matter for which the aforesaid abbot or his brethren must stand to justice in the court of the aforesaid Conon or his successors, nor shall an ecclesiastical [Col. 1570A] person be subject to the judgment of secular persons for any cause.

That this may remain valid forever, we have confirmed by the authority of our seal this document containing the grant and have caused the names of the witnesses who were present to be recorded below.

Sign of Theodoric, count of the Flemings. Sign of Conon. Sign of Arnulf, abbot of Aldenburg. Sign of Gillebert, abbot of Ename. Sign of Baldwin of Ghent. Sign of Walter of Tournai. Sign of Daniel of Termonde. Sign of Theodoric, castellan of Diksmuide. Sign of Thancmar of Straten. Sign of Christian of Gistel.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1129, indiction 7, council 1.

### V. 89 Charter of Simon, bishop of Tournai, concerning the donation of the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Aldenburg together with the entirety of the parish of Aldenburg. 1130.

[Col. 1570B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Simon, by the grace of God bishop of Tournai and Noyon, to all the faithful, present and future: grace and the blessing of everlasting salvation.

Having plainly learned that the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, situated in the town of Oudenburg, had never been supported by an abundance of resources, and that consequently the monks serving the Lord there were generally held in want, we, moved—as was fitting—with paternal compassion for them as our sons, having taken counsel with our archdeacon Robert and other worthy clerics, have given to the said monastery of Oudenburg, [Col. 1570C] and to Abbot Hariulph and the brethren entrusted to him, the church of Saint Mary situated in the same town, to be held with the entirety of the parish of Oudenburg under a personal benefice; on this condition, namely, that episcopal right shall remain intact as it existed previously, and that the person established there shall immovably pay the pontifical and synodal dues.

But to Cono, a nobleman, by whose benevolent consent and pious request we have transferred this same church to the aforesaid abbot and his monks, the person shall pay annually nine pounds in denarii to him and to his successors; from these nine pounds, however, he shall retain yearly nine shillings, from which, as has hitherto been done, he shall discharge the episcopal due. When the incumbent [Col. 1570D] departs, another is to be appointed by the will of the brethren and the abbot, and shall give only ten shillings to the bishop of Tournai. Once the customary dues established of old have been paid to the bishop and to Cono, whatever thereafter may remain of tithes, offerings, or lands belonging to the church’s endowment, we bestow upon, and by bestowing remit to, the maintenance of food and clothing for the monks of the monastery of Oudenburg, so that it may serve them by perpetual right and continually contribute to the relief of their need.

And in order that this our grant, for the honor of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, may obtain perpetual force, we have caused this written charter to be secured with our seal and strengthened by the testimony of devout clerics.

Sign of Lord Simon, bishop. Sign of Lord Robert, archdeacon of Tournai. Sign of Hugh, then present, archdeacon of Noyon. Sign of Lord Rainald, abbot of Noyon, regular canon. Sign of Novinus, canon of Tournai. Sign of Bernard, dean of Waas. Sign of Siger, canon of Noyon. Sign of Hugh, chancellor of Roeselare. Sign of Rainer, incumbent of Bredene. Sign of Balteron, incumbent of Gistel. Sign of Walter the Butler, who came to me at Bruges while I was grieving and lamenting over the murder of Count Charles in the Church of the Savior, and earnestly entreated me, with many prayers, to remit this church to the brethren of Saint Peter. Sign of Canon, brother and successor of the aforesaid Walter, who again humbly approached me at Bruges in my lodging, which was the house of Folpert Kinfaber, and asked that I remit the aforesaid church, with its personal benefice, to the abbot of Saint [Col. 1571B] Peter.

Done at Bruges, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [22 March], in the year of the Lord 1130, indiction 8.

## VI. Theodoric, Count of Flanders, remits the annual rent from certain properties set out in the charter. 1130.

I, Theodoric, by the grace of God Count of the Flemings, wish it to be known to all faithful people, present and future, that when I had entered, for the sake of prayer, the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, situated in the town of Oudenburg, the monks serving God there, with their abbot Hariulph, approached me and humbly asked that, for the salvation of my soul, I remit to them and, by indulgence, forgive a certain payment of rent which they had hitherto been obliged to render annually [Col. 1571C] to me and to our predecessors.

Moved by their humble request, and eager also to obtain the patronage of the blessed apostle Peter, I kindly granted what they asked and have perpetually pardoned, remitted, and forgiven the aforesaid annual payment of rent. In order that no deception may hereafter arise concerning its extent, we here set down an accurate account of it.

In the district of Wilram, crier for leased land: land of Saint Peter, from Animemed, 20; from Huiumed, 21; from the land of Reifrid Hassa, 8; in the port of Oudenburg, land of Ave de Pola, 9; land of Saint Peter, 6; land of Robert Baites, 8; land of Oldut, son of Elvard, 2; land of Godelie, 12; land of Rumold, son of Sibert, 8; land of Elvard, son of Elvard, 2; land of Albert of [Col. 1571D] Arka, 2; land of Tsedbert Erclis, 4; land of Gildewif, 2; land of Werembold Werric, 16; land of Arnold the Clerk.

In the four districts of William, crier for leased land: land of Hiddon and his brothers, 11. In the port of Oudenburg: land of Erembold, 14; land of Richard, 14; land of Vogal, 14; land of Saint Peter, 3; likewise land of Saint Peter, 10; land of Herred Boschmeab, 2; land of Popli, 7; land of Folbert Vogal, 12; land of Sibrand, 9; land of Follir the Jester, 6; land of Radcard, 5; land of Puerolf the priest, 5; land of Sigerd, son of Walker, 2; land of Folpt, son of Lettard, 3.

In the district of Dodin, crier for leased land: land of Bertolf son of Orpes, 18; land of Saint [Peter] from Rep, 4. From the rent at Klemskerke: land of Bertram, 6; land of [Col. 1572A] Olfrid Uldel, 7. In the district of Christian of Mor: land of Reinfrid the Bald, 27. In the district of Walter of Lisweg: land of Suildis, 15, which belonged to [lacuna] of the count. In the district of Gerard the recorder: in all, 28 shillings, 7 [denarii].

Therefore, for the remission of the sins of my fathers and for the repose of all my predecessors, and likewise for the peace and security of our county and for the salvation of all our faithful people, I have remitted and, by remitting, forgiven the annual payment of these rents to almighty God and to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, so that the monks serving God in the aforesaid place may continually implore for us the image of Christ the Lord. And in order that this our grant may obtain inviolable force, we have ordered this charter to be made [Col. 1572B] and have marked it with the signs of our faithful persons who were present, and strengthened it with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Theodoric, Count of Flanders. Sign of his wife, Countess Suanahild. Sign of Arnulph, kinsman of the counts. Sign of Godzwin of Snellegem. Sign of Gerard, chamberlain. Sign of Hubert Cubuc. Sign of Roger, provost of Bruges. Sign of Angelram, brother of Arnulph the chamberlain. Sign of Odgar Gerul, of the seal. Sign of Reinger Gelmon. Sign of Frumold the younger, recorder. Sign of Adalard, kinsman of Frumold. Sign of Gerard, recorder. Sign of Ramer Volakin. Sign of Ramer Snoges.

Done at Oudenburg, in the church of the Apostles, [Col. 1572C] on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May], indiction 9, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1130, while Louis, son of King Philip, held the kingdom of the Franks, in the twenty-third year of his reign, and in the second year of Theodoric’s countship.

## VII. Charter of Walter of Heines concerning the gifts made by his father Cono and his paternal uncle Walter. 1151.

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Since we have judged it fitting to make known to all sons of holy Mother Church, present and future, certain deeds of our times: that they should not merely not envy the actions of sons and blessed fathers, but should diligently attend to them and add something to them.

I, Walter of Heines, advocate [Col. 1572D] of the church of Saint Peter of Oudenburg, inspired by the spirit of divine love, have in like manner freely transferred, through the hand of Theodoric, Count of Flanders, to the brethren who serve Christ there, everything which my father Cono and my paternal uncle Walter gave to the aforesaid church, for the remedy of their sins, under a hereditary and perpetual rent. But because the mutability of human nature is known to be subject to the failing of forgetfulness, I have taken care to set forth this gift, commending it to enduring memory.

Namely: one third of the tithe from all the grain of the whole parish of Oudenburg; moreover, the church of Saint Mary situated at Oudenburg with all its appurtenances, that is, with another third part of the tithe and the entire small tithe [Col. 1573A] of the whole parish, and with the entire endowment of the church, namely eight measures of land; and whatever more now belongs to the endowment, or may be increased by the gifts of the faithful in the future. All this, under hereditary and perpetual rent as stated above, I have lawfully given for the perpetual use of the brethren of the aforesaid church; on this condition, namely, that the abbot of Saint Peter or the brethren of the church shall pay me and my successors annually, at three terms—namely Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—nine pounds in Flemish coin, divided into three parts according to the aforesaid terms, retaining nevertheless nine shillings from the nine pounds, with which the abbot or his brethren shall annually pay the synodal due to the bishop.

Further, once this hereditary and perpetual rent has been annually paid at the aforesaid terms, under the testimony of two ecclesiastical persons, there shall be nothing for which the abbot or his [Col. 1573B] brethren ought to stand to justice in my court or that of my successors. And in order that all these matters may remain unshaken forever, I have confirmed with the protection of my seal the charter containing the detailed account of this gift, and have caused the names of the witnesses who were present at this grant to be subscribed.

Sign of Theodoric, Count of Flanders. Sign of Roger, provost of Flanders. Sign of Desiderius, provost of Lille. Sign of Eustace, chamberlain. Sign of Henry, castellan of Oudenburg. Sign of Richard of Snellegem. Sign of Remisrid of Slype and of Rudolf his brother. Sign of Baldwin of Koekelare. Sign of Christian of Gistel.

Done at Bruges in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1151, [Col. 1573C] indiction 14, in the month of March, on the sixth day of the same month.

## VIII. Charter of Gerald, bishop of Tournai, confirming the pledge of eight pounds against Walter of Vlaardingsloo. 1154.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Gerald, by the grace of God bishop of Tournai, to future and present persons forever.

We are instructed by divine precepts and informed by apostolic admonitions that we must keep vigilant watch with untiring zeal for the well-being of churches, when we either grant new gifts to places consecrated to God and to His saints or confirm former gifts; for we believe that from God, to whom we confer these things and from whom we received them, we shall receive a reward in eternal blessedness.

Let, therefore, the diligence of the faithful know that Walter of Vlaardingsloo, in the presence of ourselves, our officials, and his own men, pledged to the abbot and monks of the aforesaid church eight pounds and eleven shillings, which the church of Saint Peter at Oudenburg customarily paid annually, under hereditary and perpetual rent, from the altar of the same town, to him as it had paid to his father Cono, for sixty marks; [Col. 1573D] on this condition, namely, that he should never be allowed to redeem the aforesaid pounds except from his own resources, and thereafter retain them for his own uses. Moreover, the said Walter kindly granted as alms to the monks all the revenues which should accrue in the meantime.

Furthermore, because the aforesaid altar is known to be held as a fief [Col. 1574A] of the count, Walter himself, Lambert of Riderford, and Eustace his brother, pledged upon faith that he would procure the count’s consent and the church’s written instrument, and that he would observe all that we have said above. Nevertheless, Walter likewise, for the remedy of his soul and that of his predecessors, with whole-hearted devotion confirmed whatever goods his brother Cono, or Walter the Butler, brother of Cono, had given to the aforesaid church of Saint Peter, as is contained in the charters of the illustrious man Theodoric, Count of Flanders.

And in order that these things may remain firm and unshaken, we have confirmed them by the impression of our seal and strengthened them by the testimony of those who were present.

Done at Bruges, in the precinct of Saint Savior, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1154.

Sign of Lord Gerald, bishop. Sign of Robert, abbot of Clairvaux. Sign of Herman, abbot of Oudenburg. Sign of Erenbald, dean of Saint Donatian. Sign of Fulcher, dean. Sign of Master Sinon. Sign of Master Walter of Antwerp. Sign of Walter, priest of Saint Savior. Sign of Richard of Torhout. Sign of Dodin of Oostkerke. Sign of Master Walter of Kortrijk. Sign of Master Remfrid. Sign of Walter of Heines. Sign of Lambert of Riderford. Sign of Eustace, his brother. Sign of Robert Colaeph. Sign of Hanegri. Sign of Rudolf Nipe.

## IX. Charter of Pope Adrian confirming all the possessions of Saint Peter at Oudenburg, namely lands, tithes, offerings, and the personal benefice. 1156.

[Col. 1574C] Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Herman, abbot of Saint Peter of Oudenburg, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: forever.

The vigor of equity and the order of reason require that just requests be granted effect, especially when compassion supports the petitioners’ wishes and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, and especially receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the monastery in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter obtain, the Lord granting, by the concession [Col. 1574D] of pontiffs, the gifts of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

One third of the tithe of the whole parish of Oudenburg; further, another third part of the tithe, and all offerings and whatsoever proceeds from the altar of Saint Mary, except the benefices which belong to the priesthood. All these, subject to an annual rent of eight pounds and eleven shillings which you are obliged to pay annually, as is contained in the privileges of the church of Tournai, we confirm to you by apostolic authority; also the tithe of Erneghem and the land which you possess at Oudenburg.

[Col. 1575A] Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved unimpaired and entire, to be of every benefit for the governance and support of those for whose use they have been granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this page of our constitution, after having been warned once, twice, or three times, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know that he is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body [Col. 1575B] and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict punishment.
