But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the day before the Kalends of January [31 December], indiction 5, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1156, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

## X. Charter of Bishop Gerald concerning the pledge of eight pounds from the altar of Saint Mary against Walter of Heines, confirmed by Count Philip. 1164.

[Col. 1575C]

In deeds which we intend to commend to enduring memory, lest they be scattered by the wind of forgetfulness, we not unwisely add the safeguard of writing. Let therefore the diligence of present and future persons know that Lord Herman, abbot of Oudenburg, pledged for sixty marks eight pounds and eleven shillings which he annually gives to Walter of Heines from the altar of the same town as a hereditary rent, as he had been accustomed to give them to Walter’s father.

This pledge was made on the following terms: that the aforesaid Walter should be permitted to redeem the same pounds and eleven shillings annually in March only; but if he redeemed them, he should pay the hereditary rent at the three terms of the year—namely Christmas, [Col. 1575D] Easter, and Pentecost—as the Church had been accustomed to do, and the redemption should take place in the presence of the Count of Flanders.

This was done at Bruges in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164, in the presence of Philip, Count of Flanders, by his counsel, assistance, and consent, and in the presence of these persons: Hugh, abbot of Saint-Amand; Desiderius, provost of Lille; Robert, provost of Aire; Haket, dean of Bruges; Walter of Dendermonde; Roger of Landast; Siger of Somergem; Eustace the Chamberlain; William of Hus—[Richard of Snellegem.

## XI. Charter of Gerald, bishop of Tournai, concerning the personal benefice of the church of Saint Mary at Oudenburg. 1165.

[Col. 1576A]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Gerald, by the grace of God bishop of Tournai, to future and present persons forever.

Since the care and solicitude for all churches in the diocese of Tournai devoted to divine worship have been entrusted to us, we must provide for them in every way, insofar as lies in our power, so that what is conferred upon them by clerics or laymen out of charity may receive pastoral protection, and so that nothing contrary to justice may be attempted in them without reasonable opposition.

We therefore wish it to be known to future and present persons that, for the remedy of [Col. 1576B] our soul and those of our predecessors, we have granted to the abbot and brethren serving God in the church of Oudenburg, to be held perpetually, the personal benefice of the church of Oudenburg, which Bernard of Waas had hitherto held and which we received from Bernard’s hand, while preserving in all things episcopal right. And so that this grant may remain firm and unshaken forever, we have confirmed it by the impression of our seal and strengthened it by the subscription of the witnesses who were present.

Sign of Lord Gerald, bishop. Sign of Walter, dean. Sign of Everard, archdeacon. Sign of Letbert, provost. Sign of Lebert, cantor. Sign of Robert, provost of Arlebecke. Sign of Thomas. Sign of Master Lambert. Sign of Walter of Jabbeke. Sign of Matthew, notary.

Done at Tournai in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1165. [Col. 1576C]

## XII. Philip of Alsace, Count of Flanders, bestows a benefit upon the abbey of Oudenburg, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Bruges.  
[Note: [Col. 1575] This charter is preserved in the archives of the Chamber of Accounts at Lille and is found published in Miraeus, vol. III.] 1173.

I, Philip, Count of Flanders and Vermandois, wish it to be known to posterity and contemporaries alike that we have given to the church of Saint [Col. 1576D] Peter at Oudenburg, to possess by hereditary right for the salvation of my soul, of my wife, and of my predecessors, all new land, both arable and pasture, which lies at Westende in Testerep, wherever it lies between the dunes, the Yser, and the sea, and all that may there in the future accrue through the sea’s alluvion.

On this condition, however: for every eight measures contained within the said land alone, that church shall pay the lord of Flanders one mark in Flemish money each year; and henceforth the aforesaid land shall remain forever free and quit of every exaction, relief, and tallage.

And in order that this my donation may hereafter remain valid and free from every danger of challenge, I have confirmed it by the authority of my seal and the testimony of those subscribed.

[Col. 1577A] Sign of Florent, Count of Holland. Sign of Robert, treasurer of Tours and chancellor of Flanders. Sign of Hugh, abbot of Saint Nicholas of Veurne. Sign of Haket, dean of Saint Donatian at Bruges. Sign of Cono, castellan of Bruges. Sign of Eustace, chamberlain. Sign of Florent of Vorren. Sign of Rason, butler. Sign of Richard Blavoet. Sign of Richard the Seneschal. Sign of Theodoric of Ypres.

Done at Ypres in the year of the Lord 1173.

## XIII. Charter of Philip, Count of Flanders and Vermandois, confirming gifts of tithes from Oudenburg, the parishes of Erneghem, Ichtegem, Koekelare, and Bovekerke. 1176.

[Col. 1577B]

Philip, by the grace of God Count of Flanders and Vermandois, to all who shall inspect this present writing: forever.

Since we believe it plainly conducive to the salvation of our soul to take care, for the security of future times, to confirm by the testimony of our seal those goods which have at some time come to churches of Christ established under our jurisdiction through the gifts of our predecessors or of other faithful people, we therefore wish it to be known to all, both posterity and contemporaries, that Herman, abbot of Oudenburg, and his brethren obtained from us by just requests that we should confirm, by the safeguard of writing and the attachment of our seal, those things which they are known to have possessed in the times of our predecessors [Col. 1577C] or still to possess in ours. To prevent any occasion for error concerning what those things are, we have thought fit to specify them:

We confirm to them, to be possessed perpetually under annual rent, one third of every tithe of the whole parish of Oudenburg; further, the church of Saint Mary situated at Oudenburg with all its appurtenances, namely with another third part of the tithe of the same town, the entire small tithe, and the whole endowment of the church, as is contained in their privileges. We also confirm the tithe of Erneghem, which certain noblemen of that town gave, from all their freehold and from all their lands cultivated and to be cultivated—as is contained in the privilege of Saint [Col. 1577D] Arnulph—by the hand of Lord Bishop Radbod, Count Robert giving consent, for the use of the aforesaid church of Saint Peter. Further, we confirm to the said brethren, free and discharged from every right of ourselves or our successors, two sheaves from the whole wilderness called in German *Fang* or *Wostyna*, in the parishes of Erneghem, Ichtegem, Koekelare, and Bovekerke, as far as the boundary of Vlaardingsloo, as is contained in the privilege of Count Charles.

Therefore, lest the same brethren or their successors suffer any wrongful injury of claim from anyone concerning these matters, we have taken care to secure the present charter containing these provisions by the authority of our seal and the attestation [Col. 1578A] of witnesses.

Sign of Hugh of Saint-Amand. Sign of Hugh, abbot of Saint Nicholas of Veurne. Sign of Haket, dean. Sign of Eustace the Chamberlain.

Given at Bruges in my house, in the year of the Lord 1176.

## XIV. Arnold, viscount of Gistel, endows the abbey of Oudenburg, with the approval of Philip of Alsace, Count of Flanders.  
[Note: [Col. 1577D] This charter is found in vol. I of Miraeus’s *Diplomata*.] 1180.

Philip, by God’s favor Count both of Flanders and Vermandois, to all sons of holy Mother Church: forever.

Since, by the benefit of divine bounty, we possess at will all that the rich fertility of this world produces, we lay up for ourselves for the future only those things which we entrust to the hands of Christ’s poor, to be carried into heavenly [Col. 1578B] treasures.

So that we may escape the hardships of earthly poverty, some of those things which are now superfluous ought to be set aside, by which both the want of Christ’s poor may meanwhile be relieved and help may be prepared for us in the future.

I have therefore taken care, by this present charter, to make known to the enduring memory of future as well as present persons that Arnold, viscount of Gistel, with his wife Agnes, surrendered into my hands, by absolute renunciation, every tithe which he held from me in fief in the parishes of Erneghem, Westkerke, Roksem, and Bekegem, between Pita and Watervalla. And I, for the cleansing of my own sins and those of my own people, have transferred that same tithe by lawful and free donation to the church of Saint Peter at Oudenburg for perpetual use.

Arnold himself, with his wife Agnes, granted to the same church of Saint Peter, to possess perpetually under the same rent payment, a certain tithe which he possessed by hereditary right, on payment yearly of half a *firton*, from the church of Saint Nicholas of Ribelmund, on the boundary of the aforesaid tithe, in place of his own right.

But lest the often-mentioned church of Saint Peter should, with the passing of time, suffer any prejudice in its property, I have thought it necessary that the aforesaid donation be committed to writing and strengthened by the protection of our seal. Present at this donation were:

Gerald, provost of Lille. [Col. 1578D] Walter, chaplain of the Count of Wijnendale. Gerard, viscount of Oudenburg. Boidin of Ravenscote. Christian of Gistel. Theodoric Damhoudera. Weitin of Jabbeke and his brothers. Henry of Paskendale. Henry of Schirvelde. Daniel of Torhout. Haket of Riddervoorde.

Given at Veurne in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1180, indiction 3, epact 17.

## XV. Charter of Count Philip of Flanders confirming the tithes of the whole parish of Oudenburg. 1183.

[Col. 1579A]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Philip, by the grace of God Count of Flanders and Vermandois, to all sons of holy Mother Church, present and future: forever.

Since the frail memory of humankind is accustomed to allow deeds performed in earlier times to be erased by forgetfulness, we judge it beneficial to our salvation that those things which came to churches of Christ established under our jurisdiction by lawful gift in our own times or those of our predecessors should be preserved unimpaired for the use of those upon whom they were conferred.

Therefore we wish by this present charter to make known to the whole body of the faithful [Col. 1579B] that Herman, abbot of Oudenburg, and the brethren of that place, have obtained from our justice by just requests that we should strengthen by the safeguard of our writing and the attachment of our seal those things which were given to the church of blessed Peter by Cono and Walter, brothers, sons of Adalard the Butler, in the time of Charles, prince of Flanders and my predecessor, and confirmed in the time of my father Theodoric, as we have learned with complete certainty from their privileges. To prevent any occasion for error concerning what those things are, we have thought fit to specify them:

Namely, one third of the tithe from all the grain of the whole parish of Oudenburg; further, the church of Saint Mary situated at Oudenburg, with all its appurtenances, namely with another [Col. 1579C] third part of the tithe, the entire small tithe of the whole parish, and the entire endowment of the church—namely eight measures of land, together with whatever more now belongs to the endowment or shall hereafter be increased by the gifts of the faithful. All this the aforesaid Cono and his brother Walter lawfully transferred, under hereditary and perpetual rent, for the perpetual use of the brethren of the aforesaid church; on this condition, namely, that the abbot of Saint Peter of Oudenburg or the brethren of the church should annually pay him and his successors, at three terms—namely Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—nine pounds in Flemish money divided into three parts according to the aforesaid terms, retaining nevertheless nine shillings from the nine pounds, with which the abbot or his brethren should annually pay the synodal due to the bishop.

Further, once this hereditary and perpetual rent has been annually paid at the aforesaid terms, under the testimony of two ecclesiastical persons, there shall be nothing for which the abbot or his [Col. 1579D] brethren ought to stand to justice in the court of the often-mentioned brothers or their successors; nor shall an ecclesiastical person be subject, for any cause, to the judgment of secular persons.

And in order that all these matters may remain unshaken with perpetual stability, we have secured, by the authority of our seal, the charter containing the detailed account of this grant, and have caused the names of the witnesses who were present at this confirmation to be recorded beneath it.

Sign of Philip, Count of Flanders. Sign of Gerald of Mesen. Sign of William, abbot [Col. 1580A] of Saint Bavo. Sign of John, provost of Ypres. Sign of Eustace the Chamberlain. Sign of William the Castellan. Sign of Audomar. Sign of Hellin of Wervik. Sign of Walter of Nevele. Sign of Arnold of Gistel. Sign of Walter of Formensel. Sign of Gerald of Landast. Sign of William of Straden, Templar.

Done at Ypres in my house, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1183.

## XVI. Charter of Everard, bishop of Tournai, concerning the agreement about the chapel of Zantvoorde and the abbot’s release from the suit of the parishioners. 1184.

I, Everard, by the grace of God bishop of Tournai, to all to whom these letters shall come: greeting.

Let it be known to you that certain parishioners of Oudenburg, coming before us, asserted [Col. 1580B] that two priests established there in the mother church were by no means sufficient to provide for the salvation of the parishioners, because of the extent and breadth of the parish and the inaccessible situation of places within it. They therefore earnestly asked us to grant them a priest in a certain chapel long established, where, as they asserted, divine services had also long been celebrated by certain priests, with no priest yet assigned or appointed, and with the right of the mother church preserved.

Having therefore taken counsel with prudent and religious men, we entrusted men of sound judgment and good reputation, with the consent of the parishioners and of the abbot who held the personal benefice of that church, to go to the place, inquire, and determine whether the salvation [Col. 1580C] of souls necessarily required the divine office to be celebrated in the aforesaid chapel. But they, after diligently investigating the truth and making an inspection, having been admonished with all strictness, reported to us that no necessity required divine services to be celebrated in the aforesaid chapel, since it was sufficiently near to the parish church and wholly unsuited to meet the needs of the more remote parishioners.

Thus sufficiently informed on these matters, after consultation with the chapter of our principal church, we have released the present abbot of Oudenburg from the aforementioned suit of the parishioners, because it was entirely without basis. If anyone should presume, in rash audacity, to oppose this our release, let him know that he will incur the sentence of anathema. We have further granted to the aforesaid abbot himself [Col. 1580D] that, should any priest celebrate divine services in that chapel without the abbot’s permission, he may, by reliance on our authority, subject that priest by name to excommunication as an evildoer. We further command that all who knowingly attend shall be subject to the same sentence, and that this sentence pronounced against both the priest and his hearers shall be promulgated by the parish priests throughout the whole deanery of Bruges.

I, Everard, bishop of Tournai, have subscribed. Likewise I, Arnold, dean of Saint Mary’s church of Tournai, together with our chapter, have subscribed under the testimony of our seal.

Sign of Gorum, archdeacon. Sign of Theodoric, provost. Sign of Gunther, archpriest. Sign of Matthew, deacon. Sign of Ghisbert and Walter, [Col. 1581A] subdeacons. Sign of Ivo, abbot of Saint Martin. Sign of Eustace, abbot of Pratis.

Given at Tournai in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1184, on the second day before the Kalends of September [31 August].

## XVII. Charter concerning all the great and small tithes of the parish of Oudenburg, adjudged to our church by Everard, bishop of Tournai.

I, Everard, bishop of Tournai, to all the faithful forever.

We have been placed [in office], and we ought to preside, in order that we may preserve to each person his rights whole and unimpaired. We make known to you all that, by command of the lord pope, which we received through the hands of the lord of Amiens and the lord of Thérouanne, concerning the controversy long conducted between Abbot Herman and the parishioners of Oudenburg, and after the chapter of Tournai had been convened, it was adjudged—as reason requires and seems just to us—in favor of the present abbot and the brethren of the church of Oudenburg [Col. 1581B] that the said parishioners [shall pay] tithes of all arable land, livestock, grain, every other crop, warrens, wastelands, thistles, and all vegetables which they may happen to sell; and of lambs and sheep, and, as of lambs, so also of wool.

If a parishioner has ten lambs, he shall be bound to give one; but if he has only nine, eight, or seven, he shall be bound either to give one or to do the abbot’s pleasure according to a reasonable valuation. But if he has fewer than seven, he shall be bound to give the tenth according to the amount of the price and the valuation of the seller or buyer; likewise, [he shall give] offerings at the Nativity [Christmas] [Col. 1581C] of the Lord, at Easter, and at Pentecost. And in order that this may be kept inviolate in future times, we bind by anathema all who may wish to act against these provisions.

And in order that this may be more strongly confirmed, we have attached our seal and that of our church, with the attestation of those who were present.

Sign of Everard, bishop of Tournai. Sign of Letbert, dean. Sign of Theodoric, priest. Sign of Masters Walter and Lambert, deacons. Sign of Walter. Sign of Winomar, subdeacon. Sign of Galter, abbot of Pratis.

## XVIII. Charter of Bishop Everard concerning Mass to be celebrated in the chapel of Zantvoorde. 1185.

[Col. 1581D] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Everard, by the grace of God bishop of Tournai, to all the faithful for ever. Since, as the Apostle says, “God has called us in peace,” whatever may overthrow the state of peace must be extinguished at its very beginning; and, lest through renewed importunity it may rise again, the manner of its extinction should be entrusted to the faithful keeping of written records. Therefore I, Everard, bishop of Tournai, make known by the present document to all present and future that, concerning the dispute which those descended from the stock of Walcher had raised in my presence against the church of St Peter of Aldenburg, over the celebration of divine offices in their chapel—known to have been built in honour of Saint Mary, ever-Virgin and Mother of God—[Col. 1582A] wishing on the one hand to safeguard the church from loss and on the other to provide for the people’s needs, I have decreed, with the assent of both parties, as follows.

A monk whom the abbot of Aldenburg appoints from the body of his own church shall celebrate only the solemnities of Mass each day in the aforesaid chapel, unless intolerable bad weather prevents him from doing so. He shall never celebrate Vespers except on principal feasts and Sundays; nor Matins except on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, the night of the Circumcision, and likewise the night of the holy Epiphany; and on the three nights preceding the day of the Lord’s Resurrection he shall be bound to celebrate there. Moreover, the aforesaid descendants of Walcher, always providing the monk with a suitable cleric, shall give the abbot one mark for the purchase of a horse for the monk’s [Col. 1582B] conveyance; and the abbot shall maintain that horse, so that it does not perish, at his own expense.

Whatever offering comes into the hand of the monk celebrating the divine offices shall all accrue to the use of the monastery of Aldenburg, except that enough of the candles shall be left in the chapel to provide the necessary lights there. Further, whatever comes to the same chapel, apart from the altar-offering, through the donations of the faithful, whether movable or immovable, one half [106] shall be reserved for the chapel’s use and the other half shall belong to the monastery. And, in order that the church of St Peter may in every respect remain free from loss, the aforesaid descendants of Walcher—namely two knights, one called Gerard Gorch and the other Walter of Beverhot—have assigned to that church one mark from their land, payable as an annual revenue: each, that is, one half. The land of Gerard upon which he assigned to St Peter half of this mark is called Everelmus Sticcortavura; Walter’s land is Nordaker and Musalms Hofsteda, which shall likewise pay one half-mark. It should be known, however, that when through the generosity of the faithful the chapel has received enough land for the revenue of the aforesaid mark to be assigned from it, the descendants of Walter shall receive their land discharged, and the monks shall receive their revenue from the chapel’s land.

They shall never require the offices of baptism and burial to be performed there; nor shall any secular priest ever presume to come there to perform divine offices except by command of the abbot. If anyone should effectively attempt to infringe any of the provisions [Col. 1582D] stated above, let him know that he incurs sentence of excommunication; and until, repenting, he has made satisfaction to the monastery as the abbot determines, the chapel shall remain deprived of divine offices. That these provisions may remain all the more unshaken and inviolate, they have been confirmed with my seal, that of the chapter of Tournai, and also that of the church of Aldenburg, and strengthened besides by the names of those present.

Sign of Arnulf, dean.  
Sign of Theodoric, priest.  
Sign of Matthew, canon.  
Sign of William, dean of Bruges.  
Sign of Nicholas, priest.  
Sign of Herman, abbot.  
Signs of Gerard, Baldwin, Walter, and Corbellus, monks.

Given at Aldenburg in the year of the incarnate Word 1185. I, Henry, by the grace of God chancellor of Tournai, have read and subscribed.

XIX. Pope Celestine receives the abbey of Aldenburg under his protection and grants various privileges. 1195.

[Col. 1583A]

Celestine, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Herman, abbot of St Peter of Aldenburg, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever. The vigour of equity and the order of reason require that just requests be granted their effect, especially when the piety of those petitioning supports their wishes and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, [Col. 1583B] strengthening it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. We have judged that the following should be expressly named: the site itself on which the aforesaid monastery stands, with all its appurtenances; one third of the tithe of the entire parish [Col. 1583C] of Aldenborgh; furthermore, one third of the tithe, all offerings, and whatever proceeds from the altar of St Mary, except the benefices belonging to the priesthood. All these, subject to an annual payment of eight pounds and eleven shillings which you must pay each year, as is contained in the privileges of the church of Tournai, we confirm to you by apostolic authority; likewise the tithe from Eerneghem; and the land which you possess at Aldenborgh.

No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive into your care clerics or laypeople, free or manumitted, fleeing the world, and retain them without any contradiction. [Col. 1583D] We further prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving that place without permission of his abbot, unless in pursuit of a stricter religious life. No one shall dare to retain one who departs without the common assurance of the brethren.

Likewise, we more strictly forbid that any bishop, archdeacon, their officials, canons, or other clerics may, under pretext of any custom, have the power or permission to demand from us a silk cope or anything else in connection with the confirmation, installation, or blessing of an abbot. If they demand anything from you on these grounds, since it is detestable and contrary to reason, you may freely deny them what they ask. [Col. 1584A] If the land is under interdict, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of the same monastery shall be free; and no one shall oppose the devotion [108] and final wish of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. When you, now abbot of that place, or any one of your successors, are in office, no one shall be set over it by any trick of usurpation or by force, except one whom the common consent of the brethren, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, has provided to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the complete benefit of the uses for whose governance or support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 1584B] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his rank and honour; let him acknowledge himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Cencius, cardinal deacon of St Lucy in Orthea, chamberlain of the lord pope, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1195, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

XX. Charter of Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, confirming the donations of all tithes and of the church of Blessed Mary at Aldenburg. 1197.

[Col. 1584D] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Baldwin, by the grace of God count of Flanders and Hainaut, to all children of holy mother Church for ever [109]. Since writing is the sole remedy for forgetfulness, imposing silence upon disputes and untying the knot of contention, we have taken care to commit to written memory certain acts performed in the time of our predecessors, lest, obscured by the cloud of forgetfulness, they should bring back the scruple of renewed doubt. Accordingly, by the testimony of the present document, we declare to all present and future that Baldwin, abbot of Aldenburg, and the brethren of that place had obtained from our justice, in response to their just petitions, that those things which had been given to the church of Blessed Peter by Cono and Walter, brothers, [Col. 1585A] sons of Adalard the Cup-bearer, predecessors of my forebears the princes of Flanders, in the time of Charles, and confirmed in the times of Theodoric, my grandfather, and of my uncle Philip, count of venerable memory—as we have learned with complete certainty from their privileges—should be confirmed by the protection of our document and the attachment of our seal.

Lest any occasion for error remain, we have judged that these should be specified: namely, one third of every tithe of grain from the whole parish of Aldenburg, free from every demand of rent; furthermore, the church of St Mary situated in Aldenburg with all its appurtenances, together with another third part of the tithe, the whole small tithe of the parish, and all the church’s endowment—namely eight [Col. 1585B] measures of land, and whatever else now belongs to the endowment or shall hereafter increase through the generosity of the faithful. All these things belong to the right of the parsonage; Cono and his brother Walter lawfully surrendered them, subject to hereditary and perpetual rent, for the perpetual use of the brethren of the aforesaid church, on the condition that the abbot of St Peter of Aldenburg and the brethren of the church pay to them and their successors every year, in three instalments—at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—nine pounds of Flemish coin, divided into three parts according to the aforesaid dates.

Nine shillings are nevertheless retained from the nine pounds, which the abbot or his brethren shall pay annually to the bishop as synodal due. Once this hereditary and perpetual rent has been paid annually at the aforesaid times, before two ecclesiastical persons as witnesses, neither the abbot nor his brethren shall have any cause to stand trial in the court of the said brothers or their successors, nor shall an ecclesiastical person be subject, for any cause, to the judgment of secular persons. [Col. 1585C] That all these provisions may remain unshaken in perpetual stability, we have strengthened with the authority of our seal the charter containing the terms of this grant, and have caused the names of the witnesses present at this confirmation to be recorded below.

Sign of Gerard, provost of Bruges and chancellor of Flanders.  
Sign of Henry, the count’s brother.  
Sign of Raso of Gavere.  
Sign of Gheerkini of Sottenghem. [110]  
Sign of Gerard, castellan of Aldenburg.  
Sign of Joseph, notary.  
Sign of William.  
Sign of Master Gunter.  
Sign of Henry of Paskendala.

Given at Male in the year of the Lord 1197.

XXI. Charter of Guy, count of Flanders, concerning all the small tithes of the whole parish of Aldenburg and Zantvoorde. 1282.

We, Guy, count of Flanders and marquis of Namur, make known to all that, whereas between the religious men, the abbot and convent of St Peter of Audenborgh on the one hand, and the parishioners of that same place of Zantvoorde on the other, there was and had been a dispute concerning the tithes of herbs called in Flemish *mede woude*, leek, onion, garlic, cabbage, and [Col. 1586A] rapeseed, which the aforesaid abbot and convent demanded from the aforesaid parishioners for the lands from which they had received and customarily received tithes of grain when those lands were and had been sown, and from which they had also received the small tithes in the aforesaid parishes. Those parishioners refused to give tithes to the aforesaid abbey and convent from these herbs because they said that no tithes had ever been collected from them. And because the aforesaid parties had submitted this dispute to our judgment and decision, having heard and understood what these parties wished to say and put before us, by the counsel of worthy persons we say and ordain that the aforesaid parishioners shall henceforward be perpetually bound to pay, [Col. 1586B] and shall pay, to the aforesaid abbey and convent the tithe due upon the herbs and lands named above lying in the aforesaid parishes. We release the aforesaid parishioners, for the sake of peace, by our judgment and ordinance, from the arrears of these same tithes.

In testimony whereof these letters were sealed with our seal. Given at Male, in the year of our Lord 1282, in the month of January.

XXII. [111] Grant of the schoolmastership of the town of Aldenburg, which belongs in full right to the abbot of Aldenburg. 1570.

Gaspar, by divine permission humble abbot of the monastery of St Peter in the town of Oudenburg, of the Order [Col. 1586C] of St Benedict in the diocese of Bruges, to our beloved in Christ, John de la Porte, cleric of the diocese of Cambrai: greeting in the Lord. The schoolmastership of the parish church of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the said town of Oudenburg, which by full right belongs and pertains to our presentation, provision, and complete disposition by reason of our right of patronage, and which is now free and vacant, we have conferred and do confer upon you in God’s name; and we provide and confer upon you the same with all its rights and appurtenances. By these our present letters we furthermore invest you with them.

Accordingly, we require and request our beloved in Christ, the dean of the Christian community of Oudenburg, or his deputy, [Col. 1586D] to place and install you, or your procurator in your name and on your behalf, in corporal, real, and actual possession of the said schoolmastership and of its rights and appurtenances, or to procure that you be so placed and installed, after the solemnities customarily employed in such matters have been observed; faithfully reporting to us what has been done in this matter. Given in the said monastery under our abbatial seal, in the year of the Lord 1570, on the eleventh day of April.

At the conclusion it read: “By order of the lord abbot.” It was subscribed: “C. J. Gillis,” with a certain manual mark.

On the back was written:

“In the year of the Lord 1570, on the first day of May, I, Peter de Palude, priest and dean of the Christian community of Oudenburg, by virtue of the foregoing letters, have in God’s name placed and installed [Col. 1587A] our John de la Porte in corporal, real, and actual possession of the schoolmastership of the church of the town of Oudenburg, in the presence there of Clotho Salomon and lord Adrian de Grutere, witnesses summoned for the aforesaid matters, as my manual mark attests.”

It was subscribed: “P. de Palude, dean of the Christian community, etc.” A seal, impressed in red wax and pierced by a double tail, was appended.

XXIII. [112] Charter concerning the union of the two portions of the pastoral cure of the church of Aldenburg, by Remigius Driutius, bishop of Bruges. 1577.

Remigius Driutius, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See bishop of Bruges, to all and each who shall inspect, read, or hear these our present letters: greeting in the Lord. We make known that, having examined the petition of the reverend father, lord Gaspar of Bovincourt, abbot of the monastery of St Peter in the town of Aldenburg, who, as patron of the parish church of Blessed Mary in that town, had petitioned and requested the union and annexation of the two portions of the aforesaid cure, or church, of St Mary of Aldenburg; and also release from the pension, or extinction of the pension, of five pounds *groot* assigned to each portion for the pastor’s maintenance from the tithes of the said parish belonging to the monastery and granted by our predecessors of pious memory in the bishopric of Bruges; [Col. 1587C] and having heard concerning that petition both the late lord Sebastian Pauwaert, rector of the said church, and the magistracy of Aldenburg and the wardens of the fabric of the said church; and having further taken account of the consent of lord Arnold Vossius, priest presented to the aforesaid cure by the said lord abbot, patron of the same church, to us as ordinary collator after the death of the aforesaid lord Sebastian, its most recent peaceful vicar:

And since the aforesaid abbot consents to a perpetual annual obligation and payment of five pounds *groot* for the larger endowment and more honourable maintenance of the pastor, from the tithes of the aforesaid parish belonging to the said monastery of St Peter, provided that the remaining five pounds *groot* mentioned above be extinguished, and that the monastery be in future released and freed from those five pounds; after diligent attention and mature consideration of all these and of the other matters to be considered by law, we, both by the authority granted to us through the decrees of the Council of Trent and by our ordinary authority, have held, decreed, and declared that the aforesaid two portions of the parish church and cure of Blessed Mary in the town of Aldenburg, now vacant, with all rights, fruits, [113] and certain and uncertain emoluments, are to be united and annexed. Accordingly, by these presents we unite the same portions in the manner and form set forth above, establish one cure from the two portions, and assign and adjudge to the pastor holding office at the time and to his successors, for more ample maintenance, from the tithes of the said parish belonging to the monastery, the sum [Col. 1588A] of five pounds *groot*.

We bind the abbot for the time being to pay that sum of five pounds *groot* every year in two instalments, namely on the feasts of our Lord Jesus Christ and on the Nativity of St John the Baptist, so that the first payment shall fall on the coming feast of St John the Baptist. We release and free the same abbot and the said monastery for the future from the remaining five pounds *groot*, saving the promise of the reverend lord Melchior Everaerts, present abbot, concerning the other five pounds payable to Arnold Vossius in respect and favour of his person during that prelate’s life. Thus we declare in these writings.

In faith and testimony whereof, we have ordered and caused these present letters to be authenticated by the appending of our seal and by the subscription of Henry Mertens. Given and enacted at Bruges, 20 April 1577. And it was signed: “By command of His Most Reverend Lordship: H. Mertens.”

XXIV. Letter of Philip IV, king of Spain, to the marquis of Caracena, stating that consideration has been given to uniting the abbey of Oudenbourg with that of the Dunes. 1663.

My cousin. The abbot of the Dunes, by the enclosed petition and for the reasons contained in it, having requested that the presently vacant abbey of Audenbourg be united and incorporated into the said abbey, I have thought fit to send you the said petition, so that you may have it examined and send me your opinion upon it; thereafter I shall order what I find suitable. So much, my cousin: may Our Lord keep you in His holy protection.

Madrid, 18 February 1663. Philip. Below: Jean Vecquer.

XXV. [114] Protest made by the abbot and religious of the abbey of St Peter at Oudenburg upon their expulsion from their house. 16 February 1797.

Liberty . . . Rights of Man . . . Personal security . . . Guarantee of property . . . Expressions, principles, maxims continually repeated and lavishly employed in the constitution of the French Republic, in the decrees of its rulers, and in the enactments of the constituted authorities: what were we not entitled to expect from them?

There is nothing in society whose choice is, and ought to be, freer for every individual than the manner of life which he wishes to embrace and follow, provided that it is not contrary to the laws or harmful to another’s rights.

We, the undersigned abbot and religious of the abbey of Oudenburg, have of our own free will chosen and embraced the manner of life established in this house since the eleventh century; we have constantly followed it until this day, and we were firmly resolved, and wished with all our hearts, to persevere in it until our last breath.

[Col. 1589A] We live peacefully upon the small income from our property held in common.

Our status, profession, and manner of life were approved and authorized by the laws of the country. Our property was guaranteed and protected by them . . . At the entry of their armies into this country, the French commissioners solemnly promised us the preservation of both . . . The French constitution, upon its publication in this country, assured and guaranteed them to us. Far from harming another’s rights, we were useful to our fellow citizens by the means of subsistence which we provided to them: by giving agricultural work and the opportunity to practise their trades, etc., to valiant Frenchmen, and by giving relief and assistance to [Col. 1589B] the needy and infirm—as the inhabitants of this commune bear witness.

Our civil existence was therefore lawful.

Yet notwithstanding this, we now find ourselves driven out and banished from our retreat, stripped of our income, and deprived of our property by a power [115] from which we flattered ourselves that we might expect every aid and protection against the unjust [Col. 1590A] invader, by a force which we cannot resist . . . We must therefore . . . and we submit.

But before leaving our beloved refuge, we declare and protest before God and the whole universe that this is against our will, and that we reserve the right and power to pursue, by every lawful means and at the proper time and place, our rights and property against whomever it may be.

Thus done in our chapter-house on 16 February 1797, and presented in duplicate to the commissioners executing this disastrous catastrophe: one copy to be attached to the official record, the other to serve us wherever it may be needed. Requesting them to give us a receipt for it, we have signed both for ourselves and [Col. 1590B] for our absent fellow religious Placide Camerlynck, vicar at Adeghem. The signatures follow.

Below was written:

“Seen by us, the commissioners for the inventory, appointed by decree of the municipal administration of the canton of Ghistelles dated the 26th of this month. Oudenburg, 28 Pluviôse, Year V of the French Republic, one and indivisible.”

And it was signed: Jean Allaert, municipal agent; J. F. Kemel, municipal agent.

ABOUT THE MIDDLE OF THE CENTURY. LISIARD, CLERIC OF TOURS

[Col. 1589]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON LISIARD.

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. IV, p. 277.)

[Col. 1589] Lisiard, Liziard, or Lictard, a cleric of Tours and dean of Laon from 1153 to 1168 [Note: [Col. 1589] D’Achery, on Guibert of Nogent, p. 820.], was, it is said, the author of the *Ordinal*, or book of ceremonies and divine office, in that church. Barth, in Book 167, chapter 7, of his *Adversaria*, and in his notes on that work [Note: [Col. 1589] In Johann Peter von Ludewig, *Reliquiae veterum monumentorum*, vol. III, p. 523.], attributes to him the *History of Jerusalem*, which Bongars published without the author’s name in *Gesta Dei per Francos*, pp. 594–621, and in which the author continues events from the year 1100 to 1124.

[Col. 1589]

HISTORY OF JERUSALEM. (THE FIRST PART HAS PERISHED.) THE SECOND PART BEGINS.

(Bongars, *Gesta Dei per Francos*, Hanover, 1611, folio, p. 594.)

[Col. 1589B] When lord Bohemond, who had returned to [Col. 1589C] Antioch and now ruled the whole city alone, after the men of Count Raymond had been expelled from it, and lord Baldwin, brother of Duke Godfrey, who himself had now gained lordship over the entire city of Edessa and the neighbouring country beyond the Euphrates, learned from reliable messengers that Christ’s holy army, which had preceded them, had, with God’s help, taken the city of Jerusalem by arms, subjugated a large part of the neighbouring country after expelling its enemies, and [Col. 1590B] more widely freed the holy places for Christ’s worship, they rejoiced greatly with their men and accordingly rendered due praise to God. With the greatest devotion they offered worthy thanksgivings to Christ, who brings His servants’ labours to prosperity and brings them to completion.

All rejoice; all exult together. Antioch triumphs with its Bohemond; Edessa dances for joy with Baldwin; the Euphrates region congratulates them both. By their rejoicing they share in so great a victory, though they had been wholly exempt from the utmost toil of battle. Bohemond and his men blush at their return; Baldwin is ashamed of his delay; each is covered with shame because the victory of highest praise is not numbered among the titles of his glory. Yet it had required the same courage and prudence to remain in order to fortify and defend regions newly conquered as to go before in order to conquer them. For it would have accomplished nothing, or little, to expel Persians and Turks from Syria and the Euphrates region as far as Persia if, when all Christians departed, those regions were left without defenders and open to enemy recapture. Indeed, it would have been the height of folly to sweat through so many and such great labours and conflicts to restore Christ’s name and worship in those regions, if they had left the lands of their homeland—lands which they had won for Christ by their own blood—to be recovered [Col. 1591B] by their enemies.

Therefore let divine providence be acknowledged to have worked both in the departure of the others and in the remaining behind of these men, so that in both cases: “Let this glory be given not to a man but to your name, O Christ. Yours is the power; yours the kingdom, Lord. You restored Jerusalem to your worshippers; you crushed the Babylonians before them. You likewise strengthened, aided, and magnified Baldwin and his men, who with a small band of your worshippers repeatedly attacked, conquered, routed, and trampled innumerable Persian multitudes on the borders of Mesopotamia.”

Finally, when the Persians learned that Baldwin and Bohemond had begun to follow their companions to Jerusalem in order to fulfil their vows to God, they again gathered together and invaded part of the region of Edessa, intending to devour with wolfish fury whatever worshippers of Christ they found there, like sheep without a shepherd. Baldwin, however, returning suddenly against them with a rather small but chosen troop of his men, unexpectedly attacked them in their camp while they were off guard and suspecting nothing less than Baldwin’s return. He broke through their camp, threw the enemy into confusion, and overcame his foes; some he killed, others he put to flight. Thus, after destroying the enemy, gaining victory, and enriching himself with abundant booty, he returned with his men to the journey he had planned and soon caught up with Bohemond, who was awaiting his return near the town called Valenium.

A certain archbishop of Pisa, named Daimbert, had arrived at the port of Laodicea, together with many Italians and Tuscans; there was also another bishop from [Col. 1591D] Apulia. All these, gathered together in considerable friendship, were estimated at twenty-five thousand horsemen and foot-soldiers. Having advanced far into Saracen territory, they endured dangers beyond description, both from attacks by pagans and from lack of provisions, affecting people and beasts alike. So pressing was the famine that many were compelled to eat the flesh of horses, asses, and even camels, so that the animals which had collapsed before completing the journey might somehow serve as food.

At times there were found certain reeds, commonly called *cannameles* [sugar-canes], from which, it is said, wild honey is made; their name seems therefore to be composed of *canna* (“reed”) and *mel* (“honey”). Those able to find them put them into their mouths and chewed them because of their honeyed taste, receiving more flavour from them than strength. The travellers were frozen by the cold of winter; continual rain weakened both people and animals. Many noblemen too, when their mounts failed, were made foot-soldiers from horsemen and were forced to walk burdened by their small packs. Some, exhausted under the very loads that they carried in order somehow to relieve themselves by means of them, were worn out almost to death.

But a people burning with longing for holy Christ conquers all things, and did not cease until, arriving at Jerusalem, it paid its vows to the Lord, worshipping Him in the place where His feet had stood. There came together the tribes of the Lord that had gone before and those which had now followed—the true testimony [Col. 1592B] of Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord. King Godfrey, duke and Baldwin’s own brother, came to meet Duke Baldwin; greeting one another with a holy kiss, they rejoiced together over each other’s safety and over the prosperous completion, so glorious, of so long a labour.

All Christ’s soldiers together fulfilled their desire and visited the holy places. They pressed most devout kisses upon the Holy Land; they could scarcely be torn away from one place except because longing and love for another compelled them to leave it. From Jerusalem they flew to Bethlehem; they flew back to Jerusalem from Bethlehem, carried now by love of the most holy sepulchre, now by love of the manger. Air and earth still reeked and were foul with the stench of freshly slain corpses; and the very vastness of that horror displayed the magnitude of the victory that Christ had granted His people over the Turks.

After men and animals had recovered there from the great exhaustion of travel and hunger, and after they had celebrated with the greatest joy at Bethlehem the annual solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity; after the aforesaid Archbishop Daimbert had been elected patriarch of Jerusalem: some chose to return to Antioch with the dukes Bohemond and Baldwin, while others chose to remain at Jerusalem with King Godfrey.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1100, the aforesaid princes Bohemond and Baldwin, returning with their followers from Jerusalem to their own lands, came through Galilee as far as Paneas. This is the place called Caesarea Philippi in the holy Gospels: a city of considerable renown, built long ago by the sons of Dan at the foot of Mount [Col. 1592D] Lebanon; but in the time of Augustus or Tiberius Caesar more carefully rebuilt by Philip, son of Herod, and surnamed Caesarea Philippi. Two springs rise there, one called Jor and the other Dan; their streams and names, joined together, form the river Jordan. It runs thence to the lake called Alphatites, or rather the Dead Sea, and there loses both its name and its character as a river. This lake—or rather a certain utterly dark and impassable abyss—is the dreadful gulf of that Pentapolis, still remaining as a witness to the destruction of the ungodly.

It is called the Dead Sea because it can neither produce anything living of itself nor sustain anything living that may happen to be introduced from elsewhere. Thus [Col. 1593A] not only has the land there been condemned with a dreadful desolation, but the water also with barrenness. For even if the soil produces something by chance, outwardly it seems pleasing in colour and solid in appearance; inwardly, however, touch or taste proves it empty. Thus it displays attractiveness outside but hides ashes within. A land once exceedingly like the paradise of God, as Moses himself testifies (Gen. 13:10), has now become a place of horror and salt; even in its very growth it is the shadow of death.

Such is the land once belonging to the lost: it still bears the marks of destruction, so that the followers of corruption and wickedness may learn from this very ordinance to what final ruin they are enslaved; or rather, that they may be afraid and cease to burn with desire for those works of lust that make them burn in everlasting fire, and may beware of being blackened by that smoke of shameful desires from which “the smoke of their torments,” as Scripture says (Rev. 14:11), “ascends for ever and ever.” But let these brief remarks suffice concerning this matter; let us now return to our subject.

Therefore, as the aforesaid princes with their companies were returning to their own territories, first through Tiberias and then through Paneas, a great multitude came out from Damascus to meet them, intending harm if they could. These Saracens were lying in wait for their passage, very confident of victory because they had learned that the travellers were unarmed and utterly exhausted by the labour of the road. Nor was their supposition concerning the Christians’ lack of weapons wholly false: our men lacked lances and had few arrows; moreover, the bows themselves, which in those regions are usually put together with glue, had been soaked by continual rains and were [Col. 1593C] almost all slack and unstrung.

Yet Christ deceived the enemies of His soldiers in their expectation of victory; and, by the skill of the princes, mercifully rescued them from the hands of those who already seemed to have seized them. Bohemond, indeed, defended the vanguard against the enemy’s encounter and attack; Baldwin, at the rear, broke the stratagems and pursuit of the wicked. At length Christ’s soldiers escaped that danger and overcame the peril so eagerly and so murderously directed against them. To have escaped in such a crisis, when they were already hemmed in and captured, was no less desirable than victory itself. For it brought no less confusion upon the enemy to lose victory in so favourable an opportunity than to flee from battle.

Accordingly, while the enemy watched from the opposite side of their fortress, called Balaac, the Christians pitched camp there for that night, intending on the next day to pass through Tortosa and Laodicea. There they still found Count Raymond, whom they had left there; but, because of the scarcity and want of provisions, they could not remain with him longer. One prince with his followers hastened to his own Edessa; the other, entering his Antioch joyfully with his followers, was received by his people with the greatest delight.

There, while Bohemond for six months vigorously exercised his customary principality, Gabriel, the leading man of the city of Melitene, made a treaty with him through envoys and agreed to surrender both himself and the city over which he presided. When Bohemond went in July with a few men to receive it, it is uncertain [Col. 1594A] at whose traitorous prompting a certain emir named Danismend, with a great Turkish force, laid an ambush not far from that city for those advancing. This accursed people suddenly surrounded Bohemond and his men on every side, rushing out from their ambushes against them as they came altogether heedlessly and incautiously, because excessively secure. The attack was so sudden and unforeseen that no one could, I do not say fight, but even seize weapons in order to fight.

Thus all were scattered and turned to flight. Alas, grief upon grief: made a sport for their enemies, very many were slain, some captured, and very few escaped by flight. They lost their arms, camp, and even their baggage, with all their possessions. Bohemond himself was taken by the Turks and carried off captive, leaving behind among his followers the most profound mourning and desolation.

While he was still held captive before Melitene, which Danismend had surrounded with siege, he cut off a lock of his hair, sent it to Baldwin by a messenger, and sent word, lamentably begging with every entreaty that Baldwin should hasten swiftly to aid him for Christ’s sake. Hearing of this most miserable disaster, Baldwin became exceedingly sorrowful: he wept for his friend, lamented his colleague, and mourned their common misfortune. Nor did this most resolute hero delay, if he could, to hurry to his friend’s aid with whatever army he could muster, joined also by the Antiochenes, exposing himself to every danger in order to free his colleague if possible.

But Danismend, forewarned that the Franks were coming together against him and fearing their courage, abandoned the city he had besieged. For three days he fled from Baldwin, who pursued him, giving him no opportunity [Col. 1594B] to assemble his forces. Thus Baldwin and his followers, their effort frustrated, returned sorrowfully; while Bohemond, as has been said, was carried away captive and kept under the strictest guard.

As Baldwin returned, Gabriel met him and surrendered himself and the city to them. Baldwin therefore confirmed friendship with Gabriel and carefully entrusted the city’s guard to his own men. The Antiochenes, bereft of their prince, returned sadly to Antioch; Baldwin returned with the Edessenes to Edessa. While enjoying peace there and some measure of prosperity, he learned from messengers all bringing word that his brother Duke Godfrey, scarcely one year having elapsed in his Jerusalemite kingdom, had died at Jerusalem [Col. 1594C] on 18 July; and that he himself had been decreed and elected by all the people of Jerusalem as successor to the kingdom.

The prince grieved, indeed, at his brother’s death, but rejoiced no less in the inheritance of the kingdom granted to him. Having shared counsel with his friends, he entrusted his own land to a kinsman, Count Baldwin, to govern and guard. He himself resolved to make for Jerusalem with about two hundred knights and seven hundred foot-soldiers. Many wondered, and his friends shuddered, that with so small an escort he should undertake so dangerous a journey, passing through so many enemy regions from which most men, frightened, had withdrawn themselves because of the dangers.

They reached Antioch, then Laodicea, then Gibel, and afterwards Arqa. Having passed through Tortosa [Col. 1595A] and the castle of Arqa, they came as far as Tripoli. The king of Tripoli, not yet a Christian but not altogether hostile to Christians, caused provisions to be abundantly supplied as a gift to Baldwin and his followers in their camp. He also informed them that Duke Duqaq, king of Damascus, and Gmahadole, king of Calipti, with many bands of Turks, Arabs, and other Saracens, had occupied the narrow passes in order to block the Christians’ route.

For not far from the city called Beirut, near the sea, there is an extremely narrow passage, yet unavoidable for travellers going that way. If one hundred men occupy its narrows beforehand, they can very easily obstruct the passage of one hundred thousand, being protected on every side by the obstacles of mountains and sea and by the hollows of caves. Therefore, when the Damascenes and Aleppans had occupied this place in advance and the Christian scouts riding ahead began immediately to attack them, those following behind, with the whole company arranged in battle-lines, prayed most devoutly that help might be granted them from heaven in so great a necessity.

Nor did the merciful goodness of the Saviour fail His own anywhere. For in the first encounter many enemies in their ambushes were immediately killed, while others were so terrified that, fearing to engage, they abandoned the fight and withdrew into the hollows of caves or the narrow mountain places, giving thought to obstructing the passage rather than to battle. Seeing this, both the prince and the standard-bearers of the Christian army placed their camp in the very place where they had begun to fight, namely lest, if they retreated even a little [Col. 1595B] for lodging, they should stir up the enemy’s broken courage against themselves again, as though they were afraid.

Almost all, men and beasts alike, spent that night sleepless, without food and without drink. They displayed boldness before the enemy, but had little confidence of life. It was dangerous to remain in camp; more dangerous to approach the narrow defile which had to be crossed; most dangerous to flee by retreating. Thus, since there was no plan for flight nor any hope of victory, almost every confidence of safety had vanished. In such anguish the Christians languished in their camp that night. The night was long to the anxious because of the bitterness of their distress; yet, because of the horror of the death they dreaded and already saw, as it were, before their eyes, they feared the coming of daylight no less. The dawn which they desired yet feared broke.

The leading men debated and all confirmed the plan either to cross the narrows or—what was more hoped for—to die gloriously in battle. Having gathered up their tents and whatever other things they had, they drove the loaded beasts before them, while armed soldiers defended them from enemies attacking on every side. They made their way towards the entrance of the pass. Saracens surrounded them as they advanced, rushing together from mountains and sea on every side; with immense shouting they assailed them with arrows and missiles, threatened them with drawn swords, and drove them from behind and from both flanks, like sheep, toward the mouth of the pass, so that when shut in there they might at will mock and destroy those thus trapped [Col. 1595C].

And they would easily have done so, had not merciful Christ, when His own were trapped in that extreme crisis, inspired a plan the more wonderful because it was the more unexpected, supplied assistance, and wonderfully deprived the enemies of His people of both advantages. For when the pious and faithful followers of Christ, amid enemies shouting on every side and wickedly brandishing their swords for the death of the godly, had occupied a plain almost adjoining those narrows, pious Jesus—present everywhere in help in time of tribulation—suddenly put such confidence into the hearts of His own that they attacked their attackers with the boldest countercharge, broke through the close-packed wedges, scattered them, and put them to flight in three directions. So completely were they routed that they could never again recover strength or re-form into battle-line.

Some fled into the mountains, while the rearmost were cut down by the swords of their pursuers; others, driven headlong from precipices or from the crags of cliffs and mountain summits, were dashed to pieces; others fled with all possible speed by skiffs or boats even across the sea, fearing that the Christians might seize their fleet as well. It was plainly wonderful to behold those fleeing by sea pursued only on land, because they believed that merely leaving the shore would not suffice to escape Christian hands unless by fleeing further they also escaped their sight. Why was this, except that it might be shown by the clearest evidence that this was nothing other than a work of power? Why, except that the Christians, true children of Israel, seeing their Lord fighting for them by land and sea, might cry in joyful harmony: “If [Col. 1596A] God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8:31).

For behold, they saw also visibly fulfilled that divine promise: “Five of you shall pursue a hundred strangers, and a hundred of you ten thousand” (Lev. 26:8). Indeed, the enemies fled even where they knew that no one could pursue them. The Almighty had sent such terror and weakness into their hearts that the wicked multitude did not dare, I will not say to attack, but not even to look back upon the few who were godly. They were so stunned with fear and almost frozen that, as though unaware why they had come, they threw down their arms and offered their unarmed right hands and bare necks to those striking them. Behold how those who boasted that they had already conquered were defeated! Victors are conquered by the conquered; captors are captured by captives; and by those whom they had thought already bound, they are bound, held captive, and divided.

After pursuing their enemies during nearly that whole day, they returned to the enemy camp, enriched with abundant spoils and having gathered the weapons of the slain. The prince judged it wiser to withdraw to a nearby but deserted fortress and, after the toil of so great a slaughter, to rest that night under olive trees and shrubs. At dawn the next day, the prince, with some of his soldiers, came to the narrows of the passage, wishing personally to discover whether any Saracens remained there who could still obstruct the crossing. But in this matter, no less than in the rest, the power of Christ showed itself: all the enemies, terrified, had completely deserted [Col. 1596B] the place, which had been impregnable.

Having carefully reconnoitred this, the prince ordered his comrades to light a fire on the mountain summit, so that, seeing the smoke as had been agreed, all who had remained in the fortress would follow. Thus, with God granting success, they all assembled and, having a free road, passed through with all their possessions. When they had lodged near Beirut, its emir, moved more by fear than affection, sent provisions on boats. The Sidonians, Tyrians, and Ptolemaians likewise feigned friendship by carrying provisions to those passing near them, though it was well known that their hearts were wicked.

The town called Caiphas, recovered that same year by the Jerusalemites, was already held by Tancred. But because he had begun to be hostile to Baldwin, the citizens, unwilling to admit him, sold bread and wine outside the walls, Tancred being absent at that time through God’s providence. Passing through Caesarea of Palestine, they came to the maritime city of Joppa, where the Franks joyfully received Duke Baldwin as their king. As they hurried thence to Jerusalem, the whole Church came out together beyond the walls and, receiving him with a most joyful procession, led him with hymns and praises as far as the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre.

There, after alliances had been confirmed with the king according to Christian custom, both the king and those who had come with him rested, by God’s and Christ’s favour, from their labour, and the people of Jerusalem from the desolation caused by the loss of their prince. Patriarch Daimbert alone, with a few others, [Col. 1596C] was absent from this very celebrated reception of the king, because he had already begun to be hated by the king and by a certain portion of both clergy and people on certain grounds. He therefore lived elsewhere, removed from his see and in a private capacity.

For this reason the ceremony of crowning the king was postponed until the following feast of the Lord’s Nativity, so that then, as was fitting, the glory of the royal crown might be made glorious by the acclaim accompanying so glorious a festival. In the meantime peace between patriarch and king, and between clergy and archbishop, was carefully negotiated and restored.

Meanwhile, after taking counsel with his leading men, the king judged it advantageous to enter the neighbouring regions of the enemy and, at the very beginning of his reign, to offer the insolence of Turkish savagery a taste, as it were, of his own valour. He considered it more expedient to attack enemies in their own lands and cities than by delay to allow them to raise their horns for attacking him. Therefore, with a select force of the Christian army, the king chose first of all to attack the people of Ascalon: a people always rebellious, hostile to Christian peace, and a nursery of every kind of malice against Christ’s servants, in and from whom there continually spring the seeds of all wars and troubles.

I think it must be believed that the Lord, as is written of ancient times, was unwilling either to destroy or to hand over this city and people to His servants, in order that Jerusalem might always be tested in them and retain the habit of fighting; lest, through idleness, Jerusalem should be more disastrously attacked and conquered by worse enemies—vicious habits. Thus, according to that saying of the satirist, truthful though he speaks in jest:

> Humble fortune preserved the chaste Latin women,
>
> And toil extending into the night, and Hannibal close to the city.

So our Jerusalemites, through the continual presence of wars and hardships, may be kept low in humility and restrained in chastity. For one is less inclined to pride where one can scarcely live; those who continually fear even death take less pleasure in fornication. External wars are therefore often the destroyers of internal wars. Visible enemies are either the restraint or the overthrow of invisible enemies. Accordingly, for our Jerusalemites the wars continually sustained against flesh and blood—that is, against the Ascalonites—must always be considered necessary against “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” [Col. 1596D].

When King Baldwin came before Ascalon with the Christian army which, under Christ’s leadership, he was leading, the enemies came out against him. He met them with so impetuous an attack that they were immediately compelled to flee back within the walls and thereafter did not dare to come out again.

Accordingly, seeing that no opportunity for battle was then offered them, the Christians preferred to range through the neighbouring territories rather than remain there longer to no purpose. Fearing them, the inhabitants of those places hid themselves, their goods, and their animals within the hiding-places of caves. Smoke was applied at the entrances of the caverns to compel them to emerge; and when it was discovered that most of them had been accustomed to commit robberies against Christians and lie in wait for travellers, they were all immediately put to the sword without delay. Syrians found among them, however, were spared because of the name of Christ, which they retain in some degree.

Having traversed and almost wholly devastated that entire region with arms and fire, it was decided also to cross into Arabia, spreading terror everywhere, sparing those who submitted, and subduing the proud. Passing through the mountains near the places famous for the tombs of the patriarchs, they came to a valley formerly, as Scripture says (Gen. 13:10), like the paradise of God, but now—or rather long ago—the shadow of death and destruction: namely, the valley of the Sodomites and Gomorrites, cities destroyed by fire and sulphur. At the place where they were swallowed up is a lake—or rather, as mentioned above, an impassable abyss.

Scripture is accustomed also to call it [Col. 1597A] the Dead Sea or the exceedingly salt sea (Josh. 3:16; Deut. 3:17 ff.), both because it can produce or sustain nothing living and because it is proved, by taste and touch, to be bitter—more bitter than anything else. It has no outlet anywhere, unless perhaps underground; it receives no river save the Jordan from the north, which is also why it is appropriately called a lake. Its length extends southward for nearly seven hundred stadia, and its breadth measures one hundred and fifty stadia.

Hence it is more reasonably believed to have been the dwelling-place of a people once criminal. When divine severity judged that the impurity of that people could no longer be endured, the earth opened with a vast chasm and swallowed up that wicked people, consumed by sulphurous fires twisted down from heaven. That gulf must then be believed to have been filled with the abyss and occupied by salinity. The king therefore, and the army with him, went around this lake and entered the mountains of Arabia from the south. They then came into a valley exceedingly fertile in every fruit of the earth. There they found also the spring which holy Moses, at the Lord’s command, is said to have drawn from a rock by striking it twice with his rod. It flows perpetually with living water, so abundantly that its stream can power very active mills and never dries up in any drought.

There they also found an oratory, still called that of Saint Aaron, situated on a mountain summit. There Aaron himself and his brother Saint Moses are said to have been accustomed to hold divine conversation. Whether it is true, however, that the meeting-place of God and the holy brothers is still said to remain there, to be seen, and to be entered, let those judge who first published such an opinion. For we perform the task proper to history, simply reporting both events and the opinions entertained concerning them.

In the aforesaid valley, abundantly supplied with every kind of provision, the Christian army could find scarcely any inhabitants. Since they were prevented from advancing farther by a very broad, utterly vast, and dreadful wilderness, they resolved to return to Jerusalem. When they had returned, the negotiation for reconciling Patriarch Daimbert with the king and the canons of the Holy Sepulchre was, by God’s favour, carefully and effectively completed. It was also agreed that the king should be crowned at Bethlehem when the day of the Lord’s Nativity [Col. 1597B] drew near, and at last all approved that the matter ought not to be further delayed.

For some argued that a human king ought not to be crowned where the King of Heaven is known to have been crowned with thorns; nor ought a man presume to take as a mark of honour the crown which Christ the Lord deigned to bear in the disgrace of mockery. But what, I ask, what does this argument matter? For whatever disgrace or labour Christ endured wholly turns to our honour. Just as Christ’s death is the cause of our life, so Christ’s mockery is our badge of honour. Is not every Christian, through that crown of Christ, made “a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9)? Certainly the fact that Christ the Lord deigned to be crowned with thorns ought to be thought of as serving rather to honour than to diminish royal honour.

Accordingly, although it was an act of praiseworthy humility that King Duke Godfrey is said, for this reason, to have refused to be crowned, it is not unreasonable that his brother Duke Baldwin was anointed in the Christian manner by Christians and crowned.

The year 1101 from the Incarnation of the Lord was therefore the first year of the second king of Jerusalem, namely Duke Baldwin. Although at the beginning of his reign he possessed few cities and did not yet have an abundant military force, nevertheless the neighbouring peoples greatly feared to attack him, knowing well that he was a most vigorous warrior. What grieved him especially was that he could not assemble as large an army as he wished. For the road was still greatly obstructed for pilgrims travelling to Jerusalem, since the enemy held every harbour except that of Joppa. Consequently passage from the western regions to the eastern was extremely difficult. The Jerusalemite region was still largely empty—not merely of defenders, but even of inhabitants. Of those whom Christian devotion led from lands beyond the sea through so many and such great dangers to see and venerate the holy places, few wished to remain there for long. Horses which those who stayed could either buy or receive as a gift from the king could scarcely be found. Therefore the royal army could scarcely possess more than three hundred knights; and it was exceedingly dangerous even to gather these from the guard-posts assigned them: both because they themselves might be intercepted one by one by the enemy on the road, and because the enemy might retake the cities or castles when almost every defender, apart from women, was absent [Col. 1597C].

For the foot-soldiers scarcely sufficed to fortify or guard Jerusalem, Ramla, Joppa, and the fortress of Caiphas. I have recalled these things so that those who read or hear them may perceive how many and how great were the labours, fears, and anguishes endured for Christ by those earliest possessors of the land or region of Jerusalem; and so that it may be understood that it was no less miraculous for so extensive a region afterwards to have been retained by such sparse possessors and defenders than it was originally to conquer it.

It is therefore evident that in all these events the gracious working of Christ the Lord may be seen, His power admired, and His mercy contemplated. For who hears that so great a country was held and defended by three hundred knights among countless and exceedingly populous enemy nations—Syria, Arabia, Egypt, Persia, and Mesopotamia—and readily believes it? This is truly incredible if human strength alone is considered. But if the Almighty is faithfully considered and devoutly acknowledged—He who does whatever He wills in heaven and on earth—it ceases indeed to seem impossible and begins rather to be wonderful: wonderful, certainly, but not pitiable.

For to labour for Christ the Lord is more glorious in proportion as it is more blessed: “Because you shall eat the labour of your hands, you are blessed,” says Scripture, “and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127:2); and the most blessed Apostle says: “If we suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, we are blessed” (1 Pet. 3:14). Therefore we too, with that same Apostle, suitably dare to call blessed those whom we know to have sweated through countless and immense labours and struggles on the road and in the Holy Land.

Nor were the Antiochenes free from the same labours—indeed, not excluded from the same rewards. They were especially distressed at that time because, after Bohemond’s capture, as mentioned above, they scarcely dared to leave their walls without their prince or leader, while also enduring the most frequent enemy raids and assaults. Therefore, providing for their abandonment, they summoned Bohemond’s kinsman Tancred by envoys in the same year and assigned to him the principality of both the city and the region, on the condition that, should Bohemond ever return by God’s mercy, nothing in his recovered duchy would be prejudiced [Col. 1597D].

When Tancred decided to depart, either from affection for his kinsman or desire for a greater principality, he made peace with King Baldwin and entrusted to his fidelity the lordship of his fortress of Caiphas and of the city of Tiberias. In the same year the Genoese Italians, wintering at Laodicea with a rather numerous fleet, sailed at the beginning of spring as far as Joppa. Having secured their ships’ station in the harbour, they proceeded with the king, who had come out to receive them most joyfully, as far as Jerusalem.
