After celebrating the Easter solemnity there, they returned to Joppa and made the following compact with the king: “When we proceed together to conquer the enemy’s cities or fortresses, the king and his men shall receive the first and second shares of money; the Genoese shall receive the third, and shall always hold one street in every captured fortress or city.” Allied in this way, they first besieged the town most hostile to pilgrims on the Holy Way, namely Arsuf, which King Godfrey had besieged but not taken.

Indeed, that king had lost there nearly one hundred Franks after a wooden tower had been brought up to the wall but had broken into pieces under the excessive weight of those climbing it, hurling them to the ground. Before the eyes of grieving Christians, the Saracens immediately crucified some of them, killed others with arrows, and put others to death by other gibbets. Those Christians who had been with King Godfrey, not forgetting this outrage prepared so cruelly against their companions, gathered so eagerly to destroy the ungodly that they drove them to despair of resistance, despite their defence with all their strength.

Knowing therefore that they could neither resist for long nor escape the punishments and deaths they deserved if captured, the inhabitants began to negotiate by envoys for surrendering the fortress to the king if their lives and money were granted them. The king and the Genoese consuls having weighed the matter in counsel, it seemed good to all that so great a danger should be removed from the besiegers and also from Christian pilgrims without risk. Thus life and possessions were granted to the townspeople. The fortress, recovered and carefully fortified, was cleared of the ungodly, who were conducted with all their belongings as far as Ascalon.

From there the siege was transferred to the very strongly fortified city of Caesarea in Palestine. The besieged Caesareans mocked the besiegers, provoking them with insults and abuse, being highly confident in their walls and defensive works. By the king’s order, engines were prepared, many ladders were brought to be set against the walls, and a wooden tower was constructed from ships’ masts, high enough to exceed the walls’ height by twenty cubits. Huge stones were hurled with force against the fortifications; the solid structures of the towers were shaken by repeated blows; and nothing thought capable of overcoming the ungodly was left untried.

Nor was the ingenuity of the besieged in defending themselves any less: by day and by night they took no rest, but were always found prepared to resist. For fifteen days the city was continually attacked, yet not taken. Wearied by so long a siege, the Christian army was ashamed and indignant that the ungodly and blasphemers were stronger in resisting a siege than they were in pressing it [Col. 1598A].

They therefore encouraged one another and challenged each other in word and example. Taking up their arms, they rushed with marvellous boldness and violence to the wall, raised ladders, climbed with their heads protected by shields, attacked the opposing enemies with swords and lances on the very battlements of the walls, slew some there, and hurled others down. They made a free way for their companions to climb after them and now fought with the enemy on equal terms. The wall became Christian, though it had just been Saracen. Thrown down from the wall, the Saracens fled swiftly to stronger positions; but the Christians pursued more swiftly.

The fleeing men were packed together, and while each strove to outstrip the other toward a hiding-place, they impeded themselves, so that a hiding-place which might have been one person’s became no one’s. Crowds were massed upon heaps of fallen slain men, and all were killed indiscriminately in slaughter, as though wheat were being threshed on a threshing-floor. Neither sex nor age was spared, so that the wrath of God might be fulfilled upon the blasphemers.

The emir of the city and the archadius—for thus the Saracens call their bishop—were captured and brought before the king. They were ordered to be kept alive and bound, I believe in hope of money rather than from any feeling of compassion. Those taken alive were first struck on the neck with fists and forced to vomit up Byzantine coins concealed inside their mouths, within their gums. Those who did not vomit them were killed, piled together in a heap, and burned, lest either gold swallowed by the wicked should be lost or the air should be corrupted by the stench rising from the bodies of the slain.

For these most wicked people were accustomed, when they foresaw that they were about to die, to swallow their gold in this way or hide it in their mouths, begrudging it to the victors even in death. Women too, more shamefully and obscenely than is fitting to relate, were compelled, as they were about to die, to expose gold coins hidden within themselves. Thus, when almost all the Caesareans had been consigned to death, very few of either sex were reserved, either to carry away and gather the corpses of the slain or to be sold into slavery. Once the city had been captured, the quantity of money, the abundance of every kind of provision, and the number, quality, beauty, and costly material of the utensils found and amassed there can scarcely be estimated, much less described. This may be sufficiently judged from the fact that many who had previously been poor thereafter became quite wealthy.

[Col. 1602D] After the city of Caesarea had been taken by storm and entrusted for guarding to prudent and valiant men, it was reported—and confirmed by all the messengers who brought the news—that the Babylonians, gathered at Ascalon, were preparing war against the Christians. Therefore the king and the Christian army hastened to the city of Ramla, near Lydda, and prepared themselves to meet the war being prepared against them. Knowing this, the Babylonians cunningly delayed coming against the Christians who were ready for them; instead, they waited to be approached near their own walls and within their own entrenchments, so that they might either conquer more easily or, if defeated, withdraw into their fortifications. When their stratagem was understood, the Christians preferred to foil cunning by comparable cunning rather than, being few and unfortified, attack innumerable enemies who were fortified. At last, seeing that their stratagem was of no avail, and wearied by delay and hunger, the Ishmaelites [Col. 1603A] dispersed in various directions. When the king and his men learned this, they returned joyfully and eagerly to Jaffa, praising Christ the Lord above all things for the benefits He had bestowed upon them.

But two months later, when the king was informed that his enemies had again assembled at Ascalon in renewed hostility against him, he too gathered at Jaffa as large an army as he could: namely, two hundred and sixty knights and nine hundred foot-soldiers. With these he was to fight against eleven thousand cavalry and twenty thousand infantry. Who can hear this without shuddering? Was this audacity, or confidence? Must it be attributed to rashness, or to courage? For it might seem that they wished not to fight, but to die. And indeed it was so: they were prepared to die, but for Him who deigned to suffer death for them. Therefore this was not audacity but faith; not rashness but charity. For, as the Apostle says, since Christ suffered in the flesh (1 Pet. 4:1), they too armed themselves with the same purpose. Hence they carried with them the wood of salvation itself, that on which Christ suffered in the flesh, having in it their particular—indeed, their whole—consolation.

The former rush forth from Ascalon; the latter advance from Jaffa. When they had now come within sight of one another, the king, having arranged his army in six divisions, addressed them in these words:

> “Come then, soldiers of Christ! You see what you sought from regions so distant, through so many and such great perils of sea and land. You came willingly to offer your lives to danger for Christ; you have found that for which you came. Let not cowardice reject what holy devotion sought and at last [Col. 1603C] found. Since you are to fight for the Lord, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of His might. The Almighty is able to save you. Always remember and fix deeply in your minds His most sweet promises, by which He most graciously consoles both your small numbers and your poverty, saying: ‘Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom’ (Luke 12:32).
>
> “If you were thinking only of the wages or gifts of an earthly king, you would rightly tremble, fearing either defeat or death. For one who knows that an eternal kingdom has been prepared by the eternal King for the dying ought rather to regard death as desirable when he goes into battle. Whether we die in this battle or escape, we cannot doubt our victory. If we seem defeated in the sight of the wicked and foolish, by dying before them and coming to Christ, our joy, we triumph more greatly over the devil and the world. But if, as our Christ has often done, He should here also wish to preserve our bodies and grant us victory over these enemies, we shall indeed meanwhile be less glorious than if we died; yet, by the gift of Christ the Lord, we shall acquire a great name, surpassing the name of the great men who are on earth. Let no one ever think of flight, for our France is far too distant from us.”

Thus encouraged by these and similar words of the king, all advanced to battle, unable to bear any longer the postponement of the encounter. The trumpets resounded, and all together cried out: “Come, O God, help us!” They plunged into the broadest and densest ranks of the enemy, striking down all whom they met. Nor did they find the enemy altogether unwarlike; rather, they found them resisting with all their strength. For the enemy enveloped the two divisions which had advanced first and, by their overwhelming numbers, almost utterly destroyed them. Many Christians fell, and more were wounded. They endured the assaults of the wicked and, attacking in turn, bravely compelled them to retreat.

The king, who had remained at the rear with his division, when he saw the denser enemy cohorts, ran up and, transforming himself wholly from king into soldier, hurled some from their horses to the ground with his lance and cleft others in two upon their saddles with his sword. He summoned his men, encouraged those pressing forward, and, having heartened them, charged against the enemy. He caused the Lord’s Cross always to be borne before them and carried into the faces of the wicked, so that by its presence the servants of the Cross might be strengthened and their enemies confounded. [Col. 1604B] Unable any longer to endure its power, just as demons cannot endure it, so too the satellites of demons, struck with a sudden heaven-sent terror, turned to flight. They began to drive one another onward, and some fell upon others. Their pursuers pressed upon the fugitives and struck down all whom they were able to overtake. Those who were with the king all rushed to the sword, he himself more bravely than all, pursuing the fugitives and cutting them down. All shouted, and with confused cries heaven itself was assailed. A tremendous din rang out from the clash of weapons, the striking of helmets, and swords; everywhere were heard the groans and wailings of the dying and the wounded.

Thus, on the side on which the saving wood of the Lord’s Cross had been borne and brought against the enemy, the enemies were defeated and driven in flight as far as Ascalon, the king and his men—or rather the Cross of Christ—pursuing them; so that the Babylonian commander himself was afterwards found there dead amid five thousand dead men. But on the other side, from which the Cross of Christ had been farther removed, the Saracens, having slain for the most part the Christians whom they encountered, advanced as far as Jaffa. Ignorant of their own men’s flight and of our side’s victory, they boasted that they had killed the king and all the Christians in battle, displaying to the people of Jaffa, watching from the wall, the arms of those who had been killed as proof of their lie. The people of Jaffa grieved deeply; yet they did not immediately surrender the city to the attackers, as the latter had vainly hoped, but waited to hear whether some sadder or happier news might come from the battle.

The king and his men, returning from pursuit of the enemy, could not reach Jaffa. Having rested that night in the enemy tents themselves, which the fugitives had left full of every kind of provision, the next day, after Mass of the Nativity of the glorious Virgin Mary had been celebrated there, he returned to Jaffa, with pack animals laden in abundant quantity with goods found in those same tents. Five hundred Arabs returning from Jaffa met those returning to Jaffa: they were the men who had rushed there the previous day as if victorious, splendidly arrayed in Christian arms collected on the battlefield, and bearing threats and some plunder which they had seized around Jaffa. The Arabs supposed that those whom they encountered were Saracens wishing, as they themselves had done, to attack Jaffa; consequently they met them not merely without fear but rejoicing. [Col. 1605A] Yet the Christians, recognizing them first, rushed most swiftly upon these unsuspecting men; they struck some down and pursued others as they turned to flee. For the enemy had not the resolve to resist even for a moment. Thus scattered, each fled as swiftly as he could. Christ, plainly, so ordained it that those who had conquered one part of His people should return only as defeated men, and that so great a victory might appear attributable only to the power of the Lord’s Cross. Yet the Christians did not pursue the fugitives longer, being exhausted by the previous day’s toil and by their wounds.

Meanwhile Christians who had escaped from the battle by night flight had come by byways to Jaffa, reporting what they themselves believed true: that the king and all the other [Col. 1605B] Christians had perished in battle. All the people of Jaffa grieved, and the queen especially was sorrowful unto death. They wrote to Tancred by a certain sea-messenger and, with every entreaty, lamentably begged him, after entrusting the principality of Antioch to another, to bring aid to the endangered people of Jerusalem, since the king and his men had now, as they thought, been slain in battle by the men of Ascalon and Babylon. Tancred grieved at the common calamity and anxiously considered how he might bring the aid requested to the people of God. The messenger bearing these reports had departed. That same day the king arrived with the remainder of the army and, by his presence, cleared away from the people of Jaffa the harsh cloud of grief and sorrow brought on by false reports. A second messenger was also sent to Tancred with news of the happy outcome, so that the anxiety caused by the earlier message might be dispelled by the later one. Then they returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and the holy Cross was honorably received and placed in the Holy Place. With the enemies, by God’s favor, thus repelled and checked, eight months followed free from the storms of war.

In the year 1102, it was heard at Jerusalem that the Babylonians had again assembled at Ascalon: some twenty thousand cavalry and ten thousand infantry, sent by the king of Babylon, not counting the camel-drivers, who led camels and asses laden with provisions while carrying both clubs and missiles in their hands for battle. All these men set out together from Ascalon and first approached Ramla, devastating all the crops already ripe, while pitching their camp [Col. 1605D] near the city. They also undertook to storm the city’s strongly fortified episcopal residence, located beside the church of St. George. When they could not prevail, they turned to attack the fifteen knights who guarded the citadel of Ramla, hating them especially because the Ascalonite raiders, owing to their frequent encounters with them, were not allowed to range freely wherever they wished.

The bishop, therefore, wishing to provide for himself and for the rescue of the city, made the matter known to the king, who was staying at Jaffa, by a swift messenger, urgently imploring speedy aid. At that time there were with the king there many distinguished and noble men: Count Stephen of Blois, Count Stephen of Burgundy, Geoffrey of Vendôme, and Hugh of Lusignan, brother of Count Raymond. Although the course of events here stretches too far back, it nevertheless seems not inappropriate to recall that all these men, together with Hugh the Great and William, count of Poitou, had in the first expedition set out for Jerusalem with the others and reached Antioch. But from there, wishing for different reasons to return to their own lands before completing the journey, they came to the farthest regions of Romania, accompanied by very numerous bodies of pilgrims. There, Soliman the Turk, not forgetting that they had taken Nicaea from him—or rather God, the righteous Judge, punishing their cowardice because they had not fulfilled the good and holy purpose of their sacred pilgrimage—destroyed one hundred thousand of them, horsemen and foot-soldiers alike, by various deaths. Those who could escape were compelled, after many and very great losses, to return once more to Antioch; Hugh the Great had earlier died at Tarsus in Cilicia.

When those travelling to Jerusalem by land had reached Tortosa, while no small portion went by sea, they undertook to storm Tortosa by land and sea. They left the captured city to Count Raymond, who preferred to remain there rather than go to Jerusalem, though he had played a sufficiently prominent part in taking it. The others then came for the first time to the Jerusalem which they had vowed to the Lord, by His ordering finally to fulfill their vow in this manner. Hearing of their arrival, King Baldwin met them at the narrow pass of Beirut, of which enough has been said above, waiting for them there for seventeen days lest, if the narrow path were first occupied by the Saracens, they should be unable to pass. Having received there the pilgrims of that second expedition and led them joyfully and gladly to the holy places at Jerusalem, many of them returned with the king to Jaffa, most awaiting a favorable wind in order to sail to France.

While they were there with the king, when he received the bishop’s report concerning aid to be brought to the people of Ramla, the king seized his weapons and, quite imprudently and with excessive impetuosity, mounted his horse, saying nothing to anyone except that they should follow him. Trumpets resounded and clarions blared. Those who could or wished followed the king, who rode on before, though they did not know where. For he relied too greatly on his own prowess and, when in such matters he ought to have depended on God alone, rashly trusted wholly in himself. His rashness was severely punished: God, who resists the proud, opposed him, so that he was not, as usual, victorious but barely escaped defeated. First, he did not cease to ride at a rapid pace as far as the enemy camp; when he saw how exceedingly extensive and crowded it was, he was struck by overwhelming terror and groaned deeply, grieving most bitterly and repenting too late of his rashness. He was reduced to such extremity that he could neither return to Jaffa, having been seen and almost surrounded by the enemy, nor, almost alone, fight against so many thousands of foes.

Still, looking back toward his men, scarcely two hundred knights of whom had been able to keep up with him as he hastened forward, he said: “Come, most valiant soldiers of Christ. Since we have come to this, that we can in no way avoid battle, let us fight bravely; nor let us die as cowards usually die. For we know that whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” [Col. 1607A] (Rom. 14:8). With these words all hurled themselves upon the enemy in a bold assault; but, surrounded on every side by wheeling Turks, they made little progress. Many fell, though not before killing many enemies. At last those who remained, no longer doubting that they were about to die unless they could save themselves by flight, temporarily withdrawing from the pressure of battle, rushed at full speed into Ramla.

But the king, and the noble and most valiant fighters who surrounded him, although they likewise could have entered Ramla, refused to do so, preferring to die rather than be shut up there. Therefore, with scarcely five knights joining him, he made for the mountains with one of them, while the remaining four were pursued by three hundred of the enemy. Thus, with God protecting him, the king meanwhile escaped, wandering through the mountains or hiding there that night. Meanwhile the enemy attacked the guardians of the fortress of Ramla and—alas, grief upon grief!—took it by storm. The bishop himself, abandoning the fortification of his episcopal residence, fled to Jaffa.

Many sufficiently distinguished and noble men fell in this battle, among them especially Stephen, the most illustrious count of the men of Blois, and Stephen, the most illustrious count of Burgundy. On the third day, the king, nearly exhausted by hunger and hardship, at last barely made his way into his town of Arsuf with only one knight and his armor-bearer. Gladly received by his people, restored by food, drink, and sleep, he recovered strength. Thus the Lord indeed chastised him justly, yet corrected him kindly: He struck down the proud man but raised him up once struck down, so that he might sing that saying of the Prophet: “The Lord has severely chastened me, but He has not delivered me over to death” (Ps. 117 [118]:18).

For on that very day on which the king escaped to Arsuf, behold, one of his nobles, Hugh of Tiberias, having received an embassy from Jerusalem instructing him to hasten to the aid of the people of Jaffa, met the king there with eighty knights and splendidly cheered his desolation and distress by however small a restoration of military strength. Yet the king did not dare to travel overland to Jaffa even with them; rather, conveyed by a small boat over the sea, he reached Jaffa before those travelling by land. He was joyfully received by his men, all rejoicing and weeping for joy because they had received safe the man whom they had mourned as dead. “The king was dead,” they said, “and has come to life; he was lost, and has been found” (Luke 15:24). Taking the knights whom he found there, he met Hugh as he approached according to their arrangement, and thus returned with them to Jaffa.

Moreover, he summoned all Christians from Jerusalem and from St. Abraham, and renewed the war against the Arabs, who were preparing even to besiege Jaffa. Yet they too suffered exceedingly dangerous enemy ambushes on the road, although nearly one hundred and one knights or horsemen assembled at Jaffa. Nevertheless, through God’s mercy they escaped and finally reached Jaffa, while the enemy pursued them as far as the gates; they were joyfully received by the king, especially because they had brought with them the unique hope and strength of all Christians—the sign of the glorious Cross, the wood of salvation. Encouraged by its presence, all were greatly invigorated, as though recovered from a severe illness. The following morning, arranged in companies by divisions, they advanced against the enemy, who had pitched their camp about three miles from the city and were there preparing their engines for the assault upon Jaffa.

When the enemy, contrary to expectation, saw the Christians advancing to battle against them, they too prepared themselves, boldly met those who came against them, and resisted in a strong fight. The innumerable surrounded the few and compelled them to hope in divine aid alone. As the Christians most devoutly prayed that this aid might be present, Christ, the merciful hearer, did not long fail those who cried to Him. Mercifully granting His own strength and protection, He miraculously terrified the enemy and turned them to flight. For the knights and cavalry, penetrating with most steadfast force the enemy masses gathered around them, then turning back toward their infantry and making a renewed charge while defending themselves most bravely, struck down those they met and scattered the crowded ranks; at last they pursued them when they had been put to flight. Thus those who shortly before had been discussing the capture of the men within the city as though already captured, as they vainly supposed, now, shamefully defeated, strove only to escape. They abandoned their camp, taking nothing from their tents, and left both their pay and weapons to the victors, glad merely to have rescued their naked bodies from danger. Finally, some died from excessive thirst while fleeing. Few would have escaped death had not the victors’ small numbers, and the toil of killing those whom they overtook, burdened the exhausted pursuers.

Thus in the later battle the enemies were defeated by those whom they themselves had defeated in the earlier one. The difference was that, in that former battle, the rashness of men trusting in themselves was confounded; whereas in this one, the faith and humility of men relying on the power of the Lord’s Cross were glorified by the triumph of their victory. “The horse,” Scripture says, “is prepared for the day of battle; but the Lord gives salvation” (Prov. 31:21). The Lord indeed gave salvation, but fittingly: saving the humble people and humbling the eyes of the proud, so that no flesh might glory before Him, instructed not to hope in its own bow and sword, but to sing with its whole heart to its Savior: “For Thou hast saved us from those who afflict us, and hast confounded those who hate us” (Ps. 53 [54]:9).

Let not pride, then, when corrected for its perversity, in its folly blame God in its heart; lest, if its arrogance murmurs against the righteous scourge, its madness deserve either to be bound in an eternal prison or tormented by everlasting punishment. Therefore let not the foolish man look to the outcome as fortune; rather, let the moderate man weigh the deserts of events, so that he may understand that there is always a just order in things, although confusion always clings to his own perverse opinion. The war having ended, and the enemy’s tents—with all their spoils and with very many camels and asses—having been collected or plundered by the victors, the king and his men returned to Jaffa with great joy, passing the whole subsequent autumn and winter peacefully, through the mercy of God and Christ, free from war.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1103, the fourth year after the City was captured—or rather recovered—when the Christians had celebrated Holy Easter at Jerusalem according to custom, [Col. 1609A] the king, with such an army as he could muster, besieged a very strongly fortified city, called formerly, as is thought, Acaron, then Ptolemais, but now named either Acre or again Acaron. Acre was then besieged by the Christians, but not taken, both because it was surrounded by a very strong wall and outer wall, and because it had many and vigorous defenders. Accordingly, the siege and assault of this city were for the moment abandoned. After destroying their crops, ravaging their gardens, and cutting down their shrubs, the king and his men returned to Jaffa.

While there he was made joyful by welcome and highly useful news: he learned that Lord Bohemond had, through God’s mercy, returned free from captivity and recovered his principality of Antioch. Bohemond also recovered Laodicea, which Tancred had later seized and which had been taken away by the men of the emperor of Constantinople; and he suitably made peace with Tancred, who had become his associate in the principality. At this time, while King Baldwin was fighting most vigorously against the Saracens as usual, it happened that, as he pursued fleeing enemies, an Ethiopian lying hidden behind a rock hurled a missile with force and inflicted a treacherous wound from behind, below his shoulder blade. Only after some time was he restored through God’s mercy; yet the scar secretly retained the nascent effect of his death, which would come much later.

In 1104, after the king and Christian army had celebrated Holy Easter at Jerusalem according to custom, they resumed the siege of Ptolemais, or Acre, which had been discontinued in the previous year. The Genoese, with a fleet of seventy beaked warships, joined them for the assault upon the city. After they had for a long time pressed it hard by land and sea, with siege engines and frequent assaults, they at last, after twenty days, compelled the besieged to surrender themselves and their city. Having expelled them, they took possession of the city, now free. It was especially necessary and altogether useful to the Christians because within its walls it possessed an excellent harbor: the sea extended into the middle of the city, and at its pleasant ebb provided an anchorage for ships. All the enemies’ goods fell to the Christians as booty; many of the enemies were killed, while some were permitted to live.

In the same year, when summer had already passed, Bohemond, handing over the principality of Antioch wholly to his colleague Tancred, himself set out for Apulia with a few men. He crossed by ship, which he did only rarely, in order to gather such military force as he could from the regions beyond the sea and bring it back with him. The venerable patriarch of Jerusalem, Daimbert, also crossed with him and, setting out for Rome in order to return to his see with the authority of the Roman pontiff, died on the journey, a pilgrim. In his place the king and people of Jerusalem then confirmed as their bishop Lord Arnulf, who had been elected long before.

In the following year, that is, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1105, Count Raymond died in his town not far from Tripoli, and his nephew William, surnamed Jordan, assumed the government of the dead man’s county. [Col. 1610A] While Tancred was administering the principality of Antioch, the king of Aleppo, named Ridwan, brought war upon him with an exceedingly large army and compelled him to meet him in battle with the Antiochenes, few indeed, but strong in Christ’s power. The battle was joined; the men of Aleppo were defeated, and the Antiochenes were victorious. Christ the Lord fought for His faithful and defended His own and their enemies so wonderfully that, although the Christian army was exceedingly small, the number of unbelievers killed by it was beyond counting. Thus those whom both their own multitude and the Christians’ small numbers had encouraged to fight against Christ, because they refused to know Christ’s power by faith, were compelled to know it in the shame of their blasphemy.

Having thus been glorified in the Antiochenes, let us continue by telling how wondrously Christ deigned to be glorified among the people of Jerusalem in that same year. For the admiral of Babylon, learning how few Christians were in the Holy Land, sent Semelmuch, commander of his forces, to Ascalon with fifteen thousand armed men, giving them these commands: that, after utterly exterminating from those lands the Christian people and name, they should also dig up with impious hands that most sacred Sepulchre of Christ the Lord and scatter it in fragments, “so that worshippers of the Buried One may no longer gather there from the western kingdoms out of love for the sepulchre.” He made those whom he sent to carry out this service of such impiety swear an oath: “never to turn their backs in battle, nor to return until the destruction of the Christians had been accomplished.”

Hearing of this obstinate malice of their enemies, the king and Christians assembled at Jaffa all throughout his kingdom who were able to bear arms, leaving only very few men in each place to guard the walls. Yet the enemy remained assembled at Ascalon and the Christians at Jaffa for some time, neither side seeking the other. At last the raging arrogance of the wicked burst forth against the people of the righteous, and the Babylonians from Ascalon and the Christians from Jaffa met near Ramla. There the king and his men, placed in the utmost anxiety, sent a messenger to the patriarch and the rest who had remained in Jerusalem, earnestly asking them not to cease in their extremity to implore divine aid for them, since they knew battle would certainly take place on the following day.

When he learned this, the patriarch gathered all the clergy and the whole people, announced the day of battle and the common danger, and urged them to seek Christ’s mercy. He exhorted them to devote themselves more earnestly on that day and the following one to fasting, prayers, and almsgiving, so that while the king and his men fought with swords, they might fight alongside them with the better weapons of prayers and alms:

> “Especially,” he said, “let us strive by visiting the sick and showing mercy to the poor to make God favorable to us; for God is won by such sacrifices.” And, as Scripture says elsewhere, “Does He leave a blessing behind Him?” (Joel 2:14).
>
> “And I,” said the patriarch, “will set out, if I can, God willing, for Ramla on the coming night, accompanied by these brethren whom you see, about [Col. 1611A] to carry with us there the unique hope and strength of the Christian people—the trophy of the most precious Cross of Christ.”

At first light, the patriarch and his party, travellers by night, reached Ramla, while the people of Jerusalem filled the churches throughout the night and the following Sunday, walked barefoot, and wept before God, omitting absolutely nothing through which they might hope to gain divine mercy. The king and his men, greatly encouraged and strengthened by the presence of the patriarch and the glorious Cross, went to the priests; each confessed his sins, prepared himself to receive death faithfully, and was strengthened by reception of the Lord’s Body and Blood. Having diligently done these things beforehand, they were drawn up for battle and advanced in divisions: scarcely five hundred knights and two thousand foot-soldiers against fifteen thousand Saracens, who had pitched their camp scarcely four miles from Ramla and were preparing, with a smaller part of their army, to advance upon Ramla, while sending the larger part to seize Jaffa, which they hoped to find empty of defenders.

But when, contrary to their expectation, they saw the king and the Christian army advancing so boldly against them so early in the morning, the cunning scheme which they had vainly contrived was scattered. Regrouping, they were compelled instead to consider immediately how to join battle. They too therefore arranged their battle-lines and boldly advanced against those who approached, trusting in their numbers. The Christians, trusting rather in Christ than in their numerical strength, entered the contest courageously with their customary cry: “Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands.” Shouting against the Saracens and assaulting them with all their strength, they made very violent charges, one against another. The many attempted to surround the very few; and especially the Turks, wheeling about from the rear, strove to enclose and strike down with arrows the Christians, who were intent upon attacking those before them.

Seeing this, the king with his division exposed himself wholly to danger. He opposed himself most resolutely to the Turks and, with God helping the right cause of the Church, compelled them to scatter in a most vigorous charge. From there he plunged into the larger and denser phalanxes of Arabs and Ethiopians; by repeated and powerful assaults he finally broke through the enemy’s densest wedges, through God’s mercy, killing some and turning the rest to flight. Those who could escape fled as far as Ascalon. The Christians, massed together behind them, pursued the fugitives and first of all killed the very admiral of Ascalon, Gemelmuch. When his death became known, Semelmuch, commander of the Babylonian king’s forces, saved his life by flight. Having abandoned all hope of victory in battle, he preferred to live as a perjurer rather than perish in keeping an accursed oath. Those who could followed their leader’s example and, as has been said, put life before their oath, fleeing wherever and by whatever route each could.

The admiral, once captured at Acre and spared by the king, had later been ransomed for twenty thousand gold pieces. The Ethiopians, because they were unable to flee, nearly all perished, slaughtered in the field. In all, four thousand slain were counted, while scarcely sixty [Col. 1612A] Christians fell. Returning from pursuit of the enemy, the Christians plundered the camp of the defeated victors and, laden with abundant spoils, returned to Jaffa with the greatest joy, praising with all their hearts God who had made Himself favorable to them and glorifying Christ, their protector and helper, in whom they had displayed great power, since their enemies had been reduced to nothing.

Things even more wonderful follow upon wonders, when Christ, glorified by victory in the land battle, deigned also to be glorified in winds and sea. For the Babylonian fleet, having arrived at Jaffa on the very day of the battle with the greater part of its army, vainly hoped, once the Christians had been destroyed in the land battle, immediately to subdue Jaffa and all the other coastal cities. But when the situation was reversed, and it learned both that its own side had been defeated and that the Christians had prevailed, after the head of Gemelmuch, admiral of Ascalon, had been cut off and hurled at it by the royal sailors, it immediately withdrew into the harbors of Tyre and Sidon. As it then strove to sail to Babylon, it was driven by a storm wind: part of it perished by shipwreck, and part, driven into the port of Jaffa, offered itself to the people of Jaffa to be seized. It is reported that twenty-five ships, full of Saracens, were captured there at that time. Thus those who hoped and prepared by land and sea to destroy all Christians were themselves destroyed by land and sea, and were made “like a wheel, and like chaff before the face of the wind” (Ps. 82 [83]:12).

But the merciful Lord, who had gladdened His people with so magnificent a consolation on the sixth day before the Kalends of September [27 August], in that same declining year, on the very eve of the Lord’s Nativity, shook the whole of Jerusalem with a very terrible earthquake and struck all hearts with overwhelming terror. He was admonishing the people of Jerusalem that, although they rejoiced in the benefits bestowed upon them by Him, they ought always to serve Him in fear.

And in the following year, namely 1106, a comet, appearing always in the evening for fifty days and more, filled the whole world at that time with astonishment and terror. It extended a pale-white ray of light toward the winter setting of the sun, like a strip of linen cloth. During the first days it appeared more flaming, but in the last it appeared dimmer, until, gradually fading away, after fifty days, as stated, it entirely ceased to be seen. [Col. 1612D] In those same days, namely in the middle of February, two things like suns appeared to the right and left of the sun. They did not shine equally with the central one, but glowed moderately with a less intense form and light. Around them two circles were seen, one enclosing the other. The outer one was wholly white; the inner, like a rainbow, was distinguished by four colors and extended from the upper side of the central Sun to the two adjoining suns in an arched embrace, while from below it ended as though divided in half. It is also reported that in the following month, one midnight, stars appeared to fall from heaven like rain. What these great and unusual prodigies portended has hitherto been less clearly established.

Yet in the regions of Jerusalem it happened in that same year that Hugh, duke of Tiberias, having twice been defeated by the Damascenes, on the third renewal of the war defeated the Damascenes so wonderfully that with one hundred and twenty fighting men he scattered four thousand armed men. Not long afterward, while on campaign with the king, he was struck down by an arrow.

In 1107 the men of Ascalon, boiling over with their accustomed fury, laid an ambush in the mountain passes for the people of Jaffa as they prepared to travel to Jerusalem, believing they could intercept and destroy them there. But the people of Jaffa, forewarned of the ambush prepared for them, sent ahead seventy-five scouts. These were suddenly so enclosed and cut off by about five hundred cavalry and a thousand infantry that they could neither return nor draw up for battle in any order other than that in which they already were. Having recognized the predicament, they chose rather, if it should happen, to die fighting than, by vainly attempting flight, to stain their death with the mark of cowardice. Praying to and at the same time hoping in Christ as their helper, they miraculously penetrated and scattered the enemy battle-line in their first assault so completely that the enemy could no longer regroup, but, by God’s will, had to strive for flight rather than battle. Many of them were killed; the rest were shamefully defeated and put to flight. Caught in the snare which they themselves had prepared, they fell into the pit which they had dug for the feet of the righteous.

In the same year, Bohemond returned from Gaul with large forces of soldiers and with a numerous fleet also prepared in the harbor of Brundisium. Sailing for Bulgaria, he at last landed at [Avlona?]; having taken it without delay, he proceeded to Dyrrhachium and besieged it. Because it was sufficiently supplied with defenders and provisions, he could not take it during a year’s siege. [Col. 1613C] Yet he was attempting, if by any means he could, to draw Emperor Alexius into war—Alexius, a most hostile enemy to Christians journeying as pilgrims to Jerusalem, and far worse and more cruel even than the Saracens themselves. When he could achieve this by no device, peace was at last both sought and confirmed through envoys: the emperor swore upon the most precious relics that thereafter he would inflict no injury upon pilgrims throughout his entire empire, but would faithfully protect and assist them; and Bohemond likewise swore peace and fealty to the emperor. This affair having been concluded, by God’s favor, Bohemond returned to Apulia with the smaller part of his army; the rest set out for Jerusalem, as they had [vowed?; *foverant* is perhaps *voverant*], [Col. 1613D] though many had been struck down and died during the siege of Dyrrhachium because of the excessive heat of the sun. Guy also died there, Bohemond’s brother. In that year Philip, king of the Franks, is said to have died, leaving his son Louis as successor to the kingdom.

In the year 1108, the eleventh after the capture of Jerusalem, Bertrand, son of Count Raymond, besieged Tripoli, having allied himself with the Genoese and their quite numerous fleet. Bertrand’s cousin William, surnamed Jordan, lord of the fortress called Mount Pilgrim, envied rather than rejoiced for Bertrand as he besieged Tripoli; he maintained that both the siege and capture of the city ought rather to be reserved and credited to himself. The one asserted a prior claim from paternal inheritance, the other from possession of the fortress. [Col. 1614A] While the siege was impeded by this discord and the capture postponed, King Baldwin came there, seeking, God willing, to win over the Genoese for the siege of Ascalon, Beirut, and Sidon. But while the king and the Genoese were negotiating to reconcile the kinsmen, Bertrand and William, William, riding by night, was struck by an arrow and killed—by whose treachery is uncertain. Thus he both ended the discord and hastened the undertaking of taking the city.

The besieged were hemmed in on every side by their besiegers and, forced to despair of life, were compelled to surrender themselves and the city. Yet they first obtained from the king, confirmed by oath, a treaty securing their lives and liberty, on these terms: after opening the gates, they were all to withdraw together into a part of the city and later go away from there wherever they wished. While this was taking place, by what event is indeed uncertain, lesser-ranking Genoese, mounting the wall amid a sudden tumult by ladders and ropes, entered the city; running about in bands, they cut down every Saracen they encountered—namely, those who had delayed in withdrawing to the place agreed upon. Indeed, the Genoese would likewise have slaughtered those who had already withdrawn, had not the king, learning of the matter, hurried to confront their fury and thus freed from death those received under his protection. Thus Count Bertrand possessed Tripoli, captured by the Christians with the king’s consent, having accordingly bound himself to the king by a compact of feudal homage. [Col. 1614B]

In the year 1110, before the month of February had passed, the king and the Christian army besieged Beirut, with Count Bertrand of Tripoli as their ally. After, I think, seventy-five days of siege, when the Christians had also shut up within the harbor with their fleet the ships which neighboring Saracens had brought to aid those enclosed, they at last took it, God helping them. They brought wooden towers against the wall, descended over the wall with marvelous boldness, leapt down from the wall into the city, and cut down every Saracen they met, whether on the walls or in the streets. Then, having opened the gates also to their companions, the entire army entered at once with full force, making a very great slaughter of the enemy and plundering all the wealth of the slain. At that time a comet again appeared for several nights, with its ray stretched far toward the south; God knows what it portended. [Col. 1614C–D]

At the same time Tancred and the Antiochenes requested the king of Jerusalem to come to their assistance against the Turks who were ravaging their territory. Crossing the Euphrates with him, they supplied Edessa more abundantly with provisions; but since the enemy gave them no opportunity to engage, the Antiochenes returned to Antioch, while the king and his men returned to Jerusalem.

Meanwhile certain Norsemen, borne from the western regions of the Ocean upon a most splendid fleet, had landed at Joppa, hastening to Jerusalem out of Christian devotion. They had as their leader the brother of the king of their own land, a very handsome young man. They were ready to remain longer in the Holy Land for Christ’s love, if the king wished, and to go with him by sea wherever he commanded, provided only that he would have necessary provisions supplied to them. The king gratefully accepted this and very willingly granted it. He therefore hastened to besiege Sidon by land, while the Norsemen besieged it by sea; having prepared engines to attack the city, they hemmed in the enemy from every side. At length, deprived both of the power to resist and of hope of escape, they compelled them to surrender, after first confirming by treaty the preservation of their lives. Thus the mercenary soldiers went away wherever they wished, while the country people remained, allied with and subject to the Christians. [Col. 1615A]

In the year 1111, a very great multitude of Turks poured out of Persia and, passing through Mesopotamia to the Euphrates, crossed the river and besieged for a long time the fortress called Turbessel, but could not take it. Departing from there and provoking Tancred and the Antiochenes with frequent raids, they compelled them again to request the aid and arrival of the king of Jerusalem. With him they went to Apamea—or rather Aleppo—a city very thoroughly taken by Tancred in the preceding year, and fortified it. Since they could not draw the Turks into battle, they compelled them to withdraw into their own territory, and each returned home.

Afterward the king besieged Tyre with much equipment and labored long to take it, but all his effort then proved ineffective. For the Saracens, in one night shooting from two towers of the wall, defended themselves with marvelous skill against the two wooden towers, taller than the wall, which had been brought up; at last they burned the engines and forced the king and his men to withdraw, greatly grieved that such prolonged labor had been wasted without result. [Col. 1615B–C]

The following year, namely 1112, the king and the people of Jerusalem enjoyed a respite from war through God’s mercy. The Antiochenes, however, found it sadder than usual, because Prince Tancred died, and his death emboldened the neighboring enemies to rise more insolently against them. Nevertheless Roger, kinsman of the deceased and made successor to the principality of Antioch, resisted the wicked men as far as he could.

In March 1113, it happened that the sun appeared from morning until the third hour as though a fourth part of its form had been removed—horned first at the upper side and then at the lower—yet it was not wholly deprived of its brightness. It is uncertain whether the sun then suffered an eclipse through the intervening conjunction of the moon on its twenty-eighth day, or whether this was some prodigy. Later, in the summer, the Turks assembled, crossed the Euphrates, passed through Syria between Damascus and Antioch, and then ranged through Phoenicia between Tyre and Pancada, which is also called Caesarea Philippi. Having also gone around the Sea of Galilee and traversed southward the lands of Naphtali and Zebulun, they finally enclosed themselves between the two rivers, the Jor and the Dan. They placed their camp upon an island, small indeed but surrounded by the rivers’ circuit and fortified on both sides by two bridges. [Col. 1615D]

This place was so advantageous and convenient for them that they could make raids from it wherever they wished, while they could not easily be attacked or hemmed in, being protected by the narrow passages of the bridges. When the king and his men, hearing of the enemy’s arrival, hurried to seize this place first, moving their army from Ptolemais, they fell into ambushes already prepared there by the enemy. The danger was so great that the king himself, having lost both his banner and his very fine tent, was forced to flee together with the patriarch; nearly thirty thousand men and twelve hundred infantrymen were killed—alas, grief upon grief! This also happened through the king’s utterly excessive and rash haste: without waiting for his troops, he had advanced far too unwisely and unconsideredly, and neither the count of Tripoli nor Roger, prince of Antioch, had yet joined him. When they arrived and heard what had happened, they blamed the king’s rashness and pitched their own camps upon the mountain overlooking the aforesaid island. [Col. 1616A]

The leader of those islanders was called Maledoctus. Having King Tuldequin of Damascus as his ally, he held that island for a long time; and they gave the Christians no opportunity to engage them. Yet the islanders could not be prevented by those on the mountain from coming out in bands, ravaging Christian lands, and carrying provisions into the island. Then even those Saracens who had been subject to the Christians deserted them, pressing them on every side and permitting no messenger to be sent from one group to another. Meanwhile the enemies seized Neapolis itself, anciently called Shechem or Sichima, and utterly plundered it. Men of Ascalon and Arabs advanced upon Jerusalem and seized the outer defensive wall of the city, setting fire to many harvests stored there; the following night they withdrew, to the rejoicing of the Jerusalemites. [Col. 1616B]

Neither those in the cities and towns nor those in the camps could learn anything about one another. So utterly confined were Christian affairs that not even the harvest—which had grown in great abundance that year—could be gathered; it was left in the fields to perish. The sea too was more disturbed than usual and denied the seacoast people even the ability to fish. The earth was shaken twice by a dreadful earthquake and threatened the ruin of buildings to mortals growing pale with fear. Deep silence possessed every Christian place; some image of death covered all the Christians there, stunned and almost bloodless with terror. All who had any sound understanding clearly recognized that this was God’s vengeance against them in his anger.

Thus afflicted for two whole months, the Christians at last recovered their breath when God had mercy, turning anger into favor. For, as forces of pilgrims arrived from beyond the sea, those islanders saw the Christian army growing day by day; terrified by God, they withdrew after two months toward Damascus, and the king and his men were able to return to Ptolemais. There the king found that the countess of Sicily had arrived, formerly the wife of Roger, brother of Robert Guiscard—later to become the king’s own wife. But Maledoctus, entering Damascus with King Tuldequin, was without delay, by God’s judgment, treacherously killed there by a certain assassin; he lost both the power of afflicting Christians and his life. He had once been a man exceedingly powerful among all the Turks in wealth and arms, and most cunning in every undertaking. [Col. 1616C–D]

[Col. 1617A] In the year 1114, first an infinite multitude of locusts flew in from the regions of Arabia and severely ravaged the territory of Jerusalem for several days. In April or May following, it was terribly shaken by an earthquake. Part of the city of Mamistra was overthrown; in the region of Antioch likewise many towns—some halfway, others entirely—were razed to the ground with part of their inhabitants. Likewise, in the city called Mariscus, the entire population was suffocated by sudden collapses of buildings and perished, alas, in a terrible and pitiable manner. In Euphratesia too, the town called Trihalec was utterly destroyed.

In 1115 the Turks returned in their customary insolence, setting up camp where they usually did between Antioch and Damascus, and again compelled the Jerusalemites and Antiochenes to unite against them. They also compelled Tuldequin, king of the Damascenes—who had become hostile to them after the death of Maledoctus, whom he had treacherously killed—to make peace with the Christians, fearing that he could not alone withstand their attack. But when the Turks learned that the Damascenes had allied themselves with the Christians and assembled for war against them, they withdrew secretly and hid in caves until they learned that the Christians had departed to Antioch, the Antiochenes [redundantly repeated in the text] to Antioch, the king with his men to Tripoli, and the Damascenes to their own homes, supposing that the Turks too had crossed the Euphrates and returned home. [Col. 1617B]

Meanwhile the men of Ascalon, thinking that the absence of the king and the Christian army had given them an opportunity to satisfy their fury, assembled against Joppa, strengthened by a Babylonian fleet of nearly seventy ships. They besieged it by land and sea and attacked it most vigorously, so that they even tried to climb the wall with ladders brought for that purpose and believed they could take the city. But although the citizens were very few and weak, they defended themselves most bravely. Since the attackers could not, under God’s protection of his own, accomplish what they vainly hoped, they set fire to and burned the city gates, then withdrew in confusion, fearing that the Jerusalemites might arrive and overwhelm them.

Yet after ten days they renewed the same siege by land and sea and attacked the city with most vigorous assaults. But God resisted these wicked men on behalf of his own; since they could achieve nothing, the impious men marveled at their own weakness and withdrew, carrying away many of their men slain there and having lost many of their horses as well. [Col. 1617C–D]

But the Turks mentioned above, learning that the Christians had departed, burst from their hiding places, again occupied the site of their customary station, and ranged through the regions of Syria, destroying by plunder and fire whatever towns or villages they could. This necessity again compelled the Antiochenes to assemble an army; they preferred to commit themselves to danger rather than be worn down so often by wicked men. Therefore, seeking and awaiting help neither from the Jerusalemites nor from the Damascenes but from God alone, although very few in number they nevertheless boldly sought out and attacked the innumerable enemy. Though the enemy resisted most fiercely, God fighting for them, they at last forced them to flee and to leave everything behind, even casting away their weapons and presenting their backs to the victors for flight. Three thousand of them were killed and very many captured. All the rest fled stripped so thoroughly of their tents, equipment, transport animals, and all their money that the captured horses, mules, and camels were beyond number; their gold was estimated at four hundred thousand pieces. Greater and more excellent than all this was the restoration of liberty to very many captive Franks and Syrians. Truly God is wonderful in all his works. [Col. 1618A]

Behold: when many Christians had been together, both Jerusalemites and Antiochenes, they either fled defeated or accomplished very little. Now that the Antiochenes were alone, though few in number, made strong by God, they routed, struck down, and captured the vast multitude of enemies whom their small number had summoned to battle. They took spoils so abundant that their quantity surpassed estimation, weight, and number. Why was this, except that the clearest signs might show that a human being ought to glory in nothing except God? For a man, powerless in himself, nevertheless dares to boast that he has accomplished valor through himself and not through God. Nothing can be more abominable or detestable before God than such presumption; conversely, nothing is more pleasing or acceptable than to understand with a truly humble and devout heart that he himself works all our works for us.

Yet he who, in mercy, so protected them by himself, also in justice chastened them by himself. In the same year he overthrew Mamistra by earthquake, shaking with similar terror that city once quite illustrious and many other places in Antiochene territory. In the same year Patriarch Arnulf was expelled from his see by a certain legate of the city of Rome; but, coming to Rome, he was restored to his see by the Roman people themselves. At this time also the king of Jerusalem went into Arabia and built a fortress upon a mountain naturally well fortified by its situation. He called this the Royal Mountain, placing suitable guards and settlers there, so that their presence might impede the raids of robbers and bandits breaking out from Arabia. The fortress is three days’ journey from the Red Sea and four days’ journey from Jerusalem. [Col. 1618B–D]

The Jerusalemites passed the year 1116 in peace from wars, God favoring them. In that year the king, traveling through Arabia with two hundred knights as far as the Red Sea itself, entered the city of Helim, the first stopping-place of the Israelites after their crossing of the Red Sea. It was then wholly empty of inhabitants, its people having entered the Red Sea in a vessel* out of fear of the king’s arrival. Having traveled along that shore of the sea and observed that the cause of its redness lay not in the water, which is very like the water of any other sea, but in the sand, the king returned with his men to the Royal Mountain and thence to Jerusalem. There, terrified by fear of death, he dismissed the countess of Sicily, whom he had not married lawfully, and was reconciled to his lawful wife, still living, whom he had dismissed because of love for a concubine. Thus the Lord reproved and corrected him, freeing one guilty of death from death through fear of death. [Col. 1618D–1619A]

But because the occasion has presented itself, this should briefly be noted concerning the location of the Red Sea: it is said to be derived from the Ocean, extending from the south toward the north, ending not far from Mount Sinai, and to lie four or five days’ journey from the Mediterranean Sea toward Joppa and Ascalon. By a very broad gulf it encloses all Egypt, Numidia, and Ethiopia on their northern side. Hence it is very remarkable how Gihon, which is also the Nile, can tend toward Egypt from Paradise, which, I think, must be believed to lie in the east; and how the Euphrates can pass through Armenia and Mesopotamia, since the Red Sea lies between the first springs of these rivers and the regions through which they are said to flow. [Col. 1619A–B]

For since, after long subterranean courses through lands, these rivers are demonstrably brought forth again upon the earth, as if from new springs, it is itself remarkable how they can pass through the Red Sea, whether by flowing between or beneath it, so as to reach the springs which they renew beyond the Red Sea. God, who can do all things, can also do this; but by what means it happens I have never been able to discover by sight, hearing, or reading. Yet we must in no way doubt the truth of Holy Scripture, which teaches that the rivers mentioned have their first origins in Paradise, from that exceedingly great fountain, and that they are themselves those which are known either to encompass or to traverse the regions already named. But whether they flow to their known places through direct but unknown channels in the midst of the Red Sea, or through however winding courses beneath the earth, since we cannot discover it, let us leave the whole matter to the providence of him whom we see give living springs to fountains upon the level summits of lofty mountains, and whom we perceive, as Scripture says, to bind waters in clouds; whom, finally, we do not doubt to have placed waters in the heights of the heavens from the beginning and to contain them continually, with this visible heaven—that is, the firmament—suspended midway in the division of the waters. But let us now return to the order of history. [Col. 1619B–C]

[Col. 1619D] In 1117, in the enemy’s place, almost the entire territory of Jerusalem was occupied by infinite multitudes of locusts. They advanced in troops, continuously, from places already devastated to devastate others, so that, after every green thing of the earth had been devoured, one could clearly perceive that the Lord had commanded the locust to consume the lands of undisciplined inhabitants—so that perhaps, returning to their senses, these perverse people might recognize that they deserved not to be ravaged by locusts but delivered to the Saracens for slaughter.

In the following month of June, after cockcrow, the moon was first seen by observers entirely red, then became dark until its light was extinguished. Whether its redness portended bloodshed, its blackness a coming famine, or it underwent its usual eclipse as it was shadowed by the interposition of the earth, made conjecturers uncertain. After nearly two hours, it recovered the full brightness of its thirteenth-day form. For around the full moon, the moon is accustomed to encounter, either wholly or in part, the earth’s shadow, extending toward it as though pointed, when the earth stands between it and the sun. Thus it suffers loss of brightness until it escapes that same shadow, which is closer to it in one place and farther off in another. The reason this does not happen at every full moon is that the moon does not always travel through the Zodiac by the same path. Thus it suffers the aforesaid loss of light only when, full, it passes through those regions of heaven toward which the shadows cast higher by the swelling of the opposing earth can extend farther, and when the moon, running above, intercepts the rays of the sun running below. [Col. 1620A]

When this occurs, it makes those ignorant of its cause marvel and suspect some portent, although the cause is then the moon’s natural course and the encounter of the earthly shadow rising higher than the moon’s path. But this having been briefly explained, let us continue, as we began, with the events of the history.

The plague of locusts was followed, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, by a most dreadful earthquake, warning that God’s anger must be appeased quickly. Buildings were shaken toward collapse, so that the hard hearts of foolish people might be shaken toward repentance. At the same time King Baldwin built a certain fortress near Tyre, situated within the fifth mile from the city, called in antiquity Scandaleon—that is, “the Field of the Lion.” Carefully repairing its ruins, the king stationed suitable guards in it, so that by their strength the raids of the Tyrians might be restrained and the future siege of that city prepared. [Col. 1620B–C]

The same year, namely in December, there followed a sign in the sky as remarkable as it was unusual. The sky itself, in the northern region, at the first silence of the night, was covered over a great part with a fiery or blood-red brightness, having rays of whitish [perhaps *albuli*, “whitish”] color intermingled from below upward, now before, now behind, and now in the middle, blended with sudden changes. The lower part of the sky, called the horizon, grew white with something like a new dawn. But a certain greater and brighter front of the same redness or whiteness preceded it, like a rising moon, so that all the surrounding places below shone more brightly everywhere, illuminated by that same radiance. [Col. 1620C–D]

Those who regarded this as a sign conjectured that it foretold either much blood to be shed in war or other terrible changes in human affairs. Those of more sober judgment warned that nothing ought rashly to be suspected, but that, “leaving the governance both of events and of times to divine providence, one must labor only to correct perversity of morals and to implore divine favor.” Yet many thought that the preceding phenomenon had signified the deaths, a year later, of several eminent persons in this world: Pope Paschal at Rome, in January; King Baldwin at Jerusalem, in April; Patriarch Arnulf; and Alexius, emperor of the Greeks; as well as the deaths at the same time of many other great men of this world. [Col. 1621A]

In the year 1118, after the month of March had passed, King Baldwin, having plundered a city situated towards Egypt which the inhabitants call Pharama, was one day travelling with his men along the banks of the Nile. Having eaten in the aforesaid town of fish from that river, he felt with great severity that the unfamiliarity of the harmful food had rekindled the pain of his old wound. Unable to ride, he lay in a litter made from the poles of tents and was carried back towards Jerusalem as far as the village called Laris. There, as the weakness caused by his incurably painful scar increased day by day, he was driven on to death; and, amid his own people, not without the great grief and mourning of all, he died, having completed eighteen years in the kingdom of Jerusalem. [Col. 1621B]

Those present carefully washed and salted his entrails, and the bearers of the funeral, all the king’s fellow-soldiers in sorrow, hastened to Jerusalem. By what I believe was God’s wonderful and unforeseen ordering, it happened that on the very day and hour when the people of Jerusalem, celebrating Palm Sunday according to custom, were conducting their solemn procession, descending from the Mount of Olives into the Valley of Jehoshaphat with palm branches, the military escort bearing the royal funeral encountered that same procession: weeping met singing, sorrow met rejoicing, groaning and wailing met exultation. But when the matter became known as it was, the whole procession of singers became a company of mourners; the entire choir was turned into lamentation. The Franks wailed, the Syrians lamented, and even the subject Saracens grieved. For who then could restrain tears, when he saw the bulwarks of the whole country fallen in a single small body?

Thus, in so great a sorrow, what remained of the funeral rites and burial was attended to. They buried him with royal magnificence on Golgotha, beside his brother, namely King Godfrey. Upon his tomb they inscribed an epitaph composed in heroic verse. Then, by a salutary decision at the outset, the men of Jerusalem immediately made the dead king’s kinsman their king—another Baldwin, likewise Count of Edessa, whom divine providence had then placed at Jerusalem in order to speak with his kinsman. But since death forestalled that conversation, he succeeded the buried king in the kingdom by common election. He was chosen by all on that very day and consecrated by royal anointing on the following Sunday of Easter. They took precautions lest, through delay, either the enemies might venture more boldly against them, or the Christians themselves, stirred by ambition, might introduce some more malign innovation. [Col. 1621C–D]

Against the new king new wars immediately arose. In the following summer, the men of Babylon and Damascus gathered their forces and resources together at Ascalon, assembling fifteen thousand cavalry and twenty thousand infantry, and prepared to exterminate both the Christian people and the Christian name. Moreover, a considerable fleet, having put in at the harbour of Tyre, had brought abundant arms and provisions for the armies.

When, therefore, the king and people of Jerusalem heard that so dangerous a war was being prepared against them, they summoned by envoys the men of Tripoli and Antioch. Having assembled all their forces from every quarter, they hastened against the enemy near Ascalon, placing their camp opposite the enemy camp so that each side could continually see and be seen by the other. But because the former were greatly formidable to the Christians by their numbers, and the latter to the Saracens by their courage, they remained continually encamped against one another for three months, each side heated for battle yet always delaying engagement. At length the Saracens, worn out by prolonged boredom, withdrew without battle. They thereby enabled the men of Jerusalem, retaining with them three hundred Antiochenes as auxiliaries, at last to return gladly to Jerusalem; while the men of Tripoli, with the remaining Antiochenes, prosperously returned home. [Col. 1622A–B]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1119, what and how great evils overwhelmed the Antiochenes, both the truth of history commands one to recount and the horror and magnitude of the disaster forbid one to relate. Yet I do not know what good it would do Christians to withhold the words describing the evils whose deeds they themselves endured. Indeed, it might even harm the lost to suppress examples of their destruction, since perhaps it may be useful even to the perverse to be deterred from imitation by their own ruin. And even if knowing how and why they perished brings no benefit to those condemned, it may nevertheless allow later generations, made aware of others’ collapses, to beware of ruinous courses.

Let it therefore not be unknown that nearly all the Antiochenes, noble and common alike, together with their prince Roger, were killed by the Turks in a single day near the town of Arcasium. Seven thousand of them are said to have been slain; but of the Turks, not even twenty men. Thus God had sold them for nothing, because they had become corrupt and abominable to him. Their prince Roger himself did not shrink from being a public adulterer; many citizens were stained by their leader’s example in this and other crimes. He even compelled the son of his lord Bohemond to live in exile in Apulia with his mother. He conducted everything not lawfully as a prince, but cruelly as a tyrant. Subject neither to God nor restrained before men, he was worthy to be set over men like himself. Thus pride and luxury had claimed everything for themselves among the Antiochenes. [Col. 1622C–D]

It is therefore no wonder if prisoners of crimes and slaves of vices were handed over to their enemies for slaughter, so that those who refuse to understand when warned in words may understand when shaken by examples of destruction that “the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). For the iniquity of the Antiochenes had come forth, as it were, from fatness; thus there was no pity for their death, since the patience of the Almighty could no longer bear the towering mass of so many evils.

Let the nation without counsel and without prudence, which does not fear to provoke the Lord’s anger, understand from this that it deserved for God to cause remembrance of it to cease from among humankind. Yet its extermination was delayed because of the anger of its enemies, lest perhaps those enemies should grow proud and say: “Our hand is exalted, and not the Lord has done all these things” (Deuteronomy 32:27). [Col. 1623A]

Nor did the Turks, the slayers of the Antiochenes, long rejoice in their victory; shortly afterwards they were defeated by a few men who had shortly before triumphed over many. How this happened must be described more fully.

When, at the Turks’ first arrival, both the prince and people of Antioch had been alarmed and had sought by envoys both the coming and assistance of the king of Jerusalem, the king, with the patriarch, was hastening toward Antioch to help them if he could arrive before the battle. In the meantime he had set aside the war which the Damascenes had undertaken against him not far from the Jordan, having first driven them in one attack from their positions and put them to flight. The Count of Tripoli came with him, as did the bishop of Caesarea, bearing the Lord’s Cross in place of the patriarch. When nearly two hundred and fifty soldiers had arrived at Antioch with the king and had learned what had already happened—the lamentable destruction of the Antiochenes—they mourned appropriately, summoned the Edessenes, and prepared to make war upon the Turks again. Nearly seven hundred soldiers assembled from every side, to fight against twenty thousand Turks. [Col. 1623B]

Who could hear this without horror? Who could fail to tremble at so unequal an array for battle? To what end was this, except that wretched mortals might understand that they ought not glory in themselves, but in him alone, for whom it makes no difference whether victory is gained through few or through many?

A certain Turk understood this to some extent. It is said that, noticing a Christian soldier who knew Persian, he reproachfully said to him:

> “What is this of yours, O Franks—not courage, but madness—that you, so very few, have dared either to meet or to fight against so many? Tomorrow you will undoubtedly be conquered by us and reduced to nothing. For we know certainly that your God has abandoned you; and since you have deserted his law, he will no longer help you. In vain do you trust in the aid of him whose law you have forsaken, preserving neither faith nor truth among yourselves as you once did. For if you kept the law and faith of your God, as you once did, you would still be terrible to us according to your custom, and moreover unconquerable.”

Alas, what shame—that the faithful are reproved for faithlessness, and by faithless men! Blush, O Christian, that transgression of the sacred law should be thrown in your face by your enemies. Blush, I say, that truth should be proclaimed to you reproachfully by children of falsehood. For if you had walked in God’s way, you would surely have dwelt in peace upon the earth. Blush then, blush, people of God; and turn with your whole heart to him who still awaits you and even invites you, through the tongues of his enemies, to turn to him. [Col. 1623C–D]

Accordingly, on the next day a most severe battle was joined, and for a long time both sides fought most fiercely. The victory was long uncertain, until at last one part was overcome by the other and put to flight in such a way that the scattered part of the Christians fled from its companions as far as Antioch, while the greater part of the Turks fled into Persia or Aleppo. But the king of Jerusalem and the count of Tripoli, strengthened with their men by the presence and power of the Lord’s Cross, never abandoned the bishop of Caesarea who bore it. They remained always unharmed and unconquered on the field of battle, until, after two days, when none of the Turks returned to battle, they went back thence to Antioch with great joy.

The patriarch and the surviving Antiochene people came out to meet the victors, giving thanks to almighty God and rendering due praises because wrath had been turned into mercy, and because, through the power of the most glorious Cross, victory over their enemies and vengeance had been restored to its worshippers. There the king, refreshed with his followers by some rest, was asked by all to become prince and lord of the whole region; he added the principality of Antioch to the kingdom of Jerusalem, holding a dominion far wider than that of any of the ancient Israelites. [Col. 1624A–B]

He entrusted the Lord’s Cross to chosen bearers and sent it back to Jerusalem, to be received on the very day of its Exaltation, by God’s ordering, in Jerusalem with a celebration of ineffable joy by all the faithful people, and to be adored. After the king had remained in Antioch for some time, assigning the lands and possessions of citizens killed in the war either to their lawful heirs or to fitting possessors, giving widows husbands and orphans protectors, he returned to Jerusalem. On the feast of the Lord’s Nativity he was crowned with his wife at Bethlehem.

[Col. 1624C] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1120, King Baldwin released all sellers of wheat or legumes within the gates of Jerusalem from every customary due, remitting the charge upon the measure called *jumagium*. But when all messengers reported that the Turks had again crossed the Euphrates and entered Syria, he did not delay in bringing the assistance requested by the Antiochenes against them. First, indeed, the Lord’s Cross was humbly requested from the clergy and patriarch of Jerusalem, and it was granted faithfully enough, but with great reluctance, because the former feared to go forth without it and the latter feared to remain when it departed. Thus the hope and devotion of the faithful people contended with one another. The side which ought to prevail—the compassion of brotherly love—prevailed; and it was judged better to meet the need of imminent danger than to follow private inclination. [Col. 1624C–D]

The patriarch, clergy, and entire people of Jerusalem accompanied it barefoot. Thus the king and his men set out with it, while the people and clergy returned weeping to the city. The Turks were already pressing Antioch on every side, most wickedly raiding throughout the entire surrounding territory and scarcely allowing the Antiochenes access or return even as far as the first stone’s throw from the city. Yet, foreseeing the king’s arrival, they immediately withdrew toward Caliptum, summoning three thousand Damascene cavalry to reinforce their army. Even so, they did not presume to meet the king or engage him.
