When the king had approached them more closely, so that arrows were cast on both sides and many everywhere fell either wounded or killed, after three days, since the Turks wholly refused to give battle, the Christians returned to Antioch and the greater part of the Turks returned to Persia. Thus, terrified by the power of the Lord’s Cross and not daring even to enter battle, the Turks left temporarily free to the Antiochenes the Syrian territory around Antioch which they had more extensively occupied. The king sent the Lord’s Cross back to Jerusalem with due honour, while he himself remained for a time at Antioch, preventing the enemies’ return by his presence. [Col. 1625A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1121, the king returned from Antioch. Having gathered all his people from Sidon to Joppa, he crossed the Jordan and compelled the king of Damascus, who with Arab allies was ravaging Christian lands toward Tiberias, to retreat into his own territory, terrified by the mere report of Baldwin’s arrival. The king pursued him for two days but could not overtake him. Returning, he besieged a certain fortress, eight miles from the Jordan, built by the Damascenes and named Jarras. Pressing it with siege-engines, he captured it, forcing its forty Turkish guards to surrender under terms guaranteeing freedom and life.

Once it had been captured, the king ordered it demolished to its foundations, perceiving that it could neither be fortified nor held except with great difficulty, and that, if recovered by the enemy, it could not be possessed without most serious injury to the Christians. This is said formerly to have been a distinguished city in Arabia, anciently called Gerasa: strong by its situation, founded high upon large squared stone and more loftily walled, near Mount Gilead, and once established in the tribe of Manasseh. The remainder of that year the Christians spent, by God’s favour, prosperously, with peace from their enemies and fertility of the soil. [Col. 1625B–C]

In the year from the Lord’s Nativity 1122, the king set his army in motion from Ptolemais and went to Tripoli, intending to suppress the contempt and rebellion of Pons, Count of Tripoli, who refused, contrary to the custom of his father Bertrand, to submit to the king of Jerusalem and to bind himself to him by the homage owed. But, by God’s will, the count adopted better counsel and rendered the king the submission due; thus king and count became reconciled and friendly.

Meanwhile a certain archbishop, bearing an embassy from the Antiochenes, arrived at Tripoli before the king, asking that assistance be brought to the Antiochenes against the Turks, who were once again ravaging and occupying the whole surrounding region far and wide without resistance. On hearing this, the king, protected by the presence of the most glorious Lord’s Cross, immediately hastened to Antioch, taking with him three hundred select soldiers and three hundred knights, while dismissing the rest to their homes. But the Turks, terrified as usual by the king’s arrival, abandoned the castle of Sardanium, which they had already besieged, and withdrew homeward. [Col. 1625C–D]

The king then went to Antioch; the Turks returned to their undertaking. The king again met them on their return. Yet even then that Parthian people, always unstable in its custom, did not offer him an opportunity to engage them—turning now its back, now its face, toward the enemy more swiftly than one could imagine, so that, when you think it fleeing, you must beware its sudden return and unexpected assaults; and where you think you have conquered it, you must take care lest you find yourself conquered. Thus that treacherous people, utterly impatient of peace, seeing the steadfastness of the king and his men and perceiving that its own cunning would avail it nothing, at length withdrew homeward, entirely avoiding battle and leaving the Christians victory without bloodshed.

And to whom other than the most glorious Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ should such a victory be attributed, in which the enemy, not daring even to engage, is overcome unharmed, while the victor, having gained victory without any loss of his own, rejoices? Who would not marvel that ten thousand armed men feared twelve hundred and, avoiding battle, departed as though defeated? [Col. 1626A–B]

Therefore let the servants of the Cross be far from glorying except in the power of the Cross (Galatians 6:14), in whose horns, as Scripture says, the Crucified One’s power is hidden. That power is expressed immediately afterwards when it says: “Before his face death shall go; the devil shall go forth before his feet” (Habakkuk 3:5). Let us understand that his feet are his bearers, worshippers, and preachers. Before them we see the devil go forth and flee in his satellites; they fear to engage and hasten to withdraw, so that the faithful of the Cross were able to return home with the Cross itself.

Accordingly, after the king had brought the Lord’s Cross as far as Tripoli, he sent it thence to Jerusalem with part of the army, while he himself returned with the rest to Antioch. Meanwhile a certain emir, Balak, second to none in cunning and malice, captured Joscelin, Count of Edessa, and with him his kinsman Galeran; both had been surrounded by an ambush, and their companions, one hundred knights, were cruelly slaughtered. The rest of that year neither Parthia nor Babylonia disturbed the Christians; through the gift of the Lord Jesus Christ it was peaceful and very fruitful in every kind of crop. [Col. 1626B–C]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1123, the long-protracted discord between Henry, emperor of Germany, and the Roman pope was at last ended by God’s will, and the empire was reconciled with the priesthood, Pope Calixtus II then acting. In the same year the Venetians vowed to visit Jerusalem with a sufficiently numerous and most splendid fleet of one hundred ships, and there either to enlarge the name and worship of Christ the Lord or to strengthen them. They had besides very many small vessels and transports, some triremes and others beaked warships; in them they carried timber of great length, suitable for constructing siege-engines wherever needed. The ships contained fifteen thousand armed men, while the horses numbered no more than three hundred. [Col. 1626C–D]

Thus they had left their land in the preceding year and wintered on the island called Corfu; but in the year now under discussion they at last arrived in Syria. Before this took place, it happened that the king of Jerusalem himself, ensnared by Balak’s ambushes, was carried off captive and placed for careful confinement in the citadel of Balak’s very strong castle at Cartapeta, together with Joscelin and Galeran. I do not know what could have happened more welcome to the Saracens, or more grievous and terrible to the Christians, than this misfortune.

When this had been publicized at Jerusalem and throughout the surrounding region, nearly all the magnates of the entire kingdom of Jerusalem assembled at Ptolemais with the patriarch, to deliberate what action was required in so great a crisis. By common counsel and election, they chose and decreed that Eustace, lord of Caesarea and Sidon, should be guardian of the whole kingdom—a man indeed vigorous in arms, honourable in character, powerful in counsel, and distinguished in nobility. The patriarch, the whole people, and all the leading men of the entire kingdom decreed that they would obey his commands until the outcome should show what God had determined concerning the king. [Col. 1627A–B]

When they learned that the men of Babylon had assembled at Ascalon by land and sea, Duke Eustace and those with him sent an embassy in very swift boats to meet the Venetian fleet, informing them of the imminent danger and urgently requesting that the expected aid be hastened to them. Meanwhile the Babylonians sailed to Joppa with a great fleet and leapt from their ships with immense clamour and piratical ferocity. Sounding bronze trumpets, shouting and howling enormously from every side, they surrounded the city and, setting up their engines, attacked its walls. With extremely powerful engines they hurled stones so forcefully that such great rocks flew beyond an arrow’s range. Arabs and Ethiopians also, of whom very many infantrymen had assembled, made mighty attacks on the walls, while others brought missiles, arrows, and stones against the citizens defending themselves from the walls as best they could. [Col. 1627B–C]

The enemy left absolutely nothing unattempted by which they hoped the besieged could be exhausted. Some began to undermine the wall in many places while others tried to drive the defenders from the battlements either with showers of arrows or storms of stones. Yet the citizens, though very few, resisted the tireless attackers without ceasing, descending from the walls neither by day nor by night. While one group of attackers relieved another, they themselves remained continually without rest at the defence of the walls. The women too, while the men laboured above, worked below: at one time supplying stones, at another missiles, to the defenders; at another offering drink to the thirsty and food to the hungry.

But after the Saracens had spent five days attempting to capture the city and had not prevailed—for God was continually strengthening his people wonderfully—and after they heard that Christians were hastening to Joppa’s aid, they did not dare remain longer there. They withdrew into their ships, dismantling their engines and taking them aboard piece by piece. There is no doubt that they would have captured the city if they had been able safely to attack it longer. For they had already undermined the wall in many places and shattered and broken down many of the battlements by the violent blows of stones hurled from their engines. [Col. 1627C–D]

The fleet, numbering about eighty vessels, then withdrew toward Ascalon and prepared for a land battle to receive the Christians advancing against them. For, at Duke Eustace’s command, nearly all Christians of the entire kingdom of Jerusalem capable of bearing arms had already assembled at Ramatha, a city once situated near Diospolis. They placed great trust in and drew strength from the presence of the glorious Cross of Christ the Lord, borne by the patriarch and clergy. Those who remained at Jerusalem devoted themselves to fasts, vigils, prayers, and almsgiving, earnestly asking God to be merciful to their brothers and to themselves, placed in so great a danger.

At first light, the duke and the magnates with him rose from Ramatha, arranged their forces in battle lines, received from the patriarch a blessing and absolution for the people, and advanced cautiously and in good order against the enemy. The enemy had gathered near Azotus, once the fifth city of the Philistines, massing themselves with the utmost preparation to join battle. [Col. 1628A–B]

The Saracens trusted in their numbers, as was their custom; the Christians placed confidence in the power of the Cross and of the Crucified One. A most severe battle was therefore joined, and the affair was fought at close quarters with swords. What more need be said? Here too it pleased Christ the Lord both to grant strength to his own and to bring confusion upon their enemies. When the soldiers of the hostile army beheld the ranks and arms of the Christian force, unable to endure their most fierce assault, they immediately turned and left their infantry to be slaughtered in the fields. As these were cut down at the pleasure of those striking them, the Christians, rejoicing in the victory granted them from heaven, pursued the fugitives as far as they could or dared, cutting down all whom they could overtake and pressing most eagerly upon the work of slaughter.

Thus six thousand enemies were killed, while the rest escaped wherever and by whatever route each could. Sixteen thousand combatants are said to have assembled, whereas the Christians are estimated at eight thousand. Once the enemy’s flight and slaughter had been effected, the victors joyfully returned to camp, enriched with abundant spoils and driving before them three hundred captured camels and five hundred asses. Christ was praised by his people; the Cross and the Crucified One were magnified, through whose power and gracious condescension the enemies had been reduced to nothing. [Col. 1628B–C]

When this war had thus been concluded by the will and grace of almighty God, and the patriarch was bringing the Lord’s Cross back to Jerusalem, where it was restored to its place amid the glorious procession of the people who came out to meet it, joyful news followed after three days from the Venetian fleet. When it had arrived at Ptolemais, the Venetian commander was informed that the Babylonian fleet, returning from Joppa, could, if he wished to meet it with his own fleet, by God’s will come within reach; and, if such were heaven’s will, be captured.

At his men’s counsel, he immediately divided his fleet into two parts. He led the smaller part swiftly toward Joppa and ordered the other to follow at a distance, knowing that the Saracens could thus be drawn unawares into battle and danger. Nor did the expectation of this shrewd man deceive him. For while the Saracens were roaming the sea and looking for any ships of pilgrims bound for Jerusalem that they might seize, they saw eighteen ships of the Venetian fleet approaching and joyfully went to meet them. In their custom they made a great din with resounding bronze trumpets, promising themselves a great profit from so many ships, as though already captured. [Col. 1628D–1629A]

The Venetians pretended to be afraid and to wish, yet be unable, to flee; they deferred battle solely in order that, when their companions arrived, they might fight more successfully. When the Saracens also saw those companions approaching, ploughing the open sea more broadly with sails and oars, those who had earlier encouraged themselves for plunder and had striven each to outstrip the other began to regret having come so near. They could now neither flee nor dare fight. Thus the Venetians, secure of victory, rushed upon the Saracen fleet; they boldly attacked the Saracens, already bloodless with fear and disordered; and they swiftly boarded their ships, cutting down everyone aboard as though harvesting grain in fields.

It may perhaps seem incredible to recount the wondrous deed said to have been done there: the blood of the slain is said to have flowed as high as the calves of those killing them, so that every deck of the ships stood filled with a dreadful flood. Finally, when the bodies of the slain had been hurled into the sea, so much blood is said to have flowed from them that the whole sea appeared red for nearly four thousand paces. [Col. 1629A–B]

Thus, after all the enemies aboard the ships had been destroyed, the Venetians captured and held all the vessels with all their arms and wealth. Then, ranging as far as Ascalon, they also captured ten other ships laden with diverse provisions and with timber of extraordinary length, prepared for the construction of siege-engines. Other ships fleeing as far as the shore they burned by casting fire upon them; others, after cutting their ropes, they brought with them to Ptolemais.

Thus the Saracens, who had assembled by land and sea to destroy the Christians, almost all perished by land and sea at the same time. They had thought those Christians unwarlike because they knew them to have no king. They learned that those people were not without a king, since they experienced that Christ the King did not fail them. They indeed held King Baldwin in chains, but they found that Christ was always the liberator of Christians. And so that he might prove even to the wicked that he is King of kings, in that same year he graciously freed King Baldwin himself from his chains in a wondrous manner and restored him, now liberated, powerfully to his kingdom. At the same time Duke Eustace died, and William of Bures was appointed in his place as guardian of the kingdom. [Col. 1629C]

But the deliverance of the king and of those who were held captive with him—Joscelin and Galeran—came about in such a manner that, since the story seems sufficiently pleasing, it ought neither to seem too long nor burdensome.

There were in the city of Edessa very valiant men who, moved, as I think must be believed, by divine inspiration, placed their lives in their hands and entered among themselves into a most courageous plan for the release of the captive king and counts. For, having bound themselves together, they came as far as Carpit; clothed in the poorest dress and laden likewise with certain very cheap wares. Pretending that they were carrying these for sale, they went throughout the whole castle, most diligently investigating by what entrance they might reach the prison, after first seizing, if possible, the inner fortification of the castle together with the citadel itself.

Having found its guards playing near the gate, they entered one after another, as though bringing a complaint before the magistrate concerning an injury done to them by the garrison. When they had first made the foremost guard attentive to their tearful complaint, they suddenly drew hidden daggers from beneath their short tunics and killed him more quickly than words can tell. Then, snatching up the lances which they found there, they slew all who were with him. A great cry arose, and all throughout the outer castle were at once thrown into confusion. Whoever entered to discover the cause of the cry was killed before he could learn what it was. Thus a hundred Turks are said to have been slain there.

Then they immediately shut the gates and, having broken open the prison, led out the king with the counts. Next, raising ladders, they climbed to the summit of the wall; and, raising the Christian banner upon the highest citadel, they cried out that the castle was theirs. Turks from every side, the neighboring people together with the garrison, assembled; besieging that inner castle together with the citadel, they carefully kept those enclosed within, lest any of them should be able to escape.

Yet the king and his companions, shut up within, consulted anxiously among themselves concerning the preservation of their lives. Joscelin, since he was a man of the greatest courage, declared himself ready, for the common danger, to expose himself to the proposed risk:

> “With only three men,” he said, “I will go out, if this pleases you, brave men and illustrious nobles. And if the merciful Lord who has begun to cooperate in our deliverance is willing, I shall go to Edessa and thence, God willing, proceed to Antioch or even Jerusalem, to seek and bring you aid as swiftly as I can.”

All the men praised the proposal. Without delay the count, with three chosen companions, set out cautiously as a nocturnal and secret traveler; passing through the hostile guards, he sent one of his men back to the king by the same route, as they had agreed together, to signify that, by God’s mercy, the way had lain open for him.

They hid by day and hurried by night through byways, and at length reached the Euphrates. Having no boat, they crossed by swimming; for the count, who did not know how to swim, they filled two skins brought along for this purpose with air and placed them beneath him. Having thus crossed the river, they hurried on hungry and thirsty. At last, entering Armenian territory, they did not dare even to seek food for themselves, since they suspected even those Christians of treachery; and therefore they feared both to be seen and to be recognized.

Placed amid such evils, they hoped only for, and prayed that there might be granted them, the aid of divine mercy. Exhausted by hunger and the toil of the journey, the count fell asleep while resting under a walnut tree, covered with brambles and leaves. Meanwhile one of the count’s companions had gone ahead, looking about to see whether he might find anything to eat anywhere. A certain Armenian peasant met him; and when, at his request, he was offering figs and a small piece of bread to the count hiding beneath the walnut tree, he recognized him:

> “Hail, Lord Joscelin,” he said, “hail, most noble count and prince most longed for by your people. What are you doing here? Why do you not come quickly?”

The count denied that he was Joscelin and still wished to conceal himself. But the peasant said:

> “Do not be afraid, lord count. Do not regard me, who know you well, as suspect. So may the Lord save me: if you command it, I shall be, to the best of my power, a helper in your safety.”

The count replied:

> “Come then, man of most generous spirit; have pity on me. I beseech you by that faith and love which you owe to Christ: do not reveal me, I pray, to any of my ill-wishers. But, if you wish to receive any reward, bring me safely, I beg you, as far as the castle of Turbessel.”

And he said:

> “I have a wife and a little daughter; henceforth I entrust myself with them to your good faith and generosity. I commend my life to your life, most noble and prudent man. If you command, I shall gladly leave my country and land for you, bringing with me my two brothers, and shall lead you with them wherever you prefer.”

Why say more? The peasant ran off and returned with all his people very quickly. The count was placed upon the peasant’s she-ass and became bearer of the little girl, the peasant’s daughter. The little girl, seated in the count’s lap, wept and wearied her bearer with continual cries. Yet the prudent man bore even this annoyance, protected by a deeper design: namely, that no traveler meeting them would believe that one carried in such a fashion, and acting as such a bearer, was anything less likely than a count.

Escorted by such a company, the count at last entered his castle of Turbessel. The reception of such guests was very joyful. All rejoiced and were glad together; his wife exulted, and the whole household offered congratulations. He who had been an exile became a count once more: consoled by his own people after having been forsaken among strangers, and now again destined both to console his own and to desolate strangers.

The peasant, the count’s fellow-traveler, received a fitting reward; and from a poor tenant-farmer he became a wealthy decurion. Thus released from exile, the count, deeply concerned and anxious for the deliverance of the captives—the king, that is, and his companions—hastened to Antioch and from there proceeded to Jerusalem. There he paid due praises to his deliverer, Christ: on Mount Calvary he offered up his own chains, hanging them there, and added others of the same weight, dedicated as a votive gift and made of silver.

He discussed with the chief men of the kingdom the means of providing for the king’s release and hastening aid to him, urging on all whom he could persuade. An army of Christians was gathered from every quarter, and all assembled at Tripoli, in order that, when every force had been brought together, they might march thence against Carpit, where the king and his companions were held enclosed. The Cross of the Lord had already been brought to Tripoli by the patriarch and clergy.

The army of Christ, which had assembled at Tripoli, then hastened to Antioch. There it took with it the forces of the Antiochenes and came as far as Turbessel. But while they were preparing to march through Armenia, they were suddenly struck by a grievous report: they heard that the king had again been captured by Balak together with the fortification in which he had been besieged. Despairing therefore of the king’s release, they wholly abandoned the aid which they had been laboring to bring him; and, lest they return empty-handed, they turned their plan toward attacking the city of Caliptum. Ravaging all through its suburbs and plundering whatever they could find, they returned as far as Ptolemais; Count Joscelin returned with his followers to Antioch.

Having crossed the Jordan, the Jerusalemites marched through the region bordering Mount Gilead and Arabia and plundered the inhabitants of the district upon whom they had arrived unexpectedly. Returning to Tiberias and thence to Jerusalem, they brought with them very many captives of both sexes and a vast spoil of camels and sheep, after the Cross of the Lord had been fittingly restored to its place.

It remains now to explain what meanwhile befell the king and those who remained shut up with him. When Balak learned that the king, whom he had left bound at Carpit with the other fellow-captives, had occupied his tower, as related above, and that Count Joscelin had escaped, he recalled to mind a dream in which he had once seen his eyes torn out by Joscelin. Greatly troubled and enraged, he hurried to Carpit with as large an army as he could muster, trying by every means in his power to recover his possession.

At first, indeed, he addressed the king gently, promising him life and liberty; he promised to pledge his word and furnish hostages for his safe conduct even to Edessa or Antioch, if only the king would restore the stronghold to him. But when the king would not consent—either because he distrusted Balak’s good faith or because he was too confident that aid would soon be brought him by Joscelin—Balak, savage in spirit, turned, according to his custom, to cunning devices. He had the rock upon which the castle stood undermined, and the foundations of the wall supported on stout timber props; then, after a greater quantity of combustible material had been brought in, he had fire applied. When all the supports had been consumed, the rock suddenly subsided in a vast chasm; and one of the towers, its wall-foundation giving way, fell with a terrible crash, shaking the king and all who were with him with extreme astonishment and terror.

Thus the king and his companions, having lost every hope not merely of liberation but even of life, surrendered themselves to Balak with the lofty tower in which they were, expecting nothing but punishment. Balak nevertheless spared the king’s life, together with that of a certain nephew of his and Galeran. But those who had aided the king he treated otherwise: some he hanged on gibbets; others he flayed alive, making them a cruel spectacle for his people; the rest he massacred with the sword. Finally, he ordered the king to be cast out of the castle and taken as far as Harran with only three of his followers.

When these events concerning the king had taken place, in the year from the Nativity of the Savior 1123, the doge of the Venetians and the Jerusalemites, after celebrating the solemnity of the Nativity of the Lord at Bethlehem according to the custom of the faithful, confirmed by common oath that, after Epiphany, they would go with all their forces to besiege either Tyre or Ascalon. The Venetians were to do this, as usual, with their fleet by sea; the Jerusalemites with their whole army, both cavalry and infantry, were to undertake it by land. Since they had few soldiers and little money, the patriarch and clergy were compelled to pawn the more precious ornaments of the Church of Jerusalem in order to hire soldiers and retainers.

Thus each army, supplied with money and carefully equipped with arms, met at Ptolemais. After mature deliberation there, they chose rather to attack Tyre, judging that its conquest would be easier. The city was therefore besieged and closely pressed on every side. It had been fortified by an abundance of wealth and by the protection of the sea, and had never been accustomed either to rule under another or to be conquered.

Meanwhile, when the Ascalonites learned that the Christian army had gone far away, they boiled over with their customary insolence and rushed to Jerusalem, believing that they could even besiege the city. Their approach having been recognized from the watchtower, the Franks and Syrians left behind to guard the city boldly came out to meet them and received their insolence in a very sharp engagement. The Saracens, who had vainly presumed that they could seize the city walls while they were empty of defenders, were compelled to concern themselves with protecting their own bodies.

A most fierce battle was fought for nearly three hours. It was especially marvelous because very few men resisted so great a multitude with such persistence in open ground, aided by the protection of no fortification, that they were not merely unable to be compelled to yield their position, but were even able to put the densely packed enemy formations to flight. Who would not recognize this as a work of divine power, visibly defending the holy people and place from the profane insolence of the impious?

Once scattered, the Ascalonites could not reform their line. They fled with such headlong haste that they gave their pursuers reason to suspect that, while fleeing, they intended perhaps to lead those pursuing them into prepared ambushes. Recalled by this suspicion or caution and given the signal to halt, the Christians turned to gathering spoil, rendering the due offerings of thanksgiving to Christ the Lord, by the protection of whose grace they had conquered. They would have thought it a great thing merely not to perish amid such danger; they rejoiced that, beyond hope, they had returned victorious too, so that they might acknowledge Christ in all things as their protector and savior.

The Ascalonites themselves too were compelled to confess this, admonished by their own confusion: astonished that they had been defeated and put to flight by men whom they had presumed would not only not dare to advance into battle, but would not even dare to open their mouths and whimper. To complete their disgrace, they left the broad open fields covered with dead; many others, wounded unto death, either fell half-dead on the road, doomed to die, or could scarcely reach their walls, dying as they went. Few indeed would have escaped, had not fear of ambush, as was said, recalled the pursuers.

Thus far our manuscript.

Daemon. See Devil. Delilah endangers Samson’s strength, 378. She denotes the multitude of the elect in a good sense, 381; in an evil sense, the sinful soul, 391. [Col. 1640] David is a figure of Christ, 19, 713; also a type of the upright man, 666. As sinner and penitent, he raises sinners to hope, 678. The defense of sin is the greatest and most diabolical sin, 774; it leads to despair and destruction, 775, 776. To consent to sinful pleasure is death, 186. Those who consent serve miserably, 69, 70. Without consent it does little harm, 512; for then it wounds but does not kill, 771. Despair and presumption are companions of the slothful and perverse person, 646. Despair grievously offends God, 650, and is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, 872. God is immutable in himself, 602; for us he became changeable in our nature, 60, in which he grows weary, 382. He is present to all, differently to the evil and differently to the good, 534. He wills all to be saved, 419. One must cooperate with him when he calls and helps, 158. He is the comforter of the just, 54, and Father for the consolation of the infirm, 482. The Devil is prince of worldly pleasures, 58, 61; he is a wolf, 439; most crafty in tempting, 734, 262, 575: against the first parents, 376; against the just and most holy, 262, 207. He tempts by introducing lukewarmness, 78, 79, 80, etc.; and often by recommending good things, 218; by doubts against faith, 409. A feast day mystically signifies the communion of believers, 116. Which day Abraham saw with exultation, 329. A day’s journey signifies the exercise of good works, 109. The finger of Christ indicates the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or the word of preaching, 807. Love is the distinguishing mark of Christ’s disciples, 492; it overcomes vices, 860; it cannot incline toward two contrary objects, 836. See Charity. Christ’s disciples doubting in faith, 409. They are truly such who labor to learn the commandments, 463. Distraction in prayer is introduced by the evil spirit and makes us without the Synagogue, 512. Christ’s divinity abandons his humanity in the Passion, 386. The division of flesh and Spirit lays waste the devil’s kingdom, 278. The rich have in the rich man at the feast what they may learn and fear, 543. True teachers are those who know how to do good and turn away from evil, 858. They are lights separating light from darkness, 625. Christ questions them concerning life and doctrine, 119. See Prelate or Preacher. The pains of sickness are the garment on which the Lord rides above the she-ass, 4. Interior pains are like hell, 550, 553. The house of the Lord is Christ’s humanity, 38; and we ourselves, 747. Yet scarcely anyone is a house of the eternal divine dwelling while in this life, 669. The house of Eli is a symbol of sinful human nature, 608. Christ himself resolves doubts entertained about his humanity, 359. Deliberation of a doubtful mind, 428. A guide or teacher is necessary for one aspiring to conversion, 260. The sweetness of the Spirit is the greatest of divine graces, 908.

## E

The Church alone is that in which Christ is found by the Jews, 119, 122. She rejoices at the conversion of the Gentiles, 263. She is Christ’s blessed field, 373; likewise, his wife, 410, and mother-in-law, 521. Eglon, being fat, signifies the enemy of the human race, 366. The elect already in heaven have no need of another’s intercession and prayers, 496. See Just or Saints. John denies that he is Elijah, 91. [Col. 1641] Elisha, requesting Elijah’s spirit, represents the soul thirsting for God, 463. Let holy prayer, reading, or meditation be our daily meal, 545. The sacrament of the Eucharist is Christ as food prepared in the Passion, 39, 585; it must be received fervently, 266. Eve’s sin is the fire of a conflagration, 57. See Adam. The Gospel is for us the beginning of conversion and perfection, 247. Why it is read about palms on the first Sunday of Advent, 15. How far its perfection excels the Law, 349. One aspiring to better things should undertake an examination of his past life, 130. What the Lord’s high places and altars are within us, 80. The excuse God accepts is acknowledgment of one’s own imperfection, 590, 591; but an excuse of the flesh against the Spirit must not be heeded, 899, 900. Examples illuminate more than words, 241. They should be taken from the Fathers of the old Law, 355. The exercise of virtues fortifies us against temptations of the flesh, 76. What departure and entrance signify mystically, 546. Funeral rites for the dead should be solemnly performed, 5.

## F

Famine of the divine word oppresses the Gentiles, 263. How *famula*, *ancilla*, and *serva* differ, and what they signify mystically, 574. When and how calling one’s brother “fool” makes one deserving of Gehenna, 686. Those celebrating the feasts of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the saints become worthy through their intercession, 523. What it is to keep a feast day mystically, 106. It is the communion of believers, 116, and is truly observed at the end of the age, 314. The fig tree is a type of the Synagogue, 47. Faith is the greatest of all virtues, 475; the compendium of the Old and New Testaments, 436; it begets us for Christ, 484. It is divided into least, moderate, and great, 147. Great faith remains the same in prosperity and adversity, 255. Without charity it profits nothing for salvation, 497, nor without works, 871. The name “potter” is not inappropriately applied to the Creator, 395. His house is Christ’s humanity and also the Blessed Virgin Mary, 396. Who are the children of light and children of the age, 755; of the Father in the Old and New Testament, 755, 776. How little children differ mystically from children, 489. One kind of weeping is useful, another useless, 779. Flowing toward Christ signifies baptism and penitence, 41. Digging is mystically interpreted, 752, 762. Who is the fountain of water springing up into eternal life? 303. Fornication may be called every sinful act, 772, 834. Fortitude casts away every delight from itself, 184; it is a gift of the Holy Spirit, 811. The strength of demons, as of those cursed by God, raises us to hope how great a strength God will give us whom he loves, 839. Woman is a mirror of human frailty, 502. Good fruits are love and fear; evil fruits, avarice and concupiscence, 738. Punishment awaits the latter, reward the former, 739. Good fruits satisfy us fourfold, 810.

## G

Let joy be common in the Church both to penitents and the innocent, 71; and to those persevering in works of penance, 616, 618. Joy is complete in heaven over subdued evil spirits, 702, 311. A groan is breath drawn from the heart with sorrow, 808. The Gentile people is denoted by Egypt, 61, and by the Samaritan, 823. Through the Spirit it is called to faith, 171, 214; he gives it what is just, 172. The Church rejoices over its conversion, 263. God’s glory must be sought in all things, 308, 479. God himself gives glory to those who seek it, 327. The tempter introduces vain glory, 223, 801. The Jews pursue it, 347. Yet it is nothing, 329; it takes away the merit of good works, 613, and is a dangerous commerce, 884. See Praise, Hypocrisy. There are five steps to salvation, 533. Grace must humbly be sought from God, 253. Without it the powers of the soul are nothing, 904; there is no understanding of the Scriptures, 763; no compunction, 236, 238, 779; no inward sweetness, 110, 863; nor merit, 167. It is instilled in us by the whole Holy Trinity, 181, in conformity with each soul, 301; flowing and overflowing, 629; it grows in us, 104; leads us to knowledge of God and ourselves, 177. [Col. 1642] It makes us God’s dwelling place, 10; strengthens us against temptations, 52; works great things in us, 100; and all things must be attributed to it, 151, 185. Therefore it requires every care, 462, and cooperation, 185. Otherwise it is in us as a widow, 103. It is denoted by the cloud, 244, and by the third day, 420. Its fullness was poured out upon humankind in Redemption, 25. Drops of Christ’s blood, likewise baptism and tears, cleanse us from sins, 26.

## H

Habakkuk bringing food to Daniel indicates the spiritual Father, 344. The slain kid represents Christ crucified, 263, etc. What is the Lord’s inheritance? 96. Heretics divide the Church, 418. Grass indicates frailty; wood, penitence and human strength, 678. Fawns are celebrated for agility and swiftness, 461. Man is a lesser world, 223, containing sun, moon, and stars, 50. The worldly person is inconstant, 458. The inner person conflicts with the outer, 790. Man is God’s image, 178, and the Lord’s priest, 568. Let him be king of himself, 34, and judge, 35. By his own powers alone he can do nothing, 904. Every person is weary, 412. He who falls among robbers represents the sinner, 814, and Christ, 821. Worldly honors draw us back from the heavenly wedding, 884. The hour of grace and divine visitation is sweet but short, 461. What barley signifies mystically, 317. The enemies of the elect will not go unpunished, 346. The human race could not expiate original guilt by its own powers and sacrifices, 609. The human race, when redeemed, is the fruit of the palm tree, 400. It is armed by God, infinitely merciful, 569, 572. Its entire adornment is Christ, 690.

Humility is called descent, 660. It is the same virtue as justice, 88. It is eminent in Christ’s assumed humanity, 30, 32, 98, and in John, 90. It belongs especially to saints, 245, and should belong to all, 319, especially to the converted, 453, 589. For it advances us toward grace, 52; frustrates temptations of pride, 90, 91, 246; is the splendor of good works, 180; teaches charity, 813; perfects penitents and the just, 907, 660, 663; and exalts them, 792, 794. It establishes Christ’s sheepfold, 449; is worthy to receive the Holy Spirit, 473; and worthy for God to join himself to it, 637. It magnifies God, 831. Other praises of humility, 95, 201. It consists not in words but in enduring injury, etc., 853. It is learned from Christ, 504. That we may learn it, God permits us to be tempted, 187; often withdraws inward consolation, 473; and allows us to fall into sin, 450. What the water jars set at Cana of Galilee signify mystically, 127, 128. Modern hypocrisy is the Church’s most grievous persecution, 214. It is suggested by the demon, 221, 641; makes the sinner utterly wicked, 284; and is figured by the Magi, 641.

## I

Idolaters dissipate the substance of the divine inheritance; all sinners are to be called such, 262, 771. The slothful, like a corpse, are handed over to infernal lions, 344. The fire of the divine Spirit kindles the penitent heart, 885. Enemies must be forgiven, 687. Whoever forgives enemies also obtains forgiveness from God, 765. When heavenly illumination ceases, there is no sweetness in prayer or understanding in reading, 763. Man is the image of God, 178. The impenitent person is like a stone, 332. Imprudence is not unlike a palisade, 780. The inconstant are excluded from spiritual marriage, 125; they easily fall back, 147, 103; endanger eternal salvation, 146; are figured in Saul, 641–654; and are very numerous in the world, 458. Inconstancy very easily throws a person down from good into evil, 267, 471, 472, 781. The infant Christ is compared to a drop, 454. Infancy signifies ignorance and the coming knowledge of divine things, 150. Christ breaks the bars of hell and brings forth the Fathers, 707. Unbelief is the greatest sin, 474. Infirmity and pain are the two disciples loosing the she-ass, 3. By “beginning” is understood the human spirit, 511; the beginning of conversion is usually from small things, 289. The innocent mystically are the rich, 544. Those intent upon heavenly sweetness are often deceived, 166. Innocence must be guarded with no less care than it is recovered, 616. [Col. 1643] Disobedience opens a door to the devil for temptations, 75. How many evils Adam brought into the world, 504. Heavenly inspirations instruct us greatly, 34; they are the first step to salvation, 533. Instruction is necessary for Christ’s future bride, 126. Understanding, a gift of the Holy Spirit, is most necessary for salvation, 297, 835. Intemperance introduces self-will and evil desires, 781. Good intention is unceasing prayer, 251. The intention of thoughts is often worse than we imagine, 735. Christ’s questioning is declaring, 707–708; arousing, 863; admonishing to penitence, 498; fervently seeking a person’s salvation, 456, 498; and acting, 872. Christ’s anger beneficially prevents sins, 371, 884. Anger directed against sins is salutary, 885, 900. Evil anger must be extinguished in the heart, 685, especially when it attempts to burst into words, 685; above all it must be avoided by a prelate, 486. What watered land signifies mystically, 374. The lower and upper springs signify charity, 765.

## J

Jacob prevails over the angel, 113. James the apostle is the brother of the Lord, 499. Fasting does not entail abstinence from every food, 209. Together with humility, it overcomes demonic temptations, 209; therefore it must be opposed to them, 643. It prepares us for Christ’s Advent, 65. Jephthah’s daughter figures Christ’s humanity, 19. Jeremiah was unmarried in the Old Testament, 394. Jeroboam’s hand stretched out against the prophet becomes stiff, 730. Jerusalem denotes the congregation of the just, or the Church, or the soul, 2, 198; it is built by Christ, 732. John the Baptist is an example of humility, 90. He is tempted concerning justice, zeal, and teaching office, 90, 91. Job is the renowned victor over adversities and temptations, 209. Joseph relating his dream is a type of the person turning toward God, 257. He acts harshly toward his brothers, 274. The Jews are Jesus’ parents, 117, yet do not believe in him, 117. They persecute his miracles, 571; are chastised according to the prophecies, 731; and condemned for pride, 350. Yet at the end of the age they will be converted, 48, 50, 63, 118, 120, 175, 264, 362, 582. They are denoted by Ethiopia, 61. Christ the Judge will come in human flesh, 33. He will strictly examine every moment, 120. His appearance will be different to the upright and the reprobate, 46. He condemns against his will, 626. A human judge must not rashly judge others, 227, whose intentions he does not know, 634; but himself, 35, 474, and his own works, so that he may sit as judge with Christ, 597, and be delivered from hell, 475. Divine judgments are an unsearchable abyss, 121, 122. The final judgment will be terrible to all, though in different ways, 874. It will reveal all hidden things, 33. Its remembrance is salutary, 755. What a beast of burden signifies mystically, 817. God’s justice and mercy must be kept together before one’s eyes, 249. There is one justice of God, another of man, another of the devil, 486. True justice is from God alone, 172. God alone is simply just, 32. He is united with the just person, 286. The just see no one but Jesus, 245. He has compassion on them, 216, and shows himself more sweetly in the sacraments to them than to the impious, 240. The mind of the just is Christ’s Mother, 97. It is figured in Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah, 77. They are rich, 544. They are often troubled over slight offenses, 14; above all others tempted by the devil, 207; and God often permits them to fall into sins, 216, for their humility, 450. Youth signifies fervor and love of virtue, 265.

## L

The tears of the penitent are compared to waves, 145. The lions’ den is mystically interpreted, 343. Joy, or gladness, of both body and soul is complete after the resurrection, 311. Sickness of soul is torpor in the love of God, 235. To praise oneself is a very great iniquity, 90. By what crowds praise and glory are announced to Christ, 22. This is done by the saints at judgment, 741, and ought always to be done by all, 797. Let one not seek one’s own praise in good works, 228, 545, 682, 761, 809. It is a stain upon good works, 684, 828. It will pursue those who flee it, 809. The thief converted on the cross manifests to all God’s immeasurable mercy, 413, 414, 716. Lazarus raised from the dead was the cause of Christ’s triumph on Palm Sunday, 363. Lazarus, being poor, is consolation to the poor, 543. Reading, meditation, and prayer should be our daily meal, 545, 553, and the bread of the soul, 652. A bed denotes the rest of the flesh, 653. Self-praise and vain glory are like leprosy, 828. [Col. 1644] Whom the leper mystically signifies, 135, etc. The ten lepers are our inner and outer senses, 828. The Levites’ task is reading, 815. Natural and written Law are Christ’s two disciples, 17, 18, 21. The Law is observed by Christ, and mercy is added, 212. Before it, under it, and under grace, some always aspired to heavenly things, 599. The tongue must be restrained, 505. Long-suffering is especially evident in the patriarchs, 729. Speech itself, or temptation, betrays the tempter, 83. To speak well is the same as to act well, 808. Washing of feet signifies compunction and cleansing of the affections, 330. Eli’s lamp mystically signifies Christ’s humanity, 603. Christ does not disdain games played by the Jews, 388. The lights of heaven signify Gospel commandments, 623. The wolf is a type of the devil, 439. Lust is a most shameful vice, 84; it is like horses, 81; the worst beast, 261; and like the idol Bel destroyed by Daniel, 341.

## M

Teachers are the mouth of the Lord, 220; likewise the pinnacle of the temple, 220. They must not be stubbornly resisted, 221. See Prelate, Preacher. The distinction between Magi and diviners, 641. The mammon of iniquity is our senses, 757. No one can serve it and God at the same time, 836. Why the commandment of love is called new, 490. See Charity. Morning and evening signify mutability, 164. The joyful dawn signifies the rising of Christ at his birth, 169. Christ’s gentleness toward the dishonored is greatest, 327. Christ himself is gentleness itself, 4, 487. Let all learn it from him, 504, especially prelates and preachers, 486, 488. It is necessary in adversity, as humility is in prosperity, 443. Its symbol is the sheep, 442. The king’s hand stretched against the prophet becomes stiff, 730. The sea denotes the penitent heart, 612. The Blessed Virgin Mary was chosen by God to complete the work of Redemption, 24, 26. She is the Lord’s sister, 24. She is immune from temptations, 28. Allegorically she is a little fortress, 17; a boat, 868; the summit of mountains, 38. Through her intercession humility is obtained, 96, and forgiveness of sins, 870. Charity arms and fortifies martyrs, 172; they in turn fortify the Church by their example and courage, 721. They receive reward in heaven, 419. Martyrdom removes all sins, 146; it is sustained by charity, 172. Christ is mediator between God and human beings, 170. Duties of the spiritual physician, 778. We are between angels and demons, 850. Meditation is the fourth step to salvation, 533, 538; let it be our daily food, 545. Remembrance of past things and consideration of future things confirm us in good, 53. All must beg spiritually in humility, 202. With the measure with which we have measured, it will be measured back to us, 628. A hireling serves from fear of being deprived of payment, 269. He benefits not the sheep but himself, 439. He flees when he is silent, 440, 447. God promises wages to workers in order to make their labor easier, 160. Every Christian fighting against the devil should be Christ’s soldier, 282. God grants his mercy to whom he wills, 168. If he denies it to a sinner, he does him no injustice, 137. Mercy shown in spiritual matters endures more than that shown in temporal matters, 9. It is always ready, 136, 332: for good and evil alike, 534; especially for sinners, 307, 482, 714, 238, 332, 897. It grants more than prayer dares to presume, 795. It must not be considered alone, but together with justice, 249; and must be adored as the Lord’s feet, 831. It is like an olive grove, 9, 17. We imitate God’s mercy if we sacrifice the spirit, 625. Prelates ought to show it to their subjects, 626. Let moderation be known to all people, 72. “A little while” is explained mystically and literally, 451 and following. A mountain denotes divinity, 38, 39; likewise apostles, and hills the just, 40. Death requires preparation in life, 7. Its hour is terrible, 154, especially because of assaults of demons, 402. But angels are present to us, 696. We must have recourse to Christ’s mercy, 3, and the end will be blessed, 4. After death neither penitence nor mercy delivers from sins, 753. Christ’s death was the death of evil spirits, 390. The death by which we die to vices and the world is truly precious, 548. [Col. 1645] Mortification gives life to the soul, 178. It is necessary for the converted, 453; fortified by humility, 825; and becomes a sweet nuptial dish for the Lord, 883. Moses and Aaron are figures of Christ, 351. Woman is a type of human frailty, 188, 502; in childbirth, of the penitent, 458; and, forgetful of the pressure of childbirth, of the blessed soul, 467. The women mourn Christ’s death, 640. They contend before Solomon: and what this signifies mystically, 748. The pure in heart are admitted to heavenly Nazareth, 104, and Jesus descends to them, 112. The world is like the sea, 312. What gift and altar are in the mystical sense, 687. Those who excessively bewail their miseries indeed murmur silently against God, 351; yet he graciously hears them, 358. Murmuring against a prelate, even a harsh one, is reproved, 226 and following. Man is subject to mutability, 267. What the speech of the mute signifies mystically, 276. He is healed by Christ, 806.

## N

Naaman is a figure of the worldly person converted to better things, 287. What being born into the world signifies mystically, 458. Christ’s two natures are figured by Hannah and Peninnah, 565. What is meritoriously done through grace must not be attributed to natural powers, 167. Christ’s little boat may be called the womb of the Blessed Virgin, 868. Simon’s boat is the symbol of the humbled soul, 661, 875. Nazareth is the heavenly garden, 104. Mist shadows forth Christ’s humanity, 42. Negligence is the root of inward affliction, 166. Saul on Mount Gilboa, and going to the woman who has a Python-spirit, are a prototype of the negligent person, 643 and following. His companions are despair and presumption, 646. *Nere* is mystically interpreted, 839. Sinews and cords are mystically explained, 378. How one ought to ask in Christ’s name, 494. The subtle suggestions of the devil deserve to be called razors, 575. Novatian the heretic attempted to divide the Church, 418. Whoever foresees his last things becomes more than a prophet, 70. Night may be called a life spent in ignorance, 662. The cloud intimates heavenly grace, 244. The number three signifies faith, hope, and charity, 237; seven, perfection, 106, 428; nine, thoughts, words, and works, 832; ten, a person’s inner and outer senses, 197, and also the ten precepts of the Decalogue, 237; eleven, transgression, 173; twelve, perfection, 106, 428; fifteen, in seven present life and in eight eternal life, 349; fifty, penitence, 464; seventy, the Decalogue and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, 348; eighty, the resurrection, 755; one hundred, perfection, 139, 905, 898; one thousand, the order of the elect in heaven, 907.

## O

Christ’s eyes were Jews and Gentiles, Adam and Eve, Peter and Judas, 386. The soul’s eyes are understanding and affection, 205. Their lifting up is intention, 903. Hatred disturbs the heart more than the other vices, 491. A good odor is a good example, 667. The Mount of Olives indicates mercy, 3, 9. The pot of flesh is concupiscence, 352. God’s omnipotence is most clearly manifested in sparing, 787. Work and holy conduct are necessary in the spiritual life, 425. What is learned through law and reading must be practiced in deed, 242. The exercise of good works is like a person’s best age, 154. God must be magnified even in the least things, 206. What prayer must be like in order to be heard, 72, 305, 495. It is often dry, 235. Without hope it is without fruit, 524. It must be made with humility and perseverance, 252; be directed toward good works, 790. True prayer is never without fruit and, like an arrow, always strikes, 867. It makes all things sweet, 513. The prayer common to the Church permits no one to perish, 804. Therefore all should be intent on praying and working, 546. An unstained life is unceasing prayer, 790. God’s ordering is that there be prelates and subjects, 632, 637. There are four orders in the Church: those who understand, the penitent, those who fight, and those who are perfected, 184; likewise three: secular persons, spiritual persons, and prelates, 657. Original sin has been dissolved through Christ, 59, 715. It is compared to a tunic, 27. The adornment of angelic nature is the confirmation of the good; that of human nature [Col. 1646] is Christ’s Incarnation and merits, 689 and following. Prelates and teachers are the Lord’s mouth, 220. To kiss one’s own hand is to praise oneself, 90. The door of the Lord’s house is the Old and New Testament, likewise baptism and penitence, 609. The idle are those who are only in desires, 160; sinners should be called such, 162; likewise those not cooperating with grace, 173. The sheep of the house of Israel are innocent souls, 251. Christ does not abandon his own living under hirelings, 440, 447. The one sheepfold of all may be understood as heaven, 441.

## P

A palm tree’s stature is added not by thinking but by conquering, 838. What the five barley loaves signify mystically, 317, and what their fragments signify, 321, etc. They indicate the five human senses, 906; the seven loaves, however, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, 699, 709. Bread from heaven is righteous people, 354. When bread is lacking, there is no perfect refreshment, 697. Paralysis signifies harmful thoughts, 154; the paralytic, one growing spiritually lukewarm, 136; the human race, 869; and the spirit weakened by sins, 876. We too may be the Lord’s parents, 108, 111. The beginnings of great conversion are generally small, 289. Christ’s Passion dissolves the bonds of hell and opens the gate of paradise, 582. It may be called Christ’s crossing over, 869. Its remembrance transfers affection to God, 855. We ought to imitate it, 824. Allegorically it is applied to our spiritual life, 399. The time of it and of Lent is more salutary than another time, 295, 339. Christ the good shepherd feeds all, and how, 438, 440. Good shepherds ought to feed sheep by preaching, works, and prayer, 446. The affection of fatherhood in God is immutable even toward sinners, 483, 509. Patience after scourges makes a person more just, 217. Patriarchs and prophets, though excelling in faith and merits, are nevertheless sent to Limbo, 723, 728. They are inferior to apostles and martyrs, 723, 729. Paul is renowned for humility, 795. The poor have consolation in Lazarus, 543. All who wish to be saved should regard themselves as poor in spirit, 560. Peace in Christ’s flesh is supreme, 115. True peace is from Christ, 425. It should flourish in the community, 153. Peace with the devil is utterly evil, 280. The inveterate sinner rises with difficulty after relapse, 238. A teacher is moved neither by word nor threats, except perhaps toward despair, 652. He is like an ox under the yoke, 590; like a leper and paralytic, 136; and should be called idle, 162. Every person is a sinner, 613. At times a person becomes such that he may learn humility, 450. He must not be proudly rejected, 211. God looks upon him with paternal affection, 483. Consolation must be given to one confessing, 229. The sighs of one aspiring to conversion, 16, and humble prayer to God, 253. Sin destroys within us God’s dwelling place, 10; binds the soul like a little cord, 10, 379. When it is committed, it mystically hands us over, mocks, scourges, and spits upon us, 200; and almost annihilates a person, 615. One descends through four stages to commit it, 679; a fifth is added, namely its defense, 769. No one in a state of pure nature could expiate sin by any number of sacrifices, 609. A preacher must above all attack sin, 165. One must repent of individual sins, 165, even lighter ones, 909, but more especially of greater ones, 597, 674. The soul’s feet are understanding and affection, 865. To travel as a pilgrim is mystically interpreted, 267. No one is simply perfect in this life, 301. There are especially three persecutions of the Church, 213. Perseverance in prosperity and adversity, 13, 102, and in temptations, 219, leads to heavenly marriage, 125. Perseverance in evil is diabolical, 162. Petitions in prayer should consist in entreating, supplicating, and giving thanks, 72. How they should be made in Christ’s name, 494. See Prayer. Saint Peter is Christ’s eye, 386. He is a model of the good shepherd, 446, 796. By his death he proves his love, 493. The penitent raises sinners to hope, 679. What and how great is the righteousness of the Pharisees, 682. Piety according to the gift of the Holy Spirit, 799. Fish intimate Christ’s hidden divinity, 318. Let us strive to please God alone, 73. Let the penitent think humbly of himself, 93. His supplication to God, 137, 904; his sighs, 139, 202. God is present to him, 659. Together with the innocent, by humility he establishes Christ’s sheepfold, 448. The Canaanite woman is his type, 248, 253, and the Samaritan woman, 302. What sort are those who repent solely through fear of Gehenna, 163.

[Col. 1647] Penitence is the way to mercy, 9. The method of performing it, 130, 138. The publican in the Temple is an example, 792. It must not be delayed, 852. It requires confession, 131. It must be undertaken with a contrite yet cheerful and steadfast mind, 617. It inclines God’s will toward human will, 138. It loosens the cords of sins, 11; covers sins, 145; always obtains forgiveness for all sinners, 237; brings joy to the soul, 618; restores strength, 653; exalts the humble in glory, 853; and teaches the soul to fly, 656. It is a supper in which God delights, 587; it is like gold, 182; standing water, 659; and fish, 906, 909. Christ the High Priest has become a bridge for us to the heavenly homeland, 323, 337. Swine are symbols of evil spirits, 268. Gospel commandments are heavenly lights, 623. Even God’s lesser commandments must be observed, 547. They are compared to keys, 429. The office of preaching must not be sought after, 485. The preaching of God’s word must be obeyed with reverence, 18. It is a two-edged sword, 365. It moves the hearer to compunction of heart, 103; inflames toward perfection, 243; and must always be attended to, 553. A preacher must first do himself what he preaches, 532. He must guard himself against vices, 325. How his life should be ordered, 231. Yet one must attend to their words, not to their examples, 447. Christ preaches in him, 190. He heals by the word, 153, like a dog licking wounds, 548. He is steward of the vineyard, 164; the gate of the mystical city, 842. Preachers are Christ’s knee, 663; servants of the Lord inviting to the wedding, 882. They must preach Christ’s humility, 98. Their zeal concerns the end of the age, 123. Prelates should benefit subjects by sound doctrine and prayer offered for them, 150, 344. The frivolity of their lives scandalizes subjects, 225. They must render an account for goods administered, squandered, etc., 750. They are winged souls, 657; light, 631; the Lord’s mouth, 220. A prelate’s bride is the congregation committed to him, 153. The prepared mountain signifies Christ, and how, 39. The pressure of the Gentiles denotes the pressure of vices, 51. First fruits must be returned to God, 798. Mystical interpretation of the pool of Bethesda, 234. Portents produce terror; signs produce love, 892. The prodigal son dissipates his substance, etc., 267, etc.; he returns to the Father, 270. Desires of the prophets awaiting Christ, 23, 37. They were written for our benefit, 37. How prophets struck the kings of Israel, 730. Prophecies concerning Christ must be spiritually fulfilled in us, 199. The resolve of spiritual life is figured in the royal official’s son, 889. Prosperity too eagerly desired establishes a chaos between us and God, 551, 561. Through it God is not found, 490. Prosperity and adversity assail us with temptations, 12, 217. For both, praise must be given to God, 797. God’s providence never forsakes his own, 273. Our neighbor is the one most in need of our help, 819. True prudence professes with the mouth what it has in the heart, 182. It fortifies us against temptations, 517. Childhood expresses fear of the Lord, 151. God’s grace helps those fighting against the devil, 198. Who are orphans mystically? 506. Purple signifies outward action, 545. The devil introduces faintheartedness by very rare deceits, 77 and following, 82, etc. It is the origin of lukewarmness and negligence, 643. The shell is mystically interpreted, 378. Pythons in the belly, and what their removal mystically signifies, 641.

## Q

Lent is a time of salvation, 295. Chariots indicate the four cardinal virtues, likewise the four Gospels, 82. What the fifteenth number signifies mystically, 349. What the number five signifies, 317.

## R
Rami — Branches cut from trees: their mystical meaning, 5. Rabsaces: a type of the devil as tempter, 75. How human reason is in the midst of the heart, 180. Through it every person is able to know God, 261. An account must be rendered to God for one’s intentions, 762. Recollection of a past life badly lived is salutary counsel for sinners, 886. Our redemption was the will of God the Father, 308. It is the greatest of divine works, 575. Its beginnings are signified by the shoot, 32. A return to one’s former life must be lamented, 107, 116. [Col. 1648] The sinner chooses a king for himself besides God, 406. The kings of the Israelites teach Catholics caution by their example, 640. To reign is to keep the commandments and practice the virtues, 73. The eternal kingdom of Christ is the Church, 422. The world was the devil’s kingdom, 407. The endowments of true religion, 505. Religious persons make a continual Lord’s Day, 233. They ought to be more righteous than clergy and laity, 682. One must preach differently to these and differently to those, 197, 585. Veneration is due to the relics of the apostles, 720. Forgiveness of an injury must be from the heart, 627. Recompense for all works will come after death, 818, 826. The rest of the divine works was the completion of Christ’s Passion, 691. But our rest is eternal, 691. Christ’s Resurrection manifests his divinity, 357. David at Siceleg is its figure, 408. Our resurrection is certain for all, either unto life or unto condemnation, 873. Perfect joy in heaven will follow it, 401, 432. Concealing sin in confession makes the human heart a den of thieves, 786. Christ is King both of himself and of others, 33. A king is one who can govern himself and his passions, 34. The distinction between *rex* (“king”) and *regulus* (“little king”), 889. Dew: a symbol of divine grace, 25. The wheel: an image of the human race, 397.

## S

Priests of the old law were strong in faith, 732, 727. Their office is to pray, 815. The sacraments present Christ differently to the perfect and to the lukewarm, 241. The world must be fled by the justified person, 179. It is called a desert, 69. Its cares are like a tomb, 549. They deprive one of the sweetness of divine visitation, 783. And of merits, 592. Its business is attended to with greater diligence than salvation, 755. Solomon’s kingdom foreshadows Christ’s eternal kingdom in heaven, 745. The salvation of the soul and the honor of God alone must be considered in all works, 670. One ascends to salvation by five steps, 533. The Samaritan woman at the well: an image of the penitent soul, 302, etc. The Samaritans were despised by the Jews, 326. The merciful Samaritan signifies Christ, 362, 372. Likewise, he signifies the people of the Gentiles converted to Christ, 823. Samson: a figure of Christ, 375. The saints intercede for the Church, 521. By their intercession we are freed from sickness of soul, 235. And from sins, 870. They remember the miseries of the world, 522. They desire the end of the world, 522. So that they may be reunited with their bodies, 670. One sees another’s thoughts, 743. They are compared to trees, 15. The beginning of true wisdom is the conquest of the passions, 34. Satisfaction must follow repentance, 593. King Saul: an example of a person turned from good to evil and despairing, 641 and following. What it is to be scandalized in Christ is explained, 68. Scandal taken from others’ lives and omissions is a dangerous temptation, 891. Knowledge: the third gift of the Holy Spirit, 799. Those possessing knowledge of a matter sin more than the ignorant, 724. It is of no benefit unless action is added, 191. Sacred Scripture provides remedies against temptations, 56, 210. Though it sounds harsh, it does not lack sweetness, 276, 857. It is compared to earth, 231; to the kingdom of God, 191; and to heaven, 808. It gives a prelate rules for living, 813; and likewise a subject, 818. Understood in a perverse sense, it blinds, 654. Scripture is more powerful than mere speech, 754, 764. Old age is denoted by the sixth age of the world, 154; by the sixth and ninth hours, 161. The senses spiritually restored by Christ, 67, 68, 161. They come under the name of Christ’s disciples, 126, 127. There are ten internal and external senses, 572. They are servants of the righteous person, 141. They are the porticoes of the soul, 234. The footstool: namely, understanding and affection, 865. They ought to cooperate in conversion, 290, 291. And they must be shut, 424. The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified by the seven loaves, 699; by the seventh hour, 894; and by the seven Sundays preached upon, 777. Likewise, the seven capital vices, 283. The seven-year period mystically explained, 102. The mystical meaning of signs in sun, moon, and stars, 43. Silence mystically explained, 796. Husks may be called the wisdom of the world, 263. Spiritual thirst of the soul arises from perseverance, 218. Mystical solitude, 697. Woman is a mirror of human frailty, 502. [Col. 1649] Hope obtains forgiveness of sins, 650. One must hold by hope what is at some time to be obtained in reality, 156. Without it prayer is fruitless, 524. The penitent must be guided by hope and fear, 229. Our hope should therefore be greater, because God left strength even to those cursed by himself, 839. Thorns are the threefold temptation of Satan, the world, and the flesh, 104. They indicate avarice for gold and honor, 736. Spiritual life is like paradise, 179. Spiritual persons are signified by the movable soul, 657. The Holy Spirit blows where he wills, 108. He rests upon the humble, 893, and the chaste, 518. He is the Consoler and Teacher of truth, 507, etc.; of the knowledge of God and of ourselves, 478. He enlightens the apostles, 476, and his Church, 601. By his coming the Gentiles are called, 171. He strengthens us against the devil, 281. He is likened to an opening, 28; to a mist covering the earth, 43; and to a book written within and without, 435. His inspiration must not be neglected, 461–462, 536. How spirit rules over flesh, 864, 898. Evil spirits are foreshadowed in Joseph’s brothers, 257, etc. Christ’s bride needs a guide, 126. She must set aside cares of the flesh, 126. Baskets are like the bodies of the elect, 701. The inn: its mystical or moral meaning, 817, 824. The warp: its mystical meaning, 378. Let each person be content with his station and lot, 632. Stars signify the apostles, 44. The robe is a symbol of divine charity, 271. Subjects are denoted by beasts of burden, 318; by darkness, 631. They should not criticize the deeds of prelates, 632. Pride is the original source of sin, 57, 201. It cast angels down from heaven, 142, 201. It is the highest and first vice, 847. It is proper to evil spirits, 838. It opens the human heart to the devil, 383, 636. It is the mother of impurity and anger, 487, and the daughter of imprudence, 781. It is the beam in one’s own eye, 633. Whoever calls a brother “fool” deserves Gehenna, 686. It is the ruin of the soul, 879. It assumes virtues in order to tempt, 89, 335, 614. When it appropriates God’s gifts to itself, it is a form of blasphemy, 877. It is ascent and descent, 348. It is broken by humility, 90, and by temptations themselves, 342. Adam is an example of pride chastised and humbled, 856. The Synagogue afflicts Christ, 570. Pride is figured in Delilah, 383. The lament of one turning late to Christ, 121. The Creed of the Apostles comprises the sacraments of Christ, 321.

## T

Temperance is an arrow against evil spirits, 184. The temple of the Lord is a holy and immaculate mind, 102. Good subjects are temples of the Lord, 220, 789. The season of the Lord’s Advent and the season of Lent are a time of grace, 23, 295. Darkness is sometimes better than light, 351. Outer darkness consists of prosperity and adversity, 887. Some temptations are good, others evil, 859. They are good if we conquer them, evil if we succumb, 250. In introducing them, the devil often renders service to God, 514. They are also a remedy against pride, 342, 187. Temptations opposed to one another are Satan’s divided kingdom, 279. They assail those renouncing the world, 11, 75 and following, 181; those struggling with death, 403 and following; everyone while we live, 224, 343, 516, 667; even the holiest, 207, 277, 465, 504, 512. Yet they are not beyond our strength, 344. Therefore the convert should not fear them excessively, 280. Although they lessen fervor, 133, they arise from adversity and prosperity, 12; from the occasion of virtues and merits, 88, 222; and in four other ways, 333. They must be resisted firmly and steadfastly, 219; by fasts and vigils, 643; by reading Holy Scripture, 56. The method of overcoming them, 12, 51, 52, 194. They are not overcome without help, 94. The gravest temptation of all is the defense of sin, 776. Lukewarmness in the exercise of virtues disarms the devil, 74. It is suggested by the devil through various deceits, 78, 79. The New Testament may be called the greater light, and the Old Testament the lesser light, 624. The theological virtues make us heirs of the heavenly kingdom, 142. They are poured into the convert, 271. They ought to be united, 331, 355. They are figured by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, 802. Thomas doubts Christ’s humanity, 359. Fear is a gift of the Holy Spirit, 777, 799. It brings the soul to perfection, 10. The movements of fear and love restrain the passions, 676. Its effects in a person are various, 45. Perfect fear ends in love, 117. Those serving on account of fear alone are hirelings, 269. Before the Last Judgment it will strike both humans and angels with terror, 49. It is foreshadowed by the age of childhood, 151. Ringing in both ears is fear of God and love, 606. Sloth arises from distrust in God, 643. It enervates virtue by filling it with flesh, 188. [Col. 1650] There is no tranquility in this life, but in the next, 148. Thistles are a symbol of concupiscence, 736. The Lord’s dining room is the threefold order of the innocent, penitents, and perfect, 131. The Holy Trinity instills grace in us, 181. It works wholly in Christ, 564, 600. One sorrow is unto death, another unto life, 472. Sorrow leading to repentance will be turned into joy, 457, 466, 899. Its effects are diverse, 466. What are the crowds rendering praise to Christ? 22.

## U

The number eleven signifies transgression, 173. Unity denotes the righteous and simple person, 428. The future unity of Jews and Gentiles at the end of the age, 174. The nail expresses perfection of life, 183.

## V

A broken potter’s vessel signifies Christ’s death, 397. The mystical meaning of coming from afar, 696. Hearing the divine word produces compunction of heart, 103. Three things impede its efficacy: hardness of heart, negligence, and avarice, 192. The spirit, not the letter, must be attended to, 734. It should be heard with a pure heart, 252. The hearer is of God, 325. He must also be a doer, 500; but a doer is rare, 174. Guarding it is life to the soul, 328. Preaching is adapted to the capacity of each person, 901, etc. It gives bread to the hungry, 230. It makes the powerless strong, 892. It is like a two-edged sword, 365. The same word often also means deed, 250. Truth is the highest knowledge of God and oneself, 478. The tender little wood-worm is Christ in his mercifulness, humility, and Passion, 715, etc. Garments indicate good subjects, 241. The wedding garment is charity, 886. What is Christ’s way and ours? 583. Christ visits his own now sweetly, now bitterly, 471, so that they may be exercised in humility, 473. Victory over the world at life’s end brings the greatest tranquility, 154. To see God is to love him, 830. The Lord can be seen in different ways, 425. The faithful soul may be called a widow, 101: leaving vanity and pleasure, 505; and bereft of the word of God, 843. The steward accused before his master is the person who abuses God’s gifts, 751, 759. The Lord’s vineyard is the Church, 159, and the heavenly paradise, 171. Wine and grain are the drink and food of human beings, 231. They do not grow without labor, 232. Mystically, they are drawn from Holy Scripture, 233. They offer compunction and sweetness of heart, 798. Together with oil they must be poured into wounds, 816. *Vir* (“man”) is so called from *virtus* (“strength”), 828. By this name the understanding is meant, 340. By woman, the senses are understood, 677. True virginity is an incorrupt mind, 102. The theological virtues: see “Theological Virtues.” The cardinal virtues are signified by the four rivers of paradise, 182, and are fitted to the four Sundays of Advent, 87. The devil assumes our virtues in order to tempt us, 88, 92. One must ascend from one virtue to another, 105, 477. How the heavens are to be moved, 46. The time of heavenly visitation must be attended to with every care, 461, 462. It is various, 782, 785. Spiritual life is like paradise, 179. David is a type of the active and contemplative life, 666. In this life we are always involved in temptations and ignorances, 224, 343, 516, 667. The present life impedes our participation in heavenly joys, 693. The capital vices were cast down by Christ’s death, 716. They must be suppressed by us, like the others, 51; likewise vicious inclinations, 427. One turning to God must mystically kill the calf, 331. The divine call is given at every age, 158, 159. It must be obeyed despite difficulty, 160. One call is gentle, another severe, 660. A good will is like light, 556. It is the beginning of perfection, 34. An evil will is like darkness, 557. Upon it depend either salvation or destruction, 557. By the will we die, either by sinning or by mortifying ourselves, 186. A will directed toward sin passes into necessity, 590. What is the death of the will? 890. There is scarcely anyone who has not sinned by will and pleasure, 457. Without grace it can do nothing, 101. It is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, 181. Worldly pleasures heap insults upon the servants of the heavenly King, 884. A voice is a being, not existing of itself, 92. The holy wounds of Christ must be bound to our hearts, 833. The five holy marks of the wounds are shown at the Judgment, 47, and to the saints in heaven, 431.
